units.la: VOD[?] post expositam Diui Pauli ad Romanos epistolam eas quoque quas idem Apostolus ad Corinthios dedit, aggressus sum, & meas in priorem Homilias sub felici Amplitudinis & Pietatis vestrae auspicio, Patres in Christo reuerendiss. & Dominis mihi haud vulgariter observandi, in lucem dare volui, nemo (opinor) me absque certa ratione fecisse dicet, qui rem propius inspexerit. Huius enim argumentum ad illius illustrationem plurimum facit, & ut eiusdem tractatio nostri saeculi hominibus imprimis conuenit: ita mihi quoque digna visa est, quae vestro iudicio atque censurae subiiceretur, quos non solum eruditione & multiplici rerum usu, verumetiam authoritate singulari Deus donauit, ut illam non modo cognoscere, sed (si ita opus sit) aduersus improbos Zoilorum dentes defendere possitis. In ea enim, quam ad Romanos scripsit Apostolus, potissimum de fide in aeternum Dei Filium IESVM CHRISTVM, disputatur, ex qua tota hominis iustificatio & universa salutis nostrae ratio dependet: In his vero, quas modo damus, vera Ecclesiae forma & legitima eiusdem oeconomia siue administratio traditur: quae nisi probe cognita & recte instituta sit, inutilis plane atque superuacanea est fidei Christianae professio. Hic enim praecipuus, quoad nos, fidei effectus est, quod per hanc iustificati & adoptionis Spiritu donati, in unum eiusdem Ecclesiae corpus coalescimus, cuius caput est IESVS CHRISTVS Dominus noster, ex quo spiritus vitae atque salus in omnia membra eius, id est, in omnes credentes deriuatur. Quamobrem Apostoli in Symbolo suo, quo suae doctrinae summam, siue (ut Tertulliani verbo utar) regulam fidei Christianae complexi sunt, hunc ordinem nobis praescripserunt, ut post unius aeterni Dei (Patris nimirum, Filij & Spiritus sancti) & eorum quae propter nos in assumpta hominis carne fecit Dei Filius, confessionem, fateamur quoque Ecclesiam Catholicam, id est, universalem, quae sanctorum, quotquot unquam fuerunt, & sunt, & in posterum nascentur, omnium communio siue societas dicitur: apud quam inestimabiles illos suae gratiae thesauros Deus depositit, Remissionem nimirum peccatorum gratuitam, laetam certamque futurae resurrectionis spem, & vitam aeternam, quae veram atque perfectam hominis beatitatem in se continet. Quorum consideratio ut inef-fabilem & plus quam paternam Dei bonitatem nobis commendat, qui ex miserra & infelici, imo deplorata humani generis massa sibi ipsi Ecclesiam certam deligere dignatus est, quam pro suo peculio, pro suo grege, suo aruo & vinea agnoscere: quam denique sanguinis sui lauacro ablutam & coniugij indissolubilis vinculo sibi desponsatam, bonorum suorum omnium consortem haberet: Ita nos quoque excitare debet, ut de conseruanda vera Ecclesiae forma & oeconomia sertio cogitemus, neque nos ab eius societate patiamur diuelli, extra quam nulla salutis spes nobis reliqua esse potest. Est enim incredibilis in illa turbanda communis nostri hostis diaboli astutia, & irrequieta improbitas, hominum vero plus quàm belluina stupiditas & oscitantia, qua decepti illius insidias vel non vident, vel etiam visas atque deprehensas contemnunt & negligunt. Utrumque periculum hoc Christus eleganti parabola depinxit, qua Ecclesiam agro confert, in quo post factam sementem inimicus dormientibus hominibus zizania superspargit, quæ mox cum tritico germinant atque succrescunt. Quod quàm vere ab illo dictum sit, omnium sæculorum historiæ infinitis exemplis docent: ex quibus con-stat, verbi Dei segetes nunquam tam feliciter germinauisse, quin inter eas hæresum quoque infelix lolium emerserit cum male virentibus pessimarum opinionum vitiis & nocentissimis scandalorum vepribus, quibus Euangelicæ doctrinæ veritas adulterata, & Ecclesiæ unitas non sine publico offendiculo scissa atque di-stracta sit.
units.tr: Having expounded the divine Apostle Paul's Epistle to the Romans, I have gone on to those which the same Apostle wrote to the Corinthians. I wished to publish my homilies on the former under the happy patronage of your Dignity and Piety, reverend fathers in Christ and lords whom I hold in no ordinary esteem. I think no one who looks at the matter more closely will say I did this without good reason. The subject of the one letter contributes greatly to the explanation of the other, and its treatment is especially suited to the people of our age. So I thought this work too deserved to be put before your judgement and criticism, since God has endowed you not only with learning and wide experience of affairs, but also with a singular authority, so that you may not only understand it but also, if need be, defend it against the savage teeth of the Zoili. The Epistle to the Romans deals chiefly with faith in the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, on which the whole justification of man and the entire basis of our salvation depends. The letters we now offer set out the true form of the Church and its lawful order or administration. Unless this is properly known and rightly established, the profession of the Christian faith is plainly useless and superfluous. For, as far as we are concerned, the chief effect of faith is this: that, justified and endowed through it with the Spirit of adoption, we grow together into one body of that Church, whose head is Jesus Christ our Lord, from whom the spirit of life and salvation flows into all its members, that is, into all believers. Therefore the Apostles, in their Creed, in which they comprised the sum of their teaching, or (to use Tertullian's word) the rule of the Christian faith, laid down for us this order: after confessing the one eternal God (Father, Son and Holy Spirit) and what the Son of God did for us in the assumed flesh of man, we also confess the Catholic Church, that is, the universal Church, which is called the communion or fellowship of all the saints, whoever have ever existed, now exist, or will be born hereafter. In it God has deposited those priceless treasures of his grace: the free forgiveness of sins, the joyful and certain hope of the future resurrection, and eternal life, which contains within itself the true and perfect blessedness of man. Consideration of these things commends to us the ineffable goodness of God, more than fatherly, who has deigned to choose for himself from the wretched and unhappy, indeed hopeless, mass of mankind a Church, to acknowledge as his own possession, his own flock, his own field and vineyard; and finally, to have as a partner in all his goods a Church washed in the bath of his blood and betrothed to himself by the indissoluble bond of marriage. In the same way it should move us also to think earnestly about preserving the true form and order of the Church, and not to allow ourselves to be torn away from its fellowship, outside which no hope of salvation can remain for us. For there is an incredible cunning in the disturbing of it on the part of our common enemy the devil, and a restless wickedness; and on the part of men, a stupidity and drowsiness more than beastly, by which they either do not see the snares of that deceiver, or, even when they have seen and detected them, despise and neglect them. Christ depicted both dangers in a fine parable, in which he compares the Church to a field where, after the sowing, the enemy sows tares over the sleeping men, which soon sprout and grow up together with the wheat. How truly this was spoken by him, the histories of all ages teach through countless examples. From them it is clear that the crops of God's Word have never sprouted so happily that the unhappy darnel of heresies has not also come up among them, with the poisonous vices of wicked opinions growing up in them and the most harmful thorns of scandals, by which the truth of the evangelical doctrine has been corrupted and the unity of the Church has been torn and divided, not without public offence.

units.la: Nam ut ab Apostolis exordiamur, quis nescit illis adhuc viuentibus & sedulo docentibus, exortos fuisse impostores nequissimos, quorum alii Legis Mosaicæ doctrinam cum Euangelio, & illius opera cum iustitia fidei commiscere, & universum IESV CHRISTI meritum euacuare: alii vero mortuorum resurrectionem, sine cuius spe religio non consistit, in dubium vocare, imo aperte negare ausi sunt. Taceo nunc horribiles Simonis Magi furores, belluinas Nicolaitarum libidines religionis fuco velatas, impia & execrationibus æternis digna Cerinthi, Hebionis & similium figmenta, quibus æternam IESV CHRISTI Deitatem & salutiferæ Incarnationis eius mysterium vellicauerunt.
units.tr: To begin with the Apostles: who does not know that while they were still living and teaching diligently, the most wicked impostors arose? Some of them dared to mix the teaching of the Mosaic Law with the Gospel, and works with the righteousness of faith, and to make void the whole merit of Jesus Christ; others dared to call in question the resurrection of the dead, without hope of which religion cannot stand, and even openly to deny it. I now pass over the dreadful frenzies of Simon Magus, the beastly lusts of the Nicolaitans veiled with a cloak of religion, and the impious fabrications of Cerinthus and Ebion and their like, which worthy of eternal curses, by which they attacked the eternal deity of Jesus Christ and the saving mystery of his incarnation.

units.la: Quæ zizania non multo post innumerabilia hæreticorum agmina pepererunt, Valentinianos nimirum, Mar-ciones, Cerdones, Apellianos, Apollinarios, Arios, Photinos, Artemones, Nesto-rios, Eutychetes, Manichæos: quorum alii personam Christi distraxerunt, alii eiusdem naturas confuderunt, alii diuinam, alii humanam negarunt, omnium vero hoc studium commune fuit, ut dum sua figmenta quisque propagare & tueri satagit, Ecclesiam in partes siue sectas distraherent: quod fieri non poterat, quin simul fidei Christianæ & salutis nostræ fundamenta, quantum in illis fuit, cum multorum exitio conuellerentur.
units.tr: Not long after, these tares gave birth to innumerable hordes of heretics: namely the Valentinians, Marcion, Cerdo, the Apellians, Apollinaris, Arius, Photinus, Artemon, Nestorius, Eutyches, and the Manichaeans. Some of them tore apart the person of Christ, some confused his natures, some denied his divinity and others his humanity. But the common aim of all of them was this: while each of them strove to propagate and defend his own fictions, they tore the Church into parties or sects. This could not happen without the foundations of the Christian faith and of our salvation being overthrown, as far as they were able, to the ruin of many.

units.la: Quia tamen istorum impietas manifestior fuit, quam ut diu latere posset, atrocior item quam ut eam Christianæ aures admittere vellent, non potuit tunc prorsus effectum dare Satan quod cupiebat, ut neque hodie potest, quamuis easdem hæreses postliminio reducere sedulo conetur. Itaque ad nouas artes conuersus, ut Ecclesiæ unitatem scinderet, alios excitauit, qui falsa absolutæ sanctimoniæ & perfectionis Christianæ persuasione fascinati, vel potius inflati, eos omnes ab Ecclesiæ societate arcendos esse docuerunt, in quibus vitium aliquod appareret, quo aliqui possent offendi. Author huius opinionis primus sub annum nati in carne Filii Dei CCLIII fuisse perhibetur Nouatus quidam, Romanæ Ecclesiæ presby-ter: qui cum natura gloriæ cupidus ad altiorem gradum aspiraret, sibique de seipso nihil non polliceretur, tandem eo usque confidentiæ progressus est, ut iis spem omnem salutis adimeret, qui inter dura persecutionum certamina & immanes tormentorum, quæ tunc Christianis adhibebantur, cruciatus lapsi essent, etiamsi seriæ pœnitentiam postea agerent. Quod cum piis omnibus durum & intolerabile (ut reuera est) videretur, qui lapsos ad pœnitentiam inuitandos potius quam ab ea absterrendos esse, ex scripturis didicerant, ille ab Ecclesia secessionem faciens multos post se traxit, quos insolenti & superbo nomine καθαροὺς, id est mundos dicebat: ita nimirum Ecclesias omnes, quæ secus sentiebant, immundas & impuras esse innuens. Damnata tunc fuit publica Concilii Romæ coacti authoritate eius sententia, nunquam tamen prorsus tolli potuit ex ea enata hæresis, quo minus episcopos proprios haberent qui eam sectabantur, idque Constantinopoli imprimis, vbi in illud usque tempus durauit, quando urbe capta Græciæ imperium ad Turcas translatum est. Et ut vulgò fieri solet, error iste multos alios ex sepê-rit[?]. Alii enim eos, qui post acceptum baptismum peccassent, per poenitentiam instaurari & servari posse negaverunt; alij à remissionis spe eos excluserunt, qui delicto aliquo voluntario legem Dei violavissent: multi inter peccata discrimina non nova finxerunt, quibus Dei gratuita misericordia, quam ille omnibus eam serio expetentibus liberaliter offert, ad paucos restringebatur. Secuti sunt posteris temporibus Donatistae, quorum furor ulterius processit, adeò ut damnata maiori orbis Christiani parte, Ecclesiam Christi angusto Aphricae angulo concluderent, neque contenti essent Ecclesias alias pro impuris damnasse, insuper colloquia quoque omnium fugerent, ne aliorum peccatis polluerentur. Fuerunt hi nocentissimi schismatis authores, quod vix multis laboribus & severis Imperatorum edictis, neque absque sanguine curari potuit, cum violentam mortem (ut Theodoretus de illis narrat) martyrium nominaret, & ad hanc pecudum instar saginati, quosvis obvios ipsis manum inferre cogerent. At ne sic quidem istorum insania potuit extingui, quo minus ea nostro saeculo in Anabaptistis revixerit, qui cum inter se vagis libidinibus indulgeant, & caedibus mutuis grassentur, & pios principes ad arma cogant, se tamen in religionis causa plus aliis profecisse sibi persuadent, & prae se omnes alios contemnunt, in quibus aliquid vitij haerere conspicantur: denique ipsi quoque ab Ecclesijs secessionem faciunt, ne (ut ipsorum verbis utar) cum aliorum sceleribus communicent. Damnant hos plerique qui purioris Euangelij doctrinam paulò diligentius inspexerunt: multos tamen ex iis quo que incosideratus iustitiae zelus atque nimius severitatis rigor aeque morosiores facit, ut quamvis in doctrinae summa nobiscum consentiant, undique tamen occasiones venentur, ut aliquem inveniant à nobis discedendi praetextum. Fit ergo, ut aliqui doctrinam causentur, si vel minimam in ea diversitatis speciem apud nos se videre putent. Qui vero nihil in ea reprehendere possunt, hi ministrorum aut doctorum vitiis se offendi aiunt, & se iustam suae ab Ecclesia discessionis causam reperisse arbitrantur, si doctrinae, quae traditur, doctorum vita & mores minus respondeant. Sunt qui de rituum diversitate queruntur, si non eundem docendi ordinem, aut eadem in Sacramentorum administratione ceremonias ubique ab omnibus observari, vel non eodem temporis momento apud omnes nostrae professionis Ecclesias coetus sacros haberi, vel preces publicas aliis atque aliis verbis concipi videant: ut iam de eorum morositate nihil dicam, qui de ministrorum habitu, de sacris vasis & aliis rebus medijs atque indifferentibus quaestiones intempestivas movent, quae lites pariunt non necessarias, & quibus totae Ecclesiae cum magno multorum scandalo turbantur. Sunt praeterea, qui cum & doctrina & totā rituum externorum oeconomia ipsis probetur, in morum tamen censura plus aequo curiosi, Christi Ecclesiam apud eos esse negant, qui vitia non pro ipsorum libito disciplina severiori coercent: & hi fere nihil non sibi contra nos licere putant, si quos manifestis sceleribus pollutos, & Christiani nominis professioni minus respondentes, ad sacrosanctam Domini Coenam cum piis accedere cernunt.
units.tr: Yet because the impiety of these men was too plain to remain hidden for long, and too monstrous for Christian ears to tolerate, Satan could not then bring about what he desired, just as he cannot today, although he diligently tries to bring back these same heresies by right of return. So he turned to new arts, in order to split the unity of the Church. He stirred up others who, bewitched, or rather puffed up, by the false persuasion of absolute holiness and Christian perfection, taught that all those in whom some fault appeared, by which some might be offended, must be excluded from the fellowship of the Church. The author of this opinion is said to have been first, about the year 253 after the Son of God was born in the flesh, a certain Novatus, an elder of the Roman Church. Eager for glory, and aspiring to a higher rank, and promising himself everything about himself, he at last advanced to such confidence that he took away all hope of salvation from those who, under the hard struggles of persecution and the savage tortures then applied to Christians, had fallen away, even if they afterwards did earnest repentance. Since this seemed harsh and intolerable to all the pious (as in truth it is), who had learned from the Scriptures that the fallen should be invited to repentance rather than kept from it, he withdrew from the Church and drew many after him, whom he called by the arrogant and proud name [καθαρούς], that is, the pure, thereby implying that all the Churches which thought otherwise were unclean and impure. Then his opinion was condemned by the public authority of a council held at Rome, yet the heresy born from it could never be entirely removed, so that they did not have their own bishops who followed it, especially at Constantinople, where it lasted until the time when, the city having been captured, the empire of Greece was transferred to the Turks. And, as commonly happens, this error gave birth to many others. Some denied that those who had sinned after receiving baptism could be restored and preserved through repentance; others excluded from the hope of forgiveness those who had violated the law of God by some deliberate offence; many invented new distinctions between sins, by which the free mercy of God, which he offers liberally to all who earnestly seek it, was restricted to a few. In later times the Donatists followed, whose frenzy went further, so that, condemning the greater part of the Christian world, they shut up the Church of Christ in a narrow corner of Africa. Not content with condemning other Churches as impure, they also avoided all conversation with others, lest they be polluted by their sins. These were the most harmful authors of schism. It could scarcely be cured with great labour and the severe edicts of the emperors, and not without bloodshed, since (as Theodoret tells us of them) they called violent death martyrdom, and, fattened like cattle for this, they forced whoever met them to lay hands on them. But even so the madness of these men could not be extinguished, so that in our age it has revived in the Anabaptists. Although they indulge in vagrant lusts among themselves and rage with mutual slaughter, and compel pious princes to take up arms, they nevertheless persuade themselves that they have made more progress in the cause of religion than others, and they despise all others in whom they see any fault. Finally, they too withdraw from the Churches, lest (to use their own words) they share in the crimes of others. Most who have examined the doctrine of the purer Gospel somewhat more carefully condemn them. Yet among these men too, an ill-considered zeal for righteousness and an excessive rigour of severity make some of them equally fastidious, so that, although they agree with us in the main points of doctrine, they hunt everywhere for occasions to find some pretext for leaving us. So it comes about that some complain of doctrine, if they think they see even the slightest kind of difference in it among us. Those who can find nothing to blame in it say they are offended by the faults of the ministers or teachers, and they think they have found a just cause for their secession from the Church if the life and morals of the teachers do not agree with the doctrine that is taught. There are some who complain of diversity in rites, if they see that the same order of teaching is not observed everywhere, or that the same ceremonies in the administration of the sacraments are not kept by all, or that the sacred assemblies are not held at the same moment among all the Churches of our profession, or that public prayers are composed in different words. I say nothing now of those over-scrupulous people who raise untimely questions about the dress of the ministers, the sacred vessels, and other adiaphora and indifferent matters, which create unnecessary quarrels and by which whole Churches are thrown into confusion, to the great scandal of many. There are also those who, although they approve both the doctrine and the whole arrangement of external rites, are nevertheless too curious in judging morals. They deny that the Church of Christ is among those who do not, by a stricter discipline, check faults according to their own whim; and these men almost think it permitted to them to do anything against us, if they see us admitting to the most holy Supper of the Lord, together with the pious, persons stained by manifest crimes and falling short of the profession of the Christian name.

units.la: Tunc enim margaritas porcis, & sanctum canibus proijci, eos vero omnes, qui cum eiusmodi hominibus Symbolis ijsdem fruuntur, peccatis alienis communicare, & proinde Ecclesiam totam impuram atque immundam esse clamant. Ex istis ergo causis aperta schismata nascuntur, & horribilis oritur non Ecclesiarum modo, verum etiam totius religionis dissipatio: qua fit, ut qui alieni delicti communicationem inconsiderato & praecipiti zelo fugiunt, eo scelere sese polluant, quo nullum gravius, nullum atrocius, nullum denique à Christianae fidei professione magis alienum designari poterat. Nam Ecclesiae desertores fiunt, & dum in hanc sibi ipsis temere iudicium sumunt, quae IESU CHRISTI sponsa est, non hanc modo, sed ipsum æternum Dei Filium in partes distrahunt, sub quo cum aliis credentibus in unum idemque corpus coalescere debebant: imo à Christo transfugæ fiunt, dum ab eorum societate sese sponte segregant, apud quos illius vox sonat, & quos ipse, quantumuis morbidos, pro suis tamen ouibus agnoscit. Falluntur hi omnes sua vel superbia & confidentia, quæ falsa absolutæ sanctimoniæ persuasione ipsos dementat: vel morositate, dum neminem ferre possunt, in quo aliquam labem Christiana professione indignam deprehendunt. Vtriusque autem mali ipsis præcipua causa est Ignorantia: quod nimirum quid sit Ecclesia, quæque eius in terris conditio sit, & ex quibus notis dignosci debeat, non intelligunt. Non ergo me rem vobis Patres in Christo reuerendiss. molestam aut iniucundam facturum puto, si de tota hac causa aliquanto diligentius dixero apud vos, ad quos (ut initio monuimus) eius cognitio imprimis pertinet. Nam licet illa vobis iampridem perspecta sit, & vobis non paruam molestiam præbuerit eiusmodi homi-num difficilis morositas, vtile tamen fuerit, si suas sententias frequenter & libere inter se conferant omnes ij, quibus hoc nouissimo sæculo Ecclesiæ suæ guber-nacula Deus commisit.
units.tr: For they cry out that pearls are being thrown to swine and what is holy given to dogs, and that all who share the same sacraments with such people partake of their sins, and therefore that the whole Church is impure and unclean. From these causes open schisms arise, and a dreadful dissolution not only of churches but of the whole of religion. So it happens that those who, in rash and headlong zeal, flee from sharing in another's crime pollute themselves with the very crime than which none could be graver, none more atrocious, and none, in short, more foreign to the profession of the Christian faith. For they become deserters of the Church, and while they rashly arrogate to themselves judgement over her, who is the bride of Jesus Christ, they tear apart not only her but the eternal Son of God himself, under whom they ought to grow together with other believers into one and the same body. Indeed they become deserters from Christ when they voluntarily separate themselves from the fellowship of those among whom his voice sounds and whom he himself acknowledges as his sheep, however diseased. All of these are deceived either by their pride and self-confidence, which drives them mad with the false persuasion of absolute holiness, or by fastidiousness, since they cannot tolerate anyone in whom they detect some stain unworthy of the Christian profession. The chief cause of both evils is ignorance: they do not understand what the Church is, what her condition is on earth, and by what marks she ought to be recognised. I therefore think I shall not be troubling or displeasing you, reverend fathers in Christ, if I speak somewhat more carefully about this whole matter before you, to whom, as I noted at the outset, its knowledge chiefly belongs. For although you have long since grasped it, and the difficult fastidiousness of such people has caused you no small trouble, it would nevertheless be useful if all those to whom God has committed the government of his Church in this last age frequently and freely compared their opinions with one another.

units.la: Ecclesia, quam in Symbolo Apostolico profitemur, proprie est omnium san-ctorum (ut supra diximus) communio siue societas. In ea soli electi censentur, qui per fidem in Christum filij Dei facti & eiusdem spiritu reuera sanctificati sunt, ideo-que soli etiam Deo nota est, qui solus nouit qui sint sui, & solus corda atq; renes hominum scrutatur. Eadem vt omnium sæculorum credentes, tam eos qui ab ipsa rerum origine fuerunt, quam eos qui hodie viuunt, & vsque ad mundi huius consummationem futuri sunt, comprehendit: ita nulli certo loco aut genti alligata per totum orbem terrarum ad omnes gentes extenditur. In præsenti tamen non de illa inuisibili (vt sic loquar) Ecclesia, sed de externa & visibili nobis sermo est, quam in vniuersalem & particulares possumus distinguere. Vniuersalis vel (si cui Græca vox magis arridet) Catholica dicitur tota illa Christianorum multitudo, quæ etsi regionum atque locorum spatijs hinc inde dispersa habitet, in vnam tamen eandemque verbi Dei doctrinam consentit & eiusdem fidei sacramentis colligatur. Hæc in se particulares omnes complectitur, quæ vt in diuersis nationibus & oppidis habitant: ita ex ijsdem nomina quoq; diuersa sortiuntur, vt alia Germanica, alia Gallica, alia Anglica, Polonica, Hungarica, vel quæ in eadem gente sunt, ab vrbibus Londinensis, Eboracensis, Tigurina &c. dicantur. Quapropter quoad nostri argumenti tractationem, Ecclesiam definimus esse societatem siue comunionem eorum, qui per Dei verbum ad IESVM CHRISTVM vocati, fidem in hunc eiusdem verbi studio & legitimo Sacramentorum vsu profitentur. Itaq; notæ Ecclesiæ visibilis sunt, verbi Dei prædicatio siue doctrina, & Sacra-mentorum vsus. Differt autem Ecclesia externa ab inuisibili, quòd vt hæc solos electos & adoptionis Spiritu donatos habet: ita in illa hypocritis quoq;, imò in-terdum flagitiosis etiam locus est, qui cùm à fide alieni sint, simulata tamen eius professione & Sacramentorum obseruatione in illius societatem sese insinuant. Ideo eam Dominus areae confert, in qua grana quidem frumenti reposita sunt, sed sub magnis palearum aceruis delitescunt, quæ suo demum tempore ipse fui iudi-cij vanno repurgata in regni sui æterni atq; cœlestis horreum transferet. Adhæc reti aut euerriculo eam similem dicit, quo omne genus piscium, viuorum & mortuorum vel semiputrium, trahuntur, non autem seliguntur, donec simul omnes in littus extracti fuerint: Agro deniq;, in quo cum bona tritici segete zizania & lolium simul succrescunt, quæ & ipsa non ante messem segregantur, id est, ante ex-tremam mundi huius consummationem. Non tamen obstat hoc, quo minus Christi Ecclesia sit illic, vbi verae fidei exercitia sunt, vtcunq; multi ea fraudulēter oba eant[?], multi etiam aperte contemnant. Nec enim fallere nos potest Christus, qui dixit: Vbicunq; duo aut tres congregati fuerint in meo nomine, ibi sum in medio eorum. Quis vero Christi coetum siue Ecclesiam esse eos negabit, qui & in eius nomine conueniunt, & salutari eiusdem praesentia fruuntur? Vel num istis fraudi erit aliorum improbitas, qui professioni suae minus respondent? Aut num ex electorum numero delebuntur ij, quorum gregi aut coetibus sese aliqui dolo malo immiscent, dum illi Dominum vocantem animo syncero & fide non simulata sequuntur? Haec certe, si paulo attentius considerentur, nimis temerarios esse patebit eos, qui propter eas, quas supra commemorauimus, causas ab Ecclesijs discedunt, in quibus purior verbi Dei doctrina sonat, & fidei Christianae symbola secundum Christi institutionem rite dispensantur.
units.tr: The Church which we profess in the Apostles' Creed is, properly speaking, the communion or fellowship of all the saints (as we said above). In it only the elect are counted, those who through faith in Christ have been made sons of God and in truth sanctified by his Spirit; and therefore it is known to God alone, who alone knows who are his, and alone searches the hearts and reins of men. This Church embraces the believers of all ages, both those who have existed from the very beginning of things and those who live today and will live until the consummation of this world; and in the same way, not bound to any fixed place or nation, it extends through the whole earth to all nations. In the present discussion, however, our concern is not with that invisible Church, as I may call it, but with the external and visible Church, which we can divide into universal and particular. The universal, or (if anyone prefers the Greek word) catholic, is that whole multitude of Christians which, though dwelling dispersed here and there across the spaces of regions and places, nevertheless agrees in one and the same doctrine of God's Word and is bound together by the sacraments of the same faith. This universal Church comprises all the particular churches, which, as they dwell in different nations and towns, so also take different names from them: some are called German, others French, others English, Polish, Hungarian, or, within the same nation, are named from cities, as the Church of London, of York, of Zurich, and so on. Therefore, for the purposes of our argument, we define the Church as the fellowship or communion of those who have been called to Jesus Christ through God's Word and who profess faith in him by studying that same Word and by the lawful use of the sacraments. Thus the marks of the visible Church are the preaching or teaching of God's Word and the use of the sacraments. The external Church differs from the invisible in this: the invisible has only the elect and those endowed with the Spirit of adoption, whereas in the external there is room also for hypocrites, and even at times for wicked men, who, though estranged from faith, insinuate themselves into its fellowship by a feigned profession and by observing the sacraments. For this reason the Lord likens it to a threshing floor, in which indeed grains of wheat are stored, but lie hidden under great heaps of chaff, which at last, in its own time, he will purge by the winnowing fan of his judgement and carry into the barn of his eternal and heavenly kingdom. He also likens it to a net or dragnet, which draws in every kind of fish, living and dead or half-rotten, and does not sort them until all have been drawn out onto the shore; and to a field in which tares and darnel grow up together with the good wheat, and which are not separated before the harvest, that is, before the final consummation of this world. Yet this does not prevent the Church of Christ from being wherever the exercises of true faith are, even though many carry them out fraudulently and many openly despise them. For Christ, who said, "Wherever two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them," cannot deceive us. And who will deny that those are the assembly or Church of Christ who gather in his name and enjoy his saving presence? Or will the wickedness of others, who fall short of their profession, be a loss to these? Or will those be erased from the number of the elect who are mixed into their flock or assemblies by deceit, while those sincerely and without pretence follow the Lord who calls them in faith? If these matters are considered somewhat more attentively, it will be plain that those are too rash who, for the reasons we have mentioned above, depart from those Churches in which the purer doctrine of God's Word sounds and the symbols of the Christian faith are rightly dispensed according to Christ's institution.

units.la: Nam vt a doctrina exordiamur, cuius diuersitas, vel potius species diuersitatis, multos offendit, fatemur equidem huius rationem praecipuam haberi debere, ne falsam pro vera admittamus. Quia enim per hanc ad Ecclesiae societatem homines vocantur, & in eade retinentur, Ecclesia vera esse non poterit, a qua vel doctrina verbi Dei exulat, vel in qua huius loco hominum traditiones praedicantur. Nec enim temere dixit Christus: Oues meae vocem MEAM audiunt, & ego cognosco eas, & sequuntur ME, alienum vero non sequuntur, sed fugient ab eo. Et Apostoli praeceptum est, ne cuiuis spiritui credamus, sed probemus spiritus num ex Deo sint. At hic meminisse oportet, distinguendum esse inter dogmata siue axiomata fidei Christianae, sine quibus ea consistere non potest, & priuatas quorundam sententias siue opiniones de rebus medijs aut indifferentibus, in quibus absque salutis periculo dissensiones oriri possunt. Axiomata fidei sunt certa & firma, Deum esse vnum, mundi huius & omnium quae in eo sunt creatorem atque gubernatorem, qui solus a nobis coli, solus item in omni necessitate inuocari debeat: Homines omnes in peccato concipi & nasci, ideoque natura peccatores esse, neque ex suis operibus quenquam seruari posse: Iustificari autem nos ex gratuita Dei misericordia per IESVM CHRISTVM, si hunc fide vera amplectamur, qui nobis a Patre factus est satisfactio, iustitia & redemptionis nostrae pretium: Christum esse verum aeternumque Dei filium, qui praefinito tempore homo factus, proque nobis in ara crucis semel immolatus, nobis perfectam & omnibus numeris absolutam peccatorum expiationem atque salutem meruerit: Hius item merito redemptos decere, vt tanto pretio partam libertatem serio tueantur, charitati & sanctimoniae studeant, & si quando ex innata vitiositate peccent, per poenitentiam ad Deum reuertantur: Animas item esse immortales, & eorum qui credunt animas ex morte in vitam aeternam, impiorum vero & infidelium in loca aeternis supplicijs destinata transfire: Fore denique corporum, quae nunc gestamus, resurrectionem, post quam omnes homines ad Christi tribunal sistentur, vt vel promissa vitae aeternae praemia recipiant, vel cum malis Angelis ad aeternos inferorum cruciatus relegentur. Debent his addi Symboli Apostolici articuli, & a Christo nobis tradita precandi formula, quibus vera fidei & inuocationis ratio siue regula continetur: Decalogi item praecepta, quae vt vitam & mores nostros formant, ita priuatim quidem oeconomias & rerum proprietatem, publice vero magistratus quoque authoritatem stabiliunt. Haec (inquam) certa & immutabilia sunt doctrinae Christianae capita, quae in sacris literis ita traduntur, vt nemini de illis aliter sentire aut loqui liceat. Quare si de his in Ecclesia aliqua ex Dei verbo recte differatur, nullam discessionis causam iustam aliquis habebit, licet in aliis nonnullis, sine quibus salus nostra constare potest, alij aliter sentiant. Idem de scripturarum interpretatione dici potest, cuius regulam Paulus esse iubet Analogiam fidei, ne videlicet aliquid huic contrarium statuatur. Etenim constat, esse quidem vniuscuiusq; loci sensum aliquem proprium atque germanum, in cuius inuestigatione doctores diligen-tes esse conuenit: sit tamen frequenter, vt locus aliquis salua fidei Analogia diuer-sos sensus admittat, qui simul omnes ad fidelium ædificationem & vitæ Christia-næ institutionem faciunt. Quòd si tunc aliqui ex ea diuersitate calumniandi & ab Ecclesia discedendi occasionem arripiant, quis illos plus æquo morosiores, imo à charitate Christiana alienos esse negauerit? Aliter certè Apostolus iubet, qui in Ecclesia liberam sententiarum collationem fieri & iudicium penes sedentes esse voluit. Eius enim verba sunt: Spiritum ne extinguatis, prophetias ne pro nihilo ducatis: omnia explorate, quod bonum fuerit, retinete.
units.tr: To begin with doctrine, whose diversity, or rather the appearance of diversity, offends many, we certainly admit that it ought chiefly to be taken into account, so that we do not accept what is false as true. For since men are called into the fellowship of the Church through doctrine and kept in it, the Church cannot be true where the doctrine of God's Word is absent, or where the traditions of men are preached in its place. Christ did not speak carelessly when he said: "My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me, but they will not follow a stranger; they will flee from him." And the Apostle commands us not to believe every spirit, but to test the spirits whether they are of God. Here, however, we must remember to distinguish between the dogmas or axioms of the Christian faith, without which it cannot stand, and the private opinions or views of certain people about matters that are indifferent or intermediate, on which disagreements may arise without danger to salvation. The axioms of the faith are these, certain and firm: that God is one, the creator and governor of this world and of all that is in it, who alone ought to be worshipped by us and alone invoked in every need; that all men are conceived and born in sin, and therefore are sinners by nature, and that no one can be saved by his own works; that we are justified by God's free mercy through Jesus Christ, if we embrace him with true faith, whom the Father has made to us the satisfaction, righteousness and price of our redemption; that Christ is the true and eternal Son of God, who, made man at the appointed time and sacrificed once for us on the altar of the cross, has merited for us a perfect and in every respect complete expiation of sins and salvation; that those redeemed by his merit ought likewise to guard earnestly the freedom bought at so great a price, to strive for love and holiness, and if at any time they sin through innate wickedness, to return to God by repentance; that souls are likewise immortal, and that the souls of those who believe pass from death into eternal life, but those of the impious and unbelieving pass into places destined for eternal punishments; finally, that there will be a resurrection of the bodies we now bear, after which all men will be brought before the tribunal of Christ, so that they may either receive the promised rewards of eternal life or be sent away with the evil angels to the eternal torments of hell. To these should be added the articles of the Apostles' Creed, and the form of prayer delivered to us by Christ, in which the true rule of faith and of invocation is contained; likewise the precepts of the Decalogue, which shape our life and morals, and which establish, in private life, household management and the ownership of property, and in public life also the authority of the magistrate. These (I say) are the certain and unchangeable heads of Christian doctrine, which are so handed down in the sacred writings that no one may hold or speak about them otherwise. Therefore, if these things are rightly taught in the Church from God's Word, no one will have a just cause for separation, even though others think differently about some other matters, without which our salvation can stand. The same may be said of the interpretation of Scripture, whose rule Paul bids us follow, namely the analogy of faith, so that nothing contrary to it is asserted. For it is certain that each passage has some proper and genuine sense, in searching out which diligent teachers ought to labour; yet it often happens that a passage, while preserving the analogy of faith, admits various senses, all of which serve the edification of the faithful and the training of Christian life. But if some people seize on this diversity as an occasion for slander and for departing from the Church, who would deny that they are more fastidious than is right, indeed alien to Christian charity? Certainly the Apostle directs otherwise, for he wished that in the Church there be free comparison of opinions, with judgement left to those who sit in office. His words are: "Do not quench the Spirit; do not despise prophecies; test all things, hold fast to what is good."

units.la: At hîc nobis corruptos ministrorum Ecclesiæ mores aliqui obiiciunt, in quo argumento Anabaptistæ præ aliis mirificè exultant. Nam cùm exæquo Ecclesiæ ministerium & magistratum politicum oderint, vtriusque ordinis abolendi plau-sibilem occasionem & causam iustissimâ se adeptos esse arbitrantur, si vel Eccle-siæ pastores vel Reipub. præfectos dissolutius viuere animaduertant. Nec enim contenti eo nomine doctores accusauisse, quòd mores ipsorum doctrinæ non re-spondeant, insuper illos ipsi etiàm doctrinæ, imò toti Ecclesiæ fraudi esse volunt, quasi neque illius veritas, neque huius puritas amplius consistere, aut quisquam in Ecclesia eiusmodi saluus fieri possit. Adhæc Sacramentis quoque apud tales suam efficaciam perire clamant. Vbi non insiciabimur, plures hodie, proh dolor, inter Ecclesiæ ministros inueniri, quorum vita & mores acerrimâ correptionem merentur, & quos præstaret secundùm IESV CHRISTI dictum, suspensa ex collo ipsorum mola asinaria in maris abyssum præcipites dari, quàm tanti scan-dali authores esse. Quòd verò alteri illi propter improbos hosce sacri ministerij prophanatores, ipsam Veritatis doctrinam vnà cum Ecclesijs damnant, id nimis insolenter & nulla cum ratione ab eis fieri, Christi verba docent, quibus de Iu-dæorum doctoribus sic ait: In cathedra Mosis sedent Scribæ & Pharisæi: Omnia ergo quæcunque iusserint vos seruare, seruate: secundùm opera autem eorum nolite facere. Dicunt enim, & non faciunt. En docere illos testatur, quæ ipsi non faciant: imò ibidem (vt multis etiam aliis in locis) multa illos improbè, multa in-iustè & impiè facere, adhæc superstitiosis patrum traditionibus populum infeli-cem grauare quæritur. Attamen quia ordinarium in Ecclesia ministerium ha-beant, illos audiri vult, quando in Mosis cathedra sedent, id est, quando non ho-minum traditiones, sed per Mosem olim tradita Dei præcepta prædicant. Ergo mores quidem doctoris improbos, fastum item, libidinem, intemperantiam, aua-ritiam detestari licet: at propter ista doctrinâ Veritatis contemnere, ipsum minis-terium proscindere, & in Ecclesia scisma facere, id verò ab hominis Christiani officio alienissimum est. Iubet quidem alibi quoque Dominus, vt nobis cauea-mus à pseudoprophetis, & seducto ribus. At non semper seductores sunt, quicun-que male viuunt, sed qui falsa docent: & in doctore probando maior doctrinæ quàm vitæ aut morum ratio haberi debet. Nam si illa vera & integra fuerit, nihil ex moribus doctoris periculi erit auditoribus, nisi qui forte proprio vitio ad ne-quitiam procliues male agendi exempla auidè arripiunt. Similiter Sacramento-rum dignitas atque virtus, non ex ministri dignitate, sed ex Dei institutione de-pendet: Qua de re olim Diuus Augustinus multa præclarè contra Donatistas dis-putauit, apud quem in Epist. 166. hæc quoque verba ex Imperatorio contra illos edicto citantur: Si in eis, qui primò initiati sunt, idcirco religio baptismatis in-dicatur infirma, quòd hi à quibus accipitur, peccatores putentur, toties renouari necesse erit traditum Sacramentum, quoties indignus fuerit inuentus eollati baptismatis administrator, & fides nostra non ex nostræ voluntatis arbitrio, neq; ex diuini muneris gratia, sed ex meritis sacerdotum & clericorum qualitate pena debit. Quibus non multo post Augustinus subiicit: Semper Dei est illa gratia, & Dei Sacramentum, hominis autem solum ministerium: qui si bonus est, adhæret Deo, & operatur cum Deo: si autem malus est, operatur per illum Deus visibilem Sacramenti formam, ipse autem donat invisibilem gratiam. Hoc sapiamus omnes, & non sint in nobis scismata, &c.
units.tr: But here some object to us the corrupt morals of the ministers of the Church, and on this argument the Anabaptists exult above all others. For since they hate the ministry of the Church and the civil magistracy alike, they think they have a plausible occasion and a most just cause for abolishing both orders, if they notice that either the ministers of the Church or the rulers of the commonwealth live too loosely. Nor are they content to have accused the teachers on this ground, that their morals do not match their doctrine; they want those men to be a snare not only to doctrine but to the whole Church, as if neither the truth of the one nor the purity of the other could any longer stand, and no one in the Church could be saved of that kind. Moreover, they cry out that among such people the sacraments also lose their efficacy. Here we will not deny that, alas, many today are found among the ministers of the Church whose life and morals deserve the sharpest correction, and whom it would be better, according to the saying of Jesus Christ, to have a great millstone hung about their neck and be cast headlong into the depths of the sea, than to be authors of so great a scandal. But that those others, on account of these wicked profaners of the sacred ministry, condemn the very doctrine of the Truth along with the Churches, that they do this too insolently and without any reason, the words of Christ teach, in which he speaks thus of the teachers of the Jews: "The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' seat. Therefore whatever they bid you observe, that observe; but do not do according to their works, for they say and do not do" (Matt. 23). Behold, he testifies that they teach things which they themselves do not do; indeed in the same place, as in many others, he complains that they act wickedly, act unjustly and impiously in many ways, and moreover burden the unhappy people with superstitious traditions of the Fathers. Yet because they hold the ordinary ministry in the Church, he wills that they be heard when they sit in Moses' seat, that is, when they preach not the traditions of men but the commandments of God once delivered through Moses. So although one may rightly detest the wicked morals of a teacher, his pride, lust, intemperance and avarice, yet to despise the doctrine of the Truth on account of these things, to tear down the ministry itself and to make a schism in the Church, is utterly alien to the duty of a Christian man. The Lord indeed commands elsewhere too that we beware of false prophets, and of those who lead us astray. But not all who live badly are seducers; those who teach falsehoods are. And in judging a teacher, a regard for his doctrine ought to be had rather than for his life or morals. For if the doctrine is true and whole, there will be no danger to the hearers from the teacher's morals, unless perhaps those who, by their own fault, are prone to wickedness eagerly seize upon bad examples. Likewise the dignity and power of the sacraments depend not on the dignity of the minister but on the institution of God. On this matter Blessed Augustine long ago disputed many things splendidly against the Donatists, and in Epistle 166 he cites against them also these words from an imperial edict: "If the religion of baptism is judged weak among those who were first initiated because those from whom they receive it are thought to be sinners, the sacrament handed down will have to be renewed as often as the administrator of the conferred baptism is found unworthy, and our faith will be owed not to the judgment of our will, nor to the grace of the divine gift, but to the merits of the priests and the quality of the clergy." Not long after these words Augustine adds: "That grace is always God's, and the sacrament is God's; the ministry alone is man's. Whoever is good cleaves to God and works with God; but if he is evil, God works through him the visible form of the sacrament, while he himself gives the invisible grace. Let us all be wise in this, and let there be no schisms among us, etc."

units.la: Sed illos quoque audiamus, qui de rituum diversitate queruntur, & propter hanc ab Ecclesijs nostris sibi discedendum esse putant. Offendit eos, aut saltem se offendi simulant, quod non eadem apud omnes observetur baptizandi formula, dum alij paruulos totos in aquam intinguunt, alij sola aspersione utuntur: alij item dum istud agitur, preces breviores, alij prolixiores fundunt. In Coena quoque Dominica hoc illis indignissime fieri videtur, quod in plerisque Ecclesijs ad mensam Domini accedunt tam viri quam mulieres, ut ex ministrorum manibus symbola sacra accipiant: in aliquibus vero eadem per sedentium subsellia circumferantur: qui illa inter se distribuunt. Quod item apud aliquos epulum istud sacrum in usu frequentiori est, cum alijs ter aut quater in anno illud usurpavisse suf-ficiat. Sunt etiam, quibus hoc quoque reprehensione dignum putatur, quod non eadem sit apud omnes Ecclesias vasorum sacrorum forma atque materia, & alij quidem ligneis, alij vitreis, multi argenteis & aureis utantur. Sunt rursus qui de ministrorum habitu lites non necessarias movent, & eo usque progrediuntur, ut propter illum viros graves & de Ecclesia atque communi Religionis causa optime meritos damnare audeant. At isti omnes non obscure suam ignorantiam (ne quid durius de illis pronuntiem) produnt: quando non intelligunt, diversitatem istam libertati Christianæ imprimis servire, & simul superstitionibus viam obstruere, quæ facile in vulgi animis locum inveniunt, si eosdem ritus ab omnibus solicite observari videant, adeo ut piaculum esse putetur, si quis a recepto apud aliquos mo-re vel latum unguem discesserit. Ita enim inter homines natura comparatum est, ut plerique externis ceremoniis addicti, quæ sub his adumbrantur mysteria eorumque usum proprium minus observent. Prodest ergo nos illarum diversitate admoneri, ut longe aliud hic agi cogitemus, quam primo intuitu appareat. Et cur diversitas ista hodie aliquem offendat, quando olim ex Christianæ libertatis iure Ecclesijs singulis licuit ijs ritibus uti, quos suæ gentis hominibus utiles esse, & pro locorum atque temporum ratione ad ædificationem plurimorum imprimis facere videbant? Multa de hac re Socrates in Ecclesiastica historia libro quinto Cap. 22[?] scribit, ubi inter alia Victorem, Romanæ Ecclesiæ antistitem, reprehendit, quod propter Paschatis solennitatem, quæ usque ad illius tempora non eodem tempore, neque eodem ritu absque omni dissensionis scandalo in Ecclesijs peracta fuerat, ipse [illegible, ~12 letters] id est, immodico fervore & zelo accensus Asiæ Ecclesias communione Christianorum privare ausus esset. Constat item in feriis & Coenæ Dominicæ usu, in precibus denique publicis, non eandem rituum externorum formam in omnibus Ecclesijs observatam fuisse. Etenim D. Hieronymus Exuperium Tholosatem episcopum laudat, quod corpus Domini in canistro vimineo, sanguinem in vitro gestaret. At quid ista de illo commemorare opus erat, si hoc ipsum alij quoque episcopi fecissent, atque eadem aut similia vasa illo seculo apud omnes in usu fuissent? Num vero hoc Exuperio aliquis vitio vertit, quod Hieronymus laude dignum putavit? Aut num ille Ecclesias alias damnavit, quæ alijs vasis utebantur? Idem de ministrorum vestibus rectissime dixeris, de quibus olim nulla unquam controversia fuit, eo quod liberum esset omnibus, ut pro more gentis suæ eo habitu uterentur, qui honestissimus habebatur. Vuala-fridus certe: qui vixit circa annum nati Christi DCC. in suo Ratio. Cap. 25. affirmat, veteres olim vsos fuisse veste vulgari, sed munda. Tandem inter sacra veste candida vti coeperunt, abscp[?] superstitione tamen: Vnde D. Hierony. aduersus Pelagianos, qui vestitum ornatiorem, vt Deo contrarium, damnabant, scripsit: Quae sunt, rogo, inimicitiae contra Deum, si tunicam habuero mundiorem? si episcopus, presbyter & diaconus, & reliquus ordo ecclesiasticus in administratione sacrificiorum candida veste processerint? Veruntamen creuit posteris temporibus cum superstitione luxus & fastus, vt sicuti immodico templorum ornatu pecatum fuit: ita habitu quoq; non minus molli & sumptuoso quam superstitioso & ad simulatam sanctitatis speciem compositio sese Episcopi ostentarint, & quicunque alij Ecclesiae ministrauerunt. Quod vt merito pij omnes damnant: ita eorum morositatem nemo qui sanae mentis & pacis amans est, probare poterit, qui dum nihil ferre volunt, quod a vulgari alicuius gentis habitu vel modicum differt, lis tibus minime necessarijs omnia turbant, & Ecclesias non sine periculosissimo scandalo in partes distrahunt. Hi dum nihil non timent, interim seipsos & Ecclesias in discrimen omnium maximum nocentissimumq; adducunt, & fit plerunq; (quod Socrates de Nouatianis, Eunomianis & aliis similibus scribit) vt qui semel ab Ecclesia secessionem fecerunt, postea ipsi quoq; inter se scindantur, neq; vllus sectarum & dissidiorum finis sit. Recte ergo Diuus Augustinus ad lanuarium scribens, cum diuersos, qui suo tempore obseruabantur, Ecclesiarum ritus exposuisset, hanc regulam Christianis hominibus tutissimam fore putauit, si in iis quae salua fide & pietate fieri possunt, sese Ecclesijs, ad quas venerint accommodent. Eius verba sunt haec: Nulla disciplina in his est melior graui prudentiaq; Christiano, quam vt eo modo agat, quo agere viderit Ecclesiam, ad quamcunq; forte deuenerit. Quod enim neq; contra fidem, neq; contra bonos mores iniungitur, indifferenter est habendum, & pro eorum inter quos viuitur societate, seruandum. Et ibidem Diui Ambrosij, de diuersitate ieiuniorum abs se interrogati, respōsum adducit, quod sibi postea semper coelestis oraculo loco fuisse scribit: Cum Romam venio, ieiuno sabbato: cum hic sum (Mediolani scilicet) non ieiuno: Sic etiam tu, ad quam forte Ecclesiam veneris, cius morem serua, si cuiquam non vis esse scandalo, nec quenquam tibi. Qua moderatione si hodie omnes vterentur, minus contentionum esset in Ecclesia, neq; superstitiosis hominum traditionibus libertas Christiana circumscriberetur. Cur vero totas Ecclesias damnant propter res indifferentes & mediias[?], qui (si Paulo obedire velint) singulorum infirmitati sese accommodare debent?
units.tr: But let us also hear those who complain of the diversity of rites, and think that on account of this they must withdraw from our Churches. It offends them, or at least they pretend to be offended, that the same baptismal formula is not observed by all: while some dip the whole infant into water, others use only sprinkling; likewise, while this is being done, some pour out shorter prayers and others longer ones. In the Lord's Supper too they see this as most unworthily done: that in most Churches both men and women come to the Lord's table to receive the sacred symbols from the hands of the ministers, while in some they are passed round through the benches of those seated, who distribute them among themselves. Likewise, that among some this sacred feast is in more frequent use, while for others it suffices to have used it three or four times a year. There are also those who think it deserving of reproof that the form and material of the sacred vessels is not the same in all Churches, and that some use wooden, others glass, many silver and gold. There are again those who stir up unnecessary disputes about the dress of ministers, and go so far that on account of it they dare to condemn men who are grave and have deserved very well of the Church and of the common cause of religion. But all these men plainly reveal their ignorance (not to say anything harsher about them), since they do not understand that this diversity serves above all Christian liberty, and at the same time blocks the way to superstitions, which easily find a place in the minds of the common people if they see the same rites diligently observed by all, so that it is thought a sin if anyone departs even a hair's breadth from the custom received among some. For it is so ordained by nature among men that most, being devoted to external ceremonies, pay less heed to the mysteries which are shadowed forth under them and to their proper use. It is therefore useful for us to be reminded by this diversity that something quite different is being done here than appears at first sight. And why should this diversity offend anyone today, when of old, by the right of Christian liberty, it was lawful for individual Churches to use those rites which they saw to be useful for the people of their own nation and, according to the circumstances of places and times, to serve above all the edification of many? Socrates writes much on this matter in the fifth book of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 22, where among other things he rebukes Victor, the bishop of the Roman Church, because on account of the solemnity of Easter, which until his time had not been celebrated in all Churches at the same time or by the same rite without any scandal of dissension, he himself, inflamed with immoderate fervour and zeal, dared to deprive the Churches of Asia of the communion of Christians. It is likewise established that in the festivals and in the use of the Lord's Supper, and finally in the public prayers, the same outward form of rites was not observed in all Churches. For Blessed Jerome praises Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, because he carried the body of the Lord in a wicker basket and the blood in a glass. But why was it necessary to mention this about him, if other bishops also did the same, and the same or similar vessels were in use among all at that time? Did anyone ever find fault with Exuperius for this, which Jerome thought worthy of praise? Or did he condemn the other Churches which used other vessels? The same you may rightly say of the dress of ministers, about which there was never any controversy in former times, because it was free for all to use, according to the custom of their own people, the garb that was regarded as most decorous. Walafrid certainly, who lived about the year 700 after the birth of Christ, in his Rationale, chapter 25, affirms that the ancients once used common but clean clothing. Afterwards they began to use white vestments in sacred service, yet without superstition. Hence Blessed Jerome, writing against the Pelagians, who condemned more ornate dress as contrary to God, wrote: "What, I ask, are the enmities against God if I have a cleaner tunic? If the bishop, the presbyter and the deacon, and the rest of the ecclesiastical order, have come forward in white garments in the administration of the sacrifices?" Yet in later times, along with superstition, luxury and pride grew, so that just as an immoderate adornment of the temples became a sin, so the bishops and all others who served the Church displayed themselves in dress no less soft and costly than superstitious and arranged to show a feigned appearance of holiness. As all the pious rightly condemn this, so no one who is sane and loves peace can approve the fussiness of those who, while they will tolerate nothing that differs even slightly from the common dress of any nation, throw everything into confusion with wholly unnecessary quarrels, and divide the Churches into factions not without the most dangerous scandal. While these men fear nothing, they meanwhile bring themselves and the Churches into the greatest and most harmful peril; and it often happens (as Socrates writes of the Novatians, the Eunomians and other like sects) that those who have once seceded from the Church afterwards split among themselves too, and there is no end to sects and dissensions. Rightly therefore Blessed Augustine, writing to Januarius, when he had set out the diverse rites of the Churches observed in his time, thought this the safest rule for Christian people: that in those things which can be done without loss of faith and piety, they accommodate themselves to the Churches to which they come. His words are these: "There is no discipline better in these matters for a Christian of grave prudence than to act in the way he sees the Church acting in whatever place he happens to arrive at. For what is enjoined neither against faith nor against good morals is to be regarded as indifferent, and to be observed for the sake of the fellowship of those among whom one lives." And in the same place he cites the answer of Blessed Ambrose, asked by him about the diversity of fasts, which he writes was ever afterwards to him a heavenly oracle: "When I come to Rome I fast on the Sabbath; when I am here (at Milan, namely) I do not fast. So also you, to whatever Church you come, keep its custom, if you do not wish to be a scandal to anyone, nor anyone to you." If all used this moderation today, there would be less contention in the Church, nor would Christian liberty be confined by the superstitious traditions of men. But why do they condemn whole Churches on account of things indifferent and in the middle, when they, if they are willing to obey Paul, ought to accommodate themselves to the weakness of individuals?

units.la: Venio nunc ad illos, qui cum & doctrinam & vniuersam alicuius Ecclesiae œconomiam probent, in eadem tamen se seruari non posse sibi ipsis persuadent, quod plerosq; in illa vitam Christiana professione indignam viuere, & malos bonis permixtos esse videant. At debebant isti nunquam non meminisse parabolarum, quibus Christus Dominus Ecclesiae suae in terris hisce militantis conditionem describit: quando illam (vt supra annotauimus) agro, areae & reti siue sagenae confert: quibus si tam veteris quam noui Testamenti exempla coniungerent, mox viderent, ne hic quidem ipsis iustam scismatis causam offerri. Quando enim vnquam ea fuit populi Dei facies siue conditio, vt nulli in illo scelerati & aperti s flagitijs infames fuerint? Num Abrahami domum ab omni vitio puram fuisse dicent? Atqui tum falsi eos arguent pastorum iurgia, Sarae vxoris abnegatio, Ismaelis proteruia, vt iam de Lothi & filiarum incestu nihil dicam. Vel num sub Isaaco & Iacobo Ecclesiam fuisse negare poterunt? Non equidem tam audaces dixero. At ille Esauum filium habuit, hominem improbe contumacem, diuini foederis & promissionum omnium contemptorem: hic vero Rubenum incestu infamem, Leui & Simeonem sanguinarios circumcisionis prophanatores, Iudam im pudentissimum scortatorem, decem denique filios plagiarios & fraterni sanguinis reos. Quid vero de Israelitis in deserto peregrinantibus dicent? Num Aaronem, Eleazarum, Phineen, Iosuam, Chalebum & horum similes damnabunt, qui ut gemmae quaedam in foedissimo illo turbae murmuratricis & omni genere scelerum pollutę[?] coeno fulserunt? Quod si ad Prophetarum tempora veniamus, illos clamantes audimus: Omne caput languet, & omne cor moeret: a planta pedis ad verticem usq; nihil est integrum: vulnus, tumor, purulentaq; plaga. Item: Macilentia mea mihi, macilentia mea mihi. Et rursus: Ecce ego & pueri, quos dedit mihi Dominus, miraculum & portentum sumus in Israele. Nisi Dominus exercituum reliquas nobis fecisset reliquias aliquas, sicuti Sodoma essemus. Quis vero dubitet reliquias istas, etsi paucae & tenues fuerint, vera tamen & germana Ecclesiae Catholicae, quam in symbolo profitemur, membra fuisset? Et cur obsecro de eo dubitaremus, quando sub impio Achabo, imperium inter Israelitas tenentibus pseudoprophetis & impuri Baalis sacerdotibus, Deus sibi septem millia piorum seruavit, quos ne Elias quidem noverat, ipse autem de illorum fide & integritate testatur? Potest idem de omnium saeculorum Ecclesiis dici, iis etiam, quae ab Apostolis collectae & institutae fuerunt: a quibus tamen nemo piorum secessionem fecisse legitur, ne aliorum malitia ipse polluereutur. Nimium ergo morosi & aequo audaciores sunt, quibus non satis est scelera & sceleratos damnauisse, nisi Ecclesias quoque, in quibus illi vivunt, immundas atque prophanas dicant, & ita eos simul damnent, quos aeternus Dei filius pro suis agnoscit.
units.tr: I come now to those who, although they approve both the doctrine and the whole order of some Church, nevertheless persuade themselves that they cannot be kept safe in it, because they see that many in it live a Christian profession unworthy of the name, and that evil men are mixed with good. But these men ought never to forget the parables by which Christ the Lord describes the condition of his Church in this militant earth, when he compares it (as we noted above) to a field, a threshing floor and a net or dragnet. If they were to join to these the examples of both the Old and the New Testament, they would soon see that not even here is a just cause of schism offered to them. For when was the face or condition of the people of God ever such that there were no wicked men in it, and none notorious for open crimes? Will they say that Abraham's household was pure of every vice? Yet then they will accuse the quarrels of the herdsmen, Sarah's denial, Ishmael's wantonness, not to mention Lot and the incest of his daughters. Or will they be able to deny that there was a Church under Isaac and Jacob? I would not dare to say so. Yet the one had a son Esau, a man shamelessly contumacious, a despiser of the divine covenant and of all the promises; the other had Reuben infamous for incest, Levi and Simeon, bloodthirsty profaners of circumcision, Judah a most shameless fornicator, and finally ten sons who were kidnappers and guilty of fraternal blood. What will they say of the Israelites wandering in the desert? Will they condemn Aaron, Eleazar, Phinehas, Joshua, Caleb and others like them, who shone like certain jewels in that most foul crowd of murmurers, polluted with every kind of crime? And if we come to the times of the prophets, we hear them crying out: "The whole head is sick, and the whole heart mourns; from the sole of the foot to the crown there is nothing whole: wound, swelling, and festering sore." Likewise: "My leanness, my leanness is upon me." And again: "Behold, I and the children whom the Lord has given me are a sign and a wonder in Israel. Unless the Lord of hosts had left us some remnant, we would have been like Sodom." Who would doubt that these remnants, though few and slender, were true and genuine members of the Catholic Church, which we profess in the creed? And why, I beg you, should we doubt this, when under the impious Ahab, with false prophets holding sway among the Israelites and priests of the unclean Baal, God preserved for himself seven thousand pious men, whom not even Elijah knew, while God himself bears witness to their faith and integrity? The same can be said of the Churches of all ages, even those which were gathered and established by the Apostles; yet we read that none of the godly withdrew from them, lest they themselves be polluted by the malice of others. Therefore those are too peevish and rather too bold, who are not content to have condemned sins and sinners, unless they also call the Churches in which those men live unclean and profane, and so condemn at once those whom the eternal Son of God acknowledges as his own.

units.la: At cùm ista dicimus, fatentur aliqui, nimium esse istorum hominum rigorem, ipsidem tamen hoc intolerabile prorsus & nulla venia dignum esse videtur, quòd qui hucusque sceleribus siue flagitijs manifestis polluti fuerunt, non modo in Ecclesiae coetibus locum habeant, verumetiam ad publicam Baptismi & Coenae Dominicae communionem admittantur. Hoc illis non iniquum modo & absurdum facinus, sed sacrilegium quoque esse videtur, quo simul omnes inquinentur, quotquot cum talibus in eundem coetum conueniunt, & ad eandem Domini Coenam accedentes, se eiusdem corporis membra cum illis esse profitentur. Et ne abs que ratione ista in nos detonare videantur, illud Pauli nobis obijciunt: Si quis cùm frater nominatur, sit scortator, aut auarus, aut idololatra, aut conuitiator, aut ebriosus, aut rapax, cum eiusmodi ne edatis quidem. Ex quibus verbis ita colligunt: Si cum palàm flagitiosis ad mensam vulgarem accedere non licet homini Christiano, multò minus illi ad Domini mensam debent admitti, ut qui verè pij & credentes sunt cum ipsis communicent. At debebant isti cogitare, aliud esse ab hominum improborum contubernio aut consuetudine non necessaria abstinere: aliud eosdem, si poenitentiam profiteantur, & cum Ecclesia mortem Domini praedicare cupiant, ab eo officio arcere, aut propter illos ab Ecclesiae societate discedere. Etenim inter duo haec Paulus ipse non obscurè distinguit. Qui enim cum sceleratis aut flagitio aliquo pollutis cibum vulgarem sumere prohibet, ut eosdem à mensa Domini reijciamus nuspiam iubet, sed quoad huius usum, ut quisque seipsum examinet praecipit, non ut nos in aliorum conscientias nobis ius aut iudicium sumamus. Enimuero graviter monet Apostolus, ne quis indignè accedens sibipsi iudicium edat & bibat: at nos in tota hac causa, quoad nostram salutem, non vult de aliorum vel hypocrisi vel apertis flagitijs solicitos esse, quasi eorum impuritate ipsi pollui possimus. Charitatis quidem hoc officium esse fatemur, ut quisque amicè & graviter eos admoneat, quos in re tanti momenti videt esse proteruiores, & de quibus periculum est, ne temere cum salutis aeternae iactura sese ingerant: At quia nos latet, qualis quisque tunc fit, quando ad mysticum hoc epulum accedit, nihil pro imperio facere, sed suo unumquenque iudicio[?] relinquere debemus. Et quia hic non de vitæ & morum, sed de sacrorum communione agitur, friuola & superuacanea est solicitudo illa, quæ aliquos discruciat, ne cum improborum peccatis communicent, aut cum ijsdem in vnum idemque corpus coalescant. Si enim qui post vitam hucusque petulanter actam ad mensam Domini accedunt, iam vere & ex animo resipuerunt, digne etiam cum piis corporis & sanguinis Christi communione fruuntur, & Ecclesiæ germana membra sunt. Sin vero hypocritæ sint improbi, Ecclesiam quidem fallere, & eius symbolis abuti possunt, ad eius vero communionem minime pertinent, & proin de nullum quoque est fidelibus cum illorum improbitate commercium: sed sibi ipsis, non aliis, tales iudicium manducant. Nec absque ratione Apostolum hoc ita constituisse putabimus. Sciebat enim quid Christus fecisset, qui discipulos multis adhuc vitiis, superbia nimirum & ambitione & inuidia & æmulatione praua infectos, confidentia item inflatos, non solum epulo paschali, verumetiam mensæ suæ mysticæ adhibuit: qui denique ne Petrum quidem exclusit, qui ipsum paulo post turpiter abnegaturus erat: vt iam de Iuda nihil dicamus, quem furem & proditorem nequissimum esse non ignorabat. Noluit ergo Paulus hero & magistro suo rigidior haberi, ne forte eos repelleret, quos ille ad suam communionem liberalissime inuitat: aut ijs externa symbola negaret, quos idem ille proprio corpore & sanguine ad vitam æternam pascere dignatur. At scio aliquos Iudam ideo non exclusum dicere, quod eius scelus adhuc lateret, neque scandalum publicum dedisset. Sed qua ratione illi hoc latuisse dicunt, cum illud æternus Dei filius, verus ille cordium scrutator, verbis non minus gravibus quam disertis detexerit? At nesciebant (inquiunt) discipuli, de quo nam ille loqueretur. Quid tum postea? Certe eo gravius erat periculum, si eius sceleris ipsi contaminari potuissent, cum proditorem audirent in mensa esse, eiusdem vero communionem, quoad cœnæ externum vsum, non possent cauere: & quamvis quis nam esset nescirent, non poterant tamen ignorare, quam horribile hoc scandalum esset futurum, si Christus a discipulo domestico proderetur. Vt vero sinamus infelicem illum, quid de aliis discipulis dicemus? Num occulta latuit eorum ambitio, quæ post tam multas tamque graves admonitiones in apertam contentionem exarsit? Et quæ obscura ratio poterit adduci, quæ nos a cœnæ vsu eos arcere iubeat, qui prius quidem enormiter peccaverunt, nunc autem vna cum seria peccati confessione seruatoris sui IESV CHRISTI studium atque fidem profitentur; quando ipse Dominus eos admisit, qui inter media sacra peccabant, & ideo redargutionem & correptionem duriorem merebantur?
units.tr: But when we say these things, some admit that the severity of these men is excessive; yet they judge it utterly intolerable and deserving of no pardon that those who until now have been defiled by manifest crimes or scandals not only have a place in the assemblies of the Church, but are even admitted to the public communion of Baptism and the Lord's Supper. This seems to them not only an unjust and absurd deed, but also a sacrilege, by which all who gather in the same assembly with such people, and who approach the same Lord's Supper, are defiled, since they profess themselves to be members of the same body with them. And lest these charges seem to thunder against us without reason, they throw at us that saying of Paul: "If anyone who is called a brother is a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or a robber, with such a one do not even eat." From these words they conclude thus: if a Christian may not eat at a common table with those who are openly wicked, much less ought such men to be admitted to the Lord's table, where true believers and the godly are to share with them. But these men ought to consider that it is one thing to abstain from the company or unnecessary custom of wicked men, and another to bar those same men from that duty, if they profess repentance and desire to proclaim the death of the Lord with the Church, or to withdraw from the fellowship of the Church on their account. For Paul himself clearly distinguishes between these two. When he forbids eating ordinary food with the wicked or with those polluted by some crime, he nowhere orders us to cast those same people from the Lord's table; rather, as regards its use, he instructs each to examine himself, not that we should take to ourselves a right or judgment over the consciences of others. Indeed the Apostle warns seriously that whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself; but in this whole matter he does not want us to be anxious about the hypocrisy or open crimes of others, as if we could be polluted by their impurity. We admit that it is a duty of charity that each should kindly and earnestly admonish those whom he sees to be more shameless in a matter of such moment, and about whom there is danger that they may rashly thrust themselves in, to the loss of eternal salvation. But because it is hidden from us what sort of person each is when he approaches this mystical feast, we ought not to act by authority, but leave each to his own judgment. And since here the question is not of the communion of life and morals but of the sacred things, that anxiety which torments some, lest they share in the sins of the wicked or be joined together into one and the same body with them, is trifling and superfluous. For if those who, after a life lived wantonly until now, approach the Lord's table have truly and from the heart repented, they enjoy worthily the communion of the body and blood of Christ with the godly, and are genuine members of the Church. But if they are wicked hypocrites, they can indeed deceive the Church and abuse its symbols, yet they do not belong at all to its communion, and therefore there is no fellowship of the faithful with their wickedness; such people eat judgment to themselves, not to others. Nor do we think the Apostle arranged this without reason. For he knew what Christ had done, who admitted to his mystical table, and not only to the paschal feast, disciples still infected with many faults, namely pride, ambition, envy and wicked rivalry, likewise puffed up with self-confidence; who finally did not even exclude Peter, who was soon to deny him shamefully, not to mention Judas, whom he knew to be a most wicked thief and traitor. Paul therefore did not wish to be thought stricter than his Lord and Master, lest perhaps he should repel those whom Christ most generously invites to his communion, or deny the outward signs to those whom Christ himself deigns to feed with his own body and blood unto eternal life. But I know that some say Judas was not excluded because his crime was still hidden and had not given public scandal. But on what ground do they say this was hidden, when the eternal Son of God, the true searcher of hearts, disclosed it in words no less grave than clear? "But the disciples did not know," they say, "of whom he was speaking." What then? Surely the danger would have been the greater if they could have been contaminated by his crime, since they heard that a traitor was at the table, and yet could not guard against sharing in the outward use of the Supper; and although they did not know who he was, they could not be ignorant how horrible a scandal it would be if Jesus Christ were betrayed by a disciple of his household. But to leave that unhappy man aside, what shall we say of the other disciples? Was their ambition hidden, which after so many and such serious admonitions flared up into open contention? And what hidden reason can be brought forward which orders us to keep from the use of the Supper those who indeed sinned grievously before, but now, together with a serious confession of sin, profess zeal and faith in their Saviour Jesus Christ; since the Lord himself admitted those who sinned in the midst of the holy things, and who therefore deserved a sharper rebuke and correction?

units.la: Sed esto fuerit occultior quædam ratio, quam tunc secutus sit Christus, & licue sit ei quod nobis non itidem licet: nemo tamen negauerit opinor, nobis hoc licere, quod Paulo ad Corinthios licuit, quando eos ad primam cœnæ Dominicæ institutionem reuocauit, & quid in huius vsu publice a tota Ecclesia, & a singulis priuatim obseruari debeat, monuit. Scimus autem Ecclesiæ illius statum corruptissimum fuisse, nec in paucis solummodo hærebat absurdissimorum errorum & grauissimorū scelerum culpa, sed totum corpus a summo capitis vertice ad imos pedes vsque erat miserrime affectum. Doctrinam certe Logodædali quidam humanæ sapientiæ figmentis adulterauerant: idem Ecclesiæ corpus in partes distraxerant: glisebant inter illos æmulationes, dissidia, rixæ, ex quibus iurgia & omnis generis iniuriæ nascebantur: litigabant multi pro rebus non magni momenti apud infidelium tribunalia, quod euidens erat charitatis frigentis & auaritiæ inexplebilis argumentum: regnabat ibidem scortandi libido, & quis stupra & adulteriorum licentiam cessauisse putet apud eos, vbi cum nouerca priuignus consuetudine impune habuit, a quo scelere plerosque ex gentibus abhorruisse scimus? Et ne quid vitij deesset, Paulum multi scurriliter ridebant, eiusdem epistolas mordaciter[?] vellicabant, cum gentium sacris, vel potius idololatria, communicabant, & daemoniorum conuiuae erant, qui cum germanis Christi cultoribus ad huius mensam accedebant: cuius vsum legitimum publice ita corruperant, vt Coena il-la, qua Christianis hominibus nihil antiquius esse debet, à conuiuio luxurioso ni-hil differret. Adde his habitum siue cultum gentilitium quo viri & mulieres in sacris coetibus vtebantur, ambitiosam donorum spiritus sancti ostentationem, scur-riles de mortuorum resurrectione disputationes, cum sexcentis aliis, quae in tanta doctrinae & sacrorum exercitiorum corruptione fieri oportuit. Inter illos tamen Ecclesiam Christi esse Paulus agnouit, nec alicui discessione ab ea suasit, & quan-do legitimum coenae vsum apud eos instaurare volebat, non curiosum scrutinium instituit, quo vel Doctores vel Seniores in aliorum conscientias penetrare, & sa-tisfactionibus nescio quibus eos qui peccassent fatigare deberent: sed hoc ipsi suf-ficere visum est, si vnusquisque seipsum examinaret, ne indigne accedendo ad epu-lum hoc sacrosanctum, seipsum corporis & sanguinis Domini reum faceret.
