Po-terat his Galatarum quoque exemplum coniungi, quos insuper extremae dementiae accusat Paulus, quod in aliud Euangelium sese passi essent transferri, & legis iusti-tiam cum fide in IESVM CHRISTVM miscendo hunc sibi ipsis inutilem reddi-dissent. Quis vero ab omni morum vitio immunes fuisse credat eos, qui qua Chri-sto dederant fidem, magna ex parte violarant, quae sola homines in officio continet? Istos certe morosi illi censores, qui hodie nobis negotiu faciunt, à fidelium commu-nione procul arcendos esse dixissent. At Paulus, qui se ad colligendum, non ad dissipandum missum esse sciebat, illos honorifico Ecclesiae Christi titulo dignatur, neque eos, qui inter illos rectius sapiebant, ideo accusat, quod coetibus ipsorum in-teressent, aut quod ad eandem cum illis mensam Domini accederent. Cur ergo no-bis vitio vertitur, si hanc Apostoli lenitatem ipsi quoque imitamur, vt melius in eius-dem fidei confessione coalescant Ecclesiae, ne qui nimia quorundam morosita-te offensi, vel apertam secessionem faciant, vel odijs mutuis ringantur, & Eccle-siam contra Christi praeceptum in partes distrahant?
units.tr: But let it be granted that there was some more hidden reason which Christ followed then, and that it is permitted to him but not to us in the same way. Yet no one, I think, will deny that we may do what was permitted to Paul among the Corinthians, when he recalled them to the original institution of the Lord's Supper and admonished them about what must be observed in its use, both publicly by the whole Church and privately by each individual. We know that the state of that Church was most corrupt, and that its fault was not confined to a few absurd errors and very grave crimes, but that the whole body, from the crown of the head to the soles of the feet, was most wretchedly diseased. Certainly some word-weavers had adulterated the doctrine with the inventions of human wisdom. The same men had torn the body of the Church into parts. Rivalries, quarrels and brawls grew up among them, from which lawsuits and every kind of injury arose. Many went to law over trifling matters before the courts of unbelievers, which was plain evidence of a cold charity and an insatiable greed. Lust for fornication reigned there, and who would think that fornication and adultery had ceased among them, when a stepson lived with his stepmother openly as a husband, a crime from which we know even many of the Gentiles shrank? And, lest any vice be lacking, many mocked Paul in a buffoonish way and sharply carped at his letters. They shared in the sacrifices of the Gentiles, or rather in idolatry, and were guests of demons, yet they came to this table alongside the true worshippers of Christ. They had so corrupted its lawful use in public that the Supper, which ought to be most sacred to Christians, differed in no way from a riotous banquet. Add to these the heathen dress or fashion in which men and women appeared in the sacred assemblies, the ambitious display of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, the frivolous disputes about the resurrection of the dead, and countless other things which were bound to happen amid such corruption of doctrine and of the exercises of worship. Yet Paul recognised among them the Church of Christ. He did not advise anyone to withdraw from it, and when he wished to restore the lawful use of the Supper among them, he did not institute a meddlesome inquisition by which the teachers or elders should penetrate into other men's consciences and wear out those who had sinned with I know not what satisfactions. He thought it enough that each one should examine himself, so that by coming unworthily to this holy feast he would not make himself guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. The example of the Galatians could also be added, whom Paul accuses of extreme folly, because they had allowed themselves to be turned over to another gospel and, by mixing the righteousness of the law with faith in Jesus Christ, had made Christ useless to themselves. But who would believe that those who had largely violated the faith they had given to Christ were free from every fault of conduct, when faith alone keeps men in their duty? Those peevish censors who trouble us today would certainly have said that such people must be kept far from the fellowship of the faithful. But Paul, who knew that he had been sent to gather, not to scatter, honours them with the respectable title of the Church of Christ. Nor does he accuse those among them who had the sounder judgement of attending their assemblies or of coming to the same table of the Lord with them. Why then are we blamed if we also imitate this gentleness of the Apostle, so that the churches may be more closely united in the confession of the same faith, and so that men offended by the excessive peevishness of some do not either make open secession or tear themselves apart with mutual hatreds, dividing the Church into parts contrary to Christ's command?

units.la: Neque ideo disciplinam abolitam aut eiectam volumus, imo vt ea solicite seruetur, optamus: quando sine hoc sale neque publica Ecclesiae salus, neque inter eius membra priuatim pax consistere potest. Eos autem non possumus probare, qui non aliam disciplinae formam constituunt, quam quae poenitentiam acturos non necessaria conscientiae carnificina excruciat, quae item olim satisfactionibus Papisticis fenestram aperuit, & magistratus legitimi authoritatem labefactauit, Episcoporum autem potentiam eo vsque euexit, vt potentissimis quoque regibus intolerabi-lis fit facta. Sunt, equidem disciplinae conseruandae rationes variae, sed inter has tutissima est, cuius forma ex Dei verbo sumitur, & quae cuiusque gentis moribus atque ingenio accommodata magistratus authoritate confirmatur, eodemque executore vtitur: cuius denique hic finis est, vt in Ecclesiae societate retineantur, quos vel opinionum diuersitas, vel morum licentia, aut etiam immoderatus nimiae seueritatis rigor alio abripere poterat. Quapropter non tam rigore, quam seuera lenitate opus est, ne vel temere resecetur aliquis à corpore Ecclesiae, vel ipsi incōsiderato ze-lo ab Ecclesijs discedamus propter eos, quos perpetuo incurabiles fore nobis non dum constat: aut si tales sint, tutius tamen ferri quam excindi possunt, sicuti in zi-zaniorum parabola Dominus admonet. Quam rationem olim sanctissimis patri-bus probatam fuisse, tum multorum aliorum testimonijs, tum ex Diuo Cypriano colligi potest, cuius haec verba extant in libro Epistolarum tertio, epist. tertia: Si vi-dentur in Ecclesia esse zizania, non tamen impediri[?] debet aut fides aut charitas nostra, vt quoniam zizania esse in Ecclesia cernimus, ipsi de Ecclesia recedamus. Nobis imo laborandum, vt frumentum esse possimus, vt cum coeperit frumenti domínicis horreis condi, fructum pro opere nostro & labore capiamus. Apostolus in epistola sua dicit: In domo autem magna non solum vasa sunt aurea & argentea, sed et lignea & fictilia, & quaedam quidem honorata, quaedam vero inhonorata. Nos operam demus, & quantum possumus laboremus, vt vas aureum vel argenteum simus. Caeterum fictilia vasa confringere Domino soli concessum est, cui & virga ferrea data est. Esse non potest maior domino suo seruus: nec quisquam sibi quod soli filio Pater tribuit, vendicare se putet, vt ad aream ventilandam & purgandam iam ferre se posse, aut a frumento vniuersa zizania humano iudicio segregare. Superba est ista obstinatio, & sacrilega praesumptio, quam sibi furor pra uus assumit. Et dum dominium sibi semper quidam plus quam mitis iustitia deposcit, assumunt, de Ecclesia pereunt. Et dum se insolenter extollunt, ipso suo tumore excaecati, veritatis lumen amittunt. Haec Cypriani sunt, quae si nostris temporibus accommodentur, facile patebit, qui nam sint, quos haec dicendo pater iste perstringat.
units.tr: Nor do we wish discipline to be abolished or cast out. Rather we desire that it be diligently maintained, since without this salt neither the public welfare of the Church nor peace among its members in private can stand. But we cannot approve of those who set up no other form of discipline than one which torments those who are to repent with a needless torture of conscience. Such a discipline once opened the way to Papistical satisfactions, weakened the authority of the lawful magistrate, and raised the power of the bishops so high that it became intolerable even to the most powerful kings. There are indeed various ways of preserving discipline, but the safest of them is the one whose form is taken from the word of God, which is adapted to the customs and character of each nation, is confirmed by the authority of the magistrate, and uses the magistrate as its executor. Its final aim is to keep within the fellowship of the Church those whom a difference of opinion, a licence of morals, or even an immoderate harshness of severity might otherwise carry away elsewhere. Therefore what is needed is not so much rigour as a severe gentleness, lest anyone be rashly cut off from the body of the Church, or we ourselves, through a thoughtless zeal, withdraw from the churches on account of those whom it is not yet clear will be incurable for ever. Or if they are such, they are nevertheless safer to be borne with than to be cut off, as the Lord warns in the parable of the tares. That this principle was approved long ago by the most holy Fathers can be gathered both from the testimonies of many others and from the divine Cyprian, whose words are found in the third book of his Epistles, epistle three: "If tares seem to be in the Church, our faith or charity should not therefore be hindered, so that because we see tares in the Church we ourselves withdraw from the Church. Rather we must labour that we may be wheat, so that when the wheat begins to be gathered into the Lord's barns we may receive fruit for our work and toil. The Apostle says in his letter: 'In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware, and some indeed are for honour, others for dishonour.' Let us take pains and labour as much as we can to be a golden or silver vessel. But it has been granted to the Lord alone to break the earthenware vessels, to whom also the iron rod has been given. A servant is not greater than his lord, nor should anyone think that he may claim for himself what the Father has given to the Son alone, so that he could now carry the winnowing fork to cleanse the threshing floor, or separate all the tares from the wheat by human judgement. That stubbornness is proud, and that sacrilegious presumption which a perverse madness takes upon itself. While some men always demand for themselves a lordship more than gentle justice, they perish from the Church. And while they insolently exalt themselves, blinded by their own swelling, they lose the light of truth." These are the words of Cyprian. If they are applied to our own times, it will easily be seen who those are whom that father condemns by these words.

units.la: Haec autem vobiscum commentari libuit, Patres in Christo reuerendiss. partim quod meam de hac re sententiam vobis non iniucundam cognitu fore putarem, quibus aliquando cum eiusmodi hominibus res fuit, qui dum nimio rigore atque zelo Ecclesias Angliae ad eam, quam ipsi animo conceperant ideam siue formam, adducere conati sunt, earum pace aliquantisper turbarunt, quam vobis ex Dei beneficio restitutam esse, ex animo gaudemus: partim quod ista Epist. huius argumento non male conuenire videbantur. In cuius enarratione quid praestiterim, ipsi iudicabitis, & vt id liberè atque ingenuè faciatis, rogo. Nec enim mihi ipsi tantum tribuere ausim, vt in opere tam vario et multis in locis obscuro, me vbique rem acu attigisse affirmem. De diligentia autem & fide mea vere testari possum. Cum enim mihi studiorum meorum scopus sit propositus, vt sacrarum literarum studiosis & muneris Ecclesiastici candidatis ad hoc viam aliquo modo sternam, a quaestionibus acutis potius & scrupulosis quam Ecclesiae necessariis consulto abstinui: in iis autem inuestigandis, quae ad Pauli sensum eruendum & illustrandum facere videbantur, nulli labori me pepercisse scio. Legi commentarios Graecorum & Latinorum, tam veteres quam recentiores, quos habere potui omnes, & illorum lectione me vehementer adiutum esse fateor: imprimis tamen eorum, qui nostro hoc saeculo in ista epistola exponenda laborarunt: ex quorum numero mihi prae aliis probantur, qui scripturas sacras nostrorum temporum moribus accommodant, vt quid in his desideretur, vtq; quae hodie pullulant in Ecclesijs vitia emendari possint, omnes intelligant. Versati sunt quidem in eo argumento alij aliis felicius, omnes tamen meo iudicio laude merentur, cum quod potuerunt pro viri praestiterint, & nullius illorum labor tam sit sterilis, qui non aliquam utilitatem ad Ecclesiae aedificationem conferat aequis & candidis lectoribus. Quod si meus quoq; conatus non omnino irritus fuerit, illud omne CHRISTI IESV beneficium esse fatebor, qui vt solus lux illa mundi, & sol iustitiae est, in cuius radijs (vt Propheta ait) salus habetur: ita idem suo etiam spiritu feruorum suorum linguas & calamum dirigit.
units.tr: I have wished to discuss these matters with you, most reverend fathers in Christ: partly because I thought my opinion on this question would not be unwelcome to you, since you have at some time had dealings with men of this kind, who, while trying with excessive rigour and zeal to bring the churches of England to that idea or form which they had conceived in their own minds, disturbed their peace for a time. We rejoice from our hearts that by God's goodness this peace has been restored to you. Partly, too, because this epistle seemed to agree well with such a subject. You yourselves will judge what I have achieved in its explanation, and I ask you to do so freely and frankly. For I would not dare to claim so much for myself as to assert that in a work so varied and so obscure in many places I have hit the mark everywhere. But of my diligence and good faith I can truly bear witness. Since the aim of my studies has been set before me to smooth in some measure the way for students of Holy Scripture and for candidates for the ecclesiastical ministry, I have deliberately refrained from sharp and scrupulous questions rather than those necessary for the Church. In investigating those matters which seemed to help in drawing out and clarifying Paul's meaning, I know I have spared no labour. I have read the commentaries of the Greeks and the Latins, both ancient and more recent, all that I could obtain, and I confess that I was greatly helped by reading them, especially those who in our own age have laboured to expound this epistle. Among these, those who adapt the sacred Scriptures to the customs of our own times are, in my judgement, more to be approved than others, so that everyone may understand what is lacking in these customs and how the faults now springing up in the churches can be corrected. Other men have worked on this subject more successfully than others, yet all of them, in my judgement, deserve praise: each has done as well as he could for a man, and no one's labour is so barren that it does not contribute some benefit to the edification of the Church for fair and candid readers. If my own effort also has not been altogether in vain, I shall confess that this is entirely the benefit of Jesus Christ, who, as he alone is that light of the world and the sun of righteousness, in whose rays (as the prophet says) salvation is found, so also by his own Spirit directs the tongues and pens of his servants.

units.la: Porro meas hasce lucubrationes vestrae pietati & amplitudini dedicare volui Patres in Christo reuerendissimi & Domini mihi plurimum obseruandi, vt meae apud vos obseruantiae pignus esset, non quod vos illis opus habere existimem. Est enim mihi satis perspecta eruditio vestra, & diligens exactaque scripturarum sacrarum notitia: quam longus & multiplex rerum vsus ita confirmauit, vt quae alij circa solam θεωρίαν aut otiosam contemplationem occupati, vix obiter & qua si per transennam inspexerunt, eorum veritatem iamprimis reipsa experti sitis, adeoque omnium quae toto hoc opere traduntur veram atque utilissimam πρᾶξιν in Ecclesia rebus tam secundis quam aduersis didiceritis. Nam quod de Philippenfibus suis Paulus scribit, illis datum fuisse in Christi causa, non solum in eum credere, verumetiam pro eo affligi, hoc ipsum de vobis verissime dici potest. Enimvero manet adhuc in recenti piorum hominum memoria, quam laeta Ecclesiae Christi lux affulserit sub serenissimo Angliae rege EDVARDO VI, eo principe nimirum, cuius similem orbis terrarum multis saeculis neminem vidit. Erat enim in bonis literis & linguarum cognitione iam inde a pueris egregie institutus, & pro aetate ita profecerat, ut nihil in eo amplius desiderari posset. In moribus eius placidissimis regia gravitas apparebat, quae ut toti Angliae visu iucunda, sic exteris quoque omnibus admirationi erat, qui in iuvene senilem prudentiam, in tam sublimi honorum & potentiae fastigio modestiam incredibilem exosculabantur. Et quod omnem huius saeculi dignitatem superat, coniunxerat istis virtutibus aeterni filii Dei IESV CHRISTI cognitionem, quem cum fide vera & constanti apprehendisset, eiusdem amore accensus, non Anglos solum suos, sed exteros simul omnes ex animo complectebatur, quoscunque vel sua eruditione communem Ecclesiae & religionis causam iuvare posse, vel e suis sedibus ejectos alieno patrocinio opus habere videbat. Florebant ergo tunc Patres reuerendis. in Anglia ve-stra bonae literae, feruebat verae pietatis studium, & ad vos ceu in asylum & portum tutissimum sub sanctissimi regis alas confluebant Germani, Galli, Hispani, Itali, Poloni, Scoti, ut illic Deo suo in fidei libertate seruirent, quam ipsis patria ingrata negabat.
units.tr: Moreover, I have wished to dedicate these my labours of night-work to your piety and dignity, reverend Fathers in Christ and lords whom I greatly honour, so that they might be a pledge of my respect towards you, not because I think you need them. For your learning is sufficiently well known to me, and your diligent and exact knowledge of the holy Scriptures, which long and varied experience of affairs has so confirmed that you have learned, by actual trial, the truth of those things which others, occupied only with theory or idle contemplation, have glanced at in passing, as if through a window; and you have learned the true and most useful practice of all that is set out in this whole work, in the Church, both in prosperous and in adverse circumstances. For what Paul writes of his Philippians, that it was granted to them in the cause of Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him, can most truly be said of you as well. Indeed, the memory of good men still remains fresh, of how joyful a light of the Church of Christ shone forth under the most serene king of England, Edward VI, that prince whom the world has not seen the like of for many ages. For he had been excellently trained from boyhood in good letters and in knowledge of languages, and for his age he had so advanced that nothing more could be desired in him. In his most gentle manners a royal dignity appeared, which, being pleasing to the sight of all England, was also an object of admiration to all foreigners, who in a young man admired a mature wisdom and an incredible modesty in so lofty a height of honour and power. And, what surpasses all the dignity of this age, he had joined to these virtues the knowledge of Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God; having laid hold of him with true and steadfast faith, kindled with love for him, he embraced with his whole heart not only his own Englishmen but all foreigners at the same time, whomever he saw could help the common cause of the Church and of religion by their learning, or who, driven from their seats, had need of another's patronage. Then, therefore, reverend Fathers, good letters flourished in your England, the zeal of true piety glowed, and Germans, French, Spanish, Italians, Poles and Scots flocked to you as to a refuge and most secure harbour under the wings of the most holy king, so that there they might serve their God in freedom of faith, which their ungrateful homeland denied them.

units.la: Tunc quoque Eduardo regi operas suas magno studio & bona fide conferebant sanctissimi Praesules, D. THOMAS CRAMMERVS Cant. Archiepisc. NICOLAVS RIDLAEVS Londinensis, D. HOPPERVS Glocestriae, Episcopi; HVGO item ille LATIMERVS, quem non tam senecta gravis quam eruditio & pietas hostibus quoque venerabilem fecerat, & infiniti alij, quorum nomina recensere longum foret, inter quos vestrum quoque omnium studium atque zelus eluxit.
units.tr: At that time the most holy prelates also devoted their labours to King Edward with great zeal and good faith: Dr Thomas Cranmer, archbishop of Canterbury; Nicholas Ridley, bishop of London; Dr Hooper, bishop of Gloucester; likewise that Hugh Latimer, whom not so much his old age as his learning and piety had made venerable even to his enemies; and countless others, whose names would be long to recite, among whom the zeal and earnestness of all of you also shone forth.

units.la: Videbatur ergo tunc orbi terrarum redire aurei saeculi felicitas, & piorum omnium animi in magnam spem erecti sibi ipsis pacem stabilem & laeta omnia polliceban-tur, frementibus e contra aduersariis, quos detectae fraudis Pontificiae & amissae existimationis dolor in rabiem accendebat. Nec dubito, quin perpetuum nobis fecisset gaudium istud Deus Opt.Max. nisi propter ingratitudinem & contumaciam suam indignus fuisset mundus, qui illo diutius frueretur. Itaque quod de Augusti Caesaris nepote Poeta olim dixit: Offendent terris hunc tantum fata, nec ultra esse sinent: id tunc quoque non sine publico totius Ecclesiae luctu accidit. Nam optimum pissimumque regem in ipso adolescentiae flore Deus terris ingratis eripuit, ut regni sui caelestis haeredem faceret: eius vero obitum perinde ut Solis occasum nox tristissima secuta est, quae exitialibus tenebris Ecclesiam fere totam involuit, & tantumnon oppressit.
units.tr: The world then seemed to be regaining the happiness of the golden age, and the minds of all the godly were raised to great hope, promising themselves a stable peace and all things joyful, while the adversaries raged on the other side, whom grief at the exposed fraud of the Papists and at their lost reputation inflamed into fury. Nor do I doubt that God the best and greatest would have made that joy perpetual for us, had not the world, on account of its ingratitude and obstinacy, been unworthy to enjoy it any longer. And so what the poet once said of the grandson of Augustus Caesar, "The fates showed him only to the lands and would not allow him to remain," came to pass at that time too, and not without public mourning of the whole Church. For God snatched that best and most excellent king from the ungrateful lands in the very flower of his youth, that he might make him heir of his heavenly kingdom; and after his death, just as after the setting of the sun, a most sorrowful night followed, which with deadly darkness enveloped almost the whole Church and nearly overwhelmed it.

units.la: Tunc in tetris carceribus infelice piorum sorte gemere coeperunt, quorum concionibus saluberrimis templa omnia prius resonuerant: tunc diris securibus multorum ceruices subiectae sunt, qui paulo ante totius regni pondus non minus pie quam feliciter sustinuerant: imo in crudelibus rogis arserunt, qui eruditione & pietate, communi patriae ceu lumina quaedam praefulserant. Multos vero alios infelix illa & sequa tempestas in exilium eiecit, & hinc inde apud exteros sedes quaerere coegit eos, qui prius omnium gentium exulibus amicum domi suae hospitium praebuerant. Tunc vos quoque Patres reuerendis. vidit Germania, & Tigurum nostrum adhuc sibi gratulatur felicitatem istam, quod tantos hospites ex vobis habuit, quorum fides & constantia nostris hominibus tunc admirationi fuit, memoria autem adhuc celebris atque iucunda est.
units.tr: Then, in foul prisons, the godly began to groan under an unhappy lot, those whose most wholesome sermons had earlier filled all the churches with sound; then the necks of many were subjected to the dreadful axes, men who a little before had borne the weight of the whole kingdom as piously as they had done it happily; indeed, those who had shone forth like lights for their country by their learning and piety were burned on cruel pyres. That unhappy and savage storm drove many others into exile and forced them to seek homes here and there among foreigners, those who before had offered a friendly hospitality at home to the exiles of all nations. Then Germany also saw you, reverend Fathers, and our Zurich still rejoices in that happiness, that it had such distinguished guests from among you, whose faith and constancy were then an object of admiration to our people, and whose memory is still famous and pleasant.

units.la: Meum certe animum mirifica cum voluptate recreat dulcissimae illius consuetudinis recordatio, ad labores autem & molestias omnis generis me alacriorem fieri sentio, quoties vestram in ferendis adversis patientiam, raram in moribus modestiam; assiduum in sacris scripturis studium, indefinentem in precibus ardorem, intrepidam denique ad omnem euentum fiduciam animo repeto. Haec certe ita Deo placuerunt, ut vestri, imo Angliae vestrae misertus, huic libertatem, vobis patriam, & vos Ecclesijs miserè afflictis restituerit, quando discussis & sublatis tenebris nouum jubar affulsit, ad regni gubernacula euecta serenissima regina E L I Z A B E T H A, de cuius pietate, prudentia, fortitudine & constantia nolo dicere, nein immensum crescat oratio, & onus humeris meis impar subijsse dicar.
units.tr: Certainly the recollection of that most sweet fellowship refreshes my mind with a wonderful pleasure, and I feel myself made more eager for labours and troubles of every kind whenever I call back to mind your patience in bearing adversities, your rare modesty in conduct, your constant study of the holy Scriptures, your unfailing fervour in prayers, and, finally, your fearless trust in every outcome. These things indeed were so pleasing to God that he, taking pity on you and on your England, restored liberty to her, your country to you, and yourselves to the wretchedly afflicted Churches, when, the darkness having been dispelled and removed, a new light dawned, Queen Elizabeth, most serene, being raised to the helm of the kingdom. Of her piety, prudence, fortitude and constancy I do not wish to speak, lest my discourse grow immense and I be said to have undertaken a burden too heavy for my shoulders.

units.la: Hoc tamen tacere non possum, illam piissimae matris instar filios extorres & longe latèque dispersos collegisse, Ecclesijs jam longa fame laborantibus fidos pastores reddidisse, leges bonas restituisse, patriam denique communem pace donauisse, quam inter omnis generis pericula, inter audacissimos hostium veritatis conatus, & multorum insidias, in hunc usque diem non sine totius orbis admiratione conseruauit. Quàm laeta verò tunc vobis Patres reuerendis. spes exorta sit, & quàm alacri animo ad opem patriae ferendam concurreritis, probè meminì: nec me laetet, quàm multi varijsq; labores vos domum reuersos exceperint, quàm graues molestiae vobis deuorandae, & noua indies subeunda fuerint certamina, vt Ecclesias instaurareris, quae prioris temporis injuria collapsae fuerant, & quarum instaurationem multi adhuc hostiliter, multi astutè & quasi aliud agentes, multi etiam consilijs intempestiuis, & zelo fortassis non malo, inconsulto tamen & plus satis morosò impediebant. Praeclara sane tunc vestrae virtutis & industriae specimina apparuerunt, constantia nimirum in excipiendis hostium conatibus, sagax in deprehendendis insidijs industria, Christiana in ferenda fratrum quorundam morositate indulgentia. Rursus ergo per vos sub serenis. reginae tutela & fida protectione Anglicana Ecclesia floret, & nouis quotidie incrementis surgit ad aeterni Dei gloriam & multorum in vera fide aedificationem.
units.tr: This, however, I cannot pass over in silence: that she, like the most pious mother, gathered together her children who were exiles and scattered far and wide; that she gave faithful ministers to the Churches which had long laboured in famine; that she restored good laws; and finally that she gave the common homeland peace, which, amid every kind of danger, amid the boldest attempts of the enemies of the truth and the plots of many, she has preserved to this day, not without the admiration of the whole world. How joyful, indeed, the hope that then arose for you, reverend Fathers, and with how eager a mind you ran to bring help to your country, I well remember; nor does it gladden me how many and varied labours received you on your return home, how grievous the troubles you had to swallow down and the struggles you had to undergo fresh each day, so that the Churches, which had collapsed through the injury of the earlier time, might be restored; and whose restoration many still hindered in a hostile spirit, many craftily and as if pursuing other aims, many also with untimely counsels and perhaps not ill-meant zeal, yet ill-advised and more than enough peevish. Then truly clear proofs of your virtue and industry appeared: constancy in withstanding the attempts of enemies, shrewd diligence in detecting plots, and Christian forbearance in bearing the peevishness of certain brothers. Thus, again, through you, under the protection and faithful guardianship of the serene queen, the English Church flourishes and rises daily with new increases, to the glory of the eternal God and the building up of many in the true faith.

units.la: Quapropter (vt ad institutum redeam) meas Homilias non ideo ad vos mitto, vt me magistro aut monitore vtamini, sed praeter eam, quam supra adduxi, longe alias habeo mei consilij rationes, quae me vt id facerem impulerunt. Primò enim operi propter argumenti varietatem laboriosò, tutoribus & patronis opus fore videbam, quorum authoritate pijs commendaretur. At hic vos Patres reuerendis. primi occurrebatis, quos hoc officium praestare posse, & mihi quantumuis nihil huius de vobis merito etiam libenter praestare velle nequaquam dubito. Etenim vt de vobis mihi nihil non pollicear, non confidentia propria, sed vestrae humanitatis fiducia adducor. Multos, sat scio, nominis vestri celebritas mouebit, vt meos labores cognitu dignos judicent, qui si omni praesidio destituti prodirent, à plerisque contemnerentur. Mouit me etiam argumenti, quod toto hoc opere tractatur, ratio. Quia enim hic de Ecclesiae constitutione & œconomia agitur, illius cognitio nemini justius & melius mandari potuit, quam vobis, qui in hac causa jam multis annis magna cum laude & nō sine felici successu estis versati. Adhaec operæpretium me facturum putaui, si nostrae in fidei doctrina & tota religionis causa consensionis publicum testimonium extaret, quo Euangelicae doctrinae virtus illustraretur: qua factum est, vt Heluetice Ecclesiae, nihil obstantibus tantis terrarum atq; Oceani interuallis, cum toto diuisis orbe Britannis in vnius eiusdemq; fidei confessione consentiant, adeoq; utrinq; vno spiritu, vna mente, & vno ore Deum Patrem per vnum mediatorem IESVM CHRISTVM innocent. Et ne quid dissimulem, me de his diligentius cogitantem & aliis de causis cunctabundum vehementer impulit amicitiae nostrae & acceptorum beneficiorum recordatio: quae jampridem monebat, vt si gratias dignas vobis referre non possem, mei tamen animi erga vos voluntatem aliquo officio sive argumento testarer. Nec enim mihi adhuc excidit, quàm benignè me ante annos triginta quinq; Anglia vestra exceperit: imo iam nunc mihi adhuc ab oculos versa-tur incredibilis illa humanitas, qua non solum studiosi iuuenes & professores doctissimi, qui tunc in Oxoniensi Academia florebant, verumetiam illustres aliquot in aula Regia viri, interq; hos immortale Angliae decus & gloriosissimus Christi martyr, D. THOMAS CRAMMERVS, Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus, me iuue-nem, peregrinum, & nullo vel rerum vsu vel splendore commendabilem, prose-cuti sunt. Accessit his postea familiaritas & diuturnior consuetudo, quae mihi cum aliquibus vestrum apud nos (vt supra dixi) agentibus intercessit, cuius me-moria tam mihi quam collegis, imo ciuibus nostris nunquam non cum voluptate singulari recurrit. Vtinam vero hanc non aliqua amaritudine aspersisset inspe-ratus D. IOANNIS IVELLI, Sarisberiensis Episcopi, obitus: qui vt vobis om-nibus procul dubio tristitiam attulit, ita eius nuntium nostros quoque animos dolore acutissimo penetrauit: eo quod vulnus hoc non ad Angliam solam, sed ad totam Christi Ecclesiam pertinere putamus, cuius ille lumen erat singulare. Sed viuit nunc spiritus eius beatus cum Christo Domino, cuius seruitio se totum con-secrauerat, in tetris vero sui desiderium & nominis gloriam immortalem reliquit. Apud vos autem Patres reuerendissimi, Gualtheri quoq; vestri memoriam non intercidisse, cum amicae literae tum alia argumenta testantur, imprimis vero sin-gularis illa planeque paterna bonitas, qua nuper filium meum, quem patris ex-emplum visendae Angliae desiderio accenderat, sic a vobis exceptum esse intelle-xi, vt me omni, quam de illo gerebam, solicitudine liberatum sentiam, & ille sibi videatur non foris inter paternos amicos, sed patres proprios viuere. Quod be-neficium ego tanti facio, quanti apud parentem non immitem & ἀσωέγοῳ[?] filius vni-cus & dilectus, ex vxore charissima, cuius defunctae recordatio mihi propter exi-mias virtutes semper pretiosa erit, natus esse debet. Ideoq; me vobis & Angliae ve-strae non hasce modo lucubrationes, sed meipsum debere libenter fateor. Acci-pietis ergo Patres in Christo reuerendissimi, hanc qualemcunque mei erga vos studij significationem eo animo, quo me iampridem complexi estis, & quo filium meum apud vos nunc agentem complectimini. Deus Opt. Max. studijs ve-stris sanctissimis benedicat, voscq; seruet ad nominis sui gloriam. Idem Reginam serenissimam, fidelem Ecclesiae suae nutricem, spiritu sapientiae, prudentiae & for-titudinis regat atque confirmet, & florentissimum Angliae regnum hisce difficil-limis temporibus aduersus diras Antichristi insidias omnemq; vim hostilem tuea-tur: Omnibus autem, qui CHRISTI IESV nomen profitentur, det idem senti-re & loqui: vt & ipse in nobis glorificetur, & regni sui pomoeria indies longe la-teq; propagentur. Amen. Datae Tiguro, primaria Heluetiorum urbe. Calend. Augusti. Anno a nato in carne aeterno Dei filio M. D. LXXII. Quando ante annos bis mille noningentos Debora, prophetico spiritu instructa Heroina, Ec-clesiam immani Chananaeorum tyrannide pressam in libertatem asseruit, & militiae Chananaicae Imperator Sisera itidem a muliere Iahele caesus, singulari exemplo dignas suae crudelitatis poenas dedit.
units.tr: Therefore (to return to my purpose), I am not sending you these Homilies so that you may use me as your teacher or adviser. Apart from the reason I mentioned above, I had quite different considerations of my own that led me to do this. First, because of the variety of its subject matter, I saw that a work of this kind would be laborious and would need guardians and patrons whose authority would commend it to the godly. You, reverend Fathers, were the first to come to mind as those able to perform this office, and I have no doubt that you would gladly do this for me, however little I deserve it. Indeed, I am moved to promise myself everything from you not by my own confidence but by trust in your kindness. I know that the renown of your names will move many to judge my labours worth reading, whereas if they came forth without such protection, most would despise them. The nature of the subject treated throughout this work also moved me. Since it deals with the constitution and government of the Church, its understanding could be entrusted to no one more justly or better than to you, who for many years have been engaged in this cause with great praise and not without happy success. Besides, I thought it would be worthwhile if there were a public testimony of agreement in the doctrine of faith and in the whole cause of religion between us, by which the power of the evangelical doctrine might be made clear. As a result, although such great distances of lands and ocean separate the Church of Helvetia from the British, who are divided from the rest of the world, they agree in one confession of the same faith, and with one spirit, one mind and one mouth they acknowledge God the Father through the one mediator Jesus Christ. And, not to conceal anything, when I was thinking about these matters more carefully and was hesitating for other reasons, the memory of our friendship and of the benefits I have received pressed me strongly. For a long time this memory had urged me that, if I could not repay you with worthy thanks, I should at least attest the goodwill of my mind towards you by some service or some work. Nor has it yet slipped from my memory how kindly your England received me thirty-five years ago. Indeed, that incredible humanity still rises before my eyes, by which not only the eager young men and the most learned professors who then flourished in the Academy of Oxford, but also several distinguished men at the royal court, and among them the immortal glory of England and most glorious martyr of Christ, Thomas Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury, treated me, a young foreigner commended by no experience of affairs or splendour. Afterwards there was added familiarity and a longer acquaintance which I had with some of you while you were residing among us (as I said above). The memory of it returns to me, to my colleagues and indeed to our fellow citizens, never without a singular pleasure. Would that the unexpected death of John Jewel, Bishop of Salisbury, had not sprinkled this pleasure with some bitterness! As it undoubtedly brought sorrow to all of you, so the news of it pierced our hearts too with the sharpest grief, because we think this wound pertains not to England alone but to the whole Church of Christ, of which he was a singular light. But his blessed spirit now lives with Christ the Lord, to whose service he had wholly consecrated himself, and he has left in the earth the longing for himself and an immortal glory of his name. Among you, most reverend Fathers, the memory of your Gualtherus has not faded, as both your friendly letters and other evidence attest. Above all, I have learned that the singular and truly fatherly goodness by which you received my son recently, who had been inflamed by his father's example with a desire to see England, has been such that I feel freed from all the anxiety I had about him, and he seems to himself to be living not abroad among paternal friends but among his own fathers. I value this kindness as highly as an only and beloved son ought to be valued by a parent who is not harsh and [an indulgent one], born of a most dear wife, whose memory will always be precious to me because of her outstanding virtues. Therefore I freely confess that I owe you and your England not only these labours but myself. Reverend Fathers in Christ, accept, then, this token of my zeal towards you, whatever its worth, in the same spirit in which you have long embraced me, and in which you now embrace my son, who is staying with you. May God, the best and greatest, bless your most holy labours and keep you to the glory of his name. May he likewise rule and strengthen the most serene Queen, the faithful nurse of his Church, with the spirit of wisdom, prudence and fortitude, and protect the flourishing kingdom of England in these most difficult times against the dire snares of Antichrist and every hostile force. And may he grant to all who profess the name of Jesus Christ the same mind and the same speech, so that he may be glorified in us too, and the borders of his kingdom may be extended daily far and wide. Amen. Given at Zurich, the chief city of the Helvetians, on the first day of August, in the year 1572 since the eternal Son of God was born in the flesh. This is when, twice a thousand and nine hundred years ago, Deborah, a heroine instructed by the prophetic spirit, freed the Church, oppressed by the savage tyranny of the Canaanites, into liberty, and Sisera, commander of the Canaanite army, likewise slain by the woman Jael, paid a penalty for his cruelty that is remarkable for its singularity.

units.tr: Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother, to the Church of God which is at Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus and called to be saints, with all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, both theirs and ours: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: INTER Diui Pauli epistolas non postremus locus priori ad Corinthios debetur, & eadem merito cum illa coniungi debet, quam ad Romanos dedit, in cuius interpretatione hucusq; occupati fuimus. Ut enim ea universam Euangelij doctrinam atq; totam humanae salutis rationem perfecte tradit: ita haec veram ecclesiae formam describit, & qua ratione vitia atq; errores, qui in illam cadunt, corrigi debeant, docet. Magna igitur semper illius apud veteres authoritas fuit, & eadem nostris temporibus optime conuenit, quando ijsdem vitijs, quibus olim laboratum fuit, & multis insuper gravioribus passim laboratur. Priusquam tamen ad Apostoli verba accedamus, quaedam de Corintho & ecclesia, quae illic fuit conditione, deinde etiam epistolae huius occasione & argumento dicenda erunt.
units.tr: Among the epistles of the divine Paul, the first to the Corinthians deserves no low place, and it ought rightly to be joined with the one he wrote to the Romans, whose exposition we have been occupied with until now. For just as that letter sets out the whole doctrine of the Gospel and the entire plan of human salvation, so this one describes the true form of the Church and teaches by what means the faults and errors that creep into it ought to be corrected. Its authority has therefore always been great among the ancients, and it fits our own times very well, since the same faults that once troubled the Church, and many graver ones besides, are everywhere troubling it. Before we come to the Apostle's words, however, some things must be said about Corinth and the condition of the Church there, and then about the occasion and subject of this letter.

units.la: Corinthus Achaiae ciuitas fuit celeberrima, & in Isthmo Peloponesi inter mare Ionium & Aegeum sita emporium habuit totius orbis nobilissimum, ad quod nationum prope omnium mercatores confluere solebant. Itaq; diuitijs & potentia eo usq; excreuit, ut Cicero eam totius Graeciae lumen, Philippus autem Macedo una cum Chalcide pedicas Graeciae dicere non veritus fuerit. Verumtamen ut vulgo fieri consueuit, cum opibus peregrinorum quoq; mores in eam irrepserunt, unde factum est, ut intemperantia, libidine & luxu immodico diffluens prouerbio locum fecerit, Non cuiuis contingit adire Corinthum. Etenim Strabo memoriae prodidit, Veneris templum illic adeo locupletatum fuisse, ut supra mille puellas Deae prostitutas caperet, quae corpore quaestum faciebant. Puniuit tantam petulantiam Deus, & annis ante natum Christum circiter centum & quadraginta quatuor, Romanos illis immisit, qui Mummio Cos. urbem coeperunt & incendio vastarunt, quo Corinthium aes ex diuersorum metallorum vasis conflatum in pretio haberi coepit: eandem tamen Augustus propter loci commoditatem instaurauit, ideoq; breui ad pristinam dignitatem simul & mores rediit, quamuis Romano Imperio parere. Venit eo Paulus, cum prius Macedoniam totam perlustrasset, & per menses octodecim illic Euangelium IESU CHRISTI magna cum difficultate praedicauit. Opponebant enim sese illi pro suo more Iudaei acerrime, & publicè etiam tumultuabantur, adeo ut de urbe relinquenda cogitaret, sed oraculo admonitus mansit. Itaq; post multos labores illic constituta est Christi ecclesia, quae viros habuit non paucos, fide & pietate singulari illustres, inter quos Gaius & Erastus fuere, quorum mentionem in postremo Cap. ad Romanos fieri audiuimus. Est autem hoc praeclarum bonitatis simul & potentiae Dei exemplum, qui urbi tot modis corruptae Euangelij sui lucem offerre dignatus est, & Ecclesiae suae illic hospitium parare potuit, ubi foedum & horrendum erat diaboli prostibulum. Soletur id nos, ne in peccatis facile desperemus. Confirmet item animos nostros huius exempli consideratio, si quando Christi regno multa obstare, adeoq; mundum totum cum suo principe aduersus illud con-jurauisse videmus. Nullae enim tam densae nebulae, nulla tam horribilis caligo, nullae tam tetrae tenebrae sunt, quas non penetret lux illa caelestis, quam in Filio suo Deus accendit. Spirat etiam ventus ille vbicunq; ipse voluerit, neq; hominum legibus astringitur: & vt turbine deiciuntur subito, quae inuicta videri poterant, sic Verbi sui praedicatione ea vincit & loco mouet Christus, quae toti mundo terrorem prius incutiebant.
units.tr: Corinth was a most famous city of Achaia. Situated on the Isthmus of the Peloponnese, between the Ionian and the Aegean Seas, it had the most noble trading place in the whole world, to which merchants from almost all nations used to flock. So it grew in wealth and power to such an extent that Cicero called it the light of all Greece, and Philip of Macedon did not hesitate to call it, together with Chalcis, the fetters of Greece. Yet, as commonly happens, the morals of foreigners crept in along with their riches. Hence intemperance, lust and immoderate luxury flowed in so freely that there arose the proverb, "It is not given to every man to go to Corinth." Indeed, Strabo has recorded that the temple of Venus there was so wealthy that it kept more than a thousand temple girls, prostitutes who earned their living by their bodies. God punished such wantonness. About one hundred and forty-four years before Christ was born, in the consulship of Mummius, He sent the Romans against Corinth, who took and burned the city; from this the Corinthian bronze, cast from the vessels of various metals, began to be prized. Augustus, however, restored the city on account of the convenience of its site, and therefore in a short time it returned to its former dignity and also to its former morals, although it obeyed the Roman Empire. Paul came there after he had first travelled through all of Macedonia, and for eighteen months he preached the Gospel of Jesus Christ there with great difficulty. The Jews, true to their custom, opposed him most fiercely, and even rioted publicly, so that he thought of leaving the city, but, warned by an oracle, he stayed. So after many labours the Church of Christ was established there, and it had not a few men, distinguished for their singular faith and piety, among whom were Gaius and Erastus, whom we heard mentioned at the end of the chapter to the Romans. This is a remarkable example of the goodness and power of God at once: He deigned to offer the light of His Gospel to a city so corrupted in so many ways, and He was able to prepare a dwelling for His Church there, where the foul and dreadful brothel of the devil had been. This should comfort us, so that we do not easily despair of sinners. The consideration of this example should also strengthen our minds whenever we see many things standing in the way of Christ's kingdom, and the whole world with its prince conspiring against it. For no clouds are so thick, no darkness so terrible, no gloom so foul, that the heavenly light which God kindled in His Son cannot penetrate them. That wind also blows where it wills and is not bound by human laws; and just as things that seemed invincible are suddenly overthrown by a whirlwind, so Christ, by the preaching of His Word, conquers and moves those things which once struck terror into the whole world.

units.la: Caeterum Paulo à Corinthiorum vrbe in Asiam digresso, in ecclesiam recens collectam & te-neram adhuc noui doctores irrepserunt, qui non tam Euangelij doctrinam corrumpere, quam sibi ipsis gloriam parare & soli prae aliis eminere conati sunt. Quod vt facilius consequerentur, sermonibus inter docendū blandis & ad ostentationem compositis vtebantur, quiduis vt cuiuis indulgebant, Paulum vero, quae nullus splendor externus commendabat, nunc nimij rigoris & seueritatis intolera-bilis, nunc insciae & ignorantiae insimulabant. Et hos facile admittebant Corinthij, quorum maior pars ex mercatoribus constabat, quod hominum genus peregrinis delectari, [?]imposturis gaudere, mollitiem sequi, disciplinae vero seueritatem detestari solet. Itaq; mox in factiones scissa est Corinthiorum ecclesia, vt alij Paulini, alij Cephistae, alij Apollonian[?] dicerentur: deinde morum quoque licentia regnare coepit, adeo vt intermoriente paulatim omni disciplina vagis libidinibus promiscuè indulgerent, incestus nimis indulgenter ferrent, lites forenses apud infidelium tribunalia ad uersus se mutuo instituerent, adhaec ad sacra quoq; gentilium accederent, & idolothytis non abstinerent, multorum scandalo vescerentur. Accessit his malis ordinis ecclesiastici confusio, vt multa in coetibus sacris indecenter, multa irreligiosè fierent, Coenae dominicae vsus peruerteretur, & praecipui doctrinae Christianae articuli, & imprimis quidem qui de mortuorum resurrectione habetur, in dubium veniret, adeoq; vix aliqua ex veris ecclesiae notis reliqua esset. De his ergo Paulus per Chloes, piae & religiosae matronae, domesticos admonitus, hanc ad illos epistolam dedit, vt tantis vitijs in tempore remedium adhiberet. Quapropter ab ipso capite exorsus factiones tollit, & vt in Christo vnum sint, hortatur. Et quia praecipui illarum authores erant, qui relicta simplici & expedita docendi ratione, sapientiam carnis & eloquentiam suam ambitiosè ostentabant, primis quatuor Capitibus de ijs diligenter eos admonet. Inde disciplinam ecclesiae restituit, vbi hominem incestum ab ecclesiae societate excludere iubet, lites forenses coercet, fcortationem & quae huic coniuncta sunt vitia grauiter prohibet, adhaec de coniugio, virginitate & coelibatu disserit. Mox à moribus ad religionem transit, & primo eos reprehendit, qui sacris alienis communicabant, & ad epulas idololatricas accedebant. Deinde ad coetus publicos ecclesiae accedens, eorum insolentiam arguit, qui vestitu indecoro vtebantur: Coena item Dominicae abusum corrigit, & primam illius institutionem renouat. Postea de sacris coetibus tractationem diligentiorem instituit, in qua donorum spiritualium vsum & legitimum docendi ordinem exacte tradit. His doctrinam de corporum resurrectione subiicit, quam argumentis multis & validissimis asserit, atq; totam eius historiam eleganter describit. Postremo de pauperum subuentione agit, & eleemosynae colligendae rationem verum tradit. Ex quibus apparet quod initio diximus, epistola hac perfectam ecclesiae formam contineri, & proinde eius le-ctionem atq; considerationem nostro seculo imprimis necessariam esse, quando de abusibus tollendis & reformatione facienda passim disputatur.
units.tr: But when Paul had departed from the city of Corinth into Asia, certain new teachers crept into the Church, which was recently gathered and still tender. They tried not so much to corrupt the doctrine of the Gospel as to win glory for themselves and to stand out above others. To achieve this more easily, they used smooth speeches, composed for display, when they taught; they indulged anyone in anything; but they accused Paul, whom no outward splendour recommended, now of intolerable harshness and severity, now of ignorance and lack of learning. The Corinthians, the greater part of whom consisted of merchants, readily admitted these men. That kind of people usually delights in foreign things, enjoys deceits, follows softness, and detests the strictness of discipline. Soon the Corinthian Church was split into factions, so that some were called Paulines, some Cephasites, and some Apollonians. Then licence in morals also began to reign. Gradually all discipline died out, they gave themselves to wandering lusts without restraint, they tolerated incest too leniently, they brought lawsuits against one another before the tribunals of unbelievers, and besides this they even went to the sacred rites of the Gentiles, did not abstain from food offered to idols, and ate it to the scandal of many. To these evils was added confusion of the ecclesiastical order, so that many things were done indecently and many irreverently in the sacred assemblies. The use of the Lord's Supper was perverted, and the chief articles of Christian doctrine, above all the teaching about the resurrection of the dead, came into doubt, so that scarcely any of the true marks of the Church remained. Therefore Paul, warned about these things by the household of Chloe, a pious and devout matron, sent this letter to them, so that he might apply a timely remedy to such great evils. For this reason he begins at the very head of the matter, removes the factions, and exhorts them to be one in Christ. And because the chief authors of these factions were men who, having abandoned a simple and straightforward manner of teaching, ambitiously displayed the wisdom of the flesh and their own eloquence, he warns them about this carefully in the first four chapters. Then he restores the discipline of the Church, where he orders that the incestuous man be excluded from fellowship with the Church, restrains lawsuits, forbids fornication and the vices connected with it, and discusses marriage, virginity and celibacy. Next he passes from morals to religion, and first he rebukes those who took part in alien rites and went to idolatrous feasts. Then, coming to the public assemblies of the Church, he reproves the arrogance of those who dressed indecorously. He also corrects the abuse of the Lord's Supper and renews its first institution. Afterwards he treats more carefully of the sacred assemblies, in which he accurately teaches the use of spiritual gifts and the proper order of teaching. To these he adds the doctrine of the resurrection of bodies, which he asserts with many very strong arguments, and he describes its whole history elegantly. Finally he deals with the relief of the poor, and he gives the true method of gathering alms. From all this it is clear, as we said at the beginning, that this letter contains the complete form of the Church, and therefore reading and considering it is especially necessary in our age, when people everywhere are arguing about removing abuses and carrying out reform.

units.la: Admonet autem nos Corinthiorum exemplum, quàm vigilanti cura atq; studio opus sit in gubernandis & seruandis ecclesijs. Nam quod in zizaniorum parabola Christus docuit, fere passim accidere videmus, vt dormientibus nobis Satan infelix lolium & zizania illis aspergat, qui bonum illud & salutiferum Verbi semen prius exceperunt. Et quamuis nō semper doctrinam Veritatis aperte oppugnet, astute tamen sese insinuat, & quasi per cuniculos irrepit, vt abolita paulatim disciplina, puriorís doctrinae fastidium nobis pariat, & superstitionibus nouis, aut etiam Epicureismo viam sternat. Et profecto mirum videri poterat, illo tempore, quando ecclesiae ab exteris hostibus vndiq; premebantur, potuisse intestinis dissidijs in factiones scindi, & in tuenda Veritatis doctrina tam negligentes esse eos, quibus animorum coniunctione & vigilantia quàm maximè opus erat, nisi hodie idem fieri videremus. Excubent ergo omnes pro publica & propria salute: Imprimis autem ecclesiarum ministri Paulum imitentur, quem neq; veterum iniuriarum memoria,neq noui labores qui indies ipsum premebant,reuocare potuerunt,quo minus ecclesiæ,à qua longius aberat,cura tangatur, & illi in tempore remedium adhibeat. Quàm enim turpe fuerit,si illi ecclesias, quarum cura ipsis peculiari vocatione demandata est, sua ignauia dissipari patiantur? Singuli ergo sibi dictum putent, quod Apostolus in Miletana Synodo Asiaticarum ecclesiarum ministris ait: Attendite vobisipsis & toti gregi,in quo vos spiritus sanctus constituit episcopos ad pascendam ecclesiam Dei, quam acquisiuit suo sanguine,&c. Neq; eos audiant, qui nescio quam simplicem & generalem docendi rationem sufficere putant: quando res ipsa docet, nihil profici,nisi doctrina singulis applicetur, & admonitionibus atque correptionibus vrgeantur,qui suæ salutis negligentiores sunt.
units.tr: The example of the Corinthians shows us how watchful care and zeal are needed in governing and preserving the churches. For what Christ taught in the parable of the tares, we see happening almost everywhere: while we sleep, the unhappy Satan sows darnel and tares among those who first received that good and saving seed of the Word. And although he does not always openly attack the doctrine of truth, he insinuates himself craftily and creeps in as if through underground passages, so that, once discipline has gradually been abolished, he produces in us a distaste for purer doctrine and paves the way for new superstitions, or even for Epicureanism. Indeed it might seem astonishing that at that time, when the churches were pressed on every side by external enemies, they could still be split into factions by internal quarrels, and that those whose union of minds and vigilance was most needed should be so careless in defending the doctrine of truth, unless we saw the same thing happening today. Let everyone therefore keep watch for the public and their own salvation. Above all, let the ministers of the churches imitate Paul, whom neither the memory of past injuries nor the new labours that pressed upon him day by day could keep from being concerned for the church, though he was far away from it, and from applying a remedy in time. How shameful it would be if the ministers allowed the churches, whose care has been entrusted to them by a special calling, to be scattered through their own laziness! Let each one therefore consider as addressed to himself what the Apostle said to the ministers of the Asian churches at the Synod of Miletus: "Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to feed the Church of God, which He purchased with His own blood," and so on. Nor should they listen to those who think that some simple and general method of teaching is enough, since the thing itself shows that nothing is accomplished unless the teaching is applied to individuals, and those who are more careless of their own salvation are pressed with admonitions and rebukes.

units.la: His præmissis ad primam epistolæ partem accedamus,quæ Inscriptionem habet his verbis comprehensam:Paulus vocatus Apostolus IESV CHRISTI per voluntatem Dei,& Sosthenes frater,Ecclesiæ Dei,quæ est Corinthi,sanctificatis in CHRISTO IESV, vocatis sanctis, cum omnibus, qui inuocant nomen Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI in quouis loco, Domini (inquam)tum ipsorum tum nostri. Gratia vobis & pax à Deo Patre nostro & Domino IESV CHRISTO. Continentur his verbis tria,quæ ex ordine videbimus.
units.tr: Having premised these things, let us come to the first part of the epistle, which opens with the salutation in these words: Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother, to the church of God which is at Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, with all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, their Lord and ours (I say). Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Three things are contained in these words, which we shall take in order.

units.la: Primùm epistolæ author indicatur, Paulus Apostolus,qui Sosthenem sibi collegam adsciscit. Vocationis autem suæ meminit,& hanc per Dei voluntatem factam esse diserte testatur,idq; propter æmulos, qui ipsum Apostolum verum aut legitimè vocatum esse negabant, quo facilius doctrinam eius in contemptum adducerent. Deinde Sosthenem sibi eoniungit,quem Synagogæ præfectum apud Corinthios fuisse Lucas in Actis scribit, vbi eundem ad Gallionis Proconsulis tribunal à Græcis pessimè tractatum & verberibus multatum fuisse legimus. Consulto igitur hunc nominat Paulus, qui & Corinthius erat, & ab illis non poterat facile contemni, cùm sub initium istius ecclesiæ tam luculentum fidei & constantiæ suæ specimen dedisset. Estq; hoc magnum modestiæ Pauli argumentum,qui hominem se longè inferiorem sibi collegam assumit:quod ab illo alibi quoq; factum audiuimus. Sosthenes autem præclarum suæ constantiæ præmium recipit,quem tanto honore dignatur Deus,vt Pauli socium faciat,eiusq; nomen in ecclesia sua æternæ memoriæ con secret. Debet huius exemplum nos quoq; excitare,quando vniuersalis promissio extat,Honorantes me honorabo. Imprimis autem curent Ecclesiarum ministri,vt suæ vocationis certi sint,neq; priuato affectu se ad istam functionem intrudant. Nam vocatio legitima & animum illis addit in periculis gravioribus,& eosdem quo minus efferantur continet. Hodie quia vocationem Dei pauci expectant,fere aut fuci ignaui ad ecclesiarum gubernacula sedent,aut superbi fidei dominatores omnia pro sua libidine versant & ecclesias dissipant.
units.tr: First, the author of the letter is named: Paul the apostle, who takes Sosthenes as his colleague. He clearly mentions his calling and testifies plainly that it came about by the will of God, and he does so because of his rivals, who denied that he was a true apostle or lawfully called, so that they might more easily bring his teaching into contempt. Then he joins Sosthenes to himself, the man whom Luke writes in the Acts was the ruler of the synagogue among the Corinthians, where we read that he was roughly handled by the Greeks before the judgment seat of the proconsul Gallio and beaten. Paul therefore names him deliberately: he was a Corinthian, and they could not easily despise him, since at the beginning of that church he had given such a splendid proof of his faith and steadfastness. This is a great sign of Paul's modesty, that he takes as colleague a man far inferior to himself, as we have heard him do elsewhere too. Sosthenes, moreover, receives the excellent reward of his steadfastness, for God deigns to honour him so greatly as to make him Paul's companion and to consecrate his name in his church to eternal memory. The example ought to stir us up as well, since the universal promise stands: "Those who honour me I will honour." Above all, let the ministers of the churches take care to be certain of their calling, and not thrust themselves into this office out of private ambition. For a lawful calling both gives them courage in more serious dangers and keeps them from being puffed up. Today, since few wait for God's calling, for the most part either lazy drones sit at the helm of the churches, or proud lords of faith manage everything as they please and scatter the churches.

units.la: Secundò, quibus epistola hæc inscripta fit,docetur. Ecclesiæ Dei nimirum, quæ tunc temporis Corinthi erat. Vt verò constaret,qui nam ad Ecclesiæ societatem pertineant,quædam subijcit,quæ Christianorum hominum descriptionem continent. Dicit enim,Sanctificatos in IESV CHRISTO & vocatos sanctos:& priori quidem membro Dei beneficium prædicat, qui nos natura impuros & peccatores sanctificauit in Filio suo, quem (vt infra dicet) nobis iustitiam & sanctificationem fecit:altero autem finem nostræ vocationis indicat, qui est, vt Deo consecrati vitam viuamus sanctam & à mundi carnisq; studijs alienam. Et hæc causa veteres mouit,vt se mutuò Sanctos dicerent:non vt sibi gloriam quandam ambitiosè vendicarent, sed vt de Dei beneficio sibi in Christo exhibito,deq; officio suo frequentius cogitandi occasionem haberent. Sanctitatis vero huius assequendæ medium nullum illi sciebant, præter fidem, quæ nos Christo inserit, & bonorum ipsius omnium participes reddit. At postquam posteris temporibus vera sanctitas inter Christiani nominis professores deficere cœpit, Romani Pontifices nouam artem excogitarunt, & Canonizationibus suis in cœlitum consortium retulerunt atq; Sanctos dixerunt, quos de ipsis bene meritos esse videbant. Sed de hoc alibi plura,nunc quod Paulus in Christianorum descriptione subijcit,videamus: Cum omnibus qui inuocant nomen Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI in quouis loco,Domini (inquam)tum ipsorum tum nostri. Ita nos locum hunc cum Chrysostomo & alijs Græcis interpretibus legendū & intelligendum esse sentimus. Nam quod plerique de loco exponunt, absurdissimum est,cùm Iudæi iam tunc per totum ferè orbem dispersi fuerint,neq; Iudæa ipsa magis[?] illorum quàm Romanorum tunc fuisse dici posset, qui eam suis præsidijs sub ditione tenebant. Sed & Paulus, qui in Cilicia natus erat, Iudæam suum locum dicere non posset. Rectius ergo ad Iudæos & gentes hoc retuleris, quibus Christum communem facit, ut obiter initio statim admoneat, nimis indignè facere eos, qui inter se factionibus scindantur, cum unū & eundem Dominum IESVM CHRISTVM, ex fide invocent.
units.tr: Second, we are taught to whom this letter is addressed: to the church of God, namely the one that was then at Corinth. So that it might be clear who belong to the fellowship of the church, he adds certain words that describe Christian people. For he says, "sanctified in Christ Jesus and called saints." In the first member he proclaims God's benefit, who sanctified us, impure and sinners by nature, in his Son, whom (as he will say below) he made our righteousness and sanctification; in the second he indicates the goal of our calling, which is that, consecrated to God, we should live a holy life, alien from the pursuits of the world and the flesh. This is also why the ancients called one another "saints", not so as to claim for themselves some ambitious glory, but so that they might have more frequent occasion to think about God's benefit given to them in Christ and about their own duty. Yet they knew of no means of attaining this holiness except faith, which joins us to Christ and makes us partakers of all his good things. But after holiness in truth began to fail among the professors of the Christian name in later times, the Roman Pontiffs devised a new art and, by their canonizations, enrolled in the fellowship of the heavenly ones, and called "saints", those whom they saw to have deserved well of themselves. But of this more elsewhere; now let us see what Paul adds in his description of Christians: "with all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, their Lord and ours (I say)." Thus we judge that this passage is to be read and understood with Chrysostom and the other Greek interpreters. For what most men explain as referring to a place is most absurd, since the Jews had by then been scattered through almost the whole world, nor could Judaea itself be said to belong to them any more than to the Romans, who then held it under their rule with their garrisons. Nor could Paul, who was born in Cilicia, call Judaea his own place. It is more correct, therefore, to refer this to Jews and Gentiles alike, to whom he makes Christ common, so that he may admonish them in passing, right at the start, that it is very unworthy of those who call upon the one and the same Lord Jesus Christ in faith to be split into factions among themselves.

units.la: Continet autem locus iste germanam Ecclesiæ definitionem, quæ eiusmodi est: Ecclesia est coetus seu communio electorum Dei, quos hic in Filio suo IESV CHRISTO sanctificauit, & quos per Euangelium vocat, ut sancte & pie viuant, atq; nomen Filij sui invocent. Fundamentum ergo Ecclesiæ in electione est, quam priusquam hic mundus conderetur factam fuisse, Paulus ad Ephesios docet. Et de hoc Sanctificatorum quoq; vocabulum nos admonet: quia nisi Deus ex corrupta & infelici atq; perdita humani generis massa nos seligat & sibi consecret, sanctificationem nostris viribus nunquam assequemur. Medium verò, quo ad Ecclesiam pertrahimur, vocatio est, quæ extrinsecus per Verbi prædicationem, intus verò per spiritus sancti tractum fit. Nam de vocatione efficaci hic loquimur, quæ nulla erit, nisi animi trahantur, secundùm illud Christi: Nemo venit ad me, nisi Pater meus traxerit illum. Ad vitæ verò sanctitatem (quem vocationis nostræ finem esse diximus) invocatio nominis IESV CHRISTI accedere debet, quæ fidei confessionem continet. Quomodo enim invocabunt eum, in quem non credunt? Fidei autem confessionem nobis necessariam esse, passim in Scripturis docemur. At quàmuis ea varie fiat, certissimum tamen eius argumentum est invocatio, ut in Martyribus est videre, qui fidem suam non alio experimento evidentius declararunt, quàm quod uno Deo patre per Christum contenti, neq; Deos alienos invocare, neq; per eorum nomina iurare (quæ ipsa quoq; invocationis species est) voluerunt. Unde apparet, Christianos germanos non esse, qui Christum quidem ore profitentur, non autem huic viuunt, neq; hunc solū invocant, sed honorem, qui ipsi debetur, in Deos cœlites transferunt. Est ergo hæc Ecclesiæ definitio probe tenenda, ne nobis ipsis inani nominis Christiani perfuasione imponamus, & ut illorum tyrannidem vitemus, qui Ecclesiæ titulum ad paucos restringunt, adeoq; sibi solis vendicant, quod hodie Pontificij præsules non sine atroci omnium Christianorum iniuria facere consueuerunt.
units.tr: This passage contains a true definition of the Church, which is of this kind: the Church is the assembly or fellowship of the elect of God, whom he has sanctified here in his Son Jesus Christ, and whom he calls through the gospel, that they may live holy and godly lives and call upon the name of his Son. The foundation of the Church, therefore, lies in election, which Paul teaches in his letter to the Ephesians was made before the world was founded. The word "sanctified" also reminds us of this, for unless God chooses us from the corrupt and wretched mass of the human race and consecrates us to himself, we shall never attain holiness by our own strength. The means by which we are drawn to the Church is the calling, which comes from outside through the preaching of the Word, and inwardly through the drawing of the Holy Spirit. For we are speaking here of effectual calling, which will be nothing unless hearts are drawn, according to Christ's words: "No one comes to me unless my Father draws him." But for the holiness of life (which we have said is the goal of our calling) the invocation of the name of Jesus Christ must be added, which contains the confession of faith. "For how will they call on him in whom they have not believed?" We are taught throughout the Scriptures that the confession of faith is necessary for us. Although it is made in various ways, the surest evidence of it is invocation, as may be seen in the martyrs, who declared their faith by no more evident proof than by being content with the one God the Father through Christ, and by refusing to call upon strange gods or to swear by their names (which is itself a kind of invocation). From this it is clear that they are not true Christians who profess Christ with their mouths but do not live by him, nor call upon him alone, but transfer the honour due to him to the heavenly gods. This definition of the Church, therefore, is to be firmly held, lest we deceive ourselves with the empty persuasion of the Christian name, and so that we may avoid the tyranny of those who restrict the title of Church to a few and so claim it for themselves alone, which the Papist prelates today customarily do, not without grievous wrong to all Christians.

units.la: net. Quomodo enim invocabunt eum, in quem non credunt?
units.tr: net. How, then, will they call upon him in whom they do not believe?

units.la: Porrò præ aliis hic obseruatu dignum est, quòd Ecclesiam Dei Paulus eos dicit, qui tot tamen grauibus (ut paulò ante dictum est) vitijs laborabant. Atqui cum admonendi & corripiendi liberas, qua erga illos usus est, ipsum ab omni adulationis suspicione satis liberet, non temere ita locutum putabimus. Etenim etsi maior pars erroribus infecta esset, reliqui tamen erant boni & pij multi, qui vitia emendari & omnia in melius restitui cupiebant, & ideo Paulum de sua conditione certiorem fecerant. Deinde locum inter illos habebant Verbi Dei prædicatio & Sacramentorum usus, quo à gentibus prophanis palàm discernebantur. Et quàmuis multa nimis licenter facerent, aliqua tamen seruabatur forma disciplinæ, ut non possent eorum similes censeri, quos Scriptura filios Belial dicere solet, eò quòd iugum omne effreni contumacia excutiunt. Quibus adde Dei oraculum, qui illi de fuga cogitanti dixerat: Ne timeas, sed loquere, & ne taceas: quoniam populus est mihi multus in hac civitate. Qui ergo sciebat Christum oves dixisse eos, qui adhuc per superstitionem & idololatriæ auia vagabantur, non temere eos à Christi grege excludere aut Ecclesiæ titulo spoliare voluit, qui Christum profitebantur, & Euangelio eius locum dabant. Utinam verò hoc Pauli exemplum propius inspicerent arrogantes illi Rhadamanti & Minoës, qui excommunicationis telum perpetuò vibrant in omnes, qui Christiani nominis professioni non per omnia respondent: neque eo contenti, Ecclesias totas damnant, in quibus nævos aut vitia quædam conspicantur. Meminerint illi, nos de colligendis potius Ecclesijs quàm dissipandis solicitos esse debere, neque eos medicos probari, qui membra morbida resecant, priusquam extremo corporis totius periculo cogantur.
units.tr: Moreover, above other things, it is worth observing here that Paul calls those the church of God who nevertheless were labouring under so many grave faults (as was said a little earlier). Since the freedom to admonish and correct them, which he used toward them, sufficiently frees him from any suspicion of flattery, we will not think he spoke thus rashly. For even if the greater part were infected with errors, there were nevertheless many good and godly people left, who wished the faults to be corrected and everything restored for the better, and for this reason they had informed Paul of their condition. Then, among them there was the preaching of the Word of God and the use of the sacraments, by which they were openly distinguished from profane nations. And although they did many things too licentiously, still some form of discipline was preserved, so that they could not be counted among those whom Scripture is wont to call sons of Belial, because they shake off every yoke with unbridled obstinacy. To these add God's oracle, who said to him when he was thinking of flight: "Do not fear, but speak, and do not keep silent, for I have many people in this city." Therefore, since he knew that Christ called his sheep even those who were still wandering astray in superstition and idolatry, he did not rashly wish to exclude from Christ's flock, or strip of the title of church, those who professed Christ and gave his gospel a place. Would that those arrogant Rhadamanthuses and Minoses would look more closely at this example of Paul, they who constantly brandish the weapon of excommunication against all who do not in every respect answer to the profession of the Christian name, and who, not content with that, condemn whole churches in which some blemishes or faults are seen. Let them remember that we ought to be concerned to gather churches rather than to scatter them, and that those are not to be approved as physicians who cut away diseased limbs before they are compelled by danger to the whole body.

units.la: Obseruari præterea debet, Ecclesiam Christi unicam esse, & eandem rectè Catholicam aut universalem dici, eò quòd per totum orbem terrarum extenditur, & ad eius societatem omnes pertinent, quotquot nomen Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI invocant, id est, quicunq; Christū talem agnoscunt, qualis in Scripturis prædicatur. Ergo locorum diuersitas Ecclesiæ unitate minimè scindit, & ut in amplo regno unius & eiusdem Regis subditi sunt, qui longissimis locorum intervallis distincti sedes diuersas habitant: ita cum Christi regnum ad fines usq; orbis terrarum extendatur, nihil obstabit gentium aut nationum distantia, quo minus omnes credentes in illius grege censeri debeant. Ideo D. Irenaeus, cum fide Christianae summam, quae Symbolo aut traditione (ut ipse lo-quitur) apostolica continetur, recensuisset, mox subdit: Hanc fidem, qui sine literis crediderunt, quantum ad sermonem nostrum Barbari sunt (loquitur enim de gentibus procul remotis, & quae literarum quoq; usu carebant) quantum autem ad sententiam & consuetudinem & conuersationē, propter fidē perquam sapientissimi sunt, & placent Deo, conuersantes in omni iustitia & castitate & sapientia, &c. Huius autem ut olim Corinthios admoneri oportuit, ne in partes scinderentur: ita hodie frequenter de hoc omnes cogitare decebat, quo minus praecipites essent in ijs damnandis, quos eiusdem fidei professio ipsis coniungit. At quae nostri saeculi infelicitas est, & hodie fere Catholici, non minus inepto quam falso nomine dicuntur, qui in hominum verba iurarunt, & a veteri illa atq; vere catholica fidei & doctrinae apostolicae regula iampridem discesserunt.
units.tr: It should further be observed that the Church of Christ is one, and is rightly called Catholic or universal, because it extends throughout the whole world, and all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ belong to its fellowship, that is, all who acknowledge Christ as he is preached in the Scriptures. Therefore the difference of places does not divide the unity of the Church; and just as the subjects of one and the same king in a vast kingdom, though separated by very great distances, dwell in different seats, so, since the kingdom of Christ extends to the ends of the earth, the distance of peoples or nations will be no hindrance to all believers being counted in his flock. Hence St. Irenaeus, after reciting the sum of the Christian faith, which is contained in the creed or in apostolic tradition (as he calls it), immediately adds: "Those who have believed this faith without letters are barbarians as far as our speech is concerned (for he speaks of peoples far removed and who lacked the use of letters), but as far as doctrine, custom and way of life are concerned, they are most wise because of their faith, and they please God, living in all righteousness, chastity and wisdom," etc. Just as the Corinthians once had to be admonished of this, lest they be split into factions, so today all ought often to reflect on it, so that they would be less hasty in condemning those whom the profession of the same faith joins to them. But what unhappiness there is in our age, that today those are commonly called Catholics, with a name no less foolish than false, who have sworn allegiance to the words of men and have long since departed from that old and truly catholic rule of faith and apostolic doctrine!

units.la: Sequitur tertium primae partis membrum, imprecatio aut salutatio apostolica, quae talis est: Gratia vobis & pax a Deo Patre & Domino IESV CHRISTO. Gratia vocabulo Dei fauorem denotari alibi diximus. Hunc ergo ipsis propitium Paulus optat. Inde pax sequitur, quae non solum prosperum vitae & rerum huius seculi successum, sed imprimis conscientiae tranquillitatem significat, quae ut omnes animi terrores, qui ex peccati sensu enascuntur, procul repellit, ita in aduersis constantes facit, & patientia Christiana nos armat, in qua animas nostras (ut Christus ait) possidemus. Pertinet huc, quod ad Roman. cap.5. scribitur: Iustificati ex fide pacem habemus apud Deum, &c. Et haec illa pax est, quae omnem huius mundi intellectum superat, eo quod in afflictionibus quoq; salua nobis maneat. Ista vero a Deo Patre illis precatur, qui bonorum omnium fons est: & eidem Christum coniungit, quo mediatore nos gratiae & salutis participes reddimur.
