At quia haec ex ipsius Christi mandato Apostoli omnibus publice & priuatim precantur, eadem nobis quoq; omnium votorū summa esse debet. Nisi enim Deo propitio utamur, & nobis cum propria conscientia recte conueniat, nullam ex opibus, honoribus, voluptatibus aut amicitijs huius seculi utilitatem consequemur. Imo haec omnia nobis veneni instar sunt, eo quod illis in proprium exitium abutimur. E contra, si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Quapropter, quae unica est salutis consequendae ratio, agnoscamus nos gratia & misericordia Dei opus habere, fide autem constan-ti amplectamur IESVM CHRISTVM, in quo vno Pater nobis reconciliatus est. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: There follows the third part of the first section, the apostolic greeting or blessing, which is this: "Grace to you and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." We have elsewhere said that by the word grace the favour of God is denoted. Paul therefore prays that he may be gracious to them. Then peace follows, which signifies not only a prosperous life and success in the things of this world, but above all tranquillity of conscience; which, as it drives far away all the terrors of the soul that spring from the sense of sin, so it makes us steadfast in adversity, and Christian patience arms us, in which we possess our souls (as Christ says). To this belongs what is written in Romans 5: "Being justified by faith, we have peace with God," etc. And this is that peace which surpasses all understanding of the world, because it remains safe for us even in afflictions. He prays that this be given by God the Father, who is the fountain of all good things, and he joins Christ to the Father, through whose mediation we are made partakers of grace and salvation. And since the apostles, by Christ's own command, pray these things publicly and privately for all, the sum of all our prayers ought likewise to be this. For unless we enjoy God's favour and our own conscience agrees with us, we shall gain no advantage from the wealth, honours, pleasures or friendships of this world. Indeed all these things are like poison to us, because we misuse them to our own destruction. On the contrary, "If God is for us, who can be against us?" Therefore, let us acknowledge, since this is the only way to obtain salvation, that we have need of the grace and mercy of God, and let us with steadfast faith embrace Jesus Christ, in whom alone the Father has been reconciled to us. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA II.
units.tr: Homily II.

units.la: Gratias ago Deo meo semper de vobis ob gratiam Dei quae data est vobis in CHRISTO IESV: Quod in omnibus ditati estis in ipso, in omni sermone & omni cognitione, prout testimonium Christi confirmatum fuit in vobis: adeo ut nullo dono deficiamini, expectantes dum reueletur Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS. Qui etiā confirmabit vos usq; ad finem inculpatos, in diem Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI. Fidelis Deus, per quem vocati estis in communionem filij ipsius, IESV CHRISTI Domini nostri.
units.tr: I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God which has been given you in Christ Jesus: that in everything you have been enriched in him, in all speech and all knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ has been confirmed among you; so that you lack no gift, as you wait for the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ. He also will confirm you to the end, blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is faithful, through whom you were called into fellowship with his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

units.la: CHRISTUS IESUS Dominus noster, Ecclesiae suae ministrum sub Oeconomi parabola describens, in illo non fidem modo & integritatem, sed prudentiam quoq; requirit, qua Verbum Dei, quo animarum cibus continetur, ita depromat atq; distribuat, ne inscitia aut importunitate eos absterreat, qui prudenti & commoda institutione lucrifieri poterant. Obseruauit hanc Christi admonitionem diligenter Paulus, tum alibi tum in huius Epistolae proemio siue exordio, quod modo recitauimus. Quia enim in Corinthijs multa reprehensurus, multa correpturus, multa etiam damnaturus erat, in praesenti sic captat beneuolentiam, ut sese omni suspicione odij & maleuolentiae liberet. Itaq; duo agit. Primum virtutes eorum & dona, quibus a Deo ornati erant, magnifice commendat. Deinde se de illis in posterum quoq; bene sperare testatur. Est hoc exemplum imitandum omnibus, qui Ecclesiæ seruiunt, ne dissimulando ea quæ laudem merentur, odium sibi ipsis conflent, aut vitia tanquam incurabilia & deplorata prorsus exagitando, eos in desperationem adducant, qui emendatione simul & consolatione opus habent. Vt vero Paulus duo hæc prudenter præmittit, sic in vtroq; prudentia singulari vtitur.
units.tr: Christ Jesus our Lord, describing the minister of his Church under the parable of the steward, requires in him not only faithfulness and integrity but also prudence, by which he should dispense and distribute the Word of God, which contains the food of souls, so that he does not frighten away by clumsiness or impatience those who could have been won over by a wise and fitting instruction. Paul observed this admonition of Christ carefully, both elsewhere and in the opening or introduction of this Epistle, which we have just read. For since he was going to rebuke many things among the Corinthians, correct many, and even condemn many, he here so wins their goodwill that he frees himself from any suspicion of hatred or ill will. He therefore does two things. First, he magnificently commends their virtues and the gifts with which God had adorned them. Then he testifies that he also hopes well of them for the future. This is an example for all who serve the Church to imitate, so that by concealing what deserves praise they do not make enemies for themselves, nor, by hammering at faults as if they were incurable and utterly hopeless, drive to despair those who need both correction and comfort at once. But just as Paul wisely puts these two things first, so he uses singular prudence in both.

units.la: Et primò quidem sic laudat Corinthios, vt neq; turpiter illis aduletur, neq; etiam sese efferen-di aut insolentius gloriandi occasionem præbeat. Nam à gratiarum actione orditur, qua donorum omnium, quibus excellebant, authorem facit Deum, partim ne ipsi illis tanquam proprijs super-biant: partim vt eorum temeritatem obiter perstringat, qui illis abutebantur, vt suo loco audie-mus. Gratias ago (inquit) Deo meo semper de vobis, ob gratiam Dei, quæ data est vobis in CHRISTO IESV. Per gratiam Dei hoc loco non fauorem modò eius, vt nuper, sed simul omnia illius effecta intelligit, qualia sunt, Remissio peccatorum, adoptio in filio Dei, salus æterna, donum spiritus peculiaria, quibus olim Ecclesiam floruisse scimus, vt pote prophetia, linguarum cognitione & miraculorum virtute. In quibus cum aliqui sibijpsis placerent, hæc illis à Deo obtigisse docet, idq; no aliquo ipsorum merito, sed in CHRISTO IESV, qui nobis hanc gratiam apud patrem meruerit.
units.tr: And first, he praises the Corinthians in such a way that he neither flatters them shamefully nor gives them an occasion to exalt themselves or to boast too insolently. For he begins with thanksgiving, by which he makes God the author of all the gifts in which they excelled, partly so that they would not be proud of them as if they were their own, and partly so that he might briefly rebuke the rashness of those who abused them, as we shall hear in its place. "I give thanks," he says, "to my God always for you, for the grace of God which has been given you in Christ Jesus." By "the grace of God" here he understands not only his favour, as just before, but at the same time all his effects, such as the remission of sins, adoption as sons of God, eternal salvation, and the special gifts of the Spirit, by which we know the Church once flourished, namely prophecy, the knowledge of tongues, and the power of miracles. Since some of them took pleasure in themselves because of these, he teaches that these things had been granted to them by God, and not by any merit of their own, but in Christ Jesus, who merited this grace for us with the Father.

units.la: Continet autem Pauli exemplum generalem doctrinam, vt nimirum Dei dona nunquam non nobis in mentem reuocemus, eorum vero authorem agnoscamus Deum, qui gratuita liberalitate in nos vtatur, & proinde illi ex animo gratias agamus. Admonet de hoc naturæ Lex; quæ non barbaris modò gentibus & à religione alienis, verumetiam brutis animantibus hunc sensum indidit, vt benefactores suos agnoscant, & quam possunt gratiam illis referant. Et gratiarum actione Deum quàm maximè delectari constat. Nam in Psal. 50. cultum suum duabus hisce partibus cōstare docet, vt in aduersis constituti ipsum invocemus, liberati autem ipsi gloriam omnem tribuamus, quod absq; gratiarum actione fieri non potest. Et Dauid cum in Psal. 69. amplissima Dei beneficia commemorauisset, tandem addit: Laudabo nomen Dei cum cantico, & extolla illud celebri laude. Gratius id erit Domino, quàm si bouem offeram aut vitulum cornibus & vngulis eximium. Neq; temere id Dauid pronuntiat. Gratiarum enim actio non solùm Deo suum honorem transcribit, verum etiam nos in officio continet, ne illius donis aut beneficijs pro nostra libidine abutamur. Debet ergo hoc in omnibus eius donis tam corporeis & externis quàm spiritualibus obseruari. Nam etsi quæ corpori seruiunt, interdum nostro labore aut industria parari videntur, reuera tamen ex Dei benedictione dependent, qui nisi ipse domū ædificarit, & agri prouentus dederit, nihil nostra cura aut labore proficitur. Quoad autem ea, quæ ad salutem æternam faciunt, ne ad cogitandum quidē idonei sumus, & si suo in nos iure Deus vtatur, sempiterno exitio multabimur. Quicquid ergo habemus boni, id omne gratuitum diuinæ liberalitatis donum est, & pro eo gratiæ Deo agendæ sunt, simulq; cauere nos decet, ne quæ ille dedit turpi abusu in nostram pernitiem conuertamus.
units.tr: Now Paul's example contains a general teaching, namely that we should never fail to call God's gifts to mind, and that we should acknowledge God as the author of them, since he uses his free liberality towards us, and that we should therefore give him thanks from the heart. The law of nature teaches this, which has implanted this feeling not only in barbarous nations and those alien to religion, but even in brute animals, so that they recognise their benefactors and repay them with whatever gratitude they can. And it is well established that God takes the greatest delight in thanksgiving. For in Psalm 50 he teaches that his worship consists of two parts: that we call upon him when we are in adversity, and that, once delivered, we ascribe all glory to him, which cannot be done without thanksgiving. And David, when in Psalm 69 he had recounted God's very great benefits, at last adds: "I will praise the name of God with a song, and magnify it with celebrated praise. This will be more pleasing to the Lord than if I offer an ox, or a calf with horns and hoofs." David does not say this rashly. For thanksgiving not only gives God his due honour, but also keeps us in our duty, so that we do not abuse his gifts and benefits according to our own lust. This must therefore be observed in all his gifts, bodily and external as well as spiritual. For although the things that serve the body sometimes seem to be obtained by our labour or industry, in truth they depend on God's blessing; unless he himself builds the house and gives the produce of the field, our care and labour accomplish nothing. As for those things which lead to eternal salvation, we are not even fit to think of them, and if God were to use his right over us, we would be punished with everlasting destruction. Whatever good we have, therefore, is all a free gift of divine liberality, and for it thanks must be rendered to God; and at the same time we ought to take care that we do not turn what he has given into our own ruin by shameful abuse.

units.la: Cæterum quod generaliùs dixerat Paulus, nunc in suas quasi species diducit, sic dicens: Quòd in omnibus ditati estis in ipso, in omni sermone & omni cognitione, prout testimonium Christi confirmatum fuit in vobis: adeò vt nullo dono deficiamini, expectantes dum reueletur Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS. Sermone autem & cognitione ipsam Verbi Dei doctrinam comprehendit, qua homines instituti cognoscunt atque intelligunt, quæcunq; ad salutem consequendam necessaria sunt. Eandemq; mox testimonium Christi dicit, vt eius certitudinem melius exprimat, & illam ab incertis hominum commentis distinguat. Sensus ergo est, Verbum Dei ita inter eos annuntiatum esse, vt vera & solida rerum cœlestium cognitione instructi, & intra animos suos plenè confirmati nullis præterea traditionibus aut donis opus habeant, sed certa atq; infallibili spe expectare possint tempus illud præfinitum, quo Christum in gloria Patris sui toti mundo reuelari oporteat. At hoc dicendo pseudoapostolos perstringit, qui hoc potissimum argumento sese apud Corinthios insinuauerant, quòd Pauli doctrinam nimis ieiunam & sterilem esse, & proinde in ipsorum ecclesia adhuc multa deesse dicerent. Est enim hoc proprium impostorum stratagema, quòd cùm Veritatis doctrinam neq; negare possint, neque illam aperte oppugnare audeant, ad hoc effugium conuertantur, & multa adhuc desiderari dicant. Quod si semel hominibus persuaserint, mox ea affulunt[?], quibus veritas obscuratur, & verus Dei cultus in superstitionem convertitur. Utuntur hac arte, qui Papatum vel retinere, vel reducere satagunt. Quibus non melius occurreris, quam si apostolos omnia plene tradidisse, & olim Ecclesiis nihil defuisse demonstres, priusquam concilia & patres illi exiterunt, quorum authoritate sese vendicant. Debent autem Pauli verba de donis necessariis intelligi, ne literam pertinacius urgendo ex hominibus Angelos fingamus, aut Paulum sibi ipsi contrarium faciamus, qui postea Corinthios ob multa vitia reprehendet, & carnales esse dicet, quibus non potuerit ut spiritualibus loqui. Etenim quoad in hac carne vivimus, non licebit nobis ad eam perfectionem venire, ut nullum prorsus donum coeleste nobis desit. At Deus pro nostro captu dona sua distribuit, & quamuis non omnibus det omnia, singulis tamen ea dat, quae ipsis ad fidem fovendam sufficere possunt usq; in eum diem, quo corporis huius vinculis soluti ad Christum colliguntur. Habet autem hic locus multa observatu dignissima.
units.tr: But what Paul had said in more general terms, he now divides, as it were, into its particular kinds, saying: "That in everything you have been enriched in him, in all speech and all knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ has been confirmed among you; so that you lack no gift, as you wait for the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ." By speech and knowledge he means the very doctrine of the Word of God, by which men who have been instructed know and understand whatever is necessary for obtaining salvation. And he at once calls this the testimony of Christ, in order to express its certainty more clearly and to distinguish it from the uncertain inventions of men. The sense, then, is that the Word of God has been so proclaimed among them that, instructed in the true and solid knowledge of heavenly things and fully confirmed in their hearts, they have no need of any further traditions or gifts, but can with a certain and infallible hope await that appointed time when Christ must be revealed to the whole world in the glory of his Father. But in saying this he takes aim at the false apostles, who had insinuated themselves among the Corinthians chiefly by this argument, saying that Paul's teaching was too meagre and barren, and that therefore many things were still lacking in their church. For it is the characteristic stratagem of impostors that, since they can neither deny the doctrine of truth nor dare openly to attack it, they take refuge in this evasion and say that many things are still wanting. If they once persuade men of this, they soon bring in those things by which the truth is obscured and the true worship of God is turned into superstition. Those who strive either to keep or to bring back the Papacy use this art. Against them you can do no better than to show that the apostles delivered everything fully, and that the Churches never lacked anything in former times, before those councils and fathers arose, by whose authority they claim their own position. Paul's words, however, must be understood of necessary gifts, lest, by urging the letter too stubbornly, we make angels out of men, or make Paul contradict himself, since he later rebukes the Corinthians for many faults and says that they are carnal, because he could not speak to them as to spiritual people. For as long as we live in this flesh, we shall not be able to attain that perfection by which no heavenly gift is lacking to us at all. But God distributes his gifts according to our capacity, and although he does not give everything to all, he gives to each one those things which can suffice for nourishing their faith until that day when, loosed from the bonds of this body, they are gathered to Christ. This passage, moreover, contains many things most worthy of observation.

units.la: Primo enim Paulus ea Corinthiorum dona praedicat, quibus pleriq; turpiter & pernitiose abutebantur. Nam in veritatis cognitione curiosi potius quam pii voluntatis divinae inuestigatores erant. Dicendi autem facultatem ostentabant, & verborum phaleris simplicem doctrinam reddebant intricatiorem. Idem de linguarum dono & infinitis aliis dici potest. At non quid illi facerent nunc spectat Apostolus, sed Dei bonitatem praedicat, ut huius consideratione excitati donis istis recte utantur. Neq; minorem laudem merentur quae per se bona & sancta sunt, quod multi illa turpi & impio abusu sibi exitialia reddant. Imo cauendum est, ne quod hominum vitio fit, nos in Dei contumeliam rapiamus. Seruit ergo Apostoli exemplum adversus inuidos, qui non contenti homines accusauisse, ipsa quoq; Dei dona audacter damnant: quod vitium hodie vulgo regnat. Hinc est, quod pauperes dum suas opes divitibus inuident, ita de illis pronuntiant, ut simul omnes exitio dignos iudicent, qui aliis opulentiores sunt. Ad eundem lapidem homines obscuri & inglorij offendunt, dum honores, qui virtuti debentur, conculcant, eo quod hos multos insolentius superbire vident. Atqui vtinam in temporarijs & terrenis bonis carpendis hac hominum malignorum licentia gradum suum sisteret, & non ulterius progressa, ea quoq; dente plus quam Theonino roderet, quae nulla cum ratione reprehendi possunt. Quam multos enim hodie audimus, qui in ipsum IESV CHRISTI Euangelium virulentas linguas acuunt, & sibi quiduis licere putant, eo quod multos sub huius praetextu licenter viuere vident? Atqui idem olim Corinthi fiebat, nihilominus tamen Paulus Deo gratias agit, quod illos omni sermone & cognitione ditare dignatus esset. Nam etsi merito accusetur eorum proteruia, qui Euangelio abutuntur, nihil tamen huic ex eo decedit, quo minus verbum reconciliationis sit, & Dei potentia ad salutem omni credenti. Quod si mihi obijcias. Et quid me aut alijs meliores sunt, qui illud audiunt, cum ipsorum vita doctrinae isti minus respondeat? in promptu est responsio: Eo ipso meliores sunt te, quod verbo Dei locum dant, quod per ipsos licet, ut alij illud cum fructu audiant, Deum pure colant & sancte viuant: cum tu non contentus propria impietate, insuper cum Deo bellum suscipias, verbum eius hostiliter persequeris, & ne hoc alij audiant obstes. Discant ergo singuli Deum pro donis suis praedicare, simulq; orent, ut ijsdem omnes digne vtantur, ne nomen eius sanctum propter nos male audiat.
units.tr: First, Paul commends those gifts of the Corinthians which many of them shamefully and destructively abused. For in knowing the truth they were more inquisitive than devout seekers of the will of God. They also showed off their power of speech and made simple doctrine more tangled with verbal ornaments. The same can be said of the gift of tongues and of countless other gifts. But the Apostle is not concerned here with what they were doing; he praises God's goodness, so that, stirred by the consideration of it, they might use those gifts rightly. Nor do things that are good and holy in themselves deserve less praise because many turn them to a foul and impious abuse. Indeed we must take care that we do not, because of human fault, cast reproach upon God. So Paul's example serves against those envious people who, not content to accuse men, also boldly condemn God's own gifts, a fault that is widespread today. Hence poor people, while they begrudge the rich their wealth, pronounce such judgments on them that they deem all who are more prosperous than others worthy of destruction. Obscure and inglorious people stumble over the same stone when they trample on the honours that are owed to virtue, because they see that many of those who have them grow more arrogantly proud. And yet, would that this licence of malicious men stopped its advance in carping at temporal and earthly goods, and did not go further, gnawing with a tooth more than Theonine even at those things that can be blamed on no reasonable ground! For how many do we hear today who sharpen their venomous tongues against the very Gospel of Jesus Christ, and think they may do whatever they please, because they see many living licentiously under the pretext of it? Yet the same thing happened at Corinth in the past, and nevertheless Paul gives thanks to God that he had deigned to enrich them with all speech and knowledge. For although the wantonness of those who abuse the Gospel is rightly censured, nothing of the Gospel's power is thereby diminished, so that the word of reconciliation is not, and God's power is not, unto salvation to everyone who believes. But if you object: "And why are those who hear it any better than I or others, when their life corresponds less to their teaching?" The answer is ready: they are better than you for this very reason, that they give room to the Word of God, that through them it is possible for others to hear it with profit, to worship God purely and live holily; whereas you, not content with your own impiety, moreover wage war against God, persecute his Word with hostility, and hinder others from hearing it. Let each one therefore learn to proclaim God for his gifts, and at the same time pray that all may use them worthily, so that his holy name is not ill spoken of on our account.

units.la: Deinde obseruabis non alias pretiosiores & magis necessarias Ecclesiae opes esse, quam verbum Dei & veram huius cognitionem, quae in nobis nascitur, si illud cum fide apprehendamus. Illud enim organum est, quo Deus suam nobis voluntatem revelat, regnum suum inter homines instaurat, nos in filios suos regenerat, & aeternae salutis thesauros nobis offert. Quo nomine illud Christus margaritae & thesauro confert, cuius ergo omnia nostra distrahere debeamus, ut illo potiri liceat. Haec autem fide animata tantorum bonorum capaces atq; participes facit. Ideo Christus Mariam, quae ad pedes ipsius sedens docentem audiebat, meliorem partem elegisse ait, Marthâ autem praehendit, quod circa multa alia occupata id negligeret, quod unum ad salutem consequendam necessarium est. Idem nos de illis dicere possumus, qui ceremonias ceremonijs accumulant, & harum observatione coelos mereri conantur, verbum autem Dei secure negligunt. Quid vero de illis dicemus, qui ut Ecclesiae decimis ditentur & annuos redditus in immensum augeant, solliciti sunt, cum interim scholarum disciplinam intercidere patiantur, & in eorundem templis Euangelij praedicatio sileat?
units.tr: Next you will observe that the Church has no treasures more precious and more necessary than the Word of God and the true knowledge of it, which is born in us if we grasp it with faith. For it is the instrument by which God reveals his will to us, restores his kingdom among men, regenerates us as his sons, and offers us the treasures of eternal salvation. For this reason Christ compares it to a pearl and a treasure, for the sake of which we ought to sell all that we have, so that we may be allowed to possess it. And this, when it is quickened by faith, makes us capable of and partakers in such great goods. So Christ says that Mary, who sat at his feet and listened to him teaching, chose the better part, but he rebuked Martha because she, busied with many other things, neglected the one thing that is necessary for obtaining salvation. We may say the same of those who heap ceremonies upon ceremonies and strive to earn heaven by observing them, while they carelessly neglect the Word of God. But what shall we say of those who are anxious to enrich the Church with tithes and to increase its annual revenues beyond measure, while meanwhile they allow the discipline of schools to perish, and the preaching of the Gospel to fall silent in their churches?

units.la: Præterea finem omnium, quæ in Ecclesia fiunt, hunc indicat Paulus, vt testimonium Christi in nobis confirmetur, cuius fructus & effectus est, quòd inter huius vitæ certamina constantes manemus, quoad gloria Christi in nobis reueletur. Dicitur autem testimonium Christi ipsum Euangelium, eò quod quis nam is sit testatur: quo nomine Apostolos ille suos testes vocat. Confirma-tur vero in nobis testimonium illud, quando Euangelio firmiter credimus, & locum in nobis inuenit πληροφορίᾳ illa, quæ nos de Dei gratia & salute certos facit, quamq; Apostoli passim nobis commendant. Est q; testimonij huius eò certior veritas, quòd ipsius Dei authoritate confirmatur, neq; aliud continet, quam quod is cœlitus pronuntiauit, dicens: Hic est filius ille meus dilectus, in quo placatus sum. Et huc facit, quod Baptista ait: Qui recipit eius testimonium, is obsignauit, quòd Deus verax sit, idest, is suo testimonio Dei promissionibus subscribit, adeoq; suo quasi sigillo confirmat quod ille de filio suo nobis pollicetur. E contra Ioannes in epistola sua Catholica dicit: Qui non credit Deo, mendacem facit eum: quia non credidit testimonio, quod testificatus est Deus de filio suo. At quæ iniuria Deo atrocior fieri potest, quàm si ipsum mendacij insimulemus, qui ipsa est veritas? Quis rursus cultus illi gratior erit, quàm si eius promissis firmiter credamus? Non igitur de re leuicula agitur, quando fidem in Christum à nobis Scriptura exigunt: hic enim simul & Dei gloria & salus nostra in periculum veniunt, si Euangelio credere detrectemus. Hic ergo nobis studiorum omnium scopus esto, vt testimonium illud Christi in nobis confirmetur, vtq; indies proficiamus in salutis fiducia, quæ ex Euangelij prædicatione hauritur. Et docent ista, quid de ijs iudices, qui de omnibus dubitant, & (vt alibi Paulus ait) quouis vento doctrinæ circumferuntur. At quales obsecro doctores sunt, qui dubitare docent, & aliquem de gratia Dei atq; propria salute certum fieri posse negant? Sunt hi non fidei, sed diffidentiæ, imò desperationis magistri, & proinde indigni, qui inter apostolicos numerentur.
units.tr: Moreover, Paul indicates that the end of all things done in the Church is this: that the testimony of Christ may be confirmed in us, and its fruit and effect is that we remain steadfast amid the struggles of this life until the glory of Christ is revealed in us. Now the testimony of Christ is the Gospel itself, because it testifies who he is; for this reason the Apostle calls his Apostles witnesses. That testimony is confirmed in us when we believe the Gospel firmly, and that full assurance [πληροφορία] finds a place in us which makes us certain of God's grace and of our salvation, and which the Apostles commend to us everywhere. And the truth of this testimony is all the more certain because it is confirmed by the authority of God himself, and it contains nothing other than what he pronounced from heaven, saying: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." And to this points what the Baptist says: "He who receives his testimony has set his seal to this, that God is true", that is, he subscribes by his testimony to the promises of God, and so, as it were, confirms with his own seal what God promises us about his Son. On the other hand John, in his Catholic epistle, says: "He who does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed the testimony that God has given of his Son." But what injury can be more atrocious to God than when we charge with lying him who is truth itself? Or again, what worship will be more pleasing to him than to believe his promises firmly? Therefore it is no trifling matter when Scripture demands from us faith in Christ; for here both the glory of God and our salvation are put in peril if we refuse to believe the Gospel. Let this, then, be the aim of all our studies: that the testimony of Christ may be confirmed in us, and that we may daily make progress in the confidence of salvation that is drawn from the preaching of the Gospel. These things also teach what you should think of those who doubt about everything and, as Paul says elsewhere, are carried about by every wind of doctrine. But what sort of teachers, I ask you, are those who teach doubt, and deny that anyone can be made certain of God's grace and of his own salvation? They are masters not of faith but of distrust, indeed of despair, and therefore unworthy to be numbered among the Apostolic teachers.

units.la: Postremò commendantur nobis hoc loco apostolicæ doctrinæ dignitas, quæ in eo maximè appa-ret, quòd nos intra animos nostros confirmare, & perfectos facere potest, ne quid nobis eorum defit, quæ salutem nobis certam afferunt, & in magnum illum dominici aduentus diem intrepidos & spe infallibili plenos reddunt. Scimus enim naturâ sic comparatum esse, vt ad mortis mentionem homines exhorrescant, iudicij verò extremi metus plane intolerabilis sit ijs, qui nihil præter huius sæculi bona nouerunt. Hinc furiæ illæ poetarum, quibus impios exagitari docent: hinc item scurrilia dicta, quibus ijdem iudicij diuini sensum eludere conantur, vt sibi ipsis contra propria conscientiæ testimonium delitias faciant. Neq; vnquam inuentus est aliquis sapientum huius sæculi, qui sua facundia aut arte terrores illos hominum mentibus eximere potuerit. Magna igitur & incredibilis fit oportet doctrina euangelica virtus, quæ sola nos confirmare potest, vt diem illum reuelationis Christi constanti animo expectemus, & ad eius mentionem læti capita attollamus, sicuti ille iubet. Quod vnum vt huius studium nobis magnificè commendat: ita eorum audaciam & impudentiam arguit, qui doctrinæ illi multa deesse aiunt, vt suis figmentis in Ecclesia locum inueniant.
units.tr: Lastly, in this place the dignity of apostolic doctrine is commended to us, which appears most of all in this, that it can confirm us in our souls and make us perfect, so that nothing of those things is lacking to us which bring us sure salvation, and render us fearless and full of unfailing hope for that great day of the Lord's coming. For we know that by nature men shudder at the mention of death, and the fear of the last judgment is utterly intolerable to those who know nothing but the goods of this age. Hence come those furies of the poets, with which they teach that the wicked are tormented; hence too those scurrilous sayings by which the same men try to evade the sense of divine judgment, so as to make themselves merry against the testimony of their own conscience. And no one among the wise of this age has ever been found who could, by his eloquence or his art, remove those terrors from men's minds. Therefore the power of evangelical doctrine must be great and incredible, since it alone can confirm us so that we await with a steady mind the day of the revelation of Christ, and at its mention lift up our heads joyfully, as he bids. This one thing not only commends its study to us magnificently, but also exposes the audacity and shamelessness of those who say that this doctrine lacks many things, so that they may find a place in the Church for their own inventions.

units.la: Quia tamen infirmioribus in fide nouissimi diei mentio aliquem metum parit, alteram huius proœmij partem subijcit Paulus, qua & se de illis in posterum quoq; bene sperare testatur, & illorum etiam spem argumento validissimo confirmat. Qui Deus (inquit) confirmabit vos vsq; ad finem inculpatos in diem Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI. Id verò probat: Fidelis enim est Deus, per quem vocati estis in communionem filij ipsius, Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI. Fidelem verò dicit Deum pro verace, quia illius fides est dictorum atq; promissorum constantia, vt è contra nostra fides erga illum assensus est animi firmus, quem ipsius verbo atq; promissis adhibemus. Argumentum Pauli eiusmodi est: Quicunq; à Deo semel vocantur in communionem Filij ipsius, ij non vnquam excidunt, sed eius spiritu confirmantur, vt in finem vsq; perseuerent: At vos vocati estis in Filij eius communionem: Ergo ab eodem confirmabimini. Ad Maioris confirma-tionem facit, quod Deus fidelis & promissorum constans, & dona eius atq; vocatio (vt ad Romanos dicitur) eiusmodi sint, vt ipsum eorum non possit pœnitere. In Minori autem de illorum vocatione, interna nimirum & efficaci, eò liberius pronuntiat, quod Deum sibi dicentem audiuisset: Est mihi in ciuitate ista populus multus. Et quia eosdem in Christo vere diligebat, non potuit non de illis bene sperare, in quibus externa electionis atq; vocationis vera signa apparebant. At quomodo Corinthijs porrò suspectus esse poterat Paulus, quem de ipsis optima quæq; sperare, & ipsorum dona tam ingenuè prædicare audiebant?
units.tr: Yet since the mention of the last day causes some fear in those who are weaker in faith, Paul adds a second part to this proem, in which he both testifies that he hopes well of them for the future and confirms their hope by a very strong argument. "God," he says, "will confirm you to the end, blameless, in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ." He proves this: "For God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ." He calls God faithful in the sense of true, because God's faithfulness is the constancy of his words and promises, just as, on the other hand, our faith toward him is the firm assent of the mind which we give to his word and promises. Paul's argument is this: whoever are once called by God into fellowship with his Son never fall away, but are confirmed by his Spirit so that they persevere to the end. But you have been called into the fellowship of his Son; therefore you will be confirmed by the same God. To strengthen the major premise, it serves that God is faithful and constant in his promises, and that his gifts and calling (as it is said in Romans) are such that he never repents of them. In the minor premise, concerning their calling, namely the inward and effective calling, he speaks all the more freely because he had heard God saying to him: "I have a great people in this city." And because he truly loved them in Christ, he could not but hope well of those in whom the outward true signs of election and calling appeared. But how could Paul be suspected by the Corinthians from now on, when they heard him hoping the best of them in every way and praising their gifts so openly?

units.la: Admonet autem nos locus iste, pios quoq; & in fide institutos iugi confirmatione opus habere, ne deficiant. Etsi enim Deus ipse in promissis constans & eiusdem dona ἀμεταμέλητα sint, ut modò diximus, manent tamen in ipsis carnis & peccati reliquiæ, quibus ita infestantur, ut sibi divino auxilio semper opus esse sentiant, sicuti proprio exemplo Paulus ad Romanos docet. Instat præterea Satan, qui novas subinde pugnas instaurat, & tentationes tam externas quam internas movet. Hic ergo assidua verbi doctrina nos in officio contineri necesse est, & preces simul adhibere oportet, ut & fidem in nobis Deus augeat, & ne nos in tentationes ducat, quarum pondere oppressi succumbamus. Imprimis autem proderit, si ipsi quoq; ex antea dictis cum Paulo argumentemur, & simul cogitemus nos vocatos esse in communionem filij Dei. Docet hoc ipse, quando ait: Qui credit in me, in me manet, & ego in illo. Et iam mortem adituru orat, ut in ipso unum simus. Potest ex hoc certa & invicta finalis perseverantiæ spes concipi. Nam fieri non potest, ut excidant qui Christo per fidem sunt insiti. Idem enim spiritum adoptionis iam conceperunt, qui salutis arrhabo est infallibilis, & fundamentum salutis in Christo habent, qui petra illa invicta est, adversus quam neque portæ quidem inferorum prævalent, & ex cuius manibus oves nemo potest rapere. Horum consideratione Paulus alibi confirmatus clamabat: Quis nos separabit à dilectione Dei, &c.? Et debent duo ista semper coniungi, ut primò quidem cogitemus nos confirmatione opus habere, & proinde in verbi studio frequentes inque precibus assidui simus: deinde vero bona spe pleni non dubitemus de Dei bonitate, qui eos nunquam deseret, quos Filij sui sanguine redimere dignatus est.
units.tr: This passage also warns us that even the godly and those instructed in the faith need constant confirmation, lest they fail. For although God himself is constant in his promises and his gifts are "without repentance," as we have just said, yet remnants of the flesh and of sin remain in them, by which they are so troubled that they always feel they need divine help, as Paul teaches by his own example in Romans. Moreover, Satan presses on, renewing his battles from time to time and stirring up temptations both external and internal. Here, therefore, we must be kept in our duty by the constant teaching of the Word, and at the same time we ought to apply prayers, so that God may increase faith in us and not lead us into temptations, under whose weight we might be overcome and give way. It will be especially helpful if we ourselves also reason with Paul from what has been said before, and at the same time consider that we have been called into the fellowship of the Son of God. He himself teaches this when he says: "He who believes in me abides in me, and I in him." And already about to face death, he prays that we may be one in him. From this a certain and unconquerable hope of final perseverance can be conceived. For it cannot happen that those who have been grafted into Christ through faith should fall away. For they have already received the Spirit of adoption, who is the infallible pledge of salvation, and they have the foundation of salvation in Christ, who is that unconquered rock against which the gates of hell do not prevail, and from whose hands no one can snatch the sheep. Paul, strengthened by the consideration of these things elsewhere, cried out: "Who shall separate us from the love of God?" etc. And these two things ought always to be joined together: first, that we consider that we need confirmation, and therefore be frequent in the study of the Word and constant in prayers; then, full of good hope, we should not doubt the goodness of God, who will never forsake those whom he has deigned to redeem with the blood of his Son.

units.la: Simul verò nostræ vocationis, adeoq; totius Christianismi finem Paulus hoc loco indicat, qui est, ut inculpati perseveremus usq; ad finem, & tales quoq; appareamus in magno illo die, quando Dei filius in gloria Patris veniet ad judicandum vivos & mortuos. Conuenit hoc cum eo, quod ad Ephes.1.cap.dicit: Elegit nos Deus in Christo priusquam mundi fundamenta jacerentur, ut essemus sancti & inculpati coram ipso per charitatem. At si nos spectes, nunquam tales invenies, qui ab omni culpa liberi reprehensionem nullam merearmur? Nam in multis labimur omnes, inquit Jacobus, & in electis quoq; peccati reliquias superesse supra ostendimus. Inculpatos autem nos facit Christus, qui si fide apprehendatur, peccata nostra tegit (ut Psalmi verbo utar) imò delet, ne apud Deum in rationem veniant, neq; nobis imputari possint. Idem verò nobis ex verbi sui semine renatis spiritum suum impertit, quo duce in viis Domini ambulamus, & quam ille nobis acquisivit sanctitatem tuemur, quatenus id humana infirmitas patitur. Hæc ut nobis justitiam & sanctitatem omnem in uno Christo monstrant ita officij quoq; nos admonent, ut vocantem nos Deum sequamur, & relictis mundi & carnis nostræ studijs illi nos sistamus viuentem hostiam. Nemo igitur eos audiat, qui Euangelij prædicatione & ipsius Dei gratia ad peccandi licentiam abutuntur, quin potius meminerimus, Filium Dei venisse in mundum, ut opera diaboli destruat, & fore aliquando diem, quo ad eius tribunal sistentur omnes, ut in corporibus suis recipiant digna vitæ & operum suorum præmia. Interim firmiter teneamus, salutis nostræ initium & complementum esse à Deo, qui ut nos in filio suo JESV CHRISTO elegit & eius merito nos redemit: ita in eodem nos confirmat & seruat in finem usq;, ut æterni & beati regni ipsius cives reddamur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: At the same time, in this place Paul indicates the goal of our calling, and so of the whole of Christianity, which is that we persevere blameless to the end, and appear such also on that great day when the Son of God will come in the glory of the Father to judge the living and the dead. This agrees with what he says in Ephesians 1: "God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him in love." But if you look at us, will you ever find such people, free from all fault, who deserve no reproof? For, as James says, "we all stumble in many things," and we have shown above that remnants of sin remain even in the elect. But Christ makes us blameless, for when he is apprehended by faith, he covers our sins (to use the word of the Psalm), indeed he blots them out, so that they do not come into account before God and cannot be imputed to us. The same Christ imparts his Spirit to us who are reborn from the seed of his Word, and under this guide we walk in the ways of the Lord and keep the holiness which he has won for us, as far as human weakness allows. Just as these things show us that all righteousness and holiness is in Christ alone, so they also remind us of our duty: that we follow God who calls us, and, leaving behind the pursuits of the world and of our flesh, present ourselves to him as a living sacrifice. Let no one, therefore, listen to those who abuse the preaching of the gospel and the very grace of God as a license to sin. Rather, let us remember that the Son of God came into the world to destroy the works of the devil, and that there will one day be a day on which all will be brought before his judgment seat, so that they may receive in their bodies the rewards due to their life and deeds. Meanwhile, let us firmly hold that the beginning and the completion of our salvation are from God, who chose us in his Son Jesus Christ and redeemed us by his merit, and so confirms and preserves us in the same to the end, that we may be made citizens of his eternal and blessed kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA III.
units.tr: HOMILY III.

units.la: Precor autem vos fratres, per nomen Domini nostri JESV CHRI-STI, ut idem loquamini omnes, & non sint inter vos dissidia, sed sitis coagmentati eadem mente & sententia. Declaratum est enim mihi de vobis fratres mei, à domesticis Chloes, quòd lites sint inter vos. Hoc autem dico, quòd unusquisq; vestrum dicit: Ego quidem sum Pauli, ego verò Apollo, ego verò Cephæ, ego verò Christi.
units.tr: I beg you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all speak the same thing, that there be no divisions among you, but that you be joined together in the same mind and the same judgment. For it has been reported to me concerning you, my brothers, by the household of Chloe, that there are quarrels among you. I mean this: that each of you says, "I am of Paul," "I am of Apollos," "I am of Cephas," "I am of Christ."

units.la: Quoniam Corinthij,insidiosis pseudoapostolorum sermonibus decepti,in Paulum animo ini-quiori erant,ut qui nimio rigore ecclesias grauaret,prudenter praefatione usus est, qua il-los sibi beneuolos redderet. Nam & dona,quibus ecclesiam eorum Deus ornauerat,magnifice laudat,& se de illis spem bonam jampridem concepisse scribit, quod in finem usq; perseveraturi sint. Suo autem exemplo doctores omnes admonet, ne temere de illis quoq; desperent, qui propter vitia non vulgaria reprehensionem acriorem merentur: sed potius ergā illos officium faciant, & (ut in po-steriori ad Timoth. monet) malos tolerent, cumq; lenitate erudiant eos qui contrarie sunt animo affecti, experiantur denique ecquando Deus illis det, ut conuersi agnoscant veritatem. Postquam vero Corinthios sibi aequiores reddidit,nunc ad primum epistola caput accedit, quo factiones, quae inter illos ortae erant, grauiter accusat, eosq; hortatur, ut procul abiectis omnibus causis dissidio-rum,unum sint in Christo atq; mutuam in ecclesia concordiam foveant. Ordine autem utitur commodissimo. Primo enim rem ipsam proponit,& summatim complectitur id,de quo dicturus erat. Deinde cur de isto eos admoneat docet,& mox malum,quo laborabant,diserte verbis accusat. Tandem rationes grauissimas adhibet, ut illi medeatur.
units.tr: Since the Corinthians, deceived by the insidious words of false apostles, were ill-disposed towards Paul, as one who seemed to burden the churches with excessive strictness, he wisely began with a preface by which he might win them to himself. For he praises magnificently the gifts with which God had adorned their church, and he writes that he had long ago conceived a good hope of them, that they would persevere to the end. By his own example he also warns all teachers not to despair rashly even of those who, on account of vices that are not ordinary, deserve a sharper rebuke; rather they should do their duty towards them and (as he advises in the later letter to Timothy) bear with the wicked, and instruct with gentleness those who are opposed in mind, and finally wait to see whether God may at some time grant them, that they may come to acknowledge the truth. Having made the Corinthians more favourable to himself, he now comes to the first chapter of the letter, in which he severely accuses the factions that had arisen among them, and exhorts them, having cast aside all the causes of division, to be one in Christ and to foster mutual harmony in the church. He uses a most fitting order. First he sets out the matter itself and sums up briefly what he is going to speak of. Then he teaches why he admonishes them about this, and at once he plainly accuses in words the evil by which they were troubled. Finally he applies the weightiest reasons to heal it.

units.la: Propositionem hic verbis comprehendit: Precor autem vos fratres, per nomen Domini nostri IESU CHRISTI, ut idem loquamini omnes, & non sint inter vos dissidia, sed sitis coagmentati eadem mente & sententia. Paucis multa dicit & grauiter, ut in breuitate ista faci-le spiritus apostolici maiestatem agnoscas cum mira lenitate coniunctam. Cum enim simpliciter monere, vel etiam jubere & mandare posset, ut concordiae studerent, obsecratione & obtestatione utitur, qua illis quasi supplex fit, qui potius culpam deprecari debebant. Ut & illa plus ponderis habeat, ipsius Christi nomen interponit, ut se non propriam, sed huius causam agere ostendat. Est hoc Apostolis admodum frequens: Nam ut in posteriori epistola scribet[?], sciebant se Christi nomine lega-tione fungi, & veluti Deo per ipsos precante, orare Christi nomine, ut Deo homines reconcilientur. Non vult ergo hic etiam aliquid priuata authoritate praecipere, imo ne quidem audiri se vult, nisi quatenus Christi minister fit. Et est hoc dignissimum obseruatu, quod in causa non minus perspi-cua quàm bona,& quàm improbare nemo nisi impudentissimus poterat, Christi authoritate Paulus utitur. Parum ergo apostolici sunt arrogantes illi fidei dominatores, qui cum aliena à fidei or-thodoxae principiis,& scripturis contraria proferunt, sibi tamen volunt simpliciter credi, moxq; extremae impietatis eos damnant, qui adversus ipsos vel mutire audent.
units.tr: Here he sums up the proposition in these words: "I beg you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all speak the same thing, that there be no divisions among you, but that you be joined together in the same mind and the same judgment." He says much in few words, and weightily, so that in this brevity you may recognise the majesty of the apostolic spirit joined with a wonderful gentleness. For although he could simply admonish, or even command and order them to pursue harmony, he uses entreaty and adjuration, by which he becomes almost a suppliant to those who ought rather to have begged pardon for their fault. And so that this may carry more weight, he invokes the very name of Christ, to show that he is pleading not his own cause but Christ's. This is very frequent with the Apostles. For, as he writes in the second letter, they knew that they discharged the office of ambassadors in the name of Christ, and, as if God were entreating through them, they prayed in Christ's name that men might be reconciled to God. Therefore he does not wish here to command anything on his own private authority; indeed he does not even wish to be heard, except insofar as he is a minister of Christ. And this is most worthy of notice: in a cause no less clear than it is good, and which no one but the most shameless could disapprove, Paul makes use of the authority of Christ. Those arrogant lords of the faith are therefore little apostolic, who put forward things alien to the principles of the orthodox faith and contrary to the Scriptures, yet want to be simply believed, and at once condemn as of the utmost impiety those who dare to murmur against them.

units.la: Quid verò illud est, quod tam graui obtestatione Paulus effectum cupit? Ut idem loquamini omnes, & non sint inter vos dissidia, sed sitis coagmentati eadem mente & sententia. His verbis primò concordiam suadet, deinde quae hanc turbare solent dissidia prohibet, postremò verae & germanae concordiae rationem tradit. Non temere autem ab hoc articulo orditur. Ut enim frustra de aliis vitiis corrigendis Corinthios admonuisset, nisi illi inter se prius uniti eius admonitiones putassent ad se pertinere: ita omnibus, qui Christiani dici aut haberi volunt, non alia re magis quàm concordia opus est. Nam totius Christianismi hunc finem esse Christus ipse testatur, ut omnes unum simus. Sic enim jam mortem adituri orat: Pater sancte, serva eos per nomen tuum, quos dedisti mihi, ut sint unum, sicut & nos. Et ne quis hoc de solis discipulis, quos tunc habebat, intelligendum putaret, paulò post subjicit. Non pro eis tantum rogo, sed & pro illis, qui credituri sunt per sermonem eorum in me: Ut omnes unum sint, sicut tu Pater in me,& ego in te, ut & ipsi in nobis unum sint. Quo etiam pertinet, quod Joannes scribit, Filium Dei mori debuisse non solum pro Judaeorum gente, sed ut filios Dei omnes, qui prius dispersi erant, cogeret in unum. Quae causa est, quod quacunq;, vel religionis Christianae exercitia, vel ad salutem consequendam adminicula sunt, Christianis omnibus eadem atq; communia sunt. Nam ut ad Ephesios Paulus scribit, unum est corpus omnium unus spiritus, una spes vocationis nostrae, unus Dominus, una fides, unum baptisma, unus denique Deus & Pater omnium, qui est super omnia, & per omnia, & in omnibus nobis. Ex quo sequitur à religione Christiana nihil tam esse alienum, quàm dissidia ferere & scisma-ta fovere in ecclesia. Imo qui hoc incessanter faciunt, pro Christi discipulis haberi non possunt, qui omnes unius gregis oves sunt sub uno pastore. Etenim cum Christus inimicos etiam diligere jubeat, qua ratione eius discipuli erunt, qui ab iis dissident, quos pro fratribus agnoscere debebant? Deinde vt corporis incolumitas in eo consistit, vt membra omnia probè inter se cohæreant, & vnumquodq; opem suam pro sui officij ratione ad corporis salutem tuendam conferat: ita ecclesiarum quoq; salus imprimis ab hoc credentium consensu dependet. Quia vbi dissidia regnant, ibi friget charitas, & dum quisq; suas res agit, publica ecclesiæ salutem interea negligit: neq; in fide multum ad-huc profecerunt, qui charitatem non colunt, per quam illa potissimum agit. Et si historias consideremus, facile patebit; ecclesias omnibus sæculis plus damni accepisse ex intestinis dissidijs quàm ex persecutionibus apertis, quibus crudelissimi hostes fidei illas euertere conati sunt. At veteribus exemplis minimè opus est, quando non sine acerbo piorum omnium dolore experimur, Euangelij cursum nostris dissensionibus maximè impediri, & has fere in causa esse, vt qui coniunctis animis publicam fidei communis causam tueri debebant, fratres in periculis turpiter negligant, imò interdum ex eorum interitu voluptatem capiant, à quibus ipsi in rebus non multum ad salutem facientibus dissentiunt. Ergo grauissimis de causis Paulus hanc epistolam ab hoc capite orditur, & idem apud alias quoq; ecclesias frequenter inculcauit. Huc enim pertinet, quod Philippensibus dicit: Tantum vt dignum est Euangelio Christi vos gerite, vt siue venero & videro vos, siue absens fuero, audiam de rebus vestris, quòd stetis in vno spiritu, vno pariter animo decertantes per fidem Euangelij. Et ad Romanos hoc eiusdem Apostoli piissimum votum habetur: Deus patientiæ & consolationis det vobis, vt eodem animo inter vos mutuò affecti sitis secundum CHRISTVM IESVM, vt concorditer vno ore glorificetis Deum ac Patrem Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI.
units.tr: But what is it that Paul desires to bring about with such a grave entreaty? "That you all speak the same thing, that there be no divisions among you, but that you be joined together in the same mind and the same judgment." By these words he first urges harmony, then forbids the divisions which are wont to disturb it, and lastly sets out the reason for true and genuine harmony. Nor does he begin from this article without cause. For just as he would have admonished the Corinthians in vain about correcting other vices, unless they first thought that his admonitions applied to them, being united among themselves, so all who wish to be or be held Christians have need of nothing more than of harmony. For Christ himself testifies that this is the end of the whole of Christianity, that all of us should be one. For so, already about to meet death, he prays: "Holy Father, keep them in your name, those whom you have given me, that they may be one, as we are." And lest anyone should think this to be understood only of the disciples whom he then had, he adds a little later: "I pray not for them only, but also for those who will believe through their word in me: that all may be one, as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us." To this also pertains what John writes, that the Son of God had to die not only for the nation of the Jews, but that he might gather into one all the children of God who had been scattered. This is the reason why whatever exercises of the Christian religion or aids to obtaining salvation there are, they are the same and common to all Christians. For, as Paul writes to the Ephesians, there is one body and one Spirit, one hope of our calling, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in us all. From this it follows that nothing is so alien to the Christian religion as to sow divisions and to foster schisms in the church. Indeed, those who do this incessantly cannot be held to be disciples of Christ, who are all sheep of one flock under one shepherd. And since Christ commands us to love even our enemies, by what reasoning will they be his disciples who dissent from those whom they ought to acknowledge as brothers? Moreover, just as the soundness of the body consists in this, that all the members cohere well together, and each contributes its aid, according to the nature of its office, to preserve the health of the body, so too the safety of the churches depends above all on this agreement of believers. For where divisions reign, there charity grows cold, and while each person pursues his own affairs, he meanwhile neglects the common safety of the church; nor have they made much progress in faith who do not cultivate charity, through which faith chiefly acts. And if we consider the histories, it will readily be clear that the churches in all ages have suffered more harm from internal dissensions than from open persecutions, by which the most cruel enemies of the faith have tried to overthrow them. But there is hardly any need for old examples, when we experience, not without bitter grief of all the godly, that the course of the Gospel is chiefly hindered by our dissensions, and that these are for the most part the cause why those who, with united minds, ought to defend the common cause of the faith, shamefully neglect their brothers in dangers, and indeed sometimes take pleasure in their ruin, from whom they dissent over matters that contribute little to salvation. Therefore, for the weightiest reasons, Paul begins this letter from this chapter, and he frequently inculcated the same among other churches as well. For to this pertains what he says to the Philippians: "Only conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the Gospel of Christ, so that whether I come and see you, or whether I am absent, I may hear of your affairs, that you stand in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the Gospel." And in Romans this same Apostle's most pious wish is recorded: "May the God of patience and consolation grant you to be of the same mind towards one another according to CHRIST JESUS, so that you may with one mouth glorify God and the Father of our Lord JESUS CHRIST.

units.la: Cæterum quod de Ecclesia dicitur ad rempub. quoq; transferri debet. Nam ipso Christo teste, omne regnum, quod in seipso diuisum fuerit, consistere non potest. Quia enim reipub. salus quoad homines maximè ex bonorum consensu dependet, qui patriam & leges patrias[?] saluas volunt, pereant oportet regna & ciuitates, in quibus dissident, qui rebus præsunt. Est hoc omnium sæculorum exemplis confirmatum. Atheniensium rempub. factiones perdiderunt, & eadem Græciam totam non solum bellis ciuilibus commiserunt, sed his attritam Persis propinarunt dilacerandam. Romanum verò imperium, cum iam toto orbe longè lateq; propagatum esset, paucorum ambitio euertit, qui factionum & bellorum ciuilium fuerunt authores: hi certè reipub. formam in Monarchiam mutarunt, quæ posteris temporibus cum vrbe imperium totum euertit. Et vt ad Græcos redeamus, quis nescit, intestinis illorum dissidijs totam illam nationem corruisse, vt iam sub dura Turcarum tyrannide seruiat, quæ aliquando totius ferè orbis imperium tenuit? Et vtinam non extarent nostrorum temporum exempla, quæ his fidem facere possunt. Quotquot ergo vel Ecclesiam vel Rempub. salvam volunt, ij sibi dictum putent, quod Corinthijs suis Paulus scribit, & procul relictis omnibus dissidijs, concordiam inter se mutuò colant atq; foueant.
units.tr: Moreover, what is said of the Church ought to be applied to the commonwealth as well. For, as Christ himself testifies, every kingdom divided against itself cannot stand. Since the safety of a commonwealth depends above all on the agreement of good men who wish to keep their country and its laws intact, kingdoms and states in which those who govern are at odds must perish. The examples of all ages confirm this. The factions of the Athenians destroyed their commonwealth, and the same discord not only delivered all of Greece to civil wars but, once it had been worn down by them, handed it over to the Persians to be torn apart. The Roman empire, though by then spread far and wide across the whole world, was overthrown by the ambition of a few men who were the authors of factions and civil wars. These men certainly changed the form of the commonwealth into a monarchy, which in later times, together with the city, overthrew the whole empire. And to return to the Greeks: who does not know that their whole nation collapsed through their internal quarrels, so that it now serves under the harsh tyranny of the Turks, although it once held rule over almost the whole world? And would that the examples of our own times did not exist, which could bear witness to these things. Therefore, all who wish either the Church or the commonwealth to be safe should take to themselves what Paul writes to his Corinthians: they should put aside all quarrels and cultivate and foster concord among themselves.

units.la: At videamus, qualem concordiam Paulus in ecclesia seruari velit. Ratione eius omnem tribus verbis comprehendit, & retrogrado ordine ab vltimo ad ipsam initium aut fontem concordiæ ascendit. Primò, vt omnes idem loquantur, requirit. Id verò de doctrina dicit, aut de fidei confessione cum publica tum priuata. Nam vt in cæteris eadem omnes dicant, neq; fieri potest, neq; etiam vtile esset, quando non omnium ea conditio aut rerum peritia est, vt de rebus grauioribus differre debeant. Ergo ad doctrinæ formam & fidei confessionem hoc restringi debet, vbi vt ijsdem locutionibus omnes vtantur imprimis necesse est, ne diuersitas rudibus & imperitis aliquam dissensionis suspicionem pariat. Fuerunt huius æqualitatis studiosissimi Apostoli, vt eorum scripta testantur, & ijdem (vt veteres tradiderunt) publicam & omnibus communem voluerunt extare confessionis formulam, quam Symbolum Apostolicum dicunt, vt illiterati quoq; homines cuiuscunq; sexus & ordinis fidem in vnum Deum per IESVM CHRISTVM ijsdem verbis profiterentur. Quem morem Sancti etiam Patres in primis Concilijs obseruarunt, & extant adhuc Symbola Nicena, Constantinopolitanæ, Ephesina & Chalcedonensis, Synodorū[?], in quibus videre est, quàm diligentes illi fuerint in seruanda eadem confessionis fidei formula inter homines Christianos. Vbi plurimum profuerit, si ipsius spiritus sancti verbis vtamur, quæ ille in scripturis prodidit. Nam vt hæc propria, plana & minimè ambigua sunt: ita à nemine eludi possunt facilè, reijci autem & contemni non possunt, nisi abijt, qui cum audacia impietatem quoque extremam coniunxerunt. Et satis constat, omnium sæculorum contentiones hinc suam originem duxisse, quòd aliqui Zelo non malo ducti phrases nouas excogitarunt, quibus ea interpretarentur, quæ ipsis in Scriptura sacra obscurius tradita esse videbantur,
units.tr: Let us now consider what kind of concord Paul wishes to be maintained in the Church. He comprehends the whole of it in three words, and, climbing in reverse order from the last to the very beginning or source of concord, he first requires that all speak the same thing. He says this of doctrine, or of the confession of faith, both public and private. For it is neither possible nor even useful that everyone say the same things about everything, since not all have the same station or expertise that would allow them to discuss weightier matters. Therefore this must be restricted to the form of doctrine and the confession of faith, where it is above all necessary that all use the same expressions, lest variation in wording give the uneducated and inexperienced some suspicion of dissension. The Apostles were most zealous for this uniformity, as their writings attest; and they (as the ancients have handed down) wanted a public confession formula common to all, which they call the Apostles' Creed, so that even unlettered people of any sex or rank might profess their faith in one God through Jesus Christ in the same words. The holy Fathers also observed this custom in the first councils, and the creeds of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus and Chalcedon still survive, in which one may see how diligent they were in preserving the same formula of confession among Christian men. This is especially useful when we use the very words of the Holy Spirit which he set down in the Scriptures. For just as these words are proper, plain and least ambiguous, so they cannot easily be mocked by anyone, nor can they be rejected and despised except by those who have joined extreme impiety to audacity. And it is well established that the contentions of all ages have drawn their origin from this: some, moved by a zeal that was not bad, devised new phrases by which to interpret those things which seemed to them to be delivered rather obscurely in holy Scripture.

units.la: Vt enim de Symbolis illis antiquis iterum dicamus, de eo, quod Apostolorum dicitur, non magna vnquam fuit contentio, neq; illius verbis haeretici abusi sunt, cùm ea omnia ex scripturis desumpta sint, & ambiguitatem in se nullam habeant. At cùm in Nicaeno Symbolo pij patres Arianorum importunitate impulsi Christum Dei filium patri ὁμοούσιον, verè quidem & rectè, vocabulo autem nouo & nusquam in scripturis vsitato, dixissent, quàm multas quamq; graues haec vna vocula concertationes peperit, & quàm multis Synodis nouis atq; Antisynodis occasionem dedit? Quod si nostri temporis de Coena dominica contentiones propius inspiciamus, non tam de re ipsa, quàm de vo-cabulis, Realiter, Substantialiter, Essentialiter, Oraliter, Corporaliter, Quantitatiue, Qualitatiue, In, Sub & cum pane, litigari videbimus. At quo nam istorum Christus vsus est, cùm Coenam in-stitueret? Aut num ita locuti sunt Apostoli, cùm ecclesias illi docerent? Quin ergo abiectis locutionibus non minus barbaris & ineptis quàm contentiosis, phrasibus Christi & Apostolorum vti-mur? Itaq; in actione de pane & vino cum Christo dicamus. Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vo-bis traditur: Hoc poculum est testamentum nouum in meo sanguine. Quod si quis de materia vel mutata vel transubstantiata interroget, rursus Symbola haec cum Paulo Panem & vinum, vel (vt Christus loquitur) fructum vitis dicamus. Vsum vero totius actionis traduxi[?], rursus Christi verba retineamus: Hoc facite in mei commemorationem. Vel vt Paulus hoc fusius exposuit: Quotiescunq; de hoc pane comederitis, aut poculum hoc biberitis, praedicate & celebrate mortem Domini, donec venerit. Haec si omnes loquerentur, iam & contentionis finis esset, & infelix populus re intellecta superstitione liberaretur, quam phrases illae nouae & ad excitandam nescio quam admirationem in hominum animis confictae pariunt.
units.tr: To speak again of those ancient creeds: concerning the so-called Apostles' Creed there was never any great dispute, nor have heretics abused its words, since all of them are taken from the Scriptures and have no ambiguity in them. But when the godly Fathers, driven by the importunity of the Arians, declared in the Nicene Creed that Christ the Son of God is consubstantial [ὁμοούσιον] with the Father, truly and rightly indeed, but with a new word that is nowhere used in the Scriptures, how many and how grave contentions this one little word produced, and how much occasion it gave to many new synods and counter-synods! And if we look more closely at the contentions of our own time concerning the Lord's Supper, we shall see that they are fought not so much over the thing itself as over words: really, substantially, essentially, orally, corporeally, quantitatively, qualitatively, in, under and with the bread. But which of these did Christ use when he instituted the Supper? Or did the Apostles speak in this way when they taught the churches? Why then, setting aside expressions no less barbarous and inept than they are contentious, do we not use the phrases of Christ and the Apostles? So in the action with the bread and wine let us say with Christ: This is my body, which is given for you; this cup is the new testament in my blood. But if anyone asks about the matter, whether it has been changed or transubstantiated, let us again, with Paul and these creeds, say bread and wine, or (as Christ speaks) the fruit of the vine. As for the use of the whole action, let us again keep the words of Christ: Do this in remembrance of me. Or, as Paul explained this more fully: as often as you eat this bread, or drink this cup, proclaim and celebrate the death of the Lord until he comes. If all men spoke in this way, the end of contention would already be at hand, and the unhappy people, once the matter was understood, would be freed from superstition, which those new phrases, invented to stir up I know not what wonder in men's minds, produce.

units.la: At frequenter fit, vt quoad verba idem aliqui loquantur, quorum tamen voluntates & animi minimè consentiunt, & vt in alijs rebus vitium hoc nimis vulgare est, ita imprimis circa religionem & doctrinam in hoc peccari solet ab ijs, qui sub fidei praetextu rebus suis student, & priuatum commodum quaerunt. Quapropter Paulus vlterius progreditur, & coagmentatos esse iubet eadem mente. Sub mentis vocabulo ipsam animi affectionem seu voluntatem intelligit, & vt ipsa voluntate inter se consentiant, monet. Et mox tertium addit, vt τῇ γνώμῃ αὐτῇ conueniant, qua locutione certam & definitâ in animo sententiam comprehendit. Itaq; gradatione ista concordia veram & minimè fucatam describit, cuius partes sunt, vt primò quidem eadem omnes loquamur, deinde verò vt eadem omnium fit voluntas, ad quam postremò animi sententia aut definitio certa accedat oportet: quia sine illa neq; voluntas nostra sibi diu constabit, & huius mutationem verbis quoq; & factis mutatis testabimur. Eos ergo omnes hac parte reprehendit Apostolus, qui cùm eadem loquantur cum alijs, non tamen eadem cum illis volunt & sentiunt: ideoq; consultò eiusmodi locutiones fingunt, quae in sensus varios & diuersos trahi possunt, & proinde à nonnullis proprie & verè cotburni dicuntur. Ludunt illi verbis, & dum idem loquuntur, occultè tamen aliud sentiunt, imò dum cum omnibus volunt conuenire, ab omnibus dissentiunt, & ne cum propria quidem mente ipsis conuenit. Est hoc hominum genus ecclesijs perieulosissimum, quia dissidiorum quidem compositionem pollicentur, sed hoc praetextu nouam indies materiam illis praebent. Nam vtrinq; magis exasperantur animi, quando se locutionibus eiusmodi illusos esse, & ab aduersa parte aliam sententiam occultè foueri cernunt. Exemplum huius rei memorabile in Synodo Syrmiensi accidit, quando fuere, qui controuersiae, quae inter orthodoxos & Arianos agitabatur, humano consilio mederi volentes, vocem ὁμοούσιον silentio obruendam, & eius loco ὅμοιον reponendam esse censuerunt. Putabant illi controuersiae illi hac ratione finem imponi posse, quia vtraq; pars IESVM CHRISTVM Dei filium esse fateretur, & quidem similem Patri. At mox senserunt orthodoxi ambiguitatem nouae istius vocis insidiosam sibi esse, cùm ipsi quidem eam de essentia similitudine intelligerent, Ariani verò solius voluntatis similitudinem assererent[?]. Mox igitur noua & prioribus grauiora certamina exorta sunt, & (vt Theodoretus scribit) περὶ τοιούτας ἀσχολουμένοι λέξεις, τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν διεστράξαν[?], id est, circa eiusmodi occupati locutiones ecclesiam distraxerunt. Quod autem illis temporibus factum fuit, hodie etiam fieri constat, quando aliqui vt concertationes de Coena Dominica semel abrumpant, locutiones fingunt nouas, quas vtraq; pars suo sensui applicare possit. At insidiosae sunt compositiones istae, & dissidia non tollunt, sed potius causa sunt, vt ad breue temporis momentum sopitum incendium,postea maiori impetu erumpat. Rectè ergo Paulus eam concordiæ rationem præscribit, quæ consensum habeat syncerum & omnis dolisiue fraudis expertem. Si enim merito reprehenduntur, qui in fœderibus & pactis ludunt (vt olim Pæni solebant) quanto scelestius fuerit hoc facere in religionis causa, ex quasi veritatem sustuleris, religio simul omnis extinguetur? Ideo καταρτισμένους[?], id est, coagmentatos nos esse iubet Apostolus, & Metaphora vtitur, quam ab humani corporis fabrica desumpsit, monens vt non aliter quàm corporis eiusdem membra inter nos cohæreamus. Atqui in membrorum constructione opus aut artificium naturæ videmus, quod admirari potius quàm verbis dignis explicare possis. Nam eiusmodi illa est, vt si vnicum membrum vel sustuleris & loco mouueris, vel etiam aliud adieceris, corpus totum deformetur. Deinde est coagmentatio illa firma & solida, vt non facile dissolui queat. Luxatio autem eius dolorem toti corpori acutissimum parit, & simul vsum membrorum tollit. Quæ omnia ecclesiæ proprijssimè conueniunt, ex quasi consensionem animorum in vera fide sustuleris, mox συμπάθεια[?] quoq, quæ ex charitate nascitur, cessabit, & nihil præter inane & inutile nomen ecclesiæ reliquum erit. Scisma vero illud siue dissidium pijs omnibus qui ecclesiæ vnitatem constanter seruant, dolorem affert intolerabilem, quem ex infelici fratrum distractione concipiunt, quando & horum salutem & Dei gloriam in periculum venire vident.
units.tr: But it often happens that some men say the same words, while their wills and minds do not agree at all; and as this fault is all too common in other matters, so it is especially wont to be committed in religion and doctrine by those who, under the pretext of faith, look after their own affairs and seek private advantage. Therefore Paul goes further and bids them be joined together in the same mind. By "mind" he understands the very affection or will of the soul, and he advises that they agree with one another in will itself. And soon he adds a third, that they be united in the same judgment [τῇ γνώμῃ αὐτῇ], an expression by which he comprehends a settled and defined opinion in the mind. Thus by this gradation he describes a true concord, not counterfeit: its parts are, first, that we all speak the same things; then, that the will of all be the same; to which, last, a firm opinion or definition of the mind must be added. For without it our will will not long remain consistent with itself, and we shall show its change by changed words as well as deeds. Therefore the Apostle rebukes all those in this respect who, while they say the same things as others, do not will and think the same things as them; and so they deliberately devise expressions that can be drawn into various and divergent senses, which, as some rightly say, are like a buskin that fits either foot. They play with words, and while they speak the same thing, they secretly feel otherwise; indeed, while they want to agree with everyone, they dissent from everyone, and they do not even agree with their own mind. This kind of men is most dangerous to churches, because they promise the settling of disagreements, yet under this pretext they supply new matter for them every day. For the minds of both sides become more exasperated when they see that they have been deceived by expressions of this kind and that the other side secretly cherishes a different opinion. A memorable example of this happened at the Synod of Sirmium, when there were some who, wishing to remedy by human counsel the controversy then being waged between the orthodox and the Arians, judged that the word homoousion should be buried in silence and that homoion should be put in its place. They thought that an end could be put to that controversy by this means, since each side would confess that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, and indeed like the Father. But soon the orthodox perceived that the ambiguity of this new word was a snare for them, since they themselves understood it of likeness of essence, while the Arians asserted only likeness of will. Straightway, therefore, new contentions arose, graver than the former ones, and (as Theodoret writes) "occupied with such expressions they tore the churches apart" [περὶ τοιούτας ἀσχολουμένοι λέξεις, τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν διεστράξαν], that is, busied with such expressions they distracted the church. What was done in those times is known to happen today as well, when some, in order to cut off contentions about the Lord's Supper at a stroke, devise new expressions which either side can apply to its own sense. But such compositions are treacherous, and they do not remove dissensions; rather, they are the cause of the fire, which, having been quieted for a brief moment, afterwards breaks out with greater force. Rightly, then, does Paul prescribe that kind of concord which has a sincere agreement, free of all deceit and fraud. For if those are rightly blamed who play tricks in covenants and pacts (as the Carthaginians once used to), how much more wicked would it be to do this in the cause of religion? If you were to remove the truth, as it were, all religion would be extinguished at once. Therefore the Apostle bids us to be "joined together" [καταρτισμένους], that is, fitted together, and he uses a metaphor which he has taken from the structure of the human body, admonishing us to cohere among ourselves in no other way than the members of one body do. Indeed, in the structure of the members we see a work or craft of nature, which you may rather wonder at than explain in worthy words. For it is such that if you take away or move out of place even a single member, or add another, the whole body is deformed. Then, this joining is so firm and solid that it cannot easily be dissolved; and its dislocation brings the most acute pain to the whole body and at the same time takes away the use of the members. All these things fit the Church most aptly. If you remove the agreement of minds in true faith, then sympathy [συμπάθεια], which is born of charity, will also cease, and nothing will remain of the Church but an empty and useless name. But that schism or dissension brings intolerable grief to all the godly who constantly keep the unity of the Church, which they conceive from the unhappy division of brothers, when they see both their salvation and the glory of God brought into danger.

units.la: Cæterum ne Paulus tam seria tamq; graui obtestatione temere vsus esse putetur, docet se non sine causa de illis solicitum esse, & ita seipsum suspicione liberat, quam de illo concipere poterant. Declaratum est enim mihi (inquit) de vobis fratres mei, à domesticis Chloes, quod lites sint inter vos. Subinde fratres suos dicit, ne se ab illo vel contemni vel odio haberi arbitrentur. Testes autem producit idoneos & procul dubio fide dignos, ne quis ipsum rumoribus temere sparsis credi-disse, aut suspicionibus incertis indulgere dicat. Suo autem exemplo docet, ne quem temere accusemus, neq; suspicionibus facile locū demus, quando de proximi fama aut salute agitur. Est enim v-trumq; alienissimū à charitatis ingenio, quæ vt omnibus bene vult, ita bene etiā sperat de omnibus. At qui suspicionibus prauis indulgent, ij & concordiam turbant, & propriam authoritatē labefactant, quando ipsa rei veritate conuincuntur: quo fit, vt pudore suffundantur, dum aliorum famæ insidias struunt. Cùm autem prius scismatum aut dissidiorum meminisset, nunc lites inter illos esse ait, quæ voce scismatis effectum exprimit. Quam primùm enim voluntatibus & sententijs dissidemus, ex eo lites apertæ & contentiones oriri consueuerunt, idq; imprimis circa religionem. Nam vt ad animorum coniunctionem nullum vinculum efficacius & fortius est, quàm consensio in religione: ita si in hac dissentiant homines, mox animi litibus nunquam finiendis accensi inimicitas graues & pertinaces concipiunt. Quo magis oportet principijs obstare, & leuissimam quoq; dissensionis speciē illico extinguere, ne ex paruis scintillis temere neglectis incendium horribile nascatur.
units.tr: Moreover, lest anyone think Paul used such a serious and weighty appeal rashly, he shows that he had good reason to be anxious about them, and so frees himself from the suspicion they might have formed about him. "For it has been declared to me, my brothers," he says, "concerning you, by those of Chloe's household, that there are quarrels among you." He calls them his brothers, so that they will not think he despises them or bears them ill will.
