Adhæc Euangelium omnem salutem nobis in Christi cruce monstrat, quæ vt doctrinæ illius argumentum est, ita nihil illa humano iudicio contemptibilius & abiectius habetur, ideoq; huius prædicationem huic humilitati conuenientem aut conformem esse oportet. Nam si eloquentia (vt D. Augustinus rectissimè definiuit) est facultas exprimendi congruenter quod sentimus, inepti & loquaces potius ostentatores quàm eloquentes sunt, qui res humiles magnificis verborum ampullis extollere & dilatare conantur. Vidit hoc olim sapientissimus ille Lacedæmoniorum Rex Agesilaus, qui cum oratorem quendam hoc nomine commendari audiret, quòd res exiguas verbis mirifice amplificaret, respondit: Ego verò ne sutorem quidem probauerim, qui paruo pedi magnum calceum inducat. At quid aliud faciunt, qui cum Christi humilis & contempti atq; crucis eius praecones dici velint, mi-rifico humanae philosophiae apparatu & verborum splendore sese venditant? Quod non ita accipi velim, quòd aliquem esse existimem, qui crucis illius victricis & triumphantis maiestatem dicendo aequare, nedum superare possit: sed quia hominibus verba fiunt, horum captui sese concionatores accommodent, ut sub humili & simplici genere dicendi, Dei virtus melius cognoscatur. Quòd si rem probè examines, rudes & artis dicendi imperitos mitti oportuit Apostolos, ut ita omnium iudicio constaret opus hoc Dei esse, & ut Euangelij doctrina ab omni fraudis & deceptionis suspicione liberaretur. Nam si Apostoli humana authoritate, regum potentia, artium cognitione, dicendi peritia prae aliis excelluissent, diceret aliquis, non difficile fuisse homines tot tantisq; donis instructos in suam sententiam pertrahere alios, qui praeter ingenij simplicitatem nihil contra ipsos in medium afferre poterant. At cum misi sint piscatores illiterati, qui ex inuisa Iudaeorum gente oriundi praesidio simul omni destituebantur, ijdem vero & Iudaeorum scribis & gentium philosophis, imo magistratibus vrbium & ipsis Romanorum Imperatoribus superiores facti sint, quis non videat illud omne virtutis diuinae opus fuisse, & in crucis praedicatione singularem se exeruisse Christi potentiam, de qua ipse iam pridem dixerat: Ego vbi exaltatus fuero à terra, omnia trahàm ad meipsum? Cum ergo crucis trophaeum tale sit, ut propria virtute sese commendet, & ipsa iam pridem de mundo & eius principe triumphauerit, stultum fuerit ad eius commendationem humani eloquij vires & philosophiae arma in medium afferre. Hoc enim perinde fuerit, ac si quis facula accensa Solis splendorem illustriorem reddere, aut Oceanum vna atq; altera aquae situla infusa augere conetur.
units.tr: In saying this, Paul not only excuses himself but at the same time shows that the preaching of the gospel has need neither of learning nor of human eloquence. For it is the word of eternal Truth, which the ancients depicted as naked, because it has nothing of which it could be ashamed, and because it commends itself sufficiently by its own native splendour. Indeed, such adornments are at odds with the power of Christ's cross, which then most evidently reveals itself when it is set forth naked and clothed with no borrowed paint. Moreover, the gospel shows us all salvation in the cross of Christ; and just as this is the argument of that doctrine, so nothing is held in greater contempt and abjection by human judgment. Therefore the preaching of it ought to be suited and conformed to this humility. For if eloquence (as St Augustine most rightly defined it) is the faculty of expressing congruently what we feel, then those who try to exalt and inflate humble things with the magnificent bombast of words are foolish and garrulous show-offs rather than eloquent men. The most wise Agesilaus, king of the Lacedaemonians, saw this long ago: when he heard a certain orator commended for this, that he wonderfully amplified trifling matters with words, he replied: "I for my part would not even approve of a cobbler who fits a great shoe to a small foot." But what else do those do who, when they wish to be called heralds of the lowly and despised Christ and of his cross, peddle themselves with the marvellous display of human philosophy and the splendour of words? I do not mean this in the sense that I think there is anyone who could match, let alone surpass, the majesty of that victorious and triumphant cross by his speech; but because speeches are made to men, preachers should adapt themselves to their capacity, so that the power of God may be better known in a humble and simple style of speaking. But if you examine the matter carefully, it was fitting that the apostles be sent as unlearned and untrained in the art of speaking, so that by everyone's judgment it would be evident that this work was God's, and so that the doctrine of the gospel might be freed from every suspicion of fraud and deception. For if the apostles had excelled others in human authority, the power of kings, knowledge of the arts, and skill in speaking, someone might say that it would not have been difficult for men so well endowed with so many great gifts to draw others to their opinion, others who, apart from simplicity of mind, could bring nothing against them. But since illiterate fishermen were sent, who, being of the hated Jewish nation, were at the same time deprived of all protection, and yet these same men were made superior to the scribes of the Jews, to the philosophers of the nations, and indeed to the magistrates of cities and to the very emperors of the Romans, who does not see that all this was a work of divine power, and that in the preaching of the cross the power of Christ showed itself singularly, of which he himself had long before said: "When I shall be lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself"? Since therefore the trophy of the cross is such that it commends itself by its own power, and has already long since triumphed over the world and its prince, it would be foolish to bring forward the powers of human eloquence and the weapons of philosophy to commend it. For this would be just as if someone, having lit a torch, tried to make the splendour of the sun brighter, or to enlarge the ocean by pouring in a bucket or two of water.

units.la: Nemo tamen existimet velim, nos bonarum artium & literarum studia damnare, aut omnes illos ab ecclesiae ministerio eiectos velle, quos eruditio & eloquentia vis commendant. Scimus enim in Verbi administris hoc quàm maximè requiri, ut docendi facultate instructi sint, quam artium studio plurimum adiuuari nemo nisi insanus negauerit. Scimus item, quòd qui initio Apostolos rudes & artium imperitos emisit ad euangelizandum, postea plures ex rhetorum & philosophorum scholis vocauit, qui egregiam in propagando Christi regno & fide defendenda operam nauarunt: quales Cyprianus, Iustinus martyr, Lactantius & plures alij fuerunt, ut iam de Augustino, Hieronymo & similibus nihil dicam. Hoc autem dicimus, quòd Deus nostra eruditione, doctrina & eloquentia minime opus habeat. Si cui vero ista ille dederit, ita ijs vtatur, vt priores semper partes Euangelio dentur, vtq; artes omnes illi seruiant: ita tamen, vt qui huic ex illis accedit ornatus, non meretricius sit, qui externos solum hominis sensus demulceat, sed sanctus & diuinus, & qui ipsius Verbi virtute animatus in cordium recessus penetret. Quod nisi obseruetur, artium ostentatio & dicendi peritia crucem Christi euacuant.
units.tr: Yet let no one think that we condemn the pursuit of the liberal arts and letters, or wish to cast out of the ministry of the Church all those whom learning and the power of eloquence commend. For we know that in the ministers of the Word this is required above all, that they be furnished with the ability to teach, which no one but a madman would deny is greatly aided by the study of the arts. We know likewise that he who at first sent out the apostles, unlearned and untrained in the arts, to preach the gospel, afterwards called many from the schools of rhetoricians and philosophers, who labored remarkably in spreading the kingdom of Christ and defending the faith: such were Cyprian, Justin Martyr, Lactantius, and many others, not to mention Augustine, Jerome and their like. But what we are saying is this: God has no need of our learning, teaching and eloquence. If, however, he has bestowed these on someone, let him use them in such a way that the first place is always given to the gospel and all the arts serve it; yet in such a way that the ornament which is added to it from these sources is not meretricious, merely tickling the outward senses of a man, but holy and divine, and one which, animated by the power of the Word itself, penetrates into the recesses of hearts. Unless this is observed, the display of arts and skill in speaking empty the cross of Christ.

units.la: At quod de istis dicitur, non minus de omnibus aliis intelligi debet, quae hominibus magnifica videntur. Idem enim fiet, si vel opum vel honorum huius seculi studium cum religione & Euangelij doctrina coniungere instituas. Nam si conatus iste succedat, fere (vt veteri proverbio dicitur) religio parit diuitias, sed filia matrem deuorat. Maximè tamen aduersus eos nobis locus iste feruit, qui Euangelij doctrinam & religionis Christianae mysteria hominum traditionibus exornare, aut externo splendore ceremoniarum, vel etiam supellectilis ecclesiasticae nitore commendabiliora reddere studeunt. Est quidem mos ille iam multorum seculorum consuetudine confirmatus, & nimium rustici multis nos videmur, apud quos in Sacramentorum vsu neq; vestes pretiosae, neque auri & argenti vel gemmarum splendor inueniuntur. At nos apud Danielem hoc Antichristo tribui scimus, quòd Deum suum Mayzim[?] auro & argento colat. De Christi autem ecclesia nihil huius legimus. Ideo nos rusticitatis istius pudere non debet, quae & Christi & veteris ecclesiae exemplo probatur. Olim certè Hieronymus Exuperium Tholosanae ecclesiae episcopum laudauit, quòd mysticam Domini Coenam canistris vimineis & poculis vitreis administraret. Et commendantur illius seculi mores, quo episcopi aurei, vasa autem templorum lignea erant. Hodie nimis infelici metamorphosi haec quidem aurea, episcopi vero vix lignei aut plumbei visuntur. Clamant illi, reuerentiam hanc Christi Sacramentis deberi. Fateor, haec reuerenter omnino tractanda esse, & quouis supplicio dignos esse, qui illa contempserint. At nos cum D. Ambrosio dicimus: Aurum Saæramenta[?] non quærunt, neq; auro placent quæ auro non emuntur. Et quæ illis debetur reuerentia, non in externo apparatu, sed in vero atq; legitimo eorum usu consistit, qui ex fide non fucata dependent. Quòd si Paulo nefas visum fuit, Euangelij virtutem non artificioso docendi genere exinanire, quando minus ferendum est, ut auro, argento, gemmis & vestibus Tragicis Sacramentorum virtus quasi obruatur, & rude vulgus ab illorum contemplatione per externi apparatus splendorem auocetur? Sed sordet[?] fortassis Pauli exemplum illorum oculis, quos aulicus splendor tam pridem perstrinxit. Satyricum ergo clamantem audiant:
units.tr: What is said of these must be understood no less of all the other things that seem magnificent to men. The same will happen if you try to join the pursuit of wealth or of the honours of this age with religion and the doctrine of the Gospel. For if that attempt succeeds, religion (as the old proverb says) generally gives birth to riches, but the daughter devours the mother. This passage, however, bears most hard against those who seek to adorn the doctrine of the Gospel and the mysteries of the Christian religion with human traditions, or to make them more commendable by the outward splendour of ceremonies or even by the polish of church furnishings. That custom is indeed confirmed by the practice of many centuries, and we seem very rustic to many, among whom neither costly garments nor the glitter of gold, silver or jewels is found in the use of the sacraments. But we know that in Daniel this is ascribed to Antichrist, that he honours his god Mayzim with gold and silver. Of Christ's Church, however, we read nothing of this sort. So we ought not be ashamed of that rusticity, which is approved by the example of Christ and of the ancient Church. Jerome certainly once praised Exuperius, bishop of the Church of Toulouse, because he administered the mystical Lord's Supper in wicker baskets and glass cups. And the customs of that age are commended, when bishops were golden but the vessels of the temples were wooden. Today, by an all too unhappy metamorphosis, the vessels are indeed golden, but the bishops are scarcely wooden or leaden. They cry out that this reverence is owed to Christ's sacraments. I grant that these things must be handled wholly reverently, and that those who despise them deserve any punishment. But we say with Ambrose: the sacraments do not seek gold, nor are they pleased by gold, things that are not bought with gold. And the reverence owed to them consists not in external display but in the true and lawful use of them by those who depend on unfeigned faith. But if it seemed wrong to Paul to empty the power of the Gospel by an artful manner of teaching, how much less bearable is it that the power of the sacraments should be, as it were, overwhelmed by gold, silver, jewels and tragic garments, and that the untutored crowd should be drawn away from contemplating them by the splendour of outward display? But perhaps Paul's example is contemptible in the eyes of those whom courtly splendour has so long dazzled. Let them therefore hear the satirist crying out:

units.la: Dicite Pontifices, in sacris quid facit aurum?
units.tr: Tell me, priests, what does gold do in sacred things?

units.la: Nempe hoc quod Veneri donata à virgine puppæ, &c.
units.tr: Namely, this: what the doll dedicated to Venus by a girl does, and so on.

units.la: Continet præterea locus iste dulcissimam consolationem, quam sibi applicare debent, qui se ad ecclesiæ ministerium vocari sentiunt, non autem villis artibus aut facultatibus ad tantum munus necessarijs sese instructos esse vident. Clamant hi sæpe cum Mose & Ieremia: Mi Domine non sum eloquens ab heri & nudiustertius. Item, Ah puer ego sum. Sed ijdem sibi quoq; à Deo dici cogitent: Quis dedit homini os? aut quis facit mutum & surdum? videntem aut cæcum? annon ego? Dominus? Vade ergo, & ego adero ori tuo, doceboq; te quæ loquaris. Item, Ego posui verba mea in os tuum, &c. Quibus addant, quod Paulus docet, non opus esse Deo, ut Euangelium Filij sui humana arte comendetur. Neq; cum Apostolis natiuam illam virtutem doctrinæ crucis vel extinctā esse, vel cessasse putent. Extant enim multorum exempla, qui posteris temporibus doctissimos philosophos & acutissimos sophistas ipsi artis rudes & indocti superarunt, ut Christi iugo colla sua submitterent. Et memorabile est, quod de philosopho quodam Eusebius scribit, qui cum episcopos arte & dicendi peritia instructos diu fatigauisset, tandem à sene simplicissimo, qui nihil præter IESUM CHRISTUM, & hunc quidem crucifixum, nouerat, ita victus est, ut publicè diceret: Dum verbis mecum actum est, verba verbis opposui, & quæ dicebantur dicendi arte confutaui: postquam verò pro verbis virtus processit ex ore docentis, non potuerunt verba resistere virtuti, nec homo aduersari potuit Deo, &c. Possent huius generis nonnulla recenseri, quæ nostro seculo facta sunt. Non est ergo, ut sibi metuant, si qui legitimè ad docendi munus vocantur. Pertinet autem consolatio ista etiam ad eos, quibus fidei suæ ratio reddenda est apud principes potentissimos & Inquisitores, qui crudeli sophistica laqueos & retia texere norunt, quibus doctissimos quosq; capiant. Sed nullis mendaciorum strophis capitur Veritas, & nequicquam Dei sapientiam vænatur carnis astutia. Et tunc in mentem nobis veniat Christi promissio: Dabo vobis os & sapientiam, cui non poterunt contradicere neq; resistere omnes, qui aduersabuntur vobis. Et dabitur vobis in illa hora quid loquamini. Non enim estis illi loquentes, sed spiritus patris vestri, qui in vobis loquitur. Vide Luc.21. Matth.10.cap.
units.tr: This passage also contains a most sweet consolation, which those should apply to themselves who feel that they are called to the ministry of the Church, but see that they are not equipped with fine arts or with the faculties necessary for so great a task. Such men often cry out with Moses and Jeremiah: "O Lord, I am not eloquent, neither yesterday nor the day before," and "Ah, I am a child." But let them also consider that God says to them: "Who gave man his mouth? Or who makes the mute and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? Is it not I, the Lord? Go therefore, and I will be with your mouth, and will teach you what you shall say." Likewise: "I have put my words in your mouth," etc. To these let them add what Paul teaches, that God has no need for the Gospel of his Son to be commended by human art. Nor let them think that the native power of the doctrine of the cross was extinguished or ceased along with the Apostles. For there are many examples of those who in later times, though untrained and unlearned in art themselves, have overcome the most learned philosophers and the sharpest sophists, so that these submitted their necks to Christ's yoke. And what Eusebius writes of a certain philosopher is memorable: when he had long wearied bishops trained in art and skill in speaking, he was at last so conquered by a most simple old man, who knew nothing but Jesus Christ, and him crucified, that he publicly said: "While we were dealing in words, I set words against words and refuted what was said by the art of speaking; but after power came forth from the mouth of the teacher instead of words, words could not resist power, nor could man oppose God," etc. Several things of this kind could be recounted which have happened in our own age. There is therefore no reason for them to fear, if they are lawfully called to the office of teaching. This consolation also pertains to those who must render an account of their faith before most powerful princes and Inquisitors, who know how to weave snares and nets with cruel sophistry, by which they catch the most learned. But Truth is caught by no twists of lies, and in vain does the cunning of the flesh hunt for God's wisdom. Let the promise of Christ then come to our mind: "I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all who oppose you will be unable to contradict or resist. And in that hour it will be given you what to say. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you." See Luke 21; Matthew 10.

units.la: Cæterum ut ad Paulum redeamus, obijceret aliquis: Atqui ita vilescit Euangelium, & apud plerosq; in contemptum venit, si nullo prorsus splendore commendetur. Præuenit ergo istam obiectionem, & ait: Nam sermo ille Crucis, id est, doctrina de Christo pro nobis crucifixo, ijs quidem qui pereunt, stultitia est: nobis autem qui seruamur, potentia Dei est. Habent ista non obscuram Concessionis speciem, & ita dicere videtur: Scio equidem quid pleriq; de Euangelio iudicent. Etenim qui carnis rationem audiunt, ijs nihil stultius, nihil absurdius putatur, quam quòd docemus, Dei Filium hominem factum esse, in terris egestatem, nuditatem, famem & alia vitæ huius incommoda sustinuisse, mortem in cruce infamem passum esse, tertio autem die à mortuis in vitam rediisse, atq; illius merito nos seruari. Videntur (inquam) hæc carni absurdissima, & ideo quæstiones mouet varias. Quomodo nimirum qui pauperrimus fuit, alios diuitijs beare: qui nudus in cruce pependit, nos vestire: qui quò caput reclinaret non habuit, nobis in cælis sedes æternas parare queat? quomodo item ex morte ad vitam resurgere potuerit, qui se quò minus occideretur, non defendit? Quærunt præterea, quæ ratio nos iubeat in Christi morte vitam, & in eiusdem cruce cœlestem gloriam sperare? At meminisse oportet, hæc illis modò stulta videri, qui pereunt: ideoq; illorum iudicia neminem offendere debent. Eadem enim prædicatio nobis, qui seruamur, est potentia Dei: quia & saluificam illam Dei virtutem nobis offert, quam in Filio suo ille exeruit: & præterea inuictam Dei potentiam mirificè illustrat. Nec enim hæc tam conspicua fuisset hominibus, si nihil huius passus esset Christus, quo seruatore gloriamur. Ut quondam illustriora suae potentiae specimina Deus edidit, quando Jonam in cœti ventre seruauit, & Danielis socios inter medias flammas defendit, quam si illos mox eripuisset, ne quid huius illis accideret: ita maior multo Dei virtus est, quod & filium ex morte restituit, & nos eiusdem morte viuificauit, quam si & illum & nos amore prorsus custodiuisset. Haec quia credentes obseruant, Euangelium illis Dei potentia est ad salutem, quod alteris illis stultitia apparet, sed quae ijsdem exitium sempiternum afferat.
units.tr: But to return to Paul: someone might object, "Yet thus the Gospel is cheapened, and among many it comes into contempt, if it is commended by no splendour at all." He anticipates this objection and says: "For the word of the cross, that is, the doctrine of Christ crucified for us, is indeed foolishness to those who perish, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God." These words have no obscure appearance of concession, and seem to say: "I know indeed what most people think of the Gospel. For to those who listen to the reasoning of the flesh nothing seems more foolish or absurd than what we teach: that the Son of God became man, endured poverty, nakedness, hunger and the other discomforts of this life on earth, suffered an infamous death on the cross, and on the third day rose from the dead to life, and that by his merit we are saved. These things (I say) seem most absurd to the flesh, and so it raises various questions. How, namely, can he who was most poor enrich others with riches; he who hung naked on the cross clothe us; he who had nowhere to lay his head prepare eternal dwellings for us in heaven? How too could he who did not defend himself from being killed rise from death to life? They also ask what reason bids us hope for life in Christ's death and for heavenly glory in his cross. But we must remember that these things seem foolish only to those who perish; therefore their judgments ought to offend no one. For the same preaching is the power of God to us who are being saved, because it offers us that saving power of God which he displayed in his Son, and moreover it marvellously illustrates the invincible power of God. For this would not have been so conspicuous to men if Christ, in whom we glory as Saviour, had suffered nothing of this kind. Just as God once gave more illustrious proofs of his power, when he preserved Jonah in the belly of the whale and defended Daniel's companions in the midst of the flames, than if he had at once snatched them away so that nothing of this befell them; so the power of God is far greater in that he both restored his Son from death and by that death quickened us, than if he had kept both him and us wholly safe from harm. Because believers observe these things, the Gospel is to them the power of God unto salvation, while to the others it appears as foolishness, but it brings them eternal destruction.

units.la: At ne hoc aliquis nouum aut insolens esse existimet, ostendit idem olim quoq; factum fuisse, & Deum has poenas tampridem omnibus decreuisse, qui ipsum audire nolunt, & propriae rationis duce sequuntur. Scriptum est enim: Abolebo sapientiam sapientum, & intelligentiam intelligentium tollam e medio. Extat locus apud Isaiam Cap.29. Accusat illic Deus populi Judaici contumaciam, imprimis autem quod humanis traditionibus ipsum colerent, & ore quidem fidem in ipsum & cultum eius profiterentur, cum cordibus ab eo quam longissime abessent. Minatur autem fore, ut qui ipsum diserte loquentem audire nolunt, tandem prorsus excaecati nihil intelligant, adeo ut Verbum eius ipsis fit instar libri obsignati in manibus hominis indocti, & ab omni litera rum cognitione alieni. Quibus tandem subiicit: Eo quod populus iste ore suo ad me accedit, & labiis suis me honorat, cor autem eius longe a me abest, & timor eorum erga me praecepto hominum doctus est, ideo en ipse quoq; addam, ut mirifice agam cum populo isto, mira scilicet & portentosa: nempe peribit sapientia sapientum eius, & intelligentia prudentum eius sese abscondet. Haec suo instituto Paulus accommodat, & quidem illi proprijssime omnia conueninnt, siue Judaeorum scribas siue gentium philosophos consideres. Noluerunt illi Christum in Euangelio loquentem audire, & suis commentis atq; traditionibus siue placitis indiuulse adhaeserunt. Factum ergo est, ut amissio rationis iudicio, extremam stultitiam putarint esse salutificam illam Dei sapientiam atq; potentiam, quae in Filio eius ipsis proponebatur. Et quod illis tunc accidit, hodie plurimi patiuntur, qui cum superstitionibus assueuerint, & propriae iustitiae fiducia efferantur, simili proteruia Euangelium rident. Causa vero erroris tam noxij est, quod regni Dei mysteria ad humanae rationis calculum reuocant, & sui ingenij acumine ea examinare & inuestigare volunt, quae omnem nostrae mentis captum excedunt. Quam vero stultum est hoc conari, cum ne eorum quidem omnium ratio reddi possit, quae naturae imprimis consentanea & in usu quotidiano sunt? Dicant enim illi nobis, si possunt, cur oculus potius quam auribus videamus, & his potius quam illis audiamus? In capite certe & cerebro utriusq; sensus organa habentur, effectus vero eorum diuersus est. Ostendant item nobis, quo vinculo anima corpori cohaereat, qua ratione per omnia membra extendatur, unde quae inter membra totius corporis est condolentia procedat? Nonne in his & infinitis aliis suam infantiam fateri cogentur? Et tamen ista nemo stulta aut absurda iudicat, nisi qui omni rationis usu destituitur. Cur ergo stulta putamus aeternae salutis mysteria, eò quod nostro intellectui minus patent? Annon certissimi interitus & exitij argumentum censeri debet ista audacia, quae sibi in ipsum Deum iudicium sumere non veretur? Imo, annon illi ipsi extremae stultitiae seipsos damnat, dum se tam stupidos rerum, dubios praebent in illis, sine quibus salus nostra non potest consiste re?
units.tr: But lest anyone think this new or strange, he shows that the same thing was done long ago too, and that God had long since decreed these punishments for all who are unwilling to hear him and follow the guidance of their own reason. For it is written: "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and bring to nothing the understanding of the understanding." There is a passage in Isaiah 29. There God accuses the people of Israel of obstinacy, especially because they worshipped him with human traditions, and professed faith in him and his worship with their mouths, while their hearts were as far from him as possible. He threatens that those who are unwilling to hear him speaking plainly will at last be utterly blinded and understand nothing, so that his Word becomes to them like a sealed book in the hands of an unlearned man, strange to all knowledge of letters. To these he finally adds: "Because this people draws near to me with its mouth and honours me with its lips, but its heart is far from me, and its fear of me is taught by human precept, therefore I will also go on to deal marvellously with this people, wonderful and portentous indeed: the wisdom of its wise men shall perish, and the understanding of its prudent men shall hide itself." Paul applies this to his own purpose, and indeed all these things fit him most aptly, whether you consider the scribes of the Jews or the philosophers of the Gentiles. They were unwilling to hear Christ speaking in the Gospel, and clung stubbornly to their own inventions and traditions or opinions. So it came about that, their judgment being lost, they thought that God's saving wisdom and power, which was set before them in his Son, was the utmost folly. What happened to them then, many suffer today, who, having grown accustomed to superstitions and puffed up with confidence in their own righteousness, mock the Gospel with similar insolence. The cause of such a harmful error is that they reduce the mysteries of God's kingdom to the reckoning of human reason, and wish to examine and investigate with the keenness of their own wit those things which exceed the whole grasp of our mind. How foolish, however, is this attempt, since the reason for even those things which are especially in harmony with nature and are in daily use cannot be given! For let them tell us, if they can, why we see with the eyes rather than the ears, and hear with these rather than those? Indeed the organs of both senses are located in the head and brain, yet their effects are different. Let them show us also by what bond the soul coheres with the body, by what reason it extends through all the members, and whence the sympathy that exists among the members of the whole body proceeds. Will they not be compelled to confess their infancy in these and countless other matters? And yet no one judges these things foolish or absurd except one who is wholly deprived of the use of reason. Why then do we think the mysteries of eternal salvation foolish, merely because they lie less open to our intellect? Ought not this audacity, which does not shrink from taking judgment upon God himself, to be regarded as a sure sign of utter ruin and destruction? Indeed, does it not condemn itself to the utmost folly, since it shows itself so dull towards the things of nature and so doubtful about those things without which our salvation cannot stand?

units.la: Recte igitur Paulus nunc quasi triumphans de humana sapientia illis insultat, & eiusdem prophetae verbis aliquanto detortis exclamat: Ubi sapiens? ubi scriba? ubi coquisitor seculi istius? Quasi diceret: Agedum in medium prodi quisquis vel inter gentes philosophiae studium, vel inter Judaeos scripturae sacrae cognitionem profiteris? Prodi etiam tu, qui totus circa huius mundi arcana occuparis, & disputationibus atq; quaestionibus acutissimis omnia inuoluis. Defendite causam vestram, si potestis, & quam ipsi vobis aspersistis extremae stultitiae notam eluite. Nonne infatuauit Deus sapientiam mundi huius? Comprehendit autem sapientia vocabulo omne id, quod homo intelligit & nouit, siue naturali acumine, siue rerum usu inuestigatum. Infatuatum vero dicit, quia illud omne nihil quam vanitas est, imo noxium est, nisi Christi cognitione regatur, quem nobis sapientiam a Patre factum esse, mox dicet. Non debet autem hoc ita accipi (ut nuper monuimus) quasi artes & harum studia in universum damnentur. Sunt enim illae etiam spiritus sancti dona, & magnus earundem usus est in ijs, quae vitae huic mortali seruiunt. At ne in aeternae salutis negotio aliquid illis tribuamus, monet Apostolus. Quid enim illic proficiat carnis sapientia, cui cælestis regni mysteria (ut modo dictum est[?]) stultitia videntur? Arguitur his ergo ingens error, qui in Christianorum scholis nimium diu regnauit: quo factum est, ut ad theologiæ studium non admissi fuerint, nisi prius philosophiæ prophanæ traditionibus imbuti & ebrij. Huic certè debemus superstitiones omnes, quæ in ecclesiam irrepserunt, & totius doctrinæ adulterationem quæ infinitas animas à recto salutis tramite abduxit. Idem enim inter Christianos, quod olim inter Iudæos sub Iasone Pontifice factum fuit. Ut enim is Hierosolymis gymnasium instituit, in quo Iu-dæa iuuentus Græcorum artibus imbueretur, & ex quo intra annos circiter quadraginta Phari-sæi, Sadducæi & Esseni prodierunt: ita in Christianorum scholis philosophi gentium auditi sunt, qui liberum hominis arbitrium, operum merita, satisfactiones pro peccatis, ignem purgatorium & sexcenta alia nobis pepererunt, quibus Christiana religio partim obscurata, partim extincta est. Arguitur præterea hic illorum quoque error, qui doctrinam fidei Christianæ hominum censuræ & iudicio subijciunt, qui præ aliis seculi huius sapientia & rerum usu instructi esse videntur. Quid vero isti hic faciant, quorum sapientiam Deus ipse iam pridem stultitiæ damnauit? Num cæci de coloribus, surdi de vocum differentijs iudicabunt? Hoc ergo nobis persuasum esto, nunquam nos aliquem in regno Dei profectum facturos esse, nisi rationem & sensus omnes Dei Verbo subijciamus per fidei obedientiam.
units.tr: Rightly, then, Paul, now as if triumphant, mocks human wisdom and, with the words of the prophet somewhat twisted, cries out: "Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the disputer of this age?" As if he said: "Come forward, whoever among the Gentiles professes the study of philosophy or among the Jews the knowledge of Holy Scripture! Come forward too, you who are wholly occupied with the secrets of this world and entangle everything in the sharpest disputations and questions. Defend your cause, if you can, and wipe away the mark of extreme folly which you yourselves have fixed upon yourselves." Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? By "wisdom" he understands everything that man understands and knows, whether discovered by natural acuteness or by experience of things. He calls it "made foolish" because all of it is nothing but vanity, indeed harmful, unless it is governed by the knowledge of Christ, whom he will shortly say was made wisdom for us by the Father. This must not, however, be taken (as we lately warned) as if the arts and their study were condemned altogether. For these too are gifts of the Holy Spirit, and they are of great use in those things which serve this mortal life. But lest we attribute anything of them to the business of eternal salvation, the Apostle warns us. For what would fleshly wisdom profit there, to which the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom seem foolishness (as has just been said)? Here, then, is refuted the great error which reigned for far too long in the schools of Christians, by which it came about that men were not admitted to the study of theology unless first they had been steeped, and drunk, in the traditions of profane philosophy. To this error we surely owe all the superstitions which crept into the Church, and the corruption of the whole doctrine which drew countless souls away from the right path of salvation. For what happened among Christians is the same as what once happened among the Jews under the high priest Jason. For as he set up a gymnasium at Jerusalem, in which Jewish youth were to be imbued with Greek arts, and from which, within about forty years, the Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes came forth, so in the schools of Christians the philosophers of the Gentiles were heard, who gave us free will, the merits of works, satisfactions for sins, purgatorial fire and six hundred other things, by which the Christian religion was partly obscured and partly extinguished. Here is also refuted the error of those who subject the doctrine of the Christian faith to the judgment and opinion of men, men who seem to be more learned than others in the wisdom of this age and in experience of affairs. But what do such men do here, whose wisdom God himself long ago condemned as folly? Will the blind judge of colours, or the deaf of differences in sounds? Let this therefore be settled in our minds: we shall never make any progress in the kingdom of God unless we submit all reason and all our senses to the Word of God through obedient faith.

units.la: Ne quis autem Deum iniquiorem & æquo duriorem esse putet, ostendit Paulus, mundum, id est[?], homines huic seculo & mundanæ sapientiæ deditos, dignos fuisse, quos ille ita tractaret. Nam postquam (inquit) in Dei sapientia mundus non cognouit Deum per sapientiam, placuit Deo per stultitiam prædicationis seruare credentes. Sapientiam Dei dicit eam, quæ in mundi fabrica, ceu in speculo limpidissimo elucet, & in qua Deus suam sapientiam cum omnipotentia coniunctam nobis contemplandam proponit. Sensus ergo loci huius est[?]: Quia sapientes huius seculi sapientia sua & ingenij acumine non recte usi sunt, ut Deum ex mundi fabrica cognoscerent, & cognitum obseruarent, colerent atq; in illo uno omnem salutis fiduciam repositam haberent: sed potius ad sua figmenta conversi Deum illum unum quasi in partes distraxerunt, & illius maiestatem cum simulachris non solum hominum, sed brutorum quoque animantium commutarunt: digni sane fuerunt, quorum sapientiam omnem ille infatuaret. Veruntamen ne genus humanum prorsus periret, placuit Deo alia via rem aggredi, & credentes seruare per stultitiam prædicationis, id est[?], per doctrinam crucis, quæ mundo stulta & absurda videtur. Et hæc dicendo Apostolus non modo iustitiam Dei asserit, sed eiusdem quoq; bonitatem commendat, qui cum nos totos nostro exitio relinquere & pro ut merueramus perdere posset, se tamen nobis accommodare, & ad nostrum captum de-mittere dignatus est[?], ut boni præceptoris instar nobiscum balbutiret, & salutis nostræ rationem, quam in sublimioribus regni sui mysterijs non poteramus percipere, in humili prædicatione Filij sui pro nobis crucifixi proponeret. Neminem ergo huius prædicationis pudere debet, quin volupe nobis sit apud mundum stultitiæ crimen sustinere, dummodo illi sapiamus. Continet autem locus hic præclarum encomium prædicationis euangelicæ, adeoq; omnium concionum, quæ ex illa dedu-cuntur. Seruantur per illam credentes. Hoc ergo organum est[?], quo Deus in nobis seruandis utitur. Ideo Angelus Cornelio dicebat: Accerse Simonem, is tibi loquetur verba, per quæ seruaris & tu & tota domus tua, &c. At non seruantur, nisi qui credunt, sicuti idem Apostolus alibi prolixè docet, imprimis ad Rom.10.cap. ubi ordinem, quem Deus obseruat, pulchrè describit, & tandem ait: Fides ex auditu est[?], auditus vero per Verbum Dei. Agnoscamus ergo tam ingens Dei beneficium, & ordini ab illo nobis tradito nos accommodemus, ut ex Euangelij prædicatione fidem discamus veram, qua seruemur in JESV CHRISTO Filio eius: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Lest anyone think that God is more unjust and harsher than is right, Paul shows that the world, that is, men devoted to this age and to worldly wisdom, were worthy to be dealt with in this way. For, he says, "since in the wisdom of God the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe." By the wisdom of God he means that which shines forth in the fabric of the world, as in a most clear mirror, and in which God sets before us his wisdom joined with his omnipotence to be contemplated. The sense of this passage, then, is this: since the wise men of this age did not rightly use their wisdom and the acuteness of their minds to know God from the fabric of the world, and having known him to observe him, worship him, and place in him alone all their hope of salvation, but rather, turning to their own inventions, they tore that one God as it were into pieces, and exchanged his majesty not only for the images of men but also for those of brute animals, they were truly worthy to have all their wisdom made foolish by him. Nevertheless, lest the human race should perish utterly, it pleased God to approach the matter by another way, and to save believers through the foolishness of preaching, that is, through the doctrine of the cross, which seems foolish and absurd to the world. And in saying these things the Apostle not only asserts the justice of God but also commends his goodness, for though he could have left us wholly to our destruction and have destroyed us as we deserved, he nevertheless deigned to accommodate himself to us and to descend to our capacity, so that, like a good teacher, he might stammer with us, and set forth in the humble preaching of his Son, crucified for us, the plan of our salvation, which we could not grasp in the higher mysteries of his kingdom. Let no one therefore be ashamed of this preaching, but let it be a joy to us to bear the charge of folly before the world, provided that we are wise in him. Moreover, this passage contains a noble encomium of evangelical preaching, and of all sermons which are derived from it. Believers are saved through it. This, therefore, is the instrument which God uses in saving us. Hence the angel said to Cornelius: "Send for Simon; he will speak to you words by which you and all your household shall be saved," and so on. But none are saved except those who believe, as the same Apostle teaches at length elsewhere, especially in Romans chapter 10, where he finely describes the order which God observes, and at last says: "Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the Word of God." Let us therefore acknowledge so great a benefit of God, and accommodate ourselves to the order he has given us, so that from the preaching of the gospel we may learn true faith, by which we are saved in Jesus Christ his Son, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA VI.
units.tr: HOMILY VI.

units.la: Quandoquidem & Iudæi signum petunt, & Græci sapientiam quærūt[?]. Nos autem prædicamus Christum crucifixum, Iudæis quidem offendiculum, Græcis vero stultitiam: ipsis autem vocatis, tum Iudæis tum Græcis, Christum Dei potentiam ac Dei sapientiam. Nam sultitia Dei sapientior est quàm homines, & infirmitas Dei vali-dior est quàm homines.
units.tr: Since both the Jews ask for a sign and the Greeks seek after wisdom, we preach Christ crucified: to the Jews indeed a stumbling block, and to the Greeks foolishness; but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. For the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.

units.la: Quoniam Corinthij in pseudoapostolis humanæ sapientiæ & eruditionis larvam, adhæc dicendi ornatum atq; splendorem nimis admirabantur, & Pauli doctrinam eo potissimum nomine contemnebant, quòd unum IESVM CHRISTVM simplici & humili dicendi genere prædicaret: diligenter admodum huic errori medetur, & graviter docet, eruditionem & eloquentiam, qua mundus hic sese ostentat, nihil prodesse ad veram æternæ salutis cognitionem, imò illam iam olim à Deo stultitiæ esse damnatam. At ne quis idcirco Deum vel iniustitiæ vel crudelitatis aut nimij rigoris accusaret, ostendit, non iustum modo & nobis salutare, verumetiam necessarium fuisse, vt sic fieret. Quia enim mundus hic sapientia, quam habebat, in Deo cognoscendo recte vti noluit, cùm vt seipsum & sapientiam atq; potentiam suam immensam in tota hac orbis cum cœlestis tum terrestris machina euidentissimè spectandam proposuisset, æquum fuit, vt Deus vniuersum humani ingenij acumen atq; eruditionem in posterum à salutis causa omnino excluderet. Eundem vero simul bonitatis suæ erga homines non immemorem fuisse demonstrat, quando ne omnes æternum perirent, malo huic remedium adhibuit per Euangelij prædicationem, quæ etsi in speciem stulta & absurda sit, credentibus tamen salutem veram & certam affert. Porro ne quis Paulum Euangelij doctrinam serio stultam dixisse putaret, nunc dicti huius declarationem subiicit, qua & Euangelicæ prædicationis dignitatem magnificè prædicat, & consilij diuini rationem diligentius exponit.
units.tr: Because the Corinthians admired in the false apostles a mask of human wisdom and learning, and also the ornament and polish of eloquence, and because they despised Paul's teaching chiefly on this ground, that he preached Jesus Christ alone in a plain and humble style, the apostle applies a careful remedy to this error and teaches earnestly that the learning and eloquence by which this world displays itself contribute nothing to the true knowledge of eternal salvation, and that God long ago condemned them as foolishness. But lest anyone should on that account accuse God of injustice, cruelty or excessive severity, he shows that this way of things was not only just and beneficial to us but even necessary. For since this world would not use the wisdom it had to know God rightly, although God had set himself and his immense wisdom and power before it, to be most plainly seen in the whole machine of heaven and earth, it was fitting that God should exclude the whole cleverness and learning of the human mind from being any cause of salvation. Yet at the same time he shows that he has not forgotten his goodness towards men, since, so that all might not perish eternally, he applied a remedy to this evil through the preaching of the gospel, which, although it seems foolish and absurd, brings true and certain salvation to those who believe. Moreover, so that no one should think Paul had seriously called the teaching of the gospel foolish, he now sets out an explanation of this saying, by which he both magnificently proclaims the dignity of the preaching of the gospel and more carefully expounds the reasoning of the divine counsel.

units.la: Et primò quidem ex hominum iudicio & moribus se locutum esse testatur, quos simul omnes in duo genera, Iudæos & gentes, distinguit, vt dictum illud verifiq; conuenire ostendat. Sic autem ait: Quandoquidem & Iudæi signum petunt, & Græci sapientiam quærunt: nos autem prædicamus Christum crucifixum, &c. Sensus verborum istorum hic est: Stultam dixi prædicationem siue doctrinam de CHRISTO IESV; non quòd revera stulta sit, sed quòd talis esse videatur omnibus, quos Dei gratia nondum illuminauit, vt sub illa latentem Dei sapientiam atq; potentiam deprehendere possint. Nam si Iudæos spectes, minimè in hanc illi intenti sunt, sed signa & miracula sibi exhiberi volunt, quibus salutifica Christi potentia oculis spectanda proponatur. Quòd si ad Græcos te conuertas, & eos maximè, qui ingenium philosophia & artium cognitione excoluerunt, hi quoq; Christi prædicationem non admittunt, eò quòd in ea humanæ sapientiæ laruam desiderent, quam solam admirari consueuerunt. At nos neq; his neq; illis satisfacere possumus. Nam nihil prædicamus, præter IESVM CHRISTVM crucifixum, qui Iudæis offendiculum est, cùm illi Messiam regni terreni magnificentia, victoriarum successu & admirabili potentia illustrem iampridem animo conceperint: at Græcis idem ille stultitia videtur. Quia enim isti sapientiæ & artium huius seculi ostentationi assuerunt, fabulam contemptu & risu dignam esse putant, quicquid de Filio Dei in crucem pro nobis suspenso prædicatur. Cæterum qualemcunq; mundus hic æstimet, idem tamen vocatis, siue illi Iudæi siue Græci fuerint, est Dei potentia & sapientia. Vocatorum autem nomine credentes intelligit, ideoq; de efficaci vocatione loquitur, sub qua gratuitam Dei bonitatem comprehendit, qui (vt alibi scribit) quos elegit & prædestinauit, eosdem suo tempore vocare etiam & trahere solet, vt in Christo iustificentur, & gloriæ cœlestis hæredes fiant. Insunt autem his verbis nonnulla, quæ diligentiorem considerationem merentur.
units.tr: And first he declares that he has spoken according to human judgement and custom, dividing all men together into two kinds, Jews and Gentiles, so that he may show that the saying fits them. He says: "Since both the Jews ask for a sign and the Greeks seek after wisdom, we preach Christ crucified," and so on. The sense of these words is this: I have called the preaching, or the teaching, about Jesus Christ foolish; not because it is truly foolish, but because it seems so to all those whom the grace of God has not yet enlightened, so that they cannot perceive the wisdom and power of God lying hidden beneath it. For if you look at the Jews, they are not at all intent on this, but want signs and miracles to be displayed to them, by which the saving power of Christ might be set before their eyes. And if you turn to the Greeks, especially those who have cultivated their minds with philosophy and knowledge of the arts, they too do not admit the preaching of Christ, because they look in it for the mask of human wisdom, which alone they are accustomed to admire. But we can satisfy neither these nor those. For we preach nothing except Jesus Christ crucified, who is a stumbling block to the Jews, who have long since conceived in their minds a Messiah renowned for the splendour of an earthly kingdom, success in victories and wonderful power; but to the Greeks the same Christ seems foolishness. For since they are accustomed to the display of the wisdom and arts of this age, they think that whatever is preached about the Son of God hung on the cross for us is a fable worthy of contempt and laughter. Yet whatever value this world may put on it, it is nevertheless, for those who are called, whether they are Jews or Greeks, the power and wisdom of God. By "those who are called" he means believers, and so he speaks of effectual calling, under which he includes the free goodness of God, who (as he writes elsewhere) is accustomed to call and draw in due time those whom he has chosen and predestined, so that they may be justified in Christ and become heirs of heavenly glory. Moreover, there are in these words some points that deserve a closer consideration.

units.la: Inter quæ primum occurrit, quibus remoris homines maximè impediantur, quò minus Chri-sto credant, & feruentur. Primam sibi ipsis obijciunt, qui Iudæorum more non in vnum Dei Verbum intenti sunt, sed signa aut miracula postulant, quibus illius doctrina confirmetur. Solet quidem Deus frequenter signa ædere, & olim erga Iudæorum gentem illis subinde vsus est, quia his opus erat illos excitare, vt reliqua mundi totius consuetudine ipsum audirent & solum colerent. Neque semper nefas aut impium est signa postulare. Hoc enim olim Gedeon fecit, & ei morem gessit Deus, eò quod non eo animo petebat, quod aut Deo dissideret, aut huic contradicendi causas quæreret, vt impij solent, sed vt in fide confirmatus eius vocationi obediret, & populum quoque in re plena periculi atq; laboris haberet obsequentiorem. Sed & Achaz rex hoc nomine à propheta corripitur acerrimè, quòd à Deo iussus signum noluit petere. Nam incredulitatis obstinata homo, neq; promissionibus Dei, neq; signis fidem habebat, & ex eorum numero erat, qui cum Deo prorsus nihil negotij sibi esse volunt. Quod non obscurè innuit propheta his verbis: An parum est, quòd hominibus molesti estis, nisi & Deo meo molestiam exhibeatis? Imò illi inuito & reluctanti signum obtrudit, vt inexcusabilis fiat illius pertinacia. Itaq; non statim impietatis damnari debent, qui signa sibi exhiberi cupiunt. At si quis ea Iudaeorum more petat, hoc certè scelus est & nulla venia dignum. Videamus ergo, vt illi signa aut miracula postularint. Primo causa petitionis istius fuit incredulitas, quae fecit vt Deum tentarent. Nam non contenti ijs argumentis, quibus se illis fruendum dabat, eius potentiam atq; voluntatem nouo & peculiari aliquo exemplo declarari cupiebant. Exemplum huius audaciae in Psalmo habebat, vbi sic scribit Asaph: Tentauerunt Deum in corde suo, cum poscerent cibum pro animarum suarum desiderio. Et contra Deum locuti sunt, dicentes: Num potest Deus mensam instruere in deserto? En petram percussit, & effluxerunt aquae & fluuij inundarunt: num panem quoq; dare poterit? num carnes poterit parare populo suo? Eius generis fuit, quòd cum Christus diuinam suam potentiam infinitis miraculis quotidie declararet, ipsi tamen illis contemptis sibi signum aliquod è caelo exhiberi cupiebant. Deinde non is postulationum eiusmodi finis ipsis propositus erat, vt in fide confirmarentur, & Deo obedirent, sed potius nouas aduersus illum murmurandi occasiones vaenabantur. Ideo quae negari non poterant in Christo negligunt, miraculum verò petunt è caelo, quod sensu minus percipi posset, & proinde facilius posset in dubium vocari. Adhaec insatiabilis erat haec illorum malitia, qua fiebat, vt signa nulla illis sufficerent, sicuti apud Mosem & in Euangelica historia est videre. Accessit his abusus nefarius, qui res sanctissimas prophanare solet. Et horum similes sunt, quicunq; etiam hodie à nobis signa & miracula aedi volunt, neq; se antea crediturôs aiunt, quàm nos apostolorum exemplo opera prodigiosa facere viderint. At quid aliud isti volunt, quàm vt aliquem praetextum inueniant, quo suam incredulitatem atq; pertinaciam excusent. Non ergo digni sunt, quorum impio desiderio Deus indulgeat. Si enim Christiani sunt quos se esse profitentur, ijs vtiq; credant necesse est, quae Euangelistae iam olim ex spiritus sancti suggestione tradiderunt. Atqui copia signorum illic maxima nobis proponitur, vt nouis minime fit opus. Quòd si illis nò credunt, iam neq; Christiani sunt. Desinant ergo tam sibijpsis quàm alijs inani & fucata fidei professione imponere. Et quoad signa, meminerimus, olim illorum vsum fuisse, cum totius orbis facies subitò mutanda erat, & doctrinae genus cum Iudaeis tum gentibus inauditum praedicaretur: at hodie non eadem necessitas nobis incumbit, qui non aliam doctrinam praedicamus, quàm quae Symbolo apostolico, quod in omnium ore est, continetur, & quam olim Apostoli miraculis innumeris confirmarunt. Imò vt alibi ex Augustino anno tauimus, vtile fuit posteris temporibus miracula cessare, ne animi nostri semper visibilia quaererent, & eorum consuetudine frigesceret genus humanum, quorum nouitate flagrauit. Quod quàm vere & prudenter ille dixerit, ex hoc Pauli testimonio apparet, qui Iudaeos signorum postulatione quàm maximè impeditos fuisse scribit, quò minus in Christum crederent.
units.tr: Among these, the first to present itself is what hindrances chiefly keep men from believing in Christ and cause them to be carried away. Those who, after the manner of the Jews, are not intent on the one Word of God but demand signs or miracles by which that teaching may be confirmed, put the first obstacle in their own way. God indeed often gives signs, and in former times he used them repeatedly towards the Jewish nation, because it was necessary to rouse that people, so that, apart from the custom of the rest of the world, they might hear him and worship him alone. Nor is it always wicked or impious to ask for signs. For Gideon once did so, and God granted his wish, because he did not ask in a spirit of distrust of God or to seek grounds for opposing him, as the wicked usually do, but so that, being strengthened in faith, he might obey his calling, and might have the people also more obedient in a matter full of danger and toil. But King Ahaz was also sharply rebuked on this account by the prophet, because when God bade him ask for a sign he refused to ask. For the unbelieving man, obstinate, had faith neither in God's promises nor in signs, and was one of those who want to have nothing at all to do with God. The prophet hints at this clearly in these words: "Is it too little for you to weary men, unless you weary my God also?" Indeed he forces a sign upon the unwilling and reluctant king, so that his obstinacy may be inexcusable. Therefore those who desire signs to be shown to them ought not to be condemned as impious at once. But if anyone asks for them in the manner of the Jews, this is certainly a crime and deserves no pardon. Let us see, then, why they demanded signs or miracles. First, the cause of this request was unbelief, which made them tempt God. For not content with the proofs by which he offered himself to be enjoyed by them, they wished his power and will to be declared by some new and peculiar example. They had an example of this boldness in the Psalm, where Asaph writes thus: "They tempted God in their heart, when they asked for food according to the desire of their souls. And they spoke against God, saying: Can God prepare a table in the wilderness? Behold, he struck the rock, and waters flowed out, and streams overflowed: can he also give bread? Can he provide flesh for his people?" Of this kind was their conduct when Christ daily displayed his divine power by countless miracles, and yet they, despising these, wanted some sign from heaven to be shown to them. Secondly, the purpose of such requests was not one set before them so that they might be confirmed in faith and obey God, but rather they hunted for new occasions for murmuring against him. Therefore they neglected what in Christ could not be denied, and sought a miracle from heaven, which could be perceived less by the senses and therefore could more easily be called in doubt. Moreover, this wickedness of theirs was insatiable, so that no signs satisfied them, as can be seen in Moses and in the gospel history. There was added to this a wicked abuse, which is wont to profane the most holy things. And those who even today want signs and miracles to be performed by us, and say they will not believe before they have seen us do prodigious works after the example of the apostles, are like them. But what else do these people want than to find some pretext by which to excuse their unbelief and obstinacy? They are therefore not worthy that God should indulge their impious desire. For if they are Christians, as they profess themselves to be, they must certainly believe those things which the evangelists long ago delivered under the prompting of the Holy Spirit. And yet the great abundance of signs is set before us there, so that there is no need of new ones. But if they do not believe those, then they are not Christians at all. Let them therefore cease to impose on themselves and on others by an empty and feigned profession of faith. As for signs, let us remember that their use belonged to former times, when the face of the whole world had to be suddenly changed and a teaching unheard of by both Jews and Gentiles was being preached. But today that same necessity does not press upon us, since we preach no other doctrine than that which is contained in the Apostles' Creed, which is on everyone's lips, and which the apostles once confirmed by countless miracles. Indeed, as we have elsewhere noted from Augustine, it was useful for later times that miracles should cease, so that our minds should not always seek visible things, and the human race should not grow cold through familiarity with those things by whose novelty it once blazed. How truly and wisely he spoke this is clear from this testimony of Paul, who writes that the Jews were most of all hindered from believing in Christ by their demand for signs.

units.la: Altera fidei remora est, si regnum Christi & aeternae salutis negotium ad humanae rationis calculū reuocemus, & nostris nos imaginationibus duci patiamur. Id verò bifariam fit. Primo, cum in Christo regnum terrenū quaeritur. Offenderunt hic etiam Iudaei, quòd promissiones & vaticinia prophetarū non rectè intelligerent, vt saepe diximus. Et hodie multis idem contingit, qui sibi ex Euangelio opes, honores, magnatum amicitias & pacem perpetuam pollicentur. Fit ergo, vt ipse sua frustrati turpiter ab incepto resiliant, & fidem nondum rectè cognitam abnegent. Deinde erratur hic ab ijs, qui nihil credere volunt, quòd non certis & inter homines receptis rationibus probetur. Hoc est cum Graecis sapientiā quaerere, aut potius sapientiam in Deo desiderare, qui ipsissima sapientia est. Sunt ergo isti eorum similes, qui in Sole meridiano facula[?] sibi accendi petunt, vt per eam de Solis splendore possint certiores fieri. Nusquam enim clarius & perfectius fulget diuinae sapientiae splendor, quàm in CHRISTO IESV & in humani generis redemptione, quae per hunc facta est. Quis enim alius praeter vnum Deum eam nostrae salutis rationem inuenire potuisset, qua & iu[?]stitiae Dei satisfieret, & eiusdem bonitatem atq; misericordiam ipsi nobis viuificà sentiremus? Fatemur tamen humanae rationi in tanti mysterij consideratione non semper satisfieri posse: sed hoc nostro vitio fit, qui ad caelestium sublimitatem vsq; penetrare non possumus: quapropter nos tunc non dubitare aut Euangelio contradicere debemus, sed potius admirari Dei consilium & æternum sapientiæ eius inexhaustæ decretum. Cogitemus item impossibile esse, vt nobis, dum in hac carne vitiamur, certa omnium consiliorum Dei ratio constet: quando nec in iis quidem, quæ ex naturæ legibus quotidie fiunt, certa & sufficiens ratio semper afferri potest. Consultissimum ergo fuerit Verbo Dei simpliciter credere, & nostræ rationis captu omniq; sensu nostro per fidei obedientiam subacto, tunc quoq; spem atq; fidem firmam animo concipere, quando nec, spes nec ratio aliqua apparet, quæ nos credere iubeat. Commendatur hoc nomine Abraham, quod præter spem sperauerit, cum ex vetula & sterili Sara sibi centenario filium nasciturum esse audiret. Debet etiam semper nobis in animo versari, quod Christus regnum suum negat esse de hoc mundo. Quæ ergo stultitia est, illud huius mundi legibus astringere, nec in illo quicquam credere, quod humanis rationibus nō possit probari? Quod si interim signis aliquibus fidem nostram Deus fulciat, aut exemplis præter omnem expectationem editis confirmet, in iis nos illius bonitatem agnoscere, ea pie obseruare atq; omnibus religiose vti conuenit ad nominis sui gloriam.
units.tr: Another hindrance to faith arises if we bring the kingdom of Christ and the business of eternal salvation back to the reckoning of human reason, and allow ourselves to be led by our own imaginings. This happens in two ways. First, when people seek an earthly kingdom in Christ. The Jews also stumbled here, because they did not rightly understand the promises and prophecies of the prophets, as we have often said. And today the same thing happens to many, who promise themselves from the Gospel wealth, honours, friendship with the great, and lasting peace. So it happens that, when their own hopes are frustrated, they shamefully withdraw from what they began and deny a faith they have not yet rightly understood. Second, people go astray here who want to believe nothing that is not proved by certain reasons accepted among men. This is to seek wisdom as the Greeks did, or rather to desire wisdom apart from God, who is wisdom itself. Such people are like those who ask for little torches to be lit for them in the midday sun, so that by them they may be better informed about the brightness of the sun. For the splendour of divine wisdom shines nowhere more clearly and perfectly than in Christ Jesus and in the redemption of the human race accomplished through him. For who besides the one God could have devised that way of our salvation, by which both the justice of God is satisfied and his goodness and mercy are felt by us as life-giving? Yet we admit that human reason cannot always be satisfied in the consideration of so great a mystery. But this is the fault of our own weakness, since we cannot penetrate to the height of heavenly things. Therefore we ought not to doubt or contradict the Gospel then, but rather to marvel at the counsel of God and at the eternal decree of his inexhaustible wisdom. Let us also consider that it is impossible for us, while we are beset by this flesh, to have a sure account of all God's counsels. For not even in those things which happen daily under the laws of nature can a certain and sufficient reason always be given. It will therefore be most wise to believe the Word of God simply, and, with our reason and every sense of ours brought under the obedience of faith, to conceive firm hope and faith in our minds even when no hope or reason appears that bids us believe. Abraham is commended on this account, that he hoped against hope, when he heard that he would have a son by the aged and barren Sarah, at the age of a hundred. We must also always keep in mind that Christ says his kingdom is not of this world. What folly, then, is it to bind that kingdom by the laws of this world, and to believe nothing in it that cannot be proved by human reasons? But if God in the meantime supports our faith with certain signs, or confirms it with examples beyond all expectation, it is fitting that we recognise his goodness in them, observe them devoutly, and use them all religiously for the glory of his name.

units.la: Obseruari quoq; debet hoc loco, quod Iudæorum & gentium peruersis de Christo iudicijs nudam & simplicem Christi prædicationem opponit. Nos (inquit) prædicamus Christum crucifixum, Iudæis quidem offendiculum, Græcis autem stultitiam, &c. Loquitur autem non in sua solum, sed in omnium Apostolorum, imò prophetarum quoq; veterum persona, qui simul omnes nihil aliud quàm Christum crucifixum nouerunt atq; prædicarunt, ut Cap.2. susius[?] demonstrabitur. Ita vero innuit, Deum propter corrupta & peruersa hominum iudicia nequaquam mutare salutis nostræ rationem, quæ æterno eius decreto nititur. Offenderunt ad Christum Iudæi & gentes: at manet ille nihilominus humani generis redemptor unicus, neq; propter temerarios illos critones[?] Apostoli prædicationis suæ argumentū aut formulam mutauerunt. Sic olim cum totus orbis sub tenebrarum potestate esset, & gentes quidem promissiones de venturo Messia prorsus ignorarent, Iudæi vero illas non rectè intelligerent, nunquam tamen illæ mutatæ sunt, sed eandem doctrinam prophetæ omnes perpetuò omnibus inculcarunt. Fiet idem omnibus seculis, & hoc non obscurè Christus docet, qui cum nouissimis temporibus pseudoprophetas & seductores plurimos oriturosq; esse dixisset, & simul de incurabili hominum contumacia discipulos diligenter admonuisset, fore tamen ait, ut Euangelium per totum orbem prædicetur. Sunt hæc propter eos obseruanda paulò attentius, qui propter aliquos, qui obstinata malitia Veritatis doctrinæ resistunt, multa concedi, multa reticeri aut dissimulari, multa item in doctrinæ capitibus mutari oportere clamant. Quasi vero in nostro arbitrio sit salutis ratio nem constituere, aut regni Dei œconomiam mutare. Quin Apostoli exemplum potius sequimur, qui & alibi ait: Christus heri & hodie, idem est etiam in secula, neq; est in quoquam alio salus. Huius item postremum mandatum est: Ite in orbem universum, & prædicate Euangelium omni creaturæ. Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, seruabitur. Qui vero non crediderit, condemnabitur.
units.tr: It must also be observed in this place that he sets against the perverse judgements of Jews and Gentiles about Christ the bare and simple preaching of Christ. "We," he says, "preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Greeks," and so on. He speaks not only in his own person but in the person of all the Apostles, and indeed of the ancient prophets too, who all knew and preached nothing other than Christ crucified, as will be shown more fully in chapter 2. He thus intimates that God, on account of men's corrupt and perverse judgements, by no means changes the manner of our salvation, which rests on his eternal decree. The Jews and the Gentiles were offended at Christ, but he remains nonetheless the sole Redeemer of the human race, and on account of those rash critics the Apostles did not change the argument or the form of their preaching. So too in former times, when the whole world was under the power of darkness, and the Gentiles were utterly ignorant of the promises about the coming Messiah, and the Jews did not rightly understand them, those promises were never changed, but all the prophets constantly impressed the same teaching on everyone. The same will happen in every age, and Christ teaches this plainly, for when he had said that in the last times many false prophets and seducers would arise, and at the same time had carefully warned his disciples about the incurable stubbornness of men, he nevertheless said that the Gospel would be preached throughout the whole world. These things must be noted rather carefully against those who, because of some who resist the doctrine of truth out of obstinate malice, cry out that many things must be conceded, many things kept quiet or passed over, and many articles of doctrine changed. As if it were in our power to set up the way of salvation, or to alter the economy of God's kingdom! Rather, let us follow the example of the Apostle, who also says elsewhere: "Christ is the same yesterday, today, and for ever, and there is no salvation in anyone else." Likewise his last command is this: "Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature. He who believes and is baptised will be saved; but he who does not believe will be condemned."

units.la: Est ergo hæc unica, certa & semper sibi constans salutis doctrina, quam Paulus (ut in posteriori ad Timotheum habetur) constanter urgeri vult in ecclesia, idq; eò magis fieri iubet, quòd sciret quàm plurimos fore, qui sanam doctrinam non recipiunt, & qui blanditiloquentia fallaci aures sibi demulceri volunt. Quod autem de salutis ratione dicitur, hoc ipsum ad omnia Dei decreta & præ-cepta debet transferri. Manet enim Verbum Domini in æternum, & illo aliquid constituente, quis illud facit irritum? Illius ergo præcepta nobis vitæ totius atq; actionum nostrarum omniū regulam constituamus, neq; putemus voluntate eius propter corruptissimos nouissimi seculi mores atq; quiduis audendi licentiam, mutatam esse, aut illum indulgentiorem fore in puniendis illis, qui leges ab ipso latas transgrediuntur. Non minus autem nos promissiones eius consolari debet aduersus mundi & principis eius minas: quando constat, illas quoq; perpetuò ratas fore. Regnabit enim Christus, ut mundus hic tumultuetur, neq; omnes eius quisquam illi ex manibus eripiet.
units.tr: This, then, is the one, certain, and always self-consistent doctrine of salvation, which Paul (as is found in his second letter to Timothy) wishes to be urged constantly in the Church. He commands this all the more because he knew that there would be very many who do not receive sound doctrine, and who want their ears to be soothed by deceitful flattery. But what is said about the way of salvation must be applied to all God's decrees and precepts. For the Word of the Lord remains for ever, and when he has decreed something, who can make it void? Let us therefore set his precepts as the rule of our whole life and all our actions, and let us not think that his will has been changed on account of the most corrupt morals of the last age and the licence to dare anything, or that he will be more lenient in punishing those who transgress the laws given by him. Still, his promises ought to comfort us no less against the threats of the world and its prince, since it is certain that these also will always stand firm. For Christ will reign, however much this world may be in tumult, and no one will snatch all his people out of his hands.

units.la: Habet prætereà locus hic egregiâ & plenam consolationis IESV CHRISTI descriptione. Nam Dei potentiam & sapientiam illum dicit Apostolus. Non loquitur autem de personæ essentia, neq; aliquid à Deo Patre abstractum imaginatur, ut neq; illius humanitatem in dubium vocat. Scimus enim illum, quoad personæ essentiam, Deum verum & hominem verum esse: Deū quidem æternū, & (ut ipse loquitur) unum cum Patre: hominem verò factum non diuinitatis abnegatione aut mutatione, sed carnis assumptione, quam præfinito tempore ex matre Virgine assumptam sibi sociauit. Itaq; locus iste de illius effectus, & fructu, qui ex illo ad nos redit, debet intelligi. Est igitur Christus Dei potentia, quia per illum saluificam suam potentiam iste exeruit, & hodie etiam efficaciter exerit, quando per illius prædicationem homines mutantur, trahuntur, regenerantur, & in eodem fortes scandala & salutis impedimenta omnia superant, in illo deniq; omnia possunt. Est idem etiam sapientia Dei, quia in eo reconditi sunt omnes scientiæ & cognitionis thesauri, neque aliquid nos sine illo in rebus diuinis intelligere aut sapere possumus. Nam ut Ioannes ait, Deum nemo vidit unquam, sed unigenitus ille Filius, qui est in sinu Patris, ille nobis enarrauit. Christus deniq; est vera illa sapientia, per quam orbis totus conditus est, & cuius lux in animis nostris accensa humanæ sapientiæ laruam detrahit, ut appareat nihil quàm vanitatem & extremam stultitiam esse, quicquid inter homines sapientiæ titulo venditatur. In horum consideratione crebrò nos versari conuenit. Usus autem considerationis istius hic nobis esto, ut illi constanter fidamus in omni tentationum genere, neque mundi huius terriculamentis nos superari patiamur. Quem enim timeant, qui Dei potentia nituntur, & supra illam petram ædificati sunt, aduersus quam ne portæ quidem inferorum prævalent? Ut verò illi fidere possimus, eum solum audire oportet, ut ex eius Verbo renati in filiorum Dei numero censeamur. Sed ô infelices, qui in Euangelio nobis loquentem Dei sapientiam fastidiunt, & incertis hominum traditionibus sese circumduci patiuntur?
units.tr: Moreover, this passage contains an excellent description of Jesus Christ, full of consolation. For the Apostle calls him the power and wisdom of God. He does not speak here of the essence of the person, nor does he imagine him as something separated from God the Father, just as he does not call his humanity into doubt. For we know that he, as to the essence of his person, is true God and true man: truly God eternal, and (as he himself says) one with the Father; and made man not by a denial or change of his divinity, but by the assumption of flesh, which in the appointed time he took from the Virgin mother and joined to himself. Therefore this passage must be understood of his effect and of the fruit which comes to us from him. Christ is thus the power of God, because through him God has exercised and today still effectively exercises his saving power, when through his preaching men are changed, drawn, and regenerated, and in him are strong to overcome all stumbling blocks and hindrances to salvation; in him, finally, they can do all things. He is also the wisdom of God, because in him are hidden all the treasures of knowledge and understanding, and without him we cannot understand or know anything in divine things. For, as John says, no one has ever seen God, but the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him to us. Christ is finally that true wisdom through which the whole world was created, and whose light, kindled in our minds, strips away the mask of human wisdom, so that it becomes plain that whatever is sold among men under the name of wisdom is nothing but vanity and utter foolishness. It is fitting that we dwell often on these things in our thoughts. The use of this consideration here should be that we trust him steadfastly in every kind of temptation, and do not allow ourselves to be overcome by the terrors of this world. For whom should those fear who rest on the power of God, and are built upon that rock against which the gates of hell do not prevail? But that we may trust him, we must hear him alone, so that, born again through his Word, we may be counted among the children of God. But oh, the unhappy men, who scorn the wisdom of God speaking to us in the Gospel, and allow themselves to be led round by the uncertain traditions of men!

units.la: At quia caro nostra videre non potest, quomodo Christus, quo nihil in mundo contemptibilius & imbecillius esse putatur, Dei potentia & sapientia fit, argumentum ex ipsius Dei natura subiicit Apostolus, quo illud probet. Nam stultitia Dei (inquit) sapientior est quàm homines, & infirmitas Dei validior est quàm homines. Quæ verba non eo sensu accipi debent, quasi in Deo aliquid vel stultum vel infirmum fit, sed hominum iudicia respicit, quibus prædicatio de cruce Christi stulta & infirma, adeoq; fabulosa & res nullius momenti aut pretii esse videtur. Et stultitiæ atque infirmitatis vocabulis utitur, ut magis amplificet quod dicere instituit. Putat autem mundus totum illud Christianæ fidei atq; religionis negotium meram stultitiam esse, eò quod rationibus humanis non potest probari, & quod homines ipsos quodammodo ad stultitiam, vel ad insaniam potius adigere putatur, ut abiectarum omnium cura, ne vitæ quidem propriæ rationem habeant, dummodo Christum apprehendere & cum illo vniri possint. Adhæc infirmitas maxima videtur, quòd fides ista & doctrina nulla hominum authoritate & potentia fulcitur, & quod omnium odijs exposita persecutiones grauissimas sustinet. Sed hæc (inquit) stultitia omnem hominum sapientiam superat, & hæc infirmitas omnem totius mundi potentiam atq; vires longe vincit. Et quod Paulus dicit, facile demonstrari potest, si ea quæ Christus ipse fecit, & quæ illius spiritu ducti Apostoli fecerunt, non oscitanter consideremus. Nam ut ab eius infantia exordiamur, qui Bethlehem in stabulo natus in præsepio iacuit, is ad sui adorationem Magos ab extremo Oriente adduxit, angelos suæ natiuitatis precones habuit, urbem Romam (ut Orosius scribit) prodigijs magnis & inusitatis terruit, & Domini nomen abdicare coegit Augustum Imperatorem, qui prius bellis ciuilibus totum orbem terrarum turbauerat, ut solus regnare posset: adhæc proditoria Herodis consilia elasit, qui vitæ ipsius crudeles insidias struebat. Postea cum vix duodecimum ætatis annum attigisset, in templo Hierosolymitano publicè docuit, & inter gentis illius eruditissimos doctores diuinæ suæ sapientiæ specimen cum summa omnium admiratione dedit. Postquam verò iam baptizatus ea obire cæpit: quorum ergo in mundum venerat, potentiam simul & sapientiam Dei exemplis tot tantisq;, declarauit, ut dies totus illis commemorandis non suffecerit. Nam diabolum in deserto vicit, & qui nullo hominum testimonio commendabatur multa discipulorum millia post se traxit: suos quàm uis nihil proprium possideret, mirificè aluit: & eosdem inter insidias & hostiles potentissimorum conatus seruauit: adhæc mari, ventis, morbis & immundis spiritibus cum imperio mandauit, sacerdotum & scribarum quæstionibus insidiosis ita respondit, ut eius quidem sapientiam omnes admirarentur, illi verò suam ignorantiam cum ignominia proderent: sed & consilia & manus hostium non semel cum miraculo euasit, cum iam ab illis comprehensus esse putaretur. Ast ubi hora illa fatalis adfuit, qua eum propter peccata nostra mori oportebat, ne tunc quidem virtutem diunam dissimulauit. Nam uno verbo cohortem totam eorum, qui ad ipsum capiendum missi erant, deiecit, innocentiam suam aduersus hostium uerfutissimorum criminationes atque calumnias ita asseruit & defendit, ut Pilatum quoq; eius testem haberet: deinde cum nudus & omnium ludibrijs expositus in cruce penderet, Solis radios extinxit, terram totam immani motu concussit, petras diffecuit, velum templi discidit, monumenta aperuit, Centurionem & multos ex militum alio-rumque speculatorum[?] numero ad sui confessionem adegit, & tandem neque Romani Imperatoris, cuius nomine sepulchri ostium obsignatum erat, authoritatem, neque militum excubantium arma moratus, a mortuis resurrexit, & resurrectione sua peccatum, mortem, diabolum atque inferos deuicit, & tandem illustri cum triumpho super nubila vectus ad Patris dextram consedit, unde spiritum sanctum misit discipulis, qui illius praedicatione totum orbem terrarum mirifico successu intra paucos annos illustrauerunt. Et hoc quidem Christi auspicijs fecere, qui numero pauci, & ob gentem suam omnibus inuisi, adhaec indocti & illiterati atque omni humano praesidio destituti erant: ij (inquam) multum reluctantibus illis, qui tunc in orbe potentissimi erant & supremam doctrinae atque sapientiae existimationem sustinebant, mutationem to-tius orbis inuexerunt, quod nemo alius unquam perficere potuit. Plato certe, quem philosophorum sapientissimum non immerito dixeris, rempublicam quidem imaginatus est nouam, sed adeo illam constituere non potuit, ut potius cum sua republica ex Sicilia eiectus vitae periculum adierit. Quid vero de Diagora, Protagora & Theodoro philosophis dicemus, qui quod Deos negarent, inter amicos graviter periclitati sunt? Et Socratem, cum omnium optimus haberetur, eadem de causa cicutam bibere coactum fuisse legimus. Neque quisquam horum suis, quod cupiebat, persuadere potuit. Quis ergo non videat Christi virtutem omni humana potentia atque sapientia maiorem esse, qui per Apostolos in toto orbe terrarum religionem simul atque rempublicam mutauit, & quamuis illi ab impijs occisi sint, mansit tamen doctrina ipsorum fructus, sicuti ille euen-turum promiserat.
