Neq; minor Christi virtus postea in Martyribus eluxit, inter quos pleriq; cum illiterati & nullo rerum usu instructi essent, tamen & fidei rationem publice reddiderunt non sine omnium admiratione, qui illos audiebant, & diros immanissimorum suppliciorum cruciatus tanta fidei constantia & animi patientia sustinuerunt, ut carnificum quidem manus fatigarent, tyrannos rerum dubios facerent, ipsi autem inuicti & immobiles ad grauiora quoque ferenda se patiratos esse ostenderent. Et haec quidem omnia Christus non inter amicos & discipulos, sed inter me-dios hostes fecit: ut plane constet ipsum esse, quem Dauid in medio inimicorum suorum regnaturum esse praedixerat. Verissime ergo ab Apostolo dictum est, stultitiam Dei sapientiorem esse hominibus, & eiusdem infirmitatem vires hominum longe superare. Neque hoc in solo Christo cernitur, sed in aliis quoque Dei operibus, quando pleraque ex iis perficit, quae aut nulla, aut iis, quae fiunt, contraria videntur. Sic totam hanc mundi machinam ex nihilo produxit, maris fluctus arena conclusit, terram aquis imposuit, & posteris temporibus ecclesiam suam tunc maxime auxit, & euexit, quando iamiam prorsus peritura videbatur. Haec ut nobis admirabilem Dei sapientiam atq; potentiam commendant, ita consolationem in aduersis & periculis dulcissimam afferunt. Terremur saepe hostium Euangelij potentia & astutia, sed tunc cogitemus, nihil his aduersus Deum profici. Qui enim per Filium suum mortali carne vestitum nos redemit, & omnibus hominum atque ipsius diaboli viribus & consilijs superior fuit, eidem facile fuerit nos tueri & fer-uare, ut in illo viuamus atque regnemus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: But because our flesh cannot see how Christ, whom the world thinks the most contemptible and feeble of all things, has become the power and wisdom of God, the Apostle brings forward an argument from the very nature of God to prove it. "For the foolishness of God," he says, "is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men." These words must not be taken as meaning that anything in God is foolish or weak. They refer to human judgements, by which the preaching of the cross of Christ seems foolish and weak, and so fabulous and of no moment or worth. He uses the words foolishness and weakness so that he may magnify more strongly what he has set out to say. The world thinks that the whole business of the Christian faith and religion is sheer folly, because it cannot be proved by human reasoning, and because it is thought to drive people almost into folly, or rather madness, so that they care nothing for all worldly things and do not even keep a rational account of their own life, provided they can grasp Christ and be united with him. Moreover, the faith and doctrine seem to be the greatest weakness, because they are supported by no human authority or power, and because, exposed to the hatred of all, they endure the most severe persecutions. But, he says, this foolishness surpasses all human wisdom, and this weakness far outdoes all the power and strength of the whole world. What Paul says can easily be shown, if we consider carefully what Christ himself did and what the Apostles, led by his Spirit, did. To begin with his infancy: he who was born in a stable at Bethlehem and lay in a manger drew the Magi from the farthest East to worship him; he had angels as heralds of his birth; he terrified the city of Rome with great and unusual portents (as Orosius writes); and he compelled the Emperor Augustus, who had earlier thrown the whole world into turmoil with civil wars so that he alone might reign, to renounce the name of Lord. He also foiled the treacherous plans of Herod, who was devising cruel plots against his life. Afterwards, when he had scarcely reached his twelfth year, he taught publicly in the temple at Jerusalem and, to the amazement of all, gave a sample of his divine wisdom among the most learned teachers of that nation. Once he had been baptized and began to carry out the tasks for which he had come into the world, he displayed the power and wisdom of God by so many and so great examples that a whole day would not suffice to recount them. He conquered the devil in the desert; he, who was commended by no human testimony, drew many thousands of disciples after him; he wonderfully nourished his followers, although he possessed nothing of his own, and preserved the same men amid the snares and hostile attempts of the most powerful. Moreover, he commanded the sea, the winds, diseases and unclean spirits with authority; he answered the crafty questions of the priests and scribes in such a way that all admired his wisdom, while they revealed their own ignorance to their shame. He also escaped the plans and hands of his enemies more than once by a miracle, when he was already thought to have been seized by them. But when that fatal hour came, in which he had to die for our sins, not even then did he conceal his divine power. With one word he threw down the whole band of those who had been sent to seize him; he asserted and defended his innocence against the accusations and calumnies of his most cunning enemies, so that even Pilate was his witness. Then, when he hung naked on the cross, exposed to the mockery of all, he extinguished the rays of the sun, shook the whole earth with a fearful tremor, split rocks, tore the veil of the temple, opened the tombs, and brought the centurion and many of the soldiers and other watchmen to confess him. Finally, neither the authority of the Roman Emperor, whose seal had been set upon the entrance of the sepulchre, nor the arms of the soldiers on guard delayed him; he rose from the dead, and by his resurrection he conquered sin, death, the devil and hell. At last, carried up in glorious triumph above the clouds, he sat down at the right hand of the Father, from where he sent the Holy Spirit to the disciples, who, within a few years, with remarkable success, illumined the whole world with their preaching. They did this under Christ's auspices, though they were few in number, hated by all because of their nation, and unlearned and unlettered and deprived of all human help. Those men (I say), while the powerful of the world, who held the highest reputation for doctrine and wisdom, struggled against them, brought about a change in the whole world, which no one else had ever been able to accomplish. Plato, whom one may rightly call the wisest of philosophers, indeed imagined a new commonwealth, but he could not establish it, so that he was rather driven out of Sicily along with his republic and faced danger to his life. What shall we say of the philosophers Diagoras, Protagoras and Theodorus, who, because they denied the gods, were in serious danger among their friends? And we read that Socrates, who was thought the best of all men, was forced for the same reason to drink hemlock. Nor could any of these persuade his own people of what he desired. Who then does not see that the power of Christ is greater than all human power and wisdom, since through the Apostles he changed both the religion and the commonwealth throughout the whole world; and although they were slain by the impious, the fruit of their teaching remained, just as he had promised it would. Nor did the power of Christ shine any less afterwards in the martyrs, among whom many, though unlettered and without any experience of affairs, nevertheless publicly gave an account of their faith, not without the amazement of all who heard them, and endured the dreadful torments of the most savage punishments with such constancy of faith and patience of mind that they wearied the hands of the executioners, left the tyrants uncertain of their purpose, and showed themselves unconquered and immovable, ready to bear even heavier things. And Christ did all these things not among friends and disciples, but among his bitterest enemies, so that it is plain that he is the one whom David foretold would reign in the midst of his enemies. Therefore the Apostle spoke most truly, that the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and his weakness far surpasses the strength of men. This is seen not only in Christ, but also in other works of God, since he brings about many things which seem to be either impossible or contrary to what is happening. Thus he brought this whole machine of the world out of nothing, enclosed the waves of the sea within the sand, set the earth upon the waters, and in later times he greatly increased and raised up his Church just when it seemed altogether about to perish. These things, while they commend to us the admirable wisdom and power of God, also bring the sweetest consolation in adversity and danger. We are often terrified by the power and cunning of the enemies of the gospel; but then let us reflect that nothing is achieved by them against God. For he who redeemed us through his Son clothed in mortal flesh, and was superior to all the strength and plans of men and of the devil himself, will easily be able to protect and preserve us, so that we may live and reign in him, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen. divine

units.la: HOMILIA VII.
units.tr: HOMILY VII.

units.la: Videtis enim vocationem vestram, fratres, quòd non multi fa-pientes secundùm carnem, non multi potentes, non multi nobiles. Verùm quæ stulta sunt in mundo elegit Deus; ut pudefaciat sa-pientes: & quæ sunt infirma in mundo, elegit Deus, ut pudefaciat robusta: & quæ ignobilia sunt in mundo, & pro nihilo habita, ele-git Deus, git Deus, & ea quae non sunt, vt ea quae sunt aboleat: Vt ne glorietur vlla caro coram eo. Sed ex ipso vos estis in CHRISTO IESV: qui factus est nobis sapientia a Deo, iustitia, & sanctificatio, & redemptio: Vt sicut scriptum est, Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur.
units.tr: For you see your calling, brethren, that not many are wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble. But God has chosen the foolish things of the world, that he might confound the wise; and God has chosen the weak things of the world, that he might confound the strong; and the base things of the world, and things that are despised, has God chosen, and things which are not, that he might bring to nought things that are: that no flesh should glory in his presence. But of him are you in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption: that, as it is written, He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord.

units.la: Etsi Deus omnem superbiam odio habeat, eam tamen imprimis detestari & horrendis exemplis deiicere aut prosternere solet, qua in iis priuatam gloriam quaerunt homines, quae ad aeternam salutem faciunt, & quae illi omnibus piis communia esse vult. Nam qui hoc facere consueuerunt, ij & gratiam illius non recte agnoscunt, & ab illo datis bonis fere ad aliorum simul atq; propriam perniciem abutuntur. Fiebat hoc apud Corinthios, idq; pseudoapostolorum vitio, qui post Pauli discessum in illam ecclesiam irrepserant. Hi enim, vt apud omnes in honore & pretio essent, sapientiae cuiusdam sublimioris existimationem venabantur, & eandem magnifico verborum apparatu ostentabant. [Quae causa erat], vt Corinthij quoq; inani persuasione delusi sibi ipsis mirifice placerent, quasi aliis ecclesijs longe praestarent: imo tantum suis illis doctoribus tribuebant, vt illorum quoq; nominibus gauderent, & ita propter illos in diuersas sectas scinderentur. Peccabatur itaq; superbia & ambitione tam a doctoribus, quam ab ecclesia & periculum erat, ne malum hoc indies latius serpendo tandem immedicabile fieret. Ideo Paulus magna diligentia illi remedium adhibet. Docet enim redemptionis & salutis humanae negotium non in sapientia humana mundi & eloquentiae ostentatione consistere, neq; Christum hisce praesidijs aut adminiculis ad regnum suum propagandum opus habere: sed longe aliam instituisse caelestis illius philosophiae rationem: Nimirum vt praedicatione in speciem stulta & absurda ad ipsum adducantur, qui ipsius sapientiam in huius mundi speculo elucentem agnoscere noluerunt: & ideo Apostolos misisse, qui non humanae philosophiae titulo, non dicendi peritia, non vllo artium praesidio instructi, sed spiritus virtute armati, Euangelium de Christo crucifixo quam simplicissime praedicauerint. His modo aliud argumentum ab ipsorum fidelium persona subijcit, quo ostendit, non solum precones Euangelij illiteratos & obscuros homines missos esse, sed maiorem quoq; credentium partem ex eodem hominum genere constare. Eratq; hoc argumentum ad deprimendam illorum confidentiam efficacissimum: quia si in seipsos descendebant, non poterant porro contemnere simplicem illam Euangelij praedicandi rationem, nisi suam quoque vocationem irritam facere vellent, aut saltem in dubium vocare. Ideo in huius argumenti tractatione multis ijsque grauissimis verbis vtitur.
units.tr: Although God hates all pride, he is especially accustomed to detest it and to cast it down or overthrow it with dreadful examples, when men seek private glory in those things which pertain to eternal salvation and which he wills to be common to all the godly. For those who are accustomed to do this do not rightly acknowledge his grace, and they abuse the gifts given by him, almost always to the ruin both of others and of themselves. This happened among the Corinthians, through the fault of the false apostles, who had crept into that church after Paul's departure. For these men, so that they might be held in honour and esteem by all, hunted after a reputation for a certain loftier wisdom and displayed it with a showy array of words. The result was that the Corinthians too, deluded by an empty persuasion, took great pleasure in themselves, as though they far excelled the other churches; indeed they attributed so much to those teachers of theirs that they took pride even in their names, and so were split into different sects on their account. Sin was therefore committed through pride and ambition, both by the teachers and by the church, and there was a danger that this evil, spreading more widely every day, would in the end become incurable. Therefore Paul applies a remedy to it with great care. For he teaches that the business of human redemption and salvation does not consist in human wisdom, in the worldly display of eloquence, nor does Christ need such props or supports to extend his kingdom; rather he has instituted a quite different method of that heavenly philosophy. Namely, by a preaching that seems foolish and absurd, people are to be brought to him, those who were unwilling to recognise his wisdom shining in the mirror of this world. And so he sent apostles who, not equipped with the title of human philosophy, nor with skill in speaking, nor with any support of the arts, but armed with the power of the Spirit, preached the gospel of Christ crucified as simply as possible. Next he adds to this another argument drawn from the very persons of the believers, by which he shows that not only were the heralds of the gospel sent as unlettered and obscure men, but that the greater part of the believers also came from the same kind of people. This argument was most effective for lowering their confidence; for if they looked into themselves, they could no longer despise that simple method of preaching the gospel, unless they wished to make their own calling void, or at least call it into doubt. Therefore in treating this argument he uses many and most weighty words.

units.la: Videtis (inquit) vocationem vestram, fratres, quòd non multi sapientes secundum carnem, non multi potentes, non multi nobiles, &c. Vocationis nomine tam ipsos vocatos, quam rationem intelligit, quam in illis vocandis Deus obseruauerat. Orationem vero sic instituit, vt ipsos quasi in rem praesentem adducat, & ipsorum testimonio probet quod dicturus erat, quae omnium certissima est demonstrandi ratio. Itaque verborum istorum sensus est: Si cui mirum aut absurdum videtur, quod de doctoribus & docendi ratione diximus, is agedum in seipsum, adeoq; ad totum qui apud vos est credentium coetum oculos conuertat, & videat diligenter, quid Deus in vobis vocandis obseruauerit, & quales ad Christi & ecclesiae eius consortium vocarit. Quid enim illic inueniet? Nimirum, quòd non multi sapientes secundum carnem, id est, non multi ea sapientia donati, quae sola carnis iudicio probatur: non multi item potentia & dignitatibus politicis illustres, nō etiam nobiles multi, qui generis sui originem ad veteres illos heroes, aut etiam Deos (vt inter gentes fieri consueuit) referre possint. Ita vero simul excludit merita & dignitatem omnem, quem vel ex generis splendore, aut quacunq; aliare hominibus accedere consueuerunt. Vnde iam colligitur nimium stultè eos facere, qui humanae sapientiae existimationem aut dignitates huius saeculi in religionis & aeternae salutis negotio aliquid momenti habere arbitrantur. Nam si rem propius inspicere libeat, adeò illa non prosunt, vt potius nobis ad salutem tendentibus impedimento sint, nisi singulari gratia Deus nos subleuet atque in officio contineat. Qui enim sapientia huius saeculi in rebus cognoscendis aut dijudicandis utuntur, ijs (ut nuper diximus) stultiffima videtur Euangelij prædicatio. Exemplum huius imprimis memorabile in Atheniensibus Lucas proponit, qui cum in vrbe sua philosophos haberent innumeros, & ibidem schola totius orbis celeberrima floreret, adeo tamen ista illis nihil profuerunt, ut vix vllos alios in religione ftultiores & ad fidem Christi admittendam magis ineptos fuisse constet. Nam & Deo ignoto aram consecrauerant, & Paulum de Christi regno & mortuorum resurrectione differentem itariferunt, ut eum nufpiam terrarum fcurrilius habitum fuisse constet. Et posteris temporibus cum philosophis plurimum semper negotij fuit Christianis doctoribus, atq; ex illorum scholis fere hæretici prodierunt, quorum curiositate & portentofis opinionibus res Christiana periculosissimè turbata fuit. At qui in repub. excellunt, ij cum Euangelium annunciari audiunt, mox doctrinam hanc reipublicæ inimicam & legibus aduersam esse putant, & quia suo honori aut famæ metuunt, illam quàm longissimè arcere conantur. Et habent illi flabella sua aulica, quæ inde seditiones & turbas enafci ipsis per suadent, &c. Et quàmuis interdum diuinæ istius lucis radij in animos illorum penetrent, obstat tamen metus ille cum politica prudentia coniunctus, ne aliquos progressus faciant. Tales olim Iudæorum principes fuisse constat, quorum aliqui rempub. nisi Christus è medio tolleretur, saluam fore negabant: alij vero etsi intra animos suos conuicti crederent, illum tamen non audebant profiteri, ne ex Synagoga eijcerentur. Quòd fi generis nobilitate & opum abundantia superbientes inspicias, ij quoq; aut Euangelium magno cum fastidio contemnunt, eò quòd iam nunc fe beatos esse, neq; alia felicitatis consequendæ ratione opus habere arbitrantur: aut fi quando ad illud audiendum veniunt, fere cum diuite illo, quem Matthæus describit, tristes discedunt, ubi quid ab ipsis requiratur, intelligunt, & femen verbi intra animos suos à spinis suffocari patiuntur. Et hæ causæ sunt, quòd omnibus istis plerunq; Euangelium abfq; fructu prædicatur.
units.tr: "You see," he says, "your calling, brethren, that not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble," and so on. By the word calling he understands both the persons who were called and the method which God had observed in calling them. He arranges the discourse so as to bring them before him as if they were present, and by their own testimony to prove what he was about to say, which is the most certain method of demonstration of all. The sense of these words is therefore this: if anyone thinks it strange or absurd that we have said these things about teachers and the manner of teaching, let him turn his eyes upon himself, and indeed upon the whole assembly of believers that is among you, and let him look carefully at what God has observed in calling you, and what sort of persons he has called to the fellowship of Christ and of his church. For what will he find there? Namely, that not many are wise according to the flesh, that is, not many endowed with that wisdom which is approved by the judgement of the flesh alone; likewise not many illustrious for power and political dignities; nor indeed are many noble, who could trace the origin of their family back to ancient heroes or even gods, as is customary among the Gentiles. Thus he excludes at the same time all merit and every dignity that men are accustomed to derive from the splendour of their birth or from any other source. From this it is now gathered how very foolishly those act who think that the esteem of human wisdom or the dignities of this age carry any weight in the business of religion and eternal salvation. For if one wishes to look at the matter more closely, these things are so far from helping that they are rather a hindrance to us as we strive for salvation, unless God raises us up by singular grace and keeps us in our duty. For to those who use the wisdom of this age in discerning and judging things, the preaching of the gospel seems most foolish (as we said a little while ago). Luke sets before us a particularly memorable example of this in the Athenians, who, although they had countless philosophers in their city, and the most famous school of the whole world flourished there, nevertheless these things profited them so little that it is clear there were scarcely any others more foolish in religion or less fit to admit the faith of Christ. For they had consecrated an altar to an unknown god, and they mocked Paul when he spoke about the kingdom of Christ and the resurrection of the dead, so that it is clear he was regarded as a babbler nowhere else on earth. And in later times Christian teachers always had a great deal of trouble with the philosophers, and heretics almost always came out of their schools, by whose curiosity and monstrous opinions the Christian cause was dangerously disturbed. But those who excel in the commonwealth, when they hear the gospel announced, at once think this doctrine hostile to the state and contrary to the laws, and because they fear for their honour or reputation, they try as far as possible to keep it away. And they have their courtly flatterers, who persuade them that seditions and disturbances arise from it, and so on. And although at times rays of this divine light penetrate their minds, that fear joined with political prudence stands in the way, so that they make no progress. It is clear that such were once the princes of the Jews, some of whom denied that the commonwealth would be safe unless Christ were removed from the midst, while others, although convinced in their hearts and believing, did not dare to confess him, lest they be cast out of the synagogue. But if you look at those who are puffed up with the nobility of their birth and their abundance of wealth, these too either despise the gospel with great disdain, because they already think themselves blessed and suppose they have no need of any other way of obtaining happiness; or if ever they come to hear it, they generally depart sad, like that rich man whom Matthew describes, when they understand what is required of them, and they allow the seed of the word to be choked by thorns within their minds. And these are the reasons why the gospel is generally preached to all such people without fruit.

units.la: Verumtamen nemo ista sic accipiat, ut neminem putet posse saluum fieri, qui aut ciuili prudentia & rerum vsu instructus, aut in magistratu constitutus, aut etiam generis nobilitate illustris est. Hanc enim opinionem Paulus ipse confutat, quando pro magistratibus iubet preces publicas facere, & hanc fui præcepti rationem affert, quòd Deus omnis loci & ordinis homines velit saluos facere. Et Christus, qui piscatores discipulos vocauit, minimè aspernatus est Nicodemum legisperitum, Iofephum Senatorem, Lazarum Bethanienfem cum sororibus, Magdalenam Ioannam, Chuzæ regij procuratoris vxorem, & plures alios, qui diuitijs & huius sæculi honoribus eximij fuerunt. Similiter prædicatione Pauli Sergium Paulum Cypri Procof. & Dionysium Areopagitam ad Christum conuersos fuisse legimus. Et inter Corinthiorum fideles numerantur Crispus Synagogæ præfectus, Gaius vir diues & totius ecclesiæ hospes, & Eraftus Quæstor. Quòd fi ad veteris testamenti libros accedamus, veri Dei germanos cultores inueniemus Abrahamum, Isaacum, Jacobum, Iosephum, Mosem, Davidem, & innumeros prophetas, quorum alij ex regijs, alij ex sacerdotalibus familijs oriundi fuerunt. Posteris item temporibus ad Christi fidem & ecclesiam clarissimi philosophi, eloquentissimi Oratores & viri politici innumeri acceffer, ut iam nihil dicamus de Imperatoribus, quorum authoritate (ut olim Isaias prædixerat) ecclesia defensa & sedulò propagata est. Nec, desunt nostro sæculo quantumuis infelici & omnibus modis corruptissimo viri egregiè doĉti, & multi ex prima nobilitate, qui rem Christianam & amplexi sunt ipsi, & studio singulari promouent. Nimis ergo odiosè hoc loco phanatici quidam abutuntur, qui omnes damnationi obnoxios esse iudicant, qui vel non stupidi prorsus, aut errores atq; mendici fuerint. Et debebant iisti verba Apostoli propius inspicere, qui non omnino neminem, sed non multos fecundum carnem sapientes, non multos potentes, non multos nobiles vocatos esse scribit. Et ita tunc fieri oportebat, ut illustrior effet crucis Christi virtus & efficacia, de qua nuper diximus. Interim non minus ea in alteris quoq; illis elucet, quando per tot obstacula penetrat, & eos quoq; ad Christi obedientiam trahit, qui humanæ sapientiæ, potentiæ, nobilitatis, diuitiarum atq; honorum huius sæculi illecebris detinentur. Itaq; illi minimè de salute sua desperare debent, simul tamen eosdem meminisse conuenit, quam diligenti cura ipsis opus fit, ne salutis suæ iacturam faciant.
units.tr: Yet no one should take these things in such a way as to think that no one can be saved who is endowed with civil prudence and experience of affairs, or who is placed in magistracy, or who is illustrious by noble birth. For Paul himself refutes this opinion when he bids public prayers be made for magistrates, and gives this reason for his command: that God wills all men of every place and rank to be saved. And Christ, who called fishermen as disciples, by no means disdained Nicodemus, a learned man of the law, Joseph, a senator, Lazarus of Bethany with his sisters, Joanna, the wife of Chuza, the king's steward, and several others who were outstanding in riches and the honours of this age. In the same way we read that through the preaching of Paul, Sergius Paulus, the proconsul of Cyprus, and Dionysius the Areopagite were converted to Christ. And among the faithful of Corinth are numbered Crispus, ruler of the synagogue, Gaius, a rich man and host of the whole church, and Erastus the treasurer. But if we turn to the books of the Old Testament, we shall find true genuine worshippers of God: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, David, and countless prophets, some of whom sprang from royal families, others from priestly families. In later times too, the most famous philosophers, most eloquent orators and countless statesmen came to the faith of Christ and to the church; not to mention the emperors, by whose authority (as Isaiah had foretold long ago) the church was defended and diligently propagated. Nor in our own age, however unhappy and most corrupt in every way, are there lacking men of outstanding learning, and many of the first nobility, who have both embraced the Christian cause themselves and promote it with singular zeal. Therefore certain fanatics abuse this passage too oddly, judging that all are liable to damnation who are not utterly stupid, or who have not been errant beggars. They ought to look more closely at the words of the Apostle, who does not write that no one at all, but that not many according to the flesh are wise, not many powerful, not many noble, are called. And so it had to happen then, that the power and efficacy of the cross of Christ, of which we spoke a little while ago, might be more illustrious. Meanwhile it shines no less in those others too, when it penetrates through so many obstacles and draws to the obedience of Christ even those who are held back by the allurements of human wisdom, power, nobility, riches, and the honours of this age. So those people ought by no means to despair of their salvation; yet at the same time it is fitting that they remember how much careful attention they need, lest they suffer the loss of their salvation.

units.la: Facit autem ad huius doctrinæ declarationem alterum huius comparationis membrum, quod multis exponit atq; illustrat Apostolus. Verum (inquit) quæ stulta sunt in mundo elegit Deus, ut pudefaciat sapientes, & quæ sunt infirma in mundo elegit Deus, vt pudefaciat robusta: & quæ ignobilia sunt in mundo, & pro nihilo habita, elegit Deus, & ea quæ non sunt, vt ea quæ sunt, aboleat, etc. Poterat stultos, infirmos et ignobiles nominare, sed stulta, infirma et ignobilia quæ in mundo sunt nominat, vt se de illis loqui testetur, in quibus nihil quam stultitia, infirmitas & ignobilitas siue obscuritas apparebat, vel qui potius ipsissima stultitia & infirmitas atq; ignobilitas videri poterant. Ea (inquit) elegit Deus, vt pudefaciat sapientes & eos, qui potentia & viribus pollent. Et ne quid omittat eorum, quæ ad diuini consilij illustrationem faciunt, eorum quoque meminit, quæ non sunt: ea nimirum intelligens, quæ non magis curantur ab hominibus, quam si non essent in rerum natura: & hæc quoq; Deu elegisse dicit, vt quæ in honore & pretio habentur aboleat. Ista vero tam diligenti enumeratione omnia remouet & excludit, quibus homines fidere aut gloriari solent: vt his procul e medio sublatis, in sola Dei gratia atq; misericordia sperandum esse intelligamus. Quid enim apud Deum mereantur, qui diuina ne intelligunt quidem, & in regni cœlorum mysterijs plus quam stulti, cæci et stupidi sunt? Quid item suis viribus effectu dabunt, qui ne ad cogitandum quidem sunt idonei, neq; aliquid possunt in ijs, quæ ad corpus pertinent? Quis enim pilum unu potest album aut nigrum facere[?]? Quis corporis staturæ cubitum aut palmum vnum addere aut detrahere potest? Quæ autem poterit eorum dignitas esse apud Deum, qui inter homines quoq; nullam habebunt, si ad primam eorum conditionem descendamus? Gentes certe olim non populus dicebantur (vt Paulus ex Hosea annotauit) eo quod a repub. Israelis exclusi, in Dei populo no magis censebantur, quam si nusquam extarent. Iudæorum autem conditio deterior fuit, eo quod maiori cum ingratitudine Dei iram contra se prouocauerunt: ideoq; non vno loco apud Prophetas gentibus incircumcisis accensentur. Quia tamen ex his omnibus ecclesiam suam Deus elegit, & vtrinq; eos fere elegit, qui mundo stultissimi & nullius pretij esse videbantur, quiq; neq; potentia neq; authoritate publica pollebant, quis non dicat eum elegisse quæ non erant, & proinde electionis suæ causam non posse aliam constitui quam gratuitam eius bonitatem atq; misericordiam?
units.tr: This second part of the comparison, which the Apostle sets out and illustrates at length, also serves to explain this teaching. "But," he says, "God has chosen the foolish things of the world, that he may shame the wise; and God has chosen the weak things of the world, that he may shame the strong; and the base things of the world, and the things that are despised, has God chosen, and things which are not, that he may bring to nought things that are." He could have called them foolish, weak and base, but he says "the foolish, weak and base things of the world," so that he shows he is speaking of those in whom nothing appeared except foolishness, weakness and baseness or obscurity, or rather those who could be seen as foolishness, weakness and baseness itself. "These," he says, "God has chosen, to shame the wise and those who are powerful and mighty." And so that he omits nothing that serves to illustrate God's purpose, he also mentions the things that are not: meaning those that men care for no more than if they did not exist in nature. God has chosen these too, he says, to bring to nothing those things that are held in honour and esteem. Yet by this so careful enumeration he removes and excludes all the things on which men are accustomed to rely or to boast, so that, with these removed from the midst, we may understand that hope must rest on the grace and mercy of God alone. For what can those merit before God who do not even understand divine things, and who in the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven are more than foolish, blind and dull? Likewise, what will those accomplish by their own strength who are not even fit to think, and can do nothing in those things which pertain to the body? For who can make one hair white or black? Who can add or take away one cubit or span of stature? Moreover, what dignity could they have before God who will have no place even among men, if we go back to their original condition? Certainly the Gentiles were once not called a people (as Paul noted from Hosea), because, excluded from the commonwealth of Israel, they were counted in the people of God no more than if they nowhere existed. The condition of the Jews was worse, because with greater ingratitude they provoked the wrath of God against themselves; therefore in more than one place the Prophets number them among the uncircumcised Gentiles. Yet since God has chosen his Church from all these, and has chosen from both peoples almost those who seemed most foolish to the world and of no worth, and who were neither powerful nor held public authority, who would not say that he has chosen things that are not, and that therefore the cause of his election can be nothing other than his free goodness and mercy?

units.la: At quæ causa fuit Deo (inquis) vt rem ita institueret? Respondet Paulus: Vt ne glorietur vlla caro coram eo. Carnis nomine utitur scriptura, quando de homine per extremum contemptum loquitur, vt eius naturam nō minus vitiosam & corruptam quam infirmam denotet. Sic enim hac voce apud Mosem Deus usus est: Nō contendet spiritus meus perpetuò cum homine, eo quod caro est. Et notum est illud propheticum: Omnis caro fœnum, & omnis gloria carnis flos agri. Sensus ergo istius loci est: Voluit hanc in vocandis hominibus rationem obseruare Deus, vt omnes videant atq; intelligant, se nihil aliud quam carnem esse, neq; aliquid habere, cuius nomine in ipsius conspectu efferantur atq; superbiant. Diserte autem dicit, CORAM EO. Nam non ignorabat Paulus, homines multa habere quibus in hoc mundo apud sui similes gloriantur, vt pote opes, honores, victorias, triumphos & alia huius generis: sed quia nihil in his omnibus solidum & stabile est, leuis quoq; & momentanea est, quæ in his quæritur gloria, neq; Deo probatur, qui superbis resistere, humilibus autem gratiam largiri consueuit.
units.tr: "But what reason did God have," you ask, "for arranging the matter in this way?" Paul answers: "That no flesh should glory before him." Scripture uses the word flesh when it speaks of man with the utmost contempt, to denote his nature as no less vicious and corrupt than weak. For God used this word in this way through Moses: "My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh." And that prophetic saying is well known: "All flesh is grass, and all the glory of flesh is as the flower of the field." The sense of this passage, then, is this: God wished to observe this principle in calling men, so that all might see and understand that they are nothing but flesh, and have nothing in whose name they may be exalted and boast in his sight. He says plainly, IN HIS SIGHT. For Paul was not unaware that men have many things in which they glory in this world among their like, such as wealth, honours, victories, triumphs and other things of this kind. But because nothing in all these is solid and stable, the glory sought in them is also fleeting and momentary, and it is not approved by God, who is accustomed to resist the proud and to give grace to the humble.

units.la: Porro cum insipientes secundum carnem, infirmos & ignobiles ideo vocatos esse Paulus scri-bat, ne quis coram Deo glorietur, non obscure innuit, illis ipsis etiam quos hic nominat, gloriandi materiam esse ereptam. Meminerint ergo illi, se non propter conditionem suam mundi iudicio vilem & contemptam saluos fieri, sed suam quoq; salutem ex mera & gratuita Dei misericordia pendere. Quod propter eos annotamus, qui ex sua egestate, infirmitate, ignobilitate & contemptissimo statu meritum fabricare consueuerunt, quasi his sibi Deum debitorem fecerint. Est horum ingens numerus hodie, qui vt sibi ipsis in sua illa conditione satis misera mirifice placent: ita nimium præcipiti iudicio omnes damnare & Orco devouere audent, quicunq; lautiori fortuna fruuntur. At meminisse eos oportebat, opes (de iustis & legitimè partis loquor) honores, dignitates, generis splendorem, inter Dei dona numerari: paupertatem verò, labores, famem, seruitutem & quæ his coniuncta sunt mala, ex peccato originem duxisse. Quod si ergo, quoad æternæ salutis causam, non licet illis gloriari, quæ præclara & eximia Dei dona sunt, quæ stultitia est in alteris istis meritum salutis constituere, quibus peccata & carnem nostram in peccatis lasciuientem Deus castigare solet.
units.tr: Moreover, since Paul writes that the foolish according to the flesh, the weak and the base have been called for this reason, that no one should glory before God, he clearly hints that the very persons he names here have been deprived of the matter of boasting. Let them therefore remember that they are not saved because of their condition, which is worthless and despised in the judgement of the world, but that their salvation also depends on the sheer and free mercy of God. We note this on account of those who are accustomed to build up merit from their poverty, weakness, obscurity and most contemptible state, as if by these they had made God their debtor. There is today a vast number of such people, who are wonderfully pleased with themselves in that condition, which is quite wretched enough; and with overhasty judgement they dare to condemn all who enjoy a more prosperous fortune and to consign them to hell. But they ought to remember that wealth (I speak of wealth justly and lawfully gained), honours, dignities and the splendour of birth are numbered among the gifts of God, whereas poverty, labours, hunger, slavery and the evils joined with these have their origin in sin. If, then, with regard to the cause of eternal salvation, it is not lawful for them to glory in those things which are the noble and excellent gifts of God, what folly it is to set up the merit of salvation in those other things, by which God is accustomed to chastise our sins and our flesh which runs riot in sin.

units.la: Debet ergo totus iste locus bifariam considerari. Primo, ut diuites & qui in mundo alijs honoratiores sunt, discant nihil sibi ipsis aut propriae dignitati tribuere, sed potius humiliari sub potenti manu Dei, qui hac gratia ipsos dignatus est. Id vero ab illis facile impetrabitur, si cogitent, quam lubrica & periculosa sit ipsorum conditio, non quidem quod Dei dona per se noxia & periculosa sint, sed quod illis caro in propriam perniciem abuti consueuit, dum pessimus suis desiderijs indulget. Vigilent ergo diligenter, & recte omnibus utantur, neque unquam animis eorum excidat, de pluribus rationem Deo reddituros esse eos, qui plura quam alij acceperunt. Deinde pauperum, infirmorum, obscurorum & contemptorum consolationi ista seruiant, ne se propter suam illam con-ditionem a Deo derelictos esse & perpetuo negligi existiment. Quin potius cogitent se maximis impedimentis liberatos, ad capessendum regnum Dei expeditiores atq; magis idoneos esse factos. Quia enim in fortuna lautiori fere spiritus maiores æquo concipimus, & elatis cristis[?] aduersus Deum quoq; proteruire audemus, neq; de futuris & cœlestibus bonis unquam serio cogitamus, necesse est omnino nos humiliari, ut vel inuiti confidentiam istam deponamus, & vere pauperes spiritu efficiamur, quibus regnum cœlorum Christus pollicetur. Vidit hoc Dauid, qui pœne mul-tas & graues afflictiones clamabat.Bonum mihi, quod humiliatus sum, ut discerem decreta tua. Item: Antequam affligerer, errabam: nunc autem eloquium tuum custodio. Et imprimis memorabile est, quod ad Romanianum, qui ex summis honoribus & lautissima fortuna in extremas miserias deiectus erat, scribit D. Augustinus: An vero si tu viueres in aedificiorum exquisitissimis molibus, in nitore balnearum, in tesseris quas honestas non respuit, in venatibus, in conuiuijs, in ore clientum, in ore ciuium, in ore denique populorum humanissimus, liberalissimus, mundissimus, fortunatissimus iactareris, quisquam tibi Romaniane, beata alterius vita, quae sola beata est, quisquam quaeso mentionem facere auderet? Quisquam tibi persuadere posset, non solum te felicem non esse, sed eo maxime miserum, quo tibi minime videreris? Quod ab Augustino verissime dictum esse omnes fatebuntur, qui in seipsos paulo altius descenderint. Et qui haec diligentius expendunt, ij non facile aduersus offenduntur, & efficacissimam ex eo consolationem sentiunt quod haec ipsis in bonum cessura esse non dubitant. Facit praeterea locus iste aduersus eos, qui hodie Euangelium hoc potissimum nomine damnant, quod ab ijs fere recipiatur, qui hominum contemptissimi sunt, eos autem hostes habeat, qui summam sapientiae existimatione sustinent, & penes quos est omnis rerum potestas. Atq; hoc olim quoq; factum audimus, & Christus idem testatur, dicens: Gratias ago tibi pater, quod abscondeUS hoc a sapientibus & prudentibus, reuelaris autem ea paruulis, &c. Vide Matth.11.cap.
units.tr: This whole passage ought therefore to be considered in two ways. First, that the rich, and those who are more esteemed than others in the world, may learn to attribute nothing to themselves or to their own dignity, but rather to be humbled under the mighty hand of God, who has deigned to bestow this grace upon them. This will easily be obtained from them if they consider how slippery and dangerous their condition is; not that the gifts of God are in themselves harmful and dangerous, but because the flesh is accustomed to abuse them to its own destruction, while it indulges its evil desires. Let them therefore watch carefully and use all things rightly, and never let it slip from their minds that those who have received more than others will have to give account to God for more. Second, let this passage serve to console the poor, the weak, the obscure and the despised, so that they may not think they have been forsaken by God and are neglected for ever because of their condition. Rather let them reflect that they have been freed from very great hindrances and made more ready and better fitted to lay hold of the kingdom of God. For since we commonly conceive greater spirits than is right in a more prosperous fortune, and dare even to act insolently against God with lifted crests, and never seriously think of future and heavenly goods, we must necessarily be humbled, so that even unwillingly we lay aside that confidence and are made truly poor in spirit, to whom Christ promises the kingdom of heaven. David saw this, who, when he was afflicted by many and grievous troubles, cried: "It is good for me that I have been humbled, that I might learn your statutes." Likewise: "Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now I keep your word." And especially memorable is what Augustine writes to Romanianus, who had been cast down from the highest honours and most splendid fortune into the greatest miseries: "But if you were living amid the most exquisite structures of buildings, in the splendour of baths, at games of dice which honourable men do not spurn, in hunting, at banquets, on the lips of clients, on the lips of citizens, and finally on the lips of peoples, being hailed as most courteous, most generous, most elegant and most fortunate, would anyone, Romanianus, dare, I ask, to make mention of the blessed life of another, which alone is blessed? Could anyone persuade you that you were not only not happy, but were most wretched precisely in the very thing in which you seemed least so?" All who examine themselves a little more deeply will admit that Augustine said this most truly. Those who weigh these things more diligently are not easily offended by them, and they feel a most effective consolation from this, because they do not doubt that these things will turn out for their good. This passage moreover speaks against those who today condemn this Gospel chiefly on this ground, that it is received mostly by those who are the most despised of men, while it has as enemies those who hold the highest reputation for wisdom and in whose hands is all power over affairs. We hear that this also happened of old, and Christ himself testifies to it, saying: "I thank you, Father, that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and have revealed them to babes," etc. See Matthew 11.

units.la: Facit ad huius consolationis confirmationem altera huius loci pars, qua doctrinam hanc pro pius applicat Corinthijs, ne propter ista, quae dixerat, salutis spem omnem abijcerent. Sed ex ipso vos estis in CHRISTO IESV, &c. Quasi diceret. Haec quidem de vobis dico, adeoq; omnibus, qui Christo nomen dederunt. Sed non propterea animum deijcere debetis, aut putare, quod haec in vestrum contemptum dicta sint. Nam licet aliquando tales fueritis, ut mortalium stultissimi, infirmissimi, abiectissimi, imo nulli prorsus videri potueritis, tamen ex Deo estis. Loquitur autem non de creatione, secundum quam omnes homines, imo etiam animantia bruta atq; res inanimatae omnes ex Deo sunt: sed de regeneratione & creatione spirituali, qua ex peccatoribus iusti, ex filijs irae filij gratiae & regni cœlorum haeredes facti sumus: Quo nomine ad Ephesios quoq; cap. 2. nos ποίημα τῶ θεῶ[?] id est, opus Dei dicit, conditos nimirum in CHRISTO IESV ad opera bona, &c. Itaq; quos paulo ante eo usq; deiecerat, ut vix hominum loco habuerit, nunc supra omnes coelos euehit, quando illos ex Deo id est, Dei filios esse dicit. Haec enim vera adeoq; unica est hominum nobilitas, quae ut non ex carne originem ducit, ita nullis etiam fortunae casibus obnoxia est, neq; ullis hominum malitiosorum iniurijs debonestatur. Ea deniq; nos fratres germanos efficit praestantissimorum hominum, quorum virtutem hodie omnes admirantur & eorundem memoriam colunt: Patriarcharum nimirum, Prophetarum, Heroum atq; Regum sanctissimorum, quotquot unquam ecclesiam Dei sua prudentia & fortitudine defenderunt, Apostolorum item & Martyrum, adeoq; omnium, qui nunc cum CHRISTO IESV in coelesti gloria viuunt & triumphant. Ne quis tamen inde novam superbiendi causam arriperet, rursus tantae dignitatis causam sive originem nobi nobis in CHRISTO IESV monstrat, extra quem nihil quàm stultitia, infirmitas, infamia, miseria & maledictio est omne id, circa quod homines occupantur. At quotquot illum recipiunt (inquit Ioannes) eis hanc dignitatem dat, vt filij Dei fiant, ijs nimirum qui credunt in nomen eius. Ita verò Paulus omnes quasi cogit, vt ad Christum recurrant & hunc fide vera apprehendant, siquidem cum Deo conciliari, & eius filij atq; hæredes fieri cupiant. Et vt fortius illos vrgeat, ostendit simul quis nam sit Christus, & quanta nobis bona in illo Pater offerat. Qui (inquit) factus est nobis sapientia à Deo, iustitia, & sanctificatio, & redemptio. Est hæc vna ex præcipuis sententijs noui testamenti, & paucis omnia comprehendit, quæ de humanæ redemptionis atque salutis negotio dici possunt, & proinde digna est, cuius singulas partes ex ordine consideremus.
units.tr: Another part of this passage helps to confirm this comfort, in which Paul applies the teaching piously to the Corinthians, so that because of what he has said they should not cast away all hope of salvation. "But of him are you in Christ Jesus," etc. As if he were saying: I say these things about you, and indeed about all who have given their name to Christ. But you ought not on that account to lose heart, or think that these things were said to your contempt. For although at some time you were such that you seemed to be the most foolish, weakest and most abject of mortals, indeed to be nothing at all, nevertheless you are of God. He speaks, however, not of creation, by which all men, indeed even brute animals and inanimate things, are of God, but of regeneration and spiritual creation, by which from sinners we have become righteous, from children of wrath children of grace and heirs of the kingdom of heaven. For this reason in Ephesians 2 also he calls us God's workmanship [ποίημα τοῦ θεοῦ], that is, the work of God, created, of course, in Christ Jesus for good works, etc. So he who a little before had cast them down so far that he scarcely counted them as men now lifts them above all the heavens, when he says that they are of God, that is, sons of God. For this is the true and only nobility of men, which, since it does not derive its origin from flesh, is so not subject to any chances of fortune, nor is it dishonoured by any injuries of malicious men. Finally, it makes us true brothers of the most excellent men, whose virtue all admire today and whose memory they honour: namely the patriarchs, prophets, heroes and most holy kings, as many as have ever defended the Church of God by their wisdom and courage, likewise the apostles and martyrs, and indeed all who now live and triumph with Christ Jesus in heavenly glory. Lest anyone, however, seize from this a new cause for pride, he again shows the cause and origin of such great dignity to us in Christ Jesus, outside whom everything with which men are occupied is nothing but folly, weakness, infamy, misery and cursing. But, says John, to as many as receive him he gives this dignity, that they should become sons of God, namely to those who believe in his name. Thus Paul in effect compels all to hasten back to Christ and to lay hold of him with true faith, since they desire to be reconciled to God and to become his sons and heirs. And to press them more strongly, he shows at the same time who Christ is and how great the goods the Father offers us in him. "Who," he says, "was made to us wisdom from God, righteousness, sanctification and redemption." This is one of the principal sayings of the New Testament, and in a few words it comprehends all that can be said about the business of human redemption and salvation, and therefore it is worthy that we consider its individual parts in order.

units.la: Primò, cùm Christum nobis sapientiam, iustitiam, sanctificationem & redemptionem factum dicit, non obscurè innuit, qui nam & quales nos simus, si ille à nobis auferatur: Stulti nimirum in omnibus ijs, quæ ad regnum Dei faciunt. Nam vt infra docebit, animalis homo non percipit ea quæ sunt spiritus Dei. Imò si quid hîc ex semetipsis statuere volunt qui hominum sapientissimi habentur, stultitiam suam ita produnt, vt nihil illis stultius & ineptius fingi possit: sicuti philosophorum exemplo demonstratur. Roman. 1. At non stulti modò sumus, verùmetiam iniusti & peccatores, & quidem natura. Quia enim in sua imagine filios suos Adam genuit, peccatum ex illo in nos omnes propagatum est, adeò, vt in peccato concipiantur & nascantur quicunque ex Adamo descendunt. Itaque latet in illis lex peccati & naturæ vitiositas, qua fit, vt figmenta cordis ipsorum prava sint ab ineunte ætate. Fieri ergo non potest (vt in Iobo scribitur) vt homo sceleris purus, & qui ex muliere natus est, mundus sit. Sequitur ex eo, quòd prophani & à Deo alieni sumus. Quia enim peccata inter hunc & nos instar maceriæ sunt, ab illo exclusi & separati sint oportet, quicunque peccatis obnoxij sunt: vt recte Paulus alibi nos sine Deo fuisse scribat. Accedit his mali omnis colophon, quod Satanæ captiui & mancipia sumus. Nam à quo quis superatur (vt Petrus ait) eiin seruitutem addicitur. Atqui vt primos parentes tentatione fraudulenta diabolus vicit: ita quotidie nos quoque vincit, dum pravis cupiditatibus, quas ille in nobis accendit, cedimus atque indulgemus. Quid ergo aliud restat, quàm quòd æterno exitio devoti sumus, nisi aliunde nobis auxilium & redemptor sese offerat?
units.tr: First, when he says that Christ was made to us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption, he clearly hints who and what we are if he is taken away from us: foolish, of course, in all those things that pertain to the kingdom of God. For, as he will teach below, the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God. Indeed, if those who are held to be the wisest among men wish to decide anything here from themselves, they betray their folly so that nothing more foolish and inept can be imagined, as is shown by the example of the philosophers (Romans 1). But we are not only foolish but also unrighteous and sinners, and that by nature. For since Adam begot his sons in his own image, sin has been propagated from him into us all, so that all who descend from Adam are conceived and born in sin. Hence there lies hidden in them the law of sin and the vicious nature, by which it comes about that the imaginations of their hearts are evil from their youth. Therefore it cannot be (as is written in Job) that a man who is born of a woman, pure from sin, should be clean. It follows from this that we are profane and alien from God. For since sins stand between him and us like a wall, all who are liable to sins must of necessity be excluded and separated from him, as Paul rightly writes elsewhere that we were without God. To these is added the crowning evil, that we are captives and slaves of Satan. For by whom a man is overcome (as Peter says), to him he is given over as a slave. And as the devil overcame our first parents by deceitful temptation, so he daily overcomes us also, while we yield and indulge the wicked desires which he kindles in us. What then remains, except that we are doomed to eternal destruction, unless a help and a redeemer offers himself to us from elsewhere?

units.la: Vbi vero ista inueniri poterunt? Paulus Christum nobis à Deo sapientiam, &c. factum esse dicit. Salus ergo nostra omnis ex vno Deo promanat, & proinde nō minus turpiter quàm perniciosè errant, quicunq; hanc vel in semetipsis, vel apud alios siue illi cœlites siue in vita superstites sint, quærunt. At quia paulò ante disertus verbis testatus est, Deum neque meriti neque dignitatis alicuius, quæ in nobis sit, respectum habuisse, sed potius ea elegisse, quæ in mundo stulta, infirma, obscura & contempta sunt, reliquum est, vt totum salutis nostræ beneficium gratuita eius misericordiæ acceptum feramus, & in hac quæramus fontes redemptionis atque vitæ æternæ. Quid enim in nobis est, quo Deus opus habeat? aut quid habemus boni, quod non ille nobis prior dederit? Et huc facit celebre illud Christi dictum: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, vt Filium suum vnigenitum pro illo daret, vt omnis qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam: Cuius expositionem Ioannes afferens, in epistola sua Catholica sic scribit: In hoc est charitas, non quòd nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quòd ipse dilexerit nos, &c. Item: Nos diligimus eum, quoniam ipse prior dilexit nos. Vide 1. Ioan. 4.
units.tr: But where can these things be found? Paul says that Christ was made to us by God wisdom, etc. Therefore all our salvation flows from the one God, and therefore those who seek it either in themselves or among others, whether among the heavenly beings or among those still living in this life, err no less shamefully than destructively. But since a little before he testified plainly in words that God had regard neither to merit nor to any dignity that is in us, but rather chose those things which are foolish, weak, obscure and despised in the world, it remains that we should receive the whole benefit of our salvation as a gift of his free mercy, and seek in him the fountains of redemption and eternal life. For what is there in us that God needs? Or what good do we have that he did not first give us? And to this purpose is that famous saying of Christ: "God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for it, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life." John, setting forth the exposition of this in his Catholic epistle, writes thus: "In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us," etc. Likewise: "We love him, because he first loved us." See 1 John 4.

units.la: At quia nobis ob conditionem nostram miseram atq; omnibus modis corruptam Mediatore apud Deum opus erat, hunc quoq; ostendit Paulus, IESVM CHRISTVM videlicet, cui ipse Pater hoc testimonium cœlitus perhibet, quod Filius ille dilectus sit, in quo ipse nobis placatus est. Ne quem verò species eius vilis atq; humilis offendat, talem esse docet, qui morbis nostris omnibus fideliter & perfectè medeatur. Quia enim nos stultos dixit, illum nobis Sapientiam factum esse admonet. Causa huius dicti est, quod in illo Pater seipsum & voluntatem suam nobis reuelauit. Deum (inquit Ioannes) nemo vidit vnquam: sed Filius ille vnigenitus, qui est in sinu Patris, ipse nobis annunciauit. Et Paulus ad Colossenses, in illo reconditos esse scribit omnes thesauros scientiæ & cognitionis Dei. Sed & ipse apud Ioannem ait: Qui me videt, Patrem videt. Item: Vos amicos dixi, quia omnia quæ audiui à Patre meo, nota vobis feci. Neq; ista temere dici[?] res ipsa do-cet, quando videmus admirabili rerum cœlestium cognitione omnes eos illuminari & confirmari, qui in Christum credunt, etiamsi mundo indocti & illiterati sint. At si Christus nobis à Patre Sapientia factus est, quid obsecro sapient aut decernent, qui cum Christum prorsus ignorent, sibi tamen iudicium omne sumunt in causa religionis & ecclesiæ?
units.tr: But because on account of our miserable condition, corrupted in every way, we needed a Mediator with God, Paul also shows this, namely Jesus Christ, to whom the Father himself bears witness from heaven that this beloved Son is the one in whom he is reconciled to us. Lest his lowly and humble appearance offend anyone, he teaches that he is such a one as will faithfully and perfectly heal all our diseases. For since he called us foolish, he reminds us that Christ has been made Wisdom for us. The reason for this saying is that in him the Father revealed himself and his will to us. "No one has ever seen God," says John, "but that only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has himself declared him to us." And Paul writes to the Colossians that in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge of God. But he himself also says in John: "He who sees me sees the Father." Likewise: "I have called you friends, because all that I heard from my Father I have made known to you." Nor is this said rashly; the thing itself teaches it, when we see that all who believe in Christ are enlightened and confirmed by a wonderful knowledge of heavenly things, even if they are unlearned and unlettered in the world. But if Christ has been made Wisdom to us by the Father, what, I beg you, will those judge wisely or decide, who know Christ not at all, and yet take to themselves every judgment in matters of religion and the Church?

units.la: Deinde iustitia quoq; nobis factus est Christus, quia & pro peccatis nostris satisfecit, & suam nobis obedientiam communicat, quæ nobis propter fidem in ipsum imputatur. Verumq; Paulus in epistola ad Romanos fusius explicat. Sicut per contumaciam unius hominis, Adami nimirum, peccatores facti sunt multi: ita per obedientiam unius Christi, iusti constituentur multi. Et in eadem epistola subinde inculcat, nos fide iustificari, eò quod fide Christum apprehendimus, qui nobis à Patre iustitia factus est.
units.tr: Then Christ was also made righteousness for us, because he both satisfied for our sins and communicates to us his obedience, which is imputed to us on account of faith in him. Paul explains this more fully in the epistle to the Romans: "As by the disobedience of one man, namely Adam, many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one, Christ, many shall be made righteous." And in the same epistle he repeatedly insists that we are justified by faith, because by faith we lay hold of Christ, who was made righteousness for us by the Father.

units.la: Accedit his tertium Sanctificatio, qua omnino opus est, ut toti Deo coniungamur. Ergo non modo nos iustificat Christus, verumetiam regenerat ex verbi femine per spiritus sancti virtutem, & (ut discipulis dicebat) ex mundo hoc selectos Patri consecrat, ut posthac non nobisipsis, multo minus aut diabolo & peccato, sed illi soli vivamus. Et hic, quoad huius vitae curriculum, proprius iustificationis fructus est, de quo ipse Christus sub vitis & palmitum parabola diligenter admonuit. Est ergo intolerabilis eorum licentia, qui sub fidei Christianæ prætextu impie & scelerate vivunt: calumniatores item virulenti sunt, qui doctrinam fidei bonis operibus inimicam esse clamant. Etsi enim his quenquam iustificari merito negemus, cum neq; proprijs viribus ea faciamus, neq; illa in nobis perfecta sint: ijsdem tamen pro virili studeant quicunq; per Christum ex peccati seruitio erepti & Deo sanctificati sunt. Quod autem multi libertate Christiana ad carnis licentiam abutuntur, & hanc fucata fidei professione palliant, minimè nobis fraudi esse debet, qui bus cum illis & vita ipsorum nequaquam conuenit. Et habebunt illi suum iudicium, quod ipsis Christus iampridem denuntiauit, ut Matth.7.cap. est videre.
units.tr: Third comes sanctification, which we absolutely need, so that we are joined wholly to God. Christ therefore not only justifies us but also regenerates us from the seed of the word through the power of the Holy Spirit, and (as he said to his disciples) consecrates us to the Father, chosen out of this world, so that henceforth we may live not to ourselves, much less to the devil and sin, but to him alone. And this is, for the course of this life, the proper fruit of justification, about which Christ himself warned diligently in the parable of the vine and the branches. It is therefore intolerable, the license of those who live impiously and wickedly under the pretext of the Christian faith. Likewise the slanderers are virulent who cry out that the doctrine of faith is hostile to good works. For although we deny that anyone is justified by these works, since we do not do them by our own strength, nor are they perfect in us, nevertheless all who have been snatched from the bondage of sin through Christ and sanctified to God should strive for them to the best of their ability. That many abuse Christian liberty for licentiousness of the flesh and cloak it with a pretended profession of faith ought in no way to harm us, whose life does not at all agree with theirs. They will have their judgment, which Christ long ago announced to them, as can be seen in Matth. 7.

units.la: Postremo illum nobis redemptionem factum esse ait. Nam seipsum pro nobis tradidit, & pro-inde sanguinis sui pretio nos ex peccati & diaboli seruitio redemit, ne quid iuris ille porro in nos habeat. Et quia peccatis noxam expiauit, simul pœnis quoq; omnibus liberat, quibus Deus humanum genus propter peccatum multauit. At hic meminisse oportet, redemptionis huius fructum in hoc sæculo tantum inchoari, dum carnis desideria spiritu suo coercet, ne peccatum in nobis dominetur: dum item aduersa omnia & afflictiones, quæ impijs peccatorum pœnæ sunt, nobis auspicatas reddit, & ita moderatur, ut nobis in bonum cedant, & salutis sint adminicula: dum denique in ipsa morte tuetur, & eam, quæ peccati pœna omnibus fuit, credentibus transitum fecit ad vitam æternam. Olim vero cum dies ille restitutionis omnium aduenerit, quo tota hæc mundi machina libe-rabitur, nostra quoq; redemptio perficietur: quia tunc corpora quoq; ad beatam immortalitatem & cœlestis regni gaudia resurgent. Ideo Christus cum infelicem nouissimi sæculi statu exposuisset unà cum signis, quæ ipsius aduentum præcedent, addit: Cum hæc fieri incipient suspicite, & attollite capita vestra, quoniam appropinquat redemptio vestra.
units.tr: Lastly he says that he has been made our redemption. For he gave himself up for us, and so by the price of his blood he redeemed us from the bondage of sin and the devil, so that the devil may have no further right over us. And since he has expiated the guilt of sins, he at the same time frees us from all the punishments with which God chastised the human race on account of sin. Here, however, we ought to remember that the fruit of this redemption is only begun in this age: while he restrains the desires of the flesh by his Spirit, so that sin does not reign in us; while he also turns all adversities and afflictions, which are punishments of sins for the wicked, into beginnings for us, and so moderates them that they turn to our good and serve as aids to salvation; and finally while he protects us in death itself and has made that death, which was the punishment of sin for all, a passage for believers to eternal life. But on that day of the restoration of all things, when this whole machine of the world will be set free, our redemption too will be completed, because then the bodies also will rise to blessed immortality and the joys of the heavenly kingdom. Therefore Christ, when he had set forth the unhappy state of the last age together with the signs that will precede his coming, adds: "When these things begin to happen, look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption draws near."

units.la: Et hæc quidem omnia nobis in Christo largitur Deus, quæ vniuersam hominis beatitudinem in se continent. Solus ergo nobis sufficere debet, neq; aliquis admittendus est in huius gloriæ consortium. Quod enim de Christo hic dicitur, hæc de nullo vel Angelorum vel hominum vspiam dici possunt, nisi dictu inveniens. Ut ergo ingratitudo magna est, si suum Christo honorem eripere, & in alios transferre audeamus: ita non minor est stultitia[?] per cisternas fissas[?] atq; pertusas ea quærere, quæ apud unum Christum, vitæ & salutis fontem perennem atq; inexhaustum inveniuntur. Hæc ergo nos in omni tentationis genere consolentur, & binc petamus argumenta, quibus Satanam profligemus, dum nos propriæ conscientiæ testimonio convincere & ad desperationem adigere conatur. Obijcit ille, nos stultos[?] esse, & nequicquam occupari circa æternæ salutis rationem, cum non percipiamus ea, quæ sunt spiritus Dei. Hic respondet: At Christus mihi factus est sapientia, & cum idem ille via & lux & veritas sit, ego si hunc sequar, aberrare non potero. Regerit quadruplator ille: At qui peccator, imò nihil nisi peccatum es: Respondè, Fateor: sed Christus mea est iustitia, quæ per fidem apprehensa me ad Dei tribunal omni reatu liberat. Obstrepit ille rursus: Quomodo autem in Dei conspectum unquam venies, qui natura prophanus & à Deo alienus es? Annon scriptura ait, sine sanctimonia nemo videbit Deum? Hic istud quoque fatere, sed adde: Christus mihi fa-ctus est sanctificatio. Quòd si jam clamet satan: At jampridem Dei sententia damnatus & exitio sempiterno devotus es, neque sententiam illam suam Deus unquam revocabit, Maledictus omnis qui non fecerit quaecunque scripta sunt in libro legis, & dicet omnis populus, Amen. Ubi respondebis: Sum equidem damnatus & filius irae, quantum in me est, sed redemptio mea est Christus, qui dilexit me, & semetipsum pro me tradidit. Et tu quis es, qui crimina intentes adversus electos Dei? Deus est qui justificat, quis est qui condemnet? Haec si animis nostris probe inscripta, & in conscientia tentationibus semper in promptu habeamus, facile victoriam reportabimus.
units.tr: God bestows on us in Christ all these things, which contain within themselves the whole happiness of man. Christ alone therefore ought to suffice us, and no one is to be admitted into the fellowship of this glory. For what is said here of Christ cannot be said of any angel or man anywhere, unless by a misuse of words. As it is great ingratitude to dare to snatch away Christ's honor and transfer it to others, so it is no less folly to seek among cracked and leaking cisterns what is found in Christ alone, the perennial and inexhaustible fountain of life and salvation. Let these things, then, console us in every kind of temptation, and let us take from here the arguments by which we may overthrow Satan, when he tries to convince us by the testimony of our own conscience and drive us to despair. He objects that we are foolish and labour in vain about the reckoning of eternal salvation, since we do not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God. Here let us answer: "But Christ has been made wisdom to me, and since he is the way, the light and the truth, if I follow him I cannot go astray." That wretched accuser retorts: "But you are a sinner, indeed nothing but sin." Answer: "I confess it; but Christ is my righteousness, which, apprehended by faith, frees me from all guilt before the tribunal of God." He barks again: "But how will you ever come into the sight of God, you who are profane by nature and alien from God? Does not Scripture say that without holiness no one will see God?" Here too confess this, but add: "Christ has been made my sanctification." And if Satan now cries out: "But you have long since been condemned by God's sentence and devoted to eternal destruction, and God will never revoke that sentence: Cursed is everyone who does not do all that is written in the book of the law; and all the people shall say, Amen." Here you will answer: "I am indeed condemned and a child of wrath, so far as lies in me, but my redemption is Christ, who loved me and gave himself up for me. And who are you, who bring charges against the elect of God? It is God who justifies; who is he who condemns?" If we have these things written well upon our minds and always ready in our consciences for temptations, we shall easily win the victory.

units.la: Porrò finem istorum omnium videamus, quem Paulus his verbis indicat: Ut sicut scriptum est, Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur. Extat locus Jeremiae 9. cap. ubi sic loquitur Dominus: Ne glorietur sapiens in sapientia sua, neque glorietur robustus in robore suo, nec glorietur dives in divitiis suis: sed in hoc glorietur qui gloriatur, quòd intelligat & cognoscat me: quoniam ego sum Dominus, qui misericordiam, justitiam & judicium facio in terra, &c. Pulchre ergo ista Pauli institutio conveniunt, qui paulò ante omnem gloriandi materiam illis eripuit, qui extra Christum, & proinde nil nisi caro sunt: nunc autem hominibus Christianis, qui per Christum renati, justificati, sanctificati & redempti sunt, ut glorientur permittit quidem, sed in Domino. Et hic finis proprius est omnium, quae Christus fecit, ut nimirum & nos servemur, & in nobis Deus glorificetur. Et hoc quidem vult ille, non quòd ipsius gloriae, quae immensa & aeterna est, aliquid per nos accedere possit: sed in eo quoque saluti nostrae consulit, ne donis & beneficijs eius gratuitis in propriam pernitiem abutamur. Admonet autem locus iste, Christiani hominis officium esse, ne quid sibi ipsi, sed omnem gloriam soli Deo per Christum transcribat. Quare in finem religionis Christianae peccant, quicunq; suis viribus, operibus item suis aut meritis aliquâ ex parte confidunt. Quin potius nos peccatores & omnibus modis miseros esse agnoscamus, deinde Dei misericordiam & gratuitam salutis beneficium toto corde & ore praedicemus: & quia huius Mediator est solus JESVS CHRISTVS, Filius ille Dei, & agnus immaculatus, qui nobis ab illo sapientia, justitia, sanctificatio & redemptio factus est, illum fide constanti amplectamur, & cum tota creatura ex animo dicamus: Sedenti in throno & agno debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Furthermore, let us look at the end of all these things, which Paul indicates in these words: "As it is written, let him who glories glory in the Lord." There is a passage in Jeremiah 9, where the Lord speaks thus: "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor let the strong man glory in his strength, nor let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he understands and knows me, for I am the Lord who exercises mercy, justice and judgment on the earth, etc." Paul's teaching therefore fits well: a little before, he took away from those outside Christ, who are therefore nothing but flesh, all matter for boasting; but now he permits Christian people, who have been reborn, justified, sanctified and redeemed through Christ, to glory, yet in the Lord. And this is the proper end of all that Christ has done: that we may indeed be saved, and that God may be glorified in us. He wills this not because anything could be added through us to his glory, which is immense and eternal, but he also looks to our salvation in this, so that we do not abuse his gratuitous gifts and benefits to our own ruin. This passage, moreover, admonishes that it is the duty of a Christian not to ascribe anything to himself, but to give all glory to God alone through Christ. Therefore those sin against the end of the Christian religion who trust in their own strength, or in their works or merits in any part. Rather let us acknowledge that we are sinners and wretched in every way, then proclaim God's mercy and the free benefit of salvation with our whole heart and mouth; and since the only Mediator of this is Jesus Christ, that Son of God and spotless Lamb, who has been made to us by him wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption, let us embrace him with a steadfast faith and say from the heart with the whole creation: "To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing, honour, glory and power forever. Amen."

units.la: CAPUT II. HOMILIA VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER II. HOMILY VIII.

units.la: ET ego cum venirem ad vos, fratres, non veni cum eminentia orationis aut sapientiae, annuntians vobis testimonium Dei. Non enim decrevi quicquam scire inter vos, nisi JESVM CHRISTVM, eũq; crucifixum. Et ego cum infirmitate, & timore ac tremore multo fui apud vos. Et oratio mea & praedicatio mea non fuit in persuasorijs humanae sapientiae verbis, sed in demonstratione spiritus & potentiae: ut fides vestra non esset in sapientia hominum, sed in potentia Dei.
units.tr: "And I, when I came to you, brethren, came not in excellency of speech or of wisdom, declaring unto you the testimony of God. For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified. And I was with you in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling. And my speech and my preaching was not in the persuasive words of man's wisdom, but in the shewing of the Spirit and of power: that your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God."

units.la: DIXIT nuper Paulus Apostolus, se non missum esse ad baptizandum, sed ad evangelizandum, non quidem cum sapientiae & eloquentiae ostentatione, sed simplici & inaffectato dicendi genere, ut in ea simplicitate virtus crucis Christi illustrior reddatur. In-de vero occasione sumpta in generale doctrinam digressus est, qua docuit, hoc esse Dei con-silium, ut electi & credentes per Evangelij praedicationem ferventur, quae mundi judicio stulta & infirma esse putatur: & huius consilij rationes grauissimas adduxit. His absolutis, redit ad suum exemplum, & sibi ista omnia accommodat, & multis exponit, se eam docendi rationem secutum esse inter eos, quam Deus instituerit, & proinde doctrinam eius minime contemni debere. Ita vero suam simplicitatem excusat, vt simul grauiter perstringat atq; confutet ostentatores illos, qui vt prae aliis omnibus eminerent, sapientiam quandam sublimiorem & aliis nondum cognita mysteria iactabant, & dicendi genere fastuoso & a communi vsu alieno vtebantur.
units.tr: Not long ago the Apostle Paul said that he was not sent to baptize but to preach the gospel, and not with any display of wisdom or eloquence, but in a plain and unaffected style of speaking, so that the power of the cross of Christ might shine the more clearly in that simplicity. Then, taking occasion from this, he digressed into a general doctrine, teaching that it is God's plan that the elect and believers are kindled by the preaching of the gospel, which in the judgment of the world is thought foolish and weak, and he brought forward the very weighty reasons for this plan. When this was finished, he returns to his own example, applies all these things to himself, and explains at length that among them he followed that manner of teaching which God had appointed, and that therefore his teaching ought by no means to be despised. He excuses his plainness in such a way that at the same time he sharply rebukes and refutes those showy men who, in order to stand out above all others, boasted of some higher wisdom and mysteries not yet known to others, and used a proud manner of speaking far removed from common usage.

units.la: Principio per concessionem hoc ingenue fatetur, cuius nomine pseudoapostoli illum accusabant, & pleriq; ipsum contemnebant: quod nimirum nihil sublimius saperet aut loqueretur: simul autem ostendit, se propterea non contemptu dignum esse, neq; ipsius doctrinam ideo debere viliorem putari, cum non aliud fecerit, quam quod cum Euangelij natura & argumento probe conueniat. Ego (inquit) cum ad vos venire, fratres, non veni cum eminentia orationis aut sapientiae, annuntians vobis testimonium Dei. Eminentia orationis vocat artificium rhetoricum & magnificum dicendi apparatum. At sapientiae sublimioris nomine intelligit omne id, quod carnis ratio tanqua eximium & supra communem hominum intellectum elatum admirari solet. Haec autem duo ita sibi adfuisse[?] negat, vt simul difer[?] te testetur, se testimonium Dei ipsis annuntiasse: in quo membri huius primi vis potissimum latet. Nam sensus est hic: Fateor me ad vos venisse non instructu ambitioso humanae sapientiae aut eloquentiae apparatu, neq; me mysteria alijs incognita et hucusq; inaudita iactasse: sed qualiscunq; venerim, & qualiscunq; fuerit, qua vsus sum, docendi ratio, tamen Dei testimonium vobis annuntiaui.
units.tr: At the outset, by way of concession, he frankly admits what the false apostles were accusing him of, and what many were despising him for: namely, that he savoured of nothing lofty and spoke in nothing lofty. At the same time he shows that for this reason he is not worthy of contempt, nor should his teaching be thought the less valuable, since he has done nothing other than what agrees well with the nature and subject matter of the gospel. "I," he says, "when I came to you, brethren, came not in excellency of speech or of wisdom, declaring unto you the testimony of God." By "excellency of speech" he means the art of rhetoric and the grand display of oratory. By "wisdom" he understands whatever human reason is accustomed to admire as remarkable and raised above the common understanding of men. He denies that these two were present with him, and at the same time testifies that he declared to them the testimony of God; in this the chief force of the first member lies. For the sense is this: "I admit that I came to you without the ambitious equipment of human wisdom or eloquence, and that I did not boast of mysteries unknown to others and hitherto unheard of. But whatever sort of man I came, and whatever the manner of teaching I used, I did nonetheless declare to you the testimony of God."

units.la: Dicit autem testimonium Dei ipsum Euangelium, eo quod non aliud eo continetur, quam quod Deus iam inde a prima rerum origine de Christo testatus est, & quod tandem publico testimonio confirmauit, coelitus clamans: Hic est Filius ille meus dilectus, in quo placatus sum, &c.
