Quibus verbis totius Euangelij & doctrinae apostolicae summa contineri, Petrus in epistola sua posteriori diligenter docet. Et est hoc dignissimum obseruatu: quia in eo maxime elucet doctrinae illius dignitas. In humanis & ciuilibus negotijs magnam esse testimoniorum authoritatem, nemo ignorat. Confirmatur ea legibus diuinis, quae causas controuersas ex ore duorum aut trium testium decidere iubent. Et vt scelus quouis supplicio dignum est, aliquem falso testimonio grauare: ita non minus periculosum est, testibus iuratis contradicere, & quod illi affirmarunt negare. Quanto igitur plus fidei meretur Euangelium, cuius precones sunt Apostoli, quos aeternus Dei Filius testes suos fecit, & qui nō aliud testati sunt, quam quod proprijs auribus ex illius ore hauserunt, proprijs oculis spectarunt, & manibus suis contrectauerunt? Quorum item verba cum ijs per omnia conueniunt, quae Deus olim Patribus promisit, quae Prophetae ex spiritus sancti suggestione praedixerunt, et quae coelesti oraculo tandem (vt modo diximus) iunt confirmata, qui denique testimonium suum non nudis verbis aut iureiurando solenni, sed proprio sanguine confirmarunt? Recte ergo Ioannes in sua epistola, eos Deum mendacij arguere scribit, qui Christo credere dedignantur, & Euangelij doctrinae contradicunt. Vnde colligimus, illos in ipsam Dei maiestatem peccare, & dignos esse, quos vltio diuina in finem vsq; perseque tur. At quid hodie vulgarius est, quam ea negare, quae Euangelij praedicatione de Christo traduntur? Docet ea, huc esse nobis a Deo doctore datu, quae omnes audire debeant: eundē Regē, Sacerdotē & caput ecclesiae vnicum esse tradit, qui suo honore nemini alteri cedat: in illo deniq, vno omne salutē repositā esse testatur, neq; aliud nomen sub coelo extare, per quod seruari possimus. At qui ista docent aut fatentur, ij non modo mendaces, sed impostores, scismatici, haeretici, sacrilegi & digni dicuntur, quorū memoria quoq; ferro & igne excindatur. Quod vnū si probe expendamus, nō mirabimur Dei iudicia, quib. mūdu totū hodie exercet & punit. Quid enim nō merentur, quorū impietas in ea vsq; rabie exarsit, vt Dei testimonium publice negare, imo conuitijs ta atrocibus proscindere audeat?
units.tr: He calls the testimony of God the gospel itself, because nothing else is contained in it than what God has borne witness concerning Christ from the very beginning of things, and what at last he confirmed by public testimony, crying from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased," etc. Peter diligently teaches in his second epistle that the sum of the whole gospel and of apostolic doctrine is contained in these words. And this is most worthy of observation, because in it especially the dignity of that teaching shines forth. That in human and civil affairs the authority of testimonies is great, no one is ignorant. It is confirmed by the divine laws, which command that controverted cases be decided by the mouth of two or three witnesses. And just as it is a crime deserving any punishment to burden someone with false testimony, so it is no less dangerous to contradict sworn witnesses and to deny what they have affirmed. How much more, then, does the gospel deserve belief, whose heralds are the apostles, whom the eternal Son of God made his witnesses, and who testified nothing other than what they had heard with their own ears from his mouth, seen with their own eyes, and handled with their own hands? Likewise, their words agree in every respect with what God long ago promised to the fathers, what the prophets foretold by the prompting of the Holy Spirit, and what was at last confirmed by the heavenly oracle (as we have just said); and, finally, they confirmed their testimony not with bare words or a solemn oath, but with their own blood. Rightly, therefore, John in his epistle writes that those make God a liar who disdain to believe Christ and contradict the doctrine of the gospel. From this we gather that they sin against the very majesty of God, and deserve to be pursued by divine vengeance to the end. But what is more common today than to deny those things which are delivered about Christ by the preaching of the gospel? It teaches those things which, it says, God the teacher has given to us, which everyone ought to hear; it declares that the same one is the sole King, Priest and head of the Church, who yields his honour to no other; finally, it testifies that all salvation is laid up in him alone, and that there is no other name under heaven by which we can be saved. But those who teach or confess these things are called not only liars, but impostors, schismatics, heretics, sacrilegious, and worthy that even their memory be cut off with fire and sword. If we weigh this one thing carefully, we shall not be surprised at the judgments of God, with which he today harasses and punishes the whole world. For what do they not deserve, whose impiety has blazed up in such a frenzy that they dare publicly to deny the testimony of God, and even to tear it apart with such atrocious insults?

units.la: Sed quia de hoc saepe aliàs dictum est, nunc Pauli exemplū obseruemus, qui hoc potissimum argumento se defendit, quod testimonium Dei annuntauerit, & proinde officio suo functus sit, ad quod ipsum Deus destinauerat. Itaque bene sibi conscius facile contempsit aduersariorum ludibria, calumnias atq; criminationes. Debent hoc ad se transferre omnis loci & ordinis homines, & eodem argumento se tueri atque consolari aduersus iniqua & peruersa hostium suorum de ipsis iudicia. Ridet & damnant nos quoque multi, quod ecclesiae ritus & dogmata multorum saeculorum vsu confirmata aboleamus, religionis formam nouam & nullo splendore commendabilem introducamus, ecclesiastici ministerij maiestatem labefactemus, deniq; quòd gratiæ Dei & gratuitæ redemptionis prædicatione multis licentiæ & securitatis fimus authores. At non debent nos ista offendere. Sufficiet enim ad defendendam nostram innocentiam, si testimonium Dei fideliter annuntiemus, & secundum huius præscriptum sacra omnia administremus. Ita frequenter pijs magistratibus negotium faciunt homines seditiosi & turbulenti, qui ut omnis disciplinæ iugum excutiant, illos rempub. nouis legibus grauare, rigore & seueritate nimia ut, & apertam tyrannidem exercere vociferantur. Sed non est, quòd ista eos moueant, qui se Dei iudicia enunciare, & non alium gubernationis suæ finem sibi propositum esse sciunt, quam ut populus in Dei cultu vero contineatur, innocentiæ & honestati studeat, & pacem atq; concordiam colat. Denique quisquis officium suum fecerit pro sua virili, eum propriæ conscientiæ testimonium excusat, & proinde non multum morari debet maleuolorum & Zoilorum dentes, qui undique quærunt calumniandi occasiones, ut ipsum vel contemptum vel exosum reddant.
units.tr: But since this has often been said elsewhere, let us now observe the example of Paul, who defends himself chiefly by this argument, that he declared the testimony of God, and so performed the office to which God had appointed him. Therefore, being well aware of this, he easily despised the mockeries, calumnies and accusations of his adversaries. All men of every place and rank ought to apply this to themselves, and to protect and console themselves by the same argument against the unjust and perverse judgments of their enemies about them. Many also mock and condemn us, because we abolish the rites and dogmas of the Church confirmed by the usage of many centuries, because we introduce a new form of religion commendable by no splendour, because we weaken the majesty of the ecclesiastical ministry, and finally because by preaching the grace of God and free redemption we have become authors of licence and carelessness for many. But these things ought not to offend us. For it will be enough to defend our innocence if we faithfully declare the testimony of God and administer all sacred things according to its rule. So too seditious and turbulent men often make trouble for godly magistrates: in order to shake off the yoke of all discipline, they cry out that the magistrates burden the commonwealth with new laws, and exercise an open tyranny through excessive rigour and severity. But those who know that they proclaim the judgments of God, and that the only goal of their government is that the people be kept in the true worship of God, pursue innocence and honesty, and cultivate peace and concord, need not be moved by these things. Finally, whoever has done his duty to the best of his ability, the testimony of his own conscience excuses him; and therefore he ought not to dwell long on the teeth of malicious men and Zoiluses, who on every side seek occasions to slander him, so as to make him either despised or hated.

units.la: Porro ad Paulum redeamus, qui causam reddit, cùr sapientiæ & eloquentiæ sublimioris o-stentationi minus studuerit. Non enim decreui, aut eximium siue etiam necessarium duxi, quicquam scire inter vos, nisi IESVM CHRISTVM, eumq; crucifixum. Quod non ita accipi debet, quasi Paulus artium & scientiarum aliarum omnino rudis fuerit, aut reuera nihil præ-ter Christum nouerit. Fuit enim in lege & Iudæorum traditionibus optimè instructus, ut qui sub Gamalielis, doctoris celeberrimi, disciplina supra omnes suos coætaneos profecerat. Adhæc in cælum tertium raptus mysteria viderat & audierat, quæ captum humani ingenij superant. Sed neq; exteros scriptores ignorauit, cum apud Athenienses Arati authoritate vsus sit, & in hac ipsa epistola Menandri locum adducat, Cretensium verò mores proprij & gentilitij ipsorum Poetæ Epimenidis verbis describat. Quantum autem dicendo potuerit, ex eo colligi potest, quòd Lystrenses illum putarunt Mercurium esse, quem gentes Deorum interpretem & eloquentiæ omnis authorem esse credebant. At quæcunq; mundus eximia putat, ille pro stercoribus, imò pro rebus noxijs habuit, ut Christum lucrifaceret, cuius cognitionem veram ad salutem sufficere sciebat. Noluit ergo Corinthios traditionibus vllis grauare, quas minime necessarias esse iampridem didicerat: multò minus autem in rebus superuacaneis & ad solam ostentationem facientibus laudem vel gloriam quærere. Emphasim verò habet, quòd Christi non simpliciter meminit in præsenti, sed crucifixum quoque dicit. Sciebat enim sub cruce vniuersum illius meritum & totum humanæ salutis rationem contineri: simul autem æmulos suos perstringit, qui circa inanes speculationes & ambitiosam sapientiæ atque eloquentiæ ostentationem sic occupabantur, ut ipsis crux Christi tantumnon sorderet. Solet enim hoc sciolis & humanæ philosophiæ addictis accidere: neque nostro sæculo desunt exempla eorum, qui cùm à Pontificijs superstitionibus abhorreant, & nobis minimè sint inimici, tamen Euangelij doctrina minus afficiuntur, quòd non nisi Christum & eius meritum perpetuò audiant inculcari. Pudet enim eos, si aut nihil præterea discant, aut ipsi quoque non aliud prædicent, cùm se maioris cuiusdam & non vulgaris eruditionis existimationem sustinere sciant. Suum ergo exemplum omnibus istis Paulus opponit, & habet locus iste non obscuram speciem protestationis, qualis ea est, qua ad Romanos vtitur: Non me pudet Euangelij IESV CHRISTI, quia potentia Dei est ad salutem omni credenti. Nam perinde est, ac si diceret: Glorientur illi sapientia plus quàm humana, & mysteriorum cognitionem verbis magnificis iactent, mihi tamen IESV CHRISTI cognitio sufficit, neque me meæ ignorantiæ in reliquis pudet, cùm sciam salutem omnem in solius crucis Christi merito contineri, & hunc solùm habere verba vitæ æternæ, &c.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who gives the reason why he was less concerned to make a show of higher wisdom and eloquence. "For I determined," he says, "and did not think it either excellent or even necessary to know anything among you save Jesus Christ, and him crucified." This ought not to be taken as if Paul were wholly ignorant of the arts and other sciences, or truly knew nothing besides Christ. For he was thoroughly instructed in the law and in the traditions of the Jews, having made progress beyond all his contemporaries under the discipline of Gamaliel, a most famous teacher. Moreover, he had been caught up into the third heaven, and had seen and heard mysteries which surpass the grasp of the human mind. Nor was he ignorant of the foreign writers: he used the authority of Aratus among the Athenians, quotes a passage of Menander in this very epistle, and describes the manners of the Cretans in the words of their own poet Epimenides. How much he could accomplish in speaking may be gathered from the fact that the people of Lystra thought him to be Mercury, whom the nations believed to be the interpreter of the gods and the author of all eloquence. But whatever the world considers excellent, he counted as dung, indeed as harmful things, so that he might gain Christ, whose true knowledge he knew was sufficient for salvation. Therefore he was unwilling to burden the Corinthians with any traditions, which he had long since learned were by no means necessary; much less did he seek praise or glory in superfluous things that serve only for display. The emphasis lies in the fact that he does not simply mention Christ in the present passage, but also says "crucified." For he knew that in the cross was contained the whole merit of Christ and the entire plan of human salvation. At the same time he rebukes his rivals, who were so occupied with empty speculations and the ambitious display of wisdom and eloquence that the cross of Christ was, so to speak, scarcely worth a thought to them. This usually happens to the superficially learned and to those devoted to human philosophy; nor in our own age are there lacking examples of men who, though they shrink from Papist superstitions and are by no means hostile to us, are nevertheless less moved by the doctrine of the gospel, because they hear nothing but Christ and his merit constantly inculcated. For they are ashamed, if they learn nothing else, or if they themselves preach nothing else, since they know they must maintain a reputation for a certain greater and uncommon learning. Paul therefore sets his own example against all these men, and this passage has something of the character of a solemn protestation, like that which he uses in the letter to the Romans: "I am not ashamed of the gospel of Jesus Christ, for it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes." For it is as if he said: "Let those glory in wisdom beyond the human, and boast of their knowledge of mysteries in magnificent words; yet the knowledge of Jesus Christ is enough for me, nor am I ashamed of my ignorance in other matters, since I know that all salvation is contained in the merit of the cross of Christ alone, and that he alone has the words of eternal life," etc.

units.la: Est autem locus hic dignißimus multa consideratione. Docet enim quis prædicationis euan-gelicæ finis aut scopus esse debeat, ad quem tàm doctores quàm auditores colliment. Is nimirum, ut in Christi cognitionem homines adducantur, & in ea quotidie proficiant, adeoq; illius discipuli fiant. Admonet de hoc ipse Christus, quando Apostolis dicit: Profecti docete omnes gentes bapti-zantes eos in nomen Patris & Filij & Spiritus sancti, docentes eos seruare omnia, quæ mandaui
units.tr: This passage is well worth careful consideration. It shows what the aim or purpose of evangelical preaching should be, the goal at which both teachers and hearers ought to aim. That aim is plainly that people be brought into the knowledge of Christ, that they make daily progress in it, and so become his disciples. Christ himself enjoins this on the Apostles when he says: "Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I have commanded you" (Matt. 28:19-20).

units.la: Euangelicæ doctrinæ argumē-tum & scopus. (side note at right, margin, not a foot note; see notes) vobis. Et haec causa est, quod initio quotquot crediderunt, Discipuli dicti sint, ut qui Christum so-lum praeceptorem & seruatorem suum agnoscerent. Et haec illa sapientia est, per quam Patres & Prophetae omnes servati sunt. De Abrahamo Christus ipse testatur, quod diem ipsius videre gesti-uerit, & in eius cognitione exultarit. Moses vero cum legis praecepta prolixe tradidisset, tandem ad magnum illum Prophetam Israelitas remisit, Christum scilicet: quod sciret, inanem fore om-nem suam doctrinam, nisi illum audirent, & reciperent. De prophetis autem omnibus Petrus scri-bit, quod duce spiritu Christi, ipsius mysteria scrutati sint. De Apostolis & Martyribus quid at-tinet dicere, quando constat, eam omnium mentem & sententiam fuisse, quam hic Paulus profite-tur. Hanc ergo sapientiam hodie etiam omnes quaerere & venari debent. Laudatur in historiis la-boriosa quorundam industria, qui regiones longinquas invisérunt, ut doctiores & sapientiores fie-rent. Hoc nomine Pythagoras in Aegyptum profectus est, ut vates Memphiticos audiret. Pla-to relictis Athenis, ubi cum laude docebat, in Italiam ad Architam Tarentinum contendit, ut a Pythagoricae sectae philosopho aliquid disceret. Apollonius autem non minori cum periculo quam labore & sumptu, extremis Indiae finibus superatis, ad Brachmanas usque profectus est, ut Hie-rarcham in throno sedentem aureo, & de Tantali fonte bibentem inter paucos discipulos (ut D. Hieronymus scribit) de natura, de moribus, & de dierum atque siderum cursu differentem audiret. Inde per Elamitas, Babylonios, Chaldaeos, Medos, Assyrios, Parthos, Syros, Phaenices, Arabes, Palestinos reversus, Alexandriam perexit, & inde in Aethiopiam penetravit, ut Gymnosophistas & toto orbe celebratam Solis mensam videret. At quid illi omnes suo studio, labore, sumptibus & peregrinationibus periculosissimis profecerunt? Magnam quidem inter homines sapientiae & doctrinae laude consecuti sunt: at quoad aeternam salutem, ea omnium fuit ignorantia, ut cum Socrate (siquidem verum fateri voluerunt) omnibus illis dicendum fuerit: Hoc unum scio, quod nihil scio. Sapientia enim unica & vera est Christum novisse, in quo omnes scientiae & cognitiones Dei thesauri reconditi sunt. Huius cognitio totum humanae salutis negotium comprehendit, neque circa illam eos aberrare finit, qui illa illuminati sunt. Eadem nos de omnibus admonet, quae ad vitae huius consuetudinem & mores faciunt. Est enim Christus omnis virtutis doctor simul & exemplar perfectissimum, in quo humilitatem, modestiam, obedientiam erga Deum, dilectionem proximi, synceram, patientiam invictam, fidem constantem, temperantiam, fortitudinem, denique omnia ea discere possumus, quae virtutis nomine comprehenduntur. In eodem quoque omnium clarissime cernitur iustitia Dei omnibus numeris absoluta, bonitas & misericordia plus quam paterna, veritas infallibilis, Sapientia infinita, omnipotentia invicta, & quaecunque alia de illo praedicantur. Ut vero huius cognitionem consequamur, neque ad Indos aut Brachmanas, neque ad Aethiopes excurrere, non etiam maria traijcere, aut in coelos (ut Mosis verbis utar) ascendere opus est. Ipse enim Christus seipsum nobis offert, ipse nobiscum in Euangelio loquitur, ipse quid credere, sentire, loqui, facere debeamus docet, & doctrinam hanc suo exemplo illustrat atque confirmat. Est ergo inexcusabilis illorum ignavia, qui illam sapientiam negligunt: execrabilis autem eorum impietas, quibus illa sordet, eo quod nullo humanae versutiae fuco coloretur. Quid autem de illorum perfidia dicemus, qui cum ecclesiarum antistites haberi velint, tamen Christo praeterito simplicem plebeculam inanibus verbis & ad augendas superstitiones compositis fabulis pascunt, et ceremoniis frigidissimis fatigant? Quam vero intolerabilis eorum audacia est, qui vel impetritis rerum, vel etiam invitis & reluctantibus, Patres nescio quos, Concilia ite & quorucunq; aliorum decreta obtrudunt. Paulus, electu[?] illud organum Dei, cum (ut ante diximus) a pueris vitae innocentia cum legis & traditionum patriarum studio coniunxisset, & coelorum quoq; arcana audisset, nihil tamen in ecclesia praeter IESUM CHRISTUM, eumq; crucifixum, scire voluit, & idem anathema pronuntiat tam homines quam angelos, qui Euangelium aliud praedicare audeant, quam quod Apostoli praedicarunt. Num ergo nostri illi novi Aristarchi, se plus quiddam scire, aut sibi in ecclesia Christi plus permissum esse arbitrantur? Discant potius omnes homines unum Chri-stum audire, unum illum sequi, & hunc novisse ipsis sufficiat, qui solus nobis a Patre sapientia, iu-stitia, sanctificatio & redemptio factus est.
units.tr: The argument and aim of evangelical doctrine. This is why, from the beginning, all who believed were called disciples, since they acknowledged Christ alone as their teacher and saviour. This is the wisdom through which all the Fathers and Prophets were saved. Christ himself testifies of Abraham that he desired to see his day and rejoiced in the knowledge of it. Moses, when he had set out the precepts of the law at length, finally sent the Israelites on to that great Prophet, namely Christ, knowing that all his teaching would be empty unless they heard and received him. Peter writes of all the Prophets that, moved by the Spirit of Christ, they searched into his mysteries. As for the Apostles and Martyrs, there is no need to say more, since it is clear that their whole mind and judgment was the one Paul here professes. This wisdom, then, all people today too ought to seek and pursue. In histories the laborious diligence of certain men is praised, who visited distant regions in order to become more learned and wiser. For this purpose Pythagoras set out for Egypt to hear the Memphite priests. Plato, leaving Athens where he taught with great renown, hastened to Italy to Archytas of Tarentum, to learn something from a philosopher of the Pythagorean school. Apollonius, not without danger, labour and expense no less great, crossed to the farthest bounds of India and went as far as the Brahmans, to hear Hierarchas, sitting on a golden throne and drinking from the spring of Tantalus, discoursing among a few disciples (as Jerome writes) on nature, morals, and the courses of the days and stars. Then, returning through the Elamites, Babylonians, Chaldeans, Medes, Assyrians, Parthians, Syrians, Phoenicians, Arabs and Palestinians, he made his way to Alexandria, and from there penetrated into Ethiopia, to see the Gymnosophists and the table of the Sun famed throughout the world. But what did all those men gain by their zeal, labour, expense and most perilous travels? They indeed obtained great praise among people for wisdom and learning; yet as regards eternal salvation, such was the ignorance of all of them that, if they were willing to tell the truth, they would have had to say with Socrates: "This one thing I know, that I know nothing." For the only true wisdom is to know Christ, in whom all the treasures of knowledge and of God are hidden. The knowledge of him comprehends the whole business of human salvation, and it does not allow those who have been enlightened by it to go astray about it. The same knowledge admonishes us about all those things that pertain to the customs and morals of this life. For Christ is at once the teacher of every virtue and the most perfect example, in whom we can learn humility, modesty, obedience towards God, love of neighbour, sincere and unconquered patience, steadfast faith, temperance, fortitude, and in short all those things that are comprehended under the name of virtue. In him too the justice of God is seen most clearly in every respect complete, goodness and mercy more than fatherly, infallible truth, infinite wisdom, invincible power, and whatever else is predicated of him. But to attain this knowledge we need not run to the Indians or the Brahmans, nor to the Ethiopians, nor cross the seas, nor (to use the words of Moses) ascend into heaven. For Christ himself offers himself to us; he himself speaks with us in the Gospel; he himself teaches what we ought to believe, think, say and do, and he illustrates and confirms this teaching by his own example. Therefore the sloth of those who neglect that wisdom is inexcusable, but the impiety of those who despise it, because it is not coloured with any cosmetic of human cunning, is execrable. What shall we say of the treachery of those who, while wishing to be regarded as bishops of the churches, nevertheless pass over Christ and feed the simple common people with empty words and fables composed to increase superstitions, and weary them with most frigid ceremonies? And how intolerable is the audacity of those who thrust upon us, whether we wish it or not, and even against our protests, certain Fathers, Councils and decrees of whomever else. Paul, that chosen instrument of God, although (as we said before) he had joined innocence of life from boyhood with zeal for the law and the traditions of the fathers, and had also heard the secrets of heaven, nevertheless wished to know nothing in the Church except Jesus Christ, and him crucified, and he pronounces the same anathema upon men and angels who dare to preach any other gospel than what the Apostles preached. Do those new Aristarchuses of ours therefore think that they know something more, or that more is permitted to them in the Church of Christ? Rather let all people learn to hear the one Christ, to follow him alone, and let it suffice them to know him, who alone has been made to us by the Father wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption.

units.la: Ut vero omnibus constet, sibi nil eorum defuisse, quae adfidei & salutis doctrinam faciunt, impedimenta quoq; enumerat Paulus, quæ omnem Euangelii profectum facile impedire potuis-sent apud Corinthios, nisi divinæ virtutis esset opus hoc totum. Sic autem scribit: Et ego cum in-firmitate, & timore ac tremore multo fui apud vos. Infirmitatis nomine docet, se nihil prorsus habuisse, quod ipsi apud Corinthios versanti præsidio esse, aut ipsum illis commendare potuerit. Quod vere ab illo dici, Lucas in Actis prolixè docet. Corinthum enim venit cum Paulo ante in Macedonia virgis cæsus & ejectus, Athenis autem à philosophis publicè derisus esset. Nihil ergo secum eo attulit præter publicæ infamiæ notas, & credibile est, in urbe mercatorum undiq; confluentium negotijs celebri, non omnino ignotum fuisse, quid illi in vicinis Græciæ locis accidisset. Corinthi verò hospitium sibi delegit apud Aquilam, Ponticum genere, hominem peregrinum, qui & ipse non multò ante cum Judæis Roma discedere jussus erat Claudij Cæsaris mandato. Quale ergo patro-cinium, quam commendationem ab hospite hoc suo sperare potuit? Quòd si vitæ genus, aut artis professionem spectes, cum Aquila tentorijs texendis occupatus fuit, & manuum labore victum sibi quæsiuit. Quid in his omnibus præter infirmitatem, contemptum, ignominiam cernitur? Aut quis hominem ejusmodi in urbe opulenta, inter cives & aduenas negotiationibus deditos, & luxu atq; libidine diffluentes aliquid effecturum putaret? Accesserunt huic impedimento pericula, quæ illi non timoris modò, verumetiam trepidationis & tremoris causa fuerunt. Cum enim diebus sabbati Synagogam ingredi & de salutis negotio disputare inciperet, mox se illi hostiliter opposuerunt Judæi, qui & gentiles erant, & propter veteres promissiones à Christo minus abhorrere debuissent. Et eò usq; illorum rabies processit, ut (quod rarissimè factum legimus) pulverem vestimentorum in illos excuteret Paulus, & non sine publica protestatione ad gentes sese conferret, qua illi magis exasperati sunt. Itaq; cum aliquos ex suis credidisse, & Crispum Synagogæ præfectum jam Christo nomen dedisse viderent, conjuratione facta Paulum comprehensum ad Gallionis Pro consulis tribunal rapiunt, & impietatis manifestæ accusant: à Gallione autem reiecti, Sosthenem ante tribunal verberibus multant. Quæ omnia Pauli mentem ita commoverunt, ut de urbe relinquenda cogitaret, & consolatione peculiari opus haberet, quam noctè illi apparens Dominus his verbis adhibuit: Ne timeas, sed loquere, & ne taceas: nam ego sum tecum, & nemo adijcíet [?] ut tibi malefaciat: quoniam populus est mihi multus in hac urbe. Magnus ergo timor Pauli fuerit oportet, quem in præsenti ingenuè fatetur, ut Dei gratiam & virtutem illustret, qua adjutus per tot obstacula Euangelii doctrinam inter illos propagavit. Simul autem pseudoapostolos rursus perstringit, qui ecclesiam tot tantisq; laboribus plantatam dolose subingressi, inani grandiloquentia sese vendebant, cùm potius cogitare deberent, quanto majori laude digni essent, qui hoc otium ipsis suo labore parauerant. Similes horum sunt hodie, qui primos evangelicæ doctrinæ instauratores, quos Deus nobis excitavit, præillis contemnunt, qui nunc nimium delicatuli inter concionandum aulicam quandam atq; forensem eloquentiam ostentant, & in suis antecessoribus nescio quam civilem prudentiam & facilitatem desiderant, qua se magnatum & vulgi moribus accommodare debuerint. Atqui longè alia fuit ô fratres rerum conditio, cùm Antichristi Camerina primum movenda esset, neque tantum otij fuit præceptoribus nostris, ut circa verborum lenocinia occuparentur, quando feuenti spiritus virtute opus erat, qua negotium istud perficeretur. Vos modò videritis, ut illorum laboribus plantatas ecclesias conservetis, & non sine sanguine partam libertatem, qua decet fide atque industria tueamini.
units.tr: So that it may be plain to everyone that nothing was lacking to him of those things that make up the doctrine of faith and salvation, Paul also enumerates the hindrances which could easily have impeded all progress of the Gospel among the Corinthians, had not this whole work been the work of divine power. He writes thus: "And I was with you in weakness, and in much fear and trembling." By the word weakness he shows that he had nothing at all to rely on while he was living among the Corinthians, nothing that could recommend him to them. Luke sets out at length in the Acts that this is truly what Paul means. For he came to Corinth after having been beaten with rods and driven out in Macedonia, and after being publicly mocked by the philosophers at Athens. He brought with him therefore nothing but the marks of public disgrace, and it is credible that in a city of merchants, thronging from every quarter and busy with commerce, what had happened to him in the neighbouring places of Greece was not wholly unknown. At Corinth he chose lodging with Aquila, a Pontian by birth, a foreigner, who himself not long before had been ordered by the decree of Emperor Claudius to leave Rome with the Jews. What patronage, then, what commendation could he hope for from this host of his? And if you look to his way of life or his trade, he was occupied with Aquila in weaving tents and sought his living by the labour of his hands. What is seen in all these things besides weakness, contempt and disgrace? Or who would think that a man of this sort would accomplish anything in a rich city, among citizens and foreigners devoted to business and flowing over with luxury and lust? Dangers were added to these hindrances, which were the cause not only of fear but of trembling and quaking. For when he began to enter the synagogue on the Sabbath days and to dispute about the business of salvation, the Jews immediately opposed him in a hostile way, Jews who were also Gentiles, and who ought to have been less averse to Christ because of the ancient promises. And their madness went so far that Paul (a thing we read was very rarely done) shook the dust from his garments against them, and, not without public protest, turned himself to the Gentiles, which exasperated them all the more. So when they saw that some of their own had believed, and that Crispus, ruler of the synagogue, had now given his name to Christ, they made a conspiracy, seized Paul and dragged him before the tribunal of the proconsul Gallio, and accused him of manifest impiety. But Gallio rejected them, and they beat Sosthenes before the tribunal. All these things so moved Paul's mind that he thought of leaving the city, and he needed a special consolation, which the Lord, appearing to him by night, gave in these words: "Do not be afraid, but speak, and do not be silent; for I am with you, and no one shall attack you to do you harm, for I have a great people in this city." Paul's fear must therefore have been great, which he frankly confesses in the present passage, so that he might make clear the grace and power of God, by whose help he propagated the teaching of the Gospel among them through so many obstacles. At the same time he again censures the false apostles, who, having secretly crept into a church planted with so many and such great labours, were selling themselves by empty boasting, whereas they ought rather to have considered how much greater praise was due to those who had prepared for them this leisure by their own toil. Those who today are like them despise the first restorers of evangelical doctrine whom God raised up for us, and who are now too delicate, displaying in their preaching a certain courtly and forensic eloquence, and in their predecessors they desire I know not what civil prudence and affability, by which they ought to have accommodated themselves to the manners of great men and of the common crowd. But, brothers, the condition of affairs was far different when the Camarina of Antichrist had first to be stirred; nor did our teachers have so much leisure that they were occupied with the flattery of words, when the power of a fervent spirit was needed, by which that task might be accomplished. Be it yours only to see that you preserve the churches planted by their labours, and that you defend with faith and diligence the liberty won not without blood, as is fitting.

units.la: Obseruabis interea in Paulo, quæ plerunq; piorum in hoc sæculo fors sit. Deficiuntur fe-rè omni humano præsidio, & simul omnium injurijs obnoxij in horas de vita periclitantur. Præ-dixit hoc Christus, quando forè ait, ut qui vos occiderit, se Deo cultum gratissimum præstitisse putet. Inter pericula autem illa pij neque lapides neque trunci sunt, qui nullo illorum sensu moveantur, qualem Stoici suum illum virum bonum & sapientem fingunt. Locum enim in illis habent affectiones, quas nobis natura indidit, & quæ per se vitiosæ non sunt, nisi aut causa illarum mala sit, aut modum excedant. Quod igitur Paulo apud Corinthios accidit, hoc etiam Mosi, & ante hunc Abrahamo, postea Josuæ, Davidi & prophetis fere omnibus accidisse scimus: ut jam nihil de Christo dicamus, qui animi sui mœrorem non minus ingenuè, quàm Paulus, apud discipulos profitetur, & in eas angustias deuenit, vt sanguineo sudore totus madeat, & Angelo consola-tore habeat opus. Et vt hoc nobis accidat necesse est: primò quidem, vt sentiamus nos sine Deo ni-hil posse, & proinde nihil nobisipsis aut nostris viribus tribuamus: deinde vt maiori studio car-nem mortificemus, quae tunc quoq; nobis negotium facit, quando spiritum solum in nobis dominari quàm maximè opus erat. Interea discamus non mox damnari debere eos, qui interdum meticulosio res sunt, neq; etiam nobis desperandum esse, si quid huius patiamur. Tunc enim non deerit nobis Deus, cuius virtus in nostra infirmitate perficitur, & hic imprimis locum habet, quod veteri proverbio dicitur: Vir fugiens denuo pugnarit.
units.tr: You will observe meanwhile in Paul what is often the lot of the godly in this age. They are stripped of almost every human support, and at the same time, exposed to the injuries of all, they are in peril of their lives hour by hour. Christ foretold this when he said that the one who kills you will think he has offered God the most acceptable worship. Among these dangers, however, the godly are not stones or tree-trunks, unmoved by any feeling, such as the Stoics imagine their wise and good man to be. For those affections which nature has implanted in us have their place in them, and they are not sinful in themselves, unless their cause is evil or they exceed due measure. What happened to Paul among the Corinthians, then, we know happened also to Moses, and before him to Abraham, afterwards to Joshua, David and almost all the prophets. Not to mention Christ himself, who openly confesses the sorrow of his soul to his disciples no less frankly than Paul, and comes into such anguish that he sweats blood all over and needs an angel to comfort him. And for this to happen to us is necessary: first, that we should feel that without God we can do nothing, and therefore ascribe nothing to ourselves or to our own strength; then, that we should with greater zeal mortify the flesh, which also gives us trouble even when the spirit most needs to rule in us. Meanwhile let us learn that those who are sometimes fearful ought not be condemned at once, nor should we despair of ourselves if we suffer something of this kind. For then God will not fail us, whose power is made perfect in our weakness; and here above all applies what the old proverb says: a man who has fled will fight again.

units.la: At pergit Paulus, & quibus armis fiue praesidijs confirmatus vicerit, docet. Vbi rursus re-petit quod initio dixerat, verbis paulo mutatis. Et oratio mea (inquit) & praedicatio mea non fuit in persuasoribus humanae sapientiae verbis, id est, nihil habui, quod homines, qui mundi authorita-te ducuntur, & carnis rationem in consilium adhibent, persuadere posset. Nam qui tales sunt, ijs (vt supra audiuimus) Christus cum omnibus quae fecit, stultitia esse videtur. Itaq; mea praedica-tio (ait Paulus) fuit in demonstratione spiritus & potentiae, id est: Quicquid feci, id spiritus vir-tute feci, qui mihi affuit, & praedicationi meae vires addidit, vt hominum mentes penetraret, atq; illis persuaderet me vera dicere. Ita factum est, vt quemadmodum ego simplici dicendi ratione ef-feci, quod hominum viribus fieri non poterat: ita illi quoq; per omnia obstacula eluctarentur, & ec-clesiae apud vos initiū darent. Id vero omne ideo sic factum fuit, vt fides vestra non esset, aut consi-steret, in hominum sapientia, sed in potentia Dei. Id est, vt omnibus constaret, fidem Christianam non ab hominum sapientia, eloquentia, virtute, authoritate pendere, sed solius Dei virtute propa-gari, & proinde nemini mortalium quicquam hic esse tribuendum. Et haec dicendo argumentum, quo aemuli ipsum grauabant, in illos retorquet, & suam authoritatem eo illustriorem reddit, dum quicquid est humanorum praesidiorum quàm longissimè abs se remouet. Quia enim neq; sapientia huius mundi, neq; eloquentia, neq; viribus aut armis, neq; aliqua authoritate publica hanc cau-sam egit Paulus, & tamen in tali vrbe fidei semina tanto cum fructu iecit, quàm plurimos ad fi-dem Christianam conuertit, ecclesiam illic constituit, vbi publicum diaboli proflibulum erat, certè diuina virtute illum armatum fuisse oportuit. Omnium vero istorum hic finis & scopus est, vt horum consideratione confirmati eam fidem constanter tueantur, quam Dei authoritate suffultam esse constet, neq; eorum grandiloquentia sese circumduci sinant, qui nihil praeter verborum ampul-las iactent, quibus crux Christi enervetur.
units.tr: But Paul goes on, and shows by what arms or defences he was strengthened and conquered. Here he repeats again what he had said at the beginning, with the words slightly changed. "And my speech," he says, "and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom," that is, I had nothing that could persuade men who are led by the authority of the world and take the reasoning of the flesh as their counsel. For such people, as we heard above, see Christ with all that he has done as foolishness. So "my preaching," says Paul, "was in demonstration of the Spirit and of power," that is: whatever I did, I did by the power of the Spirit, who was with me and gave strength to my preaching, so that it penetrated men's minds and persuaded them that I was telling the truth. So it came about that just as I, with a plain manner of speaking, accomplished what could not be done by human strength, so they too struggled through all obstacles and gave the beginning of the Church among you. All this was done in such a way so that your faith would not be, or stand, in human wisdom, but in the power of God. That is, so that it would be plain to everyone that the Christian faith depends not on human wisdom, eloquence, virtue or authority, but is propagated by the power of God alone, and therefore nothing of this kind is to be ascribed to any mortal. And in saying this he turns back upon his rivals the argument with which they burdened him, and makes his own authority the more illustrious by removing from himself as far as possible whatever human support there is. For since Paul conducted this cause neither with the wisdom of this world, nor with eloquence, nor with force or arms, nor with any public authority, and yet sowed the seeds of faith with such fruit in such a city, converted so many to the Christian faith, and established a church there where the public stronghold of the devil was, he must surely have been armed with divine power. The aim and purpose of all these things is that, being strengthened by considering them, they may steadfastly hold to that faith which is plainly supported by the authority of God, and not allow themselves to be led astray by the grand talk of those who brag of nothing but empty word-bombast, by which the cross of Christ is weakened.

units.la: Est autem hic mos Dei, quo in propaganda ecclesia & vera religione à primo rerum exor-dio vsus est: vt nimirum eos sibi ministros delegerit, qui hominum contemptissimi & infirmissi-mi videri poterant. Nà vt ab Abelo initium faciamus, qui primus verum Dei cultum exercuit, illi à vanitate nomen imposuerant parentes, nimirum quod in Caino seiam virum illum acquisi-uisse putarent, qui salutem amissam ipsis debebat instaurare. Quo praeludio adumbratum fuit, quàm contempti apud omnem posteritatem futuri essent, qui fidem in promissum illud mulieris se-men profitentur, & ex ea Deum colunt. Quod si vero Abrahamum videamus, quem patrem credentium Paulus vocat, fuit ut quidem non vulgaris authoritatis inter Chaldaeos suos: at ne quis huic aliquid daret, cum eius opera in fœdere salutis (quod in diluuio abolitum videbatur) instaurando vti vellet Deus, illum ex natali solo discedere, extorrem & peregrinum fieri, casibus diuersis iactari, & omni humana dignitate priuari voluit, vt quae femine benedicto niti debebat fides, in solaipsius gratia fundaretur. Simile quid in Ægypto factum est, cum aliquam eius re-gni reformationem facere, & ibidem ecclesiae suae hospitium praeparare instituisset. Ad eam enim rem Iosephum delegit, qui prius à fratribus infidis venditus non modo seruitutis iugum subijt, sed impudicae etiam herae calumnijs in extremum vitae periculum adductus est. Idem de Mose dicere possumus, qui priusquam Dei dux & ecclesiae, quae in Ægypto multis modis deformata fue-rat, instaurator fieret, aula eiectus ad Madianitas profugit. Extant huius generis multa in prophetis, quae omnia recensere longum foret. Et quod de seipso Paulus dicit, id ad omnes A-postolos extendi debet, quorum omnium eadem fuit conditio. Quod si ad nostra tempora de-scendamus, non alia ratione Deum in luce ex Papistica tenebris eruenda vsum esse patebit: Nam eos excitauit Verbi sui ministros, qui cum antea obscuri essent & ignobiles, neq; etiam huius mundi authoritate vel armis defenderentur, simplici tamen Euangelij praedicatione regnum Antichristi ex ipsis fundamentis labefactarunt, & multum reluctantibus potentissimis Regibus reformationis fuerunt authores, qualem ne illi ipsi quidem initio sperare fuissent ausi. Docent ista, regnum Christi non esse de hoc mundo, & proinde mundi armis non propagari, neq; etiam ijsdem euerti posse. Nemo igitur sibi in hominum authoritate praesidium quaerat, neq; aduersariorum potentia vel authoritate terreatur. Nunquam enim suis deerit Dominus, & eidem facile est res maximas per instrumenta vilissima conficere.
units.tr: Moreover, this is God's manner, which he has used in propagating the Church and the true religion from the very beginning of things: namely, that he has chosen as his ministers those who could seem most despised and weakest among men. For to begin with Abel, who first practised the true worship of God, his parents had given him a name from vanity, doubtless because they thought that in Cain they had gained the man who would restore the salvation they had lost. By this prelude was foreshadowed how despised those would be in all posterity who profess faith in that promised seed of the woman and worship God from it. And if we look at Abraham, whom Paul calls the father of believers, he indeed had no small authority among his Chaldeans; yet, so that no one would give him anything, when God wished to use his work to restore the covenant of salvation (which seemed to have been abolished in the flood), he willed that he should leave his native soil, become an exile and a stranger, be tossed about by various misfortunes, and be deprived of all human dignity, so that the faith which was to rest on the blessed seed might be founded on God's grace alone. Something similar happened in Egypt, when he had resolved to effect some reformation of that kingdom and to prepare a home there for his church. For to this task he chose Joseph, who, first sold by his faithless brothers, not only bore the yoke of servitude but was also brought to the utmost peril of his life by the false accusations of his impure mistress. The same we can say of Moses, who, before he became God's leader and the restorer of the church, which in Egypt had been disfigured in many ways, was cast out of the court and fled to the Midianites. There are many things of this kind in the prophets, which it would be long to recount in full. And what Paul says of himself ought to be extended to all the apostles, since all of them were in the same condition. And if we come down to our own times, it will be plain that God has used no other method in drawing light out of Papistical darkness. For he raised up ministers of his Word who, though before they were obscure and of low birth, and were not defended by the authority or arms of this world, nevertheless by the simple preaching of the Gospel shook the kingdom of Antichrist from its very foundations, and became the authors of reformation against the strong resistance of the most powerful kings, such as not even they themselves had dared to hope for at the start. These things teach that the kingdom of Christ is not of this world, and therefore is not propagated by the arms of the world, nor can it be overthrown by them. Let no one, then, seek a defence in human authority, nor be terrified by the power or authority of adversaries. For the Lord will never fail his own, and it is easy for him to accomplish very great things by the vilest instruments.

units.la: Admonet praeterea locus iste, fidem Christianam nulla hominum sapientia siue authoritate niti, sed in vno Deo acquiescere. Nam vt alibi ait Paulus, fides ex auditu est, auditus vero per Verbum Dei. Est hoc obseruatu cumprimis necessarium. Quia, si aliud fidei fundamentum collocetur, illam consistere impossibile est. Cum enim incerta sint hominum consilia, & eorundem voluntates in diem mutentur, nihil in fide sua certum aut stabile habebunt, quotquot ab hominum authoritate pendere volent. Adhæc inter pericula nunquam firmi & constantes erimus in fidei confessione, nisi certo nobis persuasum sit, Deum velle vt sic sentiamus, credamus & loquamur. Credidi (inquit propheta) & propterea locutus sum. Et Apostoli: Non possumus, quae vidimus & audiuimus, non loqui. Quid ergo loquentur, aut quid facient, qui non simili fidei certitudine confirmantur, quae extra Deum haberi non potest? Quod si vero in nostris viribus aut operum nostrorum meritis salutis fiduciam collocare libeat, perpetuo illa fluctuabit, cum vires nostrae nullae, opera autem nostra omnia aut mala, aut saltem vitiosa atq; imperfecta sint. Et si fides nostra non consistit in hominum sapientia, quomodo in operibus consistet, quae multo inferiora & maioris pretij sunt? Simul ergo locus hic omnes eos arguit, qui hominum authoritate pugnant, & nobis hodie Patres, Concilia, Scholas, deniq; mundi huius eruditionem, sapientiam, potentiam, opes, foedera & quae alia sunt huius generis, obijciunt. Atqui fides nostra nequaquam in his consistit, sed solius Dei virtute & authoritate nititur. Is autem aeterno decreto Filium suum vnigenitum, IESVM CHRISTVM, nobis magistrum atq; seruatorem constituit. Huic ergo nos fidere, hunc audire, colere & obseruare decet. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, this passage admonishes that the Christian faith rests on no human wisdom or authority, but rests in the one God alone. For, as Paul says elsewhere, faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the Word of God. This must be observed especially, for if any other foundation of faith is laid, it is impossible for faith to stand. For since human counsels are uncertain and men's wills change from day to day, all who wish their faith to depend on human authority will have nothing certain or stable in their faith. Besides, amid dangers we shall never be firm and steadfast in confessing the faith, unless we are fully persuaded that God wills us to think, believe and speak thus. "I believed," says the prophet, "and therefore I have spoken." And the apostles: "We cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard." What then will those say, or what will they do, who are not confirmed by the same certainty of faith, which cannot be had apart from God? But if we are pleased to place our confidence of salvation in our own strength or the merits of our works, it will waver continually, since our strength is nothing and our works are all either evil, or at least faulty and imperfect. And if our faith does not stand in human wisdom, how will it stand in works, which are much inferior and of less worth? So at once this passage refutes all those who fight for human authority, and who today object to us the Fathers, the Councils, the Schools, and finally the learning, wisdom, power, wealth, alliances of this world, and whatever else is of this kind. Yet our faith by no means rests on these things, but is founded on the power and authority of God alone. He, by an eternal decree, has appointed his only-begotten Son, JESUS CHRIST, as our teacher and saviour. It is therefore right for us to trust in him, to hear him, to worship and to obey him. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA IX.
units.tr: HOMILY IX.

units.la: Sapientiam vero loquimur inter perfectos: sapientiam autem non seculi huius, neq; principum seculi huius, qui abolentur. Sed loquimur sapientiam Dei in mysterio, occultam illam, quam praefiniuit Deus ante secula in gloriam nostram. Quam nemo principum seculi huius cognouit. Nam si cognouissent, nequaquam Dominum gloriae crucifixissent. Sed sicut scriptum est: Quae oculus non vidit, nec auris audiuit, nec in cor hominis venerunt, quae praeparauit Deus iis qui ipsum diligunt.
units.tr: But we speak wisdom among the perfect, yet not the wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are brought to nothing. We speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, the hidden wisdom which God ordained before the ages for our glory. None of the rulers of this age knew it, for if they had known it they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. But as it is written: "Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, neither has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him."

units.la: Multis hucusq; Paulus Dei decretum siue consilium exposuit, qui electos suos per Euangelij praedicationem, quae carnis iudicio stulta & absurda esse videtur, feruare, aut ad salutis per Christum acquisitae possessionem vocare solet. Et ideo ad doctrinae huius diuulgationem ordinatos esse ostendit Apostolos, qui neq; authoritate neq; huius seculi sapientia instructi sint, sed simplici & minime fucato dicendi genere vnum Christum, & hunc quidem pro nobis crucifixum praedicent. Finis horum omnium est, vt Corinthijs medeatur, qui pseudoapostolorum grandiloquentia & orationibus ad ostentationem compositis fascinati, ipsum simul atq; totam Euangelij doctrinam fastidiebant, quod nullis verborum phaleris aut dicendi artificio commendaretur. Excusat ergo suam & aliorum Apostolorum simplicitatem, & ostendit se non aliter potuisse praedicare, neq; etiam debuisse, quando hic Dei mos sit, cui se debuerit accommodare. Simul autem in genere docet, hanc docendi rationem nobis vtilissimam, adeoq; necessariam esse: vt nimirum ex ea discamus, salutis nostrae negotium, quod in Evangelio traditur, non in hominum sapientia, sed Dei solius virtute consistere. Quod si probè consideretur, iam & huic omnem gloriam tribuemus, qui ipsi gratissimus cultus est, & in tentationibus fortes atq; constantes erimus. Quia vero ista occasione multa dicenda fuerunt aduersus huius seculi sapientiam atq; dicendi artes, poterat apud nonnullos Apostolus in suspicionem venire, quasi barbarorum more liberaliores artes & omnem prudentiam ciuilem contemneret atq; damnaret: Ideo locum, quem modò recitauimus subijcit, quo & omni suspicione sinistra se liberat, & Evangelij doctrinam magnificè commendat, docens ea veram & soli-dam sapientiam contineri, quæ omnem humani ingenij captum excedat.
units.tr: Up to this point Paul has set forth God's decree or purpose, by which he is accustomed to preserve his elect through the preaching of the gospel, which by human judgement seems foolish and absurd, and to call them to possess the salvation acquired through Christ. He shows that the apostles were appointed to spread this teaching, though they were equipped neither with authority nor with the wisdom of this age, but preach one Christ, and him crucified for us, in a plain and wholly unadorned manner of speaking. The purpose of all this is to heal the Corinthians, who, dazzled by the high-flown rhetoric of the false apostles and by speeches composed for display, despised both him and the whole doctrine of the gospel, because it was not recommended by any verbal finery or artful eloquence. He therefore excuses his own simplicity and that of the other apostles, and shows that he could not have preached otherwise, nor indeed ought to have, since this is God's way, to which he ought to conform. At the same time he teaches in general that this manner of teaching is most useful and indeed necessary for us, so that we may learn from it that the business of our salvation, which is handed down in the gospel, rests not on human wisdom but on the power of God alone. If this is rightly considered, we will also give all glory to him, which is the most pleasing worship to him, and we will be brave and steadfast in temptations. But because on this occasion much had to be said against the wisdom of this age and the arts of speech, Paul might have come under suspicion among some, as though, in the manner of barbarians, he despised and condemned the liberal arts and all civil prudence. Therefore he adds the passage we have just recited, by which he also frees himself from every unfavourable suspicion and commends the teaching of the gospel magnificently, teaching that it contains a true and solid wisdom which surpasses the grasp of the human mind.

units.la: Et primò quidem Evangelium grauiter & diligenter ab omni contemptu vindicat, dicens: Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos, sapientiam autem non seculi huius, neq; principum seculi huius, qui abolentur, &c. Sensus verborum hic est: Dixi nos Apostolos inter prædicandum non vti persuasoriis humanæ sapientiæ verbis, & fidem Christianam non in hominum sapientia, sed Dei virtute seu potentia consistere. Id vero nemo sic accipiat, quasi aut sapientiam humanam (quæ & ipsa Dei donum est, & in rebus huius seculi suum vsum habet, adeoq; necessaria est) simpliciter damnem, aut ab Evangelij doctrina sapientiam omnem excludam. Nam si de re ipsa exactius loqui oporteat, dico in Evangelio veram sapientiam contineri: non quidem sapientiam huius seculi, aut eorum, qui in hoc seculo vana & caduca eminentia reliquis excellunt: sed sapientiam Dei, quæ diu quidem occultata latuit, simul tamen æterno Dei decreto præfinita est, vt inter perfectos prædicetur in nostram gloriam. Et hæc quidem non circa res huius seculi occupatur, sed ea sublimitate supra omnes cœlos attollitur, vt nemo principum huius seculi eam cognouerit.
units.tr: And first he vindicates the gospel gravely and carefully from all contempt, saying: "We speak wisdom among the perfect, yet not the wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are brought to nothing," and so on. The sense of the words is this: I said that we apostles, in preaching, do not use the persuasive words of human wisdom, and that the Christian faith rests not on human wisdom but on the power or might of God. Yet let no one take this to mean that I simply condemn human wisdom (which is itself a gift of God and has its use in the affairs of this age, and is therefore necessary), or that I exclude all wisdom from the teaching of the gospel. For if one must speak of the matter more exactly, I say that true wisdom is contained in the gospel: not indeed the wisdom of this age, or of those who excel the rest in this age through vain and fading prominence, but the wisdom of God, which for a long time lay hidden, yet was at the same time ordained by the eternal decree of God, to be preached among the perfect for our glory. And this wisdom is not occupied with the things of this age, but is raised so high above all the heavens that none of the rulers of this age has known it.

units.la: Continetur his verbis pulcherrima & plena consolationis Evangelij definitio, siue descriptio, quam sic ex illis colligemus: Evangelium est prædicatio sapientiæ Dei, quam is æterno suo decreto comprehensam apud se diu occultauit, suo autem tempore reuelauit perfectis suis, vt gloriam veram & æternam assequantur. Habes in ista definitione quæcunque de Evangelio dici possunt, & nobis cognitu necessaria sunt: quapropter non pigeat nos singulos illius partes aliquanto diligentius inspicere.
units.tr: In these words is contained a most beautiful definition, or description, of the gospel, full of consolation, which we will draw from them thus: The gospel is the preaching of the wisdom of God, which he, having comprehended it in his eternal decree, kept hidden with himself for a long time, but at its appointed time revealed to his perfect ones, so that they might obtain true and eternal glory. In this definition you have everything that can be said about the gospel and that we need to know. Therefore let us not be reluctant to examine each of its parts somewhat more carefully.

units.la: Primò prædicationem Sapientiæ Dei esse diximus. Nam IESVM CHRISTVM prædicat, quam Dei Sapientiam esse Scriptura passim docet, per quam ille omnia condidit, & quem nobis quoq; ab illo sapientiam factum esse, nuper audiuimus. Potest etiam sic dici Evangelium, quia veram sapientiam nobis tradit, qui ex nobis ipsis nihil sapimus aut videmus in illis, quæ saluti & vitæ æternæ seruiunt. Si enim sapientia (vt à veteribus Philosophis eam definitam fuisse Cicero scribit) est rerum humanarum atq; diuinarum, causarumq; quibus hæ res continentur, scientia siue cognitio, nulli rectius & meliori iure quam Evangelio, titulus iste debetur. Ex eo enim vera Dei cognitio discitur, quam nemo sapientum huius seculi vnquam inuenire potuit. Simonides certè ab Hierone interrogatus quid esset Deus, diem vnum sibi ad meditandum dari petijt. Quo elapso, cum rursus interrogaretur, biduum postulauit. Et hoc etiam concesso, rursus requisitus, triduum adhuc sibi voluit dari: & tandem ingenuè confessus est, se quò magis inquirat & cogitet, eò magis perplexum & incertum fieri. Quod ipsum aliis quoq; philosophis accidisse, ex ipsorum libris apparet, sed non omnium eadem, quæ Simonidis, fuit ingenuitas, vt ignorantiam suam & inscrutabilem diuinæ Maiestatis abyssum fateri voluerint. At Evangelij prædicatione docemur, Deum æternum & summum bonum esse, vnum essentia, personis trinum, qui Verbo suo omnia creauit & creata seruet, Filij sui merito nos redemerit, & Spiritu suo sanctificatos in filios adoptauerit. Discimus præterea, hanc Dei voluntatem esse, vt credamus in nomen Filij sui IESV CHRISTI, & vt nos mutuò diligamus. Causas item creationis & omnium quæ in mundo fiunt, in Dei prouidentia sic nobis monstrat Evangelij doctrina, vt qui in illam respiciunt, rerum certi & securi nihil præterea requirant. Adhæc æternæ salutis rationem certam & simplicem tradit, quam illiterati quoque & opifices aut rustici, imò mulieres, pueri & puellæ percipere possunt. Quoad mores autem & vitæ consuetudinem præcepta tradit numero pauca, intellectu facilia, & quorum vsus per rempub. & domesticam, adeoq; per omnia ea longè lateq; extenditur, quæ homini vel publicè vel priuatim agenda sunt. Et quem non postremum sapientiæ fructum esse, gentium philosophi agnouerunt, sola Euangelij prædicatio nos de aduersis omnibus & ipsa etiam morte re-ste[?] iudicare docet, & in omni casu nos inuictos & constantes reddit. Quis ergo illa sapientiam veram & solidam contineri neget? Quotquot ergo Euangelium audiunt, & huius cognitioni studet, ij reuera philosophi, id est, sapientiæ studiosi sunt, siue illi docti siue indocti, opifices, agricolæ, nautæ, viri, pueri, mulieres fuerint. At qui illo relicto circa veterum philosophorum scripta occupantur, & nescio quas rerum causas sui ingenij acumine scrutantur, ij philomori aut morosophi, id est, stultitiæ amatores atq; studiosi sunt. Quid enim hi aliud agunt, quam quod ipsi sibi tenebras offundunt, ne æternæ illius sapientiæ lucem intueantur, adeoq; in hoc sunt, vt cum ratione insaniant?
units.tr: First, we said that it is the preaching of the wisdom of God. For it preaches JESUS CHRIST , whom Scripture everywhere teaches to be the wisdom of God, through whom he made all things, and whom we lately heard was made wisdom for us by God. The gospel may also be called this for another reason, namely that it delivers to us true wisdom, since of ourselves we know nothing and see nothing in those matters which serve our salvation and eternal life. For if wisdom (as Cicero writes that the ancient philosophers defined it) is the knowledge or understanding of human and divine things, and of the causes by which these things are held together, then this title is due to no one more rightly and with better right than to the gospel. For from it true knowledge of God is learned, which none of the wise men of this age has ever been able to find. Simonides, when asked by Hiero what God was, certainly asked for one day to think it over. When that had passed and he was asked again, he requested two days. And when this too was granted and he was asked again, he wished for three more days; and at last he frankly confessed that the more he inquired and thought, the more confused and uncertain he became. That the same thing happened to other philosophers too is clear from their own books, but not all had the same frankness as Simonides, so as to confess their ignorance and the unsearchable abyss of the divine majesty. But by the preaching of the gospel we are taught that God is eternal and the highest good, one in essence and three in persons, who created all things by his Word and preserves what he created, who has redeemed us by the merit of his Son and, having sanctified us by his Spirit, has adopted us as sons. We learn besides that this is the will of God, that we should believe in the name of his Son JESUS CHRIST, and that we should love one another. The teaching of the gospel also shows us the causes of creation and of all that happens in the world, in God's providence, in such a way that those who look to it need nothing further, being certain and secure about things. Besides this, it hands down a sure and simple account of eternal salvation, which even the unlearned, craftsmen or farmers, indeed women, boys and girls, can grasp. As for morals and the conduct of life, it hands down precepts few in number, easy to understand, and whose use extends far and wide through the commonwealth and the household, and so through all those things which a man must do either publicly or privately. And the gentile philosophers recognised that this is no small fruit of wisdom: the mere preaching of the gospel teaches us to judge rightly about all adversities, even about death itself, and makes us unconquered and steadfast in every case. Who then would deny that true and solid wisdom is contained in it? Whoever therefore hears the gospel and applies himself to knowing it, these are in truth philosophers, that is, lovers of wisdom, whether they be learned or unlearned, craftsmen, farmers, sailors, men, boys or women. But those who, leaving this aside, occupy themselves with the writings of the ancient philosophers and, by the keenness of their wit, probe I know not what causes of things, these are philomori or morosophi, that is, lovers and students of folly. For what else do they accomplish, except that they cast darkness over themselves, so that they do not look upon the light of that eternal wisdom, and so they labour to go mad with reason?

units.la: Secundò Sapientiæ huius Euangelicæ author indicatur, Deus, qui hanc æterno suo decreto comprehensam præfiniuit. Confirmatur hoc per illud, quod quæ in illo nobis prædicantur nostræ salutis ratio, Dei electione nititur; quam priusquam mundus hic conderetur factam esse Scriptura sacra non vno loco testatur. Sed & ipsum Christum nobis redemptorem præordinatum esse Petrus docet, priusquam orbis fieret. Ideo quam primum Adam in peccatum lapsus & mortis reus factus fuit, remedium in promptu habuit Deus, & infelicem atq; trepidantem prædestinati illius redemptoris promissione confirmauit, qui præfinito tempore ex muliere nasci & serpentis caput conterere debeat. Seruiunt hæc ijs confutandis, qui Euangelij doctrinâ vel nouitatis accusant, vel humanis figmentis constare aiunt. Non erant hi modo turpiter, sed in Deum quoq; ingratissimi sunt, cuius plus quam paternam curam atq; prouidentiam agnoscere debebant. Vt enim is herbas & quæcunq; alia sunt morborum remedia creauit, priusquam morbi essent, & instar optimi patrisfamilias suis in futurum prospexit: ita cum nos lapsuros esse sciret, priusquam laberemur, eam rationem penes se decreuit, per quam miseris nobis subueniretur. Et cum Christo teste, olim omnes iusti & prophetæ ea videre & audire ardentissimè desiderauerint, quæ nostris auribus atq; oculis per Euangelij prædicationem ingeruntur, nulla venia digna eorum ingratitudo est, qui ista nunc videre & audire dedignantur. Sed solet illis fieri, quod iis qui ex oculis laborant. Vt enim hi tenebris assueti lucem ferre non possunt: ita illi cum errorum & superstitionum diuturna consuetudine irretiti sint, ex Euangelio dolorem concipiunt, & quidui faciunt, quo illud vel obscurari vel explodi posse existimant. At quia ijsdem cum Dei sapientia res est, nunquam quod volunt perficiet, sed in suis illis tenebris miserè peribunt.
units.tr: Second, the author of this gospel wisdom is pointed out, namely God, who ordained it, comprehended in his eternal decree. This is confirmed by the fact that the ground of our salvation, which is proclaimed to us in it, rests on the election of God; and Holy Scripture attests in more than one place that this election was made before this world was founded. Peter also teaches that Christ himself was foreordained to be our redeemer before the world was made. Therefore, as soon as Adam fell into sin and became liable to death, God had a remedy at hand, and he comforted the unhappy and trembling man with the promise of that predestined Redeemer, who at the appointed time should be born of a woman and crush the serpent's head. These considerations serve to refute those who accuse the teaching of the gospel of novelty or say that it consists of human inventions. They are not only shamefully wrong, but also most ungrateful toward God, whose more than paternal care and providence they ought to acknowledge. For just as he created herbs and whatever other remedies there are for diseases before the diseases existed, and like the best father of a household provided for his children in the future, so, knowing that we would fall before we fell, he decided within himself the plan by which wretched us might be helped. And since Christ bears witness that of old all the righteous and the prophets ardently desired to see and hear those things which are set before our ears and eyes through the preaching of the gospel, the ingratitude of those who now disdain to see and hear these things is worthy of no pardon. But what happens to them is what happens to those who suffer from weak eyes. For just as these, accustomed to darkness, cannot bear the light, so those who are entangled in the long-standing habit of errors and superstitions conceive pain from the gospel, and they do what they think may either obscure it or drive it out. But since they have to do with the wisdom of God, it will never accomplish what they want, but they will perish wretchedly in their own darkness.

units.la: Tertiò, ad quos sapientiæ istius cognitio pertineat, docetur. Est autem in hoc admodum diligens Paulus. Nam primùm principes seculi huius excludit, & ne quid temere dixisse putetur, bis illorum mentionem facit. Eo autem nomine omnes eos comprehendit, qui authoritate, potentia, sapientia, rerum vsu & quibuscunq; aliis donis in hoc seculo præ aliis hominibus excellunt, vt eorum principes censeri possint. Rursus ergo ad illud alludit, quod Cap. primo dixerat: Non multi sapientes secundùm carnem, non multi potentes, non multi nobiles aut genere illustres, &c. Deinde his opponit Perfectos. Sapientiam Dei loquimur (inquit) inter perfectos. At quis (inquis) inter homines perfectus est? Nemo vtiq;, cùm omnium nostrum conceptio, natiuitas, vita, polluta sit, & in multis quotidie labamur. Sed perfectos dicit Paulus eos, qui Euangelium audiunt, & IESVM CHRISTVM amplexi eius doctrinæ studeunt, quæ sola ad eam perfectionem nos deducit, quæ in hac quidem vita in nobis inchoatur, olim autem perficietur, quando corpus hoc mortale & corruptibile immortalitatem atq; incorruptibilitatem induerit, & Deus ipse erit omnia in omnibus. Respexit eòdem Paulus, quando ad Scripturæ sacræ lectionem assiduam Timotheum suum exhortans, illam hoc nomine commendat, quòd vtilis sit ad id, vt homo Dei perfectus sit, & ad omne opus bonum instructus. Itaq; Euangelium veram illam & salutarem Dei sapientiam illis solis cum fructu offert, qui illius beneficium agnoscunt & ad metam verae perfectionis tendunt, quam ille nobis in Christo præfixit. Nihil ergo ista ad porcos & canes, qui huius seculi luto immersi aduersus Deum impudenter latrant & grunniunt, neq; magis cœlestia curant, quàm gallus ille Æsopicus gemmam in sterquilinio inuentam, quæ ipsi hordei grano vilior erat. Et ideo Christus, ne doctrina hæc talibus temere proponatur, prohibet Matth.7.
units.tr: Thirdly, the passage teaches to whom the knowledge of this wisdom belongs. Paul is very careful in this matter. First he excludes the rulers of this age, and, lest it be thought he spoke rashly, he mentions them twice. By this name he takes in all who excel other men in this age in authority, power, wisdom, experience of affairs, or any other gifts, so that they may be counted as its rulers. Here again he alludes to what he had said in the first chapter: not many wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble or of illustrious birth, and so on. Then he sets the perfect against these, saying: "We speak wisdom among the perfect." But, you will ask, who among men is perfect? No one, surely, since the conception, birth and life of all of us are defiled, and we stumble daily in many things. But Paul calls perfect those who hear the Gospel and embrace Jesus Christ and study that doctrine, which alone leads us to that perfection which is begun in us in this life but will be brought to completion afterwards, when this mortal and corruptible body shall put on immortality and incorruption, and God himself will be all in all. Paul had the same in view when, urging his Timothy to the constant reading of Holy Scripture, he commends it on this ground, that it is useful for making the man of God perfect and equipped for every good work. Therefore the Gospel offers that true and saving wisdom of God with fruit only to those who acknowledge its benefit and strive toward the goal of true perfection, which he has set before us in Christ. This wisdom therefore has nothing to do with swine and dogs, who, wallowing in the mud of this age, bark and grunt impudently against God, and care no more for heavenly things than that Aesopic cockerel who, finding a gem on the dunghill, valued it less than a grain of barley. And so Christ, lest this teaching be rashly offered to such people, forbids it, Matt. 7.

units.la: Cæterum miretur aliquis, qui fiat, cur in aperta & clara Euangelij prædicatione hanc Dei sapientiam non agnoscant aut intelligant, qui præ aliis ingenio valent, & multo rerum vsu exertitati sunt? Sed occurrit huic quæstioni Paulus, dum illam in mysterio prædicari ait. Id verò non de doctrinæ huius obscuritate, quæ revera nulla est, sed eorum potius morositate & stoliditate exponi debet, qui (ut ante diximus) sibijpsis tenebras offundunt, dum humanam rationem in consilium adhibent. Horum vitio fit, ut latentia sub simplici Evangelij doctrina regni cœlorum mysteria non videant, eò quòd in sola externa intenti, nihil porrò videre aut intelligere volunt. Quæ ergo fidei oculis meridiana luce clariora sunt, ea humanæ rationi profunda & inscrutabilia mysteria esse putantur, quia longè alia sunt, quàm appareant. Itaq; illorū prædicatione & contemplatione aliter fidelis, aliter infidelis afficitur. Audit hic Dei filium in cruce mortem infamem obijsse: & quia hoc infirmitati illius tribuit, & in nudo crucis spectaculo hæret, offenditur. At dum idem illud fidelis audit, mox Dei ineffabilem bonitatem & dilectionem agnoscit, & in fide confirmatus cum Paulo exclamat: Qui proprio Filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit eum in mortem, qui non omnia nobis cum eo gratificetur? Sic huic dulcissimæ consolationis plenum & ipsi etiam rationi humanæ manifestum mysterium est, quod alteri illi scandalum & quasi sub undis delitescens scopulus est, ad quem cum fidei & salutis æternæ jactura naufragium faciat. Idem enim, si Christum à mortuis resurrexisse audiat, fabulam putabit. Qui verò fide præditus est, resurrectionis prædicatione magis confirmatur, & in ea simul mortem deuictam, diabolum profligatum & effractas inferorum portas intuetur. Eadem est Sacramentorum nostrorum ratio. Si enim alium baptismo tingi, aut mysticam Domini Cœnam in publico cœtu distribui homo prophanus videat, baptismi quidem actionem ridiculam esse, Cœnam verò nihil à conuiuio aliquo vulgari differre putabit, imò intemperantium & delicatulorum mensas atq; epulas illi longè præferet. Fidelis autem in baptismo ablutionem peccatorum, veteris Adami mortificationem, resurrectionem item ad vitæ novitatem & adoptionis nostræ per Christum facta beneficium contemplatur: in Cœna autem animo per fidem supra cœlos omnes evectio Christi carne & sanguine ad vitam æternam pascitur. Poterant hæc prolixius tractari, sed jam omnibus patere puto, cur Paulus sapientiam illam Dei in mysterio prædicari dicat. Nos autem hīs admonemur, nihil in toto hoc negotio carnis rationi tribuendum esse, sed fidei oculis hæc omnia spectari debere, quæ sola nos mysteriorum ipsiorum[?] capaces reddit.
units.tr: But someone may wonder how it comes about that those who excel others in intellect and have been trained by long experience of affairs do not recognise or understand this wisdom of God in the plain and clear preaching of the Gospel. Paul meets this question when he says that it is preached in a mystery. This must be explained not by any obscurity in the doctrine, which in truth there is none, but rather by the perverseness and stupidity of those who (as we said before) cast darkness upon themselves when they take human reason as their counsellor. Through their fault it happens that they do not see the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven lying hidden beneath the simple doctrine of the Gospel, because, intent on externals alone, they do not wish to see or understand anything further. Thus things which are clearer to the eyes of faith than the noonday light are thought by human reason to be deep and inscrutable mysteries, because they are quite other than they appear. So the preaching and contemplation of these things affect the believer and the unbeliever differently. The unbeliever hears that the Son of God died a shameful death on the cross; and because he ascribes this to weakness and dwells on the bare sight of the cross, he takes offence. But when the believer hears the same thing, he at once recognises God's ineffable goodness and love, and, confirmed in faith, cries out with Paul: "He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?" Thus to the one this mystery is full of the sweetest consolation and is even plain to human reason itself, while to the other it is a stumbling block and a rock, as it were, hidden beneath the waves, on which he suffers shipwreck with the loss of faith and eternal salvation. For the same man, if he hears that Christ rose from the dead, will think it a fable; but he who has faith is strengthened by the preaching of the resurrection, and in it he sees death conquered, the devil overthrown and the gates of hell broken open. The same is true of our sacraments. If a profane man sees someone baptised with water, or the mystical Lord's Supper distributed in a public assembly, he will think the act of baptism ridiculous, and will suppose that the Supper differs nothing from any common banquet; indeed he will far prefer to it the tables and feasts of gluttons and pampered men. But the believer, in baptism, contemplates the washing away of sins, the mortification of the old Adam, and likewise the resurrection to newness of life and the benefit of our adoption through Christ; and in the Supper, his soul by faith, lifted above all the heavens, is fed on Christ's flesh and blood unto eternal life. These things could be treated at greater length, but I think it is now plain to everyone why Paul says that the wisdom of God is preached in a mystery. We are admonished by this that nothing in the whole matter is to be ascribed to carnal reason, but that all these things must be viewed with the eyes of faith, which alone makes us capable of the mysteries themselves.

units.la: Postremò finem prædicationis evangelicæ Paulus indicat, quando totum negotium hoc ante secula in nostram gloriam præfinitum esse scribit. At gloriæ nomine tota hominis felicitas comprehenditur. Nam opponit illam Apostolus conditioni, in qua nascimur, & in qua fumus, si nos extra Christum consideres, ubi (ut supra diximus) nihil invenitur præter infamiam & ignominiam cum omni miseriarum genere conjunctam. Ut enim quoad corpus nudi cum vagitu & eiulatu in hanc lucem ex matris utero prodimus: ita quoad animam quoque plus quàm nudi sumus, eò quòd nulla in nobis justitia est, quæ peccati & mortis reos tegat. Et si qui aliquid hic conantur, non plus tamen proficiunt, quàm primi parentes, qui suam nuditatem ficus foliis nequicquam velare studuerunt. Ergo miseri & infames stamus[?] in Dei conspectu, & nisi omnem religionis sensum exuimus, nostri ipsorum nos pudet, quando nos magno nostro merito à Deo conspectu reiectos & æternæ damnationis ignominia dignos esse cogitamus.
