At hic nobis opem fert unigenitus ille Dei filius, JESVS CHRISTVS, qui (ut nuper docuit Paulus) nobis à Patre sapientia, justitia, sanctificatio & redemptio factus est. Is enim intellectum nostrum illuminat, Patris voluntatem exponit, salutis rationem monstrat, sua obedientia & justitia nuditatem nostram tegit, ex verbi sui femine renatos Deo Patri consecrat, denique proprij sanguinis pretio redimit, & spiritum adoptionis largitur, ut filij Dei facti ipsius cohæredes simus, & cum ipso in cœlesti gloria vivamus atq; regnemus. Eius enim promissio est: Ubi ego sum, illic erit etiam minister meus. Et jam moriturus dicebat: Gloriam, quam dedisti mihi ô Pater, ego dedi eis. Item: Pater, quos dedisti mihi, volo ut ubi sum ego, & illi sint mecum, ut spectent gloriam illam meam, quam dedisti mihi, &c. Jam ergo gloriæ istius gustum percipimus, quando spiritu adoptionis confirmati, nos Dei filios esse sentimus, & multùm licet reclamate mundo ad Deum clamamus: Abba pater noster qui es in cœlis, &c. Olim autem perficietur gloria ista, quàdo in totius mundi conspectu nos pro suis Christus agnoscet, & ad sui regni cofortium invitabit, dicens: Venite benedicti patris mei, possidete regnum paratum vobis à jactis fundamentis mundi. Et tanta est huius gloriæ maiestas, vt (quod alibi annotauit Paulus) huius seculi afflictiones illi nequaquam respondeant. Nam & corpora nostra mortalia gloriosò Christi corpori conformia fient, & tam animæ quam corpora nostra cœlestis regni gaudijs fruentur, quæ vt omnem humani ingenij captum excedunt, ita æterna sunt, neq; vllis fortunæ vicibus (vt in hoc seculo fieri solet) turbantur. Et de istis quidem nos certiores facit Euangelij doctrina, imò tanta bona per illam nobis Deus offert, & nos hoc medio aut instrumento ad gloriæ istius possessionem perducit.
units.tr: Lastly, Paul indicates the end of the evangelical preaching, when he writes that the whole business was predestined before the ages for our glory. Now under the name of glory the whole happiness of man is comprehended. For the Apostle sets it against the condition in which we are born and in which we are, if you consider us apart from Christ, where (as we said above) nothing is found but infamy and shame joined with every kind of misery. For just as in body we come forth naked from the mother's womb into this light, with wailing and crying, so in soul too we are more than naked, because there is no righteousness in us to cover us as guilty of sin and death. And if some men attempt anything here, they gain no more than our first parents, who tried in vain to cover their nakedness with fig leaves. So we stand wretched and infamous in the sight of God, and unless we strip off all sense of religion, we are ashamed of ourselves, when we think that we have been cast out from God's sight by our own great deserving and are worthy of the shame of eternal damnation. But here the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, brings us help, who (as Paul lately taught) has been made for us by the Father wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. For he enlightens our understanding, sets forth the Father's will, shows the way of salvation, covers our nakedness with his obedience and righteousness, consecrates to God the Father those who are born again from the seed of his word, and finally redeems us at the price of his own blood, and bestows the Spirit of adoption, so that, made sons of God, we may be his co-heirs, and live and reign with him in heavenly glory. For this is his promise: "Where I am, there shall my servant also be." And already about to die he said: "The glory which you gave me, O Father, I have given to them." Again: "Father, those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me, that they may behold my glory which you have given me," and so on. So now we taste that glory when, confirmed by the Spirit of adoption, we feel that we are sons of God, and, though the world protests greatly, we cry out to God: "Abba, Father, our Father who art in heaven," and so on. But that glory will be brought to completion afterwards, when, in the sight of the whole world, Christ will acknowledge us as his own and invite us to the fellowship of his kingdom, saying: "Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." And so great is the majesty of this glory that (as Paul noted elsewhere) the afflictions of this age bear no comparison with it. For our mortal bodies will be made conformable to the glorious body of Christ, and both our souls and our bodies will enjoy the joys of the heavenly kingdom, which, as they exceed all the grasp of human understanding, so they are eternal, and are disturbed by none of the changes of fortune, as usually happens in this age. Of these things the doctrine of the Gospel makes us certain; indeed, through it God offers us such great goods, and by this means or instrument leads us into the possession of that glory.

units.la: Hæc vt Euangelij prædicationem nobis plurimùm commendant: ita nos ad eius studium excitare debent, vt posthabitis & relictis huius seculi rebus omnibus in gloria ista quærenda assidui simus: quam facile inuenient, qui & conciones sacras frequenter audiunt, & quod audierunt diligenti meditatione & lectione priuata in animis suis confirmare studeant. Neque nos terreant suo vel exemplo vel authoritate, qui in hoc seculo reliquis præstare solent, siue illi publica potestate armati sint, siue eruditione aut aliis rebus excellant. Ignorant tales ferè hanc sapientiam, neq; sua ignorantia contenti, alios quoque impedire satagunt, quò minus ad illius cognitionem perueniant. Itaque fidis Euangelij ministris silentium indicunt, & ne quis conciones sacras accedat prohibent: adhæc cum libris quoque sacris bellum gerunt, quos aut flammis impijs tradunt, Ioakimum & Antiochum imitati, aut ex manibus laicorum temerarijs suis editis excutiunt, ne à quoquam legantur. Est horum audacia intolerabilis, cùm gigantum similes Deum ipsum, ne inter homines regnet, prohiberi posse putant: quin in ipsos cœlos sibi ius sumunt & imperium, quando obstare conantur, ne qui ad eius gloriæ possessionem veniant, quam nobis Deus in Filio suo IESV CHRISTO per Euangelium offerre solet. At neminem terrere debet Cyclopum istorum ferocia. Nam qualescunq; illi sint, abolentur tamen (vt in præsenti Paulus loquitur) & vt ipsi mortales sunt, sic caduca & momentanea est potentia, qua modò ferociunt. Omnis caro fœnum (clamat Propheta) & omnis gloria carnis flos agri. Exaruit fœnum, decidit flos, Verbum autem Dei nostri manet in æternum. Debebant ista attentius considerare Reges & principes, & veterum Regum exempla sibi frequenter ob oculos ponere, quibus infelicissimè cessit audacia sua, qua Dei ecclesiam oppugnare ausi sunt. At cùm illi neq; alienis neq; proprijs exemplis corrigantur, sed adulatorum blanditijs fascinati sibi vt Semideis quibusdam nihil non licere putent: piorum tamen est, fidem Christo datam fortiter tueri, neq; ad momentaneum secularis potentiæ splendorem ita obstupescere, vt cœlesti & æternæ gloriæ renuntient, ad cuius hæreditatem nobis in Christo aditus patet. si Euangelij doctrinam sequamur.
units.tr: These things, while they greatly commend to us the preaching of the Gospel, ought also to stir us to its study, so that, setting aside and leaving behind all the things of this world, we may be diligent in seeking that glory. Those who both hear sacred sermons frequently and take care to confirm in their minds what they have heard by diligent meditation and private reading will readily find it. Let us not be frightened by those who, in this world, are accustomed to excel the rest, whether by their example or authority, whether they are armed with public power or excel in learning or other things. Such men for the most part do not know this wisdom, and, not content with their own ignorance, they also strive to hinder others from coming to its knowledge. So they declare silence to the faithful ministers of the Gospel and forbid anyone to attend sacred sermons. Moreover, they wage war even on the holy books: some hand them over to impious flames, imitating Jehoiakim and Antiochus, others tear them from the hands of laymen, having published their own rash versions, so that they may not be read by anyone. Their audacity is intolerable, since, like giants, they think that God himself can be prevented from reigning among men; nay, they claim for themselves right and rule even over the heavens, when they try to prevent those who would come to the possession of that glory which God is wont to offer us in his Son Jesus Christ through the Gospel. But the ferocity of these Cyclopes ought to terrify no one. For whatever they may be, they will nevertheless be abolished (as Paul speaks in this place); and, being mortals themselves, the power by which they now rage is perishable and momentary. "All flesh is grass," cries the Prophet, "and all the glory of flesh is the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower falls, but the Word of our God remains for ever." Kings and princes ought to consider these things more carefully, and frequently set before their eyes the examples of the ancient kings, whose audacity, with which they dared to assail the Church of God, ended most unhappily. But since they are corrected neither by others' examples nor by their own, and, bewitched by the flatteries of courtiers, think that nothing is forbidden to them, as if they were certain demigods, it is nevertheless the duty of the godly to defend bravely the faith given to Christ, and not to be so dazzled by the momentary splendour of worldly power as to renounce the heavenly and eternal glory, to whose inheritance an entrance lies open to us in Christ, if we follow the doctrine of the Gospel.

units.la: Caterum duplici argumento probat Paulus, huius seculi principes sapientiam istā Dei ignorare. Primùm proprio ipsorum facto eos conuincit. Nam si cognouissent (inquit) nequaquam Dominum gloriæ crucifixissent. Ita verò Christum vocat, vt huius maiestatem huius seculi principibus opponat, quos cum sua authoritate aboleri dixit. Merito autè sic dicitur Christus, qui & Deus verus & vnum cum Patre est, & cui Pater omnem potestatem dedit in cœlo & in terra. Hunc (inquit Paulus) si verè cognouissent, procul dubio eundem noluissent in crucem suffigere. Atqui Christum ipsum Iudæis dixisse legimus: Qui sim scitis, & vnde sim scitis. Sed obseruabis duplicem esse Christi notitiam. Alteram vulgarem, qua illum multi Iudæorum ex operibus agnoscebant, vt vel inuiti ipsum homine maiorè esse faterentur. Et hanc illis non sine Sarcasmo tribuit apud Ioan-nem, vt ostendat illos plus scire quàm ipsis conducat, si contumaces & increduli esse pergant. Altera specialis est, quæ ad solos electos restringitur, qui illum Dei Filium, humani generis Seruatorem, Dominum cœli & terræ, victorem mortis & diaboli, adhæc vnicum vitæ authorem esse intelligunt. Quæ cognitio cum fide coniuncta est, & obedientiam parit, adeoque totum hominem Deo vendicat. Iam in præsenti principibus huius seculi Paulus negat, vt & ipse Christus, cum Pharisæis dicit: Neque me nostis, neque Patrem meum. Quod ab illo verissimè dictum suis-se, tota passionis Dominicæ historia abunde probat, imprimis autem precatio illa Christi: Pater remitte illis, quia nesciunt quid faciant. Et Petrus Apostolus Hierosolymitanos ciues hoc argumento consolatur, ne ob indignam filij Dei necem desperent, quia hoc omne per ignorantiam fecerint. Admonent ista, persecutiones omnes ex Christi & diuinæ illius sapientiæ ignorantia nasci. Videntur quidem sibi ipsis sapientissimi mortalium esse, quicunque aduersus Euangelij doctri-nam conspirant, & fere cum Caiapha alijs omnibus suam inscitiam exprobrant, quos hic minus audere vident. Et Daniel Antichristo oculos hominis tribuit, ea locutione astutiam singularem in rebus agendis denotans. Sed reuera, si aliquem diuinae & verae sapientiae gustum haberent, eam minime odissent, multo minus hostiliter persequerentur. Ideo Dauid, cum Psal.2. hostium Christi improbos conatus describisset, & ijsdem denuntiauisset, fore, ut ferreo ipsius sceptro comminuantur, mox grauem adhortationem subijcit: Sapite ergo o reges, erudimini iudices terrae. Seruite Domino in timore, & exultate cum tremore. Osculamini Filium, ne irascatur, & ne pereatis a via, &c. Debet autem horum consideratio nos excitare, ne vicissim hostes nostros odio prosequamur, sed potius eorum tangamur commiseratione, qui infelici illa ignorantia laborant, & pro illis preces ad Deum fundamus, ut & hanc audaciam illis condonet, & eorundem mentes Veritatis cognitione illuminet.
units.tr: Moreover, Paul proves by a double argument that the princes of this world are ignorant of this wisdom of God. First he convicts them by their own deed: for if they had known, he says, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. He calls Christ thus so that he may set the majesty of Christ over against the princes of this world, whom he said would be abolished by his own authority. Christ is rightly so called, since he is both true God and one with the Father, and to whom the Father has given all power in heaven and on earth. "If they had truly known him," says Paul, "without doubt they would not have nailed him to the cross." Yet we read that Christ himself said to the Jews: "You know who I am, and you know whence I am." But you will observe that there is a twofold knowledge of Christ. The one is common, by which many of the Jews recognised him from his works, so that even unwillingly they confessed him to be greater than a man. John records that he attributed this knowledge to them not without sarcasm, to show that they know more than it profits them, if they persist in being obstinate and unbelieving. The other is special, and is restricted to the elect alone, who understand him to be the Son of God, the Saviour of the human race, the Lord of heaven and earth, the conqueror of death and of the devil, and moreover the only author of life. This knowledge is joined with faith and brings forth obedience, and so claims the whole man for God. Now, in the present passage Paul denies that the princes of this world have this knowledge, just as Christ himself says to the Pharisees: "You know neither me nor my Father." That this was most truly said by him, the whole history of the Lord's passion abundantly proves, and especially that prayer of Christ: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." And the Apostle Peter comforts the citizens of Jerusalem with this argument, lest they despair over the unworthy death of the Son of God, because they did all this through ignorance. These things teach that all persecutions arise from ignorance of Christ and of that divine wisdom. Those indeed seem to themselves the wisest of mortals who conspire against the doctrine of the Gospel, and, almost with Caiaphas and all the others, reproach the ignorance of others, those whom they see here to dare less. And Daniel attributes to the Antichrist the eyes of a man, by that expression denoting his singular cunning in carrying out his purposes. But in truth, if they had any taste of divine and true wisdom, they would by no means hate it, much less persecute it so hostilely. Therefore David, when in Psalm 2 he had described the wicked attempts of the enemies of Christ, and had announced that they would be crushed by his iron sceptre, immediately adds a grave exhortation: "Be wise therefore, O kings; be instructed, you judges of the earth. Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and you perish from the way," etc. Moreover, the consideration of these things ought to stir us not to pursue our enemies with hatred in turn, but rather to be moved with pity for those who labour under that unhappy ignorance, and to pour out prayers to God for them, that he may both pardon them this audacity and illuminate their minds with the knowledge of the Truth.

units.la: Alterum argumentum ex Isaiae cap.64.adducit. Sed sicut scriptum est, quae oculus non vidit, nec auris audiuit, neq; in cor hominis venerunt, quae parauit Deus iis, qui ipsum diligunt. Leguntur haec paulo aliter apud Prophetam, sed nulla in sensu differentia est, & quaedam Paulus interserit, quae ad pleniorem loci huius explicationem faciunt. Loquitur autem illic Isaias de veteribus Dei beneficijs, & imprimis Maiestatem eius praedicat, quam toti populo in monte Sinai spectandam exhibuit, cum Legem promulgaret.
units.tr: Paul adduces the second argument from Isaiah chapter 64. "But as it is written, 'What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him.'" These words are read a little differently in the Prophet, but there is no difference in sense, and Paul inserts certain things which serve a fuller explanation of this passage. Now Isaiah there speaks of the ancient benefits of God, and above all proclaims his majesty, which he displayed for the whole people to behold on Mount Sinai, when he promulgated the Law.

units.la: Quod beneficium etiam Moses prae omnibus alijs commendat. At quia quaecunq; cum veteribus gesta sunt, Christum & in hoc nobis collata aeternae salutis beneficia adumbrarunt, recte Paulus locum istum de Christo & Euangelio eius exponit, ut ostendat huius mysteria omnem humani ingenij captum superare, & proinde non mirum esse si ista ignorent, qui praeter huius seculi eminentiam nihil sapiunt. Et sane, si ineffabilis est Dei bonitas, quam in ijs, quae ad corpus spectant, quotidie experimur, multo minus ea scrutari poterimus, quae ad regnum coelorum & salutis aeternae negotium faciunt. Et debet locus iste a nobis bifariam considerari. Primo quoad religionis & fidei Christianae causam. Quis enim tam acutus & sapiens est, ut huius mysteria humani ingenij acumine inuestiget siue excutiat? Falluntur ergo multum, qui humanam sapientiam hic in consilium adhibent, & nescio quas Scholas, Patres. Concilia nobis obijciunt, quorum authoritati in ijs etiam cedere debeamus, quae nos ex Scripturis didicimus. Deinde, quoad aeterna bona, quae nobis in coelo parata sunt, loci huius nos meminisse conuenit. Sunt enim haec quoq; eiusmodi, ut illis digne considerandis aut exponendis nulla hominis facultates sufficiat.
units.tr: Moses also commends this benefit above all others. But because whatever was done with the ancients foreshadowed Christ and the benefits of eternal salvation conferred on us in this time, Paul rightly expounds that passage concerning Christ and his Gospel, to show that the mysteries of these things surpass all the grasp of the human mind, and that therefore it is no wonder if those who know nothing beyond the eminence of this world are ignorant of them. And indeed, if the goodness of God is ineffable, which we daily experience in those things that pertain to the body, much less shall we be able to search out those things that concern the kingdom of heaven and the business of eternal salvation. And this passage ought to be considered by us in two ways. First, as regards the cause of religion and of the Christian faith. For who is so keen and wise as to investigate or examine these mysteries by the sharpness of the human mind? They are therefore greatly mistaken who here call in human wisdom as counsellor, and object to us I know not what Schools, Fathers and Councils, to whose authority we ought to yield even in those things which we have learned from the Scriptures. Next, as regards the eternal good things which are laid up for us in heaven, it is fitting that we remember this passage. For these things are of such a kind that no faculty of man is sufficient to consider or expound them worthily.

units.la: Nam in coelis nobis reposité sunt thesauri illi, quos neq; tinea arrodit, neq; vermes exedunt, neque fures aut praedones eripiunt: qui deniq; nulla vetustate deficiunt, neq; diutino & perpetuo usu aut consuetudine nobis sui fastidium pariunt. Et cum mundum hunc universum Deus Verbo suo creavit, beatam illam immortalitatem filij sui vnigeniti & aeterni sanguine acquiri nobis oportuit. Quod vnum satis admonet, eam omnibus quae in mundo sunt, sublimiorem & pretiosiorem esse. Recte ergo horum consideratione abreptus Dauid exclamat: Quam ampla sunt quae metuentibus te bona reposuisti? Quod si recte expendamus, mox patebit, quam inanis & slulta[?] sit eorum confidentia, qui salutem illam aeternam nostris viribus acquiri, aut nos operum nostrorum iustitia & propria sanctitate bona illa aeterna mereri posse docent. Si enim illa neq; sensu neq; ratione humana percipi possunt, multo minus ea nostris viribus assequi licebit. Procul ergo haec fiducia faceSSat. Interim excitet nos tantae felicitatis consideratio, ut Euangelij doctrinae credamus, & in ea nobis loquentem IESVM CHRISTVM fide vera & constanti amplexemur, qui nos & in huius vitae curriculo laborantes tuebitur, & olim regni sui coelestis participes faciet. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: For in heaven those treasures are laid up for us, which neither moth consumes, nor worms eat, nor thieves or robbers snatch away; which, finally, suffer no decay through age, and do not, through long and perpetual use or habit, breed in us any weariness of them. And since God created this whole world by his Word, that blessed immortality had to be acquired for us by the eternal blood of his only-begotten Son. This one thing sufficiently shows that it is higher and more precious than all that is in the world. Rightly, therefore, David, carried away by the consideration of these things, cries out: "How great are the good things which you have laid up for those who fear you!" If we weigh these things rightly, it will soon become plain how empty and foolish is the confidence of those who teach that that eternal salvation can be acquired by our own strength, or that by the righteousness of our works and our own holiness we can merit those eternal good things. For if they cannot be perceived either by sense or by human reason, much less will it be permitted to attain them by our own powers. Let that trust, therefore, be far away. Meanwhile, let the consideration of so great a happiness stir us to believe the doctrine of the Gospel, and to embrace in it Jesus Christ speaking to us with true and steadfast faith, who will protect us as we labour in the course of this life, and will in time make us partakers of his heavenly kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA X.
units.tr: HOMILY X.

units.la: Nobis autem Deus ea reuelauit per Spiritum suum. Spiritus enim omnia scrutatur, etiam profunditates Dei. Quis enim hominum nouit ea quae sunt hominis, nisi spiritus hominis, qui est in eo. Ita etiam ea quae sunt Dei nemo nouit nisi Spiritus Dei. Nos vero non spiritum mundi accepimus, sed Spiritum qui est ex Deo, ut sciamus quae à Deo donata sunt nobis. Quae etiam loquimur non sermonibus, quos docet humana sapientia, sed quos docet Spiritus sanctus, spiritualibus spiritualia coaptantes.
units.tr: But God has revealed these things to us through his Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. For who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man that is in him? So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. We, however, have received not the spirit of the world but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things that have been given to us by God. And we speak these things not in words taught by human wisdom, but in words taught by the Holy Spirit, fitting spiritual things to spiritual people.

units.la: UT homo propter innatam sibi naturae vitiositatem Dei donis fere omnibus in propriam perniciem abutitur: ita hoc imprimis facit quoad rationem & mentem, qua illum Deus aliis animantibus praestare voluit. Nam ardet quidem discendi & sciendi cupiditate mens nostra, in eo autem plerique errant, quod vel circa rerum inutilium cognitionem occupantur, vel quae diuina & caelestia sunt, ad suae rationis calculum revocant. Quia enim haec non capit ea, quae sunt spiritus Dei, fieri non potest, quin opiniones absurdissimas pariat, quae aut superstitionum ineptissimarum causa sunt, vel omnem religionis sensum in nobis extinguunt. Est ergo diligenti consideratione digna haec Pauli tractatio, qua primo docet, veram & salutarem sapientiam esse eam, quae Evangelii doctrina continetur: deinde illam non posse humanae rationis captu comprehendi, & proinde ab iis plerunque ignorari, qui propter eximia dona & summam authoritatem in hoc mundo principes sunt. Usus istorum nobis hic esse debet, ut relictis inutilibus & vanis huius mundi studijs, ad sapientiam hanc caelestem aspiremus, quae nos de Dei voluntate certos facit, & non solum huius vitae mortalis tutissimam regulam praescribit, verumetiam ad beatam immortalitatem nos deducit, in qua ineffabilibus regni caelorum bonis fruemur, quae nobis Christus acquisiuit. In illius tamen studio etiam atque etiam nobis cauendum est, ne quid nostri ingenij viribus aut industriae tribuamus, sed in solius Dei Verbum intenti simus, quod nos à Veritate aberrare non sinet. Et hoc plurimum facit locus iste, quem modo recitauimus. Docet enim Apostolus, quae unica ratio sit, per quam homines infelici illa & pernitiosa rerum caelestium ignorantia liberentur, & ad salutis verae cognitionem perueniant.
units.tr: Just as man, because of the wickedness innate in his nature, misuses almost all of God's gifts to his own destruction, so he does especially with reason and mind, by which God wished to set him above the other living creatures. For our mind burns with a desire to learn and to know, but most people go wrong in this: either they occupy themselves with knowing useless things, or they bring down divine and heavenly matters to the measure of their own reason. Since reason does not grasp the things of the Spirit of God, it cannot but produce the most absurd opinions, which either cause the most foolish superstitions or extinguish every sense of religion in us. This passage of Paul therefore deserves careful consideration, in which he first teaches that the true and saving wisdom is the one contained in the teaching of the Gospel; then that it cannot be grasped by the capacity of human reason, and so is for the most part unknown to those who are rulers in this world because of their outstanding gifts and great authority. We ought to take from their example that, leaving aside the useless and empty studies of this world, we should aspire to this heavenly wisdom, which makes us certain of God's will, prescribes for us the safest rule for this mortal life, and moreover leads us to blessed immortality, in which we shall enjoy the inexpressible good things of the kingdom of heaven, which Christ has won for us. In the pursuit of this wisdom, however, we must take great care again and again not to attribute anything to the powers of our own intellect or diligence, but to be intent on the Word of God alone, which will not let us stray from the truth. And this passage, which we have just recited, does this very thing. For the Apostle teaches what the only way is by which men may be freed from that wretched and harmful ignorance of heavenly things and come to the true knowledge of salvation.

units.la: Poterat enim ex iis, quae proxime dicta sunt, eiusmodi quaestio inferri: Si quae vos Apostoli praedicatis, omnem sensum simul atque humanae rationis captum superant, unde ergo vobis istorum cognitio contigit, aut quomodo illa ipsa à vobis tradi & doceri possunt? Hanc quaestionem Paulus sua responsione praeveniens, sic ait: Nobis Deus ea reuelauit per spiritum suum. Quibus verbis doctrinae apostolicae certitudinem fortiter asserit, & illam omni sinistra suspicione liberat, quasi diceret: Etsi tam sublimis & abstrusa sit haec sapientia, nemo tamen eam aut negligere debet ut cognitu impossibilem, aut de eius doctrina dubitare. Nam quae homines sui ingenij acumine aut sagacitate inuestigare non possunt, ea nobis Deus ipse per spiritum suum reuelat, ut eorum cognitio facilis & quasi oculis nostris sit exposita. Nec temere aut confidenter hoc dicit Paulus. Nouerat enim IESV CHRISTI promissionem, qua Spiritum sanctum discipulis suis pollicetur, qui ipsis omnia, quae ex illo audiuerant, in memoriam reuocare, & in omnem veritatem inducere debuit. Imo per prophetas hoc ipsum olim promiserat Deus, quod ipse Legem suam in credentium corda inscribere, & sui cognitione omnes illuminare velit. Quo nomine Isaias eos: qui Christo credunt, θεοδιδακτοὺς[?], id est, discipulos Dei vocat.
units.tr: For from what has just been said, a question of this kind might be raised: If the things you Apostles preach surpass all understanding and the grasp of human reason, how then have you come to know them, or how can they themselves be handed on and taught by you? Paul, anticipating this question with his answer, says: "God has revealed these things to us through his Spirit." By these words he firmly asserts the certainty of apostolic teaching and frees it from every unfavourable suspicion, as if he were saying: Although this wisdom is so lofty and hidden, no one ought to neglect it as impossible to know, or to doubt its teaching. For what men cannot track down by the keenness or shrewdness of their own minds, God himself reveals to us through his Spirit, so that the knowledge of these things is easy and set out, as it were, before our eyes. Paul does not say this rashly or boastfully. For he knew the promise of Jesus Christ, by which he pledged the Holy Spirit to his disciples, who was to bring back to their memory all that they had heard from him and lead them into all truth. Indeed, God had promised this same thing long before through the prophets, that he would write his law on the hearts of believers and wished to enlighten all with the knowledge of himself. For this reason Isaiah calls those who believe in Christ "taught by God" [θεοδιδακτούς], that is, disciples of God.

units.la: Admonent nos ista de bonitate & indulgentia Dei plus quam paterna: qui eo vsque se demittit, vt non per Verbum modo suum nobiscum colloqui dignetur, verumetiam spiritum suum nobis communicet, vt huius radijs ignorantiae tenebrae, quae animos hominum obnubilant, dissipentur. Nec enim ad solos Apostolos promissiones illas, quarum modo meminimus, restringi debent, sed ad Christianos omnes extendi, qui (vt in epistola ad Romanos Paulus ait) Christi non erunt, nisi eius spiritu donati sint. Et hoc negare non possunt, quicunque bonas animi suggestiones obseruant, & corda[?] sua ad Euangelij praedicationem aperiri & subito mutari sentiunt, ut ijs quàm diligentissimè attendant, à quibus prius totis animis abhorrebant. Similiter inter legendum spiritus ille cordibus piorum sese insinuat, ut saepe nouam lucem subito exoriri sentiant, quae ipsis expedita & intellectu facillima reddit, quae paulò ante Cimmerijs tenebris obscuriora videbantur. Exempla huius rei multa ex historijs adduci poterant, nisi quae quotidie fiunt sufficerent. Nos potius illa in eum finem obseruemus, ut Deo nos erudiendos praebeamus, neque extinguamus in animis nostris agentem Spiritus sancti lucem, sed Verbi studio diligenti atque precibus assiduis nos illi accommodemus, & si quem sentimus profectum, hunc omnem Deo feramus acceptum.
units.tr: These things teach us about the goodness and kindness of God, more than fatherly, who stoops so far that he deigns to speak with us not only through his Word but also imparts his Spirit to us, so that by its rays the darkness of ignorance, which clouds the minds of men, may be dispelled. For those promises, of which we have just spoken, ought not to be restricted to the Apostles alone, but extended to all Christians, who (as Paul says in his letter to the Romans) will not be Christ's unless they have been endowed with his Spirit. And this cannot be denied by those who observe the good impulses of their own minds, and feel their hearts being opened to the preaching of the Gospel and suddenly changed, so that they attend most diligently to those whom before they had abhorred with their whole soul. Likewise, while reading, that Spirit insinuates himself into the hearts of the pious, so that they often feel a new light suddenly rising, which makes plain and most easy to understand things that a little before seemed darker than Cimmerian shadows. Many examples of this could be drawn from histories, but those that happen every day are enough. Let us rather observe these things to this end: that we offer ourselves to be taught by God, and do not quench in our minds the light of the Holy Spirit at work, but by diligent study of the Word and by constant prayers we accommodate ourselves to him; and if we feel any progress, we ascribe all of it to God.

units.la: At ne quis quod Paulus dixit, difficile vel etiam impossibile putaret, hoc ipsum rationibus aut argumentis certis confirmat. Nam ad ipsa spiritus effecta nos remittens ait: Spiritus omnia scrutatur, etiam profunditates Dei. Non debent autem haec verba eo sensu intelligi, quasi Spiritus ille sanctus studio & inuestigatione opus habeat ad discendum aliqua, quae prius ignorauerit. Sed scrutandi verbo utitur, ut eam Spiritus vim esse ostendat, quae omnia penetret, ubique praesens sit, & quam nihil quantumuis arcanum & profundum possit latere. Et quod breui sententia dixit, mox per similitudinem elegantem illustrat, quam ex nostra mente aut ratione desumit: sic dicens: Quis enim hominum nouit ea quae sunt hominis, nisi spiritus hominis, qui est in eo? Ita etiam ea quae sunt Dei, nemo nouit nisi Spiritus Dei. Interrogatione utitur, ut ad horum consideratione diligentiorem magis excitet, & uno hoc simili duo comprehendit, quae ad hanc causam faciunt. Primum, ut hominum arcana nemo nouit, nisi spiritus, id est, mens hominis aut suprema illa rationis facultas, quae cogitationes cordium inspicit & moderatur: Ita quae Deus penes se statuit & decernit, nemo videre aut nouisse potest, praeter Spiritum, qui Deo proprius, & eiusdem cum illo essentiae est. Alterum, ut mentem nostram non possunt ea latere, quae in intimo cordis recessu cogitamus & intra animum nostrum voluimus: Itaque Spiritus Dei ignorare potest, quae ut iam inde ab aeterno de humani generis reparatione & salute decreuit. Sunt haec satis manifesta, neque ampliori declaratione opus habent, quia cum communi hominum sensu conueniunt. At ex ijs nos colligere oportet, Euangelij doctrinam à nobis comprehendi & intelligi non posse, nisi Spiritus sanctus animis nostris affulgeat, mentes nostras aperiat, & in eorum fide confirmet, quae in illo praedicantur. Exemplo nobis sint Apostoli, qui etsi Christo praeceptore domestico (ut sic dicam) uterentur, hunc quotidie audirent, & doctrinam eius nouis & stupendis signis itidem confirmari viderent, adeo tamen rudes & mysteriorum Christi imperiti manserunt, ut ne crassam illam & carnalem de regno eius terreno opinionem deponere possent, & non semel acerrimam correptionem meruerint. At ubi Spiritus Christi animis illorum infusus est, repente dictorum eius omnium recordati sunt, & scripturas veteres intellexerunt, & illius merito nobis partam salute non minori cum perspicuitate quàm animi constantia praedicarunt.
units.tr: But lest anyone think that what Paul said is difficult or even impossible, he confirms this very point with sure reasons and arguments. For, referring us to the effects of the Spirit itself, he says: "The Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God." These words, however, ought not to be understood as if that Holy Spirit needed study and investigation to learn some things that he had previously not known. Rather, he uses the word "searches" to show that this is the power of the Spirit, which penetrates all things, is present everywhere, and that nothing, however hidden and deep, can lie concealed from it. And what he expressed in a brief sentence he soon illustrates by an elegant comparison, which he draws from our own mind or reason, saying: "For who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man that is in him? So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God." He uses a question so as to stir us up to consider these things more carefully, and by this one comparison he takes in two points that bear on this matter. First, just as no one knows the secrets of men except the spirit, that is, the mind of man or that highest faculty of reason which looks into and governs the thoughts of the heart, so no one can see or know the things that God has determined and decreed within himself, except the Spirit, who is proper to God and of the same essence as he is. Second, just as the things we think in the innermost recesses of the heart and wish within our soul cannot remain hidden from our mind, so the Spirit of God can know what he has decreed from eternity concerning the restoration and salvation of the human race. These points are quite plain and need no further explanation, since they agree with the common sense of men. From them, however, we must conclude that the teaching of the Gospel cannot be grasped and understood by us unless the Holy Spirit shines upon our souls, opens our minds, and confirms us in faith in the things that are proclaimed in it. The Apostles are an example for us: although they had Christ as their teacher, as it were at home, heard him daily, and saw his teaching confirmed by new and wonderful signs, they nevertheless remained so slow and unskilled in the mysteries of Christ that they could not put aside their crude and carnal notion of his earthly kingdom, and more than once they earned a very sharp rebuke. But when the Spirit of Christ was poured into their souls, they suddenly remembered all his sayings, understood the ancient Scriptures, and proclaimed the salvation won for us by his merit with no less clarity than constancy of mind.

units.la: Sunt haec propter eos diligenter obseruanda, qui nos de mysterijs istis certam & solidam cognitionem habere posse negant, nisi Patrum & Conciliorum (quibus illi Ecclesiae titulum magna cum confidentia & audacia vendicant) authoritate confirmemur. Id vero nunquam dicturi essent, si rem ipsam, & quae quotidie inter homines fiunt rectius inspicerent. Etenim in Christi & salutis aeternae negotio nequaquam sufficit temere concepta opinio aut etiam coniecturis & humanis testimonijs suffulta animi persuasio: sed certo, firmo & indubitato assensu opus est, qui nos totos Christo vindicet ad fidei obedientiam. Quis vero hominum tanta aut sapientia & eruditione instructus est, aut tanta authoritate pollet, ut illum in animis nostris excitare, vel in eo nos confirmare & retinere possit? In ijs, quae ad hoc seculum spectant, aliorum sermonibus & authoritate seduci possumus: sed ut aliquid, quod non sensibus nostris ingeritur, vere cognoscamus, nullius hominis authoritate effici potest. Quae ergo dementia est, hoc in illis statuere, quae humanae rationis captum longè superant? Adde, quod ut credamus quae cum ratione & natura pugnant, nemo nos adducere potest, nisi qui in animum nostrum ius habet, & voluntatem quoq; potest mutare. Ideo infra Paulus de seipso & alijs Euangelij preconibus loquens ait: Ministri Dei sumus, per quos credidistis, prout cuiq; Dominus dedit. Quare frustra Patrum, Conciliorum, Pontificum, Regum, vel etiam totius mundi authoritatem in vnum congesseris, nisi animus intra seipsum ὑπαγοφορίαν[?] illam aut certitudinem fidei concipiat, quam solus Dei Spiritus in nobis gignit.
units.tr: These points must be carefully observed for the sake of those who deny that we can have a certain and solid knowledge of these mysteries unless we are confirmed by the authority of the Fathers and the Councils, to which they boldly and confidently claim the title of the Church. They would never say this if they looked more rightly at the matter itself and at what happens among men every day. In the business of Christ and eternal salvation, a carelessly formed opinion, or a persuasion of the mind propped up by guesswork and human testimonies, is by no means enough. What is needed is a certain, firm and undoubting assent, one that binds us wholly to Christ in obedience of faith. But which man is so instructed in wisdom and learning, or so powerful in authority, that he can stir this assent in our minds, or confirm and keep us in it? In matters that belong to this age we can be led astray by the talk and authority of others, but to know truly something that is not forced upon our senses cannot be brought about by the authority of any man. What madness, then, is it to settle such things about matters that far exceed the grasp of human reason? Add that no one can bring us to believe things that clash with reason and nature, unless he has a right over our mind and can also change our will. So Paul, speaking below of himself and the other preachers of the gospel, says: "We are ministers of God, through whom you believed, as the Lord gave to each" [1 Cor. 3.5]. Therefore you may gather together in one heap the authority of the Fathers, the Councils, the Popes, the kings, or even of the whole world, in vain, unless the mind within itself conceives that assurance [ὑπαγοφορίαν] or certainty of faith which the Spirit of God alone produces in us.

units.la: Porrò ut à Pauli instituto nonnihil digrediamur, de duobus nos hæc verba admonent. Primò, quanta conscientiæ vis sit docent. Solent pleriq; in sceleribus suis ex eo consolationem petere, quòd illa occulta esse, nec aliquem hominum ea nouisse putant. Est autem hæc consolatio vanissima, quanto ad turbandum animum plus quam satis est, si tu ea nouéris, quæ aduersus Deum delignauisti. Nam ut veteres dixere, conscientia mille testium loco est. Et tanta illius vis est, ut non ea modo nobis exprobret, quæ alioqui ob oculos nostros versantur, & dissimulari nullo modo possunt, sed profundissimos mentis recessus scrutatur, & ea nobis in memoriam reuocat, quorum ipsimet prius oblitieramus. Et quò minus id fiat, nulla arte aut consilio prohibere, aut illius exprobrationes effugere possumus. Intra nos enim illa latet, & quocunq; nos vertamus comitem agit indiuulsum, & inuitis quoq; obrepit, dum gaudia animo concipere volumus, & tam dormientes infestat, quàm vigilantes. Neq; modo in mentem reuocat, quæ præter officium à nobis facta sunt, verumetiam accusat, imò scelerís nos conuincit, ut quàmuis natura simulatores simus, & nobisipsis turpiter blandiamur, tamen nos sceleratos esse & Dei iram atq; pœnas horribiles meruisse, negare non possumus. Magna ergo huius mali vis sit oportet, & ideo illud Poëtæ per furias infernales adumbrarunt, quæ colubris armata miseros flagellent, & omnia illis infesta reddat. Huius mali vim Cainus sentit, cùm clamaret: Maior est iniquitas mea, quàm ut remittatur. Eadem Iudam coegit, ut & sceleris admissum cum publica infamia fateretur, & pecuniam, quà nihil charius habebat, redderet, & sibipsi laqueum aptaret, quo præfocatus vitam infelicem infelicius finiuit. Et hodie multos à propria conscientia vinci & in desperationis præcipitium abduci videmus, qui paulò ante neq; Dei neq; hominum metu tenebantur. Neq; à conscientiæ stimulis immunes sunt pij, quos non minus propria mens accusat, & terroribus grauissimis exagitat, ut in Dauidis, Petri & similium exemplis videmus. Melior tamen illorum sors est, quia de gratia Dei bene sperant, & adoptionis spiritu confirmantur. Nobis autem doctrina ista ad hoc seruire debet, ne impunitatis spe nos decipi patiamur: quin potius semper nobis ob oculos versetur, quod Ioannes scribit: Si condemnet nos cor nostrum, potentior est Deus corde nostro, & nouit omnia. 1[?]. Ioan. 3.
units.tr: But since we have somewhat digressed from Paul's plan, these words warn us of two things. First, they show how great is the power of conscience. Many people, in their sins, look for comfort in the thought that these are hidden and that no one among men knows of them. Yet this comfort is most vain, and far more than enough to disturb the mind, if you yourself know what you have plotted against God. For, as the ancients said, conscience is in the place of a thousand witnesses. Its power is so great that it does not merely reproach us with things that are otherwise before our eyes and cannot in any way be overlooked, but it searches the deepest recesses of the mind and recalls to our memory things we had ourselves already forgotten. And we cannot by any art or device prevent this from happening, or escape its reproaches. For conscience lies hidden within us, and wherever we turn it accompanies us inseparably; it creeps upon us even when we are unwilling, whenever we want to conceive joys in our minds, and it harasses us as much when we sleep as when we are awake. It not only recalls to mind what we have done beyond our duty, but it also accuses us, and convicts us of wickedness, so that, though by nature we are self-deceivers and shamefully flatter ourselves, we cannot deny that we are wicked and have deserved God's wrath and dreadful punishments. The power of this evil must therefore be great, and so the poets shadowed it forth through the infernal Furies, who, armed with serpents, scourge wretched men and make everything hostile to them. Cain felt the power of this evil when he cried out, "My iniquity is greater than can be forgiven" [Gen. 4.13]. The same evil compelled Judas both to confess the crime he had committed, with public infamy, and to return the money, which he held dearer than anything, and to fasten a noose for himself, by which, strangled, he ended his unhappy life more unhappily. Even today we see many men overcome by their own conscience and dragged to the precipice of despair, who a little before were restrained neither by fear of God nor of men. Nor are the godly free from the goads of conscience, since their own mind accuses them no less and torments them with the gravest terrors, as we see in the examples of David, Peter and others like them. Yet their lot is better, because they hope well of the grace of God and are strengthened by the spirit of adoption. But this doctrine ought to serve us for this purpose: that we should not allow ourselves to be deceived by hope of impunity. Rather, let us always keep before our eyes what John writes: "If our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and knows all things" [1 John 3.20].

units.la: Deinde continetur his verbis euidens[?] argumentum, quo spiritus sancti diuinitas vera & æterna probatur. Nam quæ Dei sunt, nemo præter unum Deum nouit absq; peculiari reuelatione. Quis enim (inquit alibi Apostolus) cognouit mentem Domini? At spiritus omnia scrutatur, & ipsas quoq; arcanorum Dei profunditates cognitas habet. Ergo Deus sit oportet. Adde huic argumento, quòd Paulus in epist. ad Rom. eadem loquendi formula de Deo utitur. Qui corda scrutatur Deus (inquit) nouit quis sit sensus spiritus. Et passim in scripturis hoc solius Dei proprium esse docetur, quòd corda & renes, id est, occulta omnium hominum consilia atq; desideria norit, & omnia penetret. At si diuinæ virtutis est hominum arcana nouisse, quanto maius erit ad ipsius Dei profunditates propria virtute penetrare? Atqui ea est Spiritus conditio, ut eū à Deo separare nefas sit. Ut enim homo esse definit, quando[?] spiritum ipsi eripit Deus: ita hic quoq; nullus erit, si spiritum ab eo abstuleris. Quod ipsum de Verbo etiam Dei vero & æterno sentiendum esse alibi diximus. Constat ergo nos recte & orthodoxè in Deo unitatem essentiæ, & in ea unitate personas tres suis proprietatibus distinctas agnoscere & fateri. Et sunt testimonia eiusmodi diligenter obseruanda propter eos, qui hodie Arij, Sabellij, Samosateni & Macedonij hæreses postliminio reducere conantur, & sacrosanctam atq; adorandam Trinitatis articulum oppugnantes ipsa Christianæ fidei fundamenta labefactant.
units.tr: Next, these words contain a clear argument by which the true and eternal divinity of the Holy Spirit is proved. For no one, apart from God alone, knows the things of God without a special revelation. For (as the Apostle says elsewhere) "who has known the mind of the Lord?" [Rom. 11.34]. But the Spirit searches all things, and he also has knowledge of the very depths of the secrets of God. Therefore he must be God. Add to this argument that Paul uses the same form of speech about God in his letter to the Romans: "God, who searches the hearts, knows what is the mind of the Spirit" [Rom. 8.27]. And throughout the Scriptures it is taught that this is the property of God alone, that he knows the heart and the reins, that is, the hidden counsels and desires of all men, and penetrates all things. But if it is a divine power to know the secrets of men, how much greater will it be to penetrate by one's own power into the depths of God himself? Yet such is the condition of the Spirit that it is wrong to separate him from God. For just as a man ceases to be a man when God takes his spirit from him, so here too, if you take the Spirit away from God, there will be no God. We have said elsewhere that the same must be felt about the true and eternal Word of God. It is therefore established that we rightly and orthodoxly acknowledge and confess in God a unity of essence, and in that unity three persons distinguished by their own properties. Testimonies of this kind must be carefully observed on account of those who today try to bring back the heresies of Arius, Sabellius, Paul of Samosata and Macedonius, and, by assailing the most holy and adorable article of the Trinity, undermine the very foundations of the Christian faith.

units.la: Redeamus nunc ad Pauli, qui quod dixit, nouo argumento à natura contrariorum desumpto confirmat, sic dicens: Nos verò non spiritum mundi accepimus, sed spiritum qui est ex Deo, ut sciamus quæ à Deo donata sunt nobis. Spiritus mundi hic dicit, non malum illum & impurum, per quem diabolus in impijs agit, sed mente siue rationem, qua homines naturaliter intelligunt, sapiunt, cogitant, ea deniq; faciunt, quæ naturali illa animæ facultate perfici possunt. At Dei spiritus dicitur noua illa vis, qua renatos in Christo donat Deus, & qua illi animantur & ducuntur, ut ea quoq; sapiant, cogitent & velint, quæ naturæ vires & omne humanæ rationis captū excedunt. Hunc nos accepisse ait, ut offendat non mirū cuiquam videri debere, si ea norint credentes, quæ nemo principū huius seculi intelligere potest. Et mox fine istius cognitionis indicat. Ut sciamus quæ à Deo donata sunt nobis. Loquitur autē de ijs, quæ nobis Deus per Christū & in Christo gratuita liberalitate aut misericordia donauit. Sunt hæc peccatorum remissio, reconciliatio, regeneratio, adoptio, beatæ resurrectionis spes, & vita æterna: quæ omnia nuper pauci membris complexus est, quando Iesum Christum nobis à Patre Sapientiam, Iustitiam, Sanctificationem & Redemptionem factum esse dixit. De his omnibus certos nos reddit Spiritus ille Dei, quem similiter Christus suis paracletum siue aduocatum promisit. Quia enim Veritatis spiritus est, neminem fallit, & tam certa sunt atq; infallibilia, quæ illo doctore & teste cognoscimus, vt magis certa esse non possint, quæ sensibus externis apprehenduntur, vel etiam manibus contrectantur. Imò cum oculi & aures sæpe falli soleant, & in ijs quoq; non raro decipiamur, quæ digitis proprijs tangimus, impossibile tamen est mente falli, quam Spiritus Christi illuminauit. Ea enim lucem illam veram respicit, quâ quisquis sequitur, is non ambulat in tenebris, sed habet lumen vitæ. Nec temere ergo Apostoli Spiritum illum arrhabonem salutis dicunt, eò quod Christi merito partam salutem eiusq; fiduciam intra animos nostros obsignet.
units.tr: Let us now return to Paul, who confirms what he said with a new argument drawn from the nature of contraries, speaking thus: "But we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit which is from God, so that we may know the things that have been given to us by God" [1 Cor. 2.12]. The spirit of the world here means not that evil and impure spirit by whom the devil works in the wicked, but the mind or reason by which men naturally understand, have wisdom, think, and finally do those things which can be accomplished by that natural faculty of the soul. But the Spirit of God means that new power which God bestows on those reborn in Christ, and by which they are animated and led, so that they may also have wisdom, think and will things which exceed the powers of nature and the whole measure of human reason. He says that we have received this Spirit, so that no one should think it strange if believers know those things which no ruler of this age can understand. And soon he indicates the purpose of this knowledge: "so that we may know the things that have been given to us by God." He speaks of those things which God has given us through Christ and in Christ by free bounty and mercy. These are the forgiveness of sins, reconciliation, regeneration, adoption, the hope of a blessed resurrection, and eternal life. A little earlier he briefly embraced all of these, when he said that Jesus Christ has been made to us by the Father wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. Of all these things that Spirit of God makes us certain, the same Spirit whom Christ likewise promised to his people as the Paraclete, that is, the Advocate. For, since he is the Spirit of truth, he deceives no one, and the things we know under his teaching and witness are so certain and infallible that nothing apprehended by the external senses, or even handled with the hands, can be more certain. Indeed, although eyes and ears are often wont to be deceived, and we are not seldom mistaken even about things we touch with our own fingers, it is nevertheless impossible for the mind that the Spirit of Christ has illuminated to be deceived. For it looks upon that true light, and whoever follows it does not walk in darkness but has the light of life. Nor, therefore, did the Apostles rashly call that Spirit the earnest of salvation, because he seals within our hearts the salvation won by the merit of Christ and our confidence in it.

units.la: Commendatur his plurimum Euangelicæ doctrinæ dignitas. Si enim scientiæ omnes suam dignitatem ex argumento aut materia habent, circa quam versantur, deinde ex demonstrationibus, quæ illarum certitudinem afferunt: nulla certè Euangelij doctrinæ conferri meretur. Reliquæ enim scientiæ ad res huius seculi spectant, in quibus etsi multa vtilia, multa honorifica, multa etiā ad rem pub. aut rem domesticam, vel etiam corporis valetudinem conseruandam necessaria sint, omnia tamen illa caduca, fluxa & momentanea sunt, neq; stabilis & perpetua est, quæ ex illis petitur vtilitas siue voluptas. At Euangelij doctrina cœlestium atq; æternorum bonorum thesauros nobis proponit, sine quibus felicitas hominis consistere non potest, & quæ sola nos beatos faciunt. Adhæc certa & infallibilis est illorum promissio, & quæ ex promissionibus Euangelicis dependet eorundē fiducia. Fundantur enim illæ omnes in Dei gratia siue misericordia, quam inexhaustam & æternā esse constat. Mediator autē est æternus ille & dilectus Dei filius, quem Pater aspernari non potest, cū ipse enim nobis ad hoc officiū æterno suo decreto prædestinauerit. Accedunt his testes fide dignissimi, Patriarchæ, Prophetæ, Apostoli, Martyres, Angeli denique, qui Christo nascituro, morituro, resuscitato ite & in cœlos subuecto testimonium tulerunt. Quorum fidem in dubiū vocare summæ audaciæ & extremæ impudentiæ fuerit. Superat tamen hæc omnia Spiritus sancti testimonium, qui non solum promissiones Dei nobis in mente reuocat, sed nos intra animos nostros salutis certos reddit, nostrumq; intellectu sic illustrat, vt sciamus quæ nobis à Deo donata sunt. Ideo Petrus quoq; cum fide scientia coniungens dicebat: Et nos credimus & cognouimus, quod tu es Christus, Filius ille Dei viuētis. Inculcamus hæc diligentius, ne quis impium & desperationis plenum Sophistarum figmentum admittat, qui neminem dum in hoc seculo viuit, salutis suæ certum fieri posse docent, adhæc priorū quoq; & credentium perseuerantiam dubiam & incertam faciunt. At quid hoc aliud est, quàm Euangelij promissiones in dubium vocare, Spiritus sancti testimonium negare, & ipsi Christo contradicere, qui se bonum & fortem illū pastorem esse profitetur, qui oues suas omnes probe nouerit, & ex cuius manibus illas nemo possit rapere? Procul ergo facessant à Christianis hominibus dubitationes illæ, quæ cum manifesta impietate coniunctæ sunt. Quin potius cum Paulo dicant: Nos spiritū, qui ex Deo est accepimus, vt sciamus quæ à Deo donata sunt nobis. Item: Certus & fidelis est hic sermo, & dignus quem modis omnibus amplectamur, Quòd Christus Iesus in mundum venit, vt peccatores saluos faceret. Interim ne fiducia in confidentiam, & tandem in securitatem & carnis licentiam degeneret, meminerimus semper nos non mundi huius, sed Dei spiritum accepisse, & ideo nobis annitendum esse, ne mundo & carni, sed Deo viuamus, ne (vt alibi Apostolus monet) spiritum illum Dei sanctum tristitia afficiamus. Vide Ephes.4.
units.tr: The dignity of the Gospel teaching is commended here at great length. For if all sciences derive their dignity from the subject matter with which they deal, and then from the demonstrations that establish their certainty, then certainly no science deserves to be compared with the teaching of the Gospel. The other sciences concern the affairs of this age; and although many of them are useful, many honourable, and many even necessary for the commonwealth, for the household, or for preserving bodily health, yet all of them are transitory, fleeting and momentary, and the advantage or pleasure they bring is not lasting or perpetual. But the teaching of the Gospel sets before us the treasures of heavenly and eternal goods, without which human happiness cannot exist, and which alone make us blessed. Moreover, the promise of those goods is certain and infallible, and the confidence in them depends upon the Gospel promises. For all of them are founded in the grace or mercy of God, which is known to be inexhaustible and eternal. The Mediator is that eternal and beloved Son of God, whom the Father cannot reject, since he himself has appointed him to this office by his eternal decree. To these are added the most trustworthy witnesses: the Patriarchs, the Prophets, the Apostles, the Martyrs, and finally the Angels, who bore witness to Christ's being born, dying, rising again and being taken up into heaven. To call their faith into doubt would be the height of audacity and the utmost impudence. Yet the testimony of the Holy Spirit surpasses all these things: he not only recalls to our minds the promises of God, but makes us certain of salvation within our hearts, and so illumines our understanding that we know the things that have been given us by God. Therefore Peter too, joining knowledge to faith, said: "And we have believed and have come to know that you are Christ, the Son of the living God." We stress these things more carefully so that no one should admit the impious and despair-laden fiction of the Sophists, who teach that no one living in this age can be made certain of his salvation, and who further make the perseverance even of earlier believers doubtful and uncertain. But what else is this than to call the promises of the Gospel into doubt, to deny the testimony of the Holy Spirit, and to contradict Christ himself, who professes that he is the good and strong shepherd, who knows all his sheep well, and from whose hands none can snatch them? Let those doubts, which are bound up with plain impiety, therefore keep far away from Christian people. Rather let them say with Paul: "We have received the Spirit which is from God, so that we may know the things that have been given us by God." Likewise: "This saying is certain and worthy of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners." Meanwhile, lest confidence degenerate into presumption, and finally into security and licence of the flesh, let us always remember that we have received the Spirit not of this world but of God, and that therefore we must strive to live not for the world and the flesh but for God, lest (as the Apostle warns elsewhere) we grieve that holy Spirit of God by sadness. See Ephes. 4.

units.la: Cæterum applicat tandem hæc omnia Paulus instituto suo, & sic ait: Quæ etiam loquimur, non sermonibus, quos docet humana sapientia, sed quos docet Spiritus sanctus, &c. Recte autem & non sine necessaria causa iterum de prædicatione Euangelij loquitur. Ita enim fanaticis occurrit, qui inspirationes & reuelationes nouas fingunt extra Dei Verbum, quod certissimum breuissimumq; est ad omnis generis errores atq; superstitiones compendium. Nam qui nouis inspirationibus sibi opus esse existimant, ij diabolo se illudendos propinant, qui in Angelum lucis se transformare, & absurdissimarum opinionum portenta Spiritus sancti authoritate palliare solet. Factum hoc olim in hæreticis, quos ista ratione ille decepit. Et Mahometum hoc artificio imprimis[?] usum fuisse constat, quando apud Arabes suos sibi fidem conciliare voluit. In Papatu autem hanc superstitionum fere omnium primam causam esse scimus. Nostro autem tempore Anabaptistarum Coryphaei suis inspirationibus quam plurimos seduxerunt, ut relicta Christi ecclesia illos secuti sint, qui renascentem Evangelij doctrinam quam maxime impediuerunt. Debet ergo Spiritus cum Verbi praedicatione coniungi, neque credendum est spiritui quantumuis specioso, nisi quae dictat cum Verbo Dei in scripturis revelato per omnia conveniant. Jubet hoc Paulus, quando ne Angelo quidem coelitus delapso credendum esse monet, si quid praedicet diversum ab ijs, quae Evangelio traduntur. Hoc autem non solum fanaticos illos arguit, verumetiam Conciliorum patronos, qui Patres & Episcopos in Spiritu sancto convenisse clamant, & proinde pro divinis agnosci debere, quaecunq; illi decreuerunt. At probandum erat in Spiritu sancto convenire omnes, qui hoc nomine sua venditant, & suis Sessionibus Missam de Spiritu sancto praemittunt. Probent etiam oportet, Spiritum Dei contraria docere, & sibi ipsi contradicere: quando satis constat non pauca extare Conciliorum decreta, in quibus manifesta contradictio neq; negari, neq; dissimulari potest: ut iam de ijs nihil dicamus, quae cum diserte Dei Verbis pugnant.
units.tr: Paul finally applies all these things to his purpose, and says: "Which things also we speak, not in words which human wisdom teaches, but which the Holy Spirit teaches," etc. He speaks again of the preaching of the Gospel rightly and not without necessary cause. For thus he meets the fanatics, who invent new inspirations and revelations apart from the Word of God, which is the most certain and briefest summary against every kind of error and superstition. For those who think they need new inspirations expose themselves to be deceived by the devil, who is accustomed to transform himself into an angel of light and to cloak monstrous and absurd opinions with the authority of the Holy Spirit. This happened long ago among the heretics, whom he deceived by this method. And it is well established that Mahomet especially used this artifice, when he wished to win faith for himself among his Arabs. In the Papacy, moreover, we know this to be the first cause of almost all superstitions. In our own time the leaders of the Anabaptists have led very many astray by their inspirations, so that, abandoning the Church of Christ, they followed those who most of all hindered the reviving teaching of the Gospel. The Spirit ought therefore to be joined with the preaching of the Word, and one must not believe any spirit, however specious, unless what it dictates agrees in every respect with the Word of God revealed in the Scriptures. Paul commands this when he warns that not even an Angel come down from heaven is to be believed, if he preaches anything different from what is handed down in the Gospel. This he rebukes not only in those fanatics, but also in the defenders of the Councils, who cry out that the Fathers and Bishops met in the Holy Spirit, and that therefore whatever they decreed must be acknowledged as divine. But it would have to be proved that all who vaunt their own decisions under this name have met in the Holy Spirit, and who preface their Sessions with a Mass of the Holy Spirit. They would also have to prove that the Spirit of God teaches contrary things and contradicts himself; since it is quite certain that there are not a few decrees of Councils in which a manifest contradiction can be neither denied nor concealed, not to mention those which plainly clash with the explicit words of God.

units.la: Quoad vero Pauli institutum, rursus excusat dicendi genus rude & simplex, quod ipse cum aliis Apostolis commune habebat. Nos (inquit) sermonibus utimur, non quos humana sapientia docet, quae elocutionis ornatum & figuras, amplificationum species, strophas, elenchos & paralogismos excogitavit: sed ijs potius, quos Spiritus sanctus suggerit, qui cum Veritatis spiritus sit, oratione etiam perspicua & simplici gaudet. Deniq; toti in hoc sumus, ut rebus spiritualibus verba quoq; spiritualia accommodemus, & ita rebus verba respondeant. Vocant autem spiritualia verba, in quibus nullus fucus vel Rhetoricus vel Sophisticus auditorum animos perstringit, sed in quorum simplicitate Spiritus sancti vis atq; energia elucet: quae aut nulla, aut cordatis omnibus suspecta est, quado aliquos curioso & exquisito dicendi artificio uti vident. Ejusmodi verbis Christus usus est, quando populus illum cum singulari authoritate docere animadvertit: quando item discipuli, qui Emauntem cum illo profecti fuerant, corda sua ex eius colloquio arsisse testantur. Spiritualia item verba Petrus locutus est, quando ad eius concionem multi totis animis compuncti salutis consilium sibi dari postulaverunt. Et huc pertinent quaecunq; de Apostolorum concionibus traduntur, quae etsi verbis constarent minimè artificiosis aut magnificis, spiritus tamen sancti virtutem admirabilem habuerunt conjunctam, quae auditorum animos penetravit, & totos immutavit. Ita vero rursus eos perstringit, qui simplicem Evangelij doctrinam asciticio & inani verborum fuco corrumpunt. Et debemus nos suspectos habere eos, qui hoc faciunt: imprimis autem Dei facilitatem & bonitatem agnoscamus, qui nostro captui se tam studiose accommodat. Vicissim autem nosipsos doctrinae huic accommodemus, & procul relictis humanae sapientiae ornamentis, uno JESU CHRISTO contenti simus, qui solus nobis ad salutem sufficit. Ei debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: As for Paul's purpose, he again excuses the rough and simple style of speaking, which he shared in common with the other Apostles. "We," he says, "use words not such as human wisdom teaches, which has devised the ornament of eloquence and figures, the kinds of amplification, strophes, refutations and sophisms; but rather such as the Holy Spirit suggests, who, since he is the Spirit of truth, delights also in plain and simple speech." Finally, we aim wholly at fitting spiritual words to spiritual things, so that words correspond to things. Now those are called spiritual words in which no rhetorical or sophistical gloss dazzles the minds of the hearers, but in whose simplicity the power and energy of the Holy Spirit shines forth; such words either lack that power or are suspect to all sensible people, when they see someone using a curious and far-fetched art of speaking. Christ used words of this kind when the people noticed that he taught with singular authority; likewise the disciples who had set out with him to Emmaus testify that their hearts burned from his conversation. Peter too spoke spiritual words, when many, pricked to the heart by his sermon, asked that counsel of salvation be given them. To this belongs whatever is reported of the sermons of the Apostles, which, although they consisted of words by no means artful or grand, nevertheless had the wonderful power of the Holy Spirit joined to them, which penetrated the hearts of the hearers and changed them wholly. Again, this rebukes those who corrupt the simple teaching of the Gospel with artificial and empty varnish of words. We ought to hold such people under suspicion; and above all we should acknowledge the condescension and goodness of God, who so eagerly adapts himself to our capacity. In turn, let us accommodate ourselves to this teaching, and, having put aside the ornaments of human wisdom, let us be content with Jesus Christ alone, who alone suffices for our salvation. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XI.
units.tr: Homily XI.

units.la: Animalis autem homo non est capax eorum, quae sunt spiritus Dei. Sunt enim ei stultitia, nec potest ea cognoscere, quia spiritua-liter dijudicantur. At spiritualis dijudicat quidem omnia, ipse vero a nemine dijudicatur. Quis enim novit mentem Domini, qui instru-cturus sit eum: Nos autem mentem Christi habemus.
units.tr: "The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know them, because they are spiritually discerned. But the spiritual man judges all things, yet he himself is judged by no one. For who has known the mind of the Lord, that he should instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ" (1 Cor. 2:14-16).

units.la: INter alia hominis vitia, quae nobis ex haereditaria naturae nostrae pravitate inhaerent, non po-stremum est philautiae malum. Haec enim causa est, quod omnia nostra admiramur, & contem-pta Dei gratia nos ad omnia propriis facultatibus abunde instructos esse putamus. Hic autem imprimis nos decipit sapientiae fiducia, quae ita fere nos inflat, ut non contenti in ijs, quae quotidia-na sunt & secundum naturae ordinem fiunt, ingenij nostri acumen ostentavisse, ea quoq; scrutari conemur, quae ad arcana Dei de humani generis salute consilia spectant. Est haec pestis gravissi-ma, & quae saluti plurimum officit. Ut enim in istis carnis ratio turpissime fallitur, ita graviter etiam plerique offenduntur, si quid occurrat, quod carnis iudicio absurdum aut iniquum videtur. Hinc ergo omnis generis superstitiones prodeunt, & tandem ex eadem radice omnis religionis & doctrinae syncerioris contemptus nascitur, dum omnia ad nostrae rationis calculum revocamus. Ex emplo hic nobis sunt Corinthij, quos humanae sapientiae admiratio atq; fiducia eo adduxit, ut simplicem & syncerum praedicationem de Christo fastidirent, & circa inanes speculationes occupati, veram atq; unicam salutis assequendae rationem negligerent. Necessario igitur Paulus iflam trastationem instituit, qua docet, huius mundi sapientiam & nostri ingenij acumen nihil facere ad eorum cognitionem, quae nostrae saluti serviunt. Et quamuis in eam sententiam multa dixerit hucusq;, ijs tamen haec quoque subijcit, quae modo recitavimus, quibus summam totius negotij non minus perspicue quam graviter comprehendit. Nobis autem doctrinae istius omnis usus hic esse debet. Primum, ne nostro acumini in ijs, quae ad Deum spectant, aliquid tribuamus, sed nos totos sub-ijciamus spiritus magisterio, & ita germani simus Dei discipuli, quales Christianos fore olim Isa-ias praedixit. Deinde ne offendamur, si Euangelicae Veritatis doctrina illis sordeat, qui in hoc mun-do prae aliis sapere videntur.
units.tr: Among the other vices of man that cling to us from the hereditary depravity of our nature, the evil of self-love is not the least. For this is the cause why we admire everything of our own and, despising the grace of God, think that we are abundantly equipped for everything by our own abilities. Here especially the confidence in wisdom deceives us, and it so inflates us that we are not content to have shown the keenness of our wit in those things which are everyday and happen according to the order of nature, but we also try to probe those things which pertain to the hidden counsels of God concerning the salvation of mankind. This is a most serious plague, and one that greatly harms salvation. For just as human reason is most shamefully deceived in these matters, so too many people are gravely offended if anything occurs which seems absurd or unjust to the judgment of the flesh. From this arise all kinds of superstitions, and at last from the same root springs contempt for all religion and for sound doctrine, while we bring everything back to the reckoning of our reason. The Corinthians are an example for us here, whom admiration for and confidence in human wisdom led to the point of despising the simple and sincere preaching about Christ, and, occupied with empty speculations, they neglected the true and only way of obtaining salvation. Therefore Paul necessarily undertook this discussion, in which he teaches that the wisdom of this world and the keenness of our wit contribute nothing to the knowledge of those things that serve our salvation. And although he has said much to this effect up to now, he nonetheless adds to these things what we have just recited, in which he sums up the whole matter no less clearly than gravely. Now the whole use of this teaching ought to be ours. First, that we attribute nothing to our own cleverness in those things which pertain to God, but subject ourselves wholly to the teaching of the Spirit, and so be true disciples of God, such as Isaiah foretold that Christians would be. Then, that we not be offended if the doctrine of the truth of the Gospel is despised by those who seem to be wise above others in this world.

units.la: Propositio & summa huius loci est: Animalis homo non est capax eorum, quae sunt spiritus Dei. Animalem vero hominem vocat eum, qui solis naturae facultatibus instructus suae animae, quam cum prophanis quoque & a veri Dei cognitione alienis communem habet, placitis regitur, nondum autem Dei spiritu regeneratus aut instauratus est. Ita illum Iudas Apostolus definit, quando de illis loquens, qui Euangelij doctrina & gratia Dei ad carnis licentiam abutuntur, inter alia dicit: Hi sunt qui seipsos segregant, animales, spiritum non habentes. Sensus ergo huius dicti apostolici est: Hominem, si s ibijpsi & suis facultatibus naturalibus relinquatur, non esse capacem mysteriorum spiritus Dei, neq; ea intelligere posse, quae ad regni coelorum & salutis aeternae negotium pertinent. Quod ut melius exprimat, Metaphora utitur a vasis sumpta, quae ob angu-stiam non capiunt, quae in illa infunduntur. Neq; temerarius est Paulus, qui caeco & praecipiti iudicio totam hominis naturam ignorantiae & impotentiae damnet: sed idem cum Christo dicit, qui cum discipulis suis paracletum illum verum polliceretur, nempe Spiritum Veritatis, addit: Quem mundus non potest recipere, quia non videt eum, neq; novit eum. Ubi similiter mundi nomine homines nondum renatos intelligit, qui sola naturali ratione ducuntur: & plus quiddam dicit quam Apostolus, nimirum, quod ne Spiritus quidem illius capaces sint, qui facit, ut divina intelligamus. Ex eo autem utrumque sequitur, quae hic observanda esse antea diximus. Quod nimirum neq; nostrae industriae in divinis quicquam tribuere, neq; etiam multum moveri aut offendi debeamus, si pauciores sint, qui doctrinam Euangelij admittunt. Sunt quidem ratio & intellectus praeclara & eximia Dei dona, quibus nos a brutis animantibus ille distinxit, ut his d udi & excitati, non in praesentia modo & terrena intenti simus, sed futura & coelestia bona sectemur: sed in primi parentis lapsu ita debilitatae sunt rationis & mentis nostrae vires, ut in ijs, quae ad Deum spectant, nihil videamus aut intelligamus, nisi nova Spiritus divini luce illuminemur, quae mentem humi defixam & circa huius vitae negotia occupatam ad coelestium considerationem attollat. Tam praeclaros & egregios Deos nos fecit diabolus, & haec illa tam eximia boni mali;q; scientia est, quam primus parentibus ille promisit, ut Deo inobedientes faceret. Ut ergo oculi naturalem habent videndi facultatem, ea autem sine luce uti non possunt: ita hominis quoq; anima intellectu & ratione quidem praedita est, his autem divina & coelestia videre aut intelligere non potest, nisi Spiritus sancti radijs illustretur. Itaq; si qui sine illo de divinis aliquid statuere voluntt, ij perinde faciunt, ac si quis acie oculorum fretus in medijs tenebris sine luce cernere, aut de coloribus iudicare velet.
units.tr: The proposition and summary of this passage is: The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God. By the natural man he means one who, equipped only with the faculties of nature, is ruled by the inclinations of his soul, which he shares with the profane too and with those alienated from the knowledge of the true God, and who has not yet been regenerated or renewed by the Spirit of God. So the Apostle Jude defines him, when, speaking of those who abuse the doctrine of the Gospel and the grace of God for license of the flesh, he says among other things: "These are the ones who separate themselves, natural men, not having the Spirit." The sense, then, of this apostolic saying is: a man, if he is left to himself and to his natural faculties, is not capable of the mysteries of the Spirit of God, nor can he understand those things which pertain to the business of the kingdom of heaven and eternal salvation. To express this better, he uses a metaphor taken from vessels, which because of their narrowness cannot hold what is poured into them. Nor is Paul rash, condemning the whole nature of man as ignorant and powerless by a blind and headlong judgment; rather, he says the same as Christ, who, promising his disciples that true Paraclete, namely the Spirit of truth, adds: "whom the world cannot receive, because it does not see him, nor know him." There too, by the name of the world he understands men not yet reborn, who are guided by natural reason alone; and he says something more than the Apostle, namely that not even those capable of that Spirit who makes us understand divine things can receive it. From this, however, both follow, which we said before must be observed here: that we should attribute nothing in divine matters to our own industry, and that we should not be much moved or offended if there are fewer who admit the doctrine of the Gospel. Reason and understanding are indeed excellent and remarkable gifts of God, by which he distinguished us from brute animals, so that, roused by these, we should be intent not only on present and earthly things but pursue future and heavenly goods. But in the fall of our first parent the powers of our reason and mind were so weakened that in matters pertaining to God we see and understand nothing unless we are illuminated by the new light of the divine Spirit, which lifts the mind, fixed to the ground and occupied with the affairs of this life, to the contemplation of heavenly things. The devil made us gods so distinguished and noble; this is that so remarkable knowledge of good and evil which he promised our first parents, to make them disobedient to God. Just as the eyes have the natural faculty of seeing, yet cannot use it without light, so the soul of man is indeed endowed with intellect and reason, but cannot see or understand divine and heavenly things unless it is illumined by the rays of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, if anyone wishes to determine anything about divine matters without him, they do just as if someone, relying on the sharpness of his eyes, wished to see in the midst of darkness without light, or to judge colors.

units.la: Commendatur his vehementer Euangelicae doctrinae dignitas, de qua etsi alibi dictum sit, prodest tamen nos ad eius considerationem crebro excitari, ut maiori eius studio accendamur. Magnum & praeclarum est, quod salutem veram & perfectam nobis offert, quam nulla alia scientia vere polliceri, nulla praestare potest.
