At eadem sapientiam quoq; continet, quae omnem hominis captum excedit, & circa quam sese stultissimos praebent, qui in mundo artium & sapientiae principes videntur. Apparet hoc in eo, quod qui illam recte animo conceperunt, ij soli ad ea perfectionis metam pervenerunt, quae in hac carne viventibus obtingere potest, & ad quam philosophi omnes fru-stra aspistra aspirauerunt. Nam Dei veri cognitione donantur, in Christo peccatorum remissionem inue- niunt, cum Deo se in gratia redijsse sentiunt, & ita in hoc acquiescunt, ut ad omnem fortunae euen- tum instructi & parati sint, & neq; aduersis neq; secundis à Dei dilectione diuelli queant, qua is nos in Filio suo complexus est. Sunt ergo in secundis modesti, in aduersis fortes & intrepidi, in medio hostium mites & placidi: deniq; (ut de suis discipulis Isaias pronuntiat) toti mundo por-tenti instar sunt, dum ea faciunt & ferunt, quae ratione intolerabilia esse videntur. Ad hanc ergo sa- pientiam omnes aspirare conuenit, neque eorum iudicijs offendi, quibus illa vel stulta & absurda, vel etiam reipub. inimica esse videtur. Sic enim ex ignorantia illi iudicant, cum eorum non capa- ces sint quae sunt Spiritus Dei, longe aliud dicturi, si aliquem coelestis illius philosophiae gustum per- cepissent. Hic ergo imprimis locum habet, quod proverbio dicitur: Ars non habet contemptorem, nisi ignorantem. At stultum est, eorum iudicio offendi, quos rei, de qua agitur, ignaros & im- peritos esse scias.
units.tr: The dignity of the Gospel doctrine is strongly commended by these points. Although this has been said elsewhere, it is nonetheless useful for us to be roused often to its consideration, so that we may be kindled with a greater zeal for it. It is great and excellent that it offers us true and perfect salvation, which no other science can truly promise or provide. Yet it also contains a wisdom that surpasses all human understanding, and in regard to which they show themselves most foolish who seem to be the princes of the arts and wisdom in the world. This appears in the fact that those who have rightly grasped it alone have reached that goal of perfection which can be attained by those living in this flesh, and at which all philosophers have aspired in vain. For they are granted the knowledge of the true God, they find forgiveness of sins in Christ, they feel that they have returned to God in grace, and so they rest in this, so that they are equipped and ready for every turn of fortune, and can be torn from God's love, in which he has embraced us in his Son, neither by adversity nor by prosperity. Therefore they are modest in prosperity, brave and fearless in adversity, mild and calm in the midst of enemies; finally (as Isaiah declares of his disciples) they are a wonder to the whole world, while they do and bear those things which seem intolerable by reason. We ought therefore all to aspire to this wisdom, and not be offended by the judgments of those who think it foolish and absurd, or even hostile to the commonwealth. For they judge in this way out of ignorance, since they are not capable of the things of the Spirit of God, and would speak quite differently if they had tasted some savor of that heavenly philosophy. Here, then, above all, applies the proverb: "Art has no despisers except the ignorant." But it is foolish to be offended by the judgment of those whom you know to be ignorant and inexperienced in the matter under discussion.

units.la: Porrò quod dixit Apostolus, iam duobus argumentis probat, quibus simul huius ignorantiae causam omnem in hominibus haerere docet, ne quis Deum accuset, qui ea nobis ingerere conetur, quorum nos minimè capaces esse non ignoret. Primùm, Quia sultitia sunt ei, inquit. Non ipsam Euangelij doctrinam per se sultam, sed homini animali sultitiam esse dicit, idem hic repetens, quod supra dixit, Christi crucifixi praedicationem Iudaeis quidem scandalum, Graecis verò & humanae sapientiae persuasione turgidis stultitiam esse. Etenim carnis iudicio nihil tam stultum & delirum videtur, quàm in eo salutis fiduciam ponere, qui in cruce mortis infamis supplicium su- stinuit. Atqui eadem est omnium aliorum ratio, quae in Euangelio traduntur. Nam stul- tum videtur humanae rationi docere, Quod Dei Filius in mundum venerit, ex virgine pura & inte- merata homo verus natus sit, in terris esurierit, sitierit, alserit, à discipulo proditus & in cruce suf- fixus sit: quòd item cùm ista omnia palàm sint facta, resurrectionis & ascensionis suae testes pau- cissimos esse voluerit. Cur enim haec facta sint, caro non videt, quae nihil admiratur, quàm quod mundo huic praeclarum & eximium esse videtur. Quòd si verò addas, salutis spem omnem ita in uno Christo debere collocari, ut propter eum nosipsos abnegare, charissimis & coniunctissi- mis quibusq; renuntiare, bona praesentia spe futurorum relinquere, & ad omnis generis cruciatus atq; tormenta nunquam non paratos esse oporteat: iam non stulti solum, sed insani, sed dementes, sed à communi sensu alieni & furiosi habentur mundo, qui sic docent atque sentiunt. At quae causa est, quòd tam praepostere & iniquè homo animalis iudicat? Haec nimirum, quòd in externam modo rerum speciem intentus, quae sub hac latent salutis mysteria non videt, neque etiam videre vult: imò nihil credendum & admittendum esse putat, cuius non certa ratio reddi possit ijs, qui praeter huius mundi eruditionem atque doctrinam nihil sapiunt. Praecipua ergo huius mali radix est superbia, quae ut in alijs quoque rebus homines caecos & stolidos reddit, ita in hac causa eos pror- sus dementat, ut aduersus Deum ipsum confidentissimè insurgant, neq; eius verbo rationem suam subijcere velint, ne prius errauisse videantur. Hinc illae voces aduersariorum hodie passim audi- untur: An ergo, si verum dicunt noui isti doctores, tot saeculis totus terrarum orbis erravit? An à salutis via tam turpiter deflexerunt tot Pontifices, Episcopi, Reges, principes, nobiles, docti, sa- pientes? An verò soli isti nunc sapiunt? Nulla ne tot saeculis fuit Christi ecclesia? nullus veri Dei cultus? nulla fides? religio nulla? Num tot viros prudentia, morum probitate, virtute & pietate eximios, & cum his patres, avos, proavos, atavos, maiores denique nostros omnes damnabimus? At dum ista magnis clamoribus omnium auribus ingerunt, ut nobis odium atque invidiam conflent, hoc unum efficiunt, quòd se homines animales & Spiritus Dei omnino vacuos esse testan- tur. Quid enim hic audis, quod non olim Iudaei pro sua Circumcisione, sacrificijs, imò patrum suo- rum traditionibus adduxerint? Annon ijsdem argumentis olim gentes, ut suos Deos & Idola sua tuerentur, aduersus Christianos vsi sunt? Annon hodie ijsdem, si quae esset eorum authoritas, Tur- cae suas superstitiones excusare poterant? Non aliud ergo ista, quam animalem hominem, sapiunt, & quia suam modò rationem isti audiunt, non mirum est, stultitiam ipsis videri eam doctrinam, quam Dei spiritus dictauit, & quae sola veram salutem continet.
units.tr: Moreover, as to what the Apostle said, he now proves it by two arguments, by which at the same time he teaches that the whole cause of this ignorance lies in human beings, so that no one may accuse God, who tries to force upon us things of which he knows we are by no means capable. First, "they are foolishness to him," he says. He does not call the gospel doctrine itself foolish in itself, but says it is foolishness to the natural man, repeating here what he said above: the preaching of Christ crucified is a stumbling block to the Jews, and foolishness to the Greeks, who are puffed up with the persuasion of human wisdom. For by the judgment of the flesh nothing seems so foolish and mad as to place one's hope of salvation in him who endured the punishment of an infamous death on the cross. Yet the same is true of all the other things that are handed down in the Gospel. For it seems foolish to human reason to teach that the Son of God came into the world, that a true man was born of a pure and undefiled virgin, that he hungered, thirsted, and grew cold on earth, that he was betrayed by a disciple and fastened to the cross; likewise that, although all these things were done openly, he wished to have very few witnesses of his resurrection and ascension. For the flesh, which admires nothing except what seems splendid and remarkable to this world, does not see why these things were done. And if you add that all hope of salvation must be placed in Christ alone, so that for his sake we must deny ourselves, renounce our dearest and closest relations, leave behind present goods for the hope of future ones, and always be ready for every kind of torment and torture, then men of the world regard those who teach and think this way not merely as foolish but as insane, demented, alien to common sense, and frenzied. But what is the reason that natural man judges so perversely and unjustly? Surely this: being intent only on the outward appearance of things, he does not see, and does not wish to see, the mysteries of salvation that lie hidden beneath it. Indeed, he thinks that nothing ought to be believed or admitted unless a certain reason can be given for it to those who know nothing beyond the learning and doctrine of this world. So the chief root of this evil is pride, which, as it makes men blind and stupid in other matters too, so in this case utterly maddens them, so that they rise up most boldly against God himself and are unwilling to submit their reason to his word, lest they seem to have been mistaken. Hence those voices of our opponents are heard everywhere today: "Then, if these new teachers speak the truth, has the whole world erred for so many centuries? Have so many popes, bishops, kings, princes, nobles, learned and wise men strayed so shamefully from the way of salvation? Do these men alone understand now? Has there been no Church of Christ for so many centuries? No true worship of God? No faith? No religion? Shall we condemn so many men, distinguished by prudence, uprightness of life, virtue and piety, and with them our fathers, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, great-great-grandfathers, and finally all our ancestors?" But while they pour these things into everyone's ears with loud outcries, so as to stir up hatred and envy against us, they achieve only this: they testify that they are natural men and wholly empty of the Spirit of God. For what do you hear here that the Jews did not formerly bring forward in defence of their circumcision, their sacrifices, and indeed the traditions of their fathers? Did not the Gentiles once use the same arguments against the Christians to defend their gods and their idols? Could not the Turks today use the same arguments to excuse their superstitions, if they had any authority? Therefore these men savour of nothing but natural man, and since they listen only to their own reason, it is no wonder that the doctrine dictated by the Spirit of God, and which alone contains true salvation, seems foolishness to them.

units.la: Sed alterum adhuc argumentum Paulus subijcit. Neq; potest ea cognoscere quia spiritualiter dijudicantur. Sensus est: Magna quidē humani intellectus & rationis nostrae vis est in ijs, quae nostro acumine inuestigari possunt; at quae in Euangelio traduntur, ea ad Dei regnū spectant, quòd cùm non terrenum aut mundanum, sed coelestè sit, in eius mysterijs cognoscendis, nō ratione, sed Spiritu & fide opus est, quae sola nos dirigit, vt ea internoscere, & sub hīs latentem veritatem atq; sa-lutis nostrae rationem videre possimus. Cùm autem Spiritu Dei destituantur qui adhuc toti animales sunt, impossibile est, vt in hīs aliquid intelligant. Est hoc argumentum euidens, & eodem rursus nobis commendatur doctrinae & fidei nostrae dignitas, de qua paulò ante diximus. At quoties in tali tractatione Spiritus mentionem facit Apostolus, quo nos illuminari & duci oporteat, sem-per nos in mente renocare oportet, quod nuper cum Spiritu praedicationem verbi coniunxit. Nun-quam ergo duo ista diuelli debent, neq; nobis Spiritum quendam fingere debemus, qui nos sine ver-bo doceat, aut etiam ea suggerat, quae verbo Dei, quod in Scripturis continetur, contraria sint. Sci-mus equidem in rebus agendis saepe consilia noua à Spiritu suggeri, quae in Scripturis non expri-muntur: at hīc nobis de salutis ratione sermo est, cuius dogmata certa & in sacris literis perfectè comprehensa sunt: quorum vt interpres fidissimus est Spiritus sanctus, ita à verbo illo Dei, quod ipsius inspiratione ad nos delatum est, nunquam dissentit. Quod qui non obseruant, ijdem inspira-tiones expectant nouas, satanae se illudendos propinant, & nouis quotidie erroribus implicantur, vt nuper prolixè docuimus.
units.tr: But Paul adds a second argument: "Nor can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned." The meaning is this: the power of human understanding and of our reason is great in those things which can be investigated by our keenness; but the things handed down in the Gospel pertain to the kingdom of God, and since they are not earthly or worldly but heavenly, in knowing its mysteries we need not reason but the Spirit and faith, which alone guide us so that we may discern them and see the truth hidden beneath them and the reason of our salvation. But since those who are still wholly natural are destitute of the Spirit of God, it is impossible for them to understand anything in these matters. This argument is clear, and by it again the dignity of our doctrine and faith, of which we spoke a little earlier, is commended to us. Yet whenever the Apostle, in such a discussion, mentions the Spirit by whom we must be enlightened and led, we ought always to recall to mind what he lately joined to the Spirit: the preaching of the Word. These two must never be separated, nor should we invent for ourselves some spirit who teaches us without the Word, or even suggests things contrary to the Word of God contained in the Scriptures. We indeed know that in conducting affairs new counsels are often suggested by the Spirit which are not expressed in the Scriptures; but here our discussion concerns the reason of salvation, whose doctrines are certain and fully comprehended in the holy letters. As the Holy Spirit is the most faithful interpreter of them, so he never dissents from that Word of God which was conveyed to us by his inspiration. Those who do not observe this look for new inspirations; they offer themselves to be deceived by Satan and are daily entangled in new errors, as we lately taught at length.

units.la: Caeterum obseruabis hoc loco validissimè confutari, quaecunq; in Papatu de hominis viribus, de libero arbitrio, & operum nostrorum meritis traduntur. Fingunt illi nobis hominem, qui propriae naturae facultatibus adiutus velit & possit ea praestare, quae Deo placent, & ex his fontibus doctrinam suam de hominis iustitia atq; eius merito deriuant. Atqui omnes actiones nostrae ex animae facultatibus oriuntur, inter quas facile primatum tenet mens siue intellectus. Ex hoc iudicium de rebus propositis procedit, quod deinceps in nobis voluntatem parit, & animum ad ea inclinat, quae nobis vtilia & salutaria videntur. At Paulus intellectum illum animalem, nisi Spiritus lux ac-cedat, minimè capacem esse ait eorum, quae sunt Spiritus Dei. Ergo eadem illa non intelligit, non videt, neq; etiam de illis iudicare potest. Ex quo sequitur, quod eadem quoq; non volet, neq; illis delectetur. Quis enim volet quod nescit? quin ex eo voluptatem capiat, quod ignorat? At cùm superiores illae animae facultates opera atq; actiones nostras longè vincant, nunquam certè his ea exprimemus, quae Deus vult & iubet. Itaq; vanissimum commentum est, quicquid illi de nostrorum operum iustitia & meritis garriunt. Quoad enim sibi ipsi relinquitur homo, nihil boni vnquam volet, multò minus autem faciet? Non contendet porrò Spiritus meus (inquit Deus) cum homine, quia Caro est. Item, Figmenta hominis mala sunt ab ineunte aetate. Et in posteriori ad Corinth. epistola Paulus nos ne ad cogitandum quidem idoneos esse ait. In ea autem, quam ad Romanos scripsit, in ijs etiam, qui renati sunt, adhuc legem peccati haerere testatur, quae eos praeter novi ho-minis voluntatem transversos abripiat. Quapropter licet ex regeneratione noua intellectus sanctioris lux in nobis accendatur, noua item voluntas sese proferat, & nouis viribus instructi fructum multum & minimè poenitendum feramus, tamen ne tunc quidem de aliquo merito nostro gloriari possumus. Nihil enim nostris viribus facimus, & proinde semper nobis Apostolicum illud obijci potest: Quid habes, quod non accepisti? Quod si accepisti, quid gloriaris, quasi non acceperis? Ad-hæc quia (vt modo diximus) semper in nobis manent aliquae peccati reliquiae, vitiosa & imperfecta sunt, quaecunq; secundum divinae voluntatis praescriptum facimus, ideoq; nihil per ea mereri possumus apud Deum, qui vt nostris minimè opus habet, ita gratuita bonitate erga nos vtitur, dum infirmitatibus nostris indulget. Quid ergo aliud restat, quam vt procul relicta nostrorum operum fiducia, in solius Dei gratia acquiescamus, nosq; totos subijciamus Spiritus sancti magisterio, qui & mentem nostram illuminat, & ad omne opus bonum idoneos reddit.
units.tr: Moreover, you will observe that in this passage what is taught in Popery about man's powers, free will, and the merits of our works is most powerfully refuted. They fashion for us a man who, aided by the faculties of his own nature, is willing and able to perform those things which please God, and from these sources they derive their doctrine of man's righteousness and its merit. Yet all our actions arise from the faculties of the soul, among which the mind or understanding easily holds the first place. From this, judgment about the things presented to us proceeds, which then gives birth in us to the will and inclines the soul toward those things which seem useful and salutary to us. But Paul says that the natural understanding, unless the light of the Spirit comes to it, is by no means capable of the things of the Spirit of God. Therefore it does not understand those things, does not see them, and cannot judge of them. From this it follows that it will not will them either, nor take delight in them. For who wills what he does not know? Or rather, who takes pleasure in what he is ignorant of? But since those higher faculties of the soul far surpass our works and actions, we will certainly never express by them what God wills and commands. Therefore whatever they chatter about the righteousness and merits of our works is the emptiest fiction. For as long as man is left to himself, will he ever will anything good, much less do it? "My Spirit," says God, "shall not strive with man, because he is flesh." Likewise: "The imaginations of man's heart are evil from his youth." And in the second letter to the Corinthians Paul says that we are not even fit to think. In the letter he wrote to the Romans, he testifies that even in those who have been born again the law of sin still clings, dragging them away, crooked, against the will of the new man. Wherefore, although from the new regeneration the light of a holier understanding is kindled in us, and a new will shows itself, and, equipped with new powers, we bear much fruit which we need not regret, yet even then we cannot glory in any merit of our own. For we do nothing by our own powers, and therefore that Apostolic word can always be thrown at us: "What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?" Moreover, since (as we have just said) some remnants of sin always remain in us, whatever we do according to the prescription of the divine will is faulty and imperfect; therefore we can merit nothing before God through these works. He, who has no need of our works, deals with us by free goodness while he indulges our weaknesses. What then remains, but that, with all confidence in our own works abandoned, we rest in the grace of God alone, and submit ourselves wholly to the teaching of the Holy Spirit, who both enlightens our minds and makes us fit for every good work.

units.la: Facit ad horum confirmationem, quod in Apostoli verbis sequitur: At spiritualis dijudicat quidem omnia, ipse vero à nemine dijudicatur. Spiritualem hominem animali opponit, & eum intelligit, qui in Christo renatus Dei Spiritu regitur. Is (inquit) omnia dijudicat, id est, intelligit quaecunq; cognitu necessaria sunt, & ea facultate instructus est, vt verum à falso atq; Christi vo-cem cem ab aliena discernere possit. Et vicissim idē ille à nemine dijudicatur id est, nullius præterquā solius Dei iudicio subiectus est. Ex eo autem sequitur, credentes non debere eorum iudicijs offendi aut moueri, qui de Christi doctrina audacius pronuntiant, cum eo ipso (vt supra diximus) se animales esse testentur.
units.tr: This supports the confirmation of these points, which follows in the Apostle's words: "But the spiritual man judges all things, yet he himself is judged by no one." He sets the spiritual man against the natural man, and by spiritual he means the one who, reborn in Christ, is governed by the Spirit of God. "He judges all things," he says, that is, he understands whatever is necessary to know, and he is equipped with the ability to tell the voice of Christ from a stranger's voice. And conversely, that same man is judged by no one, that is, he is subject to the judgment of no one but God alone. It follows from this that believers should not be offended or moved by the judgments of those who speak rashly about Christ's doctrine, since by that very boldness (as we said above) they show that they are natural men.

units.la: Continent hæc præclaram hominis Christiani commendationem, quæ simul officij nos admonet. Primò spirituales nos dicit, eò quòd Christi Spiritum accepimus, qui in nobis agit. Et pertinet titulus iste ad omnes, qui Christo nomen dederunt: quod propter eos obseruari debet, qui illum sibi solis vendicant, idq; propter rasuram & vnctionem, quas ecclesiasticorum notas siue characteres esse volunt. At alibi Paulus clamat: Qui Spiritum Christi non habet, is non est Christi, id est, is ne Christianus quidem est. Dum vero nos spirituales dicit, non obscurè ab illis discernit, qui in scripturis Caro dicuntur, eò quòd toti à carnis ratione atq; desiderijs pendeant. Est hæc non vulgaris dignitas, quæ simul ad afferendam nostræ salutis certitudinem plurimum facit, quando nos non amplius in eorum numero censeri constat, quibus perpetua cum Deo lis est. Deinde Christianus omnia dijudicat. Quod non ita accipi debet, quòd plenam & perfectam omnium cognitionem habeamus. Ita enim sequeretur, Christianum non esse, quisquis in aliqua re suo iudicio fallitur. Atqui dum in carne viuimus, ex parte cognoscimus, & ex parte prophetamus (vt infra dicetur) & multa quasi per speculum in ænigmate cernimus: olim autem in patria Deum facie ad faciem intuebimur, & in eodem omnia plenè & perfectè cognoscemus. Quin constat, electos sæpe falli in ijs, quæ ad huius vitæ consilia & actiones pertinent, dum præcipiti nimis iudicio secundum rationis suæ placitum de re propositâ pronuntiant, priusquam spiritus dictata audiuerunt. Exemplum huius rei in Nathano propheta habetur, qui de templo ædificando à Dauide interrogatus consilium eius pro bauit: idem vero mox Spiritus responso accepto ad Dauidem reuerti & sententiam temere prolatam retractare coactus est. Et Petrum post acceptum Spiritum sanctum in nonnullis hæsitauise adhuc legimus: nimirum, quòd carnis & suæ rationis iudicio aliquid tribueret. Ideo quod in præsenti Paulus dicit, ad ea modo restringi debet, quorum cognitio ad salutem consequendam nobis necessaria est. In his enim nos non perpetuò neq; pernitiosè falli finit Spiritus sanctus, licet non semper rei veritas nobis primo intuitu pateat, est enim hic discretionis Spiritus, qui quid à nobis eligi, quid repudiari debeat nos docet. Vnde colligimus, Christianos homines non plumbeos aut stipites esse debere, qui nihil pensi habeant: neq; rerum incertos, qui quouis vento doctrinæ, instar arundinis agitentur. Quia enim Spiritum iudicij acceperunt, eo vti debent, vt veram doctrinam à falsa, religionem veram à superstitionibus discernant, & reliquis auijs in recta salutis via pergant. Admonet de hoc Christus, quando ouibus suis hoc tribuit, quòd vocem suam agnoscant atq; sequantur, alienos autem fugiant. Et Ioannes Apostolus omnibus, qui Christi nomen profitentur, scribit: Ne cuiuis spiritui credatis, sed probate spiritus, num ex Deo sint. Multum ergo à Christianorum (quos hic spirituales Paulus nominat) ingenio absunt, qui quosuis temere sequuntur, & se excusatos arbitrantur, si simpliciter credant, id est, si absq; iudicio quæuis dogmata recipiant. Frustra ergo Apostolus ait, Spirituale omnia dijudicare. Non frustra etiam Christus nos monuit, ne cæcos duces sequamur: fore enim nisi ab illis discedamus, vt eadem perditionis fouea & nos & illos excipiat. Tertiò immunitate donantur Christiani, quando illos à nemine dijudicari dicit, & proinde non timendos esse eos, qui de illis temere pronuntiant. Etenim fides, quæ sola Christianos facit, non ab hominum authoritate pendet, sed Dei verbo nititur, quod æternum est, & sibi ipsi semper constat, vt [?]ut ab eo diuersum sentiant, qui in hoc mundo principes esse videntur. Et hæc illa immunitas est, quæ sola verè nobiles facit, & nullam reprehensionem meretur, quia & Christianum hominem in officio continet, & nemini alij grauis & molesta est.
units.tr: These words contain a remarkable commendation of the Christian, which at the same time reminds us of our duty. First, he calls us spiritual, because we have received the Spirit of Christ, who works in us. This title belongs to all who have taken the name of Christ, and it must be upheld against those who claim it for themselves alone, on the strength of the tonsure and the anointing, which they want to be the marks or characters of the clergy. But elsewhere Paul cries out: "Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ is not his," that is, such a person is not even a Christian. And when he calls us spiritual, he clearly distinguishes us from those who in the Scriptures are called flesh, because they depend wholly on the reasoning and desires of the flesh. This is no common dignity, and it greatly helps to establish the certainty of our salvation, since it is evident that we are no longer counted among those who are in a constant quarrel with God. Second, the Christian judges all things. This must not be taken to mean that we have a full and perfect knowledge of everything. For then it would follow that no one is a Christian who is mistaken in any matter by his own judgment. Yet while we live in the flesh we know in part, and we prophesy in part (as will be said below), and we see many things as through a mirror in a riddle; but in our homeland we shall see God face to face, and in that same place we shall know all things fully and perfectly. Indeed, it is clear that the elect often err in those matters which pertain to the counsels and actions of this life, when they pronounce too hastily, according to their own reasoning, on a question put before them, before they have heard the dictates of the Spirit. An example of this is found in the prophet Nathan, who, when asked by David about building the temple, approved his plan; but soon afterwards, having received an answer from the Spirit, he was compelled to go back to David and retract the opinion he had rashly given. And we read that Peter, even after receiving the Holy Spirit, still hesitated in some matters, clearly because he gave weight to the judgment of the flesh and of his own reason. Therefore what Paul says here must be restricted to those things whose knowledge is necessary for us to attain salvation. For in these the Holy Spirit does not allow us to be deceived constantly or fatally, although the truth of the matter may not always be plain to us at first glance. For this is the discerning Spirit, who teaches us what we ought to choose and what we ought to reject. From this we gather that Christians ought not to be stocks or lead, who have no weight, nor men unsettled about matters, who are blown about by every wind of doctrine like reeds. Since they have received the Spirit of judgment, they ought to use it to distinguish true doctrine from false, and true religion from superstitions, and to press on along the right way of salvation, leaving aside the other byways. Christ reminds us of this when he grants to his sheep that they know his voice and follow it, but flee from strangers. And the Apostle John writes to all who profess the name of Christ: "Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are from God." Therefore those who rashly follow whoever comes along, and think themselves excused if they simply believe, that is, if they accept any doctrines whatever without judgment, are far from the character of the Christians whom Paul here calls spiritual. Thus the Apostle says in vain that the spiritual man judges all things. Nor did Christ warn us in vain not to follow blind guides: for unless we leave them, both we and they will fall into the same pit of destruction. Third, Christians are granted an immunity, when he says that they are judged by no one, and so those who rashly pass judgment on them need not be feared. For faith, which alone makes Christians, does not depend on the authority of men but rests on the Word of God, which is eternal and always consistent with itself, so that men think otherwise than those who seem to be the rulers of this world. This is the immunity which alone truly makes men noble, and it deserves no reproach, because it both keeps the Christian man in his duty and is burdensome and troublesome to no one else.

units.la: Quia vero durius & insolentius dictum alicui videri poterat, Christianos à nemine dijudicari, probat hoc ipsum testimonio prophetico, dicens: Quis enim nouit mentem Domini, qui instructurus sit eum? Desumpta sunt hæc ex Isaiæ cap. 40. & per allusionem, vel potius comparationem adducta videntur. Illic enim redemptionem ex Babylone Propheta pollicetur, quæ quia humanæ rationi impossibilis videbatur, eam non hominum viribus, sed Dei virtute perfi-ciendam fore docet: vt certior & efficatior sit promissionis istius consolatio, Dei veritatem, potentiam, sapientiam atq; maiestatem, quae in omnibus huius mundi partibus cernitur, magnifice describit, vbi inter alia sic ait: Quis direxit Spiritum Domini? Quis à consilijs ei fuit, & eum docuit? Cum quo iniit consilium, qui eum erudiret? Quis docuit eum in semita iudicij? Quis docuit eum scientiam, & iter intelligentiae quis declarauit ei? Ex istis quaedam mutatis nonnihil verbis, nullo tamen sensus germani periculo, Paulus suo instituto accommodat, & mox subijcit: Nos autem mentem, siue Spiritum Christi habemus. Omnium ergo istorum haec mihi sententia simplicissima esse videtur: Dei spiritus à nemine dijudicari aut argui potest. Notum est enim illud Isaiae, quo patres nostros olim consolatus est: Quis direxit aut nouit Spiritum Domini, &c.? At nos CHRISTI IESV (qui verus & aeternus Dei Filius, adeoq; ille ipse est, quem Prophetae passim fere Domini nomine ornant) Spiritum aut mentem habemus: Ergo neq; nos à quoquam dijudicari aut argui possumus. Maior non solum authoritate prophetica probatur, sed sensus communis iudicio nititur, imò ipsa religionis fundamenta conuellere tentabit, qui illam negare velit. Nã ipso Deo sapientior sit oportet, qui eius Spiritum arguere, docere aut corrigere instituat. Quod cum cogitatu, nedum dictu, graue & horrendum sit, nemo in animum inducet, qui aliquo pietatis sensu tangitur. Minor probatione non opus habet, quia (vt Paulo ante diximus) nisi Christi mentem aut Spiritum teneamus, Christiani non sumus. Ex istis autem certa & infallibili consequentia concluditur, nullius hominis iudicio subiecta esse, quaecunq; Spiritu sancto doctore didicimus, & quorum fides scripturae diuinitus inspiratae testimonijs nititur. Nam qui nos propter illa reprehendere aut damnare volet, huic non nobis cum, sed cum Deo ipso lis erit, qui nos ita sentire & credere docuit.
units.tr: Because it might seem a harsh and unusual statement that Christians are judged by no one, he proves this very point by a prophetic testimony, saying: "For who has known the mind of the Lord, that he should instruct him?" These words are taken from Isaiah chapter 40, and seem to be brought in by way of allusion, or rather comparison. For there the prophet promises redemption from Babylon, and since this seemed impossible to human reason, he teaches that it would be accomplished not by human strength but by the power of God; so that the comfort of this promise might be more certain and effective, he magnificently describes the truth, power, wisdom and majesty of God, which are seen in all parts of this world, where among other things he says: "Who has directed the Spirit of the Lord? Who was his counsellor, and taught him? With whom did he take counsel, who might instruct him? Who taught him the path of judgment? Who taught him knowledge, and who showed him the way of understanding? Paul adapts some of these words to his purpose, with slight changes that do not endanger the true sense, and immediately adds: "But we have the mind, or Spirit, of Christ." So my view of all these words seems to be this most simple one: the Spirit of God can be judged or challenged by no one. For that saying of Isaiah is well known, by which he once consoled our fathers: "Who has directed or known the Spirit of the Lord?" But we have the Spirit or mind of CHRIST JESUS (who is the true and eternal Son of God, and is indeed the very one whom the prophets commonly adorn with the name of Lord). So neither can we be judged or challenged by anyone. The major premise is proved not only by prophetic authority but rests on the judgment of common sense; indeed, whoever wishes to deny it will attempt to overthrow the very foundations of religion. For he must be wiser than God himself who sets out to challenge, teach or correct his Spirit. Since this is grave and horrible even to think, let alone to say, no one will entertain it who is touched by any sense of piety. The minor premise needs no proof, because (as we said a little earlier) unless we hold the mind or Spirit of Christ, we are not Christians. From these premises, by a sure and infallible consequence, it is concluded that whatever we have learned from the Holy Spirit as our teacher, and whose faith rests on the testimonies of Scripture inspired by God, is subject to no man's judgment. For whoever wishes to rebuke or condemn us for these things will have a quarrel not with us but with God himself, who taught us to think and believe thus.

units.la: Vides igitur hoc loco, quibus argumentis fides atq; doctrina nostra fortissime defendi possit adversus eos, qui nos hodie accusant. Haeretici dicimur, quòd vnum Deum inuocandum, & vno Mediatore apud hunc vtendum esse docemus: quòd item CHRISTVM IESVM vnicum pro peccatis nostris sacrificium, vnicam iustitiam & sanctificationem esse, nosq; sola fide in illum iustificari, sanctificari atq; seruari credimus. Adhaec impios & sacrilegos, in Diuos coelites quoq; nos iniurios esse multi vociferantur, quòd hos inuocandos esse negemus, quòd illorum imagines & in ipsorum honorem facta altaria ex templis eiecerimus. Deniq; aliis licentiae & impiae securitatis magistri esse putamur, quòd neminem suorum operum meritis iustificari, & nullum ignem lustralem seu purgatorium (vt illi loquuntur) esse dicamus, in quo defunctorum animae pro delictis in hac vita commissis satisfaciant. Atqui merito nos propter ista damnarent aduersarij, si nos ea ex nostro cerebro finxissemus, & primi ista essemus locuti. Sed haec à nobis conficta, & nos primos horum auctores esse constanter negamus. Dei enim praeceptum est: Non habebis Deos alienos coram facie mea. In die tribulationis tuae inuoca me & liberabo te. Christi item vox est: Nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per me. Ioannes Baptista clamat: Ecce Agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi. Et Christus iam moriturus dicebat, Consummatum est. Vnde Apostolus concludit, illum semel oblatum peccata multorum expiauisse, neq; opus esse, vt iterum vel moriatur vel immoletur. Item Deus Pater coelitus concionatur: Hic est Filius ille meus dilectus, in quo placatus sum. Et eundem nobis à Patre iustitiam, sapientiam & sanctificationem factum esse, nuper Paulus diserte pronunciauit. Sola autem fide in illum nos iustificari & seruari toties ipsemet docet, quoties illud Euangelicum axioma repetit: Qui credit in me, habet vitam aeternam. Item: Qui crediderit et baptizatus fuerit, seruabitur. Quoad Diuos coelites, illi ipsi, ne quem praeter vnum Deum inuocemus, nos docuerunt. Neq; nostra, sed Apostolorum haec dicta sunt: Vnus Deus, vnus Mediator Dei & hominum, homo IESVS CHRISTVS. Si quis peccauerit, aduocatum habemus apud Deum, IESVM CHRISTVM, &c. Deus ipse praeterea non sine graui comminatione praecipit, ne quas imagines ad cultum proflare patiamur. Et Ioannis haec sententia est: Filioli, cauete vobis à simulachris. Altarium vero quis in nouo testamento vsus est, vbi sacrificia cessant, preces autem & gratiarum actio in Christi nomine offerri debent, qui solus ara illa aurea est, quae preces nostras Deo acceptas facit? Neq; nos, sed Christus iam moriens velum templi discidit, quo templum cum altaribus & toto illo cultu Leuitico abolendum esse significabatur, vt vero cultui locus fieret, qui inspiritu & veritate consistit. Lustralem quoq; ignem non nos, sed Christus, negauit, dicens: Qui credit in me, in iudicium non veniet, sed à morte translatus est in vitam. Et cùm latroni dixit: Hodie mecum eris in paradiso. Licentiæ verò & impiæ securitatis nos magistros dicunt, qui quid fidei fit, & quæ regenerationis effecta sint nesciunt, neq; scire volunt. Atqui eadem est omnium aliorum ratio, de quibus litem nobis mouent aduersarij. Quapropter cum ista nos ex Christi ore & spiritu hauserimus, & proinde Christi mentem habeamus, non est quod in nos sibi iudicium sumant Pontifices cum sua vnctorum & rasorum[?] cohorte. Quis enim ex illis nouit Spiritum Domini? Quis huic à consilijs fuit, cum totum nostræ salutis negotium æterno suo decreto comprehenderet? Vel ostendant illi prius, vnde hæc ipsis authoritas obtigerit, vt erroris aut falsi arguant eos, quos Spiritu Domini donatos fuisse, nemo pius vnquam negauit? Sed quicquid illi proferant, nobis vnus hic locus sufficit, quo nos aduersus illorum condemnationes tueamur.
units.tr: You see, then, from this passage with what arguments our faith and doctrine can be most strongly defended against those who accuse us today. We are called heretics because we teach that the one God is to be invoked and that we must approach him through the one Mediator; likewise because we believe that Christ Jesus is the one sacrifice for our sins, the one righteousness and sanctification, and that we are justified, sanctified and saved by faith alone in him. Besides this, many cry out that we are impious and sacrilegious, and that we wrong the heavenly saints, because we deny that they are to be invoked and because we have removed from the churches their images and the altars made in their honour. Finally, we are thought to be teachers of licence and of a reckless security, because we say that no one is justified by the merits of his works, and that there is no cleansing or purgatorial fire (as they call it) in which the souls of the dead make satisfaction for the sins committed in this life. Yet our opponents would rightly condemn us for these things if we had invented them out of our own heads and were the first to speak them. But we firmly deny that these things are made up by us and that we are the first authors of them. For the command of God is: "You shall have no other gods before my face" (Exod. 20.). "In the day of your trouble, call upon me, and I will deliver you" (Ps. 50.). The voice of Christ is: "No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14.). John the Baptist cries out: "Behold that Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world" (John 1.). And Christ, about to die, said: "It is finished" (John 19.). Hence the Apostle concludes that he, having been offered once, has expiated the sins of many, and that there is no need for him either to die again or to be sacrificed again (Heb. 9.). Likewise God the Father speaks from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Matt. 3.). And Paul recently declared plainly that the same One has been made to us by the Father wisdom, righteousness and sanctification (1 Cor. 1.). Moreover, he himself teaches again and again that we are justified and saved by faith alone in him, whenever he repeats that Gospel saying: "He who believes in me has eternal life" (John 6.). Also: "He who believes and is baptized will be saved" (Mark 16.). As for the heavenly saints, they themselves taught us to invoke no one besides the one God. These words are not ours but the Apostles': "There is one God, and one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Tim. 2.). "If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ" (1 John 2.). Moreover, God himself commands, not without a severe threat, that we allow no images to be set up for worship. And this is the saying of John: "Little children, keep yourselves from idols" (1 John 5.). But what use of altars is there in the New Testament, where sacrifices cease, and prayers and thanksgiving ought to be offered in the name of Christ, who alone is that golden altar which makes our prayers acceptable to God? Nor was it we, but Christ, who, as he was dying, rent the veil of the temple, signifying that the temple with its altars and all that Levitical worship was to be abolished, so that room might be made for worship which consists in spirit and truth. It was not we but Christ who also denied the purgatorial fire, saying: "He who believes in me does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life" (John 5.). And when he said to the thief: "Today you will be with me in paradise" (Luke 23.). But they call us teachers of licence and of a reckless security, those who do not know what faith is, nor what the effects of regeneration are, and do not wish to know. Yet the case is the same for all the others about whom our opponents raise a quarrel with us. Therefore, since we have drawn these things from the mouth and Spirit of Christ, and so have the mind of Christ, there is no reason why the pontiffs, with their cohort of anointed and shaven men, should claim judgment over us. For which of them knows the Spirit of the Lord? Who was of his counsel when he settled the whole business of our salvation by his eternal decree? Let them first show whence this authority has come to them, so that they may charge with error or falsehood those whom, as no godly man has ever denied, the Spirit of the Lord has endowed. But whatever they bring forward, this one passage is enough for us to defend ourselves against their condemnations.

units.la: At quia indomita est illorum hominum insolentia, proderit huius loci occasione amplius demonstrare, quàm atrocem toti Christianorum ecclesiæ iniuriam faciant. Primò, cùm spirituales dicat Paulus omnes, qui Christo per fidem insiti, huius verbo & Spiritu se duci patiuntur, illi (vt supra diximus) nomen illud sibi solis vendicant, eò quòd vnti & rasi sint, reliquos verò omnes igno miniosò[?] Laicorum titulo à spiritualibus discernunt. Qua in re Iudæos imitantur, qui dum se solos Dei populum esse sibi persuaserunt, alios omnes Goym appellant, quibus nihil sit cum Deo negotij. Neq; hic mihi fucum faciant calua sua excusatione, qua honorem istum ordini ecclesiastico deberi respondent, alios verò nihilominus ab ipsis pro Christianis agnoscì, & proinde non habere quod de ipsis conquerantur. Audio quidem ista iampridem à vobis dici, sed verba hæc sunt, quorum fucus vestris factis & moribus proditur. Si enim pro Christianis agnoscitis omnes, qui in Christi nomen baptizati & hunc fide amplexi sunt, cur ijsdem spiritualium nomen negatis, quod solis Christianis conuenit? Cur vos solos Clerum Domini dicendo, reliquos omnes à sorte ecclesiæ & regni Christi excluditis? Cur à librorum sacrorum lectione eosdem reijcitis vt canes & porcos, ad quos margaritæ illæ spiritus sanctì minimè pertineant? Cur calicem Domini ex Cœna mystica surripuistis, ne illo Laici illi, quos vos ita dicitis, vtantur? Cur in templo locum vobis peculiarem delegistis ne cum reliquis misceamini? Hæc certè cum iam sæculis aliquot à vobis factitata sint, & adhuc fiant, satis nota est omnibus tyrannis vestra, qua in Christi gregem debacchamini. Cur verò spiritualium nomen sibi vendicant isti? Non aliam ob causam, quàm vt hoc Pauli loco abutantur, & se à nemine mortalium iudicari debere euincant. Ita verò immunitatem sibi acquisierunt, quæ illos Regibus & Imperatoribus superiores fecit, adeoq; à totius ecclesiæ censura exemit, vt nemo mortalium sit, cuius authoritate in ordinem cogi queant.
units.tr: But because the insolence of those men is unbridled, it will be useful, on the occasion of this passage, to show more fully how atrocious an injury they do to the whole church of Christians. First, although Paul calls all spiritual who, ingrafted into Christ through faith, allow themselves to be led by his word and Spirit, they (as we said above) claim that name for themselves alone, because they are anointed and shaven, and separate all the rest from the spiritual by the shameful title of laymen. In this they imitate the Jews, who, having persuaded themselves that they alone are God's people, call all others Goyim, to whom they have no business with God. Nor let them here cover their deceit with that excuse of theirs, in which they reply that this honour is owed to the ecclesiastical order, while others nonetheless are recognised by them as Christians, and so they have no reason to complain about them. I indeed hear that these things have been said by you for some time, but these are words whose pretence is betrayed by your deeds and manners. For if you acknowledge all who have been baptized into the name of Christ and have embraced him in faith as Christians, why do you deny the name of spiritual to those same people, a name which belongs only to Christians? Why, by calling yourselves alone the clergy of the Lord, do you exclude all the rest from the lot of the church and the kingdom of Christ? Why do you cast them out from reading the sacred books, as dogs and swine, to whom those pearls of the Holy Spirit do not pertain at all? Why have you snatched the cup of the Lord from the mystical Supper, lest those laymen, as you call them, should use it? Why have you chosen for yourselves a special place in the temple, lest you be mixed with the rest? Since these things have been practised by you for several centuries and are still done, your tyrannies by which you rage against the flock of Christ are well known to all. Yet why do these men claim for themselves the name of spiritual? For no other reason than that they may abuse this passage of Paul and prove that they ought to be judged by no mortal. Thus they have obtained for themselves an immunity which has made them superior to kings and emperors, and has so exempted them from the censure of the whole church that there is no mortal by whose authority they can be brought into order.

units.la: Nec enim illos Canonis illius adhuc pudet, quo Romanum Pontificem à nemine iudicari debere clamant, etiamsi animarum myriades vna secum in gehennam abripiat. Interea verò illi sibi nō modò in omnes homines, imò Reges & Imperatores, iudicium sumunt, verumetiam in Dei verbum, in Scripturas sacras, in fidei dogmata, quæ omnia suæ libidini subijciunt, pro suo arbitrio interpretantur, & quæcunque ipsi illis contraria statuunt, non minus valere volunt, quàm ea, quæ scripturis traduntur. Quædam ergo mutant, multa item addunt, & noua quotidie fingunt, multa etiam falsi & hæresebs[?] damnant, quæ Apostolorum literis defendi possunt. Sed ita suo indicio sese produnt sorices[?] isti, quòd à Christi spiritu alieni sint, & proinde indigni, quorum iudicijs quisquam moveatur.
units.tr: For they are not yet ashamed of that canon by which they cry out that the Roman Pontiff ought to be judged by no one, even if he drags myriads of souls with him into hell. Meanwhile they claim judgment not only over all men, indeed over kings and emperors, but also over the word of God, the holy Scriptures, and the doctrines of faith, all of which they subject to their own lust, interpret at their own pleasure, and wish whatever they decree against them to carry no less weight than what is handed down in the Scriptures. Some things, therefore, they change; many they also add; and they invent new things daily; many things they even condemn as false and heretical, although they can be defended by the writings of the Apostles. But these moles betray themselves by their own judgment, in that they are estranged from the Spirit of Christ and therefore unworthy that anyone should be moved by their judgments.

units.la: Nos verò fratres charissimi, Dei bonitatem agnoscamus, qui non contentus nos redemisse per Filij sui indignam mortem, insuper Spiritu suo nos dignatur, qui nos in Dei filios regenerat, mentes nostras illuminat, docet, dirigit, & cœlestium mysteriorum (quoad necesse est nobis) capaces reddit. Excitet nos horum consideratio, vt dignitatem nostram tueamur, & procul relicta carnis sapientia atq; desiderijs, nos illi vni consecremus, & Spiritum ducem atq; verbi eius lucernà constanter sequamur. Ita & germani Dei filij erimus, & regni cœlorum hæreditate fruemur cum Filio eius vnigenito, IESV CHRISTO Domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: But we, most beloved brothers, let us acknowledge the goodness of God, who, not content to have redeemed us through the unworthy death of his Son, moreover deigns to give us his Spirit, who regenerates us as sons of God, enlightens our minds, teaches, directs, and makes us capable of heavenly mysteries (as far as is necessary for us). Let the consideration of these things stir us to guard our dignity, and, leaving behind the wisdom and desires of the flesh, let us consecrate ourselves to him alone, and constantly follow the Spirit as our guide and the lamp of his word. Thus we shall also be true sons of God, and shall enjoy the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven together with his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT III. HOMILIA XII.
units.tr: Chapter 3. Homily 12.

units.la: EGo porrò, fratres, non potui vobis loqui vt spiritualibus, sed lô cutus sum vt carnalibus, vt infantibus in Christo. Lactis potu vos alui, & non esca: nondum enim poteratis hanc ferre: imò ne nunc quidem adhuc potestis. Nam adhuc carnales estis. Cùm enim in vobis sint æmulatio, & contentio, & dissidia, nonne carnales estis, & secundum hominem incedítis? Etenim cùm dicat quidam, Ego qui dem sum Pauli: alter verò, Ego sum Apollo: nonne carnales estis?
units.tr: And I, brothers, could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but as to carnal people, as to infants in Christ. I fed you with milk, not solid food, for you were not yet able to take it. Indeed, you are not able even now, for you are still carnal. For since there is envying and strife and division among you, are you not carnal and walking according to man? For when one says, "I am of Paul," and another, "I am of Apollos," are you not carnal?

units.la: DILIGENTER hucusq; Paulus de Euangelicæ doctrinæ excellentia disseruit, & de modo docendi, quo ipse apud Corinthios vsus erat. Scopus & finis omnium hic est, quòd primò confidentes & delicatulos quosdam corrigere vult, qui pseudoapostolorum blanditijs & magnificis sermonibus delusi, Euangelium propter humile & simplex dicendi genus fastidiosè nimis contemnebant. Deinde seipsum excusat, qui non tam verborum elegantiæ & argumentandi artificio studuerit, quàm vt veritatis doctrinam Spiritus sancti virtute animatam proponeret, & reipsa doceret, se nihil absq; Spiritus suggestione proferre. Dicimus nos in ea tractatione, quæ vera illa sapientia sit, quam omnes quærere & venari debent. Non ea nimirum, quæ in philosophorum libris habetur, sed quam Euangelij doctrina nobis tradit. In hac enim ipse Dei Filius proponitur, in quo omnes sapientiæ & scientiæ thesauri reconditi sunt, quique nobis etiam à Patre sapientia factus est. Neque nos inani cognitione pascit, sed in Christo simul omnia exhibet, quæ tam ad præsentis vitæ felicitatem quàm ad salutis æternæ possessionem cognitu necessaria sunt. Docuit præterea Paulus, qua ratione illam nobis revelet Deus, & vt eadem à nobis addisci aut obtineri possint. Nimirum, si abnegata carnis ratione atque desiderijs, nos totos spiritus magisterio subijciamus, qui solus mentes nostras illuminat, vt cœlestium mysteriorum capaces sint. Et hoc faciunt, quæ nuper de homine animali & spirituali sunt dicta. At quia non satis est doctrinam aliquam in genere proposuisse, nunc ista omnia Corinthijs applicat, & suæ doctrinæ aut prædicationis ratione sic reddit, vt quod in ipso desiderabant in illos retorqueat, tales & prius fuisse & adhuc esse demonstrans, quibus docendi genus sublimius minimè conueniat. Qui locus vt apostolicæ industriæ & manssuetudinis egregium exemplum continet: ita verbi administros monet, quanta cum circumspectione & cura Euangelij prædicationem mundo debeant proponere.
units.tr: Up to this point Paul has discussed carefully the excellence of the Gospel teaching and the manner of teaching he had used among the Corinthians. His whole aim is first to correct certain overconfident and pampered people who, won over by the flattery and grand speeches of the false apostles, despised the Gospel too disdainfully because of its humble and plain manner of speaking. Then he excuses himself: he had not aimed at elegance of words or the art of argument, but at setting forth the doctrine of truth animated by the power of the Holy Spirit, and at teaching in fact that he proposed nothing apart from the prompting of the Spirit. In that discussion we have said what the true wisdom is, which everyone ought to seek and pursue. It is not what is found in the books of the philosophers, but what the teaching of the Gospel hands down to us. For in it the Son of God himself is set forth, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden, and who has been made wisdom to us from the Father. Nor does it feed us with empty knowledge; in Christ it offers all the things that need to be known, both for the happiness of the present life and for the possession of eternal salvation. Paul also taught how God reveals this to us, and how we may learn and obtain the same things: namely, if, having renounced the reasoning and desires of the flesh, we submit ourselves wholly to the teaching of the Spirit, who alone illumines our minds so that they are capable of heavenly mysteries. This is what the things said recently about the natural and the spiritual man are for. But since it is not enough to have set out some doctrine in general terms, he now applies all of this to the Corinthians. By the manner of his teaching and preaching he turns back upon them what they had desired in him, showing that they had been, and still were, the sort of people to whom a more lofty manner of teaching is not suited. This passage is an outstanding example of apostolic diligence and gentleness, and it also warns ministers of the Word with how much caution and care they ought to present the preaching of the Gospel to the world.

units.la: Et initiò quidem, cùm se à multis suspicione grauari sciret, quasi aut ignoraret, aut inuidiosè calaret, quæ pseudoapostoli plenis buccis iactabant mysteria, per Concessionis speciem pulchrè culpam omnè in illos regerit, dum ad hunc modum orditur: Ego porrò, fratres, non potui vobis loqui vt spiritualibus, sed locutus sum vt carnalibus, vel potius vt infantibus in Christo, &c. Fratrum nomine eos sæpissimè compellat, vt correptione leniat aut mitiget, quæ per se grauis & duriuscula futura erat, et quia infirmiores plus æquo poterant terreri & offendi. Et debent hoc exemplo doctores omnes imitari, vt tunc quoq; confirmandis atq; lucrifaciendis infirmioribus studeant, quando corripiendi causas habent iustissimas. Porrò hic verborum Pauli sensus est: Scio fratres, vos in me sapientia quadã altiorem desiderare, multos ita me suspectu habere, quasi consultò, vel potius prauo aliquo affectu motus quadã vos celare voluerim. At cùm CHRISTVM IESVM vobis fideliter prædicaue rim, probè mihi sum conscius, neq; maleuoloru[?] sinistris iudicijs multùm moueor. Nã Christi cognitio sapientia vere cœlestis cōtinet, qua nulla sublimior aut perfectior excogitari potest. Sed esto culpa aut reprehensione dignus videar, quòd in argumenti tam sublimis tractatione dicendi genere vsus sim humiliori et (vt multis videtur) abiecto nimis et sordido. Nō tamen ego reprehensione mereor (si quidē causa hæc tota rectius examinetur) sed vos potius, qui vt aliter vobiscū agere nō fuistis idonei, adeoq; inuitū me humi repere coegistis, qui vna vobiscum maluissem ad sublimiorem mysteriorum salutis considerationē ascendere. Quia enim vos nō spirituales, sed prorsus carnales esse vidi, minimè vobiscum ut cum spiritualibus loqui potui, sed ut vestro captui me accommodarem necesse fuit. Carnales autem dicit Corinthios, non quòd spiritu Dei prorsus destitutos putaret (initiò enim vocatos sanctos dixit, & in Christo omni sermone & cognitione abunde ditatos esse testatus est: quæ dona absque spiritus virtute efficaci in nobis locum habere non possunt) sed quòd carnis sapientiæ adhuc nimium dediti, Spiritum in se regnare non paterentur. Itaque hyperbolem sapit oratio, & carnales dici merebantur, quia tales videri poterant, si ad perfectionis Christianæ regulam examinarentur: ijdem tamen gentium respectu spirituales erant, cùm Christo nomen dedissent, & non in universum ab Euangelij doctrina abhorrerent. Ideo per expositionem subijcit: Ut infantibus in Christo: Eos nimirum intelligens, qui nondum progressus aliquos multa laude dignos in fide Christi fecissent, sed infantum instar ea adhuc ignorarent, sine quibus Christiana religio non consistit. Voluit autem istis locutionibus apud illos uti Apostolus, ut confidentiæ cristas illis deprimeret, quibus sese adversus simplicem atque synceraм Christi crucifixi prædicationem efferebant. Itaque verba hæc reprehensionem grauem continent, neque dubium est aculeos istos perquam molestos & vix tolerabiles visos fuisse illis, qui iam se supra nubes euectos esse & ipsum cœlum digito contingere sibi persuaserant.
units.tr: And at the start, since he knew he was burdened by the suspicion of many, as if he were either ignorant of the mysteries the false apostles boasted of with full mouths or was spitefully concealing them, he neatly places all the blame on them under a show of concession, beginning thus: "And I, brothers, could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but spoke as to carnal people, or rather as to infants in Christ," and so on. He very often addresses them by the name of brothers, so as to soften or mitigate a rebuke which would otherwise be severe and somewhat harsh, and because the weaker ones could be frightened and offended more than was right. All teachers ought to imitate this example, so that even when they have very just grounds for rebuke, they also take care to strengthen and win over the weaker. The sense of Paul's words is this: "I know, brothers, that you desire a certain higher wisdom from me, and that many regard me with suspicion, as if I had deliberately, or rather moved by some wicked feeling, wanted to hide things from you. But since I have faithfully preached Jesus Christ to you, I am conscious of having done so rightly, and I am not much moved by the unfavourable judgements of ill-wishers. For the knowledge of Christ contains truly heavenly wisdom, and none higher or more perfect can be imagined. But even if I seem worthy of blame or reproof because in treating so lofty a subject I have used a manner of speaking that is lowlier and (as many think) too abject and sordid, yet I do not deserve reproof (if this whole matter is examined more correctly); rather you deserve it, for you were not fit for me to deal with you otherwise, and so you forced me, against my will, to crawl along the ground, when I would gladly have ascended with you to a higher consideration of the mysteries of salvation. For since I saw that you were not spiritual but altogether carnal, I could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but I had to adapt myself to your capacity." He calls the Corinthians carnal not because he thought them utterly deprived of the Spirit of God (for at the start he called them holy by calling, and he testified that they were richly enriched in Christ in all speech and knowledge, gifts which cannot exist in us without the effective power of the Spirit), but because, still too much given over to the wisdom of the flesh, they did not allow the Spirit to reign in them. So the expression is a hyperbole, and they deserved to be called carnal because they could seem so if they were tested by the rule of Christian perfection; yet with respect to the Gentiles they were the same people as spiritual, since they had given their name to Christ and did not utterly shrink from the teaching of the Gospel. So he adds by way of explanation: as to infants in Christ, meaning those who had not yet made any progress worthy of great praise in the faith of Christ, but as infants were still ignorant of those things without which the Christian religion does not stand. The Apostle chose to use these expressions towards them so as to lower the crests of their confidence, by which they lifted themselves up against the simple and sincere preaching of Christ crucified. So these words contain a grave rebuke, and there is no doubt that these stings seemed very annoying and scarcely tolerable to those who had persuaded themselves that they had been carried above the clouds and touched heaven itself with their finger.

units.la: Mox verò modum exponit, quem in ipsis docendis secutus sit. Lactis potu vos alui (inquit) & non esca. Ita verò loquitur, ut in Metaphora perflet, qua illos infantes in Christo esse dixerat, & sensus est: Ut infantes edentulos non esca aut cibo solidiori, qui manducationem requirit, sed lacte alere atque nutrire oportet: ita vos quoque propter infantiam & imperitiam mysteriorum fidei mollius & tenerius adhuc tractandi fuistis, donec cibi solidioris capaces efficiamini. At hic diligenter observari debet, Paulum non de ipsis doctrinæ Euangelicæ capitibus & propriis fidei dogmatibus loqui, quasi alia apud Corinthios, alia apud alios prædicarit. Est enim prædicationis Euangelicæ argumentum CHRISTVS IESVS, qui ut unus & idem est heri & hodie & in seculo: sic eadem semper manet fidei doctrina, quam certis capitibus ipse comprehendit, quando in suo nomine prædicare iussit pœnitentiam & remissionem peccatorum. Neque unquam permissum fuit Apostolis, ut pro suo aut aliorum arbitrio doctrinam mutarent, articulos ex suo cerebro novos conderent, aut quicquam eorum dissimularent, quæ à Christo acceperant. Eius enim præceptum est: Docete eos servare, quæcunq; ego tradidi vobis. Ergo de modo & forma doctrinæ Paulus istud dicit, ut pseudoapostolos perstringat, qui cùm Christi & Euangelij eius præcones haberi vellent, minimè tamen in eo erant, ut propria & germana fidei Christianæ capita perspicuè traderent, sed inani verborum ostentatione sublimia quædam & mirifica eorum auribus instillabant, qui vix prima religionis rudimenta adhuc degustauerant. Et cùm idem Christus atque eadem Euangelij doctrina infantibus aut infirmis in fide lac, adultis verò & longius progressis esca aut cibus solidior sit, Paulus in præsenti lactis nomine genus docendi rude & simplex intelligit, quale in Catechismis continetur, qui breviter & perspicuè summa religionis & salutis capita tradunt, ex quibus multa alia deriuantur, quæ ad illorum illustrationem atque confirmationem facere possunt ijs, qui in primis illis non infeliciter sunt instituti. Escam verò dicit doctrinam illam solidiorem & seueriorem, qua totus homo Deo vendicatur ad fidei obedientiam, adeoq; ipsa praxis fidei & religionis Christianæ exigitur, omnesq; urgentur, ut relictis terrenis ad sola cœlestia aspirent. In qua parte multa de legis usu & abrogatione, de hominis viribus, de electione, prædestinatione, futuri seculi statu, & similibus alijs præclarè & non sine fructu dici possunt apud eos, qui in fide sunt confirmatores, modò illa sobriè & modestè tractentur: at ut ijsdem obtundantur rudes & qui minus ingenio valent, minimè opus est, cùm vera & simplex CHRISTI IESV cognitio illis ad salutem abunde sufficiat. Itaque ut paulò ante diximus, etsi utrinque idem Christus, eadem salutis humanæ ratio, eademq; fidei dogmata tradantur, in modo tamen & forma tradendi aliqua differentia est, neque idem modus omnibus convenit. Quod ergo (inquit Paulus) ego hucusq; depressum illud & humile dicendi genus secutus sum, id non mea vel ignavia vel malitia factum est, sed vestro vitio hoc omne acceptum ferri debet, siquidem in eo aliquid peccatum esse arbitramini. Nam ut aliter vobiscum agerem, non poteratis ferre, imò ne nunc quidem potestis, ut ut præ[?] aliis omnibus sapere vobis videamini, &c.
units.tr: Soon after he sets out the method he followed in teaching them: I fed you with milk (he says), and not with solid food. He speaks in such a way as to keep up the metaphor by which he had called them infants in Christ, and the sense is this: just as infants without teeth must be fed and nourished not with solid food that needs chewing, but with milk, so you too, on account of your infancy and inexperience in the mysteries of faith, had to be handled more gently and tenderly until you became able to take more solid food. But it must be carefully observed here that Paul is not speaking of the chief heads of Gospel doctrine and the proper dogmas of faith, as if he had preached one thing among the Corinthians and another among others. The subject of Gospel preaching is Jesus Christ, who is one and the same yesterday, today, and forever; so the teaching of faith remains always the same, which he himself set out under definite heads when he commanded that repentance and the remission of sins be preached in his name. Nor were the apostles ever permitted to change the teaching at their own or others' pleasure, to invent new articles from their own brains, or to conceal anything of what they had received from Christ. For his command is: Teach them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you. Therefore Paul says this about the manner and form of teaching in order to rebuke the false apostles, who, though they wished to be regarded as heralds of Christ and of his Gospel, were by no means concerned to set out clearly the proper and genuine heads of the Christian faith. Instead, by empty display of words, they poured into the ears of those who had hardly yet tasted the first elements of religion certain lofty and marvellous things. Since the same Christ and the same Gospel teaching are milk for infants or the weak in faith, but solid food for adults who have advanced further, Paul by the term milk understands a rude and simple manner of teaching, such as is contained in the catechisms, which briefly and clearly hand down the chief heads of religion and salvation, from which many other things are derived that can serve to illustrate and confirm them for those who have been fittingly instructed in these first things. By solid food he means that fuller and more demanding teaching by which the whole man is claimed for God in obedience of faith, and the very practice of faith and Christian religion is required, and all are urged to aspire to heavenly things alone, leaving earthly things behind. In this part many things about the use and abrogation of the law, about the powers of man, about election, predestination, the state of the future age, and similar matters can be said admirably and not without profit to those who are established in the faith, provided they are treated soberly and modestly. But there is no need for these to be pressed upon the untrained and those of less ability, since the true and simple knowledge of Jesus Christ is abundantly sufficient for their salvation. So, as we said a little earlier, although the same Christ, the same way of human salvation, and the same dogmas of faith are taught on both sides, there is nevertheless some difference in the manner and form of teaching, and the same manner does not suit everyone. Therefore (Paul says), the fact that I have hitherto followed that lowly and humble manner of speaking is not due to my laziness or malice, but this whole matter must be charged to your fault, if indeed you think there is some sin in it. For you could not bear my dealing with you otherwise, and even now you cannot, although you seem to yourselves to be wise above all others, etc.

units.la: Cæterum vt ista magis nostræ institutioni seruiant, præstat tam Corinthios quam Paulum propius inspicere. Corinthi enim hunc sesquianno[?] docuisse alibi diximus, neque eum in aliquo loco tam diu constitisse legimus, eò quòd per spiritum subinde ad alias gentes & vrbes vocaretur. Nihil autem illum celauisse eorum, quæ ad fidei institutionem faciunt, ex Dei mandato facile colligi poterat, qui eum loqui & non tacere iusserat. Sed & signa Apostoli inter illos non vulgaria edita fuerant cum multa patientia, miraculis & prodigijs. Successerat illi mox Apollo, vir scripturarum peritissimus & dicendi facultate præ aliis instructus, qui in confutandis Iudæis (vt Lucas scribit) diligentissimus erat, & fidelis agricolæ instar à Paulo plantatam doctrinam sedula admonitionum, correptionum & consolationum irrigatione fouebat. Quid vero omnibus hisce tanti viri profecerunt? Ecce adhuc in Christi cognitione infantes sunt, imo adhuc carnales dici merentur, eò quòd carnis sapientiæ atq; affectibus plus nimioediti, synceram de Christo crucifixo doctrinam ferre non possent. Est hoc memorabile exemplum, quo admonemur, quàm fœda & horribilis sit nostræ naturæ corruptio, & quàm turpiter fallantur, qui iam se satis instructos putant, & doctrinam de Christo & fidei nostræ fundamentis diligentiorem fastidiunt. Solet his ferè idem quod pueris confidentioribus accidere, qui in scholis ad classes altiores aspirant, cùm Grammaticæ præcepta nondum calleant. Hi ferè quæ ignorant, tanquam ijs minimè opus sit, superbè fastidiunt, & cùm coætaneis suis doctiores videri velint, suam ignorantiam tandem turpissimè produnt. Hoc ipsum Corinthijs nostris accidisse videmus. Voluerunt hi præ aliis ecclesijs eminere, & Paulum nimis insolenter contempserunt, quasi eius doctrinam iam pridem devorassent atq; concoxissent. Sed quid audiunt? Se nimirum infantes in Christo & carnales adhuc esse, qui eorum nondum capaces sint, quæ ad pleniorem salutis cognitionem imprimis sunt necessaria. Est hæc communis omnium fors, qui in fidei & salutis negotio superbiunt. Exempla hodie quotidiana occurrunt in doctoribus Seraphicis & illuminatis, qui cùm clauem scientiæ penes se solos esse putent, sæpe à mulierculis, pueris, agricolis, & opificibus vilissimis vincuntur, si cum illis de fide & religione disputationem suscipiant. Idem in pharisæis etiam nostri seculi cernitur, qui ferè se mortalium miserrimos esse sentiunt, si quæ grauior tentatio ipsorum conscientias exagitat, cùm interim inuicta fidei constantia aduersus omnes terrores peccati & mortis insurgant atque triumphent, quos illi vix hominum loco habere consueuerunt. Debent ista nos ad humilitatis & modestiæ studium excitare, vt Christo verè insiti malitia quidem pueri simus, fide autem quotidie crescamus & proficiamus.
units.tr: But so that these things may serve our instruction more closely, it is worth looking more carefully at both the Corinthians and Paul. As we have said elsewhere, Paul taught at Corinth for a year and a half, and we read that he did not stay so long in any other place, because the Spirit kept calling him on to other nations and cities. It could easily be gathered from God's command, which had bidden him speak and not keep silent, that he had concealed nothing that pertains to the instruction of faith. The Apostle also performed remarkable signs among them, with great patience, miracles and wonders. Soon after him came Apollos, a man most skilled in the Scriptures and better equipped than others in the gift of speech, who (as Luke writes) was very diligent in refuting the Jews, and who, like a faithful farmer, watered the doctrine Paul had planted with careful admonitions, rebukes and consolations. Yet what did all these things, and so great a man, achieve? Look, they are still infants in the knowledge of Christ; indeed they still deserve to be called carnal, because, being overly devoted to the wisdom and passions of the flesh, they could not bear the pure doctrine of Christ crucified. This is a memorable example, by which we are warned how foul and dreadful the corruption of our nature is, and how shamefully they are deceived who already think themselves sufficiently instructed and look down on the more careful teaching about Christ and the foundations of our faith. This usually happens to over-confident boys in schools who press on to the higher classes before they have mastered the rules of grammar. They proudly disdain what they do not know, as if they had no need of it, and wishing to seem more learned than their fellows, they finally expose their ignorance most disgracefully. We see this very thing happening to our Corinthians. They wished to stand out above other congregations, and they rather insolently despised Paul, as if they had long since devoured and digested his teaching. But what do they hear? That they are indeed infants in Christ and still carnal, not yet capable of the things most necessary for fuller knowledge of salvation. This is the common lot of all who take pride in the business of faith and salvation. Daily examples meet us today among the Seraphic teachers and the illuminati, who, thinking the key of knowledge is in their hands alone, are often bested by old women, boys, farmers and the very lowliest workmen, when they take up a dispute with them about faith and religion. The same is seen among the Pharisees of our own age, who feel themselves to be among the most wretched of mortals if some heavier temptation troubles their consciences, whereas, by the invincible constancy of faith, others rise up against all the terrors of sin and death and triumph over them, men whom the Pharisees are used to scarcely counting as human. These things ought to stir us to a zeal for humility and modesty, so that, truly engrafted into Christ, we may be children in malice, but grow and advance daily in faith.

units.la: At non minori diligentia Pauli quoque exemplum considerari debet, qui Euangelij doctrinam non obiter & quasi aliud agens proposuit, sed diligenti auditorum quos habuit ratione habita, singulorum captui & ingenio, quoad hoc salua pietate fieri poterat, sese accommodauit. Et hoc illud est, quod in ecclesiæ suæ ministro siue Oeconomo Christus requirit, vt nimirum non fidelis modo, verumetiam prudens atq; circumspectus sit, vt familiæ sibi creditæ cibum aut dimensum suum opportuno tempore depromat. Quo etiam pertinet, quòd Apostolus Timotheum suum eiusmodi ministrum esse vult, qui verbum Dei ita secet, vt omnium institutioni & ædificationi seruiat. Neq; temere hoc loco infantium in Christo mentionem fieri putabimus. Nam si fidelium conditionem diligentius inspicias, eandem quæ infantium est, esse videbis. Vt hominis principium à generatione incipit: ita vt veri homines, id est, filij Dei simus, nos in Christo renasci oportet. Nisi enim (vt ille inquit) homo renatus fuerit, non potest videre regnum Dei. Deinde vt infantes recens nati non statim cibum solidiorem capiunt, sed aliquandiu lacte aluntur, donec cum ætate vires naturales augeantur, quæ cibos quoq; alios requirunt: Ita non omnes, qui iam Christiani & ecclesiæ membra facti sunt, ideo mox perfecti sunt, & plenam omnium eorum cognitionem habent, quæ ad Christianismum pertinent, imo multa illis quoq; adhuc absurda, multa impossibilia videntur, aut etiam superuacanea: cuius rei exemplum in Apostolis habemus, qui circa veram Christi & regni eius cognitionem tam diu hallucinati sunt, vt mirum videri possit, illos sub tanto præceptore & inter tot tamq; luculenta regni eius specimina tam parum profecisse. Ideo diligenti institutione à primis fundamentis opus est. Vt enim ædificium nunquam solidum & durabile erit, quod fundamento arenoso aut alias ob causas labili superstruitur: ita neq; eorum fides atq; religio diu consistet, qui in principijs fidei Christianæ non probè instituti fuerint. Vtilissimum ergo & imprimis necessarium ecclesiæ est catechizandi exercitium, neq; in eo ministros quantumuis eximios & ad maiora idoneos alicuius industriæ aut laboris pigere debet. Nam vt nemo architectū quantumuis ingeniosum & artis suæ peritum probauerit, qui circa parietum, fenestrarum, pinnarum & tecti ornatum totus occupetur, nihil interim de fundamento ædificij solicitus: sic parum vtiles ecclesiæ sunt doctores illi, qui apud eos solos, qui in fide maiores progressus fecerunt, de rebus sublimioribus disputant, & de ecclesia sua præ aliis exornanda cogitant, non autem eorum rationem habent aliquam, quos ab ipsis fundamentis instituere oportebat. Fuerunt in eo admodum diligentes olim Episcopi, & magna eorum authoritas fuit, qui in hac re fidelem ecclesiæ operam navarunt.
units.tr: Yet the example of Paul must also be considered with no less diligence. He did not set forth the doctrine of the gospel casually, as though he were doing something else, but, taking careful account of the hearers he had, he adapted himself to the capacity and temperament of each one, so far as this could be done without compromising godliness. This is exactly what Christ requires of the minister or steward of his church: that he be not only faithful but also prudent and watchful, so that he may dispense food, or the portion due to them, to the household entrusted to him at the proper time. To this also pertains the Apostle's wish that his Timothy be such a minister, one who rightly divides the word of God so that it serves the instruction and building up of all. Nor should we think that mention of infants in Christ is made here without reason. For if you examine more closely the condition of believers, you will see that it is the same as that of infants. As a human being's life begins with birth, so we must be born again in Christ so that we may be true human beings, that is, children of God. For unless a man (as he says) is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God. Then, just as newborn infants do not at once take more solid food, but are nourished for some time on milk, until with age their natural strength grows and seeks other foods too, so not all who have already become Christians and members of the church are at once perfect, or have a full understanding of all that pertains to Christianity. Indeed, many things still seem to them absurd, impossible, or even superfluous. We have an example of this in the Apostles, who wandered so long in their grasp of the true knowledge of Christ and his kingdom that it may seem strange they made so little progress under so great a teacher and amid so many clear signs of his kingdom. Therefore careful instruction from the first foundations is needed.
