For just as a building will never be solid and durable if it is raised upon sandy foundations or is otherwise unstable, so neither will the faith and religion of those stand firm for long who have not been properly taught the principles of the Christian faith. Therefore the exercise of catechizing is most useful and above all necessary for the church, and ministers, however outstanding and fit for greater tasks, ought not to shrink from any diligence or labour in it. For no one would approve of an architect, however clever and skilled in his art, who was wholly occupied with the decoration of walls, windows, battlements and roof, and meanwhile had no concern for the foundation of the building. Likewise those teachers are of little use to the church who discuss higher matters only among those who have made greater progress in faith, and who think about adorning their own church above others, but take no account of those whom they ought to have instructed from the very foundations. In this matter the bishops of old were very diligent, and they had great authority, who devoted faithful labour to the church in this business.

units.la: Posteris temporibus vniuersus catechizandi mos abolitus est, & in eius locum fabula hi-strionica successit, quam hodie Suffraganei non sine totius religionis Christianæ ludibrio agunt. Sistitur enim puer Suffraganeo, interrogatur an baptizatus sit, & quo nomine vocetur: & si bene res cedat, fortassis orationem dominicam & Symbolum, quod Apostolicum dicunt, recitare iubetur. Quo facto, charismate frons pueri inungitur, vincitur fascia, & alapa in maxillam accepta dimittitur. Hæc fabulæ illius summa est, quam tamen illi inter Sacramenta numerant, & plausibili confirmationis titulo venditant, quasi hac ratione cõfirmatiores in fide fiant, qui prius infantes erant in Christo, nec idonei adhuc, qui ad Christianæ ecclesiæ mysteria admitterentur. Debemus ineptijs istis communem illam ignorantiam, quæ omnes ordines ita peruasit, vt inter ipsos sacerdotes vix aliquis inuentus fuerit, qui primá fidei & religionis Christianæ rudimenta teneret. Sed vt propositá infantum parabola progrediamur, vt hi non omnes quoad corporis staturâ atq; vires eosdem progressus faciunt, etiamsi eadem cura & diligentia omnes alantur atq; educentur: Ita non eadem mensura fideles omnes proficiunt, sed magna inter eos donorum spiritus diuersitas est, & alij alijs longè superiores esse consueuerunt. At hic mansuetudine & longanimitate doctores instructos esse oportet, ne de illis facile desperent, quos ab alijs longius à tergo relictos esse vident. Vt enim parentes & fidæ nutrices maiori cura atq; diligentia eos pueros educant, quos natura imbecilliores fecit: ita illi quoq; quorundam tarditatem sua industria, & interdum pia indulgentia vincere debent, ne in desperationem eos coniciant, qui aliquando non pœnitenda ecclesiæ Christi membra fieri possunt, si cõmodè tractentur. Obseruauit hoc in Apostolis suis erudiendis Dominus, & multa lenitate eos tulit, quos ineptè nimis ad eundem lapidem subinde offendere videbat. Et iam moriturus, cum illos præ mæstitia ijs, quæ dicebantur, minus attendere videret, dicebat: Adhuc multa habeo quæ vobis dicam, sed non potestis portare modò. Quæ verba Pontificij extra illius institutum detorquent, quasi multa illos cælarit, quæ posteris demum tem-poribus per Patres & Concilia reuelari oportuerit. At nihil huius voluit Christus, sed infirmitatis & tristitiæ, qua tunc grauabantur rationem habuit, simul vero Spiritum sanctum promisit, qui omnia ipsis in mentem reuocare debuit, quorum tunc non meminerant. Nihil ergo nouum & prius inauditum, sed plenam & perfectam eorum, quæ sæpe nequicquam audiuerant, declarationem expectare debuerunt. Et quod Christus fecit, hoc ipsum Apostoli omnes non minori diligentia fecerunt, imprimis autem Paulus apud Corinthios suos obseruauit. Nam etsi non tardiores modo essent in percipiendis fidei dogmatibus, sed insuper immani propria sapientiæ fiducia turgerent, quæ ipsos sanioris doctrinæ contemptores faciebat, non tamen omnem de illis spem abijcit, sed fratres suos agnoscit, infantes in Christo dicit, qui in eodem adolescere possint, & nouo studio in illis educandis & cõfirmandis vtitur. Quam rationem si omnes teneant, qui ecclesijs seruiunt, haud dubiè plus interdum proficient, quàm sperare possint: quod olim Eliæ Prophetæ accidisse scimus, qui cùm se in docendo operam omnem lusisse putaret, audit septem millia virorum in Israele superesse, qui Deum verè colant, neq; vllis superstitionibus sese polluerint. Frequenter etiam fit, vt in medijs persecutionibus præter omnem expectationem Euangelij fructus sese proferat, qui prius ita in hominum mentibus latuit, vt omnino nullus videri potuerit: & subito viros fortes se præbeant, qui paulò ante vix infantes adhuc esse putabantur. Exemplo nobis sunt Nicodemus & Iosephus Arimathæus, qui cùm occulti discipuli, & fortasse Apostolis ipsis ignoti fuissent prius, postea omnibus alijs cessantibus gloriæ Christi fortissimi vindices fuerunt, & eum honorificè [?]cunarunt sepeliri, qui ab intimis negligebatur. Et huius generis multa nostro tempore non uno in loco facta esse constat. Habet enim incrementa sua semen Verbi, & tandem ad maiora idonei sunt, qui antea infantum instar indulgentius fuerunt tractandi.
units.tr: In later times the whole custom of catechizing was abolished, and in its place succeeded a theatrical farce, which today the suffragans perform, not without mockery of the whole Christian religion. For a boy is brought before the suffragan, and asked whether he has been baptized and what name he bears. If all goes well, he is perhaps told to recite the Lord's Prayer and the creed which they call the Apostles' Creed. After this, the boy's forehead is anointed with chrism, a band is tied around him, and he is dismissed after receiving a slap on the cheek. This is the sum of that play, which they nevertheless count among the sacraments and hawk under the attractive title of confirmation, as if by this means those who were previously infants in Christ and not yet fit to be admitted to the mysteries of the Christian church become more firmly established in the faith. We must attribute to these absurdities that general ignorance which has so pervaded all orders that among the priests themselves scarcely anyone has been found who knows the first rudiments of the faith and the Christian religion. But to return to the parable of infants that we proposed: just as not all children make the same progress in bodily stature and strength, even when all are nourished and brought up with the same care and diligence, so not all believers advance by the same measure, but there is great diversity of the gifts of the Spirit among them, and some are usually far superior to others. Therefore teachers ought to be instructed to show gentleness and patience, so that they do not easily despair of those whom they see left far behind the rest. For just as parents and faithful nurses bring up with greater care and diligence those children whom nature has made weaker, so teachers too ought to overcome the slowness of some by their industry and sometimes by pious indulgence, lest they cast into despair those who may at some time become members of the church of Christ, not to be regretted, if they are handled suitably. The Lord observed this in instructing his Apostles, and with great gentleness he bore with those whom he saw were too foolish to be stirred repeatedly by the same stone. And when he was about to die, seeing that they were paying less attention to what was being said because of their sorrow, he said: "I have yet many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now." The Papists twist these words away from their proper sense, as if he had hidden many things from them which had to be revealed only in later times through the Fathers and the Councils. But Christ intended nothing of this kind; rather he took account of the weakness and sadness by which they were then burdened, and at the same time promised the Holy Spirit, who was to bring back to their minds all that they then did not remember. Therefore they were to expect nothing new and previously unheard of, but a full and perfect declaration of those things which they had often heard in vain. And what Christ did, all the Apostles did with no less diligence, and Paul especially observed this among his Corinthians. For although they were not only slower in grasping the doctrines of faith, but also swelled with an immense confidence in their own wisdom, which made them despisers of sounder teaching, he nevertheless did not give up all hope of them. He calls his brothers and infants in Christ, who could still grow up in him, and uses a new zeal in nurturing and strengthening them. If all who serve the churches hold to this method, they will undoubtedly sometimes make more progress than they could hope for. We know this happened long ago to the prophet Elijah, who, when he thought he had spent all his effort in teaching, heard that seven thousand men remained in Israel who truly worshipped God and had not polluted themselves with any superstitions. It also often happens, in the midst of persecutions, that a harvest of the gospel appears beyond all expectation, a harvest that had been so hidden in people's minds that it could not be seen at all, and suddenly men appear who a little before were thought scarcely more than infants. Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea are examples for us: though they had been secret disciples, and perhaps unknown even to the Apostles themselves before, afterwards, when all the others had withdrawn, they became the most courageous defenders of Christ's glory, and gave honourable burial to him who had been neglected by his intimates. And it is evident that many things of this kind have happened in our own time in more than one place. For the seed of the Word has its own growth, and those who were earlier to be treated with more indulgence, like infants, are at last fit for greater things.

units.la: At hic meminisse oportet, Pauli exemplum & quaecunq, de hoc dicta sunt hucusque, nequa-quam illorum ignauiæ patrocinari, qui hoc praetextu veritate dissimulant, & quamuis nonnulla non male doceant, multa tamen admiscent, quibus religio vera adulteratur, cultus Dei verus impeditur, & in superstitionibus detinentur, qui ex illis emergere cupiunt. Est horum magnus numerus hodie inter Papistas, qui cum veritatem probe norint, eam tamen aperte profiteri nolunt, ne à sacerdotijs pinguioribus deijciantur: interim tamen ne omnino nihil agere videantur, ad multa conniuent, quaedam etiam recte docent, de quibus non adeo magna est controuersia. At si illos vrgeas, vt manum ferio aratro admoueant, veritatis doctrinam liberè prædicent, & manifestos abusus atq; superstitiones è medio tollant, ecclesias denique fidei suæ commissas à sordibus Papisticis repurgent, tunc ad iflam responsionem recurrunt, quod lactis potu suos adhuc opus habere dicunt, neq; eam nunc esse temporum & locorum in quibus degunt, conditionem, vt maius quid moueri aut tentari possit. Ita vero sibijpsis delitias faciunt, dum non vno scelere sese inuoluunt. Nam primò magnam fere iniuriam faciunt suis hominibus & infantes manere cogunt vel inuitos, qui per quaeuis pericula elu&ari mallent, & progressus quotidie maiores facere. Imò infantes esse dicunt eos, qui se procul dubio viros praberent, modò ipsi non pueris & mulierculis essent meticulosiores. Deinde lactis nomine humanas traditiones, superstitiones manifestas & turpes abusus palliant, quae omnia venenum & toxica potius dici merebantur, cum multorum animæ his à Deo auocentur, & in erroribus detineantur, qui ipsis tandem exitij causa sunt. Vt ergo laudem merentur, qui prudenter & modestè panem vitæ in domo Domini dispensant: ita diligenter cauendum est, ne ignauiæ & perfidiæ patrocinium quæramus, & ne qui letalia pharmaca rerum imperitis propinent, dum lacte illos alere volunt.
units.tr: But we must remember that Paul's example, and everything said so far on this point, by no means lends support to the laziness of those who use this pretext to conceal the truth. Although some of them teach a few things correctly, they mix in much else by which true religion is corrupted, the true worship of God is hindered, and those who want to escape from superstitions are kept in them. Today there is a large number of such people among the Papists. Although they know the truth well, they are unwilling to profess it openly, lest they be cast out of their fat benefices. Meanwhile, so that they do not seem to do nothing at all, they connive at many things and teach some things correctly, about which there is not much controversy. But if you press them to put their hand to the plough, to preach the teaching of the truth freely, to remove the manifest abuses and superstitions from the midst, and finally to cleanse the churches committed to their faith of Papist filth, then they fall back on that answer: that their people still need milk, and that the present condition of the times and places in which they live is not such that anything greater can be attempted. But in this way they indulge themselves, since they entangle themselves in more than one crime. First, they do a great wrong to their people, forcing the infants to remain, even against their will, when they would rather be trained through any dangers and make greater progress every day. Indeed, they call infants those who would undoubtedly show themselves to be men, were they not more timid than boys and old women. Next, in the name of milk they cover up human traditions, manifest superstitions and shameful abuses, all of which deserve to be called poison and venom rather, since the souls of many are turned away from God by these things and kept in errors, which in the end become the cause of their ruin. Therefore, just as those deserve praise who prudently and modestly dispense the bread of life in the house of the Lord, so we must take careful heed that we do not seek a defence for laziness and faithlessness, and that those who want to feed them with milk do not hand deadly drugs to the inexperienced.

units.la: Porrò cum eò iam processisset Corinthiorum confidentia, vt non satis esset ipsis in mentem reuocauisse quales aliquando fuissent, propius illos ferit Apostolus, & quales etiam nunc sint indicat. Adhuc (inquit) carnales estis. Quasi diceret: Ferri poterat, vos olim carni plus satis dedi-tos fuisse, quando aut nulla aut perquam exigua in vobis Christi cognitio fuit. At quòd nunc quoq; tales sitis, postquam Euangelium vobis prædicatum est, & vos præ aliis eminere vultis, ad demum nulla ratione potest excusari. Ne quid verò ex priuato affectu durius loqui videretur, argumentum ab effectis aut proprijs ipsorum operibus subijcit, quae omnium efficacissima est aliquem conuincendi ratio. Sic enim ait: Cum enim in vobis sint æmulatio, & contentio, & dissidia, nonne carnales estis, & secundum hominem incedit is? Id est, ea facitis, quae ij facere solent, qui nihil quàm homines sunt, neq; adhuc Dei Spiritu ducuntur, qui bullientes carnis affectus in ipsis reflinguat. Est argumentum hoc evidentissimum. Nam vt ad Galat. scribit Paulus, carnis opera sunt, adulterium, fornicatio, impuritas, proteruia, idololatria, veneficia, inimicitiæ, lites, æmulationes, iræ, contentiones, dissidia, hæreses, inuidia, cædes, ebrietates, comessationes, & his similia. Et cum multa iflorum, vel etiam omnia Corinthijs exprobrare posset, eorum tamè solum meminit, quibus ecclesiæ vnitas scindebatur. Etenim vehementes in illis esse oportebat carnis affectus, cum his abrepti ecclesiam turbarent, cuius vnitas Christo maximè probatur, & à qua omnium salus maiori ex parte dependet. Ne quid tamen negarent, apertius adhuc eos arguit & conuincit, addens: Etenim cùm quidam dicat, Ego quidem sum Pauli: alter verò, Ego sum Apollo: nonne carnales estis? Factiones (inquit) & dissidia inter vos esse manifestum est, cùm diuersos doctores atq; magistros profiteamini. Atqui hæc absque contentionibus & rixis esse non possunt. Vnde autem hæ procedunt? Nimirum ex æmulatione, cuius causa est ambitio & inanis gloriæ cupiditas, quam proprijssimum carnis opus, adeoq; peccati omnis principium esse constat. Ita verò proprijs suorum operum indicijs eorum cristas reprimit, qui se omnes alios procul à tergo reliquisse sibijpsis persuadebant.
units.tr: Furthermore, since the boldness of the Corinthians had gone so far that it was not enough for him to remind them what they had once been, the Apostle strikes them more closely and points out what they still are. "Still," he says, "you are carnal." As if he were saying: It could be borne that you were once given over to the flesh far too much, when there was either no knowledge of Christ among you or very little. But that you are still such, now that the gospel has been preached to you and you want to stand out above others, can in no way be excused. Lest he seem to speak too harshly out of private feeling, he brings forward an argument from its effects, that is, from their own works, which is the most effective way of convicting anyone. For he says: "For since there is among you jealousy, and strife, and divisions, are you not carnal, and do you not walk according to man?" That is, you do the things that those do who are nothing but men, and who are not yet led by the Spirit of God, who would quench the boiling passions of the flesh within them. This argument is most evident. For, as Paul writes to the Galatians, the works of the flesh are adultery, fornication, uncleanness, wantonness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, emulations, wraths, contentions, divisions, heresies, envy, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. And although he could have reproached the Corinthians with many of these, or even with all of them, he mentions only those by which the unity of the Church was torn apart. For the passions of the flesh must have been strong in them, since, carried away by these, they were disturbing the Church, whose unity is most pleasing to Christ and on which the salvation of all largely depends. Lest they still deny it, he convicts and refutes them more openly, adding: "For when one says, 'I indeed am of Paul,' and another, 'I am of Apollos,' are you not carnal?" Factions and divisions, he says, are plainly among you, since you profess different teachers and masters. But these cannot exist without contentions and quarrels. Whence do they arise? Assuredly from jealousy, whose cause is ambition and the desire for empty glory, which is clearly the very work of the flesh and the beginning of all sin. In this way, by the clear signs of their own works, he humbles the pride of those who persuaded themselves that they had left all others far behind.

units.la: At nos hinc generalem doctrinam petere debemus, Carnis desideria & opera obstare nobis, quo minus in caelestis sapientiae cognitione & toto salutis aeternæ negotio progressus dignos facia-mus. mus. Pugnant enim inter se caro & Spiritus, neque fieri potest, ut hic nos vere illuminet atque regeneret, quoad illam in nobis patimur dominari. Docet hoc ipsum Christus, quando semen ver-bi iam animis conceptum per huius seculi curas & opum studium suffocari dicit. Et idem Judaeo-rum scribas non posse credere testatur, eo quod posthabita Dei gloria privatam quaerant. Et est hic multa observatione dignum, quod ea nominat Apostolus, quae plerisque leuicula & nullius momenti esse videntur. Nam si haec Corinthios carnales & ad audiendam Euangelii doctrinam ineptos fecerunt, quid de illis sentiendum est, qui longe atrocioribus flagitijs toti occupantur? Habes igitur hoc loco quid illis respondeas, qui Euangelii praedicationem hodie suspectam habent, quod ex ea pauci in melius proficiant. Atqui hoc non Euangelii vitio fit, sed eorum, qui aures & animos carnalibus desiderijs occupatos afferunt. Quod si vero qui hic laborant, Verbum nullo cum fructu audiunt, quanto minus ad praedicandum idonei erunt, qui carni student, & toti apertis flagitijs atque sceleribus serviunt. Quid ergo de toto Papatu iudicabimus, in quo caput simul & membra hoc unum agere constat, ut contentionibus, dissidijs, sectis, imo bellis apertis totus orbis turbetur? Ita enim illi crescunt, & principum discordia ad regnum suum stabiliendum abutuntur. Imo si in Monachorum claustra penetres, qui spiritualissimi haberi volunt, illic aemulatione, invidia, odio, contentionibus omnes inter se scindi & contabescere videbis.
units.tr: But from this we ought to draw a general doctrine: that the desires and works of the flesh stand in our way, so that we do not make progress worthy of the knowledge of heavenly wisdom and of the whole business of eternal salvation. For the flesh and the Spirit are at war with each other, and it cannot happen that the Spirit truly enlightens and regenerates us as long as we allow the flesh to rule in us. Christ himself teaches this, when he says that the seed of the word, already received in the minds of men, is choked by the cares of this age and the pursuit of riches. And he likewise testifies that the scribes of the Jews cannot believe, because, having set aside the glory of God, they seek their own private glory. And it is worth close attention here that the Apostle names those things which seem to most people very trivial and of no weight. For if these things made the Corinthians carnal and unfit to hear the teaching of the gospel, what must we think of those who are wholly occupied with far more atrocious crimes? Here you have, therefore, what to answer to those who today regard the preaching of the gospel with suspicion, because so few improve as a result of it. Yet this is not the fault of the gospel, but of those who bring ears and minds occupied with carnal desires. But if those who labour here hear the Word to no profit, how much less fit will they be to preach who serve the flesh and are wholly given over to open wickedness and crimes? What then shall we judge of the whole Papacy, in which it is clear that head and members alike do this one thing: to disturb the whole world with contentions, divisions, sects, and even open wars? For in this way they grow, and they abuse the discord of princes to establish their own kingdom. Indeed, if you enter the cloisters of the monks, who want to be thought the most spiritual, you will see them all torn apart and wasting away with rivalry, envy, hatred, and contentions among themselves.

units.la: Admonet praeterea locus iste, quibus gradibus ad summam ecclesiae turbationem perveniatur. Primus est aemulatio, quam ex ambitione nasci diximus. Est is dolor animi, quem ex alterius commodis concipimus. Pugnat ergo cum charitatis ingenio, quae ut omnibus bene esse cupit, ita aliorum commodis gaudet. Gravius tamen aemulatione peccant, qui huic locum dant in iis, quae ad Dei cultum & ecclesiae conservationem pertinent. Nam & Deum intra animos suos iniustitiae accusant, & ecclesiam turbant atque scindunt, quo scelere Deus maxime offenditur. Nam ab aemulatione ad contentiones proceditur, quas de rebus levissimis maximas excitant, quorum animi invidia ringuntur[?]. Sequuntur hinc factiones, quibus inter se aperte scinduntur, qui unum in Christo esse debebant. Discant ergo primum gradum cavere, qui ulterius progredi nolunt. Et ministri quidem ecclesiarum uni Christo discipulos colligant: huic autem indivulse[?] adhaereant quicunq; Euangelii doctrinam profitentur, ut in illo tandem in viros perfectos adolescant, & in caelis ad illius mensam divino illo nectare & ambrosia aeternum fruantur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: This passage also warns us of the steps by which the greatest disturbance of the Church is reached. The first is jealousy, which we said arises from ambition. It is a grief of the mind that we conceive from another's advantages. It therefore fights against the nature of charity, which, while it wishes well to all, also rejoices in the advantages of others. Yet they sin more gravely through jealousy who give it room in matters that concern the worship of God and the preservation of the Church. For they accuse God of injustice within their own minds, and they disturb and tear apart the Church, a crime by which God is especially offended. For from jealousy one proceeds to contentions, which they stir up over the most trivial matters, their minds being gnawed by envy. From these follow factions, by which those who ought to be one in Christ are openly torn apart. Let those, then, who do not wish to go further learn to guard against the first step. Ministers of the churches gather disciples to Christ alone, and whoever professes the teaching of the gospel should cling inseparably to him, so that in him they may at last grow into perfect men, and in heaven, at his table, enjoy eternally that divine nectar and ambrosia. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XIII.
units.tr: Homily 13.

units.la: Quis igitur est Paulus? quis autem Apollos, nisi ministri per quos credidistis, & ut cuique Dominus dedit: Ego plantavi, Apollos rigavit: sed Deus dedit incrementum. Itaque neque is qui plantat, est aliquid, neque is qui rigat: sed Deus, qui dat incrementum. Is vero qui plantat, & is qui rigat, unum sunt: Unusquisque vero suam mercedem accipiet secundum suum laborem. Etenim Dei sumus cooperarii, Dei arvum, Dei aedificatio estis.
units.tr: Who then is Paul? And who is Apollos? Only ministers through whom you believed, and each as the Lord gave to him. I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase. So neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God, who gives the increase. He who plants and he who waters are one; yet each will receive his own reward according to his own labour. For we are God's fellow workers; you are God's field, God's building.

units.la: Quoniam ad ecclesiae, & fidei aut religionis conservationem nihil utilius & magis necessarium est, quam credentium consensio atque concordia, Paulus non temere tam multis hoc agit, ut quae inter Corinthios glisce bant[?] dissidia & factiones componat. Causae istarum erant, partim doctorum quorundam ambitio, qui suae potius gloriae quam credentium saluti studebant: partim eorum stoliditas, qui in ostentatoribus illis humanae sapientiae & eloquentiae splendorem sic admirabantur, ut ab illis solis penderent, imo propter illos in sectas scinderentur. Ideo utrosque graviter corripuit, & nuper ostendit, ipsos factionibus illis hucusq; impeditos fuisse, ut in Euangelii doctrina non potuerint dignos progressus facere, neque habere eos quo glorientur aut superbiant, cum hoc uno argumento satis constet, ipsos adhuc carni nimium addictos esse. His commodè subijcit, quæ modò recitauimus, quibus de ministerio ecclesiastico apertius disserit, & docet, quo loco habendi sint ministri, ne ipsis plus aut minus, quàm par est, tribuamus: in quem finem item à Deo sint ordinati, & quis tam ipsis quàm auditoribus studij & laboris sui universi scopus esse debeat.
units.tr: Since nothing is more useful or necessary for the preservation of the Church and of the faith or religion than the agreement and harmony of believers, Paul does not undertake, without good reason, to settle the quarrels and factions that were growing up among the Corinthians. Their causes were partly the ambition of certain teachers, who sought their own glory rather than the salvation of believers, and partly the stupidity of those who so admired the splendour of human wisdom and eloquence in those showy men that they depended on them alone, and even split into sects on their account. So he rebuked both groups severely, and he now shows that they had been held back by these factions until now, so that they could not make worthy progress in the teaching of the Gospel, nor have anything to boast of or be proud of. This one fact is enough to show that they were still too much given over to the flesh. He fittingly adds to what we have just recited, and speaks more openly about the ecclesiastical ministry. He teaches what place ministers should be given, so that we attribute to them neither more nor less than is right; to what end they are likewise ordained by God; and what should be the aim of all their study and labour, both theirs and their hearers'.

units.la: Et primò quidem summam huius doctrinæ proponit, quæ est, Verbi præcones esse ministros Dei, quorum labore & prædicatione homines ad fidem Christi adducantur. Id verò non simpliciter nuda dicendi forma enuntiat: sed cùm nuper factionum studia illis iterum exprobrauisset, nunc non sine indignationis specie subijcit: Quis igitur est Paulus? quis autem Apollos, nisi ministri per quos credidistis? ita verò docet, id quod ab ipsis fiebat, nullo modo posse aut debere ferri in ecclesia. Prudenter verò non doctorum illorum, qui omnis mali authores erant, nomina exagitat, ne horum admiratores magis irritet, sed seipsum & Apollo producit, quos inter se coniunctissimos esse omnes sciebant, & quorum authoritatem alteri illi labefactare conabantur. Et ut aliàs diximus, credibile est non defuisse pios aliquos, qui contendendi studio & zelo non malo abrepti, contra ostentatores illos & ardeliones Pauli & Apollos authoritatem iactarent. Ut ergo simul omnes uno quasi verbo compescat, sic loquitur quasi diceret: Quid opus est vel meum vel Apollos nomen contra quenquam producere, & his abuti ad fovenda partium studia? Nec enim nostra nobis gloria curæ est, nisi quatenus ea Christo & ecclesiæ commodare potest. Et quis ego sum, qui hoc merear, ut mei potius quàm Christi discipuli dicamini[?]? Quis item Apollos, ut qui Christo debetur honor, in illum transferatur? Certè non alij, quàm ministri sumus, quorum opera & ministerio Deus uti dignatus est, ut vos à superstitionibus & impietate ad fidem Filij sui IESV CHRISTI converteret. Itaque cùm ministri modò simus, minimè convenit, ut nobis addicti sitis, quin potius in Deum respicere debetis, cuius nomine & mandato Evangelium passim prædicamus. Veruntamen ne quis ex eo, quòd Corinthios ipsorum ministerio in fide institutos esse dixit, novam sibi efferendi aut de doctoribus suis gloriandi occasionem arriperet, mox addit: Et ut cuique Dominus dedit. Quod perinde est ac si diceret: Non nos fidei vestræ sumus authores, neque in nostro arbitrio fuit hanc vobis dare, sed Dei opus istud omne est, qui fidei mensuram, prout ipsi visum est, inter vos distribuit. Et videtur Paulus diversitatis & graduum, qui inter credentes sunt, consultò meminisse, ut vel ex his colligant, nihil hic humana industria aut labore factum esse, sed negotium hoc omne uni Deo debere transcribi, qui ut in aliis donis, sic etiam in fide & Filij sui cognitione certo iudicio atque mensura utitur. Convenit cum Paulinis istis, quod Ioannes Baptista fecit. Cùm enim hunc per Legatos suos Hierosolymitani præsules interrogarent, num ipse esset Propheta ille magnus & promissus populi servator, constantissimè id negauit, & se vocem illam clamantis in deserto esse testatus est, quæ (ut olim à prophetis prædictum fuit) populum per pœnitentiæ prædicationem ad Messiam excipiendum præparare debeat. Idem cùm discipulos non sine acerba æmulatione de populi ad Christum confluentis concursu querentes audiret, simili cum stomacho[?] illis respondit: Vos ipsi mihi testes estis, quòd dixerim: Non sum ego ille Christus, sed missus sum ante eum. Qui habet sponsam sponsus est, &c. Item: Illum oportet crescere, me autem minui. cap.
units.tr: And first he sets out the sum of this teaching, which is that the heralds of the Word are God's ministers, through whose labour and preaching men are brought to faith in Christ. He does not state this as a bare form of words. Having just reproached them for their partisan zeal, he now adds, not without a show of indignation: Who then is Paul? And who is Apollos? Only ministers through whom you believed. In this way he teaches that what they were doing could in no way be tolerated or allowed in the Church. Wisely, he does not attack the names of those teachers who were the authors of all the trouble, lest he provoke their admirers the more; instead he brings forward himself and Apollos, whom everyone knew to be closely united, and whose authority the others were trying to undermine. As we have said elsewhere, it is likely that there were some godly people, carried away by a zeal for contention that was not wicked, who boasted of the authority of Paul and Apollos against those showy and restless men. So, to silence them all with a single word, he speaks as if to say: What need is there to put forward either my name or Apollos' against anyone, and to misuse them to foster party spirit? For our own glory is of no concern to us, except insofar as it can serve Christ and the Church. And who am I, that I should deserve to be called the disciples of me rather than of Christ? Likewise, who is Apollos, that the honour due to Christ should be transferred to him? Surely we are no more than ministers, whose work and ministry God has deigned to use, so that he might turn you from superstitions and impiety to faith in his Son JESUS CHRIST. So, since we are only ministers, it is by no means fitting that you should be devoted to us; rather you ought to look to God, in whose name and by whose command we preach the Gospel everywhere. But lest anyone, because he said that the Corinthians had been instructed in the faith through their ministers, should seize on this as a new occasion to exalt himself or to boast about their teachers, he immediately adds: And each as the Lord gave to him. This is just as if he were saying: We are not the authors of your faith, nor was it in our power to give it to you; it is all God's work, who distributes the measure of faith among you as he pleases. Paul seems to have deliberately mentioned the variety and the degrees that exist among believers, so that from these facts people may conclude that nothing here was done by human effort or labour, but that this whole business must be ascribed to God alone, who, as in other gifts, so also in faith and in the knowledge of his Son, uses a certain judgement and measure. What John the Baptist did agrees with these words of Paul. When the bishops of Jerusalem sent envoys to ask him whether he himself was that great Prophet and the promised saviour of the people, he firmly denied it, and testified that he was the voice of one crying in the wilderness, which (as was foretold long ago by the prophets) ought to prepare the people to receive the Messiah through the preaching of repentance. When he heard his disciples complaining, not without bitter rivalry, about the crowd flocking to Christ, he answered them with similar indignation: You yourselves are my witnesses that I said: I am not that Christ, but I am sent before him. He who has the bride is the bridegroom, etc. Likewise: He must increase, but I must decrease. chap.

units.la: Continet autem locus iste generaleam doctrinam, quid de omnibus sentire debeamus, qui unquam Deo servierunt in tradenda veritatis doctrina & hominibus ad fidem convertendis. Habeantur illi ministrorum loco, neque putemus, nos illis aliquam iniuriam facere, si eos non altius in gradum aliquem sublimiorem evehamus. Est enim hæc maxima hominis gloria, qua maior aut præstantior nulla illi obtingere potest. Præclarum multis videtur, si princeps aliquis aut Rex ipsos in aulam suam recipiat, ubi aut inter milites & corporis regij custodes numerentur, aut in canes & accipitres imperium habeant, aut in consiliariorum ordinem admissi & aureis (ut aiunt) compedibus vincti servitutem miserrimam serviant. At quantò maior dignitas censeri debet, CHRISTI IESV servum censeri, qui Rex regum est & Dominus dominantium? & qui nostra opera in illis servandis utitur, quos sanguinis sui pretio acquisiuit? Qui ergo tales olim fuisse fatentur Divos cœlites, ij sanè perquàm magnificè de illis sentiunt. Interea autem etiam atque etiam caveri debet, ne ipsis acceptum feramus, si quid eximium in mulin multorum aliorum salutem fecerunt: sed tunc illud omne Deo transcribi debet, secundum illud Christi: Nemo venit ad me, nisi Pater meus traxerit eum. Væhementer ergo errant posteri & nimij Divorum coelitum cultores, qui illos salutis suae authores, aut saltem Mediatores & aduocatos suos apud Deum esse sibi persuadent, ideoque illos in periculis inuocant, ijsdem vota faciunt, templa & aras aedificant. Isti enim, dum Divos altius euehunt, & apud eos quaerere docent quae solius Dei sunt, eosdem gloria praecipua spoliant. Nam ex Dei servis, quantum in ipsis est, Dei aemulos & aduersarios faciunt, perinde ac si quis de Rege bene merito & ob id prae aliis aulicis honoribus & dignitatibus ornatum, praeposterò & inconsulto studio in regium thronum collocare instituat. Viderunt hoc illi, cum adhuc in terris vitam degerent, & ideo indignissimè tulerunt, si qui de ipsis plus aequo senserunt, ut ex ministris Dei nouos (ut ita dicam) Deos facerent. Exempla huius rei admodum memorabilia in Petro & Ioanne, in Paulo item & Barnaba Apostolis Actorum liber continet. Et quis obsecro cogitet, eos nunc in coelis diuinos honores affectare, qui olim vitam & sanguinem proprium non alia de causa profude-runt, quàm ut uni Deo & Filio suo IESV CHRISTO gloriam suam vendicarent? At quid de Diuis dicere opus est, quando Angelos quoque nihil huius quaerere constat, quorum natura integrior & vires multò praestantiores sunt? Ioannes certè visionum magnificentia abrep-tus ad Angeli, qui Christi personam sustinebat, pedes prolapsus eum adorare voluit. Sed quid audit? Vide ne feceris (ait Angelus) conseruus tuus sum, & fratrum tuorum habentium testimo-nium IESV, Deum adora. Rectè ergo olim D. Augustinus in libro de vera Religione scripsit: Hoc etiam ipsos optimos Angelos, & excellentissima Dei ministeria, velle credamus, ut unum cum ipsis colamus Deum, cuius contemplatione beati sunt. Neque enim & nos videndo Angelos beati sumus, sed videndo Veritatem, qua etiam ipsos diligimus Angelos, & his congratulamur. Et mox: Honoramus eos charitate, non seruitute. Nec eis templa construimus. Nolunt enim se sic honorari à nobis, quia nos ipsos cum boni sumus, templa summi Dei esse nouerint. Rectè itaque scribitur, hominem ab angelo prohibitum ne se adoraret, sed unum Deum, sub quo ei esset & ille conseruus. Qui autem nos inuitant, ut SIBI seruiamus, & tanquam Deos colamus, similes sunt superbis hominibus, quibus si liceat, similiter coli volunt, &c. Quibus adde, quod idem pater alibi scripsit: Sicut impia superbia, sive hominum sive daemonum, sibi diuinos honores exhi-beri vel iubet vel cupit: ita pia humilitas vel hominum vel Angelorum sanctorum, haec sibi oblata recusavit, & cui deberetur ostendit. Haec ex Augustino recitare libuit propter eos, qui nos noui & haeretici dogmatis authores esse clamant, quod Divos neque inuocandos neque diuinis honoribus colendos esse docemus. Quod si quis obijciat, aliam esse angelorum, aliam Divorum conditionem, facilis erit responsio, utrosque Dei ministros esse, neq; diuersas esse utrorumq;[?] voluntates, cum tam hi quàm illi diuinae voluntati se accommodent, cuius expressum in sacris literis mandatum habemus, quod Deum unum & solum inuocare & colere iubet. Quod si illi negare velint, ipsa Dominicae orationis formula eos conuincet, qua rogamus: Fiat voluntas tua, quemadmodum in coelo sic etiam in terra. Idem ergo in coelo tam Angeli quàm Diui volunt, nisi eam illic quoq; studiorum dissimilitudinem & contentiones esse dicamus, quibus haec nostra vita in terris turbatur. Quod cum dictu absurdissimum sit, scripturas audiamus, quae Divos pro Dei ministris agnoscere docet, quibus ille usus est olim, ut superstitionibus deditum mundum ad verum cultum & fidei obedientiam reuocaret.
units.tr: This passage, moreover, contains a general teaching about what we ought to think of all those who have ever served God in delivering the doctrine of truth and in converting men to faith. Let them be held in the place of ministers, and let us not think that we do them any wrong if we do not raise them to some higher rank. For this is the greatest honour a man can have, and no greater or more excellent one can fall to him. It seems a splendid thing to many if some prince or king receives them into his court, where they are counted among the soldiers and bodyguards of his person, or have command over dogs and hawks, or, admitted to the order of counsellors and bound (as they say) with golden fetters, they serve a most wretched slavery. But how much greater dignity should be reckoned in being counted a servant of Christ Jesus, who is King of kings and Lord of lords, and who uses our labour in preserving those whom he has bought with the price of his own blood? Therefore those who admit that such men were once divine heavenly beings think very highly of them indeed. Meanwhile, care must be taken again and again that we do not credit them with anything remarkable they may have done for the salvation of many others, but that all of it must be ascribed to God, according to Christ's words: No one comes to me unless my Father draws him. So those later people, and excessive worshippers of the heavenly saints, are gravely mistaken, who persuade themselves that these men are the authors of their salvation, or at least their mediators and advocates with God, and therefore call on them in dangers, make vows to them, and build temples and altars to them. For while they raise the saints too high, and teach that what belongs to God alone should be sought from them, they strip God of his chief glory. For they make the servants of God, as far as they are able, rivals and adversaries of God, just as if someone were to set about, with misplaced and ill-considered zeal, to place on the royal throne a king who has deserved well and has therefore been adorned with dignities and honours above other courtiers. The saints themselves saw this while they still lived on earth, and so they took it very badly if anyone thought more of them than was right, so that they would make new gods (so to speak) out of the ministers of God. The Acts of the Apostles records remarkable examples of this in Peter and John, and likewise in Paul and Barnabas. And who, I ask, could imagine that those who once poured out their lives and their own blood for no other reason than to claim their glory for the one God and his Son Jesus Christ now claim divine honours in heaven? But why speak of the saints at all, when it is clear that the angels also seek nothing of this kind, although their nature is purer and their powers far greater? John, certainly, carried away by the magnificence of his visions, fell at the feet of an angel who bore the person of Christ, and wished to worship him. But what does he hear? See that you do not do so, said the angel; I am your fellow servant and of your brethren who hold the testimony of Jesus: worship God. Rightly, then, Augustine long ago wrote in his book On True Religion: We may believe that even the best angels and the most excellent ministries of God wish us to worship with them the one God, in whose contemplation they are blessed. For we are not blessed by seeing angels, but by seeing Truth, by which we also love the angels and rejoice with them. And soon after: We honour them with love, not with servitude. Nor do we build temples to them. For they do not wish to be honoured in this way by us, since they know that we, if we are good, are temples of the most high God. Rightly, then, it is written that a man was forbidden by an angel to worship him, but to worship the one God under whom the angel too was a fellow servant. Those, however, who invite us to serve them and to worship them as gods are like proud men, who, if they were permitted, would likewise wish to be worshipped, etc. To these add what the same father wrote elsewhere: Just as impious pride, whether of men or of demons, either commands or desires that divine honours be paid to itself, so holy humility, whether of men or of holy angels, has refused what was offered to itself and has shown to whom it is owed. It has pleased me to quote these words from Augustine for the sake of those who cry out that we are the authors of a new and heretical doctrine, because we teach that the saints are neither to be invoked nor to be worshipped with divine honours. But if anyone objects that the condition of angels is one thing and that of the saints another, the answer will be easy: both are ministers of God, and their wills are not different, since both accommodate themselves to the divine will, of which we have an explicit command in the Holy Scriptures, which bids us to invoke and worship the one and only God. If they wish to deny this, the very form of the Lord's Prayer will convict them, in which we ask: Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth. Therefore the same will is in heaven for angels and for saints, unless we say that there too is that same dissimilarity of pursuits and those same contentions by which our life here on earth is troubled. Since this is the most absurd thing to say, let us listen to the Scriptures, which teach us to acknowledge the saints as ministers of God, and which God once used to call the world, given over to superstitions, back to the true worship and obedience of faith.

units.la: Sed redeamus ad verba Pauli, qui quod in genere & paucis dixit, parabola illustrat. Et quàmuis de ministris omnibus loquatur, perstat tamen in eo quod coepit, ut sub sua & Apollo persona rem iam tractet. Ego plantaui (inquit) Apollos rigauit: sed Deus dedit incre-mentum. Itaque neque is qui plantat est aliquid, neque is qui rigat: sed Deus, qui dat incre-mentum. Plantauisse se dicit, quia primus Corinthi Euangelium praedicauit, & fidei semina iecit. Apollo autem rigationem tribuit, quia hic ipsi successerat, & studio magno in hoc fue-rat, ut Corinthiorum fidem foueret, utque hi maiores quotidie progressus facerent. Et sub duabus hisce speciebus omnes agriculturae partes comprehendit, quae plantationem, vel prætedunt [?], vel sequuntur: & per consequens, ea quoque omnia complectitur, quae ad ecclesiam ministerium pertinent. Itaque sensus est, eandem esse ministerij ecclesiastici rationem, quæ agri-culturæ est. Vt enim ad hanc agricolis omnino opus est, qui terram aratro scindant, plantent, sementem faciant, rigent, plantas & segetes aducent, ijdem tamen illi nequicquam hæc omnia faciunt, nisi cælitus detur incrementum: Ita ut ecclesiæ colligantur aut feruentur, ministros habere oportet, qui verbum prædicent, fidei semina in hominum cordibus iaciant, pietatem veram plantent, & eiusdem formam conferunt, & quod bene cœptum est ad finem suum perducant: at hi quoque omnes suo labore & industria nihil proficient, nisi Deus suo Spiritu in hominum animis agat, ut Verbum suum digne audiant, cordibus suis recondant, ut vivificatum suo tempore fructum ferat. Est parabola hæc evidens, & utraque eius pars quotidiana experientia probatur. Si enim ad fruges producendas agricolarum labor atque industria sufficeret, harum certè proventus quotannis uberrimus esset. At diversum fieri videmus, & non raro tunc quo-que agricolas spes anni fallit, quando illi in terra colenda plus solito seduli & assidui fuerunt. Oportet ergo ut ipse Dominus cœlos exaudiat ( ut Prophetæ verbis utamur ) & ita cœli terram, hæc autem fruges, & istæ rursus suos cultores exaudient, ne spe sua frustrentur. Idem in animorum cultura fieri, nemo negaverit, nisi qui quod omnibus notum est negare ausit. Etenim si hic quoque hominum in fide profectus à ministrorum aut præconum verbi diligentia pende-ret, omnes certè ad fidem converterentur, & omnes eundem in religione progressum facerent, qui Verbum audiunt. Sed longè aliud est videre, ut nimirum plerunque maior auditorum pars vel contumaciter verbo reluctetur, vel scelerata socordia illud ex animis effluere, aut pessimarum cupiditatum spinis suffocari sinat. Quod ergo de Lydia purpuraria dicitur, Deum cor eius aperuisse, ut iis attenderet, quæ à Paulo dicebantur, hoc ipsum omnibus fiat necesse est, qui Verbum cum aliquo fructu audire velint. Recte ergo Paulus, neque eum qui plantat, neque eum qui rigat, aliquid esse ait: si nimirum per se consideretur absque Spiritus sancti virtute, qui solus Verbi semen in animis nostris vivificare & fœcundum reddere potest. Usus autem istorum est, ut ne quid hominibus tribuamus in toto salutis negotio, sed nos Dei discipulos esse meminerimus, cui soli omnis gloria transcribi debeat. Quod unum si probe observetur, facilè obstabit, ne in ministrorum gratiam ecclesiæ unitatem scindamus, aut locum demus factionibus, quas homines ambitiosi pariunt. Deinde horum consideratio ad preces excitare solet, ut has cum Verbi studio coniungamus. Exempla harum in prophetis passim occurrunt, imprimis autem in illis diligens fuit Dauid, cuius hæ voces in Psalmis crebrò leguntur: Ostende mihi vias tuas Domine, assuefacito me semitis tuis. Retege oculos meos, ut videam admirabilem sapientiam, quæ recondita est in Lege tua. Da mihi, ut norim viam contestationum tuarum. Deduc me in viam decretorum tuorum Domine, & doceto me, ut retineam Legem tuam,&c.
units.tr: But let us return to the words of Paul, who illustrates in a parable what he has said in general and in few words. Although he speaks of all ministers, he keeps to the point he began, and now treats the matter under his own name and that of Apollos: "I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase. So neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God, who gives the increase" (1 Cor. 3:6-7). He says that he planted because he was the first to preach the Gospel at Corinth and sowed the seeds of faith. He assigns the watering to Apollos, because Apollos had succeeded him and had worked hard to nourish the faith of the Corinthians, so that they might make greater progress every day. Under these two images he includes all the parts of husbandry that either precede or follow planting, and consequently he also embraces everything that belongs to the ministry of the Church. The meaning, then, is that the ministry of the Church follows the same method as agriculture. Just as farmers, to be sure, must plough the land, plant, sow, water, and tend the plants and crops, yet all their work is in vain unless the increase is given from heaven, so, for churches to be gathered or preserved, there must be ministers who preach the Word, cast the seeds of faith into people's hearts, plant true godliness, bring it to its proper form, and carry what has been well begun to its end. Yet all these men accomplish nothing by their labour and diligence unless God works by his Spirit in people's minds, so that they hear his Word worthily, lay it up in their hearts, and let it, quickened, bear fruit in its season. This parable is plain, and both parts of it are confirmed by everyday experience. For if the labour and diligence of farmers were enough to produce crops, the harvests would surely be abundant every year. But we see the opposite happen, and often the farmers' hopes for the year are disappointed precisely when they have been more zealous and assiduous than usual in cultivating the land. It is necessary, therefore, that the Lord himself hear the heavens (to use the words of the prophet), and that the heavens hear the earth, and the earth the crops, and these in turn hear their cultivators, lest they be frustrated in their hope. No one will deny that the same happens in the cultivation of souls, unless he dares to deny what is known to everyone. For if progress in faith here also depended on the diligence of ministers or heralds of the Word, surely all would be converted to faith, and all who hear the Word would make the same progress in religion. But it is quite otherwise: for the greater part of the hearers, for the most part, either stubbornly resist the Word, or by wicked sloth let it slip from their minds, or allow it to be choked by the thorns of wicked desires. Therefore, what is said of Lydia, the seller of purple, that God opened her heart to attend to what Paul was saying, must necessarily happen to all who wish to hear the Word with any profit. Paul rightly says that neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, if indeed they are considered in themselves, apart from the power of the Holy Spirit, who alone can quicken the seed of the Word in our minds and make it fruitful. The purpose of this teaching is that we should attribute nothing to people in the whole business of salvation, but remember that we are disciples of God, to whom alone all glory must be given. If this one point is properly observed, it will easily prevent us from splitting the unity of the Church in favour of ministers, or giving room to the factions that ambitious men create. Next, the consideration of these things usually stirs us to prayer, so that we join prayer with the study of the Word. Examples of this occur everywhere in the prophets, and David in particular was diligent in it, whose words are often read in the Psalms: "Show me your ways, O Lord; teach me your paths. Open my eyes, that I may see the wonderful wisdom that is hidden in your law. Give me understanding, that I may know the way of your testimonies. Lead me in the path of your commandments, O Lord, and teach me, that I may keep your law," etc. (Ps. 25:4; 119:18, 27, 33-34).

units.la: Sed & ipse Christus interdum noctes totas in precibus transegit, quando populi ad ipsum audiendum concursum maiorem fieri videbat. Et laudatissimus est mos ille ecclesiæ, quo concionés sacræ à precibus inchoantur,& cum precibus finiuntur: quas qui negligunt, ij hoc ipso satis testantur, quàm malè de Dei verbo & toto Ecclesiæ ministerio sentiant. Postremò gratitudi-nem in animis nostris consideratio ista accendit. Ut enim pro uberè terræ proventu & frugibus non possunt non gratias agere Deo, qui ista ex eius benedictione sibi obtigisse sciunt, neque etiam illis facilè abutuntur,qui de hoc diligentius cogitant: Ita toti in gratiarum actionem effundi-lent,quicunque Dei beneficium, quo [?]s Verbum suum nobis revelat, rectè expendunt, & ijdem procul dubio curabunt,ne hanc gratiam ad carnis licentiam transferant.
units.tr: But Christ himself too sometimes spent whole nights in prayer, when he saw that a larger crowd was gathering to hear him. And that custom of the Church is most praiseworthy, by which sacred sermons begin with prayers and end with prayers. Those who neglect these prayers thereby sufficiently show how badly they think of the Word of God and of the whole ministry of the Church. Finally, this consideration kindles gratitude in our hearts. For just as people cannot but give thanks to God for the abundant produce of the land and the crops, knowing that these have come to them by his blessing, and just as those who think about this more carefully hardly abuse them, so all who rightly weigh the benefit of God, by which he reveals his Word to us, will be wholly poured out in thanksgiving; and without doubt they will take care not to turn this grace into licence for the flesh.

units.la: Cæterum præter ista de aliis quoque nos parabola hæc admonet, quæ ad ministerij ecclesiastici consideratiónem faciunt. Inter quæ observatu dignissimum est, quòd verbi prædicationem ecclesiæ omnino necessariam esse docemur, ut agriculturam quoq;. Posset quidem Deus, qui olim uno verbo plantas & omnis generis fructus produxit, etiam hodie nobis absque nostro labore,vel ex terra vel aliunde dare, quæ ad usum necessaria sunt. At quia Adamo dixit, In sudore vultus tui comedes panem tuum,& eidem ut terram quantùm vis malignam colat mandavit, eius ordi-nationi & mandato nos accommodemus necesse est. Nec enim ad eius providentiam aut omnipotentiam recurrere debemus, vt nostro otio consulatur, vbi quid fieri à nobis velit, satis constat. Idem ergo in animorum cultura nos obseruare conuenit. Vbi minimè negari debet, Deo nequaquam opus esse, vt in nobis instituendis vel verbi prædicatione, vel Sacramentis vtatur: Posset enim occulta Spiritus virtute & modo ineffabili nobiscum, incognito animos nostros erudire & innouare. Quia autem maledictio non minus nos quam terram premit, & proinde nos per verbi prædicationem & Sacramentorum vsum Deus ad vitam nouam & æternam coli vult, & nostrum ea in re fluidum requirit, temerarium & impium fuerit, ordinem ab illo institutum contemnere. Minimè ergo audiri debent, qui nobis nescio quem Spiritum & Verbum quoddam internum & non scriptum fingunt, quo nos instrui oporteat. Clamant illi, nos nimium stupidos & malignos diuinæ potentiæ æstimatores esse, qui illam ad Verbum externum & Sacramenta astringamus. At viderint ipsi, ne nimis temerarii in domo Dei nouatores esse deprehendantur, dum quam ipse statuit Oeconomiam abolere conantur. Neq; nos Deum aliqua necessitate astringimus, sed homines necessariò hanc illi obedientiam debere dicimus, vt eam in salutis negotio rationem sequantur, quam ille præscripsit, & quam ab ipsa rerum origine secuti sunt, quotquot illius germani cultores fuerunt.
units.tr: Moreover, this parable teaches us other things as well, which bear on the consideration of the ecclesiastical ministry. Among these, the most worthy of notice is that we are taught that the preaching of the Word is absolutely necessary to the Church, just as agriculture is. God, who once produced plants and every kind of fruit by a single word, could indeed even today give us, without our labour, whatever is necessary for use, either from the earth or from elsewhere. But because he said to Adam, "In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread," and commanded him to cultivate the earth, however unkind it might be, we must necessarily conform ourselves to that ordinance and command. For we ought not to appeal to his providence or omnipotence so that our idleness may be provided for, when it is quite clear what he wishes us to do. The same, therefore, we ought to observe in the cultivation of souls. Here it must by no means be denied that God has no need to use the preaching of the Word or the sacraments in instructing us; he could, by the hidden power of his Spirit and in an ineffable manner, teach and renew our souls without our knowing it. But since the curse presses on us no less than on the earth, and God wills that we be brought by the preaching of the Word and the use of the sacraments to a new and eternal life, and requires our diligence in this matter, it would be rash and impious to despise the order he has established. Therefore those should by no means be listened to who invent for us I know not what spirit and some inner, unwritten word, by which we must be instructed. They cry out that we are too dull and too disparaging of divine power, because we bind it to the external Word and the sacraments. But let them see to it that they are not found to be too rash innovators in the house of God, while they try to abolish the economy that he himself has established. Nor do we bind God by any necessity; rather, we say that people are necessarily bound to this obedience, to follow in the business of salvation the method that he has prescribed, and that all his true worshippers have followed from the very origin of things.

units.la: Præterea vt non sufficit terram à sentibus repurgauisse, arauisse, plantauisse, sementem fecisse, sed insuper perpetua cura & continuo labore opus est, vt quæ plantata sunt custodiantur, rigentur, æducentur, vt fructum maturum & nobis vtilem ferant: Ita in ecclesia quoque, ista omnia fieri necesse est. Vt enim inter latas segetes infelix lolium & steriles auenæ plerunque emergunt, & ex imis arborum truncis syluestria germina frutescunt, quæ superne insitos surculos excrescere non sinunt, nisi resecentur: Ita in Domini agro sua quoque zizania Satan aspergit, & subinde ex carne nostra prodeunt cogitationes & cupiditates noxiæ, quæ Verbi Dei fructum impediunt. Imò ea est hostis nostri improbitas, vt totas quoq; ecclesias aggredi, & aut securitate & fiducia incautos circumuenire, aut bene iacta & non infeliciter germinantia fidei veræ semina impijs traditionibus corrumpere soleat. Exemplo nobis sunt Corinthij nostri, quos neque accurata Pauli plantatio, neq; per Apollo factà rigatio potuit in officio continere, quin illis locum darent, aduersus quos nouo studio & labore opus fuit. Idem Galatarum quoq; ecclesijs accidisse constat, & multis alijs, quæ illo tempore fuerunt. Et quid hodie multi patiantur, commemorare superuacaneum esset, cùm id pij omnes non sine dolore ternant. Vt ergo agricola bonus modò lolium euellit, modò spinas falce resecat, modò plantas arescentes hinc inde dućtis riuis aquarum recreat, modò sæpe noua hortos munit, modò aues fugat, sæpe talpas & mures plantarum radicibus insidiantes intercipit: Ita his omnibus in æducanda & custodienda Euangelij segete fidelem ecclesiæ ministrum intentum esse conuenit. Ideò Paulus ecclesias frequenter inuisere, collapsas instaurare, animos fluctuantes confirmare, & absentes scriptis suis monere, corrigere & in viam reducere solebat. Sunt hæc propter eos obseruanda, qui conciones sacras negligunt, & sumptus inanes fieri putant in alendis ministris, qui quotidianis sermonibus populum satigent. Sed nesciunt illi, quanta sit satanæ astutia, quàm item in requietus eiusdem labor in perdendis hominibus. Fit autem non raro, vt illi ipsi grauioribus tentationibus obruti, magno suo cum periculo experiantur, nullam in hac re curam nimiam, nullum laborem superuacaneum esse.
units.tr: Furthermore, just as it is not enough to have cleared the land of brambles, ploughed it, planted it, and sown it, but there is need of constant care and unceasing labour, so that what has been planted may be guarded, watered, and nurtured, and bear mature fruit useful to us, so in the Church all these things too must be done. For just as among the broad crops the harmful darnel and barren oats often spring up, and from the lower trunks of trees wild shoots grow into bushes that do not allow the grafted twigs above to grow unless they are cut away, so in the Lord's field Satan also scatters his own tares, and from our flesh there constantly arise harmful thoughts and desires that hinder the fruit of God's Word. Indeed, it is the wickedness of our enemy to attack even whole churches, and either to beguile them when they are careless and overconfident, or to corrupt the seeds of true faith, well sown and not unhappily sprouting, with impious traditions. Our Corinthians are an example for us: neither Paul's careful planting nor the watering done by Apollos could keep them in their duty, so that they did not give room to those against whom new zeal and labour were needed. It is well established that the same thing happened to the churches of the Galatians, and to many others of that time. And to recount what many suffer today would be superfluous, since all the godly bear it not without grief. Therefore, just as a good farmer now pulls up the darnel, now cuts away the thorns with a sickle, now refreshes withering plants by channelling streams of water here and there, now often fortifies the gardens anew, now drives off the birds, and often intercepts the moles and mice that lie in wait for the roots of the plants, so it is fitting that a faithful minister of the Church should be intent on all these tasks in nurturing and guarding the crop of the Gospel. For this reason Paul was accustomed to visit the churches frequently, to restore those that had fallen, to strengthen wavering minds, and to admonish, correct, and lead back into the right way those who were absent, by his letters. These things must be noted on account of those who neglect sacred sermons and think that money is wasted in supporting ministers who wear the people out with daily sermons. But they do not know how great is Satan's cunning, and how his labour is no less restless in destroying people. Indeed, it often happens that those very people, overwhelmed by heavier temptations, learn at great cost that in this matter no care is too great and no labour superfluous.

units.la: Porrò quia Paulus inter se & Apollo discrimen aliquod fecisse & vni plus quam alteri tribuisse videri poterat, occurrit huic suspicioni, & quæcunque hactenus dicta sunt, nunc propius ad suum institutum accommodat, sic dicens: Is verò qui plantat, & is qui rigat, vnum sunt, &c. Quibus verbis minimè negat gradus illos, quos inter ministros esse alibi fatetur, vt alij quidem sint Apostoli, alij Euangelistæ, alij Prophetæ, alij Pastores, &c: sed hos omnes ita inter se coniunctos esse docet, vt omnes vnum censeri possint: eò quòd omnes vnius Domini ministri sint, in vno item & eodem opere occupentur, ad vnum & eundem finem tendant, & se mutuò iuuent, imò quòd vnusquisque aliorum ope & auxilio opus habeat. Vt ergo corpus reuera vnum est, etiamsi ex multis & inter se diuersis membris constet, quæ tamen omnia per vnam animam vivificantur, & sub vno capite conueniunt: ita ministri ecclesiæ vnum sunt, cùm omnes eodem spiritu ad eundem finem moueantur, & ab vno capite Christo dependeant. Finis autem, quem sibi omnes illi propositum habent, alibi definitur esse coagmentatio sanctorum & aedificatio corporis Christi, id est, ecclesia. Ex his autem rursus colligit Paulus, quod nemo ministrorum sese ambitiose alteri praeferre, nec quisquam propter illos ecclesiam in partes scindere debeat. Quia si hoc fiat, in ipsum ministerij finem peccabitur: & qui hoc fieri patiuntur ministri, ut suo honori privatim consulant, ij non coagmentationi sanctorum, neque aedificationi corporis Christi studeant, sed dissipationis & destructionis authores sunt. Itaq; hoc dicendo non obscure pseudoapostolos Corinthiorum Paulus perstringit, qui eo ipso, quo supra omnes volebant eminere, se indignos esse prodebant, qui ecclesiae ministri dicerentur. Vidit hoc olim Gregorius Magnus, qui cum de primatu episcoporum lis orta esset, & hunc sibi Ioannes Constantinopolitanus vendicaret, ad Mauritium Imperat. scripsit, Antichristi praecursorem esse, quisquis universalis Episcopus dici velit. At hodie, qui neq; plantant, neq; rigant, multis tamen ecclesijs simul dominari volunt. A quorum fastu non procul absunt quidam Euangelicae doctrinae professores, qui pro ter lautius stipendium sese supra eos extollunt, qui eundem cum illis Christum praedicant. At potius maiori laude digni sunt, qui frugali & tenui victu contenti, Euangelium inter mille pericula docent.
units.tr: Moreover, since Paul could seem to have made some distinction between himself and Apollos, and to have given more to one than to the other, he meets this suspicion. He now fits everything he has said so far more closely to his purpose, saying: "Now he who plants and he who waters are one, etc." In these words he does not deny the degrees that he elsewhere says exist among ministers, so that some are apostles, some evangelists, some prophets, some pastors, and so on. Rather, he teaches that all these are so joined together that they can all be counted as one. This is because they are all ministers of the one Lord, are engaged in the one and the same work, aim at the one and the same end, and help one another. Indeed, each of them needs the help and support of the others. Just as the body is truly one, though it consists of many different members, all of which are quickened by one soul and united under one head, so the ministers of the Church are one, since they are all moved by the same Spirit toward the same end and depend on one head, Christ. The end that they all have in view is elsewhere defined as "the joining together of the saints and the building up of the body of Christ," that is, the Church. From this Paul further draws the conclusion that no minister should ambitiously set himself above another, and no one should split the Church into parties on account of the ministers. For if this is done, sin is committed against the very purpose of the ministry. Those ministers who allow this to happen, so that they privately look after their own honour, are not concerned with the joining together of the saints or the building up of the body of Christ. Rather, they are authors of division and destruction. So in saying this, Paul clearly rebukes the false apostles of the Corinthians, who, by the very act of wishing to stand out above all others, showed that they were unworthy to be called ministers of the Church. Gregory the Great saw this long ago. When a dispute over the primacy of bishops arose, and John of Constantinople claimed this title for himself, Gregory wrote to the Emperor Maurice that whoever wishes to be called universal bishop is the forerunner of Antichrist. Yet today those who neither plant nor water nevertheless want to rule many churches at once. Not far from their arrogance are certain professors of the evangelical doctrine, who, because of a more generous stipend, lift themselves above those who preach the same Christ as they do. Yet those are rather worthy of greater praise who, content with a frugal and meagre diet, teach the gospel amid a thousand dangers.

units.la: At quia apud Corinthios cumprimis ambitione & laudis cupiditate nimia peccabatur, pergit Paulus & ad Deum illos remittit, qui unicuiq; mercedem redditurus sit secundum laborem suum. Quasi diceret: Quid opus est auram popularem captare & ab hominum iudicijs pendere eos, qui suorum certaminum atq; laborum iudicem & fidelissimum Agonothetem habent Deum, qui cum remunerator sit fidelissimus neminem sua mercede fraudabitur. Quin ergo hoc curant singuli, ut suum studium illi probent, & huic uni placeant? Nemo tamen quando mercedem promitti audit, ex eo operis sui meritum statuat. Nam si opera nostra spectes, nihil omnino illis meremur apud Deum: Primo, quia non ex nobis ipsis, neq; proprijs viribus ea facimus, ut qui ex nobisipsis ne ad cogitandu quidem sumus idonei, ut alibi Paulus docet. Deinde cum ex debito fiat, quicquid boni facimus, meritum nullum statui potest. Quod ipsum Christus testatur, dicens: Cum feceritis omnia, quae iniuncta sunt vobis, dicite, Serui inutiles sumus: quod debuimus facere, fecimus. Accedit his, quod vitiosa & imperfecta sunt opera nostra omnia propter insitam nobis naturae vitiositatem, quae prauis desideriis atque cogitationibus ea quoque corrumpit & Deo ingrata reddit, quae per se bona & sancta sunt. Mercedem ergo nostris operibus nullam meremur, si proprie loqui li-beat: utitur autem hoc vocabulo Deus ex paterna indulgentia, ut nos ad obsequium ipsi praestandum alacriores reddat.
units.tr: But because the Corinthians especially sinned through ambition and excessive desire for praise, Paul goes on and refers them to God, who will render to each one his reward according to his labour. As if he were saying: "Why is there any need to catch at popular applause and to depend on the judgements of men, when those who have God as the judge and most faithful rewarder of their contests and labours will not be defrauded of their wage, since he is most faithful? Why then does not each one take care to prove his zeal to him and to please him alone?" Yet when we hear that a reward is promised, no one should therefore judge that his work has merit. For if you look at our works, we deserve nothing at all from God. First, because we do them not from ourselves nor by our own strength. We are not even fit to think anything from ourselves, as Paul teaches elsewhere. Second, since whatever good we do is owed, no merit can be established. Christ himself bears witness to this, saying: "When you have done all the things that are commanded you, say, 'We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done.'" In addition, all our works are faulty and imperfect because of the inborn corruption of our nature, which, by its evil desires and thoughts, also corrupts those things that are good and holy in themselves and makes them unpleasing to God. So, if we are to speak properly, we deserve no reward for our works. God, however, uses this word out of fatherly indulgence, so that he may make us more eager to render obedience to him.

units.la: Porrò sui dicti rationem reddit, dicens: Etenim Dei sumus cooperarij, Dei aruum, Dei aedificatio estis. Quo dicto & doctores & auditores officij admonet: ut nimirum illi quidem uni Deo laborent, huic omnes adducant: hi vero similiter in illum unum respiciant, ut Dei ecclesia, non huius aut alterius factionis membra sint. Ut enim aruum domini est, non agricolae, cui eius colendi cura committitur, & proinde in domini sui usum colitur: ita ecclesia ad Christum pertinet, qui eam sanguinis sui pretio redemit, & ideo omnis qui in ea colenda impenditur labor in eum finem dirigi debet, ut omnis fructus ad Dominum redeat. Addit his aliam Metaphoram ab aedificio sumptam, ut ad ea quae sequuntur sibi transitum faciat, cuius tamen in praesenti idem sensus & usus est. Ut enim aedificium non fabrorum est, qui in eo extruendo laborant, sed eius, cui illi suam operam locauerunt: ita ecclesia Dei domus est: ideoq; ne minimam quidem eius partem sibi vendicare debent doctores, sed in eo potius esse, ut Christo, cuius ministri sunt, domum idoneam & gratam aedificent. Ex quo sequitur perfidiae reos esse omnes, qui secus agunt.
units.tr: Moreover, he gives the reason for what he has said, saying: "For we are God's fellow workers; you are God's field, God's building." By these words he reminds both teachers and hearers of their office: that the former labour for the one God alone and bring all to him, and the latter likewise look to that one, so that they are members of God's Church and not of this or that faction. For as a field belongs to the lord and not to the farmer to whom its cultivation is entrusted, and is therefore tilled for the use of its lord, so the Church belongs to Christ, who redeemed it at the price of his own blood. Therefore all the labour expended in cultivating it must be directed to this end, that all the fruit may return to the Lord. He adds to these another metaphor, taken from a building, so that he may pass on to what follows. Its sense and use in the present context is the same. For as a building belongs not to the workmen who labour in erecting it, but to the one who hired them to do the work, so the Church is God's house. Therefore teachers ought not to claim even the smallest part of it for themselves. Rather, their concern should be to build for Christ, whose ministers they are, a fit and pleasing house. From this it follows that all who act otherwise are guilty of treachery.

units.la: At est hic obseruatu dignissima Dei bonitas, qui hominibus administris vel cooperarijs uti dignatur. Est haec summa dignitas, quae non in solos verbi precones cadit, verumetiam in multos alios, quorum ministerio in ijs perficiendis utitur Deus, quae proprie ad illum solum pertinent, & non nisi eius virtute confici possunt. Eadem enim ratione, qui magistratum gerunt, Dei administri sunt: quia per hos sua iudicia ille exequitur. Tueantur ergo hanc suam dignitatem, ne si suis cupiditatibus indulgeant, in potestatem tenebrarum degenerent, ut de illis loquitur Christus, qui ad ipsum capiendum venerant. Sic Dei administri sunt coniuges in propaganpropagando & conseruando humano genere. Curent ergo, vt huic liberos generent, & ex se natos ad illius honorem æducent: ne aliter agendo sese diaboli administros faciant. Ita Dei administri sunt agricolæ, cum ipsorum opera ille vtatur in producendis terræ fructibus, quam ipsius benedictione sola fæcundari supra diximus. Ferant ergo patienter laborem omnem, & in opere suo fideles sint. Imò debet horum consideratio omnes excitare, ne ignaui torpeant. Nec enim suis administris vnquam deest Dominus, sed vt tu seruos tuos opus facientes spectare & ijsdem consilio & opera tua adesse soles: ita Deus nos omnes videt, & simul viribus instruit, vt operi nobis per ipsum mandato sufficere possimus. Neminem ergo laboris difficultas aut operis magnitudo terreat: quia si quid per nos effectu vult Deus, nihil quo minus id fiat obstare poterit. Deinde mercedem quoq; iam olim seruis suis destinauit, quam fideliter reddet ijs, qui in opere suo in finem vsq; perseuerant: sicuti in operariorum & talentorum parabolis Christus ipse docet.
units.tr: Here we must observe the most worthy goodness of God, who deigns to use men as his servants or fellow workers. This is a supreme dignity, which does not belong only to the heralds of the Word, but also to many others, through whose ministry God uses to accomplish those things which properly belong to him alone and can be done only by his power. For in the same way, those who bear the magistracy are God's ministers, because through them he carries out his judgements. Let them therefore guard this dignity, lest, if they indulge their desires, they degenerate into the power of darkness, as Christ spoke of those who came to seize him. So spouses are God's ministers in propagating and preserving the human race. Let them therefore take care to beget children for this purpose, and to bring up those born of them to his honour, lest by acting otherwise they make themselves servants of the devil. Likewise farmers are God's ministers, since he uses their work in producing the fruits of the earth, which, as we said above, is made fertile by his blessing alone. Let them therefore patiently bear every labour and be faithful in their work. Indeed, the consideration of these ministers ought to rouse everyone, so that the idle do not grow sluggish. For the Lord never fails his servants. Just as you often watch your servants at their work and are present with them by your counsel and help, so God sees us all and at the same time equips us with strength, so that we may be sufficient for the work committed to us by him. Therefore let no one be frightened by the difficulty of his labour or the greatness of his task, for if God wills anything to be accomplished through us, nothing can hinder it from being done. Moreover, he has long since appointed a reward for his servants, which he will faithfully render to those who persevere in their work to the end, as Christ himself teaches in the parables of the labourers and the talents.

units.la: Quoad vero Pauli institutum, finem omnium, quæ hucusq; dicta sunt, hunc esse meminerimus, vt vnitas & concordia in ecclesijs seruetur. Hanc nobis passim Christus commendat, & iam moriturus hoc præ aliis à Patre rogat, vt omnes in ipso vnum simus. Vt enim ædificium ruat oportet, cuius partes non rectè inter se cohærent: ita ecclesiam sine consensione fidei & charitatis mutuæ consistere impossibile est. Ideo quoties in scripturis de Christo & ecclesia sermo est, fere similibus eiusmodi Spiritus sanctus vtitur, quæ concordiam nobis commendant. Christum enim pastorem, nos eius oues aut gregem esse docet: illum sponsum, nos sponsam: illum vitem, nos palmites: illum caput, nos membra: illum primogenitum, nos fratres eius esse dicit. Quod si Decalogum inspicias, prima tabula nobis vnius Dei cultum & fidem vnam, in altera verò mutuam charitatem commendari videbis, quæ fidelissima concordiæ nutrix est. Debebant in horum consideratione omnes diligenter versari hodie, quando & ecclesiæ & respub. intestinis dissidijs passim collabuntur, quorum præcipua causa est eorum, qui rebus præsunt, insatiabilis ambitio. Sed quia hæc deplorare facilius est quam emendare, Deus Opt. Max. assiduis precibus orandus erit, vt is sopitis dissidiorum flammis spiritu suo omnium mentes dirigat, vt vnanimi fide & charitate coalescamus in CHRISTO IESV, Domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: As for Paul's purpose, let us remember that the aim of everything said so far is that unity and concord be preserved in the churches. Christ commends this to us everywhere, and even as he is about to die he asks the Father above all else that all of us may be one in him.
