Quæ omnia vt ad singulos pertinent,qui in illum credunt:ita imprimis de tota credentium ecclesia debent exponi, quam Paulus in præsenti Templum Dei, in priori autem ad Timotheum domum Dei esse dicit. Et hæc illa Ecclesia est,quam in Symbolo profitemur, quam Catholicam,id est,vniuersalem & Sanctorum communionem dicimus,eò quòd ad eam omnes pertinent, qui credunt in vnum Deum, Patrem Filium & Spiritum sanctum,quiq;per fidem illam in Christo sanctificati sunt. Hæc item domus illa spiritualis est, quæ ex nobis tanquam viuis lapidibus (vt Petrus scribit) extruitur, & in qua nobiles illi & verè pretiosi thesauri repositi sunt, Remissio peccatorum nimirum, beatæ resurrectionis spes & vita æterna, quæ & ipsa in Symbolo nostræ religionis continentur.
units.tr: Here, first of all, the admirable and more than fatherly goodness of God presents itself for our consideration, who in us deigns to choose a dwelling for himself and to live within us. For he is a power that penetrates all things and (as the Prophet says) fills heaven and earth. Indeed, that majesty is supreme, which David testifies is higher than the heavens themselves, and which the wondrous adornment of the heavenly bodies proclaims abundantly. And since he himself declares through the Prophet that heaven is his throne and the earth his footstool, it is easily gathered from this that no house can be built for him by us, nor does he have need of our works. Yet his goodness is such that he stoops so far as not only to look upon what is in heaven and on earth, but also to wish to dwell in us, and so deigns to make a temple for himself out of us, who, however we are, are mortal, wretched and deserving of any punishment. It seems a great honour if some most powerful king enrols someone among his courtly servants, or if he turns aside to someone's house and makes more familiar use of him. But what is there here that wise and thoughtful people ought rightly to admire? For a king too is a man, subject to the chances of fortune; and he turns aside to a man who can at some time help him either by counsel or even save him in peril of his life. Indeed, if we care to look at the matter more closely, we shall be even more amazed that anyone, trusting in a dignity that is temporary and exposed to so many dangers, can be so puffed up as to despise and scorn those whom he cannot deny to be partners of the same nature, unless he wishes to rave without reason. But between God and us there is no comparison at all, nor is there anything in us by which we could help him or earn some benefit from him. This is therefore a proof of incomparable goodness: that God turns aside to us not merely in passing, but also establishes for himself a seat and dwelling among us that is lasting. Because this may seem absurd to human reason, and far surpasses the grasp of our understanding, from the very beginning of things he wished us to be reminded of it and made certain of it by countless promises. The first promise, concerning the seed of the woman, teaches this, by which the head of the serpent must be crushed and we must be rescued from his tyranny. For since he willed that his Son should put on our flesh, has he not amply shown that he wishes to make use of our fellowship (so to speak)? We may say the same of the promises made to Abraham and his posterity, the sum of which is: I will be your God and the God of your seed after you. For he would not be our God unless he showed himself wholly to us and were with us for ever. And in the Law, through Moses, he said: I will set my tabernacle in the midst of you, and my soul will not loathe you. I will walk among you, and will be your God, and you shall be my people. Promises of this kind occur everywhere among the Prophets, and a whole day would not suffice to recite them. Let it be enough for us that he willed a tabernacle to be built through Moses, and afterwards a temple through Solomon, in which the ark of the covenant, the fire sent down from heaven and all that sacred furniture were kept, so that by this proof it might be established that he had made himself lord among men. But if you turn to the books of the New Testament, there you will hear Christ saying: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our abode with him. Likewise: Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age. All these things, while they pertain to each individual who believes in him, must above all be explained of the whole congregation of believers, which Paul in the present epistle calls the temple of God, and in the first to Timothy the house of God. And this is that Church which we profess in the Creed, which we call Catholic, that is, universal, and the communion of saints, because all belong to it who believe in one God, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and who through that faith have been sanctified in Christ. This is also that spiritual house which is built up out of us as living stones (as Peter writes), and in which those noble and truly precious treasures are laid up: namely the forgiveness of sins, the hope of the blessed resurrection and eternal life, which are themselves also contained in the Creed of our religion.

units.la: Commemoramus hæc eò diligentius, vt in ijs eximiam & plane incomparabilem dignitatem æstimare discamus,in quam nos Deus euexit. Nec enim nudus aut inops ad nos diuertit Deus,sed domum hanc suam donis varijs & præstantissimis exornat. Nam & peccata nostra remittit,& Filij sui Sapientiam,iustitiam & sanctitatem communicat: Spiritu item suo donat,qui omnis boni author est,& nos Dei amantes,veri reliqj studiosos,temperantes,sobrios,in secundis modestos & humiles,in aduersis inuictos atq; constantes reddit. Et cùm ij, qui in Regum aulis vitam degunt, ornatu quidem & pompa magnifica strepant,interim verò aureis compedibus vincti (vt ille dicebat) seruitutem miserrimam seruiant: Christiani homines è contra mundo quidem miseri & infelices videntur,dum omnium iniurijs expositi sunt, at ijdem verè liberi sunt ex Christi beneficio,& excusso diabolicæ seruitutis iugo Deo in Spiritu & Veritate seruiunt:quæ seruitus cum spontanea sit, etiam cum voluptate coniuncta est. Ideo Dauid ecclesiam sub reginæ persona describens, omnem eius gloriam internam esse dicit, vt quæ fide,spe,dilectione & omni virtutum genere in Dei conspectu splendeat,vtut mundo contemptissima videatur. Superat tamen hæc omnia, quòd quæ nunc Dei templum & Spiritus sancti domicilium in terris est, olim in cœlos transferetur,vt illic æternum cum sponso suo regnet atq; gaudeat.
units.tr: We recall these things the more carefully so that we may learn to value in them the outstanding and quite incomparable dignity to which God has raised us. For God does not turn to us as a poor or destitute man, but adorns this house of his with various and most excellent gifts. For he both forgives our sins and imparts to us the wisdom, righteousness and holiness of his Son; he also gives us his Spirit, who is the author of every good, and makes us lovers of God, zealous for truth and for other good things, self-controlled, sober, modest in prosperity, humble, and invincible and steadfast in adversity. And while those who live in the courts of kings, indeed, clatter with ornament and magnificent display, yet meanwhile, bound in golden fetters (as that man used to say), serve a most wretched slavery; Christians, on the contrary, indeed seem wretched and unhappy in the world, since they are exposed to the injuries of all; yet they are truly free by the benefit of Christ, and having shaken off the yoke of diabolical servitude, serve God in Spirit and in truth. And since this service is voluntary, it is also joined with joy. Therefore David, describing the Church under the person of a queen, says that all her glory is inward, since she shines in the sight of God with faith, hope, love and every kind of virtue, however utterly contemptible she may seem to the world. Yet this surpasses all else: that what is now the temple of God and the dwelling of the Holy Spirit on earth will one day be transferred into heaven, so that it may reign and rejoice there for ever with its bridegroom.

units.la: Secundò nostri officij nos ista consideratio admonet. Est enim hic mos inter homines communis,apud omnes gentes receptus & seculorum omnium consuetudine confirmatus, vt vnicuique in sua domo ius sit & imperium. Si ergo nos Dei domus sumus, eum suo iure apud nos vti & nobis imperare patiamur. Idq; eò magis fieri debet,quòd non domus aliqua priuata aut vulgaris,sed templum Dei esse dicimur. Nam vt supra diximus,magna est & fuit semper templorum religio,vt-pote quæ templa esse desinunt,si non vni Deo maneant consecrata. Christus certè cùm Hierosolymi-tanum templum à sordibus nundinatorum repurgasset, ita illud ab vsibus prophanis alienum esse voluit,vt ne vas quidem qualecunq;per illud deferre liceret. Quod cùm in eo templo obseruarit ille,quod non multò post vnà cum vrbe excindi & conflagrare debuit,quanto maior debet esse templi illius viui religio,quod Filij Dei sanguine consecrari oportuit, vt Spiritus sanctus in illo habitare posset? Quo loco duo imprimis obseruari debent. Alterum,vt templum Dei verum efficiamur atq; simus. Hic Christi regulam tenere oportet,quam supra commemorauimus, vt nimirum ipsum diligamus, & dilectionem hanc præceptorum eius obseruatione & sedulo obedientia studio testemur. Nam si quis diligit me(inquit) sermonem meum seruabit, & Pater meus diliget eum, &c. At quia de hoc sæpe dictum est, nolumus in eo explicando prolixiores esse. Alterum ergo obseruemus,quod est,ne templum istud Dei violari aut destrui patiamur. Nam vt non sufficit templum magnis impensis extruxisse, & religiose consecrauisse,nisi & ædificium eius sartum tectum seruetur,& nullis vsibus prophanis polluatur:ita in nobis etiam vtrumq; fieri necesse est, ne de nobis perinde vt de Synagoga fornicatrice olim Deus conqueri possit: eò maiori cura & diligentia hic nobis opus est, quòd non vno modo Satan templo huic viuo Dei insidias struit, vt aut totum euertat,aut impiè prophanet.
units.tr: Secondly, this consideration admonishes us of our duty. For it is a custom common among men, received among all nations and confirmed by the practice of all ages, that each person should have right and authority in his own house. If therefore we are God's house, let us allow him to use his right among us and to rule over us. And this should be done all the more, because we are called not some private or common house, but the temple of God. For, as we said above, the reverence for temples is great and has always been so, since temples cease to be temples if they are not kept consecrated to the one God alone. Certainly when Christ had cleansed the temple at Jerusalem of the filth of the moneychangers, he so wished it to be kept free from profane uses that it was not even lawful to carry any vessel whatsoever through it. Since he observed this in that temple, which not long afterwards had to be destroyed and burned together with the city, how much greater ought to be the reverence for that living temple, which had to be consecrated by the blood of the Son of God, so that the Holy Spirit might dwell in it? Two things in particular ought to be observed here. The first is that we should become and be a true temple of God. Here we must keep to the rule of Christ which we mentioned above: namely, that we love him, and bear witness to this love by keeping his precepts and by a diligent zeal for obedience. For, he says, if anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, etc. But since this has often been said, we do not wish to be too long in explaining it. Let us therefore observe the second thing, which is that we do not allow that temple of God to be violated or destroyed. For just as it is not enough to have built a temple at great expense and to have consecrated it with due ceremony, unless its building also is kept in repair and roofed, and is not polluted by any profane uses, so in us both things must necessarily be done, lest God be able to complain of us as he once complained of the adulterous synagogue. All the more care and diligence is needed here on our part, because Satan lays snares for this living temple of God in more ways than one, so as either to overthrow it entirely or to defile it impiously.

units.la: Huius enim opus est, quòd aperti fidei hostes ferro & igne aduersus ecclesiam insurgunt, vt Christum ex sua possessione deiiciant. Fuit horum magnus numerus semper, & hodie passim eorundem furor atq; crudelitas graßatur. Plus tamen nocent, qui falsam doctrinam inuehunt, & vt improbi lenones atq; lenæ solent, homines à Christo abducunt. Horum opera fit, vt loco Christi homines ambitiosi in ecclesia emineant, & per illos hæc in partes & sectas distracta, Dei templum esse desinat. Et de his imprimis Paulum in præsenti agere, totus epistolæ contextus docet. Neq; temere templi Dei violatores aut destructores illi dicuntur. Quia enim quotquot in Christum credunt, ecclesiam vnam & templum Dei vnum constituunt, imò vnū corpus sunt sub capite CHRISTO IESV, ex quo vitæ spiritus in omnia membra deriuatur: certè neq; ecclesia neq; templum Dei amplius erunt, qui loco vnius Christi capita diuersa suspiciunt & in factiones sunt scissi. Quod vnum si rectè expendatur, mox constabit, quid de Romana ecclesia iudicari debeat. Quid enim illic reperias aliud, quàm prophanationem impiam & confusionem horribilem totius religionis, adeoq; omnium rerum, quæ in ecclesia seruari debebant? Nam etsi Christum in ore habeant, talem tamen fingunt, qui vicario Pontifice vtatur, ipse nimirum otiosus rerum, quæ aguntur, spectator. Et ne Pontifice quidem contenti, sub hoc quoq; diuersos monachorum ordines, fraternitates, sodalitia finxerunt, quæ singulos suos principes aut capita agnoscunt. Et hi omnes professione, vestitu, ritibus, & multi dogmatibus quoq; inter se differunt. Taceo sacrorum nundinationem, indulgentias, sacrificia noua, missas, simulachrorum cultu, ignis purgatorij commenta, opera supererogationis & sexcenta alia, quæ omnia vt cum Euangelij doctrina palàm pugnant, ita meritum Christi euacuant. Desinant ergo illi nos ad sui Templi societatem reuocare, cuius neq; fundamentum vnum est, neque parietes inter se cohærent, & cuius tectum cum ipso fastigio ruinam iampridem minatur, quæ infelices Christi hostes & sui templi violatores male perdet. Destruunt præterea & violant Dei templum, qui disciplinam ecclesiasticam conuellunt, & hac sublata peccandi licentiam publicam inuehunt. Per hos enim fit, vt qui singuli templum Spiritus sancti esse debebant, diaboli mancipia fiant, & ideo ex Dei templo omnis libidinis & nequitiæ prostibulum faciunt. Quàmuis ergo Paulus peculiariter de sectarum authoribus in præsenti loquatur, eadem tamen admonitio aduersus omnes illos seruire debet, qui templum illud Dei violant, & proinde ca-vendum[?] est omnibus, qui Christiani dici & haberi volunt, ne talibus apud se locum dent aliquem.
units.tr: For there is need of this: openly declared enemies of the faith rise up against the Church with sword and fire, to cast Christ out of his possession. Their number has always been great, and even today their fury and cruelty rage everywhere. Yet those who introduce false doctrine do more harm, and, like wicked pimps and bawds, lead men away from Christ. Through their work it comes about that, in place of Christ, ambitious men stand out in the Church, and that the Church, torn into parties and sects, ceases to be the temple of God. That Paul is especially dealing with these people in the present passage, the whole context of the epistle shows. Nor are they rightly called violators or destroyers of God's temple without reason. For since all who believe in Christ make up one Church and one temple of God, and are indeed one body under the head, CHRIST JESUS, from whom the spirit of life flows into all the members, certainly those who, in place of the one Christ, look up to different heads and are split into factions will be neither Church nor temple of God any longer. If this one point is weighed rightly, it will soon be clear what ought to be judged of the Roman Church. For what else will you find there than impious profanation and a dreadful confusion of the whole religion, and so of all the things that ought to have been kept in the Church? For although they have Christ on their lips, they nonetheless invent a Christ who uses a vicar Pontiff, himself, of course, an idle spectator of what is going on. And not even content with the Pontiff, under him they have also devised various orders of monks, brotherhoods and fellowships, each of which acknowledges its own princes or heads. And all of these differ from one another in profession, dress, rites, and many also in doctrines. I say nothing of the trafficking in sacred things, the indulgences, the new sacrifices, the masses, the worship of images, the fictions of purgatorial fire, the works of supererogation, and six hundred other things, all of which, as they openly clash with the doctrine of the gospel, so they empty the merit of Christ. Let them therefore cease to call us back to the fellowship of their temple, whose foundation is not one, whose walls do not hold together, and whose roof with its very gable has long threatened ruin, which will utterly destroy the wretched enemies of Christ and violators of their own temple. Moreover, those also destroy and violate God's temple who overthrow ecclesiastical discipline and, once it is removed, introduce a public license to sin. For through them it comes about that those who ought each one to be the temple of the Holy Spirit become slaves of the devil, and so they make of God's temple a brothel of all lust and wickedness. Therefore, although Paul is speaking here particularly of the authors of sects, the same warning ought nonetheless to apply to all who violate that temple of God, and so everyone who wishes to be and be considered Christian must beware of giving any place to such people among themselves.

units.la: Et hinc nos excitare debet postrema huius tractationis pars, qua pœnam grauem istis omnibus minatur, dicens: Si quis templum Dei destruit, hunc destruet Deus. Est hoc horrendum valde. Quem enim Deus perdere vult, quis seruabit? Aut quò nam fugient à facie Domini, quos hic persequitur, qui vbiq; præsens est, & creaturis omnibus pro suo arbitrio imperat? At non sine gravi causa hanc tam duram sententiam Paulus pronuntiat. Constat enim omnibus seculis seuerissi-mè omnes eos punitos esse, qui externa Dei templa impiè prophanarunt. Tanti certè templum suum fecit Deus, vt illud à Davide extrui noluerit, eò quòd is bella multa gessisset, & sanguinem multum effudisset. Posteà verò eius excidium aduersus Chaldæos grauiter vltus est, & Babylonem vnà cum imperio suo toto excidit, eiusq; regem Baltazarem ab hostibus interfici voluit, cùm vasa templi, diu prius religiosè asseruata, in conuiuium luxuriosum iussisset inferri. Quid Alex-andri successoribus, & imprimis Antiocho, acciderit, qui templum violauerat, notius est, quàm vt referri oporteat. Pompeius verò, cùm capta Hierosolyma in Sanctum sanctorum nefaria curiositate ingredi & prophano intuitu ea spectare ausus esset, quæ Deus abscondita voluit, mox vltricem illius manum sensit. Nam per quindecim annos varijs fortunæ vicibus per incerta consilia iactatus, & tandem bello ciuili implicitus, postremò in Ægypto, quasi in conspectu Hierosolymæ, ab eo rege occisus est, cuius patrem in regnum restituerat. Poterant hic tristes quoq; Imperatorum aliorumq; tyrannorum exitus commemorari, qui Christianorum oratoria destruxerunt in nominis Christiani contumeliam. At si ædificij sacri prophanationem tanta seueritate Deus punit, quid obsecro merebuntur, qui viuum Dei templum violare audent? Et sunt hic quoq; exempla plurima, quæ huic comminationi fidem faciant. Nam si veteris Testamenti historiam euoluas, nullum scelus in deserto atrocius punitum fuisse reperies, quàm Coritarum, qui ecclesiam sciderunt. Et Ieroboamum cum sua stirpe mox deletum esse legimus, quòd vt in regno, sic in cultu quoq; Dei scisma fecisset. Posteris temporibus sciderunt Dei templum haeretici quoq;, inter quos primatum facilè Arius tenuit. Vt vero alij omnes nouis fere iudiciorum Dei exemplis repressi sunt: ita Arij exitus non minus turpis & foedus quàm exempli inexpectati nouitate horrendus fuit. Idem de disciplinae ecclesiasticae dissipatoribus & publicorum scandalorum authoribus dici potest: quibus iam olim Christus Vae illud horrendum denuntiauit. Et si damnatione aeterna dignus est, qui vnum ex pusillis offendit, quos pro suis agnoscit Christus, quid de illis fiet, quorum consilijs & exemplo vniuersalis peccandi licentia inuehitur? Haec vt vnitatis simul & sanctitatis studium nobis vehementer commendant: ita consolationem quoq; dulcissimam continent, qua nos aduersus tyrannorum minas atq; impios conatus armemus. Dissipant hi ecclesias & plus quàm gigantea audacia templum Dei destruunt. Ergo illos quoq; destruit Deus, & cum infelici posteritate plerunq; sic dissipat, vt nihil ex illis reliquum fiat, praeter infamem & bonis omnibus abominabilem summae eorum impietatis memoriam. Exempla sunt in veteribus historijs passim obuia, & nostro seculo multa vidimus, quae satis docent, templum suum Deo curae esse, neq; vnquam impune laturos esse, qui illi manus impias inferre audent. Ista ergo nos consolentur in periculis, & simul excitent, vt nostrae dignitatis memores eam sedulo tueamur, & Dei templum in nobis ipsis sanctum seruemus constanti fide in IESVM CHRISTVM, Dominum nostrum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: And the last part of this discussion ought to stir us up here, in which he threatens all of them with a grievous punishment, saying: If anyone destroys the temple of God, God will destroy him. This is very dreadful. For who will save the one whom God wishes to destroy? Or whither will those flee from the face of the Lord whom he pursues here, who is present everywhere and commands all creatures at his own pleasure? But Paul does not pronounce this so harsh a sentence without grave cause. For it is established that in all ages those who impiously profaned the external temples of God have been punished most severely. Certainly God made his temple of such account that he would not allow it to be built by David, because he had waged many wars and shed much blood. Afterwards indeed he avenged its destruction heavily upon the Chaldeans, and overthrew Babylon together with her whole empire, and willed that her king Belshazzar be slain by his enemies, when he had ordered the vessels of the temple, long before reverently kept, to be brought into a luxurious banquet. What befell the successors of Alexander, and above all Antiochus, who had defiled the temple, is too well known to need recounting. Pompey, however, when Jerusalem was taken and he dared, in wicked curiosity, to enter the Holy of Holies and with profane gaze to look upon those things which God had willed to be hidden, soon felt the avenging hand of God. For for fifteen years, tossed about by the varying turns of fortune and by uncertain counsels, and at last entangled in civil war, he was finally killed in Egypt, almost within sight of Jerusalem, by that king whose father he had restored to the kingdom. Here the sad ends of emperors and other tyrants, who destroyed the oratories of Christians to the reproach of the Christian name, could also be recalled. But if God punishes the profanation of a sacred building with such severity, what, I beg you, will those deserve who dare to violate the living temple of God? And there are here also very many examples that give credence to this threat. For if you unroll the history of the Old Testament, you will find no crime in the wilderness punished more harshly than that of the Korathites, who split the Church. And we read that Jeroboam with his whole line was soon destroyed, because he had made a schism not only in the kingdom but also in the worship of God. In later times heretics also have rent the temple of God, among whom Arius easily held the first place. But whereas all the others have been checked by almost new examples of God's judgments, the end of Arius was no less shameful and foul than it was dreadful through the novelty of an unexpected example. The same can be said of the scatterers of ecclesiastical discipline and the authors of public scandals, upon whom Christ long ago pronounced that dreadful Woe. And if he is worthy of eternal damnation who offends one of the little ones whom Christ acknowledges as his own, what will become of those by whose counsels and example a universal license to sin is introduced? These things, while they strongly commend to us both the zeal for unity and for holiness, also contain a most sweet consolation, with which we are to arm ourselves against the threats of tyrants and their impious attempts. These men scatter churches and, with more than gigantic audacity, destroy the temple of God. Therefore God also destroys them, and most often he so scatters them together with their unhappy posterity that nothing of them remains, except the infamous memory of their extreme impiety, abominable to all good men. Examples lie everywhere in the ancient histories, and in our own age we have seen many which sufficiently teach that God cares for his temple and that those who dare to lay impious hands upon it will never go unpunished. Let these things therefore console us in dangers, and at the same time stir us up, so that, mindful of our dignity, we may diligently guard it and keep the temple of God holy in ourselves, by steadfast faith in JESUS CHRIST, our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XVI.
units.tr: HOMILY XVI.

units.la: Nullus seipsum seducat. Si quis videtur esse sapiens inter vos in hoc seculo, stultus fiat, vt fiat sapiens. Sapientia enim mundi huius, stultitia est apud Deum. Scriptum est enim: Capit sapientes in versutia eorum. Et rursum: Dominus nouit cogitationes sapientum esse vanas. Itaq; nullus glorietur in hominibus. Omnia nanq; vestra sunt, siue Paulus siue Apollos, siue Cephas, siue mundus, siue vita, siue mors, siue praesentia, siue futura. Omnia (inquam) vestra sunt, vos autem Christi: Christus vero Dei.
units.tr: Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish, that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written: "He catches the wise in their own craftiness." And again: "The Lord knows that the thoughts of the wise are vain." Therefore let no one glory in men. For all things are yours, whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or the present, or the future. All things, I say, are yours, and you are Christ's, and Christ is God's.

units.la: Quamuis Corinthij vitijs multis laborarent, & inter haec grauissimum adeo, intolerabile erat, quod in factiones scissi, concordiam & vnitatem Christianam foedissimè turbarant, de eo tamen pro innata omnibus hominibus ingenij corruptione, leuiter admodum iudicabant, imo quasi re bene gesta singuli in sua factione superbiebant, earumq; authoribus publicè gloriabantur. Ideo Paulus nuper tanti mali atrocitatem grauiter arguit, offendens, eos templum Dei violare atq; destruere, quo vix quicquam atrocius dici vel excogitari poterat. Adhaec horribile Dei iudicium ijsdem minatus est, qui ipsi quoq; tales male perdere soleat. At quia non sufficit morbum indicauisse, nisi remedium eidem adhibeas, nunc consilium subijcit, quo docet, quid facere quidq; caeuere debeant, si poenas iam sibi imminentes subterfugere velint. Partes loci huius tres sunt. Prima summam totius negotij proponit, & omnis mali huius fontem obturat. Secunda consilium suum rationibus & argumentis confirmat. Tertia hoc omne ad causam applicat, de qua agebatur.
units.tr: Although the Corinthians were troubled by many faults, and among them this one was so grave and so intolerable that, torn into factions, they had most foully disturbed Christian concord and unity, they nevertheless judged it rather lightly, as is the way with the innate corruption of all men. Indeed, as if they had done something well, each took pride in his own faction and boasted publicly of its leaders. So Paul now sharply condemns the enormity of so great an evil, charging that they were violating and destroying the temple of God, than which scarcely anything more atrocious could be said or imagined. Besides, he threatens them with the dreadful judgment of God, which is wont to destroy such people utterly. But because it is not enough to diagnose a disease unless you also apply a remedy to it, he now adds counsel, teaching what they ought to do and what they ought to avoid if they wish to escape the punishments already hanging over them. This passage has three parts. The first sets out the sum of the whole matter and stops up the source of all this evil. The second confirms his counsel with reasons and arguments. The third applies all of this to the matter under discussion.

units.la: Primam hís verbis comprehendit: Nullus seipsum seducat: Si quis videtur esse sapiens inter vos in hoc seculo, stultus fiat, vt fiat sapiens. Est haec bipertita sententia, cuius prior pars quid caeuendum sit, monet: altera, quid fieri debeat, docet. Alloquitur autem tam doctores Corinthiorum, quàm auditores, eo quod vtrisq; remedio siue consilio opus erat. Hi enim, vt fere superbi & delicatuli solent, ne quid cum alijs ecclesijs communé habere viderentur, ostentatoribus delectabantur, qui ambitiosa sublimium mysteriorum praedicatione animos leues pascebant. Illi verò cùm se in pretio esse viderent, se prae omnibus alijs sapere sibi persuadebat, & neglecta euangelicae doctrinae simplicitate, quotidie noua quaedam comminiscebantur, vt maiorem indies eruditionis & sapientiae existimationem sibi pararet. Vtrinq; ergo inani persuasione peccabatur, quae in alijs etiam rebus plurimum obesse & nocere solet: & ideo vtrisq; monet Apostolus, vt ab illa sibi caueant, & ne sibijpsis[?] nimium tribuendo seipsos decipiant aut seducant,imò sese malè perdant,dum præ aliis volunt excellere.
units.tr: He comprehends the first in these words: "Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish, that he may become wise." This is a two-part saying, of which the first part warns what must be avoided, and the second teaches what ought to be done. He addresses both the teachers of the Corinthians and their hearers, because both needed the remedy or counsel. For these, as proud and pampered people usually are, did not want to seem to have anything in common with the other churches, and took delight in showy men who fed their shallow minds with an ambitious preaching of lofty mysteries. The teachers, seeing that they were in high esteem, persuaded themselves that they were wiser than all others, and, neglecting the simplicity of the gospel doctrine, devised new things every day, so as to win for themselves a greater reputation for learning and wisdom with each passing day. So both parties were sinning through empty self-persuasion, which is wont to do great harm and injury in other matters as well. Therefore the Apostle warns both to beware of it, and not to deceive or mislead themselves by attributing too much to themselves, but rather to ruin themselves utterly while they wish to excel above others.

units.la: Est hæc generalis admonitio, quam omnes fibijpsis accommodare debent. Nihil enim pernitiosius confidentia, imò hæc ferè perditionis & exitij causa est præsentissima omnibus, qui eius spiritus admittunt. Ideo frequenter per illam diabolus eos tentat, quos diffidentia & incredulitate vinci non posse videt. Exemplum in Christo habemus perquàm memorabile: qui cùm diffidentiæ telum, quo hostis eum aggressus fuerat, fortissimè elusisset, mox super pinnas templi constitutum sollicitat Satan, ut inde se præcipitem det, & eo facto se Dei Filium esse palàm testetur. Et ut hoc ipsi persuadeat, promissiones ex scripturis adducit, nō ut his illum fidere doceat, sed ut impia confidentia ebrium Deum tentet, & seipsum miserè perdat. Quod autem in eiusmodi casu conatur Satan, hoc ipsum in multis aliis accidere solet. In religione certè hæc præsentissima pestis est, quòd aut sui ingenij viribus freti homines de illa ex suo arbitrio statuunt, aut suæ authoritati tantum tribuunt, ut de illa leges ferant, quasi nimirum in ipsorum potestate sit Deo cultum, quem ipsi volunt, obtrudere. Offenderunt[?] ad hunc lapidem Israelitæ, quando contra expressum Dei mandatum, eius gloriam cum vituli aut bovis fœnum comedentis (ut Psalmi verbis vtar) imagine commutarunt. Ieroboamum verò nimia suijpsius fiducia decepit, ut unà cum regno summam quoq; religionis constituendæ potestatem ad se devolutam putaret, & ideo Israelitis suis idololatriæ author esset, quæ res tam ipsi quàm illis infelicissimè cessit. In utroq; gentes etiam peccauisse constat. Nam qui inter has sapientia aliis præstare voluerunt, hi ipsam Dei maiestatem proprij ingenij acumine scrutari ausi sunt, id quod eos non solum stultissimos mortalium fecit, sed in errores horribiles adduxit, qui illis immanissimorum scelerum simul & exitij causa fuerunt, ut Paulus ad Romanos docet. Romani verò cum orbi terrarum imperarent, potentia tantâ fiducia inflati, in cælos quoq; sibi ius & imperium vsurparunt, ut in Deos referrent pro suo arbitrio, quos ipsi tanto honore dignos iudicabant. Ita verò factum est, ut pro Diis colerent homines nequissimos, scortatores, adulteros, incestos, sanguinarios, parricidas, Christum verò, æternum veri Dei Filium & unicum humanæ salutis authorem, impiè reiecerent, eam imprimis ob causam, quòd Tyberius inconsulto Senatu illum pro Deo colendum esse censuisset, sicuti vetustissimus scriptor Tertullianus in suo Apologetico te-statur. Et si ad nostra tempora accedamus, quæ alia superstitionum & idololatriæ iam vbique regnantis causa fingi potest, quàm quod immani confidentia quidam eò vsq; efferuntur, ut in scripturas sacras & æternum Dei Verbum sibi cersuram sumant, & in cœlitum numerum referant eos, quos sibi vtiles aliquando expertisunt. Hinc nouum illud Canonizandi artificiū, de quo idem, quod de Romanorum audacia Tertullianus olim pronunciauit, dicere possumus: Nisi homini Deus placuerit, Deus non erit. Et homini iam Deus propitius esse debebit, ne rursus è cœlo deturbetur. At non minor in reliqua vita confidentiæ pestis est. Huic enim debetur, quòd multi maiora viribus tentant, & vt Milo ille Crotoniates, sibi ipsis exitium accersunt, dum quiduis obuiū per se confici posse sibi persuaserunt. Ex eodè fonte promanat, quòd alij de peccatis leuiter pronuntiant, & bonum malum, malum verò bonum dicunt, ideoq; pœnitere nesciij in sceleribus pergunt, quòd se nunquam pœnas daturos esse sperant. Quia enim inter homines sua vel potentia vel authoritate eò vsq; progressi sunt, ut impunè quiduis faciant, eadem impunitate se apud Deum quoq; fruituros arbitrantur. Et hæc ferè causa est, ut quasi sublato boni & mali discrimine, vitia virtutum nominibus pallientur, & è contra virtutes vitiorum titulis infames & exosæ fiant: quam reipub. pestem nocentissimam & rerum quotidie in peius ruentium certum indicium esse olim Cato ille intellexit, qui virtutis quidem & constantiæ suæ admiratores plurimos, paucos autem imitatores habuit. Adhæc admonitionum & correctionis impatientissimos reddit arrogantia: quia fieri non potest, ut aliquem æquo animo ferant, qui se sibijpsis ad omnia sufficere putant. Semper ergo in auribus & cordibus nostris sonet hoc Pauli dictum: Nullus seipsum seducat aut decipiat, &c.
units.tr: This is a general admonition, which all ought to apply to themselves. For nothing is more pernicious than self-confidence; indeed, this is almost the most immediate cause of ruin and destruction for all who admit its spirit. Therefore the devil often tempts through it those whom he sees cannot be overcome by distrust and unbelief. We have a most memorable example in Christ, who, when he had most bravely parried the dart of distrust with which the enemy had attacked him, soon after Satan tempted him to stand upon the pinnacle of the temple and throw himself down from there, and by that act openly show himself to be the Son of God. And to persuade him of this, Satan brought forward promises from Scripture, not to teach him to trust in them, but so that, drunk with impious confidence, he might tempt God and miserably destroy himself. What Satan attempts in such a case often happens in many other cases as well. In religion this is certainly the most immediate plague: either men, relying on the strength of their own wit, decide matters of religion by their own judgment, or they attribute so much to their own authority that they lay down laws about it, as if it were truly in their power to impose on God whatever worship they themselves wish. The Israelites stumbled over this stone when, against the express command of God, they exchanged his glory for the image of a calf or ox eating grass (to use the words of the Psalm). Jeroboam, however, was deceived by excessive trust in himself, so that, together with the kingdom, he thought the supreme power of establishing religion had also devolved upon him, and therefore he became the author of idolatry for his Israelites, a thing which turned out most unhappily both for him and for them. It is clear that the nations also sinned in both ways. For those among them who wished to excel others in wisdom dared to scrutinize the very majesty of God with the keenness of their own minds, which not only made them the most foolish of mortals, but led them into horrible errors, which were the cause of their most monstrous crimes and of their ruin, as Paul teaches to the Romans. The Romans, when they ruled the world, puffed up with such confidence in their power, usurped for themselves also the right and dominion over the heavens, so that they might enroll in the number of the gods whomever they judged worthy of such honor at their own pleasure. And so it came about that men worshiped as gods the most wicked, fornicators, adulterers, incestuous, murderers, and parricides, while they impiously rejected Christ, the eternal Son of the true God and the sole author of human salvation, chiefly for this reason: that Tiberius had proposed, without consulting the Senate, that he should be worshiped as God, as the most ancient writer Tertullian attests in his Apology. And if we come to our own times, what other cause of superstition and idolatry, now reigning everywhere, can be devised, than that certain men are carried away by such monstrous confidence that they take to themselves the right to correct the holy Scriptures and the eternal Word of God, and enroll in the number of the heavenly ones those whom they have at some time found useful to themselves? Hence that new art of canonizing, about which we can say what Tertullian once declared about the audacity of the Romans: "Unless God has pleased man, God will not be." And God must now be gracious to man, lest he be cast down from heaven again. But the plague of confidence is no less in the rest of life. To it is due the fact that many attempt things beyond their strength, and, like that Milo of Croton, bring ruin upon themselves, while they persuade themselves that anything whatever in their way can be accomplished by their own powers. From the same source it flows that others pronounce lightly about sins, and call good evil and evil good, and therefore persist in their crimes without learning to repent, because they hope they will never pay the penalty. For since they have advanced among men so far by their power or authority that they can do whatever they like with impunity, they think they will enjoy the same impunity before God as well. And this is almost the cause of why, as if the distinction between good and evil were removed, vices are cloaked under the names of virtues, and conversely, virtues become infamous and hateful under the titles of vices. That most harmful plague of the commonwealth, and a sure sign of affairs daily running to ruin for the worse, the famous Cato long ago understood; he had many admirers of his virtue and constancy, but few imitators. Besides, arrogance makes men most impatient of admonition and correction, because it is impossible for them to bear calmly anyone whom they think sufficient for everything in themselves. Therefore let this saying of Paul always sound in our ears and hearts: "Let no one deceive or mislead himself," and so on.

units.la: Quid verò facere debemus? Id altera huius admonitionis parte Apostolus sic docet: Si quis videtur esse sapiens inter vos in hoc seculo, id est, secundum iudicium & rationem huius seculi, stultus fiat, ut sit sapiens. Quæ verba non sic accipi debent, quasi nos quoad res huius seculi stultos rerumque inexpertos esse velit, aut ut prudentiæ omni, si quæ nobis ex Dei dono peculiari & longo rerum vsu obtigit, in vniuersum renuntiemus. Sed quia de religione & salutis ratione sermo est, monet, ne in ijs quae ad hanc spectant, nostrae sapientiae iudicium audiamus, neque a nobis-ipsis, aut ab aliquo mortalium, sed ab vno Deo pendeamus, & (vt alibi loquitur) rationem, intellectum & sensum omnem sub Verbum Dei cogamus per fidei obedientiam. Qui hoc faciunt, ij mundi iudicio hominum stultissimi sunt. Nam neglectis illis, quae ob oculos posita vident & quasi manibus suis tenent, ad futura aspirant: adhaec mundi huius amicitiam, fauorem, gloriam tantum non pedibus calcant, in se autem quorumuis odia, inimicitias & infamiam recipiunt, vt & in hoc seculo Dei gloriam prouehant, & quam Christus nobis in coelis acquisiuit, gloriam assequantur. Id vero extremam stultitiam, imo dementiam esse putant, qui nihil praeter mundum sapiunt. Sed qui ita stultescunt mundi iudicio, ij reuera sapientissimi fiunt. Nam hac ratione ad Christum venitur, qui nobis a Deo sapientia factus est, & in quo (vt Cap. secundo vidimus) iam sapientiam nobis Pater reuelat, quam nemo sapientum huius seculi cognouit: & idem diaboli quantumuis astuti insidias & artes facile eludunt, dum veram illam lucem sequuntur, quae eos in tenebris aberrare non finit. In Romana historia Iunius Brutus describitur, qui prudenti stultitiae simulatione Tarquinij superbi insidias effugit, cum is omnibus nece strueret, quos tyrannidi sua obstare posse suspicabatur. Et in scholis iactatur versiculus ille, Stultitia simulare loco sapientia summa est. At nulla hic simulatione opus est. Vere & ex animo debemus mundi sapientiam excludere, vbi de aeterna salute agitur, & quasi clausis oculis Deum sequi, qua ille nos ducit per Verbum suum, & ita vere seruabimur.
units.tr: But what ought we to do? The Apostle teaches this in the second part of this admonition: "If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age," that is, according to the judgment and reasoning of this age, "let him become foolish, that he may become wise." These words ought not to be taken as if he wished us to be foolish in the affairs of this age, or inexperienced in things, or as if he wished us to renounce altogether all prudence, if we have obtained any through a special gift of God and from long experience of affairs. But since the discussion concerns religion and the reckoning of salvation, he warns us not to listen to the judgment of our own wisdom in those matters which pertain to these, nor to depend on ourselves or on any mortal, but on the one God, and (as he speaks elsewhere) to bring every reason, understanding and sense under the Word of God through the obedience of faith. Those who do this are the most foolish in the judgment of the world's men. For, neglecting those things which they see set before their eyes and hold, as it were, in their own hands, they aspire to the things to come; moreover, they trample under foot, as it were, the friendship, favor and glory of this world, and receive upon themselves the hatred, enmities and infamy of whomever, so that in this age they may advance the glory of God, and attain the glory which Christ has acquired for us in heaven. Those who understand nothing but the world think this to be extreme folly, indeed madness. But those who become foolish in this way by the judgment of the world in fact become most wise. For by this route one comes to Christ, who has been made wisdom for us by God, and in whom (as we saw in the second chapter) the Father now reveals to us the wisdom which none of the wise of this age has known. And the snares and arts of the devil, however cunning, are easily eluded by those who follow that true light, which does not allow them to wander in darkness. In Roman history Junius Brutus is described, who by a prudent simulation of folly escaped the snares of the proud Tarquin, when he was plotting the death of all whom he suspected could stand in the way of his tyranny. And in the schools that verse is tossed about: "To simulate folly in place of wisdom is the highest wisdom." But here no simulation is needed. We ought truly and from the heart to exclude the wisdom of the world when eternal salvation is at stake, and, with our eyes as it were closed, to follow God wherever he leads us through his Word, and thus we shall truly be saved.

units.la: Venit autem hic nobis obseruanda œconomia Dei admirabilis, qua fere in omnibus suis operibus vtitur, & quae a communi hominum more alienissima est, adeoq; cum sensu communi palam pugnat. Vt enim immensam hanc mundi machinam ex nihilo, deinde vero ex luto vili hominem, creatorum omnium principem creauit (quod vtrumq; humanae rationi absurdissimum est) ita fere salutem nostram per ea prouehit & euecitur, quae huic aduersa esse videri poterant. Nam thesauros regni sui nobis per Euangelium offert, & diuitias pollicetur, quae omnem huius mundi aestimationem superant: vt vero his potiamur, pauperes spiritu nos fieri, & de nostris omnibus nos desperare iubet. Similiter victoriam de mundo & principe eius, adhaec gaudia aeterna, vitam immortalem, gloriam immarcescibilem nobis promittit: Viam autem ad haec nobis monstrat per crucem, lachrymas, mortem & infamiam. Ita sapientiam nobis praedicat per Euangelium: sed vt iflud mundo, stultitia videtur, ita ad illam non peruenire nobis licet, nisi mundo stulti fiamus, & ea dedi-mus, propter quae nos ille admiratur. Ideo Paulus, cum Legus[?] & multorum aliorum cognitione aequales suos omnes longe post se reliquisset, omnia tamen illa pro stercoribus, imo pro rebus nocentissimis duxit, vt Christum lucrifaceret. Hic ergo imprimis illud requiritur, quod in alijs artibus periti artifices obseruare solent. Qui citharâ perperam ludunt, & chordas inepte tangunt, nisi quod in vsu habuerunt dediscant, citharoedi boni nunquam fient. Ideo Timotheus quidam dupla mercedem ab illis exigebat, qui altero praeceptore aut magistro prius vsi fuerant: quod nimirum maiori cum labore dedisci videret ea, quae male didicimus, quam vera & bona doceri soleant. Ita nisi in Dei & aeternae salutis cognitione totum illud ex animo eiiciamus, quod ex nostra natura nobis adhaeret, aut quod nostro studio aut industria nobis partum est, quodq; nobis & mundo magnificum putatur, & quo diu assueuimus, nihil vnquam proficiemus. Quae causa est, quod ad caelestem hanc philosophiam ineptissimi mortalium sint, qui reliquis praestare videntur: & vt olim in Scribis & Pha-risæus, gentium itemque philosophis plurimum laborauerunt Christus & Apostoli: ita hodie plus negotij nobis exhibent, qui huius seculi sapientiam profitentur, quam homines idiotae & illiterati, quos sua simplicitas ad percipienda aeterna salutis mysteria magis idoneos reddit.
units.tr: Here we must note the wonderful economy of God, which he uses in almost all of his works. It is quite foreign to the common custom of men and openly clashes with common sense. For just as he created this immense machine of the world out of nothing, and then man, the prince of all creatures, out of worthless clay (both of which seem utterly absurd to human reason), so he generally advances and raises up our salvation through things that might seem opposed to it. He offers us the treasures of his kingdom through the Gospel and promises riches that surpass every estimate of this world. But in order to possess them, he commands us to become poor in spirit and to despair of all our own resources. Likewise, he promises us victory over the world and its prince, along with eternal joys, immortal life and unfading glory. Yet he shows us the way to these things through the cross, tears, death and disgrace. So he preaches wisdom to us through the Gospel, but just as that wisdom seems foolishness to the world, we cannot attain it unless we become foolish to the world and give up those things for which the world admires us. Therefore Paul, who had far outstripped all his equals in his knowledge of the Law and of many others, nevertheless counted all those things as dung, or rather as most harmful things, that he might gain Christ. Here, then, above all, we must observe what skilled craftsmen usually observe in other arts. Those who play the lyre badly and touch the strings clumsily will never become good lyre players unless they unlearn what they have practised. Hence a certain Timotheus used to demand double the fee from those who had previously been taught by another master, since he saw that what has been badly learned must be unlearned with greater labour than true and good things are usually taught. Likewise, unless in the knowledge of God and of eternal salvation we cast out of our minds everything that clings to us from our nature, or that we have acquired by our own zeal or industry, and that seems great both to us and to the world, and to which we have long been accustomed, we will never make any progress. This is why the most foolish of mortals are those who seem to excel the rest in this heavenly philosophy. Just as Christ and the Apostles once laboured greatly against the Scribes and Pharisees, and also against the Gentile philosophers, so today those who profess the wisdom of this age give us more trouble than simple and unlettered people, whose simplicity makes them more fit to grasp the mysteries of eternal salvation.

units.la: Caeterum ne quid temere pronunciauisse putetur Apostolus, hoc ipsum rationibus siue argumentis confirmat. Sapientia enim mundi huius (inquit) stultitia est apud Deum. Ex eo autem sequitur, non alios sapere Deo, quam qui mundo stulti putantur. Rursus, si sapientia seculi huius apud Deum stultitia est, facile apparet, illam non modo nihil nobis conferre ad regnum Dei & salutem aeternam tendentibus, verum etiam nocere & impedimento esse. Sunt quidem (vt antea quoq; diximus) praeclara Dei dona artes ingenuae & rerum experientia cum sano iudicio coniuncta, ex quibus quibus prudentia vera nascitur. Sed certis limitibus haec omnia continentur, & usum suum habet in rebus ad huius seculi vitam pertinentibus. Quoad vero regnum Dei & aeternae salutis mysteria, nihil vident aut norunt qui illis solis instructi sunt, imo talibus (ut iam saepe dictum est) stultissima videntur ea, sine quibus salus nostra consistere non potest. Itaque, si quis in regni Dei cognitione arte aut sapientia humana proficere conatur, se his plurimum impediri sentiet. Nam ut nebulae oculorum aciem impediunt, quo minus quae paulo longius distant, videre possint: ita humana ratio suis figmentis mentem nostram obscurat, ut ei dubia & incerta videantur, quaecunque, ad Dei & salutis notitiam faciunt. Imo plerunque fit, ut haec nobis nocentissima esse experiamur, eo quod fidei vehementer obstant, quo minus ijs credamus, quae Dei Verbo praedicantur. Et hunc inobedientiae omnis fontem esse, Saulis atque multorum aliorum exempla docent. Recte ergo Paulus sapientiam huius mundi apud Deum stultitiam esse ait: sed & nobis extremae stultitiae causa est, dum quae nostrum captum superant, ad nostrae rationis calculum revocamus.
units.tr: Moreover, lest it be thought that the Apostle has spoken rashly, he confirms this very point by reasons or arguments. For, he says, the wisdom of this world is foolishness before God. From this it follows that none are wise before God except those who are considered foolish by the world. Again, if the wisdom of this age is foolishness before God, it is readily apparent that it not only contributes nothing to us who strive for the kingdom of God and eternal salvation, but actually harms us and stands in our way. Indeed, the liberal arts and experience of things, joined with sound judgement, are excellent gifts of God (as we have said before), and from them true prudence is born. But all these things are confined within certain limits, and they have their use in matters pertaining to the life of this age. As for the kingdom of God and the mysteries of eternal salvation, those who are equipped with these alone see nothing and know nothing. Indeed, to such people (as has often been said already) those things without which our salvation cannot stand seem most foolish. Therefore, if anyone tries to make progress in the knowledge of God's kingdom by human art or wisdom, he will feel himself greatly hindered by them. For just as mists impede the sight of the eyes so that they cannot see things that are a little further away, so human reason, with its inventions, darkens our mind, so that whatever leads to the knowledge of God and of salvation seems doubtful and uncertain to it. Indeed, it often happens that we find these very things most harmful, because they strongly oppose faith and so prevent us from believing what is preached from the Word of God. The examples of Saul and of many others teach that this is the source of all disobedience. Rightly, then, does Paul say that the wisdom of this world is foolishness before God; but it is also the cause of extreme folly for us, when we bring back to the reckoning of our reason things that exceed our capacity.

units.la: Id vero scripturae sacrae testimoniis duobus nunc confirmat. Scriptum est enim, Capit sapientes in versutia ipsorum. Extat locus hic apud Iobum quinto Cap. & Eliphazi verba sunt, quibus uti voluit Apostolus, quia non sine Spiritus sancti suggestione dicta sunt, & praeclarum sapientiae Dei encomium continent, cuius hoc insigne argumentum est, quod sapientissimos quosque, in ipsorum versutia, id est, proprijs quasi retibus aut laqueis capit & intricat: ut nimirum sibijpsis infamiam & exitium accersant, & prae alijs stultos se esse experiantur, dum omnium sapientissimi haberi volunt. Exempla huius generis passim in historiis habentur, inter quae cumprimis memorabile est, quod de Achitophele scribitur. Et extant alia infinita, quae docent, potentissima regna fere eorum consilijs periisse, qui prius summam sapientiae laudem sustinebant, & rempub. totam sua authoritate fulciebant. Isaias certe Babylonicae Monarchiae suum interitum denuntiaturus, subinde sapientes & divinos illos exprobrat, qui illum neq; nunc praeuidere, neq; cum prae foribus fuerit, avertere possint. Et vulgo iactatur, homines sapientissimos non leviter errare, sed prae alijs maxima stultitiae argumenta praebere: neminem item in propria causa satis esse prudentem aut prouidum. Quod si hoc in externis fit, in quibus civilis prudentiae magnus & necessarius usus est, quid obsecro in religione & regno Dei fiat, ubi mens nostra nihil videre, nihil praesentire, nihil conijcere potest, nisi Spiritus virtute illuminetur? Enimuero, si Apostolorum tempora spectemus, constat Iudaeorum Scribas atq; Sacerdotes non semel consilijs proprijs ita irretitos fuisse, ut quo se verterent, videre non possent. Quid? annon totum orbem terrarum, qui tunc philosophiae & bonarum artium studijs quam maxime florebat, per piscatores illiteratos Deus erudiri & reformari voluit, ut ea ratione mundi sapientia confunderet, & de ea per suos illos servos viles & obscuros triumpharet? His adde, quod in proprijs consilijs Deus sapientes huius seculi tunc quoq; capit, quando Veritatis doctrinam & Christi regnum impedire conantur, & certam de illo sibijpsis victoriam persuadent. Typus huius rei evidentissimus olim in Balako & Balaamo praecessit. Postea hoc ipsum non semel accidit, quando Iudaeorum Seniores & Scribae insidiosis [?] quaestionibus Christum aggressi sunt, ut nulla effugij via patere videretur, nihil autem inde reportarunt quam publicam infamiam, & quod ipsimet Christo summae sapientiae laudem detulerunt.
units.tr: He now confirms this from two testimonies of holy Scripture. For it is written: "He takes the wise in their own craftiness." This passage occurs in Job, chapter 5, and they are the words of Eliphaz. The Apostle wished to use them because they were not spoken without the prompting of the Holy Spirit, and they contain a remarkable praise of the wisdom of God. A notable proof of this is that he catches and entangles the wisest of men in their own craftiness, that is, as it were, in their own nets or snares, so that they bring disgrace and ruin upon themselves, and experience themselves to be fools above others, while they wish to be considered the wisest of all. Examples of this kind are found everywhere in histories, among which the one written about Ahithophel is especially memorable. And there are countless others which teach that the most powerful kingdoms have nearly always perished by the counsels of those who had previously enjoyed the highest reputation for wisdom and who supported the whole commonwealth with their authority. Certainly Isaiah, about to announce the ruin of the Babylonian monarchy, repeatedly rebukes those wise and divine men who could neither foresee it now nor avert it when it was at the doors. And it is commonly said that the wisest men do not err slightly, but furnish the greatest proofs of folly beyond others; likewise, no one is wise or far-sighted enough in his own cause. But if this happens in external matters, in which civil prudence has great and necessary use, what, I ask, happens in religion and in the kingdom of God, where our mind can see nothing, foresee nothing, and conjecture nothing unless it is illumined by the power of the Spirit? Indeed, if we look at the times of the Apostles, it is established that the Scribes and priests of the Jews were more than once so entangled in their own counsels that they could not see where to turn. What then? Did God not wish that the whole world, which at that time flourished most of all in the study of philosophy and the good arts, be taught and reformed through unlettered fishermen, so that by this means he might confound the wisdom of the world and triumph over it through his humble and obscure servants? To these things add that God also catches the wise men of this age in their own counsels when they try to hinder the doctrine of truth and the kingdom of Christ, and persuade themselves of a sure victory over it. The most evident type of this matter came before in Balak and Balaam. Afterwards, this very thing happened more than once, when the elders and Scribes of the Jews attacked Christ with captious questions, so that no way of escape seemed open; yet they gained nothing from it except public disgrace, and they themselves conferred the highest praise of wisdom upon Christ.

units.la: Alterum testimonium ex Psalmo 94. producit Apostolus. Queritur illic Propheta de immani impiorum tyrannorum audacia & crudelitate, qui populum Dei atterant, viduas & aduenas occidant, & pupillos interficiant, idq; impunitatis spe, quod Deum ista non videre neq; intelligere dicant. His vero ad hunc modum respondet: Intelligite stupidi in populo, & o stulti quando tandem sapietis? Is qui aurem creauit, quomodo non audiret? qui oculum finxit, quomodo non videret? Qui gentes corripit, quiq; homines scientiam docet, is non argueret? Novit Dominus cogitationes hominum, quod vanae sint. Quasi diceret: Tam abest, ut quae vos palam facitis Deus ignoret, ut ne cogitationes quidem hominum ipsum latere possint. Nam has quoq; videt & novit, utpote qui corda & renes scrutatur: neq; obiter modo videt, sed vanas & irritas esse videt, id quod vos tandem magno vestro malo experiemini. Est ergo haec insignis sententia, ut quae sola sufficit ad deprimendas humanae confidentiae cristas. Nec enim de verbis temere elapsis, aut de cogitationibus, quae nobis quasi aliud agentibus leviter obrepunt, loquitur propheta, sed πῶν τῶν διαλογισμῶν, id est de cogitationibus, vel potius consultationibus, quas de rebus magnis homines instituunt, & intra animos suos diligenter versant atq; deliberant: quod Paulus observans hominum loco, de quibus propheta loquitur, sapientes posuit. Et has vanas esse dicit. Atqui vanum dicitur nō una ratione. Nam vanum est, quod aliàs inane aut vacuum dicimus. Deinde id quoq;, quod suo effectu caret, neq; ad finem suum pertingit. Adhæc, quod corruptioni obnoxium citò transit, aut perit: quo sen-su totam hanc mundi machinam Paulus vanitati obnoxiam esse scribit. Porrò sensus isti omnes hominum cogitationibus & deliberationibus optimè conueniunt. Vanissimæ enim sunt, quia nihil solidi & veri continent, & rarissimè finem suum assequuntur, denique quasi in fumum abeunt & e-vanescunt, quando impij nihil non fasturi[?] videbantur. Et vanitatis huius causam rectè dixeris, quòd ut homo natura vanus est, sic Dei freno regitur, qui illo etiam inuito consilia & conatus omnes pro suo arbitrio dirigit. Ideo Solomon dicebat: Homo proponit, Deus disponit. At Paulus ista ad suum institutum transfert, ut doceat nihil tribuendum esse nostræ sapientiæ aut industriæ, sed hanc omnem Dei verbo atq; Spiritus magisterio subijci debere.
units.tr: The Apostle produces the second testimony from Psalm 94. There the prophet complains of the monstrous audacity and cruelty of the impious tyrants who crush the people of God, kill widows and strangers, and murder orphans, and do so in the hope of impunity, because they say that God neither sees nor understands these things. To them he responds in this way: "Understand, you foolish among the people, and you fools, when will you at last be wise? He who formed the ear, shall he not hear? He who fashioned the eye, shall he not see? He who chastises the nations, he who teaches men knowledge, shall he not rebuke? The Lord knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain." As if he were saying: so far is God from being ignorant of what you do openly, that not even the thoughts of men can escape his notice. For he also sees and knows these, as he who searches hearts and reins; and he not only sees them in passing, but sees that they are vain and empty, which you will at last learn to your great cost. This, then, is a remarkable sentence, one which alone is sufficient to cut down the crests of human confidence. For the prophet is not speaking of words rashly uttered, or of thoughts that slip in lightly while we are occupied with something else, but of the thoughts [τῶν διαλογισμῶν] or rather the deliberations that men undertake about great matters, and that they turn over and weigh diligently within their minds. Paul, observing this, put "the wise" in the place of the men of whom the prophet speaks, and says that these are vain. Yet "vain" is used in more than one sense. For that is vain which we otherwise call empty or void; and also that which lacks its effect and does not reach its end; and further, that which is subject to corruption and quickly passes away or perishes. In this last sense Paul writes that this whole machine of the world is subject to vanity. Moreover, all these senses agree very well with the thoughts and deliberations of men. For they are most vain, because they contain nothing solid and true, they very rarely attain their end, and finally they pass away like smoke and vanish, when the wicked seemed ready to accomplish everything. And one may rightly say that the cause of this vanity is that, just as man is vain by nature, so he is governed by the bridle of God, who directs all counsels and endeavours according to his own will, even against man's will. Therefore Solomon said: "Man proposes, God disposes." But Paul applies these words to his own purpose, to teach that nothing is to be ascribed to our wisdom or industry, but that all of it ought to be subjected to the Word of God and the teaching of the Spirit.

units.la: Interim in aliis quoque multiplex sententiæ huius usus est. Primò enim terret nos, ne vanis, malis, impuris aut illicitis cogitationibus indulgeamus. Puderet nos earum procul dubio, si eas homines viderent aut nossent. At quantò magis nos cauere decet, ne quid cogitemus, cuius nos apud Deum pudeat, quem nihil eorum celari potest, quæ facimus? Moueat præterea, quòd vanæ sunt & noxiæ. Nam aut finem suum non attingunt, & proinde inani labore nos fatigamus: aut si attingant, sceleris alicuius nobis causa sunt, & ita miseros atque infelices reddunt. Deinde multis molestijs & curis nos liberabit diligens & assidua huius sententiæ consideratio. Nam qui se nihil proficere sentiunt, ij positis & procul relictis curis huius seculi, se totos Dei prouidentiæ comittunt, cui flores agri & auiculas cœli curæ esse norunt. Et sane cur seipsum curis inutilibus exerceat, qui cogitat, se ne latum quidem digitum corporis suæ staturæ adijcere, aut capillos suos albos vel nigros facere posse? Postremò consolationem efficacissimam suggerit, qua nos aduersus impiorum hostium fidei & ecclesiæ consilia atq; minaces conatus confirmemus. Videt enim hos quoq; ex alto Dominus, & jampridem decreuit, ut ferreo Christi sceptro comminuantur, qui saluifico Euangelij pedo[?] gubernari & defendi nolunt. Sed & in priuatis angustijs atq; periculis vehementer nos consolatur, si Deum nostras cogitationes, gemitus, suspiria nouisse credamus, quæ sæpe in nullius hominis sinum audemus deponere. Vides ergo quantum momenti ad veram huius vitæ felicitatem conferre possit unica hæc sententia, si non ofcitanter à nobis consideretur.
units.tr: Meanwhile this sentence is useful in many other ways. First, it frightens us away from indulging in vain, evil, impure or unlawful thoughts. We would surely be ashamed of such thoughts if people saw them or knew of them. How much more care should we take not to think anything of which we would be ashamed before God, from whom nothing we do can be hidden? Moreover, it should move us that such thoughts are both vain and harmful. Either they do not reach their goal, and so we wear ourselves out with fruitless labour; or if they do reach it, they become the cause of some wickedness for us, and so make us wretched and unhappy. Next, a diligent and constant consideration of this sentence will free us from many troubles and cares. Those who feel that they achieve nothing set aside the cares of this world, leave them far behind, and commit themselves wholly to God's providence, knowing that the flowers of the field and the birds of the air are his concern. And indeed, why should a man exhaust himself with useless cares when he reflects that he cannot add so much as a finger's breadth to his stature, or make his white hairs black or his black hairs white? Finally, it supplies a most effective consolation, by which we may be strengthened against the plans and threatening attempts of the enemies of the faith and the Church. For the Lord sees these enemies too from on high, and long ago decided that those who refuse to be governed by the saving yoke of the gospel shall be crushed by Christ's iron sceptre. It also comforts us greatly in private distress and danger, if we believe that God knows our thoughts, groans and sighs, which we often dare not lay in any man's bosom. You see, then, how much this single sentence can contribute to the true happiness of this life, if it is not considered carelessly by us.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui hæc omnia ad suum institutum applicat, dicens: Itaque nullus glorietur in hominibus: ut nimirum aliquem eorum pro fidei & salutis suæ authore agnoscat, & proinde ab eo denominari velit. Id verò prohibet, ut uni Christo omnem hanc gloriam deberi doceat, qui nobis à Patre sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio & redemptio factus est. Rationem verò sui dicti affert: Omnia nanq; vestra sunt, sive Paulus, sive Apollos, sive Cephas, &c. Argumentū huius verbis subest eiusmodi: Stultè & absurdè faciunt, qui seruis suis ita gloriantur, ut hos tanquam heros suos observent, seq; illis subijciant: At quotquot Euangelium vobis prædicant, ij vestri seruī sunt, sive is ego Paulus sim, sive Apollos, sive Cephas: Ergo stultè & præter decorū facitis, quòd hic quidem huius, ille alterius nomine gloriatur, & propter illos in factiones scindimini. Prudenter autem cum superbis illis ostentatoribus cristas humiliare velit, seipsum primo loco nominat, & rursus Apollo atq; Cephām sive Petrum sibi sociat, quos eodem secum animo præditos esse sciebat, ne quid ex inuidia & priuatæ gloriæ studio aduersus illos alteros dicere putetur. Est autem argumentum hoc satis euidens, & à fine ministerij ecclesiastici desumptum. Constat enim causam finalem efficienti & omnibus intermedijs præstantiorem esse. Atqui ministri propter ecclesias à Deo ordinati sunt, ut has colligant, regant, seruent: non autem ecclesiæ vocantur, ut sint, in quas illi imperium aut dominium exerceant. Ergo doctores quidem ecclesiarum seruis et ministri sunt, non aut ē his seruiliter & cum Christi contemptu subesse debent, qui ecclesia vera censeri volunt. Et convenit cū hoc loco, quod alibi dicit Paulus, potestatem doctoribus datam esse ad ædificationem, nō autē ad destructionē. Imprimis aūt huc facit, quod Petrus in sua epist. sic scribit: Presbyteros qui inter vos sunt, precor qui sum & ipse presbyter, ac testis afflictionū Christi, atq; ide gloriæ patefaciēda cōsors. Pascite gregē, qui penes vos est. est, curam illius agentes non coactè, sed libenter: non turpiter affectantes lucrū, sed prompto animo: neq; ut dominantes cleris, sed ut qui sitis (exemplaria gregis: Et cùm apparuerit ille pastorum princeps, reportabitis immarcessibilem illā gloriæ coronam. Quid in hisce Petri verbis habetur, quod dominandi cupiditatem spiret? Tales certè describit qui in ecclesia præsunt, ut eminentiā illam omnem in ministerio consistere doceat, & ecclesiam singulaq; eius membra κλῆρον, id est, forte & hæreditatem dicit, Christi nimirū, cui à Patre dictum fuit: Postula à me, dabo tibi gentes, ut sint hæreditas tua, &c. Ita verò ostendit, nō tam in ecclesiam, quàm in ipsum Christum iniurios esse eos, qui in illam sibi dominiū vendicant. Sufficiunt hæc confutandis Pontificibus, qui nobis nescio quod Petri patrimonium finxerunt, & eo prætextu ius & imperium in ecclesia omne ad se rapiunt, proq; suo arbitrio novos fidei articulos condunt, cultus novos instituunt, & de singulorum salute aut exitio dispensant. At quid huius unquam Apostoli fecerunt? Vestri sunt (inquit) Paulus, Apollos, Cephas: ne ergo his tanquā dominatoribus fidei vestræ gloriemini. At nostri illi apostolici, omnes impie damnant, quicunq; in ipsorum verba iurare nolunt, & Romanæ sedis maioritatem (ut illi loquuntur) aut supereminentiam agnoscere dedignantur. Notus est enim Bonifacij octaui Canon de Maioritate & obedientia, quem his verbis concludit. Porrò subesse Romano Pontifici omnem humanam creaturam declaramus, dicimus, definimus & pronuntiamus omnino esse de necessitate salutis.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who applies all of this to his own purpose, saying: "Therefore let no one glory in men," that is, let no one acknowledge any of them as the author of his faith and salvation, and so wish to be named after him. He forbids this, teaching that all such glory is due to Christ alone, who has been made for us by the Father wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. He gives the reason for his statement: "For all things are yours, whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, etc." The argument behind these words runs like this: They act foolishly and absurdly who boast of their servants in such a way that they regard them as their heroes and submit themselves to them. But all who preach the gospel to you are your servants, whether I, Paul, am the one, or Apollos, or Cephas. Therefore you act foolishly and improperly, in that one of you glories in the name of this man and another in the name of that one, and because of them you are split into factions. Wisely, however, since he wishes to humble the pride of those boastful show-offs, he first names himself, and then again joins Apollos and Cephas, or Peter, to himself, knowing that they had the same mind as he did, so that it should not be thought that he said anything against the others out of envy or a desire for his own glory. This argument is quite clear, and it is drawn from the end of the ecclesiastical ministry. For it is agreed that the final cause is more excellent than the efficient cause and all the intermediate means. But ministers have been appointed by God for the sake of the churches, to gather, rule and keep them; and the churches are not called into being so that the ministers may exercise command or lordship over them. Therefore the teachers of the churches are servants and ministers of them, and they ought not to be subject to them as slaves, with contempt for Christ, if they wish to be counted a true church. This agrees with what Paul says elsewhere, that the power given to teachers is for building up, not for destruction. Above all, what Peter writes in his epistle is relevant: "The elders who are among you I exhort, I who am also an elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and a partaker of the glory to be revealed: feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight of it, not by constraint but willingly, not for filthy lucre but with a ready mind; nor as lording it over the clergy, but being examples to the flock. And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the crown of glory that does not fade away." What is there in these words of Peter that breathes a desire to dominate? Certainly he describes such men as preside in the church, teaching that all eminence in the ministry consists in service, and he calls the church and each of its members the portion [κλῆρον], that is, the lot and inheritance, of Christ himself, to whom the Father said: "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance," and so on. In this way he shows that those who claim lordship over the church are wronging not so much the church as Christ himself. These points are enough to refute the Papists, who have invented for us I know not what patrimony of Peter, and under that pretext seize for themselves all right and rule in the church, and on their own authority frame new articles of faith, institute new forms of worship, and dispose of the salvation or destruction of individuals. But what did any of the apostles ever do like this? "They are yours," he says, "Paul, Apollos, Cephas: do not therefore glory in them as lords of your faith." But those men of ours who call themselves apostolic impiously condemn all who refuse to swear to their words and who disdain to acknowledge the supremacy (as they put it) or the pre-eminence of the Roman see. For the canon of Boniface VIII on the supremacy and obedience is well known, which he concludes with these words: "Moreover, we declare, say, define and pronounce that it is altogether necessary for salvation that every human creature be subject to the Roman Pontiff."

units.la: At quia satis nota est horum impudentia, nos illis omissis in Pauli verbis progrediamur, qui ut argumentū, quod propositu plus ponderis habeat, non contentus dixisse: Omnia vestra sunt, sive Paulus, sive Apollos, sive Cephas: insuper addit: Sive mundus, sive vita, sive mors, sive præsentia, sive futura. Omnia (inquam) vestra sunt, vos autem Christi, Christus verò Dei. Sunt hæc per Comparationem maioris ad minus adiecta, & sensus est: Cùm ita Deus res instituerit, ut quæ in toto mundo præstantissima sunt, ad Ecclesiæ suæ ministerium atq; defensionem destinarit, adeò ut huic vita, mors, præsentia & futura servire debeant, illa verò nullius alterius, quā Filij sui IESU CHRISTI esse velit, cui hanc instar sponsæ iam inde ab æterno elegit: quantò magis ecclesiæ ministri, non domini, censeri debent, qui peculiari vocatione Dei ad hoc destinati sunt, ut sponsam hanc (sicuti Baptista de semetipso fatetur) Christo adducant? Ut verò illos Christi, ita hunc Dei esse dicit, ut de eius officio nos admoneat. Nam à Patre is ordinatus est, ut forma servi assumpta inter illū & nos Mediatorem ageret, & nos ipsi reconciliatos eius peculiū faceret. Unde rursus apparet, quàm iniqui sint & ingrati tantæ gratiæ æstimatores, qui hominum discipulos sese faciunt, cùm ipse Dei Filius ideo in mundum venerit, ut nos Patri suo adduceret, & ab hoc uno pendere doceret. Quia enim ille unicus & solus inter Deum & nos Mediator est, hunc unum caput & magistrum nostrū agnoscamus oportet, siquidem cū Deo communionem habere volumus, in qua omnis nostra salus consistit. Ita verò docet Paulus, factionibus & sectis non solùm ecclesiæ unitatem scindi, verumetiam à Christo nos divelli, imò ipsi Deo Patri injuriam fieri, & proinde salutis jacturam facere eos omnes, qui illis student, ut homines in Christi locum evehant.
units.tr: But since the impudence of these men is well known, let us pass over them and go on to Paul's words. Not content to have said, to make his argument carry more weight, "all things are yours, whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas," he adds: "whether the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come." All things, I say, are yours, and you are Christ's, and Christ is God's. These words are added by way of comparison from the greater to the lesser, and the sense is this: since God has so arranged matters that whatever is most excellent in the whole world he has appointed for the ministry and defence of his Church, so that life, death, the present and the future must serve it, while he wills that the Church belong to no one else but his Son Jesus Christ, whom he chose from eternity as a bride for him, how much more ought the ministers of the church to be counted not its lords but its servants, who are appointed by God's special calling to bring this bride to Christ (as the Baptist confesses of himself)? Moreover, Paul says that the church belongs to Christ and Christ to God, so as to remind us of Christ's office. For he was ordained by the Father, so that, having taken the form of a servant, he might act as Mediator between him and us, and make us, reconciled to him, his own people. Hence again it appears how unjust and ungrateful are those who make themselves disciples of men, when the Son of God himself came into the world in order to bring us to his Father, and taught that everything depends on him alone. For since he is the one and only Mediator between God and us, we ought to acknowledge him alone as our head and teacher, if we wish to have communion with God, in which all our salvation consists. This is what Paul teaches: that factions and sects not only tear apart the unity of the church, but also tear us away from Christ; indeed, they do injury to God the Father himself, and so all those who devote themselves to men, raising them to the place of Christ, suffer the loss of their salvation.

units.la: Continet autem locus hic præclaram doctrinam de hominis Christiani dignitate, quæ simul incomparabilem Dei bonitatem nobis mirificè commendat. Magnum videri poterat, quòd hominem creauit Deus, qui nisi ab eo crearetur, nunquam in rerum natura futurus erat. At maius multò est, quòd mundum totum illius servitio destinauit, & in hoc omnes mundi partes occupatas esse vult. Nec enim temere mundum nostrum esse dicit Paulus.
