Nobis enim cœli pluuias & rorem destillant, nobis Sol oritur & occidit, nobis Luna fulget, nobis sydera lucent, nobis circumfusus aër omnia servat & recreat, nobis perennes aquarum fontes scaturiunt, nobis fluuij decurrunt & terram irrigant, nobis hæc ex suo penu fruges & quæcunq; ad nostrum victum pertinent depromit, nobis ignis suo calore & nativo lumine servit, ad nostrum denique obsequium veniunt iumenta, feræ, pisces, volucres, & quæcunq; alia immensus hic orbis continet. Imò propter nos mundus hic servatur, ut in eo Ecclesia domicilium habeat, donec dies ille fatalis illuxerit, quo terris hisce in nihilum redactis, illa tota in cœlos transferatur, ut cùm sponso suo æternum gaudeat. At quid minuta hæc commemoro? nostro ministerio intenti sunt cœlestes illi spiritus, quos Angelos scriptura dicit, eò quòd propter nos emittantur à Domino, ut in nostram gratiam sua munera obeant. Et ne hic quidem quievit Dei bonitas, sed cùm miseris nobis & mortem æternam meritis Filio suo opus esse videret, ut huius merito redimeremur, hunc quoq; nobis negare noluit. Venit ergo ille in mundum hunc, imo in egestatem, famem, sitim & lachrymarum vallem venit, ut nobis seruiret: seruiuit autem nobis non solum docendo & miraculosis operibus, verumetiam morte sua, quam pro nobis diram & infamem sustinuit, ut nos quoq; Dei filios & regni sui æterni coharedes faceret. Quin huic debemus, quod vitam quoq; & mortem, præsentia & futura Paulus nostra esse ait. Vt enim Christo viuimus, ita in nostrum bonum: ita eidem morimur, & mors nobis ad vitam eius beneficio transitus facta est. Similiter, ut præsentibus libere vtimur, eò quòd vsum eorum ille nobis sanctificauit: sic futura quoque bona iam spe certa & infallibili possidemus, & quo minus illis olim gaudeamus, nemo obstare poterit. Prodest in horum consideratione crebro versari. Habent enim consolationem dulcissimam, & fidem nostram mirifice confirmant, ne de Dei auxilio vnquam desperemus. Arguunt præterea mundi ingratitudinem, qui ecclesiam Christi hostiliter persequitur, cui vni debet quicquid bonorum ex Dei manu quotidie accipit. Etenim cum propter suos cultores terram ille conseruet, nulli tamen in ea difficilius locum inueniunt, nulli item mundo magis inuisi sunt. Rursus officij nostri nos ista admonent, ut magni faciamus fratres nostros, quos tantæ nobiscum dignitatis consortes Deus fecit. Imprimis autem nos hæc consideratio excitare debet, ut cum omnia nostra sint, nos autem Christi simus, huic vni nos totos consecremus, huic viuamus & moriamur, qui pro nobis mortuus & ex morte resuscitatus est, ut viuentibus atq; mortuis dominetur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: This passage contains a remarkable teaching about the dignity of the Christian man, which at the same time commends to us most wondrously the incomparable goodness of God. It might seem a great thing that God created man, who would never have come into being in nature unless he had been created by him. But it is much greater that he has destined the whole world for man's service, and wills that all parts of the world be occupied in it. Paul does not call our world that without reason. For the heavens drip rain and dew for us, the sun rises and sets for us, the moon shines for us, the stars give light for us, the air that surrounds us preserves and refreshes all things for us, perennial springs of water gush forth for us, rivers run down and water the earth for us, the earth brings forth from its store these crops and whatever pertains to our sustenance, fire serves us with its heat and native light, and finally beasts of burden, wild animals, fish, birds, and whatever else this vast world contains come to our service. Indeed this world is preserved on our account, so that the Church may have its dwelling in it until that fatal day dawns on which these lands are reduced to nothing and the whole Church is transferred into heaven, to rejoice forever with her bridegroom. But why do I recount these small things? Those heavenly spirits whom Scripture calls angels are intent on our ministry, since they are sent out by the Lord for our sake, to perform their duties for our benefit. Nor did God's goodness rest even here, but when he saw that we wretched people needed eternal death to be redeemed by the merit of his Son, he was unwilling to deny us this too. He therefore came into this world, indeed into poverty, hunger, thirst and the valley of tears, to serve us; and he served us not only by teaching and by miraculous works, but also by his death, which he endured for us as cruel and infamous, so that he might make us too sons of God and co-heirs of his eternal kingdom. Moreover, Paul says that life and death, things present and things to come, are ours, and we owe this to him. For as we live to Christ, so we live for our good; likewise we die to him, and death has become for us a passage to life by his benefit. Similarly, since he has sanctified the use of present things, we use them freely; so too we already possess future goods with certain and infallible hope, and no one will be able to prevent us from rejoicing in them one day. It is profitable to dwell often on the consideration of these things. For they hold the sweetest consolation and wondrously confirm our faith, so that we never despair of God's help. They also expose the ingratitude of the world, which hostilely persecutes the Church of Christ, though it owes to her alone whatever good things it receives each day from God's hand. For although God preserves the earth on account of his worshippers, nowhere do they find a place more difficult, and none are more hated by the world. Again, these things admonish us of our duty, that we should hold our brothers in high esteem, whom God has made partners with us in such great dignity. Above all, this consideration ought to stir us, that since all things are ours, but we are Christ's, we should wholly consecrate ourselves to him alone, live and die for him who died for us and was raised from death, that he might rule over the living and the dead. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT IIII. HOMILIA XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 4. HOMILY 17.

units.la: Sic nos æstimet homo, ut ministros Christi, & dispensatores mysteriorum Dei. Quod superest autem, illud requiritur in dispensatoribus, ut quis fidelis reperiatur.
units.tr: "Let a man so regard us as the ministers of Christ and the stewards of the mysteries of God. Moreover, it is required of stewards that one be found faithful."

units.la: MULTIS & graviter hucusque Paulus aduersus eos egit, qui ministris ecclesiæ ni-mium addicti, eò usque illos euehebant, ut pro fidei & salutis suæ authoribus agnoscerent, & Christo tantùmnon posposito ab illis denominari vellent. Erat hæc causa grauissimorum malorum: quia & doctrinæ Euangelicæ simplicitas paulatim euanescebat, & ecclesiæ unitas scindebatur, cùm in partes & sectas diuersas distraherentur. Docuit ergo Apostolus, illos omnes propter ecclesiam esse institutos, cuius caput & Dominus sit unus IESUS CHRI-STUS, qui nos sui sanguinis pretio redemptos suum peculium fecerit: ideoque omnem gloriam illi uni transcribi debere. At poterant ista a nonnullis sic accipi, quasi ministros simul & ministerium ecclesiæ deprimeret & omnibus contemnendum siue conculcandum propinaret. Quapropter omissa contentione nunc de re ipsa apertius disserit. Et quia utrinque periculum est, siue contemnantur ministri, siue plus quàm par est illis tribuatur, ita rem tractat, ut inter duo hæc præcipitia viam mediam nobis monstret, quæ nos errare non sinet. Paucis enim verbis tria comprehendit. Primùm in genere docet, quo loco haberi debeant, qui in Ecclesia docent. Deinde horum officium definit, & in quo hoc versetur indicat. Postremò monet, quid potissimùm ab illis requiratur, quid, imprimis spectare debeant.
units.tr: Paul has dealt with those at length and with severity, those who were excessively devoted to the ministers of the Church and carried them so far that they regarded them as the authors of their faith and salvation and wished to be named after them, almost setting Christ aside. This was the cause of very grave evils, for the simplicity of the Evangelical doctrine was gradually fading away, and the unity of the Church was being torn apart as people were drawn into various parties and sects. The Apostle therefore taught that all of them were instituted for the sake of the Church, whose one head and Lord is Jesus Christ, who redeemed us with the price of his blood and made us his own possession; and therefore all glory must be ascribed to him alone. But some could take these things as if he were lowering the ministers and the ministry of the Church and offering them up to be despised and trampled by all. For this reason, setting aside the contention, he now discusses the matter itself more plainly. And since there is danger on either side, whether the ministers are despised or more is attributed to them than is fitting, he handles the matter so as to show us a middle way between these two precipices, which will keep us from going astray. For in a few words he comprises three things. First, he teaches in general how those who teach in the Church ought to be regarded. Then he defines their office and indicates in what it consists. Last, he warns what above all is required of them and what they especially ought to look to.

units.la: De primo his verbis disserit: Sic nos æstimet homo, ut ministros Christi. Ministros autem vocat doctores pro veteri more scripturarum, in quibus passim Ministri aut serui dicuntur ij, quorum opera Deus utitur. Sic ipse Mosem compellat, quando eius authoritatem aduersus Aaronem & Mariam tueri voluit. Et eundem hac vita defunctum isto potissimum elogio Spiritus sanctus in principio libri Iosuæ commendat. Sacerdotes quoq; & Leuitas hoc titulo ornari videmus, quæ Isaias de Christo & bonis eius, quæ is ecclesiæ suæ confert, vaticinans, Christianis omnibus communem facit, dicens: Vos autem Sacerdotes Domini vocabimini, & Ministri Dei nostri dicetur vobis. Nec multum ab illo dissimile est, quòd Prophetæ olim viri Dei dicti fuerunt, ut qui Dei ministerio toti erant consecrati. Christus autem, quoties Apostolos de regno terreno & primatu contendentes reprimere voluit, semper suæ illos conditionis admonet, quòd nimirum ad ministrandum destinati sint, & proinde eum alijs præstantiorem fore, qui plus alijs ministrauerit. Et Paulus frequenter in epistolarum inscriptionibus se atq; collegas suos IESV CHRISTI seruos dicere consueuit. Vnde colligimus hoc nomen omnibus ijs etiam deberi, qui iam illorum partes in Ecclesia obeunt. Et recte ita dicuntur: Quia ut olim Sacerdotes, cùm Christi typum gererent, medij stabant inter Deum & populum: sic ijsti inter Christum & ecclesiam quasi locum medium tenent, & utriq; seruiunt. Christi enim ministri sunt, eò quòd is illorum ministerio & opera utitur in colligenda & seruanda ecclesia, ut ad Ephef. 4. cap. pluribus docetur. Rursus huius etiam ministri sunt, quia hac Christo, ceu sponsam, adducunt, seq; totos illi impendunt. Ut ergo paranymphus tam sponso quàm sponsæ officium præstat, dum hanc illi coiungit: ita qui Euangelium prædicant, Christo simul & ecclesiæ seruiunt: quia vero officium hoc omne potissimum Christo impenditur, à quo vocationem quoq; suam habent, ferè huius ministri dicuntur.
units.tr: He discusses the first point in these words: "Let a man so regard us as the ministers of Christ." He calls them ministers, that is, teachers, following the old manner of the Scriptures, in which everywhere those through whose work God acts are called ministers or servants. So God addresses Moses when he wished to defend his authority against Aaron and Miriam. And the Holy Spirit, at the beginning of the book of Joshua, commends the same man, now dead, above all by this title. We also see priests and Levites adorned with this title, and Isaiah, prophesying about Christ and the blessings which he confers on his Church, makes it common to all Christians, saying: "But you shall be called the priests of the Lord, and you shall be named the ministers of our God." Nor is it much different that the prophets were once called men of God, as those wholly devoted to the ministry of God. Christ, whenever he wished to restrain the apostles when they contended about an earthly kingdom and primacy, always reminded them of their condition, namely that they were appointed to minister, and that therefore he would be more excellent than the others who had ministered more. And Paul frequently used to call himself and his colleagues servants of Jesus Christ in the openings of his letters. From this we gather that this name is owed also to all those who now perform their part in the Church. And they are rightly so called: just as the priests of old, bearing the type of Christ, stood as mediators between God and the people, so these men hold a middle place between Christ and the Church, and serve both. For they are ministers of Christ, because he uses their ministry and work in gathering and preserving the Church, as is taught at length in Ephesians chapter 4. Again, they are also ministers of the Church, because they bring her to Christ as a bride and devote themselves wholly to her. Just as the best man performs the office both for the bridegroom and for the bride while he joins her to him, so those who preach the Gospel serve Christ and the Church at once; but because this whole office is chiefly performed for Christ, from whom they also have their calling, they are generally called ministers of Christ.

units.la: Est autem utilissima huius nominis aut tituli consideratio. Primò enim ambitionem doctorum reprimit, quod factu imprimis necessarium est. Ut enim omnes naturali & ex primis parentibus in nos deriuato gloriæ desiderio flagramus: ita facile hoc in flammas surgit, si nos præ alijs eminere contingat. Et quàmuis in quouis vitæ genere ambitio multorum malorum causa sit, eadem tamen in ecclesiæ ministerio nocentissima est: quia contentiones gignit, & sectas atq; partium studia inuehit, quibus ecclesiæ unitas atq; forma propria omnino dissipatur. Deinde ad asserendam illorum authoritatem plurimum facit Ministrorum titulus. Quia enim IESV CHRISTI ministri sunt, non poterunt à quoquam contemni, quin quæ ipsis irrogatur ignominia in ipsum Christum redundet. Eius enim vox est: Qui vos audit, me audit: qui vero vos reiicit, me reiicit: qui autem me reiicit, reiicit eum qui misit me. Simul ergo titulus hic consolationem dulcissimam habet, qua Euangelij prædicones sese aduersus iniqua impiorum iudicia munire possunt. Nec enim dubium est, quin in sua vocatione sedulò seruientes Christus tueatur. Itaq; cum Paulo aduersus contumaces magno animo insurgere & dicere possunt: An experimentum quæritis loquentis in nobis Christi? Præterea officij sui hoc titulo admonentur doctores. Nam si Christi serui sunt, non suas res, sed illius negotiū agere debent. Nec enim sui iuris est seruus, nec quisquam alius, qui suam operam alteri locauit. Ergo illi quoq; unum Christum respicere, huius mandata obseruare, & ut huic omnes obtemperent curare debent: imprimis autem cauendum erit, ne quid ex suo arbitrio faciant, quod illius voluntati minus conueniat. Docet item Serui aut Ministri vocabulum, ne sibiipsis vel in totam ecclesiam, vel in suos conseruos ius aut imperium vendicent. Et hoc maximè Christus obseruauit, quādo de primatu (ut paulò ante diximus) contendentes monuit, ut mutuis officijs se inuicem præuenire studeant. Grauiter autem de hoc Petrus in sua epistola disserit, cuius verba nuper adduximus. Itaq; Christo subesse discant, quicunq; in ecclesia docendi munus sustinent: & hac illius sponsam esse meminerint, cui non modò suas curas, labores, vigilias, verumetiam vitam & sanguinem debeant. Viderunt hoc Apostoli, quibus hæc summa & præcipua cura fuit, ut quàm plurimos Christo adducerent, & eos qui huic nomen dederant, in fidei puritate retinerent. Paulus certè de Corinthijs in posteriori epistola scribens, zelum Dei, quo is erga nos ardet, in se transferens ait: Ambio vos Dei zelotypia: præpa rauì enim vos, quos vni viro pro virgine pura sisterem, nempe Christo. Ut ergo qui alterius nomine procum agit, si fidelis sit, nullū officium subterfugit, quo virginem amico suo demereri se posse putat: Ita ministrorū ecclesiæ est omnem laborem subire, quo ecclesiam iuuari & promoueri posse arbitrantur, ut Christi sponsa maneat intemerata. At quæ nostri seculi infelicitas est, hodie passim peccatur. Nam qui Romanæ sedis prærogatiua, quam iactant, turgidi, se Apostolicos esse dicunt, ij quidem Serui seruorum dici volunt, at ijdem superbia intolerabili in omnes ecclesias simul atq; episcopos sibi ius atq; imperium sumunt. Quos enim pro officijs sibi factis aliquo præmio remunerare volunt, eos episcopos & ecclesiarum pastores creant, homines plerunq; ineptos, indoctos & ferè etiā moribus turpissimis infames: simul verò eosdem in sua verba iurare cogunt, & ita tam his quàm ecclesijs passim dominantur. Quòd si ad nostros transeas, multos quidem est videre, qui ecclesiæ ministerium ambiunt, sed qui ministros Christi agant non ita multos inuenies. Plerosq; enim aut stipendij amplissimi cupido, aut otij ignaui spes allicit, ut munus hoc suscipiant. At ubi iam semel obtinuerunt, iam in docendo segnes & frigidi, in hortando ignaui, in consolando nimium desidiosi sunt: & aut Mammonae seruiunt, deq; opibus colligendis cogitant, aut Bacchi mystas agunt, & alij studijs à suo munere alienissimis occupati, ecclesiam & huius curam nihil ad se pertinere putant. At omnibus hisce vitijs medebimur, si Ministri tituli nobis semper ob oculos versetur.
units.tr: Consideration of this name or title is very useful. In the first place, it restrains the ambition of teachers, which above all must be done. For just as we all burn with a natural desire for glory, derived to us from our first parents, so this readily rises into flames if it happens that we stand out above others. And although ambition in any kind of life is the cause of many evils, in the ministry of the Church it is most harmful, because it breeds contentions and brings in sects and partisan zeal, by which the unity and proper form of the Church is utterly destroyed. Next, the title of minister greatly helps to establish their authority. For since they are ministers of Jesus Christ, they cannot be despised by anyone without the insult offered to them redounding upon Christ himself. For his word is: "He who hears you hears me, and he who rejects you rejects me; and he who rejects me rejects him who sent me." Thus this title also holds the sweetest consolation, by which the preachers of the Gospel can fortify themselves against the unjust judgments of the impious. For there is no doubt that Christ defends those who serve diligently in their calling. Therefore they can rise up boldly with Paul against the obstinate and say: "Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?" Moreover, the teachers are reminded of their office by this title. For if they are servants of Christ, they ought to attend not to their own affairs but to his business. A servant is not his own master, nor is anyone else who has hired out his labour to another. Therefore they too ought to look to Christ alone, observe his commands, and take care that all obey him; above all, they must be careful not to do anything at their own pleasure that less agrees with his will. The word servant or minister also teaches them not to claim for themselves any right or rule either over the whole Church or over their fellow servants. Christ especially observed this when, as we said a little earlier, he warned those contending over primacy that they should strive to outdo one another in mutual services. Peter also discusses this seriously in his letter, whose words we lately cited. Therefore, let all who undertake the duty of teaching in the Church learn to be subject to Christ, and let them remember that they are the bride of him to whom they owe not only their cares, labours and watchings, but even their life and blood. The Apostles saw this, for whom this was the highest and chief concern, that they might bring as many as possible to Christ and keep those who had given their name to him in the purity of faith. Paul, writing to the Corinthians in his second letter, transferring to himself the zeal of God with which he burns toward us, says: "I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God; for I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ." Therefore, just as one who acts as a suitor in another's name, if he is faithful, shrinks from no duty by which he thinks he can win the virgin for his friend, so it is the duty of the ministers of the Church to undergo every labour by which they believe the Church can be helped and advanced, so that she may remain the unspotted bride of Christ. But such is the unhappiness of our age that today there is sin everywhere. For those who, puffed up with the prerogative of the Roman see which they boast of, say that they are Apostolic, indeed wish to be called servants of servants, yet at the same time, with intolerable pride, take to themselves right and rule over all churches and bishops. For those whom they wish to reward with some prize for services done to them, they appoint as bishops and pastors of churches, men generally unfit, unlearned, and almost even infamous for the most shameful morals; and at the same time they compel these same men to swear to their words, and so they lord it everywhere over both these men and the churches. But if you turn to our own people, you may see many who court the ministry of the Church, but you will find not so many who act as ministers of Christ. For most are drawn to take up this office either by a desire for an very ample stipend or by the hope of idle leisure. But once they have obtained it, they are then sluggish and cold in teaching, slack in exhorting, and far too lazy in consoling; and they either serve Mammon and think about gathering wealth, or they play the mystics of Bacchus, and others, occupied with pursuits most alien to their office, think that the Church and its care do not concern them. But we shall remedy all these vices if the title of minister is always before our eyes.

units.la: At quia ministeriorum & seruitiorum non unum genus est, apertius definit Paulus, quales ministri sint qui in Ecclesia Euangelium prædicant: Oeconomi nimirum & dispensatores mysteriorum Dei. Quo loco ad parabolam, qua Christus utitur, alludit. Is enim cum de nouissimorum temporum moribus atq; periculis disseruisset, tandem de ecclesiarum pastoribus aut ministris loquitur ad hunc modum: Quis nam est fidelis dispensator ac prudens, quem constituet Dominus super famulitium suum, ut in tempore det demensum aut alimetum? Sumitur autem parabola hæc ex ipsa ecclesiæ conditione, quam Dei domum dici, alibi quoq; docuimus. Ut enim paterfamilias domum habet, in qua habitat, ad quam item suos colligit, & in qua opes suas recondit: Ita Deus inter homines sibi domicilium deligit, ad cuius contubernium aut societatem omnes suos vocat, quos ante iacta mundi huius fundamenta in Christo elegit, ut illic suæ gratiæ diuitias illis communicet. Est domus hæc Ecclesia, quam in Symbolo Apostolico profitemur Sanctorum omnium communionem esse, & cui ibidem testamur præparatam esse remissionem peccatorum, resurrectionem carnis huius gloriosam & vitam æternam. Comprehenduntur his omnes diuinæ gratiæ thesauri, inter homines autem dispensantur per Euangelij prædicationem: & ideo qui hanc administrant, mysteriorum Dei dispensatores à Paulo dicuntur.
units.tr: But since there is not just one kind of ministry and service, Paul more clearly defines what sort of ministers those are who preach the Gospel in the Church: namely, stewards and dispensers of the mysteries of God. In this place he alludes to the parable that Christ uses. For Christ, after discoursing on the customs and dangers of the last times, finally speaks of the pastors or ministers of the churches in this manner: "Who then is the faithful and wise steward, whom the Lord has set over his household, to give them their portion of food in due season?" This parable is taken from the very condition of the Church, which we have also shown elsewhere to be called the house of God. For just as a householder has a house in which he lives, to which he gathers his people, and in which he stores up his wealth, so God has chosen for himself a dwelling place among men, into fellowship with which he calls all his own, whom before the foundation of the world he chose in Christ, so that there he may share with them the riches of his grace. This house is the Church, which we profess in the Apostles' Creed to be the communion of all the saints, and in which we testify that forgiveness of sins is prepared, and the glorious resurrection of this flesh, and eternal life. All the treasures of divine grace are contained in it, and they are dispensed among men through the preaching of the Gospel; and therefore those who administer it are called by Paul the dispensers of the mysteries of God.

units.la: Quod ergo Christus suæ familiæ demensum aut alimentum siue cibum vocat, hoc Apostolus mysterium Dei dicit. At omnibus istis non aliud quam Euangelium significatur, quo mysterium illud Dei nobis reuelatur, quod à temporibus æternis tacitum fuit (ut vlt. Cap. ad Rom. scribitur) nunc autem ex imperio æterni Dei manifestum fieri debet apud omnes gentes, ut ad fidei obedientiam adducantur, & in Christo salui fiant. Imprimis autem huc referri debet, quod ad Ephes. cap. 3. sic scribit: Audiuistis dispensationem gratiæ Dei, quæ data est mihi inter vos: Quòd scilicet Deus per reuelationem notum mihi fecerit mysterium: quod aliis æetatibus non innotuit filijs hominum, ut tunc reuelatum est sanctis Apostolis eius & Prophetis per Spiritum: Gentes scilicet esse hæredes, & concorpores consortesq; promissionis eius in Christo per Euangelium, &c. Itaq; mysteria Dei, quorum hic meminit, non alia sunt, quàm quæ per Euangelium nobis prædicantur: eadem verò familiæ Christi demensum aut cibus seu alimentum sunt, quia IESVM CHRISTVM nobis offerunt, panem illum vitæ, qui per fidem apprehensus animas nostras satiat, recreat, confortat, totum deniq; hominem seruat ad vitam æternam. Ita seipsum ille exponit, Ioan. 6. cap. dicens: Ego sum panis ille viuus, qui è cælo descendi: Si quis ederit ex hoc pane, viuet in æternum. Et rursus: Ego sum panis ille vitæ: qui venit ad me, nequaquam esuriet: & qui credit in me, nö sitiet vnquam. Idem ergo Christus & panis & fons aquæ viuæ est, & solus ad hominem alendum atq; seruandu sufficit. Hunc ergo ministri prædicare, & quæ nobis meruit bona per Euangelium omnibus offerre debent: & quia per illum nobis suam sapientiam Deus communicat, imò illum nobis sapientiam, iustitiam, sanctificationem atq; redemptionem fecit, merito ipsius Dei mysteria dispensare dicuntur, quicunq; illum sincere & vere prædicant. At Euangelij doctrinæ Sacramenta, ceu appendices, annexa esse scimus, quibus & promissiones suas Deus obsignat, & nos ad obedientiam ipsi præstandam obstringit. Illa ergo doctrinæ coniungi debent, ut ministerium omni ex parte absolutum fit. Scio Pontificios doctores per mysteria hæc sacrificium corporis & sanguinis Christi intelligere, quæ illi in Missa pro viuis & defunctis immolari fabulantur. Sed nihil huius Apostoli vnquam docuerunt, & Christus illos non ad sacrificandum, sed ad prædicandum misit. Missifices verò isti seipsos produnt, dum id docent. Si enim corpus & sanguis Christi mysteria illa sunt, quæ toti ecclesiæ dispensari debent, cur ipsi ex illis epulum priuatum faciunt? cur non quoties Missam faciunt, cum tota ecclesia communicant? cur huic poculum sanguinis Christi subducunt? Sunt igitur hæc commenta non minus impia quàm inepta.
units.tr: What Christ therefore calls the portion of food or the nourishment of his household, the Apostle calls the mystery of God. But all these terms signify nothing other than the Gospel, by which that mystery of God is revealed to us, which was hidden from eternal times (as is written at the end of the letter to the Romans), but which now, by the command of the eternal God, must be made manifest among all nations, so that they may be brought to the obedience of faith and be saved in Christ. Above all, what he writes in Ephesians 3 should be referred here: "You have heard of the stewardship of God's grace which was given to me among you: that by revelation God made known to me the mystery, which in other ages was not made known to the sons of men, as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit: namely, that the Gentiles are heirs together, and members of the same body, and partakers of his promise in Christ through the Gospel," etc. Therefore the mysteries of God, of which he speaks here, are none other than those which are preached to us through the Gospel; and these same things are the portion or food of the household of Christ, because they offer us JESUS CHRIST, that bread of life which, apprehended by faith, satisfies, refreshes and strengthens our souls, and at last preserves the whole man unto eternal life. He himself explains this in John 6, saying: "I am the living bread which came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever." And again: "I am the bread of life; he who comes to me shall never hunger, and he who believes in me shall never thirst." Christ is therefore both the bread and the fountain of living water, and alone is sufficient to nourish and preserve man. Ministers must therefore preach him, and offer to all the good things which he has merited for us through the Gospel; and because through him God communicates his wisdom to us, indeed because he has made him to be for us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption, those who preach him sincerely and truly are rightly said to dispense the mysteries of God itself. But we know that the sacraments are attached to the doctrine of the Gospel as appendages, by which God also seals his promises and binds us to render obedience to him. These must therefore be joined to the doctrine, so that the ministry may be complete in every respect. I know that the Papist teachers understand by these mysteries the sacrifice of the body and blood of Christ, which they fable is offered in the Mass for the living and the dead. But this Apostle never taught anything of the kind, and Christ sent them not to sacrifice but to preach. Those who teach this betray themselves as mass-priests. For if the body and blood of Christ are those mysteries which must be dispensed to the whole Church, why do they make a private feast of them? Why, whenever they say Mass, do they not communicate with the whole Church? Why do they withhold the cup of the blood of Christ from it? These inventions are therefore no less impious than they are absurd.

units.la: Nos potius videamus, quam magnifice Euangelium & eius praedicationem Paulus commendet, quando per hanc mysteria Dei dispensari dicit. Nec id temere dici putemus. Continetur enim illo tota Christi doctrina, quae se discipulis omnia ea manifestauisse testatur, quaecunq; à Patre acceperit. Et alibi clamat: Doctrina mea non est mea, sed Patris qui misit me. Unde colligimus, Euangelij doctrinam perfectam esse, & omnia ea continere, quae ad regnum Dei nobis cognita necessaria sunt. Neminem ergo eorum clamores moueant, qui nobis hodie Patres & Concilia obtrudunt, & quae in his decreta sunt non minus fidei mereri aiunt, quam quae Euangelio traduntur. At quia de his saepe diximus, nunc obseruemus, eos diuina sapientiae & gratiae contemptores esse, qui Euangelij praedicationem fastidiunt. Simul etiam curiositatem nostram frenare debet, quod in illo mysteria tradi audimus. Nam vt in cap. 2. audiuimus, est haec sapientia illa Dei, quae omnem humani ingenij captum superat. Quid ergo mirum, si aliqua non primo statim intuitu intelligamus? Soletur nos potius, quod ea ratione diligentiam nostram Deus excitare solet, & quod idem fidei oculis quasi coram spectanda exhibet, quae nullo hominum acumine inuestigari possunt. Et quamuis non omnia omnibus patent, tantum tamen ex suis illis mysteriis Deus cuiq; reuelat, quantum ad salutem obtinendam potest sufficere.
units.tr: Let us rather consider how magnificently Paul commends the Gospel and its preaching, when he says that through it the mysteries of God are dispensed. Nor should we think that this is said rashly. For the whole doctrine of Christ is contained in it, who testifies that he has made known to his disciples all things which he has received from the Father. And elsewhere he declares: "My doctrine is not mine, but his who sent me." From this we gather that the doctrine of the Gospel is perfect and contains all those things which are necessary for us to know concerning the kingdom of God. Therefore let not the clamours of those move us who today thrust upon us the Fathers and Councils, and say that the decrees made in them deserve no less faith than those things which are handed down in the Gospel. But since we have often spoken of these matters, let us now observe that those who scorn the preaching of the Gospel are despisers of divine wisdom and grace. At the same time, the fact that we hear mysteries delivered in it ought also to restrain our curiosity. For, as we heard in chapter 2, this is that wisdom of God which surpasses the grasp of every human intellect. What wonder, then, if we do not understand some things at the first glance? We should rather be comforted by the fact that God is wont to stir up our diligence in this way, and that he sets before the eyes of faith, as if to be beheld face to face, those things which cannot be searched out by any human keenness. And although not all things lie open to all, God nevertheless reveals to each person from these mysteries of his only so much as can suffice for obtaining salvation.

units.la: Caeterum ne qui nudo titulo contenti, otiosa & inani dignitate superbirent, plus quiddam exigi docet Apostolus. Quod superest (inquit) illud requiritur in dispensatoribus, vt quis fidelis reperiatur. Christus in sua parabola cum fide prudentiam coniungit, Paulus vtramq; vno verbo complectitur: Quia qui fidus est, is in commissio sibi munere prouidus quoq; & circumspectus, nullam huius recte obeundi occasionem negliget. In praesenti vero aemulos suos perstringit Paulus, qui in hoc vnum intenti erant, vt ipsi eminerent, ea autem facile negligebant, quibus Christi gloria & ecclesiae salus poterat promoueri. At multa comprehendit fides ista, quam in oeconomo aut dispensatore ecclesiastico requirit. Primum, ne quae Domini sunt, ipse alienet & sibi vendicet. Idenim improbi dispensatores faciunt, quos dissipatores & fures rectius dixeris. Cu-ret ergo minister, vt Christo suum in ecclesia ius integrum maneat, vt hunc omnes vnicum saluti suae authorem agnoscant, & ne vel suos vel aliorum hominum seruos faciat eos, quos Christus sui sanguinis pretio sibi acquisiuit. Fuerunt in hoc Apostoli admodum diligentes, qui ne boni quidem Zeli praetextu eorum simplicitate abusi sunt vnquam, quos sibi plus aequo tribuere videbant. De Ioanne enim & Petro scribitur, quod cum ob paralyticum miraculose sanatum omnes in illos intenti essent, illi hinc dicendi occasione arrepta concionem his verbis exorsi sunt: Viri Israelitae, quid miramini super hoc? aut quid intentos oculos in nos habetis, quasi nostra virtute aut pietate effecerimus, vt hic ambularet? Deus ille Abrahami, Isaaci & Iacobi, Deus (inquam) patrum nostrorum, glorificauit Filium suum IESVM, &c. Simile quid Paulum & Barnabam apud Lystrenses fecisse legimus. Et postulat hoc imprimis ministerij ecclesiastici finis atq; scopus, quem esse diximus, vt ecclesia Christo sponso suo pura & intemerata virgo coniungatur. Si qui ergo honorem, qui Christo debetur, vel in se vel in alios transferunt, ij leliones potius sacrilegi, quam fideles CHRISTI IESV paranymphi dici merentur. Quod vtinam expenderent, qui nobis Deos eiusmodi fingunt, qui hodie inuocari & diuinis honoribus coli volint.
units.tr: Moreover, lest anyone, content with a bare title, should grow proud of an empty and idle dignity, the Apostle teaches that something more is required. "What remains (he says) is this, that a man be found faithful." In his parable Christ joins prudence to faith; Paul embraces both in one word: for he who is faithful is also watchful and circumspect in the office entrusted to him, and will neglect no opportunity of discharging it rightly. In the present passage Paul also rebukes his rivals, who were intent on this one thing, that they themselves should stand out, but easily neglected those things by which the glory of Christ and the salvation of the Church could be promoted. Yet this faithfulness, which he requires in a steward or ecclesiastical dispenser, comprehends many things. First, that he should not alienate for himself, or claim as his own, what belongs to the Lord. For this is what wicked stewards do, whom you would more rightly call squanderers and thieves. The minister must therefore take care that the full right of Christ in the Church remains intact, that all acknowledge him as the sole author of their salvation, and that he does not make slaves of those whom Christ has acquired for himself at the price of his own blood, either of himself or of other men. The Apostles were very diligent in this; they never abused the simplicity of those whom they saw attributing to them more than was fitting, not even under the pretext of good zeal. For we read of John and Peter that, when all were intent upon them because of the paralytic who had been miraculously healed, they seized the occasion for speaking and began a sermon with these words: "Men of Israel, why do you marvel at this? Or why do you fix your eyes upon us, as though by our own power or piety we had made this man walk? The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the God, I say, of our fathers, has glorified his Son Jesus," etc. We read that Paul and Barnabas did something similar among the Lystrans. And the very aim and purpose of the ecclesiastical ministry, which we have said is this, that the Church be joined as a pure and undefiled virgin to Christ her bridegroom, demands this above all. If therefore anyone transfers to himself or to others the honour that is owed to Christ, such men deserve to be called sacrilegious procurers rather than faithful friends of the bridegroom, the best men of Jesus Christ. Would that those who today fashion for us such gods, who wish to be invoked and to be honoured with divine worship, would weigh this carefully.

units.la: Deinde fidelis erit nostra hic dispensator, si nihil tradat ecclesiae, quam quod a Domino ipse accepit, vtq; fideliter ea omnia tradat, neque eorum aliquid celet. Admonet de hoc Christus, quando discipulis dicit: Docete eos seruare, quaecunq; tradidi vobis. Et Ieremia olim dicebat Dominus: Ad omnia, ad quae te mittam, ibis: & quaecunque mandauero tibi, loqueris. Ecce ego pono verba mea in os tuum, &c. Quibus consentit, quod postea Ezechieli fuit dictum: Audies ver-bum ex ore meo, & diserte monebis eos ex me. Et huius quoq; obseruantissimi fuerunt, quotquot in suo ministerio commendantur. Moses certe cum Deo colloquebatur, & quae ex illo audiebat, bona fide ad totum populum referebat, & ideo hoc testimonio ornatus fuit a Deo, quod in tota domo eius fidelis fuerit. De prophetis nō opus est dicere, cum ipse rerū euentus de illorū fide testetur. Et Apostolos ab ijs, quae ex Christo didicerant, ne latum vngnem discessisse constat. Paulus certe in casibus dubijs inter sua consilia & expressa Dei mandata diligenter distinguit, ne vel temerarius vel male fidus in doctrina sua deprehendatur. Et cum Coenam Domini mysticam Corinthij tur-piter prophanauissent, eos ad primam institutionem revocat, nihil autem ex suo capite praescribit. Haec igitur exempla tam in doctrina quam in Sacramentorum administratione ministri omnes imitentur, & ita Christo simul atq; ecclesiae eius fideles erunt. Peccant igitur, qui noua dogmata ecclesijs obtrudunt, quae nulla Christi aut Scripturarum authoritate probari possunt. Quid enim paleae cum tritico? inquit Ieremias. Et notum est illud Isaiae, quod Christus suo testimonio confirmauit: Frustra me colunt docentes doctrinas hominum. Peccant item, qui Sacramentorum ritus mutant, aut cultus nouos instituunt, qui ad Dei quidem gloriam nihil faciunt, multorum vero conscientias grauant. Parum etiam fidi sunt, qui ut apud homines bonam gratiam ineant, ad multa connituntur, multa dissimulant, vel etiam laeta omnia pollicentur ijs, quos scelerum redargutione, & seueris poenarum comminationibus terreri oportebat. Tales olim erant Achabi prophetae, quos ipse in pretio habebat, & qui ipsi crudelis exitij authores fuerunt. Tales etiam fuerunt, qui Ieremiae refliterunt, & infelicem populum falsis pollicitationibus detinuerunt, quo minus resipisceret. Et tales fore praedixit Paulus, qui nouissimis temporibus conciones suas eorum libidini accommodant, quorum aures pruritum blandiloquentiae desiderant. Dicuntur hi omnes apud Isaiam canes muti, & eo titulo perfidiae eos arguit Spiritus sanctus. Ut enim canis infidus est, qui offa obiecta, aut etiam baculo vel minis mouetur, ut furi in aedes hori[?] sui ingressu tutu permittat: ita plus quam perfidi sunt, qui cum Christi & ecclesiae eius ministri videri velint, tamen honorum, amicitiarum & lucri illece-bris, aut minis atq; periculi alicuius metu adducuntur, ut eos perire sinant, quorum salutem ipsorum fidei Deus commendauit. Quod utinam attentius observarent, qui hodie de quorundam ministrorum seueritate & nimio rigore (ut ipsorum verbis utar) conqueruntur, & (ut olim Isaiae temporibus nonnulli solebant) fidis Christi seruis dicere audent: Ne contemplemini nobis plana, loquimini nobis blanda, contemplamini illusiones, recedite à via, declinate à semita. facite quiescere à facie nostra Sanctum Israelis. Audiuntur huius generis multa hodie: sed qui ita loquuntur & sentiunt, eorum similes sunt, qui cum morbis totum corpus foede depascentibus laborent, medico tamen praescribunt, ne aliqua acriori medendi ratione utatur, quae sola malo indies serpenti obstare poterat.
units.tr: Our steward will be faithful here only if he hands on to the Church nothing but what he has himself received from the Lord, and if he passes on all of it faithfully and conceals none of it. Christ warns of this when he says to his disciples: "Teach them to observe whatever I have delivered to you." The Lord said the same to Jeremiah long ago: "Wherever I send you, you shall go, and whatever I command you, you shall speak. Behold, I put my words in your mouth," and so on. To this agrees what was later said to Ezekiel: "You shall hear a word from my mouth, and you shall warn them plainly from me." All who are commended for their ministry have been most careful of this. Moses certainly spoke with God and in good faith reported to the whole people what he heard from him, and for this reason God honoured him with the testimony that he was faithful in all his house. There is no need to speak of the prophets, since the outcome of events itself bears witness to their faithfulness. It is also certain that the apostles did not depart by a hair's breadth from what they had learned from Christ. Paul, in doubtful cases, carefully distinguishes between his own counsel and the express commands of God, so that he might not be found either rash or unfaithful in his teaching. And when the Corinthians had shamefully profaned the mystical Supper of the Lord, he called them back to its first institution and prescribed nothing of his own invention. Let all ministers, then, imitate these examples both in teaching and in the administration of the sacraments, and so they will be faithful both to Christ and to his Church. They sin, therefore, who thrust new doctrines upon the churches, doctrines that cannot be proved by the authority of Christ or of the Scriptures. "For what has the chaff to do with the wheat?" says Jeremiah. And that saying of Isaiah, which Christ confirmed by his own testimony, is well known: "In vain do they worship me, teaching the doctrines of men." Those also sin who change the rites of the sacraments or introduce new forms of worship, which indeed contribute nothing to the glory of God but weigh heavily on the consciences of many. Those are also untrustworthy who, in order to win good favour with men, strain after many things, dissemble many things, or even promise all manner of pleasant things to those who ought rather to be terrified by the rebuke of their sins and by the severe threats of punishment. Such were the prophets of Ahab, whom he held in high esteem and who were themselves the authors of his cruel ruin. Such also were those who opposed Jeremiah and kept the unhappy people bound by false promises, so that they would not repent. And Paul foretold that such men would come in the last times, men who adapt their sermons to the lust of those whose ears crave the itching of flattering speech. In Isaiah all these are called dumb dogs, and the Holy Spirit charges them with treachery under that title. For as a dog is faithless when he is moved by a morsel thrown to him, or by a stick or threats, so that he lets a thief enter his house or garden unchallenged, so those are more than faithless who, though they wish to be seen as ministers of Christ and his Church, are yet drawn by the allurements of honours, friendships and gain, or by threats and the fear of some danger, to let perish those whose salvation God has committed to their faith. Would that those who today complain of the severity and excessive rigour of certain ministers (to use their own words) would observe this more attentively. They, like the people in Isaiah's day, dare to say to the faithful servants of Christ: "Do not look at us for what is plain; speak to us smooth things; look for illusions; turn aside from the way, leave the path; cause the Holy One of Israel to cease from before us." Many such words are heard today. But those who speak and think in this way are like those who, while suffering from diseases that foully consume the whole body, nonetheless instruct the physician not to use any sharper method of healing, although that alone could check the evil that creeps on day by day.

units.la: Postremò, tunc demum Christi minister & œconomus vere fidelem se praebebit, si omnia sua ad finem & scopum proprium ministerij dirigat. Est ũ[?] gloria Christi & salus ecclesiae. Quae duo etsi diuersa videantur, revera tamen vnum sunt: quia neq; Christus suam gloriam obtinebit, neq; ecclesia cum suis membris salua erit, nisi ille solus emineat, & sub hoc omnes in vnum corpus coalescant. Hic ergo inuigilent ministri, ne doctrinis nouis locum dent, quibus suus Christo honor eripitur, & ecclesia in sectas diuersas scinditur. Non ergo vniuersalis quaedam cura hic sufficiet, sed singulos obseruare & inspicere necesse erit, ne qui exorbitent, aut lupis praeda fiant. Quia enim toti familiae suae dispensatorem istu[?] Christus praefecit, & idem totius gregis pastor est, nunquam fidus erit Christo, si quae sua incuria perire sinat. Hic ergo ipsius Christi exemplū[?] imitari oportet, qui ouiculam vnam ex centum amissam per montes & valles quaerere satagit, & qui iam moriturus dicere potuit: Pater, quos dedisti mihi, ego custodiui, & nemo ex eis periit, nisi filius ille perditionis, ut Scriptura compleretur. Ut ergo neminem generis nobilitas, opes, honores aut quaecunq; alia sunt huius generis tuentur, quo minus verbo Dei & disciplinae ecclesiasticae subijci debeat, siquidem Christianus haberi & salutis in Christo particeps fieri velit: ita minister neminem negligere debet, siue is dives aut pauper, nobilis aut ignobilis, doctus aut indoctus, iuuenis aut senex, rusticus, nauta, opifex, vel etiam mendicus fuerit. Nam qualiscunq; fit, qui in ecclesia agit, Christi membrum, frater aut soror est: & proinde absq; Christi iniuria negligi non poterit.
units.tr: Finally, the minister and steward of Christ will then truly show himself faithful when he directs all his work to the proper end and goal of the ministry. This end is the glory of Christ and the salvation of the Church. Although these two may seem different, in truth they are one, because Christ will not obtain his glory, nor will the Church with its members be saved, unless he alone stands pre-eminent and all are joined together into one body under him. Here, then, ministers must keep watch, lest they give room to new doctrines by which Christ's honour is snatched away and the Church is torn into divided sects. A general care will not be enough here; it will be necessary to observe and look after each one individually, lest some go astray or become prey to wolves. For since Christ has set this steward over his whole household, and he is also the shepherd of the whole flock, he will never be faithful to Christ if through his carelessness he allows any to perish. Here one ought to imitate the very example of Christ, who strives to seek the one sheep out of a hundred that has gone astray over mountains and valleys, and who, about to die, could say: "Father, those whom you gave me I have kept, and none of them has perished except the son of perdition, that the Scripture might be fulfilled." Therefore, just as nobility of birth, wealth, honours, or any other such things must not shield anyone from being subjected to the word of God and the discipline of the Church, if he wishes to be counted a Christian and to share in salvation in Christ, so the minister must neglect no one, whether he be rich or poor, noble or humble, learned or unlearned, young or old, a countryman, a sailor, a craftsman, or even a beggar. For whatever he is who lives in the Church, he is a member of Christ, a brother or sister, and therefore cannot be neglected without injury to Christ.

units.la: At hic imprimis prudentia opus est, vt (quod Dominus monuit) ἐν καιρῷ[?], id est, suo & opportuno tempore omnia agat minister: quod tunc fiet, si & personarum & locorum rationem ha-beat diligentem. Ut enim cibo quidem omnes ali & seruari oportet, sed non vnum cibi genus omnibus seruit: ita verbo Dei, quod vnum & idem est, omnes homines erudiri & instrui necesse est, non tamen eadem docendi ratio omnibus conuenit, sed rudes & rerum imperitos docere, negli-gentes monere, cunctatores hortari, contumaces corripere, timidos & desperabundos consolari, deniq;[?] cibum illum (ut alibi Paulus monet) ita secare oportet, ut omnium institutioni, consolationi & aedificationi serviat. Et huc maxime referri debet gravis illa Apostoli admonitio, qua Timotheum, & sub eius persona omnes ecclesiarum ministros excitat, dicens: Obtestor ego coram Deo & Domino IESV CHRISTO, qui iudicaturus est vivos & mortuos in illustri illo suo aduen-tu & regno suo: Praedica sermonem, insta tempestiuè, intempestiuè, argue, obiurga, exhortare cum omni lenitate & doctrina. Plurimum vero hic proderit, si nunquam non cogitet minister, quanti suam ecclesiam & singula eius membra Christus fecit, & quod olim rationem ipsi omnes reddituri sint: quod non uno loco ipse docet, imprimis autem in dispensatoris parabola, ubi sic loquitur: Beatus servus ille, quem cùm venerit dominus eius, invenerit sic facientem. Amen dico vobis, super omnia bona sua constituet eum. Quod si dixerit servus ille malus in corde suo, Tardat dominus meus venire: coeperitq; verberare conservos, quin etiā edere & bibere cum ebriis: Veniet dominus servi illius in die, quo non expectat, & hora qua non novit, & dissecabit eum, partemq; eius ponet cum hypocritis, illic erit fletus & stridor dentium. Sunt hæc auditu dura, multoq; duriora, si ab eo dici cogitemus, qui ipse iudex ille venturus est, deq; cuius fide dubitari non potest, & qui olim Ezechieli quoq; dixit: Sanguinem eorum, qui pereunt, de manu tua requiram. Sed utinam in istorum meditatione frequentes hodie essent, qui ecclesiarum ministri, vel etiam antistites dici volunt. Sentirent procul dubio, tantū esse hoc onus, ut nemo huic sufficiat, nisi quem suo spiritu & gratia Deus adiuuerit, & quod hominem totum requirat, ut non possit aliis rebus vacare, quisquis in eo bona fide versari volet. Si enim, ut Paulus ait, nemo qui militat, implicatur vitæ negotiis, multò mi-nus hoc facere debent, qui ad militiam illam spiritualem à Christo delecti sunt, in qua cum diabolo bellum geritur, adversus cuius insidias ministri seipsos & ecclesiam tueri debent. At quàm parùm ista aliquos moveant, res ipsa loquitur. Episcopi certè circa huius sæculi res occupati, principum more dominantur, equorum & stipatorum apparatu superbiunt, bella gerunt, venantur, epulantur: à docendi autem munere ita abhorrent, ut grave sibi iniuriā fieri arbitrentur, si quis ipsos ecclesiæ curā suscipere iubeat. Inter nostros aut quàm plurimos inuenias, qui vel opibus colligendis intenti sunt, vel pocula sectantur, aut quibuscunq; potius studijs vacant, quàm ijs, quæ ad munus ecclesiasticum necessaria sunt: ut interim de illis nihil dicā, qui ut mundo placeant, ad omnia conniuent, imò eorum quoq; amicitiā sectantur, quos CHRISTI IESV & ecclesiæ eius hostes iuratos esse norunt. Sunt hi mercenarij illi, de quibus dicitur, quod visò lupo fugiant, & utinā nō ipsi lupis nocentiores essent, quando & negligentia sua & malo exemplo ecclesias fœdè dissipant. Sentient omnes isti aliquādo Christi iudicis manu, qui ecclesiæ suæ nunquam deesse, quò minus huic factam iniuriam dignis supplicijs vlcisceretur.
units.tr: Here above all there is need of prudence, so that the minister does everything (as the Lord warned) "in season [ἐν καιρῷ]," that is, at its proper and opportune time. This will happen if he takes careful account both of persons and of circumstances. For just as all must be fed and sustained by food, yet one kind of food does not suit everyone, so all men must be taught and instructed by the word of God, which is one and the same, yet the same method of teaching does not suit everyone. The ignorant and inexperienced must be taught, the negligent admonished, the hesitant encouraged, the stubborn rebuked, the timid and despairing comforted. Finally, that food (as Paul advises elsewhere) must be divided in such a way that it serves the instruction, comfort and building up of all. And to this should especially be referred that weighty admonition of the Apostle, by which he rouses Timothy, and in his person all the ministers of the churches, saying: "I charge you before God and the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the living and the dead at his glorious coming and in his kingdom: preach the word, be urgent in season and out of season, reprove, rebuke, exhort with all patience and teaching." It will also be of great benefit if the minister never ceases to consider how dearly Christ bought his Church and each of its members, and that all men will one day render account to him. This Christ teaches in more than one place, especially in the parable of the steward, where he speaks thus: "Blessed is that servant whom his lord, when he comes, finds so doing. Truly I say to you, he will set him over all his goods. But if that wicked servant says in his heart, 'My lord is delayed in coming,' and begins to beat his fellow servants, and even to eat and drink with the drunken, the lord of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces and appoint his portion with the hypocrites; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth." These words are hard to hear, and much harder if we consider that they are spoken by him who is himself the judge who is to come, whose faithfulness cannot be doubted, and who long ago said to Ezekiel also: "I will require their blood at your hand, of those who perish." But would that there were more today, among those who wish to be called ministers of the churches or even bishops, who were frequent in meditating on these words. Without doubt they would feel that this burden is so great that no one is equal to it unless God helps him by his Spirit and grace, and that it demands the whole man, so that whoever wishes to act in it in good faith cannot be free for other things. For if, as Paul says, no one who serves as a soldier entangles himself in the affairs of life, much less ought those to do so who have been chosen by Christ for that spiritual warfare in which a battle is waged against the devil, and against whose snares ministers must defend both themselves and the Church. But how little these things move some men, the matter itself declares. Bishops, indeed, occupied with the affairs of this age, lord it over others in the manner of princes, take pride in their display of horses and attendants, wage wars, hunt, and feast; yet they shrink so much from the duty of teaching that they consider it a grave injury if anyone bids them undertake the care of the Church. Among our own people you will find very many who are intent either on gathering wealth or on pursuing drinking cups, or on whatever pursuits they devote themselves to rather than those things which are necessary for the ecclesiastical office. I say nothing for the moment of those who, in order to please the world, connive at everything, and indeed seek the friendship of those whom they know to be sworn enemies of Christ Jesus and of his Church. These are those hirelings of whom it is said that they flee when they see the wolf; and would that they were not themselves more harmful than wolves, when by their negligence and bad example they shamefully scatter the churches. All these men will one day feel the hand of Christ the judge, who will never fail his Church, so that he will avenge with due punishment the wrong done to it.

units.la: Video me in horum tractatione prolixiorem fuisse, sed ut fieret argumenti magnitudo postulauit. Et condonabitis mihi fratres, si huius doctrinæ usum ad alios etiam extendero, quibus illa non minus seruit, quàm illis, quibus ecclesiæ cura commissa est. Nam eadem etiam illorum ratio est, qui rempub. administrant, et in magistratu constituti sunt. Sunt hi quoq; ministri Dei, & sic eos alibi vocat Apostolus. Et ex eo omnis eorum authoritas atq; gloria dependet. Ideo antiquitus ijdem & reges & sacerdotes erant, ut in Melchisedecho cernitur, & in Amo[?] suo Vergilius annotavit, quèm regem hominum & Phoebi sacerdotem fuisse scribit. Deinde ijdem dispensatores quoq; dici possunt: quia ipsis credita sunt Dei iudicia. Ergo ab illis etiam fides requiritur, ne à Deo latas leges privatā temeritate mutent, ne iudiciorum Dei loco sua placita proferant: ut item iustè iudicent, nullo personarum respectu ducantur, neminem negligant, & (quod in Psal.72. annotatur) pretiosum ducant sanguinè subditorum suorum. Finem vero sibi propositum habeant, Dei gloriam & populi salutem: ad quem tunc demum pertingent, si religionem veram tueantur, doctrinæ puritatem servari curent, impostores procul arceant, impios & blasphemos puniant, raptores, usurarios & quoscunq; alios in ordinem redigant, quos ex aliorum incommodis suum commodum quærere vident.
units.tr: I see that I have been rather lengthy in treating these matters, but the greatness of the subject required it. And, brothers, you will forgive me if I extend the use of this teaching to others as well, for it serves them no less than those to whom the care of the Church is committed. The same reasoning applies to those who administer the commonwealth and hold magistracy. They too are ministers of God, and the Apostle calls them such elsewhere. All their authority and glory depends on this. For this reason, in antiquity the same men were both kings and priests, as is seen in Melchizedek, and Virgil noted in his account of Anius that he was king of men and priest of Phoebus. Further, they may also be called stewards, since the judgments of God have been entrusted to them. Therefore faithfulness is required of them too: they must not, by their own rashness, alter the laws given by God, nor put forward their own pleasures in place of God's judgments; they must judge justly, be guided by no respect of persons, neglect no one, and (as is noted in Psalm 72) count the blood of their subjects precious. They should have as their goal the glory of God and the salvation of the people, and they will reach that goal only if they defend the true religion, take care that the purity of doctrine is preserved, keep impostors far off, punish the impious and blasphemers, and bring to order plunderers, usurers and all others whom they see seeking their own advantage from the hardships of others.

units.la: Priuatim quoq; doctrinam hanc ad se transferant, qui divitijs abundant. Curent ut Dei, non Mammonæ, ministri sint. Cogitent item se ex Dei liberalitate habere quicquid habent, neq; in illis aliquid esse, quod vel proprium dicere, aut cuius possessione perpetuā sibi polliceri possint. Omnia enim Dei sunt, at Meum & tuum (ut Chrysostomus monuit) vocabula sunt inania, quæ hominum cupiditas & auaritia excogitauit. Meminerint ergo divites, se quoq; à Deo bonorum dispensatores esse constitutos, & tales ab ipso Christo dici. Quapropter non sibi solis ea vsurpent, neque ad luxum & libidinem ijs abutantur, quae vt necessitati nostrae seruiant a Deo dari solent. Deinde non aegre ferant, si eadem vel eripiat Deus, aut ex illis aliorum necessitati subuenire iubeat. Potest enim ille de suo statuere pro suo arbitrio, imo vel inuitis omnia eripere potest, neque tamen quisquam de iniuria sibi facta potest conqueri. Nostrae autem saluti ille consulit, dum monet, vt liberalitatem spontaneam in egenos exerceamus, & pro illa nobis praemia amplissima pollicetur. Nulla igitur opum possessio tutior & stabilior, nullus earundem vsus quaestuosior est, quam si creditae nobis despensationis memores, quam plurimis subuenire, & ipsi Christo in suis membris laboranti opem ferre studeamus. Ita enim neq; abutemur ijs, quae Dominus dedit: neq; aduersus eum murmurabimus, si quod dedit iterum eripiat, sed cum Iobo dicemus: Dominus dedit, Dominus abstulit, sit nomen Domini benedictum. In horum ergo consideratione assidui simus, imprimis autem Dei bonitatem nobis subinde ob oculos ponamus, qui non contentus nobis bonorum temporariorum dispensationem credidisse, coelestia quoque & aeterna communicat, & horum dispensatores dat Euangelij praecones. Discant ergo isti fideles esse in suo munere, eosdem vero alij pro ministris IESV CHRISTI agnoscant, & huius verbum sedulo audiant, vt cum eodem olim in coelis viuant & regnent: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: This teaching also applies privately to those who abound in riches. Let them see to it that they are ministers of God, not of Mammon. Let them likewise consider that whatever they have they have from God's generosity, and that there is nothing in their possessions that they can call their own or promise themselves as a perpetual possession. For all things are God's, and "mine" and "yours" (as Chrysostom reminded us) are empty words, invented by human greed and avarice. Let the rich remember, then, that they too have been appointed stewards of goods by God, and that Christ himself calls such men stewards. Therefore they should not appropriate these things to themselves alone, nor abuse them for luxury and lust, since they are normally given by God to serve our needs. Further, they should not be aggrieved if God takes these things away, or orders them to relieve the needs of others from them. For God may decide about what is his own according to his own will; indeed he can take everything away even against our will, and yet no one can complain of an injury done to him. But he provides for our salvation when he urges us to exercise voluntary generosity toward the needy, and promises us the richest rewards in return. Therefore no possession of wealth is safer and more stable, and no use of it is more profitable, than when we, mindful of the trust committed to us, strive to help as many as possible and to bring aid to Christ himself, who suffers in his members. For in this way we shall neither abuse what the Lord has given, nor murmur against him if he takes back what he gave; rather we shall say with Job: "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord." Let us therefore be diligent in considering these things, and above all let us keep before our eyes the goodness of God, who, not content to have entrusted us with the stewardship of temporal goods, also bestows heavenly and eternal ones, and gives stewards of these, the heralds of the gospel. Let these men learn to be faithful in their office, and let others acknowledge them as ministers of JESUS CHRIST, and diligently hear his word, so that they may live and reign with him in heaven: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XVIII.

units.la: Mihi vero pro minimo est, quod à vobis dijudicer, aut ab humano die: imo nec meipsum dijudico. Nullius enim rei mihi conscius sum, sed nō per hoc iustificatus sum: sed qui me dijudicat, Dominus est. Proinde ne ante tempus quicquam iudicate vsq; dum venerit Dominus, qui & illustraturus est occulta tenebrarum, & manifesta faciet consilia cordium: ac tunc laus erit vnicuiq; à Deo.
units.tr: It is a very small matter to me that I should be judged by you, or by any human day. Indeed I do not even judge myself. For I am conscious of nothing against myself, yet I am not thereby justified; it is the Lord who judges me. Therefore judge nothing before the appointed time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the purposes of hearts; and then each one will receive his praise from God.

units.la: VT de verbi Dei doctrina recte iudicare non possunt, qui per Spiritum Christi nondum illuminati sunt: ita ijdem de administris quoque verbi perperam & iniquè pronunciant. Nam aut stolida admiratione abrepti aliquos altius quàm par est euehunt, & tantumnon pro Dijs habent: aut prophana temeritate alios ita contemnunt, vt nullum illis in ecclesia & eius ministerio locum relinquant. Fiebat vtrunq; apud Corinthios, qui vanissimos ardeliones propter magnificum humanae eloquentiae apparatum & inanem sublimioris sapientiae ostentationem in summo pretio habebant, è contra vero Paulum & alios germanos IESV CHRISTI Apostolos propter rude dicendi genus & simplicem atque synceram solius Christi praedicationem pro indoctis & ineptis nimium aspernabantur. Ideo diligenter hucusque docuit Paulus, quo loco ministri ecclesiae habendi sint, & quid illis tribui, quid non tribui debeat. At cum non ignoraret, plerosque illorum de se pessimè iudicare, & proinde hanc admonitionem illos pro ludibrio habituros esse, nunc vt suam authoritatem apud meliores tueatur, à peruersis illis & iniquis iudicibus ad Dei tribunal provocat. Quo exemplo admonemur, quid facere debeant, quotquot sese iniquis hominum iudicijs premi sentiunt.
units.tr: Just as those who have not yet been enlightened by the Spirit of Christ cannot judge rightly concerning the doctrine of God's Word, so they also judge the ministers of the Word wrongly and unjustly. For either, seized by foolish admiration, they exalt some higher than is fitting and almost treat them as gods; or, with profane rashness, they so despise others that they leave them no place in the Church or its ministry. Both of these happened among the Corinthians, who held in highest esteem the most vain office-seekers because of their splendid display of human eloquence and their empty show of a loftier wisdom, but on the other hand despised Paul and the other true Apostles of Jesus Christ too much, as untrained and inept, because of their plain style of speaking and their simple and sincere preaching of Christ alone. Therefore Paul has taught thus far, with care, in what position the ministers of the Church should be held, and what should and should not be granted to them. But since he was not unaware that many of them judged him very badly, and that they would therefore treat this admonition as a joke, he now, in order to defend his authority among the better sort, summons the matter from those perverse and unjust judges to the tribunal of God. From this example we are taught what those should do who feel themselves oppressed by the unjust judgments of men.

units.la: Propositionem huius loci his verbis comprehendit: Mihi pro minimo est, quod à vobis dijudicer, aut ab humano die. Diem pro iudicio ponit, Romanorum more, apud quos frequens erat locutio, vt dies diceretur ijs, qui ad tribunal citabantur. Et credibile est, eiusmodi locutiones apud alios quoque in vsu fuisse, qui illorum imperio & legibus parebant. Humanum autem diem vocat iudicium, in quo non ex verbi Dei praescripto, sed ex hominum arbitrio iudicatur, qui vel praeuiis affectibus abrepti, vel ignorantia & causidicorum fallacijs decepti à recto & aequo aberrant. Opponitur ergo humanus dies diei Domini, cuius multa fit mentio in sacris literis, quoties hunc de hominibus certò iudicaturum & de impijs poenas dignas sumpturum esse docent. Itaque verborum Apostoli sensus est: Scio quid de me plerique vestrum sentiant, quibus contemptui sum, tò quòd nullo splendore magnifico aut fastu me ostentem, neque doctrinam meam verborum inanium phaleris commendabilem reddā. Epistola (inquiunt) graves sunt & vehementes, sed præ-sentia corporis infirma, & sermo nihili. Sed & Apostolatum meum in dubium vocare audent, quòd ulcimus[?] ad hunc vocatus, neque (ut reliqui) cum Christo adhuc in terris agente versatus sim. Et huius generis infinita congerunt, quibus non tam me quàm doctrinam meam contemptibilem ant suspectam faciant. At non mouent ista me, qui neque vestrum, neque ullius hominis iudicium tanti facio, ut propter id animo frangar, aut mihi ab officio discedendum esse putem. Nam mihi satis superq; est, si Dei iudicio probor, qui ut me filij sui Apostolum esse voluit, meque ad hoc munus ab vtero matris meæ segregauit: ita peculiari mandato iussit, ut vobis quoque prædicarem. Est hoc magnæ fiduciæ & fortitudinis verè apostolicæ argumentum, quo simul Corinthiorum arrogantiam corripit, & æmulorum suorum vanitatem perstringit, qui toti ab hominum iudicio pendebant, de diuino autem nihil aut parum erant solliciti.
units.tr: In the statement of this passage Paul puts it in these words: "It is a very small matter to me that I should be judged by you, or by any human day." He uses "day" for judgment, after the manner of the Romans, among whom it was a common expression to speak of "day" for those who were summoned before the tribunal. And it is credible that such expressions were in use among other peoples as well who obeyed their rule and laws. He calls the judgment "human day" when judgment is made not by the prescription of God's Word but by human opinion, by those who, either carried away by prior passions, or deceived by ignorance and the sophistries of advocates, stray from what is right and fair. Thus the human day is set over against the day of the Lord, of which Holy Scripture makes frequent mention, whenever it teaches that he will judge men with certainty and will exact punishments worthy of the wicked. The sense of the Apostle's words is therefore this: I know what many of you think of me, for whom I am an object of contempt, because I do not make a show of any magnificent splendour or pomp, nor make my teaching commendable by the trappings of empty words. "The letters," they say, "are weighty and forceful, but the bodily presence is weak, and the speech is worthless." But they even dare to call my apostleship in doubt, because I was called to it late, and was not, like the others, conversant with Christ while he was still living on earth. And they heap up countless charges of this kind, by which they make not so much me as my teaching contemptible or suspect. But these things do not move me, for I do not value the judgment of you or of any man so highly that I should be broken in spirit because of it, or think that I ought to withdraw from my office. For it is enough for me, if I am approved by the judgment of God, who willed that I be the Apostle of his Son, and separated me for this office from my mother's womb, and by a special command has ordered me to preach to you also. This is a proof of great confidence and of truly apostolic courage, by which he at once rebukes the arrogance of the Corinthians and lays bare the vanity of his rivals, who depended wholly on the judgment of men, and cared little or nothing for the divine judgment.

units.la: Veruntamen quærat aliquis, cur per Corinthios de se & doctrina sua iudicium fieri nolue-rit Paulus, cum in hac ipsa epistola scribat, ecclesiam de doctoribus suis & ijs quæ ab illis propo-nuntur, iudicare debere. Et alibi, Omnia probate (inquit) quod bonum est tenete. Similiter Ioan-nes quoq; spiritus probare iubet, num ex Deo sint. Quæ omnia Christus sua authoritate confirmat, quando oibus suis spiritum discretionis tribuit, quo inter ipsius & mercenarij aut falsi pastoris vocem discernere possint. Neq; contemni debere ecclesiæ iudicium, ex eo constat, quòd Christus sua præsentiam illis pollicetur, qui in suo nomine conueniunt, & eum pro Ethnico & prophano habere iubet, qui ecclesiæ audire dedignatur. Cæterum hic meminisse oportet, Corinthiorum plerosq; inuidia & cæca æmulatione eò vsq; iam progressos fuisse, vt amplius non possent de Paulo & eius doctrina iudicare. Nam vt sæpe iam diximus, ostentatores illos ita admirabantur, vt propter eos in sectas scinderentur, & Christi nomine tantum non abiecto, ab illis denominari vellent. Adde quòd & Paulum suo præiudicio iam pridem damnauerant, & syncerum Euangelij prædicationem fastidiebant, adeò vt crux Christi iam illis sorderet præ humanæ sapientiæ saliua, quam ex pseudoapostolorum doctrina imbiberant. Non poterat ergo Paulus seipsum & doctrinam suam illorum iudicio subijcere, quin veritatem ipsam sciens volensq; (ut dicitur) proderet, idq; magno cum scandalo infirmorum, quos potius aduersus illos confirmari oportebat. De peruersis ergo illis & iniquis loquitur, neq; propterea eorum iudicium contempsit, qui rectius sapiebant. De his enim infra cap.10. dicet: Ut peritis loquor, iudicate vos quod dico. Et cap.14. Vtrumq; hoc hominum genus ita inter se distinguit, ut alteri quidem iudicium de se permittat, alterum sancta veritatis & animi bene sibi conscij fiducia contemnat. Dicit enim. Si quis videtur propheta esse aut spiritualis, agnoscat quæ scribo vobis, quòd Domini sint mandata. Qui vero ignarus est, ignarus esto.
units.tr: Yet someone may ask why Paul did not wish that judgment be made among the Corinthians concerning himself and his doctrine, when in this very letter he writes that the Church ought to judge its teachers and the things that are proposed by them. And elsewhere he says: "Prove all things; hold fast to what is good." Likewise John also bids the spirits to be tested, whether they are from God. All these things Christ confirms by his own authority, when he gives to all his people the spirit of discernment, by which they can distinguish between his voice and the voice of a hireling or false minister. That the judgment of the Church ought not to be despised is clear from the fact that Christ promises his presence to those who gather in his name, and bids that the one who refuses to hear the Church be regarded as a heathen and a publican. But here it is fitting to remember that many of the Corinthians had already advanced, through envy and blind rivalry, to the point where they could no longer judge Paul and his doctrine. For, as we have often said, they so admired those showy men that because of them they were split into factions, and wished to be named after them, the name of Christ being all but cast aside. Add to this that they had already condemned Paul beforehand by their prejudice, and loathed the pure preaching of the Gospel, so that the cross of Christ was now repugnant to them, compared with the spittle of human wisdom which they had soaked up from the teaching of the false apostles. Paul therefore could not subject himself and his doctrine to their judgment without, knowing and willing the truth itself, as they say, betraying it, and that with great scandal to the weak, who ought rather to have been strengthened against those men. He is speaking, then, of those perverse and unjust men, and he does not on that account despise the judgment of those who thought more rightly. For of these he says later, in chapter 10: "I speak as to the wise; judge what I say yourselves." And in chapter 14 he distinguishes these two kinds of men so that he grants the judgment of the one kind concerning himself, while he scorns the other kind, relying on the holy confidence of truth and of a conscience well aware of itself. For he says: "If anyone seems to be a prophet or spiritual, let him acknowledge what I write to you, that they are the commandments of the Lord. But if anyone is ignorant, let him remain ignorant."

units.la: Est autem hoc Apostoli exemplum perquàm memorabile, & multa consideratione dignissimū. Docet enim quid omnes ecclesiarum ministri in eiusmodi casibus facere debeant. Vbi primum hoc statuatur, non debere illos lucem subterfugere, quò minus doctrina ipsorum cognoscatur, & de ea iudicium fiat. Si enim vnusquisq; credentium quouis tempore instructus & paratus esse debet (ut Petrus scribit) ad reddendam fidei suæ rationem, multo magis hoc à verbi administris exigitur, qui publicum in ecclesia docendi munus sustinent. Nimium ergo superbi, imò tyrannici fidei alienæ dominatores sunt, qui sibi simpliciter credi volunt, neq; permittunt, ut quis de ipsorum doctrina iudicet. At secundo loco ecclesiarum conditionem ministri probè obseruare debent. Nam ut Christus in parabola retis piscatorij docet, non pios modò ecclesia hac in terris adhuc militantes continet, sed malos quoq; & impios illis intermixtos habet: & inter eos, qui ecclesiæ membra sunt, magnus plerunq; est infirmorum numerus, qui aut carnales nimium, aut adhuc infantes in Christo sunt. Denique plerunq; plures sunt eorum, qui aut male sentiunt de veritatis doctrina, aut ineptiores sunt, quàm ut de illa rectè iudicare possint. Talibus ergo non tantùm tribuere debent ministri, ut eorum iudicio sese subijciant, aut pro illorum arbitrio doctrinam mutent. Quòd si illi temere sibi iudicium sumant, non ideo animo frangi oportet, sed ad Dei iudicium prouocent, sui illos rationem reddituros esse Christus non vno loco docet.
units.tr: This example of the Apostle is most memorable and most worthy of close consideration. For it teaches what all the ministers of the churches ought to do in such cases. First, it establishes that they ought not to shun the light, lest their teaching be known and judged. For if every believer ought at all times to be instructed and prepared (as Peter writes) to give an account of his faith, much more is this required of the ministers of the Word, who bear the public office of teaching in the Church. Therefore those are far too proud, and indeed tyrannical lords over the faith of others, who want to be believed simply, and do not allow anyone to judge their teaching. But in the second place, ministers ought to observe carefully the condition of the churches. For, as Christ teaches in the parable of the fishing net, the Church in this world, still militant, contains not only the godly but also the evil and impious mixed among them; and among those who are members of the Church there is usually a great number of the weak, who are either too carnal or still infants in Christ. Finally, most often there are more of those who either think ill of the doctrine of truth, or are too unskilled to judge it rightly.
