Ministers ought therefore not only to yield to such people, so as to submit themselves to their judgment or to change their teaching at their pleasure. But if such people rashly assume judgment for themselves, it is not right for the minister to be broken in spirit on that account, but he should appeal to the judgment of God, since Christ teaches in more than one place that they will render account to him.

units.la: Habes igitur hoc loco, quid illis respondeas, qui petunt, vt nose t doctrinâ nostrâ Romanae fedi[?] ant Concilijs ex Pontificum sententia vel voluntate congregatis subijciamus. Prætexunt hi ecclesiæ nomen, & huius potestatem omnem penes se esse clamant, de quo nunc disputare nolumus. Sed vt hoc illis demus, non tamen ex eo sequetur, quod illi volunt. Vt enim ecclesia ex Dei verbo generatur, sic hoc vnum obseruat, sponsi sui vocem audit & agnoscit, neq; aliquid eorum admittit, quæ illi contradicunt. Quod si illi præstiterint, libenter eos audiemus. At cum constet plerosq; illorum, aut apertos verbi Dei hostes esse, aut illud prorsus ignorare, quis non diceret nos cum ratione infa-nire, si quæ ex Scripturarum fontibus nos baufisse constat, illis dijudicanda daremus? Licuit Pau-lo Corinthiorum iudicium detrectare, quos ipse primus Christo lucrifecerat, quos ecclesiæ titulo non poterat fraudare, imò quos alibi apostolatus sui sigillum, & epistolam suam vel potius Christi, dicit, quæ non atramento descripta sit, sed Spiritu Dei viui, &c. Cur ergo nobis non liceat ab eorum tribunali prouocare, qui veras germanæ ecclesiæ notas non habent, qui in sectas diuersas sciisi in eo vno conueniunt, quòd veritatis doctrinam superstitionibus variis obscurant, qui denique verbi Dei doctrinam palàm oderunt, & diris conuitijs proscindunt? Scimus equidem, illos plenis buccis Spiritum sanctum iactare, qui Concilijs ipsorum adsit, & singulorum sententias atq; suffragia regat: at nos non quid illi dicant, sed quid res ipsa loquatur, quid ue ab illis fiat, attendendum esse dicimus. Vbi mox patebit, illos non alio ordine aut progressu in Concilijs suis vti, quàm quo olim Caiaphas & alij Iudæorum Sacerdotes vsi sunt. Vt enim isti præiudicio Christum non auditum & priusquam captus esset damnarunt, & postea demum quasi iure atturi in causam eius inquisiuerunt, ita tamen, vt neq; à testibus falsis abhorruerint, neq; à vi manifesta sibi temperarint, tandem vero innocentem propter liberam & ingenuam veritatis confessionem damnquerunt: sic illi quoque dum Conciliaindicunt, in bullis suis nos damnant, quando autè ad rem venitur, omnia insidiosè agunt, neque alia illis mortis & cuiusuis supplicij causa dignior videtur, quàm si quos in CHRISTI IESV confessione syncera fortes & constantes esse cernunt. Quis ergo sanæ mentis illorum iudicio sese committat? Quis ôn veritatis desertorem aut proditorem dixerit eum, qui hoc faciat? Vel quo iure cogi poterunt Euangelij præcones, vt pro iudicibus eos agnoscant, quos iam sæculis aliquot totus fere orbis accusauit, & de quorum tyrannide pij omnes conquesti sunt? Damnent ergo illi nos, si ita libet, & hæreticos atq; excidio dignos pronuntient, eò quòd vnum IESVM CHRI-STVM prædicamus, & vnum Deum in spiritu & veritate colendum esse docemus. At nos cum Paulo dicemus: Nobis pro minimo est, quòd à vobis dijudicemur, aut ab humano die.
units.tr: You therefore have here the answer to those who ask that we submit our teaching to the Roman see, or to councils convened at the opinion or will of the Pontiffs. They put forward the name of the Church and loudly claim that all its authority rests with them, a point we do not wish to dispute now. But even if we grant them this, it does not follow what they want. For the Church is born of God's Word, and it recognises and hears the voice of its Bridegroom alone, and admits nothing that contradicts that voice. If they can show this, we will gladly listen to them. But since it is plain that most of them are either open enemies of God's Word or utterly ignorant of it, who would not say that we are out of our minds if we handed over to their judgment what we have manifestly drawn from the fountains of Scripture? Paul was free to reject the judgment of the Corinthians, whom he himself had first won to Christ, and whom he could not deprive of the name of the Church. Indeed, elsewhere he calls them the seal of his apostleship and his letter, or rather Christ's, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, and so on. Why, then, should we not be permitted to appeal from the tribunal of those who do not have the true marks of the genuine Church, who are split into diverse sects and agree in this one thing only, that they obscure the teaching of truth with various superstitions, who openly hate the doctrine of God's Word and tear it apart with dreadful insults? We know indeed that they boast with full mouths that the Holy Spirit is present at their councils and governs the opinions and votes of each member. But we say that we must attend not to what they say, but to what the matter itself declares, and to what is done by them. It will soon become clear that they use no other order or procedure in their councils than that which Caiaphas and the other priests of the Jews once used. For just as those men condemned Christ unheard, before he was taken, and afterwards at last inquired into his case as if they had a right to act in it, yet so that they neither shrank from false witnesses nor refrained from open violence, and finally condemned the innocent man for his free and frank confession of the truth, so these men too, while they summon councils, condemn us in their bulls. When it comes to the matter itself, they act treacherously in every way, and no other cause for death or any punishment seems more fitting to them than that they see some men steadfast and constant in a sincere confession of Jesus Christ. Who, then, of sound mind would commit himself to their judgment? Who could rightly call a man a deserter or traitor to the truth for refusing to do so? Or by what right could the heralds of the Gospel be compelled to acknowledge as judges those whom almost the whole world has for some centuries accused, and over whose tyranny all the godly have complained? Let them then condemn us, if they like, and pronounce us heretics worthy of destruction, because we proclaim the one Jesus Christ and teach that the one God is to be worshipped in spirit and in truth. But we shall say with Paul: "It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you, or by man's day."

units.la: Debet præterea hinc generalis doctrina peti, ne qui animo frangantur, & in suo munere tur-piter succumbant, si quando homines de ipsis iniquè iudicare, aut etiam eos ingratissimos esse sentiunt, pro quorum salute ipsi dies noctesq; vigilant. Sensit istam iniquitatem & ingratitudinem Paulus non modò apud Corinthios, verumetiam apud omnes fere, quos Christo adducere & salutis æternæ hæredes facere studuit. Et vt reliquos omnes taceamus, quas non iniurias passus est à Iudæis gentilibus suis, pro quibus ipse perpetuò ad Deum precabatur? Nū vero propterea apostolicæ functioni longum valere renuntiauit? vel num ideo animum despondit, quò minus à Deo sibi creditum munus obiret? Imò cum mundi improbitate luctatus est, eoq; fortius aduersus hostes atq; æmulos suos insurrexit, quò magis se ab illis premi sentiebat. Imitentur exemplum hoc omnes ver-bi administri, et sibi dictum putent, quod Ierem.olim dixit Deus: Ne paueas à cospectu eorū, ne paueret te faciā à conspectu eorū. Ecce enim ego te faciā hodie ciuitatē munitā, columnā ferreā, & murū æneū cōtra omnē terrā, contra reges, cōtra principes, cōtra sacerdotes, et cōtra vniuersum populū terræ, &c. Debent hoc etiam ad se transferre, quotquot magistratum gerunt. Nam his quoq;, si Deo & populo fideles sint, multis laboribus atq; periculis se premi sentient, & ferè ingratissimos experientur eos, quos maximè salvos volunt. At meminerint, nihilominus tenendam esse stationem, & inuicto animo ipsos per omnia obstacula eluctari debere, vt olim Deo sui muneris rationem reddere possint. Pertinet hæc consideratio ad singulos priuatim quoq;, ne vel benefaciendo fatigentur propter ingratorum hominum iudicia, vel aliquid contra ius & æquum faciant, si quando se minus proficere vident. Quin potius, si se ab omnibus accusari, conuitijs diris proscindi & criminibus atrocissimis grauari audiant, tribunalia autem omnia sibi clausa esse, neq; aliquem inter homines re-liquum liquò esse cernant, qui causam ipsorum vel cognoscere vel tueri possit aut velit: pergant tamen inter-center viuere & quibusuis benefacere, neq; etiam de nominis sui fama desperent. Licet enim illis ad Dei tribunal pronocare, & huic iniurias sibi factas exponere, qui afflictorum vindicem atq; patronum se esse profitetur. Vidit hoc Dauid, qui cum sub Saule grauissimis persecutionibus exercetur, & infandis criminibus premeretur, neq; ipsi liceret famam suam apud homines tueri, ad Dei tamen iudicium confugit, à quo mirificè seruatus est. Haec qui diligentius cogitant, ij in aduersis omnibus patientes sunt, & seipsos multis laboribus atq; molestijs liberant, quibus fere implicantur, qui ius suum ex priuata vindicta studio pertinacius tuentur. Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui ne te merarius & arrogans putetur, dictum iste suum rationibus grauissimis confirmat.
units.tr: Moreover, a general teaching should be drawn from this: that those who are ministers should not lose heart or basely give way in their office if at any time men judge them unjustly, or even feel that they are most ungrateful, when they themselves watch night and day for those men's salvation. Paul felt this injustice and ingratitude not only among the Corinthians but among almost all whom he strove to bring to Christ and make heirs of eternal salvation. And to say nothing of all the others, what injuries did he not suffer from his own Jewish and Gentile kinsmen, for whose sake he constantly prayed to God? Did he therefore renounce the apostolic function and bid farewell to it? Or did he lose heart, so that he would be less able to discharge the task entrusted to him by God? On the contrary, he struggled against the wickedness of the world, and rose up the more boldly against his enemies and rivals the more he felt himself pressed by them. Let all ministers of the Word imitate this example, and let them consider as said to themselves what God once said through Jeremiah: "Do not be afraid of their faces, lest I make you afraid before them. For behold, I have made you this day a fortified city, an iron pillar and a brazen wall against the whole land, against the kings, against the princes, against the priests, and against all the people of the land," and so on. All who hold magistracy should also apply this to themselves. For these too, if they are faithful to God and the people, will feel themselves pressed by many labours and dangers, and will find almost the most ungrateful those whom they most want to save. But let them remember that nonetheless their post must be held, and that with an unconquered spirit they must struggle through all obstacles, so that one day they may be able to render an account of their office to God. This consideration also applies to each private person, so that they may not grow weary of doing good because of the judgments of ungrateful men, or do anything contrary to right and justice if they see that they make little progress. Rather, if they hear that they are accused by everyone, torn apart with dreadful insults and burdened with the most atrocious charges, and if they see that every tribunal is closed to them, and that among men there is no one left who can or will either examine or defend their cause, let them nonetheless continue to live blamelessly among others and to do good to all, and not despair of the good name they bear. For they may appeal to God's tribunal and lay before him the wrongs done to them, since he professes himself the avenger and patron of the afflicted. David saw this, who, when under Saul he was harassed by the most grievous persecutions and burdened with unspeakable charges, and when it was not permitted him to defend his reputation before men, nevertheless fled to God's judgment, by whom he was wonderfully preserved. Those who think about these things more carefully are patient in all adversities, and free themselves from the many labours and troubles in which those are entangled who defend their right more stubbornly out of a zeal for private vengeance. But let us return to Paul, who, lest he be thought rash and arrogant, confirms this statement of his with very weighty reasons.

units.la: Primam ab impossibili sumit, & eam proprio exemplo probat atque illustrat, sic dicens: Imò nec meipsum dijudico. Sensus est: Quid ego aliorum de me iudicia formidem, qui nec ipse mei iudex esse possum? Et quis obsecro me tam probè nouit, atq; ego meipsum nouî? Attamen meipsum iudicare nō possum. Quomodo ergo id poterit alius? Facit ad huius argumenti confirmationem, quod cap. 2. dixit: Quis hominum nouit ea quae sunt hominis, nisi Spiritus hominis, qui est in eo? At hinc sequitur, temerarios nimis esse Corinthios, qui de aliis sibi iudicium sumunt, & eorum iudicia merito contemni, vt quae ab infscijs & rerum imperitis proficiscantur. Obseruabis autem hoc loco de ministrorum dignitate, non de moribus & vita agi. Nam quoad mores & studia, probè seipsum noverat Paulus, vt ex ijs patebit, quae mox sequentur. Sed quis nam inter Apostolos & reliquos ecclesiarum ministros alius alio praestantior esset, minimè sciebat. Hoc autem nimium audacter definiebant Corinthij. Quae enim alia causa adduci poterat, ob quam alius quidem Paulinus, alius verò Apollonianus, alius Cephista dici vellet, quam quòd quisq; suae sectae principem alijs omnibus praeferebat? At hoc iudicium caecum & incertum esse, Paulus non temere dicit. Quis enim nouit, quo quisq; animo suum munus obeat? quantum quisq; proficiat? aut qualis quisq; in finem vsq; futurus sit? Id certè constat, multos syncera fide omnia facere, qui tamen multis praeter meritum suspecti sunt: è contra verò multorum fidem & industriam praedicari, quos caeca aemulatio & ambitio, aut alij affectus praui mouent. Fit etiam, vt qui infimus & contemptissimus videtur, plures Christo lucrifaciat, quàm qui prae alijs in honore sunt & pretio. Quid? annon plerunque plus proficiunt ministri, quàm ipsi sperent? Elias certè se & alios prophetas ita in cassum laborauisse putabat, vt se solum reliquum factum diceret, qui gloriae Dei zelo duceretur. Sed quid ille audit? Superesse adhuc in Israele septem millia virorum qui ab omni superstitione & cultu illici-to se mundos & puros seruarint. Et Paulus de Corinthiorum vrbe ita desperauerat, vt de fuga aut discessu cogitaret. Sed Deus se illic populum multum habere testatur. Praeterea, non raro accidit, vt qui prae alijs feruere videbantur, vbi ad rem ventum est, subito metu fathiscant, quod tam Eliam quàm Petrum aliquando passos fuisse legimus. Rursus verò, qui diu latuerunt & cessarunt in suo munere, ij saepius praeter omnem expectationem fortissimi fiunt, quando res in extremum discrimen adducta est: cuius exempla nobis in Iosepho Arimathaeo & Nicodemo proponi, aliàs diximus. Et haec quidem tam occulta Dei dispensatione fiunt, vt nemo de seipso certum quid pronunciare possit. Recte ergo Paulus, quòd ne seipsum quidem dijudicet, ait. Quod vnum si posteri omnes obseruassent, non tam temerarij fuissent in constituendo Apostolorum principe Petro: qui error ambitionem & tyrannidem Pontificum intolerabilem peperit. Et hodie temerarijs iudicijs minus indulgerent multi, si de hac re diligentius cogitaretur.
units.tr: He takes the first from the impossible, and proves and illustrates it by his own example, saying: "Indeed I do not even judge myself." The sense is: why should I fear the judgments of others about me, when I myself cannot be my own judge? And who, I beg you, knows me as well as I know myself? Yet I cannot judge myself. How, then, could another do so? This supports the argument he had made in chapter 2: "Who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of man that is in him?" From this it follows that the Corinthians are too rash who take upon themselves to judge others, and that their judgments are rightly despised, since they come from the unlearned and those ignorant of the matter. You should observe, however, that at this point the dignity of ministers is being discussed, not their morals and life. For as regards morals and zeal, Paul knew himself well, as will be clear from what follows shortly. But he did not know at all which of the apostles and the other ministers of the churches was more excellent than another. The Corinthians, however, defined this much too boldly. For what other reason could be given why one should wish to be called a Paulinian, another an Apollonian, another a Cephasite, except that each preferred the leader of his own faction to all the others? But Paul does not rashly say that this judgment is blind and uncertain. For who knows with what spirit each man performs his office? How much each one profits, or what sort each will be until the end? This is certainly true: many do everything in sincere faith and yet are suspected beyond their deserts, while on the other hand the faith and diligence of many are praised, though blind rivalry and ambition, or other wicked passions, move them. It also happens that one who seems lowest and most despised wins more to Christ than those who are held in honour and esteem above others. What then? Do ministers not often accomplish more than they themselves hope? Elijah certainly thought that he and the other prophets had laboured in vain, so that he said he alone was left, moved by zeal for the glory of God. But what did he hear? That seven thousand men remained in Israel who had kept themselves clean and pure from all superstition and unlawful worship. And Paul had so despaired of the city of Corinth that he was thinking of flight or departure. But God declares that he has a great people there. Moreover, it is not rare that those who seemed to burn with zeal above others, when the matter came to the test, suddenly grow faint with fear, as we read happened once to Elijah as well as to Peter. Conversely, those who have long lain hidden and been idle in their office are often, beyond all expectation, the bravest when the situation is brought to its utmost peril. We have elsewhere said that examples of this are set before us in Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus. And these things happen by such hidden dispensation of God that no one can pronounce anything certain about himself. Rightly, therefore, Paul says that he does not even judge himself. If all later generations had observed this one point, they would not have been so rash in setting Peter up as the prince of the apostles, which error produced the intolerable ambition and tyranny of the Pontiffs. And today many would be less inclined to rash judgments, if this matter were considered more carefully.

units.la: Sequitur altera ratio, quae simul ad prioris confirmationem pertinet: Nullius enim rei mihi conscius sum. Argumentum est huiusmodi: Quisquis sibi ipsi bene conscius est, is facilè omnium de se iudicia contemnit: Atqui ego nullius delicti mihi conscius sum. Ergo pro minimo mihi est, quòd à vobis dijudicor, neq; etiam meipsum ego iudico aut damno. Ne quis tamen hoc arrogantius dictum putaret, & extra Pauli institutum longius extenderet, mox subijcit: Sed non propterea iustificatus sum. Sensus est. Quod nunc dico, ad hoc solum restringi debet, de quo nunc inter nos controuertitur: Nimirum ad Apostolatum aut ministerium ecclesiae Christi. In eo me sic versatum esse scio, vt de conscientiae puritate & fide mea tam apud Deum quàm homines gloriari possim. Quoad verò reliqua, scio me non propterea iustificatum esse, si Deus mecum iudicio contendere vellet: sed apud eius tribunal alia iustitia mihi opus esse, quae me tueatur. Facit ad huius dicti expositionem, quod sub finem cap.7. ad Romanos habetur: vbi sub propria persona innatam omnibus hominibus naturae vitiositatem, & quantum ea in renatis quoq; & credentibus possit, commemorat. Discimus autem hoc loco, quam ingens bonum sit mens sibi bene conscia. Nam vt apud Deum constantes & intrepidos facit: ita haec sola nos tuetur & in vocatione nostra confirmat, si quando homines de nobis iniquius iudicant. Huic ergo imprimis studere debent omnes. Frustra enim externo fuco sese apud homines venditant, quos propria mens sceleris accusat, & dormientibus quoq; obstrepit. Interim quoad Dei tribunal, nemo glorietur. Nam tanta est iustitia eius perfectio, vt ad eam nobis pertingere non liceat. Et quamuis nos, qui natura in nobis ipsis examinandis indulgentiores sumus, nihil in nobis animaduertamus reprehensione dignum, altius tamen in animi nostri recessus penetrat oculus Dei, quem nihil latere potest. Quod Dauid obseruans cla-mabat: Errores quis animaduertat? ab occultis meis libera me. Et si Paulus se iustificatum esse negat, quid de nobis fiet, qui plerunq; caecis affectibus abrepti tunc quoq; peccamus, quando officium facimus? Nec enim actioni externae animi institutum semper respondet. Confutantur igitur hoc loco validissime, qui suorum operum meritis tantum tribuunt, vt cum Pharisaeis in ipsius Dei conspectu de propria iustitia gloriari audeant.
units.tr: Follows the second reason, which also serves to confirm the first: "For I am conscious of nothing against myself." The argument runs thus: whoever is well aware of himself easily despises all judgments about himself; but I am conscious of no fault in myself. Therefore it is a very small matter to me that I am judged by you, nor do I even judge or condemn myself. Lest anyone think this said too boastfully and stretch it beyond Paul's intention, he immediately adds: "But I am not thereby justified." The sense is this: what I now say must be restricted to the matter about which we are now disputing among ourselves, namely the apostleship or the ministry of Christ's Church. In that office I know I have so conducted myself that I may glory in the purity of my conscience and my faith, both before God and before men. As for the rest, I know that I am not thereby justified if God wished to contend with me in judgment; but before his tribunal I need another righteousness that will protect me. What he says here is illuminated by what is written at the end of Romans 7, where in his own person he recounts the inborn sinfulness of all men and how far it can prevail even in the regenerate and believers. From this passage we learn how great a good it is to have a mind well aware of itself. For just as it makes us steadfast and fearless before God, so it alone protects us and confirms us in our calling when men judge us unfairly. Therefore all should chiefly strive for this. For in vain do men who are accused by their own minds of wickedness parade themselves before others with outward show, and that mind even clamours at them while they sleep. Meanwhile, as far as God's tribunal is concerned, let no one glory. For his perfect righteousness is so great that we are not permitted to attain to it. And although we, who by nature are too indulgent in examining ourselves, notice nothing in ourselves worthy of reproof, yet the eye of God, which nothing can escape, penetrates more deeply into the recesses of our minds. David, observing this, cried out: "Who will notice his errors? Free me from my hidden faults." And if Paul denies that he is justified, what will become of us, who, carried away for the most part by blind passions, sin even when we perform our duty? For outward action does not always correspond to the purpose of the mind. Therefore those are most powerfully refuted here who attribute so much to the merits of their works that they dare, with the Pharisees, to glory in their own righteousness in the very sight of God.

units.la: His tertiam rationem subiicit Paulus: Sed qui me dijudicat Dominus est. Quamuis ergo Corinthios iudices detrectaret, non tamen sibi immunitatem vendicauit Apostolus, sed iudicem se habere sensit Deum, quem in piis loquentem minime contempsit, vt in aliis locis est videre. Nunc autem huius meminit, vt Corinthiis ostendat, ipsos perperam facere, et nimium audaces esse, qui Dei partes sibi sumant, et de aliorum conscientiis velint iudicium facere. Quod autem in praesenti Paulus dicit, hoc ipsum memori mente versare debent, quotquot functionem aliquam sustinent: imo ij quoq;, qui sibi soli viuunt, et otium priuatum omnibus alijs studijs praeferunt. Non ergo decipiat eos vel propria mentis securitas, vel etiam aurae popularis fauor, si quando se hominum iudicio probari sentiunt: sed meminerint, Deum esse, qui et actiones nostras videt, et corda renesq; scrutatur, cui olim ratio reddenda erit.
units.tr: To these Paul adds a third reason: "But he who judges me is the Lord." Although he rejected the Corinthians as judges, the Apostle did not therefore claim immunity for himself, but felt that he had God as his judge, whom he by no means despised when speaking through the pious, as may be seen in other places. Now he mentions this in order to show the Corinthians that they act wrongly and are too bold, taking upon themselves the part of God and wishing to pass judgment on the consciences of others. What Paul says here, all who bear any office ought to keep in mind and fix in their memory; indeed, so should those too who live only for themselves and prefer private leisure to all other pursuits. Therefore let neither the security of their own mind nor the favour of popular applause deceive them, if at any time they feel they are approved by human judgment; but let them remember that there is God, who sees our actions, searches hearts and reins, and to whom an account will one day have to be rendered.

units.la: Debet huc referri huius loci conclusio, quae grauem admonitionem continet. Proinde (in-quit) ne ante tempus quicquam iudicate vsque dum venerit Dominus, qui & illustraturus est occulta tenebrarum, & manifesta faciet consilia cordium: ac tunc laus erit vnicuique a Deo. Sunt verba haec clara, neque multa interpretatione opus habent, ideo res ipsas potius inspiciamus. In his primum occurrit, quod certo olim iudicium erit vniuersale, in quo omnes homines sistentur, vt digna factis suis praemia recipiant. Docent hoc passim Scripturae, & Christus ipse non vno loco tam perspicue & constanter de eo concionatur, vt de eius veritate dubitare nefas sit. Petrus certe, inter prophanos & incurabiles omnis religionis atque pietatis contemptores numerat, nequam illos illusores, qui de nouissimo Christi aduentu ad iudicium ridicule & scurriliter loquuntur, vt eius fidem in dubium vocent. Etenim qui illud negant, si quantum in ipsis est, Dei iustitiam abolent. Quia enim non omnes in hac vita vel virtutis praemia recipiunt, vel scelerum supplicijs dignis multantur, nullus iustitiae Dei locus reliquus erit, nisi aliud iudicium restare dicamus, in quo ista digne & iuste dispensentur. Et hoc argumento veteres olim ad afferendam mortuorum resurrectionem & nouissimum Christi aduentum vsi sunt aduersus ethnicos, qui scripturarum auctoritatem contemnebant.
units.tr: The conclusion of this passage, which contains a grave admonition, must be referred here: "Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of hearts; and then shall each man have praise from God." These words are clear and need no lengthy interpretation, so let us rather look at the things themselves. In them, first, we meet the fact that there will one day be a universal judgment, in which all men will be brought forward to receive rewards worthy of their deeds. The Scriptures teach this everywhere, and Christ himself preaches of it in more than one place so plainly and consistently that it is wrong to doubt its truth. Peter certainly numbers among the profane and incurable despisers of all religion and piety those scoffing mockers who speak of the last coming of Christ to judgment in a ridiculous and buffoonish way, so as to call his faith into question. For those who deny it, so far as they are able, abolish the justice of God. For since not all in this life either receive the rewards of virtue or are punished with the penalties their crimes deserve, no place will remain for God's justice unless we say that another judgment remains, in which these things will be worthily and justly dispensed. With this argument the ancients once used to assert the resurrection of the dead and the last coming of Christ against the heathen, who despised the authority of the Scriptures.

units.la: Deinde quale iudicium hoc futurum sit, Paulus docet. Deus (inquit) illustrabit occulta tenebrarum, & manifestabit consilia cordium. Duobus hisce actiones simul hominum & cogitationes comprehendit. Occultorum aut meminit, quia ex eo fere impunitatis spem homines concipiunt, quod sua facinora latere & ignorari arbitrantur. Et vt in his celandis multi mire artificiosi sunt: ita abstrusissimi sunt cordium recessus, quibus consilia sua homines abscondunt. Neque temere a Propheta dictum est: Vafrum aut fallax est cor hominum, & obstinatum vel inscrutabile; quis cognoscet illud? Sed audi, quid ibidem mox respondeat Dominus? Ego & cor perscrutor, & renes exploro, vt reddam cuique secundum viam suam, & secundum fructum studiorum suorum. Quo etiam referri debet, quod de libris scribit Daniel, quos nouissimo die aperiri oportebat, ut omnium corda manifestentur, & tam boni quàm mali æquitatem diuini iudicij agnoscant. Vt verò tunc omnia patebunt, quæ nunc probè tecta & occulta putamus: ita abolebuntur prius opes, dignitates, honores, triumphi, amicitiæ, clientelæ, & quæcunq; alia sunt huius generis, quibus nunc se se tuentur, qui nihil præter mundum hunc infelicem sapiunt. Nudi enim & humano præsidio omni destituti in Dei conspectu comparebimus.
units.tr: Next, Paul teaches what kind of judgment this will be. God, he says, will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and manifest the counsels of hearts. By these two things he embraces both the actions and the thoughts of men. He mentions hidden things because men mostly conceive hope of impunity from this, that they think their crimes lie concealed and unknown. And just as many are wonderfully skilful at concealing them, so the recesses of hearts in which men hide their plans are most deeply hidden. Nor did the Prophet speak rashly when he said: "The heart of man is crafty and deceitful, and stubborn or inscrutable; who shall know it?" But hear what the Lord immediately answers in the same place: "I search the heart and try the reins, to give to each according to his way and according to the fruit of his doings." To this also should be referred what Daniel writes about the books, which were to be opened on the last day, so that the hearts of all may be made manifest, and both good and bad may acknowledge the equity of divine judgment. Just as then all things will lie open that we now think safely covered and hidden, so first will be swept away wealth, dignities, honours, triumphs, friendships, patronages, and whatever else is of this kind, by which those now shelter themselves who understand nothing beyond this unhappy world. For naked and destitute of every human protection, we shall appear in the sight of God.

units.la: Est autem huius considerationis vsus multiplex & valde necessarius. Primum in præsentia Paulus indicat, Ne quid temere de quoquam ante tempus pronuntiemus. Non quidem ciuilia aut ecclesiastica iudicia prohibentur, sine quibus hominum vita consistere non potest, propter improbos & audaces multos, quos publica authoritate coerceri necesse est. Neq; etiam admonitiones aut correptiones priuatæ abolentur, quas fraternæ charitatis opus non postremum esse constat, non autem aliquo cum fructu possunt fieri, nisi delicta arguantur, & accusentur. Sed in eo insistendum est, de quo hic agitur, ne de alicuius hominis conscientia temere iudicemus, sed quæ nos latent, Deo permittamus, qui olim occulta tenebrarum in lucem protrahet. Deinde monet etiam ista consideratio, vt vita innocentiam sectemur[?], neq; vllis fidamus huius sæculi præsidijs: quando illis Deus fle-cti non potest, quo minus iuste de nobis iudicet. Et si pudet in hominum conspectu res turpes designare, quanto magis Dei oculos nos vereri decet, quibus omnia patent, & qui ipsas quoq; cogitationes cordium intuentur[?]. Præterea habet locus iste dulcissimam consolationem, qua nos aduersus iniquam hominum improborum iudicia confirmemus. Nunc quidem sæpe calumniis opprimuntur optimi quiq;, & iniquis sententijs damnantur qui de multis bene sunt meriti, triumphantibus interea improbis, qui iustitiam cum veritate extinctam cupiunt. Sed erit aliquando rerum vicissitudo, & omnibus nota fiet piorum innocentia, ac vnicuiq; laus erit à Deo, prout in sua vocatione fidelis fuerit. Ista nos excitent o fratres, vt contemptis hominum iudicijs, IESV CHRISTO fideles simus, & in magno illo die audiamus lætam hanc sententiam: Venite benedicti patris mei, & possidete regnum paratum vobis à iactis fundamentis mundi. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: The use of this consideration is manifold and very necessary. First, in the present case Paul indicates that we should not rashly pronounce anything about anyone before the time. Not indeed that civil or ecclesiastical judgments are forbidden, without which human life cannot subsist, because of the many wicked and bold men who must be restrained by public authority. Nor are private admonitions and corrections abolished, which are agreed to be no small part of the work of fraternal charity, but which cannot be done with any profit unless faults are pointed out and accused. But what must be insisted upon is the matter of which we are speaking here: that we should not rashly judge the conscience of any man, but leave what is hidden from us to God, who will one day bring the hidden things of darkness into the light. Next, this consideration also warns us to pursue innocence of life and to trust in no defences of this age, since God cannot be turned aside from judging us justly. And if we are ashamed to point out shameful things in the sight of men, how much more ought we to revere the eyes of God, to which all things lie open, and which look upon the very thoughts of hearts. Moreover, this passage holds a most sweet consolation, by which we may strengthen ourselves against the unjust judgments of wicked men. Now indeed the best men are often overwhelmed with calumnies, and those who have deserved well of many are condemned by unjust sentences, while the wicked triumph, who desire that justice and truth be extinguished. But there will at some time be a reversal of things, and the innocence of the pious will be made known to all, and each will have praise from God according as he has been faithful in his calling. May these things stir us up, brothers, so that, despising the judgments of men, we may be faithful to Jesus Christ, and on that great day hear that joyful sentence: "Come, blessed of my Father, and possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XIX.
units.tr: HOMILY XIX.

units.la: Hæc autem, fratres, figura quadã transtuli ad meipsum & Apollo propter vos, vt in nobis discatis, supra id quod scriptum est non sapere: vt ne alius pro alio inflemini aduersus alium. Quis enim te discernit? Quid autem habes quod non acceperis? Quòd si etiam accepisti, quid gloriaris vt qui non acceperis? Iam saturati estis: iam ditati estis: absq; nobis regnum adepti estis: Atq; vtinam sane regnetis, vt & nos simul vobiscum regnemus.
units.tr: But I have transferred these things, brothers, by way of figure to myself and Apollos for your sake, so that in us you may learn not to think beyond what is written, and that none of you be puffed up in favour of one against another. For who makes you to differ? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you had not received it? Already you are full; already you are rich; you have reached the kingdom without us. And would indeed that you did reign, so that we might reign together with you.

units.la: Etsi verbi Dei prædicatores & ecclesiæ ministros ab ambitione & auræ popularis studio alienissimos esse decet, ijdem tamen ministerij sui authoritatem aduersus quosuis constanter tueri debent, ne ipsum Dei verbum & vniuersa fidei atq; salutis doctrina propter ipsos in contemptum veniat. Docet hoc Paulus admodum diligenter. Nam grauiter quidem monet, ne quod solius Dei esset sibi ipsis ministri vendicent, neq; ipsis hoc aliquid tribuat: simul autem diserte docet, quales haberi aut censeri debeant. Nimirum pro Christi ministris & mysteriorum Dei dispensatoribus, quos nemo abfq; Christi ignominia & propriæ salutis periculo contemnere possit. Et quia plerosq; ergà se tam hostili animo præditos esse sciebat, vt ipsorum iudicio se committere non satis tutum esset, ad Dei tribunal provocat, ne tota ipsius authoritas collaberetur. Vbi multa audiuimus, quæ omnium nostrûm institutioni & consolationi seruire possunt. Nunc verò ad eorum, quæ modò recitauimus, expositionem accedamus, in quibus tria agit. Primò statum huius tractationis infert, & ad hunc applicat, quæ hucusque dicta sunt. Deinde nouis argumentis eundem confirmat. Tandem graui Ironia ambitiosis illis & superbis suâ doctrinâ contemptoribus insultat, vt vel inuiti erubescant.
units.tr: Although preachers of God's Word and ministers of the Church ought to be most free from ambition and the pursuit of popular applause, they must nevertheless constantly defend the authority of their ministry against anyone whatever, lest the Word of God itself and the whole doctrine of faith and salvation be brought into contempt on their account. Paul teaches this very carefully. For he earnestly warns that ministers should not claim for themselves what belongs to God alone, nor should anyone attribute such things to them; at the same time he plainly teaches what they ought to be regarded and considered as: namely, the ministers of Christ and the stewards of God's mysteries, whom no one can despise without dishonouring Christ and endangering his own salvation. And because he knew that many were so hostile towards him that it was not safe enough for him to submit to their judgement, he appeals to the tribunal of God, lest his whole authority collapse. Here we have heard many things that can serve the instruction and consolation of us all. But now let us come to the exposition of the passage just recited, in which he does three things. First, he draws the sum of this discussion and applies to it what has been said so far. Then he confirms the same by new arguments. Finally, with a heavy irony he mocks those ambitious and proud despisers of his teaching, so that they may blush even against their will.

units.la: Statum & summa omnium sic complectitur, vt simul ostendat, cur de seipso & Apollo toties fit locutus. Nam sic ait: Haec autem, fratres, figura quadam translatio ad meipsum & Apollo propter vos, vt in nobis discatis, &c. Sensus verborum hic est: Ego quidem & Apollo nunquam in hoc fuimus, vt nobismet ipsis discipulos faceremus, neq; puto aliquos ex eorum numero, qui nostrae doctrinae recte crediderunt, inveniri, qui nostris nominibus ad sectas fouendas abutantur. Hoc enim alteri illi faciunt, quos caeca ambitio & aemulatio nobis aduersarios facit. Veruntamen ne illorum nomina traducendo alicui nouae contentionis occasionem darem, malui personas mutare, & aliorum culpam in nos transferre, idq; propter vos, vt in nobis, id est, nostro exemplo discatis humiliter & modestè agere, & sopitis contentionibus pacem & concordiam ecclesiae fouere, &c.
units.tr: He sums up the argument and the whole matter in such a way that he also shows why he has so often spoken about himself and Apollos. For he says: "But these things, brothers, I have transferred by way of figure to myself and Apollos for your sake, that in us you may learn," and so on. The sense of the words is this: Apollos and I never intended to make disciples for ourselves, nor do I think that any of those who rightly believed our teaching can be found to abuse our names in order to foster sects. For those who do this are others, whom blind ambition and rivalry make our opponents. Nevertheless, lest by naming their names I should give some occasion for new strife, I preferred to change the persons and to transfer the blame of others to ourselves, and this for your sake, so that in us, that is, by our example, you may learn to act humbly and modestly, and, having quelled contentions, to cherish peace and concord in the Church, and so on.

units.la: Continent autem haec verba memorabile exemplum Christianae modestiae, quo Paulus toti Christianorum ecclesiae praeluxit. Nam vt huius pacis atq; concordiae consuleret, ne eos quidem nominatim perstringere voluit, qui non solum reprehensione, verumetiam quouis supplicio digni erant. Adhaec inuidiam omnem in se potius transferre, & suum nomen substituere maluit, quàm nouis litibus causam praebere iis, qui iam ante plus satis dissidebant. In eo autem Christum praeceptorem imitatus est, quem eadem omnino ratione aduersus Iudam prodit, vsum fuisse nouerat. Cum enim hunc ob coniurationem cum sacerdotibus factam admonere vellet, non acerbis aut odiosis conuiciis, non correptionibus duris, quales ille merebatur, vsus est, sed securo[?] & oscitanti sceleris atrocitatem ita depinxit, vt is quidem de se agi sentiret, nullis autem contentionibus ideo turbaretur Caena mystica, quam ipse concordiae & mutuae dilectionis testeram aut vinculum esse volebat. Debent exempla ista diligenter considerari, vt de iis iudicare discamus, qui ne aliquibus inferiores esse putentur, non modo cum turbulentis hominibus seuerius & immodestius agunt, verumetiam de ecclesia bene meritos calumniis & conuiciis acerrimis proscindunt, & ecclesias simul omnes litibus nunquam finiendis innoluunt. Et tunc demum se egregie concionatos esse arbitrantur, si ex sacro fugge stu apud rudem plebeculam Zuinglianos, Caluinistas, Sacramentarios insanis clamoribus itidem ingeminarint, non sine crebra diabolorum & Satanarum repetitione. Atqui Paulus apud Corinthios ab aemulorum suorum nominibus abstinendum esse putauit, & alibi eos quoq; patienter tulit, qui aemulatione praua abrepti Christum praedicabant. Quid ergo nostri aliud faciunt, quàm quòd se a spiritu apostolico alienissimos esse produnt, et ita dum prae omnibus aliis excellere volunt, sibijpsis infamiam accersunt? Discant ergo ecclesiarum ministri modestiae studere, & nihil antiquius habeant ecclesiarum concordia, quam proprij potius sanguinis iactura tueri, quàm priuatae gloriae studio turbare debent. Idem ad se quoq; priuatim omnes alij transferant, ne dum ius suum vehementius persequuntur, dilectionis mutuae obliti[?] seipsos simul & alios turbis grauioribus implicent.
units.tr: These words, moreover, contain a memorable example of Christian modesty, by which Paul shone forth for the whole Church of Christians. For in order to secure this peace and concord, he would not name even those who deserved not only rebuke but any punishment whatever. Moreover, he preferred to draw all odium upon himself and to put forward his own name, rather than give cause for fresh quarrels to those who were already at odds more than enough. In this he imitated Christ his teacher, whom he knew to have used the very same method against Judas. For when Christ wished to warn him about his conspiracy with the priests, he did not use bitter or hateful reproaches or harsh rebukes, such as he deserved; instead, he portrayed the atrocity of the crime so carelessly and drowsily that Judas felt the matter was about himself, yet the Lord's Supper, which Christ wanted to be a token and bond of concord and mutual love, was not disturbed by any quarrels. These examples ought to be carefully considered, so that we may learn to judge those who, lest they be thought inferior to anyone, not only deal more harshly and intemperately with troublesome men, but also tear to pieces with the sharpest calumnies and insults those who have deserved well of the Church, and entangle all the churches in quarrels that never end. And they think they have preached excellently only when, from the sacred pulpit, before the simple common people, they have repeated with mad shouting, and not without frequent mention of devils and Satans, the words "Zwinglians, Calvinists, Sacramentarians." Yet Paul thought that at Corinth the names of his rivals should be passed over in silence, and elsewhere he also patiently bore with those who, carried away by a perverse rivalry, preached Christ. What, then, do our people do other than reveal that they are most alien from the apostolic spirit, and thus, while they wish to excel above all others, bring infamy upon themselves? Let ministers of the churches therefore learn to devote themselves to modesty, and let them hold nothing more precious than the concord of the churches, which they ought to defend even at the cost of their own blood, rather than disturb it for the sake of private glory. Let all others likewise apply this to themselves in private, lest, while they pursue their own right too vehemently, forgetful of mutual love, they entangle both themselves and others in more serious troubles.

units.la: Caeterum videamus paulo diligentius, quid Corinthijs Paulus in praesenti praecipiat. Primùm, vt discatis (inquit) in nobis supra id quod scriptum est non sapere. Quo loco sapiendi verbum non de rerum cognitione aut prudentia exponi debet, sed de iudicio, quod quis intra animum suum vel de seipso, vel de alio concipit. Sensus ergo est, ne de seipsis aut doctoribus suis sublimius sentiant quàm scriptura de homine sentire docet, vtq; meminerint in scripturis passim humanam naturam omnem infirmitate, caecitatis & deplorata vitiositatis damnari, commendari, aut nobis modestiam, quae omnis boni authore agnoscit Deum, & proinde non in hominibus, sed in illo vno gloriari docet. Huc ergo in primis pertinet, quod supra ex Ierem. adduxit: Ne glorietur sapiens in sapientia sua, neq; glorietur robustus in robore suo, nec glorietur dives in diuitijs suis: sed in hoc glorietur qui gloriatur, quòd intelligat & cognoscat me: quoniam ego sum Dominus, qui misericordiam, iudicium & iustitiam facio in terra, &c. Est ergo hoc Christiani hominis officium, vt suo se pede metiatur, neq; altius quid de seipso sentiat, quin potius se totum Dei verbo, quod in scripturis reuelatur, subijciat. Est hoc dictu quidem facile, sed factu durum et graue propter innata nobis ambitione et gloriae inanis studium: quod tame corrigetur in nobis, si rationes, quas paulo post adducet Paulus, nō oscitater considerauerimus.
units.tr: Moreover, let us look a little more carefully at what Paul here enjoins on the Corinthians. First, that you may learn, he says, in us not to think beyond what is written. In this place the word "to think" ought not to be explained as knowledge of things or prudence, but as the judgement which someone forms in his mind, either about himself or about another. The sense, then, is that they should not think of themselves or of their teachers more highly than Scripture teaches a human being should be thought of, and that they should remember that in the Scriptures every human nature is everywhere condemned for weakness, blindness and utterly corrupt sinfulness, or commended for it; and that Scripture teaches us modesty, which acknowledges God as the author of every good, and therefore teaches us to glory not in human beings but in him alone. To this, therefore, pertains above all what he had earlier quoted from Jeremiah: "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor let the strong man glory in his strength, nor let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he understands and knows me, for I am the Lord, who executes mercy, judgement and justice in the earth," and so on. It is therefore the duty of a Christian man to measure himself by his own foot, and not to think anything higher of himself, but rather to submit himself wholly to the Word of God, which is revealed in the Scriptures. This is easy to say, indeed, but hard and burdensome to do, on account of the ambition and the vain desire for glory that are born in us; yet this will be corrected in us if we consider carefully the reasons which Paul adduces a little later.

units.la: Sed alterum adhuc praecipit, quo prius hoc magis explicatur, quodq; ad institutum seu statum huius causae propriè pertinebat: Vt ne alius (inquit) pro alio inflemini aduersus alium. Quibus verbis hoc vult dicere, ne doctoribus suis ita superbiant, vt pro illis inter se lites suscipiant, atq; propter illos ecclesiam in sectas scindant. Recte autem inflandi verbo vtitur, vt superbiam sive ambitionem, tàm mali causam esse doceat. Est enim Metaphora, quae vel ab utribus sumitur, qui inflati turgent, & nescio quid magnum in se continere videntur, cum praeter aerem nihil habeant: vel a membris male affectis, quae ex inflammatione aut alia causa tument. Utraq; Metaphora docet quam stulte & ridicule faciant, qui spiritus eiusmodi superbos & confidentes animo concipiunt. Nam non solum inanis est tumor ille, qualis in utribus esse solet, verumetiam noxius. Ut enim in corpore inflammatio & tumor ex humoribus malis & noxijs nascuntur: ita opiniones falsae & stulta perfua-sio homines inflare solent, ut de seipsis arrogantius sapere & nihil non sibi tribuere incipiant. Et ut membra, quando primum inflammari & tumere incipiunt, videntur quidem pulsa macie priori augeri & egregie crescere, sed mox iustae proportionis mensuram excedunt, dolores novos sentiunt, & toti corpori molestiam atq; impedimentum afferunt: Ita qui arrogantiae spiritu inflantur, initio quidem aliquam virtutis speciem prae se ferunt, & magnificis Dei donis instructi videntur, at ijdem mox omnes modestiae fines transgressi tam sibi ipsis quam aliis intolerabiles fiunt. Et est hic fons omnium contentionum. Ut enim aequalitatis studium concordiam fovet: sic ambitiosa & caeca emulandi cupiditas aemulatione gignit, hoc odium parit, ex quo contentiones assiduae pullulant, quae ecclesiam & rempublicam turbant atq; evertunt. Exempla, quibus hoc probatur, in historiis cum sacris tum prophanis passim infinita habentur. Ideo Christus humilitatem & modestiam discipulis suis saepissime commendat, & quia illos pro innato omnibus hominibus gloriae & eminentiae desiderio subinde ad contentiones abripi videbat, iam moriturus omnium pedes abluit, ut exemplum illis relinqueret, cuius nunquam possent obliuisci, & quod solum superbientes spiritus posset reprimere.
units.tr: But he still gives another precept, by which the first is made clearer, and which pertained properly to the subject or state of this cause: that none of you, he says, be puffed up in favour of one against another. By these words he means that they should not be so proud of their teachers that, on their behalf, they take up quarrels among themselves and split the Church into sects because of them. He rightly uses the word "puffed up," to teach that pride or ambition is the cause of so great an evil. For it is a metaphor taken either from bladders which swell and seem to contain something great, though they have nothing but air, or from diseased limbs which swell from inflammation or some other cause. Each metaphor shows how foolish and ridiculous they are who conceive such proud and self-confident spirits. For that swelling is not only empty, as it is in bladders, but also harmful. For just as in the body inflammation and swelling arise from bad and noxious humours, so false opinions and foolish persuasion commonly puff people up, so that they begin to think more arrogantly of themselves and to attribute everything to themselves. And just as limbs, when they first begin to become inflamed and swell, seem indeed to grow remarkably, the flesh having been pushed out, but soon exceed the measure of right proportion, feel new pains, and bring discomfort and hindrance to the whole body, so those who are puffed up with the spirit of arrogance at first display some appearance of virtue and seem to be furnished with splendid gifts of God, but soon, having passed all bounds of modesty, they become intolerable both to themselves and to others. And this is the source of all contentions. For just as the desire for equality fosters concord, so blind and ambitious eagerness to rival others gives birth to rivalry, and this bears hatred, from which constant quarrels spring up, which disturb and overthrow the Church and the commonwealth. Examples proving this are found everywhere, in abundance, both in sacred and in profane histories. Therefore Christ very often commends humility and modesty to his disciples, and because he saw them being driven into contentions again and again by that desire for glory and preeminence innate in all human beings, he, about to die, washed the feet of all, so as to leave them an example which they could never forget, and which alone could restrain proud spirits.

units.la: Est autem hic probe obseruandum diaboli stratagema, qui cum plerique veritatis ministros exosos habeant, eo tamen homines adducit, ut quisque pro suo doctore cum alijs certamen suscipiat, & ita sub praetextu pietatis ecclesiae unitatem & religionem omnem turbet. Exemplum huius mali in Ioannis Bapt. discipulis habemus, quos hac ratione aduersus Christum extimulauit. Et hoc ipsum apud Corinthios factum fuisse, iam saepe dictum est. Et hodie non uno in loco idem fieri videmus, ut qui toti mundo dediti sunt, & doctrinam simul omnem extinctam cupiunt, tamen ne ab omni religione alieni esse videantur, unum aliquem ex verbi administris sibi deligunt, quem supra omnes extollunt, & pro cuius honore & authoritate sic pugnant, ut reliquis omnibus sua authoritatem derogent, simulq; verbum Dei in contemptum adducant. Habent isti fidem suam in per-sonarum respectu, quod ne fiat Iacobus graviter admodum prohibet. Atqui meminisse oportebat, neminem tantae authoritatis esse, ut ipsi aliud quam Dei verbum praedicanti credi debeat: hoc vero sua authoritatem ex seipso habere, neque absque manifesta Dei contumelia contemni posse, etiamsi ab homuncione omnium miserrimo praedicetur.
units.tr: Here we must also carefully note the devil's stratagem. Although most people hate the ministers of the truth, he still draws men into taking up a quarrel with others on behalf of their own teacher, and so, under the pretext of piety, he disturbs the unity and all the religion of the Church. We have an example of this evil among the disciples of John the Baptist, whom he stirred up in this way against Christ. That this very thing happened among the Corinthians has already often been said. Even today we see the same thing happening in more than one place: men who are wholly devoted to the world and desire all teaching to be extinguished nonetheless choose for themselves one of the ministers of the Word, so that they may not seem to be strangers to all religion. They exalt him above everyone else and fight for his honour and authority in such a way that they strip all the others of their authority and at the same time bring the Word of God into contempt. These men place their faith in regard to persons, which James strictly forbids. Yet they ought to have remembered that no one has such authority that he must be believed when he preaches anything other than the Word of God. And that authority, which belongs to the Word itself, cannot be despised without manifest insult to God, even if it is preached by the most wretched little man in the world.

units.la: Sed ad secundam huius loci partem transeamus, quanouis argumentis aduersus ambitiosos illos ostentatores eorumq; admiratores pugnat, & illa sic proponit, ut simul remedium ostendat praesentissimum, quo arrogantiae morbus coerceri possit. Argumenta duo sunt. Primum his verbis continetur: Quis te discernit? Discernere autem hoc loco idem est, quod aliquem alijs digniorem & praestantiorem aestimare, & ita ex aliorum ordine eximere. Solent enim quae pretiosiora nobis videntur ab alijs separari ac seligi. Itaq; sensus horum verborum est: Quis nam ille est tanta authoritate praeditus, qui te aut quenquam alium supra alios extollendi ius habeat, & cuius iudicio tu tantum tribuere debeas, ut te alijs praestantiorem ducas? Quasi diceret. Nemo pro suo aut aliorum placito alijs praeferri debet, nisi cui id bono iure obtigit: Atqui ius illud penes solum Deum esse docuimus, quando certum est, neminem praeter hunc de aliorum animo & fine iudicare posse. Quis ergo tu es, qui vel teipsum a communi ordine ministrorum eximis, aut te propter tuum doctorem reliquis credentibus excellentiorem putas? Seruit itaq; ratio ista tam doctoribus ambitiosis quam discipulis eorum coercendis: & hos quidem nimium stulte facere docet, qui doctoris sui authoritate freti alijs digniores haberi velint, illos autem plus quam stolidos esse, qui caeci propter vulgi temeraria iudicia eo vsque efferantur, ut locum aut gradum eminentiorem sibi in ecclesia vendicent, aut etiam eo glorientur, quod soli & vni Christo debetur. Vis igitur huius argumenti ex ordine dependet, quem Deus in ecclesia instituit. Ut enim in corpore humano membra quidem multa & diuersa sunt, nullum autem temere se alijs praefert, sed singula quicquid habent aut possunt ad totius corporis salutem conferunt: Ita in ecclesia ordines quidem & ministeria diuersa Deus instituit, sed quae omnia vni capiti subesse & ad ecclesiae totius salutem tendere debent. Et vt nulli ex membris datur, vt capitis officium sibi sumat: ita nemo ex ecclesiae ministris tantum sibi tribuere debet, vt ecclesiae caput dici, aut alios ex se denominari velit. Hinc ergo sequitur, quòd nemo seipsum discernere, sed singuli sub vno capite Christo suam stationem tenere, & quicquid eximij habeant, id in commune ad ecclesiae totius aedificationem conferre debeant.
units.tr: But let us pass on to the second part of this passage. Although Paul argues against those ambitious show-offs and their admirers, he presents his arguments in such a way that he also shows the most ready remedy by which the disease of arrogance can be restrained. There are two arguments. The first is contained in these words: "Who makes you to differ?" To make a difference here means the same as to judge someone more worthy and more excellent than others, and so to single him out from the rest. For the things that seem more precious to us are usually set apart from others and chosen. So the sense of these words is this: "Who is that man endowed with such authority that he has the right to exalt you or anyone else above the rest, and to whose judgement you ought to give so much weight that you consider yourself superior to others?" It is as if he said: No one should be preferred to others by his own or others' decision, unless he has obtained this by a good right. But we have shown that this right belongs to God alone, since it is certain that no one but God can judge the mind and purpose of others. Who then are you, who either separate yourself from the common order of ministers or think yourself more excellent than the rest of the believers because of your teacher? So this argument serves to restrain ambitious teachers as well as their disciples. It teaches that the former act very foolishly when, trusting in the authority of their teacher, they wish to be regarded as better than others; and it shows that the latter are more than foolish, who, blinded by the rash judgements of the crowd, become so puffed up that they claim for themselves a higher place or rank in the Church, or even boast of that which is owed to Christ alone and to him only. The force of this argument therefore depends on the order which God has established in the Church. For just as in the human body there are many different members, yet none of them rashly sets itself above the others, but each contributes whatever it has or can do to the health of the whole body, so in the Church God has instituted various orders and ministries, all of which must be subject to the one Head and aim at the salvation of the whole Church. And just as no member is given the office of the head, so no minister of the Church ought to claim so much for himself that he wishes to be called the head of the Church or to have others named after himself. Hence it follows that no one should make a difference for himself, but each individual should keep his place under the one Head, Christ, and should bring whatever distinction he has into the common stock for the building up of the whole Church.

units.la: At quod Corinthijs suis Paulus dicit, hoc ipsum omnibus dici potest hodie, qui sibi in ecclesia primatum vendicant, & supra omnes alios eminere volunt. Possumus ergo ijsdem verbis Romanum Pontificem compellare: Quis te discreuit ab alijs episcopis[?], vt tu potius quàm illi ecclesiae caput dici debeas? vt maiorem quàm illi peccata remittendi potestatem habeas? vt regibus & Imperatoribus praescribas, & eorum seruitio ad regnum tuum stabiliendum abutaris? vt ad pedum tuorum osculà omnes inuites? vt denique de necessitate salutis esse dicas, vt omnis anima Romanae sedi subijciatur? Quòd si respondeat, hoc se ex Petri successione habere, autem Christus discreuerit & ex aliorum discipulorum ordine segregarit, quando ei dixit: Tu es[?] Petrus, & super hanc petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam. Item, Tibi dabo claues regni coelorum: & quicquid ligaueris in terra, erit ligatum in coelis: & quicquid soluueris in terra, erit solutum in coelis. Et rursum, Pasce oues meas, &c. Si (inquam) haec & alia nobis obijciat Papa, facilè erit responsio, nihil minus voluisse Christum, quàm Petrum supra alios apostolos extollere. Nam illum non minus quàm alios hortatus est, vt procul abiecta dominandi cupiditate ad ministrandum omnibus sese accingat. Et quod illi dictum, id postea alijs omnibus Christum dixisse constat. Taceo nunc ea, quae de fabulosa Pontificum successione dici poterant, & quae alibi prolixè à nobis dicta sunt. Eadem est sacrificulorum atq; Monachorum ratio, quibus similiter dici potest: Quis vos discreuit, vt prae alijs spirituales dicamini, & Christianos reliquos omnes laicorum aut prophanorum loco habeatis? vt solis vobis librorum sacrorum lectio permissa sit? vt soli mystica Cœna Domini integra & sub vtraq; (vt loquuntur) specie vtamini? Quid obsecro habebunt illi quod respondeant? Scimus enim spiritu Christi omnes credentes donari, scimus sacras scripturas libros pijs omnibus communes semper fuisse, scimus Apostolos Cœnam totis ecclesijs tradidisse, qualem à Christo illi acceperant. Est ergo haec impia & nefaria temeritas, qua isti homines sese aduersus totum Christi gregem extollunt. Qui in repub. supra alios eminere volunt, id iure obtineant oportet: alioqui tyranni dicentur. Quanto magis hoc in ecclesia obseruari debet, vbi in CHRISTO IESV, quo ad aeternae salutis negotium, non est Iudaeus aut Graecus, non seruus aut liber, non mas aut foemina, sed omnia in omnibus Christus est? Scimus quidem verbi administros suum gradum tenere, at eosdem non vt dominentur aut capitis loco sint instituti esse dicimus, sed potius vt seruiant, & suo ministerio vnitatem ecclesiae seruent, non dissipent. Et Paulus Apostolos potestatem habere dicit ad aedificationem, non ad destructionem. Quapropter vanissima ambitiosorum hominum commenta sunt, quaecunq; illi de suo primatu & spiritualitate garriunt.
units.tr: But what Paul says to his Corinthians can be said today to all those who claim the primacy in the Church and wish to stand out above all others. We can therefore address the Roman Pontiff in the same words: "Who has made you to differ from the other bishops, so that you should rather be called the head of the Church than they? So that you should have greater power of remitting sins than they? So that you should dictate to kings and emperors and abuse their service to establish your own kingdom? So that you should invite all men to kiss your feet? So that, finally, you should say it is necessary for salvation that every soul be subject to the Roman See?" But if he replies that he has this from the succession of Peter, since Christ made a difference and separated him from the rest of the disciples when he said to him: "You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church"; and again: "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven"; and further: "Feed my sheep," and so on. If (I say) the Pope brings these and other passages against us, the answer will be easy: Christ wished no more than to exalt Peter above the other apostles. For he exhorted Peter no less than the others to cast away the desire to lord it over others and to gird himself to serve everyone. And it is established that what was said to him was afterwards said by Christ to all the others. I now pass over what might be said about the fabled succession of the Popes, and what we have discussed at length elsewhere. The same reasoning applies to the priests and monks, to whom one may likewise say: "Who has made you to differ, so that you are called spiritual above others, and so that you count all the other Christians as laymen or profane people? So that the reading of the sacred books is permitted to you alone? So that you alone use the holy Supper of the Lord whole and under both kinds (as they call it)?" What, I ask, will they have to answer? For we know that all believers are given the Spirit of Christ; we know that the holy Scriptures have always been common to all the godly; we know that the apostles handed down the Supper to all the churches just as they had received it from Christ. Therefore this is an impious and wicked rashness by which these men exalt themselves against the whole flock of Christ. Those who wish to stand out above others in the commonwealth ought to obtain this by right; otherwise they will be called tyrants. How much more ought this to be observed in the Church, where in Christ Jesus, as far as the business of eternal salvation is concerned, there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, neither male nor female, but Christ is all in all? We indeed acknowledge that the ministers of the Word hold their own rank, but we do not say that they have been appointed to lord it over others or to stand in the place of the head; rather they are to serve, and by their ministry to preserve the unity of the Church, not to scatter it. And Paul says that the apostles had power for building up, not for destroying. Therefore the most empty inventions of ambitious men are whatever they chatter about their primacy and spirituality.

units.la: Porrò ne qui propter dona peculiaria se dignos esse dicerent, qui ab alijs discernerentur, alterum argumentum subijcit Paulus: Quid autem habes, quod non acceperis? Quòd si etiam accepisti, quid gloriaris, vt qui non acceperis? Est in verbis istis non leue pondus, quod Interrogationis figura adhuc gratius reddit. Sic enim vult dicere: Stultum & ridiculum est alienis opibus superbire, seq; instar cornicula Æsopica plumis alienis ostentare. At quicquid boni & eximij habet homines, illud omne ex Deo habent. Quod si negare velis quisquis es, agedum prodi, & dic quid habeas quod non acceperis? Num corpus? num animam? nū sensus? nū reliquas corporis aut animae vires? nū eloquentiā, eruditionē, iudicij acumen? num tu ipse tibi vitium creare, num valetudinem pro tuo arbitrio tueri, corporis statuam mutare, aut vitae ad suum finem properanti diem vnum, imò horulam vnam adijcere potes? Nemo certè tam impudens, nemo tam vecors est, qui in his omnibus quicquam possit suum dicere. Cur ergo tu teipsum discernis, & pro tuo arbitrio prae alijs vis eminere? Vel cur hominibus ineptis & stolidis fidem habes, qui praecipiti suo & caeco iudicio tibi huius insolentiae authores sunt?
units.tr: Moreover, lest anyone should claim that he is worthy to be distinguished from others on account of special gifts, Paul adds a second argument: "What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?" These words carry no slight weight, and the figure of interrogation makes them more forceful still. For he means to say: It is foolish and ridiculous to be proud of other people's riches, and to show off in other people's feathers like Aesop's jackdaw. But whatever good and excellent qualities men have, they all have from God. And if you, whoever you are, want to deny this, come forward then and say what you have that you did not receive. Your body? Your soul? Your senses? The rest of the powers of body and soul? Your eloquence, learning, sharpness of judgement? Can you yourself create your own defect, or preserve your health at your own pleasure, change the stature of your body, or add to life, which is hastening towards its end, one single day, or indeed one single hour? Surely no one is so shameless, no one so senseless, that he can call anything in all these things his own. Why then do you make a difference for yourself and wish, at your own pleasure, to stand out above others? Or why do you trust foolish and stupid men, who by their rash and blind judgement are the authors of this arrogance in you?

units.la: Continent ergo hæc duo argumenta præsens remedium, quo carnis nostræ ambitionem atq; confidentiam coërcere possumus. Primum in illo erit, si quoties superbiæ spiritu titillamur, nobisipsis hanc quæstionem obiiciamus: Quis te discreuit? quo iure aut quo merito tu te alijs præfers? Ibi mox patebit, te non minus quam alios homines peccatorem, miserum, alienæ opis indigum atque mortalem esse. Quòd si tunc præclara Dei dona nobis in mentem veniant, si item conditio, quæ nobis illustrior obtigit, in oculos incurrat, tunc rursus Paulinum hoc nobisipsis occinamus: Quid autem habes, quod non acceperis? Num tu propheta natus es? num ecclesiasticam dignitatem, num regiam potentiam, num eloquentiam, eruditionem, multiplicem rerum vsum, opes, honores tecum ex vtero matris in hunc mundum intulisti? Num eadem illa, vt tibi propria, tecum hinc auferes? Quid hic aliud dicere poteris, quàm te nudum in hanc lucem venisse, & proinde hæc gratuita diuinæ bonitatis dona esse? Quæ ergo stultitia est, alienis superbire, & in ijs stabilem gloriam quærere, quæ commodato accepisti, ignarus, quando eadem sint suo largitori reddenda? Hæc certè qui probè expendunt, ij mox sentient, quantum consideratio ista ad coërcendas superbiæ cristas faciat, & procul dubio illas demittent, pauones imitati, qui caudam fulgentibus plumis sese late extollentem deijciunt, quàm primum pedes immundis & fœdis squamis turgentes conspicantur. Proderit etiam ista consideratio, ne ijs abutamur insolenter, quæ ex Dei liberalitate accepimus.
units.tr: These two arguments therefore provide a present remedy by which we can restrain the ambition and self-confidence of our flesh. The first is this: whenever we are stirred by the spirit of pride, let us put this question to ourselves: Who has made you to differ? By what right or merit do you set yourself above others? Then it will soon become clear that you are no less a sinner, wretched, in need of another's help, and mortal than other men. But if the excellent gifts of God then come to mind, or the more illustrious condition that has fallen to us, let us again sing to ourselves this saying of Paul: "What do you have that you did not receive?" Did you bring with you from your mother's womb into this world the prophetic office, ecclesiastical dignity, royal power, eloquence, learning, varied experience of affairs, wealth and honours? Will you take those same things away with you as your own? What could you say here except that you came naked into this light, and that therefore these are gratuitous gifts of divine goodness? What folly, then, is it to pride yourself on what belongs to others, and to seek lasting glory in things you have received on loan, forgetting that they must be returned to their giver? Those who weigh these things carefully will soon feel how much this consideration helps to curb the crests of pride, and without doubt they will lower them, like peacocks, who lower the tail spreading its shining feathers wide as soon as they see their feet swollen with filthy and foul scales. This consideration will also help us not to abuse insolently what we have received from God's liberality.

units.la: Et quia hæc doctrina in omnibus tam spiritualibus quàm corporalibus bonis locum habet, rectè loco isto D. Augustinus ad asserendam gratuitam iustificationem vsus est. Si enim, quoad corporis bona & externas dignitates, nihil ex nobisipsis proprium habemus, quanto minus in nostra potestate aut arbitrio sunt, quæ ad animam & æternæ salutis negotium spectant? Hic enim regeneratione, totius hominis innouatione, peccatorum remissione, sanctificatione, sapientia denique & iustitia opus est, quæ & diuina apprehendere, & ad Dei tribunal considere possint. At quis obsecro hominum seipsum regenerare, innouare & sanctificare potest? Quis Deum, vt ipsi peccata remittat, coget? Quis eam in suo intellectu lucem accendet, quæ sola mysteriorum Dei capax est? Num qui in peccato conceptus & natus est, vnquam poterit suis viribus eam iustitiam assequi, quæ Dei iudicium subire queat? Hæc certè omnes hominis vires superant, & proinde gratuita misericordiæ Dei dona sunt: à nobis autem apprehenduntur sola fide, quæ & ipsa (vt Paulus ait) Dei donum est: nimirum ad illud Christi respiciens: Nemo venit ad me, nisi Pater meus traxerit eum. Sufficit ergo vnus hic locus confutandus omnibus illis, qui pharisaico spiritu ebrij operum suorum meritis & propriæ iustitiæ fiducia in Dei conspectu superbiunt.
units.tr: And because this doctrine holds for all goods, spiritual as well as bodily, Augustine rightly used this passage to assert free justification. For if, as regards bodily goods and external dignities, we have nothing of our own, how much less are those things in our power or choice which concern the soul and the business of eternal salvation? Here there is need of regeneration, renewal of the whole man, forgiveness of sins, sanctification, and finally wisdom and righteousness, which can both grasp divine things and stand before God's tribunal. But who, I ask, can regenerate, renew and sanctify himself? Who can compel God to forgive him his sins? Who will kindle in his own understanding that light which alone is capable of the mysteries of God? Will one who has been conceived and born in sin ever be able by his own strength to attain that righteousness which can stand God's judgment? These things certainly surpass all human powers, and therefore they are gratuitous gifts of God's mercy. We apprehend them by faith alone, which too (as Paul says) is a gift of God, looking, of course, to that saying of Christ: "No one comes to me unless my Father draws him." One passage is therefore enough to refute all those who, drunk with a Pharisaic spirit, pride themselves in God's sight on the merits of their works and their confidence in their own righteousness.

units.la: Porrò quia quæ Paulus dixit tam perspicua & solida sunt, vt negari nullo modo possint, nunc iterum toti Corinthiorum ecclesiæ ista applicat, & illis cum sancta & graui Ironia insultans, docet, quàm inanis sit confidentia ipsorum, quæ tam superbos reddiderit. Iam (inquit) saturati estis, iam ditati estis, absq; nobis regnum adepti estis, &c. Saturatos, ditatos & iam reges factos esse ait, tò quòd ipsi sibi tales esse viderentur: simul autem ostendit, quantum ipsis persuasio ista noceat. Saturati enim erant, non quòd reuera salutis in Christo certi essent, sed quia verum animæ cibum, IESVM CHRISTVM, fastidirent. Nam vt hoc fruamur, esuriamus oportet, & ideo beatos ille pronunciat eos, qui iustitiam esuriunt & sitiunt. At non poterant famem istam saluberrimam sentire Corinthij, cùm se supra communem credentium mensuram profecisse putarent, & eorum similes essent, qui stomachum noxijs & pituitosis humoribus repletum habent. Vt enim illi neq; esuriunt verè, neq; naturalem edendi appetitum sentiunt, interim verò ἀτροφίᾳ [?] consumuntur, dum nutrimentum nullum habent: ita isti nihil præterea scire cupiebant, cùm tamen suis perfusionibus innixi, Christum non verè apprehendissent, qui solus panis ille vitæ est, qui nos ad vitam æternam sustentat. Simili ratione diuites iam factos esse ait, quòd non sentirent pauperiem, in qua omnes nascimur, & proinde confidentia spiritu decepti, sibi nihil porrò deesse putarent. Nam hæc etiam causa erat, quòd Christum non magni facerent, in quo vno regni cœlestis thesauri continentur, quos solis illis deberi ipse testatur, qui pauperes sunt spiritu. Opponit ergo ista Christi sententijs, quibus ille docuit, in quibus vera hominis felicitas consistat. Quasi diceret: Christus eos beatos dicit, qui pauperes spiritu iustitiam esuriunt atq; sitiunt: at vos quasi illum mendacij arguere libeat, cùm Christiani velitis dici, saturitatem & diuitias nescio quas iactatis, quarum fiducia vos eo vsq extollit, vt & supra alios omnes efferamini, & nostra etiam opera atq; ministerio vobis minimè o- pus esse putetis. Itáne ergo iam regnatis absq; nobis? & soli ne regno illo frui vultis,quod nos pri- mi vobis prædicauimus? Habent ergo verba ista acerbam exprobrationem ingratitudinis,qua eos non agnoscebant amplius, quorum laboribus ad bonorum tantorum spem primum fuerant erecti. Ne tamen quid ab ipso inuidiose dici putarent, addit per correctionrm : Atq; vtinam sane regne- tis,vt et nos simul vobiscum regnemus. Velim(inquit)ex animo vos eo vsq; progressos esse,quo vos progressos putatis. Nã vt vobis hoc salutare esset,ita ad nos quoq; gloria hæc vestra redundaret,& nos tam superatis laboribus & molestijs vniuersis, vna vobiscum regnaremus. Sed hæc dicendo, innuit illos vehementer falli, cùm ab illa perfectione adhuc procul absint, neq; aliquis dum in hac carne viuit, eo vsq; proficere possit, vt non quotidiana doctrina, admonitione,correctione & con- firmatione opus habeat.
units.tr: Moreover, since what Paul said is so clear and solid that it cannot be denied in any way, he now applies it again to the whole church of the Corinthians, and, mocking them with holy and grave irony, teaches how empty is that confidence of theirs which has made them so proud. "Now," he says, "you are satisfied, now you are rich, you have obtained the kingdom without us," and so on. He says they are satisfied, enriched and already made kings, because they seemed to themselves to be such; at the same time he shows how much this persuasion harms them. For they were satisfied not because they were truly certain of salvation in Christ, but because they loathed the true food of the soul, Jesus Christ. For to enjoy this we must hunger, and therefore he pronounces blessed those who hunger and thirst after righteousness. But the Corinthians could not feel that most wholesome hunger, since they thought they had progressed beyond the common measure of believers, and they were like those who have a stomach filled with harmful and phlegmatic humours. Just as these neither truly hunger nor feel the natural appetite for food, yet meanwhile waste away through atrophy, since they have no nourishment, so those men wanted to know nothing further, although, relying on their own infusions, they had not truly apprehended Christ, who alone is that bread of life which sustains us to eternal life.
