In a similar way he says they had already become rich, because they did not feel the poverty in which we are all born, and therefore, deceived by a spirit of confidence, they thought nothing more was lacking to them. This was also the reason they did not esteem Christ highly, in whom alone the treasures of the heavenly kingdom are contained, and which he himself testifies belong only to those who are poor in spirit. He therefore sets this against the sayings of Christ, in which he taught where true human happiness consists. As if he said: Christ calls blessed those who, poor in spirit, hunger and thirst after righteousness; but you, as if it pleased you to convict him of falsehood, though you wish to be called Christians, boast of I know not what satiety and riches, by the confidence of which you are lifted up so far that you are raised above all others, and think that even our labour and ministry are by no means needed by you. Do you therefore already reign without us? And do you alone wish to enjoy that kingdom which we first preached to you? These words therefore contain a bitter rebuke of ingratitude, because they no longer acknowledged those by whose labours they had first been raised to the hope of such great goods. Lest they think he says this out of envy, he adds by way of correction: "And I wish indeed that you reigned, so that we might also reign together with you." I would wish, he says, that you had truly advanced as far as you think you have advanced. For just as this would be salutary for you, so this glory of yours would also overflow to us, and we, after all our labours and troubles, would reign together with you. But in saying these things he hints that they are greatly mistaken, since they are still far from that perfection, and no one, while he lives in this flesh, can progress so far that he does not need daily teaching, admonition, correction and confirmation.

units.la: Quod autem Corinthijs dicitur,id non minus nostri quoq; seculi hominibus feruit. Arguitur enim his vniuersalis illa ingratitudo, qua in fidos ecclesiæ ministros ij quoq; peccant, qui Christia-nissimi dici atq; haberi volunt.Quando enim superstitionum tyrannidem & conscientiæ dolores in- tra sese sentiunt,aut alijs malis atq; periculis sese implicitos vident, tunc magno studio ad Euan- gelij præcones concurrunt, se totos illorum fidei committunt, eos in honore habent & pretio: Quàm primum verò ex angustijs emerserunt, eosdem odisse incipiunt, morositatis nimiæ accusant, & se tunc demum felicissimos fore sibi persuadent, si illis semel liberentur. Expertus est̃ hanc populi sui inconstantiam Moses. Cùm enim illis Dei promissiones denuntiaret, qui ipsos ex Ægyptiaca seruitute liberare decreuisset, proni & cernui gratias agunt, & se ad omnia obsequentes fore pro- mittunt. At ijdem quoties in deserto res minus pro votis succedebant,omnium beneficiorum obliti horrendis conuitijs atq; minis aduersus Mosem & Aaronem insurrexerunt. Eadem postea pro- phetarum quoq; sors fuit:& ideo Hoseas improbos prophetarum contemptores non temere ad ve- teres historias reuocat, vt cogitent patres olim per prophetam ex Ægypto eductos, & in deserto custoditos fuisse. Senserunt idem Apostoli omnes, & hoc illud est̃,de quo Paulus in præsenti quæ- ritur. Quid autem aliud nostro seculo tam vulgare est̃ ? Qui Euangelij promissionibus & fidei securitate fruuntur,& quoad externa otio abundant, adhæc ex Euangelio opes,honores & omnis generis fructus vberrimos metunt,ijdem fere & primos huius doctrinæ instauratores, & eos qui hodie illam prædicant,tanc & angue peius oderunt,conuitijs obruunt, eiectos volunt, vt sine illis iam in libertate euangelica exultare,& illa ad carnis atq; peccandi licentiam abuti possint.Atque vtinam vere exultarent in Domino, & vere liberi essent,quales Christus describit apud Ioannem 8.cap. Sed omnes isti eorum similes sunt,qui sine legibus regnare volunt. Vt enim horum regnum ἀνάρχίᾳ[?], vel in tyrannidem tam ipsis quàm reipub.exitialem degenerat:sic istorũ hominum Euangelium in licentiam erumpit,qua ecclesiam simul & religionem omnem pessundat. Humilie- mur ergo sub potenti manu Domini,et nos huic gratos atq; obsequentes præbeamus,vt in CHRISTO IESV vere saturi & diuites regnemus, quoad hic viuere datur, & cum eodem olim re- gnum illud beatissimum consequamur, cuius non est̃ finis, & cuius delitiae atq; opes omnem huius mundi intellectum superant.Illi debetur benedictio,honor,gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: What is said to the Corinthians applies no less to the people of our own age. For that universal ingratitude is rebuked in them, by which even those who wish to be considered most Christian sin against the faithful ministers of the church. When they feel within themselves the tyranny of superstitions and the pangs of conscience, or see themselves entangled in other evils and dangers, then with great eagerness they run to the heralds of the Gospel, commit themselves wholly to their teaching, and hold them in honour and esteem. But as soon as they have emerged from their distress, they begin to hate them, accuse them of excessive peevishness, and persuade themselves that they will be most happy once they are finally freed from them. Moses too experienced this inconstancy of his people. When he announced to them God's promises, since God had decided to free them from Egyptian servitude, they prostrated themselves and bowed low, giving thanks and promising to obey in all things. But whenever in the desert things turned out less according to their wishes, they forgot all the benefits and rose up against Moses and Aaron with dreadful reproaches and threats. Later the lot of the prophets was the same; and therefore Hosea does not lightly recall the ancient histories to rebuke the wicked despisers of the prophets, so that they may consider that their fathers were once led out of Egypt through a prophet and kept in the desert. All the Apostles experienced the same, and this is what Paul is inquiring into in the present passage. But what is so common in our own age? Those who enjoy the promises of the Gospel and the security of faith, and who abound in outward leisure, moreover reap from the Gospel riches, honours and every kind of abundant fruit, very often hate the very first restorers of this doctrine, and those who preach it today, worse than a snake. They overwhelm them with reproaches and want them cast out, so that they may exult without them in gospel liberty and abuse it for the licence of the flesh and of sinning. And would that they truly exulted in the Lord and were truly free, as Christ describes them in John chapter 8. But all these men are like those who want to reign without laws. For just as their kingdom degenerates into anarchy, or into a tyranny deadly both to themselves and to the commonwealth, so the Gospel of these men breaks out into licence, which ruins at once the church and all religion. Let us therefore humble ourselves under the mighty hand of the Lord, and show ourselves thankful and obedient to him, so that in Christ Jesus we may truly reign satisfied and rich, as long as it is given us to live here, and with him at last attain that most blessed kingdom, which has no end, and whose delights and riches surpass all understanding of this world. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XX.
units.tr: HOMILY XX.

units.la: Deus enim,puto,nos vltimos Apostolos spectandos proposuit, tanquam mortiaddictos.Nam spectaculum factisumus mundo,& Angelis & hominibus.Nos stulti propter Christum,vos autem pru- dentes in Christo:nos infirmi,vos autem validi: vos gloriosi,nos i- gnominiosi Adhanc vsq; horam & esurimus & sitimus,&nudi su- mus, & colaphis cædimur, & incertis sedibus erramus, & labora- mus operantes proprijs manibus:conuitijs affecti,bene precamur: persecutionem patientes, sustinemus: infamati,precamur; vt pia-cula mundi facti sumus,omnium sordes vsq; adhuc.
units.tr: For God, I think, has put us apostles forward as the last, like men condemned to death. For we have been made a spectacle to the world, to angels and to men. We are fools for Christ's sake, but you are wise in Christ; we are weak, but you are strong; you are honoured, but we are dishonoured. To this very hour we both hunger and thirst, and we are naked, and buffeted, and have no certain dwelling place, and we toil, working with our own hands. Being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we endure it; being defamed, we entreat. We have been made as the refuse of the world, the offscouring of all things, even until now.

units.la: VT Deus humani generis amantissimus & ad benefaciendum propensus esse: ita nos pro acceptis beneficijs gratos sibi esse vult, & vix alio scelere magis quàm ingratitudine offenditur. At hîc quàm maximè elucet nostri ingenij vitiositas. Nam etsi nos sine illo nihil posse, & ab eodem nos quicquid boni habemus accepisse constet, plerique tamen illud non modò non agnoscunt, verumetiam ab illo acceptis donis turpissimè abutuntur. Fit hoc imprimis quoad Verbum illius, per quod seipsum & omnes gratiae suae thesauros nobis liberalissimè offert: at plerique hominum aut illud impiè contemnunt, aut quasi rem nihil ad se pertinentem securi negligunt, aut si quid in eius cognitione profecerunt, mox quasi summam felicitatis arcem sua industria obtinuerunt, doctrinam praeterea omnem fastidiunt, aduersus doctores suos superbè sese extollunt, & tandem in ipsam quoq; doctrinam sibi ius & imperium sumunt. Et hoc quidem apud Corinthios factum fuisse, non semel iam diximus. Hos enim Paulus magnis laboribus & non sine grauissimis periculis ab idololatria ad qualemcunq; veri Dei & unici Seruatoris IESV CHRISTI cognitionem adduxerat. Ipsi verò æmulorum eius blanditijs & magnifica sublimioris sapientiae atq; eruditionis ostentatione fascinati, sibi nihil porrò deesse putabant, & ipsum Paulum quasi rudem & cœlestis philosophiae imperitum contemnebant. Qui contemptus quia cum manifesto salutis ipsorum periculo coniunctus erat, suam authoritatem ille diligenter asserit, & nuper non sine graui exprobratione docuit, quàm inanis & turpis sit haec illorum confidentia, qua sese aduersus fidos Euangelij praeconei extollant. At quod tunc coepit, nunc absoluit & copiosius explicat.
units.tr: God, who is most loving of the human race and inclined to do good, wishes us to be grateful to him for the benefits we receive, and he is offended by almost no crime more than by ingratitude. Here the weakness of our nature shines out most clearly. For although it is certain that we can do nothing without him, and that whatever good we have we have received from him, yet many not only fail to acknowledge this but even most shamefully abuse the gifts they have received. This happens above all with regard to his Word, through which he offers himself and all the treasures of his grace to us most freely. Yet many people either impiously despise it, or carelessly neglect it as something that has nothing to do with them; or if they have made some progress in knowing it, they at once think that by their own effort they have attained the citadel of supreme happiness. Moreover, they scorn all teaching, proudly raise themselves against their teachers, and finally claim for themselves the right and authority over the teaching itself. That this happened among the Corinthians, we have already said more than once. For Paul had brought them, with great labours and not without the most serious dangers, from idolatry to some knowledge of the true God and of the one Saviour Jesus Christ. But they, bewitched by the flattery of his rivals and by the boastful display of a higher wisdom and learning, thought they lacked nothing more, and they despised Paul himself as a rude man, ignorant of heavenly philosophy. Since this contempt was bound up with a clear danger to their salvation, he carefully vindicates his authority, and recently, with no small rebuke, he taught how empty and shameful is this confidence of theirs, by which they raise themselves against the faithful preachers of the Gospel. But what he began then, he now completes and explains more fully.

units.la: Etenim cùm dixisset: Atq; vtinam sanè regnum adepti essetis, ut & nos simul vobiscum regnemus: nunc quasi rationem huius dicti redditurus, addit: Deus enim, puto, nos vltimos Apostolos spectandos proposuit, tanquam morti addictos, &c. Quibus verbis simul non obscurè perstringit æmulos suos cum omnibus illis, qui ab ipsis excæcati germanos Christi Apostolos aspernabantur. Quasi diceret: Non immerito optarim me vobiscum regni participem fieri, quod vos iam adeptos esse existimatis. Etenim mirum est, vestris illis rem tam feliciter & absq; omni periculo succedere, vosq; tam facilè tamq; citò superatis omnibus molestijs in portum quietis appulisse, à quo nos cum reliquis adhuc tam procul absumus. Quòd si hoc vobis reuera contigit, & Euangelij praedicatio cum temporaria felicitate & huius mundi fauore omnino coniungi potest, non iniuria nos de nostra conditione queri possimus. Ea enim eiusmodi est, ut Deus videatur nos Apostolos fecisse vltimos, id est, contemptissimos, abiectissimos miserrimosq; omnium mortalium, adeoq; nos spectandos proponere omnibus populis, perinde ut de facinorosis fieri solet, qui post latam [?] in ipsos capitis sententiam per vrbem circumducuntur, mox ad crudele mortis supplicium abripiendi. Nam spectaculum factum sumus toti mundo, neq; hominibus solis, verumetiam Angelis. Iliud autem non sine causa dicit Paulus. Erat enim spectatu dignissimum, pauculos homines, ex gente infima oriundos, nulla regum authoritate & eruditionis existimatione commendatos, adhaec omni praesidio destitutos & prorsus egenos per totum orbem discurrere, apud omnes gentes nouam religionis formam inducere, veteres ritus abolere, cum sacrorum mystis, cum philosophis, cum rerumpub. gubernatoribus passim in certamen descendere, & plerunque victores abire. Hoc (inquam) spectaculum fuit, quale orbis hic nunquam vidit, & quale nemo Regum vnquam suis exhibuit. Rursus hoc quoq; spectatu dignissimum & cum totius mundi admiratione coniunctum erat, illos ipsos, cùm neminem laederent, prodessent autem omnibus, & doctrinam suam signis inauditis & nunquam visis antea, & quae plurimis salutem certam afferebant, confirmarent, omnibus tamen inuisos esse, propter ipsos fora omnia fremere, tribunalia omnia fatigari, adhaec potentissimos quosque sibi ab illis timere, qui nullis ad nocendum viribus instructi erant, neque etiam in repub. aliquid noui moliebantur. Superabat haec omnia, quod cùm vbique locorum in carceres abducerentur, virgis caderentur, publica authoritate relegarentur, saepe etiam lapidibus obruerentur, simul tamen vbique victoriosum crucis trophaeum erigebant, & illic quoq; ecclesias Christo colligebant, vnde ipsi cum ignominia eijciebantur. Fuit ergo hoc mirabile omnino theatrum, in quo ijdem & extrema quaeq; patiebantur, & de suis aduersarijs atq; horum principe diabolo gloriosè triumphabant. Spectatores autem habuerunt nõ solum homines, verumetiam Angelos. Nam hi pios Dei seruos comitari, circa hos castra figere, eosdem adiuuare, deducere & ex periculis eripere consueuerunt. Cuius rei exempla in Iacobo patriarcha, in Elisæo, Daniele, Apostolis item non pauca ha-bentur.Imo angelos ob hominum conuersionem atque salutem gaudere Christus testatur, & idem (vt ad Ephes.cap.3. Apostolus scribit)non parum proficiunt ex ea, quam cum ecclesia habent, con-suetudine. Discunt enim quæ sit multiformis illa sapientia Dei, quæque eiusdem potentia inuicta, quando gentium diuersissimarum hominum in unius fidei confessionem conuenire, & Christum in infirmis & contemptissimis seruulis suis de mundo & eius principe triumphare videnti[?]. Et ista qui-dem Corinthijs in mentem reuocat Paulus, ut intelligant, Deum longe altam sui regni rationem in terris hisce instituisse, quam ea sit, quæ ab ipsius æmulis fingebatur.
units.tr: For when he had said, "Would indeed that you had come to reign, so that we might reign with you," now, as if about to give an account of this saying, he adds: "For God, I think, has put us apostles forward as last, like men condemned to death," and so on. In these words he at the same time not obscurely strikes at his rivals and with them all those who, blinded by them, despised the true apostles of Christ. As if he were saying: "I would not wrongly wish to share the kingdom with you, which you think you have already attained. For it is remarkable that your affairs turn out so happily and without any danger, and that you have so easily and quickly overcome all troubles and reached the harbour of rest, from which we are still so far distant, along with the rest. But if this has really happened to you, and the preaching of the Gospel can be altogether united with temporary happiness and the favour of this world, then we may justly complain about our condition. For it is of such a kind that God seems to have made us apostles last, that is, the most despised, abject and wretched of all mortals, and to have put us forward as a spectacle to all peoples, just as is commonly done with criminals who, after sentence of death has been pronounced against them, are led about through the city, soon to be dragged off to a cruel death. For we have been made a spectacle to the whole world, not only to men but also to angels." Paul does not say this without cause. For it was most worthy of being watched: a few men, born of the lowest race, recommended by no royal authority or reputation for learning, and moreover destitute of every protection and utterly poor, running about through the whole world, introducing among all nations a new form of religion, abolishing the old rites, entering into conflict everywhere with the priests of the mysteries, with the philosophers, with the rulers of states, and for the most part departing as victors. This (I say) was a spectacle such as this world never saw, and such as no king ever exhibited to his own people. Again, this too was most worthy of being watched and was joined with the wonder of the whole world: that these same men, when they harmed no one but benefited all, and confirmed their teaching by unheard-of signs never seen before, which brought certain salvation to very many, were nevertheless hateful to all; that because of them all the courts raged, all the tribunals were wearied, and moreover the most powerful men feared them, though they were armed with no power to do harm and were planning nothing new in the state. What surpassed all this was that, although they were led off to prisons everywhere, beaten with rods, expelled by public authority, and often even stoned, yet at the same time everywhere they raised the victorious trophy of the cross, and there too they gathered churches for Christ, from which they themselves were thrown out in disgrace. This was therefore a truly wonderful theatre, in which the same men suffered the utmost things and triumphed gloriously over their adversaries and over their prince, the devil. Their spectators, moreover, were not only men but also angels. For these have been accustomed to accompany the pious servants of God, to pitch their camp about them, to help them, to lead them and to rescue them from dangers. Examples of this are found in the patriarch Jacob, in Elisha, in Daniel, and likewise in the apostles, and not a few. Indeed, Christ testifies that the angels rejoice over the conversion and salvation of men, and, as the Apostle writes (Ephes. 3.), they profit not a little from that fellowship which they have with the Church. For they learn what is that manifold wisdom of God, and what is his unconquered power, when men of the most diverse nations come together into the confession of one faith, and when Christ, in his weak and most despised servants, is seen to triumph over the world and its prince. Paul recalls these things to the Corinthians so that they may understand that God has established on earth a plan of his kingdom far loftier than that which was imagined by his rivals.

units.la: Est autem nobis hic non ofcitanter consideranda ministrorum Christi conditio adeoque pio-rum omnium, qui Euangelij doctrinæ credunt. Veritas (quod gentium quoque philosophi vide-runt) odium parit, & eiusdem lux mundo admodum inuisa est, eò quòd per hanc arguantur opera eius mala, & quæcunque is prætexere solet, ut suam impuritatem defendat, aut saltem abscondat. At quia lucernam hanc per ministros suos Christus accendit, & hi illam inuito etiam mundo omnium oculis ingerunt, fieri non potest, quin plerisq; hominum inuisi fiant, & persecutionibus grauissimis exerceantur. Augetur etiam odium istud, quod securè peccantibus & sibi ipsis lætâ omnia pollicentibus horribilem Dei iram & sceleribus destinatas pœnas denuntiantiquæ omnia huius seculi filijs auditu intolerabilia esse videntur. Et hoc illud est, de quo Christus discipulos suos admo-nuit. Si sermonem meum seruauerunt (inquit) & vestrum seruabunt. Si me persecuti sunt, & vos persequentur. Imo fiet, ut si quis vos occiderit, putet se cultum Deo præstare. Deniq; hæc communis Christianorum hominum regula est, ut seipsos abnegent, crucem sibi à Deo destinatam sponte tollant, & Christi exemplum constanti animo & patientia inuicta sequantur. Prodest autem nos in horum consideratione sæpius versari, ne istis tanquam nouis & insolitis offendamur: deinde ut ad proposita nobis certamina præparemur, ut in illis victores simus.
units.tr: Here we must consider, not carelessly, the condition of the ministers of Christ, and indeed of all the godly who believe the doctrine of the Gospel. Truth (as even the philosophers of the Gentiles saw) begets hatred, and its light is very hateful to the world, because by it its evil works are exposed, and whatever pretexts it is accustomed to put forward in order to defend or at least to hide its impurity. But since Christ kindles this lamp through his ministers, and they thrust it before the eyes of all, even against the will of the world, it cannot be that they should not become hateful to many men and be harassed by the most grievous persecutions. That hatred is also increased by the fact that they denounce the dreadful wrath of God and the punishments destined for sins to those who sin securely and promise themselves all happiness; things which seem intolerable to all the sons of this age when they hear them. And this is what Christ warned his disciples about: "If they have kept my word," he says, "they will keep yours. If they have persecuted me, they will persecute you. Indeed it will happen that whoever kills you will think he is offering worship to God." Finally, this is the common rule of Christian men: that they deny themselves, willingly take up the cross appointed for them by God, and follow the example of Christ with a steadfast mind and unconquered patience. It is profitable for us, moreover, to dwell often on these things, so that we may not be offended by them as if they were new and unusual, and so that we may be prepared for the struggles set before us, and be victors in them.

units.la: Hic autem tria potissimum nos semper ob oculos habere oportet, de quibus in præsenti nos Paulus admonet. Primum, Deus, puto, nos spectandos proposuit. Ergo non in hominum impijssimorum audaciam & iniustissimam tyrannorum crudelitatem, sed in Deum respexit, cuius prouidentia & æterno decreto res mortalium dispensari & gubernari credebat. Est hoc consolationis argumentum efficacissimum. Quia enim Deus (ut initio monuimus) nostri amantissimus est, nihil procul dubio nobis accidere sinit, quod non utilissimum nobis sit; & ad promouendam salutem nostram necessarium. Idem quoque cum nostram imbecillitatem probe cognitam habeat, nos supra vires nostras tentari non sinit, imo cum tentatione vires nobis sufficit, quibus confirmati ea quoq; vincimus, quæ prius inuicta videbantur. Ideo in Dei prouidentiam sanctissimi quique semper respexerunt, cuius consideratio non fortes modo & patientes, verumetiam mansuetos & iniuriarum tolerantes fecit, atque omnem priuatæ vindictæ cupiditatem in illis reflinxit. Hinc illa Iosephi facilitas & indulgentia in fratres pessimè de se meritos manauit. Illis enim pœnas dignas timentibus dicebat: Equidem vos cogitauistis aduersus me malum, at Deus cogitauit idipsum in bonum, ut faceret quemadmodum hodie apparet, & seruaret in vita populum multum. Ex eodem fonte Iobi quoque patientia profluxit, qui non quid Chaldæi fecissent, sed quid Deus de se & rebus suis fieri voluisset secum reputans, in hæc verba erupit: Deus dedit, Deus abstulit, sit nomen Domini benedictum. Et Dauid grauissima quæque certamina hoc quasi clypeo tectus superauit, quòd dies vitæ suæ apud Deum numeratos esse, & fugas quoque suas ab illo cerni, atque lachrymas om-nes ab eo colligi & in rationes ipsius adscribi crederet. Ideo Christus discipulos suos hoc potissimum argumento consolabatur, cum de periculis, quæ subituri erant, eos admonuisset, Pili capitis vestri(inquit) numerati sunt. Ite, Nonne duo passerculi denariolo veneunt? Atqui dico vobis, ne unum quidem illorum perire absque voluntate Patris mei. Est ergo Agonothetes noster Deus, qui ut certaminum species nobis præscripsit, ita eorundem euentum felicissimum ab æterno decreuit, & ad hunc omnia suæ prouidentiæ consilio dirigit. Deinde meminerimus nos in istis certaminibus spectatores habere non homines solos, sed etiam Angelos, qui non otiosi spectant, sed simul nos tuentur, & sæpe insciios, imo interdum inuitos, periculis imminentibus subducunt. Quoties ergo hostium multitudine terremur, aut periculorum agminibus obruimur, semper nobis ipsis illud Elisæi occinamus: Ne metuas,nam eorum qui nobiscum, plures sunt,quam eorum qui cum illis. Item illud Dauidis: Castra figit Angelus Domini circum eos, qui ipsum timent,& eripit eos. Addamus his tertio loco exempla veterum Martyrum, quorum certamina nostrum theatrum esse debent, ut discamus, nos non primos esse, qui in ista arena pugnamus, imitemur autem illorum patientiam, fortitudinem, constantiam, lenitatem, precandi feruorem, & quaecunque alia in illis admiratione digna sunt. Imo meminerimus, nos in ista militia ducem habere Dei Filium, qui olim mundum hunc omnem nobis vicit, & hodie suo spiritu nobis adest, ne unquam succumbamus. Qui ista diligenter cogitant, facile omnibus aduersis superiores fient, & immarcessibilem illam iustitiae coronam reportabunt.
units.tr: Moreover, there are three things especially that we must always keep before our eyes, and of these Paul reminds us in the present passage. First, God, I think, is the one we should set before us as the one to look to. So we should not fix our eyes on the boldness of the most wicked men or the most unjust cruelty of tyrants, but look to God, whose providence and eternal decree we believe govern and direct the affairs of mortals. This is a most effective source of consolation. For since God, as we noted at the beginning, loves us most dearly, he undoubtedly allows nothing to happen to us that is not most useful to us and necessary for advancing our salvation. Since he also knows our weakness well, he does not allow us to be tempted beyond our strength; indeed, along with the temptation he supplies the strength by which, being strengthened, we overcome even those things that seemed invincible before. Therefore the holiest of men have always looked to the providence of God, and the consideration of it has made them not only brave and patient but also gentle and tolerant of injuries, and has restrained in them every desire for private revenge. From this came Joseph's ready kindness and forgiveness toward his brothers, who had treated him most wickedly. For when they feared they deserved punishment, he said: "You indeed planned evil against me, but God planned the same thing for good, to bring about what appears today, and to save many people alive." From the same source came the patience of Job, who, reflecting not on what the Chaldeans had done but on what God had willed to be done to him and his possessions, burst out in these words: "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord." And David overcame all the heaviest struggles as if sheltered by this shield, because he believed that the days of his life were numbered with God, that his flights were also seen by him, and that all his tears were gathered by him and recorded in his account. Therefore Christ especially comforted his disciples with this argument, when, having warned them of the dangers they were about to face, he said: "The hairs of your head are all numbered. Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And yet I tell you, not one of them falls without the will of my Father." God, therefore, is our president of the games [ἀγωνοθέτης], who has both prescribed for us the kinds of contests and from eternity decreed their most fortunate outcome, and by the counsel of his providence directs everything toward this end. Next, let us remember that in these contests we have as spectators not only men but also angels, who do not watch idly but at the same time guard us, and often, without our knowing and sometimes even against our will, withdraw us from impending dangers. Whenever, therefore, we are terrified by the multitude of enemies or overwhelmed by hosts of dangers, let us always sing to ourselves that saying of Elisha: "Do not fear, for there are more with us than with them." Likewise that saying of David: "The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them." Let us add to these, in the third place, the examples of the ancient martyrs, whose struggles ought to be our theatre, so that we may learn that we are not the first to fight in this arena, and imitate their patience, courage, constancy, gentleness, fervour in prayer, and whatever else is admirable in them. Indeed, let us remember that in this warfare we have as our leader the Son of God, who once conquered for us this whole world, and who today is present with us by his Spirit, so that we never give way. Those who think carefully on these things will easily rise above all adversities and will win that unfading crown of righteousness.

units.la: Caeterum pergit Paulus, & Antithesi Ironica Corinthios secum & cum aliis Apostolis con-fert, ut euidentius appareat, quam absurdum & iniquum sit, ipsos superbire & insolentius efferri, cum suos magistros contemptissimos & afflictissimos esse videant, qui primi Euangelium in mundo praedicarunt. Habet Antithesis haec tria membra. Primum, Nos stulti propter Christum, vos autem prudentes in Christo. Stultos propter Christum dicit Apostolos, partim quod carnis sapientiam iampridem calcauissent, ut illum possent assequi, qui nobis a Patre Sapientia factus est: partim quod mundus eos pro stultis haberet, eo quod vnum Christum praedicarent, & propter hunc omnia contemnerent, quae in mundo eximia putantur. Atqui tales (inquit) nos sumus, neq, nos hu-ius sanctissimae stultitiae pudet: at vos iam prudentes estis in Christo. Id vero per Ironiam dicit, non quod revera prudentes essent, & Christum recte agnoscerent: sed quod carnis & mundi huius sapientiam cum Christo & fidei Christianae professione coniungere vellent, neq, viderent hanc sapientibus huius seculi extremam stultitiam putari. Hoc igitur membro innuit, ipsos dum prae aliis sapere volunt, se stultissimos declarare, quando tam cito obliti sint eius, quod Christus suo spiritui cum hoc mundo adeo non convenire ait, ut hic illum accipere non possit. Ioan.14.
units.tr: Moreover, Paul goes on, and by an ironic antithesis compares the Corinthians with himself and the other apostles, so that it may appear more clearly how absurd and unfair it is for them to be proud and to exalt themselves more insolently, when they see that their teachers, who first preached the gospel in the world, are most despised and afflicted. This antithesis has three parts. First: "We are fools for Christ's sake, but you are wise in Christ." He calls the apostles fools for Christ's sake, partly because they had long ago trampled underfoot the wisdom of the flesh so that they might attain him who was made Wisdom for us by the Father, and partly because the world regarded them as fools, since they preached Christ alone and for his sake despised everything that is thought outstanding in the world. "Yet such," he says, "we are, and we are not ashamed of this most holy folly; but you are already wise in Christ." He says this ironically, not because they were truly wise and rightly acknowledged Christ, but because they wished to join the wisdom of the flesh and of this world with Christ and the profession of the Christian faith, and did not see that this wisdom is regarded by the wise of this age as the utmost folly. By this member, therefore, he hints that while they want to be wise beyond others, they show themselves to be the greatest fools, since they had so quickly forgotten what Christ said: that his Spirit cannot agree with this world so as to be received by it. John 14.

units.la: Secundum, Nos infirmi, vos autem validi. Infirmos dicit Apostolos, quia nullo hominum praesidio defendebantur, & passim inter grauissima pericula cum timore & tremore docebant, quod ipsi apud Corinthios accidisse, Cap. secundo audiuimus. At vos (inquit) interea validi estis, scili-cet. Et hoc dicit, quod brachio carnali niterentur, & se suis ciuibus ita accommodare fluderent, ut ex illis patrocinium atque defensionem sperarent. Faciebant hoc doctores, qui cum praeter auram popularem nihil quaererent, conciones suas ita instituebant, ne quis illis offenderetur, & ideo ad multa conniuebant, quae nulla ratione poterant excusari. Similiter vulgus eorum, qui Corinthi crediderant, ne alicuius odium in se prouocarent, commercia cum omnibus habebant non necessaria, sacris quoque ethnicorum communicabant, & infinita alia faciebant a nominis Christiani professione aliena. Itaque ciuium fauore, amicitijs, opibus muniti & aduersus omne periculum abun-de instructi esse sibi videbantur. Digni itaque erant, quibus hoc exprobraret Paulus, & idem hodie merentur, qui cum Euangelij doctrina atque fide glorientur, simul tamen humanis praesidijs superbiunt, & illis scurriliter insultant, quos quorumuis libidini subiectos esse vident. Sed miserè isti omnes falli solent. Est enim infida huius mundi amicitia, & sese arundini fragili innixos esse magno suo malo sentiunt, si quod grauius certamen ecclesijs incumbit.
units.tr: Second: "We are weak, but you are strong." He calls the apostles weak because they were defended by no human protection, and everywhere, amid the gravest dangers, taught with fear and trembling, as we heard happened to them among the Corinthians in the second chapter. "But you," he says, "meanwhile are strong, of course." And he says this because they relied on an arm of flesh and were so eager to accommodate themselves to their fellow citizens that they hoped for patronage and protection from them. Teachers did this: since they sought nothing beyond popular favour, they arranged their sermons so that no one would be offended by them, and therefore overlooked many things that could not be excused on any ground. Likewise the common people among those who had believed at Corinth, so as not to stir up hatred against themselves from anyone, had unnecessary dealings with everyone, shared even in the rites of the heathen, and did countless other things foreign to the profession of the Christian name. Thus they seemed to themselves fortified by the favour of citizens, by friendships and by wealth, and abundantly equipped against every danger. They therefore deserved to be rebuked by Paul for this, and those who today glory in the doctrine and faith of the gospel, yet at the same time take pride in human supports, and mock scornfully those whom they see subject to anyone's lust, deserve the same. But all such people are usually miserably deceived. For the friendship of this world is unfaithful, and they feel to their great harm that they have been leaning on a broken reed, if some more serious conflict falls upon the churches.

units.la: Tertium membrum est: Vos gloriosi,nos ignominiosi. Dependet hoc ex eo,quod proxime praecessit, & rursus rei absurditatem hoc arguit, quòd cum Apostoli apud plerosque pro infamibus haberentur, & omne genus ignominiae sustinerent, ij gloriam huius seculi ambitiosius sectarentur, qui fidei Christianae doctrinam ex illis didicerant. Augebat vero huius insolentiae absurditatem, quòd Paulus & Apollo, & fortasis Sosthenes quoque, à Corinthijs contemnerentur, in quorum gratiam illi sese eò vsque deiecerant, ut nullas iniurias, nullam item ignominiam detrectarent. Quis enim non reprehensione dignissimum dicat filium, quem patris ad omnem laborem se offerentis pudet, cùm id pater non aliam ob causam faciat, quàm ut filio consulat, & honestè educandum curet? Debebant hoc diligentius obseruare, quos hodie ministrorum Verbi pudet, eò quod mundo inuisos & exosos esse vident: nō autem cogitant, illos odium hoc & contemptum indignissimum ideo sustinere, ut tam ipsos quàm alios ad aeternae vitae hereditatem adducant. Est autem locus iste diligenter considerandus hodie. Docet enim, quibus indicijs Apostolorum æmuli & personati eorũ successores agnosci possint. Gloriantur hoc titulo Romani Pontifices, & qui ab ipsis creantur Episcopi atq; Cardinales. At si hos omnes cum Apostolis conferas, non aliud inuenies, quàm quod in præsenti Paulus æmulis suis exprobrat. Apostoli hominum stultissimi visi sunt: at isti carnis sapientia instructissimi, profundo astu omnia agunt, ut non temere Antichristo Daniel oculos hominis tribuat, id est, prudentiam huius seculi singularem & ad omnia parata rerum agendarum peritiam. Etenim tanta hæc est, ut non tam hominis quàm Lyncis oculos habere dici possint, quando his abstrusissima quæq; scrutantur, & in ipsa regum atq; principum arcana penetrant. Deinde Apostoli infirmi atq; omni præsidio humano destituti fuerunt: illi verò terris amplißimis longè lateq; dominantur, arces munitissimas & urbes populosas, imò Romam olim totius orbis dominam, possident: vectigalia, tributa, census ingentes exigunt: sæderibus principiũ munitur: deniq; eò usq; illorum potentia iampridem excreuit, ut Regibus & Imperatoribus sint formidabiles. Nam utrumq; gladium, ecclesiasticum scilicet & politicum, sibi vendicant: & illo quidem ipsi soli pugnant, hunc verò Regibus ea conditione tribuunt, ut non nisi ad ipsorum arbitrium stringatur. Sic enim Bonifacius octauus scribit: In ecclesia eiusq; potestate duos esse gladios, spiritualem vi-delicet & temporalem, euangelicis dictis instruimur. Nam dicentibus Apostolis, Ecce duo gladij hic (in ecclesia scilicet) cùm Apostoli loquerentur, non respondit Dominus, nimis esse, sed satis.
units.tr: The third member is: "You are glorious, but we are dishonoured." This depends on what immediately preceded, and again shows the absurdity of the matter: while the apostles were regarded by many as infamous and endured every kind of disgrace, those who had learned the doctrine of the Christian faith from them pursued the glory of this age more eagerly. The absurdity of this arrogance was increased by the fact that Paul and Apollos, and perhaps Sosthenes too, were despised by the Corinthians, for whose sake they had humbled themselves so far that they refused no injuries and likewise no disgrace. For who would not say that a son deserves blame who is ashamed of a father who offers himself to every labour, when the father does this for no other reason than to look after the son and see that he is raised honourably? Those should observe this more carefully who today are ashamed of the ministers of the Word, because they see them hated and detested by the world; yet they do not consider that these men endure this hatred and most unworthy contempt so that they may bring both these people and others to the inheritance of eternal life. This passage, however, is to be considered carefully today. For it teaches by what signs the rivals of the apostles and their counterfeit successors can be recognised. The Roman Pontiffs boast of this title, and the bishops and cardinals created by them. But if you compare all of these with the apostles, you will find nothing other than what Paul in the present passage reproaches his rivals with. The apostles seemed the most foolish of men; these men, on the other hand, are most richly endowed with the wisdom of the flesh, and do everything with profound cunning, so that it is not without reason that Daniel gives Antichrist the eyes of a man, that is, an extraordinary prudence of this age and a skill in managing affairs ready for every purpose. For this skill is so great that they can be said to have the eyes not so much of a man as of a lynx, since they search out the most hidden things and penetrate into the very secrets of kings and princes. Again, the apostles were weak and destitute of every human support; but those men rule far and wide over very ample lands, possess most fortified citadels and populous cities, indeed Rome, once mistress of the whole world; they collect tolls, taxes and huge revenues; they are fortified by treaties with princes; and finally their power has grown so far that they are formidable to kings and emperors. For they claim both swords, the ecclesiastical and the political, for themselves: they themselves fight with the former alone, and they grant the latter to kings on the condition that it is drawn only at their discretion. For thus Boniface VIII writes: that there are two swords in the Church and in its power, the spiritual that is, and the temporal, we are taught by the sayings of the Gospel. For when the apostles said, "Behold, here are two swords" (that is, in the Church), the Lord did not reply that they were too many, but that they were enough.

units.la: Certè qui in potestate Petri temporalem gladium esse negat, male verbum attendit Domini proferentis: Conuerte gladium tuum in vaginam. Uterq; ergo est in potestate ecclesiæ, spiritualis scilicet gladius & materialis: Sed iis quidem pro ecclesia, ille verò ab ecclesia exercendus: Ille sacerdotis, ut manu regum & miliitum, sed ad nutum & patientiam sacerdotis, &c. Hæc (inquâ) Bonifacij verba sunt, qui ne verbis nudis ageret, reipsa hoc toti orbi testatum esse voluit. Cùm enim in festo Iubilæo, quod ipse primus è Iudaismo petitum instaurauit, Albertus Rom. Rex electionem suam illius authoritate confirmari peteret per legatos, Papa ut penes se utrumq; gladium esse doceret, legatos parum honorificè habuit, & primo quidem eius solennitatis die pontificalibus ornamentis indutus populo apostolicam benedictionem impertijt, altero autem habitu Imperiali & Cæsarea infula insignis, gladium nudatum ante se deferri iussit, & tandem in sublimi solio cõsidens alta voce testatus est: Ecce duo gladij hic. Et quod ille insolentius fecit, hoc ipsum ab aliis non minori cum fastu factum est, & extant maximorum Regum atq; Imperatorum exempla, qui inuiti & multùm relucantes Pontificum tyrannidi atq; iugo colla submittere coacti sunt. At exemplis veteribus minimè opus est, cùm hodie illorum potentiam universo terrarum orbi intolerabilem esse sentiamus. Certè de illis verissimè dici potest, quod tertio membro Paulus ait: Apostoli ignominiosi fuere, illi verò gloriosissimi sunt, quoad externum fastum, pompam, titulos, quibus nõ obscurè diuinitatis quoq; honores sibi vendicant. Quod ergo minus successit olim diabolo, quando Apostoli suo exemplo æmulorum suorum superbiam fortissimè represserunt, id posteris temporibus perfecit. Debet autè Antichristis ista probè obseruari, ut larvatos [?] illos Apostolorum successores agnoscere discamus. Interea neminem illorũ fastus atq; insolentia offendat. Nam inania spectra sunt omnia, quibus isti homines superbiunt, & ijdè olim ignominia perpetua obruentur. Ut enim Corinthij illi ardeliones [?] hodie infames sunt, celebris autem & sacrosancta est Apostolorum memoria: ita erit dies, quando Pontifices quoq; pudenda manifestabuntur, in pretio autem erunt, qui Christo & ecclesiæ eius fideliter seruierunt. Sunt enim minus corrupta posteritatis iudicia, & suo tempore in lucé Veritas emergit.
units.tr: Certainly, whoever denies that the temporal sword is in Peter's power misunderstands the Lord's words when he says, "Put your sword back into its sheath." Both swords, therefore, are in the power of the Church: the spiritual sword and the material one. The one is to be wielded for the Church, the other by the Church: the one by the hand of priests, the other by the hand of kings and soldiers, yet at the nod and sufferance of the priest, and so on. These (I say) are the words of Boniface, who, lest he act with bare words, wanted to prove this in fact to the whole world. For when, at the Jubilee festival, which he himself was the first to introduce, derived from Judaism, Albert, King of the Romans, sought through envoys that his election be confirmed by the Pope's authority, the Pope, to teach that both swords were in his own power, treated the envoys with little honour. On the first day of that solemnity, dressed in pontifical ornaments, he gave the people the apostolic blessing. On the second day, however, adorned with imperial dress and the Caesarean mitre, he ordered a drawn sword carried before him, and at last, seated on a high throne, declared in a loud voice: "Behold, two swords here." And what he did more arrogantly, others have done with no less pride. There are examples of the greatest kings and emperors who, unwillingly and struggling much, were forced to bow their necks to the tyranny and yoke of the Pontiffs. But there is no need of old examples, since today we feel their power to be intolerable to the whole world. Certainly of them it can be said most truly what Paul says in the third member: the apostles were dishonoured, but they are most glorious, in external display, pomp and titles, by which they claim divine honours for themselves not obscurely. So what less succeeded once with the devil, when the Apostles by their example most strongly repressed the pride of their rivals, he has accomplished in later times. These Antichrists ought to be carefully observed, so that we may learn to recognise those masked successors of the Apostles. Meanwhile, let none of their pride and insolence offend us. For all those things in which these men take pride are empty phantoms, and they too will one day be overwhelmed by lasting disgrace. Just as those Corinthian busybodies are infamous today, while the memory of the Apostles is famous and sacred, so there will come a day when the Pontiffs too will be exposed in their shame, while those who served Christ and his Church faithfully will be held in honour. For the judgements of posterity are less corrupt, and in its own time Truth emerges into the light.

units.la: Porrò ut magis erubesceret Corinthij, & spiritus illos feroces deponere, seq; ipsos Christi iugo atq; crucis vexillo subijcere discerent, pergit Paulus, & quæ etiam nunc sua & aliorum Apostolorũ conditio fit, docet. Ad hanc usq; horam (inquit) & esurimus & sitimus, & nudi sumus, & colaphis cædimur, & incertis sedibus erramus, & laboramus operantes proprijs manibus, &c. Quasi dicerêt. Nõ apud vos modò egeni & contempti viximus inter omnis generis pericula, sed adhuc hodie non melior est nostra conditio: ut ex ea satis constet, nos, non ut vestri illi solent, otiũ, voluptates, honores, opes quærere, sed potiùs ijs intentos esse, quæ ad vestram & multorum aliorũ salutem faciũt. Nã famelici, egeni, nudi per incertas sedes ferimur, iniurias multas & graues sustinemus, & sæpe manuũ labore victũ quærere cogimur. Hæc autem ab illo verissimè dici, Aliorũ liber abunde testatur. Nam & sua omnia iam pridem reliquerant, sæpe etiam ab impijs spoliabantur, & ecclesiæ aliæ pauperiores erant, quàm ut illis stipendium debitum numerare possent, aliæ verò tenaciores & ingratæ nimis, ut quod poterant minimè præstarent: ex quarum numero Corinthiam quoq; fuisse scimus. Postulabat item Apostolica functio, ut nullibi sedem fixam haberent, & nō raro hostium improbitate & violentia eijciebantur. Ita fiebat, ut non possent ijs frui, quæ ecclesiarum pastoribus optimo iure debentur, ut infra Cap.nono docebit. Denique, ut piacula mundi facti sumus, omnium sordes aut ramenta usq; adhuc. Quibus verbis partim extremum contemptum, partim immane odium exprimit, quo multi ita flagrent, ut Apostolorum morte & sanguine Dei iram placari, & pœnas imminentes auerti credant. Solebant enim olim quidam in publicis calamitatibus aliquos deligere, in quorum capita diras omnes congerebant, & postea per urbem circumductos in mare præcipites dabant, aut pecudum instar immolabant: qui deinde piacula aut victimæ piaculares dicebantur. Vult ergo his similibus omnia completi, quæ ad extremam miseriam faciunt, quoad huius vitæ conditionem. Et ne quis obijceret: Atqui inuiti hæc fertis, & proinde non est quòd illis gloriemini, interserit: Conuiitijs affecti bene precamur: persecutionem patientes, sustinemus: infamati, precamur. Istis autem docet, quòd alacri animo ista omnia ferant, & à vindicta cupiditate tam alieni sint, ut hostium quoque salutem pijs precibus apud Deum adiuuare satagant. Et simul grauissimè perstringit suos æmulos, qui cùm nihil horum paterentur, sed vitam in otio, voluptatibus, honore & rerum abundantia degerent, felicem euangelicæ prædicationis successum germanis Christi Apostolis inuidebant. Solent hoc fere, quicunque sub Euangelij & ministerij ecclesiastici prætextu res suas agunt. Nec enim contenti sunt, officium suum neglexisse, nisi insuper fidelibus ministris detrahant, & ijsdem scurriliter insultent.
units.tr: Moreover, so that the Corinthians might blush more and learn to lay down their fierce spirits and submit themselves to the yoke of Christ and the banner of the cross, Paul goes on to teach what the condition of his own and the other Apostles' lives is even now. "Up to this hour," he says, "we both hunger and thirst, and are naked, and are struck with fists, and wander about in unsettled dwellings, and labour, working with our own hands," and so on. It is as if he were saying: not only among you did we live poor and despised, amid dangers of every kind, but even today our condition is no better. From this it is clear enough that we do not seek, as your men do, leisure, pleasures, honours and wealth, but rather are intent on those things which further your salvation and that of many others. For we are carried about hungry, needy and naked, through uncertain dwellings; we endure many grave injuries, and often we are compelled to win our living by the labour of our hands. That these things were said by him most truly, the Book of Acts bears ample witness. For they had long since left behind all their possessions, were often plundered even by the impious, and some churches were too poor to pay the stipend owed to them, while others were too grasping and too ungrateful to give even what they could. We know that the Corinthian church was among their number. The apostolic office also required that they have no fixed seat anywhere, and not infrequently they were driven out by the wickedness and violence of enemies. So it came about that they could not enjoy those things which are rightly owed to the ministers of churches, as he will teach below in chapter nine. Finally, "we have been made as the offscouring of the world, the scrapings of all things, even until now." In these words he expresses partly extreme contempt and partly monstrous hatred, with which many burn so fiercely that they believe God's anger is appeased by the death and blood of the Apostles, and impending punishments are averted. For formerly, in public calamities, some people used to choose certain persons, heap all curses upon their heads, and afterwards lead them about the city and throw them headlong into the sea, or sacrifice them like cattle; these were then called expiations, or expiatory victims. He therefore wishes by such comparisons to signify everything that brings extreme misery as regards the condition of this life. And lest anyone object, "Yet you bear these things unwillingly, and so there is no reason for you to boast of them," he adds: "When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when defamed, we entreat." By this he teaches that they bear all these things with a cheerful mind, and are so far from any desire for revenge that they even strive to help the salvation of their enemies by pious prayers to God. At the same time he sharply censures his rivals, who, though they suffered none of these things, but spent their lives in leisure, pleasures, honour and abundance, begrudged the genuine Apostles of Christ the happy success of the preaching of the Gospel. Those who carry on their own affairs under the pretext of the Gospel and the ecclesiastical ministry are generally of this sort. For they are not content to have neglected their duty, unless they also slander faithful ministers and insult them with scurrility.

units.la: Rursus autè sors seruorum Christi nobis consideranda venit, quæ eò durior est, quòd non solum aduersa quæuis sustinent, sed ut quouis supplicio digni affliguntur. Accenditur enim hostium rabies eo potissimum argumento, quòd illos Deo exosos esse arbitrantur, qui propter illos totas respub. atque regna fame, peste, bello & seditionibus puniat. Experti hoc olim sunt prophetæ, quos multi publicorum malorum authores esse dicebant, eò quòd veteres cultus abolerent. Ieremiæ certè in faciem dicebatur: Sermonem, quem locutus es ad nos nomine Domini, non recipie-mus: sed faciemus quicquid egreditur de ore nostro, ut suffitum incendamus machinæ cœli, & libemus ei libamina, sicuti fecimus nos & patres nostri, reges nostri & principes nostri, in ciuitatibus Iuda & in plateis Ierusalem. Tum enim alimento abundabamus, & bene nobis erat, malumq; nullum videbamus. Quàm primùm autem cessauimus suffitum incendere machinæ cœli, & ei libare libamina, omnium fumus indigi, & ferro fame, consumimur, &c. Et posteris temporibus Apostolis, imò Christianis omnibus, eadem obiecta esse, patrum libri apologetici testantur. Nam religionis mutationi hoc deberi clamabant impij hostes, quòd orbis totus fame & peste laboraret, quòd prouinciarum defectione & bellis exteris Romanum Imperium labefactaretur, & quòd inter periculosissimos motus oracula cessarent, ex quibus olim maiores rerum gerendarum consilia petijssent. Ideoq; nullo non supplicio digni iudicabantur Christiani homines. Et hodie multa huius generis audimus, neque desunt, qui Regibus persuadeant, nunquam eos feliciter regnaturos, aut Turcarum arma profligaturos esse, nisi prius Euangelij doctrinam & eius sectatores stir-pitus excindant. Sed hoc illud est, de quo nos Christus prænomuit: fore nimirum, ut Deo cultum gratissimum præstare putetur, qui nos interfecerit. At tunc nos patienter omnia ferre, hostibus bene precari, & Deo gratias agere debemus, qui nos afflictionum Filij sui participes reddit, ut eiusdem olim cohæredes esse possimus. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Again, the lot of the servants of Christ must be considered by us, which is all the harder because they not only endure every kind of adversity, but are also afflicted as though they deserved any punishment. For the rage of their enemies is kindled chiefly by this argument: that they think those are hateful to God who, on their account, punish whole commonwealths and kingdoms with famine, pestilence, war and seditions. The prophets once experienced this, who were said by many to be the authors of public evils, because they overthrew the old worship. Indeed, to Jeremiah's face it was said: "We will not listen to the word which you have spoken to us in the name of the Lord; but we will do whatever goes out of our own mouth, to burn incense to the queen of heaven and pour out libations to her, as we and our fathers, our kings and our princes did, in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem. For then we had plenty of food, and it went well with us, and we saw no evil. But since we ceased to burn incense to the queen of heaven and to pour out libations to her, we have lacked all things, and are consumed by sword and famine," etc. And that in later times the same objections were raised against the Apostles, and indeed against all Christians, the apologetic books of the Fathers bear witness. For the impious enemies cried out that the change of religion was to blame for the whole world labouring under famine and pestilence, for the Roman Empire being weakened by the revolt of provinces and foreign wars, and for oracles ceasing amid the most dangerous disturbances, from which the forefathers had once sought counsel for conducting affairs. Therefore Christians were judged worthy of every punishment. And today we hear many things of this kind, nor are there lacking those who persuade kings that they will never reign happily, or overthrow the arms of the Turks, unless they first root out the doctrine of the gospel and its followers. But this is that very thing about which Christ forewarned us: that the time will come when a man will think he offers the most acceptable worship to God by killing us. Yet we ought then to bear all things patiently, to bless our enemies, and to give thanks to God, who makes us partakers of the afflictions of his Son, so that we may one day be co-heirs of the same. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXI.
units.tr: HOMILY XXI.

units.la: Non ut vos pudore suffundam hæc scribo: sed ut filios meos dilectos admoneo. Nam etsi decem millia pædagogorum habueritis in Christo, at non multos patres [habetis.] In Christo enim IESV per Euangelium ego vos genui. Precor vos igitur, imitatores mei estote.
units.tr: I do not write these things to shame you, but to admonish you as my beloved sons. For although you may have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you do not have many fathers. In Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I begot you. I beg you, therefore, be imitators of me.

units.la: ETsi Paulus ab omni ambitione alienissimus, huius saeculi gloriam atque splendorem non magni fecerit, sed potius quaecunque in mundo eximia & praeclara habebat, ut noxia abiecit, ut Christum aeternae salutis authorem apprehenderet: idem tamen passim in hoc est, ut suae functionis authoritatem contra aduersarios suos tueatur, ne huius contemptus in ipsum Christum & Euangelium eius non sine multorum exitio redundet. Et huc pertinet tota, quam hucusq; audiuimus tractatio, in qua magno studio & grauitate utitur. Vt enim fastuosos illos, qui popularis aurae fiducia turgidi ipsum scurriliter nimis contemnebant, efficatius deprimat, nuper acerbis quoq; Ironijs & exprobrationibus usus est, ita nimirum ostendens, quam indigne ipsum contemnant, qui veris & proprijs Apostoli notis praeditus sit, suos autem illos admirentur, in quibus nihil praeter inanem ostentationem videre liceat. Et debet ex Pauli exemplo doctrina generalis peti, ut quicunq; in munere aliquo publico versantur, primatu gloriam sic contemnant, ne sibi credita potestate abutantur, interim vero no prodant authoritate sua, qua illos Deus instruxit. Caeterum ne Corinthij Paulum suspicarentur hostili in ipsos animo praeditu esse, correptionem illa, quae durior videri poterat, in praesenti mitigat, sic tamen, ut nouis argumentis excitet ad officium faciendum.
units.tr: Although Paul, most free from all ambition, did not value the glory and splendour of this age, but rather cast off as harmful whatever distinguished and notable things he had in the world, so that he might lay hold of Christ, the author of eternal salvation, he nevertheless everywhere takes care to defend the authority of his office against his adversaries, lest contempt for it rebound upon Christ himself and his Gospel, to the ruin of many. The whole discussion we have heard up to now belongs to this purpose, and Paul handles it with great earnestness and gravity. To humble more effectively those haughty men, who, puffed up with confidence in popular favour, scornfully despised him, he has recently used bitter ironies and reproaches as well. In this way he shows how unworthily they despise a man endowed with the true and proper marks of an apostle, while they admire men in whom nothing but empty show can be seen. From Paul's example a general teaching should be drawn: whoever holds any public office should so despise the glory of preeminence that they do not abuse the power entrusted to them, and yet do not betray the authority with which God has equipped them. Moreover, lest the Corinthians suspect Paul of hostility towards them, he now softens the rebuke, which might have seemed harsh, yet in such a way that he stirs them to do their duty with fresh arguments.

units.la: Et primò quidem docet, quo animo haec omnia dixerit: Non ut vos pudore suffundam hac scribo, sed ut filios meos dilectos admoneo. Videtur verbis negare, quod re ipsa fecerat. Quomodo enim non possunt non pudore suffundi, qui vitia, quae negare non possunt, sibi ad hunc modum exprobrari audiunt? Et si cum verbis Pauli institutum consideres, hoc omnino voluit, ut erubescerent, & suijpsorum illos puderet: at non hic ipsi finis propositus erat, ut ex eo ignominiam aliquam referrent, sed potius, ut ipsi agnita eorum absurditate, quae hucusque fecerant, de vitijs suis corrigendis cogitarent. Itaque ut pudore suffunderentur optauit, at non noxio, non ignominioso (quem maligni & inuidi quaerunt) sed utili, & qui maioris ignominiae notas pia correctione aut poenitentia abstergat. Ideo addit: Ut filios meos dilectos admoneo. Quibus verbis se paterno in illos animo praeditum esse, & quod illos filiorum loco habeat, testatur. Admoneri autem eos voluit, ne gloriam in rebus nihili quaererent, neque germanos Christi Apostolos propter ea contemnerent, quae fidelis ipsorum industriae testimonia erant. Et hoc quidem pijs atque cordatis sufficere poterat, ut correptionem aequo animo ferrent. Nam naturae leges parentibus hoc ius tribuunt, ut filios errantes arguant, vel etiam vehementius corripiant pro delicti ratione. Eadem quoque leges hos astringunt, ut parentum correptionem patienter ferant, & illis obtemperent. Moses certè ex Dei mandato actionem capitis parentibus in filios contumaces permittit, & ut tales publicè lapidibus obruantur iubet.
units.tr: First, he teaches with what spirit he has said all these things: "I do not write these things to shame you, but to admonish you as my beloved sons." He seems to deny in words what he had in fact done. For how can those who hear their vices, which they cannot deny, so reproached to them, fail to be ashamed? Yet if you consider the purpose of Paul's words, he certainly wished them to blush and be ashamed of themselves. But this was not the goal set before them, that they should carry away some disgrace from it; rather, having recognised the absurdity of what they had done so far, they should think about correcting their faults. Therefore he wished them to be ashamed, but not with a harmful, dishonouring shame (which malicious and envious people seek), but with a useful shame, which by pious correction or repentance wipes away the marks of greater disgrace. Hence he adds: "as my beloved sons I admonish you." By these words he testifies that he has a fatherly spirit towards them and regards them as in the place of sons. He wished them to be admonished, so that they would not seek glory in worthless things, nor despise the genuine apostles of Christ for those things which were evidence of their faithful labour. This alone could suffice for the godly and sensible, to bear the correction with an even mind. For the laws of nature grant parents this right: they may reprove erring sons, or even rebuke them more sharply according to the nature of the offence. The same laws bind sons to bear their parents' correction patiently and to obey them. Moses, by God's command, certainly permits parents to bring a capital charge against stubborn sons, and orders that such sons be publicly stoned.

units.la: Vide Deut. 21.
units.tr: See Deut. 21.

units.la: Admonet autem nos suo exemplo Paulus, ut correptiones in ecclesia institui debeant. Est locus hic multa consideratione dignissimus. Nam admonitionibus & correptionibus opus esse, res ipsa docet. Vt enim ad vitia et errores natura proclives sumus: ita in nobis illa no agnoscimus, imò nobisipsis in ijs etiam blandimur, quae nos praecipites in exitiu rapiunt. Itaq; monitores esse oportet, qui vitia nostra arguat, & nos de illis corrigendis admoneant. Viderunt hoc olim gentium Philosophi, qui hanc utilitatem ex inimicis capere docuerunt, ut quando amici non semper in hac re suo officio funguntur, inimicorum exprobrationibus excitemur ad eorum consideratione, quae prius in nobis minus obseruabamus. Sed melius nobis pro sua bonitate Deus consuluit, ut nimirum in ecclesia monitores sint publici, qui non suis, sed ipsius verbis nos arguant, & pijs correptionibus in viam reducant. Et extant de hac re grauissima mandata, quibus prophetas olim Deus astrinxit. Isaiae enim sic dicebat: Clama ex gutture, ne parcas, exalta instar tubae vocem tuam, & annuntia populo meo praeuaricationem suam, et domui Iacob peccata sua. Ezechieli item: Fili hominis, speculatorem te constituit domui Israelis, audies igitur verbum ex ore meo, et diserte monebis eos ex me. Cum dixero ego impio, Certissimè morieris, atq; tu non monueris eum diserte, neque locutus fueris diserte, dehortando impium à via sua impia, ut viuat, ille quidem impius morietur in iniquitate sua, sanguinem verò eius de manu tua requira, &c. Et in nouo testamento Christus inter spiritus sancti officia primum numerat, quod mundum arguere debeat de peccato. Imò in hunc finem potissimum Lex data est, ut in eius speculo videamus, qui simus, & quae sit scelerum nostrorum atrocitas.
units.tr: Paul also admonishes us, by his own example, that corrections ought to be instituted in the Church. This passage deserves much consideration. For the thing itself shows that admonitions and corrections are needed. Just as we are naturally prone to vices and errors, so we do not recognise them in ourselves; indeed we flatter ourselves in those very things which carry us headlong into destruction. Therefore there must be monitors who may rebuke our vices and urge us to correct them. The philosophers of the nations saw this long ago, and taught that this advantage should be drawn from enemies: when friends do not always fulfil their duty in this matter, we may be stirred by the reproaches of enemies to consider what we had observed less in ourselves before. But God, in his goodness, has provided better for us, so that there should be public monitors in the Church, who reprove us not with their own words but with his, and bring us back to the right way by pious corrections. There are most weighty commands on this matter, by which God long ago bound the prophets. For Isaiah was told: "Cry aloud, do not spare; lift up your voice like a trumpet, and declare to my people their transgression, and to the house of Jacob their sins." Likewise to Ezekiel: "Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel; you shall hear the word from my mouth and warn them plainly from me. When I say to the wicked, 'You shall surely die,' and you do not warn him plainly, nor speak plainly to turn the wicked from his wicked way that he may live, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood at your hand," and so on. And in the New Testament Christ counts among the offices of the Holy Spirit, first, that he should convict the world of sin. Indeed, the Law was given chiefly for this end, that in its mirror we may see who we are and how great is the atrocity of our crimes.

units.la: Porrò ut correptio non suo fructu careat, hæc observari debent. Primùm ut certa habeatur delictorum ratio. Sunt in his alia privata & occulta plerisque, adeò ut nullum ex illis scandalū adhuc enatum sit: alia publica, & quæ non sine scandalo in omnium oculis & ore versantur. Illa privatim & mitius corripi debent, ne si per nos in publicū proferantur, ipsi scandali gravioris simus authores. Hæc autem publicè exagitari & accusari merentur, ut quod ex illis exortum est scandalum apud simplices & imperitos è medio removeatur. Et huc illud Pauli pertinet: Eos, qui peccarunt, coram omnibus argue, ut cæteri timorem habeant. Ubi tamen videndum est, ne (ut Stoici olim solebant) peccata omnia paria faciamus, & quæ levicula per se sunt, Tragicè nimis amplificemus, sed ut singulis debitæ correptiones atque minæ adhibeantur. Deinde personas quoque considerare oportet, non ut personarum respectu nos duci patiamur, aut ad aliquorū flagitia turpiter conniveamus (constat enim omnis loci & ordinis homines Verbo Dei subiectos esse) sed dispiciant prudenter ministri, quo quisque modo aut ratione flecti aut corrigi possit. Nam ut ijsdem morbis non eandem medendi rationem periti medici adhibent, sed ægrotantium naturam & complexionem (ut vocant) diligenter inspiciunt, ut huic remedia accommodent: ita non omnibus eadem monendi aut corripiendi ratio conuenit. Sunt enim aliqui mites & placidi, qui non tam malitia, quàm incogitantia & naturali atque omnibus insita ad malum proclivitate peccant. Hos mitius tractare oportet, ne in desperationem adducantur. Et hoc in Ezechia, optimo principe, Jsaias observavit. Sunt alij, qui etsi minimè proterui & contumaces sint, in vitijs tamen obstupescunt, ut ea minus agnoscant: quos sancta astutia[?] circumvenire proderit, ut ignorantibus & aliud cogitantibus peccati confessionem extorqueas, & ijsdem tunc Dei judicij ob oculos ponas. Cuius rei exemplum in Nathano propheta egregium habemus, qui hac ratione Dauidē iam quasi absorptum à peccato, & subinde in peius ruentem, in viam revocavit. Sunt rursus duri & contumaces, qui cum Deo & verbo eius litem suscepisse videri possunt. Hi acrius urgeri, et ad Dei tribunal citari debent, eòque severius cum illis agendum est, quò gravius & nocentius est scandalum, quod illi præbent. Ad hunc modum cum Achabo, impio & contumaci hypocrita, Elias agit: & huius generis cōciones passim in prophetis occurrunt, quibus eos severissimè tractarunt, quos incurabili malitia ad omne scelus ruere videbant. Denique ut pater liberorum ingenia observat, & his admonitiones atque correptiones attemperat: ita Verbi ministros severi tatem prudentia regere oportet. Finis autem non alius illis propositus sit, quàm peccatoris emendatio, non ut vel infamem faciant, aut in desperationem sive exitium adducant. Docet hoc proprio exemplo Deus, qui per Ezechielē inquit: Vivo ego, nolo morte peccatoris, sed ut convertatur, & vivat. Quod si qui hoc agunt, ut qui peccarunt, infeliciter & turpiter pereant, ij non patres, nō monitores, non item fidi ecclesiæ pastores, sed obtrectatores sunt, quibus nullus in ecclesia locus debetur. Hæc omnia si nostris temporibus applicentur, mox patebit, qua ratione hodie agendum sit. Sunt quidem adhuc piorū aliquot reliquiæ, quorū ratio diligens haberi debet. At maior hominū pars illis moribus vivit, quos novissimo sæculo regnaturos esse Christus & Apostoli prædixerunt. Accedit his, quòd alij Evangelij doctrinam contemptu plus quàm Cyclopico, alij odio immani & implacabili persequuntur. Interim omnes illi correptionem prorsus omnem fugiunt, & doctores quærunt qui blandiloquentia molli aures ipsorum fricent, & (ut Ezechiel ait) pullos consuant, quibus ipsi suaviter possint indormire. Apud tales homines nulla correptio nimia, nulla castigatio acerbior æquo esse potest. Neque etiam audiri debent, qui clamant, nullius quærendam esse infamiam, neque pudore suffundendos esse eos qui peccarunt, sed curandum potius ut emendentur. Atqui apud istos homines emendationis spes non est reliqua: ut verò pudore suffundantur periculum non est, quando iam pridem cum timore Dei pudorem quoque omnem abstulerunt, ut revera in illos dici possit, quod olim suo populo Jeremias dicebat. Frons meretricis est tibi, renuisti erubescere. Quid ergo aliud restat, quàm ut ministri qua possunt libertate infelici mundo Dei iram denuntient, & cum suis animabus paruulas hasce piorum reliquias servent?
units.tr: Moreover, so that correction may not lack its fruit, the following should be observed. First, a clear account of the offences must be taken. Some are private and hidden from most people, so that no scandal has yet arisen from them; others are public, and are in everyone's eyes and on everyone's lips, not without scandal. The former ought to be corrected privately and more gently, lest, if we bring them out into the open, we ourselves become the authors of a graver scandal. The latter, however, deserve to be publicly censured and accused, so that the scandal arising from them among simple and unskilled people may be removed. To this belongs Paul's saying: "Those who sin, rebuke before all, that the rest may have fear." Yet here we must take care not (as the Stoics once did) to make all sins equal, and to magnify with tragic exaggeration those that are slight in themselves, but rather to apply to each one the correction and threats it deserves. Next, one must also consider the persons, not so that we allow ourselves to be swayed by regard for persons, or shamefully wink at the crimes of some (for it is established that men of every place and rank are subject to the Word of God), but so that the ministers may prudently discern how each person can be bent or corrected. For just as skilled physicians do not apply the same method of healing to the same diseases, but carefully examine the nature and temperament (as they call it) of the sick, so that they may fit remedies to each, so too the same manner of admonishing or rebuking does not suit everyone. There are some who are mild and gentle, who sin not so much from malice as from thoughtlessness and that natural proneness to evil which is implanted in all. These must be treated more gently, lest they be driven to despair. Isaiah observed this in Hezekiah, an excellent prince. There are others who, although not at all shameless or stubborn, nevertheless grow numb in their vices, so that they recognise them less. With these, a holy cunning will help: you may extract a confession of sin from them while they are unaware and thinking of something else, and then set before their eyes the judgment of God. We have an outstanding example of this in the prophet Nathan, who by this method brought David back into the way, when he was already, as it were, swallowed up by sin and falling into worse. Again, there are hard and stubborn men, who may seem to have taken up a quarrel with God and his Word. These must be pressed more sharply and summoned to the tribunal of God, and the graver and more harmful the scandal they give, the more severely one must deal with them. In this way Elijah deals with Ahab, an impious and stubborn hypocrite; and sermons of this kind occur everywhere in the prophets, in which they treated most severely those whom they saw rushing into every crime through incurable malice. Finally, just as a father observes the natures of his children and adapts admonitions and corrections to them, so the ministers of the Word ought to temper severity with prudence. Let no other aim be set before them than the amendment of the sinner, not that they make him infamous, or bring him to despair and ruin. God teaches this by his own example, who says through Ezekiel: "As I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live." But if there are those who act so that those who have sinned perish unhappily and shamefully, they are not fathers, not monitors, not faithful pastors of the Church, but detractors, to whom no place in the Church is due. If all these things are applied to our times, it will soon be plain how things must be handled today. There are indeed still a few remnants of the godly, whose case must be carefully considered. But the greater part of men live by those customs which Christ and the Apostles foretold would reign in the last age. Added to this is the fact that some pursue the doctrine of the Gospel with a contempt more than Cyclopean, others with monstrous and implacable hatred. Meanwhile all of them flee from every correction, and seek teachers who may soothe their soft ears with smooth flattery and (as Ezekiel says) sew cushions under their elbows on which they may sleep sweetly. Among such men no correction can be too severe, no chastisement too harsh. Nor should those be heard who cry out that no one's infamy is to be sought, nor that those who have sinned must not be shamed, but rather that care must be taken that they be amended. Yet among these men there is no hope of amendment left; and as for their being shamed, there is no danger, since long ago, along with the fear of God, they have also cast off all shame. So it can truly be said of them what Jeremiah once said to his people: "You have the forehead of a harlot; you refused to blush." What remains, then, except that the ministers, with whatever freedom they can, proclaim the wrath of God to the unhappy world, and preserve these small remnants of the godly with their own souls?

units.la: Cæterum quia Corinthios Paulus filios dixerat, ostendit nunc se ipsorum patrem, & animo paterno in illos præditum esse. Ita verò hoc facit, ut præoccupatione ad id respondeat, quod illi poterant obijcere: Atqui hi ipsi, quos tu insectaris, etiam nos filiorum loco habent, & non minus quàm tu patres nostri sunt, nos item diligunt, & gloriâ nostram prouehere student. Etenim jâ ante diximus, Corinthios ita dementatos fuisse, ut se alijs ecclesijs præstare putarent propter doctores illos, qui inani ostentatione oculos illis perstrinxerat. Respondet ergo Paulus: Etsi decem millia pædagogorum habueritis in Christo, at non multos patres habetis, &c. Quibus verbis hoc dicere videtur: Audio quid de vestris illis sentiatis, & fateor eos esse pædagogos vestros dici in Christo, sed ut patres vestri dicantur nunquam concesserim. Nam pædagogos quidem multos inuenire potuistis, qui mercenariam operam vobis præstiterunt, sed qui patres vestri fuerint, non ita multos habuistis: neq; ego hunc titulum facile alicui permiserim, qui mihi optimo iure debetur. Ego enim is sum, qui in CHRISTO IESV per Euangelium vos genui, & ideo patris nomen merito mihi vendico, à vobis autè cõtèni et reijci nõ possum, nisi in pietatis et naturæ leges peccare libeat.
units.tr: Since Paul had called the Corinthians his sons, he now shows that he is their father and has a fatherly disposition towards them. He does this to meet in advance the objection they could raise: "Yet those whom you attack also regard us as sons, and they are no less our fathers than you are; they love us too and strive to advance our glory." For we have already said that the Corinthians were so out of their minds that they thought themselves superior to other churches because of those teachers who had dazzled their eyes with empty show. Paul therefore answers: "Even if you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, yet you do not have many fathers," etc. By these words he seems to say: I hear what you think of your men, and I admit they are called your tutors in Christ, but that they should be called your fathers I would never concede. For you could indeed find many tutors who performed hired service for you, but you did not have many who were your fathers; nor would I easily grant this title to anyone, since it is owed to me by the best right. For I am the one who begot you in Christ Jesus through the Gospel, and so I rightly claim the name of father, and cannot be denied it by you, unless you wish to sin against the laws of piety and nature.
