units.la: Quærunt hoc loco nonnulli, annon in Christi præceptum Paulus peccauerit, quod ille Matth. 23. cap. his verbis comprehendit: Patrem vestrũ neminem vocetis in terra, vnus enim est Pater vester, qui in cœlis est? Quâ quæstionem olim à Donatistis quoq; motam fuisse D. Augustinus scribit, cui catholici responderint, Paulum hoc honorificentiæ causa dixisse propter euangelicum ministerium quod dispensabat: Nã patre ad fidem salutemq; æternã non esse nisi Deũ, et proinde distin-gui debere, quid diuinæ gratiæ, quid humanæ honorificentiæ causa dicatur. Et rursus idem pater in enarratione Psal. 77. de verbis illis Christi sic scribit: Hoc non ideo dictũ est, ut hoc vocabulũ ho-noris humani de loquendi consuetudine tolleretur, sed ne gratia Dei, qua in æternam vitam regene-ramur, naturæ, vel potestati, vel etiam sanctitati cuiusquâ hominis tribueretur. Ideo cum diceret Paulus, Ego vos genui: prædixit, In Christo, & per Euangelium: ne ipsius putaretur esse, quod Dei est. Hæc August. Christus ergo aduersus eos agit, qui in populũ Dei sibi dominiũ vendicabãt, & ita patres volebant dici, ut eos in sectas distraherent, qui vnus populus et solius Dei peculiũ esse debebant. Hoc enim illo tempore Pharisæorum & Sadducæorum et Essenorum antesignanos fuisse scimus: quorum hodie similes sunt, qui in Monachorum familijs Abbates, idest, patres dicuntur. Prohibet ergo Dominus, ne quoad fidem & cœlestis regni hæreditatē, aliquē mortalium patre nobis constituamus, præter Deum, qui solus fidem nobis largitur, & nos in filios adoptat. At Paulus pro ministerij ratione loquitur, neque Deo aliquid derogat, cuius ministrum & cooperarum se esse iam ante fuit testatus. Ut ergo Deus, qui corporum quoque creator & pater est, patris ta-men nomen honoris causa illis quoque concedit, ex quibus generamur: ita eos etiam quoad fidei & salutis æternæ negotium, patres dici permittit, quorum ministerio in nobis regenerandis vi-tur. Viderint modò illi, ne sibi quicquam præter ministerium tribuant.
units.tr: Some here ask whether Paul did not sin against Christ's precept, which he set down in Matthew 23: "Call no one your father on earth; for one is your Father, who is in heaven." Augustine writes that this question was once raised by the Donatists too, and that Catholics replied that Paul said this for the sake of honour, because of the evangelical ministry he dispensed: for no one is father to faith and eternal salvation except God, and therefore one must distinguish what is said for the sake of divine grace from what is said for the sake of human honour. And again the same father, in his exposition of Psalm 77, writes concerning those words of Christ: "This was not said so that this term of human honour should be removed from the custom of speaking, but so that the grace of God, by which we are regenerated to eternal life, should not be attributed to the nature, power, or even holiness of any man. Therefore when Paul said, 'I begot you,' he added beforehand, 'in Christ, and through the Gospel,' lest it be thought to be his own what belongs to God." So far Augustine. Christ therefore acts against those who claimed lordship over God's people for themselves, and wanted to be called fathers in such a way that they divided into sects those who ought to be one people and the peculiar possession of God alone. For we know that at that time the forerunners of the Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes were of this kind; similar to them today are those who in the families of monks are called abbots, that is, fathers. The Lord therefore forbids us to make for ourselves any mortal as father, apart from God, as regards faith and the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, since God alone gives us faith and adopts us as sons. But Paul speaks according to the nature of the ministry, and takes nothing from God, whose minister and co-worker he had previously testified himself to be. Just as God, who is also the creator and father of bodies, nevertheless grants the name of father, for the sake of honour, to those from whom we are generated, so he also permits those through whose ministry we are regenerated to be called fathers, even in the matter of faith and eternal salvation. Let them only see to it that they do not claim for themselves anything beyond the ministry.

units.la: Sed reuertamur ad præsentis loci tractationem, quo Paulus inter patres & pædagogos distin-guit, ut ostendat, vehementer falli Corinthios, qui patres esse putent eos, qui non nisi pædagogi sint, quos raro ea cura & fide præditos videre liceat, qua parentes filiorum commodis inuigilare solent. Alludit ergo ad communem morem, & ex eo quod ut plurimũ fieri solet, argumentũ suũ deduxit. Pater filiũ ex se natũ, vbi literarũ & disciplinæ diligentioris jâ capace esse vidit, pædagogũ erudiendum tradit: Ita Paulus, cũm primus Corinthios in Christo per Euangelium genuisset, & eos iam aliquo vsque progressos videret, alio vocatus à spiritu doctoribus alijs commisit, qui ab ipso iacta fidei semina ad suam maturitatē æducarent, & illos perfectiores facerent. Fuit inter hos initiò Apollos, qui fidum & industriũ pædagogũ egit. Sed mox alij secuti sunt, qui quod vulgus pædagogorum solet, fecerunt. Ut enim hi plerumq; in solam mercedem intenti animos à paterno amore atque cura alienissimos habent, iisque suæ fidei creditos pueros vel indulgentia nimia corrumpunt, vel nimia seruericate in seruitutem redigunt, & seruili metu eos coercent, qui ingenuo pudore & institutione liberali ducendi erant: Ita utrumque apud Corinthios fa-stitarunt, qui in eã ecclesiã post Pauli discessum irrepserant. Nã non illorũ in vera pietate prose-stũ, sed sua modo cõmoda quærebant, ut ipsi nimirũ in honore & pretio essent, & inter ecclesiarũ certamina otiosi spectatores diuitijs augerentur. Itaq; ad multa coniuebant, in quibus seueriori di-sciplina opus erat, ut in incesti exeplo, idolothytorum cõmunione, Cænæ dominicæ abusu, cœtuum sacrorum ærasiæ & multis similibus esse videre: Rursus ijdem pecunijs omnes emungebant, in seruitutem redigebant, infames reddebant, & tantumnon in faciem quosuis caedebant, vt in po-steriori epistola apertius docet. Hi tamen Paulo, qui vt optimus pater dies noctesque pro ipso-rum salute solicitus erat, praeferebantur. Recte ergo dicit, quod etsi decem millia paedagogorum hucusque habuerint, neminem tamen pari erga ipsos cura & studio praeditum habeant.
units.tr: But let us return to the treatment of the present passage, where Paul distinguishes between fathers and tutors, to show that the Corinthians are greatly deceived who think those are fathers who are only tutors, and whom one rarely sees endowed with that care and faithfulness with which parents are accustomed to watch over the welfare of their children. He therefore alludes to common custom and draws his argument from what usually happens. A father, when he sees that the son born of him is now capable of letters and more diligent discipline, hands him over to a tutor to be educated. So Paul, when he had first begotten the Corinthians in Christ through the Gospel, and saw them already advanced to a certain point, was called elsewhere by the Spirit and committed them to other teachers, who would bring up to maturity the seeds of faith which he had sown and make them more perfect. Among these, at first, was Apollos, who acted as a faithful and diligent tutor. But soon others followed who did what the common run of tutors usually does. For as these men, being intent mostly on wages, have their minds most alien from paternal love and care, and either corrupt the boys entrusted to their charge with excessive indulgence or reduce them to servitude by excessive severity, restraining by servile fear those who ought to have been led by free-born shame and liberal instruction, so these men, who crept into that church after Paul's departure, did both among the Corinthians. For they were not concerned with true piety, but sought only their own advantage: that they themselves might be held in honour and esteem and, as idle spectators amid the contests of the churches, might be enriched with wealth. Therefore they connived at many things in which a stricter discipline was needed, as in the case of incest, the eating of idol-offerings, the abuse of the Lord's Supper, and the disorders of the sacred assemblies, and many similar things, as we see. Again, the same men drained everyone of money, reduced them to servitude, made them infamous, and nearly struck them in the face, as he teaches more openly in the second epistle. Yet these men were preferred to Paul, who, like the best of fathers, was anxious day and night for their salvation. Rightly, therefore, he says that although they have had ten thousand tutors up to now, they have no one endowed with equal care and zeal towards them.

units.la: Est autem hoc memorabile exemplum, quo docemur, quae sit filiorum huius saeculi peruersitas. Vt enim filij parum adhuc prudentes fere paedagogos ignauos & indulgentiores parentibus praeferre solent, seque ab illis seruilius tractari facile patiuntur, dummodo iuuenilis licentiae habenas ipsis laxent: Ita plerique hominum falsos doctores aut ignaua ventris & auaritiae mancipia magis colunt & amant quam fidos Dei seruos, quibus & huius gloria & ecclesiae salus quam maxime cordi est: neque aliquorum sumptuum plerosque piget, quibus grauantur ab impostoribus, modo disciplinae Christianae iugo se solui sentiant. Factum hoc olim prophetarum temporibus. Nam ex mensa regia impij Baalis sacerdotes & seductores alebantur, cum Elias & alij prophetae veri partim exularent, partim in speluncis tenuissimo victu contenti delitescerent. Sic in honore & pretio erant, qui urbe a Babylonijs obsessa impijs & poenitere nescijs laeta & fausta omnia pollicebantur: cum e contra Ieremias proditionis suspectus esset, & in tetro carcere famem grauissimam pateretur. Quid vero sub Christi aduentum, quoad sacerdotes & scribas, factum sit, notius est, quam vt multis commemorari debeat. Et hoc illud est, de quo nos Paulus ad Timoth. scribens praemonuit, fore nimirum tempus, quando sanam doctrinam non tolerabunt, sed auribus prurientes ipsi sibi pro suis cupiditatibus coacernabunt doctores, qui nimirum blanda & ipsorum desiderijs conuenientia praedicent. Quod vt in Papatu fiat, quis non videt? Nec enim ijs contenti, qui in singulis parochijs superstitiones tradunt ineptissimas, insuper Monachorum & fraterculorum examina passim alunt, qui ad fruges consumendas nati, nihil praeterea agunt, quam quod infelicem populum miserrima animarum seruitute grauant, & nocentissimis traditionibus dementant. Sunt tamen illi grati & accepti omnibus, cum interim vel exibilentur ignominiose, vel cum egestate & fame lu-stentur[?], quicunque, communi omnium saluti consultum volunt.
units.tr: This is a memorable example, by which we are taught what the perversity of the children of this age is. For as foolish sons, who are not yet very wise, are usually inclined to prefer lazy tutors who are more indulgent than their parents, and easily suffer themselves to be treated more like slaves by them, provided they loosen for them the reins of youthful licence, so most people honour and love false teachers, or slaves of the belly and of avarice, more than faithful servants of God, to whom the glory of God and the salvation of the Church are most dear. Nor do most grudge the expenses by which they are burdened by impostors, provided they feel released from the yoke of Christian discipline. This happened formerly in the times of the prophets. For at the royal table the priests of the impious Baal and seducers were fed, while Elijah and the other true prophets were partly in exile and partly hidden in caves, content with the scantiest food. Thus those were in honour and esteem who, when the city was besieged by the Babylonians, promised everything joyful and prosperous to the impious and to those who knew not how to repent; whereas Jeremiah, on the contrary, was suspected of treason and suffered the most severe hunger in a foul prison. What happened at Christ's coming with regard to the priests and scribes is better known than it needs to be recalled at length. And this is what Paul warned us of when writing to Timothy: that there would be a time when people will not tolerate sound doctrine, but, itching in their ears, will heap up for themselves teachers according to their own desires, who will preach what is pleasing and suited to their appetites. That this happens in the Papacy, who does not see? For not content with those who hand down the most foolish superstitions in individual parishes, they also feed swarms of monks and little friars everywhere, who, born only to consume the crops, do nothing else but burden the unhappy people with the most wretched slavery of souls and stupefy them with most harmful traditions. Yet these men are welcome and acceptable to all, while those who wish to consult the common salvation of all are either hissed at with disgrace, or are left to suffer poverty and hunger.

units.la: Caeterum peculiari consideratione digna sunt Pauli verba, quibus se Corinthios in IESV CHRISTO per Euangelium genuisse scribit. His enim totum regenerationis nostrae mysterium comprehendit, a quo omnis salus nostra dependet. Nam illa omnino opus esse, Christus diserte affirmat, Nicodemo dicens: Amen amen dico tibi, nisi quis fuerit genitus denuo, non poterit videre regnum Dei. Causa huius dicti satis nota est, quod natura corruptissimi sumus, quoad omnes facultates. Intellectus enim non est capax eorum, quae sunt spiritus Dei. Sequitur hinc voluntas, quae cum desiderijs omnibus ad malum procliuis & propensa est. Haec deinde opera gignit, quae vt cum Dei voluntate pugnant, ita nos ab eius regno quam longissime abstrahunt. Ergo quanti quanti sumus, caro sumus & mundus, quem spiritus sancti capacem esse Christus negat, & vt Petrus ex Isaia annotauit, faenum & gramen sumus, cuius gloria euanida est, neque consistere potest in Dei iudicio. Nisi ergo renati in alios homines transformemur, regnum Dei videre non poterimus. At in quo fit (inquis) regeneratio? Respondet Paulus, & eam nobis in Christo monstrat. Quia enim hic germanus & unigenitus est Dei filius, nos nisi huius fratres efficiamur, Dei filij nunquam erimus: & ideo ille primogenitus dicitur esse inter multos fratres, idest, in ter omnes, qui in ipso filij Dei facti sunt. Adde, quod cum in illo solo vita & salus sit, ad vitam renasci non poterunt, nisi qui huc fuerint insiti. Sequitur ergo, quod neque filij Dei, neque etiam vitae participes sint, quotquot extra Christum sunt: id quod ad religionis Christianae commendationem plurimum facit, & omnium aliarum sectarum superstitiones validissime confutat. At medium quoque regenerationis huius indicatur, Euangelium. Hoc enim nobis Christum praedicat, & ex huius auditione fides nascitur, qua sola illum apprehendimus: & ideo semen regenerationis dicitur, quia animis nostris conceptum, & spiritus virtute vivificatum, nos totos Christo vendicat, vt iam non nos viuamus, sed ille in nobis viuat & regnet. Ex quibus apparet, totum hoc negotium a sola Dei gratia pendere, neque hic aliquid nostris viribus aut meritis debere tribui. Si enim ad corporis nostri generationem nihil conferre possumus, neque in nostro arbitrio aut potestate est, ut mares aut foeminae, robusti aut infirmi, albi aut rufi nascamur: quando minus in nobis erit, ut in Dei filios renascamur, qui natura filij irae sumus?
units.tr: Moreover, the words in which Paul writes that he begot the Corinthians in Jesus Christ through the Gospel deserve special consideration. In them he comprehends the whole mystery of our regeneration, on which all our salvation depends. Christ plainly affirms that this regeneration is absolutely necessary when he says to Nicodemus: "Verily, verily I say unto thee, unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God." The reason for this saying is well known: we are wholly corrupt in all our faculties. The intellect is not capable of the things of the Spirit of God. Next comes the will, which is inclined and prone to every evil desire. This in turn produces works which, as they fight against the will of God, draw us as far as possible from his kingdom. Therefore, however great we are, we are flesh and world, which Christ declares incapable of the Holy Spirit. As Peter noted from Isaiah, we are hay and grass, whose glory fades away and cannot stand in God's judgment. Unless, then, we are reborn and transformed into other men, we cannot see the kingdom of God. But in what does this regeneration consist, you ask? Paul answers, and shows it to us in Christ. Since he is the true and only-begotten Son of God, unless we become his brothers we shall never be sons of God; and therefore he is called the firstborn among many brothers, that is, among all who have been made sons of God in him. Add that since life and salvation are in him alone, only those who have been grafted into him can be reborn to life. It follows that all who are outside Christ are neither sons of God nor partakers of life. This greatly commends the Christian religion and most powerfully refutes the superstitions of all other sects. The means of this regeneration is also indicated: it is the Gospel. The Gospel preaches Christ to us, and faith is born from hearing it, and by faith alone we lay hold of him. Therefore it is called the seed of regeneration, because, conceived in our souls and quickened by the power of the Spirit, it claims us wholly for Christ, so that it is no longer we who live, but he who lives and reigns in us. From these things it appears that this whole business depends on the grace of God alone, and that nothing here is to be attributed to our strength or merits. If we can contribute nothing to the generation of our body, and it is not in our choice or power whether we are born male or female, strong or weak, fair or red-haired, how much less will it be in us to be reborn as sons of God, we who by nature are children of wrath?

units.la: Ista vero tam ministros Verbi quam credentes, adeoq; totam ecclesiam sui officij admonet. Meminerint illi se regenerationis huius ministros, & proinde Dei cooperarios esse, & hanc solam ob causam patres dici. Curent ergo, ut patres fidos & industrios agant. Et primo quidem toti in hoc sint, ut quam plurimos regenerent in Christo, qui relictis superstitionibus & infelicis mundi consuetudine ad Dei ecclesiam accedant, & huius filij efficiantur. Vtq; parentes ex se natos non exponunt aut abijciunt, sed studiose aducant & fovent: Ita quos semel illi Christo lucrifecerunt, eos instituere & cura diligenti in verae pietatis cognitione prouehere satagant, ut aliquando in viros perfectos adolescant. Ibi doctrinam prudenter temperare opus est, ut infirmioribus lac, adultioribus autem cibus sit. Et quia frequenter degenerant, qui iam probe renati videban- tur, eos iterum parturiant (quod in Galatis suis Paulus fecit) usque quo Christus in illis formetur. Est ergo munus hoc arduum, plenum item molestiae & curarum: quod qui recte expendunt, nae illi non multum otij sibi reliquum esse sentient, quod studijs leuioribus, aut etiam impuris mundi voluptatibus vel (ut multi hodie solent) curiosis potius quam utilibus disputationibus & rixis impendant. Quare ministros quidem ecclesiarum haec excitare debent, ut officium suum sedulo faciant: reliqui vero ordini, quem Deus instituit, se non minori diligentia accommodent. Audiant itaq; Verbum Dei, & intra animos reconditu assidua meditatione foveant, ut in Christo renasci & filij Dei germani fieri possint. Id enim non fiet, nisi se totos Dei verbo subijciant per fidei obedientiam, ut iam saepe diximus. Confutatur ergo hic simul eorum commentum, qui hodie Ecclesiae authoritatem supra Scripturas aut Dei Verbum extollunt, & hoc illius testimonio confirmari oportere clamant. Quam enim absurdum hoc fit, ex eo apparet, quod nisi ex Dei Verbo Ecclesia nascatur, nulla omnino in rerum natura fuerit.
units.tr: These things admonish both the ministers of the Word and the believers, and so the whole Church, of their duty. Let the ministers remember that they are ministers of this regeneration, and therefore fellow-workers with God, and for this reason alone they are called fathers. Let them therefore take care to act as faithful and diligent fathers. First of all, let them all be intent on regenerating as many as possible in Christ, so that they, having abandoned superstitions and the customs of the unhappy world, may come to the Church of God and become its sons. Just as parents do not expose or cast off their own offspring, but diligently rear and cherish them, so let ministers strive to instruct those whom they have once won for Christ, and with careful diligence to advance them in the knowledge of true piety, so that in time they may grow into perfect men. Here the teaching must be prudently tempered, so that it is milk for the weaker and solid food for the more mature. And because those who seemed truly reborn often degenerate, they must be brought to birth again (as Paul did with his Galatians) until Christ is formed in them. This office, then, is arduous and full of trouble and cares. Those who weigh it rightly will feel that they have little leisure left for lighter studies, or for the impure pleasures of the world, or (as many do today) for curious rather than useful disputations and quarrels. Therefore these considerations ought to stir the ministers of the churches to perform their office diligently, and the rest of the order which God has instituted should apply itself with no less diligence. Let them hear the Word of God, and cherish it inwardly by constant meditation, so that they may be reborn in Christ and become true sons of God. This will not happen unless they subject themselves wholly to the Word of God through the obedience of faith, as we have often said. Hence the invention of those is also refuted who today exalt the authority of the Church above the Scriptures or the Word of God, and loudly insist that the Word must be confirmed by the Church's testimony. How absurd this is appears from the fact that, unless the Church is born from the Word of God, it would not exist at all in the nature of things.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui cum se patrem Corinthiorum dixerit, nunc infert: Precor vos igitur, imitatores mei estote. Argumentum est ex naturae legibus, quae monent, ne filij a parentum virtutibus degenerent. Quoad ergo huius tractationis statum, hic istius admonitionis sensus est. Cum me, quem patrem vestrum esse negare non potestis, videatis nullis rebus externis, sed in una Christi cruce gloriari, vos quoque idem facere convenit. Turpe enim fuerit filios insolenter superbire, & in patre sibi propositum humilitatis exemplum negligere. Precandi autem verbo utitur, ut paternum in illos animum melius exprimat, & parum ingenuos esse ostendat eos, qui patris preces contemnunt. Est autem hoc praeclarum integritatis Pauli testimonium, qui cum illis agens, quos maiori ex parte non optime de se sentire sciebat, se tamen illis in exemplum proponere auder. Praecipit hoc Petrus omnibus, qui in ecclesiae ministerio versantur, ut non superbum in hanc dominium sibi sumant, sed exemplar gregis esse studeant. Et Paulus Titum monet, ut se exemplum bonorum operum omnibus exhibeat. Timotheo autem sic scribit: Esto exemplar fidelium in sermone, in conversatione, in charitate, in spiritu, in fide, in puritate. At quod ecclesiarum ministris dicitur, sibi dictum putent omnes, qui in alios aliquod ius habent & imperium, sive illi in magistratu sint constituti, sive parentes aut publici iuuentutis praefecti sint. Etenim si isti omnes cum Paulo suis dicere possent, Imitatores nostri estote: ingens profecto ad pietatem publicam momentum accedere videremus. Sed quae non postrema est nostri saeculi calamitas, ita plerique viuunt, ut suijsorum[?] eos pudeat, quae causa est, ut peccandi licentia ad omnes ordines deriuetur.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who, having called himself the father of the Corinthians, now adds: "I beseech you therefore, be ye followers of me." The argument is drawn from the laws of nature, which teach that sons should not degenerate from the virtues of their parents. So, as to the state of this discussion, the sense of this admonition is as follows: since you see that I, whom you cannot deny to be your father, glory not in any external things but in the cross of Christ alone, it is fitting that you do the same. For it would be shameful for sons to be insolently proud and to neglect the example of humility set before them by their father. He uses the word "beseech" to express more fully his fatherly feeling towards them, and to show that those who scorn a father's entreaties are little better than ignoble. This is a notable witness to Paul's integrity: dealing with those of whom he knew that for the most part they did not think very highly of him, he nevertheless dares to set himself before them as an example. Peter gives this charge to all who are engaged in the ministry of the Church: they must not assume lordship over it, but strive to be examples to the flock. Paul likewise bids Titus show himself to all as a pattern of good works, and writes to Timothy: "Be thou an example of the faithful in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity." What is said to the ministers of the churches, let all who have some right and authority over others consider as said to themselves, whether they hold the magistracy or are parents or overseers of public youth. For if all of these could say to their own with Paul, "Be ye followers of us," we would surely see a great increase of public piety. But (and this is no small calamity of our age) most people live in such a way that they are ashamed before their own households; and this is the reason why licence to sin has spread to every rank.

units.la: At videndum est hoc loco, quam rationem in sequendis sanctorum exemplis tenere debeamus. Nam ex hoc Apostoli praecepto alij Monachorum regulas atque ordines stabilire conantur, alij quiduis sibi licere putant, cuius exemplum in aliquo sanctorum inueniunt. Fit ergo, ut ebriosi Noa & Lothum, adulteri Dauidem adducant, ut horum exemplis intemperantiae & nequitiae suae patrocinentur. Sed nihil huius vult spiritus sanctus, & infra cautionem huic praecepto Paulus adhibet, sic dicens: Imitatores mei estote, sicut ego Christi. Itaque omnis virtutis archetypus Christus est, qui in Euangelio seipsum nobis exemplum proponit, quod in tota vitae nostrae conuersatione sequantur. In hominibus etiam sanctissimis naevi & vitia sunt, ut saepe iam diximus. Videndum ergo ut quatenus illi Christum imitati sunt, nos illorum vestigiis insistamus. Non autem temere spiritus non solius Christi, sed sanctorum quoque exempla nobis proponit, ne quod ille à nobis exigit, praestita impossibile putemus: quo argumento se multi excusant. At quàm friuolè id faciant patet, si eos consideremus, qui Christum egregiè imitati sunt, & simul cogitemus, nos, qui ex nobis ipsis ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei sumus, in Christo nihil non posse, quando eius spiritu mouemur & regimur. Nemo igitur sibi ipsi delitias faciat, sed agnoscant omnes admirabilem & plus quàm paternam Dei bonitatem, qui ut nos ex Verbi semine in fi-lios suos regenerat, ita Spiritu quoque suo dignatur, & simul Filium suum unigenitum nobis perfectum omnis virtutis exemplar fecit. Hunc ergo imitemur, huic fidamus & viuamus, cui uni & soli debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: But we must consider here what method we ought to keep in following the examples of the saints. From this precept of the Apostle some try to establish the rules and orders of monks, while others think they may do whatever they find an example of in some saint. Thus drunkards bring forward Noah, and adulterers David and Lot, to defend their intemperance and wickedness by these examples. But the Holy Spirit wants nothing of this, and Paul adds a caution to his precept, speaking thus: "Be ye followers of me, even as I am of Christ." Christ, then, is the archetype of all virtue, who in the Gospel sets himself before us as an example to be followed throughout the whole course of our lives. Even in the most holy men there are blemishes and faults, as I have often said. We must therefore take care that, in so far as they imitated Christ, we follow in their footsteps. Nor without reason has the Spirit set before us the examples not only of Christ but also of the saints, lest we think that what he demands of us is impossible, which is the argument by which many excuse themselves. But how frivolously they do this is plain if we consider those who imitated Christ excellently, and at the same time reflect that we, who of ourselves are not even fit to think anything, can do all things in Christ, since we are moved and ruled by his Spirit. Let no one therefore indulge himself, but let all acknowledge the wonderful and more than fatherly goodness of God, who, as he regenerates us from the seed of the Word into his sons, also deigns to endow us with his Spirit, and has made his only-begotten Son for us a perfect pattern of all virtue. Let us therefore imitate him, trust in him and live for him, to whom alone is due blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXII,
units.tr: Homily XXII,

units.la: Propterea misi vobis Timotheum, qui est filius meus dilectus & fidelis in Domino: qui vobis in memoriam reducet quae sint viae meae in Christo, sicut ubique in omnibus ecclesiis doceo. Caeterum perinde quasi ego non sim venturus ad vos: inflati sunt quidam. Sed veniam breui ad vos, si Dominus voluerit, & cognoscam non sermonem istorum, qui inflati sunt, sed virtutem. Non enim in ser-mone situm est regnum Dei, sed in virtute. Quid vultis? Cum vir-ga veniam ad vos, an cum charitate & spiritu lenitatis?
units.tr: For this reason I have sent you Timothy, who is my beloved and faithful son in the Lord. He will remind you of my ways in Christ, just as I teach everywhere in all the churches. But as though I were not going to come to you, some have become puffed up. I will come to you shortly, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of those who are puffed up, but their power. For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power. What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a spirit of gentleness?

units.la: CUm Paulus in illis, quae proximè praecesserunt, non obscuris argumentis docuisset, se credentium, qui Corinthi erant, patrem esse, eò quòd illos primus per Euangelium in Christo genuerit, ut ex impijs & idololatris veri Dei filij efficerentur: mox eosdem grauiter monuit, ut sui imitatores essent studeant. Quo loco vidimus, qua fide in suo munere versatus sit, & quid omnes eos deceat, quibus Deus in alios homines ius & imperium aliquod concessit. Erant autem apud Corinthios duo hominum genera. Unum quod veritatis studiosos & Pauli amantes habebat, qui cum rebus afflictis consultum vellent, ipsum quàm ocyssimè aduentare cupiebant, & proinde eius mora non parum offendebantur. Alterum ex illis constabat, qui hostili in illum animo praediti hoc agebant, ut ipsius authoritate extincta prorsus, ipsi soli in illa ecclesia dominarentur. Poterant ergo priores illi obijcere: Et quid Paule, ut te imitemur, iubes, cum te neque videamus coràm, neque etiam sciamus, ubi nam locorum agas, quò tendas, aut quid facias? Quin ergo ad nos te confers, ut tua doctrina simul & exemplo coràm confirmemur? Alteri verò eius absentia & aduentus dilatione confidentiores facti, multa in illo calumniabantur, ut eum omnibus contemptum, imò inuisum atque suspectum facerent. Itaque priusquam locum hunc con-cludat, utrisque respondet, & verè paternum animum declarat: dum & pijs bonam sui aduentus spem facit, & alteros illos grauitate & seueritate apostolica territos coercet.
units.tr: When Paul, in the passage immediately before, had taught by no obscure arguments that he is the father of the believers at Corinth, because he was the first to beget them through the Gospel in Christ, so that from impious idolaters they might become sons of the true God, he then soon warned them earnestly to be eager to imitate him. In this passage we have seen with what faithfulness he carried out his office, and what befits all those to whom God has granted some right and authority over other men. Now there were two kinds of people among the Corinthians. One consisted of those who were eager for the truth and loved Paul. Wishing for help in their troubles, they longed for him to come as quickly as possible, and so were not a little offended by his delay. The other consisted of those who, endowed with a hostile spirit toward him, were acting to ensure that, with his authority utterly extinguished, they alone would rule in that church. The former could therefore object: "And Paul, why do you order us to imitate you, when we neither see you in person nor even know where you are, where you are heading, or what you are doing? Why not come to us, so that we may be confirmed both by your teaching and by your example in person?" The latter, however, made more confident by his absence and the delay of his coming, slandered him in many ways, so as to make him despised by all, indeed hateful and suspect. Therefore, before he concludes this passage, he replies to both groups and declares a truly paternal spirit: while he gives the faithful good hope of his coming, he also restrains the others, who were terrified by apostolic gravity and severity.

units.la: Ad primos pertinet quod dicit: Propterea misi vobis Timotheum, qui est filius meus dile-ctus, & fidelis in Domino, &c. Quae verba cum praecedentibus hoc sensu connectit: Iussi vos meos imitatores esse, nec dubito esse aliquos minimè malos, qui quid in me potissimum obseruare & imitari debeant, ignorent. Ne ergo dubij & suspensi haereretis, Timotheum ad vos misi, qui quod ego absens non possum, sua praesentia abunde praestabit. Est enim filius meus, vtpote per me quoque Christo genitus: neque vulgaris, sed dilectus filius est, qui mecum familiarissimè iam diu versatus, nihil eorum, quae ad me spectant, ignorare potest. Idem quoque fidelis est in Domino, id est, in omnibus negotijs Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, cuius potissimum causa hic agitur. Ita verò Timotheum à scientia rerum, quae per ipsum agendae erant, & fide commendat. Estque haec laus amplissima, in qua discimus, quibus argumentis laudari debeant ecclesiarum ministri. Primo nimirum, si apostolorum filij, id est, germani discipuli & earum rerum gnari atque periti sint, quae illi nobis de Christo & per illum parta salutis negotio tradiderunt. Quem enim docere poterunt, aut ad vitam aeternam instituere, qui ipsi ignorantes, & (vt Christius ait) caeci caecorum duces sunt? Huic autem alterum accedat, vt fideles sint in omnibus, quae ad prouehendum Christi regnum faciunt. Comprehendit igitur, his verbis Paulus, quae-cunque in suo oeconomo aut dispensatore Christus requirit, quando eum fidelem & prudentem esse iubet. Et tali quidem viro imprimis opus erat apud Corinthios, qui & nihil celaret eorum, quae cognitu necessaria sunt, & ferociora illa hominum ambitiosorum atq; confidentium ingenia commode & qua decebat moderatione tractare posset, &c.
units.tr: To the first group belongs what he says: "For this reason I have sent you Timothy, who is my beloved and faithful son in the Lord," etc. He connects these words with what precedes in this sense: "I ordered you to be my imitators, and I do not doubt that there are some, not at all wicked, who do not know what in me they ought chiefly to observe and imitate. So that you may not be doubtful and hesitant, I have sent Timothy to you, who will abundantly supply by his presence what I cannot supply while absent. For he is my son, since he too was begotten in Christ through me. He is not an ordinary but a beloved son, who, having been very closely associated with me for a long time, can be ignorant of nothing that concerns me. He is also faithful in the Lord, that is, in all the affairs of our Lord Jesus Christ, for whose sake this is chiefly being undertaken." In this way he commends Timothy by his knowledge of the matters that were to be carried out through him, and by his fidelity. This is a most ample praise, in which we learn by what marks the ministers of churches ought to be commended. First, certainly, if they are the sons of the apostles, that is, genuine disciples, and skilled and expert in those matters which the apostles have handed down to us about Christ and about the business of salvation obtained through him. For whom can they teach, or whom can they train for eternal life, if they themselves are ignorant and (as Christ says) blind guides of the blind? Let the second be added to this: that they be faithful in all the things that advance the kingdom of Christ. Paul therefore comprehends in these words whatever Christ requires of his steward or dispenser, when he commands him to be faithful and wise. Indeed, a man of this kind was especially needed among the Corinthians, one who would conceal nothing of what is necessary to know, and who could handle with fitting moderation and convenience those fiercer dispositions of ambitious and overconfident men, etc.

units.la: Habemus igitur hoc loco praeclarum prudentiae simul & charitatis apostolicae exemplum. Prudentiae enim est, quod non quemuis temere mittit, sed eum, qui ad res agendas idoneus erat, & quem illi nullo iure contemnere poterant. Et debent hoc imprimis observare, qui negotia alicuius momenti per legatos conficere instituunt. Nam quam multum referat legatos mittere, qui rerum prudentia, grauitate & fide praediti sint, gentes quoque intellexerunt, apud quas grauissimum fuit [illegible, ~12 letters] crimen, quod illis intendebatur, qui commissam sibi legationem infideliter aut negligenter obiuissent. Et non temere à Solomone dictum est, Truncat pedes & bibit violentiam, qui mittit verbum per manum stulti. Quo proverbio & abiurde nimis facere & sibi ipsis malum violenter accersere docet eos, quicunque hominibus ineptis aut malitiosis ad res arduas utuntur. Et quantum mali tales dare soleant, in illis est videre, qui ad terram Chanaanaeorum explorandam emisi, sua meticulositate & ignauia toti Israelitarum populo gravissimi sceleris simul & exitij authores fuerunt. Quibus si ex Romana historia Pompilium legatum opponas, qui incredibili grauitate Antiochum Syriae regem sic terruit, vt à Ptolemaeo infestando abstineret, & bellum, quod sibi à Romanis imminebat, declinaret: videbis vnius viri virtute duo simul regna seruata, & Romano etiam imperio quietem partam fuisse. Charitatis autem & amoris paterni argumentum est, quod eos minime negligit, à quibus procul aberat, quando ad eos Timotheum mittit, quo neminem chariorem & magis fidum habebat, & quo ipse interea non poterat carere absque magno suo incommodo. Nam vt ad Philippenses scribit, cum alij fere omnes sua modo quaerent, solus ille eodem cum Paulo animo praditus ecclesiarum res sincere & fideliter agebat. Videmus ergo Apostolum nihil antiquius habuisse ecclesiarum salute. Quod exemplum si hodie imitarentur, qui vel in ecclesia vel repub. rebus praesunt, procul dubio plus proficerent, & tam ecclesias quam respub. melius instituas haberemus. At plerique otium priuatum quaerunt, & suis atque suorum commodis student, nihil interim aut parum de publica salute soliciti. Quo fit, vt omne periculum declinandum esse putent, & dum hoc agunt, fere in extremum discrimen res adducunt, & pios quidem suo exemplo remissiores, impios vero & nouarum rerum studiosos audaciores reddunt.
units.tr: We have, therefore, in this passage a notable example of apostolic prudence and charity at once. It is prudence that he does not send just anyone at random, but one who was suited to the business at hand and whom the Corinthians could in no way rightly despise. This especially should be noted by those who undertake to conduct matters of some importance through envoys. For how much it matters to send envoys who are endowed with prudence, gravity and fidelity, even foreign peoples have understood, among whom the gravest charge was brought against those envoys who had discharged an entrusted mission faithlessly or carelessly. And it was not without reason that Solomon said: "He who sends a message by the hand of a fool cuts off his own feet and drinks violence." By this proverb he teaches that those who use inept or malicious men for difficult business both act absurdly and violently bring evil upon themselves. And how much harm such men are wont to do can be seen in those who were sent out to explore the land of Canaan: by their timidity and cowardice they became the authors both of the gravest crime and of ruin for the whole people of Israel. If against these you set, from Roman history, the envoy Popillius, who by his remarkable gravity so terrified Antiochus, king of Syria, that he refrained from attacking Ptolemy and turned aside the war that threatened him from the Romans, you will see that by the virtue of one man two kingdoms were preserved at once, and quiet was also secured for the Roman empire. But it is a sign of charity and paternal love that he does not neglect those from whom he is far away, when he sends Timothy to them, whom he held dearer than anyone and more faithful, and whom he himself could not spare in the meantime without great inconvenience to himself. For, as he writes to the Philippians, when almost all the others seek their own interests, he alone, endowed with the same spirit as Paul, handled the affairs of the churches sincerely and faithfully. We see, then, that the Apostle held nothing more important than the welfare of the churches. If those who today preside over the affairs of either church or commonwealth were to imitate this example, they would undoubtedly accomplish more, and we would have both churches and commonwealths better ordered. But most people seek private leisure and pursue their own advantage and that of their own, meanwhile being little or not at all concerned for the public safety. Hence it comes about that they think every danger must be avoided, and while they do this they bring affairs almost to the final crisis, making the godly more lax by their example, and the impious and the lovers of novelties bolder.

units.la: Quid vero illud est, quod apud Corinthios Timotheus facere debuit? Duo dicit. Primum, Is vobis in memoriam reducet, quae sint viae meae in Christo. Vias vocat scriptura viuendi rationem, quam quisque sequitur, studia item & quaecunque ex his dependent, adhaec praecepta & leges, quibus ista omnia reguntur. Ideo Dauid orabat, vt Deus ipsum suas vias doceret, inq; semitas suorum praeceptorum deduceret. Hoc ergo vult dicere: Timotheus vos certiores faciet, quid agam, quae mea sint studia, quibus rationibus regnum Christi proueham, quibus denique casibus atque periculis exercear, & qualem me inter ista omnia geram. Et hoc maxime ad id pertinet, quo vt suum exemplum imitarentur, monuerat. Atqui de his omnibus haud dubie saepius audierant, imo fesquianno toto Paulum coram viderant, vt nihil eorum deberent ignorare. Sed non sufficiebat hoc, quia tantum non obliti erant istorum omnium: & ideo hanc eorum negligentiam non obscure his verbis perstringit. Est haec ingenij humanis infirmitas, vt non semper eorum capaces simus, quae cognitu imprimis sunt necessaria: aut eadem non semper memori mente retineamus.
units.tr: What, then, was it that Timothy ought to do among the Corinthians? He names two things. First: "He will remind you of my ways in Christ." Scripture calls "ways" the manner of living that each one follows, also his pursuits and whatever depends upon these, and besides, the precepts and laws by which all these things are governed. Therefore David prayed that God would teach him his ways and lead him into the paths of his precepts. So Paul means this: Timothy will inform you what I am doing, what my pursuits are, by what methods I advance the kingdom of Christ, by what trials and dangers I am exercised, and what kind of man I show myself to be amid all these things. And this pertains especially to what he had admonished them about, that they should imitate his example. Yet they had doubtless heard about all these things more than once, indeed they had seen Paul in person for a year and a half, so that they ought to be ignorant of none of them. But this was not enough, because they had almost forgotten all of them; and therefore he touches on this negligence of theirs clearly in these words. It is a weakness of human intellect that we are not always capable of those things which are especially necessary to know, or do not always retain the same in a mindful way.

units.la: Admonet de hac Christus discipulos suos, quando se multa habere ait, quae illis dicat, ipsos autem ad ea percipienda nunc idoneos non esse, ideoque spiritum pollicetur, qui ipsis omnia suggerat, & prius audita in mentem renocet. Vnde colligimus, in ecclesia quotidianis admonitionibus, suggestionisuggestionibus, hortationibus, consolatione item frequenti, & interdum correptione etiam severiori opus esse, & rursus eorum error atque ignorantia confutatur, qui cum ista superuacanea esse putent, totum ecclesiae ministerium contemnunt atque reijciunt. Alterum, quod Timotheo apud Corinthios ex Pauli mandato agendum erat, fuit, ut illis exponeret, quae eius doctrina esset in omnibus ecclesijs, aut quam docendi rationem ubique locorum sequeretur. Videtur hoc propter illos adiectum fuisse, qui rerum imperitis & simplici plebi persuadere conabantur, illum non eadem seueritate apud omnes uti, & in nonnullis locis diuersam docendi rationem sequi, adeoque sibi non semper similem esse. Facit hoc multum ad animorum alienationem aut exasperationem, si qui putent se durius quam alios tractari: neque aliud est, quod doctoris authoritati plus deroget, quam si in suspicionem veniat, quod sibi ipsi non semper constet. Ideo ut hac culpa Paulus liberaretur, omnino necesse fuit.
units.tr: Christ admonishes his disciples of this when he says that he has many things to tell them, but that they are not yet able to receive them. Therefore he promises the Spirit, who will bring all things to their minds and recall to them what they have heard before. From this we gather that the Church needs daily admonitions, reminders, exhortations, frequent consolation, and sometimes even more severe correction. Here too the error and ignorance of those is refuted who think such things superfluous and so despise and reject the whole ministry of the Church. Second, Timothy was to carry out Paul's command among the Corinthians by explaining to them what his teaching was in all the churches, and what method of teaching he followed everywhere. This seems to have been added on account of those who tried to persuade the unlearned and simple common people that Paul did not use the same severity with everyone, and that in some places he followed a different method of teaching, and so was not always consistent with himself. This does much to alienate or embitter minds, if people think they are treated more harshly than others. Nothing else detracts more from a teacher's authority than to fall under the suspicion that he is not always consistent with himself. So, in order that Paul might be freed from this charge, it was altogether necessary.

units.la: Continet autem locus hic egregiam doctrinae apostolicae commendationem, quae in duobus hisce consistit. Primum, quod vias Christi tradit, id est, ea quae illi ab aeterno Dei Filio acceperunt, & ex spiritus sancti suggestione ubique terrarum praedicarunt. Et hoc illud est, quod Christus discipulis in mandatis dedit, ut nimirum ea omnes gentes doceant, quae ipse tradiderit. Alterum, quod in hac doctrina tradenda illi constantes, & ubique locorum sui similes fuerunt, neque genus doctrinae pro hominum diversitate mutarunt: ut facere solent, qui nihil praeter vulgi applausum aut hominum potentum atque magnatum fauorem venantur. Paulus certe tantam constantiae huius rationem habuit, ut non veritus sit dicere: Si ego Paulus, aut etiam Angelus e coelo euangelizet vobis praeter id, quod euangelizauimus vobis, anathema esto. Debet igitur hoc ante omnia obseruari ab omnibus, qui ecclesias recte constitutas esse volunt. Quia enim Dei domus est ecclesia, non alia quam Dei vox in ea audiri debet: & quia idem hic supra omnes eminet, nullius hominis tanta potestas esse authoritas siue meritum tantum, ut in eius gratiam aliquid mutetur. Arguit hoc eorum impudentiam, qui nobis sub Apostolorum nomine putidissima quaedam figmenta, & nescio quos Canones obtrudunt, in quibus nihil habetur, quod grauitatem apostolicam sapiat, multa autem insunt, quae si cum illorum scriptis conferantur, ab ijs per omnia dissentire apparebit. Damnatur etiam illorum exemplo eorum leuitas, qui in doctrinae capitibus controuersijs cothurnos fingunt, id est, locutiones ambiguas atque dubias, quibus apud diuersos auditores sensu quoq; diuerso utantur. Volunt isti homines sese omnium moribus atque ingenijs accomodare, & pacis studium praetexunt, quo suam leuitatem excusent: at interim hoc agunt, ut & Deo minus fideles sint, & fere dissensionum incendia maiora excitent, seq; ipsos labyrinthis inextricabilibus inuoluant: cuius rei exempla infinita hodie vidimus.
units.tr: This passage contains an outstanding commendation of apostolic teaching, which rests on two points. First, they handed on the ways of Christ, that is, what they had received from the eternal Son of God, and what they preached everywhere under the prompting of the Holy Spirit. This is what Christ commanded his disciples, namely that they should teach all nations what he himself had handed down. Second, in delivering this teaching they were steadfast and the same everywhere, and did not change the manner of their teaching according to the diversity of men, as those do who seek nothing beyond the applause of the crowd or the favour of powerful and great men. Paul certainly had such regard for this constancy that he did not hesitate to say: "If I, Paul, or even an angel from heaven preach to you anything beyond what we have preached to you, let him be accursed." Therefore this must above all be observed by all who wish churches to be rightly constituted. For since the Church is the house of God, nothing but the voice of God ought to be heard in it; and since this voice rises above all men, no man's power, authority, or merit is so great that anything should be changed for his sake. This exposes the impudence of those who push upon us, under the name of the Apostles, certain most foul fictions and I know not what canons, in which there is nothing that savours of apostolic gravity, but there are many things which, if they were compared with the apostles' writings, would be seen to disagree with them in every respect. The levity of those is also condemned by this example, who in the chief points of doctrine in controversies feign buskins, that is, ambiguous and doubtful expressions, which they use with a different sense before different hearers. Such men want to adapt themselves to everyone's manners and dispositions, and they put forward a zeal for peace as a pretext to excuse their levity. But meanwhile they bring it about that they are less faithful to God, and they stir up even greater fires of dissension, and entangle themselves in inextricable labyrinths. We have seen endless examples of this today.

units.la: Caeterum in Pauli verbis pergamus, qui nunc ad alteros illos sermonem conuertit, qui cum hostiliter eum odissent, eius absentia insolentiores fiebant, ut sibi quiduis in ecclesia illa licere putarent. Sic autem ait: Caeterum perinde quasi ego non sim venturus ad vos, inflati sunt quidam, &c. Haec dicendo in conscientias illorum penetrat, & non obscure docet, quod etsi ipsum improbe traducant, & contemptissime de illo loquantur, non possint tamen non eius aduentum timere, eo quod intra animos suos conuicti ipsum Spiritus virtute armatum esse sciant, cui ipsi pares esse non possint. Sensus ergo verborum est: Etsi non ignorent qui sim, & iam nunc intra animos suos non leuiter pungantur, tamen nouos quasi spiritus concipiunt, quando me nunquam posthac ad vos venturum esse sibi persuadent. Sed plurimum fallentur ipse[?] sua. Veniam enim breui, & fortassis citius quam quis putet, si Dominus voluerit. Et tunc cognoscam qui nam & quales illi sint, qui nunc tantum sibi iuris sumunt in ecclesia, ut Apostolorum quoque doctrinam insectari & contemnere non vereantur. Experimentum enim capiam, non de verbis illorum & dicendi facultate, qua illos magnifice instructos esse non ignoro: sed de virtute, an scilicet eo Spiritu armati sint, quo Christi ministros confirmari oportet, & num effectus verborum splendori & magnificis illorum promissis respondeat. Sunt autem in his quaedam nobis diligentius inspicienda.
units.tr: But let us go on with Paul's words, who now turns his discourse to those others who, though they hated him bitterly, became more insolent in his absence, so that they thought they might do whatever they pleased in that church. He says: "Now, as though I were not coming to you, some are puffed up," and so on. In saying this he penetrates their consciences, and clearly teaches that even if they wickedly slander him and speak most contemptuously of him, yet they cannot help fearing his coming, because, convicted within their own minds, they know that he is armed with the power of the Spirit, to which they cannot be equal. The sense of the words, therefore, is this: although they are not unaware of who I am, and already within their own minds are not lightly pricked, yet they conceive new kinds of spirit, as it were, when they persuade themselves that I shall never come to you again. But they are greatly mistaken in their own opinion. For I shall come soon, and perhaps sooner than anyone thinks, if the Lord wills. And then I shall learn who and what sort of men they are who now take so much licence in the church that they do not hesitate to attack and despise even the teaching of the Apostles. For I shall make trial, not of their words and their power of speech, by which, I am not unaware, they are magnificently equipped; but of their power, namely whether they are armed with that Spirit by which the ministers of Christ ought to be strengthened, and whether the effect of their words corresponds to the splendour and grand promises. There are, however, some things here that we must examine more carefully.

units.la: Primum in his est Sathanae astutia, qui ut lupus stabulis & gregibus insidiatur, quando pastores aut abesse aut dormire, vel circa alia occupari sentit: ita ille ecclesijs fere tunc malum struit, quando doctoribus fidei & indulstris destitutas esse, aut eos qui adsunt in officio suo remissiores esse videt. Et hoc illud est, de quo nos Christus præmonuit, quando inimicum sementi iam facta Zizania sua aspergere dicit, dum homines dormiunt. Et Paulus in Miletana Synodo cum Asiæ ministris agens, inter alia inquit: Noui ego hoc, quod post discessum meum ingressuri sint in vos lupi graues, non parcentes gregi: & ex vobismetipsis exorientur viri, qui loquantur peruersa, vt discipulos post se abstrahant. Quod Corinthijs accidisse, hucusque audimus, vt & multis alijs, quos Satan ad resistendum minus paratos aut instructos esse animadvertit. Et hoc Apostolos tam solicitos fecit, vt quamuis ex officio non possent in certo aliquo loco subsistere, vt qui rerum a Christo gestarum testes oculati Euangelium vbique gentium prædicare, & nouas quotidie ecclesias colligere debebant, eas tamen quas iam constituerant, crebro inuiserent, aut saltem literis suis confirmare & in officio continere studerent. At hodie, qui se Apostolicos esse gloriantur, cum ecclesiarum plurium episcopi esse velint, ne vni quidem adesse solent, vt quæ pastoris sunt obeant. Extant quidem Canones plurimi, nec non Conciliorum decreta, quibus in ecclesijs suis residere, neque ab his discedere iubentur: sed hæc facile illi contemnunt, qui interim totum terrarum orbem ferro & igne cogendum esse clamant, vt omnes Conci-liorum statutis obtemperent. Chrysostomus olim Epiphanium, virum alioqui sanctum & de Christianæ bene meritum, publice reprehendit, quod relicta Cypro, cuius episcopus erat, ad alias ecclesias excurreret, & in illis contra Canones negotia ecclesiastica obiret. Quid ergo illum hodie dicturum putas, si episcopos in aulis regum, inter heroinas aulicas, aut etiam inter ganeonum & scortorum greges, imo in medijs castris bellica negotia tractare cerneret? Porro quod de ecclesiarum pastoribus dicitur, non minus ad eos etiam pertinet, qui magistratum gerunt. Nam hi quoque imprimis cauere debent, ne quæ ipsis agenda sunt negotia per vicarios obeant. Est enim hæc reipub. pestis nocentissima, nec credibile est, alium in ijs seriò officium facturum esse, in quibus it negligentem videt, ad quem illorum cura maxime pertinet. Est præterea hoc ipsum obseruatu imprimis necessarium in re domestica ne parentes a domibus & familia sua temere absint. Vt enim illorum præsentia domesticos omnes in officio continet: ita mox lasciuiunt serui & liberi, si illos in rebus suis curandis negligentiores esse videant. Prudenter ergo veteri prouerbio omnis loci & ordinis homines admonentur, vt relictis negotijs nihil ad se pertinentibus, Spartam, quam nacti sunt, ornent. Quod si omnes facerent, melius haberent res humanæ cum priuatæ tum publicæ.
units.tr: First in these matters is the cunning of Satan, who, like a wolf, lies in wait for the folds and flocks when he perceives that the ministers are absent, or asleep, or occupied with other things. So he usually plots evil against churches when he sees that they are destitute of teachers of the faith and of diligent men, or that those who are present are more remiss in their office. This is what Christ warned us about when he says that the enemy, while men sleep, sows his tares over the seed already sown. And Paul, when he dealt with the ministers of Asia at Miletus, said among other things: "I know this, that after my departure grievous wolves will enter in among you, not sparing the flock; and from among yourselves men will arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after them." We hear that this happened to the Corinthians, and so to many others whom Satan saw to be less prepared or equipped for resisting. This made the Apostles so anxious that, although by their office they could not remain in any one place, since as eyewitnesses of the things done by Christ they had to preach the Gospel everywhere among the nations and gather new churches every day, yet they often revisited the churches they had already founded, or at least strove to confirm them by their letters and keep them in their duty. But today those who glory that they are apostolic, although they wish to be bishops of many churches, are usually not present even in one, so that they might perform the duties of a minister. There are indeed very many canons, and decrees of councils, by which they are ordered to remain in their churches and not depart from them; but those men easily scorn these, who meanwhile cry out that the whole world must be compelled by sword and fire to obey the decrees of the councils. Long ago Chrysostom publicly rebuked Epiphanius, a man otherwise holy and well deserving of the Christian cause, because he left Cyprus, of which he was bishop, and ran off to other churches, and there carried on ecclesiastical business contrary to the canons. What, then, do you think he would say today if he saw bishops conducting warlike affairs in royal courts, among courtly ladies, or even among flocks of pimps and harlots, indeed in the midst of camps? Moreover, what is said of the ministers of the churches pertains no less to those who hold the magistracy. For these too must above all take care that they do not carry out the business that is theirs to do through deputies. For this is a most harmful plague to the commonwealth, nor is it credible that another will do his duty seriously in those matters in which he sees the one to whom their care chiefly belongs to be negligent. Moreover, this itself is especially necessary to observe in domestic affairs: that parents should not rashly be absent from their homes and families. For just as their presence keeps all the household in duty, so servants and children soon run wild if they see them to be negligent in caring for their affairs. Therefore men of every place and rank are wisely admonited, by the old proverb, to leave aside business that does not concern them and adorn the Sparta which they have been allotted. If everyone did this, human affairs, both private and public, would fare better.

units.la: Deinde exemplum piæ & Christianæ modestiæ nobis Paulus exhibet. Etsi enim rem polli-ceatur per se sanctam, & quam ad suum officium pertinere sciebat, nihil tamen temere aut confidenter de seipso & voluntate sua præsumit, sed voluntati Dei omnem sui instituti euentum permittit. Veniam (inquit) ad vos breui, si Dominus voluerit. Nouerat enim nihil esse in no-stro arbitrio aut potestate, & proinde Solomonem non minus vere quam pie dixisse: Cor homi-nis deliberat de via sua, Dominus autem dirigit gressum eius. Est ergo hic fere sanctorum mos, vt in consilijs atque institutis suis semper Dei voluntatem excipiant, cum fere nobis non con-stet, num per nos confectum velit Deus, quod per se bonum est, & ad nos maxime pertinet. Et non parum prodest, vt huic mori assuescamus[?]: quia ad pietatem plurimum facit, & Dei ti-morem in animis nostris excitat, denique ceu fraeno nos continet, ne quid arroganter de nobis ipsis sentiamus. Ideo Iacobus multis & grauiter nos de hoc admonet, & secus facientes corripit, dicens: Age nunc qui dicitis, Hodie vel cras ibimus in illam vrbem, & transigemus illic annum vnum, & mercabimur, & lucrabimur: Qui ignoratis quid futurum sit postero die (quæ est enim vita vestra? vapor enim est, qui ad exiguum tempus apparet, & deinde euanescit) Pro eo quod dicere debebatis, Si Dominus voluerit & viuamus, faciemus hoc aut illud. Nunc autem gloriamini de arrogantia vestra: Omnis eiusmodi gloriatio mala est. At si malum est confidentius de illis statuere, quæ bona & quæ nostri officij sunt, quid de illis iudicare nos oportet, qui cum ea penes se statuant, quæ impia & iniusta sunt, de ijs tamen perinde pronuntiant, ac si in ipsorum arbitrio & potestate sit, illa perficere. Faciunt hoc fere, qui aduersus Christum & ecclesiam eius conspirant, & Euangelij prædicationem extinctam volunt. Horum enim sermones sunt, quos Dauid olim illis tribuit: Rumpemus vincula eorum, & lora eorum abiiciemus. Nec cogitant, Deum in coelis residere, qui ipsorum consilia ex alto irridet, & plerunq; in ipsorum exitium illa convertit. Fit ergo illis, quod Achabo, qui Michea mortem indignam minabatur, si ex Syris victoriam, quam falsi prophetae promiserant, referret: at in acie casus impiae arrogantiae poenas dedit. Similis fuit Iuliani exitus, qui cum eo animo in Parthos expeditionem faceret, ut his deuictis Christianos simul omnes aut deleret aut ad fidem abnegandam cogeret, ex improviso vulneratus & cum horribili extremae desperationis indicio mortuus, suo exemplo docuit, quid omnes eos maneat, qui simili temeritate adversus Christum aliquid tentant.
units.tr: Next, Paul sets before us an example of pious and Christian modesty. Although he promises to do something that is holy in itself and that he knew belonged to his office, he presumes nothing rashly or confidently about himself or his own will, but leaves the outcome of every plan he makes to the will of God. "I will come to you soon," he says, "if the Lord wills." He knew that nothing lies in our own choice or power, and so Solomon spoke no less truly than piously: "A man's heart plans his way, but the Lord directs his steps." It is therefore the usual custom of the saints to submit their counsels and undertakings always to the will of God, since we seldom know whether God wishes what is good in itself, and what pertains chiefly to us, to be accomplished through us. It helps greatly to accustom ourselves to this habit, for it contributes much to piety, kindles the fear of God in our minds, and, as it were, holds us back with a bridle, so that we do not think arrogantly about ourselves. For this reason James warns us of this at length and rebukes those who act otherwise, saying: "Come now, you who say, 'Today or tomorrow we will go into this city, spend a year there, trade and make a profit'; you who do not know what will happen tomorrow (for what is your life? It is a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes). Instead you ought to say, 'If the Lord wills, we shall live and do this or that.' But now you boast in your arrogance; all such boasting is evil." But if it is evil to decide with too much confidence about those things that are good and belong to our duty, what ought we to judge of those who, while they resolve upon what is impious and unjust, nevertheless speak of these things as if it lay in their own power to carry them out? Those who conspire against Christ and his Church, and wish the preaching of the Gospel extinguished, commonly do this. Their words are the ones David once attributed to them: "Let us break their bonds, and cast away their cords." They do not consider that God sits in heaven, who laughs at their counsels from on high and often turns them to their own destruction. So it happened to Ahab, who threatened Micaiah with an unworthy death if he should bring back a victory over the Syrians, which the false prophets had promised; yet in battle he paid the penalty of his impious arrogance. Julian's end was similar. He undertook his expedition against the Parthians with the intention that, once they were defeated, he would either destroy all the Christians together or force them to renounce the faith; yet he was wounded unexpectedly and died with a dreadful sign of utter despair. By his own example he taught what awaits all those who attempt anything against Christ with similar rashness.

units.la: Sed tertium quoque, quod hic proponitur, videamus: quid nimirum Paulus Corinthi facere voluerit? Cognoscam (inquit) non sermone istorum, qui inflati sunt, sed virtutem. Sermonis nomine dicendi facultatem & verborum splendorem intelligit, quo aemuli eius sese apud rude vulgus venditabant. Virtus autem efficaciam Spiritus sancti significat, quae in illis sese exerit, qui in ecclesia serio agunt Domini negotium. Sensus ergo est: Vbi ad vos venero, non multum morabor quam multa quamq; magnifica illi dicant, sed in hoc potius intentus ero, num illorum verbis coniuncta sit Spiritus sancti virtus, & quid hactenus sua illa facundia & orationis apparatu profecerint. Et huius dicti rationem subiicit: Non enim in sermone situm est regnum Dei, sed in virtute. Regnum Dei frequenter in scripturis dicitur Euangelij praedicatio, & tota illa ratio, qua homines Christo adducuntur per fidei obedientiam, ut Deum in se regnare patiantur, & tandem regni eius caelestis atque aeterni participes fiant. Hoc (inquit) omne non in verborum magnifico splendore consistit, sed in eo, ut qui Euangelij praecones sunt, armis spiritualibus instructi, Zelo ardenti & inuicto prouehendi regni Dei studio toti in hoc incumbant, ut quaecunq; huic aduersa sunt demoliantur, ea autem plantent & aedificent, quae ad Dei gloriam faciunt, utq; omnes ad Christi obsequium adducant. Neque temere hoc dicit Paulus. Vt enim Christiana religio non in otiosa <bl>ἡσυχία</bl>[?] aut contemplatione, sed potius in <bl>πρᾶξει</bl>[?] & totius vitae conversatione consistit: sic ministrorum ecclesiae conditio militiae instar est (ut in posteriori epistola docetur) cuius finis est, ut deiecto diabolo, mundo & carnis sensu atq; intellectu omni, ad fidei obedientiam omnes pertrahantur. Quapropter ut in militia non qui multa loquuntur laude digni sunt, sed qui rem strenuè ac fortiter gerunt: ita hic non verbis, sed factis res geritur, & triumphum merentur, qui ecclesias constituunt, in quibus eiecto procul Satana solus Christus imperium obtinet. Similis locutio in Epistola ad Romanos habetur: Non est regnum Dei esca & potus, sed iustitia & pax & gaudium in Spiritu sancto. Debet autem hinc generalis doctrina peti, ne vllis externis rebus ea tribuamus, quae aeternae salutis sunt, neve in ea quae ore modo fit fidei confessione acquiescamus. Si enim ad prouehendum regnum Dei nihil facit concionatorum facundia & magnificus verborum apparatus, multo minus proderit Christum in ore solo circumferre, nisi idem intra animi penetralia receptus suo Spiritu in nobis agat. Facit huc celeberrimae illius concionis, quam Christus in monte habuit, conclusio: Non omnis qui mihi dicit, Domine Domine, ingredietur in regnum meum, sed qui fecerit voluntatem Patris mei caelestis. Vtinam vero ista diligentius meditarentur cum ministri ecclesiarum tum illorum auditores. In ore quidem omnium est Christus, & magnificè docteque de illo multi dicunt & scribunt: sed quam vacui sint plerique ea Spiritus virtute, quam in praesenti Paulus requirit, non obscure docet, quae apud omnes ordines regnat, morum corruptio & effrenis quiduis designandi licentia.
units.tr: But let us also look at the third thing proposed here: what, I ask, did Paul intend to do at Corinth? "I will know," he says, "not the speech of those who are puffed up, but their power." By "speech" he means the faculty of speaking and the splendour of words, by which his rivals displayed themselves before the uneducated crowd. "Power," however, signifies the efficacy of the Holy Spirit, which shows itself in those who earnestly carry on the Lord's work in the Church. The sense, then, is this: "When I come to you, I will not spend much time on how many fine and magnificent things they say, but will rather concern myself with whether the power of the Holy Spirit is joined to their words, and what their eloquence and display of rhetoric have so far accomplished." He then gives the reason for this saying: "For the kingdom of God is not in speech, but in power." The kingdom of God is often used in Scripture for the preaching of the Gospel, and for that whole method by which men are brought to Christ through obedience of faith, so that they allow God to reign in them and at last become partakers of his heavenly and eternal kingdom. All of this, he says, does not consist in the magnificent splendour of words, but in this: that those who are heralds of the Gospel, armed with spiritual weapons, and with a burning and unconquerable zeal for advancing the kingdom of God, devote themselves wholly to this, so that they tear down whatever opposes it, and plant and build up what serves the glory of God and brings everyone to obedience to Christ. Paul does not say this rashly. For just as the Christian religion consists not in idle quiet [ἡσυχία] or contemplation, but rather in action [πρᾶξις] and in the whole conduct of life, so the office of the ministers of the Church is like military service (as is taught in the later epistle), the aim of which is that, with the devil, the world, and every sense and understanding of the flesh cast down, all men be drawn to obedience of faith. Therefore, just as in war it is not those who talk much who deserve praise, but those who carry out the business vigorously and bravely, so here the work is done not by words but by deeds, and those earn the triumph who establish churches in which Satan is driven far away and Christ alone holds rule. A similar expression occurs in the Epistle to the Romans: "The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit." From this a general doctrine ought to be drawn: we must not ascribe to external things what belongs to eternal salvation, nor rest in a confession of faith that is made only with the mouth. For if the eloquence of preachers and the magnificent display of words contribute nothing to advancing the kingdom of God, much less will it help to carry Christ about on the lips alone, unless he, received into the innermost recesses of the mind, works in us by his own Spirit. The conclusion of that most famous sermon which Christ delivered on the mount agrees with this: "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of my heavenly Father, but he who does the will of my Father." Would that both the ministers of the Churches and their hearers would consider these things more carefully! Christ is on everyone's lips, and many speak and write about him magnificently and learnedly; but how empty most are of that power of the Spirit which Paul here requires, the corruption of morals reigning among every rank and the unbridled licence of doing whatever one pleases clearly show.

units.la: Porrò concludit Paulus locum hunc graui, paterna tamen comminatione, sic dicens: Quid vultis? Cum virga veniam ad vos, an cum charitate & spiritu lenitatis? Virga authoritatem significat, qua ecclesiae pastores Deus armauit, quoad correptiones peccatorum & disciplinam in populo seruandam. Tribuitur haec Christo in Psalmis, quòd virgam potentiae suae ex Zion emissurus sit, qua omnes quidem suas colligat & defendat, rebelles vero & contumaces hircos ceu sceptro ferreo comminuat. Eam vero ex Zione emisit, quando Apostolos Verbi & Spiritus sui virtute armatos in orbem exire, & Euangelium vbique gentium praedicare iussit. Et quanta virgae huius potentia fuerit, intra paucos annos deiectus[?] terrarum orbis testatur, & imprimis horrenda illa exempla, quibus Ananiæ & Sapphiræ mendacium Petrus, Elymæ autem Magi audaciam Paulus punierunt. Hanc in præsenti quoque sibi vendicat ad-uersus eos, qui eius epistolas quidem graues, præsentiam uero infirmam esse calumniabantur: & patres imitantur, qui ubi filium contumaciorem factum esse uidet, tandem eiusmodi fere uerbis uiuntur: Age, te nebulonum & malæ frugi sociorum consortium delectat, quorum consuetudi-nem & fallacia promissa meis admonitionibus præfers, neque me eum esse putas, qui te corrigere debeam, aut cui tu obedire tenearis. Sed faxo breui intelligas quid possim, neque mihi ratio deerit, qua proteruiam tuam coerceam. Tu ergo quid facias uide, aut quid me facere uelis. Si enim mihi morem gesseris, patrem mitissimum me senties: sin secus, meo in te iure utar, ut mihi uires esse sentias, quibus te ulciscar. Tu utrum uelis elige, & penes te cogita, patre ne propitio & indul-gente potius, aut duro & aspero uti uelis? &c. Habet eiusmodi concessio[?] optionem cum acerbitate coniunctam[?], & uehementius penetrat animos generosiores, quam si pater illico uirgas aut bacu-los expediret. Tale quid Paulus quoq; in præsenti dicit: Ego uester doctor atque pater sum. In-struxit ergo me armis spiritualibus Dominus, neque mihi uirga aut pedum deest, quo proter-uientes in ordinem redigam. Et hoc quidem uos meremini, qui perinde ac si res uestræ optime habeant, inflati estis, & fidas admonitiones contemnitis: imo mea lenitate ad syncerioris doctrinæ contemptum abutimini. Sed agite, quando uobis adeo infirmus & nullus uideor, dicite qualem me esse uelitis? Num ut uirgas expediam, & me spiritus uirtute armatum esse ostendam, aut ut solita charitate & spiritus lenitate erga uos utar? At non debent ista sic accipi, quasi uirga usus & castigatio uel disciplina seuerior a charitate aliena sint (nam in his præcipua paternæ dilectionis argumenta elucent, & notum est illud Solomonis: Qui parcit uirgæ, odit filium suum) sed ex liberorum ingenio sermonem temperat, qui patres suæ lenitatis aut dilectionis immemores esse putant, quando in ipsis corrigendis seueritate debita utuntur.
units.tr: Paul then concludes this passage with a serious yet fatherly warning, saying: "What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?" The rod signifies authority, with which God has armed the ministers of the Church, for the rebuking of sins and for maintaining discipline among the people. This is ascribed to Christ in the Psalms, where he is said to send forth from Zion the rod of his power, by which he gathers and defends his own people, but crushes the rebellious and stubborn goats as with an iron sceptre. He sent it forth from Zion when he commanded his apostles, armed with the power of his Word and Spirit, to go out into the world and preach the Gospel everywhere among the nations. And how great the power of this rod was, the world, overthrown within a few years, attests; and above all those dreadful examples, by which Peter punished the lie of Ananias and Sapphira, and Paul the audacity of the magician Elymas. Paul claims this rod for himself also in the present case against those who slandered his letters as weighty but his presence as weak. The fathers imitate this when, seeing a son has become more stubborn, they at last speak in words like these: "Come, does the company of scoundrels and worthless companions delight you? Do you prefer their habits and deceitful promises to my admonitions? Do you think I am not the one who ought to correct you, or the one whom you are bound to obey? But I will make you understand soon what I can do, and I will not lack a reason by which to curb your wantonness. So see for yourself what you are doing, or what you want me to do. For if you obey me, you will find me the gentlest of fathers; but if not, I will use my right over you, so that you may feel that I have strength by which to punish you. Choose for yourself which you wish, and consider whether you would rather have a father who is kind and indulgent, or one who is harsh and severe. And so on." An offer of this kind contains a choice joined with sharpness, and it penetrates more forcefully the minds of the more spirited than if the father were at once to bring out rods or staves. Paul also says something of this sort in the present case: "I am your teacher and father. The Lord has therefore armed me with spiritual weapons, and I lack neither a rod nor a staff by which to bring the wanton back into order. And this is what you deserve, who, as if your affairs were in the best condition, have become puffed up and scorn my faithful admonitions; indeed, you abuse my gentleness to despise the purer teaching. But come, since I seem so weak and nothing to you, tell me what sort of man you want me to be. Shall I take up the rods and show that I am armed with the power of the Spirit, or shall I use my accustomed love and gentleness toward you?" Yet these things should not be understood as if the use of the rod and a stricter correction or discipline were foreign to love (for in these chiefly the signs of fatherly affection shine forth, and that saying of Solomon is well known: "He who spares the rod hates his son"). Rather, he tempers his speech according to the disposition of children, who think that fathers have forgotten their gentleness or affection when they use due severity in correcting them.

units.la: Admonet autem suo exemplo Paulus omnes ecclesiarum ministros, quo animo erga eos affecti esse debeant, qui ipsorum curæ crediti sunt. Patres se esse meminerint, & ideo patres bonos & cordatos imitentur. Sunt hi liberorum suorum amantissimi, & proinde amore atque benevolentia eos in officio continere satagunt. At si se nihil proficere, & illos lenitate ista petulanter abuti uideant, tunc seuerius cum illis agere incipiunt. Isto ordine procedant ecclesiarum pastores, & ante omnia hoc agant, ut populus se amari & omnia publicæ omnium salutis causa fieri intelligant. Si qui uero proteruiores disciplinam omnem abolere, pro sua libidine omnia instituere, & scandala publica præbere incipiunt, tum sua aduersus tales authoritate seriò utantur, & Christi in ipsis loquentis experimenta publicè præbeant.
