Hoc olim prophetas fecisse constat, qui modò plus quàm paterna indulgentia populi interitum cum lachrymis prosequuntur, modò in contumaces & pœnitere nescios minis grauissimis fulminant. Obseruauit idem Christus quoque, & quod in præsenti Paulus facit, hoc omnes alios Apostolos fecisse constat. Simul autem hic obseruabis, penes ecclesiam esse, qualis sit minister, lenis nimirum aut asper, facilis aut difficilis: eò quod hunc conciones pro illorum moribus instituere conuenit. Hodie multis nimium & durius æquo videtur, quicquid aduersus uitia & superstitiones dicitur, cùm uix virga aut pedum illis coercendis sufficiant, qui indomita ferocia disciplinam omnem turbant, & legum omnium vincula abrumpunt. Quoad uero Pauli institutum, hac clausula sibi ad secundam epistolæ partem transitum sternit, qua scelera quædam graviora accusat, & collapsam inter illos ecclesiæ disciplinam restituit. Nos in iis, quæ lucusq; dicta sunt, Dei bonitatem agnoscamus, qui ut nos per Filium suum redemit, ita doctrinam salutis facilem & perspicuam esse voluit. Hanc ergo audiamus animis ad veram pietatem compositis, ut Christum constanti fide amplexi, & ex Verbi eius semin[?] Spiritus virtute renati in illo viuamus, atque olim cum eodem regni cœlestis hæreditatem asse-quamur: cui unà cum Patre & Spiritu sancto debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Paul, by his own example, also teaches all ministers of the churches what spirit they ought to have toward those entrusted to their care. They should remember that they are fathers, and so imitate good and wise fathers. Such fathers love their children most tenderly, and therefore they take pains to keep them in duty by affection and goodwill. But if they see that their gentleness achieves nothing and that the children abuse it wantonly, then they begin to deal with them more severely. The ministers of the churches should proceed in this order, and above all they should see to it that the people understand that they are loved and that everything is done for the public welfare of all. If some who are more headstrong begin to abolish all discipline, to order everything according to their own lust, and to give public offence, then the ministers should use their authority seriously against such people, and openly display the power of Christ speaking through them. We know that the prophets did this of old: at one time they lamented the people's ruin with tears, beyond what a father's indulgence would show, and at another they thundered the gravest threats against the stubborn and those who did not know how to repent. Christ himself observed the same method, and it is clear that all the other apostles did what Paul does here. At the same time you will notice that it lies with the church to judge what sort of minister he is, whether mild or harsh, easy or difficult, since sermons ought to be shaped to the morals of the hearers. Today many think whatever is said against vices and superstitions to be too much and harsher than is fair, although the rod and the whip are scarcely enough to restrain those who, in untamed wildness, disturb all discipline and break the bonds of every law. As for Paul's purpose, this closing sentence paves the way for the second part of the epistle, in which he accuses certain more serious crimes and restores the church discipline that had collapsed among them. Let us, in what has been said so far, acknowledge the goodness of God, who, as he redeemed us through his Son, so also willed the doctrine of salvation to be easy and clear. Let us therefore hear it with minds composed to true godliness, so that, having embraced Christ with constant faith, and having been reborn by the power of the Spirit from his Word's seed, we may live in him and at length with him obtain the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom: to whom, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT V. HOMILIA XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. SERMON XXIII.

units.la: Omnino auditur esse inter vos scortatio, & eiusmodi scortatio, quæ ne inter gentes quidem nominatur: adeo vt quis vxorem patris habeat. Et vos inflati estis, & non potius luxistis, vt tolleretur è medio vestri, qui facinus hoc patrauit.
units.tr: It is reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not even named among the Gentiles: namely, that a man has his father's wife. And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that he who has done this deed might be taken away from among you.

units.la: EXPOSITA est hucusq; prima huius epistolæ pars, qua factiones & sectas, quæ in Corinthiorum ecclesia exortæ fuerant, Paulus multis & graviter reprehendit, vtq; fidei vnitatem sanctè colant, omnes hortatur. Erat autem sectarum causa præcipua, ambitio, qua & doctores, qui post Pauli discessum in illa ecclesia irrepserant, & plerique ex auditoribus laborabant. Vt enim illi auram popularem venabantur, ita hi suam ecclesiam omnibus aliis præstare putabant, imò propter suos illos doctores in partes distrahebantur. Ostendit ergo Paulus, neq; hos neq; illos habere quo glorientur, & se supra alios efferant. Argumenta, quibus aduersus illos vsus est, præcipua fuerunt, quod nihil habeant, quod non ex Dei liberalitate gratuita acceperint: item quod regnum Dei non in magnifico verborum apparatu, aut vllis rebus externis consistat, sed in virtute & efficacia spiritus, qui homines totos Deo vendicet per obedientiam fidei. At quia admodum difficile est superbiæ cristas deprimere, difficillimū verò eos, qui spiritualibus donis superbiunt, eò adducere, vt sub Dei manu humilientur, & suam inopiam siue infirmitatem agnoscant, transit modò ad alteram huius epistolæ partem Apostolus, & scelera quædam haud vul-garia arguit, quibus Corinthiorum ecclesia infamis erat, vt saltem his agnitis erubescant, & excusso inani confidentiæ spiritu humilientur, deq; illis emendandis serio cogitent, neq; posthac simplicem & syncerum Euangelij doctrinam fastidiant, quæ sola tantis malis remedium afferre potest. Suo autem exemplo omnes ecclesiarum pastores admonet, qua ratione & quo ordine aduersus eos procedere debeant, quos suijpsius fiducia decipit, vt minus proficiant in regno Dei: vt nimirum absq; omni personarum respectu illorum scelera arguant, & vel inuitos cogat Legis speculum inspicere, vt suum deformitatem intueantur. Nec enim alia efficacior ratio est, qua aut nos aut alios intra Christianæ modestiæ limites contineamus, aut etiam retrahamus eos qui iam illos transgressi sunt, quàm si diligenter consideremus, quàm procul absumus à perfectione illa, quæ Christianos homines decet, & quàm multa quamq; atrocia sint, quæ contra Christianæ fidei & professionis leges designamus. Quia verò de his pauci sua sponte cogitant, patientius ferri debent, qui nos admonendo liberius erga nos officio funguntur.
units.tr: So far the first part of this epistle has been explained, in which Paul rebukes at length and with severity the factions and sects that had arisen in the church of the Corinthians, and urges them all to keep the unity of faith holy. The chief cause of the sects was ambition, which afflicted both the teachers who had crept into that church after Paul's departure and most of the hearers. For just as those teachers hunted after popular applause, so their followers thought their own church far superior to all others, and they were divided into parties on account of those particular teachers. Paul therefore shows that neither these nor those have anything to boast of or to lift themselves above others. The arguments he used against them were chiefly these: that they have nothing that they have not received from God's free generosity; and that the kingdom of God does not consist in a splendid display of words or in any external things, but in the power and efficacy of the Spirit, which claims whole persons for God through the obedience of faith. But because it is very difficult to cut down the crests of pride, and even more difficult to bring those who are puffed up by spiritual gifts to be humbled under God's hand and to acknowledge their poverty or weakness, the Apostle now passes to the second part of this epistle and rebukes certain not inconsiderable crimes for which the church of the Corinthians was notorious. His aim is that, at least once these are acknowledged, they may blush, and, having shaken off the empty spirit of confidence, may be humbled, and think seriously about amending these faults; and that they may not henceforth despise the simple and sincere doctrine of the Gospel, which alone can bring a remedy for such great evils. By his own example, he also instructs all the ministers of the churches as to the manner and order in which they ought to proceed against those whom their own self-confidence deceives, so that they make less progress in the kingdom of God: namely, that without any regard for persons they should rebuke their sins, and force even the unwilling to look into the mirror of the Law, so that they may see their own deformity. For there is no more effective way either to keep ourselves or others within the limits of Christian modesty, or to call back those who have already overstepped them, than to consider carefully how far we are from that perfection which befits Christian people, and how many and how atrocious are the things we commit against the laws of the Christian faith and profession. But since few think about these things of their own accord, those who, by admonishing us, perform the duty of speaking more frankly to us ought to be borne with more patiently.

units.la: Orditur autem tractationem istam ab homine incesto, quem non sine publica totius ecclesiæ in-samia nimis diu tolerauerant. Et quia scelus hoc grauissimum, imò prorsus intolerabile erat, non ea, qua prius vsus fuit, lenitate rem agit, sed virgæ illius & spiritus apostolici experimentum præbere incipit, de quo sub finem proximi Cap.dixerat. Habent ergo singula verba Emphasim, & suis quasi gradibus insurgit oratio. Omnino auditur esse inter vos scortatio. Non inquit, scortationi inter vos locus est: aut, Ego vos scortationi & libidinibus vagis siue illicitis indulgere audio. Sed omnino auditur, ait: vt offendat nemini iam dubium esse quod dicitur, & sceleris huius fama iam ad exteros quoque esse diuulgatam. At hoc dicendo, ipsorum socordiam arguit, qui non obseruent id, quod in omnium ore erat. Quid verò illud est? Scortationem dicit, à qua homines Christianos alienissimos esse debere, in sequenti Capite docebit: sed hic amplificationis ergò addit: Et eiusmodi quidem scortatio, quæ ne inter gentes quidem nominatur. Quasi diceret: Christus eos, qui ipsi no-mine dederunt, è mundo hoc selectos esse vult, & hoc imprimis exigit, ne vt gentes prophanæ impura carnis studia sequatur, sed seipsos Deo sistant hostiam viuentē & sanctam: quàm ergo immane & nulla venia dignum flagitium est, inter vos ea designari, ad quorum mentionem ij quoq; exhorrescunt, qui adhuc Christum ignorant, & ab ecclesia eius alieni sunt? Et ne diutius suspensos habeat auditores, scelus mox definit: Adeò vt quis vxorem patris habeat. Id qua ratione factum fuerit, an scilicet patre adhuc superstite[?] illa abusus sit, aut illo defuncto eam concubinæ vel vxoris loco habuerit, non exprimitur, neq; id scire multum refert. Nam quicquid huius fuerit, scortatio fuit cum incestu coniuncta, neque vllo coniugij prætextu defendi sine excusari potuit. Quia enim coniugium legitima est viri & mulieris coniunctio, nihil quàm scortatio erit inter eos, qui contra leges miscentur. Et poterat Paulus nouercam nominare, sed periphrasi vti & patris vxorem dicere maluit, vt sceleris atrocitatem magis exprimeret.
units.tr: The Apostle begins this discussion with a man guilty of incest, whom they had tolerated for far too long, not without public disgrace to the whole church. And because this crime was most grave, indeed utterly intolerable, he does not deal with it in the gentle manner he had used before, but begins to put to the test the rod and the apostolic spirit, of which he had spoken near the end of the previous chapter. Each word therefore carries emphasis, and the discourse rises by its own steps. "It is reported that there is fornication among you." He does not say, "There is room for fornication among you," or, "I hear that you indulge in fornication and wandering or unlawful lusts." Rather he says, "It is reported," so that no one may doubt what is being said, and so that the fame of this crime has already spread even to outsiders. But in saying this, he rebukes their carelessness, since they did not notice what was on everyone's lips. What then is this? He calls it fornication, from which Christian people ought to be utterly far removed, as he will teach in the following chapter. Here, however, for the sake of emphasis, he adds: "and such fornication as is not even named among the Gentiles." As if he were saying: Christ wants those who have been named by his name to be chosen out of this world, and above all requires that they not follow the impure desires of the flesh like profane Gentiles, but present themselves to God as a living and holy sacrifice. How monstrous, then, and unworthy of any pardon is the disgrace, if among you there is a thing so described that even those who are still ignorant of Christ and are strangers to his church shudder at its mention? And so that he may not keep his hearers in suspense any longer, he immediately names the crime: "namely, that a man has his father's wife." By what means this happened, whether he abused her while his father was still alive, or after his death took her as a concubine or wife, is not stated, nor does it matter much to know. For whatever the case, it was fornication joined with incest, and it could not be defended or excused by any pretext of marriage. For since marriage is the lawful union of a man and a woman, those who mix against the laws will be nothing but fornicators. Paul could have called her a stepmother, but he preferred to use a circumlocution and say "his father's wife," so as to express more clearly the atrocity of the crime.

units.la: Non temere autem abisto flagitio orditur Apostolus, & illud τὰ[?] grauibus verbis exaggerat. Etsi enim, vt modò diximus, omnis scortatio homini Christiano indigna sit, ea tamen belluina libido est, quæ quem natura nobis inseuit pudorem abstergit, & simul ordinem abolet, quo inter se discernuntur, qui aliquo consanguinitatis gradu coniuncti sunt. Etenim parentibus reuerentiam summam deberi lex naturæ docet, & eadem inter fratres & sorores amorem quidem maximum seruari vult, sed talem qui cum honestate & mutui honoris cura coniunctus sit. Quo fit, vt quæ con-sanguineis infertur ignominia, eam ad nos redundare putemus, & ideo ordinariam vindictam in asserenda cognatorum fama leges ciuiles permittunt. At quis inter omnes illos reuerentiæ aut syncerę dilectionis locus erit reliquus, si cæca libidine inter sese misceantur, & quà ab alteris propulsare debebant contumeliam ipsi illis inferant? Simul ergo œconomiæ ratio omnis turbabitur, & ex tota hominum vita ordo tolletur, quo solo omnia seruantur. Nam vt iurisconsulti loquuntur, vbi non sunt iustæ nuptiæ, ibi non est matrimonium, ibi spurij, ibi nulla hæreditas, nullæ dotes. Quid ergo præter confusionem reliquum est? De his omnibus Deus in Lege nos admonitos voluit, cùm diceret: Nemo ad quascunque reliquias carnis suæ accedat, ad retegendum verenda. Reliquiæ enim carnis dicuntur relatione ad vnitatem, quæ inter cognatos & consanguineos est, eò quòd ex eadem massa omnes illi oriundi, & quasi vna eademq; caro sunt. Et eodem loco: Verenda vxoris patris tui ne retegas, nuditas enim patris tui est. Ita nimirum innuens inchestum hunc in patris contumeliam redundare, & proinde naturæ legibus contrarium esse. Alibi vero pœnam talibus constituens, sic ait: Qui dormierit cum vxore patris sui, & verenda patris sui retexerit, morte muletetur vterque, sanguis eorum sit super eos. Quod autem in Lege Deus decreuit, iam ante apud gentes non omnino barbaras receptum fuit: nimirum quòd per naturæ legem admonerentur ab eiusmodi congressibus abstinendum esse. Et constat Deum omnibus seculis horrendas pœnas de inchestis hominibus sumpsisse, si quando in illis puniendis remissiores fuerunt, ad quos ea cura pertinebat. Ruben enim primogenituræ dignitate spoliatum fuisse, & paternæ maledictionis partem in posteris quoq; hæsisse constat, quòd is patris Iacobi thorum polluisset. In Persarum historia, apud quos illicitæ nuptiæ in frequentiori vsu fuerunt, plura etiam exempla iudiciorum Dei extant. Cambyses Cyri illius Magni filius, cùm sororem in vxorem duxisset, non vulgarem vitæ exitum habuit. Nam equum ascensuro ex vagina gladius decidit & femur eius perfodit, ex quo vulnere post paucos dies est mortuus. Artaxerxes autem Mnemon, qui fratris Cyri concubinam Aspasiam ad se recepit, & eandem postea Dario filio tradidit, eundem non multò post vitæ suæ insidiatorem habuit, & domum suam parricidijs nefandis turbari sensit, & in eius filio Ocho, qui duobus fratribus occisis ad regnum peruenerat, Cyri posteritas omnis extincta est. Simile quid Seleuco Syriæ gi accidit. Is enim Antiocho filio ex insano Stratonices nouercæ amore decumbenti illam in vxorem dedit: mox autem inchestas nuptias consiliorum infelicitas secuta est, vt Monarchiæ spe illestus Ptolemæo Cerauno bellum moueret, in quo ipse cæsus vitam cum regno amisit, in quo posteri quoq; per varios casus iactati, & tandem cū regno excidsi sunt. Extant huius generis exempla in Romana historia, C. Caligulæ nimirū, Neronis, Bassiani Caracallæ, qui omnes libidinis suæ horrendas pœnas dederunt. Et vt ad sacram historiam redeamus, cùm Deus inchestas nuptias per Mosem seueris legibus prohibuisset, hanc conclusionem subiecit: In his omnibus ne polluamini, nam in hisce omnibus gentes polluuntur, quas ego eiecio ante vos: & hinc cõtaminata est terra, & ego visitaui iniquitatem eius super eam, & terra ipsa euomuit habitatores suos & rursus: Omnes istas abominationes fecerunt homines terræ illius, qui fuerunt ante vos, vt polluta sit terra. An ergo terra vos non euomet, si polluueritis eam, sicut euomuit gentem, quæ fuit ante vos? Nam quisquis fecerit aliquid ex cunctis istis abominationibus, excindentur animæ, quæ sic faciunt, è medio populi sui. Neque minas istas inanes fuisse infelix Absolonis exitus probat, ut infinita alia exempla transeamus. Apud Amos certè Deus inter grauissima flagitia, propter quæ Israëlis regnum excindere statuerit, hoc quoq; numeratur, quòd pater & filius ad eandem puellam ingressi sint, & sanctum suum nomen prophanarint. Ergo ad Dei contumeliam facit, si qui huius populus dicuntur, eiusmodi flagitia de signent. Ex eo enim impij & prophani homines occasionem arripiunt, quā verum Dei cultum cum tota fidei & æternæ salutis doctrina scurriliter proscindant. Et hæc quidem prolixius tractamus, non solum ut videamus non temere Paulum Corinthios tam grauiter corripere, qui cùm ista non possent ignorare, in tanto tamē flagitio puniendo tam ignaui & socordes fuerunt: verumetiam ut in horum consideratione diligentius versentur, qui nouissimis hisce temporibus rempub. administrant, ne sua indulgentia libidines vagas plus satis iam grassantes magis proueharent.
units.tr: The Apostle does not begin this disgraceful matter lightly, and he magnifies it with weighty words. For although, as we have just said, all fornication is unworthy of a Christian, this is a bestial lust, which wipes away the shame that nature has implanted in us, and at the same time destroys the order by which those are distinguished who are joined by some degree of kinship. For the law of nature teaches that the greatest reverence is owed to parents, and the same law wants the greatest love to be preserved between brothers and sisters, but a love joined with honour and a care for mutual respect. Hence it is that we think the disgrace inflicted on our relatives reflects on us too, and for this reason civil laws permit the ordinary vengeance in defence of the reputation of kinsfolk. But what place of reverence or sincere affection will remain among all these, if they mix with one another in blind lust, and themselves inflict upon one another the insult which they ought to have repelled from each other? Thus all the order of the household will be thrown into confusion, and the order by which all things in human life are preserved will be removed. For, as the jurists say, where there are no lawful marriages, there is no matrimony; there are illegitimate children, no inheritance, no dowries. What then remains but confusion? God wanted us to be admonished about all these things in the Law when he said: "No one shall approach any of the remnants of his flesh, to uncover nakedness." For they are called "remnants of the flesh" in relation to the unity that exists among kinsmen and blood relations, because all of them have sprung from the same mass and are, as it were, one and the same flesh. And in the same place: "You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's wife, for it is the nakedness of your father." Thus clearly he signifies that such incest reflects on the father's dishonour and is therefore contrary to the laws of nature. Elsewhere, establishing a penalty for such acts, he says: "If a man lies with his father's wife and uncovers his father's nakedness, both of them shall be put to death; their blood shall be upon them." What God decreed in the Law had already been received earlier among the nations that were not wholly barbarous, namely that by the law of nature they were warned to abstain from such unions. And it is established that God has in every age taken dreadful punishment from incestuous men, whenever those charged with punishing them have been too lenient. It is recorded that Reuben was deprived of the dignity of the firstborn, and that a part of his father's curse clung to his descendants too, because he had defiled his father Jacob's bed. In the history of the Persians, among whom unlawful marriages were in fairly frequent practice, there are also many examples of God's judgments. Cambyses, son of the great Cyrus, when he had taken his sister as his wife, did not have an ordinary end to his life. For when he was about to mount a horse, a sword fell from its sheath and pierced his thigh, and from this wound he died a few days later. Artaxerxes Mnemon, who took his brother Cyrus's concubine Aspasia to himself and afterwards handed her over to his son Darius, soon had the same man as a plotter against his life, and felt his house thrown into turmoil by unspeakable parricides; and in his son Ochus, who came to the kingdom after two brothers had been killed, the whole posterity of Cyrus was extinguished. Something similar happened to Seleucus, king of Syria. For when his son Antiochus was lying sick from a mad love for his stepmother Stratonice, he gave her to him in marriage; but soon the unhappy outcome of these incestuous nuptials followed, for Antiochus, seduced by the hope of the monarchy, made war on Ptolemy Ceraunus, in which war he himself was slain and lost his life along with his kingdom, and his descendants too, tossed about through various misfortunes, were at last driven out together with the kingdom. Examples of this kind exist in Roman history: those of Gaius Caligula, of Nero, and of Bassianus Caracalla, who all paid dreadful penalties for their lust. And to return to sacred history: when God, through Moses, had forbidden incestuous marriages with severe laws, he added this conclusion: "Do not defile yourselves in any of these things, for by all these things the nations are defiled, whom I am driving out before you; and the land has been defiled, and I have visited its iniquity upon it, and the land itself has vomited out its inhabitants." And again: "All these abominations were committed by the men of that land who were before you, so that the land has been defiled. Will not the land vomit you out also, if you defile it, just as it vomited out the nation that was before you? For whoever commits any of these abominations, those souls shall be cut off from the midst of their people." Nor was this threat empty, as the unhappy end of Absalom proves, to pass over countless other examples. Certainly in Amos, among the most grievous crimes for which God had determined to destroy the kingdom of Israel, this too is counted: that father and son went in to the same girl and profaned his holy name. Therefore it is an insult to God when those who are called his people display such crimes. For from this, impious and profane men seize the occasion to mock scurrilously the true worship of God together with the whole doctrine of faith and eternal salvation. And we treat these matters at greater length not only so that we may see that Paul did not rebuke the Corinthians so severely without reason, since they could not have been ignorant of these things and yet were so lazy and careless in punishing so great a crime, but also so that those who now administer the commonwealth in these latest times may consider these matters more carefully, lest by their indulgence they advance wandering lusts that are already spreading far too widely.

units.la: Nam ut huic exemplo adhuc insistamus, apparet in eo, quò usq; tandem scortandi licentia pro grediatur. Hanc apud Corinthios maximam fuisse, sub initium huius epistolæ diximus. Ita verò eadem viribus auêta fuit, ut ne per Euangelij quidem prædicationem coerceri aut euelli potuerit: neq; dubium est, huius fructum fuisse incestum hunc, quem in præsenti Paulus corripit. Recte ergo Deus in Lege sua statuit olim, ne sit scortū in Israel, & morte multanda esse censuit, quæ in domo patris sui libidini indulsisset, & ad virum legitimum non attulisset incorruptum virginitatis suæ florem. Nouit enim qui ipsissima est sapientia, licentiam illam turpissimæ confusionis causam esse, & vbi ea regnat, ibi honestatem publicam, imò ne iustitiam quidem consistere posse: quæ duo si è medio tollantur, simul omnia sustuleris, quæ ad seruandam humani generis societatem faciunt. Est hoc videre in omnium gentium historijs, quæ multis exemplis docent, vagas libidines fere semper grauissimorum motuum & mutationū periculosissimarum in repub. causam fuisse. At regnat illa, quàm primùm scortandi licentia permittitur. Nam absterso pudore omni, tandem & virginum & matronarum pudicitiam tentare incipiunt, qui scortationi assueuerunt. Quæ causa est, ut illis quoq; intolerabiles fiat, qui ipsis diu patrocinati sunt. Quod propter eos admonemus, qui hodie inter homines Christianos scortationem concedi debere contendunt, ne qui ad incestus & his grauiora flagitia delabātur. Quibus nos illud Pauli obijcere poteramus, Non sunt facienda mala, ut veniant bona: quando fieri non potest, ut ex radice mala atq; vitiosa aliquis fructus bonus enascatur. Et quotidianis exemplis docemur, homines indulgētia quotidie deteriores fieri, & ad grauiora flagitia viam sterni, si quæ leuiora sunt impune abeant. Est enim insatiabilis hominū cupiditas, eoq; magis accenditur, quò liberius illi indulgetur. Experti sunt hoc non sine publica ecclesiæ suæ infamia Corinthij, & hodie idem experiuntur multi, qui scortationem inter eos, qui nullis coniugij legibus astringuntur, peccatum esse negant. Huic enim licentiæ debemus, quòd leuiculū multis videtur virgini vitium offerre, ut qui inter hanc & scortum publicum nullum discrimen faciant. At neq; hic istorū libido subsistit, sed mox adulteriis quoq; habenas laxant, ut thoros alienos polluere talibus lusus iocusq; videatur. Inde verò ad incestus proximus gradus est, à quibus etiam minus abhorrent, qui priora illa cum risu prosequi iam pridem assueuerunt. Et utinam non multa hodie eius, quod dicimus, exempla passim extarent inter eos, qui Euangelio & ecclesiæ reformatione gloriantur, cùm interim disciplinam omnem reiiciant, quæ Christianos homines coerceri oportebat. Principijs ergo obstandum est, si in peius prolabi nolumus: neque audiendi sunt impuri illi ganeones, qui interrogare non verentur: Annon satius fuit cum scorto rem habere, quàm virginem ingenuam consluprare, thoro alieno insidiari, incestum committere, vel etiam Sodomiæ aut pecuniæ libidinis scelere pollui? Quis enim in repub. eum ferat, qui furandi licentiam lege sanciri velit, ne qui ad cædes & latrocinia usque progrediantur? Scimus equidem vitia alia alijs atrociora esse, sed cùm suum populum ab omni scelere purum esse velit Deus, nequaquam in nostra potestate est, ea impunita dimittere, quæ ille disertis verbis prohibuit. Et quid enim in eiusmodi casu fieri debeat, exemplo suo olim nos docuit. Cùm enim Lothus Sodomæis, qui angelis hospitibus vim nefariam inferre conabantur, filias suas offerret, ut in illis libidinis æstum restinguerent, id nequaquam fieri passus est, impuros autem illos sulphure & flammis cœlitus demissis puniuit. Et qui in Lege dixit, Ne sit scortum in Israel: idem quid de adulteriis, de incestis, de masculæ Veneris sectatoribus statui debeat, non obscurè mandauit.
units.tr: Let us stay with this example for a moment and see how far the licence of fornication will go. We said at the beginning of this letter that it was very widespread among the Corinthians. It had grown so strong that it could not be restrained or uprooted even by the preaching of the Gospel, and there is no doubt that this incest, which Paul rebukes here, was one of its fruits. God therefore rightly decreed in his Law long ago that there should be no whore in Israel, and judged that a woman who had given way to lust in her father's house, and had not brought to her lawful husband the unspoiled flower of her virginity, should be put to death. For he who is wisdom itself knows that such licence is the cause of the most shameful confusion, and that where it reigns, public decency cannot survive, nor even justice. If these two are removed, you take away everything that serves to preserve human society. This can be seen in the histories of all nations, which teach by many examples that unrestrained lust has almost always been the cause of the gravest disturbances and most dangerous upheavals in a commonwealth. Lust reigns as soon as the licence to fornicate is granted. For once shame has been wiped away entirely, those who have grown used to fornication begin at last to attack the chastity of virgins and matrons. For this reason it becomes intolerable even to those who have long defended it. We warn of this on account of those who today, among Christian men, insist that fornication ought to be allowed, lest they fall into incest and crimes worse than that. Against them we could set Paul's words: evil things are not to be done that good may come (Rom. 3.). For good fruit cannot grow from a bad and corrupt root. Daily experience also teaches us that men become worse every day through indulgence, and that a path is paved to graver crimes when lesser ones go unpunished. The desire of men is insatiable, and it is kindled all the more the more freely it is indulged. The Corinthians learned this, not without public disgrace to their church, and many today learn it too, those who deny that fornication between people who are bound by no marriage laws is a sin. Indeed, it is this licence that makes it seem to many a trifling fault to offer a virgin to a man, as if there were no difference between her and a public whore. Nor does their lust stop there. Soon they loosen the reins on adultery as well, so that defiling another man's bed seems to them merely a game and a joke. From adultery the next step is incest, and those who have long been accustomed to treat the former with laughter shrink little from the latter. Would that there were not many examples of what we are saying to be found everywhere today among those who boast of the Gospel and the reformation of the Church, while they reject all the discipline by which Christian men ought to be restrained. We must therefore resist at the beginning if we do not want to slide into worse things. Nor should we listen to those impure debauchees who do not hesitate to ask: Was it not better to have dealings with a whore than to ruin a free-born virgin, to lay snares for another man's bed, to commit incest, or even to be defiled by the crime of sodomy or the lust for money? For who in a commonwealth would tolerate a man who wanted the licence to steal to be sanctioned by law, lest people go on to murder and robbery? We know indeed that some vices are more atrocious than others, but since God wishes his people to be free from every crime, it is by no means in our power to let go unpunished what he has forbidden in plain words. And what ought to be done in such a case he long ago taught us by his own example. When Lot offered his daughters to the men of Sodom, who tried to do violence to the angels who were his guests, in order to quench the heat of their lust, God did not allow this at all, but punished those impure men with brimstone and fire sent from heaven. And he who said in the Law, There shall be no whore in Israel, did not obscurely command what should be decided about adulteries, incests, and the pursuers of male love.

units.la: Cæterum omissis impuris illis ad Paulum redeamus, in quo obseruatu dignissimum est, quòd propter vnius hominis scelus totam Corinthiorum ecclesiam, & imprimis huius præfectos & doctores, tam grauiter accusat. Poterat sanè nonnullis iniquus videri, sed ita illi merebantur, quòd in dulgentiores fuissent haC[?]tenus erga eum, quem punire poterant, & cuius libidinem coercere iam prius debuissent. Hæc enim causa est, vt vnius culpa interdum in totum populum redundet: & si consensus simplex alieni sceleris reos facit, nulla venia digni sunt, si in illo puniendo remissiores sint, quibus ea cura diuinitus commissa est, vt peccandi licentiam seueriori disciplina coerceant. Ideo quoties in Lege de puniendis hominibus sceleratis agitur, fere hæc clausula adijci solet: Tolles malum ex Israel, vel è medio tui. Quasi diceret: Ita cauebis, ne paucorum culpa toti Israeli imputetur, & totum populum ab ira Dei atq; imminenti exitio liberabis. Quod vt diligenter obseruare debet qui magistratum gerunt, ita doctorum est tales vehementer vrgere, vt officium faciant, imò acerbius quoq; reprehendi & corripi debent, si admonitionibus & hortationibus pijs non obtemperent. Fecerunt hoc olim prophetæ, vt eorum sermones re[?]stantur, & idem procul dubio Apostoli fecissent, si suo tempore principes fuissent Christiani. Qua tamen vehementia ijdem illi vsi sint erga Seniores ecclesiæ, penes quos erat disciplinæ publicæ cura, vnus hic locus abunde docet. Neq; timendum est mi-nistris Verbi, ne hic facile modum excedant hodie, quando apud omnis loci & ordinis homines pec-candi licentia regnat: neq; nimia esse potest aliqua seueritas, quæ in illis corripiendis adhibetur, qui sua indulgentia ecclesiam atq; religionem omnem impiorum ludibrijs exponunt.
units.tr: But, leaving aside those impure men, let us return to Paul. What is most worthy of observation in him is that, because of the crime of one man, he accuses the whole Corinthian church so severely, and above all its leaders and teachers. Some may have thought this unjust, but the Corinthians deserved it, since until now they had been too lenient toward the man whom they could have punished, and whose lust they ought to have restrained long before. This is the reason why the guilt of one person sometimes spreads to the whole people. If simple consent makes people guilty of another's wickedness, those to whom this care has been divinely entrusted, namely to restrain the licence to sin by stricter discipline, deserve no pardon if they are too slack in punishing it. So whenever the Law speaks of punishing wicked men, this clause is usually added: You shall take away the evil from Israel, or from the midst of you. As if it said: In this way you will take care that the fault of a few is not imputed to all Israel, and you will free the whole people from the wrath of God and impending destruction. Magistrates ought to observe this carefully, and teachers ought to press such men vigorously so that they perform their duty. Indeed, they deserve to be rebuked and reproved even more sharply if they do not obey pious admonitions and exhortations. The prophets did this in the past, so that their words might be resisted, and without doubt the Apostles would have done the same, had they been Christian rulers in their time. How vehemently they dealt with the elders of the church, to whom the care of public discipline belonged, this one passage teaches abundantly. Nor should ministers of the Word fear that they will easily exceed the proper measure today, when the licence to sin reigns among men of every place and rank. Nor can any severity be excessive that is applied in rebuking those who, by their indulgence, expose the Church and all religion to the mockery of the impious.

units.la: Et hæc causa est, quòd Apostolus in præsenti sermonem ad totam Corinthiorum ecclesiam dirigens vno reatu simul omnes inuoluit, eò quòd nemo repertus esset inter illos, qui tam immane scelus è medio tollere studeret. Accusat autem in illis non solum ignauiam, sed huic quoq; coniunctam confidentiam, qua excæcati morbum suum non agnoscebant. Et vos (inquit) inflati estis, & non potius luxistis, vt tolleretur è medio vestri, qui facinus hoc patrauit? Sensus est. Cum ista apud vos fiant, quæ ne nominari quidem oportebat, & iam in omnium ore sint, vos interim inflati estis, id est, inani exi-stimatione & vestræ dignitatis fiducia turgetis, imò quasi re bene gesta vobis ipsis placetis & alios omnes contemnitis. Atqui cum tantum dedecus vestræ ecclesiæ afferfum[?] fit, vos potius lugere & totis animis in hoc intentos esse coueniebat, vt qui publicæ infamiæ vobis author est è medio tolleretur, & ita huius infamiæ nota liberaremini. At quæ obsecro illa fiducia est, quæ vos tam elatos reddit? aut quid vobis reliquum est, quo iure aut merito glorieminì? Si enim tam eximij sunt docto-res illi vestri, quàm vos illos esse putatis, cur non hic zelum suum exerunt? cur in causa tam necessaria silent? cur non omnes sui ingenij & eloquentiæ vires intendunt, vt scandalum tam grave, tam sceleratum, tam immane è medio tollatur? Si deniq; tam bene apud vos constituta est ecclesia, vt sua alias eminere debeat, cur nemo inter vos est, qui illis cessantibus officium faciat? cur in tole-randa tanta ignominia omnes tam patientes estis, & non aliquo saltem indicio testamini vobis confusionem istam displicere? Jamne ergo vos miseros, & ijs multò inferiores esse sentitis, quos hucusque fastidiosè nimis contemp[?]tis? Lubet hic adscribere D. Augustini verba, qui quod Paulus de luctu scribit, sic interpretatur. Quare luctum potius præcipit, & non iram? Nisi quia si patitur vnum membrum, compatiuntur omnia membra: & non luctum, quia tollebatur, sed luctum (inquit) vt tolleretur, id est, vt lugentium dolor ad Deum ascenderet, & ipse tolleret hoc opus de medio eorum, sicut ipse sciret[?]: ne forte illi per inhumanam imperitiam exadicarent simul & triticum.
units.tr: This is why the Apostle, addressing his speech in this letter to the whole Corinthian church, involves them all together in one charge, because no one could be found among them who was eager to remove so monstrous a crime. He accuses them not only of negligence but also of the confidence joined to it, by which, blinded, they did not recognise their disease. And you (he says) are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, that he who has done this deed might be taken away from among you? The meaning is this: while such things are being done among you, things that ought not even to be named, and while they are already on everyone's lips, you are nonetheless puffed up. That is, you swell with empty opinion and with confidence in your own dignity, and even, as if you had done well, you please yourselves and despise all others. Yet, since so great a disgrace is brought upon your church, you ought rather to mourn and to be wholly intent on this, that the man who is the author of public infamy be removed, and so you be freed from the stain of this infamy. But what, I beg you, is that confidence which makes you so proud? Or what is left for you in which you may rightly or deservedly glory? For if those teachers of yours are as outstanding as you think them to be, why do they not show their zeal here? Why are they silent in a matter so necessary? Why do they not bend all the strength of their wit and eloquence to remove so grave, so wicked, so monstrous a scandal? Finally, if the church is so well ordered among you that it ought to stand out above the others, why is there no one among you who does the duty while they are idle? Why are you all so patient in tolerating such great shame, and do not at least show by some sign that this confusion displeases you? Do you now feel that you are wretched and far inferior to those whom until now you have despised with too much disdain? It pleases me to add here the words of Saint Augustine, who interprets what Paul writes about mourning in this way: Why does he prescribe mourning rather than anger? Surely because if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. And he says not mourning, so that it might be removed, but mourning so that it might be removed, that is, that the grief of those who mourn might rise to God, and that he himself might remove this evil from their midst, as he knew how, lest perhaps they, through inhuman inexperience, root up the wheat together with the tares.

units.la: At nos in Corinthiorum exemplo obseruare conuenit, quid ferè illis accidere soleat, qui confidentia ebrij se supra alios superbè extollunt. Nulli hominum seipsos minus norunt, quæ causa est vt inani perfuasione seipsos fallant, & in peius quotidie proficiant, dum se omni virtutis genere ornatissimos esse arbitrantur. Idem ergo talibus, quod scholasticis confidentioribus accidit. Vt enim hi dum supra coætaneos suos eminere volunt, & in classes altiores ascendunt, suam in his ignorantiam turpiter produnt, & ijs ludibrium fiunt, quos paulò ante præ se contempserunt: Ita isti securi-tate & confidentia sua dum supra omnes extollūntur, sibijpsis lapsus grauiores authores sunt, & pro laude, quam vænantur, extremā ignominiam referunt. Exemplum huius mali in Pharisæis, adeò in tota Iudæorum gente extat, qui cùm & generis & propriæ iustitiæ fiducia inflati gentes alias omnes improbè contemnerent, in eam calamitatem adducti sunt, vt mortalium omnium miserrimi contemptissimi q; habeantur. Quia enim superbis omnibus resistit Dominus, aduersus eos imprimis iustitiae suae rigore stringit, qui spiritualibus donis superbi, de ipsius gloria minus solliciti sunt. Fit ergo vt quasi sensu & ratione omni extincta in omne flagitium ruant, & ignominiam extremam sibi accersant, interim foli fere ignorent suum dedecus, quod omnium ore hinc inde vulgatur. Vtinam vero hodie etiam non idem experiremur. Vnde enim hanc morum licentiam enasci dicemus, quae apud eos regnat, qui puriorem Euangelij doctrinam profitentur? Ex eo nimirum, quod plerique iam sibi nihil amplius deesse, & externam Verbi Dei praedicationem atq; nominis Christiani professionem ad salutem sufficere putant. Hinc fit, quod ex ministris ecclesiarum multi principibus blandiuntur, quasi hi iam omni pietatis officio defuncti sint, si in suis terris Euangelio vtcunq; locum dent, & ijdem ista perfuasione confidentiores facti, iam sibi quidvis licere putant, & cum se Euangelicos esse profiteantur, simul tamen immodico fastu, libidine, intemperantia, tyrannide, exactionibus iniquis prophanos reges longè vincunt. In vulgus ergo manant exempla regentium, & ita apud omnes ordines effrenis licentia regnat, vt vix vlla videas Christianae pietatis vestigia. Passim enim occurrunt ebriosi, avari, impostores, scortatores, adulteri, vsurarij, raptores, sanguinarij Cares, sycophantae, & audiuntur passim nefaria eorum facinora, qui Euangelicae doctrinae fautores & patroni dici volunt. Exprobrant igitur haec nobis aduersarij, ex his calumniandi occasionem Pontificij amici arripiunt, vt veritatis doctrinam omnibus inuisam & suspectam reddant: propter ista ecclesias nostras damnant Anabaptistae, & ab illis secessionem faciunt: deniq; cum Euangelij vox per se laeta, iucunda & salutaris sit, nostrorum licentia fit, vt ad eius mentionem multi risum moveant, multi ringantur[?], & non pauci exhorrescant. At quotus quisq; est, quem ista moveant? qui de tam perniciosis scandalis e medio tollendis serio cogitet? aut qui propter haec imminentem nobis Dei iram & manifesta eius indicia obseruet? Quin potius plerique inflati sunt, & quasi nihil in ipsis sit reprehensione dignum in vtramq; aurem securi nimis dormiunt. Causa vero securitatis huius pestifera est, quod in otiosa Veritatis cognitione nobisipsis placemus, neq; cogitamus quae officia professione Christianam deceant. Eadem ergo correptio nobis seruit hodie, qua olim Corinthiorum suorum securam confidentiam Paulus accusauit.
units.tr: But in the example of the Corinthians we should observe what usually happens to those who, drunk with confidence, proudly raise themselves above others. No one knows himself less than such a man, and this is why he deceives himself with empty persuasion and makes worse progress every day, while he thinks himself adorned with every kind of virtue. The same thing therefore happens to such people as happens to over-confident schoolboys. When they want to stand out above their contemporaries and climb into higher classes, they disgracefully betray their ignorance and become a laughing-stock to those whom a little while before they had despised. So these men, while they exalt themselves above everyone in their security and confidence, become the authors of their own deeper falls, and instead of the praise they hunt for, they bring back the utmost shame. An example of this evil stands out across the whole Jewish nation in the Pharisees, who, puffed up with confidence in their birth and their own righteousness, shamefully despised all other nations, and were brought to such a calamity that they are now held the most wretched and most despised of all mortals. For the Lord resists all the proud, and he especially strikes with the rigour of his righteousness those who, proud of spiritual gifts, are less anxious about his glory. So it comes about that, with sense and reason as it were extinguished, they rush into every kind of shameful act and heap extreme disgrace upon themselves, while they alone almost fail to see their own dishonour, which is spread on everyone's lips on every side. Would that today we were not experiencing the same thing! For whence shall we say this licence of morals arises, which reigns among those who profess the purer doctrine of the Gospel? Undoubtedly from this, that many now think nothing more is lacking to them, and that the outward preaching of the Word of God and the profession of the Christian name is enough for salvation. Hence it happens that many ministers of the churches flatter princes, as if they had already discharged every duty of piety if they grant some place to the Gospel in their lands, and these same men, made more confident by this persuasion, now think they may do whatever they like; and while they profess themselves evangelical, at the same time by their immoderate pride, lust, intemperance, tyranny and unjust exactions they far outdo profane kings. The examples of rulers therefore seep down to the common people, and so such unbridled licence reigns among all ranks that you can scarcely see any traces of Christian piety. For everywhere drunkards, misers, cheats, whoremongers, adulterers, usurers, robbers, murderers, sycophants are met with, and everywhere are heard the wicked crimes of those who want to be called supporters and patrons of the evangelical doctrine. Our adversaries therefore throw these things in our faces, and the Papists, our friends, seize on them as an occasion for slander, so as to make the doctrine of truth hateful and suspect to all. Because of these things the Anabaptists condemn our churches and make a secession from them. Finally, although the voice of the Gospel is in itself joyful, pleasant and saving, through the licence of our people it comes about that at its mention many move to laughter, many sneer, and not a few shudder. But how few are there whom such things move? Who seriously thinks about removing such pernicious scandals from the midst? Or who on account of these things watches for the wrath of God hanging over us and its plain signs? Rather, many are puffed up, and as if there were nothing in themselves worthy of reproof, they sleep far too securely, deaf to every warning. The cause of this security, however, is deadly: we take pleasure in ourselves through idle knowledge of the Truth, and we do not consider what duties befit the Christian profession. Therefore the same rebuke serves us today by which Paul once accused the Corinthians of their careless confidence.

units.la: Quid ergo facere nos conuenit o fratres, vt huius culpae reatu liberemur? Corinthios ideo corripit Apostolus, quod non luxerint, vt e medio illorum tolleretur, qui facinus tam indignum patrauerat. Locutione vtitur ex Lege petita, qua mortis supplicium denotari notius est, quam vt demonstrari oporteat. Vide Leuit. 20. Deut. 13. 17. 19. 21. &c. Duo igitur fiant oportet. Primum luctus est, qui & publicè & priuatim suscipi debet propter publica scelera, quae cū aperto scandalo & alicuius exitio coniuncta sunt. Iubet hoc gloria Dei, cuius nos studiosissimos esse decet, & qua sceleribus eius prophanari iam ante demonstrauimus. Deinde exigit idem charitatis lex & quae inter Christianos homines est communio. Quia enim eiusdem corporis membra sumus, alij aliorum incommodis affici & condolere debet: & cum ex charitatis officio eos lugeamus, qui quoad corpus moriuntur, quanto magis eos nos deflere conuenit, qui immanibus flagitijs tam corporis quam animae exitium sibijpsis accersunt, & simul exemplo suo multis alijs incommodant? Viderunt hoc olim sanctissimi quiq;, quos acerbè admodum eos deplorauisse legimus, quos in exitium ruere videbant. Samuel certè propter Saulem maerore seipsum eò vsq; conficiebat, vt Deus illum reprehensione dignum iudicaret. Eiusdem interim quoq; Dauid iniuriarum omnium oblitus, lachrymis vberrimis prosecutus est, quod impios Dei hostes ex eo exultandi occasionem arripere videret. Et Absolonem filium idem hoc potissimum nomine luxit, quod eum in peccatis suis mortuum esse metueret. Laudem quoq; merentur discipuli, quod totis animis contristati sint, cum in suo grege eum esse audirent, qui Christum erat proditurus. Et constat hunc morem in veteri ecclesia receptum fuisse, vt publicus luctus indiceretur, si quid gravioris flagitij admissum erat, propter quod Dei iram accensam esse suspicabantur, sicuti videre est in Nabothi historia, quando Israelitae ciues ieiunium publicum indicere iubetur, eo quod ille Dei simul & regis maiestatem suis maledictis laesisset. At hodie omnium sensus obsurduerunt, alioqui haec sola consideratio sufficeret ad frenandam immoderatam lasciuiam, qua passim inter manifesta irae Dei indicia peccatur. Non tamen sufficit luctus, sed altero etiam opus est, ut malum e medio auferatur, sic ut vel emendentur qui peccauerunt, vel si nulla emendationis spes reliqua est, e medio tollantur. Quod postremum cum Corinthij secundum leges ciuiles facere non possent, eò quòd magistratus Christianum non haberent, Paulus eos ad luctum & preces remisit, quibus Dei vindictam contra sceleratum illum requirerent. Vt enim parum profuerit medicus, qui se propter alicuius morbum vehementer dolere dicit, remedium verò, quo is pellatur, nullum adhibet: ita nequaquam aliorum peccata deflentur, nisi de illis corrigendis atq; coercendis serio cogitemus. Et ut hoc fiat publica salus postulat, quando frequenter vnius hominis peccatum toti genti malum dat, ut in Achani & Ionæ multorum, alio-rum exemplis cernitur. Hic ergo singuli officium faciant pro suæ vocationis ratione. Sunt enim res media priuata, in quibus singuli sedulo esse debent. Sunt item publica, in quibus industria & seueritate imprimis opus est, ne paucorum culpa ad multos redundet. Pessimè enim reipub. & sibijpsis consulunt, qui ignaua indulgentia dissimulant ea, quæ corrigi aut puniri oportebat. Sed de his plura in sequentibus dicentur. Nunc teneamus, nos in CHRISTO IESV ab æterno electos & per Euangelium ad ecclesiæ suæ communionem vocatos esse, ut sanctè viuamus, & virtutes eius prædicemus, qui è tenebris nos vocauit in admirabilem suam lucem. Huius memores singuli scandala è medio tollant, & alios quoq; suo exemplo ad salutis huius societatem adducant. Ita ex Euangelij doctrina & fidei professione fructus optatus nobis obtinget, dum in nobis quidè glorificabitur Pater Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, & nos cum eodem regni atq; gloriæ cœlestis participes erimus. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: What then ought we to do, brothers, so that we may be freed from the guilt of this fault? The Apostle rebukes the Corinthians because they did not mourn, so that he who had committed so unworthy a crime might be removed from their midst. He uses an expression taken from the Law, by which the punishment of death is indicated, more widely known than needs to be shown. See Lev. 20; Deut. 13, 17, 19, 21, etc. Two things therefore must be done. First, there is mourning, which ought to be undertaken both publicly and privately because of public crimes, which are joined with open scandal and the ruin of someone. The glory of God demands this, and we ought to be most zealous for it, and we have already shown earlier how it is profaned by such crimes. Next, the same law of charity and the fellowship that exists among Christian people demands it. For since we are members of the same body, one ought to be affected by and to grieve for the troubles of another; and if out of duty of charity we mourn those who die in body, how much more fitting is it for us to lament those who bring upon themselves the ruin of both body and soul by monstrous crimes, and at the same time harm many others by their example? The holiest men of old saw this, and we read that they lamented very bitterly those whom they saw rushing to destruction. Samuel, certainly, because of Saul, consumed himself with grief to such a degree that God judged him worthy of reproof. Likewise David, forgetting all wrongs, followed him with the most abundant tears, because he saw the enemies of God seizing from this an occasion to exult. And he mourned his son Absalom chiefly for this reason, that he feared he was dead in his sins. The disciples also deserve praise because they were deeply grieved when they heard that one of their own flock was about to betray Christ. And it is agreed that this custom was received in the ancient Church, that a public mourning should be proclaimed if some more serious crime had been committed, on account of which they suspected the wrath of God had been kindled, as may be seen in the story of Naboth, when the citizens of Israel were ordered to proclaim a public fast, because he had injured by his curses both the majesty of God and of the king. But today the senses of all have become deadened; otherwise this consideration alone would suffice to restrain the immoderate wantonness by which sin is committed everywhere amid the plain signs of God's wrath. Yet mourning is not enough; a second thing is needed as well, that the evil be taken out of the way, so that either those who have sinned are amended, or, if no hope of amendment is left, they are removed from the midst. Since the Corinthians could not do this last thing according to the civil laws, because they had no Christian magistrate, Paul sent them back to mourning and prayers, by which they might seek God's vengeance against that wicked man. For just as a physician does little good who says that he grieves greatly over someone's disease, yet applies no remedy by which it may be driven out, so the sins of others are by no means lamented unless we seriously think about correcting and restraining them. And public welfare demands that this be done, since the sin of one man often brings evil upon a whole people, as is seen in the examples of Achan and of Jonah and of many others. Here, then, let each one do his duty according to the nature of his calling. For there are private matters, in which each must be diligent; there are also public matters, in which industry and severity are above all needed, lest the fault of a few spread to many. For those who through lazy indulgence overlook what ought to be corrected or punished are the worst counsellors both to the commonwealth and to themselves. But more on these things will be said in what follows. Now let us hold fast that we in Christ Jesus have been chosen from eternity and called through the Gospel into the fellowship of his Church, that we may live holily and proclaim the virtues of him who called us out of darkness into his marvellous light. Mindful of this, let each one remove scandals from the midst, and by his example bring others also into the fellowship of this salvation. Thus we shall obtain the desired fruit of the doctrine of the Gospel and of the profession of faith, while the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is glorified in us, and we shall be partakers with him of the heavenly kingdom and glory. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 24.

units.la: Enimuerò ego ut absens corpore, præsens autem spiritu, iam ut præsens iudicaui, ut is qui hoc ita perpetrauit, vobis & meo spiritu in nomine Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI congregatis, cum potestate Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, eiusmodi[inquâ homo] tradatur Satanæ ad interitum carnis, ut spiritus saluus sit in die Domini IESV.
units.tr: Indeed, I, though absent in body but present in spirit, have already judged, as if present, that the man who has done this thing, when you are gathered together in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, with my spirit and with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, should be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh (such a one [such a man]), so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.

units.la: QUoniam vitiorum, quibus Corinthiaca ecclesia miserè infecta atq; turbata fuit, omnium præcipua causa erat immanis confidentia, qua & reliquas ecclesias contemnebant, & fidos monitores non sine odio atq; fastidio insolenti aspernabantur, Paulus ut facilius eorum criminas[?] deprimeret, immane scelus hominis incesti, quo tota ecclesia iam apud omnes diffamata erat, publicè arguit, & (ut nuper audiuimus) multis amplificat, ut velint nolint agnoscere cogantur, se præ aliis miseros & infelices esse, qui illud hucusq; neq; obseruarint, neq; de illo tollendo cogitauerint. Simul verò benevolentiam sibi ipsi conciliat, dum ostendit, se de ipsorum salute & honore magis solicitum esse, quàm ipsi hactenus fuerint. Cæterum ut melius appareat ipsum non conuitiandi causa hoc flagitium illis exprobrauisse, nunc remedium tradit, quo ecclesiæ suæ possint succurrere. Et primò quid quid fieri debeat, docet: deinde totius negotij modum atq; rationem diligentius describit.
units.tr: Since the chief cause of the vices by which the Corinthian church was wretchedly infected and disturbed was a monstrous self-confidence, by which they despised the other churches and scorned faithful advisers with insolent hatred and disdain, Paul, in order to more easily crush their faults, publicly denounces the monstrous crime of an incestuous man, by which the whole church had already been spread abroad in infamy among everyone, and (as we heard recently) he magnifies it with many words, so that they, whether they wish it or not, are compelled to acknowledge that they are more wretched and unfortunate than others, since they have neither noticed this until now nor thought about removing it. At the same time he wins their goodwill for himself, while he shows that he is more concerned for their salvation and honour than they themselves have been until now. Moreover, so that it may appear more clearly that he has rebuked them for this shameful act not for the sake of reviling, he now gives a remedy by which his church can be helped. And first he teaches what ought to be done; then he describes more carefully the whole manner and method of the business.

units.la: Quoad primum, sic ait: Enimuerò ego ut absens corpore, præsens autem spiritu, iam ut præ-sens iudicaui, ut is qui hoc ita perpetrauit, tradatur Satanæ, &c. Quid ipse iampridem de hac causa decreuerit, exponit, ut eos qui adhuc melius sentiebant, admoneat, rem tanti momenti non esse negligendam. Et cum nonnulla (ut Cap. vndecimo audiemus) in suum aduentum vsque disponenda aut ordinanda referuet, hic nullam moram illis concedit, quia morbi vis remedium præsens postulabat. Adhæc cum simpliciter posset dicere: Hæc mea est de scelerato illo & imputo homine sententia, quam apud vos ratam esse cupio, &c: suæ simul & absentiæ & præsentiæ meminit: nimirum ut ijs terrorem incutiat, qui eius absentia freti omnia sibi licere arbitrabantur. Fatetur ergo se corpore quidem abesse, præsentem verò adesse spiritu, potiore nimirum sui parte. Neq; mihi dubium est, eum non solum de animi sui erga illos propensione & solicitudine loqui (hanc enim æmuli eius facile contemnebant) sed potius de efficaci illa Spiritus sancti virtute, quæ facit, ut sancti interdum[?] res longius difficitas norint atque intelligant. Exemplum huius in Elisteo propheta extat, qui cum Giezi seruus clam eo à Naamano Syro munera extorsisset, seq; nusquam exiuisse mentiretur, rem tamen omnem perspectam habuit, adeoq; spiritu praesens fuit, cum illud fieret, quod hisce verbis testatur: Nonne cor meum aderat, quando reuersus est homo de curru suo in occursum tui? Idem cum Naaman rex caeco & praecipiti iudicio quendam praemisisset, qui ipsum occideret, rem omnem in spiritu cognitam habens, Senioribus apud se collectis dicebat: Annon vidistis quòd latro ille miserit, vt tollat caput meum, &c? Et talem spiritus virtutem in Apostolis quoq; locum habuisse non est dubium: quae etsi non semper, tunc tamen sese exeruit, quando maior aliqua necessitas postulabat. Ipse certè Paulus illam non obscurè fatetur, ad Colossenses scribens: Etsi corpore absum, spiritu tamen sum vobiscum, gaudens ac cernens vestrum ordinem, & soliditatem vestrae in Christum fidei. Et quia haec credentibus illo tempore non potuerunt omnino ignota esse, commodè hanc spiritus praesentiam hic quoque adducit. Itaque sensus verborum est: Quoniam vos omnes cessare video, neque aliquem esse, qui in re tam graui & seria manum admoueat, ego quamuis corpore procul absum, à spiritu tamen iam pridem aurem mihi vellicari sensi, & ideo impurum illum iudicaui Satanae esse tradendum, vt vos tanta infamiae nota liberetis, & quod ex illo enatum est, scandalum è medio tollatis.
units.tr: As to the first point, he says: "Indeed, I, though absent in body but present in spirit, have already judged, as if present, that the man who has done this thing be handed over to Satan," etc. He sets out what he himself decided long ago about this matter, so as to admonish those who were still thinking more favourably, that a matter of such importance is not to be neglected. And although he reserves some things to be arranged or put in order until his coming (as we shall hear in chapter eleven), here he allows them no delay, because the force of the disease demanded an immediate remedy. Besides, although he could simply have said, "This is my judgment about that wicked and unclean man, which I want you to ratify," he mentions both his absence and his presence: namely, so that he may strike terror into those who, relying on his absence, thought that everything was permitted to them. He therefore confesses that he is indeed absent in body, but present in spirit, that is, in the more powerful part of himself. Nor am I in doubt that he is speaking not only of the inclination and concern of his mind towards them (for his rivals easily despised this), but rather of that effective power of the Holy Spirit, which makes it so that the saints sometimes know and understand things that happen far away. An example of this is found in the prophet Elisha, when his servant Gehazi secretly extorted gifts from Naaman the Syrian and lied that he had gone nowhere; yet Elisha had the whole matter clearly in view, and was present in spirit when that happened, which he attests in these words: "Did not my heart go with you, when the man turned from his chariot to meet you?" Likewise, when King Naaman, by blind and rash judgment, had sent someone ahead to kill him, Elisha, having the whole matter known to him in the Spirit, said to the elders gathered with him: "Did you not see that this son of a murderer has sent to take off my head?" And there is no doubt that such power of the Spirit was also present in the Apostles; though it did not always show itself, it did so when some greater necessity demanded it. Paul himself certainly confesses it plainly, writing to the Colossians: "Though I am absent in body, yet in spirit I am with you, rejoicing and beholding your order and the steadfastness of your faith in Christ." And since these things could not have been entirely unknown to believers at that time, he fittingly brings forward this presence of the spirit here as well. So the sense of the words is this: Since I see that you all are idle, and that there is no one who will put his hand to so grave and serious a matter, I, although far away in body, have long since felt my ear pulled by the Spirit, and therefore I have judged that this unclean man should be handed over to Satan, so that you may be freed from so great a mark of infamy, and remove the scandal that has arisen from him.

units.la: Est autem multa laude dignum Pauli exemplum, qui cessantibus illis, ad quos haec cura maxime pertinebat, ipse quamuis corpore absens, operi huic manum admouet. Est hoc magni Zeli & feruoris spiritus argumentum, cum non potuerit ignorare, quanto odio atq; inuidia seipsum grauaturus esset, si hanc Camarinam mouendo totam ecclesiam ad nouum seueriorís disciplinae exemplum edendum excitaret. Suo autem exemplo docet, quid omnes facere debeant, qui in aliqua authoritate sunt constituti. Solent inter hos plerique, in grauioribus negotijs sese aliorum ignauia excusare, & quia alij cessent, qui aut eundem aut etiam ipsis altiorem gradum tenent, sibi quoq; nihil agendum esse putant eorum, quae cum inuidia aut periculo coniuncta sunt. At non excusat nos vllorum hominum exemplum siue authoritas, si quod Deus nobis iniunxit facere negligamus. Itaq; Pauli studium imitentur quotquot ecclesiae ministerium sustinent. Turpe enim fuerit eos mundi amicitiam seruiliter captare, qui CHRISTI IESV serui sunt: aut hominum odia atq; minas timere, quibus ille suam operam iam dudum pollicitus est. Idem cogitent qui magistratum gerunt. Nam nisi hi quoq; officium fecerint, eo ipso sese accusabunt, quo se defendi posse arbitrantur. Cum enim tibi aliorum ignauia displiceat, nimium certe imprudens es, qui eandem imitaris. Quin cogita, alios fortasse ideo cessare, quia tuam operam nunc requirit Deus, & per te confectum vult illud, in quo alij magno suo malo steterunt. Itaq; cum & verbo suo & occulta spiritus suggestione tibi iam aurem vellicet Deus, alacri animo ad opus accingitor, ne eodem cum alteris illis, quos tu accusas, reatu implicieris.
units.tr: Paul's example is indeed worthy of great praise: while those to whom this care chiefly pertained were idle, he himself, though absent in body, puts his hand to this work. This is a proof of great zeal and fervour of spirit, since he could not have been ignorant of how much hatred and envy he would bring upon himself if, by stirring up this hornet's nest, he roused the whole church to a new example of stricter discipline. By his example, however, he teaches what all ought to do who have been placed in some authority. Many among such people are accustomed, in more serious matters, to excuse themselves by the idleness of others; and because others, who hold either the same rank or even a higher one than they, are doing nothing, they think that they too must do nothing of those things that are bound up with envy or danger. But the example or authority of no men excuses us if we neglect what God has enjoined upon us to do. Let therefore all who sustain the ministry of the church imitate Paul's zeal. For it would be shameful for those who are servants of Jesus Christ to court the friendship of the world in a slavish way, or to fear the hatreds and threats of men, when he had long since promised his own labour to them. Let magistrates think the same. For unless they too perform their duty, they will accuse themselves by that very thing by which they think they can defend themselves. For if the idleness of others displeases you, you are certainly very imprudent if you imitate the same. Indeed, consider that others perhaps are idle for this reason: that God now requires your work, and wills that through you be accomplished that in which others, to their great harm, have stood still. Therefore, since God now pulls your ear both by his word and by the secret suggestion of his Spirit, set about the work with a willing mind, lest you become entangled in the same guilt as those others whom you accuse.

units.la: Sed pergamus in Apostoli verbis, qui modum & mationem describit, quem in isto homine tolendo siue coercendo tenere debeant. Iudicaui (inquit) vt is, qui hoc ita perpetrauit, vobis & meo spiritu in nomine Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI congregatis, cum potestate Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, eiusmodi (inquam) homo tradatur Satanae ad interitum carnis, vt spiritus salvus sit in die Domini IESV. Primò in coetu publico agi vult hanc causam, ne quid pauculis quibusdam permittere putetur, qui sibi ius & imperium in alios ambitiosius vendicabant. Deinde suum spiritum ipsis praesente fore pollicetur, vt ostendat, se opus mandare, quod nō à quibusuis perfici possit, sed ad quod Spiritu Apostolico opus sit, qui omnia videat, & efficaciter quoq; agat contra eos, qui coerceri merentur: quo Apostolos armatos fuisse, paulò ante diximus. Hanc autem illis pollicendo simul animosiores facere vult eos, qui hucusq; nimis turpiter torpuerant. Tertiò, vt in nomine IESV CHRISTI conueniant, iubet, ne quid ex suo cerebro iubere putetur. Quartò, per expositionem addit: Cum potestate Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, nimirum miraculosa illa, qua per suos seruos (vt modò dictum est) efficaciter agit cum sanando tum castigando. Et proderat haec tam diligenter inculcari & repeti, ne se rem tantam absque effectu tentaturos, & proinde ex magno conatu nihil quàm ludibrium reportaturos esse metuerent: neue tanti flagitij reus Ecclesiae sententiam, vt improbi ac proterui homines solent, scurrili dicacitate eludere conarentur. retur. Pollicetur ergo, quòd ipse illis adesse velit ea Spiritus potestate, qua Christus Apostolos armauerit, & quæ non alia quàm ipsius Christi potestas sit, & proinde efficacissima sit ad puniendum omnes eos, qui aduersus ipsum & Ecclesiam eius cum publico scandalo proteruiunt. Summa autem & finis totius actionis est, vt impurum illum Satanæ tradant ad interitum carnis, vt spiritus saluus sit in die Domini IESV.
units.tr: But let us go on with the Apostle's words, in which he describes the manner and method that they ought to observe in removing, or rather restraining, this man. "I have judged," he says, "that the man who has done this thing, when you are gathered together, with my spirit, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, such a one (I say) be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus." First, he wants this case to be conducted in a public assembly, lest it be thought that something was being entrusted to a few men who were too ambitiously claiming for themselves right and authority over others. Second, he promises that his spirit will be present with them, so that he may show that he is entrusting them with a work that cannot be carried out by just anyone, but needs an apostolic Spirit, who sees all things and also acts effectively against those who deserve to be restrained; that the Apostles were armed with this, we said a little while ago. By promising this to them, he wishes at the same time to make more spirited those who until now had shamefully grown sluggish. Third, he orders them to gather in the name of Jesus Christ, so that it may not be thought that anything is being commanded out of his own head. Fourth, he adds by way of explanation: "with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ," that is, that miraculous power by which, through his servants (as has just been said), he acts effectively both in healing and in chastising. And it was useful that this be so carefully impressed and repeated, lest they fear that they would be attempting so great a thing without effect, and that after a great effort they would win nothing but ridicule; and lest the guilty party of so great a crime should try, as shameless and insolent men usually do, to elude the sentence of the Church with scurrilous wit. He therefore promises that he himself wishes to be present with them by that power of the Spirit with which Christ armed the Apostles, which is none other than the power of Christ himself, and therefore is most effective for punishing all those who act wantonly against him and his Church with public scandal. The sum and purpose of the whole action, however, is that they hand that unclean man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.

units.la: Est autem diligentius excutienda hæc locutio propter eos, qui Satanæ tradere non aliud esse putant, quàm ab Ecclesiæ societate & Sacramentorum vsu reijcere, quod vulgo Excommunicationem dicunt. Rationem suæ sententiæ hanc afferunt, quòd Dei saluifica virtus sese in sola Ecclesia exerat, extra hanc vero nihil nisi mundus sit, cui ex iusto Dei iudicio Satan dominetur. Fatemur autem & nos, salutem in sola Ecclesia inueniri, & sub potestate tenebrarum esse eos, qui ab illa sunt alieni: Sed in præsenti maius quiddam & grauius quam simplicem ab Ecclesiæ & sacro-rum communione exclusionem præcipi, res ipsa loquitur. Nuper enim Corinthios Paulus reprehen-dit, non quòd incestum illum hominem non excommunicassent, sed quòd non efficiebant publico luctu & precibus suis, vt è medio tolleretur. Deinde, si nihil quàm exclusionem à cœtu ecclesiæ & Cœna Domini præcepisset Apostolus, quid opus erat, vt Corinthij apud eum postea pro misero illo intercederent? Nam in illorum potestate fuisset, illum rursus ad se recipere. Aliquid ergo passum fuisse oportet, à quo ipsi eum liberare non poterant. Quæ item ratio fuisset, ob quam Paulus suæ sententiæ rigorem postea tam solicitè excusaret, quod illum fecisse in pos[?]. epist.cap.2. apparet? Ad hæc quid opus erat miraculosa illa Spiritus Apostolici præsentia, si non aliud fieri debebat, quàm quod hodie etiam cuiusuis Ecclesiæ Seniores facere possunt? Certè vnum hoc abunde docet, aliquid hic præcipi, quod sine Apostolici Spiritus virtute perfici non poterat. Scimus autè Apostolos hac etiam Spiritus potestate instructos fuisse, vt quos ita meruisse videbant, Satanæ, vt lictori & car-nifici traderent multandos, qui vel lentis morbis eos affligeret, vel etiam omnino occideret. Et sanè necessarius erat tunc lictor ille, quando Christiani magistratum non habebant, qui fontes pu-niret. Exempla, quibus hoc probetur, in Anania & Sapphira habemus, quos morte subitanea Petrus hoc modo puniuit, quòd Spiritui Sancto mentiti essent: & Elymam Magum Paulus cæcita-te percussit, idemq; Hymenæum & Alexandrum Satanæ tradidit, vt ab hoc multati discerent non maledicere. Quis verò dubitet, istos eò magis maledicturos fuisse, si à sola Ecclesiæ & Sacra-mentorum communione fuissent exclusi? Nouo igitur exemplo illos Paulus coercuit, siue à Satana morbis excruciati, siue è medio sublati fuerint. Et isto sensu hoc etiam quod in præsenti dicitur, accipi debere, finis totius actionis docet. Iubetur enim Satanæ tradi ad interitum carnis, vt spiritus saluus sit in die Domini IESV. Id est, vt quoad carnem siue corpus multetur, & ea ratione peccatum suum agnoscat, ad Deum conuertatur, & animam suam ab interitu sempiterno seruet. Scio aliquos hæc verba de mortificatione carnalium cupiditatum exponere, sed verborum proprietas hoc non patitur (vt multis demonstrari poterat) & eodem nobiscum sensu locum istum plerique veterum intellexerunt, vt pote D. Athanasius, Chrysostomus, Theodoretus, Theophylactus, & ex Latinis D. Hieronymus & Augustinus: quorum omnium verba recensere longum foret. Hic certè, etsi expositionem de affectuum mortificatione non dissimulet, eam tamen præfert, quam nos sequimur: imò mortificationem carnis inde secuturam dicit, si à Satana excruciatus in semetip-sum descendat, & scelus suum agnoscere discat. Nam lib.3. ad Parmen. epistolarum cap.5. sic scri-bit: Quid aliud agebat Apostolus, nisi vt per interitum carnis saluti spirituali consuleret? vt siue aliqua pœna, vel morte corporali, sicut Ananias & vxor eius ante pedes Apostoli ceciderunt: siue per pœnitentiam quoniam Satanæ traditus erat, interimeret in se scelera-tam carnis concupiscen-tiam, &c.? Nec est quòd aliquis obijciat, non occisum fuisse illum à Satana, sed potius Paulum postea pro eo intercessisse, vt eum in Ecclesiæ gremium reciperent. Fatemur enim hoc nos quoq; aut simuleum siue correptione duriori & comminatione dira, siue ipsa traditione Satanæ ita affecti fuisse constat, vt periculum esset, ne desperatione absorberetur. Suum ergo effectum habuit Pauli sententia, etiamsi non omnino interfectus sit, & ideo eum seriò pœnitentem in gratiam recipere iubet, inter alia argumenta hoc imprimis adducens, cauendum esse, ne Satan, cuius machinationes ipsi nō ignoret, sub nimiæ seueritatis prætextu eis imponat. Fuit ergo (vt diximus) peculiare quid, quod in praesenti praecipitur, & hoc remedio tunc opus erat, quando nulla alia ratio reliqua erat, qua scandala cum suis authoribus e medio tolli possent. Nec dubito, quin si Corinthij magistratum habuissent Christianum, Paulus huius causae cognitione nequaquam ad se pertinere putavisset, sed curasset potius, ut impurus ille sceleris tam atrocis poenas dedisset. Sciebat enim quid de talibus statuisset Deus, & leges eiusmodi per Christum minime abrogatas esse sciebat. Eius enim ad Romanos hoc dictum extat: Magistratus non temere gestat gladium. Nam Dei minister est, vltor ad iram ei, qui quod malum est, fecerit. Nunc vero durum erat ad homines prophanos & veri Dei hostes cum publico religionis Christianae ludibrio, & quo ad infelicem illum, cum aeternae salutis periculo, eius causam deferre, qui Christo nomen dederat, & de cuius conversione adhuc meliora poterant sperari. Ideo ad illud remedium recurrit Apostolus, quod tunc Ecclesia unicum habebat. At hodie cum principes Christiani sint, qui & nutritios Ecclesiae agunt, & scelera secundum leges puniunt, idque ea ratione, ut fontibus doctrina quoque & consolatio vera adhibeatur, qua instructi inter supplicia servari possint, cessare debuit miraculosa illa sceleris castigatio, quae multo cum maiori periculo coniungeretur, quam ea quae per magistratus fit, nisi apostolica prudentia & moderatione dirigeretur.
units.tr: This passage needs to be examined more carefully, because some people think that to deliver someone to Satan means nothing more than to cast him out of the fellowship of the Church and the use of the sacraments, which is commonly called excommunication.
