They support this view by arguing that God's saving power works only in the Church, and that outside it there is nothing but the world, over which Satan rules by the just judgment of God. We too admit that salvation is found only in the Church, and that those who are alien to it are under the power of darkness. But the matter itself shows that something greater and more severe is commanded here than a simple exclusion from the Church and the holy communion. Paul recently rebuked the Corinthians, not because they had failed to excommunicate that incestuous man, but because they did not, by public mourning and prayers of their own, bring it about that he was removed from their midst. Again, if the Apostle had ordered nothing more than exclusion from the assembly of the Church and the Lord's Supper, why was it necessary for the Corinthians afterwards to intercede with him on behalf of that wretched man? For it would have been within their power to receive him back again. So he must have suffered something from which they could not free him by themselves. Likewise, what reason would there have been for Paul so anxiously to excuse afterwards the severity of his sentence, as appears in the second letter, chapter 2? Besides, what need was there for that miraculous presence of the apostolic Spirit, if nothing more was to be done than what the elders of any church can do today? Surely this one thing clearly teaches that something is being commanded here which could not be carried out without the power of the apostolic Spirit. We know that the Apostles were also furnished with this power of the Spirit, so that they could hand over to Satan, as to the executioner and the hangman, those whom they saw to have deserved it, to be punished by him, either by afflicting them with lingering diseases or even by killing them outright. And indeed that executioner was necessary at a time when Christians had no magistrate to punish the sources of evil. We have examples that prove this in Ananias and Sapphira, whom Peter punished in this way with sudden death because they had lied to the Holy Spirit; and Paul struck the magician Elymas with blindness, and likewise delivered Hymenaeus and Alexander to Satan, so that, being punished by him, they might learn not to blaspheme. Who would doubt that these men would have blasphemed all the more if they had been excluded only from the communion of the Church and the sacraments? Paul therefore restrained them by a new kind of example, whether they were tormented by diseases inflicted by Satan or were taken out of the way. The end of the whole action also shows that what is said here must be understood in this sense. For he is commanded to be delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus. That is, that he may be punished as to the flesh or body, and by this means may acknowledge his sin, turn to God, and keep his soul from eternal ruin. I know that some explain these words as the mortification of carnal desires, but the proper meaning of the words does not allow this (as could be shown by many arguments), and most of the ancients understood this passage in the same sense as we do, as did St Athanasius, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Theophylact, and among the Latins St Jerome and Augustine, whose words it would be tedious to list. Here, indeed, Augustine does not hide the explanation concerning the mortification of the affections, yet he prefers the one that we follow; indeed, he says that the mortification of the flesh will follow from this, if the man, tormented by Satan, comes down into himself and learns to recognise his crime. For in the third book of his letters against Parmenianus, chapter 5, he writes thus: "What else was the Apostle doing, except to provide for the spiritual salvation of the man through the destruction of the flesh? So that either by some punishment or bodily death, as Ananias and his wife fell at the Apostle's feet, or else, since he had been delivered to Satan, through repentance he might destroy in himself the wicked lust of the flesh, etc.?" Nor should anyone object that he was not killed by Satan, but that Paul afterwards interceded for him, so that they would receive him back into the bosom of the Church. For we admit that it is certain he was either so affected by a harsher rebuke and dreadful threat, or by the very delivering to Satan, that there was danger he might be swallowed up by despair. Paul's sentence therefore had its effect, even though the man was not altogether destroyed; and so he bids them receive him back into favour as one who truly repents, adducing among other arguments this above all, that care must be taken lest Satan, whose machinations Paul knew well, should take advantage of them under the pretext of excessive severity. It was therefore (as we have said) something peculiar that is commanded here, and at that time this remedy was needed, when no other way remained by which the scandals, together with their authors, could be removed from the midst. Nor do I doubt that if the Corinthians had had a Christian magistrate, Paul would by no means have thought that the investigation of this case belonged to him, but would rather have seen to it that that impure man paid the penalties for so atrocious a crime. For he knew what God had decreed about such people, and he knew that laws of this kind had by no means been abrogated through Christ. There is, indeed, his saying to the Romans: "The magistrate does not bear the sword in vain; for he is the minister of God, an avenger to execute wrath on the one who does evil." But at that time it was hard to hand such men over, who were profane and enemies of the true God, to the public mockery of the Christian religion, and, as to that unhappy man, to deliver his cause to the peril of eternal salvation, when he had given his name to Christ and better things could still be hoped for concerning his conversion. Therefore the Apostle had recourse to that remedy, which the Church then alone possessed. But today, since there are Christian princes who both nourish the Church and punish crimes according to the laws, and do so in such a way that true doctrine and consolation are also applied to the sources of evil, so that those who are punished may be kept by these means, that miraculous punishment of sin should cease, since it would be joined with far greater danger than that which is carried out by the magistrate, unless it were directed by apostolic prudence and moderation.

units.la: Est autem hoc memorabile exemplum, quo admonemur, quam seria & diligenti cura opus sit, ut scelera, quae cum publico scandalo coniuncta sunt, digni poenis coerceantur, & ut e medio etiam tollantur, qui incurabili contumacia in illis pergunt. Quia enim natura ad peccandum proclives sumus, aliorum exemplis facile corrumpimur, idque eo magis, si quos videamus ea impune facere, quae iam ante nostris affectibus arridēt[?]. Adde, quod quae initio priuata videri possunt peccata, & in solis suis authoribus haerebant, ea publica fiunt, & suo reatu populum totum una cum magistratibus grauant, si impunita dimittantur. Ideo Deus olim, quoties in Lege sceleratis poenas capitales decernit, fere adijcere solet: Et auferes malum e medio tui. Et quam displiceat Deo impunitas & licentia peccandi, vel ex eo colligi potest, quod Ecclesiam primitivam, quae magistratibus carebat, potestate extraordinaria armare voluit, per quam homines leves & scandalorum authores Satanae multandi & affligendi traderentur. Quanto magis ergo eos, qui Respub. habent legitime constitutas, cavere decet, ne apud ipsos legum disciplina dissolvatur? Quam enim hoc necessarium sit, optimi & prudentissimi quique olim inter gentes viderunt, qui Rempub. iusta praemiorum & poenarum distributione dixerunt servari: nimirum quod his quidem a peccando homines absterrentur, illis vero ad virtutis studium alliciuntur. Et Cato, gravissimus ille morum Censor, hoc civitatis corruptae & brevi peritura argumentum esse dicebat, quod amissis virtutum & vitiorum nominibus laudem mererentur, qui omnia pro animi sui libidine facerent. Nam bona aliena largiri (dicebat) liberalitas, malarum rerum audacia, fortitudo vocatur. Nec timere debent ij, quibus haec cura commissa est, ne nimio rigore peccent, si a Deo praescriptas leges sequantur. Si enim Apostoli homines sceleratos Satanae excruciandos tradiderunt, crudelissimo humani generis hosti, quis eos peccare dixerit, qui ex Dei mandato homicidam ad necem damnant, adulterum capite plectunt, veneficos item, magos, incantatores, libidinibus item incestis & nefandis pollutos ultricibus flammis tradunt? Non (inquam) crudeles sunt, qui poenas istas de fontibus sumunt, ne malum latius grassetur: iniusti autem & crudeles sunt, qui & infelices istos in suis sceleribus perire, & eorum exemplo plures alios infici patiuntur: qui denique sua indulgentia Deum irritant, ut poenas de gente tota communes exigat, quae initio paucioribus solum debebantur. Nam vtut alij alijs delitias faciant, sibique mutuo indulgeant, non dormitat tamen Dei vindicta, & ut scelera puniantur necesse est, nisi iustitiam Dei negare prorsus libeat. Nisi ergo legitimis poenis illa castigentur, fere per extraordinaria id fieri solet, qualia sunt, fames, annonae caritas & penuria, pestes, seditiones, bella, & quae alia huius generis gentes & regna evertunt. Cogitent ergo de eo diligenter Christiani homines, quibus datum est legibus uti & magistratus habere ordinarios: ne Euangelij libertatem in carnis licentiam convertant, sed scelera dignis poenis coerceant, ne propter ipsos male audiat nomen Domini.
units.tr: This is a memorable example, by which we are warned how serious and diligent a care is needed, so that crimes which are joined with public scandal are checked by deserved punishments, and so that those also are removed from the midst who persist in them with incurable obstinacy. For since by nature we are prone to sin, we are easily corrupted by the examples of others, and all the more so if we see some doing with impunity the very things which already smile upon our passions. Add to this that sins which at first may seem private, and cling only to their own authors, become public, and burden the whole people, together with the magistrates, with their guilt, if they are left unpunished. For this reason God of old, whenever in the Law he decreed capital punishments for the wicked, was accustomed to add: "And you shall take away the evil from your midst." And how much God is displeased by impunity and licence to sin may be gathered from this, that he wished the primitive Church, which lacked magistrates, to be armed with an extraordinary power, by which light men and authors of scandals were delivered to Satan to be punished and afflicted. How much more, then, ought those who have lawfully constituted commonwealths to take care that discipline of the laws is not dissolved among them? How necessary this is, the best and wisest men among the nations of old perceived, who said that the commonwealth was preserved by a just distribution of rewards and punishments: namely, because by the one men are deterred from sinning, while by the others they are drawn to the pursuit of virtue. And Cato, that most grave censor of morals, used to say that it was a sign of a corrupted state, destined soon to perish, when those who did everything according to the desires of their own minds earned praise, the names of virtues and vices having been lost. For he said that the lavish giving away of other people's goods is called liberality, and daring in evil things is called courage. Nor should those to whom this care is committed fear that they will sin by excessive rigour, if they follow the laws prescribed by God. For if the Apostles handed wicked men over to Satan to be tormented, who would say that those sin who, by God's command, condemn a murderer to death, put an adulterer to the capital punishment, and likewise hand over poisoners, magicians, enchanters, and those polluted by incestuous and abominable lusts to avenging flames, when that most cruel enemy of the human race is the one who inflicts such torment? I say that those who take these punishments from the sources of evil are not cruel, so that the evil may not spread more widely; but those are unjust and cruel who allow these wretched men to perish in their crimes and many others to be infected by their example; and finally those who by their indulgence provoke God, so that he exacts punishment from the whole nation in common, which at first was due only to a few. For however some men pamper others and indulge one another, nevertheless the vengeance of God does not sleep, and it is necessary that crimes be punished, unless one should altogether wish to deny the justice of God. Therefore, unless these things are checked by lawful punishments, this usually happens through extraordinary means, such as famine, dearth and scarcity of food, plagues, seditions, wars, and whatever else of this kind overthrows peoples and kingdoms. Let Christian men therefore consider this carefully, to whom it has been given to use laws and to have ordinary magistrates: lest they turn the liberty of the Gospel into licence of the flesh, but restrain wickedness with due punishments, so that the name of the Lord is not ill spoken of because of them.

units.la: Imprimis autem exemplum hoc observare debent Ecclesiae, quarum eadem est conditio, quae olim fuit, quando Apostolis Euangelium in toto orbe praedicantibus, Ecclesiae passim inter medios idololatras & falsorum Deorum cultores constituebantur. Habitabant tunc Christiani inter ethnicos, & quoad res politicas Romanorum legibus utebantur, neq; illis licebat magistratus suos iudices proprios constituere, qui authoritate sua & poenis ciuilibus scelera punirent. Magna tunc quoq; & effrenis erat apud omnes gentes scelerum licentia: & quàmuis essent etiam uiri boni & honesti, qui stupra, adulteria, incestus, Venerem masculâ & alia his similia detestarentur, nemo tamen erat, qui ista publicis supplicijs digna esse iudicaret: nec impune modo hæc omnia facere licebat, sed multi libidines suas publicè etiâ decantabant, & ex scelere laudem quærebant, sicuti in illorum temporum poetis est videre. Nec dubium est multos, qui iam ad Christum conuersi erant, pristinos mores non omnino exuisse: multos etiam non tam religionis aut veritatis studio, quàm curiositate, vel priuati commodi causa (ut nimirum ex Ecclesiæ ærario alerentur) fidem professos fuisse, idq; in ijs præsertim locis, ubi maior libertas affulgebat. Ideo cura diligenti opus esse videbant Apostoli, ne eiusmodi homines intra Ecclesiam admissi, religionem Christianam gentium ludibrijs exponerent, & ijs quoq; suspectam facerent, qui iam cœperant de illa honorificentius sentire. De istis certè Iudas Iacobi frater suâ epistolâ scripsit, qua Christianos sui sæculi monet, ut ab illis sibi caueant, qui gratiam Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI transferunt ad carnis lasciuiam: eò quòd maculæ sint in ipsorum cœtibus, propter quas fides Christiana male audiat. Tales etiam fuerunt, quos alibi Paulus ἀτάκτως[?] dicit, eò quòd inordinatè & absq; omni disciplina uiuerent, & ut ijdem coerceantur iubet. Et quia Corinthi, in urbe populosa, & propter opes luxui ac voluptatibus dedita, plus erat periculi, non modo hominem illum incestum publico & prius ipsis inaudito exemplo multari[?] præcipit, uerumetiam inde occasionem arripit ipsos admonendi, ut omnium similium consortia deuitent, ne quid huius porrò accidat.
units.tr: Above all, the Churches should observe this example, since their condition is the same as it once was, when the apostles were preaching the Gospel throughout the world and Churches were being planted everywhere among idolaters and worshippers of false gods. Christians then lived among the heathen and, in civil matters, used the laws of the Romans. They were not permitted to appoint their own magistrates as judges, who might punish crimes by their own authority and with civil penalties. Then too there was great and unbridled licence for sin among all nations. Although there were good and honest men who detested fornication, adultery, incest, male lust and the like, nobody judged these things worthy of public punishment. Not only could all these things be done with impunity, but many people even sang publicly of their lusts and sought praise for their wickedness, as can be seen in the poets of that age. There is no doubt that many who had already been converted to Christ had not wholly put off their former ways. Many had professed the faith not so much from zeal for religion or truth as from curiosity, or for private gain (namely, so that they might be supported from the Church's treasury), and this especially in those places where greater freedom prevailed. So the Apostles saw that careful attention was needed, lest such men, once admitted into the Church, should expose the Christian religion to the mockery of the Gentiles and make it suspect even to those who had begun to think more highly of it. Certainly Jude, the brother of James, wrote about such men in his epistle, warning the Christians of his time to beware of those who turn the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ into lasciviousness of the flesh, because there are stains in their assemblies on account of which the Christian faith is ill spoken of. Paul also means such people elsewhere when he calls them disorderly [ἀτάκτως], because they lived without order and without any discipline, and he orders that they be restrained. And since Corinth was a populous city, given over to luxury and pleasures because of its wealth, the danger was greater there. So he not only orders the incestuous man to be punished with a public example, unheard of among them until then, but also seizes the opportunity to admonish them to avoid the company of all such persons, lest anything of this kind happen again.

units.la: Debent hoc Apostoli exemplum imitari Ecclesiæ, quæ hodie inter Papistas, vel etiam (ut in Vngaria fieri solet) inter Turcas agunt. Eadem enim plane est ipsarum conditio, qualem olim fuisse iam diximus. Et est hoc ingens Dei beneficium & præclarum diuinæ Christi potentiæ argumentum, qui in eiusmodi locis Ecclesias constituere potest. Debent ergo hæ diligenter cauere, ne, vel temere quosuis recipiant, neue etiam eos indulgentius ferant, qui morum licentiâ, aut etiam apertis sceleribus Christiani nominis professionem prophanant. Nam licet hodie etiam magistratus rari sint, qui libidines uagas & illicitas, ebrietatem & omnis generis luxum, deierationes & execrationes, aliaq; his similia, authoritate publica coerceant, manet tamen in plerisq; hominum aliquis sensus honesti, quo excitati illis offendi & animi sui indignationem non obscure testari solent. Et quia Euangelij doctrina vulgo exosa est, eò quòd sua luce mundi mala opera arguat, mox calumniandi occasionem exteri arripiunt, si quos sub illius professione petulantius & proteruius uiuere conspicentur. Quapropter de constituenda morum disciplina Christianis hominibus inter tales agentibus præcipua cura esse debet, qua nimirum in ordinem redigantur, si qui lasciuius proteruiunt. At simul uidendum est diligenter, ne quid confidentius tententur[?], & κακοῦργοι[?] peccent, dum omnia, quæ olim Apostoli fecerunt, inconsultate meritate imitari uolut. Ut enim Romani Pontifices ex hoc loco & similibus Excommunicationem suam instituerunt, quæ tyrannidis ipsorum organum fuit efficacissimum, quo non priuatos modo homines, uerumetiam Reges & Imperatores crudeliter vexarunt, bellorum denique ciuilium & seditionum fuerunt authores: Ita Anabaptistæ dum disciplinam absque Excommunicatione continere non posse sibi persuadent, Ecclesias passim turbant, & seipsos toti mundo ridiculos præbent, quando ipsi quoq; magno cum conatu eos, qui deliquerunt, Satanæ tradunt, & Apostolicam illam potestatem nullo cum effectu ostentant, qui ne pediculum quidem suis obtestationibus occidere, nedum pro imperio Satanæ aliquid mandare possunt. Iamprídem enim hoc donum cessauit, ut & multa alia: imo ne uiuentibus quidem Apostolis in tam frequenti usu fuit ut reliqua: eò quòd sufficeret uno aliquo exemplo seueriori in aliqua gente edito Apostolorum authoritatem contra ministerij Ecclesiastici contemptores asseruisse. Non igitur necesse est, ut quid simile tentetur hodie, quando neq; alia imitari possumus, quæ Apostoli miraculosè fecerunt. Eam uero disciplinæ rationem singulæ Ecclesiæ sequantur, quæ genti in qua degunt quàm maximè conuenit, quæq; pro locorum & temporum ratione omnium commodissima esse videtur. Neq; hic quisquam alijs temere præscribat, neue ad eandem formam omnes astringat. Quòd si vero aliqui in Ecclesia eiusmodi contumaciores sunt, quàm ut monendo, torripiendo, hortando in ordinem cogi possint, & ijdem insuper scurrili impudentia comminationes quoq; verbi Dei atq; poenarum denuntiationes rideant, ij ut putrida & emortua membra ab Ecclesiæ corpore prorsus resecantor, ne suo exemplo alios inficiant, neue religionem Christianam prophanorum hominum ludibrijs exponant. Quid enim aliud facere possunt ij, qui magistratu destituuntur, ad quem causas eiusmodi referant, quibus deniq; non licet poenis à Deo constitutis sceleratos & incurabiles multare? Ad istud ergo remedium recurrant necesse est, ut Ecclesiam suam suspicione liberent. Et hæc demum vera Excommunicatio dici meretur, quando nimirum ab Ecclesiæ communione vel societate in vniversum excluduntur, qui illius ciues antea habebantur. At quia hic quoq; facilis lapsus est, eo quòd pleriq; in notandis aliorum vitijs acerrimi sunt, simulq; innata homini ambitio multos abripit, ut concessa sibi potestate insolentius abutantur, diligenter observari debent huius loci circumstantiæ, & quæ hoc cap. deinceps sequuntur, ut nimirum Apostolorum & veteris Ecclesiæ vestigijs insistant, quotquot hoc remedium extremum aliquibus adhibere coguntur.
units.tr: The Churches should imitate this example of the Apostles, which today live among the Papists or even (as is customary in Hungary) among the Turks. Their condition is plainly the same as we have said it once was. This is a great blessing of God and a notable proof of the divine power of Christ, who can establish Churches in such places. They must therefore take care, both not to receive just anyone rashly and not to tolerate too indulgently those who profane the profession of the Christian name by licence of morals or by open crimes. For although today there are few magistrates who, by public authority, restrain wanton and unlawful lusts, drunkenness and every kind of luxury, oaths and curses, and things like these, most men still retain some sense of what is honourable, and when roused by such things they are accustomed to take offence and not obscurely to show their indignation. And because the doctrine of the Gospel is commonly hated, since its light exposes the evil works of the world, outsiders at once seize the chance to slander it if they see some who live too wantonly and shamelessly under its name. Therefore, among Christians living among such people, the establishment of moral discipline must be a chief concern, so that those who live too wantonly are brought back into order. But at the same time one must carefully see to it that they do not presume too boldly and sin as evildoers [κακοῦργοι] while trying to imitate without judgment and measure everything the Apostles once did. For just as the Roman Pontiffs drew from this passage and similar ones their excommunication, which was the most effective instrument of their tyranny, and with which they cruelly harassed not only private persons but even kings and emperors, and were finally the authors of civil wars and seditions, so the Anabaptists, persuading themselves that discipline cannot be maintained without excommunication, everywhere disturb the Churches and make themselves ridiculous to the whole world. They too, with great effort, hand over those who have sinned to Satan and display that apostolic power to no effect. Yet they cannot even kill a louse by their adjurations, much less command anything under the dominion of Satan. For this gift has ceased long ago, as have many others. Indeed it was not in such frequent use even while the Apostles were alive as the rest were, since one severe example given among some nation was enough to assert the authority of the Apostles against the despisers of the ecclesiastical ministry. It is therefore not necessary to attempt anything similar today, since we cannot imitate the other things the Apostles did by miracle. Let each Church follow that manner of discipline which best suits the people among whom it lives and which seems most convenient according to the circumstances of place and time. Nor should anyone rashly prescribe to others here or bind everyone to one form. But if there are some in the Church so stubborn that they cannot be brought into order by admonition, rebuke and exhortation, and who moreover with buffoonish impudence laugh at the threats of God's Word and the announcements of punishment, they should be cut off entirely from the body of the Church like rotten and dead limbs, lest they infect others by their example or expose the Christian religion to the mockery of profane men. For what else can those do who lack a magistrate to whom they may refer such cases, and who are not permitted to punish the wicked and incurable with the penalties appointed by God? They must therefore have recourse to this remedy, so that they may free their Church from suspicion. This alone deserves to be called true excommunication, when those who were previously regarded as its citizens are excluded altogether from the communion and fellowship of the Church. But because here too there is an easy slip, since most men are very sharp in noting the faults of others, and innate ambition carries many away so that they abuse the power granted them too insolently, the circumstances of this passage and what follows in this chapter must be carefully observed. In this way, whoever is compelled to apply this final remedy to some will tread in the footsteps of the Apostles and of the ancient Church.

units.la: Occurrit hic primum, quòd Paulus toti Corinthiorum Ecclesiæ scribens, vobis (inquit) congregatis. Atqui passim tunc in Ecclesijs constituerant Seniores, quorum authoritate res plerasq; gerebantur. At hanc causam non horum arbitrio permittit Apostolus, ut ipsi soli cum suis de ea statuant, sed in totius Ecclesiæ cœtu illam vult peragi. Cur enim ex paucorum sententia membrum aliquod ab Ecclesiæ corpore resecaretur? Cur pauci vulnus facerent, cuius dolor ad omnes redundaret? Et sanè prodesset tota Ecclesia conscia hæc fieri: cùm ne ministri vel alij, quorum est præcipua authoritas, invidia grauentur: tùm ut exemplo publico plures emendentur: ut deniq; coerceatur ministrorum & Seniorum ambitio, ne potestate sua imperiosius abutantur, & tandem de alijs quoq; rebus ad communem Ecclesiam pertinentibus sibi solis decernendi ius sumant, qui proximus ad tyrannidem gradus est. Quotquot ergo rem tanti momenti ad paucos referunt, vel etiam sibi solis vendicant excommunicandi potestatem, ij Ecclesiam iure suo spoliant, & tyrannidem affectant pijs intolerabilem. Idem dum morbis & vitijs mederi volunt, noua vulnera Ecclesiæ infligunt, neq; ijs medentur quos excludunt, sed potius seriores[?] reddunt, & multis alijs quiritandi occasionem præbent.
units.tr: Here first it occurs that Paul, writing to the whole Church of the Corinthians, says: "when you are gathered together." Yet at that time elders were appointed in the Churches everywhere, and by their authority most affairs were managed. But the apostle does not allow this matter to be settled by the judgment of these alone, so that they decide it by themselves with their own people; he wills it to be carried out in the assembly of the whole Church. For why should a member be cut off from the body of the Church by the opinion of a few? Why should a few inflict a wound whose pain would spread to everyone? Indeed it would be useful for the whole Church to know that these things are being done: first, so that the ministers, or others to whom the chief authority belongs, are not burdened with hatred; second, so that many may be amended by a public example; and finally, so that the ambition of ministers and elders is restrained, lest they abuse their power more imperiously and at last claim for themselves alone the right to decide other matters that pertain to the common Church, which is the nearest step to tyranny. Therefore all who refer a matter of such weight to a few, or claim for themselves alone the power of excommunication, deprive the Church of its right and aspire to a tyranny intolerable to the godly. Likewise, while they wish to heal diseases and vices, they inflict new wounds on the Church; they do not heal those whom they exclude but rather make them worse, and they give many others occasion for complaint.

units.la: Deinde ne Ecclesiam quidem temere conuenire vult Apostolus, sed ait: Vobis congregatis & Spiritu meo in nomine Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, cum potestate Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI. In nomine Christi eos conuenire iubet: nimirum ut qui hoc ius causam agere, nihil autem pro suorum affectuum libidine statuere velint. Et sui Spiritus præsentiam pollicetur, de qua nuper diximus, ut maiori cum fiducia rem agant. Et ideo etiam addit: Cum potestate Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI: respiciens nimirum ad promissionem, quæ hic pollicetur ratum fore, quicquid statuerint qui in suo nomine conueniunt. Neq; debet superuacanea cenfieri crebra hæc Spiritus, nominis, potestatis Christi repetitio. Ea enim admonet, in tota hac actione omnium mentes in vnum Christum intentas esse, omnium oculos hunc vnum respicere, omnium deniq; ora & linguas eundem vnum sonare debere. Ita vero nullum prorsus locum relinquit affectibus carnis, quos in causa tâ graui omnino sopire, imò exuere et calcare oportet, ne obstrepant. Si enim hoc magistratus facere debent, quando de re pecuniaria aut multis ad solum corpus pertinentibus agitur, quanto magis idem obseruandum est, quando animarum salus periclitatur? Minimè ergo probari debent temerarij & iracundi, qui præcipiti iudicio fulmen iflud mox in quosuis stringunt, & de excludendis hominibus ab Ecclesia potius quàm de colligedis soliciti sunt. Atqui vel solius Christi nomen, quod hic toties inculcat Paulus, huius pastoris mansuetudinem, fidem & studium erga oues suas ipsis in mentem reuocare debebat.
units.tr: Then the Apostle does not want the Church to be gathered rashly either, but says: "When you are gathered together, and my spirit, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ." He bids them gather in the name of Christ, clearly so that those who wish to take up this business plead it and decide nothing at the whim of their own passions. He also promises the presence of his Spirit, of which we spoke recently, so that they may act with greater confidence. For this reason he adds: "with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ," looking, no doubt, to the promise which here assures that whatever those decide who meet in his name will be ratified. Nor should this frequent repetition of Spirit, name and power of Christ be thought superfluous. For it reminds us that in the whole of this action the minds of all should be fixed on Christ alone, the eyes of all should look to him alone, and finally the mouths and tongues of all should sound forth the one and same thing. Thus it leaves no place at all for the affections of the flesh, which in so weighty a matter must be wholly quieted, nay, stripped off and trodden underfoot, lest they clamour. For if magistrates ought to do this when the matter is one of money or of fines touching the body alone, how much more must the same be observed when the salvation of souls is in danger? Those who are rash and quick-tempered, who in hasty judgment immediately hurl that thunderbolt at whomever, and who are more anxious to exclude people from the Church than to gather them in, ought therefore by no means to be approved. Yet the very name of Christ, which Paul so often impresses here, ought to have brought to their minds the gentleness, faithfulness and zeal of this shepherd toward his sheep.

units.la: Tertio illum quoq; quasi digito monstrat, in quem sententia ferri debeat, τὸν τοιοῦτον[?], id est, talem vel eiusmodi hominem: ita non tam illius personam, quàm qualis esset denotans: Impurus nimirum & incestus, qui nouercam vxoris loco habebat, vel alioqui illa hucusque ad nefariam libidinem abusus erat, ideoq; diuinis legibus capitis supplicium merebatur. Quo loco multa obseruatione dignum est, quòd cùm infinitis alijs quoque vitijs Corinthij laborarent, Paulus solum hunc tam graui supplicio dignum putauit. Itaque non temere in quosuis Excommunicationis sententia fer- ri debet. Sunt quidem peccata omnia, si in se aestimentur, aeternae mortis supplicio digna, & proinde à regno Dei eos excludunt, qui in illis paenitere nescij perseuerant. At quia nobis nō semper cōstat, quo animi proposito aliquis peccet, & qualis in posterum futurus sit, nō debemus temere quicquam statuere.
units.tr: Thirdly, he also points, as it were with a finger, at the one on whom sentence ought to be passed: "such a one" (τὸν τοιοῦτον), that is, such or this kind of man, so describing not so much his person as what sort he was: namely, impure and incestuous, who had his stepmother in place of a wife, or who had otherwise abused her for unlawful lust up to that time, and for this reason deserved capital punishment under the divine laws. In this place it is worth much attention that, although the Corinthians were troubled with countless other vices too, Paul judged only this one to deserve so grave a punishment. Therefore excommunication ought not to be pronounced rashly against anyone. Indeed, all sins, if they are judged in themselves, are worthy of the punishment of eternal death, and therefore they exclude from the kingdom of God those who persevere in them without learning to repent. But because we do not always know with what purpose of mind someone sins, and what he will be like in the future, we ought not to decide anything rashly.

units.la: Adhaec quia Excommunicatio publici exempli instar esse debet, nemo certè ea multandus erit, quàm qui publicum scandalum dedit, & quidè tale, quod nō alio remedio curari potest. Verùmtamen hic quoque cautione diligenti opus erit: ne videlicet propter vitium, quod genti alicui quasi proprium est, & quo maior hominum pars laborat, aliquis excommunicetur. Nam si hoc in uno fiat, in aliis quoq; idem fieri necesse erit: alioqui personas respicere dicentur, qui alterum illum excluserunt, & ita omnis vigor disciplinae intermorietur. At omnes excommunicare difficile fuerit & periculosum. Quomodo enim pauci pluribus resistent? Et quae facies erit Ecclesiae, cuius pars maior à communione excluditur? Quis item prohibebit, ne exclusi Ecclesiam propriā constituant, & ipsi quoq; Anathematismis & Excommunicationis fulmine pugnent contra eos, à quibus eiecti sunt? Vidit hoc olim D. Augustinus, qui lib. 3. contra Parmenianum sic scribit: Reuera, si contagio peccandi multitudinem inuaserit, diuinae disciplinae seuera misericordia necessaria est. Nā consilia separationis & inania sunt & pernitiosa atq; sacrilega, quia & impia & superba sunt, & plus perturbant infirmos bonos, quam corrigant animosos malos, &c. Quare tutissimum fuerit ἐπιεικείαν[?] adhibere, ne summum ius summa iniuria fiat, & Pauli modestiam imitari, qui poenas saepe quidem minatus est peccantibus, ad hanc tamen extremam rarissime descendit, nec nisi ineuitabili necessitate coactus. Nimis ergo temerarij sunt, qui vix audito scelere iras concipiunt, & anathemate eos feriunt, qui alia ratione commodiori in viam reuocari poterant.
units.tr: Moreover, since excommunication ought to be like a public example, certainly no one is to be punished with it more than the one who has given public scandal, and that of a kind which cannot be cured by any other remedy. Nevertheless, careful caution will be needed here too: lest someone be excommunicated on account of a vice which is, as it were, proper to some nation, and which the greater part of people suffer from. For if this were done in one case, the same would have to be done in others too; otherwise they will be said to have regarded persons when they excluded that one, and so all the vigour of discipline will die out. But to excommunicate everyone would be difficult and dangerous. For how would a few resist many? And what would the face of the Church be, whose greater part is cut off from communion? Who, moreover, will prevent the excluded from setting up their own church and, with anathemas and the thunderbolt of excommunication, fighting against those by whom they were cast out? Augustine saw this long ago, who in the third book against Parmenianus writes thus: "Indeed, if the contagion of sin should invade the multitude, the severe mercy of divine discipline is necessary. For plans of separation are both empty and pernicious and sacrilegious, because they are both impious and proud, and they disturb good but weak people more than they correct wicked but spirited ones," etc. Wherefore it will be safest to apply equity, lest the highest right become the highest wrong, and to imitate the moderation of Paul, who often threatened punishments against sinners, yet very rarely descended to this extreme sentence, and not unless compelled by unavoidable necessity. Therefore those are too rash who conceive anger on hearing of a crime scarcely spoken of, and strike with anathema those who could have been called back to the right way by some more suitable method.

units.la: Postremò finem totius actionis diligenter indicat, quando hunc Satanae tradere iubet ad interitum carnis, vt spiritus saluus sit in die illo Domini IESV. Ergo siue miser ille moreretur sub hac castigationis ferula, qua Satan in illum seuiturus erat, siue in vivis maneret, anima tamen eius confulcum[?] voluit Apostolus. Eundem ergo finem Ecclesia sibi proponere debet, si quando aliquem seuerius multare, vel etiam à societate sua excludere statuit: vt nimirum emendationem peccatoris quaerat, non interitum, & proinde apertas habeat semper fores gratiae, vt quandocunq; ille conuersus fuerit, absq; mora in gratiam recipiatur. Nec enim decet, vt qui Dei filij censeri volunt, Patre suo caelesti rigidiores aut duriores sint. At is non vult mortem peccatoris, quin eo ipso momento, quo is conuertitur, se ei propitium praebet: & vt idem singuli priuatim in fratribus obser- uent, qui ipsos aliquando offenderunt, Christus iubet. Si peccaverit ( inquit ) in te frater tuus, obiurga eum: & si resipuerit, remitte ei. Et si septies in die peccaverit in te, & septies in die conuersus fuerit ad te, dicens: Paenitet me: remitte ei. Quis vero dubitet, haec toti etiam Ecclesiae dici, quae ex solis Christianis constat? Non est ergo, vt operosis, diuturnis & ex parte contumeliosis satisfactionibus fatigentur ij, qui scelera sua iam agnoscunt, culpam deprecantur, paenitentiam aperte vouent, & Ecclesiae reconciliari cupiunt. Nec excusari potest eorum durities, qui tales diutius suspensos tenent, adeoq; ad desperationis praecipitia reducunt, quos cum gaudio recipere, & laetis gratiae Dei promissionibus erigere atque consolari debebant, sicuti Christus in filij perditi parabola docet. Peccauerat vt publicè in patrem, in fratrem primogenitum, in totam domum, denique in ipsos caelos: idem domi foris q; scandalum dederat. Attamen reuerso & scelus confitenti mox ignoscit pater, eodem[?] dignitati pristinae restituit, restitutum anulo reconciliationis donat, & propter ipsum mactari vult vitulũ illum saginatũ, & coniuiuiū parat, quo tota domus simul exhilaretur. Nonne Dauidi clamanti, Peccaui Domino: mox Nathan respondet: Dominus transtulit peccatum tuum? Cur ergo hodie satisfactionibus diuturnis discruciantur, qui eandem confessionem edunt, & laetis gratiae promissionibus erigi & confirmari debebant? Olim certè nocentissimum schisma in Ecclesia nimio suo rigore Nouatiani excitarunt: & quantum mali pepererint satisfactiones, quibus aliqui non malo zelo paenitentiam eorum, qui cum Ecclesia in gratiam redire cupiebant, prius probandam esse putauerunt, notius est, quàm vt multis demonstrari oporteat. Discant ergo Ecclesiae Pauli mansuetudinem imitari, qui vt primum infelicem istum respuisse audiuit, pro eodem intercesit, & ne aduersus eum longius procederetur, Corinthios grauiter monuit. Qui secus agunt, dum omnia ad vivum resecare, & Ecclesiam omnibus numeris perfectam atque impollutam constituere conantur, ij laboribus nunquam finiendis sese implicant, odia multorum praeter necessitatem sibi ipsis accersunt; adhaec principibus à fide alienis, sub quorum ditione agunt, suspecti fiunt, & eosdem saepe in rabiem accendunt, ut Ecclesijs hospitium negent, neque eos porro ferre velint, quos quotidie nouum quid parturire & mutuis condemnationibus inter se pugnare vident.
units.tr: Lastly, he carefully indicates the aim of the whole action, when he bids them deliver this man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus. Therefore, whether that wretched man should die under this rod of correction, with which Satan was going to rage against him, or whether he should remain alive, the Apostle nevertheless wished his soul to be cared for. The Church, then, ought to set this same aim before itself whenever it decides to punish someone more severely or even to exclude him from its fellowship: namely, that it seek the amendment of the sinner, not his ruin, and so always keep open the doors of grace, so that whenever he is converted he may be received back into favour without delay. For it is not fitting that those who wish to be counted sons of God should be harsher or more stern than their heavenly Father. But he does not want the death of the sinner; rather, at the very moment when he is converted, he shows himself propitious to him. And Christ bids each individual privately to observe the same toward brothers who have offended them at some time: "If your brother sin against you," he says, "rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him. And if he sin against you seven times in a day, and seven times in a day he turn back to you, saying, 'I repent,' forgive him." Who could doubt that this is said to the whole Church too, which consists solely of Christians? Therefore those who now acknowledge their crimes, beg pardon for their fault, openly vow repentance, and desire to be reconciled to the Church, ought not to be worn out with laborious, long-lasting and in part humiliating satisfactions. Nor can the hardness of those be excused who keep such people suspended for a long time, and so drive them down to the precipices of despair, whom they ought to receive with joy and raise up and console with the glad promises of the grace of God, as Christ teaches in the parable of the lost son. He had sinned publicly against his father, against his elder brother, against the whole household, and finally against heaven itself; at home and abroad he had given scandal likewise. Yet when he returned and confessed his wrong, the father at once forgave him, restored him to his former dignity, gave him back a ring as a pledge of reconciliation, and wished the fatted calf to be slaughtered for him, and prepared a banquet by which the whole household might be gladdened together. Did not Nathan answer David crying out, "I have sinned against the Lord," at once with, "The Lord has taken away your sin"? Why, then, today are those tormented with long satisfactions who make the same confession, when they ought to be raised up and strengthened by the joyful promises of grace? Certainly in former times the most harmful schism was stirred up in the Church by the excessive rigour of the Novatians; and how much evil satisfactions have brought forth, by which some, with no good zeal, thought that the repentance of those who desired to return to favour with the Church ought first to be tested, is too well known to need showing to many. Let the Churches therefore learn to imitate the gentleness of Paul, who, as soon as he heard that this unhappy man had been cast out, interceded for him, and, lest they proceed further against him, earnestly warned the Corinthians. Those who act otherwise, while they try to cut away everything to the quick and to make the Church perfect and unpolluted in every respect, entangle themselves in labours that are never to be finished, and needlessly draw upon themselves the hatred of many; moreover, they become suspect to princes alienated from the faith, under whose rule they live, and often inflame them to such fury that they deny hospitality to the Churches and no longer wish to bear with those whom they see daily giving birth to some new thing and fighting among themselves with mutual condemnations.

units.la: Et hæc quidem de Ecclesijs dicta sint, quae (ut olim Apostolorum tempore fiebat) sub principibus à fide alienis degunt. Nec enim mihi necessarium videtur, ut ista ad se trahant, qui principes habent vere Christianos, quorum authoritate morum disciplina constitui & conseruari potest. Urgent quidem Excommunicationem Anabaptistae, & quia hanc improbamus, nos Ecclesias impuras habere clamant. Sunt etiam alij, qui etsi principes habeant vere Christianos, neque leges desint, quibus morum licentia coercetur, adhuc tamen Senatu Ecclesiastico opus esse aiunt, qui in quorumuis mores animaduertat, & cui in principes quoque ius sit, ut eos qui scandalum aliquod publicum dederunt, à Coena Dominica communione arceat, & eosdem non nisi suo iudicio probatos, & praestitis prius satisfactionibus publicis, ad Ecclesiae societatem & Coenae usum rursus admittat. Quod si quis ipsorum sententiae contradicat, mox disciplinae omnis hostem esse vociferantur, & indignum cui in Ecclesia locus detur: quasi vero non illa alia disciplinae forma institui possit, quam quae ab ipsis confecta est. Sed parcant illi nobis, nec praecipiti iudicio nos damnent, qui non absque ratione ab ipsis dissentimus.
units.tr: These things may be said of the churches that, as in the days of the Apostles, live under rulers who are alien to the faith. Nor does it seem necessary to me that those who have truly Christian rulers should claim them for themselves, since under such rulers the discipline of morals can be established and preserved by their authority. The Anabaptists press for excommunication, and because we reject it, they cry out that we have impure churches. There are also others who, even where the rulers are truly Christian and laws exist to restrain licentious conduct, still say that an ecclesiastical senate is needed, one that will examine the morals of everyone, including the rulers, and that has the right to bar from the Lord's Supper those who have given some public scandal, and to readmit them to the fellowship of the Church and the use of the Supper only when they have been approved by its judgment and have first made public satisfaction. If anyone contradicts their opinion, they at once shout that he is an enemy of all discipline and unworthy of a place in the Church, as though some other form of discipline could not be instituted besides the one they have devised. But let them spare us, and not condemn us with a hasty judgment, since we dissent from them for good reason.

units.la: Distinguunt illi inter iurisdictionem Ecclesiasticam & Politicam, quoad morum disciplinam & scelerum poenas. At distinctio ista ex Pontificum officina depromta est, in Scripturis vero sacris nusquam habetur. Etenim in Nouo Testamento eandem magistratus rationem esse constat, quae olim in veteri fuit, cum Christus dixerit, se non venisse ut Legem dissoluat, sed ut impleat. At olim penes iudices & Reges fuit potestas animaduertendi in eos, qui peccauerant: neque se ei negotio Sacerdotes & Prophetae admiscebant, nisi quoad admonitiones & correptiones, quas ex Dei verbo adhibebant pro delictorum ratione. Idem ergo in Nouo Testamento obseruari debet, neque opus est, ut verbi administri Senatum habeant peculiarem, aut ut quae politici magistratus sunt, quacunq; ratione sibi vendicent. Possunt quidem morum Censores constitui, quibus in Repub. maiori omnino opus est, vbi ordinarij Magistratus non possunt negotijs omnibus sufficere. At illi ipsi non nisi ex Magistratus authoritate creari, & ex eiusdem mandato omnia agere debent, non propriam & ab ordinario Magistratu distinctam potestatem vsurpare. Distinxit enim inter politicum & Ecclesiasticum ordinem Deus, & illi quidem rerum gubernacula cum praemijs & poenis, quae vel bonis vel malis debentur, commisit: huic vero Verbi ministerium & Sacramentorum administrationem credidit. Licet ergo ministris Ecclesiae principes viros monere ex Dei verbo, vel etiam eosdem (si mereantur) durius corripere, sicuti Prophetas olim factitasse scimus: at eosdem sibi aut suo Consistorio subijcere non licet, nisi eos imitari libeat, quos Magistratus contemptui habituros, & Maiestatem Regum conuitijs petituros esse, olim Petrus praedixit. Quid multis? periculosum omnino nobis videtur, duos magistratus constituere in eodem populo: neque exemplum vllum videmus, quo istud probari possit. Et quàm hoc vtile sit, me videre non posse, libenter & ingenuè fateor. Nam qui legitimi magistratus authoritate & legibus non possunt in ordinem redigi, ij multò minus Seniorum siue Ecclesiastici Senatus imperio se coerceri patientur, quem cum toto suo apparatu ludibrio habebunt. Qui vero ex magistratibus antea in tuenda morum disciplina remissiores erant, aut indulgentiores, nunc gaudebunt oniùs hoc in alios translatu esse, & illam omnino negligent. Quid autem his cessantibus facient Seniores? Certè plerisque ludibrio erunt, dum veluti lepores (vt poëta canit) dare iura leonibus audent, conantur, truces sine vi frenare tyrannos: multi quoq; ex magistratibus ad illud non modo conniuebunt, verumetiam in sinu suo ridebunt infirmam & ridiculam noui illius Senatus dominationem. Fiet ergo, vt vbi prius aliqua saltem erat disciplina, & interdum multis atq; poenarum exemplis aliqui terrebantur: iam illa quoq; è medio sublata, impunitas regnare incipiat cum immani & publico ministerij sacri cõtemptu. Neq; hoc temere dicimus: nam hoc ita fieri exempla docent, quæ ita nota sunt om-nibus, vt plura de hac re dicere non fit opus. At si in effreni ista licentia Seniores illi excommunicat pergant omnes, qui se ipsis opponunt, periculũ est, ne aliquando maior fit excommunicatorum quàm cum Ecclesia communicantium numerus. Dicant ergo mihi Seniores, quid tunc faciendum esse cen-seant. Respondebunt, opinor: Tunc magistratus imperio opus fore, qui improbos illos coerceat, ne sua proteruia & temeritate Ecclesiã euertant. Assentior & ego huic consilio. At si tunc illud fieri debet, quando vix sine publico discrimine fieri poterit, cur non sua magistratui authoritas integra relinquitur, & ijsdem tota publicæ disciplinæ gubernatio mandatur, priusquam res ad extremũ vsq; deueniat? Possent hic multa alia dici, quæ breuitatis studio nunc prætermittimus.
units.tr: They distinguish between ecclesiastical and political jurisdiction, as far as the discipline of morals and the punishment of crimes is concerned. But that distinction has been taken from the workshop of the Popes, and it is nowhere found in the holy Scriptures. For it is clear that in the New Testament the magistrate's position is the same as it was in the Old, since Christ said that he had come not to dissolve the Law but to fulfil it. In former times the power to punish those who had sinned rested with judges and kings, and priests and prophets did not mix themselves into that business, except for the admonitions and rebukes which they applied, according to the nature of the offences, from the Word of God. The same ought therefore to be observed in the New Testament, and there is no need for the ministers of the Word to have a separate senate, or to claim for themselves, by whatever means, what belongs to the civil magistrates. Censors of morals may indeed be appointed, and a large commonwealth certainly has need of them, where the ordinary magistrates cannot suffice for all the business. But these men ought to be created only by the authority of the magistrate, and to act only on his command, not to usurp a power of their own, distinct from the ordinary magistrate. For God distinguished between the political and the ecclesiastical order: to the one he entrusted the reins of government, with the rewards and punishments due to good and bad alike; to the other he committed the ministry of the Word and the administration of the sacraments. Therefore, although it is lawful for the ministers of the Church to admonish rulers from the Word of God, and even to rebuke them more sharply if they deserve it, as we know the Prophets did in former times, it is not lawful to subject them to themselves or to their consistory, unless we are willing to imitate those whom Peter foretold would hold the magistrates in contempt and assail the majesty of kings with insults. What more is there to say? It seems to us altogether dangerous to set up two magistracies in the same people, and we see no example by which this could be proved. I freely and frankly confess that I cannot see how it could be useful. For those who cannot be brought into order by the authority and laws of the lawful magistrate will much less allow themselves to be restrained by the command of the elders or of the ecclesiastical senate, which they will hold up to ridicule along with its whole apparatus. And those magistrates who were formerly more lax or indulgent in maintaining discipline of morals will now rejoice all the more that this burden has been transferred to others, and will altogether neglect it. What, then, will the elders do when the magistrates cease? Surely they will be a laughing-stock to most people, while, like hares (as the poet sings), they dare to lay down laws for lions, and try to curb fierce tyrants without force. Many of the magistrates will not only connive at this, but will even laugh in their sleeves at the feeble and ridiculous domination of that new senate. So it will come about that where there was at least some discipline before, and sometimes some were terrified by many examples of punishment, now that discipline too is removed from the midst, impunity will begin to reign, together with a monstrous and public contempt for the sacred ministry. Nor do we say this rashly: for examples teach that this is how it happens, and they are so well known to everyone that there is no need to say more about the matter. But if those elders in this unbridled licence go on excommunicating all who oppose them, there is a danger that at some point the number of the excommunicated will exceed the number of those who communicate with the Church. Let the elders tell me, then, what they think should be done at that point. I suppose they will answer: then the power of the magistrate will be needed, to restrain those wicked men, lest by their insolence and rashness they overthrow the Church. I too agree with this counsel. But if that is to be done only when it can hardly be done without public peril, why is the magistrate's authority not left intact, and the whole governance of public discipline not entrusted to him, before the matter comes to the extreme? Many other things could be said here, which we now pass over for the sake of brevity.

units.la: Deinde, neq; hoc videre possumus, quã ratione Cœna Domini huic negotio admiscerì debeat, vt nimirũ Exclusionis organum fiat, quod Christus communionis Christianæ vinculum esse voluit. Et obstat nobis, quòd olim propter peccata à sacrificiorum & cultus diuini societate adeo nemine exclusum fuisse scimus, vt potius qui peccauerant, ad templum venire, & pro delicti ratione victimã offerre iuberentur. Neq; in Nouo testamento huius Exclusionis exemplũ vllum habetur. Et quis non videat, quàm durum sit aliquem prohibere, quo minus cum Ecclesia morte Christi annuntiet, & eidem pro exhibito redemptionis facta beneficio gratias agat? Et cur nos Symbolis externis eum indignum esse dicamus, quem ipse Christus suo corpore & sanguine alere dignatur? Dicit illi, Christum prohibuisse, ne margaritas porcis & Sanctum canibus proijciamus. Agnoscimus, & nos Christi præceptum, sed nõ ea nobis est audacia, vt canes & porcos velimus dicere eos, qui ad Ecclesiam redire, qui cum illa fide in Christum profiteri & Christi seruatoris beneficiũ publice prædicare cupiunt. At periculũ est (inquis) ne qui nos fallant. Id vero isti non tuo, sed suo periculo facient: neq; tu periculum hoc omne effugeris, si per decennium aliquem satisfactionibus theatricis fa-tigaris. Hypocritam enim sceleratum nulla temporis mora emendabit. Quàm vero periculosum sit satisfactiones exigere, quarum Scripturæ nullam mentionem faciunt, jam ante diximus, & res ipsa loquitur. Neq; nos ab ijs, qui ad Cœnam Domini accedere gestiunt, plus quiddam audemus exigere, quàm Paulus, cui sufficere visum fuit, vt quisq; seipsum probet, neque voluit vt alij in aliorum consciẽtias scrutinium facerent.
units.tr: Next, we also cannot see in what way the Lord's Supper ought to be mixed up in this business, so that it becomes an instrument of exclusion, when Christ willed it to be the bond of Christian communion. And what stands in our way is that we know that in former times no one was so excluded from the sacrifices and the fellowship of divine worship that those who had sinned were not rather ordered to come to the temple and offer a victim according to the nature of the offence. Nor is any example of such exclusion found in the New Testament. And who does not see how harsh it is to forbid anyone to proclaim the death of Christ with the Church, and to give thanks for the benefit of redemption that has been accomplished? And why should we call him unworthy of external symbols whom Christ himself deigns to nourish with his body and blood? The objector says that Christ forbade us to cast pearls before swine and what is holy before dogs. We acknowledge the precept of Christ too, but we do not have the audacity to call dogs and swine those who wish to return to the Church, who desire to profess with that faith in Christ and to proclaim publicly the benefit of Christ the Saviour. But, you say, there is a danger that they may deceive us. Yet they will do this at their own peril, not yours; nor will you escape all this danger if you wear someone out for ten years with theatrical satisfactions. For no lapse of time will reform a wicked hypocrite. How dangerous it is to demand satisfactions, of which the Scriptures make no mention, we have said before, and the thing itself speaks. Nor do we presume to require anything more of those who eagerly approach the Lord's Supper than Paul required, who thought it sufficient that each one should examine himself, and did not want others to pry into the consciences of others.

units.la: Obiiciunt nobis aliqui D. Ambrosij exemplum, qui Theodosium Imp. à templi & sacrorum communione excluserit, & culpam cum lachrymis suppliciter deprecantē per menses amplius octo suspenderit. At ego miror eos exemplo vti, cuius ipsos pudere debebat, ne in suspicionem veniant, ipsos quoq; potestate affectare, qua contra principes pro suo arbitrio abutantur. Etenim si Ambrosium cum Theodosio conferas, huius quidem pietas satis laudari nequit, illius vero vehementia (quod tanti viri pace dixerim) non potest excusari, qui absq; Ecclesiæ & collegarũ consensu, priuata authoritate tantum facinus aggressus est, quo Eccle-siæ simul & tota religio Christiana in extremũ discrimen adduci poterat, si in principem paulo ferociorem incidisset. Enimuero iniquius & durius æquo secum agi non nesciuit Theodosius, vt ex eius verbis apparet, quibus Ambrosium præcatus est, vt communis Domini IESV CHRISTI bonitatem respiciat, neq; sibi claudat fores gratiæ, quas omnibus qui resipiscunt, Christus aperuit. At pro incredibili sua pietate noluit suo iure audacius vti. Imitati sunt quidem Ambrosij exemplum Romani Pontifices, sed non sine totius orbis Christiani periculo. Coaluit enim illorum potentia hac potissimum ratione eò vsq; excreuisse, vt Regibus quoq; potentissimis intolerabilis fuerit. Notũ enim est omnibus, quàm indignus modis fortissimi Imperat. Heinrichus IIII. & huius filius Heinrichus V. Fridericus Barbarossa, Fridericus item II. Ludouicus IIII. & similes alij à Romanis Pontificibus excommunicati, qui item bellorũ motus, quot cædes, quot miserabiles vrbium euersiones & horrenda regnorũ excidia inde enata sint. Cur ergo per Euangelij prædicationem Pontificibus vix exortum Excommunicationis fulmen alijs permittatur, qui & ipsi fortasse eo abutentur? Nam vt optimi sint, qui nunc hanc causam agunt, quis nos de successoribus eorũ securos faciet? Quis ité fructus bonus ex eo sperari poterit, quod nullo Christi instituto nititur? Est etenim insatiabilis hominum ambitio, & rari inueniuntur, qui non insolentiores fiant, quando se supra alios eminere vident. Et cum euanidus huius seculi honoribus pleriq; superbiat, maius exi-lis periculum erit, quorum potestas diuini nominis authoritate commendatur. Certè qui Ecclesiasticas historias non oscitanter legerint, mox videbunt, Episcoporum ambitione omnibus seculis maximorum maximorum scandalorum causam fuisse, qui anathematismis & Excommunicationibus mutuis inter se dimicando totum orbem Christianum in partes distraxerunt, & Ecclesias multas euerterunt. Possem multa alia pericula & incommoda commemorare, sed sufficiat nunc cordatis cogitandi occasionem praebuisse. Quod si aliqui exclusionem qualemcunq; instituere velint, qua à magistratu legitimo exerceatur, & politica potius sit, quàm Ecclesiastica, cum illis nulla erit nobis contentio. Etenim nostrae quoque ciuitatis leges Excommunicatione puniunt eos, qui in audiendis concionibus & Coenae Dominicae usu negligentiores, insuper vita scelerata Ecclesiam offendunt. Tales enim, si in urbe viuant, ex tribuum societate eiiciuntur, ut commercia cum nemine habere possint, neque illis ad honores & munera publica accessus est: sin in agro habitent, à pascuorum & sylvarum communium usu arcentur. Et haec ratio nobis commodissima est. Faciant aliae urbes & gentes, quod è re sui populi esse putarint, quando constat, eandem disciplinae formam ubique locorum constitui & observari non posse. Imo ne illis quidem suam felicitatem inuidemus, qui sua illa Excommunicatione, vel exclusione potius à Coena, cum aliquo fructu uti possunt: hoc modo illos rogamus, ut intra suos fines se contineant, neque eundem calceum (quod dicitur) omnium pedibus induere conentur, & ab anathematismis abstineant, neue temere damnent Ecclesias, quibus diuersa disciplinae ratio magis probatur.
units.tr: Some object to us the example of St Ambrose, who excluded the emperor Theodosius from the communion of the temple and the sacred rites, and kept him waiting for more than eight months, though he humbly begged pardon for his fault with tears. But I wonder that they use an example which ought to make them ashamed, lest they come under suspicion of aiming at a power of their own by which they might abuse it against princes at their own discretion. For if you compare Ambrose with Theodosius, the piety of the latter cannot be praised enough, while the vehemence of the former (with due respect to so great a man) cannot be excused, since he undertook so great a deed on his own private authority, without the consent of the Church and his colleagues, a deed by which the Church and the whole Christian religion might have been brought into extreme danger, had he fallen upon a ruler somewhat fiercer. Indeed Theodosius did not fail to see that he was treated more unjustly and harshly than was right, as appears from his words, in which he begged Ambrose to regard the common goodness of the Lord Jesus Christ and not to shut against him the doors of grace, which Christ has opened to all who repent. But because of his incredible piety he was unwilling to use his right more boldly. The Roman Pontiffs did indeed imitate Ambrose's example, but not without danger to the whole Christian world. For their power grew strong, chiefly by this means, to such a height that it became intolerable even to the most powerful kings. It is known to all in what unworthy ways the most valiant emperors Henry IV, his son Henry V, Frederick Barbarossa, likewise Frederick II, Louis IV, and others like them were excommunicated by the Roman Pontiffs; how many wars and rebellions, how many slaughters, how many miserable overthrows of cities and dreadful ruins of kingdoms arose from this. Why, then, should the thunderbolt of excommunication, hardly born through the preaching of the Gospel, be granted to others by the Pontiffs, who may perhaps abuse it too? For even if those who now plead this cause are the best of men, who will make us sure of their successors? What good fruit can be hoped for from a thing that rests on no institution of Christ? For human ambition is insatiable, and few are found who do not grow more arrogant when they see themselves raised above others. And since most men swell with the empty honours of this age, the danger will be all the greater where the power is commended by the authority of the divine name. Certainly those who read the ecclesiastical histories with attention will soon see that in every age the ambition of bishops has been the cause of very great scandals, who by fighting one another with mutual anathemas and excommunications have torn the whole Christian world into factions and overthrown many churches. I could recall many other dangers and inconveniences, but for now it is enough to have given thoughtful people occasion to reflect. But if some wish to set up some kind of exclusion, provided it is exercised by the lawful magistrate and is political rather than ecclesiastical, there will be no quarrel between us and them. For the laws of our own city also punish with excommunication those who are negligent in attending sermons and in the use of the Lord's Supper, and who, moreover, offend the Church by a wicked life. For such people, if they live in the city, are expelled from the fellowship of the tribes, so that they can have dealings with no one, and they have no access to honours and public offices; if they live in the countryside, they are kept from the use of the common pastures and woods. This arrangement seems most suitable to us. Let other cities and nations do what they think is for the good of their own people, since it is clear that the same form of discipline cannot be set up and observed everywhere. Indeed we do not begrudge those their happiness who can make use, with some profit, of their own excommunication, or rather exclusion from the Supper. We ask them only to keep within their own borders, and not to try to put the same shoe (as the saying goes) on everyone's feet, and to refrain from anathemas, and not rashly condemn churches to which a different form of discipline is more pleasing.

units.la: At vos ô viri Christiani, monemus, ut Paulini exempli memores, de coercenda vitiorum licentia & constituenda morum disciplina serio cogitetis. Si enim reprehensionem & correptionem tam acrem Corinthij meruerunt, quòd vnius hominis flagitium tam diu impunitum dimiserant: nulla profectò venia digni erunt, qui hodie Euangelij quidem doctrina & verae fidei professione gloriantur, interim verò omnis generis scelera licenter grassari sinunt. Peccatur in eo fere vbique gentium. Regnat apud omnis loci & ordinis homines infame gulae studium & deformis ebrietas, qua nihil homine ingenuo turpius, nihil seruilius, nihil indecorum magis aut inhonestius fingi potest. Alios impudens & belluina scortandi & moechandi libido transuersos abripit, & multi ne ab incestis quidem nuptijs abhorrent. Multos auaritia insatiabili cupiditate inflammat, vt tam charitatis fraternae quàm iustitiae omnis immemores, monopolijs, fraudibus & voracibus vsuris quosvis grauent & expilent, vt iam de venali iure & violenta pauperum oppressione nihil dicamus. Audiuntur passim atroces blasphemiae & horribilis diuini nominis abusus, dum alij per illud execrantur & deierant, alij sub eius praetextu quosvis turpiter fallunt, multi eodem ad artes illicitas abutuntur. Ardent multi inuidia, aemulatione, odijs, vindictae cupiditate, quae simultates, inimicitias & rixas quotidianas pariunt. Sunt qui ne à sanguinis quidem effusione abhorrent, cùm militia mercenaria plerisque quaestus honestius videatur, quam merito scholam omnium scelerum dixeris. Interea verò Dei verbum à plerisque contemnitur, vel tunc modo in aliquo pretio est, quando aliqua lucri aut maioris licentiae spes ex eo affulget. Tunc fere ex Ecclesiae bonis ditescunt, qui eius labes & pestes sunt. Et ad ista dormiunt plerunq; principes viri, & multi ne ministros quidem Ecclesiae patienter ferunt, qui ista liberius accusant, multi verò ministrorum ijsdem turpiter blandiuntur. Hinc ergo horribilis confusio nascitur, quae vtriusq; ordinis statum siue authoritatem labefactat. Nam & Verbi praedicatione minus proficiunt ministri: & qui magistratum gerunt, partim pijs minus grati sunt, quia absq, Dei Verbo regnant, partim nimia indulgentia seipsos improborum ludibrijs exponunt. Sequuntur ergo scandala omnis generis. Propter ista enim Ecclesiae diffamantur, & Euangelij doctrina male audit, quasi bonis operibus inimica peccandi licentiam stabiliat. Accedit aliud longè grauius, quòd multi minimè mali, & publicae honestatis amantes, impostorum & sectariorum artibus atq; calumnijs se facilius seduci patiuntur, vt zelo, pio quidem & bono, sed inconsiderato, ab Ecclesijs secessionem faciant, & sua accessione improbos illos confirment, qui omnem Ecclesiae ordinem abolere conantur. Multi item absterrentur, quò minus Euangelium audiant, & relictis[?] superstitionibus Christo nomen dent. Isti ergo scandalis Dei ira accenditur, vt ipse eos puniat, qui seipsos iudicare & corrigere nolunt. Debet itaq; horum consideratio diligens principes simul & Ecclesiarum ministros excitare, vt in remedio istis malis adhibendo operas suas magno studio conferant: & hi quidem docere, monere, corripere, hortari, increpare, minari & quacunq; possunt ratione instare debent, vt homines peccata agnoscant, & serio ad Deum conuertantur. Qui vero ad Reipub. gubernacula sedent,ij morum licentiam bonis legibus coerceant, transgressores harum, vt par est, puniant, scandala e medio tollant, exemplo bono reliquis praeeant, denique in retinenda atque conseruanda disciplina publica acres sint & in omnem occasionem intenti.
units.tr: But you, O Christian men, we admonish to remember Paul's example and to think seriously about curbing the license of vices and establishing discipline of morals. For if the Corinthians deserved such sharp rebuke and correction, because they had allowed the shameful conduct of one man to go unpunished for so long, then those will surely be worthy of no pardon who today boast of the teaching of the Gospel and the profession of true faith, yet meanwhile allow every kind of crime to run riot unchecked. Sin is committed almost everywhere among the nations. A notorious love of gluttony and foul drunkenness reigns among men of every place and rank; nothing can be imagined more disgraceful to a free man, nothing more servile, nothing more unbecoming or dishonourable. Others a shameless and bestial lust for whoring and adultery drags off course, and many do not shrink even from incestuous marriages. Many an insatiable greed inflames, so that, forgetful of both brotherly charity and all justice, they burden and plunder everyone through monopolies, frauds and ravenous usury; not to mention the buying and selling of justice and the violent oppression of the poor. Everywhere are heard atrocious blasphemies and the horrible abuse of the divine name, while some curse and swear by it, others under its pretext deceive anyone shamefully, and many misuse it for unlawful arts. Many burn with envy, rivalry, hatred and the desire for revenge, which produce enmities, feuds and daily quarrels. There are those who do not even shrink from shedding blood, since mercenary soldiery seems to most a more honourable gain, when one might rightly call it a school of every crime. Meanwhile the Word of God is despised by many, or is held in some esteem only when some hope of gain or of greater licence shines forth from it. Then, for the most part, those who are the blight and plague of the Church grow rich from its goods. And to these things princes often turn a blind eye, and many do not patiently bear even the ministers of the Church who accuse these things more freely, while many ministers shamefully flatter the same vices. Hence arises a dreadful confusion, which weakens the state and authority of both orders. For ministers accomplish less by the preaching of the Word, and those who hold the magistracy are partly less pleasing to the godly, because they rule without the Word of God, and partly by excessive indulgence they expose themselves to the mockery of the wicked. Thus scandals of every kind follow. For on account of these things the Churches are defamed, and the teaching of the Gospel gets a bad name, as if it, hostile to good works, established licence for sinning. There is added something far more serious: many who are not at all wicked, and who love public decency, allow themselves to be more easily seduced by the arts and calumnies of impostors and sectarians, so that, with a zeal that is pious and good but ill-considered, they secede from the Churches, and by their joining confirm those wicked men who try to abolish all church order. Many likewise are deterred from hearing the Gospel and, abandoning superstitions, giving their name to Christ. Therefore the wrath of God is kindled by these scandals, so that He Himself punishes those who are unwilling to judge and correct themselves. Careful consideration of these things ought therefore to stir up princes and the ministers of the Churches alike, that they may apply their efforts with great zeal to applying a remedy to these evils: and indeed the ministers ought to teach, admonish, rebuke, exhort, reprove, threaten, and press on by every means they can, so that men may acknowledge their sins and seriously turn to God. Those who sit at the helm of the commonwealth should restrain the licence of morals by good laws, punish transgressors of these, as is fitting, remove scandals from the midst, go before the rest with a good example, and finally be keen and alert to every opportunity in retaining and preserving public discipline.

units.la: Ex hoc studio pulcherrimi fructus enascentur. Primo enim infamiae nota liberabuntur Ecclesiae, quae hactenus propter aliquorum licentiam male audiuerunt. Deinde suus quoque honor Christo afferetur, cuius Euangelium ideo multis suspectum, vel etiam exosum est, quod eius sectatores licentius viuere cernunt. Tertio emendabuntur multi & seruabuntur, qui nisi coercentur, anima simul & corpore in aeternum perirent. Quarto contagionis periculum vitabitur, ne simpliciores & infirmi aliorum exemplis malis inficiantur. Quinto ij quoque, qui naturâ ferociores sunt, exemplis eorum, qui castigantur, territi officium facient, & minus proterrient. Ex his fructus omnium exoptatissimus & saluberrimus dependet, quod nimirum Deus publico hoc studio placatur, vt peccatis hominum irasci desinat. At qui Deo propitio vtuntur, ij & in melius indies proficiunt, & huius quoq; seculi bonis atq; commodis sub illius protectione fruuntur. Habemus ergo hic veram & compendiosissimam rationem, qua nostri temporis pericula, quae vndiq; nos terrent, euitemus, & felicitatem veram atq; stabilem consequamur. Consulitur de eo à multis, & variae sunt hominum sententiae, dum quisque suo affectui indulget. Sed frustra omnes consultant, qui poenitentiae publicae & placandi Dei studium negligunt.
units.tr: From this zeal the most beautiful fruits will arise. First, the Churches will be freed from the mark of infamy, which until now have had a bad name on account of the licence of some. Second, honour will also be brought to Christ, whose Gospel is for this reason suspected by many, or even hated, because they see its followers living more licentiously. Third, many will be amended and saved, who, unless they are restrained, would perish eternally, both in soul and body. Fourth, the danger of contagion will be avoided, lest the simpler and weaker be infected with evil by the examples of others. Fifth, those also who are fiercer by nature, terrified by the examples of those who are punished, will do their duty and be less disorderly. From these things there follows the most desirable and most wholesome fruit of all, namely that God is appeased by this public zeal, so that He ceases to be angry at the sins of men. And those who enjoy God's favour also make progress for the better day by day, and under His protection they also enjoy the goods and advantages of this age. We have here, therefore, a true and most direct method by which we may avoid the dangers of our time, which terrify us on every side, and attain true and lasting happiness. Many consult about this, and opinions of men are varied, while each indulges his own inclination. But all consult in vain who neglect public repentance and the zeal of appeasing God.

units.la: Caeterum quamuis ista hodie monere & optare facilius est, quam effecta dare, & (vt Christus ipse monuit) hi nouissimorum temporum mores sunt, quos emendare vix quisquam poterit, donec ille eis finem imponat aduentu suo gloriosso, non debent tamen pij animum despondere, multo minus autem de Euangelij Veritate dubitare, aut zelo praecipiti ab Ecclesijs discedere, in quibus purior verbi diuini vox sonat, Deus per Filium sui inuocatur, & Sacramenta ex Christi instituto rite dispensantur. Agnoscant illi potius ineffabile istud Dei beneficium, qui in tanta nouissimorum temporum infelicitate aliquam saltem Ecclesiae formam nobis seruat, & principes excitat, qui etsi vitijs suis laborent, Verbo tamen suo locum dant, & abolitis superstitionibus pu-riorem Dei cultum instaurari patiuntur. Itaq; cum gratiarum actione hoc tanto beneficio fruantur, & sibi ipsis singuli disciplinam adhibeant, & quae in suis moribus vitiosa esse animaduertunt, studiose emendent: apud alios item monendo hortando & increpando instent, vt ex hoc ceu vniuersali mundi huius naufragio aliquos seruent, qui cum ipsis Deo pure seruiant, & salutem aeternam assequantur, quam nobis suae mortis merito acquisiuit IESVS CHRISTVS, Dominus noster: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Yet although it is easier to advise and wish these things today than to deliver results, and (as Christ Himself warned) these are the morals of the last times, which scarcely anyone will be able to correct until He puts an end to them by His glorious coming, the godly ought not to lose heart, much less doubt the truth of the Gospel, or in headlong zeal withdraw from those Churches in which the purer voice of the divine Word sounds, God is called upon through the Son, and the Sacraments are rightly administered according to Christ's institution. Rather let those acknowledge that ineffable benefit of God who, amid such great unhappiness of the last times, preserves for us at least some form of the Church and raises up princes who, although they labour under their own vices, nevertheless give place to His Word and allow, with the superstitions abolished, the purer worship of God to be restored.
