Therefore, since they enjoy this great benefit with thanksgiving, let each one apply discipline to himself, and diligently amend whatever he notices to be faulty in his own morals; and let them also press on with others, by admonishing, exhorting and rebuking, so that out of this, as it were the universal shipwreck of this world, they may save some who with themselves serve God purely and attain eternal salvation, which Jesus Christ our Lord acquired for us by the merit of His death: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXV.
units.tr: HOMILY XXV.

units.la: Non est bona gloriatio vestra. An nescitis, quòd paululum fermenti totam massam fermentat? Expurgate igitur vetus fermentum, vt sitis noua massa, sicut estis fermenti expertes. Etenim Pascha nostrum pro nobis sacrificatum est, nempe Christus. Itaque festum agitemus non fermento veteri, nec fermento malitiae & nequitiae, sed non fermentatis panibus synceritatis & veritatis.
units.tr: Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump? Purge out therefore the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover, is sacrificed for us. Therefore let us keep the feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

units.la: QVàmuis Corinthiorum ecclesia multis ijsq; grauissimis vitijs pollutà esset, pauci tamen illa agnoscebant, quin potius caeca ambitione & confidentia dementati aliis ecclesijs praestantiores volebant haberi. Erat hic nocentissimus error, quia poenitentia obstabat, & causa erat, vt quotidie in peius proficerent, maioremq; sibi ipsis infamiam indies conflarent. Quapropter admodum graviter cum illis Paulus agit, & ne quid negare aut dissimulare possent, nuper immane & pudendum hominis incesti scelus ipsis ob oculos posuit, quem hucusque turpi nimis indulgentia tolerauerant non sine publica ignominia totius ecclesiae & nominis Christiani quo gloriabantur. Docuit ergo quid facere ipsos deceat, vt notam iam eluant, & simul miserum illum seruent, qui alioqui periturus erat. Vidimus illic disciplinae ecclesiasticae exemplum quale olim in usu fuit, quo docemur, qua seueritate etiam hodie in expurgandis sceleribus uti debeant, quicunque ecclesiarum saluti & honori consultum volunt. At quia doctrina non omnes statim obediunt, nunc adhortationem subjicit, qua illos urget, ut in re tanti momenti serio agant, & se Christianos esse ipsis operibus testentur.
units.tr: Although the congregation of the Corinthians was polluted with many and very grave vices, few acknowledged them. Rather, blinded by ambition and overconfidence, they wanted to be considered superior to other congregations. This was a most harmful error, because it stood in the way of repentance, and it was the cause of their growing worse every day and bringing greater infamy upon themselves with each passing day. Therefore Paul deals very severely with them. So that they could deny or dissemble nothing, he has just set before their eyes the monstrous and shameful crime of a man living in incest, which they had tolerated until now with far too much indulgence, not without public disgrace to the whole church and to the Christian name in which they boasted. He therefore taught them what it behoved them to do, so that they might now wipe away the stain and at the same time save that wretched man, who otherwise was going to perish. Here we see an example of church discipline such as once was in use, by which we are taught with what severity they ought also today to proceed in purging out wickedness, whoever wish to provide for the safety and honour of the churches. But because not everyone obeys teaching at once, he now adds an exhortation, by which he urges them to act seriously in a matter of such great importance and to prove by their works that they are Christians.

units.la: Rursus autem ante omnia confidentiam illorum reprehendit, qua elati de seipsis gloriabantur, perinde ac si nihil in ipsis esset reprehensione dignum. Non est bona (inquit) gloriatio vestra. Breuis sententia, sed quae animos superbos & ambitiosos plurimum mouere potuit, quibus bonum & honestum videtur, quicquid semel instituerunt. At Paulus illos imprudenter & stulte facere ait, & honori suo pessime consulere, quando ad hunc modum superbiant. Et habet dicti sui graues atque iustas causas. Primo enim per se inhonestum & turpe est, si qui vitiis apertis infames sunt, nihilominus insolenter suas virtutes iactant, & aliis praestantiores haberi volunt. Accedebat huic vitio aliud aeque indignum, quod singuli suis modo rebus intenti, aliorum vitam atque mores nihil ad se pertinere putabant. Itaque suam innocentiam singuli iactabant, neque animadvertebant se interea in Deum simul & in charitatis Christianae leges vehementer peccare cum & Dei gloriam ignavi nimis negligerent, & sua indulgentia eos perderent, quos ab exitio debebant reuocare. Etenim quantum infelici huic, de quo potissimum hic agitur, nocuerint, res ipsa docet, quando ille quoad ipsos animam simul & corpore periturus erat, nisi Paulus sua gratuitate ipsis author fuisset, ut eum in viam salutis reducerent.
units.tr: Again, above all he rebukes their self-confidence, by which, puffed up with themselves, they boasted as if there were nothing in them worthy of reproof. "Your boasting is not good," he says. It is a brief saying, but one that could greatly stir proud and ambitious minds, to whom whatever they have once undertaken seems good and honourable. But Paul says that they are acting imprudently and foolishly, and are doing their own reputation the greatest harm, when they take such pride in this way. And he has grave and just grounds for his words. First, it is in itself dishonourable and shameful if people who are notorious for open vices nonetheless boast arrogantly of their virtues and want to be considered superior to others. To this fault was added another no less unworthy one: each, intent only upon his own affairs, thought that the lives and morals of others did not concern him. Thus each boasted of his own innocence, and did not notice that meanwhile they were sinning grievously both against God and against the laws of Christian love. For they were lazily neglecting the glory of God, and by their indulgence they were destroying those whom they ought to have called back from ruin. How much harm they had done to that unhappy man, of whom especially this passage speaks, the thing itself shows: he was going to perish in soul and body, as far as they were concerned, unless Paul, by his own kindness, had prompted them to lead him back onto the way of salvation.

units.la: Continet autem hoc Apostoli dictum generalem doctrinam sive admonitionem, frustra eos aut fide vera in Deum, aut propria vitae innocentia gloriari, qui quod ore profitentur non re ipsa praestant. Etenim fidei & religionis professio non solum ritus externos, sed totam simul hominis vitam comprehendit, cum eo ipso quod fidem in unum Deum iactamus, nos illi omnia nostra debere testemur. Deinde cum per fidem omnes sub uno capite Christo in unum corpus coalescamus, eadem fides nos ad fraternam & mutuae charitatis officia astringit: inter quae primum est, ut pijs admonitionibus & (si ita facto opus sit) correptione quoque seueriori eos ab interitu reuocemus, qui in vitijs suis perituri erant. Quomodo enim proximum diligere, & eundem pro fratre agnoscere dicetur, qui ad ea turpiter aut ofcitanter conniuet, quae illi exitium afferunt? Imo ut de religionis vinculo, quod inter homines Christianos arctissimum est, nihil dicamus, quis ciuem bonum dicet, qui vicinum perire sinit, aut in communi ciuitatis periculo otiosum spectatorem agit? Apud Lacedaemonios ex veteri instituto receptum fuit, ut qui iuniorem se praesente peccantem non reprehendisset, perinde ac si ipse peccasset plecteretur: & qui obiurgationem aut correptionem eius modi indignius tulisset, magna ignominia afficiebatur. Videbant enim grauissimi viri, quantum momenti ad rempub. & morum honestatem conseruandam eiusmodi admonitiones afferrent. Et si ad hoc officium tam promptos fecit patriae amor, quanto ardentiores in illo praestando esse conuenit Christianos homines, quos longe arctiori vinculo inter se constrinxit Dei Filius, cui in baptismo nomen dederunt? Itaq; quotquot aut Dei gloriam non eo, quo debebant, studio asserunt, aut fratres suos in sceleribus & erroribus perire sinunt, interim vero Christi nomine & verae fidei professione gloriantur, illis Paulinum istud obici debet: Non est bona gloriatio vestra, &c.
units.tr: This saying of the Apostle, moreover, contains a general doctrine or admonition: that those boast in vain either of true faith in God or of the innocence of their own life who do not show in deed what they profess with the mouth. For the profession of faith and religion comprises not only external rites but the whole of a person's life at once, since by the very fact that we boast of faith in one God, we testify that we owe all that we have to him. Then, since through faith we all grow together into one body under one head, Christ, that same faith binds us to the duties of brotherly and mutual love. Among these the first is that we call back by pious admonitions, and by stricter correction too if the case requires it, those who were going to perish in their sins. For how will someone be said to love his neighbour and to recognise him as a brother, if he winks shamefully or carelessly at the things that bring ruin upon him? Indeed, to say nothing of the bond of religion, which is the closest among Christian people, who will call a man a good citizen if he lets his neighbour perish, or plays the idle spectator in the common danger of the state? Among the Lacedaemonians it was received, by ancient custom, that whoever did not rebuke a younger man who sinned in his presence was punished as if he himself had sinned; and whoever bore such a rebuke or correction with too much indignation was held in great disgrace. For the most serious men saw how much weight such admonitions carried for preserving the commonwealth and the honesty of morals. And if love of country made them so ready for this duty, how much more eager ought Christians to be in performing it, whom the Son of God has bound to one another by a far closer bond, into whose name they were given in baptism? Therefore, whoever either do not defend the glory of God with the zeal they ought, or allow their brothers to perish in sins and errors, while meanwhile they boast in the name of Christ and in the profession of the true faith, must be confronted with that saying of Paul: "Your boasting is not good," and so on.

units.la: Quia vero Corinthios nimia suijpsorum fiducia securos quoque fecerat, ne breue hoc dictum contemnerent, periculi communis denuntiatione eos excitat, sic dicens: An nescitis, quod paulum fermenti totam massam fermentat? Interrogatione illos urget, ut ostendat quam turpis sit haec illorum ignorantia sine obliuio. Quasi diceret: Mirum est vos, qui prae aliis sapere vultis, hucusque in re tanti momenti tam securos & tam immemores vestrae salutis fuisse, cum tot exempla in quotidiano rerum usu occurrant, quae vos tam periculi, quod vobis imminet, quam officij vestri admonere possent, si animum velletis attendere. Nam ut infinita alia omittamus, cur non domi vestrae obseruatis, paululo fermenti magnam farinae subactae massam fermentari, ut inflata surgat, & acorem concipiat? Quin ergo cogitatis idem vestrae ecclesiae accidere posse, ut unius hominis exemplum, qui tantum scelus impune tulit hucusq;, multis alijs occasionem praebeat simile quid, aut etiam hoc grauiora perpetrandi? Quid vero inde sperari potest aliud, quam ut tota ecclesia in commune & extremum salutis discrimen adducatur? At haec dicendo, simul alium difciplina ecclesiastica finem sive vsum attingit, quem nos nuper ordine tertium posuimus: quòd ni- mirum scelerum contagioni obstat, ne vnius aut alterius, qui impune peccarunt, exemplo multi alij inficiantur. Nam vt Cicero dicebat, magna est peccandi illecebra, impunitatis spes: & quo- tus quisque reperitur, qui impunitate proposità, abstinere possit iniuria? At impunitatis spem ma- ximam facit peccantium multitudo. Accedit huic malo, quòd magna per se vis est exemplorum quae nobis quotidie ob oculos versantur, cuius rei causae certae adduci possunt. Prima, quòd malum suapte natura citius propagatur & crescit, quàm quod bonum est. Sic terra sponte vrticas, spinas, tribulos, lolium & alia huius generis profert, & si vel paucissima istorum semina spargantur, mox ea longè lateq; serpere & frutescere videbis: cùm frumentum & alia quae ad vitam sustentandam necessaria sunt, vix magno cum labore culta & plantata proveniant. Altera, quòd omnes homines natura ad malum proclives sunt, & ideo aliorum exemplis facilè provocantur, vt ipsi audeant facere, quod alios impune tulisse vident. Fit ergo, quòd vt scabies ab vna cute in totum gregem serpit: ita vnius ho- minis improba & impunita licentia suo exemplo ciuitatem aut ecclesiam totam inficiat. Eò maior autem exemplorum eiusmodi vis est, si vel ab ijs procedant, quorum maior est apud alios auctho- ritas, vel etiam defendantur ab illis quibus rerum potestas commissa est. Non temere ergo de hoc Corinthios Paulus admonet, vt meminerint hîc non vnius modo hominis, sed totius Ecclesiæ causam agi, adeoque cum Dei gloria publicam omnium salutem periclitari.
units.tr: But because their excessive self-confidence had made the Corinthians also careless, so that they would not despise this brief saying, he rouses them by announcing the common danger, saying: "Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump?" By this question he presses them, to show how shameful this ignorance of theirs is, and how heedless it is. As if he were saying: "It is remarkable that you, who want to be wiser than others, have until now been so secure and so forgetful of your salvation in a matter of such great importance, when so many examples occur in the daily course of affairs that could remind you both of the danger that threatens you and of your duty, if you were willing to pay attention. For, to leave aside countless other things, why do you not observe at home that a little leaven makes a great mass of kneaded flour ferment, so that it rises swollen and takes on a sour taste? Why do you not think that the same thing can happen in your congregation: that the example of one man, who has so far escaped punishment for so great a crime, may give many others an occasion for something similar, or even for committing things more serious than this? What else can be hoped from this, then, than that the whole church be brought into common and extreme peril of salvation?" But in saying these things, at the same time he also touches on another aim or use of church discipline, which we recently placed third in order: namely, that it stands in the way of the contagion of sins, so that by the example of one or two who have sinned with impunity, many others may not be infected. For, as Cicero used to say, the great enticement to sin is the hope of impunity, and how few are found who, with impunity held out, can refrain from wrongdoing? Yet the multitude of those who sin makes the hope of impunity very great. To this evil is added the fact that examples which daily meet our eyes have great force in themselves, and clear causes for this can be given. The first is that evil, by its very nature, spreads and grows more quickly than what is good. Thus the earth of its own accord brings forth nettles, thorns, caltrops, darnel, and other things of this kind; and if even a very few seeds of these are scattered, you will soon see them creeping and bushing out far and wide, whereas grain and the other things necessary for sustaining life come up only with great labour when tilled and planted. The second is that all people are by nature inclined to evil, and therefore are easily provoked by the examples of others to dare to do what they see others have got away with. So it happens, just as scabies creeps from one skin through a whole herd, so the shameless and unpunished licence of one man infects a whole state or church by his example. Moreover, the force of such examples is all the greater if they proceed from those whose authority is greater among others, or if they are even defended by those to whom the power of affairs has been entrusted. Therefore Paul does not without reason warn the Corinthians on this point, that they should remember that the cause at stake here is not that of one man only, but of the whole Church, and that therefore, together with the glory of God, the public safety of all is being put in peril.

units.la: Itaq; multiplicè doctrinam hic quoq; locus continet. Primò enim omnes admonet, & imprimis quidem eos, qui vel in Ecclesia vel in Repub. praesunt, vt vitâ sanctè & honestè instituant, ne cui mali exempli authores sint, & ita fermentum fiant, quo alij corrumpantur. Ita enim poenas illas horribiles incurrent, quas illis Christus minatur, qui alijs scandalo fuerint. Deinde docet vitan- dam esse malorum hominum consuetudinem, societatè vero & consortia cum illis inire nos debere, quorum exemplo meliores fieri possumus. Vt enim corporis vitia & gestus eorum imitamur ple- runq;, quibus cum viuimus: ita etiam in moribus fieri solet. Et memorabile est illud Solomonis di- ctum: Qui ambulat cum sapientibus, fit sapiens. E contra infinita eorum exempla produci poterant, quos hominum impiorum & malae frugis consuetudo miserè perdidit. Haec vt ad omnes pertinent, ita maximè à iuuenibus observari debent, ne in teneris annis concepta mali consuetudo in habitû & vitium immedicabile degeneret. Sed & parentes istorum consideratio excitet, vt in liberorum institutione diligentes sint, & inter alia eos quàm maximè à malorum comercijs revocent. Nam si hoc fecerint, multo simul labore & molestia seipsos liberabunt. Ideo hoc quoq; nô imprudenter à Lacedæmonijs institutum fuit, ne qui extra patriæ fines peregrinarentur. Ita enim cauere volue- runt, ne quis peregrinos & corruptos mores, quos alibi imbibisset, in ciuitatem inferret. Vide- bant enim in vicina Græcia & Asia intemperantiam, luxum, libidinem & omnis generis scelera impunè regnare: quamobrem etsi in ijsdem regionibus artium bonarum studia florerent, & qui ex- teras oras inuisunt cum multarum rerum experientia prudentiam quoq; maiorem colligant, vti- lius tamen illis visum fuit istis carere, quàm patriæ disciplinam labefactari, qua Respub. ceu ner- uis solidissimis continetur. At hodie, qui liberis suis optimè consultum volunt, eos vel in Regum aulas, vel in militiam mercenariam ablegant, vbi cum pessimis versantur, & nihil fere praeter immanem luxum & quiduis audendi libidinem inde domum referunt.
units.tr: Thus this passage also contains teaching on many points. First, it admonishes everyone, and especially those who hold office either in the Church or in the commonwealth, to order their lives holily and honourably, so that they are not authors of bad example to anyone and so do not become leaven by which others are corrupted. For they will incur those dreadful punishments which Christ threatens against those who give offence to others. Next, he teaches that we must avoid the company of wicked men, and that we ought not to enter into fellowship and association with those by whose example we could be made worse. For just as we often imitate the bodily faults and gestures of those with whom we live, so it usually happens in matters of character too. And Solomon's saying is memorable: "He who walks with the wise becomes wise." On the other side, countless examples could be brought forward of those whom the company of impious men and of bad living has wretchedly ruined. These things apply to all, but they ought especially to be observed by young people, lest a bad habit taken up in tender years should degenerate into a settled vice that cannot be cured. But let the parents of such young people also consider this, so that they may be diligent in bringing up their children and, among other things, keep them as far as possible from the company of evil men. For if they do this, they will spare themselves much toil and trouble at the same time. Hence the Lacedaemonians did not unwisely establish this rule, that none should travel abroad beyond the borders of their country. For they wished to guard against anyone bringing into the state foreign and corrupt customs that he had soaked up elsewhere. They saw that in neighbouring Greece and Asia intemperance, luxury, lust and every kind of wickedness reigned unpunished. Therefore, although the pursuit of good arts flourished in those same regions, and those who visit foreign shores gather greater wisdom from their wide experience, they judged it better to do without these things than to see the discipline of their homeland, by which the commonwealth is held together as by most solid sinews, be weakened. But today, those who wish the best for their children send them away either to royal courts or to mercenary military service, where they mix with the worst people, and bring home from there almost nothing but monstrous luxury and a lust for daring anything at all.

units.la: Cæterùm ne Corinthij se iam omni officio defunctos putarent, si impurum illum è cætu suo eiecissent, Paulus ex hac occasione sumpta in generalem doctrinam digreditur, qua simul omnes ad vitæ innocentiam & sanctitatem adhortatur, & ea omnino opus esse docet, quippe in Christo viuere & seruari velint. Et vt doctrina ista magis perspicua fit, & in animos altius penetret, perstat in fermenti parabola, & inde ad paschalis festi solennitatem transfit, quo & redemptionis nostrae communis & totius vitae Christianae typus continetur.
units.tr: Moreover, lest the Corinthians should think that they had now discharged every duty if they had cast that impure man out of their assembly, Paul, taking this occasion, passes on to general teaching, by which at the same time he exhorts everyone to innocence and holiness of life, and teaches that this is entirely necessary, since they wish to live and be saved in Christ. And so that this teaching may be clearer and penetrate more deeply into their minds, he persists in the parable of leaven, and from there passes to the solemnity of the Passover feast, in which is contained a type both of our common redemption and of the whole Christian life.

units.la: Propositio & summa totius loci est: Expurgate vetus fermentum, vt sitis nova massa, sicut estis fermenti expertes. Fermenti nomine peccatum significat, & quicquid cum illo coniunctum est: nimirum ad illud Christi respiciens, qui discipulos à fermento Pharisæorum & Herodis abstinere iussit, per illud quidem hypocrisin, per hoc verò vitam sceleratam cum manifesto Dei & admonitionum omnium contemptu coniunctam intelligens. Recte autem peccatum fermento
units.tr: The proposition and summary of the whole passage is: "Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened." By the name of leaven he signifies sin, and whatever is joined with it, plainly looking to that saying of Christ, who ordered his disciples to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod, understanding by the former hypocrisy and by the latter a wicked life joined with open contempt for God and for all admonitions. And it is rightly that sin is compared to leaven

units.la: Marc. 8. fermento confertur, quia hoc illius naturam atque effecta pulchrè adumbrat. Vt enim fermentum res quidem parua & nullius pretij videtur, mirifica tamen vi massam in gentem penetrat, seque per totam illam diffundit, vt non solum intumescat, verumetiam ex illo acorem nouum concipiat: ita peccatum primo intuitu leuiculum quid & contemptibile putatur, ex quo non multum periculi sit metuendum, at semel intra cordis penetralia admissum, hominis naturam omnem peruadit & occupat, eundem inflat, vt nouis quasi spiritibus conceptis aduersus Deum & Verbum eius extollatur, ideoque in omnibus vitae totius actionibus sese exerit, quae causa est, vt homo totus acetum sapiat, & Deo minimè gratus sit. Vetus autem fermentum dicit Apostolus, partim ad pristinam vitae in gentilismo translatae consuetudinem, partim ad innatam nobis vitiositatem respiciens. Et reuera vetus est peccatum, quia vt in primo parente coepit, ita ex illo in omnem posteritatem propagatum nobiscum concipitur & nascitur, adeò vt priusquam in Christo renascamur, nihil praeter peccatum in nobis videre possis. Quo nomine illud Apostolus veterem quoque hominem appellare consueuit. Sensus ergo verborum istorum est, expurgari & eijci oportere peccatum & quicquid prioris vitae consuetudinem sapit. Rationem verò adducit à fine religionis aut professionis Christianae desumptam: Vt sitis noua massa, sicut estis fermenti expertes. At si fermenti (inquis) expertes iam erant, quid habuerunt quod expurgarent? Vbi meminisse oportet, Paulum ad Dei gratiam respicere & vocationis ipsorum finem. Vocati enim erant singulari gratia Dei beneficio, vt noui homines fierent, & excusso omni fermento peccati atque veteris consuetudinis Deo sese omnis fermenti expertes sisterent, & quia vocanti Deo paruerant, vt Christo nomen darent, tales dicuntur, quàmuis non parua apud illos adhuc essent veteris fermenti reliquiae, quas eijci oportebat. Ita Christus discipulos suos mundos vocat propter Verbum suum, cui crediderant, & tamen eosdem, vt pe[?]les suos quotidie abluant, hortatur: per hos nimirum vitae conuersationem intelligens, cui quoad in carne viuimus, subinde aliquid ex innata vitiositate & mundi exemplo aspergitur, quod noua abstersione opus habet. Argumentum ergo Pauli ita formari poterit. Quicunq; per Euangelij praedicationem ad Christum vocati, & in hoc nouus populus atq; Dei peculium facti sunt, ij omnes peccati & veteris consuetudinis reliquias expurgare debent, vt reuera sint quod profitentur: At vos per Euangelium vocati estis, & nouus populus propter regenerationis gratiam dicimini: Ergo peccatum omne expurgare, neq; aliquid ferre debetis quod gentilismum sapiat.
units.tr: (Mark 8) with leaven, because leaven finely shadows forth its nature and effects. For just as leaven, though it seems a small thing and of no worth, by its wonderful power penetrates the whole mass and spreads itself through all of it, so that it not only swells but also takes on a new sourness, so sin, at first glance, is thought to be something slight and contemptible, from which there is not much danger to fear; yet once admitted into the innermost parts of the heart, it pervades and occupies the whole of human nature, puffs it up, so that, as if filled with new spirits, it is lifted up against God and his Word, and therefore it shows itself in all the actions of the whole of life; this is why a man as a whole tastes sour and is not at all pleasing to God. The Apostle calls it "old leaven," looking partly to the former custom of life carried over from the time of heathenism, and partly to the vice innate in us. And indeed sin is old, because, as it began in the first parent, so from him it has been propagated to all posterity, and is conceived and born with us, so that before we are born again in Christ you can see nothing in us but sin. For this reason the Apostle is also accustomed to call it the "old man." The sense of these words, therefore, is that sin and whatever savours of the former manner of life must be purged out and cast away. But he adds a reason taken from the purpose of the Christian religion or profession: "That you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened." But if (you will say) they were already unleavened, what did they have to purge? Here we must remember that Paul looks to the grace of God and to the purpose of their calling. For they had been called by the singular benefit of God's grace, so that they might become new men, and, having shaken off all the leaven of sin and of the old custom, might present themselves to God unleavened in every way; and because they had obeyed God's call to take the name of Christ, they are called such, although there still remained among them not a few remnants of the old leaven, which had to be cast out. So Christ calls his disciples clean because of his Word, which they had believed, and yet he exhorts the same men to wash their feet every day; by this he surely means the conduct of life, into which, as long as we live in the flesh, something from our innate vice and from the example of the world is from time to time sprinkled, and this needs a fresh cleansing. The argument of Paul, therefore, can be framed thus: Whoever have been called to Christ through the preaching of the Gospel, and have been made in this a new people and God's own possession, must purge away all the remnants of sin and of the old custom, so that they really are what they profess; but you have been called through the Gospel, and you are called a new people because of the grace of regeneration; therefore you ought to purge away all sin, and to bear nothing that savours of heathenism.

units.la: Obseruabis autem toto hoc loco, turpiter eos hallucinari, qui peccata vetustate & communi totius mundi exemplo excusant. Solent hi multis narrare, quae omnibus saeculis mundi huius facies aut conditio fuerit, & inde colligunt, aliter fieri non posse, & proinde non audiendos esse, qui nouam mundo faciem inducere conantur, & Deum fingunt, qui morositate quadam noua iam amplius ferre nolit, quae tot saeculis tulit. At quid opus est ô boni haec tam multis exponere? Quis enim negat, iam inde à prima rerum origine peccatum regnauisse, & mundum omnibus saeculis ambitione, auaritia, intemperantia, libidine, odijs, caedibus, rapinis & omni iniquitatis genere esse turbatum? Nonne de hoc ipse Deus per Mosem & prophetas passim queritur? Nonne hoc ipsum nos quoque fatemur? At quod vos inde colligitis, id omnino sequi negamus. Scimus enim Filium Dei in mundum venisse, vt opera diaboli destruat: inter quae cum primis locus peccatis debeatur, nequaquam his seruire debent quicunque illius nomen profitentur. Scimus illum Nicodemo dixisse: nisi quis renatus fuerit, non potest videre regnum Dei. At quid opus est regeneratione, si pristina vitae studia sectari, & carnis cupiditatibus indulgere licet? Scimus noui Testamenti primum ministrum fuisse Ioannem Baptistam: qui paenitentiae doctrina populum ad excipiendum promissae salutis Mediatorem praeparare debuit: scimus praeterea hoc in mandatis habuisse Apostolos, vt Euangelij praedicatione à paenitentiae articulo exordirentur: scimus item inter spiritus sancti officia primum recenseri vt mundum arguat de peccato. Quid verò peccati redargutione aut paenitentia opus est, si inter media peccata seruari possumus? Quod si vos iuuat veterum exemplorum commemoratio, vt bis peccandi licentiam excusetis, cur nõ eadè opera poenas & horrenda Dei iudicia commemoratis, quibus in sui numinis contemptores, in intemperantes, libidinosos, ebriosos, adulteros, scortatores, avaros, sanguinarios, raptores, ille omnibus saeculis severissimè animadvertit? Quod si exempla illa ignoratis, nam oscitanter nimis sacras literas legistis: sin verò haec vobis non ignota sunt, nimium malitiosi estis, qui impia eorum dissimulatione rudem & rerum imperitum populum decipitis: & proinde indigni estis, quibus in re tanti momenti fides habeatur. Haec fratres charissimi, hoc loco mihi omnino dicenda fuerunt propter eos, qui hodie tanta cum confidentia passim regnant & omnia turbantem scelerum immanissimorum licentiam defendunt. Ignorant isti finem Evangelij & vocationis nostrae, qui est, ut per fidei obedientiam toti Christo subijciamur, unius Deo vindicamus, qui nos Filij sui sanguine redemit
units.tr: But you will observe throughout this passage how shamefully those err who excuse sins by antiquity and by the common example of the whole world. Such people are accustomed to recount at length what the face and condition of this world has been in all ages, and from this they conclude that it cannot be otherwise, and therefore that those should not be listened to who try to bring a new face upon the world, and who imagine a God who, with a certain new peevishness, no longer wishes to bear what he has borne for so many ages. But what need is there, good people, to set out these things at such length? For who denies that sin has reigned from the very first origin of things, and that the world in every age has been disturbed by ambition, avarice, intemperance, lust, hatreds, murders, robberies and every kind of iniquity? Does not God himself complain of this everywhere through Moses and the prophets? Do we not ourselves confess this very thing? But what you infer from it, we altogether deny that it follows. For we know that the Son of God came into the world that he might destroy the works of the devil, and among these works sin must be counted first of all; those who profess his name ought in no way to serve it. We know that he said to Nicodemus: "Unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God." But what need is there of regeneration, if it is allowed to pursue our former ways of life and to indulge the desires of the flesh? We know that John the Baptist was the first minister of the New Testament, who by the teaching of repentance was to prepare the people to receive the Mediator of the promised salvation; we know moreover that the Apostles had this command, that they should begin the preaching of the Gospel with the article of repentance; we know likewise that among the offices of the Holy Spirit the first mentioned is that he convicts the world of sin. But what need is there of the convicting of sin or of repentance, if we can be preserved amid sins? And if it pleases you to recall the examples of the ancients in order to excuse your licence to sin, why do you not, in the same way, recall the punishments and the dreadful judgments of God, with which he most severely punished in all ages those who despised his majesty, the intemperate, the lustful, the drunkards, adulterers, fornicators, the greedy, murderers and robbers? But if you are ignorant of those examples, for you have read the sacred letters all too carelessly; yet if these things are not unknown to you, you are too malicious, deceiving the untutored and inexperienced people by your impious concealment of them; and therefore you are unworthy to be trusted in a matter of such great importance. These things, dearest brothers, I had to say here altogether because of those who today reign everywhere with such confidence and defend the unbridled licence of most monstrous crimes, troubling all things. They do not know the purpose of the Gospel and of our calling, which is that through the obedience of faith we should be wholly subject to Christ, and claimed for the one God, who redeemed us with the blood of his Son.

units.la: Pertinet ad hanc considerationem etiam Expurgandi verbum, quo Paulus non sine causa usus est. Poterat enim cum Christo dicere, Cauete vobis à fermento veteri, vel, Eijcite illud & deponite. Sed ita loqui voluit, ut ostenderet hic imprimis cura diligenti & labore opus esse, ut totum illud eruatur, quod vetus fermentum sapit. Quia enim ex primis natalibus nobis inhaeret lex illa peccati, non adeo facile reuellitur, quin aliquae eius radicula reliquae maneant, ex quibus mox noua mali seges prouenit, nisi illae etiam stirpitus tollantur. Nullus ergo corruptelis eiusmodi locus in nobis reliquus fieri debet, nisi cum Deo ludere, & nostri innouationem simulare potius quam serio instituere libeat. Ex imis ergo radicibus extirpentur idololatria, superstitiones, opiniones erroneae, falsa doctrina, corrupti mores, & quicquid nobis vel ex Adamo veteri, vel ex prioris vitae consuetudine adhaeret. In hoc sedulos imprimis esse conuenit Verbi administros & qui in repub. agunt: ne blandiendo & dissimulando superstitiones & vitia aperta foueant. Errant hic vehementer nostro tempore, qui dum ecclesiae & religionis reformationem instituunt, nonnulla relinquenda esse putant quae non adeo magni momenti esse videntur. His enim relictis, fit ut apud eos maioris quàm antea fieri incipiant, quorum animi superstitiosis opinionibus nondum omnino liberati sunt, ideoq; mordicus & inuicta quadam pertinacia retinere postea conantur ea, quae prius facile contemnebant. Ita vera superstitionis fomenta fiunt, quae contemptu digna esse & sine periculo negligi posse putabantur. Peccarunt in hoc ex Regibus Iuda multi non mali, quibus vitio datur, quòd crassioribus superstitionibus sublatis Excelsa reliquerint, in quibus populus contra Dei legem sacrificabit. Et quantum ex minimis veterum errorum reliquijs mali succrescat, nostris temporibus non uno loco vidimus. At quod de cultus diuini reformatione dicimus, ad vitam quoque & mores transferri debet. Quicunque enim Ecclesiae aut Reipub. disciplinam rectè constitutam, eamq; perpetuam & stabilem esse volunt, ij omnem quoque mali speciem è medio auferre satagant, ne qua occasio detur ijs, qui pristinos mores reducere cupiunt. Priuatim verò singuli discant, se tunc demum hominis Christiani officium facere, si non modò externos mores emendent, sed peccatum ex imis medullis eijcere & carnem ad hoc procliuem mortificare studeat. Si enim qui hoc pro virili faciunt, nihilominus sibi perpetuò luctandum esse sentiunt, quid obsecro ijs fiet, qui consultò multa relinquunt, quibus Satanas ad inflamanda carnis nostrae desideria abuti potest? Quàm parū ergo in religione Christiana eos profecisse putabimus, qui ea etiam excusant & defendunt, quae Dei verbo damnantur?
units.tr: This consideration also bears on the word Paul uses, "purge out" (expurgate), and he did not use it without reason. He could have said with Christ, "Beware of the old leaven," or "Cast it out and put it away." But he chose this wording to show that here, above all, careful diligence and effort are needed to pull out everything that tastes of the old leaven. Since that law of sin clings to us from our first birth, it is not easily torn away. Some small roots of it remain, and from these a fresh crop of evil soon springs up unless they too are pulled out entirely. So no place at all should be left in us for corruptions of this kind, unless we want to trifle with God and pretend to renew ourselves rather than do it in earnest. Idolatry, superstitions, erroneous opinions, false doctrine, corrupt morals, and whatever still clings to us from the old Adam or from the habits of our former life must be rooted out from the very bottom. Above all, the ministers of the Word and those who govern the commonwealth ought to be diligent in this, so that they do not foster superstitions and open vices by flattering and overlooking them. Those who, while they undertake a reform of the Church and of religion, think that some things may be left alone because they seem of little importance, are gravely mistaken in our own time. For once these things are left, those whose minds are not yet fully freed from superstitious opinions begin to hold them in greater esteem than before. Then they strive afterwards to cling to, with teeth and an unyielding obstinacy, the very things they once easily despised. In this way the real kindling of superstition is produced, things that were thought worthy of contempt and safe to neglect. Many of the kings of Judah, not wicked men, went wrong in this way, and they are blamed because, though they removed the grosser superstitions, they left the high places, in which the people went on to sacrifice against God's law. We have seen in our own times, in more than one place, how much evil grows from the smallest remnants of old errors. What we say about the reform of divine worship must also be carried over into life and morals. For those who want the discipline of the Church or of the commonwealth to be rightly established and lasting and stable should also take care to remove every appearance of evil, so that no occasion is given to those who wish to bring back their former ways. Individuals in private should learn that they then at last do the duty of a Christian, if they not only amend their outward conduct but also strive to cast out sin from the innermost marrow and to mortify the flesh, which is prone to it. For if those who do this to the best of their power still feel that they must struggle without end, what, I beg you, will become of those who deliberately keep many things by which Satan can exploit to inflame the desires of our flesh? How little progress, then, shall we think they have made in the Christian religion, who even excuse and defend the things that are condemned by God's Word?

units.la: Caeterum poterant aliqui Paulo obijcere: Quid opus est nos de fermento expurgando admonere, quos iam pridem Christus ab ijs liberauit, quae veteri populo mandata fuerunt? Ad Iudaeos ista praecepta pertinent, neq; ijs obtundi debent, qui Christo nomen dederunt. Praeoccupat ergo obiectionem istam, sic scribens: Nam Pascha nostrum pro nobis sacrificatum est, nempe Christus, &c. Quibus verbis & priorem doctrinam confirmat, & simul rationem reddit, cur locutionibus & similibus ex lege petitis apud homines Christianos utatur: ideo nimirum, quòd veteribus (ut infra dicet) omnia in figura contigerunt, cuius complementum nos in Christo habemus. Sic ergo vult dicere: Quando paschalis agni immolatione & quod ex illo fiebat epulum Deus in liberationis ex Aegypto memoriam instituit, hoc prae alijs singulari cura & seueritate observari voluit, ut omni fermento ex aedibus eiecto totos illius festi dies septem panibus non fermentatis vescerentur. Atqui nos Pascha habemus longè praestatius, ipsum scilicet Dei Filium IESVM CHRISTVM, qui ex spirituali, Pharaonis, diaboli & inferorum, tyrannide nos asseruit, & nobis epulum exhibet, quo indesinenter ad vitam aeternam pascimur atq; alimur: Ergo non minus nobis quoq; etiam atque etiam aduigilandum est, vt ab ijs abstineamus, quae per fermentum olim adumbrata sunt. Quid vero aliud voluisse putabimus Deum, quàm vt Israelitae ad terram promissam propera-turi superstitiones simul atque mores Aegyptios procul abijcerent, seq; totos ipsi consecrarent, cuius singularem gratiam tunc sentiebant? Idem ergo nobis quoque praecipi putabimus, vt reliquis & abiectis omnibus prioris vitae sordibus nunc ad coelestem patriam tendamus, & vni Christo viuamus, qui nobis libertatis multò nobilioris & praestantioris author est. Si enim ea tam diligenter obseruari debuerunt, quae typi & vmbrae fuerunt mysteriorum sublimiorum, quantò diligentiori cura in illis opus est, quae illis adumbrantur? Et si olim capitale fuit fermentum e-disse, quòd per secessum expurgatur, quanto grauior erit culpa peccato locum dedisse, quod cordibus sese insinuans nobis inhaeret, totos peruadit, inflat & à Deo prorsus abstrahit? Haec (inquam) & quaecunque alia in hanc sententiam dici possunt, Paulus his verbis comprehendit, in quibus priusquam longius progrediamur, duo obseruanda veniunt.
units.tr: Moreover, someone might object to Paul: "Why do we need to be reminded about purging out leaven? Christ has long ago freed us from the things that were commanded to the old people. These precepts pertain to the Jews, and those who have given their name to Christ should not be troubled by them." Paul anticipates this objection by writing thus: "For our Passover also has been sacrificed for us, namely Christ," and so on. By these words he both confirms his earlier teaching and at the same time gives the reason why he uses expressions taken from the law among Christians: namely, because, as he will say below, all things happened to the ancients in figure, and we have their fulfilment in Christ. So he means to say this: when God established, in memory of the deliverance from Egypt, the sacrifice of the paschal lamb and the meal made from it, he wished this to be observed with a special care and strictness above the other feasts, so that, with all leaven cast out of the houses, they should eat unleavened bread for the seven days of that feast. Yet we have a far better Passover, namely the Son of God himself, Jesus Christ, who has delivered us from the spiritual tyranny of Pharaoh, of the devil, and of hell, and sets before us a feast by which we are constantly fed and nourished unto eternal life. Therefore we too must watch all the more carefully, and keep ourselves from those things that were once foreshadowed by the leaven. And what else shall we think God wanted, but that the Israelites, hastening to the promised land, should cast far away the superstitions and the Egyptian manners, and consecrate themselves wholly to him, whose singular grace they then felt? So we too shall think that we are commanded the same thing: that, leaving aside and rejecting all the filth of our former life, we now press on toward our heavenly country and live to Christ alone, who is the author of a far nobler and more excellent liberty for us. For if those things were to be observed so diligently which were types and shadows of higher mysteries, with how much more diligent care must we attend to those things that are foreshadowed by them? And if it was once a capital matter to eat leaven, which is purged out by a secession, how much graver will the fault be of giving place to sin, which insinuates itself into our hearts, clings to us, pervades us wholly, puffs us up, and utterly draws us away from God? These things (I say) and whatever else can be said to this effect, Paul comprehends in these words. Before we go further into them, two things must be noted.

units.la: Primum est, quòd Christum Paschà nostrum dicit, & ita nos quoque non minus quàm veteres paschà habere docet, quod à nobis celebrari debeat. Neque primus hoc dicit, sed Baptistam dixisse sciebat de Christo: Ecce agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi. Et vt in praesenti Paschà nobis tribuit, et ex eo argumentum ducit quod nos de nostro officio admoneat: ita in Epistola ad Colossen. nos Circumcisionem quoque habere ait, quae non manu, sed Christi spiritu fiat, & vt huic locum demus hortatur. Simili ratione ad Hebraeos Altare etiam nobis tribuit, & inde deducit argumenta, quibus in fide vera nos instituat. E contra noui testamenti Sacramenta veteribus applicat, quando infra Cap.decimo illos & baptizatos esse, & nobiscum eandem escam spiritualem comedisse, deq; eadem nobiscum petra bibisse testatur. Est ergo certa & euidens inter veteres & nouum testamentum communio, quae docet, eandem semper fuisse salutis rationem, & quidem eam, quae in vno IESV CHRISTO habetur: quem ideo agnum ab origine mundi immolatum Ioannes vocat, quòd mortis eius meritum ad primos parentes vsq; extendi, & per hoc patres om-nes seruatos esse sciret. Quoad ergo rationem salutis & fidei principia inter nos et illos discrimen prorsus nullum est. In solo autem tempore est differentia. Illi enim Seruatorem, qui praefinito tempore venturus erat fide cōstati expectarunt, & ideo signis pluribus opus habebant, quibus in fide confirmarentur: at nobis ille iam datus est, et proinde signis quoq; paucioribus et minus operosis utimur. Vtque veteres nequaquam in externis illis ritibus salutis fiduciam collocare debuerunt, sed in Christi aduentu respicere: ita nos quoq; non in signis haerere, sed animos per fidem sursum attollere conuenit, vt Christo vere fruamur. Haec qui non obseruant, ij non modò superstitionibus nouis decipiuntur, ve-rumetiâ[?] seipsos dulcissima illa communione spoliant, quae nobis in Christo cum veteribus intercedit.
units.tr: The first is that he calls Christ our Passover, and so teaches that we too have a Passover, no less than the ancients, which ought to be celebrated by us. Nor is he the first to say this, for he knew that the Baptist had said of Christ, "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world." And just as he attributes to us the present Passover and draws from it an argument by which he reminds us of our duty, so in the Epistle to the Colossians he says that we also have a circumcision, which is made not by hand but by the Spirit of Christ, and he urges us to give place to this. In a similar way, in the Epistle to the Hebrews, he attributes an altar to us too and draws from it arguments by which he instructs us in the true faith. On the other hand, he applies the sacraments of the New Testament to the ancients, when, in the tenth chapter below, he testifies that they too were baptized, ate the same spiritual food with us, and drank from the same rock. There is therefore a certain and evident communion between the ancients and the New Testament, which teaches that the way of salvation has always been one and the same, namely that which is found in the one Jesus Christ. John calls him the lamb slain from the beginning of the world for this reason: he knew that the merit of his death extended back even to our first parents, and that through it all the fathers were saved. So as far as the way of salvation and the principles of faith are concerned, there is no difference at all between us and them. The only difference is in time. For they awaited the Saviour, who was to come at an appointed time, with a faith grounded on his promise, and so they needed more signs by which they might be confirmed in faith; but he has now been given to us, and therefore we use fewer and less laborious signs. And just as the ancients ought never to have placed their trust for salvation in those outward rites, but should look forward to the coming of Christ, so we too ought not to cling to the signs, but to lift up our minds by faith, so that we may truly enjoy Christ. Those who do not observe these things are not only deceived by new superstitions, but also, yes indeed, they rob themselves of that most sweet communion which we have with the ancients in Christ.

units.la: Alterum quòd hic obseruabis, est, quòd Paulus Christum pro nobis sacrificatum esse, non adhuc quotidie sacrificari, dicit, imò nullius praeterea noui sacrificij meminit. Atqui ad huius loci argu-mentū plurimum ponderis attulisset, si ita potuisset dicere: Quoniâ Iudaei in agni paschalis immo-latione fermentum omne ex aedibus eijcere, et totum illius festi tempus panibus nō fermentatis trāsigere debuerunt: nostri quoq; officij fuerit, per omne vitae tempus à fermento veteri abstinere, eò quòd nostrum Paschà, IESVS CHRISTVS, quotidie in Altaris sacramento nō pro nobis modò, sed pro omnibus viuis & defunctis immolatur. Fuisset certè huius argumenti vis maxima, neq; illud omisurus erat Paulus, si quid huius fieri credidisset. Sed nihil eiusmodi dicit, quia Christum iam moriturum dixisse sciebat, Consummatus est. Sciebat deniq; illum (vt ad Hebraeos scribitur) semel oblatum esse, vt multorum peccata tolleret, & vna pro peccatis oblata victima, nunc in perpetuum sede-re ad dextram Dei. Est ergo intolerabilis eorum error, qui Christi corpus et sanguinem quotidie offerri docent. Nā ita meritum crucis & mortis eius euacuant, eundem mendacij arguunt, spem salutis labefactant, & impurū sacrificiū in illius locum substituunt, imò supra ipsum longè euehunt, quàm per illum perfici credunt, quod ipse imperfectum reliquerit.
units.tr: Another thing you will observe here is that Paul says Christ has been sacrificed for us once, and is not sacrificed daily; indeed he mentions no other new sacrifice at all. Yet his argument would have carried far more weight if he could have said this: "Just as the Jews, at the immolation of the paschal lamb, had to cast out all leaven from their houses and spend the whole of that feast with unleavened bread, so it should be our duty to abstain from old leaven for the whole of our life, because our Passover, Jesus Christ, is sacrificed every day in the sacrament of the altar, not only for us but for all the living and the dead." Certainly the force of such an argument would have been very great, and Paul would not have omitted it had he believed that anything of this kind took place. But he says nothing of the sort, because he knew that Christ had said he was about to die: "It is finished." He knew too that (as is written to the Hebrews) Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many, and that, having offered one sacrifice for sins, he now sits for ever at the right hand of God. Therefore the error of those who teach that the body and blood of Christ are offered daily is intolerable. For they empty the merit of his cross and death, they make him a liar, they weaken the hope of salvation, and they put in place of it an impure sacrifice, indeed they raise it far above him, since they believe that what he left imperfect is perfected through it.

units.la: Sed omissis istis, loci huius Conclusionē audiamus: Itaque festum agitemus non fermento veteri, nec fermento malitiae et nequitiae, sed non fermentatis panibus synceritatis & veritatis. Fe-sti nomine totum vitae Christianae cursum intelligit. Vt enim nostri Agni meritu atq; virtus perpetuò durat: ita nostri quoque festi Paschalis solennitas non septem dierum spatio terminatur, sed per omne tempus nostrae vitae extenditur. Probè autem conuenit ista similitudo. Festum enim paschatis quatuor omnino partibus constabat. Primò otium habebat sacrum, & (vt in reliquis etiam festis) ab omni opere seruili feriabantur. Deinde cum gaudio & gratulatione celebra-bant memoriam redemptionis ex Aegypto. Tertiò immolabatur Agnus, qui vt beneficium patribus olim in Aegypto præstitum in mentem renocabat: ita Christi typus erat, cuius sanguis nos aduersus angeli vastatoris insidias tuebatur. Accedebant hîs quarto loco panes azymi aut non fermentati, quibus toto illo tempore vescebantur, vt præcipitis illius festinationis ex Aegypto memores sibi ab omnibus ijs cauerent, quibus tunc polluti fuerant, & libertatem suam fortiter tuerentur. Atqui hæc ipsa sunt quibus vita Christiana constat: vt nimirum à peccatis feriemur: vt perpetuò & indesinenter gaudeamus in Domino, etiamsi multa nobis aduersa sint: vt in recenti memoria nobis sit IESV CHRISTI beneficium, qui pro nobis sese obtulit, vt ex peccati seruitio & morte æterna nos redimeret: vt denique fermentum omne tam supersti-tionum veterum quàm peccati expurgemus, neue Christi beneficio abutamur ad peccandi licentiam. Recte ergo & merito vitam Christianam Pascha perpetuum dixerit.
units.tr: But setting those matters aside, let us hear the conclusion of this passage: "Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth." By the name of feast he means the whole course of the Christian life. For just as the merit and power of our Lamb endure continually, so too the solemnity of our Paschal feast is not bounded by a span of seven days, but extends through the whole time of our life. This comparison fits very well. For the feast of the passover consisted of four parts altogether. First, it had a holy rest, and (as in the other feasts too) they abstained from all servile work. Then they celebrated with joy and thanksgiving the memory of redemption from Egypt. Thirdly, the lamb was sacrificed, which called to mind the benefit once granted to the fathers in Egypt; so it was a type of Christ, whose blood guarded us against the snares of the destroying angel. To these, in the fourth place, were added the unleavened or unfermented breads, which they ate throughout that whole time, so that, mindful of the hasty departure from Egypt, they would guard themselves against all those things by which they had then been polluted, and would bravely defend their liberty. Now these very things are what the Christian life consists of: namely, that we cease from sins; that we rejoice constantly and without ceasing in the Lord, even though many adversities befall us; that the benefit of Jesus Christ, who offered himself for us to redeem us from the slavery of sin and from eternal death, be fresh in our memory; and finally that we purge out all leaven, both of the old superstitions and of sin, and do not abuse Christ's benefit as a licence to sin. Rightly and deservedly, then, he would call the Christian life a perpetual Passover.

units.la: At quia priora ad præsens Apostoli institutum minus faciunt, in postremo maximè insistit, & duobus membris comprehendit omnia, quæ Christiani homines vitare, quæue facere debent. In primo fermentum vetus denuò nominatur, per quod peccatum nobis ex originis vitio inhæ-rens & prioris vitæ consuetudinem denotari diximus. Id verò perspicuitatis causa in malitiam & nequitiam diuidit: & per illam simpliciter omne id intelligit, quod cum bona Dei voluntate pugnat, hac verò improbitatem illam denotat, qua alios etiam molestia afficimus, diaboli nimi-rum ingenium imitati, qui & ipse ideo πονηρὸς[?] dicitur. Quia verò non satis est à maleficio absti-nuisse, nisi è contra quod bonum est facias (notum est enim illud Domini per Isaiam dicentis: Cessate malefacere, discite benefacere) alterum membrum mox opponit, monens vt suæ vitæ festum in panibus non fermentatis, synceritate nimirum & veritate transsigant. Synceritate innocentiæ & sanctitatem omnem comprehendit, sine qua nemo videbit Deum. Nam huius verba sunt: Sancti estote, sicuti & ego sanctus sum. Veritas dolum atque simulationem omnem tam in cultu Dei quàm in vita & moribus excludit. Hoc ipsum ergo in præsenti dicit Apostolus, quod Christus, quando veram Dei inuocationem aut cultum in spiritu & veritate consistere docet. Nam etsi ipse de eo potissimùm agat, quales erga Deum esse debeamus, fieri tamen non potest, quin cum hominibus quoque innocenter, sancte & absque omni fraude vel simulatione agant, quicunque Deum ex animo obseruant & colunt. Et hæc quidem singuli ad se transferre debent pro sua vo-cationis ratione, vbi singuli quid agant inuenient, & pietatem veram exercendi materiam habe-bunt amplißimam. Hodie plerique Pascha agitant non tam Iudeorum quàm gentium more. At Christianum Pascha neque inanibus ceremonijs, neq; epulis aut conuiuijs luxuriosis constat, sed ijs, quæ hic Paulus præcipit. Adhæc non paucis modò diebus agitur, sed toto vitæ tempore durat. Semper ergo infelix peccati fermentum fugere, semper synceritati & veritati studere, semper in CHRISTO IESV exultare debemus, qui vt nos ex diaboli seruitio asseruit, ita nos in cæ-lesti patria semper secum viuere & regnare vult. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But because the things said earlier do less to serve the Apostle's present purpose, he dwells chiefly on the last part, and comprehends in two members everything that Christian people ought to avoid or to do. In the first, the old leaven is named again, by which we said is denoted the sin clinging to us from the corruption of our origin, and the custom of our former life. He divides this, for the sake of clarity, into malice and wickedness; by malice he understands simply everything that is opposed to the good will of God, while by wickedness he denotes that depravity by which we also afflict others with trouble, imitating the nature of the devil, who is himself for this reason called wicked. But since it is not enough to have refrained from doing evil, unless you also do what is good (for that saying of the Lord through Isaiah is well known: "Cease to do evil, learn to do good"), he immediately sets the second member against the first, urging that they keep the feast of their life with unleavened bread, that is, with sincerity and truth. By sincerity he comprehends innocence and all holiness, without which no one will see God. For these are his words: "Be holy, as I also am holy." Truth excludes all deceit and pretence, both in the worship of God and in life and conduct. So the Apostle here says the same thing that Christ does when he teaches that true invocation and worship of God consist in spirit and truth. For although he is chiefly concerned with how we ought to be towards God, it cannot but be that all who truly observe and worship God from the heart also deal with men innocently, holily, and without any fraud or pretence. Each of us ought to apply these things to himself according to the nature of his calling; there each will find what he has to do, and will have very ample material for exercising true piety. Today most people keep the Passover not so much in the manner of the Jews as in that of the Gentiles. But the Christian Passover consists neither of empty ceremonies, nor of feasts or luxurious banquets, but of those things which Paul here prescribes. Moreover it is kept not for a few days only, but lasts through the whole time of our life. Therefore we must always flee the unhappy leaven of sin, always strive after sincerity and truth, always exult in Christ Jesus, who, as he has freed us from the service of the devil, so wills that we should live and reign with him for ever in the heavenly fatherland. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXVI.
units.tr: Homily 26.

units.la: Scripsi vobis in Epistola, ne commisceamini cum scortatoribus: at non omnino cum scortatoribus mundi huius, aut cum auaris, aut cum rapacibus, aut idololatris: alioqui debetis scilicet è mundo exire. Nunc autem scripsi vobis ne commisceamini, si quis cùm frater nominetur, sit scortator, aut auarus, aut idololatra, aut conuitia-tor, aut ebriosus, aut rapax, cùm eiusmodi (inquam) ne edatis qui-dem. Quid enim mea interest etiam de extraneis iudicare? Nonne de ijs, qui intus sunt, vos iudicatis? De extraneis verò Deus iudi-cat. Tollite igitur sceleratum istum ex vobis ipsis.
units.tr: I wrote to you in my letter that you should not associate with fornicators; but I did not mean altogether with the fornicators of this world, or with the covetous, the extortioners, or idolaters, since otherwise you would have to go out of the world. But now I have written to you that you should not associate with anyone who is called a brother yet is a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or an extortioner. With such a person, I say, do not even eat. For what business is it of mine to judge outsiders? Do you not judge those who are inside? God judges outsiders. Therefore, remove that wicked person from among yourselves.

units.la: QVando Ieremiam ad docendi munus Deus vocauit, inter alia sic illi loquebatur: Ecce ego constitui te hodie super gentes & super regna, ut euellas & extirpes, ut perdas & dis-sipes, ut aedifices & plantes. Quibus verbis admonet, Verbi ministros non obiter modo aut in genere doctrinam veritatis tradere debere, sed simul boni agricolae instar omnia è medio auferre, quae illius fructum impediunt. Ut enim terra propter maledictionem, cui obnoxia est, sua sponte spinas atq; herbas inutiles, imò noxias quoq; profert: ita homines ex innato naturae vitio ea quo-tidie faciunt, quae Deo minus placent, & illos à salutis via revocant. Tanta denique est huma-nae naturae prauitas, ut in ea corrigenda non sufficiant ecclesiarum ministri quantumuis assidui & diligentes, nisi publica authoritate adiuuentur. Ideo Paulus Corinthios tam diligenter monet atque hortatur, ut quae apud illos collapsa erat, ecclesiae disciplinam instaurent, & coniunctis viribus atque unanimi consensu auferant, quaecunque vetus peccati fermentum redolent, & quibus aliqui offendi possunt. Caeterum in hac doctrina duo restabant, de quibus dubitari aut quaeri poterat. Alterum, quousque disciplina haec extendatur, & qui nam illi sint, à quorum commercijs homines Christiani abstinere debeant? Alterum quid de ijs futurum sit, qui ab ecclesiae coetu & Christianae religionis professione alieni sua licentia fruuntur, neque ullis disciplinae legibus possunt coerceri, & quoad huius saeculi conditionem omnia pro sua libidine impune faciunt. De utroque in praesenti Apostolus disserit.
units.tr: When God called Jeremiah to the office of teaching, he said to him among other things: "See, I have set you this day over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root up and to pull down, to destroy and to scatter, to build and to plant." By these words he admonishes that ministers of the Word should not merely pass on the doctrine of truth in passing or in general terms, but, like a good farmer, should also clear away everything that hinders its fruit. For just as the earth, because of the curse to which it is subject, of its own accord brings forth thorns and useless weeds, indeed harmful ones too, so people, from the inborn corruption of their nature, daily do those things that please God less and call them back from the way of salvation. Finally, human depravity is so great that ministers of the churches, however diligent and attentive they may be, are not enough to correct it unless they are supported by public authority. For this reason Paul warns and exhorts the Corinthians so earnestly, that they should restore the discipline of the church, which had collapsed among them, and with united strength and one accord remove whatever smells of the old leaven of sin and whatever may give offence to some. Moreover, two questions remained in this teaching about which doubt or inquiry could arise. The first: how far this discipline extends, and who are those whose company Christians ought to avoid? The second: what will become of those who, being strangers to the assembly of the church and to the profession of the Christian religion, enjoy their own licence and cannot be restrained by any laws of discipline, and who, as far as the condition of this age goes, do whatever they please with impunity? The Apostle addresses both questions in the present passage.

units.la: Quoad primum, Praeoccupatione utitur, qua illis respondet, qui doctrinam de vitandis improbis aut flagitiosis superuacaneum dicebant, eo quod rem praestitu impossibilem iubeat. Etenim constat inter homines secundum illud Biantis dictum οἱ πλεῖστοι κακοί[?], id est, plerosque malos & vitijs deditos esse. Quisquis ergo vitare aut declinare instituat, qui aliquid praeter Christianae religionis decorum designant cum aliorum scandalo, eum prorsus ab omnium hominum consuetudine aut commercijs abstinere oporteret, & vitam solitariam viuere, quae ut nullis legibus diuinis praecipitur, ita naturae repugnat, cum Deus hominem animal sociabile fecerit, & ideo nos mutuis charitatis officijs inter nos certare velit. Apertius ergo mentem suam Paulus explicat his verbis: Scripsi vobis in epistola, ne commisceamini cum scortatoribus: at non omnino cum scortatoribus mundi huius, aut cum auaris, aut cum rapacibus, aut idololatris: alioqui debetis scilicet e mundo exire: Nunc autem scripsi vobis, ne commisceamini, si quis cum frater nominetur, sit scortator, &c.
units.tr: As to the first, he uses an anticipation, by which he answers those who said that the teaching about avoiding the wicked or the scandalous was pointless, because it commands something impossible. For it is agreed among men, in accordance with the saying of Bias, that "the most are bad" [οἱ πλεῖστοι κακοί], that is, that most people are wicked and given over to vices. Therefore, whoever undertakes to avoid or shun all those who, beyond what befits the Christian religion, cause scandal to others, would have to abstain entirely from the company and dealings of all men and live a solitary life. This is not commanded by any divine law, and it is contrary to nature, since God made man a sociable animal and therefore wishes us to vie with one another in the mutual duties of charity. Paul therefore explains his meaning more plainly in these words: "I wrote to you in my letter that you should not associate with fornicators; but I did not mean altogether with the fornicators of this world, or with the covetous, the extortioners, or idolaters, since otherwise you would have to go out of the world. But now I have written to you that you should not associate, if anyone who is called a brother is a fornicator," and so on.

units.la: Epistolae meminit, qua iam ante illos monuerit, ne cum scortatoribus commercia habeant. At non extat illa, ut nec multae aliae, quas ad diuersas ecclesias scripsit. Nec enim dubium est, illum in scribendo assiduum & diligentissimum fuisse, cum communi omnium ecclesiarum cura subinde premeretur, & quoties per alia negotia licebat, ad eas quoque excurreret, quas sua praesentia opus habere sciebat. Cuius studij exempla non obscura in Actorum libro & eius epistolis commemorantur. Et quod de illo dicimus, hoc de alijs quoque Apostolis sentire debemus. Sed spiritus sanctus eos modo libros seruari voluit, quos ad seruandam veritatis doctrinam sufficere, & ad constituendam ecclesiae formam necessarios esse vidit: alios autem, qui illis potissimum temporibus seruiebant, intercidere passus est, ne ecclesiam scriptis non necessarijs oneraret, aut nostrae curiositati occasionem daret ea inuestigandi, quorum cognitio non multum ad nos pertinet. Quod ipsum in veteri quoque testamento factum fuisse constat. Moses etenim Libri bellorum Domini meminit, & in Regum historia frequens est Annalium mentio, qui libri hodie nulli habentur. Et Iudas siue Taddaeus in epistola sua prophetiam Henochi adducit, cuius scriptum similiter nullum extat. Haec ut paternam Dei curam nobis commendant, qui ecclesiae suae quam commodissime prospectum voluit: ita illis confutandis seruiunt, qui nobis Concilio-rum decreta & nescio quos Canones obtrudunt, quibus purior illa & Apostolorum temporibus propinquior Vetustas caruit, & nos tamen hodie illis opus habere contendunt. At cui cordato credibile videri potest, Deu voluisse ut nonnulla prophetarū & Apostolorum scripta interciderent, in eorum autem locum succederent libri, de quorum authoribus nihil certi habetur, & qui praeter superstitiosas traditiones & ceremonias non minus frigidas quam ineptas nihil continent?
units.tr: He mentions a letter in which he had already warned them earlier not to have dealings with fornicators. But that letter does not survive, nor do many others which he wrote to various churches. For there is no doubt that he was assiduous and most diligent in writing, since he was constantly burdened with the common care of all the churches, and whenever other business allowed, he also hurried to those churches which he knew needed his presence. Clear examples of this zeal are recorded in the Book of Acts and in his epistles. And what we say of him, we should also think of the other Apostles. But the Holy Spirit wished to preserve only those books which he saw were sufficient for keeping the doctrine of truth and necessary for establishing the form of the church. The others, which served those particular times, he allowed to perish, so that the church would not be burdened with unnecessary writings, nor give our curiosity an occasion to investigate things whose knowledge does not greatly concern us. It is agreed that this also happened in the Old Testament. Moses indeed mentions the Book of the Wars of the Lord, and in the history of the Kings there is frequent mention of the Annals, which books are no longer held anywhere today. And Jude, or Thaddaeus, in his epistle cites the prophecy of Enoch, whose writing likewise does not survive. These examples commend to us the fatherly care of God, who wished to provide for his church as conveniently as possible; and they serve to refute those who thrust upon us the decrees of the councils and I know not what canons, which that purer antiquity, closer to the times of the Apostles, lacked, and yet they insist that we need them today. But what sensible person can believe that God wished some writings of the prophets and Apostles to perish, while in their place there should succeed books whose authors are not known for certain, and which contain nothing beyond superstitious traditions and ceremonies, as cold as they are foolish?

units.la: At quia haec non huius loci sunt, nunc Pauli sensum videamus, qui sic vult dicere: Memini me vobis alias scripsisse, ne cum scortatoribus consuetudinem contrahatis: id vero praestitu im-possibile videtur vobis, qui in ea vrbe viuitis, quae inter gentes quoque hoc nomine male audit, quod scortandi licentia nullis omnino legibus frenetur. Sed velim vos diligentius animum attendere, vt de quibus loquar intelligatis. Nec enim hoc absolute dixi de scortatoribus mundi huius, id est, de omnibus, quotquot adhuc mundo dediti & a Christiane religionis professione omnino alie-ni sunt, et proinde communi errore in hanc licentiam abripiuntur. Ita neq; omnes eos intelligo: qui in mundo hoc auaritiae seruiunt, rapinis student, vel etiam idololatriae sequuntur. Nam fi praeceptu hoc ita vrgere velim, vt nefas putem, cum aliquo consortium habere, qui vno aut altero istorum fce-lerum pollutus est: fateor necesse omnino fore, vt ex hoc mundo digressi aliam terram, omnibus hucufq; incognitam, quaeratis: quando in hoc orbe habitabili ista passim regnant, & difficile fit ali-què inuenire, qui omnis sceleris purus fit. Itaq;, ne cui aequo rigidior videar, nunc vobis mente me-am apertius declarabo, quae haec est. Si quis cum frater nominetur, nihilominus scortatorem agit, aut auaritiae mancipium est, aut idolorum cultu polluitur, aut conuitandi rabie ardet, aut ebrie-ti & intemperantiae operam dat, aut rapinis studet, aut aliquid eiusmodi, quod cum scandalo con-iunctum est, designat: cum eo ne cibum quidem capiatis. Sunt verba haec per fe clara, quia tamen de re maximi momenti dicuntur, non inutile fuerit, ea diligentius & propius inspexisse.
units.tr: But since these matters do not belong to this place, let us now look at Paul's meaning, which is this: "I remember that I wrote to you elsewhere not to form a habit of associating with fornicators. Indeed, this seems impossible for you, who live in a city which, even among the Gentiles, has an ill reputation under this name, because the licence of fornication is restrained by no laws at all. But I would have you attend more carefully, so that you understand whom I am speaking of. For I did not say this absolutely about the fornicators of this world, that is, about all those who are still given over to the world and are entirely strangers to the profession of the Christian religion, and who therefore are swept into this licence by common error. Nor do I mean all those who in this world serve covetousness, pursue plunder, or even follow idolatry. For if I wished to press this precept so hard that I thought it wrong to have any fellowship with someone who is polluted by one or another of these crimes, I confess that you would necessarily have to depart from this world and seek another land, unknown to you until now, since these evils reign everywhere in this habitable world, and it is hard to find anyone who is pure of every crime. Therefore, lest I seem too severe to anyone, I will now declare my mind to you more plainly, and it is this: If anyone who is called a brother nevertheless is a fornicator, or is a slave to covetousness, or is defiled by the worship of idols, or burns with the rage of reviling, or devotes himself to drunkenness and intemperance, or pursues plunder, or designates something of this kind that is joined with scandal, with such a person do not even take food." These words are clear in themselves, but since they are spoken about a matter of the greatest importance, it will not be unprofitable to look at them more carefully and closely.

units.la: Occurrit in his primum, quod diserte ait: Si quis frater nominatur, id est fi, Christianum fe ef-fe profitetur, & hoc nomen vulgo obtinet. Ita vero ex communi veterum more loquitur, quo Chri-ftiani fe mutuo fratres dicebant: nimirum propter communionem, quae nobis in Christo intercedit. Vnus etenim omnium pater est Deus: vna omnium mater, Ecclesia: vnum regenerationis femen, Verbum Dei: vnus regenerationis author, Spiritus sanctus: vna denique omnium haeredi-tas, quam nobis in coelis Dei Filius acquisiuit. Et prodest Christianos homines ipso nomine ad-moneri, quo fidelius fui officij meminerint. At in praesenti Paulus professionis meminit, vt apertos Christianos ab occultis discipulis distinguat. Solent tales saepe esse in iis locis, vbi non tum est fidem veram profiteri. Et hi tunc paucis modo noti sunt, & quamuis veritatem norint, ad tempus tamen superstitionibus communicant, quia vel occasionem adhuc nullam habent discedendi, vel nondum ita confirmati sunt, vt cum aliqua rerum suarum iactura discedere velint. Peccant hi quidem non leuiter, & apud Deum excusationem nullam habent. Verum tamen cum illis cautius & mitius agendum est, ne omnino alienentur, & in desperationem veniant. Non ergo eiusmodi homines indigni iudicari debent, quibus cum versemur, sed potius alliciendi sunt, vt nostra consuetudine confirmentur, & ex occultis aperti discipuli fiant. Exemplum facilitatis huius in Christo habemus, de quo Isaias olim vaticinatus est, quod arundinem quassatam non conterat, neque linum fumigans extinguat. Nicodemum certe & Iosephum Arimathaeum patienter tulit, & discipulorum loco habuit, licet illos adhuc eius puderet, & fidem in ipsum premetu Iudeorum profiteri nollent. At ijdem postea fortissimi facti sunt, & cum ignauo & ignobili timore deuicti turpiter laterent qui prius aperti discipuli fuerant, ipsi praeter omnem expectationem prodierunt, vt Christum ab omnibus derelictum honorifice sepelirent, & eo officio fidem in illum publice testati sunt. Simile quid de Victorino Rhetore Platonico D. Augustinus narrat, quem Simplicianus diu nequicquam fatigauit, vt fidem Christum, quam iam animo conceperat, publice profiteretur, & Ecclesiae sese palam coniungeret. Solebat enim cum risu ad eiusmodi exhortationes respondere: Ergo ne parietes faciunt Christianos? At idem postea, cum nihil huius speraretur, magna cum totius Romanae ciuitatis admiratione Christi nomen professus est. Et possent huius generis nonnulla commemorari, quae nostro saeculo acciderunt. Quae tamen non in eum finem recitamus, vt qui adhuc meticu-losi & ignaui latitant, ex illis sibi patrocinium petant: sed vt quorundam rigorem temperemus, qui dum omnes nimium audacter damnant, quos adhuc inter superstitiones haerere vident, multorum animos prorsus alienos a nobis reddunt, multis item extremae desperationis authoris sunt. Est ergo diligenter obseruanda haec distinctio Christianorum, vt occultos quidem & infirmos sanctâ indulgentia alliciamus, seueritate autem digna vtamur in eos, qui fidei professionem, qua gloriantur, morum licentia prophanant.
units.tr: First there occurs to us what he plainly says: "if anyone is called a brother," that is, if he professes that he is a Christian, and this name is commonly held by him. He speaks in this way according to the common custom of the ancients, by which Christians called one another brothers, certainly on account of the communion which we have in Christ. For God is the one Father of all; the Church is the one mother of all; the Word of God is the one seed of regeneration; the Holy Spirit is the one author of regeneration; and finally, the one inheritance of all is that which the Son of God has acquired for us in heaven. And it is profitable for Christian people to be reminded by this very name, so that they may remember more faithfully their duty. But here Paul mentions the profession, so that he may distinguish open Christians from secret disciples. Such people are often found in places where it is not safe to profess the true faith. These are known to only a few, and although they know the truth, for a time they still take part in superstitions, either because they have as yet no occasion to depart, or because they are not yet so firmly established that they are willing to leave with some loss of their possessions. Indeed, these people do not sin lightly, and they have no excuse before God. Yet we must deal with them more cautiously and gently, so that they are not wholly alienated and driven to despair.
