Therefore such people ought not to be judged unworthy of our company, but rather they are to be drawn on, so that they may be strengthened by our fellowship and go from secret disciples to open ones. We have an example of this gentleness in Christ, concerning whom Isaiah long ago prophesied that he would not break a bruised reed nor quench smoking flax. Certainly he patiently endured Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea and held them in the place of disciples, although they were still ashamed of him and were unwilling to profess faith in him for fear of the Jews. Yet afterwards these same men became most courageous, and while those who had previously been open disciples lay hidden in shameful and ignoble fear, they came forward beyond all expectation to bury Christ, who had been abandoned by all, with honour, and by that duty they publicly bore witness to their faith in him. Augustine relates something similar about Victorinus, the Platonic rhetorician, whom Simplicianus long tried in vain to persuade to profess publicly the faith in Christ which he had already conceived in his mind, and to join himself openly to the Church. For Victorinus used to answer such exhortations with laughter: "Do walls then make Christians?" Yet afterwards, when nothing of this was expected, he professed the name of Christ to the great admiration of the whole Roman city. Several examples of this kind could be recalled which have happened in our own age. We do not recite them for this purpose, that those who still lurk fearful and idle may seek a defence for themselves from them; but so that we may temper the severity of some who, while they condemn all too boldly everyone whom they see still clinging to superstitions, make the minds of many wholly alienated from us, and are also the cause of extreme despair for many. Therefore this distinction among Christians must be carefully observed: that we should draw in the secret and weak with holy gentleness, but deal with severity those who profane by a licence of conduct the profession of faith in which they boast.

units.la: Videamus igitur istorum catalogum, quem Apostolus contexit. In quo rursus observari debet, de iis modò illum loqui, qui in sceleribus istis cum impio admonitionum omnium contemptu pergunt, & poenitentiae doctrinam pertinaciter aspernantur. Nam quàmuis aliqui in his aut similibus peccent, admonitione autem vel publica vel privata se in viam revocari patiantur, mox in gratiam recipi debent, nosq; de eorum conversione gaudere convenit. Ergo de iis hic loquitur Paulus, qui incurabiles & poenitere nescij peccato prorsus serviunt: quos ex ordine videbimus, ut quae vitia potissimum caveri debeant, intelligamus.
units.tr: Let us now look at the list of these vices that the Apostle has put together. Here again it must be noticed that he is speaking only of those who persist in these sins, scorning all admonition and stubbornly rejecting the teaching of repentance. For although some fall into these or similar sins, yet if they allow themselves to be called back to the right way by admonition, whether public or private, they ought at once to be received back into favour, and we should rejoice at their conversion. Paul therefore speaks here of those who are incurable, who cannot repent, and who are wholly enslaved to sin. We shall examine them in order, so that we may understand which vices above all must be guarded against.

units.la: Primo loco Scortatores nominat, partim quòd scelus hoc à vocatione nostra & nominis Christiani professione alienissimum est, ut in sequenti cap. docebit: partim quòd propter hoc imprimis in huius argumenti tractatione defenderat[?], & ab illo quàm maximè deterrendi essent Corinthij, cùm propter effrænem totius civitatis licentiam & veterem consuetudinem ij quoq; ab illo minus abhorrerent, qui iam Christo nomen dederant. Quo loco admonemur, Christianos homines ab ijs etiam vitijs abstinere debere, quae genti suae quasi propria sunt, & vix peccati loco habentur. Sunt equidem, qui illa communi exemplo excusari posse arbitrantur, & nimium morosos atque importunos eos esse dicunt, qui illa volunt disciplina severiori coercere. Sed non quid mundo videatur, aut quid in unaquaq; gente vulgò receptum sit, sed quid Deus velit spectandum est, & quid Christianae professionis leges postulent. Atqui ut omnium gentium servator est Christus: ita Evangelium omnibus praedicari, & ex eius semine omnes regenerari atq; innovari vult, ut excusso diaboli iugo libertatem, quam ipse nobis meruit apprehendamus, & in Patris sui conspectu vitam vi-vamus novâ atq; irreprehensibilem. Ut ergo publici civitatis mores & diuturna consuetudo apud Corinthios minimè excusavit scortandi licentiam: ita veniam nullam merentur, qui cùm Christiani dici & esse velint, alijs suae gentis moribus corruptis indulgent.
units.tr: In the first place he names fornicators, partly because this crime is most alien to our calling and to the profession of the Christian name, as he will teach in the following chapter, and partly because he had already dealt with this subject at length and the Corinthians had to be most strongly deterred from it. Given the unbridled license of the whole city and its long-standing custom, even those who had already given their names to Christ were less averse to it. Here we are warned that Christians must abstain even from those vices which are, as it were, peculiar to their own nation and hardly count as sin. There are indeed some who think these can be excused by common practice, and who say that those are overly fussy and troublesome who want to restrain them by stricter discipline. But what matters is not what seems right to the world, or what is commonly accepted in any nation, but what God wills and what the laws of the Christian profession demand. Christ is indeed the Saviour of all nations; so he wills that the Gospel be preached to all, and that all be born again and renewed from his seed, so that, having thrown off the yoke of the devil, we may grasp the freedom he has won for us, and live a new and blameless life in the sight of his Father. Therefore, just as the public morals of the city and the long-established custom among the Corinthians by no means excused the license of fornication, so those deserve no pardon who, while wishing to be and be called Christians, indulge in the corrupt morals of their nation.

units.la: Secundum locum avaris tribuit, in quibus πλεονεξίαν, id est, eam aviditatem reprehendit, qua aliqui plura quàm Deus dedit appetunt, neq; sua forte contenti vivunt. Videtur hoc quoq; vitium late[?] multis, & non aliqua animadversione dignum: sed sub eo multa & gravia comprehenduntur, quae singula à regno Dei excludunt, nisi ea corrigas. Nam radix eius est diffidentia, quae ut de Dei cura, qua nos prosequitur, dubitemus movet. Coniunctam verò sibi habet opum fiduciam, quae causa est, quòd alibi idololatriae species esse dicitur. Nã animum totùm à Deo abstrahit, quod Christus nõ obscurè testatur, quando fieri posse negat, ut Deo simul & Mammonae serviamus. Fructus & effecta eius sunt fraudes, doli, impostura, inhumanitas, iniqui contractus, usurae, rapinae, periuria, & quacunq; alia praeter ius & aequum fiunt, & à charitate alienissima sunt. Recte ergo avaros illos ijs Paulus adnumerat, quorum commercia Christiani fugere debent.
units.tr: In the second place he assigns the covetous, in whom he rebukes πλεονεξία, that is, that greed by which some desire more than God has given and do not live content with what they have. This vice also seems to many to be widespread and not worth any great notice, but under it are included many grave evils, each of which shuts a person out of the kingdom of God unless you correct them. For its root is distrust, which makes us doubt God's care with which he watches over us. Closely joined to it is confidence in wealth, which is the reason why elsewhere it is called a kind of idolatry. For it draws the whole mind away from God, as Christ plainly testifies when he says that it is impossible to serve God and Mammon at the same time. Its fruits and effects are deceit, trickery, fraud, inhumanity, unjust contracts, usury, robbery, perjury, and whatever else is done contrary to right and fairness and is most remote from charity. Rightly, then, Paul counts the covetous among those with whom Christians must avoid dealings.

units.la: Tertij in hoc catalogo sunt Idololatrae, quod non immerito aliquis miretur, cùm de fratribus aut Christianis agat. Absurdissimum enim ess, & quasi ἀσύνατον[?], ut quis & Christianus sit & idololatra. Sed non mirabere, si temporum illorum mores inspicias. Erant enim multi in religione ambigui, qui etiamsi fidem Christianam profiterentur, idololatria tamen sese polluebant: & id non uno modo tunc factum fuit. Alij enim quòd imaginum aliquē inter Christianos quoque usum esse putarent, ab illis minus abhorrebant. Alij sub Deorum nominibus Deum verum colì posse somniabant, & hi in illorum mysterijs mirificè philosophabantur. Inter alia autem hoc apud plerosque in usu erat, quòd à vicinis & cognatis vel amicis invitati ad sacra ethnicorum accedebant, & quàmuis non astarent sacrificantibus, epulis tamen & conviuijs intererant, quae ex carnibus sacrificiorum solebant instrui: de quibus suo loco prolixè differentem audiemus. Excusabant isti omnes factum suum multis rationibus, inter quas praecipua illis erat, quòd se in veri Dei cognitione probè instructos esse, & de falsis Dijs prorsus nihil honorificum in animo sentire dicerent. Sed Paulus eos non ex ipsorum opinione, sed ex re ipsa aestimans, idololatras esse pronuntiat: nimirum quòd tales revera sint, quicunque cultibus illicitis vel minima ex parte communicant. Similes horum sunt hodie, qui imagines defendunt, & his cū libris laicorum utendum esse censent: quotquot item quacunque alia ratione vel cum gentium vel cum Papistarum superstitionibus aut idololatria communicant. Faciunt id revera, qui sub Carnispriuiorum[?] (ut illi loquuntur) nomine Orgia Bacchi, Lupercalia & Cerealia celebrant: quae festa à gentibus olim iisdem[?] anni temporibus & eodem plane ritu celebrata fuisse constat. Item, qui Encænia retinent, quæ ut in Diuorum honorem à Papistis agi solent, ita ab illis non minori cum libertate morum retinentur, quàm apud eos fiat, quos Euangelij lux nondum illuminauit. Habent isti quoque argumenta omnis generis, quibus se excusant: sed cùm negare non possint, hæc à gentibus & Papistis originem duxisse, idololatriæ adnumerari debent quicunque ijs vacant.
units.tr: Third in this list are the idolaters. Someone may well be surprised at this, since he is speaking of brothers or Christians. For it seems most absurd, and almost impossible, that someone should be both a Christian and an idolater. But you will not be surprised if you look at the customs of those times. For there were many who were ambivalent in religion, and although they professed the Christian faith, they nevertheless defiled themselves with idolatry, and this happened in more than one way at that time. Some, thinking that the use of images was also allowed among Christians, were less averse to them. Others dreamed that the true God could be worshipped under the names of the gods, and these grew wonderfully philosophical about their mysteries. Among other things, however, it was common among many that, when invited by neighbours, relatives, or friends, they went to the sacred rites of the heathen, and although they did not stand by while the sacrifices were offered, they nevertheless took part in the feasts and banquets which were usually furnished with the flesh of the sacrifices. We shall hear about these at length in their proper place. All these men excused their action in many ways, among which their chief argument was that they were well instructed in the knowledge of the true God, and said that they held nothing honourable at all in their minds about the false gods. But Paul, judging them not by their own opinion but by the reality itself, pronounces them idolaters: clearly because they really are such, whoever shares in unlawful worship even in the smallest part. Like these are today those who defend images and think that they should be used with the books of the laity, and all who in any other way have fellowship with the superstitions or idolatry of the nations or of the Papists. Those really do this who celebrate under the name of Carnival (as they call it) the orgies of Bacchus, the Lupercalia, and the Cerealia, feasts which, as is well known, were once celebrated by the nations at the same seasons of the year and with exactly the same rites. Likewise those who keep the Encaenia, which, as the Papists usually hold them in honour of the saints, are kept by them with no less licence of morals than is found among those whom the light of the Gospel has not yet illumined. These men also have arguments of every kind by which they excuse themselves, but since they cannot deny that these customs derive their origin from the nations and the Papists, all who engage in them must be counted among the idolaters.

units.la: Quarto loco conuitiatores sequuntur, quorum scelus grave & multiplex est. Peccant enim illi in charitatis leges, quæ proximi famam atq; fortunas tueri iubent. Et vehementius fere no-cent linguæ virulentia, quàm qui vim apertâ inferunt. Quæ causa est, quòd verba eorum Dauid gladijs & sagittis acutis, imò aspidum similia esse, sub linguis autem eorum venenum ser-pentum occultari ait. Iacobus autem eiusmodi linguas ab igne infernali accendi scribit, & [illegible, ~8 letters] κακόν[?], id est, malum esse dicit, quod nulla ratione retineri aut coerceri possit. Quia autem animi index est sermo, fieri nequit, quin animos æmulatione, inuidia & odio plenos habeant, qui conuitiandi & obtrectandi libidine delectantur. At qui istis affectibus seruiunt, ij Christi spiritu nondum reguntur, & proinde fucata fidei professione se venditant, ideoq; digni sunt, quos Christiani homines suspectos habeant.
units.tr: In the fourth place come the revilers, whose sin is grave and manifold. For they offend against the laws of charity, which bid us protect the reputation and fortunes of our neighbour. And the venom of the tongue often harms more severely than those who inflict violence openly. This is why David says that their words are like swords and sharp arrows, even like the poison of asps, and that the venom of serpents lies hidden under their tongues. James also writes that such tongues are set on fire by hellfire, and says that it is an evil [κακόν], that is, a thing that cannot be restrained or curbed by any means. But since speech is the index of the mind, it cannot be otherwise than that those who delight in the lust of reviling and detracting have minds full of rivalry, envy, and hatred. But those who serve these passions are not yet ruled by the Spirit of Christ, and therefore they put on a show with a feigned profession of faith, and so they deserve to be regarded with suspicion by Christian people.

units.la: Quinti in hoc grege ebriosi numerantur. Sunt hi, qui bibendi & inebriandi habitum contraxe-runt, & in poculis omnem voluptatem sitam esse arbitrantur. Describit horum mores Isaias his verbis: Væ his qui mane se accingunt ut sectentur siceram, & id in crepusculum usq; prorogant, vino eos inflammante: in quorum conuiuijs cithara & nablum, tympanū & tibia cum vino: at in-terim opus Domini non contemplantur, neq; opus manuum eius considerant. Primò studium inebriandi assiduum illis tribuit, quando mane eos compotationes suas inchoare dicit, & easdem in noctem usque extendere. Deinde vino eos accendi & inflammari ait: nimirum ut toti carnis desiderijs ardeant, & excusso rationis iugo in omnem petulantiam ruant. Hinc ergo rixæ, conuitia, pugnæ, vulnera, cædes, illicitæ libidines & infinita alia nascuntur, quæ omnia Solomon ebriosis tribuit.
units.tr: Fifth in this flock are counted the drunkards. These are those who have acquired the habit of drinking and getting drunk, and who think that all pleasure lies in cups. Isaiah describes their manners in these words: "Woe to those who rise early in the morning to pursue strong drink, and who prolong it into the twilight, the wine inflaming them; at whose feasts are harp and lute, tambourine and flute, and wine; but they do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider the operation of his hands." First, he ascribes to them a constant zeal for drinking, when he says that in the morning they begin their drinking bouts and extend them into the night. Then he says they are kindled and inflamed by wine: clearly so that they burn wholly with the desires of the flesh, and, having thrown off the yoke of reason, rush into every wantonness. Hence quarrels, reproaches, fights, wounds, murders, unlawful lusts, and countless other evils arise, all of which Solomon attributes to drunkards.

units.la: Addit his gaudia immodica Isaias, quæ instrumentis Musicis testentur (quod Amos quoque in sui sæculi hominibus accusat) & iis maximè, quæ furorem animi magis augent, & proinde in bellis fere usum habent, qualia sunt tympanum & tibia. Et ne quis hæc leuicula putaret, addit quod grauissimum est, quod nimirum opus Domini non contemplentur, neq; opus manuum eius considerent, quibus verbis impiam securitatem cum manifesto Dei contemptu coniunctam describit: cuius hæc effecta sunt, quòd donis Dei impiè abutuntur, corporis & animi vires scientes volentes debilitant, iudiciorum Dei exempla omnia contemnunt & rident, eò deniq; delabuntur, ut qui inter illos optimi sunt pecudum instar soli ventri & gulæ seruiant: ut iam nihil de illis dicamus, qui in ursos, leones lupos, tigrides degenerare solent. Quis verò istos pro Christianis agnoscat, qui ne homines quidem dici merentur? Quis item dignos iudicet, quibus cum consuetudinem habeant, qui se totos Christo consecrauerunt?
units.tr: Isaiah adds immoderate joys, which are attested by musical instruments (as Amos also condemns in the men of his own age), and especially those that stir up the frenzy of the mind the more and so are used almost always in wars, such as the drum and the pipe. And lest anyone think these to be trifles, he adds what is most serious: namely, that they do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider the work of his hands. With these words he describes impious complacency joined with open contempt for God. The results are that such people impiously abuse God's gifts, knowingly and willingly weaken the strength of body and mind, scorn and mock all the examples of God's judgments, and finally sink so low that even the best of them, like cattle, serve only their belly and gullet. We need not say more about those who are wont to degenerate into bears, lions, wolves and tigers. Who would acknowledge such people as Christians, who do not even deserve to be called human? Who would think them worthy to have fellowship with those who have wholly consecrated themselves to Christ?

units.la: Sexto gradu rapaces collocat, de iis loquens, qui habendi & acquirendi cupiditati eò usque indulgent, ut aliena quoque ad se rapiant. Ita verò omnes rationes illicitas comprehendit, quibus quæ aliorum sunt sibi vendicant homines auari & diuitijs dediti. Ad hunc ergo titulum pertinent impostores, hæredipetæ, falsarij, fæneratores, usurarij, milites mercenarij, quos sola lucri spes ad istam lanienam trahit, & quibus (ut Poeta ait) ibi fas, ubi maxima merces. Qui hisce rebus student, ij iampridem hominem exuerunt, & cùm apud ethnicos semper male audierint, minimè digni sunt, qui inter Christianos locum habeant. Etenim nisi cum Zachæo pœnitentiam agant, & quæ iniquis modis rapuerunt restituant, fidemq; in Christum benefi-centiæ operibus testentur, regni illius cœlestis hæreditatem adire nunquam poterunt. At quia longum foret omnes enumerare, qui Christiana communione indigni sunt, uno verbo docet idem iudicium de omnibus ferri debere, quotquot his aut similibus vitiis laborant. Ali-bi certè homines ἀτάκτως, id est, inordinatos quoque excludere iubet, eos nimirum intelligens, qui cùm ex ecclesiæ ærario alantur, in turpi otio viuunt, & alienis modò intenti ipsi nihil faciunt Christiana vocatione dignum. Hi cùm Christiani nominis professionem sibi quæ-stum faciant, & ipsius Dei nomine ad otium suum tuendum abutantur, adhæc veris pauperibus & ecclesiæ quod ipsis debetur præripiant, merito certè ab ecclesiæ cœtu arcèri debent. Pertinent deniq; ad hunc catalogum, quotquot incurabili pertinacia in quocunq; peccati genere pergunt, & Christianæ disciplinæ legibus nolunt coerceri.
units.tr: In the sixth rank he places the rapacious, speaking of those who indulge their desire to have and to acquire so far that they seize even what belongs to others. In this way he comprehends all the unlawful means by which greedy men given to riches claim for themselves what is the property of others. To this category belong impostors, fortune-hunters, forgers, usurers, moneylenders, and mercenary soldiers, whom the sole hope of gain draws into that butchery, and for whom (as the poet says) it is right wherever the reward is greatest. Those who pursue these things have long since put off the man, and although among the heathen they have always had a bad reputation, they are wholly unworthy to have a place among Christians. Indeed, unless they repent with Zacchaeus, restore what they have taken by unjust means, and bear witness to their faith in Christ by works of kindness, they will never be able to enter the inheritance of that heavenly kingdom. But since it would be tedious to list all who are unworthy of Christian fellowship, he teaches in a single word that the same judgment should be passed on all who labour under these or similar vices. Elsewhere he certainly orders that the disorderly [ἀτάκτως], that is, the unruly, also be excluded, meaning those who, though they are supported from the church's funds, live in shameful idleness, and while busy with other people's affairs do nothing worthy of their Christian calling. Since they make a profit from the profession of the Christian name and abuse the very name of God to protect their idleness, and moreover snatch from the true poor and the church what is owed to them, they most deservedly ought to be shut out of the assembly of the church. Finally, to this catalogue belong all who persist in any kind of sin with incurable obstinacy and refuse to be restrained by the laws of Christian discipline.

units.la: Quid verò cum omnibus istis agendum? Cum eiusmodi (inquit Paulus) ne edatis quidem. Qua locutione familiaritatem & arctiorem consuetudinem significat, quæ aliquam consensionis speciem præ se fert. Interim quoad usum vitæ huius & commercia necessaria, nequaquam prohi-bemur, quo minus cum talibus colloquamur, contrahamus, & alia faciamus, sine quibus humana vita consistere non potest. Ubi etiam repetendum, quod alibi diximus, hoc præcepto neq; coniugia di-rimi, neq; quam subditi magistratibus & serui heris debent, fidem dissolui aut aboleri. Quia enim omnis disciplinæ hic finis & usus esse debet, vt qui peccarunt corrigantur & in viam redeant, idem omnino abijci non possunt. Ergo non disciplinam ecclesiasticam, sed tyrannidem intolerabilem & plus quàm barbaram crudelitatem exercent Pontifices, qui sub Excommunicationis prætextu, civi-tatis, tecti, aquæ & ignis omniumq; commerciorum interdictione in eos seuiunt, qui in ipsorum leges peccauerunt. Quæ enim inde utilitas ad excommunicatos redit? Quomodo item eorum exemplo alij meliores fiunt? Imò unius delictum ad multos alios propagatur, qui vt Pontificum decre-tis obtemperent, eos perire sinunt crudeliter, quos in vita seruare debebant. Ubi tamen obseruari debet, minimè probandos esse eos, qui commercia non necessaria cum illis habent, quos seueriori disciplina contineri proderat. Et intolerabilis est eorum licentia, qui cum talibus non modò edunt & bibunt, sed etiam comessantur, belluantur, ludunt, & sua illa leuitate eos obstinatiores reddunt, quo minus conuertantur, & Christianis hominibus dignam pœnitentiam agant.
units.tr: But what is to be done with all these? "With such people," says Paul, "do not even eat." By this expression he signifies familiarity and a closer intimacy, which carries with it some appearance of agreement. Meanwhile, as regards the necessary uses and dealings of this life, we are by no means forbidden to speak with such people, to have dealings with them, and to do other things without which human life cannot exist. Here it must also be repeated what we have said elsewhere: by this precept neither marriages are to be dissolved, nor the faith which subjects owe to magistrates and servants to masters is to be broken or abolished. For since the whole purpose and use of discipline ought to be that those who have sinned may be corrected and return to the right way, these people certainly cannot be cast off altogether. Therefore the Popes, who under the pretext of excommunication rage against those who have sinned against their laws, by forbidding them the city, roof, water and fire, and all commerce, are exercising not ecclesiastical discipline but an intolerable tyranny and a cruelty more than barbaric. For what benefit does this bring back to the excommunicated? Or how do others become better by their example? Indeed the offence of one spreads to many others, who, so that they may obey the decrees of the Popes, let those perish cruelly whom they ought to have preserved in life. Here, however, it must be observed that those are by no means to be commended who have unnecessary dealings with such people, whom a stricter discipline would be useful in restraining. And intolerable is the licence of those who not only eat and drink with such people, but even feast with them, revel, and play, and by their own frivolity make them more obstinate, so that they are less ready to be converted and to do penance worthy of Christians.

units.la: Quia verò huius disciplinæ usum ad solos Christianos restrinxerat Paulus, suæ sententiæ ra-tionem his verbis subijcit: Quid enim mea interest, etiam de extraneis judicare? Nonne de ijs, qui intus sunt, vos judicatis? Extraneos dicit alienos à fide, eò quòd tales adhuc extra Ecclesiæ septa vagantur, & (vt ad Ephesios de gentibus dicitur) à repub. Israelis abalienati & à pactis promis-sionum divinarum extranei sunt. Opponuntur his qui intus sunt, id est, qui per Euangelium vocati & Ecclesiæ cives facti sunt, & proinde illius privilegijs atq; bonis fruuntur. Et prodest vocabu-la ista observare, quia per illa nos Spiritus sanctus admonet, quàm infelix sit eorum conditio, qui ab Ecclesia alieni sunt. Sunt enim extranei à regno Dei, neq; ad Christi gregem pertinent, cuius ille pastor est, ideoq; luporum & ipsius diaboli insidijs patent. Petitur autem argumentum ex communi hominum consuetudine, adeoq; ex iure gentium. Vt enim civitatis legibus soli cives reguntur & coercentur, aut qui ad civium numerum pertinent: ita cum Ecclesia Dei civitas sit, in eos quoq; so-los sibi jus sumit, quos pro civibus suis agnoscit. Sensus ergo verborum Pauli est: Cum nos suæ Ec-clesiæ ministros constituerit Deus, & tota hæc disciplinæ ecclesiasticæ ratio ad illam in officio con-tinendam pertineat, minimè opus est eam vlterius ad eos extendere, qui extra Ecclesiam sunt, & nos rebus nihil ad nos pertinentibus implicare. Vt enim ridiculum esset eos à civitate excludere vel le, qui cives non sunt, neq; etiam esse cupiunt: ita stultè nimis facerent, qui ab Ecclesiæ cœtu reijcere vellent eos, qui iam ante ab illa totis animis abhorrent. Nos itaq; nostris finibus contenti de ijs iu-dicium feramus, qui intra Ecclesiæ pomœria continentur. At nō debent ista sic accipi, vt sua ver-bo Dei authoritas abrogetur, ex quo nobis licet de omnibus hominibus & factis eorum judicare. Semper enim ratum erit, iram Dei omnibus imminere, qui iniquitate seclantur[?] & absq; pœnitentia pergunt in sceleribus. Neq; unquam fallet Christi sententia: Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, seruabitur: qui non crediderit, damnabitur. Ex his ergo judicandum est de superstitionibus & om-nibus ijs, qui Christum oderunt, & ad Ecclesiæ eius societatem nolunt accedere. Adde his, quòd non raro necessitas iubet, vt extraneis quoq; concionentur verbi ministri: quando nimirum vel cum illis licenter nimis colluduntur, qui Christiani dici volunt: vel eorundem successibus & insolentia pij offenduntur: vel cùm illi in Ecclesiæ excidium coniurant, & extrema quæq; Christi culcoribus[?] mi-nantur. Et huc referri debent Prophetarum conciones, quibus illi Assyrijs, Babylonijs, Ægyptijs, Idumæis, & alijs gentibus pœnas à Deo paratas denuntiauerunt, & earundē causas prolixè enara[?] rarunt, vt vel pios aduersus illorum minas confirmarent, vel ab eorum amicitiis atque fœderibus eos retraherent, qui apud illos præsidia quærebant. Et quod illi fecerunt, bodie etiam facto opus est, neque nobis vitio verti debet, si quando de Papa & eius coniuratus verba faciamus liberius. Etsi enim illi omnes pro extraneis merito habeantur, eos tamen negligere aut silentio prorsus præterire non possumus, cum illi rebus Ecclesiæ sese immisceant, eandem modo aperta vi oppugnent, modo per insidias & cuniculos circumuenire studeant, multorum autem ex nostris tanta sit simplicitas, vt illorum artes obseruare non possint, nonnullorum quoq; ea vecordia, vt sese in eorum in-gues [?] & retia sponte ingerant.
units.tr: But since Paul had restricted the use of this discipline to Christians alone, he adds the reason for his opinion in these words: "For what is it to me to judge even those outside? Do you not judge those who are inside?" He calls "outsiders" those who are aliens from the faith, because such people still wander outside the fences of the Church and (as is said in Ephesians of the Gentiles) are alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and are strangers to the covenants of promise. They are opposed to those who are inside, that is, those who have been called through the gospel and made citizens of the Church, and therefore enjoy its privileges and goods. It is useful to observe these terms, because through them the Holy Spirit reminds us how unhappy is the condition of those who are alien to the Church. For they are strangers from the kingdom of God, and do not belong to the flock of Christ, whose shepherd he is, and therefore lie open to the snares of wolves and of the devil himself. The argument is drawn from common human custom, and thus from the law of nations. For just as only citizens are governed and restrained by the laws of the state, or those who belong to the number of citizens, so, since the Church of God is a commonwealth, it claims jurisdiction only over those whom it acknowledges as its citizens. The sense of Paul's words, therefore, is this: since God has appointed us ministers of his Church, and the whole reason of ecclesiastical discipline pertains to keeping that Church in order, there is no need to extend it further to those who are outside the Church, and to entangle ourselves in matters that do not concern us. For just as it would be ridiculous to wish to exclude from the city those who are not citizens and do not even desire to be, so it would be very foolish to wish to cast out of the assembly of the Church those who already with their whole soul abhor it. Let us therefore be content with our own bounds and pass judgment on those who are contained within the walls of the Church. But these things must not be so understood that the authority of God's word is thereby abrogated, by which we are permitted to judge all men and their deeds. For it will always be certain that the wrath of God hangs over all who pursue iniquity and persist in their wickedness without repentance. Nor will Christ's sentence ever fail: "He who believes and is baptized will be saved; he who does not believe will be condemned." From these words, therefore, we must judge concerning the superstitions and all those who hate Christ and refuse to come into fellowship with his Church. Add to this that necessity often requires that the ministers of the Word also preach to outsiders: namely, when either they play too freely with those who want to be called Christians, or the pious are offended by their successes and insolence, or when they conspire for the ruin of the Church and threaten the utmost evils against the followers of Christ. To this must be referred the sermons of the Prophets, in which they announced to the Assyrians, Babylonians, Egyptians, Edomites and other nations the punishments prepared by God, and explained their causes at length, so that they might either strengthen the pious against their threats, or draw back from their friendships and alliances those who sought protection among them. What they did, there is also need to do today, and it ought not to be counted against us if at times we speak more freely about the Pope and his conspirators. For although all of them are rightly regarded as outsiders, we cannot neglect them or pass them over in silence, since they thrust themselves into the affairs of the Church, attack it now by open force, now strive to get around it by plots and mines, while many among our own people are so simple that they cannot observe their arts, and some in their madness throw themselves willingly into their snares and nets.

units.la: Sed tempus est, vt ad alterum huius loci caput transeamus, quod paucis expedietur. Obij-ciat enim ad ista aliquis: Ergo ne impune omnia ferent, qui ab Ecclesia extranei sunt? Enimvero, si nos de illis iudicare non possumus, ijdem vero neq; per ciuiles leges coercentur, quis non videat eos immunitate quadam frui, & eorum conditionem potiorem esse, quàm piorum sit, qui & foris hostes habent crudeles, & domi disciplinæ seueriores legibus premuntur? Sed breuiter ad hanc obiectionem Apostolus respondet: De extraneis Deus iudicat. Quasi diceret: Vos quod vestrum est facite, de alteris illis non nimium solliciti. Nec enim semper impune ferent quod faciunt. Nam etsi inter homines nemo in illos animaduertat, habent tamen iudicem suum, Deum, qui vt per Legem punit eos, qui Legem acceperunt, ita absq; Lege eos iudicat, qui quam in cordibus suis descriptam habent naturæ legem, violant. Itaq; quamuis disciplinam ecclesiasticam ad illos vsq; extendi nolit Paulus, eosdem tamen ad Dei tribunal citat, & huic pœnas scelerum daturos esse minatur. Ne minem ergo licentia eiusmodi hominum offendat. Nec enim perpetua erit, qua ad tempus gaudent, impunitas, & fere præter omnem expectationem dira iustitiæ Dei exempla fiunt, qui extra omne periculum constituti esse videbantur. Poterat hoc prolixè ex historijs cum sacris tum prophanis demonstrari, vt iam de pœnis in futuro sæculo præparatis nihil dicamus.
units.tr: But it is time to turn to the second point of this passage, which can be dealt with briefly. Someone might object to this: "So will those who are outside the Church go completely unpunished?" Indeed, if we cannot judge them, and they are not restrained by civil laws, who would not see that they enjoy a certain immunity, and that their condition is better than that of the godly, who have cruel enemies abroad and are oppressed at home by a discipline more severe than the laws? But Paul answers this objection briefly: "God judges those who are outside." As if he were saying: "You do what is your business, and do not be too anxious about those others. For they will not always go unpunished for what they do. Although no man among men takes action against them, they have their own judge, God, who, as He punishes through the Law those who have received the Law, so judges without the Law those who violate the law of nature, which they have written in their hearts. Therefore, although Paul does not wish church discipline to be extended to them, he nevertheless summons them to the tribunal of God and threatens that they will pay the penalty for their crimes to Him. Let no one, therefore, be offended by the licence of such men. For the impunity in which they rejoice for a time will not be lasting, and terrible examples of God's justice often occur, almost beyond all expectation, among those who seemed to be placed beyond all danger. This could be demonstrated at length from histories, both sacred and profane, not to mention the punishments prepared for the age to come."

units.la: Restat huius tractationis conclusio, quam breuibus absoluit, vt magis referat grauitatem apo-stolicam. Tollite (inquit) sceleratum illum ex vobis ipsis. Ita vero omnes quæstiones semel abrum-pit, quas licentiæ patroni mouere poterant. Quasi diceret. Quid multis verbis opus est? Si Christiani estis, si ecclesiam puram & sanctam esse vultis, vtimini iure vestro, quo vos Christus armauit, & hominem illum tanto scelere infamem, ceu maculam & pestem e medio vestri tollite. Vtitur autem locutione, quæ frequens in Lege occurrit: Auferes malum e medio tui: ex qua rursus apparet eum non exclusionem a Cœna Domini præcipere, sed vt supplicio grauiori multandum Satanæ tradant ad carnis interitum. Simul vero docet, hoc illos suo bono facturos esse, quando sic eccle-sia pessimo contagio liberaturi sint: neq; hoc ipsis nouum aut seueritatis inauditæ exemplu debet videri, quando olim Deus in veteri populo publica scelera pœnis capitalibus punire iusserit. Admonemur igitur hac tota disputatione, per Euangelium minimè abrogari disciplinam, neq; morum licentiam per gratiæ prædicationem stabiliri. Quin suum quoq; ius magistratui integrum manet, quem Dei ministrum esse alibi Paulus docet, vt quod malum est puniat. Deniq; debet ex Eccle-sia & repub. Christiana malum auferri, vt suum in nobis regnum obtinere possit Dominus & redemptor noster IESVS CHRISTVS: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: There remains the conclusion of this discussion, which he brings to a close in a few words, so as to heighten the apostolic gravity. "Take away," he says, "that wicked man from among yourselves." In this way he cuts short at once all the questions which the patrons of licence might raise. As if he were saying: "What need is there of many words? If you are Christians, if you wish the Church to be pure and holy, use your right, with which Christ has armed you, and remove that man, infamous for so great a crime, like a stain and a plague, from your midst." He uses a phrase which occurs frequently in the Law: "You shall take away the evil from the midst of you"; from which again it appears that he is prescribing not merely exclusion from the Lord's Supper, but that they should hand him over to Satan to be punished with a heavier penalty, to the destruction of the flesh. At the same time he teaches that they will be doing this for their own good, since in this way they will free the Church from a most pernicious contagion; nor ought this to seem to them a new example or an unheard-of severity, since of old God in the ancient people commanded that public crimes be punished with capital penalties. We are therefore reminded by this whole discussion that discipline is by no means abrogated through the Gospel, nor is licence of morals established through the preaching of grace. Indeed, the right of the magistrate also remains whole, whom Paul elsewhere teaches to be the minister of God, to punish what is evil. Finally, evil must be removed from the Church and the Christian commonwealth, so that our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ may obtain His kingdom in us, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: CAPUT VI. HOMILIA XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI. SERMON XXVII.

units.la: Audet aliquis vestrum negotiũ habens cum altero, iudicio ex-periri sub iniustis, & non sub sanctis? An ignoratis, quòd sancti mundũ iudicabunt? Quòd si per vos iudicabitur mundus, indigni estis minimis iudicijs? An ignoratis fore vt Angelos iudicemus, nedum quæ ad huius vitæ vsum pertinent? Itaq; si iudicia habeatis de ijs, quæ ad huius vitæ vsum pertinent, eos qui minimi fiunt in Ecclesia, eos[inquā] in subsellijs collocate. Vt vos pudeat, vobis hoc dico. Itáne non est inter vos sapiens, ne vnus quidem, qui possit dijudicare inter fratres suos? sed frater cum fratre iudicio experiatur, idq; sub infidelibus?
units.tr: Does any of you, when he has a dispute with another, dare to go to law before the unrighteous and not before the saints? Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you unworthy to decide the smallest cases? Do you not know that we shall judge angels, to say nothing of the affairs of this life? So if you have judgments about the affairs of this life, do you seat those who are of least account in the Church to judge them? I say this to your shame. Is there not among you a single wise man who is able to decide between his brothers? But brother goes to law with brother, and before unbelievers at that?

units.la: VEMADMODVM Dominus IESVS CHRISTVS vera atque vnica mundi lux est, hanc verò suam lucem nobis per Euangelij doctrinam communicat: Ita in tenebris ambulent & inextricabilibus errorum Labyrinthis inuoluantur necesse est, quotquot reliqua doctrinæ ipsius simplicitate, vel sua vel aliorum placita & figmenta sequuntur. Exemplo hic nobis sunt Corinthij, quos in Christi & æternæ salutis cognitione per Pauli & Apollo probè institutos fuisse audiuimus. Sed cum non contenti ea institutione ambitiosis quibusdam doctoribus locum dedissent, qui mysteria nescio quæ altiora inani verborum splendore iactabant, mox errores omnis generis secuti sunt, qui vitia quoq; pepererunt, quibus tota illa ecclesia infamis facta est. Primò enim cæca æmulatione in sectas distracti, nominis Christiani professionem impie violarunt. Deinde neglecta aut potius sublata disciplina ecclesiæ, atrocissimis sceleribus atq; flagitijs fenestra patuit, adeò, vt iam ad incestas nuptias cum ingenti scandalo conniverent, qui ne scortatione quidem vulgarem ferre debebant. Sequitur nunc aliud delictum, cuius infamia non minus ad Euangelij & fidei Christianæ doctrinam redundabat. Erat hoc nimium litigandi studium, cuius ardore abrepti, ad ethnicorum tribunalia eos trahebant, qui eundem cum ipsis Christum profitebantur. Peccabatur in eo bifariam. Primum impatientia, cum qui seipsos ad patientiam & ad ferendas iniurias exercere debebant, alijs iniuriam facerent. Deinde quod apud infidelium tribunalia litigando, fidem Christianam illorum ludibrijs exponerent. Vtriusq; mali causa præcipua erat Auaritia, quæ vt artes varias excogitat ad opes augendas: ita lites quoq; & rixas infinitas parere, imò lites ex litibus quotidie nouas texere solet. Et quia hæc inter mercatores maximè dominatur, qui diuitias actionum suarum omnium fere finem constituunt, non dubium est, vitium hoc Co-rinthi, vbi mercatorum tam indigenarum quàm exterorum ingens erat numerus, admodum frequens & vulgare fuisse. Ideo in illos graviter inuehitur Paulus, vt audiemus. Nobis autem hæc tractatio plurimum seruit, eò quòd hodie etiam ad eundem lapidem sapius offendunt, qui Euangelij doctrinam puriorem profitentur. Orditur autem ab eo, quod nos secundo loco posuimus (quia id manifestius erat, neque poterat negari) vt ita commodius ad primum accedat, & id fortius vrgere possit.
units.tr: Just as the Lord Jesus Christ is the true and only light of the world, and imparts that light to us through the teaching of the Gospel, so all who follow their own or others' opinions and inventions, and leave the simplicity of his teaching, must necessarily walk in darkness and be entangled in the inextricable labyrinths of error. The Corinthians are an example for us here. We have heard that they had been well instructed by Paul and Apollos in the knowledge of Christ and eternal salvation. But when they were not content with that instruction and gave a place to certain ambitious teachers, who boasted of I know not what higher mysteries with empty splendour of words, straightway errors of every kind followed, and these also brought forth vices, by which that whole church was made infamous. For first, divided into factions by blind rivalry, they impiously violated the profession of the Christian name. Then, with discipline of the Church neglected, or rather abolished, a door was opened to the most atrocious crimes and shameful deeds, so much so that they now tolerated incestuous marriages, to the great scandal of all, although they ought not to have borne even ordinary fornication. Now there follows another offence, whose infamy reflected no less upon the teaching of the Gospel and of the Christian faith. This was an excessive zeal for litigation, and, carried away by its heat, they dragged before the tribunals of the heathen those who professed the same Christ as themselves. They sinned in this in two ways. First, through impatience, since those who ought to have trained themselves to patience and to bearing injuries were inflicting injury on others. Second, by litigating before the courts of unbelievers, they exposed the Christian faith to their mockery. The principal cause of both evils was avarice, which devises various arts to increase wealth, and so is wont to produce endless quarrels and strife, indeed to weave new lawsuits daily out of lawsuits. And since this vice rules chiefly among merchants, whose wealth is almost the sole end of all their dealings, there is no doubt that this fault was very frequent and common at Corinth, where there was a huge number of merchants, both native and foreign. Therefore Paul inveighs severely against them, as we shall hear. For us this discussion is very useful, because even today those who profess a purer doctrine of the Gospel often stumble over the same stone. Now he begins with what we have placed second, since that was more evident and could not be denied, so that he may approach the first more conveniently and press it more strongly.

units.la: Propositio totius loci præcipua & summaria est, Iniquum & indecorum esse, homines Christi-anos lites persequi sub iudicibus prophanis & à religione alienis. Id verò per interrogationem enunciat, vt rei indignitatem magis exaggeret. Audetne aliquis (inquit) vestrum, negotium habens cum altero, iudicio experiri sub iniustis, & non sub sanctis? Per iniustos intelligit alienos à fide Christiana. Quia enim Christus nobis à Patre iustitia factus est, neq; extra illum aliquis iustificari potest, iniusti sint oportet coram Deo, quicunq; illum nondum fide apprehenderunt. His autem Sanctos opponit, quo nomine credentes intelligit, qui in Christo sanctificantur, vt infra ipse docebit. Obiter autem hoc loco Apostolus omnem humanam iusticiam damnat, quacunq; authoritate, vel publica vel priuata, illa commendetur. Et fuit hoc dictu admodum graue, neq; ignorabat ipse, quàm agre id laturi essent, qui Corinthi tunc magistratum gerebant. Iniustos tamen dicit, quò magis ab eorum consuetudine abstrahat eos, qui Christo nomen dederant. Habet autem Emphasim Audendi verbum. Quasi diceret. Quæ obsecro hæc est temeritas, hominem Christianum contendendi libidine eò vsq; abripi, vt fratrem in Christo, eiusdem fidei professione gaudentem, adeoq; cohæredem suum, propter res temporarias & nullius momenti ad eorum tribunalia rapiat, qui à Christi cognitione alieni, fidem in hunc hostiliter persequuntur? Non ergo hoc reprehendit, quòd ipsi ab ethnicis citati in eorum fore comparerent (quid enim aliud facerent, qui ad hoc legibus publicis adigebantur?) sed quòd ipsi nemine cogente suos fratres inuitos eò traherent: & non potius ex suis aliquos deligerent, per quos lites eiusmodi amica cognitione aut compositione dirimeretur. Merito autem tanta cum gravitate istud pronuntiat, quia hoc fieri non poterat absq; manifesta fidei & doctrinæ Christianæ contumelia. Constat enim eos qui litigant, plerunque modum excedere, & multa in aduersarij contemptum atque odium dicere, quae animos bile potius quàm recti studio & fraterna dilectione flagrantes arguunt. Ex eo igitur ethnici occasionem arripiebant multa dicendi in Christianam religionem: Haec ne illa fides est, quae homines à terrenis auocat, vt vni Deo eosdem consecret? Haec ne religio illa est, quae sola Deum nobis conciliat? Haec ne illa charitas & pax & patientia, quam in concionibus publicis, inq; colloquijs priuatis nunquam non inculcant? Ista (inquam) & alia huius generis infinita tunc ethnici Christianis exprobrabant. Turpe igitur erat, eos isti non moueri, vt cautius agerent: vt iam de eo nihil dicamus, quòd fratres, propter fidei professionem iam ante exosos, ipsi ex priuato affectu & exigui lucri causa impiorum libidini & tyrannidi exponebant.
units.tr: The chief and summary proposition of the whole passage is that it is unfair and unbecoming for Christians to pursue lawsuits before profane judges and those alien to religion. He states this by a question, so as to heighten the indignity of the matter. "Does any of you," he says, "when he has a dispute with another, dare to go to law before the unrighteous and not before the saints?" By the unrighteous he means those alien to the Christian faith. For since Christ has been made righteousness to us by the Father, and no one can be justified apart from him, all who have not yet laid hold of him by faith must be unrighteous before God. He sets the saints over against these, by which name he means believers, who are sanctified in Christ, as he himself will teach below. Incidentally, in this place the Apostle condemns all human righteousness, by whatever authority, public or private, it is recommended. And this was a very grave thing to say, nor was he ignorant how hard it would be for those who then held the magistracy at Corinth to bear. Yet he calls them unrighteous so that he may draw more strongly away from their company those who had given their name to Christ. The word "dare" carries emphasis. As if he were saying: What, I beg you, is this recklessness, that a Christian man should be carried by the lust of contention so far as to drag a brother in Christ, who rejoices in the same profession of faith and is therefore his co-heir, before the tribunals of those who are strangers to the knowledge of Christ and hostilely persecute the faith, for temporal things of no moment? Therefore he does not rebuke them for being summoned by the heathen and appearing before them (for what else could they do, who were compelled by public laws to this?), but for bringing their brothers there against their will, without anyone compelling them, and for not rather choosing some from among their own to settle such disputes by friendly inquiry or compromise. He pronounces this with such gravity because it could not happen without manifest dishonour to the faith and the Christian doctrine. For it is agreed that those who litigate commonly exceed due measure and say many things in contempt and hatred of their opponent, which reveal minds burning with bile rather than with a zeal for what is right and with brotherly love. Thence the heathen seized the opportunity to say many things against the Christian religion: "Is this that faith which calls men away from earthly things, so as to consecrate them to the one God? Is this that religion which alone reconciles us to God? Is this that charity and peace and patience, which they never cease to inculcate in public sermons and private conversations?" These and countless other things of this kind the heathen then cast in the teeth of Christians. It was shameful, then, that these men were not moved to act more cautiously; to say nothing of the fact that they exposed to the lust and tyranny of the impious brothers who were already hateful for their profession of faith, out of private feeling and for a small gain.

units.la: At si tam grauiter reprehendi meruerunt Corinthij, quid de illis dicturus fuisset Apostolus qui propter doctrinae & fidei capita aliqua apud Antichristi satellites, vel etiam apud Tur-carum tribunalia, illis litem mouent, qui eundem cum ipsis Christum profitentur, adeoq; arma sua cum apertis fidei Christianae hostibus coniungunt, vt fratres suos opprimant? Factum hoc non semel nostro saeculo, & hic fere infelicis illius Sacramentariae contentionis fructus est, vt quoties exitio nonnullis digni videamur, eò quòd verum & naturale IESV CHRISTI corpus in coelesti gloria considere, & sola fide vere manducari, non autem manibus nostris contre-ctari, neque dentibus (vt Papa loquitur) atteri sentimus. Volunt quidem aduersarij nostri ij videri, qui soli Zelo propagandi Euangelij ardeant: sed quicunque eò vsque progrediuntur, vt cum Antichristi seruis vires suas & socia arma coniungant, ij reuera Iudaeorum similes sunt, qui ad capiendum Christum Romanis armis vsi sunt olim, & eundem apud Pilati tribunal accusarunt de iis, quae ad doctrinam & aeternae salutis negotium pertinebant. Et verendum est, ne vt Iu-daei non multo post Romanorum armis excisi sunt: ita isti quoque illos ipsos hostes nocentissimos & ecclesiarum omnium dissipatores sentiant, quorum authoritate & potentia aduersus nos abu-tuntur. Vidimus quaedam huius mali praeludia iam non vno loco, & vtinam non mox graviora sequantur.
units.tr: But if the Corinthians deserved to be rebuked so severely, what would the Apostle have said of those who, on account of some articles of doctrine and of faith, bring lawsuits against those who profess the same Christ as themselves before the satellites of Antichrist, or even before the tribunals of the Turks, and so join their arms with the open enemies of the Christian faith in order to oppress their brothers? This has happened more than once in our age, and it is almost the fruit of that unhappy sacramentarian controversy that, whenever we seem worthy of destruction for some, it is because we feel that the true and natural body of Jesus Christ sits in heavenly glory, and is truly eaten by faith alone, and is not handled with our hands, nor ground with the teeth (as the Pope puts it). Our adversaries, indeed, wish to appear to be those alone who burn with zeal for spreading the Gospel; but whoever advances so far as to join his strength and allied arms with the servants of Antichrist are in truth like the Jews, who once used Roman arms to seize Christ, and accused him before Pilate's tribunal concerning matters that pertained to doctrine and the business of eternal salvation. And it is to be feared lest, as the Jews were not long afterwards cut down by Roman arms, so these men too should experience those very enemies, most harmful and destroyers of all churches, by whose authority and power they abuse themselves against us. We have seen some preludes of this evil already in more than one place, and would that worse things do not soon follow.

units.la: Debet praeterea ex hoc loco generalis doctrina peti, ne semper faciamus quod per se licet facere, sed caueamus diligenter, ne quam calumniandi occasionem demus apertis fidei hostibus. Vt enim saluti nostrae nunquam non insidias struit Satan, ita occasiones eiusmodi per suos satellites atque seruos studiosè venatur, vt salutis doctrinam apud aliquos in contemptum & odium adducat. Et quantum hodie noceat multorum inconsulta & inconsiderata licentia, notius est quàm vt multis demonstrari oporteat. Semper ergo in nostris auribus & animis sonet illud Pauli di-ctum: Vnusquisque nostrum proximo indulgeat in bonum, ad aedificationem. Item: Omniami-hi licent, sed non omnia conducunt. Quòd si vero in ijs, quae media aut indifferentia sunt, id obseruari debet, quanto magis ab ijs nos abstinere, imò totis animis abhorrere conuenit, quae per se illicita & cum aperto scelere coniuncta sunt, & proinde sine multorum offendiculo fieri non possunt? At in eo hodie plurimum ab ijs peccatur, qui puriores doctrinae & fidei verae sectatores videri volunt. Nam laudem quidem in illis meretur veritatis professio. Quia vero ijdem aut intemperanter viuunt, aut scortantur, aut auaritiae suae indulgent, aut alijs vitijs sunt dediti, fit vt propter illos Euangelium male audiat: quae hodie omnium nocentissima est remora, qua plurimi detinentur, ne ad Christi ecclesiam accedant.
units.tr: Moreover, a general rule should be drawn from this passage: we must not always do what is in itself permitted, but take careful care not to give occasion for slander to the open enemies of the faith. Just as Satan never ceases to lay snares for our salvation, so he eagerly hunts for such opportunities through his henchmen and servants, in order to bring the doctrine of salvation into contempt and hatred among some people. How greatly the thoughtless and inconsiderate licence of many harms us today is too well known to need showing to many. Let that saying of Paul always sound in our ears and minds: "Let each of us please his neighbour for good, for edification." Likewise: "All things are lawful for me, but not all things are helpful." But if this must be observed in matters that are indifferent or intermediate, how much more should we refrain from, indeed with all our hearts shrink from, those things that are unlawful in themselves and bound up with open wickedness, and which therefore cannot be done without giving offence to many? Yet today most of the sin in this respect is committed by those who wish to be seen as the purer followers of sound doctrine and true faith. For the profession of the truth deserves praise in them. But because the same people either live intemperately, or whore, or indulge their greed, or are given over to other vices, it comes about that the Gospel is ill spoken of because of them. This is today the most harmful hindrance of all, by which very many are held back from coming to the church of Christ.

units.la: Porrò rationes adducit Paulus, quibus docet, quàm indignè iludfaciant[?] Corinthij. Prima hîs verbis continetur: An ignoratis, quòd sancti mundum iudicabunt? Quòd si per vos iudicabitur mundus, indigni ne estis minimis iudicijs? Graecè κριτήρια[?] ponuntur, quae proprie loca sunt iudicijs destinata. Et solent haec fere distingui in Repub. bene constituta, vt hic quidem causae graviores, alibi leviores agantur. Est ergo argumentum à maiori ad minus: Cùm Deus vos destinarit, vt quasi in supremis subsellijs constituti de toto mundo iudicare debeatis, num indigni aut minus idonei estis ad cognoscendum causas, quae inter vos de rebus huius saeculi incidunt? Additur his alia ratio, quae ad prioris amplificationem facit: An ignoratis fore vt Angelos iudicemus, nedum quae ad huius vitæ vsum pertinent? Loquitur autem de malis Angelis, qui etsi ob defectionem iam olim è cœlis deturbati sint, catenis tamen caliginis (vt Petrus scribit) in tartarum detrusi ad damna-tionem extremam seruantur. Et cum nunc ex iusta Dei permissione tam pijs quam impijs molesti sint, olim in magno illo die vltima in illos sententia feretur, vt vna cum suis in ignem illum inextinguibilem præcipitentur, vbi nunquam cessaturis tormentis excruciabuntur. Potest autem locus hic bifariam exponi. Nam primò mundum hunc sancti iudicant suo exemplo, dum illi omnem excusationis prætextum auferunt. Quo sensu Regina Sabæ & Niniuitæ in iudicio illo nouissimo Iudæorum gentem damnaturi esse dicuntur, quod hi quidem ad Ionæ prædicationem respuerint, illa autem Solomonis videndi & audiendi desiderio excitata per longa itinera, cum ingenti sumptu, neq; sine periculo aduenerit: ipsi vero æternum Dei Filium sponte se ipsis offerentem aspernentur. Deinde Apostolis Christus pollicetur, quod in nouissimo die iudicaturi sint duodecim tribus Israëlis. Nam etsi ipsi omne iudicium Pater dederit, assessores tamen habebit Apostolos, quorum ministerio Euangelium in toto orbe diuulgatum est. Vbi nemo humanum quid animo concipere, aut Apostolis eandem cum Christo dignitatem atq; potestatem tribuere debet. Etenim pro ministerij ratione ita loquitur Christus, & ipsos iudices fore dicit, quia ille sententiam tunc feret ex Euangelio, cuius ipsi præcones fuerunt. Quapropter cum id ad Apostolos & horum successores proprie pertineat, Paulus autem hic toti Corinthiorum ecclesiæ & (vt ita dicam) vulgo fidelium scribat, prior expositio mihi planior & simplicior videtur, quæ veterum quoq; plerisq; placuit. Quam-uis enim de eo, quod futurum fit, Paulus loquatur, pij autem iam nunc mundum suo exemplo iudicent, hoc ipsum tamen efficacius & euidentius fiet in magno illo die, quando impij, qui nunc omnia facile ridēnt[?], sese piorum exemplo conuinci videbunt, & intra conscientias suas iudicij huius rigorem iustissimum sentient: quod non obscure Christi verba de Niniuitis & Sabæ regina innuunt. Et quia idem in illo die sub damnationis impiorum sententia diabolos quoq; comprehendet, qui ex angelica dignitate propria culpa exciderunt, rectè Apostolus Angelorum quoq; meminit. Et sanè non parum grauabit illorum damnationem, quod cum naturam à terrena mole puriorem acceperint, & electorum ministerio destinati fuerint, peccato tamen locum dederunt, & eos perdere conati sunt, pro quorum salute æternus Dei Filius sese impendere dignatus est. In præsenti autem argumentis istis Paulus docet, Corinthios sibi ipsis & fratribus suis atrocem iniuriam facere, qui honorem suum, in quem ipsos Christus supra omnem mundum & Angelos euexit, in homines prophanos transferant.
units.tr: Paul next brings forward reasons by which he shows how unworthily the Corinthians behave. The first is contained in these words: "Do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you unworthy of the smallest courts?" The Greek word [κριτήρια] is used, which properly means places set aside for judgments. In a well-ordered commonwealth these are usually divided so that more serious cases are tried in one place and lighter ones in another. So the argument is from the greater to the lesser: since God has appointed you, as if seated on the highest benches, to judge the whole world, are you unworthy or unfit to decide the cases that arise among you concerning the affairs of this age? To this is added another reason, which strengthens the first: "Do you not know that we shall judge angels, let alone the matters that pertain to the use of this life?" He is speaking of the evil angels, who, though cast down from heaven long ago through their fall, are nevertheless kept, as Peter writes, bound in chains of darkness and thrust down into hell for final condemnation. And since they now harass both the godly and the ungodly by God's just permission, on that great last day sentence will be pronounced against them, so that together with their followers they will be cast into that unquenchable fire, where they will be tormented without ever ceasing. This passage can be explained in two ways. First, the saints judge this world by their example, since by their conduct they strip the wicked of every pretext for excuse. In this sense the Queen of Sheba and the Ninevites are said to condemn the Jewish nation at that last judgment: the Ninevites rejected Jonah's preaching, while the queen, moved by a desire to see and hear Solomon, came over long journeys, at great expense and not without danger; yet the Jews despised the eternal Son of God, who offered himself to them of his own accord. Then Christ promises the Apostles that they will judge the twelve tribes of Israel on the last day. For although the Father has given all judgment to him, he will have the Apostles as assessors, through whose ministry the Gospel has been spread throughout the whole world. Here no one should conceive anything human, or attribute to the Apostles the same dignity and power as to Christ. Christ speaks in this way according to the nature of their ministry, and says that they will be the judges because he will then pronounce sentence according to the Gospel, of which they were the heralds. Therefore, since this properly pertains to the Apostles and their successors, and Paul here writes to the whole church of the Corinthians and, as I may say, to the common run of the faithful, the first explanation seems to me plainer and simpler, and it has also pleased most of the ancients. For although Paul speaks of what is to come, and the godly already now judge the world by their example, this will nevertheless be done more effectively and evidently on that great day, when the ungodly, who now laugh at everything with ease, will see themselves convicted by the example of the godly, and will feel within their consciences the most just rigour of that judgment. The words of Christ about the Ninevites and the Queen of Sheba hint at this plainly. And because on that day the devils also, who fell from their angelic dignity through their own fault, will be caught up in the sentence of condemnation against the ungodly, the Apostle rightly mentions the angels too. And surely it will add no little weight to their condemnation that, though they received a nature purer than earthly matter, and were appointed to the service of the elect, they nevertheless gave place to sin and tried to destroy those for whose salvation the eternal Son of God deigned to offer himself. In the present context, by these arguments Paul teaches that the Corinthians do a grievous wrong to themselves and to their brethren when they transfer to profane men the honour into which Christ has raised them above every world and every angel.

units.la: Admonemur hoc loco, plurimum referre, vt dignitatem suam homines Christiani rectè intel-ligant, & in eius consideratione assidua versentur. Est hæc maxima & omnem huius seculi splendorem longè superat. Sunt enim fratres IESV CHRISTI, in quo ex Verbi æterni semine in filios Dei renati sunt. Sunt item eiusdem regni cum illo hæredes. Eius enim promissio est: Vbi ego sum, ibi erit & minister meus. Et cum iam moriturus de sua voluntate testari vellet, dicebat: Volo pater, vt vbi sum ego, illic etiam sint mecum, quos dedisti mihi. Itaque cum illo olim comparebunt, cum ad iudicandum venerit, & tunc eos cum admiratione simul & immani conscientiæ cruciatu spectabunt impij, qui ipsos in terris hisce afflixerunt. Vide quæ in libro Sapientiæ de hoc scribuntur Cap. 5. Ista ergo nos solentur, si quando ad impiorum tribunalia trahi iniquis sententijs damnamur. Erit enim olim rerum vicissitudo, & quod Christus Iudæorum sacerdotibus dicebat, fore vt ipsum in nubibus cœli iudicem venturum videant, qui nunc sibi in ipsum iudicium sumat: hoc ipsum nos quoq; dicere possumus, fore vt olim nostro exemplo ad sempiternos inferorum cruciatus damnentur, qui sibi nunc in nos nihil non licere putant. Imprimis autem officij nostri nos ista admoneant: ne qui ad tantam dignitatem vocati sumus, rebus terrenis & turpibus seruiliter immergamur. Cur ergo circa opes huius seculi lites mouemus? Cur propter has charitatis Christianæ leges violamus? Cur illas bonis cœlestibus atq; æternis præferimus? Cur item libidini, scortationi, intemperantiæ & fœdissimis carnis voluptatibus seruiunt, qui suo exemplo mundum & huius principem iudicare debent?
units.tr: We are reminded in this place how much it matters that Christian people rightly understand their dignity and dwell constantly upon its consideration. This dignity is the greatest, and far surpasses all the splendour of this age. For they are brethren of Jesus Christ, in whom they have been born again as sons of God from the seed of the eternal Word. They are also heirs together with him of his kingdom. For his promise is: "Where I am, there shall my servant also be." And when he was about to die and wished to make his will, he said: "Father, I will that where I am, there also may be with me those whom you have given me." Therefore they will appear with him one day, when he comes to judge, and then the ungodly, who afflicted them in this earthly life, will look upon them with wonder and with immense torment of conscience. See what is written about this in the Book of Wisdom, chapter 5. These things, then, should console us whenever we are dragged before the tribunals of the wicked and condemned by unjust sentences. For there will one day be a reversal of fortunes, and what Christ said to the priests of the Jews will come true: they will see him coming as judge in the clouds of heaven, the one who now takes judgment against himself. We too can say this: those who now think they may do anything they like against us will one day be condemned to eternal torments of hell because of our example. Above all, these things should remind us of our duty: that we, who have been called to so great a dignity, should not be sunk in earthly and base things like slaves. Why then do we stir up quarrels over the wealth of this age? Why for its sake do we violate the laws of Christian charity? Why do we prefer it to heavenly and eternal goods? Why do those serve lust, whoring, intemperance and the most foul pleasures of the flesh, who ought by their example to judge the world and its prince?

units.la: Cæterum quia non sufficit vitium aliquod arguisse, nisi eius corrigendi ratio simul tradatur, altera huius loci parte consilium præscribit, & quid fieri oportet docet his verbis: Itaq; si iudicia habeatis de ijs, quae ad huius vitae vsum pertinent, eos qui minimi fiunt in Ecclesia, eos (inquam) in subsellijs collocate. Summa consilij est, Christianos homines causas & lites suas non prophano-rum hominum iudicijs subijcere, sed ex suo coetu arbitros constituere debere, qui controversias eo-rum cognoscant, & lites amicè componant. At obijciebant aliqui, Neminem inveniri, qui ad hoc munus idoneus esset, & proinde necessario ad publica civitatis iudicia ipsos recurrere oportere. Quam obiectionem non sine Praeoccupationis specie diluit, dum eorum facit mentionem, qui in Ec-clesia minimi fiunt. Hoc enim perinde est, ac si diceret: Non est quod de vestrorum hominum prudentia aut peritia conqueramini: Qui enim inter vos minimi vel contemptissimi sunt, ij huic negotio possent sufficere, modo & ipsi animum attendere, & vos maiorem aequitatis & dilectionis quam rei privatae rationem habere velitis. In eiusmodi enim controversijs non tam prudentia & longo rerum usu, quam probitate & diligentia opus est, quae duo nunquam desunt ijs, qui serio reli-gionis sensu tanguntur. Et ut maxime errent arbitri isti, tamen rerum temporariarum modo ia-ctura fit, cum apud alteros illos ipsa religio & publica ecclesiae pax in periculum veniant. Quapro-pter cum eos qui minimi fiunt, ad causarum eiusmodi cognitionem deligere iubet, nequaquam in contemptum magistratus hoc dicit, sed per Comparationem loquitur, ut ostendat, praestare omnino, ut vel contemptissimi fidelium iudicent, quam ut sese eorum ludibrijs exponant, qui à Christiana religione alienissimi, omnem huius accusandi occasionem auidè venantur.
units.tr: But since it is not enough to have pointed out a fault unless the means of correcting it is also set forth, Paul in the second part of this passage prescribes a plan and teaches what ought to be done, in these words: "So if you have judgments concerning the things that pertain to the use of this life, set up as judges those who are least esteemed in the Church, I say, set them in the courts." The sum of his counsel is that Christian people should not submit their causes and disputes to the judgments of profane men, but should appoint from their own assembly arbiters who may examine their controversies and settle their quarrels amicably. But some objected that no one could be found who was fit for this task, and that therefore they must of necessity have recourse to the public courts of the state. Paul answers this objection, not without a semblance of anticipating it, when he speaks of those who are least esteemed in the Church. For this is as much as to say: you need not complain about the prudence or skill of your own people. Those among you who are least or most despised could be sufficient for this business, provided that they also pay attention, and that you are willing to have regard to fairness and love rather than to private advantage. For in such disputes what is needed is not so much prudence and long experience of affairs as uprightness and diligence, and these two are never lacking in those who are seriously moved by a sense of religion. And however much those arbiters might err, only some temporal goods would be lost, whereas before the others religion itself and the public peace of the church would be put in danger. Therefore, when he bids them choose those who are least esteemed to examine such cases, he does not say this in contempt of the magistrate at all, but speaks by way of comparison, to show that it is altogether better for even the most despised of the faithful to judge than for them to expose themselves to the mockery of those who are most alien to the Christian religion and eagerly hunt for every occasion of accusing it.

units.la: Observabis praeterea, hac non in eum finem dici, ut excusso legitimi magistratus iugo, quisque sibi iudicem pro suo arbitrio constituat. Nec enim Rempub. turbat Euangelij doctrina, neq; leges politicas & iudiciorum ordines abolet, qui absq; religionis detrimento retineri possunt. Adhæc non de ijs loquitur Paulus, qui a prophanis ad iudices ethnicos citabantur, neq; ut his se immorigeros praebeant, docet: sed (ut supra quoq; monuimus) quid Christianos homines in litibus inter ipsos exortis facere debeant, ostendit. Et cum ex more apud omnes recepto cuius liceat de iure suo nonnihil cedere, & litem arbitris cmitocere[?], ut amica transactione componatur: multo magis hoc Christianos facere convenit, neq; propterea magistratus authoritati quicquam derogatur. Minimè ergo lo-cus iste seditiosis reipub. turbatoribus servit, qui sub religionis praetextu licentiam quaerunt, ad iudices citati non comparent, imò magistratibus iusiurandum negant, & tenebrarum potestatem dicunt eos, qui rempub. administrant. In quorum numero hodie facile primi sunt Anabaptistae, & qui horum figmentis decepti res novas moliuntur.
units.tr: You will observe further that these words are not said for the purpose of throwing off the yoke of lawful magistrates, so that each person may set up a judge of his own choosing. The teaching of the Gospel does not disturb the commonwealth, nor does it abolish the civil laws and the order of courts, which can be retained without loss to religion. Moreover, Paul is not speaking of those who were summoned by unbelievers before heathen judges, nor does he teach them to be obedient to such men; rather (as we have also noted above) he shows what Christians ought to do in disputes that arise among themselves. And just as it is a custom accepted among all people that one may yield something of his right and refer the quarrel to arbiters, so that it may be settled by a friendly agreement, so Christians ought to do this all the more, and in doing so nothing is taken away from the authority of the magistrate. This passage therefore serves very little the seditious disturbers of the commonwealth, who under the pretext of religion seek licence, who do not appear when summoned before judges, who indeed deny an oath to magistrates and call those who govern the state the power of darkness. Among such men today the Anabaptists are easily the first, and those who, deceived by their fictions, attempt revolutionary changes.

units.la: At mirum videri poterat, ipsos homines in re plana tam turpiter offendere, & Pauli consilio abuti, nisi turpior esset episcoporum hallucinatio, qui ex hoc loco suam iurisdictionem afferere studuerunt. Est hic vetus error, quo veteres quoq; deceptos fuisse, ex Augustino patet, qui alicubi queri-tur, quod litibus audiendis bonam diei partem impendere cogatur. Ubi non negavero bonos illos patres pio zelo istud fecisse, & fortasse mouit eos fidelium fors, qui apud aulicos iudices & huiusce saeculi nimis deditos plerunque iniquius tractabantur: veruntamen non defendi potest error, quem multiplicem fuisse constat. Primo enim negotijs a sua functione alienis sese immiscuerunt, idq; contra Christi exemplum, qui a quodam requisitus ut litem, quae ipsi cum fratre de hereditate dividenda intercedebat, cognosceret, respondit: Heus tu, quis me constituit iudicem aut partitorem inter vos? Deinde auget culpam hanc, quod cum sentirent se tot negotijs minus sufficere posse, & per illa in eorum administratione impediri, quae ad ecclesiasticam functionem pertinebant, non tamen onus illud abiecerunt, neq; Apostolos imitati sunt, qui bonorum ecclesiae & pauperum curam transtulerunt in diaconos, ut ipsi liberius docendi officio vacarent. Gravius adhæc delictum fuit, quod Verbi Dei authoritate abusi sunt, & ad se rapuerunt, quod Paulus ijs, qui minimi sunt in ecclesia, committere iubet. Quibus adde, quod posteris pessimi exempli fuerunt authores. Ea enim occasione factum est, ut Episcopi Ecclesiae iurisdictionem cum politica miscuerint, quae res tyrannidem invexit toti Christiano orbi intolerabilem. Excusantur tamen veteres, quod bono zelo sibi ipsis labores imposuerunt, potestate autem sua non insolenter ad alicuius oppressionem abusi sunt. At qui hodie Episcopos profitentur, venia nulla digni sunt, cum & ecclesiasticum munus omnino negligant, & insuper fastu & tyrannidis licentia huius seculi principes vincant. Cum vero Apostolus tam graviter prohibeat, ne quis Christianus fratrem ad infidelium tri-bunalia trahat propter res ad huius vitæ usum pertinentes, quanto minus audiri debent, qui cum se Evangelicæ doctrinæ fautores atque patronos esse iactent, nos tamen ad Pontificum Concilia remittunt, ut horum cognitioni atque iudicio fidem atque doctrinam nostram subjiciamus? Est hoc non iniquum modò, sed magnæ etiam levitatis argumentum. Si enim Papam cum esse agnoscunt, qui cum suis creaturis de doctrina & fide pronunciandi ius habeat, & cui omnium, quæ in Ecclesia geruntur, ratio debeat reddi, cur ipsi illo multum reclamante ab eius obedientia defecerunt? cur eodem inuito instituerunt Ecclesiæ & religionis totius reformationem? cur Ecclesiæ bona præter eius voluntatem in usus alios transtulerunt? Sed levia sunt hæc, gravissimum vero & excusatione nulla dignum est, quod qui ita sentiunt, quantum in ipsis est, Veritatis doctrinam turpiter produnt, cum illam eorum iudicio subjicere velint, quos illius iuratos hostes esse constat, & inter quos nemini locus est, nisi qui in ipsorum verba iurauit. Sed quia de hoc sæpe diximus, nolumus nunc prolixius rem istam tractare.
units.tr: Yet it might seem strange that men should so shamefully go wrong in a plain matter and abuse the counsel of Paul, were it not that the error of the bishops is even more shameful, for they have sought to claim their jurisdiction from this passage. This is an old error, by which the ancients too were deceived, as is clear from Augustine, who somewhere complains that he was compelled to spend a good part of the day hearing lawsuits. Here I do not deny that those good Fathers did this from pious zeal, and perhaps the lot of the faithful moved them, who were for the most part treated more unjustly before courtly judges and men too much given over to this age. Nevertheless the error cannot be defended, and it is plain that it was manifold. For first, they mixed themselves into affairs foreign to their office, and this against the example of Christ, who, when a certain man asked him to decide a dispute that he had with his brother over dividing an inheritance, answered: "Man, who made me a judge or divider between you?" Next, the fault is increased by this: although they felt that they were not able to cope with so many affairs, and that they were hindered by them in the discharge of those duties which belonged to the ecclesiastical office, yet they did not cast off that burden, nor did they imitate the Apostles, who transferred the care of the goods of the Church and of the poor to deacons, so that they themselves might be more free for the office of teaching. A graver offence besides was that they abused the authority of the Word of God and seized for themselves what Paul bids to be committed to those who are of least account in the Church.
