To these add that they were the authors of a most evil example to posterity. For on that occasion it came about that the bishops of the Church mingled the jurisdiction of the Church with the civil power, a thing which introduced a tyranny intolerable to the whole Christian world. Yet the ancients are excused, in that they imposed these labours on themselves from good zeal, and they did not arrogantly abuse their power to oppress anyone. But those who today profess themselves bishops deserve no pardon, since they wholly neglect the ecclesiastical office, and moreover surpass the princes of this age in pride and in licence of tyranny. Since the Apostle forbids so gravely that any Christian should drag a brother before the tribunals of unbelievers over matters pertaining to the use of this life, how much less should they be heard, who boast that they are supporters and patrons of the Evangelical doctrine, and yet send us back to the councils of the Pontiffs, so that we may submit our faith and doctrine to their judgment and decision? This is not only unjust but also a mark of great levity. For if they acknowledge the Pope as one who has the right to pronounce on doctrine and faith together with his creatures, and to whom an account of all things done in the Church ought to be rendered, why have they, although he protests greatly, withdrawn from his obedience? Why, against his will, have they undertaken the reformation of the Church and of the whole religion? Why have they transferred the goods of the Church to other uses, contrary to his wish? But these are slight matters; the most serious thing, and one deserving no excuse, is that those who think in this way, so far as lies in them, shamefully betray the doctrine of truth, since they wish to subject it to the judgment of those whom it is plain are its sworn enemies, and among whom there is no place for anyone except one who has sworn to their words. But since we have often spoken of this, we do not wish now to treat the matter at greater length.

units.la: Audiamus nunc loci huius conclusionem, quam non sine graui exprobratione Paulus infert, dicens: Ut vos pudeat, vobis hoc dico: Itane non est inter vos sapiens, ne unus quidem, qui possit dijudicare inter fratres suos? &c. Quibus verbis ita loqui videtur: Non ægre feretis fratres, quod liberius vobiscum ago. Quia enim tanta est confidentia vestra, ut veros Christi Apostolos contemnatis, & vos præ illis sapere vobis iamdudum persuaseritis, ipsa rei necessitas requirit, ut hæc vestra delicta tam gravia & pudenda vobis ob oculos ponantur, quæ vos omnium infimos & rerum imperitissimos esse convincant. Quæ enim vobis reliqua est gloriandi occasio, cum vestro ipsorum iudicio nemo inter vos sit ea sapientia & prudentia præditus, ut quæ inter vos oriuntur lites componere possit, & ideo apud hominum prophanorum subsellia de rebus leuissimis, magna cum Christiani nominis ignominia, neq; sine scandalo litigetis? Est hoc memorabile exemplum, quo docemur, quid ferè superbis euenìat, qui confidentia tbrij[?] se aliis præferunt: Ut nimirum in rebus minimis extremam stultitiam prodant, & ita se ridiculos tunc præbeant, quando vix aliqua occasio errandi apparet. Et hoc ferè illis accidit, qui relictis ijs ad quæ diuinitus vocati sunt, res nihil ad se pertinentes tractare volunt. Faciebant hoc Corinthij, quando mysteriorum quorundam altiori speculatione detenti in ijs tam turpiter hallucinabantur, quæ ad vitæ huius usum quotidianum faciunt. Oportet autem tales Verbo Dei liberius arguere, & quasi in rem præsentem adducere, ut ipsos sui pudere incipiat, & admoniti emendentur. Laudatur in historijs Apelles pictor, qui Alexandrum Regem in officina sua de ijs, quæ ad artem pictoriam spectant, multa ineptius interrogantem tacere iussit, ne pueris, qui colores terebant, se deridendi occasione præberet. Quanto magis igitur libertate ista redarguendi Ecclesiarum ministri uti debent, ut ambitiosis & superbis cristas[?] deprimant? Quod si qui id ferre nolunt, si satis testantur, se non tam reprehensione quàm e-xibilatione[?] dignos esse.
units.tr: Let us now hear the conclusion of this passage, which Paul draws with no little reproach, saying: "I say this to your shame. Is it so that there is not among you a wise man, not even one, who is able to judge between his brethren? etc." By these words he seems to speak thus: "You will not take it ill, brethren, that I deal with you more freely. For since your confidence is so great that you despise the true Apostles of Christ, and have long persuaded yourselves that you are wiser than they, the very necessity of the matter requires that these your faults, so grave and shameful, be set before your eyes, which prove that you are the most lowly and most unskilled in affairs. For what ground of boasting is left you, when by your own judgment there is no one among you endowed with such wisdom and prudence that he can settle the disputes that arise among you, and so you go to the benches of profane men over the most trivial matters, to the great disgrace of the Christian name and not without scandal?" This is a memorable example, by which we are taught what commonly happens to the proud, who through confidence set themselves above others: namely, that in the smallest matters they show the utmost folly, and so make themselves ridiculous just when there is scarcely any occasion for error. And this happens to those who, having left aside those things to which they are called by God, want to handle matters that do not concern them. The Corinthians did this, when, held by a too lofty speculation on certain mysteries, they were so shamefully mistaken in those things which serve the daily use of this life. Such men, however, ought to be rebuked more freely by the Word of God, and as it were brought face to face with the matter, so that they may begin to feel shame and, once warned, amend themselves. In the histories the painter Apelles is praised, who ordered Alexander the King, when he was asking many foolish questions in his workshop about the things that belong to the art of painting, to be silent, lest he give the boys who ground the colours an occasion to mock him. How much more, then, ought the ministers of the Churches to use this freedom of rebuke, so that they may humble the ambitious and the proud? But if some are unwilling to bear it, they show plainly enough that they deserve not so much rebuke as mockery.

units.la: Restat hoc loco considerandum, quid in deligendis magistratibus maximè spectare debeant; qui rempub. habent in suo arbitrio & potestate constitutam. Nam quàmuis nihil hic de magistratu ex professo dicat Paulus, docet tamen quales esse debeant arbitri, qui lites inter Ecclesiæ membra exortas componant. Quod cùm ad iudices imprimis pertineat, istis[?] accommodari debet, quicquid hìc dicitur. Atqui duo imprimis vrget. Primum est, ut Christiani sint. Fides ergo in Christum requiritur, quæ Dei veri cognitionem atq; timorem, & sub his pietatem omnem comprehendit. Sunt hæc admodum necessaria. Quia nisi Dei timore coërceantur, qui in magistratu sunt, potestas illa facilè in licentiam erumpit, quæ tyrannidis mater est. Ideo frequenter admonentur iudices, ut meminerint, iudicium Dei esse, qui ipsis præsens adsit, & sententias eorum audiat. Estq; immortali laude dignissimus Tigurinæ reipub. mos, quo fidei suæ confessionem in Diacosiorum Senatu edere iubentur, quotquot ad rempub. primùm accedunt. Alterum est Sapientia, quæ ut omnium vitam & mores dirigere debet: ita maximè ea præditi sint oportet, qui alijs præsunt. Vidit hoc Solomon, qui cùm quiduis postulandi potestatem à Deo accepisset, sapientiam sibi dari voluit, ut tanto populo regendo posset sufficere. Est autem sapientiæ initium timor Domini, quem sub fide comprehendi diximus. Porrò iudicis sapientia, quoad res humanas, in hoc potissimum consistit, (quod gentium quoq; præstantissimi intellexerunt) vt non solum quid posset, sed etiam quid debeat ponderet: nec quantum sibi permissum, meminerit, sed etiam quatenus commissum sit. Sunt hæc nō ijs modò consideranda, qui iam inter iudices confident, verumetiam illis, quibus hoc beneficium contulit Deus, vt quos ipsi volunt magistratus sibi deligant. Nam si libertate ista pro libidine sua abutantur, & seipsos perdunt, & rempub. fædè dissipant. Optimè autem rebus consuletur, si hoc vnum omnes spectent, vt vbiq; regnet æternus Dei Filius, IESVS CHRISTVS, Rex regum & Dominus dominantium: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: It remains to consider in this place what they ought chiefly to look to in choosing magistrates, who hold the commonwealth established in their own will and power. For although Paul here says nothing about the magistracy as such, he nevertheless teaches what kind of arbiters ought to settle disputes arising among the members of the Church. Since this pertains above all to judges, whatever is said here must be applied to them. And yet two things above all are urged. The first is that they be Christians. Faith in Christ is therefore required, which comprehends the knowledge and fear of the true God and, under these, all piety. These are altogether necessary. For unless those who are in the magistracy are restrained by the fear of God, that power easily breaks out into licence, which is the mother of tyranny. For this reason judges are often admonished to remember that it is the judgment of God, who is present to them and hears their sentences. And most worthy of immortal praise is the custom of the Tigurine commonwealth, by which all who first come to the government are ordered to make a confession of their faith in the Senate of the Two Hundred. The second is wisdom, which ought to direct the life and conduct of all, and which especially those who preside over others ought to possess. Solomon saw this, who, when he had received from God the power to ask for whatever he wished, desired that wisdom be given him, so that he might be able to suffice for governing so great a people. Now the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, which we said is comprehended under faith. Moreover, the wisdom of a judge, as regards human affairs, consists chiefly in this (as even the most eminent of the Gentiles understood): that he weigh not only what he can do but also what he ought to do; and that he remember not only how much has been permitted to him but also how far it has been entrusted to him. These things are to be considered not only by those who already sit among the judges, but also by those to whom God has granted this benefit, that they may choose for themselves the magistrates whom they wish. For if they abuse this liberty according to their own lust, they both ruin themselves and foully scatter the commonwealth. But affairs will be best served if all look to this one thing: that the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, King of kings and Lord of lords, may reign everywhere, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXVIII.

units.la: Iam igitur omnino impotentia in vobis est, quod iudicia habetis inter vosmetipsos. Quare non potius iniuriam patimini? cur non potius damnum accipitis? At vos iniuriam facitis, & damno afficitis, idq; fratres. An nescitis, quod iniusti hæreditatem regni Dei non possidebunt?
units.tr: Now, then, it is altogether a failing in you that you have lawsuits among yourselves. Why do you not rather suffer wrong? Why do you not rather accept loss? But you yourselves do wrong and inflict loss, and that on your brothers. Do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God?

units.la: INter vitia, quibus Corinthiorum ecclesia laborabat, non postremum erat, quod lites & actiones forenses pertinaciùs sectarentur: & tanto quidem ardore, vt fratres suos ad ethnicorum tribunalia citarent. Ita enim in religionem Christianam grauissimè peccabant, cum eam prophanorum hominum ludibrijs subijcerent: & simul charitatis leges violabat, seq; maiorem opum huius seculi rationem habere testabantur, quàm arctissimæ illius communionis, quæ credentibus in Christo intercedit, & ex qua omnis nostra salus dependet. Quapropter grauiter admodum de hoc agit Paulus, & prima huius tractationis parte docuit, quàm indignè faciant, qui dignitatem, qua suos credentes Christus ornauit, tam turpiter prostituant. Adhæc consilium dedit, vt si quæ inter ipsos lites oriantur, ex suo cœtu arbitros idoneos deligant, quorum authoritate illæ componantur. His absolutis transfit modo ad alterum huius vitij caput, & ostendit lites eiusmodi per se Christianis hominibus indignas esse, eò quòd Christi legibus aduersentur, qui suos ad ferendas iniurias semper paratos, ab omni autem vindictæ studio alienissimos esse velit. Et de hoc quidem grauiter & ordine commodissimo disserit.
units.tr: Among the faults with which the church of the Corinthians was troubled, not the least was that they pursued lawsuits and legal actions so stubbornly, and with such zeal that they summoned their brothers before the courts of the heathen. In this they sinned grievously against the Christian religion, since they exposed it to the mockery of profane men. At the same time they violated the laws of love, and they showed that they regarded the wealth of this age more highly than that most intimate communion which exists between believers in Christ and on which all our salvation depends. For this reason Paul deals very seriously with this matter. In the first part of this discussion he taught how unworthily those act who so shamefully prostitute the dignity with which Christ has adorned his believers. Besides this, he gave advice that if any disputes arise among them, they should choose suitable arbiters from their own body, by whose authority such disputes may be settled. Having dealt with this, he now passes to the second head of this fault, and shows that lawsuits of this kind are in themselves unworthy of Christians, because they run counter to the laws of Christ, who wills that his people be always ready to bear wrongs and wholly far from any desire for revenge. On this he speaks seriously and in a very fitting order.

units.la: Primo enim, quia ita obstupuerant in suis vitijs, vt ea in semetipsis non agnoscerent, imò (vt suo loco vidimus) se iampridem ad Christianæ perfectionis metam peruenisse putarent, diserte docet, ipsos propter lites eiusmodi, etiamsi nihil præterea accederet, reprehensione dignos esse. Iam igitur (inquit) omnino impotentia in vobis est, quod iudicia habetis inter vosmetipsos. In Græco [illegible, ~8 letters] ponitur, quod [illegible, ~8 letters] τὸ [illegible, ~8 letters] deriuatur, & proprie defectum vel animi impotentiam significat, qua fit, vt affectibus & carnis suis desiderijs succumbant, qui illis debebant dominari. Est [?] hoc generale vocabulum, quod de omnibus vitijs dici potest, quia horum omnium vera & propria causa est, quod ab affectibus nos vinci patimur. In præsenti autem docere vult, Corinthios nondum defectu laborare, & ideo procul adhuc abesse à scopo perfectionis, ad quam Christiani homines aspirare debent. Ita vero rursus pungit ambitiosulos illos, qui quasi nihil ipsis deesset, securi in suis vitijs stertebant. Sic enim vult dicere: Videmini quidem vobis plus satis profecisse, neq; multa correctione opus habere. At qui tanta animi impotentia laborant, vt prauis affectibus tam facilè superentur, si certè de suo profectu non multum gloriari possunt. Num verò illud vobis accidere negabitis, qui huius seculi rebus ita est addicti, vt nō pudeat vos contra fratres iudicio experiri, & lites crebras instituere? Vnde enim hoc? Ex eo nimirùm, quòd nō [?] alij alijs redditis quod debetur, & quòd in feredis iniurijs nō ea patientia vtimini, quæ homines Christianos decet. Sic quasi in ipso facto deprehensos conuincit, vt sibi emendatione opus esse intelligant. Nec temere argumento hoc vtitur, quo gentium quoq; philosophi de reipub. constitutione iudicauerunt. Plato enim intemperatæ ciuitatis indicium esse dicebat, si morbi frequentes sint, & iudicium subsellia crebris litibus strepat. Morborum enim causa fere est gulæ studium & intemperantia, lites verò aut ex iniurijs acceptis nascuntur, aut ab illis temere suscipiuntur, qui ad suas res conficiendas iuris & legum prætextu improbè abuti solent. Itaq; aut præcesserit oportet iniuria, aut iam tum fit, quando lis instituitur: vt iam de eo nihil dicamus, quòd pleriq; dum bonam causam sustinet, litigandi ardore abrepti modum excedunt, & odij atq; simultatum semina concipiunt, ex quibus pessimi fructus enascuntur. Debet ergo hoc Pauli argumentum diligenter observare, qui hodie suis litibus fora & curias omnes fatigant, & tamen Christiani haberi volunt, atq; sibi ipsis iustitiæ titulo blandiuntur. Nam vt nemini iniuriam faciant, neq; quid ab aliquo præter ius & æquum postulent, animos tamen produnt à fraterna dilectione alieniores, & in patientia Christianæ schola minus exercitatos.
units.tr: First, because they had become so hardened in their vices that they did not recognise them in themselves, and indeed (as we saw in its place) they thought they had already reached the goal of Christian perfection, he plainly teaches that they deserve reproof for such lawsuits, even if nothing else were added. So, he says, it is altogether a failing in you that you have lawsuits among yourselves. In the Greek a word is used which is derived from τὸ ἡττᾶσθαι [to be defeated], and properly signifies defeat or weakness of mind, by which it comes about that people yield to their passions and fleshly desires, when they ought to rule over them. This is a general term which can be applied to all vices, because the true and proper cause of all of them is that we allow ourselves to be conquered by our passions. Here, however, he wants to teach that the Corinthians are not yet suffering from this defeat, and that for this reason they are still far from the goal of perfection, towards which Christians ought to strive. In this way he again stings those rather ambitious men who, as if they lacked nothing, slept securely in their vices. For he means to say: you seem to yourselves to have advanced quite far enough and to need no great correction. But those who suffer from such weakness of mind that they are so easily overcome by evil passions can hardly boast much of their progress, if they boast at all. Will you deny that this happens to you, who are so devoted to the affairs of this age that you are not ashamed to test your cases against your brothers in court, and to bring lawsuit after lawsuit? Whence does this come? Clearly from this, that you do not render to one another what is owed, and that in bearing injuries you do not show that patience which becomes Christians. Thus he convicts them, as if caught in the very deed, so that they understand they need to amend themselves. Nor does he use this argument rashly; by it even the philosophers of the Gentiles judged the constitution of states. For Plato used to say that it is a sign of an intemperate state if diseases are frequent and the law-courts ring with constant lawsuits. For the cause of diseases is generally a love of gluttony and intemperance, while lawsuits arise either from wrongs received or are rashly undertaken by those who are accustomed to abuse the pretext of law and statutes in order to carry out their own affairs dishonestly. So either a wrong must have gone before, or it arises at the moment when the suit is begun. To say nothing of the fact that many, while they defend a good cause, are carried away by the heat of litigation, exceed due measure, and conceive the seeds of hatred and enmity, from which the worst fruits spring. Therefore those who today wear out all the courts and tribunals with their lawsuits, and yet wish to be called Christians and flatter themselves with the title of justice, ought carefully to observe this argument of Paul. For although they do no wrong to anyone, nor demand anything from anyone beyond what is right and fair, they nevertheless betray minds too estranged from brotherly love, and too little trained in the patience of the school of Christ.

units.la: Proderit autem argumentum hoc ad omnes quoq; alias vitæ actiones extendere: vt nimirum nos in Christianæ innocentiæ aut perfectionis legeS peccare cogitemus, quoties affectibus aut carnis cupiditatibus indulgemus, nos ab illis vel modica ex parte vinci patimur. Docet hoc Christus, quando in Lege non modò dicta & facta, sed ipsam quoq; concupiscentiam prohiberi ostendit, quæ animi cogitationes ad illicita inclinat. Idem etiam nos ea conditione redemit, vt nos Deo Patri fi-steret Sacerdotes & Reges, qui carnem cum suis concupiscentijs Dei verbo iugulent, & tam sibi ipsis quàm peccato & eius desiderijs dominentur. Hic ergo certamen nobis proponitur, quo nullum gratius esse potest, & in quo victoriæ etiam omnium gloriosissimæ & felicissimæ materia offertur. Nam cum propria carne nos luctari[?] & innata nobis desideria subigere conuenit: vbi diligentia & fortitudine eo maiori opus est, quo magis sese apud nos carnis affectus insinuant nobisq; sub amabili voluptatis & felicitatis specie blandiuntur. Etenim videmus eos fere carnis cupiditatibus turpiter succumbere, qui prius aduersus acerrimos hostes per omnis generis pericula inuicti fuerunt. Rectè ergo à philosophis olim dictum fuit, eam demum gloriosissimam victoriâ esse, quæ seipsum, id est, carnis suæ desideria homo vincit. Et commendantur quidem hoc nomine nonnulli in prophanis historijs, at si rem propius consideremus, non nisi vmbra quædam virtutis fuit quæ illos alijs admirabiles fecit, & fere turpius tandem à cupiditatibus suis victi sunt, qui prius mortalium constantissimi videbantur. Ad solos ergo electos victoriæ istius gloria pertinet, qui ea per fidem potiuntur. Hac armatus Abrahamus vehementissimos illos paterni amoris motus vicit, qui ad extrema sæpe homines redigunt, quando vt Dei præcepto parëret, filium Isaacum immolare voluit. Eadem Iosephum in iuuenilis ætatis ardore aduersus herae impudicæ illecebras inuictu reddidit. Hac Dauidem confirmauit, vt neq; vindictæ desiderio, neq; ambitione aut superbia vinci potuerit, vt regnum sibi promissum ante tempus à Deo constitutum inuaderet. Hac prophetas & Apostolos mouit, vt nihil non sibi ferendum aut faciendum putauerint, quo regnum Christi propagari posse videbant. Huius deniq; fructus est, quòd credentes carni moriuntur & seipsos abnegant, vt Christo viuant. Et debent ista diligenter obseruari propter eos, qui scelera omnia hoc nomine excusant, quòd naturale sit carnis cupiditates sequi & ab illis vinci. Quæ perfuasio vera quidem est, quoad vitiosam illam hominis naturam, quæ ex primis parentibus hæreditario iure in nos deriuatur: eadem autem nos minimè excusat, qui Christo nomen dedimus: eò quòd per hunc ad vitæ nouitatem vocamur, & quòd Christiani non erimus, nisi illum fide vera apprehendamus, quæ nos omnibus desiderijs superiores facit. Quoties ergo te ab illis titillari & transuersum abripi sentis, tunc in te ἀπιστίαν[?] vel animi impotentiam esse cogita, quam in Corinthijs hic Paulus accusat, & vide, vt nouis fidei viribus confirmeris, quæ te carni non sinant succumbere.
units.tr: This argument will also be useful if extended to all the other actions of life: so that we may consider that we sin against the laws of Christian innocence or perfection whenever we indulge our passions or fleshly lusts, and allow ourselves to be overcome by them even in a small degree. Christ teaches this when, in the Law, he shows that not only deeds and words but also desire itself is forbidden, which inclines the thoughts of the mind towards unlawful things. He also redeemed us on this condition, that he might make us priests and kings to present ourselves to God the Father, who should slay the flesh with its desires by the Word of God, and rule over both themselves and sin and its lusts. Here, therefore, a contest is set before us, than which none can be more welcome, and in which the matter of the most glorious and happiest of all victories is offered. For we must wrestle with our own flesh and subdue the desires born within us, where greater diligence and courage are needed in proportion as the affections of the flesh insinuate themselves more into us and flatter us under the pleasing appearance of pleasure and happiness. Indeed we see that those who were unconquered before the most fierce enemies, through every kind of danger, usually succumb shamefully to the lusts of the flesh. So it was rightly said long ago by the philosophers that that victory is the most glorious which a man wins over himself, that is, over the desires of his own flesh. Some in profane histories are commended on this account; but if we consider the matter more closely, the constancy that made them admirable to others was no more than a kind of shadow of virtue, and those who seemed the most steadfast of mortals were often more shamefully overcome at last by their own desires. The glory of this victory belongs therefore only to the elect, who obtain it through faith. Armed with this faith, Abraham conquered those most violent movements of paternal love, which often reduce men to extremities, when he was willing to sacrifice his son Isaac in obedience to God's command. By the same faith he made Joseph invincible against the allurements of his mistress in the heat of youth. By this faith David was so strengthened that he could be conquered neither by the desire for revenge nor by ambition or pride, so that he did not seize before the time the kingdom promised to him and appointed by God. By this faith the prophets and apostles were moved to think nothing should be left unendured or undone by which they saw that the kingdom of Christ could be spread. Finally, this is the fruit of it, that believers die to the flesh and deny themselves, that they may live to Christ. And these things must be carefully observed on account of those who excuse all their crimes under this name, on the ground that it is natural to follow the desires of the flesh and to be overcome by them. This persuasion is indeed true as regards that sinful nature of man which is derived to us by hereditary right from our first parents; but it does not excuse us at all who have given our name to Christ, because through him we are called to newness of life, and because we shall not be Christians unless we grasp him with true faith, which makes us superior to all desires. Therefore, whenever you feel yourself tickled by these and dragged aside, think that there is in you unbelief [ἀπιστία] or that weakness of mind which Paul here accuses in the Corinthians, and see to it that you are strengthened with fresh powers of faith, which will not allow you to yield to the flesh.

units.la: Cæterum quod in genere & simplicius dixerat, nunc amplificatione illustrat, & simul docet, qua ratione huic malo aut defectui medeantur. Ait enim: Quare non potius iniuriam patimini? Cur nō potius damnū accipitis? At vos iniuriam facitis, & damno afficitis, idq; fratres. Interrogationibus eos vrget, vt animos fortius penetret. Quasi diceret: An ignoratis Christi præceptum, qui nos ad nouas potius iniurias paratos esse iubet, quàm vt veteres vlciscamur? Cur ergo illius immemores ista facitis? Anno præstaret iniuriam ferre, damnum accipere & rerum omnium iacturam facere, quàm ex animi impotentia charitatis simul & religionis Christianæ leges violare? At non modò impotentes estis in ferendis iniurijs, verumetiam alijs ipsi iniuriam facitis, imò ne à fratribus quidè abstinetis, quos vobis eiusdem fidei vinculum arctissimè coniunxit. At hæc dicendo multa eaq; grauissima crimina congerit. Primum, quòd impatientia peccent contra Christi præceptum, qui vt in patientia nostra animas nostras possideamus docuit. Alterum, quòd charitatis leges violent, quæ inimicos diligere, & vitam quoq; pro proximis impendere iubent, si ita facto opus fit. Tertium, quod ista in fratres designent, & ita Christianae etiam societatis vinculum, quantum in ipsis est, abrumpant. At si scelus est, quemcunq; laedere, quanto immanius flagitium fuerit eu iniuria afficere, quem vt fratrem amare & colere debebas? Et haec quidem omnia illi designabant, cum lites non necessarias susciperent, nihil autem huius in semetipsis agnoscebant, & ideo opus erat, vt liberius ab Apostolo arguerentur.
units.tr: What he had said in general and more simply, he now illustrates by amplification, and at the same time teaches by what means they may remedy this evil or defect. For he says: Why do you not rather suffer wrong? Why do you not rather accept loss? But you do wrong and inflict loss, and that on brothers. He presses them with questions so as to penetrate their minds more forcibly, as if he said: Do you not know Christ's precept, who bids us be ready for fresh wrongs rather than avenge the old? Why then do you, forgetful of that, act so? Would it not be better to bear wrong, to accept loss and to suffer the forfeit of all one's goods, than by impotence of mind to violate at once the laws of charity and of the Christian religion? But you are not only impotent in bearing wrongs; you also do wrong to others yourselves, and you do not even refrain from brothers, whom the bond of the same faith has joined to you most closely. In saying these things he heaps up many and very grave charges. First, that they sin by impatience against Christ's precept, who taught us to possess our souls by patience. Second, that they violate the laws of charity, which bid us love our enemies and even lay down our lives for our neighbours, if need be. Third, that they direct these things against brothers, and so, as far as in them lies, break even the bond of Christian fellowship. But if it is a crime to harm anyone, how much more monstrous a disgrace must it be to wrong one whom you ought to love and cherish as a brother? And indeed all these things applied to those who undertook unnecessary lawsuits, while they recognised none of this in themselves; and therefore it was needful that they be rebuked more freely by the Apostle.

units.la: Quia vero fidem medicum agere instituit, ita haec illis exprobrat, vt simul consilium suggerat, quomodo huic vitio mederi possint. Summa huius est, vt sese ad patientiam praepararet, & iniurias quantumuis graues & atroces ferre discant. Quod cum nobis difficilis sit praestitu, necesse est nos praeceptiunculis instrui, quae nos excitet atq; confirment. Primum itaq; a nobis ipsis initium faciamus, & quid ipsi mereantur, singuli cogitent. Ibi infinita occurrent, quae docebunt nobis ardentissimis ad Deum precibus & culpae deprecatione potius, quam vindictae opus esse. Et de hoc eos, qui adulteram adipsum adducebant, Christus admonuit, dicens: Qui vestrum immunis est à peccato, primus in eam lapidem proiiciat.
units.tr: Since the Apostle has undertaken to act as a physician to faith, he so reproaches them with these things that at the same time he offers counsel on how they may remedy this vice. The sum of it is that they should prepare themselves for patience and learn to bear wrongs, however grievous and savage. Since this is difficult for us to achieve, we must be instructed with little precepts which may rouse and strengthen us. Let us therefore make a beginning with ourselves, and let each consider what he himself deserves. There countless things will occur which will teach us that we have need of prayers to God, most fervent, and of confession of guilt, rather than of vengeance. Christ admonished those who were bringing the adulterous woman to him about this, saying: Let him who of you is without sin cast the first stone at her.

units.la: Deinde cogitemus, nihil nobis absq; divinae providentiae consilio accidere. Quod vnum facis ostendit, nimium temerarios nos fore, si huic relaxari libeat. Constat enim Deum nihil iniuste nobis facere, & eundem nostrae salutis studiosissimum esse, & ex illis quoq; fructum minime poenitendum vincere posse, quae homines improbi aduersus nos praeter ius & aequum instituunt. Tertio meminerimus nullum cuiusq; & breuissimum compendium esse, quo ad veram animi tranquillitatem peruenitur, quàm si in Dei providentia acquiescamus, & acceptas iniurias dissimulemus. Etsi enim haec nobis initio doleant, aegritudinem tamen illam dies mitigat, & tandem pacis solida causa erit oblivio illa iniuria voluntaria. Quod si ipses illa nos fallat, lucrum tamen inde ad nos ingens redibit, quod in patientiae portu tanquam in specula constituti tranquillo animo aliorum labores, curas, pericula & naufragia spectabimus, quae illos manent, qui pelago huic litium forensium se & fortunas suas committunt. Adde his IESV CHRISTI exemplum, qui vt omne genus iniuriarum patientissime semper tulit: ita nihil se indignum tunc quoq; dixit aut fecit, quando vestes suas inter milites immanissimos forte diuidi ex cruce spectabat. In horum consideratione si paulo diligentius versemur, iucundissimum nobis fiet hoc Christianae patientiae exercitium, quod initio durum nimis & intolerabile videbatur.
units.tr: Next let us consider that nothing happens to us apart from the counsel of divine providence. This one thing shows that we would be far too rash if we chose to relax about it. For it is certain that God does nothing unjustly to us, and that he is most zealous for our salvation, and that he can bring forth from those things also, which wicked men devise against us contrary to right and justice, a fruit by no means to be regretted. Third, let us remember that there is no surer or shorter way by which we reach true tranquillity of mind than to acquiesce in the providence of God and to overlook the wrongs we have received. For although these things may at first cause us pain, time softens that distress, and at last that voluntary forgetting of injuries will be a sure cause of peace. But if that very forgetting should deceive us, a great gain will still come back to us from it: established in the harbour of patience, as on a watchtower, we shall calmly look on the labours, cares, dangers and shipwrecks of others, which await those who entrust themselves and their fortunes to this sea of lawsuits. Add to these the example of Jesus Christ, who, though he always bore every kind of injury most patiently, said and did nothing unworthy of himself even when he saw from the cross his garments being divided among the most savage soldiers. If we dwell a little more diligently on the consideration of these things, this exercise of Christian patience, which at first seemed too hard and intolerable, will become most pleasant to us.

units.la: Caeterum quoad huius seculi fortunas, hic nobis spectanda venit auaritiae vis, quae Corinthiorum omnium ita immemores fecit, vt eos non puderet apud ethnicorum tribunalia lites suscipere contra fratres, qui eundem cum ipsis Christum profitebantur. Eadem etiam hodie hominibus omnem pietatis simul & dilectionis sensum adimit. Nam vt Christus docet, impossibile est Deo simul & Mammonae seruire. At qui Dei seruitio ceruicem suam subtraxerunt, ij nunquam adduci poterunt vt hominibus fraternae dilectionis officia praestent, si ea vel cum minima rerum fuarū ia-Stura coniuncta esse viderint. Ideo Apostolus auaritiam radicem malorum omnium esse dixit. Verum tamen aduersus morbum hunc tam pestilentem remedium in promptu erit, si de nobis ipsis simul & huius seculi diuitijs recte iudicemus. Quod nos, nudi in mundum venimus, & nudi emigrabimus, nec aliquid eorum hinc auferemus, quae stulti homines admirari & colere solent. Quod opes, haec non fluxae modo & lubricae vel incertae sunt, verumetiam ad vitam conseruandam inutiles, nec in illarum abundantia cuiusquam vita consistit, vt Christus non obscure monuit. Nec enim tam multis natura opus habet, quam ita Deus creauit, vt paucis contenta esse possit: & commodius fere viuunt, qui modico contenti nihil praeter vitae necessaria quaerunt. Et vt diuitijs rectissime vtaris, vsus tamen illarum cum vitae cursu finitur, ad cuius metam indesinenter contendimus. Ad aeterna vero vitae & regni coelorum possessionem adeo nihil conferunt opes, vt potius sarcinae immanis instar eos remorentur, quibus per angustam illam portam, cuius Christus meminit, eo esse eluctandum. Quae omnia cum in scripturis no minus vere quam diligenter tradantur, adhaec exemplis innumeris quotidie confirmentur, nimis stulte & imprudenter faciunt, qui circa huius seculi fortunas tumultuantur atq; litigant: prudentissime autem vitam & rationes suas instituunt, qui procul relicta bonorum huius seculi cura ad coelestis regni haereditatem aspirant, vbi immortales illi thesauri nobis repositi sunt, quos nullus fortuna casus eripit.
units.tr: Moreover, as regards the fortunes of this age, here the force of greed comes before us, which made all the Corinthians so forgetful that they were not ashamed to bring lawsuits against brothers, who professed the same Christ as they did, before the tribunals of the heathen. The same greed today takes from people every sense of both piety and love. For, as Christ teaches, it is impossible to serve God and Mammon at once. Those who have withdrawn their neck from the service of God will never be brought to perform the offices of brotherly love towards people if they see them joined with even the smallest loss of their possessions. Therefore the Apostle said that greed is the root of all evils. Yet against this so pestilential disease a remedy will be ready to hand, if we judge rightly both about ourselves and about the riches of this age. We came naked into the world, and naked we shall depart, and we shall carry none of those things away with us which foolish men are wont to admire and cherish. Riches are not only fleeting and slippery or uncertain, but also useless for preserving life, and no one's life consists in the abundance of them, as Christ has not obscurely warned. For nature has no need of so many things; God created it so that it can be content with few, and those who, content with a modest measure, seek nothing beyond the necessities of life generally live more comfortably. And although you use riches most rightly, their use is nevertheless ended with the course of life, towards whose goal we unceasingly press on. As for the possession of eternal life and of the kingdom of heaven, riches contribute so little that they rather hold back those who must struggle through that narrow gate of which Christ speaks, like a huge burden. Since all these things are taught in the Scriptures no less truly than diligently, and are confirmed daily by countless examples, those act most foolishly and imprudently who are in turmoil and go to law over the fortunes of this age; but those order their life and their affairs most wisely who, leaving aside the care of the goods of this age, aspire to the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, where those immortal treasures are laid up for us which no chance of fortune can snatch away.

units.la: Ioan.8.
units.tr: John 8.

units.la: Et huc referri debet loci istius Conclusio, quam non sine increpationis & comminationis specie sic infert: An nescitis, quòd iniusti hæreditatem regni Dei non possidebunt? Rursus autem interrogatione utitur, ut plus ponderis orationi accedat, & his verbis detestabilem atque nulla venia dignam eorum negligentiam accusat, qui cùm Christiani dici vellent, Christianæ religio-nis finem atque scopum adeò non observabant, ut eum aut prorsus ignorare, aut eius obliti vi-deri possent. Estis regnum Dei, cuius instaurandi causa Christus in mundum venit, & ad cuius possessionem per Euangelium vocamur, quod ideo Euangelium regni Dei, vel ipsum quoque regnum Dei dicitur. Id in eo consistit, ut dum hic vivimus, Deum suo spiritu & verbo in nobis regnantem audiamus: huius autem vitæ cursum emensi, cum illo vivamus & regnemus in cœlis, ubi nobis locum à Christo paratum esse credimus. Et de hoc intelligi debet, quod inter orandum dicimus: Adveniat regnum tuum. Hunc autem vitæ totius & actionum omnium scopum propositum esse debere, Christus his verbis docet: Quærite ante omnia regnum Dei & iustitiam eius, & reliqua omnia vobis adijcientur. Ita et in præsenti Paulus argumento à fine Christianismi desumpto utitur, quod est eiusmodi: Regnum Dei non nisi ad iustos pertinet: Ergo iniusti illud non possidebunt. Iniustorum autem nomine hic temerarios illos litigatores quoque comprehendit, quos non uno modo in iustitiæ Christianæ leges peccauisse, supra diximus. Habent ergo hæc gravissimam comminationem, qua æternæ felicitatis commercium illis negat, nisi emendentur. Ne quis autem ex contrarijs argumentando hinc colligeret, regnum Dei humanæ iustitiæ merito acquiri, consultò hæreditatis meminit. Constat enim hæreditatem filijs deberi, non quidem ex merito, sed ex generationis lege: At nos Dei filij facti sumus nullo nostro merito, sed ex gratuita adoptione, renati (ut Petrus inquit) ex semine immortali verbi Dei: Unde sequitur, regnum quoque illud nobis ex mera gratia obtingere.
units.tr: The conclusion of this passage ought also to be related to this, which he adds not without a semblance of rebuke and threat: Do you not know that the unrighteous will not possess the inheritance of the kingdom of God? Again he uses a question, so that more weight may attach to his words, and by these words he accuses the detestable negligence of those who, though they wished to be called Christians, so disregarded the end and aim of the Christian religion that they could be seen either to be utterly ignorant of it or to have forgotten it, a negligence deserving no pardon. You are the kingdom of God, for the sake of establishing which Christ came into the world, and to the possession of which we are called through the Gospel; for this reason the Gospel is called the gospel of the kingdom of God, or the kingdom of God itself. It consists in this: that while we live here we hear God reigning in us by his Spirit and Word; and, when we have finished the course of this life, we live and reign with him in heaven, where we believe a place has been prepared for us by Christ. It is of this that we must understand what we say in prayer: Thy kingdom come. And that this is to be the aim proposed for the whole of life and of all actions, Christ teaches in these words: Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you. So also in the present argument Paul uses an argument drawn from the end of Christianity, and it runs thus: The kingdom of God pertains only to the just; therefore the unjust will not possess it. Under the name of the unjust he here includes those contentious litigants also, whom, as we said above, he has offended against the laws of Christian righteousness in more than one way. These words therefore carry a most grave threat, by which he denies them a share in eternal happiness unless they amend themselves. Lest anyone, however, reasoning from the contrary, should infer from this that the kingdom of God is acquired by the merit of human righteousness, he deliberately mentions the inheritance. For it is established that an inheritance is owed to sons, not indeed on account of merit, but by the law of birth; but we have become sons of God by no merit of our own, but by gratuitous adoption, born again (as Peter says) from the immortal seed of the Word of God. Whence it follows that that kingdom also falls to us from pure grace.

units.la: Ut vero filius, etsi hæres natus sit, abdicatur tamen & ab hæreditate excidit, si se inobedientem & contumaciorem præbeat: ita nos quoque regni cœlorum hæreditatem, quæ ex adoptionis gratia nobis debetur, minimè quidem nostris operibus meremur, eandem verò nostra contumacia amittimus, & nostro magno merito abdicamur, si tantæ gratiæ iniquissimi æstimatores. Est ergo huius sententiæ usus multiplex, & proinde ad omnia vitia extendi debet, quibus in Christianæ religionis leges peccatur: ut proximo Sermone audiemus. Prudenter autem illam hic suo instituto Paulus applicat, ut ex collatione regni Dei & huius sæculi bonorum litigatores omnes intelligant, quàm malè sibi ipsis consulant, qui dum res nihili & fluxas persequuntur, ab æternorum atque cœlestium bonorum hereditate excidunt.
units.tr: As a son, although he was born an heir, is nonetheless disinherited and falls from the inheritance if he shows himself disobedient and stubborn, so we too do not deserve by our works the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven, which is owed to us through the grace of adoption. Yet by our obstinacy we lose it, and by our great fault we are disinherited, if we become the most unjust judges of so great a grace. This saying therefore has many uses, and so it must be extended to all the vices by which the laws of the Christian religion are broken, as we shall hear in the next sermon. Paul wisely applies it here to his present purpose, so that by comparing the kingdom of God with the goods of this world, all litigants may understand how badly they serve their own interests, since in pursuing worthless and fleeting things they fall away from the inheritance of eternal and heavenly goods.

units.la: Quod unum si auari diligentius expenderent, mox extingui sentirent inmanem illam sitim, quæ divitijs nullis satiari potest, sed eò magis accenditur, quò maiores illarum acervos sibi propositos esse videt. Leve quidem & vix reprehensione dignum videtur, iudicio cum aliis contendere, & aliquo prætextu in speciem honesto res alienas acquirere. At illud omne spiritus sanctus per Paulum iniustitiæ damnat, & à regno Dei eos excludit, quicunque artibus iniquis & illicitis ditescunt.
units.tr: If covetous men would weigh this one point more carefully, they would soon feel that monstrous thirst extinguished, a thirst that can never be satisfied by riches, but is kindled all the more the greater the heaps of them they see set before them. It seems a small matter, and hardly worth blame, to contend with others in court and, under some honest-looking pretext, to acquire other people's property. Yet the Holy Spirit through Paul condemns all of this as injustice, and excludes from the kingdom of God all who grow rich by unfair and unlawful arts.

units.la: Porrò ad tractationem istam quæstio pertinet: An Christianis hominibus, si ipsis iniuria fiat, & bona ipsis vel eripiantur, vel iniustè detineantur, iudicio experiri liceat? Duśputatum[?] de illa multum apud veteres, & in historijs ecclesiasticis notatur Iuliani Apostatæ scurrilis improbitas, qui Christianis de suarum facultatum direptione aut detentione quiritantibus respondere solebat, iniquas esse ipsorum querelas, cum Christi leges ipsos ad iniurias omnis generis patientes esse, & malo nequaquam resistere iubeant. Et nostro sæculo Anabaptistæ hoc ipsum quàm maximè urgent, non tàm ut litigandi studium coerceat, quàm ut magistratum è medio tollant, & leges omnes aboleant, ut quarum nullus in ecclesia Christi usus sit. Abutuntur isti hoc loco, quo Paulus iudicia simul omnia simpliciter damnare videtur: deinde Christi quoque verba citant, qui Matth. quinto Cap. dixerit: Audistis quòd dictum fuerit, Oculum pro oculo, dentem pro dente: At ego dico vobis, ne resistatis malo: sed si quis ceciderit te in dextram tuam maxillam, obverte ei & alteram: & ei qui tecum vult iudicio contendere, ac tunicam tuam capere, dimitte ei & pallium, &c. Et hæc quidem fanatici illi homines apud rude vulgus mirificè urgent, admixtis simul de charitate fraterna & spiritus libertate sermonibus, quæ duo legibus, & iudicijs,constringi nefas sit. Atqui unum hoc quærunt, ut abrogata omni magistratus authorita-te ipsis omnia miscere & impunè ex alieno vivere liceat. Et quantas turbas non uno loco dede-rint notius est, quàm ut multis demonstrari oporteat. Verumtamen propter simpliciores paucis dicemus, quæ ad huius quæstionis explicationem possunt sufficere.
units.tr: Moreover, the question belongs to this discussion: may Christians, if they suffer wrong, and their goods are either taken from them or unjustly kept from them, seek redress through the courts? Much has been disputed about this among the ancients, and the church histories record the scurrilous wickedness of Julian the Apostate, who, when Christians complained about the plundering or withholding of their property, used to answer that their complaints were unjust, since the laws of Christ bid them endure every kind of injury patiently and by no means resist evil. In our own age the Anabaptists press this very point most vigorously, not so much to restrain the eagerness for litigation as to remove the magistracy from the midst and abolish all laws, as if there were no use of them at all in the church of Christ. These men abuse this passage, where Paul seems simply to condemn all judicial proceedings. Then they also cite the words of Christ, who said in Matthew 5: "You have heard that it was said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth. But I say to you, do not resist evil; but if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also; and if anyone wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well," and so on. These fanatics press these words with great force upon the uneducated crowd, mixing in talk about brotherly love and the liberty of the Spirit, as if these two things could not be bound by laws and judgments. Yet this is all they seek: that, with all magisterial authority abrogated, they may throw everything into confusion and be free to live at others' expense with impunity. How many disturbances they have caused in more than one place is too well known to need demonstrating to many. Nevertheless, for the sake of the simpler folk, we shall say a few things that may suffice to explain this question.

units.la: Primò illud tenendum est, licere Christianis hominibus iudicum & legum præsidio uti, si quando bonitati nihil loci superesse,& amicam transactionem reijci vident. Argumenta, quibus id probetur, multa & firmissima sunt, quæ si quis omnia recitare vellet, in immensum excresce-ret oratio. Etenim ut Dei institutis seu ordinationibus utamur, nemo prohibebit, nisi qui Deo obsequium negare iubeat, aut illum aliquid instituisse dicat, quod fidei & charitatis legibus repugnet. At iudicia à Deo instituta esse, omnis scriptura docet. Moses certè iudicium Domi-ni esse ait, & ea ratione iudices admonet, ut in eo administrando bona fide agant: quo argumento Josaphatum quoque postea usum esse legimus. Et apud prophetas subinde occurrunt admonitiones illæ, quibus principes iubentur iudicium & iustitiam facere. At quid opus erat istud iubere, si iudicio experiri non licet? Scio seditiosos illos respondere, alia esse novi testamenti conditione: sed facile confutantur Pauli authoritate, qui omnem potestatem à Deo esse scribit, & magistratui obediendum esse docet, eò quòd Dei minister sit, qui non frustra gerat gladium, &c. Deinde ut judicia exerceatur, omnino necesse est. Quia enim impossibile est scelera in universum omnia è medio tollere, pœnis illa frænare & coërcere oportet. Nà nisi id fiat, intolerabilis fiet improborum licentia, neq; melior erit hominum quàm piscium conditio, qui cùm duce careant (ut propheta ait) alij alios devorant. At si unusquisq; privata authoritate jus suū tueri velit, confusio fiet, & non legibus, sed vi agetur, nō absq; manifesto optimorum periculo. Publica igitur authoritate opus est, ut et cognoscantur causæ, & suū unicuiq; reddatur. Adde hîs exempla sanctissimorum hominum, qui & judiciorum legumq; præsidio usi sunt, & ipsi magistratu gesserunt, neq; ideo minus probati fuerunt Domino, qui ad eū dignitatis gradū illos euexit. Quis enim nescit Josephū Arimathæū Hierosolymitæ ex Senatorū numero, et Paulū Sergium Cypri Proconsulem fuisse, utriusq; verò fide à spiritu sancto commendari? Et ne lœge exempla petatur, nonne ipse Paulus contra vim injustā Romanæ civitatis jure sese tutatus est, et armato etiā præsidio legitimi magistratus se defendi petijt? Magnā ergo illi injuria faciūt, qui huius loci authoritate adversus judicia publica abutūtur. Et si Apostolimè propius inspiciamus, non ipsa judicia reprehendit, sed Corinthios accusat propter vitia, quæ te merarios litigatores ferè comitātur. Imò monuit eos, ut ex credentiū numero arbitros constituāt, à quibus quæ inter ipsos incidunt lites cognoscantur. At quid hoc aliud est, quàm judicū authoritatem stabilire, adeoq; ecclesiam monere, ut proprios sibi magistratus constituant (quatenus nimirum id absque seditionis crimine fieri poterat) ne ad prophanos recurrere cogantur?
units.tr: First, this must be held: Christians may use the help of judges and laws whenever they see that there is no room left for goodwill and a friendly settlement is rejected. There are many very firm arguments by which this is proved, and if anyone wished to recite them all, my discourse would grow beyond measure. For that we may make use of the institutions or ordinances of God, no one will forbid, unless he bids us refuse obedience to God, or says that God has instituted something that contradicts the laws of faith and charity. But all Scripture teaches that judgments were instituted by God. Moses certainly says that judgment is the Lord's, and with this reason he admonishes judges to act in good faith in administering it; and we read that Jehoshaphat later also used this argument. And throughout the prophets there recur those admonitions by which princes are commanded to do judgment and justice. But why would this command be needed if one may not seek redress through the courts? I know that these seditious men reply that the conditions of the New Testament are different. But they are easily refuted by the authority of Paul, who writes that all power is from God, and teaches that the magistrate must be obeyed, because he is God's minister, who does not bear the sword in vain, and so on. Furthermore, it is entirely necessary that judgments be exercised. For since it is impossible to remove all crimes from the world, they must be restrained and checked by punishments. For unless this is done, the licence of the wicked will become intolerable, and the condition of men will be no better than that of fishes, which, lacking a leader (as the prophet says), devour one another. But if each person wished to defend his right by private authority, there would be confusion, and things would be decided by force rather than by laws, not without manifest danger to the best people. Public authority is therefore needed, both so that causes may be heard and so that to each his own may be rendered. Add to these the examples of the most holy men, who both used the protection of judgments and laws and themselves held magistracies, and were none the less approved by the Lord, who raised them to that degree of dignity. For who does not know that Joseph of Arimathea was a Jerusalemite from the number of the senators, and that Paulus Sergius was proconsul of Cyprus, and that the Holy Spirit commends the faith of both? And not to seek examples from afar, did not Paul himself protect himself by the right of the Roman citizenship against unjust violence, and ask to be defended even by an armed guard of the lawful magistrate? Those who abuse the authority of this passage against public judgments therefore do great wrong. And if we look more closely at the Apostle's words, he does not condemn the judgments themselves, but rebukes the Corinthians for the vices that usually accompany quarrelsome litigants. Indeed, he advised them to appoint arbiters from the number of the believers, by whom the disputes that arose among them might be decided. But what is this other than establishing the authority of the judges, and admonishing the church to appoint its own magistrates (so far as this could be done without the crime of sedition), so that they would not be forced to resort to the unbelievers?

units.la: Quoad Christi verba, qui ne malo resistamus, monuit, facilis est responsio. Nam si cum fanaticis illis literam urgere velimus, non Sathanæ, non falsis doctrinis, non scelerum licentia, non scandalis apertis, non latronum & sicariorum insidijs, non lenocinijs, non dolis, impostu-ris,fraudibus,resistere licebit: quia hæc omnia cum infinitis aliis sub mali censum veniunt. Imò ne precari quidem conveniet, ut Deus diaboli artes & consilia dissiper, aut improborum licentiam coërceat. Quòd si dicant, hanc non esse ipsorum mentem, ergo ipsi quoque Christi verba non rigi-dè secundum literam accipi debere fatentur: & proinde nobis quoque licebit verum eorum sensum inuestigare. Ubi primò observabis, Christum in ea concione protestatum fuisse, se non venisse, ut Legem abrogaret, sed potius ut ea impleat. Nihil ergo tradidit, quod illi contrarium censeri debeat. Deinde ut Legem de adulteriis, homicidiis & periurijs non sustulit, sed verum eius sensum contra scribas & pharisæos asseruit: ita talionis quoque legem non è medio tollere voluit, sed iis mederi, qui eius prætextu ad vindictam priuatam abutebantur. Itaque non judicibus loquitur, quorum est in puniendis malefactis regulam à Deo præscriptam observare, sed pri-uatis hominibus, quos à privata vindicta studio retrahere conatur. Deinde memineris dupli-cem esse modum resistendi malo. Primus est legitimus, quando ita urgente nos necessitate minu-rias[?] propulsamus, non nocendi studio, sed ut nos servemus, aut eos, quos nostræ fidei Deus credidit. Hūc nō licitū modò, verumetiā necessarium esse ad frænandam improborum licentiam, supra ostendimus. Alter est illegitimus, quando sola nocendi nosque ipsos ultiscendi cupiditate pari referre & vim vi repellere conamur. Hunc prohibet Christus, quia & publicam iustitiam turbat, & charitati Christianæ aduersatur, & ne unquam cum proximo in gratiam redeamus, obstat. Nemo igitur illius verba in sensum alienum rapere, & horum prætextu ad abolendas ciuiles leges abuti debet, neque statim damnandi sunt, qui iudicijs legitimis causas suas committunt, modo ab omni affectu prauo abstineant.
units.tr: As for the words of Christ, that we should not resist evil, the answer is easy. For if we wish to press the letter against those fanatics, it will not be lawful to resist Satan, false doctrines, the licence of crimes, open scandals, the snares of robbers and assassins, procurers, deceits, impostures, or frauds; for all these, with countless others, come under the heading of evil. Indeed, it would not even be fitting to pray that God would scatter the devices and plans of the devil, or restrain the licence of the wicked. But if they say that this is not their intention, then they too confess that the words of Christ must not be taken rigidly according to the letter; and therefore we too shall be free to investigate their true sense. Here you will observe first that Christ, in that sermon, declared that he had not come to abrogate the Law, but rather to fulfil it. He therefore handed down nothing that ought to be regarded as contrary to it. Next, just as he did not take away the law about adultery, murder and perjury, but asserted its true meaning against the scribes and Pharisees, so he did not wish to remove the law of retaliation from the midst, but to heal those who abused it as a pretext for private vengeance. Therefore he is not speaking to judges, whose duty is to observe in punishing wrongdoers the rule prescribed by God, but to private persons, whom he seeks to draw back from the eagerness for private vengeance. Then remember that there are two ways of resisting evil. The first is lawful, when under the pressure of necessity we repel injuries, not with the desire to harm, but in order to preserve ourselves, or those whom God has entrusted to our faith. We have shown above that this is not only lawful but necessary for restraining the licence of the wicked. The other is unlawful, when, out of the sole desire to harm and avenge ourselves, we try to repay like with like and to repel force with force. Christ forbids this, because it disturbs public justice, opposes Christian charity, and stands in the way of our ever being reconciled with our neighbour. No one, therefore, should twist his words to a foreign sense, or use them as a pretext for abolishing civil laws; nor are those to be condemned at once who commit their causes to lawful judgments, provided they abstain from every depraved passion.

units.la: Quod ut melius observetur, regulas aliquas tenere oportet, quas in agendis causis sequamur. Inter has prima esto, ne quid fiat in religionis Christianæ contumeliam. Vbi ante omnia opus est, ne hominibus magis quam Deo fidas, qui se eorum vindicem esse profitetur, qui iniurias & vim iniustam sustinent. Cauendum item: ne litibus non necessarijs fidem Christianam impiorum ludibrijs exponas: quod illi faciunt, qui fratres ad eorum tribunalia rapiunt, aut in persequendo suo iure pertinaciores sunt, neque ullum reconciliationis modum admittunt. Altera regula sit, ne temere in hanc arenam descendamus, sed lites aut actiones forenses cogitemus ex eorum remediorum numero esse, quibus non sine vitæ periculo utimur, & quæ ideo à fidis medicis non nisi in extrema necessitate adhiberi solent. Omnia ergo prius tentanda sunt, priusquam cum eo litem suscipias, qui tibi fratris loco est. Nam ut res tibi ex animi sententia succedat, multa incidunt, quæ cauere satius erat, quàm cum tenui lucro damnum maius sibi ipsi accersere. Nam (ut nunc mores sunt) lites ferè extrahuntur partim iudicum imperitia, partim causidicorum malitiosis artibus, qui ex eo quæstum uberrimum faciunt. Fit ergo, ut quod fratri negas, id omne in illos impendere cogaris, qui præter lucrum nihil quærunt. Accedunt animorum offensiones, quæ ut veteres amicitias dissoluunt, ita ne cum aduersarijs solidè in gratiam redeamus prohibent. Dum ergo pecuniam exiguam aut prædiolum tueris, amicum perdis, qui thesauri pretiosissimi instar tibi esse poterat. Tertia regula erit, ut inter litigandum charitatis perpetuò memor sis, & non tam ius tuum tueri studeas, quam fratrem iniquum quid aduersus te molientem in viam reducere, ut culpam agnoscat atque emendet. Quò imprimis pertinet, quod hic de iudicibus aut arbitris ex fidelium cœtu deligendis præcipitur. Si qui ista observent, ij non facile peccabunt. Quia verò hæc præstitu difficillima sunt propter naturæ nostræ vitiositatem, etiam atque etiam videre nos convenit, ne nos temere huic pelago committamus, in quo tam multos videmus quotidie fortunarum simul omnium & famæ suæ naufragium facere. Orent autem omnes Deum Patrem misericordiæ & pacis ut in spiritu mansuetudinis omnium mentes emolliat, in ferendis iniurijs patientes & ad omnia circumspectos reddat: ne dum in iure suo persequendo vehementiores sunt, à cœlestis regni hæreditate excidant, quam suæ mortis merito nobis acquisiuit Dominus & redemptor noster IESUS CHRISTUS: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: In order that this may be better observed, we ought to keep certain rules which we follow in conducting lawsuits. The first of these is: nothing should be done to the discredit of the Christian religion. Above all, we must take care not to trust men rather than God, who professes himself the avenger of those who suffer wrongs and unjust violence. Likewise we must beware of exposing the Christian faith to the mockery of the impious by pointless lawsuits; this is what those do who drag their brothers before their tribunals, or who are too stubborn in pursuing their rights and admit no way of reconciliation. The second rule is that we should not rush into this arena lightly, but consider that lawsuits and legal actions belong to the class of remedies that cannot be used without danger to life, and which therefore good physicians are wont to apply only in extreme necessity. Everything, then, must be tried before you take up a suit against one who is in the place of a brother to you. For although matters may turn out to your liking, many things arise which it would have been better to guard against, rather than bring a greater loss upon yourself for a small gain. For (as customs now are) lawsuits are commonly drawn out partly by the incompetence of judges, partly by the crafty tricks of advocates, who make a very rich profit from it. So it happens that you are forced to spend on those who seek nothing but gain all that you refused to your brother. Added to this are the offences given to minds, which, just as they dissolve old friendships, also prevent us from being fully reconciled with our adversaries. So while you guard a small sum of money or a little estate, you lose a friend, who could have been to you like a most precious treasure. The third rule will be that, in the course of litigating, you should always keep charity in mind, and be less eager to defend your own right than to bring back to the right path a brother who is plotting something unjust against you, so that he may acknowledge his fault and amend it. To this especially pertains what is here commanded concerning judges or arbitrators to be chosen from the assembly of the faithful. If those who observe these things, they will not easily sin. But since these things are most difficult to put into practice because of the corruption of our nature, we ought to look carefully and repeatedly, lest we rashly commit ourselves to this sea, in which we see so many every day suffer the shipwreck of all their fortunes and their reputation together. Let all pray, moreover, to God the Father of mercy and peace, that he may soften the minds of all by the spirit of meekness, make them patient in bearing injuries and watchful in all things, lest, while they are too vehement in pursuing their own right, they fall from the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, which our Lord and Redeemer JESUS CHRIST has gained for us by the merit of his death: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXIX.
units.tr: HOMILY XXIX.

units.la: Ne errate. Neque scortatores, neque idololatræ, neque moechi, neque molles, neque qui cum masculis concumbunt, neque fures, neque auari, neque ebriosi, neque conuitiatores, neque rapaces, regni Dei hæreditatem possidebunt. Et hæc eratis nonnulli: sed abluti estis, sed sanctificati estis, sed iustificati estis in nomine Domini IESU, & per Spiritum Dei nostri.
units.tr: Do not be deceived. Neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor sodomites, nor thieves, nor the covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners, will inherit the kingdom of God. And some of you were such; but you have been washed, you have been sanctified, you have been justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.

units.la: Quoniam Corinthiorum ecclesia vitiis plurimis, ijsque grauissimis, laborabat, Paulus illos non obiter modo & in genere reprehendit, sed de singulis ex ordine agit, partim quidem ut qui hactenus nimium securi fuerant, vitia illa melius agnoscant, & ad seriam ecclesiæ totius reformationem excitentur: partim ut remedium singulis adhibeat, & ostendat, qua ratione ex illis emergere & salutem in Christo acquisitam retinere possint. Itaque postquam de sectis & harum authoribus, de collapsa item ecclesiæ disciplina, deque temerarijs litigatoribus egit, nunc ad ea transitum parat, quæ ad coniugium pertinent, circa quod non vno modo peccabatur. Alij enim vagis libidinibus dediti impudentissimè scortabantur. Alij à coniugio abstinendum esse contendebant propter incommoda, quæ illud comitari solent. Multi sub religionis prætextu diuortia quærebant insidiosa & scandali plena. De his ergo omnibus differet Apostolus, initio facto à scortatione, cuius licentiæ nimis adsueuerant, & quæ aliorum vitiorum præcipua erat causa. Orditur autem in præsenti à generali reprehensione eorum scelerum, quæ præ aliis in illa ciuitate effreni licentia grassabantur: Nimirum ne qui à scortatione immunes erant, sibijpsis interea in suis flagitijs placerent, vtq; scortatores non indignius ferrent reprehensionem, quando alios non minus accusari, & eadem simul omnibus poenas denuntiari audiebant. Continet ergo locus iste generalem doctrinam, quæ hodie etiam consideratu dignissima est, quando plurimi passim sunt, qui Euangelij prætextu ad peccandi licentiam abutuntur.
units.tr: Since the church of the Corinthians was troubled by very many vices, and those most grievous, Paul does not rebuke them only briefly and in general terms, but deals with each one in order. Partly this is so that those who had hitherto been too complacent may recognise these vices better and be stirred to a serious reformation of the whole church; and partly so that he may apply a remedy to each, and show by what means they can rise out of them and keep the salvation won in Christ. So, after he has spoken of the sects and their authors, of the collapse of church discipline, and of the rash litigants, he now prepares to pass on to matters that concern marriage, in which sin was committed in more than one way. Some, given over to wandering lusts, played the harlot most shamelessly. Others insisted that one must abstain from marriage because of the troubles that usually accompany it. Many, under the pretext of religion, sought divorces that were treacherous and full of scandal. The Apostle will therefore deal with all of these, beginning with fornication, to whose licence they had grown far too accustomed, and which was the chief cause of the other vices. At present, however, he begins with a general rebuke of those crimes which, beyond the rest, ran riot in that city with unbridled licence. Clearly he does this so that those who were free from fornication should not be pleased with themselves in the meantime for their own disgraces, and so that the fornicators should not take the rebuke less hard, hearing that others were no less accused and that the same penalties were threatened to all alike. This passage, then, contains a general teaching which is most worthy of consideration today, since there are very many everywhere who abuse the pretext of the gospel to license for sinning.

units.la: Principio autem breui quidem sed graui præcepto omnis mali fontem obturat, admonens, ne falsis perfuasionibus seipsos decipiant, & ita à Veritatis atque salutis via aberrent. Ne errate, inquit. Id vero multiuariam fiebat, vt ex illorum moribus colligere licet. Plerique enim Christiani nominis professione superbi, hanc sufficere arbitrabantur, & hi cum Christum ore loquerentur, eundem vita & moribus negabant. Alij carnis & affectuum illecebris decepti, inter immanissima flagitia sibijpsis deliciis faciebant, quasi non tanta esset peccati atrocitas, quantam fingant homines morosi, qui ad viuendi rationem, quæ in scripturis traditur, omnes astringere conantur. Erant præterea qui mundi exemplo & impiorum prosperitate aut successibus offendebantur, & Deum sibi fingebant, qui facile ad omnia conniueret: quæ causa erat, vt eius longanimitate ad peccandi licentiam abuterentur. Accedebant his scurriles multorum sermones, quibus fabulæ & lusus erant, quæcunque de vita æterna, mundi fine, mortuorum resurrectione, nouissimo Christi ad iudicium aduentu, deque piorum præmijs & impiorum poenis dicuntur. Et horum voces erant, vt infra Cap.15. audiemus: Edamus & bibamus, cras enim moriemur: Post mortem frigora, flammæ. Et hæc sunt, quæ omnibus sæculis multos seduxerunt, vt inani persuasione & corrupto de peccatis et Dei iustitia aut longanimitate iudicio sibijpsis exitiū accererent. Blanditur enim sibijpsi impius (vt Dauid inquit) donec ipsi Deo exosus & detestabilis fiat, & in alio Psalmo ipse Dominus de quibusdam loquitur: Os tuum addixisti malo, & lingua tua dolo concinnat. Sedes, & contra fratre tuum loqueris, filiū matris tuæ probro afficis. Hæc fecisti, cūq; ego dissimulo, fingis me planè tui similē esse. Apud Malachiā verò quorūda sermones audiuntur. Frustra seruitur Deo: Quæ enim vtilitas, quòd custodia eius custodiuimus, et quòd humiliati coram Domino exercituū incedimus? Et enim nūc beatos dicimus superbos, quin qui impietate faciūt, ædificantur: & quiDeū tentant, liberantur. Superant hos immani audacia, quos Isaias sic loquentes inducit: Pepigimus fœdus cum morte, et cū inferis pactū fecimus: Flagellum inundans cum transierit, non peruenient ad nos. Posuimus enim mendacium refugiū nostrū, & mendacio abscōdemur. Atqui vtinam olim modò ista dicta fuissent, & nō hodie quoque passim audirentur, qui impudentissima scurrilitate omnia ea eludunt, quæ de scelerum poenis & diuini iudicij seueritate ex scripturis producuntur. Extant de his non obscura Christi & Apostolorum vaticinia, qui talesfore[?] nouissimorum temporum homines prædixerunt. Et sunt isti admodum ingeniosi, & mirificè facetijs sua condire norunt, quò facilius sese apud eos insinuent, quos adhuc aliquo pietatis sensu tangi sentiunt. Sed vno verbo ad omnia illorum argumenta Paulus respondet, dicens: Ne errate. Eo enim docet, errore non minus pernitiosum quam turpem esse omne illud, quod homines fingunt, vt peccandi licentiam atque impunitatem tueantur. Nam si fidei & religionis professionem prætexant, satis constat, regnum Dei, non in sermone, sed in virtute spiritus consistere, ex qua electi regenerantur, vt (quod Iacobus ait) fides in eorum factis aut operibus eluceat. Et notum est illud Christi: Non omnis qui dicit mihi, Domine Domine, ingredietur in regnum meum, sed qui fecerit voluntatem Patris mei, qui in cœlis est. Deinde nō ex nostris placitis aut nostro arbitrio iudicat Christus, cui omne iudicium datum est, sed ex Lege Patris sui, qui voluntatem suam nobis abunde manifestauit, vt ea nobis vitæ totius regula sit. Neque ab illo temere dictum esse putabimus: Ne existimetis quod venerim vt dissoluam Legem aut Prophetas: non veni vt dissoluam, sed vt impleam. Amen quippe dico vobis, vsque dum praeterierit cælum & terra, iota vnum aut vnus apex nequaquam praeterierit ex Lege, &c. Et notum est illud Prophetae: Verbum Domini manet in æternum. Prae aliis autem fallitur, quos impiorum hominum prosperitas offendit, & qui ideo ijsdem cum illis moribus sibi viuendum esse putant, quod eos feliciter agere videat. Est enim felicitas haec plane momentanea, & vt (Asaph dicebat) in lubrico constituti sunt, & somnij instar cum omni sua pompa atq; fastu euanescunt, quando minimè putaueris. Neq; temere à Dauide dictum est: Paulum adhuc, & nusquam erit impius: cumq; observaueris locum eius, nusquam supererit. Et rursus: Vidi impium violentum & sese diffundentem instar lauri frondosæ: Et transiui, & ecce non erat: quæsiui eum, & non est inuentus. Quod si vero nonnullos videas, qui totu huius vitæ cursum in felici otio et tranquillitate lætoq; rerum successu transigunt, cum impijssimi & quouis scelerum genere obruti sint, tamen ne horum quoque impunitas quenquam offendere debet. Ex ea enim apparet, certo fore olim vniuersalis iudicij diem quo singuli digna suis factis praemia recipiant. Nisi enim hoc demus, vniuersa Dei iustitia periclitabitur, vt alibi dictum est. Quoties ergo mundi illecebris aut carnis perfuasionibus nos tentari sentimus, semper nobis hæc Pauli admonitio in mentem veniat, &c.
units.tr: At the outset, with a brief but weighty precept, he stops up the source of every evil, warning them not to deceive themselves with false persuasions and so wander from the way of truth and salvation. "Do not be deceived," he says. This happened in many ways, as may be gathered from their conduct. For many Christians, proud of their profession of the Christian name, thought that this was enough, and while they confessed Christ with their mouths, they denied him by their life and conduct. Others, deceived by the allurements of the flesh and the passions, indulged themselves in the most monstrous crimes, as if sin were not so grave as peevish men imagine, men who try to bind everyone to the rule of life handed down in the Scriptures. There were also those who were offended by the example of the world and the prosperity or success of the wicked, and imagined a God who would easily overlook everything; this was the reason they abused his long-suffering as a licence to sin. To these were added the scurrilous talk of many, for whom everything said about eternal life, the end of the world, the resurrection of the dead, the last coming of Christ to judgment, and the rewards of the godly and punishments of the wicked, was a matter for jest and play. Their voices were such as we shall hear below in chapter 15: "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die"; "after death, cold and flames." These are the things which in every age have led many astray, so that by an empty persuasion, and by a corrupt view of sin and of God's justice, or of his patience, they brought destruction upon themselves. For the wicked man, as David says, flatters himself until he becomes hateful and detestable even to God himself. And in another psalm the Lord himself speaks of certain men: "You give your mouth to evil, and your tongue frames deceit. You sit and speak against your brother, you slander your mother's son. These things you have done, and when I keep silent, you think I am altogether like you." In Malachi, too, certain speeches are heard: "It is vain to serve God; what profit is it that we have kept his charge, and that we have walked as mourners before the Lord of hosts? For now we call the proud happy; indeed, those who work wickedness are built up, and those who tempt God are delivered." Those whom Isaiah introduces speaking thus surpass these in monstrous audacity: "We have made a covenant with death, and with hell we have made an agreement; when the overflowing scourge passes through, it shall not come to us, for we have made lies our refuge, and in falsehood we have hidden ourselves." Would that such words had been spoken only once, long ago, and were not heard today too, everywhere, from men who with the most shameless scurrility mock all those things which are drawn from the Scriptures concerning the punishments of sins and the severity of divine judgment. There are not obscure prophecies of Christ and the Apostles concerning these, who foretold that such men would arise in the last times. And these men are very clever, and know how to season their talk with wonderful witticisms, so that they may more easily insinuate themselves among those whom they perceive are still moved by some sense of piety. But Paul answers all their arguments in a single word, saying, "Do not be deceived." For by this he teaches that everything men invent in order to protect the licence and impunity of sinning is no less pernicious as error than it is shameful. For if they pretend a profession of faith and religion, it is quite clear that the kingdom of God consists not in speech but in the power of the Spirit, by which the elect are regenerated, so that (as James says) faith shines forth in their deeds or works. And that saying of Christ is well known: "Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into my kingdom, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven." Then, Christ, to whom all judgment has been given, does not judge according to our opinions or our own judgment, but according to the law of his Father, who has amply made known his will to us, so that it may be for us the rule of our whole life. Nor shall we think that he spoke rashly when he said: "Do not think that I have come to destroy the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to destroy but to fulfil. For truly I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one jot or one tittle shall in any way pass from the Law," and so on. And that saying of the Prophet is well known: "The word of the Lord endures for ever." Those are especially deceived who are offended by the prosperity of wicked men, and who therefore think they must live with the same manners as them because they see them doing well.
