For this prosperity is plainly momentary, and, as Asaph said, they are set on slippery ground, and like a dream they vanish with all their pomp and pride, when you least expect it. Nor did David speak carelessly: "Yet a little while, and the wicked shall be no more; and when you look for his place, he shall not be there." And again: "I saw the violent wicked man spreading himself like a green bay tree; I passed by, and behold, he was not; I sought him, and he could not be found." But if you see some who spend the whole course of this life in happy leisure and tranquillity and joyful success, although they are most ungodly and overwhelmed with every kind of crime, yet not even their impunity ought to offend anyone. For it shows that there will certainly be, at some time, a day of universal judgment on which each will receive rewards worthy of his deeds. For if we do not grant this, the whole justice of God will be imperilled, as has been said elsewhere. Therefore, whenever we feel ourselves tempted by the allurements of the world or the persuasions of the flesh, let this admonition of Paul always come to mind, etc.

units.la: Huic subiicit modo catalogum scelerum, quae prae aliis in Corinthiorum ciuitate regnabant. Fuit enim hæc[?] (vt initio diximus) emporium totius Graeciae nobilissimum, ad quod diuersissimarum gentium hospites atque mercatores confluebant. Hinc diuitijs augebatur, quae luxu pariunt, quem lasciuiae & libidinis authorem præcipuum esse constat. Et quia mores corruptissimi publico exemplo & consuetudine diuturna apud eos defendebantur, magna cum grauitate & commination cumprimis dira Apostolus pronuntiat: Neque scortatores, neque idololatrae, neque mœchi, neque molles, neque qui cum masculis concumbunt, neque fures, neque auari, neque ebriosi, neque conuitiatores, neque rapaces, regni Dei hæreditatem possidebunt.
units.tr: The Apostle now adds a catalogue of the sins that were especially rife in the city of Corinth. As we said at the beginning, this city was the most famous marketplace of all Greece, to which guests and merchants of very diverse peoples flocked. From this it grew rich, and its riches produced luxury, which is well known to be the chief author of wantonness and lust. Because the most corrupt morals were defended there by public example and long-standing custom, the Apostle pronounces his dreadful threat with great seriousness: "Neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor effeminate persons, nor those who lie with men, nor thieves, nor covetous persons, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners, shall inherit the kingdom of God."

units.la: Primo autem loco scortatores nominat, quia de illis potissimum differere instituit. In præsenti vero scortationi alias illicitæ libidinis species coniungit, Mœchos nimirum, qui & suis coniugibus datam fidem turpiter fallunt, & thoros alienos polluunt: Molles item, qui lasciuiam & animos impudicos quacunque re testantur: vtpote gestu, vestitu, incessu, verbis petulantibus & alijs rebus ad turpe lenocinium pertinentibus. Quibus aliqui non immerito pathicos & Cynædos coniungunt, qui prae aliis mollicie semper infames fuerunt. Addit his masculæ Veneri deditos, quod flagitium in Græcia imprimis vsitatum fuit, & hodie non in illis modo regionibus, sed inter eos quoque nimium vulgare est, qui sibi primum in Christiana ecclesia locum vendicant. Et tales quidem mortis poena Deus in Lege multare iussit, imo ipse suo exemplo quasi praeiuit & supplicij modum ostendit, quando Sodomas & Gomorrham cum toto agro vicino propter scelus igne & sulphure cælitus immisso in cineres, imo in lacum fœde olentem redegit, vt sempiterna esset exempli tam horrendi memoria. Atque digni omnino sunt, vt inusitato modo e rerum natura tollantur, quos plus quam belluina libido eo vsque exagitat, vt naturae leges violent. Est autem hic obseruatu dignissimum, quod etsi huius tam immanis flagitij meminerit Paulus, simul tamen scortationis quoque mentionem fecit, imo hanc primo loco numerauit inter ea, à quibus abstinere debent, qui ecclesiae Christi membra esse & regni Dei haeredes fieri cupiunt. Confutantur enim illius exemplo, qui hodie scortationi eo argumento patrocinantur, quod satius sit huius impunitatem permittere, quàm alicui ad foediora illa occasionem dare. Quasi vero non potius initijs scelerum obstare debeant, qui ad grauiora progredi nolunt. Etenim constat eos qui scortationi operam dare incipiunt, paulatim pudorem abstergere, vt vlterius progressi virginum pudicitiam tentent, inde matronis quoque & thalamis alienis insidias struant. Crescit ergo libidinis rabies, & tandem naturae etiam legum immemores reddit eos, qui illam indulgentia sua confirmarunt. Quae causa est, quod qui masculam Venerem ex populo suo excindere iussit, idem ne scortum in Israele sit prohibuit. Et cum Lothus bono quidem zelo, sed imprudenter filias Sodomæorum libidini prostituere vellet, ne quid illi concumeliosius in hospites eius designarent, minimè consilium illud Dominus probauit, sed sceleratos illos (vt modo diximus) cœlestibus flamis coercuit. At quia de scortatione in sequentibus plura dicentur, nunc ad alia huius Catalogi flagitia transeamus.
units.tr: He names fornicators first, because it was chiefly of them that he had undertaken to speak. In this present list, however, he joins to fornication other kinds of illicit lust: namely adulterers, who shamefully break faith with their own spouses and defile the beds of others; likewise the effeminate, who betray their wanton and shameless minds by whatever means: by bearing, dress, gait, wanton words and other things that belong to shameful enticement. Some rightly join to these the passive partners and the catamites, who above others have always been notorious for effeminacy. To these he adds those given over to male love, a vice especially common in Greece, and today not only in those regions but also among those who claim the first place in the Christian Church, where it is far too widespread. God indeed commanded such people to be punished by death under the Law; and he himself went before them, as it were, by his own example and showed the manner of punishment, when he reduced Sodom and Gomorrah, with the whole neighbouring countryside, to ashes by fire and brimstone sent down from heaven, indeed to a foul-smelling lake, so that the memory of so horrible an example might last forever. And those are wholly deserving of being removed from the order of nature in an unusual way, whom a lust more than beastly drives on so far that they violate the laws of nature. It is most worthy of notice here that, although Paul remembers this so monstrous crime, he at the same time also mentions fornication, and indeed places it first among those things from which those must abstain who wish to be members of the Church of Christ and heirs of the kingdom of God. For the example of Paul refutes those who today defend fornication on the ground that it is better to permit its impunity than to give occasion for those fouler things. As if, indeed, those who do not wish to advance to graver sins ought not rather to resist the beginnings of sins! For it is certain that those who begin to give themselves to fornication gradually wipe away shame, so that, having advanced further, they try the chastity of virgins, and from there they lay snares even for matrons and the beds of others. The rage of lust therefore grows, and at last it makes those who confirmed it by their indulgence forgetful even of the laws of nature. This is why he who ordered male love to be cut out of his people also forbade there to be a harlot in Israel. And when Lot, with a good zeal indeed but imprudently, wished to prostitute the daughters of the Sodomites to lust, so that they would not do anything more shameful to his guests, the Lord by no means approved that plan, but restrained those wicked men (as we have just said) with heavenly flames. But since more will be said about fornication in what follows, let us now pass on to the other crimes of this catalogue.

units.la: Vbi scortationi proxime subiicitur idololatria, imò hæc inter libidines illicitas quasi media interponit: Nimirum quòd scortatio sit spiritualis, & plerùque cū altera illa coniungatur. Exempla huius passim occurrunt. Quãdo enim cū Moabitarū fœminis scortari cœperunt Israelitæ, mox illarū sacris quoq; polluti sunt. Et Solomō alienigenarū uxorū atq; concubinarū blanditiis deceptus, idololatriā in regnū inuexit. Et ad Romanos Paulus non obscurè docet, iusto Dei iudicio fieri, vt sordidis libidinibus sese polluant, qui Dei maiestatem cum hominum & brutorum animantium simulachris commutare audent. Neque desunt nostri sæculi exempla, quæ istis fidem faciant.
units.tr: Directly after fornication idolatry is placed, indeed he puts it among the illicit lusts as if in the middle: namely because fornication is spiritual and is very often joined with that other sin. Examples of this occur everywhere. For when the Israelites began to commit fornication with the women of Moab, they soon were also defiled by their sacred rites. And Solomon, deceived by the allurements of foreign wives and concubines, introduced idolatry into the kingdom. And in his letter to the Romans Paul teaches plainly that it comes about by the just judgment of God that those who dare to exchange the majesty of God for images of men and brute animals defile themselves with filthy lusts. Nor are there lacking examples from our own age to bear witness to these things.

units.la: Tertiū in hoc catalogo locum iis tribuere possumus, qui quoad opes aut huius seculi facultates in proximum peccant. Inter quos vitium generale est{ Auaritia, quam plura præter ius & æquum habendi cupiditatem esse alibi diximus: & quam ad Ephes. & Colos. idololatriam esse Paulus docet, eò quod fiducia, quæ vni Deo debetur, in diuitias collocare docet. In præsenti vero hanc quoq; in suas species diducit, Fures nimirū & Rapaces. Per illos quidē eos designat, qui artibus, dolis & imposturis vtuntur, vt opes colligant: per hos autem eos, qui violenter aliena inuadūt, in quorū numero primi merito censentur mercenarij milites, qui bella sibi quastū faciunt: principes item, quos sola dominandi libido ad bella non necessaria excitat. Quarto loco Ebriosi ponuntur, de quibus Cap.quinto diximus. Quibus rectè Conuitiatores coniunxeris, quos vel vinum immodicè haustum, vel etiam odium & inuidia inebriat, vt linguam ad conuitia laxent.
units.tr: We may assign the third place in this list to those who sin against their neighbour in respect of wealth or the resources of this world. Among these the general vice is covetousness, which, as we have said elsewhere, is a desire to have more than right and justice allow; and which Paul teaches in Ephesians and Colossians to be idolatry, because it teaches men to place in riches the trust that is owed to the one God alone. In the present passage, however, he also divides this into its species, namely thieves and extortioners. By the former he designates those who use craft, tricks and deceits to gather wealth; by the latter, those who violently seize what belongs to others. Among these the first are rightly counted the mercenary soldiers, who make profit for themselves from wars; likewise princes, whom the sole lust of ruling stirs up to wars that are not necessary. In the fourth place are put drunkards, of whom we spoke in the fifth chapter. To these you may rightly join revilers, whom either wine drunk immoderately or even hatred and envy intoxicate, so that they loosen their tongues for insults.

units.la: Porrò omnibus istis denuntiatur, quòd regni Dei hæreditatem non possidebunt. Quod non ita accipi debet, quasi sententia ista in iis solis locum habeat, qui vitiis hisce simul omnibus obnoxij sunt. Nam vt D. Augustinus illam exposuit, singula enumerat Apostolus, in quibus singulis subauditur, quòd regnum Dei non possidebunt. At videtur hoc durum nonnullis, qui nos peccata omnia cum Stoicis paria facere clamant, cum & scripturæ sacræ doceant, & communi sensu constet, ingens inter illa discrimen esse. Quis enim sanæ mentis neget adulterum scortatore peiorem esse, vtrumque autem impietate superari ab iis, qui Sodomæorum nefaria libidine polluuntur? Ita minus peccant auari, qui cupiditates intra se continent, quàm fures, & his grauius delinquunt rapaces, qui ne à vi quidem manifesta abstinent. Imprimis tamen intolerabile videtur ebrietatem inter ista recenseri, ex qua hodie omnis ferè loci & ordinis homines laudem sibi quærunt, neque aliquam amicitiam stabilem aut societatem iucundam esse sentiunt, nisi quæ compotationibus immodicis sanciatur. At hic meminisse oportet, Paulum neque peccata paria facere, neque pœnarum diuersitatem aut discrimina negare, sed de eo agere, quod omnibus peccatis commune est: quòd nimirum à Dei regno excludunt. Id verò non obstat, quò minus alia aliis grauius puniantur. Sed libet hunc quoq; nodum Augustini verbis dissoluere, qui in loco, quem modò adduximus, sic scribit: Non dubitandum est ipsas pœnas, quibus cruciabuntur, qui regnū Dei non possidebunt, pro diuersitate criminū esse diuersas, & alias alijs acriores, vt in ipso igne æterno pro disparibus ponderibus peccatorum sint disparia tormenta pœnarū. Nec enim frustra ipse Dominus dicit: Tolerabilius erit Sodomis, quàm vobis, in die iudicij. Sed tamen ad non possidendum regnū Dei tantundē valet ex vitiis illis quod elegeris mitius, quantū vel plura vel vnum, quod perspexeris grauius. Hæc August. sunt. Adde his, quòd si quæ leuiora videntur diligentius examines, facilè videbis, minimè iniuriā illis fieri, qui in his incurabili contumacia perseuerant. Nā vt paulò ante diximus, auaritia idololatria est, & à Deo mentes hominum abstrahit. Scortatio templum Spiritus sancti impiè prophanat. Ebrietas scelerum grauissimorum quasi mater est, neque aliquem excusare potest, cum insania sit voluntaria, quam sibi ipsis scientes volentes accersunt, qui sana ratione vti poterat: vt iā de prophano donorū Dei abusu nihil dicatur, qui solus quouis supplicio dignus est. Nemo igitur sibi ipsi in istis delitias faciat, sed singuli potius hanc Apostoli sententiam dies noctesq; sibi occinant, quoties vitiorum illecebris sese solicitari sentiunt.
units.tr: Moreover, all these are told that they will not possess the inheritance of the kingdom of God. This ought not to be understood as if the sentence applied only to those who are liable to all these vices together. For, as Augustine explained it, the Apostle enumerates the sins one by one, and in each one is understood that they will not possess the kingdom of God. But this seems harsh to some, who cry out that we make all sins equal, as the Stoics did, although the holy Scriptures teach otherwise and common sense makes it plain that there is a huge difference between them. For who of sound mind would deny that an adulterer is worse than a fornicator, and that both are surpassed in impiety by those who are defiled with the unspeakable lust of the Sodomites? So the covetous, who keep their desires within themselves, sin less than thieves; and the extortioners, who do not even refrain from manifest violence, offend more gravely than these. Yet it seems especially intolerable that drunkenness is numbered among these things, when today almost men of every place and rank seek praise for themselves from it, and do not feel that any friendship is stable or any fellowship pleasant unless it is sealed by immoderate drinking parties. But here we ought to remember that Paul neither makes sins equal nor denies a diversity and differences of punishments, but is treating of what is common to all sins: namely that they exclude from the kingdom of God. And this does not prevent some being punished more severely than others. But I am pleased to loosen this knot also with the words of Augustine, who, in the place we have just cited, writes thus: "It is not to be doubted that the punishments themselves with which those who do not possess the kingdom of God will be tormented are diverse according to the diversity of crimes, and some are sharper than others, so that in that eternal fire itself there are unequal torments of punishment in proportion to the unequal weights of sins. For the Lord himself does not say in vain: 'It will be more tolerable for Sodom than for you in the day of judgment.'" But nevertheless, as far as not possessing the kingdom of God is concerned, whichever of those vices you choose as milder counts for as much as the more numerous or the one you see to be graver. These are Augustine's words. Add to these that if you examine more carefully those sins that seem lighter, you will easily see that no injustice is done to those who persist in them with incurable obstinacy. For, as we said a little before, covetousness is idolatry and draws men's minds away from God. Fornication impiously profanes the temple of the Holy Spirit. Drunkenness is, as it were, the mother of the gravest crimes, and cannot excuse anyone, since it is a voluntary madness, which those who could use sound reason bring upon themselves knowingly and willingly; not to mention the profane abuse of God's gifts, which alone deserves any punishment whatever. Therefore let no one indulge himself in these vices, but rather let each one sing to himself this sentence of the Apostle day and night, whenever they feel themselves enticed by the allurements of vices.

units.la: Cæterum pergit ille & argumentis eos vrget, vt reliquis omnibus vitijs, eam puritatem tue-antur, in quam Deus illos vocauit. Et hæc eratis nonnulli (inquit) sed abluti estis, sed sanctificati estis, sed iustificati estis in nomine Domini IESV, & per Spiritum Dei nostri. Continetur his verbis duplex argumentum. Primò liberè admodum & diserte priorem conditionem illis in mentem reuocat, ut eius recordatione illam horrere & abominari discant. Altero eam illi opponit, in quam Dei beneficio euecti erant, ut de ea conferuanda serio cogitent. Quoad primum, ait: Et hæc eratis nonnulli. Particulari nota vtitur, ne simul omnes immanium iflorum flagitiorum reos agere putetur, idque præter multorum meritum. Scimus enim inter gentes quoque aliquos honestatis amantiores fuisse, qui à manifestis sceleribus pro virili sibi temperauerunt. Veruntamen si ipsam hominis naturam ad viuum resecare libeat, nemo mortalium inuenietur, qui se ab horum reatu prorsus liberum aut immunem dicere possit. Latet enim in omnium carne peccatum, & vt ignis quidam in apertum lucari cupit, nisi aliqua vi maiori reprimatur. Quod & gentium philosophi non omnino ignorauerunt. Nam vt Cicero in quarto Thusc. quæst. scribit, Socrates, cum multa in conuentu vitia collegisset in eum Zopyrus quidam, qui se naturam cuiusque ex forma perspicere profitebatur, derisus est à cæteris, qui illa in Socrate vitia non agnosce-rent, ab ipso autem Socrate subleuatus est, cum illa sibi signa inesse, sed ratione à se deiecta diceret. Agnouerunt ergo naturæ vitiositatem philosophi, in eo autem hallucinati sunt, quòd eam à nobis per rationem corrigi posse putarunt. At nos scripturis edocti hoc omne ad Deum referimus, cuius gratia & virtute fit, ne quod in carne nostra delitescit peccatum pestimis apertorum scelerum fructibus se exerat. Et vt peccata quoq; suo fræno coerceat atq; moderetur diuina prouidentia necesse est, quia nisi id fiat, licentia sua totum orbem turbabunt, & pacem publicam omnino euertent. At cum Deus non facta modò hominum, sed ipsos quoq; animorum recessus in-spiciat, nos omnium flagitiorum reatu teneri constat, priusquam ex Spiritus virtute renati, inCHRISTO IESV noua iustitia donamur. Itaq; etsi Paulus atrociora illa & aperta scelera nonnullis modò tribuat, simul tamen innuit, omnium illorum eam fuisse conditionem, ut à regno Dei excludi meruerint, & verborum sensus est: Priusquam ad regni Dei hereditatem per Euangelium vocaremini, omnes simul vitijs immanissimis polluti atq; immersi fuistis. Nam vt omnes idola atq; Deos falsos coluistis: ita quoad mores & vitæ consuetudinem, alij libidines vagas secuti estis: alij auaritia accensi omne genus fraudis & iniustitiæ exercuistis, ut per fas nefasq; diuitiarum aceruos colligeretis: alij ebrietati & luxui per omnia vos addixistis, quæ vobis multorum malorum causa fuit. Neq; dubitauerim, vos iam totis animis exhorrescere, adeoq; vnumquenq; ex vobis suispsius pudere, quoties in mentem ipsi venit, quàm multa turpiter & nefariè aduersus naturæ & publicæ honestatis leges defignarit. Cæterum quæ Dei est bonitas atq; clementia, melior multò nunc vestra est conditio. Nam abluti estis, sanctificati estis, iustificati estis, & iam omne damnationis æternæ periculum effugistis. Vestri ergo officij fuerit, omni cura & studio cauere, ne ad pristinam miseriam & priores illas sordes relabamini. Hæc Pauli mens est. Conti-nent autem verba hæc generalem doctrinam, & vniuersum nostræ redemptionis negotium probè illustrant, cuius singulas partes sæpe & diligenter inspexisse plurimum prodest.
units.tr: Furthermore, he goes on and with arguments urges them to keep that purity in every other respect too, the purity to which God called them. "And such were some of you," he says, "but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit of our God." These words contain a twofold argument. First, quite freely and plainly, he recalls to their minds their former condition, so that by remembering it they may learn to shudder at and abhor it. Second, he sets against it the condition into which they were raised by God's benefit, so that they may think seriously about preserving it. As to the first, he says: "And such were some of you." He uses this qualifying mark so that he is not thought to accuse all of them of guilt for these monstrous crimes, and beyond the merit of many. For we know that among the Gentiles too there were some who loved honesty more and who, as far as they could, restrained themselves from open wickedness. Nevertheless, if one wished to cut into human nature itself to the quick, no mortal would be found who could say that he was wholly free or exempt from the guilt of these things. For sin lies hidden in the flesh of all, and like a certain fire it longs to break out into the open, unless it is held back by some greater force. The philosophers of the nations were not entirely ignorant of this either. For, as Cicero writes in the fourth book of the Tusculan Disputations, when a certain Zopyrus, who professed to discern each man's nature from his outward form, had listed many vices in Socrates, he was mocked by the others, who did not recognise those vices in Socrates. But Socrates himself came to his defence, saying that those signs were indeed in him, but that he had cast them out by reason. So the philosophers recognised the corruption of nature, but they were mistaken in thinking that it could be corrected by us through reason. We, however, taught by the Scriptures, refer all this to God, by whose grace and power it comes about that the sin hidden in our flesh does not break out in the deadly fruits of open crimes. Divine providence must also restrain and govern sins by its bridle, for unless this were done, they would by their license throw the whole world into turmoil and utterly overturn public peace. But since God looks not only at the deeds of men but at the innermost recesses of their minds, it is clear that we are all held by the guilt of every wickedness, before we are reborn by the power of the Spirit and are granted new righteousness in Christ Jesus. Therefore, although Paul attributes those more atrocious and open crimes only to some, he nevertheless implies that all of them were in such a condition that they deserved to be shut out from the kingdom of God. The sense of the words is this: before you were called to the inheritance of the kingdom of God through the Gospel, you were all together polluted and steeped in the most monstrous vices. For just as you all worshipped idols and false gods, so, as regards morals and way of life, some of you pursued wanton lusts, others, inflamed with greed, practised every kind of fraud and injustice, so as to heap up piles of riches by right and wrong alike, and others gave yourselves over entirely to drunkenness and luxury, which was the cause of many evils for you. I do not doubt that you now shudder with your whole souls, and that each of you is ashamed of himself whenever it comes into his mind how many shameful and wicked things he has done against the laws of nature and public decency. But, by the goodness and mercy of God, your condition is now far better. For you have been washed, you have been sanctified, you have been justified, and you have now escaped every danger of eternal damnation. It will therefore be your duty to take every care and pains to avoid relapsing into your former misery and those former filths. This is Paul's meaning. These words contain a general doctrine and set clearly before us the whole business of our redemption, and it greatly profits us to examine its individual parts often and diligently.

units.la: Occurrit hic primum, ut qui & quales nostra natura sumus, videamus: Nimirum, quales Paulus describit, à quibus nihil grauissimorum scelerum prorsus alienum fuerit. Clarius tamen eorundem effectus & miserabilis, quæ ex illis dependet conditio in anthithesi elucet, quando nos iam ablutos, sanctificatos & iustificatos esse scribit. Ex eo enim sequitur, nos prius pollutos & immundos, prophanos item & à Deo alienos, adhæc peccati & mortis reos fuisse. Docet id scri-ptura, quæ totam Adami posteritatem in illius corrupta imagine, adeoq; in peccato concipi & nasci testatur.Eadem peccati effectum esse docet, quòd nos instar maceriæ alicuius à Deo separet: quòd item stipendium eius sit mors, quæ per illud ingressa est. Et oportet hinc facere istius con-siderationis initium, ne quid fiduciæ in nobis collocemus, sed salutis fontem constituamus in sola Dei gratia, qui nos indignos dilexit, & nostri miserum est, ut nobis opem ferret. Et hoc non ob-scure innuit Paulus, quando non ait: Vos abluistis, vosipsos, vos sanctificastis corpora & animas vestras, &c: sed, Abluti estis, sanctificati estis, &c. Nimirum à Deo, qui hac gratia vos prosequi dignatus est, ut ex sordibus & miseria ista liberaremini.
units.tr: Here first we must consider what and of what kind we ourselves are by nature: namely, such as Paul describes, from whom nothing of the most grievous crimes would be wholly alien. The effect of these things, and the wretched condition that depends on them, shine out more clearly in the antithesis, when he writes that we are now washed, sanctified and justified. For it follows from this that we were formerly polluted and unclean, profane too, and alienated from God, and moreover guilty of sin and death. Scripture teaches this, testifying that the whole posterity of Adam is conceived and born in sin, in his corrupted image. The same Scripture teaches that the effect of sin is that it separates us from God like some wall; and that its wages are death, which entered through it. From this we must make the beginning of this consideration, so that we place no confidence in ourselves, but establish the fountain of salvation in the grace of God alone, who loved us though we were unworthy, and who was pleased to bring us help in our misery. Paul hints at this plainly when he does not say: "You washed yourselves, you sanctified your bodies and souls," and so on; but says: "You were washed, you were sanctified," and so on. Clearly this was done by God, who deigned to bestow this grace on you, so that you might be freed from these filths and this misery.

units.la: Secundò ordinem quoque exprimit, quo erga nos Deus vtitur. In quo primum est, quod qui toti immundi sumus, abluimur. Lauacrum vero hoc proprie Christi sanguis est. Sicenim Ioannes clamat: Sanguis filij Dei emundat nos ab omni peccato. Et eò David respiciens orabat: Lavame plurimum ab iniquitate mea, & à peccato meo munda me: Lavame (inquam) & nive ero candi-dior. Ablutionis autem huius sigillum est baptismus, & ideo alibi per hunc ablui & purgari dicimur. Sequitur ablutionem Sanctificatio, quia nisi toti Deo consecraremur, illa nihil prodesset. Sanctificamur autem Spiritus virtute, qua fit, ut natura vitiosa in nobis reformetur, & nos in homines novos renascamur, qui toti ab uno Deo pendeant. Accedit his iustificatio, quae gratuita peccatorum remissione constat & iustitiae Christi imputatione: quem ideo supra nobis à Patre iustitiam factum [?] esse dixit. Propter ista ergo iam pro ablutis [?], sanctis & iustis habemur, qui natura immundi, prophani & iniusti sumus. Et facit hoc vehementer ad gratiae Dei commendatio-nem, qui non solum tam enormia flagitia nobis condonat, verumetiam iustis nos titulis dignatur, qui solis filijs ipsius conueniunt. Horum igitur consideratione nosmetipsos consolemur, si quando nobis peccata nostra Satan obijcit, & meminerimus eorum qui credunt non pristina facta in rationem venire, sed tales nos à Deo aestimari, quales ipse nos ex gratia facere dignatus est.
units.tr: Secondly, he also sets out the order in which God deals with us. In this, the first thing is that we who are wholly unclean are washed. This laver is properly the blood of Christ. For so John cries out: "The blood of the Son of God cleanses us from all sin." And David, looking to this, prayed: "Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. Wash me (I say) and I shall be whiter than snow." The seal of this washing is baptism, and therefore elsewhere we are said to be washed and purged through it. Sanctification follows the washing, because unless we were consecrated wholly to God, the washing would profit nothing. We are sanctified by the power of the Spirit, by which our sinful nature is reformed in us and we are born again as new men, who depend wholly on the one God. Justification is added to these, which consists in the free remission of sins and in the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, whom for this reason the Father has made our righteousness [?]. Because of these things, then, we are now regarded as washed [?], holy and righteous, although by nature we are unclean, profane and unrighteous. This greatly serves to commend the grace of God, who not only forgives us such enormous crimes, but also deigns to call us by titles of righteousness, which belong only to his own sons. Let us therefore console ourselves with the consideration of these things, whenever Satan throws our sins in our face, and let us remember that those who believe that their former deeds do not come into account, but that we are regarded by God as he has deigned to make us by grace.

units.la: Tertiò medium & authorem totius negotij indicat. Nos enim ablutos, sanctificatos & iustificatos dicit, in nomine Domini IESV, & per Spiritum Dei nostri. Nihil hic de semetipso, vel Apollo, aut Cephas dicit Paulus, sed solius Christi meminit. Hic enim unicus & solus gratiae Dei & totius salutis Mediator est, in quo se placatum esse Pater coelitus pronunciauit. Nomen autem IESV ponit, non ut Iudaeorum more nobis nomen quoddam fingamus (quale illi suum Schem Hamphoras habent) quod vel ore pronuntiatum, vel obiter auribus receptum nos servet: sed ut ad Evangelij praedicationem nos remittat, & talem animo concipiamus Christum, qualem nobis Apostoli praedicarunt. Quia vero idem à nobis aliter, quàm per fidem apprehendi non potest, haec vero per Spiritum sanctum in nobis excitatur, rectissime huius etiam meminit, ut nos absque eius virtute prorsus examines esse & nihil posse intelligamus. Quae causa est, quòd illum Christus nobis aduocatum destinauit, qui nos in omnem veritatem inducat. Ita vero totum hoc mysterium Paulus in praesenti proponit, ut aperte satis unius veri & aeterni Dei Trinitatem exprimat. Nam negotium omne ad Deum unum authorem refert, quem proprie Patrem dicimus. Mediatorem eius indicat Filium, qui ut is posset fieri, hominem induit. Mox vero Spiritus meminit, per quem nos ad ista parari & sanctificari oporteat. Recte ergo in unum Deum baptizantur Christiani homines, Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum. Sed de hoc plura alibi.
units.tr: Thirdly, he indicates the means and the author of the whole business. For he says that we are washed, sanctified and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God. Paul says nothing here about himself, or Apollos, or Cephas, but mentions only Christ. For he alone is the unique and only Mediator of the grace of God and of all salvation, in whom the Father has declared from heaven that he is appeased. He names the name of Jesus, not so that, after the manner of the Jews, we may invent some kind of name for ourselves (such as they have in their Schem Hamphoras), which would preserve us if it were pronounced with the mouth or merely heard in passing by the ears; but so that he may send us back to the preaching of the Gospel, and so that we may conceive of Christ in our minds as the apostles preached him to us. But since this name cannot be grasped by us in any other way than through faith, and faith is in turn stirred up in us by the Holy Spirit, he rightly mentions the Spirit too, so that we may understand that without his power we are wholly powerless and can understand nothing. This is the reason why Christ appointed him to us as the Advocate, who leads us into all truth. Paul sets forth this whole mystery in the present passage in such a way that he sufficiently clearly expresses the Trinity of the one true and eternal God. For he refers the whole business to one God as its author, whom we properly call the Father. He indicates the Son as his Mediator, who, so that he could become such, put on man. Soon afterwards he mentions the Spirit, through whom we must be prepared and sanctified for these things. Rightly, then, Christian people are baptised into the one God, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. But more on this elsewhere.

units.la: Restat videre, quis istius tractationis, quoad hanc vitam, nobis finis & scopus esse debeat: Is nimirum, ut prioris conditionis plus nimis miserae & infelicis memores, dignitatem eam sedulò tueamur, in quam tanto pretio redempti & evecti sumus. Qui ex morbo letali per immanes cruciatus convaluerunt, ad illius mentionem exhorrescere solent, & (nisi non sanae mentis sint) studiosè cavent, ne in illum recidant. Et qui aere alieno amicorum beneficentia liberati sunt, vix viri boni nomen merentur, si novâ prodigalitate, & seipsos rursus perdant, & quàm parùm fecerint amicorum liberalitati [?], ea leuitate testentur: certè indignos se esse produnt, quibus quisquam in posterum subveniat. Quantò magis ista nos hic cogitare oportet, quando nos aeternae mortis reos, & iam salutis omnino deplorata, Deus proprij Filij sanguine servare, & per Spiritum suum sibi ipsi consecrare dignatus est? Nec enim ideo nos ille redemit, neq; nos per Evangelium de salute nostra ideo certos facit, ut in pristinae memoriae sordes relabamur. Cogitemus ergo sat nobis esse debere (ut Petrus ait) quòd anteactò vitae tempore pro gentium libidine & ex carnis arbi-trio vitam in omni scelerum genere transegimus: nostrum vero iam esse, ut abluti & sanctificati & iustificati, excusso infelici peccatorum iugo, vitam viuamus novam in IESV CHRISTO, Domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: It remains to see what aim and purpose this whole discussion should have for us in the present life. Namely, mindful of our former condition, which was far too wretched and unhappy, we should carefully guard the dignity into which we have been redeemed and raised at so great a price. Those who have recovered from a deadly disease after savage torments usually shudder at the mere mention of it, and (unless they are out of their minds) take great care not to relapse into it. And those who have been freed from debt by the kindness of friends scarcely deserve the name of good men if, by fresh extravagance, they ruin themselves again and by such frivolity show how little they valued their friends' generosity. Certainly they reveal themselves unworthy of anyone's help in future. How much more ought we to consider these things, since God has deigned to save us, who were guilty of eternal death and whose salvation was utterly despaired of, by the blood of his own Son, and to consecrate us to himself through his Spirit? For he did not redeem us, nor does he make us certain of our salvation through the Gospel, so that we should slip back into the filth of our former life. Let us therefore think it enough, as Peter says, that in past time we spent our life in every kind of wickedness, following the lusts of the Gentiles and the will of the flesh. It is now our task, having been washed, sanctified and justified, and having shaken off the unhappy yoke of sins, to live a new life in Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: H O M I L I A XXX.
units.tr: HOMILY XXX.

units.la: Omnia mihi licent, at non omnia conducunt: omnia mihi licent, at ego non redigar sub ullius rei potestatem. Escae ventri [de-stinatae sunt] & venter escis: Deus autem & hunc & eas abolebit:
units.tr: All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of anything. Meats are for the belly, and the belly for meats: but God shall destroy both it and them.

units.la: Corpus vero non scortationi, sed Domino, & Dominus corpori. Deus autem & Dominum suscitauit, & nos suscitabit per potentiam suam.
units.tr: Now the body is not for fornication, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. And God has both raised up the Lord, and will raise us up by his power.

units.la: Inter alia scelera, quibus Corinthiorum ciuitas polluta atque infamis erat, primatum fere tenuit scortandi licentia, cui plerique indulgebant, & impune quidem, cum nemo illam peccati loco haberet. Quæ causa fuit, ut etiam illi, qui ad Christum conuersi erant, nimium sibi adhuc in ea permitterent, ideoque multiuariam peccaretur in leges coniugij, quod Deus inter homines sacrosanctum seruari vult. Nuper ergo Paulus generali correptione usus est, qua eos monuit, ne sibi ipsis imponi paterentur ab iis, qui de peccatis leuiter judicant: sed potius pristinæ conditionis memores, curent, ne in eam relabantur: seruare autem studeant eam puritatem, quam nobis sui sanguinis pretio Christus acquisiuit. Et possunt quidem hæc argumenta sufficere hominibus Christianis, quibus Dei gratia & redemptionis per Christum facta beneficio nihil antiquius esse solet. Verum tamen obstabat Corinthijs publicæ consuetudinis exemplum, quod nunquam non in oculis eorum versabatur, & quod ipsi quoque à pueris huic licentiæ assueuissent. Hæc enim causa erat, ut (quod improbi & mundi studijsediti solent) ex consuetudine legem facerent, & ea quoque sibi putarent licere, quæ cum charitate & honestate Christiana, imò cum Christianæ religionis fine, prorsus pugnabant. Ut ergo libertate per Christum nobis parta abutebantur, quoad cibos & gulæ studium: ita illam usque ad scortandi licentiam extendebant, ut multi jam eiusdem juris esse putarent, cibis quibuslibet vesci & vagas libidines sectari. Itaque propius ad institutum Paulus accedens, errorem illum grauiter confutat, & quid in utroque potissimum observari debeat, docet.
units.tr: Among the other sins by which the city of the Corinthians was polluted and infamous, the licence of fornication held almost the first place, to which many gave themselves, and indeed with impunity, since no one counted it a sin. This was the reason why even those who had been converted to Christ still allowed themselves too much freedom in it, and so there was a manifold sinning against the laws of marriage, which God wills to be kept inviolate among men. Paul, therefore, has just used a general reproof, by which he warned them not to allow themselves to be deceived by those who judge lightly of sins, but rather, mindful of their former condition, to take care not to fall back into it, and to strive to keep that purity which Christ acquired for us at the price of his own blood. These arguments may indeed suffice for Christian men, for whom nothing is wont to be more precious than the grace of God and the benefit of redemption made through Christ. Yet the example of public custom stood in the way of the Corinthians, which was always before their eyes, and to which they themselves had been accustomed from childhood. For this was the cause why (as wicked men and those devoted to worldly pursuits are wont to do) they made custom into law, and thought that those things were also permitted to them which were wholly contrary to charity and Christian decency, indeed to the very purpose of the Christian religion. So, just as they abused the liberty won for us through Christ, in regard to foods and the pursuit of gluttony, so they extended it even to a licence for fornication, so that many now thought that they had the same right to eat any foods whatever and to pursue wandering lusts. Accordingly, drawing nearer to his subject, Paul sharply refutes that error and teaches what ought chiefly to be observed in each case.

units.la: Primum de iis agit, quæ media & indifferentia dicuntur, eò quòd illis uti vel non uti licet, & illos reprehendit, quòd his licenter nimis abuterentur. Ex his autem cibos adducit, circa quos non uno modo à Corinthijs peccabatur. Alij enim gulæ studio addicti intemperantia sua libidini materiam & fomenta subministrabant: alij vero in amicorum gratiam ad epulas ex carnibus idolothytorum instructas accedebant: utrique vero libertatem Christianam præ se ferebant, quòd nimirum per hanc quibuslibet vesci liceret, neque cibis ullis animus inquinaretur. Qua propter per Anthypophoram illorum argumento occurrens ait: Omnia mihi licent, at non omnia conducunt, &c. Quasi diceret: Audio ô boni vestras voces, quibus clamatis licere, ut absq; omni delectu cibos quoscunque edatis, & libertatis Christianæ beneficium magnificè extolli à vobis audio. Neque is ego sum, qui hoc ignorem, aut vos eo fraudare velim. Novi enim Christi dictum: Nihil quod per os ingreditur, inquinat hominem, &c. & per illum diferimina ciborum, quæ in lege olim præscripta fuerunt, iampridem abrogata esse scio: neq; permittendum esse, ut Ecclesia nouis traditionibus atq; ceremonijs grauetur. At non sufficiunt ista ad excusanda omnia, quæ sub prætextu libertatis illius fiunt. Nam non conducunt omnia quæ licent, neque statim aut tibi aut proximo utile est: quod per se salua conscientia facere potes. Adhæc videre etiam oportet, ne ego sub potestatem redigar earum rerum, quibus ceu licitis uti volo, & ita dum libertatem iacto, seruus fiam eorum, quæ mihi in bonum seruire debebant, &c.
units.tr: First he deals with those things which are called indifferent and neutral, because it is lawful to use them or not to use them, and he rebukes them because men abused these things too freely. Of these he brings forward foods, in regard to which the Corinthians did not sin in one way only. For some, given over to the pursuit of gluttony, supplied material and fuel for their own intemperance; others, to gain the favour of friends, went to feasts furnished with meats from idol sacrifices; yet both put forward Christian liberty, namely that through it they might eat anything whatever, and that the mind is not defiled by any foods. Therefore, meeting their argument by a counter-statement, he says: All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient, etc. As if he said: I hear, good men, your voices, by which you cry out that it is lawful to eat any foods whatever without any distinction, and I hear you magnify loudly the benefit of Christian liberty. Nor am I one who does not know this, or who would wish to defraud you of it. For I know the saying of Christ: Nothing that enters through the mouth defiles a man, etc., and I know that the distinctions of foods which were once prescribed in the law have long since been abrogated; nor is the Church to be burdened with new traditions and ceremonies. But these things are not enough to excuse everything that is done under the pretext of that liberty. For not all things that are lawful are expedient, nor is it at once useful to you or to your neighbour, what you can do by itself with a clear conscience. Moreover, one must also see to it that I am not brought under the power of those things which I wish to use as if they were lawful, and so, while I boast of my liberty, I become the slave of those things which ought to have served me for good, etc.

units.la: Docet ergo his verbis Paulus, quæ sit libertatis Christianæ ratio & ut pij illis uti debeant, quæ per se licita atq; permissa sunt. Est doctrina hæc utilis admodum, imò ad seruandas ecclesias necessaria: quia hic plurimum peccatur magno cum infirmorum scandalo, dum quidam libertate suam pertinacius tuentur, & ne in minimis quidem suo iure cedendum esse putant. Atqui aliud est libertas (ut quidam recte monuerunt) aliud libertatis usus: neq; statim libertate amittit, qui interdum eam prudenter & certa cum ratione dissimulat: quin potius se rerum omnium dominum reneraa[?] esse probat, qui omnibus utitur non pro carnis aut affectuum carnalium arbitrio, sed prout sibi aut aliis conducere viderit. Sunt ergo hic duo hæc probè observanda. Primum quid conducat aut utile sit, non tam nobis, quàm publicæ aliorum saluti[?] & ecclesiæ totius ædificationi. Nemo enim sibi soli natus est, sed omnibus hominibus per charitatis legem omnes obstricti sumus. Et si gentium philosophi rectè docuerunt, partem nostri sibi parentes vendicare, partem patriam, partem amicos: quanto magis Christiani homines scire debent, se totos ad Christum pertinere, qui ipsos ex peccati & mortis tyrannide in libertatem filiorum Dei asseruit, & in quo renati filij Dei facti sunt? At huius lex est, vt priuatim quidem singulorum hominum salutem pro viribus promouehamus, publicè autem ecclesiæ ædificationi studeamus, ne huius pax aut ordo per nos turbe-tur. Itaq; in rebus medijs aut indifferentibus ante omnia ædificationis rationem habere oportet, vt quam plurimos ad ecclesiæ societatem attrahamus, infirmos & nutantes confirmemus, vt ecclesia tota indies in melius proficiat. Et de hoc quidem plura sequentur deinceps, quando de idolothytorum esu prolixè Apostolus disputabit. Nunc autem meminerimus, quòd si hæc in rebus medijs & per se licitis obseruari debent, multo magis in ijs nos cautos & circumspectos esse debere, quæ illicita & Christianæ religionis legibus aduersa sunt. Confutantur ergo hic grauissimi, qui hodie ebrietatem, choreas & saltationes lasciuas, vel etiam Bacchanalium & Lupercalium reliquias prætextu libertatis excusant. Ista enim omnia non modò non conducunt, sed vehemen-ter obsunt, quando ijs multi offenduntur, ecclesiæ disciplina turbatur, & qui religionem Christianam oderunt inde calumniandi occasionem arripiunt. Non ergo est, quòd effrenem atq; impiam licentiam isti homines libertatis Christianæ nomine palliant. Secundò videndum est, ne dum libertate nostra abutimur, eorum mancipia efficiamur, in quæ nobis ius liberum esse testari volumus. Id vero fit, quando affectibus nostris non possumus imperare, quo minus absq; necessitate ea faciamus, quæ cum aliquo scandalo coniuncta sunt. Accidit hoc ijs, qui absq; iudicio quibuslibet vescuntur, neq; aliquam fratris infirmi rationem habent, qui libertatis Christianæ ius nondum intelligit. Hi enim se non ciborum dominos, sed potius gulæ & intemperantiæ mancipia esse produnt, dum se illorum illecebris seruiliter trahi patiuntur, vt in Leges charitatis fraternæ peccent.
units.tr: By these words, therefore, Paul teaches what the reasoning of Christian liberty is, and how the godly ought to use those things which are in themselves lawful and permitted. This teaching is exceedingly useful, indeed necessary for preserving the churches, because here great sin is committed, to the great scandal of the weak, while some defend their liberty more stubbornly and think that they must not yield their right even in the smallest matters. And yet liberty is one thing (as certain men have rightly observed), and the use of liberty is another; nor does he at once lose liberty who sometimes prudently and with sound reason sets it aside; rather, he proves himself master of all things who uses all things not according to the judgment of the flesh or of carnal affections, but as he sees fit for himself or for others. There are therefore two things here to be carefully observed. First, what is advantageous or useful, not so much for us as for the public salvation of others and the edification of the whole Church. For no one is born for himself alone, but we are all bound to all men by the law of charity. And if the philosophers of the nations rightly taught that parents claim one part of us, our country another, and friends another, how much more ought Christian men to know that they wholly belong to Christ, who has asserted them out of the tyranny of sin and death into the liberty of the sons of God, and in whom they have been born again and made sons of God? Now the law of this is that, privately, we should promote the salvation of individual men to the best of our powers, but publicly should strive for the edification of the Church, lest its peace or order be disturbed through us. Therefore, in matters that are indifferent or neutral, one must above all take account of edification, so that we may draw as many as possible into fellowship with the Church, strengthen the weak and wavering, and that the whole Church may make progress for the better day by day. Of this, indeed, more will follow later, when the Apostle discusses at length the eating of idol meats. But now let us remember that if these things ought to be observed in matters that are neutral and lawful in themselves, we ought to be much more cautious and circumspect in those things which are unlawful and contrary to the laws of the Christian religion. Therefore here those most serious men are refuted who today excuse drunkenness, wanton dances and revelries, or even the remnants of the Bacchanalia and Lupercalia, under the pretext of liberty. For all these things not only are not expedient, but are very harmful, since many are offended by them, the discipline of the Church is disturbed, and those who hate the Christian religion seize on them as an occasion for slander. There is therefore no reason why these men should cloak an unbridled and impious licence under the name of Christian liberty. Secondly, care must be taken that, while we abuse our liberty, we do not become the slaves of those things over which we wish to testify that we have free right. This happens when we cannot command our affections, so that we do not refrain from doing, without necessity, those things which are joined with some scandal. This happens to those who eat anything whatever without judgment, and take no account of the weak brother, who does not yet understand the right of Christian liberty. For these men show themselves to be not masters of foods, but rather slaves of gluttony and intemperance, while they allow themselves to be drawn servilely by their allurements, so that they sin against the laws of brotherly charity.

units.la: Multò magis autem hoc illis euenit, qui illicitis voluptatibus indulgent, & magna quidem cum insolentia se sui iuris esse gloriantur, interim vero affectibus turpissimis seruiunt, quos non immerito tyrannos omnium truculentissimos dixeris. Quæ enim libertas esse potest apud eos, quorum mens cupiditatibus seruit, quibus ipsa imperare debebat? Aut num liber dici debet homo, cuius pars potior atque præstantior in seruitutem redacta est? Idem de illis dicere possumus, qui vin-dictæ cupiditatem persequuntur. Putant illi se ius suum persequi, & de victoria magnificè gloriantur, vel certa huius spe decepti sibijpsis liberum in omnes alios imperium pollicentur, si iniurias inultas abire non sinant: Interim vero plus quàm miseri sunt, dum iræ mancipia fiunt, quæ rationis vsum illis adimit, & ipsorum cum animis tum corporibus dominatur. Semper ergo ista admonitio nobis in auribus sonet, cauendum esse, ne dum omnia nobis licere arbitramur, sub libertatis inani prætextu plus quam serui simus.
units.tr: Much more does this befall those who indulge in unlawful pleasures, and boast with great arrogance that they are their own masters, while meanwhile they serve the most shameful affections, which you might not unjustly call the most savage tyrants of all. For what liberty can there be among those whose mind serves desires, by which it ought itself to rule? Or can a man rightly be called free whose better and more excellent part has been reduced to servitude? The same we may say of those who pursue the desire for revenge. They think they are pursuing their own right and boast grandly of victory, or, deceived by a vain hope of it, they promise themselves free dominion over all others, if they do not allow injuries to go unavenged. Meanwhile they are more than wretched, while they become the slaves of anger, which takes from them the use of reason and rules over both their minds and their bodies. Let this admonition therefore always sound in our ears: that we must take care, while we think that all things are lawful for us, that under the empty pretext of liberty we do not become more than slaves.

units.la: Cæterum ne quis eius verba nimis late extenderet ad ea quoq;, quæ pro medijs & indifferentibus habere non possunt, declarationem subijcit, qua hoc omne ad cibos restringit, in quibus Corinthios varie peccauisse antea diximus. Escæ (inquit) ventri destinatæ sunt, & venter escæ: Deus autem & hunc & eas abolebit. Ventris nomine ipsam nutriendi vim naturalem intelligit, qua stomachus aut venter cibos excipit, exceptos concoquit & digerit, vt totum corpus ex illis alimentum habeat atque feruetur. Itaque verborum Pauli sensus est: Imprudenter & absurdè nimis facere eos, qui libertatem suam in promiscuo ciborum vsu temere ostentant. Nec enim hic (inquit) proprius ciborum vsus aut finis est, vt ijs quid nobis liceat testemur: sed ventri aut hominis alimento destinati sunt, vt quoad Deo placuerit, viuamus: & vicissim venter cibis seruire debet, vt suis organis hos excipiat atque digerat. Interim meminisse oportet, quòd neque hic neque illi perpetuò durabunt. Nam & cibos & ventrem Deus abolebit. Fit hoc etiam in hoc seculo, quando vitæ finis obrepit, & per mortem anima à corpore dissoluitur. Tunc enim aboletur vis illa vegetativa, quæ cibos attrahit atque membris omnibus dispensat, ideoq; ciborum vsus quoque, quoad nos, aboletur, cum nihil vtilitatis aut alimenti ex illis porrò recipere possimus. In futuro autem seculo membra quidem corporis omnia instaurabuntur, ne quid ad perfectam totius hominis felicitatem desit, eorundem verò vsus, qui nunc est, abolebitur. Quia vbi corruptio amplius locum non habet, ibi neque generatione opus est, & proinde ciborum quoque vsus cessabit. Ex istis verò omnibus colligit Apostolus, non debere æterna illa & cœlestia bona, quæ nobis per Euangelij prædicationem Deus in Filio suo offert, turbari propter res fluxas & breui peritu-ras: & maiorem habendam esse pacis atque concordiæ in ecclesia rationem, quando sine illa non possit salus nostra consistere, quæ omnibus huius sæculi bonis longè præferri debet.
units.tr: Furthermore, lest anyone extend his words too broadly, even to things that cannot be regarded as indifferent, he adds a clarification that restricts all of this to foods, in which we said earlier the Corinthians had sinned in various ways. "Food," he says, "is for the belly, and the belly for food: but God will destroy both this and that." By "belly" he means the natural power of nourishment itself, by which the stomach or belly receives food, digests it once received, so that the whole body has its nourishment and is kept alive from it. So the sense of Paul's words is this: those who rashly flaunt their liberty in the indiscriminate use of foods act foolishly and absurdly. For (he says) the proper use and purpose of food is not to show us what is permitted to us. Rather, food is appointed for the belly or for the nourishment of man, so that we may live as long as it pleases God; and in turn the belly ought to serve food, so that by its organs it receives and digests it. Meanwhile we must remember that neither will last forever: for God will destroy both food and belly. This happens even in this age, when the end of life creeps upon us and the soul is separated from the body by death. For then that vegetative power is destroyed, which draws in food and distributes it to all the members, and so the use of food too, as far as we are concerned, is destroyed, since we can no longer receive any benefit or nourishment from it. In the age to come, indeed, all the members of the body will be restored, so that nothing is lacking to the perfect happiness of the whole man; but the use of them that now exists will be abolished. For where corruption no longer has a place, there is no need of generation, and accordingly the use of food will also cease. From all these things the Apostle gathers that the eternal and heavenly goods which God offers us in his Son through the preaching of the Gospel should not be disturbed on account of fleeting things that will soon perish; and that greater regard should be had for peace and concord in the Church, since without them our salvation cannot stand, and it ought to be preferred far above all the goods of this age.

units.la: Admonemur igitur hoc loco, quis nobis ciborum, adeoq; externorum omnium vsus esse debeat. Is nimirum, vt necessitati seruiant ad vitam tuendam, quàm diu nos Deus in hoc sæculo superstites esse voluerit. Edendum ergo, vt viuamus: non autem viuendum, vt edamus. Et qui hunc ordinem inuertunt, ij ex hominibus in animalia bruta degenerant. Est hoc videre in ebrio-fis & gulæ deditis: qui cum Dei opera considerare, pro acceptis ab illo beneficijs gratias agere, & tâm propriam quàm aliorum salutem adiuuare debeant, canum & porcorum instar ingluuiem sectantur, & neque de Deo neque de suo officio cogitant, quo illi & alijs hominibus obstricti sunt. Neque his meliores sunt auari, qui dum neglectis regni cœlorum thesauris, circa huius sæculi opes modo occupantur, omnibus alijs molesti sunt, adhæc suum quoque genium defraudant, neque illis vti audent, sine quibus hanc vitam consistere non posse arbitrantur. Itaque Tantali instar in medijs vndis sitiunt, & in omni rerum abundantia plus quàm pauperes sunt. Quod autem mentis alienatæ certius argumentum, quàm per fas & nefas corradere vt viuas, ijsdem verò iam collectis ad vitam tuendam vti non audere? At non alia efficatior fuerit ratio ad corrigendos affectus hosce prauos & iniquos, quàm si externa omnia vnà cum eorum vsu breui abolenda esse cogitemus. Admonet de hoc alibi quoque Paulus, quando ad Timotheum scribit: Nihil intuli-mus in mundum, videlicet nec efferre quicquam possumus. Itaque habentes alimenta & quibus tegamur, contenti simus. Cùm verò in his natura paucis contenta sit, & commodius viuant qui mediocritati & temperantiæ student, nàm nimiùm stulti & infelices sunt, qui abundantiam verè noxiam & exitialem tantis laboribus affectant.
units.tr: We are therefore admonished here what the use of foods, and indeed of all external things, ought to be for us. Namely, that it should serve necessity, to sustain life, for as long as God wills us to remain alive in this age. We ought therefore to eat in order to live, not to live in order to eat. Those who reverse this order degenerate from men into brute beasts. This can be seen in drunkards and in those given over to gluttony: although they ought to consider the works of God, give thanks for the benefits received from him, and help both their own salvation and that of others, they pursue their bellies like dogs and pigs, and think neither of God nor of their duty, by which they are bound both to him and to other men. The avaricious are no better than these, who, while neglecting the treasures of the kingdom of heaven and busying themselves only with the riches of this age, are a burden to all others; moreover they defraud their own genius, and do not dare to use those things without which they think this life cannot continue. Thus, like Tantalus, they thirst in the midst of waters, and in all abundance of things they are more wretched than the poor. And what surer sign of a deranged mind is there than to heap up wealth by fair means or foul in order to live, and then, once it is gathered, not to dare to use it to sustain life? Yet there would be no more effective way of correcting these depraved and unjust affections than if we reflected that all external things, together with their use, are soon to be abolished. Paul admonishes us of this elsewhere too, when he writes to Timothy: "We brought nothing into the world, and certainly can carry nothing out. Therefore, having food and that by which we are clothed, let us be content." Since nature is content with few things in these matters, those who aim at moderation and temperance live more comfortably; for those who eagerly pursue an abundance that is truly harmful and deadly, with such great labours, are exceedingly foolish and unhappy.

units.la: Porrò transit hinc Apostolus ad scortationem, vt eos reprehendat, qui Christianæ libertatis ius ad hanc vsq; extendebant, adeò vt eandem vagarum libidinum rationem esse putarent, quæ ciborum esset. Fuit hæc fere Cynicorum sententia, qui inter actiones hominis naturales discrimen nullum constituebant, eò quòd ignorarent naturam depravatam legibus coerceri & in ordinem redigi oportere. At duobus argumentis istos confutat. Primum à fine & ordinario corporis vsu desumit, sic dicens: Corpus autem non scortationi, sed Domino: & Dominus corpori. Sensus est: Non eadem est libidinis aut scortationis ratio, quæ ciborum esse solet, neque vt hi ventri destinati sunt, & venter illis: ita corpus scortationi aut Veneri destinauit Deus: sed illud Domino Christo consecratum esse vult: & proinde nefas fuerit illud scortationi mancipare, vt contra pietatis & honestatis leges vagis libidinibus seruiat. Utq; argumenti huius efficacia aut vis maior fit, vicissim Dominum corpori nostro destinatu esse dicit. Quæ relatio ex eo deduci videtur, quòd nos per fidem Christi corpus facti sumus, hic verò caput nostrum est, ex quo vis omnis & spiritus vitæ in singula membra deriuatur: Denique vt passim scriptura docet, in eum finem nobis à Patre datus atque aptatus est, vt illo Mediatore huic conciliemur[?].
units.tr: From here the Apostle passes on to fornication, to rebuke those who extended the right of Christian liberty even to this, so that they thought the reckoning of wandering lusts was the same as that of foods. This was almost the opinion of the Cynics, who made no distinction among the natural actions of man, because they did not know that a depraved nature must be restrained by laws and brought into order. But Paul refutes them with two arguments. First he draws on the end and ordinary use of the body, saying: "The body is not for fornication, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body." The sense is this: the reckoning of lust or fornication is not the same as that which obtains for foods, nor is it the case that, as these are appointed for the belly and the belly for them, so God has appointed the body for fornication or for Venus. Rather he wills it to be consecrated to the Lord Christ; and therefore it would be wrong to hand it over to fornication, so that it serves wandering lusts against the laws of piety and decency. And so that the force and weight of this argument may be greater, he says in turn that the Lord is appointed for our body. This relation seems to be drawn from the fact that through faith in Christ we have become his body, and he is our head, from whom every power and spirit of life flows into the individual members. Finally, as Scripture teaches everywhere, we have been given and fitted by the Father for this end, that through that Mediator we may be reconciled to him.

units.la: Docent hæc Apostoli verba, quàm turpiter errent, qui scortationem peccatum esse negant, & eius licentiam eo argumento excusant vel defendunt, quòd homines naturali propensione & generandi cupiditate ad libidinem ferantur. Nec enim inde sequitur, quemuis viri cum muliere congressum secundùm naturæ leges fieri, & proinde omni culpa vacare. Et longè aliud ex præsenti argumento colligi potest. Nam vniuscuiusq; rei natura est id, ad quod eam Deus, qui naturæ omnis dominus est, destinauit. Sic ignis naturalis actio est, quòd calorem creaturis omnibus subministrat: aquæ verò, quòd ijsdem humorem necessarium sufficit. At hominem scriptura ad Dei cultum conditum, & corpus hominis Domino consecratum esse docet, ideoq; proprium & naturale hominis opus fuerit, vt Domino consecratus gloriam eius omni studio prouehat, & omnes tám corporis quàm animi facultates sub illius obedientiam redigat. Vnde sequitur non ex corporis natura, sed contra naturam esse, si à Domini seruitio abstractum scortandi licentiam sectetur. Quoad verò generandi desiderium, hoc hominibus, vt & reliquis animantibus à Deo insitum esse, & per se peccatum non esse fatemur (agnoscimus enim Dei vocem Crescite, & multiplicamini, & implete terram) at ne illud corruptæ naturæ affectibus nos transfuersos abriperet,certis legibus & coniugij sanctissimo vinculo idem Deus coerceri voluit. Huius ergo voluntati sese accommodent, qui castitatis aut virginitatis donum sibi negatum esse sentiunt. Neque hic impurissimorum hominum sermones moremur, quibus nimium & intolerabile videtur, omnes ad coniugij leges remittere, & scortationem prorsus damnare. Cur enim homini absurdum aut iniquum videatur, cuius sensum Deus in animalibus nonnullis, quae caeteris gene-rosiora sunt, extare voluit. Coniugalis certe fidei exempla in turturibus & ciconiis videmus, & admiratione singulari digna sunt, quae de elephantorum pudicitia scriptores veteres tradide-runt. Quapropter in naturam homines revera iniqui & brutis animalibus multo inferiores sunt, quotquot corpora sua absque pudore & vagas libidines proflituunt, & eadem Christo subducunt, cui consecrata esse debent.
units.tr: These words of the Apostles teach how shamefully those err who deny that fornication is a sin, and excuse or defend its licence on the ground that men are carried into lust by natural propensity and the desire to beget. For it does not follow from this that every union of man and woman takes place according to the laws of nature and is therefore free of all fault. Much else can be gathered from the present argument. For the nature of each thing is that for which God, who is lord of all nature, has appointed it. Thus the action of natural fire is to supply heat to all creatures, and that of water to supply the moisture necessary to them. But Scripture teaches that man was created for the worship of God, and that the body of man is consecrated to the Lord; therefore it is the proper and natural work of man, being consecrated to the Lord, to advance his glory with all zeal and to bring all faculties of body and soul under his obedience. Hence it follows that it is not according to the nature of the body, but contrary to nature, if, withdrawn from the Lord's service, one pursues the licence of fornication. As for the desire to beget, we confess that this, like the other living creatures, has been implanted in men by God, and that in itself it is not sin (for we acknowledge the voice of God, "Increase and multiply, and fill the earth"). But lest it carry us away, turned aside by the affections of corrupt nature, the same God wished it to be restrained by certain laws and by the most holy bond of marriage. Let therefore those who feel that the gift of chastity or virginity has been denied to them accommodate themselves to his will. Nor should we linger over the talk of the most impure men, to whom it seems excessive and intolerable to refer everything to the laws of marriage and to condemn fornication altogether. For why should it seem absurd or unjust to man what sense God wished to exist in some animals, which are more noble than the rest? Certainly we see examples of conjugal faithfulness in turtledoves and storks, and the things that ancient writers have handed down about the chastity of elephants are worthy of singular admiration. Therefore, all those who shamelessly prostitute their bodies to wandering lusts, and withdraw them from Christ, to whom they ought to be consecrated, are truly unjust to their nature and far inferior to the brute beasts.

units.la: Sed alterum quoque Pauli argumentum videamus, quod à Christi conditione petit, quam is nobiscum communem habere vult. Deus (inquit) & Dominum suscitauit, & nos suscitabit per potentiam suam. Latet sub his verbis duplex argumentum. Alterum ab exemplo Christi, quod sic formabis: Deus Filium suum excitauit ad vitam nouam & coelestem: ergo ipsum imitari, & similiter reliquis prioribus vitijs ad vitae nouitatem resurgere debent, qui illius membra aut fra-tres esse volunt. Alterum à spe beatae immortalitatis sumitur, quam ille nobis acquisiuit, quod est eiusmodi: Deus nos excitabit, vt cum Filio suo regni coelestis & aeternae beatitudinis cosortio fruamur: Ergo turpe fuerit nos impuris huius seculi studijs immergi, & scortatione pollui. Vbi rursus apparet, scortandi licentiam cum religionis Christianae legibus prorsus pugnare, & pro-inde Christianorum nomine indignos esse eos, qui huic feruiliter indulgent. At quod de illa dicitur, non minus ad omnia alia carnis & mundi studia transferri debet. Vult enim nobiscum com-munionem habere Deus, & ideo Filium suum hominem fieri voluit. Accommodemus ergo nos illius voluntati, & reliquis scelerib{us} atque vitiorum illecebris vitae sanctimoniam sectemur, vt olim coelestis gloriae capaces simus. At quia de his omnibus plura dicentur alibi, nunc consulto sumus breuiores.
units.tr: But let us also look at Paul's other argument, which he draws from Christ's condition, a condition he wants us to share with him. "God," he says, "raised up the Lord and will raise us up by his power." Two arguments lie hidden in these words. One is from Christ's example, which may be framed thus: God raised his Son to a new and heavenly life; therefore those who wish to be his members or brothers ought to imitate him and, like him, rise from their former sins to newness of life. The other is taken from the hope of blessed immortality which he has won for us, and runs like this: God will raise us up so that we may enjoy, with his Son, fellowship in the heavenly kingdom and eternal blessedness; therefore it would be shameful for us to be immersed in the impure pursuits of this age and defiled by fornication. Here again it appears that licence for fornication utterly conflicts with the laws of the Christian religion, and that those who slavishly indulge in it are therefore unworthy of the name of Christians. But what is said of that vice must be applied no less to all the other pursuits of the flesh and the world. For God wishes to have fellowship with us, and therefore he willed that his Son become man. Let us then accommodate ourselves to his will, and, setting aside the other sins and allurements of vice, pursue holiness of life, so that we may one day be capable of heavenly glory. But since more will be said about all these things elsewhere, we have deliberately been briefer now.

units.la: In praesenti tamen obseruabimus, quod de nostrorum corporum resuscitatione verba faciens, hanc Dei potentiae transscribit, qui & Christum excitarit, & nos quoque excitaturus sit. Quae verba non eo sensu accipi debent, quasi Christus non propria, sed alterius virtute suscitatus re-surrexerit. Scimus enim illum dixisse: Soluite aut destruite templum hoc, & in die tertio illud rursus extruam. Item: Potestatem habeo ponendi animam meam, & potestatem habeo rursus assumendi eam. Constat praeterea eum eiusdem cum Patre essentiae atque potestatis esse, & pro-inde opera quoque illis esse communia. Ideo scribis[?] & pharisaeis dicebat: Quæcunq; Pater facit, hæc etiam Filius pariter facit. Sicut Pater suscitat mortuos & viuificat, ita & Filius quos vult viuificat. Quæ cum Paulus minime ignoraret, nihil hic in Christi contemptum dicere voluit, sed hoc potius spectauit, vt obiter eos confutaret, qui mortuorum resurrectionem incredibilem & im-possibilem esse arbitrantur, eò quod eius rationem penes se & in hominum viribus non posse int-uenire. Ergo ad Dei potentiam eos remittit, Christum imitatus, qui in eiusdem argumenti tra-ctatione[?] Sadducaeis dixit: Erratis, ignorantes scripturas & potentiam Dei. Quod ipsum hodie etiam multis dici poterat, qui circa resurrectionem mortuorum quaestiones partim impias, partim ab-surdas & ridiculas mouent, quarum omnium non alius finis ipsis propositus est, quam vt illam in dubium vocando, sibijpsis delitias faciant, & conscientiae terrores sopiant, quibus se inuitos pungi & exagitari sentiunt. Sed & pijs interdum cogitationes eiusmodi obrepunt, quae illos aliquantum dubios & incertos reddunt. Tunc ergo cum promissis Dei & scripturarum oraculis omnipotentiam illius conferamus, & mox videbimus nos nullam habere iustam causam dubi-tandi de ijs, quae ille nobis pollicetur. Et poterit consideratio ista vehementer confirmari, si vete-ra Dei opera, & quae indies ille facit, non ofcitanter inspiciamus. Etenim si ab ipsa mundi origine initium fiat, facile patebit, Deum tunc fecisse, quod mortuorum resuscitationem longe superat. Nam ex nihilo vniuersam istam mundi totius machinam folijs Verbi sui virtute produxit. Quanto igitur facilius ei fuerit, eos qui aliquando fuerunt, & naturali dissolutione in primam materiam reuersi sunt, rursus euocare & sua illis corpora restituere? Et cur in Deo nobis nouum aut insolens videatur cuius exempla quotidie apud opifices cernimus? Possunt metallici vasorum fractorum materiam refundere, & vasa noua ex illis facere: idem in re fragilissima possunt vitri-arij, ut iam de figulis nihil dicamus, qui vnam & eandem luti massam currente rota, quoties libet, refingere possunt: & nos Deum in ea materia idem facere posse dubitabimus, ex qua primum homo factus est, & in quam omnes homines reuertuntur? Quod si sementem inspicias, eiusdem rei exemplum euidentissimum habebis, cuius ipse Christus meminit, ut & se aduersus mortis imminentis terrores consolaretur, & nos in se futurae resurrectionis confirmaret. Et ut haec fiat, Dei iustitia exigit, quae alioqui (ut alibi monuimus) consistere non potest: eo quod in hoc seculo neq; pij debita sua virtuti praemia recipiunt, neq; impij semper dignas scelerum suorum poenas exoluunt. Idem hominis quoq; dignitas requirit, qui nisi resurgat ad meliorem vitam, longe infra omnes creaturas subsidet, a quibus longaeuitate & viribus fere superatur. Nam ut terra cum reliquis elementis diu durat: ita inter feras & volucres atq; pisces inveniuntur, quae homine vivaciora sunt. Et cum animalia fere omnia sibi ipsis sufficiant, neq; aliorum ope multum indigeant, solus homo multorum servitio & auxilio opus habet, & vitam vivit brevem quidem, sed assiduis laborum atq; morborum molestijs refertam. Alterius ergo vitae spes ipsi proposita fit oportet, nisi eum inter omnia, quae in rerum natura sunt, miserrimum & calamitosissimum dicere libeat. Ridẽt quidem ista impij, & ut si-bi ipsis inter scelera delitias faciant, resurrectionem in dubium vocare & omnem eius mentionem eludere satagunt. Sed longe alia est piorum sententia: qui ut ex illa in omni aduersorum genere con-solationem petunt: ita eiusdem meditatione seipsos in officio continent, ne quid sua professione & expectatione indignum faciant, & ut olim in magno illo die salua atq; pura conscientia comparere possint, & promissa regni coelestis hereditate frui cum Domino & redemptore nostro IESV CHRISTO: cui debetur benedictio,honor,gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Yet in the present passage we shall observe that, in speaking of the resurrection of our bodies, he ascribes it to this power of God, who both raised up Christ and will also raise us. These words ought not to be taken in the sense that Christ rose not by his own power but by another's. For we know he said: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again." Likewise: "I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again." Moreover, it is agreed that he has the same essence and power as the Father, and therefore their works are also common to them. Hence he said to the scribes and Pharisees: "Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does. As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son gives life to whom he wills." Since Paul was by no means ignorant of these things, he did not wish to say anything here to Christ's disparagement, but rather aimed at this: to refute in passing those who think the resurrection of the dead incredible and impossible, because they cannot grasp its manner by their own reasoning or within human powers. So he refers them to the power of God, imitating Christ, who in treating this same argument said to the Sadducees: "You are wrong, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God." This could be said today to many who raise questions about the resurrection of the dead, some impious, some absurd and ridiculous, all of which have no other end in view than, by calling it into doubt, to make sport for themselves and to lull the terrors of conscience, by which they feel themselves unwillingly pricked and troubled. But doubts of this kind sometimes creep also into the minds of the godly, making them somewhat wavering and uncertain. Therefore let us set his omnipotence against God's promises and the oracles of Scripture, and soon we shall see that we have no just cause to doubt what he promises us. This consideration may be greatly strengthened if we do not look idly at God's ancient works and those he performs daily. For if we begin from the very origin of the world, it will be plain that God then did what far surpasses the raising of the dead. For out of nothing he brought forth this whole vast machine of the world by the power of his Word. How much easier, then, would it be for him to call back those who once existed and, through natural dissolution, have returned to primal matter, and to restore their bodies to them? And why should anything seem new or unusual in God, when we see examples of it every day among craftsmen? Metalworkers can melt down the material of broken vessels and make new vessels from it; glassmakers can do the same with a most fragile material; not to mention potters, who can remake, whenever they like, one and the same mass of clay on the turning wheel. And shall we doubt that God can do the same with that material from which man was first made and into which all men return? And if you look at seed, you will have the most evident example of this very thing, which Christ himself mentioned, both to console himself against the terrors of impending death and to confirm us in the hope of future resurrection. For this to happen, the justice of God demands it, which otherwise (as we have noted elsewhere) cannot stand: in this age the godly do not receive the rewards their virtue deserves, nor do the wicked always pay the fitting penalties for their crimes. The dignity of man also requires it: unless he rises to a better life, he sinks far below all creatures, by most of which he is surpassed in length of life and strength. For as the earth endures long with the other elements, so among the beasts, birds and fishes are found that live longer than man.
