And while nearly all animals suffice for themselves and need little help from others, man alone needs the service and aid of many, and lives a life brief indeed, but filled with the constant troubles of labours and diseases. Therefore the hope of another life must be set before him, unless one would prefer to call him the most wretched and miserable of all things in nature. Indeed the impious laugh at such things, and, that they may make sport for themselves amid their crimes, they strive to call the resurrection into doubt and to mock every mention of it. But the mind of the godly is far different: they seek consolation from it in every kind of adversity, and by meditating on it they keep themselves in their duty, lest they do anything unworthy of their profession and expectation, so that they may one day appear before that great day with a safe and pure conscience, and enjoy the promised inheritance of the heavenly kingdom with our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXI.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXI.

units.la: An ignoratis corpora vestra esse membra Christi? Num igitur tol-lens membra Christi, faciam ut sint scorti membra? Absit. An igno-ratis, eum qui agglutinatur scorto, vnum esse corpus [cum scorto]? Fient enim (inquit) qui duo erant, caro vna. Qui vero agglutinatur Domino, vnus spiritus est. Fugite fornicationem. Omne peccatum, quod fecerit homo, extra corpus est: sed qui fornicatur, in proprium corpus peccat. An ignoratis corpus vestrum esse templum Spiri-tus sancti, qui est in vobis, quem habetis a Deo? Et non estis vestri? Nam empti estis pretio. Glorificate igitur Deum in corpore vestro, & in Spiritu vestro, quae sunt Dei.
units.tr: Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a harlot? Certainly not. Do you not know that whoever is joined to a harlot is one body with her? For, it says, "the two shall become one flesh." But whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit with him. Flee fornication. Every sin a man commits is outside the body, but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body. Do you not know that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? And you are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which belong to God.

units.la: QVemadmodum aegrotus, qui morbi sui vim ignorat, multa & diligenti illius descriptione opus habet, ut medicina facilius admittat, & eandem patienter ferat: ita homines, qui peccatum quidem gravissimis obnoxij sunt, in ijsdem vero sibi ipsis mirifice blandiuntur, saepe & graviter admoneri necesse est, ut agnita delictorum suorum atrocitate, poenitentiae doctrinam studiosius audiant, & serio salutis aeternae studio accendantur. Observarunt hoc olim prophetae, & ideo in celeribus[?] argumentis atq; accusandis admodum diligentes fuerunt: quos ut ubiq; alias imitati sunt Apostoli, sic Paulus idipsum singulari quadam gravitate facit in tractatione ista, quam adversus fornicationem instituit. Quia enim apud Corinthios (ut nuper diximus) fornicandi licentia quasi dominabatur, & vix quisquam erat, qui illa in Deum peccari putaret, non contentus fornicatores inter eos numerasse, qui a regni coelorum hereditate excluduntur, ipsum scelus graphice depingit, & pluribus argumentis docet, quam illud foedum, grave & Christianis hominibus indignum sit. Et quamvis nuper quaedam dixerit, quae sufficere possunt iis, qui rem serio considerant, plura tamen subijcit, quae stupidissimos quoq; movere possunt, si vel obiter de istis cogitare velint. Ubi meminisse oportet, hac non minus nobis hodie servire, quando inter omnis loci & ordinis homines passim multi inueniuntur, qui non minori licentia, quàm olim Corinthij peccant. Et quid faciat vulgus homi-num, quando qui ecclesijs & sacris praefecti sunt, damnato prorsus coniugij usu, per omne libidi-nis genus impune volutantur? Videamus ergo, quibus argumentis Paulus scortandi licentiam dissuadeat.
units.tr: Just as a sick man who does not know the power of his disease needs a long and careful description of it, so that he may more readily accept the medicine and bear it patiently, so people who are indeed subject to the gravest sin, yet flatter themselves wonderfully in it, must often and sharply be admonished. Once they recognise the atrocity of their offences, they will listen more eagerly to the teaching of repentance and be kindled with a serious zeal for eternal salvation. The prophets observed this in their time, and so they were very diligent in arguing and accusing. The Apostles imitated them in this everywhere, and Paul does the same with singular seriousness in this treatment, which he undertakes against fornication. For since among the Corinthians (as we said recently) the licence of fornication held almost sway, and there was scarcely anyone who thought that sin was committed against God, he not only counted the fornicators among those excluded from inheritance of the kingdom of heaven, but also paints the crime itself vividly and, by many arguments, teaches how foul, grave, and unworthy of Christian people it is. And although he has said some things recently which can suffice for those who consider the matter seriously, he nevertheless adds more, which can move even the most stupid, if they are willing to think about these things even in passing. We must remember that these things serve us no less today, since among people of every place and rank many are found everywhere who sin with no less licence than the Corinthians once did. And what will the common people do, when those set over the churches and the sacred offices, having utterly condemned the use of marriage, wallow unpunished in every kind of lust? Let us see, then, by what arguments Paul dissuades the licence of fornicating.

units.la: Propositio aut status loci totius est: Fugite scortationem. Hoc autem nomine omnem illicitum viri cum muliere congressum intelligit, & illam coniugio opponit, quod coercendis libidinibus vagis à Deo institutum esse, proximo Cap.dicetur. In praesenti vero illam non solum cauere aut vitare, sed fugere iubet, ut ostendat studio & industria, vel etiam solicitudine non vulgari hic opus esse. Nā illecebris suis mirifice nos allicit malū hoc, & fugientes quoq; insequitur. Docuerunt hoc gentium poetae Sirenum fabulam, quas cantu suavissimo navigantes sopiusse fingunt, ut dormientes demergerent atq; vorarent. Ita enim meretricum mores adumbrarunt, quarum illecebras quotquot audiunt & admittunt, ij fortunarum omnium naufragio facto ad egestatem extremam re-digunter[?]. Consentit his Solomon, quando dicit: Fauus distillans labia meretricis, & nitidius oleo guttur eius, nouissima autem eius amara ut absinthium. Sunt autem eò efficaciores scortationis illecebrae, quod plerique hominum natura ad libidinem proclives sunt: quo fit, ut leuissima occasione ij quoq; capiantur, qui sapientia & virtute omnibus aliis praestant, ut in Dauidis, Solomonis & multorum aliorum inter gentes clarissimorum virorum exemplis est videre. Facilior tamen & tutior erit tanti mali fuga, si occasiones & irritamenta vitemus diligenter. Coerceri ergo debet oculorum lasciuia, ne spectandis mulierum alienarum formis intenti libidinis flammas concipiamus, aut conceptas foueamus. Notum est enim illud poetae: Ut vidi, ut perij, ut me malus abstulit error. Primi etiam mundi homines hoc in errorem abduxit, quod qui filij Dei esse debebant, filias hominum curiosius quam par erat spectarunt, & illis commixti sunt. Et hanc Dauidi cau-sam adulterij fuisse scimus, quod Bethsabeam, incautius lauantem, curiosius ipse spectauit: & ideo postea graviter monuit: Auerte oculos tuos, ne videant vanitatem. Quod prisci & orthodoxi episcopi observarunt, & ideo tanta gravitate homines Christianos à spectaculis debortati sunt, in quibus multa petulanter & impudice ad libidinem provocandam fiebant. Deinde non minor aurium cura habeatur, ne has vel cantionibus ad libidinem compositis, vel sermonibus impudicis atq; obscenis pascamus. Solent enim profundius, quàm quis putet in animos penetrare, quaecunque cum aliqua audiendi voluptate percipiuntur, & causa sunt, ut pessimis cogitationibus intenti, tandem in apertam licentiam erumpamus. Quod sapientissimus ille philosophorum Plato vidit, & ideo Poetas ex Repub. eijciendos esse censuit, quod multa ab illis dici cerneret, quae ut libidinis ignem in legentium animis accendunt, ita religionem & Deorum metum omnem paulatim restinguunt. Accedat his honestatis studium in vestitu & toto corporis habitu, vitetur autem mollities & intemperantia in victu, qua Venerem vehementer accendi notius est, quàm ut multis demonstrari oporteat. Imprimis autem otium fugiamus, quo nihil turpius, nihil nocentius homini accidere potest. Est enim illud reuera Satanae pulvinar, cui quicunque insidet, ij undique sibi occasiones ad omnem nequitiam offerri sentiunt. Nam cùm hominis mens quiescere non possit, & continuo atq; indefesso motu circa cogitationes variàs discurrat, nisi honesto aliquo negotio occupetur, ad inhonesta & turpia sponte delabitur. Quod famosissimus ille rei amatoriae magister probe observauit, quando inter amoris illiciti remedia, hoc praecipuum indicat:
units.tr: The proposition, or the state of the whole matter, is: "Flee fornication." By this word he understands every unlawful congress of a man with a woman, and he sets it against marriage, which, as will be said in the next chapter, was instituted by God to restrain wandering lusts. Here, however, he bids us not only to guard against and avoid it but to flee it, to show that here there is need of zeal and industry, and even of no ordinary anxiety. For this evil wonderfully entices us with its allurements, and it pursues those who flee it too. The poets of the nations taught this in the fable of the Sirens, whom they pretended lulled sailors with the sweetest song, so that they might drown and devour them as they slept. For in this way they portrayed the ways of harlots, whose allurements, all who hear and admit them are brought by shipwreck of all their fortunes to utmost poverty. Solomon agrees with this when he says: "The lips of a harlot drip honey, and her throat is smoother than oil; but her end is bitter as wormwood." Moreover, the allurements of fornication are all the more effective because most people are naturally inclined to lust, and so, by the slightest occasion, even those are caught who surpass all others in wisdom and virtue, as may be seen in the examples of David, Solomon, and many other most famous men among the nations. Yet the flight from so great an evil will be easier and safer if we diligently avoid the occasions and incitements. Therefore the wantonness of the eyes must be restrained, lest, intent on gazing at the forms of other men's wives, we conceive the flames of lust, or, having conceived them, nurse them. For that saying of the poet is well known: "As soon as I saw, as soon as I perished, as soon as a wicked error carried me off." This same error first led the men of the early world astray, who, being meant to be sons of God, looked upon the daughters of men more curiously than was fitting, and mingled with them. We know that this was the cause of David's adultery, since he himself looked more curiously upon Bathsheba as she bathed carelessly; and therefore he later warned sharply: "Turn away your eyes, lest they see vanity." The early and orthodox bishops observed this, and therefore with such gravity they drew Christian people away from the spectacles, in which many things were done wantonly and shamelessly to provoke lust. Next, no less care should be taken with the ears, lest we feed them either with songs composed for lust or with impure and obscene talk. For whatever is received with some pleasure of hearing tends to penetrate the minds more deeply than anyone supposes, and causes us, intent on the worst thoughts, at last to break out into open licence. The most wise of philosophers, Plato, saw this, and therefore judged that the poets should be cast out of the Republic, because he perceived that many things were said by them which, as they kindle the fire of lust in the minds of readers, so they gradually extinguish all religion and all fear of the gods. To these things let there be added a zeal for decency in dress and in the whole bearing of the body; and softness and intemperance in diet should be avoided, by which Venus is known to be kindled vehemently, more than it needs to be shown to many. Above all, let us flee idleness, than which nothing is more shameful, nothing more harmful, can befall a man. For it is truly Satan's pillow, and whoever reclines upon it feels that opportunities for every wickedness are offered to him on every side. For since the human mind cannot be at rest, but runs about among various thoughts with continuous and tireless motion, unless it is occupied with some honourable business, it will of its own accord slip into dishonourable and shameful things. The most famous master of the art of love observed this well, when among the remedies for illicit love he points out this chief one:

units.la: Otia si tollas, periere Cupidinis arcus, Contemptaeque iacent, & sine luce faces. Quaeritur, Ægistus quare fit factus adulter? In promptu causa est, desidiosus erat.
units.tr: If you take away idleness, the bows of Cupid perish, and the torches lie scorned and without light. You ask, why did Aegisthus become an adulterer? The cause is at hand: he was idle.

units.la: Quod autem de Ægisto ille dicit, hoc de multis aliis dici poterat. Nam ut ad Dauidem redeamus, hic quoque otii abundantia adulter factus est, cum suis ad Rabbam bellum gerentibus, ipse otiosus per palatium regium ambularet, & ex alto domus alienas curiosius inspiceret. Et hodie videmus otiosos homines fere scortationis laqueis intricari. Sed tempus est, ut ad Apostoli argumenta accedamus, quibus scortatores ille oppugnat, & huius peccati atrocitatem diligenter depingit.
units.tr: What the poet says of Aegisthus could be said of many others. For, to return to David, he too became an adulterer through an abundance of leisure, when his men were waging war at Rabbah, and he himself, idle, walked about the royal palace and looked more curiously from on high into other men's houses. And today we see idle people mostly entangled in the snares of fornication. But it is time to come to the Apostle's arguments, by which he assails the fornicators and diligently portrays the atrocity of this sin.

units.la: Primò in Christum peccari, & huic non leuem iniuriam fieri docet, & hîc exponit, quod nuper breuius dixerat, Corpus Domino esse destinatum, non scortationi. Argumenti summa est: In CHRISTVM IESVM peccant, quicunq; eius membra ab ipsius seruitio abstracta ad vsus ab eius instituto alienos transferunt. At qui scortantur, ij seipsos ex membris Christi membra scorti faciunt: Ergo ijdem in Christum peccant. Istud verò magna cum grauitate enuntiat, vt maius ar-gumenti pondus sit. Primò enim interrogatione vtitur, An ignoratis corpora vestra esse membra Christi? Et sic dicendo innuit, nulla venia dignos, & ad miraculum vsq; stupidos esse, si id ignoret, quod nemo Christianorum non nouit & intelligit. Deinde ne ipsis petulantius insultare putetur, rei absurditatem sub propria persona proponit, & rursus interrogando animos illorum compellat: Num igitur tollens membra Christi, faciam vt sint scorti membra? Vult autem, vt in ipso agno-scant sceleris atrocitatem, quam in seipsis agnoscere nolebant: & medicos peritos imitatur, qui fe-ipsos exempli loco sistunt aegrotis, quos ad sumenda pharmaca obstinatiores esse vident. Et hic quidem singula verba emphasim habet. Num tollens (inquit) membra Christi? &c. Quasi diceret: Num ego, qui Christi seruus sum, qui meipsum & mea omnia illi debeo, ipsi quod suum est eripiam, & faciam vt scorti membra sint, quae illius vsibus debebant seruire? At quid aliud vos facitis, quos ille proprio sanguine redemptos sibi consecrauit? Ita ergo inter se opponit Christum & scortum, vt ostendat, fieri non posse, vt quis scorti membrum fiat, nisi prius à Christo totus abstrahatur? Quae enim inter Christum & scortum communio? Ille equidem totus sanctus & omnis nequitiae aut labis expers: hoc autem libidinis, impudicitiae & impuritatis omnis sentina, adeoq; diaboli cloaca est. Quando igitur Christus vt cum scortis communionem habeat, adduci non potest, ab illo turpem secessionem faciant oportet, quicunq; scortandi licentiam sessari[?] instituerunt.
units.tr: First, he teaches that sin is committed against Christ and that no slight injury is done to him, and here he explains what he had said more briefly earlier, that the body is destined for the Lord, not for fornication. The sum of the argument is this: those who sin against CHRIST JESUS are those who transfer his members, withdrawn from his service, to uses alien to his institution. But those who fornicate make themselves members of a harlot out of the members of Christ. Therefore they sin against Christ. He states this with great seriousness, so that the weight of the argument may be greater. For first he uses a question: "Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?" And by saying this he implies that they are unworthy of any pardon and stupid to the point of wonder if they do not know what no Christian fails to know and understand. Then, lest he be thought to insult them too insolently, he sets out the absurdity of the matter in his own person, and again by questioning he addresses their minds: "Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a harlot?" He wants them to recognise in him the atrocity of the crime, which they were unwilling to recognise in themselves; and he imitates skilled physicians, who present themselves as an example to the sick whom they see more obstinate about taking medicines. And here indeed each single word carries emphasis. "Shall I then (he says) take the members of Christ?" etc. As if he were saying: "Shall I, who am the servant of Christ, who owe myself and all that is mine to him, snatch from him what is his, and make the members, which ought to serve his uses, into members of a harlot? But what else do you do, you whom he has redeemed with his own blood and consecrated to himself?" Thus he sets Christ and the harlot against each other in such a way as to show that no one can become a member of a harlot unless he is first wholly withdrawn from Christ. For what fellowship is there between Christ and a harlot? He is indeed wholly holy and free of all wickedness or stain; but she is the sink of all lust, impurity and uncleanness, and indeed the cesspool of the devil. Therefore, since Christ cannot be brought to have fellowship with harlots, those who have set out to pursue the licence of fornication must make a shameful departure from him.

units.la: Confirmat autem argumentum, & scripturae veteris testimonio probat scortatores scorti mem-bra fieri, & hic quoq; interrogando illis instat, dicens: An ignoratis, eum qui agglutinatur scorto, vnum esse corpus cum scorto? Fient enim (inquit) qui duo erant, caro vna, &c. Sunt haec Adami verba, qui cum Euam ex lateris sui costa formatam primum vidisset, non sine Spiritus sancti suggestione exclamauit: Hoc nunc os ex ossibus meis, & caro ex carne mea: ideo q; vocabitur Virago, eò quod de viro sumpta sit haec. Propterea deseret vir patrem & matrem suam, & adhaerebit vxori suae, ERUNTQUE IN CARNEM UNAM. Videtur autem Paulus loco isto abuti & in sensum alienum detorquere, cum illic de legitima viri & mulieris coniunctione sermo fit, qua olim pars viri fuit, nunc ei per matrimonium rursus copulatur, vt in vnum quasi corpus cum illo coalescat. In praesenti autem de scortatione agitur, qua nõ aliud coniugio magis aduersum aut inimicum est. Sed non obstat hoc, quia quoad carnis commixtionem, nulla inter coniugium & scortationem differentia est, nisi quod illa coniugibus ex Dei instituto licita, & proinde (vt Paulus alibi ait) impolluta, scortatoribus autem illicita, & proinde foeda atq; impura est. Qui enim secundum Dei institutum cum propria vxore in vnam carnem coalescere debebat, is ex diaboli & immo derata libidinis instinctu cum aliena (vt Solomon ait) miscetur atq; vnitur. Ita vero bifariam peccant scortatores. Primò enim coniugij leges violant, & a Deo nobis concessum beneficium foedissime conculcant. Deinde quod hic maxime urget Apostolus, Christo iniuriam faciunt, cui seipsos subducunt. Vt autem magis perspicua fit huius sceleris atrocitas, graui antithesi vtitur. Qui agglutinatur scorto, is vnum cum scorto corpus est: Qui autem agglutinatur Domino, vnus spiritus est: nimirum, quia per spiritus Dei virtutem ex Verbi femine renatus, totus spiritualis fit, neq; porro carnis desideriis imperium in suis membris permittit. Quo Christus quoq; respexit, quando de hominis regeneratione disputans dicebat: Quod genitum est ex carne, caro est: & quod genitum est ex Spiritu, spiritus est. Vbi spiritum vocat hominem vere Christianum, non quod in aliam substantiam transeat, sed quod totus a spiritu regatur, & (vt Paulus loquitur) vnus quodammodo cum Christo spiritus fiat, dum carnem cum suis desideriis crucifigit, & cogit sub spiritus obsequium. Latet ergo sub his verbis argumentum efficacissimum, quo omnes rationes confutantur, quibus homines impuri scortationem excusant aut defendunt. Si enim nefas est coniuges di-vellere, qui ex Dei instituto in vnam carnem coaluerunt, quanto grauius scelus fuerit eius coniunctionis vinculum abrumpere, quae nobis cum Christo intercedit, & qua fit, vt vnus cum illo spiritus simus? Ex quo simul evidentissimè colligitur: per scortationem non in humanas solum leges, verumetiam in religionem peccari, imò ita dissolui vinculum obligationis illius saluberrimæ, quæ nobis Deum obstringit.
units.tr: He confirms the argument and, by the testimony of the Old Testament, proves that fornicators become the members of a harlot. Here too he presses them with a question, saying: Do you not know that he who is joined to a harlot is one body with her? For, he says, the two shall become one flesh, etc. These are Adam's words. When he first saw Eve formed from a rib of his side, he exclaimed, not without the prompting of the Holy Spirit: This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; therefore she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man. Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, AND THEY SHALL BE ONE FLESH. But Paul seems to abuse that passage and twist it to a foreign sense, since there it is speaking of the lawful union of man and woman, by which she was once part of the man and is now joined back to him through marriage, so that she grows together with him into one body, as it were. Here, however, the subject is fornication, to which nothing is more opposed or hostile than marriage. But this is no obstacle, because as regards the mingling of flesh there is no difference between marriage and fornication, except that the one is lawful for spouses by God's institution, and therefore (as Paul says elsewhere) undefiled, while the other is unlawful for fornicators, and therefore foul and impure. For one who ought, according to God's institution, to grow into one flesh with his own wife is, by the impulse of the devil and unbridled lust, mixed and united with another's (as Solomon says). Thus fornicators sin in two ways. First, they violate the laws of marriage and most foully trample on the benefit granted us by God. Second, and this the Apostle especially presses, they do injury to Christ, from whom they withdraw themselves. That the atrocity of this crime may be more evident, he uses a strong antithesis: He who is joined to a harlot is one body with her; but he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit. Namely, because a man reborn through the power of God's Spirit from the seed of the Word becomes wholly spiritual, and no longer allows the desires of the flesh dominion over his members. Christ also had this in view when, discussing the regeneration of man, he said: What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit. Where he calls the truly Christian man "spirit," he does not mean that he passes into another substance, but that he is wholly ruled by the Spirit and, as Paul puts it, becomes in a manner one spirit with Christ, while he crucifies the flesh with its desires and brings it under the obedience of the Spirit. So under these words lies a most effective argument by which all the reasons are refuted with which impure men excuse or defend fornication. For if it is wrong to tear apart spouses who by God's institution have grown into one flesh, how much graver a crime would it be to break the bond of that union which exists between us and Christ, and by which we are made one spirit with him? From this it is also most clearly gathered that by fornication we sin not only against human laws but even against religion; indeed, the bond of that most wholesome obligation by which God binds us to himself is thereby dissolved.

units.la: In his autem diligenter simul observari debet, quam arcta sit, quæ nobis cum Christo intercedit communio, & quòd hæc licet spiritualis sit, tamen ad corpus quoque extendatur. Ille enim caro fieri dignatus est, & ex Virginis substantia verum Abrahami semen, id est, carnem nostram per omnia (uno peccato excepto) similem assumpsit: Vicissim vero suum spiritum nobis largitur, qui nos sibi vendicat, ut ex carnalibus spirituales reddamur, & non iam ipsi vivamus, sed in nobis vivat Christus, ut de semetipso Paulus ad Galatas loquitur. Et ideo idem ille nos corporis Christi membra ex eius carne & ossibus esse testatur. Quia vero communionis huius vinculum est spiritus, perperam nonnulli hoc Cœnæ Dominicæ tribuunt, quæ illius symbolum potius & sigillum est, quo fidem nostram Christus confirmat, ne dubitemus, nos per ipsum ad vitam æternam pasci. Plurimum autem facit ista consideratio ad totius vitæ institutionem, ut coniunctionis illius memores, non scortationem modo, sed omnia quoque alia vitia serio fugiamus, quæ nos à Christo divellunt. Adhæc consolationem dulcissimam continet, qua in omni tentatione confirmemur. Docet enim beneficium Christi ad totum hominem pertinere, & proinde fieri non posse, ut eorum velamas[?] vel corpora deferat Deus, quos vinculo tam arcto & necessario sibi coniunctos esse voluit. Sed hæc obiter annotasse sufficiat.
units.tr: In these words, moreover, we must carefully notice how close is the communion which exists between us and Christ, and that, although it is spiritual, it nevertheless extends also to the body. For he deigned to become flesh and, from the substance of the Virgin, the true seed of Abraham, that is, he took on our flesh, like ours in all things except sin. In turn he bestows on us his Spirit, who claims us for himself, so that from fleshly we become spiritual, and we no longer live ourselves, but Christ lives in us, as Paul says of himself to the Galatians. And therefore the same Paul testifies that we are members of Christ's body, of his flesh and bones. But because the bond of this communion is the Spirit, some wrongly ascribe it to the Lord's Supper, which is rather its symbol and seal, by which Christ confirms our faith, lest we doubt that we are fed by him unto eternal life. This consideration contributes greatly to the whole ordering of life: remembering that communion, we should earnestly flee not only fornication but all other vices which tear us away from Christ. Moreover, it contains a most sweet consolation by which we are strengthened in every temptation. For it teaches that the benefit of Christ pertains to the whole man, and therefore it cannot be that God should abandon, either in soul or in body, those whom he willed to be joined to himself by a bond so close and necessary. But it is enough to have noted these things in passing.

units.la: Videamus nunc alterum argumentum, quo scortationis crimen amplificatur. Constat id comparatione, quæ eos etiam excitare vult, qui religionis cura minus tanguntur. Sic enim ait: Omne peccatum, quodcunque fecerit homo, extra corpus est: Sed qui scortatur, in proprium corpus peccat. Sic autem videtur dicere: Si non cura vobis est, quòd Christo membra sua eripitis, agedum moveat vos proprium dedecus, & quæ ad vestrum corpus redundat ignominia. Nam etsi omnia peccata suam turpitudinem sibi coniunctam habeant, & simul noxia atque pernitiosa sint, alia tamen extra corpus sunt, id est, actio eorum circa res à corpore nostro alienas fere versatur, & ad alios extenditur. At qui scortatur, is in proprium corpus peccat, dum videlicet hoc polluit, & sua sanctimonia aut dignitate spoliat, ideoque sibi ipsi damnum infert irreparabile. Id vero recte dici patebis, si aliorum peccatorum conditionem examines. Avaritia quidem intra hominis animum est, effectus autem suos in opes extendit se, & circa has potissimum delinquit. Sic ira & vindicta cupiditas alijs nocere studet. Ebrietas & intemperantia donorum Dei abusu maximè peccat. Eadem fere aliorum omnium est ratio: & quamvis ex illis ad nostra etiam corpora aliquid detrimenti redeat, multò magis tamen hoc in scortatione fit, cuius quasi proprium est, quòd nota indelebili corpus, imò totum hominem polluit, dum quasi è suo gradu deiectum ea dignitate spoliat, qua nos Christus exornavit. Etenim si in generis sui nobilitatem peccat, & suam dignitatem quasi prostituit, qui uxorem sibi coniungit minus honestam: quanto turpior eorum culpa est, qui cum scorto prostituti pudoris in unam carne coale-scunt? Et qua ratione obsecro in proprii corpus peccare negabuntur, qui hoc scortis obscenissimis in servitutem mancipant, & quidem in eiusmodi servitutem, quæ omne simul rationis usum adimit, & quæ causa est, ut homo tam salutis quam dignitatis suæ obliviscatur? Sic certè David cum suo corpore regiam quoque maiestatem polluit, quando contra coniugii leges cum Uriæ uxore commixtus fuit. Et quantam sibi Solomon ignominiæ notam inflixerit, nemo ignorat, quando Legis divinæ immemor cum mulieribus alienigenis consortia habuit. Rursus igitur confutantur hoc loco, qui scortationem defendunt, quòd actio quædam sit naturalis. Hoc enim ipsi ex suo cerebro fingunt, longè aliud dicturi, si rem propius inspicerent. Nam non secundum naturam agere, sed à mente simul & communi sensu alieni esse dicuntur, qui sibi ipsis manum inferunt, & inusitata rabie in proprium corpus grassantur. Quid vero aliud facit, qui hoc scortis impurus & quavis lupa voracioribus ad sedam libidinem prostituit? Eò certè nocentior & detestabilior est illa insania, quòd dum se perdit, simul muliere quoque, aliena abutitur, & qui se mutuò ardentissimè amare videntur, in mutuum exitium sese impudenti libidine abducunt. Est ergo rabies illa prorsus diabolica, quæ eò hominem rapit, ut sciens & volens seipsum perdat, & ei quoque perditionis author fit, quam amore com-plectitur.
units.tr: Let us now consider the second argument by which the crime of fornication is magnified. It rests on a comparison, which is meant to stir even those who are less moved by concern for religion. For he says: Every sin that a man commits is outside the body; but he who fornicates sins against his own body. He seems to say: If you have no concern that you are tearing your members away from Christ, then at least let the disgrace to your own body move you, and the shame that falls back upon your own flesh. For although all sins have their own baseness attached to them and are at once harmful and pernicious, still some are outside the body; that is, their action is for the most part concerned with things foreign to our body and extends to others. But he who fornicates sins against his own body, since he thereby defiles it and strips it of its holiness and dignity, and so inflicts on himself a harm that cannot be repaired. This will indeed be seen to be rightly said if you examine the nature of other sins. Avarice, to be sure, lies within the mind of man, but it extends its effects to wealth and sins chiefly about these. So anger and the desire for revenge seek to harm others. Drunkenness and intemperance sin chiefly by abusing the gifts of God. The reasoning is nearly the same for all the others; and although some detriment from these also returns to our bodies, it happens far more so in fornication, whose peculiar mark it is that it defiles the body, indeed the whole man, with an indelible stain, since it casts him down from his own rank and strips him of that dignity with which Christ has adorned us. For if a man who marries a woman of lower standing sins against the nobility of his own kind and, as it were, prostitutes his dignity, how much more shameful is the guilt of those who, joined in one flesh with a prostitute, have cast off their modesty? And by what reasoning, I ask, will they be said not to sin against their own body, who enslave it to the most obscene harlots, and indeed to a slavery which takes away all use of reason at once, and which is the cause of a man forgetting both his salvation and his dignity? Certainly David, when he lay with Uriah's wife against the laws of marriage, defiled his own body and also his royal majesty. And no one is ignorant of how great a mark of disgrace Solomon inflicted on himself, when, forgetful of the divine Law, he kept company with foreign women. Therefore, those who defend fornication on the ground that it is a natural act are refuted once more at this point. For they invent this from their own brain, and would say something quite different if they looked more closely at the matter. For those who lay violent hands on themselves and rage against their own body with unusual frenzy are said not to act according to nature, but to be estranged from reason and common sense. And what else does he do who, impure, prostitutes himself for base lust to harlots more devouring than any she-wolf? That madness is certainly the more harmful and detestable, because while he ruins himself he also abuses another woman, and those who seem to love each other most ardently draw themselves by shameless lust into mutual destruction. That frenzy, then, is wholly diabolical, which carries a man off to the point of knowingly and willingly destroying himself, and makes him also the author of the ruin of the one whom he embraces with love.

units.la: Tertium argumentum est, quòd in Spiritum sanctum peccent qui scortantur. Non autem loquitur de illo peccato, cui remissionem prorsus negat Christus (nisi de illis hoc exponas, qui vel luina[?] & incurabili pertinacia in scortatione pergunt: & omnes admonitiones vnà cum Spiritus sancti & propriae conscientiae suggestionibus impiè eludunt) sed hoc innuit, quòd scortatores Spiritum Dei sua possessione eijciant, quam illi in nobis Christus suo merito parauit: quo sensu alibi nos admonet, ne tristitia afficiamus Spiritum sanctum Dei, per quem obsignati sumus in diem redemptionis. Hic verò rursus interrogatione utitur, vt magis in animos eorum penetret, qui libidine excaecati minus obseruant ea, quibus ipsorum salus impeditur. An ignoratis (inquit) corpus vestrum esse templum Spiritus sancti? Et cuius nam Spiritus? Eius inquam, qui est in vobis, & quem habetis à Deo, qui vos tanto honore dignatus est. Quasi diceret: Si Christiani estis, utique Spiritum Christi accepistis, qui cum adoptionis spiritus sit, in credentibus agit, vt & Deum Patrem inuocent, & huic se totos in obsequium tradant. Qui fit ergo, quòd huius immemores, corpora vestra ad libidinem prostitutionis non sine Spiritus sancti iniuria, qui sua possessione deijcitur, quam in vobis debebat tenere? Ex eo autem colligit, scortationem cum sacrilegio coniunctam, imò quo-uis sacrilegio detestabiliorem esse. Si enim scelus est templa lapidea, quae diuinis cultibus consecra-ta sunt, destruere, aut quouis alio modo prophanare, quo supplicio non dignus erit, qui Dei tem-plum viuum destruit, adeoque scipsum prophanat, vt ex Spiritus sancti templo Veneris proflibu-lum faciat? Pertinent ad huius argumenti confirmationem, quae Cap. tertio de illis diximus, qui templum Dei destruunt. Nunc autem obseruemus, unde nam illud fit, quòd scortatores absque pudore & ratione omnia faciunt, & caeco impetu in proprium exitium feruntur. Ex eo nimirum, quòd abs se Spiritum sanctum profligant, qui solus carnis affectus corruptos restinguit, aut saltem moderatur, ne hominem totum transfersum[?] abripiant. Cum enim aduersus hunc, quando nobis efficaciter adest, caro concupiscit, & saepe in sanctis quoque praevalet, quid non faciat illa, quando illo prorsus sublato aut eiecto, sibi omne imperium datum esse sentit? Sequitur quartum argumentum, quo iniustos & iniquos esse docet eos, qui scortandi licentiâ indulgent: eò quòd in rem alienâ sibi ius usurpent, & illam inuito domino in usus alienos transferrant. Nam non est ius (inquit) vestri iuris. Cur ergo pro vestra libidine vestro corpore utimini? Confirmat autem quod dixit ratione euidentissima. Nam empti estis pretio. Pleonasmo utitur (quid enim absque pretio emitur?) qui tamen ad argumenti pondus plurimum confert. Docet enim non vili aut quouis obuio pretio emptos esse, sed eo, quod Petrus per Collationem amplificat, quando nos non caducis rebus, auro nimirum & argento redemptos esse dicit, sed pretiosò sanguine agni immaculati & incontaminati IESV CHRISTI. Unde rursum sequitur, scelus istud omne in manifestam Christi ignominiam redundare, cuius sanguis & meritum à scortatoribus impiè conculcetur. Ideo Conclusionem infert: Glorificate igitur Deum in corpore vestro, & in spiritu vestro, quae sunt Dei. Quorum omnium sensus est: Seruorum est, heri sui gloriam tueri & pro virili prouehere. At vos Dei serui estis, qui vos Filij sui unigeniti sanguine redemptos sibi peculium fecit. Hunc ergo glorificate, & in eius cultum corpus simul & spiritum, id est, animam vestram impendite. Id verò fit, quando nos totos Deo consecramus, & non solum externas actiones, verumetiam mentem ipsam & omnes eius facultates accommodamus illius voluntati. Utriusq; ergo partis, ex quibus homo constat, meminit, ut hypocrisim excludat, & obedientia voluntaria opus esse extendat, quae nos totos Deo vendicet. Docet hanc Lex quoque, quando iubet, ut Dominum Deum nostrum diligamus ex toto corde, ex tota anima & totis viribus, utque nos sanctos praebeamus, quem admodum & ipse sanctus est. Neque aliud Christus praecipit, in hoc nos esse iubens, ut opera nostra luceant coram hominibus, ut his visis Patrem nostrum glorificent. Quod nos vel hoc nomine summo studio curare decet, quòd haec praecipua nostra dignitas est, quòd nobis ad hoc uti dignatur Deus, ut per nos glorificetur ipsius maiestas, quae ipsis caelis (ut Dauid inquit) est sublimior. Psalm.113. Porrò quoad praesens institutum, satis apparet, scortationem non temere inter ea scelera re-censeri, quae homines à regno Dei excludunt. Impossibile enim est, ut illius haereditatem adeant, qui Christo & adoptionis spiritu destituuntur, & iam sponte ab illo secessionem fecerunt. Ideo grauiter adeodum in Lege Deus statuit, ne scortum fit vllum ex filiabus Israel: & cum idem Vetuerit, ne Iudaei cum mulieribus alienigenis miscéantur, vtque scortationem omnem eliminatam voluit. Sed & mercedem scorti ita abominatur, vt eam in sacra inferre prohibeat. Adde his, quòd immane sit oportet scelus illud, quod idololatriae typum habet, qua nihil apud Deum abominabilius, nihil ab hominis officio alienum est. Et constat scortandi licentiam omnibus seculis grauissimè punitam esse, neq; hic officio suo defuisse Deum, si quando homines in illa coercenda cessauerunt. Haec certè vt primo mundo omnis corruptelae causa fuit, ita eidem diluuium induxit, quo ta tus[?] terrarum orbis miserabiliter afflictus fuit. In deserto autem viginti quatuor millia virorum tecidisse[?] legimus, eò quòd cum Moabitarum filiabus impudenter essent scortati. Adde his borren-dum totius fere tribus Beniamiticae excidium, cui Gabaonitarum effrenis libido causam atq; occasionem praebuit. Quòd si gentium historias euoluere libeat, tam multa tamq; horrenda huius generis exempla occurrent, vt nescias, vnde debeat narrandi initium fieri. Itaq; non sine causa Solomon in hoc malo insectando diligentissimus fuit, & cum eo, quem supra citauimus loco monuisset, cauendas esse meretricis blanditias, eò quòd earum finis absinthium sint & gladius anceps, mox subdicit rationem affert his verbis: Pedes eius descendunt in mortem, & vestigia eius tenebunt infernum. Viam vitae fortassis ponderabis, sed tam mobiles sunt gressus eius, vt scire non possis. Nunc igitur fili audite me, & ne recedatis ab eloquijs oris mei. Elonga ab ea viam tuam, & ne appropinquues ad ostium domus eius. Ne forte des alijs robur tuum, & annos tuos crudeli. Ne forte satientur alieni virtute tua, & labores tui veniant in domum extranei. Et rugias in nouissimo tuo, cùm defecerit caro tua & succus tuus, dicas: Quare odi castigationem, & c. Comprehendit his verbis Spiritus sanctus summatim poenas, quae scortationem comitari solent. Inter has primum locum habet animarum perditio, quam necessario sequi oportet, cùm à Christo abstrahat, qui salutis author est unicus. Coniuncta est illi infamia, cùm inter gentes quoq; male audierint semper, qui scortis addicti fuerunt. Nam etsi in animum inducant nihil facere, quod saluti aut honori eorum officiat, tanta tamen est meretricum astutia, tanta lenociniorum vis, vt paulatim oculos fascinent, & rationis vsum extinguant. Adhaec corporis vires debilitat, & vitam reddit breuiorem. Argumento sunt morbi, qui fere scorta & horum amatores depascuntur: inter quos horrendus est imprimis, quem Gallicum dicunt, eò quòd circiter annum 1495. in Gallorum castris, quae tunc in regno Neapolitano erant, exarsit, & inde per scortationem crudeli contagio per omnes terras sese extendit. Adde his, quòd non alia rei domesticae pestis est nocentior. Nam vt alibi dicitur, Qui pascit scorta, perdit opes. Fit ergo plerunq;, vt tandem sera nimis poenitentia seipsos discrucient, qui admonitiones salutares prius contempserunt. Excitent ista Christianos magistratus, vt scortandi licentiam disciplina seueriori coerceant. Singuli autem, qui fidem veram profitentur, sanctitati studeat, & sponsam sese castam atq; puram sistant IESV CHRISTO, cuius pretioso sanguine redempti sunt, vt cum eodem olim ad coelestes nuptias & beatae immortalitatis consortium possint ingredi. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: The third argument is that those who commit fornication sin against the Holy Spirit. He does not mean that sin for which Christ utterly denies forgiveness (unless you take this of those who persist in fornication with wanton and incurable obstinacy, and impiously mock all warnings, together with the prompts of the Spirit of God and of their own conscience). Rather, he implies that fornicators drive out the Spirit of God from the possession that Christ has won for us in him by his merit. In this sense he warns us elsewhere not to grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom we are sealed to the day of redemption. Here he again uses a question, so that it may penetrate more deeply into the minds of those who, blinded by lust, pay little heed to the things by which their own salvation is hindered. "Do you not know," he says, "that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit?" And whose Spirit? I answer: of him who is in you, whom you have from God, who has deigned to honour you so greatly. It is as if he said: If you are Christians, you have indeed received the Spirit of Christ, who, since he is the Spirit of adoption, works in believers so that they call upon God as Father and devote themselves wholly to his service. How then does it happen that, forgetful of this, you give your bodies over to the lust of prostitution, and so, not without injury to the Holy Spirit, who is driven out of the possession that he ought to keep in you? From this he concludes that fornication is joined with sacrilege, and indeed is more detestable than any sacrilege whatever. For if it is a crime to destroy or in any other way profane stone temples consecrated to divine worship, what punishment will be too great for him who destroys the living temple of God, and so profanes himself that out of the temple of the Holy Spirit he makes a brothel of Venus? To confirm this argument belong the things we said in the third chapter about those who destroy the temple of God. Now let us observe whence it comes that fornicators act without shame or reason and rush headlong, with blind impulse, to their own ruin. It arises, surely, from this: that they drive away the Holy Spirit, who alone quenches, or at least restrains, the corrupt desires of the flesh, so that they do not sweep the whole man away. For when the flesh lusts against the Spirit, while he effectively dwells in us, and often prevails even in the saints, what will it not do when, the Spirit being utterly removed or cast out, it feels that all rule has been given to itself? There follows a fourth argument, by which he teaches that those who indulge in the licence of fornication are unjust and wicked, because they claim for themselves a right over what is another's and turn it to another's use against the will of its owner. "For you are not your own," he says. Why then do you use your body for your own lust? He confirms what he has said by a most evident reason: "For you were bought with a price." He uses a pleonasm (for what is bought without a price?), yet it adds much weight to the argument. For he teaches that they were bought not with a cheap or any common price, but with that price which Peter magnifies when, comparing, he says that we were redeemed not with perishable things, gold and silver, but with the precious blood of the spotless and undefiled Lamb, Jesus Christ. Whence it again follows that all this crime redounds to the manifest dishonour of Christ, whose blood and merit are impiously trampled underfoot by fornicators. Therefore he draws the conclusion: "Glorify God, then, in your body and in your spirit, which are God's." The sense of all this is: it is the part of servants to guard the glory of their master and to advance it to the best of their power. But you are servants of God, whom he has made his own special people by the blood of his only-begotten Son. Glorify him, therefore, and devote to his worship both body and spirit, that is, your soul. This is done when we consecrate ourselves wholly to God, and bring into conformity with his will not only our outward actions but the mind itself and all its faculties. He therefore mentions both parts of which man consists, so as to exclude hypocrisy, and to extend the work of willing obedience, which claims us entirely for God. The Law also teaches this, when it bids us love the Lord our God with the whole heart, with the whole soul and with all our strength, and that we show ourselves holy, as he himself is holy. Nor does Christ command anything else, when he bids us so to let our works shine before men that, seeing them, they may glorify our Father. We ought to take the greatest care of this for this reason above all, that this is our chief dignity: God deigns to use us for this, that through us his majesty, which (as David says) is higher than the heavens, may be glorified. Psalm 113. Moreover, as far as the present purpose goes, it is clear enough that fornication is not lightly counted among those sins which exclude men from the kingdom of God. For it is impossible that those should inherit it who are destitute of Christ and of the spirit of adoption, and who have of their own accordance withdrawn from him. Therefore God, in the Law, very gravely decreed that there should be no harlot among the daughters of Israel; and when he forbade the Jews to mix with foreign women, he likewise wished all fornication to be banished. He so abhors the wages of a harlot that he forbids them to be brought into the sanctuary. Add to this that the crime must be monstrous, since it has the character of idolatry, than which nothing is more abominable before God and more alien to the duty of man. And it is established that the licence of fornication has been most severely punished in every age, and that God has not failed in his office here whenever men have ceased to restrain it. This indeed was the cause of all corruption in the first world, and so the flood brought it to an end, by which the whole orb of the earth was miserably afflicted. We read, moreover, that in the wilderness twenty-four thousand men perished because they had shamelessly fornicated with the daughters of Moab. Add to these the dreadful destruction of almost the whole tribe of Benjamin, to which the unbridled lust of the Gibeonites gave cause and occasion. If one were willing to unroll the histories of the nations, so many and so horrible examples of this kind would present themselves that you would not know where to begin the telling. Therefore it is not without reason that Solomon was most diligent in assailing this evil; and having warned, in the passage we cited above, that the flatteries of a harlot must be guarded against, because her end is wormwood and a two-edged sword, he immediately adds the reason in these words: Her feet go down to death, and her steps take hold on hell. Lest thou shouldest ponder the path of life, her ways are moveable, that thou canst not know them. Hear me now therefore, O ye children, and depart not from the words of my mouth. Remove thy way far from her, and come not nigh the door of her house: lest thou give thine honour unto others, and thy years unto the cruel: lest strangers be filled with thy wealth, and thy labours be in the house of a stranger; and thou mourn at the last, when thy flesh and thy body are consumed, and say, How have I hated instruction, and my heart despised reproof? In these words the Holy Spirit sums up briefly the punishments that usually accompany fornication. Among these the first place belongs to the destruction of souls, which must necessarily follow, since it separates men from Christ, who alone is the author of salvation. Infamy is joined with it, since those who have given themselves to harlots have always been ill spoken of even among the nations. For although they persuade themselves that they do nothing that harms their salvation or their honour, yet so great is the cunning of harlots, so great the power of their enticements, that they gradually bewitch the eyes and extinguish the use of reason. Besides, it weakens the strength of the body and makes life shorter. Proof of this are the diseases that commonly feed upon harlots and their lovers, among which the most dreadful is that which they call the French disease, since it broke out about the year 1495 in the camps of the French, which were then in the kingdom of Naples, and from there, through fornication, spread by cruel contagion through all lands. Add to this that no plague of the household is more harmful. For, as is said elsewhere, He who feeds harlots squanders his wealth. It therefore often happens that, at last, too late, they torment themselves with repentance who earlier despised the wholesome warnings. Let these things stir Christian magistrates to restrain the licence of fornication with a stricter discipline. And let each one who professes the true faith strive for holiness, and present himself as a chaste and pure bride to Jesus Christ, by whose precious blood he has been redeemed, so that he may one day enter with him into the heavenly marriage and the fellowship of blessed immortality. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT VII. HOMILIA XXXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII. HOMILY XXXII.

units.la: Cæterùm de quibus scripsistis ad me, bonum fuerit viro mulie-rem non attingere: Sed propter fornicationes suam quisq; v-xorem habeat, & proprium quæq; virum habeat.
units.tr: "Now concerning the things about which you wrote to me: it is good for a man not to touch a woman. But because of fornications, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband."

units.la: Nproximo[?] Cap. magna verborum & argumentorum grauitate in scortatores Paulus inuectus est, & ostendit, eos in ipsum Dei Filium IESVM CHRISTVM, adhaec in proprium corpus, imo in Spiritum sanctum peccare: adeoq; palàm iniquos & iniustos esse, dum seipsos à Deo alienant, qui nos Filij sui sanguine redemit, vt sibi soli consecraret. At quia frustra de morbo disseritur, nisi simul remedium adhibeas, id nunc proponit Apostolus, & hoc Capite de coniugio seu matrimonio agit: quod argumentum sic tractat, ut multas solvat quaestiones, quae de caelibatu, virginitate & multis aliis ad hanc causam pertinentibus moveri solent. Est igitur huius Capitis doctrina utilissima. Quia ut coniugium inter omnis loci & ordinis homines ex Dei instituto receptum est: ita ex eo dependet legitima humani generis propagatio, ideoq; qui hic admittitur error, longe late[?] ad multos alios redundat. Ut autem olim circa illud varie peccatum fuit: ita etiam hodie alij quidem libidinis aestro abrepti illius sanctitatem violant, alij vero sub religionis praetextu multa faciunt, quae Dei instituto & Christianae religionis legibus adversantur.
units.tr: In the preceding chapter Paul attacked fornicators with great weight of words and arguments, and showed that they sin against the Son of God Jesus Christ himself, and besides against their own body, indeed against the Holy Spirit. He showed that they are plainly wicked and unrighteous, since they estrange themselves from God, who redeemed us with the blood of his Son so that he might consecrate us to himself alone. But because it is useless to discuss a disease unless you also apply a remedy, the Apostle now sets out the remedy and in this chapter treats of marriage, or matrimony. He handles the subject in such a way that he resolves the many questions that are usually raised about celibacy, virginity and many other matters pertaining to this cause. The teaching of this chapter is therefore most useful. For just as marriage, instituted by God, is received among men of every place and rank, so the lawful propagation of the human race depends upon it, and therefore an error admitted here spreads far and wide to many other things. And just as in former times people sinned in various ways concerning it, so today some, carried away by the fever of lust, violate its holiness, while others, under the pretext of religion, do many things that are contrary to God's institution and to the laws of the Christian religion.

units.la: Occasionem huic tractationi dederunt Corinthij, qui missa ad Paulum epistola, eius super hac re sententiam rogaverunt. Nam ut suo loco videbimus, erant complures in ipsorum ecclesia, qui à coniugio abhorrebant, quod istud vitae genus curis, laboribus, incommodis & omni molestiarum genere refertum esse viderent. At ijdem, quae humani ingenij nequitia est, ne in ferendo Dei jugo impatientes esse, aut vagas libidines quaerere viderentur, religionis studium praetexebant. Haec enim hominem totum Deo vendicat, ut nimirum relictis omnibus huius saeculi studijs, illi uni & soli serviamus. Id vero vix fieri potest quorundam judicio abijs, qui in coniugio viviunt, eo quod multis negotijs atq; curis distrahantur. Accedebat his, quod illo tempore persecutiones ferverent, quae causa erat, ut multi à coniugum & liberorum complexu in carceres raperentur, multi subito solum vertere & sedes mutare cogerentur. At in his quoq; expeditiores sunt, qui à coniugij vinculis soluti nulla liberorum aut rei domesticae cura gravantur. Neq; temere Christus, cum horribiles Judaicae gentis calamitates exprimere vellet, rem eo deventuram ait, ut clament: Beati ventres, qui non genuerunt, & beata ubera, quae non lactaverunt. Ex his ergo multi colligebant, ad Christianam perfectionem facilius eos pervenire posse, qui caelibes viviunt. Hinc autem fiebat, ut multi divortia temere facerent, multi à coniugio abstinerent, & non leviter periclitarentur, cum castitatis donum non accepissent. Quia ergo multus de his sermo erat, & causa haec propter multa, quae praeter decorum fiebant, in apertas contentiones exarsisset, Pauli consilium postularunt. Unde apparet, quod etsi ingens fuerit in illa ecclesia confusio, & multi Paulum improbe contemnerent, tanta tamen eius apud maiorem partem fuit authoritas, ut eius sententiam audire vellent in re graui & quae ad omnes pertinebat.
units.tr: The Corinthians gave occasion for this discussion, for they sent a letter to Paul and asked his opinion on this matter. For, as we shall see in its place, there were several in their congregation who shrank from marriage, because they saw that this way of life was filled with cares, labours, inconveniences and every kind of trouble. Yet these same people, by that wickedness of the human mind which does not want to appear impatient in bearing God's yoke or seeking wandering lusts, pretended a zeal for religion. For this zeal claims the whole man for God, so that, having left all the pursuits of this age, we may serve him alone. Yet in the judgment of some this can hardly be done by those who live in marriage, since they are distracted by many affairs and anxieties. To this was added the fact that at that time persecutions were raging, which was the reason why many were snatched from the embrace of spouse and children and thrown into prisons, and many were suddenly forced to flee their homeland and change their dwelling. But in these circumstances too, those are more free who, released from the bonds of marriage, are not burdened by any care for children or household affairs. Nor did Christ speak rashly when, wishing to describe the dreadful calamities of the Jewish nation, he said that a time would come when people would cry out: "Blessed are the wombs that never bore, and the breasts that never gave suck." From these words many concluded that those who live unmarried can more easily attain Christian perfection. From this, however, it happened that many rashly divorced, many abstained from marriage, and they were in no small danger, since they had not received the gift of chastity. Therefore, because there was much talk about these things, and the matter, on account of the many things that were done beyond what was fitting, had flared into open contentions, they asked for Paul's counsel. From this it is clear that, although there was great disorder in that church, and many shamelessly despised Paul, nevertheless his authority with the greater part was so great that they wished to hear his judgment on a weighty matter that concerned everyone.

units.la: Est autem hic nobis observandum Satanae ingenium, quàmq; improbo & irrequieto studio in turbandis Dei institutis utatur. Quod ut in multis aliis rebus apparet, ita maximè in coniugio cernitur, quod omnibus saeculis aut in contemptum adducere, aut verum eius usum abolere conatus est. Est enim spiritus immundus & immunditiei aut impuritate gaudet, qua homines prorsus à Deo abstrahi novit, eò quod sine sanctimonia illum nemo videre aut in eius conspectu subsistere potest. At nullus immunditiei & libidini vagae locus est, ubicunq; matrimonij usus sanctè servatur, quem huic malo Deus remedium dedit. Itaq; omnibus saeculis in hoc fuit, ut coniugij legibus sublatis illicitas libidines inveheret, quibus toti prophanantur qui Spiritus sancti templa esse debebant. Ex hoc fonte polygamia manavit, quae ut inter gentes prophanas in usu fuit: ita olim inter patres quoq; sanctissimos locum invenit. Quam est Deus singulari consilio in illis tulerit, tamen neque omnino excusari potest, & illis quoque turbas dedit tantum non intolerabiles. Ad eundem authorem divortiorum licentia referri debet, quae in Dei populo eò usq; excrevit, ut eam lege de repudij libello uxoribus dando frenari oportuerit. Inter Christianos autem homines ita ab initio statim mulieres communes omnibus facere studuit, unde horribilis Nicolaitarum & Gnosticorum foeditas enata est. Postea sub religionis praetextu caelibatum obtrusit, cuius praecones & admiratores invenit inter eos quoq;, qui ecclesiae atq; fidei primi propugnatores esse videbantur. In Concilio certè Niceno fuere, qui suadebant, ut sacerdotibus coniugatis prohiberetur consuetudo coniugalis: & fortassis aliquid illi obtinuissent, nisi se illis oppositisset Paphnutius, martyrij stigma teinfignis, qui coniugia minimè dissolvenda esse docuit, & eorum coniugalem sanctum atq; impollutum esse demonstravit. At quod tunc non potuit effectum dare Satan, id posteris temporibus perfecit, & in ecclesiam per superstitiosos quosdam caelibatum invexit, ex quo inter ministros scortandi licentia enata est, quae ab illis ad omnis loci & ordinis homines propagata, simul Dei cultum omnem in extremum contemptum adduxit, vt prater inanes superstitiones nihil fere reliquum man-ferit. Non temere ergo Apostoli tanto studio coniugij dignitatem asserunt, nimirum Christi praeceptoris exemplum imitati, qui vt ipse nuptijs interesse, & eas miraculorum suorum primitijs or-nare dignatus est: ita aduersus Iudæos quoq; illam constanter defendit, cùm de repudiorum licen-tia interrogaretur. Est hoc nobis probè observandum hodie, & sufficiat aduersus omnium ratio-nes, qui cœlibatum inuehere conantur, Pauli admonitio, qui dæmoniorum doctrinam esse dicit, quæ coniugium prohibet. 1. Timoth.4.
units.tr: Here we must observe the nature of Satan, and with what wicked and restless zeal he works to disturb God's institutions. As this appears in many other matters, so it is seen most of all in marriage, which in every age he has either tried to bring into contempt or to abolish its true use. For he is an unclean spirit and delights in uncleanness or impurity, by which he knows how to draw men entirely away from God, since no one can see God or stand in his presence without holiness. But there is no place for uncleanness and wandering lust wherever the use of marriage is kept holy, which God gave as a remedy against this evil. And so in every age Satan's aim has been, once the laws of marriage were removed, to bring in unlawful lusts, by which those who ought to be temples of the Holy Spirit are wholly profaned. From this source sprang polygamy, which, as it was in use among the profane nations, so in former times it also found a place among the most holy fathers. Although God in his singular counsel bore with it in them, it still cannot be wholly excused, and it brought upon them troubles that were almost unbearable. To the same author must be referred the licence of divorce, which grew so much among the people of God that it had to be restrained by the law requiring a bill of divorce to be given to wives. Among Christians, however, from the very beginning he strove to make women common to all, from which sprang the dreadful foulness of the Nicolaitans and Gnostics. Afterwards, under the pretext of religion, he thrust celibacy upon them, and found its heralds and admirers even among those who seemed to be the first defenders of the Church and of the faith. At the Council of Nicaea certainly there were those who urged that the practice of marital intercourse be forbidden to married priests; and perhaps they would have gained something, had not Paphnutius, a man distinguished by the mark of martyrdom, opposed them. He taught that marriages were by no means to be dissolved, and he showed that the marriage bed is holy and undefiled. But what Satan could not then bring about, he accomplished in later times, and through certain superstitious men he introduced celibacy into the Church. From this arose among ministers a licence for fornication, which was spread by them to men of every place and rank, and at the same time brought the whole worship of God into the utmost contempt, so that, apart from empty superstitions, almost nothing was left. It is not without reason, then, that the Apostles defend the dignity of marriage with such zeal, imitating the example of Christ their teacher, who deigned both to be present at weddings and to adorn them with the first fruits of his miracles, and who likewise constantly defended marriage against the Jews when he was asked about the licence of divorce. We must observe this carefully today, and the admonition of Paul, who calls doctrines that forbid marriage the teachings of demons, is enough against all the arguments of those who try to bring in celibacy. 1 Timothy 4.

units.la: Debet præterea non oscitanter inspici Corinthiacæ ecclesiæ exemplum. Fuit hæc (vt iam sa-pe audiuimus) multis modis corruptissima, & pleriq; in iis quoq; erraverunt, sine quibus vera salutis ratio nõ consistit. Vicit tamen apud illos eorũ sententia, qui in causa controuersa & dubia Apostolum consulendum esse censuerunt. Ergo Apostolos agnouerunt à Deo orbis doctores datos esse, quos omnes audire debeant. Debent exemplum hoc imitari, quicunq; de fidei articulis, de salutis æternæ negotio aut quibuscunq; religionis articulis certiores fieri cupiunt. Olim ad summum Pontificem dubiæ & graviores causæ referebantur, cuius sententia contradicere scelus capitale erat: eò quòd ille Christi personam sustineret, & responsa non ex suo capite fingeret, sed à Domino accepta proferret. Et Christum magnum illum Prophetam esse, quem omnes audire debeant, Petrus & Stephanus testantur. Ille vero vt olim per Sacerdotes & Prophetas veteribus locutus est: itano-bis hodie per Apostolos loquitur, qui & historiâ illius & ex ore eius sumptam doctrinam scriptis mandarunt, deq; his ille pronunciauit: Qui vos audit, me audit, &c. Vtinam vero hoc omnes facerent hodie, & mox omnibus controuersiis finem imponi videremus, quæ de Dei vnius invocatione, de vno Mediatore Christo, de simulachris & eorum cultu, de purgatorij igne lustratione, de Sacramentis, de Ecclesiæ œconomia & clauibus, de traditionibus ecclesiasticis, de ciborum delectu[?], deniq; de omnibus aliis articulis suscitantur. At quia Apostolos audire pleriq; nolunt, & alius quidem Patrum testimonijs nititur, alius vero Concilij determinationem expectat, multi à principum authoritate pendent, quidam vero sui cerebri figmentis & acumine omnia dijudicanda putant, frustra contenditur, & latius quotidie serpunt incendia, quorum fumis religio vera obscuratur, & infirmiores vehementer offenduntur.
units.tr: Moreover, the example of the Corinthian church must be examined carefully. This church (as we have often heard) was very corrupt in many ways, and many in it also erred in matters without which the true way of salvation does not stand. Yet the opinion of those prevailed among them who judged that in a controverted and doubtful matter the Apostle should be consulted. Thus they acknowledged that the Apostles had been given by God as teachers of the world, whom all ought to hear. All who desire to be informed about the articles of faith, about the business of eternal salvation, or about any articles of religion, ought to imitate this example. In former times, weighty and doubtful cases were referred to the supreme Pontiff, and to oppose his judgment was a capital crime, because he was supposed to sustain the person of Christ and did not invent answers from his own head, but gave forth what had been received from the Lord. And Peter and Stephen bear witness that Christ is that great Prophet whom all ought to hear. But just as he formerly spoke to the ancients through priests and prophets, so today he speaks to us through the Apostles, who committed to writing both his history and the doctrine taken from his own mouth, and concerning them he declared: "He who hears you hears me," etc. Would that all did this today, and we might soon see an end put to all the controversies that are raised concerning the invocation of the one God, the one Mediator Christ, images and their worship, the cleansing of purgatorial fire, the sacraments, the economy and keys of the Church, ecclesiastical traditions, the choice of foods, and finally all the other articles. But because many do not wish to hear the Apostles, and one relies on the testimonies of the Fathers, another awaits the decision of a council, many depend on the authority of princes, and some think that everything must be judged by the figments and cleverness of their own brain, the dispute is fruitless, and the fires spread more widely every day, and by their smoke the true religion is obscured and the weaker are gravely offended.

units.la: Porrò Paulum propositæ quæstioni respondentem audiamus, qui ab initio huius causæ summam comprehendit his verbis: Bonum fuerit viro mulierem non attingere: sed propter fornicationes suam quisq; vxorem habeat, & proprium quaq; virum habeat. Vbi ante omnia videndum est, quid Boni vocabulo Apostolus intelligat. Ex eo enim olim quidam falsò collegerunt argumento à contrarijs deductò: Bonum est mulierem non attingere: Ergo malum est mulierem attingere. In quorum numero D. quoq; Hieronymus fuit, vir in multis eximius & non male meritus de re Christiana, vehementioris tamen ingenij & pertinacior in defendendis semel conceptis opinionibus. Et hodie eodem argumento aduersarij nostri vtuntur, quos non pudet cum Siricio Papa coniugium inter opera carnis numerare. Et hi quoq; in Attingendi verbo inhærentes omnem consuetudinem mulierum ita damnant, vt eas vix alloquio dignas existiment. Carthusiani verò pauimentum quoq;, quod mulier calcauit, scopis verrere consueuerunt, ne quo puluisculo aspersi polluantur. Ridiculum hominum genus, qui non vident, Paulo nunquam vel per sominum in mentem venisse, quod ipsi ex eius verbis colligunt. Nam si id voluisset, nunquam alibi coniugium dixisset honorabile esse inter quosuis, neq; episcopum vnius vxoris virum esse iussisset. Iniuriam ergo faciunt magnam Apostolo, quem non solum sibi ipsi, sed Deo contradicentem fingunt. Huius enim vox est: Non est bonum, hominem esse solum: faciam illi adiutorium, quod sit coram eo. Qua locutione non modò commendatur matrimonium, sed perpetua consuetudo coniugum docetur. Quomodo enim mulier adiutorium erit coram viro, si ei non indiuulse conuixerit? Obseruemus ergo Boni vocabulum non vno sensu accipi, & eo non solum significari quod rectum, honestum & sanctum est, verumetiam vtile & commodum. Et in hac significatione illud Paulus in præsenti vsurpat. Itaq; non opponitur malo aut iniusto siue prophano, sed incommodo & molesto aut laboriosō, & proinde verborum istorum sensus est. Commodum quidem & vtile fuerit, si vir absq; muliere viuat, neq; coniugij vinculo astringatur, aut mulier suam libertatem feruet, neq; viri imperium accersat. uersat. Nam si id faciant, multis molestiis atque incommodis liberabuntur, quæ coniugium comitari solent. Sed quia commoditas ista cum periculo coniuncta est, & multos nobis laqueos nectit Satan, quibus in scortandi licentiam & vagas atq; illicitas libidines eos pertrahit, qui castitatis domo non sunt præditi, consultissimum fuerit, vt ad vitandas fornicationes quisq; propriam vxorem habeat, & vnaquæq; cum proprio viro coniugalis thori societate coniungatur. Comparationem ergo continent hæc verba, qua potius docetur, minime committendum esse, vt vitandæ aliquius breuioris molestiæ causa nosmetipsos diaboli insidijs exponamus, deq; salute animarum periclitemur. Perinde ergo loquitur Paulus, ac si quis diceret: Bonum equidem fuerit, si quis absque cibo & potu viuere possit: at cùm hoc tentare ridiculum, præstare autem impossibile sit, eam vitæ seruandæ rationem teneamus oportet, quæ à Deo nobis præscripta est. Conuenit autem Apostoli sententia cum natura legibus, quas gentium quoque cordibus inscriptam fuisse, Metelli Numidici exemplo probatur, quem in oratione quadam sic publicè dixisse ferunt: Sisine vxore possemus viuere Quirites, omnes ea molestia careremus: sed quoniam ita natura tradit, vt nec cum iis satis commodè, nec sine illis vllo modo viui posset, saluti perpetuæ prius quàm breui voluptati consulendum est. Hæc ideo recitamus ô fratres, vt suæ arrogantiæ simul & inscitiæ pudeat hypocritas, qui non exploratis prius suis aut aliorum viribus id exigunt, quod absque peculiari gratia Dei à nemine præstari potest. Cæterum si Pauli verba propius consideremus, omnia his comprehendi videbimus, quæ de coniugio dici possunt, Itaque præcipua huius loci capita breuiter percurremus.
units.tr: Let us next hear Paul, who answers the question put to him and at the start of this matter sums it up in these words: "It is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of fornications, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband" (1 Cor. 7:1-2). Here we must first consider what Paul means by the word "good." Long ago some people drew a false conclusion from this by the argument of contraries: it is good not to touch a woman; therefore it is bad to touch a woman. Among them was St Jerome, a man outstanding in many respects and not undeserving of Christendom, but of a rather vehement temper, and too stubborn in defending opinions once he had formed them. Even today our opponents use the same argument. They are not ashamed, with Pope Siricius, to count marriage among the works of the flesh. They also cling to the word "touch" and condemn all association with women so completely that they think them scarcely worthy of conversation. The Carthusians even sweep with brooms the floor a woman has walked on, lest they be polluted by any speck of dust. What a ridiculous race of men, who do not see that Paul never even dreamed of what they draw from his words! For had he meant that, he would never have called marriage honourable among all men elsewhere, nor ordered that a bishop be the husband of one wife. They therefore do great wrong to the Apostle, whom they imagine to be contradicting not only himself but God. For this is God's word: "It is not good for man to be alone; I will make him a helper, who will be before him" (Gen. 2:18). By these words not only is marriage commended, but a lasting companionship of spouses is taught. For how will a woman be a helper before her husband if she does not live with him without separation? Let us therefore observe that the word "good" is not taken in one sense only, and that it signifies not only what is right, honourable and holy, but also what is useful and convenient. It is in this sense that Paul uses it here. So it is not opposed to what is evil or unjust or profane, but to what is inconvenient, troublesome or laborious, and so the sense of these words is this: it would indeed be convenient and useful if a man lived without a woman, and were not bound by the tie of marriage, or if a woman let her freedom boil over and did not invite a husband's rule. For if they did so, they would be freed from many troubles and inconveniences that usually accompany marriage. But because that convenience is joined with danger, and Satan spreads many snares for us, by which he draws into the licence of whoring and wandering and unlawful lusts those who are not endowed with the gift of chastity, it is most advisable that each man have his own wife to avoid fornication, and that each woman be joined in the fellowship of the marriage bed with her own husband. These words therefore contain a comparison, by which we are taught rather that we must in no way expose ourselves to the snares of the devil, and endanger the salvation of our souls, in order to avoid some briefer trouble. So Paul speaks just as if someone were to say: it would indeed be good if a man could live without food and drink; but since to attempt this is absurd and to accomplish it impossible, we must keep to that manner of preserving life which God has prescribed for us. Moreover, the Apostle's judgment agrees with the law of nature, which was written in the hearts of the Gentiles too, as is shown by the example of Metellus Numidicus, who is reported to have said publicly in a certain speech: "If we Romans could live without a wife, we would all be free of that trouble; but since nature has so ordained that one cannot live tolerably well with them, nor in any way without them, we must care for lasting well-being before fleeting pleasure." We recite these things, brothers, so that hypocrites may be ashamed of their arrogance and ignorance at once, since they demand, without first testing their own or others' strength, what no one can achieve without the special grace of God. Yet if we consider Paul's words more closely, we shall see that everything that can be said about marriage is contained in them. Therefore we shall briefly run through the principal heads of this passage.

units.la: Coniugium est legitima & diuinitus instituta viri & fœminæ coniunctio quæ cum vtriusque consensu fit, vt mutuam sibi innicem opem ferant in perferendis huius vitæ molestiis, sobolem procreent, & illicitas libidines deiiciant. Continet definitio ista ferè omnia, quæ de coniugio possunt dici. Ante omnia autem obseruandum, non quamuis viri & mulieris coniunctionem coniugium aut matrimonium esse, sed eam solùm quæ legitimè, id est, secundùm leges à Deo, primo eius authore, datas contrahitur. Ergo non statim coniugium erit, quod hoc nomine palliatur, non autem cum legibus diuinis conuenit. Inter has prima esto, vt (quod in præsenti Paulus monet) quisque vnam & propriam vxorem, similiter quæqué vnum & proprium maritum habeat. Consentit hoc cum verbis Christi, qui à Iudæis de diuortio interrogatus, ad primam coniugij institutionem eos remittit, & inter alia dicit: Annon legistis, quòd qui ab initio creauit, marem & fœminam fecit: & qui duo fuerant, erunt caro vna. Oppugnatur hîs polygamia, cuius primus author Lamech fuit, ex infelici Cainitarum prosapia oriundus. Nec est quòd nobis patriarchas, Abrahamum & Iacobum, Dauidem item aliosq; horum similes quisquam obijciat. Etsi enim quod illi fecerunt Deus peculiari indulgentia tulerit, in primam tamen coniugij legem peccarunt, & coniugia illa grauibus turbis atque molestiis referta fuisse scimus, quibus suæ institutionis violationem Deus non obscurè vltus est. Peccatur item in hanc legem, quando ea ducitur, quæ cùm alterius sit, tibi propria vxor esse non potest, aut cum ei nubit mulier, qui iure ad alteram pertinet. Fit hoc, quando alteri iam ante fides promissa est, aut temere abrupto coniugij vinculo altera ducitur. Quo Christus respiciens dicebat, adulterium ab eo committi, qui repudiatam ducit. Loquitur enim illic de repudijs temerarijs, quæ Dei iudicio rata esse non poterant, cùm ex priuato arbitrio fierent, absque causa iusta & graui. Itaque etsi dirempta esset consuetudo & cohabitationis societas, manebat tamen fidei vtrinque data vinculum, quo sibi inuicem erant obstricti, ideoque alienam sibi ducebat, quisquis cum repudiata sub matrimonij prætextu coniungebatur. Altera coniugij lex sit, ne cum iis contrahamus, quorum nuptiæ propter consanguinitatem aut affinitatem arctiorem diuinis præceptis prohibentur.
units.tr: Marriage is the lawful union of a man and a woman, instituted by God, which takes place with the consent of both, so that they may bring mutual help to one another in bearing the troubles of this life, may produce offspring, and may cast out unlawful lusts. This definition contains almost everything that can be said about marriage. Above all, however, we must observe that not every union of man and woman is marriage or matrimony, but only that which is contracted lawfully, that is, according to the laws given by God, the first author of it. Therefore whatever is cloaked under this name, but does not agree with the divine laws, will not at once be marriage. The first of these laws is, as Paul here warns, that each man have one wife, and his own, and likewise each woman have one husband, and her own.
