This agrees with the words of Christ, who, when asked about divorce by the Jews, sends them back to the first institution of marriage, and among other things says: "Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female, and said: 'the two shall become one flesh'?" (Matt. 19:4-5). Polygamy is opposed to this law. Its first author was Lamech, sprung from the unhappy stock of the Cainites. Nor should anyone object to us the patriarchs Abraham and Jacob, or David, and others like them. For although God tolerated what they did by a special indulgence, they nonetheless sinned against the first law of marriage, and we know that those marriages were full of serious disturbances and troubles, by which God did not obscurely avenge the violation of his institution. The law is also broken when a woman is taken who, since she belongs to another, cannot be your own wife, or when a woman marries a man who by right belongs to another. This happens when her faith has already been pledged to another, or when a second wife is taken after the bond of marriage has been rashly broken. Looking to this, Christ said that the man who takes a divorced woman commits adultery (Matt. 5:32). For he speaks there of rash divorces, which could not stand before God's judgment, since they were made by private choice, without a just and grave cause. Thus, although the living together and the companionship of cohabitation had been dissolved, the bond of faith given by each to the other still remained, by which they were bound to one another; and therefore whoever joined himself to a divorced woman under the pretext of marriage was taking another's wife. The other law of marriage is that we must not contract with those whose marriage is forbidden by the divine precepts on account of closer kinship or affinity.

units.la: Extant hæc in Leuitico cap. 18. & 20. Dispensant quidem in illis Romani pontifices, & horum audaciam aliqui ex iis imitantur, qui Euangelicæ doctrinæ seductores videri volunt. Sed vt isti inexcusabili temeritate sibi ipsis in Dei leges ius sumunt: ita inanis & nullius momenti est illa dispensatio. Nam etsi illi pretio aut fauore permittant consanguineorum nuptias, non tamen legitima sunt eiusmodi coniugia, & plerunq; infelix est eorundem exitus, quod multis exemplis probari poterat. Addatur hîs lex tertia, ne absq; parentum voluntate & consensu aliquid hîc faciant iuniores. Cur enim ratum sit quod in re omnium maxima ex suo arbitrio statuunt, qui ne in minimis quidem sunt sui iuris? Scio quid nobis obijciant Pontificij, qui ex matrimonio Sacramentum fecerunt, & illud Christi nobis obijciunt: Quod Deus coniunxit, homo ne separet. Inde autem colligunt, inuiolabilem esse, neque vlla ratione rescindi posse promissionem, qua inscijs quoque parentibus fidem suam filij aut filiae alijs obstringunt. At Sacramentum esse nunquam probare poterunt, & iampridem error iste confutatus est. Et quid ijdem respondebunt illi, si ego negem Deum eos coniunxisse, qui spreta parentum authoritate fidem suam alijs promittunt? Scimus quidem nihil absque Dei providentia fieri, sed non ideo omnia cum eius voluntate conueniunt, quam nobis ille in scripturis reuelauit. Et qui coniugij fidem inuiolatam seruari vult, idem ne obedientiae officio & honore debito parentes fraudemus grauissime praecepit. Quis item probare poterit ratum debere esse contractum, quo filius insciō patre domum aut agrum paternum vendit? Cur ergo rata fit promissio, qua seipsum & hereditatem simul omnem parentibus inconsultis aut inuitis quoque ad aliam transfert? Possent hic multa alia argumenta adduci, quibus istorum hominum temeritas confutatur, sed possunt haec sufficere pijs, qui Deo potius quam hominibus obedire in animum induxerunt. Et si leges, quas modo recitauimus, ratas habeant qui rempub. administrant, mox videbunt coniugia passim sanctè coli, & familias passim florere, quas nunc caeca libido misere dissipat & euertit [?].
units.tr: These things are set out in Leviticus, chapters 18 and 20. Indeed the Roman pontiffs grant dispensations in these matters, and some who wish to be seen as seducers of the evangelical doctrine imitate their audacity. But just as these men in inexcusable rashness claim for themselves a right over God's laws, so that dispensation is empty and of no weight. For even if they permit marriages of blood relatives for a price or as a favour, such unions are not lawful, and their outcome is usually unhappy, as many examples could prove. To these add a third law: that the young do nothing in this matter without the will and consent of their parents. For why should what they decide in the most important matter by their own choice be valid, when they are not even their own masters in the smallest things? I know what the Papists object to us, who have made marriage a sacrament, and who cite against us the saying of Christ: "What God has joined together, let not man put asunder" (Matt. 19:6). From this they conclude that a promise, by which sons or daughters bind their faith to others even without their parents' knowledge, is inviolable and cannot in any way be annulled. But they will never be able to prove that marriage is a sacrament, and that error was refuted long ago. And what will those same men reply, if I deny that God has joined those who, scorning their parents' authority, promise their faith to others? We indeed know that nothing happens without God's providence, but not everything that happens agrees with his will, which he has revealed to us in the Scriptures. And he who wishes the faith of marriage to be kept inviolate has also most gravely commanded that we not defraud parents of the duty of obedience and the honour due to them. Who, moreover, could prove that a contract is to be valid by which a son sells his father's house or field without his father's knowledge? Why then is a promise valid by which a son transfers himself and all his inheritance to another, without his parents being consulted or even against their will? Many other arguments could be brought forward here, by which the rashness of these men is refuted, but these may suffice for the godly, who have resolved to obey God rather than men. And if those who administer the commonwealth were to keep the laws we have just recited, they would soon see marriages everywhere honoured in holiness, and families everywhere flourishing, which unbridled lust now wretchedly scatters and overturns.

units.la: At plurimum proderit coniugij authorem semper respicere, vt illius dignitas melius cognoscatur. Est vnus & solus Deus, qui vt Adamum ex luto terrae fecit, ita Euam ex costa illius formatam ei connubio iunxit, & primus hoc munus obiuit, quod postea superstitiosi homines Iunoni pronubae & Himenaeo tribuerunt. Admonet nos de illo vetus ecclesiae mos, quo coniugia in sacro coetu confirmantur, & ijsdem Dei verbis minister benedicit, vt inde omnes intelligant, nihil hic quam diuinum agi. Imprimis tamen hic obseruari debet, tunc a Deo coniugium institutum fuisse, cum nondum peccauisset Adamus, sed dignitatem, ad quam conditus erat, adhuc retineret. Quod vnum eorum improbitatem abunde confutat, qui matrimonium inter poenas peccati numerant, & cum eius vsum non omnino damnare possint, malum esse dicunt necessarium. Quorum sententia si admittatur, Deum poenas peccati inflixisse dicemus homini priusquam ille peccauisset, adeoque et fuisse peccati authorem. Atqui aliud docent verba Dei, de quibus supra diximus, & plura suo loco dicentur. Curis quidem & molestijs plurimum coniugium refertum esse fatentur, sed tum iam ex peccato nata sint, nimium iniqui & Deo ingrati sunt, qui eius institutum per se sanctum & vtile accusant. In his autem obseruari debet matrimonij dignitas, vt hanc aduersus eos tueamur, qui Siricium Papam secuti, illud inter opera carnis numerant, & Deo placere posse negant eos, qui in coniugio viuunt. Diximus de his alibi prolixè, vt minime opus sit hic omnia repetere. Vnum hoc addimus nunc, nimium stupidos aut malitiosos esse, qui illud vitae genus damnare non verentur, in quo sanctissimos Dei seruos iam inde a prima rerum origine vixisse constat, & cuius dignitatem Deus tot tamque horrendis iudiciorum suorum exemplis apud omnes fere populos asseruit.
units.tr: But it will be of great profit always to look to the author of marriage, so that its dignity may be better recognised. There is one and only God, who, as he made Adam from the clay of the earth, so also formed Eve from Adam's rib and joined her to him in wedlock; and he first performed this office, which superstitious men afterwards assigned to Juno, the bringer of the bride, and to Hymenaeus. The ancient custom of the Church reminds us of this, by which marriages are confirmed in the holy assembly, and the minister blesses them with the very words of God, so that everyone may understand that nothing but a divine act is being done here. Yet above all it must be noted here that marriage was instituted by God at a time when Adam had not yet sinned, but still retained the dignity to which he had been created. This one fact sufficiently refutes the wickedness of those who count marriage among the punishments of sin, and, since they cannot altogether condemn its use, say that it is a necessary evil. If their opinion were admitted, we would have to say that God inflicted the punishments of sin upon man before he had sinned, and so was himself the author of sin. But the words of God, of which we spoke above, and which will be spoken of more fully in their place, teach otherwise. They confess that marriage is indeed full of cares and troubles, but since these arose from sin, those are altogether unjust and ungrateful to God who accuse its institution, which is holy and useful in itself. In these matters the dignity of marriage must be observed, so that we may defend it against those who, following Pope Siricius, count it among the works of the flesh and deny that those who live in marriage can please God. We have spoken of these things at length elsewhere, so there is no need to repeat everything here. We add only this now: they are too foolish or malicious who do not hesitate to condemn that way of life in which, as is plain, the holiest servants of God have lived from the very beginning of the world, and whose dignity God has asserted among almost all peoples by so many and such dreadful examples of his judgments.

units.la: Debet praeterea coniugij finis considerari, qui triplex est. Primo enim ideo Euam Adamo coniunxit Deus, vt adiutorium ille haberet in ferendis vitae molestijs, quas ex peccato oriturus sciebat. Atqui eadem nobis etiam hodie coniugij causa non postrema est, quando constat sine illo neque domestica feliciter curari, neque alia negotia commodè tractari, nisi curas inter se coniuges partiantur. Est autem hoc magnum diuinae bonitatis argumentum, quod qui hominem peccaturum esse sciebat, priusquam id fieret, remedium parauit, quo peccati poenae mitigarentur. Eius generis est, quod herbas creauit, quibus morbi curantur, priusquam hi ex peccato essent enati. Deinde propagando simul & seruando generi humano matrimonium seruire debuit. Nam etsi ex promiscuis quoque & illicitis congressibus liberi generentur, non tamen legitima est generatio illa, & proinde confusionem parit atque infinita alia incommoda, de quibus nunc non est dicendi locus. Hinc ergo tertius coniugij finis & vsus dependet, vt fit libidinis remedium, ne generandi cupiditas prohibitis amoribus inflammata nos abripiat, vt iustitiae & honestatis fines transiliamus. Et hunc finem in praesenti Paulus attingit, praeteritis duobus primis, qui ad eius institutum minus pertinebant. Hic autem tenere oportet, non opus esse, vt causae iustae simul omnes semper concurrant: nam vt alia cessent, vna sufficere potest, vt coniugio aliqui iungantur, quod legitimum & ratum omnino censeri debet, modo
units.tr: Furthermore, the end of marriage must be considered, which is threefold. First, God joined Eve to Adam so that he might have a helper in bearing the troubles of life, which he knew would arise from sin. And this same cause of marriage is not least even today, since it is clear that without it domestic affairs are not happily managed, nor other business conducted well, unless spouses share their cares between them. This is a great proof of divine goodness, that he who knew man would sin prepared a remedy before it happened, by which the punishments of sin might be softened. Of this kind is his creating herbs by which diseases are cured, before these arose from sin. Second, marriage ought to serve at once for propagating and preserving the human race. For although children may also be born from promiscuous and unlawful unions, that generation is not lawful, and so brings confusion and countless other harms, about which there is no place to speak now. From this comes the third end and use of marriage, that it be a remedy for lust, so that the desire to beget children, kindled by forbidden loves, may not carry us away and make us overstep the bounds of justice and honesty. And Paul touches on this end here, the two former ones, which pertained less to its institution, being set aside. But here we must hold that it is not necessary for all the just causes to concur at once: for, the others being absent, one alone can be enough for people to be joined in marriage, which ought to be judged wholly lawful and valid, provided

units.la: debet, modò non peccetur in leges, quas supra commemorauimus. Arguit hoc eorum sententiam, qui inter senes & iam effœtos matrimonium esse negant, aut qui in scortatorū numero eos habent, qui uxores ducunt, quas aut natura steriles, aut alia de causa ad pariendū non idoneas esse sciunt. Hos enim Paulus confutat, qui ut fornicationes vitentur, legitimo coniugio uti docet. Illos autem Dauidis exemplum conuincit, qui in extremo senio & iam frigidus puella Abisagam duxit, quæ quòd illi uxor fuisset legitima, Adonias mortis supplicium meruit, cum eam sibi dari vellet. Nunc potius obseruemus, eos qui coniugium oderunt, aut thoros coniugales adulterijs violant, vel stupris illicitis indulgent, non solum in sacrosanctum Dei institutum, verumetiam in humani generis societatem peccare. Tollunt enim præcipua vitæ huius auxilia, & dum minores molestias fugiunt, graviora incommoda sibi accersunt: ijdem legitimæ propagandæ posteritatis rationem impediunt, spurijs & nothis (qui publici libidinis testes sunt) domus omnes complent, denique nequitiæ fenestras aperiunt, & honestatem publicam profligant.
units.tr: provided only that no sin is committed against the laws we recalled above. This argues against the opinion of those who deny that marriage is possible between old men who are already worn out, or who count among the fornicators those who take wives whom they know to be barren by nature or otherwise unfit for bearing children. For Paul refutes the former, when he teaches that to avoid fornication one should use lawful marriage; and the example of David refutes the latter, who in extreme old age, being already cold, took the girl Abishag to wife; and because she had been his lawful wife, Adonijah earned the penalty of death when he wished to have her given to him. Now let us rather observe that those who hate marriage, or violate the marriage bed by adultery, or indulge in illicit debaucheries, sin not only against God's sacred institution but also against the fellowship of the human race. For they remove the chief aids of this life, and while they flee the lesser discomforts, they bring upon themselves graver ones. The same people hinder the lawful propagation of posterity, fill all their houses with bastards and illegitimate children (who are witnesses of public lust), and finally open the windows to wickedness and overthrow public decency.

units.la: Simul autem docet istorum consideratio, quid in contrahendo matrimonio potissimum specta-ri, & ut huius initia celebrari debeant. Quia enim eius author est Deus, prima religionis cura esse debet, ne sub coniugij prætextu à vero Dei cultu abstrahamur, & fidem illi datam negemus. Huc leges pertinent, quibus olim vetuit, ne qui eius populus dicebantur, cum prophanis gentibus miscee-rentur. Et notus est Malachiæ locus, qui sanctitatem Iuda, id est, dignitatem illam, qua popu-lum Iudaicum Deus ornauerat, ab illis prophanatam fuisse queritur, qui uxores alienigenas duxerant. Et Paulus in posteriori epistola graviter monebat, ne iugum cum infidelibus ducant: eo quòd nulla sit communio lucis cum tenebris, Christo cum Belial. Deinde cum libidinis remedium quæri debeat, curemus, ne illam ipsam in consilium vocemus, & maiorem eius quàm honestatis & rei domesticæ rationem habeamus. Itaq; sopitis affectibus prauis in unum Deum nos respicere conuenit. Admonuit is nos de isto, quando Adamum gravi somno sopiuit, cum ex latere eius costam sumere, & ex ea Euam formare voluit. Nuptias item honestè, piè & cū Dei invocatione facere oportet, adeoq; ad illas Christū ipsum vocare, ut (quod olim in Cana Galilææ fecit) omnem coniugij amaritudinem dulci sui spiritus vino, id est, piis consolationibus temperet. Hæc quia hodie plerique negligunt, quid mirum est, si infelicius cedant, quæ abs q; Deo, unico omnis boni authore, inchoantur coniugia? Reliquum est, ut de coniugum officijs dicatur, quod in sequenti Sermone commodius fiet. Nunc Deum precabimur, ut quod in rerum exordio instituit vitæ humanæ præsidium, omnibus sua benedictione felix & auspicatum faciat, imprimis autem largiatur, ut sponsa IESV CHRISTI simus casta & sancta, & cum illo viuamus atq; regnemus, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: At the same time, the consideration of these people teaches what above all is to be looked at in contracting marriage, and how its beginnings ought to be celebrated. For since God is its author, the first concern of religion must be that we are not drawn away from the true worship of God under the pretext of marriage, and deny the faith given to him. To this belong the laws by which he once forbade that those who were called his people should mix with profane nations. And the passage of Malachi is well known, where he complains that the holiness of Judah, that is, the dignity with which God had adorned the Jewish people, was profaned by those who had taken foreign wives. And Paul in his second letter sternly warned that they should not be yoked with unbelievers, because there is no fellowship of light with darkness, nor of Christ with Belial. Then, since a remedy for lust must be sought, let us take care that we do not call that very lust into counsel, and give it greater weight than honesty and domestic reason. Therefore, with depraved passions put to sleep, it is fitting that we look to the one God alone. He admonished us of this when he put Adam into a deep sleep, when he willed to take a rib from his side and form Eve from it. Likewise weddings ought to be made honourably, piously, and with the invocation of God, and so Christ himself should be called to them, so that (as he once did at Cana of Galilee) he may temper all the bitterness of marriage with the sweet wine of his Spirit, that is, with pious consolations. Since many neglect these things today, what wonder is it if those marriages turn out less happily which are begun without God, the one author of all good? It remains that the duties of spouses be spoken of, which will be done more conveniently in the following sermon. For now we will pray God that he, who in the beginning of things instituted this safeguard of human life, may make it happy and auspicious for all with his blessing, and above all grant that we may be the chaste and holy bride of Jesus Christ, and live and reign with him, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXIII.

units.la: Vxori vir debitam beneuolentiam reddat: similiter autem & vxor viro. Vxor proprium corpus non habet in potestate, sed vir: similiter autem & vir proprium corpus non habet in potestate, sed vxor. Ne fraudate alius alium, nisi si quid ex consensu ad tempus, vt vacetis ieiunio & precibus: & rursus simul conuenite, ne tentet vos Satanas propter incontinentiam vestram. Hoc autem dico ex concessione, non ex imperio. Nam velim omnes homines esse, vt & ipse sum: sed vnusquisq; proprium donum habet ex Deo, alius quidem ita, alius autem ita.
units.tr: Let the husband render to his wife the goodwill she is owed, and likewise the wife to her husband. The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to fasting and prayer; and then come together again, lest Satan tempt you because of your incontinence. I say this by way of concession, not by command. For I wish all men were as I am; but each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that.

units.la: Quemadmodum Deus ex peculiari gratia coniugium instituit, vt eius præsidio adiuti huius vitæ molestias commodius ferre & illicitas vagæ libidinis flammas facilius vitare aut restinguere possimus: ita publicus humani generis hostis omnibus sæculis in hoc fuit, vt coniugij dignitatem prophanaret, & verum eius ipsum aboleret. Non ignorat enim hoc sublato libidinibus fœdis fenestram aperiri, morum honestatem & vitæ sanctimoniam simul omnem calcari, & con-fusionem rerum omnium induci tá rei publicæ quàm domesticæ exitiale. Et quæ illius est aslutia, nô solum carni & mundo deditos intemperantiæ illecebris capit, verumetiam pijs sub ementito religionis prætextu fucum facit, vt in cœlibatu non solum commodius, verumetiam sanctius viui possint sibi persuadeant, adeoq; in illo meritum constituant, cui Deus regni sui hæreditatem promiserit.
units.tr: Just as God in his special grace instituted marriage, so that with its help we might bear the troubles of this life more easily and more readily avoid, or quench, the unlawful flames of wandering lust, so the public enemy of the human race has, in every age, set himself to profane the dignity of marriage and to abolish its true nature. For he does not fail to see that once marriage is removed, a window is opened to foul lusts, all decency of conduct and holiness of life is trampled underfoot at once, and a confusion of all things is brought about, as ruinous to the commonwealth as to the household. And it is his cunning to catch not only those who are given over to the flesh and the world with the allurements of intemperance, but also to deceive the godly under the false pretext of religion, persuading them that they can live not only more conveniently but also more holily in celibacy, and so win merit for themselves in that state, by which God will have promised the inheritance of his kingdom.

units.la: Non temere ergo scripturæ sanctæ coniugium passim magnificè commendant, & Paulus de eodem hîc diligentissimè disserit. Et initiò quidem fatetur, coniugium suas curas atq; incommoda habere, quæ ex peccato in hoc vitæ genus (vt in alia quoq; omnia) irrepserunt: quia tamen maius periculum ex fornicationis licentia nobis imminet, consultissimum esse, vt quisq; propriam vxorem, & quæq; proprium virum habeat. Vbi nuper audiuimus quid fit coniugium, quis eius author, quæ leges, quæ dignitas & in quem finem fit institutum, vt item contrahi & inchoari debeat. Quibus nunc officia coniugū subijciuntur, de quibus ordine cõmodissimo Paulus disserit, de ijs quoq; paucis dicens, de quibus sub religionis prætextu multùm contendebatur.
units.tr: Holy Scripture, then, does not without reason commend marriage everywhere in the highest terms, and Paul discusses it here with the greatest care. At the start he admits that marriage has its cares and inconveniences, which have crept into this way of life, as into everything else, through sin. Nevertheless, because a greater danger threatens us from the license of fornication, he says it is most advisable that each man have his own wife and each woman her own husband. Recently we heard what marriage is, who its author is, what its laws are, what its dignity is, and for what end it was instituted, and how it ought to be contracted and entered upon. Now the duties of spouses are set out, of which Paul treats in a most fitting order, speaking briefly of those points over which, under the pretext of religion, there was much dispute.

units.la: Principio generale præceptum præmittit, quo omnia comprehenduntur, quæ hîc dici possunt. Vxori (inquit) vir debitam benevolentiam reddat: similiter autem & vxor viro. Sensus verborum est, vt quod mutuò sibi invicem debent, fideliter vtrinq; præstent. Benevolentiæ autem vocabulo coniugalia officia omnia complectitur, vt doceat, nihil inter eos coactum esse debere, sed dilectionem & animi propensionem requiri, quæ causa est, vt nihil perinde optemus, quàm ijs rem gratam facere, quibus cum agimus. Deinde debiti meminit, vt omnem excusationis prætextum excludat, quo multi vtuntur, qui se coniugibus suis minus obstrictos esse putant, quòd vel generis nobilitate, vel fortunarum splendore ipsis nô mereantur conferri, aut etiâ ea ætate sint, quæ neq; honore neq; amore sit digna. Et hîc quidem multi sibi ipsis mirificè blandiuntur, multi etiam scurriliter ludunt in coniuges, quarum satietas eos cepit. Cæterum vt ista habeant, coniugij vinculum tam artis conditionibus fidem nostram obstringit, vt nullus alicui excusationi locus sit, quò minus præstare debeas quod promisisti. At quod hîc paucis verbis absoluit Apostolus, id in epistola ad Ephes. 5. cap.diligentius explicat, vbi & vxoris & mariti officia pulchrè distinguit. Etsi enim quoad beneuolentiam aut dilectionem æqualitas inter illos sit, in reliquis tamen vir mulieré præstat, & singulí habent quod obseruent.
units.tr: First he sets down a general precept, under which everything that can be said here is comprehended. "Let the husband," he says, "render to his wife the goodwill she is owed; and likewise the wife to her husband." The sense of the words is that they should faithfully perform towards each other what they owe one another mutually. By the word goodwill he embraces all the duties of marriage, to teach that nothing between them should be forced, but that affection and an inclination of the heart are required; and this is the reason why we should wish nothing more than to please those with whom we deal. Then he mentions what is owed, to exclude every pretext for excuse, which many use who think themselves less bound to their spouses because they do not deserve to be matched with them by the nobility of their birth or the splendour of their fortunes, or because they are of an age that is worthy neither of honour nor of love. Here indeed many flatter themselves wonderfully, and many also jest coarsely about the spouses whose company has begun to pall on them. But whatever they may have, the bond of marriage binds our faith by such strict conditions that there is no room for any excuse for not performing what you have promised. And what the Apostle concludes here in a few words, he explains more fully in Ephesians 5, where he also distinguishes admirably the duties of the wife and of the husband. For although there is equality between them as regards goodwill or love, in other matters the husband excels the woman, and each has something to observe.

units.la: De vxoribus autem sic scribit. Vxores proprijs viris subiectæ essote, vt Domino. Quo præcepto obedientiam cum debito honore aut reuerentia coniunctam requirit, qua omnino opus est, cum sexus iste infirmior fit, quàm vt sibi ipsi in omnibus sufficere possit. Ne tamen singulæ viris quibuscunq; se hoc officium debere putarent, aut viri in mulierem quancunq; temere obtuam sibi imperium sumerent, disserte monet, vt vnaquæq; suo marito obtemperet. Et quia mulieres vt plurimum superbia & ambitione peccant, rationibus aliquot hoc suum præceptum confirmat. Prima est, quod viris perinde vt Domino IESV CHRISTO parere debeant. Quo loco diuinæ institutionis eas admonet, & Dei verba in mentem reuocat, qui Euæ inter cætera dixit: Ad virum tuum erit desiderium tuum, & ipse tibi dominabitur. Vnde sequitur, non posse mulieres sibi in viros ius & imperium vendicare, quin Dei institutum violent, & huius ordinationi resistant. Quod procul dubio Sara mater mulierum credentium obseruauit, quæ (vt Petrus scribit) Abrahamum dominum suum vocare solebat, & inter assiduos labores & pericula continua nunquam se inobedientem aut contumacem præbuit. Secunda ratio à viri dignitate sumitur: Quoniam vir est caput vxoris, vt & Christus est caput ecclesiæ. Vt autem membra, adeoq; corpus totum, capiti obediant, communis sensus iubet. Magis tamen hæc ratio confirmatur Christi & ecclesiæ exemplo, dum inter coniuges eandem eminentiam & subiectionis rationem esse dicit, quæ inter Christum & ecclesiam habetur. Additur his ratio tertia: Et is est qui salutem dat corpori. Hac docet, subiectionem istam vtilem & necessariam esse. Vt enim tota ecclesia & singulorum membrorum eius salus ab vno capite Christo dependet, qui singulis spiritum vitæ distribuit: ita mulieris fama, gloria, incolumitas deniq; omnis in eo consistit, vt fidem viro inuiolatam seruet, eiusq; consilio (de viris cordatis loquitur) sese regendam præbeat, imò importunum quoq; & improbum patienter ferat: quod Abigail in suo Nabale feliciter fecisse legimus. Itaq; cùm mulieres, nisi ecclesiæ membra sint, saluæ esse non possunt, illam imitari studeant, & sicut ecclesia subiecta est Christo, ita & uxores suis viris subiectae sint in omnibus. Vbi tamen de iis modo Paulum loqui putabimus, quae viri pro suo iure imperant, & quae salua conscientia fieri possunt. Ideo ad Colossen. scribens cautionem adhibet: Vt conuenit in Domino. Quapropter si viri iure suo abutantur, & ea praecipiant, quae diuinis legibus, quoad religionem aut morum honestatem, aduersantur, minime illis obedire debent mulieres: quia eadem tunc illorum est ratio, quae impiorum magistratuum, & ideo illis apostolicum illud obijcere possunt: Oportet Deo magis obedire quam hominibus.
units.tr: He writes thus about wives: "Wives, be subject to your own husbands, as to the Lord." By this precept he requires obedience joined with due honour and reverence, which is altogether necessary, since that sex is weaker and cannot suffice for itself in all things. Lest, however, each wife should think she owes this duty to any men whatever, or husbands should rashly claim dominion over any woman whatever, he clearly admonishes that each wife obey her own husband. And because women for the most part sin through pride and ambition, he confirms this precept of his by several reasons. The first is that they ought to obey their husbands just as they obey the Lord Jesus Christ. In this place he reminds them of the divine ordinance and recalls to mind the words of God, who said to Eve among other things: "Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you." From this it follows that women cannot claim for themselves right and authority over men without violating God's institution and resisting his ordinance. Sarah, the mother of believing women, undoubtedly observed this; as Peter writes, she was accustomed to call Abraham her lord, and amid constant labours and continual dangers she never showed herself disobedient or contumacious. The second reason is taken from the dignity of the husband: "Because the husband is the head of the wife, as Christ is the head of the Church." Now that the members, and so the whole body, should obey the head, common sense dictates. Yet this reason is confirmed more strongly by the example of Christ and the Church, when he says that between spouses there is the same eminence and the same manner of subjection as obtains between Christ and the Church. To these is added a third reason: "And he is the one who gives life to the body." By this he teaches that such subjection is useful and necessary. For just as the whole Church, and the salvation of each of its members, depends on the one head, Christ, who distributes the spirit of life to each, so a woman's reputation, her glory, and in short her whole well-being consist in keeping faith inviolate with her husband, and in letting herself be ruled by his counsel (he speaks of wise men), and even in patiently bearing with him when he is troublesome and wicked, as we read that Abigail did happily with her Nabal. Therefore, since women cannot be safe unless they are members of the Church, let them strive to imitate it, and just as the Church is subject to Christ, so let wives be subject to their husbands in all things. Yet we must think that Paul speaks only of those things which husbands command by their right and which can be done with a clear conscience. Hence, writing to the Colossians, he adds a caution: "as is fitting in the Lord." Wherefore, if husbands abuse their right and command things that are contrary to the divine laws, in matters of religion or of moral decency, wives ought by no means to obey them, since their position is then the same as that of ungodly magistrates, and so they may object to them that apostolic saying: "We ought to obey God rather than men."

units.la: Inde ad mariti officium transit Paulus, dicens: Viri diligite uxores vestras. Vno verbo imperium illud, quod ipsis dedit Deus, moderatur aut temperat. Nam qui diligunt, ius suum non tyrannice vrgent cum eorum detrimento quibus praesunt, sed tam ipsis quam famae & fortunis ipsorum consultum[?] volunt. Exemplum eius rei in parentibus extat, qui cum in liberos suos imperium naturae legibus confirmatum habeant, eo tamen ita vtuntur, vt pia indulgentia illis potius seruire quam dominari videri possint, dum indefesso labore et assidua cura illorum commodis inuigilant. Quem affectum in pijs quoque magistratibus videre licet, qui tunc demum se recte imperauisse putant, si populi incolumitatem prouehant atq; tueantur. Eodem igitur animo maritos in uxores suas praeditos esse vult Apostolus: & quia inter homines vix vnquam dilectio reperitur, quae omnibus numeris absoluta sit, rursus ad Christi exemplum reuertitur, quod viris imitandum proposuit, vt quis modus ipsis tenendus sit, intelligant. Diligite (inquit) uxores vestras, sicut & Christus dilexit ecclesiam, & semetipsum exposuit pro ea, vt eam sanctificaret purgans lauacro aquae per Verbum: vt sisteret eam sibi gloriosam, Ecclesiam nimirum non habentem maculam aut rugam, aut quicquam eiusmodi, sed vt esset sancta & inculpata. Diligenter Christi exemplum tractat, quia multa continet, quae vt nos de aeterna salutis ratione admonent, ita viros euidentissime docent, quam tenere quamq; indulgenter uxores suas diligere debeant. Summi enim & tenerrimi amoris argumentum est, quod semetipsum ille pro ecclesia sua in mortem tradidit. Nemo (dicebat ipse) maiorem dilectionem habet, quam vt ponat animam suam pro amicis suis. At non pro nobis, qui amici eramus, sed pro hostibus suis ille mortuus est, vt nos sibi amicos faceret. Et vt Pauli verbis insistamus, pro ecclesia vitam suam deposuit, vt eam, quae multis modis foedata erat, & (vt in Ezechiele habetur) in sanguinibus suis proculcata iacebat, proprio sanguine ablutam sibi ipsi sponsam faceret, purum & sanctam, cum qua omnes regni sui coelestis thesauros communes haberet. Quid ergo non debent uxoribus suis mariti, si Christum ipsos imitari conuenit? Aut cur earum morositatem & quae sexui isti agnata sunt vitia impatientius ferant, quando in nostris sceleribus ferendis Christus tanta indulgentia vsus est? Cur deniq; eas fastidiant, ex quibus, licet difficillimae sint, aliquid tamen commodi recipere possunt, cum tam dura tamq; iniqua passus sit Dei Filius, vt nos sibi coiungeret, ex quibus nihil boni, quam quod ipse prius dederit, sperare possumus? Etsi vero exemplum hoc omnia contineat, quae hic dici possunt, aliud tamen addit Paulus, quod in semetipsis singuli obseruare possunt, vt no[n] opus sit oculos alio conuertere. Debent (inquit) viri diligere uxores suas, vt sua ipsorum corpora. Qui enim diligit suam uxorem, seipsum diligit, &c. Id vero non ex semetipso fingit, sed Christum de coniugibus dixisse sciebat: Erunt duo in carne una. Neq; aliter possunt sentire, qui primam mulierem ex viri latere sumptam esse, & coniuges indissolubili vinculo constringi cogitant. Itaq; in naturae leges ab illis grauissime peccatur, quicunq; coniuges suas oderunt, aut eas inhumanius tractant. Quis enim (vt in Pauli verbis pergamus) vnquam suam ipsius carnem odio habuit? Aut quis in corpus proprium mox ferrum stringit, si vel hoc totum aut aliquod eius membrum vitiosum esse viderit? Qui id faciunt, ij de semetipsis animi alienati indicium praebent, neq; in illis caput suo officio amplius fungitur. Cur ergo mentis suae compotes aut uxorum capita dicantur, qui absq; ratione in eas saeuiunt, aut eas ignominiosius habent, quas pro cofortibus suis & omnis fortunae socijs agnoscere debebant? Et cum inter ethnicos olim reperti sint, qui fidem coniugalem cum vitae periculo sanctissime custodierint, merito suae perfidiae & inhumanitatis pudere debebat eos, qui cum Christi discipulos profiteantur, eius exemplum turpissime negligunt. At cum vitium hoc nimis vulgare sit hodie, nemo opinor me accusabit, quod prolixius paulo de his egerim. Nunc tamen ad reliqua transeamus.
units.tr: Paul then turns to the duty of the husband, saying: "Husbands, love your wives." In one word he tempers, or moderates, the authority that God has given them. For those who love do not press their right tyrannically to the harm of those they rule, but look after both the persons and the reputation and fortunes of those in their charge. An example of this is found in parents, who have authority over their children, confirmed by the laws of nature, yet use it in such a way that they seem to serve their children by a dutiful indulgence rather than to lord it over them, while they watch over their welfare with tireless labour and constant care. This same affection may be seen in godly magistrates, who think they have ruled rightly only when they promote and protect the safety of the people. Therefore the Apostle wants husbands to be disposed in this same spirit towards their wives. And since among men there is hardly ever to be found a love that is perfect in every respect, he returns again to the example of Christ, which he sets before husbands to imitate, so that they may understand what measure they should keep. "Love your wives," he says, "as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself up for it, that he might sanctify it, cleansing it with the washing of water by the word, that he might present it to himself glorious, the church, that is, not having spot or wrinkle, or any such thing, but that it should be holy and blameless." He treats the example of Christ carefully, because it contains many things which remind us of the reason of our eternal salvation, and at the same time it most clearly teaches husbands how tenderly and indulgently they ought to love their wives. For it is the proof of the highest and most tender love that he delivered himself up to death for his church. "No one," he said himself, "has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends." But he died not for us, who were friends, but for his enemies, that he might make us his friends. And to keep to Paul's words: he laid down his life for the church, so that he might make for himself a bride washed with her own blood, the church which had been defiled in many ways and (as is written in Ezekiel) lay trampled in its own blood; a pure and holy bride, with whom he would share all the treasures of his heavenly kingdom. What then ought husbands not to owe to their wives, if it befits them to imitate Christ? Or why should they bear more impatiently the peevishness and the faults that belong to that sex, when Christ used such great forbearance in bearing our wickedness? Why, finally, should they despise those from whom, however difficult they may be, they can yet receive some benefit, when the Son of God suffered things so hard and so unjust in order to join us to himself, from whom we can hope for nothing good except what he has first bestowed? Although this example contains everything that can be said here, Paul adds another point, which each man can observe in himself, so that there is no need to turn our eyes elsewhere. "Husbands ought to love their wives," he says, "as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself," and so on. He does not invent this from himself, but knew that Christ had spoken of spouses: "They shall be two in one flesh." Nor can those think otherwise who consider that the first woman was taken from the side of the man, and that spouses are bound together by an indissoluble bond. Therefore those who hate their wives, or treat them too inhumanly, sin most gravely against the laws of nature. For who (to continue with Paul's words) has ever hated his own flesh? Or who immediately draws the sword against his own body if he sees that the whole of it, or some member of it, is diseased? Those who do so show the sign of a mind estranged from itself, and in them the head no longer performs its function. Why then should those be called sane, or the heads of their wives, who rage against them without reason, or treat with greater contempt those whom they ought to acknowledge as their companions and sharers in every fortune? And although among the heathen there were once found some who kept their marriage faith most faithfully even at the risk of their lives, it should shame those who profess to be disciples of Christ, yet shamefully neglect his example, for their faithlessness and inhumanity. But since this vice is far too common today, I suppose no one will accuse me of having dealt with these matters at somewhat greater length. Now, however, let us pass on to the rest.

units.la: Pergit enim Paulus, & de consuetudine ipsoq; congressu coniugali diligentius agit, de qua vehementer inter Corinthios contendebatur. Nam etsi plerique non negarent ea, quae hucusque de coniugum officijs dicta sunt, neque etiam aperte diuortium facerent, frequentius tamen secubabant: quae causa erat, vt & amor coniugalis frigesceret, & in libidines aut saltem concupiscentias foedas delaberentur. Occurrit ergo, & vt huic malo medeatur, ostendit, eos qui coniugij vinculo sese obstrinxerunt, non sui iuris, sed vnumquemque in alterius potestate esse, ideoq; non licere, vt quis ex priuato arbitrio aliquid hic statuat. Est nobis diligenter obseruanda haec Spiritus sancti diligentia, qui eo vsque se demittit, vt de ijs sermonem instituat, quae parum pudica aut honesta videri poterant: facit tamen id, quod res ita postularet. Est enim hoc fere commune vi-tium, quod qui non serio Dei timore retinentur, vbi libidinem suam expleuerunt, vxores suas fastidire & ad vagas libidines animum adijcere incipiunt. Deinde eos, qui reliquis sanctiores haberi volunt, plerunq; hypocrisis & fictae sanctimoniae fucus seducit, vt in eo meritum vitae aeter-nae consistere putent, si a coniugum congressu abstineant. Quibus adde periculum, cuius paulo ante meminimus. Nam vt D. Ambrosius annotauit, qui compendia quaerunt, saepius errare solent, & dum a licitis abstinent ad illicita & inconcessa delabuntur. Docet ergo Apostolus quid in hoc casu fieri debeat, & summa consilij aut praecepti eius est: Ne fraudate alius alium. Fraus vel fraudatio est, quando praetextu aliquo falso aut dolo malo interuertitur quod alicui debetur. Et genium fraudare dicuntur, qui quoad appetitum & honestam voluptatem non satisfaciunt naturae. Id ad debitum coniugale non inepte transfert Apostolus, vt ostendat in iustitiae & aequitatis legem eos peccare, qui a coniuge ex priuato arbitrio abstinent, nulla graui & iusta causa intercedente. Id vero probat his verbis: Vxor proprium corpus non habet in potestate, sed vir: simi-liter autem & vir proprium corpus non habet in potestate, sed vxor. Ex eo igitur colligit fraudem fieri coniugi, cui quod alter illi debet officium negatur. Facit autem hic quoque locus contra polygamiam. Si enim vir proprij corporis ius aut potestatem non habet, iniquus fuerit, si illud aut eius partem alteri addixerit. Imprimis vero adulterij quoque crimen hoc argumento amplificatur. Nec enim illud committi potest, quin aut corpus tuum, quod coniugi debetur, alteri prostituas, aut alterius corpore ad tuam libidinem abutaris. Quod si vterque coniugio astrictus fuerit, dupliciter vtrinque peccatur. Itaque adulterium cum furti crimine coniunctum est, & tanto grauius est furto, quanto pretiosius est corpus nostrum fortunis omnibus, quae vt illi seruiant destinatae sunt. Vide Proverb. 6.
units.tr: For Paul goes on, and deals more carefully with the practice of conjugal intercourse itself, about which there was great dispute among the Corinthians. For although many would not deny the things said so far about the duties of spouses, and did not openly seek divorce, they nevertheless lived apart more often, and this was the cause both of the cooling of conjugal love and of their slipping into lusts, or at least foul desires. He therefore meets the difficulty, and to remedy this evil he shows that those who have bound themselves by the bond of marriage are not their own masters, but each is in the power of the other; and therefore it is not lawful for anyone to decide this matter by private judgement. We must carefully observe this diligence of the Holy Spirit, who stoops so far as to discuss things which might seem to be little modest or honourable; yet he does so because the matter required it. For it is a fairly common vice that those who are not restrained by a serious fear of God, once they have satisfied their lust, begin to loathe their wives and to direct their minds to wandering lusts. Then those who want to be thought holier than the rest are often led astray by hypocrisy and the paint of feigned holiness, so that they think the merit of eternal life consists in this, if they abstain from intercourse with their spouses. To these add the danger we mentioned a little while ago. For, as Ambrose observed, those who seek shortcuts are wont to go wrong more often, and while they abstain from what is lawful they slip into what is unlawful and forbidden. The Apostle therefore teaches what ought to be done in this case, and the sum of his counsel or precept is: "Do not defraud one another." Defrauding, or fraud, occurs when what is owed to someone is taken away under some false pretext or by evil deceit. And men are said to defraud their own nature when they do not satisfy it in respect of appetite and honest pleasure. The Apostle aptly transfers this to the conjugal debt, to show that those sin against the law of justice and fairness who abstain from their spouse by private judgement, with no grave and just cause standing in the way. He proves this by these words: "The wife does not have power over her own body, but the husband; likewise also the husband does not have power over his own body, but the wife." From this he infers that fraud is done to a spouse when the duty which the other owes is denied. This passage also tells against polygamy. For if a husband has no right or power over his own body, he will be unjust if he gives that, or any part of it, to another. Above all, the crime of adultery too is magnified by this argument. For it cannot be committed without either prostituting your body, which is owed to your spouse, to another, or misusing another's body for your own lust. And if both are bound in marriage, each party sins doubly. Thus adultery is joined with the crime of theft, and it is as much graver than theft as our body is more precious than all the goods which are destined to serve it. See Proverbs 6.

units.la: Caeterum nunc Paulum audiamus, quid in causa hac, de qua agere coepit, obseruari debeat. Ne fraudate (inquit) alius alium, nisi si quid ex consensu ad tempus, vt vacetis ieiunio & precibus: & rursus simul conuenite, ne tentet vos Satan propter incontinentiam vestram. Non rigide praecipit, ne vnquam secubent coniuges, sed modum & rationem praescribit, ne quid periculi maioris inde nascatur, & quatuor hic obseruanda esse monet. Primum, vt ex vtriusque coniugis consensu hoc fiat, quem necessarium esse constat, cum neuter suum corpus in sua habeat potestate. Deinde ad tempus modo id facere iubet. Nihil ergo locus iste illis patrocinatur, qui nouum diuortij genus excogitarunt, vt nimirum durante quidem coniugij vinculo (quod illi indissolubile esse volunt) mensa tamen & thori consortium prorsus aboleatur. At hic de eo agitur, quod ad breue duntaxat tempus obseruari debuit. Tertiò causa quoq; exprimitur, ne quid leuiter & temere fiat, vt fere solent, quos coniugis satietas iam caepit, & ideo occasiones eiusmodi auide venantur. Itaq; vnam modo causam permittit, vt nimirum vacare possint ieiunijs & precibus. Vbi ne quis colligat perpetuò a thori consuetudine abstinendum esse, cum assiduè & indesinenter orare atq; temperantiae studere debeamus, tenendum est. Paulum de solennibus ieiunijs & precibus loqui, quae antiquitus publico ecclesiae decreto instituebantur, si vel periculum aliquod publicum imminebat, vel dere aliqua graviori & ad publicam omnium salutem pertinente erat deliberandum. Exempla eius rei apud Ioelem & Ionam habentur, quibus ea addi possunt quae in Legis promulgatione Deus fieri voluit, & quod in primitiua ecclesia obseruatum fuisse scimus, si qui ad apostolatum aut publicum ministerium ordinari debuerunt. Sciebant enim absq; Dei auxilio nihil feliciter inchoari aut perfi-ci, ad hoc autem impetrandu precibus ex fide & nō fucata animi deuotione manantibus opus esse:
units.tr: Let us now hear what Paul bids us observe in this matter, which he has begun to treat. "Do not defraud one another," he says, "except by consent for a time, that you may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again, lest Satan tempt you because of your incontinence." He does not strictly command that spouses never live apart, but he prescribes a measure and a rule, so that no greater danger arises from it, and he warns that four things are to be observed here. First, that this be done by the consent of both spouses, which is shown to be necessary, since neither has power over his own body. Second, he orders that it be done only for a time. Nothing in this passage therefore supports those who have devised a new kind of divorce, by which, while the bond of marriage remains (which they want to be indissoluble), table and bed are nonetheless wholly separated. Here the subject is what ought to be observed for a short time only. Third, a cause is also stated, so that nothing is done lightly and rashly, as usually happens with those whom satiety of their spouse has already begun to seize, and who therefore eagerly hunt for such opportunities. Thus he permits only one cause, namely that they may be free for fasting and prayer. Lest anyone conclude from this that abstinence from the marriage bed must be permanent, since we ought to pray constantly and without ceasing and to devote ourselves to temperance, it must be kept in mind that Paul speaks of solemn fasts and prayers, which in ancient times were instituted by public decree of the Church, whether some public danger was threatening or some weightier matter touching the common welfare of all had to be deliberated. Examples of this are found in Joel and Jonah, to which may be added what God wished to be done at the promulgation of the Law, and what we know was observed in the primitive Church when persons were to be ordained to the apostolate or to public ministry. For they knew that nothing could be begun or brought to a good end without the help of God, and that to obtain this help prayers were needed that flow from faith and not from feigned devotion of the mind.

units.la: Vt ergo illa feruentiores essent, ieiunia indicebant, non qualia in ciborum discrimine homines superstitiosi constituunt, sed in quibus ab omni cibo, & simul a thori consuetudine alijsque gaudijs per se licitis abstinebatur. Ideo Ioel dicebat: Egrediatur sponsus de thalamo suo, & sponsa de velo suo. Ad hunc igitur morem Paulus respiciens, permittit ut si quid huius accidat, secubare possint coniuges. At hinc nos generalem doctrinam petamus, interdum concessis quoque gaudijs & voluptatibus abstinendum esse, ut rebus diuinis liberius vacare, & preces ad Deum ardentiores fundere possimus. Est ergo detestabilis nostri seculi securitas, quando passim quidem Deus ira sua indicia exerit, & tantumnon fulminat aduersus peccata hominum, pauci tamen sunt, qui ab illis abstineant, quae diuersis Dei legibus prohibentur, & cum publico scandalo coniuncta sunt. Sed quia haec alterius loci sunt, nunc quartum videamus, quo Paulus monet, ut qui propter preces publicas ad tempus secubuerunt, mox rursus in vnum conueniant, & ita coniugij vinculum perpetuo ratum manere vult, ut & thori coniugalis consortium. Causam huic admonitioni addit: Ne tentet vos Satanas propter incontinentiam vestram. Quibus verbis ostendit, multo maius periculum nobis imminere, si quid praeter Dei institutum ex priuato arbitrio instituamus, & proinde ab hoc non temere esse discedendum.
units.tr: So, to make those prayers more fervent, they proclaimed fasts, not of the kind that superstitious men set up by distinctions of foods, but fasts in which one abstained from all food and at the same time from the use of the marriage bed and other joys that are in themselves lawful. Hence Joel said: "Let the bridegroom go out of his chamber, and the bride out of her closet." Looking back to this custom, Paul therefore permits spouses, if something of this kind should occur, to live apart. But from this let us draw a general teaching: at times one must abstain even from permitted pleasures and delights, so that we may be freer to attend to divine things and pour out our prayers to God more ardently. Therefore the security of our age is detestable, since God everywhere displays signs of his wrath and almost thunders against the sins of men, and yet there are few who abstain from those things which are forbidden by the various laws of God and are joined with public scandal. But since these matters belong to another place, let us now look at the fourth point, in which Paul advises that those who have lived apart for a time because of public prayers should soon come together again in one place; and he wants the bond of marriage to remain firm forever, and the fellowship of the marriage bed as well. He adds a reason for this admonition: "lest Satan tempt you because of your incontinence." By these words he shows that a much greater danger threatens us if we introduce anything beyond God's institution by private judgment, and therefore we must not rashly depart from this.

units.la: Est autem obseruanda diligenter locutio, qua Satanam & incontinentiam nostram coniungit. Ut enim ille mendax & homicida est, atque instar leonis rugientis quaeris quem deuoret: ita fere ex nobis captat occasiones, quibus nos circumueniat & in nassam illiciat. Ideo Iacobus dicebat, vnumquenque dum tentatur, a propria concupiscentia abstrahi atq; inescari. Multo igitur studio & excubijs assiduis opus est. Quid enim nobis tutum relinquitur, quando tunc quoq; nobis insidias struit Satan, quando circa ea occupati sumus, quae ad Dei cultum spectant, & per se sanctissima sunt? Semper ergo in animis & auribus nostris illud Christi sonet: Vigilate & orate, ne in-tretis in tentationem, &c. Quod si vero coniugibus propter preces & ieiunia publica secubantibus ita Satan insidiatur, ut non tutum sit illos diutius separari, quid obsecro apud eos fieri putemus, qui in ipso flore aetatis temerario coelibatus voto sese obstringunt, seq; ipsos illius insidijs exponunt, quando nulla grauiori causa vrgentur? Sed de hoc in sequentibus dicetur.
units.tr: The manner of speech by which he joins Satan and our incontinence must be carefully noted. For just as he is a liar and a murderer, and as a roaring lion he seeks whom he may devour, so he commonly seizes upon occasions from us by which he may get round us and lure us into his snare. Hence James said that each one, when he is tempted, is drawn away and enticed by his own lust. Much zeal and constant watchfulness are therefore needed. For what is safe for us, when Satan lays snares for us even then, when we are occupied with those things which pertain to the worship of God and are in themselves most holy? Therefore let that saying of Christ always sound in our minds and ears: "Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation," etc. But if Satan so lies in wait for spouses who live apart for public prayers and fasts that it is not safe for them to be separated for longer, what, I ask, do we suppose happens among those who in the very flower of their age bind themselves by a rash vow of celibacy, and expose themselves to his snares, when they are pressed by no weightier cause? But this will be discussed in what follows.

units.la: Nam poterant aliqui ista calumniari, quasi iis, qui per se ad libidinem nimium proni erant, habenas laxaret Apostolus: & fortassis non deerant etiam, qui hac admonitione ad immoderatum consuetudinis coniugalis vsum abuterentur: Ideo correctionem subijcit, qua hoc suum consilium moderatur & temperat, sic inquiens: Hoc autem dico ex concessione, non ex imperio, &c. Debet hoc ad ea referri, quod iusserat vnumquenq; propriam vxorem, & vnamquanq; proprium virum habere: item ne temere consuetudinem coniugalem dirimant, sed ad tempus modo, si quae maior necessitas preces ardentiores, & propter has carnis quoq; disciplinâ auste riore requirit. In Graeco [?]κατὰ συγγνώμην[?] se loqui ait, quam pleriq; indulgentiam interpretantur: sed quia haec fere in illis locum habet, quae per se vitiosa sunt, & proinde venia opus habent, ego potius Paulum ad Dei consilium respicere puto, qui coniugium nobis instar medicinae esse voluit, qua caro ad libidinem proclivius frenetur, ne quid aduersus honestatem & sanctitatem, cuius nos studiosissimos esse conuenit, designemus. Itaq; verborum sensus est: Nolim mea haec sic accipi, quasi ex imperio omnes homines ad coniugium, & ne vnquam a coniugibus suis separentur, cogere velim. Scio enim hac conditione matrimonium esse institutum, vt si quis propter singulare castitatis donum illo non habeat opus, illi ab eo prorsus abstinere liceat. At ista moneo, vt communis infirmitatis memores, non temere negligatis remedium a Deo concessum, & quo salua conscientia simul & sanctitate Christiana quilibet vti potest: ne forte nimium vobis ipsis tribuendo in grauius periculum delabamini. Interim si cui hoc diuinitus datum est, per me licet dono suo vtatur. Imo velim ego omnes homines in hac re mei similes esse: sed vnusquisq; proprium donum habet ex Deo: alius quidem vt virginitatem castam corporis simul & animi custodire possit: alius vero, vt coniugium sancte colat, & ita quoq; Deo gratus atq; acceptus sit. Quapropter quisque pro doni sui ratione vitam suam instituat, non autem temere alijs prescribat, &c. Idem ergo hic Paulus dicit, quod Christus, qui discipulis dicentibus, expedire ne quis matrimonium contrahat, respondit: Non omnes capiunt verbum hoc, sed quibus datum est. Sunt enim eunuchi, qui ex matris vtero nati sunt ita: & sunt eunuchi,qui castrati sunt ab hominibus:& sunt eunuchi,qui seipsos castrarunt propter regnum cœlorum : Qui potest capere,capiat. Quibus verbis diserte admonet,continentiæ donum peculiare esse, & proinde neminem sibi ipsi, nedum aliis legem perpetuam præscribere posse. Vnde sequitur,nimium confidentes atq; temerarios esse, qui vel alios ad continentiam perpetuam cogere instituunt,aut hanc non prius exploratis suis viribus vouent.
units.tr: For some could have calumniated these words, as if the Apostle were loosening the reins for those who were already too prone to lust, and perhaps there were not lacking those who would abuse this admonition for an immoderate use of the conjugal relation. Therefore he adds a correction by which he moderates and tempers his counsel, saying: "I say this by way of concession, not of command, etc." This must be referred to what he had enjoined, that each should have his own wife and each woman her own husband; likewise that they must not rashly break off the conjugal union, but only for a time, if some greater necessity requires more fervent prayers, and for the sake of these also a stricter discipline of the flesh. He says that he speaks "by way of concession" [κατὰ συγγνώμην], which many interpret as indulgence; but since this generally applies to those things which are in themselves faulty, and therefore need pardon, I think rather that Paul is looking to the counsel of God, who wished marriage to be for us like a medicine by which the flesh is more readily restrained from lust, so that we may not do anything against honesty and holiness, to which we ought most eagerly to devote ourselves. So the meaning of his words is this: "I would not have my words taken as if I wished by command to force all men to marriage, and to forbid them ever to be separated from their spouses. For I know that marriage was instituted on this condition, that if anyone, because of the singular gift of chastity, has no need of it, it is wholly lawful for him to abstain from it. But I advise these things so that, mindful of our common weakness, you do not rashly neglect the remedy granted by God, which anyone may use with a good conscience and with Christian holiness, lest perhaps by trusting too much in yourselves you fall into a greater danger. Meanwhile, if anyone has been given this by God, let him use his gift through me. Indeed I would wish all men to be like me in this matter; but each one has his own gift from God: one indeed so that he may keep his virginity chaste in body and mind, another so that he may holily honour marriage, and thus also be pleasing and acceptable to God. Therefore let each order his life according to the measure of his gift, and not rashly prescribe for others," etc. Paul therefore says the same thing here that Christ said, when the disciples said that it was not expedient for anyone to marry: "Not all receive this saying, but those to whom it is given. For there are eunuchs who were born so from their mother's womb; and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by men; and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven. He who is able to receive it, let him receive it." By these words he clearly warns that the gift of continence is a particular one, and therefore that no one can prescribe a perpetual law not only for others but even for himself. Whence it follows that those are too confident and rash who either undertake to compel others to perpetual continence, or vow it without first testing their own strength.

units.la: Debebant ergo istum locū diligentius inspexisse veteres,qui in celebrandis virginitatis laudibus eo usq; processerunt, ut coniugiū non obscure damnarint, quasi per se vitiosum sit,& perfectionem Christianam impediat. Abusi sunt illi exemplo Pauli qui omnes homines sibi similes esse optat: interim non observarunt, ea mox subijci, quae ipsorum sententiae aduersantur. Optauit enim hoc Apostolus, non quòd matrimonium minus sanctum esse iudicaret, sed (ut initio Cap.huius di-sum[?] est) quòd eos liberius viuere & ad ferendas persecutiones (quae tunc passim feruebant) expeditiores esse videret, quos nulla coniugum & liberorum cura grauabat. Ideo pro comuni piorum more, voluisset omnes tanti boni participes fieri. Simul tamen,ne quis suo exemplo temere abutatur,diuersitatis donorū eos admonet,& (ut paulo ante diximus) coniugium quoq; inter Dei dona numerat. Nihil ergo agunt, qui exempla huius generis vndiq; colligunt, ut impurum illum atq; infelicem caelibatum, quem Papatus genuit, vel ecclesiarum ministros, vel quibuscunq; aliis obtrudant. Nam ut maximè constaret, Mosem, Prophetas, Apostolos simul omnes & primitiuae ecclesiae episcopos caelibes vixisse, non tamen ex illorum exemplis doctrina aut generalis regula constituti posset, ad cuius observationem omnes alij astringerentur. Quoniam nulla exemplorum authoritas est, nisi quod factum est, ex Dei voluntate factum esse probaueris, & legem protuleris, quae illius imitatio alijs praecipiatur. At ut veteres omnes inspiciamus, constat Mosem & Aaronem vxores habuisse, multos item ex prophetarum numero, ut & plerosq; Apostolorum, ut infra Cap.nono Paulus ipse testatur. Quin ergo huius doctrinam potius nostri aduersarij obseruant, qua diserte monet, ut episcopus vnius vxoris consortio contentus vitam honestam transigat? Sed dum semel conceptam opinione tueri satagunt, multiplicem errorem in ecclesiam inuexerunt. Primò enim Virginitatem absq; Dei verbo ita commendarunt, ut multi in illa cultum Dei & salutis meritum consistere putauerint. Hinc factum, ut multi non exploratis suis viribus illam vouerent, aliqui etiam suos ad eiusmodi vota facienda cogerent. Et dum ecclesiarum ministris coniugio interdixerunt, puniuit Deus iniquissimam istam tyrannidem, ut & illi fœdis libidinibus totum ordinem ecclesiasticum prophanarent, & multi a ministerio hucusq; abhorruerint, qui sibi laqueum noluerunt inijci. Caruit ergo multis bonis ministris ecclesia,ijs autem referta atq; grauata[?] fuit, qui sacra omnia in contemptu adduxerunt, & toti populo pessimi exempli fuerunt authores. Moueat horum consideratio eos,qui ex sordibus istis emerserunt,ne quam illas reducendi occasionem admittant. Omnes vero in suam vocationem intenti sint, & Dei prouidentiam diligenter obseruent, qui dona sua prudenter & probe pro nostro captu distribuit: & quamuis non omnia omnibus largiatur, neminem tamen omnino negligit. Singuli ergo suis bene utantur, ut olim de illis rationem reddere possint IESV CHRISTO, Domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: The ancient writers ought therefore to have examined this passage more carefully. In praising virginity they went so far that they plainly condemned marriage, as if it were evil in itself and an obstacle to Christian perfection. They misused the example of Paul, who wishes all people to be like himself, yet they did not notice that the words immediately following contradict their opinion. For the Apostle wished this not because he judged marriage less holy, but (as at the beginning of this chapter has been said) because he saw that those whom no care of spouse and children weighed down lived more freely and were more ready to bear persecutions, which then raged everywhere. Therefore, following the common custom of the godly, he would have wished all to share in so great a good. At the same time, however, so that no one should rashly misuse his example, he reminds them of the diversity of gifts, and (as we said a little earlier) he counts marriage too among the gifts of God. Those therefore labour in vain who gather examples of this kind from everywhere, in order to press upon ministers of the Church, or upon anyone else, that impure and unhappy celibacy which the Papacy brought forth. For even if it were fully established that Moses, the Prophets, all the Apostles and the bishops of the primitive Church lived unmarried, no doctrine or general rule could be set up from their examples, binding all others to observe it. For there is no authority in examples unless you prove that what was done was done by the will of God, and bring forward a law commanding that it be imitated by others. But if we look at all the ancients, it is clear that Moses and Aaron had wives, as did many of the number of the prophets, and most of the Apostles, as Paul himself testifies in chapter nine below. Why then do our opponents not rather observe the teaching of this same Paul, who plainly bids a bishop to be content with the company of one wife and to live an honourable life? But while they strive to defend an opinion once conceived, they have introduced many errors into the Church. First, they so commended virginity apart from the Word of God that many thought the worship of God and the merit of salvation consisted in it. Hence it came about that many took vows of it without testing their own strength, and some even compelled their people to make such vows. And while they forbade marriage to the ministers of the churches, God punished this most unjust tyranny: those men profaned the whole ecclesiastical order with foul lusts, and many have until now shrunk from the ministry, not wishing to have a snare put upon them. So the Church has lacked many good ministers, and has been filled and burdened with those who brought all sacred things into contempt and became authors of a most wicked example to the whole people. Let the consideration of these men move those who have emerged from those filthy practices not to admit any occasion of bringing them back. Let all, however, be intent upon their own calling and diligently observe the providence of God, who distributes his gifts wisely and well, according to our capacity; and although he does not bestow all things on all, yet he neglects no one at all. Let each therefore use well what is his, so that one day they may be able to give account of them to Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXIIII.
units.tr: Homily 34.

units.la: Dico autem cœlibibus & viduis, bonum eis est si manserint, ut ego. Quòd si se non continent: matrimonium contrahant: nam me-lius est matrimonium contrahere, quàm uri. Iis autem qui matri-monio iuncti sunt, denuntio non ego, sed Dominus: Uxor à viro ne discedito. Quòd si etiam discesserit, maneat innupta, aut viro re-conciliator: Et vir uxorem ne dimittito.
units.tr: I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain as I am. But if they cannot contain themselves, let them marry, for it is better to marry than to burn. To those who are already joined in marriage I give this charge, not I but the Lord: let the wife not depart from her husband. But if she does depart, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. And let the husband not put away his wife.

units.la: Paulus ad quæstiones de causis quibusdam matrimonialibus à Corinthijs propositas itan-sponder[?], ut simul diligenter de omnibus differat, quæ ad matrimonium pertinent, & in eo colendo obseruari debent. Causa huius diligentiæ est, quòd hinc tota fere hominis vita adeoq; rei-pub.etiam salus dependet. Nam coniugio inter homines bene rectè constituto, liberi quoque melius educantur, affinitates fido amore coeunt, & minori negotio publica honestas conseruatur. E contra vbi coniugiorum dignitas nulla est, ibi morum licentia regnat, quæ & ecclesiam turbat, & rempub. tandem euertit. Primum igitur docuit, sicut à Deo constitutum esse, ut vitandæ for-nicationis causa quisq; propriam vxorem, & quæque proprium maritum habeat. Inde vero ad coniugum officia transitum fecit, quorum hæc summa est, ut mutuo sese ament, fidem utrinque datam sanctè colant, & meminerint se non suì iuris esse, neq; proprium corpus in potestate habere, curent denique ne quocunque prætextu seseparentur, & ita diabolo ipsos tentandi occasionem præbeant. Sequitur nunc præsens hic locus, quo de duobus disserit: de secundis nimirum nuptiis, & de iis qui temere à coniugibus secessionem faciunt.
units.tr: Paul, answering the questions the Corinthians put to him about certain matters of marriage, deals carefully with everything that pertains to marriage and ought to be observed in cultivating it. The reason for this care is that almost the whole of a person's life, and even the welfare of the commonwealth, depends on it. For when marriage between people is rightly ordered, children also are better brought up, relatives are joined in faithful love, and public decency is more easily preserved with less trouble. On the other hand, where there is no dignity in marriage, there license of morals reigns, which both disturbs the Church and in the end overturns the commonwealth. Paul therefore first taught that it was ordained by God that each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband, to avoid fornication. Then he passed on to the duties of spouses, the sum of which is this: that they love one another, keep the pledge of faith given on both sides sacredly, and remember that they are not their own masters and do not have their own bodies at their disposal; and finally, that they take care not to separate on any pretext, lest they give the devil an occasion to tempt them. Now follows the present passage, in which he discusses two matters: namely second marriages, and those who rashly make a separation from their spouses.

units.la: Erant enim, qui etsi coniugium diuinitus institutum & omnibus hominibus concessum esse, negare non possent, nefas tamen esse dicebant, post prioris coniugis mortem, ad secundas nuptias animum adiicere & nouo vinculo obstringi. Id enim incontinentiæ inexcusabilis argumentum esse putabant, si qui coniugii curas atq; molestias jam expertus erat, eidem periculo se rursus obii-cere. Et notum est Epigramma Græcum quo bis naufragium facere dicitur, qui defuncta vxore alteram ducit. Adhæc Dei exemplo abutebantur, quasi is morte coniugis testaretur, se velle ut cælebs viuat, qui superstes mansit. Vtq; inter Corinthios de hac re tunc disputari cœpit, ita posteris temporibus exorti sunt, qui causam jam magna animorum contentione egerunt, inter quos Tertullianus quoq; numeratur, scriptor alioqui nobilissimus & in multis aliis de ecclesia optimè meritus. Cæterum paucis rem omnem expedit Paulus, & his quoq; consilium, quod prius dederat, applicat his verbis. Dico autem cælibibus & viduis, bonum eis est, si manserint, ut ego: Quod si se non continent, matrimonium contrahant: nam melius est matrimonium contrahere quam uri. Primò tam viros quàm mulieres comprehendit (quod in Græco articuli appositi clare testantur) ut eandem utriusque sexus conditionem esse & idem ius ad utrosq; pertinere doceat. Deinde non ait: Deo bonum & sanctum hoc videtur, ut in eo statu maneant: sed Bonum est eis. Ergo non de eo loquitur quod Deus probat, sed quod nobis bonum, id est commodum & utile est. Itaq; sensus verborum est: Eos, qui coniugii vinculo atq; curis semel liberati sunt, commodius & minori cum molestia deinceps viuere posse, si cœlibes aut viduæ maneant: Verumtamen nihil ab illis temere esse tentandum, quin potius, si se non contineant, omnino ad coniugium reuerti debere, ut diuinitus dato remedio piè & castè utantur. Sunt ergo huius consilii partes duæ. Priori commoda commendat, quibus fruuntur qui cælibes viuunt: & hic quoq; rursus suum exemplum allegat, ne aut de re sibi ignota loqui, aut aliis præter animi sententiam suadere videatur, quod ipsemet præstare nolit. Est enim hæc efficacissima ratio in suadendo, si qui in seipsis eius rei exemplum monstrare possunt, ad quam alios hortantur. Cur enim ei fidem habeant alij, quem suis monitis contraria facere vident? Est igitur Apostoli exemplum probè obseruandum omnibus, qui in ecclesia aut repub. sibi in alios homines ius aut imperium aliquod esse volunt. Altera parte consilium mitigat, & cauet ne sui exempli commemoratione alicui laqueum iniiciat, dum permittit ut libertate sua fruatur, si cui aliter visum fuerit. Quo loco rursus admodum circumspectè loquitur. Nec enim ait: Si qui non possunt se continere, matrimonium contrahant, Sed, Quod si se non continent: Ut nimirum ostendat, in hac causa non tam spectari debere quid quis possit, quàm quid velit, quando in voluntate ista nubendi peccatum nullum est, eò quòd coniugium Deus omnibus hominibus liberum atq; licitum fecit. Et fieri potest, ut qui se continere potest, velit tamen matrimonii contrahere, vel ut liberos procreet, vel quia res eius domestica sic iubet, vel alias ob causas per se bonas & justas. Num ergo illum peccare dicemus? Nequaquam, cum non aliud faciat, quàm quod salua conscientia fieri potest, & quod per se sanctum, justum & æquum est. Quod si verò carnis concupiscentia idem ille accendatur, non modò licebit ei vxorem ducere, sed peccare dicetur, si ad restinguendam libidinem remedio legitimo uti nolit. Quod non obscurè innuit Paulus, cum dicit: Nam melius est matrimonium contrahere, quàm uri. Sed de hac re paulò post plura dicemus.
units.tr: For there were some who, while they could not deny that marriage was instituted by God and granted to all people, nevertheless said that it was wrong, after the death of a former spouse, to turn their minds to a second marriage and to bind themselves with a new tie. They thought it was an inexcusable sign of incontinence if someone who had already experienced the cares and troubles of marriage exposed himself again to the same danger. And the Greek epigram is well known, which says that a man who takes another wife after his first has died is shipwrecked twice. Moreover, they abused the example of God, as if by the death of a spouse he testified that the one who remained alive should wish to live unmarried. And just as the question began to be debated among the Corinthians at that time, so in later times there arose men who pleaded this cause with great contention of spirit, among whom Tertullian too is counted, a writer otherwise most noble and very deserving of the Church in many other respects. But Paul settles the whole matter in a few words, and applies to these people the counsel he had given earlier, in these words: "I say to the unmarried and to widows, it is good for them if they remain as I am. But if they cannot contain themselves, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn." First, he includes both men and women (as the articles placed in the Greek clearly bear witness), to teach that the condition of each sex is the same and that the same right applies to both. Second, he does not say, "This seems good and holy to God, that they remain in that state," but "It is good for them." Therefore he is not speaking of what God approves, but of what is good for us, that is, what is advantageous and useful. The sense of the words, then, is this: those who have been once freed from the bond and cares of marriage can live more conveniently and with less trouble afterwards if they remain unmarried or widowed. Yet nothing should be rashly attempted by them; rather, if they cannot contain themselves, they ought altogether to return to marriage, so that they may use the remedy given by God piously and chastely. There are therefore two parts to this counsel. In the first he commends the advantages enjoyed by those who live unmarried, and here too he again adduces his own example, lest he seem either to speak of a matter unknown to him or to urge others to something contrary to his own judgment, which he himself would not do. For this is the most effective argument in persuading, when those who exhort others to a thing can show an example of it in themselves. For why should others trust one whom they see acting contrary to his own admonitions? Therefore the example of the Apostle is to be carefully observed by all who wish to have any right or rule over other people in the Church or the commonwealth. In the other part he tempers the counsel and takes care not to cast a snare upon anyone by recalling his own example, while he permits them to enjoy their liberty if it has seemed otherwise to anyone. Here again he speaks very cautiously. For he does not say, "If any cannot contain themselves, let them marry," but, "But if they do not contain themselves": evidently to show that in this matter one should consider not so much what someone is able to do as what he wishes, since there is no sin in the will to marry, because God made marriage free and lawful for all people.
