And it can happen that one who is able to contain himself nevertheless wishes to marry, either to beget children, or because his household affairs so require, or for other causes that are good and just in themselves. Shall we then say that he sins? By no means, since he does nothing other than what can be done with a clear conscience, and what is holy, just and equitable in itself. But if the lust of the flesh is kindled in him, then not only will it be lawful for him to take a wife, but he will be said to sin if he is unwilling to use the lawful remedy for quenching his lust. Paul hints at this not obscurely when he says, "For it is better to marry than to burn." But we shall say more about this matter a little later.

units.la: Nunc enim obseruari diligenter debet illius modestia, qui etsi in caelibatu multa & magna commoda ijs proposita esse sciret, qui se continent, & ipse hoc donum a Deo accepisset, ut coniugio minime haberet opus, non tamen omnes homines ad sui exempli imitationem astringere voluit, sed cuique liberum facit quod a Deo concessum esse sciebat. Quam modestiam si obseruassent qui posterioribus temporibus ad votum perpetuae continentiae iuuenes atq; puellas in flore aetatis, aut etiam in pueritia, adegerunt, nunquam tot animae in isto flagrantis libidinis incendio tam horribiliter periclitatae essent. At quod de hac causa dicimus, in multis aliis locum habet, & simul hic confutantur quicunque Diuorum exemplis abutuntur, ut ex ijs legem publicam & omnibus necessariam obseruatu faciant, quod illi ex peculiari Dei gratia fecerunt. Errant in hoc qui ieiunium quadragesimale defendunt. Adducunt enim Mosis & Eliae exempla, quos totis diebus quadraginta absque cibo durauisse legimus. Addunt his ipsius Christi exemplum, & necessarium esse clamant, ut hoc imitentur, quotquot Christiani dici & esse volunt. At obseruare debebant isti homines, illa non vulgaria facta fuisse, sed in miraculorum numero censeri debere, ad quorum imitationem nemo astringitur, nisi qui peculiari Dei vocatione ad hoc destinatus & simili spiritus virtute donatus est. Errant praeterea, quod propriae iustitiae meritum in ieiuniis istis constituunt, cum neq; Moses neq; Elias ideo ieiunarint, sed ut ad res maiores & magis arduas praepararentur. Similis est eorum error, qui nullius doctrinae credendum esse clamant, qui non omnibus rebus suis relictis Euangelium vbiq; terrarum praedicat, & incertis hinc inde sedibus vagatur: quod olim Apostolos fecisse constat. Atqui non eadem est omnium Ecclesiae ministrorum conditio, & qui aliquos fecit Apostolos, idem alios doctores & pastores esse voluit, qui unam ecclesiam curent, neq; absque peculiari vocatione ab ea discedant. Poterant huius generis multa adduci: quae in eum finem debent obseruari, ne quem importunius urgeamus, neque vel ex nobis ipsis vel aliorum exemplis omnes homines aestimemus: sed in hoc potius simus intenti, ut quisque suo sese pede metiatur, & in Dei vocationem fideliter incumbat.
units.tr: For now the modesty of that man must be carefully observed, who, although he knew that many great advantages were set before those who contain themselves, and had himself received this gift from God, namely that he had no need of marriage, nevertheless did not wish to bind all people to imitate his example, but left each free to do what he knew God had granted. If those who in later times forced young men and maidens in the flower of their age, or even in childhood, to a vow of perpetual continence had observed this modesty, so many souls would never have been so dreadfully endangered in the blazing fire of this lust. But what we say about this cause has a place in many other matters too, and at the same time those are refuted who abuse the examples of the saints, so as to make into a public law, necessary for everyone to observe, what those saints did from a special grace of God. They err in this who defend the Lenten fast. For they adduce the examples of Moses and Elijah, whom we read to have endured forty whole days without food. They add to these the example of Christ himself, and they cry out that it is necessary for all who wish to be and to be called Christians to imitate this. But these men ought to have observed that those deeds were not common ones, but must be counted among the miracles, to whose imitation no one is bound, unless he has been destined for it by a special calling of God and endowed with a similar power of the Spirit. They err furthermore in placing the merit of their own righteousness in these fasts, since neither Moses nor Elijah fasted for that reason, but in order to be prepared for greater and more arduous tasks. Similar is the error of those who cry out that no one's teaching is to be believed who does not, having left all his possessions, preach the Gospel everywhere on earth and wander about from one uncertain dwelling to another, as the Apostles are known to have done formerly. Yet the condition of all ministers of the Church is not the same; and he who made some Apostles willed that others be teachers and pastors, who care for one church and do not depart from it without a special calling. Many things of this kind could be adduced, and they ought to be observed to this end: that we do not press anyone too importunately, nor judge all people either by ourselves or by the examples of others; but rather that we each take our own measure by our own foot, and diligently apply ourselves to the calling of God.

units.la: His interpositis, transeamus nunc ad causam coniugij, qua in praesenti Paulus affert, dicens: Nam melius est matrimonium contrahere quam uri. Conferuntur inter se matrimonium & vstio siue libidinis flagrantis aestus, & illud melius quam hoc esse dicitur. At non ita hoc accipi debet, quasi inter duas res malas comparatio fiat, & matrimonium vstione melius esse dicatur, eo quod minus malum sit: quo cauillo olim Hieronymus aduersus Iouinianum usus est. At nihil huius in mentem venire potuit Apostolo, qui (ut alibi diximus) sciebat Deum dixisse, Non est bonum, ut homo solus sit. Itaq; communi & recepto hominum more loquitur, perinde ac si quis dicat: Melius est cum Christo egere & esurire quam cum mundo diuitiis & voluptatibus diffluere.
units.tr: Having made these points, let us now turn to the reason for marriage that Paul gives here, saying: "For it is better to marry than to burn" (1 Cor. 7:9). He sets marriage and burning, that is, the fire of blazing lust, side by side, and says that the one is better than the other. But this must not be taken to mean that a comparison is being made between two evils, so that marriage is called better than burning because it is the lesser evil. Jerome used that quibble against Jovinian long ago. Yet nothing of the kind could have occurred to the Apostle, who (as we have said elsewhere) knew that God had said, "It is not good that man should be alone" (Gen. 2:18). He is therefore speaking in the common and accepted manner of men, as if someone were to say: "It is better to lack and to hunger with Christ than to overflow with the riches and pleasures of the world."

units.la: Et quo sensu Dauidi melius visum fuit deijdere [?] ad limen domus Dei, quam habitare in tentoriis impiorum. Vbi nemo sanae mentis dixerit, domum Dei & tentoria impiorum ita inter se conferri, ut vel haec ex minima parte pro bonis probentur, aut illa vituperetur. Possumus praeterea Pauli dictu ita exponere, ut tacita Anthypophora illis respondeat, qui a coniugio propter curas & molestias, quae ei coniunctae sunt, abhorrebant. Docet enim has no tam multas tamen graues esse, quin graviores sint multo, quas aestuans carnis libido parit, ideoq; melius & tolerabilius esse matrimonio etiam molestissimo implicitum viuere, quam ab illa perpetuo uri. Intelligit autem vstionis nomine vim maiorem concupiscentiae, aut (ut Chrysostomus interpretatur) libidinis tyrannidem, quae fere in illis dominatur, qui cum continentiae dono destituti sint, matrimonium tamen subterfugiunt, aut eius contrahendi facultate non habent. Ab hac ut se per coniugium liberent Christiani homines, Paulus admonet, neq; id sine grauibus causis. Nam etsi aestus ille voluntatem non semper vincat, nec in opus aliquod foedum erumpat, animum tamen grauissimè discruciat, à verbi Dei studio & coelestium bonorum meditatione reuocat, adhaec preces & quaecunque sunt alia pietatis verae exercitia impedit. Quis ergo non dicat cum Paulo melius esse quantacunque coniugij molestias subire, quam libidinis aestum ferre, quo nullus herus aut tyrannus durior & crudelior fingi potest? Sentiunt hunc, quotquot in coenobijs vitam transfigunt, & temerario continentiae voto seipsos obstrinxerunt, & poterant horrenda de quibusdam dici, nisi castis auribus parcendum esset. Neque hic sibijpsis blandiantur, qui ardorem illum ita hucusque cohibuerunt, ut nihil turpius designarint. Nec enim corpus solum nos mundi & sanctum seruare vult Deus, sed imprimis animi puritatem requirit, ut Christus docet, qui adulterium iam factum ait, quisquis mulierem alienam lasciuo oculo intuitus eius amore & cupiditate accedit. Et frustra corpus Deo consecrant, qui animum, potiorem sui partem, ei subducunt, & circa foedas ardentis libidinis cogitationes peregrinari patiuntur. Sufficiat ergo nobis locus iste aduersus omnes eorum rationes, qui vel primas vel secundas nuptias dissuadent aut prohibent: ne dum vanum religionis praetextum captantes, totis animis a Deo alienemur. Eoq; maior apud nos esse debet consilij apostolici authoritas, quod hoc ipsum in epistola ad Timotheum confirmat, vbi iuniores viduas publica authoritate ab ecclesia ad coniugium remitti vult, ne aliquando petulantiores factae alicuius scandali maioris occasionem praebeant. Quod si vero matrimonium contrahere debent, qui prauis & illicitis concupiscentiis aestuant, & proinde ad regnum Dei ineptiores sunt, quid de scortatoribus dicemus, qui se iampridem libidinibus foedis succubuisse aperta & plusquam belluina fluprorum licentia testantur? Quod vtinam diligentius expenderent, qui ecclesiarum ministros a coniugio abstinere volunt, & quibus flammis dignum scelus putatur, si Monachus aut sacrificulus vxorem ducat, aut Monialis velo deposito nubat: interim vero ad ea conniuent, quae honeste dici non possunt. Obijciunt illi nobis votum, quod rescindere nefas sit. Quasi vero non satius sit vota temeraria & iniusta rescindere, quam ea seruando scelus scele-ri accumulare. Quae item insania est, propter votum monasticum pudicitiam & puritatem eam violare, quam in baptismo vouimus? Quae item impietas est, templum Dei destruere & ex corpore tuo, quod sanguine suo Christus abluere dignatus est, scorti membrum facere, ne voti transgressor fias, quo te non minus impie quam temere obstrinxisti?
units.tr: In the same sense David thought it better to lie at the threshold of the house of God than to dwell in the tents of the wicked (Ps. 84:10). No one of sound mind would say that the house of God and the tents of the wicked are compared with each other in such a way that the latter could be approved as good in any small degree, or the former found fault with. Moreover, we may explain Paul's words so that they answer, as a kind of unspoken objection, those who shrink from marriage because of the cares and troubles bound up with it. For he teaches that these troubles, although many and grievous, are not so grievous as the far greater ones that a burning carnal lust produces. Therefore it is better and more bearable to live entangled in marriage, however troublesome, than to be burned perpetually by that lust. By "burning" he means the greater force of concupiscence, or (as Chrysostom explains it) the tyranny of lust, which generally rules over those who lack the gift of continence yet shun marriage, or do not have the means to contract it. Paul urges Christians to free themselves from this burning through marriage, and not without serious reasons. For although that fire does not always overcome the will, nor break out into some foul deed, it nevertheless tortures the mind most severely, calls it away from the study of God's Word and the meditation on heavenly goods, and besides hinders prayers and all the other exercises of true piety. Who then would not say with Paul that it is better to bear whatever troubles marriage brings than to endure the fire of lust, under which no master or tyrant could be imagined to be harsher or more cruel? All who spend their lives in monasteries and have bound themselves by a rash vow of continence feel this, and many horrible things could be said about some of them, were it not that chaste ears must be spared. Nor let those flatter themselves who have so far restrained that ardour that they have shown nothing shameful. For God wants not only the body to be kept pure and holy, but above all requires purity of mind, as Christ teaches, who says that whoever looks at another man's wife with a lustful eye and approaches her with love and desire has already committed adultery. And those consecrate their bodies to God in vain who withdraw from Him the mind, the better part of themselves, and allow it to wander among the foul thoughts of burning lust. Let this passage therefore suffice for us against all the arguments of those who dissuade or forbid either first or second marriages, lest, while grasping at a vain pretext of religion, we become wholly alienated from God in heart. And the authority of the apostolic counsel ought to carry even more weight with us, because in the epistle to Timothy he confirms this very point, where he wishes younger widows to be sent back by the Church to marriage with public authority, lest, having become wanton, they give occasion for some greater scandal (1 Tim. 5:11–14). But if those who burn with wicked and unlawful desires ought to marry, and are therefore less fit for the kingdom of God, what shall we say of the whoremongers, who by their open and more than beastly licentiousness of fornication bear witness that they long ago succumbed to foul lusts? Would that those who wish the ministers of the churches to abstain from marriage would weigh this more carefully, and consider it a crime worthy of the flames if a monk or a petty priest takes a wife, or a nun, having laid aside her veil, marries; yet meanwhile they connive at those things that cannot be named decently! They object to us the vow, which it would be a sin to break. As if it were not better to break rash and unjust vows than by keeping them to heap crime upon crime! Likewise, what madness is it to violate for the sake of a monastic vow that chastity and purity which we vowed in baptism? And what impiety is it to destroy the temple of God, and to make a member of a harlot out of your body, which Christ deigned to wash with His own blood, lest you become a transgressor of a vow by which you bound yourself no less impiously than rashly?

units.la: At quaerat hic aliquis, quid eos facere oporteat, quibus per aetatem non licet, ut matri-monium contrahant, cum adhuc sub parentum aut tutorum potestate sint, interim vero si uri & aestuare sentiant? Quibus etiam adnumerari possunt, quorum ea est vitae conditio, ut coniugio uti aut uxoribus cohabitare non possint, & proinde ne ducunt quidem, ne & has fellisse videantur, & seipsos grauioribus molestijs onerent. Num hi quidem vocationem suam deserere, illi vero spreto parentum imperio uxores ducere debent? Id equidem sacra litera nusquam iubent. Ifaacum autem nobis historia commendat, qui ad quadragesimum vsque aetatis annum coniugium distulit, ut ex patris voluntate uxorem duceret. Rursus Esau proteruiam supplicio dignam fuisse docet, qui inconsultis parentibus ex animi sui libidine coniuges sibi quaesiuit. Debent exempla ista Christianos iuuenes excitare, ne quid ex semetipsis temere statuant, et cum aetatis suae desiderijs luctentur, quoad tepus opportunum aduenerit, et ad rem domesticam idonei fiant. Nec est quod animum despondeant, et de victoria desperent. Sunt enim ipsis quoq; remedia, quibus ardores illos reflinguere, aut salte frenare poterunt, ne quid se indignum faciant. Primum fuerit, ut improborum consortia fugiant, & insidiosa puellarum colloquia declinent, earum imprimis, quas petulantiores & pudicitiae minus studiosas esse sentiunt. Deinde quod Dauid monuit, oculos suos auertant, ne vanitate spectent, neq; ex contemplandis mulierum formis voluptatem capiat. Nec enim temere Cupidine in oculis puellarum ludere, & ibi faces suas accendere olim Poetae dixerunt, & notum est illud Vergilianum: Vt vidi, vt perij, vt me malus abstulit error. Tertio ne turpi otio se dedant necesse est. Quia enim (vt alibi quoque monuimus) quiescere non potest homo, nisi quid honesti negotij agas, ad vanas cogitationes delabetur, inter quas in ea aetate ferè primae sunt, quae libidinem accendunt. Quarto in legendis scripturis & audiendo Dei verbo frequentes sint, & hic sibi familiares faciant eos scriptura locos, qui aut comminationes Dei aduersus scortatores amt horrenda in eos exempla edita continent. Illorum enim meditatione timor Dei in animis ipsorum augebitur, qui eos facile in officio continebit. Vbi plurimum proderit, si quae quotidie fiunt, diligentius obseruent. Nam hic quoque multa videbunt, quae eos a scortandi licentia reuocabunt. Addant his preces assiduas, vt spiritu sancto Deus ipsos afflare, carnis desideria reflinguere, & studia ipsorum dirigere dignetur. Qui in istis paulo diligentiores fuerint, etsi ardeant interdum, permissione tamen uri non poterunt, & procul dubio cum diuino illo Iosepho pudicitiam suam impollutam tuebuntur. Interim parenquoque & tutores hic monendi sunt, ne suo officio ipsi desint, neue insidiosa coniugij dilatione filiis suis tentationum grauiorum sint authores.
units.tr: But someone here may ask what those ought to do who, because of their age, are not yet permitted to contract marriage, since they are still under the authority of their parents or guardians, yet meanwhile feel that they are burning and inflamed. To these may be added those whose manner of life is such that they cannot make use of marriage or live with wives, and therefore do not even take them, lest they seem to have deceived these women too and burden themselves with heavier troubles. Must these men, then, abandon their calling, and those others, scorning their parents' command, take wives? Holy Scripture certainly nowhere commands this. The history commends to us Isaac, who put off marriage until his fortieth year so that he might take a wife with his father's consent (Gen. 25:20). Again, Esau's wantonness, which sought wives for himself at his own lust without consulting his parents, is shown to have deserved punishment (Gen. 26:34–35). These examples ought to rouse Christian young men not to decide anything rashly on their own, but to wrestle with the desires of their age until the opportune time arrives and they become fit for domestic life. Nor should they lose heart or despair of victory. For they too have remedies by which they can quench those burnings, or at least restrain them, so that they do nothing unworthy of themselves. (1) First, let them flee the company of the wicked and avoid the insidious conversations of girls, especially those whom they perceive to be wanton and less careful of chastity. (2) Next, as David advised, let them turn their eyes away so that they do not look upon vanity, nor take pleasure in gazing at the beauty of women (Ps. 119:37). For it was not without reason that the poets long ago said that Cupid plays in the eyes of girls and there kindles his torches, and that line of Virgil is well known: "As soon as I saw, as soon as I was lost, as soon as a wicked error carried me off." (3) Thirdly, they must avoid shameful idleness. For since (as we have also warned elsewhere) a man cannot be at rest unless he is engaged in some honest business, he slides into empty thoughts, among which at that age the first to kindle lust are usually found. (4) Fourthly, let them be frequent in reading the Scriptures and in hearing the Word of God, and let them make familiar to themselves those passages of Scripture which contain God's threats against fornicators and the dreadful examples set forth against them. For by meditating on these the fear of God will grow in their hearts, and this will easily keep them in their duty. It will help greatly if they observe more carefully what happens every day; for here too they will see many things that will call them back from the licence of fornication. Let them add to these constant prayers, that God may deign to breathe on them by the Holy Spirit, to hold back the desires of the flesh, and to direct their pursuits. Those who are a little more diligent in these things, even if they sometimes burn, will not be able to be consumed by that fire, and without doubt, like the divine Joseph, they will keep their chastity undefiled. Meanwhile, parents and guardians too must be admonished here not to fail in their duty, and not to become, by an insidious delay of marriage, the authors of greater temptations for their children.

units.la: Porrò ut ad Paulum redeamus, ne quis ex eius exemplo, & his iam repetita caelibatus commendatione ansam arriperet coniugem deserendi, vel etiam argumentum quod adduxit, in alienum sensum detorquendo inde colligeret, sibi porrò coniuge non opus esse, eo quod nullum amplius libidinis æstum sentiat: redit ad coniugij praecepta, & huius vinculum tam arctum tamq; necessarium esse docet, ut à nemine mortalium temere dissolui debeat. Sic enim ait. Jis autem qui matrimonio juncti sunt, denuntio non ego, sed Dominus: Uxor à viro ne discedito. Quod si etiam discesserit, maneat innupta, aut viro reconciliator. Et vir uxorem ne dimittito. Quo loco ante omnia observari debet, non agere hic Apostolum de divortijs legitimis, quae scripturarum & ipsius Christi authoritate defendi possunt (ut postea demonstrabitur) sed temerarijs, qualia inter Judaeos & ethnicos in usu fuisse constat. Illi enim permissione per Legem Mosis ipsis facta adeo licenter abutebantur, ut quamlibet ob causam uxoribus repudium nuntiarent. In Ezra enim & a-pud Malachiam aliqui commemorantur, qui ex Babylone reuersi uxores, quas exilij & laboris socias habuerant, non minus crudeliter quam iniuste dimittebant, ut ex vicinis gentibus alias in otio et molliter enutritas possent ducere. Inter gentes quoque, cum impune regnaret scortandi & moechandi licentia, nihil non sibi in uxores quoque mariti permittebant. Tanta denique fuit divortiorum licentia, ut in Comoedia pater, qui filio non bonae frugis uxorem petebat, non verearetur puellae parenti dicere: Incommoditas denique huc omnis redit, Si eueniat (quod Dij prohibeant) discessio. Et quid non fecisse putabimus vulgus hominum, quando in divortijs faciendis tantum non lusisse legamus eos, qui virtute & morum gravitate aliis praestare putabantur? Notum est enim Caesaris factum, qui cum Pompeiam repudiauisset, Clodium eius adulterum suo interim patrocinio & testimonio defendit, & de repudij causa interrogatus, non aliud respondit: Quia meam ne suspicionibus quidem obnoxiam esse debere existimo. Cato autem ille Uticensis Martiam uxorem ex se praegnantem Q. Hortensio ducendam permisit, & eandem postea cum Hortensij haeres scripta esset, denuo ad se recepit. Apud Corinthios autem aliud malum accedebat, quod multi libertate Christiana hic quoque abuterentur, & si vel leue aliquod dissidium aut simultas incidisset, abs se invicem discederent, & vel maritus uxorem eijceret, vel haec sua sponte abiret. Et quod gravius erat, nonnullae aliis etiam maritis nubebant. De his Paulus in praesenti agit, & quia in uno vitio multa non sine publico scandalo concurrebant, magna verborum gravitate utitur. Jis (inquit) qui matrimonio juncti sunt, denuntio non ego sed Dominus. Quae verba non ita accipi debent, quasi quae hucusque dicta sunt, ex suo cerebro finxerit, sed discernit inter ea, quae ab ipso Domino diserte vel in veteri scriptura vel in Evangelio tradita sunt, & quae ipse ex peculiari spiritus revelatione didicerat, cum prius non adeo luculenter fuissent expressa. Cuius generis multa in hac ipsa epistola habentur, qualia sunt quae de mulierum & virorum prophetantium habitu, de ordine in coetibus sacris servando, de aliis innumeris audiemus. Interim nemo Pauli authoritate sive exemplo traditiones quaecunque tveatur: quando solis Apostolis hoc datum est, ut quae ipsi nobis tradiderunt, Spiritus sancti dictata censeri debeant, quem illis Christus ideo promiserat, ut per eum in omnem veritatem inducerentur. Quod autem nunc dicturus est Paulus, id diserte ad Dominum authorem refert, ut magis perterrefaciat eos, quos ad omnem licentiam nimium proclives fuisse diximus.
units.tr: But to return to Paul: lest anyone, taking his example and the praise of celibacy he has just repeated, should seize on it as an excuse for deserting his wife, or should twist the argument he has put forward to conclude from it that he no longer needs a wife because he no longer feels any heat of lust, Paul goes back to the precepts of marriage and teaches that this bond is so close and so necessary that no mortal may dissolve it rashly. For he says: "To those who are married I give this charge, not I but the Lord: let not the wife depart from her husband. But if she does depart, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. And let not the husband put away his wife." In this passage, above all, it must be noted that the Apostle is not here speaking of lawful divorces, which can be defended both by the authority of Scripture and by that of Christ himself (as will be shown later), but of rash divorces, such as are known to have been common among the Jews and the Gentiles. For the Jews, using the permission granted them by the Law of Moses, abused it so freely that they would divorce their wives for any cause whatever. In Ezra and in Malachi we read of some who, returning from Babylon, dismissed the wives they had had as companions in exile and hardship, no less cruelly than unjustly, so that they might take wives from the neighbouring nations who had been brought up in idleness and luxury. Among the Gentiles too, since licence for whoring and adultery went unpunished, husbands allowed themselves everything with regard to their wives also. Indeed the freedom to divorce was so great that in a comedy a father, who was seeking a wife for his son of no good character, did not hesitate to say to the girl's parent: "In the end all the inconvenience comes back to this: if separation should happen (which the gods forbid)..." And what must we suppose the common run of men did, when we read that those who were thought to excel others in virtue and moral seriousness made a game of divorce? For the deed of Caesar is well known: when he had repudiated Pompeia, he defended Clodius, her adulterer, with his protection and his testimony, and when asked the reason for the divorce he gave no other answer than this: "Because I think my wife ought not even to be liable to suspicion." That famous Cato of Utica, too, allowed Martia, who was pregnant by him, to be taken as wife by Quintus Hortensius, and when Hortensius had made her his heir, he took her back to himself again. Among the Corinthians, moreover, another evil was added: many abused their Christian liberty in this matter too, and if even some slight disagreement or quarrel arose, they separated from each other, and either the husband cast out his wife or she went away of her own accord. And what was worse, some even married other husbands. Paul deals with these matters here, and because many evils came together in one fault, not without public scandal, he uses great seriousness of words. "To those who are married," he says, "I give this charge, not I but the Lord." These words should not be taken as though he had made up what he has said so far out of his own head; rather he distinguishes between those things which the Lord himself delivered clearly, either in the Old Testament writings or in the Gospel, and those which he had learned by a special revelation of the Spirit, since these had not previously been expressed so plainly. Many things of this kind are found in this very letter, such as what we shall hear about the dress of men and women who prophesy, about the order to be kept in the sacred assemblies, and about countless other matters. Meanwhile no one should defend any traditions whatever on the authority or example of Paul, since it was granted to the Apostles alone that what they delivered to us should be considered the dictates of the Holy Spirit, whom Christ had therefore promised to them, so that they would be led into all truth through him. But what Paul is about to say now, he expressly refers to the Lord as its author, so that he may frighten more strongly those whom we have said were too prone to every kind of licence.

units.la: Quid vero illud est? Uxor à viro ne discedito: Et vir uxorem ne dimittito. Haec eorum, quae proponit, summa est. Docere autem vult coniugij necessitudinem tam sanctam atq; arctam esse, ut nullius authoritate privata dissolui debeat: unde colligit, iniuste & impie facere eos, qui uxores eijciunt, ut has quoque, si à viris temere discedant. Quod si quaeras, ubi nam haec dixerit Dominus? respondemus, Paulum ad ea respicere, quae Christus Matth. quinto Cap. & 19. de coniugio & divortijs differens pronunciauit: Quod Deus coniunxit, homo ne separet. Id autem ex eo colligit, quod in ipso rerum exordio dictum fuit: Propterea deseret homo patrem suum & matrem suam, & agglutinabitur uxori suæ. Si enim coniugio pietas, quam parentibus debemus, cedere debet, nihil certè praetexere poterunt, quo suam temeritatem excusent, qui illud temere dirimunt. Addé, Adde, quod ibidem dicitur: Et qui duo erant, fient caro vna, & proinde iam non sunt duo, sed vna caro. Quod enim vnum est, fine totius destructione non potest diuidi. Denique concludit ex istis Dominus. Dico vobis, quod quisquis repudiauerit vxorem suam, nisi ob fluprum, & aliam duxerit, is adulterium committit: Et qui repudiatam duxerit, is adulterium committit. Recte ergo istud Apostolus tanta cum grauitate pronunciat. Et mox de muliere addit: Quod si etiam discesserit, maneat innupta, aut viro reconciliator. Nec enim potest legitimè cum altero coniungi, quae prioris coniugij vinculo adhuc tenetur, quod omnino ratum adhuc habet Deus, quamuis homines illud abrumpere conantur. Ea autem necessitate mulieres astringere voluit Paulus, vt cogat cum viris à quibus temere discesserunt, in gratiam redire. Nam vt multae sint, quae alterius coniugij ipsè à maritis suis diuelli cupiant, pauciores tamen sunt, quae velint aut possint absque viris viuere. Et apostolico praecepto illos astringi necesse erat, quia tunc magistratus à Christiana religione alieni erant, & ista omnia facile negligebant. Imo credibile est, multos ex gentibus hac matrimoniorum diuulsione & familiarum confusione, quae inter Christianos cernebatur, delectatos fuisse, vt maiorum haberent calumniandi occasionem. Semel ergo scandalum hoc omne sublatum voluit, dum admonet, vt coniugalis necessitudinis memores, eam sanctè colant.
units.tr: What then is that? "Let not the wife depart from her husband; and let not the husband put away his wife." This is the sum of what he sets forth. He wishes to teach that the bond of marriage is so holy and so close that it ought not to be dissolved by any private authority; from this he concludes that those who cast out their wives act unjustly and impiously, and likewise the wives too, if they depart rashly from their husbands. But if you ask where the Lord said this, we answer that Paul is looking to what Christ pronounced in Matthew chapters five and nineteen, when he discussed marriage and divorce: "What God has joined together, let not man separate." Paul draws this from what was said at the very beginning of things: "For this cause shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave to his wife." For if the duty of piety which we owe to parents must yield to marriage, certainly those who rashly break it apart will have nothing to plead in excuse of their rashness. Add that the same passage says: "And they twain shall be one flesh; so then they are no more twain, but one flesh." For what is one cannot be divided without the destruction of the whole. Finally the Lord concludes from these words: "I say to you, whoever puts away his wife, except for fornication, and marries another, commits adultery; and whoever marries her that is put away commits adultery." Rightly, therefore, the Apostle pronounces this with such great seriousness. And soon he adds concerning the woman: "But if she does depart, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband." For a woman who is still bound by the bond of a former marriage cannot lawfully be joined to another, since God still holds that bond wholly valid, though men try to break it. Paul wished to bind women by this necessity, so that he might compel them to be reconciled to the husbands from whom they had rashly departed. For although there are many women who would wish to be torn away from their husbands for another marriage, there are fewer who are willing or able to live without husbands. And it was necessary to bind them by an apostolic precept, because at that time the magistrates were alien to the Christian religion and easily neglected all these matters. Indeed it is credible that many of the Gentiles took pleasure in this tearing apart of marriages and this confusion of households which was seen among Christians, so that they might have an occasion of slandering them. Therefore he wished to remove all this scandal at once, while he admonishes them, mindful of the bond of marriage, to honour it faithfully.

units.la: Caeterum hoc loco veteres olim bifariam abusi sunt, & hodie etiam nonnulli eodem abuntur. Primò enim statuerunt, diuortium simul omne Christianis hominibus prohibitum esse. Et hi quidem literam pertinacius vrgendo hoc vnum clamant: Vxor à viro ne discedito, & vir vxorem ne dimittito. Addunt & illud Christi: Quod Deus coniunxit, homo ne separet. Item: Quisquis repudiauerit vxorem suam, & aliam duxerit, is adulterium committit. At errant isti omnes, quod non vident, de quo nam diuortij genere Christus & Paulus locuti sint: nimirum de temerarijs illis, quae priuata authoritate fiebant. De illis enim Christum à pharisaeis interrogatum fuisse Matthaeus scribit. Paulus autem non tam de diuortijs agit, quam illis, qui ob leuiorem aliquam offensam coniuges relinquebant, & ideo eos reconciliari vult, quod in diuortijs veris atque legitimis locum non habet. Deinde in Christi verbis subdolè id dissimulant, quod fluprum siue adulterium excipit, cuius causa diuortium facere licet. Neque etiam videre volunt, quod Paulus mox permittit, vt ab infideli viro vxor discedat, si ille deterior fit & iniquior in religionem Christianam. Cum ergo duas causas diuortij scriptura sacra tradat, nimium iniqui sunt illi, qui ex hoc loco regulam aut legem vniuersalem statuunt, qua diuortia simul omnia prohibentur. Clamant illi, Quod Deus coniunxerit, homo ne separet. At nos diuina authoritate eos separari dicimus, qui propter fluprum diuortium faciunt, aut à coniugibus discedunt, ne fidem Christo datam violent. Neque coniugij vinculum abrumpit, qui adulterae repudium nuntiat, sed ne vinculo quod haec prior dissoluit, amplius teneatur, curat. Quod rectè & iustè fieri communis sensus docet. Quo enim iure tenebitur fidem seruare ei, quae cum fide pudicitiam quoque profligauit? Aut quae leges iure cogere possunt virum bonum & honestum, vt vxoris adulterae lenonem agat, & eius stupra ferat aut dissimulet? At disputatione multa hic non esset opus, si officium facerent magistratus, & quod Deus iussit, adulteria capitali supplicio punirent. Cum vero illi cessent, non debet tamen eorum ignavia fraudi esse bonis, vt adulteras perpetuò ferre cogantur. Quoad religionis causam, res est expeditissima, cum Christum dixisse sciamus, parentes simul & coniuges deserendos esse, vt ipsius discipuli germani simus. Sed elucet in his diaboli astutia, qui dum falso praetextu coniugij dignitatem & indissolubilem necessitatem tuetur, hoc vnum agit, vt adulteris patrocinium deferat.
units.tr: Moreover, in this place the ancients long ago abused the passage in two ways, and some even today abuse it in the same way. First, they laid down that divorce was entirely forbidden to Christians. These men, urging the letter rather stubbornly, cry out this one thing: "Let not the wife depart from her husband, and let not the husband put away his wife." They add also the saying of Christ: "What God has joined together, let not man separate." Likewise: "Whoever puts away his wife and marries another commits adultery." But all these men are wrong, because they do not see what kind of divorce Christ and Paul were speaking of: namely those rash ones which were done on private authority. For Matthew writes that Christ was questioned about these by the Pharisees. Paul, however, is dealing not so much with divorces as with those who, on account of some slighter offence, abandoned their spouses, and therefore he wishes them to be reconciled; this does not apply to true and lawful divorces. Next, in Christ's words they dishonestly pass over the exception of fornication or adultery, on account of which it is lawful to divorce. Nor do they wish to see what Paul soon allows, that a wife may depart from an unbelieving husband if he becomes worse and more hostile to the Christian religion. Since Holy Scripture therefore sets out two causes of divorce, those are far too unjust who from this passage lay down a universal rule or law by which all divorces are forbidden together. They cry out: "What God has joined together, let not man separate." But we say that those are separated by divine authority who divorce on account of fornication, or who depart from their spouses so as not to violate the faith given to Christ. Nor does he break the bond of marriage who announces a divorce to an adulterous wife; rather he takes care that he is no longer bound by the bond which she has already dissolved. What common sense teaches is rightly and justly done. For by what right would he be bound to keep faith with one who has also cast away chastity along with faith? Or what laws could rightly compel a good and honourable man to act as pimp for his adulterous wife, and to bear or overlook her debaucheries? But there would be no need for much argument here, if the magistrates did their duty and punished adultery with capital punishment, as God has commanded. But since they have ceased to do so, their idleness ought not to be a loss to good men, so that they are forced to endure adulterous wives forever. As for the cause of religion, the matter is very easily settled, since we know that Christ said parents and spouses must be left, so that we may be his true disciples. But in these things the cunning of the devil shines forth, who, while under the false pretext of defending the dignity and indissoluble necessity of marriage, does this one thing: he grants patronage to adulterers.

units.la: Alter error eorum est, qui nouum diuortij genus excogitarunt, vt nimirum manente vinculo coniugij à thori & mensae (vt loquuntur) societate excludantur, qui repudiari meruerunt. Vrgent hi Pauli verba: Si mulier discesserit, maneat innupta, aut viro reconciliator. Sed perperam ad diuortia trahunt id, quod de temerarijs discessionibus & priuatis diuidijs dictum esse constat. Christi item authoritatem praetexunt, qui adulterium dicat fieri eum, qui repudiatam duxerit. At hunc quoque de repudijs locutum esse iam ante demonstrauimus, quae nulla iusta de causa fiebant. Addunt his, matrimonium à Paulo Sacramentum dici, & proinde eius vinculum sacrosanctum & inuiolabile esse. At iniuriam faciunt Apostolo, qui mysterium quidem magnum subesse ait, eo quòd Christi & ecclesiae coniunctionem adumbrat, eo autem sensu nusquam sacramentum dicit, quo Baptismus & Cœna Dominica Sacramenta dicuntur. Quod si vero pertinacius urgeant propter typi illius excellentiam coniugium nunquam ita dissolui debe-re, ut vel vir uxorem aliam ducat, aut mulier alteri nubat, nos eadem ratione agricolam, vinitorem, pastorem denique prohiberi dicemus, ne ad aliud vitae genus transeant, cum in ipsis quoque Christi typus sit. At quàm ridicula haec sint, nemo non videt. Accedit his, quòd suo figmento rem eò ipsi homines adduxerunt, ut insontes quidem multentur, dum uxores alias ducere non licet, his autem maior concedatur scortandi licentia, qui diuortiorum causa fuerunt. Fit denique, ut vir bonus & honestus aut uxorem adulteram cum famae suae & rerum omnium dispendio retine-re cogatur, aut semetipsum scortatione polluere, si continentiae dono destituatur. Eadem uxoris etiam pia & pudica ratio est[?], si vir illi adulter & impurus obtigerit. Itaque dum isti coniugia tueri volunt, iniusti simul & crudeles fiunt, atque inconsiderata sua tyrannide Christiani nomi-nis dignitatem turpiter prostituunt. Nemo igitur Pauli verba in sensum alienum detorqueat, malis autem & incommodis, quae hic plurima occurrunt, remedium adhibere curent ij, quorum fi-dei ecclesiae & respub. creditae sunt. Id vero facile fiet, si de matrimoniis legitimè contrahendis at-que colendis bonas leges ferant, eaedem tueantur, scortandi atque moechandi licentiam insta seve-ritate coërceant. Qui vero iam matrimonio coniuncti sunt, meminerint huius praesidem & vin-dicem esse Deum, & proinde sui officii esse, ut & fidem sibi mutuo datam sanctè colant, & totos sese IESV CHRISTO consecrent, qui nos sibi sponsam fecit carentem ruga & macula. Huic debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: The second error of these people is that they have devised a new kind of divorce, by which, while the bond of marriage remains, those who have deserved to be repudiated are shut out from what they call the fellowship of bed and board. They press the words of Paul: "If a woman has departed, let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband." But they wrongly apply to divorce what is plainly said about rash separations and private disputes. They also put forward the authority of Christ, who says that whoever marries one who has been put away commits adultery. But we have already shown that this too speaks of repudiations that were made without any just cause. To these they add that Paul calls marriage a sacrament, and therefore that its bond is sacred and inviolable. But they do Paul an injustice. He says indeed that a great mystery lies hidden in it, because it shadows the union of Christ and the Church; yet nowhere does he use the word sacrament in the sense in which Baptism and the Lord's Supper are called sacraments. And if they press more stubbornly that, on account of the excellence of that type, marriage must never be dissolved so that either the husband may take another wife or the wife marry another man, then by the same reasoning we shall say that the farmer, the vine-dresser and the minister must be forbidden to change to another way of life, since Christ is a type in them too. But how ridiculous these things are, everyone sees. Besides, by their invention these men have brought the matter to such a point that the innocent are punished, since they may not take other wives, while greater licence for whoring is granted to those who were the cause of the divorces. Finally, it comes about that a good and honourable man is forced either to keep an adulterous wife, with the loss of his reputation and of all his property, or, if he lacks the gift of continence, to defile himself with whoring. The same reasoning holds for a pious and chaste wife if she has been joined to an adulterous and impure husband. Thus, while these men want to defend marriages, they become unjust and cruel at the same time, and by their thoughtless tyranny they shamefully prostitute the dignity of the Christian name. Let no one, therefore, twist the words of Paul into a foreign sense; and let those to whom the faith of the Church and the commonwealth has been entrusted take care to apply a remedy to the many evils and inconveniences that arise here. This will easily be done if they enact good laws concerning the lawful contracting and conduct of marriages, maintain those same laws, and check the licence of whoring and adultery with strict severity. But those who are already joined in marriage should remember that God is the guardian and avenger of it, and that it is therefore their duty both to keep faithfully the pledge they have given each other, and to consecrate themselves wholly to Jesus Christ, who made us his bride, without spot or wrinkle. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXV
units.tr: HOMILIA XXXV

units.la: Reliquis autem ego dico, non Dominus: Si quis frater uxorẽ habet infidelem, quae consentiat ad habitandum cum eo, ne eam di-mittito. Et uxor, quae habet virum infidelem, qui consentiat ad habitandum cum ea, ne eum dimittito. Maritus enim infidelis sanc-tificatus est in uxore, & uxor infidelis sanctificata est in viro: alio-qui liberi vestri impuri essent: nunc autem sancti sunt. At si incredulus discedit, discedat: non est servituti subiectus frater aut soror in huiusmodi rebus: in pace autem vocauit nos Deus. Ecquid enim nosti mulier, an virum sis servaturā? aut ecquid nosti vir, an uxorem sis servaturus? Sed ut unicuique partitus est Deus, ut unumquenque vocauit Dominus, ita incedat. Et ita in ecclesiis o-mnibus constituo.
units.tr: But to the rest I say, not the Lord: If any brother has an unbelieving wife who is willing to live with him, let him not put her away. And if a woman has an unbelieving husband who is willing to live with her, let her not leave him. For the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified in the husband; otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy. But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart: a brother or a sister is not bound in servitude in such cases, for God has called us to peace. For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife? But as God has apportioned to each, as the Lord has called each, so let him walk. And so I ordain in all the churches.

units.la: UT homo pro corrupto suae carnis ingenio & innata vitiositate optima quaeque Dei institu-ta sibi ipsi per abusum impura & noxia facit: ita hoc ipsum in matrimonio potissimum si-ri[?] consueuit. Nam ut aliàs monuimus, instituit illud Deus, ut & libidinis illicitae remedium sit, & ut singuli huius vitae molestias facilius ferant. At multorum vitio fit, ut & libidini serviat, & vitam ipsis molestiorem, adeoq; acerbam reddat: cum in illo contrahendo, non in Dei volun-tatem respiciant, sed caecae carnis affectus sequantur. Non possunt enim tales sui officii meminis-se, & ideo novis quotidie laboribus sese implicant, & tandem illos coniugii quoque piget tædeŭ[?]. Omnibus ergo saeculis plurimum peccatum fuit repudiorum licentia, quae inter Iudaeos & gentes semper maxima fuit, & hodie multos sibi ipsis plus satis indulgere videmus. Recte ergo Paulus cum de coniugum officiis disseruisset, nuper graviter monuit, ne qui temere à coniugibus suis separentur, aut illas violenter eiciant: cum matrimonii vinculum sacrosanctum sit, neque aliquis authoritate privata dissolui vel abrumpi debeat.
units.tr: Just as a man, by the corruption of his flesh and his innate wickedness, turns the best institutions of God to his own harm by misusing them, so this happens especially in marriage. For, as we have noted elsewhere, God instituted marriage both as a remedy for unlawful lust and so that each person might bear the troubles of this life more easily. But through the fault of many, it comes about that marriage both serves their lust and makes their life more troublesome and even bitter, since in contracting it they do not look to the will of God but follow the blind desires of the flesh. For such people cannot remember their duty, and so they entangle themselves daily in new troubles, and at last they grow weary even of the marriage bond. Therefore, in every age there has been much sin in the freedom to divorce, which has always been very great among the Jews and the nations, and today we see many indulging themselves more than enough. Rightly, then, when Paul had discussed the duties of spouses, he recently gave a serious warning that no one should rashly separate from their spouses or violently cast them out, since the bond of marriage is sacred and no one ought to dissolve or break it by private authority.

units.la: Cæterum incidebat in hanc tractationem noua quæstio de ijs, qui impari matrimonio iun-ctì sunt. Fiebat enim Corinthi & passim inter gentes, vt ad Euangelij prædicationem, ali-quando maritus Christi cognitione & fide illustraretur, vxor autem in superstitionibus & ido-lolatria perseueraret: & è contra vxore ad fidem Christianam transeunte, maritus gentilis-mum mordicus retineret. In eiusmodi autem coniugijs non eadem erat fidelium conditio. A-liqui enim ex infidelibus ingenio mitiori præditi, consortes fideles patienter ferebant, vt nul-lam propter religionis diuersitatem ipsis molestiam facerent. Alij vero cum & Christia-næ doctrinæ odio flagrarent, & natura vehementiores essent, coniuges ad Christum conuer-sas durius tractabant, & diuortium siue discessionem minabantur, nisi ad superstitiones atque i-dololatriam redirent. In ea igitur contentione duplex periculum occurrebat. Nonnulli e-nim religionis zelo, aut saltem eius prætextu abutebantur, vt à coniugibus temere discede-rent, etiamsi per illos liceret fidei professionem illibatam seruare. Id vero absque magno & mul-tiplici scandalo fieri non poterat, cum eiusmodi diuortijs familiæ turbarentur, liberorum legiti-ma educatio impediretur, & noua coniugia vtrinque inita simultates quoque & dissidia noua parerent. Alij rursus, qui in Religione minus feruidi erant, ij vel coniugum infidelium impor-tunitate & improbis minis, aut liberorum communium amore, aut facultatum amissione & ino-piæ metu, aut qualibusque aliis causis superati fidem abnegabant, & ad superstitiones reuer-tebantur. Istis ergo malis in præsenti Paulus remedium adhibet, & docet magna hic cautione opus esse, ne qui vel religionis prætextu ad temeraria diuortia, vel coniugij necessitudine ad fi-dei abnegationem abutantur. Estq; locus hic diligenti consideratione dignissimus, quod multa con-tineat, quæ ad rem ecclesiasticam simul & domesticam pertinent.
units.tr: Moreover, a new question arose in this discussion, concerning those who are joined in a mixed marriage. For it happened at Corinth and in many places among the nations that, when the gospel was preached, sometimes the husband was enlightened by the knowledge and faith of Christ while the wife persisted in superstitions and idolatry; and conversely, when the wife passed over to the Christian faith, the husband held on stubbornly to his paganism. In such marriages, however, the condition of the believers was not the same. For some of the unbelievers, endowed with a gentler disposition, patiently bore their believing spouses, so that they caused them no trouble because of the difference of religion. Others, however, who burned with hatred of Christian teaching and were more violent by nature, treated their wives who had turned to Christ more harshly and threatened divorce or separation unless they returned to superstitions and idolatry. In this conflict, then, there were two dangers. Some, out of zeal for religion, or at least using it as a pretext, abused it to leave their spouses rashly, even though through those spouses it would have been possible to keep their profession of faith unspoiled. This, however, could not happen without great and manifold scandal, since such divorces threw families into turmoil, hindered the lawful upbringing of children, and new marriages entered into on either side would bring forth new quarrels and dissensions. Others again, who were less fervent in religion, were overcome either by the importunity and wicked threats of unbelieving spouses, or by love of their common children, or by the loss of property and fear of poverty, or by some other causes, and so they denied the faith and went back to superstitions. Against these evils Paul now applies a remedy, and teaches that great caution is needed here, lest some abuse religion as a pretext for rash divorce, or the bond of marriage as a pretext for denying the faith. And this passage is most worthy of careful consideration, because it contains much that pertains both to the affairs of the Church and to the affairs of the household.

units.la: Quia autem multos esse sciebat, qui omnia eius insidiose obseruabant, vt calumniandi occa-sionem haberent, præfatiuncula vtitur, qua quod illi cauillari poterant sponte fatetur, dicens: Reliquis autem ego dico, non Dominus. Reliquos dicit, vt inter Christianos discrimen esse often-dat, cum alij consortes quoq; thori fideles haberent, alij vero imparibus coniugijs obstricti essent. Et quia de illis nuper dixerat, nunc ad alios transit, quibus peculiari institutione opus erat, eo quòd ipsorum coniuges propter religionis diuersitatem legibus Christianis nollent subijci. Se au-tem, non Dominum, loqui testatur. Vbi nemo putauerit, Paulum hic aliquid finxisse, aut tantum sibi ipsi permisisse, vt aliquid ecclesiæ traderet à Christi doctrina alienum. Sciebat enim illum di-scipulis mandauisse: Docete seruare, quæ ego vobis tradidi. Et ipsius quoque animo hærebat Apo-stolicum illud: Si quis loquitur, loquatur vt eloquia Dei. Ideoq; in epistola ad Romanos dicebat: Nō ausim loqui quicquā, quod non effecerit Christus per me. Sed vt diximus, quia nō deerant calu-niatores, ne his occasionem daret aliquam, sub Concessionis specie sic loquitur. Quasi diceret: Age dum, fateor quæ iam dicturus sum, nusquam à Christo diuersis verbis expressa esse, sed me ista sic pronuntiare. Verumtamen nequaquam contemni debent: quia si diligentius examinetur, cū ijs om-nino ea conuenire patebit, quæ alibi Dominus de coniugio et coniugū officijs tradidit, et proinde à spiritu Christi minime aliena sunt. Et huic sensui fauet, quod sub finem Capitis totam istam tra-ctationem cum protestatione ista concludit: Puto autem, quòd & ego spiritum Dei habeam.
units.tr: Since, however, he knew there were many who watched all his words craftily so as to have an occasion for slander, he uses a little preface in which he frankly admits what they could mock, saying: "But to the rest I say, not the Lord." He says "the rest" to show that there is a distinction among Christians, since some had believing partners in the marriage bed, while others were bound by mixed marriages. And because he had spoken of the former just before, he now turns to the others, who needed a special instruction, because their spouses, on account of the difference of religion, were unwilling to submit to Christian laws. He testifies, however, that he speaks as himself and not as the Lord. Here no one should think that Paul has invented anything, or has permitted himself so much as to hand down to the Church something foreign to the teaching of Christ. For he knew that the Lord had commanded his disciples: "Teach them to keep whatever I have delivered to you." And that apostolic saying also remained fixed in his mind: "If anyone speaks, let him speak as the oracles of God." Therefore he said in the letter to the Romans: "I would not dare to speak of anything that Christ has not accomplished through me." But, as we have said, since there were no lack of slanderers, so that he would give them no occasion, he speaks in the form of a concession. As if he said: "Granted, I confess that what I am about to say has nowhere been expressed in these words by Christ, but I pronounce it thus." Yet these words must by no means be despised, because if they are examined more carefully, it will be clear that they agree entirely with what the Lord taught elsewhere about marriage and the duties of spouses, and therefore are by no means foreign to the Spirit of Christ. And this sense is supported by the fact that at the end of the chapter he concludes this whole discussion with this declaration: "But I think that I also have the Spirit of God."

units.la: Est autem multa laude dignissima Pauli modestia & ingenuitas, qui etsi sciret, hanc ipsius Christi mentem esse, non pudet tamen illum tam diserte inter ea distinguere, quæ à Christo ipso tradita sunt, & quæ ipse ex illis colligebat. Ita enim & cauere voluit, ne in ecclesia tyrannidè sibi vendicaret, & simul omnes excitare ad diligentiore eorum, quæ dicebantur, considerationem. Quam modestiam veteres quoq; & Apostolorum temporibus proximi Ecclesiæ doctores secuti sunt. Ex quo rū munero D. Augustinus fuit, quē nō puduit retractationes scribere eorū, quæ cū scripturarū ve-ritate minus conuenire videbat, ab ipso autem incōsideratius scripta fuerat. Et idè solis scripturis eum honorem deberi affirmat, vt pro indubitatis habeantur, quæ illæ tradunt, aliorum verò om-nium scripta cum iudicio legenda esse docet. Eius verba sunt ad D. Hieronymū: Ego fateor cha-ritati tuæ, solis ijs scripturarū libris, qui iā Canonici appellantur, didici hunc timore honorē, de-ferre, vt nullū eorū authore scribendo aliquid errasse firmissimè credā. Ac si aliquid in eis offende-ro literis, quod videatur contrarium veritati, nihil aliud quàm vel mendosum esse codice, vel interpretem non assecutum esse quod dictum est, vel me minime intellexisse non ambigam. Alios tem ita lego, vt quantalibet sanctitate doctrinaq; praepolleant, non ideo verum putem, quia ipsi ita senserunt: sed quia mihi vel per illos authores canonicos, vel probabili ratione, quod a vero non abhorreat, persuadere potuerunt. Nec te mi frater sentire aliquid aliter existimo: prorsus (in quā) non te arbitror sic legi tuos libros velle, tanquā prophetarū vel apostolorū, de quorū scriptis, quod omni errore careat, dubitare nefarium est, &c. Haec omnia Augusti. ex cuius libris, vt & aliorum patrum, multa huius generis adduci poterant. At hodie Pontifices, quae ipsi fingunt, pro diuinis aruculis obtrudere non verentur, vt illis contradicere scelus capitale sit, etiamsi nulla Verbi Dei authoritate probentur. Et vtinam inter eos quoque, qui puriorem Euangelij doctrinam profitentur, non plures essent, qui in suorum praeceptorum verba ita iurarunt, vt tantummnon Pythagoricum illud semper in ore habeant: αὐτὸς ἔφα[?]. At neminem istorum arrogantia moueat, quin discant singuli inter hominū traditiones et scripturae sacrae oracula distinguere, et his quidē ab sq; ylla haesitatione credant, illas vero diligenter ad Verbi Dei canonem examinent. Nunc in Pauli loco pergamus.
units.tr: Paul's modesty and candour are, however, most worthy of great praise. Although he knew that this was the very mind of Christ, he is not ashamed to distinguish so clearly between what was delivered by Christ himself and what he himself drew from those teachings. For in this way he wished both to guard against claiming tyrannical power in the Church and at the same time to stir all to a more careful consideration of what was being said. The ancient writers also followed this modesty, and the teachers of the Church who lived close to the times of the apostles. Among them was St. Augustine, who was not ashamed to write Retractations of those things which he saw did not agree well with the truth of Scripture, but which he had written too carelessly. And so he affirms that this honour is due to the Scriptures alone, that whatever they hand down be held as indubitable, while he teaches that the writings of all others are to be read with judgment. His words to St. Jerome are these: "I confess to your charity that I have learned to show this reverence and honour only to those books of Scripture which are now called canonical, so that I firmly believe that none of their authors has erred in writing anything. And if I come upon anything in those letters that seems contrary to the truth, I do not doubt that either the manuscript is faulty, or the translator has not grasped what was said, or I have not understood it at all. But the others I read in such a way that, however great their holiness and learning, I do not therefore think them true because they thought so, but because they have persuaded me, either by those canonical authors or by probable reasoning, that they do not depart from the truth. Nor do I think, my brother, that you feel otherwise. Indeed, I do not think you want your books to be read in the same way as the writings of the prophets or apostles, about whose writings it is wicked to doubt that they are free from all error," and so on. All these are the words of Augustine, from whose books, as from those of other Fathers, many passages of this kind could be quoted. Today, however, the Pontiffs do not hesitate to thrust upon us as divine oracles what they themselves have invented, so that to contradict them is a capital crime, even though they are not proved by any authority of the Word of God. And would that among those who profess the purer doctrine of the gospel there were not also many who have sworn to the words of their own teachers in such a way that they almost always keep on their lips that Pythagorean saying, "he himself has said it" [αὐτὸς ἔφα]. But let no one's arrogance prevent each from learning to distinguish between human traditions and the oracles of holy Scripture, and to believe the latter without any hesitation, while examining the former carefully by the canon of the Word of God. Now let us proceed to Paul's passage.

units.la: Primò de illis loquitur, quibus vxor aut maritus infidelis, idest, à religione Christiana omnino alienus obrigit, qui tamen ea animi moderatione vtantur, vt propter religionis diuersitatem matrimonium diuelli nolint, neque etiam coniugem ad fidei abnegationem cogere instituant. De illis sic dicit: Si quis frater vxorem habet infidelem, quae consentiat ad habitandum cum eo, ne eam dimittito. Et vxor, quae habet virum infidelem, qui consentiat ad habitandum cum ea, ne eum dimittito. Verba haec per se clara sunt, & sensus est, ne vel maritus Christianus cum vxore ethnica diuortium faciat, si haec cum eo pacifice viuere & fidem coniugalem ratam manere velit: vel vxor Christiana à marito ethnico discedat, si hic eam ferre possit, & cum ea viuere cupiat.
units.tr: First he speaks of those whose wife or husband is unbelieving, that is, wholly alien to the Christian religion, yet who show such restraint of mind that they are unwilling to dissolve the marriage because of the difference of religion, and do not intend to compel the spouse to renounce the faith. Of these he says: "If any brother has an unbelieving wife, who consents to dwell with him, let him not put her away. And the wife who has an unbelieving husband, who consents to dwell with her, let her not leave him." These words are clear in themselves, and the sense is this: a Christian husband should not divorce an ethnic wife if she is willing to live peaceably with him and to keep the marriage vow intact; nor should a Christian wife leave an ethnic husband if he is able to bear with her and wishes to live with her.

units.la: At hic probè obseruari debet, Pauli non de coniugijs contrahendis loqui, sed de illis, quae iam pridem contracta fuerant, priusquam vel maritus vel vxor ad Christi fidem peruenissent. Falso igitur hinc aliqui colligunt: Apostolus prohibuit, ne fidelis vxorem infidelem eijciat, neue vxor fidelis à marito infideli discedat: Ergo licet cum infidelibus matrimonio iungi. Nec enim semper licet facere, quod si factum iam sit tolerari potest. Et quoad coniugia iam primum contrahenda, lege diserta cauit Deus, ne qui ex ipsius populo aut ecclesia censentur, cum infidelibus iungantur. Nam Deuter. septimo Cap. sic loquitur Moses: Ne iungas cum eis affinitatem, filiam tuam ne des filio illorum, neque filiam illorum despondeas filio tuo. Et causam praecepti huius grauem subijcit: Quoniam auocabit filium tuum à me, seruientq; Dijs alijs, & commouebitur furor Domini contra vos, vt cito te deleat. Quod autem Moses monuit, hoc ipsum Deus antea ijsdem fere verbis in libro Exodi Cap. 34. praeceperat. Tanta verò fuit huius legis authoritas apud pios, vt Ezras publica poenitentia opus esse putaret, cùm qui ex Babylone reuersi fuerant, vxores ethnicas ducendo sanctitatem Iudaici populi (vt Malachias ait) prophanauissent, & coniugia illa mox rescindi iuberet, etiamsi multi iam liberos ex illis suscepissent. Nec enim sine scelere ratum esse poterat, quod contra Dei leges illi fecerant. Et constat omnibus seculis infelicissimè cessisse eiusmodi matrimonia. Ex illis olim Nephilim illi nati sunt, quorum exemplis totus orbis terrarum corruptus, diluuij aquis deleri meruit. Vxorum item alienigenarum blanditijs seductus Salomo idololatriam inuexit, quae toti Iudaeorum genti exitium attulit. Et quid hodie multis accidat, non opus est commemorare. Noluit ergo de legis diuinae rigore Paulus aliquid remittere, qui in posteriori epistola grauiter pronuntiat: Ne impari iugo copulemini cum infidelibus. Quod enim cofortiu iustitiae cu iniustitia? et quae comunio luci cu tenebris? et quae cocordia Christo cu Belial? quae pars fideli cum infideli? Et Epiphanius contra haereticos, qui Apostolici dicebantur, scribens, ab Apostolis constitutum fuisse testatur, ne Christiani suas filias Iudaeis aut gentibus nondum conuersis elocarent. Quòd si quaeras, cur ergo non Ezrae exemplum Paulus secutus est, vt coniugia ista omnino dirimeret, cùm periculum idem quod olim hic quoque posset timeri? Respondeo, non eandem fuisse Corinthiorum conditionem, quae Iudaeorum fuit. Hi enim in Dei leges peccauerant aperte vxores ethnicas ducendo, & cùm rempub. haberent propriam, errorem admissum poterant emendare. Corinthij verò in contrahendis coniugijs nihil peccarant, neque tunc aliqua fuerat religionis diversitas, sed hæc postea demum per Evangelij prædicationē inducta fuit. Deinde cum rempub. nō haberent in sua potestate, & divortia cū uxoribus ethnicis fieri non poterant, quin ignominia ad earū quoq; cognatos et parentes redundaret, res ista scandali simul et periculi plena fuisset. Adde quod spes erat eos etiā converti posse, qui adhuc in superstitionū tenebris hærebant.
units.tr: But it must be carefully observed that Paul is not speaking of marriages yet to be contracted, but of those already contracted, before either the husband or the wife had come to the faith of Christ. Some therefore wrongly infer from this: the Apostle forbade a believer to cast off an unbelieving wife, or a believing wife to separate from an unbelieving husband; therefore it is lawful to join oneself in marriage with unbelievers. For what may not always be done may nonetheless be tolerated once it has been done. And as to marriages that are yet to be contracted, God has forbidden them by a plain law, that those who are counted among his people or Church should not be joined with unbelievers. For in Deuteronomy chapter 7 Moses speaks thus: "Do not make marriages with them; do not give your daughter to their son, nor take their daughter for your son." And he gives a grave reason for this command: "For they will turn your son away from me, and serve other gods, and the anger of the Lord will be kindled against you, and he will quickly destroy you." What Moses admonished, God had earlier commanded in almost the same words in the book of Exodus chapter 34. The authority of this law was so great among the godly that Ezra thought a public repentance was needed when those who had returned from Babylon had profaned the holiness of the Jewish people (as Malachi says) by taking ethnic wives, and he ordered those marriages to be dissolved at once, even though many had already had children by them. For what they had done against the laws of God could not stand without sin. And it is agreed that in every age such marriages have turned out most unhappily. From them of old were born those Nephilim, by whose examples the whole earth was corrupted and deserved to be destroyed by the waters of the flood. Likewise Solomon, seduced by the enticements of foreign wives, introduced idolatry, which brought ruin upon the whole nation of the Jews. And there is no need to recall what happens to many today. Paul therefore would not relax anything of the rigour of the divine law, when in his later epistle he solemnly declares: "Do not be yoked unequally with unbelievers. For what fellowship has righteousness with unrighteousness? And what communion has light with darkness? And what concord has Christ with Belial? What part has the believer with the unbeliever?" And Epiphanius, writing against the heretics who were called Apostolics, testifies that it was established by the Apostles that Christians should not give their daughters in marriage to Jews or to Gentiles not yet converted. But if you ask why Paul did not follow the example of Ezra and entirely dissolve these marriages, since the same danger could be feared here as once there, I answer: the condition of the Corinthians was not the same as that of the Jews. For the Jews had clearly sinned against the laws of God by taking ethnic wives, and since they had a commonwealth of their own, they could correct the error committed. The Corinthians, however, had sinned in no way in contracting their marriages, nor was there then any difference of religion; this came in afterwards through the preaching of the Gospel. Furthermore, since they did not have the commonwealth in their own power, and divorces from ethnic wives could not be made without disgrace also falling upon their kinsfolk and parents, that matter would have been full of scandal and danger at once. Add that there was hope that even those who still stuck in the darkness of superstitions could be converted.

units.la: Porrò quod de coniugijs dicitur, hoc ipsum de fœderibus quoq; intelligi debet, quando hæc cum illis Deus in lege quam modò recitavimus, coniungit. Videndum hic, ne cum prophanis & à fide alienis fœdera ineamus, multò minus autem cum apertis fidei & veri Dei aut verbi eius hostibus. Ut enim horum commercia valde insidiosa sunt: ita fœdera eiusmodi cum fide et religione pugnant, cum nunquā fiat, quin fiducia, quæ in uno Deo nobis repositā esse debebat, in homines impios & profanos collocetur. Quæ causa est, quod in scripturis passim damnantur, quæ exemplis quoq; docent, illorum exitum fere infelicē esse. Iosaphato certè periculosa fuit Achabi idololatræ affinitas atq; fœdus. Ezechiā quoq; cum suis Ægyptij fœderis fiducia decipit, ut bellum sibi accerseret, quo de summa rerū gravissimè periclitatus est. Et si rem penitius excutiamus, Zedechias fœdere cū Idumæis, Moabitis, Ammonitis, Tyrijs & Sidonijs inito confidentior factus bello initiū dedit, quo Nabuchodonosor urbem cum templo evertit, & infelices populi reliquias in Babylonem abduxit. Possunt his accenseri Græcorum Imperatores, quibus Turcarū fœdera & ab hīs sperata auxilia exi-tium attulerunt. Quorum exemplis utinam saperent hodie, qui in re tam gravis momenti nimium leues & incircumspecti sunt. Verumtamen, sicui genti, priusquam Christi cognitione illuminata fuit, fœdus cum aliquibus adhuc à fide alienis propter viciniam aut commune periculum intercessit conditionibus minimè impijs & ad patriæ communis defensionem pertinentibus, illud quoq; non temere rescindi, neq; illis data fides violari debet, siquidè salua religione præstari possit. Observent hoc ipsum privatim serui, qui in herorum potestate sunt, qui fidem in Christum non agnoscunt: ne religionis prætextu abutantur, & dum libertatem præcipiti desiderio affectant, fidem Christianam multis suspectam faciant. Sed de his & alijs horum similibus plura suo loco dicentur.
units.tr: Moreover, what is said of marriages must also be understood of covenants, since God joins these with those in the law which we have just recited. Here we must take care that we make no covenants with profane persons and those alien to the faith, much less with the open enemies of the faith and of the true God or of his Word. For just as dealings with such people are very insidious, so covenants of this kind are at odds with faith and religion, since it never happens that the trust which ought to have been placed in the one God alone is not transferred to impious and profane men. This is why in the Scriptures such covenants are condemned everywhere, and why examples also teach that their outcome is almost always unhappy. Certainly for Jehoshaphat the alliance and covenant with the idolater Ahab was dangerous. Hezekiah too was deceived by his trust in a covenant with the Egyptians, so that he brought war upon himself, by which he was most grievously endangered for his whole kingdom. And if we examine the matter more closely, Zedekiah, made more confident by a covenant entered into with the Edomites, Moabites, Ammonites, Tyrians and Sidonians, gave the beginning of war, by which Nebuchadnezzar overthrew the city with the temple and carried the wretched remnant of the people away to Babylon. To these may be added the Emperors of the Greeks, whom the covenants with the Turks and the help hoped for from them brought to ruin. Would that they were wise today, by their examples, those who are too light and careless in a matter of such great weight! Nevertheless, if any nation, before it was enlightened by the knowledge of Christ, has entered into a covenant with some who are still alien to the faith, on account of neighbourhood or a common danger, on conditions by no means impious and pertaining to the defence of the common fatherland, that covenant too should not be rashly broken, nor should the faith given to them be violated, provided that it can be kept without harm to religion. Let servants who are under the power of masters who do not acknowledge faith in Christ observe this very thing privately: that they not abuse the pretext of religion, and by desiring liberty with headlong eagerness, make the Christian faith suspect to many. But more will be said about these matters and others like them in their proper place.

units.la: Redeamus nunc ad Paulum, cuius consilio nonnulli ad divortia facienda propensiores conta-gionis periculum obijciebant, et ex eo, quod nuper de fornicatione dixerat, per comparationem ad hunc modum argumentabantur: Qui scorto adhæret, unum cum illo corpus fit, ideoq; eius consuetudine aut coniunctione polluitur. Ergo qui uxori idololatræ adhæret, etiā cum illa in unum corpus aut unam carnem coalescit: quod fieri non potest, quin ipse quoq; idololatria eius inquinetur. Sed negat hanc consequentiam Paulus, imò hic plane diversum fieri docet. Nam maritus (inquit) infidelis sanctificatus est in uxore, & uxor infidelis sanctificata est in viro, id est, coniugis fidelis fides atq; pietas efficacior est, ut coniugium hoc, quod per se legitimè coaluit, pro sancto & puro habeatur, quàm ut alterius incredulitate aut idololatria inquinari & prophanum reddi possit. Ratio huius sententiæ alibi redditur. Quia puris omnia sunt pura, id est, ijs qui per fidem in Christum purificati sunt, ijs concessa & pura sunt, quæcunq; Deus instituit. Omnia enim (ut cap. 3. dixit) ipsorū sunt, sive mundus, sive vita, sive mors, sive præsentia, sive futura: et ideo omnibus ut proprijs utuntur, cū gratiarū actione, neq; eorū usu pollui possunt. E contra verò impijs impura sunt omnia, cum eorū mens & conscientia polluta sit, neq; in Dei institutionem respiciant, simulq; omnibus pro carnalium affectuū libidine abutantur. Ita verò soluit Apostolus argumentum, quod illi ex coniugij et scortationis collatione adducebant, & eos turpiter errare ostendit, cum nō eadem sit utriusq; ratio. Primò enim coniugium à Deo institutum & legibus divinis concessum est omnibus, qui illo uti volunt: scortatio autem semper prohibita & horrendis exemplis punita est. Deinde in scortatione utrq; peccat, & tam corpore quàm animo polluitur: in coniugijs autem imparibus nulla quoad commixtionem coniugalem culpa erat, fidelis autem neq; idololatria alterius polluebatur, cùm ei minimè communicaret. Tertiò in coniugio spes erat infidelem quoq; alterius mansuetudine & industria aliquando converti & servari posse: in scortatione autem impura & desperata sunt omnia. Quartò quo minus dissolvi deberent illa coniugia consensus & facilitas partis infidelis monebat, neq; pium fuisset dissidium non necessarium quærere, cùm salua pietate vinculum illud posset ratum manere: at in scortatione omnis ratio quæri debet, ut illicita illa stupri consuetudo dirimatur, quæ eò nocentior est, quo pertinacior inter illos consensus fuerit. Quibus adde, quòd in coniugio communicatio fit, non quoad superstitiones & idololatriam vel alia peccata, sed quoad corpora, fortunas & debita coniugii officia. Ideo coniugium etiam impar fideli sanctum, & eidem coniunx quoq; infide-lis sanctificata est, ut eius consuetudine & congressu nequaquam possit pollui.
units.tr: Let us now return to Paul. Some, who were more inclined to make divorces, were putting forward the danger of contagion on the basis of his advice, and from what he had just said about fornication they argued by comparison in this way: "He who cleaves to a harlot becomes one body with her, and is therefore defiled by her company or union. Therefore he who cleaves to an idolatrous wife also coalesces with her into one body or one flesh; and this cannot happen without his also being polluted by her idolatry." But Paul denies this consequence, and indeed teaches that the very opposite happens here. For he says: "The unbelieving husband is sanctified in the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified in the husband." That is, the faith and piety of the believing spouse are more effective, so that this marriage, which has rightly been joined together, is regarded as holy and pure, rather than being able to be defiled and made profane by the unbelief or idolatry of the other. The reason for this judgement is given elsewhere: "To the pure all things are pure," that is, to those who have been purified through faith in Christ, all things that God has instituted are granted and pure. For (as he said in chapter 3) all things are theirs, whether the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; and therefore they use all things as their own, with thanksgiving, and cannot be polluted by their use. On the contrary, to the impious all things are impure, since their mind and conscience are defiled, and they do not look to God's institution, but at the same time abuse everything for the lust of carnal affections. In this way the Apostle answers the argument which they drew from the comparison of marriage and fornication, and shows that they err shamefully, since the reason of each is not the same. For first, marriage has been instituted by God and granted by divine laws to all who wish to use it; but fornication has always been forbidden and punished by dreadful examples. Second, in fornication both parties sin, and are defiled in body as well as in mind; but in marriages between unequal partners there was no fault as regards the conjugal union, and the believer was not defiled by the idolatry of the other, since he had no fellowship with it. Third, in marriage there was hope that the unbelieving spouse too might at some time be converted and saved by the gentleness and diligence of the other; but in fornication all things are impure and hopeless.
