Fourth, the consent and willingness of the unbelieving party advised that those marriages should not be dissolved; nor would it have been godly to seek an unnecessary separation, since the bond could remain valid without loss of piety; but in fornication every reason must be sought for the dissolving of that unlawful habit of illicit intercourse, which is all the more harmful the more stubborn the consent between them has been. To these add that in marriage a sharing takes place, not in respect of superstitions and idolatry or other sins, but in respect of bodies, fortunes and the duties owed in marriage. Therefore a marriage, even one between unequal partners, is holy for the believer, and the unbelieving spouse too is sanctified by the believer, so that he or she cannot be polluted by intercourse and living together with them.

units.la: Caeterum aliud argumentum adducit Paulus, quo nullum inter coniuges eiusmodi contagio-nis periculum esse docet. Alioqui certè (inquit) liberi vestri impuri essent, nunc autem sancti sunt. Sensus est: Si per coniugii consuetudinem fidelis quoq; coniunx idololatriae & impietatis particeps atq; reus fieret, ita liberi quoq; vestri impuri & prophani essent, utpote ex parente utroq; prophano atq; alieno à Christi fide progeniti. At liberi vestri puri & sancti sunt: Ergo fidelis per infidelis coniugium non polluitur. Vbi obseruabimus, liberos eiusmodi mundos dici, non quod originis peccato careat, in quo omnes homines formari, concipi & nasci scriptura testatur, sed ad Dei foedus & eius promis-sionem respicit: Ero Deus tuus & seminis tui. Rata est autem promissio ista apud omnes credentes, etiam apud eos, quibus absq; sua culpa coniunx infidelis obtigit. Nam nihil est, quod Dei promissa abolere aut eius fidem irritam facere possit. Attollite (inquit per Prophetam) oculos vestros in cae-lum & terram subtus inspicite: quoniam caeli ut fumus deficient, & terra ut vestis vetustate pe-ribit, & qui in ea habitant ad eundem modum peribunt: salus autem mea in aeternum durabit, & iustitia mea non interibit. Et qui legem dedit, ne filij parentum culpam luant, cur ipse propter ma-tris incredulitatem infantes damnaret, quorum alter parens fidelis & per fidem in Christum sanctificatus est? Atqui iure civili liberi censentur, qui ex altero parente libero nascuntur: & nos Deum in filijs suorum cultorum rigidiorem & crudeliorem fingeremus?
units.tr: Paul brings forward another argument, by which he teaches that there is no danger of such contagion between spouses. Otherwise, he says, your children would certainly be unclean, but now they are holy. The sense is this: if a believing spouse were made a partner and accomplice in idolatry and impiety through living together in marriage, then their children too would be unclean and profane, since they were born of two profane parents, both alien to the faith of Christ. But your children are clean and holy. Therefore a believer is not polluted through marriage to an unbeliever. Here we should observe that children of this kind are called clean not because they are free from the sin of origin, in which Scripture testifies that all human beings are formed, conceived and born, but because they look to God's covenant and his promise: "I will be your God and the God of your seed" (Gen. 17). This promise holds good for all believers, including those to whom an unbelieving spouse has fallen through no fault of their own. For nothing can abolish God's promises or make his faithfulness void. "Lift up your eyes to heaven," he says through the Prophet, "and look upon the earth beneath; for the heavens shall vanish like smoke, and the earth shall wear out like a garment, and those who dwell in it shall die in the same way; but my salvation shall last for ever, and my righteousness shall not fail" (Isa. 51). And if the Lawgiver himself decreed that children should not bear the guilt of their parents, why would he condemn infants on account of their mother's unbelief, when one of their parents is faithful and has been sanctified through faith in Christ? Yet by civil law, children are reckoned free when they are born of a free parent. Would we imagine God to be harsher and more cruel toward the children of his worshippers?

units.la: Possunt autem huius loci authoritate duo insignes Anabaptistarum errores confutari: alter, quod ab ecclesijs omnibus secessionem faciunt, ne aliorum peccatis polluantur: alter, quo infantes baptizari debere negant. Vt priorem tueantur, multa de ecclesiae perfectione & sanctitate garriunt, quae neq; ruga neq; macula habere debeat, & vicissim in observandis nostrorum vitijs plus quàm Lyncei sunt, & illa mirifice amplificant, ut iustas à nobis discedendi causas se habere probent. Errant aut, quod ecclesiam talem in terris habere posse arbitrantur, qualis olim erit, quando in coelos translata ab omni corruptione liberabitur. Quanta enim optimorum quoq; vitiositas sit, quoad in hac carne viuunt, Paulus proprio exemplo ad Romanos docet, & non vno loco sanctissimi quiq; fatentur. Sufficiat nunc nobis, quod propter Christum, cui per fidem insiti sumus, pro iustis & inculpatis habemur. Quoad autem coetus ecclesiasticos, in ijs non scelerū, sed fidei & religionis communicatio fit, cuius professio & doctrina si pura & syncera fuerit, nullum nobis ex aliorum hypocrisi aut manifesta improbitate periculum est metuendum, cum illis nullo modo consentiamus. Et quod ipsi de communione membrorum ecclesiae differunt, quoad hanc causam prorsus friuolum est, negalis quem movere debet. Etenim nulla arctior inter homines coniunctio est, quàm quae inter virum & mulierem per matrimonij vinculum habetur. Est enim haec os ex ossibus viri & caro ex carne eius, & qui duo erant nunc vna caro facti sunt: deniq; vir capitis loco est, cui mulier ceu corpus subijci atq; obedire debet. Adde, quod qui ex his nascuntur liberi, utriusq; caro sunt & aequo iure ad utrumq; pertinent. Verumtamen non polluitur maritus fidelis per vxoris à fide alienae consuetudinem, neq; etiam liberi ex matris incredulitate culpam eam contrahunt, ut prophani censeri debeant. Quae ergo stultitia est, pollutionem ex illis metuere, qui qualescunq; sunt, tamen fidem profitentur in Christum, & nisi id vere & ex animo faciant, externis quidem ecclesiae ritibus communicant, eiusdem tamen membra non sunt, & proinde nihil ad nos pertinent? Deinde non polluitur alterius superstitione fidelis coniunx, quia coniugij lege tenetur, ut fidem datam non violet, imò fideli marito vxor infidelis est sanctificata per coniugij institutionem. Cur ergo non idem dee-clesiasticis coetibus sentimus, quando hos quoq; à Deo institutos & mandatos esse constat, ut nimirum hos quoq; sanctificatos esse putemus ijs, qui animo verè pio & religioso accedunt, Dei verbum in illis digne audiunt, & Sacramentis rite utuntur, etiamsi multi alij sese temere immisceant, qui secus agunt? Haec si probè expendamus, patebit, intolerabilem esse istorum hominum arrogantiam, qui ut omnes homines ceu Rhadamanti & Minoes quidam temere damnant: ita Dei gratiam & misericordiam magna ex parte euacuant, & (quod peculiare est diaboli stratagema) sub pietatis & sanctimoniae praetextu ecclesiam discerpunt, quo nullum scelus atrocius est & detestabilius. Alter quoq; error ex hoc loco facile arguitur. Est enim ecclesia (ut in Symbolo fatemur) communio Sanctorum. Quo ore ergo illi ad ecclesiam pertinere negant infantes Christianorum quando Paulus eos sanctos dicere dignatur, qui ex alterutro tantum parente Christiano nati sunt? Est ergo inexcusabilis istorum audacia, qui dum ablutionis peccatorum & sanctimoniae, quam nobis Christus acquisiuit, symbolum illis negant, eadem opera eosdem ab ecclesiae societate reijciunt, & simul illam magna suorum membrorum parte mutilant. Sed plura de his alibi.
units.tr: By the authority of this passage, two notable errors of the Anabaptists can be refuted. The first is that they secede from all the churches, lest they be polluted by the sins of others. The second is that they deny that infants ought to be baptized. To defend the first, they chatter at length about the perfection and holiness of the Church, which ought to have neither wrinkle nor spot, and in turn they are sharper-eyed than Lynceus in noticing our faults, and they magnify these wonderfully, so that they may prove they have just reasons for departing from us. But they err in thinking that the Church can be on earth such as it will one day be, when, taken up into heaven, it will be freed from all corruption. For Paul teaches by his own example in the letter to the Romans how great the sinfulness even of the best people is, while they live in this flesh, and the holiest men confess it in more than one place. For now it is enough for us that, on account of Christ, into whom we have been grafted by faith, we are counted righteous and blameless. As for ecclesiastical assemblies, what is shared in them is not wickedness but faith and religion. If their profession and teaching are pure and sincere, we need fear no danger from the hypocrisy or open wickedness of others, since we in no way consent with them. And what they argue about the communion of the members of the Church is utterly frivolous for this question, and ought to move no one. For there is no closer bond between human beings than that which exists between husband and wife through the bond of marriage. "This is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh, and the two have become one flesh"; finally, the husband is in the place of the head, to whom the wife, like a body, ought to be subject and obey. Add to this that the children born of them are flesh of both and belong equally to each. Yet a believing husband is not polluted by living with a wife who is alien to the faith, nor do the children contract that guilt from their mother's unbelief so as to be counted profane. What folly, then, is it to fear pollution from those who, whatever they are, nevertheless profess faith in Christ, and who, unless they do this truly and from the heart, take part in the external rites of the Church but are not its members, and therefore have nothing to do with us? Moreover, a believing spouse is not polluted by the superstition of the other, because they are bound by the law of marriage not to violate the faith they have pledged; indeed, for a believing husband, the unbelieving wife has been sanctified through the institution of marriage. Why then do we not think the same of ecclesiastical assemblies, since it is agreed that these too were instituted and commanded by God, so that we may surely think them sanctified for those who approach with a truly pious and religious mind, who hear the Word of God worthily in them and use the sacraments rightly, even if many others who act otherwise rashly mix themselves in? If we weigh these things carefully, it will be clear how intolerable is the arrogance of those men who, as though they were Rhadamanthus and Minos, rashly condemn everyone; and who, in great part, empty God's grace and mercy, and (which is the peculiar stratagem of the devil) under the pretext of piety and sanctity tear the Church apart, than which no crime is more atrocious or detestable. The other error is also easily refuted from this passage. For the Church is (as we confess in the Creed) "the communion of saints." With what face, then, do they deny that the children of Christians belong to the Church, when Paul deigns to call holy those who are born of only one Christian parent? Therefore the audacity of those men is inexcusable: while they deny the washing away of sins and the holiness that Christ has won for us to be a sign given to these children, by the same act they cast them out of the fellowship of the Church, and at the same time maim the Church by a great part of its members. But more on these matters elsewhere.

units.la: Nunc loci huius contextu secuti ad eos transeamus, quibus coniunx morosior & intractabilior obtigit, quam ut coniugem fideliter ferre et ei cohabitare velit. Docet hic paucis Apostolus, quid in tali casu fieri debeat, sic dicens: At si incredulus discedit, discedat. Quorum sensus est: Si vel maritus vel uxor cum fideli cohabitare nolit, & animo iam prorsus alienato diuortium omnino velit fieri, ideo& aut uxor infidelis a marito sponte discedat, aut hic uxorem fidelem crudeliter eijciat, haec quoque sors patienter ferenda est. Tunc enim infidelis & idololatrae morositas fideli nequaquam fraudi aut vitio verti poterit, & licebit huic divortium iste falsa conscientia subire. Sed hic quoque rationes adducit, quibus animos titubantes confirmet. Prima: Quia non est servituti subiectus frater aut soror in huiusmodi rebus, id est, non amplius tenentur legibus coniugij, quas alter jam violavit absq; omni ipsorum culpa. Altera: In pace autem vocavit nos Deus. Huius enim voluntas est, ut animorum pace aut tranquillitate in CHRISTO JESV fruamur, & quantum in nobis est pacem cum hominibus quoq; omnibus colamus. Quapropter quoad homines quoscunq; officio nostro erga eos fungamur, & ut omnibus alijs, ita coniugibus imprimis debitam benevolentiam praestemus: quod si autem minus proficimus, saltem de conscientiae pace retinenda laboremus, quae servari non poterit, nisi potior apud nos sit religio & fides, qua Christo obstricti sumus, quam coniugij aut ullius humani foederis necessitas. Notum enim est illud Christi: Qui amauerit patrem aut matrem supra me, non est me dignus: & qui amauerit filium aut filiam supra me, non est me dignus. Item: Si quis venit ad me, nec odit patrem suum & matrem, uxorem & liberos, et sorores, praeterea autem & animam suam, non potest meus esse discipulus. Quoties ergo rem eo deuenire videmus, ut nobis cum parentibus aut cum coniuge convenire non possit, nisi Christo relicto fidem in illum abnegemus, tunc in mentem veniat, impleri iam Christi vaticinium, qui se gladium missurum dixit in terram, quo coniunctissimi quiq; & ipsi etiam domestici abs se invicem separentur. Consoletur autem nos conscientia integritas, quod ipsi nullam dissidiorum causam praebemus, & quod retributionem liberalissimam tam in hoc quam futuro saeculo nobis Deus pollicitus est.
units.tr: Now, following the context of this passage, let us turn to those whose spouse is so stubborn and intractable that they are unwilling to bear the spouse faithfully or live with them. Here the Apostle teaches briefly what ought to be done in such a case, saying: "But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart." The sense is this: if either the husband or the wife is unwilling to live with a believing partner, and, their affection now utterly estranged, wishes the divorce to be made altogether, then either the unbelieving wife should leave her husband of her own accord, or he should cruelly cast out his believing wife. This lot too must be borne patiently. For then the obstinacy of the unbeliever and idolater can by no means be imputed to the believer as a fault, and the believer may undergo this divorce with a clear conscience. But here too he brings forward reasons by which he strengthens wavering minds. The first: "a brother or sister is not under bondage in such matters," that is, they are no longer bound by the laws of marriage, which the other has already violated without any fault on their part. The second: "God has called us to peace." For it is his will that we enjoy peace of mind and tranquillity in Christ Jesus, and, as far as lies in us, that we cultivate peace with all human beings. Therefore, in our duty toward all people, we should show the goodwill owed to all, and especially to spouses; but if we make little progress, we should at least labour to keep the peace of conscience, which cannot be kept unless religion and the faith by which we are bound to Christ are held more dear to us than the obligation of marriage or of any human covenant. For that saying of Christ is well known: "He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and he who loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me." Likewise: "If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, and indeed his own life too, he cannot be my disciple." Whenever, therefore, we see things come to the point where we cannot agree with our parents or with our spouse unless we forsake Christ and deny our faith in him, then let us call to mind that the prophecy of Christ is now being fulfilled, when he said he would bring a sword upon the earth, by which those most closely united, even members of the household, would be separated from one another. Yet our conscience of integrity will console us, since we ourselves give no cause of dissension, and since God has promised us the most generous recompense, both in this age and in the age to come.

units.la: Debet igitur haec Pauli doctrina ad omnes homines extendi, ne in aliquius gratiam aliquid faciamus, quod fidei Christianae legibus repugnet. Nam ut ante diximus, quantum in nobis est, pacem cum omnibus colere debemus. At cum de religione, fide & doctrina agitur, ista meminerimus non nostri iuris neq; in nostra potestate esse, & proinde indiuulse illis adhaereamus, quae nobis a Christo tradita esse constat. Si enim olim philosopho dicere licuit, Amicus Socrates, sed magis amica veritas: cur Christianus homo non protestari audeat, abs se quidem diligi omnes homines, sed ea conditione, ut primas semper Christus teneat, a cuius verbis vel latum pilum discedere nefas sit? Itaq; quoad de externis agitur, omnia suffert Christiana charitas, & qui hac praediti sunt, ijs nequaquam grave est, de suo iure interdum cedere: At quam primum ad Dei gloriam venitur, tunc zelum suum fides exerit, quae nihil ferre potest, quod illi aliqua ex parte deroget. At quae nostri seculi infelicitas est, plerique sub charitatis et concordiae praetextu in religionis causa frigidissimi sunt, & in hominum gratiam nihil non faciunt: ijdem vero cum quotus inimicitias irreconciliabiles suscipiunt, quando de opibus & fortunis, aut nominis ipsorum existimatione agitur.
units.tr: This teaching of Paul ought to be extended to all people, so that for the sake of anyone's favour we do nothing that conflicts with the laws of the Christian faith. For, as we said before, as far as it lies with us we ought to cultivate peace with everyone. But when matters of religion, faith and doctrine are at stake, let us remember that these are not within our right or power, and therefore we should cling without wavering to those things which are known to have been handed down to us by Christ. For if once it was permitted for a philosopher to say, "Socrates is my friend, but truth is a friend even more," why should a Christian not dare to declare that he loves all people, but on the condition that Christ always holds first place, and that it is wrong to depart from his words even by the breadth of a hair? So, as far as external matters go, Christian charity bears all things, and for those endowed with it, it is by no means burdensome to give up their own right at times. But as soon as we come to the glory of God, then faith shows its zeal, which can bear nothing that detracts from Him in any way. But it is the misfortune of our age that many, under the pretext of charity and concord, are very cold in the cause of religion and do nothing that does not serve people's favour; yet these same people, how quickly they take up irreconcilable enmities when wealth and fortunes, or the esteem of their own name, are at stake.

units.la: Porro duabus hisce rationibus novum argumentum Paulus subiicit, quo priores illos, qui ex consuetudine infidelis coniugis contagionem timebant, magis confirmat. Verba illius sunt haec: Et quid enim nosti mulier, an virum fis servatura? aut ecquid nosti vir, an uxor fis servaturus? Admonet hos, spem esse, coniugi fidelis mansuetudine & industria infidelem Christo lucrifieri posse, ideoq; vinculum coniugij non temere abrumpi debere. Simul autem docentur coniuges, non solum rei domesticae & liberorum procreationi aut educationi vacandum esse, sed hoc imprimis curandum, ut Christo vivatur, & si quid vitij in altero utro insit, id alterius prudentia et facilitate sancta emendetur. Jubet hoc ipsum graviter Petrus Apostolus, sic scribens: Uxores subditae sint suis viris, ut etiam si qui non obediunt sermoni, per uxorum conversationem absq; sermone lucrifiant, ubi viderint cum reuerentia coniunctam castam couersatione vestram. Talis olim Abigael fuit, quæ viri stolidissimum non modò patienter tulit, verumetiam præter omne suum meritum admirabili indu-stria seruauit, seipsam pro illo & fortunis eius manifesto vitæ periculo obijciens. Idem maiori cum fructu Hester fecit, quæ etsi ex gente aliena atq; omnibus inuisa originem suam duceret, & regi su-perbissimo nupta esset, sancta[?] tamen fiducia atq; humilitate legum Medicarum rigorem superauit, & Regis animum flectendo à tota Ju-dæorum gente imminēs exitium auertit. In Francorum au-tem Annalibus perquam memorabile est Gotthildis exemplum, quæ Clodouæum regem sua pieta-te & amicis colloquij mouit, vt se Christianum fore voueret, & in maximo prælij cum Alemannis periculo ad Christi opem recurreret. Possent huius generis multa colligi, & hodie etiam videmus vxorum honestate et modestia multorum ferociam domari, vt se ad omnia faciliores præbeant. Debet autem ex his doctrina generalis peti, ne de aliquius hominis salute temere desperemus. Nescimus nos, quis nam in Spiritum sanctum peccet, et sæpe ad frugi meliorem conuertuntur, quorū nequitia desperata esse videbatur. Charitas autem de omnibus optimè sperat. Quoad ergo salus hominis in dubio est, nos quoq; spem bona fouere, et erga quosuis nostro officio fungi debemus. Fecit hoc Paulus in Ju-dæorum gente, cum quorū contumacia ad extremū vsq; spiritum luctatus est, licet manifesta de eo-rū excæcatione & repudio vaticinia extare non ignoraret. Quod ipsum si hodie omnes facerent, & minus peccaretur temerarijs judicijs, & plures nostro exemplo atq; admonitionibus conuerterentur.
units.tr: Furthermore, Paul adds a new argument to these two reasons, by which he further confirms those earlier readers who feared contamination from living with an unbelieving spouse. His words are these: "For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?" He admonishes them that there is hope that an unbelieving spouse may be won to Christ by the gentleness and diligence of the believing one, and therefore the bond of marriage should not be broken rashly. At the same time, spouses are taught that they must devote themselves not only to household affairs and the bearing and rearing of children, but above all take care that they live for Christ, and if either of them has some fault, it should be holily corrected by the prudence and forbearance of the other. The apostle Peter also strongly urges this, writing thus: "Wives, be subject to your husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word through the conduct of their wives, when they see your chaste behaviour joined with reverence." Such was Abigail of old, who patiently bore with her utterly foolish husband, and beyond all her merit preserved him by admirable diligence, exposing herself, and his fortunes, to clear danger of life. Esther did the same, with greater fruit: though she was born of a foreign race, hated by all, and married to a most arrogant king, yet by holy trust and humility she overcame the rigour of the Median laws, and by bending the king's mind she turned away the impending destruction from the whole Jewish nation. In the Annals of the Franks, the example of Clotilde is quite memorable: by her piety and friendly conversation she moved King Clovis to vow that he would become a Christian, and in the greatest danger of battle with the Alemanni he had recourse to Christ's help. Many examples of this kind could be gathered, and even today we see the ferocity of many men tamed by the honesty and modesty of their wives, so that they become more pliable in all things. From these things a general teaching should be drawn: we must not rashly despair of anyone's salvation. We do not know who may sin against the Holy Spirit, and often those whose wickedness seemed beyond hope are turned to a better and more useful life. Charity, however, hopes the best of all. Therefore, while a person's salvation is in doubt, we too ought to cherish hope and fulfil our duty towards whomever it may be. Paul did this among the Jewish people, with whose obstinacy he struggled to his last breath, although he was not unaware that clear prophecies of their blindness and rejection exist. If everyone did this today, less sin would be committed through rash judgements, and more would be converted through our example and admonitions.

units.la: Cæterum concludit locum istum Paulus generali doctrina, in quam ex coniugibus petita occasione digreditur: Vt nimirum nemo temere transeat ad aliud vitæ genus, neq; statu deserat, ad quem vocatus est. Sic autem loquitur: Vt vnicuiq; partitus est Deus, vt vnusquisq; vocauit Dominus, ita incedat. Sensus verborum est: Quisq; videat ad quid vocatus sit, & quæ dona à Deo acceperit, deinde autē secundum ista vitam instituat. Et mox addit: Ita in ecclesijs omnibus constituo. Quasi diceret: Nō debet hoc vobis graue videri. Nam eandem doctrinā vbiq; trado, vt quæ consentanea sit Christi præceptis, qui neq; respub. mutat, neq; coniugiorū fidem dissoluit, neq; re domestica turbat. Hæc enim nō sunt ex eorū numero, in quibus regnū Dei aut salus hominis consistit: sed quisq; in suo statu (siquidē is per se bonus, & ipso ad eum legitimè vocatus sit) potest saluus fieri. Contentiosus autem et æquo morosior fuerit, si quis ei regulæ subijci nolit, quæ Christianis omnibus communis est.
units.tr: Moreover, Paul concludes this passage with a general teaching, to which he digresses, having taken the occasion from the spouses: namely, that no one should rashly pass over to another way of life, nor abandon the state to which he has been called. He speaks thus: "As the Lord has distributed to each, as God has called each, so let him walk." The sense of the words is: let each consider to what he has been called and what gifts he has received from God, and then order his life accordingly. And soon he adds: "So I ordain in all the churches." As if he were saying: this should not seem burdensome to you. For I teach the same doctrine everywhere, as it agrees with the precepts of Christ, who neither overturns the commonwealth, nor dissolves the faith of marriages, nor disturbs domestic affairs. For these are not among those things in which the kingdom of God or the salvation of man consists; rather, each person in his own state (provided that it is good in itself and he has been lawfully called to it) can be saved. But whoever is contentious, and more difficult than is fitting, if he is unwilling to submit to that rule which is common to all Christians, is the one at fault.

units.la: Docent hæc Apostoli verba, conditionum & statuum huius vitæ diuersitatem, non fortuitam, sed à Deo sic institutam esse. Etsi enim eadem omnium sit natiuitas, Deus tamen nos diuersis vitæ generibus destinat, secundum quæ dona sua distribuit, vt vocationi nostræ sufficere possimus. Quod ergo de ecclesiæ ministris alibi dicitur, quòd alios quidem Deus fecerit Apostolos, alios vero Prophetas, alios doctores, alios pastores, etc. hoc ipsum ad rempub. quoq; transferri debet, in qua certis ordinibus omnes distinctos esse Deus voluit, vt alij quidem in summo potestatis gradu constituti sint, alij post hos locum proximum teneant, alij judiciorum executores & publici magistratuum ministri, alij quæstores, alij ædiles, alij scribæ, & inter vulgus promiscuè alij vinitores & agricolæ, alij pastores sint, alij omnis generis opificia exerceant. Quod dū multi non obseruant, ex eo quòd natales omnium pares sunt, æqualitatem quoq; inter homines omnes constituere volunt, & non sine seditionis spiritu ad Adamū vsq; omnium originē referendo, quærunt, quis tunc nobilis, aut prætor, aut princeps rexúe fuerit, quando primi parentes terrā suis manibus coluerunt? Quibus olim Maximilianus imperator, eius nominis primus, prudenter & grauiter respondit, se quidē quoad natiuitatē et ho-minis natura à reliquis nihil diferre, à Deo autē sibi hoc datū esse, vt supra alios emineat. Et prodest in horū consideratione crebrò versari. Admonet enim, ne quæ contemnamus, neue alicui suū inuidea-mus honorē. Adhæc fortes & patientes reddit in ferendis laboribus & molestijs, quas cū nostra vocatione coniunctas esse videmus. Deniq; in officio cōtinet, ne temere deseramus stationē nobis à Deo creditā. Interim meminerimus, ista ad eos solum pertinere, qui vitæ genus sequuntur, quod cū Deo consentit, gibus conuenit, & ad quod diuinitus vocati sunt. Nihil ergo locus iste Monachis & fraterculis patrocinatur, qui ex nidis suis prodire nolunt, ne suā vocatione deseruisse videatur. Sed de his suo loco dicetur. Nūc Pauli exemplū oēs ecclesiarū ministri imitari discāt, ne quid temere ex suo capite confictū pro Dei verbo obtrudat, et vt eandē doctrinā vbiq; tradat, ne diuersitas totū religiōis negotiū suspectū reddat. Deinde cōiuges fidē sibi mutuo datā constanter feruent, & patienter ferat molestias, quibus coniungi cõdire Deo placuit. Singuli deniq; sua statione teneat, vt dū in terrenis bisce fidelis fuerint, fuerint, olim ingrediantur in regnum & gaudium Domini sui IESV CHRISTI: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: These words of the Apostles teach that the diversity of conditions and states of this life is not accidental but has been so instituted by God. For although all are born alike, God nevertheless assigns us to diverse kinds of life, and distributes his gifts according to them, so that we may be sufficient for our calling. Therefore what is said elsewhere of the ministers of the Church, that God made some apostles, others prophets, others teachers, others pastors, and so on, ought to be applied also to the commonwealth, in which God wished all to be distinguished into certain orders: some are set in the highest grade of power, others hold the next place after these, others are executors of judgements and public ministers of the magistrates, others are quaestors, others aediles, others scribes, and among the common people, some are vinedressers and farmers, some are shepherds, and some practise every kind of trade. When many do not observe this, because all are born equal, they wish to establish equality among all people, and not without a spirit of sedition, tracing everyone's origin back to Adam, they ask who was then noble, or praetor, or prince or ruler, when the first parents tilled the earth with their own hands? To such people the emperor Maximilian, the first of that name, once replied prudently and gravely, that indeed as to birth and human nature he differed in nothing from the rest, but that it had been given to him by God to stand out above others. And it is useful to dwell often on the consideration of these things. For it admonishes us not to despise what is humble, nor to envy another his honour. Moreover, it makes us strong and patient in bearing the labours and troubles which we see are bound up with our calling. Finally, it keeps us in our duty, so that we do not rashly abandon the post entrusted to us by God. Meanwhile let us remember that these things pertain only to those who follow the kind of life which agrees with God, which suits their circumstances, and to which they have been divinely called. Therefore this passage gives no support to monks and little brothers, who refuse to come out of their nests, lest they seem to have deserted their calling. But these matters will be discussed in their proper place. Now let all ministers of the churches learn to imitate Paul's example, not to thrust upon the word of God anything rashly invented from their own head, and to teach the same doctrine everywhere, so that diversity does not make the whole business of religion suspect. Then let spouses constantly keep the faith pledged to each other, and patiently bear the troubles with which God has willed that their marriage be joined. Finally, let each hold to his own station, so that, faithful in these earthly things, they may at last enter into the kingdom and joy of their Lord JESUS CHRIST, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXVI.

units.la: Circumcisus aliquis vocatus est? ne attrahat praeputium. In praeputio aliquis vocatus est? ne circumcidatur. Circumcisio nihil est, & praeputium nihil est, sed observatio mandatorum Dei. Vnusquisq; in qua vocatione vocatus fuit, in ea maneat. Seruus vocatus es? ne sit tibi curae: sed si potes etiam liber fieri, magis eo utere. Etenim qui in Domino vocatus est seruus, libertus Domini est: similiter & qui liber vocatus est, seruus est Christi. Pretio empti estis, ne estote serui hominum. Vnusquisque in quo vocatus fuit, fratres, in hoc maneat apud Deum.
units.tr: Was anyone called while circumcised? Let him not draw back his foreskin. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of God's commandments. Let each one remain in the calling in which he was called. Were you called as a slave? Let it not trouble you; but if you can become free, make the better use of it. For he who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord's freedman; likewise he who was called free is Christ's slave. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men. Brothers, let each one remain before God in the calling in which he was called.

units.la: APostolus Paulus in tota hac epistola de quaestionibus, ob quas in Corinthiorum ecclesia tendebatur, sic disserit, ut passim doctrinas & admonitiones generales interserat, quibus omnes admonentur, quid in toto religionis negotio sit faciendum. Vidimus hoc in iis, quae de sectis, de excludendo homine incesto, de litibus forensibus & de scortatione hucusq; dicta sunt. Idem vero in huius etiam cap. tractatione cernitur. De iis enim scribit, quae ad matrimonium pertinent, circa quod multi tumultuabantur: & quaestiones multas ex ordine soluit. Nuper autem de illis egit, qui coniugio impari coniuncti sunt, monens, ne quis sub religionis praetextu diuortium quaerat non necessarium. Ibidem vero generalem doctrinam subiecit, ut quisq; sua forte contentus sit, & quam Deus ipsi credidit statione diligenter teneat, & in ea tuenda bene vtatur donis, quae a Deo accepit. Id nunc exemplis illustrare pergit: quae priusquam inspiciamus, nobis duo probe sunt observanda.
units.tr: The Apostle Paul, throughout this whole letter, treats the questions that were causing disturbance in the church of the Corinthians in such a way that he everywhere interposes general teachings and admonitions, by which all are warned what must be done in the whole business of religion. We have seen this in what has been said so far about the sects, about excluding the incestuous man, about lawsuits, and about fornication. The same is seen in the treatment of this chapter. For he writes about the matters that pertain to marriage, over which many were in uproar, and he resolves many questions in order. Recently, moreover, he dealt with those who are joined in unequal marriage, warning that no one should seek a divorce under the pretext of religion when it is not necessary. Right here, however, he adds a general teaching: that each person should be content with his own lot, should diligently keep the station that God has entrusted to him, and should make good use, in preserving it, of the gifts he has received from God. He now goes on to illustrate this with examples; before we look at them, two things must be carefully observed.

units.la: Primum, quod nuper quoque attigimus, doctrinam hanc in iis modo locum habere, quae non aduersantur verbo Dei. Sub vocationis enim nomine genus vitae ordinarium intelligitur, & cum vocatio relationem habeat ad Deum, nequaquam illa ad eos extendi debet, qui ex priuato arbitrio aut stulta temeritate sibi vitae genus deligunt alienum ab eo, cui prius a Deo destinati fuerunt: vel communi errore a parentibus ad ea destinantur, quae nullis legibus diuinis probari possunt. Frustra ergo huius loci authoritate pugnant Monachi & sacrificuli in Papatu, ut otium & caelibatum suum impurum defendant, cui sese voto temerario & superstitioso obstrinxerunt, aut a suis cum adhuc pueri essent eo detrusi sunt. Nec enim possunt isti vocationem Dei praetexere, cum is nihil huius vnquam mandauerit, & pleriq; eorum relictis ijs, ad quae vocati fuerunt, hoc vitae genus sequantur, quod neq; politicum neq; ecclesiasticum est, & insuper cum oeconomia priuata pugnat, quam singuli inter suos administrare debent. Nimirum vero impudentes sunt, qui cum prius vitam vixerunt sceleribus infamem, ab ea sibi non discedendum esse putant, ne vocationem suam deseruisse videantur. Nec enim hoc agit Paulus, ut quae corpore suo turpem quaestum fecit, aut qui vsurariis artibus vacarunt, aut in otio ignauo contabuerunt, tales esse pergant: sed de iis loquitur, quorum vita & conditio diuinitus instituta est. Et cum alteri illi hucusq; diabolo & mundo vixerint, per Euangelium vero ad poenitentiam vocentur, huic vocationi quam ocyssime obtemperent necesse est.
units.tr: First, as we touched on just recently, this teaching has a place only in those matters that do not conflict with the Word of God. For by the name of calling is understood the ordinary way of life, and since a calling has a relation to God, it ought by no means to be extended to those who, by private choice or foolish rashness, select for themselves a way of life foreign to that to which they were first destined by God, or who are destined by the common error of their parents to things that cannot be approved by any divine law. Therefore the Monks and little priests in the Papacy fight in vain with the authority of this passage, when they defend their unclean idleness and celibacy, to which they have bound themselves by a rash and superstitious vow, or to which they were thrust by their people while still boys. For these men cannot pretend a calling from God, since he never commanded any such thing, and most of them, leaving those things to which they were called, follow this way of life, which is neither civil nor ecclesiastical, and moreover it conflicts with private economy, which each person ought to administer among his own. Truly they are shameless who, having previously lived a life infamous for crimes, think they must not depart from it, lest they seem to have deserted their calling. For Paul is not saying that those who have made a shameful profit with their bodies, or who have devoted themselves to usurious arts, or who have wasted away in lazy idleness, should continue to be such; he speaks of those whose life and condition have been instituted by God. And since those others have lived until now for the devil and the world, but are called to repentance through the Gospel, they must most quickly obey this calling.

units.la: Alterum hic obseruabis, non prohiberi quamuis mutationem, sed eas modo, quas absq; Dei peculiari aut noua vocatione faciunt homines, quos vel innata animi leuitas, vel lucri spes, aut alii quis alius affectus improbus abripit: qui fere & suam stationem turpiter deserunt, & publicum scandalum ponunt rerum imperitis. Alia autem est eorum conditio, qui ex vita priuata ad reipub. vel ecclesiae ministerium vocantur, quod olim Sauli, Dauidi, prophetis plerisq; & Apostolis accidisse scimus, & multis hodie accidit, qui secundum leges in vnaquaque gente receptas eliguntur, ut magistratum gerant, aut ad docendi munus legitima & secundum canones apostolicos facta electione transeunt. Nam horum quoq; vocatio diuina est. Ita non temere etiam damnandi sunt omnes, qui ab agricultura ad vrbem, aut ab opificio vno ad alterum oblata occasione meliori transeunt, ut & commodius viuant & suis melius prospiciant. Vbi tamen maiori cautio-ne opus est, ne quis sibi per cæcam carnis cupiditatem imponi patiatur. Sed ad Pauli verba, quæ modo recitata sunt, accedamus, qui regulam aut doctrinam generalem prudenter iis applicat, de quibus tunc multi importunè nimis & non sine publico scandalo tumultuabantur: Circumcisionem nimirum & Præputium, Seruitutem & Libertatem: & sub illis quidem ceremonias & ritus omnes indifferentes, sub his vero omnia vitæ genera comprehendit, quæ inter homines Deus instituit.
units.tr: Second, you will observe here that it is not any change that is forbidden, but only those changes that men make without a special or new calling from God, men whom innate levity of mind, hope of gain, or some other wicked passion carries away; these men commonly desert their station shamefully and give public scandal to the inexperienced. The condition of those who are called from private life to the ministry of the commonwealth or of the Church is different, as we know happened to Saul, David, many of the prophets, and the Apostles, and as happens to many today, who are chosen according to the laws received in each nation to bear the magistracy, or who pass to the office of teaching by a lawful election made according to the apostolic canons. For the calling of these men too is divine. Thus not all who move from farming to the city, or from one trade to another when a better opportunity is offered, are to be condemned rashly, so that they may live more conveniently and provide better for their own. Yet here greater caution is needed, so that no one allows himself to be deceived by blind desire of the flesh. But let us come to the words of Paul just recited, who wisely applies a general rule or teaching to those matters over which many were stirring up trouble, too importunately and not without public scandal: namely circumcision and uncircumcision, servitude and liberty; and under the former he includes all ceremonies and rites as indifferent, and under the latter he comprehends all the ways of life that God has instituted among men.

units.la: Non temere autem huic tractationi admonitionem de Circumcisione & Præputio interserit. De his enim plurimum contendebatur, & utrinq; peccabant multi non leuiter. Erant enim non-nulli ex Iudæis, quos gentis suæ incurabilis pertinacia atque implacabile religionis Christianæ odium adeo offendebat, ut non modo reliquas ceremonias legales immodestius damnarent, quas cum honore potius sepeliri oportuit (ut alibi monuimus) verumetiam Circumcisionem in corpore suo abolere, & præputia sibi facere conarentur, ne quid cum Iudæis commune haberent. Et quod multos sub Antiocho partim impia & scelerata leuitate, partim ex turpi metu in fidei & patriæ legis abnegationem fecisse in Machabæorum libris scribitur, id tunc nonnulli ex inconsiderato re-ligionis Christianæ zelo faciebant. Cuius facti modum & rationem Epiphanius exponit, qui Symmachum librorum veteris testamenti interpretem ex Samaritano proselytum factum, & secunda circumcisione à Iudæis circumcisum fuisse scribit. Inuenti vero huius authore ex Iudæorum traditio ne facit Efauii: quod ut ego temere affirmare nolim, ita tale quid in vsu fuisse, ex Pauli verbis mi-nifeste colligitur, ut non opus sit locum istum de toto Iudaismo aut gentilissimo exponere, ut quidam fecerunt. Fuit autem hoc egregium diaboli stratagema, qui fœderis diuini symbolum hac ratione vniuersum abolere voluit: cui non absimile est, quod hodie multi pseudochristianorum corruptis moribus & peccandi licentia offensi, baptismum & Cœnam Domini tantum non abolent, dum illum quidem per Anabaptismum euacuant, hanc vero ceu superuacaneam & inutilem prorsus negligunt. Porrò ut ad Pauli tempora redeamus, rursus alij erant, qui in expendenda Iudaicæ gentis dignitate, qua & illam & patres illorum Deus olim ornauerat, diligentiores, eorum sententiam amplectebantur, qui Circumcisionem necessariam esse iis contendebant, qui ex gentibus ad fidem Christi transirent, de quibus multus in Pauli epistolis sermo est. Nam etsi horum sententiam Aposto-li publica Synodi generalis authoritate (ut Lucas in Actis prodidit) damnauissent, multi tamen eam ecclesiis passim obtrudere ausi sunt, & discipulos inuenerunt, qui se circumcidi paterentur. Vtrisq; ergo Paulus admonitionem illam generalem, cuius supra meminimus, instar remedij adhibet, dicens: Circumcisus aliquis vocatus est? ne attrahat præputium. In præputio aliquis vocatus est? ne circumcidatur. Et huius dicti rationem reddit: Circumcisio nihil est, & præputium nihil est, sed obseruatio mandatorum Dei. Nihil ista esse ait, ut offendat, Deum illis minimè coli, neq; aliquid ad salutem momenti afferre, siue quis circumcisus, siue præputiatus fuerit, ideoq; nimium contentiosos & scrupulosos litigatores esse eos, qui de his tumultuentur, & tam sibi ipsis quàm multis aliis, adeoq; toti ecclesiæ negotium faciunt.
units.tr: He does not interpose his admonition about circumcision and uncircumcision into this discussion without reason. For there was much contention over these matters, and many on both sides sinned not lightly. For there were some of the Jews whom the incurable obstinacy of their nation and implacable hatred of the Christian religion so offended that they not only condemned the other legal ceremonies too immoderately, which ought rather to have been buried with honor (as we have noted elsewhere), but even tried to abolish circumcision in their own bodies and to make foreskins for themselves, so as to have nothing in common with the Jews. And what is written in the books of the Maccabees, that many under Antiochus fell away from faith and the law of their country, partly through impious and wicked levity, partly through shameful fear, some were then doing out of an ill-considered zeal for the Christian religion. Epiphanius explains the manner and reason of this deed, who writes that Symmachus, the translator of the books of the Old Testament, was made a proselyte from the Samaritans and was circumcised a second time by the Jews. Indeed, the tradition of the Jews does not name Esau as the author of this invention; although I am unwilling to affirm this rashly, it is plainly gathered from the words of Paul that something of this kind was in use, so that there is no need to explain this passage of all Judaism or of Gentile life, as some have done. This was an outstanding stratagem of the devil, who wished in this way to abolish entirely the symbol of the divine covenant. Not unlike this is what many pseudo-Christians today, offended by corrupt morals and license to sin, almost abolish baptism and the Lord's Supper, while they indeed empty baptism through Anabaptism, and entirely neglect the Supper as superfluous and useless. But to return to the times of Paul: again there were others who, weighing more carefully the dignity of the Jewish nation, with which God had once adorned both it and its fathers, embraced the opinion of those who insisted that circumcision was necessary for those who passed from the Gentiles to the faith of Christ, a matter about which there is much discussion in Paul's letters. For although the Apostles had condemned this opinion by the public authority of a general synod (as Luke reports in the Acts), many nevertheless dared to press it upon the churches everywhere, and they found disciples who allowed themselves to be circumcised. Paul therefore applies to both sides that general admonition, of which we have spoken above, as a remedy, saying: Was anyone called while circumcised? Let him not draw back his foreskin. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised. And he gives the reason for this saying: Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of God's commandments. He says these things are nothing, not as if God were not honored by them at all, nor because they contribute nothing of weight to salvation, whether a man has been circumcised or left uncircumcised; rather he means that those who make an uproar over them are too contentious and scrupulous litigants, and that they make trouble both for themselves and for many others, and indeed for the whole Church.

units.la: Quaerat autem aliquis non immerito, qua ratione Circumcisionem & Præputium eodem loco ponat, & illam quoq; nihil esse dicat, cum & fœderis cum Abrahamo facti (ex quo omnis hominum salus dependet) sigillum fuerit, & tanta cum seueritate illam Deus mandarit, ut ex populo suo eum extirpandum esse dicat, qui incircumcisus fuerit? Constat præterea Mosem de vita periclitatum fuisse, quòd filium sibi apud Iethronem in Madianitica terra natum non circumcidisset. Sed temporis circumstantiam obseruare nos oportet. Olim quidem Circumcisionis vsus multus erat, & eam negligere scelus erat capitale, cum a[dhu]c legis disciplina cum ceremoniis vigeret, quas ad tempus correctionis vsq; durare debuisse, Paulus alibi testatur. At cum ista scriberet, nihil amplius erat Circumcisio nisi res absq; vllo vsu, eò quòd eam Christus abrogauisset: id quod veli in templo scissio sub eius mortem facta non obscurè docebat. Itaq; sublata iam maceria illa legalium ceremoniarum, qua Iudæi à gentibus prius discernebantur, nunc neq; Circumcisio neq; Præputium quicquam ad regnum Dei & salutem æternam conferebant.
units.tr: One might fairly ask why Paul places circumcision and uncircumcision in the same place and calls circumcision nothing too, since it was the seal of the covenant made with Abraham, on which all human salvation depends, and since God commanded it with such severity that he says anyone uncircumcised must be cut off from his people. It is also well known that Moses was in danger of his life because he had not circumcised the son born to him in the land of Midian, at Jethro's home. But we must observe the circumstances of the time. Formerly the practice of circumcision was widespread, and neglecting it was a capital crime, while the discipline of the law with its ceremonies still flourished; Paul elsewhere testifies that these were to last until the time of correction. But when he wrote these words, circumcision was nothing more than an empty thing with no use at all, since Christ had abrogated it, as the tearing of the temple veil at his death clearly showed. So now that the wall of legal ceremonies, by which the Jews were formerly set apart from the Gentiles, has been removed, neither circumcision nor uncircumcision contributes anything to the kingdom of God or to eternal salvation.

units.la: Porrò singularem considerationem meretur, quòd omnes homines Paulus ad obseruationem mandatorum Dei remittit, & hanc necessariam esse docet, quæ semper & vbiq; feruetur ab omnilus, qui serūari uolunt. Conuenit hoc cum illo Solomonis: Finis uniuersi negotij est, Deum time- to & præcepta illius seruato, nam in hoc consistit omnium hominum perfectio. At hic probè tenen- dum est, quæ nam illa Dei præcepta sint, & in quonam eorum obseruatio consistat. Sunt enim qui ex hoc loco operum nostrorum iustitiam, uel meritum afferunt, & fidei iustificationem oppugnant. Sed dum hoc faciunt, duplicem errorem produnt. Primò enim non obseruant Pauli institutum, qui in præsenti nequaquam docere uult, quomodo aut per quid homines iustificentur (id enim facit, vbi Christum pro nobis peccatum & nostram iustitiam factum esse scribit, quem nos per fidem ap- prehendere oporteat) sed quid eos facere conueniat, qui iâ[?] iustificati & saluti hæredes facti sunt. Itaq; isti uerba Pauli in sensum alienum detorquent, & à causa non causa paralogizant, dum ex ef- fectu causam efficiente fingunt. Alter error est, quòd nesciunt, aut saltem scire nolunt, in quonam præceptorū Dei obseruatio consistat. Quod unum si rectè obseruetur, iustificationem fidei hoc dicto potius confirmari, quàm euerti patebit. Nam primum inter Dei præcepta est: Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus, qui eduxi te ex Ægypto, è domo seruitutis: non erunt tibi Dei alieni coram me. At quid hic aliud præcipitur, quàm fides in unum Deum, quæ si Christum Mediatorem auferas, nulla esse potest, cum sine hoc nobis, qui natura peccatores sumus, nulla cum Deo communio intercedat? Ex hoc autem præcepto, ceu fonte, reliqua omnia deriuantur. Quia qui in Deo uno & solo omnem fidu- ciam repositam habent, ij & hunc colunt ea ratione, qua coli vult, & nomen eius nullo abusu teme- rario prophanant, & cùm ab eius ore toti pendeant, hominibus quoq; singulis quæ debent officia fi- deliter præstant, quæ omnia sub charitatis præcepto comprehendi notius est, quàm ut multis de- monstrari oporteat. Et hæc quidem non ipsi ex nostro cerebro fingimus, sed dilectum illum Domini discipuli sequimur, qui cum nos à Deo omnia quæ petimus accipere dixisset, eò quòd eius præcepta custodimus, & quæ coram eo placita sunt facimus, mox subjicit: Et hoc est eius præceptum, ut cre- damus nomini filij eius IESV CHRISTI, & ut alij alios diligamus, sicuti mandauit nobis. At qui hæc præstant, ij ex uerbi semine renati sint oportet, quando nihil horum facere possumus, quoad uetus ille homo & caro in nobis viuunt aut dominantur. Itaq; optimus huius loci interpres Paulus ipse est, qui ad Galatas quoq; de Circumcisione & aliis ritibus differens, inter alia sic scri- bit: Vobis inanis factus est Christus per vos ipsos, quicunq; per Legem iustificamini: & à gratia excidistis. Nos enim Spiritu ex fide spem iustitiæ expectamus. Nam in CHRISTO IESV neq; Circumcisio quicquam valet, neq; Præputium, sed fides per charitatem agens. Et rursus. Nam in CHRISTO IESV neq; Circumcisio quicquam valet, neq; Præputium, sed noua creatio, id est, hominis totius innouatio, quam Christus regenerationem dicit, & quæ non alio medio, quoad nos, quàm fide perficitur, quæ sola semen illud Verbi apprehendit, ex quo renasci nos oportet. Ex his hominis sanctificatio quoq; dependet, cuius effectus est, ut qui prius mundo & carni viuebat, nunc toti Deo consecrati sint, huic obediant, & uasa sua cum sanctificatione & honore possideant. Hæc igitur docent, quàm fallantur, qui pro suorum operum meritis pugnant, & ad hæc tuenda huius loci authoritate abutuntur. Constat enim illos homines inter omnia opera primum locum ceremonijs tribuere, quæ ab hominibus superstitiosis uel ex Iudaismo & ueteri Lege in nouum Testamentum translatæ, uel priuata temeritate constitutæ sunt. At Paulus Circumcisionem quoq; qua olim vix quicquam sanctius & obseruatu magis necessarium erat, nunc prorsus abolitam & annihilatam esse testatur. Quæ ergo dementia est, hominum figmentis aliquid tribuere, quæ totius scripturæ authoritate damnantur?
units.tr: Moreover, the fact that Paul refers all men to the observance of God's commandments deserves special attention, and he teaches that this observance is necessary and is to be kept always and everywhere by all who wish to be saved. This agrees with Solomon's saying: "The end of the whole matter is: fear God and keep his commandments, for in this consists the perfection of all men." But here we must hold firmly which of God's commandments these are, and in which of them obedience consists. Some people take from this passage the righteousness or merit of our works, and attack the justification of faith. But in doing so they betray a double error. First, they do not observe Paul's purpose, for in this place he does not wish to teach how or by what means men are justified (he does that where he writes that Christ was made sin and our righteousness for us, and that we must lay hold of him by faith); rather, he teaches what those ought to do who are already justified and made heirs of salvation. So these men twist Paul's words into a meaning not his own, and from the effect they invent a cause, reasoning falsely from what is not the cause. The other error is that they do not know, or at least do not wish to know, in which observance of God's commandments consists. If this one point is rightly observed, it will be plain that this saying rather confirms the justification of faith than overturns it. For the first of God's commandments is: "I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. You shall have no other gods before me." But what else is commanded here than faith in the one God? Without Christ the Mediator this faith cannot exist, since we, who are sinners by nature, have no fellowship with God apart from him. From this commandment, as from a fountain, all the others flow. For those who have placed all their trust in the one and only God worship him in the manner he wills, do not profane his name by any rash abuse, and, since they depend wholly on his word, faithfully perform the duties they owe to individual men as well. It is better known than needs demonstrating that all these are included under the command of love. We do not invent these things from our own brains, but follow that beloved disciple of the Lord, who, after saying that we receive from God whatever we ask, because we keep his commandments and do what is pleasing in his sight, immediately adds: "And this is his commandment, that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another, as he has commanded us." But those who perform these things must be born again of the seed of the Word, since we can do none of these things as long as the old man and the flesh live and rule in us. Therefore the best interpreter of this passage is Paul himself, who, discussing circumcision and other rites in his letter to the Galatians, writes among other things: "Christ is of no effect to you, whoever of you are justified by the law; you have fallen from grace. For we through the Spirit by faith wait for the hope of righteousness. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love." And again: "For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation," that is, the renewal of the whole man, which Christ calls regeneration, and which, as far as we are concerned, is accomplished by no other means than faith, which alone grasps that seed of the Word from which we must be born again. On these things the sanctification of man also depends, the effect of which is that those who lived formerly to the world and the flesh are now consecrated wholly to God, obey him, and possess their vessels in sanctification and honour. These things therefore teach how wrong those are who fight for the merits of their own works and misuse the authority of this passage to defend them. For it is established that those men give the first place among all works to ceremonies, which have been carried over into the New Testament by superstitious men, either from Judaism and the old Law, or were devised by private rashness. But Paul testifies that circumcision too, which once was hardly anything holier and more necessary to observe, is now utterly abolished and annulled. What madness is it, then, to attribute something to the inventions of men, which are condemned by the authority of all Scripture?

units.la: Sed ad alterum huius loci caput transeamus, in quo de seruitute & libertate agit. Repetit au- tem propositionem: Unusquisq; in qua uocatione uocatus est, in ea maneat. Neq; superuacanea de- bet censeri ista repetitio, eò quòd illo tempore à serui & heris non parum peccabatur. Ut enim caro ubiq; licentiam quæritit, ita in religione hoc imprimis facere consueuit. Quæ causa erat, quòd qui ad fidem Christi conuertebantur serui, simul libertatis spem animo conciperent: & qui sub heris prophanis seruiebant, illis indignum & intolerabile prorsus videbatur, hominem Christianum Iudæi aut idololatræ seruitio premi: quibus uero heri contigerant Christiani, ij quoque in charitatis Christianæ leges peccari arbitrabantur, si frater in fratre imperium exerceret. Hinc fiebat, ut alij quidem seruitutis iugum impatienter ferrent, alij uero ab heris profugerent, & sua perfidia hostibus fidei egregiam eius calumniandae occasionem praebærent. E contra multi ex heris suo in servos imperio licentius abutebantur, & solitam austeritatem in eos quoque exercebant, quos pro fratribus in Christo debebant agnoscere: denique eo plus sibi contra leges Christianas licere putabant, quod ingenui & liberi nati essent. Itaque hos etiam utrinque officij admonet his verbis: Servus vocatus es? ne sit tibi cura: sed si potes etiam liber fieri, magis utere. Etenim qui in Domino vocatus est, servus, libertus Domini est: similiter & qui liber vocatus est, servus est Christi, &c. De servis diligentius agit, à quibus plus peccabatur, & partim quidem molestiam adimit, quâ ex servitutis iugo sentiebant, partim vero monet non prohiberi eos Christianis legibus, quo minus oblatum libertatis beneficium amplestantur. Si (inquit) servus vocatus es, non sit tibi cura, id est, ne propterea animo discrucieris, quasi minus gratus sis Deo, aut non simul servire & Christianum agere possis. Veruntamen quod dixi unumquenque in vocatione ea, in qua vocatus est, debere manere, non ita quisquam accipiat, quasi nefas sit manumitti & liberum fieri. Imò si quae libertatis consequendae ratio legitima occurrit, ea cum gratiarum actione utaris moneo: Quia etsi servitus non prohibeat Christianum esse, maior tamen est commoditas libertatis, & in omni pietatis officio expeditiores esse possunt, qui nullius imperio subsunt, per quod ab instituto revocentur. Scio Chrysostomum, Hieronymum & quosdam ex recentioribus postremum hoc membrum aliter exponere, ut nimirum moneat, servitute libertati praeferri debere, adeo ut potius servire velint, etiamsi libertatis occasio ipsis offeratur. Sed repugnat illorum sententiae orationis contextus & Graeci vocabuli proprietas. Nec prudenter & pie servus consuluisset Paulus, si libertatis spem omnë illis negasset, aut saltem conscientijs eorum hunc scrupulum iniecisset, quasi minus Christiane faciant, qui se manumitti patiebantur. Etenim ea fuit illorum temporum conditio, ut beneficium istud nemo respuere debuerit, cui religio cordi erat. Nam fieri poterat, ut qui hero Christiano serviebat, hoc defuncto ad haeredem impium & prophanum transfiret, cuius improbitate vel ad aperta fidei abnegationem cogebatur, vel saltem prohibebatur, quo minus religionis purioris exercitia obiret. Denique, cum servitus peccati poena, libertas autem singulare Dei beneficium sit, non absque manifesta impietatis & ingratitudinis nota poterat contemni aut negligi. Istis ergo rationibus adducor, ut eo sensu Pauli verba accipiam, qui & simplicissimus est, & plerisque interpretum probatur.
units.tr: But let us pass on to the other point of this passage, in which he speaks of slavery and liberty. He repeats the proposition: "Let each man remain in the calling in which he was called." This repetition should not be thought superfluous, since at that time masters and slaves sinned not a little. For as the flesh everywhere seeks licence, so it is especially accustomed to do this in religion. The reason was that slaves who were converted to the faith of Christ at once conceived in their minds the hope of freedom; and for those who served profane masters it seemed altogether unworthy and intolerable that a Christian man should be oppressed by the service of a Jew or an idolater. Those who had Christian masters, on the other hand, thought that sin was committed against the laws of Christian charity if a brother exercised lordship over a brother. Hence it came about that some bore the yoke of slavery impatiently, while others fled from their masters, and by their faithlessness gave the enemies of the faith a splendid opportunity to slander it. On the other side, many masters abused their power over their slaves more freely, and exercised their customary harshness even on those whom they ought to acknowledge as brothers in Christ; indeed, they thought they were allowed to do more against the Christian laws because they were born free and of free birth. So Paul admonishes both parties of their duty in these words: "Were you called as a slave? Do not be concerned about it; but if you can also become free, rather make use of it. For he who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord's freedman; likewise he who was called free is Christ's slave," and so on. He deals more carefully with slaves, since they sinned more, and partly he removes the distress they felt from the yoke of slavery, and partly he warns that they are not prevented by the Christian laws from accepting the offered benefit of freedom. "If you were called as a slave," he says, "let it not trouble you," that is, do not be tormented in mind as if you were less pleasing to God, or as if you could not at the same time serve and live as a Christian. Nevertheless, let no one take what I have said, that each should remain in the calling in which he was called, as if it were wrong to be manumitted and become free. On the contrary, I advise you, if any lawful way of obtaining liberty presents itself, to use it with thanksgiving; for although servitude does not prevent a man from being a Christian, yet the advantage of liberty is greater, and those who are subject to no one's command, by which they might be called back from their purpose, can be more free for every duty of piety. I know that Chrysostom, Jerome, and some of the more recent writers explain this last clause differently, namely that it warns that servitude should be preferred to liberty, so that men would rather remain slaves even when the opportunity of freedom is offered to them. But the context of the passage and the proper sense of the Greek word are against that view. Nor would Paul have advised wisely and piously if he had denied slaves all hope of freedom, or at least had cast this scruple into their consciences, as if those who allowed themselves to be manumitted acted less like Christians. For the condition of those times was such that no one who cared for religion ought to refuse that benefit. For it could happen that a slave of a Christian master, on that master's death, would pass to an impious and profane heir, by whose wickedness he would be compelled to a plain denial of the faith, or at least prevented from practising the exercises of purer religion. Finally, since slavery is the punishment of sin and liberty is a singular benefit of God, it could not be despised or neglected without a clear mark of impiety and ingratitude. I am therefore led by these reasons to take Paul's words in that sense, which is both the simplest and is approved by most interpreters.

units.la: Caeterum imprimis dignissima confideratu est bipertita sententia, quam rationis loco Apostolus subijcit, & qua servos quidem consolatur, herorum autem insolentiam graviter reprimit: Etenim qui in Domino vocatus est, servus (inquit) libertus Domini est: similiter & qui liber vocatus est, servus est Christi. Prima pars ad eos pertinet, qui in Domino vocantur servi, id est, qui dum servi sunt, per Euangelium ad fidem Christi vocantur. Hos etsi quoad conditionem huius seculi servi sint, tamen libertos Christi esse ait: Nimirum quia per hunc à peccato & morte liberati, ad hoc manumissi sunt, ne ut prius diabolo serviant. Altera pars de ingenuis loquitur, qui licet quoad huius vitae conditionem liberi & nullius hominis arbitrio subiecti sint, tamen Christi servi sunt, & huic omne debet obsequium, qui eos sanguinis sui pretio sibi acquisiuit. Finis & scopus omnium hic est, non esse propter haec tumultuandum, cum quoad aeternae salutis & regni Dei negotium, una sit omnium Christianorum conditio, quod nimirum Christi beneficio ex peccati & diaboli servitio liberati, illius autem servi facti sint. Docet ergo sententia haec in una eademq; hominis Christiani persona servitutem simul atq; libertatem convenire. Nam ut modò diximus, libertus Christi est, qui nos ex potestate tenebrarum in libertatem filiorum Dei transtulit: quam veram libertatem esse ipse docet, Iudaeis dicens: Si Filius vos liberauerit, verè liberi eritis. At idem Christianus homo, etiam servus Christi est, quod Paulus ad Romanos his verbis exprimit: Liberati à peccato, mancipati estis iustitiae. Et mox huius dicti rationem subiicit, sic scribens: Hominum more loquor propter infirmitatem carnis vestrae. Nempe sicut stiftis[?] membra vestra serva impuritati & iniquitati ad patranda iniquitatem: ita nunc sistite membra vestra serva iustitiae ad sanctimoniam. Sunt haec diligenter animo reponenda, quia omnis loci & ordinis hominum institutioni serviunt.
units.tr: Moreover, the twofold statement that the Apostle adds as his reason deserves especial attention. It comforts slaves and sharply checks the arrogance of free men: "For he who is called in the Lord, being a slave, is the Lord's freedman; likewise he who is called free is Christ's slave." The first part concerns those who, while still slaves, are called in the Lord, that is, are called to faith in Christ through the Gospel. Although these are slaves as far as their condition in this world goes, he says they are Christ's freedmen. Clearly this is because they have been freed by him from sin and death, and manumitted so that they no longer serve the devil as before. The second part speaks of freeborn men, who, although they are free and subject to no human's will as far as the condition of this life goes, are nonetheless Christ's slaves, and owe him all obedience, since he has acquired them for himself at the price of his own blood. The aim and purpose of the whole passage is that people should not make an uproar over these matters. As far as the business of eternal salvation and the kingdom of God is concerned, all Christians share one condition: they have been freed by Christ's benefit from the slavery of sin and the devil, and have become his slaves. This statement therefore teaches that slavery and liberty can both belong to one and the same Christian person. As we have just said, he who has transferred us from the power of darkness into the liberty of the children of God is Christ's freedman. Christ himself teaches that this is true liberty, when he says to the Jews: "If the Son shall make you free, you shall be free indeed." Yet the same Christian is also Christ's slave, which Paul expresses to the Romans in these words: "Being made free from sin, you became servants of righteousness." Soon afterwards he gives the reason for this saying, writing thus: "I speak after the manner of men because of the infirmity of your flesh. For just as you once presented your members as slaves to uncleanness and iniquity for the working of iniquity, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness for sanctification." These things must be carefully kept in mind, because they serve the instruction of every place and order of men.

units.la: Primò enim diserte docent, neminem credentium propter servilem conditionem aut rerum huius seculi inopiam à regno Dei excludi, aut minus idoneum fieri ut Christo serviat. Nec enim prohiberi potest spiritus ille Dei, quò minus spiret ubicunq; voluerit, & (ut alibi Paulus loquitur)in CHRISTO IESV non est seruus aut liber. Notum praeterea est illud Salomonis: Seruus cordatus imperabit filio herili dedecoroso, & inter fratres haereditatem diuidet. Exempla in historijs passim occurrunt eorum, qui cum serui essent, tamen & animi libertatem retinuerunt, & in eum honoris atq; dignitatis gradum euecti[?] sunt, ut suo consilio suis heris utiles, multi etiam illis superiores fuerint. Inter quos merito primus locus Iosepho debetur, quem si cum Putiphare & eius impudica coniuge conferas, ipsum utrisq; praestantiorem fuisse patebit. Illa enim abiectissimum libidinis mancipium fuit, herus autem irae & vindictae cupiditati turpiter succubuit, cum ille & iuveniles cupiditates fortiter vicerit, & inconsideratam heri rabiem incredibili modestia domuerit. Quid quod idem a Pharaone tandem in summam dignitatem euectus toti regno & simul ecclesiae Dei quae tunc erat, salutem attulit? Idem de Daniele & eius socijs dicere possumus, qui orbis victorem Nabuchodonozorem & regni Babylonici euersorem Darium vicerunt sua constantia, & fidei libertatem aduersus omnes hostium machinationes inviolatam seruarunt. Adde his Mardochaeum & infinitos alios, quorum historiae sacrae & ecclesiasticae mentionem faciunt. Nemo igitur conditionem huius seculi qualemcunq; impatientius ferat, quando etsi corpus vinciatur, algeat, esuriat, sitiat, seruiat, spiritus tamen libertas eripi non potest, quae facit, ut de totius mundi & principis eius potentia triumphemus.
units.tr: For first they clearly teach that no believer is excluded from the kingdom of God, or made less fit to serve Christ, because of servile condition or lack of this world's goods. That Spirit of God cannot be restrained from blowing wherever it wills, and (as Paul says elsewhere) "in Christ Jesus there is neither slave nor free." The saying of Solomon is also well known: "A wise servant shall rule over a son who causes shame, and shall divide the inheritance among the brothers." Examples occur everywhere in histories of those who, though they were slaves, nonetheless kept the liberty of their minds, and were raised to such a degree of honour and dignity that by their counsel they were useful to their masters, and many were even greater than them. Among these, the first place rightly belongs to Joseph. If you compare him with Potiphar and his shameless wife, it will be plain that he was superior to both of them. She was a most abject slave of lust, and her husband shamefully gave way to anger and the desire for revenge, whereas Joseph bravely conquered youthful desires and with incredible moderation tamed his master's rash fury. Moreover, was he not at last raised by Pharaoh to the highest dignity, and did he not bring salvation to the whole kingdom and at the same time to the Church of God that then existed? We may say the same of Daniel and his companions, who by their steadfastness overcame Nebuchadnezzar, the conqueror of the world, and Darius, the overthrower of the Babylonian kingdom, and kept the liberty of their faith inviolate against all the plots of their enemies. Add to these Mordecai and countless others, whom sacred and ecclesiastical histories mention. Let no one, therefore, bear with impatience whatever condition this world imposes, since, even if the body is bound, grows cold, hungers, thirsts, or serves, yet the liberty of the spirit cannot be snatched away, and this liberty makes us triumph over the power of the whole world and its prince.

units.la: Deinde heros quoq; & liberos siue ingenuos officij sui hic locus admonet, ne libertate sua abutantur, sed se Christi seruos esse meminerint. Est enim libertas (ut iurisconsultorum definitione utar) naturalis facultas eius, quod cuiq; facere libet, nisi quod vi aut iure prohibetur. Et Cicero dicebat: Libertas est potestas viuendi ut velis. Is vero (inquit) viuit ut vult, qui recta sequitur, qui gaudet officio, cui viuendi via considerata atq; prouisa est, qui ne legibus quidem propter metum paret, sed eas sequitur atq; colit, quod salutare maxime iudicat. Et rursus: Liber est [?] astimandus, qui nulli turpitudini seruit. At omnia ista uno verbo Paulus complectitur, quando seruos Christi esse iubet eos, qui libertate & ingenuitate ciuili gaudent. Hi enim soli viuunt ut volunt, quia voluntatem suam Deo conformem faciunt: & ijdem soli recta sequuntur, quia in Dei praeceptis ambulant, quae illos aberrare non sinunt: gaudent item officio, cum nihil illis tam gratum, tam iucundum & suaue sit, quam ut erga Deum simul & homines quosq; omni pietatis officio defungantur: adhaec viuendi ratio illis probe considerata atque prouisa est, quia non caecis carnis affectibus, sed Dei verbo ducuntur: neque legibus Dei ex metu parent, sed spontaneum Christo obsequium praestant(ut Dauid de illis loquitur) eo quod in eo salutem suam omnem consistere sciunt. Et hi illi ipsi sunt, quibus ipsa fortuna cedit (ut idem Cicero ait) quando per ferrum & ignes & omnia huius mundi pericula fortissime eluctantur, ut quam Christo dederunt fidem, illi sanctam & illibatam seruent. Horum ergo meminerint, qui hodie prae aliis libertate & immunitatibus superbiunt. Nisi enim Christi seruitio sese addicant, mundi quidem iudicio liberi censentur, at idem seruitutem omnium infelicissimam seruiunt, quam (ut Augustinus scribit) nunquam effugere licet, eo quod propriis cupiditatibus mancipati sunt, quae illis non minus saede quam superbe dominantur, & quas, quocunq; se vertant, secum circumferunt.
units.tr: Next, this passage also reminds free men and freeborn men of their duty, that they should not abuse their liberty but remember that they are Christ's slaves. Liberty is (to use the definition of the jurists) the natural power of doing whatever one pleases, unless it is forbidden by force or by law. And Cicero said: "Liberty is the power of living as you wish." But, he says, he lives as he wishes who follows what is right, who delights in his duty, whose way of life has been considered and foreseen, who obeys the laws not even out of fear, but follows and honours them because he judges them most salutary. And again: "He is to be counted free who serves no baseness." Paul, however, embraces all these things in one word when he commands those who rejoice in liberty and civic freedom to be Christ's slaves. For only these live as they wish, because they make their will conformed to God's; and only these follow what is right, because they walk in God's precepts, which do not allow them to wander. They also delight in their duty, since nothing is so pleasing, so agreeable and sweet to them as to discharge every office of piety towards God and towards all men. Moreover, their way of life is well considered and foreseen by them, because they are led not by blind fleshly affections but by God's Word; nor do they obey God's laws out of fear, but render a willing obedience to Christ (as David speaks of them), because they know that their whole salvation rests in him. These are the very men to whom fortune itself yields (as the same Cicero says), when they most bravely struggle through sword and fire and all the dangers of this world, so that they may keep the faith they have pledged to Christ holy and unstained. Therefore let those remember these things who today pride themselves above others in liberty and immunities. For unless they devote themselves to the service of Christ, they are indeed counted free by the judgment of the world, yet they serve the most unhappy slavery of all, which (as Augustine writes) can never be escaped, because they are enslaved to their own desires, which rule over them no less foully than proudly, and which they carry about with them wherever they turn.

units.la: Porro isti tractationi rursus generalem doctrinam siue admonitionem interserit: Pretio empti estis, ne estote serui hominum. Pertinet hoc ad omnes homines cuiuscunque loci aut ordinis. Non debet autem rigide & secundum literam accipi, quasi nulli hominum seruire debeat, qui Christi sanguine redemptus est. Quia si hoc statuamus, iam Paulum sibiipsi contradicentem fingemus, qui paulo ante seruos de sua conditione solicitos esse vetuit, & alibi seruorum officia diligenter tradit, imo Onesimum fugitiuum hero suo Philemoni remisit. Hoc igitur monet in praesenti, ne in hominum gratiam aliquid faciamus, quo redemptionis nostrae per Christum factae pretium euacuetur: & ita tacitae obiectioni occurrit eorum, qui sibi quiduis licere arbitrabantur, quod iuberent qui in ipsos ius habebant & imperium. Vult igitur ita hominibus obsequium praestent, ut semper meminerint, se plus Deo debere, qui Filij sui sanguine ipsos sibi acquisierit.
units.tr: Further, in this discussion he again inserts a general teaching, or admonition: "You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men."
