This applies to all men of whatever place or order. But it should not be taken rigidly and according to the letter, as though he who has been redeemed by Christ's blood ought to serve no man. For if we held this, we would be imagining Paul contradicting himself, since a little before he forbade slaves to be anxious about their condition, and elsewhere he carefully sets out the duties of slaves, and indeed sent Onesimus, a runaway, back to his master Philemon. Therefore in the present passage he warns us not to do anything to please men by which the price of the redemption made through Christ would be made void. In this way he meets the unspoken objection of those who thought they might do whatever those who had right and power over them commanded. He wills, therefore, that we render obedience to men in such a way that we always remember that we owe more to God, who has acquired them for himself by the blood of his Son.

units.la: Peccatur in hoc Apostoli praeceptum varie tam in religione quam in reliqua vita aut actionibus. In illa enim peccant, qui relicto aut quasi abnegato Christi nomine, ab ijs denominari volunt, quos sibi doctores atque magistros delegerunt. Faciebant hoc Corinthij, cum alius diceret, Ego sum Pauli: alius, Ego sum Petri aut Cephae: alius, Ego sum Apollo. Nam sic dicendo, se eorum servos faciebant, quos ipsorum ministerio Deus destinauerat, ut Cap. 3. audiuimus. Imitantur hos, maiori tamen cum Christiani nominis ignominia, qui hodie dicunt: Ego sum Francisci, Ego Dominici, Ego Bernhardi aut Benedicti, &c. Nam hi omnes abnegata libertate, quam nobis Christus acquisiuit, votis se obstringunt, ut ijs obediant, quibus nihil in eos ex iure diuino est imperij, & simul hominum traditionibus se subijciunt, quarum maxima pars cum Christi doctrina aperte pugnat. Potest ergo omnibus illis haec Pauli sententia occini, & sola sufficit ad confutandum rationes omnes, quibus suam superstitionem excusant. In reliqua autem vita turpissime peccatur ab ijs, qui cum libertatem ex Dei beneficio acceperint, illam tamen sponte produnt, & se aliorum seruituti mancipant. Est peccatum hoc cum summa ingratitudine coniunctum, nimis auditum vulgare hodie. Cicero dicebat adeo praeclaram esse libertatis recuperationem, ut in ea repetenda nemo mors quidem fugienda sit. Et maiores nostri, fortissimi & optimi viri, vitam atque sanguinem profundere non sunt veriti, ut seipsos & posteros in libertatem vindicarent, cuius sensum in brutis quoque animantibus videbant. Nam bestiae, quas delectationis causa concludimus, cum copiosius alantur, quam si essent liberae, non facile tamen patiuntur se contineri. At quam multos hodie est videre, qui ut gulae, libidini, ambitioni & auaritiae sua satisfaciant, libertatis nullam habent rationem, sed sponte seipsos & patria exterorum principum libidini subijciunt, quibus hoc unum cordi est, ut hominum vaenalium sanguine in conficiendis bellis suis abutantur, quae plerumque nulla, aut falsem leui de causa suscipiunt. Quibus recte eos adnumerauerit, quos gula et libido faeneratorum seruos facit, dum ab his cum manifesta suarum fortunarum omnium iactura petere coguntur unde viuant, qui prius sua turpiter profuderunt. Fuit haec semper maximarum pub. pestis, & ut Lucanus olim canebat:
units.tr: This precept of the Apostle is violated in various ways, both in religion and in the rest of life and conduct. In religion they sin who, having left or as it were renounced the name of Christ, wish to be called by the names of those whom they have chosen as their teachers and masters. The Corinthians did this when one said, "I am Paul's"; another, "I am Peter's or Cephas's"; another, "I am Apollos's." For by speaking thus they were making themselves the slaves of those whom God had appointed for their ministry, as we heard in chapter 3. Those who today say, "I am of Francis, I of Dominic, I of Bernard or Benedict," &c., imitate these, but with a greater disgrace to the Christian name. For all of them, having renounced the liberty which Christ has acquired for us, bind themselves by vows to obey those over whom they have no authority at all by divine right, and at the same time submit themselves to human traditions, the greater part of which openly fight against the doctrine of Christ. This sentence of Paul can therefore be sung against all of them, and by itself it is sufficient to refute all the reasons by which they excuse their superstition. In the rest of life, however, people sin most shamefully when, having received liberty by God's benefit, they nonetheless betray it of their own accord and hand themselves over to the slavery of others. This sin is joined with the greatest ingratitude, and it is a very common complaint today. Cicero said that the recovery of liberty was so noble a thing that no one should shrink from death in seeking it back. And our ancestors, most brave and excellent men, did not hesitate to pour out their life and blood, so that they might claim themselves and their posterity into liberty, a feeling which they even saw in brute animals. For the beasts which we shut up for pleasure, though they are fed more abundantly than if they were free, still do not easily allow themselves to be held in. But how many today may be seen who, to satisfy their gluttony, lust, ambition and avarice, have no regard for liberty, but of their own accord subject themselves and their country to the lust of foreign princes, to whom this alone is dear: to abuse the blood of mercenary men in waging their wars, which they undertake for the most part for no reason, or at least for a trifling one. Rightly are counted among them those whom gluttony and lust make slaves of usurers, when, having foolishly squandered their own goods, they are forced by these men, with the manifest loss of all their fortunes, to seek from them the means by which to live. This has always been the greatest plague of the greatest states, and as Lucan once sang:

units.la: Hinc vsura vorax, auidumque in tempore faenus,Et concussa fides, & multis vtile bellum, &c. Sed plura de his alibi.
units.tr: Hence voracious usury, and greedy interest on loans, and faith shaken, and war, which is useful to many, etc. But more on these matters elsewhere.

units.la: Restat huius loci conclusio, qua rursus statuus aut propositio primaria repetitur: Vnusquisque in quo vocatus fuit, fratres, in hoc maneat apud Deum. Tam crebra repetitionis causa est, quod homines natura ad res nouas ferri sciret Paulus, & paucos esse, qui sua forte contenti viuere possint. Opus ergo fuit idem praeceptum saepius inculcari. Hic tamen modum diligentius exprimit, quem in seruanda sua statione tenere debeant: Nimirum, ut in ea maneant apud Deum, id est, ut meminerint se in Dei conspectu versari, cui olim ratio reddenda sit. Quoad ergo seruos, facit ad huius dicti expositionem quod ad Ephes. Cap. sexto sic dicit: Serui auscultate ijs, qui Domini sunt secundum carnem, cum timore ac tremore, cum simplicitate cordis vestri, ut Christo: non ad oculum seruientes, ut qui hominibus placere studunt, sed ut serui Christi, facientes ex animo quae vult Deus: cum beneuolentia seruientes Domino, & non hominibus: Ut qui illud sciatis, singulos quicquid fecerint boni, hoc reportaturos a Deo, siue seruus fuerit, siue liber, &c. Qua clausula diserte monet, haec debere singulos ad se transferre. Etenim nullum ad coercendos carnis affectus frenum fortius & efficacius est, quam si nos in IESV CHRISTI conspectu agere cogitemus, qui olim veniet ad iudicandum, ut singulis praemia factis ipsorum digna retribuat. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: There remains the conclusion of this passage, in which the main proposition is repeated once more: Let each one abide with God in the calling in which he was called, brothers. Such frequent repetition is because Paul knew that men are naturally carried toward new things, and that few are content to live within their own lot. It was therefore necessary that the same precept be pressed home more often. Yet here he sets out more precisely the manner in which they ought to keep to their station: namely, that they remain there with God, that is, that they remember they live in the sight of God, to whom an account must one day be rendered. So far as servants are concerned, what he says in the sixth chapter of Ephesians helps to explain this saying: "Servants, obey those who are your masters according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, in the simplicity of your heart, as to Christ; not serving to the eye, as men-pleasers, but as servants of Christ, doing from the heart the will of God; serving with goodwill, as to the Lord and not to men; knowing that each one, whatever good he does, will receive the same back from God, whether he is a servant or free," etc. By this closing clause he plainly warns that each person ought to apply these things to himself. For there is no bridle stronger and more effective for restraining the desires of the flesh than to think that we act in the sight of Jesus Christ, who will one day come to judge, and will repay each one with rewards worthy of his deeds. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXVII.
units.tr: HOMILIA XXXVII.

units.la: De virginibus autem praecepti Domini non habeo, sed do quod sentio, ut qui misericordiam acceperim a Deo, ut fidelis sim. Existi-mo igitur hoc bonum esse propter instantem necessitatem, bonum (inquam) hoc esse homini, ut ita sit. Alligatus es uxori? ne quaere dissolutionem: solutus es ab uxore? ne quaere uxorem. Quod si ea-etiam duxeris uxorem, non peccasti: & si nupserit virgo, non peccauit, sed afflictionem in carne habebunt huiusmodi. Ego autem vobis parco.
units.tr: Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give my opinion, as one who has obtained mercy from God to be faithful. I think therefore that this is good because of the present distress; good, I say, that it is so for a man. Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek a dissolution. Are you loosed from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you have taken a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. Yet such will have affliction in the flesh. But I spare you.

units.la: Hactenus de coniugio & coiugum officijs, de viduis item & diuortijs Paulus diligenter disseruit, & quoad hæc probè monuit, ne qui sub religionis prætextu diuortia nō necessaria faciant. Ea autem occasione in doctrinam generalem digressus est, vt quisq; vocationem suā constan-ter sequatur, neq; abfq; certa Dei voluntate vitæ genus mutet. Poterat autem ista admonitio à quibusdam sic accipi, quasi Virgines etiam in suo statu manere, neq; vnquam matrimonium contrahere debeant, maximè si cum Virgines essent, per Euangelium ad IESV CHRISTI cognitionem atq; fidem vocati sint. Ergo nunc de illis quoq; sermonem instituit, & id quidem circumspectè admodum & cum diligenti cautione, eò quòd hoc vitæ genus imprimis lubricum & periculis multis obnoxium esse sciret. Aut enim seipsos tentationibus grauissimis exponunt, & Satanæ laqueis obijciunt, qui virginitatem suam non prius probè exploratis viribus suis tueri studuent, & dum ex coniugio pollutionem stultè metuunt, in fornicationis barathrum denoluuntur[?]: Aut si quid proficiunt in hoc suo instituto, inde gloriandi occasionem arripiunt, & se propter Virginitatem Deo magis acceptos esse sibi persuadent. Vtriusq; vitij exempla passim in gentium quoq; historijs occurrunt. Inter Christianos autem tam clara & manifesta sunt hæc, vt fateri cogamur, nos huic potissimum persuasioni debere primò libidines nefarias, quibus Christiana religio Turcis & Iudæis iampridem suspecta & infamis facta est: deinde superstitiones quoq; & insolentem propriæ dignitatis fiduciam, qua IESV CHRISTI meritum à multis euacuatur. Et inter nostri seculi miracula non postremum censeri poterat, Virginitatis tam feruentes patronos & præcones esse, qui effreni libidine familias prope omnes fœdissimè polluunt. Admiratur iflorum[?] fucatam sanctimoniam rude & imperitum vulgus: at nos Paulum ex spiritus suggestione de toto hoc negotio differentem audiamus.
units.tr: So far Paul has carefully discussed marriage and the duties of spouses, and likewise widows and divorce, and on these matters he has given sound counsel, that no one should make divorces that are not necessary under the pretext of religion. On that occasion he has passed on to a general teaching, that each person should faithfully follow his calling and not change his way of life without a certain will of God. But this admonition could be taken by some as if virgins too should remain in their state and never ought to enter marriage, especially if, being virgins, they have been called through the Gospel to the knowledge and faith of Jesus Christ. So now he takes up a discussion of them as well, and does so very circumspectly and with careful caution, because he knew that this way of life is above all slippery and exposed to many dangers. For they either expose themselves to very grave temptations and throw themselves into the snares of Satan, who foolishly seek to guard their virginity without first testing their own strength carefully, and while they foolishly fear pollution from marriage, they fall down into the abyss of fornication; or, if they make some progress in this their vow, they seize on it as an occasion for boasting and persuade themselves that they are more acceptable to God because of their virginity. Examples of both faults occur everywhere, even in the histories of the nations. Among Christians, however, these things are so clear and manifest that we are compelled to admit that we owe to this persuasion, above all, the nefarious lusts by which the Christian religion has long been suspected and made infamous among the Turks and Jews; and then also superstitions and an insolent confidence in one's own worth, by which the merit of Jesus Christ is emptied out by many. And among the miracles of our age it could not be counted least that there are such fervent patrons and heralds of virginity, who with unbridled lust foully defile almost all households. The rude and unskilled crowd marvels at their painted sanctity; but let us hear Paul, who, prompted by the Spirit, discusses this whole matter.

units.la: Principiò, ne quis ex ijs, quæ postea in Virginitatis commendationem dicturus est, præceptum fingens, sibiipsi aut alijs laqueum inijceret, protestatione vtitur, qua se nihil pro imperio mandare, sed amicè de ijs consulere docet, quæ ipsis salutaria atq; vtilia videantur. De virginibus (inquit) an scilicet Virginitatem suam perpetuò tueri, aut matrimonio iungi debeant, præceptum Domini non habeo, sed do quod sentio, id est, meam de illis sententiam profero, ne quid vos celem. At quando se præceptum Domini habere negat, duo dicit. Primum, quòd Dominus ipse nihil de Virginitate mandauerit. Alterum, quòd neque Apostolis potestatem dederit quicquam de illa constituendi. Virumq; verissimè dicitur. In Lege enim de Virginitate adeò nihil præcipitur, vt potius leges coniugij subinde inculcentur, & promissiones de posteritatis multiplicatione passim repetantur. Prophetæ etiam nihil huius vnquam docuerunt. In nouo autem Testamento Christus à discipulis interrogatus, annon satius sit à matrimonio prorsus abstinere? nihil definire, & ne ipsis quidem Apostolis legem præscribere voluit. Meminit quidem Eunuchorum, quorum alij ex vtero matris tales nati, alij ab hominibus castrati sint, quidam verò seipsos castrare soleant propter regnum Dei. At hoc non omnibus datum esse docet, & proinde non obscurè admonet, neminem debere hic aliquid statuere ex priuato arbitrio. Quòd si verò mandata eius postrema inspiciamus, quibus docendi formam Apostolis præscripsit, summa illorum est, vt quæ ab ipso acceperint, omnes homines seruare doceant. Quod illos tanto studio fecisse scimus, vt Paulus seipsum anathema pronuntiare non vereatur, si quid præterea prædicarit. Noluit autem de Virginitate aliquid mandare Deus, non modò ne nuptias aut coniugium damnare videretur (quod Diuus Augustinus & alij quoque ex veteribus annotauerunt) verumetiam ne conscientijs infirmioribus laqueum inijceret aliquid mandando, quod ad regnum Dei consequendum non est necessarium. Hoc ipsum ergo Paulus ingenuè fatetur, interim verò suam sententiam de hac re fideliter proponit, ne eos contemnere putetur, qui per ipsum instituti cupiebant.
units.tr: First, lest anyone, from what he is later going to say in praise of virginity, should make a commandment and cast a snare upon himself or others, he uses a disclaimer, by which he teaches that he commands nothing by authority, but counsels in a friendly way about those things which seem to them salutary and useful. "Concerning virgins" (he says), whether they ought to keep their virginity perpetually or be joined in marriage, "I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give my opinion," that is, I declare my judgement about them, so that I may conceal nothing from you. But when he says that he has no commandment of the Lord, he says two things. First, that the Lord himself has commanded nothing about virginity. Second, that he has not given the Apostles any power to establish anything about it. And this is said most truly. For in the Law nothing is so commanded about virginity; rather, the laws of marriage are repeatedly urged, and promises of the multiplication of posterity are constantly repeated. The prophets too never taught anything of this kind. In the New Testament, when Christ was asked by his disciples whether it was not better to abstain altogether from marriage, he chose to decide nothing, and did not prescribe a law even for the Apostles themselves. He does indeed mention eunuchs, some of whom were born such from their mother's womb, others made so by men, and some who are accustomed to castrate themselves for the sake of the kingdom of God. But he teaches that this is not given to all, and therefore he not obscurely warns that no one should establish anything here by private judgement. But if we look at his final instructions, in which he prescribed to the Apostles the form of teaching, the sum of them is that they should teach all men to observe what they had received from him. We know that they did this with such zeal that Paul does not hesitate to pronounce himself accursed if he should preach anything else. Yet God chose not to command anything about virginity, not only lest he should seem to condemn marriage or wedlock (which St Augustine and others among the ancients have also noted), but also lest he should cast a snare upon weaker consciences by commanding something that is not necessary for attaining the kingdom of God. Paul therefore frankly confesses this very thing, and meanwhile faithfully sets forth his own opinion on the matter, lest he be thought to despise those who wished to be instructed by him.

units.la: Cæterum non debent hæc verba eo sensu accipi, quasi ex suo capite aliquid proferre voluerit Paulus, quod ecclesijs obtruderet. Ita enim hunc locum Romanæ sedis propugnatores exponunt, vt eiuncant[?], Apostolos multa tradidisse, quæ in scripturis nusquam inueniantur: vnde postea colligunt, eorum quoque successoribus licere, vt ex pectoris sui scrinio nouas leges depromant, vt deinde ecclesiæ & religionis formam pro suo arbitrio constituant. Et hic ille generalis aut vniuersalis error est, qui seculis aliquot totum orbem excæcauit, & cui soli debemus immensum illud chaos humanarum traditionum, quibus purior veritatis doctrina non tam obscurata, quàm obruta atque sepulta fuit. Sed ex hoc ipso loco istorum hominum arrogantia confutari potest. Nam primò nihil hic pronuntiat Paulus, quod doctrinæ per Christum traditæ repugnet, aut saltem ab ea alienum sit: sed quod hic de Virginitatis dono in genere pronuntiauit, ipse causæ præsenti applicat, & ex circumstantijs temporum atque personarum, quibus cum agebat, colligit, quod expressæ voluntati Dei maximè consentaneum esse sciebat. Huius summa est, vt sanctè viuamus, & ipsi simus omnino addicti, neque per huius seculi studia siue aduersanos ab ipso patiamur diuelli. Ad quod cum cœlibem vitam plerisque pro illorum temporum ratione plus seruituram esse videret, non immerito tam digno præconio ornat. Deinde non vniuersalem doctrinam proponit, quam omnes promiscuè sectari debeant: sed ita agit, vt facilè constet, ipsum iis solis loqui, quibus Deus hoc dedit, vt cœlibes viuere possint. Tertiò, his tamen ipsis liberum facit, vt suæ sententiæ obediant, seu minus, prout cuique commodum esse videtur. Nam mox subijcit: Quòd si etiam duxeris vxorem, non peccasti: & si nupseris virgo, non peccauit. Quæ verba aperte docent, Virginitatis donū non ex eorum numero esse, quibus necessario vti debent qui ea accepe-runt. Nam vt matrimonij causæ finales plures sunt, ita fieri potest, vt qui nulla carnis libidine vruntur, propter alias tamen causas non possint commodè vitam transigere, nisi coniugem & sociam curarum atque laborum sibi accersant. Quòd si cum his Romanenses nostros conferas, à Pauli exemplo longè alios esse videbis. Nam ex suo capite leges condunt à Christi doctrina non modò alienas, verumetiam ei omnino contrarias, quibus optimum & vetustissimum sanctissimumq; Dei institutum inter carnis opera numeratur, & pro impuro atq; prophano habetur. Neq; ea audacia contenti, illis absq; vllo deleƈtu quosuis obstringunt, & libertatem coniugij ab ipso Deo concessam quàm plurimis eripiunt. Cogunt deniq; ad suscipiendum & feruandum cœlibatus votum eos, qui aut per ætatem quid illud sit adhuc ignorant, aut iam pridem stuprijs & libidinibus vagi toti mundo abundè testati sunt, se nihil minus posse quàm castè viuere.
units.tr: Moreover, these words must not be taken in the sense that Paul wished to bring forward something from his own head, to thrust upon the churches. For the defenders of the Roman see expound this passage in such a way that they argue the Apostles delivered many things which are nowhere to be found in the Scriptures; and from this they afterwards infer that their successors too are permitted to draw new laws from the coffer of their own breast, and then to establish the form of the Church and of religion at their own discretion. And this is that general or universal error which for several centuries blinded the whole world, and to which alone we owe that immense chaos of human traditions, by which the purer doctrine of truth was not so much obscured as overwhelmed and buried. But from this very passage the arrogance of these men can be refuted. For, first, Paul here pronounces nothing that conflicts with the doctrine handed down through Christ, or at least is foreign to it; but what he has stated here in general about the gift of virginity, he himself applies to the present case, and from the circumstances of the times and persons with whom he was dealing he infers what he knew to be most in agreement with the expressed will of God. The sum of it is that we should live holily, and be wholly devoted to him, and not allow ourselves to be torn away from him by the pursuits of this age or by adversaries. Seeing that for many the celibate life would, given the circumstances of those times, be more serviceable to this end, he not undeservedly adorns it with such worthy praise. Second, he does not propose a universal doctrine which all should indiscriminately pursue; rather, he so conducts himself that it is easily clear that he speaks only to those to whom God has given the ability to live as celibates. Third, even to these he leaves it free to obey his opinion or not, as seems more convenient to each. For he immediately adds: "But even if you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned." These words plainly teach that the gift of virginity is not among those things which those who have received it must necessarily use. For just as the final causes of marriage are several, so it can happen that those who have no use of carnal lust nevertheless, for other reasons, cannot conveniently get through life unless they take to themselves a wife, a companion in cares and labours. But if you compare our Romanists with these, you will see that they are far different from Paul's example. For they lay down laws from their own head which are not only foreign to the doctrine of Christ but altogether contrary to it, by which the best, most ancient and most holy institution of God is numbered among the works of the flesh and regarded as impure and profane. Not content with this audacity, they bind all and sundry without any distinction, and snatch away from very many the freedom of marriage granted by God himself. Finally, they compel to take up and keep the vow of celibacy those who either, because of their age, still do not know what it is, or who have long since, wandering in debauchery and lusts, testified to the whole world abundantly that they are able to live chastely in no way at all.

units.la: Obijciunt autem, nos nullo iure de illis conqueri, cùm eos solùm suis legibus astringant, qui ad ipsorum iurisdiƈtionem pertinent, ecclesiasticas nimirum personas, nihil autem præcipiant aut mandant laicis, quibus per ipsos liceat pro suo arbitrio viuere. Sed est hæc calumnia plane excusatio, quà seipsos proprio indicio vt sorices produnt. Primò enim demonstrent velim, vnde hæc illis obtigerit iurisdiƈtio, quàm sibi in alios ecclesiæ ministros vendicant? Num verò illa Christi authoritate aut Apostolorum exemplo nititur? Neutrum certè poterunt dicere, nisi frontem omnino perfricuerint. Christus enim inter discipulos æqualitatem esse voluit, & ad mutua charitatis officia eos astrinxit, vt pedes quoq; sibi inuicem abluant. Deinde quæ illa audacia est, qua se solos & quos ipsi vnxerunt [?], ecclesiasticos & spirituales faciunt, reliquos autem laicos, id est, prophanos esse dicunt? Atqui spiritum Christi omnibus dari constat, qui per fidem in illum filij Dei fiunt, neq; Christiani dici merentur, quotquot spiritum illum non habent. Adde, quòd quoad coniugium Deus nullum inter ecclesiæ ministros & reliquum vulgus aut cuiuscunq; loci & ordinis homines discrimen constituit. Nam vt in veteri Testamento summos quoq; Pontifices suas vxores habuisse constat: ita Christus in Apostolorum chorum eos adoptauit, qui & vxorati erant, & postea vxores suas secum duxerunt, vt infra Cap. nono Paulus testabitur. Et cùm matrimonium ad vitandam fornicatio-nem institutum sit, eò magis illo vti conuenit ecclesiarum ministros & doctrinæ antistites, quò tur-pius & nocentius est quod ex illorum incontinentia nascitur scandalum. Quod non oscitanter A-postolus confideraut [?], quando episcopum talem vult constitui, qui vnius vxoris maritus sit, & ne-que gentium more polygamiam, neq; vagas libidines sectetur. Est ergo audacia hæc intolerabilis, qua inepti & prostituti pudoris homines sibijpsis in ecclesiam Christi plus iuris vendicant, quàm Apostolis olim concessum fuerit, qui in hac causa non minus modesti quàm cauti & circumspe-ƈti fuerunt.
units.tr: They object that we have no right to complain about these men, since they bind by their laws only those who fall under their jurisdiction, namely ecclesiastical persons, and do not prescribe or command anything for laymen, who may live as they please under their own authority. But this objection is plainly an excuse, by which they betray themselves, like moles, through their own confession. For first I would like them to show where this jurisdiction over other ministers of the Church, which they claim for themselves, came to them. Does it rest on the authority of Christ or the example of the Apostles? They can certainly say neither, unless they have utterly hardened their brow. For Christ willed that there be equality among the disciples and bound them to mutual duties of love, so that they should wash one another's feet. Next, what audacity is it that makes themselves, and those whom they themselves have anointed, alone "ecclesiastical" and "spiritual," while they call the rest laymen, that is, profane? Yet it is clear that the Spirit of Christ is given to all who become sons of God through faith in him, and those who do not have that Spirit do not deserve to be called Christians. Add that, as regards marriage, God has set up no distinction between the ministers of the Church and the rest of the common people, or men of any place or rank. For just as it is clear that in the Old Testament even the high priests had their wives, so Christ admitted to the company of the Apostles men who were both married and afterwards took their wives with them, as Paul will bear witness below in chapter nine. And since marriage was instituted to avoid fornication, it is all the more fitting that ministers of the churches and teachers of doctrine should use it, the more shameful and harmful is the scandal that arises from their incontinence. The Apostle considered this not carelessly, when he wishes a bishop to be appointed who is the husband of one wife, and who follows neither polygamy in the manner of the nations nor wanton lusts. This audacity, therefore, is intolerable, by which men who are foolish and have lost all sense of shame claim for themselves in the Church of Christ more right than was ever granted to the Apostles, who in this matter were no less modest than cautious and circumspect.

units.la: Nemo tamen hæc nostra sic accipiat, quasi in Virginitatis contumeliam dicta sint. Vt enim merito eos admiramur, qui aliis cupiditatibus prauis minus obnoxij sunt: ita laude etiam dignisima est castitas, quæ prurienti carnis libidini resistere potest, vt tàm animum quàm corpus purum & Deo sacrum seruemus: & quibus hoc contigit, habent de quo gratias Deo agant immortales. Sed quia tadem [?] non est nostrarum virium, neque etiam ex eorum numero est, sine quibus salus nostra non potest consistere, nemini cum imperio obtrudi debet, aut ut necessaria mandari. Si qui vero propter causas alias, quæ ad huius vitæ commoditatem pertinent, vel propter undique imminentia persecutionum pericula, alicui suadere voluerint, ut vitam cœlibem degat, ij meminerint, se quoque hac ipsa protestatione uti debere, quòd nullum de hac re Dei mandatum habeant, curent denique, ne laqueum conscientijs infirmorum injciant, neue libertatem, quam Deus omnis generis hominibus concesserit, novis traditionibus & cancellis circumscribant. Quod ipsum fit in multis quoque aliis, quæ media aut indifferentia sunt, observaretur, minus in ecclesia contentionum esset, magis autem floreret pietas & concordia, sine qua ecclesiarum salus non consistit.
units.tr: Yet let no one take what we say in this way, as if it were spoken to the disgrace of virginity. For just as we rightly admire those who are less subject to other wicked desires, so chastity is also most worthy of praise when it can resist the itching lust of the flesh, so that we keep both soul and body pure and holy to God; and those to whom this has been granted have cause to give thanks to God immortal. But since this is not within our strength, and is not of the number of those things without which our salvation cannot stand, it ought to be imposed on no one with authority, nor enjoined as necessary. If, however, for other reasons, which concern the convenience of this life, or because of the dangers of persecution threatening on every side, some wish to persuade anyone to live a single life, let them remember that they too ought to use this very declaration, that they have no command of God concerning this matter. Let them take care, finally, not to cast a snare upon the consciences of the weak, nor to confine within new traditions and barriers the liberty that God has granted to men of every kind. This same thing should be observed in many other matters which are indifferent or neutral; there would then be less contention in the Church, and piety and concord would flourish more, without which the safety of the churches does not stand.

units.la: Verumtamen ut maior esset sententiæ aut consilij huius authoritas, testatur Paulus se hæc dicere non ut hominem aliquem vulgarem, qui quod in mentem venerit temere effutit, sed ut eum, quem Deus singulari misericordia prosequi dignatus fit, ut fidelis esset in eius ministerio. Et hoc quidem illi licebat dicere, cum eius fides, probitas, labores, pericula & quæcunque hactenus in Apostolatu gesserat, omnibus nota essent. Suo autem exemplo docet omnes homines, quomodo in functione sibi diuinitus commissa versari debeant. Nam quod dicit, non ad solos Verbi administros, sed ad omnes alios quoq; hominum ordines pertinet. Nec enim magna erit cuiusquam in suo munere authoritas, nisi de eius fide omnibus constet. Et utinam hodie idem cum Paulo dicere possent, qui in repub. versantur, aut qui ab his constituti functiones quascunq; obeunt. Ita enim & legibus authoritas maior accederet, & patientius ferret illorum imperiu populus, qui nunc ad res nouas passim aspirat, quando plerosq; sub reipub. prætextu res priuatas agere videt. Idem de præ-tioribus etiá dici potest, quorū authoritas hanc maximè ob causam concidit, quòd solis oppibus[?] intenti, ea minus fideliter exequuntur, quæ ad piam sanctamq; liberorum institutionem pertinent. Cur enim in honore eos esse pateretur Deus, qui ipsius honorem tàm facile negligunt?
units.tr: Yet, so that the authority of this opinion or counsel might be greater, Paul testifies that he says these things not as some ordinary man who rashly blurts out whatever comes into his mind, but as one whom God by singular mercy has deigned to favour, so that he might be faithful in his ministry. And indeed he was entitled to say this, since his faith, uprightness, labours, dangers, and all that he had hitherto accomplished in the Apostleship were known to all. Yet by his own example he teaches all men how they ought to conduct themselves in the office divinely committed to them. For what he says pertains not only to the ministers of the Word but to all the other orders of men as well. Nor will anyone's authority in his office be great unless his faithfulness is attested to all. And would that those who are engaged in the commonwealth, or who perform any functions appointed by them, could today say the same with Paul. For then the authority of the laws would also be greater, and the people would bear their rule more patiently, whereas now they aspire everywhere to new things, since they see most men pursuing private affairs under the pretext of the commonwealth. The same can be said of the magistrates, whose authority has fallen chiefly for this reason: being intent only on their wealth, they carry out less faithfully those duties which pertain to the pious and holy upbringing of children. For why would God allow those to be in honour who so easily neglect his own honour?

units.la: Est autem obseruatione multa dignum, quòd de fide sua sic gloriatur Apostolus, ut hanc non suis viribus aut industriæ suæ, sed misericordiæ Dei tribuat, qui eum, cùm Christi hostis & ecclesiæ crudelissimus persecutor esset, vocare & animum eius donis ad Apostolicam functionem necessarijs instruere dignatus fuerat. Et de hoc ipse diligentius in priori ad Timotheum scribit: Gratiam ei habeo, qui mihi has vires indidit, nimirum CHRISTO IESV Domino nostro, quòd me fidelem duxerit, dum me in ministerio collocauit, qui prius eram blasphemus & persecutor & iniuriosus: sed mei misertus est, &c. Debet hinc quoque generalis doctrina peti. Nam etiamsi non eadem sit omnium in oppugnanda veritate impietas siue audacia, qua Paulus aliquando insaniuit, omnes tamen natura peccatores sunt, & indigni, quorum ministerio Deus utatur, adhæc inepti ad omnia, quæ ex illius mandato fieri debent. Nam ut alibi Apostolus monet, ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei sumus ex nobis ipsis. Si quem ergo ad ecclesiæ minister-rium, vel ad rempub. vel quamcunq; aliam functionem Deus vocat, & ad eam digne obeundam vires largitur, hoc nullo nostro merito facit, sed omne illud misericordiæ & bonitatis diuinæ opus est, quæ cum nostro ministerio minimè opus habeat, eo tamen uti dignatur, utq; eo uti possit donis quoq; dignis instruit. Est huius misericordiæ consideratio utilissima. Nam modestos reddit, ne naturæ dignitatis aut meritorum nostrorum fiducia efferamur: adhæc in officio continet, & stimulis vehementissimis excitat, ne torpeamus in ijs, quæ per nos Deus vult perfici. At hodie Episcopi atque principes in suis edictis, & quibuscunque alijs literis tam publicis quàm priuatis, Dei gratiam & clementiam ab initio statim prætexunt, quæ ipsos in Episcopatu collocarit, aut principes Regesue esse voluerit: sed utinam id ex animo facerent, simulq; meminissent, fore aliquando diem, quando functionis suæ rationem reddere cogentur, cuius nomine nunc ad inanem modò suæ potentiæ & dignitatis ostentationem abutuntur.
units.tr: It is also worthy of much notice that the Apostle boasts of his faithfulness in such a way that he ascribes it not to his own strength or industry but to the mercy of God, who, when he was an enemy of Christ and the most cruel persecutor of the Church, deigned to call him and to furnish his mind with the gifts necessary for the Apostolic function. He writes about this more fully in his first letter to Timothy: "I give thanks to him who has given me this strength, namely to Christ Jesus our Lord, that he has counted me faithful, placing me in the ministry, I who was before a blasphemer and a persecutor and insolent; but I obtained mercy," and so on. From this a general doctrine should also be drawn. For even if all men do not share the same impiety or audacity in attacking the truth with which Paul once raged, yet all are sinners by nature and unworthy that God should use their ministry, and moreover unfit for all the things that ought to be done at his command. For, as the Apostle warns elsewhere, we are not sufficient even to think anything of ourselves. If therefore God calls anyone to the ministry of the Church, or to the commonwealth, or to any other function, and grants him the strength to discharge it worthily, he does this by no merit of ours, but it is entirely a work of divine mercy and goodness. Although God has no need of our ministry, yet he deigns to use it, and he furnishes with worthy gifts the one whom he uses. The consideration of this mercy is most useful. For it makes us modest, so that we are not puffed up by confidence in our nature, dignity, or merits; moreover, it keeps us in our duty and stirs us with most powerful goads, so that we do not grow slack in those things which God wills to be accomplished through us. But today bishops and princes, in their edicts and in whatever other letters, public or private, they write, at the very beginning put forward the grace and clemency of God, which placed them in the episcopate or willed them to be princes and kings. Would that they did this from the heart, and at the same time remembered that a day will come when they will be compelled to render an account of their office, in the name of which they now abuse it merely to display an empty show of their power and dignity.

units.la: Admonet præterea nos locus iste, euidens imprimis & præclarum bonitatis Dei argumentum esse, si quibus doctores dat fideles, qui ecclesiæ negotium agunt ex animo, & publicam salutem promotam volunt. Id certè inter præcipua beneficia ille numerat, quoties populo Israelitico suam ingratitudinem exprobrare & dignas contumaciæ pœnas denuntiare instituit. Huc enim illud pertinet, quod per Amos dicit: Excitaui de filijs vestris prophetas, & de iuuenibus vestris Nazaræos. An hoc non est ò filij Israël, dicit Dominus? Vos autem fecistis, ut Nazaræi vinum biberent, & prophetis mandauistis dicendo: Ne prophetetis. Et huic simile est, quod apud Micheam de Mose, Aarone, & Maria dicitur. Sed & ipse Christus de isto nos admonet, quando messem quidem copiosam, operarios autem paucos esse ait, simulq; iubet Deum precari, ut is mittat messores fidos ad opus suum extrudat. Quod ipsum de bonis quoque principibus intelligi debere, vel unus iudicum liber docet, in quo subinde repetitur, Deum populi sui misertù[?] excitauisse iudicem aliquem, qui illum in libertatem vendicaret. Alibi vero reges in furore suo dedisse dicitur, quando nimirum populi ingratitudinem atque contumaciam punire voluit. Exempla in utramque partem hodie passim extant. Etenim summa admiratione digna est Dei misericordia, qui nouissimis hisce temporibus, quibus per omne scelus plerique in proprium exitium ruunt, non solum fidos Euangelij praecones excitat, verumetiam principes dat, qui saniori doctrinae locum dant, & ecclesiae nutritios agunt, sicuti olim per Isaiam promisit. Rursus autem irae ipsius grauissimae argumentum est, quod multis alijs Verbi sui praedicationem eripit, & eosdem tyrannis libidine & sanguine innoxio gaudentibus dilaniandos permittit. At quae nostri saeculi infelicitas est, pauci ista obseruant, ideoq; nullis aut gratiae aut iustitiae Dei exemplis emendantur.
units.tr: Moreover, this passage admonishes us that it is an especially clear and remarkable proof of the goodness of God when he gives faithful teachers to those whose concern is the business of the Church, and who wish public welfare to be advanced. Certainly among his chief benefits he counts this whenever he sets out to reproach the Israelite people for their ingratitude and to announce the punishments due to their stubbornness. To this belongs what he says through Amos: "I raised up prophets from your sons, and Nazirites from your young men. Is this not so, O sons of Israel, says the Lord? But you made the Nazirites drink wine, and you commanded the prophets, saying: Do not prophesy." Similar to this is what is said of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam in Micah. But Christ himself also warns us about this, when he says that the harvest indeed is plentiful but the workers are few, and at the same time bids us pray God to send faithful reapers into his harvest. This same thing must also be understood of good princes, as one book of the Judges alone teaches, in which it is repeatedly said that God, pitying his people, raised up some judge who would vindicate them into liberty. Elsewhere, indeed, it is said that God gave kings in his wrath, when he wished, of course, to punish the ingratitude and stubbornness of the people. Examples of both kinds are found everywhere today. For the mercy of God is truly most worthy of the highest admiration, who in these last times, when most men rush to their own destruction through every crime, not only raises up faithful heralds of the Gospel but also gives princes who make room for sounder doctrine and act as nursing fathers to the Church, as he once promised through Isaiah. On the other hand, a most serious proof of his anger is that he takes the preaching of his Word from many others and allows them to be torn apart by tyrants who delight in lust and in innocent blood. But what unhappiness of our age it is that few observe these things, and therefore are not corrected by any examples of the grace or justice of God.

units.la: Porrò videamus, quae illa Pauli sententia sit. Existimo (inquit) hoc bonum esse propter instantem necessitatem, bonum (inquam) hoc esse homini ut ita sit. Rursus autem bonum dicit, quod alias utile & commodum dicere solemus. Et causam exprimit, cur Virginitatis statum aut vitam caelibem commodiorem esse existimet, Nimirum propter instantem necessitatem. Quo nomine aliqui putant coniugij curas & molestias intelligi, quibus fere exercentur, qui in illo vi- uunt. Quorum sententia mihi minus probari potest, quod labores illi & molestiae nequaquam causa propria censeri debent, propter quam à coniugio homines Christiani abstinere debeant: quia si hoc demus, non minus ab agricultura, opificijs manuarijs, imò à repub. abstinendum fuerit, cum in omnibus istis curae et labores omnis generis inuenanitur. Ita vero vocatione nostra desere remus, & Deo non possemus probari, qui nos ad labore destinauit, ut in libro Iobi scribitur. Ergo de persecutionibus locus iste exponi debet, quae tunc pijs multae & graues imminebant. Ad quas ferendas minus fere idonei sunt coniugati, quos & rei domesticae cura magis grauat, & dulcissima pignora detinent, ut nihil illis exilio grauius esse putetur. Sed & religionis cura praepostera tales à via reuocat, dum metuunt, ne ipsis in exilium eiectis, aut ad mortem damnatis, liberi ipsorum non modo negligantur, verumetiam in superstitionibus aeducentur[?]. Quo fit, ut multi fidem abnegent, vel saltem turpiter dissimulent, dum liberis suis consultum volunt. Haec igitur Paulus considerans, vitam caelibem non ideo commendat, quod Virginitatis apud Deum maioris sit dignitatis quàm coniugium, aut quod in illa meritum salutis aliqua expari[?] constitui debeat: sed propter huius vitae commoditatem, & pro illorum temporum ratione, quando persecutiones ubique locorum feruebant.
units.tr: Let us next see what Paul's statement is. "I think (he says) that this is good because of the present necessity; this is good, I say, for a man to be so." Again he calls it "good," which we are accustomed to call useful and convenient. He also gives the reason why he thinks the state of virginity or the unmarried life is more convenient: namely, the present necessity. Some take this to mean the cares and troubles of marriage, with which those who live in it are generally occupied. I can less readily approve this view, because those labours and troubles can by no means be regarded as a proper reason why Christians should abstain from marriage. If we granted this, men would have to abstain equally from farming, manual trades, and indeed from public life, since cares and labours of every kind are found in all of these. We would then be deserting our calling, and could not be pleasing to God, who appointed us to labour, as is written in the book of Job. Therefore this passage must be explained of the persecutions, which then pressed heavily and often upon the godly. Married people are rather poorly suited to bear these, since the care of household affairs weighs on them more, and their dearest pledges hold them back, so that nothing seems more grievous to them than exile. Also a misguided concern for religion turns such people from this path, for they fear that their children, if they themselves are cast into exile or condemned to death, will not only be neglected but even brought up in superstitions. Hence many deny the faith, or at least shamefully conceal it, while they wish to provide for their children. Considering this, Paul does not commend the single life because virginity is of greater dignity before God than marriage, or because some part of the merit of salvation should be assigned to it; he commends it for the convenience of this life and in view of the circumstances of those times, when persecutions raged everywhere.

units.la: Est autem commendatio ista eiusmodi, ut non semper & apud omnes locum habeat. Multorum enim ea est conditio, ut si vel exulare contingat, hoc illis commodius sit, si coniugem habeant laborum & periculorum sociam, quàm si solitarij viuant. Itaque Pauli sententia non uniuersaliter accipi, aut rigidius ad omnes extendi, sed pro loci, temporis & personarum ratione exponi aut applicari debet. Et de hoc ipse nos admonet in iis quae sequuntur. Ne quis enim ex illa praeceptum fingeret, cui omnes necessario obedire debeant, explicationem subijcit, qua conscientijs infirmioribus omnis scrupulus eximitur. Dicit enim: Alligatus es uxori? ne quaere dissolutionem. Solutus es ab uxore? ne quaere uxorem. Quo loco obseruabis, non eodem sensu dissolutionem aut diuortium atque coniugium prohiberi. Illud enim vere & serò prohibetur, eò quòd nefas sit quocunque praetextu diuortiù facere non necessariù: hoc autem conditionaliter accipi debet, ne quis videlicet, cui datu est Virginitatis seruàdae donù, sibiipsi temere laqueum inijciat. Et huic sensui fauet, quòd mox liberù et licitù esse docet, quod prius prohibuisse videbatur. Nam subijcit: Quòd si etiam duxeris uxorem, nō peccasti: et si nupserit virgo nō peccauit. Quod diceret, lubeo quidem, ne qui soluti et liberi sunt, coniugiu sibi accersant: sed haec nō ideo dixi, quòd si facere nefas putem, sed quòd propter huius saeculi turbas caelebs vita Christum profitentibus mihi commodior esse videtur. Quapropter nemo siue mas siue fœmina se peccare putet, si alia de causa per se honesta & bona ad coniugium accedant. Verumtamen rursus moneo, quod tales afflictionem in carne habituri sint, id est; sentient omnis generis onera atque molestias, quae coniugium comitantur, & quae nostri temporis dura conditio magis grauat. Ego autem vobis parco. Video enim vos adhuc infirmiores esse, quam ut tantis certaminibus sufficere possitis, & ideo vobis consultum cupio, ut ad omnes difficultates superandas sitis expeditiores.
units.tr: Yet this commendation is of such a kind that it does not always and for everyone hold good. For many are so situated that, if it should happen that they must go into exile, it would be more convenient for them to have a wife as a companion in labours and dangers than to live alone. Therefore Paul's statement must not be taken universally, nor extended too rigidly to all, but must be explained or applied according to the circumstances of place, time and persons. He himself warns us of this in what follows. Lest anyone should make of it a precept that all must necessarily obey, he adds an explanation by which every scruple is removed from weaker consciences. For he says: "Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek a dissolution. Are you loosed from a wife? Do not seek a wife." Here you will notice that dissolution or divorce and marriage are not forbidden in the same sense. The former is forbidden absolutely and truly, because it is wrong to divorce on any pretext whatever when it is not necessary; the latter, however, must be understood conditionally, namely that no one to whom the gift of keeping virginity has been given should rashly cast a snare upon himself. This sense is confirmed by what he immediately teaches, that what he seemed to have forbidden is free and lawful: for he adds, "But if you have taken a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin has married, she has not sinned." He means: I indeed wish that those who are free and unbound should not bring marriage upon themselves; but I did not say this because I think it wrong to marry, but because, on account of the troubles of this age, the single life seems to me more convenient for those who profess Christ. Therefore let no one, whether man or woman, think that he sins if, for some other reason, honest and good in itself, he enters into marriage. Nevertheless I warn again that such people will have affliction in the flesh, that is, they will feel all kinds of burdens and troubles that accompany marriage, which the hard condition of our time weighs upon even more. But I spare you: for I see that you are still too weak to be able to withstand such great struggles, and so I desire that you be provided for, so that you may be more ready to overcome all difficulties.

units.la: Confutantur hoc loco validissime omnes, qui perfectionem Christianam in Virginitate col-locant, & huic meritum salutis tribuunt. Facit hoc olim nimium inconsiderate D. Hieronymus, qui parabolam de femine Verbi in bona terra fructificantis ita interpretatur, ut centuplum fructum virginibus, sexagecuplum viduis & continentibus, trigecuplum verò casis coniugibus tribuat. Neque eo contentus, eorum sententiam quoque adducit, qui centuplum fructum ad martyres referebant, & addit: Quod si ita est, sancta consortia nuptiarum excluduntur à fructu bono. Quod dictu mihi non procul ab impuri Siricij Papae sententia abesse videtur, qui coniuges in carne viuere, & proinde Deo non posse placere dixit. Sed reuera nihil audacius est hypocrisi, quae vbi hominum iudicio se probari sentit, in Dei quoque Verbum sibi ius sumit & imperium. At faci le fuerit impuris illis coniugij hostibus laruam detrahere, si Pauli verba propius consideremus. Quia enim coniuges plus afflictionis in carne habituros esse dicit, non obscure innuit, maius etiā fidei & constantiae Christianae robur in sancto & Christiano coniugio inueniri, quàm apud illos, qui sibi soli viuunt. Si quid ergo hominum meritis tribuendum esset, plus certè coniugibus deberetur, quibus maiora certamina sunt propositā[?].
units.tr: In this passage are most strongly refuted all who place Christian perfection in virginity and attribute to it the merit of salvation. Jerome long ago did this rather thoughtlessly, interpreting the parable of the seed of the Word bearing fruit in good ground so that he assigns a hundredfold fruit to virgins, sixtyfold to widows and the continent, and thirtyfold to married people. Not content with this, he also cites the opinion of those who referred the hundredfold fruit to martyrs, and adds: "If this is so, the holy partnership of marriage is excluded from the good fruit." To me this seems not far removed from the opinion of the impure Pope Siricius, who said that married people live in the flesh and therefore cannot please God. But in truth nothing is more audacious than hypocrisy, which, when it perceives that it is approved by human judgement, claims for itself also the right and rule over the Word of God. Yet it would be easy to strip away the mask from those impure enemies of marriage, if we considered Paul's words more closely. For because he says that married people will have more affliction in the flesh, he clearly hints that a greater strength of faith and Christian constancy is found in holy and Christian marriage than among those who live for themselves alone. If, then, anything were to be attributed to the merits of men, more would surely be owed to married people, for whom the struggles set before them are greater.

units.la: Sunt autem rationes etiam aliae, quae coniugio plus honoris quàm Virginitati deferendum esse docent. Primo enim illud vitae genus est, quod Deus ipse in prima rerum origine instituit, & in quo sanctissimos quosque vixisse, suo loco diximus. E contra de Virginitate (vt paulò ante dictum est) nullum Domini praeceptum extat, neque de illa quicquam mandandi potestatem Apostoli habuerunt. Deinde laboribus quidem & molestiis refertum est coniugium, sed eius modi, quas Deus ipse imposuit, vt quidem nostro bono, vt libidinis frenum sint, & nos ad arduentius pietatis studium accendant. Atqui laude digniores sunt, qui à Deo iniunctos labores alacri mente suscipiunt, quàm qui eos detrectant, vt suo otio consulant. Tertio quod nonnulli thori consuetudinem horrent, superstitiosum potius quàm pium censeri debet. Illum enim castum & impollutum esse Apostolus alibi testatur: cùm e contra pernitiosè vrantur & inter cupiditates & cogitationes nefarias turpissimè astuent, qui à matrimonio sibi abstinendum esse arbitrantur. Quae causa est, vt tales ferè à regno Dei longius absint. Quid enim prodest corporis puritatem seruauisse, si animum, potiorem tui partem, in cogitationum foedissimarum caeno assiduè volutari patiaris? Quod si vtriusq;[?] status fructum consideres, vberior certè & splendidior in coniugio reperietur. Huic enim debemus generis humani propagationem, legitimas familiarum successiones, affinitates, ecclesiae item & reipub. seminaria, quae si tollas, breui vtramq; in nihilum abire videbis. Quae causa est, quod veteres de liberorum procreatione vehementer solicitos fuisse constat, & quod sterilitas probro fuit multis, imò dolorem & cruciatum attulit, vt in Rebecca, Rachelis, Annae, Zachariae et Elizabetae exemplis est videre. Inter gentes verò Legem fuisse Cicero testatur: Caelibes esse prohibento. Et apud Spartanos etsi in magno honore & pretio esset senectus, iuuenes tamen iis senibus non assurgebant, qui liberos nullos generabant, à quibus eundem honorem ipsi aliquando possent sperare. Poterant autem huius generis infinita alia adduci, quae omnia non ideo à nobis commemorantur, vt libidini immoderatae habenas laxemus, sed vt superstitiosos illos confutemus, qui Virginitatem nimijs laudibus vehendo matrimonij dignitatem maxima ex parte proculcant, & infirmis multorum malorum authores sunt: vt alibi pluribus ostendetur.
units.tr: There are also other reasons which teach that more honour is to be given to marriage than to virginity. First, marriage is the way of life that God himself instituted at the very origin of things, and in which all the most holy men lived, as we have said in its place. On the contrary, concerning virginity (as was said a little above) there is no command of the Lord, nor did the Apostles have any authority to enjoin anything about it. Next, marriage is indeed full of labours and troubles, but of such a kind as God himself has imposed, for our good, so that they may be a bridle on lust and may kindle us to a more earnest zeal for godliness. Yet those are more worthy of praise who take up with a cheerful mind the labours enjoined by God, than those who shun them in order to consult their own ease. Thirdly, that some shudder at the practice of the marriage bed ought to be judged superstitious rather than pious. For the Apostle testifies elsewhere that it is chaste and undefiled; whereas, on the contrary, those who think they must abstain from marriage are wretchedly inflamed and most shamefully seethe with desires and wicked thoughts. This is the reason why such people are generally farther from the kingdom of God. For what does it profit to have kept the purity of the body, if you allow the mind, the better part of you, to wallow continually in the filth of most foul thoughts? If you consider the fruit of each state, the fruit of marriage will certainly be found richer and more splendid. For to it we owe the propagation of the human race, the lawful succession of families, kinships, and also the seminaries of the Church and the commonwealth; take these away, and you will soon see both vanish into nothing. This is why it is well established that the ancients were greatly anxious about the procreation of children, and why sterility was a reproach to many, and even brought grief and torment, as can be seen in the examples of Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah, Zechariah and Elizabeth. Among the nations, Cicero testifies that there was a law: "Let them forbid the unmarried." And among the Spartans, although old age was held in great honour and esteem, the young nevertheless did not rise before those old men who had no children, from whom they themselves might hope for the same honour at some time. Countless other examples of this kind could be brought forward, but we do not mention these so that we may loosen the reins of immoderate lust, but so that we may refute those superstitious men who, by extolling virginity with excessive praise, largely trample underfoot the dignity of marriage, and are the authors of many evils for the weak, as will be shown more fully elsewhere.

units.la: Nunc praeter ista Pauli modestiam nos obseruare conuenit, qui totus in hoc est, vt quam mi-nimis molestijs pios grauet. Longè ergo à scribarum ingenio abfuit, qui olim sarcinas ingentes colligabant, quas populi humeris imponerent, ipsi verò eàdem ne digito quidem attingebant. Imitati sunt hos posteris temporibus, qui vota monastica & in his calibatum atque innumera alia fabricarunt, ex quibus ad ipsos quidem quæstus ingens, ad populum verò infelicem nihil quàm labor, sumptus & horribilis conscientiæ carnificina redijt. At nos Deo gratias agere decet, qui istorum artes detexit, & veterem libertatem nobis restituit. Simul verò cauere oportet, ne ea abutamur, sed vt eius nomen in nobis glorificetur, qui nos ex tenebrarum potestate vocauit in admirabilem lucem suam per IESVM CHRISTVM Dominum nostrum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Now, besides this modesty of Paul, we should observe that his whole aim is to burden the godly as little as possible with troubles. He was far from the cleverness of the scribes, who once bound up huge burdens and laid them on the shoulders of the people, while they themselves would not lift them even with a finger. Later times have imitated these men, who devised monastic vows and celibacy among them, and countless other things, from which great profit came to themselves, but to the unhappy people nothing but toil, expense, and a dreadful butchery of conscience. But we ought to give thanks to God, who has exposed their arts and restored our old liberty to us. At the same time we must take care not to abuse it, but so that his name may be glorified in us, who called us out of the power of darkness into his marvellous light through Jesus Christ our Lord: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXVIII.

units.la: Hoc autem aio fratres, quoniam tempus contractum est in posterum, vt & qui habent vxores, sint vt non habentes. Et qui flent, vt non flentes: & qui gaudent, vt non gaudentes: & qui emunt, vt non obtinentes: & qui vtuntur mundo hoc, vt non abutentes. Præterit enim species huius mundi: velim autè vos absque solicitu-dine esse. Qui cælebs est, curat ea quæ sunt Domini, quomodo placiturus sit Domino. At qui ducit vxorem curat ea quæ sunt mundi, quomodo placiturus sit vxori. Discretæ sunt ea quæ est vxor & ea quæ est virgo. Quæ est innupta, curat ea quæ sunt Domini, vt sit sancta cùm corpore tum spiritu: quæ verò nupta est, curat ea quæ sunt mundi, quomodo placitura sit viro.
units.tr: This I say, brothers: the time is short, so that from now on those who have wives should live as though they had none; those who weep, as though they did not weep; those who rejoice, as though they did not rejoice; those who buy, as though they did not possess; and those who use this world, as though they did not make full use of it. For the outward form of this world is passing away. I want you to be free from anxiety. The unmarried man is concerned with the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord. But the married man is concerned with the things of the world, how he may please his wife. The wife and the virgin also differ. The unmarried woman is concerned with the things of the Lord, that she may be holy in both body and spirit; but the married woman is concerned with the things of the world, how she may please her husband.

units.la: PAulus Apostolus non sine iustis & grauibus causis tam prolixè & diligenter de illis agit, quæ ad coniugium spectant. Vt enim circa hæc à Corinthijs varie peccabatur: ita in spiritu præuidit ille, quid nouissimis temporibus futurum esset. Vt nimirum alij quidem sub religionis prætextu matrimonium prohiberent, alij autem omni religionis sensu procul abiecto in omnem licentiam sive libidinem effunderentur. Quia ergo (vt alibi diximus) humanæ vitæ conseruatio & eiusdem honestas ex coniugio magna ex parte dependet, neque etiam sine hoc religionis dignitas consistere potest, necesse fuit, nos de toto hoc negotio probè edoceri. Et hæc causa est, quod subinde generales doctrinas siue admonitiones interserit: vt nimirum in illis videamus, hîc de omnibus agi, quæ ad vitam pie & honestè transigendam pertinent. Quo imprimis referri debet loci istius, quem modo recitauimus, pars prior, quæ breuem, simplicem & absolutam vitæ totius institutionem continet. Qua interposita, mox ad ea redit Apostolus, quæ de Virginitate & innuptarum conditione dicere cœperat.
units.tr: The Apostle Paul does not treat matters concerning marriage so fully and carefully without just and weighty reasons. For the Corinthians had gone wrong in various ways about these things, and in the Spirit he foresaw what would happen in the last times: some, under the pretext of religion, would forbid marriage, while others, casting off every sense of religion, would pour themselves out into every license and lust. Therefore, since (as we have said elsewhere) the preservation of human life and its decency depend in large part on marriage, and since the dignity of religion cannot stand without it either, it was necessary for us to be thoroughly taught about this whole matter. This is why he repeatedly inserts general teachings and admonitions, so that in them we may see that everything pertaining to living a godly and honourable life is treated here. Above all, the first part of the passage we have just recited should be noted, for it contains a brief, plain and complete outline of the whole of life. Having set this down, the Apostle returns at once to what he had begun to say about virginity and the condition of the unmarried.

units.la: Summa prioris partis est, hominem vitam & omnes eius actiones ita instituere debere, ne propter res huius sæculi bona cœlestia atque æterna negligat. Quod vt facilius impetret ab ijs, qui ex carnis natura præsentibus nimium addicti sunt, rationes & argumenta adducit, quibus excitet nos, vt de iis diligentius cogitemus. Primum his verbis proponit: Hoc autem aio fratres, quoniam tempus contractum est in posterum. Debent hæc non solùm de vitæ huius breuitate intelligi, verumetiam de totius mundi ætate (vt sic loquar) quæ nouissimo hoc tempore ad finem suum properat, vt impletis iam pridem omnibus, quæ olim prædicta sunt, nihil præter vltimum IESV CHRISTI aduentum sperare possimus, in quo mundi huius conditionem omnem aboleri oportet. Atqui communis sensus docet, eos qui rem magnam agunt, eò studiosius in eam incumbere debere, quo minus temporis sibi datum esse vident, ne circa ludicra occupati, illud abs-que fructu elabi patiantur. Sed addit huic alterum argumentum ex rerum huius sæculi conditione desumptum: Præterit autem species aut figura huius mundi. Facit hoc ad prioris confirmationem. Si enim tempus breue est, interea autem quæcunque in hoc mundo præclara & eximia putantur, paulatim, vel potius celeri & indefesso cursu transeunt, næ[?] nimium imprudentes sunt, qui aliquam temporis istius portiunculam male aut inutiliter collocant, & non totos se ad cœlestium bonorum possessionem accingunt.
units.tr: The sum of the first part is that a person must order his life and all his actions so that he does not neglect heavenly and eternal goods for the goods of this age. So that he may more easily win over those who are too much given over to present things by their fleshly nature, he brings forward reasons and arguments by which he stirs us to think about these matters more carefully. First he sets it forth in these words: "This I say, brothers, the time is short from now on." These words should be understood not only of the brevity of this life, but also of the age of the whole world (so to speak), which in this final period hastens toward its end. Since everything long foretold has already been fulfilled, we can look for nothing but the last coming of Jesus Christ, in which the whole condition of this world must be abolished. Now common sense teaches that those who are engaged in a great undertaking ought to apply themselves all the more eagerly to it, the less time they see is granted them, lest, busied with trifles, they let it slip away without profit. But he adds to this a second argument, drawn from the condition of the things of this age: "For the outward form, or figure, of this world passes away." This serves to confirm the first. For if the time is short, while meanwhile whatever is thought splendid and excellent in this world gradually passes away, or rather runs its course swiftly and without rest, then surely those are very unwise who spend some small portion of that time badly or uselessly, and do not gird themselves wholly to the possession of heavenly goods.

units.la: Figuram autem & speciem mundo tribuit, ut offendat, omnia quæ in hoc habentur, non nisi specie inani & umbris vacuis constare, non autem res esse certas & solidas, quibus aliquid tribui debeat. Quod ipsum Dauid docet, quando hominem ait in imagine viuere, id est, vitam homi-nis imaginariam esse, & circa inanes persuasiones occupari, in quibus nihil perpetuum fit aut solidum. Potest hoc prolixè demonstrari, si ex ordine omnia consideres, quæ apud homines in pretio esse solent, & quibus plerique confidunt. Etenim opes plurimi admirantur, & eos beatos prædicant, quibus datum est inter illarum thesauros vitam degere. At omne hoc imaginarium est, & inanis atque salsissima persuasio. Nam si diuitiarum usum spectes, ex congestis auri atque argenti acceruis, ex agrorum latifundijs, ex redditibus annuis & uniuerso ædificiorum, vasorum, & totius suppellectilis splendore, nihilo plus ad opulentissimum quenque redit, quam ex modicis facul-tatibus ad quemuis alium, qui sua sorte contentus viuit. Ut enim nihil in mundum intulimus, ita nihil etiam inde exportabimus, neque alius diuitiarum usus est, quàm ut nostræ necessitati quoad victum & amictum seruiant. Cum autem in his natura nostra paucis contenta sit, reliqua illa omnia inanis solummodo & superfluus splendor sunt, sub quo plerumque solicitudines & curæ latent, quæ ipsam quoque vitam homini amara reddunt. Quod si vero conditionem siue naturam diuitiarum inspicias, nihil illis incertius, nihil instabilius. Nam & casibus infinitis obnoxiæ sunt, et sæpe nobis insciis dilabuntur, adeoq; euanescunt, ut præter omnium expectationem pauper & egenus conspiciatur, quem multi Cræso ditiorem esse putabant. Eadem est honorum atq; dignitatum huius sæculi ratio, quæ etiam ipsæ præter inanem splendorem nihil continent, & ex vulgi iudicio dependent, quod in horas mutatur. Itaque omnis illa gloria fulgor ex lebete est, qui vix momento oculos perstringit, ad hominis vero felicitatem nihil prorsus confert. Denique non erraueris, si hominum vitam inter opes & honores incertis vicibus fluctuantem ludo scenico similem esse dicas. Ut enim illic theatrum ipsum aulæis undique ornatum palatia magnifica, arces & urbes refert, personæ autem, reges, heroes, belli duces esse videntur, mox autem peracta fabula, theatri splendor aufertur, & ad suam priorem conditionem reuertuntur, qui paulo ante hominum beatissimi esse putabantur: Ita breui tempore mundus hic splendorem suum magnificè ostentat, & stultos homines persuasione felicitatis inebriat, quæ mox omnis in fumum abit, & ut somnium auolat. Idem de corporis nostri bonis valetudine nimirum, viribus & forma dici potest. In quibus omnibus etsi nullus casus acerbior incidat, omnia tamen ista præterreunt, & proprio naturæ cursu singulis momentis ad finem suum properant. Nam ut Poëta ait, Tempora labuntur tacitisque senescimus annis. Item: Corpora vertuntur, nec quod fuimus fumusue Cras erimus, &c. Et hæc quidem omnes homines non modo vident atque intelligunt, verumetiam in semetipsis quotidie experiuntur & sentiunt: qui vero ea, ut decet, expendat, paucissimos esse inuenire. Recte ergo Paulus verum & salutarem huius considerationis usum nobis tradit, & in suas quasi partes aut species diducit quæcunque in hac vita fiunt, ut admonitionem hanc non minus necessariam quàm utilem singulis accommodate possimus.
units.tr: He ascribes "figure" and "form" to the world in order to show that everything found in it consists only of an empty appearance and hollow shadows, and is not made up of certain and solid things to which anything should be attributed. David himself teaches this when he says that man lives in an image, that is, that human life is imaginary, and that people are occupied with empty persuasions in which nothing is lasting or solid. This can be demonstrated at length if you consider in order all the things that are usually held in esteem among men and in which most people put their trust. Indeed, many admire riches and call those blessed to whom it has been granted to live amid their treasures. But all of this is imaginary, an empty and very foolish persuasion. For if you look at the use of wealth, the heaps of gold and silver, the broad estates, the annual revenues, and the splendour of buildings, vessels and all household goods, they bring the richest man no more than they bring any other man who lives content with his modest means. For as we have brought nothing into the world, so we will carry nothing out of it, and the only use of riches is to serve our necessity for food and clothing. Since our nature is content with few things in these matters, all the rest is nothing but empty and superfluous show, beneath which anxieties and cares usually lie hidden, which make life itself bitter for man. But if you examine the condition or nature of riches, nothing is more uncertain, nothing more unstable. For they are subject to endless accidents, and often slip away without our knowing it, and vanish so completely that a man whom many thought richer than Croesus is seen to be poor and destitute, beyond everyone's expectation. The same is true of the honours and dignities of this age. Apart from empty splendour they contain nothing either, and they depend on the judgement of the common people, which changes by the hour. So all that glory is a glitter from a bowl, which scarcely dazzles the eyes for a moment and contributes absolutely nothing to human happiness. Finally, you would not be wrong to say that human life, tossed about between wealth and honours in uncertain turns, is like a stage play. For just as the theatre itself, hung on all sides with curtains, represents magnificent palaces, citadels and cities, and the actors appear as kings, heroes and generals of war, but soon, when the play is over, the splendour of the theatre is taken away and those who a little before were thought the most blessed of men return to their former condition, so in a short time this world proudly displays its splendour and intoxicates foolish men with the persuasion of happiness, which soon all goes up in smoke and flies away like a dream. The same can be said of the goods of our body: health, strength and beauty. Even if no harsher misfortune befalls them, all these things pass away and, by the natural course of things, hasten to their end at every moment. For as the poet says: "The times glide by, and we grow old in silent years." Again: "Bodies are changed, and what we were is smoke; tomorrow we shall be…" and so on. All men not only see and understand these things, but also daily experience and feel them in themselves; yet very few are found who weigh them as they ought. Rightly, then, Paul hands down to us the true and wholesome use of this consideration, and divides into their parts or kinds whatever happens in this life, so that we may apply this admonition, no less necessary than useful, to each person fittingly.

units.la: Orditur autem à coniugibus, quia de his potissimum sermo est, & monet, ut qui uxores habent, sint ut non habentes. Quibus verbis minimè iubet, ut viri uxores negligant quasi nihil ad se pertinentes. Ita enim cum prima coniugij institutione pugnaret, in qua Lex lata est, ut homo deserti parentibus uxori suæ adhæreat. Imò sibi ipsi contradiceret, qui alibi docuit, ut viri uxores suas diligant, et ut utrinq; debitam beneuolentiam sibi mutuò reddant. In præsenti igitur hoc vult, ne uxoribus nimium additi cœlestia & quæ ad regnum Dei pertinent negligant. Hoc enim facere consueuerunt, qui (ut Thobiæ angelus dicebat) non alio animi proposito ad matrimonium accedunt, quàm ut brutorum animaliū instar libidem vacent, & proinde Deū abs se et mente sua procul excludunt. Qui cum uxoribus nō alter quàm meretricibus utuntur, coniugiū ipsum dehonestant, cui maior reuerentia debetur. Nam etsi ad fornicationes vitandas unusquisq; propriam uxorem habere debeat, in ipso tamen coniugio reuerentia & modestia seruari debet, ut meminerint singuli, uxorem dignitatis non voluptatis nomen esse: quod olim Commodum Verum Imp.dixisse historici scribunt. Peccant item, qui propter coniugium illustrium & affinitates, quas contraxerunt, efferuntur, quasi iam extra omnem teli iactum sint constituti: quod multis exitium attulisse constat. Vult ergo Paulus nos cogitare, coniugium inter vitae huius fidia[?] numerari, & proinde sic in eo vitam instituì debere, ut eius dignitatem minimè prophanemus, uxores item meminerimus nobis in Christo sorores factas esse, & ita coniugio utamur, ut inter curas, quae huic coniunctae sunt, non intermittamus vitae coelestis & aeternae felicitatis studium: denique ut in iis, quae ad Dei cultum & animarum salutem spectant, nos per coniugium non magis impediri patiamur, quam si uxores omnino nullas haberemus. Talia olim sanctorum patrum coniugia fuerunt. Abrahamum certè Sara minimè impediuit, quo minus Deum vocantem sequeretur: imò potius ei adiumento fuit, quando ipsi comes indiuulsa facta est, & labores atque aerumnas pere-grinationis sua consuetudine leviores fecit. Quod ipsum de Apostolis dicere possumus, quos uxores suas secum duxisse infra dicetur. Et qui hos imitantur, ij uxores habent perinde ac si non habeant, eo quod nullum ex illis impedimentum sentiunt, quo minus Deo obtemperent, & vitae innocentiam tueantur.
units.tr: He begins with married people, because it is chiefly of them that he is speaking, and he admonishes that those who have wives should be as though they had none. By these words he by no means orders husbands to neglect their wives as though they had nothing to do with them. For that would fight against the first institution of marriage, in which the law was laid down that a man, leaving his parents, should cleave to his wife. Indeed he would contradict himself, since he taught elsewhere that husbands should love their wives and that each should render to the other the goodwill due. His meaning here, then, is that they should not neglect heavenly things and those that pertain to the kingdom of God by being too much attached to their wives. For this is what those are accustomed to do who (as the angel said to Tobias) approach marriage with no other purpose than to indulge lust like brute animals, and so shut God out of themselves and out of their minds. Those who use their wives no differently from harlots dishonour marriage itself, which deserves greater reverence. For although each man ought to have his own wife to avoid fornication, yet within marriage itself reverence and moderation must be observed, so that each may remember that the name "wife" signifies dignity, not pleasure; historians write that the emperor Commodus Verus once said this. Those also sin who grow proud because of illustrious marriages and the connections they have made, as though they were already placed beyond the reach of any missile; it is well known that this has brought ruin to many. Paul therefore wants us to consider that marriage is counted among the frail things of this life, and so that we should order our life within it in such a way that we do not profane its dignity; that we remember also that our wives have been made our sisters in Christ; and that we use marriage in such a way that, amid the cares that are joined to it, we do not give up the pursuit of heavenly life and eternal happiness; and finally, that in those things which pertain to the worship of God and the salvation of souls, we do not allow ourselves to be hindered by marriage any more than if we had no wives at all. Such were the marriages of the holy fathers of old. Sarah certainly did not hinder Abraham from following God when He called him; rather she was a help to him, when she became his inseparable companion and by her steadfast devotion made lighter the labours and hardships of his pilgrimage. We may say the same of the Apostles, whom it will be said below that they led about their wives with them. And those who imitate them have wives as though they had none, because they feel no hindrance from them to obeying God and keeping their life blameless.

units.la: Secundo, & qui flent (inquit) sint ut non flentes: & qui gaudent, ut non gaudentes. Qua locutione utramque fortunam, secundam nimirum & adversam comprehendit.
