Permittit autem flere & gaudere, quia nos Deus non silices aut truncos creavit, qualem Stoici fingunt suum virum bonum & sapientem: sed hoc monet, ut in omni fortuna constanti fide nostram tenea-mus stationem, & quamvis dura & acerba multa accidant, quae nos dolere & ingemiscere cogunt, luctu tamen non ibi absorbeamur: Accidit hoc illis, qui in adversis & periculis gravioribus non solum fortem suam deplorant, sed insuper de Dei gratia dubitare incipiunt, deque eius providentia improbe quiritantur. Hi non tam flere dici possunt, quàm belluino ululatu tumultuari.
units.tr: Secondly, he says, "those who weep should be as though not weeping, and those who rejoice as though not rejoicing." By this expression he covers both kinds of fortune, prosperity and adversity. He permits weeping and rejoicing, because God did not create us as stones or tree trunks, as the Stoics imagine their good and wise man to be. He warns, rather, that in every fortune we should hold our position with steadfast faith. Although many hard and bitter things happen that compel us to grieve and groan, we should not be swallowed up by sorrow. This happens to those who, in adversity and in more grievous dangers, not only lament their lot but also begin to doubt God's grace and complain wickedly about his providence. Such people can hardly be said to weep so much as to howl with bestial wailing.

units.la: Itaque modum nos tenere iubet Apostolus, ut quamvis omnia nobis inimica & infesta esse videantur, non tamen de Dei gratia dubitemus, sed in medio luctu aut ploratu fiducia divinae bonitatis et aeternae salutis certa spe erecti, tristitiam omnem fortiter vincamus. Quod ergo de suo Aeneae Poeta olim dixit, Premit alto corde dolorem: hoc ipsum ad Christianos homines imprimis pertinet, ne ex nimio animi dolore aliquid dicant aut faciant, quod à fide alienum censeri possit. Idem in gaudio etiam debet observari, si quando laetior fortuna nobis arridet: ne scilicet nimia laetitia abrepti nostrae functionis obliviscamur, & coelestis vitae studia negligamus, quibus nos totos addictos esse convenit. Est hoc vitium vulgare admodum, & inter novissimi saeculi mores huius Christus meminit, quando eorum similes fore dicit, qui Noe & Lothi temporibus edebant, bibebant, uxores ducebant & nuptui dabant, immemores interea eorum, circa quae homines imprimis occupatos esse oportet. Et in horum numero fere primi sunt voluptuarij belluones, qui (ut Isaiae[?] ait) convivijs suis tympana & tibias adhibent, securi interim iudiciorum Dei, neque huius operae unquam attente considerant. Proximi his sunt, quos victoriarum successus, regnorum vires & opum splendor inebriat, ut in his sibi perpetuam felicitatem polliceantur: quibus hoc fe-re proprium est, ut tunc quoque non solum gaudeant, sed petulanti protervia lasciviant, quando plerique alij inter adversae fortunae certamina gemunt atque plorant. Quod quia à Christianae religionis legibus alienissimum est, quae nos ut eiusdem corporis membra simus conjungit, non temere de his nos Paulus admonet. Quia autem vix quicquam difficilius est, quàm in utraque fortuna modum tenere, utile simul & necessarium est instabilem & momentaneam omnium huius saeculi rerum conditionem crebrò in mentem revocare. Etenim cum & vitae huius tempus breve sit, & iam ipse mundus ad finem suum properet, non possunt diuturnae esse afflictiones, quibus hic exercemur: & consolari nos debet, quod in singulas horas aliquid ex illis decedit. Nobis quidem interdum mora longior esse putatur, sed ut qui navigio vehuntur, sive dormiant sive vigilent, edant, bibant, ludant, naufragent, singulis tamen momentis ad portum propius accedunt: ita qualiscunque sit huius vitae fortuna, ea tamen impedire non potest, quò minus tempora continuo motu labantur, & nobis vitae huius finem adducant, qui in Christum credentibus non potest non felix & beatus esse. E contra diuturnum & stabile esse non potest gaudium, quod ex huius saeculi rebus quantumvis splendidis nascitur, cum tota huius mundi facies bullae instar transeat aut evanescat. Quid? anno fere magnos successus inopina aliqua & gravis calamitas sequi solet? Quod prudenter olim Philippus Macedo observans, cum nuntium de rebus plurimis uno die felicissime felicissimè gestis accepisset, porrectis in cælum manibus exclamabat: O fortuna pro tot tantisq; bonis leui aliquo malo me affice. Et Polycrates Samiorum tyrannus, cum omnia ipsi ad miraculum usque prospere cederent, anulum cum incomparabilis pretij gemma sponte in mare abiecit, ut quam tot læti successus portendere videbantur calamitatem aliquo infortunio expiaret. Erraruntistiquidem, quod res humanas à fortuna cæca gubernari, vel potius temere ferri putarent: simul tamen solicitos fecit rerum vicissitudo, quam quasi lege perpetua subinde secunda aduersis temperare videbant. Quanto magis igitur Christianos homines in horum consideratione diligentes esse decet, ne immodico gaudio à fluant, sed in prosperis Deo quidem grati sint, & in hoc lætentur, simul verò ad ferendam crucem semper parati sint.
units.tr: Therefore the Apostle bids us keep due measure, so that, although everything seems hostile and hurtful to us, we do not doubt God's grace. Instead, in the midst of grief or tears, raised up by confidence in the divine goodness and by the sure hope of eternal salvation, we should bravely overcome all sadness. What the poet once said of his Aeneas, "He suppresses his grief in his deep heart," applies especially to Christians: they must take care that, from excess of sorrow, they do not say or do anything that can be judged foreign to the faith. The same measure must be observed in joy, when a happier fortune smiles on us. We must take care lest, carried away by excessive delight, we forget our calling and neglect the pursuits of the heavenly life, to which we ought to be wholly devoted. This is a very common vice, and Christ mentioned it among the manners of the last age, when he said that men would be like those who ate, drank, married wives and gave in marriage in the days of Noah and Lot, meanwhile forgetful of those things with which men above all ought to be occupied. Among these people the first are almost the voluptuous revellers, who (as Isaiah[?] says) have tambourines and pipes at their feasts, secure meanwhile from the judgments of God, and never attentively consider this work of theirs. Next to them are those whom the success of victories, the power of kingdoms and the splendour of wealth intoxicate, so that they promise themselves perpetual happiness in these things. It is nearly peculiar to these people that they rejoice then too, and exult with wanton insolence, when many others groan and weep amid the struggles of adverse fortune. Since this is most alien to the laws of the Christian religion, which joins us together as members of the same body, Paul does not admonish us about these matters lightly. Yet since hardly anything is more difficult than keeping measure in either fortune, it is both useful and necessary to call often to mind the unstable and momentary condition of all things in this age. For the time of this life is short, and the world itself is already hastening to its end, so afflictions by which we are tested here cannot be long-lasting. This should comfort us, that something of them departs with every hour. Indeed, the delay sometimes seems longer to us, but as those who are carried on a ship, whether they sleep or keep watch, eat, drink, play or suffer shipwreck, nevertheless draw nearer to the harbour at every moment, so, whatever the fortune of this life may be, it cannot prevent time from slipping away in continuous motion and bringing us to the end of this life, which cannot fail to be happy and blessed for those who believe in Christ. On the other hand, the joy that springs from the things of this age, however splendid they may be, cannot be lasting or stable, since the whole appearance of this world passes away or vanishes like a bubble. Why? Does some unexpected and grievous calamity not usually follow great successes almost every year? Philip of Macedon once observed this wisely: when he had received news on one very happy day that very many of his affairs had gone most successfully, he raised his hands to heaven and cried out, "O Fortune, for so many and such great blessings, afflict me with some small misfortune." And Polycrates, tyrant of Samos, when everything turned out prosperously for him, even to the point of wonder, threw into the sea of his own accord a ring with a gem of incomparable value, so that by some misfortune he might atone for the calamity that such happy successes seemed to portend. Certainly they were wrong in thinking that human affairs are governed, or rather tossed about, by blind fortune. Yet the alternation of things, which they saw temper prosperity with adversity again and again as if by a perpetual law, nevertheless made them anxious. How much more, therefore, ought Christians, who diligently consider these examples, to take care not to be carried away by immoderate joy, but to be thankful to God in prosperity and rejoice in this alone, while always being ready to bear the cross.

units.la: Tertiò de iis qui emunt sic loquitur: Et qui emunt, sint ut non obtinentes. Sub emptione & possessione universa huius vitæ negotia, contractus, rem domesticam & quæcunque sunt huius ge-neris comprehendit. Ubi observabis, quòd ut uxorem ducere, flere & gaudere permittit, ita non prohibet, quò minus etiam emamus & vendamus. Asseritur ergo hic rerum proprietas contra eos, qui inter Christianos omnia volunt esse communia. Confutantur hi etiam præcepto Dei, quo furtum prohibetur: quia huic locus nullus esse potest, ubi nihil proprium habetur. Quibus adde exempla sanctissimorum hominum veteris & noui Testamenti, qui rem domesticam probè administraverunt, cum aliis contraxerunt, & de suo in alios fuerunt benefici. Præterea cum neque uni homini omnia data sint, neque omnis fert omnia tellus, inter vicinos simul & procul dissitos mercaturæ commercia intercedant oportet. At hic duo imprimis caveri necesse est. Primum, immodica acquirendi cupiditatas, ne (quod Isaias reprehendit) domus domibus & agros agris jungamus, ut qui nos solos putemus in terris habitaturos esse. Alterum est opum fiducia, quæ facit, ut qui maximarum opum possessores videri volunt, ab illis fere ipsi possideantur, & ad Tantali exemplum in mediis undis sitiant. Accidit autem hoc iis, qui solis terrenis & temporariis bonis addicti, de cœlestibus nunquam cogitant. Itaque in contractibus & tota re domestica nunquam nobis excidat, ista omnia ad huius modò vitæ usum pertinere, qui perpetuus, aut saltem diuturnus esse non potest, cum vita ipsa brevis sit: ideoque in cœlestium bonorum spem erecti, quæ in hoc seculo nobis paravimus non magis nostra esse putemus, quàm quæ maximè à nobis aliena sunt. Qui ita animum suum instituerunt, ut neque abutuntur bonis, quæ in hoc seculo possident, neq; eorundem jacturam aut amissionem impatienti ferunt, sed cum Jobo dicunt: Dominus dedit, Dominus abstulit, sit nomen Domini benedictum.
units.tr: Thirdly, he speaks thus of those who buy: "and those who buy, as though not possessing." Under buying and possessing he comprehends all the affairs of this whole life: contracts, household management, and whatever is of this kind. Here you will observe that, just as he permits marrying, weeping and rejoicing, so he does not forbid us to buy and sell. Here, then, the private ownership of goods is affirmed against those who want all things to be held in common among Christians. These people are also refuted by God's commandment forbidding theft, since there can be no place for theft where nothing is held as one's own. To these add the examples of the most holy men of the Old and New Testaments, who administered their households well, made contracts with others, and were beneficial to others from their own goods. Moreover, since not everything has been given to one man, and no land bears everything, trade and commerce must take place between neighbours and between those who live far apart. But two things above all must be guarded against here. The first is immoderate desire for acquiring, lest (as Isaiah reproves) we join house to house and field to field, as if we alone thought we would dwell on the earth. The second is trust in wealth, which makes those who want to seem possessors of very great riches, for the most part, themselves possessed by them, and, like Tantalus, thirst amid the waters. This happens to those who are devoted only to earthly and temporary goods and never think of heavenly things. Therefore, in contracts and in the whole management of the household, let it never slip from our minds that all these things pertain only to the use of this life, which cannot be perpetual, or at least lasting, since life itself is short. Accordingly, lifting our minds to the hope of heavenly goods, let us not think the things we have acquired in this age to be ours any more than things that are most foreign to us. Those who have so disposed their minds that they neither misuse the goods they possess in this age, nor bear their loss or forfeiture impatiently, but say with Job, "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord," are the ones who do this rightly.

units.la: Postremo huius enumerationis membro omnia comprehendit, quæ in tota huius mundi machina nostris usibus serviunt, sic dicens: Et qui utuntur mundo hoc, sint ut non abutentes. Mundi vocabulo omnia huius vitæ subsidia intelligit: quibus ne utamur minimè prohibet, cum in usum hominis ista omnia creata esse Scriptura passim testetur. Faciamus hominem (inquit Deus) ad imaginem nostram, & dominetur in piscem maris, & in volucrem cœli, & in jumentum, & in omnem terram, & in omne reptile, quod reptat super terram. Et David Dei erga humanum genus bonitatem prædicans, inter alia canit: Dominum super opera manuum tuarum constituisti, cuncta eius pedibus subiecisti: Greges & armenta universa, etiam pecudes campi: volucres qui in aere, & pisces qui in aquis versantur, & quicquid per maris itinera transit. Licet ergo nobis salva conscientia, ut rebus à Deo propter nos creatis utamur: at ne iisdem abutamur, Paulus prohibet. Faciunt hoc, primùm, qui in illis spem & fiduciam suam collocant, & ita ex iis sibi Deos fingunt, quæ in ipsorum servitium divinitus sunt destinata. Deinde, qui vitam præter eam quæ hic vivitur, nullam aliam norunt, & proinde gulæ & libidini tam corpore quam animo dediti, hoc unum agunt, ut pessimis cupiditatibus per ea satisfaciant, in quibus Dei beneficentiâ agnoscere, & eius consideratione ad ardentius pietatis studium accendi debebant. Talis olim Sarda-napalus erat, cuius epitaphium eiusmodi apud Strabonem extat:
units.tr: Finally, under this last member of the enumeration he includes all the things in the whole machinery of this world that serve our uses, saying: "And those who use this world, as though not misusing it." By the word "world" he understands all the supports of this life, which he by no means forbids us to use, since Scripture everywhere testifies that all these things were created for man's use. "Let us make man (says God) in our image, and let him have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the bird of the heaven, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth." And David, proclaiming God's goodness towards the human race, sings among other things: "You have set him over the works of your hands; you have put all things under his feet: flocks and herds, all of them, even the beasts of the field; the birds of the air, and the fish that move in the waters, and whatever passes through the paths of the seas." Therefore we may use, with a clear conscience, the things created by God for our sake; but Paul forbids us to misuse them. This is done, first, by those who place their hope and trust in them, and so make for themselves gods out of things that have been divinely appointed for their service. Second, by those who know no life other than the one lived here, and therefore, given over to gluttony and lust both in body and in mind, do only this, to satisfy their worst desires through those things in which they ought to recognise God's beneficence and be kindled, by considering it, to a more ardent zeal for piety. Such was Sardanapalus of old, whose epitaph of this kind is found in Strabo:

units.la: Cum te mortalem noris, præsentibus exple Delitiis animum, post mortem nulla voluptas. Nam fue ego sum pulvis, qui nuper tanta tenebam, Hac habeo quæ edi, quæque exaturata libido
units.tr: Since you know that you are mortal, fill your mind with the pleasures at hand, for after death there is no pleasure. For I, who once held such great things, am now dust. I have what I ate, and what my lust drank in;

units.la: Hausit: at illa manent multa & præclara relictaHoc sapiens vitæ mortalibus est documentum.
units.tr: but the many fine things I left behind are not mine. This is the lesson of wisdom for mortals.

units.la: Huic non immerito Ægyptios veteres adnumerauerunt, qui in conuiuiis lautioribus cranium ho-minis mortui inferre solebant, ut eius aspectu conuiuæ fortis suæ admoniti eo intemperantius voluptati indulgerent, ne quid ipsis & vitæ huius usu decederet. Infelix plane & plus quam demens hominum genus, qui ex eo lasciuiæ occasione arripuerunt, quo ad cœlestia quærenda excitari debebant. At utinam non hodie etiam multi horum similes passim inuenirentur, qui neque huius vitæ neque rerum ad eius conseruationem creatarum usum alium nouerunt, quam ut gulæ & libidini seruiant. Atqui omnes isti mundo hoc non utuntur, sed abutuntur, vel potius diabolo sese turpissima mancipia præbent, qui illis ad proprium ipsorum exitium abutitur. Est ergo ita no-bis considerandæ rerum huius seculi incertitudo, ut simul meminerimus nos in hoc mundo peregrinos esse, patriam vero in cœlis habere, & proinde vitam esse aliam, ad quam nos contendere oportet. Itaque huius mundi bonis sic utamur, ut corpori quidem seruiant, animum vero ijsdem minime patiamur immergi, ne eorum similes simus, quos peregrinæ voluptates apud exteros detinent, adeo ut in illas consumptis & dilapidatis fortunis omnibus in patriam redire neque velint neque possint. Continet ergo locus iste veræ philosophiæ compendium, cuius doctrina omnibus vitæ generibus applicari potest, & quæ singulis viam monstrat, qua ad cœlestis patriæ possessionem possunt peruenire.
units.tr: Not undeservedly the ancient Egyptians are counted among those who used to bring the skull of a dead man into their more lavish banquets, so that, reminded of their own fate by the sight of it, the guests would indulge in pleasure all the more recklessly, lest anything be lost to them of this life and its enjoyment. Truly unhappy, and more than foolish, is that kind of men, who seized as an occasion for wantonness the very thing that ought to have roused them to seek heavenly things. Would that many like them were not found everywhere today, who know no use of this life or of the things created for its preservation except to serve their belly and their lust. Yet all such men do not use this world but abuse it, or rather they hand themselves over as the most vile slaves to the devil, who abuses them to their own destruction. So we must consider the uncertainty of the things of this age in such a way that we also remember that we are strangers in this world, that we have our homeland in heaven, and that therefore there is another life to which we ought to strive. Let us then use the goods of this world so that they serve the body, but never allow the mind to be immersed in them, lest we become like those whom the pleasures of a foreign land hold among strangers, so that, with all their fortunes spent and squandered on those pleasures, they neither wish nor are able to return to their homeland. This passage therefore contains a summary of true philosophy, whose teaching can be applied to every way of life, and which shows each person the way by which they can attain possession of the heavenly homeland.

units.la: Porrò his interpositis, ad tractationem de virginibus & innuptis redit Apostolus & his, quæ hucusque dicta sunt, applicat. Initio autem sui consilij aut sententiæ finem aut scopum præmittit, ne quis eius verba in sensum alienum detorqueat. Velim (inquit) vos absque solicitudine esse. Habent ergo ista protestationis speciem. Quasi diceret: Quæ de Virginitate & cœlibatu dixi & quæ porrò dicturus sum, nolim eo sensu accipi, quasi coniugium damnem, aut homines in eo seruari atque Deo seruire posse negem. Sed instituti aut consilij mei hæc vnica ratio est, quòd vos omni solicitudine & cura liberatos esse cupiam, ut ad vitam piè simul atque tranquillè transigendam expeditiores sitis, & quam minimo labore gravemini. Ita vero animum erga illos amicum & benevolum declarat, & qui procul absit ab impostorum moribus, qui non quid aliis commodum & salutare, sed quid ipsis quæstuosum sit spectare solent: & plerunque ut sibi consulant, oneribus gravissimis eos deprimunt, quorum conscientijs consolationem adhibere debebant. Itaque Apostoli exemplo validissimè confutantur, qui hodie eius doctrina ad impuri sui cœlibatus defensionem abutuntur. Ideo enim virginitatem suasit ille, ut solicitudine pios liberaret, qua tunc propter afflictas persecutiones premebantur, qui coniugio erant astricti. At quia in cœlibatu non potest solicitudinis expers esse, nisi qui donum illud diuinitus accepit, ut nullis immodicæ libidinis cupiditatibus uratur: inepti nimium, imò iniqui sunt illi, cùm ex eo, quod Paulus amicè consulit, præceptum fingant necessarium, ad cuius obseruationem eos etiam obstringunt, quibus nihilmo-lestius accidere poterat, quam quòd inter ardentis carnis desideria remedio diuinitus dato uti prohibentur. Non ergo ut Paulus solicitudine aliquem liberatum volunt, sed potius flammis & curis atque molestissimis turpissimisq; cogitationibus eos enecant, qui in coniugio tranquilli & quieti viuere poterant. Sed de hoc plura alibi dicentur.
units.tr: Having set these things in between, the Apostle returns to his discussion of virgins and the unmarried and applies to them what has been said so far. At the beginning of his counsel, however, he sets out the purpose or aim of his statement, so that no one may twist his words to a foreign sense. "I would have you," he says, "be free from anxiety." These words have the character of a protestation, as if he were saying: "What I have said about virginity and celibacy, and what I am about to say, I would not have taken in such a sense as if I condemned marriage or denied that people can serve God while living in it. The sole reason for my purpose and counsel is this: I want you to be freed from all anxiety and care, so that you may be more free to live a godly and at the same time peaceful life, and so that you may be burdened with as little trouble as possible." In this way he declares his friendly and kindly feeling toward them, far removed from the habits of impostors, who are accustomed to look not to what is useful and wholesome for others but to what is profitable for themselves, and who, mostly to look after their own interests, weigh down with the heaviest burdens those whose consciences they ought rather to comfort. Therefore the Apostle's example powerfully refutes those who today abuse his teaching to defend their impure celibacy. He recommended virginity so as to free the godly from that anxiety by which they were then oppressed on account of the persecutions that afflicted them, those who were bound in marriage. But since in celibacy no one can be free from anxiety unless he has received that gift from God, so that he is not burned by any immoderate desires of lust, those men are exceedingly foolish, indeed unjust, who, from what Paul advises as a kindness, fashion a necessary precept and bind to its observance even those for whom nothing could be more troublesome than being forbidden to use the remedy given by God amid the burning desires of the flesh. So they do not want those freed from anxiety as Paul was, but rather they destroy them with flames, cares, and most troublesome and shameful thoughts, when they might have lived calmly and quietly in marriage. But more about this will be said elsewhere.

units.la: Nunc istud obseruemus, non debere hinc generalem doctrinam peti, ut quis ab omni cura & solicitudine seipsum eximere conetur, & in eo Dei cultum constituere putet. Offenderunt in hoc, qui vitam Monasticam commenti sunt, & qui hanc hodie adhuc sequuntur. Aiunt illi, curas omnes procul relinquendas esse ijs, qui in rerum diuinarum contemplatione cum fructu versari, & Deo veré seruire velint. At dum hoc conantur, ex contemplatoribus vanis ignaui fuci fiunt, & ita viuunt, ut neque sibi ipsis neque vlli alij utiles sint. Quid verò huius vnquam spiritus sanctus docuit? aut cuius Prophetæ vel Apostoli exemplo hoc vitæ genus probare possunt? Quanto rectius Eliphaz ille Themanites dixit, hominem ad laborem nasci, ut auem ad volandum: Sciebat enim Adamo dictum esse: In sudore vultus tui comedes panem tuum. Et cùm in tota rerum natura nihil otiosum esse voluerit sapientissimus ille rerum opifex, stultum fuerit putare, quod hominis otio ille delectetur.
units.tr: Now let us note this: a general doctrine must not be drawn from this, namely that someone should try to free himself from all care and anxiety and think that the worship of God consists in that. Those who devised the monastic life, and those who still follow it today, have gone astray in this. They say that all cares must be left far behind by those who wish to be profitably occupied in the contemplation of divine things and to serve God truly. But while they attempt this, from empty contemplators they become idle drones, and they live in such a way that they are useful neither to themselves nor to anyone else. But what has the Holy Spirit ever taught about this? Or by whose example of a prophet or apostle can this way of life be approved? How much more rightly did that Eliphaz the Temanite say that man is born to labour as a bird is born to fly! For he knew that it had been said to Adam: "In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread." And since that most wise Maker of all things has wished nothing in the whole of nature to be idle, it would be foolish to think that he takes delight in man's idleness.

units.la: Obseruemus ergo huius vitae curas in tres species diduci posse. Prima illicitas habet & noxias, quas proprie possumus folicitudines dicere. Sunt enim cum animi anxietate coniunctae, quae ex diffidentia nascitur, cuius hic etiam effectus est, vt non contenti nostra sorte, circa res illicitas & nihil ad nos pertinentes occupemur, & nisi euentus nostro voto respondeat, aduersus Deum quoque murmurare non vereamur. Hoc curarum genus Christus gentibus tribuit, qui veri Dei cognitione destituuntur, & suos cultores ab his alienissimos esse, in Dei autem prouidentiam reiicere iubet, & (vt Dauid loquitur) sarcinas nostras omnes in illum reijcere. Secunda curas habet necessarias, quas Deus ipse hominibus imponit, & quas in publicas & priuatas distinguere possumus. Publicae enim salutis cura ministri ecclesiarum tenentur, quorum est ita suum munus obire, vt de singulis rationem possint reddere Deo, quos hic ipsorum fidei commisit. Et sane non possunt non vehementer solliciti esse & angi, quoties cogitant, sibi dici a Domino: Sanguinem eorum, qui vobis tacentibus pereunt, de manu vestra requiram. Ideo Paulus, qui se gentium Apostolum nouerat esse constitutum, omnium ecclesiarum curam sibi incumbere dicebat. Eadem est principum conditio, & omnium qui in repub. munus aliquod publicum sustinent. Quia enim hi quoque ποιμὴν λαῶν (vt Graeci poeta verbis vtar) id est pastores populorum sunt, necesse est, vt totius populi & singulorum ciuium curam ad se pertinere cogitent, & ita res atque consilia sua omnia instituant, ne quid aduersus Dei gloriam & publicam salutem designetur. At quam multa cura & labore hic opus erit, vt in officio contineantur, qui quot capita habent tot quoque diuersis sensibus atque cupiditatibus distrahuntur? Sunt deinde curae priuatae, quae ad rem domesticam pertinent, cuius diligentem rationem Paulus haberi vult, vt ethnico & infideli deteriorem esse dicat eum, qui suis non prospicit. Et vt hic imprimis laborent patresfamilias, ipsa rei necessitas exigit. Verissime enim a Graecis dictum est, in vnaquaque domo vnum nodo seruum esse, ipsum nimirum patremfamilias, qui nisi totius familiae curam in se recipiat, & ipse omnibus inseruiat, nihil aliorum omnium labore & industria efficietur. Adde his quod Christiana charitas monet, vt singuli pro aliorum salute solliciti sint, & quae fratribus accidunt aduersa in se transferant, dum illis condolent. Ab his ergo curis si qui omnino liberari volunt, ij simul Christianos se esse negant, & diuinae vocationis iugum excutiunt. Est praeterea curarum genus, quae quod modum transgrediantur vitiosae fiunt. In eo peccant, qui in commisso sibi munere industrij quidem & fideles sunt, de rei autem euentu nimium soliciti, perinde agunt, ac si per ipsos negotium omnino confici oporteat. Hi fere, si ipsi sua frustrentur, Deum quoque incusant, quasi is res suas minus curet, & in his laborantes ope sua deficiant. Solent in hoc saepe peccare optimi quique dum nimio zelo abrepti, iudiciorum Dei causas non satis diligenter expendunt. Et iistos deinde ignaui quidam imitantur, qui cum ipsi officium non faciant, interim intra animos suos discruciantur, & Deum negligentiae accusant. Hic ergo cautione diligenti opus est, vt ipsi quidem quod nostri officij est sedulo faciamus, euentum vero rei permittamus Deo: qui si eam per nos perfectam velit, facile viam inueniet: sin minus, non tamen nos frustra laborabimus, cum apud eum omnibus digna praemia repositae sint, qui opus ipsius fideliter faciunt.
units.tr: Let us note, then, that the cares of this life can be divided into three kinds. The first kind is unlawful and harmful, and these we can properly call anxieties. For they are joined with an anguish of mind, which is born of distrust, and whose effect is also this: that, not content with our lot, we busy ourselves with unlawful matters that have nothing to do with us, and, if the outcome does not match our wish, we are not ashamed to murmur even against God. Christ assigns this kind of care to the Gentiles, who are deprived of the knowledge of the true God, and he bids his own worshippers to be most distant from them and to cast all their burdens upon God's providence, as David says, "to cast all our burdens on him." The second kind has necessary cares, which God himself lays upon men, and which we can divide into public and private. For the care of public welfare is held by the ministers of the churches, whose duty it is to discharge their office in such a way that they can give an account to God for each of those whom he has entrusted to their faith here. And indeed they cannot but be greatly anxious and troubled whenever they think of the Lord saying to them: "I will require the blood of those who perish by your silence at my hand." Therefore Paul, who knew that he had been appointed apostle to the Gentiles, said that the care of all the churches lay upon him. The condition of princes is the same, and of all who bear some public office in the commonwealth. For since these too are "shepherds of the people" (to use the words of the Greek poet), that is, pastors of the people, they must think that the care of the whole people and of each citizen belongs to them, and so they must arrange all their affairs and counsels so that nothing is planned against the glory of God and the public good. But how much care and labour will be needed here to keep in duty those who, having as many heads as they have, are also pulled apart by as many different opinions and desires? Then there are private cares, which pertain to household affairs, and Paul wishes these to be carefully attended to, so that he says that one who does not provide for his own is worse than a heathen and an unbeliever. And the very necessity of the matter demands that heads of households especially labour at this. For it has been most truly said by the Greeks that in every house the one slave bound by a knot is the master of the household himself; unless he takes upon himself the care of the whole family and serves all of them himself, nothing will be accomplished by the labour and diligence of all the others. Add to these what Christian charity advises: that each should be anxious for the salvation of others, and by sympathizing with his brothers, take upon himself the adversities that befall them. Therefore, if anyone wishes to be entirely freed from these cares, he at the same time denies that he is a Christian and throws off the yoke of divine calling. There is, moreover, a kind of care which becomes faulty because it exceeds its measure. Those sin in this who, though diligent and faithful in the duty committed to them, are too anxious about the outcome of the matter, and act as if the whole business had to be completed through them alone. Such people, if their own efforts are frustrated, usually blame God as well, as if he cared little for their affairs and failed to help them in their labours. Very often the best people sin in this, when, carried away by excessive zeal, they do not weigh the reasons for God's judgments carefully enough. And some lazy people imitate them, who, although they do not perform their own duty, are nevertheless tormented in their minds and accuse God of negligence. Here, therefore, careful caution is needed, so that we diligently do what belongs to our duty, and leave the outcome of the matter to God. If he wishes it to be brought to completion through us, he will easily find a way; if not, we shall not labour in vain, since rewards worthy of all are laid up with him for those who faithfully do his work.

units.la: Quia autem difficillimum est in his modum tenere, Paulus ista ad suum institutum accommodans, se hoc cupere dicit, vt cum coniugium curis necessariis refertum fit, ipsi his liberentur, vt ad rerum caelestium studia expeditiores sint. Et mox hoc ipsum diligenti collatione explicat, in qua tam de viris quam de virginibus aut mulieribus innuptis disserit. Et de viris quidem sic loquitur: Qui caelebs est, curat ea quae sunt Domini, id est, cum liber sit a cura rei domesticae & educationis liberorum, se totum ijs impendere potest, quae ad Dei cultum pertinent, vt huic vni placeat. At qui vxorem ducit, curat ea quae sunt mundi, quomodo placiturus sit vxori. Mundi vocabulum autem non in malam partem hic vsurpatur, quo sensu fere in scripturis sumitur, quando de huius saeculi filijs & eorum studijs sermo est: sed ea intelligit Paulus, quae ad praesentis vitae conditionem, ad victum denique & familiae atque liberorum sustentationem pertinent, circa quae necessario occupari oportet omnes eos, qui in coniugio viuunt. Quibus curis haec quoque accedit, quod vxoris ingenium probe obseruari necesse est, vt ea commodiori vti possit. Ne autem haec cura ad solos viros pertinere putaretur, ad alterum quoque sexum transit, dicens: Discretae sunt ea quae est uxor, & ea quae est virgo, id est, inter virginem & nuptam siue maritatam magnum discrimen est. Nam quae innupta est, curat ea quae sunt Domini, ut sit sancta cum corpore tum spiritu, id est, ut quanta quanta est, tota Deo consecrata sit, & tam corpus quam animum purum atque castum seruet, neque ullis huius saeculi studijs contaminetur. Quae vero nupta est, curat ea quae sunt mundi, quomodo placitura sit viro. Haec autem omnia in eum finem dicuntur, ut ostendat virginitatem & caelibatum non per se laudem maiorem quam coniugium mereri, sed ideo, quod ij, quibus datum est, ut absque coniugij usu honeste & caste viuant, multis curis & negotijs seipsos exonerent, quibus coniuges non sine molestia distinentur.
units.tr: Since it is very difficult to keep to the right measure in these matters, Paul, adapting these words to his own purpose, says that he wishes this: that when marriage is filled with necessary cares, believers may be freed from them and so be less encumbered for the pursuits of heavenly things. Soon he explains this very point by a careful comparison, in which he discusses both men and virgins or unmarried women. And concerning men he speaks thus: He who is unmarried cares for the things of the Lord. That is, since he is free from the care of domestic affairs and the upbringing of children, he can devote himself wholly to those things which pertain to the worship of God, so that he may please this one alone. But he who takes a wife cares for the things of the world, how he may please his wife. The word "world" is not used here in a bad sense, as it generally is in Scripture when speaking of the sons of this age and their pursuits. Paul means rather those things which pertain to the condition of the present life: food and clothing, and the support of family and children, with which all who live in marriage must necessarily be occupied. To these cares is added that the disposition of the wife must be carefully observed, so that she may be used more conveniently. Lest this care be thought to belong only to men, he passes to the other sex, saying: The wife and the virgin differ. That is, there is a great difference between a virgin and a married or wedded woman. For she who is unmarried cares for the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy both in body and spirit: that is, that whatever she is, she be wholly consecrated to God, and keep both body and mind pure and chaste, and not be defiled by any pursuits of this age. But she who is married cares for the things of the world, how she may please her husband. All these things are said with this aim: that he shows virginity and celibacy do not in themselves merit greater praise than marriage. Rather, those to whom it is given to live honourably and chastely without the use of marriage relieve themselves of many cares and business, by which married people are not without trouble distracted.

units.la: Itaque minime audiendi sunt, qui ex Pauli verbis colligere volunt, eos qui in coniugio viuunt, Deo placere non posse, neque ea curare quae ad regnum Dei pertinent. Totus enim locus ex collatione dependet, & caelibes atque inuptas plus otij & maiorem facultatem habere docet, ut toti Deo consecrati sint, eo quod nullis aliis curis auocentur. Neque tamen hoc semper verum est, quando constat non paucos esse, qui etsi a coniugio abstineant, tamen & domum administrent, & huius saeculi curis implicentur, ita denique propter opes seipsos discrutient atque fatigent, ut non aliam ob causam a coniugio sibi temperare videri possint, quam ut aut carnis voluptati liberius indulgeant, aut quaestum maiorem faciant, dum nulla familia grauantur. E contra vero coniuges est videre, qui a Deo constanti fide pendent, huic seruiunt, & rem domesticam sic curant, ut interea adeo non negligant ea, quae ad regnum Dei pertinent, ut hoc ipso illud quam maxime promouebant, dum & sibi matrimonio iunctos Christo lucrifaciunt, & liberos sancte educant, & domi suae quasi ecclesiam habent priuatam, quam ceu antistites quidam summa cum religione gubernant. Et huc referri debet, quod supra maritum infidelem in fideli uxore, & uxorem infidelem in marito fideli aut Christiano sanctificatam esse audiuimus. Imprimis autem huc sanctorum patrum exempla pertinent, qui etsi coniuges essent, a Deo tamen uocati sunt, ut eorum opera in regno suo longe lateq; propagando uterentur: & eorum uxores Petrus sanctas uocat, easque Christianas foeminas imitandas proponit. Quid vero de Hesthera dicemus, quae & Regi marito, eoq; luxu & intemperantia infami, placuit, & simul Deo gratissimum obsequium praebuit, qui eius opera totam ecclesiam conseruare dignatus est? Neque peccat mox, quae marito placere cupit: imo ut id fiat, omnino necesse est, modo certa cum ratione fiat: ut nimirum per ea placere studeas, quae salua pietate fieri possunt, & coniugem una tecum seruare coneris. Sunt haec propter eos diligentius obseruanda, qui quaecunque in scripturis de Virginitate & caelibatu dicuntur, in eum sensum detorquent, ut coniugium Deo displicere, & idem aeternae saluti inimicum esse euincant.
units.tr: Therefore those who wish to gather from Paul's words that those who live in marriage cannot please God, nor care for the things that pertain to the kingdom of God, are by no means to be heard. For the whole passage depends on the comparison, and teaches that the unmarried and virgins have more leisure and greater opportunity to be wholly consecrated to God, because they are not drawn away by other cares. Yet this is not always true, since it is plain that there are not a few who, although they abstain from marriage, nevertheless manage a household and are entangled in the cares of this age. So they torment and wear themselves out on account of wealth, and can seem to abstain from marriage for no other reason than that they may indulge more freely in the pleasures of the flesh, or make greater gain, being burdened by no family. On the contrary, one may see married people who depend on God with steadfast faith, serve him, and manage their domestic affairs in such a way that they do not neglect the things that pertain to the kingdom of God. Rather, by this very thing they promote it most of all: they win for Christ the spouses joined to them, bring up their children holily, and have in their own home, as it were, a private church, which they govern with the greatest devotion, like certain bishops. To this must be referred what we heard above, that the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife in the believing or Christian husband. Above all, to this belong the examples of the holy Fathers, who, although they were married, were nevertheless called by God so that their work might be used in propagating his kingdom far and wide. Peter calls their wives holy and sets before Christian women that they should imitate them. But what shall we say of Esther, who pleased her husband the king, infamous for his luxury and intemperance, and at the same time offered most acceptable obedience to God, who deigned to preserve the whole Church through her work? Nor does she sin who desires to please her husband. Indeed, for this to be done it is altogether necessary, provided it is done with sound reason: namely, that you strive to please by those means which can be employed while piety is preserved, and that you endeavour to keep your wife along with yourself. These things must be observed more carefully on account of those who turn everything said in Scripture about virginity and celibacy in such a sense as to prove that marriage displeases God and is hostile to eternal salvation.

units.la: Obseruandum praeterea, Virginitatem, quae Domino probatur, non in eo consistere, ut a coniugio puella abstineat, sed alia duo magis necessaria requiri: Vnum, ut corpore simul & spiritu sancta sit. Nam ut alibi diximus, non multum in vera pietate adhuc profecerunt, quae ut corpus a libidine impollutum seruent, animum tamen illicitis cupiditatibus ardere & per vanissimas cogitationes vagari patiuntur. At quomodo de corporis quoque sanctimonia gloriari poterunt, quae illud immodico ornatu & fuco quasi prostituunt, adhaec incessu, gestu & vagis oculorum nutibus amatores alliciunt? Quis item sanctas & Deo consecratas dixerit, quae linguam & auris impudicis narrationibus & obscaenis cantilenis accommodant? Adde his vagas illas & procaces, quae domi subsistere nesciunt, per fora & theatra discurrunt, ex ludis parum honestis voluptatem capiunt, coniuiijs virorum intersunt, ea denique faciunt & loquuntur interdum, quorum coniuges honestas puderet. Abhis ergo omnibus abstineant oportet, quae cum corpore tum spiritu sanctae esse cupiunt. Alterum est, ut finem studiorum hunc unum sibi proponant, ut Domino placere possint. Id vero nunquam fiet, nisi CHRISTVM IESVM fide vera apprehendant, in quo uno pater nobis placatus est. Haec si ad eos transferas, qui in Papatu ex utroque sexu virginitatis & castitatis voto sese venditant, omnia ab his longe diuersa videbis. Quid enim Monachis auarius & rapacius? Quae item Heroina, quantumuis generosa & opulenta, tanto otio abundat & tot delitijs diffluit, quot in plerisque monialium monasterijs licet inuenire? Taceo nunc formicationes occultas, adulteria, abortus veneficio quaesitos, infantum recens natorum crudeles cædes, & infinita alia Christianis auribus indigna, & quæ animus cogitare horret. Quòd si quæ in illa schola vitam honestius instituunt, in ignavo tamen otio contabescunt, & simul circa superstitiones occupantur, quæ cùm illas à Christo avocent, Deo placere nequaquam possunt. Neminem ergo exempla ista & hypocritarum magnifici sermones decipiant, ut in eo vitæ genere pietatem & salutem consistere putet: sed singuli in suam vocationem intenti sint, & brevi huius vitæ curriculo bene utantur, imprimis autem Deo probari studeant per veram fidem in Filium eius unigenitum, IESUM CHRISTUM, Dominum nostrum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, it is to be observed that the virginity which is approved by the Lord does not consist in this, that a girl abstains from marriage. Rather, two other and more necessary things are required. The first is that she be holy in both body and spirit. For, as we have said elsewhere, those who keep the body undefiled by lust, yet allow their soul to burn with unlawful desires and wander through the most vain thoughts, have not yet made much progress in true piety. But how will those women be able to boast of holiness of body too, who by immoderate ornament and paint practically prostitute it, and who moreover entice lovers by their gait, gestures and wandering nods of the eyes? Who likewise would call holy and consecrated to God those who lend their tongues and ears to impure stories and obscene songs? Add to these those wanton and bold women who cannot stay at home, run about through marketplaces and theatres, take pleasure in rather dishonourable games, attend men's banquets, and finally do and sometimes say things at which honourable wives would blush. From all these things, therefore, those who wish to be holy in both body and spirit must abstain. The second is that they set before themselves this one aim of their pursuits: that they may be able to please the Lord. This will never happen unless they lay hold of CHRIST JESUS by true faith, in whom alone the Father has been appeased toward us. If you transfer these things to those who in Papacy sell themselves from both sexes by a vow of virginity and chastity, you will see everything very different. For what is more greedy and rapacious than the monks? Likewise, what noblewoman, however generous and wealthy, abounds with such leisure and flows with so many delights as can be found in most nunneries? I now pass over secret fornications, adulteries, abortions sought by poisoning, the cruel murders of newborn infants, and countless other things unworthy of Christian ears, which the mind shudders to think of. But if any in that school conduct their life more honourably, they still waste away in idle leisure, and at the same time are occupied with superstitions which, since they call them away from Christ, can by no means please God. Let therefore neither these examples nor the magnificent speeches of hypocrites deceive anyone into thinking that piety and salvation consist in that way of life. Rather, let each attend to his own calling and make good use of the brief course of this life, and above all study to be approved by God through true faith in his only-begotten Son, JESUS CHRIST our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXIX.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXIX.

units.la: Hoc autem dico vestri commodi gratiâ, non ut laqueum vobis injiciam: sed ut decenter & apte adhærescatis Domino absque ulla distractione. Cæterum si quis se aliquid non decens in virginem suam committere putat, si florem ætatis excedat, & ita debet fieri, quod vult faciat, non peccat: iungatur matrimonio. Qui vero stat firmus in corde, nec adigitur necessitate, sed in potestate habet propriam voluntatem, & hoc decreuit in corde suo, ut servet suam virginem, bene facit. Itaque qui dat nuptum, bene facit: qui vero non dat nuptum, melius facit. Uxor alligata est lege, quàm diu vivit vir ipsius: quod si obdormierit vir ipsius, libera est ad cui velit nubendum: tantum in Domino. Sed beatior est, si ita maneat, secundum meam sententiam: Puto autem me quoq; Spiritum Dei habere.
units.tr: I say this for your good, not to throw a noose over you, but so that you may cling to the Lord becomingly and fittingly, without any distraction. Still, if anyone thinks he is behaving unseemly toward his virgin daughter, if she is past the bloom of youth and it ought to be done, let him do what he wishes; he does not sin, let them marry. But whoever stands firm in his heart, is under no compulsion but has his own will in his power, and has decided in his heart to keep his virgin daughter, he does well. So whoever gives her in marriage does well, but whoever does not give her in marriage does better. A wife is bound by law as long as her husband lives; but if her husband falls asleep, she is free to marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. Yet she is happier if she remains so, in my judgment; and I think that I too have the Spirit of God.

units.la: Quoniam Apostoli se à CHRISTO IESU in eum finem electos esse sciebant, ut ecclesiæ eius servirent, & huius membra singula in officio continerent: admodum diligenter cavent, ne eos aliquo novarum & superstitiosarum traditionū iugo gravent, quos ille in libertatem asseruit, & sibi uni consecratos esse vult. Cur enim hominum statutis obstringantur, quos à Legis etiam veteris disciplina ille iampridem exemit? Hoc ipsum ergo in præsenti tractatione Paulus diligenter observat, in qua de vero matrimonij usu, coniugum officijs, de cœlibatu item & virginitate sic disserit, ut subinde ijs occurrat, qui aliquam erroris aut superstitionis occasionem inde captare poterant. Quæ etiam causa est, quòd cum nuper coniugij & cœlibatus collationem fecif-set, in qua huius quidem commoda & illius molestias atque curas diserte exposuit, nunc doctri-nam hanc omnem prudenter moderatur & temperat, docens nimirum, quid in utroq; statu præ-cipuè observari debeat.
units.tr: Since the Apostles knew that they had been chosen by Christ Jesus for this end, to serve his Church and to keep each of its members in their duty, they take great care not to burden with the yoke of any new and superstitious traditions those whom he set free and wishes to be consecrated to himself alone. For why should they be bound by human statutes whom he has long since released even from the discipline of the old Law? Paul therefore observes this carefully in the present discourse, in which he treats the true use of marriage, the duties of spouses, and likewise celibacy and virginity, in such a way that he continually meets those who might seize on some occasion of error or superstition from them. This is also the reason why, having recently made a comparison of marriage and celibacy, in which he clearly set out the advantages of the one and the troubles and cares of the other, he now prudently moderates and tempers all this teaching, namely by showing what ought to be especially observed in each state.

units.la: Et primò quidem consilij sui finem aut scopum indicat, & ne quis ex ijs, quæ nuper dicta sunt, cum Christi discipulis inferret: Si ita se habet causa hominis cum muliere, non confert con-trahere matrimonium, sic scribit: Hoc autem dico vestri commodi gratia, id est, ut quid vobis commodissimum sit offendam, non ut laqueum vobis injiciam, &c. Laqueum dicit doctrinam, quæ vel ad coniugium omnes rigidè cogit, vel ad cœlibatum aut virginitatem aliquos temere obstringit. Rectè autem laqueum vocat, quia quàm primùm hic absoluta necessitas statuitur, mox irretiuntur hominum conscientiæ, & quàm Christus nobis acquisiuit libertas aufertur. Sensus ergo verborum est, Se non aliud velle, quàm ut intelligant unicuique liberum esse, ut vel matrimonio iungatur, vel cœlebs maneat. Quia enim neque matrimonium neque cœlibatus ex eorum numero est, in quibus regnum Dei & hominis salus æterna consistit, temerarium fuerit & iniquum legem præscribere, ad cuius observationem omnes absque discrimine obstringi debeant. Nam ut ad cœlibatum nemo cogi debet, qui vel dono continentiæ destituitur, vel alias ob causas non potest solitarius vivere: ita neque matrimonium ceu necessarium illis debet obtrudi, qui & castè vivunt, & nulla alia causa graviori ad illud adiguntur. Sua ergo libertas cuique integra maneat, ne quod ad huius vitæ præsentis commoditatem nobis à Deo datum est, laqueus fiat, quo hominum conscientiae irretitae à regno Dei abstrahantur. Hoc autem vnicè omnes curent, vt decenter & apte adhaerescant Domino absque vlla distractione.
units.tr: First he indicates the purpose or aim of his counsel, and so that no one might draw from what was said recently the conclusion that, as the Lord's disciples had said, "if the case of a man with a woman is such, it is not good to marry," he writes thus: "I say this for your good," that is, so that I may consult what is most advantageous for you, "not to throw a noose over you," and so on. He calls a noose any teaching that either compels everyone rigidly to marriage or rashly binds some to celibacy or virginity. He rightly calls it a noose, because as soon as such an absolute necessity is laid down, men's consciences are at once entangled and the freedom that Christ has won for us is taken away. The sense of his words is therefore that he wishes nothing else than that they understand it to be free for each person either to marry or to remain single. For since neither marriage nor celibacy belongs to those things in which the kingdom of God and the eternal salvation of man consist, it would be rash and unjust to prescribe a law to which all without distinction must be bound. For just as no one ought to be forced into celibacy who lacks the gift of continence or who for other reasons cannot live alone, so neither ought marriage to be imposed as if necessary upon those who live chastely and are not driven to it by any weightier cause. Let each one's liberty therefore remain whole, so that what God has given for the convenience of this present life does not become a noose by which the entangled consciences of men are drawn away from the kingdom of God. Let all take care of this one thing alone: that they cling to the Lord becomingly and fittingly, without any distraction.

units.la: Sunt haec Apostoli verba diligenti consideratione dignissima. Admonent enim, quis in ecclesia omnium doctrinarum aut ordinationum siue canonum finis esse debeat: Nimirum credentium utilitas, quam alibi aedificationem dicit. In hac vt ante omnia Christo fundamento opus esset, cui nos inniti atque vniri oportet, ita etiam in spiritus libertate eidem seruire eos oportet, qui à salute excidere nolunt. Itaque diligenter cauere omnes debent, ne qui suis traditionibus aut statutis libertatem Christianorum in arctum redigant, & animos illaqueent. Si enim Apostoli non alia tradere debuerunt, quam quae à Christo acceperant, inexcusabilis temeritas fuerit, si qui hodie sibi ipsis plus permittere velint. At quia impostores quoque sua commenta utilitatis & publicae aedificationis nomine venditare solent, Paulus rem diligentius definit, & quae nam commoditas aut utilitas spectari debeat, docet. Haec nimirum, vt decenter & apte adhaerescamus Domino absque vlla distractione. Vt enim Deus summum bonum & omnis boni fons est, sic in eo omnis salus nostra consistit, vt huic coniuncti & vniti simus. Admonet de hoc Deus, quando Abrahamo dicebat: Ego sum El Schadai, id est: Deus omnipotens & ad omnia sufficiens, ambula coram me. Quod ipsum in Decalogi quoque initio repetitur. Et ideo Dauid recte dixit: Mihi autem Domino adhaerere bonum est, & ponere in Domino Deo spem meam. Quibus illud Petri consentit, qui interrogatus à Christo, num ipsi quoque deficere & eum relinquere vellent, respondit: Domine, ad quem ibimus? tu verba vitae aeternae habes. Vt autem illi adhaerescamus, duobus omnino opus est. Primò, vt decenter & apte id fiat. Quia enim aedificio & corpori confertur ecclesia, vt partes singulae inter se apte cohaereant necesse esse[?] est. Singuli ergo sic Christo adhaereant, vt suam vocationem sedulò sequantur, cui eos Deus destinauit. Altero, vt fide constanti armati simus, quae nos in omni tentatione superiores faciat, ne vllis periculorum terroribus aut temporarij alicuius commodi illecebris nos ab illo diuelli patiamur. Id vero cum ab omnis loci & ordinis hominibus fieri possit, non debet alicuius conscientia grauari propter externam vitae conditionem, quae per se licita & sancta est. Nam in CHRISTO IESV (vt alibi Apostolus monet) non est vir aut foemina, non liber aut seruus, non diues aut pauper, & proinde etiam non coniunx aut caelebs siue virgo. Et constat Christum, cum in terris ageret, ex omni hominum genere discipulos habuisse, & eiusdem Apostolos neminem postea temere coegisse, vt vitae genus mutaret. Et vt in praesenti causa insistamus[?], quamuis caelibatus à curis rei domesticae & infinitis aliis molestijs liberior sit, sunt tamen quibus magis profuerit coniugium, eo quod sine hoc neque illicitis cupiditatibus resistere, neque rem domesticam commodè instituere possint. Itaque quoad vitae conditionem nulla regula certa praescribi potest, ad quam omnes obstringantur: sed in hoc intenti sint ecclesiarum ministri, vt & coniuges & caelibes, principes & subditi, heri & serui, diuites & pauperes, viri, foeminae, iuuenes, senes, CHRISTVM IESVM sua salutis fundamentum agnoscant, ab hoc vno pendeant, stationem suam probè tueantur, & absque omni distractione illi adhaerescant.
units.tr: These words of the Apostle are most worthy of careful consideration. For they remind us what the end of all teachings, ordinances or canons in the Church ought to be: namely the benefit of believers, which elsewhere he calls edification. In this, just as Christ must be the foundation above all, on which we ought to rest and be united, so also in the liberty of the Spirit those who do not wish to fall from salvation ought to serve him. Therefore all must take care not to reduce the liberty of Christians to narrow limits by their own traditions or statutes, and not to ensnare souls. For if the Apostles ought to hand down nothing but what they had received from Christ, it would be inexcusable recklessness if anyone today wished to permit himself more. But since impostors too are wont to peddle their own inventions under the name of usefulness and public edification, Paul defines the matter more carefully and teaches what advantage or benefit ought to be looked to. This, namely, that we cling to the Lord becomingly and fittingly, without any distraction. For as God is the highest good and the fountain of all good, so all our salvation consists in this, that we be joined and united to him. God admonishes us of this when he said to Abraham: "I am El Shaddai," that is, "God Almighty and sufficient for all things; walk before me." The same thing is repeated at the very beginning of the Decalogue. Therefore David rightly said: "But it is good for me to cling to the Lord, and to place my hope in the Lord God." To these words Peter's agrees, who, when Christ asked whether they too wished to fall away and leave him, answered: "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life." Now to cling to him, two things are altogether needed. First, that it be done becomingly and fittingly. For since the Church is compared to a building and a body, it is necessary that the individual parts cohere fittingly with one another. Let each therefore cling to Christ in such a way that he diligently follows the calling to which God has assigned him. Second, that we be armed with a steadfast faith, which makes us superior in every temptation, so that we never allow ourselves to be torn away from him by terrors of dangers or by the allurements of some temporary advantage. Since this can be done by men of every place and rank, no one's conscience ought to be burdened on account of his external condition of life, which in itself is lawful and holy. For in Christ Jesus (as the Apostle elsewhere warns) there is neither male nor female, neither free nor slave, neither rich nor poor, and therefore neither married nor single nor virgin. And it is established that Christ, while he dwelt on earth, had disciples from every kind of man, and that his Apostles afterwards rashly compelled no one to change his way of life. And, to keep to the present matter, although celibacy is freer from the cares of domestic affairs and from countless other troubles, there are still those for whom marriage has been more profitable, because without it they can neither resist unlawful desires nor order their household affairs suitably. Therefore as regards the condition of life no fixed rule can be prescribed to which all are bound; but the ministers of the churches should see to this, that spouses and the unmarried, princes and subjects, masters and servants, rich and poor, men, women, young and old, all acknowledge Christ Jesus as the foundation of their salvation, depend on him alone, faithfully keep their own station, and cling to him without any distraction.

units.la: Caeterum quia Paulus hucusque de iis dixerat, qui cum sui iuris sint, vitam prout ipsis commodissimum videtur, instituere possunt, nouus scrupulus parentes exercere poterat, ne videlicet liberis suis male consulerent, si coniugij vinculo illos curarent obstringi, quod curis & laboribus plurimis refertum esse videbant. Nunc ergo ad illos transit, & quid ipsis facto opus sit docet. Doctrinae huius summa est, curandum ipsis esse, ne vel in periculum eos adducant, quibus donum continentiae negatum est, vel ad coniugium temere cogant eos, qui ab illo abhorrent, & sine eo caste viuere possunt. Habet ergo admonitio ista partes duas. Primam his verbis comprehendit: Si quis se aliquid non decens in virginem suam committere putat, si florem aetatis excedat, & ita debet fieri, quod vult faciat, non peccat, iungantur matrimonio. Pertinent ista ad eos, qui se in filias suas peccare putabant, si eas nuptum darent, vbi coniugij molestijs implicabantur. Illorum enim conscientijs consulit, & eos nequaquam peccare dicit, siquidem id certo & maturo consilio faciant, & ideo de duobus admonet. Primum, si quis (ait) se aliquid non decens in virginem suam committere putat, si florem aetatis excedat. Quibus verbis videre iubet, ne quid praeter officium faciant, si rem diutius differant, quàm filiarum ætas postulare videatur. Vt enim vulgò ridentur ætatis proiectioris virgines, ita multis aliis nominibus suspectæ sunt, quasi aut ad rem domesticam inutiles sint, aut superbia tumidæ procos omnes spernant, aut propter vitia latentia nullos maritos inueniant. Quis verò dixerit parentes officij sui meminisse, si filias ludibrijs & suspicionibus eiusmodi exponant? Adde hìs, quòd frequenter auaritia peccatur, quando filias ideo elocare nolunt, ne vel hæreditatem maternam reddere, vel ex suo dotem dare cogantur. Quicquid ergo huius accidit, parentum est curare, ne quam liberis suis iniuriam faciant. Deinde alterum adijcit: Et si ita debet fieri. Id verò ad ingenium & mores filiarum & filiorum referri debet: vt nimirum hos diligenter obseruent, neq; negligant à Deo datum remedium, si ad libidinem procliuiores esse sentiant. Neq; hic illorum verbis temere fides haberi debet, quia sæpe pudor obstat, ne quod animo suo cupiunt, eloqui ausint. Ideo qui prudentiores sunt, ij sæpe aut matres aut eos, quos suis familiaribus esse nouerunt, subornare solent, vt illorum voluntatem expiscentur. Qui verò non obscuris indicijs deprehendunt, tam proprio ipsorum quàm liberorum honori melius consuli, si de coniugio ho-nesto illis proficiant, ijs omnino licere dicit Paulus, vt illud faciant, neq; hic alicuius culpæ peri-culum esse timendum. Nam talis (inquit) non peccat. Et paulò post: Qui dat nuptum, bene facit. Et recte quidem hoc dicitur, quando non aliud fit, quàm quod Deus fieri voluit, & quod sanctissi-mos quosq; iam inde à prima rerum origine fecisse constat. Nam vt multos alios omittamus, quis nescit, quanto studio & industria Abrahamus olim fit vsus, vt Isaaco vxorem se dignam inueni-ret? Nec enim illi satis fuit, seruum, cuius opera vti decreuerat, diligenter admonuisse, sed eundem iureiurando obstringendum esse putauit, ne quid secus quam ipse mandabat faceret. Similem dili-gentiam postea Isaacum & Rebeccam adhibuisse legimus, dum Iacobo filio prospectum voluerunt. Tam ergo abesse, vt peccent qui vel filijs vxores desponderent, vel filias viris elocarent, vt potius peccaturi fuerint, si iubente hoc necessitate, ipsi negligentiores sese præbeant.
units.tr: But since Paul had hitherto spoken of those who, being their own masters, can order their life as seems most convenient to them, a new scruple could trouble parents, namely that they might not be dealing well with their children if they bound them with the bond of marriage, which they saw to be full of many cares and labours. So now he passes to those parents and teaches what needs to be done for them. The sum of this teaching is that they must take care not to bring into danger those to whom the gift of continence has been denied, nor rashly to compel into marriage those who shrink from it and can live chastely without it. This admonition therefore has two parts. The first he comprises in these words: "If anyone thinks he is behaving unseemly toward his virgin daughter, if she is past the bloom of youth and it ought to be done, let him do what he wishes; he does not sin, let them marry." These words pertain to those who thought they were sinning against their daughters if they gave them in marriage, when they would be entangled in the troubles of wedlock. For he takes thought for their consciences and says that they by no means sin, provided they act with certain and mature counsel; and so he gives advice on two points. The first is: "If anyone thinks he is behaving unseemly toward his virgin daughter, if she is past the bloom of youth." By these words he bids them see to it that they do nothing beyond their duty if they put off the matter longer than the age of their daughters seems to require. For just as virgins past their prime are commonly laughed at, so they are suspected on many other grounds: either as useless for household affairs, or as puffed up with pride so that they spurn all suitors, or as finding no husbands because of hidden faults. But who would say that parents remember their duty if they expose their daughters to such mockery and suspicion? Add to this that sin is often committed through avarice, when they are unwilling to marry off their daughters so that they will not be forced to hand back their mother's inheritance or to give a dowry from their own means. Whatever of this happens, it is the duty of parents to take care that they do no injury to their children. Then he adds the other point: "and it ought to be done." This must be referred to the character and morals of daughters and sons, namely that parents should observe them carefully and not neglect the remedy given by God, if they perceive them to be more inclined to lust. Nor should their words be lightly believed here, because shame often stands in the way, so that they dare not express what they desire in their hearts. Therefore the wiser parents often are wont to employ either the mothers or those whom they know to be their familiars, so that they may draw out the children's wishes. But those who detect it from unclear signs, that it is better for the honour both of themselves and of their children to be provided for by an honourable marriage, Paul says that they are altogether permitted to do so, and that there is no danger of any fault to be feared here. For such a one (he says) does not sin. And a little later: "He who gives her in marriage does well." And this is rightly said when nothing else is done than what God wished to be done, and what the most holy men from the very origin of things are known to have done. For, to omit many others, who does not know with what zeal and diligence Abraham once acted, so that he might find a wife worthy for Isaac? Indeed it was not enough for him to instruct diligently the servant by whose work he had decided to use, but he thought that the same man must be bound by an oath, so that he would do nothing otherwise than he himself commanded. We read that Isaac and Rebekah afterwards showed similar diligence when they wished to provide for their son Jacob. So far is it from being sinful for those who betroth wives to their sons, or give daughters to husbands, that rather those would be the ones who sin if, when necessity calls for it, they showed themselves too negligent.

units.la: At hic simul filij & filiæ obseruent, stabiliri hoc loco parentum in suos liberos potestatem, quæ vt in aliis rebus magna est, ita imprimis hic summam authoritatem habet, vbi de coniugio agi-tur. Etenim si illi liberis suis prospicere debent, vicissim horum fuerit illis obedire, ne horum consilia atq; voluntatem sua libidine & præcipiti audacia præuertant. Semper enim rata apud eos esse debet Lex Dei, qua parentes in honore & pretio habere iubentur. Et quam magna sit illorum in filios & filias authoritas vel ex eo patet, quòd vota illis inscijs & inconsultis facta rescindere possunt. Cùm ergo Deus ipse suo (vt sic loquar) iure cedere dignetur, neq; ratum esse velit quod ipsi pro promittitur, si aliter parentes statuant, nimium profectò temerarij & impij censeri debent, qui iuuenilia sua desideria illorum arbitrio nolunt subijcere. Nec est quod ætatem aliquis prætexat. Nec enim aliqua ætas est, quæ naturæ legibus stabilitam parentum authoritatem violare debeat. Et Paulus hoc loco de virginibus, quæ ætatis florem & nubiles annos iam excesserunt, loquitur, & nihilominus illas quoque parentum imperio subijcit, dum non quid ipsæ facere, sed quid illi de ipsis statuere debeant, docet. Obseruarunt hoc olim probè legum ciuilium authores, qui coniugia, quæ absque parentum consilio & consensu contrahuntur, irrita esse voluerunt, nisi quæ grauior causa illa rata esse iubeat. At ne quid inuiolatum relinqueret Pontificum audacia, hic quoque leges nouas induxerunt, quibus clandestina quoque coniugia, inuitis parentibus firma & rata manent. Quod quid aliud est, quàm liberorum libidini parentes subijcere, & authoritatem, qua illos Deus armauit in homines nihili & publica infamia dignos transferre, qui plerunq; ventris & gulæ gra-tia incautos iuuenes & teneras puellas suis lenocinijs seducunt, vt proprijs parentibus minus obtemperent? Prætexunt illi Sacramenti dignitatem, quæ tanta sit, vt sub eius religione facta pro-missio, rescindi nullo modo possit. Sed friuolum esse, quod de matrimonij Sacramento garriunt, a-libi demonstrauimus. Imò vt demus matrimonium inter Sacramenta referri debere, nomen tamen hoc non merebitur, nisi legitimè contractum fuerit: & vt Cœnam Domini Corinthios edisse Paulus negat, eò quòd à prima institutione desciuissent: ita nos inter eos matrimonium legiti-mum coire negabimus, qui matrimonij leges à Deo latas non obseruant. Quàm egregium ergò Sacramentum fuerit, quo & Lex Dei labefactatur, & honestas publica aboletur, & ius natü-ræ euertitur?
units.tr: Let sons and daughters also note here that the power of parents over their children is established in this passage. As it is great in other matters, so it carries the greatest authority here, where marriage is concerned. For if parents ought to provide for their children, it is in turn the children's part to obey them, so that they do not override their parents' counsel and will by their own lust and rash boldness. For God's law must always be regarded as binding among them, the law by which parents are commanded to be held in honour and esteem. And how great the authority of parents over sons and daughters is can be seen from the fact that they may annul vows made without their knowledge and consultation. Since God himself, so to speak, deigns to yield his own right, and does not wish a promise to stand if parents decide otherwise, those who refuse to subject their youthful desires to their parents' judgment must surely be considered excessively rash and impious. Nor is there any point in someone pleading his age. For there is no age that ought to violate the authority of parents, which is established by the laws of nature. Paul speaks here of virgins who have passed the bloom of youth and the years of marriageable age, and nevertheless he still places them under their parents' authority, teaching not what they themselves may do but what their parents ought to decide about them. The sound authors of the civil laws observed this in former times, when they wished marriages contracted without the counsel and consent of parents to be void, unless some weightier cause ordered them to stand. But lest the boldness of the Popes leave anything unviolated, they too have introduced new laws by which secret marriages remain firm and valid even against the wishes of parents. What is this other than to subject parents to the lust of their children, and to transfer the authority with which God armed them to men who deserve nothing but contempt and public infamy, who for the most part, for the sake of belly and gullet, seduce unwary young men and tender girls with their enticements, so that they may obey their own parents less? They pretend the dignity of the Sacrament, which is so great that a promise made under its sanction cannot in any way be annulled. But we have shown elsewhere that what they chatter about the sacrament of marriage is frivolous. Indeed, even granting that marriage ought to be counted among the sacraments, it will nevertheless not deserve that name unless it has been lawfully contracted; and just as Paul says that the Corinthians did not eat the Lord's Supper, because they had departed from its first institution, so we shall deny that those who do not observe the laws of marriage given by God contract lawful marriage among themselves. How splendid, then, is that sacrament, by which the law of God is weakened, public honesty is abolished, and the right of nature is overturned?

units.la: Sed reliquis illis, ad alteram huius admonitionis partem transeamus, quam sic proponit Paulus: Qui vero stat firmus in corde, nec adigitur necessitate, sed in potestate habet propriam voluntatem, & hoc decreuit in corde suo, ut seruet suam virginem, bene facit. Pertinent haec ad alteros, qui virgines penes se seruant, neque nuptum dant, ut earum tranquillitati consulatur: & illis quoque ut id faciant permittit. Quia tamen hoc valde periculosum est, & hominum voluntates saepe praeter omnem expectationem subito mutantur, admodum caute & circumspecte loquitur, multa requirens quae hic obseruari debeant. Primo ait: Qui stat firmus in corde suo. Docet voluntatem certa & stabili opus esse, quae absque graui & matura deliberatione concipi non potest. Haec igitur praecedat oportet, ne quid ex temerario aut praecipiti affectu statuatur, cuius aliquando poeniteat. Deinde necessitate omnem excludit, & permissione hanc ad eos modo restringit, quos nulla necessitas, ut aliter faciant, adigit. Debet autem hoc de incontinentia periculo exponi. Nam vbi hoc timetur, ibi quod parentes liberis debent officium, & liberorum honor atque salus necessario iubent, ut de coniugio illis prospiciant. Quia, ut supra dixit, satius est matrimonium contrahere, quam uri. Et huc pertinet quod tertio loco addit: Sed in potestate habet propriam voluntatem. Id enim de iis solis dicitur, qui non ab aliorum arbitrio pendent, & proinde quod volunt etiam effectum dare possunt. Id vero in praesenti causa tunc fit, quando filiae voluntas eadem est, quae patris. Itaque si illa vitam caelibem viuere nolit, non amplius suae voluntatis potestatem habet pater, & inuitus fuerit, si filiam ad vitae genus cogere velit, ad quod tuendum illa infirmior est, & ex quo hominum salus nequaquam dependet. Sequitur: Et hoc decreuit in corde suo. Quo membro non aliud dicit, quam quod iam ante dixerat. Voluit tamen Pleonasmo uti, eo quod sciret nullam diligentiam in hac causa nimiam esse posse, propter incredibilem diaboli astutiam, qui undiq; rimas & effugia quaerit, ut procul explosó coniugij honesto & legitimo usu, regnum suum per vagas libidines inter homines stabiliat. Vult ergo parentes in hac causa vigilantissimos esse, & nihil constituere absq; maturo & probe deliberato consilio. At si ista omnia concurrant (inquit) & his conditionibus quis filiam suam domi suae virginem seruarit, ut ab huius vitae curis libera Deo expeditius seruiat, is bene facit: neq; ullam reprehensionem meretur. Et mox vtrumq; membrum simul comprehendens causam istam concludit: Itaque qui dat nuptum, bene facit: qui vero non dat nuptum, melius facit: quia & quod per se licitum est, facit, & simul tranquillitati & sacro otio filia consulit, ut se totam diuinis studijs liberius consecrare possit. Semper ergo ad huius vitae commoditatem hoc omne restringi debet, quod in caelibatus & virginitatis commendationem dicitur, neque etiam ad alios extendi, quam quibus a Deo hoc datum est, ut caste viuant & nullis illicitae libidinis flammis vrantur. Nam vbi hoc fit, ibi non melius faciunt parentes, sed liberis suis pessime consulunt, quos in tanto periculo ea medicina spoliant, quam Deus illis concesserit. Potest ergo tota haec Pauli doctrina siue admonitio tribus capitibus comprehendi. Primum commodius Deo seruire & vitam hanc tranquillius agere eos, quibus continentiae donum est datum. Secundum, nihil hic statuendum esse temere, ne vel nobisipsis vel alijs laqueum iniiciamus. Postremum, licere imo necessarium esse omnibus, qui se incontinentes & in fornicationis periculo constitutos esse sentiunt, ut matrimonium contrahant.
units.tr: But leaving those matters aside, let us pass to the second part of this admonition, which Paul sets out thus: "But he that standeth stedfast in his heart, having no necessity, but hath power over his own will, and hath so decreed in his heart, that he will keep his virgin, doeth well." These words concern others who keep virgins in their power and do not give them in marriage, in order that their tranquillity may be looked after; and Paul permits them to do this as well. Yet because this is very dangerous, and men's wills often change suddenly, beyond all expectation, he speaks most cautiously and circumspectly, requiring many things to be observed here. First he says: "He that standeth stedfast in his heart." He teaches that the will must be certain and stable, which cannot be formed without grave and mature deliberation. This must therefore come first, so that nothing is decided out of a rash or headlong impulse, of which one may at some time repent. Next he excludes all necessity, and restricts this permission to those whom no necessity compels to act otherwise. But this must be understood with reference to the danger of incontinence. For where that is feared, the duty parents owe their children, and the honour and safety of the children, necessarily require that they provide for them in respect of marriage. For, as he said above, it is better to marry than to burn. To this belongs what he adds in the third place: "but hath power over his own will." For this is said only of those who do not depend on the judgment of others, and therefore can also carry out what they wish.
