In the present case this happens when the daughter's will is the same as her father's. Accordingly, if she is unwilling to live a single life, the father no longer has power over his own will, and he acts against his will if he wishes to force his daughter into a kind of life which she is too weak to sustain, and on which the salvation of men by no means depends. There follows: "and hath so decreed in his heart." In this clause he says nothing other than what he had said before. He nevertheless chose to use a pleonasm, because he knew that no diligence in this matter can be excessive, on account of the incredible cunning of the devil, who seeks cracks and escape routes on every side, so that, having cast out the honest and lawful use of marriage, he may establish his kingdom among men through wandering lusts. He therefore wills that parents be most watchful in this matter, and decide nothing without mature and carefully considered counsel. But if all these things concur, he says, and a man keeps his daughter at home as a virgin under these conditions, so that, free from the cares of this life, she may serve God more readily, he does well and deserves no reproach. And presently, embracing both clauses together, he concludes the matter: "So then he that giveth her in marriage doeth well; but he that giveth her not in marriage doeth better": because he does what is in itself lawful, and at the same time provides for the daughter's tranquillity and holy leisure, so that she may dedicate herself more freely, wholly, to divine studies. Therefore all that is said in praise of celibacy and virginity must always be restricted to the convenience of this life, and must not be extended to anyone except those to whom God has given the gift of living chastely and of not burning with the flames of unlawful lust. For where that is not the case, parents do not act better, but do the worst for their children, whom they deprive of that remedy which God has granted them in so great a danger. Thus the whole of this teaching or admonition of Paul can be comprehended under three heads. First, that those to whom the gift of continence has been given serve God more fittingly and lead this life more tranquilly. Second, that nothing is to be decided here rashly, lest we cast a snare upon ourselves or others. Last, that it is lawful, indeed necessary, for all who feel themselves incontinent and placed in danger of fornication, to contract marriage.

units.la: Porro ut ad ea redeamus, quae in virginitatis commendationem dicuntur, obseruari debet, haec omnia a Paulo sic dici, ut ne minima quidem ex parte ijs patrocinetur, qui filias suas votis monasticis obstringunt, & monasterijs includunt, adeoq; seruituti perpetuae mancipant. Nam ut paulo ante dictum est, nulla alia voluntas hic parentibus permittitur, quam quae ex filiarum arbitrio dependet, & cuius ipsi potestatem habent absq; alterius iniuria. At quia hominum voluntas in omnibus alijs rebus, tum maxime in hac causa mutabilis est, nihil certi in futurum statui poterit. Etenim videmus multos, qui in ipso aetatis flore a coniugio abhorruerunt, neque libidinum aestro infestati fuerunt: saepe praeter opinionem amore correptos insolitis flammis ardere, & non solum a caelestium meditatione auocari, verumetiam ad huius vitae studia ineptos fieri. Vbi si primum consilium aliquis pertinacius urgere velit, perinde fecerit, ac si incendio exorto aquam infundi prohibeat. Quid vero in Papatu fit aliud, quando parentes pro liberis vouent, & tam ab-sunt, ut vires & ingenia illorum prius explorent, ut saepe, nondum natos, imo ne conceptos qui-dem, dem, vitæ: nonasticæ[?] desinent? Adhæc interdum inuitos atque reluctantes votis perpetuis & in-dissolubilibus obstringunt. Deinde liberum hoc esse vult Paulus, vt vel nuptum dentur, vel minus. Illi vero necessitatem ineuitabilem fingunt. Præterea olim parentes domi suæ & in sua cu-stodia virgines suas seruabant, quod ad tuendam earum pudicitiam & ad euitandam omnis probri suspicionem tutissimum & consultissimum erat. At in Papatu parentes liberos suos publicè tantùm non abdicant, & quos ipsi seruare & tueri debebant, aliorum potestati subijciunt, quibus nihil in eos iuris à Deo est datum. Et quoad filias, plausibili quidem titulo istud fit, quando reli-giosis huius seculi studijs Christo nubere dicuntur: at vtinam non sæpe ceu ouiculæ lupis creditæ in petulantissimarum monialium potestatem deuenirent, quæ tenellos animos suo exemplo corrumpunt, & nonnunquam lenas agunt, atque crassis & libidinosis monachis eas prostituunt, quæ virginitatem perpetuam Christo vouerunt. Est igitur hoc loco imprimis admiranda diaboli astutia, qui etsi Paulus tanta verborum diligentia vtatur, & negotium hoc omne tam circumspectè proponat, tamen laqueum istum nectere potuit, quem ille abruptum & sublatum voluit. Simul autem stupore & omni reprehensione dignissima est Episcoporum & principum Christianorum stupiditas, qui laqueum hunc sua authoritate tuentur, & sacrosanctum esse volunt, etiamsi in illo tot virginum nobilium atq; plebeiarum pudicitiam periclitari, tot animarum millia perire, disciplinam ecclesiæ abrumpi, & religionem Christianam Turcarum atq; Iudæorum ludibrijs exponi videant. At quia hæc deplorare facilius est quam emendare, parentes nunc admonuisse sufficiat, vt ipsi de officio, quod liberis debent, diligentius cogitent.
units.tr: Moreover, to return to what is said in praise of virginity, it must be observed that all these things are said by Paul in such a way that they lend not even the smallest support to those who bind their daughters with monastic vows, shut them up in monasteries, and so hand them over to perpetual slavery. For, as was said a little earlier, no other will is permitted here to parents than that which depends on the daughters' judgment, and over which they themselves have power without wrong to another. But because the human will is changeable in all other things, and most of all in this matter, nothing certain can be settled for the future. For we see many who, in the very flower of their age, have shrunk from marriage and were not troubled by the heat of lusts, yet often, beyond expectation, are seized by love and burn with unaccustomed flames, and not only are drawn away from meditation on heavenly things, but also become unfit for the pursuits of this life. If anyone were to press his first resolution more stubbornly in such a case, he would act just as if, when a fire has broken out, he forbade water to be poured on it. What else, indeed, is done in Popery, when parents make vows on behalf of their children, and are so far from first testing their strength and talents that they often bind them to perpetual monastic life before they are born, or even before they are conceived? Moreover, they sometimes bind them to perpetual and indissoluble vows even against their will and while they are struggling. Next, Paul wills that it be left free for virgins either to be given in marriage or not. But the Papists invent an unavoidable necessity. Furthermore, in former times parents kept their virgin daughters at home and in their own custody, which was the safest and most prudent course for guarding their chastity and avoiding all suspicion of disgrace. But in Popery parents practically disown their children in public, and hand over to the power of others those whom they themselves ought to keep and protect, over whom God has given those others no right at all. As for daughters, this is done under a plausible title, when they are said to be wedded to Christ by religious pursuits in this age; but would that they did not often, like little sheep entrusted to wolves, fall into the power of most wanton nuns, who corrupt tender minds by their example, and sometimes act as procuresses and hand them over to gross and lustful monks, although they have vowed perpetual virginity to Christ. Therefore in this place the cunning of the devil is especially to be wondered at: although Paul uses such great care in his words and sets forth the whole matter so cautiously, nevertheless he was able to weave that snare which Paul wished to be cut off and removed. At the same time, the stupidity of the Bishops and Christian princes is to be wondered at and most worthy of reproach; they uphold this snare by their authority and wish it to be held sacrosanct, even though they see the chastity of so many noble and common virgins imperilled in it, so many thousands of souls perishing, church discipline broken, and the Christian religion exposed to the mockery of the Turks and Jews. But since it is easier to deplore these things than to amend them, it is enough for now to have admonished parents, that they may think more diligently about the duty they owe their children.

units.la: Nunc ad Paulum redeamus, qui nouum consilium de viduis subijcit, aut potius quod supra obscurius datum videri poterat, repetit atque illustrat. Nam etsi secundas nuptias absque vllo fe-xus discrimine concesserit, multis tamen à muliebris sexus decoro & honestate alienum videtur, si quæ post mariti obitum alteri iungatur. Quod inter gentes etiam reprehensione dignum multis visum fuisse constat. Nam vt Romani scriptores prodiderunt, quæ vno matrimonio contentæ e-rant, pudicitiæ corona honorabantur: quod fieri non poterat absque aliarum ignominia, quæ ad alias nuptias transfibant. Exiflimabant enim (vt Valerij verbis vtar) eum præcipuè matronæ syncera fide incorruptum esse animum, quæ post depositæ virginitatis cubile, in publicum egredi nesciret: multorum verò matrimoniorum experientiam, quasi legitimæ cuiusdam intemperantiæ signum esse credebant. Et credibile est, nonnullos vetus hoc Romanæ ciuitatis institutum perti-nacius defendisse, ne Christiani homines in hac re ab ethnicis superari viderentur. Quapropter peculiari doctrina hîc opus erat, quam Apostolus tribus capitibus comprehendit.
units.tr: Now let us return to Paul, who sets out a new counsel concerning widows, or rather repeats and clarifies what had perhaps seemed given rather obscurely above. For although he has granted second marriages without any distinction of sex, nevertheless it seems to many women to be foreign to feminine decency and honour if a woman joins herself to another man after her husband's death. It is well established that among the nations too this was thought to deserve reproach by many. For, as the Roman writers have related, women who had been content with a single marriage were honoured with the crown of chastity; and this could not happen without the disgrace of others who passed over to other marriages. For they thought (to use the words of Valerius) that a matron's mind was most unspotted by sincere faith when she did not know how to go out in public after the bed of her lost virginity; and they believed that the experience of many marriages was a sign of a kind of lawful intemperance. And it is credible that some defended this old custom of the Roman state rather stubbornly, lest Christian people should seem to be surpassed by the heathen in this matter. Therefore there was need here of a special teaching, which the Apostle embraces in three parts.

units.la: Primum his verbis proponit: Vxor alligata est lege, quàm diu viuit vir ipsius: quod si obdormierit vir ipsius, libera est ad cui velit nubendum. Sensus est, viduis liberum atque concessum esse, vt denuo nubant si velint, & proinde ne his quidem laqueum iniici debere, quo conscientiæ earum grauentur. Id autem probat argumento à contrarijs: Vxor alligata est lege dum maritus viuit: Ergo hoc defuncto soluta & libera est, neque peccat, si alteri iungatur. Est argumentum hoc clarum & firmum, neque negari potest consequentia, nisi quis coniugij vinculum inter mortuos quoque durare dicat, quod vt dictu absurdum est, ita Sadducæis olim resurrectionis negandæ occasionem præbuit. Caterùm abutuntur hoc loco Pontificij, vt nouum illud & prioribus seculis inusitatum diuortij genus defendant, quo mensæ quidem & thori separationem faciunt, matrimonij verò vinculum adhuc ratum & sanctum manere contendunt. Quæ causa est, vt ne adul-terio quidem interueniente permittant, vt alteri nubat mulier, cuius vir mæchus & adulter adhuc in viuis est. At præter id quod Christo contradicunt, qui adulterium iustam diuortij veri & per-secti causam facit, Pauli etiam verba in alienum sensum detorquent, & ex ijs plus colligunt, quàm ille dixerit. Nec enim hîc de diuortio & eius causis siue modo disserit, sed viduis licere docet, vt coniugium repetant, eo quod priores coniugij legibus non amplius teneantur. Et quia his vt plurimum per mariti mortem liberatur, huius modo meminit, non autem ideo negat, nullam aliam causam esse, quæ idem possit. Et quæ obsecro iniquitas est, insontem eo vinculo adhuc obstringere, quod alter iampridem abrupit & in nihilum redegit?
units.tr: First he sets it out in these words: "A wife is bound by law as long as her husband lives; but if her husband falls asleep, she is free to marry whom she will." The sense is that it is lawful and permitted for widows to marry again if they wish, and that therefore no snare should be laid upon them either, to burden their consciences. He proves this by an argument from the contraries: a wife is bound by the law while her husband lives; therefore when he is dead she is loosed and free, and does not sin if she joins herself to another. This argument is clear and firm, and the consequence cannot be denied, unless someone should say that the bond of marriage endures even between the dead; and as this is absurd to say, so it once gave the Sadducees an occasion for denying the resurrection. But the Papists abuse this passage in order to defend that new kind of divorce, unknown in earlier centuries, by which they make a separation of table and bed but contend that the bond of marriage still remains valid and holy. The result is that they do not permit a woman to marry another man, even when adultery has intervened, while her husband, an adulterer and fornicator, is still alive. But apart from the fact that they contradict Christ, who makes adultery the just cause of a true and complete divorce, they also twist the words of Paul into a foreign sense and gather from them more than he said. For he does not here discuss divorce or its causes or manner, but teaches that widows are free to renew marriage, because they are no longer held by the laws of marriage to the former husband. And since they are for the most part set free by the death of the husband, he mentions this alone, but he does not therefore deny that there is no other cause which could have the same effect. And, I ask, what injustice is it to bind an innocent person still with that bond which the other party long ago broke and reduced to nothing?

units.la: Secundo,quid in quaerendo nouo coniugio viduae obseruare debeant,admoneat[?]:Vt nimirum nu-bant in Domino. Fit hoc quando Deum timent & ab eo latas connubiorum leges religiosè obseruant. Inter has praecipua est, quae religionis curam habere iubet, ne cum viro prophano & à fide Christiana alieno matrimonium contrahat. Deinde vt in Dei institutionem respiciat, neque caecis affectibus sese abripi patiatur. Requiruntur item preces, quibus Dei gratia & benedictio exigitur. Quibus omnibus diligens fidei & dilectionis coniugalis cura debet accedere. Ista igitur si vidua obseruet, minimè peccabit ad nouas nuptias transeundo. At hic meminisse oportet, quod illi dicitur, non minus ad eos etiam pertinere, qui primas nuptias appetunt. Quia enim absque Dei fauore & gratia nihil nobis auspicatum esse potest, certè neque coniugia feliciter cedent, quae non in Domino contrahuntur. Exempla, quibus hoc probari possit, vndiq; occurrunt.
units.tr: Secondly, he admonishes what widows ought to observe in seeking a new marriage: namely, that they marry "in the Lord." This is done when they fear God and religiously observe the laws of marriage laid down by him. Among these the chief is that which bids them take care of religion, so that they do not contract marriage with an ungodly man, one alien to the Christian faith. Then, that they look to the institution of God and do not allow themselves to be carried away by blind affections. Prayers are also required, by which the grace and blessing of God is sought. To all these a diligent care for faith and conjugal love must be added. If, therefore, a widow observes these things, she will by no means sin in passing to new nuptials. But here we must remember that what is said to her applies no less to those who seek a first marriage. For since nothing can be auspicious for us without the favour and grace of God, certainly marriages which are not contracted in the Lord will not turn out happily. Examples by which this can be proved meet us everywhere.

units.la: Postremò addit Apostolus: Sed beatior est, si ita maneat, secundum meam sententiam. At hic quoque subintelligi debet conditio, cuius iam saepe meminimus: Si nimirum continentiae dono fit praedita. Tunc enim beatior erit, non quidem quoad sui status meritum, quod apud Deum omnino nullum est, sed quoad huius vitae commoditatem, quia minus curae habebit & molestiae. Quòd si continentiae dono caruerit, non beatior erit si vidua maneat, sed multis modis misera, imò viuens licet mortua erit, vt alibi Apostolus loquitur.
units.tr: Lastly the Apostle adds: "But she is happier if she remains so, according to my judgement." Here too a condition must be understood, which we have often mentioned already: namely, if she is endowed with the gift of continence. For then she will be happier, not indeed as to the merit of her state, which before God is altogether nothing, but as to the convenience of this life, because she will have less care and trouble. But if she has lacked the gift of continence, she will not be happier if she remains a widow, but in many ways wretched; indeed, though living, she will be dead, as the Apostle speaks elsewhere.

units.la: Quia autem hanc suam sententiam esse dixit, conclusionis loco addit: Puto autem, me quoque Spiritum Dei habere. Quae verba Ironiam sapere videntur, qua pseudoapostolos & aemulos suos perstringit, qui sublimiorus cuiusdam scientiae fiducia superbi, omnia sua sub Spiritus sancti praetextu venditabant, Pauli autem doctrinam apud rudes & rerum imperitos contemptam facere conabantur. Ostendit ergo, Spiritum Dei illis minimè alligatum esse, sed se quoque eius esse participem, neque absque huius suggestione dixisse quae hucusque dicta sunt. Vere autem ab Apostolo istud dici, res ipsa probat, quando nihil in tota eius doctrina continetur, quod ab illis diuersum sit, quae olim Deus per Mosem & Prophetas, aut per proprium Filium locutus est. Admonet autem nos breuis ista huius tractationis conclusio, neminem in ecclesia audiri debere, nisi qui Dei Spiritu praeditus ea docet, quae ab illo accepit. Interim tota huius Capitis doctrina in eum vsum nobis seruiat, vt diuini beneficij per matrimonij institutionem nobis concessi memores, puritati & castitati studeamus, imprimis autem in hoc simus, vt vera & germana membra simus ecclesiae, quam suo san-guine ablutam & purgatam sibi aeterno coniugio coniunxit Dei Filius, CHRISTVS IESVS: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Because he had said that this was his judgement, he adds by way of conclusion: "But I think that I also have the Spirit of God." These words seem to savour of irony, by which he strikes at the false apostles and his rivals, who, proud in the confidence of some lofty knowledge, boasted of all their teaching under the pretext of the Holy Spirit, and tried to make the doctrine of Paul despised among the simple and the inexperienced. He therefore shows that they were by no means bound to the Spirit of God, but that he too was a partaker of it, and that he had not said what has been said so far without the prompting of that Spirit. That this was truly said by the Apostle the thing itself proves, since nothing is contained in his whole teaching that differs from those things which God formerly spoke through Moses and the Prophets, or through his own Son. This brief conclusion of this discussion also warns us that no one ought to be heard in the Church except one who, endowed with the Spirit of God, teaches what he has received from him. Meanwhile let the whole doctrine of this chapter serve us to this end: that, mindful of the divine benefit granted to us through the institution of marriage, we may strive for purity and chastity; and above all let us be concerned that we are true and genuine members of the Church, which the Son of God, Christ Jesus, has cleansed and purified with his own blood and joined to himself in an eternal marriage: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT VIII. HOMILIA XL.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII. HOMILY XL.

units.la: CÆterum de illis quae idolis immolantur, scimus quòd omnes scientiam habemus. Scientia inflat, charitas verò aedificat. Quòd si quis sibi videtur aliquid scire, nondum quicquam novit, sicut oportet nouisse. Sed si quis diligit Deum, hic sciens ab eo factus est.
units.tr: Now concerning things sacrificed to idols: we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. But if anyone thinks he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know. But if anyone loves God, he is known by him.

units.la: Postquam Paulus Apostolus disciplinam ecclesiasticam apud Corinthios restituit, & occasione de multis egit, quae ad vitam recte instituendam & mores formandos pertinent, transfit modo ad tertiam epistolae huius partem, qua de religionis exercitijs disserit, in quibus varie peccabatur. Orditur autem à rebus medijs seu indifferentibus, in quibus multi libertate Christiana licenter nimis abutebantur, & cum multorum offensione in fidei professionem peccabat. Praecipuum hic erat, quod circa cibos fiebat. Nam vt alias monuimus, illo tempore homines Christiani ethnicis permixti habitabant, & hi quidem rerum potiebantur, eo quòd ipsorum superstitiones Romani Imperij authoritate defenderentur. Itaq; pro suo more festa agebant, Dijs suis sacri-ficabant, ex sacrificiorum carnibus epulas instituebant, ad quas frequenter Christiani quoq; vel propter vi- ciniam, vel affinitatem, aut etiam amicitiæ ergò inuitabantur. Tunc ergo multi, ne morosiores æ- quo & rigidi nimis viderentur, aut ex ethnicis amicos sibi facerent, conuiuijs eiusmodi interesse solebant: quæ res multorum scandalorum causa erat. Primò enim contra Legem Dei sacris alienis communicabant, quod fieri non poterat, quin simul in fidei Christianæ professionem peccarent. Deinde infirmiores offendebant, qui cum adhuc aliqua Deorum veterum reuerentia tenerentur, minus abhorrebant ab eorum cultu, cum sacris eiusmodi interessent ij, qui præ alijs in fide instru- cti esse videbantur. Quæ causa erat, ut multi quantumuis reclamante conscientia illos imitaren- tur. Accedebat hûs, quod exemplo suo ethnicos in superstitionibus & idololatria confirmabant, & ijsdem authores erant, ut multa de tota religione Christiana indignius loquerentur. Quia ergo multus de his sermo erat, & iam in apertam contentionem hæc causa exarserat, suam authoritatem Paulus interponit, & prolixè docet, illos indignè facere, simulq; ostendit, quid hic fieri quidue caueri debeat. Summa omnium est, Christianos homines ab omni idololatriæ communione abstinere debere, & diligenter cauere, ne vel ipsi vllis sacris illicitis polluantur, vel alios suo exemplo seducant.
units.tr: After the Apostle Paul restored church discipline among the Corinthians, and on the occasion of many matters had dealt with what pertains to ordering life rightly and forming morals, he now turns to the third part of this letter, in which he discusses the exercises of religion, in which various sins were being committed. He begins with matters that are indifferent or neutral, in which many were abusing their Christian liberty too freely and, to the offence of many, were sinning against the profession of faith. The chief issue here concerned food. For, as we have pointed out elsewhere, at that time Christians lived mingled with pagans, and these pagans held power, since their superstitions were defended by the authority of the Roman Empire. Accordingly they celebrated their festivals in their customary way, sacrificed to their gods, and held feasts from the flesh of the sacrifices, to which Christians too were often invited, whether because of nearness of dwelling, kinship, or friendship. Many therefore, lest they seem too fussy and unduly strict, or lest they make friends among the pagans, used to attend such banquets, and this was the cause of many scandals. For first, they shared in alien rites against the law of God, which could not happen without at the same time sinning against the profession of the Christian faith. Next, they offended the weaker brethren, who, still held by some reverence for the old gods, were less averse to their worship when those who seemed better instructed in the faith took part in such rites. This was the reason why many, although their conscience protested, imitated them. Moreover, by their example they confirmed the pagans in superstition and idolatry, and were the authors of the same, so that they spoke more unworthily of the whole Christian religion. Since therefore there was much talk about these matters, and this cause had already broken out into open dispute, Paul interposes his authority and teaches at length that these men were acting unworthily, and at the same time shows what ought to be done here and what ought to be guarded against. The sum of the whole is that Christians ought to abstain from every communion with idolatry, and carefully take care lest either they themselves be polluted by any unlawful rites, or they lead others astray by their example.

units.la: Est autem doctrina hæc etiam nostro seculo utilis & admodum necessaria. Nam etsi gentium superstitiones iampridem abolitæ sint, tamen solis nominibus mutatis aliæ in earum locum successerunt, & hodie passim inueniuntur, qui Dius sacra faciunt, illos inuocant, templa & aras in eorum honorem consecrant, & ijsdem festos dies agunt, in quibus multa fieri solent, partim superstitiosè, partim petulanter, quæ omnia à Christiani nominis professione alienissima sunt. At hic multos est videre, qui etsi puriorem Euangelij doctrinam profiteantur, ab illis tamen adeò non abhorrent ut sæpe per longa itinera excurrant, ut Encaniorum aliorumq; sacrorum festis intersint. Et hi quidem omnes pacis publicæ studium, amicitias item veteres & infinita alia huius generis prætexunt, at fere vnum hoc agunt, quòd infirmiores quidem multos offendunt, apertis autem & contumacioribus fidei nostræ aduersarijs calumniandi occasionem præbent, ut nostros homines non tam puriorís religionis quàm otij, ventris & gulæ studio teneri dicant. Ergo nostri quoque seculi hominibus hic concionatur Apostolus, quibus ex ista tractatione generalis doctrina petenda est, ut ab omni superstitionis specie abstineant, & libertatis per Christum partæ beneficio sic utantur, ne in licentiam degeneret cum aliorum offensione & publica nominis Christiani ignominia.
units.tr: This teaching is also useful and altogether necessary in our own age. For although the superstitions of the nations were abolished long ago, nevertheless, with only the names changed, others have taken their place, and today there are everywhere those who sacrifice to the Dii, invoke them, consecrate temples and altars in their honour, and keep festival days for them, on which many things are customarily done, partly superstitiously, partly wantonly, all of which are most alien to the profession of the Christian name. Yet here one can see many who, though they profess the purer doctrine of the Gospel, are nonetheless so little averse to those things that they often travel long journeys to attend the festivals of the Encaenia and other sacred rites. All of these people pretend a concern for public peace, and likewise old friendships and countless other such pretexts, yet they almost all accomplish this one thing: they offend many of the weaker brethren, and they give occasion for slander to open and more stubborn adversaries of our faith, so that they say our people are held not so much by zeal for a purer religion as by a love of leisure, of the belly and of the gullet. Therefore the Apostle preaches here also to the people of our own age, from whose treatment of this matter they must draw general teaching: that they abstain from every kind of superstition, and so use the benefit of the liberty obtained through Christ that it does not degenerate into licence, to the offence of others and the public disgrace of the Christian name.

units.la: Sed accedamus ad Pauli verba, qui ita rem tractat, ut argumenta, quibus aduersarij niteban- tur validissimè confutet. Est enim hæc commodissima ratio agendi cum ijs, qui à veritatis scopo aberrauerunt: quàm quia multi non sequuntur, & proprij nominis authoritatem nimis imperiosè vrgent, non mirum est, hodie minus profici in corrigendis ecclesiæ vitijs atque erroribus. Ab eo autem exorditur, qui totius mali quasi fons erat: ab opinione nimirum scientiæ, quæ plerosque ita inflabat, ut se eò vsque profecisse arbitrarentur, ut neq; epulis istis, neque vlla externa cum idololatris societate aut communione pollui possent. Et horum sermones erant: Scimus idola hæc vnà cum suis Dijs nihil quàm vana & inania nomina esse: scimus præterea Christum ciborum discrimina tamdudum aboleuisse, ut nihil quod per os ingreditur, hominis mentem atq; conscientiam possit inquinare. Itaq; cùm absq; omni Deorum fictitiorum metu aut reuerentia ad sacra illorum accedamus, neq; fidem nostram vlla superstitionum persuasione labefactari sinamus, carnibus autem immolatitijs non aliter quàm quibusuis alijs temere obuijs vescamur, nimium morosi & in nos iniqui sunt, qui nobis propter illud litem mouent, quod non nisi communis amicitiæ & publicæ pacis seranda causa facimus, &c. Agnoscis nimirum in his nostri seculi hominum verba, quibus suam leuitatem in simili causa excusant. Scimus (inquiunt) simulachra esse lignum & lapides, scimus ab hominibus facta esse, neq; tam stupidi sumus, ut in illis spem & fiduciam collocemus: scimus Deum & Dîuos externos hisce officijs nequaquam indigere: scimus Papam & totum illum clerum homines esse, &c. Deniq; infinita alia in ore habent, quorum notitiam se habere gloriantur. In quem vero finem hæc omnia dicunt? Ut superstitiones & idololatriam suam excusent, cuius tanta est absurditas, ut eius ipsos non possit non pudere.
units.tr: But let us come to the words of Paul, who treats the matter in such a way as most thoroughly to refute the arguments on which the adversaries relied. For this is the most fitting method of dealing with those who have strayed from the goal of truth; and since many do not follow it, and urge the authority of their own name too imperiously, it is no wonder that today little progress is made in correcting the faults and errors of the Church. Yet he begins with that which was, as it were, the fount of the whole evil: namely, with the opinion of knowledge, which so puffed up most people that they thought they had advanced so far that they could not be polluted either by those feasts or by any external fellowship or communion with idolaters. And these were their words: "We know that these idols, together with their gods, are nothing but vain and empty names; we know moreover that Christ has long since abolished the distinction of foods, so that nothing that enters through the mouth can defile the mind and conscience of a man. Therefore, since we approach their sacred rites without any fear or reverence for fictitious gods, and do not allow our faith to be shaken by any persuasion of superstitions, but eat meat offered to idols no differently than any other meat that comes to hand, those who bring a lawsuit against us for this, when we do it only for the sake of common friendship and public peace, are excessively scrupulous and unjust towards us," and so on. You recognise in these, of course, the words of the men of our own age, with which they excuse their levity in a similar cause. "We know," they say, "that images are wood and stones; we know they were made by men, nor are we so stupid as to place hope and trust in them; we know that God and the foreign gods have no need at all of these services; we know that the Pope and that whole clergy are men," and so on. Finally they have countless other things on their lips, of which they boast that they have knowledge. But to what end do they say all these things? To excuse their superstitions and idolatry, whose absurdity is so great that they cannot but be ashamed of it.

units.la: Quid autem ad ista Paulus? Concessione Ironica vtitur, qua argumentum hoc in ipsos retor- quet, & hac ipsa scientiæ gloriatione eos multiuariam peccare docet. Quoad ea (inquit) quæ idolis immolantur, scimus quòd omnes scientiam habemus. Fatetur & sponte hoc illis dat, quo gloria- bantur, sed hoc ipsum non tantum esse docet, vt eo superbire, & ideo sibi quiduis agendi licentiam fumere debeant. Nam non vos soli (inquit) hoc scitis, imò idem vobiscum scimus etiam nos, neque nos modò: verumetiam qui inter idololatras stupidissimi habentur, & quos nemo Christianus imi- tari volet. Ita verò loquendo innuit non satis esse, vt alicuius rei scientiam habeamus, nisi huic scientiæ actiones nostræ respondeant. Quid enim profuerit scire simulachra ex ligno, lapide, luto aut quauis alia materia constare, neque aliquid habere diuini numinis, si interim illis cultum diuinum exhibeas? Annon eò turpior erit idololatria, quà te sciens volens, omnibus cordatis non minus ridiculum præbes, quàm si quis oculis apertis & sanis in ipsa luce meridiana cæcutire se simulet & palpans oberret? Similiter, quæ vtilitas est scire vnum esse Deum, si non vnum illum inuoces, & illius prouidentia totum hunc mundum gubernari credas? Ita frustra te scire gloriaberis, Papam & sacrificulos homines esse mortales & peccatis obnoxios, cùm interim ea illis tribuas, quæ solius Christi sunt, & quæ non nisi diuina virtute possunt præstari. Quid enim aliud de te dici potest, quàm quòd cum ratione insanias? Similis est eorum arrogantia, qui de Verbi & voluntatis Dei cognitione gloriantur, vt ex eo colligant, nequaquam opus sibi esse vt verbum audiant, aut cœtibus sacris intersint, cùm interim in cultu Dei & moribus omnia faciant aduersus Christianæ professionis leges. Quasi verò inanis illa notitia ad regnum Dei sufficiat, & non potius fidei obedientia requiratur, quia reipsa præstemus, quod nos iampridem didicisse gloriamur. Ita multorum insolentiam Paulus hoc breui dicto confutat.
units.tr: But what does Paul say to these things? He uses an ironic concession, by which he turns this argument back upon them, and by this very boasting of knowledge he teaches that they sin in many ways. "Concerning those things," he says, "that are sacrificed to idols, we know that we all have knowledge." He admits it and willingly grants them what they boast of, but he teaches that this is not merely to be made proud of, and therefore that they should take to themselves a licence to do whatever they please. For, he says, you are not the only ones who know this; indeed, we also know the same thing along with you, and not only we, but even those who are considered the most foolish among the idolaters, and whom no Christian would wish to imitate. By speaking thus he implies that it is not enough for us to have knowledge of some matter unless our actions correspond to this knowledge. For what would it profit to know that images consist of wood, stone, clay or any other material, and have nothing of divine power, if meanwhile you pay divine worship to them? Will not idolatry be all the more shameful when you do it knowingly and willingly, and present yourself as no less ridiculous to all sensible people than if someone, with his eyes open and sound, in the very light of midday, pretended to be blind and wandered about groping? Likewise, what use is it to know that there is one God, if you do not call upon that one, and believe that this whole world is governed by his providence? Thus you will vainly boast that you know that the Pope and the little sacrificers are mortal men and subject to sins, while meanwhile you ascribe to them those things which belong to Christ alone and which can be accomplished only by divine power. For what else can be said of you, than that you rave with reason? Similar is the arrogance of those who glory in the knowledge of the Word and the will of God, so as to infer from it that there is no need for them to hear the word or to take part in sacred assemblies, while meanwhile in the worship of God and in their morals they do everything contrary to the laws of the Christian profession. As if that empty knowledge were enough for the kingdom of God, and obedience of faith were not rather required, because in fact we do what we boast that we have long since learned. Thus Paul refutes the arrogance of many in this brief saying.

units.la: Obseruabis autem locutionem: Cæterum de illis, quæ idolis immolantur. Ita enim loquendo, carnes illas non Dijs, sed idolis offerri innuit. Id verò ex Christianorum sententia & verè pronuntiat contra id, quod de illis ethnici sentiebant. Hi enim non tam stupidi erant, vt se simulachris lapideis aut ligneis atque anima sensuque carentibus sacra facere putarent: sed in his Deos suos colebant, quos in cœlis residere & illinc beneficia sua in homines distribuere arbitrabantur. At quia Dij illi prorsus nulli erant in rerum natura, aut certè non tales erant, quales esse credebantur, reliquum erat, vt totus ille cultus in simulachris hæreret, & proinde his solis impenderetur. Quod ipsum Spiritus sanctus in Psalmo non obscurè docet, vbi non tam simulachra quam ipsos Deos gentium nihil aliud esse testatur, quàm aurum & argentum. Patet id ex collatione, quam illic Propheta instituit. Cùm enim dixisset: Deus noster in cœlo est, qui perficit quicquid voluerit: mox subijcit: Simulachra gentium argentum & aurum sunt, opus quod hominum manibus fit: Os habent, & non loquuntur: habent oculos & non vident, &c. Moses autem apertius ad viuum rem hanc omnem resecans, eos dæmonijs sacra facere dicit, qui relicto vno vero Deo nouos Deos sibi quærunt, & gentium sacris communicant. Quem Paulus secutus infra dicit: Quæ immolant gentes, dæmonijs immolant, & non Deo. Sunt hæc propter eos obseruanda, qui indignius feruntur hodie, si idololatræ aut simulachrorum cultores esse dicantur. Et primò quidem ineptè inter idola & simulachra distinguunt, quasi verò Græcis nō idem fit idolum, quod Latinis simulachrum dicitur. Deinde multis clamoribus contendunt, se nequaquam simulachris cultum impendere, sed animis suis ad ipsum Deum & Deos cœlites respicere, quos in simulachris eiusmodi colant. At non desunt nobis argumenta, quibus falsi arguantur, cùm coram simulachris genua flectant, iisdem vota faciant, cerea accendant, denique miraculosa opera illis ascribant. Sed vt hoc illis demus quod tantopere vrgent, constat tamen neque Deum verum esse, qui aliqua imagine aut simulachro exprimi possit, neque Deos cultum eiusmodi agnoscere. Quid ergo reliquum est, quàm quòd cultus ille omnis in simulachris quasi finitur, & quod lapidum atque truncorum inanimatorum cultores sint, quicunque circa illa occupantur?
units.tr: Notice the expression, "But concerning those things which are sacrificed to idols." By speaking this way, he indicates that those meats are offered not to gods but to idols. He says this truly and in line with the view of Christians, against what the heathen thought about them. For the heathen were not so stupid as to suppose that they were sacrificing to stone or wooden images, which have no life or sense. Rather, they worshipped their gods in these images, believing that the gods sat in heaven and from there distributed their benefits among men. But since those gods were utterly nonexistent in nature, or at least were not such as they were believed to be, it followed that all that worship clung to the images and was therefore offered to them alone. The Holy Spirit clearly teaches this in the Psalm, where he says that the gods of the nations, rather than the images themselves, are nothing other than gold and silver. This is evident from the comparison the Prophet makes there. For after he had said, "Our God is in heaven; he does whatever he pleases," he immediately adds, "The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of men's hands. They have mouths, but do not speak; they have eyes, but do not see," and so on. Moses, however, cutting away the whole matter more plainly and to the quick, says that those sacrifice to demons who, having abandoned the one true God, seek new gods for themselves and share in the rites of the nations. Following him, Paul says later, "What the nations sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God." These points must be noted on account of those who today are too readily offended if they are called idolaters or worshippers of images. First, they foolishly distinguish between idols and images, as though an idol were not the same thing for the Greeks as an image is called for the Latins. Second, they loudly insist that they do not offer worship to images at all, but that their minds look up to God himself and the heavenly gods, whom they honour in such images. But we are not short of arguments to show that they are lying, since they bend their knees before images, make vows to them, light wax candles, and finally ascribe miraculous works to them. But even if we grant them what they press so hard, it is still certain that the true God cannot be expressed by any image or figure, nor do the gods acknowledge worship of that kind. What then remains, except that all such worship comes to rest, as it were, in the images, and that whoever is occupied with them are worshippers of stones and lifeless trunks?

units.la: Sed pergamus in Apostoli verbis, qui vt scientiæ fiduciam, qua illi efferebantur, magis deprimat, illam non inanem modò & inutilem, verumetiam pernitiosam esse docet. Scientia (inquit) inflat, charitas verò ædificat. Quæ verba non eo sensu accipi debent, quasi scientia per se noxia sit, aut illam Paulus damnet. Qua enim fronte hoc faceret, qui in ipso huius epistolæ exordio Deum hoc potissihoc potissimum nomine prædicauit, quòd Corinthij in ipso ditati essent omni sermone & cognitione: & qui infra eos hortabitur, ne pueri sint intelligentia? Et notum est illud Malachiæ: Labia sacerdotis custodient scientiam, & Legem ex ore eius requirent: Legatus est enim Domini exercituum. Et apud Hoseam Deus de populi simul & sacerdotum ignorantia grauiter conquerens, inter alia dicit: Ad silentium redactus est populus meus, eo quòd nihil norunt. Et mox poenam ipsam minitans infert: Quandoquidem tu scientiam repulisti, reprobaui & ego te, ne sacerdotio mihi fungaris: & quandoquidem tu oblitus es Legis Dei tui, obliuiscar & ego filiorum tuorum. Christus item suis credentibus Spiritum pollicetur, qui & aduocati & doctoris instar eos non solum in periculis consolari, verumetiam in omnem veritatem introducere debeat. Sed & Jsaias propheta aureum illud seculum & verè felicem hominum sub Christo rege conditionem multis describens, eius causam indicat his verbis: Plena enim erit terra scientia Domini: perinde ut cum aquæ maris inundant. Minimè ergo locus iste indoctis asinis & omnium disciplinarum osoribus patrocinatur, qui cùm bonas literas & linguarum cognitionem ad veram scripturæ sacræ intelligentiam plurimum conferre, hac verò patefacta superstitionei suas & quem ex illis fecerunt quæstum corruere vident, mox illud Pauli in ore habent: Scientia inflat, charitas verò ædificat. Ut autem sub scientiæ inflantis nomine veritatis cognitionem populo suspectam & invisam facere conantur, ita per charitatem non aliud quàm ignauam & oscitantem indulgentiam intelligunt, per quam ipsi liceat quiduis fingere & proprij cerebri figmenta pro oraculis indubitatis ecclesiæ obtrudere. At nihil minus voluit Paulus, qui alibi fideles monet, ne spiritum extinguant, neue prophetiam & scripturarum interpretationem pro nihilo ducant, omnia autem explorent, & quod bonum atq; veritati consentaneum esse deprehenderint, retineant. In præsenti ergo partim de inani scientiæ persuasione loquitur, qua nonnulli se aliis præferunt, partim de scientia, quæ charitate destituitur. Utriusque proprium est inflare, id est, tumidos & confidentes facere, qui deinde alios omnes præ se contemnunt. Itaq; inflat scientia, non quidem per se, sed nostro vitio, & proinde nobis hic diligenti cautione opus est, ne rem maximè utilem & necessariam nobis noxiam faciamus.
units.tr: But let us go on to the Apostle's words, who, in order to lower the confidence in knowledge with which they were puffed up, teaches that it is not only empty and useless but even harmful. "Knowledge," he says, "puffs up, but love builds up." These words must not be taken as if knowledge were harmful in itself, or as if Paul condemned it. For with what face could he do this, when at the very beginning of this letter he praised God especially under this heading, that the Corinthians had been enriched in him with all speech and knowledge; and when he will later exhort them not to be children in understanding? And the saying of Malachi is well known: "The lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth, for he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts." And in Hosea, God, complaining bitterly of the ignorance of the people and the priests alike, says among other things: "My people has been brought to silence, because they know nothing." And then, threatening the punishment itself, he adds: "Since you have rejected knowledge, I too have rejected you, so that you shall not serve me as priest; and since you have forgotten the law of your God, I too will forget your children." Christ likewise promises his believers the Spirit, who, like an advocate and a teacher, ought not only to comfort them in dangers but also to lead them into all truth. And the prophet Isaiah, describing that golden age and truly happy condition of men under Christ the king in many ways, indicates its cause in these words: "For the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea." Therefore that passage by no means supports unlearned donkeys and haters of all learning, who, when they see that good literature and the knowledge of languages contribute greatly to the true understanding of Sacred Scripture, and that once this is laid open their superstitions and the profit they have made from them collapse, at once have Paul's words on their lips: "Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up." And just as they try to make the knowledge of the truth suspect and hateful to the people under the name of knowledge that puffs up, so by "love" they understand nothing other than a lazy and yawning indulgence, by which they are free to invent whatever they like and to thrust the figments of their own brains upon the congregation as indisputable oracles. Yet Paul wanted nothing less; he elsewhere warns the faithful not to quench the Spirit, nor to despise prophecy and the interpretation of the Scriptures, but to test all things and hold fast to what they find to be good and agreeing with the truth. So in the present passage he speaks partly of the empty persuasion of knowledge, by which some set themselves above others, and partly of knowledge that lacks love. What is proper to both is to puff up, that is, to make men swollen and self-confident, who then despise all others in comparison with themselves. Knowledge therefore puffs up, not in itself, but through our fault; and so here we need careful caution, lest we make harmful what is most useful and necessary to us.

units.la: Etenim omnibus natura insitum est multa sciendi desiderium, quod ex primis parentibus in nos deriuatum esse, non est dubium: quando illi non aliam ob causam diaboli suggestionibus paruerunt, ut ex arboris vetitæ fructu comederent, quàm quòd boni & mali scientiam affectarunt, quæ illos Dei similes faceret. At desiderium hoc per se non malum duobus fere vitiis corrumpitur, curiositate nimirum & ambitione. Illa enim facit, ut non contenti iis, quæ nos scire prodest, & quæ Deus ipse nobis revelat, ea etiam quæ nihil ad nos pertinent scire velimus, & in eorum cognitionem per media illicita penetrare audeamus. Et huic malo artes divinatorias & fatidicas debemus, quibus Satan quondam orbem universum turbauit, & quarum studio etiam hodie multos à veritatis in Scriptura nobis revelatæ studio auocat. Ambitio autem causa est, ut non de vero scientiæ usu cogitemus, sed inani gloriæ studio elati supra omnes homines velimus eminere: quò fit, ut nobis solis male seruiat, quod multorum aliorum ædificationi & proue-ndæ gloriæ Dei seruire debebat. Ad hac ergo Paulus respiciens, ita argumentatur: Quic-quid non facit ad proximi & ecclesiæ totius ædificationem, id Deo placere non potest: quod si verò insuper destruat, illi invisum & exosum quoque erit. At quicquid charitate vacuum est, id non ædificat, sed potius destruit, eò quòd quæ sua sunt solum modò homines quærunt: Ergo neque vestra illa scientia Deo placere poterit, quin potius ei exosa est, eò quòd cum multorum scandalo ad communis ecclesiæ destructionem illa utimini. Hic verborum Pauli sensus est simplicissimus.
units.tr: For a desire to know many things is implanted in all people by nature, and there is no doubt that it has been passed down to us from our first parents, since they yielded to the devil's suggestion to eat the fruit of the forbidden tree for no other reason than that they coveted the knowledge of good and evil, which would make them like God. But this desire, which is not evil in itself, is corrupted by two vices, namely curiosity and ambition. Curiosity makes us, not content with those things which it profits us to know and which God himself reveals to us, want to know even those things that have nothing to do with us, and dare to penetrate into their knowledge by forbidden means. To this evil we owe the arts of divination and prophecy, by which Satan once threw the whole world into turmoil, and by whose pursuit he still today draws many away from zeal for the truth revealed to us in Scripture. Ambition, on the other hand, is the cause why we do not think about the true use of knowledge, but, carried away by a desire for empty glory, wish to stand out above all men; hence it comes about that what ought to serve the edification of many others and the advancement of God's glory serves only ourselves, and badly. Looking to these things, Paul reasons thus: whatever does not serve the edification of the neighbour and of the whole Church cannot please God; and if it moreover destroys, it will also be hateful and odious to him. But whatever is empty of love does not build up but rather destroys, because men seek only what is their own. Therefore that knowledge of yours cannot please God either; rather it is odious to him, because you use it to the destruction of the common Church, with the stumbling of many. This is the simplest sense of Paul's words.

units.la: At nos hic admonemur, in ecclesia præcipuum publicæ ædificationis studium esse debere. Nam ut alibi audiuimus, est illa domus Dei, quam cum thesaurus gratiæ suæ omnibus ille inhabitare dignatur, quem nec tota huius mundi machina capere potest. Fundamentum huius est Christus, invicta illa petra, quam neque inferorum portæ expugnare possunt. Ædificatur autem, quando in Christi & salutis per hunc nobis partæ cognitione indies proficimus, & per nos alij quoque ad eius communionem adducuntur, & qui iam antea illius membra sunt, in fide vera confirmantur. Ad hoc ergo omnes dona et facultates suas omnes in commune deferre, se invicem juvare, infirmiores sancta indulgentia fouere, & scandala è medio tollere debent: Ista vero nunquam faciunt, qui nuda scientia inflati charitate destituuntur. Recte igitur hanc illi praefert Paulus, & ipse Christus discipulis subinde humilitatem & ad quaeuis officia propensam modestiam commendat, eò quod haec fidissima charitatis nutrix sit.
units.tr: But here we are admonished that in the Church the chief concern must be for public edification. For, as we have heard elsewhere, the Church is the house of God, in which he deigns to dwell with the treasure of his grace for all, a house which the whole machinery of this world cannot contain. Its foundation is Christ, that unconquered rock, which the gates of hell cannot overcome. It is built up whenever we make progress day by day in the knowledge of Christ and of the salvation obtained for us through him, and whenever through us others also are brought to his fellowship, and those who are already his members are confirmed in the true faith. For this purpose all should bring all their gifts and resources into the common stock, help one another, cherish the weaker with holy forbearance, and remove offences from the midst. But those who are puffed up with bare knowledge and lack love never do these things. Paul therefore rightly prefers love to it, and Christ himself repeatedly commends to his disciples humility and a modesty ready for every duty, because this is the most faithful nurse of love.

units.la: Simul autem obseruabis, à charitate Christiana scientia veritatis nequaquam excludi debere. Vt enim scientia sine charitate inflat & destruit: ita nisi haec veritatis cognitione regatur, non vi[?] debit quid agat, & aut zelo immoderato & iniusto, aut indulgentia nimia peccabit. Et illius quidem exemplum Paulus in Iudaeis proponit, quos zelo Dei ardere fatetur, in eo autem peccare, quod veri scientia destituantur. Imò seipsum praepostero zelo ecclesiae persecutorem fuisse testatur, eò quod verum Legis & cultus Leuitici finem atq; vsum non intelligeret. Quantum vero eorum indulgentia ecclesiis noceat, qui in cognitione verbi Dei non satis probe instituti sunt, notius est, quàm vt multis demonstrari oporteat. Debebant ista diligentius cogitare nostri aduersarij, quorum alij scientiam, eruditionem, doctrinam, scholas & harum dignitates atq; magnificos titulos nunquam non in ore habent: alij vero charitatis fraternae & domus Dei zelo non minus super-bè gloriantur. At quae obsecro scientiae illius vtilitas, cùm quae passim occurrunt scandala non videant, aut si vident ea tamen non remouent? Quae item illa charitas, quae tot animarum periculum non animaduertit, aut saltem se ignorare fatetur rationem, qua miseris consuli possit?
units.tr: At the same time you will observe that knowledge of the truth must by no means be excluded from Christian love. For just as knowledge without love puffs up and destroys, so unless love is governed by the knowledge of the truth, a person will not know what he ought to do, and will sin either by immoderate and unjust zeal or by excessive indulgence. Paul sets out an example of the first in the Jews, whom he confesses to burn with zeal for God, but to sin in this, that they lack knowledge of the truth. Indeed he testifies that he himself was a persecutor of the Church out of misguided zeal, because he did not understand the true end and use of the Law and the Levitical worship. How greatly the indulgence of those who are not sufficiently well instructed in the knowledge of the Word of God harms the churches is too well known to need demonstrating at length. Our opponents ought to consider these things more carefully. Some of them always have on their lips learning, erudition, doctrine, schools and their dignities and grand titles; others boast no less proudly of brotherly love and of zeal for the house of God. But what, I ask, is the usefulness of that learning, when they do not see the scandals that occur everywhere, or, if they do see them, do not remove them? And what is that love which takes no notice of the danger to so many souls, or at least confesses that it does not know the method by which the wretched might be helped?

units.la: Caeterùm ne sciolis illa Corinthiorum nimium dedisse videretur Paulus, & ipse ex eo maiorem sese efferendi occasionem arripere nt, docet modò, scientiam hanc qua tantopere gloriantur, omnino nullam esse. Dicit enim: Quòd si quis sibi videtur aliquid scire, nondum quicquam nouit, sicut oportet nouisse. Sibi videntur scire, quos propria scientiae fiducia inflat. Hi reuera nihil sciunt, ut scire oportet. Omnis enim scientiae hic finis & usus est, ut homo seipsum norit primò, deinde ut Deum agnoscat, postremo ut sciat qua ratione cum illo uniri possimus, in quo uno salus & felicitas nostra omnis constistit. At qui seipsos norunt, facile vident quam nihil in ipsis sit, ex quo superbiendi & alios contemnendi occasionem arripere debeant. Similiter qui veri Dei cognitione illustrati sunt, ij eum amant, ei vni fidunt, & per fidei obedientiam sub eius manu potenti humiliantur. Rursus, qui nobis per unum IESVM viam ad Patrem apertam esse, nosq; persidem in illum cum Deo conciliari intelligunt, eos omnes superbiae pudet, eò quod Christi exemplum oculis eorum semper obuersatur, & nunquam non eius verba sibi ipsis occinunt: Discite à me, quod mitis sim & humilis corde, & inuenietis requiem animabus vestris. Ex quibus iam certò sequitur, eos reuera nihil scire quemadmodum oportet scire, quicunque suae scientiae fiducia turgidi alios prae se contemnunt, & suae potius priuatae quàm Dei gloriae studeant. Imò nulli mortalium ad discendum ineptiores sunt. Cur enim proficere studeant, qui iamdudum se omnia assecutos esse sibi persuaserunt? Verissimè ergo à Solomone olim dictum fuit: Vidisti virum sapientem in oculis suis, id est, qui ipse sibi sapere videtur: spes de stulto maior est, quàm de illo. Poterat hoc exemplis plurimis probari, & in quotidiano rerum usu subinde occurrunt, quae illi dicto fidem faciunt. Etenim ut pueris exordiaris, qui in scholis se iam eruditos & solidè doctos esse arbitrantur, priusquam Grammaticae principia probè tenent, ij nunquam ad eruditionem solidam peruenient. Ita qui artes mechanicas se iam assecutos esse sibi persuadent, nunquâ eo usq; proficiunt, ut illas cum aliquo lucro & honore exercere possint. Eadem est religionis ratio & omnium eorum, quae ad aeternam salutem faciunt. Qui enim in his se tantum progressos esse putant, ut sibi nulla institutione porrò opus esse, & sibi omnia licere dicant, ij à veritatis cognitione longissimè absunt, & vix unquam adduci possunt, ut seipsos agnoscant, nedum ut quae ipsis altiora sunt intelligant, aut eorum cognitione adiuuari propriam uti possint. Ideo alibi idem Salomon monebat: Ne sis sapiens in oculis tuis, sed Dominum time, & à malo recede: & haec sanitas erit umbilico tuo & irrigatio ossibus tuis, id est, omnia tua prospere cedent, & bene habebis quoad externum & internum hominem. Cui promissioni recte oppositum est comminationem, quae apud Isaiam habetur: Vae his, qui sapientes sunt in oculis suis: & his qui coram seipsis sunt prudentes. Quae omnia cum probe nouisset Apostolus, is praesenti infert: Sed si quis diligit Deum, hic sciens ab eo [?]cognitus est, id est, hic ex germanorum discipulorum Christi numero est, quos omnes θεοδίδακτους [?], id est, à Deo edoctos fore olim Prophe-ta prædixit. Deũ etenim nunquā diliget, qui eius cognitione fuerit destitutus: at cum hunc nemo unquam viderit, nemo etiam eum cognoscet, nisi cui ille se revelare dignatur. Dei autem dilectio cum proximi dilectione necessario coniuncta est, quia qui illum diligit, eos non potest non magni facere, quos ille proprii filii vita & sanguine chariores habuit. Hæc omnia si probè expendamus, certissima collectione sequetur, eos qui propter cibos aut quascunque res in differentes in ecclesia contentionum aut scandalorum authores sunt, Dei dilectione vacuos esse, & proinde scientia illa vera destituti, quæ sola ad salutem consequendam necessaria est. Quamuis ergo de multis glorientur, & se nihil non scire sibi ipsis persuadeant, inanis tamen atque evanida est omnis illorum gloriatio.
units.tr: Moreover, lest Paul seem to have given too much to the half-learned Corinthians, and lest they seize from it an occasion of greater self-exaltation, he now teaches that this knowledge in which they glory so greatly is altogether nothing. For he says: "If anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know." Those seem to themselves to know whom their own confidence in knowledge puffs up. These in truth know nothing as they ought to know. For the whole end and use of all knowledge is this: that a man first know himself, then that he acknowledge God, and last that he know by what means we can be united with him, in whom alone our whole salvation and happiness consists. Now those who know themselves readily see how little there is in them from which they ought to seize an occasion for pride and for despising others. Likewise those who have been enlightened by the true knowledge of God love him, trust in him alone, and through the obedience of faith are humbled under his mighty hand. Again, those who understand that through the one Jesus a way to the Father has been opened to us, and that through faith in him we are reconciled with God, are all ashamed of pride, because the example of Christ is always before their eyes, and they always sing to themselves his words: "Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls." From these things it certainly follows that those who are puffed up with confidence in their own knowledge, and who despise others in comparison with themselves, and who strive for their own private glory rather than the glory of God, truly know nothing as they ought to know. Indeed, no mortals are more unfit for learning. For why should those study to make progress who have long since persuaded themselves that they have attained everything? Rightly, therefore, Solomon said long ago: "Have you seen a man wise in his own eyes? There is more hope of a fool than of him." This could be proved by very many examples, and in the daily course of affairs there constantly occur things that bear out that saying. For example, with boys in the schools who think they are already learned and thoroughly taught before they have properly mastered the principles of grammar: these never arrive at solid learning. So too those who persuade themselves that they have already mastered the mechanical arts never advance so far that they can practise them with any profit or honour. The reasoning is the same for religion and for all those things that pertain to eternal salvation. For those who think they have advanced so far in these matters that they no longer need any instruction and that everything is permitted to them, are very far from the knowledge of the truth, and can scarcely ever be brought to recognise themselves, let alone to understand the things that are higher than themselves, or to be helped by their knowledge so as to use it for their own benefit. Therefore Solomon elsewhere warned: "Be not wise in your own eyes, but fear the Lord and depart from evil; and this will be health to your navel and moisture to your bones," that is, all your affairs will go well, and you will fare well both in outward and inward man. Rightly set against this promise is the threat found in Isaiah: "Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes, and prudent in their own sight." All these things the Apostle knew well, and therefore he adds in the present passage: "But if anyone loves God, this one is known by him," that is, this one belongs to the true number of the genuine disciples of Christ, all of whom the prophet long ago foretold would be taught by God (θεοδίδακτοι). For he who has been deprived of the knowledge of God will never love God; and since no one has ever seen him, no one will know him unless he to whom God deigns to reveal himself. Now love of God is necessarily joined with love of neighbour, because whoever loves God cannot but esteem highly those whom he has held dearer than the life and blood of his own Son. If we weigh all these things carefully, the most certain conclusion follows: that those who are the authors of contentions or scandals in the Church over foods or any other matters of indifference are empty of the love of God, and therefore destitute of that true knowledge which alone is necessary for obtaining salvation. Therefore, although they boast about many things and persuade themselves that they know everything, all their boasting is empty and vain.

units.la: Comprehendit ergo breui sententia Paulus, quæcunq; de vera scientia dici possunt, quàm vulgo sapientiam nominant, & ad quam omnes aspirare conuenit. Est hæc (vt alibi quoq; diximus) rerum diuinarum atq; humanarum, causarumq; quibus illæ continentur, notitia: & proinde omnia comprehendit, quæ tàm præsenti quàm futuræ vitæ seruiunt. Author & largitor illius est vnus & solus Deus. Quapropter grauiter errant, qui illam propria industria assequi conantur. Quàm parum enim hic videat hominis ingenium, facile apparet in philosophorum exemplis, qui etsi homines sagacissimi fuerint, & nullius eos laboris atq; diligentiæ tæduerit, in diuinorum tamen cognitione adeò nihil profecerunt, vt potius stulti facti sint (quemadmodum ad Romanos Apostolus testatur) quando illa ad humanæ rationis calculum ausi sunt reuocare. Itaq; vt Iacobus ait, si cui deest sa-pientia, postulet ab eo qui dat, nempe à Deo, qui dat omnibus benignè, nec exprobrat. Effecta eius sunt, quod Deum diligimus, eidem obedimus, & feruimus, & in illo omnes etiam homines amore syncero complexi in illos benefici sumus. Finis autem & vsus sapientiæ proprius est, vt Deo coniungamur, & in illo æternum feruemur. Ergo vt iam ante diximus, vbi Dei & proximi dilectione homines destituuntur, ibi nulla quoq; sapientia est, & ibidem error atq; ignorantia regnant, quæ miseros mortales in exitium demergunt. Quia verò seipsum Deus in Filio suo IESV CHRISTO reuelat, qui vt splendor gloriæ & character personæ illius exiflit, ita ab illo nobis sapientia factus est, hunc nos amplecti, illum vnum audire, & in eodem coalescere oportet, vt huius luce & spiritu per huius sæculi tenebras tutò dirigamur ad cœlestis illius gloriæ consortium, in qua Deum videbimus sicuti est, & salute nunquam intermoritura fruemur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Paul therefore comprehends in a brief saying whatever can be said about true knowledge, which the common people call wisdom, and to which all ought to aspire. This (as we have said also elsewhere) is the knowledge of divine and human things and of the causes by which these are contained; and therefore it embraces everything that serves both the present life and the future. Its author and giver is the one and only God. Wherefore they err gravely who try to attain it by their own industry. How little the human intellect can do in this matter is easily seen from the examples of the philosophers, who, though they were most keen-minded men and their labour and diligence never wearied, nevertheless made so little progress in the knowledge of divine things that they rather became fools (as the Apostle testifies to the Romans) when they dared to bring those things back to the reckoning of human reason. Therefore, as James says, if anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask of him who gives, namely God, who gives to all generously and does not upbraid. The effects of this wisdom are that we love God, obey and serve him, and in him embrace all men with sincere love and do good to them. The proper end and use of wisdom, however, is that we be joined to God and be preserved in him forever. Therefore, as we said before, where men are deprived of love of God and of neighbour, there is no wisdom either, and there error and ignorance reign, which plunge wretched mortals to destruction. But because God has revealed himself in his Son Jesus Christ, who is the brightness of his glory and the express image of his person, and because wisdom has been made to us by him, it is fitting that we embrace him, hear him alone, and cleave to him, so that by his light and Spirit we may be safely directed through the darkness of this age to fellowship in that heavenly glory, in which we shall see God as he is and enjoy a salvation that will never perish. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLI.
units.tr: HOMILY XLI.

units.la: De esu igitur eorum quæ idolis immolantur, scimus idolum nihil esse in mundo, & quòd nullus est Deus alius nisi vnus. Nam etiamsi sint qui dicantur Dij & in cœlo & in terra (sicut sunt Dij multi & Domini multi) nobis tamen vnus est Deus, Pater ille, ex quo omnia, & nos in ipso: & vnus Dominus IESVS CHRISTVS, per quem omnia, & nos per ipsum. Sed non in omnibus est ea scientia: nonnulli autem cum conscientia idoli vsq; ad hoc tempus tanquam idolis immolatum edunt: & conscientia eorum, infirma cum sit, polluitur.
units.tr: Concerning eating what has been sacrificed to idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is no other God but one. For even if there are those who are called gods, both in heaven and on earth (as there are many gods and many lords), yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we in him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him. But this knowledge is not in everyone; some, however, with a consciousness of the idol, still eat until now as food sacrificed to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled.

units.la: Quoniam homo animalis in Dei cognitione & diuinis omnibus cæcutire solet, neq; ea percipit quæ sunt spiritus Dei, nihil tam pernitiosum est, quàm si ex nobis sapere velimus, aut nos omnia scire nobis persuadeamus. Hæc enim causa est, quòd & circa Dei cognitionem falli-mur, & in toto salutis negotio non solùm turpiter, verumetiam cum aperto animarum discrimine à veritatis scopo aberremus. Accedit huic malo, quòd falsa & arroganti persuasione inflati quosdam alios contemnimus, & ijs scandalo sumus & exitij authores, quorum saluti ex charitatis fraternæ officio consulere debebamus. Et huius mali exemplum hic proponitur in Corinthijs, qui licenter nimis ad epulas idololatrarum ex sacrificiorum carnibus institutas accedebant, cum ipsi vnius & veri Dei cultores haberi vellent. Gloriabantur illi scientia singulari, & propter hanc sibi quidus licere existimabant. Sed Paulus gloriationem hanc aperte damnat & feueriter corripit, & ostendit scientiam hanc inutilem, imo noxiam esse, eo quod charitate non regatur, quæ sola fere obstat, ne Dei donis abutamur. Quo loco nuper didicimus, eam demum veram & salutarem scientiam esse, quæ nobis ex Deo obtingit, & in nobis Dei simul atq; proximi dilectio-nem accendit, neque alium finem sibi propositum habet, quàm vt & Deus glorificetur, & multi in eius cognitione & vera fide ad salutem æternam ædificentur. His præmissis nunc pergit Apo-stolus, & quæ illa Corinthiorum scientia fuerit exponit, qua illi sese excusabant, & eandem mox validissimè confutat.
units.tr: Since natural man is usually blind in the knowledge of God and in all divine matters, and does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, nothing is so destructive as wishing to be wise by ourselves, or persuading ourselves that we know everything. For this is the cause both of our going wrong about the knowledge of God, and of our straying, in the whole business of salvation, not only shamefully but with a plain peril to souls, from the goal of truth. To this evil is added this: puffed up by a false and arrogant conviction, we despise certain others, and become a stumbling block and a source of ruin to them, when out of the duty of brotherly love we ought to have cared for their salvation. An example of this evil is set before us here in the Corinthians, who went too freely to feasts of idolaters, held at tables of meat from sacrifices, while wishing themselves to be thought worshippers of the one and true God. They boasted of their singular knowledge, and on account of it thought they were permitted anything. But Paul openly condemns this boasting and sharply rebukes it, and shows that this knowledge is useless, nay harmful, because it is not governed by love, which alone almost stands in the way, lest we abuse the gifts of God. At this point we have recently learned that that is true and saving knowledge which comes to us from God, and kindles in us at the same time the love of God and of our neighbour, and has no other aim before it than that God may be glorified and that many may be built up to eternal salvation by knowledge of him and true faith. With these things laid down, the Apostle now goes on, and sets out what that knowledge of the Corinthians was, by which they excused themselves, and at once refutes it most strongly.

units.la: Quoad primum, verba & argumenta eorum recitat, quibus in factì sui defensionem vtebantur. De esu (inquit) eorum quæ idolis immolantur, scimus idolum nihil esse in mundo, & quòd nullus est Deus alius nisi vnus. Sensus verborum est: Scimus idola nihil esse in mundo, id est, res inanes esse, quæ nuspiam in rerum natura existunt, sed inani modò mentis imaginatione intra cogitationum discursus concipiuntur. Quid enim esse possunt idola, quando Deus vnus est, qui vt ipse nullo simulachro potest exprimi, sic neminem in diuinitatis & cultus sui societatem admittit? Ergo quæ illis immolantur carnes ex ipsis neque sanctitatem aliquam neque pollutionem concipere possunt. Ex eo autem sequitur, neque nos ex earum esu deteriores fieri, & proinde liberum cuique esse, vt in epulis eiusmodi accumbamus, seu minus. Ad antecedentis illustrationem & confirmationem facit, quod sequitur: Nam etiamsi sint qui dicantur Dij & in cœlo & in terra (sicut sunt Dij multi & Domini multi) nobis tamen vnus est Deus, Pater ille, ex quo omnia, & nos in ipso: & vnus Dominus IESVS CHRISTVS, per quem omnia, & nos per ipsum. Habent ista præoccupationis speciem, qua & gentium errori respondebant, qui Deorum multitudem affirmabant, & se ab illo alienîssimos esse testabantur, vt postea dicetur.
units.tr: As to the first point, he recites their words and arguments by which they defended their conduct. "Concerning," he says, "eating what has been sacrificed to idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is no other God but one." The sense of the words is this: we know that idols are nothing in the world, that is, they are empty things which exist nowhere in the nature of things, but are conceived only in the empty imagination of the mind, within the course of our thoughts. For what can idols be, when God is one, who, since he cannot be expressed by any image, so admits no one into the fellowship of his divinity and worship? Therefore the flesh offered to them can conceive neither any holiness nor any pollution from them. From this it follows that we are not made worse by eating it, and that it is therefore free to each to recline at such feasts, or not. What follows serves to illustrate and confirm the preceding: "For even if there are those who are called gods, both in heaven and on earth (as there are many gods and many lords), yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we in him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him." These words have the appearance of an anticipated objection, by which they also answered the error of the Gentiles, who affirmed a multitude of gods, and who professed themselves most alien from him, as will be said afterwards.

units.la: Nunc ante omnia considerari debet Pauli fides & integritas, qui aduersariorum argumenta tam diligenter & ingenuè adducit, neque aliquid dissimulat eorum, quibus illi sese defendebant. Faciunt hoc ipsum passim Apostoli, & multa huius generis videre est in epistola ad Romanos, quæ magna ex parte disputationibus in vtramque partem habitis constat. In his autem elucet doctrina apostolicæ certitudo, vt quæ neque tenebras quærat (quod impostores fere faciunt) neque calumniis & captiosis effugijs aduersus contradicentes vtatur. Quod exemplum satis docet, quo loco haberi debeant, qui hodie in nos quidem pro concionibus publicis & scriptis etiam libris virulentissimè inuehuntur, interim vero doctrinam nostram nō bona fide proponunt, argumenta item nostra vel dissimulant, vel falsò adducunt, adhæc apud principes hoc agunt, vt nostri libri proscribantur, ne videlicet fit, qui ex nostris responsionibus nostram innocentiam discat, & ipsorum fraudes atque calumnias intelligat. Habent ili præcipuum suæ doctrinæ falsæ præsidium in populi ignorantia: sed quò magis hanc fouent & augent, eò magis causam suam cordatis omnibus suspectam faciunt, neq; diu consistere potest regnum, quod ipsi lu<sci & strabi in cæcos obtinent. Tandem enim ex tenebris emergit veritas, & fulgore suo omnes mendaciorum nebulas dissipat.
units.tr: Now before all things we must consider the faithfulness and integrity of Paul, who sets out the arguments of his opponents so carefully and candidly, and conceals nothing of those by which they defended themselves. The Apostles do this everywhere, and many things of this kind can be seen in the epistle to the Romans, which for the most part consists of disputations held on both sides. In these shines the certainty of apostolic teaching, which neither seeks darkness (as impostors usually do) nor uses calumnies and captious evasions against those who contradict it. This example shows well how those should be regarded who today rail at us most virulently, both in public sermons and in written books, yet meanwhile do not set forth our doctrine in good faith, and either conceal or falsely cite our arguments; and moreover they work at the courts of princes to have our books banned, so that, of course, no one may learn from our replies our innocence, and understand their frauds and calumnies. They have as the chief defence of their false doctrine the ignorance of the people; but the more they foster and increase this, the more they make their cause suspect to all sensible men, and a kingdom which they hold over the blind, though they themselves are squint-eyed, cannot long endure. For in the end truth emerges out of darkness, and by its own brightness scatters all the clouds of lies.

units.la: Deinde elucet in hac aduersariorum Pauli argumentatione, quæ sit humani ingenij cæcitas cum prauitate & peruersitate coniunctæ. Quæcunq; enim isti dicunt, verißima sunt. Nam idola aut simulachra reuera nihil sunt, & ideo in scripturis Elilim, id est, vanitates aut res inanes atq; mendaces dicuntur. Quoad enim materiam, ex ligno plerunq; constant, in quo neq; diuinitas nüque virtus aliqua saluifica continetur. Et hic imprimis ridiculos sese præbent, qui illa vel faciunt vel colunt, quod olim probè Isaias obseruauit, qui de illis sic scripsit. Accingit se quispiam ad cædendum ligna, vt ilicem aut quercum aduehat, & corroborat se in lignis sylua: plantat pinum, quam pluuia æducat. Fit hæc homini ad incendendum ignem, & ex his calefit: quin eo incenso panem coquit, deinde & Deum ex ijsdem facit, & adorat: sculptile illud facit, & coram eo procumbit. Partem eius incendit igne, parte eius carnes coquit, assat assaturam, & satur fit: calescit quoque, & dicit: Euge caleo, & ignem sensi. Reliquum autem eius facit Deum, simulachrum (inquam). quam)sui,coram quo procumbit,quod adorat,& coram quo precatur,dicens:Libera me,nam Deus meus es tu,&c. Sunt haec tam vera tamq;manifesta,ut Poetae etiam ea videre potuerint.Anno enim cum prophetiis hisce conveniunt,quae Satyricus de suo Priapo & eius fabricatore dicit, Illum enim sic inducit loquentem:
