units.tr: Next, in this argumentation of Paul's opponents, it shines forth what blindness of the human mind is joined with wickedness and perversity. For everything these men say is most true. For idols or images are indeed nothing, and therefore in the Scriptures they are called "elilim" [Elilim], that is, vanities, or empty and false things. For as to their material, they are for the most part made of wood, in which there is neither divinity nor any saving power. And here especially they show themselves ridiculous, who either make or worship them; which Isaiah long ago rightly observed, who wrote about them thus: "A man takes wood to cut, and takes an oak or a holm-oak, and strengthens himself among the trees of the forest; he plants a pine, which the rain makes grow. This is for a man to burn for fire, and with it he warms himself; yes, when he has lit it he bakes bread; then he makes a god of the same and worships it; he makes it a graven image and falls down before it. He burns part of it in the fire, with part of it he cooks flesh, roasts a roast and is satisfied; he also warms himself and says: 'Aha, I am warm, I have felt the fire.' But the rest of it he makes into a god, his graven image, I say, before which he falls down, which he worships, and before which he prays, saying: 'Deliver me, for you are my god,' etc." These things are so true and so manifest that even the poets could see them. For indeed with these prophecies agree the things which the Satirist says about his Priapus and its maker, for he introduces him speaking thus:

units.la: Olim truncus eram ficulnus inutile lignum: Cùm faber incertus scamnum faceretne Priapum, Maluit esse Deum: Deus inde ego furum auiumq;
units.tr: "Once I was a fig-tree trunk, a useless piece of wood; when an uncertain craftsman was deciding whether to make a stool or a Priapus, he preferred that I should be a god. So I became a god, the great terror of thieves and birds," etc.

units.la: Maxima formido,&c. Quod autè de ligneis simulachris dicitur,id nō minus de lapideis,testaceis,argenteis,aureis,pictis deniq;dici potest. Nam illic etiam ex eadē massa res diversissimæ fiunt, & inter alia sæpe simulachrum Dei aut Divi alicuius prodit,unde paulo ante vas aliquod ad usus non satis honestos prodierat. Quòd si formam consideres, Dei quidem & Deorum nomina profitentur,sed professio ista vanissima & mendacissima est. Nam Dei veri forma exprimi non po-test, quando illum nemo vidit unquam, & (ut Moses loquitur) ne voluit quidem videri, ne quis ei simulachrum alicuius formae facere auderet. Dij autem illi alteri nusquam in rerum na-tura sunt,ideoq;neq;eorum simulachra esse possunt, quae hoc nomine profitantur. Vere enim à Tertulliano observatum est,simulachra ex relationum numero esse,quorum ea natura est,ut uno negato aut sublato alterum consistere non possit. Verissimè ergo à Corinthijs nostris dicebatur, idolum nihil esse: verum quoq;erat, Deum esse unum, qui ut omnia creavit, sic omnia gubernat. Neq;male ex istis colligebant,carnes victimarum ex idolis nullam vel sanctificationem vel pollutionem contrahere, & quoad essentiam aut alendi nutriendiue virtutem neq;meliores neq;deteriores fieri. At salsissimum erat,quod ex illis inferebant,licere Christiano homini epulis in idoli honorem institutis accumbere, & ne tunc quidem eos pollui,qui illis non sine infirmorum scandalo vescebantur. Unde autem ista fallacia? Ex eo nimirum,quòd illa omnia ad gulam & improbissimos carnis affectus applicabantur,& pro sua libidine abutebantur. Nec enim vera consequen-tia est: Idolum nihil est,& Deus est unus: ergo carnibus idolothytis vesci & inter idololatrarum convivia accumbere licet. Imò quia Christianos homines veritati studere,& se totos quoad corpus & animam Deo impollutos servare convenit, potius concludendum erat, ab omni idolorum & idololatrarum consortio esse abhorrendum. At in meridiana luce caecutiunt,quicunq; carnis cupiditatibus sese duci patiuntur.
units.tr: What is said of wooden images can be said no less of stone, clay, silver, gold, and finally painted ones. For there too, from the same mass, very different things are made, and among other things an image of God or of some saint often comes forth, whereas a little before a vessel for not very decent uses had come out of it. And if you consider the form, they profess the names of God and of gods, but that profession is most empty and most false. For the true form of God cannot be expressed, since no one has ever seen him, and (as Moses says) he did not even will to be seen, so that no one would dare to make an image of any form of him. But those other gods nowhere exist in the nature of things, and therefore there can be no images of them, though they profess this name. For Tertullian has rightly observed that images belong to the class of correlatives, whose nature is such that when one is denied or removed, the other cannot stand. Most truly, then, were our Corinthians saying that an idol is nothing; it was also true that God is one, who, as he created all things, so governs all things. Nor did they reason badly from these premises, that the flesh of victims from idols contracts neither sanctification nor pollution, and as to its essence or power of nourishing, they are neither better nor worse. But what they inferred from these was most absurd: that it is lawful for a Christian to recline at feasts instituted in honour of an idol, and that those who eat them, not without offence to the weak, are not even then defiled. Whence then this fallacy? Assuredly from this, that all these things were applied to the appetite and to the most wicked desires of the flesh, and were abused according to their lust. For the consequence is not true: an idol is nothing, and God is one; therefore it is lawful to eat meat offered to idols and to recline at the feasts of idolaters. Indeed, since it is fitting that Christians should strive for truth, and keep themselves wholly, in body and soul, undefiled for God, it ought rather to have been concluded that they must shrink from all fellowship with idols and idolaters. But those who allow themselves to be led by the desires of the flesh are blind in broad daylight.

units.la: Et est haec diaboli Sophistica, qui ipse etiam ex veris falsa colligit, sicuti in tentationibus adversus Christum institutis est videre. Neq; desunt huius generis exempla in multis, qui sal-lacijs eiusmodi toti ecclesiae negotium faciunt. Quid enim aliud faciunt Romanenses, quando ad ravim usque clamant, Christum dixisse, Tues Petrus, & super hanc petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam. Item: Pasce oves meas? Agnoscimus nos Christi verba, & in illis eius fidem & cu-ram plus quàm paternam exosculamur, quà ecclesiae suae prospicit, & eandem adversus omnes hostium machinationes tuetur. Ac quod illi colligunt, Romanum Pontificem ecclesiae funda-mentum, caput & universalem omnium totius orbis ecclesiarum pastorem esse, id negamus: quia nihil huius ille dixit, neq; ita eius verba Apostoli acceperunt. Similis est nostro-rum adversario-rum audacia, qui ut corporis Christi realem & crassam in Coena mystica praesentiam atq; manducationem tueantur, nunquam non illius promissionem in ore habent: Ecce ego vobiscum sum usque in consummationem seculi: adhaec de illius maiestate, omnipotentia & gloria multis con-tendunt. Atqui nos neque promissionem illius negamus, neque eiusdem omnipotentiam & maiestatem in dubium vocamus: sed haec non obstare dicimus, quo minus sua corpori eius veritas constet, & Ascensionis in coelos articulus inconcussus maneat, inque ijs etiam ille verax fit, quae de suo ex terris discessu apud discipulos est concionatus. At ista omnia adversarij nostri vel malitiosè dissimulant, vel expositionibus violentis eludunt, & in sensum alienum detor-quent. Facilè autem viderent veritatis lucem inter haec omnia sese exerentem, nisi oculos ipsis perstringeret gloriae inanis studium, quo inflati errorem veterem pertinaciter potius tueri volunt, quàm hunc fatendo nominis & honoris sui existimationem in periculum adducere. Nobis autem utilissimum est, sæpe & diligenter in horum consideratione versari, ut cautiores facti à Sophistica illa nobis caveamus, ne vel nobisipsis, vel per nos multis alijs Satan imponat, quando Dei verbum malitiosè detorquet.
units.tr: This is the sophistry of the devil, who also draws false conclusions from true premises, as can be seen in the temptations set against Christ. Nor are there lacking examples of this kind among many who make a trade of deceiving the whole Church with such tricks. For what else do the Romanists do when they shout themselves hoarse that Christ said, "You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church," and again, "Feed my sheep"? We acknowledge Christ's words, and in them we embrace with more than a father's kindness the care he takes for his Church, which he watches over and defends against all the schemes of its enemies. But what they infer from them, that the Roman Pontiff is the foundation, head and universal shepherd of the church of the whole world, that we deny, because he said nothing of the kind, nor did the Apostles understand his words in that way. Our opponents show a similar boldness. To defend a real and gross presence and eating of Christ's body in the mystical Supper, they never cease having his promise on their lips, "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age," and besides this they argue at length about his majesty, omnipotence and glory. Yet we neither deny his promise nor call into doubt his omnipotence and majesty. We say only that these things do not stand in the way of the truth of his body being established, or of the article of his ascension into heaven remaining unshaken, and that he is true also in what he preached to his disciples about his departure from the earth. But our opponents either maliciously dissimulate all these things or evade them with forced interpretations and twist them into an alien sense. They would easily see the light of truth shining forth amid all of this, if the zeal for empty glory did not dazzle their eyes, by which, puffed up, they would rather stubbornly defend the old error than risk the reputation of their name and honour by confessing it. For us, however, it is most useful to dwell often and diligently on these matters, so that, made more cautious, we may guard ourselves against that sophistry, lest Satan impose it upon us, either upon ourselves or through us upon many others, whenever he maliciously twists God's word.

units.la: Caeterum pergamus in Apostoli verbis, qui etsi in adversariorum persona loquatur, paucis tamen & dilucidè veram doctrinam de Deo & fide vera, quàs[?] colitur, comprehendit. Quod ut commodius faciat, ante omnia errorem πολυθεΐας[?], id est, de multitudine Deorum confutat. Nam etsi sunt (inquit) qui dicantur Dij & in coelo & in terra (sicut sunt Dij multi & Domini multi) nobis tamen unus est Deus, &c. Fatetur quidem Deos multos in orbe coli, & infinitos tàm in coelis quàm in terris extare, qui Deorum nomine proflent[?]. In coelis enim fulgent Sol, Luna & totus ille siderum chorus, quem scriptura exercitum coeli dicere solet. Quibus omnibus numen inesse gen-tes credebant. In terris autem plurimi fuerunt, quos ijdem in Deos retulerunt, cum homines fuisse non ignorarent. Iam pridem enim error ille obtinuerat, ut Dij crederentur, qui aut inventi aliquius praeclari, aut beneficij publici fuissent authores. Et hanc suae Deitatis originem habuerunt ut veteres[?] illi Dij, Saturnus, Rhea, Iuppiter, Osiris, Bacchus, Mercurius, Iuno, Minerva, Venus, Mars, Plutus, Neptunus, Triton, cum innumeris alijs, quos longum foret recensere. Accesserunt posteris temporibus recentiores, Quirinus, Imperatores, Reges: & ut Tertullianus scribit, eò li-centia res pervenerat, ut Senatus Romanus penes se ius illud esse vellet, ut pro Deo coleretur, quem ipse hoc nomine & honore dignatus esset, inglorius autem & obscurus maneret, quem idè illè negligendum esse decreuisset. In quibus arrogantiam ne aut stultitiam magis admirare incertum est: quando sibi in coelos ius & imperium sumpserunt, qui ne in terris quidem aliquid possunt, nisi Deus ex alto vires dederit: imò Deos facere conati sunt, qui seipsos non poterant servare, quo mi-nus à morbis infestarentur, animalia sibi noxia sentirent, tempestates item & infinita alia sibi ad-versa experirentur. Sed ne hic quidem subsistit infelix superstitio, sed ita excaecati sunt multi, ut boves, vitulos, ciconias, ibices, crocodilos, & inanimata multa, utpote porrum, cepe, al-lia pro Dijs colerent: ut non temere Iuvenalis exclamarit: O sanctas gentes, quibus hæc nascuntur in hortis Numina. Quid? annon apud Romanos lapis Terminus Deus esse creditus est, & tantus quidem, ut illi Iupiter Capitolinus cedere coactus fuerit? Et idem, cum iam rerum Domini essent, Deos esse putarunt Rubiginem, Metum, Pallorem, Febrim, Stercutium, Cloacinum: ut iam de eo nihil dicam, quod fluviis, fontibus, arboribus singulis sua numina tribuerunt, adeoque in singulis domibus Lares & Penates habuerunt, ex quorum favore totam rei domesticae administrationem putabant pendere. Deniq; eò rem progressam fuisse conflat, ut D. Augustinus ex Varrone annotarit, circiter triginta millia Deorum fuisse, quos orbis terrarum coluit: in quem tamen censum procul dubio Dij illi minores, quos modò recitavimus, non venerunt. Et hoc quidem Paulus quoque fatetur in præsenti, at simul uno verbo omnes illos reijcit atque confutat, quando Deos dici ait, non esse. Nuda ergo hæc nomina erant, & tota istorum Deorum majestas sive Deitas ex superstitiosorum hominum opinione pendebat.
units.tr: Let us go on with the words of the Apostle, who, although he speaks in the person of the opponents, nevertheless briefly and clearly sets out the true doctrine concerning God and the true faith, which is worshipped. To do this more conveniently, he first refutes the error of polytheism, that is, of a multitude of gods. For although, he says, there are those who are called gods both in heaven and on earth (as there are many gods and many lords), yet for us there is one God, and so on. He admits indeed that many gods are worshipped in the world, and that countless ones exist both in heaven and on earth who go under the name of gods. For in heaven shine the sun, the moon and that whole host of stars which Scripture is wont to call the host of heaven, and the nations believed that a divine power dwelt in all of them. On earth there were very many whom the same people counted among the gods, though they did not fail to know that they had been men. For that error had long since prevailed, that those were believed to be gods who had been the authors either of some notable discovery or of some public benefit. And those ancient gods owe their deity to this origin: Saturn, Rhea, Jupiter, Osiris, Bacchus, Mercury, Juno, Minerva, Venus, Mars, Pluto, Neptune, Triton, with countless others, too many to list. In later times more recent ones were added: Quirinus, emperors, kings. And, as Tertullian writes, matters had come to such licence that the Roman Senate wanted the right to be its own: whoever it had itself honoured with this name and dignity should be worshipped as a god, while the one it had decided to neglect should remain without glory and obscure. It is uncertain whether we should marvel more at their arrogance or their folly, since they claimed for themselves rights and dominion in heaven, though they cannot do anything even on earth unless God gives strength from on high. Indeed they tried to make gods of those who could not even protect themselves from being harassed by diseases, from being harmed by hostile animals, and from experiencing storms and countless other adversities. But not even here does wretched superstition stop. Many were so blinded that they worshipped as gods oxen, calves, storks, ibexes, crocodiles, and many inanimate things, such as leek, onion and garlic. So Juvenal did not without reason exclaim: "O holy nations, in whose gardens such divinities grow!" What of it? Was not the stone Terminus believed among the Romans to be a god, and so great that Jupiter of the Capitol was forced to yield to him? And the same people, when they were already masters of the world, thought that Rust, Fear, Pallor, Fever, Stercutius and Cloacina were gods. I say nothing of how they assigned divinities to rivers, springs and single trees, and how they had Lares and Penates in every house, on whose favour they thought the whole management of domestic affairs depended. Finally, it is established that the matter progressed so far that, as Augustine noted from Varro, the world worshipped about thirty thousand gods. Yet undoubtedly those lesser gods we have just recited were not included in that count. Paul too admits this in the present passage, but with one word he rejects and refutes all of them at once, when he says that they are not gods. These were therefore bare names, and the whole majesty or deity of those gods depended on the opinion of superstitious men.

units.la: Ut verò Christianam religionem omni vanitatis istius suspitione liberet, & ab omnibus superstitionibus distinguat, addit: Nobis tamen unus est Deus. Nimirum ad illud Mosis respiciens: Audi Israel, Dominus Deus noster Dominus unus est. Et hoc passim Propheta inculcant. Per Isaiam certè clamat ille: Ego Dominus, & hoc est nomen meum, & gloriam meam alteri non dabo, neque laudem meam sculptilibus. Et rursus: Annon ego Dominus? & non est alius Deus præter me? Deus justus & salvans nullus præter me. Respicite ad me, & salvi eritis omnes fines terræ: Ego sum Deus, & nullus præterea. Itaque hoc Christianæ religionis proprium est, quòd alijs circa multos Deos occupatis, Christiani homines unum solum agnoscunt, qui ut omnia creavit & abs se creata gubernat: ita nos per Filium suum IESVM CHRISTVM redemit, ut ipsius simus peculium, in quo ipse glorificetur. Et hanc causam olim fuisse D. Augustinus scribit, ob quam gentes, cum in novis Dijs faciendis atque colendis diligentissimi essent, CHRISTVM tamen & religionem Christianam amplexi noluerint. Sciebant enim à Socrate verissimè dictum esse, unumquemque Deum ita coli debere, sicuti ipse se colendum esse praecepit. Quapropter cùm Christianorum Deum audirent solum coli & invocari velle, neq; collegas aut rituales vllos admittere, non potuerunt facile adduci, vt vnius causa totam illam Deorum multitudinem relinquerent, quorum cultibus à pueris assuefuerant. Et quod illis accidit, hoc ipsum hodie etiam multis accidere solet, vt à vera fide in Christum non alia de causa abhorreant, quàm quòd hunc solum doceri & in eius solius merito omnia monstrari audiunt, quae nobis ad salutem sunt necessaria. Ferre enim possunt, vt quis illum nobis à Deo iustitiam, mediatorem, aduocatum, sacrificium pro peccatis factum esse dicat. Quàm primum vero ad particulam illam exclusiuam, SOLVS, venitur, & ista omnia ita soli Christo tribuuntur, vt nullus Dius[?] mediatoribus, nostrae item iustitiae, nostris satisfactionibus, vt neque Missae sacrificio aut purgatorio igni, locus reliquus fiat: mox stupent[?], & absurdum putant, omnibus aliis relictis in vno & solo Christo acquiescere. At neminem ista moueant, sed scripturas audire debent, quotquot veri Dei cultores dici & haberi volunt, & cùm Deus ipse se vnum esse profiteatur, & ne Deos alios ipsi coniungamus graviter admodum praecipiat, nemo tantum sibi ipsi permittat, vt aliquid hic sibi licere putet. Ambulabunt quidem (vt Micheas ait) omnes populi, quisque in nomine Dei sui, nos autem ambulemus in nomine Domini Dei nostri in seculum, & proinde cum Paulo dicamus: Etiamsi multi sint qui Dij dicantur & in coelo & in terra, nobis tamen Deus vnus est.
units.tr: But in order to free the Christian religion from every suspicion of this vanity, and to distinguish it from all superstitions, he adds: "Yet for us there is one God." Clearly he is looking back to that saying of Moses, "Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord." The prophets also repeat this everywhere. Through Isaiah he certainly cries out: "I am the Lord, and this is my name; I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to graven images." And again: "Is it not I, the Lord? and there is no other God besides me. A just God and a saviour; there is none besides me. Look to me, and be saved, all you ends of the earth, for I am God, and there is none else." Therefore this is peculiar to the Christian religion: while others are occupied with many gods, Christians acknowledge one alone, who both created all things and governs what he has created, and who has so redeemed us through his Son Jesus Christ that we may be his own possession, in whom he himself may be glorified. Augustine writes that this was once the reason why the nations, though most diligent in making and worshipping new gods, nevertheless refused to embrace Christ and the Christian religion. For they knew that Socrates had said most truly that each god ought to be worshipped in the way that he himself commanded. Therefore, when they heard that the God of the Christians wished to be worshipped and invoked alone, and would admit no companions or rivals, they could not easily be brought to abandon, for the sake of one, that whole multitude of gods to whose worship they had been accustomed from boyhood. What happened to them still often happens to many today, who shrink from the true faith in Christ for no other reason than that they hear that he alone is taught, and that in his merit alone are shown all the things necessary for our salvation. For they can bear it if someone says that he has been made for us righteousness from God, mediator, advocate, and sacrifice for sins. But as soon as one comes to that exclusive particle, ALONE, and all these things are so attributed to Christ alone that no room is left for other mediators, for our own righteousness, our own satisfactions, or for the sacrifice of the Mass or purgatorial fire, they are struck dumb and think it absurd to rest in Christ alone, with all else set aside. But such things should not move anyone. Whoever wishes to be, and to be considered, worshippers of the true God ought to hear the Scriptures. Since God himself professes that he is one, and sternly commands that we join no other gods to him, let no one permit himself so much as to think that anything is allowed here. "All peoples will walk," as Micah says, "each in the name of his god; but we will walk in the name of the Lord our God for ever and ever." And so, with Paul, let us say: "Even if there are many who are called gods both in heaven and on earth, yet for us there is one God."

units.la: At hic obseruabis, Paulum ita de Deo vno differere, vt in vna illa essentia personas di-stinctas esse non dissimulet. Nam & Patrem & Filium nominat, & vtrumque suis etiam proprietatibus ab altero distinguit. Nobis (inquit) vnus est Deus, Pater ille, ex quo omnia, & nos in ipso: & vnus Dominus IESVS CHRISTVS, per quem omnia, & nos per ipsum. Quem Deum vnum dixerat, mox Patrem & Filium nominat. Distinctae ergo in illa Deitate personae sunt. Nec debet hic nobis scrupulum mouere, quòd illum quidem diserte Deum, hunc vero Dominum dicit. Solent enim duo haec nomina in scripturis saepe coniungi, quoties de Deo vero & vno sermo est, vt in locis supra ex Mose & Isaia adductis cernitur: saepe etiam permutantur, vt Pater quidem Dominus simpliciter, Filius autem Deus & quidem Iehoua (quod Dei nomen essentiale & proprijssimum est) dicatur. Exempla passim occurrunt, vt illius commemorandi non opus sit insistere. Et vt Pauli verba consideremus, quemadmodum à rerum omnium dominio Patrem non excludit, licet Filio Domini nomen adscribat: ita neque Filium Deum esse negat, etiamsi Dei nomen de Patre praedicet. Quin vt distinctè loqueretur opus erat propter Iudaeos, qui personarum distinctionem nullam agnoscunt, & quaecunque de Deo vno dicuntur, in eum sensum detorquent, vt Filij Deitatem omnino negent. Ideo etsi nominibus & proprietatibus Patrem & Filium distinguat, ea tamen de vtroque dicit, quae non nisi de Deo vere & proprie dici atque intelligi possunt. Nam quoad Domini nomen, constat quidem hoc Filio fere tribui, quòd nos sanguine suo redemit, & quòd ei in carne manifestato omne iudicium & omnis potestas in coelo & in terra data sit: at simul certum est illud ipsum soli Deo proprie conue- nire, quod ipse apud Isaiam testatur. Et hoc ne gentes quidem omnino ignorauerunt, quando de Augusto scribitur, quòd se Dominum dici vetuerit: nimirum quòd nomen istud augustius & sublimius esse sentiret, quàm quod de homine mortali posset praedicari. Et huc facit in praesenti, quòd vt vnum Deum, ita vnum Dominum esse Paulus fatetur. Nam ex eo constat, ipsum non de alio Domino loqui, quàm qui idem Deus sit. At quia de personis illi sermo est, proprietatibus quoque easdem distinguit. Nam de Patre dicit: Ex quo omnia, & nos in ipso. De Filio autem: Per quem omnia, & nos per ipsum. Ex Patre omnia esse, & nos in ipso consistere & seruari dicit, vt in illo principium & essentiam rerum omnium esse doceat. Rursus per Filium omnia condita, & nos quoque per ipsum seruari ait, vt huius cum Patre inseparabilem vnionem & potestatis atque gloriae aequalitatem exprimat. Quod mysterium Ioannes non minus diligenter quàm perspicuè expressit, sic scribens: In principio erat Sermo ille, & Sermo ille erat apud Deum, & Deus erat ille Sermo. Hic Sermo erat in principio apud Deum. Omnia per illum facta sunt, & absque eo factum est nihil quod factum sit. Scimus vt ista eludant Arianae haeresis instauratores, qui Filium Deum quidem esse fatentur, sed æternum & Patri coessentialem esse negant. Fingunt ergo Patrem, qui solus æternus sit, in primo rerum exordio Filium ex se genuisse, qui prius nullus fuerit, per quem postea mundum hunc omnem creavit. Atqui aliter Ioannes loquitur, qui non modo Verbum illud in principio fuisse, & apud Deum fuisse scribit, sed etiam addit: Et Deus erat ille Sermo. Si ergo aliquando non fuit Sermo ille, & initium habuit, iam Deum quoque aliquando non fuisse, & proinde initium habere fateamur oportet. Adhæc cum omnia per Filium facta sint, & sine hoc facto nihil sit, vanissimum est quicquid illi de Filio prius in eum finem genito aut facto nugantur, ut Pater eo in mundi huius creatione uteretur. Nam si nihil sine illo factum est, ab omnium eorum numero, quæ principium habent, illum eximere oportet. Adde, quod eiusdem potentiæ & virtutis est, quod Pater omnia creavit, & quod omnia per Filium creata sunt: quod item in Patre omnia consistunt, & quod eadem per Filium consistunt. Et poterant huius generis argumenta multa adduci, sed nos iis contenti sumus, quæ ad istius loci expositionem faciunt. Sufficiat ergo monuisse, ita nos adversus gentium superstitiones & Deorum alienorum multitudinem Dei veri & vivi unitatem asserere debere, ut interea personarum in illa unitate distinctionem adversus Iudæos & Mahumetanos omnesq; sacrosanctæ & adorandæ Trinitatis hostes constanter tueamur.
units.tr: Here you will observe that Paul, in speaking of the one God, does not hide the fact that there are distinct persons within that one essence. For he names both the Father and the Son, and distinguishes each from the other by their own properties. "For us," he says, "there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we in him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him." He had called the one God, and straightway he names the Father and the Son. Therefore there are distinct persons in that one Deity. Nor should it trouble us that he calls the one God explicitly God, but the other Lord. For these two names are often joined together in the Scriptures whenever the discussion concerns the true and one God, as is seen in the passages cited above from Moses and Isaiah. They are also often interchanged, so that the Father is called simply Lord, while the Son is called God, and indeed Jehovah (which is the essential and most proper name of God). Examples occur everywhere, so there is no need to dwell on recalling them. And, to consider Paul's words, just as he does not exclude the Father from dominion over all things, though he ascribes the name of Lord to the Son, so neither does he deny that the Son is God, even though he attributes the name of God to the Father. Indeed, he needed to speak distinctly because of the Jews, who acknowledge no distinction of persons and twist whatever is said of the one God to that sense, so that they utterly deny the Deity of the Son. Therefore, although he distinguishes the Father and the Son by names and properties, he nevertheless says of each those things which can be said and understood only of God truly and properly. For as regards the name of Lord, it is certainly true that this is commonly attributed to the Son, because he redeemed us with his blood, and because all judgment and all power in heaven and on earth were given to him when he was manifested in the flesh; yet at the same time it is certain that this very thing belongs properly to God alone, as he himself testifies in Isaiah. Even the Gentiles did not altogether fail to know this, since it is written of Augustus that he forbade himself to be called Lord; clearly because he perceived that this name was more majestic and sublime than could be predicated of a mortal man. And it bears on the present point that Paul confesses there is one Lord as well as one God. For from this it is established that he is not speaking of another Lord than the one who is the same God. But because his discussion concerns persons, he also distinguishes them by their properties. For of the Father he says: "from whom are all things, and we in him." Of the Son: "through whom are all things, and we through him." He says that all things are from the Father, and that we subsist and are preserved in him, so that he teaches that in him is the principle and essence of all things. Again, he says that all things were created through the Son, and that we too are preserved through him, so that he expresses the inseparable union of this Son with the Father and the equality of power and glory. John expressed this mystery no less diligently than clearly, writing thus: "In the beginning was that Word, and that Word was with God, and God was that Word. This Word was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made." We know that the restorers of the Arian heresy, who confess that the Son is God but deny that he is eternal and coessential with the Father, try to evade these things. They therefore imagine that the Father, who alone is eternal, at the first beginning of things begot the Son from himself, who previously did not exist, and through whom he afterwards created this whole world. Yet John speaks otherwise, for he not only writes that the Word was in the beginning and was with God, but also adds: "And God was that Word." If therefore there was a time when that Word was not, and it had a beginning, we must also confess that God once was not, and so must have a beginning. Moreover, since all things were made through the Son, and nothing was made without him, it is most absurd to babble, as some do, that the Son was begotten or made before this, to the end that the Father might use him in the creation of this world. For if nothing was made without him, it is necessary to remove him from the number of those things which have a beginning. Add that it belongs to one and the same power and virtue that the Father created all things, and that all things were created through the Son; likewise that all things subsist in the Father, and that the same things subsist through the Son. Many arguments of this kind could be brought forward, but we are content with those which pertain to the explanation of this passage. It is enough, therefore, to have warned that we ought so to assert the unity of the true and living God against the superstitions of the Gentiles and the multitude of strange gods, that meanwhile we steadfastly maintain the distinction of persons within that unity against the Jews and the Mahumetans and all the enemies of the most holy and adorable Trinity.

units.la: Quòd si quæras, cur nullam Spiritus Sancti mentionem Paulus hic faciat? in promptu est responsio: quia noluit absolutam de Dei essentia & Trinitatis mysterio tractationem instituere. Sufficiebat ergo ea dixisse, quæ ad Deorum multitudinem, inter gentes receptam, confutandam poterant sufficere. Et cum magna esset Corinthiorum ignorantia atque ruditas, non confusum[?] videbatur eos in profundiorem mysteriorum, quæ omnem humani ingenij captum superant, abyssum deducere. Et hanc causam Chrysostomo quoque placuisse, eius verba testantur. Quòd si hæc non sufficit alicui, age dicat ille nobis, cur alibi Patrem & Filium & Spiritum Sanctum conjungat? Cur item Christus discipulos in nomen Patris, Filij & Spiritus Sancti baptizare iussit? Quid hic aliud responderi poterit, quàm quòd personarum iisdem sit potestas, dignitas, maiestas & gloria? imò quòd Pater, Filius & Spiritus Sanctus Deus unus sit benedictus in sæcula?
units.tr: But if you ask why Paul makes no mention of the Holy Spirit here, the answer is ready: he did not wish to undertake a full treatment of the essence of God and the mystery of the Trinity. It was therefore sufficient for him to say those things which could suffice to refute the multitude of gods received among the nations. And since the ignorance and rudeness of the Corinthians was great, it did not seem fitting to lead them into the deeper abyss of mysteries, which surpass all the grasp of the human mind. The words of Chrysostom also testify that this reason pleased him too. But if this does not satisfy anyone, let him tell us why elsewhere he joins the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit together. Why, likewise, did Christ command his disciples to baptize in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit? What else can be answered here, except that the persons have the same power, dignity, majesty and glory? Indeed, that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are one God, blessed for ever?

units.la: Restat, ut quid de Deo hoc nos potissimum credere oportet videamus, quoad ea, quæ ad nos & ad totum fidei atq; salutis nostræ negotium proprie pertinent. Primum est, quòd ex ipso sint omnia. Et huc articulus ille Symboli Apostolici pertinet, quo fatemur, Patrem creatorem esse cœli & terræ, quibus alia omnia continentur, quæ in rerum natura sunt. Est hoc Deo ita proprium, ut Prophetæ passim hoc argumento verum Deum à falsis & alienis distinguant, & ipse per Ieremiam clamet: Dij, qui non fecerunt cælum & terram, perdentur de terra, & de sub cælis ipsis. Quid ergo de philosophis dicemus, quorum alij mundi huius machinam ab æterno fuisse, alij ex atomis & quacunq; alia materia temere exorta esse tradiderunt? Annon illos omnes Dei ignorasse, & proinde in primo salutis humanæ articulo offendisse patet? Christiani ergo homines in omnibus Deum creatorem agnoscant, quod imprimis utile & necessarium est. Ita enim subinde occurrent, quæ illos in veri Dei contemplatione ducere & in fide vera confirmare poterunt. Admonet præterea hoc, minimè opus esse simulachris hominum manu factis, cum ubiq; extent Dei opera, quæ nos de eius potentia, sapientia, bonitate & veritate admonent. Secundò tenere oportet, nos & nostra omnia in hoc uno Deo consistere. Comprehendit hoc providentia eius, qua res omnes iam inde ab æterno prædestinavit, & eadem per media certa & optima ad suos fines dirigit. Extenditur hæc ad omnes mundi partes, ut neq; flores in agris nascentes, neq; coruorum pullos negligat. Et huius consideratio diligens ut nos in officio continet, ita salutis certos reddit, & in omni tentationum genere efficacissimè consolatur. Tertiò in Filium respicere convenit, quem ille æterno suo consilio prædestinavit, ut nos sui sanguinis pretio redemptos ipsi reconciliaret. Itaq; ut omnia per Filium condita sunt: ita nos quoq; per eundem non modo quoad corpus & animam creati, verumetiam Filij Dei & ipsius coheredes facti sumus. Et hæc vera atq; salutaris Dei cognitio est, adeoq; hæc fidei Christianæ summa est, in qua sola hominis vita atq; salus habetur. Et quia hæc (ut supra diximus) ita Paulus proponit, ut hanc cognitionem atq; fidem ad solos Christianos restringat, satis apparet, à fidei & religionis Christianæ scopo eos omnes aberrare, qui vel Deos alios colunt, vel alios inter Deum verum & nos Mediatores fingunt, vel Deum simulachris exprimere & colere conantur. Solus enim Deus is est, ex quo omnia sunt, & cuius virtute & providentia nos consistimus atq; seruamur. Solus autem & unicus inter illum & nos Mediator est Filius eius IESVS CHRISTVS, per quem mundus hic totus conditus est, & per quem nos eam dignitatem obtinuimus, ut Filij Dei dicamur. Vt autem Deus in sua essentia simulachro aut imagine exprimi nō potest: ita neq; Filio simulachrum fieri debet, cùm is Legem non dissoluat, sed potius compleat. Istis ergo nos instituere decet, neq; eos audire, qui nouos fidei articulos condere, & ex suo capite cultus quoq; nouos instituere audent. Abutuntur hi fere Ecclesiæ Christi authoritate, & mutato Symboli Apostolici articulo, in Ecclesiam credendum esse docent. Et cùm ipsi sibi omnem in Ecclesia potestatem vendicent, mox hæreticos & apostatas inq; matrem Ecclesiam impios esse clamant eos, qui non omnibus ipsorum statutis subscribunt. Sed nihil huius unquam Apostoli tradiderunt, & vel unus hic locus istorum tyrannidem atq; impudentiam abunde conuincit.
units.tr: It remains to see what we chiefly ought to believe about God in this respect, as far as those things pertain properly to us and to the whole business of our faith and salvation. The first is that all things are from him. To this belongs that article of the Apostles' Creed by which we confess that the Father is the creator of heaven and earth, which contain all the other things that exist in nature. This is so proper to God that the prophets everywhere distinguish the true God from false and strange gods by this argument, and he himself cries through Jeremiah: "The gods that did not make heaven and earth shall perish from the earth and from under these heavens." What then shall we say of the philosophers, some of whom have taught that the machinery of this world has existed from eternity, and others that it arose by chance from atoms or some other matter? Is it not evident that all of them were ignorant of God, and therefore stumbled at the very first article of human salvation? Let Christians therefore acknowledge God as Creator in all things, which is above all useful and necessary. For thus, from time to time, things will occur which will be able to lead them into the contemplation of the true God and confirm them in the true faith. This also warns us that there is no need at all for images made by human hands, since the works of God are everywhere present, and remind us of his power, wisdom, goodness and truth. Secondly, we ought to hold that we and all our things subsist in this one God. His providence comprehends this, by which he has predestined all things from eternity, and directs them by certain and best means to their ends. This extends to all parts of the world, so that he neglects neither the flowers springing up in the fields nor the young of the ravens. Careful consideration of this both keeps us in our duty and makes us certain of salvation, and comforts us most effectively in every kind of temptation. Thirdly, it is fitting to look to the Son, whom he in his eternal counsel predestined to reconcile us to himself, redeemed by the price of his blood. Therefore, just as all things were created through the Son, so we too through the same were not only created as to body and soul, but have also been made sons of God and his fellow heirs. And this is the true and saving knowledge of God, and therefore this is the sum of the Christian faith, in which alone the life and salvation of man is found. And because Paul sets this forth (as we said above) in such a way that he restricts this knowledge and faith to Christians alone, it is sufficiently clear that all those stray from the aim of the Christian faith and religion who either worship other gods, or feign other mediators between the true God and us, or attempt to represent God by images and worship him so. For God alone is he from whom all things are, and by whose power and providence we subsist and are preserved. Yet the only and unique Mediator between him and us is his Son Jesus Christ, through whom this whole world was created, and through whom we have obtained that dignity, that we are called sons of God. Just as God cannot be expressed in his essence by a likeness or image, so an image should not be made of the Son either, since he does not dissolve the Law but rather fulfils it. We ought therefore to be instructed in these things, and not to listen to those who dare to frame new articles of faith, and of their own head to institute new forms of worship as well. These men commonly abuse the authority of the Church of Christ, and, changing an article of the Apostles' Creed, teach that one must believe in the Church. And while they claim for themselves all power in the Church, they straightway cry out that those who do not subscribe to all their statutes are heretics and apostates and impious towards the mother Church. But the Apostles never handed down anything of this kind, and this single passage abundantly convicts the tyranny and shamelessness of these men.

units.la: At quoniam in horum mentionem incidimus, non possum mihi temperare fratres in Christo dilectissimi, quin illustrissimi Principis, Sigismundi Austriaci, qui annis ab hinc retro centum & amplius vixit, historiam recitem, ut ex ea intelligatis, non hodie demum Pontificum insolentiam principibus displicere cœpisse, sed iampridem omnibus intolerabilem fuisse visam, qui communem patriam amarunt, & gloriam Dei voluerunt promotam. Inciderat optimo principi lis cum Cardinale Cusano, quem Pius Secundus Papa (qui prius Æneas Siluius dictus fuit) Brixiæ episcopum fecerat, ut eum opibus & dignitatibus augeret. Non poterat autem Sigismundus, cùm populi sui amantissimus esset, Cardinalis auaritiam & rapacitatem diutius ferre, & cùm non aliud remedium esset, tandem in arce quadam obsessum in suam potestatem redegit, & in custodia artissima detineri curauit. Doluit hoc factum Pontifici, & Sigismundum excommunicationis fulmine ferijt, adhæc indignum iudicauit, cuius defensionem aliquis audiret. Argumentum quo nitebatur, præcipuum erat, Sigismundum fidei articulum negare, quo Christiani fateantur, se credere in unam sanctam ecclesiam catholicam, sanctorum communionem, ideoque non debere à quoquam audiri. Ad ista optimus Princeps publico scripto inter alia sic respondet: Nos certè iam inde à pueris ita à patre nostro instituti sumus, ut credamus in Deum Patrem omnipotentem, creatorem cœli & terræ, & in IESVM CHRISTVM Filium eius unicum, Dominum nostrum, & in Spiritum Sanctum: Non autem in Ecclesiam. Atqui neque Symbolo Apostolico hoc continetur, ut in aliquam creaturam credamus. Fides enim illa, quam duodecim Apostoli, milites IESV CHRISTI, cùm ad certamen aduersus idololatras & gentes descenderent, uno corde & spiritu professi sunt, qua etiam sese armarunt, ut hoc quasi scuto telli hostium aciem perrumperent, hæc verba continet: Credo in Spiritum Sanctum: Sanctam ecclesiam catholicam. In hac fide nos cum duodecim Apostolis confitimur. Ubi verò ætate progressi & cultum Dei ab ecclesia sancta institutum diligentius observare cœpimus, tunc ex Symbolo à patribus in Niceno Concilio congregatis conscripto didicimus credere in unum Deum Patrem omnipotentem, omnium visibilium & invisibilium factorem: Et in unum Dominum IESVM CHRISTVM Filium Dei unigenitum: Et in Spiritum Sanctum, Dominum vivificatorem, &c: Et sanctam ecclesiam Catholicam: Non autem, In Ecclesiam. Ea etenim creatura & opus Dei est, factoris omnium visibilium & invisibilium. Hæc omnia ex vetustissima scheda, quæ illis omnino temporibus scripta videtur, optima fide ex Germanica lingua in Latinam transtulimus, ut vel hinc constet, maiores quoque nostros & fortissimos Germanorum veterum principes, non tantum Romanis Pontificibus tribuisse, ut in eorum gratiam à simplicitate fidei & doctrinæ apostolicæ discedere voluerint.
units.tr: But since we have come upon the mention of these men, dearly beloved brethren in Christ, I cannot refrain from relating the history of the most illustrious prince Sigismund of Austria, who lived more than a hundred years ago, so that you may understand from it that the insolence of the Popes has not only now begun to displease princes, but was long ago seen as intolerable by all who loved their native land and wished God's glory to be advanced. A dispute had arisen between that excellent prince and Cardinal Cusanus, whom Pope Pius II (formerly called Aeneas Silvius) had made bishop of Brixen, so that he might enrich him with wealth and honours. Sigismund, however, who was most loving toward his people, could not bear the Cardinal's greed and rapacity any longer. As there was no other remedy, he at last seized him in a certain fortress and had him kept under the closest custody. The Pope was angered by this deed and struck Sigismund with the thunderbolt of excommunication. Moreover, he judged that no one should hear his defence, since he was unworthy of it. The principal argument on which he relied was that Sigismund denied an article of faith, by which Christians confess that they believe in one holy catholic Church, the communion of saints, and therefore he ought not to be heard by anyone. To these charges the excellent Prince replied, among other things, in a public writing as follows: "From boyhood we have certainly been so taught by our father that we believe in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth, and in Jesus Christ his only Son, our Lord, and in the Holy Spirit; but not in the Church. Yet this is not contained in the Apostles' Creed, that we should believe in any creature. For that faith which the twelve Apostles, soldiers of Jesus Christ, professed with one heart and one spirit when they went down to the battle against idolaters and the Gentiles, and by which they armed themselves so that with it, as with a shield, they might break through the battle line of their enemies, contains these words: I believe in the Holy Spirit; the holy catholic Church. In this faith we confess with the twelve Apostles. But when, having advanced in years, we began more diligently to observe the worship of God instituted by the holy Church, then from the Creed composed by the Fathers gathered at the Council of Nicaea we learned to believe in one God the Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ the only-begotten Son of God; and in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, etc.; and the holy catholic Church; but not, In the Church. For the Church is a creature and work of God, the maker of all things visible and invisible. We have translated all these things in good faith from the German language into Latin from a very ancient sheet, which seems to have been written in those very times, so that it may be clear from this too that our forefathers, and the most valiant princes of the ancient Germans, did not so yield to the Roman Pontiffs as to wish to depart from the simplicity of the faith and apostolic doctrine for their favour.

units.la: Porrò ad Paulum redeamus, qui uno verbo ad Sophisticum illud aduersariorum argumen-tum respondit, & quasi flatu uno turgentem illam inani scientiæ persuasione bullam dissipat. Sed non in omnibus (inquit) est ea scientia, &c. Quasi diceret: Audio quidem vos ista scire, & proinde carnibus istis abstinere, absq; ulla superstitione vesci: sed non omnes illi, qui vobiscum accumbunt, aut vos accumbere vident, rem perinde vt vos intelligunt. Sunt enim nonnulli, qui ad hoc vsq; tempus post tam longam & diligentem in fide Christiana institutionem, carnes idolis immolatas cum conscientia idoli comedunt, & eas ex illo pollutionem aliquam contrahere suspicantur. Cuius error is causa est, quod idolis adhuc plus quàm par sit tribuunt. Ideo conscientia eorum, cum infirma sit, polluitur. Causa huius dicti est, quod qui reclamante conscientia aliquid faciunt, ij eo ipso testantur, se suae voluntatis maiorem quàm diuinae rationem habere: imò illi suam libidinem Dei praeceptis praeferunt, cum id faciant, quod illis aduersum esse intra animos suos conscientia propria dictat. Absque fide ergo id omne faciunt: at quod absq; fide fit, peccatum est, vt ad Rom. cap.14. scribitur. Admonemur igitur hoc loco, quantum referat, animos in diuinae voluntatis cognitione rectè instructos habere. Ea enim conscientiae vis est, vt opus medium aut indifferens possit bonum aut malum facere: & de hoc intelligi debet, quod alibi Paulus dicit: Omnia quidem pura puris: sed pollutis & infidelibus nihil est purum, sed polluta est eorum mens & conscientia. Vt vero de Dei voluntate certi & intra animos nostros securi simus, fieri non potest, nisi illum in verbo suo loquentem audiamus. Nec enim hic de opinione, quam ipsi temere animis concipimus, agitur: sed de certa voluntatis Dei cognitione, quae mentes prius fluctuantes confirmat, vt quid fieri aut caueri debeat, intelligant.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who with a single word answers that sophistical argument of your opponents, and bursts that bubble swollen, as with one breath, by the empty persuasion of knowledge. "But not in all," he says, "is that knowledge," and so on. As if he were saying: I indeed hear that you know these things, and therefore abstain from such meats and eat without any superstition; but not all those who recline at table with you, or see you reclining, understand the matter in the same way as you do. For there are some who, even now, after such long and careful instruction in the Christian faith, eat meats sacrificed to idols with a conscience of the idol, and suspect that they contract some pollution from it. The cause of their error is that they still attribute more to idols than is fitting. Therefore their conscience, since it is weak, is defiled. The reason for this saying is that those who do something while their conscience protests, by that very fact bear witness that they have regard to their own will more than to the divine reason; indeed, they prefer their own lust to the precepts of God, when they do what their own conscience within their minds tells them is contrary to them. Therefore they do all this without faith; but whatever is done without faith is sin, as is written in Romans chapter 14. We are admonished, therefore, in this place, how much it matters to have minds rightly instructed in the knowledge of the divine will. For such is the power of conscience that it can make an indifferent or intermediate act good or evil; and this must be understood of what Paul says elsewhere: "To the pure all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure, but both their mind and conscience are defiled." But in order that we may be certain of God's will and secure within our minds, this cannot happen unless we hear him speaking in his word. For here we are not dealing with an opinion which we ourselves rashly conceive in our minds, but with a certain knowledge of the will of God, which confirms minds previously wavering, so that they may understand what ought to be done or avoided.

units.la: Imprimis autem hic observare debet, non sufficere, vt nos rem de qua agitur intelligamus, sed aliorum quoque rationem habendam esse, quibus cum nobis res est, aut quos in nos respicere scimus. Est enim graue peccatum alijs scandalum ponere, quos aedificare & in fide confirmare debebamus. Et notum est illud Christi: Væ homini illi, per quem scandalum venit. Quisquis offenderit vnum ex paruis istis qui in me credunt, praestiterit ei, vt suspendatur mola asinaria ad collum eius, ac demergatur in profundo maris. Probè ergo cauere nos decet, ne nostra vel scientia vel libertate abutamur apud eos, qui ampliori institutione opus habent. Peccant hic graviter, qui clamant non debere sibi fraudi esse aliorum infirmitatem, quo minus ipsi sua libertate fruantur. Quibus responderi poterat: Atqui multò minus tua scientia & fides cuiquam hominum fraudi esse debet, cum omnium donorum Dei hic nobis vsus esse debeat, vt primò quidem eius gloria, deinde proximi aedificationi & saluti seruiant. Et quia sub Christo capite omnes eiusdem corporis membra sumus, non possumus membra infirmiora negligere aut contemnere, nisi nos prius à corpore Christi alienos facere, & tam fidei quam dilectionis Christianae leges violare velimus.
units.tr: Above all, one must observe here that it is not enough for us to understand the matter in question, but we must also take account of others with whom we have to do, or whom we know to look to us. For it is a grave sin to put a stumbling block before others whom we ought to build up and confirm in the faith. And that saying of Christ is well known: "Woe to that man through whom the offence comes. Whoever shall offend one of these little ones who believe in me, it would be better for him that a millstone were hung about his neck and he were drowned in the depth of the sea." We ought therefore to take great care lest we abuse our knowledge or our liberty among those who need fuller instruction. They sin grievously who cry out that the weakness of others ought not to be a hindrance to them, so that they should not enjoy their liberty. To these it could be answered: Indeed, much less should your knowledge and faith be a hindrance to anyone, since the use of all God's gifts ought here to serve us first for his glory, and then for the building up and salvation of our neighbour. And since, under Christ the head, we are all members of the same body, we cannot neglect or despise the weaker members, unless we wish to make ourselves alien from the body of Christ and violate both the laws of faith and of Christian love.

units.la: Meminisse item oportet, ecclesiam, quoad in terris hisce militat, non posse ad perfectionem pervenire, sed magnum semper fore numerum infirmorum, & saepe in minimis adhuc eos haerere, qui prae aliis instructi esse debebant. Exemplo nobis hic esse potest ecclesia Corinthiorum. Docuerat apud eos Paulus annum integrum & menses octo. Successerat ei Apollo, vir diligens & in scripturis egregiè versatus. Erant praeterea multi etiam alij, qui doctrinam veritatis fortiter tuebantur. Non potuit tamen horum omnium fides & diligentia efficere, quin infinitis alijs naevis atque vitijs hoc quoq; accederet, quòd idolis nonnulli plus quiddam tribuerent, & idolothytorum esu offenderentur. Quid igitur de nostri seculi hominibus sperare possumus, quando zelus ille & feruor iamdudum refriguit, quo primitivae ecclesiae fideles arserunt?
units.tr: It is also fitting to remember that the Church, as long as it fights on this earth, cannot attain to perfection, but there will always be a great number of the weak, and often those who ought to have been better instructed than others still cling to the smallest matters. The Church of the Corinthians may serve us as an example here. Paul had taught among them for a whole year and eight months. Apollos, a diligent man, well versed in the Scriptures, had succeeded him. Moreover, there were many others too who stoutly defended the doctrine of truth. Yet the faith and diligence of all these could not prevent this other fault, among countless others and vices, from attaching itself as well: that some attributed a certain power to idols and were offended by the eating of food sacrificed to idols. What then can we hope of the people of our own age, when that zeal and fervour have long since grown cold with which the faithful of the primitive Church burned?

units.la: Quòd si vero in ijs, quae per se indifferentia sunt, nostro iure interdum cedere debemus, ne libertate nostra cum aliorum scandalo abutamur: quanto magis hoc observare debet in ijs, quae prorsus illicita sunt, & diuinis legibus prohibentur? Huius vtinam meminissent, qui cum euangelicae veritatis doctores & inter hos antesignani haberi velint, imagines tamen in templis prostare sinunt, & eas pertinaciter tuentur aduersus eos, qui eiectas volunt. Clamant illi: Scimus imagines nihil esse, & nemo ex nostris tam stupidus est, quin sciat, ligno & lapidi non alligandam esse gratiam Dei. Atque vtinam hoc tam vere dicerent, quam frequenter in ore habent. Sed aliud nos docent multorum exempla qui simulachris non minus, quam olim ethnici, tribuunt. Et vt nemo id faciat ex nostris, cur nostro exemplo eorum superstitionem confirmamus, qui adhuc in papisticis tenebris haerent? Denique vt scandali periculum omnino nullum fit, minimè tamen fieri debebat, quod Deus diserte & magna cum gravitate prohibuit. Dicunt, curandum potius, ut idola ex cordibus eijciantur. Fateor. Sed non ex cordibus solum, verum etiam ex templis, ex aedibus priuatis, ex triuijs denique illa tolli vult Deus. Et apud prophetam fornicationes de sinu simul & facie procul remouere iubemur[?]. Similis eorum culpa est, qui magnum illud idolum Antichristianae superstitionis, Deum Mayzim, ambiguis suis de pane mystico locutionibus tuentur, & non sine contentione eos in errore detinent, quos in veritatis cognitione & legitimo Caenae Dominicae usu instituere debebant. Quantum autem istorum pertinacia ecclesijs hucusq; nocuerit, & quam insolenter piorum Martyrum cineribus ijdem non semel insultarint, nemo sine gemitu & lachrymis referre potest. Gloriantur quidem isti omnes eruditionis & multiplicis scientiae titulis, & apud rude vulgus iampridem summam doctrinae existimationem sibi pepererunt: Sed utinam Dei & proximi dilectione haec illorum scientia gubernaretur, & ecclesiarum potius aedificationi quam ostentationi studerent. Itaq; meminerint quaeso doctores sui officij esse, ut quam plurimos Deo lucrifaciant, & ideo infirmiores non inutili sublimium mysteriorum praedicatione grauent, sed simplici veritatis doctrina instituant atque confirment. Singuli vero discant in hoc esse, ut Deum unum colant in spiritu & veritate, & unum Dominum IESVM CHRISTVM audiant atque sequantur, qui nobis ab illo factus est sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio & redemptio. Huic debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & pote-stas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: But if in matters that are indifferent in themselves we ought sometimes, by our right, to yield, lest we abuse our liberty to the scandal of others, how much more ought this to be observed in those things that are altogether unlawful and forbidden by divine laws? Would that those men had remembered this, who wish to be regarded as teachers of the gospel truth and foremost among these, yet allow images to stand in their temples, and stubbornly defend them against those who want them removed! They cry out: "We know that images are nothing, and none of ours is so stupid as not to know that the grace of God is not to be bound to wood and stone." And would that they spoke as truly as they frequently have on their lips! But the examples of many who attribute no less to statues than the heathen once did teach us otherwise. And even if none of ours does this, why do we confirm by our example the superstition of those who still remain in papistical darkness? Finally, though there is absolutely no danger of scandal, it ought in no way to be done, since God has forbidden it expressly and with great seriousness. They say that care should rather be taken that idols be cast out of hearts. I agree. But God wills that they be removed not only from hearts, but also from temples, from private houses, and finally from the crossroads. And through the prophet we are commanded to remove the fornications from the bosom and the face together [?]. Similar is the fault of those who defend that great idol of Antichristian superstition, the god Mayzim, by their ambiguous expressions about the mystical bread, and not without contention keep in error those whom they ought to instruct in the knowledge of the truth and the lawful use of the Lord's Supper. How much the obstinacy of these men has hitherto harmed the churches, and how insolently they have more than once trampled on the ashes of the pious martyrs, no one can relate without groaning and tears. Indeed, all these men boast of the titles of learning and of manifold knowledge, and have long since won for themselves among the rude common people the highest reputation for doctrine. But would that their learning were governed by love of God and of neighbour, and that they strove rather for the building up of the churches than for display. Therefore, I beg you, let the teachers remember that it is their duty to win as many as possible for God, and so not to burden the weaker with the unprofitable preaching of lofty mysteries, but to instruct and confirm them by the simple doctrine of truth. Let each one learn in this to worship the one God in spirit and in truth, and to hear and follow the one Lord Jesus Christ, who has been made for us by him wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XLIII.

units.la: Cæterum esca nos non commendat Deo. Neque enim si vescamur, abundantiores sumus: neque si non vescamur, egentiores reddimur. Sed videte, ne quo modo potestas illa vestra fit offendiculo iis, qui infirmi sunt. Etenim si quis viderit te, qui scientia præditus es, in idolo accumbere, nonne conscientia ipsius, qui infirmus est, ædificabitur ad edendum ea, quæ sunt idolis immolata? Et tua ista scientia frater, qui infirmus est, propter quem Christus mortuus est, peribit? Ita autem peccantes in fratres, & vulnerantes ipsorū conscientiam infirmam, in Christum peccatis. Quapropter si esca facit ut offendat frater meus: non vescar carnibus in æternum, nec faciam ut frater meus offendat.
units.tr: Moreover, food does not commend us to God. For if we eat, we are not the better; and if we do not eat, we are not the worse. But take heed lest this liberty of yours somehow become a stumbling block to those who are weak. For if someone sees you, who have knowledge, reclining at a table in an idol's temple, will not the conscience of him who is weak be built up to eat things sacrificed to idols? And through your knowledge will the weak brother, for whom Christ died, perish? Thus, by sinning against the brethren and wounding their weak conscience, you sin against Christ. Therefore, if food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat, so that I do not make my brother stumble.

units.la: Quamuis Deus, qui spiritus est, in spiritu & veritate vult adorari, neq; villis rebus exter-nis coli potest, de ijsdem tamen præcepta dat, & ut illis recte utamur nos imprimis vi-dere oportet, ne quæ ille in nostrum usum condidit, ipsi per abusum nobis ipsis aut aliis noxia faciamus. Admonet de hoc frequenter spiritus sanctus, eò quod hic plurimum in omnem partem peccatur. Sunt enim qui pietatem & salutem hominis omnem in externis consistere putant, & proinde his solis occupantur: quod olim temporibus Prophetarum Iudæos fecisse constat, & docentibus iam Apostolis complures hoc ipsum fecerunt, & hodie error iste longè latèq; dominatur. Alij vero ne-glectis prorsus externis omnibus, libertate per Christum nobis quæsita turpiter abutuntur cum scandalo multorum, quos ipsi in fide ædificare debebant. Et hoc illud erat, in quo à Corinthijs pecca-batur quoad epulas, quas ethnici & idololatræ ex sacrificiorum aut victimarum carnib. instruebat. His enim sæpe Christiani quoq; homines, ab amicis aut vicinis vocati intererant, & se plus satis excusatos esse arbitrabatur, quod idola Deorum nihil præter inania nomina esse scirent, & proinde nihil in eorum honorem facerent, sed amicitiæ seruandæ causa epulis istis, ut quibuscunque alijs prophanis atq; vulgaribus accumberent. Erat autem hæc illorum leuitas plena scandali, atq; suo exemplo Euangelij cursum tam apud infirmiores ex Christianorum grege, quam apud prophanas gentes vehementer impediebat. Quæ causa est, quod Paulus hanc causam multis & grauiter agit. Et nuper quidem ostendit, quàm inanis sit hæc scientiæ gloriatio, qua sese excusabant, & monuit, unumquenque aliorum etiam, quibus cum vivit, rationem habere debere. At nunc longius progreditur, & quæ hinc incommoda nascantur docet.
units.tr: Although God, who is a Spirit, wills to be worshipped in spirit and truth, and cannot be honoured by outward things, yet he gives precepts concerning them. We must above all take care to use them rightly, so that we do not, by abusing what he has established for our use, make them harmful to ourselves or to others. The Holy Spirit often warns us of this, because sin is committed on this point in very many ways. For there are some who think that all piety and human salvation consist in outward things, and so occupy themselves with these alone. This the Jews are known to have done in the times of the Prophets, and although the Apostles were teaching, many did the same, and today this error rules far and wide. Others, on the other hand, entirely neglecting all outward things, shamefully abuse the liberty won for us through Christ, to the scandal of many whom they ought to have built up in the faith. This was the very sin of the Corinthians concerning the feasts which the heathen and idolaters held with meat from sacrifices and offerings. For Christians too were often invited to these by friends or neighbours and attended, and they thought themselves more than sufficiently excused, because they knew that the idols of the gods were nothing but empty names, and so they did nothing in honour of them. They reclined at these feasts merely to keep up friendship, just as they would at any other profane and common gathering. Yet this levity of theirs was full of scandal, and by their example it greatly hindered the course of the gospel, both among the weaker part of the Christian flock and among the profane nations. This is why Paul treats this matter at length and with weight. Lately he has shown how empty is this boasting of knowledge by which they excused themselves, and has warned that each one must also have regard for others with whom he lives. But now he goes further and teaches what inconveniences arise from it.

units.la: Occurrit hic primum grauis admonitio, qua per Concessionem & Præoccupationem diluit aliud argumentum, quo aduersarij sese tuebantur. Dicebant enim: Atqui esca nos non commendat Deo, id est, cultus ille, qui nos Deo gratos & acceptos reddit, minimè in alicuius cibi esu aut abstinentia consistit. Ratio: Quia si edamus, nō sumus abundantiores, quoad ea nimirum quae ad regnum Dei pertinent: qualia sunt, remissio peccatorum, gratia Dei, iustitia, sanctificatio, & ipsa deniq; vita aeterna. Rursus, si non edamus, nihilo etiam egentiores sumus, neq; aliquid nobis deest eorum, quae modo commemorauimus. Ex his autem inferebant: Quid ergo opus est tumultuari, & propter ista nobis litem mouere? Aut quid hoc ad te aut quemuis alium, si faciamus, quod nobis licet per Christum? Vel num aliorum tarditas & superstitio nobis fraudi esse debet, quo minus libertatis Christianae beneficio fruamur? At hic rursus Sophisticae illius exemplum habemus, quae (vt nuper diximus) ex veris falsum colligit. Huius enim argumenti antecedens per se verissimum est, & cum iis conuenit, quae Dominus ipse pronuntiauit.Nam apud de ieiunio quinti & septimi mensis interrogatus, respondit: Quando ieiunastis & planxistis in quinto & septimo per hos septuaginta annos, num ieiunando mihi ieiunastis? Et cum comeditis & bibitis, annon vobis comeditis, & vobis bibitis? Quasi diceret: Nihil ista ad me, neque ego re-fris[?] cibis aut ieiunijs coli possum: sed omnis ista siue voluptas siue acerbitas in vobis haeret.Con-sentit his, quod in Euangelio Christus pronuntiauit: Non quod per os ingreditur, inquinat hominem: sed quod egreditur ex ore, hoc inquinat hominem. Et Apostolus hanc ipsam causam in epistola ad Romanos tractans, dicebat: Non est regnum Dei esca aut potus: sed iustitia & pax & gaudium in Spiritu sancto. Item ad Hebraeos: Bonum est gratia confirmari cor, non cibis, quibus non sunt adiuti, qui in ipsis versati sunt. Verissime ergo dicebant, esca nos non commendare Deo, neque alijs praestare eos qui omnibus vescuntur, neq; inferiores esse alijs eos, qui a nonnullis abstinent: At salsissimum erat, quod ex his colligebant, Licere nimirum nulla fratrum ratione habita quibuslibet vbique & semper vesci.
units.tr: Here first comes a serious admonition, by which, through concession and anticipation, he refutes another argument by which the opponents defended themselves. For they said: "Yet food does not commend us to God," that is, that worship which makes us pleasing and acceptable to God does not consist at all in the eating or abstaining from any kind of food. The reason: because if we eat, we are not more abundant in those things which pertain to the kingdom of God, such as remission of sins, the grace of God, righteousness, sanctification, and finally eternal life itself. Again, if we do not eat, we are not poorer in these things, and nothing of those we have just mentioned is lacking to us. From this they inferred: "Why then is there any need to make a commotion and to stir up strife on account of these things? What does it matter to you or to anyone else if we do what we are free to do through Christ? Or should the slowness and superstition of others be a hindrance to us, so that we may not enjoy the benefit of Christian liberty?" But here again we have an example of that sophistry which (as we said recently) draws a false conclusion from true premises. For the antecedent of this argument is in itself most true, and agrees with what the Lord himself declared. For when he was asked about the fast of the fifth and seventh month, he answered: "When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh month for these seventy years, did you truly fast for me? And when you eat and drink, do you not eat and drink for yourselves?" As if he said: "These things have nothing to do with me, nor can I be honoured by foods or fasts; but all such things, whether pleasure or bitterness, cling to you." In agreement with this is what Christ declared in the Gospel: "What goes into the mouth does not defile a man, but what comes out of the mouth defiles a man." And the Apostle, treating this very question in his letter to the Romans, said: "The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit." Likewise to the Hebrews: "It is good that the heart be strengthened by grace, not by foods, by which those who have been occupied with them have not been helped." Therefore they spoke most truly when they said that food does not commend us to God, nor do those who eat all things excel others, nor are those who abstain from some things inferior to others. But what they inferred from these premises was utterly false: namely, that it is lawful to eat anything, anywhere and always, with no regard for the brethren.

units.la: Ideo Paulus argumentum illud grauiter confutat, dicens: Sed videte, ne quo modo potestas illa vestra fit offendiculo ijs, qui infirmi sunt. Quibus verbis libertatem quidem illis concedit, eius vero vsum ita moderandu aut regendum esse docet, ne infirmiores offendant: quo nomine eos intelligit, qui in doctrina verae pietatis nondum eo vsq; profecerunt, vt non offendantur quorundam dictis aut factis, quorum rationem nondum intelligunt. Est ergo verborum istorum sensus: Fateor vos istud vere dicere, quod esca nos non commendet Deo, neq; dissimulare debemus Christi beneficium, qui Legis iu um[?] etiam quoad ciborum discrimina sustulit: at simul nos videre oportet, ne dum potestate per illum nobis facta imprudenter vtimur, ijs scandali authores simus, qui nondum satis norunt, in quo nam libertas Christiana consistat. Habent aute[?] singula verba emphasin, & proinde diligentius debent excuti. Primo, Videte ait: Ostendit ergo periculum minime contemnendum huic negotio subesse, & diaboli frequenter sub libertatis praetextu nobis insidias struere: quo magis nos vigilare conuenit, vt hostis tam vafri & versipellis laqueos euitemus. Deinde non scientiae neq; libertatis vocabulis vtitur, sed potestatis meminit, vt offendat, ipsos in hac re nimis licenter insolentiam suam prodere, quando potestatem nullis fraternae dilectionis finibus limitatam sibi vendicent, & ea deinde pro sua libidine abutantur. Et hoc facit, quod sub tacitae exprobrationis specie dicit: Potestas illa vestra. Q. d. quam ipsi sub inanis scientiae titulo vobis fingitis. Tertio, quid videre oporteat, monet. Ne potestas illa offendiculo fit ijs, qui infirmi sunt. Cuius verbis duplex scelus comprehendit: Alterum, quod non agnoscant Dei dorum[?], neq; de eius vsu vero cogitent: alterū, quod eo ipso noceant, quo plures alios debebant iuuare. Quod vnum ad arguendam huius peccati indignitatem plurimum facit. Ideo enim amplior scientia & maiores vires nonnullis dantur a Domino, vt eos qui rudiores sunt iuste instruant, & aliorum infirmitati opitulentur. Itaq; nulla venia dignum scelus est, si non solum officio suo desint, verumetiā alijs ruinae authores sint. Neq; temere tam graviter de his Paulus admonet. Sciebat enim quanta sit sceleris istius atrocitas, & quid Christus omnibus minetur, qui vel vnum ex minimis offenderint. Vide Matt.18.
units.tr: Therefore Paul refutes that argument seriously, saying: "But take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumbling block to those who are weak." In these words he indeed concedes the liberty to them, but teaches that its use must be so moderated and governed that the weaker are not made to stumble. By "the weaker" he means those who have not yet advanced so far in the doctrine of true piety that they are not offended by the words or deeds of certain people whose reasons they do not yet understand. The sense of these words, then, is this: "I admit that you rightly say that food does not commend us to God, and we ought not to dissemble the benefit of Christ, who abolished the Law even as to the distinctions of foods. Yet at the same time we must take care that, while we use imprudently the power given us through him, we do not become the authors of scandal to those who do not yet sufficiently know in what Christian liberty consists." Each word here carries emphasis and so must be examined more carefully. First, he says "Take heed": he thus shows that a danger not to be despised lies in this matter, and that the devil often lays snares for us under the pretext of liberty, so that we ought the more to be watchful, in order to avoid the snares of so crafty and shifty an enemy. Second, he does not use the words "knowledge" or "liberty," but speaks of "power," so that they may stumble; this shows that they reveal their arrogance too freely in this matter, when they claim for themselves a power limited by no bounds of brotherly love, and then abuse it at their own pleasure. He does this also when, under the appearance of tacit reproach, he says: "your power." As if to say: "which you yourselves invent for yourselves under the title of empty knowledge." Third, he admonishes what they ought to see: that this power should not become a stumbling block to those who are weak. In these words he comprehends a double wrong: the one, that they do not acknowledge the gifts of God, nor think rightly about their use; the other, that by this very thing they harm those whom they ought rather to help. This one point greatly serves to show the unworthiness of this sin. For a fuller knowledge and greater strength are given by the Lord to some so that they may justly instruct those who are more ignorant and come to the aid of the weakness of others. Therefore it is a wrong unworthy of any pardon if they not only fail in their duty but also become the authors of ruin to others. Nor does Paul warn so gravely about these things without cause. For he knew how great is the atrocity of this offence, and what Christ threatens to all who offend even one of the least. See Matt. 18.

units.la: Est autem hic multa obseruatione dignum, quod etsi Paulus amplissimā occasionem oblatam videret, vt omni idolothytorum esu Christianis hominibus interdiceret, noluit tamen temere legem ferre universalem, quæ Christianæ libertati vel minima ex parte derogaret: sed hanc va-nam ob causam à carnibus eiusmodi abstinendum esse docet, ne quibus scandalum ponamus, qui in fide nondum satis sunt instituti. Unde non obscure colligitur, carnes ipsas nihil habere quo pol-lui possit, qui illis absque scandali periculo vescitur. Est ergo intolerabilis eorum tyrannis, qui posteris temporibus noua ciborum discrimina constituerunt, & simul leges suas ad certos dies re-strinxerunt, quibus hoc aut illo cibo vesci non liceat. Pugnant illorum leges & statuta cum Christi legibus, & tota Apostolorum doctrina, quam paulo ante recitauimus: & multa simul designat, quæ singula reprehensione digna sunt. Primo enim ad Dei Verbum sua figmenta adijciunt, & dulce illud Christi iugum ipsa Lege Mosaica duriùs & intolerabiliùs reddunt, quam tamen Pe-trus patribus intolerabilem omnino fuisse testatur. Deinde conscientijs tam ante plus satis infirmis laqueum iniiciunt, & dum peccata fingunt quæ nulla sunt, simul etiam scandala augent, quæ potius ad numerum exiguum restringere, & (si fieri posset) prorsus è medio tollere oportebat. Ac cedit his crudelitas & tyrannis quando suorum decretorum authoritatem ita urgent, ut hæreticum & quouis supplicio dignum esse iudicent, qui illa transgreditur. Eo denique dementiæ progrediuntur, ut per illos rutius[?] sit Virgini stuprum inferre, thorum alienum polluere, hominem occidere, quàm diebus vetitis ouum sorbere, aut carnem edere, ut laboribus à Deo tibi mandatis possis sufficere. Sunt hæc indigna auribus Christianis, dicenda tamen sunt, quando tanta est multorum soliditas, ut nescio quidem traditionum iustarum indignitatem agnoscere velint, quarum authorem diabolum esse, Paulus alibi testatur. 1. Tim.4.
units.tr: It is worth noting here that although Paul saw a very broad opportunity to forbid Christians all eating of meat offered to idols, he did not rashly lay down a universal law that would have detracted in any degree from Christian liberty. He teaches only that such meat should be avoided for the sake of not putting a stumbling block before those who are not yet sufficiently instructed in the faith. From this it is not obscurely inferred that the meat itself has nothing by which the one who eats it without danger of giving offence can be defiled. The tyranny of those who in later times established new distinctions among foods, and at the same time restricted their laws to certain days, on which it is not lawful to eat this or that food, is therefore intolerable. Their laws and statutes conflict with the laws of Christ and with the whole teaching of the Apostles, which we recited a little earlier, and they point to many things, each of which deserves rebuke. First, they add their own inventions to the Word of God, and make that sweet yoke of Christ harsher and more intolerable even than the Law of Moses, which Peter nevertheless testifies was altogether intolerable to our fathers. Then, they cast a snare upon consciences that are already weak enough, and while they invent sins that are not sins, they at the same time increase the scandals, which it was fitting rather to reduce to a small number and, if it were possible, to remove altogether. Cruelty and tyranny are added when they press the authority of their decrees so hard that they judge anyone who transgresses them to be a heretic and deserving of any punishment whatever.
