They have finally advanced to such madness that, by their rules, it is more permissible to inflict rape on a virgin, to defile another's marriage bed, or to kill a man, than to swallow an egg or eat meat on forbidden days, so that you may be able to sustain the labours enjoined on you by God. These things are unworthy of Christian ears, yet they must be said, since many people are so hard-headed that they will not acknowledge the unworthiness of these unjust traditions, whose author, Paul testifies elsewhere, is the devil. 1 Tim. 4.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui quòd sciolos istos non facilè agnituros esse sci-ret, apertius eos arguit, & qua ratione scandalum infirmis præbeant, docet his verbis: Etenim si quis viderit te, qui scientia præditus es, in idolæo accumbere, nonne conscientia ipsius, qui infirmus est, ædificabitur ad edendum ea, quæ sunt idolis immolata? Quem locum ut omnes rectius intelligant, morem tenere oportet, quem in sacrificijs suis veteres observarunt, & quem à sanctis patribus gentes quoque acceperant. Erant sacrificiorum genera duo præcipua, quibus reliqua pos-sunt comprehendi: Expiatoria nimirum, quæ pro peccato aut aliqua immunditia quocunque modo contracta offerebantur, & Eucharistica vel Gratulatoria, quibus Deo pro accepto aliquo beneficio, vel publico vel priuato, gratiæ agebantur. In illis ferè victima tota comburebatur, quod holocaustum dicebant, aut saltem ad sacerdotes redibat quicquid non debebat comburi, qui soli ea in loco sacro comedebant. In Eucharisticis autem, renes quidem & reticulum epatis, agnæ item cauda & omnis adeps comburebantur in ara holocaustorum, armus autem dexter & pectus sacerdotis erant, reliqua ad offerentem redibant, & mox illo ipso die debebant comedi. Quia vero non semper ad ea comedenda cum suis sufficiebat, qui illa obtulerat, solebant ferè ad epulas eiusmodi inuitari vicini & amici, quibus liberius etiam lætari licebat, modò id coram Domino cum gratiarum actione facerent, & interea pauperum non obliuiscerentur. Neque mysterio mos ipse carebat. Scimus enim Christum in sacrificijs omnibus adumbratum fuisse, qui ut pro nobis hostia aut victima expiatoria factus est: ita unicus etiam est omnium quæ à Deo nobis obtin-guntur, bonorum mediator. Cum ergo ex victimis conuiuia instruere iubebat Deus, non obscure tes-tabatur, quòd sua mensa cultores suos dignari, & eosdem per Filium suum, promissum humani generis seruatorem, ad vitam æternam alere vellet. Idem ergo veteribus in sacris epulis adumbra-tur, quod nobis Cœna Dominica repræsentat: & ideo illi eandem esse spiritualem nobiscum esse dicuntur. Sed & locutionibus utebantur, quæ de hoc mysterio illos admonerent. Nam in Paschali epulo audiebant dici: Hic est transitus Domini. In publicis autem & solennibus sacris, quæ totius populi nomine fiebant, Sacerdos sanguinem populo circumstanti aspergens dicebat: Hic est sanguis fœderis aut testamenti, quod mandauit vobis Deus, &c. Quod unum si attentius observaretur, plurimum faceret ad explicationem VerborūDomini, Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis traditur: Hic est sanguis meus, qui est noui testamenti, qui pro multis effunditur in remissionem peccatorum. De quibus hodie multi digladiantur, cùm ea discipulis, quantumuis tunc adhuc rudes essent, obscura aut absurda videri non potuerunt. Nam quid aliud audiebant, quàm quod in Eucharisticis sacris, quæ publicè totius populi nomine fiebant, audiebatur? Cùm ergo verba poculi cum veteribus illis & iampridem vsitatis, quoad singulas voces & syllabas fere conuenire audirent, & de vera carnis Christi manducatione atque sanguinis eius potione antea satis esse instituti, nihil crassum aut absurdum illis in mentem venire potuit, qui alioqui in rebus minoris momenti solebant obstupescere. Sed hæc nunc obiter dixisse sufficiat. Nunc ad gentes transeamus, qui ut sacrificandi morem à Patribus sanctis acceperunt, ita diaboli præstigijs decepti per κακοζηλίαν[?], id est, stultam & impiam imitationem peccarunt. Ut enim in victimis suis expiationem peccatorum fieri putabant: ita suis illis conuiuijs & epulis sacris hoc unum agebant, ut & in superstitionum atque idololatriæ societatem sese mutuo traherent, & intemperantius epulati in omne genus lasciuiæ effunderentur. Itaque qui paulò ante Diis falsis victimas offerendo iucundum diabolo spectaculum præbuerant, mox eidem gratissimum obsequium præstabant, cum & ebriosis comessationibus indulgerent, & choros lasciuos ducerent, & stupris nefarijs polluerentur: quæ omnia sacrorum tempore imprimis factitata fuisse non potest ignorare, qui illorum historias & poëtas vel obiter inspexit. Et quid Israelitæ in vituli aurei cultu, atque inter sacra cum Moabiticis fœminis instituta fecerint, Moses non dissimulat. Neque dubium est, Corinthi, in urbe opulenta & luxuriosa in eiusmodi sacris nihil eorum omissum fuisse, quæ ad fouendam carnis libidinem faciebant. De illis ergo in præsenti Paulus loquitur, qui ad epulas idolis aut vicinis aut amicis suis, adhuc in superstitione agentibus, invitabantur, cum ipsi fidem in Christi iampridem essent professi. Et ut euidentior fit scandali, quod ex eo nascebatur, demonstratio, ad illos ipsos sermonem conuertit, qui sibi nihil non permissum putabant, quod scientia præ aliis essent instructi. Sic enim dicere videtur: Cogita quæso quisquis es, quid hic facias. Tu scientia præditus es, & eam apud omnes existimationem sustines, quòd in veri Dei & Filij eius IESV CHRISTI cognitione quàm optime sis instructus: quæ causa est, quòd multorum oculi in te respiciant, & tuo exemplo, ceu regula certa & infallibili, se duci patiantur. Quid ergo fieri arbitraris, si te in idolæo[?], id est, in templo idolorum, inter Deorum prophanorum undique profusa simulachra, inter horum item cultores & apertos Christi aduersarios, in conuiuio ex victimis aut sacris illicitis instructo accumbentem conspicetur aliquis Christianus infirmior, qui in veritatis cognitione nondum satis instructus est, & quoad libertatis Christianæ vsum adhuc intra conscientiæ dubiæ & fluctuantis cogitationes hæret? Hic certè tuo exemplo ædificatur, id est, permouetur & eò adducitur, ut ipse etiam, reluctante licet eius conscientia, ad conuiuia eiusmodi accedat, &c. Vides ergo Paulum ædificandi verbo per Catechesim, & non sine Sarcasmo aut exprobratione vti, Quasi diceret: Tuum erat fratrem infirmum ædificare in vera fide & solida IESV CHRISTI cognitione, ut rerum certus dubiæ mentis cogitationibus & conscientiæ æstuantis tentationibus resistere, & tàm corpus quàm animum sanctum atque impollutum seruare posset. Sed vah egregium ædificatorem, qui tali author est, ut præter conscientiam sacris communicet, & ijsdem polluatur? Quid hoc aliud est, quàm opus Dei destruere, veritatis cognitionem in illo obscuriorem facere, denique ruinæ & exitij causam ei præbere, cui tua scientia, & exempli tui authoritas ad fidei constantiam et religionis puritatem adiumento esse debebat? Hic loci istius sensus est, quo hoc maximè agit Apostolus, Christianis hominibus non tàm videndum esse quid ipsi facere liceat, quàm quid alij ex ipsorum exemplo colligant, & annon destructioni potius quàm ædificationi seruire possit quod ipsi faciunt. Nam ut omnia alia ad eum finem dirigi debent, ut & Dei gloriam prouehant, & publicè quidem totam ecclesiam, priuatim verò singulos ædificent: ita nisi hic quoq; libertatis Christianæ finis & scopus sit, in licentiam tam nobis ipsis quàm toti ecclesiæ exitialem erumpet. Quàmuis autem hæc doctrina generalis sit maximè, tamen illam ad se pertinere putabunt, qui multis alijs præstant, & quorum summa est apud omnes existimatio. Quò enim maior est eorum authoritas, eo efficaciora sunt exempla, quibus ipsi alijs præcunt. Quòd si verò aliquem corrumpunt, tunc aliena quoque peccata in suum caput accumulant, & simul atq; alienæ impietatis pœnas luunt. Est ergo amplus huius doctrinæ usus, et latissimè extendi debet ad omnia, quæ ad religionem aut ad mores & vitæ totius consuetudinem spectant.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who, knowing that these half-learned men would not readily acknowledge it, rebukes them more openly and teaches, in these words, how they give offence to the weak: "For if anyone sees you, who have knowledge, reclining at a meal in an idol's temple, will not the conscience of him who is weak be built up to eat things sacrificed to idols?" In order that all may understand this passage more correctly, one must keep in mind the custom that the ancients observed in their sacrifices, and which the nations also had received from the holy fathers. There were two principal kinds of sacrifice, under which the rest can be included: expiatory sacrifices, namely those offered for sin or for some uncleanness contracted in any way, and Eucharistic or thanksgiving sacrifices, by which thanks were given to God for some benefit received, whether public or private. In the former the whole victim was usually burned, which they called a holocaust; or at least whatever was not to be burned returned to the priests, who alone ate it in the holy place. In the Eucharistic sacrifices, the kidneys, the caul of the liver, the tail of the lamb and all the fat were burned on the altar of holocausts; the right shoulder and the breast belonged to the priest; the rest returned to the one offering, and was to be eaten that very day. But since the one who had offered them was not always able to eat them all with his family, neighbours and friends were usually invited to such feasts, and they were permitted to rejoice more freely, provided they did so before the Lord with thanksgiving and did not forget the poor meanwhile. Nor was the custom without mystery. For we know that Christ was foreshadowed in all the sacrifices, who was made our victim or sacrifice for expiation, and who is likewise the only mediator of all the good things we obtain from God. Therefore, when God commanded that feasts be furnished from the victims, he clearly testified that he wished to honour his worshippers at his own table, and through his Son, the promised Saviour of the human race, to nourish them to eternal life. So what is foreshadowed to the ancients in the sacred feasts is the same that the Lord's Supper represents to us, and for this reason they are said to have the same spiritual food with us. They also used expressions that reminded them of this mystery. For at the Passover feast they heard it said: "This is the passing over of the Lord." In public and solemn sacrifices, which were performed in the name of the whole people, the priest, sprinkling blood on the people standing around, said: "This is the blood of the covenant or testament that God has commanded you," etc. If this one thing were observed more attentively, it would greatly help the explanation of the words of the Lord: "This is my body, which is given for you"; "This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the forgiveness of sins." Many today contend fiercely over these words, although they could not seem obscure or absurd to the disciples, however rude they still were at that time. For what else did they hear than what was heard in the Eucharistic sacrifices, which were performed publicly in the name of the whole people? Since they heard the words of the cup agreeing almost exactly with those ancient and long-established ones, in each word and syllable, and since they had already been sufficiently instructed about the true eating of Christ's flesh and the drinking of his blood, nothing crude or absurd could come into the minds of those who otherwise were used to being astonished at matters of lesser moment. But it is enough to have said these things in passing. Now let us turn to the nations, who, although they received the custom of sacrificing from the holy fathers, were deceived by the devil's wonders and sinned through kakozelia [κακοζηλία], that is, a foolish and impious imitation. For just as they believed that expiation of sins was made by their victims, so at those feasts and sacred banquets they did this one thing: they drew each other into a fellowship of superstition and idolatry, and, eating and drinking too immoderately, they poured themselves out into every kind of lewdness. Thus those who a little before had offered victims to false gods, providing a pleasing spectacle for the devil, soon rendered him the most welcome service, indulging in drunken revels, leading lascivious dances, and defiling themselves with nefarious debaucheries. No one who has glanced even briefly at their histories and poets can be ignorant that all these things were especially practised at the time of their sacred rites. Moses does not conceal what the Israelites did in the worship of the golden calf, and among the rites instituted with the Moabite women. Nor is there any doubt that at Corinth, a rich and luxurious city, nothing of those things that fed carnal lust was omitted in such sacred rites. So Paul is speaking at present of those who were invited to feasts held in honour of idols, by their neighbours or friends who were still engaged in superstition, while they themselves had long since professed faith in Christ. And so that the demonstration of the scandal that arose from this may be clearer, he turns his speech to those very people who thought that nothing was forbidden them, because they were more instructed in knowledge than others. For he seems to say: "Consider, I beg you, whoever you are, what you are doing here. You have knowledge, and you maintain the reputation among all that you are most thoroughly instructed in the knowledge of the true God and of his Son Jesus Christ. This is why the eyes of many look upon you, and allow themselves to be led by your example, as by a sure and infallible rule. What then do you think will happen if some weaker Christian, who is not yet sufficiently instructed in the knowledge of the truth, and who as regards the use of Christian liberty still clings to the doubtful and wavering thoughts of a conscience, sees you reclining at a banquet of meat sacrificed or of unlawful rites, in an idol's temple, among the images of profane gods poured out on every side, among their worshippers and the open adversaries of Christ? Surely he is built up by your example, that is, he is moved and brought to the point that he himself, even though his conscience resists, goes to such banquets, etc." You see, then, that Paul uses the word 'build up' in the sense of catechesis, and not without sarcasm or reproach, as if he were saying: "It was your task to build up your weak brother in true faith and in solid knowledge of Jesus Christ, so that he could stand firm against the thoughts of a doubting mind and the temptations of a seething conscience, and preserve both body and soul holy and undefiled. But oh, what a splendid builder you are, who is such an author that he takes part in sacred rites, and is defiled by them! What else is this than to destroy the work of God, to make the knowledge of the truth more obscure in him, and finally to give a cause of ruin and destruction to the one whom your knowledge and the authority of your example ought to have helped toward constancy of faith and purity of religion?" This is the sense of that passage, in which the Apostle chiefly aims at this: that Christians should look not so much at what they themselves are allowed to do, as at what others gather from their example, and whether what they do may serve destruction rather than edification. For just as all other things must be directed to this end, that they advance the glory of God and build up the whole Church publicly and individuals privately, so unless this also is the goal and aim of Christian liberty, it will break out into a licence that is destructive both to ourselves and to the whole Church. Although this teaching is most general, nevertheless those who excel many others, and whose reputation is highest among all, will think it applies to them, for the greater their authority, the more effective are the examples by which they lead others. But if they corrupt someone, then they heap the sins of others also upon their own head, and at once they pay the penalties of another's impiety. The use of this teaching is therefore wide, and it ought to be extended as far as possible to all matters that concern religion, or morals and the whole conduct of life.

units.la: Sed Paulum audiamus, qui quàm graue & multiplex sit peccatum, quod ipsi designabant, diligenter offendit, sic scribens: Et tua ista scientia frater qui infirmus est, propter quem Christus mortuus est, peribit? Est hoc dictum graue admodum, & singula eius verba ad sceleris amplifi-cationem faciunt. Primò enim in quem peccetur, indicat. In fratrem nimirum. Est hoc portento simile, quando constat naturæ legem esse, vt qui ex ijsdē parentibus nati & (vt loquitur) consan-guinei sunt, se mutuò ament, & periculis eripiant eos, quos cognationis vinculo sibi obstrictos es-se sciunt. Atqui nullam cognationem aut fraternitatem arctiorem esse alibi ostendimus, quàm quæ credentibus in CHRISTO IESV intercedit. Verumtamen augetur in præsenti sce-lus, quando fratrem describens, infirmum dicit, & eum propter quem Christus sit mortuus. Inhu-manum est fratrem negligere, sed infirmum insuper perdere, plus quàm barbara crudelitas est.
units.tr: Let us hear Paul, who carefully shows how grave and manifold the sin was that they were pointing to, writing thus: "And through your knowledge shall the weak brother, for whom Christ died, perish?" This saying is very grave, and each of its words adds to the enormity of the crime. First, he indicates against whom the sin is committed: namely, against a brother. This is monstrous, since it is a law of nature that those born of the same parents, and (as they say) kinsmen, love one another and snatch from danger those whom they know to be bound to them by the tie of kinship. Yet we have shown elsewhere that no kinship or brotherhood is closer than that which exists between believers in CHRIST JESUS. And yet the crime is increased in the present case, when he describes the brother as weak, and as one for whom Christ died. It is inhuman to neglect a brother, but to destroy a weak one is more than barbaric cruelty.

units.la: At quia hoc quibusdam leue putatur, quòd fratrem non dignum iudicent, in cuius gratiam ali-quid faciant, addit: Propter quem Christus mortuus est? Quasi diceret. Falleris vehementer, si fratrem contemptu dignum iudicas. Cur enim non quouis officio dignus habeatur, quem æter-nus Dei filius sanguinis sui pretio redimere dignatus est. Deinde scelus ipsum exprimens, fra-trem illum non solum offendi, & permoueri ait, vt contra conscientiam ex carnibus sacrificiorū edat, verumetiam perire. Perdit ergo fratrem, qui ei author est, vt aliquid reclamante consciện-tia faciat. Nam quicquid ita fit, absque fide fit: at quod absque fide fit, peccatum esse alibi est de-monstratum: & quia incredulitas nos à Christo excludit, nulla potest remissionis spes esse ijs, qui fide destituuntur: quod omnibus ijs accidere oportet, qui conscientiam propriam audire nolunt.
units.tr: But because some think it a slight matter to judge a brother unworthy of the sake of whom they do anything, he adds: "for whom Christ died." As if he said: "You are gravely mistaken if you judge a brother worthy of contempt. For why should he not be thought worthy of any service, whom the eternal Son of God deigned to redeem at the price of his own blood?" Then, expressing the crime itself, he says that the brother is not only offended and provoked, so that against his conscience he eats meat from sacrifices, but is even destroyed. He destroys the brother, therefore, who is the author of his doing something while his conscience protests. For whatever is done in this way is done without faith; and that which is done without faith has been shown elsewhere to be sin. And since unbelief shuts us out from Christ, there can be no hope of forgiveness for those who lack faith. This must happen to all those who are unwilling to listen to their own conscience.

units.la: Addit his tertiò, quid illud sit, quo frater perdatur. Tua (inquit) ista scientia perit frater. Non carent semper culpa, qui fratrem per ignorantiam occidunt, & scimus publici aut sacri asyli au-thoritate olim eos defendi atque seruari oportuisse, qui securi temere & præter voluntatem ex manibus elapsa aliquem trucidauissent. Quid ergo de illis fiet, qui scientes aliquem perdunt, imò ea ipsa scientia perdunt, quā plenis buccis profitetur, et cuius hic vsus ipsis esse debebat, vt aliorū ædificationi atque saluti consulerent? Excusat medicum error absque sua culpa admissus, quales multi in re medica accidere solent. At si eo ipso ægrotum occidat, cuius se imprimis gnarum & pe-ritum profitetur, imò si tunc perdat, quando suam scientiam summo studio ostentat, quis illum ex cusatione dignum iudicabit? Atqui hoc faciebant ij, cum quibus hic Paulus agit. Cum enim cla-marent, se probè scire idolum nihil esse, interim hac scientia abutebantur, vt scandali & exitij authores fierent fratribus. Erat ergo hoc immane scelus & quouis supplicio dignum. Verumta-men ne hic quidem eius atrocitatem subsistere docet. Nam ita (inquit) peccantes in fratres, & vulnerantes ipsorum conscientiam infirmam, in Christum peccatis. In ipsum ergo Dei Filium huius audaciæ fructus infelix redundat. Is enim sibi fieri putat, quicquid ijs fit, quos ille pro suis agnoscit, & olim in magno illo die dicturus est: Quatenus fecistis vni ex istis fratribus meis mi-nimis, mihi fecistis. Neque aliter res æstimari potest, quando constat, corporis Christi membra esse omnes eos, qui fide in ipsum quantulacunque sunt illuminati. Adde, quòd dum aliquis eorum perit in eodem pretium sanguinis Christi vilescit, & quasi in nihilum redigitur. Et quod rectè hic obseruauit Chrysostomus, quod ille sanguinis sui pretio ædificauit, hoc sua temeritate & am-bitione destruunt, qui infirmitati aliorum nihil volunt concedere, etiamsi salutis periculum ipsis imminere videant. At si tot & tantorum scelerum reatu se polluunt atque grauant, qui infir-mos offendunt per ea, quæ in se licita & indifferentia sunt, quid de illis debemus sentire, qui ec-clesias totas, adeò, ipsam religionem Christianam dissamant sceleribus & effreni quiduis auden-di licentia? Est hoc nimis vulgare hodie, & constat multos pseudoeuangelicorum petulantia atque auaritia impediri, quò minus ad Euangelij lucem accedant: sed & tota Christiana religio apud Iudæos & Turcas ludibrio habetur partim propter simulachrorum cultu & frigidissimarū superstitionum exercitia, patim propter extremam morum corruptelam, quæ passim dominatur.
units.tr: He adds in the third place what it is by which the brother is destroyed: "Through your knowledge," he says, "the brother perishes." Those who kill a brother through ignorance are not always free from blame, and we know that by the authority of a public or sacred place of refuge, those were formerly to be defended and preserved who had, without care and against their will, slain someone by a weapon that slipped from their hands. What then will become of those who knowingly destroy someone, indeed destroy him by that very knowledge which they profess with full mouths, and whose use ought to have been for them to care for the edification and salvation of others? An error committed without fault excuses a physician, as often happens in medicine. But if he kills a patient by that very thing in which he professes himself especially skilled and experienced, indeed if he kills at the very time when he displays his knowledge with the greatest zeal, who will judge him worthy of excuse? Yet this is what those did with whom Paul is dealing here. For while they cried out that they knew well that an idol is nothing, meanwhile they abused this knowledge so as to become the authors of scandal and ruin to the brethren. This was therefore a monstrous crime, deserving of any punishment. Yet even here he teaches that its atrocity does not stand. For, he says, by sinning thus against the brethren and wounding their weak conscience, you sin against Christ. The unhappy fruit of this audacity therefore falls back upon the Son of God himself. For he thinks whatever is done to those whom he acknowledges as his own to be done to himself, and on that great day he is to say: "Inasmuch as you did it to one of these my brethren, the least, you did it to me." Nor can the matter be judged otherwise, since it is clear that all who are enlightened by faith in him, however slightly, are members of the body of Christ. Add that when one of them perishes, the price of Christ's blood is cheapened in that same one, and is as it were reduced to nothing. And what Chrysostom rightly observed here: that which he built up with the price of his own blood, they destroy by their rashness and ambition, those who will concede nothing to the weakness of others, even when they see danger of salvation hanging over them. But if those who offend the weak by things that are lawful and indifferent in themselves pollute and burden themselves with the guilt of so many and so great crimes, what must we think of those who defame whole congregations, and indeed the Christian religion itself, by their crimes and by an unbridled license to dare anything? This is too common today, and it is established that many are hindered from coming to the light of the Gospel by the wantonness and avarice of the pseudo-evangelicals. But also the whole Christian religion is held in mockery among the Jews and Turks, partly because of the worship of images and the practice of very cold superstitions, partly because of the extreme corruption of morals, which prevails everywhere.

units.la: At quotus quisque est inter antistites religionis (vt de vulgo iam nihil dicatur) qui illis manū admoueat, & de reformatione qua scandala ista auferantur, serio cogitet?
units.tr: But how few are there among the leaders of religion (to say nothing now of the common people) who lay a hand on these things, and seriously consider a reform by which these scandals may be removed?

units.la: Porrò concludit locum hunc Apostolus, & proprio exemplo docet, quàm durum & abominabile Christianis hominibus hoc videri debeat, de quo hactenus dixit: Quapropter (inquit) si esca sa-cit vt offendat frater meus, non vescar carnibus in æternum, ne faciam vt frater meus offendat. De idolothytis solis erat disputatio, at Paulus carnes simpliciter nominat, vt se simul omnibus potius abstinere velle offendat, quam alicuius offendiculi causam praebere. Et in aeternum, inquit quod Hyperbolen sapit. Nam neque vitam huius saeculi aeternam, neque aliquem cibi & potus usum esse sciebat in altera vita. Sic autem eorum contumaciam aut licentiam arguit, qui ne-nius quidem aut alterius convivij voluptate carere volebant, ut infirmorum fidei atque salutei consulerent. Serio autem locutum esse Apostolum non poterit dubitare, qui eius labores, curas, pericula diligentius consideraret, quae pro Christi ecclesijs sustinuit. Et cur non carnibus in perpetuum abstineret, qui alibi anathema fieri optat, ut Iudaeos feruet, quos incurabili contumacia ad exitium ruere videbat? Nec potuit aliter sentire, qui & gloriam Christi omnibus huius saeculi bonis anteponere iampridem didicerat, & non ignorabat quam horribiles poenas Christus scandalorum authoribus minitetur. Interim suo exemplo docet, non alium rerum huius saeculi usum licitum & sanctum esse, quam qui a charitate pendet, & in eum finem dirigitur, ne quae offendamus.
units.tr: Moreover, the Apostle concludes this passage, and by his own example teaches how hard and abominable this ought to seem to Christian people, about which he has spoken so far: "Wherefore," he says, "if food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I make my brother stumble." The discussion was of things offered to idols only, but Paul simply names meat, so that he may at the same time show that he is willing to abstain from everything rather than give any occasion of stumbling to anyone. "Never," he says, which savors of hyperbole. For he knew that neither this life is eternal, nor is there any use of food or drink in the next life. Thus he rebukes the obstinacy or license of those who were unwilling to forgo even the pleasure of any feast or banquet, so as to provide for the faith and salvation of the weak. Nor can anyone doubt that the Apostle spoke in earnest, if he considers more carefully his labors, cares, and dangers, which he endured for the churches of Christ. And why should he not abstain from meat forever, he who elsewhere wishes to be made an anathema for the Jews, whom he saw rushing to destruction with incurable obstinacy? Nor could he think otherwise, who had long since learned to put the glory of Christ before all the goods of this world, and was not ignorant of how terrible the punishments are that Christ threatens against the authors of scandals. Meanwhile, by his own example he teaches that no other use of the things of this world is lawful and holy than one that depends on love and is directed to the end that we give no offence.

units.la: Caeterum abutuntur quidam hoc loco bifariam. Sunt enim, qui ut suae ignaviae consulant & apud omnes bonam gratiam ineant, nihil omnino fieri debere contendunt, quod alicuius hominis offensionem pariat. Et hi non solum ad superstitiones & manifesta scelera conniVent, verumetiam Verbi administris dicendi leges praescribere audent, quam primum aliquos eorum libertate offendi audiunt. At non de animorum offensione loquitur Paulus, qua impij & huius saeculi homines irritantur, si quis vel superstitiones vel mores eorum corruptos reprehendat. Illa enim in universum caveri neque potest, propter incurabilem mundi malitiam, neque etiam debet, eo quod qui aliis praesunt, officium facere debent, & huius mundi favorem ne pili quidem facere, quemadmodum prophetarum & apostolorum, imo ipsius Christi exemplis docemur. Sunt rursus alij, qui factis illicitis palam intersunt, & sibi hoc omnino faciundum esse dicunt, ne illa negligendo aliquos offendant, aut scandalum ponant nonnullis, qui in ipsos plerunque respiciant. At mirum est istos homines sese huius loci authoritate tueri, quo vix alius est ad oppugnandum eorum impietatem evidentior & efficacior. Paulus enim omnem sacrorum alienorum usum simpliciter damnat, & ab epulis quoque sacris eos abstinere iubet, qui illis ut prophanis & vulgaribus vescebantur: illi autem cum ijs aperte communicant, quae impia & a Christiana religione alienissima esse norunt.
units.tr: Yet some abuse this passage in two ways. For some, in order to provide for their own idleness and to win good favour with everyone, contend that nothing at all should be done which would cause offence to any man. And these not only connive at superstitions and manifest crimes, but also dare to prescribe rules of speech to the ministers of the Word, as soon as they hear that some of them are offended by freedom. But Paul is not speaking of offence to minds, by which impious men and men of this world are provoked, if anyone rebukes either their superstitions or their corrupt morals. For such offence cannot be avoided in general, on account of the incurable wickedness of the world, nor indeed ought it to be, since those who are over others must do their duty and make no account of the favour of this world, as we are taught by the examples of the prophets and apostles, indeed of Christ himself. Again there are others who openly take part in unlawful deeds, and say that they must do this so that by neglecting them they do not offend some, or set a stumbling block before certain people who for the most part look to them. But it is strange that these men defend themselves by the authority of this passage, when there is hardly any other more evident and effective for overthrowing their impiety. For Paul simply condemns every use of alien sacrifices, and bids those who ate of them as profane and common food to abstain even from sacrificial feasts. But they openly take part in things which they know are impious and most alien to the Christian religion.

units.la: Deinde Paulus infirmorum in fide rationem habere vult, ne nostro exemplo in errorem abducantur: illi idololatrarum moribus sese accommodant, & ut hos in suis superstitionibus confirmant suo exemplo, ita multos infirmiores partim seducunt, partim in errore retinent. Quibus adde, quod doctrinam infirmis adhibere oportet, ut eo usque tandem proficiant, ne amplius tam facile offendantur. At egregij isti viri in docendo quidem piscem magis muti sunt, exemplo autem suo ita emicantes in multorum animis verae cognitionis & scientiae scintillas obruunt atque suffocant.
units.tr: Next, Paul wants us to take account of the weak in faith, so that they are not led into error by our example. Those men accommodate themselves to the customs of idolaters, and by their example they confirm the idolaters in their superstitions, while they also lead many of the weaker ones astray or keep them in error. To this add that teaching ought to be brought to the weak, so that they may at length advance to the point where they are no longer so easily offended. But these outstanding men are mute as fish when it comes to teaching, while by their example they blaze forth and smother and extinguish the sparks of true knowledge and understanding in the minds of many.

units.la: Atqui non opus est, ut de illis multum anxij simus, quos devotis animis in erroribus suis pergere scimus. Sinite illos (inquit Christus) quia caeci duces sunt caecorum. Et qui fordescit, fordescat adhuc. Nobis eorum salus cordi sit, in quorum animis verae fidei semina iam iacta sunt, & ne illos nostro exemplo in veritatis cursu impediamus, videre nos decet. Excitet hic omnes seria & diligens pretiosi sanguinis IESV CHRISTI consideratio, & huius memores, libertatem quam ille nobis acquisivit, sic utamur, ut & alij per nos aedificentur, & nos in illo vitam & felicitatem aeternam assequamur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Yet we need not be greatly anxious about those whom we know to persist in their errors with stubborn minds. "Let them alone," says Christ, "for they are blind guides of the blind." And "let him who is filthy be filthy still." Let our concern be for the salvation of those in whose minds the seeds of true faith have already been sown, and we ought to see to it that we do not hinder them in the course of the truth by our example. Let serious and diligent consideration of the precious blood of Jesus Christ stir up all of us, and, mindful of it, let us so use the liberty that he has won for us that others may be built up through us, and that we ourselves may attain life and eternal blessedness in him. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: CAPVT IX. HOMILIA LXIII.
units.tr: Chapter IX. Homily LXIII.

units.la: ANnon sum Apostolus? annon sum liber? Annon IESVM CHRISTVM, Dominum nostrum, vidi? Nonne opus meum vos estis in Domino? Si aliis non sum Apostolus, at certe vobis sum: Nam signillum apostolatus mei vos estis in Domino. Mea responsio apud eos qui in me inquirunt, haec est: Annon habemus po statem vescendi ac bibendi? Annon habemus potestatem sororem uxorem circumducendi, ut & reliqui Apostoli, & fratres Domini, & Cephas? An solus ego & Barnabas non habemus potestatem non operandi?
units.tr: Am I not an apostle? Am I not free? Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord? If I am not an apostle to others, yet at least I am to you, for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord. This is my answer to those who examine me: Do we not have the right to eat and drink? Do we not have the right to take about a sister as a wife, as the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas do? Or are only Barnabas and I without the right not to work?

units.la: Voniam[?] in Corinthiorum ecclesia quidam veri Dei cognitione & libertate Christiana eo usque abutebantur, ut non sine graui scandalo fratrum, qui adhuc rerum imperiti & in fide infirmiores erant, in conuiuiis, quae ex carnibus sacrificiorum instituebantur, cum idolorum & falsorum Deorum cultoribus publice accumberent: Paulus de hac re prolixam & diligentem disputationem instituit, qua illorum inconsultam petulantiam coercere studet. Summa & status illius est, Christianos homines non solum quid liceat, sed potius qui ad totius ecclesiae & singulorum fratrum aedificationem faciat, spectare debere, & simul ijsdem diligenter esse videndum, ne sacris alienis communicent, aut vllis superstitionibus polluantur. Inter alia argumenta, quibus eos confutat, nuper vltimo loco suum exemplum produxit, & scelus illud tam graue & atrox sibi videri testatus est, vt ipse potius per omnem vitam a carnibus in vniuersum omnibus abstinere malit, quam alicui scandalum dare, pro cuius salute Dei Filius sanguinem suum profundere dignatus est. At non deerant Corinthi, qui cum Paulum non magni facerent, vel etiam odissent, hoc eius dictum facile ridebant, eo quod non graue sit verbis magnificis polliceri, quod neminem abs te postulaturum esse satis nosti. Quapropter ne ardelio aliquis esse putetur, qui inanibus verbis sese venditet, nunc toto fere hoc Cap. in suum exemplum digreditur, & se iampridem plus quiddam fecisse multis docet, quam si a carnium simul omnium esu abstinuisset. Erat inter haec praecipuum, quod cum liceret Apostolis ab ecclesijs, quibus praedicabant, victum & quae praeterea necessitati seruiunt, accipere, ipse suo iure cesserat, & potius magna cum difficultate & manuum labore vitam suam duxerat, ne quam calumniandi occasionem aemulis suis praeberet, & simul euangelicae praedicationis cursum impediret. Multis vero causam hanc agit, non quidem gloriae priuatae studio, aut quod in posterum aliquid a Corinthijs extorquere cupiat, sed potius vt doctrinae suae fidem faciat, & exemplo suo eos pudefaciat, quibus adeo graue & indignum videbatur a victimarum carnibus abstinere, cum alijs epulis aeque lautis & opiparis abundarent. Simul etiam calumnias multorum praeuenit, qui eum multa exigere dicebant, quae ipsemet minus faceret.
units.tr: Since in the church of the Corinthians some, relying on their knowledge of the true God and their Christian liberty, were going so far that they reclined publicly at feasts held over meat from sacrifices, with worshippers of idols and false gods, to the serious offence of brothers who were still ignorant of such matters and weaker in faith, Paul undertook a long and careful discussion of this question, aiming to restrain their thoughtless boldness. The sum and substance of it is that Christians must consider not only what is permitted but rather what builds up the whole church and each brother, and at the same time they must take diligent care not to share in alien rites or be polluted by any superstitions. Among the other arguments by which he refutes them, he has lately put forward his own example in the last place, and he has declared that such a grave and atrocious wrong seems to him so serious that he would rather abstain from meat altogether for the rest of his life than give offence to anyone, for whose salvation the Son of God deigned to shed his blood. But there were people at Corinth who did not think much of Paul, or even hated him, and they readily laughed at this saying of his, since it is no hard thing to promise grand words, as you well know, when no one demands it of you. Therefore, lest he seem a busybody who puffs himself up with empty words, he now digresses for almost the whole of this chapter into his own example, and he shows many people that he has long done something more than if he had abstained from eating all meat together. Among these points the chief one was this: although the apostles were permitted to receive from the churches to which they preached food and whatever else serves necessity, he himself had given up this right, and had led his life instead with great difficulty and the labour of his hands, so that he would give his rivals no occasion for slander and at the same time would not hinder the course of the gospel preaching. He makes this case at length, not from a desire for private glory, nor because he wished to extract anything from the Corinthians in future, but rather to win credit for his teaching and to shame by his example those who thought it so hard and unworthy to abstain from sacrificial meat when they had plenty of other feasts just as sumptuous and lavish. At the same time he also anticipates the slanders of many who said that he demanded much from them that he himself did not do.

units.la: Est autem multa consideratione dignissima haec tractatio. Nam vt multa continet ad ecclesiae aedificationem imprimis pertinentia, de quibus singulis suo loco dicetur: ita simul docet, nihil vtilius & magis necessarium esse, quam vt doctores doctrinam suam proprio exemplo confirment, & ipsi in ijs praestandis serij atque diligentes sint, quae alijs praecipiunt. Quia enim magna est hominum licentia, & vix inueniuntur, qui ab alijs sese in ordinem redigi patienter ferant, idem plausibilem omnino occasionem sibi obtigisse arbitrantur, qua doctrinam cum eius authoribus in contemptum adducant, si quid in horum vita & moribus vident, quod illi minus conuenit. Imo exemplis multis doceri poterat, hanc praecipuam causam esse, ob quam tota religio apud multos suspecta est, apud quosdam etiam pessime audit. Cur enim illam magni facerent homines plebei & minus exercitati, quando eos absque omni religione vitam prophanam viuere conspicantur, qui de Deo & eius cultu, de caelestium bonorum praemijs & scelerum poenis sempiternis nunquam non verba faciunt? Et quis obsecro putet illos proprijs verbis credere? Recte ergo Paulus sic vitam suam instituit, vt tam in hac causa quam in alijs multis posset dicere. Imitatores mei estote: & vt idem faciant omnes ecclesiarum ministri, in epistolis ad Timotheum & Titum non vno loco hortatur. At quod illis dicitur, hoc ipsum ad se pertinere putent, quotquot magistratum aliquem gerunt & rempub. administrant. Quia tunc demum sua legibus authoritas acceder, si ijs obtemperent qui eas condiderunt. Quod si vero secus fieri videat populus, mox cum legibus authores quoq, earum contemnere & odisse incipiet. Sed quia de his dicendi locus saepe occurrit, nunc Paulum audiamus, qui primo sui apostolatus authoritatem asserit, & se Apostolum esse probat: deinde ius suum exponit, quo non minus quam alij potuerit vti. Ex quibus postea colligit, ipsos quoque vitandi scandali causa libertatis Christianae usum certis finibus circumscribere debere, ne in licentiam exitialem erumpat:
units.tr: This discussion is, however, most worthy of close consideration. For while it contains many matters which pertain above all to the building up of the church, each of which will be spoken of in its proper place, it also teaches that nothing is more useful and necessary than for teachers to confirm their teaching by their own example, and to be themselves earnest and diligent in those things which they enjoin on others. For since human licence is great, and there are hardly any who patiently bear being brought into line by others, such people think that they have been handed a wholly plausible occasion to bring the teaching, together with its authors, into contempt, if they see anything in the life and conduct of these men that does not fit well with it. Indeed, it could be shown by many examples that this is the chief cause for which the whole of religion is suspected by many and is even spoken of very badly by some. For why should ordinary and less trained people value it, when they see that those who never cease to speak of God and his worship, of the rewards of heavenly goods and the eternal punishments of sins, live a profane life without any religion? And who, I ask you, would think that such people believe their own words? Paul therefore rightly ordered his life so that, in this matter as in many others, he could say: Be imitators of me. And in his letters to Timothy and Titus he urges in more than one place that all the ministers of the churches should do the same. But what is said to them should be taken to apply also to all who hold any magistracy and administer the commonwealth. For the authority of laws is then at last established when those obey who made them. But if the people see things done otherwise, straightway they begin to despise and hate the lawgivers along with the laws. But since there is often an occasion to speak of these matters, let us now listen to Paul, who first asserts the authority of his apostleship and proves that he is an apostle, and then sets out his right, which he could use no less than the other apostles. From these things he afterwards concludes that they too, for the sake of avoiding offence, ought to limit the use of Christian liberty within certain bounds, lest it break out into deadly licence.

units.la: Orditur autem ab illis, quibus aemuli aut aduersarij authoritatem eius quam maxime eleuare conabantur. Solebant enim hi apud vulgus multa in Pauli contemptum dicere, inter quae praecipua erant: Non tantum esse eius libertatem aut potestatem in ecclesias, quantam sibi vindicaret[?]: Item neque verum aut germanum esse CHRISTI IESU Apostolum, quando satis constet, ipsum nunquam cum illo in terris agente familiariter fuisse versatum. Ex quo colligebant, ipsi non tantum licere in ecclesia, quantum aliis, quorum authoritas pluribus & firmioribus testimoniis niteretur. Est autem hoc perquam memorabile exemplum, quo docemur, quid fere praemij aut laudis referre soleant, qui pro hominum salute prae multis aliis laborant. Ex quorum numero Paulum fuisse, notius est, quam ut prolixe oporteat demonstrare. Unus certe Aliorum[?] liber nobis commentarij loco esse potest, ut ex eo intelligamus, eum neque labores neque pericula ulla detrectauisse, ut quam plurimos in Christi cognitionem & salutis aeternae societatem adduceret.
units.tr: He begins with those points on which his rivals or adversaries tried most of all to diminish his authority. For these men used to say many things among the common people to Paul's disparagement, of which the chief were these: that his liberty and his power over the churches were not as great as he claimed for himself; and likewise that he was not a true and genuine apostle of Jesus Christ, since it is well established that he had never associated familiarly with him while he was living on earth. From this they concluded that he had no more licence in the church than others, whose authority rested on more and firmer testimonies. This is a most memorable example, by which we are taught what reward or praise those commonly receive who labour for the salvation of men beyond many others. That Paul was one of this number is better known than it needs to be demonstrated at length. The book of Acts alone can serve us as a commentary, so that from it we may understand that he shrank from neither labours nor dangers, so that he might bring as many people as possible into the knowledge of Christ and the fellowship of eternal salvation.

units.la: Adde his, quae in posteriori epistola Cap. Vndecimo ipse commemorat, & miraberis unum hominem tot difficultatibus atq; molestijs sufficere potuisse. Neque de eorum fide, quae illic dicuntur, nos dubitare possumus, quando illis loquitur, qui cum eum odissent, nunquam dissimulaturi fuissent, si quid dixisset minus verum. Quid vero ex omnibus curis, laboribus, periculis, studijs & molestijs suis praemij retulit, quoad hoc saeculum? Nihil praeter contemptum, infamiam, odium, calumnias, persecutiones, denique, carceres, exilia, flagra & quaecunque in homines abiectissimos, imo scelerattissimos & quouis supplicio dignos designari, vel etiam excogitari possunt. Et haec quidem aduersus illum designarunt non modo aperti fidei & nominis Christiani hostes, sed ij quoque quinomen illud profitebantur, & qui per eius ministerium ex superstitionum tenebris utcunque emerserant. Inter alios certe iniquissime de illo Corinthij iudicauerunt, apud quos sesquianno docuerat gratis, & in quorum gratiam labores atque pericula infinita sustinuerat. Sunt autem huius generis exempla passim obuia, & in repub. quoque non multo meliorem fortem esse videmus eorum, qui pro patriae & ciuium singulorum salute dies noctesque excubant. Offendunt ista multos, qui sibi ideo licere arbitrantur, ut ab officio discedant, & tam male gratos perire sinant. Sed e mundo exeat oportet, qui hominum ingratitudinem omnem effugere velit. Coepit enim malum hoc in primis parentibus: & quid nos obiecto nobis de illis pollicebimur, qui ne Deo quidem Creatori & Redemptori suo bonam gratiam referunt? At cum hic remunerator sit fidelissimus, non est, quod iniqua de nobis mundi ingrati iudicia multum memoremur. Erit olim dies, quando occulta cordium manifestabuntur, & digna suae fidei praemia recipient, qui in sua functione diligentes fuerint. Interea, si quando Dei gloriam & multorum hominum salutem in nobis periclitari videmus, tunc aequum est, ut honorem & existimationem nostram constanter tueamur.
units.tr: Add to these things what he recounts in the later letter, in chapter eleven, and you will be amazed that one man could be sufficient for so many difficulties and troubles. Nor can we doubt the truth of those things which he says there, since he speaks to people who, because they hated him, would never have let pass anything he said that was less than true. But what reward did he receive for all his cares, labours, dangers, efforts and troubles, so far as this age is concerned? Nothing but contempt, infamy, hatred, slanders, persecutions, and finally prisons, exiles, scourgings, and whatever can be devised or imagined as punishment for the most abject, indeed the most wicked men, and worthy of any torture. And these things were inflicted upon him not only by the open enemies of the faith and of the Christian name, but also by those who professed that very name, and by those who through his ministry had emerged in some measure from the darkness of superstitions. Among others, the Corinthians judged him most unjustly, though he had taught them free of charge for a year and a half, and had endured endless labours and dangers for their sake. Examples of this kind are found everywhere, and we see in the commonwealth too that the lot of those who keep watch day and night for the safety of their country and of individual citizens is not much better. Such things offend many, who think it lawful for them on that account to withdraw from their duty and to let those so ill-thanked perish. But anyone who wishes to escape all human ingratitude must leave the world. For this evil began with our first parents; and what shall we promise ourselves concerning those who do not even return due thanks to God, their Creator and Redeemer? But since this rewarder is most faithful, there is no reason for us to dwell much on the unjust judgements of an ungrateful world. There will come a day when the hidden things of hearts will be made manifest, and those who were diligent in their office will receive rewards worthy of their faithfulness. Meanwhile, if at any time we see the glory of God and the salvation of many people endangered through us, then it is right that we steadfastly defend our honour and reputation.

units.la: Facit id Paulus in praesenti, & ut aemulos suos fortius feriat, & calumnias eorundem effi-catius arguat, crebris interrogationibus eos urget, quibus etiam invitos & reluctantes in ar-nam protrahit. Sic enim scribit: Annon sum Apostolus? annon liber? annon IESUM CHRISTUM, Dominum nostrum vidi? nonne opus meum vos estis in Domino? Quasi dicteret. Scio quid multi de me garriant, ut me indignum esse probent, cuius doctrinae & admonitionibus aliquis obtemperet. Sed agite o boni, & in medium prodite quicunque estis, & libere dicite, quid habetis, propter quod merito contemni debeam. Num Apostolum me esse negabitis? Atqui vocationem adducere possum legitimam & testibus idoneis confirmatam: & insuper Apostoli-ficium[?] ita hucusque feci, ut nihil eorum, quae ad istud faciunt, in me desiderari possit. An ergo non sum liber? Id est, annon idem mihi in ecclesias ius est, quod Apostolis suis Christus concessit? aut qua ratione vos mihi negatum esse probabitis, quod aliis concessum est? Num quod cum Christo non versatus sim, quando ille in terris egit? At multum fallimini, si me ideo aliis inferiorem existimatis putatis. Annon enim ipse etiam illum vidi? Id vero dicit, non de visione vulgari, quam multi etiam impij & infideles Christum viderunt, & qua ipse Paulus eum fortasse vidit, quando sub Gamalielis disciplina in Hierosolymorum ciuitate educatus fuit. Sed sibi plus quiddam obtigisse dicit: ut nimirum illum a mortuis resuscitatum & iam quoad carnem assumptam glorificarum viderit. Et de hoc infra Cap. 15. apertius loquitur, vbi aliquot IESV CHRISTI resuscitati apparitiones ex ordine commemorans addit: Vltimo vero omnium, velut abortiuo, vitus est etiam mihi. Imprimis tamen huc pertinere mihi videntur duae illae visiones, quarum prior ante Damascum, altera in templo facta est: eo quod in utraq; vocationis suae ad apostolatum non obscura testimonia habentur. De priori coram Agrippa rege sic disserit ipse: Die medio, Rex, in via vidi caelitus lucem, quae splendorem solis superabat, circumfulsisse me & eos, qui mecum faciebant iter. Cum autem omnes nos decidissemus in terram, audiui vocem alloquentem me, ac dicentem Hebraica lingua: Saul, Saul, quid me persequeris? durum est tibi contra stimulos calcitrare. Ego autem dixi: Quis es Domine? At ille dixit: Ego sum IESVS, quem tu persequeris. Sed exurge, & sta super pedes tuos: ad hoc enim APPARVI tibi, vt designarem te ministrum ac testem cum eorum quae vidisti, tum eorum in quibus apparebo tibi, &c. Quo loco Christum Paulo non solum locutum, verumetiam visum fuisse, imo promisisse etiam audimus, quod deinceps quoq; apparere & familiarius eum instruere velit in iis, quae per eius ministerium perfici oporteat. De altera apparitione idem ille in frequentissima populi Iudaici concione sic ait: Factum est, cum reuersus essem Hierosolymam & orarem in templo, vt raperer extra me, & VIDEREM eum dicentem mihi: Festina, & exi cito, &c. Frequenter autem Dominum Paulo apparuisse, satis patet ex iis, quae in posteriori epistola sub initium cap. 12. habentur. Non temere igitur in praesenti adversarijs suis dicit: Annon IESVM CHRISTVM, Dominum nostrum, vidi?
units.tr: Paul does this here both to strike his rivals more forcefully and to refute their slanders more effectively. He presses them with repeated questions, dragging them, even unwilling and resisting, out into the open. He writes: Am I not an apostle? Am I not free? Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord? It is as if he said: "I know what many say about me, to prove that I am unworthy for anyone to obey my teaching and admonitions. But come forward, good people, whoever you are, and say freely what you have against me, on account of which I ought rightly to be despised. Will you deny that I am an apostle? Yet I can point to a lawful calling, confirmed by competent witnesses. Moreover, I have so far carried out the apostolic office that nothing which belongs to it can be found lacking in me. Am I then not free? That is, does not the same right over the churches belong to me that Christ granted to his apostles? By what reasoning will you prove that what was granted to others has been denied to me? Is it because I was not with Christ when he lived on earth? But you are greatly mistaken if you think I am therefore inferior to others. For have I not seen him too?" He does not mean the ordinary sight which many impious and unbelieving people also had of Christ, and by which Paul himself perhaps saw him when he was brought up in the city of Jerusalem under the discipline of Gamaliel. He means that something more had befallen him: namely, that he saw Christ raised from the dead and now glorified as to his assumed flesh. He speaks of this more plainly below, in chapter 15, where, recounting in order several appearances of the risen Jesus Christ, he adds: Last of all, as to one born out of due time, he appeared to me also. Yet the two visions seem to bear most on this point: the first before Damascus, the other made in the temple, since in each there are clear testimonies of his calling to the apostleship. About the first he speaks thus before King Agrippa: At midday, O King, I saw on the road a light from heaven, which outshone the brightness of the sun, shining round me and those who journeyed with me. When we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice speaking to me and saying in the Hebrew tongue: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads. And I said: Who are you, Lord? And he said: I am Jesus, whom you persecute. But rise and stand on your feet, for to this end I have appeared to you, to appoint you minister and witness both of the things you have seen and of those in which I shall appear to you, etc. Here we hear that Christ not only spoke to Paul but was also seen by him, and indeed promised that he would afterwards appear again and instruct him more intimately in those things which were to be carried out through his ministry. About the other appearance the same man says in the very crowded assembly of the Jewish people: It happened, when I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, that I was caught up out of myself, and saw him saying to me: Make haste, and leave Jerusalem quickly, etc. That the Lord often appeared to Paul is clear enough from what is said at the beginning of chapter 12 of the second epistle. So it is no rash thing that he says to his adversaries here: Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord?

units.la: Quia tamen ista omnia minus momenti habere sciebat apud eos, quorum oculos aemulatio & odium iampridem fascinauerant, quod omnium maximum & prorsus irrefragabile erat apostolicae functionis argumentum infert: Nonne opus meum vos estis in Domino? Quasi diceret: Si verbis & rationibus non habetis fidem, saltem opus ipsum, quod in vobis per me fecit Dominus, inspicite. Annon enim per meum ministerium ad fidem IESV CHRISTI conuersi, & eius ecclesia facti estis? Aut quis, priusquam ego Corinthum venirem, Christum vobis praedicauit? Qua fronte ergo aliquis vestrum me Apostolum esse negare audet, cum veri Apostoli opus in vobis ipsis palam extet? Itaq; si aliis non sum Apostolus, at certe vobis sum. Nam sigillum apostolatus mei vos estis in Domino. Aut ergo vos Christi ecclesiam esse negare oportet, aut mihi istum honorem deferre, quod ego verus sim Apostolus. Facit autem ad huius dicti explicationem, quod in posteriori epistola loco supra citato scribit: Signa quidem Apostoli perasta fuerunt apud vos per omnem tolerantiam, & signa, & prodigia, & virtutes: Nam quid est in quo fuistis inferiores caeteris ecclesijs? Et sane, vt omnia alia silentio praetereamus, quis non insigne adeoque incomparabile summi & praestantissimi Apostoli opus fuisse dixerit, quod in ea vrbe Ecclesia IESU CHRISTI constituta fuit, in qua Satan per omne genus libidinis, per auaritiam, impofturas, fraudes & rapinas, per omnem deniq; intemperantiam regnum iam diu tenuerat? Fuit hoc omnino diuinae virtutis opus, quae per Pauli ministerium sese exeruit. Stupenda autem & execrabilis fuit istorum hominum caecitas, qui tam illustre Dei beneficium noluerunt agnoscere. Ideo Apostolus hanc demonstrationem concludens, infert: Mea responsio apud eos, qui in me inquirunt, haec est. Qua breui sententia & aduersariorum iniquitatem arguit, qui praeter eius meritum in ipsum odiosius inquirant, & suae causae bonitatem indicat, cui non opus sit multis argumentis, cum res ipsa pro eo loquatur. Perinde enim hoc est, ac si diceret: Multa quidem aduersus me aemuli mei corradunt, sed aduersus illos mihi sufficit vnicum illud, quod in vestra vrbis couersione accidit. Si enim non sum verus Christi Apostolus, si ille me pro suo non agnoscit, vnde ergo virtus illa, quae in vobis sese per meum ministerium exernit? & quo loco vos censeri debetis, qui me audito a superstitionibus & idololatria ad vnius Dei cultum transfuistis?
units.tr: Yet because he knew that all these things carried little weight with those whose eyes envy and hatred had long since bewitched, he brings forward the argument which was the greatest and wholly unanswerable proof of his apostolic office: Are you not my work in the Lord? It is as if he said: "If you do not trust my words and reasons, at least look at the work itself which the Lord has done among you through me. Were you not converted to the faith of Jesus Christ and made his church through my ministry? Or who preached Christ to you before I came to Corinth? With what face, then, does any of you dare to deny that I am an apostle, when the work of a true apostle stands openly in yourselves? So, if I am not an apostle to others, I certainly am to you. For you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord. Either you must deny that you are the church of Christ, or you must grant me this honour, that I am a true apostle." He also supports the explanation of this saying by what he writes in the second epistle in the passage cited above: The signs of an apostle were indeed wrought among you in all patience, with signs, and wonders, and mighty deeds. For what is there in which you were inferior to the other churches? And indeed, to pass over everything else in silence, who would not say that it was a remarkable and truly incomparable work of that most excellent and outstanding apostle that the church of Jesus Christ was established in that city, where Satan had long held sway through every kind of lust, through greed, deceits, frauds and robbery, and finally through every intemperance? It was entirely a work of divine power, which showed itself through Paul's ministry. Stupid and detestable, however, was the blindness of those men who refused to acknowledge so illustrious a benefit of God. So the Apostle, concluding this demonstration, adds: My answer to those who examine me is this. By this brief sentence he both charges his opponents with injustice, since they seek out faults in him more spitefully than his merits deserve, and points to the goodness of his cause, which does not need many arguments since the matter itself speaks for him. It is as if he said: "My rivals heap up many charges against me, but against them the one thing that happened in the conversion of your city is enough for me. For if I am not a true apostle of Christ, if he does not acknowledge me as his own, where then does that power come from which has shown itself among you through my ministry? And in what category must you be counted, you who, having heard me, turned from superstitions and idolatry to the worship of the one God?"

units.la: Est autem multa & diligenti consideratione dignum Pauli exemplum, qui cum se germanum Apostolum esse probare velit, non hominum authoritate, neq; titulorum inanium splendore, aut insignibus ad ostentationem conflictis sese venditat, sed res ipsas Apostolo dignas in medium adducit, adeoq;, ipso opere (quod aiunt) se artificem esse demonstrat. Praestat tamen eius argumenta, quae paucis verbis comprehendit, omnia inspicere. Est inter haec primum vocatio, cuius non obscure meminit, quando se Apostolum, id est, legatum Christi esse ait. Fieri enim non potest, ut legatus sit, quem nemo miserit. Quomodo autem missus esse dicetur, qui ne vocatus quidem aut unquam destinatus est, ut mitteretur? Secundo loco, se quoque Christum vidisse ait, non obiter quidem, sed in visione (ut audiuimus) quae ipsi causa fuit, ut in veram illius cognitionem peruenireret, deque eius voluntate certior fieret. Tertium est, Corinthiorum conuersio ad fidem. Quia enim verbum Dei (ut Isaias docet) nunquam absque fructu praedicatur, non poterit pro illius praecone agnosci, quisquis sine fructu praedicat. Fructus autem nomine non confusa sectatorum multitudo intelligi debet, quae saepe impostores nequissimi gloriantur, sed vera Dei veri cognitio, fides syncera, & quae ex hac de-pendent vita totius consuetudo. De his enim Christus loquitur, quando discipulis dicit: Constitui vos, ut abeuntes fructum afferatis, & fructus vester maneat. Haec (inquam) Paulus adducit, ut se Christi Apostolum esse euincat: quibus adnumerari poterant signa & opera miraculosa, perse-cutionum pericula, adeoque ipsius Christi stigmata, quae (ut in epistola ad Galatas scribit) in corpore suo gestabat: sed quia postrema haec non semper necessaria sunt, in praesenti eorum modo, quae prius commemorauimus, meminit. At quia haec eiusmodi sunt, ut sine illis Apostolus nemo esse possit, debebant his ipsis argumentis hodie Episcopi & Pontifices uti, qui se Apostolicos esse profitentur. Quod si autem ista quaeras, rara admodum, vel potius nulla inuenies. Vocatio certe legitima apud eos esse non potest, quibus cum Simone Mago iam pridem omnia sunt venalia. De Christi autem cognitione aut vera fide quid opus est dicere, quando tota illorum religio in ceremonijs superstitiosis & frigidis consistit, & hominum traditionibus regitur, quae a Christo quam longissime abducunt? Quae autem opera apostolicae functionis allegare poterunt, qui non modo neminem Christo lucrifaciunt, verumetiam eos, qui iam ante illi nomen dederunt, in sectas distrahunt, & hominum seruos faciunt ex illis, qui toti Christo vni & soli debebant esse consecrati? Ut ergo doctrina eorum falsa est, sic falsa sunt miracula & signa, quibus sibi fidem facere conantur. Stigmata autem IESV CHRISTI in illis reperies, qui quod illorum placitis non seruiliter obtemperant, in carceribus degunt, exulant, torquentur, ferro item & igne perduntur. Quid ergo in personatis illis Apostolicis aliud est videre, quam opes huius seculi, voluptatum studia, pompam aulicam, fastum theatricum & numerosum comitatum perditissimorum hominum, inter quos vix centesimus quisque prima fidei Christianae rudimenta intelligit? Num ergo illi vilis mortalium dicere poterunt, Sigillum apostolatus nostri vos estis? Quod cum non possint, desinant quaeso inanibus titulis se venditare hoc tempore, quando purior veritatis cognitio orbi illuxit.
units.tr: Paul's example is well worth close and careful consideration. Although he wishes to prove that he is a genuine apostle, he does not commend himself by the authority of men, by the glitter of empty titles, or by insignia contrived for display. Instead he brings forward the very things that befit an apostle and so, as the saying goes, shows himself to be a craftsman by the work itself. It is still worth looking at all of his arguments, which he sums up in a few words. First among these is his calling, which he does not fail to mention clearly when he says that he is an apostle, that is, a legate of Christ. For a man cannot be a legate whom no one has sent. But how can he be said to have been sent who was not even called, or ever destined to be sent? Second, he says that he has also seen Christ, and not merely in passing but in a vision (as we have heard), which was the reason he came to a true knowledge of him and was made more certain of his will. The third is the conversion of the Corinthians to the faith. For since the word of God (as Isaiah teaches) is never preached without fruit, whoever preaches without fruit cannot be recognised as its herald. By "fruit" we must understand not a crowd of disorderly followers, in which the most wicked impostors often boast, but the true knowledge of the true God, sincere faith, and the whole manner of life that depends on these. Christ speaks of these when he says to his disciples: I have appointed you that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain. These, I say, are what Paul brings forward to prove that he is an apostle of Christ. To them could have been added signs and miraculous works, the perils of persecutions, and indeed the marks of Christ himself, which (as he writes in the epistle to the Galatians) he bore in his body. But because these last are not always necessary, he mentions in this passage only those which we have already noted. Yet since these are of such a kind that no one can be an apostle without them, the bishops and popes who profess to be apostolic ought to use these very arguments today. If you ask them for these, you will find them very rare, or rather none at all. Certainly a lawful calling cannot exist among those for whom everything has long been for sale along with Simon Magus. And why say anything about the knowledge of Christ or true faith, when their whole religion consists in superstitious and cold ceremonies and is governed by human traditions, which lead very far away from Christ? What works of the apostolic office can they allege, who not only win no one to Christ, but even tear apart into sects those who had already given their name to him, and make servants of men out of those who ought to have been wholly consecrated to Christ alone? So just as their doctrine is false, so their miracles and signs, by which they try to win belief, are false. And the marks of Jesus Christ you will find in those who, because they do not slavishly obey their decrees, live in prisons, go into exile, are tortured, and are destroyed by sword and fire. What, then, is there to see in those masked apostles except the riches of this age, pursuits of pleasure, courtly pomp, theatrical show, and a numerous retinue of the most depraved men, among whom scarcely one in a hundred understands the first elements of the Christian faith? Could those worthless men of the world say, then, "You are the seal of our apostleship"? Since they cannot, I beg them to stop puffing themselves up with empty titles in this age, when a purer knowledge of the truth has dawned upon the world.

units.la: Obseruabis praeterea, quod Paulus Corinthiorum ecclesiam fuisse Apostolatus sigillum esse dicit. At quae nam & qualis illa ecclesia fuit? Modis omnibus (ut iam saepe diximus) corruptissima. Nam in sectas turpiter scissi erant, & tantum non abnegato Christi nomine, multi ex illis ab hominibus denominari volebant. Disciplinam ecclesiae omnem prorsus conculcarant, ut iam non ebriosis modo, fraudatoribus, scortatoribus & adulteris, verumetiam hominibus inceptis inter illos locus esset. Auaritiae & priuati commodi studio ita addicti erant, ut apud ethnicorum tribunalia lites forenses ob huius seculi fortunas persequerentur, non fine manifesta nominis Christiani contumelia. In coniugijs multa praeter decorum fiebant. Sacris idololatricis communicabant, & sua scientia ostentatione ad scandalum infirmorum abutebantur. In coetibus sacris adeo nulla erat bonae status & religionis ratio, ut sacrosanctam quoq; IESV CHRISTI Coenam in comessationem turpe & luxuriosam conuertissent. In fidei vero dogmatibus plerisq; hallucinabatur, & ipsam quoq; mortuorum resurrectionem in dubium nonnulli vocabant, sine qua falsus spes nobis consistere non potest. Omitto infinita alia, quae aduersus fidei, charitatis et honestatis Christianae leges designabantur. Neg[?]sta Paulus ignorabat, qui de his omnibus eos grauiter admonet et corripit. Nihilominus vero, quia aliquis erat inter illos priorum numerus, et alteri illi adhuc admittebat correctione, adeo nō abijcit illos, ut et ecclesia Christi in ea urbe esse agnoscat, et eadem fuit opus in Domino, sui deniq; apostolatus sigillu esse testetur. Cōfer cū hoc Pauli spiritu nostri seculi Donatistas, qui oēs coetus temere damnat, in quib. aliquos tolerari videt, qui Christiani nominis professioni minus respondent. Fingunt enim perfectionem quandam ecclesiae, quam in hoc etiam mundo absque ruga & macula esse posse fom-niant:& niant: & ideo à nostris cœtibus abhorrent, ne alienis peccatis polluantur. At quas obsecro ecclesias ynquam nobis daturi fuissent Apostoli, si eadem seueritate & rigore voluissent vti? Vel quis ille spiritus est, qui ne suam & totius humanæ naturæ imperfectionem homines agnoscant, prohibet? Aut num Christi spiritus dici poterit, qui ecclesias non colligit, sed dissipat? Poterat istius idem dici, quod olim Constantinus Imperator Acesio Nouatianorum episcopo in simili causa non minus vere quàm falsè & facetè dicebat. Ergo vos soli cœlos confscendite, & subductis pos vos scalis soli [?] illic regnate. Sed omisis ineptis illis ad Paulum redeamus.
units.tr: You will further observe that Paul says the Corinthian church was the seal of his apostleship. But what kind of church was it, and what was it like? In every respect it was most corrupt (as we have often said already). For they were shamefully split into factions, and many of them, while not quite renouncing the name of Christ, wished to be called after men. They had trampled underfoot all church discipline, so that there was room among them not only for drunkards, cheats, fornicators and adulterers, but even for men who were beginners in the faith. They were so devoted to greed and private advantage that they pursued lawsuits before the heathen courts over the wealth of this world, not without manifest disgrace to the name of Christian. Many things were done in marriages contrary to propriety. They took part in idolatrous sacrifices and used their knowledge to show off, to the scandal of the weak. In their sacred assemblies there was so little regard for good order and religion that they had turned the holy Supper of Jesus Christ into a shameful and riotous feast. In matters of doctrine most of them went astray, and some called the resurrection of the dead into doubt, though without it our hope cannot stand. I pass over the countless other things that were done against the laws of faith, charity and Christian honesty. Paul was not ignorant of all these things, and he admonishes and rebukes them severely about all of them. Nevertheless, because there was still a good number of the better sort among them, and because the others still admitted correction, he does not cast them off so completely that he fails to acknowledge that the church of Christ exists in that city; indeed, he declares that they are the work of the Lord and the seal of his apostleship. Compare with this spirit of Paul the Donatists of our own age, who rashly condemn every congregation in which they see some tolerated who answer poorly to the profession of the Christian name. For they imagine a certain perfection of the church, which they dream can exist in this world without spot or wrinkle, and therefore they shrink from our congregations, lest they be polluted by the sins of others. But tell me, what churches would the apostles have left to us at all, if they had wished to use the same severity and rigour? Or what spirit is it that forbids men to recognise their own imperfection and that of all human nature? Or can that be called the spirit of Christ which does not gather churches but scatters them? The same could be said of that man what the emperor Constantine once said, not less truly than wittily, to Acesius, bishop of the Novatians, in a similar case: "Then go up to heaven alone, take away your ladders, and reign there by yourselves." But let us set aside those silly matters and return to Paul.

units.la: Is nunc plenius rem tractat, & species aliquot enumerat eius libertatis, quâ non vsus fit pro iure suo apostolico. Rursus autem totam orationem interrogationibus figurat, vt æmulorum iniquitas melius exprimatur, & ipsi propriæ conscientiæ testimonio damnentur. Et quia propter epulas idolothytorum in istam tractationem descenderat, hic quoque ab ijs, quæ ad victum pertinent, orditur. Annon (inquit) habemus potestatem vescendi ac bibendi? Quasi diceret: Durum vobis videtur, si libertas vestra in aliquo cibi genere quacunque ob causas astringatur: at quid aliud à vobis exigo, quàm quod ipse hucusque cum apud vos tum apud alios complures præstiti? Etenim mihi quoque ex CHRISTI IESV mandato aut instituto liberum est omnibus vesci, quæ ab ijs apponuntur, quibus Euangelium prædicamus. Nam notum est illud Christi: Manete in domo, in quam diuertistis, edentes & bibentes quæ ab ipsis apposita fuerint: dignus est enim operarius mercede sua. Et rursus: In quancunque vrbem ingressi fueritis & exceperint vos, edite quæ apponuntur vobis. Verum tamen potestate hac inter vos vti noluimus, ne cui vel scandalum vel calumniandi occasionem daremus. Cum ergo nos in vniuersum ab omnibus abstinea-mus, si quando res ita videtur postulare, quæ hæc vestra est contumacia, quæ vos non patitur à victimarum carnibus abstinere? Debet ergo locus iste de stipendio ministrorum exponi, cuius hanc rationem & hos fines Christus præscripsit, vt ex suo ministerio victum habeant, qui Dei verbum docent.
units.tr: He now treats the matter more fully and lists several kinds of that liberty which he did not use by his apostolic right. Again he shapes the whole discourse by questions, so that the injustice of his rivals may be better expressed and they may be condemned by the testimony of their own conscience. And because he had come down to this discussion on account of feasts with idol-offerings, he begins here too from those things which pertain to sustenance. "Do we not have," he says, "the power to eat and to drink?" As if he were saying: It seems hard to you if your liberty is restricted in some kind of food for whatever reasons; but what else do I demand of you than what I myself have hitherto practised both among you and among many others? For by the command or ordinance of Christ Jesus, it is also free for me to eat whatever is set before me by those to whom I preach the gospel. For that saying of Christ is well known: "Remain in the house where you are lodged, eating and drinking what they set before you, for the labourer is worthy of his wages." And again: "Into whatever city you enter and they receive you, eat what is set before you." Yet we have chosen not to use this power among you, so that we should give to no one either a scandal or an occasion for slander. Since, then, we abstain altogether from all things, when the situation seems to require it, what is this obstinacy of yours, which does not allow you to abstain from the flesh of sacrificial victims? This passage ought therefore to be explained concerning the stipend of ministers, for whose purpose and limits Christ laid down this rule: that those who teach the word of God should have their livelihood from their ministry.

units.la: At hic obseruatione singulari dignum est, quòd & Christus & Apostolus solum [?] cibi aut victus meminerunt. Ex eo enim colligitur, ministris sufficere debere, si quæ ad vitam sustentandam faciunt, accipiant. Quia enim his ipse Christus contentus fuit, minimè decet, vt aut luxui & deliciis studeant, aut diuitias accumulent, qui huius præcones haberi volunt. Et si Prophetarum mores inspiciamus ex Samuelis Eliæ & Elisæi historia satis patet, illos frugalitati & temperantiæ imprimis studuisse. Quod ipsum Apostoli quoque fecerunt, & qui his proximè successerunt. Regnauit tunc in ecclesijs dicendi libertas, quando nulla habendi cupiditas aut externi splendoris & luxus studium verbi administris metum incussit, aut silentium indixit. Posteris autem temporibus religio diuitiis peperit, ex quibus luxus enatus disciplinam ecclesiasticam perdidit, & in huius locum superstitiones frigidissimæ introductæ sunt, per quas ipsa quoque religio prorsus extincta est. Quod vtinam non etiam hodie fieret multis in locis, quando constat eos, qui Euangelium prædicant, iam pridem plurimum degenerasse ab illorum moribus, qui nouissimo hoc seculo primi doctrinæ purioris instauratores fuerunt. Videmus enim plerosque de solijs stipendijs, principum fauore & priuata gloria cogitare.
