Vt ergo ciuilis libertas (quod olim Diogenes annotauit) in vescendis pulchris inuenitur, luxu autem & habendi cupiditate amittitur: Ita suam quoque libertatem doctores eiusmodi produnt, & simul omnem ecclesiæ ordinem turbant. Quod autem de verbi administris dicitur, hoc ipsum ad omnes quoque alios pertinet. Etenim si qui rempub. administrant, qui negotiantur, qui artificia manuaria exercent, ciues item & agricolæ victu & amictu contenti essent, facilius multo omnes viuerent, & iampridem luxui, vsuris & sceleribus ijs modus inuentus esset, quibus & priuatim multi pereunt, & respub. florentissimæ dissipantur.
units.tr: But here it is worth noting with special care that both Christ and the Apostle mention only food and sustenance. For from this it is gathered that it is enough for ministers to receive whatever serves to sustain life. For since Christ himself was content with these things, it is by no means fitting that those who want to be heralds of his should aim at luxury and delights, or accumulate riches. And if we look at the manners of the prophets, it is sufficiently clear from the histories of Samuel, Elijah and Elisha that they above all were devoted to frugality and temperance. The Apostles also did the same, and those who came immediately after them. Freedom of speech then reigned in the churches, when no desire for wealth, nor any pursuit of outward splendour and luxury, struck fear into the ministers of the word or imposed silence on them. But in later times religion gave birth to riches, and from these luxury sprang up and destroyed church discipline, and in its place the most frigid superstitions were introduced, through which religion itself was utterly extinguished. Would that this did not also happen today in many places, since it is evident that those who preach the gospel have long since largely degenerated from the manners of those who were the first restorers of purer doctrine in this last age. For we see most of them thinking about fat stipends, the favour of princes and private glory. Therefore, just as civil liberty (as Diogenes once remarked) is found in eating simple things, and is lost through luxury and the desire for having, so teachers of this kind betray their own liberty and at the same time throw the whole order of the church into confusion. What is said of the ministers of the word applies equally to all others as well. For if those who administer the commonwealth, those who trade, those who practise manual crafts, and likewise the citizens and farmers were content with food and clothing, everyone would live far more easily, and long ago a limit would have been set to luxury, usury and those crimes by which many perish in private life and most flourishing commonwealths are destroyed.

units.la: Secundò de coniugio ministrorum ecclesiæ Paulus disserit, dicens: Annon habemus potestatem sororem vxorem circumducendi, vt & reliqui Apostoli, & fratres Domini, & Cephas? Quibus verbis aperte docet, non ministris modo ecclesiarum, sed eorum quoque vxoribus victum deberi, & hoc iure Apostolos olim vsos fuisse. Scimus quidem sensum hunc non placuisse D. Hieronymo, qui aduersus Iouinianum disputans, Paulum de mulieribus loqui scribit, quae non quidem uxores fuerint, illos autem comitatae sint, ut eis ministrarent. Lepidum sane commentum, quo Apostoli a coniugalis consuetudinis suspicione sic liberantur, ut maiorum impuritatis notam incurrant. Quis enim viros bonos & honestos dixerit, qui mulierum quidem alienarum officia admittant, uxores autem legitimas & proprias deserant? Et quam optata haec fuisset aduersarijs calumniandi occasio, si Apostoli relictis suis uxoribus alienas circumduxissent? Placet tamen figmentum hoc Monachis & sacrificulis: nimirum, ut similes habeant labra lactucas. Vellent enim Apostolos scortatores potius quam uxoratos fuisse, ut illorum exemplo suas libidines possent excusare. Sed potior apud nos esse debet vetustissimorum scriptorum authoritas, qui cum Apostolorum temporibus vicini fuerint, omnia illorum rectius nouisse potuerunt. Ignatius certe in epistola ad Philadelph. scribit: Non detraho ceteris beatis, qui nuptijs copulati fuerunt. Opto enim Deo dignus ad vestigia eorum in regno ipsius inueniri, sicut Abraham & Isaac & Iacob, sicut Iosephi & Isaias, & ceteri prophetae: sicut Petrus & Paulus, & reliqui Apostoli, qui nuptijs fuerunt sociati, qui non libidinis causa, sed posteritatis subrogandae gratia, coniuges habuerunt. Consentit his Clemens, qui (ut Eusebius recitat) aduersus eos scribens, qui coniugiū damnabant, inter alia dicit: An & Apostolos improbant? Petrus etenim atq; Philippus & uxores habuerunt, & filias etiam viris nuptum dederunt. Sed & Paulum Apostolum non tædet in quadam epistola sua mentionem vel salutationem facere comparis suae, quam se ideo negat circumducere, ut ad praedicationem Euangelij expeditior eat. Quae omnia cum ijs consentiant, quae apud Matthaeum de socru Petri et in Actorum libro de filiabus Philippi prophetantibus dicuntur, non est quod ineptissimorum hominum superstitiosis commentis moueamur. Nam si quae in praesenti Paulus scribit propius inspiciamus, illum de uxore loqui patebit. Nam sororem nominat, quo nomine olim Christianas foeminas denotari solitas fuisse notius est, quam ut demonstrari oporteat, et circumducendi verbo potestatem innuit, quae nulli viro est nisi in eam, quae ipsi legitime iuncta est. Et hic etiam se iure suo cessisse ait, ut eos pudefaciat, qui in re leuioris momenti infirmis nihil concedendum esse putabant. In citandis autem aliorum exemplis gradatione utitur, ut vehementius fit argumentum, quod ex illis elicit. Nā primo loco Apostolos in genere nominat: deinde fratres, id est, cōsobrinos aut cognatos Christi adducit, quales Ioannem & Iacobū Simonem & Iudā, siue Thaddaeū fuisse alibi diximus: postremo Cephas aut Petrus citatur, cuius summa erat apud oēs ecclesias existimatio. Quis ergo ullis ministrorum hoc negatum dicet, quod tantis ecclesiae columnis olim licuit? Quin potius dicimus, in ipsum munus Apostolicum & Christi ecclesiam eos omnes peccare, qui hodie ministrorum coniugia damnant. Defendit haec olim vetustas, & maiores nostri per Germaniam episcopos uxoratos habuere per annos amplius mille usque ad Gregorij VII. tempora, qui totum fere orbem terrarum turbauit, ut impurum caelibatum omnibus obtruderet.
units.tr: Secondly, Paul discusses the marriage of the ministers of the church, saying: "Do we not have the power to lead about a sister as a wife, as the other Apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas do?" By these words he clearly teaches that support is owed not only to the ministers of the churches but also to their wives, and that the Apostles in former times made use of this right. We know indeed that this sense did not please Jerome, who, disputing against Jovinian, writes that Paul is speaking of women who were not wives but accompanied the Apostles in order to minister to them. A charming invention indeed, by which the Apostles are freed from the suspicion of marital intercourse only to incur the greater stain of impurity! For who would call men good and honest who admit the services of other men's women but abandon their lawful and own wives? And how welcome this would have been to the adversaries as an occasion for slander, if the Apostles had led about other men's wives after leaving their own! Yet this fiction pleases the monks and the little priests, no doubt so that they may have lips like lettuces. For they would wish the Apostles to have been fornicators rather than married men, so that by their example they might excuse their own lusts. But the authority of the most ancient writers ought to carry more weight with us, since they were close to the times of the Apostles and could more rightly know all their affairs. Ignatius certainly writes in his letter to the Philadelphians: "I do not disparage the other blessed men who were joined in marriage. For I hope that, being worthy of God, they will be found in his kingdom following in the footsteps of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, of Joseph and Isaiah, and the other prophets; as Peter and Paul and the rest of the Apostles, who were joined in marriage, and had wives not for the sake of lust but for the sake of raising up offspring." Clement agrees with these, who (as Eusebius reports) writing against those who condemned marriage, says among other things: "Do they also condemn the Apostles? For Peter and Philip had wives, and they also gave their daughters in marriage to husbands." Nor is the Apostle Paul ashamed in a certain letter of his to make mention or greeting of his companion, whom he says he does not lead about so that he may go more freely to the preaching of the gospel. All these things agree with what is said in Matthew about Peter's mother-in-law, and in the book of Acts about the daughters of Philip who prophesied. So there is no reason for us to be moved by the superstitious inventions of the most foolish men. For if we look more closely at what Paul writes here, it will be plain that he is speaking of a wife. For he names her "sister," a term by which Christian women were long customarily designated, as is too well known to need demonstration; and by the word "lead about" he signifies a right that belongs to no man except with respect to the woman who is lawfully joined to him. Here too he says that he has yielded his own right, so that he may shame those who thought that nothing should be granted to the weak in a matter of lesser importance. Moreover, in citing the examples of others he uses a gradation, so that the argument drawn from them becomes more forceful. For in the first place he names the Apostles in general; then he brings forward the brothers, that is, the cousins or kinsmen of Christ, such as we have elsewhere said James and John, Simon and Judas, or Thaddeus were; last of all Cephas or Peter is cited, whose authority was highest among all the churches. Who, then, will say that this was denied to any minister, when it was once permitted to such pillars of the church? Rather, we say that all those who today condemn the marriages of ministers sin against the very office of the Apostles and against the church of Christ. This antiquity defended, and our forefathers in Germany had married bishops for more than a thousand years, down to the time of Gregory VII, who disturbed almost the whole world in order to force an impure celibacy upon everyone.

units.la: Obseruabis autem locutionem, qua sororem uxorem dicit. Ea enim docet, qualia esse debeant coniugia fidelium. Primum in his esto, ut non nisi Christianis iungantur, qui propter eiusdem religionis societate fratres & sorores sint. Dictū de hoc sæpe, & proinde eadem repetere non est opus. Deinde eorum iunctionis suae meminerint, quae inter illos arctissima est, & quidem duplex, coniugij nimirum & religionis. Quod ergo de Sara dicitur, quod Abrahami & soror & coniunx fuerit, hoc ipsum ad omnes Christianos coniuges pertinet. Vir enim idem mulieris maritus & frater est: maritus quidem ob coniugij vinculū, frater autem in Christo, qui nos eiusdem patris filios fecit. Ita mulier una & eadem viri soror et uxor est. Quod ut amore coniugale nobis commendat, ita in coniugijs honestate quoq; feruat docet, ne alicuius turpitudinis authores simus ijs, qui nobis ita arcte coniuncti sunt. Duobus ergo vel bis Paulus oēs cōiugij leges cōprehēdit, quas multi vix infinitis voluminibus explicare potuerunt.
units.tr: You will observe the phrase by which he calls her "sister, wife." For it teaches what kind of marriages among the faithful ought to be. First, let these be such that they are joined only to Christians, who are sisters and brothers through the fellowship of the same religion. This has often been said about this matter, and so there is no need to repeat the same things. Next, let them remember the union they have with each other, which is the closest, and indeed twofold: that of marriage, namely, and that of religion. What is said of Sarah, that she was both sister and wife of Abraham, pertains to all Christian spouses in the same way. For the husband of a woman is at once her husband and her brother: her husband indeed by the bond of marriage, but her brother in Christ, who has made us sons of the same Father. Thus one and the same woman is both sister and wife to her husband. This commends to us conjugal love, and in the same way teaches that marriages are also to be preserved in honour, so that we do not become the authors of any disgrace to those who are so closely joined to us. Therefore, by these two words, or rather by this one, Paul embraces all the laws of marriage, which many could scarcely explain in infinite volumes.

units.la: Restat tertium, in quo iure suo Apostolus cessit, de quo sic scribit: An solus ego & Barnabas non habemus potestatem non operandi? Loquitur de opere manuario, quo sibi apud Corinthios victum parauit, ut etiam sæpe aliàs, sicuti Lucas in Actis, & ipse non uno loco testatur. Id vero de alijs Apostolis nusquam legitur, qui ex Euangelij ministerio vixerunt. Quod cum Paulo quoq; liceret, satis constat, eum hic quoq; noluisse libertate sua uti cum alicuius offendiculo. Coniungit autem sibi Barnabam, cui eadem gloria debebatur. Et est hoc singularis modestiae argumentum, qua illum quoque honore suo fraudare noluit, cum quo ipsi aliquando lis grauissima intercesserat. At hodie multi lites quaerunt, & nihil non in fratrum contumeliam corradunt, ut ipsis solis laus omnis cedat. In ista autem commemoratione admonemur, quanta sit mundi huius contumacia, & quam parum sua indulgentia pij ministri proficiant. Debebant Paulo animas suas Corinthij, nedum victum necessarium. At non contenti hunc negauisse, simul suos illi labores exprobrauerunt, & eo nomine eum viliorem duxerunt, quo ipsum imprimis euehere & in manibus gestare debuissent. Regnat hoc malum etiam hodie passim, & cum ecclesiae fere maiorum liberalitate ditatae sint, ut non opus sit ministros quicquam ab aliquo petere, paucos tamen esse inuenire, qui non ista quoq; stipendia illis inuideant, multi autem Iudae mores imitati ea diripiunt, quae ab alijs donata sunt. At non debet ingratitudo haec aliquem offendere. Dabunt aliquando dignas poenas, qui de verbo Dei non digne iudicant. Interea officium suum sedulo faciant ij, quibus docendi munus commissum est, & cum mundi contumacia luctentur: quod olim sanctissimos Prophetas fecisse scimus. Reliqui vero attentis animis verbum audiant, audito credant, & vitam suam secundum eius amussim instituant, ut olim aeternum feruentur in IESU CHRISTO Domino & Seruatore nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: There remains a third point, in which the Apostle yielded his right, concerning which he writes thus: "Have not I and Barnabas power to forbear working?" He speaks of manual labour, by which he provided his own living among the Corinthians, as he does often elsewhere, and as Luke also testifies in the Acts, and as he himself testifies in more than one place. But it is nowhere read that the other Apostles, who lived from the ministry of the gospel, did this. Since Paul also had the liberty to do so, it is quite clear that here too he was unwilling to use his freedom at the cost of offence to anyone. He joins Barnabas with himself, who was owed the same honour. And this is a sign of singular modesty, by which he was unwilling to defraud even him of his honour, with whom he had once had a most serious quarrel. But today many seek quarrels, and gather up everything to the reproach of their brothers, so that all praise may fall to themselves alone. In this recollection, however, we are warned how great the obstinacy of this world is, and how little the kindness of godly ministers accomplishes. The Corinthians owed him their souls, not to mention his necessary sustenance. Yet not content with having denied him this, they at the same time cast his labours in his face, and on that account thought less of him, when they ought above all to have exalted him and carried him in their hands. This evil reigns everywhere today too, and although the churches have been enriched almost by the generosity of their forebears, so that ministers need not ask anything from anyone, yet there are few to be found who do not begrudge them these stipends as well, and many, imitating the ways of Judas, plunder what has been given by others. But this ingratitude ought not to disturb anyone. Those who do not judge the word of God worthily will one day pay the proper penalties. Meanwhile, let those to whom the office of teaching has been committed diligently do their duty and struggle against the obstinacy of the world, as we know the most holy Prophets did of old. Let the rest hear the word with attentive minds, believe what they have heard, and order their lives according to its rule, so that they may be preserved eternally in Jesus Christ our Lord and Saviour, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XLIIII.

units.la: Quis militat proprijs stipendijs unquam? Quis plantat vineam, & de fructu eius non edit? Aut quis pascit gregem, & de lacte gregis non edit? Num secundum hominem haec dico? nonne etiam Lex haec dicit? Nam in Mosis Lege scriptum est: Non obligabis os bouis triturantis. Num boues curae sunt Deo? aut num propter nos omnino hoc dicit? Propter nos enim hoc scriptum est, quod sub spe debeat is qui arat arare: & qui tritu-rat sub spe, suae spei particeps esse. Si nos vobis spiritualia seminauimus, magnum ne fuerit si nos vestra carnalia messue-rimus?
units.tr: Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Or who feeds a flock and does not eat of the flock's milk? Do I say these things according to man? Does not the Law also say this? For it is written in the Law of Moses: You shall not muzzle the mouth of an ox that treads out the grain. Are oxen a concern to God? Or does he say this altogether on our account? For this was written on our account, that the one who plows should plow in hope, and the one who threshes should share in his hope. If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?

units.la: INter multa & praeclara Dei beneficia, nullum postea CHRISTUM IESUM pro nobis in mortem traditum praestantius est verbo suo. Per hoc enim voluntatem suam nobis revelat, eodem nos per huius mundi tenebras dirigit, regni sui thesauros aperit: deniq; per illud nos regenerat & adoptionis spiritu donat, ut cum filio suo regni aeterni & coelestis haeredes efficiamur. At vicissim hic sese exerit humani ingenij prauitas, & quae ex ea enascitur ingratitudo. Quia enim natura ad malum proclives sumus, & multa indies facimus, quae professionem nostram minus decent, non possumus patienter ferre nos arguentem diuinae veritatis lucem. Hinc ergo administro-rum eius odia nascuntur, ex quibus deinde omnis generis calumniae & apertae etiam aut violentae persecutiones oriri solent. Quod si qui ab illis abstinent, ij saltem inuidia ringuntur[?], & quam inique de verbo Dei simul & eius administris iudicent, hoc uno abunde ostendunt, quod nimium & iniquum esse putant, quicquid in illos confertur. Fiebant ista palam Corinthi, & tanta erat multorum malitia, ut quamuis Paulus apud illos Euangelium gratis praedicauisset, & interea temporis partim manuum labore victum sibi parauisset, partim ab aliis accepisset, qui de toto hoc negotio rectius & honorificentius sentiebant, illorum tamen dentes & calumnias effugere non potuerit. Quapropter cum ipsi demonstrandum esset, quanta facilitate & indulgentia erga illos sit usus, & in quam multis suis iure cesserit, ne Euangelij cursum aliqua ex parte remoraretur, proli-xè admodum & diligenter probat: licuisse sibi exemplo aliorum Apostolorum ab ipsis stipendium & quae vitae necessaria sunt petere. Ea autem occasione non solum authoritatem conciliat exemplo suo aduersus eos, qui Christiana libertate non sine multorum scandalo abutebantur, verum etiam turpem illorum ingratitudinem arguit, qua in Deum ipsum peccabant. Prudenter vero rem hanc omnem tractat, ne quid in aliorum Apostolorum contemptum dicere videatur, qui sub iure hucusque fuerant usi. Postquam enim nuper ostendit, sibi idem quod aliis licere, nunc hoc ipsum per se licitum & aequum esse docet, idque argumentis tribus confirmat, quae ex ordi-ne inspiciemus.
units.tr: Among the many great benefits of God, none is more outstanding than the word of Christ Jesus, who was delivered to death for us. For through it he reveals his will to us, through it he guides us through the darkness of this world, and opens the treasures of his kingdom; finally, through it he regenerates us and grants us the spirit of adoption, so that with his Son we become heirs of the eternal and heavenly kingdom. But in turn there appears the perversity of the human mind and the ingratitude that springs from it. For since we are naturally prone to evil and daily do many things that ill befit our profession, we cannot patiently bear the light of divine truth reproving us. Hence arise hatreds of its ministers, from which all kinds of calumnies and open or violent persecutions are wont to follow. But if some abstain from these, they are at least consumed by envy [?], and how unjustly they judge the word of God and its ministers together, they show abundantly by this one thing: that they think whatever is brought against them is excessive and unjust. These things were happening openly at Corinth, and the malice of many was so great that although Paul had preached the gospel among them free of charge, and in the meantime had partly provided himself a living by the labour of his hands, and partly had received support from others who judged the whole matter more rightly and honourably, he nevertheless could not escape their teeth and calumnies. Therefore, since it had to be shown to them how great an ease and indulgence he had shown towards them, and how many of his rights he had yielded so that the course of the gospel might not be hindered in any way, he proves at great length and with care that it was lawful for him, by the example of the other apostles, to ask them for a stipend and for what is necessary for life. On this occasion he not only wins authority by his own example against those who abused Christian liberty, not without great scandal to many, but also rebukes their shameful ingratitude, by which they sinned against God himself. Moreover, he handles this whole matter prudently, lest he seem to say anything in contempt of the other apostles, who until now had used this right. For after he has recently shown that what is permitted to others is permitted to him too, now he teaches that this very thing is lawful and fair in itself, and confirms it with three arguments, which we shall examine in order.

units.la: Primum ex communi hominum more sumitur, qui est, ut quisque ex eo victum habeat, ad quod legitimè vocatus est, & cui se totum impendit. Et opus erat propter iniquos & morosos illos ministerij æstimatores hinc ordiri, ut ostenderet, nihil iniquum aut absurdum hic peti, sed quod publica omnium consuetudine adeo & naturæ legibus sit receptum. Summa totius argumenti est: Unusquisque ex ea arte viuit, quam exercet: Ergo nobis quoque ex Euangelij prædicatione victus debetur. Antecedens probat per Inductionem, qua aliquos eorum enumerat, qui ex suis laboribus victum recipiunt: Milites nimirum, Vinitores aut agricolas & Pastores. Adhuc autem interrogationibus insistit, ut proprij cordis testimonio aut confessione aduersarios suos convincat. Quis militat proprijs stipendijs unquam? Quasi diceret: Quis tam iniquus fuerit, ut ab eo, qui vitam & sanguinem pro publica salute profundere paratus est, etiam hoc exigere ausit, ut proprio ære militet? Reges certe exteri & tyranni iniquissimi stipendia illis largiuntur, qui ipsorum auspiciis bella gerunt. Et notum est Sirachidis dictum, qui militem egenum inter eos numerat, quorum indigna conditio bonis & cordatis omnibus dolorem affert. Ecclef. 26. Deinde, Quis (inquit) plantat vineam, & de fructu eius non edit? Etenim Deus ipse hoc ius fecit homini-bus, ut qui terram in vultus sui sudore colunt, inde fructum recipiant. Et inter minas aut maledictiones Legis, quibus impios eius transgressores Deus territat, hæc etiam habetur: Plantabis vineam, & non primus vindemiabis eam: & ideo pugna iam instante iubebantur ex acie discedere, quicunque ex vineis suis nondum primos fructus collegerant. Addit his tertium exemplum Paulus. Aut quis pascit gregem, & de lacte gregis non edit? Pecuarij fuerunt olim sanctissimi patriarchæ, & ex suis gregibus cum tota sua familia vixerunt. Quod ipsum de Dauide, viro secundum cor Dei, dicere possumus. Et iniquus foret, qui hodie pastoribus id prohibere conaretur, &c. Latet autem sub exemplis aut parabolis hisce argumentum a comparatis cuius vis maxima in eo est, quod Euangelij præcones functionem fungiuntur, quæ cum omni suo officio ad Deum Opt. Max. refertur. Itaque etsi Paulus conclusionem ipse non inferat, cuius tamen facile est ex iis ad hunc modum colligere: Si qui regibus militant, ab iisdem stipendia accipiunt: iniquum fuerit ut suo ære viuant, qui militiam Dei exercent sub duce IESU CHRISTO, cui omnes in baptismo nomen dedimus. Si item vineæ & agri suos cultores alunt, fouium greges suis pastoribus victum suppeditant, vos ne ecclesiam, quæ Dei aruum & vinea & grex est, tam infelicem & sterilem, aut tam ingratam putabitis, ut suis cultoribus & pastoribus vitæ necessaria neget? Poterant hæc latissime diduci, & multis amplificari, sed sufficit pios paucis admonuisse, quos verbi Dei amor & studium excitat, ut huius causæ æquitatem facile intelligant. Nunc potius obseruemus, Paulum his exemplis potius uti voluisse, quam infinitis aliis, quæ in tota rerum natura & quotidiano hominum usu occurrunt. Cuius rei rationem nullam aliam reddere possumus, quam quod illis continetur, quicquid de toto Euangelij ministerio dici potest.
units.tr: The first is taken from the common custom of men, which is that each person has his living from that to which he has been lawfully called and to which he devotes himself wholly. And it was necessary to begin here, because of those unjust and fussy judges of the ministry, so that he might show that nothing unjust or absurd is sought here, but something accepted by the universal custom of all and even by the laws of nature. The sum of the whole argument is: everyone lives from the craft he practises; therefore a living is due to us also from the preaching of the gospel. He proves the premise by induction, listing some of those who receive their living from their labours: soldiers, of course, vine-dressers or farmers, and shepherds. He still presses on with questions, so that he may convince his opponents by the testimony of their own heart or by their own confession. Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? As if he were saying: who would be so unjust as to dare to demand that one who is ready to pour out his life and blood for the public safety should serve at his own cost? Certainly foreign kings and most unjust tyrants give stipends to those who wage wars under their command. And the saying of Sirach is well known, who counts the needy soldier among those whose unworthy condition causes grief to all good and sensible people. Ecclef. 26. Next: Who (he says) plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? For God himself granted this right to men, that those who cultivate the earth by the sweat of their face should receive fruit from it. And among the threats or curses of the Law, with which God terrifies its impious transgressors, this also is found: You shall plant a vineyard and not be the first to gather its grapes; and therefore, when battle was at hand, those who had not yet gathered the first fruits of their vineyards were ordered to leave the line. Paul adds a third example: Or who feeds a flock and does not eat of the flock's milk? The most holy patriarchs were once herdsmen, and they lived with their whole household from their flocks. The same we can say of David, a man after God's own heart. And he would be unjust who tried to forbid this to shepherds today, and so on. Moreover, under these examples or parables lies an argument from comparison, whose great force lies in this: the heralds of the gospel discharge a function which, with all its duties, is referred to God, the best and greatest. Therefore, although Paul does not himself draw the conclusion, it is easy to infer it from these in this way: if some serve kings, they receive stipends from them; it would be unjust that those who carry on the warfare of God under the captain Jesus Christ, whose name we all took at baptism, should live at their own cost. Likewise, if vineyards and fields feed their cultivators, and folds supply their shepherds with food, will you think the Church, which is God's field and vineyard and flock, so unfruitful and barren, or so ungrateful, that it denies its cultivators and shepherds the necessities of life? These things could be spread out very widely and amplified by many examples, but it is enough to have briefly admonished the godly, whom love and zeal for the word of God stir up, so that they may easily grasp the fairness of this cause. Now let us rather observe that Paul preferred to use these examples rather than the countless others that occur in the whole of nature and in daily human life. We can give no other reason for this than that in them is contained whatever can be said about the whole ministry of the gospel.

units.la: Primo enim quæ muneris ipsius conditio sit, adumbrat: non qualem Monachi fingunt, qui in ima ni[?] contemplatione Dei cultum consistere dicunt, & tunc se egregios IESU CHRISTI seruos esse sibi persuadent, si ut fuci ignaui nihil agant, & circa nescio quas ceremonias occupentur. Atqui tales seruos non magni facit Christus, neq; eiusmodi in sua ecclesia ministerium instituit, sed quod totum praxi aut opere constat. Est enim militiæ instar, ut in posteriori epistola Paulus annotauit. Nam cum Dei filius ideo in mundum venerit, ut communis hostis nostri opera destrueret, & eundem ex regno male occupato eiiceret, seruos quoque habere vult, qui cum hoste illo assidue pugnent, & ecclesiam suam ab eius incursionibus strenuè tueantur. Imperator militiæ huius ipse Christus est, qui iam ante hostem vicit, & suo exemplo hunc vincendi rationem monstrauit. Arma sunt non carnalia, qualia personati ipsius vicarij vibrant, sed spiritualia, verbum Dei nimirum, quod gladij ancipitis instar est, & preces, quibus & Satan terretur, & Deus ipse expugnatur, ut nobis opem ferat. Finis pugnæ aut victoria est, ut totus homo per fidei obedientiam Deo subijciatur. Quòd si cum his diaboli ingenium inquietum & improbum, deinde hominum quoque mores atque mundi infelicis studia conferas, mox videbis nullum locum socordiae aut segnitiei ministris reliquum esse, sed necessitatem ipsam exigere, ut simul & speculatores & milites agant, qui & hostis insidias observent, & populum ad resistendum excitent, & gladium Verbi Dei inde-sinenter stringant. Pertinet huc quod in Hierosolyma instauratae historia legitur, Israelitas alte-ra quidem manu muros extruxisse, altera gladios tenuisse, quibus hostes subinde irruentes profli-garent. Docet hoc ipsum vinitoris aut agricolae parabola. Nam ecclesiam Dei vineam esse Isaias docet, & Christus in Euangelio non semel hoc nomine eam appellat. Eandem supra Apostolus Dei aruum dixit. At neque aruum neque vinea cultores otiosos aut segnes requirunt, sed tales oportet esse ecclesiae ministros, qui stirpitus excindant omnia, quae segetibus nocere possunt, qui plantando & rigando fidelem operam navent, qui denique luxuriantes in hac vinea palmites falce Verbi Dei rescindant, & apud omnes instent, ut quos Deus à nobis requirit fructus ferant. Quo nomine illos Christus exactoribus quoque conseri[?]. Admonet hoc ipsum rei pecuariae aut pastori-tiae similitudo. Solet enim Christus ecclesiam suum gregem dicere, & quia hunc sui sanguinis pretio redemit, satis constat eum nihil illo pretiosiorem habere. Et quamuis ipse pastor sit verus, hominum tamen opera uti dignatur, qui Verbi doctrina gregem hunc contineant, errantes reducant, pascant, saucijs medeantur, confractos curent, lasciuientes coerceant, adhæc lupos procul arceant, aut saltem oues confirment, ne illorum minis & machinationibus succumbant. At si hic rursus consideres diaboli improbitatem, qui modò blanditijs credentes in auia abducit, modò haereticorum figmentis unitatem gregis illius scindit, plerunq; autem aperta vi totum ouile dissipare conatur: e contra autem cum hoc ouium stoliditatem, ignauiam & vaecordiam conferas, quae lupos eiusmodi vel accersunt ultrò, vel sese in eorum ungues & fauces ingerunt: rursus patebit, nunquam defore Euangelij praeconibus quod agant, siquidem hero suo fideles esse velint.
units.tr: First, he outlines what the condition of the office itself is: not the kind the monks imagine, who say that worship consists in contemplating God in the depths, and who then persuade themselves that they are excellent servants of Jesus Christ if, like idle drones, they do nothing and are occupied with I know not what ceremonies. Yet Christ does not value such servants, nor has he instituted such a ministry in his Church, but one that consists wholly in practice and work. For it is like warfare, as Paul noted in his later letter. For since the Son of God came into the world so that by his work he might destroy our common enemy and cast him out of the kingdom he had wrongfully seized, he also wants to have servants who constantly fight with that enemy and vigorously defend his Church against his attacks. The commander of this warfare is Christ himself, who has already conquered the enemy and by his own example has shown the way of conquering. The weapons are not carnal, such as his masked vicars brandish, but spiritual: namely the word of God, which is like a two-edged sword, and prayers, by which Satan is terrified and God himself is overcome, so that he may bring us help. The aim of the battle or its victory is that the whole man be subjected to God through the obedience of faith. But if you compare with these the restless and wicked nature of the devil, and then also the manners of men and the pursuits of this unhappy world, you will soon see that no room is left for sloth or laziness in the ministers, but necessity itself demands that they act both as scouts and as soldiers, who both watch for the enemy's snares and rouse the people to resist, and unceasingly brandish the sword of the word of God. To this pertains what is read in the history of Jerusalem restored: that the Israelites with one hand built the walls and with the other held swords, with which they routed the enemies rushing in upon them. The parable of the vine-dresser or farmer teaches this same thing. For Isaiah teaches that the Church of God is a vineyard, and Christ in the gospel calls it by this name more than once. The Apostle above called it God's field. But neither field nor vineyard requires idle or slothful cultivators; such ministers of the Church must be, who root out utterly everything that can harm the crops, who labour faithfully in planting and watering, who finally with the pruning-knife of God's word cut away the luxuriant shoots in this vineyard, and insist before everyone that they bear the fruit God requires of us. By this title Christ also likens them to those who exact the fruit. The same point is made by the likeness of the flock and of pastoral care. For Christ is accustomed to call the Church his flock, and since he redeemed it at the price of his own blood, it is clear enough that he holds nothing more precious. And although he himself is the true shepherd, he nevertheless deigns to use the work of men, who by the teaching of the Word keep this flock together, lead back the straying, feed them, tend the wounded, heal the broken, restrain the wanton, and moreover keep the wolves far away, or at least strengthen the sheep, so that they do not give way to their threats and schemes. But if you again consider the wickedness of the devil, who now leads the credulous astray into the wilderness by flatteries, now tears the unity of the flock apart with the fabrications of heretics, and mostly tries to scatter the whole fold by open force; and if on the other side you compare with this the stupidity, sloth and folly of the sheep, which either summon such wolves of their own accord or thrust themselves into their claws and jaws: then it will again be plain that the heralds of the gospel will never lack work to do, provided they wish to be faithful to their master.

units.la: Vt verò de laboribus & curis illos admonet Paulus, quas illos sustinere oporteat: ita merce-dem quoque eis deberi docet, sed talem, quae illos frugalitatem & temperantiam sectari debere ostendat. Nam in militiae parabola (si Graecum vocabulum inspicias Iopsoniorum meminit, id est ὀψώνιον, victus diurni, qui antiquitus militibus dari solebat. Fuit autem is frugalis, ut quem optimi quique Imperatores necessitati, non luxui aut voluptati, servire voluerunt. Apud Romanos certè, quando maximè floruit illud Imperium, militibus lentem & salem distribuere solebant, ut Plutarchus in Crassi vita annotavit. Posteris demum temporibus stipendiorum magnitudo in castra luxum invexit, & disciplinam militarem è medio sustulit, quam Valerius Maximus praecipuum decus & stabilimentum Romani Imperij dixit. Sed quia haec alterius loci sunt, sufficiat nunc ista voce frugalitatis ministros admoneri. Fit idem in vineae & rei pecuariae parabolis, in quibus non de illis loquitur Paulus, qui ex vineae fructibus comessantur & pinguiores in grege agnos mactant atque devorant: sed de ijs, qui de vineae fructu edunt, & lacte gregis contenti viuunt. Pseudoprophetis & mutis canibus Isaias tribuit, quòd convivia lautiora quaerant & comessationes ebriosas instituant. Etiam verò pane & aqua & carnibus modicis, Ioannem verò Baptistam locustis & melle sylvestri, quae desertum ipsi suppeditabant, contentum fuisse legimus. Et Apostolorum vox est: Habentes alimenta & quibus tegamur, his contenti erimus. Vt ergo locus iste ius ministerij & quae ministris debentur stipendia asserit: ita vicissim eorum improbitatem arguit, qui huius muneris praetextu turpiter & perfide abutuntur. Sunt primi in hoc ordine, qui stipendia quidem ecclesiastica ambiunt, labores autem & curas omnes detrectant, quibus ministros fideles vacare oportet. Proximi hos sequuntur, qui non contenti necessarijs, imò ne ijs quidem, quae ad vitam honestè transfigendam poterant sufficere, insuper opes ingentes accumulant, Ghezaeum illum imitati, qui Eliae heri pauperis dives servus fieri voluit. Utrisque peiores sunt, qui ut ex principum, vel etiam Episcoporum & Monachorum liberalitate stipendia lautiora accipiant, in officio suo cessare solent, & ad ea conniuent, quae palàm accusare debebant. Est magnus istorum numerus hodie, & ijs fere debemus, quòd multi ab Euangelij doctrina abhorrent, multi in eius cogni-tione minus proficiunt.
units.tr: As Paul reminds them of the labours and cares they ought to bear, so he also teaches that they are owed a reward, but one that shows they should pursue frugality and temperance. For in the parable of soldiering (if you look at the Greek word, he mentions the pay of soldiers, that is opsonion [ὀψώνιον], the daily provision that was customarily given to soldiers in ancient times), this was frugal, since the best commanders wanted it to serve necessity, not luxury or pleasure. Among the Romans, certainly, when that empire flourished most, they used to distribute lentils and salt to the soldiers, as Plutarch noted in the life of Crassus. In later times the size of pay brought luxury into the camps and removed military discipline from the midst, which Valerius Maximus called the chief glory and mainstay of the Roman empire. But since these matters belong elsewhere, let it suffice now to admonish the ministers by this word of frugality. The same happens in the parables of the vineyard and of herding, in which Paul does not speak of those who feast on the fruits of the vineyard and slaughter and devour the fatter lambs of the flock, but of those who eat the fruit of the vineyard and live content with the milk of the flock. Isaiah ascribes to the false prophets and dumb dogs that they seek more sumptuous banquets and hold drunken feasts. We read too that John the Baptist was content with locusts and wild honey, which the desert supplied him, and with bread, water and modest meat. And the word of the Apostles is: Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content. So, as this passage asserts the right of the ministry and the stipends owed to ministers, so in turn it condemns the wickedness of those who shamefully and treacherously abuse the pretext of this office. First in this order are those who seek church stipends but shun all the labours and cares that faithful ministers ought to devote themselves to. Next come those who, not content with necessities, nor even with what could suffice for living honourably, heap up huge wealth, imitating that Gehazi who wished to become the rich servant of the poor prophet Elisha. Worse than both are those who, in order to receive more lavish stipends from the liberality of princes, or even of bishops and monks, are wont to slacken in their duty and connive at things they ought to denounce openly. There is a great number of these today, and to them we largely owe it that many shrink from the doctrine of the Gospel and many make little progress in its knowledge.

units.la: Porrò poterant exempla hæc à nonnullis in ministerij ecclesiastici contemptum rapi, quasi hoc non pluris quàm militia, agricultura, aut res pecuaria fieri debeat: ideo ne solis hominum rationibus pugnare videatur Paulus, scripturæ testimonijs hoc ipsum confirmari ostendit. Quo loco ad-monemur: quæ ratio docendi in ecclesia seruari debeat. Licet quidem argumentis & similibus age-re ex rerum natura petitis: hoc enim olim Prophetas & Apostolos, adhæc ipsum Dei Filium secis-se constat: At simul videre oportet, ne quid ex illis conemur elicere, quod in Scripturis non sit expressum, aut harum authoritate non possit confirmari. Errant in hoc multi hodie, qui Pontificis Romani primatum & Diuorum intercessionem exemplis ex Regum aulis petitis probare conantur. Quibus apud Isaiam respondet Dominus: Cogitationes meæ non sunt cogitationes vestræ, neque viæ meæ sunt viæ vestræ: Sed quemadmodum cæli terra sublimiores sunt, ita excedunt viæ meæ vias vestras, &c. Exemplorum ergo & similium hic nobis vsus esto, vt quæ Dei verbo traduntur illustret & confirment, non autem vt ex illis dogmata aliena & peregrina eliciamus.
units.tr: Moreover, these examples could be seized upon by some to despise the ecclesiastical ministry, as if it ought to be valued no more highly than soldiering, farming or herding. Lest Paul seem to contend only with human reasoning, he shows that this very point is confirmed by the testimonies of Scripture. Here we are admonished as to what method of teaching ought to be observed in the Church. It is indeed permissible to argue from arguments and comparisons drawn from the nature of things, for it is established that the Prophets and Apostles, and indeed the Son of God himself, did this. Yet at the same time we must take care not to try to elicit from such things anything that is not expressed in the Scriptures or cannot be confirmed by their authority. Many today err in this, who try to prove the primacy of the Roman Pontiff and the intercession of the saints by examples taken from royal courts. To them the Lord answers through Isaiah: My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways. But as the heavens are higher than the earth, so my ways are higher than your ways, etc. Let examples and comparisons therefore be used by us here so as to illustrate and confirm what is handed down in the Word of God, and not so as to elicit from them alien and foreign dogmas.

units.la: Sed Paulus audiatur, sic loquens: Num secundum hominem hæc dico? Id est, num carnis solum sensu ducor, neque alijs nitor rationibus, quàm quæ inter homines in vsu quotidiano receptæ sunt? Nónne etiam Lex hæc dicit? Nam in Mosis Lege scriptum est: Non obligabis os bouis triturantis[?]. Extat locus Deut.25.cap. & ex illius seculi more præceptum hoc petitum est. Solebant enim veteres boum pedibus triticum aut grana ex spicis exterere, quod hodie flagellis fieri consueuit. De illis ergo legem tulit Deus, ne in illo labore agentibus os obturetur, quod haud dubie fallitarunt qui ad rem erant attentiores. At legem hanc ad Euangelij præcones Paulus extendit, & ne qui obijcerent: Quid istud ad te aut quosquam alios Euangelij ministros? Mox rem clarius exponit his verbis: Num boues curæ sunt Deo? aut num propter nos omnino hoc dicit? Boues Deo curæ esse negat, non quòd illos ab eius providentia eximere velit (sciebat enim hanc ad passeres & pullos coruorum vsq; extendi, neq; etiam illud Dauidis ignorabat: Hominem & iumentum seruabis Domine) sed non ita illum pecora curare dicit, vt in eorum gratiam leges ferre velit, cùm primas partes apud eum semper habeat homo, in cuius vsum alia omnia sunt condita. Ideo addit: Propter nos hoc scriptum est, quòd sub spe debeat vt qui arat arare: & qui triturat sub spe, sua spei particeps esse. Itaq; verborum sensus est: Quemadmodum olim legem tulit Deus, ne quis bouem triturantem à pabulo prohibeat: ita neminem mortalium idem ille sui laboris fructu fraudari vult. Itaque qui arat, sub spe arare debet, quod nimirum ex tota illa terra cultura fructum percepturus sit: & qui triturat sub spe, spei etiam suæ debet particeps fieri. At quia ecclesia Dei aruum est, & qui in illa Verbum prædicant ministri, primò quidem agricolarum instar sunt, dum homines ad sementem Verbi præparant, mox autem boues quoq; triturantes agunt, quando ad monitionibus, hortationibus, minus & quovis alio modo fructus Christiana professione dignos abominibus extorquent: minimè admittendum est, vt quoad spem salarij aut victus horum fors deterior sit, quàm agricolarum, vel etiam boum esse soleat. Quæ enim iniquitas esset homini negare quod iumento datur? aut in Christi aruo & area laborantes hominibus rusticis inferiores putare?
units.tr: But let Paul be heard, speaking thus: Do I say these things according to man? That is, am I led only by the sense of the flesh, and do I rely on no reasons other than those accepted among men in daily use? Does not the Law also say this? For it is written in the Law of Moses: You shall not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. The passage is in Deuteronomy 25, and this precept was taken from the custom of that age. For the ancients used to tread out wheat or grain from the ears with the feet of oxen, which today is commonly done with flails. God therefore gave the law concerning those oxen, that their mouths should not be bound while they laboured at that task, which those more attentive to the matter undoubtedly understood. But Paul extends this law to the heralds of the Gospel, and lest anyone object, "What has that to do with you or any other ministers of the Gospel?", he soon explains the matter more clearly in these words: Is it oxen that God cares for? Or does he say this altogether for our sake? He denies that God cares for oxen, not because he wishes to exempt them from his providence (for he knew that this extends even to the sparrows and the young ravens, nor did he overlook that saying of David: Lord, you will save man and beast), but because he does not say that God cares for cattle in such a way as to wish to make laws for their sake, since man, for whose use all other things were created, always holds the first place with him. Therefore he adds: It was written for our sake, because he who ploughs ought to plough in hope, and he who threshes in hope should share in his hope. The sense of the words, then, is this: just as God once gave the law that no one should forbid an ox treading out the corn from feeding on the straw, so that same God wishes that none of mortals be defrauded of the fruit of his labour. Thus he who ploughs ought to plough in hope, namely that he will receive the fruit from the whole cultivation of that land; and he who threshes in hope should also become a sharer in his hope. But since the Church of God is a field, and the ministers who preach the Word in it are at first like the farmers, while they prepare men for the sowing of the Word, and then also act like the oxen that tread out the corn, when they extract by admonitions, exhortations, reproofs and every other means fruit worthy of the Christian profession from the wicked, it must by no means be admitted that, as regards the hope of their salary or sustenance, their lot should be worse than that of farmers, or even of the oxen. For what injustice would it be to deny a man what is given to a beast of burden? Or to think that those who labour in Christ's field and threshing floor are inferior to rustic men?

units.la: Cæterum non immerito miretur aliquis, cur Apostolus scripturæ locum obscuriorem & hominum impiorum filio obnoxium adducere voluerit, cùm plures alij extent, qui disertis verbis illius sententiam confirmant? In Deuteronomio enim graviter præcipit Moses: Ne deferas Leuitam, qui est intra portas tuas, &c. Et in libro Numerorum decimæ & sacrificiorum partes sacerdotibus atq; Leuitis ea conditione assignantur, vt ijs non minus vti debeant, quàm si illa ex prijs agris aut horreis accepissent. Aut quid opus erat vllis veteris Instrumenti testimonijs pugnare, quando Christus (vt nuper monuimus) Apostolis liberum facit, vt ab illis victum accipiant, quibus Euangelium per ipsos prædicatur? Vel annon idem ille Verbi administris Legem naturæ & omnium gentium consensu receptam sententiam applicat, quæ operarium sua mercede dignum esse docet? Cur ergo boues triturantis potius mentionem facere voluit? Ideo nimirum, quòd comparatione ista fortius confutabatur illorum ingratitudo & malignitas, qui Christi ministris alimenta negabant, quæ ne bobus quidem & asinis negare solent, quoad aliquis eorum vsus est. Quid? annon canes domuum custodes aluntur, & quæ caueis inclusæ auiculæ aures nostras suo cantu demulcent, victum suum recipiunt? Sed o incurabilem impudentiam, quæ hodie multorum fronres[?] ita perfricuit, vt quàmuis ista verè dici non possint negare, ministros tamen egere, esurire & fa-me perire potius vellent, quàm denarium vnum aut panis buccellam egentibus largiri.
units.tr: Moreover, one might not unreasonably wonder why the Apostle wished to adduce a rather obscure passage of Scripture, one liable to the mockery of impious men, when many others exist which confirm his sentiment in plain words. For in Deuteronomy Moses strictly commands: Do not forsake the Levite who is within your gates, etc. And in the book of Numbers the tithes and portions of the sacrifices are assigned to the priests and Levites on the condition that they may use them no less than if they had received them from their own fields or barns. Or why was there any need to fight with testimonies of the Old Testament, when Christ (as we lately observed) makes it free for the Apostles to receive their food from those to whom the Gospel is preached through them? Or does not that same Paul apply to the ministers of the Word the opinion received from the law of nature and the consent of all nations, which teaches that a worker is worthy of his wages? Why then did he wish to mention the ox that treads out the corn rather than these? Surely because by this comparison the ingratitude and malice of those who denied food to Christ's ministers was more forcefully refuted, for they would not deny such things even to oxen and asses, so long as any use is had of them. What? Are not the dogs that guard our houses fed, and do not the little birds shut in cages, which soothe our ears with their song, receive their sustenance? But O incurable impudence, which today has so hardened the brows of many that, although these things cannot truly be denied, they would rather see the ministers lack, hunger and perish of famine than give one penny or a morsel of bread to the needy.

units.la: Meretur etiam hoc loco diligentem considerationem plus quàm paterna Dei providentia, qui etiamsi animalia bruta ipsum non agnoscant, de illis tamen leges ferre dignatur, & eadem propter nos alit atque conseruat: idque non eam modò ob causam, vt nobis inseruiant, sed vt virtutis quoque & pietatis documenta ex illis petamus. Hæc vt nostram spem atque fidem confirmare debent, ne nos vnquam neglectum iri putemus: ita monent, vt in præceptis omnibus, quæ brutorum aliquam mentionem faciunt, ad hominem respiciamus, propter quem illa creata sunt, & ex illis colligamus, quæ illi debeantur officia. Exempli gratia, iubet in Decalogo Deus, vt die Sabbati iumentis quoque quies permittatur, neue vllo tunc labore grauentur. Hic cogitemus, quòd vt propter hominem iumenta omnia facta sunt, ita præceptum hoc etiam hominis gratia datum esse, & proinde grauius multò peccare eos, qui seruos & ancillas otio illo sacro defraudant, quod ipsis Deus concesserit. Similiter quoties audis bouem fratris tui errantem reduci, & asinum inimici nimio onere depressum subleuari debere: mox in mentem tibi veniat, quantò magis hæc officia hominibus præstari debeant, vt nimirum erroribus seductos in viam salutis reducamus, & sceleribus grauatos subleuemus?
units.tr: It is worth careful consideration here that God's fatherly providence goes further than we might expect. Although brute animals do not acknowledge him, he nevertheless deigns to lay down laws concerning them, and he feeds and preserves them for our sake. He does this not only so that they may serve us, but also so that we may draw from them examples of virtue and piety. These examples ought to strengthen our hope and faith, so that we never suppose we will be neglected. They also teach us that, in all the precepts that make some mention of beasts, we should look to the human being for whose sake they were created, and from them gather what duties are owed to him. For example, God commands in the Decalogue that rest be granted to beasts of burden also on the Sabbath day, so that they are not burdened with any labour on that day. Let us consider here that, just as all beasts of burden were made for the sake of man, so this precept too was given for the sake of man; and therefore those who defraud their male and female servants of that holy rest, which God has granted them, sin much more gravely. Likewise, whenever you hear that your brother's ox that has strayed must be brought back, and that his ass oppressed by excessive burden must be lifted up, let it come to your mind how much more these duties ought to be performed for men: namely, that we should bring back those who have been led astray by errors into the way of salvation, and relieve those weighed down by sins?

units.la: Iubet præterea Lex, ne auem incubantem simul cum pullis suis auferamus. Vbi rursus meminisse oportet, nobis misericordiam & clementiam præcipi, qua erga homines quosuis vti debeamus: cauendum item esse ne iure nostro in quenquam seuerius vtamur: & ne licita quoq; vindicta in totius posteritatis excidium desæuiamus. Poterant huius generis exempla infinita adduci, sed sufficiat occasionem dedisse verè & piè philosophandi iis, qui scripturas non fine fructu legere & scrutari cupiunt.
units.tr: Furthermore, the Law commands that we not take away a bird sitting on her young together with the chicks. Here again we ought to remember that mercy and clemency are enjoined on us, which we ought to show toward all men whatsoever; and that we must take care not to use our right against anyone too severely, and not to rage, even in lawful vengeance, to the destruction of all posterity. Countless examples of this kind could be adduced, but let it suffice to have given an occasion for truly and piously reflecting to those who desire to read and examine the Scriptures not without profit.

units.la: Pergamus nunc in Apostoli verbis, qui quæ hucusque produxit argumenta quasi in summam colligens, ostendit præter omnem rationem de ministrorum stipendijs homines morosos & auaros conqueri, quando certum sit, ipsos plus accipere quàm illis impertiant. Id probat collatione, & in suam personam hoc omne recipit, quod inuidia & odio dignum quibusdam videbatur. Si nos (inquit) vobis spiritualia seminauimus, magnum ne fuerit si nos vestra carnalia messuerimus? Spiritualia dicit ea, quæ Verbi administri prædicant, partim quòd consistunt in rebus, quæ nullo carnis sensu, sed solo spiritu & fide percipi possunt, partim quòd non vt caro corruptioni obnoxia, sed firma & æterna sunt, nosq; ad vitam spiritualem, imò ad regnum Dei & beatam immortalitatem deducunt. Sunt hæc remissio peccatorum, gratia Dei, iustitia, sanctificatio, vita, salus & regni cœlorum hæreditas, quæ omnia per Euangelium prædicari, & legitimo Sacramentorum vsu in credentibus obsignari, satis notum est. Per carnalia autem victum[?] & amictum intelligit, quæ vt soli carni aut corpori seruiunt, ita fluxa sunt & peritura. Atqui hæc sola (inquit) a vobis accipimus, qui vobis illorum tantorum bonorum fumus administri. Quid ergo magnum datis, cuius vos merito pœnitere debeat? Voluit autem ista comparatione vti Apostolus, non quòd (vt ingrati & mala frugis ministri solent) stipendia ecclesiastica extenuare voluerit (nam quanti fecerit Philippensiū in se alendo liberalitatem, scripta ad eos epistola satis testatur) sed quia ipsi cum hominibus crassis res erat, qui cùm auaritia vt plurimum laborarent, maximi facere solebant quicquid ex suis thesauris depromere cogebantur. Nos verò obseruabimus, non cum solis Corinthijs Paulum loqui, sed simul totius mundi ingratitudinem perstringi, qui suas sordes & quisquilias tanti fere æstimat, vt nimium ei videatur, quicquid in Euangelij doctrinam & præconum eius alimoniam confertur. Est morbus hic admodum vulgaris hodie. Quàm multos enim est videre, qui cum prodigiosa prodigalitate patrimonium omne in aleam infamem, in scorta, in conuiuia luxuriosa, in insanas ædificiorum structuras, in lenones, canes, accipitres, equos, mimos denique & histriones profundant, non parci modò sunt in diuinis, sed iniuriam grauem sibi fieri queruntur, si ex sua opulentia aliquid iubeantur conferre in scholas, in sacrarum literarum studiosos iuuenes, vel in annuum sui ecclesiastis siue doctoris stipendium? Quæ vero tantæ ingratitudinis causa est? Hæc nimirum, quòd neq; opum huius seculi vsum verum, neq; Euangelij dignitatem & bonorum, quæ illo nobis prædicantur, incomparabile pretium intelligunt. Discant ergo illi sibijpsis Paulinum istud occinere, & simul cogitent, diuitiarum omnium non alium vsum esse, quàm vt vita mortali seruiant, caducas item & fluxas esse, in Euangelio autem immensum illum thesaurum & incomparabilem margaritam regni Dei contineri, cuius causa fortunas omnes diuendere, imo abijcere oportet. Potuit olim Cratem Thebanum humanae sapientiae admiratio mouere, vt opes suas omnes in mare demergeret: & quid non poterit caelestis illa sapientia, si uius excellentiam simul & vtilitatem homines recte expendant?
units.tr: Let us now proceed to the words of the Apostle, who, gathering up as it were in summary the arguments he has so far advanced, shows that men are complaining, against all reason, about the stipends of the ministers, who are morose and greedy, since it is certain that they receive far more than they give. He proves this by comparison, and takes upon himself all that seemed to some deserving of envy and hatred. "If we have sown spiritual things among you" (he says), "is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?" He calls spiritual those things which the ministers of the Word proclaim: partly because they consist in matters that can be perceived not by any sense of the flesh but by the Spirit and faith alone; and partly because they are not corruptible like the flesh, but are firm and eternal, and lead us to spiritual life, indeed to the kingdom of God and blessed immortality. These are the remission of sins, the grace of God, righteousness, sanctification, life, salvation, and the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven; it is well known that all of these are proclaimed through the Gospel and sealed in believers by the lawful use of the sacraments. By carnal things, however, he understands food and clothing, which, since they serve only the flesh or body, are as fleeting and perishable as it. "Yet these alone" (he says) "we receive from you, who are the stewards of those so great goods. What great thing do you give, of which you ought rightly to repent?" The Apostle chose to use this comparison not because (as ungrateful and sour-tempered ministers are wont to do) he wished to belittle the ecclesiastical stipends, for how highly he valued the generosity of the Philippians in supporting him is sufficiently attested by the letter he wrote to them; but because he had to deal with coarse men, who, being for the most part troubled by greed, were accustomed to value very highly whatever they were compelled to draw from their own treasuries. We, however, shall observe that Paul is speaking not with the Corinthians alone, but at the same time is censuring the ingratitude of the whole world, which values its filth and trifles so highly that whatever is contributed to the teaching of the Gospel and the maintenance of its heralds seems to it far too much. This disease is very common today. For how many are there to be seen who squander their whole patrimony with prodigious extravagance on infamous gambling, on harlots, on luxurious banquets, on insane building projects, on pimps, dogs, hawks, horses, and, in short, on mimes and actors, and who are not only stingy toward divine things, but complain of grave injury being done to them if they are ordered to contribute something out of their wealth to the schools, to young men studying the sacred letters, or to the annual stipend of their minister or teacher? And what is the cause of such great ingratitude? Surely this: that they understand neither the true use of the riches of this age, nor the dignity of the Gospel and the incomparable worth of the goods which are proclaimed to us by it. Let them therefore learn to sing that Pauline song to themselves, and at the same time let them consider that the use of all riches is none other than to serve mortal life, and that they are likewise frail and fleeting; whereas in the Gospel that immense treasure and incomparable pearl of the kingdom of God is contained, for whose sake one ought to sell off, indeed cast away, all one's fortunes. Once, the admiration for human wisdom moved Crates the Theban to plunge all his wealth into the sea; and what will not that heavenly wisdom be able to do, if men rightly weigh both its excellence and its usefulness?

units.la: At priusquam Sermonem hunc concludamus, obseruari quoque debet sementis similitudo, qua in praesenti Paulus proprijssime vtitur. Nam Verbum Dei semen est regenerationis, ex quo omnes renasci oportet, qui regnum illud caeleste videre volunt. Seminatur illud praedicatione, vt Christus in parabola docuit: & ideo recte Apostolus se & alios spiritualia illa bona apud Corinthios seminasse scribit. At sementis non sine labore fit, & multa illam praecedant oportet, quae ipsa quoque sine labore & molestia non possunt perfici: fructus autem non nisi ipse possidetur, donec vltimum illud messis futurae tempus aduenerit. Ita magno cum labore praedicatur Verbum, fructus autem non semper, qualem vellemus, apparet. Et qui in semente illa facienda plurimum laborant, ij fere in hoc mundo minimum inde praemij recipiunt. Debent tamen sub spe arare, serere, metere & triturare: quia etsi homines fallant, promissa tamen mercede Deus suos operarios minime fructrabitur, sicuti in talentorum parabola docemur. Excitent ista omnes homines ad diuinae bonitatis considerationem. Sumus omnes natura steriles & instar terrae maledictae. Inter nos tamen aruum sibi delegit Deus, quod seruorum suorum ministerio colit, & cuius sulcus semen illud caeleste committit, quos & spiritus sui virtute irrigat. Excipiant ergo singuli semen istud, & Deo sese obsequentes atque faciles praebeant, vt fructibus bonis ornati olim ad regni caelorum horrea colligantur cum IESV CHRISTO, Domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: But before we conclude this sermon, the likeness of sowing, which Paul uses here most aptly, must also be observed. For the Word of God is the seed of regeneration, from which all must be born again who wish to see that heavenly kingdom. It is sown by preaching, as Christ taught in the parable; and therefore the Apostle rightly writes that he and others have sown those spiritual goods among the Corinthians. But sowing is not done without labour, and many things must precede it, which themselves also cannot be accomplished without labour and trouble; the fruit, however, is not possessed until that last time of the future harvest has come. Thus the Word is preached with great labour, yet the fruit does not always appear as we would wish. And those who labour most in performing that sowing receive, for the most part in this world, the least reward from it. Nevertheless they must plough, sow, reap and thresh in hope; for even if men deceive them, God will by no means defraud his workers of the promised wage, as we are taught in the parable of the talents. Let these things stir all men to consider the goodness of God. We are all by nature barren and like a cursed land. Yet God has chosen for himself among us a field which he cultivates through the ministry of his servants, and into whose furrows he entrusts that heavenly seed, watering them also by the power of his Spirit. Let each one therefore receive that seed, and show himself obedient and pliant to God, so that, adorned with good fruits, he may one day be gathered into the barns of the kingdom of heaven with Jesus Christ, our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLV.
units.tr: HOMILY XLV.

units.la: Si alij sui in vos iuris participes sunt, cur non potius nos? At qui non vsi fuimus iure isto: sed omnia sustinemus, ne quid remoremur Euangelium Christi. An nescitis, quod qui sacris operantur, ex sacrario edunt? & qui altari assident, cum altari participant? Ita Dominus constituit iis qui Euangelium annuntiant, vt ex Euangelio viuant. Ego tamen nullo istorum sum vsus. Neque vero haec scripsi, vt ita fiat in me. Nam bonum est mihi mori potius, quam vt gloriationem meam aliquis inanem reddat.
units.tr: If others share this right over you, why not rather we? But we have not used this right; we endure everything, so that we may not hinder the Gospel of Christ. Do you not know that those who serve at the sacred rites eat from the temple, and those who attend the altar share in the altar? So the Lord has ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel. Yet I have made use of none of these things. Nor have I written this so that it may be done to me in this way. For it is better for me to die than for anyone to make my boasting empty.

units.la: Multis & grauibus argumentis probat Paulus, licuisse sibi a Corinthijs, quibus Euangelium annuntiauerat, stipendium ecclesiasticum accipere. Diligentiae huius causa est, quod partim suam authoritatem contra aemulos tueri vult, partim suo exemplo eorum licentiam retundere, qui libertate Christiana eo vsque abutebantur, vt non sine multorum scandalo prophanis gentium sacris communicarent, & epulis in Deorum honorem institutis vescerentur. Potest autem disputatio ista nos docere, nulla administrorum Verbi Dei diligentiam superuacaneam aut nimiam esse: quando apud eos, qui iam annis aliquot Christum professi fuerant, & multis ecclesijs praesse videbantur, tam multus opus fuit in eo demonstrando, quod communi sensu probari poterat, & de quo omnes homines Lex naturae admonet, dignum videlicet esse operarium mercede sua, & eos qui se aliorum ministerio manciparunt, ab ijsdem ali debere. Sed ea est carnis nostrae stupiditas & affectuum malitia, vt quae luce clariora sunt non videant qui hos in consilium adhibent. Exempla huius rei hodie multa in nostris ecclesijs extant, quae nos excitare debent, ne remissiores simus in ijs corrigendis, quae correctione requirere videmus. Caeterum post multa, quae hucusque produxit Apostolus, nunc proprio exemplo Corinthios conuincit, & inde propius accedit ad sua existimationis defensionem.
units.tr: Paul proves by many weighty arguments that it was lawful for him to receive ecclesiastical maintenance from the Corinthians, to whom he had proclaimed the Gospel. He takes this care partly because he wants to defend his authority against his rivals, and partly because by his own example he wishes to check the licence of those who so abused Christian liberty that they took part, not without great scandal to many, in the profane sacred rites of the Gentiles and ate at feasts held in honour of the gods. This discussion can teach us that no diligence of the ministers of God's Word is superfluous or excessive, since among those who had for some years professed Christ and seemed to preside over many churches, there was so much need to demonstrate what could be proved by common sense, and what the law of nature teaches all men: namely, that a workman is worthy of his wages, and that those who have given themselves over to the ministry of others ought to be supported by them. But such is the stupidity of our flesh and the malice of our passions that those who take such men as their counsellors do not see things that are clearer than light. Many examples of this today exist in our churches, and they ought to rouse us, so that we are not too lax in correcting those things which we see require correction. Moreover, after the many things the Apostle has brought forward so far, he now convicts the Corinthians by his own example, and from there comes closer to the defence of his reputation.

units.la: Primum hïs verbis comprehendit: Si alij sui in vos iuris participes sunt, cur non potius nos? Iuris siue τῆς ἐξουσίας[?] nomine (quam plerique potestatem interpretati sunt) intelligit facultatem viuendi aliorum sumptu & impensis: & non tam de doctoribus Corinthiorum loquitur, qui ab ecclesia victum exigebant, quàm ipsis Corinthijs, qui hunc abs se exigi patiebatur, cum in Paulum bucusq; parcissimi fuissent. Sensus ergo verborum est: Cùm alijs istud per vos liceat, quibus liberaliter numeratis plura quàm necessitas requirat, cur ego iniquus aut iniustus videar, si victum accipiam necessarium? Loquitur autem (vt Chrysostomus annotauit) de nothis & fraudulentis doctoribus, qui posteà sum dicesum apud eos irrepserant, & intolerabili insolentia, neq; sine publica ecclesiae illius contumelia res suas agebant: hiis vero seipsum opponit, qui cum Corinthiorum Apostolus esset, & primus in ea vrbe Euangelium praedicauisset, merito plus iuris apud eos debebat obtinere. Facit ergo ad huius loci expositionem, vel potius argumenti istius amplificationem, quod in posteriori epistola Cap.11. scribitur: Toleratis si quis vos in seruitutem adigit, si quis exedit, si quis accipit, si quis attollit sese, si quis vos in faciem caedit. In praesenti tamen, quòd minus necesse videretur, neq; tanta verborum grauitate in aemulos suos inuehitur, neq; suos labores arrogantius iactat: sed eo contentus est, vt sibi idem quod alijs licuisse ostendat. Est hoc magnae modestiae argumentum, & docemur Apostoli exemplo, non semper dici debere quicquid in aliqua causa dici potest: sed sufficiat ea modestè attigisse quae sufficere possunt: & cum vitiorum emendationi atq; paci ante omnia studere oporteat homines Christianos, videndum est, vt quoad eius fieri potest animorum offensio caueatur.
units.tr: First he comprehends it in these words: If others share this right over you, why not rather we? By the name of right [τῆς ἐξουσίας] (which most have interpreted as power) he means the freedom to live at the expense and cost of others; and he speaks not so much of the teachers of the Corinthians, who demanded their keep from the church, as of the Corinthians themselves, who allowed this to be demanded from them, although until now they had been most sparing towards Paul. The sense of the words, then, is this: since others are permitted this by you, to whom you have given more generously than necessity requires, why should I seem unfair or unjust if I receive what is necessary for my living? He speaks (as Chrysostom observed) of spurious and deceitful teachers, who afterwards had crept in among them, and who conducted their affairs with intolerable arrogance and not without public disgrace to that church. He sets himself against these men: since he was the Apostle of the Corinthians, and had first preached the Gospel in that city, he ought rightly to have had more right among them. What is written in the later epistle, chapter 11, therefore helps to explain this passage, or rather to amplify this argument: You suffer it, if anyone brings you into bondage, if anyone devours you, if anyone takes from you, if anyone exalts himself, if anyone strikes you in the face. Here, however, since it seemed less necessary, he does not inveigh against his rivals with such severity of words, nor does he boast of his labours more arrogantly; he is content simply to show that what was allowed to others was also allowed to himself. This is an argument of great modesty, and from the Apostle's example we are taught that one should not always say whatever can be said in a given case; it is enough to touch modestly on those things which can suffice. And since Christian people ought above all to strive for the correction of faults and for peace, care must be taken, as far as possible, that offence is not given to minds.

units.la: Apparet autem hic corruptum & peruersum mundi iudicium, qui fere benefactores odisse, aut saltem negligere, eos autem in honore & pretio habere solet, qui saluti ipsius quàm maximè officiunt. Etenim cùm Paulus apud Corinthios doceret, in amplissima & opulentissima ciuitate nemo ciuium repertus est, qui illi hospitium praeberet, aut mensa sua dignum iudicaret, praeter vnum Aquilam, qui & ipse peregrinus erat, & non ita pridem propter Claudij Caesaris edictum Romaillùc venerat. Ad hunc ergo diuertit, & dum toti vrbi caelestem animarum cibum depromit, ipse duro manuum labore sibi ipsi victum parat. At postquam ipso inde digressio vanissimi ostentatores & impostores obrepserunt, qui Christo initiatos in sectas distrahebant & hominum seruos faciebant, qui item impudenter quiduis à quibusuis postulabant, qui denique sua partim negligentia, partim improbitate ecclesiam totam infamem reddebant, mox isti omnium domus patuerunt, certatim in eos profuderunt suas fortunas, imò grauissimas quoque iniurias ab illis patienter tolerarunt. Huius generis multa olim facta sunt Prophetarum temporibus, quando hos quidem inter extremam inopiam vix vitam sustinuisse, aut etiam propter hostium insidias latuisse vel profugisse legimus, cùm interea ad regum mensas lautissimè comessarentur, qui & cultum Dei euertebant, & publici exitij erant praecipui authores. Neque melior Filij Dei in terris hisce agentis fors fuit, qui & ipse incertis sedibus hinc inde oberrauit, neque habuit quò caput inclinaret, coetus verò suorum auditorum ferè in locis desertis & littoribus coëgit, quando Sacerdotes & scribae, infelicis populi pestes, templum & Synagogas occuparant, & ex miserorum spoliis indies ditabantur. Quid verò hodie fiat notius est, quàm vt multis demonstrare necesse sit. Quis enim nescit iam seculis aliquot supremam rerum ecclesiasticarum potestatem penes eos fuisse, qui ne infima quidem ecclesiae membra dici merebantur? Et hodie passim cathedrales ecclesias (vt vocant) & augusta monasteriorum palatia cum amplissimis redditibus occupant homines aut indocti, aut etiam impuri, qui neque Veritatis doctrinam populo tradunt, neque honestè viuunt, & his tamen datur quod ad luxum & libidinem sufficit: egentibus interim & cum fame conflictantibus Christi ministris, qui vitae aeternae verbum praedicant. Est haec ingratitudo quouis supplicio digna, & ita Verbi sui contemptum Deus vlcisicitur, vt impostores & latrones sibi ipsis accersant, eosq; magnis impensis alant, qui illud nolunt audire. At non debent ista pios Christi ministros offendere. Vincet enim & in illis triumphabit nihilominus Dei Verbum, & in coelis repositia sunt illis praemia, quae nemo praeripere poterit.
units.tr: Here, moreover, appears the corrupt and perverse judgement of the world, which is accustomed almost to hate benefactors, or at least to neglect them, and to hold in honour and esteem those who most harm its welfare. For when Paul was teaching among the Corinthians, in a very large and wealthy city, no citizen was found who would offer him lodging or think him worthy of his table, except one Aquila, who was himself a foreigner and had come there from Rome not long before, because of the edict of Claudius Caesar. So Paul lodged with him, and while he dispensed the heavenly food of souls to the whole city, he himself provided his own living by the hard labour of his hands. But afterwards, when those most vain showmen and impostors had crept in after his departure, who drew those initiated into Christ into sects and made them slaves of men, who also shamelessly demanded anything at all from anyone, and who finally by their negligence in part and their wickedness in part made the whole church infamous, at once those men had their homes thrown open to them; eagerly they poured out their fortunes upon them, and indeed patiently endured even the gravest injuries from them. Many things of this kind happened long ago in the times of the Prophets, when we read that these men barely sustained life amid extreme poverty, or even hid or fled because of the plots of their enemies, while meanwhile the others feasted most sumptuously at the tables of kings, who were overturning the worship of God and were the chief authors of public ruin. Nor was the lot of the Son of God, while he lived on earth, any better. He too wandered here and there without a fixed dwelling, and had nowhere to lay his head; he gathered the assembly of his hearers almost in deserted places and on the shores, when the priests and scribes, the plagues of the unhappy people, had seized the temple and the synagogues and were growing rich daily from the spoils of the wretched. What is done today is too well known to need many proofs. For who does not know that for some centuries the supreme power in ecclesiastical affairs has rested with those who did not even deserve to be counted the lowest members of the church? And today everywhere men, either ignorant or even impure, occupy the cathedral churches (as they are called) and the stately palaces of monasteries, with the most ample revenues; they neither hand down the doctrine of truth to the people nor live honestly, and yet to them is given whatever suffices for luxury and lust, while meanwhile the ministers of Christ, who preach the word of eternal life, are in need and struggle with hunger. This ingratitude is worthy of any punishment, and God so avenges the contempt of his Word that he summons impostors and robbers to himself and feeds them at great expense, while those who refuse to hear that Word go without. But such things ought not to offend the pious ministers of Christ. For the Word of God will nevertheless conquer and triumph in them, and rewards are laid up for them in heaven, which no one will be able to snatch away.
