units.la: Itaq; Paulum imitentur, qui etsi de Corinthiorum iniquitate merito conqueri posset, nihil taMen[?] in eos durius dicit, sed id potius infert, quod ad disputationis huius statum maximè faciebat. Atqui non vsi fuimus (inquit) iure isto, sed omnia sustinemus, ne quid remoremur Euangelium Christi. Quasi diceret: Etiamsi diuinus & humanis legibus ius meum tueri, vestro denique exemplo contra vos uti possim, illud tamen persequi nolui. Nec tamen mihi aliquis obijciat, velim, me vix potuisse aliquid a vobis saluo honore meo petere, cum omnibus abundauerim, quae ad vitam beatè & lautè transigendam faciunt. Tam enim abesse, ut illud de me dici queat, ut potius constet me plerunq; in extrema necessitate constitutum esse, esuriuisse, sitiuisse, alsisse, omnia deniq; ea passum esse, quae pauperrimis & omni praesidio humano destitutis accidere solent. Qui in hunc vsq; diem (quod supra dixi) & esurimus, & sitimus, & nudi sumus, & colaphis caedimur, & incertis sedibus erra-mus. Sustinemus tamen haec omnia, & quaedam potius ferre parati sumus, quàm vel minimae ex parte Euangelicae praedicationis cursum atq; fructum remorari. At hoc dicendo, non obscurè in-nuit, quàm turpiter faciant, qui cum nulla necessitate premantur, & domi suae conuiuari possint, tamen ne ab idololatrarum quidem mensis abstinere velint, quàmuis exemplo suo infirmos offen-di, & multos ex gentibus in superstitionibus suis confirmari, & ita duplicem remo-ram Euangelio inijci videant.
units.tr: Let them therefore imitate Paul, who, although he could justly complain of the iniquity of the Corinthians, says nothing harsher against them, but rather adduces that which most served the state of this argument. But (he says) we have not used this right, but we endure all things, so that we may not hinder the Gospel of Christ. As if he were saying: even if I could defend my right by divine and human laws, and finally use your own example against you, I nevertheless did not wish to pursue it. Nor let anyone object to me that I hardly could have asked anything from you without loss of my honour, since I have abounded in all the things that make for living happily and splendidly. For it is so far from being true of me that this could be said, that it is rather clear that I have been placed very often in extreme necessity: I have hungered, thirsted, been cold, and in short suffered all those things which commonly befall the most destitute and those bereft of every human protection. Up to this very day (as I said above) we both hunger and thirst, and are naked, and are struck with fists, and wander without a fixed dwelling. Yet we endure all these things, and are ready to bear certain things rather than to hinder, even in the smallest part, the course and fruit of the Gospel preaching. But by saying this he hints not obscurely how shamefully they act who, though pressed by no necessity, and able to feast in their own homes, nevertheless are unwilling to abstain even from the tables of idolaters, although they see that by their example the weak are offended, and many from among the Gentiles are confirmed in their superstitions, and thus a double hindrance is cast in the way of the Gospel.

units.la: Quaerunt autem hoc loco nonnulli, quae illa remora fuerit, de qua Paulus loquitur, & num quid huius debuerit timeri, si a Corinthijs stipendium accepisset? Quibus nos respondemus, non su-stra timuisse Apostolum, qui ut prudentem ecclesiae ministrum docet, Corinthiorum mores attentius obseruabat. Videbat enim homines auaros & quaestui deditos vix adduci posse, ut illis ali-quid largiantur, ex quibus nihil praesentis aut terreni commodi vicissim sperare possent. Videbat rursum non deesse impostores, qui mirificis artibus sese insinuabant, ut pecunijs quam plurimos te-mungerent[?]. Inter illos ergo ius suum persequi aut obtinere non poterat, quin remoras multas Euangelio obijceret. Primo enim suo exemplo pseudoapostolorum audaciam & improbitatem confirmasset. Deinde seipsum suspectum fecisset, quasi & ipse quaestus causa omnia faceret. Tertiò multus eum seruiliter adulari, & perfidè ad vitia manifesta conniuere, multa item dissimulare oportuisset, ne eos offenderet, à quibus plurimum poterat sperari. Postremò cum gentium Apostolus esset, sui nominis existimationem non poterat in periculum adducere, quin ad omnes alias ecclesias redundaret scandalum, quod inde fuisset enatum. Imò ita sibi viam vbiq; praecluisset apud eos, qui Euangelium nondum audiuerant. Quis enim eum admittat aut patienter audiat, quem non aliud quam priuatum quaestum vanari, iam ante sibi persuasit? Et credibile est, non paucos fuisse in Corinthiorum vrbe, qui nihil non potius maluissent dare Apostolo, quàm morum disciplinam ferre, cuius ille acerrimus vindex erat, & quo nomine eum imprimis oderant. Vides ergo non inanem metum fuisse, qui illum cohibuit.
units.tr: Some people ask at this point what that hindrance was of which Paul speaks, and whether he had reason to fear anything of the kind if he had accepted support from the Corinthians. We answer that the Apostle did not fear without cause. As a wise minister of the Church, he paid close attention to the character of the Corinthians. He saw that greedy men, who were devoted to gain, could hardly be persuaded to give anything to people from whom they could expect no present or earthly advantage in return. He also saw that there was no shortage of impostors who, by remarkable tricks, insinuated themselves so that they might fleece as many people as possible of their money. So if he had insisted on his right or claimed it among such people, he would have put many obstacles in the way of the Gospel. First, by his own example he would have strengthened the boldness and wickedness of the false apostles. Second, he would have made himself suspect, as though he too were doing everything for the sake of gain. Third, he would have had to flatter people servilely, wink treacherously at manifest vices, and overlook many things, so as not to offend those from whom he could hope for much. Last, since he was the Apostle to the Gentiles, he could not risk the reputation of his name without the scandal arising from it spreading to all the other churches. Indeed, he would have closed the way for himself everywhere among those who had not yet heard the Gospel. For who would admit him or listen to him patiently, if they had already persuaded themselves that he was hunting only for private gain? It is credible that there were not a few in the city of Corinth who would rather have given anything to the Apostle than submit to the discipline of morals, of which he was the most zealous defender and for which they hated him above all. You see, then, that the fear which restrained him was not groundless.

units.la: At nos ex eius exemplo generalem doctrinam petere debemus, nobis quoque cauendum esse, ne Euangelij cursum per ea remoremur, quae nobis licita & concessa sunt, aut quocunque modo scandalum demus infirmis, qui nondum eò usque profecerunt, ut omnium quae fiunt rationem intelligant. Nam ut scandalum vitetur, non modò quid nobis liceat videndum est, verumetiam qui & quales sint, quibus cum nobis res est. Iubet hoc Dei gloria, quae Christianis hominibus commendatissima esse debet, & quae non alia re magis, quàm libera Euangelij praedicatione propagatur. Idem Lex charitatis suadet, cum ex eo omnium hominum salus dependeat, ut in Christi cognitionem adducantur. Et cùm omnium sit dona atque vires suas ad Ecclesiae Christi aedificationem conferre (quod olim Tabernaculi Mosaici extructione Israelitas fecisse legimus) ad omnis quoque loci & ordinis homines doctrina ista debet extendi. Imprimis autem minimos videre conuenit, ne dum ius suum pertinacius tuentur, multorum animos abs se & Euangelij doctrina alienent. Peccant in eo plurimum, qui in ferendis iniurijs impatientiores sunt, & sui nominis existimationem non sine aliorum contumelia tuentur. Quotquot item in exigendis stipendijs suis rigidiores, ne ijs quidem parcunt, quorum inopiam ipsi sua liberalitate subleuare debebant. Quid vero de illis dicemus, qui ut stipendia lautiora prouehantur, Episcopis & Abbatibus supplices fiunt, & ijs turpiter adulantur, quos iuratos Euangelicae veritatis hostes esse neuerunt? Est hoc hodie nimis vulgare, & eo stratagemate iam olim aduersus Christum vsus est infelix ille filius perditionis, ut ecclesias propè omnes in Monachorum & Episcoporum potestatem redegerit, qui cum decimis redditus quoque alios omnes intercipiunt, neque alios ad docendum admittunt, quàm quos prius iureiurando astringunt, ne quid praedicent, quo ipsorum tyrannis euerti, aut quem ex superstitionibus suis ipsi faciunt, quaestus diminui possit. Patiuntur haec fieri passim Christiani homines, neque vident quantum ipsis ex sua libertate decedat, & quòd pastorum loco succedunt malae frugis mercenarij & canes muti, qui offa in os iniecta tunc quoque silent, quando Christi ouile à lupis voracissimis vastatur. Hic certè satius erat Paulum imitari, neque quicquam ab illis accipere, sed quacunque aliam alendorum ministrorum rationem inire, ut sua ministerio verbi libertas integra maneret. Sed utrinque avaritia peccatur, dum luxu corruptis nullum fere stipendium sufficit, auditores autem nimium esse putant, quicquid in ministros confertur. Habent praeterea hoc loco, in cuius consideratione sese exercent Christiani principes, ne dum ipsi quoque ius suum rigidè nimis urgent, Euangelij doctrinam, cuius vindices & propugnatores videri volunt, multis suspectam & invisam reddant. Quod ipsum ad privatos quoque homines pertinet. Ut enim summum ius summa iniuria est: ita ad lucrifaciendos hominum animos nihil efficatius est facilitate & Christiana indulgentia, quae monet ut iure nostro in loco & tempore cedamus. At cùm hoc à nobis requirat Christiana religionis ratio, quàm graue & nulla venia dignum scelus fuerit, si qui in aliorum gratiam ne ab ijs quidem abstinere velint, quae sine scelere fieri non possunt. Est hoc hominum genus hodie passim obuium inter eos, qui Euangelij doctrinam profitentur, eo autem praetextu sacra & prophanarapiunt, incestis libidinibus sese polluunt, & licenter omnia faciunt, quae olim inter gentes reprehensione digna visa fuerunt. Et hi sunt, qui Euangelij cursum quàm maximè remorantur, dum infirmiores quidem grauiter offendunt, apertis verò hostibus argumenta suppeditant, quibus contra nos & veritatis doctrinam apud imperitos inuehantur.
units.tr: From his example, however, we ought to draw a general teaching: that we too must take care not to hinder the course of the Gospel through things that are lawful and permitted to us, or in any way give offence to the weak, who have not yet advanced so far as to understand the reasons for all that is done. For if offence is to be avoided, we must consider not only what is lawful for us but also who and what kind of people they are with whom we have to deal. The glory of God requires this, which ought to be most commended to Christians and which is spread by nothing more than the free preaching of the Gospel. The law of charity likewise urges it, since the salvation of all people depends on their being brought to the knowledge of Christ. And since it belongs to everyone to contribute his gifts and strength to the building up of the Church of Christ (as we read that the Israelites once did in the construction of the Mosaic tabernacle), this teaching ought to extend to people of every place and rank. Above all, however, the humblest must take care that, by defending their rights too stubbornly, they do not alienate the minds of many from themselves and from the doctrine of the Gospel. Those sin most who are more impatient in bearing injuries and who defend their own reputation without the insult of others. Likewise, those who are too strict in demanding their wages do not even spare those whose poverty they ought themselves to relieve by their generosity. But what shall we say of those who, in order to have their stipends increased, become suppliants to bishops and abbots and flatter them shamelessly, though they know these men to be sworn enemies of the truth of the Gospel? This is very common today, and that unhappy son of perdition used this same stratagem against Christ long ago, so that he reduced almost all the churches under the power of monks and bishops. These men, while they seize the tithes and all the other revenues, admit to teaching only those whom they first bind by oath not to preach anything by which their tyranny might be overthrown, or by which the profit they make from their superstitions might be diminished. Christian people everywhere suffer these things to happen, and they do not see how much of their freedom they lose, or that in place of pastors there succeed hirelings of poor quality and dumb dogs, who, when a morsel has been thrown into their mouths, keep silent even when the fold of Christ is being laid waste by the most ravenous wolves. Here it would certainly have been better to imitate Paul and accept nothing from them, but to adopt some other plan for supporting the ministers, so that the freedom of the ministry of the Word might remain intact. But sin is committed on both sides by avarice: the ministers, corrupted by luxury, are scarcely satisfied by any stipend, while the hearers think that whatever is given to the ministers is too much. Moreover, Christian princes, in considering this matter, must also take care lest, by pressing their own rights too rigidly, they make the doctrine of the Gospel, whose champions and defenders they wish to appear, suspect and hateful to many. This applies to private persons as well. For just as the highest right is the highest injustice, so nothing is more effective for winning the minds of men than kindness and Christian forbearance, which teaches us to yield our right in place and time. But since the principle of the Christian religion requires this of us, how grave and unpardonable a crime it is, if people, to please others, will not even abstain from those things which cannot be done without sin. This kind of person is found everywhere today among those who profess the doctrine of the Gospel; under that pretext they plunder sacred and profane things, defile themselves with incestuous lusts, and do freely everything that was once thought worthy of reproof among the Gentiles. And these are the ones who most of all hinder the course of the Gospel, since they gravely offend the weaker brethren, and they supply arguments to open enemies by which the doctrine of truth may be attacked among the unlearned.

units.la: Caeterum ne Paulus suo exemplo alijs Apostolis praeiudicare putaretur, & illos damnare, qui ecclesiae stipendijs viuunt, redit ad asserendum ius ministerij, & illud testimonijs scripturae euidentissimis confirmat. An nescitis, quòd qui sacris operantur, ex sacrario edunt, &c. Interrogatione utitur, quae & causa certitudinem indicat, & sciolorum malitiam arguit, qui quod omnibus notum erat audebant in dubium vocare. Perinde ergo hoc est, ac si dixisset: Quid opus est diutius in to[?] probando insistere, quod ijs quoque compertum est, qui imperitissimi esse videntur? Quid verò illud est? Quòd qui sacris operantur, ex sacrario edunt, id est, ex ijs, quae in sacrario aut templo offeruntur. Et qui altari assident, cum altari participant? Quo loco per Prosopopoeiam alteri personam affingit, eò quòd pars victimae in illo comburebatur, alia autem cedebant sacerdotibus. Duobus autem hisce membris totum cultum Leuiticum cum omnibus ijs comprehendit, qui in illo exercendo publicè ministrabant. Erant hi in duos ordines distincti. Primus inferioris sortis homines, aut vulgus Leuitarum habebat, quorum erat labores grauiores & sordidiores (si ita loqui fas est) obire. Ipsi enim ab adducentibus victimas accipiebant, eaedem mactabant, excoriabant, lauabant, secabant in partes, ligna denique struebant, quibus in altari ignis accendebatur. Adhaec templum totum cum vasis sacris purgabant & custodiebant. Alter ordo constabat sacerdotibus, quorum dignitas maior erat, quos Paulus altari assedisse ait, eò quòd ijs solis intenti essent, quae ad ipsum altare fiebant. Ipsi enim partes victimae ad sacrificium destinatas ab offerentibus accipere, coram Domino rite in altum extollere, aut in dextram & sinistram agitare, igni imponere: libamina infundere & sanguinem aspergere solebant: ad eos item pertinebat incensum, quod supra aram thymiamatis adolebatur. Etsi verò ordines illi inter se distincti, & in utroque alij alijs praestantiores essent, omnibus tamen illis, imò uxoribus quoque & liberis eorum ex suo illo munere Deus victum constituerat, ex partibus videlicet sacrificiorum, primitijs frugum ex terra nascentium, primogenitis item & decimis. Et ne ex alieno viuere, aut alijs sua eripere putarentur, non uno loco testatur Deus, ista omnia sua esse, & se ea Leuitis atque sacerdotibus dedisse, ut ex illis ceu proprijs viuant. Vide quae in hanc sententiam in libro Numerorum Cap. 18. traduntur. De his omnibus in præsenti Paulus disserit, & ne in nouo testamento ministrorum ecclesiæ con-ditio deterior esse videretur, addit: Ita Dominus constituit iis qui Euangelium annuntiant, ut ex Euangelio uiuant. Quòd si locos quæris, in quibus hoc constituerit Dominus, satis euidens est qui Matthæi decimo Cap. habetur, vbi prohibet, ne Apostoli aurum vel argentum com-parent, neque commeatum & reliqua ad iter necessaria secum ferant: eius vero mandati causam affert, quòd dignus sit operarius mercede sua. Operarijs ergo eos confert, qui ex ministerio ver-bi victum recepturi sint ab iis, quibus prædicant. Et id apertius apud Lucam exprimit dicens: Manete, edentes & bibentes quæ ab ipsis appositæ fuerint. De his in præsenti Paulus Corinthios admonet, non tam ut quid ipsi licuerit intelligant quàm ut alios Apostolos excu-set, qui ex suo ministerio uiuebant, cùm non eadem, quæ ille, necessitate constringerentur. Est ergo hoc memorabile charitatis & modestiæ Christianæ exemplum, à qua procul alieni sunt, qui si quid ipsis durius accidit, omnibus aliis fortem meliorem inuident, & odiosè de iis loquuntur, quos melius habere vident. Longè alia Pauli mens fuit, qui de sua, qua in Corinthios vsus fue-rat, indulgentia sic disserit, vt ne suspicione minima eos grauari cupiat, qui suis stipendijs frue-bantur. Quo animo si hodie omnes præditi essent, plerique essent beatiores. Sed infelices homi-nes duplicem fere miseriam sibi accersunt, dum & proprijs malis vexantur, & ex aliorum felici-tate dolorem concipiunt, ex qua potius consolationem captare debebant.
units.tr: But lest Paul, by his own example, should seem to prejudice the other Apostles and to condemn those who live from the stipends of the Church, he turns to assert the right of the ministry and confirms it by the most evident testimonies of Scripture: "Do you not know that those who serve at the sacred things eat from the sacred place, etc.?" He uses a question, which both indicates certainty and rebukes the malice of half-learned men who dared to call into doubt what was known to everyone. It is therefore as if he had said: Why is it necessary to dwell longer on proving this, which is known even to those who seem most ignorant? And what is it? That those who serve at the sacred things eat from the sacred place, that is, from those things which are offered in the sacred place or temple. And those who sit at the altar share with the altar? In this place, by prosopopoeia, he assigns a second person, because a part of the victim was burned on the altar while the other part fell to the priests. By these two members he comprehends the whole Levitical worship together with all those who publicly ministered in carrying it out. These were divided into two orders. The first consisted of men of lower rank, or the common Levites, whose task was to perform the heavier and dirtier labours (if it is permitted to speak so). For they received the victims from those who brought them, slaughtered them, flayed them, washed them, cut them into pieces, and finally piled up the wood with which the fire was kindled on the altar. Besides this, they cleaned and guarded the whole temple together with the sacred vessels. The other order consisted of the priests, whose dignity was greater, and whom Paul says sat at the altar, because they were occupied only with those things which were done at the altar itself. For they received from the offerers the parts of the victim destined for the sacrifice, lifted them up on high in the presence of the Lord according to the rite, or waved them to the right and left, and placed them on the fire; they used to pour out the drink offerings and sprinkle the blood; to them also belonged the incense which was burned upon the altar of incense. Although these orders were distinct from one another, and within each some were more eminent than others, God nevertheless assigned to all of them, and even to their wives and children, their sustenance from this office, namely from the portions of the sacrifices, the firstfruits of the grain growing from the earth, likewise the firstborn and the tithes. And lest they should be thought to live at another's expense, or to snatch from others what was theirs, God testifies in more than one place that all these things are his, and that he has given them to the Levites and priests so that they may live from them as from their own. See what is handed down to this effect in the book of Numbers, chapter 18. Paul discusses all these things in the present passage, and lest the condition of the ministers of the Church should seem worse under the New Testament, he adds: "So the Lord has ordained for those who proclaim the Gospel, that they should live from the Gospel." If you ask for passages in which the Lord has so ordained, it is clear enough from the tenth chapter of Matthew, where he forbids the Apostles to acquire gold or silver, or to carry with them provisions and the other things necessary for the journey; but he gives the reason for this command: that the workman is worthy of his wages. He therefore compares with labourers those who are to receive their sustenance from the ministry of the Word from those to whom they preach. And Luke expresses this more plainly, saying: "Remain, eating and drinking what is set before you by them." In the present passage Paul admonishes the Corinthians about these things, not so much that they might understand what was lawful for himself, as that he might excuse the other Apostles, who lived from their ministry, since they were not bound by the same necessity as he was. This, then, is a memorable example of charity and Christian moderation, from which those are far removed who, if anything falls out harder for themselves, envy everyone else a better fortune, and speak spitefully of those whom they see to be better off. Paul's mind was far different. He discusses his own forbearance, which he had shown towards the Corinthians, in such a way that he desires not even the slightest suspicion to burden those who enjoyed their stipends. If all people today were disposed in this spirit, most would be happier. But unhappy men bring upon themselves almost a double misery: they are vexed by their own troubles, and they conceive grief from the happiness of others, from which they ought rather to draw consolation.

units.la: Porrò omissis illis, uideamus paulò attentius, ut de Veteris simul & Noui Testamenti ministris Apostolus loquatur. Est hoc obseruatu utilissimum, imò necessarium quoque. Hodie enim in utramque partem vehementer peccatur, quando alij quidem solo ministerij nomine superbi, otiosos uentres agunt, & ferè fieri solet ut in opulentissimis cathedralium ecclesiarum Collegijs redditus omnes maxima ex parte intercipiant, qui non modò munus ecclesiastici ministerij nul-lum obeunt, uerumetiam vestitu & moribus testantur, indignos se esse, qui vel extremum in ec-clesia Christi locum obtineant, cùm uerissimè de illis dici possit, quod Horatius aliquos de seipsis dicentes inducit: Nos numerus sumus, & fruges consumere nati. Alij uerò, quia hic altaris & sacrificiorum mentionem fieri audiunt, nouum sacerdotium fingunt, per quod etiam hodie sa-crificia pro uiuis & defunctis offerri oporteat. Sed utrique huius loci authoritate confutan-tur. Paulus enim de iis loquitur, qui sacris operantur & altari assident. Etenim in veteri-tamento nihil otij erat sacerdotibus & leuitis, sed unicuique suum munus assignatum erat, quod summo studio obiret. Neque etiam ex primi ordinis sacerdotibus aliquis erat immunis, sed per ui-ces isti omnes requirebantur, ut per certos aliquot dies templo & altari seruirent: quod in Za-charia historia Lucas annotauit. Quoad uero noui Testamenti ministros, his Euangelij prædi-cationem tribuit Apostolus, & nullius præterea sacrificij meminit, ut nec aliarum superstitio-num, quæ posteris demum temporibus irrepserunt. Nam non ait: Ita Dominus constituit iis, qui cantillant, aquam lustralem aspergunt, cineres administrant, Missas faciunt & in ijs Chri-sto pro peccatis viuentium & mortuorum offerunt. Sed eorum modo meminit, qui Euangeli-um annuntiant. Hoc igitur uno dicto totum noui Testamenti ministerium comprehendit, quod circa solum Euangelium versatur, & quo illi demum funguntur, qui illud populo prædi-cant. Prædicationi huic, ceu appendices, Dominus adiecit Sacramenta, Baptismum & Cœnam suam mysticam: & quia prædicatio sine cœtu sacro fieri non potest, preces etiā publicæ hic com-mendantur, quibus cœtus eiusmodi inchoari & dimitti solent. Circa hæc igitur noui Testamenti ministros occupari oportet, & simul admonemur hoc loco sacrilegos, & (ut Christus loquitur) su-res atque latrones esse eos, qui aut otiosorum fucorum instar ex ecclesiæ redditibus belluantur, cùm huic nulla in re seruiant, aut rudem populum superstitionibus nouis fascinant, quibus CHRISTO IESV auocantur, in quo uno vita & salus inueniri potest. Simul autem hic quoque frugalitatis & temperantiæ ministri admonentur. Nec enim aliud illis permittit Paulus, quam ut ex Euangelio uiuant, non autem ut inde ditescant & ingentes opum thesauros colligant, quibus vel inexplebilem habendi libidinem saturare conentur, vel luxu & splendore cum iis certent, qui in mundo præ aliis eminere solent. Sed de hoc iam ante est dictum. Nunc postremam huius loci partem videamus, qua rursus de seipso agit Apostolus, qui nihil à quoquam postularit, & ne nunc quidem aliquid petat. Praeoccupatione ergo suspicionem amoli-tur, ne quis ipsum hanc causam tam multis agere putet, vt aliquid ab illis extorqueat. Sic enim ait: Neque vero haec scripsi, vt ita fiat in me. Nam bonum est mihi mori potius, quam vt gloria-tionem meam aliquis inanem reddat. Quo loco eorū verba per Mimesim imitari videtur, qui vt Christianae libertatis magni vindices esse viderentur, vitam potius se amissuros clamabat, quam passuros, vt libertas Christi sanguine parta à quoquam in angustum redigatur & finibus nouis circumscribatur. His ergo respondens vicissim ait: Atqui ego quoque mihi satius & vtilius esse putauerim, vt mortem oppetam, quam vt gloriationem meam mihi eripi; aut annihilari patiatur. Gloriatio Pauli erat, quod Euangelium fideliter & absque omni suspicione priuati commodi praedicabat. Eo autem gloriabatur non apud Deum (vt in sequentibus patebit) sed apud homines & vt haec illi gloria salua & integra esset, necesse erat propter aemulos, qui omnem occasionem captabant, qua doctrinam eius possent suspectam reddere. Itaque non tam de Pauli gloria, quam de veritatis doctrina & multorum hominum salute agebatur: & proinde serio & vere loquitur, sibi moriendum potius, quam ex ista arena cedendum esse. Sciebat enim quid ijs minitetur Dominus qui aliquos temere offendunt, aut (vt in lege Mosis ait) caeco scandalum ponunt. Quod si vero ille tanti fecit suam illam indulgentiam, qua magno suo incommodo vsus est, erga eos, qui non tam infirmi quam maligni Euangelicae doctrinae aestimatores erant: nimium certe duri & iniqui fue-runt, qui propter infirmos ab ijs nolebant abstinere, quibus Christiani nominis professio aperte polluitur. Est autem multa laude dignum Pauli studium, quo in prouehenda veritatis & communis salutis doctrina vsus est. Imitentur eius exemplum omnes ecclesiarum ministri, & cogitent nullum zelum in hoc munere nimium aut superuacaneum esse posse. Nam vt multa illis Satan obijcit, ita illos ipsos fere sibi aduersari sentiunt, quorum saluti consultum volunt. Simul autem omnes alij meminerint, sibi quoque assiduo studio opus esse in tuenda salute sua, quae tot sanctissimorum hominum laboribus in orbe propagata est, & quam sui sanguinis pretio nobis parauit Dei Filius, IESVS CHRISTVS: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Now, setting those matters aside, let us look a little more closely at how the Apostle speaks of the ministers of both the Old and the New Testament. This is most useful to observe, and indeed necessary too. For today people sin greatly in both directions. Some, proud only of the name of ministry, live as idle bellies, and it is commonly the case that in the very wealthy colleges of cathedral churches they grab nearly all the revenues, though they not only perform no part of the ecclesiastical ministry but even show by their dress and manners that they are unworthy to hold the lowest place in the Church of Christ. Of them one may most truly say what Horace makes certain men say of themselves: "We are numbers, born to consume the fruits of the earth." Others, because they hear mention made here of the altar and of sacrifices, invent a new priesthood, through which sacrifices must still today be offered for the living and the dead. But both are refuted by the authority of this passage. For Paul speaks of those who labour in sacred things and attend the altar. Indeed, in the Old Testament the priests and Levites had no leisure, but each had his own duty assigned, which he was to discharge with the greatest zeal. Nor was any even of the priests of the first order exempt, but all of them were called upon in turns to serve at the temple and the altar for certain set days; Luke noted this in the history of Zacharias. As for the ministers of the New Testament, the Apostle assigns to them the preaching of the Gospel, and he mentions no sacrifice at all, nor any of those other superstitions which crept in during later times. For he does not say: "Thus the Lord has appointed for those who chant, sprinkle holy water, administer ashes, celebrate Masses and in them offer Christ for the sins of the living and the dead." Instead he mentions only those who proclaim the Gospel. By this one word, therefore, he embraces the whole ministry of the New Testament, which is concerned with the Gospel alone, and which is discharged only by those who preach it to the people. To this preaching, as appendages, the Lord added the sacraments, Baptism and his mystical Supper; and because preaching cannot be done without a sacred assembly, public prayers are also commended here, by which such assemblies are customarily begun and dismissed. Therefore the ministers of the New Testament ought to be occupied with these things; and at the same time we are reminded here that those are sacrilegious, and (as Christ says) thieves and robbers, who either, like idle drones, gorge themselves on the revenues of the Church, though they serve it in no respect, or who bewitch the untaught people with new superstitions, by which they are drawn away from Christ Jesus, in whom alone life and salvation can be found. At the same time, the ministers are also admonished here to frugality and temperance. For Paul allows them nothing else than to live from the Gospel, not to grow rich from it and gather huge treasures of wealth, by which they either try to satisfy an insatiable lust for having, or vie in luxury and splendour with those who are wont to stand out above others in the world. But this has already been said before. Now let us look at the last part of this passage, in which the Apostle again speaks of himself, who has asked nothing from anyone and does not even now seek anything. By anticipation, therefore, he removes the suspicion that anyone might think he pleads this cause so earnestly in order to extort something from them. For he says: "Nor have I written these things so that it should be done to me in this way. For it is better for me to die than that anyone should make my boasting empty." Here he seems to imitate by mimesis the words of those who, wishing to appear great defenders of Christian liberty, cried out that they would rather lose their lives than suffer that the liberty purchased by the blood of Christ be reduced to narrow limits by anyone and hemmed in by new boundaries. Answering these men in turn, he says: "Indeed, I too would judge it better and more useful to meet death than to suffer my boasting to be snatched from me or destroyed." Paul's boasting was that he preached the Gospel faithfully and without any suspicion of private gain. He boasted of this not before God (as will become clear in what follows) but before men; and that this glory might remain safe and whole, it was necessary, on account of his rivals, who seized every occasion by which they could make his teaching suspect. Thus the matter concerned not so much Paul's glory as the doctrine of the truth and the salvation of many men; and therefore he speaks seriously and truly, that he ought to die rather than withdraw from that arena. For he knew what the Lord threatens against those who rashly give offence to some, or (as the law of Moses says) place a stumbling block before the blind. But if he set so great a value on that indulgence of his, which he exercised to his own great loss, towards those who were not so much weak as malicious judges of the Gospel doctrine, then surely they were far too hard and unjust who refused to abstain, for the sake of the weak, from those things by which the profession of the Christian name is openly defiled. Paul's zeal, by which he laboured to advance the doctrine of the truth and the common salvation, is worthy of much praise. Let all ministers of the churches imitate his example, and let them consider that no zeal in this office can be too great or superfluous. For just as Satan throws many obstacles in their way, so they often find almost the very people whose salvation they seek set against them. At the same time, let all others remember that they too need constant diligence in securing their own salvation, which has been spread through the world by the labours of so many most holy men, and which the Son of God, Jesus Christ, has won for us at the price of his own blood: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLVI.
units.tr: HOMILY XLVI.

units.la: Etenim si Euangelizem, non est quod glorier: Necessitas enim mihi incumbit: Vae autem mihi est nisi euangelizem. Nam si volens hoc faciam mercedem habeo: sin inuitus, dispensatio credita est mihi. Quae igitur mihi est merces? Vt cum euangelizem, gratuitum constituam Euangelium Christi, vt ne abutar iure meo in Euangelio.
units.tr: For if I preach the gospel, I have no ground for boasting, for necessity is laid upon me; and woe is me if I do not preach the gospel. For if I do this of my own will, I have a reward; but if against my will, a stewardship has been entrusted to me. What then is my reward? That when I preach the gospel, I make the gospel of Christ free of charge, so that I do not abuse my right in the gospel.

units.la: IN ijs quae proxime praecesserunt, copiose & diligenter ostendit Paulus, se cum in ecclesia Corinthiaca ageret, iure suo cessisse, neque aliquod ab ipsis accepisse stipendium, ne quam calumniandi occasionem daret aemulis suis, quasi sub apostolicae functionis praetextu priuatum commodum aut quaestum quaereret. Inter alia autem dixit: Bonum est mihi mori potius, quam vt gloriationem meam aliquis inanem reddat. Quae verba non animum ambitione & inanis gloriae desiderio ardentem, sed potius proueheundae veritatis & regni Christi studium atque zelum exprimunt: quo nisi ecclesiarum ministri accensi sint, nihil vnquam cum laude & fructu facient. Facile autem hic apud eos locum habebit, si Christum ex animo diligant. Ita enim non poterunt non maximi facere ecclesiam, quam is sui sanguinis pretio redemit.
units.tr: In the passages immediately preceding, Paul shows at length and with care that, while he was working in the Corinthian church, he had given up his right and had accepted no payment from them, so that he would not give his rivals any occasion for slander, as if under the pretext of his apostolic office he were seeking a private gain or profit. Among other things he said: "It is better for me to die than that anyone should make my boasting empty." These words express not a mind burning with ambition and a desire for empty glory, but rather a zeal and eagerness to advance the truth and the kingdom of Christ. Unless the ministers of the churches are kindled by this, they will never accomplish anything with praise and fruit. This zeal will readily find a place among them if they love Christ from the heart, for then they cannot fail to value highly the church that he redeemed with the price of his own blood.

units.la: Porrò diceret aliquis: Itane tantum tuo studio tribuis Paule, vt eo gloriari ausis nunc, qui alibi in solo Christo omnes gloriari iubes? Et quid vero opus fuit Paule, vt iuri tuo quoad stipendium ecclesiasticum apud nos renuntiares? aut quae causa est, quae ni illo ad huc vtaris prohibeat? [?] Cur denique tibi potius moriendum esse existimas, quam quicquam ànobis accipere? Annon sufficit tibi, si Euangelium bona fide prædices, & (quod alij Apostoli solent) quod æquum est accipias, vt vitam commodè & honestè sustentare possis? Huic obiectioni, vel quæstioni potius, in præsenti respondet, & vt sic faciat omnino necessarium esse docet, siquidem suam laudem atque gloriationem apud tam iniquos Euangelicæ doctrinæ æstimatores retinere velit aduersus æmulos suos, qui omnem ipsi obtrectandi occasionem tam solicitè obseruent. Et hoc agendo diligentius etiam exponit, quòd de sua gloriatione nuper dixerat. Sic autem ait: Etenim si Euangelizem, non est quòd glorier: necessitas enim mihi incumbit, &c. Sensus verborum hic mihi esse videtur. Est quidem res magna & præclara Euangelium, & laude simul atque præmio digni sunt, qui hoc diligenter mundo annuntiant: at non debet meum illud distum sic accipi, quasi salutis meritum in gratuita Euangelij predicatione constituatum & ea gloriæ apud Deum. Nam quia me ad hoc Deus vocauit, & peculiari mandato obstrinxit, vt gentium Apostolum agam, officio meo non potero deesse, nisi illius iram in me velim prouocare, & maledictionis sententiam incurrere. Interim verò quoad homines, ad tuendam meam & ministerij mei existimationem minimè mihi satis fuerit, si Euangelium quam fidelissimè prædicem, nisi simul omnem calumniandi occasionem æmulis meis præriipiam. Itaque in hoc mei officij summa versatur, vt volens, id est, animo libero & alacri, quem neque lucri spes neque futuri iudicij metus cogat, Euangelium vbique locorum annuntiem, & simul curem, ne quis in me eius detrectandi causam inueniat. Hoc si præstitero, mercedem habebo apud Dominum: quòd si inuitus & quasi aliud agens hoc munus obeam, dispensatio tamen mihi credita est, quæ inuitum quoque & tergiuersantem cogit, vt officio meo defungar: Interim verò mihi ministerij mei gloria atque gratia perierit apud eos, qui me suspectum habebunt, quasi non gloriæ Dei & salutis publicæ studio ducar, sed quæstum priuatum quæram. Verè igitur & merito abs me dictum est, satius hoc mihi esse, vt vitam amittam, quàm eiusmodi suspicionibus ministerium meum infrugiferum reddam, &c. Cæterum comprehendit his verbis Paulus, quæcunque de ministerio Euangelico aut ecclesiastico dici possunt, quæ singula ex ordine vidimus.
units.tr: Someone might still say: "Do you, Paul, really ascribe so much to your own zeal that you now dare to boast of it, when elsewhere you bid everyone to boast in Christ alone? And indeed, Paul, why was it necessary for you to renounce among us your right to ecclesiastical support? What reason is there that would not prevent you from still using that right? Why, finally, do you think you ought rather to die than receive anything from us? Is it not enough for you, if you preach the gospel in good faith and receive, as the other apostles usually do, what is fair, so that you may support yourself comfortably and honourably?" To this objection, or rather question, he replies at once, and he teaches that his refusal is wholly necessary, since he wishes to keep his praise and boasting before such unfair judges of the evangelical teaching, against his rivals who watch so carefully for any opportunity to disparage him. In doing this he also explains more carefully what he had said just before about his boasting. He says: "For if I preach the gospel, I have no ground for boasting; for necessity is laid upon me," and so on. The sense of these words seems to me to be this. The gospel is indeed a great and excellent thing, and those who proclaim it faithfully to the world deserve praise as well as reward. But my statement should not be taken to mean that the merit of salvation is placed in the free preaching of the gospel, and that I have glory before God for it. For since God has called me to this and bound me by a special command to be the apostle of the Gentiles, I cannot fail in my duty unless I wish to provoke his anger against me and incur the sentence of a curse. Meanwhile, as far as people are concerned, it will not be enough for me, in order to protect my own reputation and that of my ministry, to preach the gospel most faithfully, unless at the same time I also cut off from my rivals every occasion for slander. Therefore the sum of my duty lies in this: that I proclaim the gospel everywhere willingly, that is, with a free and cheerful mind, not compelled by hope of gain or fear of future judgment, and at the same time take care that no one finds in me a reason for disparaging it. If I do this, I shall have a reward with the Lord. But if I undertake this office unwillingly and as if doing something else, a stewardship has nevertheless been entrusted to me, which compels me, even unwilling and shrinking back, to perform my duty. Meanwhile the glory and the favour of my ministry will be lost in the eyes of those who will regard me with suspicion, as if I were not led by zeal for God's glory and the public salvation, but were seeking private gain. Truly and rightly, then, I have said that it is better for me to lose my life than to make my ministry fruitless by such suspicions, and so on. Moreover, in these words Paul comprehends everything that can be said about the evangelical or ecclesiastical ministry, and we have seen each of these points in order.

units.la: Primò Authorem eius denotat, quando dispensationem sibi creditam esse ait. Non igitur ipse sua sponte sibi hoc onus imposuit, sed ab alio sibi demandatum suscepit. A quo nam? A Domino nimirum, qui ipsi dixerat: Ad hoc apparui tibi, vt designarem te ministrum ac testem cum eorum quæ vidisti, tum eorum in quibus Apparebo tibi, eximens te ex hoc populo et gentibus, ad quos nunc te mitto: vt aperias oculos eorum, vt se conuertant à tenebris ad lucem, & à potestate Satanæ ad Deum, vt remissionem peccatorum & sortem inter sanctificatos accipiant per fidem, quæ est in me. Author itaq; ministerij Deus est, qui idè quos ipse voluerit ad illud destinare & vocare consueuit, & eosdem donis ad officium hoc necessarijs instruere. Nam si homines spectemus, nemo ad hoc idoneus reperietur, quando ex nobis ipsis (vt in posteriori epistola scribitur) nead cogitandum quidem idonei sumus. Imò nisi nos prior respiciat Deus, nemo hominum de regno cœlesti, deque sua aut aliorum salute vnquam cogitabit. Diuinitus ergo excitentur necesse est, qui hanc prædicent & veram eius consequendæ rationem tradant. Ideo Paulus ad Romanos scribebat: Quomodo prædicabunt, nisi missi fuerint? Potest hoc exemplis infinitis probari, si ab ipsis patriarcharum temporibus initium facias. Abrahamum certè ab ipso Deo euocatum fuisse legimus, vt hinc inde peregrinando Prophetam ageret, & salutis promissiones iampridem apud plerosque obliteratas omnibus prædicaret. Quod ipsum de Isaaco & Iacobo dicere possumus. Ita Mosem quoq;, & Aaronē diuinitus excitatos fuisse,non solùm historia sacra,sed Deus ipse longè post per Micheam testatur. Eadem fuit Prophetarum omnium conditio, quorum vocationes ferè describuntur,ad omnes autem extendi potest, quod apud citur: Excitaui de filijs vestris Prophetas, & de iuuenibus vestris Nazaræos. De Apostolis verò quid attinet dicere, quos nihil huius cogitantes Dominus vocauit, & spiritu suo donatos emisit, vt totius orbis doctores essent. At ne quis hodie aliam rerum faciem esse, aut Deum ministerij huius curam deposuisse putaret, Paulus hoc Christo perpetuum esse scribit, ut spiritus sui dona ex alto effundat, & alios quidem det Apostolos, alios vero Prophetas, alios autem Euangelistas, alios autem Pastores ac Doctores ad coagmentationem sanctorum, ad opus ministerij, denique ad ædificationem corporis sui.
units.tr: First, he indicates its author, when he says that a stewardship has been entrusted to him. He therefore did not impose this burden on himself of his own accord, but took it up as something committed to him by another. By whom, then? Surely by the Lord, who had said to him: "I have appeared to you for this purpose, to appoint you a minister and a witness both of the things you have seen and of those in which I shall appear to you, delivering you from this people and from the Gentiles, to whom I now send you, to open their eyes, that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those who are sanctified by faith in me." The author of the ministry, then, is God, who is accustomed to designate and call to it those whom he himself wills, and to equip the same with the gifts necessary for this office. For if we look at men, no one will be found fit for this, since, as is written in the second epistle, we are not even sufficient of ourselves to think anything. Indeed, unless God first looks upon us, no man will ever think about the heavenly kingdom, or about his own salvation or that of others. Those therefore who will preach this and hand down the true way of attaining it must of necessity be raised up by God. This is why Paul wrote to the Romans: "How shall they preach unless they are sent?" This can be proved by countless examples, if you begin from the very times of the patriarchs. We read that Abraham was certainly called out by God himself, so that, wandering here and there, he acted as a prophet and proclaimed to all the promises of salvation, which by then had been forgotten by many. We can say the same of Isaac and Jacob. Likewise, that Moses and Aaron were raised up by God is attested not only by sacred history but also by God himself, long afterwards, through Micah. The condition of all the prophets was the same, and their calls are for the most part described; and what is written in Amos, "I have raised up prophets from your sons, and Nazarites from your young men," can be extended to all of them. As for the apostles, what need is there to speak of them? The Lord called them when they were thinking of nothing of this kind, and having endowed them with his Spirit he sent them out to be teachers of the whole world. But lest anyone suppose that today the face of things is different, or that God has laid aside the care of this ministry, Paul writes that it is a perpetual feature of Christ to pour out the gifts of his Spirit from on high, and indeed to give some as apostles, others as prophets, others as evangelists, and others as pastors and teachers, for the equipping of the saints, for the work of the ministry, and finally for the building up of his body.

units.la: Est hoc observatu perquam necessarium. Primò enim ad communem omnium hominum institutionem facit, ut meminerint munus hoc diuinum esse, et in eo Dei bonitate agnoscant, qui nobiscum col-loqui dignatur. Christus certè se discipulos suos amicorum loco habuisse hoc argumento probat, quòd nihil eorum ipsos celauerit, quæ à Patre acceperat. Quis ergo singulare bonitatis paternæ indi-cium[?] esse neget, quòd toties à nobis repulsus & tam indignis modis habitus, adhuc suam nobis voluntatem aperit, & in eâ simul nobis offert, quæcunq; ad salutem cognitu necessaria sunt? Nostrū ergo fuerit filios bonos & ingenuos imitari, quos patris sui vox oblectat, ne dum illum in seruis suis loquentem contemnimus, contemptus ille in Deum recidat. Notum est enim illud Christi dictum: Qui vos spernit, me spernit: imò eum qui misit me. Et passim extant horrenda iudiciorum Dei exempla, quibus hic omnibus sæculis Verbi sui contemptum vindicauit.
units.tr: This is most necessary to observe. First, it serves the common instruction of all men, so that they may remember that this office is divine, and in it recognise the goodness of God, who deigns to speak with us. Christ certainly proves by this argument that he regarded his disciples as friends, because he hid nothing from them that he had received from the Father. Who then would deny that it is a singular sign of fatherly goodness that God, though repulsed by us so often and treated in such unworthy ways, still reveals his will to us, and at the same time offers us in it everything that is necessary to know for salvation? It is therefore our part to imitate good and well-born sons, whom their father's voice delights, lest, while we despise him speaking through his servants, that contempt fall back upon God. For that saying of Christ is well known: "He who rejects you rejects me, and indeed him who sent me." And everywhere there are dreadful examples of God's judgments, by which in all ages he has avenged the contempt of his Word.

units.la: Deinde ministros quoque istud in periculis & difficultatibus consolatur. Nam fieri nō po-test, ut muneri abs se instituto desit Dominus, qui omnes homines (ut alibi Paulus ait) vult salvos fieri & in veritatis cognitionem venire. Ideo Mosi ministerium hoc detrectanti dicebat: Quis dedit homini os? aut quis facit mutum & surdum? videntem & cæcum? annon ego Dominus? Vade ergo, & ego adero ori tuo, docebóq; te quæ loquaris. Ierem.1: Ego posui verba mea in os tuum. Ecce ego facio te hodie civitatem munitam, columnam ferreum, & murum æneum contra omnem terram, contra reges Iuda, contra principes eius, contra sacerdotes & contra vniuersum populum terræ. Pugnabunt contra te, sed non poterunt quicquam: ego enim tecum sum, ut te liberem, dicit Dominus. Conueniunt hîs quæ Apostolis Christus dixit: Ecce ego vobiscum sum usque in consummationem sæculi. Item: Ego dabo vobis os & sapientiam, cui non poterunt contradicere neque resistere omnes, qui se opponent vobis. Taceo nunc prolixam illam & communem omnibus consolationem, quæ apud Matthæum Cap.decimo describitur. Neque irritas esse promissiones istas, exempla infinita docent. Ferè enim fieri videmus, ut plus proficiant docendo ministri, quàm ipsi initio sperare ausi fuissent. Adhæc ijdem sæpe inter medios hostes præter omnium expectationem longissimo tempore seruantur atque docent, & non sine miraculo per mille rerum discrimina eluctantur. Cuius rei non alia causa assignari potest, quàm Dei fides atq; protectio: qui ut olim nonnullos Prophetarum diutissimè seruauit, ut alij per annos quadraginta, alij sexaginta prædicarint: ita hodie etiam suos ministros tuetur, ut multùm licet fremente mundo & principe eius, stationem tamen suam tenere possint.
units.tr: Then he also comforts ministers in dangers and difficulties. For the Lord cannot fail the office he himself has instituted, since he wills all men (as Paul says elsewhere) to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. So to Moses, when he refused this ministry, God said: "Who gave man a mouth? Or who makes the dumb and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? Is it not I, the Lord? Go therefore, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you are to say." Jeremiah 1: "I have put my words in your mouth. Behold, I make you today a fortified city, an iron pillar and a brazen wall against the whole land, against the kings of Judah, its princes, its priests and all the people of the land. They will fight against you, but they will not prevail, for I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord." These agree with what Christ said to the apostles: "Behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age." And again: "I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of those who oppose you will be able to contradict or resist." I pass over the long and common consolation described in Matthew chapter ten. That these promises are not empty, countless examples teach. For we see that ministers very often accomplish more by teaching than they had dared to hope at the outset. Moreover, these same men are often kept safe for a very long time, beyond all expectation, among enemies, and they teach and struggle through a thousand dangers, not without a miracle. No other cause can be given for this than the faithfulness and protection of God. As he once preserved some of the prophets for a very long time, some preaching for forty years and others for sixty, so today he guards his ministers, so that although the world and its prince rage greatly, they can hold their post.

units.la: Secundò, quale hoc munus siue ministerium sit, indicatur, Dispensationem enim sibi creditam esse Apostolus ait. Et huic simile est, quod supra Cap. quarto scripsit: Sic de nobis æstimet homo, ut de ministris Christi, & dispensatoribus mysteriorum Dei. Videtur autem ad parabolam alludere, in qua Christus ecclesiæ suæ ministrum Oeconomo aut dispensatori confert, quem familiæ suæ ideo præfecerit, ut illi dimensum suum in tempore depromat. At non in opum aut aliarum huius sæculi rerum distributione hæc dispensatio consistit, sed circa bona cœlestia & æterna versatur, quæ nobis Christus suæ mortis merito acquisiuit, quorum dignitas aut pretium tanto excellentius est, quanto omnibus creaturis præstat æternus Dei Filius. Fit autem dispensatio ista per Euangelij prædicationem, in qua cum Deus ipse loquatur, non possunt irritæ esse promissiones, quæ in illo continentur. Ideo Paulus se ad hoc destinatum esse ait, ut Euangelizet. Ubi tota Euangelij ratio nobis consideranda venit, de qua cùm alibi prolixè dictum sit, nunc breuius omnia perstringemus. Est autem Euangelium testimonium de IESV CHRI-STO, quo docetur hunc nobis à Deo patre secundum Prophetarum vaticinia & veteres promissiones exhibitum esse, ut nobis pœnitentiam & remissionem peccatorum afferret, & in se credentes seruaret. Subiectum ergo & argumentum Euangelij Christus est. Partes sunt pœnitentia & remissio peccatorum. Utramque verò in illius nomine prædicari oportet, quando ex nobis ipsis neque peccatorum pœnitentiam agere, neque eorundem remissionem obtinere possumus. Finis Euangelij est, ut per fidei obedientiam Christo consecrati & addicti, in ipso salutem & vitam æternam consequamur. Quicunque ergo ista annuntiant, ij mysteriorum Dei dispensatores sunt, & tales in sua ecclesia ministros Christus ipse instituit. Procul ergo facessant, qui relicta & contempta Euangelij doctrina, circa inanes & frigidas ceremonias occupantur, & infelicem populum in tenebris & conscientiæ terroribus detinent.
units.tr: Second, the nature of this office or ministry is indicated, for the Apostle says that a stewardship has been entrusted to him. Similar is what he wrote above in chapter four: "Let a man so regard us, as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God." He seems to allude to a parable in which Christ entrusts the minister of his church to a steward or manager, whom he has set over his household so that he may dispense their portion to them in due time. But this stewardship does not consist in the distribution of wealth or other things of this age; it concerns heavenly and eternal goods, which Christ won for us by the merit of his death. Their worth or price is all the more excellent in proportion as the eternal Son of God surpasses all creatures. This stewardship is carried out through the preaching of the gospel, and since God himself speaks in it, the promises contained in it cannot be empty. Therefore Paul says that he was destined for this, that he should preach the gospel. Here the whole account of the gospel must be considered by us. Since this has been discussed at length elsewhere, we will now touch on everything more briefly. The gospel is the testimony concerning Jesus Christ, by which it is taught that he has been set forth to us by God the Father, according to the prophecies of the prophets and the old promises, to bring us repentance and the remission of sins, and to save those who believe in him. The subject and matter of the gospel, therefore, is Christ. Its parts are repentance and the remission of sins. Both must be preached in his name, since from ourselves we can neither perform repentance for sins nor obtain their remission. The end of the gospel is that, consecrated and devoted to Christ through the obedience of faith, we may obtain salvation and eternal life in him. Whoever therefore announces these things is a steward of God's mysteries, and such ministers Christ himself has instituted in his church. Let those keep far away who, abandoning and despising the doctrine of the gospel, busy themselves with empty and cold ceremonies, and keep an unhappy people in darkness and terrors of conscience.

units.la: Postremo, vt in hoc munere versandum sit, suo exemplo Paulus docet. Si volens (inquit) hoc faciam, mercedem habeo. Volens prædicare dicitur, qui animo libero (vt diximus) totus in hoc incumbit, & non vllo alio affectu carnis, sed solo gloriæ Dei & salutis hominum promouendæ desiderio ducitur. Tales ministros requirit Christus, & de hoc nos frequenter admoneri opus est, quia multa sunt quæ nos auocant, si carnis rationem velimus audire. Terret enim muneris difficultas, quando constat nihil difficilius esse, quàm homines carni & mundo affectos ad cœlestium bonorum studium excitare, sceleribus item addictos ad sui mortificationem & abnegationem adducere. Multos item propriæ infirmitatis consideratio retinet, vt cum Ieremia clament: Ah puer ego sum, & loqui nescio. Accedunt his peruersa de ministris & Verbi prædicatione iudicia, quæ generosos quoque animos quàm maximè permouere solent. Quid vero de persecutionibus dicemus, quas infelix mundus excitat, quàm primùm superstitiones & scelera sua argui sentit? Sunt hæc eiusmodi, vt ijs non raro terrorem incutiant, qui Deo iubente nihil non facturi videbantur, imò eos interdum tantùmnon ex statione sua deijciunt, qui iam multis annis Domino egregiam operam nauauerunt. Exemplum eius rei in Ieremia habemus, qui post multa strenuè facta in suo munere, tandem querula & lamentabili voce exclamauit: Væ mihi o mater mea, quod me peperisti virum litigatorem & virum controuersiæ vniuersæ terræ, &c. Et quid Ionæ acciderit scimus, qui in Niniuen ad prædicandum missus admodum turpem sese dedit, cum prius sub Ioa Israelitarum rege, aut eius filio Ieroboamo Secundo Verbum Dei felicissimè annuntiauisset. Quapropter Christus sa-pe de his nos admonet, & Euangelij sui præcones ab omni carnis affectu adeo liberos esse vult, vt parentes quoque in extremis laborantes, si ita opus sit, possint relinquere. Cuidam enim dicenti: Domine, permitte mihi, vt prius abeam, & sepeliam patrem meum: Ille respon-dit, Sine vt mortui sepeliant mortuos suos: tu vero vade, & annuncia regnum Dei. In eandem sententiam alibi de vxoribus, liberis, fratribus & sororibus relinquendis nos admonet. Quæ omnia, quia carni dura, adhæc multorum iudicio non satis honesta neque pia sunt, promissionibus amplissimis illa mitigat, & efficacissimis consolationibus nos aduersus tentationum certamina abunde instruit.
units.tr: Finally, Paul teaches by his own example how one should be engaged in this office. "If I do this willingly," he says, "I have a reward." He is said to preach willingly who, with a free mind (as we have said), applies himself wholly to this and is led by no other fleshly affection, but solely by the desire to advance God's glory and the salvation of men. Christ requires such ministers, and we need to be admonished of this often, because there are many things that call us away if we wish to listen to the reasoning of the flesh. The difficulty of the office terrifies us, since it is plain that nothing is harder than to stir up men devoted to the flesh and the world to the pursuit of heavenly goods, or to lead those given over to wickedness to mortification and self-denial. Many are also held back by the consideration of their own weakness, so that they cry out with Jeremiah: "Ah, I am a boy, and I do not know how to speak." To these are added the perverse judgments about ministers and the preaching of the Word, which are wont to move even generous minds very greatly. What shall we say of the persecutions which the unhappy world stirs up as soon as it feels its superstitions and crimes being exposed? These are of such a kind that they often strike terror into those who seemed ready to do anything at God's command; indeed, sometimes they almost cast down from their post those who for many years have rendered distinguished service to the Lord. We have an example of this in Jeremiah, who, after many vigorous deeds in his office, at last cried out in a plaintive and lamentable voice: "Woe is me, my mother, that you bore me a man of strife and a man of contention to the whole land," etc. And we know what happened to Jonah, who, sent to preach in Nineveh, showed himself very base, although earlier he had announced the word of God most successfully under Joash, king of the Israelites, or his son Jeroboam the Second. Therefore Christ often admonishes us about these things, and wants the heralds of his gospel to be so free from every fleshly affection that they can even leave their parents, if they are in extremity and need requires it. For to one who said, "Lord, allow me first to go and bury my father," he replied: "Let the dead bury their own dead; but you go and proclaim the kingdom of God." To the same effect he elsewhere warns us about leaving wives, children, brothers and sisters. Since all these things are hard for the flesh, and in the judgment of many not sufficiently honourable or pious, he softens them with the most ample promises, and abundantly equips us with the most effective consolations against the struggles of temptation.

units.la: In præsenti autem Paulus, etsi promissiones iustas non ignoraret, insuper tamen minas quoque & maledictiones in mentem reuocat, quibus seruos male fidos Deus confuseuit multas. Væ mihi est (inquit) nisi euangelizem. Quæ vna sententia satis docet, quanta necessitate ministri constringantur, & quòd ijs, qui semel hoc stadium ingressi sunt, nequaquam liceat pedem iterum referre. Nam qui postquam manum (inquit Christus) aratro admouit, à tergo respexerit, is non est idoneus aut dignus regno Dei. Et exempla sunt, quæ docent Paulo non temere vocem istam excidisse, cùm non ignoraret, quàm male olim quibusdam ceciderit, qui in hoc munere operam suam Domino negarunt. Mosi Deus iratus fuisse legitur, quod aliquandiu legationem detrectaret, cui eum destinauerat. Quàm diris autem & horrendis casibus Ionas iactatus sit, quando fugæ sibi voluit consulere, ne Deo obedire cogeretur, notius est quàm vt commemorari oporteat. Tentationes certè, quibus tunc grauissimis exagitatus fuit, ipse in carmine suo minimè dissimulat. Debent ista ministros excitare, ne se ab officio reuocari patiantur, sed animo alacri & ad omnia intrepido pergant: & hoc vnum sibi pulchrum, honestum, utile & salutare ducant, si Dei mandatum exequantur, & hoc inuitis quoque ingerant. Talis olim Amos fuit, qui ipsum ne porrò Prophetæ officio fungeretur, cum authoritate mentibus respondebat: Leo si rugiat, quis non timeret? Dominus Deus locutus est, & quis non prophetaret? Quem animum alijs quoque Prophetis omnibus fuisse, eorum sermones subinde testantur. Imitati sunt hos Apostoli, qui cum Senatus Hierosolymitanus non sine genuibus minus interdiceret,ne posthac in nomine Iesu praedicarent,forti & constanti animo respon-derunt: An coram Deo iustum sit vos potius audire quàm Deum,iudicate. Non enim possumus quae vidimus & audiuimus non loqui. Volentes ergo illi omnes Euangelizauerunt, in hoc vnum intenti, vt Deo obsequium praestarent,qui munus istud ipsis demandarat. Quid enim aliud illos mouere aut cogere potuit, cum neque lucri neque honorum spes aliqua affulgeret, minae autem & horribiles hostium Christi machinationes sese auribus & oculis vndique ingererent? Inter hos autem prae aliis Paulus excelluit, qui cum non modo hostium minis peteretur, verumetiam ipsi debitum stipendium Christiani negarent, praedicare tamen non desijt, & sordido potius manuum labore victum quaerere,quam sibi creditam prouinciam relinquere maluit. Hunc animum si ecclesiarum ministri induant, tunc voluntatem suam omnem Christo consecrabunt, neque aliquid erit,quod ipsos ab officio sibi commissò[?] auocare queat.
units.tr: In the present passage Paul, although he was not unaware of the just promises, nevertheless also recalls threats and curses, with which God has often rebuked unfaithful servants. "Woe is me," he says, "unless I preach the gospel." This one sentence teaches well enough how great a necessity binds ministers, and that for those who have once entered this course it is by no means permitted to draw back a foot. For Christ says that "he who, after putting his hand to the plough, looks back, is not fit or worthy of the kingdom of God." And there are examples which show that Paul did not let that word fall rashly, since he knew how badly it once went for some who refused their service to the Lord in this office. We read that God was angry with Moses because for a while he hesitated over the commission to which he had appointed him. How dreadful and horrible were the misfortunes by which Jonah was tossed when he wished to flee, so that he would not be forced to obey God, is better known than it needs to be recalled. The temptations with which he was then most grievously harassed he by no means conceals in his own song. These things ought to stir up ministers, so that they do not allow themselves to be called back from their duty, but press on with a cheerful spirit, fearless in all things. Let them count this one thing noble, honourable, useful and salutary: to carry out God's command, and to impose it even on the unwilling. Such once was Amos, who, when they tried to stop him from further exercising the prophetic office, answered with authority: "A lion roars; who would not fear? The Lord God has spoken; who would not prophesy?" That same spirit in all the other prophets their words repeatedly attest. The apostles imitated these men. When the Senate of Jerusalem, not without threats, forbade them to preach any more in the name of Jesus, they answered with a brave and steadfast spirit: "Judge whether it is right before God to listen to you rather than to God. For we cannot but speak what we have seen and heard." All of them therefore preached willingly, intent on this one thing, that they might render obedience to God, who had entrusted this office to them. For what else could move or compel them, when no hope of gain or honours shone upon them, while threats and the dreadful schemes of Christ's enemies pressed in on eyes and ears from every side? Among these, Paul excelled beyond the others. Although he was not only attacked by the threats of enemies, but even Christians denied him the stipend due to him, he still did not cease to preach, and preferred to seek his living by the humble labour of his hands rather than abandon the province entrusted to him. If the ministers of the churches put on this spirit, they will consecrate all their will to Christ, and nothing will be able to call them away from the office committed to them.

units.la: At si demum Apostolorum imitatores sunt, qui tanta animi alacritate Euangelium annuntiant,quales obsecro censeri debent, qui Apostolicorum quidem titulo gloriantur,à nulla autem re perinde vt à praedicandi munere abhorrent? Tales autem hodie sunt Pontifices & Epi-scopi,quibus omnis ecclesiasticae dignitatis gloria in magnifico apparatu, stipatorum frequentia, luxu plus quàm Persico, denique in armorum vndique coruscantium strepitu, bombardarum tonitruis, & aliis eiusmodi rebus consistere videtur: Euangelium vero ne audire quidem possunt, nedum hoc aliis annuntiare. Clamat Paulus: Vae mihi, si non euangelizem. At istorum mores & studia eiusmodi sunt,vt si non aperta voce,certè reipsa clament: Vae nobis,si Euangelium audire cogamur. Tulit horum tyrannidem iam saeculis aliquot infelix mundus, & quamuis multi nunc passim oculos aperiant, non pudet tamen istos in medio scelere deprehensos adhuc Apostolicorum nomen sibi vendicare. Sed breui viam Dominus inueniet, qua eorum nequitiam coerceat. Interea discant Christiani homines illos declinare, patienter autem ferre fideles Chri-sti seruos, qui Euangelium qua decet libertate & constantia praedicant. Turpe enim fuerit ijs docendi leges praescribere,quos Christus loqui iussit, & qui nisi loquantur, exitium sibi sempiternum accersunt. Meminerint praeterea omnes, scelerum poenas non cessare, si Verbi praecones vel e medio tollantur, vel ad silentium ignauum redigantur: sed augeri potius, quando prioribus delictis audacia ista plus quàm diabolica accedit. Exempla, quae huc faciunt, passim sunt obuia.
units.tr: But if they are truly imitators of the Apostles, who proclaim the gospel with such eagerness, what kind of people, I ask you, ought to be judged those who boast of the Apostolic title yet shrink from nothing so much as the duty of preaching? Such are the pontiffs and bishops of today, in whom the whole glory of ecclesiastical dignity seems to lie: in magnificent display, in crowds of attendants, in luxury more than Persian, and finally in the clamour of weapons glittering on every side, the thunder of artillery, and other things of that kind. Yet they cannot even hear the gospel, much less announce it to others. Paul cries, "Woe is me if I do not preach the gospel." But the conduct and pursuits of these men are such that, if not with an open voice, then surely by their deeds they cry, "Woe to us if we are forced to hear the gospel." For some centuries now the unhappy world has endured their tyranny, and although many now everywhere are opening their eyes, these men, caught in the midst of their crimes, are still not ashamed to claim for themselves the name of the Apostles. But the Lord will soon find a way to restrain their wickedness. Meanwhile let Christians learn to avoid them, and to bear patiently the faithful servants of Christ, who preach the gospel with the freedom and steadfastness it deserves. For it would be shameful to prescribe rules for teaching to those whom Christ has ordered to speak, and who, unless they speak, bring eternal ruin upon themselves. Let all men also remember that the punishments of sins do not cease if the heralds of the Word are either removed from the midst or reduced to cowardly silence; rather, they increase, when this audacity, more than diabolical, is added to earlier offences. Examples that bear on this are everywhere to be met.

units.la: Debet praeterea ex Pauli exemplo generalis doctrina peti, vt quicunque ad munus aliquod vocati sunt à Domino, illi alacriter incumbant, neque aliquid admittant eorum, quibus in suo instituto possint impediri. Quia enim credentibus Spiritum suum Christus largitur, quem adoptionis Spiritum dicit Apostolus,solet ille ingenuos reddere, qui non seruili metu, sed potius ex amore & dilectione Patri suo caelesti obedire cupiant. Quo Dauid quoque respexisse videtur, quando populum Christi spontaneum fore vaticinatur. Scimus quidem in electis & fidelibus haerere carnis reliquias & Legem peccati,quae (vt de semetipso Paulus fatetur) interdum captiuos abripit,vt aliqua praeter officium faciant. Id vero illis praeter voluntatem interni hominis accidit,& proinde quoad hunc inuiti peccant, volentes autem Christo obtemperant, cui se totos consecrauerunt: neque illis quicquam dulcius & iucundius accidere potest, quàm si occasionem sibi offerri videant, qua officium illi gratum possint facere. Debent ista ad se transferre omnis loci & ordinis homines. Qui ergo magistratum gerunt, sibipsis Paulinum istud occinant: Vae nobis, nisi ius dicamus, nisi tueamur peregrinum, viduam & pupillum, nisi toti in hoc simus,vt nostrae fidei commissus populus Deo in veritate & sanctitate seruiat. Cogitent item quanto honore illos dignatus sit Deus, & huic gratos sese praebeant. Similiter faciant parentes, liberi, serui, & quicunque alij. Qui vero cum egestate & morbis conflictantur, aut exules incertis sedibus oberrant,si hanc ipsorum vocationem esse agnoscant, vt fidei & patientiae exempla sint, & in his voluntarium Deo obsequium praestent. Ita demum beati erunt, & Deum remuneratorem fidelissimum sentient. Poterant haec latissime diduci, sed sufficiat pijs cogitandi occasionem dedisse.
units.tr: Moreover, from Paul's example a general teaching should be drawn: that whoever has been called by the Lord to any office should apply himself to it eagerly, and admit nothing by which he might be hindered in his calling. For Christ bestows his Spirit on believers, whom the Apostle calls the Spirit of adoption, and this Spirit is accustomed to make free those who desire to obey their heavenly Father not from servile fear but from love and affection. David also seems to have had this in view when he prophesies that the people of Christ will be willing. We know indeed that remnants of the flesh and the law of sin cling to the elect and the faithful, and that this law (as Paul himself confesses of himself) sometimes carries them captive, so that they do things contrary to their duty. But this happens to them against the will of the inner man, and therefore, as far as this inner man is concerned, they sin unwillingly, while willingly they obey Christ, to whom they have wholly consecrated themselves. Nothing can happen to them that is sweeter and more pleasing than when they see an opportunity offered by which they may render a welcome service to him. Men of every place and rank ought to apply these things to themselves. Let those who bear the magistracy therefore sing to themselves that Pauline cry: "Woe to us, unless we administer justice, unless we protect the stranger, the widow and the orphan, unless we are wholly intent on this, that the people committed to our trust may serve God in truth and holiness." Let them also consider with what honour God has deigned to distinguish them, and show themselves grateful to him. Let parents, children, servants, and all others do likewise. Those who are wrestling with poverty and sickness, or wander as exiles without a fixed home, if they recognise that this is their calling, that they may be examples of faith and patience, and render voluntary obedience to God in these things, will at last be blessed, and will feel God to be the most faithful rewarder. These matters could be spread out far and wide, but let it suffice to have given the godly an occasion for thought.

units.la: Videamus nunc huius loci conclusionem, quam Paulus sic infert: Quæ igitur mihi est merces? Ut cum euangelizem, gratuitum constituam Euangelium Christi, ut ne abutar iure meo in Euangelio. Mercedem dicit, quam prius gloriationem dixerat, qua se & authoritatem suam adversus æmulos tuebatur. Hanc in duobus consistere dicit. Primum est, ut Euangelium Christi faciat ἀδάπανον[?], id est gratuitum, ut nimirum illud gratis & absque impensis audire possint quicunque volunt. Alterum, ut non abutatur iure suo in Euangelio. Poterat hoc idem cum priori videri: sed latius extenditur ius illud, & praeter stipendium ecclesiasticum plura etiam alia comprehendit, ut in iis est videre, quae proxime sequuntur. Hoc ergo se imprimis curauisse dicit, ut non quid sibi liceat videret, sed quid aliorum utilitati & aedificationi seruiat. Et est probe observanda locutio: Ut ne abutar iure meo in Euangelio. Ea enim docet, non semper recte & benefici, quod per se licitum est. Nam ut in rebus profanis summum ius summa iniuria est: ita qui in iis, quae ad religionem spectant, ius atque libertatem suam semper pertinacius tueri velit, ea non sine scandalo ad multorum destructionem abutetur. Itaque Christianæ libertatis usus, qui scandalum parit, abusus est & inexcusabilis licentia. Ista vero probe faciunt ad Pauli institutum de vitandis idolothytis & gentium superstitionibus. Suo enim exemplo admonere vult, indigne illos facere, qui ab iis abstinere nolunt, quae cum fidei Christianae professione pugnant, cum pij interdum ea vitare debeant, quae per se licita & concessa sunt. Est ergo huius etiam loci usus multiplex, & ad omnia extendi debet, quae ad vitae totius consuetudinem faciunt. Interim semper meminisse oportet, Paulum hoc omne propter Corinthios & horum similes dixisse, quorum ea erat iniquitas, ut Euangelio potius carere, quam eius causa aliquo sumptu grauari voluisset. Ideo maiorem gloriae Dei & publicae salutis quam sui iuris rationem illum habere oportuit. Sunt ergo importuni & iniqui nimium, qui hinc legem vniuersalem colligunt, ad quam omnes Verbi praecones astringi debeant. Neque vident illi se hoc absque propria ignominia facere non posse. Quia enim Paulus Corinthiorum iniquitate coactus debitum sibi stipendium non exegit, non possunt illi nos ad eius imitationem cogere, nisi seipsos in Corinthiorum locum substituant, quos iniquissimos gratiae Dei aestimatores fuisse audimus.
units.tr: Let us now look at the conclusion of this passage, which Paul draws in these words: "What then is my reward? That when I preach the gospel, I may make the gospel of Christ free of charge, so that I do not abuse my right in the gospel." He calls the reward what he had earlier called his boasting, by which he defended his authority against his rivals. He says this consists of two things. The first is that he make the gospel of Christ without cost [ἀδάπανον], that is, free, so that of course whoever wishes may hear it without expense. The second is that he not abuse his right in the gospel. This might seem the same as the first, but that right extends more widely, and includes many other things besides the ecclesiastical stipend, as can be seen in what immediately follows. So he says that his chief care was to see not what was lawful for himself, but what would serve the benefit and edification of others. And the phrase is to be carefully noted: "that I do not abuse my right in the gospel." For it teaches that what is in itself lawful is not always rightly and beneficially done. For as in secular matters the highest right is the highest injury, so whoever in matters that pertain to religion always wishes to defend his liberty and right more stubbornly will abuse it, not without scandal, to the destruction of many. Thus the use of Christian liberty that produces scandal is an abuse and an inexcusable licence. These things indeed bear well on Paul's purpose of avoiding idol-offerings and the superstitions of the Gentiles. For by his own example he wishes to warn that they act unworthily who will not abstain from those things which conflict with the profession of the Christian faith, since the godly sometimes ought to avoid things which are in themselves lawful and permitted. The use of this passage is therefore manifold, and it ought to be extended to all things that pertain to the whole custom of life.
