Meanwhile we must always remember that Paul said all this on account of the Corinthians and those like them, whose iniquity was such that they would rather go without the gospel than be burdened with any expense for its sake. Therefore he had to take more account of the glory of God and the public salvation than of his own right. So those are too importunate and unjust who gather from this a universal law to which all heralds of the Word must be bound. Nor do they see that they cannot do this without their own disgrace. For since Paul, constrained by the iniquity of the Corinthians, did not demand the stipend owed to him, they cannot force us to imitate him unless they put themselves in the place of the Corinthians, whom we hear were the most unjust assessors of the grace of God.

units.la: Abutuntur praeterea Pauli exemplo Sophistae Scholastici, ut opera supererogationis tueantur, & probent nos plus quam debemus & necesse est facere posse. Apostolus (inquiunt) hac laude & gloria excelluit, quod iure suo cedens plus fecit quam facere tenebatur: Ergo idem etiam alij poterunt, & id omnino curandum est, ut quae à nobis supra debitum fiunt, in aliorum commodum & salutem redundent. Est hoc commentum putidissimum, & indignum cuius inter hominmes Christianos aliqua ratio habeatur. At quia huic debemus non postremam partem nundinationis illius, quae religionem simul omnem iampridem pessumdedit, & eodem fere totus sacrificulorum & monachorum quaestus nititur, quem ex preculis, ieiunijs, Missis, Psalmodijs, matutinis (ut vocant) peregrinationibus, & alijs eiusmodi rebus faciunt, omnino aliquid dicendum est. Primo autem falluntur illi in gloriationis & mercedis vocabulo, dum Paulum coram Deo gloriari & ab hoc, sui operis mercedem exigere potuisse putant. Nam omne hoc ad hominum iudicium referri debet, coram quibus contra aemulos suos gloriari & authoritatem suam hoc argumento tueri poterat, quod gratis doceret. Quod si ad Dei tribunal accedamus, nihil praeter id, quod debuit, fecit Paulus. Boni enim doctoris est, non solum veritatis doctrinam tradere, verum etiam scandala cauere, & omnibus pro virili obstare, quae Euangelij professum impediunt. Quia ergo stipendium exigere non poterat, quin & authoritatem suam labefactaret, & Euangelij cursum remoraretur, non potuit non ab illo abstinere, siquidem fidelem Christi Apostolum agere voluit. Videri ergo ruinosum esse fundamentum illud, quo istorum hominum commentum nititur. Deinde si tota causa in genere agi placeat, constat opera supererogationis dici non posse, quaecunque in lege praecipiuntur: eo quod huic omnes ex officio obedire debent. At opus bonum nullum est, quod non praescribatur in Lege: imo quae non praecepta sunt à Deo, opera bona dici non possunt. Adde, quod etsi omnia faciamus, quae Lex iubet, serui tamen inutiles sumus, neque aliud quam quod facto opus est fecimus. At quem mortalium dabis, qui quaecunque in Lege mandantur, fecerit? Nonne sanctissimi quique orant: Ne ingrediaris in iudicium, Domine, cum seruo tuo? Nonne Christus precari docuit: Remitte nobis debita nostra? Est ergo tota illa doctrina de operum meritis impia & sacrilega, cum & Dei gratiam euacuet, & Christum sui meriti gloria spoliet. Vtinam vero isti homines, quibus Pauli exemplum tantopere arridere videtur, illud attentius in-tuerentur. Nam si hoc facerent, mox non modo huius figmenti, sed omnium fere illos puderet, quæ in Christi ecclesia faciunt. Apostolus hanc suam gloriationem & laborum omnium mercedem esse putauit, vt Euangelium Christi ἀδἀπανον aut gratuitum quibusuis constitueret. Quid vero illi? Annon eò vsque progressa est ipsorum auaritia, & impudens sacrorum omnium nundinatio, vt nihil in tota ecclesia gratuitum inueniatur? Ipsum ecclesiæ ministerium quæstus Episcoporum factus est, neque ad illud nisi prius numerata pecunia quisquam admittitur. Admissi vero vendunt Missas, Aquam, Ignem, Aërem, campanarum clangores, bullas, membranas, plumbum, templorum subsellia, sepulturam, & cum cœlis Christum, qui in illis residet. Denique per illos nemini vel gratis nasci, vel mori aut sepeliri licet. Quis ergo eos non dixerit magnos illos Chananæos aut negotiatores esse, quos ex ecclesia sua Christum eiecturum esse olim Zacharias prædixit? Eant ergo & ista emendent, & tunc de operibus superogationis disputent.
units.tr: Moreover, the Scholastic sophists abuse Paul's example to defend works of supererogation, and to prove that we are able to do more than we ought and than is necessary. "The Apostle," they say, "excelled in this praise and glory, that by yielding his right he did more than he was bound to do. Therefore others too will be able to do the same, and it must be taken care of entirely that what we do beyond duty should redound to the advantage and salvation of others." This is a most putrid invention, and not worthy of any consideration among Christian men. But since we owe to this no small part of that trafficking which long ago ruined all religion, and on which almost the whole gain of the priests and monks rests, which they make from prayers, fasts, Masses, psalmody, matins, pilgrimages (as they call them), and other things of that kind, something must certainly be said. First, however, those men are mistaken in the words "boasting" and "reward," since they think Paul could boast before God and demand from him the reward of his work. For all this must be referred to human judgement, before which he could boast against his rivals and defend his authority by this argument, that he taught without charge. But if we come to the tribunal of God, Paul did nothing beyond what he owed. For it is the part of a good teacher not only to hand down the doctrine of the truth, but also to beware of scandals, and to oppose with all his strength whatever hinders the progress of the gospel. Since therefore he could not demand a stipend without at the same time weakening his authority and retarding the course of the gospel, he could not but abstain from it, if he wished to act as a faithful Apostle of Christ. The foundation on which the invention of these men rests therefore seems ruinous. Next, if the whole matter is to be treated in general terms, it is plain that works of supererogation cannot be said to exist, since all things commanded in the law are owed by everyone as a matter of duty. But there is no good work that is not prescribed in the law; indeed, works that God has not commanded cannot be called good works. Add that even if we do all that the law bids, we are still unprofitable servants, and have done nothing more than what needed to be done. But which of mortals will you name who has done all that the law commands? Do not the holiest men pray, "Do not enter into judgement, O Lord, with your servant"? Did not Christ teach us to pray, "Forgive us our debts"? Therefore that whole doctrine of the merits of works is impious and sacrilegious, since it both empties the grace of God and strips Christ of the glory of his merit. Would that these men, to whom the example of Paul seems so pleasing, would look at it more attentively. For if they did, soon they would be ashamed not only of this fiction but of almost everything they do in the church of Christ. The Apostle thought his boasting and the reward of all his labours was this, that he made the gospel of Christ without cost [ἀδάπανον], or free, to whomever. But what of them? Has their avarice and shameless trafficking in all sacred things advanced so far that nothing in the whole church is free? The ministry of the church itself has become a source of gain for the bishops, and no one is admitted to it unless money has first been counted out. Those admitted in turn sell Masses, water, fire, air, the ringing of bells, bulls, parchments, lead seals, the benches of the churches, burial, and, with heaven, Christ who dwells there. In short, through them no one may be born, die, or be buried for nothing. Who then would not call them those great Canaanites or merchants whom Zechariah long ago foretold Christ would cast out of his church? Let them go, then, and amend these things, and only then let them dispute about works of supererogation.

units.la: Restat autem hic rursus doctrina generalis, quæ vera sit hominum gloria & compendiosissima hanc consequendi ratio. Est doctrina hæc vtilis & necessaria, eò quòd gloriæ studium omnibus innatum est, plerique autem Adamum secuti eam in rebus illicitis aut vanis atque inanibus quærunt. Et quàm fluxa sit omnis mundi huius & carnis gloria, facilè vident, qui quæ quotidie inter homines fiunt, non ofcitanter obseruant: In hoc igitur nobis incumbendum fuerit, vt con-temptis huius sæculi rebus, eam gloriam quæramus, quæ nos Deo commendare & in eius iudicio consistere possit. Admonet de hoc Christus, quando Pharisæorum ambitionem damnans, iubet nos non de hominum applausu solicitos esse, sed hoc agere, vt Deo patri probemur, qui suis fideliter respondeat. Id vero fiet, si ante omnia officium nostrum aut munus, cui nos Deus destinauit, probè expenderimus, & in eo obeundo fedulissimus & industrius. Interim nullius muneris dignitate nos efferri, sed sub potenti manu Dei humiliari decet: quod facilè fiet, si nos thesaurum salutis in vasis testaceis (vt Paulus ait) imò vitreis, possidere cogitemus. Actionum vero atque studiorum omnium finis nobis propositus esto, gloria Dei & multorum salus, quos hic nobis commendauit. Qui me honorauerit (inquit per Prophetam Dominus) honorabitur. Hæc ergo omnes ad se transferant, neque multum morentur hominum iudicia, quos cæcus animi affectus abripit. Nam vt vt[?] res cedat in hoc sæculo, non deerit tamen promissis suis Deus, qui fideles seruos & hic tueri, nominisque eorum memoriam conseruare solet, & eosdem gloriæ cælestis & immortalis hæredes facit cum filio suo IESV CHRISTO: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: There remains here again a general teaching, which is the true glory of men and the shortest way of attaining it. This teaching is useful and necessary, because the desire for glory is innate in all people, yet most, following Adam, seek it in unlawful or vain and empty things. And how fleeting all the glory of this world and of the flesh is, those easily see who observe carefully what happens among men every day. In this, then, we ought to labour: that, despising the things of this age, we seek that glory which can commend us to God and let us stand in his judgment. Christ admonishes us of this when, condemning the ambition of the Pharisees, he bids us not to be anxious about the applause of men, but to take care to be approved by God the Father, who will faithfully repay us. This will happen if, above all, we weigh carefully our office or duty to which God has appointed us, and are most diligent and industrious in discharging it. Meanwhile it is fitting that we not be puffed up by the dignity of any office, but be humbled under the mighty hand of God; this will easily happen if we consider that we possess the treasure of salvation in earthen vessels (as Paul says), or rather in vessels of glass. Let the aim proposed to us in all our actions and endeavours be the glory of God and the salvation of the many whom he has entrusted to us here. "Those who honour me," says the Lord through the Prophet, "will be honoured." Let all people therefore apply this to themselves, and let them not dwell long on the judgments of men, whom a blind passion of the mind carries away. For however things turn out in this age, God, who is accustomed to protect his faithful servants even here and to preserve the memory of their names, will not fail in his promises, and he makes them heirs of heavenly and immortal glory together with his Son Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLVII.
units.tr: HOMILY XLVII.

units.la: Nam cum liber sim ab omnibus, omnibus me ipsum seruum feci, vt plures lucrifaciam. Et factus sum Iudaeis, vt Iudeus, vt Iudaeos lucrifaciam: iis qui sub Lege sunt, quasi essem sub Lege, vt eos qui sub Lege sunt lucrifaciam. Exlegibus vt exlex (tametsi non sim exlex Deo, sed suplex Christo) vt lucrifaciam exleges. Factus sum infirmis vt infirmus, vt infirmos lucrifaciam. Omnibus factus sum omnia, vt omnino aliquos seruem. Hoc autem facio propter Euangelium, vt vna particeps eius fiam.
units.tr: For though I am free from all men, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might gain the more. And to the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews; to those who are under the Law, as if I were under the Law, that I might gain those who are under the Law. To those outside the Law, as one outside the Law (not being without law toward God, but subject to Christ), that I might gain those outside the Law. To the weak I became as weak, that I might gain the weak. I have become all things to all men, that I might by all means save some. And this I do for the sake of the gospel, that I may become a partaker of it with you.

units.la: PAulus diligenter & multis aduersus eos disputat, qui libertate Christiana eo vsque abute-bantur, vt gentium sacrificijs & epulis ex horum carnibus institutis communicarent. Inter alia vero argumenta suum exemplum maximè vrget, qui nullo vnquam ab illis accepto stipendio, Euangelium apud eos gratis praedicarit. Vtq, maior esset exempli sui authoritas, diligenter docuit hucusque, quid ministris suis ecclesiae debeant, & vicissim qualem ipse se praebuerit, quando manuum labore potius victum sibi voluerit quaerere, ne suo iure ad aliquorum offensionem abuteretur, & Euangelij cursum vel minima ex parte impediret. Atqui non ignorabat Apostolus, multos esse, qui omnia eius vel improbe calumniabantur, vel saltem per contemptum extenuabant: ideo in praesenti ampliorem sui exempli declarationem subijcit, qua demonstrat, se non modo quoad stipendium ecclesiasticum iure suo cessisse, verum etiam in multis aliis se demisisse ad audito‑rum captum, & omnium ingenijs atque moribus se accommodauisse, vt quam plurimorum saluti consuleret. Est autem locus iste confideratu dignissimus: quia & ecclesiarum ministros admonet, qua animi moderatione creditum sibi munus obire debeant: simulque omnes alios docet, quomodo tractandi sint fratres, qui ad pleniorem mysteriorum fidei cognitionem nondum peruenerunt.
units.tr: Paul argues this carefully and at length against those who abused Christian liberty to the point of joining in the sacrifices and feasts of the Gentiles, and of eating meat that had been offered to idols. Among his other arguments, he presses most strongly his own example, since he preached the gospel among them freely, never accepting payment from any of them. So that the authority of his example might be greater, he has until now carefully taught what the ministers of the Church are owed, and in turn what kind of man he himself has shown himself to be, since he chose rather to earn his living by the labour of his hands, lest he misuse his right to the offence of some and hinder the course of the gospel in the least degree. Yet the Apostle was not unaware that many were ready either to slander all he did in bad faith, or at least to belittle it with contempt. Therefore, in the present passage, he sets out a fuller account of his example, showing that he had not only given up his right to a church stipend, but had also in many other ways lowered himself to the level of his hearers' understanding, and had adapted himself to the abilities and customs of everyone, so that he might serve the salvation of as many as possible. This passage is most worthy of careful consideration, because it both reminds the ministers of the Church with what moderation of mind they ought to discharge the office entrusted to them, and at the same time teaches all others how brothers are to be treated who have not yet attained a fuller knowledge of the mysteries of faith.

units.la: Principio rem omnem in genere proponit, quod postea quasi in suas species diducit. Nam cum liber sim (inquit) ab omnibus, omnibus meipsum seruum feci, vt plures lucrifaciam. Liberum se dicit propter beneficium nobis a Christo collatum, qui credentes ita in libertatem asseruit, vt neque ceremonijs legalibus porro grauari debeant, neque quoad doctrinam & religionem vlli mortalium seruiliter sint obnoxij. Potest ergo dictum hoc tam ad res quam ad homines referri, & sensus est: Dixi me hoc cauisse diligenter, ne meo iure in Euangelij praedicatione & totius ministerio ecclesiastico abuterer. Id abs me non temere dictum esse, res ipsa probat. Nam etsi excommuni Christianorum iure liber sim, & simul ex apostolica functione mihi amplior quaedam potestas accedat, vt nullius iudicium mihi sit formidandum, qui libertati meae aliquid derogare & eam finibus arctioribus concludere conatur: ego tamen meipsum sponte seruum feci, idque non vni aut alteri, qui ita de me meriti esse videri poterant, sed in vniuersum omnibus: neque in eo commodum aut quaestum priuatum quaesiui, sed in hoc vnum intentus fui, vt quam plurimos Christo lucrifacerem. Istis vero inferre poterat: Quin ergo vos vestrae pudet insolentiae, qui inani nescio cuius scientiae fiducia inflati, quosuis fastiditis, & indignos iudicatis, in quorum gratiam abstineri oportet, quae vt per se illicita sunt, & fidei nostrae professioni repugnant: ita scandalum multiplex pariunt, quo multi impediuntur, ne ad Christum accedant? &c. Sed quia cuius facile erat haec & alia huius generis ex toto sermonis contextu colligere, reticet ista, ne animos eorum magis irritet, & in eo nouum eius submissionis & indulgentiae exemplum praeberet, de qua agere instituit.
units.tr: First he sets out the whole matter in general terms, which he afterwards divides, as it were, into its particular parts. For, he says, though I am free from all men, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might gain the more. He calls himself free on account of the benefit conferred on us by Christ, who so asserted believers in liberty that they must no longer be burdened by the legal ceremonies, nor be slavishly subject to any mortal in matters of doctrine and religion. This statement may therefore be referred both to things and to persons, and its sense is this: I have said that I took care in this matter, lest I misuse my right in preaching the gospel and in the whole ministry of the Church. That I have not spoken this rashly, the thing itself proves. For although, by the common right of Christians, I am free, and at the same time a certain greater authority accrues to me from the apostolic office, so that I need fear the judgement of no one who seeks to derogate from my liberty and to confine it within narrower limits, nevertheless I have of my own accord made myself a servant, and that not to one or another who might seem to have deserved it of me, but to all in general. Nor in this did I seek any advantage or private gain; I was intent upon this one thing, that I might gain as many as possible for Christ. To those men, however, he could have said: Are you not ashamed of your arrogance, you who, puffed up with the empty confidence of I know not what knowledge, despise whomsoever you please and judge them unworthy, for whose sake one ought to abstain from things which, though in themselves lawful, are contrary to the profession of our faith, and which, as they cause manifold offence, hinder many from coming to Christ? And so on. But since it was easy to gather these and other things of this kind from the whole context of the discourse, he is silent on them, lest he provoke their minds the more, and he sets forth in this a new example of condescension and indulgence, which he has undertaken to treat.

units.la: Est autem hoc praeclarum & perquam memorabile charitatis exemplum qua Paulus primo ipsum Christum, deinde in hoc omnes homines complexus est. Nam si nostri ingenij naturam & mores hominum, quibus passim viuitur, consideres, vix quicquam aliud tam indignum & iniquum videtur, quam si qui in aliquo sublimiori gradu constituti sunt, se ad aliorum arbitrium demittere, & inferioribus accommodare iubeantur. At quantus fuerit Paulus commemorare non est opus, quando hic nobis ipsius Christi testimonium sufficit, qui Ananiae de illo dixit: Instrumentum electionis est mihi iste, vt perferat nomen meum coram gentibus, & Regibus, ac filijs Israel. Verum tamen non inflari se passus est tantae dignitatis fiducia, vt sibi propriam & peculiarem Apostolici ministerij rationem fingeret, ad quam omnes astringerentur: sed potius fidelis medici aut praeceptoris instar, sese aliorum captui accommodauit, adeoque omnibus se seruum fecit. Poterat hoc prolixe demonstrari, si omnia illius facta exponere vellemus, sed ipsum audiamus in Miletana Synodo de suo ministerio differentem his verbis: Vos scitis a primo die, quo ingressus sum Asiam, quomodo vobiscum per omne tempus fuerim, seruiens Domino cum omni modestia & multis lachrymis ac tentationibus, quae mihi euenerant ex insidijs Iudaeorum: Vt nihil subfugerim eorum, quae vobis conducerent, quin ea annuntiarem vobis, & docerem vos publice ac per singulas domos. Et rursus: Argentum, aurum, aut vestem nullius concupiui: imo ipsi noftis, quod vtibus meis & his qui mecum sunt, subministrarunt manus istae. In omnibus ostendi vobis, quod sic laborantes oportet sustinere infirmos, ac meminisse verborum IESV, quoniam ipse dixit: Beatum est dare potius quam accipere. Quia ergo talem se Paulus gessit, & ipse quidem exmanuum suarum labore victum sibi parauit, omnibus autem interea Verbum vitae praedicauit, qui non videat ipsum omnibus seruum factum fuisse? At nunquam hoc facturus erat, nisi CHRI-STVM IESVM toto animo complexus, in eodem homines simul omnes tenerrime dilexisset.
units.tr: This is an outstanding and most memorable example of charity, by which Paul embraced first Christ himself, and then in him all men. For if you consider the nature of our mind and the customs of men, among whom life is lived everywhere, scarcely anything seems so unworthy and unjust as that those who have been set in some higher rank should be told to lower themselves to the judgement of others and to accommodate themselves to those beneath them. But there is no need to recount how great Paul was, since the testimony of Christ himself is sufficient for us, who said of him to Ananias: "He is a chosen vessel to me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel." Yet he did not allow himself to be puffed up with confidence in so great a dignity, so as to devise for himself a private and peculiar plan of apostolic ministry to which all should be bound. Rather, like a faithful physician or teacher, he adapted himself to the understanding of others, and so made himself a servant to all. This could be demonstrated at length if we wished to set out all his deeds, but let us hear him speaking of his ministry at the Synod of Miletus in these words: "You know, from the first day that I came into Asia, how I have been with you all the time, serving the Lord with all humility and with many tears and trials, which came upon me through the plots of the Jews; how I kept back nothing that was profitable to you, but declared it to you and taught you publicly and from house to house." And again: "I have coveted no one's silver, or gold, or clothing; indeed you yourselves know that these hands have supplied my needs and those of my companions. In all things I have shown you that by labouring in this way we ought to support the weak, and to remember the words of Jesus, who said: It is more blessed to give than to receive." Since Paul therefore conducted himself in this way, and by the labour of his own hands provided his living, while all the time he preached the Word of life to all, who would not see that he had been made a servant to all? Yet he would never have done this unless, embracing Christ Jesus with his whole mind, he had loved all men together with the tenderest affection in him.

units.la: Debent hoc eius studium omnes imitari, qui ecclesiarum pastores haberi volunt: nec est quòd verecantur, ne ex ipsorum dignitate aliquid decedat, si humilius sese omnibus accommodent. Seruitus enim haec neque ignominiosa neq; infelix est. Primò enim voluntaria est, & proinde cùm summa libertate coniuncta: quia nemo illam subibit, qui non prius carnem cum affectibus prauis subegerit, quorum imperium omni tyrannide grauius esse solet. Deinde Christo similes fiunt, qui illud faciunt. Nam is quoque serui formam suscepit, nec contentus omne officij genus docendo & sanando obiisse, sanguinem quoque suum pro nobis effudit. Finis praeterea, aut potius effectum huius seruitutis est, quòd in regno Christi maximos facit, dum quàm plurimos ei adducimus, vt in eandem nobiscum dignitatem euehantur. Admonet de hoc ille apud Matthaeum dicens: Quicunque voluerit inter vos magnus fieri, sit vester minister: & quicunque voluerit inter vos primus esse, sit vester seruus. Etenim vt in familia bene constituta eius serui praecipua est dignitas, qui prae aliis labores & curas domus sustinet: ita in ecclesia aliis praestant, qui quàm plurimis seruiunt, vt eos ad Christi cognitionem adducant.
units.tr: All who wish to be regarded as pastors of the Churches ought to imitate this zeal of his, nor need they be ashamed lest anything of their dignity be lost if they accommodate themselves more humbly to all. For this servitude is neither ignominious nor unhappy. First, it is voluntary, and therefore joined with the greatest liberty, since no one will undertake it who has not first subdued the flesh with its evil affections, whose rule is usually more burdensome than any tyranny. Secondly, those who do this become like Christ. For he too took the form of a servant, and not content to have discharged every kind of office by teaching and healing, he also poured out his blood for us. Moreover, the end or rather the effect of this servitude is that it makes us greatest in the kingdom of Christ, while we bring as many as possible to him, so that they may be raised with us to the same dignity. He warns of this in Matthew, saying: "Whoever wishes to be great among you, let him be your minister; and whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be your servant." For just as in a well-ordered household the servant who bears the labours and cares of the house before the others holds the chief dignity, so in the Church those excel the others who serve the greatest number, so as to bring them to the knowledge of Christ.

units.la: Hodie Romani Pontifices seruos seruorum se esse dicunt: sed vt in omnibus alijs mendax est Antichristus: ita hic hypocrita nequissimus, imo ne hypocrita quidem, sed potius improbus Dei & hominum illusor esse deprehenditur. Nam qui Reges potentia & opibus superat, qui ex omnibus regnis vectigalia colligit, qui Regum colla pedibus calcat, & ijsdem calceos suos deosculandos porrigit, qui in omnes ecclesias & episcopos ius & imperium sibi vendicat, qui sublimis aliorum humeris gestatur, & ex alto omnes despicit, qui denique triplici tiara redimitus se coeli, inferorum & terrae dominum esse proclamat, adhaec in ipsas quoque hominum conscientias pene-trans nouos fidei articulos condit & suis legibus omnes grauat, vt (inquam) seruum seruorum se esse profitetur. Quod quid aliud est, quàm homines simul omnes non orbis modò totius, sed ipsius etiam Satanae ludibrijs exponere? Et qualis obsecro seruus est, qui vt omnibus praecipit, ita sua figmenta ne in quaestionem quidem venire patitur, & scripturis potius sacris omnem authoritatem derogari vult, quàm vt aliqua ex ipsius traditionibus labefactetur. Non tales serui fuerunt Apostoli, neque tales suae ecclesiae Christus dedit, sed qui reipsa praestent quod dicuntur.
units.tr: Today the Roman Pontiffs say that they are the servants of servants. But as Antichrist is a liar in all other things, so in this he is a most wicked hypocrite, or rather not even a hypocrite, but is found to be a mocker of God and men. For he who surpasses kings in power and wealth, who collects tributes from all kingdoms, who tramples the necks of kings under his feet and offers his slippers to be kissed by the same, who claims for himself right and rule over all churches and bishops, who is carried aloft on the shoulders of others and looks down on all from on high, who finally, crowned with the triple tiara, proclaims himself lord of heaven, hell and earth, and moreover, penetrating even into men's consciences, frames new articles of faith and burdens all with his own laws, professes himself, I say, to be the servant of servants. What else is this than to expose all men together to the mockeries not only of the whole world but of Satan himself? And what sort of servant is he, I beg you, who commands all others, yet does not allow his own fabrications even to be called into question, and who would rather have all authority taken away from the sacred Scriptures than suffer any of his own traditions to be shaken? The Apostles were not such servants, nor did Christ give such servants to his Church, but men who in very deed do what they are called.

units.la: Sed finem aut scopum videamus, quem Paulus sibi propositum habuit: eum nimirum, vt plures lucrifaceret Christo. At Christo lucrifiunt, qui ad eius ecclesiam colliguntur, & illi sese per fidei obedientiam subijciunt. Admonet igitur locutio ista, perditos aut saltem in perditionis periculo adhuc constitutos esse omnes, quotquot à Christo exclusi & alieni sunt. Ratio huius dicti certa & irrefragabilis est, quòd in illo vno salus inuenitur. Notum est enim Apostolorum sententia: Non est in alio quoquam salus: nec enim aliud nomen est sub caelo, quod datum sit inter homines, per quod oporteat nos seruari. Et illud Baptistae: Pater diligit Filium, & omnia dedit in manum eius. Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam aeternam: qui autem non paret Filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super eum. Quibus consentit postremum Christi mandatum quo Apostolos emisit, dicens: Ite in orbem vniuersum, & praedicate Euangelium omni creaturae. Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, saluus erit: Qui non crediderit, damnabitur. Est ergo quaestus ecclesiae omnium pulcherrimus & maximus, vt homines Christo adducantur, & eius pecudum siue grex quotidie nouarum ouium accessione augeatur. Et haec illa vsura sanctissima est, quam per talenta sibi à Domino credita omnes ecclesiarum pastores exercere debent, si quidem illi probari velint. Vidit hoc fortissimus ille Christi martyr Laurentius, à quo cum quaererentur thesauri ecclesiae, promisit demonstraturum se: Sequenti autem die pauperes produxit, et interrogatus vbi essent thesauri, quos promiserat, ostendit pauperes, dicens: Hi sunt thesauri ecclesiae. Et verè thesauri (vt D. Ambrof. ait) in quibus Christus est, in quibus Christi fides est. At quod hîc de pauperibus dicitur, non minus ad omnes credentes pertinet, qui & ipsi Christum per fidem in vasis testaceis gestant, & eiusdem sunt peculium, quod ille occuli sui pupilla antiquius ducit, & quod sanguinis sui pretio redimere dignatus est. De hoc igitur lucro Verbi administros cogitare decet, & vere in Christo diuites erunt, & huius quoque opes, ceu fidi & prudentes œconomi, augebunt, quod illi officium erit longe gratissimum. At qui hodie Apostolicorum nomine gloriantur, vt nulli mortalium seruiunt (quemadmodum paulo ante diximus) ita sibi ipsis quoddam Petri patrimonium finxerunt, & eius scaphas atque retia metamorphosi plus quam Ouidiana in arces, vrbes & regnum longe lateque patens commutarunt, de quo vno augendo cogitant, auri ingentes thesauros colligunt, terras quotidie nouas coemunt, in quibus suae gentis homines principes constituant: Christiani autem ouilis atque gregis cura tam exigua tenentur, vt ne eos quidem seruare studeant, quos alij suo labore atq; studio lucrifecerunt. Dura sunt hæc & grauia dictu, sed accedit his aliud longe grauius, & quod non immerito prorsus intolerabile dixeris: quod nimirum non patiuntur Christo addictos manere, qui huic semel nomen dederunt, sed vel inuitos ad veritatis abnegationem cogunt, vel propter constantem fidei in vnum Christum confessionem crudelibus supplicijs occiduntur. Vera me dicere nemo negabit, nisi qui cum pudore sensum quoque communem exuerit: & hi tamen sunt, pro quorum tyrannide hodie reges potentissimi bella suscipiunt.
units.tr: But let us look at the end or aim that Paul set before himself: namely, that he might win more people for Christ. People are won for Christ when they are gathered into his Church and submit themselves to him in obedience of faith. This phrase therefore warns that all who are excluded from Christ and estranged from him are lost, or at least still stand in danger of perdition. The reason for this statement is certain and unanswerable: salvation is found in him alone. For the saying of the Apostles is well known: "There is no salvation in anyone else; for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved." So too is the saying of the Baptist: "The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand. He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him." The last command of Christ, by which he sent out the Apostles, agrees with this: "Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature. He who believes and is baptized will be saved; he who does not believe will be condemned." Therefore the most beautiful and greatest gain of the Church is that men are brought to Christ, and that his flock or his sheep is increased each day by the addition of new sheep. This is that most holy usury which all the ministers of the churches ought to practise with the talents entrusted to them by the Lord, if indeed they wish to be approved. The most valiant martyr of Christ, Laurence, saw this. When he was asked for the treasures of the Church, he promised to show them. The next day he brought forward the poor, and when he was asked where the treasures he had promised were, he pointed to the poor and said: "These are the treasures of the Church." And truly they are treasures (as Ambrose says) in whom Christ is, in whom the faith of Christ is. But what is said here of the poor pertains no less to all believers, who also carry Christ through faith in earthen vessels, and who are his peculiar possession, which he holds dearer than the apple of his eye, and which he deigned to redeem at the price of his blood. Ministers of the Word ought to consider this gain; then they will truly be rich in Christ, and, like faithful and wise stewards, they will increase his riches too, which will be a most welcome duty for them. But those who today boast of the name of the Apostles, so that they serve no mortal (as we said a little earlier), have likewise invented for themselves a certain patrimony of Peter, and they have changed his boats and nets, by a metamorphosis more than Ovidian, into citadels, cities and a kingdom extending far and wide. They think only of increasing this, they gather huge treasures of gold, they buy up new lands each day, in which they set up princes of their own nation. Meanwhile the care of the Christian sheepfold and flock is held so slight that they do not even strive to keep those whom others have won for Christ by their own labour and zeal. These things are harsh and grievous to speak of, but there is added to them something far more grievous, and which you may rightly call utterly intolerable: namely, they do not allow those who have once given their name to Christ to remain bound to him, but either force them unwilling to deny the truth, or, on account of their steadfast confession of faith in Christ alone, put them to death with cruel punishments. No one will deny that I speak the truth, except one who has cast off shame together with common sense; and yet these are the men for whose tyranny the most powerful kings today take up wars.

units.la: Caterum pergamus in verbis Apostoli, qui per partes explicat, vt se omnibus seruum fecerit. Primo factus sum (inquit) Iudæis, vt Iudæus, vt Iudæos lucrifaciam. Non Iudæum fe-ctum dicit (id enim sine Christiani nominis ignominia fieri non poterat) sed Iudæi similem: quia illorum moribus & ritibus se accommodauit. Factum hoc non semel: vt quando Timotheum in Iudæorum gratiam circumcidit, nimirum, vt illi apud hos docendi viam sterneret: quando item vota suscepit, capillos totondit, secundum legem purificatus est. Quibus adnumerari potest, quod diebus Sabbathorum Synagogas ingressus est & lectionibus Legis interfuit. Sed & ciborum delectum inter eos agentem habuisse credibile est, ne quem ex illis temere offenderet. Hæc (inquit) omnia feci, vt Iudæos lucrifaciam, id est, vt me illis insinuem, adeoq; ostium mihi apud eos aperiam, vt ipsis quoque Christum prædicare possim. Quod cum ab illo verissime dicatur, rursus nouum hic habemus ferventissimi zeli argumentum. Quia enim nullos hostes Iudæi acerbiores habuit, incomparabile in illo fuerit oportet promouendæ veritatis & publicæ salutis studium, quod tanta gentis illius improbitate, tot item insidijs & machinationibus non potuit restingui.
units.tr: But let us proceed in the words of the Apostle, who explains item by item how he made himself a servant to all. "To the Jews," he says, "I became as a Jew, that I might win the Jews." He does not say that he became a Jew (for that could not be done without disgrace to the Christian name), but like a Jew, because he accommodated himself to their customs and rites. He did this not once: as when he circumcised Timothy for the sake of the Jews, namely so that he might pave the way for him to teach among them; when he likewise took vows, cut his hair, and purified himself according to the law. To these may be added that he entered the synagogues on the Sabbath days and took part in the readings of the Law. It is also credible that he observed a distinction of foods among them, so as not to offend any of them rashly. "I have done all these things," he says, "that I might win the Jews," that is, that I might insinuate myself among them, and so open a door to them as well, that I might be able to preach Christ to them too. Since this is said most truly by him, we have here once again a new proof of his most fervent zeal. For since the Jews had no more bitter enemies, his zeal for advancing the truth and for public salvation must have been incomparable, for it could not be quenched by the great wickedness of that nation, nor by so many plots and machinations.

units.la: Secundo inquit: Iis qui sub lege sunt, factus sum quasi esset sub Lege, vt eos qui sub Lege sunt lucrifaciam. Videtur hoc membrum prioris expositionem continere: nonnulli tamen eos intelligi putant, qui ex Iudæis quidem ad CHRISTUM conuersi erant, verum tamen Legi & ceremonijs legalibus, quibus a pueris assuerant, adhuc nimium tribuebant. Fuit horum passim ingens multitudo, & difficile erat illo tempore Iudæos subito a Legis obseruatione in vniuersum reuocare, cum eam a Deo olim latam esse, & sub eius disciplina olim sanctissimos patres & Prophetas vixisse scirent. Cum talibus ergo sancta indulgentia vti oportuit, quod alios quoque Apostolos, & inter hos Iacobum imprimis, in Hierosolymitana ecclesia fecisse constat. Nam cum eo venisset Paulus, & Iacobo atque Senioribus exposuisset sigillatim, quæ Deus fecisset inter gentes per ministerium eius, illi quidem ijs auditis glorificauerunt Deum, at simul dixerunt Paulo: Vides frater, quot sint millia Iudæorum, qui crediderunt, suntq; omnes accensi studio Legis: audierunt autem de te ex aliorum sermone, quod defectionem doceas a Mose, &c. Et mox suadent, vt cum quibusdam, qui voto legali se obstrinxerant, sese purificet templum ingressus, & ita publice testetur, se a prophano Legis contemptu esse alienum. Quibus vt tunc morem gessit, ita non dubitarim idem sæpe alias factum fuisse. Sciebat enim ceremonias illas cum honore sepeliendas esse, & occasionem quærebat, qua tales ab obseruatione earum prorsus abductos vni Christo consecraret.
units.tr: Secondly, he says: "To those who are under the Law I became as one under the Law, that I might win those who are under the Law." This clause seems to contain an explanation of the former one. Some, however, think that by these are meant those who had indeed been converted from the Jews to Christ, but who still attributed too much to the Law and to the legal ceremonies in which they had been brought up from boyhood. There was everywhere a great multitude of these, and it was difficult at that time to call the Jews back suddenly from the observance of the Law altogether, since they knew that it had once been given by God, and that under its discipline the most holy fathers and prophets had once lived. Therefore it was fitting to use holy forbearance towards such people, as it is established that the other Apostles, and Jacob above all among them, did in the church of Jerusalem. For when Paul had come there with them, and had explained to James and the elders one by one what God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry, they indeed glorified God on hearing this, but at the same time they said to Paul: "You see, brother, how many thousands of Jews there are who have believed, and they are all zealous for the Law; but they have heard about you from the talk of others, that you teach a falling away from Moses, etc." And soon they advise that he should purify himself along with certain men who had bound themselves by a legal vow, entering the temple, and so publicly testify that he is far from any profane contempt of the Law. As he then complied with them, so I would not doubt that he often did the same on other occasions. For he knew that those ceremonies were to be buried with honour, and he sought an opportunity by which he might draw such people altogether away from the observance of them and consecrate them to Christ alone.

units.la: Tertio, exlegibus (inquit) factus sum vt exlex, vt lucrifaciam exleges. Exleges dicuntur, qui Legum expertes sunt, vel qui sine Lege aut extra Legem viuunt. Eo autem nomine gentes denotat, non quod omni lege caruerint (nam inter hos quoque legislatores fuerunt celeberrimi, Draco, Solon, Lycurgus, Minos, Numa & infiniti alij, qui & Leges condiderunt & rempub. constituerunt: imo, quod Apostolus noster ad Romanos annotauit, illi cum natura quæ Legis sunt facerent, sibijpsis Lex fuerunt, & ostenderunt opus Legis scriptum in cordibus suis) sed quod Legi Mosis non essent subiecti, quam solis Iudaeis datam fuisse scimus, quos propter promissum humani generis redemptorem a reliquis populis segregatos esse oportuit. Gentibus ergo, quibus lex Mosaica contemptui erat, se talem praebuit Apostolus, quasi ipse quoq; nullam eius rationem haberet. Cuius rei exempla sunt, quod Titum propter subreptitios falsos fratres circumcidere noluit, quod abstinebat omni ciborum delectu cum gentium credentibus versatus esset, quod deniq; Petro in faciem restitit, quando is non sine scandalo multorum Antiochiae Iudaizaret. Quibus adde, quod conciones quoq; suas illorum captui & moribus accommodauit, & omissis scripturae testimoniis (quae apud illos in nullo pretio esse sciebat) argumentis usus est, & poetarum quoq; auctoritate pugnauit, sicuti in iis est videre, quae Athenis & Lystris acta sunt. Quoad vero Legem Mosaicam, probe tenendum est, quod hic de se dicit Paulus, ad sola ceremonialia referri debere. Quae enim ad mores spectant, fere Iudaeis & gentibus communia fuerunt, cum hi quoq; in suis legibus naturae Legem sequerentur, quam Decalogo totam contineri in Epistola ad Romanos demonstrauimus. Ideo in praesenti per Parenthesim interserit: Tametsi non sim exlex Deo, sed sublex Christo. Exlegem quidem se fuisse dicit gentibus, dum Mosaicos ritus non magis, quam si ex illorum numero esset, obseruauit: at simul quoad Deum se nequaquam immunitatem captauisse testatur, cum sciret se Lege Christi teneri, cui omnes qui credunt obnoxios esse conuenit. Legem Christi alij legem fidei, alij legem charitatis esse dicunt. Ego utranque coniungendam esse arbitror. Nam a Scriba ille interrogatus de primo aut praecipuo praecepto, respondit: Diliges Domi-num Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo & ex tota anima tua, & ex tota cogitatione tua. Istud est primum & magnum mandatum. Secundum autem simile est huic: Diliges proximum tuum ut teipsum. Et ut in salutis negotio fidem unam urget & praecipit, ita quoad vitam & mores solius dilectionis meminit, qua omnia alia praecepta contineri Paulus testatur. Facit huc, quod in ultima Coena discipulis dixit: Mandatum nouum do vobis, ut alij alios diligatis, sicut (inquam) dilexi vos, ut & diligatis alij alios: Ex hoc cognoscent omnes, quod discipuli mei estis, si charitatem habueritis alij in alios. Quo Apostolus respiciens Galatis scribebat: Alij aliorum onera por-tate, & ita complete Legem Christi. Et ad Romanos: Nemini quicquam debeatis, nisi hoc ut alij alios diligatis. Sunt haec propter eos observanda, qui ubi Legem per Christum abrogatam esse audiunt, mox sibi quiduis agendi licentiam concessam esse arbitrantur. Atqui solas ceremonias veteres Christus abrogauit, & maledictionem sustulit, quae nos propter Legis transgressionem pre-mebat. Quoad caetera, Lex eadem nobis data est, quae veteribus, & ideo ille dicebat: Non veni ut dissoluam Legem, sed ut impleam. Matth.5.
units.tr: Thirdly, he says: "To those without law I became as one without law, that I might win those without law." Those are called lawless who are without laws, or who live without law or outside the law. By this name he denotes the Gentiles, not because they lacked all law (for among them too were the most famous lawgivers: Draco, Solon, Lycurgus, Minos, Numa, and countless others, who both made laws and established commonwealths; indeed, as our Apostle noted to the Romans, when they did by nature the things of the law, they were a law to themselves, and showed the work of the law written in their hearts), but because they were not subject to the Law of Moses, which we know was given to the Jews alone, who had to be set apart from the other peoples on account of the promise of the Redeemer of mankind. Therefore to the Gentiles, to whom the Mosaic law was an object of contempt, the Apostle showed himself as one who likewise had no regard for it. Examples of this are that he refused to circumcise Titus because of false brethren who had crept in; that he abstained from every distinction of foods while he lived with believers from among the Gentiles; and finally that he withstood Peter to his face when he, not without scandal to many, Judaized at Antioch. To these add that he also adapted his sermons to their understanding and customs, and, leaving aside the testimonies of Scripture (which he knew were held in no esteem among them), he used arguments and fought also with the authority of the poets, as can be seen in what was done at Athens and Lystra. But as to the Mosaic Law, it must be firmly held that what Paul says here of himself must be referred only to the ceremonial matters. For the things that concern morals were largely common to Jews and Gentiles, since these also in their laws followed the law of nature, which we have shown in the Epistle to the Romans to be wholly contained in the Decalogue. Therefore in the present passage he inserts by way of parenthesis: "Not that I am without law toward God, but under the law of Christ." He says that he was without law to the Gentiles, in that he observed the Mosaic rites no more than if he had been one of their number; but at the same time he testifies that before God he by no means sought immunity, since he knew that he was bound by the Law of Christ, to which it is fitting that all who believe be subject. Some call the law of Christ the law of faith, others the law of love. I think both should be joined together. For when a scribe asked him about the first or chief commandment, he answered: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like it: You shall love your neighbour as yourself." And just as in the matter of salvation he urges and commands one faith, so as regards life and morals he speaks only of love, in which Paul testifies that all other precepts are contained. To this belongs what he said to the disciples at the last supper: "A new commandment I give you, that you love one another; as I have loved you, so also you are to love one another. By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love one for another." Looking to this, the Apostle wrote to the Galatians: "Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ." And to the Romans: "Owe no one anything, except to love one another." These things must be noted on account of those who, when they hear that the Law has been abrogated through Christ, at once think that they have been granted licence to do whatever they please. Yet Christ abrogated only the old ceremonies, and took away the curse which pressed upon us because of the transgression of the Law. As to the rest, the same Law has been given to us that was given to the ancients; and therefore he said: "I have not come to destroy the Law, but to fulfil it." Matth. 5.

units.la: Quarto loco infirmos ponit, dicens: Factus sum infirmis, ut infirmus, ut infirmos lucrifacia. Ultimos hos facit, quia membrum hoc ad superiora genera omnia extendi debet. Eo enim exponit, quibus nam sese accommodauerit, siue illi Iudaei, siue gentes aut exleges fuerint: Nimirum non quibusuis aut omnibus promiscuè, sed infirmis. At tales dicuntur, qui etsi Christum fide appre-henderint, nondum tamen ad solidam eius cognitionē peruenerunt, sed in multis adhuc haesitant, non malitia, sed ignorantia simplici. Hi ergo institutione opus habent, & proinde indulgentius cum illis agendum est, ut metu omni (quem conscientiae infirmitas in illis parit) soluti, tandem in melius proficiant. Et de his solis totum hunc locum intelligi debere patebit, si quae circa Timo-theum & Titum gesta sunt consideremus. Illum enim propter Iudaeos, qui eum ex Graeco patre na-tum esse sciebant, circumcidit, ne scilicet isti offenderentur, si ipsum hominis incircumcisi consue-tudine & opera uti viderent: hunc autem circumcidere noluit, quod falsos aliquot fratres subrepsi-se[?] intelligeret, qui libertatem credentium subdole explorabant, ut occasione venarentur, qua illos in servitutem redigerent. Neq; hic aliquid ex priuato consilio fecit Apostolus, sed Christi praecep-toris doctrinā secutus est, qui cum Pharisaeos, quos non infirmos sed contumaces esse sciebat, suis verbis offensos esse audiret, discipulis dixit: Sinite eos, nam caeci duces sunt caecorum. Minime ergo Pauli exemplū ignauis fidei dissimulatoribus patrocinatur, qui ut securitati suae consulant, inconstantes Vertumnos & Proteos agunt, & sub Christianae indulgentiae praetextu nihil non dant hominibus improbissimis, quos apertos fidei hostes esse non ignorant, atq; in eorum gratiam multa praeter officium faciunt non sine multorum scandalo, quorum infirmitati potius erat consulendum. Debebant illi exemplum hoc diligentius inspicere, & viderent primo, Apostolum solos infirmos indulgentius tractauisse, aliorum vero adeo paruam rationem habuisse, vt supra dixerit: Mihi pro minimo est, vt a vobis diudicer, aut ab humano die. Et alibi: Si hominibus placerem, Christi seruus non essem. Deinde in solis medijs & indifferentibus hac facilitate vsus est, & tunc modo, quam diu pro indifferentibus habebantur. Quam primum enim aliqui legales ceremonias, vt ad salutem necessarias, vrgere caeperunt, hoc illi intolerabile visum fuit, sicuti voces illae testantur: Dies obseruatis, & menses, & tempora, & annos: metuo de vobis, ne frustra fatigatus sim apud vos. Item: Ecce, ego Paulus dico vobis, quod si circumcidamini, Christus nihil vos nocebit, &c. Praeterea non hoc spectauit Apostolus, vt omnibus placendo infirmitatem aliorum foueret, sed vt Christo lucrifaceret eos, qui circa nonnulla adhuc superstitiosius haerebant, vt quo illos in fide magis confirmaret. Quicunq; ergo Apostolum imitari voluerint, tria haec obseruent, vt solis infirmis indulgeant: vt in solis medijs & indifferentibus id faciant: fidei autem & salutis capita constanter propugnent: vt deniq; ad infirmorum aedificationem omnia dirigant, neminem vero in errore & superstitione confirment. Qui secus agunt, ij non infirmis consulunt, sed dum sibi amicos parant, veritatis doctrinam turpiter produnt, & infirmos offendunt.
units.tr: Fourthly, he sets down the weak, saying: "I became weak to the weak, that I might gain the weak." He puts these last because this member must be extended to all the higher kinds. For by it he explains to whom he accommodated himself, whether they were Jews, Gentiles or lawless men: not to just anyone or everyone indiscriminately, but to the weak. Such are those who, although they have laid hold of Christ by faith, have not yet come to a firm knowledge of him, but still hesitate on many points, not from malice but from simple ignorance. These need instruction, and so they must be dealt with more indulgently, so that, freed from all fear (which the weakness of conscience produces in them), they may at last make progress for the better. It will be clear that this whole passage should be understood only of such people, if we consider what was done concerning Timothy and Titus. For he circumcised Timothy on account of the Jews, who knew that he was born of a Greek father, lest those people be offended if they saw him using the custom and works of an uncircumcised man. But he would not circumcise Titus, because he understood that some false brothers had crept in, who craftily spied on the freedom of believers, so as to seize an occasion by which to reduce them to slavery. Nor did the Apostle do this from private counsel, but followed the teaching of Christ his teacher, who, when he heard that the Pharisees, whom he knew were not weak but obstinate, had been offended by his words, said to his disciples: "Leave them alone, for they are blind guides of the blind." Therefore Paul's example by no means defends the cowardly dissemblers of faith, who, to look after their own security, act like fickle Vertumnuses and Proteuses, and under the pretext of Christian indulgence give everything to the most wicked men, whom they know well to be open enemies of the faith, and for their favour do many things beyond their duty, not without the scandal of many, whose weakness ought rather to have been consulted. They ought to have examined this example more carefully, and they would have seen, first, that the Apostle treated only the weak with indulgence, but had so little regard for others that he said above: "It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you, or by man's day." And elsewhere: "If I still pleased men, I would not be the servant of Christ." Next, he used this flexibility only in matters indifferent and neutral, and then only as long as they were regarded as indifferent. For as soon as some began to press legal ceremonies as necessary to salvation, this seemed intolerable to him, as those words testify: "You observe days, and months, and times, and years; I fear for you, lest I have laboured among you in vain." Likewise: "Behold, I, Paul, tell you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing," and so on. Moreover, the Apostle did not aim to foster the weakness of others by pleasing everyone, but to gain for Christ those who still clung more superstitiously to certain things, so that he might strengthen them the more in faith. Whoever therefore wishes to imitate the Apostle should observe three things: he should indulge only the weak; he should do so only in matters indifferent and neutral, while stoutly defending the chief articles of faith and salvation; and finally he should direct everything to the building up of the weak, but never confirm anyone in error and superstition. Those who act otherwise do not consult the weak; while they make friends for themselves, they shamefully betray the doctrine of truth and offend the weak.

units.la: Porrò vt ad genus, vnde coeperat, Paulus redeat, postremo loco subijcit: Omnibus factus sum omnia, vt omnino aliquos seruem, id est, omnium ingenio atq; moribus me accommodaui, adeoq; in omnes formas me verti (quatenus salua fide in Christum fieri potuit) vt salte [?] aliquos pleniori Christi cognitione illuminatos ad salutis aeternae possessionem adducerem. Dicuntur enim Apost. seruare quando homines Christo adducunt, in quo vno vita & salus est. Quod propter eos annotamus, qui dum eiusmodi locutiones audiunt, mox vel in Deos caelites transferunt honorem, quì Christo soli debetur, vel sibi ipsis plus quiddam vendicat, quam par sit. Meminisse ergo oportet, Spiritum S. locutionibus eiusmodi ministerium Verbi nobis commendare, causam vero & rationem illarum in vno Christo quaeri debere, qui per Verbum praedicatur. Itaq; si de toto hoc negotio proprie loqui libeat, ijs insistendum erit, quae cap.3. dixit Apostolus: Ego plantaui, Apollo rigauit, Dominus dedit incrementum: Ergo neq; qui plantat neq; qui rigat est aliquid, sed Dominus, qui dat incrementum.
units.tr: Moreover, to return to the class from which he began, Paul adds last: "I have become all things to all men, that I might by all means save some." That is, I have accommodated myself to the dispositions and manners of all, and have turned myself into every shape (so far as faith in Christ allowed) so that I might at least lead some, enlightened by fuller knowledge of Christ, to the possession of eternal salvation. For the Apostles are said to save when they bring men to Christ, in whom alone is life and salvation. We note this on account of those who, when they hear such expressions, at once transfer to the heavenly gods the honour due to Christ alone, or claim for themselves something more than is fitting. We must therefore remember that the Holy Spirit, by such expressions, commends to us the ministry of the Word, but that the cause and reason of those things is to be sought in Christ alone, who is preached through the Word. Thus, if we wish to speak properly about this whole matter, we must keep to what the Apostle said in chapter 3: "I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase. So then neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase."

units.la: At hic peculiarem considerationem meretur locutio: Vt omnino aliquos seruem. Nam dicendum videbatur: Omnibus factus sum omnia, vt omnes seruem. Sed non ignorabat Apostolus, neminem in docendo tam felicem esse, vt auditoribus suis omnibus quod vult persuadeat, & omnes ad fidei obedientiam adducat. Quid enim sibi ipsi homo polliceatur, quando ipso Christo docente maior pars in incredulitate & aperta contumacia perseuerauit? Et notum est quod ille dixit, Multos quidem vocari, electos autem pauciores esse, qui vocationi ex animo obtemperent. Pertinet eodem sementis parabola, in qua aliud quidem semen in viam, aliud intra spinas, aliud in loca petricosa cecidisse dicitur, vix autem quartum quotq; in terra bona fructum tulisse optatum. Est hoc propter eos obseruandum diligenter, qui vehementer offendi solent, si non omnes ad Euangelij praedicationem emendentur & in Veritatis cognitione proficiant. Et Anabaptistas hinc fere argumentum captare scimus, quo nostras ecclesias damnent, & quae in his praedicatur doctrinam suspectam reddant. Sed falluntur omnes isti, quod Verbi aut doctrinae vitium esse putant, quod hominum vitio fit: quod item ecclesiam eiusmodi in terris fingunt, quae omni ruga & macula careat. Atqui vt intra septa agri domini loca petricosa & spineta inueniuntur, vt item publicae, in quibus frustra seminatur: ita hostis Satan dormientibus nobis, bono semini sua quoque zizania aspergit, quae ante messis diem euellere periculosum est. In his ergo tolerandis tam administris Verbi quam aliis credentibus longanimitate & patientia opus est, si quando & illi lucrifieri possint, in quibus nulla adhuc fructus spes apparet.
units.tr: Here the phrase "that I might by all means save some" deserves particular consideration. For it seemed that he should have said: "I have become all things to all, that I might save all." But the Apostle did not fail to know that no one is so successful in teaching that he persuades all his hearers of what he wishes and brings them all to obedience of faith. For what can a man promise himself, when, with Christ himself teaching, the greater part persisted in unbelief and open obstinacy? And it is well known what he said: "Many are called, but few are chosen," namely, those who obey the call from the heart. To the same point belongs the parable of the sower, in which some seed is said to have fallen by the way, some among thorns, some on rocky ground, and scarcely a fourth part in good soil bore the desired fruit. This must be carefully observed on account of those who are wont to be greatly offended if not all are moved by the preaching of the gospel and make progress in the knowledge of the truth. We know that the Anabaptists commonly seize on this as an argument by which to condemn our churches and render suspect the doctrine preached in them. But all these men are deceived in thinking that a fault which arises from the fault of men is a fault of the Word or of doctrine. Likewise they imagine a church on earth of such a kind as is free from every wrinkle and stain. Yet just as within the hedges of the Lord's field rocky places and thickets are found, and likewise public paths where seed is sown in vain, so the enemy Satan, while we sleep, sprinkles his own tares among the good seed, which it is dangerous to pull up before the day of harvest. In tolerating these, therefore, patience and forbearance are needed, both toward the ministers of the Word and toward the other believers, if at some time they too can be gained, even those in whom no hope of fruit yet appears.

units.la: Est igitur hic multa laude dignus Pauli zelus atque industria, qui etsi sciret se in multis frustra laboraturum esse, omnibus tamen sese accommodare dignatus est, vt saltem aliquos, ceu tabulas & sarcinas quascunq; ex naufragio eriperet, & Christi cognitione illuminatos seruaret. Tanti ergo Apostoli exemplum omnes ecclesiarum ministri imitentur, & meminerint boni pastoris esse non modò gregem totum pascere, sed vnius etiam ouiculae causa per montes & valles discurrere. Et vt in re domestica nunquam ditescunt [?], qui magni modò lucris intenti, minutiora & ad quotidianam domus curam pertinentia negligunt: ita Christi ecclesiam vix augebunt, quibus indignum videtur circa pauculos occupari. Arguitur his eorum ignauia, qui fere hoc praetextu sese excusant, quòd frustra praedicetur, & pauci Verbum qua decet reuerentia excipiant. Atqui hoc ipsum olim Prophetae conquesti sunt, non autem idcirco in commisso sibi munere segniores fuerunt. Quod ipsum de Christo & Apostolis simul omnibus dici potest. Quin potius nos consoletur, quòd quamuis maior vbique sit reproborum numerus, habet tamen suos quoque passim Deus, qui veri pastoris vocem agnoscunt & sequuntur. Et vt pluuia cœlitus immissa terram irrigat & fœcundam reddit, licet nequicquam compluantur petræ, silices & loca quædam sterilia: ita Verbum Domini etsi à multis non admittatur, passim tamen sunt qui id cum fructu audiunt. Vide Isa.55.Capite.
units.tr: Here, then, Paul's zeal and diligence deserve great praise. Although he knew he would labour in vain with many, he nevertheless deigned to accommodate himself to all, so that he might at least snatch some, like planks and whatever cargo from a shipwreck, and preserve them enlightened by the knowledge of Christ. Let all ministers of the churches imitate the example of so great an Apostle, and remember that it is the duty of a good shepherd not only to feed the whole flock, but also to range over mountains and valleys for the sake of a single sheep. And just as those who are intent only on great gains never grow rich in domestic affairs if they neglect the smaller things and those pertaining to the daily care of the household, so those who think it unworthy to be occupied with a few will hardly increase the church of Christ. Their idleness is exposed by those who commonly excuse themselves on this pretext, that preaching is in vain and few receive the Word with due reverence. Yet the prophets once complained of this very thing, and yet they were not on that account slacker in the office committed to them. The same may be said of Christ and all the Apostles together. Rather let this console us: although the number of the reprobate is everywhere greater, God nevertheless has his own people here and there, who recognise and follow the voice of the true shepherd. And just as rain sent from heaven waters the earth and makes it fruitful, though it falls in vain on rocks, flints and certain barren places, so the Word of the Lord, though not admitted by many, is nevertheless heard with fruit by some everywhere. See Isa. 55.

units.la: Restat postrema huius loci pars, qua studij sui finem Paulus exponit, dicens: Hoc autem fa-cio propter Euangelium, vt vna particeps eius fiam, id est, hoc ago, vt ad Euangelij propagationem aliquid conferam, neque ignauus ille & inutilis seruus sim, qui heri sui talentum defodit: sed vt particeps fiam fructus Euangelij, coronæ nimirum illius immarcessibilis, quæ credentibus in cœlis est reposita. Facit ad huius sententiæ expositionem, quod sub finem Capitis subijcit: Contundo corpus meum & in seruitutem redigo, ne quo modo cum alijs prædicarim, ipse sim reprobus. Id enim multis euenturum Christus minatur, qui munus hoc non bona fide administrant.
units.tr: The last part of this passage remains, in which Paul sets out the aim of his zeal, saying: "Now this I do for the sake of the gospel, that I may be a partaker of it with you" (1 Cor. 9.23). That is, he means: "I am doing this, that I may contribute something to the spread of the gospel, and so that I may not be like that lazy and useless servant who buried his master's talent; but that I may become a partaker of the fruit of the gospel, that is, of that unfading crown which is laid up in heaven for believers." What he adds at the end of the chapter helps to explain this meaning: "I beat my body and bring it into subjection, lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should become a castaway" (1 Cor. 9.27). For Christ threatens that this will happen to many who do not discharge this office in good faith. See Matt. 7.

units.la: Vide Matth.7. Neque fefellit spes ista Paulum, qui cum vitæ simul & ministerij sui finem non procul abesse sentiret, Spiritus testimonio confirmatus ad Timotheum scribebat: Ego iam libor,& tempus meæ resolutionis instat. Certamen illud præclarum decertaui, cursum consummaui, fidem seruaui. Quod superest, reposita est mihi iustitiæ corona, quam reddet mihi Dominus in illo die, iustus ille iudex: non solum autem mihi, sed & omnibus, qui expetunt illustrem illum ipsius aduentum. Dum autem in præsenti ait, se in hoc esse, vt vna particeps fiat Euangelij, non obscure innuit, studium hoc omnibus Christianis debere commune esse, eo quòd communione Euangelij frui non possint, qui non suam quoque operam pro virili ad propagandum regnum Christi conferant. Nec enim in eius familia quenquam otiosum esse conuenit: & vt olim in Tabernaculi constructione mulierum quoque fila ducentium & texentium opera vtilis Deo, grata erat: ita nemo tam vilis est, qui non publicam ecclesiæ causam aliquo modo iuuare possit. Nam vt omnis alia facultas deest, preces tamen suas huc quisque conferre potest, & acceptum per se est Deo pium sui regni prouehendi studium.
units.tr: That hope did not deceive Paul. Since he perceived that the end of both his life and his ministry was not far off, he was confirmed by the testimony of the Spirit and wrote to Timothy: "For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me in that day; and not to me only, but also to all who love his appearing" (2 Tim. 4.6-8). When he says here that he is intent on becoming a partaker of the gospel with others, he plainly hints that this zeal ought to be shared by all Christians, since those who do not contribute their own effort, as far as they are able, to spreading the kingdom of Christ cannot enjoy the fellowship of the gospel. For it is not fitting that anyone in his household should be idle; and just as in former times, in the building of the Tabernacle, the work of women spinning and weaving goats' hair was useful and pleasing to God, so no one is so humble that he cannot in some way help the public cause of the Church. For although every other means may be lacking, each person can still offer his prayers for this purpose, and the pious zeal for advancing his kingdom is in itself acceptable to God.

units.la: Quaerunt hic aliqui, an pium sit spe præmij seruire Deo? Sed hæc quæstio mihi curiosa magisquàm vtilis & necessaria videtur. Scimus enim populum Christi spontaneam illi obedientiam præstare: at hoc non excludit rationes quibus homines mouentur, vt spontanei fiant, nisi quis dicere velit Deum nobis frustra intellectum & mentem dedisse, quæ res propositas excutiunt, & de illis statuunt, prout salutare aut necessarium esse videtur. Et vt demus, Christi seruum non debere temporarijs commodis duci, hic tamen de vero & æterno Euangelij fructu agitur, quem omnes toto animo quærere & ambire debent. Nec temere nobis promissiones Deus in scripturis propo-suit, sed eas nobis adiumento esse vult, vt carnem facilius vincere, & hanc quoq; ad obedientiam fidei adducere possimus. Postremò, per se pijssimum est cœlestis præmij desiderio trahi, eò quòd hoc ipsum Christum comprehendit, qui nos in domo Patris sui secum esse & ad suam mensam accumbere vult, vt eiusdem cum ipso regni hæreditate fruamur. Omissis ergo otiosorum hominum quæstionibus, nosmetipsos quoad eius fieri potest, cœlestium præmiorum desiderio accendamus, & ita singuli suam vocationem obeant, vt in magno illo die lætam & beatam hanc vocem audiant: Euge serue bone & fidelis, super pauca fuisti fidelis, super multa te constituam, ingredere in gaudium domini tui. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Some ask here whether it is godly to serve God in hope of reward. But this question seems to me more curious than useful and necessary. For we know that the people of Christ render him willing obedience; yet this does not exclude the reasons by which men are moved to become willing, unless someone would say that God gave us intellect and mind in vain, by which we weigh the things set before us and decide about them, as seems wholesome or necessary. And even granting that a servant of Christ ought not to be led by temporal advantages, here we are concerned with the true and eternal fruit of the gospel, which all ought to seek and strive for with their whole heart. Nor has God set forth his promises in the Scriptures rashly; he wants them to be a help to us, so that we may more easily overcome the flesh and bring it also to the obedience of faith. Finally, it is in itself most godly to be drawn by the desire for the heavenly reward, since Christ himself embraces this, for he wants us to be with him in the house of his Father and to recline at his table, so that we may enjoy the inheritance of the kingdom together with him. Therefore, setting aside the questions of idle people, let us kindle ourselves, as far as possible, with the desire for heavenly rewards, and so let each one perform his calling that in that great day he may hear this joyful and blessed voice: "Well done, good and faithful servant; you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things; enter into the joy of your lord" (Matt. 25.21). To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XLVIII.

units.la: An ignoratis, eos qui in stadio currunt, omnes quidè currere, sed unum accipere præmium? Sic currite, ut comprehendatis. Porro quisquis certat, in omnibus est continens: illi quidem igitur, ut perituram coronam accipiant, nos autem ut incorruptam. Ego igi-tur ita curro, ut non in incertum: sic pugilem ago, ut nō aërem caedens. Sed contundo corpus meum, & in seruitutem redigo: ne quo modo cum aliis praedicarim, ipse reprobus fiam.
units.tr: Do you not know that those who run in a race all run, but only one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it. Everyone who competes exercises self-control in all things. They do it to receive a perishable crown, but we an imperishable one. So I run, not aimlessly; I box, not beating the air. But I punish my body and bring it into subjection, lest after preaching to others I myself should be rejected.

units.la: QUemadmodum homo ex innato philautiæ vitio sibi ipsi in omnibus suis dictis & factis mirificè placet: ita imprimis hoc solet fieri, si quam rerum diuinarum scientiam se præ multis aliis assecutum esse sibi persuasit. Hæc enim causa est, ut & alios omnes præ se contemnat, & quasi ipsam felicitatis arcem expugnarit, non multūm porrò de illis cogitet, quæ ad consequendum regnum Dei necessaria sunt. At hinc certissima illius ruina & salutis totius iactura sequitur. Quia enim scientiæ fiducia turgidus nihil eorum præstat, quæ ex Dei verbo didicit, fatuo illi similis fit, qui supra arenam domum ædificat, sumptuosam quidem & magnificam, sed quæ neq; ventorum turbini neq; inundantium aquarum procellis aut fluctibus resistere potest, eò quòd fundamento stabili & firmo nō nitatur. Tales omnino Corinthij fuerunt. Quia enim eorum doctores priuatæ potius gloriæ quàm ædificationis & publicæ salutis studio tenebantur, & ideo omissa simplicitate doctrinæ euangelicæ circa sublimium quorundam mysteriorum tractatione cum superba eloquentiæ ostentatione laborabant, ipsi quoq; singularis cuiusdam scientiæ persuasione ebrij, se iampridem omnia assecutos esse existimabant, & proinde rerum omnium securi, in omnem licentiam effundebantur, adeò ut (quod iam sæpe diximus) ne sacris quidem alienis abstinerent. Quapropter ostendit[?] nuper Paulus, hanc ipsorum scientiam vanam & noxiam esse, & quid ipsos deceat, suo exemplo multis docuit. Nunc autem doctrinæ huic grauem exhortationem subiicit, qua longius progreditur, ut confidentiam ipsorum fortius contundat. Docet enim eos, etsi hucusq; perfectissimi fuissent, nullum tamen ex omni studio suo fructum percepturos esse, nisi in finem usq; perseuerent. Et ne quid in hac admonitione desiderare possint, simul veram Christianæ perseuerantiæ rationem tradit, docens, quibus adminiculis nos ipsos possimus iuuare, ut indies in melius proficiamus. Omnem verò hanc doctrinam similibus appositissimis & proprio exemplo illustrat.
units.tr: As a man, through the innate vice of self-love, is wonderfully pleased with himself in all his words and deeds, so this especially tends to happen when he has persuaded himself that he has attained a knowledge of divine things beyond many others. For this is the cause why he both despises all others in comparison with himself, and, as if he had stormed the very citadel of happiness, does not think much about those things that are necessary for attaining the kingdom of God. But from this there follows his most certain ruin and the total loss of his salvation. For, puffed up with confidence in his knowledge, he performs none of those things that he has learned from the word of God, and so he becomes like the foolish man who builds a house upon the sand, a costly and magnificent house, but one that cannot withstand the gusts of the winds or the storms and waves of the flooding waters, because it does not rest upon a stable and firm foundation. The Corinthians were altogether like this. For their teachers were devoted to private glory rather than to the zeal for edification and public salvation, and therefore, neglecting the simplicity of the evangelical teaching, they laboured over the treatment of certain sublime mysteries with a proud display of eloquence. The people too, drunk with the persuasion of a peculiar kind of knowledge, believed that they had already attained everything, and therefore, secure in everything, they gave themselves over to every licence, so that (as we have often said already) they did not even abstain from strange sacred rites. Wherefore Paul lately showed that this knowledge of theirs was vain and harmful, and taught them by his own example what befits them. Now he adds a serious exhortation to this teaching, by which he goes further, so that he may more strongly crush their confidence. For he teaches them that, although they had hitherto been most perfect, they would nevertheless gain no fruit from all their zeal unless they persevered to the end. And lest they should lack anything in this admonition, he at the same time sets out the true method of Christian perseverance, teaching by what aids we may help ourselves, so that we make progress daily towards better things. He illustrates all this teaching with most fitting comparisons and with his own example.

units.la: An ignoratis (inquit) eos qui in stadio currunt, omnes quidem currere, sed unum accipere præmium? Primum simile de cursoribus est, alterum de pugilibus aut athletis, quod postea suo loco adducet. Utrumq; ex certaminibus petit, quæ olim in ludis publicis & sacris fieri solebant. Constat enim gentes ludos habuisse sacros, qui certis temporibus exhibebantur: Primatum in his habebant Olympici, quos in Iouis honorem Hercules instituerat, & qui quinto quoque anno prope Olympiam Elidis ciuitatem celebrabantur. Secundus locus Pythijs dabatur, Apollini sacris in occisi ab illo Pythij serpentis memoriam. Tertium locum tenebant Isthmij, quos Theseus Neptuno dedicauit (sicut in eius vita Plutarchus scribit) sic dicti, quòd in Isthmo Corinthiaco agerentur. Quarto loco Nemeæi erant, quibus Hercules vel (ut alij volunt) pueri Archemori memoria seruabatur. Ne autem ludi illi (quod plerunque fieri solet) in licentiam degenerarent, & in tanta hominum ad illos confluentium multitudine multa inhonestius fierent, certamina proponebantur, cursus nimirum, disci, saltus, luctæ & iaculationis. In præsenti tamen Paulus, omissis tribus reliquis, duorum modò meminit, quæ ipsius instituto maximè seruiebant. Nec temere factum putabimus, quod cùm multæ aliæ rationes & exempla multa essent, similitudines istas producere voluit. Fecit enim hoc duas ob causas potissimum: Prima est, quòd hæc omnibus notissima essent, & ne vulgus quidem quid in his certaminibus fieret, ignorare posset, cum Isthmia certamina in ipso Corinthiacæ urbis conspectu haberentur. Ideo de his dicturus ait: An ignoratis, &c? Altera, quòd excusationis prætextum omnem eripere vult ignauis & delicatis, qui iniquius secum agi queruntur, si quis carnis mortificationem, patientiam in aduersis & perseuerantiam aut constantiam ab illis requirit. Ostendit ergo nihil à nobis postulari, quàm quod huic seculo dediti sponte faciunt fluxæ voluptatis & aurae popularis vel gloriolæ momentaneæ causa. Unde sequitur, nimium turpem esse Christianorum hominum ignauiam, si in iis remissiores sint, quæ ad æternæ salutis causam faciunt. Sed ipsius Apostoli verba excutiamus.
units.tr: Do you not know, he says, that those who run in a race all run, but only one receives the prize? The first comparison is with runners, the second with boxers or athletes, which he will bring forward later in its proper place. He takes both from the contests that were once held at the public and sacred games. For it is established that the nations held sacred games, which were celebrated at fixed times.
