Among these the Olympic games held the first place, which Hercules had instituted in honour of Jupiter, and which were celebrated every fifth year near Olympia, a city of Elis. The second place was given to the Pythian games, sacred to Apollo, in memory of the serpent Python which he had slain. The third place was held by the Isthmian games, which Theseus dedicated to Neptune (as Plutarch writes in his Life of Theseus), so called because they were held on the Isthmus of Corinth. In the fourth place were the Nemean games, which were kept in memory of Hercules or, as others prefer, of the boy Archemorus. Lest these games (as usually happens) should degenerate into licence, and in such a great crowd of men flocking to them many things should be done more dishonourably, contests were set out, namely the race, the discus, the leap, wrestling and the javelin. In the present passage, however, Paul, leaving out the other three, mentions only two, which were most useful for his purpose. Nor shall we think it was done rashly, that, when there were many other reasons and many examples, he chose to bring forward these comparisons. He did this chiefly for two reasons. The first is that these were most familiar to all, and even the common people could not be ignorant of what took place in these contests, since the Isthmian contests were held in full view of the city of Corinth. Therefore, about to speak of them, he says: Do you not know, etc.? The second is that he wishes to snatch from the idle and effeminate every pretext for excuse, those who complain that they are dealt with too unfairly if anyone requires of them the mortification of the flesh, patience in adversity, and perseverance or constancy. He shows therefore that nothing is demanded of us except what those devoted to this world do willingly, for the sake of fleeting pleasure and popular applause or a momentary little glory. Whence it follows that the cowardice of Christian men is far too shameful if they are more lax in those things that serve the cause of eternal salvation. But let us examine the Apostle's own words.

units.la: A cursorum similí orditur, quod ita proponit: An ignoratis, eos qui in stadio currunt, omnes quidem currere, sed unum accipere præmium? Quæ verba non eo sensu accipi debent, quasi ex toto credentium cœtu unus modò cœlestis & æternæ vitæ brauium apprehensurus sit, quemadmodum inter eos, qui cursu certant, is solus coronatur, qui alios omnes celeritate præuertit. Sed sensus hic est: Quemadmodum in cursus certamine nemo brauium assequitur, nisi qui ad metam usque decurrit, & legitimè vincit: Ita nemo æternæ vitæ coronam accipiet, nisi qui in fide veræ & vitæ sanctimonia in finem usque perseueraverit. Vt ergo non satis est stadium ingredi, vestes deponere, inter cursores sibi locum deligere, cum illis magno impetu ex carceribus emicare & aliquousque pergere, si in medio cursu aut concidas, aut pedem sistas & ex cursore strenuo otiosus spectator fias: ita nihil proficiunt in regni Dei & salutis æternæ negotio, qui Christianis quidem sese adiungunt, verbum audiunt, Sacramentis communicant, vitæ cursum secundùm Christi præcepta aliquò usque dirigunt, tandem verò aut desessi, aut carnis cupiditatibus deuicti, aut mundi exemplo abrepti deficiunt, vel in nuda & otiosa fidei professione acquiescunt. Et de hoc hoc quidem Corinthios admoneri necesse erat, eò quòd sibi ipsis ante victoriam partam nimium placerent.
units.tr: He begins with the likeness of runners, which he sets out thus: Do you not know that those who run in a race all run, but only one receives the prize? These words ought not to be taken in the sense that, out of the whole assembly of believers, only one is going to lay hold of the prize of heavenly and eternal life, just as among those who contend in a race only the one who outstrips all the others by speed is crowned. The sense is rather this: as in a race no one attains the prize unless he runs to the goal and wins lawfully, so no one will receive the crown of eternal life unless he has persevered to the end in true faith and holiness of life. Therefore, just as it is not enough to enter the stadium, to take off one's garments, to choose a place among the runners, to dash out of the starting gates with them in a great rush and to keep going for a while, if in the middle of the course you either fall or stop your foot and, from an energetic runner, become an idle spectator, so those men achieve nothing in the business of the kingdom of God and of eternal salvation who indeed join themselves to Christians, hear the word, take part in the sacraments, and direct the course of their life for a while according to the precepts of Christ, but at last, either wearied out, or overcome by the desires of the flesh, or carried away by the example of the world, they fail, or they rest content in a bare and idle profession of faith. It was necessary that the Corinthians be admonished about this, because they were too pleased with themselves before the victory had been won.

units.la: Obseruari autem debet non indiligenter, vitæ & nominis Christiani professionem certantibus in stadio conferri. Horum cursus & certamen occulta esse non possunt, cum in conspectissima spectatorum corona currant, quorum alij eos applausu suo iuuant, alij ipsis inuident & odio rin-guntur: Ita non latere possunt Christiani homines, sed in totius mundi theatro hominibus simul & angelis (ut supra de Apostolis dictum est) spectaculum exhibent, & interea aliorum fauore & precibus iuuantur, multorum verò odijs atque machinationibus impediuntur. Et ut in stadio nullus desidiæ & quieti locus est, imò ridiculus esset, qui illic vel conuiuari, vel supinus in herba stertere vellet: Ita Christianæ fidei professio assiduos labores sibi coniunctos habet, & certaminibus continuis exercetur, à quibus sine certa salutis iactura discedere non licet. Imò ne licet quidem pedem referre aut remissius agere: quia ut primum hoc fit, mox nobis Satan instat, & læta-les ictus infert, vel cursum nostrum ita turbat & abrumpit, ut vix unquam possimus in viam redire. Non minus ergo pernitiosè quàm turpiter falluntur, qui sibi ipsis indutias fingunt, & priusquàm ad metam peruenerunt, sese ad otium & quietem componunt.
units.tr: Moreover, it must be observed, not carelessly, that the profession of life and of the Christian name is compared to those who contend in a stadium. Their running and their contest cannot be hidden, since they run before the most conspicuous crowd of spectators, some of whom help them with their applause, while others envy them and are consumed with hatred. So Christian men cannot remain hidden, but in the theatre of the whole world they present a spectacle to men and angels at once (as was said above concerning the Apostles), and meanwhile they are helped by the favour and prayers of others, but are hindered by the hatreds and machinations of many. And just as in the stadium there is no place for idleness and rest, and it would be ridiculous for anyone there to wish to feast or to snore lying on his back in the grass, so the profession of the Christian faith has continual labours joined to it, and is exercised in unceasing contests, from which one may not depart without certain loss of salvation. Indeed, one may not even draw back a foot or act more slackly, because as soon as this happens, Satan presses upon us at once and inflicts deadly blows, or so disturbs and breaks off our course that we can scarcely ever return to the way. Those who invent for themselves a truce, and before they have reached the goal settle down to idleness and rest, are deceived no less ruinously than shamefully.

units.la: Itaque Christiani hominis fuerit, sic currere ut apprehendat, sicuti ex præmissa similitudine Paulus infert. Id verò non fiet, nisi relictis à tergo omnibus prioris vitæ & huius seculi studijs, ad ea tendamus, quæ nobis propositá sunt. Nunquam ergo nos metam assecutos esse putemus, quoad in carne viuimus. Explicat hoc Paulus proprio exemplo, quando ad Philippenses de se-metipso sic scribit: Fratres, ego meipsum nondum arbitror metam apprehendisse, unum autem ago, ea quidem quæ à tergo sunt obliuiscens, ad ea verò quæ à fronte sunt contendens, scopum versus feror ad palmam supernæ vocationis Dei per CHRISTVM IESVM. Et ne quis hoc ad solos Apostolos putaret pertinere, mox infert: Quotquot itaq; perfecti sumus, hoc sentiamus. Conueniunt ista cum Christi verbis, qui eum beatum fore pronuntiat, qui in finem usque perseueraverit. Et rursus alibi dicit: Nemo, qui ubi manum admouit aratro, respexerit ad ea quæ à tergo sunt, aptus est regno Dei. Luc. 9.
units.tr: It therefore belongs to a Christian man to run in such a way that he may lay hold, as Paul infers from the comparison he has just made. This will not happen unless, leaving behind all the pursuits of his former life and of this age, we press on towards those things that are set before us. So let us never think that we have reached the goal as long as we live in the flesh. Paul explains this by his own example, when he writes to the Philippians about himself: "Brethren, I do not consider that I have yet laid hold of the goal; but this one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and straining towards what lies ahead, I press on towards the mark, for the prize of the upward call of God through CHRIST JESUS. And lest anyone think this pertains only to the Apostles, he adds at once: "Therefore let as many of us as are mature think this way." These words agree with the words of Christ, who pronounces blessed the one who perseveres to the end. And again elsewhere he says: "No one who has put his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God." Luke 9.

units.la: At hic nos excitare debet, quod dum generali præcepto Christianos omnes Paulus appellat, simul omnibus brauij apprehendendi spem facit. In hoc igitur noster cursus ab alijs differt, quòd etsi nos aliqui præuertant, & in multis nos superent, quoad donaspiritualia, ijdem tamen nos minimè impediunt, neque quod nobis destinatum est brauium præripiunt, modò ipsi quoque ad nostram metam usque constanter decurremus. Est enim una salus omnibus propositá, & una regni cœlestis hæreditas, quæ ut omnibus sufficit, ita neque diuisione in multos fratres minuitur, quando singuli totam nulla cum aliorum fraude, siue iactura possident. Ad hanc olim cursu indefesso contenderunt Patriarchæ, Moses, Prophetæ & quotquot in veteri testamento Dei vocationem secuti sunt. Successerunt his Apostoli, & quicunque illo tempore Euangelio crediderè. Proximi huius fuerunt Martyres reliqui, quorum ea fuit constantia, ut per mille mortes & crudelissimos exquisitorum tormentorum cruciatus perrumpendum sibi putarint, ut brauium sibi propositum obtinerent. At nihil illi nobis præripuerunt, sed vnà cum ipsis nos quoque per Christum acquisi-ta beatitudine fruemur. Quod si cui mirum & nouum videtur ( vt reuera humanæ rationi istud insolens est) is meminerit, nobis non certamen esse inuidiosum cum Christianis hominibus, qui in eodem nobiscum stadio currunt, sed cum diabolo, mundo, carne & corruptis eius desiderijs. Qui cum communes hostes sint, in ijs vincendis Christiani sibi mutuam opem ferunt, & singuli alios suo studio & alacritate iuuant atque confirmant. Non ergo sibi inuicem antagonistæ sunt Christiani, sed commilitones, qui quo magis proficiunt & vincunt, eò magis animum addunt alijs ad eandem victoriæ palmam aspirantibus. Ita ergo in aliorum exempla respicere debemus, vt in ijs, qui perfectissimi videntur fuisse, quantum nobis adhuc desit videamus, & ad illorum imitationem excitemur. Inter omnes verò semper nobis Christus emineat, qui & exemplo suo nobis præiuit, & nobis victoriam suo sanguine peperit, simulq; vires nouas subinde ijs suggerit, qui illum sequi instituerunt. Huc faciunt, quæ de illo & eius imitatione Apostolus ad Hebræos Capite 12. tradit,&c.
units.tr: But here we ought to be stirred up, because while Paul addresses all Christians with a general precept, at the same time he gives everyone hope of seizing the prize. In this respect our race differs from others: although some may go before us and surpass us in many respects, as regards spiritual gifts, they do not hinder us, nor do they snatch away the prize destined for us, provided that we too run steadily all the way to our own goal. For there is one salvation set before everyone, and one inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, which is sufficient for all and is not diminished by being divided among many brothers, since each one possesses the whole without fraud or loss to anyone else. The patriarchs, Moses, the prophets, and all who in the Old Testament followed God's calling once strove towards this with untiring running. The apostles succeeded them, and all who at that time believed the gospel. Next after these came the rest of the martyrs, whose steadfastness was such that they judged they must break through a thousand deaths and the most cruel torments of the tortures devised for them, so that the prize set before them they might obtain. But they have snatched nothing from us; rather, together with them we too enjoy the blessedness acquired through Christ. If anyone finds this strange and new (and indeed it is unfamiliar to human reason), let him remember that our struggle is not one of rivalry with Christians who run beside us in the same stadium, but with the devil, the world, the flesh, and its corrupt desires. Since these are our common enemies, Christians give one another mutual help in overcoming them, and each by his zeal and eagerness helps and strengthens the others. Christians, then, are not antagonists of one another but fellow soldiers, and the more they advance and conquer, the more they encourage others who aspire to the same palm of victory. Thus we ought to look to the examples of others, so that in those who seem to have been most perfect we may see how much we still lack, and be roused to imitate them. Above all, Christ should stand out to us, who both went before us by his example and won us victory by his blood, and at the same time continually supplies new strength to those who have begun to follow him. To this point belong the things the Apostle teaches about him and about imitating him in Hebrews, chapter 12, etc.

units.la: Porrò applicat nunc Paulus quod dixit ad præsentem causam de idolothytis, & simul Christianæ perseuerantiæ modum atque rationem tradit. Porrò (inquit) quisquis certat, in omnibus est continens. Loquitur de victu & diæta pugilum atque omnium eorum, qui in ludis illis solennibus certare solebant. Erat ea exquisitissima, adeò vt non solùm temperantiæ & sobrietati studerent, verumetiam ijs solis vescerentur, quæ tam animi quàm corporis vires confortare poterant: abstinebant autem ab omnibus, quæ corpus grauare & vires debilitare, vel earum vsum aliqua ex parte impedire solent. His autem infert: Illi quidem igitur vt periturum coronam accipiant continentes sunt, nos autem vt incorruptam,&c. Recte autem solius coronæ, & quidem perituræ, Paulus meminit. Quia enim veteres nihil præter honestam voluptatem in ludis illis quærebant, non pretiosa brauia ex auro vel argento, sed coronas ex frondibus aut herbis contextas solebant proponere, vt non turpis lucri, sed solius gloriæ studio iuuenes ad certamina accenderentur. Itaque qui in Olympijs vincebat, hunc oleastro coronabant. Victori autem in Pythijs laurea corona dabatur cum malis. Ex Isthmijs apio, ex Nemeæis verò pinu coronati discedebant. Coronarum autem vilitas gloriæ præconio compensabatur, cùm vulgo imprimis honorificum esse putaretur πολυςέφανον[?], id est, multis coronis redimitum dici. At hinc à Comparatis validissimè argumentatur Paulus: Si athletæ & cursores, vt cum vulgi applausu coronam breui perituram assequantur, à cibis delicatioribus & à crapulæ gulæue studio in vniuersum abstinent: quantò magis hoc facere debent homines Christiani, quibus immarcessibilem iustitiæ coronam Deus iam inde ab æterno præparauit, quam olim cum angelorum mirifico applausu atque gratulatione accipient? Comprehendit autem sub coronæ immarcessibilis nomine ipsissimum re-gnum Dei, & quæcunq; in hoc nobis per CHRISTVM IESVM parta sunt, de quibus Isaias dixit: Quæ oculus non vidit, nec auris audiuit, nec in mentem homini venerunt, ea parauit Deus illis, qui ipsum diligunt. Facit autem ad argumenti amplificationem, quòd pugiles illi simul omnes temperantiæ student, etsi sciant vnum duntaxat brauij propositi participem fore: Nam ex eo apparet, quàm turpis sit eorum negligentia, qui se cœlesti præmio minimè frustrandos norunt, si officium strenuè fecerint. At hæc dicendo acriter perstringit Corinthios, qui gulæ & ventri ita dediti erant, vt non contenti domesticis lautitijs solennes idolothytorum dapes cum publico scandalo celebrarentur: & ostendit parum aptos fore ad Christiana certamina, nisi vitæ rationem instituant, quæ Christi legibus melius conueniant.
units.tr: Next, Paul now applies what he said to the present matter concerning idol-offerings, and at the same time sets out the manner and method of Christian perseverance. "Moreover," he says, "everyone who competes is temperate in all things." He is speaking of the diet and regimen of boxers and of all who used to compete in those solemn games. It was most carefully regulated, so that they not only aimed at moderation and sobriety, but ate only those things that could strengthen the powers of both mind and body, and they abstained from all things that are wont to weigh down the body, weaken its strength, or in some measure hinder its use. He then adds: "Those indeed are temperate so that they may receive a crown that perishes, but we one that is imperishable, etc." Paul rightly mentions only a crown, and indeed a perishable one. For since the ancients sought nothing in those games beyond honourable pleasure, they used to set out as prizes not costly awards of gold or silver but crowns woven from leaves or herbs, so that young men were kindled to the contests not by the desire for base gain but by the desire for glory alone. Thus the one who won at the Olympic games was crowned with wild olive. The victor at the Pythian games was given a laurel crown, and those at the Isthmian games departed crowned with celery, and those at the Nemean games with pine. The cheapness of the crowns, however, was offset by the proclamation of glory, since it was thought especially honourable to be called [πολύστεφανον], that is, crowned with many crowns. But from this comparison Paul argues most forcefully: if athletes and runners, so that they may obtain a crown that will soon perish amid the applause of the crowd, abstain altogether from more luxurious food and from the pursuit of gluttony and drunkenness, how much more ought Christian men to do this, for whom God has prepared from eternity an unfading crown of righteousness, which they will one day receive with the wonderful applause and rejoicing of the angels? Under the name of the unfading crown he comprehends the very kingdom of God, and all the things that have been obtained for us in it through Christ Jesus, of which Isaiah said: "What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, these things God has prepared for those who love him." Moreover, to amplify the argument, it counts that those athletes all strive for temperance, although they know that only one will share in the prize set before them. For from this it appears how shameful is the negligence of those who know that they will not be deprived of the heavenly reward if they have discharged their duty vigorously. By saying these things, he sharply rebukes the Corinthians, who were so given over to gluttony and the belly that, not content with their household delicacies, they celebrated the solemn feasts of idol-offerings with public scandal; and he shows that they will be poorly suited to Christian contests unless they adopt a manner of life that better agrees with the laws of Christ.

units.la: Cæterum arguitur hoc loco infelix nostræ naturæ corruptio siue peruersitas. In ijs quæ mundo & carni seruiunt, nihil non possunt plerique ferre & facere. Pernox amator ad amicæ ostium desidet cantillans, ludibria & iannas patitur, labores nullos detrectat, periculum vitæ & fortunarum omnium dispendia pro lucro ducit, modò momentanea & turpi voluptate potiatur, cuius vel sola recordatio illi aliquando molesta futura est. Auari autem non seipsos modò & suos omnes, sed terras simul omnes atque maria fatigant, vt quæstum faciant, & opes opibus quotidie accumulent. Eadem est helluonum & ebriosorum conditio, qui voluntariam insaniam cum totius corporis debilitatione & valetudinis iactura redimunt. Quid verò de militibus loquar quibus leue videtur famem, vigilias, frigus, æstum perpeti, vulneribus 'obuiam ire, & mortem tan-tumnon accersere, modò victoriam aduersus hostes obtineant? Denique quod Satyricus dixit, vt iugulent homines, surgunt de nocte latrones. At quàm primùm Christi nomine, & pro regni cœlestis hæreditate aliquam facultatem iacturam facere, periculum aliquod subire, aut consuetis modò voluptatibus & delitijs abstinere iubemur, mox animi impatientiam indigno murmure, & sæpe atrocibus conuitijs prodimus, & nobiscum indignè, iniquè & inhumaniter agi quiritamur. Est hoc inexcusabilis peruersitatis argumentum, & debent in huius consideratione diligenter versari Christiani homines, & Paulinum hoc de pugilum continentia dictum sibijpsis crebrò occinere, vt suijpsorum eos pudeat, si quid simile in suis moribus deprehendunt.
units.tr: Moreover, in this passage the unhappy corruption or perversity of our nature is exposed. In those things that serve the world and the flesh, most men can endure and do anything. The shameless lover sits up at his mistress's door singing, endures mockery and shutting out, refuses no labours, and counts the danger of his life and the loss of all his fortune as gain, provided that he can enjoy a momentary and base pleasure, the mere recollection of which will one day be painful to him. Misers, moreover, wear out not only themselves and all their household but also lands and seas alike, in order to make profit and to heap wealth upon wealth every day. The condition of gluttons and drunkards is the same, who buy voluntary madness at the price of the weakening of the whole body and the loss of health. What shall I say of soldiers, for whom it seems a light matter to bear hunger, watches, cold and heat, to face wounds, and not even to avoid death, provided they win victory over their enemies? Finally, what the satirist said holds true: "Robbers rise at night to cut men's throats." But as soon as we are commanded to give up some property, to undergo some danger for the name of Christ and for the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, or to abstain from our usual pleasures and delights, at once we betray our impatience of spirit with unworthy grumbling and often with savage insults, and we complain that we are treated unworthily, unjustly and inhumanly. This is a proof of inexcusable perversity, and Christian men ought to dwell diligently upon it, and often to recite to themselves this saying of Paul about the self-restraint of athletes, so that they may be ashamed of themselves if they detect anything similar in their own conduct.

units.la: Vt verò plus ponderis habeat ista exhortatio, & ne Paulus ab alijs exigere putetur, quod ipse minus præstet, ad suum exemplum reuertitur, & quid ipse facere soleat, euidentius exponit his verbis: Ego igitur ita curro, vt non in incertum: sic pugilem ago, vt non aërem cædens: sed contundo corpus meum & in seruitutem redigo, &c. Duo de se dicit. Primum, quòd certum suorum studiorum atque actionum omnium scopum aut finem habeat. Non (inquit) eorum similis sum, qui absque meta currunt, & per incertas ambages nunc huc nunc illuc declectunt, & proinde ex cursu suo nihil præter totius corporis fatigationem & anhelantis pectoris æstum reportant. Neque etiam eos imitor, qui digladiando multùm quidem laborant, sed aërem solummodo feriunt, aut (quod prouerbio dicitur) cum umbra luctantur. Nam in finem certum omnia mea dirigo: vt nimirum Euangelij prædicationem longè lateque extendam, & ad ecclesiæ Christi atque singulorum credentium ædificationem plurimum conferam. Itaque fidei perfectionem declaro interdum, vt alios meo exemplo confirmem: interdum verò ad infirmorum captum me demitto, vt illos erigam: Iudæis Iudæus fio, vt hos lucrifaciam: denique nihil absque certa ratione facio, neque meum commodum, sed aliorum profectum atque salutem quæro. Ita non in incertum curro, neque vanis ictibus aërem ferio. At dum hoc de seipso dicit, simul non obscurè Corinthios perstringit, qui de libertate quidem & scientia sua multum gloriabantur, & hac fiducia freti ad sacras gentium epulas accedebant, nullum autem sui facti scopum certum habebant, imò ceu inepti gladiatores omnia turbabant, cùm & infirmiores multi illorum exemplo offenderentur, ethnici autem confirmarentur in suis superstitionibus.
units.tr: But so that this exhortation may carry more weight, and so that Paul should not be thought to demand of others what he himself does not do, he returns to his own example and sets out more plainly what he is accustomed to do, in these words: "So I run, not aimlessly; I box, not beating the air. But I beat my body and make it my slave," and so on. He says two things about himself. First, that he has a fixed goal or end for all his studies and actions. He says, in effect: I am not like those who run without a finishing line and wander about through aimless detours, now here, now there, and so gain from their running nothing but the exhaustion of the whole body and the heat of a gasping chest. Nor do I imitate those who labour hard at their sparring but only strike the air, or, as the proverb says, wrestle with a shadow. For I direct all my efforts to a definite end: namely, to extend the preaching of the gospel far and wide, and to contribute greatly to the building up of Christ's Church and of each believer. So at times I display the perfection of faith in order to strengthen others by my example; at other times I lower myself to the level of the weak in order to raise them up. I become a Jew to the Jews, that I may win them. In short, I do nothing without a sure reason, and I seek not my own advantage but the progress and salvation of others. So I run not uncertainly, and I do not strike the air with empty blows. But while he says this of himself, he at the same time quite clearly censures the Corinthians, who boasted greatly of their liberty and knowledge, and, trusting in this, went to the sacred feasts of the Gentiles, yet had no fixed aim for their conduct; rather, like clumsy gladiators, they threw everything into confusion, since many of the weaker ones were offended by their example, and the heathen were confirmed in their superstitions.

units.la: Seruit autem locus iste ijs confutandis, qui sui animi intentionem sufficere, & omnem cultum Deo probari putant, quem ipsi animo religioso instituunt. Currunt hi quidem, sed in incertum. Est enim hominis animus natura inconstans, & nouis quotidie cultibus delectatur. Deinde non possunt hominis conscientiam satiare, quæcunque extra Christum ex nostro cerebro instituimus, sicuti ille docet Samaritidi dicens: Quisquis biberit ex ista aqua, sitiet iterum: at qui biberit ex aqua, quam ego dabo, non sitiet in æternum. Sed & neque hostem nostrum diabolum cultus illi feriunt, qui incerta illa digladiatione potius delectari, quàm fugari solet. Quapropter frustra laborant, quicunque non certum scopum sibi propositum habent. At is non aliunde peti potest, quàm ex Dei verbo, quod æternum est, & eius voluntatem nobis annuntiat, quæ ipsa quoque sibi semper constat, neque in horas mutatur. Quod autem in genere de omnibus Christianis, quoad fidem & salutis æternæ negotium dicimus, hoc ipsum singuli ad suam vocationem transferre debent, vt in ea scopum, quem ipsis Deus propositum, respiciant. Nam nisi id fiat, ipsi quoque inani studio atque labore sese fatigabunt.
units.tr: This passage also serves to refute those who think that the intention of their own mind is enough, and that any worship they devise in their religious zeal pleases God. These people do run, but without a fixed goal. For the human mind is by nature unstable and delights daily in new forms of worship. Moreover, whatever we devise from our own brains apart from Christ cannot satisfy the conscience of man, just as he teaches the Samaritan woman, saying: "Whoever drinks of this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water that I shall give will never thirst for ever." Nor do those forms of worship strike our enemy the devil, who is wont rather to delight in that aimless fighting than to be put to flight by it. Therefore all those labour in vain who have no fixed goal set before them. Such a goal can be sought from nowhere else than from the word of God, which is eternal, which declares to us his will, and which is itself always consistent with itself and does not change from hour to hour. What we say in general of all Christians, as regards faith and the business of eternal salvation, each person ought to apply to his own calling, so that in it he may look to the goal that God has set before him. For unless this is done, they will weary themselves in vain zeal and labour.

units.la: Alterum, quod sibi tribuit Paulus, ex pugilum disciplina desumit, quam paulò ante attigerat. Contundo (inquit) corpus meum, & in seruitutem redigo: ὑπωπιάζω proprie est plagis aut ictibus lividum facere, quod Latini sugillare dicunt. Et hanc interpretationem D. Augustino in epist. 58. ad Dardanum placuisse vidimus. Eo autem verbo Apostolus seuerissimam disciplinam significat, & ideo per expositionem subjicit: Et in seruitutem redigo. Per corpus autem totum veterem hominem intelligit, quem alibi scriptura carnem dicit, eò quòd totus Spiritui repugnat. Ideo eum contundi & subijci necesse est, vt tandem obedire discat. Nam vt equo feroci nunquam vti possumus, nisi frænum admittat: ita neque nobismetipsis rectè vti poterimus, nisi vetus homo per fidei obedientiam Spiritui subijciatur. Vbi qua ratione id fiat, probè tenere oportet. Peccarunt enim hic vehementer aliqui ex Patribus, optimè alioqui de tota ecclesia & re Christiana meriti, qui cum hoc omne ieiunij crebris & au-steriori victus ratione perfecti putarent, eam vitæ rationem secuti sunt, qua seipsos ob valetudi-nis imbecillitatem tantùm non inutiles fecerunt publicis ecclesiæ vsibus: quod Basilio Magno & Nazianzeno accidisse legimus: & quod nocentius fuit, superstitionum authores fuerunt multis qui instituti ipsorum rationem non intellexerunt. Nos ergo Paulum ipsum sui exem-pli optimum interpretem audiamus, qui in priori ad Timotheum Cap. quarto sic scribit: Corporalis exercitatio paululum habet utilitatis: at pietas ad omnia utilis est, ut quæ promissionem habet vitæ præsentis ac futuræ. Aliquid quidem disciplinæ & exercitijs corporalibus tribuit, sed eadem sine pietate nihil prodesse docet. Et quia hanc exercitationi corporali opponit, satis euidenter docet, hanc in spirituali cultu consistere. Ideo Eusebius eam ita definiuit: [illegible, ~70 letters] ἡ κατὰ τοῦτον ζωή[?], id est, pietas est respectus ad unum solum verum Deum & secundum hunc institutam vitæ ratio. Et hunc secutus videtur D. Augustinus, qui dicit: Pietas est veracem[?] veri Dei cultus, unde omnia recte viuendi duci oportet officia. In illa igitur ante omnia Dei Verbo opus est, ut hoc nobis actionum & studiorum omnium regulam proponamus. Quod qui faciunt, & Deum ex animo eum esse agnoscunt, quem scripturæ prædicant, iustum nimirum, veracem & omnipotentem omnis malitiæ vindicem, ij mox verum illius timorem animo concipient, quo nihil ad frænandos carnis lasciuientis affectus efficacius excogitari potest. At quia hæc deliciis & intemperantia in victu ferociores fieri consueuit, externam quoque disciplinam adhiberi utile est, qua ut equo præpinguedine & otio lasciuienti pabulum, ita nos carni poteuienti libidinis & licentiæ fomenta subtrahamus. Ubi tamen diligenter cauendum est, ne omnes ad eandem victus rationem astringamus, aut eandem certis & statis temporibus alligemus: maximè autem omnium ne illi salutis meritum tribuamus. Ut enim non eodem omnes ingenio prediti sunt, ita non iisdem rebus ferociores fiunt. Ut ergo ineptus foret medicus, qui omni ætati & sexui, vel etiam omni morbo idem pharmacum adhiberet: ita imprudentes & temerarij sunt, qui eadem disciplinæ forma erga omnes utuntur. At qui in ea meritum statuunt, ij carnem non cotundunt, sed Pharisaica confidentia implent, ut aduersus Dei gratiam & huius Mediatorem, IESVM CHRISTVM, insurgere non vereatur. Sequamur ergo hic à Christo nobis præscriptam regulam de iuniijs, æterna verò salutis spem atque fiduciam in illius merito habeamus collocatam.
units.tr: The second thing that Paul claims for himself he takes from the discipline of boxers, which he touched on just before. "I bruise my body," he says, "and make it my slave." The Greek word ὑπωπιάζω properly means to make black and blue with blows, which the Latins call sugillare. We have seen that Augustine, in his letter 58 to Dardanus, approved of this interpretation. By this word the Apostle signifies a very severe discipline, and therefore he adds by way of explanation: "and bring it into servitude." By "body" he means the whole of the old man, whom Scripture elsewhere calls the flesh, because the whole of it resists the Spirit. Therefore it must be bruised and brought under, so that at last it may learn to obey. For just as we can never use a fierce horse unless it accepts the bridle, so we shall not be able to use ourselves rightly unless the old man is subjected to the Spirit through obedience of faith. We must hold firmly to the way in which this is done. For some of the Fathers, otherwise deserving very well of the whole Church and of the Christian cause, have gone seriously wrong here. Thinking that perfection lay in this, with frequent fasting and a harsher manner of diet, they followed a way of life by which they made themselves almost useless to the public service of the Church through the weakness of their health. We read that this happened to Basil the Great and to Nazianzen; and, what was more harmful, they became the authors of superstitions for many who did not understand the rationale of their practice. Let us therefore hear Paul himself, the best interpreter of his own example, who writes thus in the first letter to Timothy, chapter four: "Bodily training profits a little, but godliness is profitable for all things, since it has the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come." He grants some value to discipline and bodily exercises, but teaches that these profit nothing without godliness. And because he sets godliness against bodily exercise, he teaches quite clearly that godliness consists in spiritual worship. Therefore Eusebius defined it thus: [illegible in the scan] "ἡ κατὰ τοῦτον ζωή" [?], that is, godliness is reverence directed to the one true God and a way of life ordered according to him. Augustine seems to have followed him, when he says: "Godliness is the true worship of the true God, from which all the duties of right living ought to be drawn." Therefore, above all, we need the word of God, so that we may set this before us as the rule of all our actions and studies. Those who do this, and acknowledge that God is the one whom the Scriptures proclaim, namely just, true and almighty, the avenger of all wickedness, will straightway conceive in their minds a true fear of him, and nothing more effective for restraining the wanton desires of the flesh can be devised. But because these desires are wont to become more unruly through luxury and intemperance in food, it is useful also to apply an external discipline, by which we may withdraw from the flesh, which is lusty, the fuel of lust and licence, just as one withdraws fodder from a horse that grows wanton through excessive fatness and idleness. Yet here we must take great care not to bind everyone to the same manner of diet, or to tie them to the same fixed times; and above all, not to ascribe merit to it for salvation. For just as all men are not endowed with the same disposition, so they are not made more unruly by the same things. Thus it would be foolish for a physician to give the same medicine to every age and sex, or even to every illness; so those are imprudent and rash who use the same form of discipline towards everyone. But those who place merit in it do not subdue the flesh; they fill it with Pharisaical confidence, so that it does not hesitate to rise up against the grace of God and against his Mediator, Jesus Christ. Let us therefore follow here the rule for fasting that Christ has prescribed for us, and let us place our hope and confidence of eternal salvation in his merit.

units.la: Sed rursus causam exprimit Apostolus, cur carnem suam contundat & in seruitutem redi-gat, dicens: Ne quo modo, cùm alijs prædicarim, ipse reprobus fiam, id est, ne is esse deprehendar, cuius vita & mores doctrinæ repugnent. Quæ verba aduersarij nostri detorquent, ut doctrinam nostram de electionis certitudine euertant, & Paulum timuisse aiunt, ne reprobus fieret. At qui nihil hic de electione et vocatione ille dicit, de quarum veritate & constantia dubitare non poterat, cùm alibi ἀμεταμέλητα dicat: sed qua ratione sese in officio contineat, docet, nimirum pia & religiosa solicitudine, qua caueat, ne accusari possit de ijs, quæ cum Christiani nominis professione pugnant. Itaque cura hæc non ex dubitatione de æternæ electionis & prædestinationis decreto enata est, sed ex fidei zelo, quo electi excitantur, ut prædestinationi diuinæ inseruiant: quod tunc imprimis faciunt, quando carnem suam cum prauis desideriis contundunt, & mortificatam in ordinem redigunt. Et constat Deum electos suos spiritum timoris inferre, qui illos non de ipsius electione, sed de propria obedientia solicitos reddit, & author est, ut (quod Petrus monebat) vocationem & electionem suam firmam faciant, id est, ipsis fidei effectus declarent. Et quid obsecro hic sibi ipsi Paulus tribueret, quoad Dei tribunal, qui supra confessus est, sententiam iustificatum esse, etiamsi nullius malitiæ aut negligentiæ sibi conscius sit? Debent autem exemplum hoc ad se transferre, quicunque vel in ecclesia vel in repub. aliis præsunt. Nedum aliis præcipiunt & mandant, ipsi præter officium vitam viuant dissolutam, & suo exemplo Verbi Dei atque legum authoritatem eleuent. Meminerint ergo nullum nocentius scandalum esse, quàm quod ex ipsis nascitur, & proinde pœnas quoque graviores ipsos manere, nisi sibi diligenter caueant. At quæ nostri sæculi calamitas est, in hoc plurimum peccatur. Orandus[?] ergo est Deus Pater, vt suo spiritu omnium carnem contundat & saluberrimæ illi seruituti subijciat, in qua ipsius quidem gloriam prouehant, olim verò cum Filio suo IESV CHRISTO viuant & regnent. Huic debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But again the Apostle states the reason why he bruises his flesh and brings it into servitude, saying: "Lest by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should become a castaway," that is, lest I be found to be a man whose life and conduct contradict his teaching. Our opponents twist these words in order to overturn our doctrine of the certainty of election, and they say that Paul feared he might become a castaway. But he says nothing here about election and calling, about whose truth and steadfastness he could have no doubt, since elsewhere he calls them "without repentance" [ἀμεταμέλητα]. Rather, he teaches how he keeps himself in his duty, namely by a pious and religious anxiety, by which he takes care not to be accused of things that are at odds with the profession of the Christian name. So this care did not arise from doubt about the decree of eternal election and predestination, but from the zeal of faith, by which the elect are stirred up to serve the divine predestination. They do this especially when they bruise their flesh together with its wicked desires, and bring it, once mortified, into order. It is certain that God brings to his elect a spirit of fear, which makes them anxious not about their election itself but about their own obedience, and which prompts them (as Peter urged) to make their calling and election firm, that is, to show forth the fruits of faith. And what, I ask, would Paul claim for himself before God's judgment seat, when he has earlier confessed that he is justified by sentence, even though he is conscious of no wickedness or negligence? Yet all who are set over others in the Church or in the commonwealth ought to apply this example to themselves. Not only do they command and instruct others; they themselves live a dissolute life beyond their office, and by their example they undermine the authority of God's word and of the laws. Let them therefore remember that there is no more harmful scandal than that which arises from themselves, and that therefore heavier punishments await them as well, unless they take careful heed of themselves. But this is the calamity of our age: in this respect people sin very greatly. Therefore we must pray to God the Father that by his Spirit he bruise the flesh of all men and bring it under that most wholesome servitude, in which they may advance his glory, and at length live and reign with his Son Jesus Christ. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: HOMILIA XLIX.
units.tr: HOMILY XLIX.

units.la: NOlim autem vos ignorare, fratres, quòd patres nostri omnes sub illa nube fuerunt, & omnes per mare transiuerunt, & omnes in Mosem baptizati sunt in nube & in mari. Et omnes eandem escam spiritualem ederunt, & omnes eundem potum spiritualem biberunt. Bibebant enim ex spirituali, quæ ipsos sequebatur, petra: Petra verò erat Christus. Sed plerosque eorum non approbauit Deus. Prostrati sunt enim in deserto.
units.tr: Now I would not have you ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under that cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea. And all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and that rock was Christ. But God was not pleased with most of them, for they were laid low in the wilderness.

units.la: Thomo natura tardior est ad veræ pietatis studium: ita si quos in eo progressus fecit, mox sibipsi placet, & ijs ad suum exitium abutitur, quæ ipsi ad salutem adiumento esse debebant. Exemplum huius rei euidens in Corinthijs habemus. Cum enim hi per Paulum & Apollo bene instituti essent, & (vt initio huius epistolæ dictum est) omni cognitione & scientia abundarent, mox confidentiores facti, omisso religionis syncerioris & vitæ Christianæ studio, circa res inutiles occupari cœperunt. Secutus est hoc malum libertatis Christianæ abusus, quo eò vsque abrepti sunt, vt ad aliena etiam sacra accederent, & in his publicè comessarentur. In omnibus autem istis maximè nocebat Christianæ professionis & Sacramentorum ecclesiæ fiducia, qua persuasi, illa ad salutem prorsus sufficere arbitrabantur. Ideo Paulus nuper similibus eorum, qui in stadio cursu aut lucta certant, adhuc proprio exemplo eos hortatus est, vt à Deo sibi propositum finem respiciant, & ad hunc tendant firmo atque constanti animi proposito. At quia vix quicquam sufficit ijs, qui se iam omnia assecutos esse sibipsis persuaserunt, mo do populi Israelitici exemplum subijcit, quod ita tractat, vt simul alia quoque Corinthiorum vitia perstringat, & in genere simul omnes admoneat, quid ipsis sit expectandum, nisi professioni suæ respondeant. Summa totius loci est, Israelitis nequaquam profuisse, quod populus Dei fuerunt, & salutis Sacramenta nobiscum communia habuerunt, sed horrendis exemplis fuisse extinctos, quod Deo inobedientes essent, & in suæ fidei professionem peccarent: hoc ipsum ergo omnibus euenturum esse, quotquot Christiani nominis professione ad suam licentiam abutuntur. Partes loci sunt duæ, de quibus ex ordine dicetur.
units.tr: Man is by nature slow to pursue true godliness. So if he makes some progress in it, he soon pleases himself and misuses to his own ruin the very things that ought to have helped him toward salvation. We have a clear example of this in the Corinthians. For although they had been well instructed by Paul and Apollos, and (as was said at the beginning of this letter) abounded in all knowledge and learning, they soon became over-confident. Neglecting the study of purer religion and of the Christian life, they began to busy themselves with useless things. This evil was followed by an abuse of Christian liberty, to such a degree that they went even to the rites of other religions and feasted publicly in them. In all this, the confidence they placed in their Christian profession and in the Sacraments of the Church did the greatest harm, for they were persuaded that these things were wholly sufficient for salvation. So Paul, comparing them to runners in the stadium or wrestlers in the contest, exhorted them by his own example to look to the goal set before them by God and to press toward it with a firm and steady resolve of mind. But because little can move those who have persuaded themselves that they have already attained everything, he sets before them the example of the people of Israel. He treats it in such a way that he also strikes at the other sins of the Corinthians, and at the same time warns them all in general what they may expect if they do not live up to their profession. The sum of the whole passage is this: the Israelites were in no way helped by being the people of God and by having the sacraments of salvation in common with us; rather, they were destroyed by dreadful examples because they were disobedient to God and sinned against their profession of faith. Therefore this same thing will befall all who abuse the name of Christian profession to indulge their own licence. The passage has two parts, which will be discussed in order.

units.la: Prima pars præoccupatione constat. Nam ne obijcerent, Iudaici populi exemplum nihil ad se pertinere, quorum præstantior fit conditio, quàm illorum, qui olim sub Mose vixerunt: initiò statim probat, nullum inter hos & ipsos discrimen esse, quando Israelitæ Dei ecclesia fuerint, & Sacramenta eadem nobiscum habuerint communia. Id verò multis & diligenter probat. Nec temere præfatiunculà vtitur: Nolim autem vos ignorare fratres. Nam ita scribendo innuit, ipsos nondum satis instructos esse in ijs, quæ imprimis scire oportebat. Accidit hoc fere omnibus, qui se præ aliis profecisse putant, & sua scientia insolentius gloriantur. Exemplum, quod huc probe conuenit hodie in Anabaptistis habemus, qui cùm multa garriant de vera ecclesia & eius sanctitate ecclesias item omnes temere damnent, tamen hominum omnium indoctissimi atque ineptissimi sunt, & imprimis istud prorsus ignorant, de quo hic agitur, & quod hominibus Christianis Apostolus minimè vult esse ignotum: Quæ nimirum olim Ecclesia fuerit, quæ item semper fuerit in terris Ecclesiæ conditio, qui denique ad eam pertineant, & quid maximè spectandum sit iis, qui Ecclesiæ vera membra censeri volunt? Quin eò usque istorum hominum audacia progreditur, ut nonnulli cum Manichæis totum Vetus testamentum damnare non erubescant, & hoc nihil ad nos pertinere vociferentur. Quid verò Paulus in præsenti? Nolim vos ignorare fratres, quòd patres nostri omnes sub illa nube fuerunt, &c. Et quibus hoc dicit? Toti nimirum Corinthiorum ecclesiæ, quæ maxima parte ex gentibus constabat: & horum patres vocat Israëlitas, qui sub Mose fuerunt. Unde verò hoc? Quia omnium creden-tium pater Abraham est, quem ideo Deus multarum gentium patrem fore dixit, quòd per eius semen omnibus gentibus benedictionem obuenire, & in eius fide omnes seruari oportuit. Quia verò credentium primi sunt Israëlitæ, qui secundùm carnem ex Abrahamo pro-geniti fuerunt, iidem nostri in fide antecessores, adeoque patres merito dicuntur. Uno igitur hoc titulo, perspicuè ostendit unam & eandem esse veteris & noui testamenti ecclesiam, neque eam diuelli posse, nisi patres à filijs diuellere libeat. Verumtamen eo non contentus, aliud argumentum subijcit à Sacramentis, quibus Ecclesia colligitur, cuius hæc summa est: Ubi eadem sunt Sacramenta & fides eadem, ibi eadem quoque est Ecclesia: Atqui Israëlitæ veteres eadem nobiscum Sacramenta communia, & fidem eandem nobiscum habuerunt: Ergo eadem est veteris & noui testamenti Ecclesia. Minorem probat diligenter, dum illorum Sacra-menta cum nostris Baptismo nimirum & Cœna Dominica confert, & rem eandem utrinque contineri demonstrat. At hic, ut de singulis loquatur, attentius nos videre conuenit.
units.tr: The first part consists of an anticipation of an objection. For lest they should object that the example of the Jewish people has nothing to do with them, since their condition is better than that of those who lived under Moses long ago, he proves at once that there is no difference between these and them, since the Israelites were the Church of God and had the same sacraments in common with us. He proves this at length and with care. Nor does he use this little preface carelessly: "Now I would not have you ignorant, brothers." For in writing thus he hints that they are not yet sufficiently taught in those things which they especially ought to know. This happens almost to everyone who thinks himself more advanced than others and boasts too arrogantly of his knowledge. We have an example of this today in the Anabaptists, who, although they chatter much about the true Church and its holiness, and rashly condemn all churches, are nonetheless the most unlearned and most incompetent of all men. Above all, they are utterly ignorant of the very matter under discussion here, which the Apostle does not wish to be unknown to Christians: what the Church was in former times, what has always been the condition of the Church on earth, who belong to it, and what those who wish to be counted true members of the Church should above all look to. Indeed, the audacity of these men goes so far that some, along with the Manichaeans, are not ashamed to condemn the whole Old Testament and loudly declare that it has nothing to do with us. But what does Paul say here? "Now I would not have you ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under that cloud," and so on. To whom does he say this? Surely to the whole church of the Corinthians, which consisted for the most part of Gentiles. And he calls the fathers of these people the Israelites who were under Moses. But on what basis? Because Abraham is the father of all believers, whom God therefore said would be the father of many nations, since through his seed the blessing had to come to all nations and all had to be saved by his faith. And since the first of the believers were the Israelites, who were descended from Abraham according to the flesh, they are rightly called our forefathers in faith, and so our fathers. By this single title, then, he clearly shows that the Church of the Old and New Testaments is one and the same, and that it cannot be torn apart unless one is willing to tear fathers away from sons. Yet not content with this, he adds a second argument from the sacraments, by which the Church is gathered. Its sum is this: where the sacraments are the same and the faith is the same, there the Church is also the same. But the ancient Israelites had the same sacraments in common with us and had the same faith as we do. Therefore the Church of the Old and New Testaments is the same. He proves the minor premise carefully, while he compares their sacraments with ours, namely Baptism and the Lord's Supper, and shows that the same thing is contained in both. But here, to speak of each in turn, it is fitting that we look more attentively.

units.la: De Baptismo sic ait: Patres nostri omnes sub illa nube fuerunt, & omnes per mare transfi-uerunt, & omnes in Mosem baptizati sunt in nube & in mari. Uni baptismo symbola duo tri-buit, nubem & mare: quia duo hæc simul coniuncta fuerunt, & eadem nostri baptismi mysteri-um plenè adumbrant. Quod ut rectius intelligamus, tenendum est in baptismo tria contineri: A-quam, quæ sanguinem Christi repræsentat: Verbum Dei, quo accedente (ut Augustinus dicit) ex elemento fit Sacramentum: & Gratia, quæ nobis in peccatorum remissione exhibetur. Atqui omnia ista in hoc transitu Israëlis[?] per mare rubrum est inuenire. Etenim mare aquam baptismi refert, & ipsæ etiam actiones sibi inuicem pulchrè respondent. Ut enim nos in baptismi son-tem tingimur & rursus ex eo educimur, ita Israëlitæ intra aquarum utrinque stantium alueum descendebant, & ex eodem rursus in continentem egrediebantur. Deinde non sine Dei Verbi-[?] studio fiebat: eo enim per mare iubebantur transire, & salus certa promittebatur. Nubes autem præsentia Dei symbolum erat, à qua eiusdem gratia abesse non poterat: quin tunc quoque huius egregia testimonia extiterunt. Ex nube enim illa ipsis loquebatur Dominus, eandem viam ducem habebant, adhæc ab æstu simul atque hostibus per illam defendebantur.
units.tr: Concerning Baptism he speaks thus: "All our fathers were under that cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea." To Baptism alone he assigns two symbols, the cloud and the sea, because these two were joined together and fully foreshadow the mystery of our Baptism. So that we may understand this more rightly, we must hold that three things are contained in Baptism: the water, which represents the blood of Christ; the Word of God, by whose addition (as Augustine says) the element becomes a sacrament; and the grace, which is offered to us in the forgiveness of sins. Now all of these can be found in that passage of Israel through the Red Sea. For the sea represents the water of Baptism, and the actions themselves correspond nicely to one another. For just as we are immersed in the water of Baptism and afterwards brought out of it, so the Israelites went down into the bed of the waters standing on either side, and from it they came out again onto dry land. Moreover, this was not done without the Word of God, for they were commanded to pass through the sea, and safety was promised with certainty. The cloud, however, was a symbol of God's presence, from which his grace could not be absent; indeed, at that time too there were outstanding witnesses to this. For the Lord spoke to them out of that cloud, they had it as their guide on the way, and besides, it protected them from the heat and at the same time from their enemies.

units.la: Quod si horum omnium usum amplius spectes, rursus omnia cum baptismo conuenire vide-bis. Primo enim (ut hic Paulus ait) baptizati sunt in Mosem, id est, ea conditione, ut Mosi obe-dirent, & ei crederent, quo Deus internuntio in Legis promulgatione usus est. At quia Lex in-star pædagogi fuit ad Christum deducentis, & Moses ipse Israëlitas ad magnum illum Prophetam remisit, quem Christum esse Apostoli testantur, nemo negauerit, veteres quoque in Christum fuisse baptizatos. Quod non oscitanter Eusebius observans, non hos modò, qui sub Mosis disciplina fuerunt, verumetiam patres quotquot iam inde ab Adamo ante Mosem vixere, reipsa Christianos fuisse scribit, licet nomen illud nondum in terris vulgatū fuerit. Deinde nubis illius usus erat, quòd Israëlitas iam maris alueum transituros ab Aegyptiis separabat, illis quidem lucem præbens, his autem tenebras horribiles ingerens. Similiter baptismus nos ab infidelibus distinguit. Tessera enim est, per quam in externam Ecclesiæ societatem adoptamur, & credentes quidem iucundissima gratia nobis in Christo factæ luce exhilarat, impijs verò nihil præter caliginem affert, cùm mysterii huius profunditatem videre non possint, interim tamen in conscientijs suis Christi iudicis minas atque terrores sentiant. Tertiò maris aquæ Aegyptios merserunt & præfocarunt, Israëlitas autem reddiderunt viuos & incolumes. Eadem ratione nos quoque in Christi mortem baptizamur, cuius virtus peccatum, mortem & diabolum absorbet & tollit, nos autem in vitam veram restituit. Quarto per mare transgressus[?] plenior institutio adhibita est, quando Legem suam Deus promulgauit, & eandem per Mosem prolixè & diligenter exposuit : Ita ex Christi mandato ijs, qui iam per baptismum in eius fidem initiati sunt, doctrina perfectior adhiberi consueuit. Et huc facit folenne illud Christi mandatum, quo apostolici muneris rationem & ordinem omnem complectens ait : Profecti μαθητεύσατε[?], id est, discipulos facite (hoc enim proprie vox Græca significat) omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomen Patris & Filij & Spiritus Sancti : docentes eos feruare omnia, quæ mandaui vobis. Primum vt sibi discipulos faciant iubet, quod fiebat, quando qui prius vel Iudaicas traditiones vel ethnicorum superstitiones, aut philosophorum placita secuti erant, Christum præceptorem agnoscere incipiebant. Et hæc mihi videtur causa fuisse, ob quam sub ecclesiæ initia credentes communi vocabulo discipuli dicti fuerunt. Hos deinde publicè per baptismum initiari oportebat, quo facto mox plenior totius doctrinæ tractatio sequebatur. Postremò, vt transitus ille per mare rubrum non vnquam repeti debuit, nubes autem toto illo peregrinationis tempore nunquâ ab ijs recessit, qui mare transierant : Ita neque baptismum iterari necesse est, quando sufficit semel in eius ecclesiæ societatem adoptatum esse, à qua Dei gratia nunquam recedit, & cui à Christo gratiæ istius Mediatore dictum est : Ecce ego vobiscum sum vsque ad consummationem sæculi. Hæc omnia si probè expendamus, fatebimur omnino veteres ea omnia habuisse, quæ nobis in baptismo nostro Christus offert.
units.tr: If you look more widely at the use of all these things, you will again see that everything agrees with Baptism. First, as Paul says here, they were baptized into Moses, that is, on the condition that they obeyed Moses and believed him, through whom God acted as mediator in the promulgation of the Law. But since the Law was like a tutor leading to Christ, and Moses himself sent the Israelites on to that great Prophet, whom the Apostles testify to be Christ, no one will deny that the ancients too were baptized into Christ. Eusebius observed this carefully and wrote that not only those who lived under the discipline of Moses, but also all the fathers who lived from Adam onward before Moses, were in fact Christians, although that name was not yet widely known on earth. Next, the use of that cloud was that it separated the Israelites from the Egyptians, who were about to cross the bed of the sea, giving light to the one and bringing dreadful darkness upon the others. In the same way, Baptism distinguishes us from unbelievers. For it is the token by which we are adopted into the outward fellowship of the Church, and it gladdens believers with the most delightful light of the grace made ours in Christ, but it brings nothing but darkness to the ungodly, who cannot see the depth of this mystery, yet in their consciences feel the threats and terrors of Christ as judge. Third, the waters of the sea drowned and suffocated the Egyptians, but they gave the Israelites back alive and unharmed. In the same way we too are baptized into the death of Christ, whose power swallows up and removes sin, death and the devil, and restores us to true life. Fourth, after the crossing of the Red Sea a fuller instruction was given, when God promulgated his Law and set it out at length and diligently through Moses. So by Christ's command, a more perfect teaching is usually given to those who have already been initiated into his faith through Baptism. And to this purpose serves that solemn command of Christ, in which, embracing the whole order and method of the apostolic office, he says: "Go and make disciples [μαθητεύσατε], that is, make disciples (for the Greek word signifies exactly this) of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you." First, he commands them to make disciples, which happened when those who had previously followed either Jewish traditions or the superstitions of the Gentiles, or the opinions of philosophers, began to acknowledge Christ as their teacher. And this, it seems to me, was the reason why in the early days of the Church believers were called by the common name of disciples. Then these had to be publicly initiated through Baptism, and once this was done, a fuller treatment of the whole doctrine followed at once. Lastly, just as that crossing of the Red Sea was never to be repeated, while the cloud never left those who had crossed the sea during the whole time of their journey, so Baptism need not be repeated, since it is enough to have been adopted once into the fellowship of that Church, from which the grace of God never departs, and to which Christ, the Mediator of that grace, has said: "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age." If we weigh all these things carefully, we shall acknowledge that the ancients had everything that Christ offers us in our Baptism.

units.la: Confutantur ergo his præcipui Anabaptistarum errores, quibus illi seducti circa baptismum tumultuari solent. Primus est, quo infantes à baptismo reijciunt, & eadem opera illos ab ecclesiæ societate excludunt. Negant vspiam in scripturis inueniri, quòd infantes baptizati sint. Quòd si eos locos obijcias, in quibus totas domus aut familias baptizatas fuisse scribitur, incertum esse clamant, num in illis infantes fuerint, & vt id euidentibus testimonijs probemus, à nobis petunt. Vbi vicissim nos ab illis requirere poteramus, vt infantes nullos in illis domibus fuisse demonstrarent : sed quia hoc agendo nullus contentionum finis esset, vt ad hunc locum nobis respondeant iubemus. Testatur Paulus olim in nube & mari baptizatos fuisse quotquot per mare rubrum euaserunt. Ita autem loquendo totam populi Israelitici multitudinem comprehendit, in qua viros & mulieres, senes, iuuenes & infantes tenellos nec multò ante natos fuisse nemo negauerit, nisi qui cum ratione insanire volet. Etenim à Pharaone interro-gatus Moses, qui nam abituri essent, respondit : Cum pueris nostris & cum senibus nostris ibimus, cum filijs nostris atque filiabus nostris, cum gregibus & armentis nostris ibimus. Et idem cum pecora in Aegypto relinqui vellet Pharao, diserte ait : Etiam pecora nostra ibunt nobiscum, non relinquetur vel vngula. Quis ergo infantes aut paruulos ab illis relictos fuisse suspicari posset? Quod si ergo illorum infantes tunc baptizati, & (vt in præsenti Apostolus testatur) nostri baptismi participes facti sunt, vanissimum vtique est Anabaptistarum commentum, qui infantes nullos vnquam baptizatos fuisse contendunt. Et si veterum infantes baptizari contigit in typo, etsi iam ante per Circumcisionem in populi Dei consortium allecti erant, quæ hæc iniquitas fuerit, Christianorum infantibus hanc gratiam in vniuersum negare?
units.tr: These, then, are the chief errors of the Anabaptists, by which they are usually led astray in their clamour about baptism, and they are refuted here. The first is that they reject infants from baptism and at the same time shut them out of fellowship in the Church. They deny that anywhere in Scripture it is found that infants were baptized. If you cite those passages in which whole households or families are written of as having been baptized, they cry out that it is uncertain whether infants were among them, and they ask us to prove it by clear testimonies. In turn we could demand that they show there were no infants in those households, but since such a course would have no end to the disputing, we bid them answer this passage. Paul testifies that long ago all who escaped through the Red Sea were baptized in the cloud and the sea. In saying this he embraces the whole multitude of the Israelite people, among whom no one would deny there were men and women, old men, young men, and tender infants, not long born, unless he wished to rave while still reasoning. Indeed, when Pharaoh asked Moses who would be leaving, Moses answered: "We will go with our young and our old, with our sons and our daughters, with our flocks and herds we will go." And when Pharaoh wished the cattle to be left behind in Egypt, Moses plainly said: "Our cattle too shall go with us; not a hoof shall be left behind." Who then could suppose that infants or little children were left behind by them? If, therefore, their infants were then baptized, and (as the Apostle testifies in this passage) were made partakers of our baptism, the invention of the Anabaptists, who contend that no infants were ever baptized, is utterly vain. And if the infants of the ancients were baptized in the type, even though they had already been admitted into the fellowship of God's people through circumcision, what unrighteousness would it be to deny this grace to the infants of Christians altogether?

units.la: Clamant illi. Neminem baptizandum esse, nisi qui fidei & salutis mysteria probè intelligat, & vitæ Christianæ professionem verè iam facere possit : alioqui cum baptismo fidem & religionem omnem prophanari. Est hic alter error, quo dum priorem confirmare volunt, suam ignorantiam magis produnt. In præsenti enim Israelitarum infantes baptizatos fuisse audimus, qui quid illic ageretur prorsus ignorabant. Imò adeò obscurè illud fiebat, vt ne adultiores quidem rem intelligerent. Et Christus ijs demùm diligentius omnia suæ doctrinæ capita tradere iubet, qui iam prius in nomen Patris & Filij & Spiritus Sancti baptizati sunt. Nec statim prophanantur Sacramenta & Dei dona, si quis mysterij ignaris illa adhibeat. Circucidebantur olim octauo à natali suo die Hebræorum masculi, nec ideo Circucisio prophanari dicebatur. Et in Euangelio puerulos quosdam ad Christum allatos fuisse legimus, vt illis manus imponeret et benè precaretur : quod discipulis quidem indignum visum fuit, tantum scilicet virū circa eos occupari, qui per ætatem nihil adhuc sapere poterant : sed ijdem à Christo obiurgantur, & sibi dici audiunt : Sinite paruulos ad me venire, talium enim est regnum Dei. Quis verò Christum preces suas & ipsam Dei gratiam hunc prophanauisse putabit? At nostri illi, dum gratiæ thesauros arctiori custodia concludunt, ne qui indigniores illis potiantur, eos magna ex parte euacuant, & draconis illius mihi similes videntur, quæ aurea Hesperidum mala custodiuisse Poetæ fabulantur: simul autem Nouatianorum errorem instaurant, qui pœnitentiam & gratiam Dei illis negabant, qui post acceptum baptismum labebantur.
units.tr: They cry out: no one ought to be baptized unless he understands well the mysteries of faith and salvation and is truly able already to make profession of the Christian life; otherwise faith and all religion are profaned by baptism. This is a second error, by which, while they wish to confirm the first, they reveal their ignorance all the more. For in the present passage we hear that the infants of the Israelites were baptized, who utterly did not know what was being done there. Indeed, it was done so obscurely that not even the older ones understood the matter. And Christ bids his doctrine's heads be delivered with greater care only to those who have already been baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Nor are the sacraments and gifts of God at once profaned if someone who is ignorant of the mystery uses them. Long ago the male Hebrews were circumcised on the eighth day after their birth, and circumcision was not on that account said to be profaned. And in the Gospel we read that some little children were brought to Christ, that he might lay hands on them and bless them. This seemed unworthy to the disciples, that so great a man should be occupied with those who by their age could not yet understand anything; but these same disciples are rebuked by Christ and hear it said to them: "Suffer the little children to come to me, for of such is the kingdom of God." Who indeed would think that Christ profaned his prayers and God's very grace by this? But those men, while they shut up the treasures of grace in a tighter guard, so that none who are less worthy may possess them, largely empty them out, and they seem to me like that dragon which the poets fable guarded the golden apples of the Hesperides. At the same time they renew the error of the Novatians, who denied repentance and God's grace to those who fell after receiving baptism.

units.la: Nascitur ex his tertius error, quo baptismum iterant in ijs, qui in infantia tincti sunt: eo quòd id præter rationem fit factum, & proinde indignum sit, quòd baptismi loco habeatur. At hùc quoque errorem typus ille confutat, vt iam de Circumcisione nihil dicamus, quæ in puerulis semel facta per omnem vitam sufficiebat, vt eam ne in ijs quidem repeti opus esset, qui scelerib. atrocissimis interdum polluebantur. Et cur non sufficiat semel adscriptum esse in ecclesiæ album, quando Dei gratiam ab illa nunquam discedere constat, neque Christus, qui oues suas omnes nouit, easdè manibus suis eripi finit? Isti ergo, dum Baptismi vindices haberi volunt, & hunc turpiter prophanant, & simul Christi merito multum derogant. Poterant de his multa alia quoque dici, sed hæc pijs modo sufficiunt.
units.tr: From these a third error arises, by which they repeat baptism in those who were washed in infancy, on the ground that this was done without reason and is therefore unworthy to be counted as baptism. But that type also refutes this error. Let us say nothing now about circumcision, which, once performed on little boys, sufficed for their whole life, so that there was no need for it to be repeated even in those who were sometimes defiled by the most atrocious crimes. And why should it not suffice to have been once enrolled in the register of the Church, since it is certain that God's grace never departs from that Church, and Christ, who knows all his sheep, does not allow them to be snatched from his hands? Therefore these men, while they wish to be thought the champions of baptism, both shamefully profane it and at the same time greatly detract from the merit of Christ. Many other things could be said about these matters, but these suffice for the godly.

units.la: Pergamus ergo in Apostoli verbis, qui patribus Cænam mysticam quoque applicat, dicens: Et omnes eandem escam spiritualem ederunt, & omnes eundem potum spiritualem biberunt: Bibebant enim ex spirituali, quæ ipsos sequebatur, petra, &c. Per escam Manna intelligit, quod Christi typum fuisse mox demonstrabitur. Neq; tamen Paulus illi contradicit, qui patres in deserto verum illum panem cœlestem comedisse negat. Nam apud Ioannem Iudæos de Manna crasse vt de cibo corporis locutos fuisse constat, neque in illo aliquid sublimius spectauisse. Ideo illorum sensui[?] sese accōmodans Christus, illud ita consideratum nihil ad salutem profuisse docet. At Paulus ad typum respicit, & de illo loquitur, sicuti à Deo ordinatum erat, vt nimirum panem verum vita referret, mentes illorum in venturi seruatoris contemplatione eueheret, & fidem confirmaret. Quum[?] usum si consideres, videbis in illo omnia contineri, quæ nobis in CHRISTO IESV per Cænæ Dominicæ panè mysticam repræsentantur. Quod D. Ambrosius obseruans scripsit, iftafiguram futuri mysterij habuisse, quod nunc nos sumimus in commemoratione Christi Domini.
units.tr: Let us go on, then, with the words of the Apostle, who also applies the mystical Supper to the fathers, saying: "And all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank of the spiritual rock that followed them, etc." By the food he means the manna, which will shortly be shown to have been a type of Christ. Yet Paul does not contradict that other passage, in which he denies that the fathers in the wilderness ate the true heavenly bread. For it is clear that in John the Jews spoke of the manna in a crude way, as of bodily food, and looked for nothing more sublime in it. Therefore Christ, accommodating himself to their understanding, teaches that eating it in that considered sense profited them nothing for salvation. But Paul looks to the type and speaks of it as it had been ordained by God: namely, that it might represent the true bread of life, lift their minds to contemplation of the Saviour who was to come, and confirm their faith. If you consider its use, you will see that all those things are contained in it which are set before us in CHRIST JESUS through the mystical bread of the Lord's Supper. St. Ambrose, observing this, wrote that this figure had the same mystery that we now partake of in remembrance of the Lord Christ.

units.la: Et sanè iucunda est admodum collatio, si quæ in Manna contigerunt cum Christo conferantur. Illud gratuitum Dei donum erat, et absq; omni Israelitarum labore aut studio dabatur: Ita Christus nobis ex gratia datus est nullo interueniente nostræ dignitatis aut nostrorum meritorum respectu. Manna de cælo pluebat, & non sine miraculo: Ita Christus è cœlis in terras descendit, & miraculosè carnem humanam ex Virginis castissimæ & intemeratæ semine assumpsit, vt nostèr cibus fieret. Manna prius mundo ignotum fuit: ita Christum prius omnes ignorauerunt, & tam præsente nemo agnouit, nisi quibus illum Pater manifestare dignatus est. Manna æquali & sufficienti mensura omnibus distribuebatur: sic Christus ex æquo ad omnes credentes pertinet, & omnibus ad salutem sufficit absq; omni personarum respectu. Manna varios et iucundos sapores habuit: ita Christus omnibus sapit, qui ipsum fide vera apprehendunt, & in omni tentatione eosdem mirificè exhilarat. Manna colore candidum & quoad materiam aut substantiam omnem purissimum erat: Ita Christus absque omni labe aut macula peccati homo factus est, neque inuentus est dolus in ore eius. Manna contundi & conteri solebat, vt cibus fieret: Ita Christus in cruce carnem suam pro mundi vita dedit, vt panis vitæ nobis esset. Manna toto illo tempore datum fuit, quo Israelitæ per desertum peregrinati sunt: Ita Christus quoad in hoc sæculo peregrinamur, nos pascit & seruat. Manna cessauit, quàm primùm traiecto Iordane in terram promissam Israelitæ venerunt: Ita vbi patriam cœlestem attigerimus, tunc Sacramentorum vsus & quæcunque nunc in Christo habemus fidei adminicula cessabunt, eò quòd ijs minimè opus erit amplius, quando Dominum facie ad faciem videbimus, & in eius vultu (vt Dauid ait) omni bonorum satietate fruemur. Vides ergo non temere dici à Paulo, patres eandem nobiscum escam spiritualem comedisse. Nam vt Manna Christum adumbrauit, ita hunc verè ederunt, quotquot promissiones Dei de illo datas fide vera amplexi sunt.
units.tr: And indeed the comparison is very pleasant if we set beside Christ what happened with the manna. That was a free gift of God and was given without any labour or effort on the part of the Israelites; so Christ has been given to us from grace, with no regard to our worthiness or our merits. The manna rained down from heaven, and not without a miracle; so Christ came down from heaven to earth and miraculously took on human flesh from the seed of the most chaste and undefiled Virgin, that he might become our food. The manna was unknown to the world before; so before, all people did not know Christ, and even when he was present no one recognized him except those whom the Father deigned to reveal him to. The manna was distributed to all in an equal and sufficient measure; so Christ belongs equally to all believers, and is sufficient for the salvation of all without any respect of persons. The manna had various and pleasant tastes; so Christ tastes sweet to all who lay hold of him by true faith, and wonderfully gladdens them in every temptation. The manna was white in colour and in its matter and substance most pure; so Christ was made man without any stain or blemish of sin, and "no guile was found in his mouth." The manna was ground and crushed, that it might become food; so Christ on the cross gave his flesh for the life of the world, that he might be the bread of life for us. The manna was given during the whole time that the Israelites wandered through the desert; so as long as we are pilgrims in this age, Christ feeds and preserves us. The manna ceased as soon as the Israelites, having crossed the Jordan, came into the promised land; so when we reach our heavenly homeland, then the use of the sacraments and all the supports of faith that we now have in Christ will cease, because we shall no longer need them when we see the Lord face to face and, in his countenance (as David says), enjoy the fullness of all good things. You see, therefore, that it is not rashly said by Paul that the fathers ate the same spiritual food as we do. For just as the manna foreshadowed Christ, so all who embraced by true faith the promises of God concerning him truly ate him.

units.la: Porrò ne quid illis defuisse putemus, potum quoque eundem illos nobiscum communem habuisse ait, & expositionis loco subjicit: Bibebant enim ex spirituali, quæ ipsos sequebatur, petra: Petra verò erat Christus, id est, Christum referebat, & eius erat figura siue typus. Historia habetur in Exod.cap.17. & in lib. Num.cap.20. Paulus autem petram illam Israelitas secutam aut comita-tam fuisse scribit: nimirum quod riuus aquarum ex illa manantium toto illo tempore castra eorum secutus fuerit. Ita enim fieri oportebat, cum totum illud desertum neq; fluuios neq; fontes haberet, qui tantae hominum atq; iumentorum pecorumue multitudini sufficerent. Caeterum hic quoq; omnia cum Christo & salutis per hunc nobis exhibita beneficio optimè conueniunt. Primo enim petra Christi typus est, quo scriptura saepe utitur. Dauid certè eum lapidem dicit, qui etsi ab aedificanti-bus reprobatus esset, factus tamen sit caput anguli. Apud Isaiam verò scribitur: Ecce ego fundo in Zion lapidem, lapidem probationis, angularem, pretiosum, solidissimum fundamentum, & qui credit in eum non pudefiet. Et ipse Christus de seipso dicit: Super hanc petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam, & portae inferorum non praevalebunt aduersus eam. Rectè igitur Paulus petram hanc Christi fuisse scribit. At petram percuti oportuit, ut aperto quasi vulnere aquas profunderet: ita Christus in cruce vulneratus sanguinem profudit, quo solo astuantium conscientiarum sitis restingui-tur. Et huc imprimis pertinet, quod Ioannes testatur, ex mortui latere, cum hoc quidam lancea perfodisset, sanguinem & aquam profluxisse. Ut autem riuus ex petra emanans toti Israelitarum mul-titudini sufficere potuit: ita unius Christi sanguis omnibus ad salutem sufficit, qui ex eo bibunt per fidem veram. Et ut non opus fuit petram illam quotidie percuti, eo quod semel aperta iugi & indefinenti aquarum scaturigine omnes recreabat: Ita Christus semel mortuus nos assiduè recreat, neq; ut iterum moriatur, aut saepius immoletur necesse est. Deniq; ut petra illa populum quasi comitabatur, & quocunq; illos vocabat Deus, aquas praebebat largissimas: Ita Christus nobis per omnem vitam dux comesq; est, neq; unquam eos suae mortis fructu destituit, qui in Patris sui vocatione ambulant. Ut autem in Manna Christum perceperunt Moses, Aaron, Mariam, Iosue, Chaleb, & quicunq; alij in promissionem Dei cum fide respexere: ita in aquis illis ijdem sanguinis quoq; Christi participes facti sunt, & proinde eundem potum spiritualem nobiscum bibisse dicuntur. Priusquam verò ad id accedamus, cuius causa haec Paulus adducit, quaedam hic nobis considerandae sunt, quae ad fidei nostrae institutionem plurimum faciunt.
