units.tr: Moreover, lest we think they lacked anything, he says they also had the same drink in common with us, and by way of explanation he adds: "For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; the rock was Christ," that is, it represented Christ and was his figure or type. The story is found in Exodus chapter 17 and Numbers chapter 20. Paul writes that the Israelites were followed, or accompanied, by that rock, namely that a stream of water flowing from it followed their camp for the whole of that time. This had to happen, since the whole desert had neither rivers nor springs sufficient for such a multitude of people, beasts and cattle. Moreover, here too everything agrees well with Christ and with the salvation offered to us through him. First, the rock is a type of Christ, and Scripture often uses it in this way. David certainly calls him the stone which, though rejected by the builders, has become the head of the corner. In Isaiah it is written: "Behold, I lay in Zion a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a most sure foundation, and he who believes in him will not be put to shame." And Christ himself says of himself: "Upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." Paul therefore rightly writes that this rock was Christ. But the rock had to be struck, so that it would pour out water as from an open wound; so Christ, wounded on the cross, poured out blood, by which alone the thirst of troubled consciences is quenched. To this belongs above all what John testifies: that when a certain man pierced the side of the dead Christ with a spear, blood and water flowed out. Just as the stream issuing from the rock could suffice for the whole multitude of Israelites, so the blood of Christ alone suffices for salvation for all who drink from it through true faith. And just as there was no need for that rock to be struck every day, since once opened it refreshed them all with a constant and unfailing gush of water, so Christ, having died once, refreshes us continually, and it is not necessary for him to die again or be sacrificed more often. Finally, just as that rock accompanied the people, and gave abundant water wherever God called them, so Christ is our leader and companion throughout our whole life, and never deprives of the fruit of his death those who walk in the calling of their Father. Just as Moses, Aaron, Miriam, Joshua, Caleb, and all others who looked with faith to the promise of God, perceived Christ in the manna, so in those waters they too became partakers of the blood of Christ, and therefore they are said to have drunk the same spiritual drink as we do. But before we come to that for the sake of which Paul brings this forward, certain matters must be considered here which contribute greatly to the instruction of our faith.

units.la: Inter quae primum occurrit, unam & eandem esse Veteris & Noui testamenti ecclesiam, quam in Symbolo apostolico Catholicam dicimus, non solùm quod omnium gentium atq; locorum cre-dentes comprehendit, verumetiam quod ad omnia saecula tam elapsa, quam praesentia & futura extenditur. Ad hanc enim pertinent Adam & Eua, quibus prima promissio data fuit, & quotquot promissioni huic ante natum Christum crediderunt. Eiusdem etiam ecclesiae membra erunt, quotquot in posterum credent usq; ad consummationem saeculi huius. Et haec verè dici, res ipsa indicat. Una enim eademque salutis ratio in Veteri & Noui testamento traditur: ea nimirum, quae in CHRISTO IESV habetur, qui semen illud mulieris est, cuius virtute & merito caput serpentis conteri oportuit. Et ut in utroq; illo unus praedicatur: ita eundem tam veteribus quam nouis Sacramentis adumbrari & proponi modo audiuimus. Adhaec una & eadem est utriq; salutis percipiendae via & ratio: fides nimirum, qua sola Christus apprehenditur, ut nobis salutifer fiat. Adde, quod ad eiusdem regni haereditatem omnes vocamur, ut nimirum in coelis accumbamus cum Abrahamo, Isaaco & Iacobo. Neq; hic eos audire conuenit, qui dum pro corporali carnis Christi manducatione contendunt, nostris Sacramentis plus quiddam contineri, & ipsam Christi carnem in illis realiter & substantialiter exhiberi atq; ore etiam accipi & manducari aiunt. Est enim hoc vanissimum effugium. Nam etsi in Nouo testamento magis perspicua fit salutis ratio, eo quod umbris sublatis Veritas nobis in Christi incarnatione & morte exhibita fit, quoad tamen fa-lutem ipsam mutatio nulla facta est, neque nobis quoad rationem salutis plus tribuere possumus, quando Paulus Patres nobiscum eandem escam[?] spiritualem comedisse, & eundem potum spiritualem bibisse scribit. Et eodem pertinet, quod Christus in Apocalypsi agnus dicitur, qui im-molatus sit ab origine mundi. Cuius dicti non alia ratio affingi potest, quam quod sacrificij in ara crucis facti virtus ad primos usque parentes extensa fuit, qui illud fide amplexi & eius merito seruati sunt. Et haec causa fuit, quod cum Christo clarificationis suae specimen discipulis exhibente visi sunt Moses & Elias. Ita enim testari ille voluit, se eum esse, quem olim Lex & Prophetæ omnes prædicarint. Elucet in hac fidei Christianæ vetustas, dignitas, veritas, & in hac nostra etiam salutis certitudo: & simul patet, quàm atroci iniuria nomen Christianum afficiat, qui hodie vetus Testamentum nihil ad nos pertinere vociferantur. Eo enim commento novi quoq; Testamenti veritatem convellunt, Christi meritum contrahunt, & nobis dulcissimam illam communionem negant, quæ credentibus omnibus cum sanctissimis Patribus intercedit.
units.tr: Among these, the first to present itself is that the Church of the Old and of the New Testament is one and the same, which we call Catholic in the Apostles' Creed, not only because it embraces believers of all nations and places, but also because it extends to all ages, past, present and future. For to this Church belong Adam and Eve, to whom the first promise was given, and all who believed that promise before Christ was born. Those too will be members of the same Church who will believe in the future, until the end of this age. That these things are rightly said, the matter itself makes clear. For one and the same way of salvation is taught in the Old and the New Testament, namely that which is found in CHRIST JESUS who is the seed of the woman, by whose power and merit the head of the serpent had to be crushed. And as in both Testaments one Christ is preached, so, as we have just heard, the same Christ is foreshadowed and set forth by the sacraments of both the old and the new. Besides, there is one and the same way and method of receiving salvation for both: namely faith, by which alone Christ is laid hold of so that he becomes saving for us. Add to this that all are called to the inheritance of the same kingdom, so that we may recline in heaven with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Nor is it fitting here to listen to those who, while they contend for a bodily eating of the flesh of Christ, say that more is contained in our sacraments, and that the flesh of Christ itself is really and substantially exhibited in them, and is also received and eaten with the mouth. For this is a most vain refuge. For although the way of salvation is made clearer in the New Testament, because with the shadows removed the truth has been shown to us in the incarnation and death of Christ, nevertheless no change has been made as regards salvation itself, and we cannot attribute to ourselves more in respect of the way of salvation, since Paul writes that the fathers ate the same spiritual food with us and drank the same spiritual drink. To the same point belongs what Christ is called in the Apocalypse, the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world. No other explanation of this saying can be devised except that the power of the sacrifice made on the altar of the cross extended back even to our first parents, who embraced it by faith and were saved by its merit. And this was the reason why Moses and Elias appeared with Christ, when he showed his disciples a sample of his glory. For he wished thereby to testify that he is the one whom the Law and all the Prophets had foretold. In this the antiquity, dignity and truth of the Christian faith shine forth, and in it also the certainty of our own salvation; and at the same time it is evident how atrociously those who today loudly declare that the Old Testament has nothing to do with us wrong the Christian name. For by this device they also undermine the truth of the New Testament, diminish the merit of Christ, and deny us that most sweet communion which exists between all believers and the most holy Fathers.

units.la: Deinde observabis hoc loco, Paulum communionis & societatis huius argumentum ex Sacramentis petere. Patres enim nobis socios & eiusdem Ecclesiæ nobiscum membra esse docet, quia ijsdem nobiscum Sacramentis vsi sint. Et vt hic illis Baptismum & Cænam Dominicam tribuit: ita nobis alibi illorum Sacramenta applicat, quando nos in Christo circumcisos esse ait circumcisione, quæ fit sine manibus: quando item Christum nostrum pascha esse docet, & azymorum meminit, quibus nos quoque festum agere iubet. Et ad Hebræos scribens, nos altare etiam habere testatur, Christum intelligens, in cuius nomine orantes exaudimur. Admonent nos ista, Ecclesiam per Sacramenta colligi, & ijsdem ab aliarum sectarum hominibus discerni. Est hoc omnium sæculorum exemplis probatum, vt multa demonstratione non sit opus. Ex eo autem discimus, nequaquam contemni debere Sacramenta & quæ his coniuncta sunt religionis exercitia, Vt enim illis externa Ecclesia colligitur: ita ab huius societate sese alienant, quotquot illa per contemptum negligunt, aut impiè prophanant. Ideo olim mortis supplicium minatus est Deus iis, qui vel circumcisionem negligebant, vel paschale epulum sive festum fermento adhibito polluebant. Quòd si autem ea tanto studio observari voluit, quæ ad tempus correctionis solum durare debebant, quis non videat quanta religione nobis circa ea sit versandum, quæ mutationem nullam admittent, quoad mundus hic steterit? Rursus etiam hic Anabaptistarum temeritas confutatur, qui Ecclesias Christi esse negant in nostrorum cœtibus, etiamsi ordinaria illic sit Verbi prædicatio, & Sacramenta legitimè administrentur. Causa erroris est, quòd in solos mores hominum intenti, ta [?] negligunt, quibus ad Ecclesiæ suæ collectionem atque conseruationem Deus vitur [?]. Fatemur equidem Christianos non esse, nisi qui Christianè viuunt: Verùmtamen Christianum non vita facit, sed fides: quæ cum nobis ex Dei Verbo obtingat, & Sacramentorum vsu confirmetur, nimium temerarij sunt, qui Ecclesiam esse negant, vbi & Verbo Dei locus datur, & Sacramenta secundum Christi institutionem vsurpantur. Nec est quod eos illi nobis obiciant, qui professioni suæ minus respondent. Ferent hi suum iudicium, non autem pijs fraudi erit ipsorum improbitas: vt neque Mosi, Iosuæ, Chalebo, & horum similibus obfuit aliorum Israelitarum nequitia, qui Ecclesiæ quidem externæ admixti fuerunt, Symbolis autem & sacris omnibus turpiter abusi sunt.
units.tr: Next, you will observe in this passage that Paul draws the argument for this communion and fellowship from the sacraments. For he teaches that the Fathers are our companions and members of the same Church with us, because they used the same sacraments as we do. And just as here he ascribes to them Baptism and the Lord's Supper, so elsewhere he applies to us their sacraments, when he says that we have been circumcised in Christ with a circumcision not made with hands; when he likewise teaches that Christ is our Passover, and speaks of unleavened bread, with which he also bids us keep the feast. And writing to the Hebrews, he testifies that we also have an altar, meaning Christ, in whose name we are heard when we pray. These things remind us that the Church is gathered together through the sacraments and is distinguished by them from the people of other sects. This has been proved by the examples of all ages, so that no lengthy demonstration is needed. From this we learn that the sacraments, and the religious exercises joined to them, must by no means be despised. For just as the external Church is gathered by these, so all who neglect them through contempt, or impiously profane them, estrange themselves from its fellowship. Therefore God once threatened with the punishment of death those who either neglected circumcision or polluted the Passover meal or feast by using leaven. But if God wished these things to be observed with such zeal, which were meant to last only for a time of correction, who does not see with how great reverence we ought to treat those things which will admit of no change for as long as this world stands? Again, here the rashness of the Anabaptists is refuted, who deny that there are Churches of Christ among our assemblies, even though the ordinary preaching of the Word takes place there and the sacraments are lawfully administered. The cause of their error is that, being intent only upon the morals of men, they neglect those means by which God gathers and preserves his Church. We indeed grant that those are not Christians except those who live as Christians; but it is not life that makes a Christian, but faith, which is given to us from the Word of God and is confirmed by the use of the sacraments. Those are too rash who deny that there is a Church where the Word of God has its place and the sacraments are used according to the institution of Christ. Nor is there any reason why they should throw in our faces those who fall short of their profession. Such people will bear their own judgment, and the wickedness of these persons will not be a hindrance to the godly, just as the wickedness of other Israelites did not harm Moses, Joshua, Caleb and others like them, who were indeed mixed with the external Church but shamefully abused the symbols and all the sacred things.

units.la: Postremò non debent oscitanter prætereri locutiones, quibus veteres eandem escam spiritualem nobiscum edisse, & eundem potum spiritalem nobiscum bibisse dicit Paulus. Hæc enim docent, Sacramenta non esse vacua aut inania signa, quorum non alius vsus fit, quàm vt externæ professioni seruiant. Non enim ludit nobiscum Deus, & quia hæc suarum promissionum sigilla sunt (sicuti de circumcisione dicitur) veritas ab illis abesse non potest. Et cùm olim cum symbolis Christus coniunctus fuerit, adeoq; supra petram steterit (vt eius verba ad Mosem testantur) nefas fuit eum à Baptismo & Cœna mystica excludere. Quomodo enim in baptismo peccatorum ablutio & regenerationis beneficium obsignabitur, si hæc nusquam adsunt? Aut qua ratione Christi Cœna dicetur, si is nteque [?] præsens adest, neque nos pascit & alit? At hic meminerimus oportet, cibum & potum hunc spiritualem esse, & proinde spiritualiter quoque manducari & bibi. Vt enim quæ visibilia sunt solo visu, audibilia solo auditu, palpabilia tactu percipiuntur: ita spiritualem cibum & potum non aliter quàm spiritu apprehendere poteris, cuius os fides est. Quod D. Augustinus obseruans, de carnis Christi manducatione dicebat: Quid paras dentes & ventrem? crede, & manducasti. Quam sententiam ipse Dominus tota illa disputatione confirmat, quæ Ioan. sexto Capiti describitur. Et si ergo Christum à Sacramentis suis & legitimo eorum vsu non abesse dixerimus, non tamen vel præsentia corporalis, vel inclusio aliqua localis fingi debet. Fidei enim præsens est, quæ animum supra cœlos euehens illum apprehendit vbi reuera est, non autem illic, vbi vana hominum superstitiosorum persuasio illi locum aut domicilium finxit. Et cur alicui mirum videatur, Christi corpus & sanguinem, etsi in cœlis maneant, à nobis tamen in terra agentibus per fidem vere manducari & bibi, quando visus & auditus ea percipiunt, adeoq; nobis præsentia sistunt, quæ magno locorum interuallo à nobis distant? Quid autem de memoria & imaginatione dicemus, quæ non modò omnem loci distantiam superant, sed ea quoq; concipiunt, quæ multorum seculorum se-riis à nobis quàm longißimè remouit? Num ergo corporeis sensibus imbecilliorem esse dicemus fidem, quæ vt incomparabile Dei donum est, ita omnem hominis intellectum longè transgreditur? Et hæc causa est, quòd signis fere rei significatæ nomina tribuuntur, neq; statim Christum mendacij arguunt, qui localem aut corpoream eius cum signis coniunctionem negant. Sed quia de his plura alibi dicenda erunt, in præsenti ista sufficiant.
units.tr: Finally, we must not carelessly pass over the expressions by which Paul says that the fathers ate the same spiritual food with us and drank the same spiritual drink. For these teach that the sacraments are not empty or meaningless signs, whose only use is to serve an outward profession. God does not mock us, and since these are seals of his promises (as is said of circumcision), truth cannot be absent from them. And since Christ was once joined with the symbols, and indeed stood upon the rock (as his words concerning Moses bear witness), it would be wrong to exclude him from Baptism and the mystical Supper. For how would the washing away of sins and the benefit of regeneration be sealed in baptism, if these were nowhere present? Or on what ground would it be called the Lord's Supper, if he is neither present nor feeds and nourishes us? But here we must remember that this food and drink is spiritual, and therefore is also eaten and drunk spiritually. For just as things that are visible are perceived by sight alone, audible things by hearing alone, and tangible things by touch, so you can grasp spiritual food and drink in no other way than by the spirit, whose mouth is faith. Augustine, observing this, said of eating the flesh of Christ: "Why do you prepare teeth and belly? Believe, and you have eaten." The Lord himself confirms this opinion throughout that whole discourse which is described in John chapter 6. So if we say that Christ is not absent from his sacraments and their lawful use, neither bodily presence nor any local enclosure ought to be imagined. For it is faith that is present, which, lifting the mind above the heavens, apprehends him where he truly is, and not there, where the vain persuasion of superstitious men has fashioned a place or dwelling for him. And why should it seem strange to anyone that the body and blood of Christ, though they remain in heaven, are nonetheless truly eaten and drunk through faith by us who are living on earth? Sight and hearing perceive things and present to us what is far distant from us across a great interval of place. What then shall we say of memory and imagination, which not only overcome every distance of place but also conceive those things which a long series of many ages has removed far from us? Shall we say, then, that faith is weaker than the bodily senses, when it is an incomparable gift of God and so far surpasses all human understanding? And this is why the names of the things signified are commonly given to the signs, and why those who deny that Christ is joined to the signs locally or bodily do not at once charge him with lying. But since these matters must be discussed more fully elsewhere, let these remarks suffice for the present.

units.la: Restat, vt Pauli institutum aut scopum videamus, ad quem ista omnia diriguntur. Est vs, quòd veteribus nihil profuerit eorundem Sacramentorum communicatio. Id vero his verbis enuntiat. Sed plerosq; eorum non approbauit Deus, id est, non placuerunt Deo, quamuis hæc omnia habe-rent. Confirmat autem hoc dictu argumento ex reipsa petito, dicens: Prostrati sunt enim in deserto. Videtur autem hoc ex Christi verbis desumptum, qui Iudæis patrum exemplo gloriantibus dicebat: Patres vestri comederunt Manna in deserto, & mortui sunt. Loquitur autem non de morte naturali, quæ omnes homines manet: sed de eo, quod propter incredulitatem & contumaciam ab irato Deo deleti & extincti sint. Quod variis modis factum esse scimus. Alij enim hostili gladio ceciderunt, alios cœlitus immissus ignis absumpsit, multos lues sustulit, fuerunt ite quibus terra debiscens viuos deglutijt, alij à serpentibus occisi sunt. Deniq; pluribus & grauioribus plagis afflicti sunt, quàm Ægyptij: ex quorum tyrannide paulo ante liberati fuerant: & præter Iosuam atque Chalebum nemo eorum, qui Ægyptum reliquerant, in terra promissa possessionem venit. Ex his autem colligit Paulus, neq; nos saluos fore propter externam fidei professionem & Sacramentorum Ecclesiæ vsum, si non simul procul relictis superstitionibus vitam viuamus Christiana professione dignam. Et huc pertinet quod in epistola ad Romanos de naturalibus ramis ob incredulitatem defractis dicitur: quorum exemplo similiter probat, multo minus nobis parsurum esse Deum, si qui ex singulari gratia in oleam illam Ecclesiæ insiti sumus, Iudaici populi mores imitemur. Sed plura de his infra dicentur. Nunc omnium istorum hic nobis vsus esto, vt Dei beneficia agnoscamus, pro illis gratissimus, & non efferamur inani professionis externæ confidentia: sed fide syncera & constanti apprehendamus salutis omnis authorem, IESVM CHRISTVM, qui solus in huius vitæ peregrinatione non minus periculosa quàm laborum plena nos deducere, pascere & tueri potest, donec in cœlestis patriæ hæreditatem admissi cum eodem æternum viuamus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: It remains for us to see Paul's purpose or aim, toward which all these things are directed. It is this: the communion of these same sacraments profited the ancients nothing. He states this in these words: "But with most of them God was not well pleased," that is, they were not pleasing to God, although they had all these things. He confirms this statement with an argument drawn from the fact itself, saying: "For they were overthrown in the wilderness." This seems to be taken from the words of Christ, who said to the Jews, who boasted of the example of their fathers: "Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness, and they died." He speaks not of natural death, which awaits all men, but of those who, on account of unbelief and obstinacy, were destroyed and cut off by an angry God. We know that this happened in various ways. Some fell by the enemy's sword, others were consumed by fire sent from heaven, many were carried off by plague, some were swallowed alive when the earth opened, others were killed by serpents. Finally, they were afflicted with more numerous and grievous plagues than the Egyptians, from whose tyranny they had been freed shortly before; and apart from Joshua and Caleb, none of those who had left Egypt came into possession of the promised land. From these examples Paul concludes that we also will not be saved on account of an outward profession of faith and the use of the Church's sacraments, unless, having put aside superstitions, we also live a life worthy of the Christian profession. To this belongs also what is said in the epistle to the Romans about the natural branches broken off because of unbelief; by this example he similarly proves that God will spare us much less, if we who have been grafted into that olive of the Church by singular grace imitate the ways of the Jewish people. But more will be said about these matters below. For now, let us make this use of all these things: that we acknowledge God's benefits and be grateful for them, and not be puffed up with empty confidence in an outward profession, but with sincere and constant faith lay hold of Jesus Christ, the author of all salvation, who alone can lead us, feed us and keep us in the pilgrimage of this life, no less dangerous than it is full of toil, until, admitted to the inheritance of the heavenly fatherland, we live eternally with him. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA L.
units.tr: Homily L.

units.la: Hæc autem typi nostri fuerunt, vt ne concupiscamus res malas, sicut illi concupierunt: Neq; idololatræ sitis, sicut quidam eorum, vt scriptum est: Sedit populus ad edendum ac bibendum, ac surrexerunt ad ludendum: Neq; scortemur, sicut quidam eorum scortati sunt, & ceciderunt vno die viginti tria millia: Neque tentemus Christum, sicut quidam eorum tentarunt, & à serpentibus perierunt: Neq; murmurate, sicut quidam eorum murmurarunt, & perierunt ab Exterminatore.
units.tr: Now these things were our types, so that we should not lust after evil things, as they also lusted. Neither be idolaters, as some of them were; as it is written: "The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play." Neither let us commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication, and fell in one day twenty-three thousand. Neither let us tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him, and were destroyed by serpents. Neither murmur, as some of them murmured, and were destroyed by the Destroyer.

units.la: Spiritus sanctus in scripturis non modo fideliter & perspicuè tradit veræ fidei & vitæ morūmque præcepta, sed eadem exemplis quoq; variis illustrat & confirmat, tam piorum qui illis obsecuti Deo placuerunt, quàm impiorum qui his neglectis Dei iram prouocarunt, & grauiter mulctati sunt. Est hoc nobis non vtile modo, verumetiam necessarium propter ingenij nostri tarditatem, qua fit, vt aut non intelligamus ea quæ Deus præcipit, aut ijs non habeamus fidem quæ ab illo nobis dicuntur. Hoc ipsum ergo Paulus in præsenti tractatione de idolothytis diligēter obseruat: Et quia pleriq; Corinthiorum Christiani nominis professionem & externum Sacramentorum Ec-clesiae vsum sufficere putabant, ex eo autem sibi ipsis persuadebant, non multum peccare eos, qui amicitia & pacis colendae ergo alienis etiam sacris communicant: veteris Ecclesiae, id est, Israelitarum ex-emplis errorem istum confutat. Offendit enim illos olim eiusdem fidei professionem & eadem Sacramenta nobiscum communia habuisse, veruntamen non placuisse Deo, sed miserabiliter in deserto perijsse, eo quod professioni suae minus responderint. Inde vero Corinthios colligere vult, quod neq; ipsi feruadi sint, etiamsi Christum in Verbo suo loquentem & in Sacramentis suam gratiam nobis obsignantem habeant, atq; eunde ore profiteantur, si quoad fidem & reliqua vitae officia Deo minus obtemperet.
units.tr: The Holy Spirit in the Scriptures not only faithfully and plainly delivers the precepts of true faith, life and morals, but also illustrates and confirms them with various examples, both of the godly who obeyed them and so pleased God, and of the ungodly who neglected them, provoked God's wrath and were severely punished. This is not only useful for us but even necessary, on account of the slowness of our wit, by which it happens that we either do not understand what God commands or do not give faith to what is said to us by him. Paul therefore carefully observes this very thing in the present discussion about idol offerings: And because most of the Christians at Corinth thought that the profession of the Christian name and the outward use of the sacraments of the Church were enough, and from this persuaded themselves that those who share in alien sacred rites for the sake of friendship and of keeping the peace do not sin much, he refutes this error by the examples of the old Church, that is, of the Israelites. For he shows that they once had the same profession of faith and the same sacraments in common with us, but nevertheless did not please God, and miserably perished in the wilderness, because they did not answer their profession. From this he wishes the Corinthians to conclude that they too must not be spared, even if they have Christ speaking in his Word and sealing his grace to us in the sacraments, and confess the same with their mouth, if they obey God less in faith and the other duties of life.

units.la: Caeterum sciebat Paulus, Corinthios ista nequaquam agnoscere, quasi ad ipsos pertinerent: ideo apertius nunc agit, & Christianis omnibus applicat ea, quae olim cum veteri populo gesta fuerunt. Haec (inquit) typi nostri fuerunt. Typos vocat, quia Deus in illis, quae cum Iudaeorum patribus facta sunt, ceu in tabula quandam spectanda proponit, quae eius sit voluntas, quae item peccatorum atrocitas, & quas poenas illa merentur. Ita vero vno verbo eos confutat, qui illa tanquam nihil ad se pertinentia eludere aut reijcere conabantur. Debet autem hoc dictum nobis etiam aduersus omnes eos sufficere, qui hodie Manichaicum errorem instaurare satagunt, & scarrili dicacitate reiiciunt, quaecunq; ex veteri testamento proferuntur. Sunt inter hos facile principes Anabaptistae, qui vt primum veteris scripturae authoritate atq; exemplis sese vrgeri sentiunt, mox clamant: Et quid ista ad nos, qui non Iudaei, sed Christiani sumus? Illis ergo respondeatur: Atqui ista typi fuerunt, & quidem nostri typi, in quibus nos spectare debemus quid fieri quidue caueri debeat. Rationes, quibus hoc probetur, in promptu sunt. Primo, illos olim Dei populum fuisse constat, & quae cum ipsis egit Deus, ea non vt cum prophanis & abs se alienis egit, sed vt cum iis, quos suum peculium sibi fecerat. Quia ergo illis tandem propter incredulitatem & contumaciam eorum reiectis, nos in illorum locum successimus, non possumus a nobis aliena putare quae de illis dicuntur, nisi nos Dei peculium esse negare velimus. Deinde vt nuper diximus, eadem est salutis ratio omnium fidelium hominum proposita: ea nimirum, quae in promisso illo mulieris semine continetur, IE-SV CHRISTO, qui idem est hodie, heri & in aeternum. Adde huc, quod vt Deus aeternus est, ita voluntas eius sibi semper constat, neq; eiusdem iustitia aut veritas mutatur. Frustra igitur effugia eiusmodi captant fanatici illi, qui sibi in Ecclesia quiduis licere volunt. Obseruabis autem hoc Apostoli dictum ad omnia transferri debere, quae ad religionem & vitam siue mores spectant. Noluit olim Deus Sacramenta quae patribus dederat negligi, & scimus quàm infeliciter Mosi cesserit praetermissa filij sui circumcisio. Inde collige, peccare etiam eos, qui baptismum negligunt, aut in Caena Dominica vsu remissiores sunt. Noluit item, vt Sacramentis veteribus nimium illi tribuerent, & extant acerrimi Prophetarum sermones aduersus eos, qui salutis spem in Circumcisione, diebus festis & sacrificijs collocarunt. Ergo nobis etiam nefas videri debet, externis signis ea tribuere quae in sola Dei gratia & Christi merito quaeri debent. Puniti sunt olim, qui neglecto spirituali cultu circa externas modo ceremonias occupabantur: Ergo neq; hodie poenas effugient, qui praetermissis fidei verae officijs, Deum ritibus quantumuis magnificis colunt. Extant praeterea horrenda iudiciorum Dei exempla in homicidas, vsurarios, raptores, & alios horum similes, qui incurabili contumacia in sceleribus perrexerunt: Nemini igitur dubium sit, quin hodie etiam poenas sint daturi, qui eadem faciunt. Haec qui non oscitanter obseruant, ij multiplicem ex veteri scripturae lectione fructum referent. At quia plena horum tractatio in infinitum progrederetur, Paulus selectiora quaedam exempla producit, quae ad Corinthios, ijsdem vitijs laborantes, impri-mis pertinebant.
units.tr: Moreover, Paul knew that the Corinthians did not at all recognise these things as applying to themselves, so he now speaks more openly and applies to all Christians what was once done with the ancient people. "These things," he says, "were our types." He calls them types because God, in what was done with the fathers of the Jews, sets before us as on a painted tablet what his will is, and likewise how atrocious sins are, and what punishments they deserve. In one word, then, he refutes those who tried to mock or reject these things as having nothing to do with them. What he says should suffice for us also against all those who today strive to restore the Manichaean error, and with scurrilous wit reject whatever is brought forward from the Old Testament. Among these the Anabaptists are easily the chief, who, as soon as they feel themselves pressed by the authority and examples of the Old Scripture, at once cry out: "And what have those things to do with us, who are not Jews but Christians?" To them, therefore, let this be answered: Indeed those things were types, and indeed our types, in which we ought to look at what must be done and what must be avoided. The reasons by which this is proved are at hand. First, it is clear that they were once God's people, and that what God did with them he did not do as with profane people alien to him, but as with those whom he had made his own possession. Since, therefore, they were in the end rejected on account of their unbelief and stubbornness, and we have succeeded into their place, we cannot think that what is said of them is alien to us, unless we wish to deny that we are God's possession. Next, as we lately said, the same way of salvation is set forth for all faithful men, namely that which is contained in the promised seed of the woman, Jesus Christ, who is the same yesterday, today and for ever. Add to this that, as God is eternal, so his will always agrees with itself, and his justice or truth is not changed. Those fanatics, then, who want to be allowed anything in the Church, seek such escapes in vain. You will observe, moreover, that this saying of the Apostle must be applied to all things that pertain to religion and life or morals. God once did not wish the sacraments he had given to the fathers to be neglected, and we know how unhappily the circumcision of his son, which Moses had omitted, turned out for him. From this gather that those also sin who neglect baptism, or are too lax in the use of the Lord's Supper. Likewise he did not wish men to attribute too much to the old sacraments, and there remain the most bitter sermons of the Prophets against those who placed the hope of salvation in circumcision, feast days and sacrifices. Therefore it ought to seem to us also a wicked thing to ascribe to outward signs what must be sought in God's grace alone and the merit of Christ. Those who once neglected spiritual worship and occupied themselves only with outward ceremonies were punished; therefore those who, having neglected the true duties of faith, worship God with rites however magnificent will not escape punishment today either. Moreover, there are the dreadful examples of God's judgments against murderers, usurers, robbers, and others like them, who persisted in their crimes with incurable obstinacy. Let no one doubt, therefore, that those who do the same things will also pay the penalty today. Those who observe these things attentively will reap manifold fruit from the reading of the Old Scripture. But because a full treatment of these matters would run on to infinity, Paul brings forward some select examples, which pertained especially to the Corinthians, who were labouring under the same vices.

units.la: Primum est: Ne concupiscamus res malas, sicut illi concupierunt. Debet hoc ad historiam referri, quae in lib. Num. cap. 11. his verbis narratur. Vulgus promiscuum quod erat inter eos, concupiscentia exarserunt, & filij Israel fleuerunt, dicentes: Quis pascet nos carnibus? In mentem nobis veniunt pisces, quos comedebamus in Aegypto gratis: deinde & cucumeres & pepones, cepe & allia. Et nunc anima nostra arida est, nihilq; praeter Manna oculi nostri vident. Fuit ergo haec non vulgaris concupiscentia, sed eiusmodi, quae & Aegypti atq; pristinae conditionis desiderium in illis excitabat, & incomparabile panis angelici, quem illis Deus quotidie largiebatur, beneficium cum fastidio extenuabat. Erat utrumq; hoc coniunctum cum ingratitudine, qua nihil magis adversum est Deo, & quæ vitiorum agmina secum trahere solet, si semel hominum animis insederit. Probè autem conueniebat exemplum hoc Corinthijs, qui & ipsi immoderato gulæ studio & praua concupiscentia accensi ad nefarias idolothytorum epulas accedebant, eoq; non obscurè testabantur, quòd nondum illos ex animo pæniteret prioris conditionis, neq; etiam dignè adhuc æstimarent libertatis in Christo sibi factæ beneficium. Et consultò ab hoc ordiri voluit Apostolus, ut omnis mali fontem obturaret, quem in concupiscentia inveniri scripturæ docent, & ipsi in nobis quotidie experimur. Iacobus certè verissimè dixit: Unusquisq; tentatur, dum à propria cupiditate abstrahitur & inescatur. Et argumento nobis sunt oculi, qui si licentius circa res illicitas aut nihil ad nos pertinentes vagentur, latentem in nobis concupiscendi vim accendere solent. At hæc (ut idem Apostolus ait) postquam concepit, parit peccatum, & hoc quidem non simplex, sed quia animi humani cupiditas insatiabilis est, ad infinita extenditur, & novis in singula momenta illecebris seipsam magis accendit. Id vero fieri non potest, quin simul donorum Dei præsentium nauseam quandam sine fastidio homo concipiat. Nam qui ista magni faciunt, & illis contenti sunt, ij ad alienâ non facile animum appellunt. Et hoc illud est, in quo Israelitæ imprimis peccarunt. In eodem etiam hodie quàm plurimum peccatur quoad opes huius sæculi, quoad cibos & palati delitias, quoad libidinem, honores & quæcunq; alia sunt circa quæ hominum studia fere versantur. Recte ergo Paulus, ne Israelitas imitati res malas concupiscamus admonet. Ubi plurimùm profuerit, si ante omnia in unum Deum intenti, dona eius rectè æstimemus: quod tunc demum fiet, si nobis persuasum sit, nihil verè bonum & utile esse, nisi quod ille dederit. Deinde ut vitæ nostræ conditionem probè expendamus necesse est. Ibi enim occurret, nos in hoc sæculo peregrinos esse, patriam verò in cœlis habere, quo nobis per omnis generis prosperâ & adversa eluctandum sit. Quod unum si diligentius homo cogitet, mox videbit, stultos nimium esse eos, qui (ut de Ulyssis socijs Homerus scribit) toto huius sæculi ita sese inescari patiuntur, ut cœlestis patriæ immemores fiant. Quòd si simul fluxa & instabilia esse cogitemus, quæcunq; carni in hoc mundo magnifica videntur, haud facile nos eorum desiderio accendi aut detineri sinemus. Adde, quòd illorum cōcupiscentia noxia & exitialis est. Ut enim Israelitæ cum carnes adhuc intra dentes eorum essent, horribili clade multati sunt & locum illum suis sepulchris nobilitauerunt: Ita plerunq; fit, ut quando ea iam assecuti videmur, quæ iniustè cupiuimus, Deus pœnas à nobis exigat, & publicum iræ eius exemplum simus.
units.tr: The first is: "Let us not lust after evil things, as they also lusted." This must be referred to the history which is narrated in Numbers chapter 11 in these words: "The mixed multitude that was among them lusted greedily, and the children of Israel wept, saying: Who shall feed us with flesh? We remember the fish which we ate in Egypt freely, then also the cucumbers and melons, the leeks and the garlic. And now our soul is dry, and our eyes see nothing but the manna." This, then, was not an ordinary craving, but such that it stirred up in them a longing for Egypt and their former condition, and with disdain belittled the incomparable benefit of the angels' bread which God gave them daily. This craving was joined with ingratitude, than which nothing is more hostile to God, and which is wont to draw after it whole troops of vices once it has settled in men's minds. Now this example suited the Corinthians well, who themselves, inflamed with immoderate zeal for the belly and with a depraved desire, went to the wicked feasts of idol offerings, and by this they clearly bore witness that they had not yet repented from their heart of their former condition, nor yet valued rightly the benefit of the liberty given to them in Christ. And the Apostle deliberately wished to begin with this, so that he might stop up the source of all evil, which the Scriptures teach is to be found in concupiscence, and which we ourselves daily experience in ourselves. James certainly said most truly: "Every man is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own lust." And our eyes are proof of this, for if they wander too freely over unlawful things, or things that do not concern us, they are wont to kindle the power of desire lying hidden within us. But this, as the same Apostle says, once it has conceived, brings forth sin; and this sin is not simple, but because the desire of the human mind is insatiable, it extends to infinite things, and by fresh allurements at every moment it kindles itself the more. Now this cannot happen without a man at the same time conceiving a certain loathing, not without disdain, for the gifts of God that are present. For those who value these things highly and are content with them do not easily turn their minds to what belongs to others. And this is that in which the Israelites above all sinned. In the same way today very many sin with regard to the riches of this world, with regard to food and dainties for the palate, with regard to lust, honours, and whatever other things are those around which men's pursuits mostly revolve. Rightly, then, Paul warns us, in imitation of the Israelites, not to lust after evil things. It will be of the greatest profit if, first of all, fixing our attention on the one God, we rightly value his gifts; which will then at last come to pass if we are persuaded that nothing is truly good and useful except what he has given. Next, it is necessary that we weigh carefully the condition of our life. For there it will occur to us that we are strangers in this age, but have our homeland in heaven, to which we must struggle through every kind of prosperity and adversity. If a man thinks carefully on this one thing alone, he will soon see that those are very foolish who (as Homer writes of Ulysses' companions) allow themselves to be so enticed by the whole of this age that they become forgetful of their heavenly homeland. But if we also think that all those things which seem splendid to the flesh in this world are fleeting and unstable, we shall not easily let ourselves be kindled or held by desire for them. Add that the desire for them is harmful and deadly. For as the Israelites, while the flesh was still between their teeth, were punished with a dreadful slaughter and made that place famous by their graves, so it often happens that when we seem to have obtained those things which we have desired unjustly, God exacts punishment from us and we become a public example of his wrath.

units.la: Secundum exemplum ad idololatriam expressè refertur, de qua hic Apostolus agit. Neq; idolo-lolatræ sitis (inquit) sicut quidam eorum, ut scriptum est: Sedit populus ad edendum ac bibendum, & surrexerunt ad ludendum. Extat historia hæc in Exod.32.cap. Narratur illic populum morae, quam Moses in Dei colloquio ducebat, impatientia superatum, voluisse sibi Deos fieri, qui ipsis præirent in deserto. Collatis ergo in unum inauribus & monilibus vitulum aureum illis fecit Aaron, & festum diem indixit, quem sacrificijs publicis, conuiuijs item & ludis siue chori more gentium celebrauerunt. Plurimum autem seruiebat exemplum hoc ad confutandum Corinthiorum rationes, quibus se quoad epulas idololatrarum excusabant: & nobis etiam hodie non parum seruire potest di ligens illius consideratio. Nam si Israelitas spectes, nihil minus in animo habuerunt, quàm à vero Deo deficere, aut mutum atq; inanimatum idolum colere: sed quia de Dei præsentia non rectè iudicabant, eius simulachrum habere volebant, quo minus de eius erga se voluntate dubitarent. Ideo cùm diem festum indiceret Aaron, clamabat: Cras erit dies festus Iehouæ. Deinde nihil hic factum est priuato alicuius arbitrio, sed Aaronis summi Sacerdotis consilium secuti sunt, qui totius negotij dux & magister fuit. At nihilominus idololatras fuisse omnis Scriptura docet, & hoc in illis maximè accusat, quòd gloriam Dei immortalis commutarunt cum effigie vituli aut bouis comedentis fœnum. Conueniebant hæc omnia Corinthijs. Nam sciebant hi idolum nihil esse, neq; Diis gentium fictitijs aliquid tribuebant: & credibile est, ex doctorum suorum consilio aut saltem consensu factum fuisse, quicquid ab illis fiebat. Nihilominus tamen illos etiam idololatras Paulus adnumerat.
units.tr: The second example is expressly applied to idolatry, which is what the Apostle is treating here. "Nor be ye idolaters," he says, "as some of them were; as it is written, The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play." This history is found in Exodus 32. There we read that the people, impatient at the delay while Moses was conversing with God, wanted gods made who would go before them in the wilderness. So Aaron gathered the earrings and jewellery into one place and made them a golden calf, and he proclaimed a festival day, which they celebrated with public sacrifices, with feasting, and also with games or dancing in the manner of the Gentiles. This example serves very well to refute the Corinthians' arguments by which they excused themselves for eating at the feasts of idolaters, and a careful consideration of it can serve us no little today. For if you look at the Israelites, they had nothing less in mind than to fall away from the true God or to worship a dumb and lifeless idol. But because they did not judge rightly about God's presence, they wanted an image of him, so that they might have less doubt about his goodwill toward them. Therefore when Aaron proclaimed the feast, he cried, "Tomorrow is a feast to Jehovah." Moreover, nothing was done here at a private individual's discretion; they followed the counsel of Aaron, the high priest, who was the leader and master of the whole affair. Nevertheless, all Scripture teaches that they were idolaters, and it accuses them chiefly of this, that they exchanged the glory of the immortal God for the likeness of a calf or an ox that eats hay. All of this applied to the Corinthians. For they knew that an idol is nothing, and they attributed nothing to the fictitious gods of the Gentiles; and it is credible that whatever was done by them was done on the advice, or at least with the consent, of their teachers. Nevertheless, Paul counts even these people as idolaters.

units.la: Quo autem argumento id probat? Non alio, quàm epulis idolothytorum, quæ illi pro rebus medijs[?] dijs & indifferentibus habebant. Nam ex toto illo Israelitarum facto solum conuiuium sacrum & qui hoc secuti sunt, ludos adduxit. Sedit (inquit) populus ad edendum & bibendum, & surrexerūt ad ludendum. Quod illos ex gentium more fecisse, supra diximus. Nam etsi in populo Dei quoq; ex sacrificiorum aut victimarum carnibus epulæ solennes instituerentur, hoc tamen discrimen erat, quod gentes in conviviis istis temperantiæ fines excedebant, & ijsdem ludos coniungebat, in Diuo-rum suorum honorem institutos, in quibus multa fiebant petulanter nimis & libidinosè. Est enim hoc egregium diaboli stratagema, quod cum plerosq; mortalium ad voluptates & lasciviam proclives esse norit, cultus quoq; fingit, in quibus omnis generis illecebræ & libidinis irritamenta obijciuntur, ut facilius multos irretiat. Quod hodie etiam in plerisq; Papistarum festis est videre, quæ tunc de-mum rite peragi videntur, quando ebriosorum clamoribus, aleatorum proteruia [?], scurrarum & mimorum obscænis dicterijs, saltantium denique, & choreas ducentium [?] inhonestis atq; indecoris gestibus omnia perstrepunt. Erant ergo conuiuia illa & qui ea comitabantur ludi pars aliqua idololatriæ: & quia illis Corinthij intererant, Paulus idololatras esse docet, ficq; omnem illis excusationem eripit, cum hoc ipsum facere eos offendit, quod olim Israelitæ in vituli aurei cultu fecerunt, & quod ethnici omnes in suis sacrificijs atq; festis facere solebant. Itaq; locus iste generalem doctrinam continet, non à manifesto solum & crasso idolorum cultu, verumetiam ab omnibus quæ hunc comitantur, & uniuersis idololatrarum studijs eos debere abstinere, qui fidei verè professionem puram & synceraм retinere volunt. Polluuntur enim qui vel minima ex parte idololatrarum vel superstitionibus vel moribus communicant. Neq; etiam excusat aliquem vel animi intentio, vel antistitum aut principum authoritas, aut publicum exemplum. Nam ut impium est Deum fingere alium quam in scripturis ille seipsum revelat: ita idololatricum est omne illud, quod absq; Verbo eius instituitur. Vehementer autem huius loci authoritate confutantur quidam ex nostris, qui cum Euangelicæ doctrinæ factatores videri velint, Encæniorum tamen festis intersunt, in quibus eodem ordine omnia fiunt, quem in vituli aurei festo observatu fuisse, Moses scribit. Quod si illi viciniam, amicitias veteres et publicæ pacis studium prætexant, ego ijsdem rationibus olim Corinthios quoq; pugnauisse dicam: sed cum eas minimè admiserit Paulus, nō est quod illi has vnquà apud Deū ratas fore sibi polliceantur.
units.tr: By what argument does he prove this? By none other than the feasts of things sacrificed to idols, which they considered to be matters of indifference, neutral toward the gods. For from that whole deed of the Israelites he brought forward only the sacred banquet and the games that followed it: "The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play." We said above that they did this in the manner of the Gentiles. For although among the people of God too, solemn feasts were instituted from the flesh of sacrifices or victims, there was this difference: the Gentiles, at these banquets, exceeded the bounds of temperance, and they joined games to them, instituted in honour of their deified ones, in which many things were done excessively wantonly and lustfully. For this is an excellent stratagem of the devil: since he knows that most mortals are inclined to pleasures and wantonness, he also devises forms of worship in which every kind of enticement and incitement to lust is set before people, so that he may more easily snare many. This can be seen today too in most of the festivals of the Papists, which then seem to be properly celebrated when everything resounds with the shouts of drunkards, the reckless behaviour of gamblers, the obscene jokes of buffoons and mimes, and finally with dancers and those who lead the dances, with dishonourable and unseemly gestures. Those banquets, then, and the games that accompanied them, were a part of idolatry; and because the Corinthians took part in them, Paul teaches that they are idolaters, and so he strips them of every excuse, since he shows that they do the very thing the Israelites once did in worshipping the golden calf, and what all the heathen used to do in their sacrifices and festivals. Therefore this passage contains a general doctrine: that those who want to hold the true and pure profession of the faith must abstain not only from the manifest and gross worship of idols, but also from everything that accompanies it and from all the pursuits of idolaters. For whoever takes part, even in the smallest measure, in the superstitions or customs of idolaters, is defiled. Nor does any intention of mind excuse anyone, nor the authority of bishops or princes, nor a public example. For just as it is impious to imagine a God other than the one he reveals himself to be in the Scriptures, so everything that is instituted without his Word is idolatrous. Moreover, some among our own people are powerfully refuted by the authority of this passage: though they wish to appear to be followers of the Gospel doctrine, they nevertheless attend the festivals of the Dedications, at which everything is done in the same order that Moses writes was observed at the festival of the golden calf. If they pretend neighbourliness, old friendships, and a concern for public peace, I would say that the Corinthians too once argued with these same reasons; but since Paul by no means admitted them, there is no reason for them to promise themselves that these will ever be approved by God.

units.la: Sequitur tertium exemplum, quod ita proponitur: Neq; scortemur, sicut quidam eorum scortati sunt, & ceciderunt uno die viginti tria millia. Recte autem & prudenter hoc subijcit. Ut enim idololatriæ scortatio plerunq; coniuncta est: ita inter Corinthios hanc publicè regnauisse iam sæpe diximus, & periculum erat, ne multi libidinis æstro magis quam aliquo religionis studio impulsi, ad superstitiones & idololatriam deflecterent. Historiam verò Moses in libro Numerorum Cap. 25. describit, cuius summa est, Moabitas & Madianitas, ut Israelem Deo inuisum facerent, ex Balaami consilio filias suas illis prostituisse: quarum lenocinijs filij Israel decepti, primò cum illis scortari coeperunt impudentissimè, mox autem cum ijsdem Baalpeor sacra fecerunt. Quo scelere Deus ita excanduit, ut principes quidem publicè suspendi, reliquos verò omnes publica authoritate trucidari mandauerit. In præsenti tamen solius scortationis Paulus meminit, quod hæc tanti mali principium & causa fuisset. A Mose autem dissentire videtur in occisorum numero, quem ille viginti quatuor millium fuisse scribit. Sed facilè conciliari poterunt, si meminerimus in eiusmodi censibus sæpe millenarium totum poni, etiamsi nō plenè perfectus sit, Paulum verò, ne Tragicè nimis loqui videretur, viginti trium millium numero fuisse contentum. Est autem hoc memorabile & imprimis horrendum exemplum, quo omnem posteritatem Deus admoneri voluit, quàm graue & detestabile, quà multiplex deniq; fit scortationis scelus, quod vulgò plerisq; ludus iocusq; esse videtur. Cōfutat horū sententiam uno verbo Hoseas propheta, quando scortatione cor hominis auferre ait, adeò nimirum, ut non amplius mentis suæ compos sit, & proinde neq; velit neq; possit ea videre & intelligere, quæ ad ipsius honorē & salutem defendendam faciunt. Et videmus fere omnem pudorē eos abstergere, qui huic vitio seruire semel in animū induxerunt. Quid ergo aliud sequatur, quàm quòd nulla recti & honesti ratione habita in omne turpitudinem scientes atq; volentes ruunt? Exemplum huius impudentiæ nimis euidens hæc ipsa historia in Zamri principe tribus Simeō & Cosbi scorto Madianitico proponitur, quos in totius populi conspectu ad explendum libidinem suā festinauisse, & in ipso scelere à Phinee sacerdote, quē zelus Dei accenderat, confossos fuisse Moses narrat. Accedit malo isti plerunq; cultus diuini prophanatio, quem admodū è contra idololatriam fere scortatio & nefaria atq; incesta stuprorum licentia sequi solet, ut non immerito duo hæc scelera reciproca dici possint. sint. Exempla in utramq; partem occurrunt, quæ alibi commemorauimus. Imprimis autem pernitiosum est, quòd semel admissa scortandi licentia breui temporis spatio latissimè serpit, sicuti in præsenti historia factum videmus. Intra paucos enim dies eò vsq; vagata est libido, vt tribunum & familiarum principes fere omnes; & ex populo circiter viginti quatuor millia virorum hoc scelere se pollu-erint.
units.tr: There follows a third example, which is set forth thus: "Nor let us commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication, and in one day twenty-three thousand fell." He adds this rightly and prudently. For just as fornication is generally bound up with idolatry, so, as we have often said, fornication had publicly held sway among the Corinthians, and there was a danger that many, driven more by the frenzy of lust than by any zeal for religion, would turn aside to superstitions and idolatry. Moses describes the history in Numbers chapter 25, the sum of which is this: at Balaam's counsel, the Moabites and Midianites prostituted their daughters to them in order to make Israel hateful to God; deceived by their enticements, the sons of Israel first began to fornicate with them most shamelessly, and soon afterwards they performed sacred rites with the same women to Baal-peor. God burned with such anger at this crime that he commanded the chiefs to be publicly hanged, and all the rest to be slaughtered by public authority. In the present passage, however, Paul mentions only fornication, because it was the beginning and cause of so great an evil. He seems to differ from Moses on the number of the dead, which Moses says was twenty-four thousand. But these can easily be reconciled if we remember that in such counts the whole thousand is often put down even when it is not fully complete, and that Paul, lest he seem to speak too tragically, was content with the number twenty-three thousand. This is a memorable and above all dreadful example, by which God wished to warn all posterity how grave and detestable, and in how many forms, the sin of fornication is, which to most people commonly seems a game and a jest. The prophet Hosea refutes their opinion in one word, when he says that fornication takes away the heart of a man, so much so that he is no longer master of his mind, and therefore neither wills nor is able to see and understand the things that serve to defend his own honour and salvation. And we see that fornication wipes away almost all shame in those who have once resolved to serve this vice. What else, then, can follow, except that, having no regard for what is right and honourable, they rush into every baseness knowingly and willingly? A very clear example of this shamelessness is set before us in this same history: Zimri, a prince of the tribe of Simeon, and Cozbi, a Midianite prostitute, whom Moses tells us hurried to satisfy their lust in full view of the whole people, and who were both run through in the very act of sin by Phinehas the priest, whom the zeal of God had kindled. To this evil there is often added a profanation of divine worship, just as, conversely, idolatry is commonly followed by fornication and the unlawful, incestuous licence of debauchery, so that these two wicked things may not unjustly be called reciprocal. Examples of both kinds occur, which we have mentioned elsewhere. Above all, it is pernicious that once the licence of fornication is admitted, it spreads very widely within a short space of time, as we see happened in the present history. For within a few days lust had wandered so far that almost all the tribal and family leaders, and from the people about twenty-four thousand men, had defiled themselves with this crime.

units.la: Vt enim segetibus iam ad messem maturis immissa flamma momento discurrit et proxima quæq; corripiens indomito et præcipiti cursu totos agros populatur: ita cum natura ad libidinem proclives sint homines, si data occasione semel exarserint, nullus licentiæ modus est, & in sceleris societatem abripiuntur quos minimè putes. Quæ causa est, quòd Deus licentiam istam semper non vulgaribus pœnis, sed horrendis & latè vagantibus exemplis puniuit. Pertinent huc ciuitatis Sichemitarum miserabilis clades: Abfolomica seditio & mox secutum prælium, in quo ciuilibus & fraternis armis millia multa perierunt: Beniamitica tribus excidium, & quæ passim in omnium gentium historijs habentur. Constat enim vagas libidines multis potentissimis populis periculosissimas reipub. mutationes & regnorum euersiones peperisse. Debent in istorum consideratione diligentes esse principes Christiani, ne eorum consilia audiant, quibus ista ludus esse putantur, & qui neq; possibile neq; etiam vtile esse dicunt, vt scortatio legibus publicis prohibeatur. Est enim infelix nimium & plus quàm Tragicus ludus, qui tantorum malorum materiam præbet. Et videmus nequaquam intra scortationis limites consistere eos; qui huic semel indulgere cœperunt, sed paulatim ad stupra virginum, ad alienos thoros, ad incestus denique concubitus & his fœdiora progredi. Quòd si vero principum ignavia malum hoc eò vsq; viribus angeri patiatur, vt indomitum fiat, non tamen illud coercere impossibile fuerit Deo, qui eius puniendi rationem facile inueniet.
units.tr: Just as, when a flame is set to corn already ripe for harvest, it spreads in an instant and, seizing everything nearby, lays waste whole fields with an unrestrained and headlong course, so, since human beings are naturally inclined to lust, once they have caught fire on a given occasion there is no limit to their licence, and they are dragged into fellowship in wickedness whom you would least expect. This is why God has always punished such licence not with ordinary penalties but with dreadful examples that spread widely. To this belong the wretched destruction of the city of the Shechemites, Absalom's rebellion and the battle that followed, in which many thousands perished by civil and fratricidal arms, the destruction of the tribe of Benjamin, and the many similar cases found throughout the histories of all nations. For it is established that unrestrained lusts have brought the most dangerous upheavals of commonwealths and the overthrow of kingdoms to many mighty peoples. Christian princes ought to be careful in considering these things, lest they listen to those counsellors who regard them as a joke, and who say that it is neither possible nor even useful for fornication to be forbidden by public laws. For this is an excessively unhappy and more than tragic game, which furnishes the material for such great evils. And we see that those who have once begun to indulge in fornication by no means keep within its limits, but gradually advance to the defilement of virgins, to other men's beds, to incest and finally to intercourse and things even more foul than these. But if the sloth of princes allows this evil to gain such strength that it becomes unrestrained, it will nonetheless not be impossible for God to restrain it, since he will easily find a way of punishing it.

units.la: Quarto loco de iis agit Paulus, qui Deum aut Christum tentare non verentur, dicens: Neq; tentemus Christum, sicut quidam eorum tentarunt, & à serpentibus perierunt. Deum tentare dicuntur, qui non contenti eius verbo & operibus, quibus se nobis revelat, de eius voluntate aut potentia pro suo arbitrio periculum facere volunt, tunc nimirum credituri Deum esse bonum et omnipotentem, si hoc aut illud faciat, quod ipsi præscribunt. Fecerunt ista Israëlitæ non semel, & imprimis memorabile huius audaciæ exemplum dederunt, quando carnes sibi dari postularunt. De hoc enim Asaph in Psalmo 78. sic canit: Tentauerunt Deum in corde suo, cum poscerent cibum animabus suis, id est, pro sua libidine & gulæ desiderio. Nam contra Deum locuti sunt, dicentes: Num potest Deus mensam instruere in deserto? En petra percussit, & effluxerunt aquæ, & fluuij inundarunt: nū & panem dare poterit? num parare carnes poterit populo suo? Quibus verbis aperte docet Spiritus sanctus, hoc peccato impiam quoq; beneficiorum & miraculorum Dei extenuationem contineri, quæ cum ingratitudine summa coniuncta sit. In præsenti tamen de eo agitur, quod Moses in cap. 21. libri Numerorum sic narrat: Et profecti sunt monte in Hor per viam maris Caretlosi[?], vt circuirent terram Edom, & in via anima populi abbreuiata est, id est, præ lassitudine & tædio itineris animo defecerunt. Locutusq; est populus contra Deum & contra Mosem: Cur effecisti, vt ascenderemus ex Ægypto, vt moreremur in solitudine? Quia nec panem habemus, nec aquas, & animus noster cibum hunc vilem fastidit. Dominus igitur misit in populu serpentes vrentes, qui populum mordebant, & mortuus est ex Israële populus multus. Fuit ergo huius peccati origo ex impatientia, qua factum est, vt nō contenti diuinæ bonitatis testimonijs, quæ infinita & præclara habebant, plus quiddam postularent, neq; etiam expectare vellent tempus illud, quod quieti ipsorum Deus destinauerat, sed id quodammodo præripere aut anticipare vellent. Vere ergo Deum tentauerunt, & sub vno hoc scelere multa alia concurrisse videmus: impatientiam nimirum, ingratitudinem, sceleratum præsentium beneficiorum Dei contemptum, apertum murmur, inobedientiam deniq; & contumaciam. Itaq; quouis supplicio dignissimi fuerunt. Grauissimè autem punitos fuisse constat, quando tam citò domita fuit eorum contumacia, vt ad Mosem supplices venirent, aduersus quem paulo ante tam impudenter murmurarant.
units.tr: In the fourth place, Paul deals with those who do not shrink from tempting God or Christ, saying: "Neither let us tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him, and were destroyed by serpents." They are said to tempt God who, not content with his word and works by which he reveals himself to us, wish to make trial of his will or power according to their own judgement, being ready to believe that God is good and almighty only if he does this or that which they themselves prescribe. The Israelites did this more than once, and they gave a especially memorable example of this boldness when they demanded flesh to be given them. For Asaph sings of this in Psalm 78: "They tempted God in their heart, when they asked food for their souls," that is, according to their own lust and the desire of their gullet. For they spoke against God, saying: "Can God furnish a table in the wilderness? Behold, he struck the rock, and the waters gushed out, and the streams overflowed; can he also give bread? Can he prepare flesh for his people?" By these words the Holy Spirit clearly teaches that this sin also contains an impious belittling of God's benefits and miracles, which is joined with the greatest ingratitude. In the present passage, however, the reference is to what Moses relates in chapter 21 of Numbers: "And they set out from Mount Hor by the way of the Red Sea, to go around the land of Edom, and the soul of the people was shortened on the way," that is, through weariness and the tedium of the journey they lost heart. "And the people spoke against God and against Moses: Why have you made us come up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? For there is neither bread nor water, and our soul loathes this worthless food." Therefore the Lord sent fiery serpents among the people, which bit the people, and many of Israel died. The origin of this sin, then, lay in impatience, by which it came about that they, not content with the testimonies of divine goodness, which they had in abundance and in excellent measure, demanded something more, and were unwilling to wait for that time of rest which God had appointed for them, but wished in a way to snatch it away or anticipate it. Truly, then, they tempted God, and we see that many other things came together under this one sin: namely impatience, ingratitude, contempt for God's present benefits, open murmuring, and finally disobedience and obstinacy. Therefore they were worthy of any punishment whatever. It is agreed that they were punished most severely, since their obstinacy was broken so quickly that they came as suppliants to Moses, against whom a little before they had murmured so shamelessly.

units.la: Porrò obseruatu dignissimum est, quòd Paulus Christum ab illis tentatum fuisse scribit. Rationem huius dicti D. Ambrosius hanc adducit: Quia is erat, qui cum Mose loquebatur. Quo etiam referri debet, quòd supra Christu petram dixit, quæ illos comitata fuerit. Is ergo fuit Angelus ille, qui Mosi apparuit, & qui iam inde ab origine rerum ecclesiæ suæ ducem & protectorem sese[?] præbuit. Est autem hoc euidens & irrefragabile diuinitatis Christi testimonium. Moses enim illos aduersus Deum murmurauisse scribit, & ipsi se in Iehoua (quod nomen Dei essentiale est, neque vllì creaturæ communicatur) peccauisse fatentur. Id vero omne Paulus Christo tribuit, quod sine sacrilegio fieri non poterat, nisi is Deus sit, Patri coæternus & coessentialis. Et huius generis argumenta multa colligi possunt, si veteris testamenti scripturas cum Nouo non oscitanter conferamus.
units.tr: Moreover, it is most worthy of notice that Paul writes that Christ was tempted by them. The reason for this statement is given by Saint Ambrose: "Because it was he who spoke with Moses." To this too should be referred what he said above, that Christ was the rock which accompanied them. He, then, was that Angel who appeared to Moses, and who from the beginning of things showed himself the leader and protector of his Church. This is a clear and irrefutable testimony to the divinity of Christ. For Moses writes that they murmured against God, and they themselves confess that they had sinned against Jehovah (which is the essential name of God, and is communicated to no creature). Paul, moreover, ascribes to Christ all that could not be done without sacrilege unless he were God, coeternal and coessential with the Father. And many arguments of this kind can be gathered, if we compare the Scriptures of the Old Testament with the New with careful attention.

units.la: Interim meminerimus, hanc admonitionem imprimis ad nos pertinere, ne videlicet tentemus Christum. Faciunt hoc primum, qui non contenti eius voluntate, quam nobis ille in terris agens reuelauit, & postea per Apostolos suos plenius exposuit, noua mysteria fingunt, & nouas quotidie salutis rationes comminiscuntur. Deinde qui nouos cultus instituunt, & iugum Legis rursus sibi aut aliis accersunt, quod per Christum auferri oportuit, quod à nemine mortalium ferri posset. De hoc graviter admodum Petrus in Hierosolymitana Synodo pronunciauit aduersus eos, qui gentibus Circumcisionem obtrudere conabantur. At quid hodie frequentius fit, quando suis viribus & suorum operum meritis cœlum sibi acquirere docentur, qui ex semetipsis ne ad cogitandum quidem sunt idonei? Deum tentare diceretur, qui in altum euolare vellet, aut ex alto sese præcipitare. At quid aliud faciunt, qui cœlos ipsos conscendere conantur absq; Christo, qui solus via est & veritas? Sunt hi Icaro audaciores, & quemadmodum ille fecit, ita ipsi quoq; sua temeritate seipsos infames faciunt, & simul omnem suæ doctrinæ professionem proprio exitio nobilitant. Christum quoq; tentare dicuntur, qui eius bonitatem sua contumacia irritant, & eius fiducia (si modo hoc nomen meretur) ad peccandi licentiam abutuntur. Peccabant in omnibus istis Corinthij, cum & nouos doctores audirent, & religionem Christianam externo splendore & propria dignitate metirentur, interim præcipiti licentia in omne scelus ruerent. Et hodie passim idem faciunt, qui Christianissimi dici & haberi volunt. Sed meminerint omnes isti, iam ipsis quoq; pœnas paratas esse à Domino. Permittuntur enim veteris serpentis potestati, qui venenatos morsus subinde inferens, nouis quotidie cupiditatibus accendit, quibus absumpti horribiliter pereunt. Remedium tanti mali vnicum & præsentissimum est, vt in vna Dei voluntate acquiescamus, de illius fide & bonitate nihil dubitemus, patientes simus in aduersis, & si quid humanum patimur, ad CHRISTVM IESVM recurramus, qui (quod olim in æneo serpente adumbrabatur) in crucem suffixus diabolum vicit, & salutem meruit omnibus, qui in ipsum credunt.
units.tr: Meanwhile let us remember that this warning pertains chiefly to us, namely that we should not tempt Christ. They do this first who, not content with his will, which he revealed to us while living on earth and afterwards explained more fully through his Apostles, invent new mysteries and devise new ways of salvation every day. Next, those who institute new forms of worship, and bring back upon themselves or upon others the yoke of the Law, which had to be removed through Christ, and which no mortal could bear. Peter spoke most weightily about this at the Synod of Jerusalem against those who tried to force circumcision upon the Gentiles. But what is done more often today, when men are taught to acquire heaven for themselves by their own strength and the merits of their works, though of themselves they are not even fit to think anything? One would be said to tempt God who wished to fly up on high, or to throw himself down from a height. But what else do those do who try to climb into the heavens themselves without Christ, who alone is the way and the truth? These men are bolder than Icarus, and just as he did, so they too by their rashness make themselves infamous, and at the same time bring renown to every profession of their doctrine by their own ruin. They are also said to tempt Christ who provoke his goodness by their obstinacy, and who abuse his trust (if indeed it deserves this name) as a licence for sinning. The Corinthians sinned in all these ways, when they both listened to new teachers and measured the Christian religion by outward show and personal dignity, while in the meantime they rushed headlong into every crime through reckless licence. And today too, those who wish to be and to be thought the most Christian do the same everywhere. But let all of them remember that punishment is already prepared for them by the Lord. For they are given over to the power of the old serpent, who, inflicting venomous bites from time to time, inflames them with new desires every day, by which they are consumed and perish dreadfully. The only and most ready remedy for so great an evil is that we should rest in the one will of God, have no doubt about his faithfulness and goodness, be patient in adversity, and, if we suffer anything human, have recourse to CHRIST JESUS, who, lifted up on the cross (as was foreshadowed long ago by the bronze serpent), overcame the devil and won salvation for all who believe in him.

units.la: Restat postremum exemplum, quod his verbis Paulus proponit: Neq; murmurate, sicut quidam eorum murmurarunt, & perierunt ab Exterminatore. Murmur dicitur in hac causa, quando de Deo & eius gubernatione aut prouidentia homines queruntur. Est hoc homini proprium, eo quod natura impatientes sumus, si quid nobis præter animi voluntatem accidit. Peccarunt in hoc sapis-sime filij Israelis toto illo tempore, quo per desertum peregrinati sunt. Quia vero hic Exterminatoris meminit, videtur ad historiam seditionis per Core & eius socios, Dathanum atq; Abiram, excitatæ respicere. Extat hæc diligenter descripta in lib. Numerorum cap. 16. Causa seditionis & murmuris fuit ambitio, qua illi extimulati Mosem & Aaronem ex eo gradu deiicere conabantur, in quem eos Dominus euexerat. Affute autem crimen hoc in Dei seruos transferunt, & se populi causam agere simulant, quem tyrannide illa semel liberari oporteat. Aiunt enim: Satis superq; vobis: omnes in cœtu sancti sunt: & Dominus est in medio eorum: cur efferimini supra congregationem Domini? Territ hic illorum conatus Mosem vehementer, quod non ignoraret, quid inde nasciturum esset, nisi in tempore adhiberetur remedium. Itaq; magna cum grauitate causam hanc egit, & Deus ipse nouo & inaudito prius exemplo illorum audaciam puniuit, vt nimirum terra ipsis debisceret, & viui descenderent ad inferos cum omnibus suis domesticis atq; facultatibus: Sed & ignis à Domino egressus viros, qui cum illis coniurauerant, ducentos quinquaginta absumpsit. At non potuit omnium contumaciam flectere tanti supplicij atrocitas, quin mox crastino die multi infl aurato aduersus Mosem & Aaronem murmure dicerent: Vos interfecistis populū Domini. Quare cum res ad maiorem motum spectare videretur, mox sese interposuit Dominus, & cladem subitam immisit, qua breui temporis momento quatuordecim millia hominum & septingenti perierunt. Facta fuit hæc cædes per Angelum, quem Paulus in præsenti Exterminatorem nominat. Probe autem ser-viebat exemplum hoc Corinthijs, qui & ipsi aduersus Paulum & fidos Christi ministros murmu-rabant. rabant. Neq; minus nobis hodie feruit, quando peccatum hoc passim regnat. Quam multos enim est audire, qui aduersus Dei verbum murmurant, & ambitiosae atq; intolerabilis tyrannidis eius administros accusant, si quid ex illo proferatur, quo suam petulantiam perstringi aut coerceri sentiunt? Quid vero de illis dicemus, qui (quod Prophetarum quoq; temporibus factum fuit olim) dicendi leges verbi administris audent praescribere? At omnibus istis non cum Dei seruis, sed cum ipso Deo lis est, qui causae suae nunquam deerit. Notum est enim illud Christi: Qui vos reijcit, me reijcit: qui autem reijcit me, reijcit eum qui misit me. Sceleratior autem est eorum impudentia, qui quas ipsi suis sceleribus meruerunt calamitates, verbo Dei & huius praeconibus acceptas ferre confuerunt: quod ipsum Israelitas quoq; in deserto non semel fecisse scimus. Et Ieremiae quidam in faciem dicebant: Sermonem Domini, quem locutus es ad nos nomine Domini, non recipiemus, sed faciemus quicquid egreditur de ore nostro: ut suffitum incendamus machinae coeli, & libemus ei libamina, sicut fecimus nos & patres nostri, reges nostri & principes nostri in ciuitatibus Iuda & in plateis Ierusalem: tunc enim & alimento abundabamus, bene nobis erat, & malum nullum videbamus: Ut primum autem cessauimus suffitum incendere machinae coeli, omnium sumus indigi, & fero ac fame consumimur, etc. Agnoscis opinor hic eorum verba, qui hodie prorem[?] suam felicitatem nobis magnifice narrant, praesentis vero seculi calamitates Tragice amplificant, causam vero istarum esse clamant mutationem doctrinae & religionis, quae ex verbi Dei praescripto facta est. Sed est haec summa impietas. Nam qui ita sentiunt, ij Deum omnis mali authorem fingunt. Quid ergo ipsis quoq; aliud fiat, quam ut Exterminatori diabolo illos tradat Dominus? Discant ergo singuli exempla ista ad se transferre, & horum consideratione territi concupiscentijs prauis frenum injiciant, superstitiones & cultus illicitos fugiant, fornicationi & impuritati omni longum valere renuntient, Deo tentare desinant, & absq; murmure sese totos regendos praebeant Filio eius IESV CHRISTO, quem ille nobis Regem & Sacerdotem vnicum aeternum, esse voluit. Huic debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: The last example is the one Paul sets before us in these words: "Neither murmur, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed by the Destroyer." Murmuring, in this sense, is when people complain about God, his government or his providence. This is a natural human failing, since we are by nature impatient whenever anything happens to us against our will. The children of Israel sinned in this way most grievously throughout the whole time they wandered in the desert. Since Paul mentions the Destroyer here, he seems to have in mind the story of the sedition raised by Korah and his companions, Dathan and Abiram. It is described carefully in the book of Numbers, chapter 16. The cause of the sedition and the murmuring was ambition: stirred up by it, these men tried to thrust Moses and Aaron down from the rank to which the Lord had raised them. Cunningly, they transferred this charge onto the servants of God, pretending to plead the cause of the people, who ought to be freed from such tyranny. "You have gone too far," they said. "All the congregation are holy, and the Lord is among them. Why then do you lift yourselves up above the assembly of the Lord?" This attempt terrified Moses greatly, because he knew what would follow unless a remedy was applied in time. So he pleaded the case with great seriousness, and God himself, by a new and hitherto unheard-of example, punished their audacity: the earth opened beneath them, and they went down alive into the pit with all their households and possessions. Fire also came out from the Lord and consumed the two hundred and fifty men who had conspired with them. Yet the severity of such punishment could not bend the obstinacy of them all; on the very next day many, inflamed with murmuring, said against Moses and Aaron, "You have killed the people of the Lord." Since the matter seemed likely to lead to a greater uprising, the Lord at once intervened and sent a sudden plague, by which in the space of a moment fourteen thousand and seven hundred people perished. This slaughter was carried out by the Angel, whom Paul here calls the Destroyer. This example was very fitting for the Corinthians, who were themselves also murmuring against Paul and the faithful ministers of Christ. This sin is no less rife among us today, when it reigns everywhere. How many people are there to be heard who murmur against the Word of God and accuse the ministers of its ambitious and intolerable tyranny, if anything is brought forward from it by which they feel their own wantonness is rebuked or restrained? What shall we say of those who (as was also done in the time of the Prophets) dare to prescribe laws to the ministers of the Word about what they may say? But for all such people the quarrel is not with the servants of God but with God himself, who will never lack a cause to defend.
