For that saying of Christ is well known: "He who rejects you rejects me, and he who rejects me rejects him who sent me." Yet more wicked still is the impudence of those who are accustomed to lay the calamities they have deserved by their own crimes at the door of the Word of God and of its heralds. We know that the Israelites too did this more than once in the desert. Some people also said to Jeremiah's face: "We will not listen to the word which you have spoken to us in the name of the Lord, but we will do whatever comes out of our own mouths: we will burn incense to the queen of heaven and pour out drink offerings to her, as we and our fathers, our kings and our princes did in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem. For then we had plenty of food, we prospered, and we saw no evil. But since we stopped burning incense to the queen of heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we are in want of everything and are consumed by sword and famine," and so on. I think you recognise here the words of those who today loudly boast to us of their own happiness, and magnify with tragic exaggeration the calamities of the present age, crying out that the cause of them is the change of doctrine and religion that has been made according to the prescription of God's Word. But this is the height of impiety. For those who think this way make God the author of all evil. What else then will happen to them, but that the Lord hands them over to the Destroyer, the devil? Let each one therefore learn to apply these examples to himself, and by considering them, being terrified, let him bridle his depraved desires, flee superstitions and illicit worship, renounce fornication and every impurity, cease to tempt God, and without murmuring offer himself wholly to be ruled by his Son, Jesus Christ, whom God willed to be our only, eternal King and Priest. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LI.
units.tr: HOMILY LI.

units.la: Haec autem omnia typice eueniebant eis, scripta vero sunt ad nostri admonitionem, in quos fines seculorum occurrerunt. Itaq; qui sibi videtur stare, videat ne cadat. Tentatio vos non coepit nisi humana: Fidelis autem est Deus, qui non sinet vos tentari supra id quod potestis: sed praestabit vna cum tentatione etiam euasionem, vt possitis sufferre.
units.tr: Now all these things happened to them as types, but they were written for our admonition, on whom the ends of the ages have come. Therefore let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall. No temptation has taken you but what is human; but God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to bear it.

units.la: Quamuis Deus voluntatem suam nobis in Scriptura sancta abunde revelet, & perspicue omnia tradat, quae nos tam in religione quam vita & moribus instituere possunt, non tamen omnes fructum, quem debebant, inde referunt. Causa huius mali est, quod plerique ea, quae olim dicta & gesta sunt, nihil ad se pertinere putant, ideoq; dum scripturas legunt vel audiunt, curiositati potius suae indulgent, quam ut ea discere studeant, quae ad salutem necessaria sunt cognitu. Est ergo diligenti consideratione dignissima prima huius cap. pars, qua Paulus veterum Israelitarum exemplis Corinthios dehortari instituit, ne cum idololatrarum sacris aliquid commune habeant. Nam ut id maiori cum fructu faciat, diligenter ostendit veterum exempla ad nos pertinere, eo quod eadem illorum religio fuerit, quae nostra est, quodq; in suis Sacramentis eundem Christum fide perceperint, quem nos in nostris habemus.
units.tr: Although God abundantly reveals his will in holy Scripture, and sets out clearly everything that can instruct us both in religion and in life and conduct, nevertheless not all draw from it the fruit they ought. The cause of this evil is that most people think those things that were said and done long ago do not pertain to them. So when they read or hear the Scriptures, they indulge their curiosity rather than strive to learn what is necessary for salvation to know. The first part of this chapter is therefore most worthy of careful consideration. In it Paul sets out to dissuade the Corinthians, by the examples of the ancient Israelites, from having anything in common with the rites of idolaters. To do this with greater profit, he carefully shows that the examples of the ancients pertain to us, because their religion was the same as ours, and because in their sacraments they received by faith the same Christ whom we have in ours.

units.la: At non poterat ignorare, difficulter hoc omnibus persuaderi, & frequenter fieri, ut qui optime de religione & toto humanae salutis negotio sentire videntur, minus tamen animum attendant ijs, quae de veterum rebus gestis dicuntur. Ideo quod nuper dixerat, nunc repetit: Haec autem omnia typice eueniebant eis, scripta vero sunt ad nostri admonitionem, in quos fines seculorum occurrerunt. Typos siue figuras vocat, quae vulgo exempla dicuntur. Et ita olim locum istum Tertullianus interpretatus est. Quod propter phanaticos quosdam admonemus, qui quacunq; de veteribus scribuntur, ea umbras solummodò & typos eorum, quæ posteris demum temporibus reipsa implerì aut perfici debuerint, fuisse contendunt: inde vero aliud magis absurdum colligunt, veteres neq; veram Dei Ecclesiam fuisse, neq; cultum habuisse aut Sacramenta, quæ Deo probarentur. Ex quo tertius quoque error deriuatur, non deberi ex veterum historijs argumenta aut exempla peti eorum, quæ hodie post Christum exhibitum in Ecclesia & religione fieri debent. Et hoc effugio Anaba-ptistæ fere utuntur. Si enim ad afferendum baptismum infantium Legem Dei de masculis octauo die circumcidendis adducas, & inde colligas baptismum, qui in Circumcisionis locum successit, par uulis[?] negari non debere: aut si Israelitarum patres unà cum suis infantibus baptizatos fuisse di-cas, quando nube tecti per maris rubri alueum euaserunt: mox illos vociferari audies: Hæc omnia umbræ & typi fuerunt, & ideo ad nos minimè pertinent, quibus veritas ipsa in Christo exhibita est. Atqui fatemur nos quoq; ista Israelitis typos & figuras fuisse beneficiorum, quæ præfinito tempore Christus collaturus erat: at typi isti non inanes fuerunt, qui præter umbram aliquam nihil continerent. Nam ut promissiones de Christo & salute humani generis per hunc instauranda habuerunt veras & minimè ambiguas: ita promissionum istarum sigilla quoq; vera fuerunt, quæcunq; in toto illo cultu Leuitico fiebant, ut iam de alijs, quæ extraordinariè facta sunt, nihil dicamus. Et in is-dem illos eundem Christum nobiscum percepisse, Paulus supra verbis disertis docuit. Nam qua fide Abrahamus Christi diem vidit, eadem posteri quoque eius illum viderunt & complexi sunt. Quæ omnia cùm vere & reipsa facta sint, illos quoq; Ecclesiam Dei veram fuisse nemo negauerit, nisi qui cum ratione insanire volet, aut tempus aliquod fingere, quo nulla prorsus Ecclesia fuerit. Recte ergo Apostolus asserit, hæc ita cum patribus gesta fuisse, ut simul Deus exempla publica pro posuerit, ex quibus tota posteritas disceret, quid fieri quidue caueri debeat ab iis, qui Ecclesiæ dignitatem tueri, & pœnas incredulis atq; immorigeris iam olim constitutas declinare cupiant. Et ideo expositionis loco addit: Scripta vero sunt ad nostri admonitionem, in quos fines seculorum occurrerunt.
units.tr: But he could not be unaware that this is hard to persuade everyone of, and that it often happens that those who seem to think most rightly about religion and the whole business of human salvation pay less attention to what is said of the deeds of the ancients. Therefore he now repeats what he said a little before: "Now all these things happened to them as types, but they were written for our admonition, on whom the ends of the ages have come." He calls them types or figures, which are commonly called examples. Tertullian long ago interpreted this passage in the same way. We note this on account of certain fanatics, who contend that whatever is written of the ancients was only shadows and types of things which were to be really fulfilled or accomplished in later times. From this they draw something even more absurd: that the ancients were neither the true Church of God, nor had worship or sacraments that were pleasing to God. From this a third error also follows: that arguments and examples for what ought to be done today in the Church and religion after Christ has been revealed should not be sought from the histories of the ancients. The Anabaptists mostly use this escape. For if you bring forward God's law that males were to be circumcised on the eighth day, in order to assert infant baptism, and conclude from it that baptism, which succeeded circumcision, ought not to be denied to little ones; or if you say that the fathers of Israel, together with their infants, were baptized when they passed through the bed of the Red Sea under the cloud: straightway you will hear them cry out, "All these were shadows and types, and therefore do not pertain to us, to whom the truth itself has been exhibited in Christ." Yet we admit that those things too were types and figures for the Israelites of the benefits which Christ was to bestow at the appointed time. But those types were not empty, containing nothing beyond some shadow. For just as they had true and by no means doubtful promises concerning Christ and the salvation of the human race to be restored through him, so the seals of those promises were also true, whatever was done in that whole Levitical worship, to say nothing now of other things that were done extraordinarily. And Paul taught in the words above that they received the same Christ as we do. For by the faith by which Abraham saw the day of Christ, by that same faith his posterity also saw him and embraced him. Since all these things were truly and really done, no one will deny that they too had the true Church of God, unless he wishes to be irrationally mad, or to invent some time in which there was altogether no Church. Rightly therefore the Apostle asserts that these things were so done to the fathers that God at the same time set forth public examples, from which all posterity might learn what ought to be done, or avoided, by those who desire to uphold the dignity of the Church and to escape the punishments laid down long ago for unbelievers and the disobedient. And so, by way of explanation, he adds: "But they were written for our admonition, on whom the ends of the ages have come."

units.la: Fines seculorum dicit nouissimam mundi ætatem, quæ alias nouissimum tempus, aut nouissi-ma hora dicitur. Ut enim homo certos ætatum gradus habet, per quos ad suæ vitæ finem decurrit: ita mundus quoq; aut totum illud mundi tempus, in ætates certas potest distingui, & singularum tam initium quàm finem ex scripturis possumus colligere. D. Augustinus ætates sex numerat, die-rum numerum secutus, quibus cœlum terramq;, & quæ his continentur, Deus condidit. Primam ab Adamo ad Noa siue diluuium extendit, quam infantiæ confert. Secundam à diluuio ad Abra-hamum usq; quam pueritiam dicit. Tertiam ab Abrahamo ad Davidem, quæ adolescentia mun-di ipsi esse videtur. Quartam à Davide ad captiuitatem Babylonicam, quæ virili ætati respondeat. Quintam à captiuitate illa usq; ad Christum. Inde sextam numerat, quæ finem habeat ipsam seculi huius consummationem, & quam sequatur æternum illud Sabbatu[?], in quo electi[?] quieté et gaudio cœlesti in æternum fruentur. Mihi tamen videtur totum mundi tempus secundum insigniores, quæ in illo factæ sunt, mutationes, commodius & simplicius in quatuor solummodo ætates posse diuidi. Quarum prima annos mille sexcentos & quinquaginta sex continet, qui ab origine rerum ad diluuium usq; effluxerunt. Hanc verè possumus mundi infantiam vel pueritiam dicere, quia & artes tunc primùm inuentæ sunt, & primis promissionibus de salute instauranda pij contenti, Deum quoq; ritu simplicissimo coluerunt. Secunda à diluuio ad Legis promulgationem usq; extenditur, quam non immeritò adolescentiam mundi dixeris. Tunc enim homines longè lateq; per omnes ter-ras diuisi, & gentium termini constituti sunt: tunc respub. cœperunt, & primæ Monarchiæ initium factum est: tunc denique fœdus salutis cum Abrahamo instauravit Deus, Messiæ genus & stirpem designauit, & futuræ uniuersalis redemptionis exemplum in liberatione populi sui ex Ægypto ex-hibuit. Tertiam ætatem Christus ipse ad suum usq; in carnem aduentum extendit, dicens: Lex & Prophetæ usq; ad Ioannem, ab eo tempore regnum Dei annunciatur. Fuit hæc mundi virilis ætas: quia tunc Dei voluntas scriptis comprehensa est, promissiones ceremonijs pluribus obsignatæ & Prophetarum varicinijs illustratæ sunt. Et ut ætatem virilem labores & pericula graviora comi-tantur: ita illud quoq; tempus multas grauissimasq; regnorum mutationes & totius orbis motus horribiles habuit. Sequitur hanc quarta ætas, quæ Filium Dei in carne manifestatum vidit, & quæ ad finem sæculorum usque durabit. Hanc nouissimam horam ( ut supra quoque annota-vimus) & plenitudinem temporis Apostoli vocant, eò quòd impletis iam omnibus quæ de huma-ni generis redemptione olim promissa & prædicta fuerunt, nihil restat præter postremum Christi aduentum, qui toti huius mundi machinæ finem imponet, atque conditionem omnem præsenti sæculi prorsus abolebit. Senectuti autem rectè conferetur, quia ut senibus diuturniores vitæ spes nulla esse potest, cùm & non procul absint à fine vitæ, & cursum suum assiduis curis, morbis & omnis generis molestiis accelerari sentiant: ita de mundo toto nihil porrò nobis possumus polliceri, quòd aut diu duraturus, aut eius conditio in melius commutanda sit, cùm in peius quotidie proficiat, adeoque in proprium exitium præceps ruat. De Hoc tempore Paulus in præsenti loquitur, & nos hæc diligentius annotamus, quia multum prodest frequenter cogitare, nos in fines sæculorum incidisse.
units.tr: By "the ends of the ages" he means the last age of the world, which elsewhere is called the last time or the last hour. For just as a man passes through certain stages of life on his way to the end of his life, so the world, or that whole time of the world, can be divided into certain ages, and from the Scriptures we can gather both the beginning and the end of each. Saint Augustine counts six ages, following the number of days in which God created heaven and earth and the things contained in them. He extends the first from Adam to Noah, or the Flood, and assigns it to infancy. The second, from the Flood to Abraham, he calls boyhood. The third, from Abraham to David, seems to be the adolescence of the world itself. The fourth, from David to the Babylonian captivity, corresponds to manhood. The fifth runs from that captivity to Christ. He then numbers a sixth, which has as its end the very consummation of this age, and which is followed by that eternal Sabbath, in which the elect enjoy heavenly rest and joy forever. It seems to me, however, that the whole time of the world can more conveniently and simply be divided, according to its more notable changes, into four ages only. The first of these contains 1656 years, which ran from the beginning of things to the Flood. This we can truly call the infancy or childhood of the world, because the arts were first invented then, and the godly, content with the first promises of salvation to be restored, worshiped God also with the simplest rite. The second extends from the Flood to the promulgation of the Law, and this you may not unreasonably call the adolescence of the world. For then men were scattered far and wide over all lands, and the boundaries of nations were established; then commonwealths began, and the first monarchies were founded; then at last God renewed the covenant of salvation with Abraham, designated the line and stock of the Messiah, and in the liberation of his people from Egypt set forth an example of the future universal redemption. Christ himself extended the third age to his coming in the flesh, saying, "The Law and the Prophets until John; from that time the kingdom of God is preached." This was the manly age of the world, because then the will of God was comprehended in writing, the promises were sealed by many ceremonies, and were illustrated by the prophecies of the Prophets. And just as manhood is accompanied by heavier labours and dangers, so that time too had many very grievous changes of kingdoms and dreadful upheavals of the whole world. There follows the fourth age, which has seen the Son of God manifested in the flesh, and which will endure until the end of the ages. This last hour (as we have also noted above) the Apostles call the fullness of time, because all things that were of old promised and foretold concerning the redemption of the human race have now been fulfilled, and nothing remains except the last coming of Christ, who will put an end to the whole machinery of this world and utterly abolish every condition of the present age. It is rightly compared to old age. Just as the old can have no longer hope of life, since they are not far from the end of life and feel their course being hastened by constant cares, sicknesses and every kind of trouble, so concerning the whole world we can promise ourselves nothing further: that it will last long, or that its condition is to be changed for the better. It advances daily for the worse, and so rushes headlong to its own destruction. Paul speaks of this time in the present passage, and we note these things more carefully because it is very profitable to think often that we have fallen upon the ends of the ages.

units.la: Primum enim admonet, ne offendamur mundi improbitate, nequitia, turbis, & periculosis omniumferè populorum atque rerum pub. mutationibus. Cur enim his offendamur, de quibus nos iam pridem Christus admonuit? Eius certè verba sunt de temporibus hisce: Multiplicabitur iniquitas, & refrigescet charitas multorum. Et cùm venerit Filius hominis, num reperturus est fidem in terra? Item: Audietis bella & rumores bellorum, videte ne turbemini: oportet enim omnia fieri, sed nondum est finis. Surget enim gens in gentem, & regnum in regnum: & erunt pestilentiæ & famis, & terræmotus in singulis locis. Hæc autem omnia principium sunt dolorum, &c. Idem verò in tantis malis eam inter homines securitatem regnaturam testatur, quam olim Noë & Lothi temporibus regnauisse Moses scribit. Cur ergo alicui nouum videatur, si quid huius hodie euenit? Aut cur miramur, si mundus hic iam senescens quotidie nouis vitiis laboret? Inter nos senectus ipsa morbus est, & quæcunque in rerum natura sunt, vetustate deteriora fiunt, & nos de mundo nobis aliquid melius pollicebimur, qui & Satanam principem habet, & totus in malo iacet, ut Apostoli verbis utar? Deinde nos ad vigilandum excitare debet ista consideratio. Quia enim hæc nouissima hora est, nescimus quando venturus sit Dei filius, ad cuius tribunal nos omnes sisti oportet. Procul certè abesse non poterit, cùm iam pridem plerâque impleta sint, quæ de signis nouissimum eius aduentu præcessuris Spiritus sanctus prædixit, & quæ adhuc reliqua sunt quotidie impleantur. Semper ergo in auribus nostris sonet vox eius: Vigilate, nescitis enim quando dominus veniet, sero, an medio noctis, an in gallicinio, an mane: Ne cùm veniret repente, inueniat vos dormientes. Quæ autem dico vobis, omnibus dico: Vigilate. Præterea consolationem quoque efficacissimam hinc petere licet, quando cogitamus, hæc quæ impijs & spem melioris vitæ ignorantibus terrorem incutiunt, mundi ad suum finem properantis indicia esse. Ex eò colligimus, neque diuturna esse posse mala, quibus nunc exercemur, neque nos procul à portu abesse, in quo quies nobis sempiterna obueniet. Ideo Christus dicebat: Cùm hæc fieri incipient, suspicite, et attollite capita vestra, quoniam appropinquat redemptio vestra. Ad cuius promissionis confirmationem facit, quod idem alibi ait; dies illos nonissimos decurtandos fore propter electos. Luc.21. Matth.24.
units.tr: First, he warns us not to be offended by the wickedness, iniquity, disturbances, and dangerous political upheavals of almost every people and every thing in the world. For why should we be offended by things about which Christ warned us long ago? These are surely his words about these times: "Iniquity will be multiplied, and the love of many will grow cold. And when the Son of man comes, will he find faith on earth?" Likewise: "You will hear of wars and rumours of wars; see that you are not troubled, for these things must happen, but the end is not yet. For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be pestilences, famines and earthquakes in various places. But all these things are the beginning of sorrows," and so on. He also testifies that in such great evils there will reign among men the same security that Moses writes reigned in the days of Noah and Lot. Why, then, should anything that happens today seem new to anyone? Or why do we wonder if this world, now growing old, suffers daily from new vices? Among us, old age is itself a disease, and whatever exists in nature grows worse with age. Shall we then promise ourselves something better from the world, which has Satan as its prince and lies wholly in evil, to use the Apostle's words? Next, this consideration ought to rouse us to watch. For since this is the last hour, we do not know when the Son of God will come, before whose judgment seat we must all stand. Certainly he cannot be far off, since most of the things the Holy Spirit foretold would precede his last coming as signs have long since been fulfilled, and what remains is being fulfilled every day. Let his voice therefore always sound in our ears: "Watch, for you do not know when the Lord will come, whether in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow, or in the morning; lest, coming suddenly, he find you sleeping. What I say to you, I say to all: watch." Moreover, we may also draw a most effective consolation from this, when we reflect that these things, which strike terror into the wicked who are ignorant of the hope of a better life, are signs of a world hastening to its end. From this we conclude that the evils with which we are now exercised cannot be lasting, nor are we far from the harbour in which everlasting rest will come to us. Therefore Christ said: "When these things begin to happen, look up and lift up your heads, for your redemption draws near." What he says elsewhere also confirms this promise: that those last days will be shortened for the sake of the elect. Luc. 21. Matth. 24.

units.la: Imprimis autem proderit vsum scripturæ sacræ observauisse, quem nobis Paulus hoc loco monstrat. Hæc enim non propter eos data est, qui iam olim mortui sunt, priusquam Moses historiam sacrâ literis mandaret (quid enim ad illos utilitatis inde redeat?) sed propter nos qui in vivis sa-mus[?], & quibus illa legere vel audire datur. In quem verò finem data est? Ad nostri admonitionem. In Græco νουθεσία scribitur, quæ eiusmodi admonitione significat, quā mens ipsa excitatur, ut de iis quæ dicuntur diligentius cogitet, & ad se omnia transferat, ijsq; ad doctrinam & vitæ institutionem utatur. Itaque uno verbo hic dicit Paulus, quod alibi pluribus explicat. Nam ad Romanos Cap.15. sic scribit: Quæ ante scripta sunt, in nostram doctrinam scripta sunt, ut per patientiam & consolationem Scripturarum spem habeamus. Et in posteriori ad Timotheum Cap.3. Tota Scriptura diuinitus est inspirata, & utilis ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem quæ est in iustitia: Ut perfectus sit homo Dei ad omne opus bonum perfecte instructus. In præsenti autem temporis circumstantia bonitatem Dei vehementer commendat. Est enim hoc singulare beneficium, quòd qui sciebat quæ aliquando futura essent rerum conditionobis priusquam essemus antidotum parauit, & de singulis admonuit, ne quid improuisum nobis accideret. Adde huic aliud, quòd nimirum scripturæ sacræ libros inter tot tamq; graues orbis terrarũ mutationes non sine miraculo in hunc vsq; diem seruauit, & eosdem in omnes linguas transferri vo-luit, ne aliqua gens per ignorantiã perire posset. Cœpit hoc fieri anno ante natum Christũ ducente-simo sexagesimo septimo, quando Ptolemæus Philadelphus, Ægypti rex, Hierosolyma accer-siuit Septuaginta interpretes, vt Veteris testamenti libros, quibus historiam certam rerum ab ipsa mundi origine gestarum contineri audiuerat, Græco sermone redderent. Instruxit Rex ille biblio-thecam totius mundi celeberrimam, in qua septingenta millia librorum fuisse historici tradunt. At illa post annos ducentos viginti quatuor tota flammis exusta in cineres abijt, & cùm tunc pror-sus interierint infiniti scriptores, quorum opera tot reges & principes seruata voluerunt, non tamen perierunt Mosis & Prophetarum libri, qui iam Græcè loquentes multorum passim manibus terebantur. Quòd si simul cogites, quàm multi libros iflos abolere conati sint olim, & quàm multi potentia & authoritate graues hoc ipsum hodie conentur, fatearis oportet, diuino numine eos con-seruari & indies per omnes linguas magis atq; magis diffundi.
units.tr: Above all, it will be profitable to observe the use of Holy Scripture, which Paul shows us in this place. For it was given not for those who died long ago, before Moses committed the sacred history to writing (for what use would it be to them?), but for us who are alive and to whom it is given to read or hear it. For what end was it given? For our admonition. In Greek it is written νουθεσία [nouthesia], which signifies an admonition by which the mind itself is stirred to think more carefully about what is said, to apply everything to itself, and to use it for teaching and the training of life. Thus Paul here says in one word what he explains at greater length elsewhere. For in Romans chapter 15 he writes: "Whatever was written before was written for our instruction, that through patience and the comfort of the Scriptures we might have hope." And in the second letter to Timothy, chapter 3: "All Scripture is divinely inspired and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work." In the present circumstances he commends very strongly the goodness of God. For this is a singular benefit: that he who knew what conditions would one day come upon us prepared a remedy before we existed, and warned us about each thing, lest anything befall us unforeseen. Add to this another thing: that he preserved the books of Holy Scripture, amid such great and grave upheavals of the world, not without a miracle, down to this day, and willed that they be translated into all languages, lest any nation perish through ignorance. This began to be done in the year 267 before the birth of Christ, when Ptolemy Philadelphus, king of Egypt, summoned the Seventy interpreters from Jerusalem to render the books of the Old Testament into Greek, for he had heard that they contained a certain history of things done from the very origin of the world. That king furnished the most famous library in the whole world, in which, historians report, there were seven hundred thousand books. But after two hundred and twenty-four years that library was entirely consumed by flames and went up in ashes. Although then countless writers perished, whose works so many kings and princes had wished to preserve, the books of Moses and the Prophets did not perish; already in Greek, they were handled everywhere by the hands of many. If you also consider how many have tried in the past to abolish these books, and how many, powerful and influential, try the same today, you must confess that they are preserved by divine power and are spread more and more every day through all tongues.

units.la: Admonent nos ista, vt tantum Dei beneficium agnoscamus, & in legendis scripturis simus diligentes. Id verò tunc demum cum fructu fiet, si ea in illis obseruemus, quæ ad nostram institutionem atq; admonitionem faciunt: non autem curiositati nostræ indulgendo circa ea occupemur, quæ nihil ad nos pertinent. Peccant in eo, qui propheta-rum oracula altius scrutantur, & ea ex illis eruere volunt, quæ nos scire noluit Deus, & quorum cognitio non inutilis modo, sed etiam noxia no-bis esset. Nostrum fuerit in hoc incumbere, vt ad vitæ vsum transferamus, quæ nos Scriptura docet. Quòd si quæ occurrunt obscuriora, & quæ de rebus futuris potius quàm præteritis aut præsentibus dicta videntur, tunc meminerimus, prophetias (quod Augustinus quoq; monuit) citius impleri, quàm intelligi. Quòd si opus erit vt quæ prius nos latebant intelligamus, non deerit nobis suo tempore Spiritus Domini, cuius reuelationem nos pio & obsequenti animo expectare decet. Interim sufficit vnus hic locus aduersus omnes phanaticorum clamores, qui Vetus testamenti nihil ad nos pertinere contendunt. Hos enim Paulo palàm contradicere notius est quàm vt demonstrari oporteat. Confutatur præterea eorum tyrannis & audacia, qui laicos (vt ipsi loquuntur) à lectione scripturarum arcent, & has in vulgares linguas transferri nolunt. Sunt hi generis humani hostes nocentissimi. Dum enim doctrinam verbi Dei eripiunt miseris, simul authores sunt, vt multi in-gnorantiæ tenebris incerti rerum oberrent atque pereant. Quod enim de Sadducæis Christus dicit, Erratis ignorantes scripturas: hoc ipsum de omnibus dicitur, qui absq; harum cognitione aliquid instituunt.
units.tr: These things admonish us to acknowledge so great a benefit of God and to be diligent in reading the Scriptures. This will be done with profit only if we observe in them those things which serve our instruction and admonition, and do not occupy ourselves, indulging our curiosity, with things that have nothing to do with us. They err who scrutinise the oracles of the prophets too deeply and wish to draw out of them things which God did not want us to know, and whose knowledge would be not only useless but harmful to us. Let it be our task to apply to the use of life what Scripture teaches us. But if any more obscure passages occur, which seem to speak of future things rather than past or present, then let us remember that prophecies (as Augustine also warned) are fulfilled sooner than they are understood. And if it is necessary that we understand what previously lay hidden from us, the Spirit of the Lord will not be wanting to us in his time, and we ought to await his revelation with a devout and obedient mind. Meanwhile, one passage is enough against all the clamours of the fanatics, who contend that the Old Testament has nothing to do with us. For it is better known that they openly contradict Paul than that it needs to be demonstrated. Moreover, the tyranny and audacity of those is refuted who keep the laity (as they themselves put it) from reading the Scriptures and are unwilling to have them translated into the vernacular tongues. These are the most harmful enemies of the human race. For while they snatch the teaching of God's Word from the wretched, they are at the same time the authors of the fact that many wander and perish, uncertain, in the darkness of ignorance. For what Christ says of the Sadducees, "You err, not knowing the Scriptures," is said of all who undertake anything without knowledge of them.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui exempla, quæ nuper recitauit, suo instituto & causæ præsenti applicat, dicens: Itaq; qui sibi videtur stare, videat ne cadat. Stare sibi videbantur, qui (vt cap. 8. audiuimus) inani scientiæ plenioris fiducia turgidi, se eò vsq; profecisse putabant, vt quàmuis ad idololatrarum sacra accederent, & eorundem epulis atq; ludis interessent, nihil tamen læderentur quoad fidem & conscientiam. Admonet ergo nos, ne ista perfuasione seipsos decipiant, sed cogitent potius, quid multis acciderit alijs, & quòd cùm homines sint, nihil humanum ab ipsis sit alienum. Quare sensus verborum est: Scio quæ sit quorundam inter vos fiducia, qui nihil minus animo cogitant quàm quòd à fide deficere, aut in idololatriam prolabi velint. Nam ad constantiam fidei plus satis instructos esse sibi persuadent. Sed velim illos in Israëlitarum exempla propius intueri. Annon enim hi quoq; sibi stare visi sunt? Neq; id immerito. Etenim Israëlem filium Dei primogenitum esse, & se Dei peculium & regnum sacerdotale dici audiebant. Fuit præterea in illis non vulgare fidei argumentum, quòd Mosem & Aaronem in re difficillima secuti sunt, quòd se cum vxoribus, paruulis liberis et senibus decrepitis itineri commiserunt ignoto, laboris pleno & cuius finem nemo vnquam viderat: quòd deniq; pendentes vtrinq; in sublime surgentium aquarum parietes subierunt. Adde his tot diuinæ virtutis & præsentiæ testimonia, Legis promulgationem maiestatis & horroris plenam, tot sacra & ritus, quæ singula eos in officio continere poterant, si animum attendere voluissent. Verumtamen quando rerum securi, suæ carnis cupiditatibus obsecuti sunt, hæc & alia infinita accidererunt, quæ modo commemorauimus. Ne ergo vos sitis confidentiores: sed vigilate diligenter, & salutem cum timore & tremore operemini, neq; vos eam aliter retinere posse cogitetis, quàm si ab omni etiam specie mali abstineatis.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who applies the examples he has just recited to his present purpose and cause, saying: "Therefore let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall." Those seemed to themselves to stand who, as we heard in chapter 8, puffed up with the vain confidence of fuller knowledge, thought they had advanced so far that, although they came to the rites of idolaters and took part in their feasts and games, they would suffer no harm to their faith or conscience. He therefore warns us not to deceive ourselves with this persuasion, but rather to consider what has happened to many others, and that, since they are men, nothing human is foreign to them. Hence the sense of the words is this: I know what confidence some of you have, who think of nothing less than falling from the faith or slipping into idolatry. For they persuade themselves that they are sufficiently equipped for the constancy of faith. But I would have them look more closely at the examples of the Israelites. Did not they too seem to themselves to stand? And not undeservedly. For they heard that Israel was the firstborn son of God, and that they were called God's own possession and a kingdom of priests. Moreover, there was in them no small proof of faith, in that they followed Moses and Aaron in a most difficult matter, that they committed themselves, with their wives, little children and decrepit old men, to an unknown journey full of toil, whose end no one had ever seen; and finally that they passed between the walls of water rising up on either side. Add to these so many testimonies of divine power and presence, the promulgation of the Law full of majesty and dread, and so many sacred rites, each of which could have kept them in their duty had they been willing to attend. Nevertheless, when they grew careless and yielded to the desires of their flesh, these things happened, along with the countless others we have just mentioned. Therefore do not be more confident: but watch diligently, and work out your salvation with fear and trembling, and do not think you can keep it in any other way than by abstaining from every appearance of evil.

units.la: Continet ergo locus iste generalem doctrinam, ne quis sibi ipsi aut viribus suis confidat, aut propter praesentem rerum suarum statum sibi in posterum quoq; omnia tuta polliceatur. Hinc e-nim securitas nascitur, quae nos diaboli insidijs exponit, & quae saepius praestantissimis Dei servis nocuit, ut in Davidis & Petri exemplis videmus. Ut enim in bellis victoriam, quae iam in ma-nibus est, amittere solent, qui securiores & remissiores facti hostibus rei gerendae occasionem prae-bent: ita plerunque praeter omnem expectationem diaboli artibus prosternuntur, qui adversus omne genus tentationis invictì stare putabantur. Quid vero de privatis hominibus dicere opus est, quando totis ecclesijs idem accidit? Nam si omnium seculorum historias evoluamus, Ecclesiam omni tempore plus damni ex otio quam ex persecutionibus accepisse patebit. His enim ad ardens defendendae veritatis studium omnes accenduntur, ut preces & omnes vires coniungant: illo autem pleriq; non modò remissiores fiunt, verumetiam aemulatione abrepti contentiones & dissensiones inte-stinas mouent, quae certum ecclesijs exitium pariunt. Semper ergo meminerimus quae nostra conditio sit. Carnem infirmam & ad lapsum procliuem esse Christus ipse testatur, ut spiritus ad officium omne promptus & velox sit. Accedit huic inte-stino malo Satan, qui quiescere non potest, sed Leonis rugientis instar oberrans indesinenter quaerit quem deuoret. Opem huic fert infelix mundus, qui varias tentationum species per secunda simul & adversa nobis obijcit. Quae omnia cum in semetipsis omnes experiantur, debet nos excitare horum consideratio, ne unquam somno aut securitati locum demus. Nunquam enim extra teli iactum sumus, quoad in hac carne viuimus: sed huius demum vinculis solutos beatae immortalitatis portus excipit.
units.tr: This passage therefore sets out a general teaching: no one should trust in himself or in his own strength, or promise himself that everything will be safe in future because of his present condition. From this false security arises a carelessness that exposes us to the snares of the devil, and it has often harmed the most excellent servants of God, as we see in the examples of David and Peter. In wars, those who grow too confident and careless, and so offer the enemy an opportunity to act, often lose a victory that is already in their hands. In the same way, beyond all expectation, by the arts of the devil, those are often overthrown who seemed to stand unconquered against every kind of temptation. Why should I speak of private individuals, when the same thing happens to whole churches? If we run through the histories of all ages, it will be plain that the Church has at all times suffered more harm from idleness than from persecutions. For persecutions kindle everyone to an ardent zeal for defending the truth, so that they join their prayers and all their strength. Idleness, on the other hand, not only makes most people more lax, but, carried away by rivalry, it stirs up quarrels and internal dissensions, which bring certain ruin to the churches. Let us therefore always remember what our condition is. Christ himself testifies that the flesh is weak and prone to fall, so that the spirit may be ready and quick for every duty. Satan adds to this inner evil; he cannot rest, but roams like a roaring lion, constantly seeking someone to devour. The unhappy world gives him help, presenting us with various kinds of temptation through both prosperity and adversity. Since everyone experiences all these things in themselves, the consideration of them ought to rouse us, so that we never give place to sleep or security. For as long as we live in this flesh we are never beyond the range of the weapon; only when loosed from its chains does the harbour of blessed immortality receive us.

units.la: At hic observabis interea, locum istum nequaquam iis patrocinari, qui hominem de gratia Dei & propria salute, quoad hic viuit, certum fieri posse negant. Quae doctrina ut divinae electionis certitudinem evertit: ita hominum fidem vehementer labefactat, & infirmis in fide desperationis argumenta suggerit, illis autem admodum quaestuosa est: quia hac territi infelices, ad illorum opem confugiunt, & ut ipsorum precibus atq; meritis post mortem quoq; iuvantur, illos magno pretio conducunt. At nihil huius docere voluit Apostolus, qui alibi salutem nostram certam & nulli periculo iacturae obnoxiam esse demonstrat. Facile autem fuerit istorum fallaciam deprehendere, si inter fiduciam distinguas, quam in salutis negotio homines concipiunt. Alia enim Dei promissionibus & gratia nititur, quam revera sanctam & salutarem, adhaec certam minimeq; fallacem dicere possumus. Concipi autem haec non potest ab hypocritis & carni addictis, sed a solis electis, qui fide supra omnem hominis sensum euecti, gratiam Dei vere degustant, & eius do-na ἀμεταμέλητα[?], id est, eiusmodi esse agnoscunt, quorum Deum nunquam possit poenitere. Ideo pleni fiducia cum Paulo clamant: Quis nos separabit a dilectione Dei, &c? Fiducia autem ista non securitatem parit, sed potius divinae gratiae sensu ita inflammatur, ut maius pietatis studium concipiat, neq; velit ab illo Deo hominem separari, in quo eum viuere & servari sentit. Altera fiducia est, qua propriis viribus & suorum operum dignitate atq; meritis homines nituntur, quae confidentia potius dici debet, eo quod ex inani opinione concepta animum inflat, & exitiali illa securitate implet, de qua paulo ante diximus. Et hi sunt, de quibus in praesenti Paulus loquitur. Hi enim sibi ipsis videntur stare, cum revera non stent, sed ex cereis plumis, instar Icari inter caelum & terras pendeant: quae etiam causa est, ut quo sublimius efferuntur, eo graviori lapsu ruant. Quia vero persuasio ista interdum apud electos quoq; locum invenit, ex cognato ipsis carnis vitio, ut ab ea sibi caveant, Apostolus admonet. At Sophistae nostri extra septa salientes, admonitionem istam ad sanctam illam fiduciam transferunt, & bis impij sunt, dum & Dei gratiam evacuant, & electos salutari illa gloriatione exultare prohibent, quae sola in tentationibus invictos, & toti mundo atq; principi eius admirandos reddit. Caeterum omissis impostoribus illis, hoc potius observemus, quod si admonitione tam graui opus habent, qui tam sibi ipsis quam aliis videntur stare, quid cum illis agendum erit, qui ne stant quidem in speciem, sed iampridem diffidentia & cupiditatum telis confossi iacent, & per omne scelus volutantur? In horum censu sunt auari raptores, quos totos sibi Mammon vindicauit: ebriosi canes, qui se totos Baccho consecrarunt: fornicatores item improbi, quibus Venus nefaria animum abstulit: quotquot deniq; abiecta pœnitentia in peccatis pergunt. His altiori tuba propheticas illas comminationes intonare oportet: Audite cæ-li, auscultate tellus, quoniam Dominus loquitur. Filios educaui & euexi, ipsi autem perfide de-fecerunt à me. Heu gentem scelestam, populum iniquitate onustum, semen malitiosum. Frons mulieris meretricis facta est tibi, renuisti erubescere. Num sic cadunt homines vt non resurgant? Num sic aliquis deflectit, vt non redeat? Quid fit ergo vt isti auertantur auersione tam pertinaci? &c. Haec (inquam) & alia huius generis merentur multi nostro seculo, qui tamen omnem seuerum disciplinam fastidiunt.
units.tr: Here, however, you will observe in the meantime that this passage in no way supports those who deny that a man can be made certain, while he lives here, of God's grace and of his own salvation. That doctrine overturns the certainty of divine election, and it greatly weakens people's faith, supplying the weak in faith with arguments for despair; yet it is very profitable to those others, because the wretched people, frightened by it, flee to their aid, and are helped, as they think, after death by their prayers and merits, and so hire them at a great price. But the Apostle wished to teach none of this, since elsewhere he shows that our salvation is sure and not liable to any danger of loss. It will be easy to detect the deceit of these men if you distinguish between the kinds of confidence that people have in the matter of salvation. For one kind rests on God's promises and grace; we can call this truly holy and saving, and moreover sure and by no means deceptive. Yet this confidence cannot be conceived by hypocrites and those given over to the flesh, but only by the elect, who, raised by faith above all human understanding, truly taste the grace of God and recognise his gifts as irrevocable [ἀμεταμέλητα], that is, of such a kind that God can never regret them. Therefore, full of confidence, they cry out with Paul: "Who shall separate us from the love of God?" (Rom. 8.35). This confidence does not produce security, but rather, through a sense of divine grace, it is so inflamed that it conceives a greater zeal for godliness, and does not wish that the man be separated from that God in whom he feels himself to live and be preserved. The other confidence is that by which men rely on their own powers and on the worth and merits of their works. This ought rather to be called presumption, because it puffs up the mind with an empty opinion and fills it with that deadly security of which we spoke a little before. These are the people of whom Paul speaks here. For they seem to themselves to stand, when in truth they do not stand, but hang between heaven and earth like Icarus on waxen wings. This is also the reason why the higher they are lifted up, the harder they fall. But because this persuasion sometimes finds a place even among the elect, the Apostle warns them to beware of it, since it springs from the corruption of the flesh that is in them as well. Our Sophists, however, leaping outside the fold, transfer this warning to that holy confidence; and they are doubly impious, since they both empty the grace of God and forbid the elect to rejoice in that saving boasting, which alone makes them invincible in temptations and admirable to the whole world and its prince. But, setting aside those impostors, let us rather observe this: if those who seem to stand as much to themselves as to others need so severe a warning, what shall be done with those who do not even seem to stand, but lie long since pierced through by diffidence and the darts of their lusts, and wallow in every sin? Among these are the greedy plunderers, whom Mammon has claimed wholly for himself; the drunken dogs, who have wholly consecrated themselves to Bacchus; likewise the wicked fornicators, whom accursed Venus has robbed of their minds; and, in short, all who, having cast off repentance, persist in their sins. To these the prophetic threats must be thundered with a louder trumpet: "Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord speaks. I have nourished and brought up children, but they have rebelled against me. Alas, a wicked nation, a people laden with iniquity, a malicious seed. The brow of a harlot is yours; you refused to blush" (Isa. 1.2–4; Jer. 3.3). "Do men fall so as not to rise again? Does anyone turn aside so as not to return? Why then do these turn away with so stubborn an aversion?" etc. These things, I say, and others of this kind, many in our age deserve to hear, who nevertheless despise all strict discipline.

units.la: Porrò ne horribili illa & graui exemplorum veterum commemoratione territi, de venia & salute propria desperarent, consolationem subijcit, qua eos in certam salutis spem erigit. Est hoc boni doctoris officium, vt (quod de Deo ipso scribitur) sic vulnera infligat conscientiis securus & confidentibus, vt simul medicinam & μαλάγματα[?] adhibeat ijs, quos iam territos & de gratia Dei solicitos esse videt. Hoc olim Nathanum. Isaiam & reliquos prophetas fecisse scimus. Sunt autem consolationis partes duae, quarum prior admissorum scelerum condonationem pollicetur, altera in futurum illis spem facit, ne quid grauius metuant. Primam his verbis absoluit: Tentatio vos non cepit, nisi humana: Id est, nihil vobis accidit, quam quod hominibus omnibus accidere solet, & cuius quotidiana sunt exempla. Humanum enim est errare, mundi insidijs circumueniri, & à carnis securitate opprimi. Haec enim omnia sanctissimis quoq; Dei seruis accidisse constat, quorum non vulgares lapsus in Scripturis leguntur. Videte modo, vt excusso errore in viam redeatis, & salua vobis erunt omnia.
units.tr: Moreover, lest they be frightened by that dreadful and grave recital of the examples of the ancients and despair of pardon and their own salvation, he adds a consolation, by which he raises them to a sure hope of salvation. It is the office of a good teacher, as is written of God himself, to inflict wounds on consciences that are secure and confident, and at the same time to apply soothing remedies [μαλάγματα] to those whom he sees already frightened and anxious about the grace of God. We know that Nathan, Isaiah and the other prophets did this of old. The consolation has two parts: the first promises the forgiveness of sins already committed, the second gives them hope for the future, so that they need fear nothing more grievous. He settles the first with these words: "No temptation has taken you except a human one" (1 Cor. 10.13). That is, nothing has befallen you except what usually befalls all men, and of which there are daily examples. For it is human to err, to be beset by the snares of the world, and to be overcome by the carelessness of the flesh. It is certain that all these things have happened even to the holiest servants of God, whose not ordinary falls are read of in the Scriptures. Only see to it that, once the error is shaken off, you return to the way, and all will be well for you.

units.la: Sunt verba haec nobis diligentius consideranda. Docent enim vt nostræ consolationi seruire debeat communis hominum fors, quoad peccata & poenas peccatorum. In peccatis quidem Satan fere nos ad desperationem adducere conatur, dum Deum nobis fingit durum & inexorabilem, simulq; eorum exemplis nos territat, qui in suis peccatis mortui miserè perierunt. At tunc ad alium exempla respicere proderit, & quidem sanctorum imprimis, qui & ipsi interdum carnis suæ desiderijs superati peccarunt. Ita videbimus nobis nihil quàm quod humanum est accidisse, & ex eo spem veniæ concipiemus, quæ mox confirmabitur, si diligentior promissionum Dei & meriti Christi consideratio accedat. Rursus, si quando aduersis nos exerceri contingat, similiter impatientiæ stimulis nos diabolus exagitat, vt nos omnium mortalium miserrimos & ipsi Deo inuisos esse clamemus. Sed tunc quoq; nobis in mentem veniat, tentationes eiusmodi humanas esse, & quàm multi eadem, aut etiam his graviora patiantur videamus: & sic facile patebit, nos iustam de Deo quiritandi occasionem nullam habere. Posset hæc doctrina latissimè diduci. At hodie in vtramq; partem peccatur. Alij enim vt scelera sua excusent, humanum quidem esse dicunt errare: sed ex eo colligunt, sibi nunquam in viam redeundum esse: quod iam non humanum, sed diaboli cum censeri debet. Alij vero solis ijs intenti, quæ ipsi patiuntur, de alijs hominibus nunquam cogitant: quæ perpetui murmuris & impatientiæ inexcusabilis causa est.
units.tr: These words must be considered more carefully by us. For they teach that the common lot of men should serve our consolation, both as regards sins and the punishments of sins. In sins indeed Satan tries almost always to bring us to despair, pretending to us that God is hard and unyielding, and at the same time terrifying us with the examples of those who died in their sins and perished wretchedly. But then it will be useful to look to others, and especially to the saints, who themselves sometimes sinned, overcome by the desires of their flesh. So we shall see that nothing has happened to us but what is human, and from this we shall conceive hope of pardon, which will be confirmed soon enough if we consider more carefully the promises of God and the merit of Christ. Again, if it should happen that we are exercised by adversities, the devil likewise goads us with the stings of impatience, so that we cry out that we are the most wretched of all mortals and hated by God himself. But then too let it come to mind that temptations of this kind are human, and let us see how many suffer the same things, or even heavier ones; and thus it will easily be plain that we have no just occasion to complain against God. This teaching could be spread out very widely. But today people sin in both directions. Some, to excuse their wicked deeds, say that it is indeed human to err, but from this they conclude that they must never return to the way; which ought now to be judged not human but of the devil. Others, intent only on those things which they themselves suffer, never think about other men; and this is the cause of perpetual murmuring and of an inexcusable impatience.

units.la: Sed alteram quoq; Consolationis huius partem videamus, quam sic proponit: Fidelis autem est Deus, qui non sinet vos tentari supra id quod poteritis: sed præstabit vnà cum tentatione etiam euasionem, vt possitis sufferre. Quibus verbis hoc dicere videtur: Quod si quid grauius vobis posthac accidat, tamen ne tunc quidem vos animum desponderé velim, sed in Dei naturam siue ingenium respicere. Est enim is fidelis, & proinde non sinet oneribus vos vllis grauari, quæ vestras vires superent. Comprehendit paucis hîce verbis Apostolus, quicquid de tentationibus aut afflictionibus qualibuscunq; dici potest. Primum de authore illarum admonet, quando dicit: Deus non sinet vos tentari. Ergo nihil nobis accidere poterit, nisi ita volente aut permittente Deo, cuius prouidentia res omnes gubernantur, qui capitis quoq; nostri pilos numeratos habet. Quod vnum si observent homines, iam neq; terrebuntur afflictionibus, neque aduersus Deum insolentius murmurabunt. Mox enim occurret, quod hic de Deo Paulus pronuntiat, Fidelem scilicet esse, Quâ voce non solùm veracem esse offendit in promissis, sed fidum quoque suorum custodem atque tutorem. Et hanc Dei fidem Dauid in Psalmo 103. pulchrè describit: Vt pater miseretur liberorum, rum, ita Deus miseretur timentium ipsum. Ipse enim nouit conditionem nostram, recordans quod sumus puluis. Et ipse Deus apud Isaiam dicit: Num obliuioni tradit mulier infantem suum, quò misereatur filij vteri sui? Sed esto, obliuiscantur illæ, ego tamen tui non obliuiscar. Ecce in manibus istis ambabus insculpsi te, &c. Quò etiam pertinet, quod per Zachariam clamat: Qui vos tangit, tangit pupillam oculi mei. Argumentum autem huius fidei & amoris plus quàm paterni (vt infinita alia transeamus) cumprimis euidens est, quòd ne Filio quidem suo vnigeni- to pepercit, sed pro nobis eum tradidit, nosque eius fecit cohæredes. Ex hoc autem duo colligit Apostolus. Primum, quòd non supra vires nos tentari sinat. Quod ab illo verissimè dici, frequen- ter ipsi experimur, in morbis maximè, qui interdum eò vsque augentur, vt vires nos deficere vi- deantur, sed tunc aliquam respirandi occasionem Deus ferè ex improuiso offert. Errant ergo, qui in suis viribus explorandis siue ponderandis curiosiores sunt, si quid ex Dei mandato est faciendum. Debet quidem illud fieri, si quid proprio animi motu aggredi volumus, ne idem nobis quod Miloni Crotoniatæ euenit. At si quid Deus iubet aut imponit, certò nobis persuasum esse debet, illum vires nostras non ignorare, nosq; nouis viribus armaturum esse, si oneri succumbentes videat. Itaque si quando nos grauiori tentationum pondere grauari sinit, nostro bono illud facit, vt propriæ infirmitatis sensu territi ardentiores ad illum preces fundamus, & in posterum minus simus confidentes. Alterum est, quòd cum tentatione faciat euasionem, vt & onus impositum sustinere, & cum illo ad metam nobis propositam euadere possimus. Ergo modum quoque tentationibus nostris Deus statuit, ne diutius quàm par est illis premamur. Vbi meminisse prodest, nos singulis momentis ad finem tendere, Deo item infinitas esse rationes, quibus viam euadendi nobis aperiat, etiamsi nos nullam cernere possimus. Qui enim per medium mare olim populum suum educere potuit, vt nos quoque per morbos, famem, gladios & ipsam mortem in tutum potest collocare. Quid, quòd non raro hostium opera in suis seruandis vtitur? Dauidem certè per Philisteos è Saulis manu liberatum fuisse legimus, cùm nulla alia effugij via pateret. Et huc pertinet, quod in Apocalypsi scribitur, de terra, quæ fluuium absorbuit, quem draco euomuerat, vt Ecclesiam abriperet atque extingueret. Fit hoc, quando homines terreni & carnales hostium Ecclesiæ consilia turbant, & eorundem vires frangunt, non quidem iuuandæ veritatis studio, sed suis affectibus duĉti. Sic olim Parthi multas ab Ecclesiæ ceruicibus persecutiones remouerunt. Et nostro seculo quot flumina impiorum, qui aduersus veritatem conspirauerant, vel Turcarum subitæ irruptiones, vel inter ipsos coniuratos exorta bella absorbuerunt? Debet horum consideratio nos excitare, vt tam fideli Deo ipsi quoque fideles simus: deinde constantes reddat in tentationibus, neque de euentu dubitemus. Ita enim afflictionum IESV CHRISTI socij efficimur, vt cum eodem olim regnemus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: But let us also look at the other part of this consolation, which he sets out thus: "God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear, but with the temptation will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it." By these words he seems to say: if anything more grievous happens to you hereafter, I would not have you lose heart even then, but look to the nature and disposition of God. For he is faithful, and therefore will not allow you to be weighed down by any burdens that exceed your strength. In a few words the Apostle here covers whatever can be said about temptations or afflictions of any kind. First, he warns us about their author, when he says: "God will not allow you to be tempted." Therefore nothing can befall us unless God wills or permits it, God by whose providence all things are governed, and who has even the hairs of our head numbered. If people would hold to this one truth, they would neither be terrified by afflictions nor murmur more insolently against God. For there immediately follows what Paul here says of God, namely that he is faithful. By this word he shows that God is not only true in his promises, but also a faithful keeper and guardian of his own. David in Psalm 103 describes this faithfulness of God beautifully: "As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear him. For he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust." And God himself says through Isaiah: "Can a woman forget her infant, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb? Yet even if these forget, yet I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands," and so on. To this also belongs what he cries out through Zechariah: "He who touches you touches the apple of my eye." Moreover, the proof of this faithfulness and of a love more than paternal (to pass over countless other instances) is especially clear in the fact that he did not spare even his only-begotten Son, but gave him up for us, and made us his co-heirs. From this, however, the Apostle draws two conclusions. First, that God does not allow us to be tempted beyond our strength. This we ourselves often experience to be most truly said, especially in sicknesses, which sometimes grow to such a point that our strength seems to fail us; but then God, almost unexpectedly, offers some opportunity to breathe again. Those therefore are wrong who are too curious in testing or weighing their own strength when something is to be done at God's command. Indeed, such testing ought to be made if we wish to undertake something by our own impulse, lest what happened to Milo of Croton should happen to us as well. But if God commands or imposes something, we ought to be firmly persuaded that he does not ignore our strength, and that he will arm us with new strength if he sees us giving way under the burden. Thus, if at any time he allows us to be weighed down by a heavier load of temptations, he does so for our good: that, struck with a sense of our own weakness, we may pour out more fervent prayers to him, and be less self-confident in time to come. The second conclusion is that, along with the temptation, he makes a way out, so that we may both bear the burden laid upon us and, with it, get through to the goal set before us. Therefore God also sets a limit to our temptations, so that we are not pressed by them longer than is fitting. Here it is useful to remember that we are moving toward the end every moment, and that God also has countless means by which he can open a way of escape for us, even though we cannot see any. For he who once was able to lead his people through the middle of the sea can also bring us safely through diseases, famine, swords, and death itself. Why should I mention that he often uses the work of enemies in preserving his own? We read that David was certainly delivered by the Philistines from the hand of Saul, when no other way of escape lay open. This also relates to what is written in the Apocalypse about the earth which swallowed up the river that the dragon had poured out, in order to snatch away and destroy the Church. This happens when earthly and carnal men throw the counsels of the enemies of the Church into confusion and break their strength, not indeed from zeal for helping the truth, but driven by their own passions. So in former times the Parthians removed many persecutions from the necks of the Church. And in our own age, how many rivers of the wicked, who had conspired against the truth, have been swallowed up either by sudden incursions of the Turks or by wars that arose among the conspirators themselves? The consideration of these things ought to stir us up, so that we may also be faithful to so faithful a God; and it makes us steadfast in temptations, so that we do not doubt the outcome. For thus we become partners in the afflictions of Jesus Christ, so that we may reign with him in time to come. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LII.
units.tr: HOMILY LII.

units.la: Quapropter dilecti mei, fugite ab idololatria. Vt peritis loquor, iudicate vos quod dico. Poculum benedictionis, cui benedicimus, nonne communio sanguinis Christi est? Panis, quem frangimus, nonne communio corporis Christi est? Quoniam vnus panis, vnum corpus multi sumus: nam omnes ex vno pane participamus.
units.tr: Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry. I speak as to wise men; judge for yourselves what I say. The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? For we being many are one bread, one body: for we are all partakers of that one bread.

units.la: Diligenter & prolixè Paulus aduersus eos disputat, qui ad superstitionem instituti idololatrarum epulis communicabant. Et vt maiori cum fructu disputationem perficiat, ab eorum argumentis exorsus est, quibus illi factum suum tuebantur. Præcipuum hic erat, quod absque conscientia idoli & nulla superstitiosa opinione imbuti accederent, ideoq; carnibus illis non aliter quàm vulgaribus & prophanis vescerentur. Alterum, quòd hoc omne facerent amicitiæ & pacis conseruandæ studio, ne cives suos & Romanos magistratus irritarent, sed his omnibus magi propitiis vterentur. Iisdem ergo rationibus illi pugnarunt, quibus hodie multi sua cum alienis superstitionibus consortia excusant. At Paulus ad illas sic respondet, ut quamuis per Concessionem conuiuia illa inter res medias aut indifferentes numerare videatur, ipsis tamen non conuenire debeat, ut illis intersint: eo quod Christiani hominis sit, fratrum infirmorum rationem habere, & a licitis quoq; interdum abstinere, ne quem illorum suo exemplo offendat. Quae admonitio ut efficacior esset, generalem doctrinam grauissimis veterum Israelitarum exemplis confirmatam interposuit, qua eorum confidentiam reprimit, qui se eo usq; profecisse arbitrabantur, ut nullum ex lapsu fidei periculum ipsis esset timendum. His absolutis, nunc propius cum illis congreditur, & id quod faciebant, reuera idololatriae speciem esse docet, & proinde etsi nullum praeterea scandalum accedat, nulla ratione excusari posse. Quamuis autem grauitas sceleris reprehensionem acerbissimam mereretur, eam tamen prudentia & lenitate sic temperat, ne qui inter illos erant morosiores, irritati prorsus resiliant.
units.tr: Paul disputes against those who joined in the feasts of idolaters, a practice established for superstition, diligently and at length. In order to carry out the argument to greater profit, he begins from the arguments by which they defended their conduct. The chief of these was that they took part without any thought of the idol and without being imbued with any superstitious opinion, and therefore ate that meat no differently from ordinary and profane food. The second was that they did all this out of a zeal for friendship and for keeping the peace, so as not to irritate their fellow citizens and the Roman magistrates, but that they would treat all of them more favourably. They therefore fought with the same arguments with which many today excuse their fellowship with the superstitions of others. But Paul answers them in such a way that, although those feasts may seem by concession to be counted among indifferent or neutral things, it is nonetheless not fitting for them to be present at them; because it belongs to a Christian to have regard for weak brothers, and sometimes to abstain even from lawful things, lest he offend any of them by his example. So that this admonition might be more effective, he inserted a general doctrine confirmed by the most serious examples of the ancient Israelites, by which he checks the confidence of those who thought they had advanced so far that there was no danger to them of falling from the faith. With these matters settled, he now engages them more closely, and teaches that what they were doing was in truth the appearance of idolatry, and therefore, even if no other scandal arose, it could be excused in no way. Although the gravity of the offence deserved a very bitter rebuke, he tempers it with such prudence and gentleness that those among them who were more stubborn should not be utterly provoked and turn back.

units.la: Propositio aut status omnium, quae sequuntur, est, ut ab omni cultu illicito aut idololatrico Christiani homines sibi caveant. Id vero non sine amica fraterni amoris significatione enuntiat, & ex illis, quae hucusque dicta sunt, sic infert: Quapropter dilecti mei, fugite ab idololatria. Quod perinde est, ac si dixisset: Cum demonstratum sit abunde, quam grauibus & horrendis exemplis Deus sui populi lenitatem & contumaciam olim punierit, & quo delapsi sint, qui omnibus verae pietatis adminiculis aduersus omne genus tentationum suffulti esse videbantur: nullius certe vobis socordiae locus reliquus est, sed omni cura atque studio vos anniti decet, ut ab idololatria procul fugiatis. Fugiendi autem verbo uti voluit, cum mitiora magisq; vulgaria non deessent, ut offenderet eos qui Christo nomen dederunt, idololatriam, ceu scelus nocentissimum, cum animi horrore detestari debere. Atqui non ignorabat, illos neque Diis gentium, neque simulachris eorum, quicquam tribuere: sed solis conuiuiis illis & ludis interesse, quae in sacris gentium (ut supra diximus) instituebantur. Nihilominus tamen idololatriam esse dicit, quam fugere & abominari debeant. Ubi nemo illam acerbius locutum esse putauerit. Nam dicti huius ratio (si rem penitus intueamur) facile patebit. Ut enim homo ex anima & corpore constat: ita utramq; partem Deus sibi vendicat. Duplex ergo Dei cultus est: Internus, qui in veritate & Spiritu consistit: Externus, qui circa ceremonias siue actiones externas versatur. Et quamuis interno Deus praecipue & vere delectetur, externum tamen propter nos instituit, ut per hunc animus, qui fere terrenis fluidijs immersus haeret, ad caelestia excitetur, & ut quam animo concepimus religionem, externis actionibus testemur. Quia ergo cultus ille externus ad fidei confessionem facit, quam necessariam esse alibi docuimus, nullo modo omitti debet. Eadem est idololatriae & superstitionum ratio, in quibus similiter simulachrorum cultum internum & externum videre licet. Internus enim est, quando praeter Deum unum & verum animo aliquid concipitur, cui fidimus, in quo speramus, & quod cultu diuino dignum esse sentimus. Externus multiplex est, & cum sacrificijs omnia alia continet, quae circa creaturarum & idolorum cultum fieri consueuerunt: qualia sunt, dies festi, epulae sacrae, ludi, genuflexiones, capitis apertio, insolitus aedium & viarum ornatus, & quaecunque alia sunt huius ordinis. Ut ergo Deum verum colere dicitur, qui cultui per illum instituto cum pijs operam dat, & ea facit, quibus ille internam religionem testari iussit: Ita idololatra reus est, quisquis idolorum cultui & idololatrarum sacris vel minima ex parte communicat. Et quamuis alter ille hypocrisi peccare possit, dum veri Dei cultum falso simulat, & animum ab eo alienum habet: hic tamen culpa non liberatur, etiamsi animo ab idolis abhorreat, quia corpus quoque ab horum cultu subducere, & soli Deo consecrare debemus. Huic enim negatur, quicquid simulachris impenditur. At in hoc Corinthij palam peccabant, cum conuiuijs & ludis interessent, quos idololatriae appendices, imo non minimam illius partem fuisse, supra ostendimus. Recte ergo clamat Paulus: Dilecti mei, fugite ab idololatria: & paucis verbis diserte docet, non posse eos veros Christianos agere, nisi totis animis abhorreant a superstitionibus universis, seque ipsos quoad corpus & animum puros & immaculatos seruent.
units.tr: The proposition, or the main point, of all that follows is that Christians should guard themselves against every unlawful or idolatrous worship. He states this not without a friendly expression of brotherly love, and from what has been said so far he draws the conclusion: Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry. This is just as if he had said: Since it has been shown abundantly by how grievous and dreadful examples God has in times past punished the leniency and obstinacy of his people, and into what falls those have come who seemed to be supported by all the aids of true piety against every kind of temptation, surely there is no place left for your carelessness, but it becomes you to strive with all care and zeal to flee far from idolatry. He chose the word flee, although milder and more common words were not lacking, so that he might shock those who had given their name to Christ, and make them detest idolatry, as the most harmful crime, with a horror of mind. Yet he was not unaware that those men attributed nothing to the gods of the Gentiles or to their images, but only took part in those feasts and games which were held in the sacred rites of the Gentiles, as we said above. Nevertheless he says that it is idolatry, which they ought to flee and abominate. No one would think he had spoken more bitterly about it. For the reason for this saying will easily be clear (if we look at the matter thoroughly). For just as a man consists of soul and body, so God claims both parts for himself. There is therefore a twofold worship of God: internal, which consists in truth and in the Spirit; external, which is concerned with ceremonies or outward actions. And although God is chiefly and truly delighted by the internal, nevertheless he has instituted the external for our sake, so that by this the mind, which clings almost immersed in earthly fluids, may be stirred up to heavenly things, and so that we may bear witness by outward actions to the religion which we have conceived in our mind. Since therefore that external worship serves the confession of faith, which we have shown elsewhere to be necessary, it ought in no way to be omitted. The same is the reasoning concerning idolatry and superstitions, in which one may likewise see the internal and external worship of images. For the internal is when, apart from the one and true God, something is conceived in the mind, in which we trust, in which we hope, and which we judge worthy of divine worship. The external is manifold, and includes along with sacrifices all the other things which are customarily done in the worship of creatures and idols: such as festival days, sacred feasts, games, genuflections, uncovering of the head, unusual decorations of houses and streets, and whatever else is of this kind. Therefore, just as he is said to worship the true God who gives his labour to the worship instituted by him along with the godly, and does those things by which he commanded that inward religion be attested, so he who shares even in the smallest part in the worship of idols and in the rites of idolaters is guilty of idolatry. And although the other may sin by hypocrisy, while he feigns the worship of the true God and has a mind alienated from it, yet this man is not freed from guilt, even if in his mind he abhors idols, because we ought also to withdraw the body from their worship and consecrate it to God alone. For whatever is bestowed on images is denied to him. But in this the Corinthians were openly sinning, when they were present at feasts and games, which we have shown above to be appendages of idolatry, indeed not the least part of it. Rightly therefore Paul cries out: My beloved, flee from idolatry; and in a few words he clearly teaches that they cannot be true Christians unless they abhor all superstitions with their whole souls, and keep themselves pure and unspotted in both body and mind.

units.la: Nos autem obseruemus, idem omnibus dici, qui hodie vel Missas in aliorum gratiam audiunt, vel quibuscunque alijs sacris Papisticis intersunt. Excusant quidem illi animum suum, & hunc & hunc ab omni superstitionis consensu alienum, uni autem vero Deo consecratum esse gloriantur. At quia Deo externum quoq; cultum debemus, non excusari possunt actiones externae, si alio dirigantur. Frustra autem illi puritatem animi jactant. Qui enim hanc vere custodiunt, iis visu & auditu intolerabile est, quicquid Deo displicere, & in veri cultus contumeliam fieri sciunt. Et ut quae vere casta & mariti sui amans est, nihil patienter audire potest, quo pudicitiam suam tentari sentit: ita qui animos suos Deo vere consecraverunt, iis horrori est quicquam videre, quo mens ab illo avocatur. Exempla, quae huc faciunt, multa & illustria in Martyribus habemus, qui eo vehementius in gentium idololatriam invehere soliti fuerunt olim, quo magis se ad illam sollicitari & urgeri sentiebant. Tantus certe in illis verae fidei & religionis ardor fuit, ut non levissima aliqua actiuncula, imo ne dissimulatione quidem aut silentio ignavo superstitiones idololatrarum probare voluerint.
units.tr: Let us note, however, that the same is said to all who today either hear Masses for the sake of others, or take part in whatever other Papistical rites. Those men indeed excuse their mind, and boast that this mind is free from all consent to superstition and consecrated to the one true God alone. But since we owe God external worship as well, outward actions cannot be excused if they are directed to another. Yet they vainly boast of the purity of their mind. For those who truly keep it find it intolerable to see or hear whatever they know displeases God and is done to the insult of true worship. And just as a woman who is truly chaste and loves her husband can endure nothing to be heard by which she feels her modesty is being tested, so those who have truly consecrated their souls to God are horrified to see anything by which the mind is drawn away from him. We have many clear and illustrious examples of this in the Martyrs, who were accustomed in times past to inveigh the more vehemently against the idolatry of the Gentiles the more they felt themselves provoked and urged towards it. Certainly there was so great a fervour of true faith and religion in them that they would not allow any slightest little action, or even dissimulation or cowardly silence, to appear to approve the superstitions of idolaters.

units.la: At ne praeter causam Corinthios idololatriae accusare putetur, argumentis grauissimis il-los convincere instituit, quae ut plus apud eos ponderis habeant, praefatiuncula utitur, qua benevolos simul & attentos facit. Dicit enim: Ut peritis loquor, Judicate vos quod dico. Peritos vocat, eo quod mysteriorum religionis nostrae, quae sub Sacramentis teguntur, non ignaros esse sciret. Simul autem sciolos illos, quos nimia suae scientiae fiducia inflabat, ut illa recte utantur admonet, & causae suae bonitatem demonstrat, quando eiusmodi esse docet, ut non vereatur judicium de ea illis ipsis deferre, quos accusabat. Itaque verborum sensus est: Scio vos intelligere quid in Sacramentis nostris profiteamur, & quid nominis Christiani professio requirat. Liberius ergo agentem ferte quaeso, & cur non feratis me, cum vos ipsos non detrectem huius causae judices habere? Equidem facile, quid hic statui debeat, intelligetis, si animi oculos aliquantisper a cupiditatum carnalium illecebris attollere libeat.
units.tr: But lest he be thought to accuse the Corinthians of idolatry without cause, he undertakes to convict them by the most serious arguments; and so that these may carry more weight with them, he uses a short preface, by which he makes them at once well-disposed and attentive. For he says: I speak as to wise men; judge for yourselves what I say. He calls them wise because he knew they were not ignorant of the mysteries of our religion, which are veiled under the sacraments. At the same time he warns those half-learned men, whom an excessive confidence in their own knowledge puffed up, to use that knowledge rightly, and he demonstrates the goodness of his cause, since he teaches that it is of such a kind that he does not hesitate to refer the judgement of it to the very men whom he was accusing. So the sense of the words is: I know that you understand what we profess in our sacraments, and what the profession of the Christian name requires. Please, then, bear with me as I speak more freely; and why should you not bear with me, since I do not refuse to have you as judges of this cause? Indeed you will easily understand what ought to be decided here, if you are willing to lift up the eyes of your mind for a little while from the allurements of carnal desires.

units.la: Suo autem exemplo nos docet Apostolus, verbum Dei in Ecclesia sic proponi & tractari debere, ut adversariis quoque notum fiat, nos verum & rectum docere. Nam nisi illorum animi convincantur, nihil unquam proficiemus. At hominem eo adducere tam difficile est, quam sepiam capere. Quia ut haec suo atramento se occultat, ut piscatoris manu elabatur: ita ex semetipso subinde aliquid parturit homo, quo tam sibi ipsi quam aliis nebulas offundat, & agnitam quoque veritatem obscuret, ne hanc fateri & se victum esse agnoscere cogatur. Hic igitur multo studio & exquisita diligentia opus est verbi administris, ut praehensum arctius stringant, & in lucem protrahant, ut proprii animi judicio damnetur, & ita resipiscat. Verumtamen eosdem animum probe intendere oportet, ne exemplum Pauli temere imitando seipsos & veritatem in periculum adducant. Fit hoc, quando de rebus controversis judicium illis defertur, quos eo usque in impietate profecisse constat, ut eis non grave sit propriae conscientiae dictatis contradicere. Observandum hoc propter eos, qui a nobis hodie contendunt, ut Episcoporum & Cardinalium judicio, qui in Conciliis ex Pontificis Romani authoritate confident[?], doctrinam nostram submittamus, neque hoc nobis debere iniquum aut grave videri, quando Paulus adversarios suos causae praesentis judices constituat. Atqui dispar multum est ratio. Primum enim Apostolo res fuit cum peritis rerum, & qui gentium Deos cum suis idolis jampridem damnaverant, sola autem levitate, vel incogitantia potius peccabant. Nobis autem cum illis lis est, qui veritatem vel ignorant, vel ignorare consulto & affectate volunt, ideoque superstitiones apertas contra propriae mentis sententiam perfricta fronte tuentur. Deinde hanc solam causam, quae ad ipsos potissimum pertinebat, illorum judicio defert: nostri autem illi hoc flagitant, ut totius doctrinae nostrae, imo Sacrae etiam Scripturae judices ipsos agnoscamus.
