Quod cum absque manifesta divini nominis contumelia, & totius Ecclesiae periculo fieri non possit, cautione & prudentia singulari opus est.
units.tr: The Apostle, by his own example, teaches us that the Word of God ought to be set forth and handled in the Church in such a way that even our opponents come to know that we teach what is true and right. For unless their minds are convinced, we will never make any progress. Yet bringing a person to that point is as hard as catching a cuttlefish. Just as the cuttlefish hides itself in its own ink and slips out of the fisherman's hand, so a man keeps producing some new thing from within himself, casting mists over himself and others, and obscuring even a truth he has recognised, so that he will not be forced to admit it and acknowledge that he has been beaten. Here, therefore, ministers of the Word need great care and exact diligence, so that they can grip the man tightly once he is caught and drag him into the light, and so that he is condemned by his own judgement and comes to repentance. Yet they must also take care not to put themselves and the truth in danger by rashly imitating Paul's example. This happens when the decision on disputed matters is handed over to those who are known to have advanced so far in impiety that it is no burden to them to contradict the dictates of their own conscience. This must be observed on account of those who today insist that we should submit our teaching to the judgement of the bishops and cardinals who meet in councils under the authority of the Roman Pontiff, and who say that this ought not to seem unfair or burdensome to us, since Paul appoints his adversaries as judges of the present cause. But the situation is very different. First, the Apostle had to deal with men skilled in these matters, who had long since condemned the gods of the nations along with their idols, and who sinned only through levity or, rather, thoughtlessness. We, however, have a dispute with those who either do not know the truth or deliberately and purposefully wish not to know it, and who therefore defend open superstitions against the judgement of their own minds with brazen faces. Second, Paul handed over to them only this one question, which pertained chiefly to them; our opponents, on the other hand, demand that we acknowledge them as judges of our whole doctrine, and even of Holy Scripture itself. Since this cannot be done without a plain insult to the divine name and danger to the whole Church, it requires singular caution and prudence.

units.la: Quid vero illud est, de quo Corinthios judicare jubet Apostolus? Argumentum ex usu Coenae Dominicae sumptum adducit, & ut quod dicit probe penes se expendant hortatur. Non est autem nobis hoc oscitanter praetereundum, quod ex Sacramentis argumentatur. Est enim hoc vulgare admodum Apostolis. Nam simili ratione cap. 1. per Baptismum eos confutat, qui in sectas scissi, alio quam solius Christi nomine gloriabantur. Et in epistola ad Romanos, eiusdem Baptismi mysterium interpretans docet, Christiani hominis esse, vt in Christi mortem sepultus peccato moriatur, & cum illo ad vitae nouitatem resurgat. Et ad Colossenses cum Baptismo circumcisionem coniungens, hoc ipsum grauiter suadet. Quid, quòd supra ex paschali epulo argumentum profert, quo monet, vt expurgato & procul eiecto veteris hominis siue peccati fermento, vitam omnem in azymis veritatis & synceritatis transfigant? Taceo infinitos alios locos. Quòd si veteris Ecclesiae Patrum siue doctorum libros euoluamus, huius generis multa esse inuenire. Nec enim solum vitae & morum praecepta ex Sacramentorum vsu deriuant, verumetiam contra haereticos ex illis rationes depromunt, quibus praecipua fidei nostrae capita, Christi diuinitatem mirum & veram incarnationem, adhaec vtriusque naturae in vna persona proprietates & inconfusam distinctionem, tuentur. Ex quibus apparet, Sacramentorum cognitionem olim omnibus vulgarem fuisse, & hodie etiam quae in illis fiunt, vulgo quibusuis Christum profitentibus nota esse debere. Quia enim vt nostrae tarditati succurrant data sunt, & ijsdem Deus suas promissiones obsignat, nosq; nostri officij admonet, deniq; cùm Christianae societatis (vt mox dicetur) tefera sint, nihil turpius, indignius & absurdius fingi potest, quàm si illorum sensum & vsum non intelligant, qui Christiani dici & haberi volunt. Confutatur ergo veteris & Apostolicae Ecclesiae exemplo Pontificum tyrannis, qui cùm validissimum fui regni praesidium in vulgi ignorantia & inani persuasione consistere sciant, Sacramenta quoque obscura & omnibus ignota esse voluerunt. Et vt populo persuaderent, nemini licere, vt ea penitius cognoscat, miracula in illis finxerunt, quae neque sensu neque ratione comprehendi possint, adhaec in eorum administratione lingua peregrina vsi sunt, cuiusfurros [?], gesticulationes & tantumnon saltationes theatricas admiscuerunt, quae apud rerum imperitos nihil praeter fluporem quendam & rei non intellectae stultam admirationem pariunt. Et ne ab aliquo iniuriarum genere abstineant, hanc suam audaciam Christi dicto excusant, qui Sanctum canibus proijci prohibuerit. Ergo illis canum loco sunt ij, in quorum gratiam aeternus Dei Filius non solum Sacramenta instituere, verumetiam proprium corpus & sanguinem pro peccatis eorum hostiam facere dignatus est. Et hi sunt, qui nos hodie sacrilegos dicunt, quoniam infelix mundus colit & adorat.
units.tr: But what is that matter on which the Apostle bids the Corinthians judge? He brings forward an argument taken from the use of the Lord's Supper, and urges them to weigh carefully what he says. We must not pass over lightly the fact that he argues from the sacraments. For this was quite common with the Apostles. In a similar way, in chapter 1, he refutes by means of Baptism those who, divided into sects, boasted in a name other than that of Christ alone. And in the epistle to the Romans, interpreting the mystery of this same Baptism, he teaches that it is the duty of a Christian man to be buried with Christ in his death, so that he dies to sin and rises with him to newness of life. And in the epistle to the Colossians, joining circumcision with Baptism, he urges this very thing earnestly. What of the fact that above he brings an argument from the Passover feast, by which he warns that, once the leaven of the old man or of sin has been purged out and cast far away, they should spend their whole life in the unleavened bread of truth and sincerity? I pass over countless other places. And if we turn over the books of the ancient Fathers or teachers of the Church, we will find many things of this kind. For they draw precepts of life and morals not only from the use of the sacraments, but also against heretics they draw from them arguments by which the chief articles of our faith are defended: Christ's wondrous divinity and true incarnation, and further the properties of each nature in the one person, and their unconfused distinction. From these things it is evident that the knowledge of the sacraments was once common to all, and that today too, what is done in them ought to be known by the common people, to anyone who professes Christ. For since they have been given to help our slowness, and God seals his promises by them, and since they also remind us of our duty, and finally since they are the tokens of Christian fellowship (as will be said shortly), nothing more shameful, unworthy and absurd can be imagined than for those who wish to be and be called Christians not to understand their meaning and use. The tyranny of the Popes is therefore refuted by the example of the ancient and Apostolic Church. Since they know that the strongest bulwark of their kingdom rests on the ignorance and empty persuasion of the common people, they have wished the sacraments also to be obscure and unknown to all. And in order to persuade the people that no one is allowed to know them more deeply, they have invented miracles in them that can be grasped neither by sense nor by reason; moreover, in their administration they use a foreign tongue and mix in gestures and almost theatrical dances, which among those unskilled in these things produce nothing but a certain stupor and a foolish admiration for a thing not understood. And so that they may abstain from no kind of outrage, they excuse this audacity by the saying of Christ, who forbade that what is holy be thrown to dogs. Therefore those for whose sake the eternal Son of God not only instituted the sacraments but also deigned to make his own body and blood a sacrifice for their sins are, in their eyes, in the place of dogs. And these are the men who today call us sacrilegious, because we refuse to worship what the wretched world worships.

units.la: Sed audiamus Pauli argumentum, cuius Antecedens in praesenti his verbis proponit: Poculum benedictionis, cui benedicimus, nonne communio sanguinis Christi est? Panis, quem frangimus, nonne communio corporis Christi est? Quibus postea infert: Non debetis ergo de poculo daemonum quoque bibere, neq; eorundem mensa edere. At nunc ante omnia obseruari debet, Latinos interpretes hic communicationis vocabulo vsos esse, quo rei alicuius in multos distributio significatur. Inde verò error exortus est, vt Paulum de corporis & sanguinis Christi distributione loqui plerique putauerint, quae per Ministri manus fiat. At Graeca vox κοινωνία, non communicationem, sed potius communionem significat, quam aliqui ex iure aut pacto inter se habent, & ideo rectius per Societatis vocabulum redditur. Et ita à Latinis quoque scriptoribus vsurpari constat: Notum est enim illud Ciceronis: Inter quos est communio Legis, inter eos communio iuris est. Itaque communio proprie societatem eorum significat, qui certis legibus & conditionibus rem aliquam participant, aut inter se communem habent. Sic communio aut societas mercatorum esse dicitur, qui eiusdem negotiationis socij lucrum & damnum, quod negotiando faciunt, ex pacto commune habent. Et milites communionem inter se habent, qui ea conditione armorum societatem inierunt, vt praeda vel spolia per ipsos acquisita in commune deponi, & in singulos distribui debeant. Neq; aliter Apostolos hac voce vti, multis testimonijs probari potest. Nam huius epistolae cap. 1. scribitur: Fidelis Deus, per quem vocati estis in communionem Filij ipsius, IESV CHRISTI. Quo loco Vetus interpres Societatem dixit. Et in epist. ad Galatas Iacobus, Cephas & Ioannes Paulo & Barnabae dextras κοινωνίας dediisse dicuntur societate nimirum his legibus inita, vt hi quidem inter gentes, ipsi verò inter Iudaeos Euangelium praedicarent. Et pro Philippensibus gratias agit Deo Apostolus, quòd in communionem Euangelij peruenerint, id est, bonorum omnium socij facti sint, quae nobis per illud in Christo offeruntur. Ioannes quoq; in sua Catholica cap.1. κοινωνίας vocem eodem sensu subinde repetit, & hunc finem Apostolis propositum esse ait: Vt & vos communionem habeatis nobiscum, & communio nostra sit cum Patre, & cum Filio eius IESV CHRISTO. Et mox: Si dixerimus nos κοινωνίαν, id est, societatem habere cum eo, & in tenebris incedimus, mentimur. Quibus adde quod Paulus in posteriore ad Corinth.: se à Macedonibus rogatum esse scribit, vt susciperet κοινωνίαν, id est societatem ministerij illius, per quod ipsi egenis in Syria fratribus praesidium pecuniarij submittere decreuerat. Sunt huius generis etiam alij loci, sed sufficiunt isti ad demonstrandum proprium huius vocabuli sensum. Quod si quis obijciat, Communicatione cum communione aut societate coniunctam esse, vt pote quae huius effectum sit: id nos minime negamus, imò in eo maximè gloriamur, quòd Christi corpus & sanguinem nobis communicari scimus. Communicationem vero illam non externis symbolis aut actioni, quae in Coena fit, alligandam esse dicimus, eò quòd tota spiritu perficiatur, & à nobis non aliter quàm fide possit percipi, sicuti suo loco pluribus dicetur.
units.tr: But let us hear the argument of Paul, whose antecedent he sets out in the present passage in these words: "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?" From which he afterwards infers: "You ought not therefore to drink of the cup of demons, nor to eat at their table." Now, first of all, it must be observed that the Latin translators have used here the word communicatio, by which the distribution of something among many is signified. From this error has arisen, so that many have thought Paul is speaking of the distribution of the body and blood of Christ, which is made by the hand of the minister. But the Greek word κοινωνία signifies not communicatio but rather communio, which some have with one another by right or by agreement, and therefore it is more properly rendered by the word societas (fellowship). And it is established that Latin writers too have used it in this sense: for that saying of Cicero is well known: "Among those between whom there is a communion of law, there is a communion of right." Thus communio properly signifies the fellowship of those who share something on certain laws and conditions, or hold something in common with one another. So we say that a communion or partnership of merchants exists, those who as partners in the same business hold by agreement the gain and loss which they make in trading in common. And soldiers have a communion among themselves, who on this condition enter a partnership in arms, that the booty or spoils acquired by them shall be placed in common and distributed to each. Nor can it be proved by many testimonies that the Apostles use this word in any other way. For in chapter 1 of this epistle it is written: "God is faithful, by whom you were called into the communion of his Son, Jesus Christ." In this place the Old interpreter rendered it societas. And in the epistle to the Galatians, it is said that James, Cephas and John gave to Paul and Barnabas the right hands of κοινωνία [fellowship], that is, they entered into a partnership under these terms: that these indeed should preach the Gospel among the Gentiles, and they themselves among the Jews. And the Apostle gives thanks to God for the Philippians, because they have come into the communion of the Gospel, that is, they have been made partners in all the good things which are offered to us in Christ through it. John too, in his catholic epistle, chapter 1, repeats the word κοινωνία in the same sense, and says that this was the aim set before the Apostles: "That you also may have communion with us, and our communion may be with the Father, and with his Son Jesus Christ." And soon after: "If we say that we have κοινωνία, that is, fellowship, with him, and walk in darkness, we lie." To these add that Paul, in the second epistle to the Corinthians, writes that he was asked by the Macedonians to receive the κοινωνία, that is, the partnership in that ministry by which they had decided to send financial help to the needy brethren in Syria. There are other places of this kind too, but these suffice to show the proper sense of this word. But if someone objects that communicatio is joined with communio or societas, as being its effect, we by no means deny this; indeed we glory especially in this, that we know the body and blood of Christ are communicated to us. But we say that this communication is not to be tied to the external symbols or to the action which takes place in the Supper, since it is wholly accomplished by the Spirit and can be received by us only by faith, as will be said in more detail in its proper place.

units.la: Vt autem nunc ad praesentis loci tractationem accedamus, Communio sanguinis & corporis Chri-sti dicitur credentium societas vel coetus & Ecclesia, qui cum Christi corpore & sanguine communionem habent, eò quòd his in cruce pro illis traditis redempti sint, & ijsdem alantur ad vitam aeternam. Cuius communionis non symbolum modò, sed vinculum quoq; externum, est Coena Dominica, & ideo ex hac argumentum suum Apostolus deducit. Vtq; hoc firmius sit & efficatius, de poculo & pane seorsim & distinctè loquitur, vtroq; nimirum symbolo eandem communionem denotari docens. Poculum (inquit) benedictionis, cui benedicimus, id est, poculum illud, quod ab ipso Christo nobis destinatum est, & quo nos ex eius institutione vtimur, vt illo cum solenni gratiarum actione ipsius beneficium celebremus, qui sanguinem suum pro nobis fundere, & ex peccati mortisq; seruitio redemptos sibi coheredes facere dignatus est: nonne est communio sanguinis eius? Similiter panis, quem in eadem Coena frangimus, nonne est communio corporis eius? Id est, nonne hoc ipso, quod ex vno poculo omnes bibimus, & ex vno pane omnes edimus, publicè testamur, nos ad vnam & eandem societatem aut coetum pertinere, & quidem ad eorum coetum, qui CHRISTI IESV corpore & sanguine redempti sunt, vt & cum illo & ipsi inter se communionem habeant? Et hunc verborum suorum sensum Paulus ipse ostendit, quando Expositionis loco subjicit: Quoniam vnus panis, vnum corpus multi sumus, id est, Quemadmodum vnus panis in Coena mystica apponitur, & hic ex multis granis vnus panis factus est: ita nos quoq; etsi multi, & quoad alias conditiones multiq; quoq; inter nos diuersi sumus, vnus tamen coetus, vna societas, vna Ecclesia, imò vnū corpus sumus. Et mox huius quoq; dicti rationem reddit: Quia ex vno pane participamus: ex eo nimirum, qui Christum, verum illum panem vitae, nobis repraesentat, & sigillum seu tessera est salutiferae illius communionis, quae nobis cum illo primùm, deinde in illo cum omnibus credentibus intercedit. Iam ergo verborum Pauli sensum tenemus, quae ab alijs aliter explicari non ignoro, sed hunc & simplicissimum & à superstitiosis multorum de Coena mystica opinionibus alienissimum esse, fatebuntur opinor, quicunque rem ipsam, de qua agitur, propius inspexerint.
units.tr: Now to come to the treatment of the present passage: the communion of the blood and body of Christ is called the fellowship or assembly of believers, the Church, who have communion with the body and blood of Christ, because they were redeemed by them when they were delivered up on the cross for them, and are nourished by them to eternal life. The Lord's Supper is not only a symbol of this communion but also its external bond, and so the Apostle derives his argument from it. To make this firmer and more effective, he speaks of the cup and the bread separately and distinctly, teaching that each symbol signifies the same communion. "The cup of blessing (he says) which we bless," that is, the cup which Christ himself appointed for us and which we use by his institution, so that with solemn thanksgiving we may celebrate his benefit, who deigned to shed his blood for us and to make us, redeemed from the slavery of sin and death, his co-heirs: is it not the communion of his blood? Likewise, "the bread which we break in the same Supper, is it not the communion of his body?" That is, is it not by this very fact, that we all drink from one cup and all eat from one bread, that we publicly testify that we belong to one and the same fellowship or assembly, and indeed to the assembly of those who have been redeemed by the body and blood of Jesus Christ, so that they may have communion both with him and among themselves? Paul himself shows this sense of his words when, by way of explanation, he adds: "Because we, being many, are one bread, one body." That is: just as one bread is set before us in the mystical Supper, and here one bread is made from many grains, so we also, though many, and in other respects many and diverse among ourselves, are nevertheless one assembly, one fellowship, one Church, indeed one body. And soon he gives the reason for this saying: "because we partake of one bread." This is that bread which represents to us Christ, the true bread of life, and is a seal or token of that saving communion which exists between us and him first, and then in him with all believers. So we hold the sense of Paul's words. I am not unaware that others explain them differently, but those who examine the matter itself more closely will, I think, admit that this sense is both the simplest and the most remote from the superstitious opinions of many about the mystical Supper.

units.la: Quoad vero institutum Apostoli, argumentum in ijs demum, quae proximè sequitur, absoluitur. Id vero eiusmodi est: Quicunq; cum Christi corpore & sanguine communionem habent, & in illo cum tota credentium multitudine vnum corpus facti sunt, ij sacris alienis nequaquam communicare debent, neq; etiam salua religione Christiana id facere possunt: Atqui vos cum Christi corpore & sanguine communionem habetis, & vnum corpus cum credentium Ecclesia iam pridem estis facti: Ergo nefas fuerit aliquam cum idololatrarū sacris habere communionem. Maiorem non probabat, quia omnibus satis nota est, & ad eius confirmationem hoc vnum sufficit, quòd Deus nos totos sibi vendicat, neq; aliqua nostri pars in nostro arbitrio est sita, vt eam ab illo vel in specie alienare liceat. Adde tamen & hoc, quod qui alienis sacris communicant, ij in vtramq; partem claudicando, primùm quidem professionem Christianam violant, deinde verò Ecclesiae vnitatem scindunt, & confusionis authores sunt, quae vt multos infirmiores offendit, ita tandem prophanū omnis religionis contemptum parit. In Minore autem probanda insistit, & huc totus hic locus pertinet. Nam proprio testimonio eos conuincit, quando communionem hanc cum Christo & Ecclesia eius publicè testantur, quoties ad mensam Domini cum alijs credentibus accedunt. Ita vero animos eorum magis ferit, & simul sceleris atrocitatem amplificat, quòd mensae daemoniorum (vt infra loquetur) participes fiant, qui cum Christi mensa communionem habere velint.
units.tr: As for the Apostle's argument, it is completed in what follows immediately. It runs thus: whoever have communion with the body and blood of Christ, and have become one body with him and with the whole multitude of believers, ought by no means to communicate in alien rites, nor can they do so while keeping the Christian religion. But you have communion with the body and blood of Christ, and have long since become one body with the Church of believers. Therefore it would be wrong to have any communion with the rites of idolaters. He does not prove the major premise, because it is well enough known to all; and to confirm it this one thing suffices, that God claims us wholly for himself, and no part of us lies at our own disposal so that it may be lawful to alienate it from him, even in appearance. Add also this: those who communicate in alien rites, limping to both sides, first violate the Christian profession, then split the unity of the Church, and become authors of confusion. This offends many weaker people, and in the end gives birth to a profane contempt of all religion. But he dwells on proving the minor premise, and this whole passage pertains to that. For he convicts them by their own testimony, when they publicly attest this communion with Christ and his Church, as often as they approach the Lord's table with other believers. He wounds their minds all the more, and at the same time magnifies the atrocity of the crime, by saying that they become partakers of the tables of demons (as he will say below), when they wish to have communion with the table of Christ.

units.la: Est autem totus hic locus multa consideratione dignissimus, eò quòd præcipua Ecclesiae my-steria continet, ex quibus & Sacramentorum proprius usus, & universa salus nostra dependet. Et primò quidem admonemur, credentium omnium unam modò esse Ecclesiam, quae ideo in Symbolo Apostolico Catholica, id est, universalis dicitur, quòd ad eius societatem omnes omnium nationum homines pertineant, quotquot eam fidem profitentur, quae in illius articulis traditur. Et hoc illud est, quod vetustissimus scriptor Irenaeus, Barbaros quoq; & ab omni literarū cognitione alienos, qui ex Apostolorum traditione ita credunt & sentiunt, Ecclesiae germana membra esse, & Deo probari scribit. Admonet hoc, quàm diligenter sibi à sectis cauere debeant, qui Ecclesiae titulo gloriantur. Quia enim haec (ut diximus) una est, imò corpus unum est, ipsa quidem lacerari non poterit, ab eius autem societate separentur oportet, quicunque in sectas abeunt. Ab ea autem separari non possumus, nisi etiam bonorum tam corporalium quàm spiritualium, quae credentibus communia sunt, participatione nosmetipsos spoliemus.
units.tr: This whole passage is most worthy of careful consideration, because it contains the principal mysteries of the Church, on which both the proper use of the Sacraments and our whole salvation depend. First, we are reminded that there is only one Church of all believers. It is therefore called catholic, that is universal, in the Apostles' Creed, because all men of all nations belong to its fellowship, as many as profess that faith which is set out in its articles. This is what the very ancient writer Irenaeus means when he writes that barbarians too, and those alien from all knowledge of letters, who believe and think according to the tradition of the Apostles, are genuine members of the Church and are approved by God. This teaches how carefully those who glory in the title of Church ought to guard themselves against sects. For since this Church is one (as we have said), indeed one body, it cannot itself be torn; but those who go off into sects must necessarily be separated from its fellowship. Nor can we be separated from it unless we also strip ourselves of participation in the goods, both bodily and spiritual, which are common to believers.

units.la: Secundò vinculum unitatis aut communionis illius verum & internum nobis in Christo mon-stratur, qui corporis & sanguinis sui pretio redemptos ita sibi con[?]fecrat & unit, ut ijdem inter se quoque per unum & eundem spiritum coalescant. Quæ causa est, quòd ille non fundamentum modò ecclesiae, verumetiam angularis lapis, & quidem supremus, imò caput ipsum dicitur: ut ni-mirum eum esse sciamus, qui Ecclesiae membra omnia, summa, media, infima, inter se commodissi-mè connectit, & eadem suo spiritu vivificat & gubernat. Exponit mysterium hoc Paulus dili-genter in Epistola ad Ephesios his verbis: Christus est caput, ex quo totum corpus congruenter coagmentatum, & compactum per omnes suppeditatas commissuras, ex vi intus agente pro mensura uniuscuiusque membri, incrementum capit corpori conveniens, ad suiipsius extructionem per charitatem. Ex quibus satis constat, nos non posse inter nos coalescere, nisi singuli prius Christo uniantur, adeoque incorporentur: quod non alia ratione fieri potest, quàm per fidem, quæ ita nos ei inserit, ut ipse in nobis agat, & nos in illo vivamus. Id verò ut consolationem dulcissi-mam affert piis & vere credentibus (quomodo enim de salute sua dubitent, aut mundi conatibus sive minis terreantur, qui se Christi membra esse sciunt) ita omnes eos arguit, qui ecclesiae membra dici & haberi volunt, ita verò vivunt, ut se à Christo & eius spiritu alienissimos esse ni-mis aperte testentur. Putrescunt membra, in quibus vitales spiritus agere desinunt, & qui non totum corpus perire volunt, ea resecare solent: Ita qui Christi spiritu non reguntur, ij neque vi-tam in seipsis habent, neque pro membris suis eos ille agnoscit, sed procul abiectos æterni ignis supplicio multat.
units.tr: Secondly, the true and inward bond of this unity or communion is shown to us in Christ, who so consecrates and unites to himself those redeemed by the price of his body and blood that they also grow together with one another through one and the same Spirit. This is why he is called not only the foundation of the Church but also the corner stone, and indeed the chief, nay the very head: so that we may know him to be the one who most fittingly connects all the members of the Church, high, middle and low, with one another, and enlivens and governs them all by his Spirit. Paul explains this mystery diligently in the Epistle to the Ephesians, in these words: "Christ is the head, from whom the whole body, fitly framed and knit together through every joint that supplies, by the working of each part in due measure, makes the increase of the body, to the building up of itself in love." From these words it is clear enough that we cannot grow together among ourselves unless each of us is first united to Christ and so incorporated into him. This cannot be done in any other way than through faith, which so engrafts us into him that he works in us and we live in him. This indeed brings the sweetest consolation to the pious and truly believing (for how could they doubt their salvation, or be terrified by the efforts or threats of the world, when they know themselves to be members of Christ?). And it accuses all those who wish to be called and considered members of the Church, yet live in such a way as to testify all too plainly that they are utterly alien from Christ and his Spirit. Members rot in which the vital spirits cease to act, and those who wish the whole body not to perish are accustomed to cut such members away. So those who are not ruled by the Spirit of Christ neither have life in themselves, nor does he acknowledge them as his members; casting them far away, he punishes them with the torment of eternal fire.

units.la: Cæterum quia homines sumus, qui externis rebus duci & moveri solent, tam in colligenda quàm conservanda Ecclesia sua externis ritibus atque symbolis utitur. Nam ut D. Augu-stinus contra Faustum Manichaeum scribit: In nullum nomen religionis, seu verum seu falsum, coagulari homines possunt, nisi aliquo signaculorum vel Sacramentorum visibilium consortio colligentur: quorum Sacramentorum vis inenarrabiliter valet plurimum: & ideo contempta sacrilegos facit. Impiè quippe contemnitur, sine qua non potest perfici pietas. Et sanè si omnium gentium historias evoluamus, nulla fuit unquam, quæ non certis quibusdam ritibus sive cæremoniis in religionis eiusdem communionem vel societatem externè coaluerit. Et habuit olim vetus Ecclesia sub Mose circumcisionem, Paschale epulum, dies festos & sacrificia, quæ omnia unita-tis symbola erant, ne in diversos greges distraherentur: & imprimis hoc faciebat, quod uno templo & uno altari contentos esse voluit Deus, ne ipse etiam religionis promovendæ zelus schisma aut sectas inveheret. In novo autem testamento vetera quidem illa sublata sunt, quia quæ illis adumbrabantur Christus adventu suo impleuit, alia autem instituta sunt (ut rursus Augustini verbis utar) virtute maiora, utilitate meliora, actu faciliora, numero pauciora, Baptismus nimirum & Cœna mystica. Quæ veteribus efficaciora & utiliora dicit Augustinus, quia quæ illa futura adumbrabantur, ea nostris hisce iam exhibita & præstita esse docentur. At si verum & proprium Sacramentorum usum spectes, idem nostrorum est, qui olim veterum fuit, & quem tribus capitibus completi possumus. Primò enim Dei promissiones & secundum has præstitum in CHRISTO IESV humanae redemptionis beneficium, communionem denique illam indissolubilem, quam cum Christo, vt membra cum capite suo habent obsignant. Quod quia non imaginariè, sed verè faciunt, fidem simul confirmant, & fidei contemplatione nobis præsentia sistunt ea, quæ maximis locorum spatijs distant. Secundo gratiarum actioni seruiunt, de quo Chri-stus in Cænæ suæ institutione diserte loquitur, quando his dixit: Hoc facite in mei commemorationem. Quæ verba Paulus sic exponit: Quotiescunque ederitis panem hunc, & poculum hoc bi-beritis, mortem Domini annuntiate vsquequo venerit. Ideo Paulus poculum benedictionis dixit, & veteres Cœnam totam ab hoc vsu Eucharistiam vocarunt, quod Latinis Gratiarum actio-nem significat. Et panum benedictionis meminit Socrates lib.7. cap.12. de Chrysantho Nouatianorum Episcopo loquens. Quia autem gratiarum actio Deo gratissimæ victimæ instar est, ijdem frequenter Sacrificij nomen Cœnæ tribuunt, non quòd ibi Christum aut quiduis aliud pro peccatis nostris offerri crediderint, sed quòd exhibitum salutis beneficium sacrificio laudis cele-brari scirent. Continet hic Cœnæ vsus confessionem publicam fidei, quando nos CHRISTVM IESVM redemptorem & seruatorem nostrum agnoscere profitemur: simulque admonet, ne alienis sacris communicemus.
units.tr: Moreover, since we are men, who are wont to be led and moved by external things, he uses external rites and symbols both in gathering and in preserving his Church. For as St Augustine writes against the Manichaean Faustus, men cannot be gathered into any name of religion, whether true or false, unless they are brought together by some partnership in visible signs or sacraments. The power of these sacraments is ineffably great, and therefore contempt for them makes men sacrilegious: for that is impiously despised without which piety cannot be made perfect. Indeed, if we unroll the histories of all nations, there has never been one which has not come together outwardly into communion or fellowship of its religion by certain rites or ceremonies. The old Church under Moses had circumcision, the Passover feast, festal days and sacrifices, all of which were symbols of unity, lest the people be scattered into divided flocks. Above all, God did this when he wished them to be content with one temple and one altar, lest even zeal for promoting religion should bring in schism or sects. In the New Testament those old things were indeed taken away, because Christ by his coming fulfilled what they foreshadowed; but other things were instituted, (to use Augustine's words again) greater in power, better in usefulness, easier in practice, fewer in number: namely Baptism and the mystical Supper. Augustine says these are more effective and useful than the old rites, because those things which were foreshadowed as future are taught to have now been exhibited and accomplished in these. But if you regard the true and proper use of the Sacraments, it is the same for us as it once was for the ancients, and it can be summed up under three heads. First, they seal God's promises, and according to these the benefit of human redemption accomplished in Jesus Christ, and finally that indissoluble communion, which they have with Christ as members with their head. Because they do this not imaginarily but truly, they at the same time confirm faith, and by the contemplation of faith they set before us as present those things which are separated by the greatest spaces of place. Secondly, they serve thanksgiving, about which Christ speaks plainly in the institution of his Supper, when he said to them: "Do this in remembrance of me." Paul explains these words thus: "As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes." Therefore Paul called it the cup of blessing, and the ancients called the whole Supper from this use Eucharist, which in Latin means thanksgiving. Socrates, in book 7, chapter 12, speaking of Chrysanthus, bishop of the Novatians, also mentions the blessing of the bread. And because thanksgiving is like a most pleasing sacrifice to God, the same writers often give the name of sacrifice to the Supper: not because they believed that Christ or anything else is offered there for our sins, but because they knew that the benefit of salvation which has been exhibited is celebrated with a sacrifice of praise. This use of the Supper contains a public confession of faith, when we profess that we acknowledge Jesus Christ as our Redeemer and Saviour; and at the same time it admonishes us not to communicate in alien rites.

units.la: Postremò Sacramenta Ecclesiam visibiliter colligunt, vt modò ex Augustino docuimus. Etenim per Baptismum in huius societatem adoptantur, quicunque huius membra sunt: & ijdem postea societatis illius & communionis studium publicè testari solent, quoties cum alijs credentibus ex vno eodemque pane edunt, & ex eodem poculo bibunt. Quod si verè & non fucato animo faciant, verè etiam membra corporis Christi sunt, & eius spiritu viuunt. Ideo D. Augustinus, cum hæc Pauli verba adduxisset, Vnus panis, vnum corpus multi sumus, subitò exclamat: O Sacramentum pietatis, ô signum vnitatis, ô vinculum charitatis. Qui vult viuere, habet vbi viuat, habet vnde viuat: accedat, credat, incorporetur vt viuificetur, &c.
units.tr: Lastly, the sacraments visibly gather the Church together, as we have just taught from Augustine. For through Baptism all who are its members are adopted into this fellowship; and afterwards they are wont to bear public witness to their fellowship and communion whenever they eat from the one and the same bread with other believers and drink from the same cup. If they do this truly and with an unfeigned heart, they are truly members of the body of Christ and live by his Spirit. Therefore Augustine, when he had quoted these words of Paul, "We, being many, are one bread, one body," suddenly exclaims: "O sacrament of godliness, O sign of unity, O bond of charity! He who wishes to live has a place where he may live, has something from which he may live: let him draw near, let him believe, let him be incorporated that he may be quickened," and so on.

units.la: Ista verò eorum sententiam confutant, qui cum Christum sola fide apprehendi audiunt, mox Sacramenta pro inutilibus atque superuacuis negligunt. Gloriantur quidem illi de fidei virtute, sed à fide se alienissimos esse produnt, cum ea contemnant, quæ vt fidei exercitium & nostræ in ipso communionis externum vinculum sint, Christus instituit. Quid verò de illis dicemus, qui non contenti ecclesiam factiosis Lutheranorum, Zuinglianorum & Caluinistarum nominibus in sectas scidisse, ipsa Cœna, quæ Christianæ communionis vinculum esse debebat, ad contentiones instaurandas atque fouendas abutuntur? Dedit horum intemperies plus mali ecclesiæ, quàm illis piorum lachrymis pro merito deplorari posset. Vtinam illis vel nunc tandem illud Pauli in mentem veniat: Si alius alium mordetis & deuoratis, videte ne vicissim alius ab alio consumamini. Agnoscant ergo singuli ineffabile Dei beneficium, qui nos Filij sui vnigeniti morte redimere, & in hoc vnum corpus facere dignatus est. Tueantur ergo huius corporis vnitatem, neque alienis sacris se polluant: sed vnum IESVM CHRISTVM salutis suæ authorem agnoscant, huic vni fidant, hunc colant & obseruent, vt illius spiritu viuant, & cum eodem in cœlis regnent: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: But those who hear that Christ is apprehended by faith alone, and at once neglect the sacraments as useless and superfluous, refute this opinion of theirs. Indeed they boast of the power of faith, but they show themselves most alien to faith when they despise the things which Christ instituted as the exercise of faith and the outward bond of our communion in him. But what shall we say of those who, not content that the Church has been torn into sects by the factious names of Lutherans, Zwinglians and Calvinists, misuse the Lord's Supper itself, which ought to be the bond of Christian communion, to stir up and foster quarrels? The intemperance of these men has done the Church more harm than the tears of the godly could lament as it deserves. Would that Paul's words might now at last come to their minds: "If you bite and devour one another, take heed that you be not consumed by one another." Let each one therefore acknowledge the unspeakable benefit of God, who has deigned to redeem us by the death of his only-begotten Son and to make us into this one body. Let them therefore guard the unity of this body, and not defile themselves with strange rites; but let them acknowledge the one Jesus Christ as the author of their salvation, trust in him alone, worship and observe him, that they may live by his Spirit and reign with him in heaven, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LIII.
units.tr: HOMILY LIII.

units.la: Videte Israelem, qui est secundum carnem: Nonne qui edunt victimas, participes sunt altaris? Quid ergo dico? idolum aliquid esse, aut quod idolis immolatum est, aliquid esse? Imò quæ immolant gentes, dæmonijs immolant, & non Deo: nolim autem vos participes dæmoniorum esse. Non potestis poculum Domini bibere, & poculum dæmoniorum: non potestis mensæ Domini participes esse, & mensæ dæmoniorum. An prouocamus ad æmulationem Dominum? num validiores illo sumus?
units.tr: Behold Israel after the flesh: are not they which eat of the sacrifices partakers of the altar? What say I then? that the idol is any thing, or that which is offered to idols is any thing? But I say, that the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils, and not to God: and I would not that ye should have fellowship with devils. Ye cannot drink the cup of the Lord, and the cup of devils: ye cannot be partakers of the Lord's table, and of the table of devils. Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? are we stronger than he?

units.la: ETsi Deus hominem ab initio rerum statim ad cultum suum destinarit, & religio (vt La-ctantius & alij veterum rectè definierunt) sola verè proprium illud sit hominis, quo à brutis animalibus distinguitur: non tamen alia in re frequentius & turpius, quàm in illa, errari con-sueuit. Causa errorum est, quòd plerique carnis rationem sequuntur, quae non modò Deos falsos concipiunt, & cultus quoque ex semetipsa quotidie nouos fingit, verumetiam suadet, ut religionem ex hominum arbitrio & priuata vtilitate metiamur, ideoq; in aliorum gratiam, quorum fauor & amicitia nobis commoda & necessaria videtur, multa admittamus, quae verum Dei cultum corrumpunt, aut etiam omnino euertunt. Peccant in eo multi hodie, & maxima fere illorum secta est, quibus stultum videtur ad vnam eandemque religionis formam omnes homines astringere velle, cum in vnaquaque Deus coli & placari possit. Ita vero religionem inter res medias & indifferentes numerant, in quibus licet pro nostro arbitrio ludere: quod non aliud est, quàm religionem omnem tollere, vt alibi demonstrauimus. Et in illo Corinthij quoque vehementer falsi sunt. Vt enim ethnicis & idololatris, quibus permixti viuebant, magis propitijs vterentur, ad sacrificiorum epulas accedebant, idque non sine graui infirmorum scandalo. Et habebant isti eadem plane argumenta, quibus hodie sese excusant, qui papisticis sacris communicare non verentur. Sed Paulus omnia illa graviter admodum confutat, & nuper demonstrare coepit, salua religione fieri non posse, vt qui Christo per fidem insiti, Ecclesiae Sacramentis communicant, alienorum quoque sacrorum sese participes faciant. Id vero in praesenti amplius confirmat, & ita huius argumenti tractationem concludit.
units.tr: Although God from the beginning of the world appointed man for his own worship, and religion (as Lactantius and other ancient writers rightly defined it) is alone truly the proper mark of man, by which he is distinguished from the brute animals, yet in no other matter do men commonly err more frequently and more shamefully than in this one. The cause of these errors is that most people follow the reasoning of the flesh, which not only conceives false gods and daily devises new forms of worship out of itself, but also persuades us to measure religion by human judgement and private advantage. And so, for the sake of others whose favour and friendship seem useful and necessary to us, we admit many things which corrupt, or even utterly overthrow, the true worship of God. Many today sin in this way, and almost the greatest sect of them are those who think it foolish to bind all men to one and the same form of religion, since God can be worshipped and appeased in every form. Thus they count religion among things indifferent and neutral, with which one may play as one pleases; and this is nothing other than to abolish all religion, as I have shown elsewhere. The Corinthians too were grievously mistaken in this matter. In order to be on better terms with the heathen and idolaters among whom they lived, they attended the feasts of the sacrifices, and this not without grave offence to the weak. They had exactly the same arguments with which those today excuse themselves who do not hesitate to take part in Papist rites. But Paul refutes all those arguments most severely, and has begun to show that, religion being preserved, it cannot happen that those who are grafted into Christ by faith and share in the sacraments of the Church should not also make themselves partakers of other men's rites. He confirms this further now, and so concludes his discussion of this matter.

units.la: Quia enim quod nuper dixerat, idololatriae participes fieri eos, qui ad conuiuia idololatrarum accedunt, durius dictum videri poterat, probat modò eos omnes, qui alienis aut externis sacris quacunque ratione communicant, totius etiam religionis, cuius illa sacra sunt, socios atque consortes fieri. Et vt nuper communionem Coenae Dominicae adduxit, ita nunc in Iudaeorum sacrificijs idem fieri docet, vt eandem omnium religionum rationem esse ostendat, quoad sacrorum externorum communionem. Videte (inquit) Israelem, qui est secundum carnem, &c. Sic vocat Iudaeos, qui illo tempore viuebant, & sacra Leuitica mordicus retinebant: quibus alibi opponuntur veri Israelitae, quos filios promissionis dicit, quia promissiones de Christo vera fide amplexi erat. In praesenti autem simul obiter inanem illorum gloriationem, qua sese venditabant, perstringit. Superbiebant enim primò natalibus, quòd ex patribus sanctissimus origine ducerent: deinde sacris, quae olim ab ipso Deo per Mosem maioribus ipsorum tradita fuerunt. Vtrunq; vero carnale erat: quia neq; fidem patrum imitabantur, neq; sacrorum illorum finem atq; scopum obseruabant, Christum videlicet: quem si ab illis auferas, nihil praeter expiationes & iustificationes carnis continent, quae ad animam minimè pertinent, vt prolixè in epistola ad Hebraeos Apostolus docet. Consulto autem sic loquitur de Iudaeis, qui tunc erant, ne illorum sacris aliquid tribuere putetur, quae in Christi morte abrogata esse sciebat. Inde vero generalis doctrina peti debet, inanem esse coram Deo omnem carnis gloriationem, neq; ad salutem aliquid facere, ex quibus nam nati sumus, aut quales dicamur: sed in hoc versari salutis cardinem, vt in Christo renati, veros & germanos Dei filios nos esse demonstremus. Demonstrationis autem huius argumenta sunt, constans & syncera fides in Christum, & quae ex hac nascitur vitae sanctitas atq; dilectio non simulata. Qui his destituuntur, ij Christiani secundum carnem sunt, & quoad ipsos non nisi carnale est, quicquid circa religionem faciunt.
units.tr: For what he had said a little before, that those who come to the banquets of idolaters become partakers of idolatry, might seem a harsh saying, he now proves that all who in any way share in strange or external rites also become associates and fellows of the whole religion to which those rites belong. And as he lately adduced the communion of the Lord's Supper, so now he teaches that the same holds in the sacrifices of the Jews, so as to show that the reasoning is the same for all religions as regards communion in external rites. "Behold," he says, "Israel after the flesh," and so on. So he calls the Jews who lived at that time, and who clung stubbornly to the Levitical rites; elsewhere true Israelites are set over against them, whom he calls children of promise, because they embraced by true faith the promises concerning Christ. In the present passage, however, he at the same time briefly strikes at their empty boasting, with which they vaunted themselves. For they were proud, first of their birth, because they traced their origin from the most holy fathers; then of the rites which God himself had long before delivered to their forefathers through Moses. Both of these were carnal, because they neither imitated the faith of the fathers nor observed the end and aim of those rites, namely Christ; and if you take him away from them, they contain nothing but expiations and purifications of the flesh, which do not pertain to the soul at all, as the Apostle teaches at length in the Epistle to the Hebrews. He speaks deliberately in this way of the Jews who then existed, lest it be thought that he ascribes anything to their rites, which he knew had been abrogated by the death of Christ. From this, however, a general doctrine must be drawn: all boasting of the flesh is empty before God, and neither that from which we were born nor what sort of people we are called contributes anything to salvation; but the hinge of salvation lies in this, that, being born again in Christ, we show ourselves to be true and genuine sons of God. The proofs of this demonstration are a constant and sincere faith in Christ, and the holiness of life and unfeigned love which springs from this faith. Those who lack these are Christians only according to the flesh, and so far as they are concerned, whatever they do in religion is nothing but carnal.

units.la: At quia haec alterius loci sunt, audiamus quid de illis Paulus dicat. Nonne qui edunt vi-ctimas, participes aut socij sunt altaris? Altaris nomine religionem Iudaicam vniuersam intelligit, qua illi simul omnes in vnum Ecclesiae corpus colligebantur. Ideo enim vnicum templum, & vnicum altare illis esse voluit Deus, vt in religionis vnitate facilius contineri possent. Ideo cum Rubenitae, Gaditae & dimidia Manasseorum tribus post occupatam & diuisam terram Chanaan ad sua redeuntes ad Iordanis limitem aram ingentem & altissimam aedificauissent, reliqui Israelitae illos dignos putarunt, quos ob violatam religionem à Deo traditam bello aggrederentur, neq; prius illis placati sunt, quàm vbi aram illam, non vt illic sacrificia fierent, aedificatam esse audiuerunt, sed potius, vt posteritati instar testimonij publici esset, quòd Transiordani quoq; Iudaei ad tabernaculum Domini, quod in terra Chanaan locum habebat, pertinerent. Itaq; verborum Pauli sensus est, eos qui ad Iudaeorum epulas sacras, quas illi (vt supra diximus) ex sacrificijs gratulatorijs instituebant, accumbunt, eo ipso totam Iudæorum religionem probare, seq; huius socios atq; consortes profiteri. Nam nisi id facerent, imò nisi secundum Legem rite prius purificarentur, nunquam fuissent admissi. Ex eo autem Corinthios colligere vult, ipsos similiter superstitionum atq; totius idololatriæ gentium consortes fieri, si cum his festa conuiuia celebrent. Id verò per interrogationem enuntiat, vt vehementius arguat sciolos illos, qui cum sublimioris scientiæ gloriatione turgerent, nondum eo vsque profecerant, vt proprium vsum externorum sacrorum intelligerent: qui est, quòd consensus in religione symbolum sunt, nosq; visibili (vt sic dicam) vinculo constringunt cum illis, quorum sacris communicamus. Facit etiam ad argumenti vim, quòd aperte de illis Iudæis loquitur, qui tunc suis ceremonijs contumaciter addicti, Christianam religionem vbiq; locorum persequebantur. Perinde enim hoc est, ac si diceret: Sat scio, si quis vos, qui Christum profitemini, Hierosolymam proficisci, sacrificijs Iudæorum solennibus adesse, & conuiuijs quoq; eorundem sacris accumbere iuberet, vos id nunquam esse facturos. Nolletis enim altaris, id est, religionis Iudæorum participes aut socij videri. Cur ergo ô boni, non eadem ratione vtimini, quoad gentium sacra & idololatriam? Annon enim idolorum quoq; participes estis, si ad conuiuia accederitis, quæ in illorum honorem instituuntur? Etenim si Ecclesiæ Christianæ socij censentur, qui ad eandem Christi mensam cum alijs credentibus accedunt: si item Iudaicarum superstitionum consortes fiunt, qui illorum sacrificijs communicant: fieri non potest, quin cum ethnicis quoque & idololatris communionem habeant, quotquot illorum epulis sacris intersunt. Nam cùm inter homines salis & mensæ communio amicitiæ arctioris symbolum sit, hoc ipsum in religione quoq; observari debet, tam propter veterem & communem omnium gentium in hoc more consensum, quàm quòd Deus ipse communionem religionis, cùm in veteri testamento tum in novo conuiuijs sacris adumbrari voluerit. In summa hoc omnium animis infixum esse vult Apostolus, externa sacra communionem habere cum tota illa religione, cuius sacra sunt. Sententiæ huius ratio certa & evidens est, quòd ceremoniæ omnes ad fidei confessionem pertinent, & communionis vinculum sunt externum. Falluntur ergo vehementer, quicunq; externa illa nequaquam ad animam vsq; pertingere putant, & hanc ab omni superstitionis labe puram & immunem esse sibi ipsis persuadent, licet eosdem cum impijs dies festos agant, ritusq; eosdem exerceant. Atqui fieri non potest, quin polluantur, quotquot sacris alienis communicando in eam societatem siue communionem peccant, quæ nobis in Christo, omnis sanctificationis authore & mediatore, cum tota credentium Ecclesia intercedit. Quod vnum si paulò attentius & maiore cum studio alii qui obseruarent, minus haud dubiè indulgerent sibi ipsis in ijs, quæ contra religionis Christianæ leges faciunt.
units.tr: But since these matters belong to another place, let us hear what Paul says about them: "Are not they which eat of the sacrifices partakers or fellows of the altar?" By the name of the altar he understands the whole Jewish religion, by which they were all gathered together into one body of the Church. For God willed that they should have one temple and one altar, so that they might more easily be kept together in the unity of religion. Hence, when the tribes of Reuben, Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh, returning to their homes after the land of Canaan had been occupied and divided, built a great and very high altar at the boundary of the Jordan, the remaining Israelites thought them worthy to be attacked in war for violating the religion delivered by God, and they were not appeased until they heard that the altar had been built not for sacrifices to be offered there, but rather so that it might serve as a public witness to posterity that the Jews beyond the Jordan also belonged to the tabernacle of the Lord, which had its place in the land of Canaan. Therefore the sense of Paul's words is this: those who sit down at the sacred feasts of the Jews, which they (as we said above) held from the thank-offerings, by that very act approve the whole Jewish religion and profess themselves its associates and fellows. For unless they did this, or unless they first were duly purified according to the Law, they would never have been admitted. From this, however, he wishes the Corinthians to conclude that they likewise become partners in superstitions and in the whole idolatry of the Gentiles if they celebrate festive banquets with them. He states this by way of a question, so that he may argue more vehemently against those smatterers who swelled with the boast of a more lofty knowledge, yet had not advanced so far as to understand the proper use of external rites. That use is that agreement in religion is a sign, and binds us, to speak visibly, with a bond to those whose rites we share. The force of the argument is also helped by the fact that he speaks plainly of those Jews who, stubbornly devoted at that time to their ceremonies, persecuted the Christian religion wherever they could. For this is just as if he said: "I know well that if anyone ordered you, who profess Christ, to go up to Jerusalem, to be present at the solemn sacrifices of the Jews, and to recline at their sacred banquets too, you would never do it. For you would not wish to appear to be partners or fellows of the altar, that is, of the Jewish religion. Why then, good people, do you not use the same reasoning in regard to the rites and idolatry of the Gentiles? Are you not also partakers of idols, if you go to the feasts that are instituted in their honour? For if those who come to the same table of Christ with other believers are reckoned fellows of the Christian Church, and if those who share in the Jewish sacrifices become partners of Jewish superstitions, it cannot be that all who take part in the sacred feasts of the heathen and idolaters should not have fellowship with them." For since the sharing of salt and table is among men a sign of closer friendship, this same thing ought to be observed in religion too, both because of the ancient and common agreement of all nations in this custom, and because God himself willed the communion of religion to be shadowed forth by sacred feasts, both in the Old Testament and in the New. In sum, the Apostle wishes this to be fixed in the minds of all: that external rites carry communion with the whole religion to which they belong. The reason for this opinion is certain and evident: all ceremonies pertain to the confession of faith, and are an external bond of communion. Therefore those are gravely mistaken who think that such external things do not reach the soul at all, and persuade themselves that the soul is pure and free from every stain of superstition, though they keep the same festivals as the impious and perform the same rites. And yet it cannot be that all who sin by communicating in alien rites are not defiled, since they sin against that fellowship which, in Christ, the author and mediator of all sanctification, binds us with the whole Church of believers. If only others would observe this one thing a little more carefully and with greater zeal, they would surely indulge themselves less in those things which are done against the laws of the Christian religion.

units.la: Sed est hic obseruatu digna locutio, qua altaris participes fieri, aut cum altari eos commu-nicare dicit, qui victimas edunt. Respondet hæc ijs, quibus supra vsus est, cùm de pane & poculo mystico Cœnæ Dominicæ loqueretur. Illic enim κοινωνίαν vel communionis vocem posuit, hic κοινωνὸς [?] dicit, eorum nimirum, qui ad communionem pertinent. Et perinde est, ac si hic quoque dixisset: Nonne epulum sacrum, quod ex victimis gratulatorijs instruitur, communio altaris est? At quomodo epulum illud aut eius esus communio altaris erat? Num quòd in eo ipsum altare comederent realiter, essentialiter & substantialiter? Nequaquam: Sed quòd ita testarentur se illius Ecclesiæ membra esse, cuius vinculum externum (vt supra monuimus) altare illud erat, & quæ suam sanctificationem, salutem & vitam ex ipso altari deriuari credebat. Ad eundem ergo modum nos quoque cum Christi corpore & sanguine communionem habemus, quando panem mysticum edimus, & poculum illud benedictionis bibimus: non quòd corpus illius naturale essentialiter & oraliter (vt quidam loquuntur) manducemus, & verum eiusdem sanguinem, qui ex vulneribus eius fluxit, realiter bibamus: sed quòd eius ecclesiæ membra sumus, quæ Christi corpore & sanguine redempta, ex eodem vitæ spiritum haurit, qui in singula eius membra redundat. Quod propter eos annotamus, qui ex locutionibus cùm Christi tum Apostolorum de Cœna carnis Christi corporalem præsentiam atque manducationem colligere satagunt, nobis autem Tropum obijcientibus perinde vociferantur, ac si nihil huius in scripturis vspiam dicatur, in cuius expositione Tropum quærere oporteat.
units.tr: But there is a notable expression here, in which he says that those who eat the sacrifices are partakers of the altar, or have communion with the altar. This answers to the words he used above when speaking of the bread and the mystical cup of the Lord's Supper. There he used the word communion [κοινωνία], but here he says partakers [κοινωνοὶ], meaning those who belong to the communion. It is as if he had said here too: Is not the sacred feast, which is prepared from the thank offerings, a communion of the altar? But how was that feast, or the eating of it, a communion of the altar? Not because they really, essentially and substantially ate the altar itself. By no means. Rather, by it they professed themselves to be members of that church, whose external bond (as we noted above) was that altar, and which believed that its sanctification, salvation and life were derived from the altar itself. In the same way we too have communion with the body and blood of Christ when we eat the mystical bread and drink that cup of blessing: not because we eat his natural body essentially and orally (as some put it), and really drink the true blood that flowed from his wounds, but because we are members of that church which, redeemed by the body and blood of Christ, draws from the same source the spirit of life that flows into each of its members. We note this on account of those who strive to infer a bodily presence and a manducation of Christ's flesh in the Supper from the words of Christ and the Apostles, and who, when we object a trope, cry out as if nothing of this were said anywhere in Scripture, so that a trope should have to be sought in its interpretation.

units.la: At poterant Paulo Corinthij obijcere: Si eadem est idolothytorum, quibus ethnici in suis epulis vescuntur, quae Mosaicarum victimarum & Coenae Dominicae ratio, ideoq; nos illorum esus idolorum & idololatriae consortes facit, & polluit, certè idolis vim aliquam inesse necesse est, neque omnino nihil erit, quod de Diis gentium, in quorum honorem illa prostant, passim dicitur. Quapropter ne sibi ipsi contrarius esse putetur, qui supra dixerat idolum nihil esse, inania quoque esse Deorum fictitiorum nomina: nunc isti etiam obiectioni occurrit, & ex eo quod idola nihil sunt, non id sequi docet, quòd indifferens sit carnium sacrificatarum eius, sed longè aliud, quo nihil gravius & atrocius fingi poterat: nimirum, quod daemoniorum consortes fiant, qui illis vescuntur. Et ne quid dissimulare putetur, ipse sibi obijcit, quod illi dicturi erant. Quid ergo dico? idolum aliquid esse? aut quod idolis immolatum est, aliquid esse? &c. Quasi diceret: Nolim ex meis verbis aliud, quàm ego dixerim, colligi. Iam antea enim vobiscum testatus sum, idola nihil esse in mundo, & proinde carnes quoque, quae illis immolantur, quoad essentiam suam, non mutari, neque ex idolis aut eorum Diis, qui nusquam in rerum natura sunt, aliquam vim vel polluendi vel sanctificandi contrahere. Et quod nuper dixi, hoc ipsum adhuc constanter affirmo. Quod autem vos inde colligitis, licere victimarum, quae illis immolantur, carnibus perinde ut aliis vulgaribus vesci, id ego pernego. Imò quia neque idola, neque Dii illorum aliquid sunt, ex eo ego pronuntio, quòd quae gentes immolant, daemoniis immolent, & non Deo: Ego autem nolim vos participes daemoniorum esse. Fuit hoc gravissimum dictu, quod & ethnicos & Christianos vehementer offendere potuit. Nam ut alias diximus, gentium religio Romani Imperij authoritate nitebatur, & in ipsa Corinthiorum urbe cum imperio erat Achaiae Procos. Romanus, penes quem omnis erat rerum potestas. Quam verò indigne hoc illos tulisse putamus, qui in Deorum cultu nati & enutriti erant? Quas item multorum Christianorum voces fuisse putas, quando hoc dici audiebant, quod solum poterat omnium ethnicorum animos contra ipsos in rabiem accendere? Verumtamen dicit istud Paulus, quem nihil horum latebat, quia sic dicto opus erat propter effrenem multorum licentiam, qui nihil non sibi permittebant. Prudenter autem usque ad finem huius tractationis dictum istud differre voluit, ut prius rationes dilueret, quibus adversarij nitebantur, & eorundem animos ad penitius agnoscendam sceleris atrocitatem praepararet.
units.tr: But the Corinthians could have objected to Paul: If the meat offered to idols, which the heathen eat at their feasts, is of the same nature as the Mosaic sacrifices and the Lord's Supper, and so makes us partners and defiles us in the eating of those idols and in idolatry, then the idols must certainly have some power, and what is said everywhere about the gods of the nations, in whose honour those offerings are made, will not be altogether nothing. Therefore, lest he be thought to contradict himself, since he had said above that an idol is nothing and that the names of the fictitious gods are empty, he now meets this objection too. From the fact that idols are nothing, he teaches that it does not follow that the eating of meat sacrificed to them is a matter of indifference, but something far different, and nothing more grave and atrocious could be imagined: namely, that those who eat them become partners of demons. And lest he be thought to dissemble, he raises the objection they were going to make: What do I say then? That an idol is anything? Or that what is sacrificed to idols is anything? etc. As if he said: I would not have anything inferred from my words other than what I have said. For I have already testified to you that idols are nothing in the world, and therefore the meats that are offered to them are not changed in their essence, nor do they acquire from the idols, or from their gods who exist nowhere in nature, any power either to defile or to sanctify. And what I said recently, I still constantly affirm. But as for what you infer from this, that it is lawful to eat the flesh of the sacrifices offered to them just as other ordinary flesh, that I flatly deny. Indeed, because neither the idols nor their gods are anything, I declare on that ground that what the nations sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God; and I would not have you become partners of demons. This was a very grave thing to say, which could greatly offend both the heathen and the Christians. For, as we have said elsewhere, the religion of the nations rested on the authority of the Roman Empire, and in the very city of Corinth the Roman proconsul of Achaia held office, in whose hands lay all power. How indignantly do we suppose those men took this, who had been born and reared in the worship of the gods? And what do you think were the complaints of many Christians when they heard this said, which alone could inflame the minds of all the heathen to fury against them? Yet Paul, who was aware of none of these things, said it, because such a saying was needed on account of the unbridled licence of many who permitted themselves everything. But he wisely chose to defer that saying until the end of this discussion, so that he might first dissolve the arguments on which his opponents relied, and prepare their minds to recognise more fully the atrocity of the sin.

units.la: Est ergo hoc memorabile libertatis ecclesiasticae cum vera prudentia coniunctae exemplum, quod ministri ecclesiarum sibi proponant. Ne quid autem in aliquem aequo gravius dicant, ob-servent Paulum nihil hic dicere, quam quod prius in sacris literis dictum fuisse sciebat. Nam in Leuitico Deus dicit: Ne ultra sacrificent sacrificia sua Seirim, post quos scortati sunt. Hebraeis autem Seirim daemones dicuntur, & ii quidem proprie, qui cultoribus suis hirsuti & villosi instar hircorum apparere solebant, quales in poetarum fabulis Panes & Satyri describuntur. Et Moses in Cantico suo Israelitis defectionem a vero Deo ad Deorum fictitiorum cultum exprobrans, inter alia inquit: Sacrificaverunt daemonibus, non Deo. Mox vero rem apertius explicans addit: Diis, quos non noverunt, novis item qui nuper exorti sunt, quos patres vestri nihil revereri sunt. Nihil ergo ex suo capite finxit Paulus, neque disputationis fervore abreptus tam gravem sententiam pronuntiavit, sed (quod olim Prophetis dictum fuit) ex ore Domini verbum sumpsit, id est, ex scripturis, per quas nobis Deus loquitur.
units.tr: This is therefore a memorable example of ecclesiastical liberty joined with true prudence, which the ministers of the churches should set before themselves. Lest they say anything more harshly against anyone than is fitting, let them observe that Paul says here nothing other than what he knew had been said earlier in the sacred letters. For in Leviticus God says: "Let them no longer sacrifice their sacrifices to the Seirim [שעירים], after whom they have played the harlot." Now among the Hebrews the Seirim are called demons, and properly so, those which used to appear to their worshippers hairy and shaggy like goats, such as the Pans and Satyrs are described in the poets' fables. And Moses, in his Song, reproaching the Israelites for their defection from the true God to the worship of fictitious gods, says among other things: "They sacrificed to demons, not to God." Then, explaining the matter more plainly, he adds: "To gods whom they did not know, to new ones too that have recently arisen, whom your fathers did not revere." Paul therefore invented nothing of his own, nor, carried away by the heat of debate, did he pronounce so grave a sentence, but (as was said of old to the Prophets) he took the word from the mouth of the Lord, that is, from the Scriptures, through which God speaks to us.

units.la: Non autem temere gentes daemoniis sacrificavisse dicuntur. Nam etiamsi longe alia fuerit animi ipsorum intentio, ut nimirum Deo vero cultum exhiberent, minimè tamen id assecuti sunt, cùm in Dei cognitione errarent, religio autem sive cultus absque illius cognitione non possit consistere. Deum enim eiusmodi finxerunt (de melioribus & sanioribus loquor) qui ipse solus non omnibus sufficiat, quae ad totius mundi gubernationem pertinent, sed qui Diis subsidiariis utatur, inter quos partes mundi & quae in hoc fiunt, ceu provincias quasdam distribuerunt, ut alibi fusius est dictum. Deinde tam summum illum Deum, quàm alteros illos simulachris variis adumbrare & exprimere conati sunt, idque tanta cum licentia & temeritate, ut non hominum modò, verumetiam quadrupedum, volatilium, serpentum, piscium denique formas illis tribuerent. At quia Deus eiusmodi nullus est, Dii verò illi subsidiarij multò minus sunt, nihil etiam fuerunt simulachra; quae illis ponebantur. Quorsum ergo tendebat totus ille cultus templorum, altarium, dierum festorum, sacrificiorum, conviviorum solennium, omnium denique, quae ab hominibus superstitiosis solebant fieri? Non utique ad verum illum Deum, omnium Creatorem & gubernatorem, qui ista non potuit probare, cum eius naturae & voluntati aperte repugnarent. At neque falsi illi Dii & ficticii istis rebus colebantur, cum illi nusquam in rerum natura essent. Reliquum ergo est, ut totum hunc cultum ad se rapuerint mali daemones, qui miseris errorum & superstitionum authores erant, & simulachris sese insinuabant, ut alia quidem loco moverentur, alia quaerentibus responsa darent, multa sudarent, minaci gestu capita concuterent, & infinita alia facerent, quae homines vel terrore & metu, vel spe bona & gaudio replebant. Sic ergo sub religionis & divini cultus praetextu hoc demum effectum dedit Satan, quod iam inde ab origine rerum ambiit, ut nimirum Deo similis fieret, & eius loco ipse coleretur. Id autem iusto iudicio permisit Deus, ut infelix mundus poenas daret suae contumaciae, qua ipsum neque in operibus suis sese manifestantem agnoscere, neque in Verbo suo loquentem audire voluit. Dignus ergo fuit, qui in reprobum sensum traditus diaboli ludibrium fieret: & ideo non per sceleris amplificationem, sed vere & proprie loquitur Spiritus Sanctus, quando gentes daemonibus sacra fecisse ait.
units.tr: Nor are the nations said to have sacrificed to demons rashly. For even though the intention of their minds was quite different, namely to render worship to the true God, they by no means achieved it, since they erred in the knowledge of God, and religion or worship cannot exist without that knowledge. For they fashioned a God of such a kind (I speak of the better and saner among them) that he alone does not suffice for all the matters that pertain to the government of the whole world, but makes use of subordinate gods, among whom they distributed the parts of the world and the things that happen in it, as if they were certain provinces, as has been said more fully elsewhere. Then they tried to portray and express that supreme God, as well as those others, by various images, and did so with such licence and recklessness that they assigned to them the forms not only of men, but also of quadrupeds, birds, serpents and finally fishes. But since no God of this kind exists, and those subordinate gods are far less, the images that were set up for them were also nothing. To what end, then, did all that worship of temples, altars, festival days, sacrifices and solemn banquets, in short all that superstitious men used to perform, tend? Certainly not to that true God, the Creator and governor of all, who could not approve of these things, since they were plainly contrary to his nature and will. Nor were they worshipped as fictitious gods, since those gods existed nowhere in nature. It remains, then, that the evil demons seized upon all this worship, they who were the authors of wretched errors and superstitions, and insinuated themselves into the images, so that some of them were moved from place to place, some gave answers to those who inquired, some sweated, some shook their heads with threatening gestures, and did countless other things which filled men either with terror and fear or with good hope and joy. Thus, under the pretext of religion and divine worship, Satan achieved this end, which he had aimed at from the very beginning of things: namely, to become like God and to be worshipped in his place. God, by a just judgment, permitted this, so that the unhappy world might pay the penalty for its obstinacy, by which it was unwilling to recognise him manifesting himself in his works, or to hear him speaking in his Word. It was therefore worthy that it should be given over to a reprobate mind and become the sport of the devil; and so the Holy Spirit speaks not by way of exaggeration of the sin, but truly and properly, when he says that the nations sacrificed to demons.

units.la: Continet autem haec consideratio generalem doctrinam, & utilissimam cognitu: Ne de re-ligione & Dei cultu secundum nostri animi aut aliorum intentionem iudicemus. Deus enim cum per se invisibilis & humanae etiam menti incomprehensibilis sit (quo nomine lucem in-accessam habitare dicitur) non aliter a nobis quam in Verbo suo vere & certo cognosci po-test. Unde sequitur, neque etiam vere illum coli posse, nisi ea ratione, quam nobis in Verbo suo revelavit. Itaque cultus falsus, erroneus, superstitiosus, vanus & noxius est, quemcunque homines ex semetipsis instituunt. Nam quaecunque, aut qualiscunque sit eorum intentio, cultus tamen eiusmodi omnis ad diabolum redundat, qui solus illo oblectatur, eo quod ex hominum erroribus atque interitu voluptatem capiat. Id vero non de prisca modo gentium idololatria, aut eorum superstitionibus intelligi debet, qui hodie inter Orientales populos & terras nuper inventas Deos falsos sub horribili imaginum terrificarum specie colunt: verum etiam de illis cultibus, qui inter Christianos quoque iam aliquot saeculis in usu fuerunt. Nam hi quoque Deum sibi fingunt, qui imagine exprimi possit, & qui ex hominibus Semideos quosdam satiat, quorum opera in rerum administratione utatur. Cultum ergo exercent, qui totos fere simulachrorum cultura, altarium & templorum ornatu, Missae sacrificio, suffitibus crebris, diebus festis, cantu, organorum multipici harmonia, ludis denique & omnibus aliis rebus constat, quibus olim gentes suos Deos colebant. Et cultum illum partim Deo vero impendunt, partim in Divos coelites & Angelos distribuunt. At non recipit illum Deus, qui iam olim talia ipsi obtrudentibus dixit: Quis requisivit ista de manibus vestris? Et Angelos divinis honoribus coli nolle eius testimonio probatur, qui olim Ioanni visionum maiestate abrepto, ut ad pedes ipsius se prosterneret, dicebat: Vide ne feceris,conservus enim tuus sum, & fratrum tuorum Prophetarum, & eorum qui servant verba prophetiae libri huius: Deum adora. Et ApostolusAngelos scribit ministratores spiritus esse, qui ministerii causa mittuntur propter eos, qui haeredes erunt salutis. Quoad Divos, ii quidem cum in terris viverent, egregiam Deo operam navarunt, ut quam plurimos ad veram eius cognitionem atque cultum adducerent, se autem adorari & coli adeo noluerunt, ut intolerabile scelus illis visum sit, si quos tale quid tentare viderent, sicuti Ioannis & Petri, Pauli & Barnabae ex-empla testantur: at nunc in coelis ab omni rerum humanarum cura liberi beata immortalitate fru-untur. Magnam ergo illis iniuriam faciunt, qui cunque tales iam esse fingunt, qui divinos honores ambiant, & a nobis invocari velint, cum neminem defunctorum unquam ab aliquo veri Dei cultore invocatum fuisse legamus. Cum ergo neque Deus, neque Angeli, neque Sancti qui in coelis agunt, ea ratione coli velint aut possint, quid restat, quam ut cum D. Ambrosio dicamus, sub tegmine simulachrorum diabolum coli, cuius per eiusmodi cultum lusus iucundus & optatus exhibetur? Qui plura de hac re audire volet, D. Augustinum legat in Enarratione Psal. 96: ubi de Angelis simul & Sanctis eorum, cultu prolixe disputat.
units.tr: This consideration contains a general doctrine, and one most useful to know: that we must not judge about religion and the worship of God according to the intention of our own mind or of others. For God, being invisible in himself and incomprehensible even to the human mind (for which reason he is said to dwell in unapproachable light), can be known by us truly and certainly only in his Word. It follows that he cannot truly be worshipped either, except in the manner he has revealed to us in his Word. Therefore any worship that men devise from themselves is false, erroneous, superstitious, vain and harmful. For whatever their intention, and whatever its kind, all such worship redounds to the devil, who alone delights in it, because he takes pleasure in men's errors and ruin. This must be understood not only of the ancient idolatry of the nations, or of the superstitions of those who today among eastern peoples and in lands lately discovered worship false gods under the horrible appearance of frightful images, but also of those forms of worship which have been in use among Christians for some centuries now. For these too fashion for themselves a God who can be expressed by an image, and who has certain demigods made from men, whose services he uses in the government of things. So they carry on a worship which consists almost entirely of the worship of statues, the adornment of altars and temples, the sacrifice of the Mass, frequent incense, festival days, singing, the manifold harmony of organs, and finally games and all the other things by which the nations of old worshipped their gods. And they offer that worship partly to the true God and partly distribute it among the heavenly divinities and angels. But God does not accept that worship, for long ago he said to those who thrust such things upon him: "Who has required these things at your hands?" That God is unwilling to be worshipped with divine honours by angels is proved by the testimony of him who once, when John had been carried away by the majesty of the visions and threw himself at his feet to prostrate himself before him, said: "See that you do not do it; for I am your fellow servant, and of your brethren the prophets, and of those who keep the words of the prophecy of this book: worship God." And the Apostle writes that angels are ministering spirits, sent for the sake of ministry to those who will be heirs of salvation. As for the saints departed, indeed while they lived on earth they laboured splendidly for God, to bring as many as possible to the true knowledge and worship of him; yet they were so unwilling to be adored and worshipped themselves that it seemed an intolerable crime to them if they saw anyone attempting such a thing, as the examples of John and Peter, Paul and Barnabas attest. Now in heaven, free from all care of human affairs, they enjoy blessed immortality. Therefore they do great injury to those who imagine that such saints now exist, who seek divine honours and wish to be invoked by us, since we read that no one of the departed was ever invoked by any worshipper of the true God.
