Since neither God, nor the angels, nor the saints who dwell in heaven wish or are able to be worshipped in this way, what remains but that we say with Ambrose that under the covering of images the devil is worshipped, to whom a pleasant and desired sport is provided by such worship? Whoever wishes to hear more on this matter, let him read Augustine's exposition of Psalm 96, where he discusses at length the worship of the angels together with that of their saints.

units.la: Porrò Conclusionem huius argumentationis infert Apostolus, quasi simul exponit quod dixerat, Nolim vos participes daemoniorum esse. Et ne ipsum satis pro imperio loqui putarent, neque aliqua certa ratione niti, mox subjicit: Non potestis poculum Domini bibere, & poculum daemoniorum: Non potestis mensae Domini participes esse, & mensae daemoniorum. Vbi quis miretur, quomodo eos id posse neget, quod subinde faciebant? Imò hoc nomine illos ipse accusat, quòd cum ad Coenam Christi mysticam accederent, & in illa fidem Christianam profiterentur, nihilominus tamen idololatrarum sacris communicarent. Sed in praesenti non tam de externa actione Coenae loquitur, quàm de vera communione Christi & Ecclesiae, quam in Coena nobis referri & visibiliter confirmari supra diximus. Perinde ergo ista dicuntur, ac si quis mulieri dicat: Non potes in thoro coniugali iacere, simulque vagis libidinibus vacare: Item: Non potes annulum, coniugij arrham, gestare, & simul amatorum munusculis superbire. Eodem sensu Corinthij admonentur, veram illam communionem, quae credentibus cum Christo intercedit, ipsis constare non posse, quoad daemoniorum participes aut confortes fuerint. Vt enim nulla communio est Christi et Belial: ita illi fidem feruare non possumus, si vel minima ex parte huic adhaereamus. Et ex Eliae Prophetae dicto constat, Deu[?] non probare eos cultores, qui in vtrumquelatus claudicat, & non ipsum solum ex toto corde & tota anima diligunt. Vides hoc loco, quam procul Prophetae & Apostoli ab eorum sententia abfuerint, qui hodie impios & indignos corpus Christi edere, & eiusdem sanguine bibere contenduns. Vt enim Christo simul & diabolo communicemus, impossibile dicit esse Paulus: At impij cum diabolo communicant: Ergo ijsdem cum Christi corpore & sanguine communio nulla esse potest.
units.tr: Moreover, the Apostle draws the conclusion of this argument, as if at the same time explaining what he had said: "I would not have you become partners with demons." And lest they think he speaks merely by authority, resting on no sure reason, he soon adds: "You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; you cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons." Here someone might wonder how he can say they cannot do what they constantly did. Indeed he accuses them on exactly this ground: that when they came to the mystical Supper of Christ and professed the Christian faith in it, they nevertheless shared in the sacred rites of idolaters. But at present he is speaking not so much of the external action of the Supper as of the true communion of Christ and the Church, which we said above is set before us in the Supper and visibly confirmed. These things are said just as if someone should tell a wife: "You cannot lie in the marriage bed and at the same time give yourself to wanton lusts"; likewise: "You cannot wear the ring, the pledge of marriage, and at the same time pride yourself on the little gifts of lovers." In the same sense the Corinthians are admonished that the true communion which exists between believers and Christ cannot stand for them, insofar as they have been partakers or companions of demons. For as there is no communion between Christ and Belial, so we cannot keep faith with him if we cling to the devil even in the smallest part. And from the saying of the prophet Elijah it is clear that God does not approve those worshippers who limp towards both sides, and do not love him alone with the whole heart and the whole soul. You see here how far the Prophets and Apostles were from the opinion of those who today contend that the impious and unworthy eat the body of Christ and drink his blood. For Paul says it is impossible to communicate both with Christ and with the devil; but the impious communicate with the devil; therefore there can be no communion with the body and blood of Christ for the same people.

units.la: Pulchre autem Conclusionem vtrique symbolo Coenae Dominicae applicat, vt euidentius confirmet diaboli astutia, qui in constituendo idolorum cultu morem sanctorum patrum, imò ipsius Christi exemplum secutus est, quod is in Coena sua observari voluit. Vt enim patres olim in suis epulis sacris à calice gratiarum actionis exordiebantur, cuius Dauides quoque in Psalmis meminit, & quo Christum Coenam paschalem exorsum fuisse Lucas scribit: ita ethnici quoque in sacrificijs suis & conuiuijs, quae ex carnibus immolatis instituebantur, libationibus certis Deos illos inuocare & placare solebant, in quorum honorem sacrificium totum vnà cum conuiuio illo erat institutum. Exempla & testimonia huius rei in scriptoribus, & quidem in Poëtis maxime, passim sunt obuia, vt eorum commemoratione nequaquam fit opus. Libationes ergo illas poculum daemoniorum dicit, sicuti epulum illud vniuersum mensam daemoniorum appellat. Nec temere daemoniorum mentionem tertio repetit, cum haec sola ab omni alienae superstitionis commertio eos absterrere possit, qui non omnem religionis sensum exuerunt. Non possunt enim non ad diaboli recordationem exhorrescere homines Christiani, qui Dei Filium ideo in mundum venisse sciunt, vt illius opera destrueret, & nos sui sanguinis pretio ex illius tyrannide liberaret.
units.tr: He applies the conclusion beautifully to both symbols of the Lord's Supper, so as to confirm more clearly the cunning of the devil, who in establishing the worship of idols followed the custom of the holy Fathers, indeed the very example of Christ, which he wished to be observed in his Supper. For as the Fathers of old began their sacred feasts with the cup of thanksgiving, of which David also speaks in the Psalms, and with which Luke writes that Christ began the paschal supper, so the heathen too, in their sacrifices and banquets, which were arranged from the flesh of the victims, were accustomed to invoke and placate those gods with certain libations, in whose honour the whole sacrifice together with the feast had been instituted. Examples and testimonies of this are found everywhere in the writers, and especially in the poets, so there is no need to recall them. Those libations, therefore, he calls the cup of demons, just as he calls the whole feast the table of demons. Nor does he repeat the mention of demons a third time carelessly, since this alone can deter from all contact with alien superstition those who have not cast off every sense of religion. For Christian men, who know that the Son of God came into the world for this purpose, to destroy the works of the devil and to free us from his tyranny at the price of his own blood, cannot but shudder at the remembrance of the devil.

units.la: At meminisse oportet, Paulum hoc loco nobis quoque loqui. Nec enim nos ad suam communionem Christus admittet, nisi prius alienis superstitionibus ex animo renuntiemus. Nam cum semetipsos abnegare debeant qui germani illius discipuli esse volunt, quanto magis alia omnia relinquant oportet, quae fidem in ipsum aliquo modo labefactare possunt? Vidit hoc olim Iacob patriarcha, qui cum tota familia ascensurus in Bethel, vt ibi facta faceret Deo, qui eodem in loco promissionem venturi Christi cum ipso instaurauerat, hoc ante omnia curauit, vt Deos alienos & quaecunque ad hotum cultum faciebant abijcerent. Et Samuel Dei foedus cum populo innouaturus, ab hoc ipso initium fieri voluit, & ideo dicebat: Si toto corde vestro reuertimini ad Dominum, auferte Deos alienos & Astaroth é medio vestri, & praeparate cor vestrum ad Dominum, & ei soli seruite. Sunt ergo reuera miseri & infelices, qui hodie in hominum superstitiosissimorum gratiam Missas audiunt & alijs simulachrorum cultibus communicant, simul autem ad Domini quoque Coenam accedunt, & cum illo communionem habere volunt. Possent quidem illi sese impudenter in Ecclesiae consortium ingerere, Christianorum nomen nobis inuitis vsurpare, Sacramento corporis & sanguinis Christi communicari, cum ipso Christo autem communionem veram habere non poterunt, neque eius corpore & sanguine ad vitam aeternam frui, cum fide vera destituantur, quae sola communionis illius verae vinculum est. Quid igitur illi aliud faciunt, quàm quòd semetipsos ab ea communione excludunt, & ex qua omnis nostra salus dependet? Recte ergo olim sanctissimi Reges sacra aliena extirparunt, ut solius veri Dei cultus locum haberet. Recte olim Constantinus & Theodosius fecere, quorum ille quidem templa idolorum clausit, hic vero sub Juliano rursus aperta funditus evertit. Recte D. Ambrosius Symmachose [?] opposuit, qui Romanorum nomine apud Imperatores petebat, ut sacra vetera, & inter haec Victoriae aram instaurare liceret. Et hodie Christianos magistratus pro suo populo imprimis excubare convenit, ut non obiter modò Veritatis doctrina praedicetur, verumetiam omnis superstitionis species atque occasio tollatur.
units.tr: But we ought to remember that Paul here speaks to us also. For Christ will not admit us to his communion unless first we renounce alien superstitions from the heart. For since those who wish to be his true disciples must deny themselves, how much more must they leave aside all the other things that can in any way weaken faith in him? Jacob the patriarch saw this long ago, who, when he was about to go up to Bethel with his whole household, to make offerings there to God, who at that very place had renewed with him the promise of the coming Christ, took care above all that they should cast away the strange gods and whatever they had used for that worship. And Samuel, about to renew God's covenant with the people, wished to begin from this very point, and therefore said: "If you return to the Lord with your whole heart, put away the strange gods and Ashtaroth from among you, prepare your hearts for the Lord, and serve him alone." Therefore they are truly wretched and unhappy who today, to please the most superstitious of men, hear Masses and join in other worship of images, and at the same time approach the Lord's Supper too and wish to have communion with him. They might indeed shamelessly thrust themselves into the fellowship of the Church against our will, usurp the name of Christians, and partake of the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ; but they cannot have true communion with Christ himself, nor enjoy his body and blood unto eternal life, since they lack the true faith, which alone is the true bond of that communion. What, then, do they do but exclude themselves from that communion, on which all our salvation depends? Rightly did the most holy kings of old root out alien rites, so that the worship of the one true God alone might have its place. Rightly did Constantine and Theodosius act: the former closed the temples of idols, and the latter, when they had been reopened under Julian, utterly overthrew them. Rightly did Ambrose oppose Symmachus, who in the name of the Romans sought from the emperors permission to restore the ancient rites, and among them the altar of Victory. And today it is fitting that Christian magistrates above all keep watch over their people, so that not merely the doctrine of the truth may be preached in passing, but every form and occasion of superstition may be removed.

units.la: Ceterùm non ignorabat Paulus, multis haec omnia leuicula putari, & hos adhuc suis rationibus insistere, quibus factum suum tuebantur: quapropter altius nunc insurgens, graui & horribili sententia illos territat. An (inquit) provocamus ad aemulationem Dominum? num validiores illo sumus? Quasi diceret. Cùm ista sic sese habeant, & non solùm manifesto Dei verbo, verumetiam omnium saeculorum exemplis abunde probata sint, quid opus est rationibus atque argumentis humanis contendere? An nondum intelligitis, obis [?] non mecum, neque cum ullo alio mortalium, sed cum ipso Deo rem esse? Num igitur cum illo litigare, & ita illum ad aemulationem & iram justam provocare vultis? Et si hic vobis animus est, dicite quaeso, quibus argumentis eius veritatem expugnare, aut quibus viribus & armis illius potentiam vincere possitis, si semel justa ira inflammatus suum judicium in vos stringere incipiat? Stultus & insanus putatur, qui hostem se potentiorem lacessit: & vos Deum, qui nutu suo caelum terramque concutit, in certamen provocare non veremini? Proprie autem verbo παραζηλοῦν[?] utitur, quod de iis dicitur, qui non ad iram quamlibet, sed ad aemulationem provocant aliquem, quae iram justam parit. Faciunt illud impudicae mulieres, quae non contentae fidem coniugale violasse, insuper in mariti conspectu cum adulteris suis comessantur, ludunt, & quidquid faciunt, quo illos irritari sciunt. Et servit toti huic negotio Metaphora ista, propter coniugium spirituale, quod nobis cum Deo intercedit, qui ut in Lege prohibet, ne Deos alienos coram facie eius nobis fingamus, ita se zelotypum esse profitetur, qui istud nullo modo ferre possit aut velit. Quid vero aliud faciebant Corinthij, quando à mensa Domini ad Deorum falsorum sacra atque conviuia transibant? Annon similes erant adulterae, quae à viri mensa vel etiam thoro coniugali surgens cum adultero palam miscetur? Neque poterant hanc perfidiam excusare aut extenuare, cum in simili causa ijsdem verbis Moses contra Judaeos utatur, ad quae Paulus in praesenti alludit. Vide Deuter.32.
units.tr: Paul, however, was not unaware that many people thought all these things rather trivial, and that some still clung to their own arguments by which they defended what they had done. So, rising higher now, he frightens them with a grave and dreadful sentence. "Or do we provoke the Lord to jealousy?" he says. "Are we stronger than he?" As if he were saying: since these matters stand as they do, and have been abundantly proved not only by the plain Word of God but also by the examples of all ages, what need is there to contend with human reasons and arguments? Do you not yet understand that the matter is not with me, nor with any other mortal, but with God himself? Do you therefore want to contend with him and so provoke him to jealousy and righteous anger? And if you have this intention, tell me, I beg you, by what arguments you could overthrow his truth, or by what strength and weapons you could conquer his power, if once inflamed with righteous wrath he begins to bring his judgment to bear upon you. A man is thought foolish and mad who challenges a more powerful enemy; and do you not fear to challenge to battle God, who shakes heaven and earth with a nod? Now he uses the word "to provoke to jealousy" [παραζηλοῦν] properly, which is said of those who provoke someone not to just any anger but to jealousy, and jealousy begets righteous anger. Shameless women do this: not content to have violated their marriage faith, they feast and play with their lovers right in front of their husbands, and do whatever they know will make them angry. This metaphor fits the whole business, because of the spiritual marriage that exists between us and God. As he forbids in the Law that we should make strange gods in his sight, so he declares himself a jealous God, who can in no way bear or wish to bear such a thing. And what else were the Corinthians doing when they passed from the Lord's table to the feasts and banquets of false gods? Were they not like adulterous wives, who leave their husband's table or even marriage bed and openly mix with a lover? Nor could they excuse or extenuate this treachery, since Moses, in a similar case, uses against the Jews the same words to which Paul here alludes. See Deut. 32.]

units.la: Rursus autem observabis, hoc ipsum omnibus dici, qui ea in disceptationem vocant, quae Deus in Verbo suo diserte pronuntiavit. Ult enim is nobis firmum ratumque esse, quicquid dixerit, & eius voluntas nobis summae rationis loco esse debet, ad quam confirmandam nullis praeterea argumentis opus sit. Nefas ergo fuerit cum illo disputationem instituere, quasi nos aliquid melius, utilius aut commodius excogitare possimus. Est autem huius doctrinae usus multiplex. Et primo quidem ad vitam & mores debet accommodari. Sunt enim hic multi nimium artificiosi in excusandis sceleribus, quae contra expressam Dei voluntatem designant. Sed tunc cogitare oportet, humanum quidem esse peccare: at peccatum defendere velle id vero θεομαχεῖν[?] ἐστ[?], id est, cum ipso Deo bellum suscipere. Fecit hoc olim Cain & postea hunc Pharao, Saul & plures alij, quorum omnium infelix fuit exitus. Imprimis autem in religione hoc observari debet, quae nisi ad Dei nutum instituatur, ne nomine quidem hoc digna est. At hanc omnem certis capitibus olim Deus comprehendit, quorum summa in Decalogo & in Symbolo quod Apostolorum vocant, continetur. Quàm multos autem hodie est videre, qui illa palàm negant, aut spinosis disputationibus involvunt, ut eorum loco sua figmenta possint rudi vulgo obtrudere? Quid vero de illis dicemus, qui cùm se rationibus & argumentis destitui sentiant, ad vim conversi ferro & igne de iis decerni volunt, quae ad Dei cultum & aeternae salutis negotium pertinent? Fit istud passim hodie, & isti fere rationibus pugnant, qui Romani Pontificis primatum, Missae sacrificium, imaginum cultum, ignem purgatorium, indulgentias papae les & fexcenta alia aduersus manifestum Dei Verbum tuentur. Sed omnes isti Deum ad æmulationem prouocant, & aliquando magno suo malo experientur, quàm nullæ ipsis aduersus illum vires sint. Nec enim dormit, qui olim per Dauidem dixit: Zelus domus tuæ comedit me. Et exempla sunt cùm veteratum recentia, quæ his fidem possunt facere. Debet ergo hoc Apostoli dictum semper in auribus & animis nostris sonare, vt partim nos admoneat, quid in re quaque facto opus sit: partim vt ex eo consolationem petamus aduersus eos, qui nobis propter fidem in vnum Deum & propter verbum eius negotium faciunt. Nec enim nobiscum, qui vt omnes [?]mactationis sumus, illius res est, sed cum æterno Dei Filio, IESV CHRISTO, cui omne iudicium dedit Pater, & potestatem omnem in cœlo & in terra. Huic facile fuerit, & illorum proterui-am frangere, & ecclesiam suam tueri, quam sanguinis sui pretio redemptam sibi despondit. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Again, you will observe that this same thing is said to all who bring into dispute those things which God has plainly declared in his Word. For he wills that whatever he has said be firm and ratified for us, and his will ought to stand for us as the highest reason, and nothing further is needed to confirm it. It would therefore be wrong to enter into debate with him, as if we could devise something better, more useful or more fitting. Now the use of this teaching is manifold. First, it ought to be applied to life and morals. For there are many here who are overly ingenious in excusing crimes which are committed against the express will of God. But we ought then to consider that it is human to sin, but to wish to defend sin is indeed to fight against God [θεομαχεῖν ἐστι], that is, to wage war with God himself. Cain did this of old, and afterwards Pharaoh, Saul and many others, and the outcome for all of them was unhappy. Above all, this must be observed in religion, which, unless it is instituted at the nod of God, is not even worthy of the name. But God long ago comprehended all of this under certain heads, the sum of which is contained in the Decalogue and in the Creed which they call the Apostles'. How many people today are there to be seen who openly deny those things, or wrap them in thorny disputations, so that they can foist their own fictions on the ignorant crowd in their place? And what shall we say of those who, feeling themselves lacking in reasons and arguments, turn to force and want matters pertaining to the worship of God and the business of eternal salvation to be decided by sword and fire? This happens everywhere today, and those who fight with arguments are almost the ones who defend, against the manifest Word of God, the primacy of the Roman Pontiff, the sacrifice of the Mass, the worship of images, purgatorial fire, papal indulgences and countless other things. But all these men provoke God to jealousy, and sometimes they will learn to their great cost how powerless they are against him. For he does not sleep, who said long ago through David: "The zeal of your house has consumed me." And there are recent examples, as well as old ones, which can give credit to these words. This saying of the Apostle ought therefore always to sound in our ears and minds, so that partly it may admonish us what must be done in each matter, and partly that we may draw consolation from it against those who make trouble for us on account of our faith in the one God and his Word. For the matter is not with us, who are as all mortals are, but with the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, to whom the Father has given all judgment and all power in heaven and on earth. To him it will be easy both to break the insolence of those men and to protect his Church, which he has betrothed to himself, redeemed by the price of his own blood. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY LIIII.

units.la: Omnia mihi licent, at non omnia conducunt: omnia mihi licent, sed non omnia aedificant. Nemo quod suum est quaerat, sed quisque quod alterius est. Quicquid in macello venditur, edite, nihil interrogantes propter conscientiam. Domini enim est terra & plenitudo eius. Quod si quis infidelium vos vocat, & vultis ire, quicquid apponitur vobis, edite, nihil interrogantes propter conscientiam. At si quis vobis dixerit, Hoc idolis immolatum est: ne edite, propter illum qui indicauit, & propter conscientiam. Domini enim est terra & plenitudo eius. Conscientiam autem dico, non tuam, sed illius alterius: Cur enim libertas mea iudicatur ab alia conscientia? Et si ego per gratiam participo, cur ob id mihi maledicitur, pro quo ego gratias ago?
units.tr: "All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient: all things are lawful for me, but not all things edify. Let no one seek his own, but each man what is another's. Whatever is sold in the meat market, eat, asking no question for conscience' sake. For the earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof. But if any of the unbelievers invites you, and you are willing to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no question for conscience' sake. But if anyone says to you, 'This has been offered in sacrifice to idols,' do not eat it, for the sake of him who informed you, and for conscience' sake. For the earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof. Now I say conscience, not your own, but that of the other. For why is my liberty judged by another's conscience? And if I partake with thanksgiving, why am I reviled for that for which I give thanks?"

units.la: Quamuis Deus, qui spiritus est, mente & spiritu adorari atque coli velit, plurimum tamen refert, ut externa religio recte instituta sit: partim quidem propter nos, quos externis exercitijs in coelestium & spiritualium contemplationem excitari oportet: partim propter ipsum Deum, qui cum ipsa sit veritas, nihil à nobis fictum aut simulatum vult fieri. Vehementer ergo & pernitiose errant qui de animi integritate & fidei synceritate ita gloriantur, ut in externis sibi nihil non licere putent, & quorumuis arbitrio sese accommodent. Quia enim illa ad fidei quoque confessionem faciunt, in qua ingenuam fortitudinem atque constantiam Christus requirit, magno studio nos anniti decet, ne quid dicamus vel faciamus, quo haec labefactetur, aut cum alio rum scandalo in suspicionem veniat. Et huc referri à nobis debet tota haec Pauli Apostoli de idolothytis tractatio: In qua nuper offendit, eos qui circa illa sibi indulgent, rem praestitu impossibilem tentare, ut nimirum germana Ecclesiæ Christi membra sint, & simul daemoniorum participes fiant: & ut huius audaciæ atrocitatem melius exprimeret, diserte pronunciauit, eos qui id faciunt, ipsum Dominum ad æmulationem & quasi ad certamen prouocare, cuius non posset non infelicissimus, quoad ipsos, euentus expectari. Poterat haec comminatio [?]abunde suffi-cere ijs, qui serio pietatis & gloriae Dei studio tanguntur: at quia aduersarij noua quotidie effu-gia captabant, rursus ad praecipuas eorum obiectiones respondet.
units.tr: Although God, who is a Spirit, wishes to be worshipped and honoured in mind and spirit, it nonetheless matters greatly that outward religion be rightly ordered: partly indeed for our own sake, since we must be stirred by outward exercises to the contemplation of heavenly and spiritual things; and partly for God himself, who, being truth itself, wills that nothing feigned or pretended be done by us. Therefore those people err grievously and destructively who boast of integrity of heart and sincerity of faith in such a way that they think they may do anything they like in outward matters and accommodate themselves to whatever anyone pleases. For since these outward matters also bear upon the confession of faith, in which Christ requires a noble courage and constancy, we ought to strive eagerly that we say or do nothing by which this confession is weakened, or by which it comes under suspicion to the scandal of others. And to this end the whole discussion of Paul the Apostle concerning things sacrificed to idols must be referred by us. In it he has recently shown that those who indulge themselves in such things attempt an impossible feat, namely to be genuine members of the Church of Christ and at the same time to become partakers of demons; and, to express more clearly the atrocity of this audacity, he plainly declared that those who do this provoke the Lord himself to rivalry, or as it were to a contest, and that an outcome most unhappy for themselves cannot but be expected. This threat might have been enough for those who are seriously moved by devotion to godliness and the glory of God; but since the adversaries kept seeking new escapes every day, he again answers their principal objections.

units.la: Initio autem ad illud redit, quod in tota hac causa aduersarij nunquam non in ore habe-bant: Christianis nimirum hominibus ex iure libertatis per Christum partæ licere omnibus, quæ à Deo data sunt, tutò uti, neque illos ullis legibus, quoad ciborum delectum, teneri. De quo etsi supra quoque Cap. sexto & nono dixerit, hic tamen quæ tunc dicta sunt repetit: eò quòd vix quicquam tam difficile est, quàm fræno certo carnem continere, ne libertate Christiana in licentiam abutatur. Vt vero minus odij habeat tractatio, in seipsum hoc omne transfert, & in propria persona loquens ait: Omnia mihi licent, at non omnia conducunt: omnia mihi licent, sed non omnia ædificant. Primum libere & ingenuè fatetur quod illi iactabant, vt offendat, se Christianorum libertati nihil prorsus derogatum velle, quò minus hæc pijs salua maneat. At ex altera parte mox docet, non ideo quidiu esse faciendum, neque Christianum hominem decere, vt suæ libertatis iure semper & apud omnes vtatur. Causam huius exceptionis allegat, quòd non omnia conducant, neque etiam omnia ædificent. Potest autem hæc causæ redditio tam ad eos, qui libertate suâ licentius vtuntur, quàm ad alios extendi, quibus cum illis res est. Quoad illos enim, satis constat, non semper ipsis vtile esse, vt faciant quicquid licet: sed vtilius interdum esse, vt cupiditates suas arctioribus habenis coerceant. Quia quò magis indulgemus carnis nostræ desiderijs, eò magis illa accendimus, vt tandem in illicitis quoque nobis dominentur. Fit ergo plerunque quod Clemens olim prudenter admodum & verè dixit. Qui faciunt quicquid licet, huc cito delabuntur, vt faciant quod non licet. Est enim (vt aliâs monuimus) insatiabilis hominum cupiditas, & vt flamma vorax, quoad materiam sibi obiectam habet, subindè latius serpens, absque omni discrimine proxima quæque corripit: ita carnis affectus modum nesciunt, & indulgentia nimia confirmati, ne ab illis quidem abstinent, quæ tam diuinis quàm humanis legibus prohibentur. Ita vero libertas in turpissimam seruitutem degenerat, quæ facit vt carnis & affectuum plus quàm belluinorum mancipia fiant, qui in spiritus libertate soli Deo seruire & propriæ saluti consulere debebant. Quem ergo fructum ex libertate sua recipit, qui eius persuasione deceptus ea designat, quorum ipsum non potest non pudere, si respiciat, & quæ præsens illi exitium attulerunt, si in ijs pergat? Quoad alios autem, res est manifestior: quia qui adhuc in fide infirmiores sunt ij non possunt non offendi, si quos absque omni ratione licentius agere videant: qui verò à fide prorsus sunt alieni, ij ex eo calumniandi occasionem arripiunt. Utrumque verò non ædificat, sed destruit potius, & Euangelicæ doctrinæ cursum remoratur. Vult ergo, vt gratis quidem animis agnoscamus libertatis per Christum nobis quæsitæ beneficium, eius verò vsum pro temporum, locorum & personarum ratione restringamus, vt tam nostræ quàm multorum aliorum vtilitati seruiat: & ne quis etiam vtilitatis nomine abutatur, de ea se loqui docet, quæ cum ædificatione in vera fide coniuncta est. Etenim si bonus paterfamilias, etsi merum in sua domo imperium habeat, non tamen temere quidquam facit, sed familiæ et totius rei domesticæ rationem habet ne quid huic incommodet: quanto magis hoc Christianos homines obseruare decet, qui etsi in domum Dei adoptati sint, vt spiritu filiorum Dei & communi cum his honorum cœlestium hæreditate fruantur, Christo tamen subiecti sunt, qui ferre non potest, vt vel domus suæ ordo & administratio turbetur, vel quisquam ex ipsius domesticis nostra licentia pereat?
units.tr: At the beginning, however, he returns to that point which the adversaries always had in their mouths throughout this whole cause: that, namely, by the right of liberty won through Christ, all things given by God may be used safely by Christian people, and that they are not bound by any laws concerning the choice of foods. Although he has said something about this above, in chapters six and nine, he here repeats what was said then, because there is scarcely anything so difficult as to restrain the flesh with a sure bridle, so that it does not abuse Christian liberty into licence. But so that the discussion may cause less offence, he transfers the whole matter to himself and, speaking in his own person, says: "All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient: all things are lawful for me, but not all things edify." First, he frankly and openly concedes what they were boasting, so that he may not offend them: he wishes nothing at all to be taken away from the liberty of Christians, so far as it remains safe for the godly. But on the other side he at once teaches that for this reason it is not to be done at every point, nor does it befit a Christian man to use his right of liberty always and before everyone. He gives the reason for this exception: that not all things are expedient, nor do all things edify. This reason of his may be extended both to those who use their liberty too licentiously and to others who have dealings with them. As for the former, it is quite clear that it is not always useful for them to do whatever is allowed; rather, it is at times more useful for them to restrain their desires with tighter reins. For the more we indulge the desires of our flesh, the more we inflame them, so that at last they rule over us even in unlawful things. So it generally happens what Clement once said very wisely and truly: those who do whatever is permitted quickly slide into doing what is not permitted. For (as we have pointed out elsewhere) the desire of men is insatiable, and like a voracious flame, which, so long as it has matter laid before it, creeps ever more widely and seizes whatever is nearest without any distinction, so the affections of the flesh know no measure, and, strengthened by excessive indulgence, they do not abstain even from those things which are forbidden both by divine and by human laws. Thus liberty degenerates into the most shameful slavery, which makes men slaves of the flesh and of passions more than beastly, when they ought in the liberty of the Spirit to serve God alone and to care for their own salvation. What fruit, then, does he gain from his liberty who, deceived by its persuasion, pursues those things of which he cannot but be ashamed if he looks back, and which have brought ruin upon him at present if he persists in them? As for others, the matter is more evident: for those who are still weaker in faith cannot but be offended if they see others acting with too much licence without any reason; and those who are wholly estranged from the faith seize on this as an occasion for slander. Both of these do not edify but rather destroy, and they hinder the course of the Gospel teaching. He therefore wishes us to acknowledge with grateful minds the benefit of the liberty won for us through Christ, but to restrain its use according to the circumstances of times, places and persons, so that it serves the advantage both of ourselves and of many others. And lest anyone abuse even the name of advantage, he teaches that it is the advantage which is joined with edification in true faith that is meant. For if a good householder, though he has absolute authority in his own house, nevertheless does nothing rashly, but takes account of his family and of the whole domestic economy, lest anything harm it; how much more ought Christian people to observe this, who, although they have been adopted into the house of God, so that by the Spirit of the sons of God they may enjoy a common heavenly inheritance with the others, are nevertheless subject to Christ, who cannot bear that the order and management of his house should be disturbed, or that any of his household should perish through our licence?

units.la: Ideo generalem sententiam subijcit Paulus, qua omne id comprehendit, quod in hac causa dici poterat. Nemo (inquit) quod suum est quærat, sed quisque quod alterius est. Suâ quæriere dicuntur, qui suis modò commodis student, nulla aliorum ratione habita. Est hoc commune vitium nobis à natura insitum, vt (quod Comicus olim obseruauit) omnes sibi melius esse velint, quàm alteri. Et tanta huius philautiæ vis est, vt religionem quoque corrumpat, quo nullum fingi potest efficatius vnitatis & communionis vinculum. Facit enim, vt sub huius prætextu plerique priuatum commodum quærant, & suam licentiam saluti aliorum præferant. At hunc affectum à Christianis hominibus Paulus alienissimum esse vult, vt qui aliorum potius quàm suis priuatis commodis intenti esse debeant. Et huius præcepti sui rationes grauissimas adducere poterat, quas tamen breuitatis causa omittit. Primò enim (quod philosophi quoque monuerunt) constat, neminem mortalium sibi soli natum esse, sed partem nostri sibi vendicare parentes, partem aliam natale solum, partem verò amicos. Imò eos demum Dijs similimos fieri dixerunt, qui quàm plurimis benefaciunt. Ergo in communes humanitatis leges peccare dicimus eos, quicunque ita sibijpsis soli priuatim viuunt, vt alios omnes securè negligant. Deinde vrget nos charitatis fraternæ Lex, quam ea conditione nobis Christus commendauit, vt tunc demum nos discipulorum & amicorum loco habituros sit, si alij alios diligamus, sicuti ipse nos dilexit. Ideo Paulus, cum hanc ipsam causam in epistola ad Romanos ageret, Christi exemplum adducit, quod omnes imitari debeant. Debemus (inquit) nos qui firmi sumus, imbecillitates infirmorum portare, ac non indulgere nobis ipsis. Vnusquisque enim nostrum proximo indulgere debet in bonum, ad aedificationem: Nam & Christus non indulsit sibiipsi, &c. Et sane si huius exemplum diligenter excutiamus, illum nihil suipsius causa, sed omnia propter nos fecisse videbimus. Propter nos enim cum in forma Dei & Patri aequalis esset, humiliauit se, & non homo solum factus est, sed servi formam assumpsit, ut nos Dei filios & suos coheredes faceret. Propter nos peregre & sub censu natus est, ut patriam nobis in caelis pararet, & ex diaboli tyrannide miseros eriperet, virgamque exactoris illius improbissimi (ut olim Isaias promiserat) confringeret. Propter nos pauper factus est, ut nos aeternis regni caelestis thesauris beatos faceret. Propter nos genus omne iniuriarum sustinuit, ut nos aeternae damnationis ignominia liberaret. Propter nos denique acerbam & infamem in ara crucis mortem subijt, & pro nobis peccatum factus est, ut nos per ipsum iustitia Dei efficeremur. Ad tanti ergo exempli imitationem sese accingere debent, quicunque germani eius discipuli esse volunt: & pudeat ipsis aliquid graue & iniquum videri, quod Dei Filium pro nostra salute fecisse vident. Deniq; aedificatio nobis studiorum & actionum omnium finis atque scopus sit, & ita a salutis tramite nequaquam aberrabimus. Sunt haec quidem dictu facilia, & (cum in genere traduntur) auditu quoque iucunda sunt: at si cum his nostri saeculi mores conferas, paucos reperies, qui abilicitis[?] & inconcessis abstinere velint in eorum gratiam, quos publica multorum licentia offendi audiunt. Sentient illi aliquando, quid sit Christi nomine ad eorum destructionem abuti, quos ille proprij sanguinis pretio redimere dignatus est.
units.tr: Therefore Paul subjoins a general sentence which comprehends all that could be said in this cause: "Let no one," he says, "seek his own, but each man what is another's." They are said to seek their own who are concerned only with their own advantage, with no regard had to others. This is a common vice implanted in us by nature, so that (as the comic poet once observed) everyone wishes himself to be better off than another. And the power of this self-love is so great that it corrupts even religion, though no bond of unity and fellowship can be devised more effective than religion. For it makes many people, under its pretext, seek private advantage and place their own licence before the salvation of others. But Paul wishes this disposition to be most alien from Christian people, who ought to be intent upon the advantage of others rather than of their own private concerns. He could have adduced very weighty reasons for this precept of his, which, for the sake of brevity, he omits. For first (as the philosophers too have taught) it is clear that no mortal is born for himself alone, but parents claim a part of us, the native land another part, and friends a further part. Indeed, they said that those men at last become most like the gods who do good to the greatest number. Therefore we say that those who live so privately for themselves alone, while carelessly neglecting all others, sin against the common laws of humanity. Next, the law of fraternal charity presses upon us, which Christ commended to us on this condition, that he would then at last count us among his disciples and friends if we love one another, as he himself loved us. So Paul, when he treated this very cause in his epistle to the Romans, brings forward the example of Christ, which all ought to imitate. "We who are strong," he says, "ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves. For each of us ought to please his neighbour for good, unto edification. For Christ also did not please himself," etc. And indeed, if we examine his example diligently, we shall see that he did nothing for his own sake, but did all things for our sake. For for our sake, though he was equal to the Father in the form of God, he humbled himself, and was made not only man, but took the form of a servant, so that he might make us sons of God and his co-heirs. For our sake he was born in a foreign land and under a census, so that he might prepare for us a fatherland in heaven, and snatch us wretched people from the tyranny of the devil, and break the rod of that most wicked exactor (as Isaiah had once promised). For our sake he became poor, so that he might make us blessed with the eternal treasures of the heavenly kingdom. For our sake he endured every kind of injury, so that he might free us from the disgrace of eternal damnation. For our sake, finally, he underwent a bitter and infamous death on the altar of the cross, and was made sin for us, so that through him we might be made the righteousness of God. Therefore all who wish to be his true disciples ought to gird themselves to imitate so great an example; and they should be ashamed to regard as grievous and unjust anything which they see the Son of God has done for our salvation. Finally, let edification be the aim and goal of all our studies and actions, and so we shall by no means wander from the path of salvation. These things are indeed easy to say, and when they are delivered in general terms they are also pleasing to hear; but if you compare with them the manners of our own age, you will find few who are willing to abstain from unlawful and unbecoming things for the sake of those whom they hear are offended by the public licence of many. They will one day feel what it is to abuse the name of Christ for the destruction of those whom he deigned to redeem at the price of his own blood.

units.la: Caeterum vt ad Pauli institutum & praesentis argumenti tractationem redeamus, noua dif-ficultas & periculum ineuitabile ex publico more pijs obijciebatur, quae noua obiectiones aut quaestiones pariebant. Nam vt in historijs est videre, solebant interdum sacrificia liberalium & tanta cum multitudine victimarum fieri, vt earum carnes in epulo sacro simul omnes absumi non possent. Tunc ergo quae reliquae fiebant, in macello publice vendebantur, & ex his collecta pecunia ad sacerdotes redibat. Et huius moris D. Augustinus in expositione propositionis 78. ex epistola ad Romanos meminit. Accedebat huic moris alius quod aliqui ex carnibus victimarum partem aliquam domum deferrent, vt domesticos suos, qui epulo sacro non potuerant interesse, eius ita participes facerent. Ex quo inter Christianos consuetudinem natam esse verisimile est, vt ex pane & poculo Coenae Dominicae aliquid ad eos, qui domi aegrotabant, allatum fuerit: quod non aliud fuit, quam ex Coena publica priuatam facere, & multis superstitionibus occasionem praebuit. Erant itaque immolatitiarum carnium tam in foro quam in aedibus priuatis omnia plena, vt illarum esum omnino vitare impossibile esset. Hinc ergo quidam occasionem arripiebant, vt Pauli rē obseruatu impossibile & Christianis hominibus indigna praecipere clamaret. Quia enim et in macello immolatitiae carnes inter vulgares promiscue venditur[?] (dicebant) et in priuatis quoq; conuiuijs apponuntur, in vniuersum caueri non poterunt, nisi ab omni carnium esu abstinere, adhaec omnem hominum consuetudinem fugere libeat. At quid hoc aliud est, quam libertatem Christianam prorsus abrogare, & quoad ciborum delectu Christianis iugu[?] imponere Mosaico illo longe intolerabilius, eo quod simul amicitiae inter homines e medio auferat? Habebat haec magnu[?] momentu[?] apud rerum imperitos, nec dubium est hisce clamoribus multos vehementer offensos fuisse, vt Pauli doctrinam indignius ferrent. Quapropter ne quid intactum relinquat, quo vel infirmiores offendi, vel gulae dediti calumniandi et tergiuersandi occasionem arripere possent, doctrinam hanc quaestionibus istis applicat, & quid in vtroque casu Christiani obseruare debeant, diligenter docet.
units.tr: But to return to Paul's plan and the treatment of the present subject: a new difficulty and an unavoidable danger were being thrown in the face of the godly by the public custom, and these gave rise to new objections and questions. For, as one can see in the histories, sacrifices to the gods of the liberal arts were sometimes carried out with such a multitude of victims that their flesh could not all be consumed at the sacred feast. Then what was left over was sold publicly in the meat market, and the money collected from this went back to the priests. Blessed Augustine also mentions this custom in his exposition of the seventy-eighth proposition from the Epistle to the Romans. Another custom was added to this: some people carried part of the flesh of the victims home, so as to make their household members, who could not be present at the sacred feast, partakers of it. From this it is likely that the custom arose among Christians of carrying some of the bread and cup of the Lord's Supper to those who were sick at home; this was nothing other than making a private thing out of a public one, and it gave occasion to many superstitions. Thus everything was full of meat offered to idols, both in the market and in private houses, so that it was utterly impossible to avoid eating it. Hence some seized the opportunity to cry out that Paul was prescribing something impossible to observe and unworthy of Christian people. For, they said, since meat offered to idols is sold among ordinary goods in the market and is also served at private dinners, it cannot be avoided in general unless one abstains from all eating of meat and, moreover, is willing to flee all human society. But what is this other than to abolish Christian liberty altogether, and to impose on Christians, in regard to the choice of foods, a burden far more intolerable than that of Moses, in that it would also take away friendship between people? This argument carried great weight with the inexperienced, and there is no doubt that many were deeply offended by these outcries, so that they took Paul's teaching more indignantly. Therefore, so as to leave nothing untouched by which either the weaker might be offended or those given over to their bellies might seize the opportunity to slander and evade, he applies this teaching to those questions and carefully teaches what Christians ought to observe in each case.

units.la: Et de primo quidem breuius agit his verbis: Quicquid in macello venditur, edite, nihil inter-rogantes propter conscientiam: Domini enim est terra & plenitudo eius. Distinguit inter ido-leum siue templum idolis consecratum, de quo supra, & macellum seu forum publicum, in quo omnis generis carnes venduntur. Illud enim pro sacro habebatur, & absque controuersia sacrae dicebantur carnes, quae illic apponi solebant: macellum vero inter locos prophanos numeratur, & in eo cuiuis licet emere, quae vitae sustentandae seruiunt. Quoad ergo macellum, conscientias omni metu & solicitudine liberat, & aperte monet, ea quae hucusq; de vitandis carnibus immolatitiis dicta sunt, non debere in forum vsq; extendi, vbi quod in idoleo sacrum erat, iam omnium vsui expositum est, & proinde sacrum esse & haberi desijt. Imò edite (inquit) quicquid illic venditur, nihil interrogantes propter conscientiam. In Graeco ἀνακρίνοντες habetur, quod est intra semetipsum haerere, & in vtramq; partem ratiocinari, liceat ne an minus aliquid facere. Eiusmodi ergo haesitatione in ijs, quae publicè venduntur, nequaquam opus esse ait, propter conscientiam, id est, quoad causam religionis, & quatenus ipsis cum Deo res fit, qui animi puritatem maximè requirit. At quia impossibile est, hominem in animo suo securum & tranquillum fieri, nisi de Dei voluntate certus sit, doctrinam hanc spiritus sancti testimonio confirmat, quod in Psalmo 24. habetur. Composuit illum Dauid, cum templi sedem aut locum ipsi Deus monstrauisset: ideoq; prima eius parte eorum superstitioni occurrit, qui religionem certis locis alligare student, & vt illorum opinionem falsi arguat, dicit: Domini est terra & plenitudo eius: orbis & qui eum inhabitant: Ipse enim super maria fundauit eam, & super flumina praeparauit eam. Quia autem plenitudo terrae Hebræis omnem rerum creatarum abundantiam significat, qua Deus illam ornauit & instruxit, non praeter rationem Paulus dictum istud huic causae accommodat, in qua de libero ciborum quorumuis esu disserit. Caeterum primo intuitu non admodum bona aut probabilis consequentia esse videtur. Domini est terra & plenitudo eius, Ergo omne quod in foro venit edite, nihil interrogantes propter conscientiam. Diceret enim illusor aliquis Lucianicus: Quid ad te ô bone, quod omnis terra & quaecunq; ea continentur, Domini sunt? Num ideo tibi omnibus illis, vt proprijs, vti licebit? Quin potius illa tua esse demonstras?
units.tr: He deals with the first case rather briefly, in these words: "Whatever is sold in the meat market, eat, asking nothing for the sake of conscience; for the earth is the Lord's and its fullness." He distinguishes between an idol-temple, or a place consecrated to idols, of which he spoke above, and the meat market or public marketplace, where meats of every kind are sold. The former was regarded as sacred, and the meats customarily set out there were without controversy called sacred; but the meat market is counted among profane places, and in it anyone may buy whatever serves to sustain life. So as regards the market, he frees consciences from all fear and anxiety, and plainly warns that what has been said hitherto about avoiding meat offered to idols should not be extended to the market, where what was sacred in the idol-temple has now been exposed to the use of all and therefore has ceased to be sacred and to be regarded as such. Indeed, he says, eat whatever is sold there, asking nothing for the sake of conscience. The Greek has ἀνακρίνοντες, which means to hesitate within oneself and to reason on both sides whether one may do or leave undone something. He says, then, that there is by no means need for such hesitation about things sold publicly, for the sake of conscience, that is, as regards the cause of religion, and insofar as the matter lies between a person and God, who above all requires purity of heart. But since it is impossible for a man to become secure and tranquil in his mind unless he is certain of God's will, he confirms this teaching by the testimony of the Holy Spirit, which is found in Psalm 24. David composed it when God had shown him the site or place of the temple; therefore, in its first part, he meets the superstition of those who strive to bind religion to certain places, and to refute their opinion as false, he says: "The earth is the Lord's and its fullness; the world and those who dwell in it. For he founded it upon the seas and prepared it upon the rivers." Now since "fullness of the earth" signifies to the Hebrews the whole abundance of created things with which God adorned and furnished it, Paul is not unreasonably applying this saying to this case, in which he discusses the free eating of any foods whatever. Yet at first glance the consequence does not seem very good or plausible: "The earth is the Lord's and its fullness; therefore eat whatever comes to the market, asking nothing for the sake of conscience." For some mocking Lucianic character might say: "What is it to you, good sir, that the whole earth and all that it contains belong to the Lord? Will you therefore be allowed to use all those things as if they were your own? Or rather, do you not show that they are yours?"

units.la: At hic duo oportet tenere, & mox patebit Pauli argumentum validissimum esse. Primum, quod ideo haec omnia Domini esse dixit Dauid, quia ille omnium creator est & conditor. Constat autem Deum quaecunq; fecisse bona fecisse, ita vt ex semetipsis nihil impurum aut vitiosum habuerint. Nam vidit Deus (inquit Moses) omne quod fecerat, & ecce erat valde bonum. Cùm ergo res creatae omnes per se bonae sint, & eadem in Dei possessione atq; protectione maneant, vt illis homines mali abutantur, in semetipsis pollui non possunt, quin pijs bonae sint. Istud ergo superstitioni eorum medetur, qui carnes ex idolis aut immolatione, quae idolis fiebat, aliquam pollutionem contrahere suspicabantur, & ideo ab illis abhorrebant, etiamsi vel in macello venderentur, aut in priuatis conuiuijs apponerentur. Alterum, quod quae Domini sunt, ad eos quoque pertinent, quos ille pro suis agnoscit. Nam initiò omnia propter hominem facta sunt, & Deum tunc scimus dixisse: Faciamus hominem in imaginem nostram, secundùm similitudinem nostram, & dominetur in piscem maris & in volucrem coeli, & in iumentum, & in omnem terram, & in omne reptile, quod reptat super terram, &c. Quam Dei bonitatem Dauid in Psalmis considerans, exclamat: Ecquid est homo mortalis, vt eius memineris? & filius hominis, vt eum inuisas? Paululum siquidem est, quod Deo inferiorem illum fecisti, gloria & decore cinxisti eum: Constituisti eum dominum super opera manuum tuarum, cuncta pedibus eius subiecisti: Greges & armenta vniuersa, etiam pecora campi, &c. Et quàmuis dignitas ista per peccatum euersa sit, inq; eius locum successerit maledictio, quae hominibus omnia infesta reddit: haec tamen nunc in solis impijs haeret, pijs autem & credentibus ius illud antiquum restituit Christus, qui nos sanguinis sui lauacro purificatos Patri ita reconciliauit, vt ex eius manu nos accipere sciamus, quaecunq; ad huius vitae sustentationem faciunt, ideoq; nobis pura, & proinde licita & concessa sunt omnia, quae cum gratiarum actione sumimus. Quibus adde, nos ea conditione in filios adoptatos esse à Deo, vt Christi fratres atq; coheredes simus. Quia ergo illi omnis potestas data est in coelo & in terra, nosq; coelestis regni haereditatem olim cum illo possidebimus, aequum certè est, vt quoad in terris viuimus, rebus creatis libere fruamur, quoad illis ad vitae nostrae sustentationem opus fuerit. Verè ergo & recte Paulus argumentatur.
units.tr: But here two things must be held fast, and it will soon be clear that Paul's argument is most valid. First, David said that all these things belong to the Lord because he is the creator and maker of all. It is certain that God made whatever he made good, so that they have nothing impure or faulty in themselves. For God, says Moses, saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good. Since therefore all created things are good in themselves, and remain in God's possession and protection, they cannot be polluted in themselves, however wicked men may abuse them; so they are good for the godly. This therefore remedies the superstition of those who suspected that meat from idols, or from the sacrifice that was made to idols, contracted some pollution, and therefore shrank from it, even if it was sold in the market or set out at private dinners. Second, that what belongs to the Lord pertains also to those whom he acknowledges as his own. For at the beginning all things were made on account of man, and we know that God then said: "Let us make man in our image, according to our likeness, and let him have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the heaven, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth," and so on. David, considering this goodness of God in the Psalms, cries out: "What is mortal man, that you should remember him? And the son of man, that you should visit him? For you have made him a little lower than God, you have crowned him with glory and honor. You have made him ruler over the works of your hands; you have put all things under his feet: all flocks and herds, and the beasts of the field," and so on. And although that dignity was overthrown through sin, and a curse, which makes all things hostile to men, has taken its place, nevertheless this curse now clings only to the wicked, while Christ restores that ancient right to the godly and believers. He, having cleansed us by the washing of his blood, has so reconciled us to the Father that we know we receive from his hand whatever serves the sustaining of this life; therefore all things that we take with thanksgiving are pure to us, and consequently lawful and permitted. Add to this that we have been adopted by God as sons on the condition that we should be brethren and co-heirs with Christ. Since therefore all power has been given to him in heaven and on earth, and since we shall one day possess the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom together with him, it is surely right that, as long as we live on earth, we should freely enjoy created things, so far as they are needed for the sustaining of our life. Thus Paul argues truly and rightly.

units.la: Debet autem ex hoc loco generalis doctrina peti, nullius conscientiam novis legibus de ciborum delectu aut discrimine esse grauandam. Si enim carnes, quae prius impijs vsibus & idololatriae con-secratae erant, Christianis hominibus licitae fuerunt & mundae, quanto minus ea prohiberi debent, quae ne abusu quidem vllo polluta sunt? Et cùm Deus ipse homini omnium, quae ipse creauit, vsus fecerit, sacrilegij species est, id cuiquam negare aut eripere, quod Deus dedit. Rursus, quia regnum Dei non est cibus aut potus, temeritas inexcusabilis fuerit illud absq; Dei verbo in ciborum quorumcunq; abstinentia monstrare. Qui enim nos sumus, vt in regno Dei leges condamus nouas, eatq; Dei legibus contrarias? Non temere igitur Apostolus in priori ad Timotheum daemonio- rum doctrinam esse dicit, quae à cibis certis abstinere iubet, quos in nostrum vsum Deus condidit. Atq; vnum hoc abunde arguit incurabilem Pontificum contumaciam, qui in tam clara Euangelij luce, quae vulgo omnibus nota est, adhuc traditiones suas firmas & ratas esse volunt: Nimirum ergo simplices sunt, qui illos in suis Concilijs de reformanda ecclesia serio cogitare putant.
units.tr: From this passage a general doctrine should be drawn: no one's conscience is to be burdened with new laws about the choice or distinction of foods. If meats that were formerly consecrated to impious uses and idolatry were lawful and clean for Christians, how much less should those be forbidden that have not been polluted by any misuse at all? And since God himself has given man the use of all the things he created, it is a sort of sacrilege to deny or snatch from anyone what God has given. Again, since the kingdom of God is not food or drink, it is an inexcusable rashness to point out, without the word of God, abstinence from any kind of food whatever. For who are we to frame new laws for the kingdom of God, and so set them against God's laws? It was not without reason that the Apostle, in his first letter to Timothy, called the doctrine that forbids certain foods, which God has created for our use, a doctrine of demons. This one thing amply proves the incurable obstinacy of the Papists, who, in such a clear light of the Gospel, which is known to everyone, still want their traditions to stand firm and valid. Surely, then, those are simple-minded who think that they seriously consider reforming the Church in their councils.

units.la: Porro ad alteram quaestionem de conuiuijs priuatis accedamus, quam pluribus & diligentius tractat. Sic enim scribit: Quod si quis infidelium vos vocat (videlicet domum suam, non in idolaeum aut epulum sacrum) & vultis ire, quicquid apponitur vobis, edite, nihil interrogantes propter conscientiam: At si quis vobis dixerit, Hoc idolis immolatum est: ne edite, propter illum qui indicauit, & propter conscientiam, &c. Primo, si vultis ire, inquit. Ergo liberum illis facit, vt ad eiusmodi conuiuia honoraria & amica accedant, vel minus, prout ipsis commodum videtur. Locutione autem ista admonet, vt probe apud se dispiciant, & nihil faciant absq; certo consilio. Nam in vniuersum ab omni infidelium congressu abstinere, minime consultum est: quia qui hoc faciunt, simul omnem ipsos lucrifaciendi occasionem negligant, oportet. Rursus qui hic temerarij & leues sunt, ij fere periculis sese implicant, & interdum fidei naufragium faciunt inter pocula, dum multa praeter officium dicunt & faciunt ipsi, ad multa etiam impie facta conniuent, multa item turpiter dissimulant, ne parum commodi aut grati hospites videantur. Verus ergo & proprius conuiuiorum vsus spectari[?] debet, qui est, vt primo quidem amicitia conseruetur: deinde vt occasionem habeamus in viam reducendi eos, qui hactenus aberrauerunt, vtq; maiori erga eos libertate possimus vti. Instituuntur interdum etiam, vt cum amicis gratias agamus Deo pro singulari aliquo beneficio, quo nos ornare dignatus est. Sic Abrahamus conuiuium magnum instruxisse legitur, cum filium Isaacum Sara ablactaret. Et huius generis multa inter pios & sanctos olim facta fuisse & adhuc hodie fieri videmus. Neq; peccant statim, qui ab infidelibus vocati veniunt. Nam Christum eiusmodi conuiuijs non semel interfuisse scimus, quando à Scribis & Pharisaeis vocabatur. Licet ergo etiam hodie Christianis hominibus eodem animo & instituto ad eorum mensam accedere, qui à nobis in religione dissentiunt, non tamen omnino hostiliter affecti sunt, sed nostram praesentiam atq; colloquia ferre possunt. Et constat hic saepe optatas occasiones offerri, quibus multi ad Christum adducuntur, multi mitiores fiunt & Veritati magis propitij. Vbi vero spes nulla est aliquos lucrifaciendi, periculum autem multiplex sese offert, ne quid à nostra professione alienum facere aut ferre cogamur, satius fuerit à conuiuijs & reliquis commercijs impiorum non necessarijs abstinere. Haec si hodie omnes diligentius expenderent, mox viderent quid ipsis in hoc casu sit obseruandum, & fortassis minus delectarentur eorum mensis, quos constat omnia insidiose agere, & omnem quaerere opprimendae veritatis occasionem.
units.tr: Next let us turn to the second question, about private banquets, which he treats more fully and carefully. He writes: "If any of those who do not believe invite you (namely to their home, not to an idol feast or a sacred banquet), and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking nothing for conscience' sake. But if anyone says to you, 'This has been offered to idols,' do not eat it, for the sake of the one who pointed it out, and for conscience' sake, etc." First, he says, "if you wish to go." Therefore he leaves it free to them to attend such banquets of honour and friendship, or not, as seems good to them. By this wording, however, he warns them to weigh the matter carefully within themselves and to do nothing without sound counsel. For it is by no means advisable to avoid all contact with unbelievers altogether, since those who do so must necessarily also neglect every opportunity of winning them. On the other hand, those who are rash and light-minded are often entangled in dangers and sometimes make shipwreck of their faith over their cups, while they themselves say and do many things beyond their duty, connive at many impious deeds, and shamefully dissemble many things, so as not to seem poor or ungrateful guests. The true and proper use of banquets, then, should be observed: first, that friendship be kept; then, that we have an opportunity of leading back those who have hitherto gone astray, and that we may use greater freedom towards them. Sometimes banquets are also held so that we may give thanks to God with friends for some singular benefit with which he has deigned to honour us. So Abraham is read to have prepared a great feast when he weaned his son Isaac. We see that many things of this kind were done of old among the pious and holy, and are still done today. Nor do those who come when invited by unbelievers sin at once. For we know that Christ was present at such banquets more than once, when he was invited by the scribes and Pharisees. Therefore it is lawful even today for Christians to come to the table of those who differ from us in religion, with the same intention and purpose; not that they are altogether hostile, but that they can bear our presence and conversation. And it is clear that here opportunities often arise, eagerly desired, by which many are brought to Christ, and many become milder and more favourable to the truth. But where there is no hope of winning anyone, and many dangers present themselves, lest we be compelled to do or endure something foreign to our profession, it will be better to abstain from banquets and other unnecessary dealings with the ungodly. If everyone considered these things more carefully today, they would soon see what must be observed by them in this case, and perhaps they would take less pleasure at the tables of those who are known to do everything treacherously and to seek every occasion of suppressing the truth.

units.la: Caeterum distinguit inter ista conuiuia Paulus, & casum ponit duplicem. Primus est, quando nulla de cibis mouetur quaestio aut controuersia, sed hi omnes apponuntur vt vulgares & soliti cibi. Tunc (inquit) edite, nihil interrogantes propter conscientiam. Sensus est: Nolim vos curiosos aut solicitos esse, quaenam aut quales sint carnes quae apponuntur. Nam siue immolatitiae fuerint, seu minus, vobis tamen fraudi esse non possunt, cum vt vulgares ex solito more apponantur, & vos ijsdem absq; omni superstitione, vt vulgaribus vescamini. Ita vero & conscientijs Christianorum consulit, & simul monet, ne ipsi conuiuia, quae honoris aut amicitiae ergo instituta sunt, temere turbent, & ex illis rixandi materiam vanentur. Meminerint ergo Christiani homines, hoc loco generalem regulam praescribi, ne ipsi sine causa lites moueant inter eos, qui amicitiae siue honoris causa ipsos vocarunt. Solent hoc quidam morosiores aequo, qui vt singularis sanctimoniae & pietatis existimationem sibi parent, nihil non in quaestionem vocant, disputationes intempestiuas passim instituunt, & tantum non rationes totius oeconomiae exigunt ab ijs, à quibus amicè vocati sunt. Solent isti morositate sua saepe eos offendere, qui attrahi & lucrifieri poterant, si ipsi se commodiores praeberent. Quam vero ridiculi sunt Anabaptistae, qui si lautioris fortunae homines ipsis hospitium praebeant, & cibos quoq; delicatiores apponant, aliude[?] quidem illis ventres suos farciunt, nihil interrogantes propter conscientiam: at ubi eo devenitur, ut hospiti pro accepto beneficio gratias agere debeant, tunc aliquem ex suo grege subornant, qui vultu ad severitatem & tristitiam compositio, in delicias invehitur, temperantiam Apostolicam laudat, & tandem infelicem illum hospitem accusat, ut acerrima reprehensione dignum propter ea, quibus illi gulam & ventrem suum distenderunt. Mirificum hominum genus, quibus merito Satyricum illud occinas:
units.tr: Moreover, Paul distinguishes between these banquets and sets out a twofold case. The first is when no question or controversy about the food is raised, but everything is served as ordinary and customary fare. "Then," he says, "eat, asking nothing for conscience' sake." The sense is: I would not have you be inquisitive or anxious about what sort of meats are set before you. For whether they were offered to idols or not, they can do you no harm, since they are served in the ordinary way and you eat them without any superstition, as ordinary food. In this way he consults the consciences of Christians, and at the same time warns them not to disturb rashly the banquets that have been arranged out of honour or friendship, nor to hunt for material for quarrels in them. Let Christians therefore remember that this passage prescribes a general rule: that they themselves should not stir up quarrels without cause among those who have invited them out of friendship or honour. Certain men who are more morose than is right are accustomed to do this. Wishing to win for themselves a reputation for singular holiness and piety, they call everything into question, start untimely disputations everywhere, and all but demand an account of the whole household management from those by whom they have been kindly invited. Such men by their moroseness often offend those who could have been drawn in and won, had they shown themselves more accommodating. How ridiculous the Anabaptists are! If men of better fortune offer them hospitality and set more dainty foods before them, they stuff their bellies on these, asking nothing for conscience' sake. But when it comes to the point that they ought to thank their host for the kindness received, they then suborn someone from their flock, who, with a face composed to severity and gloom, inveighs against luxury, praises apostolic temperance, and finally accuses that unhappy host, as one deserving the sharpest rebuke, for those very things with which they themselves have distended their gullet and belly. A wonderful race of men, to whom one may fitly apply that line of the satirist:

units.la: Qui Curios simulant, & Bacchanalia viunt.
units.tr: Who pretend to be Curii, and live Bacchanalian lives.

units.la: Sed alterum casum videamus, quem sic proponit: At si quis vobis dixerit, Hoc idolis immolatum est: ne edite. Abstinere iubet, si quis alius de cibi genere sermonem moveat, qui disputationi aut controversiæ occasionem præbere posset. Causam vero adducit: Ne scilicet edant propter illum qui indicavit, & propter conscientiam. At ne sibipsi contrarius putetur, mox Expositionis loco subiicit: Conscientiam autem dico, non tuam, sed illius alterius. Ergo ne hic quidem propter cibum alicuius conscientiæ laqueum iniicere vult, & quamvis abstinere iubeat a cibo posse eiusmodi indicium factum, diserte tamen testatur, hoc non ideo fieri debere, quòd cibus per se immundus & illicitus sit, sed ne quæ scandali occasio illi detur, qui istud indicium fecit. Is enim aut Christianus erit, aut ethnicus. Si Christianus, haud dubiè infirmus erit, cùm quæstionem de cibo moveat, & ideo cavendum erit, ne per nos offendatur. Sin ethnicus fuerit, periculum est ne maligne & insidiò se captet calumniandi occasionem, qua & suam idololatriam defendat, & Christianam religionem omnium ludibrio exponat. Et verisimile est, frequentes in multorum ore fuisse sermones istos: Videtis ne qualis sit nova hæc Christianorum religio? Deos nostros publicè proscindunt, imagines hic positas detestantur, sacra quoq; fugiunt, neq; in templis nostris volunt accumbere. At si qui illis domum suam vocatis carnes ex victimis reservatas apponant, iam hic vesci nulla ipsis religio est. Quis ergo non videat, homines istos gulæ potius & ventris studio quàm religione duci? Hæc (inquam) & his similia tunc vulgò ferebantur: & ideo rectè admonet Paulus, ut abstineant, quàm primùm de cibo quæstio mota fuerit, ne scientes volentes idolorum sacrificijs vel minimâ ex parte communicare videantur. Et rationem subiicit gravem: Cur enim libertas mea iudicatur ab alia conscientia? Id est, cur ego occasionem dem, qua vel infirmus in fide, vel ethnicus, quorum conscientia nondum probè instituta est, in libertatem nostram sibi iudicium sumant, & eam suis cavillis proscindant atque damnent? Damnabatur enim, quando illi gulæ & ventris studio eos duci dicebant, qui sua libertate inconsultius utebantur. Addit: Et si ego per gratiam participo, cur ob id mihi maledicitur, pro quo ego gratias ago? Per gratiam nos participare dicit cibis, ut singulare illud Christi beneficium exprimat, qui & maledictione sublata, & legis maceria disrupta, fecit, ut creatorum omnium usus iam nobis licitus & sanctus fit. Vult ergo ne tantum beneficium, quo cum gratiarum actione uti debemus, nostra licentia & abusu calumniis eorum exponamus, qui omnem nos calumniandi occasionem vænantur, ut nos impios sacrorum omnium contemptores esse probent. His vero rursus interserit testimonium Psalmi, quod prius adduxerat: Ut nimirum doceat, tam eos qui edunt, quàm qui non edunt, nunquam non meminisse debere, cibos omnes nobis ex Dei manu obtingere. Hoc enim ut ad gratiarum actionem nos excitat, & temperantiam commendat: ita superstitioni quoq; medetur, ne cibum aut potum qualemcunq; aliquid ad æternam salutem conferre putemus. Cur enim hoc credat, qui cibos omnes à Deo esse, & ex huius benedictione sanctos esse novit? Sed & consolationi servit dictum illud: quia admonet, non deesse nobis victum in hoc penu Domini, tam magnificè instructo, licet à quibusdam abstineamus, quæ non sine scandalo à nobis usurpari possunt.
units.tr: But let us look at the second case, which he sets out thus: "But if anyone says to you, 'This has been offered to idols,' do not eat it." He bids them abstain if anyone raises a discussion about a kind of food that could give occasion for dispute or controversy. He gives the reason: namely, that they should not eat it for the sake of the one who pointed it out, and for conscience' sake. But lest he be thought to contradict himself, he at once adds, by way of explanation: "But I say conscience, not your own, but that of the other." So here too he does not wish to lay a snare for anyone's conscience on account of food; and although he bids them abstain from food when such an indication has been made, he clearly testifies that this should not be done because the food is unclean and unlawful in itself, but lest a occasion of offence be given to the one who made the indication. For that person will be either a Christian or a heathen. If a Christian, he will doubtless be weak, since he raises a question about food, and so care must be taken that he is not offended by us. But if he is a heathen, there is a danger that he will maliciously and craftily seize on the chance to slander, both to defend his own idolatry and to expose the Christian religion to the mockery of all. And it is likely that such words were frequently on the lips of many: "Do you see what kind of new religion this of the Christians is? They publicly tear down our gods, they detest the images set up here, they shun the sacred rites too, and they will not recline in our temples. Yet if some of them, when invited to their homes, set before them meats kept over from the victims, then they have no scruple at all about eating them. Who then does not see that these men are led by a desire for gluttony and the belly rather than by religion?" These things, I say, and things like them were then commonly spread about. And so Paul rightly advises them to abstain as soon as the question about food has been raised, lest they seem knowingly and willingly to share, even in the smallest part, in the sacrifices to idols. And he adds a weighty reason: "For why is my liberty judged by another conscience?" That is, why should I give occasion for a weak person in the faith, or a heathen whose conscience is not yet properly instructed, to take upon themselves the judgement of our liberty, and to tear it apart and condemn it with their quibbles? For it was condemned when they said that those who used their liberty too carelessly were led by a desire for gluttony and the belly. He adds: "And if I partake with thanksgiving, why am I evil spoken of for that for which I give thanks?" He says that we partake of foods "with thanksgiving," to express that singular benefit of Christ, who, by taking away the curse and breaking down the wall of the law, has made the use of all created things lawful and holy for us. He therefore wishes that we not expose so great a benefit, which we ought to use with thanksgiving, by our licence and abuse, to the calumnies of those who hunt for every occasion to slander us, in order to prove that we are impious despisers of all sacred things. He then again inserts the testimony of the Psalm that he had cited before: "The earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof" (Psalm 24). This is to teach that both those who eat and those who do not eat must never forget that all foods come to us from the hand of God. For this both stirs us to thanksgiving and commends temperance, and at the same time it remedies superstition, lest we think that any food or drink whatever contributes to eternal salvation. For why should anyone believe that, who knows that all foods are from God and are made holy by his blessing? And the saying also serves for consolation, because it reminds us that we shall not lack sustenance in this storehouse of the Lord, so richly furnished, even if we abstain from certain things which cannot be used by us without offence.

units.la: Rursus vero doctrinam generalem nobis Apostolus proponit, quæ in omnibus Dei donis observari debet: Ut nimirum illis cum gratiarum actione utamur, & ita quidem, ut usus hic noster aliorum quoq; bono serviat. Hoc enim charitatis lex monet, illud autem religio exigit, quæ Deum omnis boni largitorem agnoscere docet. De his autem nos sæpius admoneri utile est, quia hic vulgò peccatur. Est enim (ut alibi monuimus) infinita hominis cupiditas, & quàm primùm à Deo oculos revocat, variis illecebris inescata, facit, ut ad fastum & voluptates illicitas ijs abutamur, quibus ante omnia Dei gloriam, deinde nostram atq; aliorum salutem proevehere debebamus. Fit hoc non in ijs modò, quæ ad victum pertinet, verumetiam in opibus, honoribus, corporis forma & valetudine bona, deniq; in omnibus, quæ nobis ex Dei gratuita liberalitate obvenerunt. Est̄ hoc sce- lus graue admodum, & non postrema causa est̄ malorum, quibus mundum ingratum Deus affli- git. Si enim supplicio digni sunt, qui dona regia turpiter polluunt, quis extra culpam eos esse dixe- rit, qui Dei donis tam turpiter abuti non verentur? Quod vero præcipuum huius loci caput est̄, docemur, ita cum infidelibus esse versandum, ne minima ex parte fidei nostræ confessionem labefa- ctemus: quin testemur potius dictis & factis, nos ab omnibus abhorrere, quæ Christi merito & fi- dei in illum quicquam derogant. Quam regulam si sibi observandam proponant, qui hodie ad men- sas Monachorum & Abbatum ut muscæ ad multa convolare solent, mox sentient, se non ad- modum gratos convivas esse. Quid multis? Actionum & studiorum nostrorum omnium finis & scopus nobis sit gloria Dei, & ut nos CHRISTO IESU approbemus, in magno illo die, quo veniet ad judicandum vivos & mortuos. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æter- num, Amen.
units.tr: Again, the Apostle sets before us a general principle which ought to be observed in all of God's gifts: namely, that we should use them with thanksgiving, and in such a way that this use of ours also serves the good of others. For the law of charity requires the one, and piety, which teaches us to acknowledge God as the giver of every good, demands the other. It is useful for us to be reminded of these things often, because this is where people commonly go wrong. For human desire (as we have noted elsewhere) is boundless, and as soon as it turns its eyes away from God, it is baited by various enticements and makes us abuse, for pride and illicit pleasures, those things by which we ought above all to advance the glory of God and then our own salvation and that of others. This happens not only in matters of food, but also in wealth, honours, bodily beauty and good health, and finally in everything that has come to us from God's free generosity. This is a very grave sin, and it is no small cause of the evils with which God afflicts an ungrateful world. For if those are worthy of punishment who shamefully defile royal gifts, who would say that those are free from blame who do not hesitate to abuse the gifts of God so shamefully? The chief point of this passage, however, is that we are taught how we must live among unbelievers, so that we do not weaken the confession of our faith in the smallest degree; rather, by our words and deeds we should testify that we shrink from all things that detract in any way from the merit of Christ and from faith in him. If those who today flock like flies to the tables of the monks and abbots, as they often do, would take this rule as something to observe for themselves, they would soon realise that they are not very welcome guests. What more need be said? Let the end and aim of all our actions and studies be the glory of God, and that we may be approved in Christ Jesus on that great day when he will come to judge the living and the dead. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LV.
units.tr: HOMILY LV.
