units.la: Siue igitur editis, siue bibitis, siue quid facitis, omnia in gloriam Dei facite. Estote sine offendiculo & Judæis & Græcis, & Ecclesiæ Dei, sicut & ego per omnia omnibus placeo, non quærens meam ipsius utilitatem, sed multorum, ut serventur. Imitatores mei estote, sicut ego Christi.
units.tr: Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God. Be blameless both to the Jews and to the Greeks, and to the Church of God, even as I please all men in all things, not seeking my own profit, but the profit of many, that they may be saved. Be followers of me, even as I am of Christ.

units.la: QVoniam Paulus epistolam hanc ideo scripsit, ut qui in Corinthiacam ecclesiam irrepse- rant errores corrigeret, multis hucusq; de iis disseruit, qui contra fidei Christianæ professio- nem idololatrarum sacris communicabant, cum ad convivia illorum accederent, quæ ab illis in Deo- rum suorum honorem instituebantur. Erat vitium hoc non graue modo, verumetiam vulgo apud plerosq; in usu erat, & plausibili libertatis Christianæ prætextu, deinde pacis etiam publicæ & cha- ritatis studio defendebatur. Ideo multis & gravibus argumentis docuit, ipsos rem Christianis ho- minibus indignissimam facere. Nam primo ostendit Christianæ libertatis ius nequaquam in eo consistere, ut quæcunq; libet faciamus, sed ut externis & indifferentibus utamur, prout nobis & fratribus videmus conducere. Ex eo igitur concludit, quòd est per se licitum esset ad convivia eius- modi accedere, Christianorum tamen esse, ut ab illis abstineant, quando constet infirmiores quidem in fide hoc exemplo offendi, gentes autem & idololatras in suis superstitionibus confirmari. Dein- de rem ipsam aggressus, docuit societatem hanc alienorum sacrorum per se impiam ac detestabi- lem esse: Per hanc enim eos participes fieri mensæ dæmoniorum, & aperte in fidei confessionem pec- care, quam Christiani in omni casu puram & illibatam servare debeant. Postremò ad quæstiones quæ hic moveri poterant, respondit, quid nimirum in foro, quid item in convivis privatis observari debeat. At videbatur res ista nonnullis levior & minoris momenti esse, quàm quæ tam proli- xè & solicitè tractari deberet. Idcirco nunc epilogum inducit, quo docet, non temere se de his tam diligenter egisse: quando hac tractatione continentur, quæcunque ad vitam recte & sanctè instituendam faciunt. Primò enim a specie ad genus transit, & regulam præscribit universalem, quam in omnibus actionibus suis debeant observare. Deinde hanc proprio exemplo confirmat. Postremò suum quoque exemplum breui sententia illustrat, quæ totius Christianismi summam continet.
units.tr: Because Paul wrote this epistle in order to correct the errors that had crept into the Corinthian church, he has until now discussed at length those who, against their profession of the Christian faith, took part in the sacrificial feasts of idolaters when they attended the banquets held in honour of their gods. This vice was not a light one, and it was common practice among many, and it was defended under the plausible pretext of Christian liberty and then also of public peace and the zeal of charity. So he taught, with many weighty arguments, that such people were making themselves most unworthy of Christians. First, he showed that the right of Christian liberty does not consist in our doing whatever we please, but in using indifferent things as we see that they are useful to us and to our brothers. From this he concludes that although it was in itself lawful to attend such banquets, it is nevertheless the duty of Christians to abstain from them, since it is clear that the weaker in faith are offended by such an example, while the heathen and idolaters are confirmed in their superstitions. Then, taking up the matter itself, he taught that this fellowship with strange worship is in itself impious and detestable, for through it they become partakers of the table of demons and sin openly against the confession of faith, which Christians ought to keep pure and unstained in every case. Finally, he answered the questions that could be raised here, namely what ought to be observed in the law courts and likewise at private banquets. But that matter seemed to some to be lighter and of less moment than something that ought to be treated so fully and so carefully. Therefore he now introduces an epilogue, in which he teaches that he had not discussed these things so diligently without reason, since this treatment contains everything that serves to order our life rightly and holily. For first he passes from the particular to the general, and prescribes a universal rule that they ought to observe in all their actions. Then he confirms this by his own example. Lastly, he illustrates his own example with a brief saying, which contains the sum of all Christianity.

units.la: Primum his verbis explicat: Siue igitur, editis, siue bibitis, siue quid facitis, omnia in gloriam Dei facite: Estote sine offendiculo & Judæis, & Græcis, & Ecclesiæ Dei. Sub Edendi & Bibendi vocabulis Synecdochicè omnes hominum actiones quotidianas, & quæ ob vulgarem usum plerisque nullius momenti esse videntur, comprehendit. Horum autem potius quàm aliorum meminit, quia de idolothytorum esu hucusq; disseruit, & ut ostendat Christianos homines sui officij in illis etiam meminisse debere, quæ nobis, quoad externum usum, cum impiis quoq; & incredulis communia sunt. Ut ne minutioribus illis intentus, alia quæ graviora sunt, negligere putaretur, addit: Siue quid
units.tr: He first explains this in these words: "Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God. Be blameless both to the Jews and to the Greeks and to the Church of God." Under the words eating and drinking he comprehends, by synecdoche, all the daily actions of men, including those which seem to be of no importance to most people because of their ordinary use. He mentions these rather than others because he has so far discussed the eating of food offered to idols, and in order to show that Christians ought to remember their duty also in those matters which, as far as outward use goes, are common to us with the impious and the unbelieving. Lest he should be thought to be so intent on these smaller matters as to neglect others that are weightier, he adds: "or whatever you do."

units.la: faciitis facitis, qualecunq; scilicet illud fit, siue magnum, siue paruum, siue ad Dei cultum, siue ad vitae consuetudinem & mores pertineat. Verborum ergo sensus est hic: Possum fortasse quibusdam aequo curiosior videri, qui de cibis tam prolixe disputarim. Sed si rem ipsam expenderitis, & quis homini actionum omnium scopus esse debeat probe consideraueritis, nihil absq; grani causa abs me dictum esse intelligetis. Est enim homo ad Dei gloriam conditus, de qua cum hic agatur, huius vtiq; ratio mirimis erit tenenda. Adhaec Christiani hominis est cauere, ne quem dicto aut facto offendat. At eo, quod hactenus fecistis, tam Iudaeos quam Graecos, imo multos etiam ex Ecclesiae membris adhuc infirmioribus, offenditis. Annon ergo digna est res, quae diligentius consideretur, ne libertas in licentiam abeat, & ne dum hominum amicitiae studetis, a Dei gratia excidatis? Non temere autem Iudaeorum, Graecorum & Ecclesiae Dei meminit. Scimus enim Iudaeos illo tempore passim ethnicis permixtos habitasse. At non poterant illi non offendi, quando Christianos, qui religionem suam Mosis & Prophetarum testimonijs niti gloriabantur, videbant ad idolothytorum epulas accedere. Cogitabant enim, illos Mosem & Prophetas falso allegare, cum altaria & idola non horrerent, quae illi excindere, & ne aurum quidem, quod aliquando idolorum cultui seruijt, in vsus priuatos transferre iuuerunt. Similiter exemplum hoc ethnicos quoq; remorabatur, quo minus reliquis erroribus ad Christum transfirent. Ex illo enim colligebat, simulachrorum cultum non adeo graue scelus esse, & Christianos morositate potius quam religione aliqua illum damnare. Ad ecclesiam deniq; scandalum iste redundabat, quia (vt modo diximus) infirmiores in fide offendebantur, qui potius confirmari debebant, & simul hostibus dabatur occasio, qua religionem Christianam calumnijs suis vulgo suspectam & inuisam facerent.
units.tr: "Whatever you do," that is, whatever it may be, whether great or small, whether it pertains to the worship of God or to the customs and conduct of life. The sense of his words, then, is this: "Perhaps I may seem to some rather too scrupulous, since I have disputed so at length about foods. But if you weigh the matter itself, and consider carefully what the aim of all of a man's actions ought to be, you will understand that nothing has been said by me without weighty cause. For man was created for the glory of God, and since that is what is here at issue, its reasoning is surely to be held in the highest regard. Moreover, it is the duty of a Christian man to take care not to offend anyone by word or deed. But by what you have done up to now you have offended both Jews and Greeks, and indeed many even of the more infirm members of the Church. Is not this matter, then, worthy of more careful consideration, lest liberty turn into license, and lest, while you strive for the friendship of men, you fall away from the grace of God?" He does not mention the Jews, the Greeks and the Church of God without reason. For we know that the Jews at that time lived scattered and mixed among the heathen. But they could not help being offended when they saw Christians, who boasted that their religion rested on the testimonies of Moses and the Prophets, going to feasts of food offered to idols. For they thought that these Christians were falsely appealing to Moses and the Prophets, since they did not shrink from altars and idols, which the Jews had not been able to tear down, nor even to turn to private use the gold that had once served the worship of idols. In a similar way this example also hindered the heathen from passing over to Christ from their other errors. For from it they concluded that the worship of images was not so grave a crime, and that Christians condemned it out of peevishness rather than from any religious conviction. Finally, this scandal reflected back upon the Church, because (as we have just said) the weaker in faith were offended, when they ought rather to have been strengthened, and at the same time the enemies were given an occasion by which they might make the Christian religion, already commonly suspected and hated, the object of their slanders.

units.la: Est autem haec admonitio nobis diligentius consideranda, eo quod duobus capitibus omnia complectitur, quae in omnibus vitae nostrae actionibus atq; studijs obseruari debent. Primum est, vt omnia faciamus ad gloriam Dei. Ab hac autem oritur, quia qui huius studio tenentur, ij nunquam admittent, vt beneficiorum Dei aut libertatis Christianae abusu illa in periculum veniat, & hostium calumnijs exponatur. Vt vero illi ante omnia studeamus, Lex naturae admonet, quae praecipit, vt filij suos parentes, serui suos heros in honore & pretio habeant. Quanto autem maiori iure hoc a nobis Deus requirit, qui nos cum nulli essemus, creauit, & ex luto factos in summam dignitatem euexit, adeoq; in homine omnium creaturarum domino, suae potentiae & maiestatis simulachrum extare voluit? Superat tamen haec omnia, quod perfide lapsum non modo in dignitatem suam restituit, sed cum aliter nobis succurrere non posset, quam Filij vnigeniti sanguine, hunc pro nobis in mortem tradere dignatus est, imo hunc potius flagellatum, conspurcatum, spinis coronatum, denique in sublimi cruce inter latrones nudum videre maluit, quam nos in exitio relinquere, quod ipsi nostris sceleribus nobis accersiueramus. Nec enim eam modo dignitatem restituit, ex qua Adamus exciderat, sed in filiorum numerum adoptauit, & Filij vnigeniti coheredes fecit. Merito igitur Paulus monet, vt vicissim nos quoq; illi totos consecremus, & omnia faciamus ad ipsius gloriam. Conuenit admonitio haec cum Christi praecepto, qui discipulis in Euangelio dixit: Vos estis lux mundi: Splendeat ergo lux vestra coram hominibus, vt videant opera vestra bona, & glorifi-cent Patrem vestrum, qui in caelis est. Fit hoc, quando vera Dei & voluntatis eius cognitione illuminati, affectus carnis subigimus, omnia vero facimus ad illius praescriptum, vt nostro exemplo illi quam plurimos adducamus.
units.tr: This admonition, moreover, is for us to consider more carefully, because it embraces in two heads everything that ought to be observed in all the actions and pursuits of our life. The first is that we do everything to the glory of God. From this follows the second: those who are devoted to this aim will never allow the gifts of God or the liberty of a Christian to be abused so as to bring them into danger and expose them to the slanders of enemies. And that we should above all strive for this, the law of nature admonishes us, which commands that children honour and esteem their parents, and servants their masters. But with how much greater right does God require this of us, who created us when we were nothing, and raised us from clay to the highest dignity, and willed that in man, the lord of all creatures, there should stand an image of his own power and majesty? Yet all this is surpassed by the fact that, when we had fallen into perfidy, he not only restored us to our dignity, but, since he could not otherwise come to our aid than by the blood of his only-begotten Son, he deigned to deliver him to death for us; nay rather, he was willing to see him scourged, defiled, crowned with thorns, and finally naked on the high cross among thieves, rather than to leave us in the ruin which we had brought upon ourselves by our own crimes. For he restored not only that dignity from which Adam had fallen, but also adopted us into the number of his sons and made us co-heirs with his only-begotten Son. Rightly, therefore, Paul admonishes that in turn we should also wholly consecrate ourselves to him, and do all things to his glory. This admonition agrees with the precept of Christ, who said to his disciples in the Gospel: "You are the light of the world. Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven" [Matt. 5.14, 16]. This happens when, enlightened by the true knowledge of God and of his will, we subdue the affections of the flesh, and do all things according to his precept, so that by our example we may bring very many to him.

units.la: Potest ergo hoc latissime per omnes huius vitae actiones extendi. Nam vt ab eo, de quo hic agitur, exordiamur, glorificatur Deus edendo & bibendo, si illum cibi atq; potus largitorem agnoscimus, eidem pro hisce donis gratias agimus & eius beneficentiam praedicamus: si item illis temperanter vtimur, & nostro exemplo alijs authores sumus similia faciendi: deniq;, si ex nostra abundantia pauperum inopiam subleuamus, vt hi quoq; nobiscum laetari, & pro ijs, quae a nobis acceperunt, Deo gratias agere possint. Secus fit, si diuites illos auaros & epulones, quorum Christus meminit, imitati, gulae & ebrietati studeamus, vsum donorum Dei nobis solis vendicemus, & egenos atq; famelicos, ceu nihil ad nos pertinentes, negligamus. Tunc enim & ipsi multa facimus, quibus Dei gloria obscuratur, & pauperibus, qui iam ante iugum egestatis impatientius ferunt, occasionem damus, vt aduersus Deum murmurare & eius dispensationem, ceu iniquam accusare audeat. Potest idem de coniugiis dici. Glorificatur enim in his quoq; Deus, quando hic eorum author esse agnoscitur, quando secundum leges ab ipso latas contrahuntur, quando coniuges illi seruiunt, domum bene administrant, liberos in Dei cognitione & timore educant, denique quando toti in hoc sunt, ut ipsi pie vivant, & posteros sui similes relinquant, in quibus Dei veri notitia atque cultus conseruetur. His rebus olim Abraham studuit, & hoc nomine plus laudis meruit, quam ullì mortalium utriusque sexus, qui in caelibatu aut virginitate vitam suam transegerunt. At qui bellarum instar solo libidinis aestro impulsi coniuenunt[?], aut divitiarum atque honorum amore potius quam pietatis & sobolis studio ducuntur, ii plerunque ita vivunt, ut & in ipsis religio Christiana male audiat, & posteros relinquant Dei & sacrorum omnium contemptores. Quod de his dicitur, hoc ipsum ad opifices & agricolas pertinet, quibus uberrima Deum glorificandi materia proposita est. Meminerint modo isti, Deum esse, qui sua benedictione labores ipsorum fecundos atque felices reddat, & absque illius nutu nihil nobis feliciter succedere. Ita enim intelligent, pietati studendum esse, & simul ab omni dolo atque impostura abstinebunt, & in unum Deum intenti, alios quoque suo exemplo ad huius cultum provocabunt. At qui istorum[?] obliti, suo labore atque industria opes coacervare student, ii plerunque multa iniquè & iniustè contra charitatis leges designant[?], eoque plures offendunt, quo maiori audacia fidem in Deum veram sunt professi. Imprimis autem huius regulæ aut admonitionis meminisse debent ii, quos ideo supra alios homines Deus eminere voluit, ut suæ gloriæ vindices atq; tutores constitueret. De Ecclesiarum ministris & principibus loquor, adeoq; omnibus, qui in aliquo reipub. gradu constituti sunt. Discant illi nona-lium suæ gubernationis finem ipsis propositum esse debere, quam ut Deus emineat, Verbum eius locum habeat, & illius legibus omnes vivant. Hoc si effectum dare studeant, maximam ex eo au-thoritatem sibi accedere sentient. Dei siquidem promissio est: Honorantes me honorabo. Sed uti-nam hoc omnibus persuadere tam facile esset, quam dicere. Queruntur quidem de collapsa ministerii dignitate qui in Ecclesia docent: magistratus item & legum existimationem iam pridem languisse clamant, qui rempublicam administrant. Et merito quidem atque vere istud utrinque dicitur. Sed unde o boni, contemptus iste nascitur? Magna quidem populi licentia est: sed nem vobis maior fit videte. Quotus quisq; vestrum quæcunq; facit, ad gloriam Dei facit? Annon ple-riq; divitiis cumulandis inhiant, ludis & voluptatibus sunt dediti, Dei gloriam negligunt, & religionem vel omnino aspernantur, vel sub eius plausibili prætextu aliena invadunt, & ferè ne a sacrilegiis quidem abstinent? Vident hos fures multi ex Verbi ministris, & currit cum illis, sicut Deus in Psalmo loquitur. Hæc & alia huius generis fiunt, & adhuc de conculcata ordinum superiorum authoritate quiritamur?
units.tr: This can therefore be extended very widely over all the actions of this life. To begin with the matter under discussion, God is glorified in eating and drinking if we acknowledge him as the giver of food and drink, give him thanks for these gifts and proclaim his goodness; likewise if we use them temperately and by our example encourage others to do the same; and finally, if from our abundance we relieve the poverty of the poor, so that they too may rejoice with us and be able to give thanks to God for what they have received from us. It is otherwise if we imitate those rich, greedy feasters of whom Christ speaks, devote ourselves to gluttony and drunkenness, claim the use of God's gifts for ourselves alone, and neglect the needy and the hungry as if they had nothing to do with us. For then we ourselves do many things by which the glory of God is obscured, and we give the poor, who already bear the yoke of want with impatience, an occasion to dare to murmur against God and to accuse his dispensation as unjust. The same can be said of marriages. For God is glorified in these too when he is acknowledged as their author; when they are contracted according to the laws he has given; when the spouses serve each other, manage their household well, and bring up their children in the knowledge and fear of God; and finally when they are wholly intent on living godly lives themselves and leaving behind descendants like themselves, in whom the knowledge and worship of the true God may be preserved. Abraham once laboured at these things, and for this reason he earned more praise than any mortal of either sex who spent his life in celibacy or virginity. But those who, driven like beasts by the heat of lust alone, come together, or who are led by love of riches and honours rather than by zeal for piety and offspring, usually live in such a way that the Christian religion itself is badly spoken of because of them, and they leave behind descendants who despise God and all sacred things. What is said of these applies also to craftsmen and farmers, for whom a most abundant material for glorifying God is set before them. Let them only remember that it is God who, by his blessing, makes their labours fruitful and prosperous, and that nothing succeeds for us happily without his nod. For so they will understand that they must strive after piety, and at the same time they will abstain from all deceit and fraud; and intent on the one God, they will also stir others to his worship by their example. But those who forget these things and strive to heap up wealth by their own toil and industry usually devise many things unjustly and wrongly against the laws of charity, and they offend the more, the more boldly they have professed the true faith in God. Above all, those whom God wished to stand out above other men, in order to appoint them as defenders and guardians of his glory, ought to remember this rule or admonition. I speak of the ministers and rulers of the Churches, and indeed of all who hold any rank in the commonwealth. Let them learn that the sole end proposed to them in governing is that God be exalted, his Word hold its place, and all live by his laws. If they earnestly strive to bring this about, they will feel that the greatest authority accrues to them from it. For this is God's promise: "Those who honour me, I will honour." But would that it were as easy to persuade everyone of this as it is to say it. Those who teach in the Church indeed complain of the fallen dignity of the ministry; and those who administer the commonwealth cry out that the esteem of the magistracy and of the laws has long been failing. And rightly and truly is this said on both sides. But, good people, from where does this contempt arise? The licence of the people is indeed great; but see whether it is not greater in you. How few of you do anything whatever for the glory of God? Do not most of you crave to pile up riches, are given over to games and pleasures, neglect God's glory, and either despise religion altogether or, under its specious pretext, seize what belongs to others, and hardly abstain even from sacrilege? Many of the ministers of the Word see these thieves, and they run with them, as God says in the Psalm. These things and others of this kind are done, and yet do we still complain about the trampled authority of the higher orders?

units.la: Alterum huius admonitionis caput est, ut sine offendiculo simus. In Graeco ἀπροσκόπους[?] esse iubet, id est, tales, ad quorum exemplum nemo offendere, aut in eo mali ansam arripere possit. Erat autem necessarium hoc adici, siquidem prius illud, de quo iam diximus, locum habere debet. Nam impossibile est ad Dei gloriam id fieri, quod alios in illius cognitione & cultu deteriores reddit, aut saltem remoratur. Sed ut primo membro Dei gloriam nos ante omnia quærere docuit: ita hoc secundo Legem charitatis fraternæ nobis commendat, qua imprimis ad hoc nos astringit, ut nemini alicuius scandali simus authores. Pertinet huc, quod in Lege Deus pronuntiat: Ne maledicas surdo, neque offendiculum ponas coram cæco, quin potius timebis Deum tuum. Quod si vero scelus est cæco lapsus aut ruina causam dedisse: quanto grauius peccare eos putabimus, qui ignorantes & rerum imperitos suo exemplo in errores præcipitant, qui animæ exitium pariunt? Et debet hic diligenter observari distinctio, qua Paulus veluti sufficienti partium enumeratione utitur. Estote (inquit) sine offendiculo & Iudæis, & Græcis, & Ecclesiæ Dei. Ita enim omnia, quæ tunc erant, hominum genera nominare voluit, ne quem adeo vilem aut abiectum putemus, ut nobis quidvis in illum liceat. In hoc enim à plerisque peccatur, quod vix aliquem dignum arbitrantur, ut in suis rebus agendis aliquam eius habeant rationem. In alio enim vetus gentis odium, in alio familiæ ignobilitatem, in alio veteres iniurias & nescio quæ sexcenta alia causantur. At Paulus in præsenti Iudæos nominat, qui ut religionis Christianæ hostes acerrimi, & proinde odio digni erant: ita impunè contemni & negligi poterant, cum Romanū[?] & reliquis gentibus æquè inuisi essent. Deinde Græcorum meminit, quo nomine ethnicos homines & adhuc Deorum fictitiorum cultibus deditos intelligi, sæpe diximus. Erant ergò hi Tur-cis qui hodie regnant, peiores. His coniungit Ecclesiam Dei, vt ostendat non modò fratrum rationem esse habendam, ne per nos offendantur, verumetiam exterorum, qui negligi salua pietate non possunt, quando nostrum est nouos subinde Christo discipulos adducere. Ecclesiam verò in genere dicit, quia tunc illa offenditur, quando alicui ex eius membris scandalum præbetur. Vt enim qui digitum vulnerauit, corpus hominis læsisse dicitur, & verè quidem, quando digitus corporis pars est, quæ absq; illius mutilatione truncari nequit: ita Ecclesiam offendit, quisquis vilissimo illius membro lapsus author est. Differtè verò Ecclesiam Dei nominat, vt cogitemus, iniuriam istam ad hunc redundare, qui illam Filij sui sanguine redemptam suum fecit peculium.
units.tr: The second point of this admonition is that we be without offence. In Greek he bids us be "without offence [ἀπροσκόπους]," that is, such people that no one can take offence at their example or seize on it as an occasion for evil. It was necessary to add this, since the first point, of which we have already spoken, ought to hold good. For it is impossible for that to be done for the glory of God which makes others worse in the knowledge and worship of him, or at least hinders them. But just as in the first part he taught us to seek God's glory above all things, so in this second part he commends to us the law of brotherly charity, by which he binds us above all to be the authors of no scandal to anyone. To this belongs what God pronounces in the Law: "You shall not curse the deaf, nor put a stumbling block before the blind, but you shall fear your God." If it is a crime to give the blind man a cause of stumbling or falling, how much more grievously shall we think those sin who, by their example, hurl into error the ignorant and inexperienced and bring about the ruin of souls? And here the distinction which Paul uses, as a kind of full enumeration of the parts, must be carefully noted. "Be," he says, "without offence both to the Jews and to the Greeks and to the Church of God." For he wished to name all the kinds of men then existing, so that we should not think anyone so base or abject that we may do whatever we like to him. For most people sin in this respect, that they hardly think anyone worthy that they should take any account of him in their dealings. In one case they plead an old hatred of a nation, in another the lowly birth of a family, in another old injuries and I know not how many other excuses. But in the present passage Paul names the Jews, who, as the bitterest enemies of the Christian religion, and therefore deserving of hatred, could be despised and neglected with impunity, since they were equally hateful to the Romans and the other nations. Then he mentions the Greeks, by which name we have often said that the heathen are meant, still given over to the worship of fictitious gods. These, then, were worse than the Turks who rule today. To these he joins the Church of God, to show that we must have regard not only for the brethren, lest they be offended by us, but also for outsiders, who cannot be neglected without loss of godliness, since it is our task to bring new disciples continually to Christ. He speaks of the Church in general because it is offended whenever a scandal is given to any of its members. For just as one who has wounded a finger is said to have injured the body of a man, and truly so, since the finger is a part of the body which cannot be cut off without its mutilation, so whoever is the cause of a fall to the most insignificant member of the Church offends the Church. Moreover, he pointedly calls it the Church of God, so that we may consider that this injury redounds to him who made it his own possession, redeemed by the blood of his Son.

units.la: In horum consideratione hodie versari debebant Christiani homines, & viderent, quàm procul absimus à regula Christianismi, quam nobis omnibus Apostolus præscribit. Constat omnibus simulachrorum cultu tam Iudæos quàm Turcas offendi, & hanc præcipuam esse causam odij implacabilis, quo Christianam religionem prosequuntur. At quis obsecro principum Christianorum, imò quis ex Episcoporum aut Pontificum numero hucusq; prodijt, qui de scandalo hoc contra Dei verbum inducto, remouendo cogitarit? Idem de impuro sacerdotum cælibatu, de Abbatum mollitie, de Episcoporum fastu & potentia dicere possumus, & infinitis alijs, quæ cùm per se impia, nefaria, scelerata sint, & insuper Iudæos, Turcas & plurimos ex Christianis offendant, tamen non feruntur modò, sed suos quoq; defensores habent, per quos tutius fuerit nouas superstitiones inuehere, aut quouis alio scelere in Christianæ charitatis & sanctitatis leges peccare, quàm de illis abolendis sermonem facere. His adde eos, qui cùm in repub. & Ecclesiæ ministerio constituti sint, & purioris doctrinæ studium profiteantur: ita tamen viuunt, vt illorum exemplis bonæ leges eneruentur, & omnis ministerij ecclesiastici authoritas paulatim intermoriatur. Nolunt hi omnes Paulum amicè concionantem & monentem audire: sed nunquam effugient illud Christi tonitru, dicentis: Væ homini illi, per quem scandalum venit. Item: Quisquis offenderit vnum ex parvulis istis, qui in me credunt, præstiterit ei, vt suspendatur mola asinaria in collum eius, ac demergatur in profundo maris. Vide Matth.18.
units.tr: Christian people ought to be occupied today with the consideration of these things, and they should see how far we are from the rule of Christianity which the Apostle prescribes for us all. It is agreed by all that the Jews are offended by the worship of images no less than the Turks, and that this is the chief cause of the implacable hatred with which they pursue the Christian religion. But which, I ask you, of the Christian princes, or indeed which of the number of bishops or popes has so far come forward, who has thought of removing this scandal introduced against the Word of God? The same can be said of the impure celibacy of the priests, of the effeminacy of the abbots, of the pride and power of the bishops, and of infinite other things which, since they are in themselves impious, abominable and wicked, and moreover offend the Jews, the Turks and very many of the Christians, nevertheless are not only tolerated but have their defenders too, through whom it would be safer to introduce new superstitions, or to sin in any other wickedness against the laws of Christian charity and holiness, than to speak of abolishing them. To these add those who, though placed in the commonwealth and in the ministry of the Church, and though they profess zeal for purer doctrine, nevertheless so live that by their examples good laws are weakened, and the whole authority of the ecclesiastical ministry gradually dies out. All these men are unwilling to hear Paul preaching and admonishing them in a friendly way; yet they will never escape that thunderclap of Christ, saying: "Woe to that man through whom the scandal comes." Likewise: "Whoever shall offend one of these little ones who believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone be hung about his neck and he be drowned in the depth of the sea." See Matthew 18.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui abs se præscriptam Legem siue regulam proprio exemplo con-firmat: id verò non arroganter facit, sed partim ex officio, vt qui gentium doctor & magister esse à Deo constitutus: partim quia sic res exigebat, eo quòd multi quererentur abs se plus quam ab alijs postulari. Dicit ergo: Sicut & ego per omnia omnibus placeo, non quærens meam ipsius vtilitatem, sed multorum, vt seruentur. Quibus verbis ita dicere videtur: Non debet cuiquam vestrum graue aut iniquum videri, quod iubeo. Iniqua enim & intolerabilia mandare vel dici possunt, qui ipsi nihil eorum præstant quæ iubent. At qui ipse suo exemplo alijs præit, illo no mine accusari non potest. Id verò me hucusque fecisse cùm apud vos tum apud alios, nemo opinor negabit. Nam per omnia omnibus placeo, id est, omnibus indulgeo & placere studeo, neq; meam ipsius vtilitatem aut commodum priuatum quaero, sed ita me omnium moribus accommodo, vt ipsi salutis in Christo participes fiant. Et hæc quidem absq; vanitatis & arrogantiæ suspicione illi dicere liberum & tutum erat, cùm hæc omnibus nota essent, omniumq; animis adhuc hæreret exemplum singulare zeli apostolici, quo per sesquiannum inter illos vsus erat, cùm nulla priuati commodi spes affulgeret.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who confirms by his own example the rule or law he has set down. He does not do this arrogantly. He does it partly because of his office, as one appointed by God to be teacher and master of the Gentiles, and partly because the situation demanded it, since many complained that more was asked of them than of others. So he says: "Even as I please all men in all things, not seeking my own profit, but the profit of many, that they may be saved" (1 Cor. 10:33). By these words he seems to say: "None of you should think it grievous or unjust that I command what I command. For only those who themselves do none of the things they order could be said to command unjust and intolerable things. But one who goes before others by his own example cannot be accused on that ground." That he has done this until now, both among you and among others, I think no one will deny. For "I please all men in all things" means that I yield to all and strive to please them, that I do not seek my own advantage or private gain, but so adapt myself to everyone's ways that they may become partakers of salvation in Christ. He could say this freely and safely, without any suspicion of vanity or arrogance, since these things were known to all, and the memory of his singular apostolic zeal, which he had shown among them for a year and a half, when no hope of private gain shone upon him, still clung to everyone's mind.

units.la: Quo loco rursus admonemur, quàm referat, vt qui aliis præsunt, non authoritate modò & imperio vtantur seuerius, sed potius pastorum aut viæ ducum instar exemplo suo præeant. Nihil enim ad mouendos vulgi animos efficatius est. Rursus, cùm omnes homines natura licentiæ appetentes sint, vndiq; causas obseruare atq; etiam auidè venari solent, quibus suam rebellionem atq; inobedientiam excusent. Inter has autem iustissimas & sufficientes esse putant, si illos ipsos licentius videant viuere, qui alios in officio continere debebant. Ergo si hi ipsi in officio faciendo diligentes sint, & quod ab alijs exigunt ipsi sedulò præstent, tunc non modò occasionem calumniandi proterui illis & rebellibus eripiunt, verumetiam eos, in quibus spiritus generosioris scintilla aliqua adhuc reliqua est, suo exemplo accendunt, & simul ignauis & terguersatoribus pudorem aspergunt, qui inuitos cogit officium facere. Exempla huius rei in militia passim occurrunt, vbi ducis aut imperatoris tolerantia atq; fortitudo frequenter omne laboris tædium atq; omnem mortis metum ijs abstergit, qui stationem suam iamiam deserturi esse videbantur. C. Marium certè Plutarchus scribit, cum Metelli legatus esset in bello Iugurtino, militum animos sibi denuinxisse, quòd eodem cum illis pane vesceretur, humi inter illos cubaret, & in fossis vel aggeribus ducendis operam communem præstaret, inq; periculis ab hoste imminentibus inter primos semper conspiceretur. His enim exemplis adducti, illum sibi Imperatorem dari postulauerunt, & ipse ijsdem postea ad omnes labores atq; pericula promptus & strenuus vsus est. Atqui eadem est militiæ spiritualis ratio, cuius duces populo suo verbi administros Christus constituit. Sibijpsis ergo illi ista accommodent, ne de ipsis idem quod de Iudæorum scribis dici possit: quòd nimirum farci-nas graues & portatu difficiles aliorum humeris dessinent, quas tamen ipsi ne minimo quidem digito attingant. Cogitent aut: hanc inexcusabilem esse doctrinæ & verbi Dei prophanationem, si quod magno conatu docent, proprio exemplo destruant. Hinc enim verbi contemptus nascitur, quem Deus in ipsis punire solet, sicuti in Iudæorum sacerdotibus apud Malachiam & in Euangelica historia est videre. At non minus ista ad se transferre debent, qui magistratum gerunt, vt & ipsi populo boni exempli authores sint, & quam ab alijs requirunt vitæ honestatem ipsi indicis suis præstare studeant. Hic obedientiæ publicæ fons simul atq; nerus est validissimus. Nec enim vlla disciplina tam arcta fuerit, quam non patienter ferat populus, si principes suos ijsdem secum legibus viuere videat. At qui sibi propter dignitatem, qua supra alios eminent, plus licere putant, hoc vnum inde referunt, quòd & legibus suis authoritatem derogant, & seipsos non contemptos modò, verumetiam inuisos & exosos reddunt. Possumus idem de parentibus dicere, & omnibus ijs, quorum curæ tenera ætas commissa est. Tunc enim pueri obedientiæ & virtutis re-cte assuescunt, si non modò præcepta audiant, sed huius viuum exemplar in illis sibi propositum videant, à quibus instituuntur. Interim verò quicunq; aliorum imperio subsunt, meminisse debent, non ideo sibi quiduis licere, si illi licentius agant, à quibus ipsi reguntur. Manet enim nihilominus ordo à Deo institutus, & malis quoque præpositis obtemperandum est in ijs, quæ bene præcipiunt, aut quæ salua pietate & conscientia possunt fieri. Ideo Christus de scribis in Mosis cathedra sedentibus dicebat: Omnia quæ dixerint vobis vt seruetis, seruate & facite: sed secundum opera eorum ne feceritis. Et in repub. raro feliciter cedunt seditiones, quæ contra principes quantumuis malos & improbos excitantur. Deus enim propter aliquorum malitiam ordinem abs se institutum turbari non vult: neque tamen ipsi rationes desunt, quibus tyrannorum petulantiam coerceat.
units.tr: Here again we are reminded how much it matters that those who preside over others should not rely only on authority and command, and be rather severe, but should go before them by their example, like shepherds or guides on the road. For nothing is more effective in moving the minds of the common people. Again, since all men by nature desire licence, they usually look everywhere for reasons, and even eagerly hunt for them, by which to excuse their rebellion and disobedience. Among these they think the most just and sufficient are these: when they see those very men who ought to keep others in line living more licentiously themselves. Therefore, if these same men are diligent in performing their duty, and diligently practise what they demand of others, then they not only take away from the insolent and rebellious the occasion of slander, but they also kindle with their example whatever spark of nobler spirit remains in those who are still capable of it, and at the same time they cover the idle and shirkers with shame, compelling them to do their duty even against their will. Examples of this are found everywhere in military life, where the endurance and courage of a leader or general often wipes away from those who were about to desert their post all weariness of labour and all fear of death. Plutarch certainly writes that Gaius Marius, when he was legate of Metellus in the Jugurthine war, won the hearts of the soldiers because he ate the same bread as they did, lay on the ground among them, shared in the common labour of digging trenches and raising earthworks, and was always seen among the first in dangers threatened by the enemy. Moved by such examples, the soldiers demanded him as their commander, and he himself afterwards used the same readiness and vigour in facing every labour and danger. Yet the same is the rule of spiritual warfare, whose leaders Christ has appointed as ministers of the Word for his people. Let them therefore apply these things to themselves, lest what is said of the scribes of the Jews could be said of them too: that they lay heavy burdens, hard to carry, on the shoulders of others, while they themselves will not touch them even with a finger. Let them consider that it is an inexcusable profanation of doctrine and the Word of God if they destroy by their own example what they teach with great effort. For from this comes contempt for the Word, which God is accustomed to punish in such men, as can be seen in the priests of the Jews in Malachi and in the Gospel story. But those who hold the magistracy ought no less to apply these things to themselves, so that they too may be authors of good example to the people, and may strive to show in their own lives the uprightness of life that they demand of others. Here is the strongest source and sinew of public obedience. For no discipline is so strict that the people will not patiently bear it if they see their rulers living under the same laws as themselves. But those who think they may do more because of the dignity by which they stand out above others, bring about only this result: they both detract from the authority of their own laws, and make themselves not merely despised, but hated and loathed. We can say the same of parents, and of all those to whom a tender age is entrusted. For children learn obedience and virtue rightly only if they hear precepts and also see before them a living model of them in those by whom they are taught. Meanwhile, those who are under the command of others ought to remember that they are not therefore free to do whatever they like if those by whom they are ruled act more licentiously. For the order instituted by God remains nonetheless, and even wicked men set over us must be obeyed in those things that they command rightly, or that can be done without violating piety and conscience. Thus Christ said of the scribes sitting in Moses' seat: "Whatever they tell you to observe, observe and do; but do not do according to their works" (Matt. 23:3). And in the commonwealth, seditions raised against rulers, however bad and wicked they may be, seldom turn out well. For God does not wish the order he has instituted to be disturbed because of the wickedness of some; nor does he lack reasons by which he can restrain the insolence of tyrants.

units.la: Cæterum in præsenti diligentius paulo videre oportet, quomodo Apostolus per omnia omnibus placuerit. Sunt enim qui eius exemplo abutuntur, vt ea excusent, quæ in hominum gratiam præter omne officium faciunt. Sed ad ipsos pertinet, quod idem Paulus ad Galatas scribit: Si hominibus placerem, Christi seruus non essem. Ad huius verò loci interpretationem facit, quod supra cap. 9. dixit: Cum liber sim ab omnibus, omnibus me ipsum seruum feci, vt plures lucrifaciam. Et factus sum Iudæis vt Iudæus, vt Iudæos lucrifaciam: iis qui sub Lege sunt, ac si essem sub Lege, vt eos qui sub Lege sunt lucrifaciam. Ex legibus vt ex lex (cum non sim ex lex Deo, sed sublex Christo) vt lucrifaciam eos qui sunt exleges. Factus sum infirmis vt infirmus, vt infirmos lucrifaciam: Denique omnibus factus sum omnia, vt omnino aliquos seruem. In quibus primo obseruabis, Paulum ista fecisse tantum in rebus medijs atque indifferentibus, & tunc quidem, quando absque aliquo scandalo infirmioribus indulgere potuit. Itaque in præsenti loco Paulus per vtilitatem suam non aliud quam libertatem intelligit, qua (vt eodem cap. audiimus) ex Christi instituto non minus quam reliqui Apostoli vti poterat. Sed in eo omnibus placere studuit, quando libertate sua quasi neglecta sese instar serui omnium captui atque moribus accommodauit, ne cui ad salutem tendenti impedimento esset. Deinde quando suum commodum se quæsiuisse negat, diserte sese ab adulatorum numero eximi, qui dum omnibus indulgent & gratificantur, non nisi quod suum est quærunt: vt nimirum amicos sibi parent, in honore sint & pretio, imprimis autem vt ex alieno otiosi viuant. Tales olim pseudoprophetæ fuerunt, & quos Paulus alibi canes dicit, eò quòd præter ventrē nihil aliud quærant. At isti dū omnibus blandiun-tur, & sibi bene esse volunt, plerunq; seipsos atq; alios in exitiū adducunt. Ideo de illis Deus per Isaiam olim dicebat: Populemi, qui te beatum dicunt, ipsi te decipiunt, & viam gressuum tuorū dissi-pant. Postremò, quid illud est, quod aliis conferre voluit Paulus sua indulgentia? Ut feruentur, inquit. Non ergo ullorum hominum prauis cupiditatibus inseruiuit, sed eorum salutem sibi om-nium suarum actionum atq; studiorum finem siue scopum proposuit. Hæc singulī obseruare de-bent, ne arbitrentur locum hunc ijs patrocinari, qui in religione leues & ambigui, pro potentiorum arbitrio in singulas horas mutantur. In ijs quidem, quæ nostri iuris sunt, laudem meretur facili-tas atq; indulgentia: at vbi expressum Dei mandatum intercedit, ibi meminerimus non licere no-bis ab eo latum unguem vel ad dextram vel ad sinistram deflectere.
units.tr: For the present, however, we should look a little more carefully at how the Apostle pleased all men in all things. There are those who abuse his example to excuse things they do to win men's favour beyond all duty. But what Paul writes to the Galatians applies to them: "If I still pleased men, I would not be a servant of Christ" (Gal. 1:10). What he said in chapter 9 above helps to interpret this passage: "Though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might gain the more. And I became to the Jews as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews; to those who are under the Law, as if I were under the Law, that I might gain those who are under the Law; to those who are without law, as if I were without law (not being without law toward God, but under law toward Christ), that I might gain those who are without law. I became weak to the weak, that I might gain the weak. I have become all things to all men, that I might by all means save some" (1 Cor. 9:19–22). In these words you will observe, first, that Paul did these things only in matters that are indifferent and neutral, and then only when he could yield to the weaker without any scandal. So in the present passage Paul by "my profit" means nothing other than the liberty which (as we heard in the same chapter) he could use by Christ's institution no less than the other apostles. But in this he strove to please all: when he had, as it were, set his liberty aside, he made himself a servant of all, adapting himself to their understanding and customs, so that he would be a hindrance to no one who was seeking salvation. Next, when he denies that he sought his own advantage, he clearly distinguishes himself from the company of flatterers, who, while they indulge and humour everyone, seek only what is their own: namely, to make friends for themselves, to be held in honour and esteem, and above all to live idly at another's expense. Such men were once the false prophets, whom Paul elsewhere calls dogs, because they seek nothing but their belly. But while these men flatter everyone and wish to be comfortable themselves, they very often lead both themselves and others to ruin. Therefore God once said of such people through Isaiah: "O my people, those who call you blessed deceive you, and they destroy the way of your steps" (Isa. 3:12). Last of all, what did Paul want to bring to others by his indulgence? "That they may be saved," he says. So he did not serve the wicked desires of any men, but set their salvation before himself as the end and aim of all his actions and endeavours. Each of us should observe this, lest they think this passage supports those who are light and wavering in religion, and who change from hour to hour at the pleasure of the more powerful. In matters that belong to our own right, ready compliance and indulgence deserve praise; but where a clear command of God stands in the way, we must remember that we are not permitted to deviate from it by so much as a hair's breadth, either to the right or to the left.

units.la: Obseruemus præterea hoc loco communem vitæ Christianæ regulam præscribi; quæ est, ut quisque non suam, sed aliorum utilitatem quærat, & pro virili omnium salutem adiuuare stu-deat. Hoc enim (ut mox audiemus) nos Christo simillimos facit, & nisi hoc studio tenéamur, in-utilia erunt quæcunq; alia facimus. Docet hoc Christus non obscurè in talentorum parabola. Il-lic enim seruus inutilis & æterno exitio dignus iudicatur, qui neque heri bona suffuratus erat, ne-que turpiter dilapidauerat, sed humi defossa seruarat, ut sortem integram restitueret. Damnatur tamen quòd otio suo consuluit, neque cum lucro ad herum retulit, quod negotiandi causa accepe-rat. Vult ergo nos Deus non de nostra solum, verumetiam aliorum salute solicitos esse: & ideo itares hominum mutuo quasi nodo inter se constrinxit, ut in aliorum commodis nostrum inclu-sum sit, & ij demum sibi ipsis optimè consulant, qui aliorum utilitati studeant. Sic opifices, etsi di-uersa artificia exerceant, alij tamen alios iuuant, & pauci sunt, qui aliorum opera & auxilio ca-rere possint. Idem in repub. cernitur, ubi ordines quidem diuersi sunt, singuli tamen ab alijs iuuen-tur oportet, siquidem suam dignitatem seruare velint. Qui vero ut sibi ipsis consulant, alios ne-gligunt, ijs fere accidit quod illis, qui incendio in vicinia exorto domi suæ sese includunt, ne cum aliqua sua molestia ijs locum dare cogantur, qui incendiū restinguere conantur. Ut enim flammis iam tecta omnia superantibus ad illos quoque incendium diffunditur, ut cum fortunis omnibus pereant: ita qui aliorum utilitatis & salutis causa nihil molestiæ aut periculi subire volunt, fe-rè periculis inextricabilibus sua illa ignauia sese implicant. Semper ergo animis nostris obseruse-tur Pauli exemplum, qui de aliorum potius quàm propria utilitate solicitus, quàm plurimos ser-uauit, & sibi ipsi cum salute gloriam immortalem acquisiuit.
units.tr: Let us also note in this passage that it prescribes a general rule of Christian life: each person should seek not his own advantage but that of others, and strive to help the salvation of everyone as far as he can. For this (as we shall hear shortly) makes us most like Christ, and unless we are held by this zeal, whatever else we do will be useless. Christ teaches this plainly in the parable of the talents. There the servant is judged useless and worthy of eternal destruction, though he had neither stolen his master's goods the day before nor wastefully squandered them, but had kept what was entrusted to him buried in the ground so as to return the whole amount. Yet he is condemned because he looked after his own leisure and did not bring back to his master, with profit, what he had received for trading. God therefore wants us to be concerned not only for our own salvation but also for that of others. So he has bound human beings to one another by mutual need, like a knot, so that our own interest is enclosed within the interests of others, and those who aim at the advantage of others are the ones who in the end best serve themselves. Thus craftsmen, though they practise different arts, nevertheless help one another, and there are few who can do without the work and help of others. The same is seen in the commonwealth, where the ranks are indeed different, yet each must be helped by the others if they wish to keep their dignity. Those who neglect others in order to look after themselves are for the most part in the position of those who, when a fire breaks out in the neighbourhood, shut themselves up in their houses so as not to be forced, with some inconvenience to themselves, to make room for those who try to put out the fire. For when the flames already overcome all the roofs, the fire spreads to these people too, so that they perish along with all their goods. In the same way, those who wish to undergo no trouble or danger for the sake of others' advantage and salvation often entangle themselves, by that very laziness, in dangers from which there is no escape. Let us therefore always keep before our minds the example of Paul, who, concerned for the advantage of others rather than his own, saved very many, and won for himself immortal glory together with his own salvation.

units.la: At ne quis illum arrogantiorem diceret, qui suum exemplum omnibus proponeret imitan-dum, aut aliqui simpliciores eodem per κανόνλιυ[?], id est, stultam aut prauam imitationem abu-terentur, diligentius rem explicat, & tam seipsum quàm omnes alios ad Christum remittit, di-cens: Imitatores mei estote, sicut & ego Christi. Breue dictum, quo totam philosophiam Christia-nam comprehendit, & seipsum communi cum alijs regulæ subijcit, simulq; multis superstitionibus occurrit. Sunt enim, qui prisco-rum sanctorum admiratione capti, nihil non sibi faciendum es-se putant, quod illos fecisse audiunt. Quæ causa est, quòd multa inepte, multa ridiculè, & (quod pessimum est) multa superstitiosè faciant. Et hinc fere originem habuit vita monastica, quam multi ideo amplexi sunt, quòd olim sanctissimos homines in locis desertis vixisse & miraculis cla-ruisse audirent. Sed ut de primis illis siue Monachis siue Eremitis nihil dicamus, quos partim temporum illorum iniquitas & immanis tyrannorum crudelitas, partim propria fidei imbecilli-tas & tormentorum metus eò adduxit: hoc solum quæro, quid unquam huius CHRISTVS IE-SVS fecerit? Num hic quoque ab hominum consuetudine abhorruit? Num solitarius vixit? Certè neminem tam impudentem esse arbitror, qui hoc ausit affirmare. Quicunq; ergo hoc vitæ ge-nus hodie sequuntur, ij neq; veri Sanctorum imitatores sunt, neque huic regulæ insistunt, quam in præsenti Paulus præscribit, & cuius summa est, ut quisque non suam ipsius utilitatem quærat, sed aliorum, ut seruentur. Debet autem huius eò maior apud nos esse authoritas, quod cum Chri-sti regula conuenit, in Euangelio dicens: Si quis vult post me venire, abneget semetipsum, & tollat crucem suam quotidie, & sequatur me. Unde sequitur, nullius hominis, quantumuis sancti & de re Christiana optimè meriti, exemplum nobis imitandum esse, nisi quatenus illum Christi vestigia secutum esse videmus. Itaque iudicio certo & diligenti hic opus est, ne temere ab exegi-plo argumentemur. Nam si id liceat, jam aperta quoq; scelera suam excusationem habent, cum in sanctis aliquando locum invenerint. Semper ergo meminerimus, in sanctis quoq; suos esse ve-nos, quos Scriptura commemorat, non ut imitemur, sed ut illorum consideratio nos cautiores red-dat. Vitae vero exemplum omnibus numeris absolutum nobis in Christo propositum esse sciamus, quod & nos imitari, & ad eius regulam omnia aliorum dicta & facta examinare debemus.
units.tr: But lest anyone should call him too arrogant, for setting his own example before everyone to imitate, or lest some simpler people should abuse it through misguided imitation [κακοζηλίαν], that is, foolish or perverse copying, he explains the matter more carefully, and refers both himself and all others to Christ, saying: "Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ." It is a brief saying, in which he sums up the whole Christian philosophy, subjects himself to the common rule along with others, and at the same time meets many superstitions. For there are some who, captivated by admiration for the holy men of old, think that they must do whatever they hear those men did. This is why many people act foolishly, many ridiculously, and (worst of all) many superstitiously. Monastic life largely had its origin in this, and many embraced it for the reason that they heard that holy men of old lived in desert places and were famous for miracles. But let us say nothing of those first monks or hermits, whom partly the wickedness of those times and the savage cruelty of tyrants, partly their own weakness of faith and fear of torments, drove to that way of life. I ask only this: what did Christ Jesus ever do of this kind? Did he too shrink from human company? Did he live a solitary life? I certainly think no one is so shameless as to dare to affirm this. Therefore those who follow this kind of life today are neither true imitators of the saints nor adherents of the rule which Paul prescribes here, and whose sum is that each person should seek not his own advantage but that of others, so that they may be saved. This rule ought to carry all the more authority with us because it agrees with the rule of Christ, who says in the Gospel: "If anyone wants to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me." From this it follows that the example of no human being, however holy and however well deserving of the Christian cause, is to be imitated by us, except insofar as we see that he followed the steps of Christ. Therefore careful and diligent judgment is needed here, so that we do not argue hastily from an example. For if this were allowed, even open crimes would have their excuse, since they have sometimes found a place among the saints. Let us therefore always remember that Scripture records among the saints also men who are our own, not to be imitated, but so that the consideration of their failings may make us more cautious. Let us know that the example of life, complete in every respect, has been set before us in Christ, and that we ought both to imitate it and to test all the sayings and deeds of others by its rule.

units.la: Porrò non minus consideratione opus est, quid nam in Christi exemplo imitari debeamus. Errant enim hic nonnulli vehementer, qui ex iis leges fingunt, quae ille aut miraculose fecit, aut pro sua vocationis ratione: Prioris generis est, quod ieiunium quadragesimale omnibus obtrudunt, eo quod Christus in deserto diebus quadraginta ieiunauisse legitur. At hoc non sine miraculo factum fuit, quod non magis imitari possumus, quam si ad illius exemplum leprosos mundare, paralyticos sanare aut mortuos excitare conemur. Deinde ut demus illum simul exemplum praebuisse, noluit tamen ieiunii formam, quae tempore certo & ciborum superstitioso delectu definia-tur, praescribere, sed perpetuum temperantiæ & sobrietatis studium commendare omnibus, qui in huius vitæ palæstra versantur. Nō ergo ulla Christi institutum extendi debet illius exemplum, sed in ieiuniis regula seruetur, quam Matth. 9. cap. discipulis tradidit. Alterius generis est cœlibatus Christi, quo multi impurum illud vitæ genus tueri student, quod in Papatu monachi & sacrificuli sequuntur magna cum thori coniugalis ignominia. Atqui ut cœlebs viveret Christus, peculiaris eius vocatio requirebat, quæ fuit, ut germanos Dei filios procrearet, qui non ex viri aut mulieris voluntate, neque ex ulla carnis commixtione, sed ex verbi immortalis semine per-spi-ritus virtutem generari solent. Nihil ergo hoc ad cœlibatus monastici commendationem, quasi in hoc sita sit hominis Christiani perfectio. Itaque ad ea solum regula ista extendi debet, quae Christum nobis in exemplum fecisse constat. Loquitur de his ipse apud Matthaeum dicens: Di-scite à me, quod mitis sum & humilis corde. Et Zebedæi filiis primatum in suo regno ambientibus exemplum suum proponit, ut quemadmodum ipse non venerit ut sibi ab hominibus in mundo ministraretur: sed ut ipse aliis ministraret, ita illi non ut supra alios eminere[?] quaerere, sed in hoc potius esse debeant, ut quam plurimis inserviant. Quæ omnia postremò confirmant, quando discipulorum pedes abluit, & se exemplum illis præbuisse ait, ut quod ipsum fecisse vident, ipsi quoq; faciant. Pertinent autem hæc omnia ad dilectionem fraternam, cuius fidissima nutrix est humilitas & officiosum sibi mutuò inserviendi studium, ideoq; rectissimè à Paulo exponuntur, qui ad Philip. sic scribit. Explete gaudium meum, ut idem sitis affecti, eandem charitatem habentes, unanimes, & sententiis uni. Nihil gerite per contentionem, aut per inanem gloriam, sed ex modestia alium quisque se præstantiorem existimet: ne sua quisque spectetis, sed unusquisque etiam quæ sunt aliorum. Enimvero is fit affectus in vobis, qui fuit, & in IESV CHRISTO, &c. Continetur sub his vitæ innocentia, quæ in toto Christi exemplo elucet. Adhæc in morte, resurrectione & ascensione idem exemplum nobis præbuit, ut nimirum ipsi quoq; carnem crucifigamus, peccato moriamur, in ipso autem resurgamus ad vitæ novitatem, in qua terrenis omnibus calcatis ad cœlestia contendamus. Adde his patientiam in adversis, quae s[?]militer in illo perfectissima fuit. Hæc & alia huius generis olim sancti Dei cultores sibi imitanda propo-suerunt, in quibus & nos eorum imitatores esse conuenit. Ita vero absoluit Paulus tractationem de idolothytis, cuius hic nobis usus esse debet, ne libertate nostra abutamur ad carnis licentiam, & primo quidem fidem in IESVM CHRISTVM puram, eiusq; confessionem illibatam seruemus: deinde nemini demus aliquam scandali occasionem, sed quoad eius fieri potest, infirmorum ædificationi studeamus, no-stri[?]q; indies ei adducamus discipulos. Sic Paulum vere imitabimur, imò ipsius CHRISTI IE-SV imitatores erimus, qui spiritu suo animatos ad regni sui cœlestis hæreditatem euehet. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Furthermore, no less consideration is needed as to what we ought to imitate in the example of Christ. Some men err greatly here, who make laws from those things which he did either miraculously or according to his particular calling. Of the first kind is the Lenten fast, which they impose on everyone, because it is read that Christ fasted in the desert for forty days. But this happened not without a miracle, and we can no more imitate it than if we tried, after his example, to cleanse lepers, heal paralytics, or raise the dead. Moreover, even granting that he at the same time gave an example of this, he nevertheless did not wish to prescribe a form of fasting defined by a fixed time and a superstitious choice of foods, but commended to all who engage in the struggle of this life a perpetual zeal for self-control and sobriety. Therefore Christ's example should not be extended into an institution; rather the rule of fasting should be kept, which he gave to the disciples in Matthew chapter 9. Of the second kind is the celibacy of Christ, by which many strive to defend that impure way of life which the monks and little priests in Popery follow, to the great disgrace of the marriage bed. Yet if Christ lived unmarried, his particular calling required it, which was that he should beget true sons of God, who are generated not from the will of man or woman, nor from any mingling of flesh, but from the immortal seed of the Word, through the power of the Spirit. So this has nothing to do with commending monastic celibacy, as if the perfection of a Christian consisted in it. Therefore this rule ought to be extended only to those things which it is clear that Christ did as an example for us. He speaks of these himself in Matthew, saying: "Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart." And to the sons of Zebedee, who were seeking the first place in his kingdom, he sets his own example before them: just as he did not come to be served by men in the world, but to serve others, so they too should not seek to stand out above others, but should rather be such as to serve as many as possible. All these things finally are confirmed when he washed the disciples' feet, and said that he had given them an example, so that they should do as they saw him do. All these things pertain to brotherly love, whose most faithful nurse is humility and an eager, dutiful readiness to serve one another. Therefore Paul rightly explains them, writing to the Philippians thus: "Fulfil my joy, that you may be of the same mind, having the same love, being of one accord and of one judgment. Do nothing through contention or vainglory, but in humility let each esteem others better than himself. Let each look not to his own things, but each also to the things of others. For let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus," etc. Under these heads is included the innocence of life, which shines throughout the whole example of Christ. Besides, in his death, resurrection and ascension he has likewise given us an example, that we too should crucify the flesh, die to sin, and rise again in him to newness of life, in which, having trampled underfoot all earthly things, we should strive toward heavenly things. Add to these his patience in adversity, which was likewise most perfect in him. These and other things of this kind the holy worshippers of God in former times set forth for imitation, and in these we ought to be their imitators as well. Paul concludes his discussion of meat offered to idols in such a way that its use should be for us: that we should not abuse our liberty for licence of the flesh; and, first, that we should keep our faith in Jesus Christ pure and our confession of him unblemished; then that we should give no one any occasion of offence, but, as far as it can be done, should work for the building up of the weak, and daily bring our own disciples to him. In this way we shall truly imitate Paul, indeed we shall be imitators of Christ Jesus himself, who, having quickened those animated by his Spirit, will bring them to the inheritance of his heavenly kingdom. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: HOMILIA LVI.
units.tr: HOMILY LVI.

units.la: LAudo autem vos, fratres, quòd omnia mea meministis, & sicut tradidi vobis, traditiones retinetis. Velim autē vos nosse, quòd omnis viri caput Christus est, caput autem mulieris vir, caput verò Christi Deus. Omnis vir orans aut prophetans operto capite, dedecorat caput suum. Omnis verò mulier orans aut prophetans non operto capite, dedecorat caput suum. Nam id unum ac idemest ac sirasa esset. Nam si non velatur mulier, etiam tondeatur. Quòd si turpe mulieri tonderi aut radi, veletur.
units.tr: I commend you, brothers, that you remember me in all things and hold fast to the traditions just as I delivered them to you. But I want you to know that Christ is the head of every man, the man is the head of the woman, and God is the head of Christ. Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonours his head. But every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonours her head, for it is one and the same as if she had been shaved. For if a woman is not veiled, let her also be shorn. But if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaved, let her be veiled.

units.la: DISPUTAVIT huiusq; Paulus adversus eos, qui contra professionis Christianæ leges sacris ethnicorum, aut saltem festis atq; sacris eorum conuiuijs communicabant. Sequitur nunc quarta huius epistolæ pars, in qua cœtus ecclesiasticos instituit, & diligenter de omnibus agit, quæ in illis præter decorum fiebant. Primum vitium in vestitu erat, in quo à viris simul & mulieribus partim superstitione, partim luxu & mollitie vehementer peccabatur. Nam vt aliàs diximus, Corinthi emporium fuit totius orbis celeberrimum. Undiq; ergo illuc confluentibus peregrinis, luxus indies augebatur, tum in aliis rebus, tum maximè in vestitu, in quo ex innata leuitate sibipsis nimiùm licenter indulgere solent, qui diuitijs abundant, & præ aliis eminere volunt. Maior tamen erat superstitionis culpa, quòd nimirum eodem habitu, & fortasse ijsdem quoq; gestibus, in cœtibus sacris uterentur, quibus à pueris in gentilis-mo assueuerant. Et hoc potissimum spectasse videtur Apostolus, quando viros aperto capite, mulieres autem velato orare & prophetare iubet. Nam vt Plutarchus in Problematibus scribit, solebant viri inter gentes, & imprimis quidem ij, qui Romanorum legibus viuebant, Deos suos velatis capitibus adorare, & inter sacra vestem ad aures vsq; attollere, partim quidem, vt eo gestu & habitu se humiliores redderent: partim ne inter precandum triste quid aut ignominiosum aliunde auribus occurreret, quo animi deuotio turbaretur. Meminit huius ritus Vergilius quoq;, qui Helenum Æneæ sic dicentem introducit: Purpureo velare comas adopertus amictu, Ne qua inter sanctos ignes in honore Deorum Hostilis facies occurrat, & omnia turbet. Hunc socij morem sacrorum, hunc ipse teneto, Hac casti maneant in religione nepotes.
units.tr: Paul has been arguing against those who, contrary to the laws of the Christian profession, took part in the rites of the heathen, or at least in their festivals and sacred feasts. Now comes the fourth part of this letter, in which he sets out the assemblies of the Church and deals carefully with everything that was being done in them contrary to decency. The first fault was in dress, in which men and women alike sinned greatly, partly from superstition and partly from luxury and softness. For, as we have said elsewhere, Corinth was the most famous trading centre in the whole world. With strangers flocking there from every direction, luxury grew daily, both in other things and above all in clothing, where people who abound in wealth and want to stand out from others are accustomed to indulge themselves too freely, from their natural frivolity. Yet the fault of superstition was greater: namely, that they used the same dress, and perhaps the same gestures too, in their sacred assemblies as they had grown accustomed to from childhood in heathenism. The Apostle seems to have had this chiefly in view when he orders men to pray and prophesy with heads uncovered, and women with heads veiled. For, as Plutarch writes in his Problems, among the nations, and especially those who lived under Roman law, men used to worship their gods with heads veiled, and during the sacred rites they drew their garment up to their ears; partly so that by this posture and dress they would make themselves more humble, and partly so that nothing sad or ill-omened might reach their ears from elsewhere during prayer and disturb the devotion of their minds. Virgil also mentions this custom, introducing Helenus speaking thus to Aeneas: With a purple cloak drawn over your hair, lest any hostile face appear among the holy fires in the honour of the gods and disturb everything. Let your companions and yourself keep this custom of the rites; let your chaste descendants remain in this religion.

units.la: E contra mulieres ferè passim capillis sacra celebrauisse, cùm ex aliis locis, tum ex eodè Poëta colligi potest[?], qui funus Polydoro instauratū & circa hoc facta sacrificia describens, inter alia dicit: Et circum Iliades crinem de more solutæ.
units.tr: On the other hand, women commonly performed the sacred rites with their hair loose; this can be gathered both from other places and from the same poet, who, describing the funeral of Polydorus renewed and the sacrifices offered around it, says among other things: And around, the Trojan women with their hair loose, as is the custom.

units.la: Quia ergo non tam luxu quàm superstitione peccabatur, & hac etiam in re ethnicorum atq; infi-delium similes erant ij, qui iam Christo nomen dederant, Paulus hanc causam diligenter & gravi-ter tractat, docens tam viros quàm mulieres decere, ut modestiæ & honestati in habitu quoq; studeant, imprimis autē, ut inter sacra Christiana ne habitū quidē gerant cum infidelibus & idololatris commune. Estq; doctrina hæc hodie etiā non minus necessaria quàm utilis: quando multi eorum, qui Euangelium profitentur, inter orandum Papistas imitantur, ad nolarum pulsum capita aperiunt, & vix à Diuorum inuocatione sibi temperant: multi vestes quoq; Papisticis superstitionibus consecratas Ecclesijs ad Euangelij regulam reformatis obtrudunt: pleriq; verò in vestitu quotidiano non infidelium modò quibus cum viuunt, similes sunt, verumetiā Turcas & quos-uis alios vestitu referunt. In quo non fastu modò peccatur, sed effreni petulantia et impudentia ita luditur à plerisq;, ut nesciam si quid ante hac unquam Sol viderit, quod cum illorū leuitate conferri queat. Videntur quidem ista non magni momenti, & ideo ridentur ferè virorum gravium admonitiones. Sed aliter iudicabunt, qui Paulum de his agentem diligentius audiuerint.
units.tr: Since, then, people sinned not so much from luxury as from superstition, and in this matter too those who had now given their name to Christ were like the heathen and unbelievers, Paul treats this cause carefully and seriously, teaching that both men and women should be concerned with modesty and decency in dress as well, and above all that in Christian assemblies they should not even wear anything in common with unbelievers and idolaters. This teaching is no less necessary and useful today: for many of those who profess the gospel imitate the Papists while praying, uncover their heads at the sound of the bell, and can scarcely refrain from invoking the saints. Many also thrust upon the churches, reformed by the rule of the gospel, vestments consecrated by Papistical superstitions. Most, indeed, in their everyday dress not only resemble the unbelievers among whom they live, but even copy the Turks and any others whatever in their clothing. In this they sin not only through pride, but through unbridled wantonness and shamelessness, and many play so with it that I do not know whether the sun has ever seen anything comparable to their frivolity. These matters seem of little importance, and so the admonitions of serious men are mostly laughed at. But those who listen more carefully to Paul when he treats of these things will judge otherwise.

units.la: Orditur autem tractationem hanc à laudibus Corinthiorum, ut eos magis attentos & sibi benevolos reddat, qui propter ea, quae hucusq; dicta sunt, animo alieniori esse poterant. Lauao[?] vero vos, fratres (inquit) quod omnia mea meministis, & sicut tradidi vobis, traditiones retinetis. Duo in illis praedicat. Primum, quod omnium meminerint, quae ab ipso acceperant. Est hoc in totore-ligionis[?] & salutis nostrae negotio imprimis necessarium. Nam praecipuum, quod à nobis exigitur, est obedientia fidei. At quomodo hanc praestabit, qui eorum ne recordatur quidem, quae in mandatis accepit? Ideo Christus in sementis parabola primum genus eorum, qui verbum absque fructu audiunt, eos facit, qui semen excipiunt in viam, ubi ab avibus devoratur, aut hominum illac iter facientium pedibus conculcatur: eos nimirum intelligens, qui vel pravis cogitationibus, vel diaboli suggestionibus, aut impiorum illusorum dicterijs[?] locum dant, quae omnia eò illos adducunt, ut verbi Dei prorsus obliuiscantur, neque dignum putent, in cuius considerationem intenti esse debeant. Alterum est, quod traditiones retineant, sicuti eas illis tradiderat. Quilus[?] verbis vera obedientiae Christianae ratio aut modus exprimitur. Sunt enim qui in genere quidem retinent quae ab Apostolis tradita sunt, sed non eo modo retinent, quem illi praescripserunt. Exempla huius passim hodie occurrunt, & in hoc fere errant, qui prae aliis apostolici dici & haberi volunt. Causa huius mali est carnis nostrae confidentia, quae non contenta suis finibus, in diuinis quoq; vult sapere, & ea pro suo arbitrio mutat & detorquet, prout sibi commodu esse videtur. Meminerimus ergo nos nihil dum praestitisse, nisi quae Deus nobis mandat, ea ratione & modo exequamur, quem idem ille nobis praescripsit: nec licere nobis in diuinis aliquid mutare, vel addere vel adimere: sicut non vno loco Moses admonet.
units.tr: He begins this discussion with praise of the Corinthians, so as to make them more attentive and well disposed to himself, since on account of what has been said so far they might have been rather hostile. "I commend you, brothers," he says, "that you remember all my teaching and hold fast to the traditions as I delivered them to you." He commends two things in them. First, that they remember all that they had received from him. This is especially necessary in the business of our whole religion and salvation. For the chief thing required of us is the obedience of faith. But how will he render this who does not even remember what he has received in commands? Therefore Christ, in the parable of the sower, first describes the kind of people who hear the word without fruit: those who receive the seed by the way, where it is devoured by birds or trampled under the feet of men passing that way. He clearly means those who give place to evil thoughts, or to the suggestions of the devil, or to the mockeries of the ungodly, all of which lead them to forget the word of God altogether and not to think it worth their while to give it attention. The second thing is that they hold fast to the traditions just as he had delivered them. By these words the true rule and manner of Christian obedience is expressed. For there are some who in general do hold fast what was handed down by the Apostles, but do not hold it in the way they prescribed. Examples of this occur everywhere today, and those who want to be called and considered apostolic are mostly in error in this respect. The cause of this evil is the self-confidence of our flesh, which, not content with its own limits, wants to be wise in divine matters too, and changes and twists them at its own pleasure, as it seems convenient to itself. Let us remember, then, that we have done nothing yet, unless we carry out what God commands us, in the manner and way which he himself has prescribed; and that it is not lawful for us to change, add or take away anything in divine matters, as Moses admonishes us in more than one place.

units.la: Caeterum abutuntur hoc loco aduersarij nostri, quibus cum Scriptura Sacra lis est. Nam Paulum traditionum meminisse aiunt, earum videlicet, quas non scripto, sed viua voce tradiderit, & quas deinceps posteri à suis maioribus quasi per manus acceperint. Ex eo autem colligunt, Apostolos non omnia literis comprehendisse, quae creditu & obseruatu necessaria sunt. Quo fundamento iacto, mox illi superstruunt suas Missas, confessionem auricularem, absolutionem priuatam, satisfactiones, purgatorii ignem, Diuorum merita atq; intercessionem, simulachrorum cultum, caelibatu, ieiunia, & sexcenta alia, quae nulla scripturarum authoritate probari posse sciunt. Quicquid enim nullis Apostolicorum scriptorum testimonijs defendi potest, id traditionem Apostolicam esse aiunt, quae non minorem authoritatem mereatur, quàm ea, quae in illorum libris habentur. Adhaec Corinthios hoc potissimum nomine commendari dicunt, quod traditiones Apostoli retinuerint. Quibus & illud addunt, quod idè ad Thes. scribit: State fratres, & tenete traditiones, quas edocti estis sive per sermonem sive per epistolam nostram. Et his quidem facile fucum faciunt simplicioribus atq; rerum imperitis. Sed si rem ipsam propius inspiciamus, facilis est ad ista responsio. Primò enim traditionum illarum certum numerum nobis ostendi petimus ex vetustis Ecclesiae scriptoribus, & vt id fiat omnino opus est, ne in immensum illae excrescant, & verae à falsis obruantur. Quod si vero hoc illi conati fuerint, quas objecto illi nobis dabunt, quae hodie ab illis ipsis obseruentur? Dicant ergo nobis, cur eas ipsi aboleuerint? cur non reduci curent abolitas? Deinde dicimus, traditiones Apostolicas, vel consentire ijs, quae illi scripserunt, vel ab ijs differentire[?]. Si conueniunt, cur non scriptis eorum contenti sumus? & quae stultitia est, ab incerto traditionum titulo pendere, & non potius ijs insistere, quae in sacris literis diserte exprimuntur? Quòd si traditiones aliquae tum doctrina Scripturae sacrae pugnant, nos illas Apostolicas esse negamus, Apostoli enim Spiritum veritatis acceperunt, qui sibi ipsi contrarius esse non potest, nisi ex eo mendacij Spiritum fingere libeat.
