At si omnia ea, quae hodie sub traditionum Apostolicarum nomine venditantur, ex ordine consideres, multa ineptiora esse videbis, quam quae Apostolorum gravitati conueniant, pleraq; autem cum ijs ex diametro pugnare, quae in illorum scriptis continentur.
units.tr: But our adversaries, with whom we have a quarrel over Holy Scripture, misuse this passage. For they say that Paul remembers traditions, namely those which he handed down not in writing but by the living voice, and which later generations received, as it were, by hand from their ancestors. From this they conclude that the Apostles did not set down in writing everything that is necessary to believe and to observe. Once this foundation is laid, they immediately build upon it their Masses, auricular confession, private absolution, satisfactions, the fire of purgatory, the merits and intercession of the saints, the worship of images, celibacy, fasts, and six hundred other things which they know cannot be proved by the authority of the Scriptures. For whatever cannot be defended by any testimony of the Apostolic writings, they say is an Apostolic tradition, which deserves no less authority than what is found in their books. Moreover, they say the Corinthians were commended chiefly on this ground, that they held fast to the traditions of the Apostle. To these they also add what he writes to the Thessalonians: "Stand fast, brothers, and hold the traditions which you have been taught, whether by word or by our letter." And by these things they easily deceive the simpler sort and those inexperienced in affairs. But if we look more closely at the matter itself, the answer to these claims is easy. For, first, we ask them to show us a certain number of those traditions from the ancient writers of the Church, and this must certainly be done, lest they grow to an immense size and the true be overwhelmed by the false. But if they attempt this, what objects will they give us which are observed today by those very people? Let them tell us, then, why they themselves have abolished them? Why do they not take care to restore those that have been abolished? Next, we say that Apostolic traditions either agree with what they wrote or differ from it. If they agree, why are we not content with their writings? And what folly is it to depend on the uncertain title of traditions, and not rather to rest on those things which are expressly set out in the sacred letters? But if any traditions clash with the teaching of Holy Scripture, we deny that they are Apostolic, for the Apostles received the Spirit of truth, who cannot be contrary to himself, unless one should choose to invent a spirit of lying. But if you consider in order all those things which are today peddled under the name of Apostolic traditions, you will see that many of them are more trivial than suits the dignity of the Apostles, and most of them openly contradict what is contained in their writings.

units.la: Quod si veteres audire libeat, qui Apostolorum temporibus proximi vixerunt, non alias illi Traditiones agnouerunt, quoad doctrinam, quam fidei Christianae articulos, qui Symbolo continentur, quod vulgò Apostolorum dicimus. Cuius rei testimonia luculentissima apud Irenaeum habentur. Nam lib. 1. cap. 2. sic scribit: Ecclesia per vniuersum orbem vsq; ad fines terrae dispersa, ab Apo-
units.tr: If we care to hear the ancient writers who lived closest to the time of the Apostles, they recognised no traditions, so far as doctrine goes, other than the articles of the Christian faith contained in the Creed, which we commonly call the Apostles'. The clearest testimony to this is in Irenaeus. In book 1, chapter 2, he writes as follows: The Church, scattered throughout the whole world, even to the ends of the earth, received from the Apostles and their disciples the faith

units.la: ab Apostolis ac ipsorum discipulis eam accepit fidem, quæ est in vnum Deum, Patrem omnipotentem, qui fecit cœlum & terram, mare & omnia quæ in eis sunt: Et in vnum IESVM CHRISTVM, Filium Dei, incarnatum pro nostra salute. Et in Spiritum Sanctum, qui per Prophetas prædicauit dispensationis mysterium & aduentum, &c. Et idem Libro tertio, capite quarto, aperte ostendit, fidem hanc esse traditionem illam Apostolicam, quæ à fidelibus passim retineatur. Nam inter alia sic dicit: Quid autem si neque Apostoli quidem scripturas reliquissent nobis, nonne oportebat ordinem sequi TRADITIONIS, quam tradiderunt iis, quibus committebant ecclesias? cui ordinationi assentiunt multæ gentes Barbarorum, eorum qui in Christum credunt, sine charactere vel atramento scriptam habentes per spiritum in cordibus suis salutem & veterem TRADITIONEM diligenter custodientes: In vnum Deum credentes, fabricatorem cœli & terræ, & omnium quæ in eis sunt, per CHRISTVM IESVM, Dei Filium: qui propter eminentissimam erga figmentum suum dilectionem, eam quæ esset ex Virgine generationem sustinuit, &c. Conueniunt his per omnia, quæ D. Cyprianus Martyr de Symbolo Apostolicæ fidei, & ante hunc Tertullianus in libro de præscriptionibus hæreticorum, de Regula fidei, tradidit. Ergo quoad fidei & salutis doctrinam traditiones Apostolorum nullas agnoscimus, quàm quæ Symbolo continentur, quod totius doctrinæ illorum Compendium aut Epitomen dicere possumus. Quoad verò externam Ecclesiæ formam non inficiamur, illos passim multa tradidisse de ordine cœtuum ecclesiasticorum, de Sacramentorum administratione & tota Ecclesiæ Oeconomia. In quibus cùm non posset eadem vbique gentium forma obseruari, sic illa instituerunt, prout vrbis aut gentis alicuius conditionem requirere videbant. Et constat omnibus seculis, Ecclesias in his libertate sua vsas fuisse, & proinde iniquos nimium esse, qui hodie vel sub traditionum Apostolicarum nomine, vel quocunque alio prætextu omnes ad eandem formam astringere conantur.
units.tr: in one God, the Father almighty, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them; and in one Jesus Christ, the Son of God, made flesh for our salvation; and in the Holy Spirit, who through the Prophets proclaimed the mystery and the coming of the dispensation, etc. In book 3, chapter 4, he likewise plainly shows that this faith is that Apostolic tradition which is held everywhere by the faithful. Among other things he says: "But what if the Apostles themselves had left us no Scriptures? Ought we not to follow the order of the TRADITION, which they handed down to those to whom they committed the churches? To this order many nations of barbarians who believe in Christ agree, having salvation written in their hearts by the Spirit without paper or ink, and diligently guarding the ancient TRADITION: believing in one God, maker of heaven and earth and all that is in them, through Christ Jesus, the Son of God, who, out of his most excellent love for his handiwork, submitted to be born of a Virgin, etc." In every respect, Cyprian the martyr agrees with these things in his treatment of the Creed of the Apostolic faith, and before him Tertullian in his book on the prescription of heretics, concerning the rule of faith. Therefore, so far as the teaching of faith and salvation goes, we acknowledge no traditions of the Apostles except those contained in the Creed, which we may call the summary or epitome of all their teaching. As for the external form of the Church, we do not deny that they handed down much about the order of ecclesiastical assemblies, the administration of the sacraments and the whole economy of the Church. Since the same form could not be observed everywhere among the nations, they arranged these things as they saw the condition of each city or nation required. And it is evident that in all ages the churches have used their liberty in these matters; therefore those are too unjust who today, whether under the name of Apostolic traditions or under any other pretext, try to bind everyone to the same form.

units.la: Nunc peculiari consideratione dignum est, quòd etsi Corinthiorum Ecclesia tot vitijs atque erroribus polluta esset, eam tamen Paulus non solum Ecclesiæ titulo dignatur, verumetiam laude dignam iudicat, eò quòd abs se traditam fidei Christianæ summam & Ecclesiæ formam hucusque retinuissent. Quo exemplo didicimus, propter quorundam publica vitia, non debere totas ecclesias damnari, aut bonos quoque abijci, qui cum illis versantur. Debent quidem ecclesiarum vitia obseruari & notari, sed in eum finem, vt emendentur. Ideo Verbi sui administros Episcoporum & Speculatorum titulis exornat. At vitia non alio animi proposito obseruare, quàm vt aduersus bonos quoque, & aduersus totas ecclesias calumniandi occasionem inuenias, id verò diabolicum est. Nam diabolum hac ratione in canillandis [?] Dei operibus vti constat, quòd quæ in illis aliunde irrepserunt vitia in ipsius opificis contumeliam exagitat. Nunquam autem nobis excidere debet, Ecclesiam Dei aruum siue agrum esse, neque aliam esse eius conditionem, quoad in terris militauerit, quàm quæ nostrorum agrorum est. Vt hi ex maledictione, qua terram Deus multauit, sua sponte herbas noxias & inutiles gignunt: ita ex innata nobis vitiositate pessimi fructus nasci solent, & quidem in sanctissimis quoque hominibus, qui hoc minime diffitentur. Accedit huic domestico malo hostis Satan, qui si vel tantillum dormiamus, Zizania sua spargit, quæ vnà cum bono semine succrescunt, & in toto hoc agro sæpius dominari videntur. Nunquam ergo absque næuis & vitijs grauioribus est Ecclesia: quod prolixè demonstrari poterat, si quis eius historiam iam inde à Patriarcharum temporibus vellet percurrere. Sed sufficiat nobis eius Ecclesiolæ exemplum, quam ipse Dei Filius, IESVS CHRISTVS, in terris agens habuit. In qua procul dubio optimi omnium fuerunt discipuli, quos vt orbis terrarum doctores essent, destinauerat. Quàm multus verò, quamque grauibus vitijs illi simul omnes laborarunt? Verumtamen hos mundos esse dicit propter Verbum suum, cui locum dabant, & quod fide apprehenderant. Quid ergo obstat, quò minus hodie etiam Ecclesiam inter eos esse sentiamus, qui etsi multa habeant reprehensione digna, Verbo tamen Euangelij locum dant, & à Christo traditam fidei atque religionis formam retinent?
units.tr: It is worth considering especially that although the Corinthian Church was defiled by so many vices and errors, Paul nonetheless not only honours it with the name of Church but also judges it worthy of praise, because it had so far kept the sum of the Christian faith and the form of the Church that he had handed down. From this example we learn that because of the public vices of some, whole churches ought not to be condemned, nor the good who live among them cast out. The faults of churches ought indeed to be observed and noted, but with the aim of their being corrected. For this reason Paul adorns his ministers of the Word with the titles of bishops and watchmen. But to observe faults with no other purpose than to find an occasion for slandering the good as well as whole churches is truly diabolical. For it is evident that the devil uses this method in slandering God's works: he hurls at the Creator himself the faults that have crept into them from elsewhere. Yet we must never forget that the Church of God is a field, and that while it serves on earth its condition is the same as that of our fields. Just as these, by the curse with which God punished the earth, spontaneously produce noxious and useless herbs, so from our inborn vitiousness the worst fruits are wont to spring, even in the holiest men, who do not deny this at all. To this domestic evil is added the enemy Satan, who, if we sleep even a little, sows his tares, which grow up together with the good seed and often seem to dominate the whole field. The Church is therefore never without blemishes and grave faults; this could be demonstrated at length if anyone wished to run through its history from the times of the Patriarchs onward. But let the example of that little church suffice for us, which the Son of God himself, Jesus Christ, had while he dwelt on earth. In it, without doubt, the disciples were the best of all, whom he had appointed to be teachers of the world. Yet how many faults, and how grave, did they all labour under together? Nevertheless, he calls them clean because of his Word, to which they gave place and which they had grasped by faith. What then prevents us from thinking that today also the Church is among those who, although they have many things worthy of reproof, nevertheless give place to the Word of the Gospel and keep the form of faith and religion handed down by Christ?

units.la: Debebant ista diligentius considerare, nostri temporis Donatistæ, qui temere nimis totas vrbes & gentes damnant, in quibus Dei Verbum prædicatur, Sacramenta rite administrantur, præces publicæ habentur, & pauperibus non illiberaliter subuenitur, legibus denique bonis & sanctis scelera prohibentur atque puniuntur. Hæc omnia illi pro nihilo ducunt, nisi nouus quidam magistratus constituatur, cui in ipsos quoq; principes ius sit, eos non modo corripiendi, verumetiam excommunicandi. At velim vnum saltem exemplum ab eis produci vel Veteris vel Noui Testamenti, quo suam illam dictatura probare possint. A prophetis quidem reges magna cum libertate officij admonitos, & propter sua vitia correptos fuisse scimus: at ab ijsdem nullum vnquam à sacrorum communione exclusum fuisse legimus. Nec quicquam huius Apostoli fecerunt, & qui his proximi successerunt. Obiciunt illi nobis D. Ambrosium, qui Theodosium Imperatorem excommunicarit, vt octo totis mensibus à templi ingressu arceretur. Sed qui historiæ eius circumstantias omnes expenderit, Theodosij pietatem potius quam Ambrosij factum probabit, qui optimū & de Ecclesia præclarè meritum Imperatorem Thessalonicensium seditiosorum & spurcissimorum Sodomiæ propugnatorum ludibrijs obiecit. Sed quia de his alibi dictum est, nolo nunc plura addere.
units.tr: The Donatists of our own time ought to have considered these things more carefully. They rashly condemn whole cities and nations in which the Word of God is preached, the sacraments are rightly administered, public prayers are offered, the poor are relieved with no small generosity, and crimes are finally forbidden and punished by good and holy laws. They count all these things as nothing unless some new magistracy is set up with the right not only to rebuke but even to excommunicate the princes themselves. But I would like them to produce at least one example from the Old or New Testament by which they could prove this dictatorship of theirs. We know that kings were admonished by the prophets with great freedom in their office and rebuked for their vices; but we never read that any of them was excluded from the communion of the sacred things by the same prophets. Nor did the Apostles do anything of the kind, nor those who came closest to them. They object to us Ambrose, who excommunicated the Emperor Theodosius so that he was kept from entering the church for eight whole months. But whoever weighs all the circumstances of that story will commend the piety of Theodosius rather than the deed of Ambrose, since Ambrose exposed to the mockery of the seditious and most filthy defenders of sodomy at Thessalonica an emperor who was excellent and had deserved very well of the Church. But since I have spoken of these matters elsewhere, I do not wish to add more now.

units.la: Sed ad Pauli doctrinam de virorum & mulierum habitu accedamus, cuius hæc summa est: Viri dum orant & prophetant, caput aperire debent: è contra mulieres inter orandum & prophetandum sint capite operto siue velato. De hoc autem potissimùm agit, quia (vt initiò monuimus) in eo maximè peccabatur. Nos verò hinc generalem doctrinam petere debemus: decoro & honestati studendum esse in cœtibus ecclesiasticis. Qui in regum conspectum prodeunt, vt coram illis de rebus alicuius momenti differant, non modò verba probè meditantur, sed vestitu quoq; & gestibus vtuntur decenter, ne illorum oculos offendant. Atqui in Ecclesiæ cœtibus Christus ipse præsens adest, Rex & Sacerdos summus atq; æternus: & in ijsdem de rebus agitur omnium maximis, ex quibus omnis nostra salus dependet. Procul ergo abesse debet omnis leuitas & petulantia, qua homines mundo dediti in vestitu vti consueuerunt. Cur enim hic nobis indulgeamus, quando Deus ipsa quoq; loca, in quibus propter religionis exercitia conuenitur, sacrosanctâ esse vult, & ab omni prophano vsu aliena? Christus certè cùm templum Hierosolymitanum repurgauisset, ne vas quidem qualecunque per illud gestare permisit. Cur ergo corpora sua, quæ viua Spiritus sancti templa sunt, immodico ornatu & superbiæ armis dedecorent, qui in cœtus sacros veniunt, vt in Dei conspectu appareant?
units.tr: But let us come to Paul's teaching about the dress of men and women, the substance of which is this: men ought to uncover their heads when they pray and prophesy; on the contrary, women during prayer and prophecy ought to have their heads covered or veiled. Paul treats this matter chiefly because, as we noted at the beginning, the fault was most common in this respect. But from here we ought to draw a general teaching: that decorum and propriety must be cultivated in ecclesiastical assemblies. Those who come into the presence of kings, in order to speak with them about matters of some importance, not only carefully weigh their words but also use dress and gestures becomingly, so as not to offend the eyes of those men. Yet in the assemblies of the Church Christ himself is present, the King and the eternal and supreme Priest, and in them are discussed the greatest matters of all, on which our whole salvation depends. Therefore all levity and wantonness, in which worldly people are accustomed to indulge in dress, must be far removed. For why should we indulge it here, when God wills even the places in which people gather for the exercise of religion to be holy and free from every profane use? Certainly Christ, when he had cleansed the temple at Jerusalem, did not permit even an ordinary vessel to be carried through it. Why then do those who come to holy assemblies, in order to appear in the sight of God, disgrace their bodies, which while alive are temples of the Holy Spirit, with immoderate adornment and the weapons of pride?

units.la: Interim obiter nos hic locus admonet, quæ externa veteris Ecclesiæ exercitia fuerint. Duorum enim meminit Paulus, ad quæ olim in cœtus sacros Christiani conuenerunt. Primum, Orationis aut precum. Nam etsi priuatim in his assidui esse debeamus, prodest tamen publicè multorum preces simul coniungi, vt (quod olim Tertullianus dixit) quasi manu facta & coniunctis copijs Deo inflemus, cui vis hæc imprimis grata est, vt quæ fidei ardentis indicia habet, & quod mutuis exemplis singuli magis accenduntur atq; confirmantur. Alterum est Prophetia. Est hæc non modo futurorum prædictio, aut huius facultas, sed etiam Scripturæ sacræ tractatio, vt infra Cap.14. audiemus. At quia hæc non minus ad auditores quàm ad doctores pertinet, prophetare etiam dicuntur, qui Scripturarum interpretes audiunt. Et ideò hic mulierum prophetantium meminit, quibus tamen in cœtibus publicis loqui non permittit Apostolus, vt suo loco videbimus, Est autem verbum Dei præcipuum, quod Ecclesia habet. Nam vt per hoc suum animum atq; voluntatem nobis Deus declarat: ita neq; vllus cultus neq; preces illi gratæ sunt, nisi secundum illius præscriptum dirigantur. Porro appendices Verbi sunt Sacramenta, quorum hic non meminit, cùm quia sub Verbo comprehenduntur, adeoq; Verba sunt visibilia: tum quia hic de ijs solis agit, quæ quotidie debent in Ecclesia fieri. Nam non semper administrari possunt Sacramenta, neque etiam vt quotidie administrentur opus est. Imò prodest in his modum adhibere, ne relicto Verbo externis hisce symbolis superstitiosè inhæreamus, vel nimius vsus contemptum pariat. Alia autem est precum & Verbi Dei ratio, in quibus nihil huius timeri potest. Semper enim precibus est opus, & quo magis in his assidui sumus, eò magis in fide confirmamur. Semper etiam nos doceri, admoneri, corripi & consolationibus piis confirmari oportet: neq; potest Verbi nauseatio fastidium facile nasci, cùm in illo iucundissima sit varietas, qua nostro ingenio Deus sese accommodat. Quid multis? Veterem illam simplicitatem in Ecclesia retinere studeant, qui Deo probari volunt: procul autem arceantur, qui noua figmenta obtrudunt, & reliquis grauioribus illis maxime necessarijs, circa res vanißimas & prorsus inutiles occupantur. Sed tempus est, vt argumenta videamus, quibus suam hanc traditionem Paulus confirmat.
units.tr: Meanwhile, this passage briefly reminds us what the external practices of the early Church were. For Paul mentions two things for which Christians once gathered in sacred assemblies. The first is prayer or supplication. For although we ought to be constant in these in private, it is still useful for the prayers of many to be joined together in public, so that (as Tertullian once said) we may, as it were, make an assault upon God with a united band and combined forces, which he especially welcomes, since it is a sign of burning faith, and because individuals are more inflamed and strengthened by one another's examples. The second is prophecy. This is not only the foretelling of future things, or the gift of doing so, but also the handling of Holy Scripture, as we shall hear below in chapter 14. But since this concerns hearers no less than teachers, those who listen to the interpreters of Scripture are also said to prophesy. And so here he mentions the prophesying women, though the Apostle does not permit them to speak in public assemblies, as we shall see in its place. The chief thing the Church has, however, is the Word of God. For just as God declares to us through it his mind and will, so no worship and no prayers are pleasing to him unless they are directed according to his prescription. Moreover, the appendages of the Word are the sacraments, which he does not mention here, both because they are included under the Word, and so are visible words, and because here he treats only of those things which ought to take place in the Church every day. For the sacraments cannot always be administered, nor is it necessary that they be administered every day. Indeed, it is useful to observe a measure in them, lest, leaving the Word, we cling superstitiously to these external symbols, or excessive use breed contempt. But the case of prayer and of the Word of God is different, and in these nothing of this kind is to be feared. For there is always need of prayers, and the more constant we are in them, the more we are confirmed in faith. Likewise we always ought to be taught, admonished, rebuked and strengthened by pious consolations; nor can weariness of the Word easily arise, since in it there is the most delightful variety, by which God adapts himself to our disposition. What more is there to say? Let those who wish to please God strive to keep in the Church that ancient simplicity; but let those who thrust in new inventions be kept far away, and who busy themselves with empty and altogether useless matters, while neglecting those weightier things which are most necessary. But it is time to see the arguments by which Paul confirms this tradition of his.

units.la: Primum à Dei instituto & ordinatione desumit, quæ est, vt nullus inter homines gradus sit aut ordo, qui non caput habeat proprium, cui subesse, & quod pro virili ornare & colere debeat. Verba eius sunt hæc: Velim autem vos nosse, quòd omnis viri caput Christus est, caput autem mulieris vir, caput verò Christi Deus. Christum omnis viri caput esse dicit, quia ille in hoc sexu supra omnes eminet: vt si quis quæråt, quis virorum omnium princeps merito dici debeat? non alius, quàm Christus nominari possit. Itaq; dictum hoc non ita accipi debet, quasi Christum ad solos viros pertinere, Apostolus docere velit. Hic enim non de salutis æternæ negotio agit, sed de solo externo & politico ordine, quo inter homines Deus distinxit, & Christum propter sexum viris adnumerat. Quoad verò regnum illius spirituale, ex quo salus nostra dependet, in illo non est vir nec fœmina (vt alibi Paulus docet) & ad omnes credentes ille pertinet, cuiuscunq; sexus, loci aut ordinis fuerint. Similiter (inquit) caput mulieris est vir. Ita enim Deus instituit, cùm Euæ diceret: Ad virum erit respectus tuus, & ipse tibi dominabitur. Et quod hic uno verbo dicit Apostolus, id in epistola ad Ephef. multis exponit. Dicitur autem vir caput mulieris, non modò propter imperium, aut quòd hæc ancillæ aut mancipij loco ei esse debeat, sed quòd cum virtute & sapientia præesse, & capitis instar tam sibi ipsi quàm uxori, quæ unum cum ipso corpus est, consulere debet.
units.tr: First, he draws it from God's institution and ordinance, which is that there is no grade or order among men that does not have its own head, to which it should be subject, and which it should, as far as it can, adorn and honour. His words are these: "I would have you know that the head of every man is Christ, and the head of the woman is the man, and the head of Christ is God." He says that Christ is the head of every man, because in this sex he surpasses all others; so that if anyone asks who ought rightly to be called the prince of all men, no one else can be named but Christ. Therefore this saying ought not to be understood as if the Apostle wished to teach that Christ pertains only to men. For here he is not dealing with the business of eternal salvation, but only with the external and political order which God has established among men, and he counts Christ among men on account of his sex. As for his spiritual kingdom, on which our salvation depends, in that there is neither male nor female (as Paul teaches elsewhere), and he pertains to all believers, of whatever sex, place or rank they may be. "Likewise," he says, "the head of the woman is the man." For thus God instituted it, when he said to Eve: "Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you." And what the Apostle says here in one word, he sets out at length in the epistle to the Ephesians. Now the man is called the head of the woman not only on account of authority, nor because she ought to be to him in the place of a maidservant or slave, but because he ought to preside with virtue and wisdom, and to care for her, as the head does for the body, as much as for himself, since she is one body with him.

units.la: Addit his tertium gradum: Caput Christi Deus. Quod dictum Ariani olim & Eunomiani extra Pauli institutū detorquentes, Filium creaturam & non eiusdem essentiæ atq; dignitatis cum Patre esse contendebant. At noluit hic Paulus de Patris & Filij divinitate verba facere: sed quod dicit, id ad personam Mediatoris referre oportet, secundum quam Filius assumpta humanitate sese Patri subiecit, vt & hunc se maiorem, imò ab hoc se missum esse, & doctrinâ suam, non suam sed Patris esse testetur. Ea igitur ratione Deus caput Christi est. Quòd si Deitate ipsam consideres, ibi nihil alio vel maius vel minus occurret, sed ipsum Christum audies dicentem: Ego & Pater unū sumus: Qui me vidit, Patrem vidit, &c. Non debent ergo Pauli verba ab eius instituto in alienum sensum trahi. Videtur autem Christi mentionem ideo facere, ut argumentum, quod hinc ducere instituit, magis amplificet propter eos, qui politicos & œconomicos ordines per Christum sublatos esse arbitrantur. Quasi diceret: Deus adeò nemine inter homines esse voluit, qui non capiti certo subesset, ut ne Filius quidem Dei in carne manifestatus hanc gloriam usurparit. Quanto magis igitur aliorum hominũ fuerit, ut singuli caput suum agnoscant, idq; debito honore & [?]culturpro sequantur? Hoc autè fundamento iacto infert: Omnis vir orans aut prophetans operto capite, dedecorat caput suum: Omnis verò mulier orans aut prophetans non operto capite, dedecorat caput suum. Argumentum ita formare poteris: Nemo caput suum dedecorare debet, ne à Deo instituto ordinem turbet, de quo modò diximus: At vir operto aut tecto capite orans sive prophetans caput suū dedecorat, & hoc ipsum mulier facit, quæ nudato capite orat aut prophetat: Ergo viri quidē aperto, mulieres autē operto sive velato capite orare et sacra omnia peragere debent.
units.tr: He adds a third grade: "the head of Christ is God." Arians and Eunomians once twisted this saying outside Paul's purpose, contending that the Son is a creature and not of the same essence and dignity as the Father. But Paul did not wish to speak here about the divinity of the Father and the Son, but what he says must be referred to the person of the Mediator, in respect of which the Son, having assumed humanity, subjected himself to the Father, so that he might also testify that the Father is greater than he, indeed that he was sent by him, and that his teaching is not his own but the Father's. For this reason, then, God is the head of Christ. But if you consider the deity itself, nothing either greater or lesser will appear there, but you will hear Christ himself saying: "I and the Father are one; he who has seen me has seen the Father," etc. Therefore the words of Paul ought not to be drawn from his purpose into an alien sense. He seems, however, to mention Christ for this reason, so as to amplify more the argument which he has undertaken to draw from this, on account of those who think that the political and domestic orders have been abolished through Christ. As if he were saying: God so willed that there be no one among men who is not subject to some definite head, that not even the Son of God, made manifest in the flesh, usurped this glory. How much more, then, ought it to be for other men that each acknowledge his own head, and render him due honour and [?]... Having laid this foundation, he infers: "Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonours his head; but every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonours her head." You may frame the argument thus: No one ought to dishonour his head, lest he disturb the order instituted by God, of which we have just spoken; but a man who prays or prophesies with his head covered or veiled dishonours his head, and the woman does the same when she prays or prophesies with her head bare. Therefore men ought to pray and perform all sacred duties with the head uncovered, and women with the head covered or veiled.

units.la: Sed hic quæstio nascitur: Quomodo vir caput suū dedecorare dicatur, si illud operiat aut tegat? quomodo item mulier suū caput dedecoret, si illud denudet aut aperiat? Respondeo Paulum ex illius seculi consuetudine argumentum petere. Nam illo tempore capitis apertio dignitatis & imperij symbolum erat, velum verò subiectionis. Itaq; verborum istorum sensus est: Viros sibi ipsis injuriam facere, si caput velando in sacris cœtibus dignitatẽ & eminentiam suam, qua eos Deus ornauit, dissiteantur: injuriam verò illâ in ipsum Christum redundare, quem totius virilis sexus caput & principem esse, supra dixit. Potest his addi, quod Christus nobis hanc gratiam & dignitatem meruit, ut justificati ex fide pacem habeamus apud Deum, & proinde in eius conspectu intrepidi possimus comparere. Eam ergo dignitate inter orandum & in cœtibus sacris viri aperto capite profiteri debent, ne eam dissimulando beneficium à Christo nobis collatū negare, aut saltem extenuare videantur. Similiter mulier (inquit) suū caput ignominia afficit: quia dum aperto aut nudo capite incedit, sibi quodammodo jus & imperium in virum vendicat, & tantumnon publicè suam rebellionē profitetur, quòd nimirum excusso jugo divinæ ordinationis pro suo arbitrio omnia velit agere. Id verò fieri non potest absq; manifesta viri contumelia, quem pro suo capite & domino debeat agnoscere.
units.tr: But here a question arises: how is a man said to dishonour his head if he covers or veils it? And likewise how does a woman dishonour her head if she bares or uncovers it? I answer that Paul takes his argument from the custom of that age. For at that time the uncovering of the head was a sign of dignity and authority, but the veil a sign of subjection. Therefore the sense of these words is this: men do an injury to themselves if, by veiling their heads in sacred assemblies, they conceal the dignity and pre-eminence with which God has adorned them; and that injury redounds upon Christ himself, whom he said above to be the head and prince of the whole male sex. To this may be added that Christ has merited for us this grace and dignity, that, justified by faith, we have peace with God, and therefore may appear fearlessly in his presence. Men ought therefore to profess that dignity by going bareheaded while praying and in sacred assemblies, lest by dissembling it they seem to deny, or at least to diminish, the benefit conferred upon us by Christ. Likewise, he says, the woman puts her head to shame: for while she goes about with her head uncovered or bare, she in some measure claims for herself a right and authority over the man, and as good as publicly professes her rebellion, namely because, having shaken off the yoke of divine ordinance, she wishes to do everything at her own pleasure. Yet this cannot happen without a manifest insult to the man, whom she ought to acknowledge as her head and lord.

units.la: Videntur haec leuicula & vix digna esse, de quibus publicè in Ecclesia sermo fiat. Sed rem propius considerantibus mox patebit, haec & maximum momentum habere, & nostris temporibus imprimis conuenire. Viros enim Apostolus suam dignitatem profituere, & Christum ignominia afficere dicit, qui more patrio pileati & velato aut inuoluto capite in coetibus ecclesiasticis comparebant. Quid ergo illum dicturum putabimus, si hodie ministros Ecclesiarum vel Papistico habitu uti, vel militari veste, aut mercatoria, vel etiâ militariter incedere: vulgus vero Christianorum cum luxu petulantiam extremam coniungere videret: dum horum alij plumis struthionum, gallorum, caponum & gruum pileos suos exornant: alij ijsdem cornua aut auriculas asininas affingunt: alij gentium peregrinarum & Christiani nominis hostium vestitu superbiunt? Nam ut de solis Germanis nostris dicamus, non sufficiunt amplius petulantissimis hominibus, quae iamdudum ab Italis, Hispanis, Gallis & aliis finitimis gentibus quasi mutuò sumpserunt, nisi ex Tartaris & Turcis galeros in portentosam altitudinem acuminatos accersant, quibus ita superbiunt, quasi & corporis statura aliquid inde accedat, & victoriae aduersus Turcas trophaea capitibus suis gestent. Est hoc magnae leuitatis argumentum, & utinam non peius aliquod omen subsit. Si enim capitis velatio subiectionis symbolum est, vereor Turcarum tyrannidi subijciendos tandem fore eos, qui illorum pileos sibi ipsis sponte accersunt.
units.tr: These matters seem trivial and hardly worth discussing publicly in the Church. But anyone who considers the matter more closely will soon see that they are of the greatest importance and especially suited to our own times. For the Apostle says that men who appeared in the church assemblies wearing hats, or with their heads veiled or wrapped in the native manner, dishonour their own dignity and dishonour Christ. What, then, do we think he would say if he saw ministers of the Churches today dressed either in Papist garb, or in military or merchant's clothing, or even strutting about like soldiers; and if he saw the common run of Christians joining extreme wantonness to luxury? Some of them adorn their hats with the feathers of ostriches, cocks, capons and cranes; others fix horns or donkey's ears to them; others take pride in the dress of foreign peoples and enemies of the Christian name. To speak only of our own Germans: they are no longer satisfied with the most outrageous fashions which they have long since borrowed, as it were, from Italians, Spaniards, French and other neighbouring peoples. Instead they send for hats from Tartars and Turks, shaped into a monstrous height at the peak, and they take such pride in them as if their stature were increased thereby, and they wear on their heads the trophies of victory over the Turks. This is a sign of great frivolity, and I wish it did not portend something worse. For if the covering of the head is a symbol of subjection, I fear that those who voluntarily fetch Turkish hats for themselves will in the end be made subject to the tyranny of the Turks.

units.la: Habet praeterea locus ille generalem doctrinam, in Christum ipsum iniurios esse viros, qui inhonestius & indecentius sese gerunt. Nam dignitatem suam profituuntur, in quam ipsos Deus euexit, & in qua ergà suas uxores viuum Christi simulachrum esse debebant. Erat hoc illis diligentius considerandum, qui non solum indecoro vestitu sese ridiculos praebent, verumetiam uxores suas adeò iniquè & inhumaniter tractant, ut diaboli exemplum sibi imitandum propositum videri possint. Similiter mulieres hic discant, sibi non laudi, sed summo dedecori esse, si viris suis dominari velint, & suum illud dominium vestitu, moribus, gestu, aut etiam verbis asperioribus ostentent. Dum enim viros aliorum contemptui & ludibrijs exponunt, simul sibi ipsis proteruae impudentiae & impiae temeritatis notam inurunt. Quis enim pias, religiosas, pudicas dixerit eas, quae à Deo institutum ordinem tam petulanter conculcant? Quanto rectius Sara, quae cum Abrahamo suo omne genus molestiae patienter tulit, & hunc suum dominum agnouit? Hoc certe nomine illam Spiritus sanctus per Petrum Apostolum commendat. Nec est quod virorum duritiem & iniquitatem praetexant, quae dominium impatientius ferunt. Nec enim maritorum vitijs ipsarum superbia & arrogantia excusatur. Nam qualis qualis sit vir, caput tamen est mulieris. Quin ergo ad proprij corporis constitutionem respiciunt superbiae illae, quae omnem dominandi occasionem tam aùdè venantur? Annon suis quoque vitijs & morbis caput laborat? Num verò propterea à manibus laceratur? num aduersus illud pedes extolluntur. Imò quo periculosiores illius morbi sunt, eò promptius in illo curando & fouendo reliqua membra suum officium faciunt. Idem ergo mulieres obseruent, quibus cum viris iniquioribus res est. Exemplum habent in Abigaele, quae immortalem laudem meruit sua modestia, qua virum Nabalem, durum & ineptum patienter tulit.
units.tr: Moreover, that passage contains a general teaching: men who conduct themselves in a more dishonourable and indecent way do wrong to Christ himself. For they profess the dignity to which God has raised them, and in which they ought to be a living image of Christ towards their wives. Those men should consider this more carefully who not only make themselves ridiculous by their indecent dress, but also treat their wives so unjustly and inhumanly that they seem to have the devil's example set before them for imitation. Likewise, let women learn here that it is no credit to them, but a great disgrace, if they wish to lord it over their husbands, and display that domination by their dress, their manners, their bearing, or even by harsh words. For by exposing their husbands to the contempt and mockery of others, they at the same time brand themselves with the mark of brazen impudence and impious rashness. For who would call pious, religious and chaste those women who so wantonly trample underfoot the order instituted by God? How much more rightly did Sarah act, who patiently bore every kind of hardship with her Abraham and acknowledged him as her lord? The Holy Spirit certainly commends her by the name of this virtue through the Apostle Peter. Nor is there any reason for them to pretend that their husbands are harsh and unjust, when they bear the authority of the husband with greater impatience. For a wife's pride and arrogance are not excused by the faults of her husband. For whatever sort of man he is, he is still the head of the woman. Why, then, do those proud women not look to the constitution of their own body, which gives them every opportunity for dominating? Does not the head suffer from its own faults and diseases? Yet is it therefore torn by the hands? Are the feet raised up against it? Indeed, the more dangerous those diseases of the head are, the more readily do the other members perform their duty in curing and cherishing it. Let women in the same way observe this who have to do with more unjust husbands. They have an example in Abigail, who earned immortal praise by her modesty, by which she patiently bore her husband Nabal, who was harsh and foolish.

units.la: At quia mulierum superbia difficilius domatur, de his prolixius disserit Paulus, & in praesenti aliud argumentum subijcit ex communi sensu desumptum, quo docet, quàm indecorum & absurdum, adeoque naturae legibus aduersum sit, si mulier nudo aut non velato capite in publicos coetus prodeat. Nam hoc (inquit) unum & idem est, ac si rasa esset. Et id exponens addit: Nam si non velatur mulier, etiam tondeatur. Quod si turpe mulieri tonderi aut radi, veletur. Argumentum est eiusmodi: Turpe & indecorum nimis censetur mulierem radi, quam natura capillis longioribus ornauit: At quae non velatur, rasae similis est: Ergo caput velare aut tegere debent. Videri poterat argumentum hoc non satis firmum, vel etiam ridiculum esse, cùm quae aperto capite prodire gaudent, in capillis nutriendis & ornandis tam curiosae & solicitae sint, ut nihil minus quàm rasae possint censeri. Sed Paulus non quid mundo videatur, sed quid Deus velit atque iubeat, respicit. Is enim (ut paulò ante diximus) mulierem viri imperio subesse vult, & capillis densioribus demissioribusq; sexum illum donauit, ut naturalis veli loco sint, & quò minus illas subiectionis illius pudeat. Si quae ergo velum capitis, quod usitatum subiectionis symbolum est, abijcit, abjicit, ea certè eodem iure capillos quoque, qui velum naturale sunt, abjicere poterat. Et quàm-uis id non faciat, quin potius calamistris & odoribus comas mirificè plantet atq; exornet, in Dei tamen conspectu pro rasa reputatur, id est, pro ea, quae excusso jugo sibi imperium & dominium vendicet, & proinde ea sibi sumat, quae penes virum esse debent. Haec (inquam) Paulus expendens, non sine indignantis specie dicit: Si non velatur mulier, etiam tondeatur. Nec temere tanta gravitate & vehementia utitur, cum sciret olim Deum per Mosem ejusmodi Legem tulisse: Mulier ne gerat arma vel habitum viri, neque vir induatur veste muliebri: quoniam abo-minandus est Domino Deo tuo, quisquis illa fecerit. Deut.22.cap.
units.tr: But because the pride of women is more difficult to tame, Paul discourses on them at greater length, and in the present passage he adds another argument, drawn from common sense, by which he teaches how unseemly and absurd it is, and therefore contrary to the laws of nature, for a woman to come into public assemblies with her head bare or uncovered. For he says, "This is one and the same thing as if she were shaven." And explaining this he adds: "For if a woman is not covered, let her also be shorn. But if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaved, let her be covered." The argument runs thus: it is judged too shameful and indecent for a woman to be shaved, when nature has adorned her with longer hair; but a woman who is not covered is like one who is shaven; therefore women ought to cover or veil their heads. This argument might seem not very strong, or even ridiculous, since women who delight in going about with their heads uncovered are so careful and anxious in growing and adorning their hair that they could be thought to be anything but shaven. But Paul looks not at what seems right to the world, but at what God wills and commands. For God (as we said a little while ago) wants woman to be subject to the rule of man, and has given that sex longer and thicker hair, so that it might serve in place of a natural veil, and so that women might be less ashamed of that subjection. If, therefore, a woman casts off the veil of the head, which is the customary symbol of subjection, she could by the same right also cast off her hair, which is a natural veil. And although she does not do this, but rather curls and perfumes her locks and adorns them wonderfully, in the sight of God she is still reckoned as shaven, that is, as one who, having shaken off the yoke, claims for herself the rule and dominion, and therefore takes to herself what ought to belong to the husband. Weighing these things (I say), Paul says, not without a show of indignation: "If a woman is not covered, let her also be shorn." Nor does he use such seriousness and vehemence rashly, since he knew that God had long before given by Moses a law of this kind: "A woman shall not wear a man's weapons or dress, nor shall a man put on a woman's garment; for whoever does these things is an abomination to the Lord your God." Deut. 22.

units.la: Haec ut insolentem mulierum nostri seculi luxum arguunt: ita foedam & absurdam Papistarum superstitionem confutant, qua in virginibus Christo consecrandis utuntur. Paulus mu-lieres velatis capitibus esse vult, nimirum more patrio & honesto, & absurdissimum turpissimumque esse dicit, si quae tondeatur aut radatur. At in Papatu novum pro virginibus coniugium commenti sunt, quo illae Christo desponsantur. Quod dum fit, velum quidem peculiare accipiunt, crines autem abscindunt, quibus natura eas velari voluit. Id vero ad coniunctionem illam spiritualem cum Christo necessarium esse aiunt, & non minimam meriti partem in hac tonsura collocant. Quis vero non videat, quàm hoc pugnet cum Apostolorum traditionibus, quas isti homines nunquam non in ore habent? Paulus enim (ut modò diximus) cum indignatione & Sarcasmo mulieres tonderi jubet, si velari nolint: illi vero hoc seriò & sub religionis praetextu praecipiunt. At quid de Apostolis dico, quorum authoritatem illi jampridem conculcarunt? (ut non Conciliorum Canones audiunt, quibus quod faciunt diserte prohibetur?) Tradunt enim historiae sub annum Christi CCCLX. regnante Constantio, Eustathium quendam Sebastiae Armeniorum episcopum de vitando coniugio & carnium esu, & ne mulieres comam haberent, leges tulisse. Conuenerunt adversus illum episcopi alij in Gangrensi Synodo, inter cuius Canones decimus septimus sic habet: αἵ τις γυναικῶν ὅσα [?] τῶν νομιζομένων [?] ἀσχημοσύνῃ [?] ἀποκείρεσθαι τὰς κόμας [?], οὐκ ἔδωκεν [?] ὁ θεὸς ἐς ὑπόμνησιν τῆς ὑποταγῆς, ὡς ἀναλύσασα τὸ πρόσχυμα τῆς ὑποταγῆς, ἀνάθεμα ἔστω [?]. Quorum verborum sensus est: Si quae mulier propter putatitium religionis exercitium capillos tondeat, quos Deus ut per nos subjectionis admoneatur dedit, ea ut quae praeceptum subjectionis dissoluerit, anathema esto. Haec ideo commemorare libuit, ut omnes videant, quomodo res subinde in peius prolapsae sint, & quòd nos non primi hominum ineptissimorum superstitiones damnemus, sed olim damnatas prohibeamus [?]. At quoad hujus loci institutum agnoscere nos decet singulare Dei beneficium, qui coetus sacros instituit, quibus ipse medius interesse, & suorum praeces audire solet. In his assidui sint (Christiani homines, & ita sese gerant, ut tam mares quàm foeminae dignitatem suam tueantur, quam illis meruit JESVS CHRISTVS: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Just as these words rebuke the excessive luxury of the women of our age, so they also refute the foul and absurd superstition of the Papists, which they use in consecrating virgins to Christ. Paul wants women to have their heads veiled, of course in the native and honourable manner, and he says it is most absurd and shameful if a woman is shorn or shaved. But in the Papacy they have invented a new kind of marriage for virgins, by which they are betrothed to Christ. When this is done, they indeed receive a special veil, but they cut off the hair with which nature wished them to be covered. They say this shearing is necessary for that spiritual union with Christ, and they place no small part of its merit in this tonsure. Yet who does not see how much this conflicts with the traditions of the Apostles, which these men never cease to have on their lips? For Paul (as we have just said) orders women to be shorn, with indignation and sarcasm, if they will not be veiled; but they enjoin this in earnest and under the pretext of religion. But why do I speak of the Apostles, whose authority those men trampled underfoot long ago? (Do they not hear the canons of the Councils, which expressly forbid what they do?) For histories relate that in about the year of Christ 360, in the reign of Constantius, a certain Eustathius, bishop of Sebaste in Armenia, passed laws about avoiding marriage and eating meat, and that women should not keep their hair. Other bishops met in the Synod of Gangra against him, and among its canons the seventeenth says: [αἵ τις γυναικῶν ὅσα τῶν νομιζομένων ἀσχημοσύνῃ ἀποκείρεσθαι τὰς κόμας, οὐκ ἔδωκεν ὁ θεὸς ἐς ὑπόμνησιν τῆς ὑποταγῆς, ὡς ἀναλύσασα τὸ πρόσχυμα τῆς ὑποταγῆς, ἀνάθεμα ἔστω]. The sense of these words is: If any woman, under the pretext of religious observance, shears her hair, which God gave as a reminder of subjection, let her be anathema, as one who has dissolved the obligation of subjection. I have been pleased to mention these things so that everyone may see how matters have from time to time slipped into worse, and that we do not condemn for the first time the superstitions of the most foolish men, but forbid things long since condemned. But as far as the purpose of this passage is concerned, we ought to acknowledge the singular blessing of God, who instituted sacred assemblies, in which he himself is wont to be present in the midst and to hear the prayers of his people. Let Christians be diligent in these, and let them so conduct themselves that both men and women maintain that dignity which Jesus Christ has earned for them, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LVII.
units.tr: HOMILY LVII.

units.la: Vir enim non debet velare caput, cùm is imago sit & gloria Dei: at mulier gloria viri est. Non enim est vir ex muliere, sed mulier ex viro. Neque enim conditus est vir propter mulierem, sed mulier propter virum. Propter hoc debet mulier potestatem habere in capite propter Angelos. Verumtamen neque vir absque muliere, neque mulier absque viro, in Domino. Sicut enim mulier ex viro est: ita & vir per mulierem: omnia vero ex Deo. Apud vosipsos judicate, num decorum sit mulierem non velatam Deum orare? Anne natura quidem ipsa hoc vos docet, quod viro quidem, comatum esse dedecori sit: contra mulieri, comatam esse gloriae sit? Nam coma pro velamine data est ei. Quod si quis videtur contentiosus esse, nos ejusmodi consuetudinem non habemus, neque Ecclesiae Dei.
units.tr: For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of the man. For the man is not from the woman, but the woman from the man. Neither was the man created for the woman, but the woman for the man. For this reason the woman ought to have authority on her head, because of the angels. Nevertheless, neither is the man without the woman, nor the woman without the man, in the Lord. For as the woman is from the man, so also is the man through the woman; but all things are from God. Judge among yourselves: is it seemly that a woman should pray to God uncovered? Does not nature itself teach you that for a man to wear long hair is a disgrace, but for a woman it is a glory? For her hair has been given to her as a covering. But if anyone seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God.

units.la: Christianos quidem homines omni loco & tempore honestati studere decet, & curare ne quid sua professione indignum faciant: imprimis tamen hoc observandum est in coetibus Ecclesiasticis publicis. Nam ut in his ad preces & Dei cultum conveniuntur: ita promissione IESV CHRI-STI habemus, quod ipse nobis adesse, & quae illic fiunt Patri accepta facere velit. Qua causa est, quod in Lege multa de coetibus praecipiuntur, & Prophetae non uno loco graviter eos accusant, qui ad sacra publica non ea fide & reverentia veniebant, quam Deus requirit. Non temere ergo Paulus, cum Corinthiorum Ecclesiam a vitiis, quae in eam irrepserant, repurgare instituisset, de coetibus ecclesiasticis peculiari studio & diligentia agit, & quaecunque in his perperam fiebant, corrigit. Primum in his erat, quod tam viri quam foeminae habitu verterentur, qui Christianam professionem minus decebat: illis quidem caput operientibus eo ritu, cui in gentilismo adsueverant, & qui (ut nuper diximus) cum luxu superstitionem quoque coniunctam habebat: his vero petulanter nimis aperto capite & superbo capillorum ornatu formam suam ostentantibus. De viris ergo graviter agit, & ab initio ostendit, Deum ita instituisse, ut unusquisque hominum ordo caput habeat, quod honore & cultu debeat prosequi: Non decere igitur viros, ut suum caput, Christum, hoc ritu gentilitio dedecorent: neque mulieres, ut in sexus virilis contumeliam sibi id sumant, quod virorum est, quos pro suo capite debeant agnoscere. Sequuntur alia argumenta, quibus & viros & mulieres fortius urget, & simul locum illum absoluit.
units.tr: Christians ought to study decency in every place and at every time, and take care not to do anything unworthy of their profession; yet this must be observed above all in the public assemblies of the Church. For since they gather in them for prayer and the worship of God, we have the promise of Jesus Christ that he himself will be present with us and will be pleased to make acceptable to the Father whatever is done there. For this reason the Law prescribes many things concerning assemblies, and the Prophets in more than one place sharply accuse those who came to the public sacred gatherings without that faith and reverence which God requires. Not without reason, therefore, when Paul had undertaken to purge the Corinthian Church of the faults that had crept into it, does he treat of the ecclesiastical assemblies with special care and diligence, and correct whatever was being done wrongly in them. The first fault was that both men and women were dressed in a manner unbefitting the Christian profession: the men covering their heads with the rite to which they had grown accustomed in heathenism, which (as we said recently) was joined with luxury and also with superstition; the women, on the other hand, displaying their figure too boldly with uncovered heads and a proud arrangement of their hair. He therefore deals sternly with the men, and shows at the outset that God has so ordained that every order of men should have a head, which they ought to honour and reverence. It is not fitting, then, for men to dishonour their head, Christ, by this heathen rite; nor for women to take to themselves, to the shame of the male sex, what belongs to men, whom they ought to acknowledge as their head. There follow other arguments by which he presses both men and women more strongly, and at the same time completes that passage.

units.la: Primum ad viros redit, & quid illos deceat, ostendit: Vir non debet velare caput, quando nimirum in Dei conspectum venit ad orandum aut prophetandum. Ratio: Quia imago Dei est & gloria Dei. Loquitur autem Paulus, non de illa imagine Dei, quae in hominis mente potissimum sita est, & quam in primi parentis lapsu deflructam & obliteratam Christus postea in nobis instaurauit (quoad hanc enim, etiam mulieres piae & Christianae imago Dei sunt) sed de principatu & eminentia, in quam Deus virum constituit, ut non solum in alias creaturas, verumetiam in mulierem ius habeat & imperium, adeoque mulieri Deus fit, dum illam regit, tuetur & illius saluti atque honori consulit. Sic Moses Pharaoni in Deum datus fuisse dicitur, eo quod divina authoritate armatus cum illo agebat. Ut vero argumentum, quo hic Apostolus utitur, illustrius & efficatius fit, virum gloriam Dei quoque esse ait. Causa huius dicti est, quod Dei gloria maxime elucet in principatu illo & potestate, in quam homo evectus, ab omnibus creaturis suspicitur, colitur, observatur, timetur, veneratur. Quantam enim eius maiestatem, authoritatem, potentiam, sapientiam esse oportet, qui hominem caducum, mortalem, infinitis casibus obnoxium & (si corporis vires spectemus) reliquis animalibus longe inferiorem, ad tam sublime fastigium evehere, & authoritate armare potuit, quae truculentissimis quoque bestiis formidabilis est? Ex eo certe apparet, illum revera Dominum exercituum esse, qui omnibus creatis pro suo nutu utatur. Ut ergo Reges gloria sunt principes & praefecti provinciarum, qui cum authoritate praesunt: ita merito gloria Dei vir dicitur, qui suae dignitatis memor, eam, ut par est, tuetur. Hinc autem colligit Apostolus, non debere viros suae dignitatis insignia negligere, neque ethnicorum similes fieri, qui cum neque Deum neque suam gloriam recte agnoscant, praeferulimeu [?] velatis capitibus sua sacra peragunt: sed potius ingenua & liberali capitis apertione suam illam praeeminentiam testari. Quemadmodum enim coram rege in maiestatis solio sedente provinciarum praesides, praefecti, tribuni, militiae duces, equestris ordinis viri & quicunque alij cum sui ordinis aut muneris insignibus apparent, neque probaretur, qui praepositerae [?] humilitatis praetextu illa tunc absconderet, quando ad regis gloriam ea proferre decebat: ita Christiani homines in sacris coetibus, in quibus sumus ille Rex regum praesidet, sua etiam dignitatis insignia nequaquam dissimulare, sed ijs uti ad illustrandam eius maiestatem, qui illos tanto honore & gloria dignatus est.
units.tr: First he returns to the men and shows what befits them: A man ought not to cover his head, namely when he comes into the presence of God to pray or to prophesy. The reason: because he is the image and glory of God. Paul is speaking, however, not of that image of God which lies chiefly in the mind of man, and which, destroyed and effaced in the fall of our first parent, Christ afterwards restored in us (for in respect of this, even pious and Christian women are the image of God), but of the principality and pre-eminence into which God has set the man, so that he has right and dominion not only over the other creatures but also over the woman; and thus the man becomes God to the woman, while he rules her, protects her, and cares for her salvation and honour. So Moses is said to have been given as a god to Pharaoh, because he dealt with him armed with divine authority. In order to make the argument which the Apostle uses here clearer and more forceful, he says that man is also the glory of God. The reason for this saying is that the glory of God shines most brightly in that principality and power to which man, raised up, is looked up to, worshipped, obeyed, feared and venerated by all creatures. For how great must be the majesty, authority, power and wisdom of him who could raise a frail, mortal man, subject to countless accidents and (if we consider the strength of his body) far inferior to the other animals, to so lofty a height, and arm him with an authority which is feared even by the fiercest beasts? From this it certainly appears that he is truly the Lord of hosts, who uses all created things at his bidding. Therefore, just as kings are the glory of princes and governors of provinces who preside with authority, so the man who, mindful of his dignity, maintains it as is fitting, is rightly called the glory of God. From this the Apostle draws the conclusion that men ought not to neglect the badges of their dignity, nor become like the heathen, who, not rightly acknowledging either God or their own glory, perform their sacred rites with heads covered in a kind of perverse humility; but rather that they should bear witness to that pre-eminence by the free and noble uncovering of the head. For just as, before a king seated on the throne of majesty, provincial presidents, prefects, tribunes, commanders of the army, men of the equestrian order, and any others appear with the insignia of their order or office, and no one would be approved who, under the pretext of a misplaced humility, concealed those insignia when it was fitting to display them for the king's glory; so Christians in sacred assemblies, in which the King of kings presides, ought by no means to hide the insignia of their dignity, but use them to illustrate the majesty of him who has deigned to honour and glorify them so greatly.

units.la: Venit nobis hoc loco consideranda admirabilis & plus quam paterna bonitas Dei, qui cum nullius egeat, hominem tamen ad suam imaginem condere dignatus est, & in eodem suam gloriam vult elucere: imo hunc suam gloriam dicere dignatur, qui nisi ipse eum fecisset, nullus erat in rerum natura. Magnum hoc, si primam hominis originem & unde is desumptus sit, consideres. Maius autem multo est, quod imaginem hanc, quam nostra culpa deleueramus, Filij sui sangui-ne instaune instauravit, qui ne quid gloriæ veræ & solidæ nobis deesset, nos sibi fratres & regni sui cœlestis cohæredes facere dignatus est. Superant hæc rationis humanæ captum, quia inter homines nemo invenietur, qui pro filio rebelli & contumaci tantum facere vellet. Dauid equidem prioris illius dignitatis, quam omnium creaturarum princeps homo factus est, consideratione abreptus exclamat: Et quid est homo mortalis, vt memoriam eius habeas, & Filius hominis, vt eum invisas? Quid ergo nos dicere convenit? Aut quibus verbis, imo quibus cogitationibus eam, quæ in CHRISTO IESV nobis facta est, Dei beneficentiam prosequi poterimus? Veruntamen etsi nos hæc verba simul & animi facultates deficiant, prodest tamen de his sæpe cogitare: Vt nimirum nostræ dignitatis memores, hanc nulla re indecora aut inhonesta prophanemus. Prophanatur hæc (vt alias monuimus) intemperantia & ebrietate, libidine & fcortatione atque adulteriis, avaritia & nimio rerum huius seculi studio. Qui enim his indulgent, ij animos quasi è cœlis detractos in lutum fœdissimum immergunt, & excusso spiritu adoptionis, qui idem libertatis spiritus est, seipsos diaboli mancipia faciunt, quibus nihil fœdius, nihil miserius, nihil infelicius excogitari potest. Prophanant quoque dignitatem suam, qui vestitu indecoro aut etiam superstitioso vtuntur. Vt enim ma-tronalis decori non magnam rationem habet, quæ meretricio cultu sese venditat: ita non magni faciunt Christiani hominis dignitatem, qui vestibus sese ornant, quæ Christianam professionem minus decent. Atqui tales sunt, quæ vel superbiæ & libidini seruiunt, vel superstitiosam cultus diuini perfuasionem coniunctam habent. Et hoc videns Paulus, de capitis habitu, qui non magni momenti esse videri poterat, tam diligenter disserit. Quod si verò ille Apostolo dignus visus est reprehensione, quid de illis dicemus, qui formas vestium quotidie peregrinas accersunt, aut ipsi novas excogitant, quibus forma quoque totius corporis ita mutatur, vt quiduis aliud potius quàm homines videri possint? Fuit leuitas ista omnibus seculis non solum extremæ corruptionis, verum etiam imminentis excidij argumentum. Exemplo nobis sit Hierichuntis excidium, inter cultus spolia chlamys Babylonica numeratur, ita nimirum luxum & fastum in vestitu perstringente Spiritu sancto, quo præter alia scelera peccarunt. In Romana historia Lucullus habetur, vir alioqui eximius & bene de republica meritus, qui purpureas chlamydes ducentas ad spectacula scenica Prætori commodato misit. Quo exemplo historici docent, qui tunc Romanæ vrbis mores fuerint, quando plurimarum gentium spoliis ditati, luxu & fastu omnes diffluebant. At mox secuta sunt ciuilia bella, quæ finem non habuerunt, donec res ad Monarchiam devenit, quæ penes homines crudelissimos plerunque fuit, qui sua libidine tandem seipsos & Romanum Imperium pessundederunt. Et vt ad sacra redeamus, nonne Sophonias Propheta minatur, Dominum visitaturum esse omnes eos, qui habitu peregrino vestiuntur? Quæ omnia si cum nostri seculi moribus conferantur, facile videbunt cordati quique, quid nobis hodie sperandum sit, quando alij quidem insolito & monstrifico vestitu religionem metiuntur, alij vero ea in vestium formis petulantia ludunt, vt cum pudore sensum quoque communem abiecisse videri possint. Debebant hic suam auctoritatem interponere Christiani principes, quando ad Verbi Dei prædicationem plerique obsurduerunt. Sed quid de illis dicere opus est, quando monstra eiusmodi fere ex aulis eorum, ceu ex equo Troiano, prodeunt?
units.tr: Here we must consider the admirable and more than paternal goodness of God, who, though he needs nothing, has yet deigned to make man in his own image and wills that his glory shine forth in him; indeed he deigns to call him his glory, who, unless he had made him, would not exist in the nature of things. This is great if you consider the first origin of man and whence he was taken. Much greater, however, is that he restored this image, which we had blotted out by our fault, with the blood of his own Son, and that he deigned, so that nothing of true and solid glory might be lacking to us, to make us his brothers and co-heirs of his heavenly kingdom. These things surpass the grasp of human reason, because among men no one will be found who would be willing to do so much for a rebellious and obstinate son. David, indeed, carried away by the consideration of that former dignity, which man was made to have as prince of all creatures, cries out: "What is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you visit him?" What, then, is it fitting for us to say? Or in what words, or rather in what thoughts, shall we be able to pursue the kindness of God which has been shown to us in Christ Jesus? Yet, even if our words and powers of mind fail us in these matters, it is nonetheless profitable to think often about them: so that, mindful of our dignity, we may profane it by nothing unseemly or dishonourable. It is profaned (as we have warned elsewhere) by intemperance and drunkenness, by lust and fornication and adultery, by greed and excessive devotion to the things of this world. For those who indulge in these things plunge their souls, as it were dragged down from heaven, into the most foul mire, and, having cast off the spirit of adoption, which is the same as the spirit of freedom, they make themselves slaves of the devil, than whom nothing more foul, more wretched, or more unhappy can be imagined. They also profane their dignity who use indecent or even superstitious clothing. For just as a matron has little regard for decorum when she offers herself for sale in a harlot's dress, so Christians do not esteem the dignity of a Christian man highly when they adorn themselves with garments that are unbecoming to the Christian profession. Yet such are those garments which either serve pride and lust, or are joined with a superstitious persuasion of divine worship. Paul, seeing this, argues so carefully about the habit of the head, which might seem to be of little moment. But if that was thought worthy of rebuke by the Apostle, what shall we say of those who summon up new foreign fashions of clothing every day, or devise new ones themselves, by which the form of the whole body is so changed that they can appear as anything rather than men? This levity has been a sign, in every age, not only of extreme corruption but also of impending ruin. Let the destruction of Jericho be an example to us: among the spoils of the worship there is counted a Babylonian cloak, the Holy Spirit thus censuring the luxury and pride in clothing by which, among other sins, they had sinned. In Roman history Lucullus is recorded, a man otherwise distinguished and well deserving of the republic, who sent two hundred purple cloaks to the praetor, lent for the stage plays. By this example the historians show what the manners of the city of Rome were then, when, enriched by the spoils of very many nations, all people were dissolving in luxury and pride. But soon civil wars followed, which had no end, until affairs came to a monarchy, which for the most part rested in the hands of the most cruel men, who in the end, through their own lust, ruined both themselves and the Roman Empire. And to return to sacred matters: does not the prophet Zephaniah threaten that the Lord will visit all those who clothe themselves in foreign dress? If all these things are compared with the morals of our own age, thoughtful people will easily see what we ought to hope for today, when some measure religion by a strange and monstrous clothing, and others play with such wantonness in the forms of their clothes that they seem to have cast off, along with shame, even common sense. Here Christian princes ought to have interposed their authority, since so many have grown deaf to the preaching of the Word of God. But why need we speak of them, since monsters of this kind issue almost from their courts, as from the Trojan horse?

units.la: Cæterum ad Paulum reuertamur, qui denuo mulieres aggreditur, & aduersus has plura argumenta adducit; eo quod sexus iste (vt nuper monuimus) & procliuior est ad luxum atque fastum, & in eo defendendo contumacior. Olim certè propter legem Oppiam publicè tumultuatum fuit à mulieribus Romanis, adeò vt absq; pudore per forum & omnes vrbis regiones discurrerent, quosuis obuios prehensarent, hoc vnum rogantes, vt ipsis auro & purpura pro suo arbitrio vti, & vehiculis sumptuosis per vrbem vehi liceret. Et qui fœminarum in Græcia mores fuerint, quanta item licentia Corinthi regnauerit, historiæ non vno loco testantur. Recte ergo Paulus singulari studio in causam istam incumbit. Propositio & summa doctrinæ eius est: Mulier potestatem habere debet in capite. Potestatis vocabulo Metonomicè vtitur, per rem signatam signum intelligens. Ita enim dicit Velum capitis, quod subiectionis, vel potestatis viri in mulierem symbolum esse, alibi diximus. Quòd si verò mulieres in ornatu capitis, quæ præstantissima corporis pars est, modestiam & humilitatem profiteri debent, quanto magis in reliquo corporis cultu hoc fieri conuenit? Ideo Isaias Propheta, cùm fui seculi mulierum luxum & mollitiem reprehensurus, à capite exorsus esset, inde per totum corpus ad imos pedes vsq; descendit, & singulorum membrorum ornatum commemorat, quem Deus ab illis ablaturus sit, vt pro musco sit tabes, pro cinctura dissolutio, pro opere calamistri caluitium, pro fascia pectorali saccus, & pro venustate adustio. Arguit autem hic locus indomitam mulierum nostri seculi petulantiam. Iubet Paulus, ut potestatem, cui subsunt, capitis velo tegantur, & ita seipsas ad humilitatem commonefaciant. At hodie vix alia corporis parte magis ad fastum ornantur. Alia enim crispantibus capillorum cincinnis faciem totam ad lenocinium componunt: alia myrtis aut vittis aureis atq; gemmatis capillos includunt: alia pileolis virilibus utuntur, quibus frequenter plumas quoq; addunt, ne quid desit, quod ad testandam animi leuitatem faciat: multae fibiipsis tantum non cornua fingunt, dignae quae fœnū in cornibus illis gestarent, ut proverbio dicitur. Sunt hae omnes Apostolici praecepti parum memores, & dum prae aliis superbiunt, hoc unum inde praemij reportant, quod se à Christiana modestia alienissimas esse testantur, & proinde indignas, quae in Ecclesia locum habeant. Sed audiamus rationes, quibus sententiam suam Paulus probat.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who once more takes up the women and brings several arguments against them, because this sex (as we noted recently) is both more prone to luxury and pride and more stubborn in defending them. Formerly, indeed, on account of the Oppian law, the Roman women rioted openly, so that without shame they ran through the forum and all the districts of the city, accosting whoever they met and asking only this: that they be allowed to use gold and purple as they pleased, and to be carried through the city in costly carriages. And histories in more than one place testify what manners women had in Greece, and how great the licence that reigned at Corinth. Rightly, then, Paul applies himself with special zeal to this cause. The proposition and summary of his teaching is: "A woman ought to have power on her head." He uses the word "power" by metonymy, understanding the sign through the thing signified. For he speaks here of the veil on the head, which we have said elsewhere is a sign of subjection, or of the husband's power over the wife. But if women ought to profess modesty and humility in the adornment of the head, which is the most excellent part of the body, how much more fitting is it that this be done in the rest of their dress? So the prophet Isaiah, when he was about to rebuke the luxury and softness of the women of his age, began at the head and then descended through the whole body to the very feet, recounting the adornment of each member which God would take away from them: instead of perfume there would be rottenness, instead of a girdle, loosening; instead of skilfully curled hair, baldness; instead of a breast-band, sackcloth; and instead of beauty, branding. This passage exposes the unbridled wantonness of the women of our own age. Paul bids them cover with a veil on the head the power to which they are subject, and so remind themselves of humility. Yet today they hardly adorn any other part of the body more for show. Some arrange their whole face for allurement with curled ringlets of hair; others bind their hair with myrtle, or golden fillets and jewelled bands; others wear men's caps, to which they often add feathers too, lest anything be lacking that might attest the lightness of their minds; many shape for themselves almost horns, fit to carry hay on those horns, as the proverb goes. All these women are little mindful of the apostolic precept, and while they vaunt themselves above others, they gain from it only this reward: they prove themselves most alien to Christian modesty, and therefore unworthy to have a place in the Church. But let us hear the reasons by which Paul proves his opinion.

units.la: Prima est, quòd ut vir gloria Dei est, ita mulierem gloriam viri esse dicit. Ratio huius di-sti[?] est, quòd in muliere apparet, quanti virum faciat Deus, quando ei talem vitae omnisque fortunae sociam & tale adiutorium coniungere voluit. Vt enim subditorum opulentia, industria, di-gnitas, maiestatem principis qui in tales imperium habet, maximè commendat: ita viri digni-tas inter ea, quae ad huius vitae vsum spectant, maximè in eo elucet, quòd hanc illi subiecit Deus, quae & ipsa immortalitatis capax est, & olim cœlestis regni hæreditatem possidebit. Id vero in eum finem Paulus adduxit, ut mulieres sui officij memores, re ipsa praestent quod dicuntur, & omnia sua ad illustrandam & prouehendam viri gloriam conferant. Vbi imprimis obedientia opus est, qua sibi ipsis quoque gloriam parant. Vt enim subditorum honor & gloria praecipua est, si magistratui aut principibus suis sese obedientes praebeant: ita mulieris decus summum est viro obsequi eiusque iussis parere. Obedientia coniuncta sit sedulitas & industria in re domestica, cuius cura mulieres imprimis decet, & quae ad augendam mariti gloriam plurimum confert. Ideo Propheta, cum matronam sedulam & fidelem multis commendauisset, tandem infert: Nobilis est in porta maritus eius, dum sedet inter senatores regionis. Exempla, quibus id probari poterat, quotidie multa occurrunt. E contra videmus multos omnibus contemptui esse propter vxorum fastum, petulantiam & negligentem rei domesticae administrationem. Quia vero contemptus ille in illas ipsas redundat, imò ipsis omnium hominum odia parit, & pleriq; tales mulieres extrema detestatione dignas iudicant, foeminas Christianas semper meminisse conuenit, suam gloriam cum viri gloria coniunctam esse, & proinde huic ipsas debere studere.
units.tr: The first is that, as man is the glory of God, so he says woman is the glory of man. The reason for this saying is that in woman appears how highly God values man, since he willed to join to him such a companion for life and for every fortune, and such a helper. For just as the wealth, diligence and dignity of subjects most commend the majesty of a prince who rules over such people, so the dignity of man, among those things that pertain to the use of this life, shines out most in this: that God has made subject to him one who is herself capable of immortality and will one day possess the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. Paul adduced this to the end that women, mindful of their duty, should in deed make good what they are called, and direct all their efforts to illustrating and advancing the husband's glory. Here, above all, obedience is needed, by which they also win glory for themselves. For as the chief honour and glory of subjects is to show themselves obedient to the magistrate or their princes, so a woman's highest grace is to obey her husband and carry out his commands. Let obedience be joined with diligence and industry in household affairs, the care of which especially befits women and which contributes greatly to increasing the husband's glory. So the Prophet, after commending a diligent and faithful matron to many, finally adds: "Her husband is known in the gates, when he sits among the elders of the land." Examples by which this could be proved occur every day in abundance. On the contrary, we see many men held in contempt by everyone because of their wives' pride, wantonness and careless management of the household. But since that contempt rebounds upon the women themselves, and indeed brings them the hatred of all men, and most judge such women worthy of the utmost detestation, Christian women ought always to remember that their glory is joined with the glory of their husband, and therefore they ought to strive to serve it.

units.la: Secundam rationem ex creatione communis omnium nostrum matris, Euae desumit, sic dicens: Non est enim vir ex muliere, sed mulier ex viro: Neque enim conditus est vir propter mulierem, sed mulier propter virum. Quibus verbis ad primam originem mulieres remittit, ut vnde sint, & in quem finem conditae sint, meminerint, & proinde minus superbiant. Simul autem duo argumenta comprehendit, quorum alterum à causa materiali, alterum à finali sumitur. At vtriusque confirmationem facit creationis historiam, quam Moses sic describit: Et dixit Dominus Deus: Non est bonum, ut homo solus sit: faciam illi adiutorium, quod sit coram illo. Et paulò post: Immisit Dominus Deus somnum in Adamum, qui obdormiuit: & tulit vnam ex costis eius, carne eius locum concludens: & aedificauit Dominus Deus costam, quam sumpserat de homine, in mulierem, & adduxit eam ad hominem, &c. Vere igitur in praesenti Paulus dicit, mulierem ex viro originem ducere, & propter virum esse conditam. Atqui communi sensu constat, causam finalem omnibus alijs praestare. Quanto igitur vir mulieri praestabit, qui materiam quoq; ex qua illa formaretur praebuit? Inde vero sequitur, intolerabilem esse insolentiam, si foeminae contra viros efferantur, & subiectionis symbola reijciant.
units.tr: The second reason he takes from the creation of Eve, the mother common to us all, saying: "For man is not of woman, but woman of man; neither was man created for woman, but woman for man." By these words he sends women back to their first origin, that they may remember whence they are and for what end they were made, and so be less proud. At the same time he embraces two arguments, one taken from the material cause and the other from the final cause. He confirms both by the account of creation which Moses describes thus: "And the LORD God said: It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him." And a little later: "The LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept; and he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh instead thereof; and the rib, which the LORD God had taken from the man, made he a woman, and brought her unto the man," etc. Truly, then, Paul here says that woman derives her origin from man and was created for man.
