Yet it is a matter of common sense that the final cause surpasses all the others. How much more, then, will man surpass woman, he who also supplied the material out of which she was formed? From this it follows that it is intolerable insolence if women rise up against men and cast off the signs of subjection.

units.la: At hic obseruemus, ista de toto sexu dici, & proinde ad virgines quoq; & viduas debere extendi. Nam etsi hae viros proprios non habeant, quibus coniugalia officia praestent, viros tamen omnes propter sexus eminentiam reuereri, & modestè atque humiliter cum illis versari debent, neq; ea ntq;[?] ea illis negare officia, quae saluo pudore praestari possunt. Talem virginem olim Rebeccam fuisse legimus, & eas viduas Paulus commendat, quae hospitales sint, quae item sanctorum pedes ab luant, & afflictis subueniant. Hodie à multis peccatur, quâ non alium suae virginitatis aut coeli-batus finem sibi propositum habent, quàm ut liberius, imò licentius & petulantius viuant, virosq; simul & iuuenes omnes ludibrio habeant. Quod autem mulieres suae originis atq; finis Apostolus ad monet, hoc ipsum omnes homines ad se debent transferre, ut nunquam nō cogitent, quae ipsorum origo aut pristina vitae conditio fuerit, & ad quid nunc à Deo destinati sint. Haec meditatio Dauidem posse amplissimas victorias inter opes & delitias regni in officio continuit: quod nimirum cogitaret, se ex opilione ad fastigium illud euectum esse, non ut sibi viueret aut genio suo indulgeret, sed ut populum Domini pasceret. Quod si idem semper animo voluant qui vel in repub. vel Ecclesia praesunt, mox videbunt, sibi nihil otij concessum esse, multò minus autem licere, ut populi simplicitate abutantur, cùm ipsi propter populum, non hic propter ipsos, ordinati sint.
units.tr: But here let us observe that these things are said of the whole sex, and therefore ought to be extended to virgins and widows too. For although these have no husbands of their own to whom they owe the duties of marriage, yet on account of the eminence of their sex they ought to revere all men, deal with them modestly and humbly, and not deny them those services which can be rendered without loss of modesty. We read that Rebecca was such a virgin once, and Paul commends those widows who are hospitable, who likewise wash the feet of the saints and help the afflicted. Today many sin in this, since they have no other aim set before them in their virginity or celibacy than to live more freely, indeed more licentiously and wantonly, and to make a mockery of men and young men alike. But what the Apostle admonishes women about their origin and end, all men too ought to apply to themselves: they should never cease to consider what their own origin or former condition of life was, and for what purpose they are now destined by God. This meditation kept David, amid the wealth and delights of the kingdom and amid his most ample victories, in his duty; for he considered that he had been raised from a shepherd to that height not so that he might live for himself or indulge his own inclinations, but that he might feed the people of the Lord. If those who preside either in the commonwealth or in the Church would always turn this over in their minds, they would soon see that no leisure is granted to them, and much less is it lawful for them to take advantage of the simplicity of the people, since they themselves are appointed for the sake of the people, not the people for their own sake.

units.la: Tertiae rationis loco Angelos adducit Paulus, propter quos mulier caput velare debeat. Quem locum alij aliter exponunt: ego simpliciter de bonis Angelis hoc dici sentio, quos Ecclesiae praesides aut tutores à Deo datos esse, ex Daniele constat, & quos singulis piorum adesse, scriptura non vno loco testatur. Notum enim est quod in Psalmis dicitur: Castrametatur Angelus Domini circa eos, qui ipsum timent, & eripit eos. Item Angelis suis praecipiet de te, ut in omnibus viis tuis te custodiant: Manibus suis gestabunt te, ne ad lapidem pes tuus offendat. Quibus adde illud Apostoli, qui de Angelis dicit: Nonne omnes sunt ministratores spiritus, qui ministerij causa mittuntur pro pter eos, qui haeredes erunt salutis? Consentit hîs omnibus quod Christus de paruulis in Euangelio pronuntiat: Angeli eorum in coelis semper vident faciem Patris mei, qui in coelis est. Sunt haec testimonia non clara modo, sed infinitis exemplis confirmata, quae cùm alibi commemorauerimus, hîc breuitatis studio omittimus. Meminit autem istorum Paulus, ut eas fortius compescat, quae sibi nihil non licere putant, neq; rationes facilè admittunt. Perinde enim hoc est, ac si diceret: Si quam non mouet suae creationis consideratio & hominum respectus, saltem Angelos vereatur, & pudeat hos suae petulantiae testes facere, qui piorum coetibus interfuunt, & qui ut ordine & decoro gaudent, ita confusione & inhonestis rebus offenduntur.
units.tr: In the third reason Paul adduces the angels, on whose account a woman ought to cover her head. Other writers explain this place differently, but I simply take it that this is said of the good angels. From Daniel it is clear that they were given by God as guardians or overseers of the Church, and Scripture testifies in more than one place that they are present with each of the faithful. For it is well known what is said in the Psalms: "The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them." Likewise: "He will give his angels charge over you, to keep you in all your ways. They shall bear you up in their hands, lest you dash your foot against a stone." Add to these the Apostle's words about the angels: "Are they not all ministering spirits, sent to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?" What Christ says of little children in the Gospel agrees with all of these: "Their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven." These testimonies are not only clear but confirmed by countless examples, which, since I have mentioned them elsewhere, I omit here for the sake of brevity. Paul mentions them so that he may more forcefully restrain those who think they may do anything at all and are not easily moved by reasons. It is as if he said: "If the consideration of your creation and regard for other people do not move you, at least let the angels make you fear, and let it shame you to make them witnesses of your wantonness, since they attend the assemblies of the godly, and as they delight in order and decency, so they are offended by disorder and dishonourable conduct."

units.la: Rursus autem hoc loco consideranda nobis venit hominis dignitas, cuius praeclarum & illustre argumentum est, quod Angelos suos nobis Deus custodes atque ministros dedit: quasi parum esset, quod hominem creaturarum, quae in terris sunt, omnium principem constituit. Soletur hoc nos in omni periculorum genere. Nullum enim tam graue est, quod non facile unicus aliquis Angelus, si ita velit Deus, propulsare possit. Simul autem istorum meditatione vtamur, ut Apostolus monet: Ut nimirum honestati & sanctitati studeamus in omnibus, ne nos nostra petulantia tam sancto, tamq; necessario Angelorum praesidio spoliemus. Nam hoc sublato, quid reliquum est, quàm ut communis hostis diaboli insidijs expositi animâ & corpore perdamur? Poterat feria huius rei consideratio nos à multis absterrere, ad quae praecipites ferimur: sed ea est multorum stupiditas, ut derebus maximè necessarijs nunquam cogitent, & ideo in ipsius Christi & Angelorum eius conspectu impudenter designent, quorum eos coram hominibus vel minima authoritate praeditis, imò vilissimis quoq; puderet.
units.tr: Here again the dignity of man comes before us, of which a splendid and illustrious proof is that God has given us his angels as guardians and ministers. It is as if it were not enough that he has made man the chief of the creatures that are on earth. This should comfort us in every kind of danger. For there is no danger so grave that a single angel, if God so wills, cannot easily repel it. At the same time let us make use of the meditation on them, as the Apostle advises, so that we may indeed strive for honesty and holiness in all things, and not by our wantonness deprive ourselves of so holy and so necessary a protection of the angels. For if this is taken away, what remains but that we, exposed to the snares of the common enemy the devil, should perish in soul and body? The consideration of this matter could have turned us away from many things to which we are rushing headlong. But such is the stupidity of many that they never think about the most necessary matters, and so they shamelessly do in the sight of Christ and his angels what would shame them to do before men of even the least authority, or indeed before the most worthless of men.

units.la: At non ignorabat Paulus, esse nonnullos, qui quacunq; in hanc sententiam dicuntur, insolentius in mulieb-ris sexus contemptum rapere solent, mulieres quoque nonnullas his ita deiici, ut se Deo minus curae esse arbitrentur, qui proximus ad impatientiam & desperationem gradus est. Ideo per digressiunculam interserit admonitionem, qua & viros ferociores reprimit, & mulieres infirmiores consolatur. Veruntamen (inquit) neq; vir absq; muliere, neq; mulier absq; viro in Domino: Sicut enim mulier ex viro est, ita & vir per mulierem: omnia vero ex Deo. Quorum verborum hic sensus est. Quàmuis haec ita se habeant, ut hactenus dixi, non tamen idcirco viri feroces efferri debent, & mulieribus ceu vilissimis mancipijs abuti, quasi non in alium finem conditae sint, quàm ut ipsorum libidini seruiant. Nam olim quidem in primorum parentum creatione hoc factum, ut mulier ex viro desumpta atq; formata sit: at nunc si Domini institutum respiciamus, neque vir absque muliere, neque haec sine viro consistit. Imò ut mulier ex viro primam originem duxit:sic vicissim vir per mulierem generatur: omnium vero author Deus est, qui & viros & feminas creat, & utrisque suum officium praescripsit. Est argumentum hoc eius simile, quo hodie fere utimur aduersus insolentes & scurriles muliebris sexus contemptores atque osores, quando eos interrogamus: Annon ipsorum quoque mater foemina fuerit? Quamuis quod hic dicitur, neq; virum absq; muliere, neque hanc absq; illo esse in Domino, ad redemptionem per Christum factam referri possit. Quia enim in totius generis humani seruator est, viri autem huius dimidia tantummodo pars sunt, nequaquam a Christo excludi debent mulieres, ex quibus ipse homo natus est, & quas (ut alibi monuimus) sibi familiarissimas habere dignatus est, ut non solum miraculorum, verumetiam mortis & resurrectionis suae testes essent. Quam ergo indigna & inexcusabilis petulantia est, eas aspernari & insectari scurrilius, quas pro sororibus in Christo agnoscas oportet, siquidem ipse per illum seruari vult? Interim admonet nos locus iste, tam virorum quam mulierum esse, ut ad Dei institutum respiciant, & secundum hoc utrinq; fortem suam sedulo tueatur. Occurrit hic primum, quod neq; vir absq; muliere, neq; haec absq; illo consistit. Vterq; ergo sexus alterius opera & auxilio indiget. Id vero non debet malum necessarium dici (ut quidam ex gentium sapientibus olim senserunt) sed singulare Dei beneficium agnoscatur, qui ut humano generi & communi paci consuleret, viros & mulieres ita erga se inuicem obstringi voluit. Ex hoc ergo alterum sequitur, quod ut vnius eiusdemq; corporis membra utrinque officij sui meminisse debent, sic ut vir quidem capitis officium fideliter praestet, mulier vero instar corporis hunc obseruet, colat & adiuuet sedulo. Utrinque autem fide & charitate temperent molestias, quas coniugium secum trahit. Sed de his alibi plura diximus.
units.tr: But Paul was not unaware that there are some who, whatever is said to this effect, are accustomed to turn it more insolently into contempt for the female sex, and that some women too are so cast down by such talk that they think God cares little for them, which is the step nearest to impatience and despair. Therefore, in a brief digression, he inserts a warning by which he both restrains the fiercer men and comforts the weaker women. "Nevertheless," he says, "neither is the man without the woman, nor the woman without the man, in the Lord. For as the woman is from the man, so also the man is through the woman; but all things are from God." The sense of these words is this: although things stand as I have said so far, men must not on that account become proud and abuse women as the most worthless slaves, as if they had been made for no other purpose than to serve their lust. For indeed, in the creation of our first parents, it was done this way, that the woman was taken from the man and formed from him. But now, if we consider the Lord's institution, neither does the man exist without the woman, nor the woman without the man. Indeed, just as the woman drew her first origin from the man, so in turn the man is born through the woman; but the author of all is God, who creates both men and women, and has prescribed to each their duty. This argument is similar to one we use today against insolent and scurrilous despisers and haters of the female sex, when we ask them: "Was not your own mother a woman?" Although what is said here, that neither is the man without the woman nor the woman without the man in the Lord, can also be referred to the redemption made through Christ. For since he is the Saviour of the whole human race, and men are only half of it, women must by no means be excluded from Christ, from whom he himself was born as man, and whom (as I have noted elsewhere) he deigned to have as his most intimate companions, so that they might be witnesses not only of his miracles but also of his death and resurrection. How unworthy and inexcusable, then, is the wantonness of despising and harassing with scurrilous talk those whom you ought to acknowledge as sisters in Christ, since he himself wishes to be saved through them? Meanwhile this passage admonishes us that men and women alike should look to God's institution and, according to it, each carefully maintain their own strength. First it occurs that neither the man is without the woman, nor the woman without the man. Both sexes therefore need the work and help of the other. This ought not to be called a necessary evil (as some of the wise men of the Gentiles once thought), but recognised as a singular benefit of God, who, to provide for the human race and common peace, willed that men and women be bound to one another in this way. From this, then, another consequence follows: just as the members of one and the same body ought each to remember their duty, so the man should faithfully perform the office of the head, while the woman, like the body, should observe, cherish and diligently help him. And on both sides, let faith and love temper the troubles that marriage brings with it. But I have said more about these things elsewhere.

units.la: Caeterum quia Corinthiorum licentia eo usq; excreuerat, ut Paulus sibi ipsi satisfacere non pos-sit, post digressiunculam istam ad institutum redit, & ad naturam magistram eos remittit, qui rationes ex Verbo Dei petitas hucusq; noluerant obseruare. Et quod solent qui causam optimam sustinent, illos ipsos iudices facit, dicens: Apud vosipsos iudicate, num decorum sit, mulierem non velatam Deum orare? Annon natura ipsa hoc vos docet, quod viro quidem comatum esse dedecori sit: contra mulieri comatam esse gloriae sit? Nam coma pro velamine data est ei. Quo loco comatos dicere videtur eos, qui in nutrienda coma sunt delicatiores. Alioqui apud Graecos comam gestare per se dedecori non erat. Homerus enim Achiuos frequenter καρηκομόωντας, id est, capite comatos dicit. Et notum est Lycurgi institutum, qui ne Spartani comam deponerent prohibuit: quod illa formosis quidem maiorem gratiam addat, deformes autem terribiliores reddat. Apud Romanos autem tondendi mos sero demum admissus est, quando teste Plutarcho tonsores anno demum ab urbe condita CCCCLIIII. ex Sicilia P. Ticinius Mena adduxit. Meo igitur iudicio locus hic de molliculis intelligi debet, quos veteri proverbio notatos fuisse legimus: Vnico digitulo scalpit caput. Hos autem ab ipsa natura damnari Paulus non temere pronuntiat. Quid enim minus virile est, quam re fluxa & inani, imo corporis excrementis superbire, quae si quid strenuum & arduum agere oporteat, plus incomodi quam commodi affert? Quis enim Absolomum nescit, cui ad miraculi usq; enutrita caesaries tandem laquei loco fuit, ex quo suspensus miserè periit? Alia autem mulierum ratio est, quas natura pluribus & longioribus capillis exornauit, idq; non sine causa. Nam coma (inquit Paulus) mulieri pro velamine data est. Ista vero ad illius institutum probè faciunt. Si enim viro non licet naturali coma superbire, multo minus peregrina & superba capitis ornamenta aliunde accersere debet. Rursus cum Deus comam mulieri pro velamine dederit, eo ipso satis aperte illam admonere voluit, eam minimè decere, ut nudo & aperto capite sese ostentet, sed potius ut subiectionis memor, Dei instituto sese accommodet.
units.tr: Moreover, since the licence of the Corinthians had grown so far that Paul could not satisfy himself, after this brief digression he returns to his subject, and he refers to nature as the teacher those who had hitherto refused to observe reasons drawn from the Word of God. And, as those who defend an excellent cause are accustomed to do, he makes them the judges themselves, saying: "Judge for yourselves: is it fitting that a woman pray to God uncovered? Does not nature itself teach you that for a man to wear long hair is a disgrace, but for a woman to wear long hair is her glory? For her hair is given to her as a covering." By the phrase "long-haired" he seems to mean those who are more effeminate in growing their hair. Otherwise, among the Greeks, to wear long hair was not in itself a disgrace. For Homer frequently calls the Achaeans karēkomōntas [καρηκομόωντας], that is, long-haired. And the institution of Lycurgus is well known, who forbade the Spartans to cut their hair; it adds greater grace to the beautiful, and makes the ugly more terrifying. Among the Romans, however, the custom of shaving was admitted only late, when, according to Plutarch, barbers were first brought from Sicily by P. Ticinius Mena in the four hundred and fifty-fourth year from the founding of the city. In my judgment, therefore, this place should be understood of the effeminate, whom we read were marked by the old proverb: "He scratches his head with one little finger." Paul does not rashly pronounce that these are condemned by nature itself. For what is less manly than to pride oneself on a flimsy and empty thing, indeed on a mere excrescence of the body, which, if one must do something vigorous and arduous, brings more inconvenience than advantage? For who does not know Absalom, whose hair, nurtured to a marvel, became at last a noose for him, from which he hung and perished miserably? Women, however, are another case: nature has adorned them with more and longer hair, and not without reason. For hair (says Paul) is given to a woman as a covering. These things fit well with his teaching. For if a man may not pride himself on his natural hair, much less should he bring in foreign and showy ornaments for the head from elsewhere. Again, since God has given hair to a woman as a covering, by that very fact he wished to admonish her quite plainly that it does not become her to display herself with a bare and uncovered head, but rather, mindful of subjection, to conform herself to God's institution.

units.la: In genere autem admonemur, quam parum excusationis habeant, qui aliquid praeter officium faciunt. Quod enim in praesenti causa Paulus dicit, hoc in multis aliis est videre. Annô natura per corporis nostri formam eos arguit & accusat, qui terrenis modo studijs immersi diuina & coelestia negligunt? Potuit hoc Ouidius obseruare, qui hominem cum aliis animantibus conferens ait:
units.tr: In general we are warned how little excuse those have who do anything beyond their duty. What Paul says in the present matter can be seen in many other cases. Does not nature itself, through the form of our body, reproach and accuse those who, immersed only in earthly pursuits, neglect things divine and heavenly? Ovid could observe this, when comparing man with the other living creatures, he says:

units.la: Pronaque cum spectent animalia cætera terram, Os homini sublime dedit cœlumque tueri Iußit, & erectos ad sidera tollere vultus, &c. Similiter annon apes & formicæ ignauos accusant, qui in otio torpent, deinde vero circa aliorum opes tumultuantur? Adde, quòd natura duce omnes eos peccati pudet, qui non hominem prorsus exerunt. Senserunt pudorem hunc primi parentes, & hodie intra semetipsos eo suffunduntur scelera-tissimi quiq; imò hæc illis causa est, quòd Euangelij lucem oderunt, quia (vt Christus ait) operæ sua prava nolunt argui. Quæ ergo excusatio illis reliqua est, si ea nihilominus designant, quorum ipsos pudet, & de quibus à propria conscientia accusantur? Quòd si ad præsentem causam accedat, nonne natura nos admonet, ne vestitu immodico & luxuriosò superbiamus? Quem enim facinoro-sum dabis, quem vinculorum suorum non pudeat? At quid aliud sunt vestes, quibus tunc demum primos parentes quasi vinctos & inuolutos fuisse scimus, postquam peccati sui conscios suæ nuditatis puderet, cùm prius ipsis propria innocentia aduersus omnem ignominiæ metum sufficeret? Quæ ergo dementia est in illis gloriam & honorem quærere, quæ nos nostræ vitiositatis & pœna-rum, quas meruimus, admonere debebant? Rursus, & quod nam in rerum natura est animal, quod sui corporis formam mutatam velit? Simia certè, qua nullum animal est deformius, nihil huius conatur, imò sua illa forma, vt præstantissima delectari solet. Quis ergo sanæ mentis dicat eos homines, qui vestitu peregrino & petulanti formam corporis nouam sibi accersunt, & monstra potiùs quàm homines videri malunt? Possent huius generis multa adduci, sed sufficiat occasionem dedis-seijs[?], qui salutis curam non omnem abiecerunt.
units.tr: "While the other animals look down upon the earth, he gave man a face raised up, and bade him look at the heavens, and lift his upright countenance to the stars, etc." Likewise, do not bees and ants condemn the idle who grow sluggish in leisure, and then bustle about the wealth of others? Add that, under nature's guidance, all those are ashamed of their sin who do not fully bring forth the man. Our first parents felt this shame, and today the most wicked are suffused with it within themselves; indeed this is the reason they hate the light of the Gospel, because (as Christ says) they do not want their wicked works to be reproved. What excuse, then, is left to them, if they nonetheless display those things of which they are ashamed and for which their own conscience accuses them? But if we come to the present matter, does not nature warn us not to take pride in immodest and luxurious clothing? For who would call a criminal happy, one who is not ashamed of his chains? Yet what else are clothes, by which we know our first parents were then, as it were, bound and wrapped, after they, aware of their sin, were ashamed of their nakedness, when before their own innocence had sufficed for them against all fear of disgrace? What madness, then, is it to seek glory and honour in those things which ought to remind us of our faults and of the punishments we have deserved? Again, what animal in nature wishes its bodily form changed? The ape, certainly, than which no animal is more misshapen, attempts nothing of this kind, but rather delights in its own form, as is customary for the most excellent creatures. Who, then, of sound mind would say that those men are sane who, by foreign and wanton dress, procure a new form for their bodies, and prefer to appear as monsters rather than as men? Many examples of this kind could be brought forward, but let it suffice to have given occasion to those who have not wholly abandoned concern for their salvation.

units.la: Nunc cū Paulo vela colligamus, qui brevi & gravi sententia eos coërcet, quos sciebat in vrbe opulenta & voluptatibus deditā non facilè adduci posse, vt mores longa consuetudine inveteratos mutarent, aut petulantiæ suæ modum præscribi paterentur. Sic autem dicit: Quòd si quis videtur contentiosus esse, nos eiusmodi consuetudinem non habemus, neq; Ecclesiæ Dei. In Græco φιλόνεικος habetur, quæ vox litium & contentionum amantem seu cupidum significat. Sunt tales, qui contradicendi studio delectantur, neq; tacere possunt, etiamsi rationibus & testimonijs idoneis sese destituti videant. Effecta huius vitij sunt, quòd novitati studeant, ritus receptos & bonos absq; causa è medio sublatos volunt, in quæstionem quoq; vocant quæ per se minimè ambigua sunt, deniq; ceu Acte quædam pomum contentionis per omnes ecclesias circumferunt. Si qui inter vos (inquit Apostolus) sunt tales, quibus non sufficiunt rationes ex Dei instituto, ex communi sensu & naturæ legibus pro dubio, cum illis porrò contendere non libet: sed hoc unum eis respondemus, neq; nos Apostolos, neque Ecclesias hanc consuetudinem habere, vt cum rixatoribus contentionis restim ducamus, & omissis ijs quæ ad Ecclesiæ ædificationem faciunt, circa lites inutiles & nunquam finiendas occupemur. At hæc dicendo simul docet, eiusmodi homines indignos esse, quibus respondeatur. Nos ergo Pauli exemplo discamus, quid hodie agendum, quando eiusmodi rixatorum plena sunt, omnia, quibus nihil arridet quod veteris Ecclesiæ simplicitatem respipit, sed suis argutijs omnia inuoluunt & obscurant. Urgeantur tales Verbi Dei authoritate & firmis rationibus, vt intra animos suos convincantur. Quòd si cedere nolunt, reliquantur Domini iudicio, ne cum ipsis litigando occasionem meliora agendi negligamus. Nihil etenim apud illos proficias, qui Marcelli similes ceteri possunt, de quo Hannibal dicebat, sibi cum eo hoste rem esse, qui neq; vincor neq; vincus quiescere posset. Imò verè stulti illi sunt, quorum similes fiunt (vt Solomon inquit) qui ipsis secundum stultitiam eorum respondent. Hoc si nostro seculo in multis controuersijs esset observatum, minus esset scandalorum in Ecclesia. Cæterum quoad Pauli institutum, discant Christiani homines honestati studere, & superstitionis omnem speciem fugere. Quod vt semper fieri debet, ita maximè in sacris cœtibus. In his manus puras & castas attollere convenit, & ita nos gerere, vt digni censeamur, quos Pater ille cœlestis exaudiat propter nomen Filij sui unigeniti, IESU CHRISTI, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Now, with Paul, let us furl our sails, who, in a brief and weighty sentence, restrains those whom he knew, in a wealthy city given over to pleasures, could not easily be brought to change customs long ingrained by habit, or to allow the limits of their wantonness to be prescribed. He speaks thus: "But if anyone seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God." In the Greek it is philoneikos [φιλόνεικος], a word signifying one who loves or is eager for quarrels and disputes. There are such people who delight in the zeal for contradicting, and cannot keep silent even when they see themselves lacking adequate reasons and testimonies. Marks of this vice are that they pursue novelty, want received and good rites removed without cause, call into question matters that are in themselves by no means doubtful, and finally, like Acte, carry the apple of discord through all the churches. "If there are any among you," says the Apostle, "who are such that reasons drawn from God's institution, from common sense and the laws of nature, do not suffice for them, and who think the matter doubtful, it is not our pleasure to contend further with them; but to them we give this one answer: neither we Apostles nor the Churches have this custom, of dragging brawlers of contention on a rope, and, neglecting those things which serve the building up of the Church, of occupying ourselves with useless and never-ending quarrels." But in saying this he also teaches that such men are unworthy to be answered. Let us therefore learn from Paul's example what must be done today, when all things are full of such brawlers, to whom nothing pleases that looks back to the simplicity of the ancient Church, but who wrap and obscure everything with their subtleties. Let such men be pressed with the authority of the Word of God and with firm reasons, so that they may be convinced within their own minds. But if they refuse to yield, let them be left to the Lord's judgment, lest by quarrelling with them we neglect the opportunity of doing better things. For you will achieve nothing with those who can be like Marcellus, of whom Hannibal used to say that he had to do with an enemy who could neither be conquered nor rest from conquering. Indeed, those are truly foolish whose likeness men become, as Solomon says, when they answer them according to their folly. If this had been observed in many controversies in our age, there would be less scandal in the Church. But as for Paul's purpose, let Christians learn to pursue honesty and to flee every appearance of superstition. This ought always to be done, but most of all in sacred assemblies. In these it is fitting to lift up pure and chaste hands, and so to conduct ourselves that we may be deemed worthy to be heard by that heavenly Father for the sake of his only-begotten Son, JESUS CHRIST, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY LVIII.

units.la: Hoc vero denuntians non laudo, quòd non in melius, sed in deterius convenitis. Primùm enim cùm convenitis in Ecclesia, audio dissidia inter vos esse; & aliquam partem credo. Oportet enim etiā hæreses inter vos esse, ut qui probati sunt, manifesti fiant inter vos. Itaque cùm conuenitis in unum, hoc non est Dominicam Coenam edere: Nam unusquisque propriam coenam præoccupat in edendo: & hic quidem esurit, ille vero ebrius est. Enimuero num domos non habetis ad edendum? aut Ecclesiam Dei contemnitis, & pudefacitis eos qui non habent? Quid vobis dicam? Laudabo vos? In hoc non laudo.
units.tr: But in announcing this, I do not praise you, because you come together not for the better but for the worse. For first, when you come together in the Church, I hear that there are divisions among you, and I partly believe it. For there must be factions among you as well, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you. So when you come together as one, it is not to eat the Lord's Supper, for each of you goes ahead and eats his own supper: one goes hungry while another is drunk. Do you not have houses in which to eat? Or do you despise the Church of God and shame those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise you.

units.la: Prima huius Capitis parte cum illis egit Apostolus, qui in cœtibus sacris habitu à Christiana professione alieno utebantur, & multis argumentis docuit, quid hic tam viros quàm mulieres deceat. Nunc ad aliud transit, quod grauioris momenti erat: Nimirum ad Coenam IESV CHRISTI mysticam, in qua non minus luxu & fastu peccabant, & eò usq; progressi erant, ut quod faciebant, non amplius Coena Dominica dici mereretur. Opus ergo erat diligenti & acriori medicina, quam hoc ordine adhibet. Primò vitium aut abusum Coenæ, quem inuexerant, arguit & grauiter accusat. Deinde primam Coenæ institutionem exponit, & ad huius formulam eos reuocat. Postremò monet, quid singuli facere debeant, ut hoc sacro epulo digne & cum fructu fruantur. Est autem in tota hac tractatione nobis obseruanda diaboli improbitas, qui huic Sacramento tam citò insidiatus est, & verum eius usum peruertere ac abolere studuit. Vidit enim eo gratam & cum fide coniunctam mortis Christi commemorationem contineri: quæ & fidem nostram confirmat, & nos in officio continet, ne vel Christo neglecto post superstitiones exorbitemus, vel subil-lius velamine & prætextu licentiæ carnis indulgeamus. Quapropter viuentibus adhuc Apostolis, oculatis Christi testibus, hoc conari ausus est: & quàmuis Paulus hoc Cap. Corinthios, & cum his omnes Christianos ad primam Coenæ institutionem reuocet, & huic quasi astrictos esse velit, non tamen tanta fuit apud posteros eius authoritas, quò minus multa zelo quidem pio & bono, inconsul-to tamen, facta sint, quæ tandem superstitiones nocentissimas pepererunt. Romanis certè Episcopis hunc morem fuisse Irenæus apud Eusebium testatur, ut Episcopis aliarum Ecclesiarum Romam venientibus Eucharistiam, ceu pacis & consensionis symbolum, solenniter transmitterent. Tertullianus verò in libro de Monogamia mulierculas Eucharistiæ reliquias in cistis asseruare solitas fuisse scribit: cuius rei Cyprianus quoq; meminit: Hesychius autem in Leuitico, illas à quibusdam exustas fuisse, Nicephorus verò Constantinopoli à pueris è ludo euocatis consumptas tradit. Hieronymus author est, aliquos voluisse, ut in nuptijs illa in ædes priuatas deferretur, nimirum ut illas auspicationes faceret. Ambrosius item fratrem suum Satyrum inter nauigandum Eucharistiam ex collo gestauisse narrat. Cypriani verò temporibus eadem infantibus quoq; data est: quod Caroli Magni temporibus adhuc aliquibus in locis obseruatum esse legitur. Quid, quod aliqui mortuos baptizarunt, & Eucharistiam ijsdem in os dederunt? qui mos in Concilio Carthaginensi abrogatus est. Fuerunt item, qui ut se à crimine obiecto purgarent & suam testarentur innocentiam, Eucharistiam cum solenni protestatione sumebant. Instituti quoq; (ut alibi monuimus) presbyteri pœnitentiarij, qui ad Coenam Domini accessuros probarent. At quid horum Christus docuit, cùm illam in suæ mortis commemorationem institueret? Aut quid huius tradiderunt Apostoli? Fuerunt ergo hæc præludia superstitionis maioris & idololatriæ, quæ tandem secuta est, quando Eucharistiam in ædiculis sacris adseruare, adorare, in processionibus circumferre, festo in eius honorem instituto colere Innocentius III. & Honorius III. atq; Urbanus IIII. Pontifices mandarunt. Hæc ideo commemoramus, ne cui mirum videatur, posteris temporibus horribilem illam Coenæ prophanationem introductam fuisse, quæ totum Christi meritum euertit: neue offendamur, si etiam hodie inter eos, qui Euangelij doctrinam profitentur, multi contentionum & implacabilium inimicitiarum materiam arripiunt ex illa, quæ concordiæ & unitatis Christianæ vinculum esse debebat? Excitemur potius horum consideratione, ut diligentes simus in retinenda apostolica doctrina, quæ nobis hodie non minus, quàm olim, necessaria est. In præsenti primam huius tractationis partem videbimus, in qua primum in genere Corinthios Paulus accusat: deinde ad species defendit, & quibus vitijs Coenam polluant, docet: tandem acerrime in illos inuehitur. Quoad primum, hoc in illis reprehendit, quòd cœtus ecclesiasticos, absque fructu agant, nec ad eum finem dirigant, propter quem sunt instituti. Vtitur autem graui praefatiuncula, quam huius Capitis initio opponit: Hoc vero denuntians non laudo, &c. Quasi diceret: Laudaui quidem vos, quòd traditiones meas in reliquis obseruetis, at quod nunc vobis denuntiaturus sum, id eiusmodi est, vt laudare nullo modo possim. Quid vero illud est? Quòd non in melius, sed in deterius conuenitis: vel quòd non cum emolumento, sed cum detrimento conuenitis, id est, quòd cœtus vestros ita agitis, vt non proficiatis in vera pietate (quod vnicè erat spectandum) sed potius ex illis redditis deteriores. Quo loco ante omnia obseruabimus, non statim omnino irreprehensibiles & in omnibus perfectos esse, qui in aliquibus à Spiritu sancto commendantur. Laudauit super Corinthios Paulus, & merito quidem, quòd ab ipso traditam doctrinae formam retinerent: at eosdem nunc acriter reprehendit, & vituperio dignos esse docet, quòd in re maximi momenti scopum, qui omnibus Christianis propositus esse debet, non respicerent. Ita non vno loco Israelitæ laudantur, et hos Deus modò suum filium primogenitum, suum peculium, suum regnum sacerdotale dicit: ijdē vero alibi filij defectores & degeneres, populus Gomorrhæus, & Chananæorum Amorrhæorum-que similes dicuntur. Quod ipsum de Dauide dicere possumus, quem alibi Deus virum esse testatur secundum cor suum: sed idem postea in adulterium lapsus grauem correptionem meruit.
units.tr: In the first part of this chapter the Apostle dealt with those who, in the sacred assemblies, wore dress foreign to the Christian profession, and he taught by many arguments what is fitting for men and women alike in this matter. Now he turns to another matter, of greater weight: namely the mystical Supper of Jesus Christ, in which they were sinning no less through luxury and pride, and had advanced so far that what they were doing no longer deserved to be called the Lord's Supper. A careful and sharper remedy was therefore needed, and he applies it in this order. First he points out and sharply accuses the fault or abuse of the Supper that they had introduced. Then he sets out the original institution of the Supper and recalls them to its pattern. Lastly he advises what each individual ought to do so that they may partake of this sacred feast worthily and with profit. In this whole discussion we must also observe the wickedness of the devil, who so quickly laid snares for this sacrament and strove to pervert and abolish its true use. For he saw that it contained a grateful remembrance of Christ's death, joined with faith; this both confirms our faith and keeps us in our duty, lest, neglecting Christ, we stray again into superstitions, or indulge the flesh under the cover and pretext of liberty. Therefore, while the Apostles were still living, the eyewitnesses of Christ, he dared to attempt this; and although Paul recalls the Corinthians, and with them all Christians, to the original institution of the Supper, and wishes them to be bound to it, nevertheless his authority was not so great among later generations that many things were not done, by a pious and good zeal indeed but without due deliberation, which in the end gave birth to most harmful superstitions. Irenaeus, as reported by Eusebius, testifies that it was certainly the custom of the Roman bishops that, when bishops of other churches came to Rome, they would solemnly send them the Eucharist as a symbol of peace and agreement. Tertullian, however, in his book on monogamy, writes that little women were accustomed to keep remnants of the Eucharist in boxes; Cyprian also mentions this matter. Hesychius, on Leviticus, reports that some of these remnants were burned, and Nicephorus relates that at Constantinople they were consumed by boys called away from school. Jerome is the authority that some wished it to be carried into private houses at weddings, namely to make it a omen of good fortune. Ambrose likewise relates that his brother Satyrus, while sailing, wore the Eucharist around his neck. In the time of Cyprian the same was also given to infants, which is read to have been observed in some places even in the time of Charlemagne. What of the fact that some baptized the dead and placed the Eucharist in their mouths? This custom was abrogated by the Council of Carthage. There were also some who, to purge themselves of an alleged crime and to testify to their innocence, took the Eucharist with a solemn protestation. Penitentiary elders were also appointed (as we have noted elsewhere), who would test those who were about to approach the Lord's Supper. But what of these things did Christ teach when he instituted it in remembrance of his death? Or what did the Apostles hand down about them? These things were therefore the prelude to a greater superstition and idolatry, which in the end followed, when Innocent III, Honorius III and Urban IV commanded that the Eucharist be reserved in sacred shrines, adored, carried about in processions, and honored by a feast instituted in its honor. We recall these things so that no one should think it strange that in later times that dreadful profanation of the Supper was introduced, which overturns the whole merit of Christ; and so that we are not offended if even today, among those who profess the doctrine of the Gospel, many seize upon the very thing that ought to be the bond of Christian concord and unity as the material of quarrels and implacable enmities. Rather, let us be stirred by considering these things to be diligent in retaining apostolic doctrine, which is no less necessary for us today than it was of old. In the present discussion we shall see the first part of this treatment, in which Paul first accuses the Corinthians in general; then he defends them against particular charges and teaches with what faults they pollute the Supper; and finally he inveighs most sharply against them. As to the first, he rebukes them in this, that they hold ecclesiastical assemblies without profit, and do not direct them to the end for which they were instituted. He uses a weighty little preface, which he places at the beginning of this chapter: "But in announcing this, I do not praise you," and so on. As if he said: I did praise you indeed, because you keep my traditions in the other matters; but what I am now about to announce to you is of such a kind that I can by no means praise it. What is it, then? That you come together not for the better but for the worse; or, that you do not come together with advantage but with harm, that is, that you conduct your assemblies in such a way that you do not advance in true piety (which alone ought to have been the aim), but rather come away from them worse. At this point we must first observe that those who are commended by the Holy Spirit in some matters are not at once wholly blameless and perfect in everything. Paul praised the Corinthians, and rightly so, because they kept the form of doctrine handed down by him; but now he sharply rebukes the same people and teaches that they deserve blame, because in a matter of the greatest importance they did not regard the goal that should be set before all Christians. So in more than one place the Israelites are praised, and God calls them now his firstborn son, his peculiar people, his kingdom of priests; yet elsewhere they are called faithless and degenerate sons, a people like Gomorrah, and like the Canaanites and Amorites. The same we may say of David, whom God elsewhere testifies to be a man after his own heart; yet the same man, after he fell into adultery, earned a severe rebuke.

units.la: Seruiunt hæc nobis aduersus Romanenses, qui quòd Paulus eius Ecclesiæ fidem in toto orbe prædicari dixit, sibi eam prærogatiuam vendicant, quòd errare non possint, & quod omnes Ecclesiæ Romanis Pontificibus parere, & eorum doctrinam atque placita sequi debeant. Sed probandum prius erat, eandem esse adhuc in Romana ecclesia doctrinæ & fidei formam, quæ olim fuit, quando illam tanto præconio dignam Paulus iudicauit. Quod cùm nunquam probaturi sint, & res ipsa diuersum loquatur, non est quòd maiorum laudes ad se rapiant.
units.tr: These things serve us against the Romanists, who, because Paul said that the faith of that church was proclaimed throughout the whole world, claim for themselves the prerogative that they cannot err, and that all churches must obey the Roman Pontiffs and follow their doctrine and decrees. But it had first to be proved that the form of doctrine and faith in the Roman church is still the same as it was when Paul judged it worthy of such praise. Since they will never prove this, and the thing itself speaks otherwise, there is no reason for them to snatch the praises of their forebears for themselves.

units.la: Imprimis autem Verbi administri exemplum Pauli imitari discant: vt quæ laude digna sunt laudent, vt sic fortius excitentur, & facilius in officio contineantur, qui ingenui sunt: simul autem diligenter curent, ne ad ea conniueant, aut etiam turpi adulatione excusent, quæ reprehensionem merentur. Peccant in hoc multi hodie, qui in magnis viris propter priora merita in rem pub. & Ecclesiam ea non excusant modò, sed tantùm non laudibus vehunt[?], quæ publicè & magna cum libertate corripi debebant, vt quod ex illorum exemplo nascitur scandalum, è medio tollere-tur. Sunt hi canes muti, qui vt Heroum & principum amicitijs sese insinuent, ministerij libertatem produnt, & perfidiosa indulgentia eos perdunt, quorum honori & existimationi se consulere aiunt. Longè aliter olim Prophetæ, vt Paulo ante de Dauide diximus, quem postquam tot labores, pericula, victorias, triumphos & egregia in populum Dei merita, Nathan ob adulterij & homicidij scelus durissime corripuit, & ita in viam salutis reuocauit eum, qui rerum securus alioqui perijsset. Sic cum Ezechia, laudatissimo principe, Isaiam egisse legimus. Quid, quòd Christus Petrum, quem paulò ante beatum pronunciauerat ob fidei verae confessionem, mox Satanam dicit, eò quòd ipsum à morte ex Patris decreto subeunda deberet? Hæc exempla Ecclesiarum ministri sibi imitanda proponant. Etenim cum inter amicos fidos & ingenuos admonendi & reprehendi libertas seruari soleat, & eadem amicitiæ vinculum sit firmissimum, quanto magis illa Ecclesiæ pastores seruare debent, & illa suum erga illam amorem atque fidem testari?
units.tr: Above all, let the ministers of the Word learn to imitate Paul's example: that they praise what deserves praise, so that those who are well-disposed may be more strongly stirred up and more easily kept in their duty; but at the same time let them take care not to connive at, or even excuse with base flattery, those things that deserve rebuke. Many today sin in this respect: on account of earlier services to the commonwealth and the Church, they not only excuse great men in their faults but almost carry them along with praise [?], when those faults ought to be corrected publicly and with great frankness, so that the scandal that arises from their example might be removed. These are dumb dogs, who, in order to insinuate themselves into the friendship of heroes and princes, betray the freedom of their ministry, and by a treacherous indulgence destroy those whose honour and reputation they say they are looking after. Far otherwise did the prophets of old act, as we said before of David: after so many labours, dangers, victories, triumphs and outstanding services to the people of God, Nathan rebuked him most severely for the crime of adultery and murder, and so called back to the way of salvation a man who otherwise, being secure in his position, would have perished. So we read that Isaiah dealt with Hezekiah, a most praiseworthy prince. And what of the fact that Christ, who had shortly before pronounced Peter blessed for his true confession of faith, soon called him Satan, because he was trying to turn him away from the death he had to undergo by the Father's decree? Let the ministers of the Churches set these examples before themselves to imitate. For since freedom to admonish and rebuke is usually preserved among faithful and frank friends, and this is the firmest bond of friendship, how much more ought the pastors of the Church to preserve it, and to attest their love and faithfulness toward her?

units.la: Præterea diligenti obseruatione dignum est, quòd Paulus Corinthios non hoc nomine reprehendit, quòd in conuentibus ecclesiasticis frequentandis negligentiores essent, sed quòd nihil proficerent in illis, neque meliores inde redirent. Sunt enim cœtus sacri propter nos instituti, & quæcunq; in illis fiunt, à Deo tradita sunt, vt nobis adiumento sint ad pietatem & salutem æternam. Possunt ista omnia tribus capitibus comprehendi, Verbi Dei prædicatione, Sacramentorum vsu & Precibus publicis. At prædicationis verbi vsus est, vt in Dei cognitione proficiamus, vt cognitio hæc fidem in Deum & timorem eiusdem in nobis augeat, ex quibus deinde vitæ nouitas & vena sanctimonia nascuntur. Sacramenta autem Verbi appendices sunt, quibus Deus promissiones suas obsignat, & quæ nobis in Christo Filio suo exhibuit beneficia, sensibus quoque externis repræsentat. Ergo illa quoque si rite vsurpentur, fidem nostram iucundissima contemplatione exercent atq; confirmant, simulque nos obstringunt ad fraternæ dilectionis & sanctimoniæ studium. Precum verò exactissima formula est, quæ in Oratione Dominica habetur, quæ ut omnia complectitur, quæ nobis publicè & priuatim quoad corpus & animam necessaria sunt: ita epitome vel compendium dici potest omnium Psalmorum & precationum, quibus olim sanctissimi homines apud Deum usi sunt. At quid aliud illa docet, quàm ut unum Deum, qui in cœlis est, pro patre nostro agnoscamus, illum unû colamus, nominatim eius gloriam illustrare studeamus, regno illius locum demus, voluntati eius iustæ & bonæ nos totos submittamus: ut denique ab illo accepto corporis & animæ alimento, inter suos mutua dilectione coalescamus, inuidiam, odium & vindictæ cupiditatem totis animis profligemus: denique tentationibus prauis & harum authori, diabolo, omnibus tam animi quam corporis viribus resistamus? Hæc (inquâ) cùm in sacris cœtibus tractetur, nō possunt nō meliores fieri, qui his animum attendunt, neque circa vanas aut turpes quoque cogitationes peregrinantur. At est hoc vitium nimis vulgare, quemadmodum in sementis parabola Christus admonet. Et olim apud Prophetas Deus de Iudæis non semel conquestus est, quòd ad sacra quidem publica & ad Verbum eius audiendum conuenirent, nihil autem proficerent in solida pietate. Ideo per Isaiam clamabat: Quum venitis ut coram me compareatis, quis id postulat à manu vestra, ut conculcetis atria mea? Et apud Ezechielem eiusmodi hypocritarum mores graphicè describit his verbis: Et tu fili hominis, filij populi tui colloquuntur tecum iuxta parietes & in ostijs domorum loquitur alter ad alterum, quisque videlicet ad proximum suum dicendo: Venite quæso, & audite, quod nam Verbum egressum sit à Domino. Et veniunt ad te secundum ingressum populi (id est, turmatim sicuti populus ad opus aliquod publicum confluere solet) sedentque coram te populus meus, & audiunt sermones tuos, quos tamen non faciunt: quandoquidem subsannationes ore suo concinnant, et post auariciam suam vadit cor eorum. Et ecce tu illis es ut author carminis amatorij voce suavi modulans, & ut instrumentum musicum, quod scitè pulsatur: audiunt ergo verba tua, sed ea non faciunt, &c. Quæ verba si ad nostri seculi mores transferas, videbis nihil aptius, nihil verius & magis proprium de illis dici posse. Et tales fere sunt, qui reliquis meliores possunt censeri. Cæterum quia Corinthij non modò securitate & Verbi contemptu peccabant, sed aliis quoque vitijs corrupti ex cœtibus suis deteriores abibant, nunc illa Paulus recenseт, ut quid hic ipsis cauendum sit, intelligant.
units.tr: Moreover, it is worth careful notice that Paul does not rebuke the Corinthians for being too careless about attending the church assemblies, but because they gained nothing from them and came back from them no better. The sacred gatherings were instituted for our sake, and whatever takes place in them has been handed down by God, so that they may help us towards godliness and eternal salvation. All of this can be comprised under three heads: the preaching of the Word of God, the use of the Sacraments, and public prayers. The purpose of the preaching of the Word is that we may make progress in the knowledge of God, and that this knowledge may increase faith in God and fear of him in us, from which newness of life and holiness of conduct then spring. The Sacraments, moreover, are appendages of the Word, by which God seals his promises and represents to our outward senses the benefits he has bestowed on us in Christ his Son. So, if they are rightly used, they exercise our faith in the most delightful contemplation, and they confirm it, and at the same time bind us to the pursuit of brotherly love and holiness. The most exact form of prayer is the one contained in the Lord's Prayer, which embraces all that we need, publicly and privately, for body and soul. It may be called an epitome or summary of all the Psalms and prayers by which the holiest men of old made their appeal to God. And what else does it teach, than that we should acknowledge the one God who is in heaven as our Father, worship him alone, take care to make his glory known, give his kingdom room, submit ourselves wholly to his just and good will; that, finally, having received from him the nourishment of body and soul, we should grow together among our own people in mutual love, and with all our hearts put down envy, hatred and the desire for revenge; and, lastly, that we should resist with all the strength of soul and body wicked temptations and the diabolical author of them? When these things (I say) are treated in the sacred assemblies, those who give their minds to them cannot fail to become better, nor do they wander off into empty or base thoughts. But this fault is all too common, as Christ warns in the parable of the sower. And long ago, among the Prophets, God complained of the Jews more than once, that they gathered indeed for the public worship and to hear his Word, but made no progress in true piety. So through Isaiah he cried out: "When you come to appear before me, who has required this at your hand, that you trample my courts?" And in Ezekiel he describes the conduct of such hypocrites vividly in these words: "And you, son of man, the sons of your people talk with you beside the walls and in the doorways of the houses, one speaking to another, each saying to his neighbour: Come, I pray you, and hear what word has come forth from the Lord. And they come to you as the people usually come, and they sit before you, my people, and they hear your sermons, which yet they do not do; for they make mockeries with their mouths, and their heart goes after their covetousness. And behold, you are to them like the author of a love song, singing with a sweet voice, or like a musical instrument played skilfully: so they hear your words, but do not do them," and so on. If you transfer these words to the manners of our own age, you will see that nothing more fitting, nothing truer, and nothing more applicable could be said of them. And such people are nearly the kind who might be counted better than the rest. But since the Corinthians were sinning not only by their complacency and contempt of the Word, but also, corrupted by other vices, were leaving their assemblies worse than they came, Paul now lists those vices, so that they may understand what they must guard against.

units.la: Primum hîs verbis enuntiat: Primùm enim cùm conuenitis in ecclesia, audio dissidia inter vos esse, et aliquam partem credo. In Græco σχίσματα habetur, quæ vox Latinis quoque Theologis in usu est. Quæ verò scismata ista sint, siue dissidia Corinthiorum fuerint, sub initium epistolæ audiuimus: quòd nimirum in sectas scissi à doctoribus suis denominari volebant. Scribit enim illic Apostolus: Declaratum est mihi de vobis, fratres, à domesticis Chloes, quòd lites sint inter vos: Hoc autem dico, quod vnusquisque vestrum dicit, Ego quidem sum Pauli, ego verò Apollos, ego vero Cephæ, &c. In præsenti autem ad culpæ aggrauationem facit, quòd dissidia ista ab ipsis in Ecclesiam, imò in Cœnam mysticam inferri dicit, quæ concordiæ symbolum est, vbi vno spiritu omnes tanquam eiusdem corporis membra animari & idem in Christo sentire debebant. Atqui solet hoc fieri, vt qui semel inter se scissi partium studia fouere incipiunt, non in externis modò & profanis rebus, verumetiam in ipsa religione, & in ijs, sine quibus salus nostra non consistit, dissidia & scismata illa exerceant. Exemplum huius mali nimium infelix hodie nobis exhibet Sacramentaria contentio, quæ factiosis Lutheranorum & Zuinglianorum, siue Caluinianorum nominibus eò vsque exarsit, vt alij alios communione Cœnæ indignos iudicent, & eos pro fratribus agnoscere nolint, qui eundem cum ipsis Christum profitentur. Ideo Christus iam mortem aditurus tam diligenter & solicitè precabatur Patrem, vt suos omnes vnum faceret. Et admodum necesse est, vt summo studio vigilemus aduersus insidias diaboli, qui hoc imprimis effectum cupit, vt nos quacunque occasione in partes scissos ab Ecclesiæ vnitate, & sic eadem opera à Christo capite & vnico omnis salutis authore auellat. Nam ex hisce Apostoli verbis satis constat, inania esse externa religionis exercitia, vbicunque scismata regnant: imò non solùm nihil proficiunt in cœtibus sacris homines factiosi & litibus dediti, verumetiam deteriores fiunt. Abutuntur enim ad scismatum defensionem Verbo Dei & sacris symbolis, & quia hæc omnia pro se facere arbitrantur, obstinatiores fiunt in-dies, dicti, & simul contendendi libidine sensus religionis paulatim extinguitur. Passime ergo de tota Christi Ecclesia hodie merentur, qui infelix illud de re Sacramentaria dissidium fouent, & authores sunt multis, vt etsi ad eandem mensam Domini accedant, diuersis tamen nominibus appellari velint, & eos odio prosequantur, quos pro fratribus in Christo debebant agnoscere. Quid enim illi aliud faciunt, quam quòd progressus multorum in vera pietate impediunt, & ijsdem noxia red dunt quae nobis salutis adminicula esse debebant?
units.tr: First, he expresses it in these words: "For first of all, when you come together in the church, I hear that there are divisions among you, and I partly believe it." In the Greek it is schismata [σχίσματα], a word that is also in use among Latin theologians. What these schisms or divisions of the Corinthians were, we heard at the beginning of the letter: namely, that they were split into sects and wished to be named after their teachers. For the Apostle writes there: "It has been declared to me concerning you, brethren, by those of the household of Chloe, that there are quarrels among you. Now I say this, that each one of you says: I am of Paul, and I of Apollos, and I of Cephas, and so on." In the present passage, he increases the blame by saying that these divisions are brought by them into the Church, indeed into the mystical Supper, which is the symbol of concord, where all ought to be animated by one Spirit as members of the same body and to think the same thing in Christ. Yet it commonly happens that those who once begin to split up among themselves and to foster partisan zeal exercise these divisions and schisms not only in external and profane matters, but even in religion itself, and in those things without which our salvation does not stand. The most unhappy example of this evil that is set before us today is the sacramentarian controversy, which has so inflamed the factious parties of the Lutherans, the Zwinglians, or the Calvinists, that each judges the others unworthy of communion in the Lord's Supper, and refuses to acknowledge as brethren those who profess the same Christ as they do. Therefore Christ, about to go to his death, prayed to the Father so diligently and earnestly that he might make all his people one. And it is very necessary that we watch with the greatest care against the snares of the devil, who especially desires this result, that on whatever occasion we should be split into parties and torn away from the unity of the Church, and so at the same time from Christ the Head and the sole author of all salvation. For from these words of the Apostle it is clear enough that the external exercises of religion are empty wherever schisms reign: indeed, factious men and those given to quarrels not only make no progress in the sacred assemblies, but become worse. For they abuse the Word of God and the sacred symbols in defence of their schisms, and because they think that all these things favour their side, they become more obstinate day by day, and gradually, through the lust of contending, the sense of religion is extinguished. Therefore they deserve very ill of the whole Church of Christ today who foster that unhappy division concerning the sacraments, and are the cause for many that, even though they approach the same table of the Lord, they nonetheless wish to be called by different names, and pursue with hatred those whom they ought to acknowledge as brethren in Christ. For what else do they do, than hinder the progress of many in true godliness, and make harmful to them those things which ought to have been helps to their salvation?

units.la: At ne Apostolus durius quid dixisse & omnes vno reatu inuoluisse videretur, simul dicti huius mitigationem subijcit, qua insontes à culpa eximit, & infirmos consolatur, ne offensi vel deflerent, vel ecclesiam deserant. Et aliquam partem (inquit) credo. Quasi diceret: Non quidem vos simul omnes dissidijs studere puto, verumtamen non omnino vanum esse credo, quod tam cer-tis authoribus didici: neque mihi dubium est, esse inter vos, qui dudum suscepta partium studia fouere pergant. Id verò probat, addens: Oportet enim etiam haereses inter vos esse, vt qui probati sunt, manifesti fiant inter vos. Haeresis vox grauior & atrocior est quàm scismatis. Hoc enim ex quacunque alienatione animorum nascitur, vt cùm aliqui vel ex odio pastorum aut moro-sitate propria illos audire nolunt, vel cum his aut illis sacra communia habere dedignantur, & ita secessionem ab Ecclesia faciunt. At haeresis ex dissensione in doctrina nascitur, & pertinaciam coniunctam habet, qua quod semel aliqui tradiderunt, tueri satagunt, & alios quoque in errorem abducendo apertas sectas inuehunt. Vult ergo Paulus sic dicere: Non nouum aut insolens mihi videtur quod de vobis audio, neque quisquam priorum istis dissidijs ita offendi debet, vt propter ea vel de Euangelij veritate dubitare, vel Ecclesiae societatem relinquere velit. Nec enim vestra sors potior est quàm aliarum ecclesiarum, quae grauioribus quoque malis sunt obnoxiae. Nam vt Christus ipse monuit, est quidem Ecclesia Dei ager, sed in hunc sua zizania quoque Satan se-minat, & proinde in hoc saeculo seges ab omni vitio pura sperari non potest. Et vos ipsos adhuc graviora certamina manebunt, quando malè feriati quidam portentosis dogmatibus ecclesias in partes distrahent. At tunc meminerit is, hoc ita fieri oportere, & non sine certo prouidentiae Dei consilio fieri, qui talia permittit, vt qui probati, id est, in fide verè instructi & constantes sunt, manifesti fiant inter vos. Quoad enim in otio & alta pace ecclesiae degunt, veri Christiani hypocritis & probi rèprobis permixti viuunt, & nonnunquam hi illis meliores videntur. At cùm graciores aliqui doctrinae articuli & ipsa fidei Christianae capita in contentionem veniunt, mox apparet qui nam Christū verè & ex animo amplexi sint, qui item falsa & inani fidei professione hactenus Ecclesiae fucum fecerint. Neminem ergo aliorum siue leuitas siue contumacia offendere debet, sed curent singuli, vt huic remedio, quo suam Ecclesiam Deus purgare & pios ab impijs simulatoribus secernere solet, sese animo forti & inuicta fidei constantia accommodent.
units.tr: But lest the Apostle should seem to have said something too harsh, and to have included everyone in one charge, he adds at once a softening of his statement, by which he frees the innocent from blame and comforts the weak, so that they will not either be grieved by offence or desert the Church. "And I partly believe it," he says. As if he were saying: "I do not think indeed that all of you are devoted to divisions, but still I believe that what I have learned from such trustworthy authorities is not entirely groundless; nor is it doubtful to me that there are among you some who continue to foster the party allegiances they took up long ago." He proves this by adding: "For there must also be heresies among you, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you." The word heresy is graver and more atrocious than schism. For schism arises from whatever estrangement of minds, when some either refuse to hear the ministers, out of hatred for them or from their own peevishness, or disdain to share the common sacred rites with this or that person, and so make a secession from the Church. But heresy arises from disagreement in doctrine, and has obstinacy joined to it, by which men strive to defend whatever they have once taught, and by leading others also into error, they bring in open sects. Paul therefore wishes to say this: "What I hear about you does not seem new or strange to me, and none of the earlier ones should be so offended by these divisions as to doubt the truth of the Gospel because of them, or to wish to leave the fellowship of the Church. For your lot is no better than that of other churches, which are also liable to graver evils. For, as Christ himself warned, the Church of God is indeed a field, but Satan also sows his tares in it, and therefore in this age a crop pure from every fault cannot be hoped for. And you yourselves will still face even graver conflicts, when certain men, badly struck, will divide the churches with monstrous doctrines. But then let the one who permits such things to happen, not without a definite purpose of God's providence, be mindful that it must be so, so that those who are approved, that is, those who are truly instructed and constant in faith, may become manifest among you. For as long as the churches live in leisure and deep peace, true Christians live mixed with hypocrites and the upright with the wicked, and sometimes these latter seem better than the former. But when certain more serious articles of doctrine and the very heads of the Christian faith come into contention, it soon appears who have embraced Christ truly and from the heart, and who, likewise, have so far deceived the Church by a false and empty profession of faith. Therefore let the levity or the stubbornness of others offend no one; rather let each one take care to adapt himself, with a strong mind and an unconquered constancy of faith, to that remedy by which God is accustomed to purge his Church and to separate the godly from the impious pretenders."

units.la: Est autem diligentius expendenda locutio Apostoli: Oportet etiam haereses inter vos esse, &c. Hac enim & aliis similibus multi abutuntur, vt haereses & quaevis alia scelera excusent. Si (inquiunt) haec aut ista fieri oportet, quis quo minus fiant prohibebit? Et cùm necessitate ad ista homines feruntur, cur illos accusamus, aut supplicio dignos censemus? Denique cùm ista omnia piorum bono fiant, cur de illis querimur? At Paulus sic loquendo nos nequaquam ad diuinae prouidentiae arcana remittere voluit, sed potius necessitatis huius causas in ipsis hominibus monstrare, & simul Dei bonitatem commendare, qui rei mala euentum bonum facere consueuit. Nam vt modo diximus, in Ecclesia externa semper probis & germanis Christi discipulis reprobi quidam permixti sunt. Non item feriatur Satan, qui vt omnem nobis nocendi occasionem auidè captat, ita vbique eos inuenit, qui ipsi aures simul & animum praebent. Quid verò hinc aliud sperari potest, quàm vt dissidia, factiones, haereses & graues ecclesiarum motus sequantur? Est ergo locutio haec ei similis, qua Christus vtitur dicens: Necesse est, vt veniant scandala. Vbi necessitatis istius causas non in Deo altius scrutari opus est. Quid enim aliud fiat, quando malorum & improborum maximus vbique est numerus, & qui illis sunt meliores ad malum tamen natura proclives sunt, & proinde malorum exemplis facilè permouentur? Sed mirum est istos homines scripturae locutionibus tam pertinaciter abuti, cùm multae similes nobis in quotidiano vsu sint. De to enim, qui perpotat, ludit, scortatur, inutilem seruorum turbam alit, & alia huius generis facit, dicimus: Hunc hominem ad inopiam & egestatem redigi necesse est. De intemperanter item vi-uentibus: Hos oportet in febres, podagram, intercutem & alios morbos incidere. Quis vero hæc audiens de occulta Dei prouidentia disputationem instituit, vt iustos excusæt? Cur ergo id facimus in ijs, quæ ad animam spectant, vbi scelerum & perditionis causa non minus euidentes sunt in hominibus, quàm in alteris illis inopia & morborum causas hærere nemo negat? Quod vero ex scandalis, dissidijs, hæresibus ad electos bonus aliquis fructus redundat, hoc non illis acceptum ferri debet, neque ideo iustorum culpa liberantur: sed Dei bonitati & sapientiæ illud omne transcribendum est, qui sic res omnes gubernat & moderatur, vt quæ per se mala, scelerata & noxia sunt, ijs qui ipsum diligunt adiumento sint ad bonum. Exempla, quibus hoc illustrari poterat, passim occurrunt, & imprimis huc pertinent, quæ in Iosephi à fratribus venditi, & Christi per Iudam prodití historia habentur. Fratribus certe culpam deprecantibus Iosephus dicit: Vos equidem cogitauistis ad-uersus me malum, at Deus cogitauit idipsum in bonum, vt faceret quemadmodum hodie apparet, & seruaret in vita populum multum. Christus quoque se ex æterno Patris decreto per discipulum prodi & infami supplicio mori oportere non vno loco testatur. At idem in vltima Cœna ait: Væ homini illi, per quem Filius hominis proditur, &c. In publicis quoque ecclesiæ persecutionibus hoc ipsum cernitur, quas accidere necesse est propter nos, vt hypocritæ eiciantur, & qui dormitant excitentur, adhæc electorum fides illustrior fulgeat: nec ideo excusati sunt impij tyranni, quos innatum veritatis odium in rabiem iam adduxit. Discant ergo singuli intra hos limites se continere, vt Deum quidem mali nullius authorem faciant, eius vero bonitatem & sapientiam exosculentur, qui quod malum est nobis in bonum convertere potest: & ex eo in omni genere tentationum consolationem capiant.
units.tr: We must also weigh more carefully the Apostle's words: "There must be heresies among you also," and so on. Many people abuse this and similar sayings to excuse heresies and every other kind of wickedness. "If these things or those must happen," they say, "who can prevent them from happening? And since men are driven to these things by necessity, why do we accuse them or think them worthy of punishment? Finally, since all these things happen for the good of the godly, why do we complain about them?" Paul did not mean by such words to refer us to the hidden counsels of divine providence, but rather to show the causes of this necessity in men themselves, and at the same time to commend the goodness of God, who is accustomed to turn the evil outcome of a matter to good. For, as we have just said, in the outward Church some reprobate are always mixed in with the upright and genuine disciples of Christ. Nor does Satan take a holiday: as he eagerly seizes every opportunity to harm us, so he finds everywhere those who give him both their ears and their minds. What else can be expected from this than that quarrels, factions, heresies and serious disturbances in the churches should follow? So this saying is like the one in which Christ says, "It must needs be that offences come." There is no need to search deeper into God for the causes of this necessity. For what else would happen when the number of evil and wicked people is everywhere very large, and those who are better than them are nevertheless by nature inclined to evil, and so are easily moved by the examples of the wicked? But it is remarkable that these men abuse the expressions of Scripture so stubbornly, when many similar ones are in everyday use among us. For of one who drinks heavily, gambles, whores, keeps a useless crowd of servants and does other things of this kind, we say, "This man must necessarily be reduced to poverty and want." Likewise of those who live intemperately: "These must fall into fevers, gout, dropsy and other diseases." Yet who, hearing these things, would start a discussion about the hidden providence of God in order to excuse the men concerned? Why then do we do this in matters that concern the soul, where the causes of crime and ruin are no less evident in men than, as no one denies, the causes of poverty and disease lie in the other cases? As for any good result that flows from scandals, dissensions and heresies to the elect, this must not be credited to those who cause them, nor are the upright thereby freed from blame; rather, all of it must be ascribed to the goodness and wisdom of God, who so governs and directs all things that what is in itself evil, wicked and harmful becomes a help to good for those who love him. Examples by which this could be illustrated are found everywhere, and especially those belonging to the histories of Joseph, sold by his brothers, and of Christ, betrayed through Judas. When his brothers begged pardon for their fault, Joseph says: "You indeed thought evil against me, but God meant the same thing for good, to bring about what appears today, and to save many people alive." Christ also testifies in more than one place that by the eternal decree of the Father he must be betrayed by a disciple and die a shameful death. Yet at the last supper he also says, "Woe to that man through whom the Son of man is betrayed," and so on. This same thing is seen in the public persecutions of the Church, which must come about on our account, so that hypocrites may be cast out, the sleepers roused, and the faith of the elect shine more brightly. Nor on that account are the impious tyrants excused, whom their innate hatred of the truth has already driven to madness. Let each one therefore keep himself within these limits: so that he does not make God the author of any evil, but embraces his goodness and wisdom, who can turn to good for us whatever is evil, and from this draws comfort in every kind of temptation.

units.la: Videamus nunc alterum vitium, quo circa Cœnam Corinthij peccabant. Erat hoc totius Cœnæ immutatio quædam, & talis quidem vt non amplius Cœna Dominica dici mereretur, quam illi agebant. Id his verbis enuntiat: Itaque cùm conuenitis in vnum, hoc non est Dominicam Cœnam edere, &c. Quasi diceret: Conuenitis quidem in Ecclesiam, vt qui mensæ Christi participare, mortis eius memoriam celebrare, vos mutuo ad fidem & dilectionem fraternam excitare atque exercere velitis: Sed quod tunc facitis nihil minus est quàm Cœna Domini, neque eam vos manducatis. Id probat argumento à contrarijs: Nam vnusquisque propriam Cœnam præoccupat in edendo, & hic quidem esurit, ille vero ebrius est. Ostendit ipsorum ritum à Christi institutione alienissimum esse, & adhuc modum argumentatur: Christus vnam & eandem mensam omnibus suis communem esse voluit, & adeò non distinxit inter diuites & pauperes, vt ne inter seipsum quidem & discipulos, quoad externa symbola, discrimen esse voluerit. Quid, quòd ne Iudam quidem, iam proditorem & hostem, exclusit? At vnusquisque vestrum pro suarum facultatum ratione aut animi sui arbitrio Cœnam propriam instituit, ad quam quos ipse vult inuitat, & hi deinde commessantur intemperatissimè, multis interim esurientibus, qui & ipsi nihil habent, & à vobis, qui opulentiores estis, negliguntur: Ergo vestra hæc conuiuia nihil cum Christi Cœna habent commune. Vel si breuius velis, argumentum ita formabis: Christi Cœna, non priuata aut alicui propria, sed toti Ecclesiæ communis est: Vos Cœnas habetis priuatas aut proprias: Ergo non editis Cœnam Domini.
units.tr: Let us now look at the other fault by which the Corinthians sinned in regard to the Supper. This was a kind of alteration of the whole Supper, such that what they were doing no longer deserved to be called the Lord's Supper. He states this in these words: "When therefore you come together in one place, this is not to eat the Lord's Supper," and so on. As if he were saying: you certainly come together in the Church, wishing to share in the table of Christ, to celebrate the remembrance of his death, and to stir up and exercise one another in faith and brotherly love. But what you do then is anything but the Lord's Supper, and you do not eat it as such. He proves this by an argument from contraries: for each one goes ahead with his own supper in eating, and one indeed is hungry while another is drunk. He shows that their rite is most alien to the institution of Christ, and he argues further in this way: Christ wished one and the same table to be common to all his people, and he did not so distinguish between rich and poor that he wished there to be no difference, as regards the outward signs, even between himself and the disciples. Why, he did not even exclude Judas, already a betrayer and enemy! But each of you, according to his means or his own judgment, arranges a supper of his own, to which he invites whom he wishes; then these people feast most intemperately, while many go hungry, who have nothing themselves and are neglected by you who are wealthier. Therefore your banquets have nothing in common with the Supper of Christ. Or, if you want it more briefly, you may frame the argument thus: the Supper of Christ is not private or belonging to any one person, but common to the whole Church. You have private or proper suppers. Therefore you do not eat the Lord's Supper.

units.la: Cæterum vt rem omnem rectius intelligamus, primitiuæ aut veteris Ecclesiæ morem nouisse oportet, ex quo prophanus iste abusus Cœnæ apud Corinthios enatus fuit. Solebant Iudæi (vt alias diximus) ex Dei instituto gratulatorijs sacrificijs conuiuia coniungere, ad quæ amicos & vicinos vocabant: & imprimis pauperum rationem illos habere iusserat Deus, si ad hunc modum in eius conspectu conuiuari vellent. Imitati sunt hunc morem per κοινωνίαν[?] gentes, vt in festis & sacrificijs celebrioribus publicas epulas instituerent: quibus vtiscerationes possunt adnumerari, quæ apud Romanos in feriis, quas Latinas dicebant, et in funeribus seu exequijs illustrium personarum solebant facere. Hinc occasionem arripuerunt Christiani homines, & ne in læta hac redemptionis per Christum factæ commemoratione, quoad pauperum curam, Iudæis & gentibus inferiores viderentur, qui inter illos opulentiores erant, domo afferebant epulas, ad quas postea peractam Cœnam Domini tota Ecclesia vocabatur, & in his promiscuè diuites cum pauperibus discumbebant. bant. Dicebantur conuiuia illa Agapæ, id est, charitates, tanquam charitatis fraternæ symbolum & tesseræ. Meminit illarum in sua epistola Iudas Apostolus, & Petrus in posteriori, Cap. secundo. Et earundem Tertullianus quoque diligentem mentionem facit, vt quæ ipsius tempore adhuc in vsu fuerunt. Habuit ergo res ista initium ex bono zelo, sed (vt inter opulentos, fastui & deliciis affluetos, fieri solet) apud Corinthios mox in fœdum abusum degeneravit. Opulentiores enim neglecto proprio Cœnæ Dominicæ vsu, sub illius prætextu sua sympofia agebant, & soli cum suis (vt diximus) luxuriosè nimis conuiuabantur, illis interim non sine publica contumelia famescentibus, in quorum gratiam potissimùm Agapæ illæ initiò institutæ fuerant. Itaque in vno facto multiplex scelus concurrebat. Primò enim non alienum à culpa fuit, quod Christi instituto aliquid addiderant, & cùm infinitæ aliæ rationes essent subueniendi pauperibus, hanc delegerant, quæ ab exemplo Christi alienissima erat, qui cùm Cœnam suam instituere vellet, Paschale epulum prius abrogauit. Alter error fuit, quod ex publica & communi Cœna priuatam quisque sibi fingebat. Sequebatur ex hoc gulæ & ventris studium, quod cùm in omni reliqua vita vituperio dignum sit, in sacris execrationem extremam meretur. Erat hîs coniunctus pauperum contemptus, quos non negligebant modò, verumetiam pudefaciebant, cùm vel ipsa Cœna eos hîc sui officij admonere posset. Nam vt decimo Cap. dixit Apostolus, vnum corpus sunt, qui ex vno pane Domino edentes vnam & eandem in illum fidem profitentur. Hæc omnia Paulus in præsenti accusat, & eos Cœnam Dominicam habere negat.
units.tr: But that we may understand the whole matter more rightly, we must know the custom of the primitive or early Church, from which that profane abuse of the Supper arose among the Corinthians. The Jews (as we have said elsewhere) were accustomed, by God's appointment, to join banquets to thank-offerings, to which they invited friends and neighbours; and God had especially commanded them to take account of the poor, if they wished to feast in this way in his sight.
