The Gentiles imitated this custom through fellowship [κοινωνίαν], so that at festivals and more famous sacrifices they held public feasts. To these may be added the entertainments that the Romans were accustomed to give at the Latin holidays, as they were called, and at the funerals or obsequies of illustrious persons. Seizing on this occasion, Christians, so that in this joyful remembrance of the redemption made through Christ they should not appear inferior to Jews and Gentiles in care for the poor, brought food from home, those among them who were wealthier; and afterwards the whole Church was invited to these feasts, once the Lord's Supper had been celebrated, and in them rich and poor reclined together without distinction. Those banquets were called Agapae, that is, loves, as a sign and token of brotherly love. The apostle Jude mentions them in his epistle, and Peter in his second epistle, chapter two. Tertullian also makes careful mention of them, since they were still in use in his time. So this practice had its beginning in good zeal, but (as commonly happens among the wealthy, who abound in luxury and pleasures) among the Corinthians it soon degenerated into a shameful abuse. For the wealthier, neglecting the proper use of the Lord's Supper, held their own drinking parties under its pretext, and feasted too luxuriously, as we have said, only with their own people, while others went hungry in public disgrace, and it was chiefly for their sake that those Agapae had been instituted at the beginning. Thus several sins came together in one deed. First, it was not free from fault that they had added something to Christ's institution; and though there were countless other ways of helping the poor, they had chosen this one, which was most alien to the example of Christ, who, when he wished to institute his own supper, first abrogated the Passover feast. The second error was that each person made a private supper for himself out of the public and common Supper. From this came a zeal for gluttony and the belly, which, although it deserves reproach in every other part of life, merits the utmost execration in sacred things. Joined to this was contempt for the poor, whom they not only neglected but even shamed, although the Supper itself could have reminded them of their duty here. For, as the Apostle said in chapter ten, "we are one body, since we who eat of one bread to the Lord profess one and the same faith in him." Paul accuses them of all these things in the present passage, and denies that they eat the Lord's Supper.

units.la: Est hoc memorabile exemplum, quo docemur, quàm periculosum sit diuinis institutis aliquid ex nostra rationis placito siue arbitrio assuere[?]. Solet enim nobis hîc imprimis insidiari Satan, vt externis sacris vel mutatis vel abolitis religionem quoque internam ex animis nostris aboleat. Neque hîc quid velit, aperte semper significat, sed in angelum lucis transformatus pietatem simulat, & sub huius prætextu persuadet, vt à Deo traditos ritus vel mutare, vel additionibus aut adeptionibus nostris corrumpere audeamus. At quàm primùm hîc sibi aliquid homo permittit, indies longius progreditur. Est enim insatiabilis humani ingenij audacia, & mirificè suis inuentis circa Dei cultum delectatur. Exempla in veteri testamento plurima habentur, quæ docent, quousq; illorum etiâ licentia progredi soleat, qui Dei verbo nô omnino desistuntur[?]. Quid vero posteris temporibus acciderit, notius est, quàm vt multis commemorari oporteat. Non temere ergo Deus humanas traditiones passim damnat, & inutiles sibique abominabiles esse testatur omnes cultus, qui secundùm illas instituuntur. Semper ergo meminerimus, non esse faciendum quod nobis bonum videtur in oculis nostris, sed Dei verbo esse insistendum, à quo nefas sit ad dextram vel ad sinistram deflectere. Vide Numer. 15. Deut. 4. & 12.
units.tr: This is a memorable example, by which we are taught how dangerous it is to add anything to divine institutions by the decision or judgment of our own reason. For Satan usually lays his snares for us here above all, so that by changing or abolishing external rites he may also destroy inner religion from our minds. Nor does he always openly show what he wants, but transformed into an angel of light he feigns piety, and under this pretext persuades us to dare to change the rites handed down by God, or to corrupt them by our additions or subtractions. But as soon as a man permits himself something here, he advances further day by day. For the boldness of the human mind is insatiable, and it delights wonderfully in its own inventions about the worship of God. Many examples in the Old Testament show how far the license of those who do not wholly desist from the word of God is wont to go. What happened in later times is too well known to need recounting at length. Therefore God does not rashly condemn human traditions everywhere, and he testifies that all worship instituted according to them is useless and abominable to him. Let us always remember, then, that we must not do what seems good in our own eyes, but must cling to the word of God, from which it is wrong to turn aside to right or left. See Numbers 15, Deut. 4 and 12.

units.la: Præ alijs autem hîc considerari paulò attentius debet, quòd diserte negat Corinthios edere Cœnam Dominicam. Visum hoc fuit haud dubiè plerisque durum dictu. Dicit tamen, & dicti sui rationem habet sufficientem, quòd non sequerentur Christi institutum, quo vera & perfecta Cœnæ agendæ ratio continetur. Enimuero communi sensu hæc ratio nititur. Cur enim Dominicum dicatur, quod a Domini voluntate & institutione discrepat? Pertinet igitur hoc ad omnes, qui vel in Cœna sacra, vel in alijs Dei ordinationibus ab illius verbo discedunt. Quid ergo de Missa dicemus, quam Cœnæ Dominicæ loco sacrificuli celebrant, quæ non modò ipsis propria & priuata facta est, sed sic mutata quoq; vt neq; nomen Cœnæ retinuerit, neq; aliquod huius vestigium in illa appareat? Et quod in præsenti Paulus reprehendit, illic cum maiori sit impudentia. Quis enim nescit luxum vestitus sacri plus quàm theatricum, altarium & in hus prostantium imaginum ornatum, candelabrorum & calicum multo auro rutilantium splendorem? quæ omnia superstitiosi homines contra veteris Ecclesiæ morem inuexerunt. Quis verò ex illa edit & bibit? Soli sacrificuli, spectante tota Ecclesia, cui nihil quàm oculos non nisi breui momento pascere licet. Quòd si quâdo publicæ & solennis communionis dies adest, iam ne tunc quidem Cœna integra populo distribuitur. Alteram enim speciem (vt vocant) poculum videlicet benedictionis subtraxerunt iampridem contra Christi mandatu, qui de poculo dixit: Diuidite hoc inter vos, & bibite ex eo omnes. Quàm turpiter verò ex Missa sua belluetur & comessentur, omnes norūt, qui funera ab illis deduci, exequias, octauas, tricesimas et nunquâ nô redeuntia anniuersaria festa celebrari viderūt. Hîc ceu ad cadauer corui & vultures convolant, magno cum boatu defunctum cient, inde ad pocula & epulas ruunt, à quibus raro nisi prius bene madidi & distenti discedunt, sefurientibus[?] sæpe & luctu conta-bescentibus viduis & orphanis, qui ad ista impensas conferunt. Quid, quod hoc prætextu frequenter totas hæreditates intercipiunt? Negent ista fieri, si possint. At qua fronte negabunt, quod in totius mundi theatro iam sæculis aliquot factum est, & quod hodie adhuc fieri omnes vident? Quid ergo Paulum ad ista dicturum putas, si ea videret? Num hos Cœnam Dominicam manducare[?] diceret? Non equidem arbitror. Et hi tamen sunt, qui nos Sacramentorum hostes & sacrile-gos esse dicunt, eò quod primam Christi institutionem revocamus. At non soli illi in culpa sunt, sed ex nostris etiam nonnulli eodem reatu tenentur, qui novam Cœnæ peragendæ formam instituunt, panis fractionem prorsus auferunt, fines denique & usus illius mysterij fingunt, quorum nullam mentionem Christus unquam fecit, cum illud institueret. Videant illi, ne dum aliquid emendare volunt in Domini instituto, idem illis dici possit, quod in præsenti Corinthijs dicitur.
units.tr: Above all, we should consider here a little more carefully that he plainly denies that the Corinthians are eating the Lord's Supper. This doubtless seemed hard to many to hear. Yet he says it, and he has sufficient reason for his saying, because they did not follow Christ's institution, in which the true and perfect manner of celebrating the Supper is contained. Indeed this reasoning rests on common sense. For why should something be called the Lord's if it differs from the will and institution of the Lord? This therefore applies to all who depart from his word, whether in the holy Supper or in other ordinances of God. What then shall we say of the Mass, which priests celebrate in place of the Lord's Supper, and which has become not only their own private property but has been changed so much that it has kept neither the name of Supper nor any trace of it? And what Paul rebukes here is found there with greater impudence. For who does not know the luxury of sacred vestments, more than theatrical, the decoration of altars and of the images standing on them, the splendour of candlesticks and chalices gleaming with much gold? All these things superstitious men have introduced contrary to the custom of the ancient Church. And who eats and drinks from it? Only the priests, while the whole Church watches, and the Church is allowed only to feed its eyes for a brief moment. But if a day of public and solemn communion arrives, even then the whole Supper is not distributed to the people. For they have long since withdrawn the other kind (as they call it), namely the cup of blessing, against Christ's command, who said of the cup: "Divide this among yourselves and drink from it, all of you." How shamefully they feast and gorge themselves on their Mass, everyone knows who has seen funerals led by them, and obsequies, octaves, thirtieths and anniversary feasts celebrated that never cease to return. Here, like ravens and vultures gathering around a corpse, they summon the dead with great noise, then rush to cups and feasts, from which they rarely depart unless first well soaked and stuffed, while widows and orphans, who pay the expenses for these things, often rage and waste away in grief. What of the fact that under this pretext they frequently seize whole inheritances? Let them deny these things if they can. But with what face will they deny what has been done for centuries on the stage of the whole world, and what all see being done even today? What then do you think Paul would say to these things if he saw them? Would he say that these men eat the Lord's Supper? I certainly do not think so. And yet these are the ones who call us enemies and profaners of the sacraments, because we call back Christ's first institution. But they are not the only ones at fault; some of our own people are also bound by the same guilt, who devise a new form of celebrating the Supper, remove the breaking of bread altogether, and finally invent purposes and uses of that mystery, of which Christ never made any mention when he instituted it. Let them see to it that, while they wish to correct something in the Lord's institution, the same may not be said to them as is said to the Corinthians in the present passage.

units.la: Sed redeamus ad Pauli verba, qui rei indignitate motus acerrime & plenus (quod aiunt) ve-hementer in illos invehitur. Primum: Enimuero num domos non habetis ad edendum? Offendit hoc illos præter omnem necessitatem facere, cùm (si omnino convivari velint) non desint domus aliæ privatæ & publicæ, in quibus id facere possint. Et ita loquendo simul docet non hunc Cœnæ dominicæ usum esse, ut in ea edamus & bibamus ad corporis satietatem, sed ut animis altius elevatis cibum quæramus, qui & ipse non perit, et eos, qui ipsum vere edunt, pascit et alit ad vitam æternam. Denique hoc dicto Agapas quoque illas, de quibus supra diximus, e loco sacro & cœtibus ecclesiasticis omnino sublatas esse vult, quàm uis eas bono & sancto zelo institutas esse sciret. Ubi admonemur, non debere aliquem pudere, si mutare aut abrogare jubeatur, quod sine Dei Verbo institutum aliquam boni speciem habet. Si enim quæ Deus ipse instituit, Satan pervertere & in usum pessimum detorquere potest, quid de nostris institutis nobis polliceri possumus, quæ bonæ etiam intentionis excusationem amittunt, si per Dei Verbum meliora edocti cedere nolumus? Sed pergit Paulus, & vehementius sermonem intendens ait: Num ecclesiam Dei contemnitis? Ergo contumelia hæc non in paucis hærebat, sed in totam Ecclesiam redundabat, cum & hanc Sacramento omnium nobilissimo spoliarent, & in eius conspectu turpissimis cupiditatibus indulgerent. Atqui idem omnibus dicitur, qui Dei instituta pervertunt, & in Ecclesiam invehunt quæ ipsorum affectibus arrideнт[?]. Quid ergo de illis dicemus, qui sacra omnia venalia habent, & omnes ritus eo dirigunt, ut suæ avaritiæ & libidini satisfiat? Gloriantur isti Ecclesiæ titulo, & huius passores[?] habere volunt: sed si unquam de illa serio cogitarent, eam non ita haberent ludibrio. Non fallent autem oculos Domini, qui Sponsæ suæ factam iniuriam, inultam abire non sinet. Addit ad hanc amplificationem Apostolus: Et pudefacitis eos, qui non habent. Scelus est graue pauperem negligere. At eundem ludibrio habere flagitium est nulla venia dignum. Qui pauperi illudit (inquit Solomon) probro afficit factorem eius. Augetur tamen & hoc scelus, si ipsum inter media sa-cra, & in Ecclesiæ conspectu fiat, ubi nullum divitis & pauperis, docti[?] & indocti, nobilis & plebei discrimen esse debet, quoad mysteriorum regni Dei communionem. Observabis autem hic eos quoque perstringi, qui in Ecclesia vestium luxu superbiunt, in subsellijs altioribus sese toti cœtui, ut Semideos quosdam, conspicuos ostentant, & ijsdem arma seu gentis suæ insignia affigunt. Habent hi suos defensores, imo (ne quid intactum impollutumque Antichristus relinqueret) adiuuerunt istorum fastum sacrifici & monachi, & pretio illis vendiderunt loca illa, ex quibus sese ostentarent. Habent isti omnes fidem Domini nostri JESV CHRISTI cum respectu personarum: quod quàm à fidei ingenio alienum sit Apostoli passim docent, imprimis autem hoc faciunt, quæ Jacobus in sua epistola sub initium Cap. secundi prolixè tradidit. Deinde ijdem pauperes, non solum pudefaciunt, sed ijsdem impatientiæ etiam authores sunt, ut Dei judicia & eius providentiam audacius accusare incipiant. Vides ergo quàm multa scelera in uno concurrant, & demonstratione ampliori non opus est, ubi res ipsa loquitur.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul's words. He, moved by the unworthiness of the matter, attacks them most bitterly and, as they say, with full vehemence. First: "What? Have you no houses in which to eat?" This shows that they did it beyond all necessity, since, if they really wished to feast together, there were other private and public houses in which they could do it. And in speaking thus he also teaches at the same time that this is not the use of the Lord's Supper, that we should eat and drink to bodily satiety in it, but that with minds raised high we should seek the food which does not perish, and which feeds and nourishes to eternal life those who truly eat it. Finally, by this saying he wants those Agapes also, of which we spoke above, to be entirely removed from the holy place and from ecclesiastical assemblies, although he knew they were instituted with good and holy zeal. Here we are reminded that no one should be ashamed if he is ordered to change or abolish something which, though instituted without the word of God, has some appearance of goodness. For if Satan can pervert what God himself instituted and turn it to the worst use, what can we promise ourselves about our own institutions, which lose even the excuse of good intention if, having been taught better through the word of God, we are unwilling to yield? But Paul goes on, and stretching his speech more vehemently, says: "Or do you despise the Church of God?" Therefore this insult did not cling to a few, but overflowed upon the whole Church, since they both robbed it of the most noble of all sacraments and indulged their most shameful desires in its sight. Yet the same is said to all who pervert God's institutions and bring into the Church things which please their own passions. What then shall we say of those who hold all sacred things for sale, and direct all rites so that their greed and lust are satisfied? They boast of the title of the Church and want to have its ministers, but if they ever thought seriously about it they would not treat it as a mockery. Yet they will not deceive the eyes of the Lord, who will not let the injury done to his Bride go unavenged. The Apostle adds to this amplification: "And you shame those who have nothing." It is a grave sin to neglect the poor. But to make them a laughing-stock is a shameful crime deserving no pardon. "He who mocks the poor," says Solomon, "insults his Maker." Yet this crime is increased if it is done in the midst of the holy things and in the sight of the Church, where there should be no distinction between rich and poor, learned and unlearned, noble and common, so far as communion in the mysteries of God's kingdom is concerned. You will observe here that those also are rebuked who take pride in the luxury of their clothing in the Church, who display themselves conspicuously to the whole assembly from the higher seats, like certain demigods, and fix their arms or family crests upon them. These men have their defenders; indeed (lest Antichrist leave anything untouched and unpolluted) priests and monks have aided this arrogance of theirs, and have sold them for a price those places from which they might show themselves off. All these men hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ with respect of persons, which the Apostles everywhere teach is far from the nature of faith; James, at the beginning of the second chapter of his epistle, has set this out at length. Moreover, the same men not only shame the poor, but are also the authors of impatience in them, so that they begin to accuse God's judgments and his providence more boldly. You see, then, how many crimes come together in one, and there is no need for a fuller demonstration where the matter itself speaks.

units.la: Audiamus Paulum ita concludentem: Quid vobis dicam? Laudabo vos? In hoc non laudo. Atqui in huius epistolæ exordio, eos non laudauit modo, verum etiam dignos judicauit, quorum nomine gratias ageret Deo, qui illos omni scientia & cognitione liberaliter donauisset. Et sub buius cap.initium eos laudauit, quòd ab ipso acceptas traditiones fideliter seruarent. In eò autem, de quo hic agitur illos laudare non potuit. Causa, quia quod faciebant, id ab instituto Christi alienum erat, vt ex ijs patebit, quae proximè sequuntur. Meminerint exempli huius ministri Ecclesiarum, vt neq; laudent neque defendant quod cum verbo Dei non conuenit, quocunq; exemplo & praetextu, aut quibuscunque rationibus pallietur. Vt enim verbum suum in Ecclesia Deus audiri vult, ita nihil sibi gratum & acceptum habet, quod illi aduersatur. Discant praeterea omnes alij quoque, ab eodem verbo pendere, & in sacrorum symbolorum perceptione per fidem in vnum IESVM CHRISTVM respicere, vt per hunc alantur & feruentur, qui solus panis ille viuus est, in quo vita vera potestas inueniri. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let us hear Paul concluding in this way: "What shall I say to you? Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise you." Yet at the beginning of this letter he did not merely praise them; he also judged them worthy of thanks to God, who had generously given them all knowledge and understanding. And at the beginning of this chapter he praised them because they faithfully kept the traditions they had received from him. But in the matter of which he is speaking here, he could not praise them, because what they were doing was foreign to the institution of Christ, as will be clear from what follows immediately. Let the ministers of the Churches remember this example, so that they neither praise nor defend what does not agree with the Word of God, whatever example, pretext or reasons may be offered to cover it. For just as God wills his Word to be heard in the Church, so he holds nothing pleasing and acceptable that opposes it. Let all others also learn to depend on that same Word, and in receiving the holy symbols to look by faith to the one Jesus Christ, so that they may be nourished and strengthened by him, who alone is that living bread in whom true life and power are found. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LIX.
units.tr: HOMILY LIX.

units.la: Ego enim accepi à Domino, quod & tradidi vobis: quòd Dominus IESVS ea nocte, qua proditus est, accepit panem, & gratijs actis fregit, ac dixit. Accipite, edite, hoc meum est corpus, quod pro vobis frangitur: hoc facite ad mei recordationem. Itidem & poculum, postquam cænassent, dicendo: Hoc poculum est Nouum illud testamentum in meo sanguine: hoc facite, quotiescunque biberitis, ad mei recordationem. Quotiescunque enim ederitis panem hunc, & poculum hoc biberitis, mortem Domini annuntiatis, donec venerit.
units.tr: For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you: that the Lord Jesus, the same night in which he was betrayed, took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and said: Take, eat; this is my body, which is broken for you; do this in remembrance of me. In the same way also he took the cup, after supper, saying: This cup is the new testament in my blood; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me. For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes.

units.la: QVamuis Deus, qui spiritus est, in spiritu adorari & coli velit, neque ullis officijs corporeis opus habeat, idem tamen propter nos ritus aliquos externos tradidit, quibus promissiones suas obsignat, beneficiorum ab ipso acceptorum memoriam commendat, & nos nostri officij admoneret. In illis igitur magna diligentia opus est, ne eos vel impiè negligamus, vel aliquo abusu siue prophano siue superstitioso corrumpamus. Quàm primum enim hoc fit, interna quoque animi religio consistere non potest, ideoq; sensim omnis Dei cultus intermoritur. Exempla huius generis in Veteri testamento passim occurrunt, quae commemorare longum foret. Imprimis autem memorabile est, quod in Corinthiorum Ecclesia accidit. Cùm enim illi primùm bono zelo Cænae Domini mysticae aliquid addidissent, mox eò vsque progressi sunt, vt Paulus eorum intemperantiam grauissimis & tantumnon Tragicis verbis reprehendendam esse duxerit. Fuit inter haec grauissimum, quòd eos non Dominicam Cænam edere, sed comessando & conuiuando propriae gulae & ventri indulgere dixit. Hoc vt abs se verè dictum esse demonstret, & simul rationem ostendat, qua tam turpem & pernitiosum errorem corrigere possint, nunc eos ad primam huius Sacramenti institutionem reuocat, & eandem diligenter exponit, vt ex huius consideratione discant, quàm procul ab eo recesserint, quod Christus in sua Ecclesia perpetuò voluit observari.
units.tr: Although God, who is a spirit, wishes to be worshipped and honoured in spirit, and has no need of any bodily services, he nevertheless, for our sake, has handed down certain outward rites, by which he seals his promises, commends to us the memory of the benefits received from him, and reminds us of our duty. In these rites, therefore, great care is needed, lest we either carelessly neglect them or corrupt them by some abuse, whether profane or superstitious. For as soon as this happens, the inward devotion of the mind also cannot stand, and so by degrees all worship of God dies out. Examples of this kind occur everywhere in the Old Testament, and it would be tedious to recount them. Especially memorable, however, is what happened in the church of the Corinthians. For when they had at first, with good zeal, added something to the mystical Lord's Supper, they soon advanced so far that Paul thought their intemperance must be rebuked in the most severe words, almost tragic ones. Among these faults the gravest was that, as he says, they did not eat the Lord's Supper but indulged their own gluttony and belly in feasting and revelry. To show that he has spoken truly in this, and at the same time to show the method by which they might correct so shameful and pernicious an error, he now calls them back to the first institution of this sacrament and carefully expounds it, so that from considering it they may learn how far they have departed from what Christ wished to be observed always in his Church.

units.la: Priusquam verò rem ipsam aggrediamur, singulari consideratione dignum est Pauli exemplum, quo vera ratio abolendi siue corrigendi abusus omnes continetur. Est haec, vt relicta prorsus omni humana ratione siue authoritate ad Dei verbum recurramus, & quid ille constituerit, quidue à nobis fieri velit consideremus. De hac olim Deus populum in Lege admonuit, quando iussit, vt causas obscuriores aut difficiliores ad locum Tabernaculi aut Templi referrent, & de illis Sacerdotem summum consulerent, quem ipse inter se & illos quasi internuntium aut interpretem constituisset. Et ideo Malachias dicebat: Labia Sacerdotis custodient scientiam, & legem ex ore eius requirent: Nam Legatus est Domini exercituum. Isaias item sui seculi homines, sub Achaz rege ad Deorum alienorum oracula & illorum mystas[?] siue diuinatores confugientes, his verbis compellat: Quòd si dixerint vobis, Scisciscamini à Pythonicis, diuinis, qui mussitant, & susurrant: Annon quaeq; gens suos Deos consulit? Num pro viuis ad mortuos? Ad Legem & testimonium. Qui non dixerint secundum verbum hoc, ijs non erit lux matutina. Quodsi Christum ipsum spectemus, hunc quoque hanc regulam secutum fuisse patebit, licet aeterna Patris sapientia sit, & pro imperio ac propria authoritate de quibusuis pronuntiare posset. De diuortijs enim interrogatus, ad primam coniugij institutionem aduersarios suos remittit, & vt haec piis cum nibus rata & salua esse debeat, docet: neque hic aliquid vel publico exemplo, vel veteri consuetudini tribuit, quae absque populi odio atque inuidia non poterat aboleri. Similiter à Sadducaeis de mortuorum resurrectione requisitus, non rationibus aut argumentis agit, quae infinita & firmissima afferre poterat, sed Deum Patrem inducit, qui defunctos viuere, & se illorum Deum esse, olim testatus est. Idem fecit, quando Scriba quidam de primo mandato quaestionem mouit. Ne Apostoli sibi plus quiddam licere putarent, peculiari Lege illos astrinxit, ne quid docerent, quam quod ab ipso traditum acceperint. Recte ergo Paulus, Corinthijs in Coenae mysticae negotio erranti bus primam huius institutionem ob oculos ponit, & huic cedere vult receptum & plerorumq; authoritate confirmatum illius Ecclesiae morem. Quod exemplum si hodie omnes sequerentur, qui nostri seculi de doctrina & religione controuersias componere student, mox pacem & concordiam ecclesijs restitutam videremus. At quia pleriq; vetustatem, Patres, Concilia, Principes, Reges, Pontifices & nescio quam Apostolicam successionem tonant, non mirum est, paucos illorum statutis & decretis obedire, errores autem & abusus quotidie confirmari. Solent enim qui vere pij sunt, ad solum Deum respicere, & nisi huius vocem audiant, acquiescere non possunt. Vani autem & quos Regum mundiq; fauor transfuersos abripit, illorum decretis sibi standum esse arbitrantur, quos prae alijs authoritate & potentia eminere vident. Posset hic latissime extendi oratio, & Pauli exemplum controuersijs articulis omnibus applicari, sed sufficiat cordatis ansam praebuisse. Omnes autem administri verbi, ita sibi in suo munere versandum esse meminerint, vt cum Paulo apud ecclesias suae fidei creditas dicere possint, se nihil tradidisse, quam quod à Domino IESV CHRISTO acceperint. Nunc ad rem ipsam accedemus, in qua explicanda breuiores erimus, eo quod pleraq; quae hic dici poterant, iam ante in D. D. Marci & Ioannis, Euangelistarum expositione dicta sint. Comprehendemus autem totam hanc causam tribus capitibus. Primo, quid sit de quo hic agitur, & quid nobis Christus tradiderit, docebimus. Secundo ritum & ordinem, quo Christus in hoc mysterio vsus est, inspiciemus: vt ex eo nobis constet, quis ritus hodie etiam in ecclesia obseruari debeat. Tertium, quod nostrum hic fit officium explicabit.
units.tr: Before we take up the matter itself, the example of Paul deserves special consideration, since it contains the true method of abolishing or correcting all abuses. It is this: that, setting aside entirely all human reason and authority, we return to the word of God and consider what he has ordained and what he wishes to be done by us. God once admonished the people of this in the Law, when he commanded that more obscure or difficult questions be referred to the place of the Tabernacle or the Temple, and that they consult about them the high priest, whom he had appointed as a kind of go-between and interpreter between himself and them. And therefore Malachi said: The lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth, for he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts. Isaiah likewise, addressing the people of his own age who, under King Ahaz, fled to the oracles of alien gods and to their initiates or diviners, speaks to them in these words: "If they say to you, 'Consult the mediums and the wizards, who chirp and mutter,' should not a people consult its gods? Should the living consult the dead? To the law and to the testimony! If they do not speak according to this word, there will be no morning light for them." If we look at Christ himself, it will be plain that he too followed this rule, although he is the eternal wisdom of the Father and could have pronounced on anything whatever by his own command and authority. For when he was asked about divorce, he refers his opponents back to the first institution of marriage, and teaches that it ought to remain valid and safe for the godly; nor does he grant anything here either to public example or to ancient custom, which could not have been abolished without the hatred and envy of the people. Likewise, when he was questioned by the Sadducees about the resurrection of the dead, he did not argue with reasons or arguments, which he could have brought forward in endless and most solid number, but brought forward God the Father, who had once declared that the dead live and that he is their God. He did the same when a certain scribe raised a question about the first commandment. Lest the apostles should think they might do something more, he bound them by a special law not to teach anything except what they had received from him. Rightly, therefore, Paul, when the Corinthians were going astray in the matter of the mystical Supper, sets before their eyes the first institution of it, and wishes the custom of that church, received and confirmed by the authority of most people, to give way to it. If all who in our own age strive to settle controversies about doctrine and religion would follow this example today, we would soon see peace and concord restored to the churches. But because most people thunder about antiquity, the Fathers, the Councils, princes, kings, pontifices, and I know not what Apostolic succession, it is no wonder that few obey their statutes and decrees, while errors and abuses are confirmed every day. For those who are truly godly are accustomed to look to God alone, and unless they hear his voice they cannot rest content. But the vain, whom the favour of kings and the world carries off in its wake, think that they must abide by the decrees of those whom they see to stand out above others in authority and power. This discussion could be extended very widely, and Paul's example applied to all the controverted articles, but it is enough to have given the sensible an occasion. All ministers of the Word, however, should remember that in their office they must so conduct themselves that, like Paul, they can say to the churches entrusted to their faith that they have handed on nothing except what they received from the Lord Jesus Christ. Now we shall come to the matter itself, and in explaining it we shall be briefer, because much that could be said here has already been said in the exposition of the Evangelists Mark and John. We will, however, comprehend this whole cause under three heads. First, we will teach what the matter is with which we are dealing here, and what Christ has handed down to us. Second, we will examine the rite and order which Christ used in this mystery, so that it may be clear to us what rite ought to be observed even today in the church. Third, it will explain what our duty here is.

units.la: Quoad primum, vulgo inter Christianos Coenae nomen obtinuit, & Paulus ipse hoc cap. Coenam Dominicam dixit. Causa nominis est, quod Christus illam post tempus vespertinum, iam nocte imminente instituit. In quo nos non ita haerere oportet, vt hodie etiam non nisi nocte eam celebrari debere putemus, ne nomen cum re ipsa pugnare videatur. Quod enim Christus fecit, non sine certis rationibus factum est. Primo enim paschale epulum, cui illa subfititui debuit, non alio tempore, quam sub noctem agere licebat: qua de re expressum Domini praeceptum apud Mosem extat. Deinde in postremum vitae suae actum huius mysterij institutionem differre voluit propter discipulos, quos tunc habebat, & nos: vt illi quidem mox in eius morte impleri viderent, quod nunc mystica hac actione adumbrabatur: nos vero in maiori pretio & honore habeamus, quod nobis à Filio Dei tunc traditum esse audimus, quando imminens vitae periculum illum de propria salute potius quam de nobis instituendis cogitare iubebat. Itaque merito apud Apostolos & omnem posteritatem tanta fuit exempli Christi authoritas, vt actionem hanc, quocunque tempore celebretur, κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν[?] Coenam Dominicam dixerint. Idem tamen eius celebrationem ad tempus noctutnum aut vespertinum astringere noluerunt: eo quod scirent, Christum nos à diurnum obseruatione liberauisse, vt liberum sit iam Christianis hominibus sacra mysteria obire, quandocunque sibi commodissimum esse, & ad aedificationem quam maxime seruire vident. Vt ergo non peccarunt veteres Christiani, qui persecutionis tempore nocturnos coetus egerunt, vt verbum Dei audirent, simul precarentur, & mensae Domini communicarent (quod hodie etiam pij multis in locis ob tyrannorum in ecclesiam grassantium iniquitatem facere coguntur) ita neque nos peccamus, qui tempore matutino, coetibus ecclesiasticis destinato & ad omnia seria magis idoneo, Coenam hanc sacram sumimus.
units.tr: As to the first point: among Christians the name "Supper" has commonly prevailed, and Paul himself in this chapter calls it the Lord's Supper. The reason for the name is that Christ instituted it after evening, when night was already approaching. We ought not to cling to this so closely that we think it must not be celebrated today except at night, lest the name seem to fight with the thing itself. For what Christ did was not done without definite reasons. First, the paschal feast, for which this rite was to be substituted, could be held at no other time than toward night; and an express command of the Lord on this point stands in Moses. Next, he wished to defer the institution of this mystery to the final act of his life, on account of the disciples he then had, and on account of us: so that they might see soon fulfilled in his death what was now foreshadowed by this mystical action, and we might hold in greater price and honour that it was handed down to us by the Son of God at a time when the imminent danger to his life bade him think of his own safety rather than of establishing it for us. And so, rightly, the authority of Christ's example was so great among the apostles and all posterity that they called this action, at whatever time it is celebrated, the Lord's Supper par excellence [κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν]. Nevertheless, they were unwilling to bind its celebration to the night-time or evening, because they knew that Christ had freed us from observance of days, so that it is now lawful for Christians to perform the sacred mysteries whenever they see it most convenient and most serviceable to edification. Thus the ancient Christians did not sin when, in time of persecution, they held nightly assemblies to hear the word of God, to pray together, and to partake of the table of the Lord (which godly people are even today compelled to do in many places, because of the iniquity of tyrants who rage against the church); so neither do we sin who receive this holy Supper in the morning, at the hour set apart for ecclesiastical assemblies and better suited to all serious matters.

units.la: Nunc illud potius tenere conuenit, Cœnam istam minimè vulgarem, sed IESV CHRI-STI Cœnam esse, quæ sub vilißimorum symbolorum specie mysteria saluberrima comprehen-dat. Docent hoc ipsius Domini verba, qui idem præceptum bis inculcat, dicens: Hoc facite ad mei recordationem. Quod item de pane dicit: Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis frangitur. Et de poculo: Hoc poculum est Nouum illud testamentum in meo sanguine. Vel vt Marcus recitat: Hic est sanguis meus, qui est Noui testamenti: qui pro multis effunditur. Quæ omnia si probè considerentur, quid sit Cœna docent, & definitionem eius nobis constituunt veram, simplicem & perfectam, quæ eiusmodi est: Cœna est actio sacra, in qua ex Christi mandato panem & vinum inter nos distribuimus & sumimus, ad recordationem mortis ipsius, qua is Nouum testamentum compleuit ratumq; fecit.
units.tr: It is better now to hold firmly to this: this Supper is by no means ordinary, but the Supper of Jesus Christ, which under the appearance of the humblest symbols contains the most saving mysteries. The words of the Lord himself teach this, when he twice impresses the same command, saying: "Do this in remembrance of me." He says likewise of the bread: "This is my body, which is broken for you." And of the cup: "This cup is the New Testament in my blood." Or as Mark recounts it: "This is my blood of the New Testament, which is poured out for many." If all these words are carefully considered, they teach what the Supper is, and they set before us a true, simple and complete definition of it, which is this: the Supper is a sacred action, in which, by Christ's command, we distribute and receive among ourselves bread and wine, in remembrance of his death, by which he fulfilled and ratified the New Testament.

units.la: Quo loco Noui testamenti ratio nobis consideranda venit, quam Paulus in epistola ad Hebræos diligenter ex Ieremia explicat. Quia enim veteres Iudæi fœdus siue testamentum Dei, quod cum patribus ipsorum fecerat, sua perfidia & inobedientia violarant, nouo opus erat. Id per Ieremiam Dominus pollicetur, cuius summa est: Ego ero Deus eorum, & ipsi erunt mihi populus, id est, peculium meum & filiorum instar, quos & in hac vita mea gratiæ donis ornabo atq; tuebor, & olim regni mei cœlestis hæredes faciam. Et quia huic promissioni obstare poterant peccata, quibus nos à Dei regno excludi omnes scripturæ testantur, addit: Propitius ero iniquitatibus eorum, & peccatorum ipsorum nō recordabor amplius. Atqui nihil aliud his omnibus continetur, quàm quod olim Abrahamo & reliquis patribus promissum fuit. Cur ergo testamentum Nouum dicitur? Primum, propter instaurationem veteris illius pacti siue testamenti, cuius Deus omnino oblitus esse videbatur, cùm populo in Babylonem abducto vrbs & templum in ruinis iacerent, & fœda esset cùm reipub. tum Ecclesiæ totius dissipatio. Deinde, quòd nouum populum Deus adoptare, & Filij sui regnum per omnes gentes extendere voluit. Postremò, propter nouam Ecclesiæ & externæ religionis faciem. Oportebat enim abolitis tristibus & cruentis ceremonijs, & operosa illa cultus Leuitici celebratione sublata, religionis formam faciliorem & Sacramenta iucundiora & mitiora substitui. Quod Christum in ipsa Cœna facere cœpisse videmus, quando in locum epuli paschalis & sanguinis agni, qui postibus aspergebatur, lætam suæ mortis recordationem sub panis & vini symbolis instituit. Non temere igitur Nouum testamentum dicitur pactum illud, quo salutem & vitam æternam Deus nobis promisit. At quia totam hanc salutis nostræ rationem testamento compleƈti voluit, mortem testatoris intercedere necesse erat, quando ad promissæ aut legatæ hæreditatis possessionem nemo venire potest, quoad ille in viuis fuerit. Porrò Deum mori impossibile erat, cuius vera & essentialis proprietas est, non modò immortalem, sed ἀφθαρτον [?], id est, nulli prorsus corruptioni obnoxium esse. Filium ergo Dei vnigenitum, & Patri coëssentialem, in mundum venire & hominem fieri oportuit ex æterno Patris consilio, vt qui Deus verus æternus & immortalis est, in assumpta hominis natura mortem subiret, & morte sua testamentum illud ratum faceret, nosque in regni cœlestis possessionem induceret.
units.tr: Here we must consider the nature of the New Testament, which Paul carefully explains from Jeremiah in his epistle to the Hebrews. For the ancient Jews had violated the covenant or testament of God, which he had made with their fathers, by their faithlessness and disobedience, so a new one was needed. The Lord promises this through Jeremiah, and its sum is: "I will be their God, and they shall be my people," that is, my own possession and like my children, whom I will adorn and protect with the gifts of grace in this life of mine, and one day make the heirs of my heavenly kingdom. And because sins, by which all of us are shut out of God's kingdom, as all the Scriptures testify, could stand in the way of this promise, he adds: "I will be merciful to their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more." Yet all of this contains nothing other than what was once promised to Abraham and the other fathers. Why, then, is it called the New Testament? First, because of the renewal of that old covenant or testament, of which God seemed utterly to have forgotten, when the city and temple lay in ruins, the people had been carried off to Babylon, and the dispersion both of the commonwealth and of the whole Church was miserable. Second, because God wished to adopt a new people and to extend the kingdom of his Son through all nations. Last, because of the new face of the Church and of external religion. For it was fitting that, with the sad and bloody ceremonies abolished, and with that laborious celebration of Levitical worship taken away, a simpler form of religion and more pleasant and gentle sacraments should be put in their place. We see Christ beginning to do this in the Supper itself, when, in place of the paschal feast and the blood of the lamb that was sprinkled on the doorposts, he instituted, under the symbols of bread and wine, a joyful remembrance of his death. It is therefore not without reason that the covenant by which God promised us salvation and eternal life is called the New Testament. But since he wished to complete this whole plan of our salvation by a testament, the death of the testator had necessarily to intervene, since no one can come into possession of a promised or bequeathed inheritance while the one who bequeathed it is still alive. Moreover, it was impossible for God to die, whose true and essential property is not only to be immortal but [ἄφθαρτον], that is, to be utterly subject to no corruption. Therefore, by the eternal counsel of the Father, the only-begotten Son of God, coessential with the Father, had to come into the world and become man, so that he who is the true, eternal and immortal God might undergo death in the nature of man he had taken on, and by his death might ratify that testament and bring us into possession of the heavenly kingdom.

units.la: De hoc igitur nos Christus admonet, quando Nouum testamentum in sanguine suo fundari dicit, & huius symbolum in poculo mystico nobis propinat. Verborum itaque eius hic sensus esse videtur: Scitis quæ humani generis calamitas fuerit, quod propter peccata à regno Dei exclusum, & ad inferos damnatum fuit. Remedium in humanis nullum est. Vnica autem salutis spes in Noui illius testamenti promissione habebatur, quam per Prophetas vobis Deus proposuit. At dilata hucusque res fuit, & quamuis legata esset miseris mortalibus æternæ salutis hæreditas, ad hanc tamen nemo admittebatur, cùm testamentum illud nondum confirmatum aut ratum esset. Nunc verò optatus ille dies illuxit, nunc tempus illud diu expectatum appropinquauit, quo ego mei corporis & sanguinis pretio totius mundi peccata redimā, & meæ mortis intercessione testamentum illud complebo, vt posthac liber vobis sit ad regni cœlestis & vitæ æternæ hæreditatem aditus. Vtq; minus dubitetis, en vobis meæ mortis, imò corporis & sanguinis mei, certissima symbola. Accipite ergo panem hunc, & edite: accipite poculum hoc, & ex eo bibite: quodq; nunc facitis, id vobis solenne fit, & in posterum quoq; ex meo mandato facite. Quotiescunq; autem feceritis, meminisse vos velim, vos mei corporis & sanguinis pretio redemptos, & salutem omnibus nume-rus perfectam per me vobis partam esse, deniq; vos in me habere panem & potum vitæ, qui vos in-ter huius seculi palæstram alat, recreet & feruet ad vitam æternam. Itaq; non in symbolis istis hærete, sed quando panem & poculum sumitis, simul corpus & sanguinem meum fideli mente concipite, quæ pro vobis in mortem tradita salutem vobis instaurarunt, &c.
units.tr: Christ therefore reminds us of this when he says that the New Testament is founded in his blood, and offers us its symbol in the mystical cup. The sense of his words therefore seems to be this: "You know what a calamity for the human race it was that, on account of sins, it was shut out of the kingdom of God and condemned to hell. There is no remedy among men. The only hope of salvation, however, lay in the promise of that New Testament, which God set before you through the prophets. But the matter has been deferred until now, and although the inheritance of eternal salvation was bequeathed to wretched mortals, no one was admitted to it, since that testament was not yet confirmed or ratified. But now that longed-for day has dawned, now that time, long awaited, has drawn near, when I shall redeem the sins of the whole world by the price of my body and blood, and fulfil that testament by the intercession of my death, so that from now on the way to the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom and eternal life may be open to you. And so that you may have less doubt, behold, the most certain symbols of my death, indeed of my body and blood. Take therefore this bread and eat; take this cup and drink from it; and what you now do shall become a solemn custom for you, and in future also do it at my command. Whenever you do so, I would have you remember that you have been redeemed by the price of my body and blood, that complete salvation has been won for you through me, and finally that you have in me the bread and drink of life, which will nourish you amid the struggle of this age, refresh you and sustain you unto eternal life. Therefore do not cling to these symbols, but when you take the bread and cup, at the same time conceive with a faithful mind my body and blood, which were given up to death for you and restored your salvation, etc."

units.la: Hæc & quæcunq; præterea in hanc sententiam dici possunt, paucis hisce verbis Christus com-prehendit. Ex quibus colligimus præcipuum Cœnæ huius finem atq; usum esse recordationem & commemorationem mortis Domini. Vbi nemo putauerit, nos de otiosa & inani recordatione lo-qui, qualis est rerum nihil ad nos pertinentium: sed eam intelligimus, quæ per fidem in Christi morte intenta, illum ipsum cum omnibus bonis suis apprehendit, adeo ut nobis unitus nos alat & feruet ad vitam æternam. Hunc autem usum & finem Cœnæ proprium & principalem esse dici-mus, quia huius solius Christus meminit, his dicens: Hoc facite ad mei recordationem. Et Paulus post expositam institutionis Cœnæ historiam illud ipsum repetens ait: Quotiescunq; ederitis panem hunc, & poculum hoc biberitis, mortem Domini annunciatis, donec veniat. Viderunt hoc veteres, qui actioni huic Eucharistiæ nomen indiderunt, quod gratiarum actionem sonat. Cæterum ex hoc fine alij dependent, vel potius cum eo coniuncti sunt. Inter quos primus est fidei in Christum professio publica. Secundus, quod in unum Ecclesiæ corpus colligimur, & (ut supra Paulus dixit) multi unus panis efficimur: quo nomine illam veteres σύνδειπνον dixerunt. Tertius, quod nos officij multiuariam admonet. Docet enim, eos qui Christum redemptorem profitentur, & de eius mensa edunt atq; bibunt, nullis alienis sacris communicare debere: quando fieri non potest, ut simul mensæ Christi & mensæ dæmoniorum participes simus. Deinde innocentiæ & sanctitatis studium nobis Cœna hæc commendat. Si enim serio profitemur, nos pretiosò Christi corpore & sanguine redemptos esse, simul utiq; intelligemus, annitinos[?] debere, ut sanctitatem & dignitatem illam sedulò tueamur, in quam nos ille collocauit. Præterea ad fouendam & feruandam charitatem Cœnæ usus plurimum prodest. Quomodo enim possunt odium & simultates admittere, qui se in Christo eiusdē corporis membra factos esse cogitant? Quomodo item non omne odium ex corde expuant, qui non fida[?] fide cum reliquis eundem Christum profitentibus ad eius mensam accedunt? Exhibet ergo nobis Cœna amplissimam cogitandi nosq; ipsos exercendi materiam in omnibus ijs, quæ tam præsenti quam futuræ vitæ seruiunt, in qua qui diligentiores Paulo fuerint, ij nunquam dicent, nos nihil præter otiosam mortis dominicæ commemorationem agnoscere.
units.tr: Christ sums up all of this, and whatever else may be said to the same effect, in these few words. From them we gather that the chief purpose and use of this Supper is the remembrance and commemoration of the Lord's death. No one should suppose that we mean an idle and empty remembrance, such as of things that have nothing to do with us. We mean that remembrance which, through faith, is fixed on Christ's death and lays hold of him himself with all his benefits, so that, united to us, he nourishes us and keeps us alive to eternal life. We call this the proper and principal use and purpose of the Supper, because Christ mentions only this one, saying: "Do this in remembrance of me." Paul also, after setting out the account of the institution of the Supper, repeats the same thing and says: "As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes." The ancients saw this, and they gave this action the name Eucharist, which means thanksgiving. Moreover, other purposes depend on this one, or rather are joined with it. The first of these is the public profession of faith in Christ. The second is that we are gathered into one body of the Church and (as Paul said above) are made one bread, a name by which the ancients called it a synaxis [σύνδειπνον]. The third is that it reminds us of our duty in many ways. For it teaches that those who profess Christ as Redeemer and eat and drink at his table must not share in any alien rites, since it is impossible for us to be partakers both of the table of Christ and of the table of demons. Next, this Supper commends to us a zeal for innocence and holiness. For if we seriously profess that we have been redeemed by the precious body and blood of Christ, we will at the same time understand that we ought to strive to guard carefully that holiness and dignity in which he has placed us. Furthermore, the use of the Supper greatly helps to foster and preserve love. For how can those who think of themselves as members of the same body of Christ admit hatred and quarrels? Likewise, how can those who approach his table without sincere faith alongside the others fail to spit out all hatred from their heart? The Supper therefore gives us a very broad matter for thought and for exercising ourselves in all those things that serve both the present life and the life to come. Those who are more diligent than Paul will never say that we recognise nothing beyond an idle commemoration of the Lord's death.

units.la: Confutantur autem hoc loco, qui alios Cœnæ Dominicæ fines atq; usus fingunt, aut ab alijs confictos defendunt. Inter quos detestabilis maximè est eorum audacia, qui illam totam in sacrificium commutarunt, in quo Christum quotidie pro peccatis vivorum & mortuorum immolari aiunt. Quod quid aliud est, quàm sacrificium corporis & sanguinis Christi in cruce factu evacuare et irritum reddere? Proximi his sunt, qui etsi illos tă impij erroris pudeat, & Christu denuo sacrificari negent, sacrificij tamè per illu facti applicationem fieri contendunt. At ne hoc quidè in Cœnæ sua institutione ille docuit. Sacrificium autem & omne meritum Christi nobis per Evangelium applicari, à nobis autem fide apprehendi constat, juxta illud: Prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ, qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, servabitur. Errant etiam, qui corpora nostra pane & vino hoc mystico ad resurrectionem pasci docent: quasi vero non eorum quoq; corpora resurrectura sint, qui & Cœnæ nunquam communicarunt, & à fide Christiana prorsus alieni sunt. Similis prope illorum error est, qui ex Cœna viaticum quoddam finxerunt, quo iam morituros instrui oporteat, & ij in domos priuatas illam deferentes ex publica priuatam faciunt. Quod ipsum quoq; ab Apostolis nuspiam factitatum esse legimus. Iacobus quidem ad ægrotantes presbyteros aut verbi ministros accersiri iubet, qui pro illis orare & eos oleo inungere debeant in nomine Domini (quod sanationis symbolum fuit olim, cum adhuc dona illa peculiaria & miraculosa vigerent) at Eucharistiæ ad eosdem deferendæ mentionem facit nullam. Scimus quidem superstitionem hanc vetustissimam esse, & huius mentionem apud Cyprianum quoq; fieri: sed quia eam Apostoli ignorarunt, nos eam merito reiicimus, ut & multa alia, quæ olim quidam vel superstitione vel zelo inconsulto decepti fecerunt. Nostro autem seculo omnium abusuum circa Cœnam causa est præcipua, falsa & erronea Pontificum doctrina, qua toti mundo persuadere conati sunt, ipsissimum Christi corpus verum & naturale in Cœna ministrorum manibus contrectari & exhiberi, sumi item & vere atq; corporaliter edi ab omnibus, qui ad illam accedunt. Quorum errorem multi etiam ex nostris prosi-tentur, qui corporalem IESV CHRISTI præsentiā finem Cœnæ præcipuum esse clamant, quasi ideo hæc instituta sit, ut in ea à nobis corporaliter inveniri, prehendi, palpari, ore deniq; percipi & manducari queat. Et hi dum illis contradicimus, nos testamentum filij Dei violare, & Christum mendacij arguere vociferantur. Hinc deniq; sub renascentis Euangelij lucem exorta est infelix illa contentio de Sacramentis, quæ multorum oculos ita perstringit, ut in sola symbola & quam ipsi sibi imaginantur corporis Christi præsentiā intenti, Cœnæ usum proprium negligant, & in charitatem fraternam maximè peccent, cuius illa vinculum esse debebat. At quid obsecro horum dixit Christus? Certè si eius verba examines, nihil huius sonant, neque nobis aliud ille mandauit, quàm ut hoc faciamus ad sui recordationem.
units.tr: These words refute those who invent other ends and uses of the Lord's Supper, or who defend such inventions made by others. Most detestable among them is the audacity of those who have turned the whole Supper into a sacrifice, in which they say Christ is daily immolated for the sins of the living and the dead. What else is this than to empty the sacrifice of the body and blood of Christ made on the cross and render it void? Close to these are those who, though ashamed of such impious error and denying that Christ is sacrificed again, nevertheless contend that the sacrifice made by him is applied through the Supper. But he did not teach even this in the institution of his Supper. That the sacrifice and every merit of Christ are applied to us through the Gospel, and apprehended by us through faith, is established by the saying: "Preach the Gospel to every creature; he who believes and is baptized shall be saved." Those also err who teach that our bodies are nourished to resurrection by this mystical bread and wine, as if the bodies of those who never communicated in the Supper and are wholly alien to the Christian faith were not also to rise again. Similar to this is the error of those who have invented from the Supper a kind of viaticum, by which those about to die ought to be fortified, and who, carrying it to private houses, make a private thing out of a public one. We read nowhere that the Apostles ever practised this. James indeed bids the elders or ministers of the Word to be summoned to the sick, who ought to pray for them and anoint them with oil in the name of the Lord (which was once a sign of healing, when those peculiar and miraculous gifts still flourished); but he makes no mention of carrying the Eucharist to the same sick. We know indeed that this superstition is very ancient, and that mention of it is made also in Cyprian; but because the Apostles did not know it, we rightly reject it, as also many other things which some in former times did, deceived either by superstition or by ill-considered zeal. In our own age, however, the chief cause of all abuses concerning the Supper is the false and erroneous doctrine of the Papists, by which they have tried to persuade the whole world that the very body of Christ, true and natural, is handled and offered in the hands of the ministers in the Supper, and likewise that it is eaten truly and bodily by all who approach it. Many even of our own people profess this error, who cry out that the bodily presence of Jesus Christ is the chief end of the Supper, as if it had been instituted so that in it he might be bodily found, grasped, touched, and finally received and eaten by the mouth. And while we contradict them, these men shout that we violate the testament of the Son of God and charge Christ with lying. Hence, finally, under the light of the renewed Gospel, that unhappy contention about the sacraments has arisen, which so dazzles the eyes of many that, intent only on the signs and on the bodily presence of Christ as they imagine it, they neglect the proper use of the Supper and sin most grievously against fraternal charity, of which the Supper ought to be the bond. But what, I ask, did Christ say of these things? Certainly, if you examine his words, they sound nothing of this, nor did he enjoin anything on us except that we do this in remembrance of him.

units.la: Objiciunt nobis adversarij: Atqui de pane loquens dixit: Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vo-bis traditur. De poculo item: Hic est sanguis meus, &c. Sunt hæc verba clara, perspicua, diserta, & verbum substantiuum, Est, omnem Tropum excludit, ut aliter quàm sonant, accipi non possint. Agnoscimus et nos Christi verba, neq; ea mutata, multò minus sublata volumus, ut quidā impudentissimè calumniantur. Quod autem illi per verbū substantiuum, Est, Tropum omnem ex-cludi aiunt, id illis dare non possumus. Ioannes Euangelista dixit, Verbum caro factū est. Quæ locutio plus quiddā sonat, quam si verbū carnem esse dixisset. Si quis tamen literam pertinacius urgere velit, in hæresim incidet, & Christi Deitatē abnegabit, ut quæ mutationem passa, & in humanam naturam conversa sit. Necessario igitur ad Tropū confugere oportet, & cum Paulo locutionem istā exponere, qui æternum Dei Filium semen Abrahami assumpsisse scribit. Itaq; verbum caro factum dicetur, non conversione (quam verborum litera exprimit) sed assumptione carnis ut jam Deus & homo fit, qui prius homo solummodo erat. Et quia huius generis de semetipso multa dixit, in quibus literam urgere absurdum foret, hic quoq; res ipsa, de qua agitur, propius inspici debet, ut ex ea verborum sensum proprium colligamus. Atqui in eo nobis cum adversarijs conuenit, Christum hic Sacramentum instituisse. Ergo locutiones istæ Sacramentales sunt, & pro communi Sacramentorum ratione exponi debent. Constant autem Sacramenta duabus rebus, Signo externo & Reinterna seu spirituali, quæ per signum adumbratur: & quia inter duo hæc analogia est proprissima arctissimaq;, fit, ut signo rei signatæ nomē communicetur. Potest hoc infinitis Scripturæ testimonijs & exemplis demonstrari. Hac enim ratione Circumcisio fœdus Domini, epulum paschale transitus Domini, sacrificia peccata & peccatorum expiatio, arca deniq; testimonij Dominus exercituum dicuntur. Quid, quòd Paulus in proximo cap. petram, quæ Israelitis desertum errantibus potum profudit, Christum fuisse dixit? Baptismum item regenerationis & innouationis lauacrum, deniq; peccatorum ablutionem Apostoli dicere consueuerunt: quod secundum literam nō accipi debere, eorum vita probat, qui etsi baptizati sint, veterem tamen hominem in se regnare patiuntur, & toti peccatis seruiunt. Neq; tamen falsi arguitur Spiritus sanctus. Reuera enim ablutionis peccatorum & regenerationis certissimum sigillum & pignus est Baptismus, eiusdem vero fructus nō nisi in electis et credentibus se exerit. Hæc cum in locutionibus illis omnes observare possint, neque de ijs aliqua sit controuersia, cur absurda & impia expositio videtur, si panem corpus Christi, & vinum sanguinem eiusdem dici dicamus, eò quòd corporis & sanguinis eius symbola sint, quæ totum mortis Christi fructum nobis & adumbrant & obsignant?
units.tr: Our opponents object: "Yet speaking of the bread he said: 'This is my body, which is given for you.' Likewise of the cup: 'This is my blood,' etc. These words are clear, plain, and explicit, and the substantive verb 'is' excludes every trope, so that they cannot be taken otherwise than they sound." We too acknowledge the words of Christ, and we wish them neither changed nor, much less, removed, as some most shamelessly calumniate us. But that they say the substantive verb 'is' excludes every trope, we cannot grant them. John the Evangelist said: "The Word was made flesh." This expression means something more than if he had said the Word is flesh. If anyone, however, wishes to press the letter more stubbornly, he will fall into heresy and deny the deity of Christ, as if it had undergone a change and been converted into human nature. It is necessary therefore to take refuge in a trope, and with Paul to explain that expression, who writes that the eternal Son of God took on the seed of Abraham. Thus "the Word was made flesh" will be said not by conversion (which the letter of the words expresses) but by the assumption of flesh, so that he who previously was only man now is both God and man. And since he said many things of this kind about himself, in which it would be absurd to press the letter, here too the matter itself under discussion ought to be examined more closely, so that from it we may gather the proper sense of the words. Yet in this we agree with our opponents, that Christ here instituted a sacrament. Therefore these expressions are sacramental, and ought to be explained according to the common manner of the sacraments. Now sacraments consist of two things, an external sign and an internal or spiritual reality, which is shadowed forth by the sign; and because between these two there is a most proper and close analogy, it comes about that the name of the thing signified is communicated to the sign. This can be demonstrated by countless testimonies and examples of Scripture. For in this way circumcision is called the covenant of the Lord, the paschal feast the Lord's passover, sacrifices are called sins and the expiation of sins, and finally the ark is called the Lord of hosts, the ark of testimony. What of the fact that Paul, in the chapter immediately preceding, said that the rock which poured out drink for the Israelites wandering in the desert was Christ? The Apostles also were accustomed to call baptism the washing of regeneration and renewal, and finally the cleansing of sins; that this ought not to be taken according to the letter, the life of those proves who, though baptized, nevertheless allow the old man to reign in themselves and wholly serve their sins. Yet the Holy Spirit is not thereby charged with falsehood. For baptism is indeed the most certain seal and pledge of the cleansing of sins and of regeneration, but its fruit shows itself only in the elect and believers. Since all can observe these things in those expressions, and there is no controversy about them, why should it seem an absurd and impious exposition if we say that the bread is called the body of Christ, and the wine his blood, because they are the signs of his body and blood, which both shadow forth and seal for us the whole fruit of the death of Christ?

units.la: Respondent ad ista adversarij: Veteris quidem testamenti locutiones figuratas esse & secundum analogiā, quæ inter signa & res signatas est, exponi debere fatemur. Illic enim res tam manifesta est, ut de eo ambigere nemo possit, nisi qui plus quàm Judaico errore velit salutē in pecudū sanguine & rebus periturís collocare. At hic nulla ratio nos cogit, ut quæ Christus iam moriturus locutus est, aliter quàm verba sonant, intelligamus, ideoq; nefas fuerit alium sensum illis affingere. His responderi poterat, nos necessitate cogi, ut in locutionibus Christi de Cœna Tropum statuamus: quia nisi id fiat, flagitium jubere videbuntur: qua nota figuratas locutiones agnoscere docet Augustinus lib. 3. de doctrina Christiana cap. 16. Sed quid dicetis ô fratres, si demonstremus nos rationibus grauissimis cogi, ut locutiones Christi de pane & vino Cœna per Tropum exponantur, & nisi id fiat, præcipuos fidei Christianæ articulos labefactari & salutis nostræ fundamenta concuelli[?]? Exordiamur autem ab his verbis, de quibus controuertitur, in quibus Diuos Euangelistas Tropum & figuratam locutionem agnouisse, vel ex eo patet, quòd in ijs recitandis non ea curiositate vsi sunt, ut ijsdem omnino verbis & syllabis omnes insistendum putarint, sed alij alijs breuiores sunt, alij verba quædam mutarunt, aut aliter reddiderunt, sicuti in ijs fieri solet, quæ figurate dicta, alium quam literalem sensum requirunt. Matthæus enim & Marcus, Christum de pane dixisse scribunt: Accipite, edite, hoc est corpus meum: nec quicquam præterea addunt. Lucas autem adijcit: Quod pro vobis datur. Quam particulam Paulus quoq, aliter reddit, nimirum: Quod pro vobis frangitur. Priores ergo duo panem simpliciter à Christo corpus suum dictum esse testantur. Lucas autem, ne quis in panis symbolo hæreret, ad mortem Christi nos remittit, & huius corpus pro nobis traditum esse ostendit, ut intelligamus fructum huius mysterij non ex actione ista mystica, sed ex morte pendere, in quam seipsum[?] Filius Dei pro nobis tradidit. Paulus item fractionis meminit. Hoc est (inquit) corpus meum, quod pro vobis frangitur: Quod absque Metonymia exponi non potest. Nam corpus Christi neque frangi debuisse, neque etiam fractum fuisse in cruce, Ioannes Euangelista testatur. Paulus ergo ad corpus Christi transfert, quod in eius symbolo, panem nimirum, fit quando Cœna peragitur: ut ita nos distributionis & communionis admoneat, qua credentes omnes tam illo quàm bonis eius omnibus fruuntur. Scio aliquos fractionis vocabulum ad acerbissimum illud mortis genus referre, quo corpus eius tantum non contusum atq; contritum fit: sed neq; hi Tropum omnem effugiunt, quia tunc Paulus amplificatione aut hyperbole vsus dicetur ad exprimendam mortis Christi acerbitatem. At ego non libenter quocunq; sensu corpori eius fractionem tribuerim, cùm hanc Spiritus sanctus tam diserte neget, ut typum quoq; olim in agno paschali extare voluerit, quo verum agnum Dei nihil huius passurum esse adumbrabatur.
units.tr: Our opponents reply to these things: "We grant indeed that the figurative expressions of the Old Testament are to be explained according to the analogy that exists between signs and the things signified. For there the matter is so plain that no one can doubt it, unless he wishes to place salvation in the blood of beasts and in perishable things, which is more than Jewish error. But here no reason compels us to understand what Christ, about to die, spoke otherwise than the words sound; and therefore it would be wrong to attach another sense to them." To this it could be answered that we are compelled by necessity to posit a trope in Christ's words about the Supper: for unless this is done, he would seem to command a crime; by this mark Augustine teaches us to recognise figurative expressions, in book 3 of On Christian Doctrine, chapter 16. But what will you say, brethren, if we demonstrate that we are compelled by the weightiest reasons to explain Christ's words about the bread and wine of the Supper by a trope, and that unless this is done the chief articles of the Christian faith are weakened and the foundations of our salvation shaken? Let us begin, however, with those words about which there is controversy, in which it is plain that the divine evangelists recognised a trope and a figurative expression, from the fact that in reciting them they did not use such scrupulous care as to think everyone must keep to exactly the same words and syllables; rather, some are briefer than others, some changed certain words or rendered them differently, as is customary in those expressions which, being spoken figuratively, require a sense other than the literal. For Matthew and Mark write that Christ spoke of the bread: "Take, eat; this is my body," and add nothing further. Luke, however, adds: "which is given for you." Paul too renders this particle differently, namely: "which is broken for you." The first two therefore testify that Christ simply called the bread his body. Luke, however, lest anyone should stick at the sign of the bread, refers us to the death of Christ and shows that his body was given for us, so that we may understand that the fruit of this mystery depends not on that mystical action but on the death into which the Son of God delivered himself for us. Paul also mentions the breaking: "This is (he says) my body, which is broken for you," which cannot be explained without metonymy. For John the Evangelist testifies that the body of Christ ought not to have been broken, nor was it broken on the cross. Paul therefore transfers to the body of Christ what is done to its sign, namely the bread, when the Supper is celebrated; so that he may remind us of the distribution and communion by which all believers enjoy both him and all his goods. I know that some refer the word breaking to that most bitter kind of death, by which his body was almost bruised and crushed; but these too do not escape every trope, since then Paul will be said to have used amplification or hyperbole to express the bitterness of Christ's death. But I, for my part, would not gladly ascribe breaking to his body in any sense, since the Holy Spirit denies it so plainly, and even willed that there should be a type of it in the paschal lamb, by which it was foreshadowed that the true Lamb of God would suffer nothing of the kind.

units.la: Quòd si ad poculi verba veniamus, illic & maior diuersitas, & Tropi plures occurrunt, ut mirum sit aliquos tam vecordes esse, ut nos odio dignos dicere audeant, qui illa figuratè accipienda esse dicimus. Nam Matthæus illa sic enunciat: Hic est sanguis meus, qui est Noui testamenti, qui pro multis effunditur, in peccatorum remissionem. Marcus cum illo per omnia consentit, nisi quòd posteremam de remissione peccatorum particulam omittit. Lucas verò verba ista sic recitat: Hoc poculum est Nouum illud testamentum in sanguine meo qui pro vobis effunditur. Et cum hoc idem omnino Paulus dicit, omissa tamen etiam posterema illa particula, Qui pro vobis effunditur. Quid ergo hic faciemus ô fratres? Clamabimus ne: Verba sunt diserta, propria, rotunda, neque aliter quàm secundum literam debent accipi? Atqui Euangelistarum & Apostolorum authoritas hoc dicere non finit, qui illa aliter atque aliter recitauerunt. Num verò aliquos eorum vel memoria lapsos esse, vel priuata temeritate quædam mutauisse, aut alia suppositisse dicemus? Absit. Ita enim tota, quam nobis tradiderunt & proprio sanguine obsignarunt, salutis ratio in dubium veniret? Quid ergo restat, quàm ut fateamur, hoc ex singulari spiritus sancti consilio factum esse, qui futuras super hac re contentiones & multorum superstitionem præuidens, admonere nos voluit, ut neque in literam, neque in externa symbola nimis intenti simus, sed rem ipsam propius inspiciamus, de qua agitur. Ideo quod Matthæus & Marcus pro communi Sacramentalium locutionum more simpliciter enuntiarunt, id Paulus & Lucas Spiritu dictante sic reddiderunt, ut & Tropum in Christi verbis latentem ceu digito monstrarent, & totius negotij fructum traderent, denique nobis authores essent animos altius euehendi ad eorum contemplationem, quæ per symbola panis & vini significantur. Primò enim poculi voce vtuntur, continente nimirum pro re quæ continetur: quæ aperta Metonymiæ species est. Deinde quod alibi dicitur: Hic est sanguis meus, qui est Noui testamenti: illi reddunt: Hoc poculum est Nouum illud testamentum in meo sanguine, qui pro vobis effunditur. At sic loquendo nos tantumnon excitant & monent, ut non tam ad effusi sanguinis historiam, quàm ad illius fructum siue effectum respiciamus, qui in peccatorum nostrorum remissione consistit, ex qua Noui testamenti completio, de qua ante diximus, dependet. At quis hic non videt effectum pro causa efficiente aut materiali poni? Frustra ergo illi homines nobis succenfent, quòd Christi verba mutemus, & Tropum obtrudamus, vbi rei veritas nullum admittat. Quin potius Euangelistis & Apostolis litem moueant, qui Christi verba sic interpretantur, vt nos à crassis corporeæ manducationis & potationis cogitationibus ad veram & salutarem Christi & bonorum eius perceptionem excitent, quæ in spiritu per solam fidem fit.
units.tr: But if we come to the words of the cup, there is again greater variation and several tropes appear, so that it is remarkable that some are so mad as to dare to call us worthy of hatred because we say these words are to be taken figuratively. For Matthew sets them out thus: "This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins." Mark agrees with him in every respect, except that he omits the final clause about the remission of sins. Luke recites the words thus: "This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you." Paul says the very same thing, though he also omits that final clause, "which is shed for you." What shall we do here, brethren? Shall we cry out that the words are plain, proper and exact, and must be taken only according to the letter? Yet the authority of the Evangelists and Apostles does not allow us to say this, since they recited the words in different ways. Shall we say that some of them slipped in memory, or by private rashness changed certain things, or inserted others? Far from it. For then the whole plan of salvation which they handed down to us and sealed with their own blood would come into doubt. What remains, then, but to confess that this was done by the singular counsel of the Holy Spirit, who, foreseeing the future disputes over this matter and the superstition of many, wished to warn us not to be overly intent upon the letter or the outward signs, but to look more closely at the thing itself under discussion. Therefore, what Matthew and Mark stated simply, according to the common manner of sacramental speech, Paul and Luke rendered under the Spirit's dictation in such a way that they both pointed out, as with a finger, the trope lying hidden in Christ's words, and handed down the fruit of the whole matter, and finally became our authorities for raising our minds higher to contemplate those things which are signified by the symbols of bread and wine. For first they use the word "cup," which of course contains for the thing contained, which is a clear kind of metonymy. Next, where elsewhere it is said, "This is my blood, which is of the new testament," they render it: "This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you." But by speaking thus they almost urge and admonish us to look not so much to the history of the blood shed as to its fruit or effect, which consists in the remission of our sins, on which the fulfilment of the new testament, of which we spoke before, depends. But who does not see here that the effect is put for the efficient or material cause? In vain, then, do those men take offence at us because we change Christ's words and force a trope upon them where the truth of the matter admits none. Rather let them bring their quarrel against the Evangelists and Apostles, who so interpret Christ's words that they lead us away from the gross thoughts of corporeal eating and drinking to the true and saving reception of Christ and his benefits, which is made in the spirit through faith alone.

units.la: Deinde non verborum modò horum varietas, sed ipsius etiam Cænæ finis & vsus nos cogunt, vt à crasso & literali sensu recedamus. Hic enim non corporis, sed animæ negotium agitur, neque ad vitam hanc corruptibilem, sed ad cœlestem atque æternam alimur. Atqui vt anima non carne aut sanguine vescitur: ita neque cibo vllo corporeo ad cœlestem & spiritualem illam vitam opus est, & ad hanc per Christum sustentemur oportet, qui panis ille vitæ nobis est factus, quatenus è cœlo in mundum veniens ex nobis carnem assumpsit, quam pro nobis in mortem tradidit, vt ipse hoc mysterium Ioan.6.cap. interpretatur. Quid ergo de corporali manducatione, quæ ore & dentibus fiat (vt quidam nostrorum aduersariorum loquuntur) contendimus? Deinde præcipuum Cænæ finem, Christi & mortis eius recordationem & cum fide coniunctam commemorationem esse nuper audiuimus, in qua nos exerceri conuenit, donec ille (vt Paulus mox docebit) è cœlo veniet ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos. Quid verò opus erat vel præsentis corporis memoriam instituere, vel venturum expectare, si hoc ipso corpore nobiscum tam agit, quod ex Virgine assumpsit, & in quo nobis salutem vitamq; æternam meruit?
units.tr: Furthermore, not only this variety of words but also the very purpose and use of the Supper compel us to depart from the crude and literal sense. For here what is at stake is the soul's business, not the body's, and we are fed not to this corruptible life but to a heavenly and eternal one. Now as the soul feeds not on flesh or blood, so there is no need of any corporeal food for that heavenly and spiritual life, and we must be sustained by Christ for it, who has been made for us the bread of life, inasmuch as, coming down from heaven into the world, he took our flesh, which he delivered up to death for us, as John 6 itself explains this mystery. Why, then, do we contend about a corporeal eating, which is done with the mouth and teeth (as some of our adversaries speak)? Furthermore, we have lately heard that the chief purpose of the Supper is the remembrance of Christ and of his death, and the commemoration of it joined with faith, in which we ought to exercise ourselves until he (as Paul will soon teach) comes from heaven to judge the living and the dead. But what need was there either to institute a memorial of a body present, or to wait for one who is to come, if he deals with us by this very body which he took from the Virgin, and in which he merited for us salvation and eternal life?

units.la: Adde his tertio loco finem incarnationis Christi, quem non alium constituere possumus aut debemus, quàm qui ab ipso nobis in vtriusque testamenti libris monstratur. Est is, quod ex nobis illum funere oportuit, quod pro peccatis nostris offerret, & vt morte sua Nouo Testamento suum quasi effectum daret, quo cœlestis regni hæredes scripti eramus.
