Nullus ergo carnis Christi vsus est extra nostræ redemptionis negotium, quod ipsius verbis probatur, qui de crassa carnis suæ manducatione disceptantibus dicebat: Spiritus est qui viuificat, Caro non prodest quicquam, &c. At redemptionem humani generis plenam & omnibus numeris absolutam in ara crucis factam esse, ipse iam moriturus diserte testatus est. Vnde sequitur Carnis eius præsentiam in terris posthac minimè necessariam esse, & proinde eos nimium[?] ridiculos sese præbere, qui pro re non necessaria tam hostiliter digladiantur. Confirmatur hoc argumentum ipsius Christi verbis, qui nobis expedire dicit, ne posthac in mundo sit: quod non aliter quam de corporali præsentia potest intelligi: eò quòd nisi sua diuinitate, virtute & merito nobis perpetuò adsit, perimus.
units.tr: Add to these, in the third place, the purpose of Christ's incarnation, which we can and ought to set down as none other than that which he himself shows us in the books of both Testaments. It was necessary that he be offered in death for our sins, and that by his death he should give to the New Testament, as it were, its effect, by which we were written down as heirs of the heavenly kingdom. Therefore there is no use of Christ's flesh outside the business of our redemption, which is proved by his own words, when he said to those who disputed about the gross eating of his flesh: "It is the Spirit who quickens; the flesh profits nothing," and so on. But he himself, about to die, plainly testified that the redemption of mankind was full and complete in every respect and was accomplished on the altar of the cross. Hence it follows that the presence of his flesh on earth is hereafter by no means necessary, and that therefore those men make themselves very ridiculous who fight so bitterly over a thing that is not necessary. This argument is confirmed by Christ's own words, when he says that it is expedient for us that he should not be in the world any longer, which cannot be understood otherwise than of a bodily presence, since unless he is present with us continually by his divinity, power and merit, we perish.

units.la: Postremò corporis Christi conditio nos cogit, vt quod de pane & vino Eucharistico dicitur, per Metonymiæ tropum exponamus. Verum enim corpus ille ex Virgine assumpsit, cui nihil eorum defuit, quæ corporibus humanis propria sunt. Fuit enim ex membris suis compactum, ossibus suffultum, neruis & iuncturis inter se colligatum, carne denique & pelle vestitum. Idem cibo, potu, quiete & somno opus habuit. Adhæc quæ proprissima est corporum proprietas, suo semper & certo in loco fuit, vt nemo illud vnquam vel miraculose, vel ex peculiari quadam prærogatiua, ad aliquod temporis momentum simul pluribus in locis visum fuisse dicere posset. Etsi verò in resurrectione infirmitates, quæ ex peccato nobis inhærent, exuerit, & proinde glorificatum iam neque cibo & potu, neque quiete aut somno, illi sit opus, carnem tamen & ossa vnà cum membris omnibus retinuit, eaque non visibilia solùm, verumetiam palpabilia discipulis coràm exhibuit, eorumque veritatem per totos dies quadraginta infinitis argumentis tam apud discipulos, quàm apud alios fratres (vt Cap.15. dicetur) probauit. At quò nam abiit tandem corpus illud? Num euanuit nullo posse relicto testimonio, quo docemur vbi posthac quæri debeat? Nequaquam. Sed videntibus discipulis in cœlum, æternæ nimirum beatitudinis mansiones (sicuti prius promiserat) ascendit, & Angelos posse reliquit, qui hæsitantibus rem omnem exponerent. De quo adeò non dubitarunt Apostoli, vt Petrus dixerit, eum oportere cœlo capi vsque ad diem restitutionis omnium. Et Paulus alibi nos illum è cœlo expectare ait, vt mortalia nostra corpora conformia faciat corpori suo glorioso. Neque hic eos audire oportet, qui per nescio quam dispensationè hæc facta dicunt, & Ascensionem non aliud quàm priorus, quam in terris hisce habuit, conditionis mutatione fuisse somniant. Horum enim narratio cum tota Euangelicæ historiæ expositione coniungitur: ut si quid hic non vere factum dicamus, iam illam totam in suspitionem & dubium vocauerimus. Et inter fidei apostolicæ articulos hi ex ordine censentur, quibus illum ipsum Christum, qui crucifixus, mortuus, sepultus & tertio die resuscitatus est, in cœlum ascendisse fatemur, illic autem sedere ad dextram Patris omnipotentis, & venturum esse ad iudicandum vivos & mortuos. Non possumus ergo crassam corporis eius præsentiam vllam in terris statuere, sive in Cœna sive extra Cœnam, nisi aut illum cœlo detrahere, aut corporis eius veritatem negare, & illud omnipræsens, sive (vt cum crassis & ineptis inepte loquamur.) Vbiquarium fingere velimus. Scimus aduersarios ad personalem humanitatis & diuinitatis vnionem, deinde ad Dei omnipotentiam & ad miraculum confugere. Sed ad illam iampridem abunde responsum est: quoad illa vero, respondemus, ridiculum esse omnipotentiam vrgere, vbi de voluntate Dei nobis non certo constat: miracula autem fingere, quæ nulla visuntur aut sentiuntur, & quorum scriptura nusquam meminit, plus quam scurrilis & circulatoria audacia est. Itaque iustis & gravibus causis moti, dicimus, Panem & Vinum Cœnæ Dominicæ corpus & sanguinem Christi appellari, eo quod horum symbola & certa nostræ redemptionis per Christi mortem factæ sigilla sint: & (vt cum Apostolo nostro loquamur) quia communio sunt corporis & sanguinis Christi, id est, eius communionis sigilla sunt, quæ nobis cum Christo intercedit, qui vt caput nostrum est, ita nos suum corpus fecit, vt simus caro ex carne eius, & os ex ossibus eius. Monemus autem Christianos homines, ne signa pro rebus accipiant, quam miserrimam animarum seruitutem esse, Augustinus docet: neq; in signis Christum quærant, sed animis supra cœlum euectis, illic eum fide apprehendant. Ita enim salutariter manducatur, quod ipsum quoq; Augustinus monuit, dicens: Quid paras dentes & ventrem? crede, & manducasti. Poterant autem quæ hucusque diximus infinitis veterum patrum testimoniis probari: sed quia hæc alibi recitauimus, eadem hic repetere non est opus. Nunc ad reliqua progrediamur.
units.tr: Lastly, the condition of Christ's body compels us to explain by the trope of metonymy what is said of the bread and wine of the Eucharist. For he took from the Virgin a true body, which lacked none of those things that belong to human bodies. For it was held together by its members, supported by bones, bound together by sinews and joints, and finally clothed with flesh and skin. He had need of food, drink, rest and sleep. Moreover, what is the most proper property of bodies, it was always in its own and definite place, so that no one could say that it was ever seen at one and the same moment in several places, whether miraculously or by some peculiar prerogative. Although indeed in the resurrection he put off the infirmities which cling to us from sin, and so, now glorified, has no need of food and drink, nor of rest or sleep, he nevertheless kept his flesh and bones along with all his members, and he showed these to the disciples before their eyes, not only visible but also tangible, and for forty days, by infinite proofs, he demonstrated their truth both to the disciples and to other brethren (as will be said in chapter 15). But where, finally, did that body go? Did it vanish, leaving no testimony by which we are taught where we ought to seek it hereafter? By no means. But while the disciples watched, he ascended into heaven, into the mansions of eternal blessedness (as he had promised before), and he left angels who would explain the whole matter to those who hesitated. The Apostles had no doubt about this, so that Peter said that he must be received into heaven until the day of the restoration of all things. And Paul elsewhere says that we await him from heaven, so that he may make our mortal bodies conformable to his glorious body. Nor ought we to hear those who say that these things were done by some dispensation and dream that the Ascension was nothing other than a change of condition from the earthly state he had before. For their account is joined with the whole exposition of the Gospel history, so that if we say anything here was not truly done, we shall have cast that whole history into suspicion and doubt. And among the articles of the apostolic faith these are listed in order: that we confess that the very Christ who was crucified, dead, buried, and raised on the third day, ascended into heaven, and sits there at the right hand of God the Father Almighty, and will come to judge the living and the dead. We cannot, therefore, posit any gross bodily presence of his on earth, whether in the Supper or outside the Supper, unless we either drag him down from heaven, or deny the truth of his body, and want to feign that body to be omnipresent, or (to speak foolishly with the gross and foolish) "ubiquitarian." We know that our adversaries take refuge in the personal union of the humanity and divinity, and then in God's omnipotence and in a miracle. But to the first a sufficient answer was given long ago; as for the rest, we answer that it is ridiculous to urge omnipotence where we are not certain of God's will; and to invent miracles which are neither seen nor felt, and which Scripture nowhere mentions, is more than buffoonish and charlatan-like audacity. Therefore, moved by just and weighty causes, we say that the bread and wine of the Lord's Supper are called the body and blood of Christ because they are symbols of these things and sure seals of our redemption made by the death of Christ; and (to speak with our Apostle) because they are the communion of the body and blood of Christ, that is, the seals of that communion which intervenes between us and Christ, who, as he is our head, so has made us his body, so that we are flesh of his flesh and bone of his bones. We warn Christian people, however, not to take signs for things, which Augustine teaches is a most wretched slavery of souls; nor should they seek Christ in the signs, but, with their minds lifted above heaven, there apprehend him by faith. For so is he eaten to salvation, as Augustine also admonished, saying: "Why do you prepare teeth and belly? Believe, and you have eaten." Now what we have said so far could be proved by countless testimonies of the ancient Fathers, but since we have recited these elsewhere, there is no need to repeat them here. Let us now proceed to the remaining matters.

units.la: Sequitur enim in Christi actione considerandum, quo ordine & ritu solennem hanc suæ mortis recordationem instituerit. Conuenit cum discipulis in certum locum. Cœtum itaq; egit sacrum, in quo de rebus diuinis & maximè seriis tractaretur. Deinde ab epulo paschali exorsus, inter edendum de sua morte & eius fructu, de fidei constantia, de charitate, patientia in cruce & aliis multis concionatus est, quæ in ipso seruari volentibus necessaria sunt. Inter hæc accepit panem, gratias egit, fregit, fractumq; discipulis distribuit, quos iussit accipere, edere, ea verba addens quæ hucusque exposuimus. Inde similiter poculum quoq;, illis porrexit, in quo maiori diligentia mo-nuit, imò iussit, vt ex eo omnes biberent: Nimirum quod præuideret, nouissimis temporibus venturos, qui sacrilego ausu poculum mysticum vulgo Christianorum surriperent: quod vt iam pridem nonnulli conati fuerant: ita in Constantiensi Concilio publica authoritate sanciuerunt, vt posthac sub altera modo specie laici communicent. Postremo, vbi hymnum dixissent, cum discipulis ad montem olearum exiuit, vbi sibi ab hostibus insidias structas esse non ignorabat. Et hæc quidem Christus fecit. Docent autem ista, quis Cœnæ ritus sit optimus, & qui in Ecclesia perpetuo retineri debeat. Is nimirum, quo Christus vsus est, & quem Apostoli ab illo acceptum ecclesiis tradiderunt, vt in præsenti Paulus testatur. Debet igitur in cœtu sacro Cœna celebrari, quia nihil hic priuatum agitur. Præcedat concio sacra de iis, quæ ad huius mysterij expositionem & verum eius usum maxime pertinent. Inde ea ratione panis & poculum Domini distribuantur, qua ipse illa distribuit. Ea autem fideles suis manibus excipiant, edant & bibant cum gratiarum actione: quæ cum omnibus epulis semper adhiberi debeat, hic fine scelere negligi non potest.
units.tr: For in considering Christ's action, the next point is the order and ritual by which he instituted this solemn remembrance of his death. He met with his disciples in a certain place. He therefore held a sacred assembly, in which divine and most serious matters were discussed. Then, beginning from the Passover feast, while they were eating he preached to them about his death and its fruit, about constancy of faith, about love, about patience on the cross, and about many other things that are necessary for those who wish to be preserved in him. In the course of this he took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and distributed the broken bread to the disciples, bidding them take and eat it, and adding the words that we have explained above. In the same way he then handed them the cup, and with even greater care he admonished them, indeed commanded them, that all should drink from it. Clearly he foresaw that in the last times there would come those who, with sacrilegious daring, would snatch the mystical cup from the common run of Christians. Some had already attempted this long ago, and so the Council of Constance by public authority decreed that henceforth the laity should communicate under one kind only. Finally, when they had sung a hymn, he went out with the disciples to the Mount of Olives, where he knew that snares had been laid for him by his enemies. Christ did these things. Moreover, these things teach what the best rite of the Lord's Supper is, and what ought to be kept perpetually in the Church. That is, of course, the rite Christ used, and which the Apostles, having received it from him, handed down to the churches, as Paul testifies in the present passage. Therefore the Supper ought to be celebrated in a sacred assembly, because nothing private is done here. Let a sermon come first, on those matters which pertain most to the explanation of this mystery and its true use. Then let the bread and the cup of the Lord be distributed in the same manner in which he himself distributed them. Let the faithful receive them with their own hands, eat and drink them with thanksgiving; and since this should always be observed at all feasts, it cannot be neglected here without sin.

units.la: Videtur quidem ritus iste simplicior & abiectior, quam qui tanto mysterio respondeat: imò multi nos rusticos & inciuiles nimium esse aiunt, dum ista secundum Christi exemplum peragimus. Sed non debent hæc quenquam mouere. Nec enim humano splendore regni Dei mysteria commendantur: & si ritum hunc diligentius excutiamus, plenum maximorum mysteriorum ueniemus, quæ singula nos & officij admonere, & consolationibus dulcissimis in fide confirmare possunt. Panis & vinum enim Christum nobis figurant, qui & panis vitæ, & vinum illud dulcissimè est, de quo solo verè dicitur, quòd Deum & homines exhilaret. Hæc dum nos Christus ac-cipere iubet, non obscurè seipsum nobis offert, & tam certum est illum cum bonis suis omnibus no-strum esse velle, quàm symbola hæc manibus nostris tenemus. Non dubites ergo, ut manibus pa-nem & poculum tenes, ita te per fidem ipsum Christum habere. Fractio autem panis ut Christi mor-tem adumbrat, ita dum per nos fit, peccatorum confessioni seruit, & nos eos esse admonet, qui mor-tis illius authores fuerimus, quando propter nos illum mori oportuit. Et dum ista inter se distri-buunt fideles, communionis admonentur, quæ ipsis in Christo intercedit: docentur item, ne singuli propriam modò salutem curent, sed alios quoq; in Christi & salutis societatem adducere studeant. At non modò manibus suis sacra symbola accipiunt pii, sed ex Christi mandato illa edunt & bi-bunt. Quo docemur, non sufficere ut Sacramenta sumamus, aut Christi nomen vel ore, vel quo-cunq; alio modo circumferamus: sed salutis nostræ cardinem in hoc versari, ut Christus fide vera apprehensus in nobis viuat & agat, nosq; toti in illū transformemur. Hæc & alia huius generis ritus iste Cœnæ continet, qui primo aspectu contemptus, vel etiā ridiculus videtur. Et in hunc pec-cant, qui ex Cœna publica priuatā faciunt, qui sine Verbi prædicatione eam celebrant, qui fractio-nem panis ex illa auferunt, & rotundas crustulas prius domi parant, quibus in eius administra-tione utantur: qui distributionē quoq; abolent, dum ipsi singulis panem in os ingerunt, & ipsi po-culum aliorum labijs admouent, nec patiuntur, ut quis ex vulgo sacra symbola contingat: qui de-nique extra usum Cœnæ illa asseruant, auro & gemmis venerantur, adhæc cum theatrica pompa circumgestant. Quid enim horum Christus fecit? aut quid huius ecclesijs tradiderunt Apostoli? Excusant illi ista, quòd sic honorem & authoritatē Sacramentis conciliare oporteat. At nostrum non est Dei institutis aliquid addere, quæ nisi hominibus ob illius authoritatem in pretio sint, nos ascitio[?] illo fuco nihil proficiemus. Videant autē illi, ne dum à Christi formula & exemplo discedant, idem illis dici possit, quod Corinthiis: quod nimirum non manducent Cœnam Domini, & ne loco Christi Deum illum Mayzim adorent, quem Daniel Antichristo tribuit, qui illum auro, argento, gemmis & aliis rebus pretiosis veneraturus sit.
units.tr: Admittedly this rite seems rather plain and humble, not befitting so great a mystery. Indeed, many say that we are too rustic and uncivilised in performing these things according to Christ's example. But these objections ought not to move anyone. For the mysteries of the kingdom of God are not commended by human splendour; and if we examine this rite more carefully, we will find it full of very great mysteries, each of which can both remind us of our duty and confirm us in faith with the sweetest consolations. For bread and wine represent Christ to us: he is the bread of life, and he is that wine, most sweet, of which alone it is truly said that it gladdens God and men. When Christ bids us take these things, he offers himself to us quite plainly; and it is as certain that he wishes to be ours with all his good things as it is that we hold these symbols in our hands. Do not doubt, then, that just as you hold the bread and cup in your hands, so through faith you have Christ himself. The breaking of the bread, moreover, as it foreshadows Christ's death, so when it is done by us it serves as confession of sins, and reminds us that we are those who were the authors of his death, since it was necessary for him to die on our account. And while the faithful distribute these things among themselves, they are reminded of the fellowship which they have with one another in Christ; they are also taught not merely to care for their own salvation alone, but to strive to bring others too into the fellowship of Christ and of salvation. Nor do the godly merely receive the sacred symbols into their own hands, but in obedience to Christ's command they eat and drink them. By this we are taught that it is not enough to receive the sacraments, or to carry the name of Christ about on the lips or in any other way; rather, the hinge of our salvation lies in this, that Christ, truly apprehended by faith, lives and acts in us, and that we ourselves are transformed into him. This rite of the Supper contains these and other things of this kind, though at first sight it seems contemptible, or even ridiculous. And they sin against it who make a private thing of the public Supper, who celebrate it without the preaching of the Word, who take away from it the breaking of bread, and who prepare beforehand round little wafers at home to use in its administration; who also abolish the distribution, while they themselves put the bread into each person's mouth and bring the cup to the lips of others, and do not allow anyone from the common people to touch the sacred symbols; and finally, who keep those things apart from the use of the Supper, venerate them with gold and gems, and carry them about with theatrical pomp. For did Christ do any of these things? Or did the Apostles hand down any of them to the churches? They excuse these practices on the ground that the sacraments must thus be given honour and authority. But it is not for us to add anything to God's institutions; and unless these things are held in esteem by men on account of God's authority, we shall gain nothing by such addition and paint. Let those men see to it, however, lest, while they depart from Christ's form and example, the same thing be said to them that was said to the Corinthians: namely, that they do not eat the Lord's Supper; and that instead of Christ they worship that god Mayzim, whom Daniel ascribes to Antichrist, who will honour him with gold, silver, gems and other precious things.

units.la: Accedamus nunc ad tertium & postremum nostræ tractationis caput, quod est de nostro in Cœna peragenda officio. Etsi enim ritum externum probè obseruemus, nihil tamen hoc profuerit, nisi id præstemus, cuius causa actio hæc instituta est. Id verò Christus ipse non disertis modò verbis, sed etiam iterum repetitis exprimit, dicens: Hoc facite ad mei recordationem. Quæ verba Paulus exponens ait: Quotiscunque ederitis panem hunc, & poculum hoc biberitis, mortem Domini annuntiate, donec venerit. Sub morte comprehenduntur quæcunque hanc præcesserunt & secuta sunt. Nam ut mori posset, hominem fieri oportuit. Non autem profuisset nobis illius mors, nisi secuta fuisset resurrectio ex mortuis & ascensio in cœlos. Agitur ergo hic de toto nostræ redemptionis mysterio, ideoq; pie & prudenter à maioribus nostris institutum est, ut in actione Cœnæ Symbolum, quod Apostolicum vocant, recitetur, quò facilius omnes in memoriam renocent, quæ propter nos æternus De Filius fecit & passus est. Recordationi autem publica beneficij tanti prædicatio & pro eodem gratiarumactio accedat. Eam tamen non in solis verbis consistere putabimus, sed animum totum à nobis requirit Dominus, neque illi satis grati erimus, nisi nos ita ei addicamus, ut quemadmodum ille pro nobis vitam & sanguinem profudit: ita nos quoq; omnia nostra pro ipso impendere, & pro eius gloria mori parati simus. Huc veteres respexe-runt, quando Cœnam Eucharistiam dixere, unde etiā apud illos Sacrificium dicta fuit: non quòd in ea Christum sacrificari, aut sacrificium eius, quod in ara crucis factum est, nobis applicari senti-rent: sed quòd gratiarumactionem Deo sacrificium omnium gratissimum esse scripturæ passim doceant. In hoc ergo nos intentos esse decet, quoties Cœnā hanc celebramus, ut animo syncero & san-ctafide prædicemus mortem Domini, qua ille nos ex peccatis, morte, inferis & universa diaboli tyrannide redemit. Etenim tam eximium, tam salutare, tam multiplex est beneficium istud, ut nulla hominum linguæ illud digne, & ut par est, laudare possint. Quod ergo nobis deest, solen-ni hac actione farciamus, quam ipse nobis in eum finem commendauit. Quòd si verò mortem Domini annuntiare debemus, nimium importuni & inepti sunt, qui Cœnæ negotium mirificè de Christi maiestate, corporis glorificati omnipresentia, sessione item eiusdem ad dexteram Patrū disputationibus ita implicant & involuūt, ut pleriq; & mortis eius obliviscantur, & neglecto huius mysterij sine charitatis Christianæ vinculum abrumpant. Sed eo deveniant oportet, qui in Dei institutis plus sapere aut videre volunt, quàm ipse per Verbum suum nobis tradiderit.
units.tr: Let us now come to the third and final head of our discussion, which concerns our duty in celebrating the Supper. For even if we carefully observe the outward rite, it will profit nothing unless we perform that for the sake of which this action was instituted. Christ himself expresses this not only in plain words but also by repeating them: Do this in remembrance of me. Paul, expounding these words, says: As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes. Under the death are included all the things that went before it and followed it. For in order to be able to die, he had to become a man. Nor would his death have profited us unless his resurrection from the dead and his ascension into heaven had followed. Therefore this rite concerns the whole mystery of our redemption; and so it was piously and wisely instituted by our forefathers that in the celebration of the Supper the creed which they call the Apostles' Creed should be recited, so that all may more easily call to mind what the eternal Son of God did and suffered for us. Let public proclamation of so great a benefit, and thanksgiving for it, accompany the remembrance. Yet we should not think that this consists only in words: the Lord requires the whole heart from us, and we shall not be sufficiently grateful to him unless we devote ourselves to him in such a way that, just as he poured out his life and blood for us, so we too are ready to spend all that we have for him, and to die for his glory. The ancients had this in view when they called the Supper the Eucharist, whence it was also called by them a sacrifice: not because they believed that Christ is sacrificed in it, or that his sacrifice, made on the altar of the cross, is applied to us; but because the Scriptures everywhere teach that thanksgiving is the most acceptable sacrifice to God. Therefore we ought to be intent on this whenever we celebrate this Supper: that with a sincere mind and holy faith we proclaim the death of the Lord, by which he redeemed us from sins, death, hell and the whole tyranny of the devil. For this benefit is so outstanding, so saving, and so manifold that no human tongue can praise it worthily and as it deserves. Therefore let us supply by this solemn action what is lacking in us, since he himself commended it to us for that end. But if we ought to proclaim the Lord's death, those are excessively troublesome and foolish who so entangle and involve the business of the Supper in disputations about the majesty of Christ, the omnipresence of his glorified body, and likewise his sitting at the right hand of the Father, that many forget even his death, and, neglecting the meaning of this mystery, break the bond of Christian love. Yet those must come to this who wish to be wiser, or to see more, in God's institutions than he himself has handed down to us through his Word.

units.la: Porrò obseruabimus Paulum hic omnibus Christianis loqui, & proinde præceptum hoc ge-nerale esse, quo iubet, ut actionem hanc mysticam in memoriam & gratam prædicationem mortis Christi celebremus. Quoad enim in hac vitiosa et mortali carne viuimus, multa sunt, quæ sanctif-simos quoq; in salutis via remorantur. Ideo fidei nostra nunquàm non opus habet Verbi & Sacramentorum adminiculis. Quapropter vehementer errant, qui ista ceu superuacanea aut minus necessaria negligunt. Faciunt hoc multi nostro seculo, qui Verbum quoddam internum fingunt, quod neq; ex scripturis neq; alicuius hominis voce, sed solius spiritus reuelatione discatur. Eo autem prætextu deceptos Satan immani et perniciosa persuasione inebriat, ut se Verbũ illud assecutos esse, & ad perfectionis Christianæ metà peruenisse arbitrentur. Itaq; ecclesias omnes præ se contemnunt, Verbi prædicationem negligunt, Sacramentorum usum rident, deniq; omnia pietatis & religionis exercitia pro puerilibus quibusdam hominum nondum in Christo perfectorum crepundijs ducunt. Sed dum alijs præstare volunt isti homines, se ab omni religione alienissimos esse produnt. Quis enim vel cognitione Dei vera imbutos, vel serio illius timore præditos esse dixerit eos, qui eius insti-tuta pro inutilibus aut superuacaneis contemnunt? Longè aliter senserunt veteres illi cultores Dei, quorum fidem scriptura tam magnificè prædicat. Sacrificandi more minimè neglexit Abra-hamus, quem à patribus acceperat, & idem iam prope centenarius circumcisione admittere non recusauit, licet fidem suâ Deo iam prìdem probatam, seq; propter hanc iustificatū esse non ignoraret. Dauid quoq; vir secundum cor Dei, in exilio suo nihil molestius sensit, quàm quòd à sacris cæti-bus & externi cultus exercitio se exclusum videret. Et Paulus etsi non definiat quoties in anno Corinthij Cœnam celebrare debeant, tamen cùm, QVOTIESCVNQVE, dicit, nō obscurè innuit, ipsos una Cœna in anno nequaquà contentos esse debere. Cùm enim in vera religione nimiùm fri-gidi simus natura, & licet multi nobis stimuli adhibeantur, vix tamen in officio contineri possimus, quid de nobis fiet, si sponte abijciamus quæ nobis Deus adhibet adminicula? Neminem ergo istorum hominum exempla moueant, qui magno suo malo sibi ipsis blanditias faciunt: quin potius meminerimus nullam in vera religionis exercitijs diligentiam nimiam, & nemini quantumuis perfecto Cœnæ Dominicæ usum superuacaneū esse posse. Nam ut rectè in hunc locum Theodoretus annotavit, post adventum Domini demum nō amplius opus erit symbolis, aut signes[?] corporis, cùm scilicet ipsum corpus apparebit. Et ideo Paulum iussisse idem testatur, ut Cœna hæc utamur donec ille venerit. Facit tamen particula ista etiâ ad fidei & spei nostræ cöfirmationem, quando cogitamus nos non circa eius memoriam occupari, qui nostri immemor nunquam ad nos rediturū fit, sed illius, qui etsi corpus ex hoc infelici & periturō mundo supra omnes cœlos in beatæ immortalitatis locum euexerit, nobis tamen suo spiritu & virtute adest, ut nos alat, seruet atq; tueatur: quique olim è cœlis venturus est in nubibus, ut nos ad se transferat. In omnibus ergo istis Dei bonitatem agnoscamus & prædicemus, qui nostræ saluti simul & fidei infirmitati tam variè con-sultum voluit. Accommodemus autè nos eius institutis, & externis hisce fidei exercitijs ita va-cemus, ut interim animis supra cœlos euectis per fidem CHRISTO IESV verè fruamur ad vitam æternam. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Furthermore, we shall observe that Paul here speaks to all Christians, and therefore this is a general precept, by which he bids us celebrate this mystical action in memory of and in grateful proclamation of the death of Christ. For as long as we live in this sinful and mortal flesh, there are many things which hold back even the most holy in the way of salvation. Therefore our faith always has need of the aids of the Word and the Sacraments. Wherefore those err greatly who neglect these things as superfluous or less necessary. Many in our age do this, who invent a certain inward Word, which is learned neither from the Scriptures nor from the voice of any man, but by the revelation of the Spirit alone. Under this pretext Satan, with monstrous and destructive persuasion, intoxicates those he has deceived, so that they think they have attained that Word and reached the goal of Christian perfection. Accordingly they despise all the churches, neglect the preaching of the Word, mock the use of the Sacraments, and finally regard all the exercises of piety and religion as the childish toys of men not yet perfect in Christ. But while these men want to appear superior to others, they reveal that they are most alien from all religion. For who would say that those are imbued with a true knowledge of God, or endowed with a serious fear of him, who despise his institutions as useless or superfluous? The ancient worshippers of God, whose faith Scripture praises so magnificently, thought very differently. Abraham, whom he had received from the fathers, by no means neglected the manner of sacrificing, and though nearly a hundred years old he did not refuse to admit circumcision, although he knew that his faith had long since been proved to God and that he had been justified on account of it. David also, a man after God's own heart, in his exile felt nothing more painful than seeing himself shut out from the holy assemblies and the exercise of external worship. And Paul, although he does not define how often in the year the Corinthians ought to celebrate the Supper, yet when he says AS OFTEN AS, he plainly hints that they ought by no means to be content with one Supper in the year. For since we are by nature too cold in true religion, and although many spurs are applied to us, we can scarcely be kept in duty, what will become of us if we willingly cast away the aids God offers us? Let the examples of those men, who flatter themselves to their great harm, move none of us; rather let us remember that there can be no excessive diligence in the exercises of true religion, and that the use of the Lord's Supper cannot be superfluous for anyone, however perfect. For as Theodoret rightly observed on this passage, after the coming of the Lord there will no longer be any need of symbols or signs of the body, when the body itself shall appear. And he attests that Paul therefore commanded us to use this Supper until he comes. Yet this particle also serves to confirm our faith and hope, when we consider that we are occupied not with the memory of one who, mindful of us, will never return to us, but with him who, although he has lifted his body from this unhappy and perishing world above all the heavens into the place of blessed immortality, is nevertheless present with us by his Spirit and power, to nourish, preserve and keep us; and who one day will come down from heaven in the clouds to transfer us to himself. In all these things, then, let us acknowledge and proclaim the goodness of God, who has provided so variously both for our salvation and for the weakness of our faith. Let us accommodate ourselves to his institutions, and so devote ourselves to these external exercises of faith that, meanwhile, with our minds lifted above the heavens, we may truly enjoy CHRIST JESUS through faith unto eternal life. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LX.
units.tr: HOMILY LX.

units.la: Itaq; quisquis ederit panem hunc, aut biberit hoc poculū Domini indignè reus tenebitur corporis & sanguinis Domini. Probet autem seipsum homo, & ita de pane illo edat, & de poculo illo bibat. Nam qui edit & bibit indignè, iudicium sibi ipsi edit & bibit, non discernens corpus Domini.
units.tr: Therefore whoever eats this bread or drinks this cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup. For he who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgement to himself, not discerning the body of the Lord.

units.la: QVoniam Corinthij sacrosanctam Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI Cœnam fœde & turpiter prophanarunt, ut iam nihil minus quàm Cœnam Dominicam edere viderentur, Paulus vt tanto malo medeatur, primò quidem eos grauissimè corripit, deinde verò ad primam huius Sacramenti institutionem eos reuocat, ita nimirum monens, vt formam & ritum à Christo traditum constanter seruent, neque hunc vllis additionibus corrumpi aut mutari sinant. Est hoc obseruandum in omnibus Dei institutis, neque alia est tutior & certior expeditiorque er-rores & abusus tollendi ratio, quàm vt videamus, non quid hominum iudicio probetur, aut longo vsu receptum atque confirmatum sit, sed quid Deus instituerit, & quid is fieri velit. At quia difficile est homines à publicis erroribus in viam reducere, subijcit modò grauem admonitio-nem, qua primum in genere agit de vitio, quo circa Cœnam peccatur, & quanta sit illius atroci-tas docet: deinde remedium siue consilium adhibet: postremò supplicij comminatione terret eos, qui contumaciores erant. Est autem locus hic eò maiori diligentia considerandus, quòd genera-lem & imprimis necessariam doctrinam continet, quomodo vnusquisque ad Cœnam aut mensam Domini sese præparare debeat.
units.tr: Since the Corinthians had foully and shamefully profaned the most holy Supper of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they seemed to eat nothing less than the Lord's Supper, Paul, in order to remedy so great an evil, first rebukes them very severely, then calls them back to the first institution of this sacrament, plainly warning them to keep constantly the form and rite handed down by Christ, and not to allow it to be corrupted or changed by any additions. This must be observed in all God's institutions. There is no safer, surer or quicker way of removing errors and abuses than to look not at what is approved by human judgement, or what has been received and confirmed by long use, but at what God has instituted and what he wishes to be done. But because it is hard to lead men back from public errors, he now adds a grave admonition, in which he first deals in general with the fault by which the Supper is sinned against, and shows how atrocious it is; then he applies a remedy or counsel; and finally he frightens with a threat of punishment those who were more stubborn. This passage deserves all the more careful consideration because it contains a general and especially necessary teaching on how each person ought to prepare himself for the Supper, or the table of the Lord.

units.la: Generale in hac causa vitium, quo alia omnia continentur, est indignè edere & bibere de mensa Domini mystica. De hoc Paulus sic pronuntiat: Itaque quisquis ederit panem hunc, aut biberit hoc poculum Domini indignè, reus tenebitur corporis & sanguinis Domini. Infert ista commodè ex ijs, quæ proximè præcesserunt, quasi diceret: Cùm æternus Dei Filius, qui pro nobis homo fieri nosq; mortis suæ merito seruare dignatus est, Cœnam hanc ad sui recordationem instituerit, nostrum verò in ea celebranda officium sit, eius mortem cum fideli & seria gratiarum actione prædicare: denique cùm panem hunc & hoc poculum corporis & sanguinis sui sacra symbola esse voluerit, & ea corpus suum & sanguinem suum dicere dignetur, etiam atq; etiam vobis cauendum erit, ne ea indignè vsurpetis. Si enim sapientissimus ille Solomon prudenter monuit, vt qui ad principis mensam accumbunt, diligenter aduertant, quæ coram ipsis apponuntur: quanto magis hic cura & diligentia opus est, quando ad mensam Regis regum & Domini dominantium inuitamur, vt cogitemus quid isthic agatur, qualis cibus nobis apponatur, & qua reuerentia in eo sumendo debeamus uti? Qui enim hic indignè ederit aut biberit, is non in panem aut vinum peccat, sed in ipsum Domini corpus & sanguinem, &c.
units.tr: The general fault in this matter, which contains all the others, is to eat and drink unworthily at the mystical table of the Lord. Paul pronounces concerning this: "Therefore whoever eats this bread, or drinks this cup of the Lord, unworthily, will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord." He draws this fittingly from what immediately precedes, as if he were saying: Since the eternal Son of God, who deigned to become man for us and to save us by the merit of his death, instituted this Supper in remembrance of himself, and since our task in celebrating it is to proclaim his death with faithful and earnest thanksgiving; and finally, since he willed this bread and this cup to be the holy symbols of his body and blood, and deigns to call them his body and his blood, you must take heed again and again that you do not use them unworthily. For if that most wise Solomon prudently advised that those who sit down at a prince's table should carefully notice what is set before them, how much more care and diligence is needed when we are invited to the table of the King of kings and Lord of lords, so that we may consider what is being done there, what food is set before us, and with what reverence we ought to take it? For whoever eats or drinks unworthily here sins not against bread or wine, but against the very body and blood of the Lord, etc.

units.la: Hic ante omnia tenere oportet, quid sit indignè edere & bibere ex Cœna Domini. Potest id ex contrario facillimè intelligi. Dignè vsurpari dicitur res aliqua, quando ad vsum suum pro-prium destinatur, idq; legitimo suo modo & ordine. Sic dignè vestibus vtuntur, qui obseruata decori & honesti ratione ijs corpus aduersus cœli iniuriam muniunt, & ea tegunt, quæ natura tegere voluit. Cibis item reliquis dignè vescuntur, qui illis corporis vires sustentant, & eosdem sumunt temperanter & cum gratiarum actione. Et coniugium dignè contrahunt, qui in Dei institutum intenti hoc spectant, vt illicitas libidines deuitent, sobolem legitimam Deo procreent, & vitæ sociam habeant, qua adiuti fortunam omnem facilius & patientius ferant. Eadem est omnium aliorum ratio. In religione autem dignè fit, quod ex fide fit secundum verbi Dei præscriptum. Quicquid autem absque fide fit, vel ex nostri capitis arbitrio, vel secundum hominum traditiones, id omne peccatum est, erroneum est, & Deo non potest placere. Transferamus ista nunc ad Cœnæ institutionem, & mox res omnis patebit. Est hæc actio sacra (vt nuper diximus) in qua ex Christi instituto panem & vinum inter nos distribuimus & sumimus ad recordationem mortis ipsius, quam is Novo Testamento suum effectum atque complementum dedit, vt coheredes ipsius efficeremur. Seruit ergo Cœna hæc, quoad nostrum in ea officium, professioni fidei, & eadem ad sanctitatis, innocentiæ vitæ & dilectionis mutuæ studium obstringimur. Quoad verò eius ritum & ordinem, hunc ipse Christus tradidit, quem ab illo acceptum Euangelistæ & Apostoli diligenter descripserunt. Dignè igitur edunt & bibunt, qui ritum à Christo traditum obseruant, fidem verò quam profitentur, reuera animo conceperût & tenent, atq; eandem morum innocentia, dilectionis fraternæ officijs, tota denique vita exprimunt. E contra indignè de mensa ista edunt & bibunt, primò qui à Christi institutione discedunt, dum vel ritum externæ actionis mutant, vel fines Cœnæ alios constituunt. Fit hoc multiuariàm, vt in præcedenti sermone dixi-mus. At omnes isti non edunt Cœnam Domini, quando talis dici non potest, quæ non secundum formam ab ipso præscriptam peragitur. Proximi hi sunt, qui fide destituuntur, qui non eiusdem sunt ordinis. Alij enim ne historicam quidem fidem habent, sed pro fabulis & figmentis ducunt, quæcunq; ex scripturis prædicari audiunt: alij verò etsi Christum hominem factum esse, miraculis claruisse, & tandem à suis proditum & in cruce crudeliter occisum esse minimè negent, hæc tamen ipsa ad se nihil pertinere putant, & proinde eorum commemoratione non magis quàm alicuius peregrinæ historiæ commouentur. His coniungi debent, qui etsi hæc omnia fateantur, adeò tamen non gratos se præbent Domino, vt potius vitæ impuritate & effreni morum licentia meritum eius, quantum in ipsis est, conculcent, adeoq; ipsum (vt in epistola ad Hebræos scribitur) denuo crucifigant. Ad horum ordinem pertinent, qui in quocunq; scelere absq; pœnitentia pergunt, & quàmuis in Cœna fidem & innocentiæ studium cum aliis piis profiteantur, mox tamen vt canes ad vomitum redeunt, & ijsdem quibus antea sceleribus vacant. Faciunt hoc, qui ebrietati & gulæ studio ita addicti sunt, vt ne illo ipso die, quo Cœnæ communicarunt, à comessationibus abstineant: quò fit, vt sæpe vino superati ea dicant, & faciant, quæ non homine decent, nedum Christianum hominem. Qui pharmacum sumunt, solent eo die ab omnibus abstinere, quibus pharmaci vis & operatio impediri potest. At isti cum pharmacum sumant, quo nullum in rerum natura pretiosius & salutarius est, quo nimirum fides exercetur & confirmatur, quo conscientiæ afflictæ exhilarantur, & quo totus homo ad Christianæ pietatis officia obeunda alacer & strenuus redditur: mox tamen cum ratione pudore etiam excusso, ad pocula ruunt, ibi cum sui similibus ad diabolicum inebriandi certamen descendunt, impudicis cantilenis seipsos & alios ad libidinem accendunt, insanis item clamoribus, execrationibus & deierationibus tàm sibijpsis quàm toti vicinia molesti sunt. Quis obsecro tales panem hunc mysticum digne edere, & ex Domini poculo digne bibere dixerit? Maior est eorum impudentia, qui illo ipso tempore ad scorta reuertuntur, vt stupris & adulteriis Veneri cultum exhibeant, qui paulò ante se Christi membra esse professi sunt. Pertinent ad eundem catalogum auari, qui etsi cum pauperibus communicent ad mensam Domini, eosdem tamen pro fratribus non agnoscunt, clamores eorum surdis auribus transfire sinunt, adhæc vsurarijs suis artibus atq; impostoris populum vniuersum crudeliter spoliant atque deglubunt. De his omnibus loquitur Augustinus lib. 2. contra literas Petil. cap. 55. scribens: Indignè manducant, qui corpus & sanguinem Christi in Sacramento manducant & bibunt, membra autem eius toto orbe diffusa in Euangelio non agnoscunt. Sed quid opus est singulos ex ordine recensere? Indignè bibedunt [?] & bibunt, quicunque pœnitere nescij ita viuunt, vt diaboli potius quàm Christi membra aut serui censeri possint. Nam etiamsi tales Christianam fidem profitentur, Sacramentis communicent, & vel volentes vel coacti ad nuptiale illud conuiuium Christi veniant, carent tamen veste nuptiali, & proinde in tenebras exteriores suo tempore eijcientur.
units.tr: Here above all we must grasp what it is to eat and drink unworthily from the Lord's Supper. This can be understood most easily by the opposite. A thing is said to be used worthily when it is directed to its proper use, and that in its lawful manner and order. Thus those use clothing worthily who, observing the rule of decency and honesty, cover the body against the injuries of the sky and conceal what nature willed to be concealed. Likewise they eat other foods worthily who sustain the strength of the body by them and take them temperately and with thanksgiving. And they contract marriage worthily who, intent on God's institution, aim at this: to avoid unlawful lusts, to beget lawful offspring for God, and to have a companion of life, by whose help they may bear every fortune more easily and patiently. The reasoning is the same for all other things. In religion, however, a thing is done worthily when it is done from faith according to the prescription of God's Word. Whatever is done without faith, either by the decision of our own head or according to human traditions, all that is sin, is erroneous, and cannot please God. Let us now transfer these points to the institution of the Supper, and soon the whole matter will be plain. This is a sacred action (as we said recently) in which, by Christ's institution, we distribute among ourselves and take bread and wine in remembrance of his death, which he gave its effect and fulfilment in the New Testament, so that we might become his co-heirs. So this Supper serves, as far as our part in it goes, as a profession of faith, and by it we are bound to a zeal for holiness, innocence of life and mutual love. As for its rite and order, Christ himself handed it down, and the Evangelists and Apostles carefully described what they had received from him. Those therefore eat and drink worthily who observe the rite handed down by Christ, and who truly conceive and hold in their minds the faith they profess, and express it in innocence of manners, in the duties of brotherly love, and finally in their whole life. On the contrary, they eat and drink unworthily from this table who first depart from Christ's institution, either by changing the external form of the action or by setting up other ends for the Supper. This happens in many ways, as I said in the previous sermon. But all these do not eat the Lord's Supper, since that cannot be called such which is not carried out according to the form prescribed by him. Nearest to these are those who lack faith, who are not of the same order. For some do not even have historical faith, but regard as fables and fictions whatever they hear preached from the Scriptures; others, though they do not deny that Christ became man, shone with miracles, was at last betrayed by his own people and cruelly killed on the cross, nevertheless think that these things do not concern them at all, and so are no more moved by their remembrance than by the story of some foreign land. To these must be joined those who, although they confess all these things, nevertheless show themselves so ungrateful to the Lord that by the impurity of their lives and their unbridled licence of manners they trample underfoot, so far as in them lies, his merit, and so (as is written in the Epistle to the Hebrews) crucify him afresh. In this rank are those who persist in any wickedness without repentance, and although at the Supper they profess faith and zeal for innocence with other pious people, yet soon they return like dogs to their vomit and devote themselves to the same wickednesses as before. They do this who are so addicted to drunkenness and gluttony that they do not abstain from carousing even on that very day on which they have communicated; hence it happens that, overcome by wine, they often say and do things unbecoming to a man, let alone a Christian man. Those who take medicine are accustomed on that day to abstain from everything by which the power and operation of the medicine could be hindered. But these men, when they take a medicine than which there is nothing more precious and more healthful in the nature of things, by which faith is indeed exercised and strengthened, by which afflicted consciences are cheered, and by which the whole man is made eager and energetic for performing the duties of Christian piety, soon, with reason and even shame cast off, rush to their cups, there descend with their like into a devilish contest of drinking, inflame themselves and others to lust with shameless songs, and by insane shouts, curses and oaths are a nuisance both to themselves and to the whole neighbourhood. Who, I beg you, would say that such people eat this mystical bread worthily and drink worthily from the Lord's cup? Greater is the impudence of those who at that very time return to harlots, to pay worship to Venus with fornications and adulteries, though a little before they professed themselves members of Christ. In the same catalogue are the covetous, who, though they communicate with the poor at the Lord's table, do not acknowledge them as brothers, allow their cries to pass by deaf ears, and moreover cruelly strip and flay the whole people with their usurious tricks and deceptions. Augustine speaks of all these in book 2 against the letters of Petilianus, chapter 55, writing: "They eat unworthily who eat and drink the body and blood of Christ in the Sacrament, but do not acknowledge his members spread throughout the world in the Gospel." But what need is there to list each one in order? Those who eat and drink unworthily are all who, not knowing how to repent, live in such a way that they can be counted rather as members or servants of the devil than of Christ. For even if such people profess the Christian faith, communicate in the sacraments, and come, whether willingly or under compulsion, to that wedding feast of Christ, yet they lack the wedding garment, and therefore in due time will be cast out into outer darkness.

units.la: Scio hoc nonnullis durius dictum videri, qui Christiani nominis professione ad omnia scelera tegenda & excusanda sufficere putant. Sed audiant illi Paulū huius sceleris grauitatem exponentes, & mox videbunt nihil temere aut præcipitantius à nobis pronunciatū esse. Quisquis ederit panem hunc, aut biberit hoc poculū Domini indignè, reus tenebitur corporis & sanguinis Domini. Id est eiusdem criminis reatu tenebitur cum Iuda, qui Christum prodidit: cum Iudæis & militibus, qui eius corpus flagellarunt, conspuerunt, vulnerarunt, in crucem suffixerunt, & eiusdem sanguinem fuderunt. Est hoc quoq; dictu & auditu grauissimum, ratio tamen huius pronunciati certa est, & communi sensu confirmata. Vt enim qui Imperatoris aut Regis statuam euerit, coronam cum sceptro in lutum abijcit, tabulas regias cum suis sigillis discerpit & conculcat, læsæ maiestatis crimen incurrit, & non in saxa, aurum, gemmas, membranas & ceram, sed in ipsum Regem siue Imperatorem peccauisse iudicatur: Ita qui Sacramenta indigno atq; impio abusu prophanant, non in panem & vinum, sed in illorum authorem, Dominum iniurij sunt, & ea ipsa Dei dona conculcant atq; polluunt, quæ his repræsentantur & obsignantur. Ideo qui olim Circumcisione abusi sunt, ij fœdus salutis violauisse, & in ipsum Deum perfidi fuisse dicuntur. Et cùm Christus sibi factum iudicet, quod vni alicui suorum fit, num aliter æstimaturum putamus Cœnæ sua abusum, quo sacra sui corporis & sanguinis symbola & redemptionis nostræ, quæ per ipsum facta est, sigilla prophanantur? Non temere igitur hoc dictum Paulo excidit, quod reatu corporis & sanguinis Christi teneatur, qui hunc panem indignè ederit, & poculū hoc Domini indignè biberit. Caterum Cæterùm ex eo colligunt nonnulli, corpus & sanguinem Christi symbolis ita connexa esse, vt illa impij quoque cum his verè & realiter edant atque bibant. Nam qua alià ratione (inquiunt) reus sanguinis & corporis Christi fit impius, nisi illa ederit & biberit? Sed est hoc nimis friuolum, & non contentiosis sufficere poterant similia siue exempla, quæ paulò ante adduximus. Nec est quòd illi occlament[?], exempla ista esse de rebus prophanis, longè aliam verò esse rationem diuinorum atque cœlestium mysteriorum. Nam vt discrimen, quod inter diuina & humana est, minimè negamus: ita in scripturis tam Veteris quàm Noui testamenti obseruauimus, Spiritum sanctum humano more nobiscum loqui, & in tradendis Sacramentorum mysteriis non solum captui nostro, verumetiam receptæ inter homines consuetudini sese accommodare. Quid autem tam vulgare & vsitatum est, quàm quòd reus læsæ maiestatis dicitur, qui principis sigillum siue statuam violauit, etiamsi principem ipsum nunquam attigerit, & fortassis ne viderit quidem? Quo sensu hæc etiam Apostoli verba accipi debere, multæ graueque rationes nos admonent. Prima est, quòd Paulus Christi venturi, non autem iam corporaliter præsentis meminit. Secunda, quòd in tota hac tractatione panem & poculum nominat. Quoties hunc panem ederitis, & poculum hoc biberitis, &c. Et hic: Quisquis ederit panem hunc, & biberit hoc poculum Domini indignè, &c.Et mox: Probet seipsum homo, & ita de pane illo edat, & de poculo illo bibat. Ita verò loquitur Apostolus, quàmuis sibi cum ijs rem esse sciret, qui de Cœna hac minus honorificè sentiebant, adeò vt nihil discriminis fere facerent inter hanc & vulgare aliquod siue prophanum epulum.
units.tr: I know that some will think this said too harshly, those who imagine that the mere profession of the Christian name is enough to cover and excuse every crime. But let them hear Paul setting out the gravity of this sin, and they will soon see that nothing has been declared rashly or too hastily by us. "Whoever eats this bread, or drinks this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord." That is, he will be held guilty of the same crime as Judas, who betrayed Christ; as the Jews and soldiers who scourged his body, spat upon it, wounded it, nailed it to the cross and poured out his blood. This statement is most grave to say and to hear, yet the reasoning behind it is sound and is confirmed by common sense. For whoever overthrows the statue of an Emperor or King, casts his crown and sceptre into the mud, tears up and tramples the royal documents with their seals, incurs the charge of treason, and is judged to have sinned not against gold, gems, parchment and wax, but against the King or Emperor himself. So those who profane the sacraments by an unworthy and impious abuse do wrong not to the bread and wine, but to their author, the Lord, and trample on and defile those gifts of God which they represent and seal. So too those who in former times abused circumcision are said to have violated the covenant of salvation and to have been faithless towards God himself. And since Christ judges that what is done to any one of his own is done to himself, do we think he will judge otherwise of the abuse of his Supper, by which the holy symbols of his body and blood, and the seals of our redemption, which was accomplished through him, are profaned? Paul therefore did not say rashly that whoever eats this bread unworthily and drinks this cup of the Lord unworthily is guilty of the body and blood of Christ. But some infer from this that the body and blood of Christ are so joined to the symbols that the wicked too truly and really eat and drink them along with them. For, they say, how else is the impious man guilty of the body and blood of Christ, unless he eats and drinks them? But this is far too trifling, and the similar examples which we cited a little earlier should have been enough for the quarrelsome. Nor is there any point in their crying out that these examples are drawn from profane things, while the reasoning about divine and heavenly mysteries is quite different. For while we by no means deny the difference between the divine and the human, we have observed in the Scriptures of both the Old and New Testaments that the Holy Spirit speaks with us in a human manner, and in delivering the mysteries of the sacraments accommodates himself not only to our capacity but also to the custom received among men. Now what is so common and usual as this: that a man is said to be guilty of treason who violates the seal or statue of a prince, even though he has never touched the prince himself, and perhaps has not even seen him? Several weighty reasons remind us that these words of the Apostle must be understood in this sense. The first is that Paul speaks of the Christ who is to come, not of one now bodily present. The second is that throughout this whole discussion he names the bread and the cup: "As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup," etc. And here: "Whoever eats this bread and drinks this cup of the Lord unworthily," etc. And soon after: "Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup." The Apostle speaks in this way, although he knew that he had to do with those who thought less honourably of this Supper, to such an extent that they made almost no distinction between it and any ordinary or profane feast.

units.la: At quantum ponderis admonitioni huic accessurum erat, si dixisset: An nescitis ipsum Christum realiter, corporaliter & substantialiter vobis præsentem adesse? adeoque panem hunc iam non amplius panem, sed ipsissimum corpus Christi esse, in poculo autem hoc non vinum, sed ipsissimum Christi sanguinem, quo redempti estis, contineri? Cur ergo tam indignè ista tractatis? Cur vos tanto scelere polluitis, sacrosanctum illud corpus indignè manducando, & sanguinem eiusdem indignè bibendo? Hæc & huius generis multa dici poterant, si eadem Pauli de hoc mysterio, quæ hodie multorum est, fuisset sententia. Sed noluit hyperbolicis locutionibus vti, ex quibus superstitionis aliqua occasio enasci poterat: & si huius exemplum aliqui ex patribus secuti fuissent, qui vt Cœnæ mysticæ authoritatem maiorem conciliarent, crassè nimis locuti sunt, minus errorum & superstitionum in Ecclesiam irrepsisset.
units.tr: But how much weight would this admonition have carried, if he had said: "Do you not know that Christ himself is really, bodily and substantially present with you? And so this bread is no longer bread, but the very body of Christ, and in this cup there is not wine, but the very blood of Christ, by which you have been redeemed. Why then do you treat these things so unworthily? Why do you defile yourselves with so great a crime, by eating unworthily that most holy body, and by drinking unworthily its blood?" Many such things could have been said, if Paul's opinion about this mystery had been the same as that of many people today. But he chose not to use hyperbolic expressions, from which some occasion of superstition might arise. And if some of the Fathers had followed this example, instead of speaking too crudely in order to win greater authority for the mystical Supper, fewer errors and superstitions would have crept into the Church.

units.la: Sed de his alias: quoad verò præsens institutum, docent locutiones istæ Apostolicæ, impios in Cœna præter panem & vinum nihil accipere, nihilominus tamen corporis & sanguinis Christi reatu teneri. Probatur id tertia ratione euidentissimè, quæ est, quòd Christi caro & sanguis non aliter quàm per fidem eduntur & bibuntur. Docet hoc ipse Ioan. sexto Cap. vbi promisciuè edendi, bibendi & credendi verbis pro ijsdem subinde vtitur. At impios fide destitutos, notius est quàm vt demonstrari debeat. Quomodo igitur corpus Christi edent, & eius sanguinem bibent, cùm os illud non habeant, quo solo hæc edi & bibi possunt? Adde hîs quarto loco, quòd Christi corpus nunquam inutiliter, multò minus cum pernitie aut ad hominis exitium sumitur. Est enim huic coniunctus Spiritus Christi, qui porrò ab illo separari non potest. Quisquis ergo illud accipit, idem Spiritum quoque Christi accipiat oportet, quo animatur, vt in illo vitam nouam viuat. Ideo ipse in loco supra citato dicebat: Qui edit meam carnem, & bibit meum sanguinem, in me manet, & ego in ipso. Sicut me misit Viuens ille Pater, & ego viuo per Patrem: ita & qui ederit me, viuet ipse quoque propter me. At impij neque Christum in seipsis manentem habent, neque ipsi in illo manent, multoque minus in illo viuunt: Ergo neque eius corpus edunt, neque sanguinem bibunt, licet externis symbolis communicent.
units.tr: But of these things elsewhere; as for the present subject, these Apostolic words teach that the wicked in the Supper receive nothing beyond bread and wine, and yet are nonetheless held guilty of the body and blood of Christ. This is proved most clearly by a third reason, namely that the flesh and blood of Christ are eaten and drunk only through faith. The Lord himself teaches this in John chapter 6, where he uses the words eating, drinking and believing interchangeably for the same thing. But that the wicked lack faith is too well known to need demonstration. How then will they eat the body of Christ and drink his blood, since they do not have that mouth by which alone these can be eaten and drunk? Add to this, in the fourth place, that the body of Christ is never taken in vain, much less with ruin or to a man's destruction. For the Spirit of Christ is joined to it, and cannot in turn be separated from him. Whoever therefore receives it must also receive the Spirit of Christ, by whom it is quickened, so that he may live a new life in him. So he himself said in the place cited above: "He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him. As the living Father sent me, and I live through the Father, so he who eats me shall live also through me." But the wicked neither have Christ abiding in themselves, nor do they abide in him, and much less do they live in him. Therefore they neither eat his body nor drink his blood, although they share in the outward symbols.

units.la: Quòd si autem de impiorum manducatione omnino digladiari libet ijs, qui puriorem Euangelij doctrinam profitentur, quid adhuc Scholasticos Doctores & ineptos Monachos ridemus, qui disputare solent, quid mures & tineæ comedant, quando panem Sacramenti arrodunt? quid itemcanes, aucicula, simiæ & quæcunque alia sunt animalia? Quis enim nescit impios omnibus animantibus brutis deteriori loco esse? Ipse etenim Deus hæc illis longè præfert, quando per Prophetas ait: Agnouit bos herum suum, & asinus præsepe domini sui: at Israel non agnoscit, populus meus se non intelligit. Item Ciconia in aëre nouit tempora sua: turtur, grus & hirundo observant tempus profectionis suæ: at populus meus non agnoscit iudicium Domini. Quod si dicas: Cœnam Dominicam propter homines, non autem propter animalia bruta institutam esse, & proinde superuacaneas esse quæstiones, quæ de illis mouentur: idem ipse tecum fateor, at simul me iam habere dico quod quærebam. Quia enim Cœna non propter impios, sed solos electos & fideles instituta est, perperam & intempestiuè disputatur, quid in hoc sacro epulo impij comedant, in quo nulla ipsius pars est, & ad quod neque os illud neque attractuam[?] illam facultatem afferunt, quibus solis caro & sanguis Christi percipiuntur. Ingerunt quidem sese vt subdola vulpes hypocritæ, impudenter canum instar sese intrudunt scelerati multi & pœnitere nescij, violenter etiam vt lupi & leones multi irrumpunt, quos nullæ admonitiones neque comminationes mini-strorum abstterrere possunt, quo minus Cœna Dominica abutantur: sed hi omnes cum à fide alienti sint, nihilo plus inueniunt, quàm bruta illa, quorum ingenium & mores referunt. Imò eo perniciosior illis est esus ipse, quia reatu corporis & sanguinis Domini sese alligant, vt damnationi & exitio ipsis seruiat, quod pijs ad salutem est traditum.
units.tr: But if those who profess the purer doctrine of the Gospel wish to fight at length about the eating of the wicked, why do we still laugh at the Scholastic doctors and foolish monks, who are wont to dispute what mice and moths eat when they gnaw the bread of the Sacrament? What of dogs, jackdaws, apes and any other animals? For who does not know that the wicked are in a worse position than all brute animals? God himself ranks these far above them when he says through the Prophets: "The ox knows its owner, and the ass the manger of its master; but Israel does not know, my people does not understand." Likewise the stork in the air knows its seasons; the turtle-dove, the crane and the swallow observe the time of their departure; but my people does not know the judgement of the Lord. But if you say that the Lord's Supper was instituted for men, not for brute animals, and that therefore the questions raised about them are superfluous, I agree with you on this point, but at the same time I say that I now have what I was seeking. For since the Supper was instituted not for the wicked but only for the elect and faithful, it is foolish and ill-timed to dispute what the wicked eat in this sacred feast, in which they have no part, and to which they bring neither that mouth nor that power of receiving by which alone the flesh and blood of Christ are perceived. Indeed, many wicked and impenitent men push themselves in like cunning foxes or hypocrites, shamelessly like dogs, and many force their way in violently like wolves and lions, whom no admonitions or warnings from the ministers can deter from abusing the Lord's Supper. But all of these, since they are alienated from faith, find nothing more than those brute animals whose nature and habits they reflect. Indeed the eating itself is more destructive for them, because by it they bind themselves to the guilt of the body and blood of the Lord, so that what was handed down for the salvation of the godly serves for their own damnation and ruin.

units.la: Obiiciunt hîc rursus aliqui: Ergo Sacramentorum virtus & ipsius Dei fides ab hominibus pendet? Quibus ego respondeo, Nequaquam: Noui enim illud Pauli de Iudæis dicentis: Quid tum si quidam illorum fuerunt increduli? num incredulitas eorum fidem Dei facit irritam? Absit. Imò sit Deus verax, omnis autem homo mendax. Vt ergo Deus per Euangelium in Filio suo IESV CHRISTO salutem omnibus vere offert, eius autem non nisi credentes participes fiunt, reliquis proprio vitio in sua incredulitate & pertinacia pereuntibus: Ita Sacramenta redemptionis per Christum facta sigilla sunt vera & certa, quibus gratiæ suæ promissiones Deus omnibus hominibus obsignat, quibus item Christus toti mortalium generi testatur, se esse panem illum & potum vitæ, quo vno ad vitam æternam feruemur: fructum tamen illorum soli ij percipiunt, qui ore fidei simul Christum apprehendunt: non autem illi, qui impia nausea pleni cibum illum vitæ respuunt, symbolis autem alias ob causas pro sua libidine abutuntur. In ipsis ergo perditionis culpa hæret, & neque Deo neque Verbi eius aut Sacramentorum impotentiæ adscribi debet. Poterant hæc multis Scripturæ & patrum testimonijs probari, sed cum quæ hucusque dicta sunt sufficere possint ijs qui veritatis cognitionem ex animo quærunt, ad alteram huius loci partem transfibimus.
units.tr: Here some again object: "Then does the power of the sacraments, and even the faith of God himself, depend on men?" To them I answer: By no means. For I recall Paul's words about the Jews: "What if some of them were unbelieving? Does their unbelief make the faith of God without effect? God forbid. Let God be true, but every man a liar." Just as God truly offers salvation to all men through the Gospel in his Son Jesus Christ, yet only believers become partakers of it, while the rest perish through their own fault in their unbelief and obstinacy, so the sacraments of redemption made through Christ are true and certain seals, by which God confirms to all men the promises of his grace. In them Christ likewise testifies to the whole human race that he is that bread and drink of life by which alone we are nourished to eternal life. Yet only those receive its fruit who at the same time lay hold of Christ with the mouth of faith. Those who, full of impious loathing, spit out that food of life, and who abuse the symbols for other reasons, as their lust dictates, do not receive it. The guilt of destruction therefore lies in them, and it must not be ascribed to God's impotence, or to his Word or sacraments. These things could be proved by many testimonies of Scripture and the Fathers, but since what has been said so far is enough for those who seek the knowledge of truth from the heart, we will pass to the other part of this passage.

units.la: Pergit enim Paulus & vitio huic generali remedium quoque aut consilium generale adhibet, in cuius cognitione omnes diligenter versari necesse est. Nisi enim hic probe instructi fimus, facile fuerit, dum vnum vitium vitare volumus in contraria multa incurrere: quod hodie non pauci accidere videmus. Quando enim proponuntur hæc, quæ hucusque exposuimus, multi scelerum aut propriæ indignitatis conscientia territi, à Cœnæ huius vsu prorsus abstinent, ne corporis & sanguinis Domini reos sese faciant. Alij vero, quos propriæ iustitiæ fiducia confidentiores facit, communionem publicam fugiunt propter sceleratos aliquos, qui in Ecclesijs passim visuntur. Metuunt illi, ne eandem cum his Cœnam fumentes simul sceleribus quoque eorum communicent. Et hinc olim Confessio auricularis suum initium habuit, qua nonnulli putabant hoc caveri posse, ne quis indignè ad mensam Domini accederet. Cui errori hodie nouam occasionem struunt, qui sub plausibili disciplinæ ecclesiasticæ cpræextu[?] Excommunicatione tuentur & vrgent, quia à Sacramentorum societate eos excludant, qui ipsis minus probati videntur. Sed quid Paulus, qui in Corinthiaca Ecclesia omnis generis vitia atque scelera regnare sciebat? Vno verbo rem maximi momenti expedit, si multi omnium istorum erroneas sententias iugulat. Probet (inquit) seipsum homo, et ita de pane illo edat, & de poculo illo bibat. Hominis vocabulo vtitur phrasi Hebraica, pro eo quod nos vnusquisque dicimus. Sensus ergo est, non opus esse, vt Christiani homines hinc inde sciscitantum discurrant, num ad Cœnam satis idonei sint, vel in aliorum personis solliciti hæreant, num tuto cum illis possint communicare: sed vnumquemque in seipsum descendere & seipsum explorare debere, priusquam ad hanc mensam accedat.
units.tr: For Paul goes on, and he also applies to this general vice a general remedy or counsel, and it is necessary for everyone to study it carefully. For unless we are thoroughly instructed here, it will be easy, while we want to avoid one vice, to fall into many contrary ones, as we see happening today to not a few. For when the things we have set out so far are proposed, many, terrified by the consciousness of their crimes or of their own unworthiness, abstain altogether from the use of this Supper, lest they make themselves guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. Others, whom confidence in their own righteousness makes more bold, shun public communion because of certain wicked people who are seen everywhere in the churches. They fear that by taking the same Supper with these people they will at the same time share in their sins. From this, long ago, auricular confession took its beginning, by which some thought it could be guarded against that anyone should approach the Lord's table unworthily. Those who now defend and press excommunication under the plausible pretext of church discipline are preparing a new occasion for this same error, since they exclude from fellowship in the sacraments those who seem to them less approved. But what did Paul do, who knew that every kind of vice and crime reigned in the Corinthian church? In one word he settles a matter of the greatest importance, and cuts the throat of all those erroneous opinions: "Let a man," he says, "examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup." He uses the word "man" in a Hebrew manner of speaking, in the sense of what we each say. The meaning, therefore, is that Christians need not run here and there inquiring whether they are fit enough for the Supper, or hang anxiously upon the persons of others, to see whether they can safely communicate with them. Rather, each must descend into himself and examine himself before he approaches this table.

units.la: Confutatur hoc loco, qui alios potius quàm seipsos probare satagunt, et si quos ad Cœnam admittunt videt, quos ipsi indignos iudicant, mox præcipiti iudicio totam illam Ecclesiam damnant, & ab ea secessionè[?] faciunt. Tales olim Donatistæ fuerunt, quorum errore hodie Anabaptistæ instaurat, qui multos sub plausibili sanctitatis prætextu seducunt, quibus persuadent, ita omnino fieri oportere, ne cum sceleratis unum corpus fiant, & eorum peccatis communicent. Faciunt hi quod nuspiam iubentur. Nec enim vt aliorum vitam & conscientias exploremus iubet Paulus, sed vt singuli seipsos probent. Et notum est illud Christi: Ne iudicate, vt ne iudicemini. Et cum Cœna charitatis frater-næ vinculum externum esse nobis debeat: faciunt isti quod ab illa est alienissimum. Charitas enim non temere damnat, sed bene sperat de omnibus: non abijcit, sed colligit: non eraducit [?] fratrum scelera,neque theatrica ex illis qui ea agnoscunt spectacula facit, sed multitudinem quoq; peccatorum operit, vt ex Solomone Petrus annotauit. Conantur denique quod factu impossibile est. Quis e-nim nouit ea quæ sunt in homine præter spiritum hominis, qui in ipso est? Et Deum solum cordium & renum scrutatorem esse scriptura passim docent. Damnantur præterea illi totius Veteris & Noui testamenti consensu, atque omnium sæculorum exemplis. Quis enim sanctorum olim propter alios, quos vitæ minus probatæ esse videbat, vel à Circumcisione vel ab alijs sacris vnquam abstinuit? Et vt Prophetas taceamus, qui cum illis ipsis sacrificia & dies festos egerunt, quorum scelera suis concionibus grauissimè accusabant, nonne Christus ad dies festos Hierosolymam ascendit, sacris interfuit, & Pascha cuius celebrauit, quos propter indomitam contumaciam exitio suo proximos esse sciebat? Idē nec Ioannes baptismū horruit, quem multi hypocritæ, multi palam flagitiosi recipiebant, quo deniq; tingebantur, quos ipse Ioannes progeniem viperarum vocabat. Quod si ad primam Cœnam accedamus, quales obsecro primi Christi conuiuæ, discipuli nimirum fuerunt? Et nonne illis Iudas interfuit, fur & proditor? Neque tamen hunc Christus exclusit, neque propter illum à mensa alij discipuli abierunt. Scio quid hic aduersarij obiciant, Iudæ peccatum adhuc occultum fuisse, & ideo illum neque à Christo eijci debuisse, neque à discipulis communionem cum illo potuisse vitari. Sed mirum est, homines doctos & iudicio præditos effugia huiusmodi quærere. Num verò Christus Iudæ scelus ignorabat? Attamen illum epulo paschali primum, deinde suæ etiam Cœnæ adhibere dignatus est. Adhæc discipulos quoque scelus hoc non latuit, cum Christus illud tam diserte verbis argueret, & ipsi ex eo dolorem vehementem conciperent. Sed sceleris auctorem non agnoscebant, inquis. Hoc vt demus, adeò nihil iuuat aduersarios, vt potius ex eo plus periculi fuerit, si cum impijs Sacramentorum communione vti nefas esset, cum nescirent à quo potissimum sibi deberent cauere. Nihil ergo est quod illi dicunt, ne primæ Cœnæ exemplo conuincantur. Sed imponit plerisque falsa persuasio, in Sacramentorum vsu ita vniri & coniungi homines, vt aliorum quoque peccatis communicent, qui cum malis & impijs Cœnam Christi mysticam celebrant. Est autem persuasio hæc vanissima. Nec enim hic scelerum communio fit, sed earum rerum, à quibus salus nostra dependet, & quæ ad fidei confessionem faciunt. Hic etiamsi Ecclesiæ oculos fallant impij, hoc tamen pijs fraudi esse non potest, quando illi præter externa symbola nihil acceperunt, alienissimi autem sunt ab ijs, quibus pij sub Christo capite in vnum corpus coalescunt. Et hoc Paulus probè intellexit, qui ideo mox dicit: Qui edit & bibit indignè, iudicium sibi ipsi edit & bibit. En sibi ipsi iudicium edit impius hypocrita, non tibi, non mihi, non vlli alij priorum, qui sacra hæc cum fide & vt par est vsurpant. Hæc diligentius expendant omnes, quos vel propriæ iustitiæ fiducia, vel inutilis & præposterus metus decipit, vt sibi à publica communione abstinendum, vel ab Ecclesijs discedendum esse putent, ne aliorum peccatis polluantur. De seipsis potius omnes soliciti sint, seipsos probent & examinent serio, Dei autem iudicio relinquant eos, quos abs se corrigi non posse vident.
units.tr: This passage refutes those who strive to test others rather than themselves, and if they see that some whom they judge unworthy are admitted to the Supper, they at once condemn that whole church with hasty judgment and withdraw from it in separation. Such were the Donatists of old, and by their error the Anabaptists now renew it. Under the plausible pretext of holiness they lead many astray, persuading them that it must altogether be so, lest they become one body with the wicked and share in their sins. These people do what they are nowhere commanded to do. For Paul does not bid us to explore the lives and consciences of others, but that each should test himself. And the saying of Christ is well known: "Judge not, that you be not judged." And since the Supper ought to be for us the outward bond of brotherly love, these people do what is most alien to it. For love does not rashly condemn but hopes well of all things; it does not cast away but gathers together; it does not lay bare the crimes of brothers, nor make a theatrical spectacle of them for those who recognise them, but, as Peter noted from Solomon, it covers the multitude of sins. Finally, they attempt what is impossible to do. For who knows the things that are in a man except the spirit of the man that is in him? And Scripture everywhere teaches that God alone is the searcher of hearts and reins. Moreover, those people are condemned by the agreement of the whole Old and New Testament and by the examples of all ages. For which of the saints in former times ever abstained from circumcision or other sacred rites on account of others whom he saw to be of less approved life? And to say nothing of the prophets, who celebrated sacrifices and feast days with those very men whose crimes they accused most severely in their sermons, did not Christ himself go up to Jerusalem for the feast days, take part in the sacred rites, and celebrate the Passover, though he knew that those men, because of their untamed obstinacy, were near to their own destruction? Likewise John did not shrink from baptising, which many hypocrites, and many openly wicked men, received, and by which they were washed, those whom John himself called a brood of vipers. But if we come to the first Supper, what sort of guests, I beg you, did Christ have there, namely his disciples? And was not Judas, the thief and traitor, present among them? Yet Christ did not exclude him, nor did the other disciples leave the table because of him. I know what our opponents object here: that Judas's sin was still hidden, and therefore he ought neither to have been cast out by Christ, nor could communion with him be avoided by the disciples.
