But it is strange that learned men of judgment seek such escapes. Did Christ, then, not know Judas's crime? Yet he deigned to admit him first to the Passover feast, and then to his own Supper. Moreover, the disciples too were not unaware of this crime, since Christ rebuked it so plainly in words, and they themselves were filled with great grief because of it. But, you say, they did not recognise the author of the crime. Grant this: it helps our opponents so little that it would rather have been more dangerous, if it were wrong to share the sacraments with the impious, since they did not know from whom they most needed to guard themselves. So there is nothing in what they say that can be shown false by the example of the first Supper. But a false persuasion deceives most people, that in the use of the sacraments men are so united and joined that they share also in the sins of others who celebrate Christ's mystical Supper with the evil and impious. This persuasion, however, is most vain. For here no communion of sins takes place, but of those things on which our salvation depends and which pertain to the confession of faith. Here, even if the impious deceive the eyes of the Church, this cannot be a loss to the godly, since the wicked have received nothing beyond the outward symbols, and they are utterly alien to those in whom the godly, under Christ the head, grow together into one body. Paul understood this well, which is why he soon says: "He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself." See, the impious hypocrite eats judgment to himself, not to you, not to me, not to any of the others who receive these holy things with faith and as is fitting. Let all those consider these things more carefully who are deceived either by confidence in their own righteousness, or by a useless and perverse fear, so that they think they must abstain from public communion or depart from the churches, lest they be polluted by the sins of others. Rather let all be anxious about themselves, let them test and examine themselves seriously, and leave to God's judgment those whom they see they cannot correct.

units.la: Confutantur præterea hoc Pauli consilio, qui priuatam singulorum præparationem ad Cœnā vrgent, cuius præcipuam partem constituunt Confessionem auricularem, per quam in cordium quoque & cogitationum arcana penetrant. Quorum tanta est in suo hoc more tuendo seueritas, vt neminem ad huius Sacramenti communionem admittant, nisi qui prius delicta sua, sacerdoti confessus sit, & ab eo absolutionem priuatā acceperit. Quid verò huius in præsenti Paulus iubet, cum ex professo docere instituerit, vt singuli sese præparare debeant, ne indignè de mensa Domini edant & bibant? Aut quid simile factum in veteris populi ecclesia, vbi purificationes & præparationes frequentiores simul & operosiores fuisse scimus? Ibi tamen nulla vnquam in vsu fuit priuata peccatorum confessio, neque aliquem propter peccata à communione sacrorum vnquam exclusum fuisse legimus. In primitiua quoque Ecclesia nihil huius inuenitur, neque ex scripturis probari potest, vnquam penes ministros eam potestatem fuisse, vt ipsi examen priuatum haberent eorum, qui communicaturi erant, & vt ipsi qui nam digni, quiue indigni essent, pronuntiarent. Valuit enim apud omnes Spiritus Sancti consilium, qui per Paulum monuit, vt vnusquisque seipsum probet atque scrutetur. Posteris demum temporibus, quando crescente superstitione Sacramentis nimium tribui captum, tunc exclusiones eorum institutae sunt, qui publice peccauissent. Additae simul satisfactiones, quibus non Deo, sed Ecclesiae satisfieret, priusquam ad eius communionem rursus admitterentur. Et vt Sozomenus scribit, episcopi Nouatianorum importunitate coacti presbyteros ordinarunt, qui poenitentiam agentibus praeessent. Erant hi spectatae pietatis viri, prudentes & commissi arcani fideles custodes. His priuatim confitebantur, qui peccatorum conscientia sese premi sentiebant. Praescribebant illi satisfactionum formam, & certum poenitentiae illius tempus definiebant, quo euoluto ad Caenae communionem denuo illis accessus patebat. Habuit ergo mos iste initium non malum, & bono zelo moti episcopi ista constituerunt, vt Nouatianis silentium imponerent, qui orthodoxas Ecclesias pro impuris damnabant. At quia suum potius zelum, quam Dei Verbum secuti sunt, & totum hoc institutum, non diuinum, sed humanum fuit, mox fructus quoque peperit, ex quibus plus scandali enatum est, quam ex sceleribus publicis, quae illi hac ratione coercere voluerunt. Cum enim in Constantinopolitana urbe mulier quaedam genere illustris a presbytero poenitentiario iussa esset ieiuniis & precibus frequentioribus vacare, & ideo in templo praeter morem diutius & saepius moraretur, accidit vt cum diacono stupri consuetudinem haberet, & in hoc tam turpi flagitio deprehenderetur. Commouit tanti sceleris indignitas totum populum, & ministerii ecclesiastici dignitatem vehementer labefactauit. Quapropter Nectarius, eius vrbis Episcopus & diaconum scortatorem loco mouit, & presbyteros poenitentiarios sustulit, monentibus nonnullis, vt vnumquemque propriae conscientiae relinqueret, neque aliquam remoram poneret iis, qui ad Caenam Domini mysticam accedere volunt. Mansit tamen mos iste (vt idem author perhibet) in Occidentalibus Ecclesiis, & imprimis Romae, quae iam tunc incipiebat mysterium iniquitatis operari, & postea hoc fere medio tyrannidem in omnium hominum conscientias obtinuit. Mox autem grauiores multo errores secuti sunt, inter quos intolerabilis est, quod satisfactionibus, quae in Confessione auriculari mandantur, meritum adscripserunt, & iisdem peccata expiauerunt. Quid, quod hac ratione, quasi per cuniculos, in Regum, Imperatorum & quorumuis aliorum arcana penetrarunt Pontifices, quod vnum toti mundo formidabiles facere potuit? Si quis vero stupra, adulteria, incestus, rapinas, haereditatum interceptiones, & alia huius generis enumerare velit, quae Sacrificuli & Monachi impuri sub Confessionis praetextu designarunt, dicendi exordium citius quam finem inueniet. At hi sunt humanorum inuentorum fructus. Et cum haec lippis atque tonsoribus nota sint, mirum est, non modo Pontificios tantum errorem tueri, verumetiam in reformatis Ecclesiis inueniri aliquos, qui ad illum viam denuo sternant suis priuatis praeparationibus & priuatis absolutionibus, quas pertinaciter defendunt.
units.tr: Moreover, this teaching of Paul is refuted by those who insist on private preparation of each individual for the Supper. The chief part of that preparation, they maintain, is auricular confession, through which they penetrate even into the secrets of the heart and the thoughts. In defending this custom they are so severe that they admit no one to communion in this Sacrament unless he has first confessed his sins to a priest and received private absolution from him. But what does Paul here command, when he set out to teach expressly that each person should prepare himself, so that he does not eat and drink unworthily at the Lord's table? Or what similar practice was there in the Church of the old people, where we know that purifications and preparations were both more frequent and more laborious? Yet there was never any private confession of sins in use there, nor do we read that anyone was ever excluded from the sacred rites on account of sins. Nothing of this is found in the primitive Church either, and it cannot be proved from Scripture that the ministers ever had the power to hold a private examination of those who were about to communicate, and to declare who were worthy and who unworthy. For the counsel of the Holy Spirit, who through Paul admonished that each one should prove and examine himself, held sway among all. In later times, when superstition grew and far too much was ascribed to the Sacraments, then exclusions were instituted for those who had sinned publicly. At the same time satisfactions were added, by which satisfaction was made not to God but to the Church, before they were readmitted to its communion. And as Sozomen writes, the bishops, compelled by the importunity of the Novatians, appointed presbyters who would preside over those doing penance. These were men of proven piety, prudent and faithful guardians of the secrets entrusted to them. Those whose consciences felt burdened by sins confessed to them privately. They prescribed the form of satisfactions and fixed a definite period of penance, at the end of which access to the communion of the Supper was opened to them again. This custom, then, had a not bad beginning, and the bishops who established these things were moved by a good zeal, to impose silence on the Novatians, who condemned the orthodox Churches as impure. But because they followed their own zeal rather than the Word of God, and this whole institution was human, not divine, it soon also bore fruit, from which more scandal arose than from the public crimes which they wished to restrain in this way. For when in the city of Constantinople a certain woman of noble birth was ordered by a penitentiary presbyter to devote herself to fasting and frequent prayers, and therefore lingered in the church longer and more often than was customary, it happened that she had an illicit relationship with a deacon and was caught in this so shameful disgrace. The unworthiness of so great a crime stirred the whole people and greatly undermined the dignity of the ecclesiastical ministry. Therefore Nectarius, bishop of that city, removed the deacon who was a fornicator from his place, and abolished the penitentiary presbyters, some advising that each person be left to his own conscience and that no hindrance be placed in the way of those who wish to come to the mystical Supper of the Lord. Nevertheless this custom remained (as the same author reports) in the Western Churches, and especially at Rome, which was already then beginning to work the mystery of iniquity, and afterwards by this means it gained almost tyrannical power over the consciences of all men. Soon, however, much graver errors followed, among which is intolerable the fact that they ascribed merit to the satisfactions which are enjoined in auricular confession, and by these expiated sins. What of the fact that by this method, as though through mines, the Pontiffs penetrated into the secrets of kings, emperors and any others whatever, a thing which alone could make them formidable to the whole world? If anyone wished to list the adulteries, fornications, incests, robberies, interceptions of inheritances, and other things of this kind, which impure priests and monks have brought to light under the pretext of confession, he would find the beginning of his speech sooner than its end. But these are the fruits of human inventions. And since these things are known even to bleary-eyed folk and barbers, it is a wonder that not only the Papists defend this error, but that in the reformed Churches there are also some who, by their private preparations and private absolutions, which they stubbornly defend, pave the way for it again.

units.la: Fatemur equidem, saepe homines ita perplexos esse, vt vel ministrorum Ecclesiae vel aliorum consilio eos subleuari necesse sit. Quos monemus, vt quando sibi ipsis non satisfaciunt, ab illis consilium petant, qui instructiores sunt, neque ad priuatam sui Pastoris institutionem recurrant. Vt ve-ro Ecclesiarum ministri aliquem cogant, & nouum sibi in hominum conscientias ius atque imperium vendicent, nullo modo probare possumus. Quin potius Paulum nobis etiam loqui putamus, qui si quid huius deberet fieri, minime id taciturus erat, maxime cum ad eam Ecclesiam scri-bat, in qua scelera grauissima regnabant, & in qua a plerisque prophano Caenae abusu hucusque peccatum fuerat. Vult tamen ille, vt quisque seipsum probet, nec aliquem vlterius grauari vult. Hoc enim examen vt tutissimum, sic etiam certissimum est. Quis enim suam ipsius conscientiam fallere poterit? Enimuero etsi hoc interdum conentur impii & scelerati homines, nihilominus proficiunt. Inuitis enim illa obrepit, accusat, arguit, convincit, vt non temere eam mille testium loco esse veteres dixerint. In aliis vero hominibus examinandis facile fallimur. Vascrum est enim cor hominis & inscrutabile inquit Ieremias. Ideo & illi nobis imponere possunt, & pœnitentiam simulare, quæ apud ipsos nulla est, & vt iam verum nobis fateantur, tamen qui & quales in posterum futuri sint, scire non possumus. Adde his, quòd qui ad Ecclesiam & Sacramentorum communionem allici debebant, importunis illis & iniquis exclusionibus arcentur: prohibentur denique peccatores, ne cum reliquis mortem Domini prædicent, quod opus Deo gratissimum est, & ab omnibus exigitur, qui Christo nomen dederunt. Fit denique, vt fere Pharisæi hypocritæ omnium optimi iudicentur, qui superbis illis alienæ fidei dominatoribus sese approbare possunt, excludantur autem publicani, qui animo vere contrito clamant: Domine, propitius esto mihi peccatori. Verum me dicere fatebuntur, quotquot Ecclesias illas propius inspexerint, in quibus illi dominantur. Quotquot ergo & priuatæ singulorum saluti, & publicæ Ecclesiarum paci aut quieti consultum volunt, ij Pauli consilium sanctum ratum habeant, neque aliquos ab vsu mensæ Dominicæ arceant, quàm eos, qui seipsos probare non possunt: quales sunt infantes & pueri, furiosi & rationis vsu destituti, & qui à Christiana religione prorsus alieni sunt, aut saltem prima eius rudimenta nondum intelligunt.
units.tr: We admit indeed that people are often so perplexed that they must be relieved by the counsel of the ministers of the Church or of others. We advise such people that, when they are not satisfied with themselves, they should seek counsel from those who are better instructed, and not have recourse to the private instruction of their own pastor. But that the ministers of the Churches should compel anyone, and claim for themselves a new right and rule over men's consciences, we cannot in any way approve. Rather we think that Paul speaks to us also, for if anything of this kind ought to be done, he would certainly not have kept silent about it, especially since he was writing to that Church in which the gravest crimes reigned, and in which, through the profane abuse of the Supper by very many, sin had been committed up to that time. Yet he wills that each one examine himself, and he does not wish anyone to be burdened further. For this examination is as safe as it is certain. For who can deceive his own conscience? Indeed, although wicked and criminal men sometimes try to do this, they nonetheless fail. For against their will that conscience creeps up on them, accuses, convicts, and condemns them, so that the ancients rightly said it is worth a thousand witnesses. But in examining other men we are easily mistaken. For the heart of man is deceitful and inscrutable, says Jeremiah. Therefore they can also impose upon us and feign a repentance which they do not in fact have, and even if they now confess the truth to us, we still cannot know what sort of people they will be in future. Add to this that those who ought to be drawn to the Church and to communion in the Sacraments are kept away by those troublesome and unjust exclusions. Finally, sinners are forbidden to proclaim the Lord's death with the rest, which is a work most pleasing to God and is required of all who have given their name to Christ. In the end it comes about that, almost, the Pharisees, the hypocrites, are judged the best of all, since they can recommend themselves to those proud lords of another's faith, while the tax collectors, who cry out with a heart truly contrite, "Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner," are shut out. All who have looked more closely at those Churches in which these men rule will confess that I speak the truth. Therefore, all who wish to provide both for the private salvation of individuals and for the public peace or quiet of the Churches should hold Paul's counsel to be holy and approved, and should keep from the use of the Lord's table none but those who cannot prove themselves: such as infants and children, the insane and those deprived of the use of reason, and those who are wholly alien to the Christian religion, or at least do not yet understand its first rudiments.

units.la: Porrò hic singuli intelligant oportet, in quo nam probatio nostri ipsius consistat, & quomodo fieri debeat. Qui aurum probare volunt, Lydio lapide & igne vtuntur, quibus explorant, num adsint ea, quæ auri propria sunt. Ita hic ad Verbi Dei ignem, qui simul indicis aut lapidis Lydij instar est, nosmetipsos examinari oportet, num ea nobis insint, quæ in Cœna profitemur. Sunt hæc (vt nuper audiuimus) fides in vnum IESVM CHRISTVM, sine qua recordatio & prædicatio vera mortis eius fieri non potest: abnegatio superstitionum & falsorum cultuum, vitæ innocentia morumque sanctitas, dilectio item mutua & fraterna, qua qui multi sumus, in vnum corpus coalescimus, adeoque panis vnus efficimur. Hæc si in nobis non ficta aut simulata deprehendamus, periculum non est, qui tuto & cum fructu ad sacram hanc & salutarem mensam possimus accedere.
units.tr: Furthermore, each person ought to understand here in what our own self-examination consists and how it ought to be done. Those who wish to test gold use the Lydian stone and fire, by which they find out whether those qualities which are proper to gold are present. So here we ought to be examined, ourselves, by the fire of the Word of God, which at the same time is like the touchstone of the Lydians, to see whether those things which we profess in the Supper are present in us. These are (as we heard recently): faith in the one Jesus Christ, without which a true remembrance and proclamation of his death cannot take place; renunciation of superstitions and false worship; innocence of life and holiness of manners; likewise mutual and brotherly love, by which we who are many coalesce into one body, and so are made one bread. If we find these things in ourselves not feigned or pretended, there is no danger that we may approach this holy and saving table safely and with profit.

units.la: Vbi simul obseruari debet, non requiri à nobis perfectionem angelicam. Nec enim Angelis aut spiritib. cœlestibus Cœna à Domino instituta est, sed hominibus, qui vt omnes in peccato concepti et nati sunt: ita etiâ natura infirmi atq; imperfecti sunt. Ideo in præsenti Paulus non ait, Qui indignus hûc panē edit, &c: sed, Quisquis ederit panē hunc, & hoc poculû Domini biberit indigne, &c. Ad actionem ergo Cœnæ, non ad edentium & bibentium personas indignitatem hanc restringit. Nam si nos respicias, quis obsecro dignus inuenietur, quem æternus Dei Filius suo corpore et sanguine pascat & alat ad vitam æternam? Nonne omnes cum Centurione illo Euangelico exclamare cogemur, Domine, non sumus digni, sub quorum tectum tu ingrediaris? In hoc ergo huius rei tardo versatur, ne indignè tanta tractemus mysteria, licet nos indignissimi simus, quibus illa committantur. Id vero cauebitur, si (vt diximus) nihil dolo malo fiat, & non falsa aut hypocritica sit, quam illic facimus, professio: & si peccatum non patiamur regnare in mortali corpore nostro, sed aduersus illud gladio Verbi Dei pugnemus, & in precibus feruentes simus, quibus & remissionem peccatorum, & Spiritus sancti gratiâ & fidei augmentum à Deo petamus. Qui ita in suum conspectum veniunt, eos non abijciet Dominus, qui vt laborantes & oneratos ad se vocat: ita neminem ad se venientem reijcit, & linum fumigans non extinguit, neque arundinem quassatam conterit. Exempla in Euangelio passim occurrunt, sed sufficere nobis potest, quod in prima Cœna proponitur. Quales enim tunc fuerunt discipuli? Certè vt Iudam nunc omittamus, reliqui omnes magnis & grauibus peccatis obnoxij fuere, imò inter cœnandum enormiter peccarunt. Nam contentionem de primatu, toties à Christo sopitam, instaurant; quæ animos ambitiosos, superbos & contentiosos arguit. Et tanta apud eos fuit istorum affectuum vis, vt nec tristissima mortis Christi iam imminentis commemoratio, quam ille tunc faciebat, ambitiosos illos spiritus reprimere potuerit. Accessit mox confidentia, qua elati Christo de ipsorum fuga & dispersione concionanti contradicunt: Vbi Petrus non modò Domino sese contumaciter opponit, verum etiam insolenter se omnibus alijs præfert, eosque pro fratribus debebat agnoscere. Taceo nunc turpem fugam, qua post pauculas horas dispersi, Christum inter medios hostes reliquerunt. Taceo turpiorem & cum aperta impietate coniunctam Petri abnegationem, qua Christum etiam abiurauit. Attamen hos omnes ille non mensa modo sua dignatus est, verumetiam mundos esse dicit propter Verbum suum, quod ipsis annuntiarat, & cuius semina illi intra animos suos constanter seruabant, vt vt ab innata vitiositate superati subinde delinquerent. Neminem ergo sua vel infirmitas vel imperfectio, imò neque ante commissorum scelerum recordatio terreat. Patent verè & ex animo poenitentibus diuinae gratiae fores. Et fides quantulacunque sit, ad Christum apprehendendum satis potens est & efficax, qui quae nobis desunt sua perfectione farcit atque supplet, peccata autem nostra sanguine suo eluit, ne in rationem apud Deum veniant, simulque gratiae huius sigillum atque testimonium sensibile in Coena nobis exhibet, qua nos intrepidè & fide certa vti conuenit.
units.tr: Here it should be observed at the same time that no angelic perfection is required of us. The Supper was not instituted by the Lord for angels or heavenly spirits, but for men, who, since all are conceived and born in sin, are also weak and imperfect by nature. Therefore Paul does not say here, "He who eats this bread unworthily," etc., but, "Whoever eats this bread and drinks this cup of the Lord unworthily," etc. He thus restricts this unworthiness to the action of the Supper, not to the persons who eat and drink. For if you look at us, who, I ask, will be found worthy, whom the eternal Son of God would feed and nourish with his body and blood unto eternal life? Shall we not all be compelled to cry out with that Gospel centurion, "Lord, we are not worthy that you should enter under our roof"? The point at issue, then, is this: that we should not handle such great mysteries unworthily, although we are most unworthy to whom they are entrusted. This will indeed be guarded against if (as we have said) nothing is done with evil intent, and the profession we make there is not false or hypocritical; and if we do not allow sin to reign in our mortal body, but fight against it with the sword of the Word of God, and are fervent in prayer, asking God for the forgiveness of sins, for the grace of the Holy Spirit, and for an increase of faith. The Lord will not cast out those who come into his sight in this way, for he calls the labouring and burdened to himself; so he rejects no one who comes to him, and does not quench the smoking flax nor break the bruised reed. Examples occur everywhere in the Gospel, but what is set before us in the first Supper may suffice. What kind of disciples were they then? Certainly, to leave Judas aside for now, all the rest were liable to great and grave sins; indeed, during the supper they sinned grievously. For they renewed the contention about primacy, which Christ had so often quelled, and this proves their minds to be ambitious, proud and quarrelsome. Such was the force of these passions among them that not even the most sorrowful commemoration of Christ's death, which he was then making and which was now imminent, could restrain those ambitious spirits. Soon confidence followed, by which, puffed up, they contradicted Christ when he preached about their flight and dispersal; here Peter not only stubbornly opposes the Lord, but also insolently sets himself above all the others, whom he ought to have acknowledged as brothers. I now pass over the shameful flight by which, scattered within a few hours, they left Christ among his enemies. I pass over Peter's more shameful denial, joined with open impiety, by which he even renounced Christ. Yet he did not deign to count all these only at his table, but even says they are clean on account of his Word, which he had announced to them, and whose seeds they constantly kept within their hearts, although, overcome by their innate sinfulness, they sometimes offended. Let no one therefore be terrified by his weakness or imperfection, or even by the recollection of past sins. The doors of divine grace are truly open to those who repent from the heart. And faith, however small, is powerful and effective enough to lay hold of Christ, who supplies by his perfection what is lacking in us, and washes away our sins with his blood, so that they do not come into account before God. At the same time, in the Supper he presents to us the seal and visible testimony of this grace, which we ought to use fearlessly and with a sure faith.

units.la: Quoniam verò omnibus saeculis inueniuntur, quos non multùm mouet sceleris atrocitas, tales Paulus ad Dei tribunal citat, & supplicij denuntiatione terret, dicens: Nam qui edit & bibit indignè, iudicium sibi edit & bibit, non discernens corpus Domini. Iudicij nomine poenam ipsam intelligit, quae partim aeterna est, quae impij & poenitere nescij multantur: partim temporaria, quae pij in hoc saeculo castigantur, quando indignius Coenam tractant. Et hoc Corinthijs accidit, quos lue & peste punitos fuisse audiemus propter huius Sacramenti abusum. Causam verò poenae subijcit his verbis: Non discernens corpus Domini. Corpus Domini vocat panem mysticum, quem corporis Christi Sacramentum esse iam ante diximus. Discernunt ergo corpus Domini in Coena, qui dignitatem tanti mysterij rectè expendunt, & panem hunc à reliquis cibis vulgaribus distinguunt, sic vt eo non ad corporis alimoniam vtantur, sed animae causam hac agi cogitent, adeoque credunt hic nobis Christi symbola proponi, quibus hic testatur, se panem illum vitae esse, qui suos alat & feruet ad vitam aeternam. Non discernunt autem corpus Domini, qui panem hunc à vulgari nihil differre putant, & ad Coenam perinde vt ad epulum prophanum ruunt, quod Corinthios fecisse supra audiuimus. Iudicium itaque tales sibi edunt & bibunt, non quòd panis ipse & hoc poculum per se mali aut noxij quid contineant, sed quòd illi abusu prophano sibi noxia reddunt, quae Dominus salutis nostrae ergo inflixit. Ita huius loci sensum D. Augustinus in libris de Baptismo contra Donatistas ex-posuit, vbi inter alia sic scribit: Sicut Iudas, cui buccellam tradidit Dominus, non malum accipiendo, sed malè accipiendo locum in se diabolo praebuit: sic indignè quisque sumens dominicum Sacramentum non efficit, vt quia ipse malus est, malum fit: aut quia non ad salutem accipit, nihil acceperit. Corpus enim Domini & sanguinis Domini nihilominus erat etiam illis, quibus dicebat Apostolus, Qui manducat indignè, iudicium sibi manducat. Corpus & sanguinem Domini etiam indignè manducantibus fuisse dicit, quia Sacramenta ipsa in se non mutantur, etiamsi impij (vt supra demonstrauimus) res ipsas non percipiant. Vnde idem Pater alibi dicit Iudam accepisse quidem panem Domini, non autem panem Dominum. Quod verò iudicium & poenas minatur Paulus ijs, qui indignè edunt & bibunt, non temerè facit, & multis exemplis id probari poterat. Quia tamen domestico exemplo Corinthiorum huic comminationi fidem faciet, nunc plura adducere non est opus. Hoc potius non oscitanter consideremus, quid hodie nobis sperandum sit, quando alij Coenam Domini sibi ipsis quaestum faciunt, alij sacrificium ex ea fabricant in meriti Christi contumeliam, multi verò ex eadem rixandi materiam venantur: plerique autem illam aut contemnunt, aut superstitiosius externis symbolis tribuunt, quae apud vnum Christum quaeri debebant? Haec nobis emendanda erant, siquidem vndique nobis imminentem Dei iram placare aut effugere vellemus. Hic ergo studium omne intendant cum verbi administris Christiani principes. Coniunctis autem precibus omnes Deum orent, vt hic omnium mentes illuminare & ad verae pietatis atque pacis studium flectere dignetur, vt idem sentiant & loquantur in Filio eius & redemptore nostro IESV CHRISTO: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: But since in every age there are found those whom the atrocity of a crime does not much move, Paul summons such men to the tribunal of God and terrifies them with the threat of punishment, saying: "For he who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgement to himself, not discerning the body of the Lord." By judgement he means the punishment itself, which is partly eternal, with which the wicked and those who cannot repent are punished; and partly temporal, with which the godly are chastised in this age when they handle the Supper unworthily. This happened to the Corinthians, who, we shall hear, were punished with plague and pestilence on account of their abuse of this sacrament. He states the cause of the punishment in these words: "not discerning the body of the Lord." He calls the mystical bread the body of the Lord, which we have already said is the sacrament of Christ's body. Those therefore discern the body of the Lord in the Supper who rightly weigh the dignity of so great a mystery and distinguish this bread from other common foods, so that they do not use it for nourishing the body, but think that the cause of the soul is being pursued here, and believe that Christ's symbols are set before us here, by which he testifies that he is that bread of life which feeds and nourishes his own unto eternal life. But those do not discern the body of the Lord who think this bread differs in nothing from ordinary bread, and rush to the Supper just as to a profane feast, which we heard above the Corinthians did. Such people eat and drink judgement to themselves, not because the bread itself and this cup contain anything evil or harmful in themselves, but because by profane abuse they make harmful for themselves what the Lord instituted for our salvation. Augustine expounded the sense of this passage in the same way against the Donatists in his books on Baptism, where among other things he writes: "As Judas, to whom the Lord gave the morsel, offered a place in himself to the devil not by receiving evil but by receiving badly, so each one who receives the Lord's sacrament unworthily does not make it evil because he himself is evil, nor receive nothing because he does not receive it to salvation. For the body of the Lord and the blood of the Lord were nonetheless also for those to whom the Apostle said, 'He who eats unworthily eats judgement to himself.'" He says that the body and blood of the Lord were also for those who eat unworthily, because the sacraments are not changed in themselves, even if the impious (as we showed above) do not receive the things themselves. Hence the same Father elsewhere says that Judas indeed received the bread of the Lord, but not the Lord's bread. That Paul threatens judgement and punishment to those who eat and drink unworthily he does not do rashly, and this could be proved by many examples. Yet since he will make this threat credible by the domestic example of the Corinthians, there is no need now to bring forward more. Rather let us consider carefully, and not carelessly, what we may hope for today, when some make gain for themselves from the Lord's Supper, others fashion a sacrifice out of it to the insult of Christ's merit, many hunt material for quarrelling from the same, and most either despise it or superstitiously ascribe to external symbols what ought to be sought in Christ alone. These things had to be amended by us, if we wished to placate or escape the wrath of God hanging over us on every side. Therefore let Christian princes, together with the ministers of the Word, apply all their zeal here. And with joined prayers let everyone pray God that he may deign to enlighten the minds of all and bend them to the pursuit of true piety and peace, so that they may think and speak the same in his Son, our redeemer Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXI.
units.tr: HOMILY LXI.

units.la: Propterea multi inter vos sunt infirmi & inualidi, & dor-miunt multi. Etenim si nosipsos dijudicaremus, non iudicaremur. Sed cum iudicamur, a Domino erudimur, ne cum mundo condemnemur. Itaque fratres mei, cum convenitis ad vescendum, alius alium expectate. Quod si quis esurit, domi edat: ne ad iudicium conveniatis. Reliqua vero, cum venero, constituam.
units.tr: For this reason many among you are weak and sickly, and many sleep. For if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged. But when we are judged, we are chastened by the Lord, so that we are not condemned with the world. So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you do not come together for judgment. The rest I will set in order when I come.

units.la: Quoniam Corinthij Cœnam Domini nostri Eucharisticam fœdissime prophanauerant, ut iam à prophano, vel etiam luxurioso convivio nihil differret, Paulus multa hucusq; adduxit, quibus hoc vitium corrigere studuit. Primo enim graviter eos reprehendit, quòd opulentiores cum pauperum & totius Ecclesiæ contemptu sub Cœnæ prætextu ventri & gulæ indulgerent, adeò ut multis esurientibus ipsi inebriarentur. Inde primam huius Sacramenti institutionem exposuit, ut ex ea illius verum usum simul & dignitatem intelligerent. Tertiò, ut singuli sese ad hoc epulum sacrum præparare debeant, docuit, ne indignè ad hoc accedendo in ipsum Christum peccent, seq; ipsos corporis & sanguinis eius reos faciant. Postremò, quia aliquos scelerum atrocitate non multum moveri sciebat, ostendit eos, qui de mensa Domini indignè edunt & bibunt, sibi ipsis iudicium accersere, & proinde pœnas graves Deo esse daturos. Docet autem hic ordo Pauli, in Ecclesia abusus & errores sic accusari debere, ut simul ad Dei instituta homines remittantur, adhæcq; rationibus validis urgeantur, ut sese illis accommodent. Observarunt hunc ordinem olim Prophetæ, & in multis aliis causis Apostoli: & nisi eundem sequantur qui hodie docent, non multum proficient.
units.tr: Since the Corinthians had most foully profaned the Eucharistic Supper of our Lord, so that it differed in nothing from a profane or even a riotous banquet, Paul has so far brought forward many arguments by which he has sought to correct this fault. First, he rebukes them severely because the wealthier members, with contempt for the poor and for the whole Church, indulged their bellies and their gluttony under the pretext of the Supper, so that while many went hungry, they themselves got drunk. Next he sets out the first institution of this Sacrament, so that from it they might understand both its true use and its dignity. Third, he teaches that each person ought to prepare himself for this sacred feast, lest by approaching it unworthily he sin against Christ himself and make himself guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. Last, because he knew that some were not much moved by the atrociousness of their sins, he shows that those who eat and drink unworthily at the table of the Lord bring judgment upon themselves, and that they will therefore pay heavy penalties to God. This order of Paul's teaches that abuses and errors in the Church should be accused in such a way that at the same time people are sent back to God's institutions, and are pressed with solid reasons so that they accommodate themselves to them. The prophets observed this order long ago, and the apostles in many other matters; and unless those who teach today follow the same order, they will achieve little.

units.la: Quia verò quod de iudicio & pœna dixerat, à nonnullis facilè poterat eludi & rideri, præsenti & domestico exemplo eos convincit, & se non temerè hoc dixisse probat. Propterea (inquit) multi sunt inter vos infirmi, & invalidi, & dormiunt multi. Quasi diceret: Ne putetis me sine causa vestrum hoc delictum tam multis exaggerare, & minas pœnasq; fingere, quibus vos immerentes terream. Scio enim quanti Deus faciat abs se instituta sacra, & quòd illa contemni aut prophanari nequaquam patiatur. Et vos nisi toti obstupuissetis, poteratis manifesta iudicij & iræ diuinæ indicia inter vos animaduertere, quæ vos de Deo placando admonerent. Unde enim evenit, quòd multi inter vos gravibus, adhæc novis & insolitis morbis excruciantur? quòd lectis quasi affixi diutissimè decumbunt, nec ulla remediorum ope possunt subleuari? quòd denique multi dormiunt, id est, morte immatura & præpropera è medio tolluntur? Ex eo nimirum, quòd professioni vestræ minus respondetis, & cum in multis aliis officium negligitis, tum maximè in Cœna Dominica, quam abusu non minus impio quàm turpi atq; inhonesto prophanauistis. Voluit autem tam diserte loqui Apostolus, quòd videret eos neq; peccatum suum agnoscere, neq; causam pœnarum, quas iam tunc luebant, observare. Ea est enim nostri ingenij corruptio, ut quemadmodum in peccatis nobis ipsis blandimur, ita quando à nobis pœnas exigit Deus, quiduis potius quàm eas peccatorum pœnas esse fatemur. Plerique enim, qui ad Epicureismum inclinant, omnia fortuito fieri sibi ipsis persuadent. Alij sese aliorum exemplis excusant, qui nihil huius patiuntur, cum eadem faciant. Quod si qui pœnas propter peccata infligi credunt, ij in alios potius quàm seipsos respiciunt, quorum scelera suis graviora esse arbitrantur. Denique ut malæ indolis pueros pudet fateri se virgis cæsos esse, eosdem verò suæ nequitiæ & contumaciæ non pudet, quò minus in illa pergant: Ita plerique hominum affecti sunt, ut absque Dei & piorum reverentia suis cupiditatibus indulgeant, & peccata peccatis accumulent, nolint autem ex eorum numero videri, propter quos Deus calamitates publicas immittat. Hic ergo ministros animo præsenti & ingenua dicendi libertate armatos esse oportet, ut peccata arguant, pœnarum causas apertè prodant, & improbos illos hypocritas sive tergiversatores in rem præsentem adducant, ne quid amplius negare possint. Sic olim Prophetas fecisse scimus. Cum enim sub Achabo Deus Israeliticam terram siccitate & fame annorum aliquot affligeret propter impios cultus, quos Baali instituerant, nequaquam illud propterea fieri putabat Achab, qui præcipuus erat tanti mali author, sed Eliæ obvius factus huic omnem hanc calamitatem acceptam ferens, clamabat: Tu ne ille es, qui conturbas Israelem? Quid verò ad hoc Propheta? Ego non turbo Israelem, sed tu & domus patris tui, cùm deseruerit is præcepta Domini, & tu incedis post Baalim. Et mox convocatis totius populi comitijs, publicè ostendit quantum hucusq; peccauerint, & quid porrò facere debeant. Exempla huius generis multa passim apud Prophetas inueniuntur, quorum fortitudinem & libertatem Apostolos quoq; imitatos fuisse, non hic modò locus, verumetiam primæ illorum conciones tenuerunt, quibus Hierosolymæ Senioribus, sacerdotibus totiq; populo indignum facinus, quod in Filium Dei commiserant publicè exprobrarunt non sine graui poenarum comminatione, quas non aliter quam per poenitentiam effugere possint. Et sanè hæc compendiosissima ratio est; qua homines adduci possunt, vt peccata sua agnoscant, deq; Deo placando cogitent.
units.tr: But since what he had said about judgment and punishment could easily be mocked and laughed off by some, he convinces them by a present and domestic example, and proves that he has not spoken rashly. Therefore, he says, many among you are weak and feeble, and many sleep. It is as if he were saying: Do not think that I am magnifying your offence so greatly without cause, or inventing threats and punishments with which I frighten you though you do not deserve it. For I know how highly God values the sacred institutions he has given, and that he will by no means suffer them to be despised or profaned. And unless you had been utterly stupefied, you could have noticed among yourselves the plain signs of divine judgment and wrath, which should have reminded you to appease God. For whence does it come that many among you are racked by grave and moreover new and unusual diseases? Why do they lie almost fixed to their beds for a very long time, and cannot be relieved by any remedy? Why, finally, do many sleep, that is, are taken from the midst of life by an untimely and premature death? Surely this is because you respond poorly to your profession, and while you neglect your duty in many other matters, you do so most of all at the Lord's Supper, which you have profaned by an abuse no less impious than shameful and dishonourable. The apostle wished to speak so plainly because he saw that they neither acknowledged their sin nor observed the cause of the punishments they were already suffering. For such is the corruption of our nature that, just as we flatter ourselves about our sins, so when God exacts punishment from us, we confess that these are anything rather than punishments for sins. Most of those who lean towards Epicureanism persuade themselves that everything happens by chance. Others excuse themselves by the examples of those who suffer nothing of this kind although they do the same things. But if some believe that punishments are inflicted on account of sins, they look rather at others than at themselves, and think that the crimes of others are graver than their own. Finally, just as badly brought-up boys are ashamed to admit that they have been beaten with rods, yet are not ashamed of their own wickedness and obstinacy, so that they do not desist from it, so most people are so disposed that they indulge their desires without reverence for God and the godly, and heap sins upon sins, yet they do not want to be counted among those on account of whom God sends public calamities. Therefore ministers ought to be armed with a bold spirit and a frank freedom of speech, so that they may denounce sins, openly reveal the causes of punishments, and bring those wicked hypocrites or evaders face to face with the present matter, so that they can deny nothing further. We know that the prophets did this in former times. For when under Ahab God afflicted the land of Israel with drought and famine for several years on account of the impious worship which they had established for Baal, Ahab, who was the chief author of so great an evil, did not think at all that this came about because of him; but when he met Elijah and laid all this calamity at his door, he cried: Are you the one who troubles Israel? What did the prophet answer? I do not trouble Israel, but you and your father's house, since you have forsaken the commandments of the Lord and you follow after Baalim. And soon, after calling together an assembly of the whole people, he publicly showed how greatly they had sinned up to that point and what they ought to do next. Many examples of this kind are found everywhere among the prophets; and it is not only this place but also the first sermons of the apostles that show that they too imitated their courage and freedom. In these sermons they publicly reproached the elders, priests and the whole people of Jerusalem for the unworthy deed they had committed against the Son of God, not without a grave threat of punishments, which they could escape in no other way than by repentance. And indeed this is the most compendious method by which men can be brought to acknowledge their sins and to think about appeasing God.

units.la: Debet autem ex hoc loco generalis doctrina peti, Deum Sacramentorum abusum atq; prophanationem impunitam non dimittere. Olim certè Circumcisionem sub capitis poena fanciuit[?], & exemplum cumprimis memorabile in Mosem ædidit, quem ex Madian in Ægyptum redeuntem interficere voluit, quòd filium sibi apud exteros natum non circumcidisset. Aaronis autem filij, Nadab & Abihu, igne cœlitus immisso crudeliter combusti sunt, eò quòd ignem alienum seu prophanum ausi essent intra tabernaculum in Dei conspectum afferre. Quid verò Israelitis acciderit, qui arcam fœderis, præsentiæ diuinæ symbolum, proprio instinctu in castra detulerunt: quid item Philistæi passi sint, qui eandem bello captam in templum Dagonis collocarunt, in primo Samuelis libro prolixè describitur. Et in Prophetarum sermonibus satis euidenter apparet, quàm indignè tulerit Deus, si quando Iudæi templo & sacrificijs abs se institutis ad peccandi licentiam abusi sunt, vt in ijs sceleruin[?] suorum prætextum quærerent. Quid ergo nostri seculi calamitates miramur, quando horribilis omnium Sacramentorum abusus vna cum prophano Verbi contemptu vbiq; dominatur?
units.tr: From this passage a general doctrine should be drawn: that God does not let the abuse and profanation of the sacraments go unpunished. Long ago he certainly decreed circumcision under pain of death, and he gave a most memorable example in Moses, whom he wished to kill as he was returning from Midian to Egypt, because he had not circumcised a son born to him among foreigners. The sons of Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, were cruelly burned by fire sent from heaven, because they had dared to bring strange or profane fire into the tabernacle in the sight of God. What happened to the Israelites, who carried the ark of the covenant, the symbol of God's presence, into the camp by their own impulse, and what likewise the Philistines suffered, who after capturing it in war placed it in the temple of Dagon, are described at length in the first book of Samuel. And it is quite plain from the sayings of the prophets how indignantly God took it when the Jews abused the temple and the sacrifices he had instituted as a licence for sinning, so that they sought in them a pretext for their crimes. Why then do we wonder at the calamities of our own age, when the horrible abuse of all the sacraments reigns everywhere together with a profane contempt for the Word?

units.la: Nam vt à Baptismo exordiamur, quot modis ille vitiatus adeoq; prophanatus est apud eos, qui se solos Ecclesiam esse sibi persuaserunt? Instituit hunc per Ioannem Baptistam Dominus, quem simplici ritu in Iordane ad se venientes tinxisse legimus. Et Christus eius formulam discipulis præscribens baptizare iussit in nomen Patris, Filij & Spiritus sancti. Quem ritum absq; omni superstitione seruarunt Apostoli, adeò vt non in ædibus modò priuatis, verumetiam ex itinere aqua temere oblata eos baptizarint, quos iam fide illuminatos esse videbant. Quod non ideo dico, quòd hodie idem fieri velim, vbi Ecclesiæ constitutæ sint, & festinatione illa nequaquam opus est: sed vt ostendam quàm studiosi sanctæ simplicitatis fuerint Apostoli. At quid hodie in Papatu fit? Exorcismus primò peculiaribus aqua præparatur, deinde admiscentur sal, oleum, sputum denique, ne quid sordium desit. Vbi verò ad actionem ventum est, iam rursus noui exorcismi infanti, tanquam à dæmone obsesso adhibentur, & multa superstitiosè, multa impiè, multa ridiculè fiunt, quæ si omnia commemorare vellem, in immensum extenderetur oratio. Vnum tamen omitti non potest, quòd contra Pauli doctrinam (quam Cap. 14. audiemus) omnia hæc lingua peregrina fiunt, quæ à nemine astantium, & sæpe ne ab ipsis quidem sacrificulis Baptismum administrantibus, intelligitur. Quòd si ad nos transfeas, quis non damnet leuitatem, qua in testibus, quos patrinos & matrinas vocant, adhibendis multi vtuntur, qui vel solum quæstum captant, vel inani gloriæ student?
units.tr: For to begin with Baptism: in how many ways has it been corrupted and profaned among those who have persuaded themselves that they alone are the Church? The Lord instituted it through John the Baptist, whom we read baptized with a simple rite in the Jordan those who came to him. And Christ, prescribing its formula to his disciples, ordered them to baptize in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The apostles kept this rite free from all superstition, so much so that they baptized, not only in private houses, but also on the way, with water rashly at hand, those whom they saw already enlightened by faith. I do not say this because I wish the same to be done today, where churches have been established, and there is no need for such haste; but to show how earnest the apostles were for holy simplicity. But what happens today in the Papacy? First the water is prepared with special exorcisms, then salt, oil and finally spittle are mixed in, so that nothing of filth may be lacking. And when it comes to the action itself, new exorcisms are again applied to the infant as if it were possessed by a demon, and many things are done superstitiously, many impiously, many ridiculously; if I wished to recount all of them, my discourse would extend without end. One thing, however, cannot be omitted: that, contrary to Paul's teaching (which we shall hear in chapter 14), all these things are done in a foreign tongue, which none of the bystanders understands, and often not even the little priests who administer the baptism. And if you pass over to us, who would not condemn the levity with which many use the witnesses whom they call godfathers and godmothers, who either seek only profit or are eager for empty glory?

units.la: In Cœna autem quanta prob Deum corruptio, cuius species vix quisquam omnes enumerauerit. Ex Cœna enim publica priuatum epulum fecerunt, quo vnus solus reliquis spectantibus fruitur. Deinde hoc quoq; in sacrificium commutarunt non sine notoria sacrificij Christi in cruce oblati contumelia. Adde his quæstum, quem inde vberrimum faciunt, & vt is vberior fit, mortuis applicant, quod non nisi viuentibus à Christo est traditum. Omitto nunc luxum vestium, altarium ornatu plus quàm prophanum, & non sine sacrilegio ademptum laicis poculi Dominici vsum, & infinita alia, quæ totam illam actionem ita deformant, vt ne minimum quidem Cœnæ Dominicæ vestigium illic videas. Imò ne quis hanc apud eos requirat, nomen quoq; mutarunt, vt iam Missa dicatur, quod Apostoli modò Cœnam Domini, modò Fractionem panis, veteres autem propter vsum & finem eius Eucharistiam & Synaxim dixerunt. Quòd si verò illos ipsos de Missæ vocabulo interroges, vix habent quod respondeant, & non vna eademq; est omnium sententia. Alij etiam illud Hebræum esse aiunt, & oblationem spontaneam significare. Alij doctiores à gentibus nomen hoc desumptum esse affirmant, apud quos peractis sacris præco publicus, quem grammatea dicebant, clamabat, λαοῖς ἀφιέναι[?], id est, populis missio, scilicet datur, vt ad sua singuli redeant. Hinc morem apud Christianos quoq; obtinuisse dicunt, ut finito hoc nouo sacro, per Diaconum pronuntiatur: Ite, missa est: & inde toti huic actioni nomen esse inditum. Quis vero probauerit, homines Christianos ritus aliquos ab idololatris & ethnicis mutuari, imò sacris suis inde nomina accersere? Et quid hæc aliud quàm extremam Cænæ Dominicæ prophanationem arguunt? At ne hic quidem subsitit istorum hominum temeritas, qui ut quæstum facerent maiorem, ex semetipsis Sacramenta noua finxerunt, in quibus eadem corruptio deprehenderetur, si ea ad Verbi Dei regulam examines. Quòd si autem rursus ad nos oculos conuertas, qui puriores doctrinæ & reformationis nomine gloriamur, paucos certè reperies, qui ad Cænam Domini ea reuerentia, qua opus erat, accedant, cum apud plerosq; hypocrisis & securitas nimia, apud alios petulantia effrenis dominetur. Hinc ergo est, quòd bellis & seditionibus assiduis, fame rerumq; penuria, morbis incognitis, peste deniq; continua, & infinitis aliis calamitatibus infelicem mundum Deus affligit. Quæ omnia aduersarij Euangelio accepta ferunt & nobis, qui veteres ritus aboleuerimus. At ut nos non omnino extra culpam esse iam ante fassi sumus, ita illam in nobis hærere, nullo autem modo Euangelicæ doctrinæ adscribi debere testamur. Utrinq; tamen urgens nos Dei iudicium dissimulare aut negare non possumus, quando non ijs modò plagis multamur, quas paulò ante recitauimus, verumetiam ea videmus fieri, quæ Paulus gentibus propter idololatriam accidisse scribit, ut nimirum in reprobum sensum traditi seipsos ignominia afficerent. Fit hoc apud aduersarios, quando parentes liberos suos in monasteria detrusos tantumnon scientes ad omnem libidinem prostituunt. Et nos simile quid sentimus, quando qui idem sentiunt, idem tamen non possunt loqui, & cum magno suo dedecore digladiantes hostibus iucundissimum spectaculum præbent. Erant igitur abusus & errores illi corrigendi, si nosipsos pœnis, & Christianum nomen publica ignominia liberari vellemus.
units.tr: Yet how great is the corruption of the Lord's Supper before God, the forms of which no one could list in full. They have turned the public Supper into a private feast, of which one man alone partakes while the others look on. Then they have also changed it into a sacrifice, not without a notorious insult to the sacrifice of Christ offered on the cross. Add to this the very rich profit they make from it, and, so that the profit may be larger, they apply it to the dead, although Christ handed it down only to the living. I now pass over the luxury of vestments, the ornamentation of the altars beyond what is even profane, the use of the Lord's cup taken away from the laity, not without sacrilege, and countless other things that so deform that whole action that you can see there not the smallest trace of the Lord's Supper. Indeed, lest anyone look for it among them, they have even changed the name, so that it is now called the Mass, whereas the Apostles spoke of the Lord's Supper or the breaking of bread, and the ancients called it the Eucharist and the Synaxis because of its use and purpose. But if you ask those very men about the word Mass, they scarcely have an answer, and there is not one and the same opinion among them all. Some say that it is a Hebrew word and signifies a voluntary offering. Other, more learned men affirm that the name was taken from the Gentiles, among whom, when the sacred rites were finished, a public herald, whom they called the grammateus, cried out [λαοῖς ἀφιέναι], that is, "the people are dismissed," so that each may return to his own home. From this, they say, the custom also prevailed among Christians that, when this new sacred rite is finished, it is announced through the deacon: "Go, it is the dismissal" [Ite, missa est], and from this the whole action received its name. But who would approve that Christian men borrow certain rites from idolaters and pagans, and indeed draw names for their sacred actions from them? And what do these things prove except the utmost profanation of the Lord's Supper? Yet even here the rashness of these men does not stop, for in order to make greater profit they have invented new sacraments out of their own heads, in which the same corruption would be found if you tested them by the rule of the Word of God. But if you turn your eyes back to us, who boast of being purer in doctrine and of the name of reformation, you will surely find few who approach the Lord's Supper with the reverence that was required, since among many hypocrisy and excessive complacency reign, and among others unbridled wantonness. Hence it is that God afflicts the unhappy world with constant wars and seditions, with famine and scarcity of goods, with unknown diseases, finally with continual plague, and with countless other calamities. The adversaries bring all these things to the charge of the Gospel and of us, who have abolished the old rites. But just as we have already confessed that we are not wholly free from blame, so we testify that this blame clings to us, yet that it ought in no way to be ascribed to evangelical doctrine. Nevertheless, we cannot dissemble or deny the pressing judgement of God upon us on both sides, since we are punished not only by those plagues which we recited a little earlier, but also because we see happening those things which Paul writes befell the Gentiles on account of their idolatry, namely that, given over to a reprobate mind, they brought dishonour upon themselves. This happens among our adversaries when parents thrust their children into monasteries and, almost without knowing it, prostitute them to every lust. And we feel something similar when those who think the same cannot speak the same, and, fighting with great dishonour to themselves, offer the most pleasing spectacle to their enemies. Those abuses and errors therefore needed to be corrected, if we wished to be freed from punishments and from public disgrace to the Christian name.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui morborum & luis inter Corinthios grassantis causam apertius exprimit, & sic quidem, ut simul remedium & consolationem dulcissimam adhibeat, dicens: Etenim si nosipsos dijudicaremus, non iudicaremur. Seipsum iudicat, qui vitam & mores totumque suæ naturæ ingenium rectè inspicit, seq; cum omnibus suis studijs & actionibus ad præceptorum Dei regulam examinat, peccata sua agnoscit, & ea in semetipso damnat, deniq; ex ea cognitione humiliatus in Dei conspectu resipiscit. Ita semetipsum Paulus dijudicauit, quando carnem & huius cupiditates cum Lege Dei conferens dicebat: Nouì quod non habitet in me, id est, in carne mea bonum. Sensus ergo verborum eius in præsenti est: Si ipsi peccata nostra agnoscerimus, deq; illis emendandis serio cogitaremus, non opus esset ut suum iudicium in nos exerceret Deus, & flagellis meritis castigaret. Ita verò socordiam illorum accusat, qua cogant Deum in ipsos seuerius animaduertere. Ne tamen pij hinc colligerent, ipsis simul omnibus pereundum esse (quis enim coram Deo consistat, si is iudicio nobiscum velit contendere?) mox consolationem subjicit: Sed cum iudicamur, id est, cum iusto & seueriori Dei iudicio affligimur, tunc à Domino erudimur, ne cum mundo condemnemur. Erudiendi verbo paternum in nos Dei affectum simul & utilitatem afflictionum exprimit, ut posthac pluribus dicetur. Continet enim locus hic doctrinam non minus necessariam quàm utilem de afflictionibus, quæ tam pijs quàm impijs in hoc seculo accidunt, cuius partes ex ordine considerabimus: Quis eas immittat? Deinde quæ illarum causa sit quoad nos? Tertiò, in quem finem nobis immittantur? Postremò, qua ratione illas præuenire possimus ne incidant, vel iam imminentes auertere?
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who sets out more plainly the cause of the sicknesses and of the plague raging among the Corinthians, and does so in such a way that at the same time he applies a remedy and a most sweet consolation, saying: "For if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged." He judges himself who rightly examines his life and morals and the whole disposition of his nature, and who tests himself, with all his pursuits and actions, by the rule of God's precepts; he recognises his sins, condemns them in himself, and finally, humbled by that knowledge, repents in the sight of God. So Paul judged himself when, comparing the flesh and its desires with the Law of God, he said: "I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, there dwells no good thing." The sense of his words, then, in the present passage is this: if we acknowledged our sins and seriously considered amending them, there would be no need for God to exercise his judgement upon us and chastise us with deserved scourges. He thus accuses them of that carelessness by which they compel God to punish them more severely. Yet lest the godly should conclude from this that all of them must perish together (for who would stand before God if he wished to contend with us in judgement?), he immediately adds the consolation: "But when we are judged, that is, when we are afflicted by the just and more severe judgement of God, then we are taught by the Lord, so that we are not condemned with the world." By the word "taught" he expresses at once God's fatherly affection towards us and the usefulness of afflictions, as will be said more fully later. For this passage contains a doctrine no less necessary than useful concerning the afflictions which befall both the godly and the wicked in this age, and we shall consider its parts in order: Who sends them? Then, what is their cause as far as we are concerned? Third, for what end are they sent to us? Lastly, by what method can we forestall them so that they do not fall upon us, or turn them aside when they already threaten?

units.la: Primum diserte & uno verbo Paulus explicat, dicens: Cùm iudicamur, à Domino erudimur. Deus ergo is est, qui castigat & affligit, nec aliquid hic fortuitù censeri debet. Est enim is creator & gubernator rerum omnium, neq; eorum opificum similis est, qui ædificia magno quidem labore & industria extruunt, eadem verò deinceps ut nihil ad se pertinentia negligunt: sed quæ ille condidit, seruat quoq; & singula certo consilio & ordine ad suum finem destinat. Itaq; ut Christus ipse in Euangelio docet, eius providentia ad auiculas, ad coruorum pullos, ad flores in agris nascentes, imò ad capillos capitis nostri extenditur, ut hos quoq; in numerato habeat. Num ergo ille bella, famem, pestem, feras, tempestates aduersas, & quæ aliæ sunt huius generis calamitates in nos temere grassari pateretur? Aut num aliquid absq; eius permissione in nos posset Satan? Ideo Amos dicebat,non esse malum,id est, calamitatem aut infortunium aliquod in civitate,quod non faciat Deus. Et passim in Prophetis ille hostes è longinquis regionibus sibilo euocare,locustas,brucos,famem,pestem & sterilitatem adducere dicitur. Et Anna mater Samuelis canit: Dominus occidit, & viuificat:deijcit in barathrum,& rursus euehit. Est hoc diligenter tenendum,quia si nulla alia consolatio accedat,hoc vnum nos ad patientiam erudire & in omnibus aduersis plurimum confirmare potest. Quia enim iustus est Deus,nemini iniuriam facit, neq; dubitare debemus,nos quecunq; mala accidunt multiuariam meruisse,licet ipsi propter philautiam, quae nos excaecat,illorum causas non semper possimus in nobis ipsis animaduertere. Rursus cum pater sit,& quidem humani generis amantissimus,minimè nos perditos vult,sed vt postea sequetur,omnia eò dirigit,vt saluti nostrae prouehendae seruiant. Recte igitur Iob,fortissimus ille patientiae athleta in suis calamitatibus non ad hostes Chaldaeos & Sabaeos respiciebat,neque in ventorum & tempestatum procellis haerebat,sed in Dei prouidentiam intentus dicebat: Dominus dedit, Dominus abstulit, sit nomen Domini benedictum. Quem Dauid imitatus, Semei maledici hominis conuicia patientissime tulit, quòd Deum impiorum quoq; linguas in sua potestate habere, & illis ad suorum correptionem vti sciret. Quòd si nos inspicias,hunc omnis impatientiae & fremitus aut murmuris fontem esse patebit, quòd plerique in proximis causis haerentes summum omnium quae fiunt authorem Deum negligunt.
units.tr: First, Paul explains this plainly and in a single word, saying: "When we are judged, we are taught by the Lord." God, therefore, is the one who chastises and afflicts, and nothing here should be regarded as happening by chance. For he is the creator and governor of all things, and is not like those craftsmen who build houses with great labour and diligence, and then afterwards neglect them as if they had nothing to do with them; rather, he also preserves what he has made and directs each thing to its end by a fixed plan and order. Accordingly, as Christ himself teaches in the Gospel, his providence extends to the little birds, to the young of the ravens, to the flowers growing in the fields, indeed even to the hairs of our head, so that he holds these too in account. Would he then allow wars, famine, plague, wild beasts, adverse storms, and other calamities of this kind to rage against us at random? Or could Satan do anything against us without his permission? For this reason Amos said that there is no evil, that is, no calamity or misfortune in a city, which God does not do. And throughout the Prophets it is said that he summons enemies from distant regions with a whistle, and brings locusts, caterpillars, famine, plague and barrenness. And Hannah, the mother of Samuel, sings: "The Lord kills and makes alive; he brings down to the pit and brings up again." This must be held carefully, because if no other consolation is at hand, this alone can teach us to patience and greatly strengthen us in all adversities. For since God is just, he does wrong to no one, and we ought not to doubt that whatever evils befall us we have deserved in many ways, although, on account of self-love, which blinds us, we cannot always perceive their causes in ourselves. Again, since he is a father, and indeed the most loving of the human race, he by no means wishes us to perish, but, as will follow later, he directs all things so that they serve the advancement of our salvation. Rightly, then, Job, that most courageous athlete of patience, in his calamities did not look to the Chaldean and Sabaean enemies, nor cling to the gusts of the winds and storms, but, fixed on the providence of God, said: "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord." David imitated him when he bore most patiently the reproaches of the cursing man Shimei, because he knew that God holds even the tongues of the wicked in his power and knows how to use them for the correction of his own people. But if you look at us, it will be plain that the source of all impatience, grumbling and murmuring is this: that many, fixed on proximate causes, neglect God, the supreme author of all that happens.

units.la: At quia Deus (vt modò diximus) iustus est, non temere calamitates & aduersa immittit, neq; aliquem immerentem affligit. Ideo quae afflictionum causae sint quoad nos,secundo loco videndum est. Has etiam in praesenti Paulus indicat, peccata nimirum, & quòd homines non seipsos iudicant,id est,securi rerum peccata sua nō agnoscunt,sed quasi re bene gesta sibi ipsis tunc quoq; blandiuntur, quando Dei oculos quàm maximè offendunt. Consentit hic tota scriptura sacra,quae per peccatum mortem, & quaecunq; hanc comitantur,in mundum ingressa esse docet,vt pote terrae sterilitatem, agriculturae labores,curas rei domesticae, partus dolores,educationis liberorum molestias,famem,bella,aeris incommoda,tempestates & alia,quae singula referre longum foret. Et vt ad singularia exempla descendamus,propter primi mundi scelera diluuium immissum fuisse, non solùm Moses,verumetiam prophani scriptores testantur. Libido item effrenis,pauperum contemptus,inhospitalitas & quiduis agendi licentia Sodomis & vicinis vrbibus excidium coelitus attulit. Pharaonem quoq; cum Aegyptijs suis propter innocentis populi crudelem oppressionem borrendis plagis à Deo multatos fuisse legimus. Ita Chananaeos propter incestus,venefitia,fatidicas artes, iniustas caedes, rapinas & alia huiusmodi scelera excisos fuisse Dominus per Mosem non uno loco docet. Et ne quis ista & alia huius generis singularia quaedam exempla putaret,ex quibus vniuersalis doctrina minimè peti debeat, in Lege multis docetur, Deum morbis insolitis, coelitemperie,gladio,fame,peste, deniq; ferarum incursionibus in omnes eos animaduersurum esse,qui ipsius praecepta improbè transgressi fuerint. Et Legis interpretes Prophetae hoc ipsum vnanimi consensu testantur. Ieremias certè cum sui populi scelera recensuisset,mox infert: An super his non visitarem,ait Dominus,& gentem huic similem non vlcisceretur anima mea? Sed quid multa opus est,quando hanc notitiam omnium hominum animis ita inscripsit Deus, vt gentes quoq; ipsum minimè ignorauerint? Ideo enim in publicis & priuatis calamitatibus ad libros Sibyllinos, ad Deorum oracula,ad vates & Sacerdotes suos recurrebant,vt scirent,quo scelere potissimum Deos suos offendissent,& qua ratione ijdem possent placari. Hoc ipsum ergo nobis certò persuasum fit[?], quicquid aduersi accidit,id nos peccatis nostris meruisse. Quod adeò verum est,vt ne in sanctissimis quidem negari posset. Et hoc in semetipso Dauid obseruans,non solum propter adulterium & indignam Uriae caedem se supplicio dignum esse fatebatur, verumetiam propter innatam vitiositatem,in qua conceptus & nacus erat. Et notae sunt illae sanctorum preces: Ne intres in iudicium cum seruo tuo Domine:quoniam in tuo conspectu nulla caro iustificabitur. Item:Si iniquitates obseruaueris Domine,quis consistet[?]? Neq; opus est,vt manifesta semper sint scelera. Sufficit enim, quòd haec in carne nostra latent,& frequenter ne illa erumpant, Deus aliqua calamitate illa praevenire & carnis cupiditates coërcere solet. Ista ergo nobis in mentem veniant,quoties aut morbi, aut fame,aut facultatum nostrarum iactura,aut tempestatibus noxijs,aut bello,aut persecutioni-bus, bus, exilio, vel quacunq; alio aduersorum genere multamur. Ita enim deprehendimus nobis iniuriam non fieri, quando hæc & his grauiora partim peccatis, partim nostra in his corrigendis socor-dia meremur. Et revera stulti atq; iniqui sunt, qui quasi ipsos iniquius tractet Deus, quærunt, vbi hæc aut ista meruerint. Quin tuam conceptionem, natales, pueritiam, cogitationes, cupiditates, sermones, studia, & actiones omnes inspice, & Dei longanimitatem potius miraberis, qui talem hucusq; tulit, & nunc non pro meritis punire, sed ad pœnitentiam inuitare satagit.
units.tr: And since God (as we have just said) is just, he does not rashly send calamities and adversities, nor afflict anyone who has done nothing to deserve it. So we must now consider, in the second place, what the causes of afflictions are as far as we are concerned. Paul indicates these also in the present passage: namely sins, and the fact that men do not judge themselves, that is, being secure, they do not acknowledge their sins, but as if they had done well they flatter themselves even when they most grievously offend the eyes of God. The whole of holy Scripture agrees here, teaching that through sin death and all that accompanies it entered the world: barrenness of the earth, the labours of farming, the cares of household affairs, the pains of childbirth, the troubles of raising children, famine, wars, inclemencies of the air, storms, and other things which would take too long to list one by one. And to come down to particular examples: that the flood was sent on account of the crimes of the first world is attested not only by Moses but also by profane writers. Likewise unbridled lust, contempt for the poor, inhospitality, and licence to do whatever one pleases brought destruction from heaven upon Sodom and the neighbouring cities. We also read that Pharaoh and his Egyptians were punished by God with dreadful plagues on account of their cruel oppression of an innocent people. So too the Canaanites, on account of incest, poisoning, sorcery, unjust murders, robberies and other crimes of this kind, were cut off, as the Lord teaches through Moses in more than one place. And lest anyone think these and other particular examples of this kind should not be the basis of a universal doctrine, the Law teaches in many places that God will punish all who have wickedly transgressed his precepts with unusual diseases, the weather, the sword, famine, plague, and finally the attacks of wild beasts. The Prophets, the interpreters of the Law, testify to this same thing with one accord. Jeremiah, after he had recounted the sins of his people, immediately adds: "Shall I not visit these things, says the Lord, and shall not my soul avenge itself on such a nation as this?" But why need many words, since God has inscribed this knowledge on the minds of all men, so that even the Gentiles did not altogether ignore it? For this reason, in public and private calamities, they had recourse to the Sibylline books, to the oracles of their gods, and to their seers and priests, so that they might learn by what crime they had especially offended their gods, and by what means those gods might be appeased. Therefore this is firmly persuaded to us: whatever adversity befalls us, we have deserved it by our sins. This is so true that it cannot be denied even of the most holy. David, observing this in himself, confessed that he deserved punishment not only on account of his adultery and the unworthy murder of Uriah, but also on account of the innate vitiousness in which he had been conceived and born. And those prayers of the saints are well known: "Enter not into judgment with your servant, O Lord, for in your sight no flesh shall be justified." Likewise: "If you, Lord, should mark iniquities, who shall stand?" Nor is it necessary that the sins be always manifest. It is enough that they lie hidden in our flesh, and that God, to prevent them from frequently breaking out, is accustomed to forestall them by some calamity and restrain the desires of the flesh. Let these things therefore come to mind whenever we are punished with sickness, or famine, or loss of our property, or harmful storms, or war, or persecutions, or exile, or whatever other kind of adversity. For thus we find that no injustice is done to us, since we deserve these and worse things, partly by our sins, partly by our negligence in correcting them. Truly they are foolish and unjust who ask, as if God were treating them more unfairly, where they have deserved this or that. Nay, examine your conception, birth, childhood, thoughts, desires, words, studies and all your actions, and you will rather marvel at the long-suffering of God, who has borne with such a person until now, and now, instead of punishing him according to his deserts, takes pains to invite him to repentance.

units.la: Et hoc illud est, quod tertio loco considerandum esse diximus, in quem finem videlicet Deus nos afflictionibus & aduersis exerceat. Cum iudicamur (inquit Paulus) à Domino erudimur, ne cum mundo condemnemur. Græcum verbum παιδευειν[?] eiusmodi eruditionem siue institutionem significat, qualem parentes liberis suis adhibere solent, quæ plerunq; cum correptione & castigatione coniuncta est. Exprimitur autem hoc loco discrimen, quod est inter afflictiones piorum & impiorum. Peccant enim tam hi quàm illi, & sæpe eadem flagitia designant. Sed impij mera malitia & affectuum libidine abripiuntur, neq; aliquo tanguntur pœnitentiæ sensu. Imo admoniti & correpti recalcitrant, & aduersus ipsum quoq; Deum insurgunt. Quæ causa est, quòd illos fere libidini suæ Deus permittit, vt (quod de Amorrhæis dicitur) iniquitatis mensuram impleant, & tandem digni pœnis, id est, exitio sempiterno multentur. Pij verò non devota malitia, sed ex carnis infirmitate & quæ omnibus innata est natura corruptione peccant, & quia semen filiorum Dei (vt Ioannes inquit) in ipsis manet, admonitionem & correptionem admittunt, quæ illos in peccatis perseuerare non finit. Quia tamen interdum securiores sunt, tunc suas virgas Deus exerit, quibus ad peccati agnitionem & pœnitentiam illos excitat. Et hoc illud est, quod Petrus dicit, iudicium a domo Dei incipere, & vt ita fiat omnino necesse est. Primùm ne Deus iudex iniquus esse videatur, qui quod in alijs punit, in suis dissimulet, aut etiam probet. Deinde, vt in suis toti mundo exemplum proponat, quod eludere aut contemnere nemo possit, secundùm illud: Si hoc fit in viridi, in arido quid fiet? Et si iustus vix seruatur, impius vbi comparebit? Postremò, vt priusquam impiorum excidium appropinquat, suos erudiat ad pœnitentiam, ne cum infelici mundo condemnati æternis inferorum cruciatibus multentur. Quapropter duo ex hoc loco colligi debent, cognitu & obseruatu admodum necessaria.
units.tr: This is what we said should be considered in the third place, namely to what end God exercises us with afflictions and adversities. "When we are judged," says Paul, "we are instructed by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world." The Greek word παιδεύειν [paideuein] signifies that kind of training or instruction which parents are wont to give their children, and which is usually joined with correction and chastisement. Now a difference between the afflictions of the godly and of the wicked is expressed in this passage. For both the one and the other sin, and often they commit the same wicked deeds. But the wicked are carried away by sheer malice and the lust of their passions, and are moved by no sense of repentance at all. Indeed, when admonished and corrected, they kick back, and rise up even against God himself. This is why God generally allows them to indulge their lust, so that (as is said of the Amorites) they may fill up the measure of their iniquity, and at last be punished, that is, with eternal destruction, as they deserve. But the godly sin not from settled malice, but from the weakness of the flesh and the corruption of nature which is innate in all; and because the seed of the sons of God (as John says) remains in them, they admit admonition and correction, which does not allow them to persist in their sins. Yet because they are sometimes too secure, God then stretches out his rods, by which he rouses them to acknowledge their sin and to repent. This is what Peter means when he says that judgment begins at the house of God, and that it must necessarily be so. First, lest God appear to be an unjust judge, who would punish in others what he overlooks or even approves in his own. Then, so that he may set before the whole world an example among his own people which no one can mock or despise, according to that saying: "If this is done in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?" And "if the righteous is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly appear?" Lastly, so that, before the destruction of the wicked draws near, he may train his own people to repentance, lest they be condemned together with the unhappy world and punished with eternal torments of hell. Therefore two things ought to be gathered from this passage, which are very necessary to know and to observe.

units.la: Primùm, afflictiones piorum non esse irati Dei argumentum, qui perdere velit, sed potius paternas virgas & remedia necessaria, quibus carnis & affectuum peculantia coerceatur. Inscitur[?] quidem suos quoq; Deus, sed vt pater filijs, & in ipsa ira misericordiæ suæ memor est. Nouit enim (vt Dauid inquit) nos terram & puluerem esse. Quia tamen indulgentia nimia perituri eramus, amorem & misericordiam salutari seueritate temperat. Et huc pertinet, quod in epistola ad Hebræos scribitur: Quem diligit Dominus, castigat: & flagellat omnem filium, quem recipit. Si castigationem sustinetis, vt filijs ita se offert Deus. Quis enim est filius, quem non castiget pater? Quòd iestis[?] absq; castigatione, cuius participes sunt omnes, nempe spurij estis, & non filij. Deinde corporum nostrorum habuimus castigatores patres, ac reueriti sumus: annon multò magis subijciemur Patri spirituum, & viuemus? Nam illi ad paucos dies, prout ipsis videbatur, nos castigabant: hic autem ad commodum nostrum, ad hoc vt participes simus sanctimoniæ ipsius. Omnis autem castigatio in præsens quidem non videtur esse gaudij, sed tristitiæ: at postea fructum tranquillum iustitiæ reddit ijs, qui per illam fuerint exercitati, & c. Hæc qui attentius considerant, ij in omni tentatione dulcissimam consolationem sentiunt, quæ ipsos succumbere non finit.
units.tr: First, the afflictions of the godly are not a sign of the anger of a God who wishes to destroy, but rather paternal rods and necessary remedies, by which the wantonness of the flesh and of the passions is restrained. God indeed trains his own people too, but as a father trains his sons, and even in his anger he remembers his mercy. For he knows (as David says) that we are dust and ashes. Yet because we would perish through excessive indulgence, he tempers his love and mercy with salutary severity. To this belongs what is written in the Epistle to the Hebrews: "Whom the Lord loves he chastens, and scourges every son whom he receives. If you endure chastening, God deals with you as with sons; for what son is there whom the father does not chasten? But if you are without chastening, of which all are partakers, then you are bastards and not sons. Moreover, we have had earthly fathers who chastened us, and we respected them; shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits, and live?
