For they chastened us for a few days, as seemed good to them; but he does so for our profit, that we may be partakers of his holiness. Now all chastening seems for the present not to be joyous but grievous; yet afterwards it yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness to those who have been exercised by it," and so on. Those who consider these things more attentively feel in every temptation the sweetest consolation, which does not allow them to succumb.

units.la: Alterum est, ne filiorum huius seculi prosperitate offendamur, aut hac illecti illorum sectemur amicitia & studia. Quia enim vasa iræ & ad interitum destinati sunt, vt porci saginantur, & tanq; magis ad interitum festinant, quò felicius (vt carni videtur) carnis voluptatibus indulgent. Exempla passim occurrunt eorum, qui cum suo splendore & fortunis omnibus subitò pereunt, quando hominum beatissimi esse videntur. Idemq; omnes cum Dauide dicere possumus: Vidi impium fortem, & sese diffundentem instar lauri virentis: Et transiuit, & ecce non erat: quæsiui eum, & non est inuentus. Recte igitur Asaph, cum impiorum gloriam, successus & splendorem multis expositum, tandem illorum sorte diligentius perspecta infert: Certè velut in lubrico constituisti eos, deijcies illos præcipites, vt planè vastentur. Vt vastati sunt, pene in momento temporis? perierunt, & terroribus consumpti sunt. Non aliter quàm somnium, quod auolat postquam quis euigilaue-rit, despicatas reddes Domine in ciuitate imagines illorum, &c. Horum consideratio nos excitet, ut impijs suam illam momentaneam prosperitatem relinquamus, ipsi autem Mosen imitati malimus affligi cum electis Dei, & patienter feramus quæcunq; is imponit, ut nostræ saluti consulat.
units.tr: The second is that we should not be offended by the prosperity of the sons of this age, nor, allured by it, follow their friendship and pursuits. For since they are vessels of wrath and destined for destruction, they are fattened like swine, and the more happily (as it seems to the flesh) they indulge the pleasures of the flesh, the more hastily they hurry to destruction. Examples of those who suddenly perish with all their splendour and fortunes, when they seem most blessed of men, occur everywhere. And we can all say with David: "I saw the wicked in great power, spreading himself like a green bay tree. Yet he passed away, and lo, he was not; I sought him, but he could not be found." Rightly therefore Asaph, after setting out at length the glory, success and splendour of the wicked, at last, having more carefully looked into their lot, adds: "Surely you set them in slippery places; you cast them down into destruction, so that they are utterly laid waste. How are they laid waste in a moment? They perish, and are consumed with terrors. Like a dream when one awakes, so, Lord, when you awake you shall despise their images in the city," etc. Let the consideration of these things stir us to leave to the wicked their fleeting prosperity, and rather, imitating Moses, to choose to be afflicted with the people of God, and patiently to bear whatever he lays upon us, so that he may provide for our salvation.

units.la: At non obstat hoc, quò minus aduersa auertere aut declinare studeamus, modò id rectà cum ratione fiat. Disputatur de eo multis hodie, sed ab omnibus fere erratur. Alij enim ad externa præsidia confugiunt, & quasi cum Deo certamen suscepturi, eius iudicijs se subducere conantur. Alij propria nituntur industria. Multi suis meritis, aut etiam inani ceremoniarum splendore Deum placare student. Sed vana & inutilia sunt hæc omnia. Itaq; Paulum audiamus, qui sic ait: Si nosipsos dijudicaremus, non iudicaremur, id est, tunc non cogeretur Deus suo iudicio in nos animad-uertere, & plagis seuerioribus socordiam nostram punire. Intelligit autem Paulus pœnitentiam, cuius hoc principium est, si in seipsos descendant homines, peccata sua agnoscant, & illa in semetipsis damnent. Hinc enim fit, ut ad Deum conuertantur, qui ad se conuersos facilè in gratiam recipit. Est hæc generalis doctrina, & unica declinandæ iræ Dei ratio, quam scriptura passim præscribit. In Lege certè Deus se plagas denuo ablaturum esse pollicetur, si illis emolliti & domiti ad ipsum conuertantur. In Prophetis autem non semel clamat: Conuertimini ad me, & ego conuertar ad vos. Et apud Ezechielem, se peccatorum non amplius recordaturum ait, si peccator vias suas emendauerit. In nouo autem Testamento Ioannes Baptista à pœnitentiæ doctrina prædicandi initium fecit, & hunc secutus Christus Apostolis ut idem facerent præcepit. Estq; doctrina hæc confirmata omnium seculorum exemplis, sed potest hic nobis sufficere unicus Iudicum liber, qui Israelitas quoties à Deo recesserunt, in hostium manus traditos esse, eosdem verò semper liberatos esse testatur, quàm primùm ad illum redierunt. Erat hoc nobis publicè & priuatim obseruandum hodie, & mox finem videremus calamitatum, quæ totum fere orbem Christianum affligunt. At quia hic nimium socordes sumus, & pauci sunt qui seipsos iudicent, non mirum est, si idem nobis, quod Corinthijs accidat.
units.tr: Yet this does not prevent us from striving to turn away or avoid adversity, provided it is done rightly and with reason. Many people discuss this today, but almost all of them go wrong. Some take refuge in external protections and, as if about to contend with God, try to escape his judgments. Others rely on their own industry. Many seek to appease God by their merits or by the empty splendour of ceremonies. But all of these are vain and useless. Let us therefore hear Paul, who says: "If we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged" (1 Cor. 11). That is, God would not be compelled to pass judgment on us and to punish our carelessness with more severe blows. Paul means repentance, whose beginning is this: when people descend into themselves, they acknowledge their sins and condemn them within themselves. For from this they turn to God, who readily receives into grace those who have turned to him. This is the general doctrine and the only way of averting the wrath of God, and Scripture prescribes it everywhere. In the Law, God certainly promises that he will take away the plagues again if the people, softened and tamed by them, turn back to him. In the Prophets he cries out more than once: "Turn to me, and I will turn to you" (Zech. 1; Mal. 3). And in Ezekiel he says that he will no longer remember the sins of the sinner if he amends his ways. In the New Testament, John the Baptist began to preach the doctrine of repentance, and Christ, following him, commanded the Apostles to do the same. This doctrine is confirmed by the examples of all ages, but the single book of Judges may suffice for us here, which testifies that the Israelites, whenever they fell away from God, were handed over into the hands of their enemies, and that they were always set free as soon as they returned to him. This ought to have been observed by us today, both publicly and privately, and we would soon see an end to the calamities that afflict almost the whole Christian world. But because we are so careless here, and few are those who judge themselves, it is no wonder if we suffer the same thing that happened to the Corinthians.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui & ipse ad hypothesim redit, & huic admonitionem hanc amicè admodum accommodat: Itaq; fratres mei, cum conuenitis ad vescendum, alius alium expectate, &c. Quasi diceret: Cùm Deus in Ecclesia sua velit omnia cum decoro & ordine fieri, & CHRI-STVS IESVS Cœnam suam, ut toti Ecclesiæ communis, non paucorum priuatum epulum fit, instituerit, huius instituto vos accommodate, ut quæ iam vobis imminent mala possitis auertere. Quare quoties conuenitis in cœtum sacrum, ut Eucharisticum hoc epulum celebretis, alij alios expectate, ne conuentus & actio illa vobis in iudicium & condemnationem cedat, dum à Christo institutum ordinem turbatis. Quòd si quis esurit, aut ea est valetudine, ut diutius expectare non possit, is domi prius edat, ne quid in cœtu sacro Christiana religione indignum facere cogatur. Docet autem hæc repetitio, quàm necesse sit, ut in Ecclesia, & quidem imprimis in Sacramentorum administratione, omnia decenter fiant, néue à Christi ordinatione discedatur. Id enim fieri non potest, quin nos illo sapientiores putemus, & simul cum inobedientia manifesta coniunctum est.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who himself also returns to his proposition and very kindly applies this admonition to it: "So then, my brethren, when you come together to eat, wait for one another" (1 Cor. 11:33). As if he were saying: since God wishes everything in his Church to be done with decency and order, and since Christ Jesus instituted his Supper to be a common feast of the whole Church, not a private banquet of a few, conform yourselves to his institution, so that you may avert the evils now hanging over you. Therefore, whenever you come together in the sacred assembly to celebrate this Eucharistic feast, wait for one another, lest that gathering and that action turn to your judgment and condemnation, while you disturb the order instituted by Christ. But if anyone is hungry, or is in such health that he cannot wait longer, let him eat at home first, lest he be compelled to do anything unworthy of the Christian religion in the sacred assembly. This repetition teaches how necessary it is that everything be done decently in the Church, and especially in the administration of the sacraments, and that no one depart from the ordinance of Christ. For this cannot happen without our thinking ourselves wiser than he, and it is joined with manifest disobedience.

units.la: Est autem hic obseruatu dignum, quòd non rigidè exigit, ut non nisi ieiuni ad Cœnam Domini accedant: sed permittit, ut si necessitas aut corporis valetudo sic moneat, aliquid cibi prius domi sumatur. Arguit ergo Paulus suo exemplo eorum superstitionem, qui peccatum mortale esse aiunt, si quis ante communionem aliquid edat. Non probandi quidem qui solius ventris & gulæ studio prius comessantur, & vix satis sobrij ad sacrum hoc Christi epulum veniunt. Id enim animos parum religiosos arguit. At si valetudo, aut alia necessitas sic iubeat, nimis temerarium fuerit id damnare, quod Deus nusquam prohibuit. Hoc potius curent singuli, ut mens ipsis sit sobria quàm neq; malarum cupiditatum vertigo hinc inde rapiat, neque superstitio aut incredulitas à veritatis via abducat.
units.tr: It is worth observing here that he does not rigidly demand that none approach the Lord's Supper except the fasting; rather, he allows that, if necessity or the condition of the body so advises, something of food be taken at home beforehand. Paul therefore by his own example refutes the superstition of those who say that it is a mortal sin if anyone eats anything before communion. Certainly those are not to be approved who feast themselves beforehand out of zeal for belly and gluttony, and come to this sacred feast of Christ scarcely sober. For this shows minds that are little reverent. But if health or another necessity so requires, it would be too rash to condemn what God nowhere forbids. Rather, let each one take care that his mind be sober, so that neither the giddiness of wicked desires carries him hither and thither, nor superstition or unbelief leads him away from the way of truth.

units.la: Restat huius tractationis conclusio: Reliqua verò, cùm venero, constituam. Aduentus fui me-mihi, ut studiosius corrigant quæ hucusq; in ipsis reprehenderat. Abuntur autem hac clausula Papistæ, ut Missam suam tueantur, quam à Paulo apud Corinthios tunc institutam fuisse contendunt. Sed est hoc nimis ridiculum. Cur enim ad primam Cœnæ Dominicæ institutionem eos reuocauisset, vocauisset, si quid voluisset instituere ab illa prorsus alienum? Deinde si Missam instituerunt Apostoli, qui fit, quòd veterissimi scriptores, & qui ad illorum tempora proximè accesserunt, nullam eius rei mentionem faciunt? Et si aduersariorum historicos audiamus, illi ipsi Missam non ad vnum authorem referunt, sed centonis instar à multis Pontificibus confutam & nouis subinde additamentis auctam esse scribunt, donec formam, quam nunc habet, obtinuit. Loquitur ergo Paulus de iis, quae ad decorum & ordinem in Ecclesia pertinent, quoad docendi aut praedicandi modum, Sacramentorum administrationem, preces publicas, & quae alia sunt eius generis. Non potest in his idem ordo & eadem forma seruari, sed pro ratione locorum, temporum, hominum illa constitui debent, prout maximè videbitur ad aedificationem facere. Id vero quia nemo facile fecerit, nisi coram Ecclesia aut populi alicuius conditionem videat, Paulus in suum aduentum istud reijcit. Rursus autem suo exemplo eos arguit, qui Ecclesijs quae nunquam viderunt, pro imperio praescribunt, & ad vnam eandemque formam omnes reducere conantur. Ita vero libertatem Ecclesiarum euertunt, quam in externis illis seruari vtile & necessarium est, quò minus illorum obseruatio in superstitionem degeneret, & in isdem salutis fiduciam collocent homines, quae in vnius Christi merito nobis reposita esse debet. Nos vero ex his, quae hucusque de Caena Domini ab Apostolo dicta sunt, discamus in omni externo cultu ad Dei voluntatem & huius institutionem respicere. Externa autem haec meminerimus fidei exercitia & promissionum Dei atque exhibita in Christo salutis sigilla esse. Ita ergo illis vtamur, vt nihil cum prophano contemptu aut turbulenta confusione fiat. Salutis vero authorem agnoscamus vnum solumque IESVM CHRISTVM, qui hanc nobis sanguinis sui pretio acquisiuit, & in se credentes suo spiritu in illius via dirigit, ne vnquam excidant, sed in ipso aeternum seruentur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potentia in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: There remains the conclusion of this discussion: "The rest I will set in order when I come" (1 Cor. 11:34). Paul adds this clause, remembering his coming, so that they may more diligently amend what he had hitherto rebuked in them. The Papists abuse this clause to defend their Mass, which they contend Paul then instituted among the Corinthians. But this is far too ridiculous. For why would he have recalled them to the first institution of the Lord's Supper, if he had wished to institute something wholly foreign to it? Next, if the Apostles instituted the Mass, how is it that the most ancient writers, and those who came closest to their times, make no mention of such a thing? And if we listen to the historians of our adversaries, they themselves do not ascribe the Mass to one author, but write that, like a patchwork, it was put together, refuted by many pontiffs, and increased by new additions from time to time, until it attained the form it now has. Paul therefore speaks of those things that pertain to decency and order in the Church, as to the manner of teaching or preaching, the administration of the sacraments, public prayers, and other things of that kind. In these the same order and the same form cannot be kept; rather, they ought to be established according to the circumstances of places, times and people, as seems most conducive to edification. But since no one would easily do this unless he saw the condition of the Church or of a particular people, Paul defers it to his coming. Again, by his own example he rebukes those who prescribe by authority for churches they have never seen, and try to reduce all to one and the same form. Thus they overturn the liberty of the Churches, which it is useful and necessary to preserve in these external matters, lest their observance degenerate into superstition, and men place in them a confidence of salvation that ought to be reposed in the merit of Christ alone. But let us from what the Apostle has said so far about the Lord's Supper learn to look, in all external worship, to the will of God and to his institution. Let us remember that these external things are exercises of faith and seals of the promises of God and of salvation exhibited in Christ. Let us so use them that nothing is done with profane contempt or disorderly confusion. Let us acknowledge the one and only author of salvation, Jesus Christ, who acquired it for us at the price of his blood, and who, in those who believe in him, directs them by his Spirit in his way, so that they never fall away, but are kept eternally in him. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XII. HOMILIA LXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII. HOMILY LXII.

units.la: Porrò de spiritualibus [donis] fratres, nolim vos in ignorantia[?] versari. Scitis quòd Gentes eratis, qui ad idola illa muta, prout rapi contigisset, abripiebamini. Quapropter notum vobis facio, quòd nullus per Spiritum Dei loquens dicit IESVM anathema: & nemo potest dicere IESVM dominum, nisi per Spiritum sanctum.
units.tr: Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I would not have you ignorant. You know that you were Gentiles, carried away to those dumb idols, however you happened to be led. Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking by the Spirit of God says "Jesus is anathema," and no one can say "Jesus is Lord" except by the Holy Spirit.

units.la: QVARTA[?] huius epistolae parte Paulus de caeremonijs ecclesiasticis & vitijs illis agit, qui- bus illorum verum vsum Corinthij corruperant: & haetenus quidem de vestitu indecoro primùm, deinde de Caena Domini nostri IESVM CHRISTI disseruit. Nunc verò de donis spiritualibus incipit agere, vt quae illic concurrebant vitia corrigat. Quae tractatio per tria capita proximè sequentia extenditur, & (vt Chrysostomus quoq; annotauit) multis obscurior, nonnullis autem superuacanea esse videtur, quia dona ista non in tam frequenti vsu sunt hodie vt olim, multa autem prorsus cessarunt. Olim enim cum Baptismo Spiritum sanctum recipiebant credentes, qui se signis externis & operibus eximijs declarabant: inter quae præ alijs vsitata erant donum linguarum & prophetia, quae non solùm vulgarem Scripturarum cognitionem, verumetiam eas interpretandi & ex illis vaticinandi facultatem continebat. Exempla eius rei Lucas proponit in Cornelio Centurione atque domesticis eius, in Ephesijs item & Samaritanis ciuibus: & eodem referri debet, quod Paulus Galatis dicit: Hoc solum cupio discere à vobis, Ex operibus Legis Spiritum accepistis, an ex praedicatione fidei? Arguit enim eorum stupiditatem, quòd à pseudoapostolis se ad Legis opera reduci paterentur, cum fidei doctrinam Spiritus sancti missione & huius excellentissimi doni confirmari sensissent, quale nihil vnquam circa Legis doctrinam fieri viderant. Nam praeter ea, quorum modo meminimus, multa alia accedebant, & (vt infra dicetur) alij quidem dabatur sermo sapientiae, alij sermo cognitionis, alij dona sanationum, alij miraculorum facultas, alij discretio spirituum: adhaec aliis plura simul, aliis pauciora obtingebant. Hic autem non vno modo peccabatur. Alij enim dona ista ambitiose ostentabant, & propter ea sibi in fratres imperium sumebant, & ita simul Deum, à quo illa acceperant, sua gloria fraudabant, Ecclesiam vero eorundem vsu priuabant. Alij vero insolentia illorum irritati ipsis inuidebant. Multi quoque pusillanimitate sua superati, se à Deo neglegi, neq; germanae Ecclesiae membra esse arbitrabantur. Itaq; dissidiorum & scismatum causa erant dona ista, in quibus ipsi simul omnes Dei gratiam agnoscere, & per illa in vnum corpus arctiori vinculo coalescere debuissent. Accedebat aliud quoq; vitium, quod in illorum deletu peccarent, & vel ostentationis vel commodi ali cuius priuati causa affectarent vilio ra & minus vtilia, neglectis praestantioribus, ex quibus publica Ecclesiae aedificatio & priuata singulorum salus maxima ex parte dependet. Hic ergo diligenti institutione opus erat, & ideo Paulus causam istam prolixè tractat. Primo enim authorem istorum donorum nobis ostendit, Deum, qui Spiritus sui virtute ea conferat. Deinde eorundem diuersitatem exponit. Tertio quae inter illa alias praestent, docet. Postremo de vero illorum vsu disserit. Neq; nobis hodie doctrina ista inutilis & superuacanea videri debet. Nam etiamsi miraculosa illa dona, quorum nunc non tantus porro vsus est, fere omnino cessauerint, nec etiam absq; nostro labore & industria subito nobis obtingat rerum agendarum cognitio atq; facultas: sunt tamen adhuc dona, quibus & Ecclesiarum ministros & singulos credentes instructos esse oportet, & qua nostro labore atq; studio nunquam obtinebimus, nisi his Dominus Spiritus sui virtute benedicat. Et quia hodie non minus ambitione, inuidia, pusillanimitate alijsq; vitijs peccatur, nobis etiam remedio opus est, quo omnibus istis occurratur.
units.tr: In the fourth part of this letter Paul treats of ecclesiastical ceremonies and of the abuses by which the Corinthians had corrupted their true use. Up to this point he has discussed first the unseemly clothing and then the Lord's Supper of our Lord Jesus Christ. Now he begins to treat of spiritual gifts, so as to correct the faults that had gathered around them there. This discussion extends through the next three chapters and, as Chrysostom also noted, is more obscure to many and seems superfluous to some, because these gifts are not in such frequent use today as formerly, and many have altogether ceased. For in former times believers received the Holy Spirit at baptism, and they declared this by external signs and remarkable works. Among these, the gift of tongues and prophecy were more commonly used than the others, and these included not only ordinary knowledge of the Scriptures but also the ability to interpret them and to prophesy from them. Luke sets out examples of this in Cornelius the centurion and his household, and likewise in the Ephesians and the Samaritan citizens. To the same matter belongs what Paul says to the Galatians: "This only I want to learn from you: did you receive the Spirit by the works of the Law, or by the preaching of faith?" For he rebukes their stupidity, in that they allowed themselves to be led back to the works of the Law by false apostles, when they had perceived that the doctrine of faith was confirmed by the sending of the Holy Spirit and by this most excellent gift, something they had never seen happen in connection with the doctrine of the Law. Besides those things we have just mentioned, many other gifts were added. As will be said below, to one was given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another gifts of healing, to another the power of working miracles, to another the discerning of spirits; moreover, some received several of these together and others fewer. Yet the abuses here were not of one kind. For some displayed these gifts ambitiously, and on that account claimed dominion over the brothers, and so at the same time robbed God, from whom they had received them, of his glory, and deprived the Church of their use. Others, provoked by the arrogance of these, envied them. Many too, overcome by their own timidity, thought that God neglected them and that they were not true members of the Church. Thus these gifts became the cause of divisions and schisms, when they ought all to have acknowledged God's grace in them and through them to have been joined into one body by a closer bond. There was also another fault: in their use of these gifts they sinned, and out of ostentation or some private advantage they pursued lesser and less useful things, neglecting the more excellent ones, on which the public building up of the Church and the private salvation of individuals depend for the most part. Here therefore careful instruction was needed, and so Paul treats this matter at length. First he shows us the author of these gifts, God, who bestows them by the power of his Spirit. Then he sets out their diversity. Third, he teaches which of them excel the others. Last, he discourses on their true use. Nor should this doctrine seem to us today useless and superfluous. For even if those miraculous gifts, whose use is no longer so great, have almost wholly ceased, and even if the knowledge and ability to do things do not come to us suddenly and without our own labour and diligence, there are still gifts with which the ministers of the Churches and individual believers ought to be equipped, and these we shall never obtain by our labour and zeal unless the Lord blesses us with them by the power of his Spirit. And because today sin is committed no less through ambition, envy, timidity and other faults, we also need a remedy by which all these may be checked.

units.la: Orditur autem à breui praefatiuncula, qua doctrinam istam, vt cognitu dignam atque necessariam commendat. Quod verò (inquit) dona illa spiritualia fratres, nolim vos in ignorantia versari, sed potius vos illorum authorem finem & vsum scire velim, vt quid in illis potissimum spectari debeat, intelligatis. Nec temere hoc dicit Apostolus. Hinc enim omnium rerum abusus originem ducit, quod pauci Deum omnis boni largitorem agnoscunt, neque in quem finem is omnia nobis largiatur, obseruant. Et quis obsecro tam impudens esset, vt vel frugibus ad ebrietatem & intemperantiam, vel corporis forma atque valetudine ad libidinem, vel opibus ad luxum, vel sapientia ad impostauras, vel potentia & authoritate ad communis patriae oppressionem abuteretur, si ista omnia à Deo dari, & in eum finem dari cogitaret, vt & ipsius gloriam nobis illustretur, & ijsdem Ecclesia aedificetur, & multi alij adiuuentur? At quia haec paucissimi intelligunt, aut saltem intelligere & obseruare nolunt, fit, vt se non Deo aut alijs hominibus, sed sibi soli natos putent, & proinde donis omnibus pro sua libidine abutantur. Semper ergo hanc cantilenam omnes sibi occinant. Vnde habes ea, quibus ante alios excellis? In què vsum illa data sunt? Cur ergo ea tibi soli vendicas? Cur nulla vel Dei vel hominum ratione habita, ijs pro tuo arbitrio abuteris?
units.tr: He begins with a brief preface, by which he commends this doctrine as worth knowing and necessary. When he says, "Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I would not have you ignorant," he means that he wishes you to know their author, their end and their use, so that you may understand what ought chiefly to be looked to in them. The Apostle does not say this rashly. For from this source comes the abuse of all things: few acknowledge God as the giver of every good, and few observe for what end he bestows all things on us. And who, I beg you, would be so shameless as to abuse the fruits of the earth for drunkenness and intemperance, bodily beauty and health for lust, wealth for luxury, wisdom for deceit, or power and authority for the oppression of the common fatherland, if he thought that all these things were given by God, and given to this end: that God's glory might be made known through us, that the Church might be built up by them, and that many others might be helped? But because very few understand these things, or at least are unwilling to understand and observe them, it comes about that men think they are born not for God or for other men but for themselves alone, and therefore abuse all their gifts as their lust dictates. So they all sing this same tune: "Where did you get the things by which you excel above others? For what use were they given? Why then do you claim them for yourself alone? Why do you abuse them at your own pleasure, taking no account of God or of men?"

units.la: Est praeterea obseruatu dignissimum Pauli exemplum, qui de donis spiritualibus verba facturus, non paucos aliquos sibi deligit, quos solos dignos iudicet, qui illorum rationem omnem atque vsum intelligant: sed totam Ecclesiam instituit, & neminem, qui illius membrum fit, in ignorantia vult versari. Eadem omnium Apostolorum mens fuit atq; sententia, qui quaecunq; ad Regni Dei cognitionem & aeternam hominis salutem faciunt, publicè omnibus praedicauerunt. Sciebant enim sibi à Christo dictum esse: Docete eos seruare omnia, quae mandaui vobis. Et quia iidem nouerant, Christi Spiritu omnes eos donatos esse, quotquot in illum credunt, neminem eorum cognitione indignum iudicarunt, quae Spiritus ille in electis operatur. Posteris demum temporibus exorti sunt Pontifices & horum assentatores, qui non minus impium quàm odiosum & contumeliosum dicrimen illud Laicorum & Spiritualium inuexerunt, & horum quidem titulo eos solos dignati sunt, qui rasi & vncti in illorum verba iurarunt, reliquum verò Christianorum vulgus tanquam profanum & Christi Spiritu destitutum illorum libidini subiecerunt. Et quasi hoc parum esset, locum quoq; peculiarem sibi ipsis in templis delegerunt, à quo ferreis cancellis inclusos reliquos omnes excluderent. derent. Adhæc libros sacros ex vulgi manibus excusserunt, indignum rati, vt diuinæ voluntatis mysteria ab alijs legerentur, quàm quos ipsi illorum cognitione dignos iudicauissent. Sunt hæc tyrannica plane, eoq; intolerabiliora, quia non de fortunis & huius seculi vita, sed de æterna hominum totius salute agitur. Ita vero fieri oportebat ab ijs, quorum regnum maximè in populi ignorantia consistit. Quis enim illorum tyrannidem patienter ferat, qui Christianæ libertatis cognitionem vel mediocrem habeat? Quapropter vt primum aliquos ad Scripturæ sacræ lectionem attentiores esse, aut de salutis ratione diligentius inquirere sentiunt, mox verba ista audias: Hæc spiritualia plane sunt, & proinde eorum tractatio ad solos spirituales pertinet, &c. At cur non cum Paulo dicit: Quoad dona spiritualia, nolumus vos in ignorantia versari?
units.tr: Moreover, Paul's example is most worthy of notice. When he is about to speak of spiritual gifts, he does not choose a few men whom he alone judges worthy to understand their whole reason and use; he addresses the whole Church, and he does not want anyone who becomes a member of it to remain in ignorance. This was the mind and opinion of all the Apostles, who publicly preached to all everything that contributes to the knowledge of the kingdom of God and the eternal salvation of man. For they knew that Christ had said to them: "Teach them to observe all that I have commanded you." And since they knew that all who believe in him are endowed with the Spirit of Christ, they judged none unworthy of knowing what that Spirit works in the elect. Later times, however, produced Popes and their flatterers, who introduced no less impiously than odiously and insultingly that distinction between laity and "spiritual" persons. Under the title of the spiritual they deemed worthy only those who, shaven and anointed, had sworn to their words, and they subjected the rest of the Christian crowd to their lust as profane and destitute of the Spirit of Christ. And as if this were too little, they also chose for themselves a special place in the churches, from which they shut out all the rest, enclosed behind iron railings. Furthermore, they snatched the holy books out of the hands of the common people, judging it unworthy that the mysteries of the divine will should be read by others than those whom they themselves had judged worthy of knowing them. These things are plainly tyrannical, and all the more intolerable because what is at stake is not fortunes and the life of this age but the eternal salvation of all mankind. Yet this was bound to happen from those whose kingdom consists chiefly in the ignorance of the people. For who could patiently bear the tyranny of these men if he had even a moderate knowledge of Christian liberty? Therefore, as soon as they perceive that some are more attentive to reading Holy Scripture or inquire more diligently into the way of salvation, you will at once hear these words: "These things are plainly spiritual, and so their treatment pertains only to the spiritual," and so on. But why do they not say with Paul: "Concerning spiritual gifts, we would not have you ignorant"?

units.la: Sed ad rem ipsam Apostolus accedit, & ab authore sive efficiente causa donorum omnium exorsus, hunc ostendit esse vnum Deum, qui illa nobis ex gratuita misericordia largiatur. Ex eo autem concludere vult, illis nos pie & religiosè vti debere. Itaq; summa argumenti eius est: Quæcunque hominibus ex Dei gratia obtinguntur, ijs nemo ad ostentationem siue priuatam gloriam cum aliorum contemptu debet abuti: Atqui spiritualia illa dona, vt pote cognitio linguarum, prophetia, spirituum discretio & quæcunq; sunt alia huius generis, nobis ex gratuita Dei liberalitate dantur. Ergo non ambitiosius ostentari, nec quisquam, qui illis minus instructus est, ideo insolentius contemni debet. Simul autem authoris omnium donorum cognitio alterum quoq; illis seruiebat, qui ijs inuidebant, quos pluribus & excellentioribus donis cernebant esse instructos. Nemini enim ea, quæ ipsi à Deo donata sunt, inuidere possumus, nisi simul Deum iniquitatis & insipientiæ accusare libeat, qui sua dona iniustè aut imprudenter dispenset. Cæterum dona illa omnia à Deo dari, duobus argumentis Apostolus demonstrat.
units.tr: But the Apostle comes to the matter itself. Beginning from the author or efficient cause of all gifts, he shows that there is one God, who bestows them on us out of free mercy. From this he wishes to conclude that we ought to use them piously and religiously. So the sum of his argument is this: no one should abuse whatever is obtained by men through the grace of God for display or private glory, to the contempt of others. But those spiritual gifts, such as the knowledge of tongues, prophecy, the discerning of spirits, and whatever other gifts there are of this kind, are given to us by God's free generosity. Therefore they should not be displayed more ambitiously, nor should anyone who has less knowledge of them be despised the more insolently. At the same time, the knowledge of the author of all gifts served another purpose too, against those who envied others whom they saw to be endowed with more and more excellent gifts. For we cannot envy anyone for what God has given him, unless we are willing at the same time to accuse God of injustice or folly, as if he distributed his gifts unfairly or without judgement. Moreover, the Apostle proves by two arguments that all those gifts are given by God.

units.la: Primum ex pristina eorum conditione petit, dicens: Scitis quòd Gentes eratis, qui ad idola illa muta, prout rapi contigisset, abripiebamini. Gentes dicit fuisse, vt vna voce comprehendat veri Dei ignorantiam, superstitiosos cultus, & quòd tanquam abdicati à Deo nullam æternæ salutis societatem cum filijs eius habuerant. Ita enim gentes alibi describit, vt quando Ephesijs dicit: Mementote vos aliquando Gentes in carne, qui dicebamini Præputium ab ea quæ vocatur Circumcisio in carne, & quæ manibus fit: Vos (inquâ) illo tempore fuisse absq; Christo, alienatos à republ. Israelis, & extraneos à pactis promissionis, spem non habentes, & Dei expertes in mundo. Et rursum eosdem ad vitam professione Christiana dignam exhortans, ait: Obtestor vos per Dominum, ne amplius versemini sicuti reliquæ Gentes versantur in vanitate mentis suæ, cogitationem habentes obscuratam, & alienati à vita Dei, propter ignorantiam, quæ est in ipsis ex obduratione cordis ipsorum: Qui posteaquam dedoluerunt, semetipsos dediderunt proteruiæ ad patrandam impuritatem omnem certatim, &c. Et hæc omnia in præsenti vno quasi verbo comprehendens dicit, eos ad idola muta abreptos fuisse temere, prout rapi contigisset, id est, absq; omni consideratione rectè ne an perperam ducerentur. Illorum autem eos admonet, non vt ignominiosè illis insultet pristinæ conditionem exprobrando: sed vt Dei gratiam illis commendet, & efficacius exhortetur, vt in donis illis spiritualibus officium suum fideliter faciant. Ex his enim argumentum præsenti instituto commodissimè seruiens colligi potest ad hunc modum: Quicunq; ad idola muta absq; ratione abripiuntur, ij ex semetipsis non percipiunt ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, neq; propria industria aut virtute dona illa spiritualia possunt assequi: Atqui vos ad idola muta abripiebamini temere, nec quicquâ ea in re pensi habebatis: Ergo nihil donorum spiritualium ex vobisipsis habetis [?], sed quicquid horum apud vos extat, id ex Dei dono & liberalitate accepistis.
units.tr: First, he appeals to their former condition, saying: "You know that you were Gentiles, carried away to those dumb idols, however you happened to be led." He calls them Gentiles to comprehend in one word their ignorance of the true God, their superstitious worship, and the fact that, as cut off from God, they had no fellowship in eternal salvation with his sons. He describes Gentiles in this way elsewhere too, as when he says to the Ephesians: "Remember that you were once Gentiles in the flesh, who were called the uncircumcision by those who are called the circumcision, which is made in the flesh by hands. You (I say) were at that time without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world." And again, urging these same people to a life worthy of the Christian profession, he says: "I beseech you in the Lord that you no longer walk as the other Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their minds, having their understanding darkened, alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them because of the hardening of their hearts; who, having become past feeling, have given themselves over to wantonness, to work all impurity greedily," and so on. Summing all this up in the present passage in one word, he says that they were carried away to dumb idols rashly, however they happened to be led, that is, without any consideration whether they were being led rightly or wrongly. He reminds them of this, however, not to insult them with reproaches of their former condition, but to commend the grace of God to them, and to exhort them more effectively to faithfully perform their duty in those spiritual gifts. From this, an argument serving the present purpose very aptly can be drawn in this way: whoever are carried off to dumb idols without reason do not by themselves receive the things that are of the Spirit of God, nor can they obtain those spiritual gifts by their own industry or virtue. But you were carried off to dumb idols rashly, and took no thought at all in that matter. Therefore you have none of the spiritual gifts from yourselves [?], but whatever of these is among you, you have received by the gift and generosity of God.

units.la: Quòd verò eos ad muta idola abreptos fuisse dicit, id non vno modo factū fuisse patebit, si gentium mores & studia diligentius consideremus. Primò enim huc oracula pertinent, secundum quæ Reges quoq; potentissimi & qui respub. clarissimas administrabant, omnia sua dirigere soliti fuerunt. Reddebantur ea apud simulachra ferè ea, quæ vel vetustate, vel opere & artificio, vel loci celebritate, aut etiam miraculis commendabantur: & mirificè in his cum hominibus superstitiosis Satan lusit. Nam vt modò diximus, ijs etiam, qui authoritate & potentia præstabant, author fuit, vt simulachra muta consulerent. Id verò non absurdum modò, verumetiam à communi sensu alienum erat. Qui enim muti sunt, ij plerunq; surdi etiam esse consueuerunt. Simulachra autem cùm ex inanimata materia constarent, non modò muta & surda erant, sed simul omni alio quoq; sensu atq; motu destituebantur, ut non temere de illis divinus ille Psaltes[?] dicat: Os habent, & non loquuntur: oculos habent, & nō vident. Aures habent, & non audiunt: habent nasum, nec odorantur. Manus habent, nec palpant: pedes habent, nec ambulant, neq; sonum edunt suo gutture. Quid verò stultius est, quid absurdius & risu dignius, quàm eum de re aliqua magni momenti interrogare, qui neque audit quod dicitur, neq; ad quæstionem propositam potest respondere? Cùm autem id fecerint qui consilio, prudentia & rerum usu præ aliis excellebant, quos obsecro negauerint eos diabolica virtute aut tyrannide temere abreptos fuisse? Quod eò manifestius apparet, quod sæpe non contenti uno oraculo, plura quæsiuerunt, nec viderunt se fidem derogare iis, quos primò sciscitati fuerant. Est eius rei memorabile exemplum in Lacedæmoniorum historia. Cùm enim Agesilaus bellum contra Persas animo concepisset, ut Græcos, qui Asiam incolebant, in libertate assereret, primò Iouis Dodonæi oraculum consuluit: qui ut rem ipsam pro sui animi sententia gereret, iussit. Id verò responsum non suf ficere putarunt Ephori, quorum consilio ipsi etiam reges regebantur. Itaq;, ut Delphicum quoq; oraculum quæreret, iusserunt, & ita Agesilaum à patre Ioue ad filium Apollinem remiserunt, inq; dubium vocarunt eius fidem atq; authoritatem, quem gentes omnes publicè patrem hominumq; Deumq; esse pro fitebantur. Quid hic stultius, quid à religione & pietate magis alienum fieri poterat? Ipse certè Agesilaus, quo erat ingenij acumine præditus, tam Ephororum superstitiosam stultitiam, quàm oraculorum simul omnium fidem ludibrio habuit, quando ad Delphos profectus, quæstione ita propositâ: Apollo, idem ne tibi videtur quod patri? Et huius generis exempla plura adduci poterant, quæ vel cæcam illorum hominum stupiditatem, vel etiam voluntariam insaniam arguunt: utriusq; autem illis author fuit diabolus, ut vel scientes vel nescientes in pericula ruerent, & imposturis atque fraudibus delectarentur.
units.tr: That they were carried away to dumb idols will be clear to have happened in more than one way, if we consider more carefully the customs and pursuits of the Gentiles. In the first place, oracles pertain here, according to which even the most powerful kings and those who administered the most famous commonwealths were accustomed to direct all their affairs. These were given at images which were commended for the most part either by their antiquity, their workmanship and craftsmanship, the fame of the place, or even by miracles; and in these matters Satan played wonderfully with superstitious men. For, as we have just said, he was also the author of persuading even those who excelled in authority and power to consult mute images. And this was not only absurd but even alien to common sense. For those who are mute are commonly deaf too. Images, moreover, since they were made of inanimate matter, were not only mute and deaf but also deprived of every other sense and motion; so that the divine Psalmist does not speak lightly of them when he says: "They have mouths, but they do not speak; they have eyes, but they do not see; they have ears, but they do not hear; they have noses, but they do not smell; they have hands, but they do not feel; they have feet, but they do not walk; nor do they make any sound in their throat." What indeed is more foolish, more absurd and worthy of laughter, than to ask about some matter of great importance one who neither hears what is said nor can answer the question put to him? And since those who excelled others in counsel, prudence and experience of affairs did this, I ask whom they would deny to have been rashly carried away by diabolical power or tyranny? This appears all the clearer because they often were not content with one oracle, but sought several, and did not see that they were thereby casting doubt on those whom they had first consulted. There is a memorable example of this in the history of the Lacedaemonians. For when Agesilaus had conceived in his mind the plan of making war on the Persians, so as to assert the liberty of the Greeks who inhabited Asia, he first consulted the oracle of Jupiter at Dodona, which ordered him to carry out the matter according to his own inclination. But the Ephors, by whose counsel even the kings themselves were ruled, did not think this response sufficient. So they ordered him to seek the oracle at Delphi too, and thus they sent Agesilaus from the father Jupiter to the son Apollo, and called into doubt the faith and authority of him whom all the nations publicly professed to be the father of men and of gods. What could be more foolish here, or more alien from religion and piety? Agesilaus himself, endowed with the sharpness of wit that he had, mocked the superstitious folly of the Ephors as much as the trustworthiness of all the oracles together, when, having gone to Delphi, he put the question in this way: "Apollo, does it seem to you the same as to your father?" Many more examples of this kind could be brought forward, which prove either the blind stupidity of those men or even their voluntary madness; and of both the devil was the author, so that, whether knowingly or unknowingly, they rushed into dangers and delighted in deceptions and frauds.

units.la: Quòd si verò ad eos transfeas, quorum opera & ministerio diabolus in reddendis oraculis usus est, manifestior erit infelix illa tyrannis, qua in homines miseros desæuijt. In Delphico enim oraculo Pythia mulier divaricatis cruribus tripodi impositâ Spiritu diabolico (quem infelices illi Deum suum Apollinem esse putabant) implebatur, & huius impatiens cotaq; mente alienata, eum excutere cupiebat, modò caput horrendo gestu & ore spumanti concutiens, modò voce fremens, tandemq; vi-Ela versus[?] fundebat obscuros & ambiguos, quos ne ipsa quidem intelligebat, & ex quibus sensus certus vix unquam poterat elici. In aliis etsi diuersæ esse conciperent spiritus vaticinantis formæ, furor tamen idem fuit, qui ita omnes exagitauit, ut eorum quæ dixerant nunquam recordarentur. Fuit ergo raptus iste verè violentus, & non alij quàm diabolico spiritui tribuendus, cùm constet, Deum suos vates non crudeliter tractare, nec furoribus horrendis exagitare, sed Spiritus sanctus ce dirigere, quæ rationis usum illis nequaquam adimit, & tam illos ipsos quàm alios ipsorum opera eorum cognitione instruit, quæ ipsos scire refert.
units.tr: But if you turn to those through whose work and ministry the devil was used in giving the oracles, that wretched tyranny by which he raged against miserable men will be clearer still. For at the Delphic oracle the Pythia, a woman with legs spread apart and seated on the tripod, was filled with a diabolical spirit (which those wretches believed to be their god Apollo). Unable to endure this, and with her mind alienated, she wished to shake it off, now tossing her head with a horrible gesture and foaming mouth, now roaring with her voice; and at last, with difficulty, she poured out obscure and ambiguous words, which she herself did not even understand, and from which a clear sense could scarcely ever be drawn. In others, although they conceived the forms of the prophesying spirit to be different, the frenzy was nevertheless the same, which so agitated them all that they never remembered what they had said. That rapture, then, was truly violent, and must be attributed to no other spirit than the diabolical one, since it is established that God does not treat his prophets cruelly, nor stir them up with dreadful frenzies, but the Holy Spirit directs them in such a way that it by no means takes away the use of reason from them, and instructs both them and others by their work with that knowledge which it relates they should know.

units.la: At quid de vatibus dicere opus est, quando in ipso cultu Deorum non obscura argumenta inueniuntur, quibus diaboli tyrannis agnosci potest, qua miseri illi exagitati & oppressi fuerunt? Constat enim sacra quædam & dies festos non ab aliis celebratos fuisse, quàm ab iis, qui aut verè furoribus tunc temporis corripiebantur, aut saltem se furere ac insanire simulabant: qualia lupercalia fuerunt, in quibus iuuenes caprinis pellibus velati & faciem sanguine inuncti discurrebant, obuios quosq; & imprimis fœminas tam steriles quàm grauidas loris cædentes, ut hæ quidem facilius partu leuarentur, illæ verò fecundæ fierent: Bacchanalia item, in quibus mulieres thyrsis armatæ & pellibus vestitæ non per urbis modo, pudore omni abiecto, verumetiam per campos & syluas discurrebant, furiosis clamoribus Bacchum cientes, ideoq; Græcis Mænades, quasi furentes, dictæ sunt. Multa quoque horum similia in aliis etiam sacris acciderunt, quorum maxima pars semper petulantibus ludis ac impudicis saltationibus peracta fuit, ut iam de conuiuijs luxuriosis & plus quàm barbara humanarum victimarum crudelitate nihil dicamus; cùm alij hospites temere oblatos, alij seruos, alij homines maleficos, multi proprios liberos in Deorum honorem immolarent. Et ut nihil horum falsum fuisset unquam, simplex tamen ille idolorum cultus, non obscurum argumentum fuit, homines illos neq; sanæ mentis & rationis motu, neq; Dei spiritu duc-tos, sed spiritu malo & humani generis inimico raptos fuisse: quando incorpoream & incorruptibilem æterni numinis naturam materia corruptibili & humana arte, eiusdem verò mores & facultates forma hominis caduci, aut etiam bruti animalis, exprimere conati sunt. Et quis obsecro sana mente eum uti dixerit, qui manuum suarum opus colit & adorat? qui lapidi aut ligno loqui-tur? qui ab eo opem petit, in quo ne motus quidem ille est, quem in culice aut vermiculo omnium minutissimo esse videmus? Non temere certè à Propheta dictum est, Simulachrorum similes fie-ri eos, qui illa colunt.
units.tr: But why should we speak of the prophets, when the very worship of the gods offers clear evidence by which the tyranny of the devil, under which those wretched men were driven out of their minds and oppressed, can be recognized? For it is established that certain sacred rites and festival days were celebrated by none but those who were either truly seized by frenzy at the time or at least pretended to rave and go mad. Such were the Lupercalia, in which young men, wrapped in goatskins and smeared with blood on the face, ran about striking with thongs whomever they met, especially women, both barren and pregnant, so that the former might be eased more easily in childbirth and the latter might become fruitful. Likewise the Bacchanalia, in which women armed with thyrsi and clad in animal skins, having cast off all shame, ran not only through the city but also through the fields and woods, calling on Bacchus with frenzied cries; for this reason the Greeks called them Maenads, as if raving. Many things similar to these also happened in other rites, the greater part of which were always carried out with wanton games and immodest dances, not to mention luxurious banquets and a cruelty toward human victims beyond even barbarous measure, when some sacrificed strangers who had been rashly offered, others slaves, others wicked men, and many their own children in honour of the gods. And although none of these things had ever been false, that plain worship of idols was nonetheless a clear proof that those men were moved neither by a sound mind and reason nor by the Spirit of God, but were seized by an evil spirit, the enemy of the human race, since they tried to express the incorporeal and incorruptible nature of the eternal deity by corruptible matter and human art, and its character and powers by the form of frail man or even of a brute animal. And who, I ask, of sound mind would say that someone worships and adores the work of his own hands? who speaks to stone or wood? who seeks help from one in whom there is not even that motion which we see in a gnat or the smallest of worms? Surely not without reason did the Prophet say that those who worship them become like the idols.

units.la: Porrò non debet hoc loco negligi, quòd cùm Paulus crassissimos gentium errores & turpissima quaq; scelera producere posset, quibus probaret eos nihil boni habere, quod non ex gratuita Dei mi-sericordia seu liberalitate accepissent, eorum tamen solummodo meminit, quæ circa idolorum cul-tum acciderunt. Est enim idololatria omnium scelerum gravissimum, & multorum aliorum fæcundissima mater. Primùm enim hominem totum à Deo abducit, & ideo fornicatio spiritualis di-citur. Deinde cultum omnem evertit, qui (ut olim Lactantius monuit) nullus esse potest, ubicunq; simulachra sunt. Quia enim hæc cum mendacio coniuncta sunt (sicuti ex nomine eorum apparet) ille autem ipsissima & æterna Veritas est, fieri nequit, ut hic illis colatur. Adde his, quòd cultus ille omnis (ut Cap. decimo prolixè demonstravimus) dæmonijs impenditur, quæ hac ratione sese in-sinuare solent, ut quod iam inde ab origine rerum ambiuerunt, ita impetrent. Præterea animum hominis ab idolis transfuersum abripi, vel etiam totum auferri, Hoseas testatur, & res ipsa abunde docet, quando (ut modò diximus) ea fiunt, quæ non à ratione solùm, verumetiam à communi sensu & pudore aliena sunt. Deniq;, quia tales Dei gloriam atq; maiestatem commutant cum forma ho-minis mortalis & peccatoris, imò cum formis brutorum animalium, dignissimi certè sunt, qui in sensum reprobum traditi seipsos sceleribus atrocissimis turpissimisq; polluant, sicuti Apostolus ad Romanos testatur. Ista autem ita considerari debent ô fratres, ut non solum quæ olim fuit, infelicem gentium conditionem & immensam Dei gratiam, qui tales ex erroribus & interitu eripere, & donis sui Spiritus ornare dignatus est, agnoscamus: verumetiam intelligamus hæc omnia non minus ad nos pertinere, qui & ex gentibus oriundi sumus, & postremis hisce temporibus in similes tenebras demersi, Dei similem clementiam experti sumus, qui nos quoq; in lucem & libertatem af-feruit, & Filij sui cognitione illuminauit, in quo salutem veram Regnumq; sui hereditatem posside-bimus. Quæ consideratio nos excitare debet, ut dignitate nostra minimè superbiamus, sed donis accep-tis utamur ad Dei gloriam & multorum ædificationem: fugiamus autem veteres illas idolo-latriæ & superstitionum sordes, in quibus pereundum nobis erat, nisi inde illius gratuito beneficio essemus extracti.
units.tr: Moreover, it should not be overlooked in this place that, although Paul could have brought forward the grossest errors of the Gentiles and their most shameful crimes, by which he might prove that they had nothing good which they had not received from God's free mercy and bounty, he mentions only those things which happened in connection with the worship of idols. For idolatry is the gravest of all sins and the most fruitful mother of many others. First, it draws the whole man away from God, and therefore it is called spiritual fornication. Then it overturns all true worship, which (as Lactantius once warned) cannot exist wherever there are images. For since these are joined with falsehood (as the very name of them shows), while He is the very and eternal Truth, it cannot happen that He is worshipped among them. Add to these that all such worship (as we demonstrated at length in chapter ten) is offered to demons, who are accustomed to insinuate themselves in this way, so that they obtain what they have sought since the beginning of things. Moreover, Hosea testifies that the mind of man is carried off and even wholly taken away from God by idols, and the thing itself teaches abundantly when (as we have just said) those things are done which are alien not only to reason but also to common sense and modesty. Finally, since such people exchange the glory and majesty of God for the form of mortal and sinful man, indeed for the forms of brute animals, they are most worthy, as the Apostle testifies to the Romans, to be given over to a reprobate mind and to defile themselves with the most atrocious and most shameful crimes. Brethren, these things ought to be considered in such a way that we acknowledge not only the wretched condition of the Gentiles of old and the immense grace of God, who deigned to snatch such people from error and destruction and to adorn them with the gifts of his Spirit; but also that we understand all these things pertain to us no less, who too are descended from the Gentiles, and who, plunged in the last times into similar darkness, have experienced the like clemency of God, who has also rescued us into light and liberty, and enlightened us with the knowledge of his Son, in whom we shall possess true salvation and the inheritance of his kingdom. This consideration ought to stir us up, so that we do not puff ourselves up with our dignity, but use the gifts we have received for the glory of God and the edification of many; and let us flee those old filths of idolatry and superstitions, in which we had to perish, unless we had been drawn out of them by his free kindness.

units.la: Sed transeamus ad alterum argumentum, quo Paulus probat dona spiritualia à solo Deo no-bis dari. Infert hoc ex priori, dicens: Quapropter notum vobis facio, quòd nullus per Spiritum Dei loquens, &c. Sensus est:Quoniam hæc fuit vestra conditio, eademq; omnium est, qui Christi Spi-ritu adhuc destituuntur, hoc vobis persuasissimum esse volo, quòd ut nemo, qui per Dei Spiritum loquitur, IESUM anathema dicit:ita vicissim nemo eundem potest dominum dicere, nisi per Spiritum sanctum illuminetur, qui eius linguam excitet & regat. Anathema sumitur pro eo, qui execratione & exitio dignus est. Itaq; IESUM anathema dicere idem est, quod blasphemiam aut conuitium contra illum proferre, aut eius merito vel gloriæ quocunque modo detrabe-re[?]. At eundem dominum dicere est, non modò honorificè de eo loqui, sed ex animo agnoscere, quòd Dominus, id est, vindex & redemptor noster sit, cui nos fidem, amorem, reuerentiam & obedientiam debeamus, secundùm illud: Ego Dominus, hoc est nomen meum, & gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Intempestiuè ergo hoc loco aliqui quæstionem de impijs aut hypocritis mouent, num hi quoq; Spiritu sancto ducantur, quando Christum dominum dicunt? & cur eos ille pro suis non agnoscat, sicuti apud Matth. 7. Cap. habetur? Hic enim de verè pijs sermo est, qui quod ore prosi-tentur, ex animo credunt, & argumentum formatur à comparatis, quòd cùm Christum ne prosi-teri quidem possimus absq; Spiritus sancti virtute, multò minus nos ex nobisipsis habere dona il-la, quibus ille cultores suos exornat. Quoad hypocritas, non negamus, hoc etiam Spiritus sancti o-pus esse, qui linguas eorum propter alios moderatur & regit, ut Christo testimonium ferant, etiamsi ipsi à fide alieni sint. Nec enim plena virtute apud omnes agit Spiritus ille, & aliud est donum cognitionis illius vulgaris, quae non semper cum fide coniuncta est, aliud vero donum regenerationis, quae totum hominem Christo vendicat. Illud olim Iudas habuit, & non nisi ex Spiritus virtute Christi Euangelium praedicauit, sicut & illi, de quibus ad Philippenses scribit Paulus, quòd per aemulationem & contentionem Christum praedicent. Et commendatur in eo Spiritus sancti virtus, qui impiorum quoq; & hypocritarum linguis ad illustrandam Dei gloriam potest vtiliter abuti. Quid ni enim hoc faceret, qui diabolo quoq; veri confessionem extorquere potest, & ex ore infantium atq; lactentium laudes Dei elicere?
units.tr: But let us pass on to the other argument, by which Paul proves that spiritual gifts are given to us by God alone. He infers this from the previous one, saying: "Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking by the Spirit of God," etc. The sense is this: since this was your condition, and it is the same for all who are still destitute of the Spirit of Christ, I want you to be fully persuaded of this: just as no one who speaks by the Spirit of God says "Jesus is anathema," so in turn no one can say that He is Lord unless he is enlightened by the Holy Spirit, who stirs up and governs his tongue. "Anathema" is taken for one who deserves execration and destruction. Therefore to say "Jesus is anathema" is the same as to utter blasphemy or insult against Him, or in any way to detract from His merit or glory. But to say that He is Lord is not only to speak of Him honourably, but to acknowledge from the heart that the Lord, that is, our avenger and redeemer, is He to whom we owe faith, love, reverence and obedience, according to that saying: "I am the Lord; this is my name, and I will not give my glory to another." Therefore some raise, out of place here, the question concerning the impious or hypocrites, whether these also are led by the Holy Spirit when they say that Christ is Lord, and why He does not acknowledge them as His own, as is found in Matthew chapter 7? For here the discussion concerns those who are truly godly, who believe from the heart what they profess with their mouth, and the argument is drawn from comparison: since we cannot even profess Christ without the power of the Holy Spirit, much less do we have those gifts from ourselves with which He adorns His worshippers. As for hypocrites, we do not deny that this also is the work of the Holy Spirit, who for the sake of others restrains and rules their tongues so that they bear witness to Christ, even though they themselves are alien to faith. For that Spirit does not act with full power among all, and there is one thing, the gift of that common knowledge, which is not always joined with faith; and there is another, the gift of regeneration, which claims the whole man for Christ. Judas once had the former, and he preached the Gospel only by the power of the Spirit, as did those of whom Paul writes to the Philippians, that they preach Christ out of rivalry and strife. And the power of the Holy Spirit is commended in this, that it can usefully make use even of the tongues of the impious and hypocrites for the illustration of God's glory. For why should He not do this, who can even wring the confession of the truth from the devil, and draw praises of God from the mouths of infants and sucklings?

units.la: Docet autem nos locus iste, quanta sit nostra imbecillitas & natura nostra depravatio, quanadone[?] ore quidem Christum profiteri possumus, nisi Spiritus sanctus nos excitet, & linguam nostram moderetur. Probatur id exemplis sanctissimorum hominum. Querebatur Moses, se linguae esse impeditioris, nec posse loqui. Sed eidem respondet Dominus: Quis dedit homini os? & quis facit mutum ac surdum? videntem & caecum? nonne ego Dominus? Vade ergo, & ego adero ori tuo, docebóq; te quae loquaris. Quicquid ergo Moses recte fecit & locutus est, hoc Dei opus fuit, qui Spiritu suo eius mentem atq; linguam direxit. Idem de Ieremia, Isaia & reliquis Prophetis, ipsis denique Apostolis scriptum legimus: ideoque David olim orabat: Aperi Domine labia mea, ut os meum laudem tuam annuntiet. Et Paulus communibus Ecclesiae precibus se adiuuari voluit, ut sibi daretur apertio oris, id est, facultas libere & commode dicendi ea, quae dici oportebat. Etenim quid ex nobismetipsis faceremus in vera fide praedicatione aut confessione, qui nisi diuinitus illuminemur, neque Deum Patrem, neque Filium eius IESVM CHRISTVM nouimus? Huius enim verba sunt: Nemo venit ad me, nisi Pater meus traxerit eum. Item: Nemo scit quis sit Filius, nisi Pater: & quis sit Pater, nisi Filius, & cui voluerit Filius revelare. Nisi ergo Dei Spiritus sese animis nostris insinuet, & linguas nostras regat, quod de illo loquamur non habebimus. Admonent nos ista, ne meritum statuamus in operibus nostris, & ne in ijs quidem, quae ex fide promanant, aut ipsa etiam fidei confessione. Quia enim fides ipsa donum Dei est, abeodem accipiamus oportet, quicquid ex fide recte aut bene facimus. Quid ergo gloriamur operibus nostris, quasi ex propria virtute aut industria fiant? Docet praeterea locus iste, ne aliorum quidem donis tantum tribui debere, ut illis feruiliter adhaereamus, aut propter illos in sectas scindamur: quod apud Corinthios factum fuisse, initio Epistolae huius vidimus. Quin potius in omnibus illis Dei bonitatem atque gratiam praedicemus, cui vni omnis gloria debetur.
units.tr: This passage teaches us how great our weakness is and how depraved our nature, since we could not profess Christ with our mouths unless the Holy Spirit stirred us up and governed our tongues. This is proved by the examples of the most holy men. Moses complained that he was slow of speech and could not speak; but the Lord answered him: "Who made man's mouth? or who makes the dumb and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? Is it not I, the Lord? Go therefore, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you are to say." Whatever Moses rightly did and said, therefore, was the work of God, who directed his mind and tongue by his Spirit. We read the same written of Jeremiah, Isaiah and the other prophets, and finally of the Apostles themselves; and so David once prayed: "Open my lips, O Lord, that my mouth may declare your praise." And Paul wished to be helped by the common prayers of the Church, that there might be given to him the opening of the mouth, that is, the ability to speak freely and fittingly what ought to be said. For what could we do of ourselves in the true preaching or confession of the faith, we who, unless we are enlightened from heaven, know neither God the Father nor His Son Jesus Christ? For His words are: "No one comes to me unless my Father draws him." Likewise: "No one knows who the Son is except the Father, and who the Father is except the Son, and to whom the Son wills to reveal Him." Therefore, unless the Spirit of God insinuates Himself into our minds and governs our tongues, we shall not have anything to say about Him. These things warn us not to count merit in our works, nor even in those which flow from faith, or even in the very confession of faith. For since faith itself is a gift of God, whatever we do rightly or well from faith we must receive from the same source. Why then do we boast in our works, as if they were done by our own power or industry? This passage further teaches that not even the gifts of others should be so highly prized that we cling to them slavishly, or are split into factions on their account, as we saw at the beginning of this Epistle that happened among the Corinthians. Rather, in all those gifts let us proclaim the goodness and grace of God, to whom alone all glory is owed.

units.la: Proponitur item nobis hoc loco regula, ad quam nos ipsos probemus & alios, num Spiritu sancto ducamur. Est haec non vtilis modo, verum etiam necessaria, siue nos ipsos siue alios spectemus. Nam quoad nos, nisi Spiritum Christi habeamus, non sumus eius membra siue fratres. Imo quia idem ille adoptionis Spiritus est, neq; Dei filij erimus, nisi per illum excitati clamemus: Abba pater. Expendant ista non hypocritae modo, qui Christi nomine nequicquam gloriantur, verumetiam qui conscientiae angustia oppressi de electione sua dubitant, & Dei arcana curiosius scrutantur. Nam vt id facias minimè opus est: In teipsum descendito, & quid de Christo sentias vide. Hic enim est liber ille ciuitatis Dei, in quo ciuium Regni coelestis nomina adscripta sunt: quia in illo electi sumus (vt alibi Paulus ait) priusquam mundus hic conderetur. Itaq; si illum dominum tuum agnoscas atq; fatearis, ampliori cura minimè opus erit, cum illud Spiritus sancti in te agentis opus sit. Id ergo tibi sufficiat, teq; consoletur, etiamsi quoad reliqua dona, te multis aliis inferiorem esse sentias. Nam quantulacunq; sit fides nostra, ad Christum amplectendum sufficiens erit, qui nostras infirmitates farciet, peccata nostra conteget, & nos ex manibus suis eripi nunquam patietur. Quod si quibus donis alijs opus erit aliquando propter aliorum salutem, quos per nos Deus sibi vult lucrifacere, illa quoq; adijcientur. Interim nostra forte contenti, nostro nos pede metiamur, nec plus affectemus quàm Dominus dederit.
units.tr: Also set before us in this place is a rule by which we may test ourselves and others, to see whether we are led by the Holy Spirit. This rule is not only useful but necessary, whether we look at ourselves or at others. As for ourselves, unless we have the Spirit of Christ, we are not his members or brothers. Indeed, since it is the same Spirit of adoption, we will not be children of God unless, stirred up by him, we cry: "Abba, Father." Let not only hypocrites, who vainly boast in the name of Christ, consider these things, but also those who, oppressed by anguish of conscience, doubt their election and scrutinize the secrets of God too curiously. For there is no need at all to do this: go down into yourself and see what you think of Christ. For this is that book of the city of God in which the names of the citizens of the heavenly kingdom are written, because in him we were chosen (as Paul says elsewhere) before this world was founded. So if you acknowledge and confess him as your Lord, there will be no need for more anxious care, since that is the work of the Holy Spirit acting in you. Let that be enough for you and console you, even if you feel yourself inferior to many others in the remaining gifts. For however small our faith is, it will be sufficient to embrace Christ, who will make up for our weaknesses, cover our sins, and will never allow us to be snatched from his hands. But if other gifts are at some time needed for the salvation of others, whom God wishes to win through us, those too will be added. Meanwhile, content perhaps with what is ours, let us measure ourselves by our own foot, and not aim at more than the Lord has given.

units.la: Deinde regula ista propter doctores opus est, ne qui nos fallant. Nam alibi quidem monet Apostolus, ne extinguamus spiritum, neue prophetiam contemnamus, idem vero omnia probare in bet, & quod bonum fuerit tenere. Et Ioannes praeceptum est: Dilecti, ne cuiuis spiritui credatis, sed probate spiritus an ex Deo sint. Et mox regulam huius probationis istam tradit: Omnis spiritus, qui confitetur Iesum Christum in carne venisse, ex Deo est: At quicunque spiritus non confitetur IESUM CHRISTUM in carne venisse, is ex Deo non est, &c. Conveniunt ista plane cum eo, quod in praesenti Paulus dicit. Nam incarnationis mysterio Ioannes omnia com-plectitur, quae in carne assumpta Christus fecit & passus est, quorum omnium hic finis & scopus ipsi fuit, ut noster dominus fieret, id est, ut nos ex peccato & morte redemptos suum peculium, imo sponsam suam Regnique sui coheredes faceret. Si qui ergo huius Spiritu aguntur, ii omnem doctrinam ad eum scopum dirigent, ut ille solus emineat, & ab omnibus agnoscatur Dominus, Rex & Sacerdos, in quo uno salus mundo parta fit. Quotquot autem huius gloriam atque me-ritum nostrorum operum meritis obscurant, ab illo abducunt, & alias salutis consequendae ratio-nes comminiscuntur, ii mendacij spiritu aguntur, impostores & Antichristi sunt, quos nemo au-dire debet, nisi qui sciens perire velit. Discant etiam ex hoc loco omnes homines de vita & mori-bus tam suis quam aliorum iudicare. Nam qui his Christum referunt, & huic Domino suo obse-quium omne fideliter praestant, eos illius Spiritu regi certissimum est. Si qui vero eius Verbum fastidiunt, nomen eius proscindunt, vel eo ad execrationes & deierationes abutuntur, fidei denique Christianae profes-sionem scelerum licentia prophanant, ii Spiritu Dei destituantur oportet: imo hi Spiritus impuri & diabolici organa sunt, quorum neq; exemplo neq; successibus quisquam offendi debet. Porro qui praecipuus & verus huius loci scopus est, quicunque se Christi cognitione illu-minatos esse sentiunt, & hunc profitentur, ii sibi istud ex Dei gratia obtigisse cogitent. Huic ergo grati sint, & in fide constantes donis illius utantur ad eius gloriam atque aliorum aedificationem. orent autem indesinenter pro fidei augmento, ut per omnia aduersa eluctari, & tandem ad por-tum aeternae felicitatis appellere possint, quam nobis ille sui sanguinis pretio acquisiuit, cui debe-tur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Next, this rule is needed on account of teachers, lest they deceive us. For elsewhere the Apostle indeed warns us not to quench the Spirit or despise prophesying, but he also says that we must prove all things and hold fast what is good. John too is commanded: "Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are from God." And soon he gives the rule of this testing: "Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God; but whatever spirit does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not from God," etc. These things plainly agree with what Paul says here. For John embraces in the mystery of the incarnation all the things that Christ did and suffered in the flesh he assumed, and the whole aim and goal of all of these was that he should become our Lord, that is, that he should make us, redeemed from sin and death, his own possession, indeed his bride and co-heirs of his kingdom. If therefore those are led by his Spirit, they will direct all teaching to that goal, so that he alone stands out and is acknowledged by all as Lord, King and Priest, in whom alone salvation has been won for the world. But whoever obscure his glory and merit by the merits of our works, lead people away from him, and devise other ways of obtaining salvation, they are driven by the spirit of lying; they are impostors and Antichrists, whom no one should hear, unless he wishes to perish knowingly. Let all people also learn from this place to judge both their own life and morals and those of others. For those who refer these things to Christ, and faithfully render every obedience to this their Lord, it is quite certain that they are ruled by his Spirit. But if any despise his Word, tear apart his name, abuse it for curses and oaths, or finally profane the profession of the Christian faith by a license to sin, these must be lacking the Spirit of God; indeed they are instruments of an impure and diabolical spirit, and no one should be offended by their example or their success. Moreover, the chief and true aim of this place is that whoever feel themselves enlightened by the knowledge of Christ and profess it should think that this has come to them by the grace of God. Let them therefore be thankful for it, stand firm in faith, and use his gifts for his glory and the building up of others. Let them also pray unceasingly for the increase of their faith, so that they may struggle through all adversities and at last reach the harbour of eternal happiness, which he acquired for us at the price of his blood, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power forever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY LXIII.

units.la: Discrimina autem donorum sunt, sed idem Spiritus: & discri-mina ministeriorum sunt, sed idem Dominus: & discrimina facul-tatum sunt, sed idem est Deus efficiens omnia in omnibus. Uni-cuique vero datur declaratio Spiritus ad utilitatem. Nam huic quidem per Spiritum datur sermo sapientiae: alii vero sermo cognitionis per eundem Spiritum: alii vero fides per eundem Spiritum: alii vero dona sanationum per eundem Spiritum: alii vero facul-tates potentiarum: alii vero Prophetia: alii vero discretiones spiri-tuum: alii vero genera linguarum: alii vero interpretatio lingua-rum. Sed omnia haec efficit unus ille & idem Spiritus, distribuens privatim unicuique sicut vult.
units.tr: Now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are differences of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God who worketh all in all. But to every man is given the manifestation of the Spirit to profit withal. For to one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge by the same Spirit; to another faith by the same Spirit; to another the gifts of healing by the same Spirit; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discerning of spirits; to another divers kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of tongues. But all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will.

units.la: Quemadmodum Deus bona sua, imo seipsum quoque totum, nobis gratuita liberalitate offert atque communicat: ita ut nos illis recte & pie utamur praecipit, neque ulla re perinde ut ingratitudine & donorum suorum abusu offenditur. Exempla, quae hoc probent, in omnibus historiis occurrunt, & quotidie multa fiunt, quae docent, eos plerunque & sibiipsis & aliis nocere, qui in illis suam potius libidinem quam Dei voluntatem sequuntur. Caeterum hic quam maxime elucet nostrae naturae pravitas, quae neq; beneficiorum Dei consideratione, neq; aliorum exemplis corrigi potest, quo minus hic multiuariam peccetur. Alii enim dona eius prorsus contemnunt, & imprimis quidem ea, quae ad animum excolendum faciunt. Alii tanquam propriis superbiunt, & non contenti Deum sua laude spoliauisse, simul illis ad proximi contemptu atque depressionem abutuntur. Rursus alii horum insolentia irritati aduersus Deum murmurant. Fit ergo, ut quae concordiae & pacis vinculu esse debebant, dissensiones & dissipationis Ecclesiae causa sint. Quod apud Corinthios factum fuisse, nuper audiuimus. Ideo Paulus hanc causam multis ac diligenter agit. Et initiū[?] statim docuit, omnis boni authorem in nobis esse Deum, nos autem nisi eius Spiritu innouemur atque regamur, ne linguam quidem in Christi laudes aut nominis sui confessionem posse soluere. Poterat hoc unum modestiam & gratitudinem iis suadere, qui serio gloriae Dei studio tanguntur. Sed quia multos diuersitas donorum & quæ in eorum distributione cernitur inæqualitas offendit, nunc de hac etiam disserit, vt demonstret, hanc non obstare, quo minus illa concordiæ & publicæ omnium ædificationi seruire debeant.
units.tr: As God offers and communicates his goods, indeed himself wholly, to us in free generosity, so he commands that we use them rightly and piously, and nothing offends God so much as ingratitude and the abuse of his gifts. Examples proving this occur in all histories, and every day many things happen that teach that those who in these gifts follow their own lust rather than the will of God mostly harm both themselves and others. Moreover here the wickedness of our nature shines forth most of all, which can be corrected neither by consideration of God's benefits nor by the examples of others, so that here sin is committed in many ways. For some utterly despise his gifts, especially those that serve to cultivate the mind. Others pride themselves as if they were their own, and not content to have stripped God of his praise, they at the same time abuse them for the contempt and depression of their neighbour. Again others, provoked by the insolence of these, murmur against God. So it comes about that what ought to have been bonds of concord and peace become the causes of dissensions and the scattering of the Church. That this happened among the Corinthians we heard recently. Therefore Paul pursues this cause at length and carefully. And at the outset he taught at once that the author of every good is God within us, and that unless we are renewed and ruled by his Spirit, we cannot even loosen our tongue to praise Christ or to confess his name. This one point could have persuaded those who are seriously moved by zeal for God's glory to modesty and gratitude. But because the diversity of gifts and the inequality seen in their distribution offend many, he now discusses this too, to show that it does not stand in the way of these gifts serving concord and the common edification of all.

units.la: Primò fatetur dona ista diuersa esse, & diuersitatem istam in genere exponit, dicens: Discrimina autem donorum sunt, sed idem Spiritus: & discrimina ministeriorum sunt, sed idem Dominus: & discrimina facultatum sunt, sed idem est Deus, qui efficit omnia in omnibus. Discrimina esse ait, partim quod ipsa dona non sunt eadem, neque eiusdem generis: partim quod non vni omnia, neque eadem omnibus dantur. Habent autem verba hæc non omnino obscuram præoccupationis speciem, qua illis respondet, qui de inæqualitate querebantur, & ita dicere videtur Apostolus: Scio ipse & fateor etiam quod obijcitis. Sed si discrimina donorum videtis, cur non simul illa omnia ex vno eodemque Spiritu manare animadvertitis? Si ministeria diuersa esse cernitis, cur non omnibus illis vni & eidem Domino seruiri obseruatis? Si denique facultatum discrimina vobis indigna videntur, cur non Dei virtutem agnoscitis, quæ sola in omnibus illis omnia efficit? Sed præstat singula, quæ hic dicuntur, inspicere.
