units.tr: First he admits that these gifts are diverse, and sets out this diversity in general terms, saying: "Now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are differences of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God who worketh all in all." He says there are diversities partly because the gifts themselves are not the same nor of the same kind, and partly because not all things are given to one person, nor the same things to all. These words have a not wholly obscure appearance of anticipation, by which he answers those who complained of inequality, and the Apostle seems to say: "I myself know and admit what you object. But if you see diversities of gifts, why do you not also notice that all of them flow from one and the same Spirit? If you see diverse ministries, why do you not observe that they all serve one and the same Lord? If finally the diversities of powers seem unworthy to you, why do you not acknowledge the power of God, which alone works all things in all of them?" But it is better to look at the individual points made here.

units.la: Vbi rursus primo loco author istorum omnium occurrit, in quo diuersis vocabulis siue nominibus vtitur. Nam primò Spiritum, deinde Dominum, postremò Deum nominat omnia in omnibus efficientem. Ex his mysterium Trinitatis quidam ex Patribus non male collegerunt. Nam Deum vnum esse constat, & nunquam non verissimum erit quod Moses dicit: Au-di Israël, Dominus Deus tuus, Deus vnus est. Et idem Paulus aperte hic fatetur, quando Deum esse ait, qui omnia in omnibus agat. Verumtamen idem hic personas euidentissime distinguit, dum Spiritum nominat, deinde Dominum, tertio Deum, Patrem nimirum intelligens: non quidem eo sensu, quod Spiritum & filium neget Deum esse, sed potius, vt omnia ad Deum illum vnum referre doceat, cuius vnitas in personis trinis consistit, inter quas nulla aliis vel minor est, vel dignitate inferior. Nam etsi inter illas distinguat, eandem tamen dignitatem & potentiam omnibus tribuit.
units.tr: Here again, first, the author meets us, using different names for all of these. For first he names the Spirit, then the Lord, last God, who works all in all. From these some of the Fathers rightly drew the mystery of the Trinity. For it is established that God is one, and what Moses says will always be most true: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord thy God is one God." And Paul likewise openly confesses this here, when he says that it is God who works all in all. Yet at the same time he most clearly distinguishes the persons, while he names the Spirit, then the Lord, and thirdly God, meaning the Father of course. He does this not in the sense that he denies that the Spirit and the Son are God, but rather to teach that all things are referred to that one God, whose unity consists in three persons, among whom none is lesser or inferior in dignity to the others. For although he distinguishes between them, he yet attributes the same dignity and power to all.

units.la: Est ergo hic nobis observandum discrimen inter religionem veram & falsam. Hæc in diuersitate illa donorum tam spiritualium quam corporalium, & eorundem diuersis effectus, non potest Deum vnum agnoscere, sed multis Diis opus esse arbitratur, & ideo non multos modo, verumetiam fere inter se dissidentes fingit. Sic olim gentes totam hanc mundi machinam, vt patrimonium quoddam, inter Saturni filios distribuerunt, Jouem quidem cæli & orbium cælestium, Plutonem terræ, Neptunum maris dominum constituentes, & istorum sororem Junoni, aerem addixerunt, eo quid hic omnibus illis simul inseruiat. Et rursus ne isti singuli in suis illis prouinciis nimium occuparentur, plures alios eis addiderunt, quorum alius igni, alius morbis, alii frugibus, alii rebus bellicis præessent: adeo vt nihil in rerum natura fuerit, quod non ab aliquo proprio Deo conseruari & regi fingerent. Quis enim omnes Deos Maiores, Minores, Medioxumos, Panes, Naiades, Dryades, Hamadryades, omnia denique fluuiorum, fontium, lucorum, vrbium numina enumeret? Nec tamen hoc satis fuit hominibus superstitiosis, nisi Deos quoque inter se am-bitiosè diffidentes atque pugnantes fingerent. Poetæ equidem Junonem, Venerem & Palladem sub iudice Paride de forma contendentes describunt. Homerus Deos è cœlis in castra & ad arma vocat, & hos quidem pro Troianis, illos verò pro Græcis dimicantes inducit. Vergilius Neptunum Æolo iratum fingit, quod ipso inscio maria ventis turbauisset: & idem Junoni perpetuam cum Venere litem tribuit, dum hæc Æneam seruare & imperio donare, illa verò eundem perdere studet. Ridicula hæc sunt, obseruatu tamen digna, vt videamus nihil à religione tam alienum esse, quàm Deorum multitudinem statuere: quia vt primùm hæc admittitur, confusio illa & ambitiosæ concertationes non possunt euitari. Quapropter non aliud certius falsæ religionis argumentum est, quàm si mundi huius gubernatio non ad vnum Deum refertur, sed in plures distribuitur. Quod cum in Papatu quoque fiat, vnum hoc nos abunde docet, quid de illo iudicare debeamus. Etenim vera religio vnum Deum in adorando & sacrosancto Trinitatis mysterio agnoscit, Patrem, Filium & Spiritum Sanctum, qui vt omnium creator est, sic omnia gubernat & seruat, omnia denique agit in omnibus, cùm in ipso viuamus, moueamur & simus. Et qua is natura atque essentia vnus est: sic vna quoque sibique perpetuò constans illius voluntas est, quam per Verbum suum in Scripturis manifestauit, vna quoque & perpetua est cultus diuini totiusque gubernationis Ecclesiasticae ratio siue forma, quam idem ille nobis praescripsit.
units.tr: Here then we must observe the distinction between true and false religion. The latter, in that diversity of gifts, both spiritual and bodily, and their diverse effects, cannot acknowledge one God, but thinks that many gods are needed, and so it feigns not only many but almost mutually discordant ones. Thus of old the nations divided this whole machine of the world, as a sort of patrimony, among the sons of Saturn, appointing Jove to rule heaven and the heavenly spheres, Pluto the earth, Neptune the lord of the sea, and assigning their sister Juno the air, so that what is here serves all of them together. And again, lest these individuals be too busy in their own provinces, they added many others to them, of whom one presided over fire, another over diseases, others over crops, others over warfare; so that there was nothing in nature which they did not imagine to be preserved and ruled by some particular god. For who could list all the gods: the Greater, the Lesser, the Middling, the Fauns, Pans, Naiads, Dryads, Hamadryads, in short all the divinities of rivers, springs, groves and cities? Nor was even this enough for superstitious men, unless they also imagined gods ambitiously at odds and fighting among themselves. The poets indeed describe Juno, Venus and Pallas contending about beauty under the judgment of Paris. Homer calls the gods from heaven to camp and to arms, and brings in some fighting for the Trojans, others for the Greeks. Virgil imagines Neptune angry with Aeolus because he had, without his knowledge, stirred the seas with winds; and he assigns to Juno a perpetual quarrel with Venus, since the one strives to save Aeneas and grant him empire, the other to destroy him. These things are ridiculous, yet worth noting, so that we may see that nothing is so alien to religion as positing a multitude of gods; for as soon as this is admitted, that confusion and ambitious strife cannot be avoided. Therefore there is no surer sign of false religion than when the governance of this world is not referred to one God, but is divided among many. Since this also happens in Papacy, this one thing teaches us abundantly what we ought to judge of it. For true religion acknowledges one God in worship and in the sacred mystery of the Trinity: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, who as creator of all, so also governs and preserves all, and finally works all in all, since in him we live, move and have our being. And as he is one in nature and essence, so also his will is one and constantly the same, which he has manifested through his Word in the Scriptures; one and constant too is the manner or form of divine worship and of the whole ecclesiastical government, which he himself has prescribed to us.

units.la: Quoad ergo praesentis loci argumentum, ista consideratio plurimum facit ad seruandam Ecclesiae concordiam. Quia enim vnus Deus omnium donorum author est, vnus omnium in Ecclesia ministeriorum siue functionum dominus, vna omnium facultatum siue effectorum causa efficiens, quis non intelligat, omnium facultates atque studia ad vnum eundemque scopum dirigi aut collimari debere? Quamobrem ex diuersitate illa donorum non dissensionis materia peti debet, sed potius consensus studium accendi, vt singuli quod habent ad publicam communis Ecclesiae salutem conferant. Exempla, quibus istud docemur, in natura rerum & ijs etiam, quae humana industria fiunt, plurima habentur. Nam si tellurem inspicias, quàm multa plantarum genera in eodem horto reperies, quae cùm colore, odore, forma, altitudine multum inter se differant, adeò tamen nullam confusionem pariunt; vt potius hortum totum varietate ista mirifica, quasi veste varia exornent, & amoeniorem reddant. Similiter quanta est inter voces Musicae differentia, quàm multiplex in instrumentis Musicis chordarum diuersitas, quam varium in tubis atque tibijs sonorum discrimen? At si ista omnia recte gubernentur, admirabili symphonia siue concentu aures demulcent; & licet vox alia altius assurgat, alia submissius feratur, haec tardiori quasi passu cunctetur, illa volubili quadam celeritate varietur, vnum tamen concentum eumque suauissimum efficiunt. Quae ergo insania est, ex vnius Dei donis diuersis dissensionum materiam petere, aut Deum, qui vnitatis atque concordiae verus author est, talem fingere, qui diuersitate ista Ecclesiam scindere aut inter homines contentionum semina spargere cupiat? Discant ergo singuli, non solum quid ipsis datum sit videre, verumetiam aliorum dona obseruent, & omnium istorum donorum vnum esse cogitent: & mox sentient, omnium idem studium, studiorum omnium eundem scopum esse debere. Est hoc ad deprimendas superbiae cristas efficacissimum argumentum. Cur enim aduersus alios insolentius efferatur, qui & se nihil ex seipso habere sentit, & alios quosque homines Deo non minus cordi esse videt? Eadem consideratio simul in officio nos continet; ne cui inuideamus, quae ipsi à Deo data sunt, neque impatientius feramus nostram tenuitatem. Nam licet non eadem mensura omnibus dona sua Deus distribuat, neminem tamen idem ille praeterit, quin vnicuique det, quod ad salutem consequendam & ad obeundam functionem, quam sustinet, potest sufficere. Placent sibi ipsis mirificè qui à magnis Regibus munera honoraria accipiunt, & eam sibi gloriam praecipuam esse putant, quod ab his digni iudicentur, qui ipsorum liberalitate ornari merentur. Quanto autem excellentior gloria est, hominem miserum & mortalem diuinis atque spiritualibus donis à Deo donari, qui vt iustus, sic etiam sapientissimus est, vt indicio suo falli non possit? Certè qui hoc vnum non oscitanter expendunt, ij mox videbunt, se adeò nullam habere de sua tenuitate quaerendi occasionem, vt potius gratijs digne agendis non possint sufficere: neque iam alijs plura illa & excellentiora dona inuidebunt, sed potius illud Christi in mentem reuocabunt: Omni habenti dabitur, ab eo autem qui non habet, etiam quod habet auferetur. Itaque toti in eo erunt, vt suo dono quantulocunque bene vtantur: quae vnica & facillima est ratio, qua Dei dona in nobis augeri solent.
units.tr: As to the argument of the present passage, this consideration contributes greatly to preserving the concord of the Church. For since one God is the author of all gifts, one Lord of all ministries or functions in the Church, one efficient cause of all powers or effects, who would not understand that the abilities and endeavours of all must be directed or aimed at one and the same goal? Therefore from this diversity of gifts the matter of dissension must not be sought, but rather the zeal for agreement must be kindled, so that each contributes what he has to the public salvation of the common Church. There are many examples in nature, and in those things also which are done by human industry, by which we are taught this. For if you look at the earth, how many kinds of plants you will find in the same garden, which, though they differ much among themselves in colour, smell, shape and height, yet produce no confusion at all; rather they adorn the whole garden with that wonderful variety, as with a varied robe, and make it more pleasant. Similarly how great is the difference between musical voices, how manifold the diversity of strings in musical instruments, how varied the distinction of sounds in trumpets and flutes! But if all these are rightly governed, they soothe the ears with a wonderful harmony or concert; and although one voice rises higher, another is carried more softly, this one lingers as if at a slower pace, that one varies with a certain rapid fluency, yet they make one concert, and a most sweet one. What madness is it, then, to seek the material of dissensions in the diverse gifts of the one God, or to imagine God, the true author of unity and concord, as one who would wish to split the Church by this diversity or to scatter the seeds of strife among men? Let each therefore learn not only to see what has been given to himself, but also to observe the gifts of others, and to think that all these gifts are one; and soon they will feel that all have the same zeal and that all zeal ought to have the same goal. This is a most effective argument for bringing down the crests of pride. For why should someone be puffed up more insolently against others, when he feels that he has nothing of himself, and sees that all other men are no less dear to God? The same consideration at once keeps us in our duty: that we should not envy anyone what God has given to them, nor bear our own meagreness with too much impatience. For although God does not distribute his gifts in the same measure to all, yet he passes over no one without giving each what can suffice for attaining salvation and for performing the office he undertakes. Those who receive honorary gifts from great kings are wonderfully pleased with themselves, and think it a chief glory that they are judged worthy by them, to be adorned by their generosity. But how much more excellent is the glory of a wretched and mortal man being endowed by God with divine and spiritual gifts, who is as just as he is most wise, so that he cannot be deceived in his judgment? Certainly those who weigh this one thing with care will soon see that they have so little occasion to boast of their meagreness that they cannot even suffice for giving thanks worthily; nor will they now envy others those many and more excellent gifts, but rather they will call to mind that saying of Christ: "To him that hath shall be given, and from him that hath not, even that he hath shall be taken away." So they will all devote themselves to using well whatever small gift they have; and this is the only and easiest way by which God's gifts are wont to be increased in us.

units.la: Sed videamus etiam, quod alterum huius loci caput est, quibus nominibus dona illa Apostolus describat, de quibus hic agitur. Primùm χαρίσματα dicit, vt gratuita Dei misericordia & liberalitate ea nobis conferri ostendat. Eo autem nomine sapientiam, scientiam, prophetiam, linguarum cognitionem & alia comprehendit, quae postea ex ordine enumerabuntur. Commendatur autem hoc loco Dei bonitas atque fides plane paterna, qui Ecclesiam suam ab initio statim donis necessarijs atque mirificis instruere voluit, vt scandalo mederetur, quod ex illius contemptibili specie aut lenibus principijs nasceretur. Faciunt huc quae de Apostolis & primitiva Ecclesia in Actorum libro scribuntur. Etenim res ridicula & absurda videri poterat, IESVM hunc Dei Filium & humani generis redemptorem dicere, quem ante dies quinquaginta omnes in cruce mori viderant, & cuius resurrectionis nullis idoneis testibus (si mundi iudicio causam examines) probabatur, negabatur autem a militibus, quibus contradicere non erat tutum. Huic igitur scandalo remedium adhibuit Deus, linguarum donum, solidam item Scripturae veteris cognitionem, atque miracula: quae ipsos etiam sacerdotes & Seniores perplexos fecerunt, quando ista in illis cernebant, quos ab ineunte aetate homines idiotas & illiteratos fuisse constabat. Similiter odio & excidio digna videri poterat tota illa credentium multitudo, qui primi Christo nomen dederant, & procul dubio armis praesidium subito oppressa fuisset (quod illo tempore multis accidisse scimus, qui impostores & pseudoprophetas secuti in locis desertis confluebant) nisi illos authoritate singulari Deus armauisset, adeo ut in ipso templo possent turò versari, & ita formidabiles esse ut nemo aliorum se illis coniungere auderet. Quam multa autem fuerunt, quae Ecclesiae exitium minabantur, & quae effugere nunquam potuissent, nisi aliquos prophetico Spiritu donasset Deus, qui Ecclesiam de insidiis hostium, de periculis, de famae futura admonebant: qualem Agabum fuisse legimus & alios, qui Antiochiae eodem dono excelluerunt. Et huius generis exempla in historijs Ecclesiasticis passim habentur, nec desunt nostro saeculo, quae Ecclesiam Deo non minus curae esse docent, quando inter medios hostes tuto degit, aut insidias sibi structas admirabili industria eludit, denique sub crucis vexillo perpetuos quasi triumphos agit de hostibus suis. Ex his ergo consolationem petamus publice & privatim, ne vel de Ecclesiae salute dubitemus, vel segniores simus in iis obeundis, ad quae nos Dominus vocat. Qui enim nos negotiis magnis destinat, idem donis quoque instruet ad illa necessaria. Nec est, quod aliquem sua terreat indignitas: quia enim χαρισματα sunt, non quid ipsi mereamur videt Dominus, sed quibus opus sit nobis, per quos aliquid effectum dare vult. Id vero nos simul oficij admonere debet, ne quod meritum hic statuamus, & propria dignitati fiducia elati aduersus Deum aut homines superbiamus. Et debet hoc ad omnia extendi, quaecunque vel in animo vel in corpore, aut etiam reliquis fortunis, eximia & praeclara habemus. Quid enim ex omnibus his nostrum dicere possumus, qui nudi ex utero matris nascimur, nec quicquam proprium in hanc lucem afferimus, praeter naturae totius vitiositatem, quae ex Adamo in nos omnes est propagata? Recte ergo supra dictum fuit ab Apostolo: Quid habes, quod non accepisti? Quod si accepisti, quid gloriaris, ac si non acceperis? Admoneat ergo nos χαρισματων, id est donorum gratuitorum vocabulum, ut modestia studeamus, & Deo grati simus, deque vero potius donorum omnium usu, quam nostra gloria cogitemus.
units.tr: But let us also consider the second point of this passage: by what names the Apostle describes the gifts he is discussing here. First he calls them charismata [χαρίσματα], to show that they are given to us by God's free mercy and generosity. Under this name he includes wisdom, knowledge, prophecy, the knowledge of tongues and the others, which he will list in order afterwards. In this place God's goodness is also commended, together with a truly fatherly faithfulness, since he willed from the very beginning to equip his Church with necessary and wonderful gifts, to remedy the scandal that might arise from its contemptible appearance or its humble beginnings. What is written in the Acts of the Apostles about the Apostles and the primitive Church bears on this. For it could seem a ridiculous and absurd thing to call this Jesus the Son of God and redeemer of the human race, whom all had seen die on the cross fifty days before, and whose resurrection was attested by no reliable witnesses (if you judge the case by the verdict of the world), and was denied by the soldiers, whom it was not safe to contradict. God therefore applied a remedy to this scandal: the gift of tongues, likewise a solid knowledge of the Old Scripture, and miracles. These astonished even the priests and elders, when they saw such things in men whom everyone knew to have been uneducated and illiterate from early youth. In the same way the whole multitude of believers, who had first given their names to Christ, might have seemed worthy of hatred and destruction, and would undoubtedly have been suddenly crushed by force of arms (as we know happened to many at that time who followed impostors and false prophets and gathered in deserted places), unless God had armed them with a singular authority, so that they could move about in the temple itself and were so formidable that no one else dared to join them. How many were the dangers that threatened the ruin of the Church, and which could never have been escaped unless God had endowed some men with the prophetic Spirit, who warned the Church of the snares and perils of its enemies and of future famine! We read that Agabus was such a man, and others who excelled in the same gift at Antioch. Examples of this kind are found everywhere in the ecclesiastical histories, and they are not lacking in our own age; these show that the Church is no less a concern to God, when it lives safely in the midst of enemies, or cleverly evades the snares laid for it, or finally, under the banner of the cross, wins what are almost continual triumphs over its foes. Let us therefore draw consolation from this, both publicly and privately, so that we neither doubt the salvation of the Church nor become slack in performing the tasks to which the Lord calls us. For he who appoints us to great undertakings will also equip us with the gifts necessary for them. Nor should anyone be frightened by his own unworthiness: since they are charismata [χαρίσματα], the Lord does not look at what we deserve, but at what we need, and through whom he wishes something to be accomplished. This ought at the same time to remind us of our duty, that we should not set up any merit here, nor, puffed up by confidence in our own dignity, grow proud against God or men. And this should be extended to everything that we have as outstanding and distinguished, whether in mind or body, or even in other fortunes. For what of all these things can we call our own? We are born naked from our mother's womb, and bring nothing of our own into this light, except the corruption of the whole of nature, which has been propagated from Adam to us all. Rightly, then, the Apostle said above: "What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast, as if you had not received it?" Let the word charismata [χαρίσματα], that is, free gifts, admonish us to cultivate modesty, to be grateful to God, and to think about the true use of all gifts rather than our own glory.

units.la: Secundo loco discrimina ministeriorum Paulus numerat: quo nomine functiones ecclesiasticas intelligit, quas non eiusdem generis esse alibi ostendit, ubi alios quidem Apostolos, alios vero Evangelistas, alios autem Prophetas, alios doctores aut Pastores fieri scribit. Omnium vero istorum functionum, & quaecunque aliae sunt eius generis, ministeriorum voce comprehendit, quia per illas Deo & Ecclesiae servitur: quod in epistola ad Ephesios clarius explicat. Nam cum functiones istas ex ordine recensuisset, eas institutas ait ad coagmentationem sanctorum, ad opus ministerii, ad aedificationem corporis Christi, &c. Rursus vero hoc solum sufficere poterat, ne quis vel insolentius efferatur, aut aliis suam conditionem invideat. Si enim ministeria sunt gradus isti omnes, quos in Ecclesia sua Deus instituit, ministri & servi sint oportet, quicunque in illis sunt constituti. At quid turpius est, quam servum insolentiorem esse, & adversus domesticos aut conservos suos superbire? Intolerabilia certe bonis & cordatis omnibus videntur esse servorum imperia, & eadem multis regnis exitium peperisse, historiae testantur. Rursus quam stulti sunt, qui alicui suum in Ecclesia gradum invident, cum hunc ille retinere non possit, nisi & tibi & mihi, omnibus denique serviat, qui Ecclesiae Christi membra sunt? Debent autem huius probe meminisse omnes, quibus gubernacula Ecclesiae credita sunt, ne ex ministerio suo dominium sive imperium faciant. Quia enim illa Christi haereditas sive κληρος est (quo nomine Petrus quoque eam appellat) nemo absque scelere eius dominium sibi vendicare poteris. Et qui illud audent, mali illi atque perfidi coloni sunt, qui (ut in parabola Christus admonet) ipsum occisum volunt, ut hæreditatem & possessionem vineæ possint sibi vendica-re. Quod vero de Ecclesiæ ministris dicitur, id etiam ad se pertinere sciant viri principes, qui Reipub. gubernant. Nam licet illos authoritate & potentia Deus armaverit, ijdem tamen (ut ad Romanos Paulus docet) ministri Dei sunt: ministerium vero eorum in eo consistit, ut populi pastores agant, quorum cura atque studio ille conservetur. Est hæc illorum gloria præcipua, quia seipsos spoliant, quicunque sibi tale ius & imperium usurpant, ut omnia sibi licere existiment, & nunquam non tyrannicum illud in ore habeant: Sic volo, sic iubeo, sit pro ratione voluntas. Quid enim in illis reliquum manet, cuius nomine coli & observari mereantur, si Dei servi & pacis sive salutis publicæ ministri esse nolunt?
units.tr: In the second place Paul enumerates the differences of ministries, by which name he understands ecclesiastical offices. He shows elsewhere that these are not all of the same kind, since he writes that some are made apostles, others evangelists, others prophets, others teachers or pastors. He comprehends all these offices, and whatever others are of the same kind, under the word ministries, because through them God and the Church are served; he explains this more clearly in the Epistle to the Ephesians. For after listing these offices in order, he says that they were instituted for the building up of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edification of the body of Christ, and so on. Again, this alone could be enough to stop anyone from becoming too arrogant, or from envying others their position. For if these ministries are all the grades that God has established in his Church, then whoever is placed in them must be ministers and servants. But what is more shameful than for a servant to be too insolent and to lord it over his fellow household members or fellow servants? The histories certainly testify that the commands of servants seem intolerable to all good and sensible people, and that the same has brought ruin to many kingdoms. Again, how foolish are those who envy someone else his rank in the Church, since he cannot keep it unless he also serves you and me, indeed all who are members of Christ's Church! All those to whom the government of the Church has been entrusted ought to remember this well, so that they do not turn their ministry into lordship or dominion. For since that inheritance of Christ is a klēros [κληρος] (a name by which Peter also calls it), no one can claim its dominion for himself without sin. And those who dare to do so are those wicked and faithless tenants who, as Christ warns in the parable, wish to kill him so that they may claim the inheritance and possession of the vineyard for themselves. What is said of the ministers of the Church, let the princes who govern the commonwealth also know to apply to themselves. For although God has armed them with authority and power, they are nonetheless (as Paul teaches to the Romans) ministers of God; their ministry consists in this, that they act as shepherds of the people, whose safety and welfare they should preserve by their care and diligence. This is their chief glory. Those who claim for themselves such a right and power, so that they think everything is allowed to them and always have that tyrannical saying on their lips, "Thus I wish, thus I command, let my will stand in place of reason," strip themselves of this glory. For what remains in them by which they could deserve to be honoured and obeyed, if they are unwilling to be servants of God and ministers of peace and public welfare?

units.la: Cæterum quoad Ecclesiæ gubernationem, observabis eum donis ministeria coniungi. Ut ergo donorum usus circa ministerium versatur, ut sic illorum fructus ad multos alios redundet: ita cavendum est, ne quod ministerium temere alicui credatur, nisi quem donis ad illud necessarijs satis instructum esse constet. Si enim in familia bene constituta non cuique servulo quodlibet officium committitur, sed industriæ, ingenij & virium corporis diligens ratio habetur: quanto magis hoc in Dei familia observari debet, ubi de publica & privata plurimorum salute agitur? Viderunt hoc Apostoli & primitiuæ Ecclesiæ fideles, qui in ministrorum ordinatione precibus ac ieiunijs vacabant, etiamsi eorum qui ordinari debebant probitas atque fides omnibus abunde perspecta esset. Quod si hodie etiam observaretur, Ecclesias melius constitutas haberemus, & maiori cum fructu Verbum Dei prædicaretur.
units.tr: Moreover, as regards the government of the Church, you will observe that Paul joins ministries to gifts. Just as the use of the gifts is directed to the ministry, so that their fruit may overflow to many others, so care must be taken that no ministry is entrusted to anyone carelessly, unless he is known to be sufficiently equipped with the gifts necessary for it. For in a well-ordered household, the task is not assigned to any servant at random, but a careful account is taken of his diligence, his ability and the strength of his body. How much more should this be observed in God's household, where the public and private welfare of very many people is at stake! The Apostles and the faithful of the primitive Church saw this, and they devoted themselves to prayers and fasting in the ordination of ministers, even when the honesty and faith of those who were to be ordained were already fully known to all. If this were still observed today, we would have better organised churches, and the Word of God would be preached with greater fruit.

units.la: Admonet præterea locus iste neminem debere alienam functionem temere invadere: Quia enim ministeriorum discrimina sunt, unusquisque suo se pede metiatur, & Spartam suam ex-ornet. Nam nisi functionum discrimina retineantur, ipsius Dei ordo turbatur, & res tandem in tyrannidem erumpit, aut saltem in ἀναρχίαν [?], sive confusam quidem audendi licentiam, quæ omni tyrannide est nocentior. Etenim quantum mali hæc pariat in Reipub. nemo ignorat. In Ecclesia autem eo gravius est periculum, quod cum fortunis totus homo, quoad corpus & animam, periclitatur. Quod si vero ad hunc locum Ecclesiæ Papisticæ constitutionem examines, quantum Deus bone, quamque horribilem rerum omnium confusionem atque licentiam reperies. Ministeriorum quidem titulis adeo gloriantur, ut ipse etiam Pontifex Maximus Seruus feruorum velit dici: qui tamen aliorum humeris sublimis gestatur corona triplici redimitus, qua triplex imperium in cœlos, terram atque inferos ostentat. Neque eo contentus, Reges quoque potentissimos ad pedum suorum oscula inuitat, & si quos ad obsequium hoc contumaciores esse videt, eos anathematis fulmine percussos pedibus quoque impuris conculcat. Nec multo modestiores sunt, qui ab illo dignitatibus ecclesiasticis exornantur. Quod si ministeria ipsorum consideres, præter vetera illa, quorum supra ex Paulo meminimus, alia in-numera illi confinxerunt. Sunt enim inter eos Ostiarij, Acoluthi, Exorcistæ, Suffraganei, Decani, Archipresbyteri, Confessores, Cantores, Diaconi, Archidiaconi, Subdiaconi, Presbyteri, Sacellani, & nescio qui alij sexcenti, quorum nomina recensere longum foret. Et quamvis ministeria hæc inter se distincta esse ipsi quoque fateantur, in ijsdem tamen admirabilis confusio cernitur: quando non raro unus aliquis in ecclesijs procul distitis diuersas functiones, aut potius inanes diuersarum functionum titulos sustinet, & in hac quidem Ecclesia Præpositum, in illa Decanum, alibi vero Archidiaconum, & rursus alibi alium gradum dignitatis occupat. Cum autem omnium locorum Ecclesiæ unicam illam constituant, quam ideo Catholicam dicimus, quis obsecro dicere poterit, illos discrimina hæc ministeriorum observare, de quibus hoc loco Paulus loquitur?
units.tr: This passage also warns that no one should rashly usurp another's office. Since the ministries are distinct, each person should measure himself by his own foot and adorn his own Sparta. If the distinctions between functions are not maintained, God's own order is thrown into confusion, and affairs finally break out into tyranny, or at least into anarchy [ἀναρχία], that is, a disordered license to dare anything, which is more harmful than any tyranny. Nobody is unaware how much evil this produces in the commonwealth. In the Church the danger is greater still, since the whole person, body and soul, is endangered along with his fortunes. If you examine the constitution of the Papistical Church on this point, good God, what a horrible confusion and license of every kind you will find! They glory so much in the titles of ministries that the Supreme Pontiff himself wishes to be called "servant of servants," yet he is carried high on the shoulders of others, crowned with a triple crown, which displays a threefold rule over heaven, earth and hell. Not content with this, he invites the most powerful kings to kiss his feet, and if he sees any who are too stubborn in this obedience, he strikes them with the thunderbolt of anathema and tramples them under his unclean feet. Those who are adorned by him with ecclesiastical dignities are not much more modest. If you consider their ministries, besides those ancient ones of which we have spoken above from Paul, they have invented countless others. Among them are doorkeepers, acolytes, exorcists, suffragans, deans, archpriests, confessors, cantors, deacons, archdeacons, subdeacons, presbyters, chaplains, and I know not how many other hundreds, whose names would be too long to list. And although they themselves admit that these ministries are distinct from one another, an astonishing confusion is seen in them, since not rarely one and the same man, in churches far apart, holds diverse functions, or rather the empty titles of diverse functions: in this church he is provost, in that one dean, elsewhere archdeacon, and again elsewhere he holds another grade of dignity. Yet since these churches of every place make up that one church which we therefore call Catholic, who, I beg you, can say that they observe those distinctions of ministries of which Paul speaks in this place?

units.la: Tertium vero duobus istis addit, discrimina facultatum. In Graeco χαρισμάτα [?] ponitur, quæ vox internam illam Spiritus Sancti virtutem denotat, quæ ministros ad functiones suas aptos atque idoneos reddit, imo quæ in illis agit, ut quod in mandatis habent, fideliter & magno cum successu perficiant. Et quia hanc quoque isto loco numerat, ubi de donis Dei Spiritualibus disserit, quæ ad Ecclesiæ gubernationem necessaria sunt, non obscure docet, illam quoque non nostri iuris aut arbitrij esse, sed totam ex Dei arbitrio pendere. Facit huius consideratio multum ad deprimendum confidentiae cristas. Nam etiamsi in Ecclesia locum honoratiorem obtineas, & donis necessarijs instructus sis, nihil tamen proficies, nisi diuina illa Spiritus Sancti vis accedat, quae ministerium tuum efficax reddat. Non est enim aliquid qui plantat vel rigat, nisi Deus incrementum dederit. Et nisi Dominus aedificauerit domum, nequicquam fatigantur quotquot eam augere volent. Itaque si quid per nos recte & cum laude fiat, gloriam hanc omnem Deo tribuamus, qui nobis Spiritus sui [?]ἐνεργήματα dedit, ut ministerium nostrum efficax esset.
units.tr: Paul adds a third distinction to these two, that of gifts [χαρίσματα]. The Greek term is charismata, a word which denotes that inner power of the Holy Spirit which makes ministers apt and fit for their functions, indeed which works in them so that they carry out faithfully and with great success what they have been entrusted to do. Since he counts this among the spiritual gifts of God, which are necessary for the government of the Church, when he discusses them, he clearly teaches that this too is not subject to our right or choice, but depends entirely on the will of God. Considering this greatly helps to lower the crest of self-confidence. For even if you hold a more honourable place in the Church and are equipped with the necessary gifts, you will accomplish nothing unless that divine power of the Holy Spirit is added, which makes your ministry effective. For "neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth, but God that giveth the increase," and "unless the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it." Therefore, if anything is done rightly and commendably through us, let us ascribe all this glory to God, who has given us the workings [ἐνεργήματα] of his Spirit so that our ministry might be effective.

units.la: Seruiat hoc quoque consolationi, ne temere offendamur, si quando vel nosipsos vel alios in Ecclesiae ministerio minus videamus proficere. Quid enim nos aliud quam laborem & industriam nostram conferre possumus, ita nos mouente & agente Dei Spiritu, sine quo ne illud quidem possumus? Sufficiat ergo hic nobis, si de nostra fide & industria nobis bene confcissimus [?], euentum vero omnem Deo permittamus, qui labores nostros & studia ad eum, quem ipse sibi proposuit, scopum diriget. Nam etsi nullus, aut perquam exiguus nostri studii fructus sequatur, non tamen primi fumus, quibus hoc accidit, sed fors ista nobis cum sanctissimis Dei Seruis, Prophetis atque Apostolis, communis est: quos non semel de auditorum suorum vel contumacia vel etiam paucitate conquestos fuisse legimus. Quid autem de illis dico, quando tam paucos fuisse constat, qui Christo docenti crediderint, cum ut doctrinam suam miraculis infinitis confirmaret? Debebant istorum meminisse, qui hodie de Euangelii doctrina ex auditorum moribus iudicant, imo illam aperte damnant, quod non omnes ab erroribus superstitionum & scelerum licentia conuertantur. Objiciunt hoc nobis multi, qui & ipsi nulla siue religionis siue poenitentiae cura tanguntur: & imprimis hic sibi ipsis applaudunt Anabaptistae, & eo argumento doctrinam nostram omnem erroris convinci posse putant, quod paucissimi ab ea discedant meliores. Quos omnes nos ad Christum & Prophetas atque Apostolos remittimus, ut cum illis disceptent, priusquam nobis litem moueant.
units.tr: This also serves for consolation, so that we are not rashly offended if at any time we see either ourselves or others making little progress in the ministry of the Church. For what else can we contribute than our labour and diligence, when we are moved and driven by the Spirit of God, without whom we cannot even do that? It is enough for us, therefore, if we are conscious of our faith and diligence, and we leave the outcome entirely to God, who directs our labours and efforts to the goal which he has set for himself. For even if no fruit, or very little fruit, of our effort follows, we are not the first to whom this has happened. This misfortune is shared with the most holy servants of God, the prophets and apostles, who, as we read, more than once complained of the obstinacy or even the small number of their hearers. But why do I speak of them, when it is well established that so few believed Christ teaching, even though he confirmed his doctrine with countless miracles? Those who today judge the doctrine of the Gospel by the morals of its hearers ought to remember these examples, indeed openly condemn it because not all are converted from the errors of superstition and from licentious living. Many people object this to us, who themselves are not moved by any care either for religion or for repentance. Above all the Anabaptists congratulate themselves on this, and they think that all our doctrine can be convicted of error by this argument, that very few of its adherents turn out better. We send all of them back to Christ and the prophets and apostles, so that they may dispute with them before they bring their quarrel against us.

units.la: Porro finem tam donorum quam ministeriorum atque facultatum omnium Paulus subiicit, dicens: Unicuique vero datur declaratio Spiritus ad utilitatem. Habent haec aliquam praeoccupationis speciem, quae illis occurrit, qui sua dona minoris faciunt, eo quod se pauciori-bus instructos esse vident. Cur enim contemnatur, quod certo Dei consilio in usum bonum atque utilem nobis datum esse audimus, quantulumcunque illud sit? Vocat autem declarationem seu manifestationem Spiritus ipsa dona & horum effectus, eo quod qui in cordibus credentium habitat Spiritus Sanctus, per illa sese exerit, ut aliis quoque hominibus eius gratia siue virtus innotescat. Nec enim otiatur ille, aut ignauus quiescit, sed effectis diuinam eius virtutem referentibus sese declarat. Unde colligimus, Spiritu Christi omnino destitutos esse omnes eos, qui vitam vi-uunt impuram & ab ijs studijs alienam, quae nobis ille in Scripturis praecipit. Loquitur autem Apostolus de publica utilitate, quae in Ecclesiae augmento siue aedificatione habetur, de qua supra ex Epistola ad Ephesios diximus. Non potest ea consistere nisi paci & concordiae publicae omnes studeant: & hic maxime locum habet, quod historicus ille Romanus olim dixit: Concordia parvae res crescunt, discordia magnae dilabuntur. Unde sequitur, eos Dei donis turpissime, & non sine sacrilegio abuti, qui illa insolenter ostentando authores sunt, ut Ecclesia in partes aut sectas scindatur. Semper ergo hic nobis scopus propositus sit, ut quaecunque nobis a Deo data sunt dona, non nobis solis data esse cogitemus, & proinde illa in eum finem dirigamus, ut multi alii per nos lucrifiant, & Ecclesia nouis quotidie augmentis crescat.
units.tr: Furthermore, Paul states the purpose of all gifts, ministries and faculties, saying: "But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal." These words have a certain appearance of an objection which comes to mind for those who think little of their own gifts because they see themselves equipped with fewer than others. For why should we despise what we hear has been given to us for a good and useful purpose by the certain counsel of God, however small it may be? He calls the gifts themselves and their effects the declaration or manifestation of the Spirit, because the Holy Spirit, who dwells in the hearts of believers, shows himself through them, so that his grace or power also becomes known to other people. For he is not idle or lies inactive, but declares himself through effects which reflect his divine power. From this we gather that all those are wholly destitute of the Spirit of Christ who live an impure life, alien from those pursuits which he commands us in the Scriptures. The Apostle, moreover, speaks of the public usefulness which is found in the increase or building up of the Church, of which we spoke above from the Epistle to the Ephesians. This cannot exist unless everyone strives for public peace and concord, and what that Roman historian once said applies here most of all: "By concord small things grow great, by discord great things fall to ruin." It follows that those who ostentatiously display gifts and so become the authors of a division of the Church into parties or sects abuse God's gifts most shamefully and not without sacrilege. Let this always be our aim, then: to consider that whatever gifts God has given us have not been given to us alone, and so to direct them to that end, that many others may gain through us and the Church may grow daily with new increases.

units.la: Pergit autem Paulus et dona illa Spiritualia quasi per partes enumeratione exponit: non quidem omnia, sed quae potissima & Ecclesiae prae aliis necessaria sunt, in quibus etiam a Corinthiis maxime peccabatur aemulatione atque contentionibus. Sic enim ait: Nam huic quidem per Spiritum datur sermo sapientiae, alii vero sermo cognitionis per eundem Spiritum, &c. Repetit subinde Spiritum omnium illorum datorem, quia quod hunc minus respi-cerent Corinthii, illis hucusq; ad ostentationem cum multorum contemptu atq; scandalo abusi fuerant.
units.tr: Paul goes on to set out those spiritual gifts by enumeration, as it were part by part. He does not give all of them, but those which are chief and more necessary for the Church than others, and in which the Corinthians especially sinned through emulation and contentions. For he says: "For to one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge by the same Spirit," and so on. He repeatedly names the Spirit as the giver of all those things, because the Corinthians had paid less attention to him, and until now they had abused those gifts for ostentation, to the contempt and scandal of many.

units.la: Primo autem loco sermonem sapientiæ ponit phrasi Hebraica, pro ipsa sapientia: secundo sermonem scientiæ siue cognitionis. Quæ duo etsi idem significare videantur, differunt tamen inter se. Scientia enim circa rerum scitu necessariarum cognitionem versatur: Sapientia vero earundem vsum quoq; comprehendit, & docet vt illas vtiliter ad suum scopum siue finem dirigere debeamus. Neq; semper in omnibus duæ istæ dotes ingenij coniunctæ sunt. Vt enim Hannibalem vincere quidem posse dicebat quidam, nescire autem victoria vti: ita multos esse videre, qui rerum scientia & cognitione præclara præditi sunt, qui tamen iudicio destituuntur, & ijs etiam ad aliorum ædificationem & Ecclesiæ vtilitatem nesciunt vti, quæ probè intelligunt. Est ergo vtrunq; donum Ecclesiæ necessarium, eò quod Regnum Dei non in sermone consistit, sed in virtute. Et admonet hoc sciolos, ne rerum scientia superbiant, sed ijs locum dent, quos rerum vsu & prudentia magis instructos esse vident.
units.tr: The first place he gives to "the word of wisdom," using a Hebrew idiom for wisdom itself; the second is "the word of knowledge," or understanding. Although these two may seem to mean the same thing, they differ. Knowledge is concerned with the understanding of things that must be known, but wisdom also includes the use of them, and teaches us how to direct them usefully to their proper goal or end. Nor are these two gifts of mind always joined together in the same people. Someone once said that Hannibal could win victories but did not know how to use them. So too we see many who are endowed with excellent knowledge and understanding of things, yet lack judgment, and do not know how to use what they understand well, for the building up of others and the benefit of the Church. Both gifts are therefore necessary to the Church, since the Kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power. He also warns the half-learned not to be proud of their knowledge, but to give place to those whom they see to be better instructed in practical experience and prudence.

units.la: Tertia in hoc catalogo fides est: non quidem iustificans illa, qua Christum iustitiæ & salutis authorem vnicum apprehendimus (hæc enim omnibus Christianis communis est, neq; sine illa aliquis seruatur) sed ea, per quam miracula fiunt, de qua etiam in sequenti capite dicetur: Si habeam fidem totam, adeo vt montes transferam, charitatem autem non habeam, nihil sum. Et ista fidei virtus non omnibus datur, sed ijs solis, quorum opera & ministerio peculiari ad alios lucrifaciendum Deus vult vti.
units.tr: The third gift in this list is faith: not the justifying faith by which we lay hold of Christ as the sole author of righteousness and salvation (for this is common to all Christians, and no one is saved without it), but the faith through which miracles are wrought, which will also be discussed in the next chapter: "If I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing." This power of faith is not given to everyone, but only to those through whose work and ministry God wills to gain others for himself by a special means.

units.la: Quarto loco dona sanationum ponuntur, quæ fidei huius, de qua diximus, effecta dicere licebit, sicuti ex Christi verbis patet: Signa eos, qui crediderint, hæc sequentur: Per nomen meum dæmonia eijcient, linguis loquentur nouis, serpentes tollent, & si quid letale biberint, non nocebit eis, super ægrotos manus imponent, & bene habebunt, &c. Et olim quidem miraculosis illis sanationibus opus erat, vt Christi virtus clarius innotesceret, & plures ad eum amplectendum excitarentur: hodie autem inter Christianos homines illis minime opus est, qui Euangelij doctrinam profitentur, cuius illa quasi sigilla fuerunt. Qui ergo illa adhuc requirunt, ij se ne principia quidem Christianæ religionis adhuc tenere produnt, & proinde non digni sunt, qui Christianorum nomine censeantur.
units.tr: Fourthly come the gifts of healings, which we may call the effects of that faith of which we have spoken, as is clear from the words of Christ: "These signs will follow those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons, they will speak with new tongues, they will take up serpents, and if they drink anything deadly it will not harm them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will recover," and so on. In former times there was need of those miraculous healings, so that the power of Christ might become more clearly known and more people might be stirred to embrace him. Today, however, there is no need of them among Christians, who profess the teaching of the Gospel, of which those miracles were as it were the seals. Those who still seek them show that they do not yet hold even the first principles of the Christian religion, and therefore they are not worthy to be counted among Christians.

units.la: Quintum locu facultatibus potentiarum tribuit. In Graeco δυνάμεις[?] leguntur, quæ vox excellentiorem illa & potentiorem Spiritus Sancti virtutem denotat, quæ non solum morbis medetur, verumetiam malos homines pœnis coercet, & dæmonia expellit. Huius exemplu Petrus edidit, quando Ananias et Sapphira vxor eius, eò quod Spiritui Sancto mentiti essent, morte subitanea corruerunt: Paulus item, quando Elymæ Magi cæcitate percussit, & quando puellæ tacere coegit, quæ malo dæmone agitata ipsi & Syllæ collegæ suis clamoribus infesta erat. Huc deniq; mihi pertinere videtur, quod de quibusdã Satanæ tradendis scribitur. Nisi enim mox manifestum aliquod vindictæ diuinæ exemplum secutum fuisset, impijs facile erat minas omnes scurrilitate sua eludere. Et voluit olim Ecclesiam suam hac potestate armare Deus, cum nondum penes Christianos esset ius gladij, neq; alia ratione vel hypocritæ vel palam improbi ac scelerati coerceri possent. Hodie illa minus opus est, apud eos, qui rempub. habent, in qua principes præsident Christiani, qui omnes illos pœnis ciuilibus, quas Deus in Lege nobis præscripsit, vel in ordinem redigunt, vel (si ita opus sit) e medio tollunt. Scio quidem Anabaptistas hanc potentiam Spiritus ostentare, quando Satanæ tradi eos vociferantur, quos à sua Ecclesia aut communione excludunt: et eos multi imitantur, qui in rebuspub. bene constitutis hoc fieri oportere putant, quod in Ecclesijs sub impiorum tyrannide periclitantibus necessario obseruatur. Sed caveant illi diligenter, ne dum non necessaria, inuehere studeant, respub. turbent, & Ecclesias dissipent potius quam colligant.
units.tr: Fifthly, he assigns the workings of powers [δυνάμεις]. In the Greek the word is δυνάμεις, which denotes the more excellent and powerful virtue of the Holy Spirit, which not only heals diseases but also punishes wicked men and casts out demons. Peter gave an example of this when Ananias and his wife Sapphira fell down dead at once, because they had lied to the Holy Spirit. Paul did likewise when he struck the magician Elymas with blindness, and when he compelled a girl, who was possessed by an evil spirit and was troubling him and his colleague Silas with her shouting, to be silent. Finally, I think this also belongs here: what is written about the handing over of certain men to Satan. For unless some clear example of divine vengeance had quickly followed, it would have been easy for the impious to mock all their threats. God once wished to arm his Church with this power, when the sword of justice was not yet in the hands of Christians, and when hypocrites or openly wicked and criminal men could be restrained in no other way. Today it is less necessary, among those who have a commonwealth in which Christian princes preside, who either bring all such people into order by the civil penalties that God has prescribed for us in the Law, or (if need be) remove them altogether. I know that the Anabaptists display this power of the Spirit when they cry out that those whom they exclude from their Church or communion are to be handed over to Satan. Many imitate them, thinking that what is necessarily done in Churches endangered under the tyranny of the impious ought to be done in well-ordered commonwealths. But let them take care not to disturb the commonwealth and scatter the Churches rather than gather them, while they eagerly introduce what is not necessary.

units.la: Sexta in hoc numero Prophetia est, quæ alibi quidem Scripturæ Sacræ interpretationem & eius ad rem præsentem applicationem significat: hic autem ea facultas intelligitur, qua ex reuelatione Spiritus futura cognoscuntur, de quibus vel totam Ecclesiam vel aliquos priuatim admoneri necesse est. Hoc dono Apostolorum temporibus Agabus excelluit, & plures alij, qui Paulum Hierosolymam ascendentem in omnibus propè ciuitatibus de vinculis & afflictionibus admonebant, quas illic passurus esset. In quorum ordine etiam Philippi filiæ censeri debent, de quibus Lucas in Actis disserit. Singulare item prophetiæ exemplu fuit, quod instante obsidione vrbis Hierosolymæ, Ecclesia oraculo admonita trans Iordanem Pellam usque emigrauit. Duraui huius doni usus diu in veteri Ecclesia, quando insidiarum plena erant omnia, & multa restarent ex prisciis vaticinijs, quæ nondum erant impleta. Hodie facilius illo possumus carere, quando pleraq; iam finem suum attigerunt, ex Scripturis autem peti possunt, quæcunque nobis scitu necessaria sunt. Hic autem diaboli audacia atque astutia sese prodit, qui cùm humani ingenij curiositatem probè perspectam habeat, sibi hanc facultatem vendicat & ipse suos prophetas excitat nimirum ariolos, astrologos, et illicitarum artium sectatores, quos olim Deus in Lege sua damnauit, & quibus in Christi Ecclesiæ locum fore Micheas Propheta negat. Et mirum est, inter Euangelicæ fidei professores inueniri aliquos, qui iudiciariæ astrologiæ ita addicti sunt, ut in rebus arduis ex ea potius quàm ex Sacris literis consilium petant. At qui hoc faciunt, ferè idem patiuntur, quod Babyloniorum ariolis atq; magis Isaias minatur.
units.tr: The sixth in this number is prophecy, which elsewhere means the interpretation of Holy Scripture and its application to the present matter. Here, however, it is understood as that ability by which future things are known through a revelation of the Spirit, things about which either the whole Church or certain individuals must be warned. In the time of the Apostles Agabus excelled in this gift, and several others who warned Paul, as he went up to Jerusalem, in almost every city about the chains and afflictions that awaited him there. The daughters of Philip, about whom Luke writes in the Acts, should also be counted in this company. There was also a notable example of prophecy when, with the siege of Jerusalem impending, the Church, warned by an oracle, migrated across the Jordan to Pella. The use of this gift continued for a long time in the ancient Church, when everything was full of snares, and many of the earlier prophecies, not yet fulfilled, still remained. Today we can more easily do without it, since most of them have already reached their end, and whatever we need to know can be sought from the Scriptures. Here, however, the boldness and cunning of the devil are revealed. Since he has a thorough knowledge of the curiosity of the human mind, he claims this ability for himself and raises up his own prophets, namely soothsayers, astrologers, and followers of forbidden arts, whom God once condemned in his Law, and of whom the prophet Micah says there is to be no place in the Church of Christ. It is remarkable that some professors of the evangelical faith are found to be so devoted to judicial astrology that in difficult matters they seek counsel from it rather than from the sacred letters. Those who do this suffer nearly the same thing that Isaiah threatens against the soothsayers of the Babylonians, and even more.

units.la: Septimo loco discretiones spirituum ponuntur, & donum illud intelligitur, quo doctores veros à falsis discernimus. Est hoc imprimis necessarium, eò quòd Christus non uno loco falsos doctores fugere iubet, & quòd ijdem absque manifesto salutis periculo admitti non possunt. Ergo commune hoc præceptum est, quo omnibus Christianis mandat Apostolus, ne cuiusq; spiritui credant, sed spiritus probent, num ex Deo sint. Et spiritus vocabulo hic Apostoli utuntur, quia nihil tam vulgare & tritum est, quàm quòd impostores Spiritum Dei iactare, & suis figmentis illius authoritatem prætexere consueuerunt. Et quia ijdem pellibus ouium quoq; vestiuntur, non facilè ab omnibus agnosci possunt, & quotidie multos de eo conqueri audimus, quòd nesciant, quem in tanta doctorum inter se dissidentium turba debeant audire ac sequi. At isti ferè sibi ipsis difficultates fingunt, dum in homines respiciunt, quæ vel nullæ omnino, vel certè pauciores essent, si unû Deum audirent nobis per Filium suum in Euangelio loquentem. Oues meæ (inquit Christus) vocem meam audiunt. Et quia ipse est via, veritas & vita, idem etiam certissima & infallibilis est discretionis istius regula: ut nimirum Dei Spiritu eum duci sentiamus, qui unum Christum prædicat, & salutem omnem in illo monstrat, rursus autem non dubitemus maligni spiritus organa esse omnes eos, qui nobis extra Christum noua salutis rationes, & nouos fidei articulos [?]cemmi nifcuntur. Quia tamen omnis ista facultas hoc loco inter dona spiritualia numeratur, verbi Dei studio preces coniungere nos oportet, ut Deus suo Spiritu mentes nostras illuminet, ut ipsum nobis loquentem audiamus atq; agnoscamus.
units.tr: Seventhly, the discernings of spirits are listed, and this is understood as the gift by which we distinguish true teachers from false ones. This is especially necessary, because Christ bids us flee false teachers in more than one place, and they cannot be admitted without manifest peril to salvation. Therefore the Apostle gives this common command to all Christians, that they should not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are from God. The Apostles use the word "spirit" here, because nothing is more common and worn out than that impostors are accustomed to boast of the Spirit of God and to cover their fabrications with his authority. And since they also clothe themselves in sheep's skins, they cannot easily be recognised by everyone, and we hear many daily complain that they do not know whom, in so great a crowd of teachers at odds with one another, they ought to hear and follow. But such people largely create difficulties for themselves when they look to men, difficulties which would be none at all, or at least far fewer, if they heard the one God speaking to us in the Gospel through his Son. "My sheep," says Christ, "hear my voice." And since he is the way, the truth and the life, the same is also the most certain and infallible rule of this discernment: namely, that we perceive ourselves to be led by the Spirit of God when he preaches the one Christ and shows all salvation in him; and conversely, that we do not doubt that all those are instruments of an evil spirit who strive to devise for us new ways of salvation and new articles of faith apart from Christ. Yet because all this ability is numbered here among the spiritual gifts, we ought to join prayer to our study of the Word of God, so that God may illuminate our minds by his Spirit, and that we may hear and recognise him as he speaks to us.

units.la: Octauum locum in hoc catalogo linguarum genera obtinent, quarum cognitio olim necessaria fuit, quando ex Iudæa egressi Apostoli ac viri Apostolici omnibus gentibus prædicare iubebantur: at hodie donum hoc non tam necessarium est, eò quòd iam omnes Ecclesiæ uno ore & una lingua unum Christum sonant, & lingua Chananæa loquuntur, ut Isaias olim dixit de Ægyptiorum ad fidem Christianam conuersione vaticinans. Supplet doni huius defectum hodie admirabile illud & plane diuinum artis Typographicæ inuentum, quo fit, ut minimo sumptu & labore libri sacri & horum interpretes latissime sparguntur, & unus aliquis domi suæ residens eodem temporis momento inter gentes procul dissitas concionetur.
units.tr: The eighth place in this catalogue is held by the kinds of languages, a knowledge of which was once necessary, when the Apostles and apostolic men, going out from Judaea, were commanded to preach to all nations. Today, however, this gift is not so necessary, because all the Churches now sound with one mouth and one tongue the one Christ, and speak the language of Canaan, as Isaiah once prophesied when he foretold the conversion of the Egyptians to the Christian faith. The admirable and plainly divine invention of printing now makes up for the lack of this gift: at very little cost and labour, sacred books and their interpreters are spread very widely, and a single man sitting at home can, in the same moment, preach to nations far apart.

units.la: Addit his postremo loco interpretationem linguarum, quæ cum priori idem esse videtur, ab eo tamen differt, quòd prius istud simplicem linguarum cognitionem denotat, hic autem ea facultas notatur, qua quæ ipsi intelligimus, alijs etiam interpretari, & in multorum usum accommodare possumus: quod nisi fiat, non multum utilitatis linguarum notitia nobis adferet. Et olim quidem miraculose donum istud linguarum conferebatur, quando prædicandi vel Euangelizandi necessitas nullam moram admittebat: hodie autem etiamsi miraculosa illa omnium linguarum cognitio non amplius necessaria sit, tamen Hebraeæ & 'Græcæ linguæ usu Ecclesia omnino carere non potest, eò quòd his nobis descripti sint libri sacri, quibus Dei verbum & per illum nobis manifestata salutis ratio continetur. Et notum est illud Augustini, quod inter decreta sua Pontifices referri voluerunt: Ut veterum librorum fides de Hebraeis voluminibus examinanda est: ita nouorum veritas Græci sermonis normam desiderat. Quia autem nullius cognitio miraculose absque nostra industria atque studio nobis obtingit, scholas aperiri oportet, in quibus viri docti & pij tam linguas quam artes alios tradunt, quibus Ecclesia Dei ædificatur. tur. Vidit hoc olim Iulianus apostata, qui Christianos procul à scholis arceri voluit, vt tandem propria ignorantia seipsos & fidem Christianam euerterent. Quare non minus prudenter quàm pie à maioribus institutum est, vt scholae passim Ecclesijs celebrioribus coniunctæ essent, ex quibus doctores subinde noui defunctis aut rude donatis succederent. Quæ cura hodie etiam cum Ecclesiarum pastoribus tum principibus Christianis commendatissima esse debet. Interim meminerint omnes, ne nunc quidem absque Spiritus gratia aliquem vel linguæ peregrinæ cognitionem, vel germanum Scripturæ sensum consequi posse. Christum ergo, qui nobis à Patre sapientia factus est, scholarum suarum præsidem agnoscant Christiani homines, & qui in illis versantur, precibus assiduis à Deo lucem illam ingenij flagitent, quæ eorum cognitionem nobis reuelat, quæ cognitu necessaria sunt. Quod ipsum de omnibus alijs donis debet intelligi, in quibus nostra industria sine studium nostrum hodie requiritur. Nam perpetuò ratum manet, quod alibi Paulus dixit: Quid habes, quod non acceperis? &c.
units.tr: Last of all, he adds the interpretation of languages. This seems to be the same as the former, but it differs from it in this respect: the former denotes a simple knowledge of languages, whereas this denotes the ability by which we can also interpret to others what we ourselves understand, and adapt it for the use of many. Unless this is done, a knowledge of languages will bring us little benefit. Once this gift of tongues was bestowed miraculously, when the necessity of preaching or evangelising allowed no delay. Today, even though that miraculous knowledge of all languages is no longer necessary, the Church certainly cannot do without the use of Hebrew and Greek, since our sacred books, in which the word of God and the way of salvation revealed through it are contained, were written down for us in these languages. Well known is the saying of Augustine, which the Pontiffs wished to have included among their decrees: "As the faith of the old books must be tested by the Hebrew volumes, so the truth of the new books requires the standard of the Greek language." But since no one's knowledge comes to him miraculously, without his own diligence and zeal, schools ought to be opened, in which learned and godly men teach both languages and arts, by which the Church of God is built up. Julian the Apostate saw this long ago; he wanted Christians kept far from the schools, so that by their own ignorance they would at last ruin themselves and the Christian faith. Therefore it was instituted by our ancestors no less wisely than piously that schools should be joined everywhere to the more famous churches, from which teachers would from time to time succeed those who had died or been dismissed. Today this care ought to be most strongly commended both to the ministers of the Churches and to Christian princes. Meanwhile, let all remember that, even now, no one can attain a knowledge of a foreign language or the true sense of Scripture without the grace of the Spirit. Therefore let Christian people acknowledge Christ, who has been made wisdom for us by the Father, as the patron of their schools; and let those who labour in them ask from God, by constant prayer, that light of mind which reveals to them what is necessary to know. This must be understood of all the other gifts as well, in which our diligence and study are required today. For what Paul said elsewhere always remains true: "What do you have that you did not receive?" etc.

units.la: Nunc autem obseruabis, eiusmodi donorum distributionem hic describi, quæ nemini mortalium omnia, sed singula singulis, aut saltem aliqua modò singulis tribuit. Vt ergo non omnis fert omnia tellus: ita neminem inuenies facile, qui omnibus donis Spiritus Sancti instructus sit. Nam licet alij alijs plura accipiant pro suæ vocationis ratione (vt in talentorum parabola Christus docet) omnibus tamen certa mensura datur Spiritus, solus autem Christus est dilectus ille & vnigenitus Dei Filius, qui absque omni mensura Spiritus plenitudinem possidet, de qua nos omnes accepimus. Est hoc notius quàm vt multis demonstrari oporteat. Facit autem ista consideratio multum ad deprimendam eorum insolentiam, qui dum se præ alijs omnibus instructos esse sibi persuaserunt, sibi solis viuere incipiunt, & omnes homines nimium insolenter præ se contemnunt. Nam vt plurima habeas, quibus alij destituuntur, habent tamen hi quoq; nonnulla, quæ tibi desunt, & propter quæ ipsorum ministerio tibi opus est. Potuerunt hoc in ijs quæ soli corpori seruiunt, obseruare Poetæ & Philosophi, qui mutui huius auxilij necessitatem percæci & claudi typum adumbrarunt, quorum hic quidem ab altero gestatur, ille verò huius oculis aut visu regitur. Itaque mutuat hic oculos, mutuat ille pedes. Quod cum in omnibus alijs rebus fiat, nimiùm stulti sunt, qui perinde superbiunt, ac si sibi ipsis ad omnia sufficerent. Quin potius in ista donorum inæqualitate consilium Dei agnoscimus, qui hoc quasi ineuitabili necessitatis vinculo nos ad concordiam obstringere voluit. Cur enim huius studium negligant, qui nisi ab alijs iuuentur, suam functionem feliciter obire non possunt?
units.tr: Now you will observe that the distribution of such gifts described here is not given to any mortal all together, but to each one singly, or at least to each only some. Therefore, just as not every land bears everything, so you will not easily find anyone who is furnished with all the gifts of the Holy Spirit. For although some receive more than others according to the measure of their calling (as Christ teaches in the parable of the talents), yet a certain measure of the Spirit is given to all; only Christ, that beloved and only-begotten Son of God, possesses the fullness of the Spirit without any measure, and "of his fullness we have all received." This is too well known to need demonstrating to many. This consideration, moreover, goes a long way to humbling the insolence of those who, having persuaded themselves that they are more fully equipped than all others, begin to live for themselves alone and to despise all other men with excessive arrogance. For although you may have many things which others lack, these also have some things which you lack, and for which you need their ministry. Poets and philosophers, who saw this in those things which serve the body alone, observed the necessity of this mutual help, and in their blindness and lameness they symbolised it: the one is carried by the other, and the other is guided by the eyes or sight of the first. So one lends his eyes, another lends his feet. Since this happens in all other things, they are very foolish who take such pride as if they were sufficient for everything in themselves. Rather, in this inequality of gifts we recognise the counsel of God, who wished to bind us to harmony by this, as it were, unavoidable chain of necessity. For why should those neglect the pursuit of this who, unless they are helped by others, cannot fulfil their function happily?

units.la: Sed audiamus huius loci conclusionem: Sed omnia hæc efficit vnus ille & idem Spiritus, distribuens priuatim vnicuique, sicuti vult. Repetit vnicum istorum omnium authorem atque datorem, Spiritum Sanctum, cuius diuinitas rursus exprimitur, quando eum ista efficere ait: in eiusdem verò libera voluntate siue arbitrio omnem huius distributionis atque inæqualitatis causam commonstrat. Spiritus vnus & idem (inquit) ista efficit, & vnicuique vel singulis distribuit, non prout nos volumus, sed sicuti ipse vult. Est hoc breue dictum, sed quod omnia complectitur, quæ ad huius causæ cognitionem pertinent. Primò enim ne ijs superbiamus admonet, quæ ex Spiritus Dei liberalitate accepimus: sed potius de vero illorum usu soliciti simus. Deinde ses prohibet, ne secessionem ab Ecclesia faciant, qui nisi cum vno illo & eodem Spiritu, qui in credentibus agit, communicent, filij Dei non erunt. Postremò ne quis alteri inuideat, monet, aut de donorum inæqualitate conqueratur. Tu enim quis es, qui Deo obloquaris, aut Spiritum Sanctum ad rationem reddendam adigas? Num oblitus es, nos lutum esse in manu figuli illius, qui primum hominem creauit? Cur ergo lutum figulo dicit, Quare me sic fecisti, illum verò sic? Vel num oculus tuus ideo malus est, quòd ille beneficus sit? Cogitent ergo omnes, nos de donis istis quiritari non posse, nisi simul horum largitorem, Deum in ius vocemus. Quod cum non modò absurdum & inhonestum, verumetiam impijssimum sit, illius potius agnoscamus beneficentiam donis autem eius sic vtamur, vt ijs & Ecclesia ædificetur, & in nobis glorificetur nomen Domini & Seruatoris nostri IESV CHRISTI: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: But let us hear the conclusion of this passage: "But all these things one and the same Spirit works, distributing to each one individually as he wills." He repeats the one author and giver of all these things, the Holy Spirit, whose divinity is again expressed when he says that the Spirit effects these things; and by pointing to the Spirit's free will or choice, he shows the cause of all this distribution and inequality. "One and the same Spirit," he says, "works these things and distributes them to each one or to all, not as we wish, but as he himself wills." This is a short saying, yet it embraces everything that pertains to the knowledge of this matter. For first, it warns us not to be proud of those things which we have received from the generosity of God's Spirit, but rather to be concerned about their right use. Next, it forbids those who would withdraw from the Church to do so, since they will not be children of God unless they share with that one and the same Spirit who works in believers. Finally, it warns anyone against envying another, or complaining about the inequality of the gifts. For who are you, that you answer back to God, or that you bring the Holy Spirit to give an account? Have you forgotten that we are clay in the hand of that potter who created the first man? "Why does the clay say to the potter, 'Why have you made me thus, and him otherwise?'" Or is your eye evil because that one is generous? Let everyone therefore consider that we cannot complain about these gifts unless at the same time we summon their giver, God, to judgement. Since this is not only absurd and dishonourable but even most impious, let us rather acknowledge his kindness, and so use his gifts that the Church is built up by them and the name of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ is glorified in us, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: Sicut autem corpus vnum est, & membra habet multa, omnia vero membra corporis vnius multa cum sint, vnum sunt corpus: ita & Christus. Etenim per vnum Spiritum nos omnes in vnum corpus baptizati sumus: sive Iudaei, sive Graeci, sive serui, sive liberi: & omnes in vnum Spiritum potati sumus. Etenim corpus non est vnum membrum, sed multa. Si dicat pes, Quia non sum manus, non sum ex corpore: num ob id non est ex corpore? Et si dicat auris, Quia non sum oculus, non sum ex corpore: num ob id non est ex corpore? Si totum corpus oculus, vbi auditus? Si totum auditus, vbi odoratus? Nunc autem Deus collocauit membra singula sigillatim in corpore, sicut voluit. Quod si omnia essent vnum membrum, vbi corpus? Nunc vero multa quidem membra sunt, vnum vero corpus.
units.tr: "For as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the one body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ. For by one Spirit we were all baptised into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves or free, and we were all made to drink of one Spirit. For the body is not one member, but many. If the foot should say, 'Because I am not a hand, I am not of the body,' is it therefore not of the body? And if the ear should say, 'Because I am not an eye, I am not of the body,' is it therefore not of the body? If the whole body were an eye, where would be the hearing? If the whole were hearing, where would be the smell? But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, as he wished. If all were one member, where would the body be? But now there are many members, yet one body."

units.la: Sicuti Deus bonitatem suam eo argumento potissimum declarat, quod seipsum & bona sua spiritualia nobis communicat: ita hoc euidens imprimis est nostrae prauitatis indicium, quod ex eius donis aduersus ipsum & quosuis alios homines tumultuandi occasionem arripimus, quae nos tam ipsi Deo quam hominibus obstringere debebant. Est vitium hoc admodum frequens. Quia enim dona Spiritus non eadem mensura omnibus distribuuntur, fit, ut qui plus acceperunt, alios contemnant: qui vero minus, invidia ringantur [?], adhaec contra Deum murmurent, & ab Ecclesia secessionem faciant. Fiebant ista omnia apud Corinthios. Ideo Paulus causam hanc diligenter tractat: & nuper docuit, esse quidem discrimina donorum, & eadem inaequaliter a Deo distribui, id vero non obstare, quo minus illa concordiae seruire debeant. Hanc doctrinam nunc simili ex rerum natura desumpto illustrat, de corporis humani fabrica, quo in epistola ad Romanos etiam cap. 10. [?] est vsus. Licet enim ijs, qui salutis mysteria tractant, argumentis atq; similibus ex rerum natura petitis uti. Hoc enim frequenter olim prophetae & Christus facitarunt [?]. Imo est hoc quoque praeclarum bonitatis Dei argumentum, qui ut nostro captui se accommodat, nihil a nobis exigit, quam cuius exempla in rebus vulgo cognitis ac vsitatis habentur. Hic autem cautio adhibere debet, ne exemplis ex hominum consuetudine petitis ea probare velimus, quae in sacris literis nusquam traduntur. Faciunt hoc, qui hodie Diuorum intercessionem similibus ex Regum aula desumptis afferunt: Quibus alibi ex Isaia respondimus, per quem Dominus ait. Cogitationes meae non sunt cogitationes vestrae, neq; viae meae sunt viae vestrae, &c. Vide Isa. 55.
units.tr: Just as God chiefly shows his goodness by giving himself and his spiritual blessings to us, so it is a clear sign of our wickedness that we seize on his gifts as an occasion for quarrelling both with him and with other people, when those gifts ought to bind us to God and to other people alike. This vice is very common. Because the gifts of the Spirit are not distributed to everyone in the same measure, those who have received more despise others, while those who have received less snarl with envy, murmur against God, and secede from the Church. All of this was happening among the Corinthians. Therefore Paul treats this matter carefully. A little earlier he taught that there are differences among the gifts, and that God distributes them unequally, but that this does not stop them from serving harmony. Now he illustrates this teaching with an example taken from nature, the structure of the human body, which he also used in his Epistle to the Romans, chapter 10 [?]. For it is permitted to those who handle the mysteries of salvation to use arguments and comparisons drawn from nature. The prophets and Christ himself often did this in former times. Indeed this is also a notable proof of the goodness of God, who adapts himself to our capacity and asks nothing of us except what is found in examples from things commonly known and familiar. Here, however, caution must be applied, lest we wish to prove from examples taken from human custom those things which are nowhere handed down in the sacred letters. Those do this who today bring forward the intercession of the saints, using comparisons drawn from the courts of kings. We have answered them elsewhere from Isaiah, through whom the Lord says: My thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are my ways your ways, etc. See Isa. 55.

units.la: Sed accedamus ad locum Pauli, cuius summa est: Sicut corpus vnum est, & membra habet multa, omnia vero membra corporis vnius, multa cum sint, vnum sunt corpus: ita & Christus. Continetur his verbis propositio bipertita, cuius pars prima est: Vnum corpus, multa habet membra. Altera, multa membra vnum sunt corpus. Vtramq; partem vno verbo ad causam praesentem applicat: Ita & Christus. Christi enim nomine non eam modo personam, quae Deus & homo est, sed totum illud corpus Ecclesiae mysticum intelligit, quod non ex solis fidelibus, verumetiam capite constat. Nam quemadmodum (vt Chrysostomi verbis vtar) corpus & caput vnum hominem constituunt: sic Ecclesia & Christus vnum sunt. Et vt non proprie corpus, sed truncus dicitur, cui caput ablatum est: ita non amplius Ecclesia dici meretur, quae capiti Christo non cohaeret, sed ab hoc aulsa eius etiam spiritu destituitur. Itaq; huius dicti sensus est: Christum esse instar corporis, quod ex multis membris constet, quae vni capiti adhaerent siue connexa sunt. Ex eo autem postea hoc quoq; colligit, quod Ecclesia sit vnica, etiamsi fideles sint multi, qui donis & functionibus differant, imo Ecclesiae vnitatem ex hac fidelium diuersitate constare.
