Ex quo rursus sequitur quod ad hanc causam imprimis pertinet, ipsum Christum diuidi & distrahi, quando propter membrorum atq; donorum discrimina aut diuersitatem Ecclesia distrahitur. Ideo supra sectarijs dixit Apostolus: Num diuisus est Christus? Quod vtinam diligentius expenderent, qui hodie Christianam Ecclesiam in Benedictinorum, Bernardinorum, Franciscanorum & aliorum sexcentorum ordines distrahunt.
units.tr: But let us come to Paul's passage, whose sum is this: As the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the one body, though they are many, are one body, so also is Christ. This sentence contains a two-part proposition. The first part is: one body has many members. The second: the many members are one body. He applies both parts to the present cause in one word: so also is Christ. For by the name of Christ he understands not only that person who is God and man, but the whole mystical body of the Church, which consists not only of the faithful but also of the head. For just as (to use the words of Chrysostom) the body and the head make up one man, so the Church and Christ are one. And just as a trunk, not a body properly speaking, is what has lost its head, so that is no longer worthy to be called the Church which does not cling to Christ its head, but is cut off from him and is therefore deprived of his Spirit. Hence the sense of this saying is this: Christ is like a body which consists of many members that cling to, or are joined to, the one head. From this he afterwards also draws the conclusion that the Church is one, even though the faithful are many and differ in gifts and functions; indeed the unity of the Church consists in this very diversity of the faithful. From this follows again what especially pertains to this cause: when the Church is torn apart because of the differences or diversity of members and gifts, Christ himself is divided and torn. Therefore the Apostle said above to the sectarians: Is Christ divided? I wish that those who today tear the Christian Church into the orders of the Benedictines, Bernardines, Franciscans and six hundred others would weigh this more carefully.

units.la: Debet igitur hoc loco considerari articulus fidei, quem in symbolo apostolico profitemur: Cre-do sanctam Ecclesiam catholicam, sanctorum communionem. Vnam fatemur esse Ecclesiam, non plures. Ideo articulus iste in Constantinopolitano Symbolo sic habetur: Credo in spiritum sanctum, qui locutus est per Prophetas in VNAM catholicam & apostolicam Ecclesiam. Vt enim Chri-stus caput est vnicum, ita corpus quoq; vnicum habet. At corpus illud est Ecclesia, quod in Scri-pturis tam diserte traditur, vt demonstratione ampliori nequaquam fit opus. Ergo illam vnam esse, necessario sequitur. Et ideo eam vulgo catholicam, id est, vniuersalem dixerunt, quia etsi propter locorum aut gentium discrimina, haec quidem Corinthiorum, illa Romanorum, hae item Macedonicae, illae Asiaticae, Germanicae, Anglicae, Gallicae, Polonicae Ecclesiae dicantur, omnes tamen illae ad vnicam illam pertinent, ad hanc vnam respiciunt, in eadem omnes conueniunt sub vno capite IESV CHRISTO, cuius singuli fideles ita vniuntur, vt non solum omnes eius spiritu viuant & regantur, verumetiam (quod alibi Paulus annotauit) sint os ex ossibus eius, & caro ex carne eius. Et haec illa coniunctio est, quam Scriptura Veteris & noui testamenti per coniugium adumbrat.
units.tr: Here we ought to consider the article of faith which we profess in the Apostles' Creed: I believe in the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints. We confess that the Church is one, not many. Therefore this article stands in the Constantinopolitan Creed in this form: I believe in the Holy Spirit, who spoke through the prophets, in ONE holy catholic and apostolic Church. For just as Christ is one head, so he also has one body. That body is the Church, which is taught so plainly in the Scriptures that no lengthy demonstration is needed. Therefore it necessarily follows that it is one. And so they commonly called it catholic, that is, universal, because although on account of differences of places or nations some are called the Church of the Corinthians, others of the Romans, these likewise of Macedonia, those of Asia, the Churches of Germany, England, France, or Poland, yet all of them belong to that one Church, look to this one, and all come together in the same under one head, Jesus Christ, to whom individual believers are so united that they not only live and are ruled by his Spirit, but (as Paul noted elsewhere) are bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh. And this is that union which Scripture of the Old and New Testament portrays through marriage.

units.la: Quo in loco imprimis tenendum est, connexionem atq; vnionem istam spiritus virtute con-flare, non autem corporali aut carnali praesentia. Nam spiritus virtute fit, vt quemadmodum qui in diuersis loci habitant fideles, omnes vnum corpus sunt & eiusdem Patris filij: ita ijdem omnes Christo quoq; cohaereant, qui suo corpore in coelis agit, quo illum ascendere viderunt Apo-stoli. Et cur hoc alicui absurdum videatur, quando in coniugij, quod inter homines intercedit, consideratione simile quid occurrit? Nam qui illo vinculo semel constringuntur, ij iam non duo sunt, sed vna caro (vt Christi verbis vtar) nec ulla locorum distantia obstat, quo minus vna caro aut corpus vnum dicantur, etiamsi interdum diuersis in locis degant, imo alter coniugum ab altero longis terrarum & nationum interuallis disiungatur. Quod si vero coniugalis vinculi tanta vis est, quod cum vitae huius curriculo tandem abrumpitur, an minorem putabimus esse mystici illius coniugij dignitatem atq; efficatiam, quod aeternum manet, & quod per mortem adeò non dissolui-tur, vt hac interueniente propius & arctius cum Christo sponso nostro coniungamur? Quod vnum si rectius expenderent omnes, mox pateret, quam crassus atq; absurdus illorum error sit, qui de carnali & reali aut essentiali corporis Christi in pane mystico praesentia contendunt. Atqui vt nobis Christus praesens sit, vt q; nobis cohaereat potius quam panem necesse est, & eundem nobis ceu caput corpori connexum esse atq; indiuulse adhaerere Scriptura docet. Quis vero siue veterum siue recentium, qui sano iudicio vsi sunt, vnquam disputauit, An nos simus reale illud & naturale Christi corpus, quod ex Maria virgine natum est, quod in crucem suffixum mundi peccata expiauit, quod in sepulchro ad tertij vsq; diei exortum iacuit, & quod nunc in coelis gloriosum & incorrup-tibile viuit atq; triumphat? Quis (inquam) hominum vnquam ita delirauit, vt tale quid ei vel per somnium in mentem venerit? Quae ergo dementia est, panem, qui ore perceptus & dentibus contritus in stomachum transmittitur, in eam dignitatem euehere, vt ipsissimum Christi corpus esse putetur, pro ipso deniq; Christo, Deo & homine, adoretur?
units.tr: In this place it is above all to be held that this connection and union is brought about by the power of the Spirit, not by a bodily or fleshly presence. For by the power of the Spirit it comes about that, just as the faithful who dwell in different places are all one body and children of the same Father, so these same people also cling to Christ, who acts in heaven with his body, into which the Apostles saw him ascend. And why should this seem absurd to anyone, when something similar occurs in considering the marriage that takes place between human beings? For those who are once bound by that tie are no longer two, but one flesh (to use Christ's words), and no distance of places stands in the way of their being called one flesh or one body, even if they sometimes live in different places, indeed even if one spouse is separated from the other by long intervals of lands and nations. But if the bond of marriage has such force that it is at last broken when the course of this life ends, shall we think that the dignity and efficacy of that mystical marriage is less, since it remains eternal, and since it is not dissolved by death, but rather, through death intervening, we are joined more closely and tightly to Christ our bridegroom? If everyone weighed this one point more rightly, it would soon be plain how gross and absurd is the error of those who contend for a carnal, real, or essential presence of the body of Christ in the mystical bread. Yet, for Christ to be present to us and to cling to us, it is necessary, as Scripture teaches, that he be joined to us as the head is joined to the body, and cling to us inseparably, rather than the bread. Who, among the ancients or the moderns, who has used sound judgement, has ever disputed whether we are that real and natural body of Christ which was born of the Virgin Mary, which was fastened to the cross and expiated the sins of the world, which lay in the tomb until the rising on the third day, and which now lives and triumphs in heaven, glorious and incorruptible? Who (I say) of men has ever gone so mad as to have such a thing come into his mind even in a dream? What madness, then, is it to raise to such dignity bread, which is taken into the mouth, crushed by the teeth, and sent down into the stomach, so that it is thought to be the very body of Christ, and is finally adored in place of Christ himself, God and man?

units.la: Sed vt ad tractationem de Ecclesia redeamus, simul huius quoq; dignitatem Paulus expri-mit, quae recte cognita dulcissimam consolationem parit. Nam non modo corpus Christi, sed ipse Christus dicitur. Quia enim hic in omnibus & singulis membris suis agit, in ijsdem etiam ipse agnosci & censeri vult. Et ideo sibi factum reputat, quod suis fit, qui ipsi per fidem sunt insiti. Hinc locutiones istae in Scripturis habentur: Qui vos tangit, tangit pupillam oculi mei. Item, Saul Saul, quid me persequeris? Et rursus: Quod vni ex minimis hisce fecistis, mihi fecistis. Ista nos consolentur, ne vnquam Christum, qui nunc in coelis residet, nostri immemorem esse putemus. Quomodo enim suijpsius, id est, corporis sui ille obliuiscatur? Sed ne quidem dubitare debemus, nos eius protectione iam nunc frui, dum in huius mundi stadio certamus, olim vero omnibus malis exemptos vitam in coelis immortale et vere beata actuaros esse cum illo, qui discipulis dixit: Vbi ego sum, ibi erit & minister meus. Item: Volo Pater, vt vbi ego sum, illic etiam sint quos dedisti mihi. Ioan.12. & 17[?].
units.tr: But to return to the discussion of the Church, Paul at the same time expresses its dignity, which, rightly understood, brings the sweetest consolation. For he is called not only the body of Christ but Christ himself. For since Christ acts in all and each of his members, he also wishes to be recognised and reckoned in them. And so he counts as done to himself whatever is done to those who are grafted into him through faith. Hence these sayings are found in the Scriptures: He who touches you touches the apple of my eye. Likewise: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? And again: What you did to one of these least, you did to me. Let these things comfort us, so that we never think that Christ, who now sits in heaven, is forgetful of us. For how could he forget himself, that is, his own body? Nor ought we even to doubt that we now enjoy his protection while we contend in the arena of this world, and that one day, freed from all evils, we shall live with him in heaven, immortal and truly blessed, he who said to his disciples: Where I am, there shall my servant also be. Likewise: Father, I desire that where I am, there also may be those whom you have given me. John 12 and 17 [?].

units.la: Confutatur etiam huius loci consideratione Pontificum insolentia, qui se caput Ecclesiæ esse dicitant. Si enim CHRISTUS IESUS Ecclesiæ suæ ita coniunctus sive unitus est, ut cum ea unum & idem corpus esse dicatur, eius caput Papa esse aut dici non potest, nisi Christi quoq; caput sit. Quid vero magis absurdum magisq; insolens fingi vel excogitari potest? Ex eo enim colligeretur, Christum ex Pontifice spiritum vitæ haurire, adeoq; ex illo vitam motumq; accipere. Quod si hoc negent, iam Christum quoq; caput Ecclesiæ fatendo, hanc bicipitem constituent. Itaq; si non ullum aliud argumentum extaret, unum hoc sufficeret ad demonstrandum, sub Pontificum titulo latere, imò potius palam se exerere [?]ἀντικείμενον illum & magnum Christi atque Ecclesiæ suæ aduersarium, qui se extollit aduersus omne id, quod Dei aut numinis nomine censetur 2. Thessal. 2.
units.tr: This passage also refutes the arrogance of the Pontiffs, who call themselves the head of the Church. For if Christ Jesus is so joined and united to his Church that the two are said to be one and the same body, the Pope cannot be, or be called, its head unless Christ is its head too. What could be imagined or devised that is more absurd and more arrogant? For it would follow that Christ draws the Spirit of life from the Pope, and receives life and motion from him. But if they deny this, and so confess Christ as head of the Church as well, they make the Church two-headed. Therefore, even if there were no other argument, this one alone would suffice to show that the title of Pontiff conceals that great adversary of Christ and his Church, who "exalts himself above everything that is called God or worship" (2 Thess. 2) [ἀντικείμενον], and who in fact shows himself openly under that title.

units.la: Porrò quod proposuit Paulus, demonstrare incipit, & primò unum corpus ex multis membris constare, aut multa membra habere docet, quæ prima propositionis pars fuit. Etenim in uno Spiritu (inquit) nos omnes in unum corpus baptizati sumus, sive Iudæi, sive Græci, sive servi, sive liberi: & omnes in unum Spiritum potati sumus. Ex Sacramentis argumentatur, quæ Ecclesiæ tesserae & gratiæ Dei atq; totius redemptionis nostræ sigilla sunt. Et primò quidem de baptismo loquens, nos omnes in uno Spiritu baptizatos esse scribit, ea locutione totum baptismum comprehendens, qui non sola aqua, sed etiam huic coniuncta Spiritus virtute constat. Hac enim fit, ut qui externo aquæ baptismo in externam Ecclesiæ societatem adoptantur, simul etiam vere inserantur in corpus Christi mysticum, & huius germana membra fiant. Ideo ad Romanos scribens, nos in Christi mortem baptizari dixit, & ita cum eo coalescere, ut tam mortis quàm resurrectionis eius participes efficiamur. Et in epistola ad Ephesios unitatem illam diligentius exprimens ait: Unum est corpus, unus Spiritus, sicut & vocati estis in unam spem vocationis vestræ: Unus Dominus, una fides, unus baptismus, unus Deus & Pater omnium, &c. In præsenti autem particulam universalem, OMNES, per distributionem explicat, addens: Sive Iudæi sive Græci, sive servi sive liberi. Duobus membris maxima, quæ tunc erant, personarum discrimina comprehendit: Alterum erat nationis, quo omnes totius orbis populi in Iudæos & Gentes sive Græcos dividebantur: Alterum conditionis, quòd alij liberi essent, alij servi. Quòd si vero ista non possunt Ecclesiæ unitatem scindere, quò minus ex istis unum corpus coalescat, quanto minus igitur donorum diversitas obstabit, quæ ex eodem Spiritu promanant, & eiusdem fidei symbola sunt atq; administriculæ? Debet ergo istorum consideratio nos admonere, quàm putida ac detestabilis sit eorum superbia, qui aliquos propter gentem, ex qua natus est, vel conditionem obscuram & abiectam, non autem impiam, ut sua societate aut communione indignum fastidiunt, quem non fastidit Deus, & quem sui corporis membrum Christus agnoscere dignatur.
units.tr: Next, Paul begins to prove what he has put forward. First he teaches that one body consists of many members, or has many members, which was the first part of his proposition. For, he says, "In one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves or free; and we were all made to drink of one Spirit." He argues from the sacraments, which are the tokens of the Church and the seals of God's grace and of our whole redemption. Speaking first of baptism, he writes that we were all baptized in one Spirit, a phrase that takes in the whole of baptism, which consists not only of water but also of the power of the Spirit joined to it. For by this it happens that those who are admitted by the outward baptism of water into the outward fellowship of the Church are at the same time truly grafted into the mystical body of Christ and become its true members. So, writing to the Romans, he said that we are baptized into the death of Christ, and so grow together with him that we become partakers both of his death and of his resurrection. And in the letter to the Ephesians, expressing that unity more fully, he says: "There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called into one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all," and so on. In the present passage he explains the universal word ALL by distribution, adding: "whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves or free." By two members he takes in the greatest distinctions of persons that then existed. The first was of nation, by which all the peoples of the whole world were divided into Jews and Gentiles or Greeks. The second was of condition, namely that some were free and others slaves. But if these distinctions cannot split the unity of the Church, so that a single body is not formed from them, how much less will the diversity of gifts stand in the way, since these flow from the same Spirit and are tokens and helps of the same faith? Therefore the consideration of these things ought to remind us how foul and detestable is the pride of those who scorn some people, because of the nation from which they were born, or because of a lowly and humble condition (not an impious one), as unworthy of their company or fellowship, when God does not scorn them and Christ deigns to acknowledge them as members of his body.

units.la: Cæterum ex Cæna quoque Dominica argumentum adducit: Et omnes in unum Spiritum potati sumus. Alij ex Græcis Scholijs legunt [?]ἐν πόμα ἀποτισθῆμεν εἰς ἓν πνεῦμα, id est, uno poculo potati sumus in Spiritum: vel εἰς ἐν πόμα, id est, in unam potionem, sive in unum poculum. Sed nolim temere mutare usitatam & receptam lectionem, cùm non inutilis aut ab instituto Apostoli aliena sit antithesis corporis & Spiritus. Ut ego prius nos in unum corpus baptizatos esse dixit, ita nunc in unum quoque potatos esse scribit: quod præsenti argumento probe feruit. Docet enim nos ita unum corpus in Christo factos esse, ut uno quoque & eodem Spiritu omnes vivamus atque ducamur. De eo autem nos Cæna Domini mystica admonet, in qua ex uno poculo omnes bibimus, ut ita testemur nos unum corpus esse, & omnes uno Christi Spiritu recreari atque animari ad vitam æternam. Per Synecdochen vero solius poculi meminit, non ut Cænam distrahat, aut alterutram speciem (ut vulgò loquuntur) ceu superuacaneam & inutilem negligi posse doceat (quod nouissimis temporibus Pontificij doctores tradiderunt) sed quia poculi symbolum præsenti instituto melius seruiebat: cùm in sanguine, qui per poculum adumbratur, spiritus vitæ sedem habeat. Notum est enim illud Dei dictum, quo sanguinem ipsam animam esse pronuntiat. In præsenti autem sic ista Paulus proponit, ut ostendat, eos in professionem fidei & nominis Christiani peccare, qui propter donorum diversitatem inter se scinduntur, & Christianæ societatis seu unitatis vinculum abrumpunt. Est enim unus & idem omnium credentium Spiritus, vna item eademque omnium anima, quae & συμπαθείας illius mirifica causa est, de qua suo loco dicetur. Ad hunc ergo locum referri debent admonitiones & adhortationes apostolicae, quibus vnitatem fidei & sententiarum nobis Spiritus sanctus commendat. Ad Philippenses certè Paulus scribens: Tantum (inquit) vt dignum est Euangelio Christi vos gerite, vt siue venero & videro vos, siue absens fucro, audiam de rebus vestris, quòd stetis in vno spiritu, vno pariter animo decertantes per fidem Euangelij. Et paulò post: Explete gaudium meum, vt idem sitis affecti, eandem charitatem habentes vnanimes & sententijs vni. Similiter Ephesios quoque studere iubet, vt seruent vnitatem spiritus per vinculum pacis. Sunt hae admonitiones hodie admodum necessariae, & vtinam earum diligentius meminissent, qui vt vel suae vel eorum existimationi consulant, in quorum verba semel iuraverunt, Ecclesias omnes rixis & contentionibus nunquam finiendis turbare solent.
units.tr: Moreover, Paul also draws an argument from the Lord's Supper: "and we were all made to drink of one Spirit." Others read from the Greek scholia, ἐν πόμα ἀποτισθῆμεν εἰς ἓν πνεῦμα, that is, "we were made to drink in one draught into one Spirit"; or εἰς ἐν πόμα, that is, "into one drink," or "into one cup." But I would not rashly change the usual and accepted reading, since the antithesis of body and Spirit is neither useless nor foreign to the apostle's purpose. Just as he said that we were baptized into one body, so now he writes that we were made to drink into one, which suits the present argument very well. For he teaches that we have been made one body in Christ, so that all of us live and are led by one and the same Spirit. The mystical Lord's Supper reminds us of this, in which we all drink from one cup, so that we may thereby testify that we are one body, and that all of us are renewed and quickened by the one Spirit of Christ to eternal life. By synecdoche he mentions only the cup, not to tear the Supper apart, nor to teach that one of the two kinds may be neglected as superfluous and useless (as the Papist teachers have taught in recent times, as they commonly put it), but because the symbol of the cup served the present purpose better, since the seat of the spirit of life is in the blood, which is pictured by the cup. For that saying of God is well known, by which he declares that the blood is the soul itself. But here Paul sets these things before us so that he may show that those sin against their profession of faith and their Christian name who tear themselves apart from one another because of the diversity of gifts, and break the bond of Christian fellowship or unity. For there is one and the same Spirit of all believers, and likewise one and the same soul of all, which is also the wonderful cause of their sympathy, about which it will be spoken in its own place. Therefore to this passage must be referred the apostolic admonitions and exhortations by which the Holy Spirit commends to us unity of faith and of opinion. Writing certainly to the Philippians, Paul says: "Only let your conduct be worthy of the gospel of Christ, so that whether I come and see you, or am absent, I may hear of your affairs, that you stand in one spirit, striving side by side with one mind for the faith of the gospel." And a little later: "Fulfil my joy, that you may be of the same mind, having the same love, being of one accord and one judgment." Similarly he bids the Ephesians to take care to keep the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace. These admonitions are very necessary today, and would that those who swore allegiance to the words of certain men would more diligently remember them. For in order to look after their own reputation, or that of those men, they are accustomed to trouble all the churches with quarrels and contentions that are never ended.

units.la: At in toto hoc pauli argumento singularem consideratione meretur, quod in baptismo simul & Coena spiritus mentionem facit. Nam in vno Spiritu omnes baptizari, & in vnum Spiritum omnes potari scribit. Quibus locutionibus admonemur, omnem Sacramentorum efficaciam siue virtutem à Spiritu promanare, non autem in externis symbolis aut ceremoniarum actione consistere. Nam per Baptismum quidem cooptamur in externam ecclesiae societatem, sed corpori Christi mystico non inserimur, vt germana eius membra simus, nisi Spiritus virtutem in nobis agentem sentiamus. Sic in Coena, panis & vinum symbola quidem sunt vnitatis nostrae, sed eadem nihil ad salutem aeternam conferunt, nisi per alimentum illud mysticum, quod nobis Christus in seipso exhibet, in vnum corpus vnumque spiritum coalescamus. Denique vt regeneratio, quae per Baptismum adumbratur, spiritu constat: ita alimento quoque spirituali nos ad vitam aeternam ali atque sustentari necesse est. Ideò Christus Capernaitas (vt alibi quoque monuimus) de carnali esu seu manducatione altercantes, ad spiritum remittit, dicens: Spiritus est qui viuificat, caro non prodest: quicquam: verba quae ego loquor vobis, spiritus & vita sunt. Et Petrus cùm nos per Baptismum seruari dixisset, mox subiecit: non quo sordes carnis abijciuntur, sed quo fit, vt conscientia ab vno Deo pendeat, & in hoc vno acquiescat. Paulus item cùm de lauacro regenerationis verba fecisset, ei illico addit renouationem Spiritus sancti: ita nimirum docens, lauacri nomine Spiritum, per regenerationem verò non aliud quàm hominis totius innouationem intelligi debere. Sunt hæc diligentius obseruanda propter eos, qui symbolis aut elementis omnem vim siue efficaciam tribuunt, & illa pro rebus, quae ijs adumbrantur, accipiunt: Est hæc animarum seruitus miserrima, vt D. Augustini verbis vtar. Quid enim miserius aut infelicius animâ accidere potest, quàm si elementis adhaereat ipsa, quae spiritus est omnibus elementis praestantior? propter illa denique terris adfixa maneat, quorum adminiculis totus homo ad spiritum deduci debebat?
units.tr: But in the whole of this argument of Paul, one thing deserves particular consideration: that he mentions the Spirit both in baptism and in the Supper. For he writes that all are baptized into one Spirit and all are made to drink into one Spirit. By these expressions we are reminded that all the efficacy and power of the sacraments flows from the Spirit, and does not consist in outward tokens or in the performance of ceremonies. For through baptism we are indeed admitted into the outward fellowship of the Church, but we are not grafted into the mystical body of Christ so as to be its true members unless we feel the power of the Spirit working in us. So in the Supper, bread and wine are indeed tokens of our unity, but they contribute nothing to eternal salvation unless, through that mystical food which Christ offers us in himself, we grow together into one body and one spirit. Finally, as the regeneration pictured by baptism consists in the Spirit, so we must also be nourished and sustained by spiritual food for eternal life. This is why Christ, when the Capernaites quarrelled about carnal eating or manducation (as we have also noted elsewhere), sends them back to the Spirit, saying: "It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing; the words that I speak to you are spirit and life." And Peter, after saying that we are saved through baptism, immediately added: not because the filth of the flesh is put away, but because the conscience depends on the one God and rests in him alone. Likewise Paul, after speaking of the washing of regeneration, immediately adds the renewal of the Holy Spirit, thereby teaching, of course, that by the name of washing the Spirit is to be understood, and by regeneration nothing other than the renewal of the whole man. These matters must be observed more carefully on account of those who ascribe all power and efficacy to symbols or elements, and take those things for the realities that are pictured by them. This, in the words of St Augustine, is the most wretched slavery of souls. For what can happen to a soul more wretched or unhappy than to cling to the elements, when it is itself a spirit, which is superior to all elements, and to remain fixed to the earth for the sake of those things by whose aid the whole man ought to have been led up to the Spirit?

units.la: Sed & Anabaptistarum sacrilega temeritas hic confutatur, qui ne Baptismus infantibus communicetur prohibent. Atqui tota illius virtus atque dignitas ex Spiritu dependet, cuius illos participes esse, supra Cap. septimo docuimus. Quae ergo stultitia est aquam illis negare, quos Dei Spiritus abluere & potare dignatur? Quanto rectius Petrus, qui Cornelium cum domesticis suis ideo baptizandum esse putaut, quòd eos Spiritu iam donatos esse videret? Quid verò de Pontificum audacia dicemus, qui poculum benedictionis mysticum Laicis surripuerunt? Paulus eodem nos vno poculo in vnum Spiritum potari dicit, vt eo argumento demonstret, omnes qui credunt, summos, medios, infimos, doctos & indoctos, vnam esse Ecclesiam, & vnum in Christo corpus constituere.
units.tr: The sacrilegious rashness of the Anabaptists is also refuted here, since they forbid baptism to be given to infants. Yet the whole virtue and dignity of baptism depends on the Spirit, and we showed above in chapter seven that infants are partakers of the Spirit. What folly is it, then, to deny water to those whom the Spirit of God deigns to cleanse and water? How much more rightly Peter reasoned when he thought that Cornelius and his household ought to be baptized because he saw that they had already received the Spirit! And what shall we say of the audacity of the Papists, who have snatched the mystical cup of blessing from the laity? Paul says that we are all given to drink of one cup into one Spirit, so that by this argument he may show that all who believe, whether high or middling or low, learned or unlearned, are one Church and make up one body in Christ.

units.la: Sed ad alteram propositionis suae partem confirmandam transit Apostolus, qua docet multa & diuersa membra vnum corpus constituere, & diuersitatem iflam adeò non scindere corpus aut distrahere, vt potius illud feruet: cùm è contra aquabilitas illa, quam nonnulli inconsultius vrgent, illi exitialis foret, si semel admitteretur. Etenim corpus (inquit) non est vnum membrum, sed multa. Argumentum hoc subest à necessario, quod postea diligentiori expolitione illustrat. Nunc iflorum sensus est: Quemadmodum corpus non vno tantum membro constat, sed multis, imò non posset corpus dici, nisi membra haberet multa, quorum vsus & multiplex & necessarium est: Ita Ecclesia non ex uno homine, aut unico hominum genere constituitur, sed ex multis, neq; Ecclesia dici merebitur, nisi ex multis collecta fuerit. At concurrunt hic duo hominum genera, quibus singulis occurri oportebat. Primum eorum est, qui quòd se paucioribus domis instructos & in inferiori loco constitutos vident, impatientia & pusillanimitate superati, secessionem ab Ecclesia faciunt, & quia in illa non possunt eminere, ne membra quidem eius esse volunt. Est hoc hominum genus nocentissimum tam in Ecclesia quàm in Republ. Tales enim apud Romanos fuerunt Marius, Pompeius & similes, qui rempub. primò turbarunt, deinde totam euerterunt. Simili ambitione Arius olim accensus Ebionitarum & Samosateni haresim instauravit, & nocentissimi dissidij author extitit. Et nostro seculo non alia causa Anabaptistarum duces mouit, ut renascentem Euangelij lucem suis furoribus turbauerint. Alterum genus eorum est, qui cum donis maioribus se praestare sentiant, & in loco eminentiori sint constituti, omnes alios praese con-temnunt, nec aliquem emergere patiuntur, ut eandem cum ipsis dignitatem teneat: quales olim in Republ. Sylla & Iulius Caesar fuisse leguntur, & ijsdem vestigijs in Ecclesia hodie cum suo purpuratorum Senatu Pontifices insistunt. Vtrique generi doctrinam hanc applicat Paulus.
units.tr: But the Apostle turns to confirm the other part of his proposition, which teaches that many and diverse members make up one body, and that this diversity does not tear or divide the body but rather keeps it alive. The opposite is true of that levelling which some press too rashly, for it would be ruinous if it were ever admitted. For the body (he says) is not one member but many. This argument rests on a necessity, which he afterwards illustrates with a more careful elaboration. Its sense is this: just as the body does not consist of one member only but of many, and indeed could not be called a body unless it had many members, whose uses are both manifold and necessary, so the Church is not constituted of one man or one kind of men, but of many, and it could not deserve to be called a Church unless it were gathered from many. But two kinds of people come together here, and each must be met. The first kind is of those who, seeing that they are furnished with fewer gifts and placed in a lower position, are overcome by impatience and pusillanimity, and withdraw from the Church; and because they cannot stand out in it, they do not even want to be its members. This kind of men is most harmful both in the Church and in the commonwealth. Such were Marius, Pompey and others like them among the Romans, who first disturbed the commonwealth and then overthrew it entirely. With the same ambition Arius once, being inflamed, revived the heresy of the Ebionites and of Samosata, and became the author of a most pernicious schism. And in our own age no other cause moved the leaders of the Anabaptists, so that with their frenzies they have troubled the light of the gospel as it was rising again. The second kind is of those who feel that they excel in greater gifts and are placed in a more prominent position; they despise all others and do not suffer anyone to rise up so as to hold the same dignity as themselves. Such, we read, were Sulla and Julius Caesar in the commonwealth, and the popes today, with their purple-clad senate, follow the same footsteps in the Church. Paul applies this teaching to both kinds.

units.la: Et in praesenti quidem de primis illis agit, vtq; minus inuidiae habeat oratio, prosopopoeia vtitur, qua membris in humano corpore constitutis litem hanc adfingit, ita nimirum ambitiosos illos ad naturam, optimam rerum magistram, remittens. Primum igitur pedes cum manibus conferens ait: Si dicat pes, Quia non sum manus, non sum ex corpore, id est, nihil mihi cum corpore commune est: num ob id non est ex corpore? Quasi diceret: Nequaquam id recte colligeret pes: nam etiamsi non fit manus, nihilominus tamen ad corpus pertinet, & cum spiritu vitae participat, qui in alijs membris sese exerit: neque propterea pro inutili aut superuacaneo excluditur, quòd infimum in corpore locum obtineat. Inde ad membra superiora transit, & aures cum oculis confert, dicens: Si dicat auris, Quia non sum oculus, non sum ex corpore: id est, nihil mihi cum corpore commune est: num ob id non est ex corpore? Vt ergo pedi non obstat, quod non sit manus: ita neq; auri, quod non sit oculus. Iste vero nos alteram similitudinis partem subijcere oportet, vt pro pedes intelligamus eos, qui infimum in Ecclesia locum habent, & donis paucioribus siue ignobilioribus sunt instructi: pro manibus autem eos, quorum ministerio plures iuuantur: pro auribus & oculis Verbi administros, episcopos, magistratus, & quicunque toti Ecclesiae prospiciunt, & ad quos querelae tam publicae quam priuatae deferuntur. Itaque huius loci status est: vt ne quem suae conditionis pudeat, neue propter tenuitatem suam desperet, aut se Deo minus curae esse arbitretur. Vt enim situs non obstat, quo minus vnumquodq; membrum, corporis pars sit: ita neque gradus indignitas cuiquam vitio erit, quo minus inter Ecclesiae ciues numerari debeat. Siue enim summus, siue infimus, siue medioxumus fis, Ecclesiae membrum es: & vt caput, etsi corporis totius arcem teneat, pedes tamen minime negligit: ita Christus, qui Ecclesiae suae caput est, ne infimos quidem & hominum iudicio contemptissimos aspernatur: quin potius ijs gaudet, qui in mundo vilissimi habentur. Sufficiat vnicuiq;, quod Ecclesiae membrum sit. Quae enim maior aut excellentior dignitas homini potest obtingere, quàm si inter Dei domesticos adscribatur? Quae item felicitas & beatitudo certior atque perfectior? Vidit istud Dauid, & ideo canebat: Quàm sunt amabilia Domine exercituum, tabernacula tua? Ardet, & etiam deperit anima mea ad atria Domini: cor meum & caro mea ad Deum viuum clamarunt. Quia potior est dies in atrijs tuis, quàm alij mille: malo ad limen desidere domus Dei, quàm habitare in tentoriis impiorum. Hoc idem votum si in omnium animis arderet, procul dubio tales efficeret, qui & sua forte contenti nihil praeterea cuperent, & ad quæuis officia proximo praestanda propensissimi essent. Itaq; neq; aduersus Deum murmurarent, neq; alicui suam fortunam inuiderent. Discant ergo singuli in partium corporis sui consideratione diligentius versari. Quis vnquam pedes contra caput insurgere, aut manus in oculos inuolare vidit? Cur ergo tu, qui inferiori loco constitutus es, te superioribus suum gradum inuides? cur in eos odium concipis? cur deiectos & oppressos cupis? Quin potius tu ijs quoque officium praestas, qui te superbè negligunt? Iuua igitur hos quoque, & si non aliud illis potes impendere, saltem precibus à Deo hoc eis impetrare studeto, vt suae sortis & officij memores suis donis atq; dignitate non abutantur. Cæterum doctrinam istam amplius confirmat Paulus, & ostendit aliter fieri non posse, siquidem Ecclesia debeat salua & incolumis consistere. Si totum corpus (inquit) oculus, vbi auditus? Si totum auditus, vbi odoratus? Ab absurdo argumentatur, æqualitatem non posse induci, nisi multæ aliæ functiones aboleantur, quibus Ecclesia carere non potest. Vt enim si totum corpus, oculo solo constaret, neque auribus, neque manibus, neque pedibus, imò nullis alijs membris locus esset, quæ non minus necessaria sunt: Ita si in Ecclesia omnes Prophetæ essent, iam & magistratus & agricolæ & opifices cessarent, cum infinitis alijs, quorum opera ad vitæ huius conseruationem necessario requiritur. Quod ipsum de Repub. quoque potest dici. Est ergo necessaria prorsus dominorum atq; ministeriorum inæqualitas, quia æqualitas cum præsenti exitio coniunctam confusionem pareret. Etenim vt neque corpus neque membra consistere diu poterunt, si horum diuersæ functiones aboleantur: ita Ecclesiam simul & singula huius membra destruunt, qui sublatis gradibus donorum atque functionum, æqualitatem inuehere student, ex qua præter horribilem ἀταξίαν[?] nihil nascitur. Plato quidem olim in Repub. æqualitatem inter cives, & bonorum omnium, imò mulierum quoque & liberorum communionem vtilem & necessariam putauit: sed sua ratione multum falsus est, & eius sententiam sapientissimi quique reprobauerunt. Respub. enim absque diuersis functionibus consistere non potest, hæ autem æqualitatem illam atque communionem procul excludunt. Vinculum verò Reipub. tutissimum atque firmissimum est, Legum & publicæ disciplinæ semper sibi constans & æqualis administratio. Eadem est Ecclesiæ conditio, in qua sufficit fidem omnium eandem esse, & ijsdem fidei atque innocentiæ Christianæ legibus omnes astringi.
units.tr: In the present passage he deals with the first kind, and so that his speech may carry less odium, he uses a prosopopoeia, by which he attributes this dispute to the members set in the human body, thus sending those ambitious men back to nature, the best teacher of things. First, then, comparing the feet with the hands, he says: If the foot shall say, Because I am not the hand, I am not of the body, that is, I have nothing in common with the body: is it therefore not of the body? As if he were saying: the foot would by no means draw the right conclusion; for even though it is not a hand, it nonetheless belongs to the body and shares in the life-giving Spirit, which shows itself in the other members; nor is it cast out as useless or superfluous because it holds the lowest place in the body. Then he passes to the higher members and compares the ears with the eyes, saying: If the ear shall say, Because I am not the eye, I am not of the body, that is, I have nothing in common with the body: is it therefore not of the body? Just as, therefore, it is no obstacle to the foot that it is not a hand, so it is no obstacle to the ear that it is not an eye. We must, however, apply the other part of the comparison, so that by the feet we understand those who hold the lowest place in the Church and are furnished with fewer or humbler gifts; by the hands, those by whose ministry many are helped; and by the eyes and ears the ministers of the Word, the bishops, the magistrates, and whoever watch over the whole Church and to whom both public and private complaints are brought. The meaning of this passage, therefore, is this: that no one should be ashamed of his condition, nor despair because of his lowliness, nor think that he is of less concern to God. For just as position is no obstacle to each member being a part of the body, so the unworthiness of a rank will be no fault that prevents anyone from being counted among the citizens of the Church. For whether you are highest, lowest or middling, you are a member of the Church; and just as the head, though it holds the citadel of the whole body, nonetheless does not neglect the feet, so Christ, who is the head of his Church, does not spurn even the lowest and those most despised in human judgment; rather, he delights in those who are held most worthless in the world. It is enough for each one that he is a member of the Church. For what greater or more excellent dignity can fall to a man than to be enrolled among God's household? What happiness and blessedness could be more certain or more perfect? David saw this, and therefore he sang: How lovely are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul burns and even faints for the courts of the Lord; my heart and my flesh have cried out to the living God. For a day in your courts is better than a thousand others; I would rather sit at the threshold of the house of God than dwell in the tents of the wicked. If this same desire burned in the hearts of all, it would doubtless make them such that, content perhaps with their own lot, they would desire nothing more, and be most ready for whatever duties they must perform for their neighbour. Thus they would neither murmur against God nor envy anyone his fortune. Let each one therefore learn to attend more carefully to the consideration of the parts of his own body. Who has ever seen the feet rise up against the head, or the hands fly at the eyes? Why then do you, who are placed in a lower position, envy those above you their rank? Why do you conceive hatred against them? Why do you wish them cast down and oppressed? Rather, do you not perform your duty even to those who proudly neglect you? Help them, then, and if you can give them nothing else, at least strive to obtain for them from God, through your prayers, that mindful of their lot and their office they may not abuse their gifts and dignity. Paul, moreover, confirms this teaching further and shows that it cannot be otherwise, if the Church is to remain safe and whole. If the whole body (he says) were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the smelling be? He argues from the absurd: equality cannot be introduced unless many other functions are abolished, which the Church cannot do without. For if the whole body consisted of the eye alone, with no ears, no hands, no feet, and indeed no room for the other members, which are no less necessary, then likewise, if all in the Church were prophets, the magistrates, the farmers and the craftsmen would cease, along with infinitely many others whose work is necessarily required for the preservation of this life. The same can also be said of the commonwealth. Therefore an inequality of ranks and ministries is entirely necessary, because equality would bring about a confusion joined with present ruin. For just as neither the body nor its members can stand for long if their diverse functions are abolished, so those who, once the grades of gifts and functions are removed, strive to bring in equality destroy the Church and each of its members at once; from such equality nothing arises except a dreadful disorder [ἀταξία]. Plato once thought, in his Republic, that equality among citizens, and a communion of all goods and even of women and children, was useful and necessary; but he was greatly mistaken in his reasoning, and the wisest men have rejected his opinion. For a commonwealth cannot exist without diverse functions, and these utterly exclude that equality and communion. The safest and firmest bond of a commonwealth, however, is the constant and even administration of its laws and public discipline. The condition of the Church is the same: it is enough that all have the same faith, and that all are bound by the same laws of faith and Christian innocence.

units.la: Confutantur etiam hoc loco Anabaptistæ, qui vt omnes ad prophetandi munus admitti volunt, ita vicissim omnes ad fluuium & opificia manuaria remittunt. Rationes illorum sunt, ex vno Adamo patre omnes nos esse progenitos, vnum corpus esse in Christo, in quo non sit liber aut seruus, mas aut fæmina, vnam denique omnium esse naturam atq; conditionem mortalem. At non debent cum natura & æterna salutis mysterio confundi externæ functiones, quarum in alijs vitæ huius negotijs multiplex & necessarius vsus est. Nam vt exemplum sumamus ex vulgo, inter Christianos coniuges eiusdem naturæ & salutis in Christo partæ communio est: nihilominus tamen ex Dei decreto vir mulieri imperat, & hæc illius iussis obedire debet. Atqui eandem rationem in Ecclesia & Repub. esse, ex infinitis scripturæ locis notius est, quam vt prolixè demonstrari debeat. Non est ergo, quod curbatores istos aliquis audiat, qui sub religionis plausibili prætextu omnem ordinem tam politicum quàm ecclesiasticum fædè dissipant.
units.tr: The Anabaptists are also refuted at this point. They want everyone admitted to the office of prophesying, yet in turn they send everyone back to the river and to manual trades. Their reasons are these: that we are all descended from one father, Adam; that there is one body in Christ, in which there is neither free nor slave, male nor female; and finally that all have one nature and one mortal condition. But outward functions ought not to be confused with nature and with the mystery of eternal salvation, and these functions have a manifold and necessary use in the other affairs of this life. To take an example from common life: among Christians, husband and wife share the same nature and the same salvation obtained in Christ; nevertheless, by God's decree the husband commands the wife, and she ought to obey his orders. Yet that the same reasoning holds in the Church and in the commonwealth is better known from countless passages of Scripture than it needs to be proved at length. There is therefore no reason for anyone to listen to those disturbers who, under the plausible pretext of religion, shamefully destroy every order, political as well as ecclesiastical.

units.la: Redeamus nunc ad Pauli verba, qui partem istam concludens ait: Nunc autem Deus collocauit membra singula sigillatim in corpore, sicut voluit. Rursus tamen propter morosos & contentiosos quosdam repetit, quod iam ante dixerat, sic omnino fieri oportere. Nam dicit: Quòd si omnia essent vnum membrum, vbi corpus? Equidem huius conditio eiusmodi est, vt absque membris multis & multum inter se diuersis constare non possit. Vicissim & membra, quamuis inter se donis & officijs differant, vnum tamen corpus sunt, & se mutuò iuuant, vt postea sequetur. Quod ipsum in Ecclesia quoque fieri innuit, & propterea nostrum esse, vt diuinæ ordinationi nos accommodemus. Obseruabis autem hic eandem rationem adduci, quam prius allegarat, & eius non aliam causam assignari, quàm liberam Dei voluntatem, cui ita facere visum fit. Eadem ergo nobis quoque sufficere debet. Cum illo enim litigare, impium est. Oremus potius illum, ne ipse contra nos litem suscipiat, & seuerius à nobis exigat nostræ functionis rationem. Memineri-mus ergo nos terram esse, agnoscamus autem IESV CHRISTI beneficium, qui nos corporis sui membra fecit, & proinde fideles simus ei, qui nos tanto honore dignatus est. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Let us now return to the words of Paul, who, concluding this part, says: "But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, as he pleased." Yet again, on account of certain stubborn and quarrelsome people, he repeats what he had said before, that it must altogether be so. For he says: "If all were one member, where would the body be?" Indeed, the body's condition is such that it cannot exist without many members, differing greatly among themselves. Conversely, the members, although they differ among themselves in gifts and offices, are nevertheless one body and help one another, as will follow afterwards. He hints that this is also to be done in the Church, and therefore it is our part to accommodate ourselves to the divine ordering. You will observe here, however, that the same reasoning is brought forward which he had earlier set out, and that no other cause is assigned for it than the free will of God, to which it has seemed good to act thus. That, therefore, ought to be enough for us as well. For to dispute with him is impious. Rather let us pray him not to take up a suit against us himself, and not to demand from us a more severe account of our office. Let us remember that we are dust, but let us acknowledge the benefit of Jesus Christ, who made us members of his body; and therefore let us be faithful to him who has deigned to honour us so greatly. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXV.
units.tr: HOMILY 65.

units.la: Non potest autem oculus dicere manui, Non est mihi opus te: aut rursum caput pedibus, Non est mihi vobis opus. Imò multo potius,quæ videntur membra corporis infirmiora esse, necessaria sunt: & quæ putamus in corpore inhonestiora esse, iis honorem ampliorem circumponimus: & quæ sunt in nobis indecora, copio siorem decorem habent. Nam quæ sunt in nobis decora, iis decore non est opus: sed Deus simul temperauit corpus, ei cui deerat, copiosiore tributo honore: Vt ne sit dissidium in corpore, sed membra idem curent alia pro aliis. Itaque siue patitur vnum membrum, simul dolent omnia membra: siue honore afficitur vnum membrum, simul gaudent omnia membra.
units.tr: The eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you; nor again the head to the feet, I have no need of you. Rather, on the contrary, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary; and those which we think less honourable in the body we clothe with greater honour; and those which are unseemly in us have a more abundant comeliness. For what is comely in us has no need of comeliness, but God has so tempered the body together, giving more abundant honour to the part that lacked it, that there should be no division in the body, but that the members should have the same care for one another. So if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; if one member is honoured, all the members rejoice with it.

units.la: Nihil inter homines tam vulgare est, quàm quòd à Deo acceptis donis, tam corporalibus quàm spiritualibus, ad suam simul & aliorum pernitiem abutuntur. Fiebat hoc apud Corinthios quoque, & ideo Paulus de donorum Dei ratione & vsu vero diligenter disserit, & doctrinam suam simili corporis humani atque membrorum illustrat, vt nunquam non nobis occurrat de his cogitandi occasio. Id vero sic proponit, vt fidi medici instar simul vitijs occurrat, quibus in hac causa maximè peccatur. Primum, eorum est, qui paucioribus donis instructi, sè in gradu inferiori constitutos esse vident. Hi ferè suam sortem impatientius ferunt, & ideo alijs inuidènt, & quasi non pertineant ad Ecclesiam, omnium aliorum commercia atq; consuetudinem fugiunt: imò frequenter aduersus Deum quoq; murmurant, quasi vt iniquè dona sua inter homines partiatur. De his nuper dixit, & quid eos deceat, docuit. Alterum vitium eorum est, qui donorum excellentia & functionis suæ dignitate multis alijs præstant. Hi ferè sibi ipsis placent, & quasi sibi ipsis sufficiant, alios contemnunt, quasi eorum nullus sit vsus in Ecclesia. Hinc lites acerbissimæ & dissidia exitialia nascuntur: quia natura sic comparatum est, vt ij quoq; qui sua forte contenti viuere norunt, ab alijs tamen contemni & insolentius negligi nolint. Pergit ergo in propositâ parabola Apostolus, & nunc cum istis quoq; agit, & eos grauiter admonet, ne quem se inferiorem contemnant. Estq; pars ista dignissima diligentiori consideratione: quia vt horum insolentiam deprimit, ita alteros illos efficacissimè consolatur.
units.tr: Nothing is so common among men as that they abuse the gifts received from God, both bodily and spiritual, to their own ruin and that of others. This happened among the Corinthians too, and therefore Paul discusses carefully the true nature and use of God's gifts, and illustrates his teaching by the likeness of the human body and its members, so that we may never lack an occasion to think about these things. He sets this out so that, like a faithful physician, he meets at once the faults by which people most sin in this matter. The first belongs to those who, being furnished with fewer gifts, see that they stand in a lower rank. These usually bear their lot too impatiently; and so they envy others, and as if they did not belong to the Church, they shun the company and fellowship of all the others; indeed they often also murmur against God, as if he distributed his gifts among men unjustly. Of these he spoke a little while ago, and taught what befits them. The second fault belongs to those who surpass many others in the excellence of their gifts and the dignity of their office. These usually please themselves, and as if they were sufficient to themselves, they despise others, as if none of them were of any use in the Church. From this the bitterest quarrels and ruinous divisions arise; for it is the nature of things that even those who know how to be content with their own lot do not want to be despised by others or neglected more arrogantly. So the Apostle, continuing his parable, now deals with these men as well, and seriously admonishes them not to despise anyone as inferior to themselves. And this part deserves very careful consideration, because as it humbles the insolence of the one sort, so it most effectively comforts the others.

units.la: Propositio est, neminem contemni debere, vel potius aliqua iusta ratione contemni posse, quem Deus fide donare & Ecclesiæ suæ membrum facere dignatus est. Id vero rursus per Pro-sopopœiam explicat, dum membris sermonem tribuit. Non potest (inquit) oculus dicere manui, Non est mihi opus te: Aut rursum caput pedibus, Non est mihi vobis opus. Per oculos possunt doctores intelligi, quos in Ecclesia speculatorum loco positos esse, ex Ezechiele constat, & idem Episcopi vocabulum euidenter docet. Manus sunt, quorum opera in rebus administrandis opus est, opifices item & quicunq; alij sunt eius ordinis. Capitis loco sunt omnes, qui in eminentiori dignitate constituti alijs imperant. Per pedes autem vulgus promiscuum recte intelligemus. Itaque verborum istorum sensus erit: Quemadmodum inter oculos & manus, caput & pedes ingens differimen est, siue situm membrorum siue eorundem vires atque dignitatem considerent, nullum autem alterius opera & ministerio carere potest: Sic in Ecclesia multum quidem inter se differunt credentes, omnium tamen vsus est aliquis non vtilis modo, verumetiam ad Ecclesiæ constitutionem atque conseruationem necessarius. Et debet obseruari locutio, Non potest oculus dicere manui, &c. Supra enim scripserat Apostolus: Si dicat pes, Si dicat auris, &c. Illic enim inuidorum aut ex pusillanimitate desperantium verba atque mores expressit, qui affectu superati multa inepte & absurde dicunt & faciunt. At hic cum superbis & arrogantibus ipsi res est, qui & ipsi multa huius generis dicere solent, ostendit autem hoc illos nulla cum ratione iusta aut saltem probabili facere posse, cum quotidianus rerum usus eos convincat: quo abunde docemur, neminem esse, qui non interdum opus habeat hominum abiectissimorum opera atque ministerio. Sed quod propositum fuit Paulus, rationibus quoque confirmat, quas ita adducit, vt simul argumenta confutet, quibus confidentes illi seipsos decipiunt.
units.tr: The proposition is that no one ought to be despised, or rather that no one can justly be despised, whom God has deigned to endow with faith and to make a member of his Church. He explains this again by prosopopoeia, in that he gives speech to the members: The eye, he says, cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you; or again the head to the feet, I have no need of you. By the eyes can be understood the teachers, who, as is clear from Ezekiel, are placed in the Church in the position of watchmen, and the very word bishop plainly teaches the same. The hands are those whose work is needed in administering affairs, likewise craftsmen and all others of that order. All who are set in a more eminent dignity and rule over others take the place of the head. By the feet we shall rightly understand the common crowd. The sense of these words, then, will be this: just as between the eyes and the hands, and between the head and the feet, there is a great difference, whether one considers the position of the members or their strength and dignity, yet none of them can do without the work and service of another, so in the Church the believers differ greatly among themselves, yet the service of each is not only useful but even necessary for the building up and preservation of the Church. And we ought to notice the wording, The eye cannot say to the hand, etc. For earlier the Apostle had written: If the foot should say, If the ear should say, etc. There he expressed the words and conduct of the envious, or of those who despair through timidity; these, overcome by feeling, say and do many foolish and absurd things. But here he deals with the proud and arrogant, who are accustomed to say many things of this kind themselves; and he shows that they cannot do this with any just or even plausible reason, since the everyday use of things convicts them. From this we are amply taught that there is no one who does not at times need the work and service of the most lowly men. But Paul also confirms with reasons what he has proposed, reasons which he so brings forward that at the same time he refutes the arguments by which those self-confident men deceive themselves.

units.la: Primum inter illa est, quòd suam excellentiam cùm aliorum tenuitatè conferentes, stulta & stolida persuasione sibijpsis persuadent, nihil vtilitatis ad ipsos redire posse ex contemptu illis & obscuris, qui fere toti ab aliorum authoritate atque consilio pendent. Illis ergo respondent, dicens: Imò multò potius, quae videntur membra corporis infirmiora esse, necessaria sunt. Est hoc nimis evidens, neque id aliquis negauerit, qui corporis constitutionem diligentius consideràt. Infirmissimae huius partes sunt caput, oculi, aures, nares. Illud enim doloribus & morbis infinitis obnoxium suo languore frequenter totum corpus debilitat, haec autem facillimè laeduntur, neque habent quo se à vi externa defendant. Quid vero ijsdem magis necessarium? Quid enim sine capite reliquum corpus erit aliud quàm truncus exanimis atque putrescens? Quid vero videbunt, audient, odorabuntur manus, tibiae, pedes, si oculos, aures & nares auferas? Rursus etsi caput cum oculis atque auribus supremum in corpore gradum teneant, membris tamen se multò inferioribus non possunt vllo modo carere. Eadem omnino est ratio inter Ecclesiae membra. Quid in hac contemptius & infirmius fere est doctoribus, qui oculorum vices (vt paulò ante diximus) obeunt? Nos (inquit Apostolus) stulti propter Christum, vos autem prudentes in Christo: nos infirmi, vos autem validi: nos ignominiosi, vos gloriosi: Ad hoc vsque tempus & esurimus & sitimus, & nudi sumus, & colaphis caedimur, & incertis sedibus erramus, &c. Quod autem de seipso & Apostolis reliquis dixit, hoc imprimis locum habet in aliis, qui ne inter Christiani quidem nominis professores eam dignitatem obtinent, qua olim Apostoli excelluerunt. Quid vero tam necessarium est quàm Verbi praedicatio, quae si ministros & doctores è medio tollas, nulla erit? Cessante prophetia (Solomon olim dicebat) dissipatur populus. Quia enim per Verbi doctrinam Ecclesia colligitur, eam consistere impossibile est, si illa cesset. Exemplum eius rei memorabile nobis tempora Heli Sacerdotis exhibent, quando populi Israelitici status infelicissimus fuit, eius autem causa indicatur, quòd Verbum Domini pretiosum, id est, rarum esset: ijs nimirum in suo munere cessantibus, qui illud annuntiare debebant. Rebus autem afflictis tunc consulturus Deus Samuelem excitauit, per quem Verbi praedicatio instauraretur. Et Amos propheta extremum exitium populo denuntiare volens, famem Verbi Dei minatur, quae infelices hinc inde discurrere cogat, vt aliquam animarum suarum refocillationem inueniant. Id vero Iudaeis, qui nostro tempore viuunt, accidere videmus. Quia enim legitima Verbi praedicatione destituti sunt, per foetidas Rabbinorum paludes atque lacunas volutantur, & exitiali coeno seipsos demergunt, dum animi aestuantis sitim volunt restinguere. Quid multis hodie euenit, qui cùm Christiani dicantur, Verbum tamen Dei audire nolunt, vel ab eo audiendo principum edictis arcentur, notius est quàm vt commemorare opus sit. Sed vt ad institutum redeamus, etiamsi ijdem doctores quoad suae conditionis gradum alijs Ecclesiae membris excellentiores sint, his ipsis tamen carere nequaquam possunt. Quid enim erit doctor absque discipulis? Idem quod pastor absque ouibus, & quod imperator absque militibus. Denique vt in tota rerum natura fere maior & frequentior vsus est eorum, quae minus pretiosa sunt (etenim ferro magis quàm auro, lignis magis quàm argento ad res necessarias vtimur: frugibus item multò minus quàm gemmis carere possumus) ita in Repub. & Ecclesia res maximae plerunque per inferioris gradus homines perfici consueuerunt. Nam vt ad vulgaria descendamus, quis non videt, magis nos ad vitae communis vsum opus habere agricolis, opificibus, nautis & alijs qui mercede conducti opus faciunt, quàm otiosis illis, qui generis nobilitatem luxu vestium, fastuoso incessu & superbo aliorum contemptu ostentant. Et vt summatim dicamus quod res est, qui divitijs abundant minus sibijpsis possunt sufficere, quàm pauperes, quos sua egestas ingeniosos & ad quemuis laborem industrios atque tolerantes facit: cum alteri illi omne praesidium in pecuniis habeant, quibus alios conducere coguntur, quorum ministerio res suas conficiant. Sunt etiam exempla, quae docent, Deum saepius in populo suo seruando hominum abiectissimorum opera vsum fuisse: vt pote Mosis, Gedeonis, Dauidis, vt de mulieribus nunc nihil dicamus, quarum singularis virtus aliquando eluxit, turpiter cessantibus viris, qui fortissimi & sapientissimi esse videbantur. Quoties item viri multo rerum vsu exercitati non vident neque intelligunt ea, quae pueris aut hominibus plebeis nota atque perspecta sunt? Id certè in religionis & aeternae salutis[?] causa tam vulgare aut frequens est, ut Christus non dubitarit gratias agere Deo Patri, qui mysteria Regni sui celarit huius seculi sapientibus, revelauerit autem pueris siue infantibus. Quotquot ergo cognitione ista illuminati sunt, ij imprimis necessarij sunt, licet quoad alia homines contemptissimi videantur, nec aliquis est, qui vere dicere possit, se vel hoc vel illo non opus habere. Turpiter autem seipsos fallunt, qui suarum virium atque donorum fiducia ebrij aliquem prae se contemnunt. Poterant hos, nisi communi sensu destituerentur, potentissimorum Regum exempla terrere, qui frequenter vilissimorum hominum ope seruantur: quod olim Xerxi quoque accidisse, historici testantur.
units.tr: First among these is this: when they compare their own excellence with the meanness of others, they persuade themselves with a foolish and stupid conviction that no advantage can come back to them from despising those who are humble and obscure, who almost wholly depend on the authority and counsel of others. To these he replies, saying: Rather, on the contrary, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary. This is most evident, and no one who considers the constitution of the body more carefully would deny it. The weakest parts of it are the head, the eyes, the ears and the nostrils. For the head, subject to endless pains and diseases, often weakens the whole body by its sickness, while these parts are very easily injured and have no means of defending themselves against external violence. Yet what is more necessary to the body than these? For what would the rest of the body be without a head but a lifeless and rotting trunk? And what will the hands, shins and feet see, hear or smell if you take away the eyes, ears and nostrils? Again, although the head with the eyes and ears holds the highest place in the body, yet it can by no means do without the much lower members. The reasoning is entirely the same among the members of the Church. What is more despised and weaker than the teachers, who (as we said a little earlier) perform the office of the eyes? We (says the Apostle) are fools for Christ's sake, but you are wise in Christ; we are weak, but you are strong; we are dishonoured, but you are glorious. To this present hour we both hunger and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and wander about without a fixed home, etc. What he said of himself and the other Apostles applies especially to others, who do not even among the professors of the Christian name hold that dignity which the Apostles once excelled in. And what is so necessary as the preaching of the Word, which, if you remove the ministers and teachers from the midst, will not exist? When prophecy ceases, the people perish (Solomon said long ago). For since the Church is gathered by the teaching of the Word, it is impossible for it to stand if that ceases. The memorable example of this is given to us by the times of Eli the priest, when the state of the people of Israel was most unhappy, and the cause of it is stated to be that the word of the Lord was precious, that is, rare: namely, because those who ought to proclaim it had ceased from their office. Then, God, about to consult the afflicted state of things, raised up Samuel, through whom the preaching of the Word was restored. And the prophet Amos, wishing to announce utter destruction to the people, threatens a famine of the Word of God, which will drive the unhappy folk to run hither and thither to find some refreshment for their souls. We see this happening to the Jews who live in our own time. For since they are deprived of the lawful preaching of the Word, they wallow through the foul marshes and pools of the rabbis, and drown themselves in deadly mire, while they wish to quench the thirst of their restless minds. What happens today to many who, though they are called Christians, nevertheless refuse to hear the Word of God, or are kept from hearing it by the edicts of princes, is too well known to need recounting. But to return to our purpose: even if these same teachers are more excellent than the other members of the Church in the degree of their station, yet they can by no means do without these very members. For what will a teacher be without pupils? The same as a minister without sheep, and a commander without soldiers. Finally, as throughout the whole of nature the more common and frequent use is of things that are less precious (for we use iron more than gold, and wood more than silver for necessary purposes; likewise we can do far less without crops than without gems), so in the commonwealth and the Church the greatest matters are usually carried out by men of the lower rank. For to descend to ordinary things, who does not see that we have more need, for the common use of life, of farmers, craftsmen, sailors and others who work for hire, than of those idle men who display the nobility of their birth by the luxury of their clothes, their proud gait and their haughty contempt for others? And, to sum up the matter as it really is: those who abound in riches can less often suffice for themselves than the poor, whom their want makes clever, industrious for any labour, and enduring; whereas the rich have all their protection in money, with which they are forced to hire others, by whose service they get their affairs done. There are also examples which teach that God, in preserving his people, has more often used the work of the most lowly men: such as Moses, Gideon and David; not to speak now of women, whose singular courage has sometimes shone out when the men, who seemed most brave and wise, shamefully failed. How often, too, do men practised by long experience of affairs not see or understand what is known and plain to boys or common folk? Certainly in the matter of religion and eternal salvation this is so common and frequent that Christ did not hesitate to give thanks to God the Father, who hid the mysteries of his kingdom from the wise of this age and revealed them to babes and infants. Therefore all who have been enlightened in that knowledge are above all necessary, even if in other respects they seem most contemptible; and there is no one who can truly say that he has no need of this or that. But those men deceive themselves shamefully who, drunk with confidence in their own powers and gifts, despise someone in comparison with themselves. If they were not deprived of common sense, the examples of the most powerful kings should terrify them, who have often been saved by the help of the vilest men; as historians attest that once happened even to Xerxes.

units.la: Caeterum aliud praeterea vitium est, quo confidentes illi sibi ipsis imponunt. Nam aliorum saepe illos pudet, vel quod illos egestate premi, vel peccatis aut sceleribus infames esse vident. Rursus ergo hic quoque nos ad corporis nostri fabricam remittit. Nam in illo etiam partes aliquae indecorae sunt, quarum nos pudet. Num vero eas abijcimus? num ignominiosius eadem tractamus? Imo, inquit Paulus, quae putamus in corpore inhonestiora esse, ijs honorem ampliorem circumponimus: et quae sunt in nobis indecora, copiosiorem decorem habent. Prudenter autem ait, Quae putamus in corpore inhonestiora esse. Quia Deus nihil fecit aut creauit, quod per se turpe aut inhonestum sit: propter peccatum autem fit, ut nos nunc membrorum quorundam pudeat, quae vel generationi vel excrementorum euacuationi seruiunt. Ideo de primis parentibus priusquam peccassent, scribitur: Erant uterq; nudus, nec erubescebant. Quam primum vero ad vetiti pomi esum oculi eorum aperti sunt, pudore suffusi ficuum folia contexuerunt, quibus partes illas velarent. Et durat mos iste etiam hodie, ut non modo tegantur, verumetiam (quod Paulus in praesenti annotauit) ornatu aut decore asciticio ornentur, ne aliqua in illis turpitudo appareat.
units.tr: Moreover, there is another fault by which those self-confident people deceive themselves. Often they are ashamed before others, either because they see that they are oppressed by poverty or that they are notorious for sins and crimes. Here again, then, he refers us to the structure of our own body. For in the body too there are some unseemly parts, and we are ashamed of them. Do we then cast them away? Do we handle them with less honour? No, says Paul: we put greater honour upon those parts that we think more unseemly in the body, and those in us that are unseemly have a fuller comeliness. He wisely says, "those that we think more unseemly in the body." God made and created nothing that is shameful or unseemly in itself. It is because of sin that we are now ashamed of certain members, those that serve generation or the evacuation of waste. So of our first parents, before they sinned, it is written: "They were both naked, and were not ashamed." But as soon as their eyes were opened to the eating of the forbidden fruit, overcome with shame they sewed fig leaves together to cover those parts. This custom persists even today, so that these parts are not only covered but also adorned with added ornament or decoration, lest any ugliness appear in them, as Paul noted in the present passage.

units.la: Et cur idem non in alijs quoque membris fiat, docet: quia quae in nobis decora sunt, ijs decore aut ornatu alieno non est opus. Adhaec, ne quid hic temere fieri putemus, Dei constitutionem allegat, qui corpus nostrum ita temperauerit, ut membris quibus naturalis decor deest, copiosiorem tribuerit honorem. Docet hoc communis sensus, cuius non obscura indicia in barbaris etiam hominibus apparent, qui cum propter caeli clementiam, aut nimium calorem corpore nudi incedant, partes tamen illas velo aliquo velare consueuerunt. Unde colligimus in naturae leges peccaria[?] Cy-nicis illis, qui membra ista vel non tegunt, vel tegendo sic exprimunt, ut non situs modo illorum evidentior fit, verumetiam forma turpior appareat, quam si prorsus nudarentur. Regnat petulantia ista hodie passim inter viros & mulieres. Quis enim illorum brachas ignorat, quas vel pyramidum instar acuunt, vel ad formam belluini alicuius capitis effigiant, aut ea figura repraesentant, quam pictores diabolo affingere solent? Possunt foeditatem istam Turcae in Christianis hominibus detestari: at nostris principibus oculi desunt, quibus ista videant, imo utinam non ipsi quoque procul abiecto pudore idem facerent. De mulierum lasciuia pudet dicere, quae non sunt contentae mammas & femur quoq;, vestitu meretricio ostentasse, nisi incessu quoq; libidinem tam suam quam spectatorum suorum irritent. Sed sunt hi nouissimorum temporum mores, quibus olim finem imponet Dominus aduentu suo glorioso.
units.tr: He teaches why the same is not done with the other members as well: because those parts that are comely in us have no need of foreign decoration or ornament. Furthermore, lest we think anything here is done carelessly, he appeals to God's arrangement, who so tempered our body that he gave greater honour to the members that lack natural comeliness. Common sense teaches this, and its clear signs appear even among barbarian peoples who, though they go about naked because of the mildness of the climate or excessive heat, nonetheless are accustomed to cover those parts with some veil. From this we gather that the Cynics, who either leave these members uncovered or cover them in such a way that not only is their position more plainly visible but their shape appears uglier than if they were wholly bare, offend against the laws of nature. This wantonness reigns today everywhere among men and women. Who does not know the breeches that they either sharpen into the likeness of pyramids, or shape into the form of some monstrous head, or represent in that figure which painters are wont to give the devil? The Turks may detest this foulness in Christian men, but our princes lack eyes to see these things. Indeed, would that they themselves, having cast off all shame, did not do the same! I am ashamed to speak of the wantonness of women, who are not content to display their breasts and thighs in harlot's dress, unless by their very gait they also stir up lust, both their own and that of their onlookers. But these are the customs of the last times, which the Lord will bring to an end at his glorious coming.

units.la: Admonemur autem toto hoc loco, quid ijs debeamus, quorum multos pudet, qui Ecclesiae con-ditionem non recte considerant. Sunt inter illos praecipui, pauperes & peccatores. Utrumque istud hominum genus prae alijs curari debet. Nam quoad pauperes, iuuari debent, ne publica egestatis exempla fiant: quia si negligantur, id sine totius Ecclesiae ignominia fieri non potest. Discurrunt enim & passim quiritando duritiem accusant. Quod si vero ad Papistas usque excurrant, multiplex hic calumniandi occasio praebetur: nec possunt pro germanis Christi discipulis agnosci, qui fidei domesticos inopes atque famelicos oberrare patiuntur. Accedit his, quod ex mendicis fere ἀγύρται[?] vel inordinati illi homines prodeunt, qui omni tam Ecclesiasticae quam politicae disciplinae iugo excusso vagantur, & similes sui posteros generant, qui Christiani nominis labes & totius populis tandem oneri sunt. Ideo Deus olim mandauit, ne quis in Israel mendicus esset, ita vero egenis prospiceretur, ne ostiatim victum mendicare cogerentur. Quod quam diligenter obseruarit primitiua Ecclesia, alibi diximus. Meminisse ergo nos oportet, pauperes Ecclesiae & eiusdem nobiscum corporis membra esse, inhonestiora quidem mundi iudicio, sed talia quibus nos carere nullo modo possimus. Christi enim vox est, quam ex Lege repetitam promulgauit: Pauperes semper habebitis: & vt eos habeamus necesse est. Primum vt in illis occurrat semper Christi imago, qui pro nobis in hoc mundo egestatem & famem perpessus est. Deinde vt occasio nobis fit exer-cenda charitatis, quem ille discipulorum suorum tesseram esse dixit, ex qua agnosci possint. Deniq; vt in illis ipsum Christum nostra beneficentia recreare queamus, qui se in suas rationes adscribe-re velle pollicetur, quicquid in illos collatum fuerit. Quod ergo in velandis[?] & exornandis nostri corporis membris inhonestioribus facere solemus, id ipsum in pauperibus iuuandis atq; alendis fa-ciamus, ne egestas eorum nobis aut Ecclesiae totius fit dedecori.
units.tr: Throughout this passage, however, we are reminded what we owe to those whom many are ashamed of, those who do not rightly consider the condition of the Church. Among them the chief are the poor and the sinners. Each of these kinds of people ought to be cared for before others. As for the poor, they must be helped, lest they become public examples of want; for if they are neglected, this cannot happen without shame to the whole Church. They wander about everywhere, complaining loudly and accusing us of hardness. And if they run as far as the Papists, a manifold occasion for slander is given; nor can those be recognised as true disciples of Christ who allow the needy and the hungry of their own faith to wander about. Added to this is that from beggars there often come forth vagrant beggars [ἀγύρται] and disorderly men who, having shaken off the yoke of all church and civil discipline, wander about and beget offspring like themselves, who in the end become a stain on the Christian name and a burden to the whole people. Therefore God once commanded that there be no beggar in Israel, and that the needy be so provided for that they would not be forced to beg food from door to door. How diligently the primitive Church observed this, we have said elsewhere. We ought therefore to remember that the poor are members of the Church and of the same body as ourselves, more unseemly indeed in the judgement of the world, but such that we can in no way do without them. For it is Christ's word, which he repeated from the Law and proclaimed: "You will always have the poor, and it is necessary that we have them." First, so that the image of Christ may always meet us in them, who for our sake suffered want and hunger in this world. Second, so that an occasion may be given us to exercise charity, which he called the token of his disciples by which they may be recognised. Finally, so that by our kindness we may refresh Christ himself in them, who promises that he will count to his own account whatever is bestowed upon them. What we are wont to do in covering and adorning the more unseemly members of our body, let us do the same in helping and feeding the poor, so that their want may not be a disgrace to us or to the whole Church.

units.la: Quoad vero peccatores & aliquo graviori delicto infames, magna quidem peccati turpitudo est, cuius illos ipsos tandem pudet, qui aliquando suis desiderijs licentius indulgent. Quam ob rem Paulus recte dicebat: Quem fructum habebatis ex ijs, de quibus nunc erubescitis? Et supra audi-imus, flagitia publica lustu[?] etiam publico prosequenda esse. Verumtamen charitatis est illa non odiose divulgare, sed tegere potius, quoad eius potest fieri, & amicis admonitionibus corrigere, adhaec consolationibus eos confirmare, quos illorum cognitione iam perculsos & territos esse videmus.
