Et hic in Ecclesia admonitionum quoque publicarum & increpationum scopus esse debet. Quod si qui priuatim in nos peccauerunt, illis quoque offensam omnem condonare Christus iussit, & ipsi nos ad illud proprijs precibus obstringimus, dicentes: Remitte nobis debita nostra, sicut & nos remittimus debitoribus nostris. Neque id facere cuiquam graue aut iniquum videtur. Nam qui nos iniuria affecit, aut frater est, aut à fide & religione vera alienus. Quod si frater est, eum vlcisci non potes, nisi teipsum laedas, aut saltem aliqua infamia notam tibi aspergas. Quod si Christi ignarus totus, prophanus est, quid mirum est, si petulantius & insolentius tecum egerit? De Socrate fertur, cum per forum ambulanti quidam colaphum impegisset, & amici proteruum illum in ius trahere iuberent, illum respondisse. Et quid mihi faciendum esse censeretis ô boni, si me asinus calce ferijsset? an hunc quoque apud iudices accusare deberem? Videbat sapiens vir, hominem absque ratione proteru[?]entem nihil ab asino differre. Quid ergo nos de ijs sentire oportet, qui religionis quoque cura nulla ducuntur? Quia tamen Paulo de ijs sermo est, qui Ecclesiae nobiscum membra sunt, eos amore prosequamur tunc quoque, quando aliquid sua professione indignum fecerunt, & curemus ne ipsorum nomen atque fama per nos in periculum grauius adducatur.
units.tr: As for sinners, and those notorious for some more serious offence, there is indeed great shamefulness in sin, of which those very men are at last ashamed, who once indulged their desires rather licentiously. For this reason Paul rightly said: "What fruit did you have from those things of which you now are ashamed?" And above we heard that public scandals must also be pursued with public mourning. Nevertheless, it is the mark of charity not to spread them abroad with hatred, but rather to cover them, as far as that can be done, and to correct them with friendly admonitions, and moreover to strengthen with consolations those whom we see already struck down and terrified by the knowledge of their fault. And here in the Church public admonitions and rebukes ought also to have their aim. If some have sinned against us privately, Christ also commanded us to pardon every offence to them, and we ourselves bind ourselves to this by our own prayers, saying: "Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors." Nor does this seem hard or unjust to anyone. For whoever has wronged us is either a brother or a stranger to the true faith and religion. If he is a brother, you cannot take vengeance on him without harming yourself, or at least without staining yourself with some infamy. But if he is wholly ignorant of Christ and profane, what wonder is it if he has dealt with you more wantonly and insolently? It is related of Socrates that when someone had struck him with a blow as he walked through the marketplace, and his friends urged him to drag the shameless fellow into court, he replied: "And what do you think I ought to do, good sirs, if an ass had kicked me? Ought I to accuse this creature too before the judges?" The wise man saw that a man who acts shamelessly without reason differs in no way from an ass. What then ought we to think of those who are not moved by any concern for religion? Yet since Paul is speaking of those who are members of the Church along with us, let us love them even when they have done something unworthy of their profession, and let us take care that through us their name and reputation are not brought into greater danger.

units.la: Sed praestat finem huius doctrinae inspicere, quem Apostolus his verbis indicat: Vt ne sit dis-sidium[?] in corpore, sed membra idem curent alia pro alijs. Subest his argumentum à necessario: Si enim mutua haec cura & solicitudine opus est, ne scisma fiat, id omnino fiat oportet, vbi illa negligitur. At scisma inter membra fieri non potest absque totius corporis destructione. Ergo illud necessario cauere debent, qui corporis saluti consulere volunt. Vidit hoc ipsum olim Menenius Agrippa, quando populum Romanum, qui secessionem ex vrbe fecerat, apologo simili de membris corporis humani cum ventre dissidentibus, rursus cum Patribus conciliauit. Quod ideo commemoramus, vt tanto maior sit apud nos huius doctrinae authoritas, quando gentes illam agnoscere potuerunt. Etenim eandem esse Ecclesiae & Reipub. conditionem, quae corporis & membrorum est, Christus docet his verbis: Omne regnum partitum aduersus sese vastatur: & domus aduersus sese partita, cadit. Et notum est illud Pauli: Si alius alium mordetis & devoratis, videte ne vicissim alius ab alio consumamini. Exempla, quibus hoc confirmatur, passim in historijs occurrunt, & vtinam non hodie iam sentiremus cum praesenti potentissimarum nationum & inter has agentium Ecclesiarum periculo.
units.tr: But it is worth looking at the aim of this teaching, which the Apostle indicates in these words: "That there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another." There is an argument from necessity here: if this mutual care and concern is needed so that no schism arises, then surely it must occur where that care is neglected. But a schism among the members cannot occur without the destruction of the whole body. Therefore those who wish to provide for the health of the body must necessarily guard against it. Menenius Agrippa saw this same thing long ago, when he reconciled the Roman people, who had seceded from the city, with the Fathers again by a similar fable about the members of the human body quarrelling with the belly. We mention this so that the authority of this teaching may be all the greater among us, since even the Gentiles were able to recognise it. Indeed, Christ teaches that the condition of the Church and of the commonwealth is the same as that of the body and its members, in these words: "Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a house divided against itself falls." And that saying of Paul is well known: "If you bite and devour one another, take care lest you are consumed by one another in turn." Examples confirming this occur everywhere in histories; and would that we did not already feel it today, with the present danger to the most powerful nations and to the Churches acting among them.

units.la: Est ergo diligenter nobis obseruandum Apostoli de vitandis dissidijs consilium, quod sub-ijcit: Membra idem curent alia pro alijs. Et mox infert: Itaque siue patitur vnum membrum, si-mul dolent omnia membra: siue honore afficitur vnum membrum, simul gaudent omnia membra. Duo praecipit. Primum, vt alij aliorum curam habeant, & non arbitrentur aliorum res nihil ad se pertinere. Cur enim hoc sibi aliquis persuadeat, cum eadem omnium origo, eadem natura, & ijsdem omnes casibus obnoxij simus, nec aliquis sibi ipsi possit sufficere? Imo vt membrum pereat oportet, & simul alia quoque perdat, quod sua quasi statione relicta opem quam alijs debet, negat: Ita seipsos & alios in periculum adducunt, quotquot alios omnes negligunt, & sibi soli viuere instituunt. Quapropter alterum quoq; præcipit Apostolus, quo hîc imprimis opus est: συμπα-θεαν nimirum: siue compassionem, qua fit, vt alius aliorum commodis atq; incommodis afficiatur. Et huius quoque typum in corporis humani atque membrorum constitutione proponit. Siue (inquit) patitur vnum membrum, simul dolent omnia membra: siue honore afficitur vnum membrum, simul gaudent omnia membra. Indefinitè loquitur, vt simul membra omnia & quæcunque his accidere solent comprehendat. Est autem omnibus notum quod hîc dicitur, & in semetipsis singuli quotidie ista experiuntur. Etenim si pes offenderit, aut eius planta spina infixa hæreat, mox omnia corporis membra ad opem ferendam properant. Incuruatur dorsum, vt caput ad pedem se propius possit demittere, manus eundè molliter contrectat, intuentur loci affectum oculi, fœtorem eius nares non fastidiunt. Similiter si oculus periclitetur, manus clypei loco sese obtendunt: & eadè tanto studio membris omnibus adsunt, vt in prouerbiû ea res abierit: Vbi dolor, ibi manus. Non autem ista modò obseruari vult Paulus, sed dum membra in se mutuo συμπάσχειν, id est, συγχαίρειν [?] compati vel condolere & congaudere scribit, non obscurè innuit, affectiones illas corporis ad ipsum quoque animum pertingere. Etenim cruciatus membrorum animo dolorem afferre, & ideo nobis horrori esse, nemo est qui non in semetipso sentiat. Vicissim animo dolente, ex præcordijs & pulmonibus suspiria siue gemitus ducuntur, collachrymantur oculi, debilitatur caput, cibos fastidit stomachus, corpus denique totum languet, & melancholia frequenter letales morbi surgunt. Quòd si animo bene sit & gaudio exultet, mox gaudij ista signa in vultu, sermone, incessu & gestibus apparent. Ideo à Salomone non minus vere quam pru-denter dictum est: Cor lætum bonam parit valetudinem, mens autem tristis exiccat ossa. Vt ergo hoc ipsum inter homines Christianos obseruari Apostolus, vt nimirum alij aliorum damnis atque ægritudinibus afficiantur, & rursus aliorum quoque gaudijs gaudeant. Est hæc causa amoris mutui, & verissima amicitiarum conciliatrix inter eos etiam, qui prius sibi mutuò vix noti erant. Vbi verò secus fit, ibi simultates glisceunt, odia accenduntur, & hæc tandem in apertas inimicitias & dissidia cum publico Ecclesiæ malo erumpunt. Vitabunt hæc omnia facilè, qui diligentius cogitant, quàm arctâ cognatione homines inter se Deus constrinxerit. Potuerunt hanc obseruare qui inter gentes mentis oculos paulò altius extulerunt in eorum considerationem, quæ nos facere decet. Etenim memorabilis est M. Antonini Imperatoris sententia, quam contra eos differens, qui aliorum vel ingratitudine vel malitia se à benefaciendo & amando auocari sinunt, inter alia sic scribit: Ego, qui naturam boni perspectam habeo, quòd honestum sit, & mali quòd turpe sit, ipsamq; eius qui peccat naturam, quod mihi sit cognata (non quia eiusdem carnis est aut seminis, sed mentis & diuinæ particulæ particeps) à nullo eorum lædi possum. Neque enim in me turpitudinem aliquam quisquam coniiciet. Ei porrò quod mihi cognatum est, neque irasci possum, neque infensus esse: Vt enim vnus alterum iuuaret in suo opere, eò nati sumus, vt manus, vt pedes, vt palpebræ, vt superiorum inferiorumq; dentium ordines. Quare contra naturam est, vt inuicè nobis repugnemus: atqui succensere & auersari se inuicè, id quidem est repugnare. Hæc Antoninus, qui in Christianos persecutionem aliquando mouerat, sentire & loqui potuit, quæ hodie à plerisque aut ignorantur, aut saltem contemnuntur, qui in Christi schola præ aliis profecisse videri volunt. Est ergo locus iste totus multa & diligenti consideratione dignissimus. Docet enim nos iudicare de nostri seculi moribus atque studijs, quando omnes fere homines sibi solis viuunt, sibi prospiciunt, alios verò periclitantes securi negligunt, vt non tam Christianæ cognationis quàm humanitatis atque communis sensus obliti esse videri possint. Quid verò de priuatis multorum calamitatibus dico, quæ paucissimos mouent, quando plerique Ecclesiarum ruinas & quæ passim toti nomini Christiano incumbunt pericula siccis oculis intuentur? Et hi quidem optimi sunt, si cum illis conferantur, qui insuper periclitantibus insultant, & afflictis afflictionem addunt. Isti verò quid aliud faciunt, quàm quod Christum in cruce pendentem aceto & felle potant? Meditemur ergo diligenter ô fratres, quid per corporis nostri fabricam nos Dei prouidentia doceat: & cùm nos eodem necessitatis atque naturæ vinculo obstrictos esse conflet, nemo alterum vt nihil ad se pertinentem negligat, sed quisque alium se præstantiorem putet, aliorum commodis studeat, afflictis autem & calamitosis condoleat: potissima autem nobis cura sit, ne Ecclesiae unitatem aemulatione aut contendendi libidine, aut superbo aliorum contemptu scindamus: sed itidem affecti: eandem charitatem habeamus idemque sentiamus in CHRISTO IESV, Domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: We must therefore carefully observe the Apostle's advice about avoiding divisions, which he adds: "Let the members have the same care one for another." He then infers: "And so, if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; if one member is honoured, all the members rejoice with it." He gives two instructions. The first is that they should each care for the others and not think that the affairs of others have nothing to do with them. For why should anyone persuade himself of this, since all of us have the same origin and the same nature, are all subject to the same misfortunes, and no one can be wholly self-sufficient? Indeed, if a member withholds the help it owes to the others, as though it had left its place, it must perish, and at the same time destroy the others as well. So those who neglect all others and resolve to live for themselves alone bring both themselves and others into danger. Therefore the Apostle also prescribes a second thing, which is especially needed here: namely sympathy [συμπάθειαν], or compassion, by which one person is affected by the advantages and disadvantages of another. He sets forth a figure of this too in the structure of the human body and its members. "If one member suffers," he says, "all the members suffer with it; if one member is honoured, all the members rejoice with it." He speaks indefinitely, so as to include all the members together and whatever usually happens to them. Everyone knows what is said here, and each of us experiences these things every day in himself. For if a foot strikes something, or a thorn sticks in its sole, at once all the parts of the body hasten to bring help. The back bends so that the head can lower itself closer to the foot; the hand gently handles the place; the eyes look at the condition of the spot; the nostrils do not shrink from its stench. Likewise, if the eye is in danger, the hands present themselves as a shield; and they attend to all the members with such zeal that the matter has passed into the proverb: "Where there is pain, there is the hand." Paul wishes us to observe not only this, but when he writes that the members suffer together [συμπάσχειν], that is, rejoice together [συγχαίρειν], to be compassionate or to grieve with one another and to rejoice with one another, he clearly hints that those bodily feelings reach the mind itself as well. Indeed, no one fails to feel in himself that the pains of the members bring sorrow to the mind, and for this reason are dreadful to us. In turn, when the mind grieves, sighs and groans are drawn up from the heart and lungs, the eyes shed tears together, the head grows weak, the stomach loathes food, and finally the whole body languishes; and often deadly diseases arise from melancholy. But if the mind is well and exults with joy, at once the signs of joy appear in the face, speech, gait and gestures. Therefore Solomon said, no less truly than wisely: "A cheerful heart makes good health, but a sad mind dries up the bones." Thus the Apostle wishes this same thing to be observed among Christian people: that some should be affected by the losses and sicknesses of others, and in turn should rejoice in the joys of others as well. This is the cause of mutual love, and the truest reconciler of friendships, even among those who previously were hardly known to one another. Where it happens otherwise, there enmities grow, hatreds are kindled, and at last these break out into open hostility and quarrels, to the public harm of the Church. All these things will be easily avoided by those who think more carefully how closely God has bound men to one another by kinship. Those among the Gentiles who lifted the eyes of their minds somewhat higher to the consideration of what we ought to do could observe this. Indeed, the saying of the Emperor Marcus Antoninus is memorable, which, in arguing against those who allow themselves to be called away from doing good and loving others by the ingratitude or malice of others, he writes among other things as follows: "I, who have a clear view that the nature of the good is what is honourable, and the nature of evil is what is shameful, and that the nature of the one who does wrong is akin to mine (not because it is of the same flesh or seed, but because it shares in the same mind and a particle of the divine), cannot be harmed by any of them. For no one will bring any disgrace upon me. Nor can I be angry with or hostile to what is akin to me. For we were born to help one another in our work, just as the hands, the feet, the eyelids, and the rows of upper and lower teeth. Therefore it is against nature that we should oppose one another; yet to be angry with and turn away from one another is surely to oppose." So wrote Antoninus, who at one time had stirred up persecution against the Christians, and he was able to feel and speak these things, which today are either unknown to many people, or at least despised, though they wish to seem to have made progress above others in the school of Christ. This passage, then, is altogether most worthy of much and careful consideration. For it teaches us to judge the morals and pursuits of our own age, when nearly all men live for themselves alone, look out for themselves, and carelessly neglect others who are in danger, so that they may seem to have forgotten not so much the Christian kinship as humanity itself and the common feeling. But why do I speak of the private calamities of many, which move very few, when most people look upon the ruin of the Churches, and the dangers that hang everywhere over the whole Christian name, with dry eyes? And these indeed are the best, if they are compared with those who moreover mock those in danger and add affliction to the afflicted. But what else do these men do than give Christ, hanging on the cross, vinegar and gall to drink? Let us therefore, brothers, diligently meditate on what God's providence teaches us through the structure of our body. Since it is clear that we are bound by the same chain of necessity and nature, let no one neglect another as if he had nothing to do with him; rather let each consider the other more excellent than himself, seek the advantage of others, and grieve with the afflicted and the calamitous. Let our chief care be that we do not rend the unity of the Church through rivalry or a lust for contention, or through proud contempt of others; but, being similarly disposed, let us have the same love and think the same in CHRIST JESUS, our Lord, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY LXVI.

units.la: Vos autem estis corpus Christi, & membra ex parte. Et alios quidem constituit Deus in Ecclesia primum Apostolos, deinde Prophetas, tertio Doctores: inde Potestates, deinde dona sanationum, opitulationes, gubernationes, genera linguarum. Num omnes Apostoli? num omnes Prophetae? num omnes Doctores? num omnes sunt Potestates? num omnes donum habent sanationum? num omnes linguis loquuntur? num omnes interpretantur?
units.tr: But you are the body of Christ, and members in part. And God has indeed set some in the Church: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers; then powers, then gifts of healing, helps, governments, and kinds of tongues. Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all have powers? Do all have the gift of healing? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?

units.la: Exposuit hucusque Paulus diligenter parabolam de corpore humano & membrorū eius con-sensu. Summa illius est, illud etiamsi ex multis membris constet, vnicum tamen esse, mem-bra autem ista inter se vnitatem & concordiam colere, adeò vt nullum alteri inuideat, nullum aduersus alterum insurgat, sed potius alia alijs condolere & congaudere: Omnia vero ista in eum finem dicuntur, vt doceat, idem omnino inter homines Christianos obseruari debere, ne propter donorum & functionum diuersitatem inter se scindantur, sed potius vnanimi studio in commune deponant quicquid à Domino acceperunt, & ita officijs mutuis Ecclesiam adiuuent atque conser-uent. Caeterum poterant ad ista Corinthij obijcere: Multis tu quidem ô Paule, ista declamas & vrges: quid vero illa ad nos? Etenim fiunt ista in humano corpore motu quodam naturali, cu-ius ratio non alia afferri potest, nisi quòd vna est atque continua totius corporis omniumq; e-ius membrorum essentia atque connexio, quodque ab vnius mentis consilio omnia illa dependent. Atqui longè alia est ratio hominum, inter quos nihil huius est videre. Nam vt personis se-parati & distincti sumus: ita singuli suo etiam sensu abundant, & non alienae, sed propriae men-tis consilio atq; motu feruntur, nec temere proverbio dicitur: Quot homines, tot sententiae, suus cuiq; mos est. Itaq; Paulus quae dixit, nunc causae praesenti applicat.
units.tr: Paul has so far carefully set out the parable of the human body and the harmony of its members. Its sum is this: though it is made up of many members, it is nevertheless one, and these members cultivate unity and concord among themselves, so that none envies another, none rises against another, but rather they grieve with one another and rejoice with one another. All these things are said with this aim, that he may teach that the same thing ought to be observed among Christian men, so that they are not torn apart from one another by the diversity of gifts and offices, but rather, with united zeal, place in common whatever they have received from the Lord, and so help and preserve the Church by mutual services. Yet the Corinthians could object to this: "You, Paul, declaim and press these things on us many times; but what do they have to do with us?" For these things happen in the human body by a natural movement, the reason for which cannot be given other than that the essence and connection of the whole body and all its members is one and continuous, and that all those things depend on the counsel of one mind. But the situation of men is quite different, and nothing of this kind can be seen among them. For, just as we are separate and distinct in persons, so each one also abounds in his own feeling, and is moved not by the counsel and motion of another mind but of his own. Nor is it said for nothing in the proverb: "As many men, so many opinions; each has his own way." Therefore Paul now applies to the present case what he has said.

units.la: Vos autem (inquit) estis corpus Christi, & membra ex parte. Quae verba cum ijs, quae prae-cesserunt, sic cohaerent, vt argumentum ex illis eiusmodi formare possis: Quotquot corpus sunt vnum, ij vt membra inter se vnitati & concordiae studere debent, neque aliquam ob causam te-mere scindi: Vos estis corpus Christi, & ex parte membra, nimirum Christi & corporis eius, pro-ut cuique datum est pro sui muneris aut officij ratione: Ergo vnanimi consensu vnitatem cole-re debetis, vt neque inuidia vel odio, neque superbo aut insolenti aliorum contemptu à vobis in-uicem diuellamini. Si enim naturae tanta vis est in omnium animantium corporibus, vt membra inter se consentiant, quanto maior esse debet gratiae & Spiritus Dei, qui in credentibus a-git? Dicitur autem Ecclesia corpus Christi, quia hic illius caput est, ex quo singuli fideles spi-ritum vitae, lucis verae cognitionem, motum denique & bene operandi vires hauriunt. Ex quo sequitur, impios & quotquot à fide alieni sunt, non esse Ecclesiae membra, etiamsi in eius externa societate agant. Vt enim membrum corporis non amplius dici meretur, quod arefactum aut mortuum non communicat cum spiritu vitali, qui per omnia corporis membra diffunditur: ita fieri non potest, vt Ecclesiae & Christi membrum sit ille, in quo Christus non agit suo Spiritu, quiq; vitae illius communis, quam credentes ex illo hauriunt, non est particeps. Debent hoc omnes diligenter expendere ne seipsos inani professionis externa fiducia decipiant, & hoc ad salu-tem sufficere putent, si propter Sacramentorum communionem inter Ecclesiae cives censeantur. Confutatur etiam hic Anabaptistarum error, qui pios & vere credentes pollui putant, si in Sacramentorum usu cum impijs aut incurabilibus hypocritis communicent. Quia enim hi non sunt germana Ecclesiae membra, non poterit ipsorum improbitas illis fraudi esse, qui vera fide praediti sunt, & Christi Spiritu ducuntur.
units.tr: "But you," he says, "are the body of Christ, and members in part." These words so cohere with what went before that you can form from them an argument of this kind: All who are one body ought, as members, to strive for unity and concord among themselves, and not be torn apart for any reason at random. You are the body of Christ, and members in part, namely of Christ and of his body, according as each has been given according to the nature of his gift or office. Therefore you ought to cultivate unity with one consent, so that you are not pulled apart from one another by envy or hatred, or by proud or insolent contempt of others. For if nature has such power in the bodies of all living things that the members agree among themselves, how much greater ought the grace and Spirit of God to be, who works in believers? The Church is called the body of Christ because he is its head, from whom individual believers draw the spirit of life, the knowledge of the true light, and finally motion and the power to do good works. It follows from this that the impious, and all who are alien from faith, are not members of the Church, even if they take part in its external fellowship. For just as a part of the body no longer deserves to be called a member if it has dried up or died and no longer shares in the vital spirit that flows through all the members of the body, so it cannot be that he in whom Christ does not work by his Spirit, and who does not share in that common life which believers draw from him, is a member of the Church and of Christ. All should weigh this carefully, lest they deceive themselves with the empty confidence of an outward profession, and think it enough for salvation to be counted among the citizens of the Church because of communion in the sacraments. Here also the error of the Anabaptists is refuted, who think that the godly and truly believing are defiled if they communicate in the use of the sacraments with the ungodly or with incurable hypocrites. For since these are not true members of the Church, their wickedness cannot harm those who are endowed with true faith and are led by the Spirit of Christ.

units.la: Caeterum praestat hoc loco diligentius considerare incredibilem Dei bonitatem, qui homines in tam sublimem dignitatem euexit, ut Filij sui vnigeniti corpus & membra dicantur. Etenim ne coeli quidem illum capiunt, & (ut Propheta canit) eius gloria atque maiestas coelis sublimior est. Idem tamen se eo usque demittit, ut nos inhabitare dignetur, & nos templum sibi faciat. Dictum de hoc supra cap. sexto. At non contentus hac nos dignitate exornauisse, insuper nos Filio suo despondit, ut sicuti per coniugium duo fiunt una caro: ita nos cum CHRISTO IESV coalescamus, imo eius corpus simus, os ex ossibus eius, & caro ex carne eius, ut ad Ephesios Paulus scribit. Hoc ut mysterium est excellentissimum, quod captum humani ingenij omnem superat: ita beneficium quoque est, cui explicando & praedicando nulla hominis eloquentia sufficit. Finge Regem aliquem potentissimum uxorem sibi deligere humili & obscuro loco natam, quam sincero amore completatur, & dignitatis suae bonorumq; omnium consortem habeat. Quis non hoc factum admirabitur? Quis illius bonitatem non praedicabit? Attamen hoc ipsum nihil fuerit, si cum hac Dei bonitate conferatur. Illic enim fortunarum modo diversitas est, eadem autem est natura utrinque, cum utraque homo sit, & vel forma, vel morum similitudo, aut virtutum pulcherrimarum consideratio principem movere potest, ut talem potius quam inani natalium & divitiarum splendore superbientem sibi desponsare velit. At si nos cum Deo conferas, nihil horum reperies. Nos enim variis casibus obnoxij, omnium indigentes, mortales, adhaec iniusti, impuri, mendaces, & propter inhaerentem nobis naturae vitiositatem aeternis inferorum cruciatibus digni sumus, nec idonei, qui ex nobis ipsis aliquid vel cogitemus: Ille vero aeternus & extra omnem fortunae casum constitutus, adhaec bonorum omnium copiacorum, immortalis, iustus, sanctus, verax, ipsa denique iustitia atque veritas est, sibique ipsi solus ad omnia sufficit. Quid ergo illum movere potuit, ut nos infelices & impuris sanguinibus immersos (ut per Ezech.loquitur) eligeret, & sanguine Filij sui ablutos sibi desponsaret? Nihil certe praeter bonitatem & misericordiam, cuius simile exemplum nullum unquam Sol ipse spectavit. Seruiat ista consideratio nobis in omni tentationum genere, ut ex ea consolatione petamus. Quis enim de Dei clementia dubitet, aut nos ei minus curae esse arbitretur, qui nos tam arcto tamq; fido vinculo sibi copulauit?
units.tr: Moreover, it is better to consider here more carefully the incredible goodness of God, who has raised men to so high a dignity that they are called the body and members of his only-begotten Son. For the heavens do not even contain him, and (as the Prophet sings) his glory and majesty is higher than the heavens. Yet he still humbles himself so far as to deign to dwell in us and to make us his temple. This was spoken of above in chapter six. But not content to have adorned us with this dignity, he has moreover betrothed us to his Son, so that, just as through marriage two become one flesh, so we may be joined with Christ Jesus, indeed that we may be his body, bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh, as Paul writes to the Ephesians. As this is a most excellent mystery, which surpasses all the grasp of the human mind, so it is also a benefit for which no eloquence of man is sufficient to explain and proclaim it. Imagine some most powerful king choosing as his wife a woman born in a humble and obscure place, whom he cherishes with sincere love and makes a partner of his dignity and of all his goods. Who would not marvel at this deed? Who would not proclaim his kindness? Yet this would be nothing if it were compared with this goodness of God. For there the difference is only one of fortune, but the nature is the same on both sides, since both are human; and either the beauty or the similarity of character, or the consideration of the most excellent virtues, can move a prince to wish to betroth himself to such a woman rather than to one who is proud of the empty splendour of birth and riches. But if you compare us with God, you will find none of these things. For we are subject to various misfortunes, lacking all things, mortal, moreover unjust, impure, deceitful, and on account of the wickedness of nature inherent in us we are worthy of the eternal torments of hell, and we are not fit to think anything of ourselves. But he is eternal and placed beyond every chance of fortune, moreover possessed of all good things, immortal, just, holy, true, indeed justice and truth itself, and alone sufficient to himself for all things. What, then, could move him to choose us, wretched and immersed in impure blood (as he speaks through Ezekiel), and to betroth us to himself washed in the blood of his Son? Certainly nothing but goodness and mercy, whose like the sun itself has never seen. Let this consideration serve us in every kind of temptation, so that we may seek consolation from it. For who would doubt God's mercy, or think that we are of less concern to him, when he has joined us to himself with so close and so faithful a bond?

units.la: At simul nos ista officij admonere debent, quod in duobus potissimum consistit. Primum est, ut CHRISTO IESV, Filio Dei aeterno, fidem seruemus inuiolatam. Haec enim coniunctionis istius vinculum est, neq; aliud medium inuenitur, quo ille a nobis apprehendi & retineri possit. Seruant autem illi fidem, qui ut sponsum suum colunt & obseruant, qui ab illo uno pendent, & in ipso uno sibi reposita esse sciunt, quaecunque nobis ad salutem aeternam necessaria sunt. Quotquot ergo fiduciam salutis alio transferunt, & alios sibi seruatores atque vindices fingunt, siue illos ex viuentium siue defunctorum numero deligant, ij vinculum sanctissimi illius coniugij non tam scelerata quam sacrilega perfidia abrumpunt. Et haec spiritualis illa fornicatio est, de qua Deus frequenter per Prophetas cum Israelitarum gente expostulat, & propter quam dignos iudicauit, quos abdicatos horribili excidio perderet. Ut autem quae fidem coniugalem fallere suamque pudicitiam obscaenis amatoribus prostituere audent, simul rem domesticam foede dissipant: ita qui a Christo deficiunt & idololatriae atque superstitionum spiritu ducuntur, ijdem vitam viuunt ab illius spiritu alienam, & vel in omnem scelerum licentiam impudentissime effunduntur, vel impia hypocrisi Deo & hominibus fucum facere studeant. Quamuis ergo in externa Ecclesiae societate aliquem locum habeant, vera tamen illius membra non sunt, neque in Christi corpore censentur. Alterum est, ut singuli meminerint, se esse membra ex parte, id est, non eos esse, qui vel soli totum corpus constituant, vel sibi ipsis ad omnia sufficiant: sed aliorum opera indigere, quibus ipsi vicissim suam operam praestare debeant. Itaque Christiani hominis officium duabus his sese partibus comprehenditur, ut primum Christo, animarum nostrarum vnico sponso, fidelis sit: deinde ut per charitatem siue dilectionem omnibus pro sua virili seruiat atq; benefaciat.
units.tr: But at the same time these things ought to remind us of our duty, which consists mainly in two things. The first is that we keep faith inviolate with Christ Jesus, the eternal Son of God. For this is the bond of that union, and no other means is found by which he can be apprehended and retained by us. Those keep faith who honour and observe him as their bridegroom, who depend on him alone, and who know that whatever is necessary for us to eternal salvation has been laid up for them in him alone. Therefore, all who transfer their confidence of salvation to another, and invent for themselves other saviours and defenders, whether they choose them from the number of the living or of the dead, break the bond of that most holy marriage by a perfidy that is not so much wicked as sacrilegious. And this is that spiritual fornication, for which God often complains through the Prophets against the nation of Israel, and on account of which he judged them worthy to be cast off and destroyed by a dreadful destruction. And just as those who dare to betray the marriage faith and prostitute their chastity to obscene lovers at the same time foully ruin the household, so those who fall away from Christ and are led by the spirit of idolatry and superstitions likewise live a life alien to his Spirit, and either pour themselves out most shamelessly into every licence of crime, or strive to deceive God and men with impious hypocrisy. Therefore, although they have some place in the external fellowship of the Church, they are nonetheless not its true members, nor are they counted in the body of Christ. The second is that each remember that he is a member in part, that is, that he is not one who alone constitutes the whole body, or who is sufficient to himself for all things, but needs the work of others, to whom in turn he ought to render his own service. Thus the duty of a Christian man is comprised in these two parts: first, that he be faithful to Christ, the one spouse of our souls; then, that through charity, or love, he serve and do good to all, according to his strength.

units.la: Priusquam vero hinc discedamus, non inutile fuerit, Chrysostomi expositionem audire, qui postremum hoc membrum, Et estis membra ex parte: ad totam Corinthiorum Ecclesiam extendit, quasi hanc Paulus admoneat, ut meminerint, se non solos esse Christi Ecclesiam, sed membrum solummodo Ecclesiae illius universalis, quae per omnia tempora ab origine rerum usque ad finem seculi, per loca item omnia sive gentes & nationes omnes extenditur. Est sensus iste ab instituto Pauli non omnino alienus, & docet inter Ecclesias quoque non debere locum dari stultae & ambitiosae aemulationi, qua alia alij praeferatur, aut una aliqua in alias omnes sibi primatum vendicet. Est enim (ut saepe iam diximus) unica Christi Ecclesia, quam ideo Catholicam, id est, universalem dicimus, quia omnium seculorum atque locorum credentes complectitur. Huius membra maiora & generaliora (ut sic loquar) dici possunt Ecclesiae, quae per orbem terrarum dispersae locis distinguuntur. Inter istas quamuis interdum alia alijs praestet atque celebrior sit propter credentium multitudinem, praeclaras Spiritus Sancti dotes, & eximios, qui in ea sunt, Christi servos, id tamen perpetuum non est, neque aliqua sibi propterea apud posteros quoque eam laudem aut gradum debet vendicare. Solet enim Deus dotes illas saepe alio transferre, & subitas mutationes facere, ne Spiritum alicui loco astrictum aut alligatum esse putemus. Sic Apostolorum temporibus initio Hierosolymorum Ecclesia excelluit, cum in ea illi adhuc omnes docerent. Mox huic praeferri potuit Antiochena, quae (ut Lucas scribit) prophetis & doctoribus abundauit, & ex qua Paulus atque Barnabas per Spiritum vocati Euangelium inter gentes longe lateq; praedicauerunt. Sed & Paulus Macedonum Ecclesias, Thessalonicensem videlicet & Philippensem, prae aliis laudat. Posteris temporibus Alexandrina aliquandiu quam maxime floruit. Quid quod Hippo, non amplum neque nobile Africae oppidum, multis aliis praeferri meruit, cum illic D. Augustinus agens, omnes sui temporis episcopos doctrinae puritate, studio & diligentia vinceret? Et huius generis exempla plura enumerari possent, quae docent, Christum in terris hisce nullum sibi locum delegisse, in quo Ecclesiae suae perpetua & primaria sedes constitui debeat: quales in regnis huius mundi haberi solent. Id vero omnibus Ecclesijs proprium atque perpetuum est, quod CHRISTUM IESUM, caput & sponsum habent, & huius corpus atque membra sunt. Qui vero dominium & imperium in alias Ecclesias affectant, ij spiritu Antichristi aguntur, & huic viam sternunt. Imo, ut historia docens, ista aemulatio Antichristum nobis peperit. Viderunt hoc olim optimi quique, & ideo resistendum esse putarunt ijs, qui in Ecclesijs alienis nimium audebant. Sic Chrysostomus Ephi-phanio sese opposuit, viro alias docto & bene merito, quod in causa librorum Origenis per Ecclesias discurreret, & multa faceret contra Canones, Synodos cogendo & suffragia colligendo, in-consultis vel etiam inuitis legitimis Episcopis. Sed & Gregorius ille Magnus Ioanni Constantinopolitano, titulum universalis Patriarchae aut Episcopi ambienti, fortissimè restitit: & ad ipsum scripta epistola graviter monet, neminem praeter unum Christum debere universalem Episcopum dici, negatq; ullos ante se Episcopos hunc titulum usurpasse. Titulum item dicit esse nonum, stultum, superbum, peruersum, scelestum, prophanum: in quem consentire perinde sit atque fidem abnegare. Et rursus: Ego autem fideliter dico, quia quisquis se universalem Sacerdotem vocari, vel vocari desiderat, in elatione sua Antichristum praecurrit. Et hoc quidem ab eo verissime dictum est. Nam Ioannes ille Constantinopolitanus non multo post occasionem dedit Bonifacio III. ut honorem istum a Phoca impetraret, eoq; impetrato Antichristus fieret.
units.tr: Before we leave this point, it will not be unprofitable to hear Chrysostom's exposition, who extends this last clause, "And you are members in part," to the whole Corinthian Church, as if Paul were warning them to remember that they are not the only Church of Christ, but only a member of that universal Church, which extends through all times from the beginning of things to the end of the age, and likewise through all places, that is, all peoples and nations. This sense is not wholly foreign to Paul's purpose, and it teaches that among Churches too no place should be given to foolish and ambitious rivalry, by which one is preferred to another, or one Church claims the primacy over all the others. For there is (as we have often said already) one Church of Christ, which we call Catholic, that is, universal, because it embraces believers of all ages and places. Its members may be called, to speak so, the larger and more general Churches, which are scattered through the world and distinguished by their locations. Among these, although one sometimes surpasses the others and is more celebrated because of the number of believers, the outstanding gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the eminent servants of Christ who are in it, this is not permanent, and on that account no Church may claim that praise or rank for itself even with posterity. For God often transfers those gifts to another place and makes sudden changes, so that we may not think the Spirit is bound or tied to any place. Thus in the time of the Apostles the Church of Jerusalem excelled at the beginning, when all of them were still teaching in it. Soon the Church of Antioch could be preferred to it, which (as Luke writes) abounded in prophets and teachers, and from which Paul and Barnabas, called by the Spirit, preached the gospel far and wide among the Gentiles. But Paul also praises the Churches of Macedonia, namely those of Thessalonica and Philippi, above others. In later times the Church of Alexandria flourished for a while exceedingly. Why should I mention that Hippo, not a large or noble town of Africa, deserved to be preferred to many others, when Augustine, working there, surpassed all the bishops of his time in purity of teaching, zeal and diligence? Many other examples of this kind could be listed, which show that Christ has chosen for himself no place on these earth in which his Church ought to have a perpetual and chief seat, such as are usually held in the kingdoms of this world. What is proper and perpetual to all Churches is that they have Christ Jesus as their head and bridegroom, and are his body and members. But those who aspire to dominion and empire over other Churches are driven by the spirit of Antichrist and pave the way for him. Indeed, as history teaches, this rivalry has given birth to Antichrist for us. The best men of old saw this, and therefore thought that those who presumed too much in other people's Churches must be resisted. Thus Chrysostom opposed Epiphanius, a man otherwise learned and well deserving, because he ran about through the Churches in the cause of Origen's books and did much against the canons, convening synods and collecting votes, without consulting, or even against the wishes of, the lawful bishops. But also that great Gregory strongly resisted John of Constantinople, who was seeking the title of universal patriarch or bishop, and writing to him in a letter he admonishes him severely that no one except Christ alone ought to be called universal bishop, and he denies that any bishops before him had used this title. He also says that the title is profane, foolish, proud, perverse, wicked and impious, and that to consent to it is just as much as to deny the faith. And again: "I say faithfully that whoever wishes to be called, or is called, universal priest, runs before Antichrist in his pride." And this was said by him most truly. For that John of Constantinople, not long afterwards, gave occasion to Boniface III to obtain that honour from Phocas, and once it was obtained, he became Antichrist.

units.la: Sed redeamus ad Paulum, qui praecipua corporis huius mystici, Ecclesiae Christi nimirum, membra enumerat una cum suis ministerijs, ad quae destinata sint. Et alios quidem constituit Deus in Ecclesia, primum Apostolos, deinde Prophetas, &c. Quo loco ante omnia ordo debet observari, quo Apostolus in ista tractatione utitur. Huiusq; enim de donis spiritualibus disseruit, & membra etiam docuit esse diuersa. His nunc demum ministeria & functiones ecclesiasticas subijcit. Ita vero nos de ordine admonet, quem Deus solet observare, qui non ordinat Ecclesiae suae ministros, nisi quos prius donis necessarijs instruxit. Exempla, quae huc faciunt, passim habentur in Mose, Aarone, Bezaleele, prophetis deniq; Veteris testamenti omnibus. Quibus Apostoli & Septuaginta illi discipuli adnumerari debent. Imo etsi Apostoli priusquam Christus moreretur, alii[?] quod prædicationis Euangelicæ tyrocinium inter Iudæos dedissent, eosdem tamen ab Hierofoly-ma discedere & inter gentes docere noluit, donec Spiritus donis ùberioribus abunde essent instructi. Obseruarunt præceptoris sui exemplum Apostoli in primitiua Ecclesia, sicuti in Matthia electione, Pauli item & Barnabæ missione ad gentes esse videre. Idem ergo hodie etiam obseruent, qui ius ordinandi ministros penes se esse volunt, ne quem muneri huic non minus periculoso quàm sancto & necessario destinent, nisi quem donis necessariis instructum esse norint. In eum enim Spiritus Sanctus ab Apostolis Canones certos describi voluit, non fictitios illos & superstitionum ineptissimarum plenos, quos aduersarij nostri pro tuenda Romani Pontificis authoritate nunquam non in ore habent, sed qui apud Paulum in priori ad Timoth. cap. 3. & ad Tit. 1. extant. Quibus merito adnumeraueris, quæ Petrus postremo cap. prioris suæ epistolæ tradidit.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who enumerates the chief members of this mystical body, that is, of Christ's Church, together with their ministries, for which they are appointed. "And God indeed has set some in the Church: first apostles, second prophets, etc." In this passage the order which the Apostle uses in this discussion must above all be observed. For he has discussed the spiritual gifts and has also taught that the members are diverse. Now at last he subjoins the ministries and ecclesiastical functions to these. He thus reminds us of the order which God usually observes, who does not appoint ministers for his Church unless he has first furnished them with the necessary gifts. Examples that bear on this are found everywhere in Moses, Aaron, Bezaleel, and finally in all the prophets of the Old Testament. To these the Apostles and those seventy disciples must be added. Indeed, although the Apostles, before Christ died, had given their first practice in evangelical preaching among the Jews, he nevertheless did not want them to depart from Jerusalem and teach among the Gentiles until they were abundantly instructed with richer gifts of the Spirit. The Apostles in the primitive Church followed the example of their teacher, as is seen in the choice of Matthias and in the sending of Paul and Barnabas to the Gentiles. Let those therefore who want the right of ordaining ministers to rest with them observe the same today, so that they do not appoint to this office, which is no less dangerous than holy and necessary, anyone whom they do not know to be instructed with the necessary gifts. For the Holy Spirit wanted the Apostles to set down certain fixed canons for this, not those fictitious ones full of most foolish superstitions, which our adversaries always have in their mouths to defend the authority of the Roman Pontiff, but those which are found in Paul, in the first epistle to Timothy, chapter 3, and in Titus 1. To these may rightly be added what Peter delivered in the last chapter of his first epistle.

units.la: Arguunt ista phanaticorum quorundam impudentiam atque temeritatem, qui cum neque literas norint, neque fidei dogmata ex ordine teneant, ad docendum excurrunt. Et imprimis Anabapti-starum furores locus iste confutat, qui veterem Ecclesiarum morem reductum volunt, quo sæpe plu-res in cœtibus sacris prophetabant ex ordine, neque vident dona illa iampridem cessauisse, quibus Ecclesia tunc floruit. Quia enim ministeria cum donis suis coniuncta vult esse Deus, nemo ad illa aspirare debet, qui non hæc prius sit assecutus. Sed videamus, quæ nam ministeria illa aut functiones sint, quibus Ecclesia olim opus habuit, & quæ hodie etiam retineri debent.
units.tr: These things expose the impudence and rashness of certain fanatics, who, although they know neither letters nor the doctrines of the faith in order, rush forth to teach. And above all this passage refutes the madness of the Anabaptists, who want the ancient custom of the Churches restored, by which often several in the sacred assemblies prophesied in turn, and who do not see that those gifts by which the Church then flourished have long since ceased. For since God wills ministries to be joined with their gifts, no one ought to aspire to them who has not first obtained these. But let us see what those ministries or functions are, which the Church once needed and which should still be retained today.

units.la: Primus locus Apostolis tribuitur, non quidem aliquo ambitionis affectu, sed quia olim per hoc prædicationis initium fieri oportuit. Nomen habent à mittendo, quia IESV CHRISTI legati fuerunt, quos ad omnes gentes per totum orbem proficisci oportuit, ut vbiq; rerum ab illo gestarum testes essent, & Ecclesias passim nouas plantarent. Sub his in præsenti Paulus Euangelistas quoq; comprehendit, quorum peculiarem mentionem facit ad Ephef. 4. cap. Et illis quidem olim opus fuit, quando ne nomen quidem Christi notum erat gentibus: hodie non item, cum Euangelij doctrina totum orbem personuerit, neq; si illis opus sit, ab aliquo ordinari possunt, eò quòd tales donis linguarum & miraculorum instructos esse oportet, quæ neq; ab homine dari, neq; propria industria acquiri possunt. Quòd si Deo ita visum fuerit, ut Euangelij buccina adhuc semel totus terrarum orbis ante nouissimum Christi finem ad pœnitentiam & fidem veram excitetur, facile ei fuerit deligere, quos ad tantum munus idoneos faciat. Nunc autem obseruemus, quàm impudenter Romani Pontifices cum suis Cardinalibus & Episcopis Apostolicorum nomen sibi arrogent, dum Petri successores dici volunt, in cuius cathedra ipsi sedeant. Atqui cum certis locis illi sedeant, qua ratione eorum titulos vsurpant, qui quòd legati essent, ita dici meruerunt? Fingunt quidem Petrum totis annis viginti quatuor Romæ resedisse: sed atrocem illi faciunt iniuriam: quia hoc præter omne officium fecisset, cum eodem quo alij Apostoli mandato esset obstrictus. Sed ipsa Actorum Apostolicorum serie figmentum hoc facile cõfutatur, ut alibi demonstrauimus.
units.tr: The first place is given to the Apostles, not indeed from any motive of ambition, but because by them the beginning of preaching had to be made in former times. They have their name from being sent, because they were the legates of Jesus Christ, whom it was necessary to send to all nations throughout the whole world, so that they might be witnesses everywhere of the things done by him, and might plant new Churches in many places. Under these, for the present, Paul also includes the evangelists, whom he mentions specifically in Ephesians, chapter 4. Indeed there was once need of them, when not even the name of Christ was known to the Gentiles; today it is not so, since the teaching of the gospel has resounded through the whole world, and if there were need of them, they could not be ordained by anyone, because such men must be furnished with gifts of tongues and miracles, which can be given neither by man nor acquired by one's own industry. But if it should seem good to God that the whole circle of the earth should once more be roused to repentance and true faith by the trumpet of the gospel before the last end of Christ, it will be easy for him to choose those whom he makes fit for so great a task. Now, however, let us observe how shamelessly the Roman Pontiffs, with their cardinals and bishops, claim for themselves the name of Apostolic, while they want to be called successors of Peter, in whose chair they sit. Yet since they sit in certain places, by what reasoning do they usurp the titles of those who were called such because they were legates? They indeed invent that Peter sat at Rome for twenty-four whole years, but they do him a grievous injury, because he would have done this beyond all his duty, since he was bound by the same commission as the other Apostles. But this fiction is easily refuted by the very sequence of the Acts of the Apostles, as we have demonstrated elsewhere.

units.la: Secundo loco Prophetæ collocantur. Dicuntur hi proprie vates, qui spiritu vaticinandi prædicti[?] de futuris & cognitu necessarijs admonent, quo dono veterem Ecclesiam floruisse, iam sæpe diximus. At quia in hoc catalogo nullam facit Paulus pastorum mentionem, quos in epistola ad Ephesios Apostolis & Euangelistis proximè subijcit, Prophetæ nomen hic generalius accipi debere videtur (ut etiam infra cap. 14.) ut nimirum sub eo ordinarios Ecclesiæ Episcopos & pastores comprehendamus, qui populo à sacris concionibus sunt, & Scripturarum arcana dextrè enucleando omnia pro temporum & locorum ratione ad præsentem vsum accommodant. Et huic sensui fauent Commentarij, qui D. Hieronymo tribuuntur. In illis enim sic legimus: Prophetæ sunt, qui explanant obscura Prophetarum, & qui homines exhortantur, sicut alibi dicit: Nam qui prophetat, hominibus loquitur ædificationem, exhortationem & consolationem. Et istis quidem perpetuò opus est, ideoq; Apostoli in Ecclesijs abs sese collectis & plantatis episcopos & seniores constituisse leguntur. Vide Actor. 14. Tit. 1.
units.tr: Secondly, the prophets are placed. These are properly called seers, who, endowed with the Spirit of prophecy, warn of future things and of things needful to know. We have often said that the ancient Church flourished with this gift. But since Paul makes no mention of ministers in this list, whom in the epistle to the Ephesians he places immediately after the apostles and evangelists, the name prophets seems to be taken here more generally (as also below, chap. 14), so that under it we understand the ordinary bishops and ministers of the Church, who preach to the people in the sacred sermons and, by expounding the hidden things of Scripture rightly, adapt everything to present use according to time and place. The commentaries ascribed to St Jerome favour this sense. For there we read: "The prophets are those who explain the obscure things of the prophets, and who exhort men, as elsewhere it says: 'For he who prophesies speaks to men for edification, exhortation and consolation.'" And indeed the Church always has need of these, and therefore the apostles are read to have appointed bishops and elders in the churches they gathered and planted. See Acts 14; Titus 1.

units.la: Tertij in hoc catalogo Doctores sunt. Intelliguntur ij, qui in scholis agunt, & Scripturas scholastico more interpretantur. Fecerunt hoc olim Prophetæ, qui non publicè modo ad populum concionati sunt, verumetiam scholas & collegia instituerunt, in quibus priuatim discipulos instituebant, qui Prophetarum filij dicebantur: sicuti in Samuelis & Helisæi historia esse videre. Videbant enim sanctissimi homines quàm referret temporibus illis corruptissimis, quando Sacerdotes & Leuitæ in suo officio cessabant, aliquos à pueris institui, qui populum de Dei voluntate docerent. Et duravit mos iste inter Iudæos usque ad Apostolorum tempora, ut tunc quoque fuerint, qui Mosis legem diebus Sabbati in Synagogis exponerent: ut Iacobus Actorum 15.cap. testatur. Quem morem à Iudæis ad Christianos translatum postea fuisse, D. Ambrosius annotavit, & tam ex isto loco quàm alijs similibus satis evidenter apparet. Antiochenam certè Ecclesiam hoc potissimum nomine Lucas commendat, quòd doctores & Prophetæ eiusmodi plures in ea fuerint. In Alexandria quoque scholam fuisse legimus, in qua Panthemius, Clemens, Origenes & alij floruerunt. Et Nicomediæ schola atque collegium Christianæ iuuentutis fuit, in quo Iulianus institutus, postea ecclesiæ illius lector factus est. Itaque vetustissimum est in Ecclesijs scholarum publicarum institutum, & in hanc curam principes Christiani imprimis incumbere debebant, ut in celebrioribus Ecclesijs schola essent, in quibus religionis dogmata diligenter traderentur, & morum disciplina vigeret. Hæc enim fœcundissima sunt Ecclesiæ seminaria: quia ex his prodeunt non modò Verbi Dei prædones, verum etiam reipub. gubernatores, qui cum rerum usu atque prudentia pietatem coniunxerunt. At hodie plerique curam illam abs se alienam putant, & in re maximè necessaria sumptibus parcunt: utinam verò ijdem non fere Ecclesiarum redditus in usus prophanos, vel etiam inhonestos, transferrent. In scholis autem, quæ habentur, partim effrenis morum licentia regnat, cuius authores sunt non raro ipsi professores, qui ebrietati & intemperantiæediti suo exemplo Christo & Musis consecratos iuuenes corrumpunt: partim stulta & indocta ambitio dominatur. Qui enim non nisi titulotenus Doctores sunt, discipulos quoque sui similes faciunt, qui nihil præter inanes & pretio emptos titulos fastumque intolerabilem ad Ecclesiæ gubernacula adferunt. His maxima ex parte debemus collapsam ubique gentium disciplinam, immanem scelerum licentiam, & contentiones, quibus Ecclesiæ lacerantur, & religio Christiana impiorum ludibrijs exponitur. Orandus erg est Deus, ut ipse Doctores det fidos, & ut veterem Scholarum disciplinam instauret.
units.tr: Third in this list are teachers. These are understood to be those who work in schools and interpret the Scriptures in the scholastic manner. The prophets of old did this too, who not only preached publicly to the people but also established schools and colleges, in which they privately instructed disciples, who were called sons of the prophets, as can be seen in the histories of Samuel and Elisha. For the most holy men saw how much it mattered in those most corrupt times, when priests and Levites neglected their office, that some should be trained from boyhood to teach the people the will of God. This custom lasted among the Jews right down to the time of the apostles, so that even then there were those who expounded the law of Moses in the synagogues on the Sabbath days, as James testifies in Acts 15. That this custom was afterwards transferred from the Jews to the Christians, St Ambrose has noted, and it appears quite clearly both from that passage and from others like it. Luke certainly commends the church of Antioch chiefly on this account, because there were many teachers and prophets of this kind in it. We read also that there was a school in Alexandria, in which Pantaenus, Clement, Origen and others flourished. And at Nicomedia there was a school and college of Christian youth, in which Julian was educated, and afterwards became reader of that church. Thus the institution of public schools in the churches is very ancient, and Christian princes ought above all to bend their efforts to this care, that in the more famous churches there should be schools in which the doctrines of religion are diligently taught and the discipline of morals flourishes. For these are the most fruitful seminaries of the Church, since from them come forth not only heralds of the Word of God but also governors of the commonwealth, who have joined piety with practical experience and prudence. But today most people think that this care is none of their business, and they stint expense on a matter most necessary. Would that the same people did not largely divert the revenues of the churches to profane, or even disgraceful, uses. In the schools that do exist, partly an unbridled licence of morals reigns, whose authors are not rarely the professors themselves, who, given to drunkenness and intemperance, corrupt by their example the youths consecrated to Christ and the Muses; partly foolish and untaught ambition holds sway. For those who are teachers only in name make their pupils like themselves, who bring to the helm of the Church nothing but empty titles bought with money and intolerable pride. For the most part we owe to these men the collapse of discipline everywhere among the nations, the monstrous licence of sins, the quarrels by which the churches are torn, and the exposure of the Christian religion to the mockery of the impious. God must therefore be prayed to give faithful teachers and to restore the old discipline of the schools.

units.la: Quarto loco Potestates numerantur, pro ijs, qui potestatem in Ecclesia legitimam exercent. Erant hi Seniores, qui disciplinæ præfecti eos corrigebant qui aliquid contra hominis Christiani officium fecissent: impios verò & contumaces maiori Spiritus virtute cohibebant. Erant enim dono singulari armati, ut diabolo quoque affligendos traderent eos, qui admonitionibus & correptionibus non poterant corrigi. Exempla huius potestatis antiquitus ab Elia & Helisæo edita sunt, quorum ille quidem milites ad se capiendum missos flammis cœlitus immissis combusit, hic verò vrsos euocauit, qui pueros ipsi petulantius illudentes discerpserunt. Eadem virtute aut potestate Petrus Ananiam & Sapphiram occidit, qui Spiritui sancto mentiri ausi fuerant, Simonem item Magum exitio tradidit. Paulus quoque hac potestate aduersus Elymam Magum usus est, quem oculis priuauit, quod Proconsulem Cypri suis mendacijs decipere pergeret. Idem Hymenæum & Alexandrum se Satanæ tradidisse scribit, ut aliquo supplicio affecti discerent porrò non blasphemare. Et huc etiam referri debet quod in posteriori ad Corinth. contumacibus quibusdam minitabundis dicit: Quòd si venero denuo, non parcam: quandoquidem experimentum quæritis in me loquentis Christi. His enim non obscurè innuit, se cum verbis coniunctam habere virtutem perficiendi quod dicit, & contemptores suos cohercendi. Atq; olim hac Spiritus facultate omnino opus erat, cum magistratum non haberent Ecclesiæ, & proinde iure gladij non possent uti. Hodie illam requirere non necesse est, quando donum istud Spiritus cessauit, & principes atq; magistratus sunt Christiani qui legibus & publica authoritate quosuis in officio continent, contumaciores verò & præfractos puniunt. Sunt quidem nonnulli, qui ad veteris & primitiuæ Ecclesiæ exemplum Seniores siue Senatum ecclesiasticum instituere volunt, qui in ipsos quoq; magistratus imperium habeat, si quando illi officium non fecerint. Sed prius illos demonstrare oportebat, suis illis Senioribus hanc potestatem esse, de qua in præsenti Paulus loquitur. Quod cum nullo argumento constet, & nihilominus Satanæ tradant quos volunt, perinde faciunt, ac si qui leprosos mundare, mortuos excitare & alia opera miraculosa facere conantur, eò quod illa olim in primitiva Ecclesia vulgò facta sunt.
units.tr: Fourth in the list are the authorities, meaning those who exercise lawful authority in the Church. These were the elders, who, set over discipline, corrected those who had done anything contrary to the duty of a Christian; but the impious and stubborn they restrained by a greater power of the Spirit. For they were armed with a singular gift, so that they might even hand over to the devil for affliction those who could not be corrected by admonitions and rebukes. Examples of this power were displayed of old by Elijah and Elisha. Elijah burned with fire sent from heaven the soldiers sent to seize him, while Elisha called forth bears which tore apart boys who were mocking him too insolently. By the same power or authority Peter put to death Ananias and Sapphira, who had dared to lie to the Holy Spirit; he also delivered Simon the Magician to destruction. Paul too used this power against Elymas the magician, whom he struck blind because he persisted in deceiving the proconsul of Cyprus with his lies. He likewise writes that he had handed over Hymenaeus and Alexander to Satan, so that, punished with some suffering, they might learn not to blaspheme further. To this also should be referred what he says in the second letter to the Corinthians to certain stubborn and threatening people: "If I come again, I will not spare, since you seek proof of Christ speaking in me." For by these words he clearly hints that he had power joined to his words to accomplish what he says and to restrain his despisers. Indeed, of old there was altogether need of this gift of the Spirit, since the Church did not have magistrates and therefore could not use the right of the sword. Today there is no need to seek it, since that gift of the Spirit has ceased, and there are Christian princes and magistrates who by laws and public authority keep everyone in duty, and punish the more stubborn and unruly. There are indeed some who want to set up elders or an ecclesiastical senate after the example of the old and primitive Church, which would also have authority over the magistrates themselves if ever they failed in their duty. But they ought first to demonstrate that this power of which Paul speaks in the present passage belongs to their elders. Since this is established by no argument, and nevertheless they hand over to Satan whomever they wish, they do just as if men tried to cleanse lepers, raise the dead and do other miraculous works, merely because those things were commonly done in the primitive Church of old.

units.la: Quintum locum habent dona sanationum, id est, ij qui dono sanandi praediti erant. Fuit enim hoc quoque inter Christianos homines admodum frequens, & ideo Iacobus in sua epistola monebat: Infirmatur quis inter vos? accersat presbyteros Ecclesiae, & orent pro eo, unguentes eum oleo in nomine Domini: & oratio fidei seruabit laborantem. Oleo autem illi aegrotos inungebant, quod sanationis symbolum fuisse, ex Marci sexto Capite apparet: & ideo ne qui in externa illa unctione superstitiosius haerent, inuocatio nominis Dei ex fide illi coniungebatur. Ubi obiter discimus, quam praeclaris testimonijs olim fidem Christianam Deus exornauerit, quando homines Christiani in uno Christo repositam sibi habuerunt, quae prophani & insolentes huius seculi filij magnis laboribus atque impensis quaerunt. Extant adhuc hodie Magni illius Persarum Regis Artaxerxis epistolae, quibus Hippocratem medicum magnis propositis praemijs ad se euocauit, ut autem ille veniret, ab eo impetrare non potuit. Quanto melius ergo Deus illo tempore Christianis consuluit, qui cum omnium mortalium abiectissimi essent, tam fidum & certum suae valetudinis praesidium habuerunt in illis, quibus medendi facultas miraculosa data erat, & ea quidem conditione, ut quod gratis acceperant, gratis darent? Etsi vero hoc quoque donum cessauerit, constat tamen medicinam, quae per media naturalia exercetur, diuinitus conferri: & ea Christianis hominibus uti licet, modo curent, ne quae in uno Deo collocari debet fiducia, in externis illis haereat. Ita enim olim Asam[?] Regem peccauisse legimus. Et opus est in Repub. bene constituta medicos fidos & rerum peritos habere, qui consilio suo adsint male habentibus, ne vel in impostores veneficos incidant, vel ad artes superstitiosas siue illicitas se fe[?] conuertant.
units.tr: The fifth place is held by the gifts of healings, that is, those who were endowed with the gift of healing. For this too was quite common among Christians, and so James in his epistle admonished: "Is anyone sick among you? Let him call for the elders of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the one who is labouring." They used to anoint the sick with oil, which was a sign of healing, as appears from Mark chapter 6; and so that people should not cling superstitiously to that external anointing, the invocation of the name of God from faith was joined to it. Here we learn incidentally with what splendid testimonies God once adorned the Christian faith, when Christians had in one Christ the things which the profane and arrogant sons of this age seek with great labour and expense. The letters of the great Persian king Artaxerxes still survive today, in which he summoned the physician Hippocrates to himself with great promised rewards; yet he could not obtain him, though he came. How much better, then, did God provide for Christians in that time, who, though they were the most abject of all mortals, had so faithful and sure a safeguard for their health in those who were given the miraculous power of healing, and that on the condition that what they had received freely they should give freely? Even if this gift too has ceased, it is nevertheless established that medicine, which is practised through natural means, is conferred by God; and Christians may use it, provided only they take care not to rest the trust, which ought to be placed in the one God alone, upon external things. For we read that king Asa once sinned in just this way. And in a well-ordered commonwealth it is necessary to have trustworthy physicians skilled in their craft, who may assist with their counsel those who are unwell, lest they fall into quacks and poisoners, or turn themselves to superstitious or unlawful arts.

units.la: Sextus locus opitulationes habet: eorum nimirum, qui egentibus opem ferunt, siue illi Ecclesiae domestici, siue peregrini fuerint. Erant hi quoque admodum necessarij olim, quando ferentibus ubique gentium persecutionibus multi sedibus patrijs pellebantur, multi fortunis spoliabantur, multi morbis correpti neminem ex suis habebant, qui ipsorum curam susciperet. Tunc ergo Diaconos instituerunt Apostoli, penes quos erat pecuniae publicae dispensatio. Idem viduas ecclesiasticas ad eiusmodi fratrum egentium subsidia destinabant, hospitia item designabant peregrinis. Conueniebat hoc cum Dei instituto, qui mandarat olim, ne mendicus esset in Israele. Et hodie hoc ipsum obseruari debet, quando passim inueniuntur, qui publico Ecclesiae subsidio opus habent. Itaque laudabile prorsus est Xenodochiorum institutum, in quibus excipiuntur homines peregrini, & morbis affecti curantur, simulque multorum aliorum egestati subuenitur. Meminerint ergo qui illis praefecti sunt, se munus a Deo institutum & maxime necessarium obire, & proinde in illius administratione fideles sint, & praemium in magno illo die a Christo recipient amplissimum.
units.tr: The sixth category comprises those who bring help to the needy, whether they belong to the household of the Church or are strangers. These too were very necessary in former times, when, with persecutions raging everywhere among the nations, many were driven from their homeland, many were stripped of their goods, and many, struck down by sickness, had no one of their own to take care of them. Therefore the apostles appointed deacons, in whose charge was the distribution of public funds. Likewise they assigned churchly widows to the support of such needy brothers, and also designated hospices for strangers. This accorded with God's institution, who commanded long ago that there should be no beggar in Israel. And today the same thing ought to be observed, since everywhere are found those who need the public help of the Church. Thus the institution of hospitals is truly praiseworthy, in which strangers are received, the sick are cared for, and at the same time relief is given to the poverty of many others. Let those who are set over them remember that they perform a ministry instituted by God and most necessary, and therefore they should be faithful in its administration, and they will receive a very ample reward from Christ on that great day.

units.la: Septimus in hoc ordine Gubernationes ponit, quibus comprehenduntur viri politici, qui in rebus huius seculi quosuis iuuabant, & causas cognoscebant, si quae inter Christianos orirentur. Nam ut Capite sexto dictum est, nolebant Apostoli, ut qui Christum profitebantur apud ethnicorum tribunalia de fortunis suis alijsque rebus ad hanc vitam pertinentibus litigarent. Praeficiebantur ergo eiusmodi causis viri prudentes & rerum usu exercitati, quorum authoritate & consilio lites dirimerentur. Idem publice etiam aderant Ecclesiae, si quid apud Proconsules aut Praesides agendum erat: quod frequenter accidisse, non est dubium. Denique ut nauclerı quidam Ecclesias inter varia rerum discrimina fluctuantes suis consilijs atque prudentia gubernabant. Hodie talibus in publico non ita opus est, quando (ut supra diximus) magistratus Christiani sunt, quorum authoritate ista omnia felicius possunt transfigi. Et agnoscere debemus singulare Dei beneficium, qui nouissimis hisce temporibus Ecclesiae suae gubernatores cum politicos tum ecclesiasticos dare dignatur, sicuti olim per Isaiam promisit. Nemo igitur ordinem a Deo institutum facile turbet, ut calcata principum & magistratuum authoritate Senatum nouum instituat, qui in illos sibi ius & imperium vendicet. Fecerunt hoc olim Episcopi quidam bono fortasse zelo: sed ea res tandem in tyrannidem pontificiam degeneravit, & paucorum ambitio rem Christianam prorsus euertit. Agnoscant vicissim principes, se Ecclesiae membra, non dominos esse: & proinde suo imperio ad illius defensionem utantur, atque consilia sua omnia ad hunc scopum dirigant, ut eius ordo atque incolumitas seruetur.
units.tr: Seventh in this order he places governments, under which are included political men who helped in the affairs of this age, whoever they were, and examined cases if any arose among Christians. For, as was said in chapter six, the apostles did not want those who professed Christ to litigate before pagan tribunals about their goods and other matters pertaining to this life. Therefore men who were prudent and practised in affairs were put in charge of such cases, by whose authority and counsel disputes were settled. Likewise they stood publicly beside the Church, if anything had to be pursued before proconsuls or governors; that this often happened there is no doubt. Finally, like certain pilots, they steered the churches, which were tossed about amid various perils, by their counsels and prudence. Today there is not so much need of such men in public, since (as we said above) the magistrates are Christian, and by their authority all these things can be carried through more happily. And we ought to acknowledge the singular benefit of God, who in these latest times deigns to give his Church governors, both political and ecclesiastical, just as he promised long ago through Isaiah. Let no one therefore lightly disturb the order instituted by God, by trampling on the authority of princes and magistrates in order to set up a new senate which claims for itself right and rule over them. Some bishops did this long ago, perhaps with good zeal; but the matter eventually degenerated into papal tyranny, and the ambition of a few utterly overthrew the Christian cause. In turn, let princes acknowledge that they are members of the Church, not its lords; and therefore let them use their power for its defence, and direct all their counsels to this goal, that its order and safety may be preserved.

units.la: Postremo loco genera linguarum ponuntur, sub quibus interpretationis quod, donum comprehenditur, de quo supra dictum est. Erat utrumque donum tunc necessarium, quando Euangelij doctrina per paucos Apostolos virosque Apostolicos in toto orbe diuulgari debebat. Hodie sufficit fere eas linguas tenuisse, quibus in Scripturis exarandis Spiritus Sanctus vsus est, Hebræam nimirum & Græcam: quibus Latinam propter exterarum Ecclesiarum commercium coniungere oportet. Agnoscimus tamen hoc quoque Deo acceptum ferri debere, si cui datum est diuersarum gentium linguis loqui, quæ hodie in vsu sunt. Consultò autem Paulus linguas vltimo in gradu collocat, vt vel hoc argumento doceat, quam stulte faciant Corinthij, dum circa illas tumultuentur, neglectis aliis multis, quæ magis erant necessaria. Obseruabimus autem istos gradus ita enumerari, vt omnium author indicetur Deus. In hunc ergo omnes respicere debent, vt suam fidem atque industriam illi approbent.
units.tr: Last in the list are kinds of tongues, under which is included the gift of interpretation, concerning which we have spoken above. Both gifts were then necessary, when the doctrine of the gospel had to be spread throughout the whole world by a few apostles and apostolic men. Today it is almost enough to have mastered those languages in which the Holy Spirit used to write the Scriptures, namely Hebrew and Greek; to these it is fitting to add Latin, because of commerce with foreign churches. Yet we acknowledge that this too must be credited to God, if anyone has been granted to speak the languages of the various peoples that are in use today. But Paul deliberately places tongues in the last rank, so that by this very argument he may teach how foolishly the Corinthians act, while they make a tumult over these things and neglect many others that were more necessary. We shall observe, moreover, that these ranks are enumerated in such a way that God is shown to be the author of all. Therefore all should look to him, so that they may commend their faith and diligence to him.

units.la: Porrò non temere aliquis miretur, cùm Paulo propositum fuerit Ecclesiæ ordines recensere, quibus in eius gubernatione seu administratione opus est, nullam ab eo illorum mentionem fieri, quos in Papatu sub Sacramenti titulo iactare solent. Sunt hi septem numero, Ostiarij, Lectores, Exorcistæ, Acoluthi, Subdiaconi, Diaconi, Sacerdotes. Isidorus Lectoribus Psalmistas addit, quos postea Cantores dixerunt. Omnes vero istos non modò ab Apostolis institutos olim esse fabulantur, sed ipsum quoque Christum illorum officia obijsse contendunt, quem Ostiarium fuisse aiunt, quando vendentes & ementes templo eiecit: Lectorem, quando in Synagoga Nazarethana locum Isaiæ recitauit: Exorcistam, quando homini muto & surdo adhibita saliua & dicto, Ephphatha, auditum atque loquendi facultatem reddidit: Acoluthum, cùm dixit: Qui sequitur me, non ambulat in tenebris: Subdiaconum, quando linteo succinctus discipulorum pedes abluit: Diaconum, quando corpus & sanguinem in Cœna distribuit: Sacerdotem quando seipsum Patri in cruce obtulit. Quod postremum vt nemo nostrum negat, ita reliqua illa tam putida & ridicula sunt, vt confutatione nequaquam opus habeant. Certè vnus hic locus illis conuincendis sufficit. Cur enim istos ordines ab Apostolo omissos esse dicemus, nisi quòd tunc omnibus ignoti, & ne in rerum quidem natura fuerunt? Quod ipsum de Pontificibus Max. de Metropolitanis siue Archiepiscopis, de Cardinalibus, Sacellanis, Monachis & tota ra[?]forum atq; vnctorum colluuie dicimus. Omnes enim illi Antichristi creaturæ sunt, nec digni, qui in Ecclesia locum aliquem habeant. Nobis sufficiat, si in Ecclesia fidi & idonei Pastores atq; Doctores sint, Scholarum item præfecti industrij, magistratus pij, qui & Dei cultum tueantur, & ius dicant, improbos & contumaces digni modis coerceant, bonos defendant, pauperes vero sibi habeant commendatos.
units.tr: Moreover, let no one be rashly surprised that, although Paul proposed to recount the orders of the Church that are needed for its government and administration, he makes no mention of those whom they are wont to boast of in Papistry under the title of sacrament. There are seven of these: doorkeepers, readers, exorcists, acolytes, subdeacons, deacons, and priests. Isidore adds psalmists to the readers, whom they later called cantors. But they not only fable that all these were instituted long ago by the apostles, they also maintain that Christ himself performed their offices: they say he was a doorkeeper when he drove out those buying and selling from the temple; a reader when in the synagogue of Nazareth he read the passage from Isaiah; an exorcist when, applying spittle and the word Ephphatha to a man who was deaf and mute, he restored his hearing and power of speech; an acolyte when he said: He who follows me does not walk in darkness; a subdeacon when, girded with a towel, he washed the disciples' feet; a deacon when at the Supper he distributed body and blood; a priest when on the cross he offered himself to the Father. As none of us denies this last point, so the rest is so foul and ridiculous that it needs no refutation. Certainly this one place is enough to convict them. For why should we say those orders were omitted by the apostle, unless because at that time they were unknown to all and did not even exist in the nature of things?
