We say the same of the Supreme Pontiffs, of the metropolitans or archbishops, of cardinals, chaplains, monks, and the whole sewer of shaven and anointed men. For all of them are creatures of Antichrist, and not worthy to hold any place in the Church. It is enough for us if the Church has faithful and fit ministers and teachers, likewise diligent heads of schools, and pious magistrates who both guard the worship of God and administer justice, restrain the wicked and obstinate by fitting measures, defend the good, and hold the poor committed to their care.

units.la: Porrò concludit locum istum Paulus, & docet nemini dona ista simul omnia esse, nec aliquem inueniri, qui omnibus illis ministerijs obeundis sufficiat. Num (inquit) omnes Apostoli? num omnes Prophetæ? num omnes Doctores? num omnes sunt Potestates? num omnes donum habent sanationum? num omnes linguis loquuntur? num omnes interpretantur? Interrogationibus vrget, vt proprio testimonio eos couincat. Quasi diceret: Nemo mei ista ex meo cerebro fingere arbitretur: Res ipsa loquitur. Inspicite enim omnes, qui passim sunt, Christianos, vnà cum ijs qui in Ecclesijs hinc inde ministrant: & mox videbitis, nullum ex istis ministerijs esse, ad quod omnes vocentur. Quis enim Ecclesiam nobis dabit, in qua omnes sint Apostoli, omnes prophetent, omnes docendi facultatem habeant, omnes morbis miraculosè medeantur, omnes linguis loquantur, aut interpretandi dono sint præditi? Quid verò hinc colligit Apostolus? Primum, quòd nullum ex donis siue ministerijs istis per se sufficiat ad Ecclesiam constituendam & feruandam. Nam si hoc daremus, iam superuacanea forent reliqua omnia. Vnde rursus sequitur, alios aliorum opera atq; auxilio opus habere: & proinde neminem insolentius efferri debere cum aliorum contemptu, aut cuiquam suum gradum siue dona inuidere. Et hoc facit, quòd minora quoque dona repetit, vt vel ea non omnibus communia esse doceat. Exemplo sint nobis ipsi Apostoli: qui etiamsi donis ferè omnibus instructi essent, opus tamen habuerunt Pastoribus, Episcopis, Diaconis, Senioribus, Doctoribus: sine quibus ab illis plantatæ Ecclesiæ non potuissent consistere. Ea denique Ecclesiæ conditio est, quæ Reipublicæ in qua distinctos munerum publicorum gradus esse oportet, quando ne sapientissimus quidem omnia solus obire potest. Deinde hoc quoque ex Pauli verbis colligitur, dona & ministeria illa non esse eiusmodi, ut sine illis salus nobis constare non possit. Si enim non omnes qui credunt, simul etiam Apostoli aut Prophetae sunt, licet utique credere & salvum fieri, etiamsi neque doctorem agas, neque linguarum dono instructus fis. Iustius etenim sua fide vivit, & omnis qui credit in me (inquit Christus) habet vitam aeternam: & in Christo non est ullus personarum respectus. Sunt ergo nimium stulti, qui non necessaria ambitiosius affectant, aut illa aliis invidendo seipsos labore & curis inutilibus, imo noxiis, conficiunt. Ideo deinceps hortabitur Paulus Corinthios, ut procul abiectis invidiae & ambitionis affectibus, animum appellant ad dona excellentiora, quae ad salutem consequendam magis necessaria sunt. Applicent ista sibi ipsis singuli, & sua forte contenti Spartam, quam nacti sunt, diligenter ornent: salutis vero fiduciam omnem collocent in uno JESV CHRISTO, qui suos dum hic vivunt abunde instruit, & tandem ad se collectos vera felicitate beat. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, Paul concludes this passage and teaches that these gifts are not all together in anyone, nor is anyone to be found who suffices for performing all those ministries. Are all apostles? (he says) Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all powers? Do all have the gift of healings? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret? He presses with questions, so as to convince them by their own testimony, as if he were saying: let no one think I am inventing these things from my own brain; the thing itself speaks. For look at all the Christians who are scattered about, together with those who minister here and there in the churches, and you will soon see that there is no one of these ministries to which all are called. For who will give us a Church in which all are apostles, all prophesy, all have the ability to teach, all heal the sick miraculously, all speak in tongues, or are endowed with the gift of interpretation? But what does the apostle gather from this? First, that none of these gifts or ministries is by itself sufficient to establish and preserve the Church. For if we granted this, all the rest would already be superfluous. Whence it follows again that some need the work and help of others, and therefore no one ought to be puffed up more insolently to the contempt of others, or envy anyone his rank or gifts. He does this also by mentioning the lesser gifts, so that he may teach that even these are not common to all. Let the apostles themselves be our examples: although they were furnished with almost all the gifts, they nevertheless needed pastors, bishops, deacons, elders, and teachers, without whom the churches they had planted could not have held together. Finally, this is the condition of the Church, which is like a commonwealth, in which distinct grades of public offices ought to exist, since not even the wisest man can perform everything alone. Then this too is gathered from the words of Paul: those gifts and ministries are not of such a kind that without them our salvation cannot stand. For if not all who believe are at the same time apostles or prophets, it is certainly possible to believe and be saved, even if you are neither a teacher nor endowed with the gift of tongues. For the righteous lives by his faith, and everyone who believes in me (says Christ) has eternal life; and in Christ there is no respect of persons. Therefore they are too foolish who eagerly pursue things that are not necessary, or who, by envying others, wear themselves out with useless, indeed harmful, labours and cares. Therefore Paul will afterwards exhort the Corinthians that, casting away the affections of envy and ambition, they should turn their minds to the more excellent gifts, which are more necessary for obtaining salvation. Let each apply those things to himself, and, content with the lot he has been given, diligently adorn it; but let them place all their trust for salvation in the one Jesus Christ, who abundantly instructs his own while they live here, and at last, gathering them to himself, blesses them with true happiness. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XIII. HOMILIA LXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII. HOMILY LXVII.

units.la: AMbite autem dona potiora, & adhuc viam ad excellentiam vobis indicabo. Si linguis hominum loquar & Angelorum, charitatem autem non habeam, factus sum aes resonans, aut cymbalum tinniens. Et si habeam prophetiam, & noverim mysteria omnia omnemq; scientiam, & si habeam omnem fidem, adeo ut montes transferam: charitatem autem non habeam, nihil sum. Et si infumam in alimoniam omnes facultates meas: & si tradam corpus meum ut comburar: charitatem autem non habeam, nihil mihi prodest.
units.tr: But earnestly desire the better gifts, and I will show you a still more excellent way. If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not charity, I am become as sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal. And if I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing. And if I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but have not charity, it profits me nothing.

units.la: V[?]oniam Corinthij propter dona spiritualia pernitiose tumultuabantur, adeo ut in sectas scinderentur propter ea, quae mutuae charitatis vinculum esse debebant, Paulus diligenter & prolixe de tota ista causa disserit. Et nuper docuit, ita rem esse a Deo institutam, ut nemo credentium donis simul omnibus instructus sit, aut ministerijs sive functionibus simul omnibus adhibeatur. Ex quo satis evidenter colligitur, omnia ista eiusmodi esse, ut ad Ecclesiae quidem gubernationem atque conservationem faciant, non autem ad singulorum salutem privatim necessaria sint: imo sine illis servari posse eos, qui per fidem in Christum Deo vere reconciliati sunt. Faciebat hoc plurimum ad Pauli institutum, ne qui aliis dona sua inviderent, aut insolentius superbirent, si pluribus instructi & in altiori gradu constituti essent. His commodè subijcit doctrinam sive adhortationem de donis excellentioribus, quae omnibus ex aequo necessaria sunt, & quae omnia sub charitatis titulo comprehendit. Utilis admodum locus, & multa consideratione dignissimus, quia communi hominum vitio medetur. Ut enim in ijs, quae ad hanc vitam pertinent, plerique ea affectant, quae voluptati potius & ostentationi, quam honestati & valetudini serviunt: Ita in spiritualibus etiam solet evenire, ut a plerisque pluris fiant quae carnis curiositati satisfaciunt (qualia sunt vaticinandi facultas, linguarum cognitio, miracula, & quae alia sunt huius generis) quam excellentia illa & vere necessaria dona, sine quibus salus nostra non potest consistere: qualia sunt, fides in Deum, Verbum Dei, charitas, vitae innocentia, patientia & constantia. Et tanta hic fere iudicij inopia laborat, ut multi ex illis doctores quoque aestiment, ipsam vero doctrinam minus expendant. Audiamus ergo Apostolum de hac re graviter & pulchre differentem.
units.tr: Since the Corinthians were being thrown into dangerous turmoil over spiritual gifts, so that they were split into factions over the very things that ought to have been the bond of mutual charity, Paul treats this whole matter carefully and at length. Just before, he taught that God has so arranged things that no believer is endowed with all the gifts at once, or charged with all the ministries or functions at once. From this it is quite clearly gathered that all these things are such as serve the government and preservation of the Church, but are not individually necessary for each person's salvation. Indeed, those who are truly reconciled to God through faith in Christ can be saved without them. This served Paul's purpose very much, namely that those who were richer in gifts and set in a higher rank should not envy others, nor be puffed up more insolently. To this he fittingly adds his teaching, or exhortation, about the more excellent gifts, which are necessary for all alike, and which he comprehends under the name of charity. It is a most useful passage and deserves the closest consideration, because it remedies a common human fault. For just as, in matters pertaining to this life, most people pursue those things that serve pleasure and display rather than decency and health, so in spiritual matters it often happens that by most people those things are valued more which gratify the curiosity of the flesh (such as the power of prophesying, knowledge of languages, miracles, and others of this kind) than those excellent and truly necessary gifts without which our salvation cannot stand. These are faith in God, the Word of God, charity, innocence of life, patience and constancy. And there is almost such a lack of judgement here that many think those who have these gifts are teachers, yet they weigh the doctrine itself less. Let us then hear the Apostle, who discusses this matter seriously and beautifully.

units.la: Propositio sive summa adhortationis est: Ambite dona potiora. In Graecis ζηλοῦτε[?] habetur, quo verbo aemulationem requirit. Est haec cum serio aliquid consequendi studio coniuncta, & ferē inuidiam parit, si quos alios eodem potiri aut frui videat. Attamen Paulus, cum inuidiae & odio mederi instituerit, aemulationem sanctam praecipit, quae nemini inuidet, & non nisi ea quae nobis necessaria sunt, & absq; alicuius incommodo possunt obtineri, affectat, vt & officium faciamus in credito nobis munere, & vnà cum aliis electis salutem consequamur. Sic igitur dicendo caecam illorum ambitionem perstringit, qua accensi circa linguarum ostentationem toti occupabantur, neglectis aliis multis, quae magis erant necessaria. Et sensus est: Video vos zelo & aemulatione ardere, & vnumquemque in hoc esse vt prae aliis excellat: & id quidem ferri posset, si absq; invidia & odio fieret: sed cum vos scindi videam, hoc vestrum studium non possum probare. Quare si & publicae concordiae & priuatae saluti consultum vultis, hoc agite, vt donis potioribus excellatis, & ijsdem ad Ecclesiae totius aedificationem vtamini. Et ne dubii aut perplexi haererent, & nouas quaestiones nectererent, mox addit: Et adhuc viam ad excellentiam vobis indicabo, id est, monstrabo vobis, qua ratione eo euectì possitis, vt reuera excellatis, & donis qualibuscunq; cum fructu tam vestro quam aliorum positus vti. Id vero de charitate dicit, quae vere omnibus aliis praestat. Si enim bona quaevis eo praestantiora sunt, quo magis communia sunt & plures iuuant, vix aliquid inuenietur quod cum illa conferri queat. Omnibus enim credentibus communis nota sive tessera est, ex qua pro Christi discipulis agnoscuntur: cum reliqua dona non nisi pro ministerij ratione distribuantur, ad quod vnumquenque Deus destinauit. Deinde haec fere dissidiorum causa sive materia sunt, propter inhaerentem nobis naturae vitiositatem: Charitas autem omnes vnit & constringit, vt idem sentiant atq; loquantur. Adhaec monet nos, vt omnes nostras facultates in publicum conferamus ad prouehendam Dei gloriam & aliorum salutem. Itaq; sanctae illius communionis vinculum est charitas, dum nemini quod suum est eripit, omnibus autem quae ipsa habet liberalissimè communicat. Quo nomine nonnulli eam virtutum omnium vitam dixerunt, & ideo Paulus eandem rectè commendat, vt per illam excellere studeamus.
units.tr: The proposition, or summary, of the exhortation is: Earnestly desire the better gifts. In the Greek it is ζηλοῦτε, which requires emulation. This is joined with a serious zeal for attaining something, and almost gives rise to envy if one sees others possessing or enjoying the same thing. Yet Paul, since he sets out to cure envy and hatred, commands a holy emulation, which envies no one and aims only at those things that are necessary for us and can be obtained without harm to anyone, so that we both perform our duty in the office entrusted to us and attain salvation together with the other elect. So by saying this he censures their blind ambition, by which those inflamed about the display of tongues were wholly occupied, neglecting many other things that were more necessary. And the sense is: I see you burning with zeal and rivalry, each one striving to excel the others. This could be borne if it were done without envy and hatred; but since I see you being split apart, I cannot approve this eagerness of yours. Therefore, if you wish to provide for both public harmony and private salvation, see to it that you excel in the better gifts and use the same for the building up of the whole Church. And lest they remain doubtful or perplexed, and weave new questions, he immediately adds: And I will show you a still more excellent way, that is, I will show you by what means you may be raised so as to truly excel, and so that, whatever gifts you have, you may use them with profit both to yourselves and to others. He says this about charity, which truly surpasses all other things. For if any goods are the more excellent the more they are shared and the more they help many, scarcely anything will be found that can be compared with it. For it is a common mark or token for all believers, by which they are recognised as disciples of Christ; whereas the other gifts are distributed only according to the measure of ministry for which God has destined each one. Moreover, the other gifts are almost always the cause or matter of quarrels, on account of the vice of corruption inherent in our nature; but charity unites and binds all, so that they think and speak the same. Besides, it admonishes us to bring all our resources into the common good, to advance the glory of God and the salvation of others. Thus charity is the bond of that holy communion, since it takes away from no one what is his own, but shares most generously with all what it itself possesses. For this reason some have called it the life of all the virtues, and therefore Paul rightly commends it, so that we may strive to excel through it.

units.la: At hic tenere oportet, quae vera sit illam ambiendi ratio. Etenim in nobis nihil huius inueniri, quos innata philautia vrget, vt nostris potius quam aliorum commodis studeamus. Itaq; si primam eius originem scrutari libeat, Dei donum est, vt & fides, ex qua enasci aut deriuari solet. Sunt tamen exercitia quaedam, quibus eam assequi & augere possumus. Inter haec primum est, vt in Dei conspectu humiliemur, & nostri ipsius consideratione fratli contremiscamus ad verbum eius, sicuti Isaias docet. Nam qui ita affecti sunt, apud eos locum habere non potest ambitio, quae aemulationem atq; inuidiam parit. Accedat frequens beneficiorum Dei recordatio, qui ita dilexit nos, vt Filium suum vnigenitum pro nobis dederit. Quod qui non oscitanter expendunt, ij Deum vicissim diligunt, & proinde in eo omnes quoq; alios complectuntur, quos ille eodem fauore & studio prosequi dignatus est. Et hic diligenter meditari oportet, quanta sit hominis dignitas apud Deum, etiamsi mundi iudicio vilis & contemptissimus esse putetur. Tanti enim illum fecit Deus, vt Filij sanguine salutem eius redimere voluerit. Imò etiamsi aliquis peccator sit, non tamen illum mox abiicit Deus, sed amicè fouet & suffert, & cum vita hac creatorum quoq; simul omnium vsum illi concedit. Quod vnum eorum inhumanitate arguit, qui proximum detestantur, & Deo sanctiores videri volunt, dum illum suo amore indignum iudicant. Coniungatur istis mutuae necessitatis consideratio, qua nos ita constrinxit Deus, vt alius alterius auxilio atq; opera opus habeat, nec aliquis à nobis absq; nostro incommodo siue periculo possit negligi. Istas meditationes commentantur preces feriae atque indefinentes, vt Deus suo spiritu nos fulcire & carnis cupiditates noxias ac illicitas restinguere dignetur. Qui (inquam) hisce exercitijs occupantur, ij se indies proficere, & in charitatis studio confirmari sentiunt.
units.tr: But here we must hold fast to what the true way of pursuing it is. For in us, whom innate self-love presses to seek our own advantage rather than that of others, nothing of this is to be found. Therefore, if we wish to examine its first origin, it is a gift of God, as faith is, from which it is wont to be born or derived. There are nevertheless certain exercises by which we can attain and increase it. Among these the first is that we humble ourselves in the sight of God, and, considering ourselves, tremble at his word, as Isaiah teaches. For those who are so disposed, ambition, which gives rise to rivalry and envy, cannot have a place among them. Let there be added the frequent remembrance of God's benefits, who so loved us that he gave his only-begotten Son for us. Those who weigh this attentively love God in return, and consequently embrace in him also all others whom he has deigned to favour and cherish with the same kindness. And here we must diligently meditate on how great is the dignity of a man before God, even if he is judged vile and most despised in the opinion of the world. For God esteemed him so highly that he willed to redeem his salvation with the blood of his Son. Indeed, even if someone is a sinner, God does not immediately cast him away, but cherishes and bears with him kindly, and grants him, together with this life, the use of all created things. This alone condemns the inhumanity of those who detest their neighbour and wish to seem holier than God, while they judge him unworthy of their love. Let to these be joined the consideration of mutual need, by which God has bound us so that one man has need of another's help and labour, and no one can be neglected by us without loss or danger to ourselves. Daily and unceasing prayers accompany these meditations, that God may deign to strengthen us by his Spirit and quench the harmful and unlawful desires of the flesh. Those who, I say, are occupied in these exercises feel that they advance day by day and are confirmed in the pursuit of charity.

units.la: Quia vero Paulus nos in hac causa tardiores esse nouit, qui stimulis & incitamentis opus habeamus, praeclarum & magnificum charitatis encomium subjicit. Argumentum huius primum est à necessario. Docet enim sine illa aliorum donorum, quantumuis praestantissimorum, vsum omnino nullum esse: quo loco comparationem horum & illius facit memorabilem. Deinde ex propriis notis sive effectis eam commendat. Postremò ad comparationem prius institutam rediens, illam cum fide & spe confert, quae donorum praestantissima habentur, & in quo his etiam illa excellat, docet.
units.tr: But since Paul knows that we are slow in this matter, and need spurs and incitements, he adds a remarkable and magnificent encomium of charity. The first argument for it is drawn from necessity. For he teaches that without it there is no use at all of the other gifts, however excellent they may be; in this place he makes a memorable comparison between these and it. Next, he commends it by its own marks, or effects. Lastly, returning to the comparison set up earlier, he compares it with faith and hope, which are held to be the most excellent of the gifts, and shows in what respect it also surpasses these.

units.la: Primum charitatem cum dono linguarum confert, deq; eo magnificè admodum loquitur, vt illam magis extollat. Ab eo autem orditur, quia linguis maximè superbiebant. Si linguis (inquit) hominum (omnium videlicet, quæ sub cælo viuunt, gentium) loquar, & Angelorum, &c. Prudenter verò sermonem in seipsum transfert, ne alios insolentius contemnere videatur. Et cum hominibus Angelos coniungit, non quòd hi vel corpora habeant, vel linguis loquantur, sed vt dicendi facultatem humanam excellentiorem, adeoq; verè cœlestem exprimat. Itaq; cum innumeras guarum cognitione eloquentiam omnem comprehendit, & fortasse eos quoque perstrinxit, qui visiones Angelorum & colloquia cum spiritibus æthereis iactabant, de quibus in epistola ad Coloss. etiam aliquid dixisse videtur; vbi vt à talibus caueamus monet, qui res nunquam abse visas magna cum audacia & quasi pro imperio ingerunt & obtrudunt. Fecerunt enim hoc olim inter gentes, qui præ aliis excellere volebant, vt alibi de Minoë, Numa, Sertorio & similibus est dictum. Sectarijs item hoc omnibus seculis familiare fuit. Mahumet certè Alcoranum suum, quo nihil ineptius, nihil magis insulsum magisve impium excogitari poterat, Angeli Gabrielis nomine venditauit, quo cum sibi colloquia priuata intercedere simulabat. De Monachis quid dicere attinet, qui de coelesti Hierarchia & Angelorum choris, deq; Mariæ Virginis & Diuorum intercessionibus apud Christum tanta confidentia nugantur, vt maiori non possent, si multis annis rerum, quæ in cœlis aguntur, spectatores fuissent. Similis est Anabaptistarum insania, qui Patris reuelationes & voluntatem omnibus suis commentis prætexunt. Sed omnibus iis in præsenti Paulus loquitur: Si linguis hominum loquar & Angelorum, charitatem autem non habeam, factus sum æs resonans, aut cymbalum tinniens siue ἀλαλάζων enim sonum confusum & tumultuarium edere significat. Loquitur autem de tota charitate, Dei nimirum & hominum, qualis in electis & verè credentibus habetur: qui vt Deum supra omnia diligunt, ita in illo omnes quoq; homines complectuntur. Estq; in singulis comparationis huius membris obseruandum, ne ea accipiamus abs q; conditione, quam de charitate itidem repetit: neue Dei dona absolutè aut temere damnemus, quorum vsus magnus & vtilissimus est, si charitatis regula gubernentur.
units.tr: First he compares love with the gift of tongues, and he speaks of it in very lofty terms, so as to raise love higher. He begins with tongues because those who had them were especially proud of them. "If I speak," he says, "with the tongues of men (that is, of all the nations that live under heaven) and of angels, etc." He wisely turns the discussion onto himself, so that he does not seem to despise others too arrogantly. He joins angels with men, not because angels have bodies or speak with tongues, but to express a human power of speech that is more excellent and truly heavenly. So by "tongues" he takes in all eloquence, and perhaps he also touches those who boasted of visions of angels and conversations with heavenly spirits, about whom he seems to have said something in his letter to the Colossians, where he warns us to beware of those who thrust upon us and force on us, with great boldness and almost by authority, things they have never seen. People did this of old among the nations, those who wished to excel above others, as is said elsewhere of Minos, Numa, Sertorius and others like them. Sectaries have always been prone to the same thing. Mahomet certainly peddled his Koran, than which nothing could be devised more absurd, more insipid or more impious, under the name of the angel Gabriel, pretending that private conversations passed between himself and the angel. What need is there to speak of the monks, who babble with such confidence about the heavenly hierarchy and the choirs of angels, and about the intercessions of the Virgin Mary and the saints with Christ, that they could not do so more confidently had they been spectators of what goes on in heaven for many years? Similar is the madness of the Anabaptists, who cover all their inventions with pretended revelations and the will of the Father. But Paul is speaking in the present passage to all of these: "If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I have become sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal" [alalazōn]. For the word means to make a confused and tumultuous noise. Moreover he speaks of the whole of love, that is, of love toward God and toward men, such as is found in the elect and truly believing, who, as they love God above all things, so in him embrace all men too. And in each member of this comparison we must observe that we should not take these things without the condition that he repeats concerning love; nor should we condemn the gifts of God absolutely or rashly, since their use is great and very useful if they are governed by the rule of love.

units.la: Admonemur igitur hoc loco, quid de linguarum cognitione & tota dicendi facultate sentire debeamus. Initiò terram vnius labij fuisse, Moses tradit: sed propter hominum insolentiam, qui Dei decreto sese contumaciter opposuerunt (quos gentium poeta per gigantomachiæ fabulam describunt) linguarum diuersitas immissa est, quæ malè susceptum consilium turbauit. Vt ergo tunc peccati poena fuit, & etiamnum hodie est (quod probè experiuntur, qui inter gentes peregrinas agunt) ita singulare Dei donum est, si cui contingat vt plures linguas audire & profari possit. Et hoc dono olim Apostolos instrui oportuit, vt Euangelium in toto orbe prædicarent, & gentes diuersis superstitionibus inter se scissas ad fidei Christianæ vnitatem adducere possent. Est præterea non minus vtilis quàm præclara facultas bene dicendi, qua commodè & prudenter animi sensus explicatur. Quare hanc quoque discipulis suis Christus pollicetur, & securos esse iubet, si quando fidei & doctrinæ suæ rationem reddere cogantur apud hostes, quos potentia & doctrinæ existimatio formidabiles facit. Et quanta vis sit orationis omnium gentium historiæ exemplis plurimis testantur. Quod enim de Hercule Gallico siue Ogmio Lucianus prodidit, qui homines ab aure reuinctos catenulis ex lingua sua protensis ducat quo velit, hoc ipsum de omnibus intelligi debet, qui totas respub. sua facundia rexerunt, & populi animos pro vt ipsis libebat in quamcunq; partem inclinarunt: qualis apud Athenienses Pericles fuit, in cuius labijs ipsa Pitho siue Suadela residere dicebatur, apud Romanos autem Cicero cum multis alijs. Constat certè hanc philosophiæ partem imprimis excultam semper fuisse ab ijs, qui in Repub. alijs præstare voluerunt. Athic meminisse oportet, dicendi regulam optimâ tutissimamq; esse charitatem. Nisi enim hæc orationi præsideat vt gubernatrix quædam, non inutile modò erit donum iflud, verumetiam noxium: quia affectuum libidine abrepta lingua aduersus Deum simul & homines effreni impetu fertur. Exempla huius audaciæ in ijs quotidie cernuntur, qui deierationibus & execrationibus temerarijs affuerunt: quos si vel verbulo vno laseris, illos horribiles diras & impiissimas voces pleno ore tonare audies. Imò qui hominum cordatissimi & prudentissimi habentur, nisi charitatis regulam sibi sequendam proponant, facundia sua saepe rempub. in extrema pericula abdu-cunt, cunt, dum suis potius commodis quam patriae consulunt: quod olim Graciae Oratores fecisse confiat. Possunt his falsi prophetae adnumerari & quotquot alij doctrinam suis affectibus accommodant: qui eo plus nocent, quo plus dicendo possunt. Recte igitur Prophetae & Apostoli admonent, ut linguam frenemus & ori nostro custodiam imponamus. Quod etsi omnibus praecipiatur, maxime tamen ad Verbi Dei administros pertinet, qui nisi charitate toti ardeant, nihil proficient docendo. Ideo Christus Petrum abnegatorem non prius in integrum restituit, quam illum de sui dilectione diligentius examinauisset. Et quam tenere populum amarint prophetae, non modo sermones illorum docent, quibus errantes in viam revocarunt, verumetiam querelas acerbissimas, quibus hominum contumacium interitum deplorauerunt. Quid, quod Paulus anathema fieri cupiebat a Christo, ut Iudaei converterentur? Et hos procul dubio imitabuntur, quotquot diligentius expenderint qualis grex sit Ecclesia & quanti eam faciat Deus, qui ipsam Filij sui sanguine redemptam voluit. Non poterunt enim non illam amore summo complecti, qui hoc cogitant, & ita simul ijdem non inani tinnitu aerem verberabunt, sed verba proferent, quae charitatis igne ardentia & spiritus virtute armata in intimos usque cordium recessus penetrabunt, & eos quoque convincent, quorum contumacia insuperabilis esse videbatur.
units.tr: We are therefore admonished in this place about what we ought to think of the knowledge of languages and of the whole faculty of speech. Moses tells us that at first the earth had one language; but because of the arrogance of men, who stubbornly set themselves against God's decree (whom the poet of the nations describes in the fable of the gigantomachy), the diversity of tongues was sent in, which upset the ill-conceived plan. Thus, as it was then a punishment for sin, and still is today (as those know well who live among foreign nations), so it is a singular gift of God if someone should happen to be able to hear and speak several languages. And the Apostles needed to be equipped with this gift, so that they might preach the gospel throughout the whole world and be able to bring the nations, divided among themselves by various superstitions, to the unity of the Christian faith. Moreover, the skill of speaking well, by which the feelings of the mind are explained fittingly and wisely, is no less useful than it is distinguished. Therefore Christ also promises this to his disciples, and bids them be unafraid whenever they are forced to give an account of their faith and teaching before enemies whom power and a reputation for learning make formidable. And how great a force eloquence has, the examples of the histories of all nations bear witness in very many cases. For what Lucian reported of the Gallic Hercules, or Ogmios, who leads men by the ear, bound with little chains stretched out from his tongue, wherever he wishes, this same thing must be understood of all those who have governed entire commonwealths by their eloquence, and turned the minds of the people in whatever direction they pleased. Such was Pericles among the Athenians, on whose lips Peitho or Suadela herself was said to dwell; and among the Romans Cicero, along with many others. It is certainly agreed that this part of philosophy has always been especially cultivated by those who wished to excel others in the commonwealth. Here we must remember that the best and safest rule of speaking is love. For unless love presides over speech as a kind of guide, that gift will not only be useless but harmful, because the tongue, carried away by the lust of the passions, rushes with unbridled force against God and men alike. Examples of this boldness can be seen every day in those who take part in rash oaths and curses; if you merely touch them with a single word, you will hear them thunder forth horrible, dreadful and most impious words with full mouths. Indeed, even those who are considered the most sensible and prudent men, unless they set before themselves the rule of love to follow, often lead the commonwealth by their eloquence into the greatest dangers, while they look to their own advantage rather than to the good of the fatherland; as the orators of Greece are known to have done of old. False prophets may be counted among these, and all others who adapt doctrine to their passions; they do the more harm, the more they are able to say. Rightly, then, the Prophets and Apostles admonish us to bridle the tongue and to set a guard over our mouth. And although this is commanded of all, it pertains most of all to the ministers of the Word of God, who, unless they burn wholly with love, accomplish nothing by teaching. Thus Christ did not restore Peter, who had denied him, to his place until he had examined him more carefully about his love for him. And how tenderly the prophets loved the people, their sermons teach us, by which they called back those who had strayed onto the way, and also their most bitter lamentations, in which they mourned the destruction of stubborn men. What of the fact that Paul wished to be made an anathema by Christ, so that the Jews might be converted? Without doubt, all who weigh carefully what sort of flock the Church is, and how highly God values her, whom he willed to redeem with the blood of his Son, will imitate them. For those who think of this cannot but embrace her with the greatest love, and so at the same time they will not beat the air with empty noise, but will speak words that, burning with the fire of love and armed with the power of the Spirit, will penetrate even to the innermost recesses of hearts, and will convince even those whose obstinacy seemed invincible.

units.la: Quoniam autem hoc loco Paulus de linguarum dono potissimum disputat, possunt ista commodissime aduersus eos proferri, qui linguas peregrinas in Ecclesiam inducunt. Coepit id iam olim fieri, quando mysterium iniquitatis Antichristus operari incepit, & non sine contentione primatum in Ecclesijs omnibus obtinuit. Vt enim Romani antiquitus in provincijs sua lingua ius dicebant, quae ea ratione omnibus passim obtrudebatur: ita posteris temporibus Pontifices, ut suum in omnes imperium testarentur, Latinae linguae usum in Ecclesijs inuexerunt. Tunc ergo passim lectiones & cantiones Latinae instituta, & eadem lingua Sacramenta administrata sunt. Quod non absq; Spiritus sancti suggestione praeuidens Irenaeus, vetustissimus & vere orthodoxus Scriptor, Antichristi nomen fore dixit, Latinus. Atqui id praeter charitatis regulam factum esse, res ipsa loquitur. Qui enim illa ducuntur, ij in dicendo Dei gloriam quaerunt, & populi salutem atque aedificationem suarum actionum omnium scopum sibi proponunt. At quis hoc de illis affirmare possit, qui ita loquuntur, & canunt, ut a nemine intelligi velint? Ergo ut nunc taceamus Diuorum invocationes, scripturarum detorsiones, operum merita & infinitas alias superstitiones, quae illic regnant, [?]vt nicus iste Latini sermonis usus reprehensionem grauem meretur, & totum illum sacrificorum atque monachorum gregem iure aera tinnientia & cymbala vlulantia dixeris, quorum nullus in Ecclesia usus sit. Nec puto absq; Dei prouidentia factum esse, ut suo indicio [?]foricres isti sese proderent, quando organorum concentus & campanarum sonitus non postremam cultus diuini partem fecerunt. Poterat tamen ferri stolida istorum hominum arrogantia, nisi tantis Ecclesiae sumptibus alerentur, & non tam cymbala inaniter tinnientia, quam vtriculares tibiae essent, ut qui non nisi bene saginati & distenti sonum ædunt.
units.tr: Since, however, Paul is disputing here chiefly about the gift of tongues, these things can most fittingly be brought forward against those who introduce foreign tongues into the Church. This began long ago, when Antichrist began to work the mystery of iniquity and, not without contention, obtained primacy in all the churches. For just as the Romans of old administered justice in the provinces in their own language, which was thus forced upon everyone everywhere, so in later times the Pontiffs, to bear witness to their power over all, introduced the use of the Latin language into the churches. Then readings and chants were everywhere instituted in Latin, and the sacraments were administered in the same language. Foreseeing this, not without the prompting of the Holy Spirit, Irenaeus, a most ancient and truly orthodox writer, said that the name of Antichrist would be Latinus. Yet the thing itself shows that this was done apart from the rule of love. For those who are led by love seek the glory of God in speaking, and set before themselves the salvation and edification of the people as the aim of all their actions. But who could affirm this of those who speak and sing in such a way that they wish to be understood by no one? So, to say nothing for now of the invocations of the saints, the distortions of Scripture, the merits of works and the countless other superstitions that reign there, this single use of the Latin language deserves grave censure; and you could rightly call that whole flock of priests and monks clanging bronze and howling cymbals, for whom there is no use in the Church. Nor do I think it happened without the providence of God that those fellows betrayed themselves by their own sign, when the harmony of the organs and the sound of the bells made up no small part of divine worship. Still, the foolish arrogance of these men could be tolerated, were they not nourished at such great expense to the Church, and were they not, rather than cymbals ringing emptily, like bagpipes, which give out a sound only when they are well fed and swollen.

units.la: Sed ad institutam comparationem redeamus, cuius secundo membro Paulus charitatem cum ijs donis Spiritus sancti confert, sine quibus neq; Ecclesia conseruari, neq; priuata cuiusquam salus consistere potest. Inter ea primum locum prophetiae tribuit, quam in sequenti Cap. linguis longe praeferet. Continet illa Scripturarum interpretationem, vna cum dono vaticinandi, quod in prima Ecclesia diu floruisse, alibi diximus. Secundo cognitionem mysteriorum & omnem scientiam ponit. Quibus vocabulis sapientiam intelligit, quam rerum omnium tam humanarum quam diuinarum scientiam dixerunt. Tertio fidem ipsam nominat, vbi obseruare oportet, fidem bifariam accipi. Primum pro fiducia gratuita misericordiae Dei, & firmo animi assensu, quo promissiones salutis aut vitae aeternae apprehendimus. Hac quia in his Christum apprehendit, qui nobis a Patre iustitia et salus factus est, iustificare & seruare dicitur. Ideo Habakuk dicebat: Iustus fide sua viuet. Et Isaias de Christo: Scientia sua multos iustificabit seruus meus, quorum iniquitates ipse gestabit. De illa item exponi debent omnes illae promissiones euangelicae: Qui credit in me, habet vitam aeternam. Item: Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, seruabitur. Et haec illa fides quam Paulus per charitatem agere dicit, ut illam a mortua & inani persuasione distinguat, Deinde est fides quaedam particularis, quae in Christo nihil praeter facultatem edendorum miraculorum apprehendit: & haec interdum hypocritis quoque datur, ut ex Christi verbis patet, qui in nouissimo die multos discturos ait: Domine Domine nonne per nomen tuum prophetauimus, & per nomen tuum daemonia eiecimus, & per nomen tuum multas virtutes fecimus? Quibus ipse respondebit: Nunquam noui vos, &c. De hac fide particulari Apostolus in praesenti loquitur, ut ex adiecta conditione apparet: Adeo ut montes transferā. Hac enim ad verba Christi alludit, in E-uangelio dicentis: Quicunque dixerit monti huic, Tollitor & proiicitor in mare: & non dis-ceptauerit in corde suo, sed crediderit quod fiant quae dicit, erit ei quicquid dixerit. Est hoc obseruandum propter Sophistarum argutias, qui hoc loco abutuntur, ut iustificationem charitati adscribant, aut saltem hanc fidei σωκάτιον[?] faciant contra Apostolorum doctrinam, qui hominem sola fide iustificari tradunt. Sed extra oleas currunt illi, quando Paulus hic non de iustificatione, sed de vsu donorum spiritualium, & de Ecclesiae oeconomia siue administratione loquitur. Nec etiam observant, iustificationem fidei adscribi, non propter charitatem aut eius opera, sed quia medium vnicum est, quo Christum & in hoc iustitiam & vitam apprehendimus. Obijciunt illi, Paulum loqui de omni fide, & ideo iustificantem quoque illam simul completi. At nos respondemus, vniuersales particulas non semper ad omnes species alicuius generis extendi, sed frequentius ad eas modo, de quibus agitur, restringi debere. Quia ergo de ea fidei specie hic sermo est, qua miracula edun-tur, Apostolus quoad hanc dixit omnem fidem, pro plena & perfecta. Sic sub initium huius epistolae Corinthios omni cognitione & scientia plenos esse dixit. Quae verba si quis ad omnium artium tam liberalium quam mechanicarum scientiam, aut ad rerum omnium, quae in natura sunt, cognitionem velit extendere, ne nimium ille ineptus erit aut ridiculus. Sufficiant ista pijs, qui à contendendi studio abhorrent. Nunc ergo quid de fide ista miraculorum dicatur, audiamus: (Si inquit) habeam omnem fidem, adeo ut montes transferam, charitatem autem non habeam, nihil sum. Caute & prudenter admodum loquitur, ne Dei donis aliquid detrahere videatur. Nec enim hoc nihil esse dicit, sed se nihil adeoque nullum fore, si charitate destituatur, quae sola facit, ut reliquis donis recte vtamur.
units.tr: But let us return to the comparison we set out. In its second part, Paul sets love against those gifts of the Holy Spirit without which neither the Church can be preserved nor the salvation of any individual can stand. He places prophecy first among them, which he will rank far above tongues in the following chapter. It consists in the interpretation of Scripture, together with the gift of prophesying, which, as we have said elsewhere, flourished for a long time in the early Church. Second, he names the knowledge of mysteries and all knowledge. By these words he means wisdom, which they have called the knowledge of all things, both human and divine. Third, he names faith itself. Here we must note that faith is understood in two ways. First, as the free confidence in God's mercy and the firm assent of the mind by which we grasp the promises of salvation or of eternal life. Because by this faith we lay hold of Christ, who has been made for us by the Father righteousness and salvation, it is said to justify and to save. So Habakkuk said: "The just shall live by his faith." And Isaiah, of Christ: "My servant, by his knowledge, shall justify many, bearing their iniquities." All the gospel promises should be explained in this sense as well: "He who believes in me has eternal life." Likewise: "He who believes and is baptized will be saved." This is the faith that Paul says works through love, distinguishing it from a dead and empty persuasion. Then there is a certain particular faith, which in Christ apprehends nothing beyond the power of working miracles. This is sometimes given even to hypocrites, as is clear from the words of Christ, who says that on the last day many will say: "Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in your name, and cast out devils in your name, and done many mighty works in your name?" To whom he will answer: "I never knew you," etc. It is of this particular faith that the Apostle is speaking here, as the added condition shows: "so that I could remove mountains." For he alludes to the words of Christ in the Gospel, saying: "Whoever says to this mountain, Be taken up and cast into the sea, and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says will come to pass, it will be done for him, whatever he says." This must be observed because of the subtleties of the Sophists, who misuse this passage to ascribe justification to love, or at least to make this faith a mere support for love, against the teaching of the Apostles, who declare that a man is justified by faith alone. But they go astray outside the olive grove, since Paul is not speaking here of justification but of the use of spiritual gifts and of the economy or administration of the Church. Nor do they notice that justification is ascribed to faith not because of love or its works, but because it is the only means by which we lay hold of Christ, and in him righteousness and life. They object that Paul speaks of all faith, and therefore that the justifying faith is also included. But we reply that universal particles do not always extend to all the species of a genus, but more often ought to be restricted to those of which the discussion is concerned. Since, then, the talk here is of that kind of faith by which miracles are worked, the Apostle, as far as this goes, said "all faith" to mean full and perfect faith. So at the beginning of this letter he said the Corinthians were full of all utterance and all knowledge. If anyone wished to extend these words to the knowledge of all the liberal and mechanical arts, or to the knowledge of all things that exist in nature, he would be too absurd or ridiculous. These things are enough for the godly, who shrink from the desire to quarrel. Now let us hear what is said about this faith of miracles: "If," he says, "I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing." He speaks very cautiously and prudently, lest he seem to take anything away from God's gifts. For he does not say that these are nothing, but that he himself would be nothing, and indeed no one at all, if he were destitute of love, which alone makes us use the other gifts rightly.

units.la: Docemur igitur hoc loco, quid in cognitione rerum coelestium & salutis aeternae, quid item in toto Ecclesiae ministerio potissimum spectari debeat: Nimirum, ut charitatis regulam in omnibus sequamur. Est sane Verbi ministerium inter huius saeculi munera longe praestantissimum. Nam qui illo fungitur, eum legatum Domini exercituum, dicit Propheta. Et notum est illud Christi: Qui vos audit, me audit, &c. Praeclarum item est rerum futurarum & earum quae salutis sunt, cognitio. Sed nisi charitate gubernetur, neque priuatae neq. publicae aliorum saluti quicquam conferet. Nam aut ambitionis spiritu homine inflant (quod supra de scientia Paulus dixit) aut ab auaritia ad turpe quaestum detorquentur. Exemplum huius rei memorabile extat in Balaamo. Fuit is vir totius Orientis celeberrimus, & fatidico spiritu oraculum de Christo et gente Israelitica verissimum edidit. Sed quia charitatem non habuit, auaritiae & quaestus turpis studio superatus, adeo nullus fuit in Dei conspectu, ut eum ab asina argui & corripi voluerit: & tandem gladio caesus dignas suae impietatis poenas luit. Idem de Caiapha & reliquis Iudaeorum sacerdotibus atq; scribis dici poterat: quibus rectissimè Simonem quoque Magum adnumeraueris. Quod autem de Ecclesiasticis viris dicitur, non minus ijs conuenit qui in Repub. versantur, qui si à charitate alieni sint, sapientiam simul & rerum vsum in suum & totius reipub. exitium conuertunt. Exempla huius generis in Saule, Ieroboamo, Iuliano, Sylla, Mario, Pompeio, Caesare, Alcibiade & similibus habentur. Et vtinam nostra tempora nihil simile vidissent.
units.tr: We are taught in this place, therefore, what ought above all to be regarded in the knowledge of heavenly things and of eternal salvation, and likewise in the whole ministry of the Church: namely, that we should follow the rule of love in all things. Indeed the ministry of the Word is by far the most excellent of the offices of this age. For the one who discharges it, the Prophet calls an ambassador of the Lord of hosts. And that saying of Christ is well known: "He who hears you hears me," etc. The knowledge of future things and of those that pertain to salvation is also excellent. But unless it is governed by love, it will contribute nothing to the salvation of others, either private or public. For either it puffs a man up with the spirit of ambition (as Paul said above of knowledge), or it is turned by greed to shameful gain. A memorable example of this exists in Balaam. He was the most famous man in all the East, and by a prophetic spirit he gave the most true oracle about Christ and the Israelite nation. But because he did not have love, and was overcome by the desire of greed and base profit, he was so far from being in God's sight that God wished him to be rebuked and corrected by an ass; and at last, struck down by the sword, he paid the penalty his impiety deserved. The same could be said of Caiaphas and the rest of the Jewish priests and scribes; and you could rightly count Simon the Magician among them as well. What is said of churchmen applies no less to those who engage in the commonwealth: if they are estranged from love, they turn their wisdom and their experience of affairs to their own ruin and that of the whole commonwealth. Examples of this kind are found in Saul, Jeroboam, Julian, Sulla, Marius, Pompey, Caesar, Alcibiades and others like them. And would that our own times had seen nothing similar.

units.la: Erant haec diligentius obseruanda ijs, penes quos est ministrorum Ecclesiae & Magistratuum electio. Solent hi fere generis splendorem, diuitias, vel etiam eruditionem aut eloquentiam suspicere, vel titulis inanibus sese fascinari sinunt. Alij miracula requirunt: quae vt ab impostoribus saepe fiunt, ita neque illos ipsos iuuant, qui neglecta charitatis Lege[?] non hoc vnum spectant, vt proximus quisque aedificetur, & Dei gloria promoveatur. Atqui miraculorum & signorum omnium praestantissimum est charitas: quia ex ea germani Christi discipuli dignoscuntur. Quis autem in Ecclesiae ministerio charitatis studiosos esse dixerit eos, qui locum subinde mutant, & quàm primùm pinguioris stipendij spes sese offert, oues suae fidei creditas de-serunt? Quis item Reipub. fidos putauerit, qui lucri studio ducti ad noua quotidie munera aspirant? E contra magni facere discamus doctores & magistratus fidos, qui vel hoc uno argumento charitatem suam declarant, quod multorum inuidiae & odijs se subijciunt, ut aliorum commodis atque saluti consulant.
units.tr: These things ought to have been observed more carefully by those in whose power is the choice of the ministers of the Church and of the magistrates. Such men are usually in awe of splendour of birth, riches, or even learning and eloquence, or they allow themselves to be bewitched by empty titles. Others seek miracles; and as these are often performed by impostors, so they do not help even those who, neglecting the law of love, do not look to this one thing, that each neighbour be edified and God's glory advanced. Yet of all signs and miracles, love is the most excellent, for by it true disciples of Christ are known. Who, then, would say that those are zealous for love in the ministry of the Church who change their place from time to time, and abandon the sheep committed to their faith as soon as the hope of a fatter stipend presents itself? Who again would think faithful to the commonwealth those who, led by the desire for gain, aspire every day to new offices? On the contrary, let us learn to value highly those teachers and magistrates who declare their love by this one proof, that they submit themselves to the envy and hatred of many in order to look after the advantage and salvation of others.

units.la: Sequitur tertium & quartum istius Comparationis membrum, quo ea comprehenduntur, quae charitatis effecta videri poterant. Inter haec primum est: Si insumam in alimoniam omnes facultates meas, &c. Potest hoc latissime extendi: Ut nimirum de epulis publicis & largitionibus intelligatur, quibus multi apud gentes olim populi fauorem venabantur; & huc pertinent viscerationes, sacrificia publica, congiaria, conuiuia, & alia huius generis. Simile quid postea inter Christianos factum fuit quoad ἀγάπας[?], id est, epulas, quae in coetibus sacris apponebantur, ut supra Cap. undecimo diximus. Imprimis tamen huc pertinet, quae sub eleemosynae praetextu in so-los pauperes distribuuntur. Et consulto videtur verbo ὑπωπίζειν[?] uti Apostolus, quod non alere modò, sed cibum minutim concisum quasi in os ingerere significat. Ita vero cum impensis quae fiunt ministerium promptum ac diligens coniungit: quod Chrysostomus annotauit. At quamuis id faciam (inquit Paulus) nullus inde ad me fructus redibit, si absque charitate id fecero. Quia eleemosynae à misericordia nomen habent, quae proprium & germanum charitatis effectum est, hypocriticum sit oportet, quicquid huius sine charitate fit. Exempla passim occurrunt, quae docent fucatam beneficentiam Deo minime probari: & huc referri debent quae de Pharisaeis Chri-stus apud Matthaeum pronuntiat: quae item de Anania & Sapphira Lucas in Actis prodidit. Quid ergo de illis dicemus, qui ex alieno liberales sunt, & dum misericordes videri volunt, crudeliter aliorum fortunas diripiunt, aut usuris fraudulentis intercipiunt? Volunt isti praedam cum Deo partiri, ut hoc propitio utantur: sed nunquam eos ille probabit, qui manus sanguine plenas ita abominatur, ut à talium precibus quoque oculos auertat. Recte ergo Thobias filium suum monebat, ut de suis facultatibus beneficentiam faceret.
units.tr: There follows the third and fourth part of this comparison, in which those things are included that might seem to be effects of love. The first among these is: "If I bestow all my goods to feed the poor," etc. This can be extended very widely, so that it is understood of public feasts and largesses, by which many peoples among the nations of old sought the favour of the populace; to this belong public banquets, sacrifices, distributions of corn and oil, dinners, and other things of this kind. Something similar was later done among Christians with the agapae, that is, the feasts that were set out in the sacred assemblies, as we said above in chapter eleven. Yet chiefly this refers to what is distributed to the poor alone under the pretext of alms. And the Apostle seems to have used the word "to bruise" advisedly, which means not merely to feed, but to put food in the mouth, as it were, in small pieces. In this way he joins to the expenses the ready and diligent service, as Chrysostom observed. But, says Paul, although I do this, no fruit will come back to me from it if I do it without love. Because alms take their name from mercy, which is the proper and genuine effect of love, whatever is done of this kind without love must be hypocritical. Examples occur everywhere that teach that feigned beneficence is by no means pleasing to God; and to this must be referred what Christ pronounces of the Pharisees in Matthew, and what Luke has related in Acts about Ananias and Sapphira. What then shall we say of those who are generous with what belongs to others, and, while wishing to seem merciful, cruelly plunder the fortunes of others or seize them by fraudulent usury? Such men want to share their plunder with God, so that they may use his favour; but he will never approve of those whose hands are so full of blood that he turns his eyes away even from their prayers. Rightly, therefore, Tobit admonished his son to do acts of beneficence from his own substance.

units.la: Confutantur praeterea huius loci authoritate, qui opera praeparationis excogitarunt, quibus primam gratiam (ut illi loquuntur) mereamur, aut propter quae fidem nobis Deus largiatur. Nam qualiacunque illa sint, nihil proderunt, si absque charitate fiant. Atqui ex charitate non possunt alii quid facere, quotquot fide destituuntur: & alibi peccatum esse pronuntiat Paulus, quicquid absque fide fit. Quae ergo illa praeparatio, quae non nisi peccatis constat? Quae vero stultitia fuerit, vel insania potius, in peccato meritum fidei aut salutis constituere? Quid autem de illis dicemus, qui eam demum charitatem caelos mereri docent, si qui multa in sacrificos & Monachos conferant, ideoque iam moriturus suadent, ut fraudatis legitimis haeredibus, ignauos illos ventres in bonorum suorum possessionem succedere patiantur? Sunt hi nequissimi impostores, qui & fidei fundamenta conuellunt, & charitatem è medio auferunt.
units.tr: Moreover, by the authority of this passage, those are refuted who have devised works of preparation by which (as they put it) we may merit the first grace, or on account of which God bestows faith upon us. For whatever such works are, they will profit nothing if they are done without charity. But those who lack faith cannot do anything from charity, and Paul elsewhere pronounces that whatever is done without faith is sin. What, then, is that preparation which consists of nothing but sins? And what folly, or rather madness, is it to set up the merit of faith or of salvation in sin? But what shall we say of those who teach that a charity of this sort merits heaven, if they bestow much upon priests and monks, and therefore, about to die, urge that the rightful heirs be defrauded and those lazy bellies be allowed to succeed to possession of their goods? These are most wicked impostors, who both overthrow the foundations of faith and remove charity from the midst.

units.la: Sed postremum huius Comparationis membrum videamus: Si tradam corpus meum ut com-burar, charitatem autem non habeam, nihil mihi proderit. Pleriq; hoc de martyrio exponunt, deq; ijs, qui morte & sanguine suo testimonium fidei suae Christo perhibent. At quia tales charitate non possunt destitui, de ijsdem locus iste non potest exponi, nisi Paulum hyperbolicè locutum fuisse dicamus. Itaque de illis potius hic agi puto, qui neque fide neque charitate moti, sed caeco carnis affectu abrepti seipsos in vitae discrimen manifestum coniiciunt. Fecerunt hoc olim apud Romanos Curtij, Horatij & Decij, qui vitam suam pro patria impendisse videri volebant, cum priuatae gloriae studio potius abriperentur. Sunt etiam, quos iniuria acceptae impatientia, aut vindictae cupiditas eò adducit, ut sibi ipsis mortem conscisc ant: quod olim Lucretia Romae & apud Carthaginenses uxor Hasdrubalis fecerunt. Empedocles ambitiosa affectatae scientiae libidine superatus in Aetnae craterae sese coniecit, & ita periit. Indicae foemina, ut pudicitiae suae & fidei coniugalis existimationem afferant, in maritorum defunctorum rogos insiliunt. Quibus adnumerari possunt, qui ut superstitionibus suis fidem faciant, diros cruciatus & mortem voluntariam subeunt, ut olim Baalis sacerdotes, qui cultellis seipsos fodiebant, & postea Donatistae & Circumcelliones, qui percussores quaerebant, à quibus occiderentur. Imitantur hos ex parte nostro saeculo Anabaptista[?],furiosum & contumax hominum genus, qui martyrijs gloriantur, quando sua figmenta Scripturis confirmare non possunt. Digni erant omnes isti quibus idem fieret, quod olim quibusdam ex Donatistis accidisse Theodoretus scribit. Cum enim generosum quendam iuuenem esse porrecto rogarent, vt ipsos occideret, ille prius vinciendos esse dixit, ne qui visa sociorum cæde pœnitentia ductì in ipsum ruerent. Itaque vinculis astrictos virgis egregie cecidit, & mox illis ita reliquit abijt. Sed vt in Pauli verbis progrediamur, istos quoque omnes nullum inde fructum reportaturos esse ait, si absque charitate talia patiantur. Nam vt aliàs ex D. Augustino annotauimus, causa facit martyrem, non supplicium.
units.tr: But let us look at the last member of this comparison: "If I give my body to be burned, but have not charity, it profits me nothing." Most people expound this of martyrdom, and of those who bear witness to their faith in Christ by their death and blood. But since such men cannot be destitute of charity, this passage cannot be explained of them, unless we say that Paul spoke hyperbolically. So I think rather that what is meant here is those who, moved neither by faith nor by charity, but carried away by blind fleshly affection, throw themselves into manifest danger of life. The Curtii, Horatii and Decii among the Romans did this, who wished to seem to have spent their lives for their country, when they were rather swept away by the desire for private glory. There are also those whom impatience at an injury received, or the lust for revenge, leads to bring death upon themselves, as Lucretia did at Rome and the wife of Hasdrubal among the Carthaginians. Empedocles, overcome by the ambitious lust of pretended learning, threw himself into the crater of Etna and so perished. Indian women, to vouch for the good repute of their chastity and conjugal faithfulness, leap onto the funeral pyres of their dead husbands. To these may be added those who, to confirm their superstitions, undergo dreadful torments and voluntary death, as the priests of Baal once did, who gashed themselves with knives, and afterwards the Donatists and Circumcellions, who sought out killers by whom they might be slain. In our own age the Anabaptists, a furious and obstinate kind of men, who boast of martyrdoms when they cannot confirm their fictions by the Scriptures, imitate these in part. All of those would have deserved what, Theodoret writes, once happened to some of the Donatists. For when they asked a certain noble young man to kill them, he said that they must first be bound, lest, moved by repentance at the sight of the slaughter of their companions, they rush upon him. So, bound with chains, they were thoroughly flogged with rods, and then he left them and went away. But to proceed with Paul's words: he says that all these too will gain no fruit from it, if they suffer such things without charity. For, as we have noted elsewhere from Augustine, the cause makes the martyr, not the punishment.

units.la: Confutantur igitur hoc loco omnes cultus electitij, qui in corporis castigatione aut exercitijs molestioribus consistunt. Si enim nihil iuuantur qui seipsos in ignem tradunt, quid prodesse poterit, si ieiunijs, vigilijs, cilicijs, chameunijs, peregrinationibus teipsum conficias? Non vult sacrificium Deus, sed obedientiam. At huius summa charitas comprehendit. Nam qui diligit alterum, Lege im pleuit, &c. Roma.13. Et alibi Apostolus corporale exercitationem parum utilitatis habere ait, pietatem vero ad omnia utilem esse, vt quae promissionem habeat vitae praesentis & futurae. Huic ergo omnes studeant, quae vt omnium virtutum parens est, ita nihil vitij coniunctū habet, & durissima quaeque nobis leuia & iucunda reddit, imò Deo conformes facit, qui ipsa charitas est. Adhuc quia ex fide emanat, huic testimonium reddit, nosq; germanos IESV CHRISTI discipulos esse demonstrat. Huic debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Therefore in this passage all chosen forms of worship which consist in castigating the body or in more burdensome exercises are refuted. For if those who give themselves over to the fire gain nothing, what can it profit you if you wear yourself out with fasts, vigils, hair shirts, lying on the ground, and pilgrimages? God does not want sacrifice but obedience, and the sum of obedience is comprehended in charity. For he who loves another has fulfilled the law, etc. (Rom. 13.) And elsewhere the Apostle says that bodily exercise has little usefulness, but godliness is useful for all things, since it holds the promise of the life present and of the life to come. Let all therefore strive for this charity, which, as the parent of all virtues, has no vice joined with it, and which makes every hardest thing light and pleasant for us, and indeed makes us conformed to God, who is charity itself. Moreover, since it springs from faith, it bears witness to that faith and shows us to be true disciples of Jesus Christ. To this charity be due blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY LXVIII.

units.la: Charitas longanimis est, comis est: charitas non æmulatur, charitas non agit perperā, non inflatur, non agit indecorè, non quærit quæ sua sunt, nō irritatur, non cogitat malum, non gaudet iniustitia, congaudet autem veritati: Omnia suffert, omnia credit, omnia sperat, omnia sustinet.
units.tr: Charity is patient and kind. Charity does not envy, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, does not behave unbecomingly, does not seek its own things, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice in injustice, but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.

units.la: Omnis quidem Scriptura propter nos data est, et multa tradit, quae ad vitā rectè instituendā necessaria sunt: Inter ea autem nihil frequentius & diligentius inculcat quàm charitatē, monens passim, vt hanc non ore solum & verbis, sed reipsa aut factis testemur. Hanc certè totius Legis summā esse Christus testatur, et hoc ipsum Apostoli nō absq; causa diligentissimè docent. Nā etsi nobis nihil magis necessarium est charitate, eadem tamen nobis admodum difficulter persuaderi potest propter ingenitum nobis philautiae malū, ex quo inuidia, simultates, odia, contentiones et rixae, imò frequenter Ecclesiarū & rerumpub. dissipationes nascuntur. Est ergo locus iste consideratu dignissimus. Postquam enim Paulus charitatē omnibus antepositū, quae vere eximia et praeclara sunt, nunc eande ab effectis & fructibus commendat, & pulcherrimas eius virtutes ex ordine enumerat, quas Corinthiorum vitijs opponit. Ita vero docet, nihil illa vtilius & magis necessarium esse, ad Ecclesiae & vnitatis ecclesiasticae conseruationem. Nobis autem huius loci hic vsus esse debet, vt in hoc quasi speculo nosipsos contemplemur, & discamus, quantum quisque in re Christiana profecerit, quidue sibi adhuc desit. Sed & antidotum saluberrimum hic nobis proponi cogitemus aduersus animi vitia, quae plerosque infestant. Etenim qui in illius consideratione se diligentius exercuerint, si sese neque vindictae cupiditate, neque ira praecipiti, neque inuidia aut odio, neque superbia aut confidentia, nullo denique caeco affectu abripi vel superari patientur. Non pigeat ergo singula verba siue membra diligentius excutere.
units.tr: Scripture, indeed, was given for our sake in its entirety, and it teaches much that is necessary for ordering our life rightly. Among these teachings, however, it urges nothing more frequently or more earnestly than charity, everywhere admonishing us to bear witness to it not only with the mouth and in words, but in deed and in fact. Christ testifies that this is the sum of the whole Law, and the Apostles teach this very thing most diligently, and not without cause. For although nothing is more necessary for us than charity, it can be persuaded upon us only with great difficulty, on account of the self-love that is born in us, from which envy, rivalries, hatreds, contentions and quarrels arise, and indeed frequently the break-up of churches and commonwealths. This passage is therefore most worthy of consideration. For after Paul has placed charity above all things, which are truly outstanding and excellent, he now commends it from its effects and fruits, and lists in order its most beautiful qualities, which he sets against the vices of the Corinthians. He teaches in this way that nothing is more useful or more necessary for the preservation of the Church and of ecclesiastical unity. We ought, however, to use this passage so that we may contemplate ourselves in it as in a mirror, and learn how far each of us has advanced in the Christian matter, and what is still lacking to us. But let us also consider that a most wholesome antidote is set before us here against the vices of the mind that infest most people. For those who have exercised themselves more diligently in the consideration of it will not allow themselves to be carried off or overcome either by the desire for revenge, or by headlong anger, or by envy or hatred, or by pride or self-confidence, in short by any blind passion. Let us not be weary, then, of examining each word and clause more carefully.

units.la: Primò charitatem longanimē esse ait. In Graeco enim habetur, μακροθυμεῖ[?] quod ἀπὸ τῆς θυμοῦ[?] deducitur. Est autem θυμὸς efferuescentia sanguinis circa cor cum vindictae cupiditate coniuncta. Inde μακροθυμῶς[?] siue longaniminiter agere dicitur, qui etsi iniurijs prouocetur, primum tamen illum bilis feruorem & animi motum reprimit, & magnanimitate quadam ijs quoque mitem atque beneuolum sese praebet, qui peiora de ipso meriti videbantur. Est haec patientiae causa, & ideo interpretes aliqui membrum hoc exposuerunt: Charitas patiens est. Ab eo autem orditur[?] Paulus propter Corinthios, quos diuturna rixa & factiones inueterata irritabiles secerant ut leues ob causas fratribus succenserent. Ideo remedium huic malo adhibere, & fontem contentionum obturare voluit. Interim meminerimus, nobis quoque hanc curam primam esse debere: Quia nihil tam officit charitati, quam animus ad iram praeceps & vindictae cupiditas. Sunt enim omnia offensarum plena, ideoque nunquam non occasionem irascedi ac tumultuandi invenient, qui affectui indulgere voluerint. Semper ergo cogitemus, vindictam ad Dei ius pertinere, nos autem ad beneficentiam ab illo esse conditos. Facile autem sibi temperabunt, qui vel modicam moram interposuerint irae, ubi hanc in corde suo ardere senserint. Nam ut subito accenditur, ita mox extingui potest, si non ipsi illam dictis acerbis & improbis sive crudelibus ausis amplius accendamus. Vidit hoc olim Athenodorus philosophus qui, Augustum monebat, ne iratus aliquid diceret aut faceret, nisi prius recitatis ex ordine vigintiquatuor literarum elementis.
units.tr: First, he says that charity is long-suffering. In Greek the word is μακροθυμεῖ [makrothymei], which is derived from θυμός [thymos]. Now θυμός is the boiling of the blood about the heart, joined with the desire for revenge. Hence μακροθύμως [makrothymōs] means to act with long-suffering, that is, one who, though provoked by injuries, nevertheless restrains that first heat of bile and emotion of mind, and with a certain magnanimity shows himself mild and benevolent even toward those who seemed to deserve worse from him. This is the cause of patience, and therefore some translators have rendered this clause: "Charity is patient." Paul begins with this on account of the Corinthians, whom a long-standing quarrel and deep-rooted factions had made so irritable that they took offence at their brothers for slight reasons. Therefore he wished to apply a remedy to this evil and to stop up the source of the contentions. Meanwhile let us remember that this must also be our first concern, because nothing so hinders charity as a mind rushing headlong into anger and the desire for revenge. For everything is full of offences, and so those who wish to indulge their passion will never fail to find an occasion for becoming angry and stirring up tumult. Let us therefore always consider that vengeance belongs to the right of God, while we have been made by him for beneficence. Those who, when they have felt this anger burning in their heart, interpose even a short delay, will easily restrain themselves. For as it is kindled suddenly, so it can be quickly extinguished, if we do not fan it further by bitter and wicked or cruel words and deeds. The philosopher Athenodorus saw this long ago, when he advised Augustus that, if he was angry, he should not say or do anything until he had first recited in order the twenty-four letters of the alphabet.

units.la: Secundò, Comis est charitas. In Graeco habetur χρηστεύεται [?], id est comem, placidam, comodam, facilem & utilem omnibus sese praebet. At qui tales sunt, ijdem omnia facile ferunt, & quaecunque fiunt in partem meliorem interpretantur. Contrarium huius virtutis est morositas & asperitas ingenij, qua fit, ut neque nos alios ferre possimus, neque alijs nobiscum convenire possit. Quia autem charitas communis Christianorum nota est, parum adhuc in religione Christiana morosi illi profecerunt, & proinde ipsis emendatione seria opus est. Conferet ad hanc plurimum, si primo unusquisque in seipsum descendat, & proprios mores atque animi affectus diligentius examinet. Mox enim inueniet se quoque hominem & nihil humanum abs se alienum esse. Peccavit itaque in te frater, aut vitio corporis sive animi laborat, propter quod tibi merito displicere debeat. At fortasse tibi quoque idem vitium, aut simile, aut etiam illo maius adhaeret: & quod illi accidit, tibi quoq; vel volenti vel inuito accidere potest. Succurrat ergo tibi naturae Lex: Quod tibi non vis fieri, alteri ne feceris. Huic meditationi alteram de Dei longanimitate coniungito, qualis nimirum ille erga nos fit, & quam clementer nostris vitiis atque infirmitatibus ignoscat. Quo cumprimis pertinet precatio: Remitte nobis debita nostra, sicuti nos remittimus debitoribus nostris: Quam unā qui serio expendunt, ij se omnibus faciles & propitios praebent.
units.tr: Second, charity is kind. In Greek the word is χρηστεύεται [chrēsteuetai], that is, it shows itself courteous, mild, obliging, easy to deal with, and useful to all. Those who are such also bear all things easily and interpret whatever happens in the better sense. The opposite of this virtue is moroseness and roughness of disposition, by which it comes about that we can neither bear with others nor can others get along with us. But since charity is the common mark of Christians, those morose people have made little progress in the Christian religion, and therefore they need serious correction. It will contribute greatly to this if each one first goes down into himself and examines more carefully his own manners and the affections of his mind. For he will soon find that he too is a man, and that nothing human is alien to him. Your brother has therefore sinned against you, or suffers from a bodily or mental fault, on account of which he ought rightly to displease you. But perhaps the same fault, or a similar one, or even a greater one, clings to you too; and what has happened to him can happen to you as well, whether you wish it or not. Let the law of nature therefore come to your aid: What you do not want done to you, do not do to another. Join to this meditation another one on the long-suffering of God, namely how he is toward us, and how mercifully he pardons our faults and weaknesses. To this especially belongs the prayer: Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. Those who weigh this one thing seriously show themselves easy and gracious to everyone.

units.la: Tertiò ait, Charitas ζηλοῖ [?], id est, non aemulatur. Est autem ζηλοῦν aliquid cum vehementiori animi affectu desiderare: & tam in bonam quam malam partem sumitur. In bonam partem, quando eorum, quos bene & fideliter agere videmus, similes fieri cupimus: aut etiā eos iuuare atque prouehere, quos amamus. Sic Corinthios Paulus aemulabatur, ut eos Christo sisteret virginem puram & incorruptam. Et ista aemulatio charitati proprie convenit. In malam vero partem sumitur aemulatio, quando idem est quod φθονεῖν, id est, invidere. Id enim ex caro nostri ipsius amore nascitur, qui homines movet, ut non modo appetant meliorem fortem, verum etiam ex aliorum felicitate dolorem concipiant. Et tales Corinthios fuisse audiuimus, quos Paulus supra carnales adhuc esse ostendit, quod zelo sive aemulationi, contentionibus item ac dissidijs locum darent. Ista autem aemulationis genere non in charitatem modo sed in ipsum quo que Deum peccatur, quasi is iniquus bonorum suorum dispensator sit, qui indignis ea largiatur, nobis autem multo dignioribus illa neget. Estque hoc vitium eo nocentius, quod omnibus naturā insitum sit, adeo ut eius scintillas, imo effecta potius non obscura, in infantibus quoque appareant. Remedium ergo tanti mali diligenter quaeri debet. Ubi primo cogitasse proderit, quod Capite duodecimo Paulus subinde inculcauit, Deum videlicet donorum simul & ministeriorum omnium esse authorem. Quis ergo illum accusare audeat, qui & sapientissimus est, & omnia iustissime administrat? Deinde hoc etiam animo reputabis, dona quae iam accepisti praestantiora esse, quam ut gratijs Deo agendis possis sufficere. Nam ut omnia alia taceamus, quos vnquam illi fatis gratus fuit, quod ab ipso homo creatus & anima rationali atque immortali donatus sit? Fertur pastor quidam conspecto bufone foedo & immani in largissimum fletum erupisse: quem cum magni nominis praesul praeteruectus interrogaret cur ita fleret, respondit ille: Se suam ingratitudinem, qua Deum hactenus offenderit, deplorare, qui videlicet nunquam expenderit, quantum hoc sit Dei beneficium, qui ipsum hominem, non bufonem, crearit. Quanto putas pauperculū illū meliorē fuisse omnibus illis, qui praeter hoc amplissimis fortunis ac dignitatibus ornati, de gratijs Deo agendis nunquā cogitant: insuper vero indigne ferunt, si quos ab illo benignius respici vident? Cogitent illi praeterea sibi nihil mali aut detrimenti accedere ex aliorū cōmodis, hos autem propter ista & Deo & ipsis magis quam antea esse obstrictos. Nam ea lege nobis sua bona Dominus largitur, ut ea in commune deponamus, & ut alij per nos iuuentur. Quid,quòd qui inuidia ringuntur, sibi ipsis nocent, non aliis? Nam vitam sibi ipsis amaram reddunt, iucundo honorum quae acceperunt usu seipsos spoliant, & cor proprium exedendo inuidia affectum cibo omnium pretiosissimo saturare studēt. Quod Satyricus obseruauit, cum scriberet:
units.tr: Third, he says, charity ζηλοῖ [zēloi], that is, it does not envy. To be zealous for something [ζηλοῦν, zēloun] is to desire it with a more vehement emotion of the mind, and the word is taken in a good sense as well as a bad. It is taken in a good sense when we wish to become like those whom we see acting well and faithfully, or also when we wish to help and advance those whom we love. In this sense Paul was zealous for the Corinthians, so that he might present them to Christ as a pure and uncorrupted virgin. And this zeal properly belongs to charity. But the word is taken in a bad sense when it means the same as φθονεῖν [phthonein], that is, to envy. For this arises from love of one's own flesh, which moves men not only to desire a better lot, but also to be grieved at the happiness of others. And we have heard that the Corinthians were such people, whom Paul shows above to be still carnal, because they gave room to zeal or emulation, and likewise to contentions and dissensions. Now by this kind of emulation sin is committed not only against charity but also against God himself, as if he were an unjust dispenser of his goods, who bestows them on the unworthy and denies them to us, who are far more worthy. And this vice is the more harmful because it is implanted in all by nature, so much so that its sparks, or rather its clear effects, appear even in infants. A remedy for so great an evil must therefore be diligently sought. Here it will be useful first to reflect on what Paul repeatedly urged in the twelfth chapter, namely that God is the author of all gifts and of all ministries together. Who then would dare to accuse him, who is both most wise and administers all things most justly? Next, you will also consider in your mind that the gifts you have already received are too great for you to be able to repay them with thanks to God. For, to pass over all other things, when has any man been sufficiently grateful to him for having been created by him and endowed with a rational and immortal soul?
