It is told that a certain minister, on seeing a foul and monstrous toad, burst into a flood of tears; when a prelate of great name, passing by, asked why he wept so, he replied that he was lamenting his ingratitude, by which he had hitherto offended God, since he had never considered how great a benefit of God it was that he had created him a man and not a toad. How much better do you think that poor fellow was than all those who, though adorned with the greatest fortunes and dignities apart from this, never think of giving thanks to God, and, what is more, take it ill if they see others regarded more kindly by him? Let them also consider that no harm or loss comes to them from the advantages of others; rather, on account of these very gifts they are bound more than before both to God and to themselves. For the Lord bestows his goods on us on this condition, that we should lay them up for the common good, and that others may be helped through us. Moreover, those who are consumed by envy harm themselves, not others. For they make their own life bitter, they deprive themselves of the pleasant use of the honours they have received, and by gnawing at their own heart they strive to satisfy envy with the most unpalatable of all foods. This the satirist observed when he wrote:

units.la: Inuidia Siculi non inuenere tyranni Tormentum maius.
units.tr: Envy did not invent a greater torment than the tyrants of Sicily.

units.la: Superat tamen haec omnia, quòd iidem illi Dei iram contra se prouocant, & huius benedictio-ne seipsos priuant: cuius rei exempla in Caino, Saule & similibus horrenda extant. Cum è con-tra felicissimè vitam degant, quotquot sua forte contenti pietatem colunt, & simul aliorum felici-tati congratulantur. Vidit hoc Solon, qui à Croeso rogatus ut aliquem beatum ipsi proderet, A-glaum quendam nominauit, qui patrii agelli fines nunquam excesserat, suo nimirum contentus & à curis aliorum omnium liber. At hodie qui Christiani dici volunt, plerisque aliis suam felici-tatem inuident, neque se felices fore arbitrantur, nisi illos miseros & infelices videant.
units.tr: Yet all these things are surpassed by this: such people provoke the anger of God against themselves and deprive themselves of his blessing. Examples of this stand out, horrible ones, in Cain, Saul and others like them. On the contrary, all who are content with what they have and cultivate godliness, and at the same time rejoice in the happiness of others, live most happily. Solon saw this, when Croesus asked him to name someone happy. He named a certain Aglaus, who had never left the boundaries of his ancestral field, content with his own and free of the cares of everyone else. Yet today those who wish to be called Christians envy most others their happiness, and do not think they will be happy unless they see those others wretched and unhappy.

units.la: Quartò dicit Paulus: Charitas nō agit perperā, vel ut Graecè scribitur, ἀ περπερεύεται[?]. Chrysostomus id exponens idem esse dicit, quod ἀπροπετεύονται[?] quae Metaphora est ab auibus desumpta, quae implumes adhuc volare nituntur. Ea ergo voce insolentia notatur & proteruia, quam confi-dentia parit in iis, qui sibi omnia licere, seque sibi ipsis ad omnia sufficere putant. Tales fere absque ratione omnia faciunt, inque eo sibi ipsis potissimum placent, quòd plus aliis ausint. Sunt ingenia ista reipub. nocentissima, eò quòd unum hoc vitium virtutes & dotes omnes obscurat atque cor-rumpit. Laborauit eo olim Alcybiades, & eo abreptus seipsum perdidit, & ingenij animique do-tes praestantissimas foedissimè polluit, atque insuper patriam in extremum discrimen adduxit. Si-milis huic apud Romanos Catilina fuit cum suis coniuratis: quos fere imitantur hodie, qui gene-ris nobilitate & opibus confisi insolentius agunt, & sibi quiduis audendi licentiam pollicentur. Qui vero in Ecclesia tantum sibi arrogant, si fere cum disciplina ordinem omnem & sacra omnia euertunt. Exemplo sunt Corinthij, qui epulas lautiores in coetus sacros inferendo pauperioribus im-patientiae & murmuris authores fuerunt, & IESV CHRISTI Coenam mysticam turpiter prophanarunt. Sunt hi omnes à charitatis ingenio alienissimi. Illa enim, quia neminem contemnit, nihil sibi insolentius arrogat: & ideo Paulus hoc loco Corinthijs modestiam commendat: quae homi-num mentes ceu fraeno continet, ne cotumaciter efferantur. Hic autem ante omnia opus est, ut quisque seipsum probe noverit, seque non minus quam qui cotemptissimi habentur, Dei gratia et Christi-rito opus habere intelligat. Meminerint praeterea omnes communionem, quae nobis cum omnibus credentibus in Christo intercedit, pluris fieri debere quàm generis nobilitatem aut quaecunque alia sunt huius saeculi priuilegia. Etenim Christi leges universales sunt, & ex aequo omnes obstringūt, qui illi semel nomen dederunt. Omnium vero illarum caput siue summa est charitas. Itaque in Ecclesia ij demum praestantissimi sunt, qui quàm plurimi feruunt.
units.tr: Fourthly, Paul says: Charity does not act perversely, or, as it is written in Greek, [περπερεύεται]. Chrysostom, explaining this, says it means the same as [ἀπροπετεύονται], a metaphor taken from birds that, still unfledged, strive to fly. By this word, then, is noted the insolence and arrogance that confidence produces in those who think everything is allowed them and that they are sufficient for everything by themselves. Such people almost always act without reason, and they please themselves most in this, that they dare more than others. Such dispositions are most harmful to the commonwealth, because this one vice obscures and corrupts all virtues and gifts. Alcibiades once suffered from it, and, carried away by it, ruined himself, foully polluted the most outstanding gifts of mind and character, and moreover brought his country to the utmost peril. Similar to him among the Romans was Catiline with his fellow conspirators; and today those imitate them almost exactly who, trusting in noble birth and wealth, behave more insolently and promise themselves a licence to dare anything. Those who in the Church claim so much for themselves overturn almost all order and discipline and all sacred things. The Corinthians are an example: by bringing more lavish feasts into the sacred assemblies, they became the authors of impatience and murmuring among the poorer folk, and they foully profaned the mystical Supper of Jesus Christ. All these are most alien to the nature of charity. For charity, since it despises no one, claims nothing for itself too insolently; and so Paul here commends modesty to the Corinthians, which restrains men's minds as with a bridle, lest they be carried away in stubbornness. Here, however, above all, each must know himself well, and understand that he needs the grace of God and the merit of Christ no less than those who are held most contemptible. Let all also remember that the fellowship which we have with all who believe in Christ ought to be valued more highly than nobility of birth or any other privilege of this age. For the laws of Christ are universal, and bind all equally who have once given their name to him. The head, or chief, of all these laws is charity. Therefore in the Church those are truly most outstanding who are most fervent.

units.la: Quintò, Non inflatur Charitas. Est hoc cum priori coniunctum, vel potius est eius antecedens. Unde enim insolentia illa, quam quòd aliqui inflantur? Est autem locutio haec Metaphorica, sumpta vel ab utribus, qui inflati vento turgent: vel à membris vitiosis, quae ex inflammatione aut noxijs humoribus intumescunt. Transfertur hoc ad animum, & superbis tribuitur, quos propria persuasio & sui ipsius fiducia decipit, ut nihil non sibi tribuant, & ideo se contra omnes extollant. Ex horum numero scioli illi Corinthiorum fuerunt, de quibus Cap. secundo & octauo dixi-mus. Et horum similes hodie multi sunt, qui quasi dictaturam in Ecclesia gerant, omnibus pro imperio praescribunt, & anathematisimis devouent eos, qui ipsis non in omnibus assentiuntur. Sunt hi quoque alienissimi à charitate, quae facit ut quisque de semetipso modestissimè sentiat, & alios quoq; omnes amore fido complectatur. Est igitur huius vitij remedium praestantissimum, si nosipsos rectius excutiamus. Tunc enim apparet, nos utriū inflatorū aut partium corporis ex in-flammatione tumescentium similimos esse. Illud enim, cuius fiducia plerique turgent, aut inanis flatus est, aut humor noxius siue sanies, vel etiā pestifera aut letalis inflamatio. Ad prius pertinent opes, honores, dignitates, forma, ipsa deniq; vita hominis, quàm Iacobus vaporem esse scribit ad exiguum tempus apparentem & mox euanescentem. Ad alterum caeca illa persuasio, quae ipsum animum extollit altius. Quia enim aduersus ipsum Deum extollitur, non potest non coram illo fætere, unde nobis praesens interitus nascitur. Rectè ergo superbia initium peccati dicitur, & exempla sunt in potentissimis Regibus, quae docent, quàm illa exitialis sit.
units.tr: Fifthly, charity is not puffed up. This is connected with the previous point, or rather it comes before it. For whence does that insolence arise, if not because some are puffed up? This expression is metaphorical, taken either from bellows, which swell with wind, or from diseased limbs, which swell from inflammation or harmful humours. This is transferred to the mind, and it is applied to the proud, whom their own persuasion and self-confidence deceive, so that they attribute everything to themselves and therefore exalt themselves against all others. Among these were those self-styled know-alls of the Corinthians, of whom I spoke in the second and eighth chapters. There are many today like them, who act as if they were dictators in the Church, prescribe to everyone as if by command, and devote to anathema those who do not agree with them in everything. These people too are most alien to charity, which causes each person to think of himself with the greatest modesty and to embrace all others with faithful love. The best remedy for this vice, then, is to examine ourselves more carefully. For then it becomes clear that we are very like the bellows or the swollen parts of the body that swell from inflammation. For that in which most people swell with confidence is either empty wind, or harmful humour, that is, pus, or even a deadly and pestilent inflammation. To the first belong riches, honours, dignities, beauty, and indeed the very life of man, which James writes is a vapour appearing for a short time and soon vanishing away. To the second belongs that blind persuasion which lifts up the mind itself too high. For because it is lifted up against God himself, it cannot but stink before him, whence present ruin arises for us. Rightly, then, pride is called the beginning of sin, and examples among the most powerful kings teach how deadly it is.

units.la: Sexto, Charitas non agit indecorè. In Graeco est, ἐκ ἀχημονα[?]. Vsus est eadem voce Apostolus supra Cap. septimo de parentibus, qui praeter quàm ipsos deceat, filias suas apud se detinent, ne eas nuptui dent. Est autem duplex huius vocabuli significatio. Prima, vt idem fit quod indecorè seu indecenter agere. In eo peccant, qui sui sexus, aetatis, conditionis nullam habent rationem, & ne eorum quidem, quibus cum agunt: quod fere proterui illis & inflati accidit, de quibus diximus. Altera, vt pro fastidire ponatur, & tunc potest ad homines & ad res transferri. Itaq; secundum hanc significationem peccatur ab ijs, qui vix aliquem dignum esse putant, cui ipsi inferiantur: quosq; eorum pudet, quae ex officio facere debebant. In omnibus istis peccabant Corinthij, cum multa praeter Christianae professionis decorū facerent, indoctos contemnerent, & pauperes fastidirent, adeo vt ne in Coena quidem mystica cum illis vellent communicare. Et vtinam hodie non magnus esset eorum numerus, qui similia faciunt. At istis quoq; malis charitas medetur. Qui enim hanc habent, hi & seipsos inspiciunt diligentius, & simul alios obseruant, ne quem suo officio fraudent: & ideo per illam Apostolus Legem impleri dicit. Deinde quia omnes sibi fratres esse norunt, neminem ita fastidire possunt, vt suo seruitio indignum esse putent. Imò nullius rei ipsos pudet, quàm si quid abs se praeter officium factum esse senserint. Et cur non tunc nos nostripsius pudeat, quando tales ab ipsa rerum natura arguuntur, cuius singulae partes officio suo quam diligentissimè funguntur? Haec certè causa est, quòd prophetae ad boues & asinos, ad volucres deniq; eos remittunt, qui in Dei schola erudiri nolunt. Quoad homines verò, non possunt illi aliquem fastidire aut contemnere, cuius operam sibi aliquando vtilem aut necessariam fore cogitant. Quod enim de Leone narrant fabularum scriptores, quem laqueo captum mus liberauit, hoc ipsum multis Regibus accidisse constat, qui hominum vilissimorum beneficio in summis periculis seruati sunt. Xerxes certè, qui mare totum nauibus vt ponte straverat, paulò post piscatoris opera seruatus est, qui sua scapha exceptum in Asiam traiecit. Et cur nos alicuius hominis pudeat, qui Christum peccatores simul & miserrimos quosque tam benignè complexum esse legimus? Quid verò de illis dicemus, quos rectè facere pudet, & sibi intolerabilem iniuriam fieri clamant, si liberius moneantur, vt officium faciant?
units.tr: Sixthly, charity does not behave unseemly. In Greek it is [ἀσχημονεῖ]. The Apostle used the same word above in chapter seven, of parents who keep their daughters at home, not giving them in marriage, beyond what is becoming to them. This word has a twofold meaning. The first is that it amounts to acting indecorously or indecently. They sin in this who take no account of their sex, age or condition, nor even of those with whom they deal; this happens almost always to the arrogant and puffed-up, of whom we have spoken. The second is that it is used for to despise, and then it can be applied to persons and to things. According to this meaning, those sin who think hardly anyone worthy that they should serve him, and who are ashamed of the things they ought to do by virtue of their duty. In all these things the Corinthians were sinning, when they did many things unbecoming to the Christian profession, despised the unlearned, and scorned the poor, so much so that they did not even want to share the mystical Supper with them. And would that today the number of those who do similar things were not great! But charity heals these evils too. For those who have it both examine themselves more diligently and at the same time observe others, lest they defraud anyone of his duty; and so the Apostle says through it the law is fulfilled. Then, because they know that all are brothers to them, they cannot so despise anyone as to think him unworthy of their service. Indeed they are ashamed of nothing so much as if they perceive that they have done anything beyond their duty. And why should we not be ashamed of ourselves, when such people are shamed by nature itself, each part of which performs its office most diligently? This is certainly the reason why the prophets send to oxen and asses, and finally to birds, those who do not wish to be taught in God's school. As for human beings, they cannot despise or contemn anyone whose service they think will someday be useful or necessary to them. For what the writers of fables tell of the lion, whom a mouse freed when he had been caught in a snare, is established to have happened to many kings, who were saved in the greatest dangers by the help of the lowliest men. Xerxes certainly, who had covered the whole sea with ships as with a bridge, was saved shortly afterwards by the work of a fisherman, who in his little boat ferried him over to Asia. And why should we be ashamed of any man, when we read that Christ embraced sinners and the most wretched so kindly? But what shall we say of those who are ashamed to do right, and cry out that a intolerable injury is done to them if they are admonished more freely to do their duty?

units.la: Septimo, Non quærit charitas quæ sua sunt. Sua quærere & curare per se peccatum non est: quin decet potius vt vnusquisq; salutem suam cum timore & tremore operetur: adhæc infideliorem dicit Apostolus eum, qui suis non prospicit. At hic sua quærere dicuntur, qui non nisi suis commodis student, alios verò omnes inhumaniter negligunt, imò (quod crudelius est) ex aliorum damnis suum commodum venantur. Est hic proprius fructus philautiae, quae charitati ex diametro opponitur. Ex illa enim nascuntur calumniae, vsurae, rapinae, furta, obtrectationes & venalia iura. Hinc bella non necessaria, seditiones & Reipub. dissipationes prodeunt. Deniq; de MEO & TVO omnes lites oriuntur, quibus fora & iudicum subsellia perstrepunt. Et si Corinthios spectemus, ex hoc fonte apud ipsos sectae manarunt, quibus tota eorum Ecclesia scissa fuit, actiones item illae forenses, quas apud ethnicorum tribunalia instituebant. Est autem hoc vitium eo nocentius & incurabilius, quod omnibus innatum sit, sicuti in infantibus est videre. Itaq; magno studio hic opus est. Vix enim quicquam tam difficile est, quàm cauere ne quis à seipso fallatur: quia impostor ille nunquam discedit, vt Plato quoq; monuit. Proderit autem vehementer, si cogitemus, nā-tura sic comparatum esse, vt nostrum commodum in alterius commodo inculsum sit. Nam eadem inter homines ratio est communionis, quae inter corporis membra: quo simili supra Paulus vsus est. Et vt incendio exorto, nisi quisq; suum negotium agi putet, & ad illud restinguendum accurrat, facile tota vrbs flammis absumitur: ita si vel in ciuitate, vel Ecclesia, vel re domestica, alij alios negligant, dum singuli suis intenti sint, omnia pessum eant oportet. Romanis certè philautia bellorum ciuilium causa fuit, quae Rempublicam totam euerterunt. Eadem in Ecclesia olim haereses & factiones peperit, quæ illam miserè conuulserunt: quod vnius Arij exemplum abunde probat. Et quid hodie passim fiat, omnes vident. Rectè ergo Paulus ad Philippenses scribebat: Ne sua quisq; spectetis, sed vnusquisq; etiam quæ sunt aliorum. Quo loco Christi exemplum magnifice propont & illustrat, vt maius fit huius admonitionis pondus. Vide Philip.2.
units.tr: Seventh, love does not seek its own things. To seek and look after one's own interests is not in itself a sin; indeed, everyone ought rather to work out his own salvation with fear and trembling, and the Apostle also calls the man who does not provide for his own worse than an unbeliever. But those are said to seek their own things who study only their own advantage, treat all others with inhuman neglect, and, what is more cruel, hunt for their own gain from the losses of others. This is the proper fruit of self-love, which is directly opposed to charity. From it spring slander, usury, robbery, theft, detraction and venal justice. From it come unnecessary wars, seditions and the ruin of commonwealths. Finally, all lawsuits arise from the words "mine" and "yours," and the courts and judges' benches resound with them. If we look at the Corinthians, from this source sects flowed among them, by which their whole congregation was torn apart, and also those lawsuits which they brought before the tribunals of the heathen. This vice is all the more harmful and incurable because it is innate in everyone, as can be seen in infants. Therefore great effort is needed here. For there is scarcely anything as difficult as guarding against being deceived by oneself, because that deceiver never leaves us, as Plato also warned. It will greatly help, however, if we consider that nature has so ordered things that our own advantage is bound up with the advantage of others. For the same bond of fellowship exists among men as among the members of the body, a comparison which Paul used above. And just as, when a fire breaks out, unless each man thinks that his own business is being attended to and runs to put it out, the whole city is easily consumed by the flames, so, if in the state, or in the Church, or in the household, people neglect one another while each is intent only on his own affairs, everything must perish. Certainly self-love was the cause of the civil wars among the Romans, which overthrew the whole commonwealth. The same self-love once bore heresies and factions in the Church, which tore it wretchedly apart; the example of Arius alone proves this abundantly. And what is done today everywhere, all can see. Rightly, therefore, Paul wrote to the Philippians: "Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others." In that passage he sets forth and illustrates the example of Christ in a remarkable way, so that the weight of this admonition may be greater. See Philip. 2.

units.la: Octauo, Charitatem non irritari dicit. Pertinet hoc ad primi membri expositionem de longa nimitate. In præsenti verò per ἀπολογίαν[?] siue causæ reddition em subijcit: Non cogitat malum, id est, aliena est à prauis & sinistris suspicionibus. Ex quo hoc quoq; sequitur, quod neq; vindicta cupida sit, neq; malum malo rependere studeat. Est autem hoc membrum consideratu dignissimum: quia nulla pestis nocentior, nulla charitatis remora efficacior est animo ad suspiciones proclivi. Est verò hoc quoq; vitium nobis innatum, & philautiæ fructus est, de qua modo diximus. Vt enim qui furantur, fallunt, libidinibus vagis indulgent, aut alijs vitijs laborant, omnes homines idem studijs delectari putant: ita quia nostri amantes sumus & nostris commodis studemus, ex nostro ingenio alios omnes æstimantes, eos quoq; non nisi sua quærere, & proinde nobis inuidere, bonis nostris insidiari, deniq; eadem quæ nos affectare suspicamur. At qui huic affectui indulgent, hi amicitias arctissimas dissoluunt, neq; vllis beneficijs emolliri possunt, vt meliora de ijs sibi pollicentur, quos suspectos habent. Exempla quotidie inter coniuges æduntur[?], quos zelotypia urit, qui quo magis se mutuo amant, eò magis intra animos suos excruciantur, vt amore etiam illo frui nequeant. Quare non imprudenter Cæsar dicebat, se velle domum suam à suspicionibus quoq; liberam esse. In Repub. nihil suspicione nocentius esse, omnium seculorum exemplis abunde probatum est. Hæc Pharaoni & Ægyptijs sæuissimæ illius tyrannidis causa fuit, quæ postea exitium ipsis attulit. Hæc Saulem contra Dauidem extimulauit, imò mouit, vt aduersus Deum impiè insurgeret. Hæc iudiciorum maxima corruptela est, quia iudicum aures calumnijs patefacit, quod olim Apelles typo non minus eleganti quam vero docuit. Iudicem pingebat pro tribunali sedentem auribus patentissimis, cui à tergo quidem Ignorantia, à sinistris autem Suspicio assistebat: ad huius tribunal hominem innocentem per capillos attrahebat Calumnia facem ardentem gestans, quam Invidia, Fraus & Insidiæ comitabantur. Procul verò has sequebantur Veritas & Pænitentia. Ita nimirum innuens eorum innocentiam, qui suspicionibus & calumnijs circumuenti à iudicibus ignorantibus damnantur, serò tandem patefieri, & tunc inutili fere pœnitentia duci eos, qui suspicioni nimium indulserunt. Et vt ad homines priuatos redeamus, vt suspicio omnia in malam partem rapit, ita causa est vt amicitiæ semel dissutæ vix vnquam possint iterum coalescere. Ideo rectè à Menandro dictum est, Τὸ δ’ ὑποκεῖν διαβολὴν ἔχει μέλλω τὰ ποιοῦν[?]: innuens ex suspicionibus calumnias plures & grauiores, quàm ex ipsis factis enasci. Nec dubium est hoc vitium apud Corinthios vulgare fuisse, cùm singuli suam sectam euehere studerent. Nos verò teneamus, suspiciones charitati imprimis aduersas esse, & proinde procul arceri debere, ne animis insideant. Cauebitur hoc facile, si in quibuslibet monendis ingenua libertate vtamur, quam Christus commendat, neq; simultates aut odiorum scintillas admittamus. Interim Christianorum quoq; est, ita se gerere, ne quam alijs male de se suspicandi occasionem præbeant, per quam charitatis vinculum possit abrumpi.
units.tr: Eighth, he says that love is not provoked. This pertains to the explanation of the first clause, concerning long-suffering. Here, however, by way of defence [ἀπολογίαν], or by giving the reason for the matter, he adds that love "thinks no evil," that is, it is a stranger to wicked and sinister suspicions. From this it also follows that it is not eager for revenge, nor does it strive to repay evil with evil. This clause is most worthy of careful consideration, because no plague is more harmful, and no hindrance to love more effective, than a mind prone to suspicion. This vice too is innate in us, and it is a fruit of the self-love of which we have just spoken. For just as those who steal, deceive, indulge in wandering lusts, or suffer from other vices, think that all men are delighted by the same pursuits, so, because we love ourselves and study our own advantage, judging all others by our own nature, we suspect that they too seek only their own things, and therefore envy us, lay snares for our goods, and finally aim at the very things we ourselves aim at. But those who indulge this feeling dissolve the closest friendships, and cannot be softened by any kindnesses so that they promise themselves better things from those whom they hold under suspicion. Every day examples are seen among married couples, whom jealousy burns, and who, the more they love each other, the more they are tormented in their minds, so that they cannot even enjoy that love. Therefore Caesar was not unwise in saying that he wished his own house to be free even from suspicions. That nothing is more harmful in a commonwealth than suspicion has been abundantly proved by the examples of all ages. This was the cause of Pharaoh's and the Egyptians' most savage tyranny, which afterwards brought ruin upon them. This stirred up Saul, indeed moved him, to rise up impiously against David and against God. This is the greatest corruption of judgments, because it opens the ears of judges to calumnies; Apelles once taught this in a picture no less elegant than true. He painted a judge sitting on the tribunal with very open ears; behind him stood Ignorance, and on his left Suspicion. To this tribunal Calumny dragged an innocent man by the hair, carrying a burning torch, and Envy, Fraud and Snares accompanied her. Far behind them followed Truth and Repentance. Thus he indicated, of course, that the innocence of those who are overwhelmed by suspicions and calumnies and condemned by ignorant judges is revealed too late, and that then those who have indulged suspicion too much are led to a repentance that is almost useless. And to return to private persons: just as suspicion twists everything into a bad sense, so it is the cause that friendships once torn apart can scarcely ever be joined together again. Therefore Menander rightly said: "Τὸ δ’ ὑποκεῖν διαβολὴν ἔχει μέλλω τὰ ποιοῦν," implying that more and graver slanders arise from suspicions than from the deeds themselves. And there is no doubt that this vice was common among the Corinthians, since each man strove to exalt his own sect. But let us hold fast that suspicions are above all opposed to charity, and therefore must be kept far off, lest they settle in our minds. This will be easily avoided if, in admonishing anyone, we use the frank liberty which Christ commends, and do not admit quarrels or sparks of hatred. Meanwhile it is also the duty of Christians so to conduct themselves that they give others no occasion to suspect them unjustly, by which the bond of charity could be broken.

units.la: Nono, non gaudet charitas iniustitia, congaudet autem veritati. Potest hoc bifariam ex-poni. Primò, quod qui vera dilectione ardent, non gaudeant aliorum sceleribus aut malefactis, quod inuidi solent. Quia enim cupiunt perire eos, quibus male volunt, ex eorundem delictis atque sceleribus delectationem capiunt, quibus illos sibi ipsis odia multorum & exitium accersere videant. At longè alius charitatis affectus est, quæ veritate gaudet, id est, tunc sibi & alijs gratulatur, quando omnia integrè & syncere fieri videt. Quia enim Deum & homines completitur, non potest non voluptatem ex eo maximam capere, si Dei cultum florere & iustitiæ omnes studere conspicetur. E contra verò ex aliorum interitu tristitiam & dolorem concipit, vt in Samuele, qui Saulis repulsam lugebat, & in Lotho ob Sodomæorum flagitia seipsum exeruciante est videre. Quam ergo procul à charitate absunt, qui ex benefactis calumniandi occasionem arripiunt? Deinde potest membrum hoc ijs etiam opponi, qui sub charitatis prætextu sceleribus patrocinantur, & quibus impunè fieri sinunt. At hæc non charitas est, sed perniciosa negligentia siue indulgentia. Nam pater filium, quem diligit castigat. Et Deus, qui ipsissima est charitas, sæpe alienum opus facit (vt Isaia verbis vtar) vt opus suum facere possit, id est, iratus nobis poenas infligit, vt gratiae suae & bonitati apud nos locum faciat. Quot quot ergo ferre possunt, vt aliqui inter scelerum licentiam perreant, quoad fortunas suas & corpora, ij profecto hominum aut negligentissimi, aut crudelissimi sunt. At quos Christianae charitatis ardor inflammauit, ij à delinquentibus poenas exigunt, sed cum dolore & gemitu, atq; in eo patres pios fidosq; imitantur. Aduersus vtrumq; huius membri sensum Corinthij peccabant, qui & scelera grauissima impune designari patiebantur, & sibijpsis placebant, quando lugere potius debuissent, vt in incesti illius exemplo supra vidimus. Obseruare hoc debent diligenter omnes, qui in publica authoritate constituti sunt, ne vel negligentius agant, vel modum iustae seueritatis excedant: sed vinitores & agricolas inducstrios imitentur, qui noxias quidem herbas euellunt, & palmites luxuriantes siue arescentes resecant, cauent autem ne ipsis frugibus malum dent. At moderationis huius regula tutissima est charitas, quae poenas quantumuis graues, ijs qui deliquerunt leues & salutares facit.
units.tr: Ninth, love does not rejoice in injustice, but rejoices with the truth. This can be explained in two ways. First, those who burn with true love do not rejoice in the crimes or misdeeds of others, as the envious are wont to do. For since they desire that those whom they wish ill should perish, they take delight in the offences and crimes of those men, by which they see hatred and ruin being brought upon them from many quarters. But the affection of charity is quite different: it rejoices in the truth, that is, it congratulates itself and others when it sees all things being done wholly and sincerely. For since it embraces God and men, it cannot but take the greatest pleasure if it sees the worship of God flourishing and all men striving for justice. On the contrary, it conceives sorrow and grief at the ruin of others, as can be seen in Samuel, who mourned Saul's rejection, and in Lot, who tormented himself over the wickedness of the Sodomites. How far, then, are those from charity who seize upon the good deeds of others as an occasion for slander? Next, this clause may also be opposed to those who, under the pretext of charity, defend crimes and allow them to go unpunished. But this is not charity, but a ruinous negligence or indulgence. For a father chastises the son whom he loves. And God, who is love itself, often does "his strange work" (to use Isaiah's words) so that he may do his own work, that is, he inflicts punishments upon us in anger so that he may make room for his grace and goodness among us. Therefore, all those who can bear that wicked men should go on in their licence, as far as their property and bodies are concerned, are certainly either the most careless or the most cruel of men. But those whom the fire of Christian charity has inflamed exact punishment from offenders, yet with grief and groaning, and in this they imitate pious and faithful fathers. The Corinthians sinned against both senses of this clause: they allowed the gravest crimes to be overlooked with impunity, and they were pleased with themselves, when they ought rather to have mourned, as we saw above in the example of that incest. All who hold public authority ought to take careful note of this, lest they act either too negligently or exceed the measure of just severity; rather they should imitate diligent vinedressers and farmers, who indeed pull up noxious weeds and cut back luxuriant or withered shoots, but take care not to do harm to the crops themselves. The safest rule of this moderation is charity, which makes punishments, however severe, light and wholesome for those who have offended.

units.la: Decimo, Omnia suffert Charitas. In Graeco est verbum στέγω [?], quod tegere & ferre aut aliquid sustinere significat, Metaphora ab aedificijs sumpta, quae fulcris sustinentur & tectis impositis teguntur. Vtrumq; pulchre seruit charitatis ingenio. Haec enim vt Solomon dicebat, tegit multitudinem peccatorum, nec temere cum proximi ignominia diuulgat, quae ab ipso praeter officium fiunt. Fert item patienter non aduersa modo, verum etiam iniurias & quaecunq; salua pietate ferri possunt, eo quod Christo & spe praemij futuri nititur. Exemplu huius facilitatis eximiū in Iosepho habetur, qui atroces à fratribus suis & Putiphares [?] vxore sibi factas iniurias ita tulit, vt illorum honori quoq; consuluerit. Similis fuit Mosis erga Israelitas, homines ingratissimos iniquissimosq;, patientia. Quibus merito Dauidem adnumerauerit, qui Saulis iniustam vim tanta lenitate pertulit, vt cum maxime posset, nihil in illum vellet hostiliter facere. Imprimis tamen hic nobis Christus spectandus venit, qui vt sua iustitia omnium hominum peccata tegit, ita hostes quoq; fert, & ad se conuersos in gratiam recipit. Arguuntur igitur hoc membro, primum ij, qui aliorum vitia odiose diuulgant, imo amplificant quoq;, vt maiorem illis ignominiam conflent. Deinde hi quoq;, qui nihil ferre volunt, & leuissimis iniurijs prouocati non solum aduersus homines insurgunt, verumetiam contra Deum murmurant, nisi in illico vindicem aut vltricem manum exerat. Solent ijdem fere ea ferre & defendere, quae minime ferri debebant: dum neq; gloriae Dei zelo vruntur, neque aliquam habent publicae honestatis rationem. Ita vero sese produnt, quod neque Dei neque hominum amore syncero teneantur.
units.tr: Tenthly, "Charity bears all things." In the Greek the word is στέγω [?], which means to cover, and also to bear or to sustain something. The metaphor is taken from buildings, which are held up by supports and covered by a roof laid on top. Both senses fit the nature of charity admirably. For charity, as Solomon said, covers a multitude of sins, and it does not rashly spread abroad the disgrace of a neighbour for things that have been done to it beyond what duty requires. Likewise it bears patiently not only adversities but also injuries, and whatever else can be borne without loss of godliness, because it rests on Christ and on the hope of future reward. An outstanding example of this ready endurance is found in Joseph, who bore the savage injuries done to him by his brothers and by Potiphar's wife in such a way that he also took care for their honour. Moses showed a similar patience towards the Israelites, a most ungrateful and unjust people; Paul rightly counts David among such men, who endured Saul's unjust violence with such gentleness that, though he could most easily have done so, he would not act in hostility against him. Above all, however, Christ is set before us here, who, as by his righteousness he covers the sins of all men, so also bears with his enemies and receives into favour those who turn to him. In this clause, therefore, are rebuked first those who spread abroad the faults of others hatefully, indeed even magnify them, so that they may heap greater shame upon them. Then also those who will bear nothing, and who, provoked by the slightest injuries, not only rise up against men but also murmur against God unless he immediately stretches out his avenging or punishing hand. These same people commonly bear with and defend things that by no means ought to be borne, since they have neither zeal for the glory of God nor any regard for public honesty. Indeed, by this they betray that they are not held by a sincere love either of God or of men.

units.la: Vndecimo, Omnia credere dicitur charitas. Id vero non debet de ijs intelligi, quae ad fidei & salutis dogmata pertinent. Haec enim ex Scripturis peti debent, & ne cuiuis spiritui credamus, Iohannes admonet. Adhaec quia charitas ex fide emanat, à Dei Verbo separari non potest, neq; aliquid admittere, quod ab hoc dissentiat. Ad ea ergo hoc restringi debet, quae nobis in proximi laudem referuntur, aut si qui nobis de sua erga nos voluntate benigne promittunt. In his charitas facilis ac credulos facit, cum à sinistris suspicionibus (vt modo dictum est) sit aliena. Rursus ergo arguuntur, qui nemini fidunt, & semel conceptam suspicionem pertinaciter fouent. Interim nemo putauerit, damnari hic piam illam prudentiam, qua nos serpentum similes fieri iubet Christus in prospiciendis & cauendis periculis, quae nobis à fidei hostibus struuntur. Haec enim vt charitati nihil derogat: ita huius legi ad illam astringuntur omnes, quorum fidei publica falsa credita est.
units.tr: Eleventhly, "Charity is said to believe all things." This must not be understood of those things which pertain to the doctrines of faith and salvation. For these ought to be sought from the Scriptures, and John warns us not to believe every spirit. Moreover, since charity flows from faith, it cannot be separated from the Word of God, nor admit anything that dissents from it. This statement must therefore be restricted to those things which are referred to us in praise of a neighbour, or to those who kindly promise us their good will towards us. In these matters charity makes us easy and ready to believe, since it is far from sinister suspicions (as was just said). Again, therefore, those are rebuked who trust no one and obstinately nurture a suspicion once conceived. Meanwhile, let no one think that that pious prudence is condemned here, by which Christ bids us become like serpents in foreseeing and guarding against the dangers that are laid for us by the enemies of the faith. For as this takes nothing away from charity, so all those whose public faith has been falsely believed are bound by its law to that charity.

units.la: Duodecimo, Omnia sperat charitas: omnia scilicet quae de aliquo sperare licet. Non ergo eos probat Paulus, qui temere spes pro sua libidine concipiunt, & vt amantes solent, ipsi sibi somnia fingunt. Sed debet hoc partim ad eos referri, qui nobis reconciliari cupiunt, partim ad quosuis, qui se peccatorum poenitentia duci testantur, seq; in posterum meliores fore vouent. Imo non obstat pietas, quo minus bene speremus de illis, qui adhuc in peccatis contumaciter pergunt, vel etiam apertum cum Deo bellum gerunt. Sunt enim exempla, quibus docemur, Deum subinde eos conuertere & in gratiam recipere, in quibus nulla poenitentia argumenta cernebantur: neq; nos scire possumus facile, qui nam in Spiritum sanctum peccent, aut quid de vnoquoq; Deus statuerit. Quoad ergo nobis non reuelatum adhuc est Dei iudicium de aliquo (vt olim Samueli de Saule) meliora de illo spe rare licet. Fecit hoc Moses cum Israelitis suis, quem postea Paulus imitatus indesinenter pro Iudæu[?] precabatur. Minimè ergo probari debent, rigidi illi & seueri Catones, qui mox desperant de eorum salute, quos turpius aliquanto lapsos esse vident, & ideo excommunicationes spirant, quando de reducendis peccatoribus cogitare debebant. Tales olim Nouatiani fuerunt, & hos imi-tantur Anabaptistæ, seditiosum & turbulentum hominum genus, qui sua scelera aliorum excom-municationibus & fucatis de disciplina Ecclesiæ instauranda sermonibus palliare solent. Aliter Christus, qui septuagies septies fratri ignoscere iubet. Et Paulus alibi ministrum eiusmodi requi-rit, qui malos etiam tolerare possit, & cum lenitate erudire aduersarios, si quando illis det Deus, vt conuersi agnoscant veritatem. Etenim si medici non ante membra resecant, quàm vbi toti corpori exitium imminere vident: nemo cordatus eum pastorem probauerit, qui ab Ecclesiæ corpore illum reijcere volet, qui hoc saluo diutius ferri poterat.
units.tr: Twelfthly, "Charity hopes all things": that is, all those things which it is lawful to hope for concerning someone. Paul therefore does not approve of those who rashly form hopes according to their own lust, and, as lovers are wont to do, fashion dreams for themselves. Rather, this ought to be referred partly to those who desire to be reconciled to us, partly to anyone who testifies that he is led to repentance for his sins and vows that he will be better in future. Indeed, piety does not prevent us from hoping well of those who still persist stubbornly in sin, or even wage open war against God. For there are examples by which we are taught that God from time to time converts such people and receives them into favour, though no signs of repentance were visible in them; nor can we easily know who sin against the Holy Spirit, or what God has decreed concerning each one. Therefore, as long as God's judgment concerning someone has not yet been revealed to us (as once to Samuel concerning Saul), it is permitted to hope better things of him. Moses did this with his Israelites, and Paul, imitating him, afterwards prayed unceasingly for the Jews. Those stern and severe Catos, therefore, who at once despair of the salvation of those whom they see to have fallen somewhat more shamefully, and who for this reason breathe out excommunications when they ought to be thinking about bringing sinners back, deserve no approval. Such were the Novatians of old, and the Anabaptists imitate them, a seditious and turbulent kind of men, who are wont to cloak their own crimes with the excommunications of others and with pretended speeches about restoring church discipline. Christ acts otherwise, who bids us forgive a brother seventy times seven times. And Paul elsewhere requires such a minister as can even tolerate bad men, and instruct opponents with gentleness, if at any time God gives them the grace to recognise the truth when converted. For if physicians do not cut off limbs until they see that ruin is threatening the whole body, no sensible person will approve of the minister who wishes to cast out of the body of the Church one who could be borne longer while this remained safe.

units.la: Postremò additur, Charitate omnia sustinere. ὑπομένει[?] dicuntur Græcis, qui sub onere impo-fito perseuerant, nec vnquam deficiunt. Solet hoc charitas, quæ sibi ipsi nunquam satisfacit, & pro-inde non defatigatur, etiamsi se erga multos frustra laborare videat. Exemplain[?] rebus vulgaribus occurrunt, vbi amore & studio homines detinentur, vt nullius laboris ipsos pigeat. Quòd si hoc in fide fiat, hæc illa patientia est, qua animas nostras possidere nos iubet Dominus. Eadem moueret etiam, ne benefaciendo defatigemur, quàmuis multos ingratos sentiamus. Deniq; hæc virtutes in nobis omnes perficit, & ideo apud Chrysostomum charitas ἀχρῆς[?] ἀπάσης[?] ἀνυσσέγος[?] dicitur. Huic ergo studeant, quicunq; Christiani dici & haberi volunt, & hic ipsius Christi exemplum sibi imitandum proponant, qui suos in finem vsq; dilexit, & se pro illis in mortem tradidit. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Lastly, it is added, "Charity endures all things" (sustinere). Those are called by the Greeks ὑπομένει [?] who persevere under a burden laid upon them and never give way. Charity is wont to do this, since it is never satisfied with itself, and therefore is not wearied, even if it sees that it labours in vain towards many. Examples of this occur in ordinary affairs, where people are held by love and zeal so that no labour of any kind irks them. But if this is done in faith, this is that patience by which the Lord bids us possess our souls. The same charity would also move us not to grow weary in doing good, although we perceive many to be ungrateful. Finally, charity brings all the virtues in us to perfection, and therefore in Chrysostom charity is called ἀχρῆς [?] ἀπάσης [?] ἀνυσσέγος [?]. Let therefore all who wish to be and be called Christians strive after this, and let them set before themselves the example of Christ himself, to be imitated, who loved his own to the end and gave himself up to death for them. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXIX.
units.tr: HOMILY LXIX.

units.la: Charitas nunquam excidit, siue prophetiæ abolebuntur, siue linguæ cessabunt, siue cognitio abolebitur. Ex parte enim cognoscimus, & ex parte prophetamus: Cùm autem aduenerit quod perfectum est, tunc quod ex parte est abolebitur. Cùm essem infans, vt infans loquebar, vt infans cogitabam, vt infans sentiebam: postquam autem factus sum vir, abolevi quæ infantis erant. Cernimus enim nunc per speculum & per ænigma, tunc autem coràm: nunc cognosco ex parte, tunc verò cognoscam prout cognitus fuero. Nunc verò manet fides, spes, charitas, tria hæc: maxima autem harum charitas.
units.tr: Charity never fails, whether prophecies are abolished, or tongues cease, or knowledge is abolished. For we know in part and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part will be abolished. When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I thought as a child, I felt as a child; but when I became a man, I put away the things of a child. For now we see through a mirror and in a riddle, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known. And now faith, hope and charity remain, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.

units.la: Inter ea quæ charitatis vinculum abrumpunt, nihil nocentius est æmulatione & arrogantia. Hæc enim omnes superbè fastidit, illa verò quibusuis inuidet ea, quæ ipsis diuinitus data sunt. Vtroq; autem vitio tunc nocentissimè peccatur, quando in dona spiritualia cadunt, quæ ad Ecclesiæ gubernationem pertinent. Nam præter id quòd donorum istorum abusus inde nascitur, hinc simul dissensiones prodeunt, quibus Ecclesiæ vnitas scinditur, & hi se mutuò mordent atq; laniant, qui in Christo vnum esse debebant. Exemplo sunt Corinthij, & hodie multa huius generis non sine summo piorum dolore fiunt, quando aliorum quidem ambitione, aliorum autem inuidia contentiones quotidie nouæ excitantur, quibus Euangelij cursus & multorum fides impeditur. Est igitur diligenti consideratione dignissima huius Cap.doctrina, qua Paulus charitatem sic commendat, vt magnificentius commendari non possit. Primò enim hanc cum donis præstantissimis conferet, & ijsdem longè præfert. Deinde eiusdem dotes siue effecta omnia ex ordine recensuit, quibus omnia comprehenduntur, quæ priuatim ad vitam rectè instituendam, & publicè ad seruandam pacem Ecclesiæ faciunt. Sequitur tertium argumentum à perpetuitate, quod nimirum omnibus aliis donis cessantibus ipsa maneat atq; duret.
units.tr: Among the things that break the bond of charity, nothing is more harmful than rivalry and arrogance. Arrogance proudly despises all others, while rivalry envies others the gifts that have been divinely given to them. Both vices do the greatest harm when they fasten upon the spiritual gifts that pertain to the government of the Church. For besides the abuse of those gifts that arises from this, dissensions also break out, by which the unity of the Church is torn apart, and those who ought to be one in Christ bite and tear at one another. The Corinthians are an example of this, and today many things of this kind happen, not without the great grief of the godly, when new quarrels are stirred up daily, some through the ambition of some, others through the envy of others, and by these the course of the gospel and the faith of many are hindered. This teaching of the chapter is therefore most worthy of careful consideration, in which Paul commends charity in such a way that it could not be commended more magnificently. For first he compares it with the most excellent gifts and places it far above them. Then he runs through in order its qualities, or effects, by which all those things are comprehended that serve to order life rightly in private and to preserve the peace of the Church in public. There follows a third argument, drawn from its perpetuity: namely, that when all the other gifts have ceased, it alone remains and endures.

units.la: Propositio totius loci est, Charitas non excidit. Exponunt hoc nonnulli, quòd nunquam fallatur aut exorbitet in veri inquisitione, eò quòd etsi nō semper sensum germanum attingamus, non tamen perniciose errare possint quotquot charitatis regulam in suo sensu sequuntur. Sed si quae sequuntur propius considerentur, hoc potius dicitur, quod nunquam cesset charitas, sed perpetuò du- ret. Nam ad collationem donorum spiritualium rediens, per expositionem addit: Sive prophetiae abolebuntur, sive linguae cessabunt, sive cognitio abolebitur. Quae verba Aposiopesis speciem habent, quae sic suppleri potest: Charitas tamen non abolebitur, neque intercidet. Et hic sensus plerisque veterum placuit. Hieronymus enim exponit: Ipsa sola permanet in futuro: aut certè quae vera est, non finitur. Ambrosius autem: Haec est, quae & in praesenti prodest, & in aeternum cum Deo perma- net. Abolendas autem dicit prophetias, & cessaturas linguas atque cognitionem: quia ubi impletae fuerint prophetiae, illis non opus erit amplius: ut neque linguarum aut cognitionis usus erit aliquis, ubi perfectionis statum omnes attigerimus. Abolebuntur ergo & cessabunt ista, perinde ut Sole super Orizontem euectio aurora cessare aut euanescere dicitur. Neque ideo quaerere opus est: An ergo non locuturi sint sancti coelites? Vel an nulla tunc futura sit rerum cognitio? Quis enim mutos fore dixerit eos, quibus omnia membra restituentur? Aut num truncorum loco eos fore putabimus, qui omnibus exoptatam beatitatem iam sunt assecuti? Per linguas autem in praesenti diversitas illa linguarum intelligitur, quae nunc cum molestia & incommoditate coniuncta est. Cognitionis autem nomen relatiuè ponitur, pro ipsa cognoscendi ratione, quam vulgò μάθησιν dicit. Ergo quamuis in futuro seculo coelites neque muti neque rerum ignari erunt, non tamen illa quae nunc est linguarum diversitas erit, ut neque ea discendi ratio, qua hodie exercemur. Quia enim dona illa omnia huic vitae serviunt, et ideo dantur, ut nobis ad fidem excolendam adiumento sint, tunc autem abolita huius seculi conditione salutem plenam assequemur, nulla porro opus erit institutione, nullo item cognitionis assequendae studio. Itaq; nihil tunc doctius & eruditius decedet, sed quod nunc laboriosè quaerunt & non nisi fide percipiunt, id tunc revera inuenient atq; possidebunt. Denique quia linguarum diversitas inter peccati poenas numeratur, nullus illi locus esse poterit amplius, quando perfecta felicitate in coelesti patria fruemur. Et cur illic linguis diversis sancti vterentur, quando Ecclesiae in terris agenti hoc Isaias tribuit, quod omnes lingua una locuturi sint: non quidem quo- ad idioma, sed quoad fidei sensum & Dei glorificandi studium. Quod autem idioma illud futurum sit, & qualem tunc cognitionem habituri sint sancti, quaerere curiosum, non autem scitu necessarium est. Quare omissis eiusmodi quaestionibus, hoc potius agamus, ut olim aeternis illis bonis frui nobis liceat, quae suae mortis merito Christus electis suis acquisiuit.
units.tr: The proposition of the whole passage is: Charity never fails. Some explain this as meaning that charity never goes wrong or strays from the search for truth, because even if we do not always reach the true sense, those who follow the rule of charity in their understanding cannot err to their ruin. But if the words that follow are considered more closely, what is said is rather that charity never ceases, but endures forever. For returning to the list of spiritual gifts, he adds by way of explanation: "whether prophecies shall be abolished, or tongues shall cease, or knowledge shall be abolished." These words have the form of an aposiopesis, which can be supplied thus: "charity, however, will not be abolished, nor will it perish." And this sense has pleased most of the ancients. For Jerome explains: "It alone remains in the future"; or at least, "what is true is not brought to an end." Ambrose says: "This is the charity which both profits in the present and remains with God for eternity." He says that prophecies will be abolished, and tongues and knowledge will cease, because when prophecies have been fulfilled, they will no longer be needed; likewise there will be no use of languages or knowledge once we have all attained the state of perfection. These things, therefore, will be abolished and will cease, just as the dawn is said to cease or vanish when the sun rises above the horizon. Nor need we on that account ask: Will the holy inhabitants of heaven then not speak? Or will there then be no knowledge of things? For who would say that those will be mute to whom all their members are restored? Or shall we think that they will be like trunks, those who have already attained the blessedness that all desire? By "tongues" in the present, however, is understood that diversity of languages, which is now attended with trouble and inconvenience. The word "knowledge" is used relatively, for the very method of knowing, which is commonly called [máthēsin] learning. Therefore, although in the future age the heavenly inhabitants will be neither mute nor ignorant of things, yet that diversity of languages which now exists will not be there, nor that method of learning by which we are exercised today. For all those gifts serve this life, and they are given so that they may help us to cultivate faith; but when the condition of this age has been abolished, we shall attain full salvation, and then there will be no need of instruction, nor of any eagerness to acquire knowledge. Hence nothing then will be lost through being less learned or less instructed; rather, what they now seek with labour and grasp only by faith, they will then truly find and possess. Finally, since the diversity of languages is counted among the punishments of sin, there can be no place for it any longer when we enjoy perfect happiness in the heavenly homeland. And why should the saints there use different languages, when Isaiah assigns to the Church on earth that all shall speak with one tongue: not indeed as to idiom, but as to the sense of the faith and the zeal for glorifying God? As to what that idiom will be, and what kind of knowledge the saints will then have, to inquire into it is curious, and not necessary to know. Therefore, setting aside questions of this kind, let us rather attend to this, that we may one day be permitted to enjoy those eternal goods which Christ, by the merit of his death, has obtained for his elect.

units.la: Pulchrè autem seruit Pauli iustituto hoc dictum. Nam Corinthiorum stultitiam perstringit, qui propter dona illa, quae mox abolebuntur, inter se ambitiosè contendebant, neglectio eo, quod aeternum est, & sine quo ne hic quidem commodè vitam degere possumus. Debet autem hinc generalis doctrina peti, ut ipsi quoq; non similiter stultitia neglectis bonis aeternis ac immortalibus, circa euanida huius seculi bona occupemur. Quod unum si diligentius omnes expenderent, plurimum ad veram pietatem momenti se assecutos esse sentirent. Quid enim in toto hoc mundo stabile inuenitur? Omnis caro fœnis (Clamat ex Domini iussu Isaias propheta) & omnis gloria carnis flos agri. Cui Solomon consentiens, postea omnium, quae magnifica videntur, accuratissimam considerationem dixit: Vanitas vanitatum, & omnia vanitas. Et Paulus supra mundo speciem siue figuram euanidam ac praetereuntem tribuit. Quod si vero Corinthios reprehensione dignos putauit, qui charitate neglecta, circa linguas & prophetiam aliaq; dona Dei minimè contemnenda occupabantur, quid de illis dicendum erit, qui opes, honores, voluptates deniq; huius seculi bonis aeternis atq; coelestibus praeferunt? Quàm enim malefida sit opum possessio, exemplis quotidianis docemur. Honores fluxi sunt, & à vulgi fauore pendent, quo nihil mobilius & instabilius fingi potest. Voluptates verò ut plerunque cum fœditate quadam coniunctae sunt, ita pudendam sui memoriam relinquunt, ut non possint non erubescere (ut alibi Paulus inquit) qui vitae in his transactae recordantur. Nihil ergo homini Christiano dignius, nihil utilius, nihil salutarius fuerit, quàm ut regulae Christi memor, omnibus aliis posthabitis Regnum Dei quaerat, & thesaurum sibi in coelis recondat. Matth.6.
units.tr: This saying serves Paul's purpose well. For he censures the folly of the Corinthians, who on account of those gifts that will soon be abolished were ambitiously contending among themselves, neglecting that which is eternal and without which we cannot even live well here. From this a general doctrine ought to be drawn, that we too, not less foolishly, should not, neglecting eternal and immortal goods, be occupied with the fading goods of this age. If all people weighed this one matter more carefully, they would feel that they had gained very much in true piety. For what is found that is stable in all this world? "All flesh is grass" (so the prophet Isaiah cries out at the Lord's command), "and all the glory of flesh is the flower of the field." Solomon agrees, and afterwards gave the most careful consideration of all things that seem magnificent, saying: "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity." And Paul above ascribes to the world an appearance or figure that is fading and passing away. But if he thought the Corinthians deserved rebuke, who, neglecting charity, were occupied with tongues and prophecy and other gifts of God by no means to be despised, what must be said of those who prefer riches, honours and pleasures, in short the goods of this age, to the eternal and heavenly goods? For how treacherous the possession of wealth is we learn from daily examples. Honours are fleeting and depend on the favour of the crowd, than which nothing more changeable and unstable can be imagined. Pleasures, however, as they are for the most part joined with a certain foulness, so they leave a memory of themselves that is shameful, so that those who recall the life spent in them cannot help blushing (as Paul says elsewhere). Nothing therefore is more worthy of a Christian, nothing more useful or more salutary, than to remember the rule of Christ, and, all other things set aside, to seek the Kingdom of God and to lay up for himself a treasure in heaven. Matt. 6.

units.la: Abutuntur autem hoc loco aduersarij, ut Diuorum intercessionem afferant, ex qua deinde eorundem invocationem colligunt, & sic argumentantur: Abolitis & cessantibus donis aliis omnibus durat charitas in altero quoq; seculo: Charitatis autem opus proprium est bene velle omnibus, & salutem omnium iuuare dictis, factis, precando & intercedendo: Ergo sancti coelites pro nobis intercedunt, & per consequens etiam à nobis debent inuocari. Sed est hic paralogismus à dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter. Nam ad omnia charitatis officia extendunt & singuli id applicant, quod de illa simpliciter dicitur. Itaque extra oleas vagantur, dum non insistunt Apostoli institutio. Etenim quamuis charitas in sanctis maneat, quorum animae iam in caelis agunt, non tamen omnia illic faciunt, quae hic fecerunt, & quae nunc in terris ex illius Lege fieri solent. Quia alia est huius praesentis, alia futura vitae ratio. In hac vita charitatis opera sunt, cibum dare esurientibus & sitientibus potum, vestire nudos, hospitio excipere peregrinos & incertis sedibus vagantes, adesse aegrotantibus, tueri viduas ac pupillos, & quae alia sunt huius generis. In caelis autem nihil huius fieri potest, vbi nullus fami, siti, egestati, exilio, morbis & miseriis locus est. Deinde inter coelites summus in voluntate Dei consensus est, quem in oratione Dominica fatemur. Non possunt ergo postulare aliquid, quod cum illa pugnet, sed in ea vna acquiescunt, & ex eadem voluptatem capiunt. Nec ideo minus amant: quia ad seruandam charitatem sufficit, si nobis in genere bene velint, & Dei nomen inter homines sanctificari & glorificari cupiant. Adde hic quod incertum plane est, an singulorum, qui in terris agunt, res norint. Solomon certe rationem redditurus, cur solus Deus inuocari debeat, hanc affert, quod solus corda scrutetur, & solus omnium vota exaudiat. Quod ipsum Propheta non vno loco annotarunt. Et si statum illum beatitudinis propius con-sideres, nihil cum eo minus conuenire posset, quam vt nostris curis & miseriis caelites occupentur. Quid quod Davidem suo seculo deseruisse, Paulus in Actis dicit? ita nimirum innuens, illum non habere porro inter ea quae in terris geruntur, quod ad ipsius curam pertineat. Atqui eadem est omnium ratio, qui ex hac vita emigrant, quos ideo defunctos dicunt, quod iam omnibus curis & miseriis exempti atq; liberati sunt. Constat praeterea, illorum invocationem nullis vel testimonijs Scripturae vel probatorum Dei seruorum exemplis probari posse. Davidem certe in Psalmo 107. omnium fere catalogum contexens, qui vel domi vel peregrinae in aquis aut in terra periclitantur, vel cum morbis, cum egestate aut aliis aduersis conflictantur, omnibus hoc vnum tribuit, quod ad Dominum clamauerint, & per hunc ex omnibus angustijs suis liberati sint. Et recte quidem hoc dicitur, quia si qui aliter facerent, ij in Dei praeceptum peccarent, dicentis: In die tribulationis inuocame, & liberabo te, &c. Quod si vero de intercessione verba facere libeat, haec ad vnum Christum pertinet, qui vnicus Mediator est inter Deum & homines: apud illum vero intermedijs aduocatis nequaquam opus est, qui omnes eos qui laborant atq; onerati sunt, recta ad se venire iubet, & neminem ad se venientem reijcit.
units.tr: Our opponents, however, abuse this passage to bring forward the intercession of the saints, from which they then infer the invocation of the same, and argue thus: "When the other gifts are abolished and have ceased, charity endures in the other age too. But it is the proper work of charity to wish well to all and to help the salvation of all by words, deeds, prayer and intercession. Therefore the saints in heaven intercede for us, and consequently they ought also to be invoked by us." But this is a paralogism, from a statement qualified in one respect to a statement taken absolutely. For they extend to all the offices of charity and each applies to the saints what is said absolutely of charity. Thus they wander outside the olive grove, since they do not keep to the teaching of the Apostle. For although charity remains in the saints, whose souls now dwell in heaven, yet they do not there do all the things they did here, and which are now usually done on earth under the law of charity. For the manner of the present life is one thing, and that of the future life another. In this life there are works of charity: to give food to the hungry and drink to the thirsty, to clothe the naked, to receive strangers and wanderers without fixed abode into one's house, to attend the sick, to protect widows and orphans, and other things of this kind. In heaven, however, nothing of this kind can happen, where there is no place for hunger, thirst, want, exile, sickness and miseries. Further, among the heavenly inhabitants there is the highest agreement with the will of God, which we confess in the Lord's Prayer. They cannot therefore ask for anything that conflicts with that will, but they rest in that one thing alone and take their delight from it. Nor do they love any the less on that account: for to preserve charity it is enough if they wish us well in general, and desire that the name of God be sanctified and glorified among men. Add to this that it is quite uncertain whether they know the affairs of individuals who are living on earth. Solomon, at any rate, when giving the reason why God alone ought to be invoked, brings this forward: that he alone searches the hearts, and he alone hears the vows of all. The prophets also noted this in more than one place. And if you consider more closely that state of blessedness, nothing could be less consistent with it than that the heavenly inhabitants should be occupied with our cares and miseries. What of the fact that Paul in the Acts says that David in his own generation fell asleep? Clearly thereby implying that he no longer has any concern for what is done on earth that pertains to him. Yet the case is the same for all who depart from this life, whom they therefore call "the departed," because they are now freed and released from all cares and miseries. Moreover, it is established that their invocation cannot be proved either by testimonies of Scripture or by the examples of approved servants of God. David certainly, in Psalm 107, weaving together an almost complete catalogue of those who are in danger at home or abroad, on the waters or on land, or who are struggling with sickness, want or other adversities, ascribes to all this one thing: that they cried to the Lord, and through him were delivered from all their distresses. And this is rightly said, because if anyone did otherwise, he would sin against the command of God, who says: "Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you," etc. But if one wishes to speak of intercession, this pertains to Christ alone, who is the only Mediator between God and men. With him there is certainly no need of intervening advocates, for he bids all who labour and are burdened to come straight to him, and he rejects no one who comes to him.

units.la: Quia vero de hac causa alibi quoq; diximus, nunc ad Paulum revertamur, qui rationem adducit, cur dona illa prophetiae, linguarum & cognitionis in futuro seculo aboleri dixerit. Est enim: Ex parte enim cognoscimus, & ex parte prophetamus: cum autem aduenerit quod perfectum est, tunc quod ex parte est abolebitur. Ex parte aliquid nouisse idem est quod non totum nouisse. At non omnia nunc a nobis cognosci probat, quia ex parte quoq; prophetemus. Per prophetiam enim mysteriorum & voluntatis Dei reuelatio intelligitur. Quia vero Spiritus nunc ea sola reuelat, quae nobis in hac vita agentibus cognitu necessaria sunt, sequitur tam reuelationem quam cognitionem quae nunc nobis obtingunt, particulares modo, non omnibus numeris absolutas atq; perfectas esse, quibus omnia Regni Dei mysteria comprehendantur. Potest hoc probari exemplis sanctissimorum hominum, quibus multa defuisse ex eo apparet, quod interdum graviter lapsi sunt, singulari Dei gratia eos instaurari atq; erigi oportuerit. At vbi venerit (inquit Paulus) quod perfectum est, id est, postquam ad statum perfectionis peruenerimus, tunc quod ex parte est, id est, particularis illa cognoscendi simul & tradendi ratio abolebitur. Debet vero hoc de eo statu intelligi, qui mox a morte inchoatur, perficietur autem in nouissimo die, quando corpora quoq; nostra restituentur, vt totus homo vere felix atq; in aeternum beatus sit, neq; vllis scholarum linguarum aut institutionis adminiculis porro opus habeat. Debent autem ista ad Pauli institutum referri, quod est, ne qui dona sua superbi alios prae se contemnant, aut illa alijs maligne inuideant. Cur nim alios contemnat, qui ipse adhuc multis destituitur? Aut cur alicui inuideas dona ista, quae ipsa imperfecta sunt? Adiuuent potius alij alios, vt simul omnes quotidie in melius proficiamus. Quod si vero in spiritualibus hisce donis imperfectio tam multa est, quid de ijs dicemus, quae praesenti tantum seculo seruiunt, per se autem caduca & fluxa sunt? Sunt ergo revera stulti & miseri, qui neglectis cœlestibus & æternis bonis circa illa toti occupantur.
units.tr: Since I have discussed this point elsewhere too, let us now return to Paul, who gives the reason why he said that the gifts of prophecy, tongues and knowledge would be abolished in the age to come. His words are: "For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part will be done away" (1 Cor. 13:9-10). To know something in part is the same as not to know it wholly. Paul proves that we do not now know everything, since we also prophesy only in part. Prophecy here means the revelation of the mysteries and will of God. Because the Spirit now reveals only those things which we need to know while we live in this life, it follows that both the revelation and the knowledge we now receive are only partial, not complete and perfect in every respect, so that all the mysteries of the kingdom of God would be grasped by them. This can be shown from the examples of the holiest men, who plainly lacked many things, since at times they fell badly and had to be restored and raised up by the singular grace of God. But when, Paul says, "that which is perfect has come", that is, once we have reached the state of perfection, "then that which is in part" will be abolished, that is, that partial manner of knowing and of teaching. This must be understood of the state which begins immediately after death and will be completed on the last day, when our bodies too will be restored, so that the whole man may be truly happy and blessed for ever, and no longer need the aids of schools, languages or instruction. These things should be referred to Paul's purpose, which is that those who are proud of their gifts should not despise others in comparison with themselves, nor maliciously envy them their gifts. For why should someone despise others when he himself still lacks much? Or why should you envy someone these gifts, which are themselves imperfect? Rather, let us help one another, so that all of us may make daily progress for the better. But if in these spiritual gifts there is so much imperfection, what shall we say of those things which serve only the present age and are in themselves frail and fleeting? They are truly foolish and wretched, therefore, who, neglecting heavenly and eternal goods, occupy themselves wholly with those things.

units.la: Cæterum quia hæc nonnullis absurda videri poterant, & quidem imprimis sciolis, qui indignissime ferunt humanæ sapientiæ supercilium detrahi, propositionem suam Paulus similibus illustrat. Primum a gradibus ætatum sumit, quibus vulgo homines proficiunt quoad corpus & animum. Cum essem infans (inquit) ut infans loquebar, ut infans cogitabam, ut infans sentiebam: Postquam autem factus sum vir, abolevi quæ infantis erant. Huius seculi vitam infantiæ aut pueritiæ confert. Ut enim ætas ista propter imperfectionem, quæ ei coniuncta est, non nisi puerilia sapit, puerilia item cogitat & loquitur, imo balbutit potius: ita nos quoque dum in hac carne vivimus, eius mole & sensibus impediti, non possumus sensus & cogitationes nostras altius attollere, ut cœlestia sapiamus & loquamur, nisi quantum nobis Spiritus Dei largitur, qui ut pueros adhuc infirmis poplitibus vacillantes manu ducit, & mentes nostras, quantum nunc opus est, illuminat. In sua autem persona ista proponit, ut invidiam declinet, ne de aliis tantum hoc dicere, seipsum vero a communi hominum sorte eximere putetur. Nam ut Paulo ante diximus, in sanctissimis quoque huius imperfectionis aut infirmitatis exempla passim occurrunt. Et quid de aliis aut nobis dicere attinet, quando Paulus, electissimum illud organum gratiæ Dei, qui in tertium cœlum raptus ineffabilia Regni cœlestis mysteria viderat, se infantem esse fatetur comparatione perfectionis illius gloriosæ, quam in altero seculo assequemur? Potest autem ex eo æstimari beatitudinis illius cœlestis excellentia, de qua verissime Isaias pronuntiavit: Quæ oculus non vidit, nec auris audivit, neque in mentem hominis venerunt, ea præparauit Deus iis, qui ipsum diligunt. Neminem ergo huius seculi afflictiones terreant, quæ (ut alibi Paulus ait) cum futura illa gloria nullo modo conferri merentur. Sed neque huius vitæ delitiis nos inescari patiamur, ut propter eas velimus cœlestia negligere. Nam qui hoc faciunt, ii revera stolidi illi Lotophagi & infelices Circes socii sunt, qui in hortis & caulis atque ferarum septis volutari malunt, quam ad patriam illam beatissimam contendere.
units.tr: But since these things could seem absurd to some, and especially to the half-learned, who take it very badly that the pride of human wisdom is pulled down, Paul illustrates his proposition with similar examples. First he takes it from the stages of life through which people commonly pass in body and mind: "When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I thought as a child, I felt as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things" (1 Cor. 13:11). He compares the life of this age to infancy or childhood. Just as that stage, because of the imperfection that belongs to it, savours of nothing but childish things, thinks and speaks in a childish way, and indeed rather stammers, so we too, while we live in this flesh, hampered by its weight and senses, cannot raise our feelings and thoughts higher, so as to savour and speak of heavenly things, except as far as the Spirit of God grants us, who leads us by the hand, as children still wobbling on weak knees, and illuminates our minds as far as is needed now. He puts this forward in his own person so as to avoid ill will, lest it be thought that he says this only of others and exempts himself from the common lot of mankind. For, as we said before, examples of this imperfection and weakness occur everywhere even among the holiest men. And what need is there to speak of others or of ourselves, when Paul, that most chosen instrument of the grace of God, who was caught up into the third heaven and had seen the unspeakable mysteries of the heavenly kingdom, confesses that he is a child in comparison with the glorious perfection which we shall attain in the other age? From this one may estimate the excellence of that heavenly blessedness, of which Isaiah spoke most truly: "Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him" (Isa. 64:4; 1 Cor. 2:9). Let no one, then, be frightened by the afflictions of this age, which, as Paul says elsewhere, are in no way worthy to be compared with that future glory (Rom. 8:18). Nor let us allow ourselves to be enticed by the delights of this life, so that for their sake we would neglect heavenly things. For those who do this are truly companions of those foolish Lotus-eaters and the unhappy companions of Circe, who prefer to wallow in gardens, sheepfolds and animal pens rather than hasten to that most blessed homeland.

units.la: Sequitur alterum simile, quo infantilis huius aut puerilis cognitionis rationem reddit, dicens: Cernimus enim nunc per speculum & per ænigma, tunc autem coram, videlicet cernemus: Et mox hoc ipsum exponens addit. Nunc agnosco ex parte, tunc autem agnoscam prout cognitus fuero. Duo tribuit cognitioni, quam nunc habemus. Primum, quod similis sit visioni, quæ in speculo cernitur. Id vero non ipsas res, sed imagines rerum videndas exhibet. Alterum, quod ænigmatica sit. Est autem ænigma oratio sive quæstio obscurior, quæ verbis tropicis res tegit, ut planiori interpretatione opus habeant. Utrumque negotio de quo hic agitur, probe convenit. Deus enim, qui natura invisibilis est, nobis dum in carne vivimus, seipsum per verbum & opera sua revelat. Sub verbo Sacramenta quoque comprehendimus. At omnis ista cognitio tenuior, imo obscura & quasi ænigmatica est, sicut cum perfecta illa conferatur, qua olim donabimur. Tunc enim coram Deum ipsum intuebimur facie ad faciem, sicuti est. Et facit ad huius loci expositionem quod Ioannes in sua epistola scribit: Charissimi, nunc filii Dei sumus, sed nondum apparuit quod erimus: scimus autem quod cum ipse patefactus fuerit, similes ei erimus: quoniam videbimus eum sicuti est. Et in præsenti Paulus addit: Imo tunc cognoscam, prout cognitus fuero, id est, sicuti edocebor ab eo, qui & nunc me novit, & cognitione, quæ huic vitæ congruat, dignatur, tunc autem se totum mihi revelabit, ut (quod Davidi olim dixit) in eius vultu gaudiorum atque bonorum omnium satietate fruar. De qua visione illud etiam Iobi exponi debere videtur: Spectabo Deum e carne mea, quem ego mihi contemplabor, & non alius: quod unicum meum est desiderium. Iob.19.cap. Scio quosdam multis disputare de facie Dei, & num contemplatio illa mente sola, aut simul etiam oculis corporis fiat. Sed sunt hæ hominum otiosorum disputationes. Sufficiat nobis, quod Scripturæ docent, felicitatem illam non minus ad corpus quam ad animum pertinere, & proinde illius quoque sensibus (qui tunc purissimi & ab omni affectu vitioso purgatissimi erunt) perceptum iri. Nam quod illi obijciunt, Deum oculis corporeis non posse videri: nequaquam ad alterum seculum extendi debet, in quo omnis illa infirmitas abolebitur, qua nunc impedimur, quo minus a nobis ille conspici possit.
units.tr: There follows a second comparison, by which he gives the reason for this childish or infantile knowledge, saying: "For now we see through a mirror, in a riddle, but then face to face; now I know in part, but then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known" (1 Cor. 13:12). He attributes two things to the knowledge we now have. First, that it is like the sight seen in a mirror. This shows not the things themselves but images of things to be seen. Second, that it is enigmatic. An enigma is a speech or question that is rather obscure, which hides things under figurative words so that they need a plainer explanation. Both fit well the matter under discussion. For God, who is invisible by nature, reveals himself to us, while we live in the flesh, through his word and his works. Under the word we also include the sacraments. But all this knowledge is thin, indeed obscure and almost enigmatic, when it is compared with that perfect knowledge with which we shall be gifted one day. For then we shall look upon God himself face to face, as he is. This passage is also helped by what John writes in his letter: "Beloved, now we are the children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be; we know that when he is revealed we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is" (1 John 3:2). In the present passage Paul adds: "Yes, then I shall know as I have been known", that is, as I shall be taught by him who knows me now and deigns to give me knowledge suited to this life; then he will reveal himself to me wholly, so that (as he once said to David) I may enjoy the fullness of joys and of all good things in his presence. It seems that the words of Job should also be explained of this vision: "I shall see God in my flesh, whom I shall behold for myself, and not another; this is my only desire" (Job 19:26-27). I know that some dispute at length about the face of God, and whether that contemplation is made by the mind alone or also by the eyes of the body. But these are the idle disputes of idle men. It is enough for us that the Scriptures teach that that happiness pertains to the body no less than to the soul, and therefore will be perceived also by its senses, which then will be most pure and wholly cleansed of every sinful affection. As for their objection, that God cannot be seen with bodily eyes, it ought by no means to be extended to the other age, in which all that weakness that now hinders us from seeing him will be abolished.

units.la: Est tamen Paulo diligentius excutiendum, quod dicitur nos nunc ex parte duntaxat, & ut in speculo aut ænigmate, id est, obscurius & imperfectius cernere. Ex eo enim aduersarij nostri occasionem arripiunt oblatrandi Scripturis, quasi hæc doctrinam contineant obscuram, imperfectam, imò dubiam & incertam: Quo fundamento non minus impiè quàm infeliciter iacto, duos errores illi superstruunt pernitiosissimos: Unum, laicos à Scripturarum lectione procul arceri debere, ne rerum dubij opiniones falsas de religione concipiant, & hæretici fiant. Alterum traditionibus opus esse, & certam mysteriorum Scripturæ cognitionem ab ijs petendam esse, qui Ecclesiæ gubernaculis præsident.
