Hinc illa de scrinio pectoris summi Pontificis, deq; Patrum & Conciliorum authoritate, cui ipsas Scripturas subijciunt. Sed facile illa diluuntur. Paulus enim hoc loco ex collatione præsentis & futuri seculi loquitur, non autem dubiam vel imperfectam esse docet eam cognitionem, quæ ex sacris libris petitur, quoad salutis consequendæ rationem, & ea quæ nunc nobis cognitu necessaria sunt, futuram verò illam certiorem, pleniorem & perfectionem fore dicit, ut quæ non solùm coràm videbit & intelliget omnia, Verumetiam apprehendet, Deoq; præsenti fruetur, qui omnis felicitatis est ℭ Colophon.
units.tr: Yet what Paul says needs to be examined more carefully: that we now see only in part, and as in a mirror or a riddle, that is, more obscurely and imperfectly. Our adversaries seize on this as an occasion to bark against the Scriptures, as if they contained an obscure, imperfect, indeed doubtful and uncertain doctrine. Having laid this foundation no less impiously than unhappily, they build upon it two most pernicious errors. The first is that laypeople must be kept far from reading the Scriptures, lest, being uncertain about the matters, they form false opinions about religion and become heretics. The second is that traditions are necessary, and that a certain knowledge of the mysteries of Scripture must be sought from those who preside over the government of the Church. Hence come those notions about the hidden bosom of the supreme Pontiff, and about the authority of the Fathers and the Councils, to which they subject the Scriptures themselves. But these notions are easily refuted. For Paul in this place speaks by way of comparison between the present and the future age; he does not teach that the knowledge which is drawn from the sacred books is doubtful or imperfect as to the way of attaining salvation and as to those things which we now need to know. He says rather that the future knowledge will be more certain, fuller and perfect, so that we shall see and understand all things face to face, and indeed shall grasp them, and enjoy the presence of God, who is the source of all happiness.

units.la: Quòd si de Scripturarum dignitate & authoritate dicendum sit, non potest negari, has doctri-nã perfectam & sufficientem continere. De Legalibus enim præceptis dicitur, quòd in eis vitā beat quisquis illa fecerit. Quòd ergo ex eis vita non haurimus, nõ Legi, sed nostræ vitiositati acceptũ ferri debet, qua impediti nõ facimus quæ Lex iubet. Verumtamen hic quoq; nobis Scriptura succurrit, dum Christum tradit, qui nobis à Deo sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio & redemptio factus est. Ideo Paulus totam Scripturam diuinitus inspiratam, & proinde vtilem esse dicebat ad id, ut homo Dei perfectus sit, & ad omne opus bonum instructus. Quoad homines quantùmuis præstantissimos, nihil illi nos docere possunt, quàm quod reuelante Spiritu ex Scripturis sacris hauserunt.
units.tr: But if we are to speak of the dignity and authority of the Scriptures, it cannot be denied that they contain a perfect and sufficient doctrine. For of the legal precepts it is said that whoever does them shall live in them. If, therefore, we do not draw life from them, the fault lies not with the Law but with our own wickedness, which hinders us from doing what the Law commands. Yet here too Scripture comes to our aid, in that it delivers Christ, who has been made for us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. So Paul said that all Scripture is divinely inspired and therefore profitable, so that the man of God may be perfect and equipped for every good work. As for men, however outstanding, they can teach us nothing except what they have drawn from the holy Scriptures by the revelation of the Spirit.

units.la: Ideo Prophetæ olim verbum ex ore Domini petere iubebantur, & Apostolis Christus dicebat: Docete gentes, quæ ego vobis tradidi. Quòd si qui diuersum quid tradant, si Paulo teste, anathema censeri debent. Et hominum traditiones ad cultum Dei nihil conferre, Christus ex Isaia aperte testatur. Itaq; obseruemus diligenter & exosculemur Dei bonitatem, qui ut nostræ infirmitati consuleret, discendi rationem tutissimam nobis proposuit. Etenim si per Angelos nobiscum ageret, facile nobis imponere poterat Satan, qui se in Angelum lucis potest transformare. Sin verò occultis reuelationibus & somnijs uteretur, hic quoq; non raro cogitationes propriæ fucum facerent: & exempla sunt, quid multis accidere solet, qui mente alienati aut debilitati sibi ipsis imaginationes mirificas fingunt. Ergo ne quid huius pateremur, certis capitibus siue principijs omnem fidei & salutis nostræ doctrinam Deus complexus est, Decalogo nimirum, Oratione Dominica & Symbolo Apostolico. Eadem quoq; literis mandata prolixè exposuit, & exemplis infinitis illustrauit. Instituit item ordinarium Ecclesiæ ministerium per quod doctrina ista publicè prædicetur: iudicium verò penes Ecclesiæ esse voluit, ne qui plus æquo sibi tribuerent. Ut deniq; fraus omnis facilius caueretur, lingua vulgari in his semper vsus est. Hanc ergo rationem sequamur, & Deo gratissimus.
units.tr: Therefore the prophets were once commanded to seek the word from the mouth of the Lord, and Christ said to the apostles: Teach the nations what I have delivered to you. But if anyone teach something different, then, by Paul's testimony, he ought to be counted accursed. And Christ clearly testifies from Isaiah that human traditions contribute nothing to the worship of God. Let us therefore observe this diligently and embrace the goodness of God, who, to provide for our weakness, set before us the safest method of learning. For if he dealt with us through angels, Satan, who can transform himself into an angel of light, could easily deceive us. But if he used hidden revelations and dreams, then our own thoughts would often counterfeit them as well; and there are examples of what commonly happens to many who, deranged in mind or weakened, fashion for themselves wonderful imaginings. Therefore, lest we suffer any of this, God has comprised the whole doctrine of our faith and salvation under certain headings or principles, namely the Decalogue, the Lord's Prayer and the Apostles' Creed. He has also set out the same things at length in writing, and illustrated them with countless examples. He likewise instituted the ordinary ministry of the Church, through which this doctrine is publicly proclaimed; but he willed that judgement rest with the Church, lest any should claim more for themselves than is fitting. Finally, so that every fraud might be more easily guarded against, he has always used the common tongue in these matters. Let us therefore follow this method, and so be most pleasing to God.

units.la: Quòd si quid nunc nobis obscurius videtur, neminè id offendat: quando in alijs omnibus, quæ creditu & cognitu necessaria sunt, nihil obscurum est, nihil ambiguum, nihil imperfectum: qualia sunt, Deum esse qui omnia creauit, quiq; abs se creata gubernat & seruat. Filium Dei pro nobis hominem factum esse, eundem nos mortis suæ merito redemisse, resurrectione sua morte vicisse, ascensione cælorum portas reclusisse, & illic nostrum aduocatum agere, qui Ecclesiam simul sua tueatur. Hæc & alia huius generis, plenè & dilucidè in Scripturis traduntur. Quis autè & qualis Deus sit in sua essentia, quis incarnationis Filij Dei modus, quæ Regni cælestis forma & œconomia, vel Hierarchia, ea etsi nusquam exprimantur, neminè id mouere debet. Nã ut illa sciamus, nunc minimè opus est, consoleatur aut nos, quod olim coràm omnia spectabimus, quando in Regni Dei possessione veniemus.
units.tr: But if anything now seems rather obscure to us, let no one be troubled by it, since in all the other things that we must believe and know there is nothing obscure, nothing ambiguous, nothing incomplete. Such things are these: that God is the one who created all things and who governs and preserves what he has created; that the Son of God was made man for us, that by the merit of his death he redeemed us, by his resurrection overcame death, by his ascension opened the gates of heaven, and there acts as our advocate, who at the same time protects his Church. These and other things of this kind are set forth fully and clearly in the Scriptures. But as for what God is in his essence, what the manner of the incarnation of the Son of God is, what the form and economy or hierarchy of the heavenly kingdom is, although these are nowhere expressed, no one should be disturbed by this. For there is by no means any need for us to know these things now; and we may be comforted by the fact that we shall one day see all things face to face, when we come into possession of the kingdom of God.

units.la: Porrò concludit Paulus encomium istud charitatis, in quod digressus fuit: Nunc verò manet fides, spes, charitas, tria hæc: maxima autem harum charitas. Manere dicit hæc tria respectu aliorum donorum: quia etsi in hac carne viuentibus neq; linguarum cognitio, neq; prophetia, neq; miraculorum facultas, aut vllum aliud simile obtingat, tria tamen ista Christi serues nunquam destituunt, imo necessaria sunt, simulq; ad salutem consequendam ipsis possunt sufficere: cùm è contra alia illa multis conferantur, quos æternum exitium manet, ut iam sæpe diximus. Itaq; sensus istorum verborum est: Si omnium donorū ratio subducatur exactissima, omnibus cessantibus haec nobis summa reliqua erit, neq; aliorum alius usus est, quam ut fidei & spei confirmandae serviant, & charitatis organa sint, per quae illa quam plurimos adiuvet. Et haec illa sunt, quibus carere non possunt unquam, qui Deo servire & servari volunt. Fides enim est animi assensus, qui certa & indubitata fiducia CHRISTVM IESVM, & in hoc promissiones Dei omnes, simul& Deū ipsum apprehendit. Spes vero perseverantia est, qua bona, quae nobis promissa sunt, expectamus: & illa ut ex fide nascitur, ita hanc vicissim erigit atq; confirmat, ne tentationum ponderi succumbamus. Per charitatem autem fides agit, et eadem actionum omnium fidissima est moderatrix. Ideo de hac in praesenti adijcit: Maxima autem harum trium charitas.
units.tr: Furthermore, Paul concludes that encomium on love into which he digressed: "But now abide faith, hope, love, these three; but the greatest of these is love." He says that these three abide in respect of the other gifts, because, although for those living in this flesh neither the knowledge of tongues, nor prophecy, nor the power of miracles, nor any other like thing is granted, yet these three never fail those who serve Christ; indeed they are necessary, and at the same time can suffice for obtaining salvation; whereas, on the contrary, those other gifts are often bestowed upon many who await eternal destruction, as we have said many times already. Therefore the sense of these words is this: if the account of all gifts is cast up most exactly, once all have ceased, these three will remain to us as the sum, and the other gifts have no use except to serve the confirming of faith and hope and to be instruments of love, by which love may help as many people as possible. And these are the things that those who wish to serve God and be saved can never do without. For faith is the assent of the mind which, with a sure and undoubting trust, apprehends Christ Jesus, and in him all the promises of God, and God himself as well. Hope, however, is the steadfastness by which we await the good things promised to us; and just as it is born of faith, so in turn it raises up and strengthens faith, lest we succumb under the weight of temptations. Faith, moreover, works through love, and love is the most faithful guide of all actions. Therefore, concerning this, he adds in the present passage: "But the greatest of these three is love."

units.la: Quod dictum non debet simpliciter accipi, sed respectu eorum quae praecesserunt, ne ab Apostoli in-stituto discedamus. Loquitur enim de Ecclesiae oeconomia aut gubernatione, deq; ratione pacis in Ecclesia conseruandae, quae simul mores & totius vitae actiones in se comprehendit. In his palmam charitati tribuit, quia omnes alias dotes Spiritus moderatur, ut aliorum aedificationi & saluti serviant. Quod si de ipso salutis mysterio & illius causis exactius differere libeat, fides supra omnia alia longe excellit. Ex hac enim charitas illa gemina Dei & hominum nascitur, quae aut nulla aut su[?]cata erit, si fide sustuleris. Haec quoq; sola Christi apprehendit, qui nobis a Deo iustitia, sanctificatio & redemptio factus est, & in quo uno vita salusq; omnis habetur. Fides item victoria nostra est, qua mundū vincimus, & per omnia salutis obstacula eluctamur. Per hanc quoq; solam in filios Dei renascimur, & Regni caelorum efficimur haeredes. Debent ergo Pauli verba non ultra scopum, ad quem ille respexit, extendi: & proinde turpiter paralogizant, qui illis ad euertenda fidei iustificationem abutuntur. Charitas (inquiunt) maior aut praestantior est quam fides & spes: ergo charitas iustificat, aut saltem ad iustificationem plus confert quam fides. Est haec quoq; fallacia dicti secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter, perinde ac si quis argumentetur: Aurum pretiosius est pane: Ergo melius alit & nutrit hominem aurum quam panis. Item, Rex praestat sutore: Ergo melius quam hic conficere poterit calceos. Iurisperitus excellit nauta: Ergo ad nauim gubernandam magis idoneus erit. Quis vero no rideret ita argumentantem, aut communi sensu destitutum negaret? At no minus ridicule isti colligunt. Paulus enim de Ecclesiae gubernatione disserit, in qua licet charitas fidem excellat, non debet tamen hoc ad iustificationem trahi, in qua omnis gloria fidei debetur, no propter ullum opus externum, sed propter assensum illum animi, quo Christu[?], qui nostra iustitia & vita est, apprehendit. Quia vero de his saepe dictum est, ista modo sufficiant. Discamus potius hoc loco, quibus potissimum studere debeant Christiani homines. Prima ijs cura sit, ut Christum vera fide amplexi ex eius verbo regenerentur in filios Dei. Deinde, ut spe firma suffulti per omnes huius vitae procellas atq; certamina eluctentur. Postremo, ut charitate duce actiones suas omnes sic instituant, ne per ipsos vel priuatae amicitiae dissoluantur, vel Ecclesiae pax turbetur. Haec propria sunt religionis Christianae exercitia, quibus si qui vacant, ij & in hoc seculo vitam beatam & tranquillam degunt, & olim in caelis viuent atq; regnabunt cum CHRISTO IESV, Domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: That statement must not be taken simply, but with reference to what has gone before, lest we depart from the apostle's purpose. For he is speaking of the economy or government of the Church, and of the means of preserving peace in the Church, which together comprise morals and the whole conduct of life. In these matters he gives the palm to love, because it governs all the other gifts of the Spirit so that they serve the edification and salvation of others. But if we wish to discuss more precisely the very mystery of salvation and its causes, faith far surpasses all other things. For from faith is born that twofold love of God and of men, which would be either nonexistent or stifled if you took away faith. Faith alone also apprehends Christ, who has been made for us by God righteousness, sanctification and redemption, and in whom alone all life and salvation are found. Faith is also our victory, by which we overcome the world and struggle through all the obstacles to salvation. Only through faith are we also born again as children of God and made heirs of the kingdom of heaven. Paul's words therefore ought not to be extended beyond the aim at which he was looking; and so those who misuse them to overthrow the justification of faith reason basely. "Love," they say, "is greater or more excellent than faith and hope; therefore love justifies, or at least contributes more to justification than faith." This is also a fallacy of an argument made in a certain respect being applied to the argument made absolutely, just as if someone were to argue: "Gold is more precious than bread; therefore gold nourishes and sustains a man better than bread." Likewise: "A king surpasses a cobbler; therefore he will be able to make shoes better than the cobbler can." "A jurist excels a sailor; therefore he will be more fitted to steer a ship." Who, indeed, would not laugh at someone reasoning in this way, or deny that he lacks common sense? Yet those men infer no less ridiculously. For Paul is discussing the government of the Church, in which, although love excels faith, this ought not to be drawn over to justification, in which all the glory is owed to faith, not on account of any external work, but on account of that assent of the mind by which Christ, who is our righteousness and life, is apprehended. But since these things have often been said, let these suffice. Let us rather learn here what Christians ought chiefly to devote themselves to. First, their care should be that, having embraced Christ in true faith, they be born again through his word as children of God. Next, that, supported by a firm hope, they struggle through all the storms and conflicts of this life. Last, that, with love as their guide, they so order all their actions that they are not dissolved by private friendships or the peace of the Church disturbed. These are the proper exercises of the Christian religion, and whoever devotes himself to them lives a blessed and tranquil life in this age, and hereafter will live and reign in heaven with Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XIIII. HOMILIA LXX.
units.tr: Chapter 14. Homily 70.

units.la: Sectamini charitatem, ambite autem spiritualia, magis tamen ut prophetetis. Nam qui loquitur lingua, non hominibus loquitur, sed Deo: nullus enim audit, spiritu vero loquitur mysteria. Qui autem prophetat, hominibus loquitur aedificationem, & exhortationem, & consolationem. Qui loquitur lingua, seipsum aedificat: qui vero prophetat, Ecclesiam aedificat. Velim autem omnes vos loqui linguis, magis tamen ut prophetetis: Maior enim est qui prophetat, quam qui loquitur linguis, nisi si interpretetur: ut Ecclesia aedificationem accipiat.
units.tr: Follow after charity, and desire spiritual gifts, but rather that you may prophesy. For he who speaks in a tongue does not speak to men but to God, for no one understands him, although in the Spirit he speaks mysteries. But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, exhortation and comfort. He who speaks in a tongue edifies himself, but he who prophesies edifies the Church. I would indeed that you all spoke with tongues, but rather that you prophesied; for greater is he who prophesies than he who speaks with tongues, unless he also interprets, so that the Church may receive edification.

units.la: PAVLVS Apostolus diligenter admodum & prolixè disserit de donis spiritualibus, quibus Ecclesiam suam Deus exornat & instruit. Causa illi fuit, quòd Corinthij propter illa inter se crebris rixis & contentionibus tumultuarentur, cùm alij quidem insolentius ostentarent, alij verò ea ipsis inuiderent. Primò igitur docuit, authorem illorum esse Deum, qui ea per suum spiritum conferat, quiq omnium sit Dominus. Inde colligit, hunc vnum ante omnia spectari debere, vt illis ad huius gloriam vtantur: Deinde diuersa esse ostendit, & à Deo non sine certa ratione inaequaliter distribui, vt charitatis vinculum sint, dum quisq alterius opera indiget. Et ea occasione in charitatis laudes digressus est, quas magnificè celebrauit. Sequitur tertia huius tractationis pars, qua docetur, quae nam inter dona illa alijs praestient, & quod nō praecipuum sit, cui reliqua omnia debeant seruire. Et hic palmam tribuit Prophetiae aut Scripturarum tractationi, de cuius vero vsu atq; ratione differet, quae perpetuò in Ecclesia seruari debeat.
units.tr: The Apostle Paul treats the spiritual gifts, with which God adorns and instructs his Church, very carefully and at considerable length. His occasion was that the Corinthians were stirred up by frequent quarrels and contentions among themselves over these gifts: some displayed them too arrogantly, while others envied those who had them. First, therefore, he taught that God is the author of these gifts, since he bestows them through his Spirit and is the Lord of all. From this he concludes that, above all, one ought to look to God alone, so that the gifts are used for his glory. Then he shows that the gifts are diverse, and that God distributes them unequally, not without a sure reason, so that they become a bond of love, since each one needs the work of another. On this occasion he digresses into the praise of charity, which he celebrates magnificently. Then follows the third part of this discussion, in which he teaches which of those gifts surpass the others, and that the one to which all the rest ought to serve is not the chief one. Here he awards the palm to prophecy, or to the exposition of the Scriptures, and he goes on to discuss its right use and purpose, which ought always to be maintained in the Church.

units.la: Transitione verò vtitur commodissima, qua praecedentia cum ijs, quae sequuntur, pulchrè connectit, dicens: Sectamini charitatem, ambite autem spiritualia, magis tamen vt prophetetis. In Graeco legitur ζηλοῦτε, quod nō obiter aliquid sectari, sed persequi significat. Ergo ardentissimum charitatis studium illus commendat, quasi diceret: Cum tantus tamq; necessarius illius vsus sit, vt ei merito in Ecclesiae gubernatione prima gloria tribuatur, veltrum fuerit, illam omni studio sectari, & (quod proverbio dicitur) vela & remos intendere vt eam assequamini: quod tum fiet, si ipsi omnibus alijs charitatis officia praestetis, & ita illos ad vos redamandum pelliciatis. Hoc enim verè Christianum certamen est, quando mutuis amicitiae officijs certatur, & nemo ab altero vinci vult. Neq; obstabit hoc, quò minus alia quoq; dona spiritus sectemini, imò vt ea quoq; zelo & aemulatione sancta ambiatis iubeo, cùm illa quoque à Deo dentur, & suum habeant vsum in Ecclesia. Imprimis tamen hoc agite, vt prophetetis. Ita verò admonet, prophetia inter dona spiritualia praestantissimum esse, cui illa omnia recillari[?] debeant: id quod huius tractationis caput est.
units.tr: He uses a most fitting transition, by which he neatly connects what precedes with what follows, saying: "Pursue charity, and earnestly desire spiritual gifts, but rather that you may prophesy." In the Greek it is written ζηλοῦτε [zēloute], which means not to pursue something in passing, but to chase after it. He therefore commends an ardent zeal for charity, as if he were saying: since its use is so great and so necessary that rightly the first glory in the governing of the Church is given to it, it would be worth your while to pursue it with every effort, and (as the proverb says) to spread sail and ply oars to reach it. This will happen if you yourselves render the duties of charity to all others, and so draw them to love you in return. For this is truly a Christian contest, when people vie with one another in the mutual duties of friendship, and no one wishes to be outdone by the other. Nor does this stop you from pursuing the other gifts of the Spirit as well; indeed, I bid you to seek them too with holy zeal and emulation, since these also are given by God and have their use in the Church. Above all, however, make this your aim: that you prophesy. He thus warns that prophecy is the most outstanding of the spiritual gifts, and that all the others must be referred to it. This is the point of the whole discussion.

units.la: At nunc obseruemus, charitatem sic à Paulo laudari, vt interim non damnet alia dona, quibus Corinthij turpissimè abutebantur. Quae enim Deus in vsum bonum largitur, ea non debent pro malis aut noxijs abijci propter eos, qui ijsdem ad suum aut aliorum exitium abutuntur. Nā si id facere semel instituamus, iam omnes tam animi quàm corporis dotes, vnà cum fortunis omnibus & toto terrae prouentu damnare cogemur. Quàm multos enim est videre, qui prudentia, rerum vsu, eloquentia & authoritate sua rempub. euertunt? Quàm multis verò sua forma & integra valetudo libidini & fastui seruit? Et quanta cum ingratitudine multi frugibus ad turpem quaestum abutantur, aut intemperanti earum abusu seipsos impiè perdant, non opus est commemo rare, cùm hoc neminem latere possit. Eadem est aliarum quoq; rerum ratio. Olim enim artium ijs & bonis artibus homines ambitiose superstitiosi abusi sunt, dum humanis traditionibus Ecclesiam grauarunt non sine luculento purioris religionis dispendio. At si ista omnia propterea damnare libeat, iam ingratitudine peccabimus, & Deum faciemus scelerum authorem, quod sine manifesta impietate fieri non potest. Tutissimum ergo fuerit regulam à Paulo nobis praescriptam sequi, vt quaeuis Dei dona pio & ardenti zelo sectemur, quatenus id nostra nobis vocatio permittit, omnibus verò vtamur ex charitatis praescripto, quae nos falli aut errare non patietur. In huius autem studio summam industriam adhibeamus necesse est, cùm tam multa sint, quae charitatem turbare possunt. Nam vt de iniurijs nihil dicamus, quarum plena sunt omnia, plurimum hic nocet philautiae affectus, qui ita fere in nobis dominatur, vt tunc quoq; nostrum commodum quaeramus, quando alijs benefacere aut prodesse videri volumus.
units.tr: Now let us observe that Paul praises charity in such a way that at the same time he does not condemn the other gifts, which the Corinthians shamefully abused. For the gifts that God bestows for a good use ought not to be cast aside as evil or harmful because of those who abuse them to their own or others' ruin. For if we once began to do this, we would be forced to condemn all the endowments of mind and body, together with every kind of wealth and the whole produce of the earth. How many are there to be seen who overthrow the commonwealth by their prudence, their experience in affairs, their eloquence and their authority? And how many use their beauty and sound health as servants of lust and pride? It is not necessary to recount how many, with great ingratitude, abuse the fruits of the earth for shameful gain, or by intemperate use of them ruin themselves impiously; this can be hidden from no one. The same is true of other things. For in the past, ambitious and superstitious men have also abused the arts and good learning, when they burdened the Church with human traditions, to the clear loss of purer religion. But if we were to wish to condemn all these things for this reason, we would then sin through ingratitude, and make God the author of wickedness, which cannot happen without manifest impiety. It will therefore be safest to follow the rule prescribed to us by Paul: that we pursue every gift of God with pious and ardent zeal, so far as our calling permits, and that we use all of them according to the precept of charity, which will not allow us to be deceived or to err. In pursuing this, we must indeed apply the greatest diligence, since there are so many things that can disturb charity. For, to say nothing of injuries, with which everything is full, the feeling of self-love does great harm here; it so commonly rules within us that we seek our own advantage even when we wish to seem to do good or be of help to others.

units.la: Quia verò prophetiae donum omnibus alijs anteposuit, nunc eius rationem reddit, & hanc omnibus Ecclesiae exercitijs longè excellentiorem esse argumentis solidissimis probat. Intelligitur (ut ex eius verbis mox patebit) non miraculosum illud vaticinandi donum, quod tunc in vsu fuisse scimus, sed publicam Scripturarum tractationem, adeoq; totum munus docendi, quo Dei voluntas exponitur ad Ecclesiae totius ac singulorum membrorum eius institutionem & aedificationem. Utq[?] illustrior sit illius dignitas siue praestantia, eam cum dono linguarum confert diligenter: quod ideo inter alia potissimum deligit, quòd circa linguas imprimis occupantur Corinthij, vt quae ostentationi & ambitioni eorum maximè seruirent. Ita enim natura comparatum est, vt ignobile vulgus maximi faciat quæ non intelligit, & proinde sæpius contemptius doni præstantioribus, ea quæ minoris momenti sunt, stolida ignorantia admiretur. Quid verò Paulus? Qui loquitur lingua, scilicet peregrina seu aliena, is non hominibus loquitur, sed Deo. Et huius dicti rationem subiicit: Quia nullus audit, id est, nemo intelligit, vt vel sensum eorum quæ dicuntur, aut aliam aliquam vtilitatem ex illis percipiat. Sed spiritu, id est, afflatu doni illius spiritualis loquitur mysteria. Ita verò dicit vel res prorsus arcanas & à nemine cognitas, vel ipsa salutis mysteria, quæ in Ecclesia non celari, sed publicè proponi debent, & sic quidem, vt ab omnibus intelligantur. At qui prophetat, is loquitur hominibus, id est, in vsum & vtilitatem hominum: & loquitur ædificationem, & exhortationem, & consolationem, id est, ea loquitur, quibus homines ædificantur in Dei cognitione, quibus item excitantur ad pietatem, & quæ ipsos in periculis & tentationibus confirmant. Et hoc ipsum clarius exponens subiicit: Qui loquitur, seipsum ædificat sibi soli vtilis: at qui prophetat, Ecclesiam ædificat. Quantum ergo (vt Chrysostomus ait) discrimen est inter vnum hominem & totam Ecclesiam, tanto præstantior est prophetia dono linguarum.
units.tr: Since Paul has placed the gift of prophecy above all the others, he now gives the reason for this, and proves by most solid arguments that it is far more excellent than all the other exercises of the Church. It is understood (as will soon be clear from his words) that he is not speaking of that miraculous gift of foretelling which we know was then in use, but of the public exposition of the Scriptures, and so of the whole office of teaching, by which the will of God is set forth for the instruction and edification of the whole Church and of its individual members. And so that the dignity or excellence of this office may appear more clearly, he carefully compares it with the gift of tongues. He chooses this above the others chiefly because the Corinthians were especially occupied with tongues, which served their display and ambition. For it is the nature of ignorant people to value highly what they do not understand, and so, with foolish ignorance, to admire the things of lesser importance more often than the more excellent gifts. What then does Paul say? He who speaks in a tongue, that is, a foreign or strange one, does not speak to men but to God. And he gives the reason for this saying: because no one hears, that is, no one understands, so that they might grasp either the sense of what is said or any other usefulness from it. But in the Spirit, that is, by the inspiration of that spiritual gift, he speaks mysteries. He means either things entirely hidden and known to no one, or the mysteries of salvation themselves, which ought not to be concealed in the Church but publicly set forth, and in such a way that they may be understood by all. But he who prophesies speaks to men, that is, for the use and profit of men; and he speaks edification, exhortation and consolation, that is, he speaks those things by which men are built up in the knowledge of God, by which they are likewise stirred up to godliness, and which strengthen them in dangers and temptations. Explaining this even more clearly, he adds: he who speaks in a tongue edifies himself, useful only to himself; but he who prophesies edifies the Church. Therefore, as Chrysostom says, as great as the difference is between one man and the whole Church, so much more excellent is the gift of prophecy than the gift of tongues.

units.la: Admonemur igitur hoc loco, nihil in Ecclesia præstantius & excellentius habere prædicatione verbi Dei. Per hanc enim ille nobiscum loquitur, & voluntatem suam nobis reuelans se nos amicorum loco habere testatur. Per eandem nos alit, pascit, dirigit & confirmat in consiliis et actio-nibus omnibus. Ideo vt huic functioni authoritas maior accederet, Deus ipse primũ doctorem egit in Paradiso, quando primos parentes in peccatu fœdè prolapsos verbo suo de forte futura admonuit, & feminis ex muliere nasciturí promissione consolatus est. Deinde omnibus seculis idē ad hoc munus homines præstantissimos et sibi præ aliis charos destinauit: quales Patriarchæ fuerunt, deinde Moses, post hunc Prophetæ, quos Petrus sanctos Dei homines dixit. Taceo nunc Dauid-dem et Solomonem , quorum hic Regum opulentissimus, ille verò victoriosissimus fuit, vterq; autè plus gloriæ ex doctrina verbi Dei habent, quam Psalmis & aliis scriptis comprehensam ad posteros transmiserunt, quàm ex suis victorijs, triumphis, thesauris & toto illo apparatu, quo suam magnificentiam ostentarunt. Hæc enim omnia, etsi toti mundo olim admirationi fuerint, iampridem tamen vnà cum ipsis extincta sunt: doctrina autem eorum adhuc hodie in omnium ore & manibus versatur, & omnibus ad vitam piè instituendam & æternam felicitatē consequendam vtilissima est. Quòd si ad noui Testamenti historiam accedamus, ipse Dei Filius in carne manifestatus docendi ac prædicandi munerí imprimis vacauit, & eius gratia se in mundum venisse testatur: quo nomine olim à Mose magnus ille Propheta dictus fuit, quem omnes audire debeant.
units.tr: We are therefore admonished in this passage that there is nothing in the Church more excellent and outstanding than the preaching of the Word of God. For through it God speaks with us, and by revealing his will to us he testifies that he regards us as his friends. Through the same Word he nourishes, feeds, directs and strengthens us in all our counsels and actions. So that this office might have greater authority, God himself first acted as teacher in Paradise, when he admonished our first parents, grievously fallen into sin, by his Word concerning the seed that was to come, and comforted them with the promise of the offspring to be born of a woman. Then, in every age, he appointed to this same office men most excellent and dear to him above others: such were the Patriarchs, then Moses, and after him the Prophets, whom Peter called the holy men of God. I pass over David and Solomon, of whom the one was the most wealthy and the other the most victorious of kings. Yet both of them have more glory from the teaching of the Word of God, which they handed down to posterity contained in the Psalms and their other writings, than from their victories, triumphs, treasures and all that display by which they showed off their magnificence. For all these things, though once they were admired by the whole world, have long since perished together with them; but their teaching is still in the mouths and hands of everyone today, and is most useful for living piously and attaining eternal happiness. And if we come to the history of the New Testament, the Son of God himself, made manifest in the flesh, devoted himself above all to the office of teaching and preaching, and testifies that he came into the world for this purpose; for this reason he was once called by Moses that great Prophet whom all ought to hear.

units.la: Idem illi postea discipulos destinauit, quos peculij instar sibi ex toto hominum genere selegerat, & ijsdem de Regno suo sciscitantibus hoc regnum ipsorum fore respondit, vt Euangelium in toto orbe terrarum prædicent, & ita omnibus æternæ salutis administri sint, qui illud fide vera amplectuntur. Discant ergo omnes magni facere tantum Dei beneficium, qui verò ad hoc munus destinati sunt, non moueantur iniquis hominum iudicijs, qui illud explosum aut extinctum vellent. Quia enim per illud salutem nobis offert Deus, Satan illi omnibus seculis insidiatus est, & huius ingenium referunt, qui hodie calumnijs suis verbi prædicationem exosam, & eius ministros omnibus suspectos facere studēt. Sed neminem ista offendant. Fit enim in hac idem, quod in multis alijs. Nam si communis vitæ studia inspiciamus, pluris fiunt mercatores opulenti, quàm opifices, qui manuum labore victum sibi quæritant: maior item est apud plerosq; militum sanguinarium quàm agricolarum dignitas. At si rem ipsam æstimemus, hi omnibus illis digniores, honestiores, reipub. item vtiliores & magis necessarij sunt. Quod etsi omnes norint atq; sentiant, proprio tamen iudicio pleriq; seipsos fallunt. Quid ergo miramur, si simile quid fiat in ijs, quæ ad salutem æternam spectant, cuius mysteria humani ingenij captum longè excedunt?
units.tr: Likewise he afterwards appointed disciples, whom he had chosen for himself as a peculiar people from the whole human race. When they asked him about his kingdom, he answered that it would be theirs, so that they should preach the gospel throughout the whole world and thus be ministers of eternal salvation to all who embrace it in true faith. Let everyone therefore learn to value this great benefit of God. But those who are appointed to this office should not be moved by the unjust judgements of men who would have it rejected or extinguished. For since God offers us salvation through it, Satan has lain in wait against it in every age, and those who today by their slanders strive to make the preaching of the word hateful and its ministers suspect to all share his disposition. But let no one be offended by these things. The same thing happens in this matter as in many others. If we look at the pursuits of common life, wealthy merchants are held in higher esteem than the craftsmen who seek their living by manual labour; likewise among most people the bloodthirsty soldier has greater dignity than the farmer. Yet if we weigh the matter itself, these others are more worthy, more honourable, and also more useful and more necessary to the commonwealth than all those. Although everyone knows and feels this, most people nevertheless deceive themselves by their own judgement. Why then do we wonder if something similar happens in those things which concern eternal salvation, whose mysteries far exceed the grasp of the human mind?

units.la: Docet prætereà locus iste, quibus partibus constet ministrorum Ecclesiæ aut doctorum officium. Vbi ante omnia obseruari debet, quòd hominibus loqui debent, non sibi ipsis, aut lignis siue lapidibus, neq; inani verborum strepitu aërem ferire, sed in hoc esse, vt omnia ad auditorum captum atq; institutionem accommodent. In ipso igitur limine (quod dicitur) offenduntur, qui suis commodis studendo totum ministerium sibi quæstum faciunt. Quid verò loqui debeant, tribus capitibus Paulus comprehendit. Primum est ædificatio, id est doctrina, quæ ad ædificationem fi-cit.[?] Ea est quæ Dei cognitio plantatur, fides ite, timor & cultus Dei, & quæcunq; alia ad pietatem & vitæ Christianam pertinent. Vitur autem ædificandi Metaphora Apostolus, quia Ecclesia domus Dei est, quæ in eum finem verbi prædicatione & Sacramentis colligitur, ut in ea Deus suo Spiritu agat, & illic Regni sui thesauros deponat, quos in Symbolo Apostolico sub Remissione peccatorum gratuita, futuræ Resurrectionis spe & vita æterna comprehendimus. Fundamentum unius ædificij Christus est, ut ipse apud Matth. testatur, & supra cap.3. Paulus demonstrauit. Huic per Euangelij doctrinā ceu vivi lapides superstruuntur quotquot credunt: quia per fidem ipsi insertur, & in eo coalescunt. Hinc doctores in Scripturis ædificantes dicuntur, et Apostolus ideo ipsum architectum vocat. Horum est ante omnia curare, ut bonum fundamentum ponant, ipsum ut delicet Christum, qui alibi fundamentum Prophetarum & Apostolorum dicitur. Deinde ut super illud unum ædificent, neq; ei admisceant stipulas, fœnu, arundines, ligna aut quicquam aliud à Christo alienum. Adhæc operi sedulo insistent, et simul curent, ne illud clàm actis cuniculus Satan suffodiat, neue tempestatum turbinibus & procellis euertatur, ne deniq; aliqui ut arena sine calce suaspontè labantur atq; deficiant. Meminerint itē ministri assidua & perpetua ædificatione opus esse, partim quòd credentium infirmitas nouam quotidie instaurationem requirit: partim quòd nouos subinde lapides sancto huic ædificio imponi oportet, ut plures ad Christi indies colligantur, & Regnum eius perpetuò propagetur. Sed elucet hoc loco Satanæ astutia, qui ut omnes homines in hoc studio remissiores atq; segniores faceret, ædificia quædam templorum, turrium, collegiorum & sacellorum excogitauit, quæ æterna dicuntur, et magnis impensis struuntur, neglecto interim hoc spirituali templo Domini, quod fere in ruinis totū iacet illic, ubi insana ista ædificandi libido dominatur. Nam aut ædificatores omnino nulli sunt, aut perfidi sunt, qui (ut de Iudæorum Sacerdotibus Scriptura loquitur) reiecto illo pretioso lapide fundamenti, salutis præsidiū omne in rebus inutilibus atq; pernitiosis monstrant. Caueant ergo sibi ab istorum exemplo, qui ædificationem loqui voluerint. Alterum ministerij ecclesiastici caput est Exhortatio. Opus hac propter eos, qui non statim obediunt quando edocentur de ijs, quæ ad salutē consequendam necessaria sunt. Natura enim tardiores sumus ad cœlestia, & (quod nocentius est) insuper peccatis & erroribus delectamur. Opus igitur peccatorū & errorū redargutione, opus increpatione, correptione & adhortatione: cuius exempla gratissima habemus in Prophetis, quos Deus olim speculatorū instar tubā verbi sui inflare iussit, ut quosuis ad officiū faciendū excitarent. Imitati sunt hos passim Apostoli, ut nunc de Christo nihil dicamus, cuius adhortationes grauissimæ apud Euangelistas leguntur. Vehementer ergo errant, qui hodie nihil huius volunt fieri, sed quasi nuda simplexq; doctrina sufficiat, indignissimè ferunt omnem correptionem atq; adhortationem. Quàm verò hæ necessariæ sint, crescens quotidie immanissimorum scelerum licentia & omnium hominum mores corruptissimi abunde testantur. Quia verò Ecclesia multos habet, qui tentationibus & omni afflictionum genere exercentur, tertium caput adijcitur, Consolatio: ad quam pertinent, quæ de boni & fidi pastoris officio apud Ezechielem dicuntur, quando se illum fore pollicetur Dominus, qui perditas oues requirat, expulsas reducat, fauicas liget & infirmas roboret. Et in horum consideratione ministri Ecclesiarū sic versari debent, ut semper meminerint, se tunc demum fideles Deo fore, si in populi studia atq; mores totis animis intenti, pro auditorum & temporum ratione ista omnia quam diligentissimè proponant, ut simplices quidem & rerum ignari erudiantur, tardiores vero & obstinati urgeantur, afflicti vero & trepidi consolationibus pijs erecti spem bonam concipiant. Huc referri debent, quæ de verbo Dei recte secundo Paulus Timotheo scribit, & quæ Christus sub œconomi sui parabola tradidit 2. Timoth. 2. Matth. 24.
units.tr: Moreover, this passage teaches of what parts the office of the ministers of the Church or of teachers consists. Here, above all, it must be observed that they ought to speak to men, not to themselves, nor to wood or stones, nor to strike the air with empty noise of words; rather, they should aim to adapt everything to the understanding and instruction of their hearers. Those, then, stumble right at the threshold, as it is said, who, seeking their own advantage, make the whole ministry a source of gain for themselves. Paul summarises under three heads what they ought to speak. The first is edification, that is, teaching which contributes to edification. This is the teaching by which the knowledge of God is planted, faith, hope, the fear and worship of God, and whatever else pertains to godliness and the Christian life. The Apostle uses the metaphor of building because the Church is the house of God, gathered together for this end by the preaching of the word and the sacraments, so that God may work in it by his Spirit and there lay up the treasures of his kingdom, which we comprehend in the Apostles' Creed under the free forgiveness of sins, the hope of the future resurrection, and eternal life. Christ is the foundation of this one building, as he himself testifies in Matthew, and as Paul showed above in chapter 3. Upon this foundation, through the doctrine of the gospel, all who believe are built up like living stones, because they are joined to it by faith and grow together in it. Hence teachers are said to build up by the Scriptures, and the Apostle therefore calls him the architect. It is their first duty to take care that they lay a good foundation, namely Christ himself, who elsewhere is called the foundation of the prophets and apostles. Then they should build upon that one foundation alone, and not mix with it stubble, hay, reeds, wood, or anything else foreign to Christ. Besides, they must apply themselves diligently to the work and at the same time take care that Satan does not secretly dig a mine beneath it, nor that it is overturned by the whirlwinds and storms of tempests, and finally that some do not slip away and fail, like sand without lime. Ministers should also remember that edification must be constant and perpetual, partly because the weakness of believers requires a fresh restoration every day, and partly because new stones must continually be placed in this holy building, so that more may be gathered to Christ day by day and his kingdom may be perpetually extended. But here Satan's cunning is apparent. In order to make all men slacker and more lax in this pursuit, he has devised certain buildings of temples, towers, colleges and chapels, which are called eternal and are erected at great expense, while meanwhile this spiritual temple of the Lord is neglected, lying almost wholly in ruins where that mad lust for building holds sway. For either there are no builders at all, or they are faithless, who (as Scripture says of the priests of the Jews) having rejected that precious cornerstone of the foundation, point to every means of salvation in useless and pernicious things. Let them therefore beware of following the example of such men, who wish to speak of edification. The second head of the ecclesiastical ministry is exhortation. It is needed for those who do not at once obey when they are taught about the things necessary for obtaining salvation. For by nature we are slow towards heavenly things, and (what is more harmful) we take delight in sins and errors. Therefore there is need for the rebuke of sins and errors, need for reproof, correction and exhortation. We have most welcome examples of this in the prophets, whom God once commanded to sound the trumpet of his word like watchmen, so that they might rouse anyone to do his duty. The apostles everywhere imitated them, not to mention Christ himself, whose most weighty exhortations are read in the evangelists. Those therefore greatly err who today want none of this done, but think that plain and simple doctrine is enough, and who take it very ill that any rebuke or exhortation is given. How necessary these are, the ever-growing licence of monstrous crimes and the thoroughly corrupt morals of all men bear ample witness. But since the Church has many who are exercised by temptations and every kind of affliction, a third head is added: consolation. To this belong the things said by Ezekiel about the duty of a good and faithful shepherd, when the Lord promises that he will himself be such a one: to seek the lost sheep, bring back those driven away, bind up the broken, and strengthen the weak. In considering these things, the ministers of the Churches ought so to conduct themselves that they always remember they will then at last be faithful to God if, wholly intent upon the studies and morals of the people, they set forth all these things as carefully as possible according to the capacity of their hearers and the needs of the times: so that the simple and ignorant may be taught, the slower and obstinate may be pressed, and the afflicted and anxious, raised up by godly consolations, may conceive good hope. To this belong the things Paul rightly wrote to Timothy about handling the word of God, and what Christ delivered in the parable of his steward (2 Tim. 2; Matt. 24).

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui ne linguas in genere aut simpliciter damnare putetur, per Præoccupationem subijcit: Velim autem omnes vos loqui linguis, magis tamen ut prophetetis. Etenim credibile est, multos qui linguarum cognitionem & excellentiorem doctrinam alijs inuidebant, hanc occasionem captauisse, ut quæcunque sunt huius generis dona pro inutilibus, vel etiam noxijs eijcerent: quales hodie etiam inueniuntur homines barbari, linguarum & bonarum artium hostes, qui ut propriam ignorantiam tegere possint, in literarum studia & scholas perinde inuehuntur, ac si non aliæ nocentiores sint veræ religionis pestes. Quibus omnibus hoc Pauli votum possumus opponere, qui ut omnes linguis loquerentur optauit. Habuit autem eius voti causas multas & graues. Erat enim hoc præclarum & memorabile donum Dei, non Apostolis modò & viris apostolicis necessarium, sed non minus vulgo credentium vtilissimum. Commendabat enim Euangelicæ doctrinæ excellentiam, & testabatur eam diuinam esse, & totam huius causam cælitus gubernari. Deinde ad Scripturæ veram intelligentiam plurimùm fa-cit linguarum cognitio, qua qui destituuntur, ij cæcorum & claudorum instar alienis oculis vident, & alienis pedibus ambulant. Præterea nullus inuidiæ ac æmulationi locus reliquus esse po-terat, si omnes eodem dono fuissent instructi. Quia ergo hodie etiam in eruendis Scripturarum arcanis magnus Hebræa & Græca linguæ vsus est, ut iam de mutuis hominum & gentium di-uersarum commerciis nihil dicam, nimiùm profecto barbari sunt, qui scholas & bonarum artium studia odiosius exagitare non verentur.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who, lest he should seem to condemn tongues in general or without qualification, adds by way of anticipation: "I would indeed that you all spoke with tongues, but rather that you prophesied." For it is credible that many who begrudged others their knowledge of languages and their superior learning seized upon this occasion to cast out, as useless or even harmful, every gift of this kind. Such men are to be found today too: barbarians, enemies of languages and of the liberal arts, who, in order to cover their own ignorance, rail against the study of letters and the schools, as though there were no other and more harmful pests of true religion. To all of them we may oppose this wish of Paul, who desired that all should speak with tongues. He had many weighty reasons for this wish. For this was an excellent and memorable gift of God, necessary not only for the apostles and apostolic men, but no less most useful for the common body of believers. It commended the excellence of the evangelical doctrine and bore witness that it was divine and that its whole cause was governed from heaven. Next, knowledge of languages contributes greatly to a true understanding of Scripture; those who lack it see with the eyes of others, like the blind and lame, and walk on the feet of others. Moreover, there could be no room left for envy and rivalry if all had been equipped with the same gift. Therefore, since today too great a use of Hebrew and Greek is needed for unlocking the hidden things of the Scriptures, to say nothing of the mutual dealings between men and different nations, they are surely too barbarous who do not hesitate to attack with excessive hostility the schools and the study of the liberal arts.

units.la: Elucet autem in Pauli exemplo syncera charitatis ingenium revera ἀφθονον. Qui enim ea ardent, ij quæ bona & vtilia sunt, omnibus communia esse cupiunt, ut ad plures eorum fructus redeat. Ita Moses olim omnes Israelitas Spiritu Dei donari optabat, ut ad prophetandum idonei fierent. Neque Elizæo Elias succensuit, quando suum spiritum in se duplicari petebat. Et quanto studio Prophetæ simul omnes & Apostoli sibi revelatam diuinæ voluntatis cognitionem toti populo communicauerint, eorum scripta & conciones abunde testantur. Arguit hoc Ponti-ficum arrogantiam, qui quæcunque sunt huius generis sibi soli & suis creaturis vendicant, Sacrificis nimirum, quos tonsura & unctio ab ipsis excogitata à vulgo Christianorum segregat aut distinguit. His enim soli per illos Scripturas sacras legere, & ijsdem soli totam Cœnam Domini usurpare licet. Imò hos solos spirituales dicunt, & ijsdem locum quoque in templo proprium dicarunt, ut gradibus aliquot altiorem, ita ferè ferreis quoque cancellis interseptum. Denique ut soli dominari possint, non optant cum Paulo Apostolo, ut omnes linguis loquantur & pro-phetent, sed contra proprios Canones linguarum cognitionem omnino sepultam volunt, & ijsdem nefas videtur, si quis ex populo Christiano de fidei mysterijs & religione orationem instituat. Vident enim fortissimum sui regni fulcrum in populi ignorantia positum esse, & ideo illum aliqua cognitione instrui non possunt ferre.
units.tr: Indeed, in Paul's example the genuine character of sincere love shines forth, which is truly without envy. For those who burn with this love wish the things that are good and useful to be common to all, so that their fruit may flow back to many. Thus Moses once wished that all the Israelites might be endowed with the Spirit of God, so that they might become fit to prophesy. Nor was Elijah angry with Elisha when Elisha asked that a double portion of his spirit be given to him. And how eagerly the Prophets and Apostles, all together, shared with the whole people the knowledge of the divine will revealed to them, their writings and sermons abundantly testify. This refutes the arrogance of the Pontiffs, who claim for themselves alone, and for their creatures, whatever things are of this kind: namely the priests, whom a tonsure and anointing invented by themselves separate and distinguish from the common multitude of Christians. For to these alone it is permitted to read the holy Scriptures through their own medium, and to these alone to make use of the whole Lord's Supper. Indeed they call these alone spiritual, and have also dedicated to them a place of their own in the temple, raised a few steps higher and, as it were, enclosed with iron railings. Finally, so that they alone may be able to lord it over others, they do not wish, with the Apostle Paul, that all should speak in tongues and prophesy; but, contrary to their own canons, they want the knowledge of languages altogether buried, and it seems to them an outrage if anyone from the Christian people should hold a discussion about the mysteries of the faith and religion. For they see that the strongest prop of their kingdom rests on the ignorance of the people, and therefore they cannot bear that the people be instructed by any knowledge.

units.la: Porro omissis iis, Paulum rursus audiamus, qui ne hoc suo voto eorum ambitionem confirmare videretur, qui linguas superbè & cum aliorum contemptu ostentabant, illud moderatur addita correctione: Magis tamen ut prophetetis. Et huius quoque rationem reddit: Maior enim est qui prophetat (nimirum, quia toti Ecclesiæ loquitur) quàm qui linguis loquitur, nisi si interpretetur ut Ecclesia ædificationem accipiat. Interpretatio enim clavis instar est, quæ nisi adhibeatur, non aliquis usus esse potest Verbi Dei lingua peregrina & ignota prædicati aut propositi: Imò thesauri abstrusi instar erit, quem omnes ignorant, aut ad quem nemo poterit penetrare. Simul apparet in Apostoli verbis, non unum idemq; donum fuisse tunc temporis Linguis loqui & Interpretari: ut & hodie multos invenias, qui linguas norunt, nihil tamen præstare possunt, si animi sui sensum in publico proferre debeant.
units.tr: But, setting those things aside, let us hear Paul again, who, lest he seem to confirm by his wish the ambition of those who displayed tongues proudly and with contempt for others, moderates it by adding a correction: "Yet rather that you may prophesy." And he also gives the reason for this: "For he who prophesies is greater" (namely, because he speaks to the whole Church) "than he who speaks in tongues, unless he interprets, so that the Church may receive edification." For interpretation is like a key, which, unless it is applied, the use of the Word of God preached or set forth in a foreign and unknown tongue cannot be of any benefit. Indeed, it will be like a hidden treasure, which everyone ignores, or into which no one can penetrate. At the same time it appears from the Apostle's words that speaking in tongues and interpreting were not one and the same gift at that time; just as today you will find many who know languages, yet can accomplish nothing if they must express the sense of their mind in public.

units.la: Primùm autem nos de proprio & germano linguarum usu hic locus admonet, qui est ut prophetiæ, id est, Scripturarum interpretationi seruiant, & sic Ecclesiæ ædificationem adiuvent. Confutatur ergo illarum abusus, qui ita in Papatu obtinuit, ut in Ecclesiasticis cœtibus omnia linguis peregrinis, Latina præsertim, peragantur. Est is cum multiplici errore coniunctus. Primò enim pugnat cum fine, in quem cœtus sacri à Deo instituti sunt. Est ille, ut homines Verbo Dei doceantur quæ huius voluntas, quæ item vera sit salutis consequendæ ratio: deinde ut Sacramenta administrentur cum publica beneficiorum Dei & redemptionis per Christum factæ commemoratione: ut item preces fiant publicæ, & simul Deo gratiæ agantur, & eius nomen prædicando aliis exemplo sumus, quo & ipsi ad eius cognitionem atque cultum excitentur. Quid autem horum lingua peregrina fieri poterit? Deinde sepelitur hac ratione Verbum Dei, ut plerique illud ignorent. Quod quid aliud est, quàm lucem ipsam obscurare, & pios gladio illo spirituali exarmare, quo solo diabolus profligatur & vincitur? Præterea contra Dei & Angelorum exemplum istud fit. Ille enim lingua vulgari olim cum patribus priuatim & cum toto populo publicè locum est: & (vt infra audiemus) poenam minitaturus, se lingua peregrina vsurum esse dicit. Et de Angelis nusquam legitur eos alia lingua locutos fuisse, quàm quæ illis nota erat, quibus cum agebant. Adde his, quòd cum Deo luditur, si in eius domo lingua loquamur, quam eius domestici non intelligunt: imò quàm sæpe ne illi quidem intelligunt, qui ea inter legendum & canendum verun-tur. Esset hoc in bene constituta domo intolerabile alicui patrifamilias, si quid huius œconomi sa-cerent & qui aliis rebus agendis præfecti sunt. Num verò Deum id ferre posse aut velle putabi-mus? Denique nihil huius unquam in veteri Ecclesia factitatum est, nisi hoc allegare libeat quod in præsenti Paulus tanta cum grauitate reprehendit: & qui hodie in Græcia, in Ægypto & Æthiopia, in toto denique Oriente agunt Christiani, sacra sua idiomate vulgari ac omnibus noto peragunt. Solus Romanus Pontifex Occidentalibus Ecclesijs, quarum caput seipsum constituit, Latini sermonis usum obtrufit: ut vel hoc argumento constet, illum Antichristum dici debere, cui Latini nomen fore, olim Irenæus, vetustissimus & orthodoxus Ecclesiæ scriptor, præ-dixit. Neque satis illi visum est, si sacrifici Latinè loquerentur & canerent, sed à rudi etiam vulgo preces priuatas eadem lingua recitari voluit. Sunt hæc absurdissima, si vel communem sensum iudicem adhibeas. Excusant tamen illi factum, vel potius pertinaciter defendunt. Dicunt enim, multa in sacris libris contineri, quæ populo edicere non satis tutum fit, inter precandum verò sufficere bonam animi intentione, etiamsi quid preceris non intelligas. Sed prius illud falsum & blasphemum est, postremum verò hoc adeò puerile & ridiculum, ut mirum sit tale quid posse in mentem venire hominibus, qui soli sapere videri volunt. Nec enim fieri potest, ut bona sit animi intentio absque attentione diligenti & seria deuotione. Quid verò attendet, aut quo medio animi deuotionem excitabit, qui quid ipse loquatur, aut quid alij dicant nō intelligit? Itaque unum hoc abunde docet, quàm fallantur ipse sua, qui sibi ipsis de isto hominum genere aliquid boni pollicentur, quasi serio Ecclesiæ reformandæ studio flagrent, quando tot iam annis ab instaurata Euangelij doctrina adduci non potuerunt, ut abusum hunc tam manifestum, tam crassum & absurdum corrigere in animum induxerint.
units.tr: First, however, this passage reminds us of the proper and genuine use of languages, which is that they should serve prophecy, that is, the interpretation of the Scriptures, and so help the edification of the Church. Therefore the abuse of them is refuted, which has prevailed so strongly in Papacy that in ecclesiastical assemblies everything is carried on in foreign tongues, Latin especially. This is connected with many errors. For first, it conflicts with the purpose for which sacred assemblies were instituted by God. That purpose is that men be taught by the Word of God what his will is, and also what the true way of obtaining salvation is; then that the sacraments be administered with a public commemoration of God's benefits and of the redemption accomplished through Christ; likewise that public prayers be made and thanks be given to God at the same time, and that by proclaiming his name we become an example to others, so that they too may be stirred up to his knowledge and worship. But how can any of these be done in a foreign tongue? Next, the Word of God is buried in this way, so that most people are ignorant of it. What else is this than to darken the light itself, and to disarm the godly of that spiritual sword by which alone the devil is put to flight and conquered? Moreover, this practice is contrary to the example of God and the Angels. For God once spoke in the common tongue with the fathers privately and with the whole people publicly; and (as we shall hear below) when he was about to threaten punishment, he says that he will use a foreign tongue. And nowhere is it read that the Angels spoke in any language other than the one known to those with whom they dealt. Add to these that we mock God if we speak in his house in a language which his household does not understand; indeed, how often even those do not understand who mutter it while reading and singing. In a well-ordered house this would be intolerable to any head of a family, if the servants who are placed in charge of other business did such a thing to their master's household. Will we then think that God can or will bear this? Finally, nothing of this kind was ever practised in the ancient Church, unless one is willing to allege what Paul here rebukes with such severity; and those Christians who today act in Greece, in Egypt and Ethiopia, and indeed in the whole East, perform their sacred rites in the vernacular, known to all. The Roman Pontiff alone has forced the use of the Latin language on the Western Churches, of which he has made himself the head; so that by this argument alone it is established that he ought to be called Antichrist, the one for whom Irenaeus, the most ancient and orthodox writer of the Church, once foretold the name of Latinus. Nor did it seem enough to them that the priests spoke and sang in Latin; they also wished private prayers to be recited in the same language by the untutored common people. These things are most absurd, if you bring in even common sense as judge. Yet they excuse the practice, or rather stubbornly defend it. For they say that many things are contained in the sacred books which it is not safe enough to declare to the people, while in praying it is sufficient to have a good intention of mind, even if you do not understand what you pray. But the first claim is false and blasphemous, and the last is so childish and ridiculous that it is astonishing such a thing could come into the minds of men who alone wish to seem wise. For a good intention of mind cannot exist without diligent attention and earnest devotion. But what will he attend to, or by what means will he stir up devotion of mind, who does not understand what he himself says or what others say? Thus this alone sufficiently shows how much those men deceive themselves who promise themselves some good from such a class of men, as if they were eagerly devoted to the serious reform of the Church, when for so many years since the restored doctrine of the Gospel they have not been brought to resolve to correct an abuse so manifest, so gross and absurd.

units.la: Priusquam verò dicendi finem faciamus, videndum etiam quis verè magnus, aut etiam reliquis maior sit in Ecclesia, vel Christi Regno. Est hoc confideratu dignissimum. De eo enim olim pugnatum inter Apostolos, cùm huius rationem adhuc ignorarent. Et hanc ipsam concertationem in veteri Ecclesia magnos motus dedisse scimus, dum inter Episcopos alij alijs præstantiores esse voluerunt. Tandem dignitatem hanc partim artibus insidiosis, partim aperta vi obtinuerunt Romani Pontifices, qui hodie Maximi & Ecclesiæ Caput dicuntur: & extat Bonifacij octaui Canon de Maioritate & obedientia, cuius summa est, supremam rerum potestatem penes Pontificem esse, & proinde de necessitate salutis esse, ut illi omnis anima subiecta sit. Et ne Reges & Imperatores se exemptos putent, gladios duos fingit, quorum alter in Pontificis solius, alter verò in Imperatoris quidem manu sit, sed non nisi pro Pontificis arbitrio moueri aut exerceri debeat. Similiter Pontificem Luminare maius siue Solem, Imperatorem verò Luminare minus aut Lunam dicit, ut illum supra hunc eminere ostendat. Sed longè aliter Christus, qui eum in Ecclesia sua alijs maiorem fore olim docuit, qui omnibus alijs seruiat. Quis verò ille est? Id in præsenti Paulus docet, quando eum qui prophetat omnibus alijs eo nomine præfert, quòd toti Ecclesiæ loquatur, quæ ex ipso ædificationem accipiat. Quò Christus quoque respexit, quando Ioannem Baptistam prophetis omnibus anteposuit: nimirum quòd etsi hi omnes docuerint sui seculi homines, ille tamen ipsum propius monstrauerit, & totam diu expectatæ salutis rationem clarius exposuerit. Maioritas ergo (ut illorum vocabulo utar) non in huius seculi dignitatibus aut opum splendore consistit, neque certo alicui loco alligata est, sed ex ministerij fide & docendi sedulitate tota dependet, & alijs præferri meretur, qui maiori cum fructu docet, & plures Christo lucrifacit. At si ad hanc regulam examinentur Romani Pontifices, mox appa-rebit eos ne minimos quidem, imò omnino nullos esse in Ecclesia, cùm nemini seruiant, nemínem doceant, sed plus quàm barbarico fastu sese supra omnes alios extollant, adhæc ceu canes quidam in præsepi diris latratibus & morsibus crudelissimis obstent, ne quis alius docendi munus fideliter theat. Neminem ergo illorum insolentia moueat, gratias autem agamus Deo, qui nos ex istorum tyrannide liberauit, inq; libertate illa constanter seruiamus Domino & seruatori nostro IESV CHRISTO: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Before we make an end of speaking, we must also consider who is truly great, or even greater than the rest, in the Church or in the Kingdom of Christ. This is most worthy of consideration. For this was once disputed among the Apostles, when they still did not know the reason for it. And we know that this very contention in the ancient Church gave rise to great disturbances, when some among the Bishops wished to be more distinguished than others. At last the Roman Pontiffs obtained this dignity, partly by insidious arts and partly by open force; they who today are called the Greatest and the Head of the Church. And there exists the Canon of Boniface VIII concerning Majority and obedience, the sum of which is that the supreme power of things rests with the Pontiff, and that therefore it is necessary for salvation that every soul be subject to him. And lest kings and emperors think themselves exempt, he imagines two swords, of which one is in the hand of the Pontiff alone, and the other indeed in the hand of the Emperor, but which must be moved or wielded only at the Pontiff's pleasure. Similarly he calls the Pontiff the greater light, or the Sun, and the Emperor the lesser light, or the Moon, so as to show that the former rises above the latter. But Christ teaches quite otherwise, who once taught that the one who is greater in his Church should be the one who serves all the others. Who then is he? Paul teaches this at present, when he prefers to all others on this account the one who prophesies, because he speaks to the whole Church, which receives edification from him. To this Christ also looked when he placed John the Baptist before all the prophets: namely because, although all of them taught the men of their age, yet he pointed out the very One more closely and set forth more clearly the whole manner of the long-awaited salvation. Greatness, then (to use their term), does not consist in the dignities of this age or in the splendour of wealth, nor is it bound to any particular place, but depends entirely on faithfulness in the ministry and diligence in teaching, and deserves to be preferred to others, he who teaches with greater fruit and gains more people for Christ. But if the Roman Pontiffs are examined by this rule, it will soon appear that they are not even the least, indeed that they are altogether nothing in the Church, since they serve no one and teach no one, but with more than barbarian haughtiness raise themselves above all others; moreover, like certain dogs in a manger, they stand in the way with dreadful barking and most cruel bites, lest anyone else should faithfully perform the office of teaching. Let no one, therefore, be moved by their insolence; but let us give thanks to God, who has freed us from the tyranny of these men, and in that liberty let us constantly serve the Lord and our Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXXI.
units.tr: HOMILY LXXXI.

units.la: Nunc vero fratres, si veniam ad vos linguis loquens, quid vos profuabo, nisi vobis loquar aut per reuelationem, aut per cognitionem, aut per prophetiam, aut per doctrinam? Atqui inanima quæ sonum edunt, siue tibia sit siue cithara, nisi distinctionem tonis dederint, quo modo cognoscetur quod tibia canitur aut cithara? Etenim si incertum sonum tuba dederit, quis apparabitur ad bellum? Ita & vos nisi bene significantem sermonem edider/ itis, quomodo intelligetur quod dicitur? Eritis enim in aerem loquentes. Tot, prout incide-rit, genera vocum sunt in mundo, & nihil est mutum. Nisi igitur sciero vim vocis, ero ei qui loquitur barbarus, & qui loquitur, apud me barbarus fuerit: Ita & vos.
units.tr: But now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what good will I do you, unless I speak to you either by revelation, or by knowledge, or by prophecy, or by teaching? Yet lifeless things that give sound, whether a flute or a harp, unless they produce a distinction of notes, how will it be known what is being played on the flute or the harp? For if the trumpet gives an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for battle? So also you, unless you utter speech that clearly conveys its meaning, how will what is said be understood? For you will be speaking into the air. There are, however many kinds of voices there may be in the world, and none is without voice. If then I do not know the force of a voice, I shall be a barbarian to the one who speaks, and the one who speaks will be a barbarian to me. So also with you.

units.la: Vt homo propter naturæ suæ vitiositatem, quæ ex primo parente in nos deriuata est, nihil boni habet ex semetipso: ita neque donis à Deo acceptis bene uti potest, nisi singulari Spiritus luce gubernetur: & plerique vel negligentia peccant, dum sibi creditum talentum cum malo illo seruo defodiunt: vel malitia, dum illis ad quæstum siue ad inanem ostentationem abutuntur. Quod si hoc in iis fiat, quæ ad Ecclesiam pertinent, nihil huic nocentius potest accidere. Tunc enim Veritatis doctrina depravatur, ordo omnis turbatur, & confusio inducitur cum horribili dissipatione cum sacrorum omnium tum ipsorum fidelium coniunctia. Exemplum huius mali in Corinthijs habemus, quorum Ecclesiam omni cognitione & scientia excelluisse, & præclaris donis à Deo ornatam fuisse, iam sæpe audiuimus. Inter illa autem linguarum quoq; donum fuit, quo tunc temporis Euangelij sui prædicationem Christus commendabat. At quia illi his ambitiose abusi sunt, non modo in sectas scissi fuerunt, verumetiam in cœtibus sacris & toto religionis externæ exercitio omnia confuse & absque fructu faciebant. Ideo Paulus hoc Capite multis hanc causam agit, hoc imprimis vrgens, ne linguas inutiliter ostentent, sed his prophetiam longè præferant, per quam Ecclesia in veritatis cognitione, fide & pietate ædificetur. Et quia linguas, nisi ad hunc finem dirigantur, nuper inutiles esse dixerat, id nunc exemplis atque similibus confirmat.
units.tr: Just as a man, because of the corruption of his nature, which has been derived to us from our first parent, has nothing good from himself, so he cannot make good use of the gifts received from God unless he is guided by the singular light of the Spirit. Many sin either through negligence, when they bury the talent entrusted to them together with that wicked servant, or through malice, when they abuse those gifts for gain or for empty display. If this happens in matters that concern the Church, nothing more harmful can befall it. For then the doctrine of the truth is corrupted, all order is disturbed, and confusion is introduced, with terrible scattering of both all the sacred things and the faithful themselves who are bound together. We have an example of this evil among the Corinthians, whose Church, as we have often heard, excelled in all knowledge and learning and was adorned with splendid gifts from God. Among these was also the gift of tongues, by which Christ at that time commended the preaching of his gospel. But because they abused this ambitiously, they were not only split into factions, but in their sacred assemblies and in the whole outward exercise of religion they did everything in confusion and without profit. Therefore Paul in this chapter argues this case at length, urging above all that they must not display tongues uselessly, but must greatly prefer prophecy to them, through which the Church is built up in the knowledge of the truth, in faith and in piety. And because he had said recently that tongues are useless unless they are directed to this end, he now confirms this by examples and comparisons.

units.la: Ordiitur autem à seipso, & proprium exemplum adducit, vt causa hæc minus inuidiæ ac odij habeat. Nunc vero fratres (inquit) si veniam ad vos linguis loquens, quid vos iuuabo, nisi vobis loquar aut per reuelationem, aut per cognitionem, aut per prophetiam, aut per doctrinam? Poterat dicere Apostolus: Scio veniisse ad vos post meum discessum, & quotidie in cœtibus vestris prodire sciolos quosdam, qui linguarum variarum cognitione sese venditant, suamq; eruditione sermone peregrino non sine magna omnium admiratione ostentant: sed scire velim, quid nam omnes isti vobis prosint, & quam ex illis vtilitatem capiatis? At quia hoc odiosum fuisset, & ipse simul insuspicionem incurrere poterat, quasi odio suorum æmulorum talia diceret, & Ecclesiæ ipsorum hanc laudem inuideret, hoc omne in se transfert. Si ego (inquit) nunc ad vos redirem, & omnium earum gentium linguis vobis concionarer, quas toto mei apostolatus tempore lustraui, quis inde obsecro ad vos fructus rediret? Sed nolo ego de eo pronuntiare, vos ipsos appello, vos in hac causa testes simul & iudices audire cupio. Certe nihil ex meis concionibus meliores abibitis, neq; profectum aliquem facietis, nisi vobis loquar (lingua videlicet vestra vulgari) aut per reuelationem, aut per cognitionem, &c. Fuit hoc argumentum vt euidens, ita satis firmum & efficax ad conuincendam illorum insaniam, qui inani linguarum ostentatione superbiebant. At nos hodie ex verbis istis non minus valide argumentari possumus: Si tantus Apostolus absq; fructu Ecclesiæ lingua peregrina loqueretur, quanto minus præstabunt stupidi illi Alcinoi & ignaui Penelopes sponsi, qui hodie in templis boant, & Psalmodias atq; lectiones Latinas faciunt?
units.tr: He begins from himself and brings forward his own example, so that this cause may have less envy and hatred. "But now, brothers," he says, "if I come to you speaking in tongues, what good will I do you, unless I speak to you either by revelation, or by knowledge, or by prophecy, or by teaching?" The apostle could have said: "I know that since my departure there have come among you, and every day in your assemblies there appear, certain half-learned men who boast of their knowledge of various tongues and display their learning in foreign speech, not without great admiration from all. But I should like to know what good all these men do you, and what profit you derive from them." But because this would have been offensive, and he himself might at the same time have incurred suspicion, as if he were speaking out of hatred for his rivals and begrudging their Church this praise, he turns the whole matter upon himself. "If I," he says, "were now to return to you and preach to you in the tongues of all those nations which I have traversed throughout my whole apostolic ministry, what, I beg you, would be the fruit that would come to you from that? But I do not wish to pronounce on this; I call on you yourselves, I wish you to hear, in this matter, both witnesses and judges. Surely you would go away from my sermons no better, and you would make no progress at all, unless I speak to you (in your own vernacular, of course) by revelation, or by knowledge, etc." This argument was as clear as it was firm and effective enough to convict the madness of those who were puffed up with the empty display of tongues. But today we may argue no less forcefully from these words: if so great an apostle spoke in a foreign tongue without benefit to the Church, how much less will those dull Alcinoi and idle suitors of Penelope accomplish, who today bawl in the churches and recite psalms and lessons in Latin?

units.la: Interim suo exemplo Paulus omnes Verbi administros sui officij admonet: ut nimirum non alio animo aut instituto ad Ecclesiam veniant, quam ut huic prosint, & eam aedificent. Etenim multi currunt & in ministerium seipsos intrudunt, non autem ut alijs fructum aliquem afferant, sed ut quaestum sibi faciant & suas res agant. Tales olim Prophetarum tempore fuerunt, de quibus per Ieremiam & Ezechielem Deus queritur: Currebant, & non mittebam eos. Item, Vae pastoribus, qui pascunt seipsos, &c. Et Apostolis adhuc docentibus non defuerunt canes muti, quorum Deus venter erat, & qui nullo vel Dei vel Ecclesiae zelo ducti per aemulationem & contentionem concionabantur, de quibus in epistola ad Philippen. graviter Paulus pios admonet. Et hodie in Papatu multi veniunt ad Episcopatus, Canonicatus & ad Ecclesiarum pinguissima pendia, sed quotus quisque cum Paulo seipsum aut alios interrogat: Quid vobis prosum[?] quae mei est in Ecclesia utilitas? Quid autem de illis dico, quando neque inter nostros, qui Euangelij precones haberi volunt, omnes haec cura tangit? Si enim de eo vel semel serio cogitarent, non possent tantum temporis ignavo otio, infructuosis peregrinationibus, vel discursionibus potius, quam item & comessationibus tribuere. Meminerint ergo omnes isti, se ideo missos & ordinatos esse, ut aliquam Ecclesiae utilitatem afferant. Est haec CHRISTI IESV sponsa, quam cum proprij sanguinis pretio redemerit, eam inutilibus nugis lacerari non sinet. Itaque hanc quaestionem nobis semper occinamus o fratres: Quid proficis haec aut ista dicendo? Quid juvant Ecclesiam concertationes istae de rebus abstrusis, quae paucissimi intelligunt? quid utilitatis capiunt pij ex ceremonijs theatricis, ex imaginibus, ex organorum strepitu, ex sumptuoso templorum ornatu? Quod autem de Ecclesiarum ministris dicimus, non minus ad se pertinere putabunt viri principes, & quotquot ad Rempub. administrandam vocati sunt. Ita enim ipsi quoque seipsos ad curam diligentiorem excitabunt, & ad publicam salutem plurimum conferent.
