units.tr: Meanwhile, by his own example, Paul admonishes all the ministers of the Word of their office: namely, that they should come to the Church with no other purpose or plan than to be of service to it and to build it up. For many run and thrust themselves into the ministry, not so as to bring any benefit to others, but to make gain for themselves and to attend to their own affairs. Such men there were in the time of the prophets, of whom God complains through Jeremiah and Ezekiel: "They ran, and I did not send them." Likewise: "Woe to the ministers who feed themselves," etc. And while the apostles were still teaching, there were not lacking dumb dogs, whose god was their belly, and who, moved by no zeal either for God or for the Church, preached out of rivalry and contention, concerning whom Paul seriously admonishes the godly in his epistle to the Philippians. And today in the Papacy many come to bishoprics, canonries and the richest revenues of the churches, but how few ask themselves and others with Paul: "What good am I to you? What is my usefulness in the Church?" But why do I speak of them, when this concern does not touch all of our own men either, who wish to be regarded as heralds of the gospel? For if they once seriously thought about it, they could not give so much time to lazy idleness, to unfruitful journeys or rather wanderings, and to feasting as well. Let all of them therefore remember that they have been sent and ordained so that they may bring some benefit to the Church. This is the bride of Jesus Christ, whom he redeemed with the price of his own blood; he will not allow her to be torn by useless trifles. Therefore, brothers, let us always sing this question to ourselves: What good do these or those statements do? What use are those disputes about abstruse matters, which very few understand, to the Church? What benefit do the godly derive from theatrical ceremonies, from images, from the noise of organs, from the costly adornment of churches? What we say about the ministers of the churches, the princes and all who have been called to administer the commonwealth will think applies no less to themselves. For thus they too will stir themselves to more diligent care, and will contribute greatly to public welfare.

units.la: Obseruabis praeterea hoc loco, quas partes faciat Apostolus praedicationis Euangelicae, aut quomodo huius ordinem atque finem definiat. Nisi (inquit) vobis loquar per revelationem, aut per cognitionem, aut per prophetiam, aut per doctrinam. Ambrosius haec omnia unum & idem esse existimat, sed non temere inter ea Apostolus distinguit, ut simul de ordine admoneret, quo minister debet progredi inter docendum, ut ad finem eum perveniat, quem Deus ipse ministerio Ecclesiastico praefixit. Ante omnia revelatione opus est. Quid enim ex semetipso docebit alios, qui nisi divinitus illuminetur, neque Deum Patrem neque Filium nosse potest? Nemo novit (ait Christus) quis sit Filius, nisi Pater: & quis sit Pater nisi Filius, & cuicunq; voluerit Filius revelare. Et idem Petro qui ipsum ingenue erat confessus, dicebat: Caro & sanguis non revelarunt tibi, sed Pater meus, qui in coelis est. Ideo olim Prophetae Verbum ex ore Domini petere iussi sunt, & Apostolis Spiritus Veritatis datus est, qui ipsis suggereret ea, quae populo proponerent. Hic ergo preces nobis commendantur, quibus non modo generalem Verbi Dei cognitionem petimus, verum etiam quid quovis loco & tempore facto & dicto opus sit. Revelationem cognitio sequitur, quam illius effectum rectissime dixeris. Et haec quoq; no minus necessaria est. Quid enim dicet, qui nihil novit, nihil intelligit? Ideo Apostolis dicebat Christus: Discipulos facite omnes gentes, docentes eos servare quae ego vobis tradidi. Requiritur autem hic Scripturae sacrae studium, quia per illam nobis loquitur Deus, & ideo Paulus Timotheum suum, quem a pueris in sacris literis institutum esse sciebat, graviter monet, ut lectioni sedulo incumbat. Tertium locum habet prophetia, quae dextera est & propria Scripturarum interpretatio, per quam Dei voluntas eruitur & revelatur, futuri quoque rerum eventus non obscure praedicuntur, ut ex his consilia quoque de rebus agendis peti possint. At nullus istorum omnium usus est, nisi alij de ijsdem edoceantur. Nam ut Solomon ait, sapientiae reconditae & thesauri abstrusi nulla est utilitas: cui Satyricum illud consentit: Scire tuum nihil est, nisi te scire hoc sciat alter. Ideo doctrinam quoque subijcit Paulus, quae singula ista auditoribus applicat pro locorum & temporum ratione, ut singulorum institutioni, vitae denique & morum emendationi serviant. Et haec illa pars est, in qua Ecclesiae & singulorum eius membrorum aedificatio potissimum consistit. In istis ergo ministri omnes sese exerceant: nam sine his nihil proficient, imo ab illis requiretur sanguis eorum qui in suis sive sceleribus sive superstitionibus pereunt.
units.tr: You will observe moreover in this passage what parts the apostle assigns to the preaching of the gospel, or how he defines its order and its end. "Unless," he says, "I speak to you by revelation, or by knowledge, or by prophecy, or by teaching." Ambrose thinks all these are one and the same thing, but the apostle does not distinguish between them without reason, so that at the same time he might admonish about the order in which a minister ought to proceed in teaching, so as to reach that end which God himself has set before ecclesiastical ministry. Above all, revelation is necessary. For how will one who is not enlightened from above teach others from himself? Such a one can know neither God the Father nor the Son. "No one knows," says Christ, "who the Son is, except the Father, and who the Father is, except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him." And to Peter, who had openly confessed him, he said: "Flesh and blood have not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven." Therefore of old the prophets were commanded to seek the Word from the mouth of the Lord, and the Spirit of truth was given to the apostles, to suggest to them what they were to set before the people. Here, then, we are commended to prayer, by which we seek not only a general knowledge of the Word of God, but also what is needed in any place and time, in deed and word. Knowledge follows revelation, which you would rightly call its effect. And this too is no less necessary. For what will one say who knows nothing and understands nothing? Therefore Christ said to the apostles: "Make disciples of all nations, teaching them to observe what I have delivered to you." Here the study of Holy Scripture is required, because through it God speaks to us; and so Paul seriously urges his Timothy, whom he knew to have been trained in the sacred letters from boyhood, to apply himself diligently to reading. Third in place is prophecy, which is the right and proper interpretation of the Scriptures, through which the will of God is drawn out and revealed, and the outcome of future events is also plainly foretold, so that counsel about things to be done may also be sought from them. But none of all these has any use unless others are taught about the same things. For, as Solomon says, there is no benefit in hidden wisdom and buried treasure; to this the satirist's saying agrees: "To know something is nothing, unless another knows that you know it." Therefore Paul also adds teaching, which applies each of these things to the hearers according to the circumstances of places and times, so that they serve the instruction of individuals, and finally the amendment of life and morals. And this is the part in which the building up of the Church and of each of its members chiefly consists. In these, then, let all ministers exercise themselves: for without them they will accomplish nothing; indeed, the blood of those who perish in their sins or in their superstitions will be required of them.

units.la: Quod autem proprio exemplo docuit Paulus, id per simile illustrat, quod ab instrumentis Musicis est desumptum. Dicit enim: Atqui inanima, quae sonum edunt, id est, quae humano artificio sic fiunt, ut vel inflata vel tacta sonent, utpote tibia aut cithara, aut quodcunq; aliud huius generis, nisi distinctionem tonis dederint, quomodo cognoscetur quod tibia canitur aut cithara? id est, quis intelliget, quid sonus iste velit? Et ut de tuba loquar, cuius multiplex usus est, dum ea vel signum praelij ineundi datur, vel receptui canitur, vel coetus publici convocantur, quis obris occini consueuit? Ita & vos nisi bene significantem sermonem addideritis[?], quomodo intelligetur quod dicitur? Certe eritis in aerem loquentes, id est, frustra & absque omni fructu loquemini, ut qui vestris orationibus non in auditorum animos penetrabitis, sed aerem solum inutili verborum a nemine intellectorum strepitu feritis. Subest autem huic similitudini argumentum comparationis, siue a minori ad maius: Si in Musicis instrumentis hoc requiritur, ut quamuis vocem non edant articulatam, distinctam tamen edant, ut cuius argumenti fit tantus ille intelligatur? quanto magis in Ecclesia Dei hoc observari debet, ut omnes quid illic dicatur & agatur intelligant? Hic enim caelestis illa & divina Musica exercetur, de qua vere dici potest, quod de Orpheo & Amphione olim poeta fabulati sunt: quod scilicet feras cantu suo cicurauerint, quod fluminum cursus inhibuerint, saxa traxerint & arborum truncos. Namper Dei Verbum, si diu ignè[?] tractetur, belluini animorum motus & minas aestuantia corda placantur, ruentes in vindictam animi cohibentur, & in misericordiam mutuam & concordiam trahuntur, qui prius lapidibus duriores & truncis stupidiores videri poterant. Adde huic argumento alterum quoque: Si homo tibijs, cithara, lyra, tubae & similibus instrumentis vocem certam magno studio & labore affingit, qua toni eorum dignosci possint: quam absurdum & ridiculum fuerit, si homines vocibus incertis & ignotis linguis confusum quid sonent, quod a nemine intelligatur? Item: si inanima ista sonum edunt, quem auditores intelligunt, quis non graui reprehensione dignos iudicet homines, qui cum anima immortali & rationali a Deo donati sint, ita tamen loqui gaudent, ut quid nam dicant ignoretur?
units.tr: What Paul taught by his own example, he illustrates by a comparison drawn from musical instruments. He says: "Yet lifeless things that give sound, that is, things made by human skill so that they sound when blown or struck, such as the pipe or the lyre or anything else of this kind, unless they give a distinction of tones, how will it be known what is piped or played on the lyre? That is, who will understand what the sound means? And to speak of the trumpet, which has many uses, when it is sounded as the signal to join battle, or to sound the retreat, or when public assemblies are called, who does not know what it is being sounded for? So you too, unless you add speech that signifies well, how will what you say be understood? Surely you will be speaking into the air, that is, you will speak in vain and without any fruit, since you will not penetrate your hearers' minds with your words, but will only strike the air with a useless noise of words that no one understands." The comparison also carries an argument from the lesser to the greater. If, in musical instruments, this is required, that although they do not produce articulate voice they nevertheless produce a distinct one, so that the tune they play is understood, how much more must this be observed in the Church of God, that everyone understands what is said and done there? For there that heavenly and divine music is practised, of which one may truly say what the poets once fabled of Orpheus and Amphion: that they tamed wild beasts with their song, checked the courses of rivers, and moved rocks and tree trunks. Indeed, if the Word of God is handled for long, the savage stirrings and threats of minds are calmed, and hearts that seemed harder than stones and more stupid than tree trunks are drawn to mutual mercy and concord, while minds rushing toward vengeance are restrained. Add to this argument another: if a man, with great study and labour, gives a fixed voice to pipes, lyre, harp, trumpets and similar instruments so that their tones can be distinguished, how absurd and ridiculous it would be if men, with uncertain voices and in unknown tongues, sounded something confused that no one understands! Likewise: if these lifeless things give a sound that hearers understand, who would not judge worthy of grave rebuke men who, endowed by God with an immortal and rational soul, nevertheless delight to speak in such a way that no one knows what they are saying?

units.la: Non temere autem hoc simili Paulum usum esse putabimus. Probe enim & eleganter ecclesiastici ministerij usum & ministrorum officium adumbrat. Tibia multos & varios canendi modos admittit, variis itemque chordis cithara aut lyra constat. Ita non unus est praedicandi Verbi Dei modus, sed in una saepe concione mirifica cum harmonia concurrunt doctrina, admonitiones, hortationes, increpationes, comminationes & consolationes. Deinde ut non satis est temere inflauisse tubam aut tibiam, vel incerto tactu digitorum citharae chordas percurrisse, sed illas distincte inflare, has autem certo ordine tangi oportet: Ita non dum officio suo defuncti sunt, qui Dei Verbum utcunque praedicant, aut ex Scripturis detonant quicquid illis in buccam venit: sed cordate & prudenter ea afferre oportet quibus maxime opus est, quaeq; loco praesenti & tempore depromat.
units.tr: We shall not think that Paul used this comparison rashly. For it admirably and elegantly sketches the use of the ecclesiastical ministry and the office of ministers. The pipe admits many and various modes of playing, and the lyre or harp consists of various strings. So there is not one mode of preaching the Word of God; in a single sermon there often concur, in wonderful harmony, teaching, admonitions, exhortations, rebukes, warnings and consolations. Next, as it is not enough to blow the trumpet or pipe carelessly, or to run over the strings of the lyre with an uncertain touch of the fingers, but the former must be blown distinctly and the latter touched in a fixed order, so those who in any way preach the Word of God, or sing out from Scripture whatever comes into their mouth, have not yet discharged their office. They ought rather to bring forward, thoughtfully and wisely, those things that are most needed and that suit the present place and time.

units.la: Imprimis tamen huc pertinet tubae similitudo. Huius usum praecipuum in militia esse constat. Atqui militia est vita hominis super terram, eo quod hostem habemus communem, quo nemo crudelior, nemo improbior, nemo magis inquietus aut melius instructus fingi potest. Est Satan, qui & primos parentes in exitium adduxit, & nunquam non rugientis leonis instar oberrans quaerit quem devoret. Habet is a partibus suis mundum hunc, per quem modo illecebritas atq; astutia, ipsis quoq; cordibus nostris sese insinuat, ut nostrae carnis affectibus, imo nostra ratione & intellectu, in nobis oppugnandis utatur. Quamuis autem hic tota salus nostra periclitatur, multi tamen securi nimis dormiunt, multi metu superati aut voluptatum illecebris ducti turpiter deserunt, multi animo plus quam proditorio cum hoste pacificuntur, & non con-tum[?] quo ne inducias quidem vnius horae Christiano homini habere licet. Hic ergo speculatores & tubicines suos Deus constituit, qui securos & dormientes excitent, qui oscitantes de periculo admoneant, qui de statione deserenda cogitantibus prælij ineundi signum dent, qui cum hoste col-ludentes aut pacisentes arguant, & ubiq; insistent, ne improbus ille hostis de Christi Ecclesia tri-umphare possit. Tubicines illi precones Verbi sunt, quibus apud Prophetam dicitur: Clama ex gutture, ne parcas, exalta instar tubæ vocem tuam, & annuntia populo meo præuaricationem suam. Item: Ad palatum tuum adhibe buccinam. Ab omnibus ergo istis hoc requiritur, ut clarè & distinctè prædicent, & quod res est dicant, ne quis ipsorum negligentia aut perfidia pereat. Huc pertinent, quæ prolixè traduntur. Ezech.3. & 33. Cap.
units.tr: Above all, however, the comparison of the trumpet applies here. It is well known that its chief use is in war. Now the life of man upon earth is a warfare, since we have a common enemy, than whom none can be imagined more cruel, more wicked, more restless or better equipped. He is Satan, who led our first parents to ruin and who, like a roaring lion, ever prowls about seeking whom he may devour. He has this world as his ally, through which he insinuates himself by enticement and cunning even into our very hearts, so that he may use the passions of our flesh, indeed our reason and understanding, to assail us. Although our whole salvation is imperilled here, many sleep far too securely; many, overcome by fear or led on by the allurements of pleasure, shamefully desert their post; many make peace with the enemy in a spirit more than treacherous, and do not take up arms against him, though a Christian may not even have a truce for a single hour. Here, therefore, God has appointed his watchmen and trumpeters, who rouse the secure and sleeping, who warn the drowsy of danger, who give the signal for battle to those thinking of abandoning their post, who rebuke those who collude with or make peace with the enemy, and who stand firm everywhere so that that wicked enemy may not triumph over the Church of Christ. Those trumpeters are the heralds of the Word, of whom the Prophet says: "Cry aloud from the throat, do not spare; lift up your voice like a trumpet, and declare to my people their transgression." Also: "Set the trumpet to your mouth." All of them, therefore, are required to preach clearly and distinctly, and to say what the matter is, lest anyone perish through their negligence or treachery. To this pertain the things related at length in Ezek. 3 and 33 chap.

units.la: Possumus autem totum hunc locum non absq; certa ratione contra eos proferre, qui in Papatu cantum peregrinum in Ecclesiam inuexerunt, & imprimis quidem contra vsum organorum in templis. Pauli enim argumentum in eo consistit, quòd Musicæ ignotæ & non intellectæ nullus vsus sit. Quod communi omnium consensu ita receptum est, vt in proverbium abierit, quo dicimus, Occultâ Musices nullum esse respectum. Cui Ouidianum illud consentit: Tu licet & Thamyram superes atque Orphea cantu, Non erit ignota gratia magna Lyrae.
units.tr: We may use this whole passage, not without sound reason, against those who in the Papacy brought foreign chant into the Church, and especially against the use of organs in churches. Paul's argument rests on this, that music which is unknown and not understood is of no use. This is so generally accepted by universal consent that it has passed into a proverb, by which we say: "Hidden music has no regard." To this the line of Ovid agrees: "Even if you surpass Thamyras and Orpheus in song, the great charm of the lyre will not go unknown."

units.la: Atqui à Musicâ ignota siue occulta nihil differt cantus qualiscunq;, qui non intelligitur. Quis vero alius est totus ille, qui in Papatu auditur? Est equidem mos canendi in Ecclesia vetustissimus, apud Orientales imprimis. Et Plinius Secundus, cum ad Traianum Imperatorem scriberet de Christianis, hoc inter alia eis tribuit, quòd Christo Deo suo antelucanos hymnos canant. Sed cantus ille primum lingua vulgari fiebat, deinde voce modicum modò deflexa, vt à simplici verborum recitatione non multum differret: cuius rei mentionem facit luculentam D. Augustinus, qui D. Athanasium Alexandriæ episcopum hoc nomine commendat. Et D. Hieronymus in Commentarijs in epistolam Pauli ad Ephesios, Musicam illam artificialem aperte damnat, vt quæ theatris potius quàm Ecclesiæ conueniat, vbi Regni cœlorum mysteria tractantur. Eius verba sunt: Canere & psallere & laudare Dominum magis animo quàm voce debemus. Hoc est quippe quod dicitur: Cantantes & psallentes in cordibus vestris Domino. Audiant hæc adolescentuli: audiant hæc quibus Psallendi in Ecclesia officium est, Deo non voce, sed corde cantandum: nec in Tragædorum modum guttur & fauces dulci medicamine colliniendas, vt in Ecclesia theatrales moduli audiantur & cantica, &c. Quæ verba Pontifices inter decretorum suorum Canones referri debere censuerunt: à quibus non multum abludunt, quæ ijdem ex Gregorio suo Magno adducunt: qui non obscurè fatetur, non raro fieri, vt cantor minister Deum moribus corruptus mulet aut irritet, dum populum voce blanda delectat. At hodie in Papatu non linguis modò peregrinis canitur, verumetiā voces tanto artificio miscentur, vt ne cantores quidem ipsi verba numeris suis semper applicare possint. Neq; hoc satis visum fuit, nisi organa quoq; inueheret, vere & proprie sic dicta, quando in vno opere organico omnia fere instrumenta Musica habentur, quæ vocibus infinitis & harmonia admirabili simul perstrepunt. Id verò inuentum esse non adeo vetustum, ex historijs apparet. Nam vt Marianus Scotus annotauit, sub annū Domini DCCLVI. organa eiusmodi, prius in Occidente nunquam visa Constantinus, cognomento Copronimus, Pipino misit, quando Romana etiam Ecclesiæ ritus & ceremoniæ primùm in Franciam translatæ & suscepta sunt. Illorum verò concentum artificiosum quotus quisq; ex sacrificiorum numero intelligit, vt nunc de rudi vulgo nihil dicam? Obijciunt illi nobis Davidis exemplum, & illa ex Psalmis adducunt: Laudate Deum clangore tubæ, laudate eum nablo & cithara: Laudate eum tympano & tibia, laudate eum in choris & organo: laudate eum in cymbalis bene sonantibus, &c. Sed nos simpliciter respondemus, non decere vt ceremoniæ Veteris Testamenti in nouum transferantur, cum nullum eius rei exemplum Apostoli nobis præbuerint, & vetus Ecclesia ceremonijs simplicissimis contenta non alium quoq; cantum habuerit, quàm qui pronuntiationi similior fuit quàm cantioni. Verumtamen quoad cantum ecclesiasticum, scimus D. Augustinum olim dubium hæsisse, an vtilius sit eum in Ecclesia retineri, aut inde eijci: quando constat, pios quidem illo vehementer affici, & sæpe ex eo nouam fidei alacritatem concipere: alios autem, qui mundi voluptatibus addicti sunt, non aliud quærere, quàm vt aures inani oblectatione demulceant. Potest tamen non inutiliter ferri meo iudicio, modò locorum & gentis cuiusq; diligens ratio habeatur, tria hæc obseruentur. Primum, ut non fit immodicus, neue canendo absumatur tempus quod Ver-bi prædicationi debebat impendi. Alterum, ut lingua vulgari canatur, quam omnes intelligant. Po-stremum, ut numeri sint simplicissimi, qui nec verba atq; sententias artificiosa nimium vocum volubilitate obscurent, neq; animi attentionem remorentur, aut hunc alio abripiant.
units.tr: But a song that is not understood differs in nothing from unknown or hidden music, whatever kind it is. And what else is all that chanting which is heard in the Papacy? There is indeed a most ancient custom of singing in the Church, especially among the Easterners. And Pliny the Younger, when writing to the Emperor Trajan about the Christians, ascribed to them, among other things, that they sang hymns before dawn to Christ their God. But that chant was at first done in the vernacular tongue, and then with the voice only slightly inflected, so that it did not differ much from the plain recitation of words. St Augustine makes a clear mention of this, and on this account he commends St Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria. And St Jerome, in his Commentaries on Paul's Epistle to the Ephesians, openly condemns that artificial music as fitting theatres rather than the Church, where the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven are handled. His words are: "We ought to sing and psalm and praise the Lord more with the mind than with the voice. This is indeed what is said: singing and psalming in your hearts to the Lord." Let young men hear this; let those whose duty it is to psalm in the Church hear this: God is to be sung to with the heart, not the voice; nor should the throat and jaws be smeared with sweet ointment in the manner of tragic actors, so that theatrical tunes and songs are heard in the Church, and so on. The Pontiffs thought these words should be included among the canons of their decrees, and what they cite from their Gregory the Great does not differ much from them. He openly admits that it often happens that a singing minister, corrupt in his morals, provokes or angers God while delighting the people with a seductive voice. But today in the Papacy not only is it sung in foreign tongues, but the voices are mixed with such artifice that the singers themselves cannot always fit the words to their notes. Nor did this seem enough unless they also brought in organs, truly and properly so called, since in one organ work almost all musical instruments are contained, which together resound with endless voices and admirable harmony. That this invention is not very ancient appears from the histories. For, as Marianus Scotus noted, in the year of the Lord 756 Constantine, surnamed Copronymus, sent such organs, never before seen in the West, to Pepin, when the rites and ceremonies of the Roman Church were first carried over into France and received there. But how many of the sacrificing class understand their artificial harmony, not to mention the untutored common people? They object to us the example of David and adduce those passages from the Psalms: "Praise God with the sound of the trumpet; praise him with psaltery and harp; praise him with timbrel and pipe; praise him with strings and organs; praise him with well-sounding cymbals," and so on. But we simply answer that it is not fitting for the ceremonies of the Old Testament to be transferred into the New, since the Apostles have given us no example of this, and the ancient Church, content with the simplest ceremonies, had no other chant than one more like recitation than singing. Nevertheless, as regards ecclesiastical chant, we know that St Augustine once hesitated whether it was more useful to retain it in the Church or to cast it out, since it is clear that the pious are strongly moved by it and often conceive from it a fresh eagerness of faith, while others, given over to worldly pleasures, seek nothing but to soothe their ears with empty delight. Yet in my judgement it may be borne without harm, provided that the circumstances of each place and people are carefully considered and these three things are observed. First, that it not be excessive, nor consume the time that ought to be given to preaching the Word. Second, that it be sung in the vernacular, which all understand. Last, that the tunes be most simple, so that they do not obscure words and sentences by an overly artificial fluency of voices, nor delay the attention of the mind or draw it elsewhere.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui tertio loco communem omnium vocum rationem adducit, inquiens: Tot, prout inciderit, genera vocum sunt in mundo, & nihil est mutum. Id est, Natura sic est comparatum, ut & gentes singulæ suam habeant linguam peculiarem, & animalia singula vo-cem edant, qua dignoscuntur, imò inanimatis quoq; (ut modò diximus) voces affingi solent cer-ta, distincta & quæ à quouis intelligi possunt: denique nihil in tota fere rerum natura mutum est; quod scilicet non intelligatur. Hus[?] infert: Nisi igitur sciero vim vocis, ero ei qui loquitur barba-rus, & qui loquitur, apud me barbarus fuerit: Ita & vos. Quibus verbis hoc omnino dicere videtur: Quàm ergo absurdum & indignum fuerit, homines Christianos, qui eiusdem gentis sunt & si-mul agunt, non habere inter se linguam, quæ ab omnibus percipi & intelligi possit? Quæ enim gens ita desipit, ut ius sibi dici velit lingua peregrina? Quæ igitur dementia est, in Ecclesia iura & le-ges Dei, ex quibus vniuersa salus humani generis depender, linguis ignotis proferri? Sed & animalia bruta ex suis vocibus dignoscuntur, dum boues mugiunt, leones rugiunt, canes latrant, lupi vlulant, ursi[?] uncánt, pantheres cauriunt, lynces orcant, apri frendunt, cerui glocitant, equi hinni-unt, asini rudunt, oues balant. sues grunniunt, vulpes ganniunt, mures mintrant[?], serpentes sibilar[?], ranæ coaxant, & inter aues quoq; suis singulæ vocibus vtuntur. Cur ergo sic loquatur homo, ut quis sit, aut quid sibi velit, nemo intelligat? Cæterum sic ista pronuntiat Paulus, ut simul acriter pungat Corinthiorum stultitiam, qui dum inani linguarum ostentatione laudem & gloriam vena-bantur, sibi ipsis infamiam atter·sebant[?]. Nam addit: Nisi sciero vim vocis, ero ei qui loquitur bar-barus, & qui loquitur apud me barbarus fuerit. Ita & vos, scilicet barbari vobis inuicem eritis, si quæ dicuntur ignoret's. Ita loci huic olim aliquot distinxisse, Theophylactus testatur, & ipse con-textus distinctionem hanc requirit, si attentius ista cum iis quæ sequuntur, conferamus.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who in the third place brings forward the common nature of all voices, saying: "There are so many kinds of voices in the world, as it happens, and none is without meaning." That is to say, nature has so ordered things that each nation has its own peculiar language, and each animal utters a voice by which it is recognised; indeed, even to inanimate things (as we have just said) certain voices, distinct and such as anyone can understand, are commonly attributed. In short, almost nothing in the whole of nature is mute, that is, unintelligible. He then concludes: "If therefore I do not know the meaning of the voice, I shall be a barbarian to the one who speaks, and the one who speaks will be a barbarian to me. So also you." By these words he seems to say plainly: How absurd and unworthy it would be for Christian men, who belong to the same people and act together, not to have among themselves a language that all can perceive and understand! For what nation is so foolish as to want law pronounced to it in a foreign tongue? What madness, then, is it to utter in the Church in unknown tongues the laws and commands of God, on which the whole salvation of the human race depends? Yet even brute animals are known by their voices: oxen low, lions roar, dogs bark, wolves howl, bears growl, panthers snarl, lynxes purr, boars grunt, stags bellow, horses neigh, asses bray, sheep bleat, pigs grunt, foxes yelp, mice squeak, serpents hiss, frogs croak, and among birds too each kind uses its own cries. Why then should a man speak in such a way that no one understands who he is or what he wants? Paul, moreover, delivers these words so as to sting sharply the folly of the Corinthians, who, while they hunted after praise and glory through a vain display of tongues, were bringing infamy upon themselves. For he adds: "If I do not know the meaning of the voice, I shall be a barbarian to the one who speaks, and the one who speaks will be a barbarian to me. So also you," that is, you will be barbarians to one another, if you do not know what is said. Theophylact testifies that some of the ancients divided the passage in this way, and the context itself requires this division if we compare these words more carefully with what follows.

units.la: Cæterum ut Strabo Geographiæ suæ libro 14. de Caribus scribens testatur, barbari olim di-cebantur sillo[?] vocabulo ad soni imitationem, qui verba Græca duriter & difficulter pronuntia-bant: quod fere peregrinis omnibus solet accidere. Quia autem Græci propter bonarum artium stu-dia & eloquentiam soli sibi videbantur diserti esse & ornatè dicere, & reliquas gentes pre se con-temnebant, easdem simul omnes per ignominiam barbaras vocabant. Quod ipsum postea Romani quoq; fecerunt, quando rerum domini facti imperium suum per totum fere orbem terrarum longè lateq; extenderunt. Tunc enim barbari à Latinis quoq; dici cœperunt, quotquot illud non agnosce-bant. Pulchrè autem & in loco Paulus Corinthiorum sciolos de isto admonet. Quasi diceret: Videte quaso diligentius, quàm egregiam laudem ex vestra hac linguarum ostentatione referatis. An-non vos Græci ignominioso vocabulo soletis barbaros dicere peregrinos omnes, qui aut male pronuntiant Græca verba, aut eadem omnino non intelligunt? Quæ igitur stultitia est, vosipsos ex disertis Græcis barbaros facere, adeò ut non exteris, sed vestris hominibus tales esse merito vi-deamini? Si enim vobis barbarus est, qui lingua ignota loquitur, eadem omnino ratione vos quoq; barbari eritis, dum lingua vtimini, quam vestra gentis homines non intelligunt. Nam quæ tunc quoad sermonis vsum, inter vos & peregrinos est differentia? Aut quid respondebitis, si quis vos vocum naturam & vsum inuertere dicat? Has etenim ideo inuentas & datas esse vestri quo-que philosophi tradiderunt, ut affectionum in animo latentium signa sint, quibus illæ exprimantur. Quis ergo vos loqui aut sermone vti dixerit, si à nemine intelligamini? Fuit argumentum hoc haud dubiè efficacissimum apud eos, qui summam laudem in multiplici rerum disciplina & elo-quentia collocabat. Solet autem hoc ipsum omnibus iis accidere, qui peregrinitatem in sermone aut pronuntiatione, in vestitu, in moribus deniq; affectant. Faciunt id fere nostro seculo, qui generis no-bilitate & vetustate gloriantur, & in sua gente aborigines haberi volunt. At cùm ijdem neq; patrio vestitu induantur, neq; recepta apud suos pronuntiatione vtantur, adhæc mores peregrinos & plerunq; non satis laudatos inuehere studeant, quis obsecro pro talibus agnoscat, quales videri vo-lunt? quis eos non dixerit odio & contemptu dignos esse?
units.tr: Moreover, as Strabo writes in book 14 of his Geography concerning the Carians, the word "barbarians" was once used, by an imitation of sound, of those who pronounced Greek words harshly and with difficulty, as nearly all foreigners are wont to do. But because the Greeks, on account of their devotion to the liberal arts and their eloquence, alone seemed to themselves to speak learnedly and elegantly, and despised the other nations in comparison with themselves, they called all of them together barbarians by way of reproach. The Romans afterwards did the same thing too, when, having become masters of the world, they extended their empire far and wide over almost the whole earth. For then the Latins too began to call barbarians all who did not know their language. Paul rightly and fittingly warns the smatterers of Corinth about this. As if he said: Please consider more carefully what outstanding praise you win from this display of tongues. Do not you Greeks habitually use the disgraceful word "barbarians" of all foreigners who either pronounce Greek words badly or do not understand them at all? What folly, then, is it to make yourselves barbarians out of learned Greeks, so that you seem rightly to be such not to foreigners but to your own people? For if he is a barbarian to you who speaks an unknown language, then by exactly the same reasoning you too will be barbarians while you use a language which the men of your own people do not understand. For what difference, then, in the use of speech is there between you and foreigners? Or what will you answer if someone says that you invert the nature and use of voices? For your own philosophers too have taught that voices were invented and given for this very purpose, that they should be signs of the feelings hidden in the mind, by which those feelings are expressed. Who, then, would say that you speak or use speech if no one understands you? This argument was undoubtedly most effective among those who placed the highest praise in a manifold learning and eloquence. Yet this same thing happens to all who affect foreignness in speech or pronunciation, in dress, and finally in manners. Those who in our own age glory in the nobility and antiquity of their stock, and wish to be regarded as the native-born of their nation, do much the same. But when these same people neither clothe themselves in the native dress, nor use the pronunciation received among their own people, and moreover take pains to import foreign customs, usually not very praiseworthy, who, I ask, would acknowledge them as the sort of people they wish to appear? Who would not say that they are worthy of hatred and contempt?

units.la: Quoad vero huius loci argumentum, non obscure colligi poterit, nihil ab Ecclesia Christiana magis alienum esse, quam vsum linguae peregrinae & incognitae. Ecclesia enim (vt alibi dictum est) corpori confertur, in quo membra omnia inter se communionem habent eiusdem spiritus, eiusdem naturae, simul & fortunae. Ita enim in Ecclesia quoq; pij omnes de eodem spiritu, eadem doctrina & iisdem Sacramentis communicant, imò eiusdem vitae & salutis cohaeredes sunt. Vt, in externis aut prophanis hominum commercijs vinculum communionis sermo est: ita illic quoq; per Euangelij praedicationem omnes gentes ad societatem hanc spiritualem vocantur, vt cum electis Dei omnia Regni coelestis bona communia habeant: & ijdem simul omnes vno corde in vnum Christum credunt, vno spiritu eundem colunt, & ore vno confitentur. Quo Isaias respiciens olim Aegyptios quoque lingua Chananaea, id est lingua populi Dei locuturos praedicebat, vbi ad Christum effent conuersi. Quotquot ergo lingua peregrina docent, aut in Sacramentorum administratione sermone ignoto vtuntur, nonne communionis Christianae vinculum, quantum in ipsis est, abrumpunt? non ne seipsos ex Christi ciuibus barbaros faciunt? aut saltem alios pro barbaris habent, à quibus ipsi nolunt intelligi? Desinant ergo nobis litem mouere Romanenses Episcopi, quod ab eorum Ecclesia defecerimus. Ipsi enim dum in templis Latinè loquuntur, Latinè canunt, Latinè Missant, Latinè baptizant, Latinè denique sacra omnia administrant, omnium nationum homines barbarorum loco habent, qui indigni sint quibus cum sacrorum commercium habeant. De L. Philippo Consule in Romana historia scribitur, eum aliquando arrogantius dixisse, sibi Senatu alio opus esse. Cùm verò dictum hoc indignius ferret L. Crassus, eidem mox ille manum iniecit iussit. At Crassus reiecto litore, Non es mihi (inquit) Philippe Consul, quia nec ego tibi Senator sum. Laudata fuit & hodie adhuc laudem meretur libertas ista, qua vir grauissimus ad tuendam Senatorij ordinis & Reipub. dignitatem vsus est. Cur ergo nobis non liceat Romanensibus illis & horum Creaturis dicere: Non estis nobis Pontifices aut Episcopi, quia nos vobis non sumus Christiani? Aut cur vos pro pastoribus agnoscerémus, qui nos ouium loco non habetis? Vel num do-ctores[?] nostros putabimus eos, qui à nobis non volunt intelligi? Ferunt quidem illi indignissimè hanc nostram libertatem, vt qui regno male vsurpato nimis diu assueuerunt. At pijs non minus graue est, si linguis ignotis obtundantur, si Verbo Dei spolientur, aut id sepeliri, vel quacunq; ratione obscurari sentiant. Neminem ergo istorum clamores moueant, meminerimus potius nos oues IESV CHRISTI esse, & proinde huius vocem sequamur, qui pastor non minus fortis & potens quàm bonus est, qui q; nos ex manibus suis eripi nunquam patietur. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: As for the argument of this passage, it may be readily gathered that nothing is more foreign to the Christian Church than the use of a foreign and unknown language. For the Church (as has been said elsewhere) is compared to a body, in which all the members have fellowship with one another in the same Spirit, the same nature and the same fortune. For in the Church too all the godly share the same Spirit, the same doctrine and the same Sacraments, and indeed are fellow heirs of the same life and salvation. Just as in the external or profane dealings of men speech is the bond of fellowship, so there too through the preaching of the Gospel all nations are called to this spiritual society, so that with the elect of God they may hold all the goods of the heavenly kingdom in common; and all of them together, with one heart, believe in the one Christ, worship him with one Spirit, and confess with one mouth. Looking to this, Isaiah long ago foretold that the Egyptians too would speak the Canaanite tongue, that is, the language of the people of God, when they were converted to Christ. Whoever therefore teaches in a foreign tongue, or uses an unknown language in the administration of the Sacraments, does he not, so far as lies in him, break the bond of Christian communion? Does he not make himself a barbarian among the citizens of Christ? Or at least does he not regard as barbarians those by whom he does not wish to be understood? Let the Roman bishops therefore cease to press their charge against us, that we have departed from their Church. For while they speak Latin in their temples, sing Latin, say Mass in Latin, baptise in Latin, and in short administer all sacred rites in Latin, they hold the men of all nations as barbarians, unworthy to have fellowship with them in holy things. It is written in Roman history that the consul Lucius Philippus once spoke rather arrogantly, saying that he had no need of the Senate. When Lucius Crassus took this remark more indignantly, Philippus soon ordered him to be seized by the hand. But Crassus, shaking off the hand, said: "You are not my consul, Philippus, since I am not your senator." That freedom, by which a most dignified man defended the dignity of the senatorial order and of the commonwealth, has been praised, and still today deserves praise. Why then should it not be lawful for us to say to those Romanists and their creatures: You are not our pontiffs or bishops, since we are not your Christians? Or why should we acknowledge you as pastors, when you do not count us as your sheep? Or shall we think of those as our teachers who do not wish to be understood by us? Those men indeed take this freedom of ours very ill, as men who have too long been accustomed to a kingdom wrongly seized. But it is no less grievous to the godly to be stunned with unknown tongues, to be deprived of the Word of God, or to feel that it is buried or obscured in any way. Let no one be moved, then, by the outcries of these men; let us rather remember that we are the sheep of Jesus Christ, and therefore let us follow the voice of him who is as strong and powerful a shepherd as he is good, and who will never suffer us to be snatched out of his hands. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXII.
units.tr: HOMILY LXXII.

units.la: Quandoquidem spiritus ambitis, ad aedificationem Ecclesiae quaerite ut excellatis. Quapropter qui loquitur lingua, precetur ut interpretetur. Nam si precer lingua, spiritus meus precatur, sed mens mea est infructuosa. Quid est igitur? Precabor spiritu, sed precabor etiam mente: psallam spiritu, sed psallam etiam mente. Quandoquidem si benedixeris spiritu, is qui implet locum idiotae, quomodo dicturus est Amen ad tuam gratiarum actionem? siquidem quid dicas nescit. Nam tu quidem bene gratias agis, sed alius non aedificatur. Gratias ago Deo meo, quod magis quam vos omnes linguis loquar: Sed in Ecclesia malim quinq; verba mente mea loqui, vt & alios instituam, quam decem millia verborum lingua.
units.tr: Since you are eager for spiritual gifts, seek to excel in those that build up the Church. Therefore let whoever speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret. For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful. What then? I will pray with the spirit, but I will pray with the mind also; I will sing with the spirit, but I will sing with the mind also. For if you bless with the spirit, how will the one who fills the place of the untrained say Amen to your thanksgiving, since he does not know what you are saying? For you indeed give thanks well, but the other person is not built up. I thank my God that I speak in tongues more than you all; but in the Church I would rather speak five words with my mind, so that I may also teach others, than ten thousand words in a tongue.

units.la: PAulus aduersus ambitiosam peregrinarum linguarum ostentationem, qua pleriq; Corinthio-rum vehementer peccabant, sic agit, vt illas quidem non damnet, sed suum eis inter χαρίσματα seu gratuita Spiritus sancti dona locum relinquat, monet autem eas ideo dari, vt Scripturarum interpretationi & doctrinae seruiant: vnde colligit, hoc potius spectari[?] debere, vt illis per prophetiam ad publicam Ecclesiæ ædificationem utantur. Et hactenus quidem similibus & exemplis docuit, linguas omnino inutiles esse, nisi ad illum finem & scopum dirigantur. Istis verò locum hunc, quem modò recitauimus, subjicit, quo hoc ipsum multis explicat, & apertius quid fieri debeat docet.
units.tr: Paul, against the ambitious display of foreign tongues, in which many of the Corinthians sinned greatly, proceeds in such a way that he does not condemn the tongues, but leaves them their place among the charismata [χαρίσματα], that is, the free gifts of the Holy Spirit. He warns, however, that they are given so that they may serve the interpretation of the Scriptures and teaching. From this he concludes that the chief concern should be that they be used through prophecy for the public building up of the Church. Up to this point he has taught, by similar examples and illustrations, that tongues are altogether useless unless they are directed to that end and aim. He then adds the passage we have just recited, in which he explains this very point at length and teaches more plainly what ought to be done.

units.la: Principiò ex iis, quæ proximè præcesserunt, infert denuò statum huius tractationis. Quando-quidem spiritus ambitis, ad ædificationem Ecclesiæ quærite ut excellatis. Spiritus dicit ipsa dona Spiritus sancti, & imprimis quidem linguas, de quibus in præsenti agitur, & quarū cognitionem, seu potius ostentationem, illi ambitiosius affectabant. Habent autem verbà hæc grauem admoni-tionem, quam sub specie Concessionis acriorem facit, quasi diceret: Non æquidem obsto, quo minus quævis charismata sive dona Spiritus ambiatis: imò ab initio illa magno studio & zelo sancto quærere iussi. Sed hic velim vos in eum finem respicere, qui omnibus in Ecclesia Christi servienti-bus propositus esse debet. Est ea ædificatio Ecclesiæ tam totius quàm singulorum, qui in ea agunt: & in eum quoq; finem Deus dona sua largitur, non ut nostræ ostentationi aut gloriæ priuatæ ser-viant. Quapropter si omnino excellere libet, aut multis aliis præstare, hoc agite, ut ad ædificatio-nem excellatis. Ut enim in Regni administratione aliis præstantior est, qui illius fines legitimè propagat: & ut in Scholis merito is præfertur, qui sua industria plures reddit doctiores: Ita in Ecclesia vere excellunt, qui quàm plurimos adducunt ad illius societatem, & iam ante adductos in agnita veritate confirmat. Hic verborum Apostoli sensus est: ideoq; non suadet eis ambitiosam supra alios eminendi cupiditatem: sed præposterum illorum studium corrigit, ut intelligant, quàm procul adhuc absint ab ea gloria, quàm vanabantur: cùm hactenus sua potius gloria, quàm alio-rum ædificationi & publicæ multorum saluti studuerint.
units.tr: First, from what has just gone before, he again draws out the subject of this discussion: Since you are eager for spiritual gifts, seek to excel in those that build up the Church. By spiritual gifts he means the gifts of the Holy Spirit themselves, and above all the tongues, which are the subject here, and whose knowledge, or rather whose display, they were pursuing too eagerly. These words carry a serious warning, which under the guise of a concession he makes sharper, as if he said: "I do not object to your eagerness for any charismata or gifts of the Spirit; indeed, from the beginning I bade you seek them with great zeal and holy ardour. But here I would have you look to the end that ought to be set before all who serve Christ in the Church. The building up of the Church, both of the whole and of the individuals who act in it, is that end, and God bestows his gifts for this end too, not so that they may serve our display or private glory. Therefore, if you wish to excel altogether, or to surpass many others, do this: excel in building up." For just as in the administration of a kingdom he is the more outstanding who lawfully extends its boundaries, and just as in schools he is rightly preferred who by his diligence makes more men learned, so in the Church those truly excel who bring as many as possible into its fellowship, and who confirm in the acknowledged truth those already brought in. This is the sense of the Apostle's words. He therefore does not urge on them an ambitious desire to stand out above others, but corrects their misguided zeal, so that they may understand how far they still are from that glory for which they were vainly striving, since hitherto they have pursued their own glory rather than the building up of others and the public salvation of many.

units.la: Concinetur ergo his verbis axioma cumprimis memorabile, quod omnium Christianorum animis inscriptum esse debet, imprimis autem eorum, qui vel in Repub. supra alios eminere cupiunt, vel ad Ecclesiæ gubernacula sedent. Est enim gloriæ studium omnibus natura insitum, & ut Ci-cero scribebat philosophos illis ipsis libris, quos de contemnenda gloria scribunt, nomina sua inscribere, & eo ipso gloriam vanari: ita eos etiam hac cupiditate ritillari videmus, qui mundo mortui videntur, & qui de carnis & affectuum mortificatione nunquam non disputant. Nascitur autem ex hoc principio pessimorum vitiorum seges, ut pote fastidiosus aliorum contemptus, simulta-tes, odia, contentiones & infinita alia, quibus Reipub. tranquillitas & Ecclesiarum pax turbatur. Fons autem sive origo omnis mali est, quod plerique sibi persuadent, se nisi aliis oppressis, eminere aut excellere non posse. Itaq; si omnes intelligant, veram & tutissimam excellendi rationem in alio-rum ædificatione consistere, & ut quisq; quàm plurimùm prosit, mox vitij huius remedium habebunt præsentissimum. Nam Dei gloriam suæ præferent. Deinde proximum quenq; juvare incipient, & quò diligentius istud fecerint, eò clarius intelligent quàm procul adhuc absint à meta perse-ctionis: imò videbunt sibi singulis momentis aliquod novum negotium incidere, quod novos labores & curas novas requirat.
units.tr: Therefore a principle especially worth remembering should be sung into these words, a principle that ought to be written on the minds of all Christians, and above all of those who either wish to stand out above others in the commonwealth or sit at the helm of the Church. For the desire for glory is implanted in all by nature. As Cicero wrote, philosophers put their own names on the very books in which they write about despising glory, and so by that very act they seek glory. Likewise we see that those also are tickled by this passion who seem dead to the world and who never cease to discuss the mortification of the flesh and of the affections. From this principle there springs a crop of the worst vices: a disdainful contempt of others, quarrels, hatreds, strife, and countless others, by which the tranquillity of the commonwealth and the peace of the churches are disturbed. The source or origin of every evil is that most people persuade themselves that they cannot stand out or excel unless others are crushed. So if everyone understood that the true and surest way to excel consists in building up others, and that each should benefit as many as possible, they would soon have the most ready remedy for this vice. For they would set God's glory before their own. Then they would begin to help each neighbour, and the more diligently they did this, the more clearly they would understand how far they still are from the goal of perfection. Indeed, they would see that some new task presents itself to them at every moment, one that calls for fresh labours and fresh cares.

units.la: Cæterum dicat aliquis Paulo: Quid ergo faciam? An linguarum donum prorsus inutile & infructuosum est? Num contemni debet & abijci? Hanc quæstionem ille præoccupat, dicens: Quapropter qui loquitur lingua, precetur, ut interpretetur. Sensus est: Non dico donum hoc vel inutile, vel aliqua ex parte contemnendum esse. Cur enim hoc dicerem, cùm Deus Euangelii prædicationem hoc miraculo quasi obsignet, & eius usus nobis, qui inter gentes diversas prædicamus, non modò utilis, verumetiam necessarius fit? Sed nè inutiliter & ad solam ostentationem eo utamini, moneo. Id verò ne fiat, consultissimum fuerit, ut qui se linguarū cognitione et usu donatum sentit, Deum sedulò precetur, ut interpretandi quoq; donum obtineat, & ita Ecclesiæ toti exponere possit, quod lingua peregrina locutus est. Ita verò rursus non obscurè innuit, linguæ incognitæ nullum usum esse, nisi interpres accedat: quod ex quotidiana experientia tam notum est omnibus, ut ampliori demonstratione non fit opus.
units.tr: But someone may say to Paul: "What then shall I do? Is the gift of tongues altogether useless and unfruitful? Ought it to be despised and cast aside?" Paul anticipates this question, saying: Therefore let whoever speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret. The sense is: I do not say that this gift is useless, or that it should in any way be despised. For why should I say this, since God, as it were, seals the preaching of the gospel by this miracle, and its use is not only useful but even necessary for us who preach among diverse nations? But I warn you not to use it uselessly and merely for display. To make sure this does not happen, it will be most advisable that whoever feels himself endowed with the knowledge and use of tongues should earnestly pray God that he may also obtain the gift of interpreting, and so be able to expound to the whole Church what he has spoken in a foreign tongue. Here again he hints clearly that an unknown tongue has no use unless an interpreter comes forward; this is so well known to everyone from daily experience that no lengthier demonstration is needed.

units.la: Est autem hic dignissimum observatu, quòd ad preces illos remittit, quibus donum interpre-tandi impetrare à Deo debeant. Facit hoc secundum Christi promissionem, qua docet, non negatu-rum illum nobis Spiritu sanctum, si eum votis ardentibus & sedulis flagitemus. Cui Jacobus Apostolus cõsentiens scribit: Si cui deest sapientia, postulet ab eo qui dat, nempe Deo, qui dat (inquam) omnibus benignè, nec exprobrat, & dabitur ei. Et aliquanto post huius præcepti rationem hanc affert: Omnis donatio bona & omne donum perfectum superne est, descendens à Patre luminum, &c. Et voluit huius in præsenti meminisse Paulus, quia id faciebat ad deprimendum cristas superborum: quia ostendit illos nihil habere in se boni, quàm quod ex Dei liberalitate acceperint. Interim nemo existimet, damnari hoc loco studia bonarum artium, quibus hodie in linguarū cognitione & interpretatione proficitur. Paulus enim pro sui seculi conditione loquitur, quando cognitio ista per peculiarem Spiritus sancti operationem miraculosè dabatur, & ideo simpliciter ad preces remittit eos, qui illa cupiunt in Ecclesia excellere. Hodie cessavit quidem hoc donum, neq; ut quis omnes linguas noverit opus est, veruntamen necessaria adhuc est Latinæ, Græcæ & Hebrææ cognitio (quod & D. Augustinus in libris de Doctrina Christiana annotauit) quæ non absq; nostro studio & industria acquiritur. Itaq; istam rationem iuuenes diligenter sequi debent, & simul studijs suis preces coniungere, quando sine Spiritus virtute nihil proficitur. Orent autem, ut non modò istarum cognitionem assequantur, sed etiam ut ijsdem aliquando uti possint ad Ecclesiæ ædificationem. Debet hoc ipsum in omnibus alijs Dei donis obseruari, utpote prudentia, eloquentia, opibus, bona corporis valetudine, & si quæ alia sunt huius generis. Quia nisi illis digne utamur, neq; nobis ipsis neq; alijs prosunt: imò nostram ignauiam siue malitiam arguunt, qui cum malo illo servo Domini talentum defodimus. Nunquam autem illis rectè utemur, nisi hoc quoq; nobis det Deus, & vitiosos carnis affectus corrigat, quibus transfuersi abripimur.
units.tr: It is worth noting here, most deserving of attention, that he refers them to prayers by which they ought to obtain from God the gift of interpreting. He does this in keeping with Christ's promise, in which he teaches that the Holy Spirit will not be denied us if we ask for him with ardent and earnest prayers. The Apostle James, agreeing with this, writes: If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of him who gives, namely God, who gives (I say) to all generously and does not reproach, and it will be given him. And a little later he gives this reason for the precept: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, etc. Paul wished to recall this here because he was doing so to humble the pride of the arrogant, since he shows that they have nothing good in themselves except what they have received from God's bounty. Meanwhile, let no one think that the study of the liberal arts, by which progress is made today in the knowledge and interpretation of languages, is condemned in this passage. For Paul speaks according to the condition of his own age, when that knowledge was given miraculously through a special operation of the Holy Spirit; and so he simply refers to prayer those who desire to excel in the Church in these things. Today this gift has ceased, and it is not necessary that anyone know all tongues; nevertheless a knowledge of Latin, Greek and Hebrew is still needful (as Augustine also noted in his books On Christian Doctrine), and this is not acquired without our own study and industry. Therefore young people ought diligently to follow this method and at the same time join prayers to their studies, since nothing is accomplished without the power of the Spirit. Let them pray not only that they may attain a knowledge of these things, but also that they may at some time be able to use them for the building up of the Church. The same must be observed in all the other gifts of God, such as prudence, eloquence, wealth, good bodily health, and whatever others there are of this kind. For unless we use them worthily, they profit neither ourselves nor others; indeed they expose our idleness or malice, when we bury the talent like that wicked servant of the Lord. But we will never use them rightly unless God also grants us this, and corrects the vicious affections of the flesh by which we are carried away crookedly.

units.la: Porrò rationem huius præcepti reddit Apostolus: quia nisi interpretatio accedat, inutile & infructuosum sit, quicquid lingua exotica siue peregrina dicitur. Id verò ita proponit, ut ea occasione ad alterum vitium transeat, quo in hac causa Corinthij peccabant, cùm preces quoq; publicas in linguis peregrinis conciperent. Et quia non orationis modò, veruntamen Psalmorum mentionem facit Paulus, credibile est, multos non tam ostentationis quàm superstitionis ergò Psalmos & orationem Dominicam idiomate Hebræo recitasse: eò quòd lingua ista in populo Dei omnium vetustissima, imò prima fuit, & etiam hodie non immeritò Sancta dicitur, quòd ea Deus ipse olim cum patribus locutus est, in qua Legem quoq; descriptam eis tradidit, deniq; quòd eadem æternus Dei Filius, dum in terris ageret, populum docuit. Dicit ergo Paulus: Si precer lingua, id est, peregrino idiomate, spiritus meus precatur, sed mens mea est infructuosa. Torquent se hoc loco interpretes, & pleriq; ex nostris spiritū pro flatu & anhelitu oris accipiunt, mentem verò pro ea hominis facultate, qua intelligimus. Et isti Paulum de illis loqui arbitrantur, qui linguis sibi ipsis quoq; ignotis precabantur (quod hodie multi ex Monachis & Monialib. faciunt) & id tunc vulgare fuisse aiunt, ut qui donū linguarū haberet, nō tamē semper intelligerent quæ ipsi dicebant. Sed fuisset id indignū religione Christiana, & nō immeritò ridiculi vili fuissent auditoribus Christiani, si phitacorum [?] & picarum similes verba non intellecta protulissent. Imò qui diuino hoc Spiritus sancti afflatu agebantur, non dissimiles fuissent eorum, quos malignus spiritus agit, ut res arcanas & sibiipsis incognitas cum auditorum admiratione enuntient, quales olim Phœbades & ἐνθουσιαστικοὶ [?] fuerunt. Denique non linguarum variarum dono Christianos homines instruxisset Deus, sed potius verum & necessarium sermonis usum illis abstulisset. Quapropter spiritus vocabulum non alio sensu hic accipi debet, quàm quo Apostolus toto hoc Capite eo utitur: pro ipso nimirum charisfmate aut dono linguarum. Mens verò siue νοῦς (ut Theodoretus exponit) est eorum quæ dicuntur manifestatio, quam alij intelligentiam dixerunt. Et huic sensui sanè quod non multo post Paulus dicet: Malo quinque verba loqui mente mea ut alios instituam (id est, sic ut mea mens atq; distorum sensus ab omnibus intelligatur) quàm decem millia verborum lingua, id est, sermone peregrino, quem nemo auditorum intelligit. Itaq; huius loci sensus hic est: Si preces concipiam peregrino & alijs incognito idiomate, Spiritus quidem Dei per donum illud, quod mihi datum est, officio suo fungitur, & verba mihi suggerit idonea, precesque quoad meum sensum & animi intentionem bene dirigit, sed quoad mentem & sententiam precationis, ea infructuosa erit auditoribus, neq; aliquis ex ea ad Ecclesiam fructus redibit. Ideo quòd mentem infructuosam fore dicit, ad auditores extendi debet, non ad ipsum precatem restringi. Patet hoc factis evidenter ex eo, quod supra dixit: Qui lingua loquitur seipsum aedificat. At quomodo seipsum aedificabit, qui psitta[?]-ci instar verba non intellecta deblaterat? Constat praeterea quoad preces priuatas, nihil referre quæ quis lingua loquatur, modo ex fide precetur, & eo sermone siue idiomate vtatur, qua mentem suam siue animi intentionem se efficacius exprimere posse existimat. In præsenti autem de publicis precibus agitur, aut potius precum publicarum formula, qua ministri populo præeunt. Ista si lingua ignota concipiantur, nemo eas intelliget præter eum, qui illas recitat, infructuosæ autem erunt auditoribus, quia quid illis postuletur nesciunt. Et hunc sensum ipsa etiam vox ἀκάρπως innuit, qua Paulus vtitur. ἄκαρπος enim vel fruges terræ vel arborum plantarumve fructum aut prouentum significat. At illæ non sibi ipsis, sed hominibus & animalibus fructum ferunt. Latinis fructus a fruendo dicitur, & idem Carpendi & Decerpendi vocabula ἐκ τῶ ἄκαρπα deriuauisse videntur, quando illis non aliud significatur, quam fructum aut utilitatem ex re aliqua percipere. Græci autem proprie ἄκαρπα dicunt, quæ alias ἄγονα vocantur, eo quod nihil gignant. Quamobrem propria significatione mentem siue intelligentiam ἀκάρπου Paulus dixit, ex qua nullum fructum percipit Ecclesia, etiamsi qui loquitur, probe intelligat quæ dicit. Potest huc non inepte omnino accommodari quod Christus dicit, se Apostolos mittere vt fructum ferant (non quidem sibi ipsis, sed Deo & hominibus) & fructus ipsorum maneat.
units.tr: The Apostle gives the reason for this command: unless interpretation is added, whatever is said in a foreign or strange tongue is useless and unfruitful. He puts it this way so that he can move on, on this occasion, to the other fault by which the Corinthians were sinning in this matter, namely that they offered public prayers in foreign tongues. And since Paul mentions not only prayer but also the Psalms, it is likely that many recited the Psalms and the Lord's Prayer in the Hebrew language, not so much for show as out of superstition. This is because that language was the oldest of all among the people of God, indeed the first; it is still rightly called holy today, because God himself once spoke with the fathers in it, gave them the Law written in it, and finally because the eternal Son of God taught the people in it while he lived on earth. Paul therefore says: "If I pray in a tongue, that is, in a foreign idiom, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful." Here the interpreters twist themselves in knots, and many of our own men take "spirit" to mean the breath and breathing of the mouth, and "mind" to mean that faculty of man by which we understand. They think Paul is speaking of those who prayed in tongues unknown even to themselves (which many monks and nuns do today), and they say that this was common at that time: whoever had the gift of tongues did not always understand what he himself was saying. But that would have been unworthy of the Christian religion, and Christians would rightly have been mocked by their hearers if they had uttered words they did not understand, like parrots and magpies. Indeed, those who were moved by the divine breath of the Holy Spirit would not have been unlike those whom an evil spirit drives, who pronounce hidden things unknown to themselves, to the amazement of their hearers, as the Pythian priestesses and the [ἐνθουσιαστικοί] of old did. In short, God would not have equipped Christians with the gift of various tongues, but would rather have taken away from them the true and necessary use of speech. So the word "spirit" must not be taken here in any other sense than that in which the Apostle uses it throughout this chapter: namely, the gift itself, or the gift of tongues. "Mind," however, or [νοῦς] (as Theodoret explains it), is the making clear of what is said, which others have called understanding. And to this sense Paul certainly refers when he says shortly afterwards: "I would rather speak five words with my mind, so as to instruct others" (that is, so that my mind and the meaning of others may be understood by all), "than ten thousand words in a tongue", that is, in a foreign speech which none of the hearers understands. So the sense of this passage is this: "If I make prayers in a foreign idiom, unknown to others, the Spirit of God indeed, through that gift which has been given to me, performs his office and supplies me with suitable words, and rightly directs my prayers as far as my own understanding and the intention of my mind are concerned; but as far as the mind and meaning of the prayer are concerned, it will be unfruitful for the hearers, and no fruit will come from it to the Church." The phrase "his mind is unfruitful" must be extended to the hearers, not confined to the one who prays. This is shown clearly by what he said above: "He who speaks in a tongue edifies himself." But how will he edify himself, if he babbles words he does not understand, like a parrot? It is also clear that, with regard to private prayers, it makes no difference in what tongue someone speaks, provided he prays in faith and uses the language in which he thinks he can express his mind or the intention of his heart more effectively. But here we are speaking of public prayers, or rather the form of public prayers by which the ministers lead the people. If these are composed in an unknown tongue, no one will understand them except the one who recites them, and they will be unfruitful for the hearers, because they do not know what is being asked of them. The very word [ἀκάρπως], which Paul uses, also points to this meaning. [ἄκαρπος] signifies either the crops of the earth or the fruit or yield of trees and plants. But these do not bear fruit for themselves, but for men and animals. In Latin, "fruit" is named from "enjoying", and the words "carp" and "pluck" seem to have been derived from [ἄκαρπα], since these words mean nothing other than to receive fruit or profit from something. The Greeks properly call [ἄκαρπα] those things which are otherwise called [ἄγονα], because they produce nothing. Therefore Paul, in the proper sense, called the mind or understanding [ἀκάρπου], from which the Church receives no fruit, even if the speaker understands well what he says. What Christ says may fitly be applied here: that he sends the Apostles to bear fruit (not indeed for themselves, but for God and men), and that their fruit should remain.

units.la: Hæc diligentius aliquanto dicenda fuerunt, ne præter rationem ab eorum sententia recessisse putemur, quibus alioqui propter suam eruditionem & præclara in Ecclesiam merita plurimum tribuimus. Continet autem locus iste memorabilem doctrinam, non satis esse, vt ipsi in spiritu Deum precemur atq; colamus, sed in Ecclesia hoc requiri, vt alij quoq; quid fiat aut dicatur intelligant: ne quoad illos infructuosum siue inutile sit quod nos facimus. Sufficiunt ista abundè aduersus precum demurmurationes & Psalmodias, quæ in Papatu fiunt lingua Latina. Si enim infructuosum est quicquid non intelligunt auditores, siue id precatio fit, siue cantus, siue quæcunque alia oratio: quid de illis dici debet, qui ne ipsi quidem quid dicant aut canant intelligunt? Id verò de maiori numero sacrificulorum, monachorum & nonnarum siue monialium verissimè dicitur, quorum omnium inscitia iam olim in proverbium abijt. Quid, quòd in plerisq; nationibus ex Romanensium Pontificum instituto rustici & opifices orationem Dominicam, Salutationem Angelicam, & Symbolum Apostolicum Latinè proferunt? At si huic errori nulla superstitio neque ullus alius abusus accederet, inutilis tamen est labor iste omnis, neque excusari potest ulla ratione quod à Paulo in præsenti tam manifestè damnatur. Non tamen hîc pedem fislit hominum superstitiosissimorum audacia, quin multa his accedunt, partim inepta & absurda, partim etiam impia. Etenim maior precationum atq; Psalmodiarum pars Diuus nuncupatur, & sæpe tota feré hora in Litaniis decantandis absumitur, in quibus Diui ex ordine nominantur. Id verò cum manifesto Dei præcepto pugnat, dicentis: In die tribulationis tuæ invoca ME, & eripiam te. Cui Christus consentiens, dicebat: Cùm oratis, dicite, Pater noster qui es in cœlis, &c. Sed & meritum preculis illis astringitur, & in numero quoque superstitiose nimis ineptiunt: quod pharifaicum esse Christus testatur, & ideo multiloquium vitandum esse docet. Adhæc defunctis applicantur preces & Psalmodiæ, & vt olim in funeribus ethnici tibicines adhibebant, ita hodie aliis serio lugentibus conducuntur, qui voce quidem flebili cantillent, corde autem læto iubilent, & in sinu suo gaudeant, quando hic illis quæstus est ùberrimus. Id verò non sine manifesta Christi contumelia fit, cuius merito omne illud derogatur, quod illi suis istis precibus & cantionibus tribuunt. Quàm au-tem hoc alienum fit à Dei instituto, vel ex eo apparet, quòd Lex Dei Sacerdotes procul à funeribus abesse iubet, ne eorum contactu polluantur. At isti vt vultures ad cadauera mortuorum vndiq; conuolant, & non voce modò sua, verùmetiam nolarum siue campanarum sonitu ipsum æthera fatigant. Accedit hîs, quòd hoc prætextu domus viduarum & pupillorum devorant, quo nomineolim Christus Iudæorum sacerdotes acerrimè reprehendit. Et ista quidem defendunt pertinacissimè, qui Apostolorum successores dici volunt: & quàmuis Paulum ista de semetipso dicentem audiant, adduci tamen non possunt, vt errorem tam manifestū tamq; atrocem corrigere in animum inducant. Seruit enim illorum commodo populi ignorantia, qui facilè oculos aperiret, si vel solam orationem Dominicam aut Symboli apostolici articulos rectè intelligeret. Fuit ergo hoc singulare Dei beneficium, quod Germanis semper suo sermone precari & fidem suam confiteri licuit: imò præsagium fuit, ex ea gente exorituros esse tandem, qui superstitiosæ illius tyrannidis fulcra revellerent. Agnoscite ergo ô Germani hanc gloriam vestram, & Deo grati sitis, nec multum mo-veamini impiorum illorum pertinacia, qui quæstum suum publicæ omnium aliorum saluti anteponunt.
units.tr: These things had to be said somewhat more carefully, lest we be thought to have departed from reason in opposing the opinion of those to whom, otherwise, we attribute much because of their learning and their distinguished services to the Church. This passage contains a memorable teaching: it is not enough that we ourselves pray to God and worship him in the Spirit, but it is also required in the Church that others understand what is done or said, so that what we do is not unfruitful or useless for them. These points are more than enough against the mumbling of prayers and the psalmody which are done in Latin under the Papacy. For if whatever the hearers do not understand is unfruitful, whether it be prayer, song, or any other speech, what must be said of those who do not even understand what they themselves say or sing? This is most truly said of the greater part of the priests, monks, and nuns, whose ignorance has long since passed into a proverb. And what of the fact that in many nations, by the custom of the Roman Pontiffs, peasants and craftsmen recite the Lord's Prayer, the Angelic Salutation, and the Apostles' Creed in Latin? But even if no superstition or other abuse were added to this error, this whole labour would still be useless, and it cannot be excused by any reason, since it is so plainly condemned here by Paul. Yet the boldness of these most superstitious men does not stop here; many things are added to it, some foolish and absurd, some even impious. For the greater part of their prayers and psalmody is addressed to the so-called saints, and often almost a whole hour is spent in chanting litanies, in which the saints are named one after another. This clearly conflicts with the plain command of God, who says: "In the day of your trouble call upon me, and I will deliver you." Christ, agreeing with this, said: "When you pray, say, Our Father who art in heaven, etc." But merit is also attributed to these prayers, and they are superstitiously foolish even in the number of their repetitions; Christ testifies that this is Pharisaical, and therefore teaches that much speaking must be avoided. Moreover, prayers and psalmody are applied to the dead, and just as in former times the pagans hired flute-players at funerals, so today singers are hired by others who are seriously mourning; they chant with a tearful voice, but rejoice and exult in their hearts, since this is a very rich source of profit for them. And this is done not without a clear insult to Christ, to whose merit all that they attribute to their prayers and chants is wrongly transferred. How far this is from God's ordinance appears from the fact that God's Law commands the priests to keep far from funerals, so that they are not polluted by contact with them. But these men, like vultures, swarm from every side to corpses, and tire the very air not only with their voices but also with the ringing of bells. In addition, under this pretext they devour the houses of widows and orphans, the very thing for which Christ once so sharply rebuked the priests of the Jews. These men defend such practices most stubbornly, and they wish to be called the successors of the Apostles; and although they hear Paul speaking these words about himself, they cannot be brought to resolve to correct so plain and so shameful an error. For the ignorance of the people serves their advantage; it would easily open their eyes if it understood even the Lord's Prayer or the articles of the Apostles' Creed properly. This was therefore a singular benefit of God, that the Germans have always been allowed to pray and to confess their faith in their own language: indeed it was a foreshadowing that from that nation would at last arise men who would tear out the props of that superstitious tyranny. Acknowledge, then, O Germans, this your glory, and be grateful to God, and do not be much moved by the obstinacy of those impious men who put their own gain before the public salvation of all others.

units.la: Etenim Paulus hic in sua persona loquens longe alios fingit piorum mores, quando mox quæstionem infert: Quid est igitur? Solent enim filij Dei, quàm primùm se errare aut inutiliter laborare sentiunt, quærere, quid Deus velit, & quid ipsos facere conueniat? Ita Iosias Dominum quæsiisse legitur, quod illi omnis pietatis principium fuit. Et de primis credentibus scribitur, quòd cùm se reos occisi Filij Dei factos esse audirent, totis cordibus compuncti, Apostolis dixerint: Quid faciemus, viri fratres? Ipse denique Paulus, quando fulgure prostratus Dominum sibi intonantem audiebat: Saul Saul, cur me persequeris? Durum est tibi contra stimulum calcitrare: illico interrogauit: Quis es Domine? Item: Domine, quid me vis facere? Hoc ipsum ergo in præsenti docet omnes Christianos, quando ipse quid in hac causa fieri debeat, quærit. Licet autem hic obiter videre corruptissimum nostri sæculi statum. Accusantur quotidie superstitiones & abusus horribiles, qui iam seculis aliquot religionem veram depravarunt, obruerunt & extinxerunt. Ita vero arguuntur, ut plerique eos agnoscant & fateantur. Quis vero ex horum ducibus siue magistris quærit: Quid est igitur? Quid nos facere iubet Deus? Imò plerique illos defendunt, & cùm id rationibus & Scripturarum authoritate non possint, faces & gladios proferunt aduersus eos, qui de Dei voluntate inquirunt. Eadem ratione scelera quo q; accusantur & desperata illa morum corruptio, quæ publicè apud omnis loci & ordinis homines obtinuit. Fatentur hanc quoq; plerique, & emendatione omnino opus esse aiunt. Quis autem à semetipso exorsus interrogat, quid faciendum sibi sit? aut qua ratione cum Deo in gratiam possit redire? Quin potius quod Deus nobis sponte offert salutis consilium, plerique contemnunt atq; exibilant. Quid ergo miramur mundum in pejus proficere, & Dei iram aduersus omnes populos indies magis magis q; accendi?
units.tr: For Paul, speaking here in his own person, depicts quite different habits in the pious when he at once raises the question: "What is it then?" The sons of God are accustomed, as soon as they feel they are going astray or labouring to no purpose, to ask what God wills and what it befits them to do. So we read that Josiah sought the Lord, which was for him the beginning of all piety. And of the first believers it is written that, hearing they had become guilty of the death of the Son of God, they were pricked in their hearts and said to the Apostles: "What shall we do, brethren?" Lastly, Paul himself, when he was struck down by lightning and heard the Lord thundering at him, "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad," at once asked: "Who are you, Lord?" and again: "Lord, what do you want me to do?" So he now teaches all Christians by asking what ought to be done in this matter. Here, however, one may incidentally see the thoroughly corrupt state of our own age. Daily, superstitions and dreadful abuses are denounced, which for some centuries have corrupted, overwhelmed and extinguished true religion. And they are so clearly convicted that most acknowledge and confess them. But who among their leaders or masters asks: "What is it then? What does God bid us do?" Indeed, most defend these things, and when they cannot do so by reason and the authority of Scripture, they bring out torches and swords against those who inquire into God's will. By the same reasoning, they are charged with crimes, and with that desperate corruption of morals which has prevailed openly among people of every place and rank. Most also admit this and say that amendment is altogether needed. But who, starting with himself, asks what must be done for him, or by what means he can be reconciled to God? Rather, most despise and hiss at the counsel of salvation that God freely offers us. Why then do we wonder that the world grows worse, and that God's wrath is kindled more and more each day against all peoples?

units.la: Sed Paulum sibi ipsi respondentem audiamus: Precabor spiritu, sed precabor etiam mente: psallam spiritu, sed psallam etiam mente. Coniungit spiritum, id est, donum illud spiritus, quo linguis diuersis multi loquebantur, cum mente siue intelligentia, ne linguarum vsum prorsus contemnere videatur, & sensus istorum verborum est: Si omnino libeat peregrina lingua preces concipere aut Psalmos cantare, tunc simul adhibebo intelligentiam, id est, curabo ut interpretem quæ agam, & ut omnes quod dico intelligant.
