Et cur ita fieri oporteat, rursus graui argumento docet: Quando quidem si benedixeris spiritu, is qui implet locum idiota, quomodo dicturus est Amen ad tuam gratiarum actionem? siquidem quid dicas nescit. Argumentum est eiusmodi. In precibus publicis & gratiarum actione consensus requiritur, ut idem sit omnium animus, eadem mens atq; voluntas. Nec enim temere à Christo dictum est: Si duo ex vobis consenserint in terra, de omnire[?] quamcunq; petierint, fiet eis à Patre meo, qui in cœlis est. Atqui inter precantes consensus esse non potest, nisi omnes quid dicatur intelligant: Unde sequitur, eos qui preces lingua peregrina concipiunt, simul omnem illarum fructum e medio auferre. Id verò probat publico & recepto apud omnes more Ecclesiæ, qui fuit, ut minister precando præiret, reliqui verò omnes sub finem subijcerent, Amen. Est autem hæc vox Hebræa, nobis idem sonans quod, Ita fiat. Erat ergo nota confirmationis, qua non obiter modò consensum suum testabantur, verumetiam optabant ratum fieri id, quod ille erat precatus, qui formulam illam orationis conceperat. Et constat hunc vetustissimum morem fuisse, ut tota Ecclesia in publicis cœtibus, qui de rebus grauioribus & maioris momenti agebantur, suum consensum præberet antistiti, qui vel precabatur, vel quid Deus vellet promulgabat. Ob-seruarunt hoc ex Mosis præscripto Israelitæ, quando terram ingressi promissam, benedictiones illas solennes Dei & execrationes publicè & solenniter pronuntiari curauerunt. Idem sub Ezra quoque factum fuisse postea, quando hic Legem ex Babylone reuersis proposuit, in libro Nehemiæ scribitur. Et quia initiò Ecclesiæ fere ex Iudæis colligebatur, à quibus prædicandi initium faciebant Apostoli, idem ille mos in illam quoque introductus, & Hebræa vox AMEN inter Christianos homines seruata est, ut & aliæ quædam, quæ à vulgo intelligebantur, ut D. Augustinus in loco, quem supra adduximus, admonet. Quia vero hic benedictionis publicae meminit, non absque causa aliqui existimant, Paulum non de solis quotidianis precibus, sed imprimis de Coena dominica actione loqui. Ut enim hanc Christus in gratiam & solennem suae mortis commemorationem instituit: ita non debet eadem absque publica & solenni benedictione sive gratiarum actione celebrari: quam primitivam Ecclesiam usam fuisse, supra Cap. decimo audiuimus. Et memorabilis de hac re locus habetur apud Iustinum Martyrem in secundo Apologetico ad Antoninum Pium Imp. circa finem.
units.tr: But let us hear Paul answering himself: "I will pray with the spirit, but I will also pray with the mind; I will sing with the spirit, but I will also sing with the mind." He joins spirit, that is, that gift of the Spirit by which many spoke in various tongues, with mind or understanding, so that he does not seem to despise the use of tongues altogether. The sense of his words is this: if it should please anyone to frame prayers or sing psalms in a foreign tongue, then at the same time I will add understanding, that is, I will take care that there is an interpreter of what I am doing, and that everyone understands what I say. And he teaches again, with a weighty argument, why this ought to be done: "For if you bless with the spirit, how will the one who fills the place of the untrained say Amen to your thanksgiving, since he does not know what you are saying?" The argument runs thus. In public prayers and thanksgiving agreement is required, so that all have the same mind, the same understanding and will. For Christ did not speak rashly when he said: "If two of you agree on earth concerning anything whatever they ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven." But there cannot be agreement among those who pray unless all understand what is being said. Hence it follows that those who frame prayers in a foreign tongue take away all the fruit of them. This he proves by the public and accepted custom of the Church, which was that the minister led the prayer, and all the others at the end added, Amen. This word is Hebrew [אָמֵן], sounding to us the same as "So be it." It was therefore a mark of confirmation, by which they not only testified their assent in passing, but also wished that what he had prayed, the one who had composed that form of prayer, might be ratified. And it is clear that this very ancient custom was that the whole Church in public assemblies, where matters of greater weight and importance were dealt with, gave its consent to the one presiding, who either prayed or declared what God wished. The Israelites observed this by the prescription of Moses, when, having entered the promised land, they took care that God's solemn blessings and curses were pronounced publicly and solemnly. That the same was done afterwards under Ezra, when he set forth the Law to those returning from Babylon, is written in the book of Nehemiah. And because the Church at its beginning was gathered mostly from Jews, from whom the Apostles began their preaching, that same custom was carried over into it, and the Hebrew word AMEN was kept among Christians, as were certain other things which were understood by the common people, as St. Augustine reminds us in the passage we cited above. Since Paul here mentions the public blessing, some not without reason think he speaks not only of daily prayers but chiefly of the celebration of the Lord's Supper. For just as Christ instituted it as a thanksgiving and solemn remembrance of his death, so it ought not to be celebrated without a public and solemn blessing or thanksgiving, which we heard the primitive Church used, above in chapter ten. There is also a memorable passage on this matter in Justin Martyr, in his Second Apology to the emperor Antoninus Pius, near the end.

units.la: Quod si vero ista propius consideremus, abunde patebit, eos qui linguas peregrinas in coetus Ecclesiae inuehunt, simul & preces publicas impedire, vel inefficaces reddere, & Sacramentorum usum legitimum impedire. Utrumque in Papatu fieri tam manifestum est, ut superuacaneum fuerit id velle demonstrare. Scio quid illi obiiciant, sufficere bonam animi intentionem, & cum actiones illae per se sanctae, verba item similiter sancta sint, neque de eo populus dubitet, posse unumquemque tuto & salua conscientia ijs succinere vel subscribere, quae illic dicuntur & aguntur. Sed est hac plus quam calua excusatio, qua Paulus, quasi istorum temeritate praeuiderit, paucis verbis confutat. Tu quidem (inquit) bene gratias agis, sed alius non aedificatur. Ergo non sufficit, ut tu aliquid bene facias & loquaris, nisi per illud alij quoque aedificentur. Ac qualis aedificatio speari potest illic, vbi ignorantia regnum obtinet. Idem certe istis responderi poterat, quod Samaritidi Christus dixit: Vos nescitis quid adoratis. Vide Ioan. 4. cap.
units.tr: If we consider these things more closely, it will be abundantly clear that those who introduce foreign tongues into the assemblies of the Church at the same time hinder public prayers or render them ineffective, and impede the lawful use of the sacraments. That both happen in the Papacy is so manifest that it would be superfluous to wish to demonstrate it. I know what they object: that a good intention of mind is sufficient, and since those actions are holy in themselves, and the words likewise holy, and the people need not doubt that anyone may safely and with a clear conscience join in saying or subscribing to what is said and done there. But this is more than a bald excuse, which Paul, as if foreseeing their rashness, refutes in a few words: "You indeed give thanks well, but the other is not edified." Therefore it is not enough that you do something and speak well, unless others are also edified by it. And what edification can be hoped for where ignorance holds sway? Certainly the same answer could be given to them that Christ gave to the Samaritan woman: "You do not know what you worship." See John 4.

units.la: Priusquam vero hinc discedamus, propius quoque inspici debet locutio ista Pauli: Is qui implet locum idiotae. Nam vox ista proprie homine priuatum significat, qui nullo officio seu munere publico fungitur. Ideo ut Theodoretus scribit, hoc nomine eos quoque appellabant, qui a militia remoti sibi solis viuebant. Sumitur ergo hic pro toto populo Ecclesiae, quae ab ijs distinguit, qui interpretum & doctorum, siue pastorum locum tenebant. Obseruari hoc debet propter Anabaptistas, qui toto hoc capite abutuntur, ut euincant omnibus in Ecclesia dicendi potestate fieri debere. At Paulus de illis loquitur, quibus hoc datum erat, quod & donis instructi essent, et legitime ordinati: Reliquo populo hoc tribuit, ut omnes dicant Amen, & ita quae a primis illis bene & recte dicta sunt suo assensu probent. Quod autem postea sequitur, Poteritis omnes singillatim prophetare: id propter charismata sive dona illa peculiaria Spiritus sancti dicitur, quae tunc admodum vulgaria erant. Quia vero eadem hodie cessauerunt, ridiculi nimium sunt, qui quod olim pro illorum temporum & Christianismi primum nascentis ratione factitatum est, nunc etiam tentare volunt.
units.tr: Before we depart from this point, the expression of Paul, "the one who fills the place of the untrained," must also be examined more closely. For that word properly signifies a private man, one who discharges no office or public function. Hence, as Theodoret writes, they also called by this name those who had withdrawn from military service and lived for themselves alone. Here, then, it is taken for the whole people of the Church, which is distinguished from those who held the place of interpreters, teachers or pastors. This must be noted because of the Anabaptists, who abuse this whole chapter in order to prove that everyone in the Church ought to have the power of speaking. But Paul speaks of those to whom this had been given, both because they were furnished with gifts and because they were lawfully ordained. To the rest of the people he assigns this, that they all say Amen, and so by their assent approve what was well and rightly said by those first ones. As for what follows, "You can all prophesy one by one," this is said on account of those special gifts or charisms of the Holy Spirit, which were then quite common. But since these have now ceased, they are altogether ridiculous who wish to attempt now what was once practised for the reasons of those times and of the first beginnings of Christianity.

units.la: Quia autem calumniatorum plena sunt omnia, & aliqui dicere poterant, Paulum ex inuidia hoc dicere, quod ipse linguarum ignarus earundem cognitionem atque usum alijs inuideret: praeoccupatione suspicionem iam declinat, & simul suo exemplo docet quid omnes facere conueniat. Scribit enim sic: Gratias ago Deo meo, quod magis quam vos omnes linguis loquar. Sed in Ecclesia malim quinque verba mente mea loqui, etc. Quo loco hoc dicere videtur: Nemo putet me meo honori hic consultum velle, ne qui me eruditiores habeantur. Nam si de linguis certandum sit, ego affirmare possum, me in harum cognitione vobis omnibus esse praestantiorem, & id reipsa hactenus probaui, quando doctrina de IESV CHRISTO per meum ministerium in tota Syria, Arabia, Asia, Graecia, in insulis denique longe lateque propagata est. Possem ergo hoc dono me etiam apud vos ostentare. Sed tam abest a superba & inani ostentatione animus meus, ut in Ecclesiae coetibus malim quinque verba mente mea loqui, idest, intelligibiliter, ut mentis meae sensum omnes percipiant, utque alios ipse instituam, quam decem millia verborum lingua sive idomate peregrino atque incognito.
units.tr: Since slanderers are everywhere, and some might say that Paul says this out of envy, that he, ignorant of languages himself, begrudged others the knowledge and use of them, he forestalls the suspicion in advance and at the same time teaches by his own example what all should do. For he writes thus: "I thank my God that I speak with tongues more than you all. But in the Church I would rather speak five words with my mind, etc." Here he seems to say: let no one think I am seeking my own honour here, as if I wished to be regarded as more learned. For if there is to be a contest about tongues, I can affirm that in their knowledge I surpass you all, and I have proved this in fact hitherto, since the doctrine of Jesus Christ has been spread far and wide through my ministry throughout all Syria, Arabia, Asia, Greece, and finally in the islands. I could therefore show off to you by this gift. But my mind is so far from proud and empty ostentation that in the assemblies of the Church I would rather speak five words with my mind, that is, intelligibly, so that all may grasp the sense of my mind and I may instruct others, than ten thousand words in a foreign and unknown tongue or idiom.

units.la: Est autem hoc Apostoli exemplum obseruatu admodum memorabile. Eo etenim admonemur, quatenus & quomodo nobis Dei donis gloriari liceat. Fecit hoc alias quoque Paulus, quando in Euangelij contemptum ipsius persona sive authoritas oppugnabatur. Sed tunc videre oportet, ut gloriationem nostram ea modestia & pietate temperemus, qua Paulus in praesenti utitur. Primo nihil suae industriae aut labori tribuit, sed ad Deum authorem omnia refert, & huic se gratias debere fatetur. Est hoc principium recti & legitimi usus donorum omnium. Quod unum si diligentius observauissent Corinthij, donis suis nunquam tam turpiter tamq; insolenter fuissent abusi. Deinde non sui honoris respectum habuit Paulus, sed totius Ecclesiae, ut hanc aedificaret, & plures quotidie Christo adduceret. Ideo extra Ecclesiam haud dubie cum omnibus lingua ipsorum vsus est: in coetibus autem sacris ea, quae vulgaris et pro ratione gentis omnibus nota erat. Diuersum plane hodie Monachi & Sacrificuli faciunt. Nam extra templum nunquam aut raro Latine loquuntur, imo fere vsum eius linguae non habet aliquem, & ridiculi fiunt, si in homines eruditos incidant, qui eos Latine loqui cogunt: In templis autem inter homines idiotas, cerdones, furores, nautas, foeminas & pueros Latine canunt, Latine legunt, Latine missant, baptizant, adiurant, precantur, Latine denique omnia dicunt & faciunt. Postremo Paulus eousq; demittit, ut infirmorum quoque institutioni se accommodet. Nam vtitur verbo κατηχίζειν[?], quod de illa proprie dicitur. Non ergo eorum similis fuit, qui dicunt ut dicant, id est, ut tempus extrahant, vel ut suam ostentent eloquentiam siue eruditionem. Atqui nihil illi profiiciunt, ut alibi est demonstratum. Debet autem generalis doctrina hinc peti, quam singuli sibi ipsis accommodent. Agnoscant se diuinitus accepisse quicquid boni habent. Eo deinde vtantur, non ad ostentationem aut quaestum, sed in commune deponant, ut toti Ecclesiae prosint, aut saltem priuatim aliquorum saluti promoveant. Ita fideles IESV CHRISTI serui erunt, & olim in magno illo die in Regni eius hereditatem & societatem adoptabuntur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: This example of the Apostle is indeed most worthy of notice. For by it we are admonished how far and in what way we may glory in the gifts of God. Paul did this also elsewhere, when his person and authority were attacked to the contempt of the Gospel. But then we ought to temper our boasting with that modesty and piety which Paul uses here. First, he attributes nothing to his own industry or labour, but refers everything to God as the author, and confesses that he owes thanks to him. This is the principle of the right and lawful use of all gifts. If the Corinthians had observed this one thing more carefully, they would never have abused their gifts so shamefully and so insolently. Next, Paul had regard not to his own honour but to that of the whole Church, that he might build it up and bring more people daily to Christ. Therefore outside the Church he undoubtedly used their language with everyone, but in the sacred assemblies he used that which was common and known to all according to the custom of the people. Monks and priests today do quite the opposite. For outside the temple they never or rarely speak Latin; indeed, they hardly have any use of that language at all, and they become ridiculous if they meet learned men who force them to speak Latin. But in the temples, among ignorant people, cobblers, weavers, sailors, women and children, they sing in Latin, read in Latin, say Mass in Latin, baptize, exorcise, pray in Latin, and in short say and do everything in Latin. Finally, Paul stoops so low as to accommodate himself even to the instruction of the weak. For he uses the word katēchizein [κατηχίζειν], which is properly said of that kind of teaching. He was therefore not like those who speak in order to talk, that is, to pass the time, or to show off their eloquence or learning. Yet they achieve nothing by this, as has been shown elsewhere. A general doctrine ought to be drawn from this, which each may apply to himself. Let them acknowledge that whatever good they have they have received from God. Let them then use it not for display or gain, but put it at the common disposal, so that they may profit the whole Church, or at least advance the salvation of some in private. Thus the faithful will be servants of Jesus Christ, and at that great day to come they will be adopted into the inheritance and fellowship of his kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 73.

units.la: Fratres, ne estote pueri intelligentia, sed malitia pueri, intelligentia vero perfecti estote. In Lege scriptum est: Propterea per diuersas linguas & aliis labiis loquar populo huic, & ne sic quidem me audient, dicit Dominus. Linguae igitur sunt signum, non iis qui credunt, sed infidelibus: prophetia vero non infidelibus, sed credentibus. Itaque si eodem conuenerit tota Ecclesia, & omnes linguis loquantur, ingrediantur autem idiotae, vel infideles, nonne dicent vos furere ? Sed si omnes prophetent, ingrediatur autem infidelis quispiam, aut idiota, arguitur ab omnibus, diiudicatur ab omnibus: & ita occulta cordis eius manifesta fiunt: atque ita procidens in faciem, adorabit renuntians Deum vere in vobis esse.
units.tr: Brethren, do not be children in understanding, but be children in malice, and in understanding be mature. In the Law it is written: "With other tongues and with other lips will I speak to this people, and even so they will not hear me, says the Lord." Tongues, therefore, are a sign not for those who believe but for unbelievers, whereas prophecy is not for unbelievers but for believers. So if the whole Church comes together and all speak in tongues, and untaught or unbelieving people come in, will they not say that you are mad? But if all prophesy, and some unbelieving or untaught person comes in, he is convicted by all and judged by all, and the secrets of his heart are made manifest; and so, falling on his face, he will worship God and declare that God is truly among you.

units.la: IN tota hac tractatione de linguis peregrinis & earum vsu in Ecclesia, praeter statum ad quem omnia pertinent, obseruatu dignissimum est, quod viuentibus adhuc Apostolis tam multa[?] quae graues errores atque abusus in Ecclesias passim irrepserunt. Fuit enim Corinthiorum Ecclesia (vt alias diximus) optime instituta, & quam sedulam atque diligentem absentium quoque curam habuerit Apostolus, totus fere Actorum liber & eiusdem epistolae testantur. Attamen nō modo foeda morum vitia illic succreuerunt, verumetiam coetus sacri, siue habitum externum virorum atque mulierum, siue Sacramentorum vsum & docendi modum spectes, ita fuerunt corrupti, vt nihil in illis integrum esset. Nam gentilitio habitu viri & mulieres vestiebantur, Coena Dominica in epulum conuersa fuit luxuriosum, in locum autem prophetiae vel doctrinae prophanae & ambitiosa linguarum peregrinarum ostentatio successerat, qua illa tantum non prorsus abolebatur. Sunt haec obseruanda, ne offendamur, si quid huius etiam hodie accidit, neue iis aures praebeamus, qui mox clamant, Ecclesias omnes impuras esse, & ideo secessionem fieri, aut saltem omnes a sacrorum communione eiici vel excludi debere, quotquot vitiis eiusmodi infecti sunt. Quin potius quid Paulus fecerit videamus. Is nemini secessionem suadet, nec aliquem eiicere iussit praeter vnum illum, qui ob scelus capitale mortis supplicium merebatur: vitia autem illa corrigi & e medio auferri curat. Factum hoc in multis aliis hucusque, & idem in ista quoq; tractatione fieri videmus. Poterat ea operosior videri, sed si cogitemus, quantum nocuerit abusus ille linguarum, cum praedicationem Verbi impediret, qua nihil praestantius, nihil magis necessarium habet Ecclesia, quantum item hodie etiam peregrinæ linguæ vsus obsit religioni, mox patebit, hanc Apostoli diligentiam & olim necessariam fuisse, & nos hodie non minus opus habere diligenti omnium, quæ hic dicuntur, consideratione. Postquam autem multis ostendit, quàm inutilis, absurda & noxia sit hæc linguarum ostentatio, nunc ab ea dehortatur, & quidem magno serio, quia id necessitas exigebat.
units.tr: In this whole discussion of foreign tongues and their use in the Church, apart from the condition to which all these matters belong, the most noteworthy point is that, while the Apostles were still alive, so many serious errors and abuses crept into the churches everywhere. For the Church of the Corinthians was, as we have said elsewhere, very well organised, and the whole book of Acts and the Apostle's own letter bear witness to how careful and diligent he was even in caring for those who were absent. Yet not only did shameful moral vices grow up there, but the sacred assemblies, whether you look at the outward dress of men and women, at the use of the Sacraments, or at the manner of teaching, were so corrupted that nothing in them was sound. For men and women dressed in the fashion of the Gentiles; the Lord's Supper had been turned into a luxurious feast; and in place of prophecy or sound teaching there had come a vain and ambitious display of foreign tongues, by which the very thing was almost entirely abolished. These things must be observed, so that we are not offended if anything of the kind happens today, and so that we do not lend our ears to those who immediately cry out that all Churches are impure, and that therefore separation must be made, or at least that all who are infected with such vices must be cast out and excluded from the communion of the sacred things. Rather, let us see what Paul did. He does not urge anyone to separate, nor did he order anyone to be cast out except that one man who deserved the punishment of death for a capital crime; but he takes care that those vices are corrected and removed. This has been done by many others up to now, and we see the same thing being done in this discussion too. It might seem to be a more laborious task, but if we consider how greatly that abuse of tongues harmed things, since it hindered the preaching of the Word, than which the Church has nothing more excellent or more necessary, and how much the use of a foreign tongue likewise harms religion even today, it will soon be clear that this diligence of the Apostle was necessary in his own time, and that we today have no less need of careful consideration of all that is said here. Now, having shown at length how useless, absurd and harmful this display of tongues is, he now dissuades them from it, and indeed with great earnestness, because the necessity of the matter demanded it.

units.la: Propositio huius loci est: Fratres, ne estote pueri intelligentia, sed malitia pueri, intelligentia autem perfecti sive adulti estote, qui iudicio vtamini in rebus agendis graui & maturo. Fratres dicit, quod nomen Christianorum commune est, & sanctissimæ illius communionis vinculum exprimit, quo illi omnes, vt vnius Dei filij, in Christo colliguntur. Ita verò beneuolentiam sibi conciliat, ne se ab ipso prorsus reiectos & damnatos esse putarent. Monet autem, ne pueri sint intelligentia, id est, ne res suas tanquam pueriliter instituant, vt merito cordatioribus quibusque ridiculi sint. Erat admonitio ista vtilissima & perquam necessaria. Fuerunt enim Græci natura leuiores, & (quod plerique historici testantur) ad res seriās minus idonei: adeò vt inter ipsos quoque (vt Chrysostomus alibi annotauit) proverbium publicum iactaretur, Ἕλλως ἀεὶ παῖδες, ἢ γέρων Ἕλλως[?], id est, Græci semper pueri, & nemo Græcus senex. In pueris enim ignorantia est, qua fit, vt res sibi vtiles minus perspiciant, imò de his differentes ægre ferant, ipsi verò molesta & inepta garrulitate omnium aures obtundant. Idem, quia iudicio nondum sunt confirmato, facilè sibi quiduis persuaderi sinunt: adhæc pictoris, puppis & similibus ineptijs delectantur, denique ab omnibus ea probari volunt, quæ ipsis magnifica videntur. At his vitijs Græcos fere laborauisse constat. Cicero certè in libris de Oratore, hac eos ineptia laborare scribit, qua nulla maior fit, quòd nimirum quocunque in loco & quoscunque inter homines vsum fit, de rebus aut difficillimis, aut non necessarijs differant. Quo nomine apud Lacedæmonios, qui oratione graui & breui delectabantur, illi semper male audierunt. Hi certè Ctesifontem eiecisse scribuntur, quòd profiteretur, se de re quauis totum diem posse dicere. Dicebant enim, boni oratoris esse, orationem habere rebus parem. Et alius Græculo cuidam de re quauis prolixam orationem pollicenti respondit: Ego ne sutorem quidem probauerim, qui paruo pedi magnum inducit calceum. Quæ ineptia cum procul dubio inter Corinthios quoque regnaret, seipsos tamen quodammodo superabant, cùm in cœtibus Ecclesiæ de rebus sacris & ad æternam hominis salutem pertinentibus sermone peregrino dissererent, adhæc preces quoque linguis non intellectis conciperent: Quasi verò toti cœtui probari deberet sermonis exotici ostentatio, qua ipsi superbiebant. Rectè igitur & magno illorum merito Paulus eos hortatur, ne pueri sint intelligentia, sed Christianæ grauitatis memores current, ne puerili & vanæ ostentationi indulgendo non tam seipsos quàm religionem omnem impiorum ludibrijs exponant. Nam hoc eos fecisse, ex ijs, quæ mox sequentur, patebit.
units.tr: The proposition of this passage is: Brethren, do not be children in understanding, but in understanding be mature or grown up, so that you use a serious and mature judgement in the things you do. He says "brethren," a name common to Christians, which expresses the bond of that most holy communion by which all of them are gathered together in Christ as sons of the one God. In this way he wins their goodwill, so that they do not think they have been utterly rejected and condemned by him. He warns them not to be children in understanding, that is, not to order their affairs in a childish way, so that they become justly ridiculous to all the more sensible people. This admonition was most useful and very necessary. For the Greeks were by nature rather frivolous and (as most historians testify) less suited to serious matters; so much so that among themselves too (as Chrysostom observed elsewhere) a public proverb was in circulation: "Greeks are always children, and no Greek is an old man" [Ἕλλως ἀεὶ παῖδες, ἢ γέρων Ἕλλως], that is, "Greeks are always children." For children have ignorance, which means they do not see clearly what is useful to them, and indeed, disagreeing about such things, they bear it poorly, while they themselves weary everyone's ears with tiresome and foolish chatter. Likewise, because their judgement is not yet settled, they let themselves be easily persuaded of anything at all; moreover they delight in paintings, ships and similar trifles, and finally they want everything to be approved by all which seems splendid to themselves. It is certain that the Greeks were largely afflicted with these faults. Cicero, at least in his books On the Orator, writes that they suffered from this folly, which is the greatest of all, namely that wherever they are and among whatever people they happen to be, they discuss matters that are either very difficult or not necessary. For this reason the Lacedaemonians, who delighted in grave and brief speech, always spoke ill of them. They are certainly written of as having expelled Ctesiphon, because he professed that he could speak for a whole day on any subject. For they said that it was the mark of a good orator to have a speech equal to the subject. And another man answered a certain little Greek who promised a long speech on any subject: "I would not even approve of a shoemaker who puts a big shoe on a small foot." Since this folly undoubtedly reigned among the Corinthians too, they nevertheless in some way surpassed themselves, when in the assemblies of the Church they discoursed in a foreign tongue on sacred matters and things pertaining to the eternal salvation of man, and moreover made their prayers in tongues not understood. As if the whole assembly ought to approve of a display of exotic speech, in which they themselves took pride! Rightly, therefore, and with great credit to them, Paul exhorts them not to be children in understanding, but to remember Christian gravity and to run, lest by indulging in childish and vain display they expose not so much themselves as all religion to the mockery of the impious. For that they had done this will be clear from what follows immediately.

units.la: Eadem autè opera simul illis occurrit, qui ad Christiani nominis professionem sufficere arbitrabantur, si cœtibus sacris interessent, & quæ illic proponebantur audirent, preces item suas cum aliorum precibus coniungerent, neque necessarium esse, vt omnes quæ dicuntur intelligant. Quæ persuasio hodie etiam multos dementat, & Pontifices per suos emissarios hoc præcipuè vrgent, simpliciter esse credendum, & eorum conditionem tutissimam esse, qui inter nostri sæculi controversias fide Ecclesiæ contenti, nihil præterea quærunt aut scrutantur. Per fidem verò Ecclesiæ Romanas ceremonias & ineptias intelligunt. Quò fit, vt multi cæci duces cæcos sequantur, admonitionis Christi immemores, qui ambos in foueam cadere dicit. Ergo nobis quoque Paulum loqui putemus, quando eadem iudicij inopia multi laborant. Debet etiam huc referri, quod Paulus ad Ephesios scribit, ne pueri simus, qui fluctuemus & circumferamur quouis vento doctrinæ: & quod Ioannes monuit, ne temere cuiuis spiritui credamus, sed probemus spiritus, num ex Deo sint. Quid verò de ijs dicemus, qui hodie, cùm pro adultis & perfectis haberi velint, ad pueriles Papistarum sordes relabuntur, dum in aliorum labore & industria reformatas Ecclesias inutilem templorum ornatum, imagines, organa, cantum figuratum (vt vocant) & histrionicum ministrorum vestitum reducunt? Sunt hæc inutilia prorsus ô fratres, & vtinam non simul noxia quoque essent: Dei Verbum semen illud regenerationis est, in quo adolescere conueniet eos, qui aliquando verè sa-pere & in viros perfectos in Christo euadere cupiunt. Nihil ad hoc conferunt organorum concentus & Musica artificiosa voluptas, nihil item prosunt vestes theatricae, imagines vero animos di-strahunt, & absque idololatriae suspicione vix unquam ferri aut retineri possunt.
units.tr: At the same time he meets those who thought it enough for the profession of the Christian name that they attend the sacred assemblies and hear what is set before them there, and likewise join their own prayers with the prayers of others, and that it was not necessary for everything that is said to be understood. This persuasion still drives many people out of their minds today, and the Papists through their agents press this especially, that one must simply believe, and that the condition of those is safest who, amid the controversies of our age, are content with the faith of the Church and seek or search into nothing further. They understand the Roman ceremonies and foolish trifles by "the faith of the Church." The result is that many blind leaders are followed by the blind, forgetful of the warning of Christ, who says that both will fall into the pit. Therefore let us also think that Paul is speaking to us, since many suffer from the same lack of judgement. What Paul writes to the Ephesians should also be referred here: that we should not be children, tossed about and carried round by every wind of doctrine; and what John warned: that we should not believe every spirit rashly, but test the spirits, whether they are from God. But what shall we say of those who today, though they wish to be regarded as adults and perfect, relapse into the childish filth of the Papists, and while others have reformed the Churches by their labour and diligence, bring back the useless adornment of the temples, images, organs, so-called figured and theatrical singing, and the theatrical vestments of the ministers? These things are utterly useless, brethren, and would that they were not at the same time harmful too! The Word of God is that seed of regeneration in which those who at some time wish truly to be wise and to grow into perfect men in Christ ought to grow. The harmonies of organs and the artful delight of music contribute nothing to this, and theatrical garments likewise do no good; images indeed distract the minds, and can scarcely ever be tolerated or retained without the suspicion of idolatry.

units.la: Caeterum probat Paulus, Corinthios pueriliter agere, & proinde admonitione ista opus habe-re. In Lege scriptum est, Propterea per diuersas linguas & alijs labijs loquar populo huic, & nè sic quidem me audient, dicit Dominus, &c. Argumenti ex his verbis ita potest formari: Pu-rile est id affectare, aut in eo gloriam quaerere, quod irati Dei argumentum & impietatis paena est: Atqui linguae peregrinae irati Dei indicium sunt, & illis hic fere sui Verbi contemptum olim vitus est: Ergo plus quam pueri est, dum circa illas tanta cum contentione occupamini. Minorem probat ipsius Dei verbis ex Isaiae 28. Cap. desumptis. Ea autem sub legis titulo adducit, sicuti & Christus apud Ioannem Psalmi 82.testimonium, quia Prophetae germani ac veri sunt Legis interpretes. Accusat illic Deus incurabilem eorum contumaciam, qui verbum eius scurriliter contemnebant. Minatur praeterea, si illis posthac loqui velle lingua peregrina, id est, hostes e longinquis regionibus adducere, quorum linguam non intelligant, & hos ipsorum concionatores, vel potius concionum atque minarum propheticarum executores fore. Id vero cum minis legalibus con-uenit, inter quas ista quoque apud Mosem habetur: Excitabit contra te Dominus gentem e lon-ginquo, ab extremitate terrae, quae inuolabit vt aquila, gentem cuius linguam tu non intelliges, gen-tem impudentem facie, quae faciem senis non reuerebitur, nec miserebitur adolescentis. Ista ergo Paulus Corinthijs applicat, vt intelligant quam stulti sint, sponte id sibijpsis accersendo, quod Deus olim impijs Verbi sui contemptoribus sit minatus. Nec est quod aliquis obijciat, in No-uo testamento linguas gratia Dei testimonium, & necessarium organum fuisse, per quod Euange-lij praedicatio per totum orbem terrarum longè lateque diffusa est. Quia enim Corinthij linguis non in eum finem vtebantur, vt Euangelium ad exteros propagarent, sed eius doctrinam inter su-os homines, quantum in ipsis erat, illarum vsu obscurabant, certè sibijpsis supplicium struebant ex eo, quod Deus vt salutis plurium seruiret, dederat.
units.tr: Paul also proves that the Corinthians behave like children, and that they therefore need this admonition. It is written in the Law: "By men of other tongues and by other lips will I speak to this people, and even so they will not hear me, says the Lord," and so on. The argument can be formed from these words as follows. To strive after something, or to seek glory in it, is childish when it is a sign of God's anger and a punishment for impiety. But foreign tongues are a sign of God's anger, and by them God once punished the contempt of his Word. Therefore it is more than childish for you to be occupied with them with such great eagerness. He proves the minor premise from the words of God himself, taken from Isaiah chapter 28. He cites these words under the title of the Law, just as Christ cites Psalm 82 in John, because the Prophets are the true and genuine interpreters of the Law. There God accuses the incurable obstinacy of those who scornfully despised his Word. He threatens moreover that if they should henceforth wish to speak in a foreign tongue, that is, to bring in enemies from distant regions whose language they do not understand, these enemies will be their preachers, or rather the executors of the prophetic sermons and threats. This agrees with the threats of the Law, among which this also is found in Moses: "The Lord will bring a nation against you from afar, from the end of the earth, which will swoop down like an eagle, a nation whose language you will not understand, a nation shameless of face, which will not respect the face of the old nor pity the young." Paul therefore applies these things to the Corinthians, so that they may understand how foolish they are, bringing upon themselves of their own accord what God once threatened against the impious despisers of his Word. Nor is there any reason for someone to object that in the New Testament the gift of tongues was a testimony of God's grace and a necessary instrument by which the preaching of the Gospel was spread far and wide across the whole world. For the Corinthians did not use tongues with the aim of propagating the Gospel among outsiders, but by their use they obscured its teaching among their own people, as far as they were able. Certainly they were preparing punishment for themselves by abusing what God had given to serve the salvation of many.

units.la: Solet hoc ipsum omnibus accidere, qui alia quoque Dei dona non digne aestimant, sed ijs pro af-fectuum suorum libidine vel ad fastum & inanem ostentationem, vel ad quaestum abutuntur. Exe-pla huius rei quotidie occurrunt in diuitibus. Etenim opes Dei donum sunt, quo suos quoque cultores interdum remunerat, vt in Abrahamo, Isaaco & similibus est videre. Eadem si quis bene illis vtatur, egregium vtilissimumque sunt[?] omnis virtutis organum, imprimis autem beneficentiae & misericordiae. Et his conueniunt promissiones, quod sibi thesaurum in caelis recondant, & a-micos sibi parent, à quibus olim in tabernacula aeterna recipiantur. At si qui ex illis luxuriantur & superbiunt, aut illis freti alios opprimunt, vel etiam insatiabili earum cupiditate accensi vsu-ras voraces & toti reipub. noxias exercent, bi sibijpsis maledictionem, ignominiam & exitium aeter-num accersunt. Istis enim seruiunt Legis maledictiones, & quod Christus in Euangelio cla-mat: Vae vobis diuitibus, quia recepistis consolationem vestram: Vae vobis qui saturati estis, quo-niam esurietis, &c. Et illud Iacobi: Agite nunc diuites, plorate vlulantes super miserijs vestris, quae aduenient vobis, &c. Eadem ratio est honorum atque dignitatum. Qui his bene vtuntur, Deum sibijpsis indies magis conciliant, qui per prophetam dixit, Honorantes me honorabo. Qui autem his superbi tyrannos agunt, & aduersus ipsum quoque Deum insurgunt, hi ab eo tandem e sedibus suis deturbantur, sicuti Diua Virgo cecinit. Luc.1.
units.tr: The same thing happens to all those who do not value the other gifts of God rightly, but abuse them for the sake of their passions, either for pride and empty display, or for profit. Examples of this occur every day among the rich. For riches are a gift of God, by which he sometimes rewards even his own worshippers, as can be seen in Abraham, Isaac and others like them. If anyone uses these well, they are an excellent and most useful instrument of every virtue, above all of beneficence and mercy. And to these belong the promises that they lay up for themselves a treasure in heaven and make friends for themselves, who will one day receive them into the everlasting tabernacles. But if some of them live in luxury and grow proud, or relying on their wealth oppress others, or even, inflamed by an insatiable desire for it, practise ravenous usury and harm the whole commonwealth, they bring upon themselves curse, shame and eternal destruction. For the curses of the Law apply to them, and what Christ cries out in the Gospel: "Woe to you rich, for you have received your consolation! Woe to you who are full, for you shall hunger," and so on. And that of James: "Come now, you rich, weep and howl over your miseries that are coming upon you," and so on. The same reasoning applies to honours and dignities. Those who use them well win God's favour for themselves more and more each day, for he said through the prophet: "I will honour those who honour me." But those who, proud of these things, play the tyrant, and rise up against God himself, are at last cast down from their seats by him, as the Blessed Virgin sang. Luke 1.

units.la: Sed in Apostoli verbis pergamus, qui ex ijs quae modo dixit, argumentum infert eiusmodi: Linguae igitur sunt signum, non ijs qui credunt, sed infidelibus: prophetia vero non infidelibus, sed credentibus. Ex sine[?] aut vsu linguarum atque prophetiae argumentatur. Signum enim hoc loco in partem meliorem sumit pro miraculosa gratia diuina testimonio, & ideo illud tam linguis quam prophetiae accommodat, quae ambo dona non sine miraculo dabantur. Infideles autem non dicit hic reprobos & prorsus alienos à Dei familia, sed eos qui etsi sint ex electorum numero, adhuc tamen ad credendum difficiliores sunt, & proinde signis opus habent, quibus excitentur: quibus non amplius trahi aut moueri opus est alios, qui iam crediderunt. Itaque argumentum Pauli est: Qui vere sapiunt & non pueriliter leuitate rapiuntur, ij quid ipsis conueniat vident, & omnibus ad-finem vtuntur, cui sunt destinata: At lingua à Deo ideo data sunt, vt incredulos excitent, & vt ex eorum miraculoso usu appareat, Euangelio cœlestem atque diuinam doctrinam contineri? Non debent ergo circa has occupari, qui fidem iam assecuti sunt. In quorum numero cum vos procul dubio haberi velitis, non inani & inutili iam vobis linguarum ostentatione superbire, sed vos totos prophetiae impendere debebatis, quae credentibus data est, vt ea sese exerceant, & ex ea petant quae ipsorum institutioni, consolationi & aedificationi seruiunt. Ita vero aperte ostendit, minimum pueriliter eos agere, dum non obseruant quis vtriusque doni finis sit. Vt enim non postremae sapientiae pars est, causas & fines rerum obseruare, vt illis recte vtaris: ita plus quam puerilis stultitia est, istud negligere et quiduis temere obuiū arripere. Qui enim ad faciunt, ij ineptis opificibus similes sunt, qui quouis instrumento temere vtuntur, nulla vel operis sui, quod faciunt, vel instrumenti ratione habita. Erat autem eo turpior Corinthiorum stultitia, quod cum aliis Ecclesijs præstare cuperent, cæca ambitione sese ad ea deijcerent, quæ infidelium aut infirmorum adminicula, vel potius prima rudimenta esse debent.
units.tr: But let us go on with the words of the Apostle, who from what he has just said draws this argument: "Tongues, therefore, are a sign not for those who believe, but for unbelievers; prophecy, however, is not for unbelievers but for believers." He argues from the use of tongues and of prophecy. Here he takes "sign" in its better sense, for a miraculous testimony of divine grace, and so he applies it to tongues as much as to prophecy, both of which gifts were given not without a miracle. By "unbelievers" he does not mean here the reprobate and those utterly alien to God's household, but those who, although they are among the number of the elect, are still more difficult to bring to belief, and therefore need signs by which they may be stirred up. Those who have already believed do not need to be drawn or moved in this way any more. So Paul's argument is this: those who truly have wisdom and are not carried away by childish levity, see what is fitting for them, and use everything for the end to which it is appointed. But tongues were given by God so as to rouse unbelievers, and so that by their miraculous use it might appear that the heavenly and divine doctrine is contained in the Gospel. Therefore those who have already attained faith ought not to be occupied with them. Since you undoubtedly wish to be counted among their number, you should not now take pride in the empty and useless display of tongues, but devote yourselves wholly to prophecy, which was given to believers, so that they may exercise themselves in it and seek from it what serves their instruction, consolation and edification. In this way he clearly shows that they act in a rather childish manner, in that they do not observe what the end of each gift is. For just as it is no small part of wisdom to observe the causes and ends of things, so that you may use them rightly, so it is more than childish folly to neglect this and to snatch up at random whatever happens to be at hand. For those who act in this way are like clumsy workmen who use any tool at random, with no regard either for the work they are doing or for the purpose of the tool. The folly of the Corinthians was all the more shameful because, while they wished to excel the other congregations, they blindly threw themselves into those things which ought to be the crutches of unbelievers or of the weak, or rather their first rudiments.

units.la: Est autem hic diligenti obseruatione dignum, quod Prophetiam ad eos pertinere dicit, qui iam crediderunt, & quidem ad eos imprimis, qui iam non amplius pueri, sed adulti sunt in Christo. Confutat hoc eorum errorem, qui vbi fidem assecuti sunt, inque ea aliquo vsque profecerunt, ita sibi placent, vt & Verbi doctrinam & quaecunque alia sunt fidei atque pietatis exercitia contemnant. Habent hi argumenta, quibus suam impietatem palliant. Fides (inquiunt) sola iustificat, sola item saluos facit. At haec Dei donum est, neque est volentis aut currentis, sed miserentis Dei, neque ad Christum venit aliquis, nisi quem Pater traxerit. Item: Nihil est qui plantat, aut qui rigat, sed qui incrementum dat, Deus. Sunt haec omnia per se verissima: Sed quod illi ex hiis colligunt, ideo non opus esse Verbi praedicatione, Sacramentis, precibus publicis, id vero salsissimum est. Fidem enim per Verbi praedicationem dari, Paulus diserte docet, ad Romanos scribens: Quomodo credent ei, de quo non audiuerunt? quomodo audient absque praedicante? Et mox infert: Fides ex auditu est, auditus autem per Verbum Dei. Ideo Christus Apostolis dicebat: Ite in totum orbem, & praedicate Euangelium omni creaturae. Et tunc demum infert: Qui crediderit, & baptizatus fuerit, saluus erit. Per eandem praedicationem Spiritus quoque confertur, qui trahit, qui volentes & spontaneos facit ex nolentibus, qui currentes instigat, qui denique, semen illud regenerationis viuificat & vegetat. Adhæc, quia in credentibus manent peccati reliquiae, quibus fit, vt frequenter labamur, quotidiana etiam doctrina, admonitione, hortatione, increpatione et consolatione opus est. Id pij & electi in semetipsis ita agnoscunt, vt non necessaria modo putent doctrinam Verbi Dei, verumetiam illa nihil suauius, nihil iucundius habeant. De illa certe Dauid pronuntiat, quod magis expetibilis sit, quam aurum praestantissimum, dulcior ite fauis multo melle stillantibus. Ideo precibus quoq; suis hoc subinde postulant, vt Deus vias suas ipsis notas faciat, & in semitis suis eos assuefaciat. Sed & Christus hoc filijs Dei proprium esse ait, quod Verbum eius audiant, Pharisaeos autem eo argumento probat, non Dei, sed diaboli filios esse, quod Verbum eius audire dedignarentur. Recte igitur Paulus, prophetiam in signum gratiae Dei datam esse ait, quod non possunt hi contemnere, qui gratiae illius saluberrimam suauitatem semel degustauerunt. Quotquot vero illam fastidiunt & negligunt, ij dum aliis perfectiores volunt videri, seipsos adhuc a Deo alienos, neque dignos esse produnt, qui in eius familia, siue Ecclesia, censeantur.
units.tr: Here it is worth careful observation that he says prophecy pertains to those who have already believed, and indeed above all to those who are no longer children but are grown up in Christ. He refutes the error of those who, once they have attained faith and made some progress in it, become so pleased with themselves that they despise both the teaching of the Word and all the other exercises of faith and piety. They have arguments by which they cloak their impiety. "Faith alone," they say, "justifies, and faith alone also saves. But this is the gift of God, and it is not of him who wills or runs, but of God who has mercy; and no one comes to Christ unless the Father draws him." Likewise: "Neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase." All these things are most true in themselves. But what they infer from them, namely that there is no need of the preaching of the Word, the sacraments or public prayers, is utterly false. For Paul clearly teaches that faith is given through the preaching of the Word, writing to the Romans: "How will they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without a preacher?" And shortly afterwards he concludes: "Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the Word of God." Therefore Christ said to the Apostles: "Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature." And only then does he add: "He who believes and is baptized will be saved." By this same preaching the Spirit too is conferred, who draws, who makes the unwilling willing and eager, who spurs on those who run, and who finally quickens and enlivens that seed of regeneration. Besides, because remnants of sin remain in believers, through which it happens that we often stumble, they need daily teaching, admonition, exhortation, rebuke and consolation as well. The pious and the elect recognise this in themselves, so that they not only think the doctrine of God's Word necessary, but find nothing sweeter and more delightful than it. Of it David certainly declares that it is more to be desired than the finest gold, and sweeter than honey dripping from the honeycomb. Therefore they also ask in their prayers from time to time that God would make known to them his ways and train them in his paths. Christ also says that it is a mark of the children of God that they hear his Word, and he proves by this argument that the Pharisees were sons not of God but of the devil, because they disdained to hear his Word. Paul rightly says, then, that prophecy was given as a sign of God's grace, because those who have once tasted the most wholesome sweetness of that grace cannot despise it. But all who loathe and neglect it, while they wish to appear more perfect than others, show that they are still alien from God and not worthy to be counted in his family, or Church.

units.la: Porrò quod antea dixit Apostolus; nunc ὑποδείγματι siue exemplo ceu demonstratione ad oculum facta, confirmat & illustrat. Sumitur autem exemplum ab ijs, quae quotidie fiebant. Quia enim Christiani homines ethnicis permixti habitabant, frequenter accidebat, vt aliqui vel propria curiositate moti, vel a vicinis & amicis rogati, multi etiam occulta numinis vi dulli in eorum coetibus venirent, vt quae illic agebantur & dicebantur viderent. Ex eo igitur casum duplicem fingit Apostolus. Primus ad abusum linguarum refertur, quae hucusq;, reprehendit. Esto (inquit) vbi tota vestra Ecclesia in vnum locum conuenerit, ingrediantur aliqui idiotae aut infideles, qui neq; linguas vllas praeter vulgarem norint, neq; fidem adhuc siue Christi cognitionem habeant aliquam: & hi vos omnes audiat vel simul vel alternis loqui linguis peregrinis, ita vt nec ipsi vos mutuo intelligatis: quae obsecro vos, illorum de vobis erit sententia? quid dicet? Certe vos furere aut insanire dicet. Nec enim fani hominis est, velle in publico coetu sic loqui, vt à nemine intelligatur; & loquendo seipsum simul & auditores inaniter fatigare. Quanto minus autem ratione sana vti dicentur, qui multi promiscue id ipsum faciunt? Id vero non temere dixit Apostolus. Sciebat enim, quid in die Pentecostes accidisset, quando Apostoli multis musto pleni esse visi sunt, cum linguis peregrinis subito loquerentur. Et credibile est, apud Corinthios non semel simile quid contigisse, cum in urbe luxu & libidine perdita magnus esset hominum prophanorum & perditissimorum numerus. De eo igitur illos admonet, ne temere risum moveant auditoribus, & religionem Christianam flultitiæ & dementiæ suspectam reddant. Et habent ista acrem infamiæ puerilis exprobrationem, quando tales esse ostendit, qui non observare possint ea, quorum absurditatem homines prophani & a religione alieni facile animadvertant.
units.tr: The Apostle now confirms and illustrates what he said before by an example [ὑποδείγματι], a demonstration made as if before the eyes. The example is taken from what happened every day. Because Christians lived mixed among pagans, it often happened that some, moved by their own curiosity or asked by neighbours and friends, and many also drawn by some hidden power of God, came into their assemblies to see what was done and said there. From this the Apostle imagines a twofold case. The first concerns the abuse of tongues, which he has so far rebuked. Suppose, he says, that when your whole Church has come together in one place, some unlearned or unbelieving people come in, who know no language but the common one and have no faith or knowledge of Christ at all; and they hear you all speaking together, or in turn, in foreign tongues, so that you do not even understand one another. What, I ask you, will their judgement of you be? What will they say? Surely they will say that you are raving or mad. For it is not the mark of a sane man to wish to speak in public in such a way that no one understands him, wearying both himself and his hearers to no purpose. How much less will they think that those use sound reason who do this together, all of them at once? The Apostle did not say this rashly. He knew what had happened on the day of Pentecost, when the Apostles seemed to many to be full of new wine, because they suddenly spoke in foreign tongues. It is credible that something similar had happened among the Corinthians more than once, since in a city of luxury and dissolute lust there was a great number of profane and most depraved people. He therefore warns them about this, lest they carelessly provoke laughter in their hearers and make the Christian religion suspected of folly and madness. These things carry a sharp rebuke of childish disgrace, since they show that these people cannot observe what profane men and those alien to religion will easily notice as absurd.

units.la: Debent autem ex his generalem doctrinam petere omnes, qui Christi nomen profitentur, ne quid in tota sua vita faciant, quod fidei professionem vel minima ex parte lædat. Meminerint ergo, non temere nos a Christo civitati conferri, quæ in alti montis cacumine sita latere non potest, et proinde curent, ut operibus suis Deum patrem glorificent. Quia item nos ex hoc mundo Christus selegit, non poterunt excusari, qui cum huius discipuli dici velint, mundo simul conformes esse pergunt. Lacon quidam interrogatus, cur barbam prolixam nutriret? respondit: Vt canos videns nihil his indignum faciam. Quin ergo sibi ipsis occinunt subinde Christiani homines: Cur Christianus diceris? Cur in Christi nomen baptizatus es? Cur cœtus sacros ingrederis? Cur Cœnę mysticæ cum aliis Christi professoribus communicas? Num ut mundo immersus maneas? ut hominum ambitiosorum & superstitiosorum stultitiæ sis admirator? ut in caupona, in ganeo inter diaboli fœda mancipia computrescas? ut simul menses dæmoniorum communices cum iis, qui Christi membrum tum iampridem conculcaverunt? Annon potius, ut Christi membrum sis, hunc ore & vita tota loquaris, nec quicquam facias a gravitate Christiana alienum? Etenim si cauere nos decet, ne quid stulte facere aut furere videamur, quanto magis videndum fuerit, ne carnis libidinem, aut turpem quæstum, vel otium ignavum sectemur? Proderit hic etiam aliorum de nobis iudicia audire & inquirere, ut ex illis agnoscamus vitia, quæ in nobis ipsis non animadvertimus: quam utilitatem ex inimicis etiam caperet docuerunt olim gentium philosophi.
units.tr: From these things everyone who professes the name of Christ ought to draw a general teaching: that in the whole of their life they should do nothing that harms the profession of faith, even in the smallest part. Let them remember that we have not been compared to a city by Christ without reason, a city set on the peak of a high mountain, which cannot be hidden; and therefore let them take care to glorify God the Father by their works. Likewise, since Christ has chosen us out of this world, they cannot be excused who, while wishing to be called his disciples, still go on conforming themselves to the world. A certain Spartan, asked why he grew a long beard, replied: so that, seeing my grey hairs, I may do nothing unworthy of them. Why then do Christians not repeat these questions to themselves: Why are you called a Christian? Why were you baptized in the name of Christ? Why do you enter sacred assemblies? Why do you share the mystical Supper with other professors of Christ? Is it so that you may remain immersed in the world? So that you may admire the folly of ambitious and superstitious men? So that you may rot in a tavern, among the filthy slaves of the devil, among the drinkers? So that you may share the feasts of demons with those who long ago trampled the member of Christ underfoot? Should you not rather, being a member of Christ, speak this with your mouth and your whole life, and do nothing foreign to Christian gravity? For if we ought to take care not to seem to act foolishly or to rave, how much more must we watch lest we pursue fleshly lust, shameful gain or idle sloth? It will also be useful here to hear and inquire into the judgements of others about us, so that from them we may recognise faults that we do not notice in ourselves. The philosophers of the nations long ago taught what benefit we can even draw from enemies in this way.

units.la: Sed alterum quoque casum ponit Apostolus, qui ad prophetiæ commendationem pertinet: Si omnes (inquit) prophetent (non quidem simul omnes, sed per vices & eo ordine, quem mox tradet) ingrediatur autem infidelis aliquis aut idiota, arguitur ab omnibus, dijudicatur ab omnibus, id est, intra animum suum propriæ conscientiæ testimonio convincitur, & ipsi iam manifesta fiunt, quæ prius in corde eius occulta latebant. Est enim Verbum Dei vivum & penetrantius quovis gladio ancipiti, & pertingit usque ad divisionem animæ simul ac spiritus, compagumque & medullarum, discretor item est cogitationum & intentionum cordis. Exemplum huius rei evidens in potentissimo Babyloniorum Monarcha extat. Is cum omni sui visione perturbatus sese[?] expedire non posset, nec quisquam sapientum Chaldæorum illius historiam atque interpretationem proferret, utrumque autem Spiritu vere divino atque prophetico Daniel exponeret, mox intra animum suum conversus in faciem procidit, exclamans: Vere Deus vester omnium Deorum excellentissimus est, & Dominus Regum, & aperiens arcana, &c. Cui simile est quod Hierosolymis ad primam Petri concionem accidisse Lucas in Actis scribit, multos nimirum illo die animis compunctos consilium salutis postulavisse, & baptizatos Christo nomen dedisse. Et cur quis de Verbi Dei effectu dubitet, quando inter ethnicos philosophiæ puriorus fructus non contemnendos aliquando extitisse constat? Erat olim Athenis Polemon[?] quidam perdita luxuria adolescens & infamia gaudens. Is cum aliquando tota noctem perpotasset, & post ortu demum Solis e conviuio domum reverteret, Xenocratis scholam ingrederetur, irridendi potius quam disputandi studio, ille autem omissa re, quam tractabat, de modestia & temperantia differere inciperet: Polemon mox gravitate sermonis resipiscere coactus, primum coronam capite detractam proiecit, paulo post brachium intra palliū reduxit, denique procedente tempore oris coniuvialis hilaritatem depositi, ad ultimum luxuriam omnem exuit. Et quis dubitet multa olim huius generis facta fuisse, quando Ecclesia mirificis donis florebat, cum hodie in multis magni Euangelicæ doctrinæ effectus cernantur? Ipsius vero Paulus Corinthios puerilis ineptiæ convincit, qui tam stupidi sint, ut hæc non observent, sed potius circa ea occupentur, quæ ipsis stultitiæ extremæ suspicionem conflare possint: Qui haud dubiè acutissimus stimulus fuit apud eos, qui præ multis aliis sapere videri volebant.
units.tr: But the Apostle also sets out a second case, which pertains to the commendation of prophecy: "If all prophesy" (not all at once, but in turn and in the order he will shortly give), "and some unbeliever or unlearned man comes in, he is convicted by all, judged by all." That is, he is convinced within his own mind by the testimony of his conscience, and the things that were hidden in his heart before become manifest to him. For the Word of God is living and more piercing than any two-edged sword, and it reaches even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and it discerns the thoughts and intentions of the heart. A clear example of this is found in the most powerful monarch of the Babylonians. When he was disturbed by his own vision and could not explain it, and none of the wise men of the Chaldeans could recount and interpret his story, but Daniel expounded both by the truly divine and prophetic Spirit, he at once turned within himself and fell on his face, crying out: "Truly your God is the most excellent of gods, and the Lord of kings, and the revealer of secrets," etc. Similar to this is what Luke writes in the Acts happened at Jerusalem at Peter's first sermon: many, pricked in heart that very day, asked for counsel of salvation and, being baptized, gave their names to Christ. Why should anyone doubt the effect of God's Word, when it is certain that among the pagans purer fruits of philosophy, not to be despised, have sometimes appeared? Once at Athens there was a certain young man, Polemon, given over to dissolute luxury and rejoicing in infamy. When he had once drunk through the whole night, and at last after sunrise was returning home from the drinking party, he entered the school of Xenocrates with the eagerness to mock rather than to dispute. But the other, leaving aside the matter he was treating, began to discourse on modesty and temperance. Polemon, compelled by the gravity of the speech, was soon brought to his senses: first he threw the garland off his head, a little later he drew his arm back under his cloak, then as time went on he laid aside the cheerfulness of his banquet face, and at last he shed all luxury. And who would doubt that many things of this kind happened long ago, when the Church flourished with wonderful gifts, when today too many great effects of the evangelical doctrine are seen? Paul convicts the Corinthians of childish silliness, for they are so stupid that they do not observe these things, but rather busy themselves with what can stir up suspicion of utter folly in others. This was no doubt a most sharp goad among those who wished to seem wiser than many others.

units.la: Porrò simul de vero prophetiæ usu nos locus iste edocet. Nō est illa simplex recitatio & interpretatio Scripturarum, sed (vt initio huius Cap. audiuimus) eiusmodi quæ cū adhortatione & consolatione ad ædificationem totius Ecclesiæ & singulorum applicatur. Debet ergo sic exerceri, vt in animos penetret, arguat de peccato (quod proprium Spiritus sancti in Apostolis opus fore Christus dixit) ita deniq; agat, vt omnes de se dici intelligant. Est enim cor hominis profundū et inscrutabile, & qui grauissimè peccauerunt, fere sibi ipsis delitias faciunt, vt propria scelera non agnoscant, aut saltem aliquatenus dissimulent. Vt enim non videmus naues, qui in facie aut oculis nostris hærent: ita plerique non vident quæ in ipsis vitiosa & reprehensione digna sunt. Imò vt multi cum deformissimi sint, cultu tamen aspectitio & fuco formā sibi ipsis conciliare studeant: Ita qui toti vitijs addicti & polluti sunt, mira arte illa tegere & occultare consueuerunt. Vtriq; ergo alijs opus habent, quispeculum Verbi Dei vel inuitis obtendant, qui fucum abstergant, larvam detrahant, & laterales quærentes ad Dei tribunal citent. Docet hoc Dauidis exemplum, qui cum turpi libidine thorum alienum polluisset, & ex adultero nefarius homicida atque populi Dei proditor factus esset, culpam tamen non agnouit, donec per Nathanam conuictus est. Hinc illa prophetarum libertas, quæ ex Dei mandato in sceleribus arguendis vsi sunt, & quorum imitatores Apostoli quoq; fuerunt. Atqui hoc illud est, quod totum Verbi ministerium mundo inuisum facit. Sed nihilominus pergere, & cum propheta dicere oportet: Leo si rugiat, quis non expauescat? Dominus Deus locutus est, quis non prophetet? Cui illud apostolicum conuenit: Oportet Deo magis obedire, quàm hominibus. Itaque ignaui fuci, & ministerij proditores sunt, qui ad scelera conniuent, cum scelerata colludunt, perpotant, voluptuantur, & ijsdem puluillos consuunt, quibus molliter indormiant. Vide Matth. 24. Ezech. 13.
units.tr: Moreover, this passage also teaches us the true use of prophecy. It is not a simple recitation and interpretation of the Scriptures but, as we heard at the beginning of this chapter, a application that is joined with exhortation and consolation for the edification of the whole Church and of each individual. It ought therefore to be exercised so that it penetrates the minds of hearers, convicts of sin (which Christ said would be the proper work of the Holy Spirit in the Apostles), and finally acts so that all understand it to be said of themselves. For the heart of man is deep and unsearchable, and those who have sinned most gravely almost make pleasures for themselves, so that they do not acknowledge their own crimes, or at least partly dissemble them. For just as we do not see the beams that stick in our face or eyes, so most people do not see what in themselves is faulty and worthy of reproof. Indeed, just as many who are very deformed nonetheless strive to win a good appearance for themselves by showy dress and paint, so those who are wholly given over and polluted by vices are accustomed to cover them with a wonderful art. Both therefore need others who will hold up the mirror of the Word of God even against their will, who will wipe off the paint, strip away the mask, and summon the crooked ones to God's judgement seat. David's example teaches this: when he had polluted another man's bed with shameful lust, and from an adulterer had become a wicked murderer and betrayer of God's people, he nonetheless did not acknowledge his guilt until he was convicted through Nathan. Hence came the freedom of the prophets, who by God's command used it in rebuking crimes, and whose imitators the Apostles also were. Yet this is precisely what makes the whole ministry of the Word hateful to the world. But one must nonetheless persist, and say with the prophet: "The lion has roared; who will not be afraid? The Lord God has spoken; who will not prophesy?" To this the apostolic saying applies: "We ought to obey God rather than men." Thus they are idle drones and traitors to the ministry who connive at crimes, who collude with wicked men, drink, indulge in pleasures, and sew cushions for the same men on which they sleep softly. See Matth. 24. Ezech. 13.

units.la: Postremò fui etiam officij auditores hic admonentur. Agnoscant illi de se agi, neque reluctentur conscientiæ, si quando hæc per Dei Verbum excitata illis scelera sua exprobrare incipit: quin potius confiteantur ea, vt Dauid, qui eo se quietem inuenisse & de peccatorum remissione certū fa-ctus fuisse testatur. Deinde prosternantur in faciem, id est, humiliter in conspectu Dei. Hoc enim gratissimum est sacrificium Deo, qui cor contritum & contritum (vt idem Dauid canit) non negliger. Et hæc vera contritio est, quæ non cilicijs, ieiunijs superstitiosis, aut chameunijs, sed cordis sanctatristitia atq; dolore secundū Deū (vt Pauli verbis vtar) constat. Tertiò Deū adorent, & huius seruitio se totos consecrent. Quod si fecerint, iam procul relictō mundo & huius studijs, Dei misericordiam atque gratiam implorabunt. Deniq; testentur Deū esse in sua Ecclesia, & ita publicum Veritati testimonium ferant. Hodie vtring; peccatur. Multi enim ex ministris non agunt seriò, qui vero hos iuuare & instigare debebant, illis etiam frigidiores sunt. Si qui vero aliquantulum feruent, ij plerisq; exosi sunt, nec multum proficiunt apud eos, quorum animos pessimorum affectuum præiudicia occupauerunt. Atqui ista ingratitudine & contumacia Deus maximè offenditur, & ideo fere linguis peregrinis loquitur, & concionatores adducit longè rigidiores, vt supra ex Isaia dictum est. Meminerimus ergo Verbi prædicationem non humanum commentum, sed ipsum Dei Filium, IESVM CHRISTVM, cum suo ministerio coniunctum esse, qui olim non temere dixerit: Qui vos audit, me audit: & qui vos reiicit, me reiicit: qui autem me reiicit, reiicit eum qui misit me. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Lastly, the hearers of the office are admonished here. Let them recognise that this is about them, and not resist their conscience if, whenever these things are stirred up by the Word of God, it begins to rebuke them for their sins. Rather, let them confess those sins, as David did, who testifies that he found rest in this and was made certain of the forgiveness of sins. Then let them fall down on their faces, that is, humble themselves in the sight of God. For this is the most acceptable sacrifice to God, who does not despise a broken and humbled heart (as David sings in the same place). This is true contrition, which consists not in sackcloth, superstitious fasts, or sleeping on the ground, but in holy sorrow and grief of heart according to God (to use the words of Paul). Third, let them worship God and consecrate themselves wholly to his service. If they do this, then, having left the world and its pursuits far behind, they will implore the mercy and grace of God. Finally, let them bear witness that God is in his Church, and so bear public testimony to the truth. Today both sides sin. For many of the ministers do not act in earnest, and those who ought to help and spur them on are even colder than they are. And if some do burn a little, these are for the most part hated, and they accomplish little among those whose minds have been taken over by the prejudices of the worst affections. Yet God is most greatly offended by this ingratitude and obstinacy, and therefore he speaks, for the most part, in foreign tongues, and brings in preachers far harsher, as was said above from Isaiah. Let us remember, then, that the preaching of the Word is not a human invention, but is joined to its ministry by Jesus Christ, the Son of God himself, who once said, not without reason: "He who hears you hears me, and he who rejects you rejects me; but he who rejects me rejects him who sent me." To him alone belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILIA LXXIIII.

units.la: Quid igitur est fratres? Quoties conuenitis, quisq; vestrum canticum habet, doctrinam habet, linguam habet, reuelationē habet, interpretationem habet, omnia ad ædificationē fiant. Siue lingua quis loquitur, fiat per binos, aut ad plurimum per ternos, & vicissim: vnus autem interpretetur. Quòd si non fit interpres, taceat in Ecclesia, sibi ipsi vero loquatur & Deo.
units.tr: What then is the case, brothers? Whenever you come together, each of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has a tongue, has a revelation, has an interpretation. Let all things be done for edification. If anyone speaks in a tongue, let it be done by two, or at most three, and in turn; and let one interpret. But if there is no interpreter, let him keep silent in the Church, and let him speak to himself and to God.

units.la: INter externa religionis exercitia nihil præstatius habet Ecclesia quàm sacros cœtus in quibus Verbum Dei prædicatur, Sacramenta administrantur & preces publicæ fiunt. Non absq; causa ergo Satan, qui hominum perditione gaudet, illis omni tempore insidiatus est, ut eos aut dissipa ret, aut ordinem eorum everteret. Olim enim tyrannos excitavit ex Regum & Imperatorum numero, qui gravibus edictis prohibuerunt, ne qui publicè convenirent: & illorum vestigiis multi etiā hodie insistunt, qui quovis supplicio dignum scelus esse putant, si qui cœtus agant, in quibus de vera religione disseritur. Satanæ item opus est, quod multi sublatis veræ pietatis & religionis exercitijs hominum figmenta inuehunt, quæ aut superstitioni aut vanissimæ oblectationi serviunt. Accedit hïs, quòd turbulentorum quorundam hominum intempestivis contentionibus nō raro in partes populus distrahitur, qui vno corde & vno ore Christū profiteri & colere debebat. Facta sunt hæc omnia a postolorum temporibus, & Exempli huius rei memorabile in Corinthijs habetur, qui cùm libertate aliqua præ alijs gentium Ecclesijs frueretur, ambitione et æmulatione mutua plurimum peccarunt. Fuit autè inter alia imprimis reprehensione dignum, quòd immodico & intempestiuo peregrinarum linguarum vsu prophetiā siue Verbi Dei interpretationem impediebant, qua nihil vtilius, nihil Ecclesiæ magis necessarium est. Ideo Paulus rem istam serio ac diligenter tractat: & hactenus quidem multis docuit, quantum incommodi ex isto abusu ad totam Ecclesiam, & ad singulos priuatim redundet, quàm item pueriliter totam religionem Christianam omnium ludibrijs exponant, & sibijpsis infamiam ponte accersant, dum intempestiuè nimis linguarum dono superbiunt. Istius nunc subijcit doctrinam, qua quicquid de sacris cœtibus rectè & bene instituendis dici potest, breuiter & dilucidè duobus capitibus complectitur: quorum altero finem omnium exercitiorum Ecclesiæ indicat, altero ordinem & formam siue rationem tradit, quam pij sectari in illis debeant.
units.tr: Among the external exercises of religion the Church has nothing more excellent than the sacred assemblies, in which the Word of God is preached, the sacraments are administered, and public prayers are offered. It is not without reason, then, that Satan, who delights in the destruction of men, has always lain in wait for them, to scatter them or to overturn their order. For in former times he raised up tyrants from among kings and emperors, who by severe edicts forbade anyone to gather publicly; and many today follow in their footsteps, who think it a crime deserving any punishment if people hold meetings at which true religion is discussed. It is also Satan's work that, with the exercises of true piety and religion abolished, many introduce human inventions, which serve either superstition or the emptiest amusement. In addition, the people are often divided into factions by the untimely quarrels of certain troublesome men, though they ought to profess and worship Christ with one heart and one mouth. All these things have happened since the time of the apostles, and a notable example of this is found in the Corinthians, who, while they enjoyed a certain liberty beyond the other churches of the Gentiles, sinned greatly through rivalry and mutual emulation. Among other things, it was especially worthy of rebuke that by an immoderate and untimely use of foreign tongues they hindered prophecy, that is, the interpretation of the Word of God, than which nothing is more useful or more necessary to the Church. Therefore Paul treats this matter seriously and carefully. Thus far he has shown at length how much harm from this abuse redounds to the whole Church and to individuals privately, and how childishly they expose the whole Christian religion to the mockery of all, and bring infamy upon themselves, while they vainly boast beyond measure of the gift of tongues. Now he sets out his teaching on this, and in two chapters he briefly and clearly embraces all that can rightly and well be said about the ordering of sacred assemblies: in the one he indicates the end of all the Church's exercises, and in the other he hands down the order and form, or rule, which the godly ought to follow in them.

units.la: Ad primum pertinet interrogatio, cui ipse mox respondet. Quid igitur est, fratres? Quasi diceret: Cùm non possitis negare, à vobis non vno modo esse peccatum, certè emendatione seria & reformatione matura opus erit: Quid ergo fieri oportebit? Ditam[?] paucis: Cùm conueniatis, quisque vestrū canticum habet, doctrinam habet, linguam habet, revelationem habet, interpretationem habet, omnia ad ædificationem fiant. Loquitur pro conditione eius sæculi, quando tanta erat inter credentes donorum Spiritus sancti ubertas, ut nemo in cœtus sacros veniret ἀσύμβολος, qui non aliquid in commune deponeret, quo alij possent ædificari. Oportebat enim ita fieri, ut magis commendaretur Noui testamenti gratia, & Christi Regnum inter mille obstacula, quæ Satan undique obijciebat, felicius propagaretur. Quàm verò iucundum fuisse putabimus spectaculum, quo pulcherrimum hoc saluberrimumque donorum suorum certamen Deus exhibebat? Hæc vtinam nobis reflituerent hodie, qui veterum cœtuum formam reducant[?], & cuius dicendi potestatem fieri volunt. Quid enim dicant hodie in publicis cœtibus, qui vix inter amicos priuatim de rebus sacris possunt paucissima effari, quin vel ignorantiam suam, vel balbutiem & infantiam prodant? Fateor quidem nostra culpa ex parte fieri, quòd minus liberaliter Spiritus dona in nos effunduntur, quando plerique in afferenda Dei gloria frigent: at simul non debet dissimulari, hodie non tanta illorum copia opus esse, quando Euangelij doctrina abundè satis confirmata est. Sed quia hæc alterius loci sunt, nunc Pauli verba excutiamus: qui ista sic proponit, ut tantum non protestetur, se dona ista nemini inuidere, neque hoc agere, ut ea ab Ecclesia explodantur, sed ut rectus & legitimus obseruetur illorum vsus, ne inani modo ostentationi, vel etiam æmulationi cæca seruiant. Hoc ergo vult dicere: Nō equidem improbo, quòd tam multis tamque præclaris donis instructi conueniunt, ut vnusquisque aliquid in commune afferat, neque alicui suam laudem inuideo: sed hoc solum moneo, ut vestri summul officij & communis salutis memores omnia faciatis ad ædificationem.
units.tr: To the first point belongs the question, which he himself immediately answers: What then is the case, brothers? As if he were saying: Since you cannot deny that you have sinned in more ways than one, there will certainly need to be serious amendment and mature reformation. What then ought to be done? To put it briefly: When you come together, each of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has a tongue, has a revelation, has an interpretation; let all things be done for edification. He speaks in accordance with the condition of that age, when there was such an abundance of the gifts of the Holy Spirit among believers that no one came to the sacred assemblies empty-handed, without contributing something to the common good by which others could be built up. For it was fitting that it should happen in this way, so that the grace of the New Testament might be more commended, and the kingdom of Christ, amid the countless obstacles which Satan threw up on every side, might be propagated more happily. And how delightful we may suppose that spectacle was, in which God displayed this most beautiful and most wholesome contest of his gifts! Would that those who wish to restore the form of the old assemblies, and to give them the power of speaking, would today return these gifts to us! For what would they say today in public meetings, who can scarcely utter a few words in private among friends about sacred things without betraying either their ignorance or their stammering and infancy?
