I admit that in part it is our own fault that the gifts of the Spirit are poured out upon us less generously, since most people grow cold in proclaiming the glory of God; but at the same time it ought not to be overlooked that today there is no need of so great an abundance of such gifts, since the doctrine of the Gospel has been amply confirmed. But since these matters belong to another place, let us now examine Paul's words, who sets this out in such a way that he almost protests that he begrudges these gifts to no one, and that he is not aiming at their being cast out of the Church, but that their right and lawful use be observed, so that they do not serve empty display or even blind rivalry. So he means this: I do not indeed disapprove that people endowed with so many and such excellent gifts come together, so that each one brings something for the common good, nor do I begrudge anyone his praise; but I only warn you that, mindful of your mutual duty and the common salvation, you do all things for edification.

units.la: Discimus igitur hoc loco, quis omnium, quæ in Ecclesia fiunt, finis siue scopus esse debeat: Ædificatio nimirum, quam toto hoc Cap. vrget Apostolus. Ea autem in hoc consistit, ut omnes proficiant in cognitione IESV CHRISTI ac veræ fidei, vtq; noui quotidie discipuli accedant, & qui iam ante crediderunt, magis confirmentur. Ita enim ceu viui lapides (vt Petri verbis vtar) coalescunt omnes in domum illam spiritualem, quam Deus ipse inhabitare dignatur. Obseruabis autem particulam, Vnusquisq; vestrum. Est enim hic scopus vnicus & communis omnibus, ad quem omnes loci & ordines homines collimare debent, non soli Verbi administri, quos Scriptura huius sanctissimi ædificij architectos dicere confuerit, vt alibi diximus. Ergo ad magistratus quoq; & principes haec cura pertinet, quorum haec praecipua gloria est, quod Deus illos Ecclesiae suae nutritios constituit: quo officio tunc demum probe fungentur, si curent vt sarta tecta maneat ea aedificij huius forma, quam nobis Apostoli, veri illi Bezaleeles, ab ipso Christo traditam reliquerunt. Possunt hic etiam plurim&um praestare patresfamilias, si priuatim domum suam fideliter instituant, imprimis autem liberos suos, quos merito Ecclesiae seminarium dixeris. Extant de hoc praecepta Dei, quae alibi recitauimus. Et in eo diligentissimos fuisse scimus sanctos patres, qui prolis studio & amore hanc ob causam potissimum arserunt, quod quam plurimos ex se nasci cuperent, qui veri Dei cultores essent, & per quos huius cognitio atque cultus ad posteritatem perfutura quoque saecula propagaretur. Sed & priuatim hoc Dei aedificium iuuare possunt, qui cum amicis, cum hospitibus, cum quibusuis obuijs data occasione de religione differunt, qui errantes in viam reuocant, peccatis deditos ad poenitentiam hortantur. Imprimis tamen in coetibus sacris hoc obseruari debet, vbi non aliud quam Christi & Ecclesiae negotium agitur. Ex quo etiam hoc colligi potest, nihil in illis fieri aut ferri debere, quod ad aedificationem aliorum non faciat. Quod vnum argumentum suf-ficiet pijs contra imagines in templis prostantes, contra theatricum Missa spectaculum, contra lectiones Latinas, contra cantum artificialem siue compositum, organorum concentum, suffitus, lampades, cerea, & sexcenta alia, quae vel oculos solos pascunt, vel aures delinunt, ad solidam veram pietatem nihil conferunt.
units.tr: Let us learn from this passage, then, what the end or aim of all that is done in the Church ought to be: namely edification, which the Apostle urges throughout this whole chapter. This consists in all making progress in the knowledge of Jesus Christ and of true faith, and in new disciples being added daily, and in those who had already believed being more strongly confirmed. For thus, like living stones (to use Peter's words), all are joined together into that spiritual house which God himself deigns to dwell in. Note the phrase, each one of you. For this is the one aim, common to all, toward which all men of every place and rank ought to aim, not only the ministers of the Word, whom Scripture is accustomed to call the architects of this most holy building, as we have said elsewhere. Therefore this care pertains also to the magistrates and princes, whose chief glory it is that God has appointed them nursing fathers of his Church; they will discharge this office properly only if they take care that the form of this building remains whole and intact, which the apostles, those true Bezalels, have handed down to us as received from Christ himself. Heads of households too can contribute very much here, if they faithfully order their own houses in private, and above all their children, whom you may rightly call the seminary of the Church. The precepts of God on this have been recited by us elsewhere. And we know that the holy fathers were most diligent in this, who burned especially for this reason with a zeal and love for offspring, because they desired that as many as possible born of them should be worshippers of the true God, and through whom the knowledge and worship of him might be propagated to posterity, to endure for ages to come. But private persons too can help this building of God, who, when occasion offers, discuss religion with friends, with guests, with whomever they meet, who call back those who go astray into the way, and exhort those given to sin to repentance. Above all, however, this must be observed in the sacred assemblies, where nothing but the business of Christ and the Church is transacted. From this it can also be gathered that nothing ought to be done or brought in those assemblies which does not serve the edification of others. This one argument will suffice for the godly against images standing in the churches, against the theatrical spectacle of the Mass, against Latin readings, against artificial or composed singing, the harmony of organs, incense, lamps, wax candles, and six hundred other things, which either only feed the eyes or tickle the ears, and contribute nothing to solid and true piety.

units.la: Deinde obseruabis etiam hoc loco, quae nam illa sint, quae a Paulo commemorantur ceu instrumenta huius aedificationis. Primo Psalmos nominat. Erant enim tunc, qui non propha-no obscaenorum poetarum furore, sed vere diuino spiritu agitati hoc dono pollebant, vt hymnos & cantica meditarentur, quibus & Dei laudes praedicabant, & animos auditorum ad alacri-tatem in obeundo veri Dei cultu accendebant, conscientias item afflictas consolabantur. Et hoc Spiritus sancti opus esse, in Dauide apparet & pluribus aliis Veteris testamenti prophetis: quibus ex Nouo recte Zachariam, Simeonem, Matrem virginem & alios connumerauerit, de quibus in praesenti Paulus loquitur. Arguunt autem veterum exempla nostri saeculi poetastros, qui non horum vestigijs insistunt, sed tunc demum ex sua poësi laudem eximiam sibi pollicentur, si veterum Graecorum & Latinorum poetarum obscaenitatem vincant: eos item, qui linguis vulgaribus cantiones fingunt de impuris atque illicitis amoribus, de stuprii item & adulterijs, quae inter Christianos ne nominari quidem debebant. Secundo loco doctrina ponitur, per quam ipsa docendi facultas, vel etiam dogma aliquod intelligi potest, quod pro temporis ratione clari-us explicari & illustrari necesse erat. Nam licet certa & perspicua sint fidei capita & axiomata religionis Christianae, saepe tamen casus incidit, in quo admonitione & doctrina siue institutione peculiari opus est. Tertio lingua nominatur, ipsum videlicet donum linguae alicuius peregrinae: de quo nunc plura dicere superuacuum esset, cum toto fere hoc Cap. de illo differatur. Quartum locum Reuelatio habet, quae nimirum peculiari aliquo Spiritus sancti motu siue operatione fit, cuius exemplum in Agabi vaticinio extat, quo Ecclesiam de fame sub Claudio futura admonuit. Idem Pauli quoque vincula praedixit, quibus illum Iudaei conflicturi essent. Erat autem hoc quoq; donum illo tempore admodum necessarium propter hostium crebras insidias & infinita pericula, quibus Ecclesia tunc obnoxia erat. Quinto subiicitur Interpretatio, quae tam ad linguas quam ad obscuriores Scripturae locos potest referri, de qua alibi quoq; dixi-mus, & plura paulo post sequentur. Sunt autem insuper alia dona Spiritus sancti, sed Paulo in praesenti satis fuit praecipua & quae magis communia erant recensere, sub quibus reliqua om-nia comprehendit.
units.tr: Next, observe also at this point what those things are which Paul mentions as the instruments of this edification. First he names psalms. For there were then men who, moved not by the profane frenzy of obscene poets but by a truly divine Spirit, excelled in this gift, so that they meditated on hymns and canticles, by which they proclaimed the praises of God, kindled the minds of the hearers to eagerness in rendering the worship of the true God, and likewise comforted afflicted consciences. That this is a work of the Holy Spirit appears in David and in many other prophets of the Old Testament; to these from the New one may rightly add Zechariah, Simeon, the Virgin Mother, and others, of whom Paul is speaking at present. The examples of the ancients, however, expose the versifiers of our own age, who do not follow in their footsteps but promise themselves extraordinary praise from their poetry only if they surpass the obscenity of the old Greek and Latin poets; and likewise those who compose songs in the vulgar tongues about impure and unlawful loves, and about debauchery and adultery, which ought not even to be named among Christians. In the second place, teaching is set down, by which is meant the very faculty of teaching, or also some doctrine, which had to be explained and illustrated more clearly according to the needs of the time. For although the articles of faith and the axioms of the Christian religion are certain and plain, yet it often happens that a particular admonition and instruction is needed. Third, tongue is named, that is, the very gift of some foreign language; to say more about this now would be superfluous, since almost this whole chapter treats of it. The fourth place is held by revelation, which certainly comes about by some particular motion or operation of the Holy Spirit; an example of this is found in the prophecy of Agabus, by which he warned the Church of the coming famine under Claudius. He likewise foretold Paul's chains, with which the Jews were about to assail him. Moreover, this gift was at that time also very necessary, on account of the frequent plots of enemies and the endless dangers to which the Church was then exposed. Fifth is added interpretation, which may refer both to tongues and to the more obscure passages of Scripture; we have also spoken of this elsewhere, and more will follow a little later. There are, moreover, other gifts of the Holy Spirit; but for the present Paul was content to recount the chief and more common ones, under which he comprehends all the rest.

units.la: Et rursus debent ista diligentius obseruari propter eos, qui sub praetextu aedificationis quidam obtrudunt hominibus imperitis, & ea quoque ad iustum finem instituti posse clamitant, quorum nulla vspiam in Scripturis fit mentio. Hoc enim sophismate imagines, cerea, ipsam denique Missam & omnia alia tuentur, quae paulo ante recitauimus. At non dicit Paulus: Quoties conuenitis, vnusquisque imaginem habet, cereum habet, Missam habet, Requiem canit pro defunctis, Litaniam habet, &c. Nam quia Ecclesia super Christum solum fundatur, & non nisi ex Verbi Dei semine nascitur, nunquam poterit ad eius ædificationem facere, quod à Verbi doctrina alienum est. Quotquot vero eiusmodi commenta ad ædificium illud attulerunt, ij si non perfidi, saltem inepti illi & ridiculi architecti sunt, de quibus Cap. tertio diximus, qui cum Christi nomen profitentur, & Apostolos atque Prophetas in ore habeant, super fundamentu tamen, quod illi posuerunt, stipulas, arundines, ligna putria, vetustate exesos lapides, aut arena quoq; sine calce cogerunt. Nobis ergo sufficiant, quæ Apostolis sufficientia & vere idonea visa sunt.
units.tr: And again these things must be observed more carefully on account of those who, under the pretext of edification, force certain things upon unlearned people, and loudly claim that such things also serve a just end of the institution, though nothing of them is anywhere mentioned in the Scriptures. For by this sophistry they defend images, wax candles, the Mass itself and all the other things we recited a little earlier. But Paul does not say: "Whenever you come together, each one has an image, has a wax candle, has a Mass, sings a Requiem for the dead, has a Litany," and so on. For since the Church is founded on Christ alone, and is born only from the seed of the Word of God, it can never do anything for its edification that is foreign to the doctrine of the Word. As for all those who have brought such inventions to that building, if they are not treacherous, they are at least foolish and ridiculous architects, of whom we spoke in the third chapter, who, while they profess the name of Christ and have the Apostles and Prophets on their lips, nevertheless build upon the foundation they have laid straw, reeds, rotten wood, stones eaten away by age, or even sand without lime. Let those things suffice for us which seemed sufficient and truly fit to the Apostles.

units.la: Cæterum non satis est ea in Ecclesiam afferre, quæ proprie & vere ad huius ædificationem faciunt, nisi eadem recto & legitimo ordine proponantur, ut huic scopo possint convenire. Ideo applicat nunc doctrinam istam ijs, quæ tunc præcipua erant, Linguis nimirum & Prophetiæ, ostendens quomodo utroque uti debeant. De linguis sic præcipit: Siue lingua, id est idiomate peregrino quis loquitur, fiat per binos, aut, &c. Quo loco ante omnia obseruabis, Paulum conditionaliter loqui, ut doceat, quid debeat fieri, si omnino velint linguis uti, non autem expressè iubere vel mandare ut illis loquantur. Potest enim Ecclesia fidem habere puram & sanctam, singuli item seruari possunt, etiamsi nemo sit, qui linguarum peregrinarum cognitionem atque usum habeat. Non enim in sermone situm est Regnum Dei, sed in virtute. Verumtamen quia tunc doni illius usus erat non contemnendus quoad Apostolos, qui illo non poterant carere, deinde quoad infirmiores in fide, quos signis & miraculis confirmari oportebat, denique singulare ornamentum Ecclesiæ & publicum testimonium erat, quo Deus significabat, se totius negotij Euangelici esse authorem, nequaquam contemni siue explodi debuit. Ideo illud in medio relinquit Paulus, & Corinthijs libertatem facit, ut in suis cœtibus doni illius usum exerceant, seu minus, prout sibi utile fore putent. Quia vero hucusq; peccauerat ambitione, et tempus inutiliter consumpserant, quod exercitijs magis necessarijs debuerat impendi, certam formam siue modu præscribit, quem sequantur, & hunc tribus regulis comprehendit. Prima est, ne plures loquantur quam duo aut tres. Quia enim tunc vulgare admodum erat donum istud, si omnes linguis loqui voluissent, qui poterant, totum illud tempus cœtuum sacrorum illis oportuisset tribuere, & ita populus absque fructu discedere sit. Altera ut per vices loquantur, ne videlicet confusio fiat: quæ non poterat cauere, si multis simul dicendi potestas detur. Imo hoc illud erat propter quod Christiani furere putabantur ijs, qui Deigratiam in illis agentem non agnoscebant. Tertia, ut quod lingua peregrina dictum est, aliquis interpretetur. Nam nisi id fiat, nullus ex eo ad Ecclesiam potest fructus redire. Ideo mox diuersis verbis subijcit Apostolus: Quod si non fit interpres, taceat in Ecclesia: Nimirum hoc volens, ne quis peregrino & alijs incognito idiomate obstrepat ijs, qui circa meliora occupati sunt. Et ne quis obijceret: Ergo ne sepelire debeo donum Dei? per correctionem addit: Sibijpsi vero loquatur & Deo. Id est, penes se intra animum suum meditetur quacunque lingua velit, quod ad pietatem & religionis exercitium facere putauerit, & Deo gratias agat, proq; fidei incremento oret.
units.tr: Moreover, it is not enough to bring into the Church those things which properly and truly serve its edification, unless they are set forth in a right and lawful order, so that they can agree with this aim. Therefore Paul now applies this doctrine to those things which were then prominent, namely tongues and prophecy, showing how each should be used. Concerning tongues he instructs thus: "If anyone speaks in a tongue, that is, in a foreign language, let it be done by two, or," etc. In this place you will observe above all that Paul speaks conditionally, so that he may teach what ought to be done if they should wish to use tongues at all, and does not expressly command or order them to speak in tongues. For the Church can have a pure and holy faith, and individuals can likewise be preserved, even if there is no one who has knowledge and use of foreign languages. For the Kingdom of God does not consist in speech but in power. Nevertheless, since the use of that gift was not to be despised as far as the Apostles were concerned, who could not do without it, and then as far as the weaker in faith were concerned, who had to be confirmed by signs and miracles, and finally since it was a singular ornament of the Church and a public testimony by which God showed that he was the author of the whole Gospel business, it ought by no means to have been despised or rejected. Therefore Paul leaves that matter undecided and gives the Corinthians freedom to exercise the use of that gift in their assemblies, or less, as they think useful for themselves. But because until now they had sinned through ambition, and had uselessly consumed time that ought to have been spent on more necessary exercises, he prescribes a certain form or manner which they should follow, and he comprises this in three rules. The first is that not more than two or three should speak. For since that gift was then quite common, if all who could speak in tongues had wished to do so, the whole time of the sacred assemblies would have had to be given to them, and so the people would depart without profit. The second is that they should speak in turn, so that confusion does not arise, which could not be guarded against if the power of speaking were granted to many at once. Indeed, this was precisely why Christians were thought to be mad by those who did not recognize the grace of God working in them. The third is that what has been said in a foreign tongue should be interpreted by someone. For unless this is done, no fruit can return from it to the Church. Therefore the Apostle immediately adds in different words: "But if there is no interpreter, let him keep silent in the Church," clearly wishing that no one should drown out, with a foreign language unknown to others, those who are occupied with better things. And lest anyone should object: "Then ought I to bury the gift of God?" he adds by way of correction: "But let him speak to himself and to God." That is, let him meditate inwardly within himself, in whatever tongue he likes, on whatever he thinks will serve piety and the exercise of religion, and let him give thanks to God and pray for the increase of faith.

units.la: Quod si ad has Pauli regulas examines quæ in Papatu fiunt, vix quicquam videbis quod apostolicum dici mereatur. Nec enim contenti sunt linguam peregrinam inuexisse, sed insuper multi simul canunt, & plerumque artificio tam vario & volubili, ut ne ab ijs quidem verba percipi possint, qui linguam Latinam probè nouerunt. Similiter in eodem templo multi simul eodem tempore Missas suas faciunt, ut sæpe vix apud se aliqui constituere possint, quem nam præ alijs spectare siue audire debeant. Et omnia ista sine interprete faciunt, & plerunque tanta est sacrificulorum & Monachorum inscitia, ut seipsos non intelligant. Istis vero ineptijs tempus ita teritur, ut tandem populus absque omni doctrina & consolatione dimittatur. Quis ergo hos Apostolorum successores dixerit, qui tam manifestos abusus pertinaciter tuentur? Quis non populi infelicis calamitatem deploret, qui ab istis quasi nasò suspenditur, & superstitionibus non minus ineptis quam noxijs delectatur?
units.tr: If you test what is done in Papacy by these rules of Paul, you will scarcely see anything that deserves to be called apostolic. For they are not content to have introduced a foreign tongue, but moreover many sing together at once, and mostly with such varied and rapid artifice that the words cannot even be perceived by those who know the Latin tongue well. Likewise, in the same temple, many perform their Masses together at the same time, so that often some can scarcely decide for themselves which of the others they ought to look at or listen to. And they do all these things without an interpreter, and for the most part such is the ignorance of the little sacrificers and monks that they do not understand themselves. By these follies time is so wasted that at last the people are dismissed without any teaching or consolation. Who, then, would call these the successors of the Apostles, who stubbornly defend such manifest abuses? Who would not lament the calamity of the unhappy people, who are held in suspense by these men as if by the nose, and delight in superstitions no less foolish than harmful?

units.la: Sed priusquam dicendi finem faciamus, discere nos conuenit hoc loco, quid fieri debet, si quando donis, quæ nobis à Deo collata sunt, non licet in publico uti? Non ideo illa abijcere, aut in terram defodere debemus, sicuti de ignauo illo & malæ frugis seruo Christus loquitur. Multo minus autem animum despondere aut contra Dei murmurare debemus. Hoc enim superbi et ambitiosi lent,qui sibi intolerabilem iniuriam fieri arbitrantur, si nulla sese occasio offerat, qua fortitudi-nem aut peritiam & potentiam suam ostentent, alijs interim multa cum laude triumphantibus. Talis olim Alexander Macedo fuit, qui ob patris Philippi victorias animo discruciabatur, quòd timeret, eum nihil sibi reliquum facturum esse, in quo facinus aliquod magnum & memorabi-le aederet. Et Cæsare illachrymatuisse scribunt visis Alexandri statuis, & lectis eius gestis, quòd se iam prætergressum illius ætatem nihil adhuc fecisse cogitaret, quod cum illius virtute posset co-ferri. At longe alia piorum mens est. Hi enim Deo sese gratos præbent pro acceptis ab illo beneficiis: & si his non aliter uti possunt, pia eorum meditatione seipsos recreant, & in omnem occasionem parati sunt, ut per illa omnibus prosint, nemini autem noceant. Fit ergo, ut dona sua apud tales Deus nequaquam intermori aut perire patiatur, & sæpe præter omnem expectationem pulcherrimas illis utendi occasiones ipsis offerat, quibus illi sic utuntur, ut aperta inde referant fidei & industriæ suæ testimonia, & tandem in gaudium Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI admissi, cum eodem vivant & regnent. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But before we make an end of speaking, it is fitting for us to learn in this place what ought to be done if, at any time, the gifts that have been bestowed upon us by God may not be used in public? We ought not on that account to cast them away or bury them in the ground, as Christ speaks of that idle and unprofitable servant. Much less ought we to lose heart or murmur against God. For this is what the proud and ambitious do, who think they suffer an intolerable injury if no occasion presents itself by which they may display their courage, skill and power, while others in the meantime triumph with great praise. Such was once Alexander of Macedon, who was tormented in mind by the victories of his father Philip, because he feared that his father would leave him nothing to do by which he might perform some great and memorable deed. And they write that Caesar wept when he saw the statues of Alexander and read his deeds, because he thought that he had already passed the age of Alexander and had done nothing yet that could be compared with his valour. But the mind of the godly is quite different. For they show themselves grateful to God for the benefits received from him; and if they cannot use these gifts in any other way, they refresh themselves by pious meditation, and they are ready for every opportunity to benefit all by these gifts, but to harm no one. Thus it comes about that God does not allow their gifts to die out or perish in such people, and often, beyond all expectation, offers them most splendid occasions of using them, which they so use that they bring back from them open testimonies of their faith and diligence, and at last, admitted into the joy of our Lord Jesus Christ, they live and reign with him. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXV.
units.tr: HOMILY LXXV.

units.la: Prophetæ autē duo aut tres loquantur & alij dijudicent. Quòd si quid alij patefactum fuerit assidenti, prior taceat. Potestis enim sigillatim omnes prophetare, ut omnes discant, & omnes consolationem accipiant: Et spiritus prophetarum prophetis subiiciuntur. Non enim est confusionis author Deus, sed pacis, ut in omnibus Ecclesiis sanctorum.
units.tr: "Let the prophets speak, two or three, and let the others judge. But if anything is revealed to another who is sitting by, let the first keep silent. For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all may be comforted. And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets. For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all the churches of the saints."

units.la: Postquam Paulus ambitionem Corinthiorum, qua donis spiritualibus, & imprimis quidē linguis & prophetia abutebantur, graviter corripuit, concludit tandē totâ istam tractatione generali doctrina, qua docet, quis ipsis omnium donorum finis esse debeat, & quæ vera atque tutissima sit illis rectè utendi ratio. Finem verò omnibus propositū esse vult, ædificatione. Quia enim nō nobis solū nati, adhæc eiusdē corporis membra sumus, in commune debet deponi quicquid nobis à Deo datur. Deinde de usu et exercitio linguarum paucis disseruit, ita tamen, ut abunde comprehendat, quæcunque de illo dici possunt. Nunc ad prophetandi ratione accedit, quæ diligentius inspici debet propter Anabaptistas, qui hodie veterem illam formam reductam volunt, & nisi ea restituatur, sed iustam & grauem causam habere arbitrantur, ut ab Ecclesiis nostris secessionem faciant.
units.tr: After Paul had severely rebuked the Corinthians' ambition, by which they abused the spiritual gifts, and especially tongues and prophecy, he finally concludes this whole discussion with a general teaching. He shows what the true end of all the gifts ought to be, and what the surest way of using them rightly is. He wills that the end proposed for all of them be edification. For since we are not born for ourselves alone, and are moreover members of the same body, whatever is given to us by God ought to be laid down for the common good. Next he has briefly discussed the use and exercise of tongues, yet in such a way that he fully covers everything that can be said about them. Now he comes to the manner of prophesying, which must be examined more carefully on account of the Anabaptists, who today want that old form brought back, and who think that unless it is restored they have a just and serious reason for separating from our churches.

units.la: Obseruari autem ante omnia debet, quod quid fieri debeat, simpliciter docet Apostolus, neque hic quicquam illorum arbitrio liberum permittit, ut prius fecerat, quando de linguis & earū usu locutus est. Ibi enim in medio quasi reliquit, ut illis utantur, seu non utantur. In præsenti autem & in tota hac tractatione de prophetia sic disserit, ut necessario eam exerceri debere doceat. Causam si quæras, ea in promptu est: quia sine doctrina, quæ exhortationem & consolationem comprehendit, neq; Ecclesia aliqua colligi, neque prius collecta gubernari & conservari potest. Quod sapientissimus ille Regum observans, dixit: Cessante prophetia dissipatur populus. Vult ergo Paulus ut prophetent Corinthij; imò ut id omnes possent in votis habuit, quemadmodum Moses olim, qui inconsultum Iosuæ sui zelum reprimens dicebat: Quis det ut omnis populus prophetet, & det Dominus spiritum suum super eos? Præscribit autem Paulus diligenter ordinem & modum prophetandi, & ita quidem hunc tradit, ut & confusionem omnem declinet, & simul suam Ecclesiæ libertatem tueatur, neque tanti tamque necessarij doni effectum siue fructum impediat. Nos singula ex ordine examinemus.
units.tr: First of all it must be observed that the Apostle teaches simply what ought to be done, and here he leaves nothing to the choice of individuals, as he had done before when he spoke of tongues and their use. There he left matters, as it were, in the middle, so that people might use them or not. But in the present passage and in this whole discussion of prophecy he argues in such a way that he teaches it must necessarily be exercised. If you ask the reason, it lies close at hand: without teaching, which includes exhortation and comfort, no church can be gathered, and once gathered it cannot be governed and preserved. The wisest of kings observed this and said: "Where there is no prophecy, the people is scattered." Paul therefore wants the Corinthians to prophesy; indeed he wished that all might be able to do so, just as Moses did long ago, who, restraining the ill-considered zeal of his Joshua, said: "Would that all the people prophesied, and that the Lord would put his Spirit upon them!" Paul prescribes carefully the order and manner of prophesying, and he hands it down in such a way that he both avoids all confusion and at the same time protects the liberty of the Church, without hindering the effect or fruit of so great and so necessary a gift. Let us examine the particulars one by one.

units.la: Primò, qui nam munus hoc obire debeant, docet. Prophetæ autem (inquit) duo aut tres loquantur. Non ait, duo aut tres ex Ecclesia loquantur: sed Prophetas nominat, de ijs nimirum loquens, qui dono prophetiæ instructi, & ab Ecclesia legitimè ad docendi munus ordinati sunt. Fuisse enim Prophetas in Ecclesia ordinarios ministros, à communi credentium turbadistinctos[?], alibi diserte docet, quando ait, Christum alios quidem dedisse Apostolos, alios vero Prophetas, &c. Porrò hos quoque ad certum numerum astringit, ne si plures ad dicendum fur-gant, confusio oriatur, & populus diutius quàm par est fatigetur. Obseruabis autem Apostolum loqui pro illorum temporum conditione, quando Christiani ethnicis permixti habitabant, imò magistratibus ethnicis & à fide alienis subiecti erant, & ideo propter pericula, quae ex hostium fi-dei insidijs nunquam non ipsis imminebant, non poterant frequentius conuenire in coetum sacrum. Itaque si quando sese occasio offerret, tunc per horas aliquot conuentus illi extrahebantur, & sepe totam noctem aut diem durabant, ut videre est in iis, quae de coetu Troadis habito in Actis scri-buntur. Quare necesse erat, ut plures essent, qui per vices verba facerent aut docerent, quia unus non potuisset solus tot horis sufficere. Ij vero non difficulter haberi poterant in tanta, quae tunc erat, donorum Spiritus ubertate: quando (ut Ioel fore praedixerat) ille liberalissime ef-fundebatur, & passim in omni aetate & sexu inueniebantur, qui prophetandi dono erant in-structi. Vbi simul hoc quoque obseruatum fuit, ut quoties in coetum Christiani conuenirent, cer-ti aliqui deligerentur, qui tunc docendi vices obirent: & ne quis negligeretur, modò hoc modò illis partes istae dabantur. Quem morem suo adhuc saeculo seruatum fuisse, Theodoretus scri-bit, ut ex ordinarijs Ecclesiae doctoribus alij quidem in hac concione, alij in alia ad popu-lum loquerentur. Quae ideò monemus, ne quis hodie quoque pluribus ministris putet opus esse, & plures ex ordine ad docendum surgere debere, quando ordinarij coetus in urbibus & a-lijs locis frequentiores, vel etiam quotidiani habentur, & difficile sit populum ultra unius horae spatium in templis detinere. Nunc autem hoc loco praecipuè obseruabis, Paulum docendi partes Prophetis tribuere, id est, ordinarijs, & legitimis Ecclesiae ministris, nec velle ut quiuis temere ad dicendum prorumpat. Nam si hoc permittatur, iam superuacanea & prorsus inutilia sunt, quaecunque de missione & vocatione ministrorum tam in Veteri quàm Nouo testamento dicuntur.
units.tr: First, he teaches who ought to discharge this office. "Let the prophets," he says, "speak, two or three." He does not say "let two or three from the church speak," but names the prophets, plainly speaking of those who, instructed with the gift of prophecy and lawfully appointed by the Church to the office of teaching. That there were prophets in the Church as ordinary ministers, set apart from the common body of believers, he teaches clearly elsewhere, where he says that Christ gave some apostles, and some prophets, and so on. Moreover, he also limits these to a fixed number, lest if many rose to speak, confusion should arise and the people be wearied longer than is fitting. You will observe, however, that the Apostle speaks according to the circumstances of those times, when Christians lived mixed with pagans, indeed were subject to pagan magistrates who were foreign to the faith, and therefore, because of the dangers which never ceased to threaten them from the snares of the enemies of the faith, they could not meet in the holy assembly more often. So whenever an opportunity offered itself, those gatherings were prolonged for some hours, and often lasted a whole night or day, as can be seen in what is written in Acts about the assembly held at Troas. Hence it was necessary that there be several who would speak or teach in turn, since one alone could not have sufficed for so many hours. Such men could be found without difficulty in that abundance of the gifts of the Spirit which then prevailed, when (as Joel had foretold) the Spirit was poured out most bountifully, and everywhere, in every age and sex, there were those who were instructed in the gift of prophecy. Here it was also observed that whenever Christians came together in assembly, certain men were chosen who then took their turns at teaching, and so that no one should be neglected, these duties were given now to one, now to another. Theodoret writes that this custom was still kept in his own age, so that of the ordinary teachers of the Church, some spoke to the people in this assembly, others in another. We note this so that no one may think today too that several ministers are needed, and that several must rise in turn to teach, when ordinary gatherings are held more frequently in cities and other places, or even daily, and it is difficult to keep the people in the churches beyond the space of one hour. But here you should observe especially that Paul assigns the teaching to the prophets, that is, to the ordinary and lawful ministers of the Church, and does not want anyone to rush forward rashly to speak. For if this were permitted, then everything that is said in both the Old and the New Testament about the sending and calling of ministers would be superfluous and altogether useless.

units.la: Secundò quid alij faciant, indicat. Alij dijudicent (inquit) num ex Dei Verbo deprompta sit, quae à Prophetis proponitur, doctrina. Id verò factu imprimis necessarium est. Primum, quia Satan mille artifex sese in Angelum lucis transformare potest. Deinde, quia nihil tam vulgare est, quàm quod impostores Dei nomen atque Spiritum praetexunt. Sic olim pseudoprophetae Achabi & Iezabelis temporibus, quando tanta fuit Zedechiae impostoris temeritas, ut Michaeam diuersa à se dicentem in faciem percuteret, adiectis his verbis: Quà nam transiuit Spiritus Domini à me, ut tibi loqueretur? Et apud Ieremiam de illis queritur Dominus, qui quasi ab eo in consilium admissi essent, populo pacem pollicebantur, quem ipse iam gladio & exilio destinauerat. Quid verò nobis hodie sperandum sit, Christus ipse docuit, quando praedixit nouissimis temporibus pseudoprophetas & pseudochristos exituros esse, qui plurimos seducturi sint. Sed aliud quoque periculum est, quod nos cautos & prouidos esse cogit: Nimirum quòd sancti quoque & fideles Dei serui interdum falluntur & errant, quando affectibus suis indulgent, & zelo abrepti sua consilia praecipitant. Exemplum eius rei memorabile in Nathano habemus, qui quod de templo aedificando Dauidi dederat consilium, eadem hora reuocare iussus est, quòd illud inconsulto Domino, suum modò zelum per se bonum & sanctum secutus dedisset. Magna etiam timoris & aliorum affectuum vis est, à quibus ne sancti quidem liberi sunt: qui etiamsi non errent in dogmatibus fidei, in aliis tamen, quae ad Ecclesiae gubernationem pertinent, non raro fallūtur. Quapropter necesse omnino est, ut doctrinae dijudicentur, & extant ea de re alibi quoque prae-cepta apostolica. In priori enim ad Thessalonicen. scribit Apostolus: Prophetias ne pro ni-hilo habeatis: omnia explorate, quod bonum est tenete. Et notum est illud Ioannis: Dilecti, ne cuiuis spiritui credatis, sed probate spiritus, an ex Deo sint. Sunt autem hic quaedam di-ligentius excutienda.
units.tr: Second, he shows what the others are to do. "Let the others judge" (he says), whether the teaching put forward by the prophets is drawn from the Word of God. This is indeed especially necessary. First, because Satan, the master of a thousand tricks, can transform himself into an angel of light. Next, because nothing is so common as impostors pretending the name and Spirit of God. Thus long ago, in the times of Ahab and Jezebel, the false prophets, when the impostor Zedekiah had such boldness that he struck Micaiah, who was saying things contrary to himself, in the face, adding these words: "By what way did the Spirit of the Lord pass from me to speak to you?" And in Jeremiah the Lord complains of those who, as if they had been admitted into his counsel, promised peace to the people whom he himself had already doomed to the sword and exile. What we are to expect today Christ himself taught, when he foretold that in the last times false prophets and false christs would arise, who would lead many astray. But there is another danger too, which compels us to be cautious and watchful: namely, that even the holy and faithful servants of God sometimes are deceived and err, when they indulge their feelings and, carried away by zeal, rush headlong with their plans. We have a memorable example of this in Nathan, who was ordered to recall at once the advice he had given David about building the temple, because he had given it following his own zeal, which was good and holy in itself, without consulting the Lord. There is also a great power of fear and of other passions, from which not even the saints are free: and although they may not err in the doctrines of faith, yet in other matters, which pertain to the government of the Church, they are not seldom mistaken. Therefore it is altogether necessary that doctrines be judged, and the apostolic precepts on this matter are found elsewhere too. For in the first letter to the Thessalonians the Apostle writes: "Do not despise prophecies; test all things, hold fast to what is good." And the well-known saying of John is familiar: "Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are from God." But there are certain points here that must be examined more carefully.

units.la: Primum, qui nam doctrinas dijudicare aut probare debeat? Nam alij quod in praesenti dicitur, ad eos solos restringunt, qui & ipsi Prophetae sunt, aut donis peculiaribus instructi in Ecclesia prae aliis excellunt. In qua sententia ex veteribus Theodoretus fuit, qui dijudicandi officium ad eos pertinere scribit, qui donum habent discretionis, quod peculiare & non omnibus commune fuisse, supra Cap. duodecimo vidimus: vbi illud ab aliis distinguit, & prophetiae proximo gradu subjicit. Alij verò hoc omnium esse aiunt, qui docentes audiunt. Et horum sententia probabilior mihi quoq; videtur, quia hic de communi omnium salute agitur, & absurdum foret, quenquam ab alterius quàm solius spiritus iudicio pendere. Ita enim nobis alios constitueremus nostrae fidei magistros, neque nobis de illius certitudine certum quid possemus polliceri. Sed & Christus Dominus ouibus suis omnibus hoc proprium esse ait, quòd vocem suam norint, hanc solam sequantur, aliorum non item.
units.tr: First, who ought to judge or test doctrines? Some restrict what is said here to those who are themselves prophets, or who are endowed with special gifts and stand out among others in the Church. Among the ancients Theodoret held this view: he writes that the duty of judging belongs to those who have the gift of discernment, which, as we saw above in chapter twelve, was a special gift and not common to all. There he distinguishes it from the others and places it in the rank next to prophecy. Others say that it belongs to everyone who hears teachers. This opinion seems to me the more probable, because the common salvation of all is at stake here, and it would be absurd for anyone to depend on the judgment of another's spirit rather than his own alone. Otherwise we would be appointing others as the masters of our faith, and we could never be certain of its certainty. Christ the Lord also says that it is the proper mark of all his sheep that they know his voice and follow it alone, and not that of others.

units.la: Secundum, quo vsq; iudicium hoc siue examen doctrinarum extendi debeat? Nam sunt qui clament, si hoc statuatur, iam Verbum Dei hominum iudicio subijci. At non hoc vult Apostolus, sed vt de Scripturarum interpretatione & ijs quae Verbi Dei nomine proponuntur, iudicium fiat. An scilicet quod à Prophetis illis dicitur, cum Verbo Dei conueniat? Quod vt primum constite-rit, iam omnis censura cessare debet, neq; aliud reliquum est, quàm vt omnes per fidei obedientiam sese Verbo submittant, etiamsi omnis sensus siue intellectus nostrae rationis reclamet. Quo loco simul Sophistarum vanitas arguitur, qui Verbo Dei suam authoritatem ex Ecclesiae iudicio conflare garriunt. Atqui nos potius vere dicimus, Ecclesiam non esse nisi eam, quae ex Dei Verbo renata, hoc solum audit & probat. Vide 1.Pet.4.
units.tr: Second, how far should this judgment, or examination of doctrines, extend? Some cry out that if this is laid down, the Word of God will be subjected to human judgment. But the Apostle does not mean this. Rather, judgment should be made about the interpretation of Scripture and about those things that are put forward in the name of the Word of God: namely, whether what those prophets say agrees with the Word of God. Once that is established, all scrutiny must cease, and nothing remains but for everyone to submit himself to the Word through obedient faith, even if every sense or understanding of our reason protests. Here the vanity of the Sophists is also exposed, who babble that their authority over the Word of God is drawn from the judgment of the Church. We rather say truly that the Church is nothing other than that which, born again of the Word of God, hears and approves this alone. See 1 Pet. 4.

units.la: Tertium est, vt huius probationis siue examinis regulam videamus. Propria quidem & communis est Scriptura sacra, quam alibi Paulus θεόπνευστον[?] dicit, quòd à Dei Spiritu inspirati homines sancti illius oracula literis mandarunt. Et certum est, falsum atque adulterinum esse, quicquid non ex illa depromitur, aut illius testimonijs firmiter ac solide probatur. Sed quia Scripturae latius patent, quàm vt quivis possit ex illis de doctrina quavis iudicium facere, repetendum est hoc loco, quòd Apostolus ad Romanos prophetiae regulam constituit Analogiam siue Propor-tionem fidei: ne scilicet aliquid dicatur, quod pugnet cum huius principijs, quae in Decalogo, Oratione Dominica & Symbolo Apostolico (quod communem illam & verè Apostolicam traditionem de vera fide esse, Irenaeus testatur) continentur. Horum certa notitia, qua nemo Christianus carere potest & debet, cum diligenti consideratione coniuncta non patietur aliquem facilè falli: quando nemo tam stupidus est, quin mox videre possit, an de vno solo Deo adorando & invocando per vnicum Mediatorem IESVM CHRISTVM sermo fit, vel num Dij plures, & Mediatores etiam alij, novae item & diuersae salutis acquirendae rationes commonstrentur?
units.tr: Third, let us see the rule of this testing or examination. Sacred Scripture is its own and common rule, which Paul elsewhere calls theopneustos [θεόπνευστον], because holy men, inspired by the Spirit of God, committed its oracles to writing. And it is certain that whatever is not drawn from it, or is not firmly and solidly proved by its testimonies, is false and adulterate. But because the Scriptures extend too widely for anyone to make a judgment on any doctrine from them, it must be repeated here that the Apostle to the Romans set up the rule of prophecy: the analogy or proportion of faith. This is so that nothing is said that conflicts with its principles, which are contained in the Decalogue, the Lord's Prayer and the Apostles' Creed (which Irenaeus testifies is that common and truly apostolic tradition of the true faith). Certain knowledge of these, which no Christian can or should lack, joined with careful consideration, will not allow anyone to be easily deceived. For no one is so dull that he cannot at once see whether the discourse concerns the one God to be adored and invoked through the one Mediator, Jesus Christ, or whether many gods and other mediators are being shown, and new and different ways of obtaining salvation.

units.la: Arguitur itaque toto hoc loco Pontificum tyrannis, qui Ecclesiam hac sua libertate prorsus spoliauerunt, non minus quàm Pharao olim Israelitas, quos priuilegijs exuit, quae priores reges illis propter Iosephi merita donauerant. Primò enim penes se esse dicunt totius Scripturae interpretationem, nec alicui licere, vt ab ipsis edita sententia contradicat. Deinde facultatem docendi siue donum prophetiae suo chrismati & confurae[?] alligarunt, vt nisi quis ipsorum characterem accepe-rit, huic in eorum Ecclesia (vt in Apocalypsi traditur) neque emere neque vendere liceat. Tertiò, hos ipsos in sua verba iurare cogunt: quò fit, vt si quando in Veritatis cognitionem peruenerint, ea tamen quae bene sentiunt, proferre non audeant. Postremò, eosdem sacrosanctos fecerunt, quibus nemo contradicere audet, & quos nefas sit dicto aut facto laedere. Et quia non potuerunt ignorare hominum conscientijs non ita facilè satisfieri, vt aliorum placitis omnibus acquiescant, fidem finxerunt implicitam, quae cuiuis ad salutem sufficiat: Si videlicet maneat in fide Ecclesiae, & se cum suo pastore aut Episcopo sentire dicat, etiamsi quae horum sententia sit, ignoret. Hinc portenta illa errorum, superstitionum, idololatriae, omnis item licentiae & nequitiae prodierunt, quibus colluuies illa rasorum[?] & vnctorum totam Christiani nominis professionem conspurcauit. Neque malorum finis sperari poterit, nisi sua Ecclesiae libertas restituatur, quae eam Christus donauit. Clamant quidem illi indignum esse vt Laici de spiritualibus iudicent, quia inde horribilis nascitura sit omnis ordinis confusio, & fexcenta alia fingunt, quae non aliter deuitari possint, nisi ipsis licentia ista salua maneat. Sed vnico argumento, quod hic nobis Paulus suggerit, omnes istorum paralogismi dissolui & confutari possunt. Voluit Deus vt de suis Prophetis & Apostolis iudicium fieret, de quorum vocatione & missione omnibus constabat: Ergo multò magis de istis iudicari debet, qui toti mundo innumeras ob causas suspecti sunt. Quod autem illi de populi ignorantia querun-tur, eo suam ignauiam atq; perfidiam produnt, qui eos tam turpiter neglexerunt, quos ipsi in fidei principijs instituere debebant, ne iudicando falli possent.
units.tr: So in this whole passage the tyranny of the Pontiffs is exposed. They have utterly robbed the Church of this liberty, no less than Pharaoh of old robbed the Israelites of the privileges which earlier kings had granted them on account of Joseph's merits. For first, they say that the interpretation of all Scripture rests with them alone, and that it is not permitted for anyone to contradict a judgment issued by them. Second, they have tied the faculty of teaching, or the gift of prophecy, to their chrism and censure, so that unless someone has received their mark, he may not buy or sell in their Church (as the Apocalypse tells us). Third, they compel these same men to swear to their words, with the result that if ever they come to know the truth, they still do not dare to put forward what they rightly think. Last, they have made sacrosanct those very men whom no one dares to contradict and whom it is wrong to harm by word or deed. And since they could not be unaware that men's consciences are not so easily satisfied as to acquiesce in all the opinions of others, they invented an implicit faith, which suffices for salvation for anyone: namely, if he remains in the faith of the Church and says that he agrees with his minister or bishop, even if he does not know what their opinion is. Hence those monstrous errors, superstitions and idolatries have arisen, as well as every licence and wickedness, by which that filth of shaven and anointed men has defiled the whole profession of the Christian name. Nor can an end to these evils be hoped for unless the Church's own liberty, which Christ gave her, is restored. Those men indeed cry out that it is unworthy for laymen to judge spiritual matters, because from this a horrible confusion of every order would arise; and they invent six hundred other things which, they say, cannot be avoided unless that licence remains intact for them. But by the single argument which Paul here puts before us, all their paralogisms can be dissolved and refuted. God willed that judgment be made about his Prophets and Apostles, whose calling and mission were known to all. Therefore much more ought judgment to be made about these men, who are suspect to the whole world for countless reasons. As for their complaint about the ignorance of the people, that betrays their own sloth and faithlessness, since they have so shamefully neglected those whom they ought to have instructed in the principles of faith, so that they would not be deceived when judging.

units.la: Caeterum ut ad locum praesentem redeamus, fiebat interdum, ut ordinarij illi Prophetae loci propositi sensum germanum non omnino attingerent, aut non omnia dicerent, quae de illo utiliter dici poterant, vel etiam ut alicui ex assidentibus auditoribus subita & peculiari revelatione innotesceret, quod praesenti tempore imprimis feriebat. Docet ergo Apostolus, quid tunc quoque fieri debeat, & sic dicit: Quod si quid alij patefactum fuerit assidenti, prior taceat. Sedentes dicit ipsos auditores, idque ex veteri more. Solebant enim considere in sacris coetibus, qui ad audiendum Verbum Dei convenerant, ut ipso corporis habitu admonerentur, composito & sedatis affectibus omnibus ipsos in solius Dei voluntatem intentos esse debere. Sic Maria ad pedes IESV sedisse dicitur, ut docentem audiret. Diuus Ambrosius trium ordinum & distinctorum in templis subselliorum meminit: sed id minus convenit cum simplicitate veteris Ecclesiae, quando ab emulatiofa eminendi aut excellendi affectatione ministri alienissimi fuerunt: illius autem temporibus convenire potest, quando locum proprium & cancellis interstinctum sacerdotes sibi vindicarunt, quem ne Imperatoribus quidem ingredi licebat, ut in historia Theodosij ab illo excommunicati & post octo menses poenitentiam indignissime reiecti apparet. Proderit tamen observare veterem morem, ut eo etiam arguatur Papistarum peruersitas, qui summam religionem in eo consistere arbitrantur, si non uno in loco sese contineant, sed per templa discurrant, modo ad hoc, modo ad illud altare missam audiant, nunc huic, nunc illi statuae cereae suffigant, imo per multa quoque templa vagentur. Quoad vero praesentis loci statum, vult Paulus ijs quoque dicendi potestatem fieri, qui ex vulgo sunt Christianorum, & ne cui cedere dedignetur, qui prior coeperat verba facere.
units.tr: But to return to the present place: it sometimes happened that those ordinary prophets did not fully grasp the genuine sense of the passage in hand, or did not say everything that could usefully be said about it; or else that something was made known by a sudden and special revelation to one of the hearers sitting among them, which especially struck the present time. The Apostle therefore teaches what ought to be done in that case too, and says: "If anything is revealed to another who is sitting, let the first be silent." He calls the hearers "sitting," and this comes from the ancient custom. For those who had come together in sacred assemblies to hear the Word of God used to sit, so that by the very posture of the body they might be reminded that, with composed and calm affections, they ought all to be intent on the will of God alone. Thus Mary is said to have sat at the feet of Jesus, so that she might hear him teaching. Saint Ambrose mentions three orders of distinct benches in the churches; but this agrees less with the simplicity of the ancient Church, when the ministers were most remote from the emulous desire to stand out or excel. It could fit later times, when priests claimed for themselves a place of their own, set apart by railings, which not even emperors were permitted to enter, as appears in the history of Theodosius, who was excommunicated by him and, after eight months, most unworthily refused repentance. Still, it will be useful to observe the ancient custom, so that the perversity of the Papists may also be exposed by it. They think supreme religion consists in this: that they do not keep to one place but run through the churches, now hearing mass at this altar, now at that, now fixing wax candles before this statue, now before that, and even wandering through many churches. As for the state of the present passage, Paul wills that the power of speaking be granted also to those who belong to the common sort of Christians, and that no one who had begun to speak first disdain to yield.

units.la: Est autem locus iste diligenter inspiciendus propter Anabaptistas, qui eius authoritate potissimum nituntur, ut Ecclesias nostras non Apostolicas esse probent. Sed observabis primum, Paulum loqui pro sui temporis ratione, quando Ecclesiae non tam frequentes erant, maior autem erat donorum Spiritus ubertas. Stultum ergo fuerit, ea velle hodie instituere, quae olim usitata fuerunt, cum longe alia sit nostrorum temporum ratio. Deinde non permittitur sedenti, ut ad dicendum surgat, nisi Propheta ordinarius sensum loci propositi non attigerit, aut omiserit quae dicenda erant. Adhaec revelationis mentio fit. Ergo non licuit cuiusvis pro suo arbitrio prorumpere, neque semper hoc licuit: sed singularis revelatio debuit expectari, quae haud dubie non facile esset, nisi quando ita necessitas exigebat: ut si quando Prophetae in officio segniores erant, aut causa aliqua gravior incideret. Adde, quod in propria modo Ecclesia id licuit, & quidem observato diligenter ordinis decoro. Patet hoc in Apostolorum, Pauli & Barnabae, exemplo, qui erant a Deo doctores gentium ordinati & publica Ecclesiae authoritate ad praedicandum emissi essent, Antiochiae tamen Synagogam ingressi non antea ad dicendum surrexerunt, quam postquam ordinariam Legis ac Prophetarum lectionem a principibus Synagogae inuitarentur. Denique non in eo consistit hominum salus, ut omnes sint doctores, sed ut veri ac germani sint Christi discipuli, qui Euangelij doctrinam diligenter audiant, eidem credant & vitam viuant Christiana professione dignam. In his periculum nullum est, imo ex his salus nostra dependet, & haec pietas illa est, cui tam huius quam futurae vitae promissiones datas esse, Apostolus docet: Docentium autem conditio periculosissima est, quia in multis labimur omnes, & vix quisquam tam humanum est, quam errare & falli, ex doctorum autem manibus sanguis omnium eorum requiretur, quos illi negligentia aut incuria sua perdiderint. Recte igitur Iacobus monebat: Ne sitis multi magistri fratres mei, scientes quod gravius iudicium auferemus, &c. Haec diligentius considerata satis docent, neq; posse hodie commode fieri id quod fanatici illi requirunt, neq; si omnino fieri deberet, hanc causam esse sufficientem, ob quam ab Ecclesijs nostris discedant. Quod si qui locum hunc pertinacius urgere volent, nos eos rogamus, ut revelationes quas iactant, illis indicijs probent, quibus se a Spiritu Dei agi olim probarunt, qui docendi partes sibi vendicabant. Quod cum non faciant, neq; possint facere, quid reliquat, quam ut eos ambitionis spiritu exagitari dicamus, quem ab Ecclesia Paulus procul vult eiectum esse. Porrò quoad Corinthios, credibile est, ambitiosos illos, quorum magnus illic numerus erat, non facilè locum dedisse inferioribus, si quid eis esset revelatum: Ideo quod dixit, nunc rationibus confirmat. Sunt hæ quatuor numero. Prima, Potestis enim omnes sigillatim prophetare, ut omnes discant, & omnes consolationem accipiant. Loquitur autem de Spiritus virtute, qui (ut Christus ait) ubi vult spirat, neque ullis personis aut locis alligatus est, quo minus libere agat in omnibus, quos sibi ut organa sua delegerit. Si enim Sauli datus fuit Spiritus Domini, & multos ex reprobis in suo nomine prophetare Christus testatur, quis obstabit, quo minus Spiritus sancti virtus in electis sese exerat, quos ille omnes Deo Patri suo Reges ac Sacerdotes fecit? Imò est hoc (ut alibi monuimus) votum commune piorum omnium, qui non vulgarem consolationem ex eo concipiunt, si quàm plurimos donis Spiritus excellere, & ijsdem bene uti videant. Quia enim toti ardent studio gloriæ Dei, priuatæ gloriæ cupiditatem nequaquam in se dominari patiuntur, ut infelices illi, qui invidia contabescunt, si qui doctrina aut aliis virtutibus excellunt. Repetit autem Apostolus finem prophetiæ, quem nuper sub ædificationis vocabulo comprehendit, nunc autem huius partes constituit duas: Doctrinam, qua homines in Dei cognitione & vera fide instituuntur: & Consolationem, qua fidelium animi aduersus tentationum certamina confirmantur. Nec temere fieri putemus, quòd bis repetitur nota universalis, cùm dicit: Ut OMNES discant, & OMNES consolationem accipiant. Nemo enim tam doctus est, qui non ex obscuris & vilissimis possit aliquid discere. Diogenes, cùm puerum aquam manu haurire & ita bibere videret, ab illo didicit, scutella sibi nequaquam opus esse: Ita qui vulgarium hominum dicta & facta non oscitanter observant, semper invenient, quo doctiores fiant & magis confirmentur. Diuus Augustinus se in Scripturis plura nescire quàm scire fatebatur. Et præclarè admodum idem ille Au-xilio Episcopo juveni scribebat: En adsum senex à juvene coëpiscopo, & Episcopus tot annorum à collega necdum anniculo paratus sum discere. Quod exemplum utinam observent, qui eò arrogantiæ progressi sunt, ut symmystas suos omnes contemnant. Similiter nemo est, qui non consolatione quoque opus habeat: quia in propriis periculis fere labascunt & rerum incerti hærent, qui aliis consilio adesse noverunt.
units.tr: This passage needs careful examination because of the Anabaptists, who rely chiefly on its authority to prove that our churches are not apostolic. But first you should observe that Paul speaks according to the circumstances of his own time, when churches were not so numerous and the abundance of the gifts of the Spirit was greater. It would therefore be foolish to want to institute today what was once customary, since the circumstances of our own times are quite different. Next, a seated person is not permitted to rise to speak unless the ordinary prophet has not touched on the sense of the text proposed, or has left out what ought to have been said. Moreover, mention is made of revelation. So it was not permitted for anyone to break forth at his own pleasure, nor was it always permitted even then; rather, a special revelation had to be awaited, which would undoubtedly not be easy to receive unless necessity demanded it, as when the prophets were rather slack in their duty or some more serious cause arose. Add that this was permitted only in one's own church, and even then with careful observance of good order. This is clear from the example of the apostles Paul and Barnabas, who, though they had been ordained by God as teachers of the Gentiles and sent out to preach by the public authority of the church, nevertheless, when they entered the synagogue at Antioch, did not rise to speak until the rulers of the synagogue invited them to speak after the customary reading of the Law and the Prophets. Finally, human salvation does not consist in everyone being a teacher, but in being true and genuine disciples of Christ, who listen diligently to the doctrine of the Gospel, believe it, and live a life worthy of the Christian profession. In these things there is no danger; indeed, our salvation depends on them, and this is the godliness to which, as the Apostle teaches, the promises both of this life and of the life to come have been given. But the condition of teachers is most perilous, because we all stumble in many things, and hardly anyone is so free from human weakness that he does not err and fall; and the blood of all those whom they have lost through their negligence or carelessness will be required at the hands of teachers. Rightly, then, James warned: "Let not many of you become teachers, my brothers, knowing that we shall receive a heavier judgment," etc. These things, considered more carefully, sufficiently show both that what those fanatics demand cannot conveniently be done today, and that, even if it ought to be done altogether, this would not be a sufficient cause for them to withdraw from our churches. But if any want to press this passage more stubbornly, we ask them to prove the revelations they boast of by those marks by which those who once claimed the role of teaching proved that they were driven by the Spirit of God. Since they do not do this, and cannot do it, what remains but for us to say that they are driven by the spirit of ambition, which Paul wants cast far from the Church? Further, as to the Corinthians, it is credible that those ambitious men, of whom there was a large number there, were not willing to yield the place to their inferiors if anything had been revealed to them. Therefore, what he said he now confirms with reasons. There are four of these. The first: "For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all may be comforted." He speaks of the power of the Spirit, who (as Christ says) breathes where he wills, and is bound to no persons or places, so that he cannot act freely in all whom he has chosen as his instruments. For if the Spirit of the Lord was given to Saul, and Christ testifies that many of the reprobate prophesied in his name, who will stand in the way, that the power of the Holy Spirit should not display itself in the elect, whom he has made all kings and priests to God the Father? Indeed, as we have noted elsewhere, this is the common prayer of all the godly, who derive no ordinary comfort from it if they see very many excelling in the gifts of the Spirit and using them well. For since they burn wholly with zeal for the glory of God, they by no means allow the desire for private glory to rule over them, unlike those unhappy men who waste away with envy if anyone excels in learning or other virtues. The Apostle, moreover, repeats the purpose of prophecy, which he had just comprehended under the name of edification, but now he sets out its two parts: teaching, by which men are instructed in the knowledge of God and in true faith; and comfort, by which the minds of the faithful are strengthened against the struggles of temptations. Nor should we think it rashly done that the universal mark is repeated twice when he says: "that ALL may learn, and ALL may be comforted." For no one is so learned that he cannot learn something from obscure and very humble people. When Diogenes saw a boy scoop up water in his hand and drink it that way, he learned from him that he had no need of a bowl; so those who do not carelessly observe the sayings and deeds of ordinary people will always find something by which they become more learned and are more confirmed. Saint Augustine confessed that in the Scriptures he knew more things that he did not know than things that he knew. And that same Augustine very admirably wrote to Auxilius, a young bishop: "Behold, I am an old man writing to a young fellow-bishop, and I, a bishop of so many years, am prepared to learn even from a colleague who is not yet a year old." I wish those would follow this example who have advanced to such arrogance that they despise all their fellow-believers. Likewise, there is no one who does not also need comfort, since those who know how to give counsel to others often wobble in their own dangers and hang in uncertainty about their affairs.

units.la: Secunda ratio est: Et spiritus Prophetarum Prophetis subjiciuntur. Alij hoc dictum de ipsis Prophetis exponunt, qui spiritu miti & placido præditi, non præfractè aut contumaciter sese efferunt, sed libenter locum dent meliora monentibus. Talis Petrus fuit, qui Paulum sibi in faciem resistentem patienter tulit. Sunt qui de singulis hoc interpretantur, quod Spiritus sui potentes sint, nō non autem arreptitijs similes, qui sibi ipsis temperare non possint, de quo alibi diximus. Alij spiritus pro doctrina accipiunt, ut Joannes in loco, quem supra citavimus. Hæc (inquiunt) censura & examini subiecta esse debet. Est enim hoc præceptum Dei perpetuum ut doctrinæ probentur, num ex Deo sint. Omnes hi sensus pij sunt, nec aliquid habent absurdi. Postremus tamen instituto Pauli melius convenit. Vult enim ostendere, neminem tantæ authoritatis esse, ut à censura Ecclesiæ eximi debeat: utq; emphasim majorem habeat oratio, spiritum potius quàm doctrinam posuit, quem admodum alibi Angelum anathema pronuntiat, qui Euangelium aliud ausit prædicare. Nemo tamen hinc colligat, aliquem Prophetam in alios ius habere aut dominium: quia non de subiectione violenta, sed voluntaria sermo est, qua fit, ut se mutuo audiant, & operas suas studiosè conferant ad Christi regnum ampliandum: sicuti inter fidos milites solet fieri, quos nulla imperatoris severitas aut disciplinæ metus cogit, sed propria fortitudo excitat, ut rem strenuè gerant, seq; mutuum juvent. Quis ergo Pontifices Dei spiritu agi dixerit, qui nemini subesse, & à nemine dijudicari volunt? Ita certè Baalami spiritum referunt, qui ne Dei quidem admonitionibus flecti potuit, ut ab infestandis Israelitis abstineret. Sed ut ille ab asina correptus fuit, ita frequenter fit, ut insolentes illi ab ijs arguantur, quos paulò ante vix asinorum loco habuerunt. Et hoc dignum est insolentiæ stipendium: quod fere in repub. quoque & priuatim omnes recipiunt, qui sese supra omnes alios superbè extollunt. Quia enim superbis resistit Dominus, fieri nequit, ut ijdem Dei Spiritu ducantur.
units.tr: The second reason is: "And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets." Some explain this of the prophets themselves, who, endowed with a gentle and calm spirit, do not carry themselves forward stubbornly or obstinately, but willingly give way to those who advise better things. Peter was such a man, who patiently bore Paul resisting him to his face. Some interpret it of individuals, that they are masters of their own spirit, and not like the possessed, who cannot restrain themselves, about which we have spoken elsewhere. Others take "spirits" for doctrine, as John does in the passage that we cited above: these (they say) must be subjected to censure and examination, for it is a perpetual precept of God that doctrines should be tested to see whether they are from God. All these senses are godly, and none of them contains anything absurd. Yet the last agrees better with Paul's purpose. For he wants to show that no one is of such authority that he ought to be exempt from the censure of the Church; and so that the statement may have greater emphasis, he has put "spirit" rather than "doctrine", just as elsewhere he pronounces an angel who dares to preach another gospel accursed. No one, however, should conclude from this that any prophet has right or dominion over others, because the discourse is not about violent subjection but voluntary subjection, by which it happens that they listen to one another and diligently contribute their labours to enlarge the kingdom of Christ, just as usually happens among faithful soldiers, whom no severity of a commander or fear of discipline compels, but their own courage stirs up so that they may act vigorously and help one another. Who, then, would say that the pontiffs are driven by the Spirit of God, when they wish to be subject to no one and to be judged by no one? Certainly they reproduce the spirit of Balaam, who could not be turned even by God's admonitions from harassing the Israelites. But just as he was rebuked by the donkey, so it often happens that those arrogant men are reproved by those whom shortly before they scarcely regarded as better than donkeys. And this is a fitting wage for arrogance, which almost everyone receives in the commonwealth and in private life, all who proudly exalt themselves above all others. For since the Lord resists the proud, it cannot happen that those same men are led by the Spirit of God.

units.la: Tertia ratio est, quòd ita velit Deus. Non est enim (inquit) confusionis author Deus, sed pacis. In Græco legitur ἀκαταστασία[?], quæ tunc facta dicitur, quando res non manent in statu suo legitimo & ordinario. Talis in repub. est, quando nemo alium audit, nemo alteri cedit. In Eccle-sia vero rectè ἀκαταστασίαν [?] dixerit, si qui omnibus alijs imperare volut, & pro suo arbitrio quibus-dam praescribunt. Turbatur tunc vera Ecclesiae constitutio, quia consistere non potest συνταξίαν [?] illa membrorum, de qua Cap. duodecimo diximus. Simul autem ἀνθυποφορὰν [?] occultam habet hoc di-ctum, quia illis occurrit, qui confusionem & omnis status turbationem nasciturum esse metuunt, si qui inferiores sunt, antistiti suo contradicant. Docet enim, nihil huius eventurum esse, si omnia ex Spiritus Dei suggestione gerantur, sed mutuo audiant. Qui enim omnia creauit in mensura & pon-dere, quia certa cum ratione omnia regit, idem facile inter eos consensum conciliabit, qui ipsius prae-ceptis se accommodant. Et quemadmodum firmissimum amicitiae retinendae vinculum est, si liberè & amicè se mutuò moneant, qui se offensos esse sentiunt: ita Ecclesiae consensus tunc demum vere retinetur, quando suas sententias inter se conferunt, qui dissentire videntur. Simul autem admonemur hoc loco, eos nequaquam à Dei Spiritu gubernari, qui turbis & contentionibus flu-dent, & has sua insolentia fouent. Vult enim nos in ipso unum esse Christum Dominum. Objiciunt quidem nobis Papistae hunc locum, vt Euangelicae doctrinae instauratores Dei Spiritu actos fuisse negent, eò quòd Ecclesiae pacem turbauerint, & dissidiorum in orbe Christiano fuerint authores. Sed non mouet nos huius criminis exprobratio: quia de pace ea loquimur, quae ex Deo est, & cuius regula est Dei Verbum. Nihil ergo hoc ad eos, qui contra Deum coniurarunt. Vt enim olim turris Babylonicae aedificatores turbari & scindi vtile fuit: ita istorum quoque consensum turbari o-portuit, quia sub huius praetextu horribilis omnium rerum ἀκαταστασία latuit. Quis enim nescit homines relicto Creatore circa creaturarum cultus occupatos, populum Christianum in sedes vni-tatis distractum, prophanam sacrorum omnium nundinationem introductam fuisse, deniq; impu-rissimos lenones sibi in IESV CHRISTI sponsam ius & imperium vendicauisse, adhaec to-tum illum Clerum vnctum & rasum, immunitate fictitia & male vsurpata superbum, contra legi-timos magistratus conspirauisse? Oportuit ergo salutiferum illum gladium mitti, qui discordem il-lam atq; inordinatam concordiam dirimeret, vt omnes in vno Christo conuenire possent. Huc perti-nent, quae habentur Matth.10. & Luc.12.cap.
units.tr: The third reason is that God so wills. For God (he says) is not the author of confusion but of peace. In the Greek it reads ἀκαταστασία [akatastasia], which is said to happen when things do not remain in their proper and ordinary state. In the commonwealth this is the case when no one listens to another and no one yields to another. In the Church one may rightly speak of ἀκαταστασία [akatastasia] if some wish to command all the others and prescribe things to certain people at their own pleasure. The true constitution of the Church is then thrown into disorder, because that ordered arrangement [συνταξία, syntaxia] of the members, of which we spoke in the twelfth chapter, cannot stand. At the same time this saying contains a hidden rebuke [ἀνθυποφορά, anthyposphora], for it meets those who fear that confusion and a disturbance of the whole order will arise if inferiors contradict their superior. For it teaches that nothing of the kind will happen if all things are done at the prompting of God's Spirit and they listen to one another. For he who created all things in measure and weight, because he governs all things with a certain reason, will easily bring about agreement among those who accommodate themselves to his precepts. And just as the firmest bond for keeping a friendship is that those who feel offended admonish one another freely and in a friendly way, so the consensus of the Church is truly preserved only when those who seem to disagree confer their opinions with one another. At the same time we are reminded in this place that those who are carried away into tumults and contentions, and foster them by their insolence, are by no means governed by the Spirit of God. For he wills us to be one in Christ the Lord. The Papists indeed object to us this passage, so that they may deny that the restorers of the evangelical doctrine were moved by the Spirit of God, because they disturbed the peace of the Church and were the authors of dissensions in the Christian world. But the reproach of this charge does not move us, because we are speaking of that peace which is from God, and whose rule is the Word of God. This therefore has nothing to do with those who have conspired against God. For just as it was once useful that the builders of the Babylonian tower be confounded and scattered, so the consensus of those men had to be broken up, because under its pretext the horrible disorder of all things lay hidden. For who does not know that men, having abandoned the Creator, were occupied with the worship of creatures; that the Christian people had been torn apart into factions opposed to unity; that a profane trade in all holy things had been introduced; that shameless pimps had claimed for themselves the right and dominion over the bride of Jesus Christ; and besides, that the whole clergy, anointed and shaven, proud through a fictitious and wrongly usurped immunity, had conspired against the lawful magistrates? It was therefore necessary that that saving sword be sent, which would break up that discordant and disorderly concord, so that all might be able to come together in the one Christ. To this pertain the things that are found in Matthew 10 and Luke 12.

units.la: Restat quarta & postrema ratio, quam his verbis comprehendit: Vt in omnibus Ecclesijs sanctorum, scilicet ego doceo, aut fieri consueuit. Potest enim vtroq; sensu hoc accipi: Vel, quod nihil aliud illis praecipiat, quàm quod alijs quoq; Ecclesijs hactenus mandarit: Vel, quod non aliud ab ipsis requirat, quàm quod passim omnes Christiani obseruent. Theodoretus ita exponit: Nihil noui statuimus, sed vos Ecclesiarum leges docemus, quas ipse statuit pacis magister Dominus. Est ergo argumentum ab exemplo, vt nihil habeant ab alijs Ecclesijs diuersum: sed quoad eius fieri potest, se aliarum ritibus atq; moribus accommodent. Scimus quidem libertatem esse in eiusmodi rebus, neq; eandem ecclesiasticam œconomiam formam omnibus Ecclesijs conuenire: Veruntamen non contemni debent aliorum exempla, ne dissensionis suspicio tum scandalo coniunctâ infirmis ac rudioribus oboriatur. Tutissimû autem fuerit ad veteris & primitiuae Ecclesiae formam respicere, in qua credentium omnium fuit cor vnum, cùm non aliam fidei sua & totius œconomiae regulam baberent quàm Apostolorum doctrinam, quam hi Spiritu authore proponebant. Interim non obscuram exprobrationem habent Pauli verba, qua Corinthiorum ambitionem reprehendit, qui vt supra alios eminerent, singulare quid affectabant: & ideo hortatur, vt alijs sese conformes facere studeant, ne dum peculiare quid sectantur, odium & inuidiam sibi apud omnes Ecclesias conciliënt. Faxit Deus Pater concordiae & vnitatis, vt hoc nostro afflictissimo seculo distant tandem omnes vno corde, vno spiritu & ore profiteri IESVM CHRISTVM, qui solus est via, vita & veritas. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: There remains the fourth and last reason, which he comprehends in these words: as in all the Churches of the saints, namely, I teach, or as is customary. This can be taken in either sense: either that he commands them nothing other than what he has hitherto enjoined on the other Churches as well; or that he requires of them nothing other than what all Christians everywhere observe. Theodoret explains it thus: We establish nothing new, but teach you the laws of the Churches, which the Lord, the teacher of peace, himself established. There is therefore an argument from example, that they should have nothing different from the other Churches, but, as far as it can be done, accommodate themselves to the rites and customs of the others. We indeed know that there is liberty in matters of this kind, and that the same form of ecclesiastical order does not suit all Churches; nevertheless the examples of others ought not to be despised, lest a suspicion of dissension, joined with scandal, arise among the weak and the more ignorant. Moreover, it will be safest to look to the form of the ancient and primitive Church, in which all the believers had one heart, since they had no other rule of their faith and of the whole order than the doctrine of the Apostles, which they set forth under the inspiration of the Spirit. Meanwhile Paul's words contain no obscure rebuke, in which he censures the ambition of the Corinthians, who, wishing to stand out above the others, sought after something singular; and therefore he urges them to strive to conform themselves to the others, lest by pursuing something peculiar they win hatred and envy for themselves among all the Churches. May God the Father of concord and unity grant that in this most afflicted age of ours all may at last with one heart, one spirit and one mouth profess Jesus Christ, who alone is the way, the life and the truth. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXVI.
units.tr: HOMILIA LXXVI.

units.la: Mulieres vestrae in coetibus sileant: nec enim permissum est eis vtloquantur, sed vt subditae sint, sicut & Lex dicit. Quòd si quid discere volunt, domi suos viros interrogent: Nam turpe est mulieribus[?] in coetu loqui. An à vobis sermo Dei profectus est? an ad vos solos deuenit? Si quis videtur Propheta esse, aut spiritualis, agnoscat quae scribo vobis, quod Domini mandata sunt. Qui vero ignarus est, ignarus esto. Itaque fratres hoc ambite, vt prophetetis, & loqui linguis ne prohibete. Omnia vero decenter & ordine fiant.
units.tr: Let your women keep silent in the churches, for it is not permitted for them to speak, but they are to be subject, as the Law also says. But if they wish to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home, for it is shameful for women to speak in the congregation. Did the word of God come out from you?
