Or has it come to you alone? If anyone seems to be a prophet, or spiritual, let him acknowledge that what I write to you are the commandments of the Lord. But if anyone is ignorant, let him remain ignorant. So, brothers, strive to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. But let all things be done decently and in order.

units.la: INijt[?] quae proximè praecesserunt diligenter & perspicuè docuit Paulus, quo ordine & qua ratione in sacris coetibus proponi debeant, quae ad publicam omnium institutionem & aedificationem faciunt. Quia autem magna tunc donorum spiritualium vbertas erat, ne aliquibus obstare videatur, quò minus dono suo vtantur, inter alia dixit: Potestis singillatim omnes prophetare, vt omnes discant, & omnes consolationem accipiant. Id vero sic accipi poterat, quasi mulieribus quoq; in coetu sacro loquendi potestatem faceret: Et credibile est in Corinthiorum Ecclesia ex gentilismo hoc etiam vitium irrepsisse, vt mulieres quoq; docendi partes sibi sumerent. Solebant enim inter gentes fere oracula Deorum per mulieres edi, vt nunc de Sybillis nihil dicam, quarum maxima fuit authoritas. Similiter sacra quaedam solis mulieribus credebantur: qualia fuerunt, Ignis Vestae, Bonae Deae, Cereris item apud Catinenses in Sicilia, & alia infinita. Facile ergo fuit mulierem ambitionem in Christi quoq; Ecclesia aliquid tentare. Pergit ergo Paulus, & quid mulieres Christianas deceat, docet: deinde tractationem istam de sacris coetibus tandem absoluit.
units.tr: Up to this point Paul has taught carefully and clearly in what order and by what method those things that serve the public instruction and edification of all should be set forth in the sacred assemblies. But because at that time there was a great abundance of spiritual gifts, so that he would not seem to hinder anyone from using his gift, he said among other things: You can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all may receive comfort. This could be taken as though he were granting women too the power to speak in the sacred assembly. And it is credible that this fault also crept into the Church of the Corinthians from their heathenism, so that women also took upon themselves the role of teaching. For among the Gentiles the oracles of the gods were nearly always uttered through women, not to mention the Sibyls, whose authority was very great. Likewise certain sacred rites were entrusted to women alone, such as the fire of Vesta, the rites of the Good Goddess, and of Ceres among the people of Catana in Sicily, and countless others. It was therefore easy for women to attempt some ambitious act even in the Church of Christ. Paul therefore goes on, teaches what befits Christian women, and finally brings his discussion of the sacred assemblies to a close.

units.la: Quoad causam mulierum, status sive propositio est: Mulieres vestrae in coetibus sileant. Poterat hoc durius dictum videri, quasi satis fuisset monuisse, vt modestè, pudicè, caute & breuiter dicant quod volunt: Sed simpliciter & absolutè praecipit vt sileant. Id vero de ordinaria functione intelligi debet, ne videlicet sibi ius sumant docendi aut disputandi in Ecclesia. Non est ergo, vt hic aliquis Paulo obijciat Mariam sororem Mosis, Deboram, Annam prophetissam, & si quae aliae his similes inueniuntur. Quod enim istae fecerunt, id singulari Dei consilio factum est, & suum vsum habuit peculiarem: & ideo nemo inde colligere debet, quibusuis idem licere, quas sua libido aut garrulitas ad dicendum excitat. Sed rationes audiamus, quibus Apostolus suam Propositionem probat.
units.tr: As regards the cause of the women, the issue or proposition is: Let your women keep silent in the churches. This might seem a harsher saying, as if it had been enough to advise them to say what they wish modestly, chastely, cautiously and briefly. But he simply and absolutely commands them to be silent. This must be understood of the ordinary office, namely, that they should not claim for themselves a right to teach or to dispute in the Church. Therefore no one should object here to Paul with Miriam the sister of Moses, Deborah, Anna the prophetess, and any others like them that are found. For what these women did, they did by a singular counsel of God, and it had its own peculiar use; and so no one should infer from this that it is permitted to anyone whom his own lust or garrulity stirs up to speak. But let us hear the reasons by which the Apostle proves his proposition.

units.la: Prima est, quod mulieres in coetu loqui nefas sit, eò quòd aliud iubeat Lex Dei, qua praecipitur vt subditae sint. Argumentum est à repugnantibus, eiusmodi: Dei institutum est, vt mulier viro sit subdita: At docendi munus in Ecclesia species est praefecturae, & eminentiam sibi coniunctam habet: Ergo ad illud mulieres non debent admitti. Absurdum enim foret, eam in totum Ecclesiae corpus ius aliquod sibi sumere, quae ne viro quidem proprio dominari aut imperare debet.
units.tr: The first is that it is wrong for women to speak in the congregation, because the Law of God, which commands that they be subject, says otherwise. The argument is from the opposite, of this sort: It is God's institution that the woman be subject to the man; but the office of teaching in the Church has the appearance of authority and carries eminence with it; therefore women ought not to be admitted to that office. For it would be absurd for a woman to take to herself any right over the whole body of the Church, when she ought not even to rule or command her own husband.

units.la: Quòd si Lege requiris, de qua Paulus loquitur, extat ea in Genesi, vbi Deus Euae, quae viro transgressionis causa fuerat, dicit: Dolorem tuum & conceptum tuum multiplicabo, in dolore paries filios, & ad virum tuum erit respectus tuus, & ipse dominabitur tibi. Est autem obseruatu dignum, quòd ex subiectionis iure Apostolus colligit, mulieres silentiù decere. Eo enim admonemur, hanc demum veram esse subiectionem, si ne loquamur quidem aduersus eum, cui nos Deus subditos esse voluit. Talis est eius subiectionis conditio, qua nos sibi Deus subiecit. Ideo Dauid dicebat: Vtiq; ad Deum silens respicit anima mea. Item: Tibi ô Deus silentium, laus in Zion, &c. Et apud Isaiam contumaciae detestabilis argumentum adducitur eorum audacia, qui ad Dei Verbum adeò non silebant, vt potius ipsi eius praeconibus silentium mandarent. Quod ipsum qui hodie faciunt, ij satis aperte produnt, se Deo debitam obedientiam negare, & proinde in murmuratorum loco censeri debere, de quibus Cap. 10. huius Epistolae diximus. Debet autem hoc non modò in praeceptis aut mandatis Dei obseruari, ne aduersus illa disputare libeat, verumetiam in morbis, egestate, persecutionibus, exilio & omnibus aliis periculis, ne de illis ita conqueramur, vt Dei iustitia siue bonitas à nobis accusetur. Eadem est magistratuum & subditorum, parentum & liberorum, mariti & vxoris, herorum & seruorum conditio. Nec enim verè subditi esse dici possunt, quicunq; obloqui audent illis, quos ipsis Lex Dei praefecit.
units.tr: But if you ask for the Law of which Paul speaks, it is found in Genesis, where God says to Eve, who had been the cause of the transgression for the man: I will multiply your sorrow and your conception; in sorrow you shall bear children, and your desire shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you. It is worth noting that the Apostle infers from the right of subjection that women ought to keep silence. For we are reminded by this that that is true subjection only if we do not even speak against the one to whom God willed us to be subject. Such is the condition of that subjection by which God has made us subject to himself. Therefore David said: Truly my soul waits in silence upon God. Likewise: Silence becomes you, O God, praise in Zion, etc. And in Isaiah the detestable obstinacy of those is cited, whose audacity was such that they did not keep silent before the Word of God, but rather commanded silence to its very heralds. Those who do the same today sufficiently reveal that they deny the obedience owed to God, and therefore ought to be counted among the murmurers of whom we spoke in chapter 10 of this Epistle. This must be observed not only in the precepts or commands of God, so that we do not desire to dispute against them, but also in diseases, poverty, persecutions, exile and all other dangers, so that we do not complain of them in such a way that the justice or goodness of God is accused by us. The condition of magistrates and subjects, of parents and children, of husband and wife, of masters and servants, is the same. For those who dare to speak against those whom the Law of God has set over them cannot truly be called subjects.

units.la: Altera ratio est: Nam turpe est mulieribus in coetu loqui. Turpe dicitur, quod fit contra legem naturae & morem receptum. Vtrumque in hac causa locum habet. Quia enim Deus mulieres subditas esse voluit (vt modò demonstratum est) certè contra Legem naturæ, quæ non alia quàm Dei Lex est, peccant, quotquot in publico dicendi potestatem sibi vendicant. Deinde constat ex historijs, γυναικοκρατείαν[?] apud omnes fere populos male audiuisse. Hoc nomine apud Geographos Ægyptij taxantur, quòd mulieres eorum forum & negotia tractarent, viri pensa & domos curarent. Numa Rex sapientissimus, mulieres curiosas esse prohibuit, sobrietatem verò illis præcepit, & ne de necessarijs quoque rebus absente viro loquerentur. Quare cùm posteris temporibus mulier quædam propriam causam in foro dixisset, id portento simile visum est Patribus, & legati missi consultum Deos, quid ea res ciuitati portenderet. Heliogabali quoque imperium cùm multis aliis de causis, tum ob hanc etiam infame fuit, quòd matri permisisset mulierum Senatum instituere, quem per ludibrium Senatulum dixere. At si de feriis mulierem in publico loqui turpe est, quanto grauius reprehendi debent, quæ impudenter hinc inde discurrunt, in publico canunt, mimas agunt, ludunt, saltant, quæq; in conuiuijs inter viros garrulitate sua omnes obtundunt, & ne ab obscœnis quidem dicteriis siue narrationibus abstinent?
units.tr: The second reason is: For it is shameful for women to speak in the congregation. Something is called shameful when it is done against the law of nature and accepted custom. Both apply in this matter. For since God willed women to be subject (as has just been shown), certainly all who claim for themselves the power of speaking in public sin against the law of nature, which is nothing other than the Law of God. Further, it is clear from histories that gynaecocracy [γυναικοκρατίαν] was ill regarded among almost all peoples. On this account the Egyptians are censured by the geographers, because their women conducted the marketplace and business, while the men looked after the spinning and the households. King Numa, the wisest of kings, forbade women to be inquisitive, but prescribed sobriety for them, and that they should not speak even about necessary matters in their husband's absence. Therefore, when in later times a certain woman pleaded her own cause in the forum, this seemed to the Fathers a portent like a prodigy, and envoys were sent to consult the gods as to what this event portended for the state. The reign of Heliogabalus was infamous for many other reasons, but also for this, that he allowed his mother to establish a senate of women, which in mockery they called the little senate. But if it is shameful for a woman to speak in public about holidays, how much more gravely ought they to be rebuked who run about shamelessly here and there, sing in public, act in mimes, play, dance, and who in banquets wear out all the men with their chatter, and do not even refrain from obscene jokes or stories?

units.la: Admonet autem nos hic quoq; locus, quid de Papatu & tota, quæ illic exercetur, religione iudices. Ibi enim mulieres in templis canunt, & quidem lingua peregrina, vt nimirum vna actione duo Apostoli præcepta violent. Abbatissæ item sub religionis prætextu ius dicunt, leges condunt, & in ijs quæ ad hoc seculum spectant, viris insolenter dominantur: adhæc Ecclesiarum præfecturas ad se rapiunt, & illarum curam pro suo arbitrio quibus volunt committunt: deniq; mulieribus permittitur, vt in ædibus priuatis baptismum administrent. Sed quid non faciant illic mulieres, vbi Scorto licuit per omnes dignitatis gradus in ipsam sedem Papalem vsq; ascendere? Et hæc cùm iam seculis aliquot facta sint, & adhuc fiant, adeò tamen pleriq; insaniunt, vt Romanam sedem errare posse negent. Quòd si verò mulieribus ecclesiastica negotia tractare nefas est, quid de viris iudicari debet, qui cùm Ecclesiæ antistites haberi velint, muliebria tractant & viris indigna faciunt? In horum numero sunt, qui plus quàm muliebriter in Ecclesia nugantur, cantillant, comuntur, & ceremonijs non minus ineptis quàm anilibus atque nolliculis religionem totam corrumpunt. Sunt hæc indigna ijs, qui publicum grauitatis exemplum omnibus præbere debebant, & præ alijs Legem Dei obseruare, quæ prohibet, ne viri muliebri habitu sexum suum dedecorent. Vide Deuter.22.cap.
units.tr: But this passage also reminds us what to judge of the Papacy and of the whole religion practised there. For there women sing in the temples, and indeed in a foreign tongue, so that by one action they violate two precepts of the Apostle. Likewise abbesses, under the pretext of religion, pronounce judgments, enact laws, and rule insolently over men in matters that pertain to this age; moreover they seize for themselves the governance of the churches and commit their care to whomever they wish at their own discretion; finally women are permitted to administer baptism in private houses. But what will women not do there, where a harlot was permitted to climb through every grade of dignity to the Papal seat itself? And although these things have been done for several centuries and are still being done, yet many are so mad that they deny that the Roman see can err. But if it is wrong for women to handle ecclesiastical affairs, what ought to be judged of men who, while wishing to be considered leaders of the Church, handle womanly matters and do things unworthy of men? Among their number are those who trifle in the Church more than womanishly, sing little songs, adorn themselves, and corrupt the whole religion with ceremonies no less silly than those of old women and little effeminates. These things are unworthy of those who ought to offer a public example of gravity to all, and above others to keep the Law of God, which forbids men to dishonour their sex by women's dress. See Deut. 22.

units.la: Caterùm vt ad Pauli constitutionem redeamus, obijceret aliquis: Quid verò, si mulier aliqua non intelligat ea, quæ à ministris in publico cœtu dicuntur, aut de re aliqua grauì & cognita necessaria dubitet? Annon licebit tunc quæstiones mouere, quibus alij quoque instituantur? Ad ista Paulus per Præoccupationem respondet, dum rationibus, quas modò audiuimus, interserit: Quòd si quid discere volunt, domi suos viros interrogent. Non prohibet, quò minus interrogent de ijs, quæ nondum intelligunt. Est enim sexus ille infirmior, & non modò tentationibus pluribus obnoxius, verumetiam ad superstitiones proclivior. Ideo magistris opus habent, quibus cum familiaribus conferre possint. Hos ergo illis destinat Paulus: non quidem Ecclesiarum ministros, vt hodie quidam faciunt, qui in omnium ædes penetrant, examina priuata mulierculârum & puellarum instituunt (id enim alibi impostoribus proprium esse ait, à quibus sibi cauere debeant) sed proprios maritos: vt & illarum pudicitiæ atque honori consulat, & coniugum concordiam foueat, hos autem reddat attentiores in audiendis sacris concionibus. Licet quidem mulieri alios etiam viros graues & peritos rerum, si quæ occasio honesta sese offerat, interrogare, vel etiam interdum Ecclesiæ ministrum accedere, vt ab eo instituatur, vel consolationem accipiat. Sed neq; frequentius id fieri debet, neque insciis maritis, aut saltem ijs, quibus aliquod in eas ius est atq; imperium. Habet quædam de hac re non indigna obseruatu D. Hieronymus in epistola ad Nepotianum, quem imprimis monet, ne absque arbitris secreta cum muliere quacunque colloquia habeat. Et exempla sunt, quæ docent, quantum mali dederit Confessio auricularis, sub cuius prætextu Sacerdotes & Monachi in mulierum & puellarum arcana penetrarunt, & sæpe cum pudicitia iusta eas dimiserunt abs se, quæ ob leuem aliquam culpam illos conuenerant. Inter nostros autem inueniuntur fœminæ opulentiores, quæ quorundam Ecclesiæ ministrorum amicitiam & familiaritatem eam potissimum ob causam ambiunt atque colunt, vt eorum authoritate luxum atque fa-stum stum suum adversus alios ministros tueantur, qui in illo corripiendo liberiores sive acriores sunt. Nihil ergo tam ministris quam mulieribus tutius est hac Pauli regula, ut nimirum hæ conditionis suæ memores domi se contineant, de rebus cognitu necessariis viros suos interrogent, & horum voluntati sese accommodent.
units.tr: But to return to Paul's ruling, someone might object: what if a woman does not understand what the ministers say in the public assembly, or doubts some serious and well-known matter that she needs to grasp? Will it not then be permitted to raise questions, by which others too may be instructed? To this Paul responds by anticipation, inserting among the reasons we have just heard: "If they want to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home." He does not forbid them to ask about things they do not yet understand. That sex is weaker, and not only more exposed to many temptations but also more prone to superstitions. So they need teachers with whom they can confer within the household. Paul assigns these to them: not the ministers of the churches, as some do today, who enter everyone's houses and hold private examinations of women and girls (for he says elsewhere that this is characteristic of impostors, against whom they ought to be on guard), but their own husbands. In this way he looks after their chastity and honour, fosters harmony between spouses, and makes the husbands more attentive in hearing the sacred sermons. A woman may indeed also ask other grave and experienced men, if a fitting opportunity presents itself, or even at times approach a minister of the Church to be instructed by him or to receive comfort. But this should not be done too often, nor without the knowledge of their husbands, or at least of those who have some right and authority over them. Saint Jerome, in his letter to Nepotianus, whom he above all warns not to hold secret conversations with any woman without witnesses, has some remarks on this matter that are worth noting. And there are examples which show how much harm auricular confession has done, under whose pretext priests and monks have penetrated the secrets of women and girls, and often dismissed from their presence with their chastity ruined those who had come to them over some slight fault. Among our own people, however, there are wealthier women who court and cultivate the friendship and intimacy of certain ministers of the Church, chiefly for this reason: that by their authority they may defend their luxury and pride against other ministers, who are more free or sharp in rebuking them. Nothing, then, is safer for ministers and women alike than this rule of Paul: that women, mindful of their condition, keep themselves at home, ask their husbands about matters necessary to know, and accommodate themselves to their husbands' wishes.

units.la: Admonet etiam locus iste, quales esse conveniat Christianorum hominum familias. Ecclesiæ & scholæ sint (ut ita dicam) particulares, quibus (ut alibi Paulus admonet) materfamilias suos liberos, socrus, nurum, anus, fæminas, iuvenculas, maritus uxorem & totam reliquam familiam instituat inque officio contineat. Talem olim Abrahami domum fuisse, Deus ipse testatur. Et huc pertinent, quæ passim in Scripturis de liberorum institutione in Lege Dei & Sa-crorum usu habentur. Asaph certè carmine divino vetera Dei beneficia & iudiciorum eius exempla complexurus, præfatur se hoc ex Dei mandato facere, ut posteri omnes inde virtutis & pietatis documentum petant. Constituit (inquit) Dominus testatione in Iacob, & legem tulit in Israële, quam præcepit patribus nostris, ut ea nota facerent filijs suis: ut cognoscat ætas postera, filij scilicet qui nati sunt, cum adoleverint, narrent eadem filijs suis: ideoque fiduciam suam in Deo ponant, nec obliviscantur operum Dei, & mandata eius observent. Istud ubi observatur, ibi in pietate proficitur: quia singuli salis illius evangelici loco sunt alijs, dum pijs admonitionibus eos condiunt, ne in vitijs & erroribus computrescant. At quæ nostri seculi infelicitas est, hodie sal omnis infatuatus est, & ideo collapsa iacet eorum authoritas, qui alios ad pietatem erudire debebant: regnant autem apud omnes ordines petulantia, & in peius pleriique proficiunt.
units.tr: This passage also shows what sort of households Christian families ought to be. Let them be, so to speak, particular churches and schools, in which the mother of the household instructs her children, her mother-in-law, daughters-in-law, old women, women and young girls, as Paul admonishes elsewhere; in which the husband instructs his wife and the whole rest of the household and keeps them to their duty. God himself testifies that Abraham's house was once such. And to this belong the many passages throughout Scripture about instructing children in the law of God and in the use of the sacred rites. Asaph, indeed, about to recount God's former benefits and examples of his judgments in a divine song, begins by saying that he does this by God's command, so that all posterity may draw from it a lesson in virtue and piety. "The Lord," he says, "established a testimony in Jacob and set a law in Israel, which he commanded our fathers to make known to their sons; so that the next generation might know it, the children who would be born, and in turn might tell it to their own sons; so that they might put their confidence in God, not forget the works of God, and keep his commandments" (Ps. 78). Where this is observed, there is progress in piety, because each person is like the salt of the gospel to others, seasoning them with godly admonitions so that they do not rot in vices and errors. But such is the unhappiness of our age that today all the salt has lost its savour, and therefore the authority of those who ought to train others in piety lies in ruins; meanwhile wantonness reigns among all ranks, and most people make progress for the worse.

units.la: Sequitur postrema capitis huius pars, qua totam tractationem de cœtibus sacris absoluit. Eam verò Corinthiorum ingenio atque moribus prudenter accommodat. Erant enim illi ambi-tiosi nimis atque arrogantes, & indignum putabant, se Apostolorum legibus sive statutis subijci, adeoque sibi licere ut suam Ecclesiam, nulla aliarum ratione habita, pro suo arbitrio regerent. Ergo doctrinæ suæ authoritatem magna cum gravitate astruit, & ab increpatione exorsus ait: An à vobis sermo Dei profectus est? an ad vos solos devenit? Id est, an à vobis cœpit verbum Dei, adeo ut nullum prius in mundo fuerit? Num hoc ipsum in vobis desijt, ut ad nullos præterea cursum suum extenderit? Num vos soli Christiani estis? aut num in vobis Christianismus totus deficiet? Annon aliæ etiam sunt Ecclesiæ, quæ vobis priores ad Christum conversæ sunt, & hodie adhuc celebres in fide excellunt? Quæ ergo hæc vestra arrogantia est, qua illas omnes contemnitis, & quasi soli sapiatis, contra aliorum morem, quidvis cuius permittitis?
units.tr: There follows the last part of this chapter, with which he finishes the whole discussion of sacred assemblies. He adapts it wisely to the character and manners of the Corinthians. For they were overly ambitious and arrogant, and thought it beneath them to be subject to the laws or ordinances of the Apostles, and so considered it permissible to govern their Church as they pleased, without regard for the practice of the other churches. Therefore he asserts the authority of his teaching with great seriousness, and beginning with a rebuke, says: "Did the word of God go out from you? Or has it come to you alone?" That is, did the word of God begin with you, so that there was nothing before it in the world? Has this very thing ended with you, so that it has extended its course to no others? Are you the only Christians? Or will all of Christianity fail in you? Are there not also other churches, which were converted to Christ before you, and which today still flourish in faith? What, then, is this arrogance of yours, by which you despise all of them, and act as if you alone were wise, permitting yourselves whatever you like, contrary to the custom of others?

units.la: Est autem hæc generalis doctrina, ne aliarum Ecclesiarum iudicia & exempla temere con- temnamus. Scimus equidem, libertatem aliquam concessam esse in externis ritibus, pro cuiusque gentis & loci ratione. At illius usus finis præcipuus est, ut superstitio caveatur, ne quis Dei cultum externis hisce alligatum esse putet, non autem, ut unusquisque pro suo arbitrio omnia faciat cum superbo & fastidioso aliorum omnium contemptu. Si enim, ut Paulus in epistola ad Romanos monuit, singuli se mutuò προσλαμβάνειν[?], id est, amicè sibi adiungere debent, quanto ma-gis totas Ecclesias observare debemus, ne vel insolentius contemnantur, vel scandalum aliquod ex nobis accipiant? Aut quis tolerabilem putet esse eorum insolentiam, qui sibi ipsis in omnes Ecclesias ius sumunt, & eas sibi serviliter subiectas esse volunt? Quod ergo in præsenti Paulus Corinthijs dicit, hoc ipsum hodie meliori iure Romanensibus dici poterat, qui suis legibus omnes subijci volunt, & de necessitate salutis esse dicunt, ut omnes animæ Romano Pontifici subijciantur. Sed & in eos ista conveniunt, qui quosvis in sui magistri verba iurare cogunt, quasi nefas sit ab ijs vel latum unguem discedere, quæ ille semel effutuit. Nec minus illorum quoque ambitio hic arguitur, qui omnes Ecclesias ad suæ œconomiæ sive disciplinæ formam reducere conantur, & disciplinam illic nullam haberi clamant, ubi non omnia ipsorum traditionibus sive statutis respondent. Sed ijdem dignas suæ arrogantiæ pœnas exoluunt, quando qui ab illis veniunt ad externos, petulantia quosvis alios superant, nec aliquid domo secum adferunt, quàm immanem & intolerabilem optimorum quorumque contemptum, neq; vllis aliorum admonitionibus se coerceri sinunt. Potest idem illis etiam dici, qui in libera Repub. nobilitatem suam morum petulantia ostentant, & ut se à vulgo hominum differre demonstrent, leges omnes procul abs se reijciunt. Quis enim illis non dicat: Soli ne cives estis? soli ne in hac urbe nati estis? an ad vos solos iura & priuilegia publica pertinent? Vos ne soli ciuitatem constituitis? soli ne eam seruatis atque defenditis?
units.tr: This is a general teaching: that we should not rashly despise the judgments and examples of other churches. We know, to be sure, that some freedom is granted in external rites, according to the circumstances of each nation and place. But the chief purpose of that freedom is that superstition be avoided, so that no one may think the worship of God is bound to these externals; not that each person should do everything as he pleases, with a proud and disdainful contempt for all others. For if, as Paul admonished in his letter to the Romans, each ought to receive one another [προσλαμβάνεσθε], that is, to join one another in friendship, how much more ought we to take care for whole churches, lest they be despised with insolence or receive some scandal from us? Or who would think tolerable the insolence of those who claim for themselves a right over all churches and want them to be servilely subject to them? So what Paul says here to the Corinthians could today be said with much better right to the Romanists, who want all to be subject to their laws, and say that it is necessary for salvation that every soul be subject to the Roman Pontiff. But these words also apply to those who force people to swear to the words of their master, as if it were a sin to depart from a single hair's breadth of what he once blurted out. Their ambition, too, is rebuked here, those who try to bring all churches into the form of their own economy or discipline, and cry out that there is no discipline anywhere that does not agree with their traditions and ordinances. Yet these same people pay the penalty their arrogance deserves: when those who come from them to outsiders surpass everyone else in wantonness, and bring nothing with them but a monstrous and intolerable contempt for all the best men, and do not allow themselves to be restrained by any admonitions from others. The same can also be said of those who, in a free commonwealth, display their nobility by the wantonness of their conduct, and in order to show that they differ from the common herd, cast all laws far from themselves. For who would not say to them: Are you alone citizens? Are you alone born in this city? Do public rights and privileges pertain to you alone? Do you alone constitute the state? Do you alone preserve and defend it?

units.la: Cæterùm obijciebant Corinthij: Verumtamen spirituales sumus, & tu ipse dixisti, spiritua-lem omnia dijudicare, ipsum autem à nemine iudicari? Id verò in ipsos retorquet Apostolus, dicens: Si quis videtur Propheta esse, aut Spiritualis, id est, si quis se eò usque profecisse arbitratur, ut reuera Propheta aut Spiritualis dici possit, is agnoscat quae scribo vobis, quòd Domini mandata sunt, id est, eo ipso se talem esse probet, quòd Domini mandata agnoscit, & ijsdè obtemperat. Quia enim singulae oues vocem pastoris sui, IESV CHRISTI, agnoscere debent, multò ma-gis hoc eos decet, qui prae aliis excellere volunt, dum sibi in Ecclesia Prophetarum & Spiritua-lium ius omne vendicant. Ita verò superbos illos ostentatores perstringit, quibus nihil in Ecclesia nocentius est & exitialius. Et addit: Qui verò ignarus est, ignarus esto. Quasi dicat: Si quis non vult agnoscere mandata Domini, age maneat ille qui est: ego nolim cum eo praeterea conten-dere, cùm Ecclesiae illam consuetudinem non habeant.
units.tr: But the Corinthians objected: "Nevertheless we are spiritual, and you yourself said that the spiritual man judges all things, yet he himself is judged by no one." Paul turns this against them, saying: "If anyone thinks himself to be a prophet, or spiritual, that is, if anyone considers that he has advanced so far that he can truly be called a prophet or spiritual, let him acknowledge what I write to you, that they are the commandments of the Lord." That is, let him prove himself such by this very thing, that he acknowledges the commandments of the Lord and obeys them. For just as each sheep ought to recognise the voice of its shepherd, Jesus Christ, so much more should this be fitting for those who wish to excel above others, while they claim for themselves all the right of prophets and spiritual men in the Church. Thus Paul strikes at those proud show-offs, than whom nothing in the Church is more harmful and ruinous. And he adds: "But if anyone is ignorant, let him be ignorant." As if to say: If anyone does not wish to acknowledge the commandments of the Lord, let him remain as he is. I would not want to contend further with such a person, since they do not have that custom of the Church.

units.la: Est hic multa obseruatione dignum, quòd Dei authoritatem sciolis istis arrogantibus obijcit, & huic uni insistiens eos fortiter urget, ut Dei mandata agnoscant. Dei autem mandata dicit ea, quae ex Scripturis & recepto paßim Ecclesiarum more produxit, quaeque videbat ad Ecclesiae aedificationem atque conseruationem facere. Licuit hoc illi, quia Christi Apostolus erat, & praesenti Spiritus sancti virtute ducebatur. Eius autem exemplo admonemur, Dei authoritate pugnandum esse aduersus omnes, qui se doctrinae faniori opponunt. Qui enim illam contemnunt, eos certum est, non esse Dei Spiritu praeditos. Qui ex Deo est, audit Dei verba. Possumus ergo ideo hodie spiritualibus illis in Papistica Ecclesia dicere: Si spirituales verè estis, cur non agnoscitis ea, quae olim Prophetae & Apostoli ex Spiritus reuelatione tradiderunt? Cur doctrinam illorum de uno solo Deo inuocando, de uno Mediatore Christo, de mortis eius merito, de fidei iustificatione & similibus articulis, falsi & haereseos accusatis? Quòd si illi reluctari pergant, & ignorantiam suam arrogantius tueantur, suae illos contumaciae relinquamus, secundum illud Christi: Sinite eos, nam sunt duces caeci caecorum. Quid enim porro ijs facias, quos aeternae veritatis verbum non mouet? Nec est, quòd illorum iudicia pij doctores multùm morentur. Paulus pro minimo ducebat, ut iudicaretur ab humano die. Et in posteriori epistola proteruis illis Euangelicae doctrinae contemptoribus dicet: Num experimentum quaeritis loquentis in me Christi? Eadem ratione cum illis etiam agi debet, qui Scripturae sacrae authoritatem in dubium vocant, & ipsa fidei atq; religionis principia negant. Philosophorum axioma est, Contra eum non disputandum esse, qui principia negauerit. Nimium ergo stultus fuerit, qui cum eo contendere velit, qui à Deo ipso tradita salutis fundamenta conuellere audet.
units.tr: Here is something worthy of close attention: he sets the authority of God against these arrogant half-learned men, and, insisting on this one point, presses them hard to acknowledge the commandments of God. By the commandments of God he means those things which he has drawn from the Scriptures and from the custom received throughout the churches, and which he saw were conducive to the building up and preservation of the Church. He could do this because he was an Apostle of Christ and was guided by the present power of the Holy Spirit. By his example we are admonished that we must fight with the authority of God against all who set themselves against sounder doctrine. For those who despise that doctrine are certainly not endowed with the Spirit of God. He who is of God hears the words of God. We may therefore say today to those spiritual men in the Papist Church: If you are truly spiritual, why do you not acknowledge what the Prophets and Apostles of old delivered by the revelation of the Spirit? Why do you accuse their doctrine of calling upon the one God alone, of the one Mediator Christ, of the merit of his death, of justification by faith, and of similar articles, of being false and heretical? But if they persist in resisting, and defend their ignorance more arrogantly, let us leave them to their own obstinacy, according to that saying of Christ: "Let them alone; they are blind guides of the blind." For what can you further do with those whom the word of eternal truth does not move? Nor is there any reason why faithful teachers should dwell long upon their judgments. Paul regarded it as a very small thing to be judged by the human day. And in the later epistle he will say to those insolent despisers of the evangelical doctrine: "Do you seek a proof of Christ speaking in me?" The same method ought to be used with those too who call the authority of holy Scripture into doubt and deny the very principles of faith and religion. It is a maxim of the philosophers that one should not dispute with a man who has denied the first principles. It would therefore be exceedingly foolish for anyone to wish to contend with one who dares to overthrow the foundations of salvation delivered by God himself.

units.la: Porrò concludit locum Paulus de usu donorum spiritualium, & summam eorum repetit, quae de prophetia & linguis dixerat: Itaque fratres, hoc ambite, ut prophetetis, & loqui linguis ne prohibete. Fratres dicit, ut increpationem, qua modò usus erat, mitiget: & suo exemplo docet, sic obiurgari debere eos qui errant, ne interea fraternitatis illius obliuiscamur, cuius vinculo nos omnes Christus constrinxit. Rursus autem prae omnibus donis spiritualibus & exercitijs ecclesiasticis prophetiam commendat: nimirum, quòd haec imprimis facit ad Ecclesiae aedificationem, cui omnia alia seruire debent. Caeterùm ne qui imperitiores & elegantioris eruditionis hostes hinc occasione arrepta, linguas prorsus abijcerent, diligenter monet, harum quoque usum nequaquam prohiberi debere. Nam ut alibi diximus, donum Dei erant singulare, quo Euangelij praedicatio vehementer adiuuabatur. At hodie eius longè alia est ratio, neq; eius aliquis usus esse potest in publicis Ecclesiae coetibus: itaque paralogizant papistici doctores, quando ex hoc loco colligunt, non debere aliquem prohiberi, quo minus Latine canat in templis, aut Latino sermone in Missa, siue in baptismi administratione utatur. Sed de his abundè satis iam ante dictum est. Hoc tamen obseruabis, corrigi quidem à Paulo abusum linguarum, eàsdem verò nequaquam prorsus aboleri aut reiici. Tenenda haec regula in omnibus, quae per se bona & licita sunt: ut nimirum abusus tollatur, si quis obrepsit, illa autem seruentur proq; Dei donis agnoscantur: Peccant in eo multi, qui bonas & sanctas Dei constitutiones temere damnant, quando aliquos illis abuti vident. Ita coniugium olim damnarunt aliqui, quos hodie Pontifices sequuntur. Sic eruditionem omnem & scholas abijciunt barbari quidam, quos multorum arrogantia & Sophistice offendit. Multi quoque Magistratum è medio tolli debere clamant, quòd illius potestas saepe in tyrannidem degeneret. At id non est errores & abusus corrigere, sed Dei ordinationes euertere, quod absq; scelere fieri nō potest. Singula igitur ad primam institutionem revocari debent, & ita utilitate magnam adferent.
units.tr: Finally, Paul concludes the passage on the use of spiritual gifts and repeats the sum of what he had said about prophecy and tongues: "Therefore, brothers, desire this, that you prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues." He says "brothers" to soften the rebuke he had just been using, and by his own example he teaches that those who err should be reproved in this way, lest in the meantime we forget that brotherhood, to the bond of which Christ has bound us all. Again, above all the spiritual gifts and ecclesiastical exercises he commends prophecy, namely because this above all serves the building up of the Church, to which all other things ought to be subordinate. Yet lest any of the less skilled and enemies of a more elegant learning should seize the occasion from this and utterly cast away tongues, he diligently warns that the use of these too must by no means be forbidden. For, as we have said elsewhere, they were a singular gift of God, by which the preaching of the gospel was greatly helped. But today their case is quite different, and there can be no use of them in the public assemblies of the Church. Therefore the Papist teachers reason fallaciously when they conclude from this passage that no one ought to be prevented from singing in Latin in the churches, or from using Latin speech in the Mass or in the administration of baptism. But enough has already been said about these matters. You should, however, observe this: Paul indeed corrected the abuse of tongues, but he by no means abolished or rejected them altogether. This rule must be held in all things which are good and lawful in themselves: namely, that the abuse is removed if any has crept in, while those things are kept and acknowledged as gifts of God. Many sin in this, who rashly condemn good and holy ordinances of God whenever they see some people abusing them. Thus some once condemned marriage, whom the Pontiffs today follow. So certain barbarians cast away all learning and schools, offended by the arrogance and sophistry of many. Many also cry out that the magistrate must be removed from the midst, because its power often degenerates into tyranny. But that is not to correct errors and abuses, but to overturn the ordinances of God, which cannot be done without wickedness. Each thing therefore ought to be brought back to its first institution, and so they will bring great benefit.

units.la: Restat vniuersalis conclusio, quae ad omnia pertinet, quae hucusq; ab initio cap. Vndecimi de sacris coetibus dicta sunt: Omnia decenter & ordine fiant. Duo requirit. Primum est, Decorum. Id à philosophis sic definiri Cicero scribit, ut decorum esse velint, quod ita naturae consentaneum fit, ut in eo moderatio & temperantia appareat cum specie quadam liberali. Porrò decorum, de quo hic agitur, multi in externo templorum apparatu, altarium ornatu, theatrico ministrorum vestitu, luminaribus, imaginum cultu, & similibus alijs constituunt. At non possunt ista proprie sic dici, quia cultui diuino minimè consentanea sunt, quem Christus in Spiritu & veritate, non in externis eiusmodi rebus consistere docet. Itaq; hoc potius praecipit Apostolus, ut omnia fiant pro ratione personarum atq; rerum praesentium. Huc ergo pertinebat, ut viri aperto capite, mulieres autem velato orent, ne quid cum superstitiosis gentium moribus commune habere videantur: ut Caena Domini publica sit totius Ecclesiae, non privata unius siue alterius: ut in eadem sobrietati omnes studeant, neue aliqui propter tenuiorem suam conditionem negligantur: ut item qui donis instructi sunt pluribus & excellentioribus, non contemnant se inferiores, hi verò vicissim illis non inuideant, neq; impudentius oblatrent. Et hodie Christiani hominem decet, videre quid agat, & quibus cum agat. In coetu res sacrae tractantur, auditur verbū Dei, administrantur Sacramenta, fiunt preces publicae: Ergo non ve[?]nandum illuc habitu scurrili, non garriendum in templis, non ludendum, nec quicquam admittendum, quod cum sacris illis exercitijs minus conueniat. Similiter Sabbatum Deus sibi sacrum esse voluit: Ergo nihil eo tempore fieri debet à Dei voluntate & cultu alienum. Ecclesiarum ministros salem terrae & lucem mundi esse Christus ait: Decet ergo hos moderata & circumspecta dicendi libertas, morum gravitas, rerum peritia & singularis fidei virtus atq; constantia. Magistratus Deorum instar fecit Dominus, & eosdem Deorum nomine dignatus est: Horum ergo fuerit, Dei iudicia enuntiare, huius beneficentiam imitari, & dignitatem suam sanctaq; seueritate, sapientia, consilio tueri. Christiani deniq; singuli domi forisq; professionis suae memores, omnibus quae ipsis debentur officia fideliter praestent. Haec omnia uno decori vocabulo Paulus comprehendit.
units.tr: There remains the general conclusion, which pertains to all that has been said from the beginning of the eleventh chapter about sacred assemblies: "Let all things be done decently and in order." He requires two things. The first is propriety. Cicero writes that the philosophers so defined propriety as that which agrees with nature in such a way that moderation and temperance appear in it together with a certain liberal grace. Now the propriety of which we are speaking here, many place in the external outfitting of churches, the adornment of altars, the theatrical dress of ministers, lights, the veneration of images, and other such things. But these cannot properly be called that, because they are by no means consistent with divine worship, which Christ teaches consists in spirit and truth, not in external things of this kind. Rather, the Apostle prescribes this: that all things be done according to the nature of the persons and of the present circumstances. To this therefore belonged the rule that men should pray with bare head and women with head covered, so that they might not seem to share anything with the superstitious customs of the Gentiles; that the Lord's Supper be public to the whole Church, not private to one or another; that in it all should strive for sobriety, and that none be neglected on account of his humbler condition; likewise that those who are endowed with more and more excellent gifts should not despise those beneath them, and these in turn should not envy them nor bark at them more shamelessly. And today it becomes a Christian to see what he is doing and in whose presence he is doing it. In the assembly sacred matters are handled, the word of God is heard, the sacraments are administered, public prayers are made. Therefore one must not come there in a buffoon's dress, must not chatter in the churches, must not play, nor admit anything that is less fitting to those sacred exercises. Likewise God wished the Sabbath to be holy to himself; therefore nothing ought to be done on that day that is alien to the will and worship of God. Christ says that the ministers of the churches are the salt of the earth and the light of the world; therefore moderate and circumspect freedom of speech, gravity of conduct, skill in affairs, and singular virtue and constancy of faith become them. The Lord made magistrates like gods, and has deigned to honour them with the name of gods; therefore it is their task to declare the judgments of God, to imitate his beneficence, and to guard their dignity by holy severity, wisdom and counsel. Finally, let each Christian, mindful of his profession at home and abroad, faithfully render all the duties that are owed to him. Paul comprehends all these things under the single word "propriety."

units.la: Alterum est, Ordo. Nec enim satis est, ut fiat quod fieri debet, sed ut ordine certo & legitimo fiat necesse est. Exempla sunt in quotidiano rerum usu, quibus hoc probetur. Nunquam opus suscep-tum feliciter perficiet opifex, nisi ordine recto progrediatur. In agricultura aratio sementem praecedat necesse est, alioqui labor & impensa omnis perierit. In rerum natura nisi ordinarii siderum motus & temporum vices sibi inuicem succedant, mox tota mundi machina dissoluetur. In Repub. item ordine & officiorum distinctione opus esse, nemo non videt. Similiter in re domestica, nisi ordo seruetur, mox omnia turbabuntur, & confusio exitialis sequetur. Idem ut in Ecclesia observetur, admodum necesse est. Itaque ut à minimis initium fiat, infantes statim Christo adducuntor, & in Ecclesiae societatem adoptantor: inde ubi aetate aliquò usq; progressi sunt, in Catechesi instituuntor, & ad coetus sacros assuefiant. In his loca sive sedilia sint distincta virorum atq; mulierum: suum quoq; locum ordinarium doctores habeant, ex quo ab Ecclesia tota conspici & audiri possint. In docendo item ordo seruetur, quoad scripturarū interpretationem, ne per illas temere vagentur ministri, & frustillatim modo hunc modo illum locum decerpant, quasi alia nequicquam à Spiritu sancto sint tradita. Praecedant preces ad Deum, & ijsdem conciones sacrae claudantor. In Sacramentorum administratione ordo, quem Christus tradidit, observetur. Nisi enim id fiat, partim superstitione, partim tumultuaria & exitiali confusione peccabitur. Ut ergo ipsi quoq; locum hunc concludamus, meminerint Christiani homines, coetus sacros insigne & præclarum esse Dei beneficium: ideo de illis recte cogendis & seruandis serio cogitent: orent ati[?]tem indesinenter Deum, vt hisce turbulentissimis temporibus Ecclesias vbique gentium seruet, & hanc pacem concedat, vt pijs tuto conuenire liceat ad prædicandum nomen filij sui IESV CHRISTI, quem ille nobis redemptorem dedit, vt in ipso coalescamus, & huius vitæ curriculum emensi cum eodem viuamus in cœlis: Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: The second is order. For it is not enough that what ought to be done is done; it must also be done in a fixed and lawful order. Examples from the everyday practice of life show this. A craftsman will never bring a undertaken work to a successful end unless he proceeds in right order. In farming, ploughing must come before sowing, or all the labour and expense will be lost. In the natural world, unless the regular motions of the stars and the changing seasons follow one another in turn, the whole machinery of the universe would soon fall apart. Likewise, everyone sees that the commonwealth too needs order and a distinction of offices. Similarly in household affairs, unless order is kept, all things will soon be thrown into confusion and ruinous disorder will follow. It is absolutely necessary that the same be observed in the Church. Thus, to begin with the smallest, infants are at once brought to Christ and adopted into the fellowship of the Church; then, when they have advanced to a certain age, they are instructed in the catechism and accustomed to the sacred assemblies. In these assemblies let the places or seats of men and women be kept separate; let the teachers also have their fixed place, from which they can be seen and heard by the whole Church. In teaching too, order must be kept as regards the interpretation of Scripture, so that the ministers do not wander rashly through it, plucking out now this passage and now that in scraps, as if the other things had been handed down by the Holy Spirit in vain. Prayers should go before, and the sacred sermons should be closed with them. In the administration of the sacraments, the order that Christ delivered must be observed; for unless this is done, sin will be committed partly through superstition and partly through tumultuous and ruinous confusion. So, to bring this section to a close as well, let Christian people remember that sacred assemblies are a remarkable and splendid benefit of God; therefore let them think seriously about gathering and keeping them rightly. Let them pray to God without ceasing that in these most turbulent times he would preserve the Churches everywhere among the nations, and grant such peace that the godly may safely be permitted to meet together to proclaim the name of his Son Jesus Christ, whom he has given us as Redeemer, so that we may be joined together in him, and, having run the course of this life, may live with him in heaven. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XV. HOMILIA LXXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV. HOMILY LXXVII.

units.la: Declaro autem vobis, fratres, Euangelium quod euangelizaui vobis, quod & accepistis, in quo etiam statis, per quod etiam, siquidem retinetis quo sermone vobis euangelizauerim, seruamini, nisi si frustra credidistis. Tradidi enim vobis in primis quod & acceperam: quod nimirum Christus mortuus est pro peccatis nostris, secundum scripturas: & quod sepultus est, & excitatus tertio die, secundum scripturas.
units.tr: Now I declare to you, brothers, the gospel which I preached to you, which you also received, in which you also stand, through which you are also saved, if you hold fast to the word by which I preached it to you, unless you have believed in vain. For I delivered to you first of all what I also received: namely, that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures.

units.la: CONTINETVR hoc capite quinta huius epistolæ pars, qua de mortuorum resurrectione Paulus disserit, et eam multis validissimis demonstrationibus confirmat. Occasionem illi de hac dicendi dederunt, qui eam inter Corinthios vel aperte negabant, vel saltem in dubium vocabant. Poterat autem mirum videri, inter eos, qui Christi nomen profitebantur, inueniri potuisse, qui præcipuum fidei & religionis Christianæ articulum non reciperent. Sed meminisse oportet, Ecclesias penè omnes tunc temporis ex Iudæis & gentibus fuisse collectas. Inter gentes autem summam doctrinæ existimationem sustinebant philosophi, quorum pleriq; de animarum immortalitate & toto defunctorum statu dubiè loquebantur, nullian[?]tem corporum resurrectionem credebant. Argumentum eius rei euidens est, quod cum Paulus Athenis, in schola totius orbis celeberrima, concionem haberet, & in mentionem resurrectionis ex mortuis incidisset, à plerisque cum risu & ludibrio exceptus est. Apud Iudæos autem rerum tunc potiebantur Sadducæi, quibus corpora resuscitari adeo absurdum videbatur, vt animarum quoque immortalitatem, & cum hac spiritus simul omnes tam bonos quam malos negarent. Facile ergo fuit hunc errorem illis aspergere, qui iampridem à simplici doctrina Euangelij recesserant, & circa inanes atque curiosas humanæ sapientiæ speculationes occupabantur. Est igitur hoc Corinthiorum exemplum perquàm memorabile, quo docemur, quàm periculosum sit à verbi Dei doctrina vel modicum deflectere. Quia enim illo vno continentur recte credendi atque viuendi regula, fieri non potest, qui nin[?] auia & horribiles tenebras adducantur, quicunque illo relicto, suis n[?]tiocinacionibus indulgent. Et solet ita Deus verbi sui contemptum ulcisci: cuius iusto iudicio factum est, vt in præcipuo fidei & salutis communis articulo errarint Corinthij, qui præ aliis Ecclesijs sapere voluerunt, cum simplex Euangelij doctrina ipsis sorderet.
units.tr: This chapter contains the fifth part of this epistle, in which Paul discourses on the resurrection of the dead and confirms it by many very strong demonstrations. The occasion for speaking about it was given by those who, among the Corinthians, either openly denied it or at least called it into doubt. It might seem strange that among those who professed the name of Christ there could be found some who did not accept a chief article of the Christian faith and religion. But we must remember that nearly all the churches of that time were gathered from Jews and Gentiles. Among the Gentiles, the philosophers held the highest reputation for learning, and most of them spoke uncertainly about the immortality of souls and the whole condition of the dead, and did not believe in the resurrection of bodies. Clear evidence of this is that when Paul preached at Athens, in the most famous school in the whole world, and came to mention the resurrection from the dead, he was received by most with laughter and mockery. Among the Jews, meanwhile, the Sadducees held power, and the resurrection of bodies seemed to them so absurd that they denied the immortality of souls too, and with it the existence of spirits, both good and bad. It was therefore easy to infect with this error those who had long since turned aside from the simple doctrine of the gospel and were occupied with empty and curious speculations of human wisdom. This example of the Corinthians is therefore most memorable, and it teaches us how dangerous it is to deviate even slightly from the doctrine of God's word. For since the rule of right believing and living is contained wholly in that word, it cannot be otherwise than that those who abandon it and indulge in their own reasonings are led into pathless and dreadful darkness. And God is accustomed to avenge contempt of his word in this way. By his just judgment it came about that the Corinthians, who wished to be wiser than the other churches while the simple doctrine of the gospel was distasteful to them, went astray in the chief article of faith and common salvation.

units.la: Quia autem circa hunc articulum tota religio periclitatur, Paulus tanti erroris principijs grauiter & magno studio occurrit. Et primò quidem ipsius IESV CHRISTI Resurrectionem multis testimonijs asserit. Deinde ex ea firmiter colligit, nostra quoq; corpora resurrectura esse, & illic aduersariorum obiectiones confutat, quibus hi illam in dubium vocare audent. Prætera modum & ordinem futuræ Resurrectionis exponit. Postremò doctrinam hanc concludit cum graui exhortatione, qua omnes ad fidei constantiam excitat.
units.tr: But since the whole of religion is endangered over this article, Paul resists the beginnings of so great an error with weighty effort and great zeal. First, he asserts the resurrection of Jesus Christ himself by many testimonies. Then from it he firmly concludes that our bodies also will rise, and there he refutes the objections of the adversaries, by which these men dare to call it into doubt. Besides, he sets out the manner and order of the future resurrection. Lastly, he concludes this teaching with a grave exhortation, by which he rouses all to constancy in faith.

units.la: Oritur à transitione, & quia in dogmatibus fidei atq; religionis nouitas quàm maximè exosa est, initiò statim docet, se nihil nouum afferre, ipsos autem à cœpto fidei cursu deflexisse, quod inconstantiæ seu leuitatis culpa non careat. Declaro autem vobis, fratres, Euangelium quod euangelizaui vobis, quod & accepistis, &c. In Græco contextu verbum γνωρίζω ponitur, nō quidem in propria propria significatione, quasi rem prius inauditam & ipsis incognitam praedicet, sed pro eo quod est in mentem revocare (qui sensus Chrysostomo placuit) vel pro eo quod aliàs declarare & prolixius sive apertius explicare significat. Itaq; sensus verborum est: Audiuistis & didicistis iampridem quaecunq; cognitu necessaria sunt: quia verò non retinuistis, noua & diligentiori explicatione opus est. Diserte autem ad Euangelium eos remittit, vt non aliam doctrinam se iam proponere velle ostendat, quàm quae iam ante ab ipso praedicata & ab illis recepta sit. Et habent singula verba Emphasim. Nam declaro (inquit) vobis Euangelium, cuius nimirum praedicationi nos Apostolos Christus destinauit. Et quod nam Euangelium? Primò, quod ego vobis euangelizaui. Deinde, quod vos accepistis, id est, quod vt verum probauistis, & cui credidistis. Tertiò, in quo statis, id est, cuius doctrinam & fidem adhuc profitemini. Nam si proprie loqui voluisset, non equidem stare in Euangelio Corinthij dici poterant, cum & in Resurrectionis articulo, & multis alijs ab eius simplicitate & veritate deflexissent. Quibus quarto loco addit: Per quod etiam fer-uamini, si quidem retinuistis quo sermone vobis Euangelizauerim, & non frustra siue inutiliter credidistis. Ita verò paucis verbis tria agit. Primum, ignorantiae praetextum adimit. Secundò inconstantiam & leuitatem eorum perstringit, qui tam cito se abduci passi sint ab ea doctrina, quam receperint, quam adhuc profiteatur. Postremò, de periculo eos admonet, nimirum, quod salus ipsis non possit constare, ideoq; fides atq; professio eorum prorsus inutilis futura fit, nisi articulum hunc de mortuorum Resurrectione constanter teneant. Itaq; verborum istorum sensus est: Cùm ego vobis Euangelium plene & perfecte praedicauerim, non aliqua vobis est ignorantiae excusatio: cùm autem vos doctrinam illam amplexi fueritis, quae illa leuitas est, vt eandem modò negetis? Deniq;, cùm illa sola vitae aeternae rationem tradat, cur eam reijciendo spontaneum vobis ipsis exitium accersitis?
units.tr: He begins with a transition, and since novelty is most hateful in the articles of faith and religion, he teaches at once at the outset that he brings nothing new, but that they themselves have turned aside from the course of faith they had begun, which is not free from the fault of inconstancy or levity. "Now I declare to you, brothers, the gospel which I preached to you, which you also received," and so on. In the Greek the verb γνωρίζω [gnōrizō] is used, not in its proper meaning, as though he were announcing something previously unheard and unknown to them, but in the sense of calling to mind (which meaning pleased Chrysostom), or in the sense it otherwise has, of declaring and explaining more fully and plainly. The sense of the words, then, is this: you heard and learned long ago everything that needs to be known; but since you have not held on to it, there is need of a fresh and more careful explanation. He expressly refers them to the gospel so as to show that he wishes to propose no other doctrine now than that which he had already preached before and they had received. Each word also carries emphasis. For he says, "I declare to you the gospel," the very gospel to whose preaching Christ appointed us apostles. And what gospel is it? First, the one I preached to you. Second, the one you received, that is, the one you approved as true and believed. Third, the one in which you stand, that is, whose teaching and faith you still profess. For if he had wished to speak strictly, the Corinthians could not properly be said to stand in the gospel, since they had already turned away from its simplicity and truth in the article of the resurrection and in many other matters. To these he adds, in a fourth place: "through which also you are saved, if indeed you hold fast to the word by which I preached it to you, and have not believed in vain or to no purpose." In these few words he deals with three things. First, he takes away the pretext of ignorance. Second, he censures the fickleness and levity of those who have allowed themselves to be drawn away so quickly from the teaching they had received and still profess. Lastly, he warns them of the danger, namely that their salvation cannot stand, and therefore their faith and profession will be altogether useless, unless they constantly hold to this article concerning the resurrection of the dead. So the sense of these words is: since I have preached the gospel to you fully and perfectly, you have no excuse of ignorance; but when you have embraced that doctrine, what kind of levity is it that you now deny the same? Finally, since that gospel alone sets out the way of eternal life, why by rejecting it do you bring upon yourselves a destruction of your own choosing?

units.la: Est autem obseruatu dignissimum, quòd in re maximi momenti, non noua figmenta pro-fert, neq; ad hominum quorumcunq; decreta, sed ad simplicem Euangelij doctrinam eos remittit, & quae prius ipsis tradiderat repetit. Idem supra fecit in Caenae negotio, quam illi turpissimè pro-phanauerant. Nam cùm illorum audaciam acriter corripuisset, tandem infert: Ego quod à Domino accepi, vobis tradidi. Et mox primam Caenae institutionem exponit, & vt huius formulam à Christo traditam feruent, praecipit. Sic Christum fecisse legimus, quando quaestionem de libello repudij siue de diuortijs aliqui mouerunt, vt calumniandi occasionem inuenirent. Debet ergo hoc ipsum in omnibus alijs obseruari, quae ad fidei & religionis causam pertinent, & de quibus certa Dei praecepta siue statuta habentur. Etenim Euangelij doctrinam certam & perfectam esse constat, cùm eam Dei Filius à Patre acceptam fidelissimè nobis tradiderit. Eius enim verba sunt: Doctrina mea, non est mea, sed Patris qui misit me. Quo dicto eam ab hominum traditionibus ita discernit, vt ne seipsum quidem, quatenus homo est, eius authorem faciat. Et idem in vltima Caena discipulis ait: Omnia, quae audiui ex Patre meo, nota feci vobis: adhaec Spiritum suum illis submisit, qui ab ipso tradita fidelissimè suggesserit, vt nihil eorum exciderit. Quibus adde, quod Paulus Scripturam θεόπνευστον [?] esse ait, id est, diuinitus inspiratam, & vtilem esse ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem quae est in iustitia: vt perfectus sit homo Dei, ad omne opus bonum perfecte instructus. Itaque nulla poterit incidere controuersia, quae non facile dirimi possit ex Dei verbo, quod in Scripturis reuelatur. Poterat hoc exemplis plurimis illustrari, si ex ordine omnes articulos excutere vellemus, qui hodie sunt in controuersia. Sed quia id nimis prolixum foret, hoc in praesenti monuisse sufficiat: hanc ad veritatis cognitionem viam esse compendiosissimam tutissimamq;, si Dei verbum Ecclesiae ministri sedulò inculcent & illud vnum praedicent, id verò auditores patienter ferant, & eius dictatis sese per fidei obedientiam subijciant. Neq; hic aliqua doctorum diligentia debet nimia censeri: quando ea est ingenij humani prauitas atq; tarditas, vt vix quicquam sufficere possit ad reprimendam curiositatem eius, cui plerunq; affectus quoq; pessimi concurrunt, quae ipsam quoq; mentem transfuerfum abripiunt. Non pigeat ergo doctores crebrò repetere ea, quae cognitu & obseruatu imprimis necessaria sunt. Obseruauit hoc Paulus cùm alibi, tum quando Philippensibus dicebat: Eadem scribere vobis, me quidem haud piget, vobis autem tutum est. Et cur eadem semper proferre & inculcare nos pudeat, quando idem Prophetae & Apostoli fallitarunt, & Paulus anathema eum esse dicat, qui praeter ea euangelizare audet, quae Apostoli nobis tradiderunt. Solet illis, qui illud faciunt, accidere, ut circa sua rationis aut aliorum hominum commenta occupati, non attendant ijs, quae magis necessaria sunt.
units.tr: It is also most worthy of notice that in a matter of the greatest importance he does not bring forward new inventions, nor refer them to the decrees of any men, but refers them to the simple doctrine of the gospel and repeats what he had delivered to them before. He did the same above in the matter of the Lord's Supper, which they had most shamefully profaned. For after sharply rebuking their audacity, he finally adds: "For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you." And soon after he sets out the first institution of the Supper and commands that its form, handed down by Christ, be kept. So we read that Christ also acted when some raised a question about a bill of divorce, or about divorces, in order to find an occasion for calumny. This same principle ought to be observed in all other matters that pertain to the cause of faith and religion, and about which God's certain commands or statutes are given. For it is certain that the doctrine of the gospel is sure and perfect, since the Son of God received it from the Father and delivered it to us most faithfully. For his words are: "My doctrine is not mine, but his who sent me." By these words he so distinguishes it from human traditions that he does not make himself its author, even insofar as he is man. And in the last Supper he says to his disciples: "All things that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you." Besides this, he sent his Spirit to them, who would most faithfully bring to their minds what had been handed down by him, so that nothing of it would slip away. To these add that Paul says Scripture is God-breathed [θεόπνευστον], that is, divinely inspired, and useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, so that the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly equipped for every good work. Therefore no controversy can arise that cannot easily be settled from God's word, which is revealed in the Scriptures. This could be illustrated by very many examples if we wished to go through in order all the articles that are in dispute today. But since that would be too lengthy, it is enough to have pointed out in the present place that this is the shortest and safest way to the knowledge of the truth: if the ministers of the Church diligently impress the word of God and preach that alone, and if the hearers patiently bear it and submit themselves to its dictates by the obedience of faith. Nor should the diligence of teachers in this be considered excessive, since human nature is so perverse and slow that scarcely anything can suffice to restrain its curiosity, to which very bad feelings often join, and which carry the mind itself off in a perverse direction. Let teachers therefore not be ashamed to repeat often those things that are most necessary to know and to observe. Paul observed this both elsewhere and when he said to the Philippians: "To write the same things to you is no trouble to me, but for you it is safe." And why should we be ashamed to bring forward and impress the same things always, when the same prophets and apostles have taught them, and Paul says that he is accursed who dares to preach anything beside what the apostles have delivered to us? It usually happens to those who do otherwise that, occupied with the inventions of their own reason or of other men, they do not attend to the things that are more necessary.

units.la: Debet etiam obseruari, quod Paulus de Euangelio abs se praedicato loquens ait: in quo seruamini. Conuenit hoc cum verbis Angeli, qui Cornelio Centurioni praecipiens, ut Petrum Ioppa ad se accerseret, mox adiecit: Is tibi dicturus est per quae seruaris & tu & tota domus tua. Et ipsi Paulo Angelus ille Macedonum nomine in somnis apparens, dicebat: Veni, & succurre nobis. Recte igitur hac locutione in praesenti vtitur, cum ad Romanos scribens dixisset, Euangelium potentiam Dei esse ad salutem omni credenti. Debent ergo locutiones de Euangelio intelligi, quatenus IESVM CHRISTVM praedicat, qui cum vita & salus fit, omnes eos viuificat & seruat, qui ipsum fide vera apprehendunt. Vnde simul colligimus, nullum aliud esse doctrinae genus, in quo salus inueniri possit, praeter Euangelium, per quod ipse Christus nobiscum loquitur, & nobis seipsum atque salutem offert. Quo nomine Petrus illi dicebat: Domine, quo ibimus? tu verba vitae aeternae habes.
units.tr: It should also be observed that Paul, speaking of the gospel he preached, says: "in which you are being saved." This agrees with the words of the angel who, instructing the centurion Cornelius to send for Peter from Joppa, soon added: "He will tell you by what words you and all your household are saved." And that same angel who appeared to Paul in a dream in the name of the Macedonians said: "Come over and help us." Rightly, then, he uses this expression here, since in writing to the Romans he had said that the gospel is the power of God unto salvation for everyone who believes. So statements about the gospel must be understood insofar as it preaches Jesus Christ, who, as life and salvation, gives life to and saves all those who grasp him by true faith. From this we gather at the same time that there is no other kind of teaching in which salvation can be found apart from the gospel, through which Christ himself speaks with us and offers us himself and salvation. In this sense Peter said to him: "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life."

units.la: At hic non ofcitanter attendere oportet, quid fieri oporteat, ut salutem illam assequamur? Paulus se praedicauisse, Corinthios autem Euangelium accepisse, & in illo stare scribit, seruari autem, siquidem retineant quo sermone ipsis praedicauerit. Primo igitur praedicatione opus est. Quomodo enim credent ei, de quo nihil audierint? quomodo autem audient absq; praedicante? Deinde praedicationi credere, & Christum, qui praedicatur, cum fide amplesti[?] oportet. Fidei autem confessio accedere debet, ne ex eorum numero simus, quos sui seruatores pudet. Sunt hi eorum similes, qui cum ab alijs beneficia crebra accipiant, & ipsis omnino opus habeant, tales tamen videri nolunt, & studiose cauent, ne quid accepisse videantur. Sunt hi hominum ingratissimi, & indigni quibus benefiat. At quanto detestabilior eorum ingratitudo est, quos aeterni Filij Dei pudet, qui se totum pro ipsis tradidit? Ideo Apostolus in loco paulo ante citato fidei confessionem coniungens scribit: Hoc est verbum illud fidei, quod praedicamus: Nempe, quod si confessus fueris ore tuo Dominum IESVM, & credideris in corde tuo, quod Deus illum excitauit ex mortuis, seruaberis. Corde enim creditur ad iustitiam, ore autem confessio fit ad salutem. Nemo tamen professionem externam sufficere putet, sed ut in ea constantes simus, videndum est. Sunt enim qui verbum audiunt, & animo semen illud aliquo modo concipiunt, sed non retinent, neq; fructum ex eo aliquem ferunt, quia (ut in sementis parabola Dominus admonet) vel in viam, vel in spinas, vel in loca petricosa excipiunt: dum videlicet corda adferunt vel patentia quibusuis diaboli & carnis suggestionibus, vel curis huius seculi prorsus obsita, vel dura nimis, aut etiam praecocia, quae semen illud radices agere non patiuntur. Ideo in praesenti Paulus Corinthios per Euangelium seruari dicit, siquidem illud retineant, & non frustra crediderint. Itaq; animo honesto opus est, quod discendi cupiditate sancta ardeat, semen verbi conceptum feruet, & fructum suum ferat per patientiam. Si enim Corinthijs non profuit, quod Euangelium Christi profitebantur, & in eo videbantur stare, certe nobis quoq; inutilis erit professio externa, nisi in fide constantes simus, nosq; in Euangelio stare re ipsa demonstremus. Non igitur frustra ab Apostolo dictum esse putabimus: Ostende mihi fidem tuam ex factis tuis. Et a Christo: Qui perseuerauerit in finem, saluus erit: At qui postquam manum aratro admouit, respexerit a tergo, non est idoneus ad Regnum Dei. Matt.24.Luc.9.
units.tr: Here we must pay close attention, not carelessly, to what must be done so that we may attain that salvation. Paul writes that he preached, that the Corinthians received the gospel and stand in it, and that they are saved, provided they hold fast to the word by which he preached to them. First, then, preaching is needed. For how will they believe him of whom they have heard nothing? And how will they hear without someone preaching? Next, one must believe the preaching and embrace with faith Christ who is preached. Confession of faith must also follow, so that we are not among those whom their Saviour is ashamed of. There are those like people who receive many benefits from others, and really need them, yet do not want to appear so, and take great care not to seem to have received anything. They are the most ungrateful of men, and unworthy to be benefited. But how much more detestable is the ingratitude of those whom the eternal Son of God is ashamed of, he who gave himself wholly for them? Therefore the Apostle, in the passage cited shortly before, joining confession of faith, writes: "This is the word of faith which we preach: namely, that if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." Yet let no one think that an external profession is enough; we must see to it that we remain constant in it. For there are those who hear the word and in some way take that seed into their minds, but do not retain it, nor bear any fruit from it, because (as the Lord warns in the parable of the sower) they receive it either on the path, or among thorns, or in rocky places: that is, when they bring hearts either open to whatever suggestions of the devil and the flesh, or utterly choked by the cares of this age, or too hard, or even too premature, which do not allow that seed to put down roots. Therefore in the present passage Paul says that the Corinthians are saved through the gospel, provided they hold it fast and have not believed in vain. So an honest mind is needed, which burns with a holy desire to learn, in which the conceived seed of the word is kept warm and bears its fruit through patience. For if it did not profit the Corinthians that they professed the gospel of Christ and seemed to stand in it, certainly our external profession too will be useless unless we remain constant in faith and show in fact that we stand in the gospel. Therefore we shall not think it said by the Apostle in vain: "Show me your faith by your works." And by Christ: "He who perseveres to the end will be saved." But "whoever puts his hand to the plough and looks back is not fit for the kingdom of God." Matt.24.Luc.9.

units.la: Caeterum, quia in Euangelij mentionem semel incidit Paulus, mox summam quoq; eius repetit, ut ea occasione ad praesentis argumenti seu causae tractationem accedat. Tradidi enim vobis (inquit) in primis quod & acceperam: quod nimirum Christus mortuus est pro peccatis nostris, secundum scripturas: & quod sepultus est, & excitatus tertio die, secundum scripturas. Quo loco rursus ante omnia obseruari debet, quod non aliud se Corinthijs tradidisse scribit, quam quod acceperit a Domino, nimirum, quem unicum sui Euangelij authorem & magistrum fuisse, in epistola ad Gal. multis demonstrat. Ita vero decet verbi administros. Quia enim hos suae domus dispensatores Deus constituit, nihil huius familiae depromere debent, quam quod ex illius penu petitum sit. Et cur aliena obtrudat, cui herus tam dives tamq; liberalis obtigit, qui suis nihil defieri patitur, & suum potius Filium pro illis tradere voluit, quàm eos esurientes & egenos relinquere? Adde quod quæcunque aliunde petuntur, reuera non cibus sunt (vt Isaias ait) neque animas saturare possunt: imò plerunq; veneni & toxici instar sunt, quo infelices miserè contabescunt. Ideo Prophetæ olim iussi sunt ex ore Dei Verbum petere: & Apostolos certo mandato Dominus astringebat, vt ea suos auditores seruare docerent, quæ ipse eis tradidisset. Frustra ergo nobis hodie quidam traditiones Patrum aut Ecclesiæ obtrudere conantur. Cur enim patres agnosceremus alios, quàm Apostolos, qui mundum hunc totum (vt supra Paulus de Corinthijs dicebat) in Christo per Euangelium genuerunt? Nimium verò impudentes sunt, qui suis aut aliorum figmentis nomen Ecclesiæ prætexere audent. Quia enim Ecclesia ex Dei Verbo nascitur, & IESV CHRISTI sponsa est, ipsa Leges ab hoc accipere, non autem ex suo cerebro nouas conscribere solet, quas suis obtrudat. Nam probè nouit sibi iam olim dictum esse: Audi filia, & vide, inclina aurem tuam: obliuiscere populi tui, & domus patris tui. Neque etiam ignorare potest illud, quod ex Isaia Christus repetijt: Frustra me colunt docentes doctrinas hominum. Quapropter nemo eorum nugas audire debet, qui sua figmenta proferunt: neque sibi ipsi aliquis sub ignorantiæ aut simplicitatis Christianæ prætextu delitias faciat. Nam etsi nos simplices esse velit Dominus, id tamen admorum ingenuitatem & animos doli expertes restringi debet: in doctrinis autem dijudicandis nos solertes & prouidos esse conuenit, ne impostorum commentis nos seduci patiamur. Sed plura de hac re alibi dicta sunt.
units.tr: Moreover, because Paul mentioned the gospel only once, he soon repeats its summary, so that on that occasion he may come to the treatment of the present subject or cause. "For I delivered to you," he says, "first of all what I also received: namely, that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and raised on the third day according to the Scriptures." Here again, above all, it must be observed that he writes he handed on to the Corinthians nothing other than what he had received from the Lord, whom he shows in the epistle to the Galatians to have been the sole author and teacher of his gospel. This is indeed how the ministers of the Word ought to behave. For since God has appointed them as stewards of his household, they ought to bring forth nothing from this household except what has been drawn from its store. And why should someone push foreign goods on others, when he has been given so rich and so generous a master, who allows nothing to be lacking to his own, and preferred to give his own Son for them rather than leave them hungry and needy? Add that whatever is sought elsewhere is in truth not food (as Isaiah says), nor can it satisfy souls; indeed for the most part it is like poison and venom, by which the unhappy waste away wretchedly. Therefore the prophets were of old commanded to seek the word from the mouth of God; and the Lord bound the Apostles by a definite command to teach their hearers to keep those things which he himself had handed on to them. In vain, therefore, some men today try to force upon us the traditions of the Fathers or of the Church. For why should we acknowledge any fathers other than the Apostles, who begot this whole world in Christ through the gospel (as Paul said above of the Corinthians)? Truly they are too shameless who dare to put forward the name of the Church as a cover for their own or others' inventions. For since the Church is born of God's Word, and is the spouse of Jesus Christ, she is accustomed to receive her laws from him, not to write new ones out of her own brain to impose on her people. For she knows well that it was said to her long ago: "Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear: forget your people and your father's house." Nor can she be ignorant of what Christ repeated from Isaiah: "In vain do they worship me, teaching the doctrines of men." Wherefore no one should listen to the trifles of those who put forward their own fictions, nor should anyone indulge himself under the pretext of ignorance or Christian simplicity.
