For although the Lord wishes us to be simple, that simplicity must be restrained by the frankness of men and minds free of deceit; but in judging doctrines it is fitting for us to be shrewd and watchful, so that we do not allow ourselves to be led astray by the inventions of impostors. But more has been said on this matter elsewhere.

units.la: Nunc quæ illa Euangelicæ doctrinæ summa sit, videamus, quam Corinthijs Paulus tradidit. Comprehenditur ea duobus Capitibus. Primum est, quòd Christus mortuus sit secundum scripturas. Christi voce promissum humani generis seruatorem denotari, sæpe iam diximus: & ad hoc significatum in præsenti etiam Apostolus respicit. Itaque hic verborum istorum sensus est: Docui Messiam illum siue Christum, quem patribus olim Deus promisit, debuisse mori pro hominum peccatis, idq; præstitum esse in hoc IESV, qui ex Maria Virgine hominem assumpsit, & quem nos prædicamus: & hunc non fortuito, aut hostium vi oppressum mortem obijsse, sed secundum scripturas, quibus æternum Dei consilium de humani generis redemptione exponitur, &c. Id verò luculenter & perspicuè doceri imprimis opus erat. Nam IESVM mortuum esse, nemo negabat: imò hoc illud erat, quo Iudæi quàm maximè offendebantur, & propter quod Euangelij prædicatio Græcis stultitia erat, vt primo Cap. audiuimus. De eo autem contendebatur, an Messiam illum mori oportuerit ex æterno Dei consilio, & an Christus infamis & diræ mortis merito peccata mundi expiarit. Id verò Iudæi pertinacissimè negabant, & prophetijs perperam intellectis ad sui erroris confirmationem abutebantur: quales nimirum sunt, quæ de Messiæ & Regni eius perpetuitate habentur. In Psalmis enim scribitur: Dixit Dominus Domino meo, Sede à dextris meis, donec posuero inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum. Item: Semel per sanctitate meam iuraui, neque quaquam Dauidem fefellero: Semen eius in æternum erit, folium eius coram me vt Sol perstabit: firmum vt Luna manebit, quæ est certus in æthere testis, &c. Cuius generis multa adduci poterant, quæ omnia cùm Iudæi secundum literam de regno terreno exponerent, nihil absurdius fingi posse ipsis videbatur, quàm si quis IESVM hunc Messiam esse diceret, quem nõ solùm regno caruisse, sed medium inter latrones infamem in ara crucis mortem perpessum fuisse omnibus constabat. Ideo ipse Dominus quoties de sua morte apud discipulos disseruit, semper fere scripturarum meminit, in quibus illa sit prædicta. Et huc imprimis pertinent prolixæ illæ demonstrationes, quas à mortuis resuscitatus propositu, quarum summam tandem comprehendit his verbis: Ita scriptum est, & ita oportuit Christum pati, & resurgere à mortuis tertio die, & prædicari in eius nomine resipiscentiam & remissionem peccatorum, &c. Recte ergo magistri sui exemplum Apostoli imitati sunt, quando ipsi quoque, vt crucis scandalum remouerent, Christum ex æterno Patris decreto, quod in Scripturis reuelatum est, mortuum esse demonstrauerunt. Loci, quibus hoc probetur, passim occurrunt, & imprimis memorabiles atque perspicui sunt, qui extant, Isaiæ 53. Psalm.22. Danielis 9. Zacha.3. & 13. vt iam de typis nihil dicam, qui in Isaaci immolatione, in æneo serpente, agno paschali & omnibus alijs sacrificijs habentur. At quia de his alibi dictum est, ista iam prolixius exponere superuacaneum foret.
units.tr: Now let us see what is the sum of that evangelical doctrine which Paul handed on to the Corinthians. It is contained under two heads. The first is that Christ died according to the Scriptures. That by the word "Christ" the promised Saviour of the human race is meant, we have often said already, and to this meaning the Apostle also looks here. So the sense of these words is: I taught that the Messiah, or Christ, whom God promised to the fathers of old, had to die for the sins of men, and that this was accomplished in this Jesus, who took on man from the Virgin Mary, and whom we preach; and that he did not meet death by chance, or by being overcome by the violence of enemies, but according to the Scriptures, in which the eternal counsel of God concerning the redemption of the human race is set forth, and so on. This indeed needed above all to be taught clearly and plainly. For no one denied that Jesus had died; indeed this was the very thing by which the Jews were most offended, and on account of which the preaching of the gospel was foolishness to the Greeks, as we heard in the first chapter. But the dispute was whether that Messiah ought to die by the eternal counsel of God, and whether Christ, by the merit of an infamous and dreadful death, expiated the sins of the world. The Jews stubbornly denied this, and abused prophecies wrongly understood to confirm their error; such are, namely, those which are held concerning the perpetuity of the Messiah and his kingdom. For in the Psalms it is written: "The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet." Likewise: "Once I have sworn by my holiness, I will not lie to David: his seed shall endure forever, his throne shall stand before me like the sun, firm like the moon, which is a faithful witness in the sky." Many passages of this kind could be brought forward, and since the Jews explained all of them literally of an earthly kingdom, nothing seemed to them more absurd to imagine than if someone said that this Jesus was the Messiah, who, as everyone knew, not only lacked a kingdom but had suffered an infamous death on the cross between thieves. Therefore the Lord himself, whenever he spoke to his disciples about his death, almost always recalled the Scriptures in which it had been foretold. And to this especially pertain those lengthy demonstrations which he set out after he had been raised from the dead, the sum of which he finally gathered up in these words: "Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins be preached in his name," and so on. Rightly, then, the Apostles imitated the example of their master when, in order to remove the scandal of the cross, they too demonstrated that Christ died according to the eternal decree of the Father, which is revealed in the Scriptures. Passages by which this is proved occur everywhere, and those that exist are especially memorable and clear: Isaiah 53, Psalm 22, Daniel 9, Zechariah 3 and 13; not to speak now of the types, which are found in the sacrifice of Isaac, in the bronze serpent, the paschal lamb and all the other sacrifices. But since these things have been said elsewhere, it would be superfluous to set them out more fully here.

units.la: Alterum praedicationis euangelicae caput est, quod sepultus sit Christus, & idem tertio die resurrexerit secundum Scripturas. Sepulturae mentionem facit, quia ut haec illum vere mortuum esse probat, ita resurrectionis gloriam & quae in hac eluxit diuinam Christi virtutem vehementer illustrat. Oportuit autem Christum, qui pro peccatis nostris victima factus fuerat in ara crucis, a mortuis resurgere, ut mortem deuinceret, & redemptionem nostram compleret: de quo infra suo loco plura dicentur. Et haec causa est, quod illius mors & resurrectio semper coniunguntur, eo quod neque haec neque illa nobis seruandis sola sufficeret. Rursus vero Scripturarum meminit, quae illum resurrecturum esse olim praedixerint. Locos alibi annotauimus, & quia sacras literas legentibus nunquam non occurrunt, illos hic repetere nequaquam opus est. Nunc teneamus, duobus hisce capitibus non modo Euangelium totum, verum etiam summam redemptionis & salutis nostrae contineri. Quia ergo Christus pro peccatis nostris mortuus est, nos omnes peccatores esse fateamur oportet. Nam qui id negare velit, is Christum quoque pro se mortuum esse neget necesse est. Id vero peccati atrocitatem arguit, quae non potest non maxima & admodum detestabilis esse, quando non aliter quam morte Filii Dei expiari potuit. Quod ut blanditias peccati & carnis procul repellit, nos[?], ne illis locum demus monemur: ita omnes alias satisfactiones & omnia merita confutat, quibus homines superstitiosi se seruari posse sibi persuadent. Et sane stultissimi & mortalium infelicissimi sunt, qui ut plus sapiant quam Apostoli, quos Deus totius orbis doctores constituit, non contenti doctrina hac simplici & syncera, eam nouis quotidie commentis adulterant. Nos ergo, ne idem nobis quod Corinthijs accidat, stemus[?] in agnita Veritate, & salutis fiduciam collocemus in solius IESV CHRISTI merito, qui pro peccatis nostris secundum Scripturas mortuus est, & tertio die ex mortuis resuscitatus totam humani generis redemptionem plenissime absoluit. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: The second head of the evangelical preaching is that Christ was buried and that on the third day he rose again according to the Scriptures. He mentions the burial because, just as this proves that he truly died, so it greatly illustrates the glory of the resurrection and the divine power of Christ that shone forth in it. Christ, who had been made a victim for our sins on the altar of the cross, had to rise from the dead, so that he might overcome death and complete our redemption; more on this will be said in its proper place below. And this is the reason why his death and resurrection are always joined together, since neither of them alone would be sufficient for our salvation. Again, he recalls the Scriptures, which long ago foretold that he would rise. We have noted the passages elsewhere, and since they never fail to meet those who read the sacred letters, there is no need at all to repeat them here. Let us hold to this: that these two heads contain not only the whole Gospel but also the sum of our redemption and salvation. Therefore, since Christ died for our sins, we must confess that we are all sinners. For whoever wishes to deny this must necessarily deny that Christ also died for him. Indeed, this argues the atrocity of sin, which cannot but be very great and altogether detestable, since it could not be expiated in any other way than by the death of the Son of God. As this drives far away the flatteries of sin and of the flesh, and warns us not to give them any room, so it refutes all other satisfactions and all merits by which superstitious men persuade themselves they can be saved. And truly they are most foolish and the most unhappy of mortals, who, wishing to be wiser than the Apostles, whom God appointed as teachers of the whole world, are not content with this simple and sincere doctrine, but corrupt it every day with new inventions. Let us therefore, lest the same thing happen to us that happened to the Corinthians, stand firm in the acknowledged truth, and place our confidence of salvation in the merit of Jesus Christ alone, who died for our sins according to the Scriptures and, raised from the dead on the third day, has most fully accomplished the redemption of the human race. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY LXXVIII.

units.la: Et quod visus sit Cephae, deinde duodecim illis: Postea visus est amplius quam quingentis fratribus semel: ex quibus plerique manent usque adhuc, quidam autem obdormierunt. Postea visus est Iacobo, deinde Apostolis omnibus: Ultimo autem omnium veluti abortiuo, visus est etiam mihi. Ego enim sum minimus Apostolorum, qui non sum dignus vocari Apostolus, propterea quod perse-cutus sim Ecclesiam Dei: Sed gratia Dei sum id quod sum: & gratia eius erga me non fuit inanis, sed amplius quam illi omnes laborauì: non ego tamen, sed gratia Dei quae mecum est. Et ego igitur & illi ita praedicamus, & ita credidistis.
units.tr: "And that he was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve. After that he was seen of above five hundred brethren at once, of whom the greater part remain unto this present, but some are fallen asleep. After that he was seen of James, then of all the apostles. And last of all he was seen of me also, as of one born out of due time. For I am the least of the apostles, that am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am: and his grace which was bestowed upon me was not in vain; but I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me. Therefore whether it were I or they, so we preach, and so ye believed."

units.la: INter fidei Christianae articulos non temere prae aliis inculcatur passim in Scripturis, quo Resurrectionem corporum nostrorum ex mortuis profitemur. Est enim huius multiplex usus siue fructus. Primo nos plene redemptos atque seruatos esse docet, quando ne morte quidem vinci aut detineri possumus. Deinde aduersus mortis terrores consolatur, ne his superati aliquid faciamus nostra professione indignum. Adhaec dolorem atque luctum moderatur, quem ex nostrorum obitu concipimus. Praeterea voluptatum irritamenta restinguit, & mundi illecebris obstat, ne has aeternae vitae bonis praeferamus. Postremo patientiae basis siue fulcrum est firmissimum, quo sustentati per omnia aduersa & tentationum varios assultus eluctamur. Huius etenim spe con-firmatus Iobus inter dura illa, quae undique instabant, certamina, constans in fide perstitit, ut alibi quoque diximus. Eiusdem consideratione Paulus ipse recreatus mortem intrepido animo expectauit, quando Romae sub Nerone, libidinis & crudelitatis monstro, in carcere detinebatur. Et prophetae non raro ex mortuorum resurrectione argumenta petunt, quibus eos consolantur, quos in Babylonem abduci oportebat, aut qui iam illic extorres atque per omnes eius regni provincias dispersi affligebantur. Ideo huic doctrinae omnibus seculis Satan insidiatus est. Nam ut nihil de gentibus dicatur, inter quas vix aliqua eius mentio facta est, inter eos quoque, qui de animorum immortalitate aliquid disseruerunt, inter Iudæos certè, qui Dei peculium esse debebant, Sadducæos fuisse scimus, qui & corporum resurrectionem & animorum immortalitatem apertè negauerunt. Postea inter Christiani nominis professores, apostolis adhuc viuentibus, exorti sunt Hymenæus & Philetus, qui resurrectionem iam factam esse docebant, & ita futuræ illius spem omnem tollebant. Quorum vestigijs hodie Libertini insistunt. Taceo nunc eos, qui etsi illam faterentur, corporum tamen resuscitatorum veritatem negarunt, à quibus non multum differunt, qui nostro seculo Eutychetis de corpore Christi Deificato hæresin instaurant. Scit enim Satan, hoc fundamento euerso, religionem simul omnem corruere, & huic ex hominum animis sublatæ vel Epicuræam quiduis audendi licentiam, vel desperationem exitialem succedere. Quæ causa est, quòd cum apud Corinthios quoque articulus iste in dubium venisset, Paulus de illo multis & prolixè disserit. Et vt doctrinæ isti authoritas maior accederet, initio statim illam Euangelio contineri testatus est, cuius summa duobus hisce articulis, Christi nimirum morte & resurrectione comprehendatur. Quia autem in resurrectione Christi nostræ fundamentum est, illam argumentis pluribus astruit. Initio enim illum secundum Scripturas resurrexisse dixit, ne quid nouum aut insolens afferre putetur. Nunc testes producit, qui illum resuscitatum viderint.
units.tr: Among the articles of the Christian faith, the resurrection of our bodies from the dead is not lightly pressed above the others, yet it is pressed everywhere in the Scriptures. It has many uses and fruits. First, it teaches that we have been fully redeemed and saved, since not even death can overcome or hold us. Second, it comforts us against the terrors of death, lest, overcome by them, we do anything unworthy of our profession. Besides this, it tempers the grief and mourning we feel at the death of our own people. Furthermore, it quenches the incentives of pleasure and resists the allurements of the world, so that we do not prefer them to the good things of eternal life. Lastly, it is the firmest foundation and support of patience, by which, sustained through all adversities and the various assaults of temptations, we struggle on. For Job, confirmed by this hope, persevered constant in faith amid those harsh conflicts that pressed on him from every side, as we have said elsewhere. By the same consideration Paul himself, refreshed, awaited death with a fearless spirit, when at Rome under Nero, that monster of lust and cruelty, he was held in prison. And the prophets often draw arguments from the resurrection of the dead, by which they console those who were to be led away to Babylon, or who were already exiles there and afflicted, scattered through all the provinces of that kingdom. For this reason Satan has always laid snares for this doctrine. To say nothing of the Gentiles, among whom there is scarcely any mention of it, even among those who discoursed on the immortality of souls, and certainly among the Jews, who ought to have been God's peculiar people, we know there were Sadducees, who openly denied both the resurrection of bodies and the immortality of souls. Later, among the professors of the Christian name, while the apostles were still living, Hymenaeus and Philetus arose, who taught that the resurrection had already taken place, and so removed all hope of the future one. Today the Libertines follow in their footsteps. I say nothing now of those who, though they confessed the resurrection, denied the truth of the raising of bodies; these do not differ much from those who in our age revive the heresy of Eutyches about the deified body of Christ. Satan knows that once this foundation is overthrown, all religion collapses together with it, and that in place of it, from men's minds, there succeeds either an Epicurean license to dare anything, or deadly despair. This is why, when this article was also called into doubt among the Corinthians, Paul disputes about it at length and with many arguments. And so that greater authority might attach to this doctrine, he at once testified at the outset that it is contained in the Gospel, the sum of which is comprehended in these two articles, namely the death and resurrection of Christ. Because our hope rests on the resurrection of Christ, he establishes it by several arguments. For first he said that Christ rose again according to the Scriptures, lest anything new or strange be thought to be brought forward. Now he produces witnesses who saw him raised.

units.la: Debet autem hic ordo in dogmatibus ecclesiasticis obseruari, vt primus locus Scripturis sacris detur, per quas nobis Deus loquitur. Sine his enim nulla erit testium qualiumcunque authoritas, qui cum illis pugnantia dicunt. Nihil ergo hodie proficiunt, qui Patres, Concilia, Canones & sexcenta alia tonant. Ex Dei Verbo controuersiæ de fide & religione decidi debent, cuius Oraculum certum non alibi quàm in Scripturis inuenitur.
units.tr: In doctrines of the Church this order ought to be observed, that the first place be given to the holy Scriptures, through which God speaks to us. For without these there will be no authority of any witnesses, however they may be, who say things contrary to them. Therefore those who now thunder about the Fathers, the Councils, the canons and six hundred other things accomplish nothing. Controversies about faith and religion ought to be decided from the Word of God, whose sure oracle is found nowhere but in the Scriptures.

units.la: Obseruabis autem toto hoc loco, Paulum non alios quàm oculatos testes adducere, cùm & pro-phetarum oraculis & argumentis siue rationibus firmissimis causam suam probare posset. Ita enim quæstiones curiosorum hominum simul omnes præcidere voluit, simulq; docere, Christum vero & naturali suo corpore verè & realiter, siue etiam corporaliter, resurrexisse, neque aliquid hîc fingi debere spirituale, quod eius resurrectionem in dubium vocare posset. Quæ enim spiritualia sunt, & non verè fiunt, sensibus nostris non possunt percipi: at quæ oculis cernuntur, tactui item subiacent, ea reuera sint oportet. Ideo Christus se ex mortuis rediuiuum discipulis suis videndum atq; contrectandum præbuit, ne se spectrum aut spiritum videre existimarent. Et Apostoli, se illum non modò vidisse, verumetiam contrectauisse, adhæc cum illo comedisse & bibisse testantur.
units.tr: Observe throughout this passage that Paul adduces none but eyewitnesses, although he could have proved his cause by the oracles of the prophets and by most firm arguments or reasons. For he wished in this way to cut off at once all the questions of curious men, and at the same time to teach that Christ rose truly and really, or even bodily, with his natural body, and that nothing spiritual ought to be imagined here which could call his resurrection into doubt. For things that are spiritual and do not truly happen cannot be perceived by our senses; but things that are seen by the eyes and are also subject to touch must truly be so. Therefore Christ showed himself to his disciples, risen from the dead, to be seen and handled, lest they should think they saw a ghost or a spirit. And the apostles testify that they not only saw him but also touched him, and moreover ate and drank with him.
Luke 24. John 20, 21. Acts 1 and 10.

units.la: Porro videamus testes istos, qui nam sint, & quo ordine à Paulo producantur. Ex Euangelica enim historia, illum mulieribus primis visum fuisse, constat, quæ ad corpus eius pro more gentis unctura ad sepulchrum exiuerant: vt se eius etiam sexus seruatorem esse doceret, per quem peccatum & mors introuerant. At Paulus virorum solummodo meminit, ne illusoribus testimonia ista eludendi aliquam occasionem præbeat: quod gratuitatis & prudentiæ apostolicæ exemplum est. Constat enim multis exemplis, causam per se bonam interdum propter testes suspectam fieri, si tales producantur, quorum fides dubia & incerta est. Et historiæ docent, quàm graviter in testibus vel admittendis vel reijciendis olim Romani egerint, qui illo tempore rerum potiebantur. Quoad autem huius loci historiam, non temere factum putabimus, quòd Christus non initio statim discipulis suis simul omnibus, sed per interualla nunc his nunc illis se visendum præbuit. Ita enim causam hanc, per se creditu difficilem, agi oportuit, vt primi quique (quod Chrysostomus quoque annotauit) alteris viam sternerent ad tanti mysterij fidem atq; cognitionem.
units.tr: Let us look further at who these witnesses are and in what order Paul produces them. From the Gospel history it is clear that he first appeared to the women, who had gone out to the sepulchre to anoint his body according to the custom of their people; so that he might show himself to be the Saviour also of that sex through which sin and death had entered. But Paul mentions only men, so that he may not give the mockers any occasion to evade the testimony; this is an example of apostolic candour and prudence. For it is established by many examples that a cause which is good in itself is sometimes made suspect because of the witnesses, if such are brought forward whose faith is doubtful and uncertain. And histories teach how gravely the Romans, who at that time held power over affairs, were wont to proceed in admitting or rejecting witnesses. As for the history of this passage, we shall not think it happened by chance that Christ did not show himself at once to all his disciples together, but at intervals, now to these, now to those. For this matter, difficult to believe in itself, had to be handled in such a way that the first ones (as Chrysostom also observed) should pave the way for the others toward faith in and knowledge of so great a mystery.

units.la: Primus autem sistitur Cephas, quem eundem cum Petro esse ex verbis Ioannis Euangelistæ constat, quæ primo Cap. habentur. Facit autem huius rei mentionem Lucas quoque, quando vndecim apostolos duobus discipulis Emmaunte reuersis dixisse scribit: Surrexit Dominus verè, & apparuit Simoni. Est hoc singulare exemplum gratiæ quo Christum ideo in mundum venisse docemur, vt peccatores saluos faceret. Fuit enim Petrus abnegator Christi, & proinde indignus, quem ille porro pro suo agnosceret. Verumtamen & Angeli huic imprimis illius resurrectionem mulieres nuntiare iubent, & eidem primo inter discipulos idem ille apparet. Debent ex eo consolationem petere, quotquot peccatorum suorum conscientia grauantur, ne Christi meritum nihil ad se pertinere existiment: at ijdem Petri studium imitentur, qui etsi ex carnis infirmitate illum abnegauisset, mox tamen peccatum suum amaris lachrymis defleuit, relicto item impiorum impij Pontificis satellitum consortio ad Ecclesiam redijt, alijsque feruentior primus ad sepulchrum excurrit, cùm illum resuscitatum esse audiuisset. Vide Ioan.20.
units.tr: Now Cephas is the first to be set forth, and it is clear from the words of the Evangelist John, which occur in the first chapter, that he is the same as Peter. Luke too makes mention of this matter, when he writes that the eleven apostles said to the two disciples who returned from Emmaus: "The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon." This is a singular example of grace, by which we are taught that Christ came into the world in order to save sinners. For Peter was a denier of Christ, and therefore unworthy that Christ should still acknowledge him as his own. Yet the angels above all bid the women announce to him the resurrection, and to him Christ first appears among the disciples. From this, all who are weighed down by the awareness of their sins should take comfort, lest they think the merit of Christ has nothing to do with them. And let them imitate the zeal of Peter, who, though by the weakness of the flesh he had denied him, soon bewailed his sin with bitter tears, and, having left the company of the impious servants of the wicked high priest, returned to the Church; and he, more fervent than the others, was the first to run to the sepulchre when he heard that Christ had risen. See John 20.

units.la: Habemus praeterea in Paulo praeclarum modestiae exemplum. Sciebat is multos inter Corinthios inueniri, qui Petri authoritate & nomine aduersus ipsum abutebantur: adhaec eidem aliquando in faciem resistere coactus fuit, cùm illum ignaua dissimulatione uti videret, qua multorum fides labefactabatur, Iudaei autem in suis superstitionibus magis confirmabantur. Attamen neque proprij honoris studio neque veteris controuersiae memoria vinci potest, ut ea dissimulet, quae ad tanti Apostoli commendationem faciebant. Quod si simili animorum moderatione hodie omnes vterentur, qui ad Ecclesiae gubernacula sedent, minus dissidiorum esset, & maioribus incrementis Christi regnum surgeret, quod nunc ambitiosis Theologastrorum quorundam concertationibus magna cum multorum offensione distrahitur. Quam vero alieni sunt a Pauli spiritu, qui in viros optime de Ecclesia meritos, & quorum fides in oppugnandis communibus Christi aduersarijs perquam egregia eluxit, & qui iampridem in Christo obdormierunt, dentes Theoninos stringunt, memoriam illorum odiose laniant, & neminem ferre possunt, qui de illis honorificè sentit aut loquitur? Non sunt haec apostolici spiritus sed pectoris ambitiosi & liuidi argumenta.
units.tr: Moreover, in Paul we have a notable example of modesty. He knew that among the Corinthians there were many who abused the authority and name of Peter against him; besides, he was once compelled to resist Peter to his face, when he saw him using a lazy dissimulation, by which the faith of many was weakened, while the Jews were confirmed the more in their superstitions. Yet neither the zeal for his own honour nor the memory of an old quarrel could prevail on him to pass over in silence those things that tended to the commendation of so great an apostle. If all those who now sit at the helm of the Church would use the same moderation of mind, there would be fewer dissensions, and the kingdom of Christ would rise with greater growth, which now is torn apart by the ambitious contentions of certain little theologians, to the great offence of many. How far are they from the spirit of Paul, who grind their Theonine teeth against men who have deserved very well of the Church, and whose faith shone forth most excellently in opposing the common adversaries of Christ, and who long ago fell asleep in Christ; who viciously tear their memory to pieces, and cannot bear anyone who thinks or speaks honourably of them? These are not signs of an apostolic spirit but of an ambitious and envious heart.

units.la: Secundo loco Duodecim simul producit Paulus, quorum nomine discipulos illos peculiares intelligit, quos sibi prae alijs Christus elegit, ut eorum opera in Euangelij sui praedicatione per totum orbem diuulganda vteretur: vnde etiam Apostoli dicti fuerunt. Loquitur autem de ea apparitione, quae in ipso resurrectionis die facta fuit, & cuius historia Lucae vlt. & Ioannis Cap.20. describitur. Praecessit tamen quod cum Cleopa & eius comite in itinere Emmauntino accidit. Neque pugnat cum Paulo, quod Ioannes Thomam tunc abfuisse scribit, & quod Iudas proditor iam ante e medio fuit sublatus. Quia enim duodenarius numerus apud omnes obtinuerat, solent Duodecim dici, etiamsi vnus aut alter ex eo numero desiderentur: neque id ab vsitata dicendi consuetudine alienum est. Apud Romanos certe olim Centumuiri dicebantur, qui iudicijs praefecti erant, cùm in eo ordine viri centum & quinque numerarentur: & Centumuirorum authoritate siue decreto pronuntiata dicebatur sententia, etiamsi plures ex illis non interfuissent. Et in nostra Repub. Diacosiorum siue Ducentorum nomine publica edicta promulgantur, licet raro contingat, ut non aliqui ex eo numero desint. Ergo minimè opus est hoc loco nodū in scirpo quaerere, aut ad solutiones argutas magis quam solidas confugere, ut vel Matthia, vel alium aliquem adfuisse dicamus, quando non tam de numero hic agitur, quam de ordine eorum, quibus tunc Dominus visus fuit. Nos potius illius bonitatem & fidem consideremus, qui cùm discipulos inter spem & metum fluctuare sciret, illos diutius suspensos tenere noluit: sed eo ipso die suam ex mortuis resurrectionem ita demonstrauit, ut de eius veritate non possent amplius dubitare. Idem ergo neque nobis deerit, si ab eo institui & confirmari cupiamus.
units.tr: Second, Paul brings forward the Twelve together. By this name he means those chosen disciples whom Christ picked out above the rest so that, through their work, his gospel might be spread throughout the whole world; that is why they were also called Apostles. He is speaking of the appearance that took place on the very day of the resurrection, which is described in the last chapter of Luke and in John chapter 20. But something came before it, namely what happened with Cleopas and his companion on the road to Emmaus. Nor does it conflict with Paul that John writes that Thomas was then absent, or that Judas the traitor had already been removed from the group. Since the number twelve had become established among everyone, they are commonly called the Twelve even when one or another of that number is missing, and this is not foreign to ordinary usage. Among the Romans, certainly, those who presided over the courts were once called the Centumviri, although that body numbered one hundred and five men; and a sentence was said to be pronounced by the authority or decree of the Centumviri even when several of them had not been present. Likewise in our own commonwealth, public edicts are issued in the name of the Two Hundred, although it rarely happens that some of that number are not absent. So there is absolutely no need here to seek a knot in a rush, or to take refuge in subtle rather than solid explanations, saying that Matthias or some other person was present, since the question here concerns not so much the number as the company of those to whom the Lord then showed himself. Let us rather consider his goodness and faithfulness, for he knew that the disciples were wavering between hope and fear, and he was unwilling to keep them in suspense for long. Instead, on that same day he demonstrated his resurrection from the dead in such a way that they could no longer doubt its truth. Therefore the same goodness will not be lacking to us, if we desire to be instructed and confirmed by him.

units.la: Tertiò, visus est (inquit) amplius quam quingentis fratribus semel, ex quibus plerique manent vsque adhuc, quidam autem obdormierunt. Debet hoc de celebri illo conuentu intelligi, quo discipulos in Galilaea simul omnes collegit, ut inter eos de tota Regni sui administratione dissereret, & Apostolis praedicandi Euangelij munus commendaret: quod ad fidem ipsis conciliandam imprimis faciebat. Describit actionem illam Matthaeus sub finem Euangelici sui operis, unde tota eius historia peti debet. Apparuit autem in ea IESV CHRISTI inuicta planè diuina potentia, & euidens regni sui per totum orbem terrarum propagandi argumentum. Illum enim, cùm ad montem Oliueti caperetur, ab omnibus relictum & desertum fuisse scimus: morienti verò nemo praeter Ioannem adfuit, & Virgo mater cum mulierculis aliquot & notis quibusdam eius, qui eminus spectabant. At nunc paucorum dierum spatio eò vsque excreuit credentium numerus, ut quingenti numerentur, quos Spiritus Sanctus fratres, id est, verè fideles & germanos Christi discipulos dicere dignatur. Plures ergo tunc fuerunt, quàm quando miraculis clarus docebat. hat. Adde his, quòd inter fauissimas[?] persecutionum procellas, & undique impendentia pericula istos omnes ita seruauit vt plerique eorum tunc adhuc in vinis fuerint, cùm epistolam hanc Paulus scriberet, quod anno ab Ascensione Christi circiter vigesimo factum fuisse ex coniecturis minimè incertis potest colligi. Itaque per Crucem ille triumphat (vt aliàs diximus) & tunc efficacissimè agit in hominum cordibus, quando extinctus & sepultus esse putatur. Horum ergo meminerimus, quando res Christiana in angustum redacta esse videtur, & omnia nobis exitium inevitabile minantur. Vt enim olim ex parvis atque ignobilibus reliquijs, quas in Judæorum gente Deus sibi seruauerat, Ecclesia in immensum creuit: ita posteris quoque temporibus idem factum esse legimus, & hodie multa fiunt, quæ nobis spem istam possunt confirmare. Nunquam ergo nobis excidat, Regnum Christi non hominum viribus siue authoritate niti, sed totum à Dei potentia siue nutu pendere.
units.tr: Third, he says, he was seen by more than five hundred brethren at one time, of whom most remain until now, though some have fallen asleep. This must be understood of that famous gathering in which he brought all the disciples together in Galilee, in order to speak with them about the whole administration of his kingdom and to commend to the Apostles the duty of preaching the gospel, which was especially useful for securing their faith. Matthew describes that event at the end of his Gospel, and from there his whole account should be sought. In it there appeared the altogether invincible divine power of Jesus Christ, and clear evidence that his kingdom would be spread throughout the whole world. For we know that when he was seized at the Mount of Olives, he was abandoned and deserted by all; and at his death none was present except John, and his mother the Virgin with a few women and certain acquaintances who watched from a distance. But now, within a span of a few days, the number of believers had grown so much that five hundred are counted, whom the Holy Spirit deigns to call brethren, that is, truly faithful and genuine disciples of Christ. There were therefore more then than when he taught, famous for his miracles. Add to this that, amid the most savage storms of persecution and dangers hanging over them on every side, he so preserved all these people that many of them were still alive when Paul wrote this letter; this can be gathered from conjectures that are by no means uncertain, to have happened about twenty years after the Ascension of Christ. Thus he triumphs through the Cross (as we have said elsewhere), and he is most effective in men's hearts precisely when he is thought to be extinguished and buried. Let us therefore remember these things when the Christian cause seems reduced to a narrow state and all things threaten us with inevitable ruin. For just as the Church once grew immensely from small and humble remnants that God had preserved for himself among the Jewish nation, so we read that the same has happened in later times, and today many things are happening which can confirm this hope in us. Let it never slip from our minds that the kingdom of Christ rests not on the strength or authority of men, but depends entirely on the power and will of God.

units.la: Quartus producitur Jacobus, cui Christus visus sit. Plerique eum intelligunt, quem fratrem Domini dixerunt, cognomento Justum, & quem Hierosolymorum episcopum fuisse veteres tradunt. Quod si verum est, non fuit ille ex duodecim Apostolorum numero, quibus minimè licuit sedes certas siue fixas habere, cùm Euangelium hinc inde per totum orbem prædicare deberent. Et Paulus ad Ephesios scribens, inter Apostolos & Pastores (qui & Episcopi dicuntur) euidenter distinguit. At si Hierosolymæ episcopus fuit Jacobus ille, hoc etiam non contemnendum est bonitatis Dei argumentum, qui huic Filium suum ex morte restitutum peculiari visione innotescere voluit, quem ad munus imprimis arduum & periculosum destinauerat. Quis enim non videat, quàm graue & durum fuerit in ea ciuitate Ecclesiam regere, in qua Christi latrones, præsidum Romanorum potentia atque authoritate armati, dominabantur? Quid non illic videre & audire oportuit fidos Christi cultores? Quàm multis quamq; acerbis piorum querelis eum fatigatum fuisse putabimus, qui illic pastorem gregis Christiani agebat? Sed solet Deus viribus & donis necessarijs armare eos, quos rebus magnis destinat.
units.tr: Fourth, James is brought forward, to whom Christ appeared. Most understand him to be the one whom they called the brother of the Lord, surnamed the Just, and whom the ancients report to have been bishop of Jerusalem. If this is true, he was not one of the number of the twelve Apostles, who were by no means permitted to have fixed or settled seats, since they were to preach the gospel here and there throughout the whole world. And Paul, writing to the Ephesians, clearly distinguishes between Apostles and Pastors (who are also called Bishops). But if that James was bishop of Jerusalem, this too is no small evidence of God's goodness, who wished to make known by a special vision to this man his Son restored from death, whom he had destined above all for a task that was very hard and dangerous. For who does not see how grave and harsh it must have been to rule the Church in that city, where the robbers of Christ, armed with the power and authority of the Roman governors, held sway? What must the faithful worshippers of Christ have had to see and hear there? How many and how bitter the complaints of the godly must have wearied him, who there served as pastor of the Christian flock? But God is accustomed to arm with the necessary strength and gifts those whom he destines for great things.

units.la: Quinto loco Apostoli simul omnes producuntur: quo nomine discipulos quoq; Septuaginta comprehendit, quos similiter ad prædicandum emissos fuisse Lucas scribit: nec dubium est, quin eosdem postea sibi adiunxerint Duodecim illi, & prædicandi prouincias inter illos distribuerint, prout rei necessitas postulabat. Quapropter necesse fuit, vt Christus ipsis quoque familiarius innotesceret, & vt testes αὐτόπται siue oculati possent esse Resurrectionis suæ, de qua potissimùm controuertebatur. Vbi obseruatione dignum est, quòd etiamsi Apostoli, quoad dona Spiritus, aliis præstantiores fuerint, tamen quoad salutarem & necessariam hominibus Christi cognitionem, æquales aut pares fuerunt, sed ipsum ille omnibus manifestare dignatus est, vt eadem esset doctrinæ, quæ ab illis prædicabatur, authoritas. Admonemur isto argumento, ne de illa ex hominum respectu iudicemus. Vt enim olim omnes, qui Apostoli erant, & Christum viderant, fidem merebantur: ita hodie etiam quicunque vera Christi cognitione instructi sunt, & legitimè ad docendi munus vocati ab illo accepta prædicant, ii audiri debent. Omnibus enim illis seruit, quod Dominus dixit: Qui vos audit, me audit, &c. Luc.10.
units.tr: Fifth, all the Apostles together are brought forward. By this name he also includes the Seventy disciples, whom Luke writes were likewise sent out to preach. Nor is there any doubt that the Twelve afterwards joined them to themselves and distributed among them the provinces for preaching, as the need of the matter required. Therefore it was necessary for Christ to become more familiarly known to them too, and for them to be eyewitnesses [αὐτόπται] of his resurrection, which was the chief point under dispute. Here it is worth noting that although the Apostles were more outstanding than the others in respect of the gifts of the Spirit, nevertheless in respect of the saving and necessary knowledge of Christ which men need, they were equal or on a par with them; and he deigned to make himself manifest to all of them, so that the authority of the teaching proclaimed by them would be the same. This argument warns us not to judge that teaching by regard for persons. For just as once all who were Apostles and had seen Christ deserved faith, so today also whoever has been instructed in the true knowledge of Christ and, lawfully called to the office of teaching, proclaims what he has received from him, ought to be heard. For what the Lord said applies to all of them: "He who hears you hears me," etc. Luke 10.

units.la: Postremò testium, quos vidimus, catalogo seipsum quoque Paulus adnumerat, ne ex aliorum relatione de re sibi non satis perspecta loqui videatur: idq; propter æmulos facit, qui vt eius authoritatem eleuarent, ipsum cum Christo versatum esse & hunc vidisse negabant. Ergo eum ex mortuis rediuiuum abs se quoque conspectum fuisse ait. Quando autem id factum sit, non satis constat. Illud tamen certum est, Christum Paulo visum esse ad Damasci vrbem, & eidem tunc pro-misisse, quòd in posterum quoque ipsi apparere velit. Hoc enim in præclara illa oratione, quam coram Agrippa Rege & Festo præside habuit, diserte testatur. Similiter in alia oratione ad populum Hierosolymitanū, illum sibi in templo oranti apparuisse dicit, & mandatum dedisse, vt rebludæis ad gentes prædicatum abiret. Ex posteriori item ad Corinth. epistola patet, ipsum crebris visionibus confirmatum fuisse, quando laborum & periculorum necessitas tale quid postulabat. Nam quod antea diximus, solet Deus suis seruis adesse, quos rebus grauibus destinauit, ne supra quàm ferre possint, tententur.
units.tr: Last of all, Paul also counts himself in the catalogue of the witnesses whom they have seen, so that he might not seem to speak of a matter not sufficiently known to him from the report of others. He does this on account of his rivals, who, in order to diminish his authority, denied that he had lived with Christ and had seen him. Therefore he says that he too saw him risen again from the dead. When this happened is not altogether clear. Yet this is certain: Christ appeared to Paul near the city of Damascus, and then promised him that he would wish to appear to him again in the future. He clearly testifies to this in that famous speech which he gave before King Agrippa and the governor Festus. Similarly, in another speech to the people of Jerusalem, he says that Christ appeared to him while he was praying in the temple and gave him the command to depart and preach to the Gentiles far from the Jews. It is also evident from the later letter to the Corinthians that he was strengthened by frequent visions whenever the necessity of his labours and dangers demanded something of this kind. For, as we said before, God is accustomed to be present with his servants whom he has destined for weighty tasks, so that they are not tried beyond what they can bear.

units.la: Scio quid hic aliqui obiciant: Christum à Paulo videri non potuisse, si ille corpore suo in cœlis, id est, extra hunc mundum corruptibilem agat, & proinde vel hinc patere, Ascensionem non de motu aliquo ex loco in locum alium intelligi debere, sed de mutata corporis Christi qualitate & œconomia, qua factum fit, ut qui prius visibiliter & ratione huius seculi in terris agebat, nunc quidem eas minimè reliquerit, sed vero suo corpore nunc ubique nobis præsens adsit, seq; nobis quando vult videndum, aut etiam contrectandum præbeat. Nam si in cœlis esset corpus Christi (aiunt) neq; Paulus neque Stephanus illic eum videre potuissent, cum oraculorum acies nec nubes quidem, nedum orbes cœlestes simul omnes penetrare possit. Quibus ego respondeo, Paulum non tam imprudentem disputatorem fuisse, ut corporis Christi resurrectionem eiusmodi argumento aferere voluerit, quo aut corporis veritas aut eiusdem Ascensio negetur. Cur enim hoc faceret, qui non uno loco Christum nobis in cœlo, & quidem in supernis locis, id est, in cœlo quod supra nos est, monstrat, & eidem corpus verum tribuit, cui nostra corpora olim conformia fieri oporteat? Non possumus ergo eius verba aliter accipere quam sonant, cum de fidei articulo agatur, qui si bifariam resurrectionis & corporis Christi veritatem eiusq; naturales siue essentiales proprietates negemus, confiteri non poterit. Etsi ergo nobis non constet, quando, aut ubi, qua denique ratione Christum Paulus viderit, illum tamen ab eo visum esse certum est, neq; propterea opus fuerit, corpus Christi vel è cœlis detrahere, vel Ubiquarium siue Utopicum fingere. Qui enim priusquam Paulum ad fidem converteretur, cœlos findere & Stephani oculos ita acuere potuit, ut ipsum à dextris Dei stantem & quasi ad vindictam paratum cerneret: hoc ipsum in Paulo quoq; potuit præstare: eoq; efficacior fuit consolatio, si in cœlis agentem vidit, quem cœlitus voce sua intonantem audiuerat: Saul Saul, cur me persequeris? Sed omissis contentiosis illis, qui corpus ipsum Christi totum potuit negauerint, quàm pro eius corporali in terris præsentia & eiusdem Capernaitica manducatione contendere desinant, Paulum de ista Christi apparitione loquentem audiamus.
units.tr: I know what some here will object: Paul could not have seen Christ if Christ's body is in heaven, that is, beyond this corruptible world. From this they conclude that the Ascension should not be understood as a movement from one place to another, but as a change in the quality and economy of Christ's body. By that change he no longer dwells visibly on earth in the manner of this age, but his true body is now present everywhere with us, and he allows himself to be seen or even touched by us when he wills. For (they say) if Christ's body were in heaven, neither Paul nor Stephen could have seen him there, since no sharpness of sight can penetrate even the clouds, much less all the heavenly spheres. To these I reply: Paul was not so careless a reasoner that he would argue for the resurrection of Christ's body by an argument that denies either the truth of the body or its Ascension. Why would he do so, when in more than one place he shows Christ to us in heaven, indeed in the highest places, that is, in the heaven that is above us, and ascribes to him a true body, to which our own bodies must one day be made like? So we cannot take his words otherwise than they sound, since the matter concerns an article of faith. If we deny the truth of Christ's resurrection and body, and its natural or essential properties, in either way, we shall not be able to confess the faith. So even though we do not know when, where, or by what means Paul saw Christ, it is certain that he was seen by him, and there is no need either to drag Christ's body down from heaven or to invent a ubiquitous, or Utopian, body. For if he who could, before Paul was converted to the faith, cleave the heavens and sharpen Stephen's eyes so that he saw him standing at God's right hand, as if ready for vengeance, could do the same for Paul too; and the consolation was all the more effective if Paul saw him acting in heaven, whom he had heard thundering from heaven with his own voice: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? But let us set aside those contentious men who have been able to deny the whole body of Christ, and stop contending for his bodily presence on earth and for that Capernaitic eating of him. Let us hear Paul speaking of this appearance of Christ.

units.la: Vltimo autem omnium veluti abortiuo visus est etiam mihi, ἐκτρώμα, id est, abortum, fœtum abortiuum se vocat ratione sui apostolatus siue minisserij. Proprie enim sic dicitur fœtus, qui intra diem à conceptione quadragesimum extruditur aliqua violenta naturæ operatione. Iidem [?] aliorum Apostolorum respectu, qui cum Christo diutius versati & institutione ordinaria quasi fuerant ad docendi munus, potuit Paulus reuera ἐκτρώμα siue abortus dici, qui præter omnem expectationem vocatus, & subitò Christi cognitione illuminatus, adeoq; singulari vi Spiritus Sancti extrusus fuit, ut ex lupo pastor factus, Euangelium magna cum omnium admiratione prædicaret. Voluit autem ita loqui propter æmulos suos, ut ofendat, se quàmuis reliquis Apostolis libenter concedat dignitatem illam, quam ex diuturniori cum Christo consuetudine habeant, tamen, se quoq; eiusdem veteri fœtum, id est, germanum Christi Apostolum esse. Est autem hoc memorabile exemplum gratiæ Dei, quo docemur, quàm facilè huic fit vasa gratiæ suæ facere ex illè, qui iræ & ignominiæ vasa esse videbantur. Quod ut nos aduersus conscientiæ terrores consolatur: ita simul admonere debet, ne de alicuius conuersione aut salute temere desperemus.
units.tr: Last of all, as if to one born out of due time, he appeared to me also, ἐκτρώμα [ekthrōma], that is, an abortion; with respect to his apostleship or ministry he calls himself an abortive foetus. Properly, that is called a foetus which is expelled before the fortieth day from conception by some violent operation of nature. In comparison with the other apostles, who had been with Christ for a longer time and had been prepared for the office of teaching by ordinary instruction, Paul could indeed be called an ἐκτρώμα [ekthrōma], or abortion, since he was called contrary to all expectation, was suddenly enlightened by the knowledge of Christ, and was thrust forth by the singular power of the Holy Spirit, so that from a wolf he became a shepherd and preached the gospel to the great amazement of all. He chose to speak in this way because of his rivals, so that he might show that, although he willingly grants to the other apostles the dignity that they have from longer companionship with Christ, nevertheless he too is a true apostle of Christ, a foetus of the same kind, that is, a genuine apostle. This is a memorable example of the grace of God, by which we are taught how easily he makes vessels of his grace out of those who seemed to be vessels of wrath and dishonour. This should comfort us against the terrors of conscience, and at the same time it should warn us not to despair rashly of anyone's conversion or salvation.

units.la: Cæterum non ignorabat Paulus, æmulos suos hoc imprimis agere, ut ipsius testimonium el-uarent [?]: quapropter non minus modestè quàm grauiter eius authoritate siue fidem confirmat. Nam debent quidem ministri humilitati & modestiæ studere, ne quid de seipsis arrogantius loquantur aut sentiant: ijdem tamen suam authoritatem aduersus malignos Verbi Dei contemptores constanter tueri atque asserere debent, ne hoc propter ipsos in contemptum veniat. Hoc olim Prophetas fastitauisse [?] scimus, & Christus, quo nemo mortalium modestior fuit & humilior, id ipsum non semel obseruauit. Vt autem res tota fit dilucidior, confert Paulus priorem suam conditionem cum ea, quam tunc sustinebat. Ad priorem pertinet, quod ait: Ego enim sum minimus Apostolorum qui non sum dignus vocari Apostolus. Et mox causam ipse subjicit: Propterea quod persecutus sum Ecclesiam Dei. Ex animo igitur & seriò loquitur, non ut Monachi & Pontifices, qui se Minimos & Seruos seruorum dicunt, cùm hoc vnum agant, ut sub inani humilitatis specie omnibus dominentur atque imperent. Eam enim causam adducit, qua verissimè probat quod dicit. Quis enim Ecclesiæ persecutorem dignum esse dixerit, qui subito Apostolus fiat? Quis lupum, ut pastorem agat, idoneum iudicet? Solet autem Paulus frequenter sui pristini status meminisse, ut Dei gratiam magis commendet: Ideo in præsenti culpam suam minime extenuat, & eandem absq; omni exceptione sibi soli adscribit. Poterat enim dicere: Nemo me impium Ecclesiae hostem fuisse putet, qui sciens volens cum Deo bellum susceperim. Quicquid enim feci, ideo feci, ut ijs morem gererem, qui tunc in populo Dei regnabant, & ab his accepto mandato eos persecutus sum, quos illi scismaticos [?], impios & quouis supplicio dignos iudicabant. Et ut id facerem, zelus gloriae Dei me momordit, cuius Legem & veterem cultum aboleri videbam, &c. Haec (inquam) & alia huius generis poterat dicere, si effugia captauisset: sed simpliciter, se Ecclesiam Dei persecutum esse ait: eam nimirum, quam alibi pretioso Dei sanguine redemptam esse testatur. Itaq; scelus longè atrocissimum in semetipso agnoscit, quod hodie etiam in omnibus haeret, qui Euangelicae doctrinae sectatores hostiliter persequuntur. Nec enim hic aliquem excusant Pontificum aut quorumcunque hominum de nobis iudicia: sed ratum erit, quod olim Christus per Prophetam dixit: Qui vos tangit, tangit pupillam oculi mei. Et quod ipsi Paulo dictum fuit: Saul Saul, quid me persequeris?
units.tr: Moreover, Paul was not unaware that his rivals were chiefly doing this, namely, trying to undermine his testimony; therefore he confirms his authority no less modestly than seriously. For ministers ought indeed to strive for humility and modesty, so that they say or think nothing too arrogant about themselves; yet at the same time they must constantly defend and assert their authority against the malicious despisers of God's Word, lest it come into contempt on their account. We know that the prophets were despised in this way in former times, and Christ, than whom no mortal was more modest or humble, observed the same thing more than once. So that the whole matter may be clearer, Paul compares his former condition with the one he was then enduring. To the former belongs what he says: "For I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle." And soon after he adds the reason: "Because I persecuted the Church of God." He speaks therefore from the heart and seriously, not as the monks and pontiffs do, who call themselves "the least" and "servants of servants," while they do only this, that under the empty show of humility they may dominate and rule over everyone. For Paul gives a reason by which he most truly proves what he says. Who would say that a persecutor of the Church is worthy to become an apostle all at once? Who would judge a wolf fit to act as a shepherd? Paul often recalls his earlier state, so that he may commend God's grace the more; therefore in the present passage he by no means minimises his own fault, and ascribes it wholly and without exception to himself alone. For he could have said: "Let no one think that I was an impious enemy of the Church, since I knowingly and willingly waged war against God. Whatever I did, I did in order to please those who then ruled among the people of God, and having received the mandate from them I persecuted those whom they judged to be schismatics, impious, and worthy of any punishment. And in doing this, zeal for the glory of God stung me, whose Law and ancient worship I saw being abolished," and so on. These things, I say, and others of this kind he could have said, if he had sought excuses. But he simply says that he persecuted the Church of God, that Church which he elsewhere testifies was redeemed by the precious blood of God. Thus he recognises in himself a crime by far the most atrocious, a crime which still clings today to all who hostilely persecute the followers of the evangelical doctrine. For here the judgments of the Pontiffs or of any men about us excuse no one; rather, what Christ once said through the prophet will stand firm: "He who touches you touches the apple of my eye." And what was said to Paul himself: "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?"

units.la: Continet autem hoc Apostoli exemplum generalem doctrinam, ut qui in gratiam à Deo recepti sunt, nunquam non meminerint, qui & quales aliquando fuerint. Ista enim recordatio partim plurimum facit ad illustrandam Dei gratiam, quae unicum nostrae salutis fundamentum est: partim modestiae admonet, & nos in officio continet, ne vel contra Deum, vel contra aliquem mortalium insolentius efferamur. Vidit hoc Dauid olim, qui frequenter domus patris sui & caulae meminit, ex qua desumptus & ad throni regalis fastigium euectus fuerat: cuius recordatio illum docilem & disciplinae atq; admonitionum patientem fecit. Quod si illi Saulem opponas, mox videbis hunc, qui se aliquando agasonem fuisse oblitus fuerat, intolerabili insolentia aduersus Deum simul & optimos quosq; proteruijsse. Est ergo doctrina haec admodum necessaria, quam quia pauci observant, plurimum peccatur priuatim simul & publicè.
units.tr: This example of the apostle contains a general teaching: that those who have been received into God's favour should never forget who and what sort of people they once were. Such remembrance partly contributes greatly to illustrating the grace of God, which is the sole foundation of our salvation; and partly it reminds us of humility and keeps us in our duty, so that we do not become too insolently proud either against God or against any mortal. David long ago saw this, who often recalls the house of his father and the sheepfold from which he had been taken and raised to the height of the royal throne; this remembrance made him teachable and patient of discipline and admonition. But if you set Saul against him, you will soon see that Saul, who had forgotten that he had once been a herdsman, behaved with intolerable insolence against God and against all the best men. This teaching is therefore very necessary, and because few observe it, much sin is committed both in private and in public.

units.la: Priori autem conditioni Paulus praesentem opponit, de qua sic loquitur: Sed gratia Dei sum id quod sum: & gratia eius erga me non fuit inanis, sed amplius quàm illi omnes laborauì: non ego tamen, sed gratia Dei, quae mecum est. Per Dei gratiam non aliquas animi facultates sibi diuinitus datas intelligit, quibus ipse deinde pro suo arbitrio usus sit (ut olim Pelagius exponebat) sed gratuitam Dei misericordiam, qui ipsum nihil tale meritum respicere & vas gloriae ex ipso facere dignatus erat. Quae enim dignitas, aut quod meritum in ipso esse potuit, qui exhibitam nobis in Christo Dei gratiam hostiliter persequebatur? Praemittit autem hoc membrum, Gratia Dei sum id quod sum, ne vel minimum quid sibi ipsi arrogantius tribuere videatur. Rursus autem suo exemplo generalem doctrinam comprehendit, ut nos quoq; quicquid sumus aut habemus, id nos ex gratuita Dei liberalitate habere sentiamus. Hoc enim frenum est, quo arrogantia nostra coercetur, & quo continemur, ne Dei donis insolenter abutamur. Hodie vulgò obtinuit, ut principes & episcopi in titulos suos Dei gratiam praetexant: sed quàm leuiter de illa cogitent, facta eorum abunde testantur. Nam si ex animo faterentur, se regna sua & episcopatus ex Dei gratuito fauore habere, qui indignos in hoc fastigium euexerit, nunquam factu immani superbirent, & multò minus populum suae fidei creditum tyrannide opprimerent, exactionibus iniquissimis excoriarent, aut traditionibus superstitiosis grauarent. Praecipuus tamen huius dicti usus est in salutis aeternae causa, aduersus meritorum suorum ostentatores. Illam enim à sola Dei gratia pendere Paulus alibi ita docet, ut gratiam operibus opponens, illi nullum porrò locum fore dicat, si haec admittantur. Nam ad Ephesios scribit: Gratia estis seruati per fidem, idq; non ex vobis. Dei donum est, non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur. Et ad Rom.ii.cap. Quod si per gratiam (scilicet seruati estis) non iam ex operibus: Quandoquidem gratia iam non est gratia. Sin ex operibus, iam non est gratia: Quandoquidem opus iam non est opus.
units.tr: To his former condition Paul opposes his present one, of which he speaks thus: "But by the grace of God I am what I am; and his grace toward me was not in vain, but I laboured more abundantly than they all; yet not I, but the grace of God which is with me." By the grace of God he does not mean some faculties of mind given to him by God, which he then used at his own discretion (as Pelagius once explained), but the free mercy of God, who deigned to regard in him no such merit and to make him a vessel of glory. For what dignity, or what merit, could there have been in him, who hostilely persecuted the grace of God shown to us in Christ? He puts this clause first, "By the grace of God I am what I am," so that he may seem to ascribe to himself not even the smallest thing too arrogantly. Again, by his own example he embraces a general teaching, so that we too may feel that whatever we are or have, we have it from God's free bounty. For this is the bridle by which our arrogance is restrained, and by which we are kept from insolently abusing the gifts of God. Today it has become common for princes and bishops to put forward the grace of God as a pretext for their titles; but how lightly they think of it, their deeds amply testify. For if they confessed from the heart that they hold their kingdoms and bishoprics by God's free favour, who has raised the unworthy to this height, they would never grow so monstrously proud, and much less would they oppress with tyranny the people entrusted to their faith, flay them with most unjust exactions, or burden them with superstitious traditions. Yet the chief use of this saying is in the cause of eternal salvation, against those who boast of their own merits. For Paul teaches elsewhere that salvation depends on God's grace alone, and, setting grace against works, he says that there is no further place for grace if works are admitted. For he writes to the Ephesians: "By grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, lest anyone should boast." And in Romans (chapter ii): "But if it is by grace, then it is no longer by works; since grace is no longer grace. But if it is by works, then it is no longer grace; since work is no longer work."

units.la: Sed & gratiae Dei effectum Paulus praedicat, dicens: Et gratia eius erga me non fuit inanis, sed amplius quàm illi omnes laborauì: Id vero non ideo dicit, quod cum Apostolis contentionem sibi scipere voluerit, sed propter aemulos, qui Apostolorum authoritate ad ipsum opprimendum abutebantur. Id autem ab ipso verè dictum fuisse Actorum liber abunde testatur, & quae alibi de Euangelio per ipsius ministerium ab Arabia ad Illyricum usq; longè latèq; propagato leguntur. Neq; ei tutum fuisset tale quid dicere apud Corinthios, inter quos infiniti erant qui omnia eius calumniabantur, nisi labores eius omnibus cogniti & perspecti fuissent. Rursus autem illo exemplo admonentur ij, qui gratia Dei gloriantur, vt eius specimina certa in suis factis siue operibus exerant. Nam nisi id faciant, tam seipsos quàm alios decipiunt. Accidit hoc ijs, qui fidei professione & gra-tuita iustificatione superbiunt, cùm nulli in ipsis fidei verae effectus, nulla iustificationis argumenta in omni ipsorum vita appareant.
units.tr: Paul also proclaims the effect of God's grace, saying: "And his grace toward me was not in vain, but I laboured more abundantly than they all" (1 Cor. 15:10). He does not say this because he wanted to set himself in rivalry with the Apostles, but because of rivals who abused the authority of the Apostles to oppress him. That he truly said this the book of Acts amply attests, and so do the things read elsewhere about the Gospel, spread through his ministry far and wide from Arabia to Illyricum. Nor would it have been safe for him to say such a thing among the Corinthians, among whom there were countless people who slandered all his doings, unless his labours were known and observed by everyone. Again, those who boast in the grace of God are admonished by this example to display certain proofs of it in their deeds and works. For unless they do so, they deceive both themselves and others. This happens to those who pride themselves on the profession of faith and on free justification, when no true effects of faith and no signs of justification appear in their whole life.

units.la: Caeterum ne hic quoq, aliquid sibi ipsi arrogantius tribuere videatur, per Correctionē subij-cit: Non ego tamen, sed gratia Dei quæ mecum est. Vbi docemur, Dei gratiam ita à nobis agnosci & prædicari debere, vt quicquid à nobis iam fide donatis et ex Dei verbo renatis rectè fit, ad hanc vnam referamus. Nam vt Paulo ante monuimus, non ita nos Deus sua gratia donat, vt nos deinde nostro arbitrio permittat, qui ex nobis ipsis aliquid facere aut mereri possimus. Etenim si istud fieret, facilis esset salutis nostræ iactura, cùm thesaurum gratiæ Dei (vt in posteriori epistola scribitur) in testaceis vasculis gestemus, & vitæ huius via lubrica fit, multaq; indies nobis obiician-tur, ad quæ pedes nostri possunt offendere. Itaq; continua gratiæ Dei operatione nobis opus est, & qui iam fide illuminati sunt, nihil ex seipsis, sed (vt ille dicebat) acti agunt, ideoq; nihil habent, quo in Dei conspectu gloriari possint.
units.tr: But lest he seem to ascribe something too arrogant to himself here too, he adds by way of correction: "Yet not I, but the grace of God which is with me." Here we are taught that the grace of God ought to be acknowledged and proclaimed in such a way that whatever we rightly do, we who have already been given faith and reborn through God's word, we refer to this one thing alone. For, as we noted a little earlier, God does not so bestow his grace on us that he then leaves us to our own judgment, as if we could do or merit anything of ourselves. For if that were so, the loss of our salvation would be easy. We carry the treasure of God's grace (as is written in the second letter) in earthen vessels, the way of this life is slippery, and many things are daily thrown in our path, over which our feet may stumble. Therefore we need the continual working of God's grace, and those who are already enlightened by faith do nothing of themselves but, as he said, are acted upon, and so have nothing in which they may glory before God.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui locum hunc concludit his verbis: Et ego igitur & illi ita prædicamus, & ita credidistis. In vnum colligit testimonia, quæ hucusque produxit, omnia, & quàmuis se plus aliis laborauisse dixerit, tamen quoad doctrinam Apostolos omnes æquales facit. Itaque verborum istorum sensus est: Non est quòd vel meum vel cuiusquam alterius testimonium reijciatis, quasi minus fidei mereatur. Nam siue me, siue quemcunque alium ex Apostolorum choro audiatis, omnes idem prædicamus: Christum videlicet & mortuum esse secundum Scripturas, & resurrexisse ex mortuis, sicuti eadem Scripturæ prædixerant. Neque ista semel modò prædicauimus, sed in hunc vsque diem eadem prædicamus, neque doctrina hæc vnquam mutabitur. Sed & ipsi ita credidistis, siue Paulini sitis, siue Petrini, siue Apollonii. Non poteritis ergo inconstantiæ & leuitatis notam effugere, si à doctrina & fide semel recepta deficiatis.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who concludes this place with these words: "Therefore whether it was I or they, so we preach and so you have believed." He gathers into one all the testimonies he has brought forward so far, and although he has said that he laboured more than the others, nevertheless, as regards doctrine, he makes all the Apostles equal. So the sense of these words is this: there is no reason for you to reject either my testimony or that of anyone else, as if it deserved less credit. For whether you hear me or any other from the company of the Apostles, we all preach the same thing: namely that Christ died according to the Scriptures and rose from the dead, just as the same Scriptures had foretold. Nor have we preached these things only once, but to this day we preach the same, and this doctrine will never change. You too have believed so, whether you are of Paul's party, or Peter's, or Apollos'. You will therefore not be able to escape the mark of inconstancy and fickleness if you fall away from the doctrine and faith once received.

units.la: Apparet ex hisce verbis Apostolos omnes eandem doctrinam tradidisse, vt qui eodem Chri-sti mandato omnes astricti fuerunt, vt nimirum docerent, quæ ab illo accepissent. Id verò non de sola Resurrectione intelligi, sed ad omnes quoque alios articulos extendi debet. Nec incredibile est, quod de Symboli apostolici articulis ex communi illorum omnium consensu conscri-ptis vetustissimi Scriptores, Irenæus & Cyprianus tradiderunt. Voluerunt enim hanc fidei regulam esse (vt Tertulliani verbo vtar) quam omnes sequerentur, qui Christiani dici & haberi volunt. In primis certè concionibus eorum, quæ Actorum secundo, & tertio capite describuntur, articulos hosce omnes inuenire possunt, qui rem propius inspexerint. Quod si caput religionis Christianæ consideraueris, Iustificationem nimirum fidei, mirificus in ea doctrina omnium illorum consensus apparebit. Eò autem maior apud nos esse debet doctrina apostolicæ authoritas, quòd eidem Veteris testamenti Scriptores, Moses & Prophetæ consentiunt. Sunt ergo ridiculi nimis (ne quid grauius dicam) qui nobis hodie paucorum sæculorum præscriptione confirmatum Romanensium consensum obiiciunt, aut noua Concilij alicu-ius determinatione opus esse aiunt, qua de fide & religione certum quid statuatur, quod omnes re-cipere & sequi debeant.
units.tr: From these words it appears that all the Apostles handed down the same doctrine, since all were bound by the same command of Christ to teach what they had received from him. This must be understood not only of the resurrection but must be extended to all the other articles as well. Nor is it incredible what the most ancient writers, Irenaeus and Cyprian, have handed down about the articles of the Apostles' Creed, drawn up by the common consent of all of them. For they wished this to be the rule of faith (to use Tertullian's word) which all should follow who wish to be called and considered Christians. Certainly, anyone who has looked into the matter closely can find all these articles in the first sermons described in the second and third chapters of Acts. And if you consider the chief point of the Christian religion, namely justification by faith, a remarkable agreement of all those men will appear in that teaching. The authority of apostolic doctrine ought to be all the greater for us because the writers of the Old Testament, Moses and the Prophets, agree with it. Therefore they are far too ridiculous (to say nothing harsher) who today object to us the consensus of the Romanists, confirmed by the prescription of a few centuries, or who say that some new determination of a council is needed, by which something certain concerning faith and religion may be laid down that all must accept and follow.

units.la: Illud potiùs tenendum erit, non aliam doctrinam in Ecclesia prædicari & audiri debere, quàm quæ ab Apostolis ex Spiritus Christi suggestione tradita est: Qui verò illam semel receperunt, in ea constantes in finem vsque perseuerare debent, ne puerorum instar sese à quouis vento circumagitari patiantur. Leuitas enim vt in quauis alia re reprehensionem meretur, ita in religione prorsus inexcusabilis est, vbi de æterna hominis salute agitur, & vbi semel admissus error non aliter corrigi potest, quàm vt ad communem illam fidei regulam redeant, qui vel latum culmum ab ea deflexerunt. Si quis verò hic audeat fidem Deo datam fallere, quid obsecro ille faciet in alijs, quando ei cum solis hominibus res est? Vidit hoc olim laudatissimus princeps Constantinus, Constantini Magni parens, qui exauthorandos esse censuit milites, qui cum ante Christi religione professi fuissent, in ipsius gratiam Diis thura adoleuerant. Quis enim Regi (dicebat) fidelis fideles fore putauerit eos, qui in supremum numen ingrati sunt? Simus ergo constantes, neq; nos di-uelli patiamur ab aeterno Dei Filio, IESV CHRISTO, qui & pro peccatis nostris mortuus est, & morte per resurrectionem deuicta nobis salutem veram & regni coelestis hereditatem meruit. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Rather, we must hold to this: that no other doctrine ought to be preached and heard in the Church than that which was handed down by the Apostles through the prompting of Christ's Spirit. Those who have once received it ought to persevere in it steadfastly to the end, and not allow themselves to be tossed about by every wind like children. For fickleness, though it deserves blame in any other matter, is wholly inexcusable in religion, where the eternal salvation of man is at stake, and where an error once admitted cannot be corrected except by returning to that common rule of faith, by those who have turned aside from it even by a hair's breadth. But if anyone here dares to betray the faith given to God, what, I ask, will he do in other matters, when he has to do only with men? The most praiseworthy prince Constantine, father of Constantine the Great, saw this long ago, and judged that soldiers who had once professed the Christian religion, but had burned incense to the gods to win his favour, should be dismissed. For who, he said, would think that those who are ungrateful to the supreme Godhead would be faithful to the king? Let us therefore be steadfast, and let us not allow ourselves to be torn away from the eternal Son of God, JESUS CHRIST, who both died for our sins and, by overcoming death through the resurrection, earned for us true salvation and the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXIX.
units.tr: Homily 79.

units.la: Quod si vero Christus praedicatur ex mortuis excitatus esse, quomodo dicunt quidam inter vos, non esse resurrectionem mortuorum? Nam si resurrectio mortuorum non est, Christus quoq; non est excitatus. Quod si vero Christus non est excitatus, inanis sane est praedicatio nostra, inanis autem est etiam fides vestra: Reperimur autem etiam falsi testes Dei; quoniam de Deo testificati sumus, quod excitarit Christum, quem non excitavit, si videlicet mortui non excitantur. Nam si mortui non excitantur, Christus quoq; non est excitatus. Quod si Christus non est excitatus, inanis est fides vestra, adhuc estis in peccatis vestris: Nempe & qui obdormierunt in Christo, perierunt. Si in hac solum vita speramus in Christum, miserrimi omnium hominum sumus.
units.tr: But if Christ is preached as raised from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? For if there is no resurrection of the dead, neither is Christ raised. And if Christ is not raised, then our preaching is empty and your faith is empty too. Moreover we are found to be false witnesses of God, because we have testified of God that he raised up Christ, whom he did not raise, if indeed the dead are not raised. For if the dead are not raised, neither is Christ raised. And if Christ is not raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins. Indeed, those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If we hope in Christ in this life only, we are of all men the most miserable.

units.la: Omnes quidem fidei Christianae articuli diligenter cognosci & frequenti meditatione exerceri debent, ut in illis confirmemur: Verum tamen singulari studio in eo opus est, qui de mortuorum, vel potius corporum nostrorum resurrectione habetur. Ut enim ex eo plurimum consolationis hauritur in omni tentationum genere: ita non alius est, qui ad vitam recte pieq; instituendam magis conducat. Quia enim praecipua licentiae scelerum causa est, quod plerique huius vitae commodis intenti, futura aut nunquam aut quam rarissime cogitant: fieri e contra non potest, ut praesentis vitae deliciis & studiis sese inescari atque seduci patiantur, quicunque longius prospiciunt, & piis promissa aeternae vitae praemia, simulq; impiis destinatos horribiles atque sempiternos cruciatus frequenter animo repetunt. Adde hus[?], quod hic fundatur religionis Christianae & salutis nostrae summa. Et hoc potissimum Paulus spectat in tota cap. huius tractatione, quam adversus eos instituit, qui mortuorum resurrectionem negabant. Docuit ergo primum, hanc esse Evangelicae doctrinae summam, quod CHRISTVS IESVS pro peccatis nostris mortuus, propter nostri autem iustificationem ex mortuis excitatus fit. Deinde hanc quoque unanimem esse totius Scripturae sacrae doctrinam, quae in Veteris testamenti libris passim inveniantur, & quam Apostoli uno ore praedicent. His praemissis nunc ad rem ipsam propius accedit, & adversarios argumentis validissimis confutat.
units.tr: All the articles of the Christian faith ought to be carefully learned and practised by frequent meditation, so that we may be confirmed in them. Yet there is special need for study of the doctrine concerning the resurrection of the dead, or rather of our bodies. For just as a great deal of comfort is drawn from it in every kind of temptation, so there is no other teaching that better equips us to live rightly and piously. For the chief cause of licence in sin is that most people, intent on the advantages of this life, think of the future either never or very rarely. On the contrary, it cannot happen that those who look further ahead allow themselves to be enticed and led astray by the pleasures and pursuits of the present life, when they often call to mind the promised rewards of eternal life for the pious and the terrible and everlasting torments destined for the impious. Add to this that the sum of the Christian religion and of our salvation is founded here. Paul chiefly has this in view throughout this chapter, in the discussion he undertakes against those who denied the resurrection of the dead. He therefore taught first that this is the sum of the Gospel doctrine: that CHRIST JESUS died for our sins, and was raised from the dead for our justification. Then he taught that this doctrine is also the unanimous teaching of the whole of holy Scripture, which is found everywhere in the books of the Old Testament, and which the apostles proclaim with one voice. With these things set out, he now comes closer to the matter itself and refutes his opponents with the strongest arguments.

units.la: Primo ex ijs,quae proxime praecesserunt,sic infert: Quod si vero Christus praedicatur ex mortuis excitatus esse,quomodo dicunt quidam inter vos,nō esse resurrectionem mortuorum? Id est, resurrectionem esse inane commentum, ut quae neq; sit,neq; unquam futura sit. Ita vero docet,eos qui resurrectionem negant, simul Evangelio & huius ministris siue praeconibus contradicere. Et est hic observatu dignissimum, quòd cum simplici dicendi forma uti posset, interrogatione ordinem figurat, ut apertius exprimatur rei absurditas & adversariorum audacia siue impudentia. Emphasim quoque habet particula, Quomodo dicunt quidam inter vos, &c? Nam hoc perinde est ac si diceret: Tolerabile foret, aliquos qui Christiana fidei mysteria prorsus ignorant, intra cordis sui sensus dubitare de mortuorum resurrectione, ut quae rationis & intellectus nostri captum longè excedit: sed inveniri aliquos, qui hoc diserte dicant, & quidem inter vos, qui iam-pridem Christo nomen dedistis, qui in eius cognitione summa cum diligentia instituti scientia & cognitione omni abundavistis, qui deniq; aliis ecclesiis praestantiores videri vultis, id vero nulla ratione vel ferri vel excusari potest.
