units.tr: First, he draws an inference from what has just gone before, in this way: "But if Christ is preached as raised from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?" That is, the resurrection is an empty invention, as if it neither is nor ever will be. He teaches that those who deny the resurrection at the same time contradict the Gospel and its ministers or heralds. And it is most worthy of notice here that, although he could have used a plain form of speech, he shapes the order of his words as a question, so that the absurdity of the thing and the boldness or shamelessness of the opponents may be expressed more plainly. The particle in "How do some among you say, etc.?" also carries emphasis. For this is just as if he were saying: It would be tolerable if some who are wholly ignorant of the mysteries of the Christian faith should doubt in their own minds the resurrection of the dead, since it far exceeds the grasp of our reason and understanding. But that some should be found who state this openly, and that among you, who have long since taken Christ's name, who have been instructed in his knowledge with the greatest diligence and abound in all learning and knowledge of him, who in the end wish to seem superior to other churches, this can in no way be borne or excused.

units.la: Est autem perquàm memorabile Pauli exemplum, qui nihil dissimulandum esse putavit, quàm germanum fidei dogma sive articulum aliqui negare & aduersus cum disputare non sunt veriti. Sciebat enim eiusmodi sermones virus suum quàm latissimè diffundere, & (ut ipse scribit) cancri instar serpere, donec omnem ex cordibus hominum fidei verae notitiam atque gustum depascat. Fecerunt hoc ipsum in aliis quoque articulis Apostoli, & tales Paulus verbi administros, sive Ecclesiarum pastores constitui vult, qui non modo veritatis doctrinam proponere, verum etiam huic contradicentes rationibus idoneis atque firmis confutare possint. Neque oscitantius negligi debet ordo ille, quo primum Apostolorum de Christo resuscitato doctrinam prepofuit, deinde vero huic aduersariorum sententiam opposuit, ut ex collatione ista appareat, quàm absurdum sit, aliquid ab illa discrepans proferri ab iis qui Christiani dici & haberi velint. Eodem ordine etiam hodie procedi debet aduersus omnes eos, qui quodcunque axioma sive dogma Christianae fidei, quod Apostoli olim unanimi consensu tradiderunt, negare aut oppugnare audent. Exempli gratia: Si quis nos sola fide iustificari neget, mox illi dicatur: Quomodo ergo Apo-stoli dixerunt, fide corda purificari? Quid item sibi voluit Paulus, cum de Christo apud Antiochenos concionem habens, inter alia dixit: Per IESVM hunc vobis annuntiatur peccatorum remissio, & ab omnibus, à quibus non potuistis per legem Mosis iustificari, per hunc omnis qui credit iustificatur? Item: Scimus non iustificari hominem, nisi per fidem IESV CHRISTI: & nos in CHRISTVM IESVM credidimus, ut iustificaremur ex fide Christi, & non ex operibus legis. Itaque quis praeter Christum plures alios apud Deum mediatores esse contendat, huic etiam mox obijciatur: Quid igitur Christo respondebis dicenti: Nemo venit ad Patrem, nisi per me? Quid Paulo, qui scripsit: Unus Deus, unus Mediator Dei & hominum, homo CHRISTVS IESVS? Quid Ioanni dilecto discipulo, qui cùm Christus ipsi matrem Virginem commendarit, tamen nō dubitauit dicere: Si quis peccauerit, aduocatum apud Deum habemus, IESVM CHRISTVM iustum. Eadem ratione confutari possunt, qui Christum in resurrectione naturales & essentiales corporis proprietates deposuisse, neq; illud in certum beatae immortalitatis locum extra hunc mundum corruptibilem euexisse, sed omniprasens fuisse garriunt. Quomodo ergo Angelus corpus illud in sepulchro fuisse negat? quomodo ille à discipulis visus & contrectatus est? quomodo Apostoli illum superne in coelis agere, & olim inde reditururum esse praedicant? Et sanè non minus insolens est hodie inter Christianae fidei propugnatores inueniri, qui nouas istas de Christi corpore Deificato chimaeras fingunt, quàm quod olim apud Corinthios fuerunt, qui mortuorum resurrectionem negare audebant. Utinam vero ad hunc modum sua commenta omnia examinarent nostri aduersarij, qui pro Diuorum cultu nobiscum certamen susceperunt, cùm ipsi plerosq; fidei articulos oppugnent, quos illi non ore modo confessi sunt, verumetiam sanguine suo obsignarunt.
units.tr: Paul's example is indeed most memorable. He thought nothing should be concealed, however genuine a dogma or article of the faith some men might deny, and they were not afraid to argue against it. For he knew that such talk spreads its poison as widely as possible and, as he himself writes, creeps like a cancer until it eats away all true knowledge and taste of the faith from people's hearts. The apostles did the same in other articles too, and Paul wants such men appointed as ministers of the Word, or pastors of the churches, who can not only set forth the doctrine of the truth but also refute those who contradict it with suitable and firm arguments. Nor should we carelessly overlook the order by which he first set out the apostles' teaching about the risen Christ and then opposed to it the view of his adversaries, so that from this comparison it may appear how absurd it is for anyone who wishes to be and be called a Christian to put forward anything at odds with that teaching. The same order ought to be followed today against all who dare to deny or attack any axiom or dogma of the Christian faith which the apostles once handed down with one accord. For example: if anyone denies that we are justified by faith alone, let him at once be asked: "How then did the apostles say that hearts are purified by faith?" Likewise, what did Paul mean when, preaching about Christ at Antioch, he said among other things: "Through this Jesus forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and through him everyone who believes is justified from all things from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses" (Acts 13:38-39)? Again: "We know that a man is not justified except through faith in Jesus Christ; and we have believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law" (Gal. 2:16). So if anyone contends that there are other mediators before God besides Christ, let him at once be confronted: "What then will you answer Christ, who says: No one comes to the Father except through me (John 14:6)? What will you answer Paul, who wrote: One God, one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5)? What will you answer John, the beloved disciple, who, although Christ had commended his mother the Virgin to him, nevertheless did not hesitate to say: If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1)?" In the same way can be refuted those who babble that in the resurrection Christ laid aside the natural and essential properties of his body, and did not lift it up into a definite place of blessed immortality beyond this corruptible world, but was everywhere present. For how then does the angel deny that the body was in the tomb? How was he seen and touched by the disciples? How do the apostles proclaim that he is now acting above in heaven, and that he will one day return from there? And indeed it is no less outrageous to find today, among the defenders of the Christian faith, men who invent those new fancies about the deified body of Christ, than it was once among the Corinthians, who dared to deny the resurrection of the dead. Would that our adversaries, who have taken up the contest with us on behalf of the worship of the saints, would examine all their own inventions in this way, since they themselves attack many articles of the faith which those men not only confessed with their mouths but also sealed with their blood.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui suos aduersarios ipsius Christi exemplo confutat. Si resurrectio mortuorum (inquit) non est, Christus quoque non est excitatus. Id verò euidentissima et validissima ratione colligit. Nam secundum dialecticorum regulas, quae cum sensu communi consentiunt, valet consequentia ab universali ad particulare negatiue, ut si dicas: Si nulla caro ex suis meritis in Dei iudicio iustificatur, ne Dauid quidem suis meritis iustificatus est. Ad eundem mo-dum in praesenti Apostolus argumentatur: Si nulla prorsus est resurrectio mortuorum, & inane figmentum est quicquid de illa dicitur, certè neq; Christus neq; quisquam alius resurrexerit oportet: At Christum resurrexisse Scriptura docet, & nos testibus plurimis fideq; dignissimis modo probauimus: Ergo est mortuorum resurrectio. Poterat autem aliquod esse huius argumenti pondus, quia cum illis Paulo res erat, qui Christum resurrexisse non poterant negare, cum Christiani dici & haberi vellent. Cum impijs & à professione Christiana alienis aliter fuisset agendum, qui nisi rationibus & argumentis ex rerum natura desumptis conuincantur, nunquam credent.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who refutes his adversaries by the example of Christ himself. "If there is no resurrection of the dead," he says, "neither is Christ raised." He draws this conclusion by a most evident and forceful argument. For according to the rules of the dialecticians, which agree with common sense, the inference holds from a universal to a particular in the negative form, as when you say: If no flesh is justified before God's judgment by its own merits, then David too was not justified by his own merits. In the same way the Apostle argues here: If there is absolutely no resurrection of the dead, and whatever is said about it is an empty fiction, then certainly neither Christ nor anyone else can have risen. But Scripture teaches that Christ has risen, and we have just proved this by many witnesses who are most worthy of trust. Therefore there is a resurrection of the dead. Now this argument could have real weight, because Paul was dealing with men who could not deny that Christ had risen, since they wished to be and be called Christians. With the impious, and those alien to the Christian profession, another method would have to be used, since they will never believe unless they are convinced by arguments and proofs drawn from the nature of things.

units.la: Potest autem nostrorum corporum resurrectio per Christi resurrectionem validissimè probari. Primò, quia ille caput nostrum est, nos verò eius corpus sumus, quod eius spiritu animatur. Et huc faciunt alij loci, in quibus Apostolus argumentum hoc euidentius tractat. Nam ad Romanos octauo capite sic scribit: Si Christus in vobis est, corpus quidem mortuum est propter peccatum, spiritus autem vita est propter iustificationem. Quibus mox subijcit: Si spiritus eius, qui excitauit IESVM à mortuis, habitat in vobis: is qui excitauit Christum ex mortuis, viuificabit & mortalia corpora vestra per inhabitantem eius spiritum in vobis. Et cap. sexto: Si coaluimus conformatione mortis eius, nimirum etiam resurrectionis conformatione coalescemus. E-tenim nisi ista consequentia valeat, Ecclesiam constituemus, cuius caput viuet, membra autem erunt mortua. Deinde, quaecunque Christus fecit & passus est, propter nos fecit & passus est, vtpote Mediator Dei & hominum, & ideo illorum omnium effectus in nos redundat, cum ipse nullius horum indigeret. Vt ergo ipse Filius hominis factus est, vt nos faceret filios Dei: pauper, vt nos bonis caelestibus ditaret: exul & peregrinus in terris, vt nobis ciuitatem permanentem & patriam in caelis pararet: contemptus & abiectus, vt nos ad gloriam caelestem euheheret: vt denique facinorosi instar mortuus est, vt nos a peccati noxa liberatos seruaret: Ita a mortuis resurrexit quoque vt eum destrueret, qui mortis habebat imperium, & vt nos in ipso aeternum viuamus. Ideo Paulus rursus in eadem ad Romanos epistola cap. octauo dicebat: Quos praescuit, eosdem & praedestinauit conformes fieri imagini Filij sui: vt is sit primogenitus inter multos fratres.
units.tr: Moreover, the resurrection of our bodies can be most powerfully proved from Christ's resurrection. First, because he is our head and we are his body, which is quickened by his Spirit. Other passages also bear on this, in which the Apostle treats the argument more clearly. In Romans chapter 8 he writes: "If Christ is in you, the body is indeed dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of justification." He immediately adds: "If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also quicken your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you." And in chapter 6: "If we have grown together in the likeness of his death, we shall certainly also grow together in the likeness of his resurrection." For unless this consequence holds, we would be constituting a church whose head lives while its members are dead. Next, whatever Christ did and suffered, he did and suffered for us, as Mediator between God and men, so the effects of all these things flow over to us, although he himself needed none of them. Just as the Son of man was made man that he might make us sons of God; became poor that he might enrich us with heavenly goods; was an exile and stranger on earth that he might prepare for us an enduring city and a fatherland in heaven; was despised and cast down that he might raise us to heavenly glory; and finally died like a criminal that he might save us, freed from the harm of sin, so he also rose from the dead, to destroy him who had the power of death and that we might live eternally in him. Paul therefore says again in the same epistle to the Romans, chapter 8: "Those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers."

units.la: Sunt haec diligentius obseruanda propter eos, qui exemplum resurrectionis Christi nihil ad nos pertinere clamant: quia ille non solum homo, sed insuper Deus quoque sit, qui seipsum pro-pria virtute potuerit excitare: quia item ἀναμαρτητος, id est, ab omni peccato immunis fuerit, ideoque minus etiam iuris in ipsum habuerit mors, quam per peccatum ingressam esse Scriptura docet. Nec enim vt Deus resurrexit, sed vt homo, secundum quem & mortuus fuerat. Recte enim Tertullianus hoc mysterium explicans inter alia scripsit: Quomodo autem Christus resur-rexit? in carne, an non? Sine dubio, si mortuum, si sepultum audis secundum Scripturas, non aliter quam in carne, aeque resuscitatum in carne concedis. Ipsum enim quod cecidit in morte, quod iacuit in sepultura, hoc & resurrexit, non tam Christus in carne, quam caro in Christo. Deinde etsi ipse peccatum nullum fecerit, & vere ἀναμαρτητος dicatur, non tamen sine peccato mortuus fuit, cum Pater omnium nostrum peccata in ipsum transtulerit, & (vt alibi Paulus scribit) ipsum pro nobis peccatum fecerit, vt nos essemus iustitia Dei in eo. Vt vero quae ipsi imputata fuerunt mundi totius peccata, eum non potuerunt detinere in morte: ita neque nos nostra peccata detinere poterunt, quae illius morte iampridem expiata sunt, & ideo nobis porro non imputantur. Cur ergo (inquis) adhuc morimur? Propter haerentes adhuc in carne nostra peccati reli-quias, quarum tamen non tantae vires sunt, vt in morte aeterna nos possint detinere. Deinde quia mortale hoc & corruptibile, in quo nascimur, aboleri oportet, vt olim immortales & incor-ruptibiles resurgamus. Postremo, etsi nosipsos non possimus propria virtute excitare, ipsius tamen potentia excitabimur, qua ille sibi omnia potest subijcere. Est ergo hoc Pauli argumentum longe firmissimum: eo quod Christi resurrectio non solum nostrae exemplum, sed potius causa efficiens est cum diuina & omnipotente eius virtute coniuncta.
units.tr: These things must be observed more carefully on account of those who loudly claim that the example of Christ's resurrection has nothing to do with us: because he was not only man but also God, and so could raise himself by his own power; and because he was ἀναμαρτητος [sinless], that is, free from all sin, and so death had less right over him, which Scripture teaches entered through sin. For he rose not as God but as man, the nature in which he had also died. Tertullian rightly, explaining this mystery, wrote among other things: "But how did Christ rise? In the flesh, or not? Undoubtedly, if you hear that he died and was buried according to the Scriptures, you must concede that he was raised in the flesh, no differently than he died in the flesh. For that very thing which fell in death, which lay in the burial, this also rose; not so much Christ in the flesh as flesh in Christ." Next, although he committed no sin and is truly called ἀναμαρτητος [sinless], he did not die without sin, since the Father of us all transferred our sins to him, and (as Paul writes elsewhere) made him sin for us, that we might be the righteousness of God in him. But just as the sins of the whole world, imputed to him, could not hold him in death, so our sins will not hold us, since they were expiated long ago by his death and therefore are no longer imputed to us. Why then, you ask, do we still die? Because remnants of sin still cling to our flesh, but these are not strong enough to hold us in eternal death. Further, this mortal and corruptible nature in which we are born must be abolished, so that we may rise immortal and incorruptible. Lastly, although we cannot raise ourselves by our own power, we shall be raised by his power, by which he can subject all things to himself. Therefore this argument of Paul is by far the firmest: Christ's resurrection is not merely the example of ours but rather its efficient cause, joined with his divine and almighty power.

units.la: Faciunt autem ad argumenti huius confirmationem quae sequuntur. Nam absurda recen-set, quae admittere oporteat, si Christum resurrexisse negemus. Quod si Christus (inquit) non est excitatus, inanis sane est praedicatio nostra, inanis autem est etiam fides vestra, &c. Primo praedicationem Apostolorum inanem, id est, fallacem fore dicit, quae ad scopum suum non pertingat. Loquitur autem de tota doctrina Euangelij, quae in Christi resurrectione maxima ex parte refertur: Vt enim resurgeret, prius illum mori oportuit: vt vero mori posset, hominem fieri necesse erat. E contra, vt & incarnatio & mors eius nobis fructuosa & salutaris esset, resurrectionem omnino accedere oportebat. Quis enim iam moriturus vitam sibi ex eo polliceretur, qui hanc sibi ipsi non posset reddere? Itaque quotquot illum resurrexisse negant, si simul eius quoque incarnationem atque mortem, aut saltem (quod magis absurdum magisque impium est) utriusque fructum siue meritum negant. Recte ergo Paulus colligit, totam Euangelij praedicationem inanem fieri, si Christi resurrectionem e medio auferamus. Ex eo autem absurdum alterum colligit: Inanis autem est etiam fides vestra. Sunt enim relatiua: Praedicatio & Fides, se-cundum illud: Quomodo credent ei, de quo non audierunt? Item Fides ex auditu est, auditus autem per verbum Dei. Quibus postremum illud Christi mandatum consentiit: Profecti in totum orbem, praedicate Euangelium omni creaturae: Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, salvus erit. Adde his, quod in mortis articulo nulla fidei certitudo esse poterit, si ipsem vitae tollas, quae ex sola resurrectione concipitur. Fieri ergo non potest, quin hac negata, fidem simul inanem & incertam, vel potius nullam fecerit. His vero tertium absurdum Paulus infert: Reperimur autem etiam falsi testes Dei: quoniam de Deo testificati sumus, quod excitarit Christum, quem non excitavit, si videlicet mortui non excitantur. Ita vero loquitur, quia Euangelium (ut alias diximus) non simplex narratio est, sed testimonium de Filio Dei, ad quod dicendum Apostoli delecti sunt, quos ipse Christus testes suos vocat. Vos (inquit) eritis mihi testes Hierosolymae, & in tota Iudaea, &c. Non temere autem inter alia absurda, quae resurrectionem negantibus obijcit Paulus, hoc etiam numerat, quod per illos Apostoli insimulentur, quasi falsum de Christo testimonium dixerint. Et Dei testes eos dicit, ut iniuriam hanc in ipsum Deum redundare ostendat.
units.tr: Moreover, the following points serve to confirm this argument, for Paul lists the absurdities we must admit if we deny that Christ has risen. "If Christ," he says, "has not been raised, then our preaching is surely empty, and your faith is empty also," and so on. First, he says the apostolic preaching would be empty, that is, deceptive, since it would not reach its goal. He is speaking of the whole doctrine of the gospel, which for the most part is directed toward Christ's resurrection. For he had to die before he could rise, and to be able to die it was necessary that he become man. On the other hand, for both his incarnation and his death to be fruitful and saving for us, the resurrection altogether had to follow. For who would now promise himself life from one who was about to die, if he could not restore that life to himself? Therefore, all who deny that he rose also deny, at the same time, his incarnation and death, or at least (what is more absurd and more impious) the fruit and merit of both. Rightly, then, Paul concludes that the whole preaching of the gospel becomes empty if we take away Christ's resurrection. From this he draws a second absurdity: "your faith is also empty." For preaching and faith are correlatives, according to that saying: "How will they believe him of whom they have not heard?" Likewise, "faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God." Christ's final command agrees with these: "Go into all the world, preach the gospel to every creature; whoever believes and is baptized will be saved." Add to these that at the point of death there can be no certainty of faith if you remove the life which is conceived from the resurrection alone. It cannot happen, then, that by denying this one does not make faith at once empty and uncertain, or rather nothing at all. To these Paul adds a third absurdity: "We are also found to be false witnesses of God, since we have testified of God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise, if indeed the dead are not raised." He speaks thus because the gospel (as we have said elsewhere) is not a simple narrative but a testimony concerning the Son of God, for which the apostles were chosen, whom Christ himself calls his witnesses: "You," he says, "will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea," and so on. Nor without reason does Paul, among the other absurdities he charges against those who deny the resurrection, count this too: that by these means the apostles are accused of having given false testimony about Christ. And he calls them witnesses of God, to show that this injury redounds upon God himself.

units.la: Ex eo autem generalis doctrina siue admonitio peti debet, quam videlicet periculosum sit ea negare, aut in dubium vocare, quae in Euangelio traduntur. Quia enim huius praecones Apostoli ipsius Dei testes sunt, non potest illud fieri, quin Deus ipse mendacij arguatur. Vidit hoc discipulus ille discipulus, qui ideo sic scripsit: Qui credit in Filium Dei, habet testimonium in seipso: Qui non credit Deo, mendacem fecit eum: quia non credidit testimonio, quod testificatus est Deus de Filio suo. At quid hodie vulgarius est? quam ea negare, quae de CHRISTO IESV unico humani generis Seruatore ex Apostolorum & Prophetarum libris praedicantur? Quid? nonne inueniuntur, qui Scripturas simul omnes simpliciter negant, & plus quam scurrili dicacitate explodunt, dum mendacia perinde ut quae vera sunt, scribi posse clamant? Quid ergo Dei irati flagella admiramur? Inter homines nullum conuitium turpius & illiberalius esse iudicatur, quam quo quis mendacij insimulatur: quia (ut Cicero olim dicebat) in bonum virum non cadit mentiri emolumenti sui causa. Cur ergo hoc Deo tribuatur, ad quem nihil ex nobis redire potest, si nos quam maxime fallere vellet?
units.tr: From this a general doctrine or admonition should be drawn: how dangerous it is to deny or call into doubt the things handed down in the gospel. For since the apostles, the heralds of this message, are witnesses of God himself, it cannot happen that God is not thereby charged with lying. That disciple saw this, who therefore wrote: "He who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself; he who does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed the testimony which God has borne concerning his Son." Yet what is more commonplace today than to deny those things which are preached from the books of the apostles and prophets about CHRIST JESUS, the one Saviour of the human race? Indeed, are there not those who flatly deny all the Scriptures together, and mock them with more than buffoonish wit, while they cry out that lies can be written just as well as truths? Why then do we wonder at the scourges of an angry God? Among men no insult is judged more shameful and ungentlemanly than being charged with lying, because (as Cicero once said) it does not befit a good man to lie for his own advantage. Why then should this be attributed to God, to whom nothing can return from us, if he wanted above all to deceive us?

units.la: Sed pergamus in Pauli verbis, qui per Expolitionem repetit, quod paulo ante dixerat, ut apertius demonstret, totum fidei & salutis nostrae negotium euacuari, si Resurrectio mortuorum negatur. Rursus autem suis quasi gradibus oratio ascendit, ut evidentius pateat aduersariae sententiae absurditas. Primo sic ait: Nam si mortui non excitantur, Christus quoq; non est suscitatus. Idque libere dici poterat, quia Christum mortuum esse, ne hostes quidem acerrimi religionis Christianae negabant. Secundo autem infert: Quod si Christus non est excitatus, inanis est fides vestra, &c. Huius etenim articulus praecipuus est, quo illum resurrexisse fatemur. Quid autem praeteriquitur? Adhuc estis in peccatis vestris. Id est, tenemini adhuc reatu peccatorum vestrorum, nec eorum remissionem adhuc obtinuistis. Id autem verissime dicitur, quando per solam eam fidem iustificamur, qua Christum resurrexisse credimus, & ex eo colligimus illum nostrum esse redemptorem. Ita enim in epist. ad Rom. 10. cap. hoc exponit Paulus, dicens: Hoc est verbum Fidei quod praedicamus: Quod si confessus fueris ore tuo Dominum IESVM, & credideris in corde tuo, quod Deus illum excitavit a mortuis, seruaberis. Praeterea, si in ijs falsi conuincantur Christus, quae de sua resurrectione dixit, quam nostrae fundamentum esse iam ante diximus, mox omnibus eius promissis fides derogabitur. Adde, quod si non resurrexit, ne mortuus quidem erit, & proinde peccata quoq; nostra nondum erunt expiata, nosq; eorum reatu adhuc tenebimur. Sed aliud subijcit Paulus, quod ista omnia longe superat: Nempe & qui obdormierunt in Christo, perierunt. In Christo obdormire dicuntur, qui ea fide decedunt, quod ille pro ipsis satisfecerit, & quod per ipsum ex hac lachrymarum valle in vitam aeternam transeant, sicut ipse non vno loco pollicetur. Nam Ioan. 5. cap. ait: Amen dico vobis, qui verbum meum audit, & credit ei qui misit me, habet vitam aeternam: & in iudicium non veniet, sed transiuit a morte in vitam. Item cap. 6. Haec est voluntas eius qui misit me, ut omnis qui videt Filium, & credit in eum, habeat vitam aeternam, & ego suscitabo eu in vltimo illo die. Et rursus cap. 11. Ego sum resurrectio & vita: qui credit in me, etiamsi mortuus fuerit, viuet. Et omnis qui viuit, & credit in me, non morietur in aeternum. At si ipse Christus (inquit Paulus) non est excitatus, omnes qui in ista fide obdormierunt, perierint oportet. Na spe sua turpiter falsi sunt, quando neq; peccata (vt modò diximus) expiata, neq; mors, quæ per peccatum ingressa fuit, deuicta est. Ita vero ostendit, per illusores istos, qui mortuorum resurrectionem negant, in periculum siue dubium simul vocari omnium eorum salutem atq; famam, qui unte[?] nos decesserunt. Id vero optimum quenq; vehementer mouet. Durum enim est damnare tot bonos viros, qui virtutibus & rebus præclarè gestis insignes fuerunt, & vnà cum illis maiores quoq; nostros, quorum memoria apud nos merito grata est & honorifica. Ideo nobis hodie argumentum istud obijciunt aduersarij nostri, qui papisticas superstitiones contra Euangelij doctrinam tuentur. Si (inquiunt) falsa est religio, quam hucusq; secuti sumus, perierunt utriq;[?] maiores nostri & infinita hominum millia, qui iam seculis aliquot mortui sunt, priusquam [illegible, ~3 letters] istud Euangelium prædicaretur, quo Papatus totus oppugnatur.
units.tr: But let us press on with Paul's words. By way of repetition (expolitio) he restates what he had said a little earlier, so that he may show more plainly that the whole business of our faith and salvation is annulled if the resurrection of the dead is denied. Again, the argument climbs as if by its own steps, so that the absurdity of the opposing view may appear more clearly. First he says: "For if the dead are not raised, neither is Christ raised." This could be said freely, since not even the bitterest enemies of the Christian religion denied that Christ had died. Second, he infers: "And if Christ is not raised, your faith is vain," etc. For the chief article of faith is this, that we confess he rose again. And what follows? "You are still in your sins." That is, you are still bound by the guilt of your sins, and you have not yet obtained their forgiveness. This is said most truly, since we are justified by that faith alone, by which we believe that Christ rose again and from this conclude that he is our Redeemer. For Paul explains this in the tenth chapter of Romans in just this way: "This is the word of faith which we preach: if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved." Moreover, if Christ is shown to be false in those things which he said about his own resurrection, which we have already said is the foundation of ours, then straightway his whole promise will lose its credit. Add that if he has not risen, he is not even dead, and therefore our sins will not yet be expiated, and we will still be held by their guilt. But Paul adds something else which far surpasses all these: "Indeed, those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished." They are said to fall asleep in Christ who depart in that faith, that he has made satisfaction for them, and that through him they pass from this valley of tears into eternal life, as he himself promises in more than one place. For in John 5 he says: "Truly I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and will not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life." Likewise in chapter 6: "This is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day." And again in chapter 11: "I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me, even if he dies, will live. And everyone who lives and believes in me will never die." But if Christ himself (says Paul) has not been raised, then all who have fallen asleep in this faith must have perished. For they have been shamefully deceived in their hope, since neither have their sins been expiated (as we have just said), nor has death, which entered through sin, been overcome. Thus he shows that, through these mockers who deny the resurrection of the dead, the salvation and good name of all those who have died before us are placed simultaneously in peril or doubt. This moves every good man very strongly. For it is hard to condemn so many good men, who were distinguished by their virtues and noble deeds, and together with them our forefathers too, whose memory among us is rightly pleasing and honourable. Therefore our opponents, who defend the Papist superstitions against the doctrine of the Gospel, bring this argument against us today. "If," they say, "the religion which we have followed until now is false, then our forefathers and countless thousands of men have perished, who have been dead for several centuries before this Gospel was preached, by which the whole Papacy is assailed."

units.la: Quis vero nostrum illud vnquam dixit? Aut quis tam temerarius, tam inhumanus & barbarus fuerit, vt omnes eos qui toto illo tempore, quo superstitiones Romanæ floruerunt, extincti sunt, simpliciter aut absque omni exceptione damnare audet? Hoc autem dicimus & constanter affirmamus, per eas superstitiones neminem seruari posse: neque nos pudet cum Apostolis de Christo pronuntiare: Non est in alio quoquam salus: nec enim aliud nomen est sub cœlo, quod datum sit inter homines, per quod oporteat nos seruari. Neque ipsum Christum mendacij arguere libet, dicentem: Nemo venit ad Patrem nisi per me. Interim non negamus, toto illo tempore multos in Christo obdormiuisse, id est, in ea fide decessisse, quæ solius Christi pro nobis crucifixi merito nititur, perque illam esse seruatos. Et vt hoc speremus, mouet nos singularis Dei bonitas, qui quæ in Decalogo & Oratione Dominica inque Symbolo Apostolico habentur fidei & religionis Christianæ principia, in tenebris istis conseruauit, vt nunquam ex hominum cognitione aut memoria prorsus deleta fuerint. Sed & hodie plerisque in locis ipsi Papistæ iam moritu-ris Symboli recitatione præire solent, in cuius confessione multi eorum ex hac vita demigrant. Quotquot ergo fundamentum illud hucusque tenuerunt, quàmuis propter temporum istorum iniuriam superstruxerint multa, quæ merito paleas & stipulas, aut si quid his vilius est, dixeris, attamen in Christo tandem obdormiuerunt, & proinde seruati sunt, sed vt per ignem: quando nimirum in extremo illo mortis agone experti sunt vanam fuisse aliorum omnium fiduciam, salutis verò authorem atque mediatorem esse vnicum IESVM CHRISTVM, qui neminem ad se venientem foras eijcit. Et huius generis exempla hodie passim videmus. Non est ergo quod nobis aduersarij suis calumnijs inuidiam atque odium concilient. Ipsi potius viderint, qua temeritate nos damnent propter eam doctrinam atque fidem, quam à Prophetis & Apostolis accepimus, & in qua omnes Veteris Testamenti patres obdormierunt, quamq; Martyrum infinita millia sanguine suo obsignarunt. Quoad verò huius loci argumentum, istud firmiter teneamus, salutem nobis constare non posse absque mortuorum resurrectione, quæ in Christo fundata est. Quotquot autem in huius fide moriuntur, ij reuera non moriuntur, sed obdormiunt, olim ad gloriam cœlestem resurrecturi, vt alibi diximus.
units.tr: But which of us has ever said that? Or who would be so rash, so inhuman and barbarous, as to dare to condemn simply, or without any exception, all those who died during the whole time when the Roman superstitions flourished? We do say, and firmly affirm, that no one can be saved by those superstitions; nor are we ashamed to pronounce with the Apostles concerning Christ: "There is salvation in no one else; for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved." Nor do we wish to accuse Christ himself of lying when he says: "No one comes to the Father except through me." Meanwhile we do not deny that during all that time many fell asleep in Christ, that is, departed in that faith which rests solely on the merit of Christ crucified for us, and were saved through it. And that we may hope this, the singular goodness of God moves us, who in those darkness preserved the principles of the Christian faith and religion contained in the Decalogue, the Lord's Prayer and the Apostles' Creed, so that they were never utterly blotted out of human knowledge or memory. Indeed, even today in very many places the Papists themselves are accustomed to have the dying recite the Creed, and in its confession many of them depart from this life. Therefore, however much they have built upon that foundation, which they have held until now, with much that, because of the injury of those times, may rightly be called straw and stubble, or anything worse than this, yet they have at last fallen asleep in Christ, and so have been saved, but as through fire; since in that final struggle of death they have learned that the trust of all others was vain, and that the sole author and mediator of salvation is Jesus Christ, who casts out no one who comes to him. And we see examples of this kind everywhere today. There is therefore no reason why our opponents should win hatred and odium for themselves by their calumnies. Rather let them see with what rashness they condemn us on account of that doctrine and faith which we have received from the Prophets and Apostles, and in which all the fathers of the Old Testament fell asleep, and which countless thousands of martyrs have sealed with their blood. As for the argument of this passage, let us hold firmly to this: that salvation cannot stand for us without the resurrection of the dead, which is founded in Christ. Moreover, all who die in the faith of this are not truly dead, but fall asleep, destined to rise one day to heavenly glory, as we have said elsewhere.

units.la: Porrò addit his postremum quoque Paulus, quo aduersariorum sententiam validissimè con- futat. Si (inquit) in hac solum vita speramus in Christum, id est, si fides & spes nostra, quam in Christo habemus, non vltra huius vitæ terminum extenditur, neq; fructum aliquem in altero seculo vberiorem percipiemus, miserrimi sumus omnium hominum. Ratio huius dicti euidentissima est. Nec enim communes modò calamitates cum alijs hominibus piè ferunt, verumetiâ seipsos vt plurimum vitæ præsentis commodis spoliant, vt futuram illam & æternam assequantur. At nulla huius spes reliqua esse potest, si mortuorum resurrectio nulla sit. Erat argumentum istud tunc temporis efficacissimum, quando nihil tam exosum, nihil cum tot tantisq; periculis coniunctum erat, atq; Christiani nominis professio: vt hodie quoq; eadem multis in locis nullo non supplicio digna esse videtur. Nos autem in hac crucis atq; persecutionum palæstra teneamus, Christianorum hominum felicitatem nequaquam huius vitæ spacijs terminari. In mundo peregrini sumus patriam in cœlis habemus. Quid ergo mirum, si inter impios peregrinantibus multa tristitia, multa præter opinionem accidant? Soletur autem nos, quod olim in cœlis simus regnaturi: Neq; eos audiamus, qui spem illam quacunque ratione labefactare conantur. Sunt hi in Deum blasphemi & in omnes huius cul- tores iniuria, qui in fide ista obdormierunt, & proinde indigni, qui cum alijs hominibus aere cum- muni fruantur. Sed olim digna illi recipient suae impietatis praemia: nobis autem perpetuo rata erit JESV CHRISTI promissio: Volo ut ubi ego sum, ibi etiam sit minister meus. Illi debe- tur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Furthermore, Paul adds to these last words as well, by which he most powerfully refutes the opinion of the adversaries. "If," he says, "we hope in Christ only in this life, that is, if our faith and hope which we have in Christ do not extend beyond the limit of this life, and we shall not receive any richer fruit in the other age, we are the most wretched of all men." The reasoning of this saying is most evident. For not only do godly men bear common calamities with other men, but they also, for the most part, deprive themselves of the advantages of the present life, so that they may attain that future and eternal life. But no such hope can remain if there is no resurrection of the dead. This argument was most effective at that time, when nothing was so hated, nothing so bound up with so many and such great dangers, as the profession of the Christian name; as today too, in many places, the same profession seems worthy of no less than capital punishment. But let us hold our ground in this arena of the cross and persecutions, and remember that the happiness of Christian people is by no means limited by the span of this life. We are pilgrims in the world; we have our homeland in heaven. What wonder, then, if many sorrows and many things beyond expectation befall us as we journey among the impious? Let us be comforted by the fact that one day we shall reign in heaven; and let us not listen to those who try by any means to shake that hope. They are blasphemers against God and wrongdoers to all who worship him; they who have fallen asleep in this faith are therefore unworthy to enjoy the common air with other men. But one day they will receive the rewards of their impiety, which they deserve; while for us the promise of Jesus Christ will stand forever: "I wish that where I am, there also my servant may be." To him be blessing, honour, glory and dominion for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXX.
units.tr: HOMILY 80.

units.la: & Nunc autem, Christus excitatus est ex mortuis, & primitiae eo- rum qui obdormierunt factus est. Quia enim per hominem mors, per hominem quoque resurrectio mortuorum. Sicut enim in Ada- mo omnes moriuntur: ita & in Christo omnes vivificabuntur. Vn- usquisque autem suo ordine: primitiae Christus, postea qui sunt Christi, in aduentu ipsius.
units.tr: And now Christ is risen from the dead, and has become the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. For since death came by man, by man also comes the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive. But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, afterwards those who are Christ's, at his coming.

units.la: Quoniam totus in hoc seculo vitae humanae cursus laborum & molestiarum plenus est, pij & sancti cultores Dei omnes iam inde ab exordio rerum spem & fiduciam omnem in su- turae vitae expectatione collocatam habuerunt: quae causa est, quod ex mortuorum resurrectione praecipua sumpserunt consolationis argumenta, quibus seipsos in omni tentationum genere con- firmarent. Ergo quicunque resurrectionem negant, iidem illos simul omnes damnant, & religi- onis Christianae fundamenta convellunt. Docuit id nuper Paulus disertis verbis, quando dixit: Si resurrectio mortuorum non est, neque Christus quoque non est excitatus. Quod si vero is non excI- tatus est, sed a morte victus ad huc detinetur, inanis utique est fides vestra, inanis etiam est Euangelij praedicatio, & nos falsi testimonij crimine tenebimur, idque non sine manifesta Dei con- tumelia, qui nos sibi testes fecit: Denique qui Christo fidunt & vivunt, omnium mortalium mi- serrimi erunt, cum & huius vitae commodis seipsos priuent, & simul ab omni spe futurae remune- rationis excidant. Ex quibus sequitur, nullam esse blasphemiam atrociorem ea, qua mortuorum resurrectio negatur. Ideo Apostoli illam deploratis illis nouissimorum temporum illusoribus tri- buunt, ad quorum sermones pij aures obturare debeant. At postquam Paulus tot absurdorum enumeratione aduersariorum ora obturauit, nunc propius ad rem ipsam accedens, mortuorum re- surrectionem duobus argumentis validissimis confirmat, & inde transit ad eorum descriptionem, quae illam comitabantur, &c.
units.tr: Since the whole course of human life in this world is full of labours and troubles, the godly and holy worshippers of God have from the beginning of things placed all their hope and trust in the expectation of a future life. For this reason they drew their chief arguments for comfort from the resurrection of the dead, by which they might strengthen themselves against every kind of temptation. Therefore whoever denies the resurrection condemns all of them together and overturns the foundations of the Christian religion. Paul taught this recently in plain words, when he said: "If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ is not risen either. And if Christ is not risen, then our preaching is vain and your faith is also vain; yes, and we are found false witnesses of God, because we have testified of God that he raised up Christ, whom he did not raise up, if indeed the dead rise not." Moreover, those who trust in Christ and live for him will be the most wretched of all mortals, since they deprive themselves of the advantages of this life and at the same time fall from all hope of future reward. From these things it follows that there is no blasphemy more outrageous than the denial of the resurrection of the dead. Therefore the Apostles assign it to those despairing mockers of the last times, whose speeches godly ears ought to stop. But after Paul had silenced the mouths of his opponents by listing so many absurdities, he now comes closer to the matter itself and confirms the resurrection of the dead by two very strong arguments, and from there he passes to a description of the things that accompany it, etc.

units.la: Primum argumentum ex iis, quae proxime praecesserunt, infert: Nunc autem Christus ex- citatus est ex mortuis, & primitiae eorum qui obdormierunt factus est. Quasi diceret: Cum ita se res habeat, hoc inter homines Christianos firmum ratumq; tenere debet, JESVM CHRISTVM non modo pro peccatis nostris mortuum, verumetiam ex mortuis resuscitatum esse, & ideo nos quoque eiusdem virtute olim resurrecturos esse. Id autem probat simili siue exemplo, quando illum primitias eorum factum esse dicit, qui obdormierunt. Alludit enim ad Legem de primitijs, quae Deuteronomij Cap. 26. prolixè describitur. Secundum hanc frugum primitiae Deo offerebantur cum publica & solenni gratiarum actione. Ea autem fruges reliquae omnes sanctificabantur, ut iis tuto & salubriter frui possent. Constat enim, terram cum omni prouentu suo propter peccatum maledictioni obnoxiam esse, & proinde impuris atque prophanis omnia impura esse. Ut ergo pijs eadem pura atque salubria fiant, Deus se omnium datorem agnoscit vult. Quod qui norunt, si hoc ipsum publicè cum gratiarum actione testantur, ideoque omnibus ex iure divino salubriter utun- tur. Quo Paulus respexit, quando in priori ad Timotheum de illis vaticinans, qui ciborum di- scrimina tradituri sint, inter alia scribit: Quicquid creauit Deus, bonum est: nec quicquam abiiciendum est, si cum gratiarum actione sumatur: Sanctificatur enim per Verbum Dei & precationem. Itaque in primitiarum oblatione praecipuum erat olim gratiarum actio & frugum simul omnium sanctificatio. Illas autem mox plena messis sequebatur. Conuenit autem simile siue exemplum hoc praesenti causae. Nam ut Theodoretus scribit, primitiae eandem habent cognationem cum eo, tuius sunt primitiae: Ita etiam Christus carnem suam ex nobis assumpsit, & proinde eiusdem naturae particeps factus est. Dum vero illam ex mortuis excitauit, simul totam humanam naturam, quae prius mortalitati obnoxia erat, sanctificauit siue praeparauit, ut immortalitatis capax sit, quae olim suo tempore, seu messis quaedam universalis sequetur. Quo referri debet, quod ipse Christus huius saeculi finem & mortuorum resurrectionem messi confert. Habent ergo frugum primitiae non solum similitudinem aliquam cum Christi resurrectione, verumetiam ostendunt (quod nuper quoque monuimus) hanc nostrae resurrectionis fundamentum, vel potius causam esse efficientem. Ideo Theodoretus, Christum primitias eorum qui obdormierunt factum esse dicit, quia primus mortis potentiam soluerit, & ideo eius resurrectionem tota humani generis massa sequetur.
units.tr: He draws the first argument from what has immediately gone before: "But now Christ is risen from the dead, and has become the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep." As if he were saying: since things stand thus, Christians ought to hold firmly and securely that Jesus Christ was not only dead for our sins but also raised from the dead, and that therefore we too shall one day rise by his power. He proves this by a similar example, when he says that Christ has been made the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. For he alludes to the law of the firstfruits, which is described at length in Deuteronomy chapter 26. According to this law the firstfruits of the crops were offered to God with a public and solemn thanksgiving. The remaining crops were then sanctified, so that they could be enjoyed safely and wholesomely. For it is established that the earth with all its produce is liable to the curse on account of sin, and therefore all things are impure to the impure and profane. So that these same things may become pure and wholesome for the godly, God acknowledges himself to be the giver of all things and wills that it be so. Those who know this, if they testify to it publicly with thanksgiving, therefore use everything wholesomely by divine right. Paul had this in view when, in his first letter to Timothy, prophesying about those who would teach distinctions of foods, he writes among other things: "Whatever God has created is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer." Thus in the offering of the firstfruits, the thanksgiving and the sanctification of all the crops were formerly the chief things; and the full harvest soon followed them. This likeness or example also fits the present matter. For, as Theodoret writes, the firstfruits have the same kinship with that whose firstfruits they are. So Christ too took his flesh from us, and so became a partaker of the same nature. But when he raised that flesh from the dead, he at the same time sanctified and prepared the whole human nature, which before was subject to mortality, so that it might be capable of immortality, which will follow at its appointed time, as a kind of universal harvest. To this must be referred the fact that Christ himself links the end of this age and the resurrection of the dead with the harvest. The firstfruits of the crops therefore not only have some likeness to Christ's resurrection, but also show (as we pointed out recently too) that his resurrection is the foundation, or rather the efficient cause, of ours. Therefore Theodoret says that Christ has been made the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, because he was the first to loose the power of death, and so the whole mass of mankind will follow his resurrection.

units.la: Ut vero maior fit huius argumenti fides, Paulus non temere in tota hac causa subinde obdormiendi verbo utitur, quando de mortuis agit. Est enim locutio frequens admodum in Scripturis, & ea Christum quoque de Iairi filia & Lazaro Bethanien-si usum fuisse legimus. Neq; illam gentes omnino ignoraverunt. Homerus certe mortem somni fratrem dixit, nimirum propter similitudinem. Ut enim somnus quieti consecratus totum corpus recreat: sic sola mors nobis in vitae huius curriculo laborantibus quietem conciliat, & corpora praeparat, ut exuta mortali conditione ad immortalitatem resurgere possint. Ideo Angelus in Apocal. clamat: Beati mortui, qui posthac in Domino moriuntur: Etiam dicit Spiritus, quoniam requiescunt à laboribus suis. Deinde, ut somnus non est perpetuus: ita neq; mors corpora nostra perpetuò detinet. Et ut somnus fere clamore aut agitatione aliqua corporis excutitur: ita olim Christus totius mundi concussione & tuba Dei aut voce archangeli (ut alibi Paulus scribit) mortem discutiet, & hac prorsus abolita corporibus nostris vitam restituet immortalem atq; sempiternam. Debent ista frequenter considerari, ut certam habeamus adversus mortis terrores consolationem: qua qui deficiuntur, ij fere illis superati ab officio discedunt. At qui in ista meditatione diligentiores sunt, eos mortis recordatio ad officium faciendum magis extimulat, & alacriores reddit. Quoties ergo cubitum imus & quoties mane e lecto surgimus, ista nobis in mentem veniant, ex quibus mox magnum ad veram pietatem momentum nobis accedere sentiemus.
units.tr: So that the faith in this argument may be greater, Paul does not carelessly keep using the word "fallen asleep" throughout this whole discussion when he speaks of the dead. For it is a very common expression in the Scriptures, and we read that Christ also used it of Jairus's daughter and of Lazarus of Bethany. Nor did the Gentiles altogether fail to know it. Homer certainly called death the brother of sleep, no doubt because of the likeness. For as sleep, dedicated to rest, restores the whole body, so death alone brings rest to us who labour in the course of this life, and prepares our bodies so that, laid aside their mortal condition, they may rise again to immortality. Therefore the angel in the Apocalypse cries out: "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on. Yes, says the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours." Again, just as sleep is not perpetual, so neither does death hold our bodies for ever. And just as sleep is usually broken by some noise or movement of the body, so one day Christ will shake the whole world, with the trumpet of God and the voice of the archangel (as Paul writes elsewhere), and will dispel death; and with death utterly abolished, he will restore our bodies to immortal and everlasting life. These things ought often to be considered, so that we may have a sure comfort against the terrors of death. Those who lack this comfort are mostly overcome by those terrors and withdraw from their duty. But those who are more diligent in this meditation are more spurred on by the remembrance of death to do their duty, and are made more eager. So whenever we go to bed and whenever we rise from our beds in the morning, let these things come to our minds; and we shall soon feel that a great help toward true godliness is added to us.

units.la: Sed ad alterum huius loci argumentum accedamus, quod etiam exemplo à contrarijs desumpto constat. Quia enim per hominem mors, per hominem quoq; resurrectio mortuorum: Sicut enim in Adamo omnes moriuntur: ita & in Christo omnes vivificabuntur. Finis huius argumenti est, ut ostendat, non debere cuiquam impossibilem videri mortuorum resurrectionem. In hoc enim fere offendit ratio humana, quod ipse Paulus non indiligenter observavit, quando coram Agrippa rege de fide Christiana differens, hac vehementissima apostrophe usus est: Quid? incredibile vdicatur apud vos, quòd Deus mortuos excitet? Docet ergo in praesenti, hoc non debere alicui novum aut insolens videri, cùm in hominis lapsu & interitu tale quid acciderit. Per hominem enim unum (inquit) mors totum genus humanum invasit. Quid ergo novum aut à ratione alienum, si per unum e contra nobis omnibus resurgendi facultas parta est? Et ut id rectius intelligatur, per Expositionem subjicit: Sicut enim in Adamo omnes moriuntur: ita & in Christo omnes vivificabuntur. Opponit inter se Adamum, primum parentem nostrum, & Christum, qui alibi alter Adamus dicitur, & hunc simpliciter hominem modò dicit, non ut Deum esse neget, sed quia mors & resurrectio solius humanae naturae sunt, divina autem ut non moritur, ita neq; resurrectione opus habet. Adhaec ad argumenti vim facit hominis Christi vocabulum. Sensus enim est: Si unius hominis Adami peccatum atq; lapsus potuit omnem posteritatem morti obnoxiam facere, cur cuiquam impossibile videatur unius Christi iustitiam atq; resurrectionem potuisse omnibus hominibus resurgendi facultatem acquirere? Etenim si hoc negetur, maior peccati per Adamum inuectiuus erit, quam iustitiae Dei nobis in Christo exhibitae. Ut tamen argumenti praecipuè in eo sita est, quòd ut Adam non sibi soli peccator factus est, & mortuus, sed posteros simul omnes secum in exitium traxit: Ita Christus quoque non sibi soli mortuus est & ex mortuis resuscitatus, sed (ut nuper diximus) quicquid fecit, ex aeterno Patris decreto propter nos fecit, ut quam nos meruéramus peccati poenam ipse lueret. Si ergo tantum potuit ius naturae, vt qui peccator factus erat & morti obnoxius, ex se non alios quam peccatores & mortales gi-gneret: non minoris efficacia aut virtutis censeri debet Dei decretum, qui Filij sui vnigeniti mortem & resurrectionem cum omnibus suis effectis ad nos extendi voluit: vt quemadmodum ille ex mortuis in vitam restitutus est: ita nos quoque effractis & abolitis eius merito mortis claustris, olim ad vitam immortalem resurgamus. In Epistola ad Romanos quinto Capite etiam hoc argumentum prolixè tractatur, sed eo loci de vita spirituali & salute aeterna per Christum nobis restituta potissimum agitur: at hoc loco de corporum resurrectione disputat Paulus: & quia haec impijs quoque & à Christo alienis contingeret[?], simpliciter illam ad omnes homines extendit, vt quemadmodum omnes in Adamo mortui sunt, ita omnes quoad corpora olim in Christo resuscitentur.
units.tr: But let us come to the second argument of this passage, which also rests on an example drawn from the contrary. "For since death came by man, by man also comes the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive." The aim of this argument is to show that the resurrection of the dead ought not to seem impossible to anyone. For human reason mostly stumbles at this point, which Paul himself did not overlook when, speaking about the Christian faith before King Agrippa, he used this very forceful exclamation: "Why should it be thought incredible with you that God should raise the dead?" So here he teaches that this ought not to seem new or strange to anyone, since something of this kind has happened in the fall and death of man. For (he says) through one man death has seized the whole human race. What then is new or contrary to reason if, on the other hand, through one man the ability to rise has been won for us all? And so that this may be understood more correctly, he adds by way of explanation: "For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive." He sets Adam, our first parent, over against Christ, who elsewhere is called the second Adam, and here he calls him simply a man, not to deny that he is God, but because death and resurrection belong only to human nature, whereas the divine nature neither dies nor needs to rise. Moreover, the word "man" of Christ adds weight to the argument. For the sense is this: if the sin and fall of one man Adam could make all posterity liable to death, why should it seem impossible that the righteousness and resurrection of the one Christ could win for all men the ability to rise? For if this is denied, the harm brought by sin through Adam will be greater than the righteousness of God shown to us in Christ. Yet the main force of the argument lies in this: as Adam became a sinner and died not for himself alone, but dragged all his descendants together with him into ruin, so Christ too did not die and rise again for himself alone, but (as we said recently) whatever he did, he did for us by the eternal decree of the Father, so that he himself might pay the penalty of sin which we had deserved. If therefore the law of nature was able to make it so that one who had become a sinner and liable to death could beget from himself none but sinners and mortals, then the decree of God, who willed that the death and resurrection of his only-begotten Son, with all its effects, should extend to us, must be judged of no less efficacy and power; so that, just as he was restored from the dead to life, so we too, the bars of death having been broken and destroyed by his merit, shall one day rise to immortal life. In the Epistle to the Romans, chapter five, this argument is also treated at length, but there the discussion concerns above all the spiritual life and eternal salvation restored to us through Christ; here, however, Paul is disputing about the resurrection of bodies. And because this would happen also to the impious and to those alienated from Christ, he extends it simply to all men: as all died in Adam, so all in Christ shall one day be raised in their bodies.

units.la: Obseruabis tamen discrimen in resurrectione illa vniuersali ingens fore, quia pij & qui CHRISTVM IESVM vera fide amplexi fuerunt, ad coelestem vitam & sempiterna regni coelorum gaudia, impij vero & in peccatis suis mortui ad aeternos inferorum cruciatus resurgent, verumtamen tam hi quam illi non alia quam Christi virtute excitabuntur. Frustra igitur hic nonnulli nodum in scirpo quaerunt, dum quaestionem mouent, qua ratione aut quo sensu Paulus omnes per Christum viuificari dicat, cum plures olim ad mortem aeternam damnandi sint, illo nimirum dicente: Multi quidem sunt vocati, pauci vero electi? Sed solent in eiusmodi quaestiones incidere, & sibiipsis retia nectere, qui extra oleas currunt, nec attendunt diligenter quae de re in vno quoque loco agatur. Hic enim de sola corporum resurrectione sermo est, cuius author est Christus, qui vt impiorum quoque iudex erit, ita horum quoque corpora ex mortuis suscitabit, & immortalia faciet, vt poenis siue tormentis nunquam finiendis possint sufficere. Obseruauit hoc in Apostoli verbis Theodoretus, vetus & orthodoxus Scriptor, qui in Epitome diuinorum decretorum sic scripsit: Sicut omnes in Adamo moriuntur, sic etiam in Christo omnes viuificabuntur. Et non dixit, Seruabuntur: sed, Viuificabuntur. Communis est enim resurrectio, post resurrectionem autem fiet distinctio. Et hoc declarauit subiungens: Vnusquisque autem in proprio ordine. Multi enim sunt & eorum qui puniuntur, & eorum qui seruantur, ordines. Pro qualitate enim & quantitate iustitiae praebebuntur donorum remunerationes: Similiter autem & pro peccatorum differentia, erunt supplicia. Haec Theodoret.
units.tr: You will note, however, that the difference will be great in that general resurrection: the godly, and those who embraced Christ Jesus with true faith, will rise to heavenly life and the everlasting joys of the kingdom of heaven, but the wicked, who die in their sins, will rise to eternal torments of hell. Yet both alike will be raised by no power other than the power of Christ. It is therefore in vain that some here seek a knot in a rush, when they raise the question by what reason, or in what sense, Paul says that all are made alive through Christ, since many are to be condemned to eternal death: the words, "Many are called, but few are chosen," seem to them to contradict this. But those who run outside the olive groves are wont to fall into such questions and to weave nets for themselves, and they do not attend carefully to what is being treated in each place. For here the subject is only the resurrection of bodies, whose author is Christ. As he will be the judge of the wicked too, so he will raise up their bodies from the dead and make them immortal, so that they may be able to endure punishments or torments that will never end. Theodoret, an ancient and orthodox writer, observed this in the Apostle's words, and in his Epitome of the divine decrees he wrote thus: "As all die in Adam, so also in Christ all will be made alive." He did not say, "They will be preserved," but, "They will be made alive." For the resurrection is common, but after the resurrection the distinction will be made. And he made this plain by adding: "But each in his own order." For there are many orders both of those who are punished and of those who are preserved. For rewards will be given according to the quality and quantity of righteousness; likewise, too, punishments will be according to the difference of sins. So Theodoret.

units.la: Cæterum comprehendit hoc loco Paulus summam Christianæ fidei, adeoque eorum omnium, quae de toto salutis nostrae negotio possunt dici. Capita huius tractationis duo sunt. Primum est, quod omnes in Adamo moriantur. Atqui mortem peccati stipendium esse, omnis Scriptura docet: Ergo ex Adamo peccatores nascimur omnes. In Adamo enim mori dicimur, non quod ipsi extra omnem culpam constituti illius delictum luamus, sed quod ex illo in nos deriuata natura vitiositas, nos quoque peccatores facit, qui ex semetipsis non aliud possunt quam peccare. Et consulto hac locutione Spiritus sanctus vti voluit, vt peccati vim exprimat, & vt nos ea perspecta, magis ab illo abhorreamus. Et facit ad huius loci explicationem, quod idem Apostolus ad Romanos Capite quinto scribit, Mortem ab Adamo vsque ad Mosem regnauisse inter eos quoque, qui non peccauerant ad similitudinem transgressionis Adami. Obseruarunt hoc diligenter veteres, & inter hos Augustinus imprimis, quando per mortem infantium demonstrauerunt peccatum originis & huius atrocitatem, quam Pelagiani extenuare conabantur, vt vires hominis atque arbitrij nostri libertatem stabilirent: quod hodie Anabaptistae quidam maiori impudentia faciunt, dum se ab omni peccato immunes viuere posse affirmant. Quia enim infantes saepius in ipso partu extinguntur, saepius non multis a partu mensibus vitam finiunt, mors autem peccati stipendium sit, illos quoque peccatores esse fateamur oportet, nisi Deum iniustitiae aut crudelitatis accusare velimus, qui nihil tale adhuc meritos occidat. At illos actu nondum peccare posse constat. Restat ergo, vt potentia peccatores sint, & propter naturae vitiositatem, quam ex Adamo primo parente omnes contraximus, morte mulctentur[?], & merito quidem, cum vitiositas illa ipsis propria sit, & ipsorum cordibus atque medullis (vt ita loquar) insideat, sicuti ex effectis videre licet, quibus illam abunde produnt, quam primum cogitare, sapere, loqui aut aliud quid facere incipiunt. Figmentum enim cordis humani, ipso Deo teste, prauum est à pueritia sua. At si morte digni sunt infantes, quid de adultis dicemus, quorum peccata tam conspicua sunt, vt ne versutissimi[?] quidem hypocritæ illa dissimulare aut prorsus negare queant? Id vero vt nostræ iustitiæ meritum euertit, ita salutem nobis ex gratuita Dei misericordia obtingere docet.
units.tr: Moreover, in this place Paul comprehends the sum of the Christian faith, and so of all that can be said about the whole business of our salvation. There are two heads of this discussion. The first is that all die in Adam. Now all Scripture teaches that death is the wages of sin; therefore we are all born sinners from Adam. For we are said to die in Adam not because we, being ourselves free from all guilt, pay for his offence, but because the corruption of nature derived from him makes us sinners too, since of ourselves we can do nothing but sin. And the Holy Spirit deliberately chose to use this expression, both to express the force of sin and so that, having seen it clearly, we may shrink from it all the more. It also helps to explain this place that the same Apostle writes in Romans chapter five that death reigned from Adam to Moses even over those who had not sinned after the likeness of Adam's transgression. The ancients observed this carefully, and among them Augustine above all, when they showed by the death of infants both original sin and its atrocity, which the Pelagians tried to minimise in order to establish the powers of man and the freedom of our will. Some Anabaptists do the same today, with greater shamelessness, when they affirm that they can live free from all sin. For infants are often extinguished in the very act of birth, and often end their life a few months after birth; and since death is the wages of sin, we must confess that they too are sinners, unless we wish to accuse God of injustice or cruelty, who would kill them when they had merited nothing of the kind. But it is clear that they cannot yet actually sin. It remains, then, that they are sinners potentially, and because of the corruption of nature which we all contracted from our first parent Adam, they are punished with death, and rightly so, since that corruption is proper to them and dwells, so to speak, in their hearts and marrow. This can be seen from its effects, by which it reveals itself abundantly as soon as they begin to think, to understand, to speak, or to do anything else. For "the imagination of the human heart is evil from its youth," as God himself testifies. But if infants deserve death, what shall we say of adults, whose sins are so obvious that not even the most cunning hypocrites can dissemble them or deny them altogether? This doctrine overturns any merit of our own righteousness, and teaches that salvation comes to us from the free mercy of God.

units.la: Alterum huius doctrinæ caput est, omnes viuificari in Christo, & in solo quidem illo. Nam etsi hoc loco de corporum resurrectione agatur, potest tamen quod hic dicitur rectissime de vtraque hominis vita exponi, quando quod nobis in Christo collatum est beneficium, ad totum hominem extenditur. Nam vt mortis suæ merito peccatum mundi expiauit: ita sua resurrectione mortem deuicit atque exarmauit, vt in suos nihil præterea iuris aut imperij habeat. Quotquot ergo ei per fidem veram insiti sunt, ijdem eius spiritu animati ad vitæ nouitatem resurgunt, & tandem in vniuersali illa resurrectione quoad corpora quoque viuificabuntur, vt tam hæc quàm animæ eorum vita cœlesti & æterna fruantur. Ideo Christus olim Marthæ dicebat: Ego sum resurrectio & vita: Estque Christi beneficium multiplex admodum & prorsus liberale. Primò enim homo factus naturam nostram, qua nihil tunc miserius & infelicius erat, sibi vniuit: vt quæ in Adamo tota perierat, suo merito & virtute tota seruaretur. Deinde mortem sua peccatum sustulit, quæ nostræ perditionis causa erat, & eadem ratione Legis maledictionem aboleuit. Postremò idem ille tam corpora quàm animas nostras viuificat, vt & in hoc seculo vitam viuamus cœlestem, & olim toti cum illo regnemus. Iure ergo omnes homines ad se imitat, vt in suo merito quærant quæ sibi ad salutem consequendam necessaria esse sentiunt.
units.tr: The second head of this doctrine is that all are made alive in Christ, and in him alone. For although the subject here is the resurrection of bodies, what is said here may most rightly be applied to both lives of the man, since the benefit conferred on us in Christ extends to the whole man. For just as by the merit of his death he made expiation for the sin of the world, so by his resurrection he overcame and disarmed death, so that he has no further right or dominion over his own. Therefore, all who have been grafted into him by true faith, animated by his Spirit, rise to newness of life, and at last in that general resurrection they will be made alive also in body, so that both their bodies and their souls may enjoy heavenly and eternal life. Hence Christ once said to Martha: "I am the resurrection and the life." And the benefit of Christ is exceedingly manifold and altogether generous. For first, having been made man, he united our nature to himself, a nature than which nothing was then more wretched and unhappy, so that what had wholly perished in Adam might by his merit and power be wholly preserved. Then he took away the sin that was the cause of our destruction, and by the same means abolished the curse of the Law. Lastly, the same one makes alive both our bodies and our souls, so that we may live a heavenly life in this age and at last reign wholly with him. Rightly, therefore, he invites all men to himself, that they may seek in his merit what they feel to be necessary for obtaining salvation.

units.la: Sunt autem hominum stultissimi & ingratissimi, quotquot illo relicto, qui solus fons est aquæ viuentis, hinc inde vagantur, & cisternas sibi fodiunt arentes atque pertusas, quæ aquam nec continere quidem possunt. Et hi ferè dignas suæ ingratitudinis pœnas luunt. Vt enim non nisi in Adamo omnes moriuntur: ita non nisi in solo Christo vita obtingit illis, qui eum fide vera & constanti apprehendunt. Itaque dum hunc illi respuunt, simul à vita excidant oportet, seque ipsos labore inani & impensis inutilibus fatigant. Rectè ergo in hunc Pauli locum D. Augustinus olim scripsit: Per hanc apostolicam diuinam claramque sententiam satis euidenter elucet, nemi-nem ire in mortem, nisi per Adam, neminem ire in vitam æternam, nisi per Christum. Hoc est quippe Omnes & Omnes: Quia sicut omnes homines per primam, hoc est, per carnalem generationem pertinent ad Adam: sic omnes homines ad secundam, id est, spiritalem regenerationem veniunt, quicunque ad Christum peruéniunt[?]. Ideo ergo dictum est & hic Omnes, & ibi Omnes quia sicut omnes qui moriuntur, non nisi in Adam moriuntur: ita omnes qui viuificabuntur, non nisi in Christo viuificabuntur. Ac per hoc, quisquis nobis dixerit, quenquam in resurrectione mortuorum viuificari posse nisi in Christo, tanquam pestis communis fidei detestandus est. Hæc omnia Augustini sunt, quæ ideo recitauimus, vt obiter simul doceremus, non nos primos esse, qui homines non nisi per Christum iustitiam atque salutem consequi affirmant, sed hunc veterem & orthodoxum esse Ecclesiæ consensum, quem tunc Christiani doctores tenuerunt, quan-do minus fuit superstitionum, fidei autem & pietatis zelus ardentior, quàm posteris temporibus, quando vetus apostolicæ ecclesiæ simplicitas paulatim extincta est. Nec periculum est, ne quis ex ista doctrina licentiæ aut impiæ securitatis ansam arripiat. Nam qui illam verè receperunt, ij dum in hoc corpore mortali sunt, sic viuunt, vt iam nunc Christi viuificantis virtus in eis appareat, dum peccato mortui vitam viuunt nouam & verè Christianam. Vide ad Romanos sextum Caput.
units.tr: Yet the most foolish and ungrateful of men are those who, leaving him, who alone is the fountain of living water, wander hither and thither and dig for themselves cisterns that are dry and cracked, which cannot even hold water. And these generally pay the penalty their ingratitude deserves. For just as all die only in Adam, so life comes to those who lay hold of him with true and steadfast faith only in Christ alone. Therefore, while they reject him, they must at the same time fall away from life, and wear themselves out with fruitless labour and useless expense. Rightly, then, did St Augustine once write on this passage of Paul: "Through this apostolic, divine, and clear sentence it shines forth sufficiently plainly that no one goes to death except through Adam, and no one goes to eternal life except through Christ. For this is the meaning of 'all' and 'all': just as all men belong to the first, that is, the carnal generation, to Adam, so all men who come to Christ come to the second, that is, the spiritual regeneration. Therefore 'all' is said both here and there, because just as all who die die only in Adam, so all who will be made alive will be made alive only in Christ. And so, whoever tells us that anyone can be made alive in the resurrection of the dead except in Christ is to be detested as a common plague of the faith." These are the words of Augustine, which we have recited so that we might teach in passing that we are not the first to affirm that men obtain righteousness and salvation only through Christ, but that this is the old and orthodox consensus of the Church, which the Christian teachers of that time held, when there was less superstition and a more ardent zeal for faith and piety than in later times, when the old simplicity of the apostolic Church was gradually extinguished. Nor is there any danger that anyone will seize from this doctrine an occasion for licence or wicked security. For those who have truly received it, while they are in this mortal body, so live that even now the power of the life-giving Christ appears in them, since they, dead to sin, live a new and truly Christian life. See Romans chapter six.

units.la: Caeterum obiiciat aliquis: Si Christus nostræ resurrectionis author est, & in eo omnes viuificantur, cur ergo non, vt ille, tertio nos etiam statim die resurgimus? Cur corpora nostra computrescunt & dissoluuntur? Respondet ergo Paulus huic obiectioni per Præoccupationem: Unusquisque autem suo ordine, &c. Quasi diceret: Etsi verissimum sit quod dixi, Deus tamen certum resurrectionis ordinem constituit, quem turbari nefas est. Si enim naturæ ordo in omnibus constantissimè seruatur, & certis vicibus hiemi ver succedit, hoc vero æstas exci-pit, quam autumnus sequitur, qui mox hiemi locum denuò præbet: cur non certus ordo seruetur in eo, quo nihil maius, nihil miraculosius, nihil denique homini salutarius est? Et cum tellurit proventum patienter expectemus, ut suo tempore illum colligamus, multo magis hunc optatissimum fidei nostrae fructum cum aeterna salute coniunctum, non cum praecipiti & impatienti desiderio anticipare velle debemus, sed firma & constanti spe tempus illud expectare, quod Deus tanto negotio destinavit, qui ex ordine abs se constituto nihil prorsus decedere, neque ullo modo eum interrumpi patietur.
units.tr: But someone may object: If Christ is the author of our resurrection, and in him all are made alive, why then do we not rise on the third day immediately, as he did? Why do our bodies decay and dissolve? Paul answers this objection by anticipation: "But every man in his own order," and so on. As if he said: Although what I have said is most true, God has nonetheless established a certain order of resurrection, which it is wrong to disturb. For if the order of nature is most constantly kept in all things, and in fixed turns winter gives way to spring, and this is followed by summer, which autumn follows, and autumn soon gives place again to winter: why should a fixed order not be kept in that which is nothing greater, nothing more wonderful, and nothing, in short, more salutary for man? And just as we patiently await the produce of the earth, so that we may gather it in its own time, much more ought we not to wish to anticipate with headlong and impatient desire this most longed-for fruit of our faith, joined with eternal salvation, but with firm and constant hope to await that time which God has appointed for so great a business, since he will suffer nothing at all to depart from the order he has established, nor in any way to be broken.

units.la: Quis vero ille ordo est? Primitiae (inquit) Christus, postea qui sunt Christi in adventu ipsius. Primitias Christum dicit, ut hunc primum resurgere debuisse ostendat: partim quidem ut membra, id est, singuli homines ex suo capite ipsum resurgendi certum concipere: partim in huius resurrectione pateret, qualis nostra olim futura sit: vera nimirum, quae ea ipsa corpora, quae nunc gestamus, nobis vere restituentur. Quae causa est, quod non modo surrexit Christus, verumetiam a resurrectione se discipulis videndum & contrectandum praebuit, adeoque infinitis demonstrationibus probavit, se corpore suo vero, quod ex Maria virgine assumpsit quodque suis partibus constat, resurrexisse, non alio aut essentialibus suis proprietatibus exuto: quae de re alibi plura diximus.
units.tr: But what is that order? "Christ the firstfruits," he says, "afterward those who are Christ's at his coming." He calls Christ the firstfruits to show that Christ ought to have risen first, partly so that, as members, that is, individual men, they might grasp from their head the certainty of his rising, and partly so that in his resurrection it might be made plain what ours will one day be: namely, that these very bodies which we now bear will truly be restored to us. This is why Christ not only rose, but also offered himself to be seen and touched by his disciples after his resurrection, and proved by countless demonstrations that he had risen in his true body, which he took from the virgin Mary and which consists of its own parts, and not in some other body stripped of its essential properties. We have said more about this matter elsewhere.

units.la: Quaerunt autem aliqui, qua ratione Christus primus ex mortuis resurrexisse dicatur, cum ante eius in carnem adventum aliqui in vitam restituti sint, utpote filius Sunamitidis, quem Helisaei precibus resuscitatum legimus, & alter ille, qui in eiusdem prophetae sepulchrum abiit. Eius reuixit, cum illius ossa attigisset. Et ipse Christus priusquam moreretur Iairi filiam, quae paulo antequam ad eam venisset, expirauerat, viduae item Naimiticae filium, qui iam efferebatur, & post hos Lazarum iam quartum in sepulchro diem agentem excitavit. Sed observabis hic de ea resurrectione agi, qua ad vitam caelestem & immortalem excitabimur. In ea certe primus locus Christo debetur, cum alteri illi non nisi ad terrenam hanc vitam resurrexerint denuo morituri. Adde, quod primitias resurrectionis recte dicit Christum, quia huius virtute omnes illi resurrexerunt, qui ante ipsum excitati sunt.
