Ut enim mortis eius meritum ad veteris Testamenti patres, imo ad primum parentem nostrum extenditur (quo nomine agnus dicitur mactatus ab origine mundi) ita eiusdem resurrectio, quoad eius meritum & effectum, islos quoque omnes praecessisse dici potest. Et haec quidem propter eos dicta sint, qui aequo curiosiores undique quaestiones captant, & saepe non multum necessarias.
units.tr: Some ask, however, in what sense Christ is said to have risen first from the dead, since before his coming in the flesh some were restored to life, such as the son of the Shunammite woman, whom we read was raised by the prayers of Elisha, and that other man who was laid in the prophet's tomb. He revived when his bones touched the prophet's bones. And Christ himself, before he died, raised Jairus's daughter, who had breathed her last shortly before he came to her; likewise the son of the widow of Nain, who was already being carried out; and after these he raised Lazarus, who had already been four days in the tomb. But you will observe that here the subject is that resurrection by which we shall be raised to heavenly and immortal life. In that resurrection the first place certainly belongs to Christ, since those others rose only to this earthly life, to die again. Add to this that Christ is rightly called the firstfruits of the resurrection, because all who were raised before him rose by his power. For just as the merit of his death extends to the fathers of the Old Testament, indeed to our first parent (for which reason he is called the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world), so the merit and effect of his resurrection can be said to have preceded all of them too. These things have been said for the sake of those who are overly curious and seize on questions from every side, and often questions that are not very necessary.

units.la: Sed ut ad ordinem resurrectionis redeamus, secundum locum illis tribuit Paulus, qui Christi sunt in eius adventu, id est, vere credentibus, quos ille cunc pro suis agnoscet, & sibi coharedes faciet. Ita ipse se exponit in priori ad Thessalonicenses, ubi sic scribit: Qui mortui fuerint in Christo resurgent primum: deinde nos vivi, qui reliqui erimus, rapiemur simul cum eis in nubes, in occursum Domini in aera, &c. Ergo eos Christi esse dicit, qui in fide Christi decesserunt, quia id certissimum electionis argumentum, & infallibilis filiorum Dei nota est, si in ipso mortis articulo vitam in Christo speramus, adeo ut neque vita neque mors nos ab ea dilectione separare possit, qua nos Deus in illo complexus est. Horum resuscitationem sequetur mox subita eorum mutatio, quos dies ille vivos deprehenderit: de quibus infra dicetur. Fruentur ergo tunc ista quoque praerogativa fideles, ut Christi vivificantis virtus ad ipsos primos redundet, & eos iam vita restitutos visuri[?] sint impij, ubi ipsi ex morte prodierint, qui tunc ex eorum conspectu dolorem & horribilem conscientiae cruciatum concipient, sicuti in libro Sapientiae scribitur. Addit hic in praesenti Paulus: Deinde erit finis mundi scilicet tuus[?], & omnium quae in mundo sunt. Ita vero impatientiae medetur, quae plerunque in aduersis & calamitatibus oboritur, & eo nos adducit, ut cum his vitam simul abrumpere cupiamus. Ea autem occasione in statum futuri saeculi digreditur, de quo in sequenti sermone dicemus. Faxit Deus, Pater misericordiae, ut Filii sui unigeniti vera cognitione illuminati vitam nostram ita instituamus, & in eius fide constanti moriamur, ut olim eiusdem virtute ad caelestis patriae haereditatem excitemur, cumq; illo vivamus & regnemus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen. Deinde erit finis, cum tradiderit regnum Deo ac Patri, cum abſoleuerit[?] omne imperium, & omnem potentiam & virtutem. Nam oportet eum regnare vsquequo omnes inimicos subiecerit pedibus eius. Vltimus autem hostis aboletur mors. Nam omnia subiecit sub pedes eius. Cum autem dicit omnia ei esse subiecta, palam est (hoc dici excepto eo, qui subiecit ei omnia. Postquam vero subiecta ei fuerint omnia, tunc & ipse Filius subiicietur ei, qui subiecit ipsi omnia, vt sit Deus omnia in omnibus.
units.tr: But to return to the order of the resurrection: Paul assigns the second place to those who are Christ's at his coming, that is, to those who truly believe, whom he will acknowledge as his own and make co-heirs with himself. He himself explains this in his first letter to the Thessalonians, where he writes thus: "The dead in Christ shall rise first; then we who are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air," etc. Therefore he says that those are Christ's who have died in the faith of Christ, because this is the most certain proof of election and the infallible mark of the sons of God, if at the very moment of death we hope for life in Christ, so that neither life nor death can separate us from that love by which God has embraced us in him. Their resurrection will be followed soon by the sudden transformation of those whom that day finds alive, of whom more will be said below. The faithful will therefore then enjoy this privilege as well, so that the life-giving power of Christ flows first into them; and the wicked, when they come out of death, will see them already restored to life, and at the sight of them will feel grief and the dreadful torment of conscience, as is written in the Book of Wisdom. Here Paul adds: "Then comes the end of the world," that is, of this world and of all that is in it. In this way he cures impatience, which commonly arises in adversity and calamities and leads us to wish to cut life short along with them. On this occasion he turns to the state of the age to come, about which we shall speak in the following sermon. May God, the Father of mercies, grant that we, enlightened by the true knowledge of his only begotten Son, so order our lives and so die steadfast in his faith, that by his power we may one day be raised to the inheritance of the heavenly fatherland, and live and reign with him, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen. "Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God and the Father, when he has put down all rule, and all authority and power. For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death. For he has put all things under his feet. But when he says that all things are put under him, it is plain that this does not include him who put all things under him. When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things under him, so that God may be all in all."

units.la: Inter alia, quae resurrectionis fidem impediunt, praecipuum est, quod ratio humana inter praesentis & futuri seculi statum non discernit, & in futuro quoque eam putat rerum conditionem fore, quae nunc in mundo cernitur. Ibi enim absurda multa occurrunt, quae non aliter declinari posse videntur, quam si mortuorum resurrectio prorsus negetur. Exemplum huius rei Euangelica historia in Sadducaeis proponit, qui contentiones & lites inter coniuges polygamos oriturac putarunt, si mortui aliquando resurgerent: & ideo quaestionem de muliere, quae septem ex ordine fratribus secundum Legem nupserat, Christo moverunt. Et horum similes hodie sunt multi, qui quaerere audent: Si omnino futura est mortuorum resurrectio, quis tunc erit rerum status? Volent singuli ad sua redire, & rursus occupare quae prius habuerunt, & in quorum possessionem ipsis defunctis successerunt alij. Ita vero lites nascentur de opibus, dignitatibus, coniugijs, imperijs, regnis. Quid autem de pijs fiet? Hi certe ad eadem certamina rapientur, quae nunc iustinent, aut etiam his graviora. Rursus ergo opus erit precibus, Sacramentis, protectore Christo, deniq; iudicibus & magistratu. Et tale quid gentes olim somniauisse videntur, quando Minoem, Aeacum & Rhadamantem[?] finxerunt, qui apud inferos iudiciorum praefecti sint. Sed omnibus hisce quaestionibus Paulus occurrit, & primo quidem nullum omnino litibus locum fore docet: deinde futuri seculi statum siue conditionem describit.
units.tr: Among the other things that hinder faith in the resurrection, the chief is that human reason does not distinguish between the state of the present age and that of the age to come, and thinks that the condition of things in the future will be what is seen in the world now. For then many absurdities present themselves, which seem unavoidable unless the resurrection of the dead is denied altogether. The gospel history offers an example of this in the Sadducees, who thought that quarrels and lawsuits would arise between polygamous spouses if the dead ever rose; and so they put to Christ the question about the woman who had married seven brothers in turn according to the Law. Today there are many like them who dare to ask: If the resurrection of the dead is to come at all, what will the state of things be then? Each man will want to return to his own, and to reclaim what he once had, and of which others succeeded to possession after he died. Thus lawsuits will arise over wealth, dignities, marriages, empires and kingdoms. And what will become of the godly? They will surely be dragged into the same contests they now endure, or even into worse ones. Then there will again be need of prayers, sacraments, Christ as protector, and finally judges and the magistrate. Something like this the nations seem to have dreamed long ago, when they imagined Minos, Aeacus and Rhadamanthus as presiding over judgements in the underworld. But Paul meets all these questions: first, he teaches that there will be no room at all for lawsuits; then he describes the state or condition of the age to come.

units.la: Primum vno verbo absoluit: Deinde erit finis, scilicet mundi huius & omnium quae in mundo sunt. Quia enim resuscitatis mortuis, & immutatis ijs quos dies ille viuos deprehenderit, & singulis ad loca, quae ipsis debentur, remissis, impleta erunt omnia, nihil quod porro fiat reliquum erit. Cremabitur ergo tota huius mundi machina, & (vt Petrus scribit) caeli cum stridore praeteribunt, elementa vero aestuantia soluentur, terraque & quae in ea sunt opera exurentur. Vnde sequitur nullas de ijs, quae nunc inter homines vsitata sunt, lites fore aut contentiones. Sunt ergo absurda prorsus neque vllo responsio digna, quae illusores scurrae suis quaestionibus in medium afferunt, vt mortuorum resurrectionem negent, siue in dubium vocent. Confutantur item philosophi, qui mundum hunc aeternum esse tradiderunt, vt qui neque creatus sit vnquam, neque etiam finem suum fit habituruS. Atqui creatum olim fuisse, & quidem ex nihilo, Moses diserte ex Spiritus revelatione prodidit: Finis autem in praesenti Paulus meminit, vt & Christus consummationis huius seculi. Neminem ergo curiosorum & audacium hominum argutiae moueant, qui vt conscientiae latranti blanditias faciant, ad eiusmodi commenta conuertuntur. Porro considerationis huius vsus est duplex.
units.tr: First, he settles the matter in one word: "Then comes the end," namely of this world and of all that is in it. When the dead have been raised, those whom that day finds alive have been changed, and each has been sent to the place that is owed to him, everything will be completed and nothing further will remain to be done. So the whole frame of this world will be burned up, and (as Peter writes) the heavens will pass away with a roar, the elements will be dissolved by burning heat, and the earth and the works in it will be consumed. It follows that there will be no lawsuits or disputes of the kind now common among men. Therefore the questions that mocking jesters bring forward to ridicule the resurrection of the dead, or to call it into doubt, are utterly absurd and not worth any answer. The philosophers who taught that this world is eternal are also refuted, since on their view it was never created and will never have an end. Yet Moses plainly tells us, from the revelation of the Spirit, that it was created long ago, and indeed out of nothing. Paul, for his part, mentions the end, as Christ does, of the consummation of this age. Let the subtleties of curious and daring men therefore not disturb anyone. They turn to such inventions only to flatter a barking conscience. Moreover, this consideration is useful in two ways.

units.la: Primo consolationi seruit in omni aduersorum siue tentationum genere. Quia enim mundo huic suus iam finis constitutus est; afflictiones quoque & calamitates aliquando desinant oportet. Imo ne diuturnae quidem esse poterunt, cum vitae huius curriculum breue sit, vltra quod illae non extenduntur. Tunc autem momentaneas huius vitae aduersitates, aeternum & ipsa (vt ita dicam) aeternitate aeternius pondus caelestis gloriae excipiet, vt Apostolus hic noster in posterioris Epistolae Cap.quarto diligentius docebit.
units.tr: First, it serves for consolation in every kind of adversity or temptation. For since an end has already been set for this world, afflictions and calamities must also come to an end at some point. Indeed they cannot even be lasting, since the course of this life is short, and they do not extend beyond it. Then, for the momentary troubles of this life, an eternal weight of heavenly glory, eternal in its own right (so to speak), will take their place, as our Apostle will teach more fully in the fourth chapter of his second Epistle.

units.la: Deinde vitae totius institutioni ista seruire debent, vt reliquis procul huius mundi studijs ad caelestem vitam aspiremus. Docuit istud Paulus eodem planè argumento supra Capite septimo, vbi mundo nihil praeter figuram breui transituram tribuit: Et Petrus cum ea, quae modo citauimus dixisset, mox infert: Cum igitur haec omnia soluantur, quales oportet esse vos in sanctis con-uersationibus & pietatis officijs, expectantes & properantes ad aduentum diei Dei, in quo caeli conflagrantes dissoluentur, & elementa aestuantia liquescent? Et mox haec quoque subjicit: Sed caelos nouos & terram nouam secundum promissum expectamus, in quibus iustitia inhabitat. Quapropter dilecti, haec expectantes, studete, vt immaculati & incontaminati ab eo reperiamini in pace, &c.
units.tr: Second, this understanding ought to shape the whole of our life, so that, putting aside all other pursuits of this world, we aspire to the heavenly life. Paul taught this very same argument above in the seventh chapter, where he assigns to the world nothing but a figure that will soon pass away. And when Peter had said the things we have just cited, he immediately adds: "Since, then, all these things are to be dissolved, what manner of persons ought you to be in holy conduct and acts of piety, waiting for and hastening toward the coming of the day of God, in which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved, and the burning elements will melt?" And soon he adds this as well: "But according to his promise we look for new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells. Therefore, beloved, while you wait for these things, be diligent that you may be found by him spotless and blameless in peace," and so on.

units.la: Debet autem longius quoque extendi ista doctrina, ne caeco carnis affectu decepti eos aemulemur, qui in hoc saeculo felices esse videntur. Est haec admonitio admodum necessaria, quia ad hunc lapidem saepe, qui optimi & pijssimi sunt, offendunt, vt Asaphi & Ieremiae exempla testantur. Sed finge aliquem in navi ornatissima, secundo flumine & aura leniter crispante deferri, quem scias mox ex improuiso naufragium passurum esse: Num quaso illi voluptatulam istam inuideris? num te eadem navi vehi optabis? Annon potius te beatum & felicem diceres, cui con-tigisset in portu subsistere? Item si domum habitares commodam quidem, sed quam breui conflagra-turam aut ruituram esse certo constaret, num in ea securus delitiari posses? Non equidem arbi-tror. Atqui eadem est mundi huius conditio, imo multo infelicior est. Nam non modo ruina & incendium illud vniuersale eum manet, sed ne nunc quidem, dum maxime floret & triumphat, quicquam habet, quo animus hominis satiari possit. Non id opes possunt, non dignitates, non voluptates: imo omnia ista nos insatiabili cupiditate eo magis accendunt, quo vberius affluunt: & insuper aut curas mordacissimas sibi continuas habent, aut cum dolore & lachrymis finiuntur. Incumbit praeterea omnibus inuitabilis moriendi necessitas, hora autem mortis incertissima nos ne momento quidem temporis securos aut otiosos esse patitur: cum fere nihil tale opinantibus obrepere soleat. Et si detur vsque ad nouissimum Christi aduentum vitae dies extendere, attamen tunc finis erit omnium, quae nunc in mundo nobis tam chara & pretiosa habentur, cum illis autem miserè pereunt & aeternum lamentabuntur omnes, qui ijs nimium addicti caelestia neglexerunt. Hac qui aliquanto diligentius meditantur, ijs non facile persuaderi poterit, vt terrena haec caelestibus & aeternis anteponant.
units.tr: This teaching ought also to be extended further, so that we do not, deceived by blind fleshly desire, imitate those who seem happy in this age. This warning is very necessary, because the best and most godly people often stumble over this stone, as the examples of Asaph and Jeremiah bear witness. But imagine someone being carried in a most splendid ship, with a fair wind and a gentle breeze, while you know he will soon suffer shipwreck without warning. Would you begrudge him that little pleasure? Would you wish to be carried in the same ship? Would you not rather call him blessed and fortunate who had managed to reach harbour? Likewise, if you lived in a comfortable house, but it was certain that it would soon be burned or collapse, could you take your pleasure in it without anxiety? I do not think so. Yet the condition of this world is the same, indeed far more wretched. For not only does that universal ruin and fire await it, but even now, while it flourishes and triumphs most of all, it has nothing with which the human mind can be satisfied. Wealth cannot do it, nor honours, nor pleasures. Indeed all these things kindle us with insatiable desire the more abundantly they flow in, and besides, they either keep us constantly under the most biting cares, or they end in grief and tears. Moreover, the inescapable necessity of dying lies upon everyone, and the uncertainty of the hour of death does not allow us to be secure or idle even for a moment, since it usually creeps upon those who suspect nothing of the sort. And even if life were granted to be extended to the last coming of Christ, still there will be an end of all the things that are now held so dear and precious to us in the world. Along with them, all who have clung too closely to these things and neglected heavenly things will perish wretchedly and lament forever. Those who meditate on these things with some diligence will not easily be persuaded to prefer these earthly things to the heavenly and eternal ones.

units.la: Sed transeamus ad alterum huius loci caput, quo quod de fine huius saeculi dixit, plenius explicatur, & totus futuri saeculi status describitur. Duo autem dicit. Primum: Christus tradet regnum Deo ac Patri, id est, ei, ex quo ipse ab aeterno genitus est. Nec enim locutio ista accipi debet, quasi alius sit Deus, alius Pater: cum potius Deum verum Paulus a falsis & fictitijs distinguere voluerit. Abusi autem sunt olim hoc loco Ariani & Eunomiani, vt Filium Patre minorem esse euincerent, & ita argumentabantur: Filius tradet regnum Deo Patri: Ergo quod habet nunc, non nisi a Patre acceptum habet. Item: Qui quod habet, alteri tradere tenetur, eo minor fit oportet: Filius regnum Patri olim tradet: Ergo Patre minor est. At non viderunt Paulum de Christo loqui, quatenus Mediator est inter Deum & homines, & locutiones eiusmodi ad humanam naturam, quam is assumpsit, potissimum referri debere. Imo non viderunt turbulentissimi homines eodem suo argumento Patrem longe infra Filium deijci. Si enim hic olim regnum ita tradet, vt ipse quoad diuinam quoque naturam regnare desinat, fateamur oportet, Patrem tam nunc non regnare, cum dies ille nondum aduenerit, neque regnum vnquam habiturum nisi a Filio acceptum. Quid ergo respondebunt huic dicenti: Omnia mihi data sunt a Patre meo? Item: Data est mihi omnis potestas in caelo & in terra? &c. Num Patrem Filio inferiorem facit dicent, quasi regnum & potestatem ita in hunc transtulerit, vt ipse nunc ijs prorsus careat? Quin potius cum Diuo Augustino dicamus, inseparabilem esse Patris & Filij operationem. Vt ergo Pater Filio omnia dedit, nihil interim sibi ipsi adimens: ita vicissim Filius olim Patri regnum tradet, vt tamen ipsius diuinitati & potentiae nihil decedat. Etenim perpetuo verum ratumque manet quod dixit Christus: Ego & Pater vnum sumus. Item: In principio erat Verbum, & Verbum illud erat apud Deum, & Deus erat Verbum, &c.
units.tr: But let us pass to the second head of this passage, by which what he said about the end of this age is more fully explained, and the whole state of the coming age is described. He says two things. The first: "Christ will hand over the kingdom to God and Father," that is, to him from whom he was begotten from eternity. For this phrase must not be understood as if God were one and the Father another, since Paul rather wished to distinguish the true God from false and fictitious ones. The Arians and Eunomians of old abused this passage to prove that the Son is less than the Father, and they argued thus: "The Son will hand over the kingdom to God the Father; therefore what he now has, he has received only from the Father." Again: "He who must hand over to another what he has must be less than that other; the Son will one day hand over the kingdom to the Father; therefore he is less than the Father." But they did not see that Paul is speaking of Christ as far as he is Mediator between God and men, and that such expressions must be referred chiefly to the human nature which he assumed. Indeed those most turbulent men did not see that by this same argument the Father would be thrown far below the Son. For if the Son were one day to hand over the kingdom in such a way that he himself ceased to reign even as regards the divine nature, we would have to confess that the Father does not reign now either, since that day has not yet come, and that he will never have a kingdom except one received from the Son. What then will they answer to him who says: "All things have been given to me by my Father"? Or: "All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me," and so on? Will they say that he makes the Father inferior to the Son, as if he had so transferred the kingdom and power to the Son that he now lacks them altogether? Rather, let us say with the divine Augustine that the operation of the Father and the Son is inseparable. Just as the Father gave all things to the Son while losing nothing for himself, so in turn the Son will one day hand the kingdom over to the Father, yet nothing will be taken away from his own divinity and power. For what Christ said remains true and firm forever: "I and the Father are one." And: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God," and so on.

units.la: Sed debet ante omnia Pauli institutum siue scopus respici, qui hoc loco non hoc agit, vt ostendat Pater ne aut Filius maior fit, sed quae regni Dei in altero seculo conditio futura sit, docere vult. Itaque locus iste bifariam exponi potest. Primum, vt Regnum sumatur pro populo regni, id est, pro tota electorum omnium Ecclesia. Hos omnes suo olim sanguine redemptos Christus Pa-tri tradet, vt in ijs tunc regnet Deus, in quibus per vitia prius regnarat diabolus. Quem sensum Commentaria quoque exprimunt, quæ D. Hieronymo adscribuntur. Et fauent ei promissiones: In domo Patris mei mansiones multæ sunt, sin minus, dixissem vobis. Vado paraturus vobis locum. Et cùm abiero, & parauero vobis locum, rursus veniam, & assumam vos ad meipsum, vt vbi sum e-go, & vos sitis. Item: Ego pacisc[?]or vobis prout pactus est mihi Pater regnum, vt edatis & bi-batis super mensam meam in regno meo. Et rursum: Pater, quos dedisti mihi, volo vt vbi sum e-go, & illi sint mecum, vt spectent gloriam illam, quam dedisti mihi, &c. Deinde de regni Christi administratione Apostoli verba intelligi possunt. Est enim illud duplex, Gratia nimirum & Gloria. Gratia regnum ad huius seculi conditionem pertinet, in qua pro nobis adhuc intercedit ille, nosque Patri suo reconciliat: quod facto opus est, quando nouis quotidie delictis Dei oculos of-fendimus. Sequetur autem in nouissimo eius aduentu regnum gloriæ, quâ nos quoque (sicuti pro-misit) fruemur, & in quo nobis porro neque aduocato neque vlla intercessione opus erit. Erit enim tunc Deus omnia in omnibus, quem ipsi quoque coràm intuebimur, vt ex ipso bonorum omnium fa-cultatem longè beatissimam habeamus. Possunt autem duo isti sensus facile inter se conciliari, cùm reipsa conueniant, & alter ex altero dependeat. D. Augustinus certè, acutissimus mysteriorum Scripturæ sacræ indagator, vtrumque coniungit, sic scribens: Cùm ergo tradiderit regnum Deo ac Patri, id est, cùm credentes & viuentes ex fide, pro quibus nunc Mediator interpellat, produxerit ad contemplationem, cui percipiendæ suspiramus & gemimus, & tranferit labor & ge-mitus, iam non interpellabit pro nobis tradito regno Deo ac Patri. Itaque ista regni traditio, de qua in præsenti Paulus loquitur, non aliud erit, quàm administrationis regni Dei, quoad nos, in melius mutatio: quia sublato peccato, carnis vitiositate, mundo item & morte, omnibusque obsta-culis, quæ nunc nos remorantur, nulla nobis vllius intercessione, neque aliquo alio salutis præsidio opus erit: eò quòd perfecta pace & beatitate sempiterna nullisque fortunæ vicibus obnoxia liber-rimè fruemur. Nam vt Regis filius ad tumultuantem prouinciam missus, rebus probè compositis & fracta rebellium contumacia, bonos & fidos regni subditos, quos eadem tempestas simul ab-ripuerat, ad se colligit, totamque prouinciam Patri tranquillam atque pacatam tradit, neque ea traditione ipse minor aut contemptibilior, sed multò gloriosior redditur, vt quæ triumphus potius quàm imperij derogatio dici mereatur: Ita Christus quoque plenè iam peractis omnibus, quæ ad humani generis redemptionem & ad Regni Dei ab æterno decretam constitutionem pertinebant, illud Patri sic trader, vt ipse cum eodem viuat & regnet in sempiternum. Nec enim irritum fiet vnquam, quod & Prophetæ olim, & postea Angelus Gabriel de regno Christi nunquam fi-niendo sunt vaticinati.
units.tr: But before all else, Paul's purpose or scope must be considered. He is not here aiming to show that the Father or the Son becomes greater, but wants to teach what the condition of God's kingdom will be in the other age. So this passage can be explained in two ways. First, "kingdom" may be taken for the people of the kingdom, that is, for the whole Church of all the elect. Christ will hand over all these, once redeemed by his own blood, to the Father, so that God may then reign in those in whom the devil formerly reigned through sins. The commentaries attributed to Jerome also express this sense. And the promises favour it: "In my Father's house there are many mansions; if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you. And when I have gone and prepared a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you may be too." Again: "I covenant with you, just as my Father has covenanted with me a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom." And again: "Father, those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they may be with me, so that they may behold that glory which you have given me," and so on. Second, the words of the Apostle can be understood of the administration of Christ's kingdom. For this is twofold, namely of grace and of glory. The kingdom of grace belongs to the condition of this age, in which he still intercedes for us and reconciles us to his Father, which must be done since we offend God's eyes with fresh sins every day. But in his final coming there will follow the kingdom of glory, in which we too (as he promised) will enjoy, and in which we will have no further need of an advocate or any intercession. For then God will be all in all, and we shall see him face to face, so that from him we may have the most blessed possession of all good things. These two senses can easily be reconciled with each other, since in fact they agree and the one depends on the other. Augustine certainly, the most acute investigator of the mysteries of holy Scripture, joins both, writing thus: "When, therefore, he will have handed over the kingdom to God and Father, that is, when he will have brought believers who live by faith, for whom he now intercedes as Mediator, to the contemplation which we sigh and groan to attain, and when labour and groaning have passed away, he will no longer intercede for us, since the kingdom has been handed over to God and Father." Therefore this handing over of the kingdom, of which Paul is speaking here, will be nothing other than a change for the better in the administration of God's kingdom as regards us. For when sin, the corruption of the flesh, the world and death, and all the obstacles which now hold us back, have been removed, we will need no intercession of anyone, nor any other safeguard of salvation, since we will enjoy perfect peace and eternal blessedness, subject to no changes of fortune. For just as a king's son, sent to a province in tumult, when matters have been well settled and the stubbornness of the rebels broken, gathers together the good and faithful subjects of the kingdom whom the same storm had carried away, and hands the whole province over to his Father calm and pacified, and is not made less or more contemptible by that handing over, but much more glorious, so that it deserves to be called a triumph rather than a diminution of his rule; so Christ too, once all things have been fully accomplished which pertained to the redemption of mankind and to the constitution of God's kingdom decreed from eternity, hands that kingdom over to the Father in such a way that he himself lives and reigns with the same Father forever. For what the prophets of old, and afterwards the angel Gabriel, prophesied about the never-ending kingdom of Christ will never become void.

units.la: Simul autem locus iste nos admonet, omnem nostræ salutis causam siue gloriam vni illi tribu-scribi debere. Huius enim vox est, quæ nunquam fallet siue mutabitur: Nemo venit ad Patrem, nisi per me. Etenim dum in hac carne viuimus, Deum neq; videmus neque agnoscimus nisi in illo, qui est splendor & genuinus aut essentialis character Patris. Deinde cum eodem neq; in gratiam redire possumus nisi per illum, in quo solo nobis Pater placatus est: Olim quoq; in magno illo die nemo nos eidem acceptos fisset, vt regni cœlorum hæredes simus, præter ipsum vnum, cuius iudicio omnes homines aut stabunt aut cadent. In illo deniq; vno æternum seruabimur. Sunt ergo stultissi-mi miserrimiq; omnium hominum, qui hoc relicto circa vanissima sui capitis figmenta occupan-tur, quæ ad salutem & animarum tranquillitatem nihil conferunt.
units.tr: At the same time this passage reminds us that the whole cause and glory of our salvation must be attributed to him alone. His is the word that will never fail or change: No one comes to the Father except through me. For while we live in this flesh, we neither see nor know God except in him, who is the brightness and the true or essential image of the Father. Moreover, we cannot be restored to favour with the Father except through him, in whom alone the Father has been reconciled to us. Likewise, on that great day, no one could be accepted by God as an heir of the kingdom of heaven apart from him alone, by whose judgment all people will either stand or fall. In him alone we shall be preserved for ever. Therefore they are the most foolish and wretched of all people who, leaving this aside, busy themselves with the vain fictions of their own minds, which contribute nothing to salvation or to the peace of their souls.

units.la: Sequitur alterum, quod de futuri seculi conditione Paulus dicit, Quòd nimirum Christus a-bolebit omne imperium, & omnem potentiam & virtutem. Tribus vocabulis omnia comprehen-dit, quæ nunc magnifica & eximia habentur. Sunt enim imperia siue principatus Angelorum, de quibus multus apud Danielem sermo est: & horum quidem alij boni, alij mali sunt. In terris item sunt Reges, principes, vrbium magistratus, præsides, iudices & horum omnium ministri. At omnes isti abolebuntur, quoad suas functiones, quarum tunc nullus vsus erit amplius. Quæcunque enim huius generis sunt, ad vita huius præsentis conseruationem & Ecclesiæ in terris adhuc mi-litantis gubernationem faciunt. Itaque abolita prorsus huius seculi conditione & tota hac mundi machina,illa etiam omnia simul cessabunt. Nam Angelorum honorum ministerijs deinceps minime opus erit, sed hi nobiscum nosque cum illis in Dei conspectu Regni aeterni gaudijs fruemur: mali vero omnes cum suo principe ad tartara detrusi cruciabuntur, neque alicui porro negotium facient. Ita neque magistratibus tunc opus erit, cum nemo futurus sit qui iniuriam patiatur, & defensionem requirat. Disciplinam quoque sive ecclesiasticam sive politicam aut civilem instituere superuacaneum foret, quando vna omnium in coelis gaudentium voluntas, vtrum desiderium, vnus affectus erit, cum Dei voluntate per omnia conueniens. Tyranni autem & iniqui principes suas quoque poenas exoluent apud inferos cum omnibus colleEti, qui (vt Propheta ait) terrorem suum posuerunt in terra viuentium. Eadem erit tunc quoq; ministrorum Verbi Dei ratio. Quidenim illi docendo faciant, quando nemo erit qui aliquid ignoret, aut quem officij immemorem admonitionibus siue correptione seueriori vrgere oporteat? Quicunque autem in illo munere fideles fuerunt, stellarum instar tunc splendebunt (vt Daniel praedixit) ignavi vero & impostores cum hypocritis poenas dabunt. Daniel.12. Matth.24.
units.tr: Next comes what Paul says about the condition of the age to come: namely, that Christ will abolish every rule, every authority and power. In three words he embraces everything that is now regarded as grand and excellent. For there are dominions or principalities of angels, of which Daniel speaks at length; and some of these are good, others evil. Likewise on earth there are kings, princes, the magistrates of cities, governors, judges, and the ministers of all of these. But all of them will be abolished so far as their functions are concerned, for those functions will then have no further use. For whatever belongs to this kind serves the preservation of this present life and the government of the Church still militant on earth. Therefore, once the condition of this age and the whole machinery of this world have been utterly abolished, all these things will cease together. For there will be no further need for the ministry of the good angels, but they will share with us, and we with them, in the joys of the eternal kingdom in the sight of God; while all the evil ones, together with their prince, will be thrust down to hell and tormented, and will no longer cause trouble for anyone. So too there will then be no need of magistrates, since no one will be left who suffers wrong and requires defence. It would also be superfluous to establish discipline, whether ecclesiastical or political or civil, since there will be one will, one desire and one affection in all who rejoice in heaven, agreeing in every way with the will of God. But tyrants and unjust princes will also pay their penalties in the lower world, together with all who (as the Prophet says) have set their terror in the land of the living. The same will hold for the ministers of the Word of God. For what would they do by teaching, when there will be no one who is ignorant of anything, or whom it is necessary to urge by warnings or by sterner correction, because he has forgotten his duty? Yet those who were faithful in that office will then shine like the stars (as Daniel foretold), while the slothful and deceitful will pay the penalty with the hypocrites. Dan. 12. Matt. 24.

units.la: Ista officij admonent omnes eos, qui in aliquo eminentiori gradu constituti sunt. Meminerint, potestatem suam huius modo seculi negotijs seruire, non autem perpetuam fore, diem quoque aliquando venturum esse, quo rationem reddere iubebuntur de omnibus, quae fecerunt. Bene ergo tantum potestate illa, & hoc vnum agant, vt quando abolitis omnibus istis dignitatibus ad Christi tribunal stabunt, laetam illam & beatam vocem audiant: Euge serue bone, in pauco fidelis fuisti, super multa te constituam: Intra in gaudium heri tui. Terreat illos vicissim quod tunc ignavi & infidis dicetur, qui in tenebras exteriores eijcientur. Nihil enim tunc praesidij ipsis erit in ea potestate, quae priusquam sistentur, omnis abolebitur.
units.tr: These things admonish all those who are placed in any more eminent rank. Let them remember that their power serves only the affairs of this age and is not everlasting, and that a day will come when they will be commanded to give an account of all that they have done. Let them therefore use that power well, and do this one thing: that when all those dignities have been abolished and they stand before the judgment seat of Christ, they may hear that joyful and blessed word: Well done, good and faithful servant; you have been faithful in a few things, I will set you over many things; enter into the joy of your lord. In turn, let it terrify those who are slothful and faithless, who will be told then, and cast into outer darkness. For then there will be no protection for them in that power, which will be wholly taken away before they are brought to trial.

units.la: Confutantur praeterea hoc loco Anabaptistae & horum sectatores, qui principatus & magistratus iam nunc abolitos volunt, & Isaiae de regno Christi vaticinio abuntur, qui lupos, leones, vrsos, aspides & basiliscos cum bobus, agnis, haedis & infantibus commoraturos esse praedixit absque omni periculi metu. Nam de iis loquitur Propheta, qui mores in melius mutant, & Euangelij praedicatione illuminati atque emolliti, ex feris & truculentis bestijs in mites Christi agnos transformantur. At quia interim nunquam deerunt hypocritae, qui dolo malo se in Ecclesiae gremium insinuant, improbi item & temerarij disciplinae Christianae contemptores, legum freno opus est, & proinde ijs etiam, qui iudiciorum executione illos coerceant. Quod autem de pacatissimo illo statu & vniuersali Ecclesiae pace ipsi somniant, in nouissimo demum Christi adventu implebitur. Interea ijs nos accommodemus, quae Apostoli de magistratibus tradiderunt. Nam ita facto opus esse, exempla quotidiana docent, quae nemo, nisi impudentissimus sit, negare potest.
units.tr: Moreover, in this passage the Anabaptists and their followers are refuted, who want principalities and magistrates to be abolished already now, and who abuse Isaiah's prophecy about the kingdom of Christ, in which he foretold that wolves, lions, bears, asps and basilisks would dwell with oxen, lambs, kids and infants, without any fear of danger. For the Prophet is speaking of those who change their ways for the better, and who, enlightened and softened by the preaching of the Gospel, are transformed from wild and savage beasts into gentle lambs of Christ. But since in the meantime there will never be lack of hypocrites, who with evil intent insinuate themselves into the bosom of the Church, and likewise of wicked and reckless despisers of Christian discipline, there is need for the restraint of laws, and therefore also for those who restrain them by carrying out judgments. As for the perfectly peaceful state and universal peace of the Church, which they dream of themselves, it will be fulfilled only at the last coming of Christ. Meanwhile let us accommodate ourselves to what the Apostles have handed down about magistrates. For daily examples teach that this is necessary, and no one except the most shameless can deny it.

units.la: Caeterum quaerat aliquis: Cur vero non statim a resurrectione sua Christus ista praestitit? aut cur adhuc differt, quo minus istud faciat? num sua Ecclesiae immemor, aut num tam infirmus & impotens est, vt nunc ista perficere non possit? Respondet ergo huic quaestioni Paulus per Praeoccupationem. Nam oportet eum (inquit) regnare vsquequo omnes inimicos subiecerit pedibus eius: Vltimus autem hostis aboletur, mors, &c. Quibus verbis docet, eum neq; suorum immemorem, neq; etiam aliqua impotentia aut imbecillitate impediri: sed hoc aeternum Dei decretum esse, vt hoc Christi regnum, quale nunc est, duret vsquequo omnes hostes suos subegerit. Id vero probat authoritate Psalmi 8. aut 110. in quo hoc praedictum esse constat, fore, vt omnes inimici pedum eius scabellum fiant. Ex eo loco ad hunc modum argumentatur: Christus per Euangelium & media quae ad huius propagationem faciunt, regnabit eo vsq; donec hostes suos omnes pedibus suis subiecerit. At vltimus hostium erit mors, quae ante finem huius seculi aboleri non poterit. (Est enim via omnis terrae, & quam diu corruptibilis ista huius mundi facies duraverit, illam quoq; durare nec esse est.) Ergo mutatio illa regni Christi, aut administrationis eius, in melius non antea fieri potest, quam illa quoq; fuerit demutata, sub finem videlicet huius seculi.
units.tr: But someone may ask: Why did Christ not accomplish these things immediately after his resurrection? Or why does he still delay doing them? Is he forgetful of his Church, or is he so weak and powerless that he cannot now bring these things to completion? Paul answers this question by anticipating it. For he says: He must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be abolished is death, and so on. By these words he teaches that he is neither forgetful of his own nor hindered by any powerlessness or weakness; but it is the eternal decree of God that this reign of Christ, such as it now is, shall last until he has subdued all his enemies. He proves this by the authority of Psalm 8 or 110, in which it is plainly foretold that all enemies will become a footstool for his feet. From that passage he argues in this way: Christ will reign through the Gospel and the means that serve its propagation until he has put all his enemies under his feet. But the last of the enemies will be death, which cannot be abolished before the end of this age. (For it is the way of all the earth, and as long as this corruptible face of the world endures, death too must endure and cannot cease.) Therefore that change in the reign of Christ, or in his administration, cannot take place for the better before that too has been changed, namely at the end of this age.

units.la: Non debet autem oscitanter negligi, quod mortem in numero hostium Christi Paulus recenset. Possunt huius causae plures afferri. Prima, quod diaboli inuidia per peccatum introducta est, & altera, quod primo Dei instituto aduersatur, qui hominem vt aeternum viueret creavit[?], & ideo in medio paradisi arbore mvitæ[?] plantauerat. Postrema, quia huius telo Satan utitur contra Dei seruos, ut vel a bsferreat[?] eos, quo minus officium faciant, vel etiam e medio tollat, ne ipsius conatibus sese opponant. Et postremus hostis dicitur, quia ut postrema superuenit, cum iam peccauissent Adamus, ita durabit quoq; (ut modo diximus) usq; ad nouissimum Christi aduentum. Est ergo mors per se mala, & ideo horrorem coniunctum habet, quo plerunq; sanctissimi quiq; ita percellun-tur, ut eius declinandæ consilia ineant, aut saltem illam deprecentur, sicuti in Abrahami, Mosis, Dauidis, imprimis autem IESV CHRISTI exemplis est videre. Quæ nos admonere debet, ne vel de nobisipsis desperemus, si quid huius sentimus in nobis: vel alios temere abijciamus, qui mortem metuunt. Nam ut modo diximus, hoc in sanctos quoq; Dei cultores cadit, & hic maxime locum habet proverbium: Vir fugiens denuo pugnabit. Agnoscamus autem ingens Christi beneficium, qui viret eius ita contudit, ut nullum ius in animas nostras habeat, sed solum corpus petat, animabus autem transitus fit ad vitam æternam. Olim autem per eundem tota abolebitur, quando corpora quoq; nostra resurgent, & beata immortalitate donabuntur. Huius ergo spe nosipsos in omni periculo consolemur.
units.tr: Nor should it be carelessly overlooked that Paul counts death among the enemies of Christ. Several reasons for this can be given. First, because death was introduced through the envy of the devil and sin, and second, because it opposes God's first institution, who created man to live for ever, and therefore had planted him in the midst of the tree of life in paradise. Last, because Satan uses this weapon against the servants of God, either to drive them away so that they do not perform their duty, or even to remove them from the scene so that they cannot oppose his attempts. And death is called the last enemy because, like a last arrival, it came after Adam had already sinned; and so it will endure (as we have just said) until the final coming of Christ. Death is therefore evil in itself, and so it carries with it a horror by which very holy people are often so struck that they plan ways to avoid it, or at least pray to be spared from it, as can be seen in the examples of Abraham, Moses, David, and especially of Jesus Christ himself. This should admonish us not to despair of ourselves if we feel something of this in ourselves, nor to rashly cast off others who fear death. For, as we have just said, this falls also upon the holy worshippers of God, and here the proverb applies most of all: A man who flees will fight again. Let us acknowledge the great benefit of Christ, who by his power has so crushed death that it has no right over our souls, but seeks only the body, while for souls there is a passage to eternal life. And in time, through the same Christ, death will be entirely abolished, when our bodies too will rise and be granted the blessed immortality. Let us therefore console ourselves in every danger with the hope of this.

units.la: Sed præter alia hoc loco imprimis dignum est obseruatu, quod Christum in hoc etiam sæculo regnaturum esse audimus, donec omnes hostes ipsi subijciantur. In hoc censu numerantur Satan, peccatum, mors, quam innumeri comites undique stipant, omnes denique, qui Satanæ suam operam locant in regno Christi oppugnando, quale sunt Antichristus cum suis satellitibus hæreticis, impostoribus, tyrannis & horum ministris. Hi omnes (inquam) Christi hostes sunt, quia hunc persequitur, dum Verbum eius & huic credentes extinctos volunt. Quod si vero eos Christi pedibus subijci oportet, nunquam sane efficient quod volunt, ut consultando & machinando omnem lapidem moueant. Nam de omnibus his intelligi debet, quod in Psalmo secundo scribitur, fremere quidem gentes, & reges collecti sua conferre consilia, ut jugum excutiant, sed omnium istorum conatus irritos fore, & Christum tandem ferreo sceptro, id est, inuincibili potentia ipsos confrangeturum esse ut vasa fictilia siue testacea. Exempla, quibus istud confirmetur, multa in historijs passim occurrunt, & nostro sæculo multis hoc infelicissimè cessisse vidimus, quod aduersus Christum coniurauerunt. Possumus his connumerare peccatorum licentiam & quæ ubique nobis obijciuntur scandala, quo minus in regno Christi proficiamus. Nam hæc quoque Christus quotidie judicium suorum seueritate coercet, ne indomitum grassentur, eadem vero olim simul collecta igni æterno tradentur, sicut ipse in parabola ζιζανίων docet. Ex istis ergo consolationem petamus in tentationibus, nec dubitemus, suo tempore cessatura esse, quæ nunc nobis negotium faciunt. Regnat enim jam nunc in cœlis Christus, & regnum eius sempiternum est, in hoc autem sæculo per crucem triumphat, quam olim gloria æterna sequetur.
units.tr: But apart from other matters, one point in this passage deserves particular attention: we hear that Christ will reign even in this age, until all enemies are placed under his feet. Among these enemies are Satan, sin, and death, which is attended on every side by countless companions, and finally all those who hire themselves out to Satan to fight against Christ's kingdom. Such are the Antichrist with his hireling heretics, impostors, and tyrants, and their ministers. I say that all of these are Christ's enemies, because they persecute him while they seek to destroy his Word and those who believe in it. Yet even if they must be subjected to Christ's feet, they will certainly never achieve what they want, however much they plot and scheme and stir every stone. What is written in the second Psalm must be understood of all of them: the nations rage and the kings take counsel together to cast off the yoke, but the efforts of all of them will come to nothing, and Christ will at last break them with an iron sceptre, that is, with invincible power, like potters' vessels. Many examples of this are found scattered through the histories, and in our own age we have seen many who conspired against Christ come to a most unhappy end. To these we may add the licence of sinners and the scandals that are everywhere thrown in our faces, which hinder our progress in Christ's kingdom. Christ also restrains these things daily by the severity of his judgement, so that they do not run riot unchecked; but one day they will all be gathered together and handed over to eternal fire, as he teaches himself in the parable of the tares [ζιζανίων]. Let us therefore seek consolation from these things in our temptations, and not doubt that what now gives us trouble will cease in its own time. For Christ already reigns in heaven, and his kingdom is everlasting; in this age he triumphs through the cross, which will one day be followed by eternal glory.

units.la: Quia autem Christi pedibus omnia subijci oportere dixerat, periculum erat, ne quis Deum Patrem quoq; illi seruiliter subijciendum suspicaretur. Nam gentibus hæc dicebat Paulus, inter quas vulgo tritæ erant fabulæ de Saturno a Joue & aliis filijs regno suo eiecto. Interserit ergo non- nulla quibus huic errori siue suspicioni medeatur, & ex Psalmi verbis, quæ adduxerat, argumen- tum sic colligit: Cum autem dicit, omnia ei esse subiecta, palam est hoc dici excepto eo, qui subiecit ei omnia. Quasi diceret: Qui omnia alteri subijcit, seipsum utique non subijcit, neque potestate sua priuatur. (Nam nisi omnipotens sit, omnia cuiquam subijcere nō potest.) At Pater omnia subiecit Filio: Ergo ille huic subiectus non est. Imo tam abest, ut per subiectionem ista diuinæ Patris maiestati aut potentiæ aliquid derogetur, ut potius Filius sese illi subiecturus sit, idq; in tum finem, ut Deus sit omnia in omnibus.
units.tr: But since Paul had said that all things must be placed under Christ's feet, there was a danger that someone might suppose that God the Father too must be made subject to him in a servile way. Paul was speaking to the Gentiles, among whom the stories were commonplace about Saturn being driven from his kingdom by Jove and his other sons. So he inserts some remarks to correct this error or suspicion, and from the words of the Psalm he has quoted he draws his argument thus: "When he says that all things are subjected to him, it is plain that this is said with the exception of the one who subjected all things to him." As if he were saying: "The one who subjects all things to another does not himself become subject, nor is he deprived of his power. (For unless he were almighty, he could not subject all things to anyone.) But the Father has subjected all things to the Son; therefore he himself is not subject to him." Indeed, far from this subjection detracting in any way from the majesty or power of the divine Father, it is rather that the Son himself will submit to him, and to this end, that God may be all in all.

units.la: Est autem diligentius considerandum, qua ratione Christus Patri subijciendus esse dicatur. Diuus Augustinus hoc de humana natura interpretatur: nimirum ut Ariani respondeat, qui ex hoc dicto aduersus Christi diuinitatem argumentabantur, ut eum Patre minorem esse euincerent. Sed quoad carnem, initio statim sese Patri subiecit, quando forma serui assumpta, sese exinaniuit, & obediens factus est usque ad mortem crucis: hic autem de subiectione, quæ nouissimo demum die futura sit, agitur. Itaque rectius hoc de Mediatoris officio intelligi debet, quo se tunc abdicabit, ut non amplius necessario. Quod si vero id in fine sæculi demum fiet, fungetur ille procul dubio interea hoc munere, & proinde nimium iniqui sunt, qui eo illum nunc spoliant, vel hoc in Dinos[?] transferunt. Cessabit autem tunc Christi Mediatoris officium, ut Deus sit omnia in omnibus. Est quidem nunc quoque Deus omnia in omnibus, quia in illo viuimus, mouemur & sumus, sed eo sensu hoc dicitur, quia tunc immediatè absque omnibus adminiculis regnabit, quibus nunc propter nostram infirmitatem vtitur: nosque ab eo immediatè omnia ea percipiemus, quae nunc partim creaturarum ministerio, partim Christi intercessione accipimus. Itaque ad solum Deum omnia referentur, verum videlicet illum Deum, in cuius vna substantia (vt ex aliis Scripturae locis patet) sunt Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus. Et tunc quoque nostra perfectietur felicitas, quia & Dei dilectio in nobis consummabitur, nosque cum redemptore nostro IESV CHRISTO, viuemus atque regnabimus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: We must consider more carefully in what sense Christ is said to be subject to the Father. Saint Augustine interprets this of his human nature, chiefly in order to answer the Arians, who used this saying to argue against Christ's divinity, in order to prove that he is less than the Father. But as regards his flesh, he subjected himself to the Father at once from the beginning, when, having taken the form of a servant, he emptied himself and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Here, however, the subjection that will take place at the last day is under discussion. Therefore it ought rather to be understood of the office of Mediator, which he will then lay down, so that it is no longer necessary. But if this is to happen only at the end of the age, he will undoubtedly still discharge that office in the meantime, and so those are very unjust who now strip him of it or transfer it to God. The office of Christ the Mediator will then cease, so that God may be all in all. God is indeed even now all in all, since in him we live, move, and have our being; but this is said in a different sense, because then he will reign immediately, without all the aids which he now uses on account of our weakness, and we shall receive immediately from him all those things which we now receive partly through the ministry of creatures and partly through the intercession of Christ. Thus all things will be referred to God alone, that is, to that God in whose one substance (as other passages of Scripture make plain) are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. And then too our happiness will be made perfect, because the love of God will be brought to completion in us, and we shall live and reign with our Redeemer Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory, and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXXII,
units.tr: HOMILY LXXXII,

units.la: Alioqui quid facient qui baptizantur pro mortuis, si omnino mortui non excitantur? & cur baptizantur pro mortuis? Et cur nos periclitamur omni hora? In dies morior per gloriationem nostram, quam habeo in CHRISTO IESV Domino nostro. Si secundum hominem aduersus bestias pugnaui Ephesi, quae mihi vtilitas, si mortui non excitantur? Edamus & bibamus, cras enim morimur. Ne errate. Mores boni commercia corrumpunt mala. Euigilate iuste, & ne peccate. Quidam enim Deum non norunt. Ad pudorem vobis loquor.
units.tr: Otherwise, what will those do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise at all? And why are they baptized for the dead? And why are we in danger every hour? I die daily, through the boasting I have in Christ Jesus our Lord. If, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what good is it to me, if the dead do not rise? "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die." Do not be deceived. "Evil companions corrupt good morals." Wake up righteously, and do not sin. For some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.

units.la: ETsi[?] resurrectionis mortuorum articulus non solum in Veteris & Noui testamenti scripturis tradatur, verum etiam exemplis infinitis, quae in rerum natura fiunt, confirmetur, non possunt tamen illi fidem habere ij, qui sola carnis ratione ducuntur. Imò ijdem fere vndique argumenta conquiruut, quibus illum in dubium vocent, & incredulitatem suam foueant. Quia vero plerung, ad absurda confugiunt, quae ex resurrectione consequi videntur, Paulus vicissim absurda plura & maiora congerit, quae omnino sequi necesse fit, si illa negetur. Et initio quidem ea recensuit, quibus tota religio Christiana cum suis principijs euertitur. Si enim mortui (inquit) non resurgunt, nec Christus quidem resurrexit. At si hic non resurrexit, inanis est praedicatio nostra, inanis etiam est fides vestra, adhuc estis in peccatis vestris, & quotquot in Christo obdormierunt, perierunt. Subiecit his deinde argumenta quaedam, quibus Christi virtus & meritum illustratur, eaque occasione in statum futuri seculi & regni Dei administrationem digressus est. Nunc redit ad absurdorum enumerationem, vt euidentius doceat, quam fallantur suis rationibus, qui resurrectionem negare audent.
units.tr: Although the article on the resurrection of the dead is taught not only in the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments but is also confirmed by countless examples from the course of nature, yet those who are guided by mere human reason cannot believe it. Indeed, almost the same people gather arguments from every side by which they call it into doubt and nourish their unbelief. Because they often take refuge in the absurdities that seem to follow from the resurrection, Paul in turn heaps up still more and greater absurdities, which must necessarily follow if it is denied. At first he listed those by which the whole Christian religion, with its foundations, is overthrown. For, he says, "If the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen. But if Christ has not risen, our preaching is empty, your faith is also empty, you are still in your sins, and all who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished." After this he added certain arguments by which the power and merit of Christ are set forth, and on that occasion he digressed into the state of the future age and the administration of the kingdom of God. Now he returns to the enumeration of absurdities, so that he may more clearly teach how those are deceived by their own reasoning who dare to deny the resurrection.

units.la: Primum ritu baptismi, qui tunc in vsu erat, aduersarios confutat, sic dicens: Alioqui quid facient qui pro mortuis baptizantur, si omnino mortui non excitantur? cur & baptizantur pro mortuis? Quae verba plerique veterum de ijs exponunt, qui nomine aut loco suorum, qui iam defuncti erant, baptizabantur, quasi id illis aliqua ratione prodesset. Et Chrysostomus non minus ridiculum quam impium Marcionitarum errorem exponit, qui si quem priusquam baptizatus esset mori contingeret, lecto eius aliquem supponere solebant, qui interrogatus num baptizari vellet, pro mortuo respondebat, & simul baptizabatur. Sed credibile non est, Apostolum errorem tam foedum tamque ludicram baptismi prophanationem dissimulaturum fuisse, qui vitia multo leviora huius grauissimè corripuit. Si enim fides aliena neminem seruat, sed iustus sua fide viuit, quanto minus ad salutem alicuius proderit, si quis alius pro ipso vel baptizetur, vel Coenae mysticae communicet? Deinde pugnat hoc cum totius Scripturae sacrae consensu, in qua nulla prorsus sacra pro defunctis nulli ritus, deniq; nihil omnino traditur, per quod defunctorum saluti consulatur.
units.tr: First, he refutes the opponents by the rite of baptism then in use, saying: "Otherwise, what will they do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise at all? Why then are they also baptized for the dead?" Most of the ancients explain these words of those who were baptized in the name or place of their own kin who had already died, as if this helped them in some way. And Chrysostom describes the error of the Marcionites as no less ridiculous than impious: if someone was about to die before he was baptized, they used to place someone on his bed who, when asked whether he wished to be baptized, answered on behalf of the dead man, and at the same time he was baptized. But it is not credible that the Apostle would have passed over in silence so foul and so absurd a profanation of baptism, when he rebuked far lighter faults most severely. For if another's faith saves no one, but "the just lives by his own faith," how much less will it profit anyone's salvation if someone else is baptized for him, or receives the mystical Supper on his behalf? Moreover, this conflicts with the agreement of all Holy Scripture, in which no holy rite is handed down for the dead, and nothing at all by which the salvation of the dead is provided for.

units.la: Alij à fine baptismi argumentum duci exi-stimant, qui est, vt aduersus mortem remedij loco fit, eò quòd regenerationis symbolum continet, sine qua salus nobis constare non potest. His pro mor-tuis baptizari idem est, quod baptizari in resurrectionem à mortuis. Et hi ritus veteris memine-runt, quo de mortuorum resurrectione olim potissimum interrogati sint, qui baptizabantur. Sed nullis Scripturæ exemplis demonstrari potest, hoc primùs illis Ecclesiæ nascentis temporibus vsi-tatum fuisse, hîc autem de actione quadam peculiari agitur, quæ etsi in vsu fuerit, non tamen omni-bus communis erat, sicuti ex Pauli verbis diligentius inspectis deprehenditur, quæ certam quorun-dam baptismum denotant, in cuius forma & vsu nihil ille reprehendit.
units.tr: Others think the argument is drawn from the purpose of baptism, which is that it serves as a remedy against death, since it contains the symbol of regeneration, without which our salvation cannot stand. For them, to be baptized for the dead means the same as to be baptized unto the resurrection from the dead. They also recall the old custom by which those who were baptized were chiefly asked about the resurrection of the dead. But it cannot be shown from any example of Scripture that this practice was in use at the very beginning of the nascent Church; and here a certain peculiar action is under discussion, which, even if it was in use, was not common to all. This is clear from a closer look at Paul's words, which denote the baptism of certain persons, and in whose form and practice he finds no fault.

units.la: Quapropter mihi præ aliis eorum sententia probatur, qui eos notari existimant, qui cum Christi cognitione & fide imbuti essent, baptismum tamen vel metu vel aliis de causis dilulerant, donec morbo præuenti illum requirebant, & Ecclesiæ atque Christo tunc demum nomen dabant, ne absque publico salutis testimonio, quo credentes Dominus initiari voluit, ex hac vita emigrarent. Erat is pius affectus, & quamuis mora ista suis cunctatio reprehensionem mereretur, non tamen ab Ecclesiæ societate arceri aliquo iure poterant, qui vel sero tandem fidem in Christum prosi-teri instituebant.
units.tr: Therefore, among the other views, I approve the opinion of those who think that he is referring to those who, though instructed in the knowledge and faith of Christ, had nonetheless postponed baptism, whether from fear or for other reasons, until, overtaken by sickness, they sought it and only then gave their name to the Church and to Christ, so that they would not depart from this life without the public testimony of salvation, by which the Lord willed believers to be initiated. This was a pious feeling, and although such delay and hesitation deserved reproof, still those who at last, even late, began to profess faith in Christ could not by any right be shut out from the fellowship of the Church.

units.la: Scimus quidem posteris temporibus eorum superstitionem exortam fuisse, qui baptismum ad horam mortis vsque consulto differebant, nepost illum acceptum rursus peccarent. Dicebantur hi Clinici, eò quòd in lectis decumbentes & iam morituri baptizarentur, eorum nimirum traditionibus decepti, qui post baptismum in peccatum relapsis veniam & remis-sionem negabant. Et erat quidem istorum superstitio inexcusabilis, cùm & gratiam Dei in dubium vocaret, & merito Christi derogaret, adhæc desperandi occasionem ijs præberet, qui pijs consolationibus erigi atque confirmari debebant. At quid hoc ad id, quod Apostolorum tempore alijs de causis & absque superstitione vsitatum fuit? Etenim credibile est, multos sub mortis articulum ita animo suo coarctatos fuisse, vt quam hucusque dissimularant fidem in Christum, tunc profiterentur, & huius confirmandæ causa baptizari vellent.
units.tr: We know indeed that in later times a superstition arose among those who deliberately deferred baptism until the hour of death, so that they might not sin again after receiving it. These were called Clinics, because they were baptized while lying in bed and about to die, deceived no doubt by the traditions of those who denied pardon and forgiveness to those who had relapsed into sin after baptism. And indeed the superstition of these men was inexcusable, since it both called into doubt the grace of God and detracted from the merit of Christ, and besides gave an occasion of despair to those who ought to have been raised up and strengthened by pious consolations. But what has this to do with the practice that was in use in the time of the Apostles, for other reasons and without superstition? For it is credible that many, so distressed in mind at the approach of death, then professed the faith in Christ that they had hitherto concealed, and wished to be baptized in order to confirm it.

units.la: Exempla huius generis multa in Turcarum sacerdotibus edi aiunt, qui fere in Christianæ fidei confessione moriuntur, & iam morituri baptismum flagitant, multi quoque seipsos baptizant, quando nemo est qui hoc officium illis præstet. Tales autem olim pro mortuis baptizari dicebantur, quia cùm vita eorum desperata esset, pro mortuis potius quàm vivis censeri poterant: deinde, quòd baptismi fructu in morte demum perciperent, quo toto vitæ suæ curriculo hucusque caruerant. Ex ea igitur consuetudine Paulus argumentum ducit, quo eorum absurditate arguit, qui mortuorum resurrectionem negabant. Si (inquit) mortui omnino non excitantur, quid facient, qui iam morituri demum baptismum accipiunt? Hic sane illis quoad hanc vitam inutilis est, cùm mox hinc emigrent. Nisi autem aliquando resurgant, nec mortuis quidem ille profuerit. Quid ergo sequetur aliud, quàm illos inani ludo seipsos fatigare? Nam etsi quis dicat, non perire baptismi huius fructum, eò quòd ad animam pertingat, quæ immortalis est: nihil tamen dixerit. Paulus enim ex natura & dignitate Sacramentorum argumentatur, quæ salutis plenæ & perfectæ signilla sunt, & proinde non minus corpori quàm animæ seruiunt. Sunt enim symbola salutis in Christo exhibita, quem idò hominem verum factum esse constat, vt tam corporum quàm animarum redemptor atq; seruator fieret. Ita verò consuetudine & ex emplo proprio eos confutat Apostolus, qui resurrectionem ex mortuis vellicabant. Solet huius generis multa accidere ijs, qui fidei articulis siue principijs contradicunt. Ita qui hodie salutis spe in creaturis collocant, Deos inuocant, indulgentias Romanas pecunijs redimunt, sacra pro defunctis instituunt, ij omnes proprij oris testimonio confutantur, quando Apostolici symboli articulos nobiscum recitant, quibus se in vnum Deum credere profitentur, qui Filium suum pro nobis hominem fieri voluit, vt pro nostris peccatis in ara Crucis immolatus remissione peccatorum & vitam æternam nobis mereretur. Sed non mirum est, si seipsos ludibrio exponant, quicunque in cœlum expuere audent.
units.tr: They say that many examples of this kind occur among the priests of the Turks, who mostly die while confessing the Christian faith, and, being about to die, beg for baptism; many also baptize themselves when no one is at hand to perform this office for them. Such persons were formerly said to be baptized for the dead, because, since their life was despaired of, they could be counted among the dead rather than the living; and further, because they received the fruit of baptism only at death, of which they had been deprived throughout the whole course of their life. Paul therefore draws an argument from this custom, by which he proves the absurdity of those who denied the resurrection of the dead. "If," he says, "the dead do not rise at all, what will they do who, though about to die, receive baptism at last? It is certainly useless to them as far as this life goes, since they will soon depart hence. Unless they rise again at some time, it will not even profit the dead. What else, then, follows but that they weary themselves in an empty game?" For even if someone says that the fruit of this baptism does not perish, because it reaches the soul, which is immortal, he would say nothing. For Paul argues from the nature and dignity of the sacraments, which are signs of full and perfect salvation, and therefore serve the body no less than the soul. For they are symbols of the salvation exhibited in Christ, who, as is well known, became a true man so that he might be the redeemer and saviour of both bodies and souls. In this way the Apostle refutes, by custom and by their own example, those who were carping at the resurrection from the dead. Many such things usually happen to those who contradict the articles or principles of faith. Thus those who today place their hope of salvation in creatures, invoke gods, buy Roman indulgences with money, and institute rites for the dead, are all refuted by the testimony of their own mouths, when they recite with us the articles of the Apostles' Creed, in which they profess to believe in one God, who willed his Son to become man for us, so that, sacrificed for our sins on the altar of the Cross, he might win for us the forgiveness of sins and eternal life. But it is no wonder if those who dare to spit toward heaven expose themselves to mockery.

units.la: Cæterum admonet nos mos iste veteru, non temere negligi debere vsum Sacramentorum. Nam etsi salus nostra externis symbolis minimè alligata sit, & sine his seruari possunt, qui necessitate ab eorum vsu excluduntur, non tamen absq; scelere & manifesto salutis periculo negligi possunt à nobis, si eorum vsus liber nobis concedatur. Nec enim temere à Christo dictum est: Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, seruabitur. Itë: Hoc facite in mei commemorationem. Nec ignotum est, quàm ca seueritate olim vetera mandauerit Deus, qui mortis supplicium ijs constituit, qui vel Circumcisionem con-tempsiffent, vel sabbatum violassent, vel ignem alienum intulissent ad sacrificium, aut quodcunque aliud fecissent praeter ritus ab ipso praescriptos. Adde his exempla primitiuae et apostolicae ecclesiae, in qua Apostoli absque omni mora baptizandos esse censuerunt, quos fidem in Christum[?] amplexos esse et salutis desiderio ardere videbant: quales Hierosolymitani fuerunt, qui ad primam Pentecostes concionem conuersi sunt, Eunuchus item Aethiops, Cornelij familia et alij, quorum mentio fit in Actis. Seruit hoc confutandis Anabaptistis, qui paruulos baptizari nolunt, quia fidem in Christum nondum profiteantur: non autem obseruant, eosdem a Christo in credentium numero censeri, et hunc mandasse, ut ad se adducantur: denique quod foedere Dei comprehensi, a populi Dei fecie-tate[?] reijci non possunt, nisi illud violare, aut saltem angustioribus finibus, quam ipse velit, circum-scribere libeat. Eadem est Cœnæ Dominicæ ratio, quam minime intermittere decet eos, quibus eius vsus liber et tutus obtigit. Si qui enim hic negligentiores sunt, ne illi non satis digne æstimant mortis Christi beneficium, in cuius memoriam illa instituta est. Peccant ergo non parum, qui papistica superstitione adhuc detenti sufficere putant, si semel in anno sub festum Paschatis communicent: quasi vero semel tantum pro redemptione nobis per Christum facta gratiæ agi debeant. At ijdem iam morituri Cœnam sibi priuatim administrari volunt, quam cum valetudine integra frequentarent, cum alijs publice sumere noluerunt.
units.tr: Moreover, this ancient custom reminds us that the use of the Sacraments should not be carelessly neglected. For although our salvation is not tied to outward signs, and those who are excluded from their use by necessity can be saved without them, yet we cannot neglect them without sin and manifest danger to our salvation when their use is freely offered to us. Christ did not speak carelessly when He said: "Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved." Likewise: "Do this in remembrance of me." Nor is it unknown how severely God in former times commanded that those who despised circumcision, broke the Sabbath, or offered strange fire in sacrifice, or did anything else apart from the rites He had prescribed, should be put to death. Add to these the examples of the primitive and apostolic Church, in which the Apostles judged that those whom they saw embracing faith in Christ and burning with desire for salvation should be baptized without any delay. Such were the men of Jerusalem who were converted at the first sermon of Pentecost, also the Ethiopian eunuch, the household of Cornelius, and others mentioned in the Acts. This serves to refute the Anabaptists, who do not want infants baptized because they do not yet profess faith in Christ. They do not observe that these same infants are counted by Christ among believers, and that He commanded that they be brought to Him; and finally, that being included in the covenant of God, they cannot be cast out from the fellowship of God's people unless one chooses to break that covenant or, at least, to limit it within narrower bounds than He Himself wills. The same reasoning applies to the Lord's Supper, which those to whom its use is free and safe should by no means neglect. If some are rather careless about it here, they do not sufficiently value the benefit of Christ's death, in remembrance of which it was instituted. Therefore those do not sin lightly who, still held by Papist superstition, think it enough to communicate once a year at the feast of Easter, as if thanks should be given for the redemption made for us through Christ only once. And yet these same people, when about to die, want the Supper administered to them privately, though when in good health they were unwilling to receive it publicly with others.

units.la: Sed in Pauli verbis pergamus, qui alterum absurdum ab Apostolorum aliorumque feruoris Christi exemplo adduxit, quorum labores omnes pereant & pericula sint superuacanea, si refurre-ctionis spes e medio tollatur. Et cur nos periclitamur (inquit) omni hora, si scilicet mortui non resurgunt? Conuenit hoc cum eo, quod supra dixit perijsse omnes, quotquot in Christo obdormierunt, si nulla sperari debeat resurrectio ex mortuis. Est autem hoc non absurdum modo, verumetiam dictu & cogitatu durissimum. Quis enim de re Christiana honorifice sentire dicat eos, qui huius do-ctores Apostolos, & eiusdem familiarissimos atque grauissimos testes, sese præter omnem rationem & abs retributionis spe tantum laboribus atque periculis obiecisse dicunt? At quæ causa iusta & grauis adduci, quæ retributionis spes monstrari poterit, si nulla sit mortuorū resurrectio? Nam si quis animam seruari dicat, mox respondebitur: Atqui retributio illa manca & imperfecta, imo ex par-te iniqua fuerit, cum maior laborum pars ad corpus pertineat, quod illi ab omni remuneratione spe excluduntur. Ita ergo non Apostoli modo & sancti Martyres suo honore spoliabuntur, verumetiam Dei iustitia periclitabitur.
units.tr: But let us go on with the words of Paul, who adduced a second absurdity from the example of the Apostles and others who were zealous for Christ, whose labours would all perish and whose dangers would be pointless if the hope of the resurrection were removed. "And why do we face danger every hour" (he says), "if indeed the dead do not rise?" This agrees with what he said above, that all who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished, if no hope of resurrection from the dead should be held out. Yet this is not only absurd but, even to say or think, most harsh. For who would say, with any respect for the Christian religion, that those who were teachers of this religion, the Apostles and its most intimate and most serious witnesses, exposed themselves to labours and dangers beyond all reason, with no hope of reward? But what just and weighty cause can be advanced, what hope of reward can be shown, if there is no resurrection of the dead? For if someone should say that the soul is saved, it will at once be answered: that reward would be incomplete and imperfect, indeed in part unjust, since the greater part of the labours belongs to the body, which would be excluded from every hope of recompense. So then not only the Apostles and holy martyrs would be robbed of their honour, but the justice of God itself would be put in jeopardy.

units.la: Ne tamen Paulus in aliorum modo persona loqui putetur, ipse ignauus & otiosus spectator, & extra omnem teli iactum constitutus, hoc ipsum exemplo proprio illustrat & confirmat: Indies morior per gloriationem nostram. Iusiurandum interponit, quia causa grauis erat, ex qua Dei gloria simul & salus nostra omnis dependet. Iurat autem per gloriationem communem Christianorū, quam habet in IESV CHRISTO, quem in cælis ad dexteram Patris regnare, & nouissimo die ad iudicium venturum esse sciunt, vt tam corporibus quam animabus eorum, qui in ipsum crediderunt, digna fidei & pietatis præmia retribuat. Nec aliud intelligi debere per gloriationem illam ex alijs locis constat, quibus idem Paulus se nihil quam IESVM CHRISTVM nouit, se testatur, & insuper addit: Absit, vt glorier præterquam in cruce IESV CHRISTI, &c. A cruce autem & morte eius resurrectionem minime separari debere, notius est quam vt demonstrari debeat. Prudenter autem & graviter per hoc ipsum iurat, de quo controuertebatur, vt ostendat, quam hoc illi certum atque persuasum sit. Quid vero iurat? Indies morior, id est, periculis indies nouis & ipsa morte grauioribus exerceor. Et licebat ei hoc dicere, cum eius labores omnibus noti essent, adeo vt ne hostes quidem & æmuli illos possent negare.
units.tr: Yet lest Paul be thought to be speaking only in the person of others, while he himself is an idle and lazy spectator, placed beyond the reach of any missile, he illustrates and confirms this very point by his own example: "I die daily through our boasting." He adds an oath, because the matter was weighty, and on it depends both the glory of God and all our salvation. He swears by the boasting common to Christians, which they have in Jesus Christ, whom they know reigns in heaven at the right hand of the Father and will come to judgement on the last day, so as to render worthy rewards of faith and piety to the bodies and souls alike of those who believed in Him. Nor is it clear from other passages that this boasting ought to be understood otherwise, where Paul likewise testifies that he knows nothing but Jesus Christ, and adds: "God forbid that I should glory, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ," and so on. That the resurrection should by no means be separated from His cross and death is more widely known than needs to be demonstrated.
