Moreover, he swears wisely and seriously by that very thing about which the dispute was, in order to show how certain and persuaded he is of it. And what does he swear? "I die daily," that is, I am exercised daily by new dangers, more grievous even than death itself. He could say this, since his labours were known to all, so that not even his enemies and rivals could deny them.

units.la: Porrò ex multis exemplum subijcit cumprimis memorabile, quod non ita pridem Ephesi acci-derat, vnde epistolam hanc misit. Si (inquit) secundum hominem, id est, non alia grauiori aut sublimiori causa quam humano affectu, vt pote ambitione aut temeritate confidentiori abreptus, aduersus bestias pugnaui Ephesi, quæ mihi vtilitas, si mortui non excitantur? Exponit hoc quidam de hostibus, quos Ephesi grauissimos & truculentissimos habuit, à quibus seditionem publicam aduersus illum authore Demetrio aurifabro excitatam fuisse, Lucas in Actis scribit. Et hos bestias dici putant propter indomitum furorem, quo in illum ferebantur. Mouet eos ad hanc sententiam amplectendum, quòd nullius historiæ Lucas meminerit, ad quam hæc verba, si proprie accipiatur, possint referri. Atqui idem ne eorum quidem mentionem facit, quæ in posteriori epistola Cap. 11. & 12. habentur. Nec enim omnia singillatim describere voluit Lucas, cui satis fuit eorum seriem contexere, quæ ad Euangelij longe lateque per orbem propagati historiam pertinebant. Et si Lucæ tale quid narranti crederent, cur non potius Paulo ipsi fides habeatur hoc de se dicenti? Etenim non credibile est, illum labores suos & pericula locutionibus figuratis amplificare voluisse apud eos, quos iniquius de se sentire, & omnes calumniandi occasiones avidè venari non ignorabat. Ego igitur hæc ab illo vere & germano sensu dici existimo, cum de periculo loquatur, quo ipse potissimum petitus sit, quale nihil illum passum esse in seditione per Demetrium excitata, ex historia satis apparet. Nam à discipulis simul atque Asiæ primatibus prohibitus fuit, ne se furentis populi manibus obijceret. Fuit autem vulgare illo sæculo, ut qui mortem meruisse videbantur, vel nudi bestijs obijcerentur mox ab his laniandi (quod D. Ignatio & alijs Martyribus accidisse scimus) vel armati cum bestijs pugnare cogerentur, ut populo spectaculum exhiberent: & hos solebat bestiarios dicere. Erat hus[?] quidem spes aliqua vitæ propositá, si vincerent, ea tamen pauci potiebantur, eò quòd bestijs devictis novæ succederent, cum quibus pugnam instaurare oportebat. Fuit ergo hoc genus supplicij cum aperto vitæ discrimine simul & infamia coniunctum. At quæ mihi ex eo utilitas (inquit Paulus) si resurrectio nihil præter inane figmentum est? Aut quis me vel quenquam alium humano affectu rapi putet ad ea, ex quibus neque commodum neque gloria aliqua potest sperari? Ita verò exemplo proprio doctrinam suam confirmat, quod imprimis facto opus est. Nihil enim ad persuadendum efficacius est, quàm si exemplum in doctore aut monitore suo homines sibi propositum esse videant.
units.tr: Furthermore, he adds from many examples one especially memorable, which had happened not long before at Ephesus, from where he sent this letter. "If," he says, "according to man, that is, not for any weightier or higher cause than human feeling, such as ambition or a rash and bold temper carried me away, I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what good is it to me if the dead are not raised?" Some explain this of the enemies whom he had at Ephesus, very serious and savage men, by whom, as Luke writes in the Acts, a public uproar was stirred against him, under the leadership of Demetrius the silversmith. And some think these men are called beasts because of their untamed fury with which they rushed upon him. They are moved to adopt this opinion because Luke makes no mention of any history to which these words, if taken literally, could refer. Yet the same Luke does not mention the things that are found in the second letter, chapters 11 and 12, either. For Luke did not wish to describe everything one by one; it was enough for him to set out the sequence of events that pertained to the history of the Gospel spreading far and wide through the world. And if they believe Luke when he relates such a thing, why not rather trust Paul himself, who says this about himself? For it is not credible that he wished to magnify his labours and dangers by figurative expressions before those whom he knew to judge him unfairly and to eagerly hunt for every occasion to slander him. I therefore think these words are spoken by him in their true and genuine sense, since he speaks of the danger in which he was especially sought out, and it is clear enough from history that he suffered nothing of the kind in the uproar stirred up by Demetrius. For he was forbidden by the disciples, as well as by the leading men of Asia, to throw himself into the hands of the raging people. It was, moreover, a common practice in that age that those who seemed to have deserved death were either thrown naked to beasts to be torn apart at once (as we know happened to Ignatius and other martyrs), or were forced to fight armed against beasts, to provide a spectacle for the people; and such men were usually called beast-fighters. There was indeed some hope of life set before them, if they conquered; yet few obtained it, because when the beasts were overcome, new ones came on, with whom the fight had to be renewed. This kind of punishment was therefore joined with an open peril to life and with infamy. "What good is it to me, then" (says Paul), "if the resurrection is nothing but an empty fiction? Or who would think that I, or anyone else, am carried by human feeling to things from which neither profit nor any glory can be hoped for?" In this way he confirms his teaching by his own example, which is above all necessary. For nothing is more effective in persuading than when people see an example set before them in their teacher or adviser.

units.la: Interim obseruare debemus hoc loco indignam in hoc mundo piorum sortem. Quod enim Pau-lo accidit, quem ad dirum & triste hoc supplicij genus Deus passus est abripi, id commune & vulgare fuit tunc temporis, ut videre est in Tertulliani Apologetico: & hodie si non eadem, non tamen hoc mitiora exempla edunt. Nec temere ab Apostolo nostro dictum est, omnes eos persecutionem pati, qui in Christo piè viuere instituunt. Neminem ergo offendat nostri sæculi ingratitu-do & crudelitas. Cui enim parceret mundus hic, qui ne Christo quidè[?], æterno Dei Filio, pepercit? Quoad autem veterum Martyrum supplicia, meminerimus illa totidem argumenta esse, quibus suam de salute æterna fidem atque doctrinam confirmauerunt. Non poterit ergo ea negari, nisi simul illos extremæ stultitiæ & vanitatis accusare libeat. Quòd si verò nobis aliquid simile ferendum sit, non graue nobis videatur tam sancto & gloriosō veterum Christi sodalitio accenseri. Soletur autem nos, quòd Deus facilè, si velit, suos poterit ex tentatione eripere. Sin verò nolit, non est quod quiritentur: quando semel emensi huius vitæ curriculum, ad cœlestes sedes colliguntur, in quibus animæ viuunt & gaudent, dum corpora spe lætæ resurrectionis ab omni labore suo quiescunt. Qui verò ipsos persequuntur, ijdem Dei quoque hostes sunt, & olim ad æternos cruciatus detrudentur cum principe suo diabolo, cui nunc seruiunt.
units.tr: Meanwhile we ought to observe here the unworthy lot of the godly in this world. For what happened to Paul, whom God allowed to be dragged off to this dreadful and miserable kind of punishment, was common and ordinary at that time, as may be seen in Tertullian's Apology. Even today, if the examples are not the same, they are no milder. Nor did our Apostle speak carelessly when he said that all who resolve to live godly lives in Christ suffer persecution. Let no one, then, be shocked by the ingratitude and cruelty of our own age. For why should this world spare us, when it did not spare Christ himself, the eternal Son of God? As for the punishments of the early martyrs, let us remember that they are as many proofs by which they confirmed their faith and teaching concerning eternal salvation. Therefore these cannot be denied, unless one is willing at the same time to accuse those men of the utmost folly and vanity. But if we ourselves must bear something similar, let it not seem a burden to us to be counted among the holy and glorious fellowship of Christ's men of old. Yet this consoles us: God can easily, if he wishes, snatch his people out of temptation. But if he does not wish it, there is no reason for them to complain, since, once they have run the course of this life, they are gathered to the heavenly seats, where their souls live and rejoice, while their bodies rest from all their labour in the hope of a joyful resurrection. As for those who persecute them, they are also enemies of God, and in time they will be thrust down to eternal torments with their prince, the devil, whom they now serve.

units.la: Sed ex eo, quod dixit, tertium absurdum colligit Paulus: nimirum sublata spe resurrectionis, non modo piorum patientiam & constantiam damnari, verumetiam mundo & carni deditis fenestram, siue ostium potius, ad omnem licentiam & nequitiam aperiri. Id verò per Mimesim enuntiat, Epicuræorum verbis vtens, quibus hi admonitiones sobriorum & temperantiæ præcepta eludunt, dicentes: Edamus & bibamus, cras enim morimur. Itaque verborum istorum sensus est: Si nulla nobis est resurrectionis spes, quid obstat, quo minus ventri & gulæ dediti, Epicuræos illos imitemur, qui quòd se morituros esse sciunt, futuræ autem vitæ spe nulla habent, omnem tempus sibi perijsse arbitrantur, quod voluptatibus fœdis non impenditur? Tales apud Isaiam Cap.22. describuntur: Vocauit Dominus Deus exercituum in illa die ad fletum & planctum, ad calluitium & ad cinctura[?] sacci: & en[?] lætitia & gaudiu, cædendo boues, mactando oues, edendo carnes & bibendo vi nu[?],edere, bibere, cras enim moriemur. Ad quæ verba in præsenti Paulus alludit: & prudenter quidem, quando inter gentes omnibus sæculis plurimi fuerunt, qui idè sentirent & dicerent. Ægyptij certè in conuiuia hominis dudum mortui cranium inferre solebant, ut eo visu fortis suæ mortalis recordarentur, eoq; studiosius genio indulgerent, ne quod tempus ipsis inutiliter periret. Etm.[?] ta est Sardanapali, vltimi Assyriorum regis, historia, cuius hoc Epitaphium apud Strabonem legitur: Sardanapalus, Anacyndaraxis filius, Anchiadem[?] & Tarsum vna die condidit: Et in hospes ede, bibe, lude.
units.tr: But from what he has said, Paul draws a third absurdity: namely, if the hope of resurrection is taken away, not only is the patience and constancy of the godly condemned, but a window, or rather a door, is opened to all licence and wickedness for those given over to the world and the flesh. He expresses this by way of mimesis, using the words of the Epicureans, by which they mock the admonitions of sober men and the precepts of temperance, saying: "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die." So the sense of these words is this: If we have no hope of resurrection, what prevents us from giving ourselves to the belly and the throat and imitating those Epicureans who, knowing that they must die and having no hope of a future life, think that all the time is lost which is not spent on base pleasures? Such people are described in Isaiah 22: "In that day the Lord God of hosts called to weeping and mourning, to baldness and to girding with sackcloth; and behold joy and gladness, slaying oxen, killing sheep, eating flesh and drinking wine: 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.'" Paul alludes to these words in the present passage, and wisely so, since among the nations in every age there have been many who thought and said the same. The Egyptians, certainly, used to bring the skull of a man long dead into their banquets, so that by this sight they would remember their own mortality and therefore indulge the spirit more eagerly, lest any time should be wasted unprofitably. Such too is the story of Sardanapalus, the last king of the Assyrians, whose epitaph is read in Strabo: "Sardanapalus, son of Anacyndaraxes, founded Anchialus and Tarsus in one day. Stranger, eat, drink, play."

units.la: Item:
units.tr: Likewise:

units.la: Cùm te mortalem noris, præsentibus exple Delitijs animum, post mortem nulla voluptas. Namque ego sum pulvis, qui nuper tanta tenebam: Hæc habeo quæ edi, quæque exaturata libido Hausit: at illa manent multa & præclara relicta. Hoc sapiens vitæ mortalibus est documentum.
units.tr: Since you know you are mortal, fill your spirit with the delights present to you; after death there is no pleasure. For I am dust, who lately held so much: I have these things, which I have eaten, and which unbounded desire has swallowed; but those many and splendid things I left behind remain. This is the lesson of life that the wise give to mortals.

units.la: Apparet in istis horribilis naturæ & ingenij humani corruptio. Quotquot communi sensu ad huc integro utuntur, ij mortis consideratione ita fere terreri solent, ut huius sæculi delitijs non multùm moveantur, & mordaci quadam cura atque sollicitudine seipsos discruciént. Ideò sapientissi-mus ille mortalium Solomon dicebat: Melius est adire domum funeris, quàm domum conuiuij. Illic enim cernitur finis omnium hominum, & viuentes id reponit in corde suo. Et alter ille sapiens: In omnibus factis tuis memento finis, & in æternum non peccabis. At ea est multorum peruersitas, ut ideo sibi quidvis licere putent, quod mortales sint, mortis vero horam ignorent. Et hi sunt illusores illi, quos nouissimis temporibus exorituros esse Petrus olim prædixit, & quorum vestigia hodie passim audiuntur: Et quis nouit quando nobis moriendum sit? quis ultimum mortalium sepulturus sit? aut quæ nam sit vitæ futuræ conditio? Quin ergo præsenti fruimur, futuram tetri[?] cu[?] & curiosi[?] illis relinquentes, qui ne cælum ruat, metuunt, &c. Sed ijdem meminerint ad se imprimis pertinere, quod sui[?] sæculi illusoribus Isaias in loco supra citato respondet: Reuelatum est hoc in auribus Domini exercituum, non expietur vobis hæc iniquitas, donec moriamini, dicit Dominus Deus exercituum. Quibus adde, quæ in Apostolicis & euangelicis scripturis de repentino & improuiso Christi ad iudicium aduentu dicuntur. Matth.24.1. Thess.5.2. Petr.3.
units.tr: In these words there appears the corruption of a horrible nature and of human understanding. Whoever still uses sound common sense is usually so terrified by the thought of death that he is not much moved by the delights of this age, and he tortures himself with a biting care and anxiety. Therefore that wisest of mortals, Solomon, said: "It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting; for there is the end of all men, and the living lays it to his heart." And that other wise man: "In all your deeds remember the end, and you will never sin." But such is the perversity of many that they think they may do whatever they like because they are mortal, yet they do not know the hour of death. These are the mockers whom Peter long ago foretold would arise in the last times, and whose footsteps are heard everywhere today: "And who knows when we must die? Who will bury the last of mortals? Or what is the condition of the future life? Why not then enjoy the present, leaving the future to those gloomy and curious men who fear that the sky will fall," and so on. But let these men remember that what Isaiah answers in the passage cited above to the mockers of his own age pertains chiefly to them: "This has been revealed in the ears of the Lord of hosts: this iniquity will not be atoned for you until you die, says the Lord God of hosts." To these add what is said in the apostolic and evangelical Scriptures about the sudden and unexpected coming of Christ to judgement: Matthew 24; 1 Thessalonians 5; 1 Peter 3.

units.la: Ideo grauem admonitionem Paulus hoc loco subijcit: Ne errate. Id est, ne fallatis vosipsos, neque locum dei[?] eiusmodi illusorum sermonibus. Et mox causam adducit: Mores boni commercia corrumpunt mala. Est hic Senarius Iambicus, quem plerique Menandri esse tradunt, at Socrates Ecclesiasticæ historiæ scriptor illum Euripidi tribuit. Voluit autem eo ut Paulus, cum similia multa ex sacris literis proferre posset, partim quia verissimè hoc dictum est, partim quia Corinthijs id non ignotum esse poterat, qui in theatris hæc & alia huius generis non raro audiebant. Et licet interdum exterorum exemplis aut testimonijs uti, si ita res ferat. Semper enim sibi constat veritas, per quemcunq; prædicetur: & multa Deus gentium cordibus inscripsit, quæ poëtæ & philosophi illustrarunt, ne prorsus exleges indomitum furerent. Proderat etiam Corinthiorum negligentiam argui, qui in re tam graui tamq; seria scurrilibus hominum leuissimorum dictis locum dabant, quæ in quotidiana vitæ consuetudine vitanda & explodenda esse, poëta docet.
units.tr: Therefore Paul adds here a serious warning: "Do not be deceived." That is, do not deceive yourselves, nor give a place to such mockers' talk. And he soon adds the reason: "Evil company corrupts good morals." This is an iambic senarius, which most attribute to Menander, but Socrates, the writer of the Ecclesiastical History, assigns it to Euripides. Paul chose to use it, although he could have brought forward many similar things from the sacred letters, partly because it is most truly said, and partly because it could not be unknown to the Corinthians, who often heard such sayings and others of this kind in the theatres. And it is sometimes permitted to use the examples or testimonies of outsiders, if the matter so requires. For truth always agrees with itself, by whomever it is proclaimed; and God has written many things on the hearts of the nations, which poets and philosophers have made clear, so that they might not rage utterly lawless and unrestrained. It was also useful to rebuke the carelessness of the Corinthians, who in a matter so grave and serious gave a place to the scurrilous words of the most frivolous men, which the poet teaches must be avoided and rejected in ordinary daily life.

units.la: Et sane debet hæc admonitio ad omnes sermones & omnia commercia extendi. Quod enim in [?]Resurrectionis articulo fit, hoc ipsum in omnibus aliis solet fieri. Cuius mali causa est, quod animus noster originali & hereditaria vitiositate corruptus facile accenditur, ut desideria illicita & cogitationes malas concipiat. Et ut sermo animi nostri index est, ita in aliorum quoque animos efficacissimè penetrat, ut eo ad malum excitentur. Exempla eius rei quotidie occurrunt in iracundis, qui uno verbulo irritati fulminant & cælum terræ miscere conantur: in libidinosis, qui dicto aut cantu lasciuiori accensi turpissima designant. Ideo scriptura nō uno loco iubent, ut oris nostro claustrum, linguæ autem frænum iniiciamus, ne temere cum aliorum offensione vagetur: & grauissima est Christi admonitio, qui nos de quouis verbo otioso olim rationem redditurus[?] ait. Cuius vtinam diligentius meminissent, qui nulla vel Dei vel auditorum ratione habita, quicquid in buccam venit, temere effutiunt. Quorum licentia cùm maior sit, quàm ut facile coërceri possit, discant saltem pij[?] à talium commercijs sibi cauere, & si id non omnino licet, aures saltem obturare, ne quid boni moribus inimicum, aut à pietate alienum, per has in animos usque descendat.
units.tr: And indeed this warning ought to be extended to all conversation and all dealings. For what happens in the article of the resurrection happens in fact in all other matters as well. The cause of this evil is that our mind, corrupted by original and hereditary vice, is easily inflamed so as to conceive illicit desires and wicked thoughts. And as speech is the index of our mind, so it penetrates most effectively into the minds of others, so that they too are stirred to evil. Examples of this occur every day among the angry, who, provoked by a single little word, thunder and try to turn heaven and earth upside down; among the lustful, who, kindled by a wanton word or song, devise the most shameful things. Therefore the Scriptures in more than one place command us to set a guard over our mouth and a bridle on our tongue, lest it wander rashly to the offence of others; and Christ's warning is most serious, who said that we shall one day give account of every idle word. I wish they had remembered this more carefully, those who, without any regard either for God or for their hearers, rashly pour out whatever comes into their mouth. Since their licence is too great to be easily restrained, let the godly at least learn to guard themselves against the company of such men, and if this cannot be done altogether, at least to stop their ears, lest anything hostile to good morals, or foreign to piety, should pass through these channels down into their minds.

units.la: Facit autem ad breuis huius admonitionis confirmationem quod sequitur: Euigilate iuste, ne peccate. In Graeco est ἐκνήφειν[?], quod proprie dicitur de ebrijs, vbi crapulam edormierunt. Conueniebat autem Metaphora haec probe ijs, qui nimium socordes & somnolenti scurrarum impiorum dicterijs se inebriari patiebantur, ut ipsi quoque sui ingenij vires in eo obtentarent, si eluderent mirificè, quae de mortuorum resurrectione & fine mundi dicuntur. Hortatur ergo, ut tandem excusso hoc tam pestilenti veterno, iuste euigilent, id est, ita, ut non in malo solertes & acuti sint, sed in ijs ingenij vires exerceant, quae professionem Christianam decent, & ad mutuam in fide aedificationem faciunt. Et ne hoc frustra monere putetur, addit: Quidam enim Deum non norunt: Ad pudorem vobis, vel ad vestri confusionem loquor. Quasi diceret: Vos quidem vobis hominum sapientissimi & acutissimi videmini, quando argumenta eiusmodi disputationis ergo profertis: sed reuera extremam stultitiam proditis, & quod ne eam quidem Dei cognitionem assecuti sitis, quam vulgares Christiani habere debebant: imo prima adhuc rudimenta religionis Christianae ignoratis. Id vero dico, ut vos pudore suffundam, & ut in posterum modestius & religiosius sapere discatis. Ita ergo etiam hodie eos tractare oportet, qui cum sublimium mysteriorum cognitionem sibi vendicent, de ijsdem audacius disputando ita hallucinantur, ut ad principia religionis turpissimè offendant. Si enim Christus Cleopam & comitem huius stultos dixit, qui bono & pio zelo tirea ipsius resurrectionem haesitabant, quid non merentur audire, qui consultò ea inficiari audent, ex quibus salus nostra omnis dependet?
units.tr: Wake up righteously, and do not sin. The Greek is ἐκνήφειν [eknephein], a word properly used of drunkards who have slept off their drunkenness. This metaphor fitted well those who were too careless and drowsy, and who let themselves be intoxicated by the jokes of impious jesters, so that they wasted their own mental powers in mocking what is said about the resurrection of the dead and the end of the world. He urges them, therefore, to shake off at last this pestilent lethargy and to wake up righteously. That is, they should not be clever and sharp in evil, but should exercise their mental powers on things that befit the Christian profession and build up one another in the faith. Lest this warning seem to be given in vain, he adds: For some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame, or to your confusion. As if he said: You seem to yourselves the wisest and sharpest of men when you bring forward arguments of this kind for disputation. But in truth you show extreme folly, and you have not even attained that knowledge of God which ordinary Christians ought to have; indeed you do not yet know the first rudiments of the Christian religion. I say this so that I may make you blush, and so that in future you may learn to think more modestly and piously. So too today we ought to deal with those who, while claiming for themselves the knowledge of lofty mysteries, dispute about them so boldly that they go astray and stumble most shamefully over the first principles of religion. For if Christ called Cleophas and his companion foolish, who with a good and pious zeal doubted his resurrection, what do they not deserve to hear who dare deliberately to deny those things on which our whole salvation depends?

units.la: Simul autem admonemur hoc loco, veri Dei ignorantiam, causam esse eius incredulitatis, qua mortuorum resurrectio negatur. Nam qui Deum vere noverunt, ij eius voluntatem, iustitiam & omnipotentiam ignorare non possunt. Atqui tria haec in articulo isto concurrunt. Et voluntatem quidem suam iam olim in Verbo suo expressit, quo se mortuorum quoque Deum esse testatur, & ijsdem resurrectionem pollicetur. Loca Scripturae nunc citare non opus est, cum hanc legentibus passim occurrant. Prae aliis tamen illustria & indubia sunt, quae extant Psal.16. Isa.25. Ezech.37. Daniel.12. Ioan.5. Matth.24. & 25. Ac voluntatis huius fundamentum est iustitia, quae retributionem tam bonu quam malis dispensat. At haec in praesenti saeculo aut nulla aut rarissima est, quod optimorum etiam querelae testantur. Ergo in altero saeculo fiat oportet, & ut eadem perfecta & aequa sit, corpora quoque excitari necesse est, quae nobis tam ad pietatis officia, quam ad scelera feruerunt. Cum ergo velit simul & debeat Deus nos in vitam restituere, non aliud restat, quam ut hoc illum posse intelligamus. Atqui Dominus exercituum & omnipotens est, qui omnipotentiam suam iam inde a prima rerum origine factis & operibus innumeris declarauit. Nam solius Verbi sui virtute universam hanc mundi fabricam ex nihilo produxit, & de illo verissimè illud canitur: Deus noster in coelo est, omnia quae voluit, fecit. Poterit ergo idem ille cadavera in pulveres & cineres conversa nobis reddere, & ijsdem vitam quoque restituere. De quo neminem pium & cordatum dubitare patiuntur, quae in rerum natura videmus, exempla. Ut enim à nobis ipsis incipiamus, annon foetus in matris utero animam vitalem hauriens, & suo tempore in hanc lucem prodiens, resurrectionis nostrae typus est evidentissimus? Nonne terra cum plantis suis hyberno tempore mortua, vere autem novo quasi reviviscens, eandem nobis adumbrat? Quid de frumenti grano dicemus, quod nisi terra mandatum emoriatur, fructum non feret? Sed & diem suis vicibus mori & viuere, id est, occidere & oriri videmus. Quae ergo dementia fuerit, homini, creatorum omnium principi, id negare, quod terrae, quod feminibus, quod omnibus prope inanimatis concessum est? Num his omnibus suo modo reviviscentibus, solus homo semel extinctus perpetua morte premetur? Certe, qui ita sentiunt, ij neque iustitiam neque omnipotentiam Dei agnoscunt: quod olim Christus quoque Sadducaeis exprobrauit. Hi denique veri illi Nabales sunt, qui si non ore semper, in cordibus tamen suis dicunt, Non est Deus. Itaque horum memores, confirmemur in fide IESV CHRISTI, qui ideo mortuus est & resurrexit, ut vivis & mortuis dominetur, & in se credentes servet quoad corpus & animam. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: At the same time we are reminded in this place that ignorance of the true God is the cause of that unbelief by which the resurrection of the dead is denied. For those who truly know God cannot be ignorant of his will, his justice and his omnipotence. Yet all three come together in this article. He has long since expressed his will in his Word, in which he testifies that he is also the God of the dead, and promises them the resurrection. It is not necessary now to cite passages of Scripture, since they occur everywhere to those who read it. Yet those that are found in Psalm 16, Isaiah 25, Ezekiel 37, Daniel 12, John 5, and Matthew 24 and 25 are especially clear and unquestionable. The foundation of this will is justice, which distributes reward to good and bad alike. But in the present age this justice is either non-existent or extremely rare, as even the complaints of the best men testify. Therefore it must take place in another age, and for it to be complete and equal, the bodies must also be raised, which have burned for us both in the duties of piety and in crimes. Since God therefore both wills and ought to restore us to life, nothing remains but that we understand that he is able to do this. Now the Lord of hosts is also omnipotent, and has declared his omnipotence from the very beginning of things by countless deeds and works. For by the power of his Word alone he brought this whole fabric of the world out of nothing, and of him that most truly is sung: "Our God is in heaven; whatever he has willed, he has done." He will therefore be able to restore to us the corpses that have been turned into dust and ashes, and to restore life to them as well. That nothing pious and sensible man can doubt this, the examples we see in nature compel us. For to begin with ourselves: does not the foetus in the mother's womb, drawing in the breath of life and at its time coming forth into this light, serve as a most evident type of our resurrection? Does not the earth, with its plants dead in winter and as it were coming back to life in the new spring, shadow forth the same thing to us? What shall we say of the grain of wheat, which, unless it is committed to the earth and dies, will not bear fruit? Moreover, we see the day die and live in its turns, that is, set and rise. What madness would it be, then, to deny to man, the prince of all creatures, what has been granted to the earth, to seeds, and to almost all inanimate things? If all these revive in their own way, will man alone, once extinguished, be held down by perpetual death? Certainly those who think this way acknowledge neither the justice nor the omnipotence of God, which Christ long ago also reproached the Sadducees for. Finally, they are those true Nabals who, if not always with their mouth, yet in their hearts say: "There is no God." Therefore, mindful of these men, let us be strengthened in the faith of Jesus Christ, who for this reason died and rose again, that he might rule over the living and the dead, and preserve in himself those who believe, both in body and soul. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: At dicet aliquis: Quomodo suscitantur mortui? quali autem corpore prodeunt? Demens, quod tu seminas, non viuiscit, nisi mortuum fuerit. Et quod seminas, non corpus nasciturum seminas, sed nudum granum, prout inciderit, tritici aut alicuius ex reliquis: Sed Deus ei dat corpus ut voluit, & singulis seminibus suum corpus.
units.tr: But someone will say: How are the dead raised? And with what kind of body do they come forth? Fool, what you sow is not made alive unless it dies. And what you sow is not the body that is to spring up, but a bare grain, as it may chance to fall, of wheat or of some other of the rest. But God gives it a body as he has willed, and to each seed its own body.

units.la: INter fidei Christianae articulos vix alius est, à quo humana ratio magis abhorreat, quàm in quo corporum nostrorum resurrectionem ex mortuis profitemur. Ut enim caro nostra mortem natura metuit & abominatur: ita aliquem ex ea in vitam restitui impossibile esse sibi persuadet. Ideo frequenter de illa Spiritus Sanctus in Scripturis disserit, & eandem Apostoli in suis concionibus atque scriptis prae aliis articulis urgent. Omnium vero diligentissimus in hac causa est Paulus hoc Cap. quo prolixè illis respondet, qui illam apud Corinthios negabant. Et hactenus qui dem argumentis solidissimis probauit, eam negari non posse, nisi omnia religionis Christianae principia convellere, & indomitae vel belluinae potius, scelerum licentiae fenestras aperire libeat. Quibus absolutis, nunc iis respondet, qui eam quaestionibus non minus impijs quam scurrilibus indu-bium vocabant.
units.tr: Among the articles of the Christian faith there is hardly any other from which human reason shrinks more than that in which we profess the resurrection of our bodies from the dead. For just as our flesh by nature fears and abhors death, so it persuades itself that it is impossible for anyone to be restored from it to life. Therefore the Holy Spirit often speaks of this in the Scriptures, and the apostles in their sermons and writings press it more than the other articles. But Paul is the most diligent of all in this matter in this chapter, in which he answers at length those who denied it among the Corinthians. And so far, indeed, he has proved by the most solid arguments that it cannot be denied unless one overturns all the principles of the Christian religion and opens the windows to the untamed, or rather bestial, licence of crimes. Having finished these, he now answers those who called it into doubt with questions no less impious than scurrilous.

units.la: Principio quaestiones illorum[?] ipse proponit, ne quid in causa tanti momenti dissimulare videatur. Est hoc candoris apostolici argumentum, qualia multa in illorum scriptis occurrunt. Qui auditores sive lectores fallere instituerunt, ij consulto non attingunt ea, quae sententiae suae adversari vident. At qui in docendo fideles & Veritatis amantes sunt, illa quoque studiose adducunt, & quàm infirma sint, aut quibus rationibus dilui sive confutari possint, demonstrant. Id ipsum ergo in praesenti Paulus observans ait: Quomodo suscitantur mortui? quali autem corpore prodeunt? Duas quaestiones coniungit: Alteram de resurrectionis modo: Alteram de corporum resuscitatorum qualitate aut conditione. Utramque ita proponunt impij & Epicurei illusores, ut simul ab impossibili evincere conentur, inane figmentum esse, quicquid de mortuorum resurrectione dicitur. Ad priorem pertinet, quod dicunt: Qui obsecro fieri potest, ut omnium eorum corpora, qui diversis lo-cis[?] generibus iam inde ab origine rerum absumpti sunt, & porro in fine saeculi usque tollentur, olim resurgat, et quidē ea corpora, quorum alia in terra defossa coputruerunt, alia in aquis perierunt, alia flammis in cineres redacta, alia a bestijs diversis discerpta et devorata sunt? Quis non videat quàm horribilis tumultus & inextricabilis rerum confusio oritura sit, si omnia corporis alicuius membra ad locum suum reverti debeant? Quod si vero quis Dei omnipotentiam opponat, cui hoc facile sit, & quàm negare nimis impudens est, mox ad alteram quaestionem transeunt: Dic ergo, si mortui omnino resurgent, qualia illorum corpora tunc erunt? Etenim in praesenti multum inter se differunt forma & habitu, alia aliis praestant, & alia aliis vitiosiora sunt: In morte autem ita defaedantur, ut non formam modo priorem, verumetiam membrorum usum amittant, imo ne ab amicis quidem facile agnoscantur. Adhaec aspectu & foetore nauseam movent: quae causa est, ut plerunque illico veste sepulchrali induantur occlusis prius illorum oculis, multi etiam jam morituri amicos & domesticos suos rogent, ne post mortem a quoquam videantur: quod de Cyro suo Xenophon annotavit. Quod si ergo haec ipsa corpora nobis restituuntur, qualia prius fuerunt, nec non multum est, quòd de resurrectione illorum aliquid gloriemur. Si alia, jam non erit corporum nostrorum resur-rectio, & stulti nimis sunt, qui ea praesentis saeculi commodis fraudant spe futurorum bonorum, quae illa nunquam percipient: adhaec qualia nam corpora illa futura sint, scire cupimus. Haec & alia huius generis olim Apostolis & Christianis omnibus a philosophis & impijs vitae futurae contempto-ribus objici solebant. Multi quoque, ut omnem resurrectionis spem everterent, Martyrum cineres dissipare, vel etiam in mare aut in profluentem abijcere solebant: Hodie etiam eiusmodi multa fi-unt & dicuntur a fidei nostrae adversarijs.
units.tr: First he himself puts forward their questions, so that he may not seem to be concealing anything in a matter of such great importance. This is a mark of apostolic candour, of which many examples occur in their writings. Those who have set out to deceive their hearers or readers deliberately avoid touching on those things which they see are opposed to their opinion. But those who are faithful in teaching and lovers of truth also bring forward those objections diligently, and demonstrate how weak they are, or by what arguments they can be dissolved or refuted. Paul, then, observing this very thing in the present case, says: How are the dead raised? And with what kind of body do they come forth? He joins two questions: one concerning the manner of the resurrection, the other concerning the quality or condition of the bodies raised. The impious and Epicurean mockers propose both in such a way that they try at the same time to prove from impossibility that whatever is said about the resurrection of the dead is an empty fiction. To the first belongs what they say: "I beg you, how can it come about that the bodies of all those who have been consumed in various ways from the beginning of things, and who will be lifted up at the end of the age, should rise again at some time? And indeed those bodies, of which some have rotted in the earth when buried, some have perished in the waters, some have been reduced to ashes by flames, and some have been torn apart and devoured by various beasts? Who does not see what a horrible tumult and inextricable confusion of things will arise if every member of a body must return to its own place?" But if someone should object the omnipotence of God, to whom this would be easy, and it is too shameless to deny this, they immediately pass on to the second question: "Tell us, then, if the dead will rise at all, what kind of bodies will they have then? For in the present life they differ greatly in form and appearance; some excel others, and some are more blemished than others. But in death they are so disfigured that they lose not only their former form but also the use of their limbs; indeed they are not easily recognised even by friends. Besides, they cause nausea by their sight and stench. This is why very often they are at once clothed in grave-clothes, after their eyes have first been closed; many, even when about to die, ask their friends and household not to be seen by anyone after death." Xenophon noted this of his Cyrus. Now if these very bodies are restored to us just as they were before, there is not much to boast about in the resurrection of them. If they are different, the resurrection of our bodies will no longer be the same, and they are too foolish who deprive themselves of the advantages of the present age for the hope of future goods, which they will never receive. Moreover, we want to know what kind of bodies those will be. These and other objections of this kind were once thrown at the apostles and all Christians by philosophers and impious despisers of the future life. Many also, in order to overturn all hope of resurrection, used to scatter the ashes of the martyrs, or even cast them into the sea or into a flowing river. Today, too, many things of this kind are done and said by the adversaries of our faith.

units.la: Caeterum ad utramque quaestionem graviter admodum Paulus respondet, Non autem vel Dei potentiam simpliciter allegat, vel Scripturae veteris oracula, nec etiam ad revelationes confugit, quas multas & eximias poterat adducere: quia cum illis ipsi res erat, qui haec omnia ludibrio habuissent. Itaque argumenta ex rerum natura profert, ut iflorum fluporem belluinum arguat, quibus id impossibile videbatur, cuius exempla viua quotidie in terra prouentu cernebat. Est autem hoc doctoris boni officium, ut non fideliter modo, verumetiam circumspectè & prudenter ea proferat in medium, quae maxime idonea sunt pro locorum & temporum ratione, siue auditorum captu. Hoc enim Christus praecipit, quando nos oeconomos confert fidis & prudentibus, qui familiae suae dimen-sum suum in tempore depromere debeant: quo Paulus quoque respiciens doctorem requirit, qui Verbum Dei recte secare norit. Nec enim satis est dixisse quod verum est, nisi idem hoc praesenti causa & auditorum aedificationi seruiat: ne nobis illud prouerbio in ineptos Oratores iactatum dici possit: Omnia quidem bene, sed quorsum istud tuum tam bene? Alioqui & illud Solomonis innos conueniet: Vt spina crescens in manu ebrij, sic parabola in ore stultorum. Proverb. 26.
units.tr: Paul answers both questions very gravely, yet he does not simply appeal to God's power, or to the oracles of the Old Testament, nor does he take refuge in revelations, though he could have cited many striking ones, because he was dealing with men who had treated all these things as a joke. So he brings forward arguments from the nature of things, to rebuke the brutish stupidity of those for whom this seemed impossible, when he saw living examples of it every day on earth. It is the duty of a good teacher to set forth what he says not only faithfully but also circumspectly and prudently, choosing what is most suitable to the circumstances of places and times and to the grasp of the hearers. Christ commands this when he calls us stewards who must be faithful and wise, to bring out their household's portion in due time; Paul, looking to this too, asks for a teacher who knows how to divide the word of God rightly. For it is not enough to say what is true, unless it also serves the present cause and the edification of the hearers, lest the proverb thrown at inept orators could be said of us: "All very well, but what is the point of your being so good?" Otherwise that saying of Solomon would fit us too: "As a thorn goes up into the hand of a drunkard, so is a parable in the mouth of fools." Proverbs 26.

units.la: Admonemur praeterea Pauli exemplo, omnium esse, ut quae in rerum natura fiunt, diligentius obseruent. Illic enim non solum quae corpori & vitae sustentandae seruiunt proponit Spiritus sanctus, verumetiam exempla, quibus fides nostra confirmetur, nosque simul officij in rebus agendis aut vitandis admoneamur. Nouit enim Deus quam tardi simus ad ea percipienda, quae in salutis negotio cognitu quam maxime necessaria sunt: quam item facile eorum obliuio nobis obrepat, sine quibus salus nobis non potest constare. Quae causa est, quod plerumque parabolarum, quibus nos erudit, argumenta ex rebus quotidianis & vulgo vsitatis sumit, ut quocunque oculos vertimus, ea nobis occurrant, quae nos indesinenter cogitare conuenit. Et hi sunt libri illi laicorum, quibus tuto & cum fructu uti possumus: non autem imagines, quas homines superstitiosi isto honore & titulo dignantur. Sed quia de his alibi, nunc Paulum ad quaestiones istas respondentem audiamus.
units.tr: We are also admonished by Paul's example to observe more carefully all that happens in the nature of things. There the Holy Spirit sets forth not only what serves the body and the sustaining of life, but also examples by which our faith is confirmed and by which we are reminded at the same time of our duty in what we should do or avoid. For God knows how slow we are to grasp those things which are most necessary to know in the business of salvation, and how easily the forgetting of those things creeps upon us without which our salvation cannot stand. This is why, in teaching us, he mostly takes the arguments of his parables from everyday and common things, so that wherever we turn our eyes, those things meet us which we ought to think about unceasingly. And these are those books of the laity which we can use safely and with profit, not the images which superstitious men honour with that dignity and title. But since we have dealt with these elsewhere, let us now hear Paul answering these questions.

units.la: Ad primam pertinet quod dicit: Demens, quod tu feminas, non viuiscit, nisi mortuum fuerit. Primo dementes aut stultos dicit eos, qui de corporum nostrorum resurrectione, ut re absurda & impossibili, quaerunt. Neq; ideo in Christi praeceptum peccasse putandus est, quo gehennae incendio digni pronuntiantur, qui fratres fatuos dixerint. Ibi enim de illis agitur, qui pravo odij affectu aut vindictae cupiditate abrepti fratres couitiantur. At Paulus hoc agit, ut eos ad meliorem mentem reducat, qui carnis prudentiam secuti mysteria tanta ad suae rationis calculum revocabant: & Christi exemplum imitatur, qui similiter stultos dixit Emmauntinos illos discipulos, quibus sua Resurrectio dubia videbatur. Monet ergo, ne suam stultitiam prodant, dum mortalium acutissimi videri volunt. Et quis non fatuos & dementes dixerit eos, qui neque Dei voluntatem, neque eius iustitiam, neq; omnipotentiam nouerunt, quae omnia in hac causa concurrere, nuper diximus? Quis item stupidissimos esse negauerit, qui in semetipsis non observant, quod in rerum natura quotidie occurrit?
units.tr: To the first question belongs what he says: "Fool, what you sow is not made alive unless it dies." First, he calls fools those who ask about the resurrection of our bodies as if it were an absurd and impossible thing. Nor should he be thought to have sinned against Christ's precept, by which those who call their brothers fools are pronounced worthy of the fire of hell. For there the concern is with those who, carried away by a wicked feeling of hatred or a desire for revenge, revile their brothers. But Paul does this so as to bring back to a better mind those who, following the wisdom of the flesh, reduced such great mysteries to the reckoning of their own reason; and he imitates the example of Christ, who likewise called the Emmaus disciples fools, for whom his own resurrection seemed doubtful. So he warns them not to betray their folly while they wish to seem the sharpest of mortals. And who would not call fools and madmen those who know neither God's will, nor his justice, nor his omnipotence, all of which, as we said recently, come together in this matter? Who again would deny that they are most stupid, who do not notice in themselves what happens every day in the nature of things?

units.la: Ideo in ipsos argumentum retorquet, & quia eis impossibile videtur, ut corpus mortuum & putrefactione iampridem resolutum reuiuiscat, sementis exemplo docet, morte & resolutione illa resurrectionem adeo non impediri, ut potius per illam adiuuetur & promoueatur. Argumentabatur illi ad hunc modum: Impossibile est ea corpora in vitam restitui & resurgere, quae iampridem mortua & putrefactione omnino resoluta sunt. Ergo nulla est mortuorum resurrectio. Inuertit hoc argumentum Paulus, & ideo resurrecturā dicit corpora nostra, quia moriantur & putrefiant. Est enim haec natura lex, ut corruptio generationem praecedat. In exemplum vero sementem adducit, in qua illud euidentissimè cernitur. Nec dubium est, illum ad Christi verba respexisse, qui de sua morte & resurrectione eiusq; fructu loquens, ait: Amen amen dico vobis, nisi granum frumenti proiectum in terram mortuum fuerit, ipsum solum manet: Si vero mortuum fuerit, multum fructum affert. Nec est quod aliquis excipiat, seminibus naturale germinandi vim inesse, qua cum corpora nostra destituantur, non posse de eis idem quod de illis dici. Nec enim nostra virtute resurgemus, sed Spiritus Christi virtute, qua hic excitatus est. Quod alibi his verbis Paulus enuntiat: Si Spiritus eius, qui excitauit IESVM à mortuis, habitat in vobis, is qui excitauit Christum ex mortuis, viuificabit & mortalia corpora vestra per inhabitantem eius Spiritum in vobis. Et ipse Christus yocùs[?] suæ meminit, ad cuius mandatum, qui in monumentis iacent, sint surrecturi. Quo pertinet, quod alibi de tuba Dei & voce Archangeli dicitur. Quibus adde, quòd qui feminibus vim illam generandi & germinandi insseuit, idem nostra quoque corpora resurgendi facultate donare potuit. Ideo Paulus argumentum illud in præsenti ita proponit, ut singula verba Emphasim habeant. Tu (inquit) quod feminas, &c. Quasi diceret: Tu, qui homo es peccator, mortalis, infirmus & nullis non casibus obnoxius, sementem facis, & quæ tu sulcis aut hortis mandas femina, viviſcunt, postquam emortua & corruptionem passa fuerint. Quæ ergo dementia fuerit, de corporum nostrorum resurrectione dubitare, quæ Deus ille omnipotens, immortalis & æternus seminat, & ea inter ram, unde primitus sumpta sunt, ea conditione vult reuerti, ut tandem ad vitam immortalem & nulli corruptioni obnoxiam resurgant? An ergo Dei sementem minor, quàm tuam, effectus sequetur? Et num quod tu seris, cum fœnore germinabit, quod autem Deus seminat, æterna morte sepultum iacebit? Hic verborum Apostoli sensus est.
units.tr: So he turns the argument back upon them. Because it seems impossible to them that a dead body, long since dissolved by putrefaction, should come back to life, he teaches by the example of seed that death and that dissolution do not hinder the resurrection at all, but rather help and advance it. They argued in this way: "It is impossible that those bodies should be restored to life and rise again which have long been dead and wholly dissolved by putrefaction. Therefore there is no resurrection of the dead." Paul inverts this argument and says that our bodies will rise precisely because they die and decay. For this is the law of nature, that corruption goes before generation. He brings in seed as an example, in which this is most plainly seen. And there is no doubt he had in mind the words of Christ, who, speaking of his death and resurrection and its fruit, says: "Amen, amen, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit." Nor should anyone object that seeds have a natural power to germinate, which our bodies lack, so that what is said of them cannot be said of us. For we shall rise not by our own power but by the power of the Spirit of Christ, by which he himself was raised. Paul states this elsewhere in these words: "If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you." And Christ himself recalls his voice, at whose command those who lie in the tombs shall rise. To this pertains what is said elsewhere of the trumpet of God and the voice of the archangel. Add to these that he who gave seeds that power of generating and germinating can also grant our bodies the ability to rise again. So Paul sets out the argument in the present passage in such a way that each word carries emphasis. "You," he says, "what you sow..." as if he said: You, who are a sinful, mortal, weak man, subject to every kind of mishap, you sow seed, and what you entrust to furrows or gardens is made alive after it has died and suffered corruption. What madness, then, is it to doubt the resurrection of our bodies, which that almighty, immortal and eternal God sows, and wills to return into the earth from which they were first taken, on this condition, that at last they rise to immortal life, subject to no corruption? Or will the outcome of God's sowing be less than yours? Will what you sow sprout with increase, but what God sows lie buried in eternal death? This is the sense of the Apostle's words.

units.la: Est autem hîc obseruatu dignissima admirabilis Dei prouidentia, cuius singulare & proprium opus est per ea agere siue operari, quæ rationi prorsus contraria & aduersa videntur. Hic enim in prima rerum origine ex tenebris lucem eduxit. Hic fulgura & ignes ex aquis elicit, & per has discurrere facit, ut in Psalmo scribitur. Idem ut sanet, vulnerat: ut vivificet, occidit: de-nique per mortem ea perficit, quæ vitæ nostræ sustentandæ seruiunt. Terra certè hybernis frigoribus mortificata, ubi sub niuibus aliquandiu sepulta latuit, vere novo rediuiua emicans fruges omnis generis ad humani generis & aliorum animalium alimoniam producit. Animalia item, nisi mactentur, nobis cibum & alimentum præbere non possunt. Quid, quòd nec Christi caro nobis pa-nis vitæ esse potuit, nisi pro mundi vita daretur, quod in ara crucis factum esse scimus? Debent nos ista consolari in omni tentationum genere. Quid enim fuerit, à quo nobis merito timeamus, quando ex ipsa morte spes vitæ certa affulget?
units.tr: Here we must observe most worthily the admirable providence of God, whose singular and proper work it is to act and operate through things that seem wholly contrary and opposed to reason. For in the first origin of things he brought light out of darkness. He draws lightnings and fires out of the waters and makes them run through these, as is written in the Psalm. The same God wounds in order to heal, and kills in order to make alive; finally, through death he brings to completion those things which serve to sustain our life. The earth, deadened by winter frosts, where it lay hidden for a while buried under the snows, rises again with the new spring shining forth and produces fruits of every kind for the food of mankind and of other animals. Likewise animals, unless they are slaughtered, cannot give us food and nourishment. What of it, that Christ's flesh could not be the bread of life for us unless it were given for the life of the world, which we know was done on the altar of the cross? These things ought to console us in every kind of temptation. For what is there to fear from anything, when from death itself the sure hope of life shines forth?

units.la: Venit etiam hoc loco consideranda sepulturæ ratio, ne illa nobis horrorem aut metum incutiat. Est ea sementis Dei. Ut enim femina sulcis mandantur, ut cum fœnore crescant: ita nostra quoque corpora ex Dei instituto sepeliuntur, ut olim præstantiora & nobiliora nobis reliquantur. Viderunt hoc inter ethnicos quoque, quotquot sapientiæ studio accensi animos suos à terris paulò altius sustulerunt. Hinc Lucanus olim canebat: Tabes ne cadauera soluat, An rogus, haud refert, placido natura recepta Cuncta sinu. Et Paulo post: Capit omnia tellus, Quæ genuit, &c.
units.tr: Here the manner of burial must also be considered, lest it strike horror or fear into us. It is God's sowing. For as seed is entrusted to furrows so that it may grow with increase, so our bodies too are buried by God's appointment, so that they may be left to us afterwards more excellent and more noble. The pagans too have seen this, as many as, kindled with the love of wisdom, have raised their minds somewhat higher above the earth. Hence Lucan once sang: "Whether decay dissolves the corpses or the pyre, it makes no difference, since nature takes all things back into her gentle bosom." And a little later: "The earth receives all the things that it has brought forth, etc."

units.la: Apud Xenophontem verò Cyrus iam morti vicinus sic loquitur: Meum corpus, ô charissimi fili, neq; in auro condite, neque in argento, neque in alia re prorsus vlla: sed illud terra reddite quàm primùm. Quid enim hac re beatius, quàm terra misceri, quæ pulchra omnia, bona omnia gignit & nutrit? Christiani quoque homines ex vetustissimo more adhuc nostro sæculo loca sepeliendis defunctorum corporibus destinata, agros Dei & Cæmiteria, quasi Dormitoria vocitant: ut nimirum recordentur sepulturam sementis instar esse, quasi satta[?], corpora à laboribus suis somno profundissimo & securissimo quiescant, olim surrectura, vbi vniuersalis illa messis aduenerit, qua qui Dei triticum sunt, in cœlestis regni horrea colligentur, palea autem inutiles abijcientur, ut æternum in gehennæ ignibus ardeant. Illorum[?] meminerint Christiani homines, quando suorum[?] su-nera efferuntur. Agricola feminis iacturam cum gaudio facit, quia in messis venturæ spem totus animo intentus est. Cur ergo nos doleamus, si vel parentes, vel amicos, vel dulcissima pignora agro dominico credimus, unde olim corporum nostrorum messis multò uberior atque beatior colligetur? Enimuero si feminibus aut sensus inesset, aut sermonis vsus daretur, non possent sementem sua dolere, quin potius hanc cum gaudij suauissimi significatione sustinerent propter mox sequentem lætissimam sui generationem. Cur ergo nos quiritamur, quibus spes certior multò & fe-liciore est proposita? Sed de his plura adhuc in iis, quæ sequuntur, dicenda venient.
units.tr: Xenophon's Cyrus, already near death, speaks thus: "My body, dearest sons, do not place in gold, nor in silver, nor in anything at all, but return it to the earth as quickly as possible. For what is more blessed than to be mingled with the earth, which produces and nourishes all things beautiful and good?" Christians too, following a very ancient custom that persists even in our own age, call the places set aside for burying the dead fields of God and cemeteries, as if they were dormitories. They do this so that they may remember that burial is like sowing, and that the bodies, released from their labours, rest in the deepest and most secure sleep, destined to rise one day when that universal harvest comes. Then those who are God's wheat will be gathered into the barns of the heavenly kingdom, while the useless chaff will be cast away to burn for ever in the fires of hell. Christians should keep this in mind whenever their dead are carried out for burial. A farmer throws away seed with joy, because his whole mind is fixed on the hope of the coming harvest. Why then should we grieve, if we entrust our parents, friends or dearest pledges to the Lord's field, from which one day a far richer and happier harvest of our bodies will be gathered? Indeed, if seeds had feeling or the power of speech, they could not grieve over their sowing; they would rather bear it with a sign of the sweetest joy, because of the most joyful generation that soon follows. Why then do we lament, when a much surer and happier hope is set before us? But more on these matters will be said in what follows.

units.la: Transit enim Paulus ad alteram quæstionem, ut quo nam & quali corpore mortui olim resurgant. Sic autem ait: Et quod feminas, non corpus nasciturum feminas, sed nudum granū, prout inciderit, tritici aut alicuius ex reliquis: Sed Deus dat ei corpus ut voluit, et singulis feminibus suum corpus. Dicit, non seminari corpus illud, quod nasciturum fit: quae verba non ita accipi debent, quasi quoad substantiam corporis, aliud seminetur, aliud germinet aut surgat. Hic enim de qualitate corporum resuscitandorum sermo est, cum illa omnino resurrectura esse, abunde demonstrauerit. Itaque hoc vult dicere Apostolus: Quemadmodum non totam spicam siue plan-tam totam seminas, qualis ea est cu sua radice, caule, foliis & flore atq; inde nasciturô fructu, sed nu-dum granum vel femen, id vero germinans radices agit & excrescit in sua quidem substantia, lon-ge tamen pulchrius, praestantius, uberius atq; copiosius: Ita etiam de nostris corporibus fiet. Nam quae nunc gestamus terrae mandantur, & eadem illa, non alia horum loco resurgent, non autem qua-lia nunc sunt, infirma, morbida, mortalia, sed clarificata & eximiis dotibus ornata. Et ita locum hunc Chrysostomus intellexit, cuius haec verba sunt: Idem corpus, quod sepultum fuit, surget, & non idé: idem quo ad substantiam: non idem, quoad qualitatem. Videtur autem sub Pauli verbis argu-mentum latere à comparatis, quo corporum clarificatio confirmatur: Si nudum granum tanto cũ fœnore germinat & è terra surgit, quanto magis hoc de nostris corporibus sperare debemus? Sed de gloria corporum resuscitatorum infra pluribus agetur, nunc quae huius loci sunt cõsiderabimus. Habent enim singula verba quod diligentius obseruetur.
units.tr: Paul now passes to the second question, namely with what kind of body and of what sort the dead will rise. He says: "And as for what you sow, you do not sow the body that is to be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of some other kind. But God gives it a body as he pleases, and to each seed its own body." He says that the body which is to be does not get sown. These words should not be taken as if, so far as the substance of the body is concerned, one thing is sown and another sprouts or rises. Here the discussion concerns the quality of the bodies to be raised, since he has already sufficiently shown that they will certainly rise. So the Apostle means this: just as you do not sow the whole ear or the whole plant, such as it is with its root, stalk, leaves and flower, and the fruit that will come from it, but a bare grain or seed, and this, sprouting, puts out roots and grows, in its substance indeed the same, yet far more beautiful, excellent, abundant and plentiful, so it will also be with our bodies. For what we now carry is committed to the earth, and that same body, not another, will rise in its place, yet not such as it now is, weak, diseased and mortal, but glorified and adorned with outstanding gifts. Chrysostom understood the passage in this way; his words are: "The same body that was buried will rise, and yet not the same: the same as to substance, not the same as to quality." Moreover, under Paul's words there seems to lie an argument from comparison, by which the glorification of bodies is confirmed: if a bare grain sprouts with such increase and rises from the earth, how much more ought we to hope this for our bodies? But the glory of the raised bodies will be discussed at greater length below; now let us consider the points of this passage. Each word has something that should be observed more carefully.

units.la: Occurrit hic primum, quod corpora nostra granis aut feminibus cofert. Ergo qualescunq, simus in hoc saeculo, divites, pauperes, nobiles, obscuri, docti, indocti, liberi, serui, senes, iuuenes, beati, miseri, Dei tamen gratia [?] sumus. Nam vt non solius frumenti aut tritici meminit, sed in genere de quo-uis femine loquitur, quorum nullum negligit Deus, quo minus ipsum quoq; germinet & excrescat: Ita neque personarum diuersitas obstabit, quo minus omnium corpora in nouissimo die suscitetur. Obseruabis etiam, nihil hic de caelestibus influentijs, aut Luna, Sole aliisque coftellationibus dici, sed Deum solum nominari, cuius virtute semina germinent & crescant. Hic enim solus in tota rerum natura operatur, hic fruges in hominum vsum, & faenum quoq; pecoribus producit, sicuti in Psalmis docemur: & nihil est qui plantat, nihil qui rigat, Deo autem omnis illa virtus adscribi debet, qui dat incrementum. Ita in resurrectionis etiam negotio, non in nostrae personae conditionem, neque occultiore aliquam naturae virtutem, sed solum Deum respicere debemus. Huius enim virtute (vt supra dictum est) totum istud negotium perficietur: qui vt singulis seminibus corpus dedit prout voluit: ita nobis quoque corpora nostra restituet, & talia quidem, vt gloriae coelestis capacia esse possint. Et vnum hoc piis sufficere debet contra quaestiones curiosorum hominum, & obiectiones siue argumenta, quae illi ab Impossibili adducunt.
units.tr: Here we first notice that he compares our bodies to grains or seeds. Therefore, whatever we are in this age, rich or poor, noble or obscure, learned or unlearned, free or slave, old or young, happy or wretched, we are nonetheless God's field. For he speaks not only of wheat or grain, but in general of any seed whatever, and God neglects none of them, so that each may sprout and grow. So too the diversity of persons will not stand in the way of all bodies being raised on the last day. You will also observe that nothing is said here about heavenly influences, or the moon, sun or other constellations, but that God alone is named, by whose power seeds sprout and grow. For he alone works in the whole of nature; he alone produces crops for human use and hay for the cattle, as we are taught in the Psalms; and there is nothing in him who plants, nothing in him who waters, but all that power must be ascribed to God, who gives the increase. So also in the business of the resurrection we ought to look not to the condition of our own person, nor to some hidden power of nature, but to God alone. For by his power (as was said above) that whole work will be accomplished; he who gave each seed its body as he willed will likewise restore our bodies to us, and such bodies as can be capable of heavenly glory. And this one thing should suffice the godly against the questions of curious men and the objections or arguments which they bring from the impossible.

units.la: Deinde nudum granum seminari dicit Apostolus, quia non coniunctā habet folia, caulem, ramos. Ad eundem modum corpora quoque nuda sepulturae mandantur. Induuntur quidem veste fe-pulchrali, & vt id fiat, humanitatis sensus & publicae honestatis ratio monet. Sed quacunque nobis in hoc saeculo agentibus splendore aliquem addunt, ea omnia nos in morte deflituunt, vt nullus exillis decor nobis porro accedat. Nullus enim tunc vsus est amicitiarum, dignitatum, opū: defluit formae flos, vires deficiunt, torpor letalis membra omnia astringit, & vt vita recedit, sic omni etiam motu & membrorum vsu exuimur. Oportet enim impleri quod Deus olim pronunciauit: Terra es, & in terram reuerteris. Ideo mors omnes homines aequare dicitur, qui dum in hoc saeculo viuunt, alij alijs plurimum praestare putantur. Etenim ad omnes pertinet, quod Iobus [?] de semetipso dixit: Nudus egressus sum de vtero matris meae, nudus etiam eo reuertar. Et illud apostoli-cum: Nihil intulimus in mundum, videlicet nec efferre quicquam possumus. Prodeste de his frequenter cogitare, ne mundi huius caduci & infelicis splendore nos capi patiamur. Vtamur eo, dum hoc a Domino nobis datur: non autem illo abutamur, memores, nos peregrinos esse, quibus migrationis aut profectionis hora a Deo constituta sit, quam nemo subterfugiet.
units.tr: Next, the Apostle says that a bare grain is sown because it does not have leaves, stalk and branches joined to it. In the same way, bare bodies are committed to burial. They are indeed clothed in funeral garments, and the sense of humanity and the reasonable respect of public decency urge that this be done. But whatever splendour they add to us while we live in this age, all of it abandons us in death, so that no adornment of that kind is added to us any longer. For then there is no use of friendships, dignities or wealth; the flower of beauty falls away, strength fails, deadly numbness binds all the limbs, and as life departs we are stripped also of all motion and use of the members. For what God once declared must be fulfilled: "You are earth, and to earth you shall return." Therefore death is said to make all men equal, though while they live in this age some are thought to excel others greatly. For what Job said of himself applies to all: "Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked I shall return there." And the Apostle's saying: "We brought nothing into the world," clearly means that we can carry nothing out either. It is useful to think often on these things, lest we allow ourselves to be captivated by the splendour of this fading and unhappy world. Let us use it while the Lord grants it to us, but not abuse it, mindful that we are strangers, for whom the hour of departure or migration has been appointed by God, and that no one will escape it.

units.la: Imprimis autem breui hoc dicto immanis ille sepulturae & sepulchrorum fastus confutatur, quo nihil inanius, nihil stultius, nihil homine Christiano indignius excogitari potest. Debent quidè funera honorifice duci, & honeste sepeliri corpora, quae cum in vius essent, Spiritus Sancti templa fuerunt, & nunc in beatae resurrectionis spe quiescunt. Sed & in communem humanitatis sensum pec-cant, qui vel mortuorum cadauera ignominiosius tractant (quod in Moabitis olim Deus grauissimè puniuit) vel eorundē [?] sepulchra violat: quod scelus gentibus quoq; atrocissimū esse visum fuit, qui publicis legibus pœnas statuerunt τυμβωρύχοις,id est sepulchrorum effosoribus. Interea tamen fa-stus omnis à funeribus & sepulchris procul abesse debet, ne in ipso etiam mortis articulo super-bum quid adhuc spirauisse, vel etiam nunc spirare videamur. Quid enim stultius quàm tunc super-bire, vel potius superbiæ pristinæ speciem inanem ostentare, quando neque manus neque pedes ossi-cium faciunt, & cum membrorum usu sensum quoque omnem amisisti? Quid vero tam ridiculum, quàm armis conspicuas imagines sepulchris imponi eorum, qui à vermibus demorantur, aut tabe fœ-dissima consumuntur? Quid tam alienum à pietate, quàm sanguinis studium, cædes, rapinas in tem-plis, imò in Dei conspectu ostentare, qui precantium quoque manus, si sanguine pollutas videat, a-uersatur? At hac hodie gloriam sibi vendicàt nobiles & principes, & præ aliis quidem imprimis, qui nihil unquam vel pro patria vel communi religione egregium & laude dignum gesserunt.
units.tr: Above all, by this brief saying, that monstrous display in funerals and tombs is refuted, than which nothing can be devised more empty, more foolish, or more unworthy of a Christian man. Indeed funerals ought to be conducted with honour, and bodies decently buried, since while they were alive they were temples of the Holy Spirit, and now rest in the hope of a blessed resurrection. But those also sin against the common sense of humanity who treat the corpses of the dead more shamefully (a thing God once punished most severely in the Moabites), or violate their tombs; a crime which even the Gentiles thought most atrocious, and who by public laws set penalties for tomb-robbers [τυμβωρύχοις], that is, those who dig up graves. Meanwhile, all ostentation must be kept far away from funerals and tombs, lest we seem to have breathed some proud thing even at the very moment of death, or still to breathe it now. For what is more foolish than to show pride then, or rather to make an empty display of former pride, when neither hands nor feet perform their office, and when, with the use of the limbs, you have also lost all feeling? And what is more ridiculous than to place on tombs images made conspicuous with arms, of men who are being consumed by worms or wasted by most foul decay? What is more alien to godliness than to parade a zeal for blood, slaughter and plunder, even in temples, indeed in the sight of God, who turns away from the hands of those who pray, if he sees them polluted with blood? Yet today nobles and princes claim this glory for themselves, and above others especially those who have never done anything outstanding or worthy of praise, either for their country or for the common religion.

units.la: Postremò addit Paulus, Deum singulis feminibus suum corpus dare. Ergo nobis quoque no-stra restituentur, non autem alienis donabimur. Oportuit hoc addi propter ea, quæ prius dixerat: Tu quod feminas, non corpus nasciturum feminas. In hoc enim disputationis huius cardo versa-tur, ut ea ipsa corpora, quæ nunc gestamus, quæ cum Deo visum est moriuntur & terræ credi-ta resoluuntur & putrefiunt, olim resurrectura esse demonstret. Ideo disertè istud pronunciat: Deus ei dat corpus ut voluit, & singulis feminibus suum corpus: In Dei quidem nutu & manu sicum est, singulis creatis corpora dare prout ipsi libuerit, neque nunc nostrorum corporum for-mam, staturam & effigiem mutare possumus. Ut autem ea quæ seruntur semina germinant, & in suo quidem genere, neque pro tritico lolium, aut pro faba pisum siue hordeum nascitur: ita non alia, quàm quæ sepulta sunt, corpora resurgent, & unicuique suum restituetur, in quo olim uixit. Seruit hoc iis confutandis, qui nescio quam corporum & membrorum confusionem me-tuunt, & ne animabus corpora aliena obtingant (quod olim Pythagoræi de sua μετεμψυχώσει[?] somniarunt, quos inter gentes quoque doctissimi quique risu & ludibrio dignos putarunt) aut corporibus quoque partes aliquæ aut membra ipsis non conuenientia addantur. Qui enim singu-lis feminibus suum corpus dare potest, ut singula esi[?] confusa & promiscua in eodem agro ferã-tur, in suo genere exerescant: idem ille hic quoque facile cauebit, ne quæ confusio aut membrorum permixtio absurda siue inordinata incidas.
units.tr: Finally, Paul adds that God gives to each seed its own body. Therefore our own bodies will be restored to us, and we will not be given other people's. This had to be added because of what he had said earlier, "Thou sowest not that body that shall be." The hinge of this argument is to show that those very bodies we now bear, which die when God pleases, are committed to the earth, and dissolve and rot, will one day rise again. So he states it plainly: "God giveth it a body as it hath pleased him, and to every seed his own body." It lies in God's will and hand to give bodies to each created thing as he pleases, and we cannot now change the form, stature and likeness of our bodies. Just as the seeds that are sown sprout each in its own kind, so that wheat does not grow as darnel, nor a bean as a pea or barley, so the bodies that rise will be none other than those that were buried, and each will be restored in the body in which he lived. This serves to refute those who fear some confusion of bodies and limbs, and that alien bodies might be attached to souls (as the Pythagoreans long ago dreamed under their metempsychosis [μετεμψυχώσει], which the most learned men among the nations also thought worthy of laughter and mockery), or that some parts or limbs not fitting the bodies themselves might be added to them. For he who can give each seed its own body, so that single seeds sown together in the same field, though mixed, grow up each in its own kind, will easily guard against any confused or absurd mixing of limbs.

units.la: Et ut ita sentiamus atque credamus, argumenta multa & firmissima nos admonent. Et primò quidem ipsa Resurgendi & Resurrectionis vocabula, quibus in hac causa Spiritus San-ctus utitur. Resurgere enim dicitur quod cecidit, nec id proprie de eo, quod nunquam cecidit, di-ci potest. At in morte corpora nostra cadunt, ad quæ sola mortis uis penetrat, animabus illo-rum vinculo solutis & adsuetis sedes emigrantibus. Illa ergo eadem resurgant necesse est, nisi Spiri-tum Sanctum inanibus uocabulis nos ludere, uelimus suspicari. Etenim nisi hoc demus, neq; pro-prie neque uere à Paulo dictum est, Deum unicuique suum corpus dare. Deinde in nouissimo die mors abolebitur & victoria omni spoliabitur, quam eò usque obtinuisse videri poterit. Id ve-rò nunquam fiet, nisi eos restituere cogatur, quos abstulit siue absorbuit. Tertio, nec ad Christi exemplum resurrecturos esse, Scriptura testatur. At hic in corpore suo vero re-surrexit, in quo crucifixus & mortuus fuerat, ideoque clauorum vestigia retinuit, ut discipulis ea ostendere, & ijsdem veram sui corporis resurrectionem ad oculum (quod aiunt) demonstrare posset. Quòd si qui istud adhuc negare audent, age dicant illi nobis, unde Christus corpus illud alienum habuerit, quod discipuli viderunt & contrectarunt? Scriptura certè nullius alterius corporis meminerunt, quàm quod ex Maria Virgine natum, cum ætatis progressu adoleuit, & quod in cruce suffixum, mortuum atque sepultum, tertio postdie resurrexit. Quartò typus, qui in Iona præcessit, hoc ipsum confirmat. Illum enim tam suæ quàm omnium nostrûm resurrectionis exemplum fuisse, Christus testatur. At e-undem Ionam, quem lamia absorbuit, non alium, terris redditum fuisse scimus. Addebis, quòd nisi nostra corpora nobis restituantur, ne retributio quidem erit, quam olim futuram esse omnes credimus, & sine qua (vt alibi diximus) iustitia Dei consistere non potest. Hæc enim exigit, vt quæ peccarunt corpora puniantur, & quæ pro pietatis causa labores atque pericula sustinuerunt, gloria cœlesti coronentur. Cæterum quæ corporum nostrorum gloria olim futura sit, mox sequetur. Nunc teneamus, certò fore corporum resurrectionem in nouissimo die, neque alia quàm quæ nunc habemus, resurrectura esse. Ea igitur spe confirmati, animos nostros à mundi praui s studijs reuocemus, ita verò viuamus, vt dies ille nobis lætus illucescat, & ad cœlestis regni gaudia colligamur cum Seruatore nostro IESV CHRISTO, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Many very firm arguments also urge us to think and believe this. First, there are the very words "rise again" (resurgere) and "resurrection," which the Holy Spirit uses in this matter. For that is said to rise again which has fallen, and this cannot properly be said of what never fell. But in death our bodies fall, the only part on which the power of death acts, when the souls, their bond loosed, depart to their accustomed seats. Those same bodies must therefore rise again, unless we are willing to suspect that the Holy Spirit is playing with empty words. For unless we grant this, Paul has not spoken properly or truly when he says that God gives each his own body. Second, on the last day death will be abolished and stripped of the victory it seems to have held until then. This will never happen unless death is compelled to restore those whom it carried off or swallowed up. Third, Scripture testifies that we shall rise according to the example of Christ. But he truly rose in the body in which he had been crucified and had died, and therefore kept the marks of the nails, so that he could show them to the disciples and, as they say, demonstrate before their eyes the true resurrection of his own body. But if anyone still dares to deny this, let them tell us whence Christ had that alien body which the disciples saw and handled. Scripture certainly mentions no other body than the one born of the Virgin Mary, which grew with advancing age, and which, hanged on the cross, dead and buried, rose on the third day. Fourth, the type which went before in Jonah confirms this very thing. For Christ testifies that Jonah was an example both of his own resurrection and of ours. But we know that the same Jonah whom the sea monster swallowed was returned to dry land, and no other. You will add that unless our bodies are restored to us, there will be no retribution, which we all believe will come, and without which (as we have said elsewhere) the justice of God cannot stand. For this demands that the bodies which sinned be punished, and that those which endured labours and dangers for the cause of piety be crowned with heavenly glory. As for what the glory of our bodies will one day be, that will follow shortly. For now let us hold that there will certainly be a resurrection of bodies on the last day, and that they will rise as none other than those we now have. Confirmed in this hope, let us recall our minds from the wicked pursuits of the world, and so live that that day may dawn joyfully upon us, and that we may be gathered into the joys of the heavenly kingdom with our Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 84.

units.la: Non omnis caro, eadem caro: sed alia quidem caro hominum, alia verò caro pecorum, alia verò piscium, alia verò volucrum. Et sunt corpora cœlestia, & sunt corpora terrestria: sed alia quidem cœlestium gloria, alia verò terrestrium. Alia gloria Solis, & alia gloria Lunæ, & alia gloria stellarum: Stella enim à stella differt in gloria. Ita & resurrectio mortuorum. Seminatur in corruptione, excitatur in incorruptibilitate: Seminatur in ignominia, excitatur in gloria: Seminatur in infirmitate, excitatur in potentia: Seminatur corpus animale, excitatur corpus spirituale: Est corpus animale, & est corpus spirituale.
units.tr: Not all flesh is the same flesh: but there is one flesh of men, another flesh of beasts, another of fishes, and another of birds. There are also celestial bodies and terrestrial bodies: but the glory of the celestial is one, and the glory of the terrestrial is another. One is the glory of the sun, another the glory of the moon, and another the glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory. So also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption. It is sown in dishonour, it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness, it is raised in power. It is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body.

units.la: REspondit nuper Paulus ad illusorium quæstiones, quibus illi mortuorum resurrectionem in dubium vocare, vel potius ludibrio habere solent.
