Et quia eis impossibile & absurdum videtur, ea tunc nobis corpora restitui, quæ nunc vitijs plurimis obnoxia sunt: femetis[?] parabola docuit, idem omnino corpus, quod sepultum fuit, resurrecturum esse, quoad substantiam, longe tamen præstantius & nobilius, quoad nouas qualitates, quibus ornabitur. At hic obijceret aliquis: Qua autem ratione corpora eadem, quæ nunc gestamus, surgere dicemus, si non eadem tunc futura est illorum qualitas siue conditio? Itaque quod paucis dixerat, nunc plenius exponit, & demonstrat, hoc neque nouum neque insolens cuiquam videri debere, si manente corporum substantia, mutatio tamen fiat in melius.
units.tr: Paul lately answered the frivolous questions by which men are accustomed to call the resurrection of the dead into doubt, or rather to mock it. Since it seems to them impossible and absurd that those bodies, which are now subject to so many defects, should be restored to us, he taught by the parable of the seed that the very same body which was buried will rise again, as to its substance, yet far more excellent and noble as to the new qualities with which it will be adorned. But someone might object here: By what reasoning shall we say that the same bodies which we now carry will rise, if their quality or condition is not to be the same then? Therefore what he had said briefly he now explains more fully and shows that this should seem neither new nor strange to anyone, that, while the substance of the bodies remains, a change for the better should nevertheless take place.

units.la: Rursus autem similibus vtitur ex rerum natura desumptis, quæ multa adduci poterant, vt pote de metallis, auro, argento, ferro & similibus, quæ in mille formas finguntur & refinguntur, cum nihil interea substantiæ eorū decedat. Ita eadē luti massa pro figuli arbitrio nunc hanc nunc illā figurā recipit. Quod ipsum de cera & quauis alia molliori aut ductili materia dici potest. At his omnibus relictis, ea exempla profert, quæ huic causæ propius & melius conueniunt. Et primò quidem ex ipsa carnis natura argumentatur, sic dicens: Non omnis caro, eadem caro: sed alia quidem caro hominum, alia verò caro pecorum, alia verò piscium, alia verò volucrum. Caro vocabulum vt genus ponit, cui suas species subijcit, humanam videlicet, pecuinam, piscium item & volucrum. Et sensus verborum est: Quemadmodum omnis caro, siue ea hominum, siue pecorum, siue piscium, siue auium sit, si substantiam & naturam spectes, non aliud quàm caro est, neque aliter potest aut debet dici, specie tamen & qualitate saporis alia ab alia differt: Ita in resurrectione mortuorum eadem caro, quam nunc gestamus, suscitabitur quoad suam substantiam, neque ei quicquam derogabit mutatio illa, quæ ipsi gloriam & conditionem præstantiorem conferet. Si enim in hoc corruptibili mundo inter hominum & animalium carnes tanta est differentia, quæ tamen non obstat, quo minus illa omnia carnem habere dicantur: absurdum fuerit, hoc impossibile putare in hominibus, quos Deus iam inde ab initio ad sortem præstantiorem condidit, qua cetera animantia excellant. Adde his, quòd si nunc vitam hanc miseram & mortalem viuentibus nihil ex corporis substantia decedit: quando ægroti ex morbo conualescunt, pauperes diuitijs, inglorij honoribus & dignitatibus ornantur, vel etiam homo priuatus ad regni fastigium euehitur: annon olim quoque in regeneratione illa vniuersali, manente eadem quæ nunc est corporum substantia, conditio felicior & præstantior nobis possit obtingere? Quid quòd Deus Adamum propter primam originem adhuc terram dixit, quando nihil minus quàm terra esse videbatur? Et etiam nobis idem dictum conuenit, Terra es, & in terram reuerteris? Quòd si terrena adhuc est corporum nostrorum substantia, licet anima viuente donata formam quoque digniorem acceperit, quid obstat, quò minus in resurrectione carnis substantia nobis salua maneat, quàmuis eadem immortalitate & gloria cœlesti donetur? Possent huius generis multa adduci, quæ euidentissimè demonstrant, corporum nostrorum resurrectionem, quàmuis humanæ rationis captum excedat, non tamen pugnare cum naturæ legibus quibus corpora subijciuntur.
units.tr: Again he uses similar examples drawn from nature, of which many could be brought forward, such as metals, gold, silver, iron and the like, which are shaped and reshaped into a thousand forms while none of their substance is lost in the process. So the same mass of clay takes now this shape, now that, at the will of the potter. The same can be said of wax and of any other softer or malleable material. But leaving all these aside, he brings forward examples which fit this cause more closely and aptly. And first he argues from the very nature of flesh, saying: Not all flesh is the same flesh: but there is one flesh of men, another flesh of beasts, another of fishes, and another of birds. He sets the word "flesh" down as a genus, under which he places its species, namely human, animal, and likewise fish and birds. The sense of the words is this: just as all flesh, whether of men, beasts, fishes or birds, when you regard its substance and nature, is nothing other than flesh, and cannot or should not be called anything else, yet differs from one kind to another in its form and the quality of its make-up, so in the resurrection of the dead the same flesh which we now carry will be raised as to its substance, and that change, which will confer on it a more excellent glory and condition, will take nothing away from it. For if in this corruptible world there is so great a difference between the flesh of men and of animals, which nevertheless does not prevent all of them from being said to have flesh, it would be absurd to think this impossible in men, whom God from the beginning created for a more excellent lot, by which they surpass the other living creatures. Add to this that if this miserable and mortal life loses nothing of the substance of the body for the living: when the sick recover from illness, the poor are enriched, the obscure are adorned with honours and dignities, or even a private man is raised to the heights of royal power, could not a happier and more excellent condition also fall to us at that general regeneration, the substance of our bodies remaining the same as it now is? What of the fact that God said to Adam, on account of his first origin, that he was still earth, when he seemed to be anything but earth? And does the same saying also fit us: You are earth, and you shall return to the earth? But if the substance of our bodies is still earthly, although, with the soul living within it, it has received a more worthy form too, what hinders the substance of the flesh from remaining safe for us in the resurrection, although it is granted the same immortality and heavenly glory? Many things of this kind could be brought forward, which most clearly demonstrate that the resurrection of our bodies, although it exceeds the grasp of human reason, does not nevertheless conflict with the laws of nature to which bodies are subject.

units.la: Porrò vt à Pauli instituto & argumenti huius tractatione aliquantulum digrediamur, non indignum est obseruatu, inter ea, quæ carnem habent, piscès quoque recenseri. Alia (inquit) est caro pecorum, alia vero piscium, alia vero volatilium. Nec enim Apostolo dictum hoc temere, vt homini idiotæ & rerum naturalium imperito, excidisse putabimus, cùm eadem omnium sit physicorum sententia, qui de animalium historia diligentius scripserunt. Plinius certè de lupus piscibus scribit: Luporum laudatissimi, qui appellantur lanati, à candore molli-tiaque carnis. Item de mullis: Alga vescuntur & ostreis, & limo, & aliorum piscium carne. Et verè quidem carnem piscibus tribui, res ipsa docet, si totam corporis ipsorum constitutionem inspicias. Arguit hoc Pontificum stultitiam, qui cùm à carnium esu interdicant, inque ea abstinentia omnem ieiuniorum suorum religionem consistere arbitrentur, piscibus tamen quosdam permittunt. Imò ab operibus lactarijs & ouis abstinendum esse docent, ne quid edatur quod aliqua ex parte cum carnis natura siue substantia communicet, interim piscibus omnes saturari sinunt. Quòd si respondeant, instituti sui hanc esse rationem, ne carni lasciuienti libidinis irritamenta subministrentur, sed vt voluptas immodica fræno quodam coerceatur, facilius est adidre sponsio. Pisces enim carnibus reliquis lautiores sunt, & à plerisq; in delitijs habentur: ita denique in cibum parantur atque conditiuntur, vt libidinem vehementius quàm quadrupedum aut volatilium carnes accendant: vt iam de vino nihil dicamus, quod cum bis meracius & liberalius libitur. Atqui id (inquiunt) non vulgò fit, quia plerique impensis tam magnis non sufficiunt. Ridiculum. Ergo ieiuniorum legibus soli pauperes tenentur, quibus illis minimè opus est, cùm vt lint nolint frequentius ieiunent, quàm corporis vires ferre possint. Ita seipsam prodit superstitio, vt appareat Paulum non temere hoc doctrinæ genus ad diabolum authorem referre, cuius primum est ex hominum insertu voluptatem capere. Nobis sufficiat, quòd Christus cibórum discrimina cum alijs Legis ceremonijs abrogauit, neque ijs quæ per os ingrediuntur quemquam polluì docuit. Nec excidat nobis illud Apostoli: Non est regnum Dei esca aut potus: sed iustitia & pax & gaudium in Spiritu sancto. Sed quia hæc alterius loci sunt, nolumus ijs nunc diu-tius insistere.
units.tr: Furthermore, to digress a little from Paul's plan and from the treatment of this argument, it is not unworthy of notice that fishes too are counted among the things that have flesh. "Another," he says, "is the flesh of beasts, another of fishes, another of birds." Nor should we think that this was said carelessly by the Apostle, as if it had slipped from a layman ignorant of natural things, since all the natural philosophers who wrote more carefully about the history of animals hold the same view. Pliny certainly writes about the sea-bass: the most praised of the sea-bass are those called "woolly," for the whiteness and softness of their flesh. Likewise about mullets: they feed on seaweed and oysters, and on mud, and on the flesh of other fishes. And indeed that fishes have flesh the thing itself teaches, if you look at the whole constitution of their bodies. This shows the folly of the Papists, who, while they forbid the eating of flesh, and think that all the religion of their fasts consists in that abstinence, nevertheless allow certain fishes. Indeed they teach that dairy foods and eggs must be avoided, lest anything be eaten which in any part shares in the nature or substance of flesh, while meanwhile they let everyone gorge on fish. If they answer that the reason for their rule is that the lustful flesh should not be given incitements to lust, but that immoderate pleasure should be restrained by a kind of bridle, then it is easy to offer the counter-argument. For fishes are more delicate than other flesh and are held by most people as delicacies; they are prepared and seasoned as food in such a way that they kindle desire more fiercely than the flesh of quadrupeds or birds, not to mention wine, which is poured out both stronger and more freely with them. Yet they say that this is not done commonly, because most people cannot afford such great expense. Ridiculous. So only the poor are bound by the laws of fasting, and they have no need of them, since, whether they like it or not, they fast more often than their bodily strength can bear. Thus superstition betrays itself, so that it appears that Paul did not carelessly refer this kind of teaching to the devil, whose first concern is to take pleasure in the invention of men. It is enough for us that Christ abolished the distinctions of foods along with the other ceremonies of the Law, and taught that no one is defiled by what enters through the mouth. Nor should that saying of the Apostle escape us: The kingdom of God is not meat and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. But since these matters belong to another place, we do not wish to dwell on them any longer now.

units.la: Redeamus ergo ad Pauli institutum, qui aliud argumentum ex ipsa corporum natura profert, quæ ipsa quoque in varias atque diuersas species distinguantur, nihil obstante eorum substantia, quæ ipsis salua & integra manent. Et sunt (inquit) corpora cœlestia, & sunt corpora terrestria: sed alia quidem cœlestium gloria, alia vero terrestrium &c. Hoc autem vult dicere: Si corpora in genere spectemus, ea primùm in cœlestia & terrestria distinguuntur, attamen tam hæc quàm illa, si substantiam consideres, corpora sunt, & quò minus corpora dici debeant, neque loci distantia, neque quod inter illa est gloria siue dignitatis discrimen prohibet. Quid ergo obstabit, quò minus nostrorum corporum substantia salua & integra maneat, vt verè corpora dicantur, licet nouam qualitatem & dignitatem excellentiorem accipiant? Imò vt iam de solis cœlestibus dicamus, quæ cum ad idem genus pertineant, & substantiæ atque naturæ sint eiusdem, tamen alia alijs præstant. Alia enim est gloria Solis, alia Lunæ, alia stellarum: Sed & inter stellas videmus alias alijs maiori splendore fulgere, vt iam de earundem diuersis mo-tibus nihil dicamus. Num ergo impossibile fuerit, tale quid in nostris etiam corporibus fieri, vt quàmuis non euacuetur eorum substantia, neque aboleatur, qualitate tamen & conditione præstantiori ornentur, qua differant ab ijs quæ nunc sunt? Et hic quidem proprius huius loci sensus est, quoad corporum nostrorum resurrectionem, de qua Paulus in præsenti disputat, vt demon-stret[?], stret[?], quale discrimen futurum sit inter corpora, quae nunc gestamus vitiosa & infirmitatibus va-rijs obnoxia, & incorruptibilia illa, quae olim nobis restituentur.
units.tr: Let us then return to Paul's plan, who brings forward another argument from the very nature of bodies, which are themselves also divided into various and different kinds, without any harm to their substance, which remains safe and whole for them. "There are celestial bodies," he says, "and there are terrestrial bodies: but the glory of the celestial is one, and of the terrestrial another," and so on. He wishes to say this: if we regard bodies in general, they are first divided into celestial and terrestrial; yet both these and those, if you consider their substance, are bodies, and neither the distance of place nor the difference of glory or dignity between them prevents them from being rightly called bodies. What then will hinder the substance of our bodies from remaining safe and whole, so that they may truly be called bodies, even though they receive a new quality and a more excellent dignity? Indeed, to say nothing yet of the various motions of the stars, let us speak of the heavenly bodies alone: although they belong to the same genus and are of the same substance and nature, yet some surpass others. For the glory of the sun is one, of the moon another, of the stars another; and among the stars we see some shining with greater splendour than others. Would it then be impossible for something of this kind to happen also to our bodies, so that, although their substance is not emptied or abolished, they may be adorned with a more excellent quality and condition, by which they differ from what they are now? And this is indeed the proper sense of this passage, as far as the resurrection of our bodies is concerned, about which Paul is disputing here, showing what difference there will be between the bodies we now carry, which are faulty and subject to various infirmities, and those incorruptible ones which will one day be restored to us.

units.la: Verūntamen nolim dissimulare, plerosq; ex veteribus postremum hoc, vel potius totum hunc locum interpretari de diuersis corporum resuscitatorum conditionibus, adeoq; de praemiorum & poenarum, quae in altero seculo nobis obuentura sunt, diuersitate. Quod licet cum huius disputationis statu non per omnia conueniat, ab hac tamen tractatione non omnino alienum est. Quoad ergo illorum sententiam, ista observabis. Primum: Vt nunc inter coelestia & terrestria ingens discrimen est: ita tunc quoq; erit inter eos, qui in hoc seculo terrenis fluidis immersi fuerunt, & eos, qui animis supra hunc mundum corruptibilem euectis coelestia sectati sunt. Ex eo igitur consolationem petamus contra scandalum, quod ex impari aut iniqua huius seculi conditione nascitur. Offendit ea multos, vt nunquam non in ore habeant: Inaequaliter inter homines comparatum est, aliis feliciter agentibus & omni bonorum genere affluentibus, dum alii cum extremis miseriis perpetuo conflictantur. Quod etsi vere dicatur, & plerunq; optimi quiq; in hoc seculo laborent atque egeant, impii vero sacrorum omnium illusores sua temeritate quidvis pro voto conficiant: neminem tamen ista debent offendere: sed tunc futuri seculi conditio nobis in mentem veniat, vbi non minori inaequalitate, iusto tamen & aequissimo iudicio, praemia & poenas Dominus distribuet, quando agni ab haedis discernentur, & hi quidem aeternis inferorum cruciatibus mancipabuntur, illis cum Christo aeternum gaudentibus. Neq; alicui mora ista, qua suum aduentum Christus differt, molesta esse debet. Sentiunt enim discrimen hoc ingens animae nostrae, quam primum huius vitae vinculis solutae ex corporis ergastulo emigrant. Admonet nos de eo Christus, quando in diuiti epulonis & Lazari mendici parabola Abrahamum epuloni respondentem inducit: Fili, memento, quod recepisti bona tua in vita tua, & Lazarus similiter mala: nunc autem hic solatio fruitur, tu vero cruciaris. Luc.16.
units.tr: I would not, however, conceal that many of the ancient writers interpret this last point, or rather this whole passage, as referring to the different conditions of the raised bodies, and so to the difference between the rewards and punishments that await us in the next age. Although this does not agree in every respect with the purpose of the present discussion, it is not entirely foreign to it. So, as to their view, you should note the following. First, just as there is now a vast difference between heavenly and earthly things, so then there will be a difference between those who in this age were immersed in earthly pleasures and those who, with their minds lifted above this corruptible world, pursued heavenly things. Let us therefore draw comfort from this against the offence that arises from the unequal condition of this age. It offends many people, so that they are never done complaining: among men, things are unequally arranged, some prospering and abounding in every kind of good, while others are constantly wrestling with the utmost misery. Even if this is truly said, and the best people in this age often labour and go in need, while the wicked, mockers of all holy things, carry out whatever they wish through their recklessness, still these things ought not to offend anyone. Instead, let us call to mind the condition of the future age, where the Lord will distribute rewards and punishments with no less inequality, yet with a just and most equitable judgement, when the sheep are separated from the goats, and the one group will be given over to the eternal torments of hell, while the others rejoice eternally with Christ. Nor should this delay by which Christ postpones his coming trouble anyone. For our souls perceive this vast difference as soon as they are freed from the bonds of this life and depart from the prison of the body. Christ reminds us of this when, in the parable of the rich man and the beggar Lazarus, he introduces Abraham answering the rich man: "Son, remember that you received your good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted here, while you are tormented." Luke 16.

units.la: Deinde obseruabis in vtroq; genere, piorum scilicet & impiorum, rursus discrimen fore, quoad poenarum & praemiorum diuersitatem. Quia qui grauius peccarunt, grauius quoq; multabuntur, & rursus prae aliis gloria coronabuntur, qui fide maiori donati in Dei seruitio plus aliis praestiterunt. Docet hoc non obscure Dominus. Nam apud Lucam ait: Ille seruus, qui nouit volunta-tem domini sui, nec se comparauit, nec fecit ex voluntate eius, caedetur multis plagis: Qui autem non nouit, & fecit digna plagis, caedetur paucioribus. Cuicunq; verò multum datum est, multum quaeretur ab eo: & apud quem deposuerunt multum, amplius petent ab eo. Idem de ciuitate loquens, quae Euangelij praedicationi locum dare dedignatur, inter alia inquit: Dico vobis, quòd Sodomis & Gomorrhae tolerabilius erit in die iudicij, quàm illi ciuitati. Quod pio[?] verò, satis notum est, quòd Apostolis suis non obscure praerogatiuam insignem tribuit, quando in duodecim thronis consessuros ait, vt iudicent duodecim tribus Israël's[?]. Nam etsi locutio illa figurata sit, nemo tamen negare poterit, excellentiorem fore in illo die eorum gloriam, quorum ministerio Dei Filius in toto terrarum orbe reformando vti dignatus est. Id enim Danielem quoq; diserte olim docuit Angelum, dicens: Doctores splendebunt vt splendor firmamenti: & qui multos ad iustitiam adducunt, vt stellae sempiternis temporibus. Et huc nonnulli ex orthodoxis Patribus Christi etiam dictum retulerunt, quo in domo Patris sui mansiones multae esse testatur. Nemo tamen hic Mahumeticum quid somniare debet, aut seruilem aliquam inter beatos subiectionem fingere, quae cum aemulatione siue inuidia coniuncta sit. Quia enim omnes in Dei conspectu agent, in quo beata satietate gaudiorum fruentur, nullus aemulationi locus erit, neq; aliquis affectus carnalis felicitatem illam perfectissimam turbabit.
units.tr: Next, you will observe that in each of the two groups, namely of the godly and of the ungodly, there will again be a difference with respect to the diversity of punishments and rewards. For those who have sinned more gravely will also be punished more gravely, and conversely, those who, endowed with greater faith, have done more in the service of God will be crowned with greater glory than others. The Lord teaches this plainly. For in Luke he says: "That servant who knew his lord's will, and neither prepared himself nor acted according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes; but he who did not know it, and did things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with fewer. And from everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required; and from the one with whom they have deposited much, they will demand more." Speaking of a city that refuses to give room to the preaching of the gospel, he says among other things: "I tell you that it will be more bearable for Sodom and Gomorrah in the day of judgement than for that city." As for what is true, it is well enough known that he clearly granted an outstanding pre-eminence to his apostles, when he said that they would sit on twelve thrones to judge the twelve tribes of Israel. For although that expression is figurative, no one can deny that the glory of those through whose ministry the Son of God has deigned to reform the whole world will be greater on that day. Daniel too once taught this plainly, when the angel said: "Teachers will shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars for ever and ever." Some of the orthodox Fathers have also referred to this the saying of Christ in which he testifies that there are many rooms in his Father's house. Yet no one should dream here of anything Mahometan, or invent some servile subjection among the blessed, joined with rivalry or envy. For since all will act in the sight of God, in whose blessed fullness of joys they will rejoice, there will be no place for rivalry, and no carnal feeling will disturb that most perfect happiness.

units.la: Quòd si quis obiciat, Ergo aliquid tribui debet nostris meritis? Id constanter & diserte negamus, neq; tale quid hinc colligi potest. Poenae quidem impiis & sceleratis ex merito designantur, quia ex propria malitia peccamus: beatitudo autem siue felicitas illa aeterna nequaquam nostrorum operum meritis debetur: quia nihil boni ex nobis ipsis facimus, imò ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei sumus, sed Dei opus est, quicquid boni facimus, qui Verbo & Spiritu in nobis agere dignatur. Nihil ergo ille in nobis quàm sua dona coronat: & quoties sacra litera mercedis aut praemij meminerunt, quo Deus bona opera remuneretur, tunc partim Dei iustitiam & veritatem, partim eiusdem gratuitam bonitatem commendant, ut nos ad serium[?] pietatis studium ma-gis excitent.
units.tr: But if someone objects: "Then should something be ascribed to our merits?", we constantly and plainly deny this, and nothing of the kind can be inferred from it. Punishments are indeed appointed for the wicked and the criminal as their due, because we sin from our own malice. But that eternal blessedness or happiness is in no way owed to the merits of our works, because we do nothing good of ourselves; indeed we are not even fit to think, but whatever good we do is the work of God, who deigns to work in us through his Word and Spirit. Therefore he crowns nothing in us but his own gifts. And whenever the sacred letters mention the reward or prize by which God recompenses good works, they then commend partly the justice and truth of God, and partly his free goodness, so that they may rouse us the more to a earnest zeal for godliness.

units.la: Caeterum redit Paulus ad sementis parabolam, ut amplius demonstret quae & qualis corporum resuscitatorum conditio futura sit. Ita (inquit) erit etiam resurrectio mortuorum. Ut enim illud ipsum semen germinat & surgit, quod per sementem sulcis mandatum est, non autem nudum surgit & contemptibile, quale seminatum fuit, sed praestantius multò & ornatius: Ita de nostris quoq; corporibus agetur, quae eadem quidem suscitabuntur, non autem qualia nunc sunt, corruptibilia, vitiosa, infirma & infinitis casibus obnoxia. Id vero mox elegānti comparatione illustrat, quae tribus aut quatuor membris omnes corporum clarificatorum dotes comprehendit.
units.tr: Moreover, Paul returns to the parable of sowing, to demonstrate more fully what and what kind of condition the raised bodies will have. "So," he says, "will also be the resurrection of the dead. For just as that very seed sprouts and rises, which was committed to the furrows, yet it does not rise naked and contemptible, as it was sown, but far more excellent and adorned: so it will be also with our bodies, which will indeed be raised the same, but not as they now are, corruptible, faulty, weak and subject to endless accidents." He then illustrates this at once with an elegant comparison, which includes in three or four members all the endowments of glorified bodies.

units.la: Primum est: Seminatur in corruptione, excitatur in incorruptibilitate. Perstat in sementis parabola, ut sepultura huius instar esse doceat, de quo nuper diximus ex Christi verbis, quae Ioan. 12.cap.leguntur. Corruptionis autem nomine non solum putrefactionem corporum intelligit, sed ipsam corruptibilitatem, quae illis agnata est, adeoq; sepultura finem, qui est, ut secundum Dei sententiam, quae Adamo denunciata fuit, in terram, unde sumpti sumus, reuertamur. Itaq; primi huius membri sensus est: Seminatur sive sepelitur corpus, quod sua natura corruptibile est, & ideo sepelitur, ut putrefactione resolutum ad suam originem, terram videlicet, red at: Idem vero excitatur suo tempore in incorruptibilitate, id est, nulli casui aut corruptioni amplius obnoxium. En suscitatur, inquit, de eo ipso corpore loquens, quod seminari dixerat, ne quod aliud aut diversum ab eo imaginemur.
units.tr: The first is: "It is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruptibility." The parable of the seed continues, to teach that this is like burial, about which we lately spoke from the words of Christ, which are read in John chapter 12. By the name of corruption he means not only the putrefaction of bodies, but the corruptibility itself which has grown into them, and so the end of burial, which is that, according to the sentence of God pronounced on Adam, we return to the earth from which we were taken. So the meaning of this first member is: the body is sown or buried, which by its nature is corruptible, and is therefore buried, so that, dissolved by putrefaction, it may return to its origin, namely the earth. But the same body is raised in its time in incorruptibility, that is, no longer subject to any accident or corruption. Behold, he says, it is raised, speaking of the very body that he had said was sown, lest we imagine something else or different from it.

units.la: Prudenter vero Paulus cum corporum corruptione sementem sive seminatione coniungit. Ita enim simul iis respondet iterum, qui resurrectionem fieri posse negant, eo quod corpora corrumpi, adeoque (ut ipsis videtur) in nihilum redigi conspicantur. Ostendit ergo, hic vere impleri quod physici dicunt, Unius corruptionem esse generationem alterius. Non tamen in id incumbit, quod resurrectio causis sive principiis physicis nitatur: sed ut eius exempla in rerum natura commonstret, & eorum ignorantiam atque stupiditatem arguat, qui hic non observant Dei potentiam, quae passim exemplis similibus se nobis conspiciendam praebet. Ut ergo sepultura impiis & prophanis hominibus spem resurrectionis omnem aufert, quia in eius solius spectaculo, quod carni tristissimum est, subsistunt: ita pii ex illa spem firmiorem concipiunt, quando eam sementis instar esse cogitant.
units.tr: Paul wisely joins the sowing or the seeding with the corruption of bodies. For thus he answers at the same time those who deny that the resurrection can happen, because they see bodies corrupted and so, as it seems to them, reduced to nothing. He shows, therefore, that what the natural philosophers say is truly fulfilled here: the corruption of one thing is the generation of another. He does not, however, lean on the claim that the resurrection rests on physical causes or principles; rather, he points out its examples in the nature of things, and rebukes the ignorance and dullness of those who here do not observe the power of God, which everywhere presents itself to us to be seen in similar examples. Therefore, just as burial takes away every hope of resurrection from impious and profane men, because they rest only in the sight of that which is most sorrowful to the flesh, so the godly conceive a firmer hope from it, when they think of it as a kind of seed.

units.la: Itaque imprimis eorum consolationi servit hoc membrum, quibus indignum & molestum videtur, corpus istud corrumpi & computrescere, quod nunc formae flore lepidissimo commendatur, & viribus quam maxime pollet. Audiuntur istiusmodi hominum querulae & lachrymabiles voces. Ergo membra ista tam robusta dissoluentur? ergo forma haec tam amabilis abolebitur? ergo facies ista tanto lepore radians vermibus esca fiet, quae oculos tam suaue micantes extinguent, lumen tam facundam exedent, & carnes tam delicatas depascentur? Quid ni ò stulte? quandoquidem istaeunque ista sint, corruptibilia sunt, nec in alium finem sepeliuntur, quàm ut in primam suam materiam redeant. Quin Dei beneficium agnoscis, qui illa tibi hucusque sua virtute seruauit, ne te viuente adhuc computruerint, aut à vermibus erosa sint: quod olim Antiocho, Syllae, Herodi & similibus accidisse scimus, quorum impiam & confidentem superbiam tam diro tamque tetro supplicio Deus olim ultus est? Cogita, ista, dum corrumpuntur, ad finem suum tendere, ut olim ab omni corruptione liberata resurgant, & beata incorruptibilitate donentur. Itaque, ut D.Chrysostomi verbis utar, quando oculos vides fractos, os contractum, corpus immobile, ne cogitaveris, os istud nunquam porrò loquuturum, oculos istos nihil unquam spectaturos, neque pedes amplius iter facturos esse, quia omnia simul corrupta sint & in nihilum redacta. Ne (inquam) haec dixeris, sed his contraria potius: Os istud aliquando melius loquetur, oculi isti praestantiora his spectabunt, pedes isti supra nubes extollentur, & corpus istud corruptum immortalitatem induet. Hoc qui diligentius expendunt, ii patienter ferunt omnem huius saeculi molestiam, qua multi superantur, ut vitam quoque sibi ipsis amaram faciant. In annalibus nostris scribitur, quendam olim sub annum à Christo nato millesimum ducentesimum & vigesimum, Steina (quod celebre est Tigurinorum municipium) in Rhenum desiliisse, ut vitam hanc abrumperet, cuius non alium usum esse dicebat, quàm edere, bibere, cacare, meiere, indui, exui, dormire & rursum à somno surgere. Nefeiebat infelix homo incorruptibilitatis spem, quae omnibus esse [?] proposita, neque suas cogitatio-nes ultra huius vitae metas extendebat: quod qui faciunt, ijs leuiculi & iucundi videntur labores, quibus finem tam laetum a Deo destinatum esse norunt. Simul autem ista consideratio carnis illi-cebras cupiditates in nobis frenare, & a scelerum licentia nos abstinere debet. Ut enim piorum corpora olim incorruptibilitate donabuntur, ut aeternae vitae gaudijs frui possint: ita impio-rum quoque immortalia fient, neque aboleri amplius poterunt, ut aeternis gehennae flam-mis sufficiant.
units.tr: Therefore this member especially serves the comfort of those to whom it seems unworthy and grievous that this body, which now is commended for the most charming bloom of its beauty and is very strong in its powers, should be corrupted and rot. Such complaints and tearful voices of people are heard: "Shall these members, so robust, be dissolved? Shall this form, so lovely, be abolished? Shall this face, shining with such charm, become food for worms, which will extinguish eyes that sparkle so sweetly, devour a light so graceful, and feed upon flesh so delicate?" Why not, you fool? Since these things are what they are, they are corruptible, and they are buried for no other end than that they may return to their first matter. Indeed, acknowledge God's kindness, who has so far preserved them for you by his power, so that while you are still alive they have not rotted or been eaten away by worms. We know this once happened to Antiochus, Sulla, Herod and similar men, whose impious and arrogant pride God once punished with such a dire and foul torment. Consider that these things, while they are corrupted, are tending to their end, so that they may rise again once freed from all corruption and be endowed with blessed incorruptibility. Therefore, to use the words of St Chrysostom: when you see the eyes broken, the mouth twisted, the body immovable, do not think that this mouth will never speak again, that these eyes will never see anything, and that these feet will no longer walk, because everything has been corrupted together and reduced to nothing. Do not, I say, say these things, but rather their opposites: this mouth will one day speak better, these eyes will see things more excellent than these, these feet will be lifted above the clouds, and this corrupted body will put on immortality. Those who weigh this more carefully bear patiently every trouble of this age, by which many are overcome, so that they make even their own life bitter. In our annals it is written that a certain man, around the year of our Lord 1220, leapt into the Rhine from Stein (a well-known town of the Zurichers) in order to end this life, of which, he said, there was no other use than to eat, drink, defecate, urinate, dress, undress, sleep and rise again from sleep. That unhappy man did not know the hope of incorruptibility, which is set before all, nor did he extend his thoughts beyond the limits of this life. Those who do know it find their labours light and pleasant, since they know that God has appointed for them so joyful an end. At the same time, this consideration ought to restrain the allurements of the flesh and desires within us, and keep us from the license of wickedness. For just as the bodies of the godly will one day be endowed with incorruptibility, so that they may enjoy the joys of eternal life, so the bodies of the ungodly will also become immortal, and will no longer be able to be destroyed, so that they may suffice for the eternal flames of hell.

units.la: Sequitur secundum huius comparationis membrum: Seminatur in ignominia, excitatur in gloria. In ignominia seminari dicit, non ut doceat defunctorum corpora contemptim abijcere, aut contumeliosius tractare (id enim cum communi humanitatis sensu pugnat, & Deo quam maxime displicet, ut alibi ostendimus) sed quae corporis hac vita defuncti conditio sit docet. Etenim omni ornatu atque decore exutum in terram defoditur, adeo ut si spem resurrectionis auferas, a brutorum cadaueribus nihil differat. Qui ergo prius in honore & pretio erant, quibus omne genus officij magno cum honore deferebatur, qui vestitu sumptuoso & molli superbiebant, qui in cubiculis ad omnem temporis vicissitudinem magnifice & commode extructis delitiabantur, ij postquam animam exhalarunt, linteo inuoluti non ex cubiculis modo, verumetiam ex aedibus, imo frequenter extra urbium quoque moenia exportantur, & vel terrae mandantur, vel mausoleis sumptuosis quidem, sed tetro foetore plenis, instar facinorosorum concluduntur, ne viuentium oculos aspectu, nares foetore offendant. Fit etiam plerumque ut cum vita simul omnis quoque eorum authoritas concidat, & multorum cogitationes retegantur: dum qui ipsis viuentibus odium suum egregie celabant, nunc ex eorundem morte ipsis insultandi occasionem arripiunt. Exempla cumprimis memorabilia sunt in Imperatorum quorundam historijs, qui cum pro foemideis adorarentur, mox ubi vitam hanc infelicem finierunt, unco tracti, & in cloacas vel profluentem abiecti sunt. Quibus ex sacris literis Solomonem possumus addere, qui ornatu & splendore omnes totius orbis reges ita superauit, ut Christus de incomparabili magnificentia dicturus, eius exemplo utatur. Quam vero il-le ex sua gloria, opibus & apparatu laudem retulit? aut quem fructum ex eius in totum populum munificentia atque beneficijs posteri perceperunt? Eum ex populi ad Roboamum filium vocibus agnoscere licet: Pater tuus aggrauauit iugum nostrum. Item: Quae pars nobis in Dauide? Non est nobis haereditas in filio Isai: Ad tentoria tua o Israel, provide domi tuae Dauid. Et si verum dicere oporteat, infelicior est hac parte regum & principum potentissimorum conditio, quam hominum priuatorum atq; tenuium: quia plus his amittunt, & plurimorum odijs exponuntur, a quibus immunes & satis tuti sunt, qui vitam suam in tenui aut mediocri fortuna transigunt. Prudenter ergo Cyrus iam moriens suos admonuit, ne mortui corpus spectandum exponerent: non ignorans scilicet, quantum hominis authoritati mors deroget. Quod unum si omnes frequentius cogitarent, prob Deum immortalem, quantum decederet fastui, superbiae, corporis curae, luxui & voluptatum studijs, quibus stultissimi homines seipsos simul & alios nequicquam fatigant?
units.tr: Next comes the second member of this comparison: "It is sown in dishonour, it is raised in glory." Paul says it is sown in dishonour, not to teach that the bodies of the dead should be cast off with contempt or handled with insult (that is contrary to common human feeling and displeases God most of all, as we have shown elsewhere), but to show what state the body is in once a person has died in this life. For stripped of all ornament and dignity, it is buried in the earth, so that if you take away the hope of resurrection, it differs in nothing from the carcasses of beasts. Those who were formerly held in honour and esteem, who were served with every kind of service and great deference, who took pride in sumptuous and soft clothing and delighted in bedchambers magnificently and comfortably built against every change of season: once they have breathed their last, they are wrapped in linen and carried out, not only from their bedchambers but from their houses, and often even beyond the walls of the cities, and are either committed to the earth or shut up, like criminals, in tombs that are indeed sumptuous but full of foul stench, so that their smell may not offend the eyes and noses of the living. It also commonly happens that with life all their authority falls away too, and the thoughts of many are laid bare: those who, while the men were alive, carefully concealed their hatred, now seize the chance to insult them at their death. The most memorable examples are in the histories of certain emperors, who, while they were worshipped as gods, were soon after their unhappy lives ended dragged with hooks and thrown into the sewers or into the flowing river. To these from Holy Scripture we may add Solomon, who surpassed all the kings of the whole world in ornament and splendour, so that Christ, when he speaks of incomparable magnificence, uses his example. But what praise did he gain from his glory, his riches and his display? Or what fruit did posterity receive from his generosity and benefits to the whole people? We may recognise this from the words of the people to Rehoboam his son: "Your father made our yoke heavy." Likewise: "What portion have we in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, O Israel; now look to your own house, David" (1 Kings 12:16). And, if one must speak the truth, the condition of kings and most powerful princes is more unhappy in this respect than that of private and humble men, because they lose more, and are exposed to the hatred of many, from which those who pass their lives in a modest or middling fortune are free and fairly safe. Wisely, then, Cyrus, as he was dying, admonished his people not to expose his dead body for viewing, being evidently well aware how much death takes away from a man's authority. If all men thought more often of this one thing alone, good God, how much pride, arrogance, care for the body, luxury and devotion to pleasures would it take away, with which the most foolish men wear out both themselves and others to no purpose?

units.la: At quia haec frustra dicuntur carni & mundo deditis, audiant pij, quod de ipsorum corpori-bus olim resuscitandis opponitur: Excitatur (inquit) in gloria. Non debet hoc de huius seculi gloria intelligi, quae tunc nulla erit amplius: sed de coelesti, quam Christus nobis suae mortis merito ac-quisiuit. Erit ea multiplex. Nam corpora nostra ab omni vitio & corruptibilitate liberata glorio-si Christi corpori (ut ad Philippenses noster Apostolus scribit) conformia fient. Eadem illam quoque gloriam percipient, quam (ut prophetae verbis utar) oculus non vidit, auris non audiuit, & quae omnem humani intellectus captum longe excedit. Accedit his, quod tunc patebit toti mundo Dei filios esse eos, qui nunc hominum scelerati-ssimi habentur, & omni contumeliarum atq; conuiciorum genere obruuntur. Vide Sap.4.& 5.cap. Item 1.Joan.3.
units.tr: But since these things are said in vain to those given over to the flesh and the world, let the godly hear what is set against the future raising of their own bodies: "It is raised in glory," he says. This must not be understood of the glory of this age, which will then be no more at all, but of the heavenly glory which Christ has won for us by the merit of his death. This glory will be manifold. For our bodies, freed from every defect and corruptibility, will be made conformable to the glorious body of Christ (as our Apostle writes to the Philippians). They will also receive that glory which (to use the words of the prophet) "eye has not seen, nor ear heard," and which far surpasses the grasp of the human mind. In addition to this, it will then be plain to the whole world that those who are now counted the most wicked of men, and are overwhelmed with every kind of insult and abuse, are the sons of God. See Wisdom 4 and 5. Likewise 1 John 3.

units.la: Debent ista nobis consolationem afferre, si quando nos tam nobisipsis quam alijs hominibus fastidio vel nauseae esse sentimus: aut quando propter fidei verae confessionem, aut admonendi li-beratem indigni iudicamur, quibus cum aliquis commercium siue consuetudinem habeat. Erit enim aliquando rerum vicissitudo. Auferetur tunc omne illud, quod nunc corpori dedecus parit, aut fastidium: siue illud morbus sit, siue senectus, siue quodcunq; aliud vitium. Hominum vero in-dicia sic mutabuntur, vt qui nunc nos odio dignos iudicant, tunc non sint manifesta acerbissimi do-loris significatione honorifice de nobis sentiant & loquantur. Et cur de eo dubitemus, quod in no-uissimo die certo fiet, quando huius generis multa bodie, dum mundus hic infelix dominari vide-tur, fieri cernimus? Raro enim fallit, quod Dauid & Solomon dixerunt: Memoria iusti vsq; durabit. Item: Memoria iusti laudem habet. Psal. 112. Prouerb. 10.
units.tr: These things ought to console us whenever we feel that we are a disgust and a nausea both to ourselves and to other men, or when, on account of the confession of the true faith, or of freedom in admonishing, we are judged unworthy of any fellowship or association with someone. For there will at some time be a reversal of circumstances. Then all that now brings dishonour or distaste to the body will be taken away, whether it be sickness, old age, or any other defect. The judgements of men, too, will change, so that those who now judge us worthy of hatred will then not be able to speak and think of us honourably without a clear sign of the bitterest grief. And why should we doubt what will certainly happen on the last day, when we see many things of this kind happening today, while this unhappy world seems to hold sway? For what David and Solomon said rarely fails: "The memory of the just will last for ever." Likewise: "The memory of the just has praise" (Ps. 112; Prov. 10).

units.la: Tertium comparationis huius membrum est: Seminatur in infirmitate, excitatur in potentia. Loquitur Paulus de ipsius naturae nostrae infirmitate, cui corpora nostra ita subiecta sunt, vt ne nunc quidem dum viuunt resistere possint morbis, fami, siti, lassitudini, senectae & infinitis aliis affectionibus, quae nobis negotium faciunt. Quis enim ne vnquam aegrotet, efficere poterit? Equidem praeter omnem expectationem morbi obrepunt, qui corpus totum debilitant. Ita fames & sitis inuitos quoque lacessunt. Senectus vero nihil huius cogitantibus obrepit, tacitisque senescimus annis, vt Poeta dicebat. Quid, quod ne dormire quidem, neque ventris excrementis nos quoties libet leuare possumus, adeo vt saepe medicos & pharmacopolas omnes hic fatigari oporteat? Qui vero suæ voluntati imperare potest? quis affectus suos exuere, quo minus ea subinde animo occursent quae minime vult? Sunt haec magna infirmitatis nostrae argumenta, quae nemo negare potest. Accedit tamen his mors, quam omnis terra viam olim dixit Dauid, quia moriendi necessitas omnibus incumbit, quam neque consilio, neque corporis viribus aut celeritate, subterfugere, neque nominis nostri existimatione vel authoritate depellere à nobis possumus. Sola enim neque potentia & dignitate mouetur, neque muneribus placatur. Quid multis? Ea est natura nostrae infirmitas, vt non temere olim ex Domini mandato Propheta exclamauerit: Omnis caro fænum, & omnis gloria carnis flos agri. Est de his frequenter cogitandum, ne securi superbia-mus, aut huius vitae studijs addicti coelestia negligamus.
units.tr: The third member of this comparison is: "It is sown in weakness, it is raised in power." Paul speaks of the weakness of our very nature, to which our bodies are so subject that, even now while they live, they cannot resist sicknesses, hunger, thirst, weariness, old age and countless other afflictions which give us trouble. For who can ensure that he never falls ill? Indeed, diseases creep upon us beyond all expectation and weaken the whole body. So hunger and thirst assail even the unwilling. Old age creeps upon those who think of none of this, and we grow old with years that pass in silence, as the poet used to say. And what of the fact that we cannot even sleep, nor relieve the excretions of the belly whenever we wish, so that physicians and apothecaries must often be worn out here altogether? Who can command his own will? Who can strip off his feelings, so that things he does not want do not from time to time spring up in his mind? These are great proofs of our weakness, which no one can deny. Added to them is death, which David once said is the way of all the earth, because the necessity of dying lies upon all men, and which we cannot escape by counsel, by bodily strength or by speed, nor drive away from ourselves by the reputation or authority of our name. For death is moved neither by power nor by rank, and is not appeased by gifts. Why say more? Such is the weakness of our nature that the prophet, at the command of the Lord, once rightly cried out: "All flesh is grass, and all the glory of flesh is the flower of the field." We ought to think of these things often, lest we become complacent in pride, or, given over to the pursuits of this life, neglect heavenly things.

units.la: Ut vero ista mortem nobis leuem faciunt, per quam infirmitate ista molestissima libera-mur: ita consolationem efficacissimam habet, quod huic opponitur. Excitatur in potentia. Lo-quitur enim non de Dei potentia, qua olim nos excitandos fore alibi diximus, sed de ea potentia, qua tunc corpora nostra donabuntur, quando nullis porro affectionibus siue casibus obnoxia, de omnibus triumphabunt in beata illa immortalitate, quae nunc nobis infesta sunt. Tunc enim cef-sabit gemitus omnis, tunc omnes lachrymae abstergentur, tunc etiam finem habebunt dolor, cura, folicitudines: tunc fracta & extincta iacebunt Satana, peccati & mortis vires. Quid ergo nunc dolemus & tristamur propter ea, quibus resistere non possumus? Impotentia equidem huius se-culi propria est, & hanc cum regibus quoque, qui potentissimi videntur, communem habemus. Feramus ergo patienter quod mutari non potest, certam vero & firmam concipiamus eius po-tentiae spem, quae ad seculum futurum pertinet, quam similiter nemo impedire poterit, quo minus ea nobis in Christo vindice & seruatore nostro obtingat.
units.tr: But just as these things make death light for us, through which we are freed from this most troublesome weakness, so the opposite point holds the most powerful consolation: "It is raised in power." For he speaks not of the power of God, by which we shall be raised, as we have said elsewhere, but of that power by which our bodies will then be endowed, when, no longer subject to any affections or accidents, they will triumph over all things in that blessed immortality, which now are hostile to us. For then all groaning will cease, then all tears will be wiped away, then pain, care and anxieties will also have an end; then the powers of Satan, of sin and of death will lie broken and extinguished. Why, then, do we now grieve and sorrow over things we cannot resist? Weakness is indeed the mark of this age, and we share it even with kings, who seem the most powerful. Let us therefore bear patiently what cannot be changed, but let us conceive a certain and firm hope of that power which belongs to the age to come, which likewise no one will be able to prevent from being granted to us in Christ, our defender and saviour.

units.la: Porrò quia longum esset omnes corporis infirmitates recensere, quibus in huius vitae stadio currentes obnoxij sumus, & futuri seculi dotes atque gaudia, quae nostrae etiam rationis captum superant, summatim & uno (quod aiunt) verbo omnia quae hic dici possunt complectens [?], dicit: Seminatur corpus animale, excitatur corpus spirituale. Et ne de re, quae nuspiam in rerum natura extet, loqui videatur, huius dicti rationem hanc affert: Est corpus animale, & est corpus spirituale. Animale corpus dicit, ut etiam hominem animalem, quod solius anima naturalis facultatibus viuit, regitur & feruatur, eaque ablata concidit atque aboletur. Id vero quia ipsum sibi non sufficit, adminiculis siue subsidijs naturalibus opus habet, ut pote cibo, potu, somno, vestibus, remedijs & alijs similibus: Huic opponitur corpus spirituale, sic dictum, non quod spirituali substantia constet, sed quod animam quidem suam seruabit (haec enim & immortalis est) & cum corpore in coelis aeterni gaudij consors erit, ut alibi diximus) at simul spiritus virtute excel-lentiori donabitur, quae illud reget & seruabit absque adminiculis illis, quibus nunc sustenta-mur. Idem cessantibus quoq; affectibus alijs, quae nunc spiritui repugnant, huic volens & non sine gaudio atque exultatione obtemperabit. Ita veteres olim hoc dictum interpretati sunt. Augustinus enim in Epist. 146. corpus spirituale dici ait, quia spiritui inseparabiliter copulatu maneat. Et lib. de Ciuitate Dei 13. Cap. 22. Spiritualia erunt, non quia corpora esse desistent, sed quia spiritu viuificante subsistent. Item Cap. 20. Sicut spiritus carni seruiens non incongrue carnalis: ita caro spiritui seruiens recte appellatur spiritualis: non quod in spiritu conuertetur, sicuti nonnulli putant ex eo quod scriptum est: Seminatur corpus animale, suscitatur spirituale. D. Ambrosius ita definit: Animale corpus est, dum cibis sustentatur, ut viuat: spirituale autem, dum horum nihil indigebit, conuersum in vitam. Omnia supra dicta hoc sensu clauduntur. Non enim corpus anima-le semper hic habere potest Spiritum sanctum: tunc vero, id est, in resurrectione semper manebit in sanctis. Theodoretus autem ita scribit: Animale corpus, quod ab anima gubernatur: spirituale, quod a spiritu regitur. Chrysostomus sic interpretatur: Nunc gratia spiritus saepe magna ex parte recedit peccantibus quibusdam: & quamvis spiritus animae adsit, vita tamen carnis est. Tunc autem perpetuo manebit cum carne iustorum, & huius erit robur simul praesente anima. Epiphanius vero contra Origenem Adamant. haec prodidit: Non aliud corpus est spirituale, & aliud anima-le: sed idem animale, idemque spirituale. Quando enim sumus in mundo, & corruptibilia carnis opera facimus, corpora sunt animalia. Seruimus enim animae in mundo in absurditatibus. Quando autem resurgimus, non amplius est animae seruitus: sed spiritus consequentia, hinc iam habens arrha-bonem, per hoc quod dictum est: Si viuimus spiritu, spiritu etiam ambulemus: Si vero etiam spiritu ambulamus, actiones corporis mortificantes viuemus. Haec ex veterum scriptis adducere libuit propter eos, qui hodie nouum dogma, & eruditae illi sanctaeq; vetustati ignotum, inuehunt de corporibus clarificatis, quae proprietatibus naturalibus spoliant, & loco contineri negant. At ni-hil horum neque Scriptura tradit, neque veteres senserunt, quos spiritualis corporis tres hasce do-tes agnouisse apparet: Primam, quod diuini spiritus virtute absque externis adminiculis feruetur & subsistat. Alteram, quod a spiritu nunquam deseratur. Tertiam, quod eidem obtemperet, ces-santibus iam animalis hominis passionibus atque cupiditatibus. Atqui nulla harum corporis substantiae quicquam derogat. Si enim in corpore corruptibili & mortali potuerunt Moses & Elias per dies quadraginta absque cibo viuere, manente tamen corporum veritate, quanto magis illa, vbi clarificata fuerint, absque cibo aut alimento durare poterunt? Si item nunc Spiritui sancto in corporibus nostris locus est, vt in electis regnet & agat, multo magis hoc fiet postquam peccatum & Satan defecerint. Sunt ergo nimium ridiculi, qui ex hoc loco occasionem arripiunt contendendi de corpore quodam spirituali, cuius substantia mutetur, quodque naturalibus proprietatibus exu-tum natura sua neque palpabile sit, neque visibile, neque loco certo contineatur. Conuincuntur hi exemplo Christi, cuius corpori glorioso nostra oportere conformia fieri, Paulus testatur. At ille se spiritum esse negat, carnem & ossa se habere affirmat, & quamuis neque cibo neque potu opus haberet, edit tamen & bibit, ne de corporis eius veri restitutione discipuli dubitarent. Itaque nos omissis curiosis & superuacaneis disputationibus, Dei bonitatem agnoscamus, qui corpora haec nostra corruptibilia, ignominiosa, infirma & animalia olim tanto honore dignabitur, vt incorruptibilia, gloriosa, valida & nullis porro casibus siue vitijs obnoxia fiant: & hac spe confirmati, patienter feramus huius seculi incommoda atque molestias, quibus coelestis & aeterna gloria tandem succedet, quam in CHRISTO IESV obtinebimus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum ; Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, since it would take too long to list all the bodily infirmities to which we are subject as we run the race of this life, and since the endowments and joys of the age to come surpass even the grasp of our reason, Paul sums up everything that can be said here in a single phrase, saying: "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body." So that he may not seem to speak of something that exists nowhere in nature, he gives the reason for this saying: there is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body. He calls it a natural body because a natural man lives by the faculties of the natural soul alone, is governed and preserved by them, and falls apart and perishes when they are taken away. Since this body is not sufficient for itself, it needs natural aids or supports, such as food, drink, sleep, clothing, remedies and the like. Opposed to this is the spiritual body, so called not because it consists of a spiritual substance, but because it will keep its soul (for the soul is immortal too), and will share with the body in eternal joy in heaven, as we have said elsewhere. At the same time, it will be given a more excellent power of the spirit, which will govern and preserve it without those supports on which we now depend. Likewise, when the other affections that now resist the spirit have ceased, the body will obey the spirit willingly and with joy and exultation. The ancients interpreted this saying in this way. For Augustine, in Epistle 146, says that the body is called spiritual because it remains inseparably joined to the spirit. And in book 13 of The City of God, chapter 22, he says: "They will be spiritual, not because they cease to be bodies, but because they subsist by the life-giving spirit." Likewise, in chapter 20: "Just as a spirit serving the flesh is not inappropriately called fleshly, so flesh serving the spirit is rightly called spiritual, not because it will be turned into spirit, as some think from the words written: 'It is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body.'" Ambrose defines it thus: the body is natural while it is sustained by foods so that it may live, but spiritual when it needs none of these and has been turned into life. All the things said above are contained in this sense. For the natural body cannot always have the Holy Spirit here; but then, that is, in the resurrection, it will always remain in the saints. Theodoret writes: the natural body is the one governed by the soul; the spiritual body is the one ruled by the spirit. Chrysostom explains it thus: now the grace of the Spirit often withdraws, to a great extent, from some who sin, and although the spirit is present with the soul, the life is that of the flesh; but then it will remain forever with the flesh of the righteous, and the strength of the flesh will be theirs, the soul being present at the same time. Epiphanius, however, in his work against Origen (the Adamantius), set out this: the spiritual body is not one thing and the natural body another, but the same body is both natural and spiritual. For while we are in the world and do the works of the corruptible flesh, the bodies are natural, since we serve the soul in the world in its follies. But when we rise again, there is no longer servitude to the soul, but a consequence of the spirit, already having the earnest of it in the words: "If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit; and if we walk by the Spirit, by the Spirit we shall mortify the deeds of the body and live." I have thought it worthwhile to bring forward these things from the writings of the ancients, on account of those who today introduce a new doctrine, unknown to that learned and holy antiquity, concerning glorified bodies, which they strip of their natural properties and deny to be contained in any place. But neither Scripture teaches this, nor did the ancients think so; they clearly recognised three marks of the spiritual body: first, that it is preserved and subsists by the power of the divine Spirit without external aids; second, that it is never forsaken by the Spirit; third, that it obeys the Spirit, the passions and desires of the natural man having now ceased. Yet none of these takes anything away from the substance of the body. For if Moses and Elijah could live for forty days without food while in corruptible and mortal bodies, the reality of their bodies remaining, how much more could those bodies, once they have been made glorious, last without food or nourishment? Likewise, if the Holy Spirit now has a place in our bodies so that he may reign and act in the elect, much more will this happen after sin and Satan have ceased. Therefore those men are very ridiculous who seize on this passage as an occasion to contend about a certain spiritual body whose substance is changed, and which, stripped of its natural properties, is by its nature neither palpable, nor visible, nor contained in a fixed place. Such men are refuted by the example of Christ, to whose glorious body Paul testifies that ours must be made conformable. Yet Christ denies that he is a spirit, affirms that he has flesh and bones, and although he had no need of food or drink, he nevertheless ate and drank, so that his disciples might not doubt the true restoration of his body. Therefore, setting aside curious and superfluous disputations, let us acknowledge the goodness of God, who will one day honour these our corruptible, dishonourable, weak and natural bodies with such great honour that they will become incorruptible, glorious, strong, and no longer subject to any accidents or vices; and, confirmed by this hope, let us patiently bear the troubles and annoyances of this age, after which heavenly and eternal glory will at last follow, which we shall obtain in Christ Jesus, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXXV.
units.tr: HOMILY LXXXV.

units.la: Ita enim scriptum est: Factus est primus homo Adam in animā viuentem: posterior autem Adam in spiritum viuificantem. At non prius quod spirituale, sed animale, deinde spirituale. Primus homo e terra, terrenus: secundus homo, ipse Dominus e coelo. Qualis terrenus ille, tales & qui terreni sunt: & qualis ille coelestis, tales & qui coelestes sunt. Et sicut gestauimus imaginem terreni, gestabimus etiam imaginem coelestis. Hoc autem dico fratres, carnem & sanguinem non posse regni Dei haereditatem consequi, neq; corruptio incorruptibilitatis haereditatem accipit.
units.tr: For it is written: "The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit. Yet the spiritual was not first, but the natural, and afterwards the spiritual. The first man is of the earth, earthy; the second man is the Lord from heaven. As is the earthy, so are they also who are earthy; and as is the heavenly, so are they also who are heavenly. And as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly. Now this I say, brethren, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does corruption inherit incorruption."

units.la: Quemadmodum sancti cultores Dei omnes, se in terris peregrinos esse, neq; civitatem permanentem habere confessi sunt, ita omnes huius vitae labores atq; pericula spe futurae resurre-ctionis & vitae aeternae superarunt. Exempla eorum nobis passim scriptura proponit, ut ea imitemur. Atqui spem iam vehementer labefactat mortis & quae hanc sequuntur corruptionis corporum nostrorum consideratio: quia ut ea nobis restituantur, & gloriosiora fiant, carnis rationi impossi-bile esse videtur. Ideo Paulus non modo nos resurrecturos esse argumentis validissimis demonstrat, verumetiam diligenter docet, qualia olim corpora nostra futura sint, ut quam ex horum corruptione fœda & abominabili concipimus, dubitatio, gloriosae illorum & beatae instaurationis consideratione discutiatur. Et huc faciunt imprimis, quae nuper dicta sunt: Seminatur in corruptione, excitatur in incorruptibilitate: Seminatur in ignominia, excitatur in gloria, &c. Utq; uno verbo causam hanc absolveret, tandem subiecit: Seminatur corpus animale, excitatur corpus spirituale: quo dicto omnia comprehendit, quae de corporum clarificatorum gloria & perfectissima conditione dici possunt. Id vero quia multis obscurius dictum videri poterat, nunc diligentius interpretatur, eiusq; rationes certas & solidas reddit.
units.tr: Just as all the holy worshippers of God confessed that they were strangers on earth and had no lasting city, so all the labours and dangers of this life have been overcome by the hope of the future resurrection and eternal life. Scripture sets their examples before us everywhere, that we may imitate them. Yet the consideration of death, and of the corruption of our bodies that follows it, already greatly weakens this hope, since it seems impossible to human reason that these bodies should be restored to us and made more glorious. Therefore Paul not only demonstrates by the most forceful arguments that we shall rise again, but also carefully teaches what our bodies will be like, so that the doubt which arises from the foul and loathsome corruption of these bodies may be dispelled by considering their glorious and blessed restoration. To this purpose especially belong the words said just before: "It is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption; it is sown in dishonour, it is raised in glory," and so on. And so that he might settle the whole matter in a single phrase, he finally added: "It is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body." In these words he comprehends everything that can be said about the glory and most perfect condition of glorified bodies. Since this statement might seem rather obscure to many, he now explains it more carefully and gives sure and solid reasons for it.

units.la: Et initio quidem, ne qui locutionibus istis offenderentur, tanquam novis & in humani generis contumeliam confictis, quasi homines nihil a brutis differant, docet eas ex Scriptura & religionis nostrae arcanis esse petitas, sic dicens: Ita enim scriptum est: Factus est primus homo Adam in animam viventem. Extat locus Genes. secundo Cap. ubi sic describitur primi parentis nostri creatio: Fecit Dominus Deus hominem, pulverem sive lutum de terra, & inflavit in nares eius spiritum vitae, factusq; est homo in animam viventem. Ex his verbis occasione arrepta, Christum cum Adamo conferens, mox subiicit: Posterior autem Adam in spiritum vivificantem. Id vero facit Apostolus, ut ex prima generis nostri origine discamus, quid Adam, quidue Christus nobis contulerint, & unde discrimen illud corporis animalis & spiritualis enascatur. Est ergo utrumque nobis considerandus.
units.tr: At the outset, so that no one might take offence at these expressions, as though they were new and invented to the disgrace of the human race, as if men differed in nothing from the brutes, he shows that they are drawn from Scripture and from the secrets of our religion, saying: "For it is written: The first man Adam was made a living soul." There is a passage in the second chapter of Genesis where the creation of our first parent is described thus: "The Lord God formed man, dust or clay from the earth, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and man became a living soul." Taking occasion from these words, comparing Christ with Adam, he immediately adds: "The last Adam a life-giving spirit." The Apostle does this so that from the first origin of our race we may learn what Adam and what Christ have conferred upon us, and whence that difference between the natural and the spiritual body arises. Both, then, must be considered by us.

units.la: Adamum primum hominem dicit, non eam modo ob causam, quòd primus conditus est, sed quòd humani generis principium & author est, ex quo omnes homines originem suam duxerunt. Hunc autem proponit, ut in eo agnoscamus conditionem nostram, quam fere in nobis ipsis non agnoscimus. Plerique enim sibi persuadent, se semideos quosdam esse, & suis viribus suique arbitrij libertate gloriantur, quasi sibipsis ad omnia possint sufficere. Vult ergo ut originem nostram diligentius expendamus. Vbi primum occurrit ipsa Adami creatio. Vnde vero ille ortum habuit? Num Verbi aeterni virtute ex nihilo, ut reliquae mundi partes, creatus est? Nequaquam, sed ex materia omnium contemptissima, sordidissimaque illius corpus formauit Dominus. Vnde autem eidem spiritus vitae? Num hunc ex semetipso habuit? Ne hoc quidem, sed Deus sufflauit in nares eius, & sic lutea illa & inanimis massa, quae & sensu & ratione carebat, facta est in animam viuentem, id est, animal viuum. Ex Deo ergo habemus, quòd homines sumus, quòd viuimus, spiramus & movemur. Neque de Adamo & posteris eius aliud dicitur, quàm quod de piscibus, reptilibus & omnibus alijs bestijs sive pecoribus scriptum invenitur in creationis mundi & diluuij historia. Ergo quoad primam nostram originem, ex Adamo nihil aliud habemus, quàm quòd homines sumus animales, infirmi, mortales & omnis generis affectionibus obnoxij. Brutis vero animantibus non alia in re differimus, quàm quòd animae nostrae immortales & cognitionis Dei capaces sunt. Non temere igitur a Lactantio dictum est, hominem a brutis aut reliquis animalibus neque ratione neque sermonis usu, sed sola religione differre, quae ex vera Dei cognitione dependet. Rationis enim usum in animalibus quoque videmus, quando & pericula evitare, & in futurum prospicere sibi norunt. Nec proprie muta dici possunt pleraque ex illis, cum & voces suas habeant, & eas quidem non eiusdem semper soni, seq; mutuo intelligant. Quid, quòd aues quaedam humanas quoque voces sonare discunt, quas ita proferunt, ut eas rationis usu prorsus carere, nemo sanus dixerit. Mira sane de luscinijs Plinius scribit, superant tamen ista omnia, quæ nostro seculo acciderunt, quando illas humana vōtē[?] de rebus feriis diu multumq; collocutas fuisse constat. Quòd si de iis dicere libeat, quæ ad victum parandum & ad vitæ conseruationem per|tinent, multùm in illis nos pleraq; alia animalia superant, quæ & facilius & commodius viuunt. In horum consideratione nos frequentius versari conueniebat, quæ & superbiæ spiritum validissi-mè reprimeret, & nos ad cœlestis atq; melioris vitæ studium excitaret.
units.tr: He calls Adam the first man, not only for the reason that he was created first, but because he is the beginning and author of the human race, from whom all men have derived their origin. He sets him before us so that in him we may recognise our condition, which we scarcely recognise in ourselves. For most people persuade themselves that they are a kind of demigods, and they glory in their own powers and in the freedom of their own will, as if they were sufficient for everything by themselves. He wishes us therefore to weigh our origin more carefully. Here first comes the very creation of Adam. But whence did he receive his beginning? Was he created out of nothing by the power of the eternal Word, like the other parts of the world? By no means; the Lord formed his body out of the most despised and filthiest material. And whence did he receive the breath of life? Did he have it from himself? Not even this, but God breathed into his nostrils, and so that clay and lifeless mass, which lacked both sense and reason, became a living soul, that is, a living animal. We have it from God, therefore, that we are men, that we live, breathe and move. Nor is anything said of Adam and his posterity other than what is found written of fishes, reptiles and all other beasts or cattle in the history of the creation of the world and of the flood. So, as regards our first origin, from Adam we have nothing more than that we are natural, weak, mortal men, subject to every kind of affliction. Indeed, we differ from the brute animals in nothing else than that our souls are immortal and capable of knowing God. It was not without reason, then, that Lactantius said that man differs from the brutes and the other animals not by reason or the use of speech, but by religion alone, which depends on the true knowledge of God. For we see the use of reason even in animals, since they know how both to avoid dangers and to provide for the future. Nor can many of them be properly called mute, since they have their own voices, and these not always of the same sound, and they understand one another. What of the fact that some birds also learn to utter human words, which they pronounce in such a way that no sane person would say they lack the use of reason? Plinius writes marvellous things about nightingales. Yet all these are surpassed by what happened in our own age, when it is known that certain birds conversed at length with human voice about ordinary matters. But if one wishes to speak of those things which pertain to procuring food and preserving life, in many of these we are surpassed by other animals, which live both more easily and more comfortably. It would have been fitting for us to dwell more often on the consideration of these things, which would powerfully restrain the spirit of pride and stir us to the pursuit of a heavenly and better life.

units.la: Nunc ad Christum veniamus, de quo sic scribit Paulus: Posterior, siue posteremus[?] Adam factus est in spiritum viuificantem. Adamum dicit, vt hominem verum factum esse doceat, & quam nobiscum habet naturæ nostræ communionem exprimat: quo sensu Lucas etiam eius genealogiam ad primum Adamum ipsum deducit, & ipse ne quid dubitemus se Filium hominis dicere consueuit. Posteriùs vero Adamum dicit, non ordinis causa, quasi nemo posteriùs[?] homo natus sit, sed vt eum ostendat alterum esse humani generis instauratorem, & solum quidem, posteriorem nullus alius in posterum expectari debeat. Quo vno multæ superstitiones confutantur. Quia enim duo tantum sunt humani generis patres, quorum alter nobis vitæ animalis author est, & ideo primus Adam dicitur: alter spiritualis & æternæ; quem ideo posterius Adamum Scriptura vocat, sequitur, turpiter errare Iudæos, qui post hunc exhibitum adhuc alium Messiam ipsi Seruatorem expectant: turpius item Turcas falli, qui Mahumetem illi præferunt, quasi is perfectiorem salutem pepererit. Deniq; omnes alij erroris continentur, quotquot nō vno illo contenti, alia comminiscuntur, per quæ nos seruari oporteat.
units.tr: Now let us come to Christ, of whom Paul writes thus: "The last Adam was made a life-giving spirit." He calls him Adam in order to teach that he was made a true man and to express the communion of nature that he has with us. In this sense Luke also traces his genealogy back to the first Adam himself, and Christ himself was accustomed to call himself the Son of Man, so that we should have no doubt about it. He calls him the last Adam, not for the sake of order, as though no man had been born after him, but to show that he is the other restorer of the human race, and that no other is to be expected in the future. By this one point many superstitions are refuted. For since there are only two fathers of the human race, of whom the one is the author of our animal life and is therefore called the first Adam, and the other of spiritual and eternal life, whom Scripture for that reason calls the last Adam, it follows that the Jews err shamefully who, after this one has been revealed, still look for another Messiah and Saviour; and the Turks are deceived more shamefully still, who prefer Mahomet to him, as though he had brought forth a more perfect salvation. Finally, all others are caught in error, however many, not content with that one, invent other means by which we ought to be saved.

units.la: Quid autem de Christo dicit Paulus? Is factus est in spiritum viuificantem. Quæ verba non ita accipi debent, quasi anima rationali Christus caruerit, eius verò locum supplemerit Dei Spiri-|tus siue diuina natura, vt Apollinaris olim fabulabatur. Nam scimus Christum vere hominem factum fuisse, & animæ suæ mentionem facere, quam contristari fatetur, quod in diuinam naturam minimè cadit. In Spiritum ergo viuificantem factus esse dicitur, quia non solum animam habuit, vt nos, sed cum illa coniunctum simul Spiritum Dei, qui corporaliter (vt ita cum Paulo loquamur) in illo habitauit, vt non seipsum modò propria virtute à mortuis excitarit, sed simul omnes homines excitare posset ad vitam immortalem. Ideo Ioannes de illo scripsit: In ipso vita erat, & vita erat lux illa hominum. Vt ergo in Adamo, primo parente nostro, tota hominis natura, quoad corpus & animam, collapsa fuit: ita in Christo, qui alter nobis vitæ author est, totus homo instauratur. Ex illo enim habemus spiritum viuificantem, qui vt ex Verbi semine renatos illuminat & vita noua donat, quam secundum Dei voluntatem viuimus: ita olim corpora quoq; ad vitam immortalem reuocabit, vt æternis regni sui cœlestis gaudijs fruantur. Facit ergo ad huius loci expositionem, quod Paulus ad Rom. scribit octauo cap. Si Christus in vobis est, corpus quidem mortuum est propter peccatum, (id est, corpus iflud animale, quod ex Adamo accepimus, adhuc morti obnoxium est propter peccati fomitem & reliquias, quæ electis quoq; inhærent, quoad in hoc seculo vixerint) spiritus autem vita est propter iustitiam, id est, spiritu viuitis propter iustitiam, quam nobis Christus acquisiuit, & quam fide estis amplexi. Et mox ad corpora quoq; nostra hoc illius beneficium extendens, hæc subiungit: Sed si spiritus eius, qui excitauit IESVM à mortuis, habitat in vobis, is qui excitauit Christum ex mortuis, viuificabit & mortalia corpora vestra per inhabitantem eius Spiritum in vobis. Ita verò illustratur discrimen illud hominis animalis & spiritualis, quod item in corporibus nostris indicatur quoad præsens hoc & futurum seculum. Vt enim ex Adamo animales, corruptibiles & mortales nascimur: ita in Christo renati ex verbi semine per spiritum eius spirituales, incorruptibiles, immortales & conditionis cœlestis capaces efficimur.
units.tr: But what does Paul say about Christ? "He was made a life-giving spirit." These words must not be taken as though Christ lacked a rational soul, and that the Spirit of God or the divine nature took its place, as Apollinaris once fabled. For we know that Christ was truly made man, and he speaks of his soul, which he confesses was sorrowful, something which by no means applies to the divine nature. He is said to have been made a life-giving spirit because he had not only a soul, as we do, but with it the Spirit of God joined together, who dwelt in him bodily (to speak thus with Paul), so that he could not only raise himself from the dead by his own power, but could also raise all men to immortal life. Therefore John wrote of him: "In him was life, and that life was the light of men." Just as in Adam, our first parent, the whole nature of man, as to body and soul, fell, so in Christ, who is the other author of our life, the whole man is restored. For from him we have a life-giving spirit, who enlightens those reborn from the seed of the Word and gives a new life, by which we live according to the will of God; and in the same way he will one day also restore our bodies to immortal life, so that they may enjoy the eternal joys of his heavenly kingdom. This is what Paul writes in Romans chapter eight, which helps to explain this passage: "If Christ is in you, the body is dead because of sin" (that is, that natural body which we received from Adam is still subject to death because of the tinder of sin and the remnants which cling even to the elect, as long as they live in this age), "but the spirit is life because of righteousness" (that is, the spirit lives because of the righteousness which Christ has obtained for us and which you have embraced by faith).
