And presently, extending this benefit of his to our bodies too, he adds: "But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you." Thus is illustrated that difference between the natural and the spiritual man, which is likewise indicated in our bodies, both in this present age and in the age to come. For just as we are born from Adam natural, corruptible and mortal, so, reborn in Christ from the seed of the Word, through his Spirit we are made spiritual, incorruptible, immortal and capable of a heavenly condition.

units.la: Commendatur hîs plus quàm paterna Dei bonitas, quam & in primo parente nostro Adamo, & postea in posteris eius abunde declarauit. Illum ex luto terræ desumptum, & quoad vitam huius seculi nihilo præstantiorem aliis animalibus, in summam dignitatem euexit, & creatorum omnium principem constituit. Nos autem, qui in illo lapsi & perditi, imò filij iræ facti eramus, vna cum illo in vitam restituit per Filium suum IESVM CHRISTVM, quem & in mundum hunc venire & hominem fieri voluit, & eundem pro nobis in mortem tradidit. Imò plus nobis in eo præstitit, quàm in Adamo amiseramus. Hic enim in terris modò imperiū tenebat, corpus verò habebat mortale, quod per fructum arboris vitae conseruabatur, simulque tentationibus obnoxium erat: At Christus nobis regnum in coelis acquisiuit, in quo vitam viuemus verè beatam, quae ut nullis huius seculi adminiculis opus habebit, ita ab omni tentationum periculo liberá aeternum durabit. Excitet nos istorum consideratio, ut dignitatis tantae memores, stationem nostram constanter tueamur, & nos gratos ei praebeamus, qui nos in hoc fastigium euehere dignatus est.
units.tr: God's paternal goodness, which he has shown abundantly in our first parent Adam and afterwards in his posterity, is commended here even more. He raised Adam, taken from the clay of the earth and in respect of the life of this age no better than the other animals, to the highest dignity and made him prince of all created things. But us, who had fallen and perished in him, indeed had become children of wrath, he restored to life together with him through his Son Jesus Christ, whom he willed to come into this world and become man, and whom he delivered up to death for us. Indeed, in him he has bestowed more upon us than we had lost in Adam. For Adam held dominion only on earth, and had a mortal body, which was preserved by the fruit of the tree of life and was at the same time liable to temptations. But Christ has acquired for us a kingdom in heaven, in which we shall live a truly blessed life. As this life will need no aids of this age, so it will endure forever, free from every danger of temptation. Let the consideration of these things stir us, so that, mindful of so great a dignity, we may constantly guard our position and show ourselves grateful to him who has deigned to raise us to this height.

units.la: Caeterum quaerat aliquis: Cur verò non nunc nobis corpus datur spirituale? cur item tam diu in hoc animali corpore luctamur atq; affligimur? Respondet ergo Paulus: At non prius, quod est spirituale, sed quod animale, deinde spirituale. Ad Dei prouidentiam remittit nos, qui hunc ordinem constituerit, & ita uno quasi ictu omnes quaestionum eiusmodi curiosarum nodos abrumpit, quibus hodie multi seipsos & alios irretiunt. Quales fere sunt: Cur Deus non talem initio fecit Adamum, qui non potuit labi, & neque morte neq; hanc comitantibus miserijs esset opus? Cur item non ita redemerit nos in Christo, ut totam naturam peccatricem aboleret, ne posthac peccatores nascerentur? Vel, cur non in Christi morte mundo huic corruptibili finem imposuerit? Sunt haec temeraria nimis, neque ad pietatem neque ad salutem hominis quicquam conferunt. Sufficiat Christiano homini, Deum ita rem constituisse, de cuius bonitate, iustitia, veritate, sapientia dubitare nefas sit. Vel respondeant nobis curiosi illi nugatores, cur non ver perpetuum Deus fecerit? cur semente opus sit, quando sine hac Deus messem dare possit? cur hyberno frigore terra torpeat, priusquam vernalibus Zephyris emollita suo vigori restituatur? Verumtamen si quis sobrie & simul in consilium adhibito Dei timore causas huius rei inquirere velit, satis graues inueniet, quae pijs & moderatis ingenijs sufficiant. Prima, cum in Adamo toti animales facti sumus, non possunt eodem tempore duae istae diuersae naturae concurrere, ut simul corpus animale & spirituale gestemus, sed ut una alteram praecedat, necesse est. Deinde, priorem non prorsus abolori oportuit, ne Dei iustitia periclitaretur, quae ut peccata debitis poenis castigentur, postulat. Praeterea, proprium sapientiae opus est, mutatio in melius. Postremo ad diuinae bonitatis & misericordiae commendationem facit, ut huius vitae miserias experti ad coelestis regni gaudia transferamur. Nisi enim illa praecederent, nemo nosse posset beneficij diuini magnitudinem. Stultè ergo & iniquè faciunt, qui in hoc seculo perpetuam felicitatem sibi pollicentur, aut saltem omnibus molestijs liberari volunt. Gestamus enim animale corpus, quod multis indiget, ideoq; vita haec laborum atq; curarum plena est: utq; his omnino liberemur, neq; corporum quae nunc habemus, conditio, neq; ratio huius seculi permittit. Et ut Solomon ait, omnia tempus habent, cui sese prudentes & cordati accommodant. Nunc patientia opus est, qua animas nostras possidebimus, si nosipsos spe futurae & beatae immortalitatis confirmemus.
units.tr: Someone may ask: why is a spiritual body not given to us now? Why too do we struggle and suffer for so long in this animal body? Paul answers: "But that was not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural, and afterwards that which is spiritual." He refers us to the providence of God, who appointed this order, and so with one stroke he cuts through all the knots of such curious questions, by which many today entangle themselves and others. Such questions are roughly these: Why did God not make Adam at the beginning such that he could not fall, so that there would be no need of death and the miseries that accompany it? Why, too, did he not so redeem us in Christ as to abolish the whole sinful nature, so that people would no longer be born sinners? Or why did he not, by Christ's death, put an end to this corruptible world? These questions are too rash, and contribute nothing either to piety or to a man's salvation. It is enough for a Christian to know that God has so arranged the matter, and it is wrong to doubt his goodness, justice, truth or wisdom. Or let those curious trifflers answer us: why did God not make a perpetual spring? Why is seed needed, when God could give a harvest without it? Why does the earth lie numb in winter's cold until, softened by the spring breezes, it is restored to its vigour? Nevertheless, if anyone wishes to inquire soberly into the causes of this matter, with the fear of God taken as counsellor, he will find them weighty enough to satisfy godly and moderate minds. (1) First: since we were all made natural in Adam, these two different natures cannot coincide at the same time, so that we bear at once an animal and a spiritual body; one must necessarily precede the other. (2) Second: the former could not be wholly abolished, lest God's justice be endangered, which requires that sins be punished with due penalties. (3) Moreover, it is a mark of wisdom to change for the better. (4) Last, it contributes to the commendation of divine goodness and mercy that, having experienced the miseries of this life, we be transferred to the joys of the heavenly kingdom. For unless those miseries went before, no one could know the greatness of the divine benefit. Foolishly and unjustly, then, do those act who promise themselves perpetual happiness in this age, or at least wish to be freed from all troubles. For we bear an animal body, which needs many things, and therefore this life is full of labours and cares; neither the condition of the bodies we now have nor the order of this age allows us to be wholly free of these. As Solomon says, "All things have their time," and the prudent and wise accommodate themselves to it. Now patience is needed, by which we shall possess our souls, if we strengthen ourselves with the hope of future and blessed immortality.

units.la: Porro redit Paulus ad institutam Adami & Christi comparationem, & quod obscurius dictum videri poterat, clarius exponit & illustrat. Primus homo (inquit) è terra, terrenus: secundus homo, ipse Dominus è coelo. Abusi sunt olim hoc loco haeretici, Apollinaris & Manichaei, ut Christum non ex Maria virgine corpus verum assumpsisse, sed coelestè quoddam coelitus attulisse probarent. Sed fefellit infelices homines, quod non animaduerterunt, Paulum hic non de corporum substantia, sed potius de ea qualitate & conditione loqui, quam corpora nostra in resurrectione mortuorum ex Christi beneficio obtinebunt. Et ideo Christum diserte hominem dicit, quod non alia ratione, quam propter assumptam veri hominis naturam dicitur, secundum quam illum ex Iudaeis genus suum ducere ad Romanos scribit. Itaque statum huius loci spectare oportet, qui est, ut demonstret, conditionem cuius nobis author est Christus, & in quam nouissimo die transferemur, multò praestantiorem & beatiorem fore ea, quae ex Adamo in nos propagata est, & in qua nunc vitam infinitis calamitatibus obnoxiam viuimus. Quod ut ad oculum (quod dicitur) demonstret, Adamum & Christum inter se confert, dicens: Primus homo è terra, terrenus: secundus homo, ipse Dominus è coelo. In Graeco legitur χοϊκός, quod proprie coenosum aut lutosum, siue in coeno & luto versantem, significat, ideoq; non tam originem & materiam, ex qua homo factus est, quam eius conditionem, siue ingenium & naturam denotat. Ut è contra ἐπουράνιος dicitur, non qui ex materia coelesti factus est, sed qui coelestibus solis addictus circa ea occupatur. Ita, sensus verborum est. Quemadmodum Adam, qui ex terrena materia originem ducit, terrenus est: ita quotquot ex illo nati sunt, terreni sunt (nam in sua imagine eum liberos suos genuisse Moses scribit) & proinde terrena sapiunt, terrena loquuntur, terrenis student & vacant, simulq; vicissitudini rerum & variis huius seculi casibus (vt omnia alia in terris) sunt obnoxij. Rursus, quemadmodum Christus, qui è coelo descendit, vt ex virgine homo factus nos redimeret & seruaret, coelestia sapuit, coelestia docuit, & tandem carnem quoque ab omni corruptibilis naturæ vitio liberatam coelis intulit, vbi & ipsa nunc vitam vivit coelestem nullisq; huius seculi casibus obnoxiam: Ita quotquot ex eius verbo renascuntur, ijdem coelestes fiunt, coelestia sapiunt, quæ-runt, tractant, & olim tam anima quàm corpore patriam in coelis possidebunt. Hunc sensum Paulus ipse nobis monstrat, quando subijcit: Et sicut gestauimus imaginem terreni, id est, sicuti Adamo parenti nostro similes fuimus vitam hanc mortalem in terris viuentes: ita tunc imaginem coelestis gestabimus, & Christi similes efficiemur, vbi corruptibile hoc corpus incorruptibi-litate donatum fuerit. Vbi obseruabimus, Paulum non de inani imagine loqui, sed tali, cui res ipsa coniuncta fit. Nam vt non inanem Adami imaginem gestamus, sed reuera eius similes sumus, quoad labores, curas, miseram vitæ huius conditionem & morti obnoxiam: Ita Christo etiam vere conformes effieicmur, eiusdem videlicet dignitatis & beatitudinis cum illo participes, & corporum quoque immortalitate donati. Sic locum hunc Theodoretus olim exposuit, cuius hæc verba sunt: Vt terreni primi parentis execrationis & mortis participes fuimus: ita participes quoq; erimus gloriæ Domini coelestis. Nihil ergo hic aliud dicit Apostolus, quàm quod in epistola ad Philippenses dicitur: Ciuitas fiue municipium nostrum in coelis est: vnde etiam Seruatorem expectamus, Dominum IESVM CHRISTVM: Qui transformabit corpus nostrum humile, vt conforme fiat corpori suo glorioso, &c. Vide cap.3.
units.tr: Paul now returns to the comparison of Adam and Christ and explains more clearly what might seem obscurely said. "The first man," he says, "is of the earth, earthy; the second man is the Lord from heaven." Heretics of old, Apollinaris and the Manichaeans, abused this passage to prove that Christ did not assume a true body from the virgin Mary, but brought a certain heavenly body down from heaven. But they deceived themselves, because they did not notice that Paul is speaking here not of the substance of bodies, but of that quality and condition which our bodies will obtain in the resurrection of the dead through Christ's benefit. And so he calls Christ plainly "man", for no other reason than the assumed nature of a true man, according to which he writes to the Romans that Christ's lineage is from the Jews. We must therefore look to the purpose of this place, which is to show the condition of which Christ is the author for us, and into which we shall be transferred on the last day, and that it will be far more excellent and blessed than that which has been propagated into us from Adam, and in which we now live a life liable to infinite calamities. To make this clear, as they say, to the eye, he compares Adam and Christ with each other, saying: "The first man is of the earth, earthy; the second man is the Lord from heaven." In the Greek it reads [χοϊκός], which properly means muddy or miry, or dwelling in mud and clay, and so denotes not so much the origin and material from which man was made as his condition, or disposition and nature. Conversely, [ἐπουράνιος] is said not of one made from heavenly material, but of one devoted to heavenly things and occupied with them. So the sense of the words is this: just as Adam, who derives his origin from earthly material, is earthly, so all who have been born from him are earthly (for Moses writes that he begot his children in his own image), and accordingly they savour of earthly things, speak earthly things, are devoted and given to earthly things, and at the same time are subject to the changes of things and the various chances of this age, like all other things on earth. Again, just as Christ, who came down from heaven so that, made man of a virgin, he might redeem and save us, savoured of heavenly things, taught heavenly things, and at last carried his flesh too, freed from every defect of corruptible nature, into the heavens, where it now lives a heavenly life, subject to no chances of this age, so all who are reborn by his word become heavenly, savour of heavenly things, seek and handle them, and in time will possess a fatherland in heaven, both in soul and in body. Paul himself shows us this sense when he adds: "And as we have borne the image of the earthy, that is, as we were like our parent Adam, living this mortal life on earth, so then we shall bear the image of the heavenly, and shall be made like Christ, when this corruptible body has been endowed with incorruptibility." Here we observe that Paul is not speaking of an empty image, but of one to which the reality itself is joined. For as we bear not an empty image of Adam, but are truly like him in labours, cares, the wretched condition of this life and liability to death, so we shall also truly be conformed to Christ, that is, made partakers with him of the same dignity and blessedness, and endowed with immortality of body too. Theodoret long ago expounded this passage in this way, and his words are: "As we have been partakers of the curse and death of our first earthly parent, so we shall also be partakers of the glory of the heavenly Lord." So the Apostle here says nothing other than what is said in the epistle to the Philippians: "Our citizenship is in heaven, from where we also await the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform our lowly body to be conformed to his glorious body," etc. Vide cap.3.

units.la: Quo loco rursus obseruari debet diligenter ingens Christi beneficium. Finge aliquem ex for-dida & ruinam in horas minante casa in regium palatium transferri, & ex egestate extrema ad opes maximas euehi & honores amplissimos: quis non de illo optimè agi dixerit? quis non laudauerit eorum liberalitatem, qui inopem & miserum tam benignè tractent? Atqui maiora multo nobis Christus contulit, qui infelices & à Dei conspectu exultantes cum eo in gratiam reduxit, qui corporis huius tabernaculum ruinosum olim instaurabit & immortale faciet, qui denique ius regni Dei nobis meruit, vt in eo omnibus cœlorum thesauris fruamur. Nec est, quòd de istis dubitemus. Ita enim Christum describit Apostolus, vt eum hæc præstare velle & posse, luculenter doceat. Nam hominem dicit, & hominem verè factum esse constat. Itaq; nostræ naturæ particeps & nostras miserias expertus nobis condolere potest, & simul iuuare volet. Adhæc quia frater noster est, iure causam nostram suscipere, & vindicem agere potest: quo nomine illum Iohns [?] olim appellauit: Scio, quòd vindex meus viuit, &c. Deinde idem ille Dominus est, & quidem de coelo. Ergo imperium habet legitimum & ordinarium, quod non ipse violenter sibi vsurpauit, sed secū coelitus in terras attulit. Testatur hoc ipse, quando omnia sibi à Patre tradita esse ait. Itè: Data est mihi potestas omnis in coelo & in terra. Id verò infinitis miraculis declarauit, quando mortuos, ventos, fluctus, dæmones pro imperio corripuit, & eos qui vita hac defuncti erant, ex mortis faucibus reduxit. Est ergo reuera Dominus coeli & terræ, imò resurrectio & vita est, & proinde in nouissimo etiam die præstare poterit quod hic nobis Apostolus ex ipsius ore pollicetur.
units.tr: Here again we should carefully notice Christ's great benefit. Imagine someone taken from a squalid hovel, one threatening to collapse at any hour, and carried into a royal palace, raised from extreme poverty to great wealth and very high honours. Who would not say that he had been treated very well? Who would not praise the generosity of those who treat a poor and wretched man so kindly? Yet Christ has bestowed far greater things on us. He has reconciled to himself us who were wretched and cast out from the sight of God. He will one day restore this ruinous tabernacle of the body and make it immortal. In short, he has merited for us the right to the kingdom of God, so that in it we may enjoy all the treasures of heaven. Nor is there any reason for us to doubt these things. For the Apostle describes Christ in such a way that he clearly teaches that he is both willing and able to bring them about. He calls him a man, and it is agreed that he truly became man. Therefore, having shared our nature and experienced our miseries, he can sympathise with us and will at the same time wish to help us. Moreover, because he is our brother, he can rightly take up our cause and act as our avenger. Job once called him by this name: "I know that my avenger lives," and so on. Then, he is the same Lord, and indeed Lord from heaven. Therefore he has a lawful and ordinary authority, which he did not seize for himself by force, but brought with him from heaven to earth. He testifies to this himself when he says that all things have been handed over to him by the Father, and again: "All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth." He has declared this by countless miracles, when he commanded the dead, the winds, the waves and the demons, and brought back from the jaws of death those who had departed this life. He is therefore truly the Lord of heaven and earth; indeed he is the resurrection and the life, and so on the last day he will be able to do what the Apostle here promises us from his own mouth.

units.la: Porrò rationem quoq; istius mutationis audiamus, cur nimirū nos cœlestes & Christo similes fieri oporteat? Hoc autem dico fratres, carnem & sanguinem non posse regni Dei hæreditatem consequi, neque corruptionem incorruptibilitatis hæreditatem accipere. Carnem & sanguinem dicit totam hominis naturam atque conditionem, qualis nunc est quoad corpus & animam. Hoc infirmum, caducum corruptibile & mortale est, atque de eo simul & omnibus ad illud spectantibus verissimè olim Propheta exclamauit: Omnis caro fœnum, & omnis gloria carnis flos agri. Anima verò non affectibus modo & desiderijs prauis obnoxia, verumetiam diuinorum ignara est, neque etiam ea percipere potest suo intellectu quæ sunt spiritus Dei, quod Paulus supra secundo cap. diserte affirmauit. Et eodem Christus respiciens, Petro qui ipsum verum & æternum Dei Filium atque humani generis Seruatorem esse confessus erat, respondit: Beatus es Simon, Bar Ionæ, caro & sanguis non reuelauit tibi, sed Pater meus, qui in cœlis est. Denique tanta est hominis in hoc corpore agentis infirmitas, vt ne gustum quidem leuissimum cœlestis gloriæ ferre possit, sicuti in prophetarum & Apostolorum exemplis est videre, quos consternatos & totos exanimes factos fuisse legimus, si quando Deus illis propius apparuit. Nec temere iis Mosi ipsum coram videre cupienti dicebat: Non poteris videre faciem meam: nec enim videbit me homo, & viuet. Quæ cum ita sint, sequitur, totius hominis mutationem & innouationem omnino necessariam esse, qua & anima affectuum caligine atque tenebris liberata, luce maiori illustretur, & corpus ab omni infirmitate exemptum cœlestis illius conuersationis capax fiat. Quia, vt in præsenti seipsum exponit Paulus, corruptio, id est, natura hæc corruptibilis & caduca, quoad talis manserit, incorruptibilitatis non potest particeps fieri.
units.tr: Next, let us hear the reason for this change, and why it is necessary that we be made heavenly and like Christ. "Now this I say, brethren, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does corruption inherit incorruptibility." By flesh and blood he means the whole nature and condition of man as it now is, in body and soul. This is weak, frail, corruptible and mortal, and of it, and of everything that pertains to it, the prophet once cried out most truly: "All flesh is grass, and all the glory of flesh is the flower of the field." The soul, moreover, is not only liable to evil affections and desires, but is also ignorant of divine things, nor can it by its own understanding perceive the things of the Spirit of God, as Paul plainly affirmed above in the second chapter. Christ, too, addressing Peter, who had confessed him to be the true and eternal Son of God and Saviour of the human race, answered: "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah. Flesh and blood have not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven." Finally, so great is the weakness of a man living in this body that he cannot bear even the slightest taste of heavenly glory. We see this in the examples of the prophets and apostles, whom we read were dismayed and utterly overcome whenever God appeared to them more closely. Nor without reason did he say to Moses, who longed to see him face to face: "You cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live." Since these things are so, it follows that a change and renewal of the whole man is altogether necessary, by which the soul, freed from the darkness and shadows of the affections, may be illumined by a greater light, and the body, freed from every infirmity, may become capable of that heavenly way of life. For, as Paul himself sets out in this passage, corruption, that is, this corruptible and perishable nature, as long as it remains such, cannot become a partaker of incorruptibility.

units.la: Nemo tamen ista sic accipiat, quasi mutatio hæc corporum substantiam aboleat siue euacuet. Ita olim quidam huius loci authoritate turpiter abusi sunt, vt probarent, in nouissimo die non nostra, quæ nunc gestamus, corpora resurrectura esse, sed eorum loco cœlestia quædam siue aëria. Conuincuntur hi aliis Scripturæ locis, à quibus Apostolum dissentire, vel potius sibi ipsi contradicere voluisse, nemo sanæ mentis dixerit. Daniel certè, eos qui in puluere dormiunt, Christus verò in monumentis agentes surrecturos dicit. Et in Symboli Apostolici articulis huius carnis resurrectionem profitemur. Itaque verus & orthodoxus verborum Pauli sensus est: Nos quoad nihil quàm[?] caro & sanguis, id est, caduci, infirmi, corruptibiles, mortales, cœlestium ignorantes & prauis cupiditatibus obnoxij sumus, non posse hæreditatem & possessionem regni cœlorum adire. Corruptibilis enim natura, nisi aboleatur, incorruptibilitati locum non dabit: neque fieri potest, vt mors & vita inter se concilientur.
units.tr: No one, however, should take these words as if this change abolished or destroyed the substance of our bodies. Some men once shamefully abused the authority of this passage to prove that on the last day it is not our present bodies that will rise, but certain heavenly or aerial bodies in their place. No one of sound mind would say that these men are refuted by other passages of Scripture, or that the Apostle wished to dissent from them, or rather to contradict himself. Daniel certainly says that those who sleep in the dust will rise, and Christ says that those who are in the tombs will rise. And in the articles of the Apostles' Creed we profess the resurrection of this flesh. Therefore the true and orthodox sense of Paul's words is this: that we, insofar as we are nothing but flesh and blood, that is, frail, weak, corruptible, mortal, ignorant of heavenly things and subject to evil desires, cannot enter upon the inheritance and possession of the kingdom of heaven. For corruptible nature, unless it is abolished, will not make room for incorruptibility, nor can death and life be reconciled with each other.

units.la: Primùm igitur admonemur hoc loco, in cœlesti patria neque corporis neque animi affectionibus locum fore. Vt enim mortalitas cessabit, ita dolor quoque, luctus, cura, & multò magis inordinatæ & illicitæ cupiditates prorsus abolebuntur. Nam ipso Christo teste, Angelis similes erimus, non quidem quoad corporum substantiam, sed quoad conditionem cœlestem gloriosi & ab omni huius seculi casu liberati. Debet hoc diligenter teneri propter Sadducæos, & quoscunque alios illusores, qui (vt alibi dictum est) resurrectionis spem in dubium vocare nituntur, dum cœlestem vitam ex huius præsentis conditione æstimant, & illam ideo negant, quòd absurda quædam ipsi fingunt, quæ tunc omnino nulla erunt, cùm longè alia sit regni cœlorum quàm vitæ huius mortalis & caducæ conditio.
units.tr: First, then, we are reminded in this place that in the heavenly fatherland there will be room neither for affections of the body nor for affections of the mind. For just as mortality will cease, so too pain, grief and anxiety will cease, and much more so disordered and unlawful desires will be utterly abolished. For, Christ himself being witness, we shall be like the angels, not indeed in the substance of our bodies, but in a heavenly condition, glorious and freed from every fall of this age. This must be firmly held on account of the Sadducees and any other mockers who, as has been said elsewhere, strive to call the hope of the resurrection into doubt. They judge the heavenly life by the present condition of this life, and deny it because they invent certain absurdities for it, which will then not exist at all, since the condition of the kingdom of heaven is far different from the condition of this mortal and frail life.

units.la: Interim singuli meminerint, officij nostri esse, vt iam nunc cœlestibus assuescamus, & (vt Paulus ad Colossenses scribit) superna curemus, non terrestria. Resistamus ergo carni & sanguini, & mortificemus membra nostra terrestria, fornicationem, impuritatem, mollitiem, cupiditates malas, & malorum omnium radicem auaritiam. Debent quidem in hac meditatione omnes versari quotidie, præ alijs tamen ij, quibus Ecclesiæ & verbi sui ministerium Deus credidit. Est enim hodie causa licentiæ scelerum & vniuersalis illius corruptionis morum apud omnes ordines præcipua, quòd pauci credunt, & pleriq; vix vnquam de ijsdem cogitant. Vrgeant ergo constanter doctrinam istam, vt saltem aliqui veterno illo exitiali excusso, relictis terrenis studijs ad cœlestia bona aspirent, quæ nobis meruit IESVS CHRISTVS Dominus noster, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Meanwhile, let each one remember that it is our duty to accustom ourselves now to heavenly things, and (as Paul writes to the Colossians) to seek the things that are above, not the things that are on earth. Let us therefore resist flesh and blood, and mortify our earthly members: fornication, uncleanness, softness, evil desires, and covetousness, the root of all evils. All should indeed dwell on this meditation daily, but especially those to whom God has entrusted the ministry of the Church and of his Word. For today the chief cause of licence in sin and of that universal corruption of morals among all orders is that few believe, and most scarcely ever think about these things. Let them therefore press this doctrine constantly, so that at least some, having shaken off that deadly drowsiness and left earthly pursuits, may aspire to the heavenly goods which our Lord Jesus Christ has merited for us, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXXVI
units.tr: HOMILY LXXXVI

units.la: Ecce mysterium vobis dico: Non omnes quidem dormie-mus, sed omnes mutabimur, momento & iactu oculi ad vlti-mam tubam (canet enim tuba) & mortui suscitabuntur in-corrupti, & nos mutabimur. Oportet enim hoc corruptibi-le induere incorruptibilitatem, & mortale hoc induere im-mortalitatem.
units.tr: Behold, I tell you a mystery: We shall not all indeed sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet (for the trumpet will sound), and the dead will be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible must put on incorruptibility, and this mortal must put on immortality.

units.la: Hassenm[?]
units.tr: Hassenm[?]

units.la: Hactenus multis & prolixè docuit Paulus, fore in nouissimo die universalem ex mortuis resurrectionem, simulq; diligenter respondit ad captiosas aduersariorum quæstiones, quibus illam in dubium vocant, dum quærunt, quomodo & quo nam corpore mortui resurrecturi sint. Sequitur ergo postrema pars huius tractationis, in qua primùm tota resurrectionis historia describitur, sic ut rursus demonstretur, quæ futura sit corporum resuscitatorum conditio. Deinde quid à resurrectione futurum sit docetur. Tandem doctrinam hanc Corinthijs, vel potius Christianis omnibus accommodat, ut ea confirmati, in fide vera constanter perseuerent, nec sese ab ea dimoueri patiantur.
units.tr: Up to this point Paul has taught at length and in many words that there will be a universal resurrection of the dead on the last day, and at the same time he has carefully answered the adversaries' captious questions by which they call it into doubt, asking how and with what body the dead will rise. There follows, then, the final part of this discussion. In it, first, the whole history of the resurrection is described, so that it may again be shown what the condition of the raised bodies will be. Then it is taught what will happen after the resurrection. Finally, he applies this teaching to the Corinthians, or rather to all Christians, so that, being strengthened by it, they may persevere constantly in the true faith and not allow themselves to be moved away from it.

units.la: Exordium breue præmittit: Ecce mysterium dico vobis. Demonstrandi particula utitur, ut attentos reddat in re maximi momenti: hanc verò mysterium dicit, ut sibi beneuolos faciat, quando ea quidem ipsos celare velit, quæ non omnibus vulgo cognita sint. Solent enim mysteria dici, quæ efferri non licet, & à quibusdam definitur: Mysterium est contemplatio spiritualis, quæ multorum captum siue intellectum fugit. Latini arcana dicunt, cuius vocabuli sensus latius patet, cum quàmuis rem occultiorem, etiam prophanam, comprehendat: mysterium autem ad sola sacra pertineat. Ita verò in præsenti Apostolus vocat totam resurrectionis historiam, quà eius ordo atq; modus describitur: partim quidem, quòd ista prius nunquam tam diserte & perspicuè exposita fuerunt: partim verò ut Corinthios admoneat, ne de re omnium difficillima & sacratissima, quæ humani ingenij captum excedit, temere pronuntient, neq; etiam in eius consideratione oscitantius versentur. Hæc enim illis hucusq; præcipua erroris causa fuerat, quòd ardua hæc regni Dei mysteria ad suæ rationis calculum reuocarent. Quid enim hic possit homo animalis, qui non percipit ea, quæ sunt spiritus Dei? imò qui ne ijs quidem, quæ ad corpus spectant, futura prospicit?
units.tr: He prefaces the account with a brief introduction: "Behold, I tell you a mystery." He uses the particle of pointing out, to make his hearers attentive to a matter of the greatest importance. He calls it a mystery in order to win their goodwill, since he wishes to set forth things that are not commonly known to everyone. For those things are usually called mysteries which may not be publicly declared, and someone has defined a mystery as a spiritual contemplation which escapes the grasp or understanding of many. The Latins call such things secrets (arcana), a word whose meaning extends more widely, since it includes any more hidden matter, even a profane one, whereas mystery pertains only to sacred things. Now the Apostle here calls the whole history of the resurrection, in which its order and manner are described, a mystery: partly because these things had never before been set out so clearly and plainly, and partly so that he may warn the Corinthians not to pronounce rashly on a matter that is the most difficult and most sacred of all, one that exceeds the grasp of the human intellect, nor to engage in its consideration too carelessly. For hitherto the chief cause of their error had been that they reduced these lofty mysteries of the kingdom of God to the reckoning of their own reason. For what can a natural man do here, who does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God? Indeed, he does not even foresee the things that concern the body?

units.la: Debet autem considerari hoc loco Dei consilium, qui pleniorem huius rei cognitionem per Paulum demum toti mundo innotescere voluit. Veteribus quidem non ignotam fuisse resurrectionis spem, antea non semel demonstrauimus: Sed poterat illis sufficere, quòd illa omnino fore scirent & crederent, etiàsi eius modum & ordinem ignorarent. At quia Corinthij cum alijs gentibus humanæ philosophiæ rationibus decepti de illa dubitabant, & nouissimis temporibus non minus argutos quàm impios illusores orituros esse Spiritus Sanctus præuidebat, qui eius fidem argumentis undiq; conquisitis oppugnarent, mysterium istud diligentius explicari, & imprimis ad quæstiones illas responderi oportuit, quas illi mouere solent. Sic multa alia veteribus obscurius tradita fuerunt, si totum IESV CHRISTI negotium spectes: quæ postea illo in carne exhibito euidentius patuerunt. Ideo ille discipulis dicebat: Vestri beati sunt oculi, quia vident: & aures vestræ, quia audiunt. Amen & enim dico vobis, quòd multi prophetæ & iusti desiderauerunt videre quæ videtis, non viderunt: & audire quæ auditis, & non audierunt. Quò etiam referri debet, quòd Ioannes in Christo nobis non vitam modò, verumetiam lucem exhibitam esse scribit, quæ suo in mundum aduentu omnes homines illuminet. Debemus ergo diligenter obseruare prærogatiuam nostram, qua nos Deus dignatus est, ut nos illi pro tanto beneficio gratos præbeamus, & constanter retineamus lucem illam veritatis salutiferam, quæ nobis in Euangelij prædicatione affulget. Alexander Macedo, infelix ambitionis & gloriæ popularis mancipium, Achillem felicè pronun tiabat, quòd viuenti Patroclus fidelissimus amicus, mortuo autè Homerus laudum suarum præco obtigisset. At quanto feliciores sunt, qui in tempora Euangelij renascentis inciderunt, cuius prædicatio nobis salutem æternam affert, ipsum deniq; Deum nobis conciliat, qui nobis Filium suum vindicem dedit, qui nos amicorum & fratrum loco habere dignatur, quos inter regni sui coharedes adscribat. Discamus præterea tanti beneficij consideratione ingenij nostri curiositatem atq; audaciam frænare, ne velimus sapere supra id quod in Scripturis sacris reuelatur. Solet enim Deus manifestare quantum cuiq; satis est: quòd si quid præterea scire necesse fuerit pro temporis & loci ratione, id quoq; non celabit, quando hæc eius voluntas est, ut omnes homines salui fiant, & in veritatis cognitionem perueniant. Philip. 3. & 1. Timoth. 2.
units.tr: Moreover, in this passage we should consider the counsel of God, who willed that a fuller knowledge of this matter should at last become known to the whole world through Paul. We have already shown more than once that the hope of resurrection was not unknown to the ancients. But it could suffice for them that they knew and believed that it would certainly come to pass, even if they were ignorant of its manner and order. But because the Corinthians, deceived by the reasonings of human philosophy along with other nations, were doubting it, and because the Holy Spirit foresaw that in the last times there would arise scoffers no less subtle than impious, who would attack its faith with arguments gathered from every side, it was necessary that this mystery be explained more carefully, and above all that answers be given to those questions which such men are accustomed to raise. Thus many other things were handed down more obscurely to the ancients, if you look at the whole business of Jesus Christ; these became clearer afterwards, when he had been revealed in the flesh. Therefore he said to his disciples: "Blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear. For truly I say to you, that many prophets and righteous men desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it." To this also should be referred what John writes, that in Christ there has been given to us not only life but also light, which by its coming into the world enlightens all men. We ought therefore to observe carefully the privilege by which God has deigned to honour us, so that we may show ourselves grateful to him for so great a benefit, and constantly hold fast to that saving light of truth which shines upon us in the preaching of the Gospel. Alexander the Macedonian, the unhappy slave of ambition and popular glory, used to pronounce Achilles fortunate because he had the most faithful friend, Patroclus, while he lived, and Homer, the herald of his praises, after he died. But how much happier are those who have fallen into the times of the renewed Gospel, whose preaching brings us eternal salvation, reconciles us at last to God himself, who has given us his Son as our champion, and who deigns to count us in place of friends and brothers, and to enroll us among the co-heirs of his kingdom. Let us learn further, from consideration of so great a benefit, to restrain the curiosity and boldness of our wit, so that we do not wish to be wise beyond what is revealed in the holy Scriptures. For God is accustomed to make known as much to each as is enough; and if anything more needs to be known, according to the circumstances of time and place, he will not conceal that either, since this is his will, that all men be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. Philip. 3. and 1 Tim. 2.

units.la: Porrò audiamus Paulum de resurrectionis historia differentem: Non omnes quidem (ait) dormiemus, sed omnes mutabimur momento & iactu oculi ad ultimam tubam (canet enim tuba) & mortui suscitabuntur incorrupti, & nos mutabimur. Debent his coniungi, quæ in priori ad Thessalonicens. 4. cap. paulo fusius tradit, sic scribens: Hoc vobis dicimus verbo Domini (nemo igitur ista hominis figmentu esse arbitretur) quod nos vivi, qui reliqui (sive superstites) erimus in adventu Domini, non prævenie-mus eos qui obdormierunt. Nam ipse Dominus cum hortationis clamore & voce Archangeli ac tuba Dei descendet de cœlo, & qui mortui fuerint in Christo, resurgent primùm: Deinde nos vivi, qui reliqui erimus, rapiemur simul cum eis in nubes in occursum Domini in aerem: & ita semper cum Domino erimus. Sunt verba hæc plana & perspicua, neq; [?] audiendi sunt, qui subtilius de his philosophando mira quædam fingunt de resuscitatorum conditio-ne, deq; cœlis & electorum felicitate. Nos potius rem ipsam, de qua agitur, consideremus: & primò quidem, de quibus in præsenti sermo fiat: deinde quid de omnibus tunc futurum sit, sive prius hac vita defuncti, sive superstites fuerint: postremò, qua ratione aut quibus medijs ista omnia per-fici oporteat.
units.tr: Let us then listen to Paul discoursing on the history of the resurrection: "We shall not all indeed sleep, but we shall all be changed in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet (for the trumpet will sound), and the dead will be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed." These words should be joined with what he hands down rather more fully in his earlier letter to the Thessalonians, chapter 4, writing thus: "This we tell you by the word of the Lord (let no one therefore think these things to be the invention of man), that we who are alive, who remain (or survive) at the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself, with a shout of command and the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God, shall descend from heaven, and those who have died in Christ shall rise first. Then we who are alive, who remain, shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord." These words are plain and clear, and those should not be listened to who, philosophising more subtly about these things, invent wondrous tales about the condition of the raised, about the heavens and the happiness of the elect. Let us rather consider the matter itself under discussion: and first, of whom the discourse is being made; then what will happen to all of them then, whether they have died before this life or are survivors; lastly, by what method, or by what means, all these things ought to be brought about.

units.la: Quoad primum, sic scribit Apostolus: Non omnes quidem dormiemus, sed omnes mutabimur momento & ictu oculi, &c. Item: Nos vivi, qui reliqui erimus in adventu Domini, non præue-niemus eos qui obdormierunt. Dividit totum genus humanum in viuentes & mortuos, quæ distinctio etiam in Symbolo Apostolico habetur, ubi Christum fatemur venturum ad iudicandum vi-vos & mortuos. Et de illis quidem diserte pronuntiat: Non omnes dormiemus: Item, Nos vivi, qui reliqui erimus. Ergo multi illo die superstites erunt, quod Christus quoque non obscure docet, quando de novissimi temporis moribus & suo ad iudicium adventu differens, inter alia sic dicit: Sicut erant dies Noæ, ita erit & adventus Filij hominis. Ut enim erant in diebus, qui præcesserunt diluvium, edentes & bibentes, contrahentes matrimonium & nuptum dantes usq; ad eum diem, quo intravit Noa in arcam, & non cognoverunt, donec venisset diluvium, & sustulisset universos: ita erit & adventus Filij hominis. Tunc duo erunt in agro, unus assumetur, & alter relinquetur: duæ molentes in mola, una assumetur, & altera relinquetur: Vigilate ergo, quia nescitis qua hora Dominus vester venturus sit. Quò etiam facit, quod Paulus ad Thessal. scribit: Cum dixerint, Pax pax, & tuta omnia, tunc repentinum eis imminet exitium, sicut dolor partus mulieri prægnanti. Frustra item & ridiculè nos ad vigilandum hortaretur Dominus, ne dies ille ex improviso nobis incidat, si moriendum esset omnibus priusquam ille illucescet. Confutantur igitur hoc loco falsæ illæ prædictiones de signis novissimum Christi adventum præcessuris, inter quæ hoc etiam numeratur, quod omnes homines uno die moriturisint [?]. Sunt hæc ferè monachorum figmenta, quibus volupe est, hominum mentes perterrefacere: non quidem ut ad pœnitentiam veram & salutarem excitent, sed ut ipsi quæstum faciant maiorem.
units.tr: As to the first point, the Apostle writes thus: "We shall not all indeed sleep, but we shall all be changed in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye," etc. Likewise: "We who are alive, who remain at the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have fallen asleep." He divides the whole human race into the living and the dead, a distinction which is also found in the Apostles' Creed, where we confess that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead. And about the former he pronounces plainly: "We shall not all sleep"; likewise, "We who are alive, who remain." Therefore many will survive on that day, which Christ also teaches not obscurely, when, speaking of the morals of the last time and of his coming to judgment, he says among other things: "As were the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. For as in the days before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day that Noah entered the ark, and they did not know until the flood came and swept them all away, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. Then two will be in the field: one will be taken, and the other left; two women grinding at the mill: one will be taken, and the other left. Watch therefore, for you do not know at what hour your Lord will come." To this also Paul's writing to the Thessalonians pertains: "When they say, 'Peace, peace, and all is safe,' then sudden destruction will overtake them, like the pain of labour upon a pregnant woman." Likewise the Lord would be exhorting us to watch in vain and ridiculously, lest that day come upon us unexpectedly, if all men were to die before it dawns. Therefore the false predictions of signs that are to precede the last coming of Christ are refuted here, among which this is also counted, that all men will die on one day. These are almost the fabrications of the monks, in which they delight to terrify men's minds, not indeed to rouse them to true and saving repentance, but so that they themselves may make greater gain.

units.la: Habet præterea locus iste dulcissimam [?] consolationem, qua nos in omnibus adversis sive periculis, imprimis autem adversus crudeles tyrannorum conatus confirmemus, qui fidem in unum Christum & cum ea Ecclesiam simul extinctam volunt. Quia enim sub novissimum Christi adventum adhuc aliqui superstites erunt, qui tunc ad gloriæ æternæ possessionem immutabuntur, nō obscurè apparet, Ecclesiam ad finem usq; seculi mansuram esse: quod Dominus ipse testatur, quando apud Matthæum ait: Ego vobiscum sum usq; in consummationem seculi. Queritur quidem alibi de corruptissimis novissimorum temporum moribus & credentium paucitate, at simul aliquos fore dicit, quorum rationem habiturus sit, ut dies illos decurtet, ne vel pravo mundi exemplo cor-rumpantur, vel malorum tunc grassantium mole superentur. Et ad istos hæc efficacissima conso-latio pertinet: Cum hæc fieri incipient, suspicite, & attollite capita vestra: quoniam appropinquat redemptio vestra. Facit ad horum confirmationem, quòd ita de hac re Paulus disserit, ut seipsum inter eos numeret, quos dies ille superstites deprehensurus sit, & quos ad gloriam cœlestem immu-tari oporteat. Nos vivi (inquit) qui reliqui erimus in adventu Domini, &c. Quæ non ita accipi debent, quasi vana confidentia aut fitto quodam oraculo delusus hæc dicat (nam eosdem Thessa-lonicenses in posteriori epistola graviter admonet, ne impostoribus fidem habeant, qui diem illum iamiam venturum dicebant: quia prius defectionem fieri, & Antichristum revelari oporteat) sed ex electorum more loquitur, qui cùm certò sciant fore finem huius mundi, & venturum omni-no Christum iudicem, ad cuius adventum nos in omnes horas paratos esse conveniat, ita de istis co-gitant, ac si certò ipsis constaret, iamiam diem illum in foribus adesse. Ita enim nobis ipse Dominus praecipit, apud Lucam his verbis: Sint lumbi vestri praecincti, & lucernae accensae, & vos similes hominibus expectantibus quando dominus suus reuertatur à nuptijs: vt cum venerit ac pulsauerit, confestim aperiant ei. Et paulo post: Vos igitur estote parati, quia qua hora non putatis, Filius hominis veniet. Et sane vt ita fiat plus quam necesse est, eo quòd nihil nocentius est ea persuasione, qua Christus moras nectere, aut aduentus eius adhuc procul abesse putatur. Illam enim ipse seruo illi malo & proditorio tribuit, qui in familia sua tyrannidem exercet, & poenas dignas tandem dabit cum hypocritis. Nostro etiam seculo praecipua securitatis, qua totus mundus perit, causa est, quòd de Christi aduentu pauci serio cogitant. Remedium vero eius praesentissimum erit, si de eo cum Paulo loqui assuescamus, perinde ac si iam iam nostris capitibus ille immineat.
units.tr: This passage also offers a most sweet consolation, by which we may strengthen ourselves in all adversities and dangers, and especially against the cruel attempts of tyrants, who want faith in Christ, and the Church along with it, extinguished. For since at the last coming of Christ there will still be some survivors who will then be changed into the possession of eternal glory, it is not obscurely shown that the Church will remain until the end of the world. The Lord himself testifies to this when he says in Matthew: I am with you always, even to the end of the world. Elsewhere he does complain of the most corrupt morals of the last times and the paucity of believers, but at the same time he says that there will be some for whose sake he will shorten those days, so that they are not corrupted by the wicked example of the world or overwhelmed by the mass of evils then raging. To these people belongs this most effective consolation: "When these things begin to happen, look up and lift up your heads, for your redemption draws near." What also serves to confirm them is that Paul discusses this matter in such a way that he counts himself among those whom that day will find surviving and who must be changed into heavenly glory. "We who are alive," he says, "who remain until the coming of the Lord, etc." These words should not be taken as if he said this out of vain confidence or deluded by some false oracle (for in his second letter he seriously warns the same Thessalonians not to believe impostors who were saying that day was already at hand, since a falling away must first occur and the Antichrist must be revealed). Rather he speaks in the manner of the elect, who, knowing for certain that this world will end and that Christ will surely come as judge, for whose coming we ought to be prepared at all hours, think about these things as if it were certain to them that that day was already at the doors. For the Lord himself commands us this way, in Luke, in these words: "Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning, and be like men waiting for their lord to return from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks, they may open to him at once." And a little later: "Therefore you also be ready, for at an hour you do not expect the Son of Man will come." And indeed, to make it happen this way, more than is necessary, since nothing is more harmful than the belief by which people think that Christ delays or that his coming is still far off. For he himself assigns that belief to the wicked and treacherous servant who exercises tyranny in his household, and he will at last give him the punishment due to hypocrites. In our own age too, the chief cause of that security in which the whole world perishes is that few think seriously about the coming of Christ. Its most immediate remedy will be if we grow accustomed to speaking about it with Paul, just as if it were already hanging over our heads.

units.la: Porrò ad alterum huius loci caput accedamus, quo quid tunc de omnibus futurum sit doceatur, siue illi tunc superstites sint, siue iam ante mortui fuerint. Non omnes (inquit) moriemur, sed omnes mutabimur momento & ictu oculi, &c. Et mox: Mortui suscitabuntur incorrupti, & nos mutabimur. Ad Thessalonicen. vero ordinem huius negotij distinctius explicat, dicens: Nos viui, qui reliqui erimus in aduentu Domini, non praeueniemus eos, qui obdormierunt: Sed qui mortui fuerint in Christo, resurgent primùm: deinde nos viui, qui reliqui erimus, rapiemur simul cum eis in occursum Domini in aërem: vbi nimirum mutatio illa praecesserit, de qua in praesenti loquitur. Ergo qui superstites fuerint in illo die, mutabuntur, quoad nimirum corporum qualitatem & conditionem, vt incorruptibiles et immortales fiant: mortui verò incorrupti fient, & similiter incorruptibilitate ac immortalitate donabuntur: inde quotquot tam ex his quàm illis ex electorum & filiorum Dei numero fuerint, simul omnes in occursum Domini in aërem rapientur, vt aeternum cum illo viuant & regnent. Caeterum quoad primos, cùm mors via omnis terrae in Scripturis dicatur, & Apostolus alibi dicat, hoc omnes homines manere, vt semel moriantur, poterat videri sibipsi contradicere, quando aliquos superstites fore scribit in illo die, qui non morituri, sed subitò in meliorem conditionem mutandi sint. Sed obseruabis, subitam iflam mutationem loco mortis fore, & aliqua ratione mortem dici posse, quia idem in nobis agit, quod ista. Auferet enim ex corporibus nostris omnem corruptibilitatem atque mortalitatem vnà cum vitijs, quae cum his coniuncta sunt. Quod factu necessarium esse, nuper diximus, & in praesenti idem repetens Paulus ait: Oportet enim hoc corruptibile induere incorruptibilitatem, & mortale hoc induere immortalitatem: Nimirum, quia caro & sanguis, id est, homo qualis nunc est in hac corrupta natura, regni Dei haereditatem adire non potest. Etsi verò Paulus hic de solis pijs loquatur, qui aeternum cum Christo erunt (quia ad credentes scribebat, aut saltem ad fidei verae professores, de quibus omnibus charitas Christiana piè ac bene sperare solet) constat tamen, mutationem iflam etiam in impijs fieri oportere. Quemadmodum enim pij & credentes mutabuntur, vt ab omni corruptibilis naturae vitio atque impedimento liberati, in Christi occursum tendere, & aeternis regni coelorum bonis frui possint: ita impiorum quoque corpora incorruptibilia fieri necesse est, vt aeternis supplicijs queant sufficere. Vt igitur in hoc seculo quae pijs ac Deum diligentibus salutifera sunt, impijs sua culpa exitium afferunt: ita in futuro quoque fiet, vt conditionis corruptibilis in incorruptibilem mutatio pijs ad aeterni regni & gaudij beatam possessionem, impijs verò ad nunquam finiendos infernalium poenarum siue tormentorum cruciatus seruiat.
units.tr: Now let us come to the second part of this passage, in which it is taught what will then happen to all, whether they are still alive at that time or have died before. "We shall not all die," he says, "but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, etc." And soon after: "The dead will be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed." But in the letter to the Thessalonians he explains the order of this matter more clearly, saying: "We who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have fallen asleep. But those who have died in Christ will rise first; then we who are alive and remain will be caught up together with them to meet the Lord in the air," where, of course, that change which he is speaking of in the present passage will have come first. Therefore those who survive on that day will be changed, as regards the quality and condition of their bodies, so that they become incorruptible and immortal; and the dead will be raised incorruptible and likewise will be given incorruptibility and immortality. Then all who, whether from these or those, belong to the number of the elect and sons of God will be caught up together in the air to meet the Lord, so that they may live and reign with him forever. But as for the first group, since death is called the way of all the earth in the Scriptures, and the Apostle elsewhere says that it is appointed for all men once to die, one might think he contradicts himself when he writes that there will be survivors on that day who are not going to die but are suddenly to be changed into a better condition. But you will observe that this sudden change will take the place of death, and in some sense can be called death, because it works in us the same thing that death does. For it will remove from our bodies all corruptibility and mortality, together with the vices joined to them. We said recently that this must necessarily happen, and repeating the same point now Paul says: "For this corruptible must put on incorruptibility, and this mortal must put on immortality." Of course, because flesh and blood, that is, man as he now is in this corrupt nature, cannot inherit the kingdom of God. Although Paul here speaks only of the godly, who will be with Christ forever (because he was writing to believers, or at least to those who truly profess the faith, of whom Christian charity is accustomed to hope well and good), it is nevertheless clear that this change must also take place in the wicked. For just as the godly and believers will be changed, freed from every defect and hindrance of corruptible nature, so that they can press on to meet Christ and enjoy the eternal goods of the kingdom of heaven, so too the bodies of the wicked must become incorruptible, so that they may be able to endure eternal punishments. Therefore, just as in this age the things that are salutary for the godly and for those who love God bring destruction to the wicked through their own fault, so it will also be in the future: the change from a corruptible to an incorruptible condition will serve the godly for the blessed possession of the eternal kingdom and joy, but for the wicked it will serve the torments of infernal punishments that are never to end.

units.la: Imprimis autem hoc loco obseruatu dignum est, quae nam corpora à mortuis resurrectura sint. Nam etsi de eo iam saepius dictum sit, prodest tamen hoc ipsum frequentius repetere, vt efficacior sit consolatio, quam ex resurrectionis spe concipimus, ne illa eorum somnijs labefactetur, qui hodie Origenianis speculationibusediti de corporum clarificatione subtilius philosophantur, quae ὕλα, id est, omnis materiae expertia, & proinde insensibilia quoque, fore fingunt. Nam corpora (inquiunt) clarificata erunt incorruptibilia: At materia omnis corruptibilis est: Ergo corpora illa in clarificatione materiam omnem deponent. Cuius figmenti ipsis causa est, vnica, vt Christi corpus nunc quoque tale esse doceant, & ex eo probent, idem vbique esse, imò nullo loco contineri. Quòd si obijcias: Num ergo negent eadem, quae nunc gestamus corpora, & quidem in sua substantia resuscitanda fore? Id plane affirmant, sed substantiam corporum & carnis dicunt esse animam. Mirum sane & nouum theologiae genus, quod illi ex philosophorum adytis prose-runt, quos à Dei simul & regni coelorum cognitione alienissimos fuisse constat. Et quis unquam veterum dixit animam esse corporum substantiam? Si de viuis corporibus loquantur, ea quidem anima consistere & viuere fatemur. Interim ratum semper manet, quod philosophi quoque sanio-res tradiderunt, hominem duabus partibus, corpore nimirum & anima constare, ex quibus haec quidem nobis cum Diis immortalibus, illud vero cum belluis commune est. Quod discrimen sa-crae literae etiam nobis indicant, quae corpus ex terra desumptum & formatum fuisse docent, cui Deus spiritum vitae inspiraverit. Itaque viuere quidem definit corpus, quando ex eo anima emigrat, at non propterea corpus esse definit, neque etiam substantia sua spoliatur, quam ex terra accepit, in quam reuertitur.
units.tr: Above all, in this passage it is worth noting which bodies are to rise from the dead. For although this has been said many times already, it is nonetheless useful to repeat it more often, so that the consolation we draw from the hope of the resurrection may be more effective, and so that it is not shaken by the dreams of those who today, devoted to Origenist speculations, philosophize more subtly about the clarification of bodies, and feign that they will become hyla [ὕλα], that is, free of all matter, and therefore also insensible. For they say: "Bodies will be incorruptible when they are clarified; but all matter is corruptible; therefore those bodies, in their clarification, will lay aside all matter." The only reason they have for this fiction is to teach that the body of Christ is even now of this kind, and from this to prove that it is everywhere, indeed that it is contained in no place. But if you object: "Do they then deny that the very bodies we now bear will be raised in their own substance?" They plainly affirm it, but they say that the substance of bodies and of flesh is the soul. A strange and new kind of theology, which they have drawn out of the inner sanctuaries of the philosophers, who are known to have been most alien to the knowledge of God and of the kingdom of heaven. And which of the ancients ever said that the soul is the substance of bodies? If they are speaking of living bodies, we grant that a soul subsists and lives in them. Meanwhile it always remains valid what even the wiser philosophers have handed down: that man consists of two parts, namely body and soul, of which the one is common to us with the immortal gods, the other with the beasts. The sacred letters also show us this difference, teaching that the body was taken and formed from the earth, into which God breathed the breath of life. Thus the body ceases to live when the soul departs from it, but it does not therefore cease to be a body, nor is it stripped of the substance it received from the earth, into which it returns.

units.la: Sed Paulum loquentem audiamus, qui cum dixisset: Mortui suscitabuntur incorrupti, & nos mutabimur: Mox huius dicti rationem reddens & seipsum exponens subjicit: Oportet enim hoc corruptibile induere incorruptibilitatem, & mortale hoc induere immortalitatem. Primum [?]ait:HOC corruptibile, & HOC mortale: quasi ad illud Iobi dictum respexerit: Postquam circumdederint HOC mea cute, &c. Non igitur de alio corpore loquitur, quàm quod in morte cadit, & corruptioni obnoxium in terram aut puluerem dissoluitur. Deinde mutationem, non abolitionem ei tribuit, qua in nihilum redigatur, aut [?] sive omnis materia sensibilis expers fiat. Tertiò mutationis huius rationem definit Induendi verbo: Oportet (inquit) hoc corruptibile induere incorruptibilitatem, &c. Et eodem verbo in posteriori epistola beatae immortalitatis spem explicat, dicens: In hoc suspiramus, expetentes domicilio nostro, quod è coelo est, superindui. Et mox: Etenim qui sumus in hoc tabernaculo suspiramus onerati: in quo non cupimus exui, sed superindui, vt absorbeatur mortalitas à vita. Nemo igitur istorum argumenta admittat, quae de materia corruptibili proferunt, vt corpus clarificatum [?] esse, aut ex nulla materia constare probent. Id enim oppugnant & negant, circa quod resurrectionis cardo versatur. Fatemur nos quoque omnem materiam, quae nunc in rerum natura est, corruptioni obnoxiam esse. At in illo die mutatio in melius fiet, qui ideo dies instaurationis omnium & regenerationis dicitur. Itaque manente eadem substantia & materia corporum, ipsa tamen incorruptibilitatem & immortalitatem induent: Nec est vt propter materiam, quae ex elementis petita est, corruptionem nouam metuamus: quia haec locum amplius habere non poterit, quando ipsa mors absorbebitur, & vires eius omnes abolebuntur, vt in sequenti Sermone dicetur. Quod nisi fateamur, dicant quaeso illi disputatores, in quo Dei Filij ab huius mundi machina differant, quae & ipsa abolebitur, vt seruitute, sub qua nunc gemit, liberetur: si non eadem corpora, quoad substantiam & materiam, qualitate autem & conditione beatiori ipsis restituentur. Quomodo autem idem corpus dici poterit, cuius neque forma neque materia est eadem, quae prius fuit? Respondeant item Christo, qui corpus clarificatum ex partibus & materia definiens, dum manus, latus, pedes, carnem & ossa nominat, & idem ex spirituum numero eximens discipulis spectandum & contrectandum exhibuit. Hoc (inquiunt) per dispensationem factum est. Quaero autem quae & qualis haec dispensatio fuerit? aut num alium se illis exhibuerit, quàm reuera esset? Si dicant, spectandum & contrectandum se praebuisse, cùm corpus haberet omnis materiae expers & insensibile: iam illum nobis praestigiatorem facient, qui falso spectro discipulorum sensus ludificarit. Et quae obsecro est illa consequentia: Christus à resurrectione in corpore clarificato se discipulis videndum & palpandum praebuit, vt se verè resurrexisse probaret: Ergo corpus Christi clarificatum est [?] & insensibile? Quis non praestigias iflas verborum abominetur? Aut quae vnquam Sophistica in fidei & religionis Christianae mysterijs impudentius lusit, aut petulantius populi rudis simplicitati insultauit? Denique vt finiamus hanc disputationem, quae praemia corporibus debuntur, aut quas poenas eadem subibunt, si & materia & sensu destituuntur? Procul ergo facessant haec commenta non minus impia quàm absurda, quibus tota salutis spes euertitur, & Christi pro nobis incarnati, mortui, resuscitati & nunc quoad humanam quoq; naturam in coelo regnantis mysterium prorsus euacuatur. Nos autem his omissis ad tertium huius loci caput transeamus. Nam exponit etiam Paulus, quo medio & qua ratione mortui excitandi sint. Qui locus con-fideratu dignissimus est, eò quòd resurrectio plerisque hac sola de causa impossibilis videtur, quia qua ratione perfici debeat non intelligunt, aut saltem non qua decebat diligentia expendunt. Præstat autè ante omnia Christum audire, qui negotium hoc omne sic narrat: Statim post affli-ctionem dierum illorum Sol obscurabitur, & Luna non dabit lumen suum, & stellæ cadent è cœlo, & potestates cœlorum agitabuntur: Et tunc apparebit signum Filij hominis in cœlo, & tunc plangent omnes tribus terræ, & videbunt Filium hominis venientem in nubibus cœli cum potestate & gloria multa. Et is mittet angelos suos cum tuba voce magna, qui cogent electos eius à quatuor ventis, à cœlorum extremo ad eorum extremum. Et apud Ioannem idem sic ait: Veniet hora, in qua omnes, qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem Filij Dei, & prodibunt: qui bona fecerunt in resurrectionem vitæ: qui verò mala egerunt, in resurrectionem iudicij. Ex Christi ore ergo desumpsit Paulus quod hic ait: Canet tuba, & mortui suscitabuntur incorrupti, & nos mutabimur. Quod ipsum in epistola ad Thessalonicenses pluribus explicat, quem locum supra recitauimus. Quæ omnia si diligentius considerentur, mox patebit, non adeò difficile fore, quod nunc nobis impossibile videtur. Nam Regi potenti in bellum contra hostes profecturo se confert Christus. Solent autem reges primum signa militaria expedire, præcones & tubicines mittere, qui milites ad arma excitent, & ad locum constitutum vocent. Estq; tanta istorum authoritas, vt milites mox relictis aliis rebus omnibus arma corripiant, & ad signa sua concurrant. Quia ergo Christus, qui Rex regum est, & Dominus dominantium, in nouissimo die idem faciet, non minoris efficaciæ erit signi, quod ille in cœlis expediet, conspectus, & tubæ illius cœlestis clangor, quem suam vocem dicit, quia ipsius virtute & auspiciis omnia gerentur. Etenim qui verbi sui virtute mundum hunc totum creare, & quæ non erant, ex nihilo producere potuit, vtique minori cum negotio mortuos ex terræ visceribus euocabit, vt ad ipsius tribunal sistantur. Vocat autem vltimam tubam Paulus respectu eorum, quæ de septem tubis in Apocalypsi leguntur, per quas Ecclesiæ certamina Spiritus Sanctus denotat, quibus omnibus postrema hæc finem imponet, eò quòd tunc Christus iudex in nubibus cœli comparebit, & optatissimum illum iubileum[?] electis suis adducet, quem olim sub Lege tubarum argentearum clangor denotabat, & quo ad amissam regni cœlorum possessionem rursus admittemur.
units.tr: But let us hear Paul speaking. After saying, "The dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed," he gives the reason for this and explains himself: "For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality." First he says "THIS corruptible" and "THIS mortal," as if he had in mind that saying of Job: "After they have destroyed THIS my skin, etc." So he speaks of no other body than the one that falls in death and, being subject to corruption, is dissolved into earth or dust. Next he attributes to it a change, not an abolition by which it would be reduced to nothing or made wholly devoid of all sensible matter. Thirdly, he defines the manner of this change by the word "put on": "For this corruptible must put on incorruption," etc. And in the later epistle he explains the hope of blessed immortality with the same word, saying: "In this we groan, desiring to be clothed upon with our habitation, which is from heaven." And soon after: "For we who are in this tabernacle groan, being burdened, not that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon, so that mortality may be swallowed up by life." Therefore let none of those men admit the arguments they bring forward about corruptible matter, to prove that the glorified body is either not a body or is made of no matter at all. For they attack and deny that very thing on which the hinge of the resurrection turns. We too grant that all the matter which now exists in nature is subject to corruption. But on that day there will be a change for the better, which is therefore called the day of the restoration of all things and of regeneration. Thus, while the same substance and matter of bodies remain, they will nevertheless put on incorruptibility and immortality. Nor is there any reason for us to fear a new corruption on account of the matter, which is taken from the elements, since corruption will no longer have place when death itself is swallowed up and all its powers are abolished, as will be said in the following sermon. Unless we grant this, let those disputers tell us, I beg, in what the bodies of the Son of God differ from the machinery of this world, which will also be abolished so that it may be freed from the servitude under which it now groans, if the same bodies are not restored to them, as to substance and matter, but in a happier quality and condition. And how can it be called the same body, whose form and matter are not the same as before? Let them also answer concerning Christ, who, defining his glorified body by its parts and matter, while he names hands, side, feet, flesh and bones, and, removing it from the number of spirits, showed it to the disciples to be seen and handled. "This," they say, "was done by dispensation." But I ask what and of what kind this dispensation was. Did he show himself to them otherwise than he really was? If they say that he offered himself to be seen and handled, though he had a body devoid of all matter and insensible, then they will make him for us a trickster, who deceived the senses of the disciples with a false phantom. And what, I beg, is that inference: "Christ, after the resurrection, showed himself in a glorified body to be seen and touched by the disciples, to prove that he had truly risen; therefore the body of Christ is glorified and insensible"? Who does not abhor those verbal tricks? Or what sophistry has ever played more shamelessly with the mysteries of the Christian faith and religion, or more insolently mocked the simplicity of the unlearned people? Finally, to end this discussion: what rewards are owed to bodies, or what punishments will they undergo, if they are deprived both of matter and of sense? Let these inventions, no less impious than absurd, depart far from us, by which the whole hope of salvation is overturned and the mystery of Christ, incarnate, dead, raised, and now reigning in heaven also in his human nature, is utterly emptied. But we, leaving these aside, pass on to the third point of this passage. For Paul also explains by what means and in what manner the dead are to be raised. This passage is most worthy of consideration, because the resurrection seems impossible to many for this reason alone: they do not understand in what way it ought to be accomplished, or at least do not weigh it with the care it deserves. Above all, it is best to hear Christ, who relates the whole matter thus: "Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give her light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken. And then the sign of the Son of man will appear in heaven, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. And he will send his angels with a great trumpet voice, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other." And in John he says the same thing: "The hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God and will come forth: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment." Paul therefore took from the mouth of Christ what he says here: "The trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed." He explains this at greater length in the epistle to the Thessalonians, which passage we cited above. If all these things are considered more carefully, it will soon be clear that what now seems impossible to us will not be so very difficult. For Christ betakes himself like a powerful king setting out to war against enemies. Kings usually first send out their military standards, and dispatch heralds and trumpeters, who rouse the soldiers to arms and summon them to an appointed place. And their authority is so great that the soldiers, leaving all other things at once, seize their arms and run together to their standards. Therefore, since Christ, who is King of kings and Lord of lords, will do the same on the last day, the sight of the sign which he will set up in heaven, and the blast of that heavenly trumpet, which he calls his voice because everything will be done by his power and under his auspices, will be no less effective. For he who by the power of his word was able to create this whole world and to bring into being from nothing things that were not, will certainly with less trouble call the dead out from the bowels of the earth, so that they may stand before his judgment seat. Paul calls it the last trumpet with respect to those trumpets of which we read in the Apocalypse, the seven trumpets, by which the Holy Spirit signifies the conflicts of the Church; this last trumpet will put an end to all of them, because then Christ the judge will appear in the clouds of heaven and will bring to his elect that most desired jubilee, which the sound of the silver trumpets under the Law once signified, and by which we shall be readmitted to the lost possession of the kingdom of heaven.

units.la: Ista verò inuictam & diuinam IESV CHRISTI potentiam nobis commendant, cuius multa argumenta hic simul congeruntur. Primum est ipsa corporum nostrorum resurrectio, quæ vires hominis omnes longè superat. Alterum, quòd eadem corpora resurgent, quæ nunc gestamus, & quæ per mortem extincta in terram redierunt. Superat vtrumq;, quòd illa nobis præstantiora & incorruptibilia restituentur. Imprimis verò stupendum diuinæ omnipotentiæ opus est, quòd ista omnia momento & iactu oculi fient. Quod etsi nostræ rationis captum excedat, nemini tamen impossibile videri debet. Si enim nos iactu oculi visum longè lateque extendere, & res innumeras longeque dissitas cernere possumus: si item vna vox multorum millium aures vno momento penetrat: annon maiorem esse oportet vocis diuinæ & cœlestis illius tubæ efficaciam? Seruiant ista consolationi aduersus crudeles tyrannorum conatus, quibus illi fidem & salutem nostram oppugnant. Simul autem nos officij admoneat magni illius diei consideratio, qui vt omnibus illucebit, ita nemo subterfugere, nemo iudicem illum reicere, nemo ab illo prouocare poterit. Non proderunt tunc opes, non honores, non eruditio, non dicendi facultas, non potentia, non amici, clientes, patroni, nihil denique quod nunc eximium habetur. Soli autem seruabuntur, quod propter fidem veram, qua ipsum amplexi sunt, pro suis agnoscet æternus Dei Filius IESVS CHRISTVS: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: These things commend to us the invincible and divine power of Jesus Christ, of which many proofs are here gathered together at once. The first is the resurrection of our bodies themselves, which far surpasses all human powers. The second is that the very same bodies which we now bear, and which by death have been extinguished and returned to the earth, will rise again. Both are surpassed by this, that they will be restored to us in a more excellent and incorruptible state. Above all, it is a stupendous work of divine omnipotence that all these things will happen in a moment and in the twinkling of an eye. Although this exceeds the grasp of our reason, it ought to seem impossible to no one. For if by a glance of the eye we can extend our sight far and wide, and see countless things lying far apart; and likewise if a single voice penetrates the ears of many thousands in one moment, must not the efficacy of the divine voice and of that heavenly trumpet be greater? Let these things serve for consolation against the cruel attempts of tyrants, by which they assail our faith and salvation. At the same time, let the consideration of that great day admonish us of our duty. For as it will shine on all, so no one will be able to escape it, no one will be able to reject that judge, no one will be able to appeal from him. Then riches will not avail, nor honours, nor learning, nor skill in speaking, nor power, nor friends, clients, or patrons; in short, nothing that is now held in esteem. Only those will be saved whom the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, shall acknowledge as his own, because of the true faith by which they embraced him. To him be blessing, honour, glory and dominion for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXXVII.
units.tr: Homily 87.

units.la: Cüm autem hoc corruptibile induerit incorruptibilitatem, & mortale hoc induerit immortalitatem, tunc fiet illud quod scriptum est: Absorpta est mors in victoriam. Vbi tuus ô mors aculeus:[?] vbi tua ô inferne, victoria? Aculeus vero mortis, peccatum: vis autem peccati, lex. Sed Deo sit gratia, qui dedit nobis victoriam per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum.
units.tr: When this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written: Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory? The sting of death is sin, and the strength of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Quoniam plerique resurrectionem ex mortuis impossibilem arbitrantur esse, eo quod eius modum siue rationem & cuius virtute perficiatur ignorant, vel saltem non diligenter expendunt, Paulus nuper eius historiam & ordinem expo-suit. Summa est, Christum de coelo descensurum esse in postrema tuba cum voce Archangeli, & tunc eos qui ante illum diem mortui fuerunt resurrecturos, inde mox alios, qui adhuc superstites fuerint, mutationem subituros esse, ut simul omnes incorruptibiles & immortales fiant. Omnia vero ad Dei omnipotentiam refert, ut primam mundi creationem nobis in mentem reducat, in qua nouae huius restitutionis exemplum euidens praecesserit. Habet autem historia duo, quae nos plurimum consolantur. Primum, quod multos ex electorum numero dies ille superstites deprehendet. Ex eo colligimus, Ecclesiam perpetuo duraturam esse in terris usque in huius seculi consummationem. Irriti ergo erunt omnium eorum conatus, qui illam oppressam & extinctam volent. Qui vero inter persecutionum fluctus in fide constantes perseuerauerint, iis dies ille laetus & salutifer illucescet. Alterum, quod mutatio fiet in melius.
