Nemini ergo molesta & intolerabilis videri debet, quae nunc in corporibus nostris haeret vitiositas, neque de resurrectione aliquis ideo dubitet, quod corpora corrupti & computrescere videt. Nam ita fieri necesse est, ut olim nobis incorruptibilia restitui possint. Simul autem illic eorum fultitia arguitur, qui corpori suo delitias faciunt, quasi in eo aeternum victuri sint, & eadem post mortem quoque conseruare studeant atque sepulchrorum sumptuoso apparatu superbiunt. Discant potius Christiani homines ad beatam illam immortalitatem aspirare, quam non assequemur, nisi quicquid in nobis corruptibile est vel per mortem, vel per subitam illam mutationem aboleatur. Porro his absolutis ad alterum huius historiae caput transit, quo quid a resurrectione futurum sit docetur, & ita amplissimum eius fructum exponit, quo perfecta totius humanae naturae redemptio continetur.
units.tr: Since many people think that the resurrection of the dead is impossible, because they do not know the manner or the means by which it is accomplished, or at least do not examine them carefully, Paul has recently set out its history and order. In summary: Christ will descend from heaven at the last trumpet, with the voice of the archangel; then those who died before that day will rise again, and soon after, those who are still alive will undergo the change, so that all of them together become incorruptible and immortal. Paul refers all these things to the omnipotence of God, so that he may call to mind the first creation of the world, in which an clear example of this new restoration preceded. The account contains two points that greatly comfort us. First, that day will find many of the number of the elect still alive. From this we gather that the Church will endure on earth continuously until the end of this age. Therefore all the attempts of those who wish to crush and extinguish it will come to nothing. But for those who remain steadfast in faith amid the waves of persecution, that day will dawn joyful and saving. Second, the change will be for the better. Therefore no one should regard as troublesome or intolerable the corruption that now clings to our bodies, nor should anyone doubt the resurrection because he sees bodies decay and rot. For it must happen in this way, so that they may one day be restored to us incorruptible. At the same time, the folly of those is exposed who indulge their bodies with luxuries, as if they were going to live in them for ever, and who strive to preserve them even after death and take pride in the costly furnishing of tombs. Rather, Christian people should learn to aspire to that blessed immortality, which we shall not attain unless whatever in us is corruptible is abolished, either through death or through that sudden change. Now, with these things settled, he passes to the second point of this account, in which it is taught what will follow the resurrection, and so sets out its most ample fruit, in which the complete redemption of the whole of human nature is contained.

units.la: Principio sic ait: Cum autem hoc corruptibile induerit incorruptibilitatem, & mortale hoc induerit immortalitatem, tunc fiet illud quod scriptum est: Absorpta est mors in victoriam, &c. Non temere repetit voces istas, HOC corruptibile, & HOC mortale. Oportet enim probe tenere non aliam, quam corporum quae nunc habemus, resurrectionem esse sperandam. Et mirum est inter Christianos homines inueniri hodie, qui de eo subtilius philosophentur, quod Apostolus toties verbis disertis repetit, & tantum non ad nauseam usque inculcat. Ne autem aliquid ex suo cerebro fingere putetur, futuri seculi conditionem non suis, sed Veteris Scripturae verbis exponit. Ita enim solent Apostoli in causis difficilioribus, & suo exemplo temerarios somniatores arguunt, qui quicquid ipsis in buccam venit effutiunt, & Ecclesiae sua figmenta pro indubiis Verbi Dei oraculis obtrudunt. Argumentum vero Pauli est eiusmodi. Ex Scripturis constat, mortem oportere absorberi in victoriam, id est, ita vinci, ut nulla porro fit, adeoque, ut nobis ei simul & inferi insultare liceat. Id vero fieri nequit, quoad corpora nostra per illam detinentur: Ergo ea resurgant oportet, & incorruptibilia fiant. Tunc enim nullus porro morti locus erit, neque aliquid ius in nos habebunt inferi, & proinde vita immortali, gaudio item & felicitate aeterna absque omnis periculi metu fruemur. Quod si vero mors tota absorbebitur, nullum periculum erit, ne corpora nostra adhuc corruptioni obnoxia sint, etiamsi materia & substantia sua, quam prius habuerunt, non exuantur. Sed in Apostoli verbis pergamus, qui duos Scripturae locos coniungit.
units.tr: In the beginning he speaks thus: When this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written: Death is swallowed up in victory, etc. He does not repeat these words, THIS corruptible and THIS mortal, rashly. For it is necessary to hold firmly that the only resurrection to be hoped for is that of the bodies we now have. And it is strange that among Christian people today there are some who philosophize more subtly about this than the Apostle, who repeats it so often in plain words, and almost drives it home to the point of nausea. Lest he be thought to invent something from his own brain, he sets out the condition of the future age not in his own words but in the words of the Old Scripture. This is how the Apostles are accustomed to act in more difficult matters, and by their example they refute rash dreamers, who babble whatever comes into their mouths and foist their own fancies on the Church as if they were the indubitable oracles of the Word of God. Paul's argument is of this kind. It is established from the Scriptures that death must be swallowed up in victory, that is, be so conquered that it no longer exists, and so that we may also mock it, and hell along with it. This cannot happen as long as our bodies are held by death. Therefore they must rise and become incorruptible. For then there will be no place left for death, and hell will have no right over us, and so we shall enjoy immortal life, and likewise joy and eternal happiness, without fear of any danger. But if death is swallowed up entirely, there will be no danger that our bodies, even if they retain the matter and substance they previously had, are still subject to corruption. But let us proceed with the words of the Apostle, who joins two passages of Scripture.

units.la: Primus extat apud Isaiam, qui cum vigesimo quarto Cap. vniuersale Dei iudicium describeret, quo omnibus seculis mundi scelera puniturus fit, mox sequenti Cap. de credentium liberatione vaticinatur, ne quis inter horribiles omnium gentium motus Ecclesiam quoque periturampu-taret. Et quia liberatio haec solius Christi merito nititur, qui idem vnicus eius author est, ita hanc causam tractat, ut illius beneficia commemoret. Inter ea autem praecipuum est, quod ex mortis tyrannide nos eripuit, de quo sic loquitur: Mortem absorbebit in victoria, & abstergit[?] Dominus Dominus Deus lachrymam à cunctis faciebus, & opprobrium populi sui auferet ab vniuersa terra.
units.tr: The first is found in Isaiah, who, when in chapter twenty-four he describes the universal judgment of God, by which he will punish the sins of the world in all ages, in the following chapter he prophesies the deliverance of believers, so that no one, amid the terrible upheavals of all nations, should think that the Church too will perish. And because this deliverance rests solely on the merit of Christ, who is its only author, he treats the matter in such a way as to recall his benefits. Among these the chief is that he has rescued us from the tyranny of death, of which he speaks thus: The Lord GOD will swallow up death in victory, and will wipe away tears from all faces, and will take away the reproach of his people from the whole earth.

units.la: Quo loco diligenter obseruari debet, Prophetas quoties bona temporaria populo pollicentur, horum quoq; authorem siue mediatorem facere Christum, & ea occasione de æternis quoque admonere, & ita in vniuersam humani generis liberationem siue redemptionem digredi. Exempla passim occurrunt, vt ea commemorare non sit opus. Nobis autem eorum hic vsus esse debet, vt ipsi quoq; quæcunq; nobis pro voto & feliciter accidunt, ad Christum authorem referamus, qui nobis Patrem placauit, vt nobis propitius fit, qui prius peccatis nostris irascebatur. Interim meminerimus, præstantiora hisce temporariis bonis nobis in Christo reposita esse, in quorum plenam possessionem olim venturi sumus, quando nobis ex morte resuscitatis vnà cum morte omnis diaboli atque inferorum potestas prorsus destruetur & abolebitur. Itafiet, vt neque in huius seculi commodis acquiescamus (quod plerique cum certa salutis æternæ iactura faciunt) neque etiam aduersis ex improuiso incidentibus offensi à fide deficiamus. Nam beatæ resurrectionis spe confirmati ad æterna & cœlestia bona aspiramus, huius autem vitæ incommoda, vt momentanea & leuicula facilè contemnemus.
units.tr: Here it must be carefully observed that whenever the Prophets promise temporal goods to the people, they make Christ the author or mediator of these also, and on that occasion they also admonish about eternal things, and so digress into the deliverance or redemption of the whole human race. Examples occur everywhere, so there is no need to recall them. But we ought to use them in this way: that we too should refer to Christ, as author, whatever happens to us according to our wish and happily, since he has appeased the Father for us, so that he who was previously angry at our sins may be propitious to us. Meanwhile let us remember that better things than these temporal goods are laid up for us in Christ, into whose full possession we shall one day come, when, having been raised from death, the power of the devil and of hell, together with death itself, will be utterly destroyed and abolished. Thus it will come about that we shall neither rest content in the advantages of this age (which many do, with the certain loss of eternal salvation), nor, offended by adversities that fall upon us unexpectedly, fall away from the faith. For, strengthened by the hope of the blessed resurrection, we aspire to eternal and heavenly goods, and the troubles of this life we will easily despise as momentary and trifling.

units.la: Alterum locum ex Hoseæ Cap. XIII. adducit Paulus. Corripuit illic Deus grauiter Israelitarum contumaciam, & vt magis moueat, simul docet, quàm felices & beati futuri sint, si seipsos ei reformandos & corrigendos præbeant. Inter alia igitur hæc quoq; dicit: E manu sepulchri redimam eos, ex morte vindicabo illos, id est, licet morte absumpti in sepulchris delitescant, & ad inferos vsque detrudantur, tamen inde quoq; eos eripiam. Et mox prosopopœia eleganti mortem & inferos hostes fingit, quibus insultans, vel potius minitabundus dicit: Ero pestis tua ô mors, & ero excidium tuum ô inferne. At quia promissionum omnium basis atq; fundamentum est Christus, in quo etiam eadem sunt Etiam & Amen, Paulus verba ista nonnihil immutans ea Christo ad iudicium venturo tribuit, & quasi iam nunc impleta sint omnia ipsum loquentem inducit, perinde ac si quis hosti deuicto & prostrato insolentes minas & armorum apparatum, victorias item priores & quæcunque alia confidentes homines iactare solent, exprobret. Itaque illum dicentem fingit: Multùm quidem & diu hucusque ô mors sæuisti in humanum genus, & per te Satan plane dominari visus es, quando tu omnis loci & ordinis homines promiscuè abripuisti. At nunc dies ille aduenit, quem olim tibi per Prophetas meos denunciaui: fore nimirum vt te destruam, & simul inferos quoque deuincam. Ubi ergo nunc tua illa victoria? ubi triumphi? ubi aculeus ille tuus, quo omnes perdidisti? Ubi inferorum potestas, quibus tu seruire videbaris? Annnon te debellatam & exarmatam esse sentis, quando vitæ restitutos & prorsus incorruptibiles atque immortales factos esse vides, quos prius perdidisse videbaris? Iam ne me eum esse agnoscis, quem Pater ab æterno vitæ & mortis dominum constituit? Hæc & quæcunq; sunt huius generis paucis hisce verbis comprehenduntur, adeoq; gloriosus Christi triumphus illis denotatur, quem ille tunc de morte, diabolo & inferis aget.
units.tr: Paul brings forward the second passage from Hosea chapter thirteen. There God severely rebukes the obstinacy of the Israelites, and to move them more strongly he teaches at the same time how happy and blessed they will be if they allow themselves to be reformed and corrected by him. Among other things, then, he also says: I will redeem them from the hand of the grave; I will deliver them from death. That is, although they may lie hidden in graves, consumed by death, and be thrust down even to the underworld, nevertheless I will snatch them away from there too. And soon after, with an elegant prosopopoeia, he imagines death and hell as enemies, and, insulting them, or rather threatening them, says: I will be your plague, O death, and I will be your destruction, O hell. But because Christ is the basis and foundation of all promises, in whom the Yes and the Amen are the same, Paul, slightly altering these words, attributes them to Christ as he will come to judgment, and, as if all things were already fulfilled, introduces him speaking, just as people are accustomed to taunt an enemy who has been conquered and thrown down with insolent threats, a display of arms, and boasts of former victories and whatever else confident men are used to boast. So he imagines him speaking thus: Much and long, hitherto, O death, you have raged against the human race, and you, Satan, have clearly seemed to rule through death, since you have snatched away people of every rank and station indiscriminately. But now that day has come, which I long ago announced to you through my Prophets: that I shall certainly destroy you, and at the same time conquer hell as well. Where, then, is your victory now? Where are your triumphs? Where is that sting of yours, by which you destroyed everyone? Where is the power of hell, to which you seemed to be enslaved? Do you not perceive that you have been defeated and disarmed, when you see restored to life and made wholly incorruptible and immortal those whom you seemed to have destroyed? Do you not yet recognize me as the one whom the Father from eternity appointed lord of life and death? These things, and whatever is of this kind, are comprehended in these few words, and by them is signified the glorious triumph of Christ, which he will then win over death, the devil, and hell.

units.la: At hic meminerimus, ista Christo propter nos tribui, vt certò sciamus, mortem iam nunc ab illo ita deuictam esse, vt nequaquam nobis porrò formidabilis esse debeat. Manet quidem adhuc omnes homines moriendi necessitas: at credentibus mors non amplius exitio est, sed ostium potius siue transitus ex vita hac misera & mortali in patriam cœlestem, vbi æterna gaudia nobis præparata sunt. Nec quicquam obstabit, quin olim corpora quoque nostra resuscitentur, & fiat, quod olim per prophetas & apostolos prædictum est. Quis ergo morte porrò horreat? Quin potius ea timemus quæ morte graviora sunt? Quæ verò illa? Num exilium? num morbi? num egestas? num libertatis oppressio? Non equidem si verum fateri libeat. Nam omnia ista cum morte coniuncta sunt, quæ ijsdem aliquando finem imponet. Omnibus autem istis & ipsa morte grauius atque intolerabilius est à Christo diuelli, & ita vitæ æternæ iacturam facere. Agnouerunt hoc omnes sancti, quorum pietas in scripturis probatur. Huius doloris sensu perculsus Petrus olim clamauit: Domine quò ibimus? tu verba vitæ æternæ habes. Quod ipsum Paulus sentiens omnia, quæ in mundo præclara & eximia habebat, pro damnis duxit, vt Christum apprehenderet. Eiusdem impatientissimo desiderio Martyres accensi mille rogos subire, & diris quorumuis tormentorum cruciatibus subijci maluerunt quàm fidem in Christum abnegare.
units.tr: But let us remember here that these things are attributed to Christ on our account, so that we may know for certain that death has already been so conquered by him that it ought in no way to be dreadful to us any longer. Indeed the necessity of dying still remains for all men; but to believers death is no longer destruction, but rather a door or passage out of this wretched and mortal life into the heavenly homeland, where eternal joys are prepared for us. Nothing will stand in the way of our bodies also being raised one day, and what was foretold of old by the prophets and apostles will come to pass. Who, then, should still shrink from death? Or rather, what do we fear that is worse than death? And what is that? Exile? Disease? Poverty? The oppression of liberty? Not really, if we are willing to speak the truth. For all these are bound up with death, which will one day put an end to them. But to be torn away from Christ, and so to suffer the loss of eternal life, is more grievous and more intolerable than all of them, even than death itself. All the saints, whose godliness is attested in the Scriptures, have acknowledged this. Struck by the feeling of this sorrow, Peter once cried out: "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life." Paul, feeling this very thing, counted all the splendid and excellent things he had in the world as loss, that he might lay hold of Christ. Kindled by the same most impatient longing, the martyrs preferred to undergo a thousand fires and to submit to the dreadful torments of whatever kind rather than deny their faith in Christ.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui ut certior & efficacior fit consolatio ista, evidentius docet, quis sit ille mortis aculeus, quae item inferorum victoria, & qua ratione horum potestas eversa, illius autem virus sublatum atque extinctum sit. Aculeus mortis (inquit) est peccatum: vis autem peccati, Lex. Sed Deo sit gratia, qui dedit nobis victoriam per Dominum nostrum IESUM CHRISTUM. Diabolum, communem generis humani hostem, immani serpenti aut bestiae confert, quae aculeo mortis, id est, mortifero omnes homines occidat. Et aculeum hunc dicit esse peccatum. Per peccatum enim mors ingressa est, & ut primos parentes Satan serpente tectus occidit, quando eis ut Dei mandatum transgrederentur persuasit: ita omnibus illorum posteris peccandi idem author est, unde exitium nostrum emanat. Unde vero (inquis) tanta peccati vis? Id uno verbo Paulus docet, Legem nominans: non quod Lex suapte natura letifera sit[?] exitialis sit, sed quod peccatum (ut ab Ioanne Apostolo definitur) Legis transgressio sit, quae mortem meretur. Quod si Legem per se aestimes, sancta iusta & bona est. Quia autem ubi nulla Lex, ibi neque transgressio ulla est; nos vero Legem habemus quidem, sed eidem obedire aut satisfacere non possumus, illa peccatum simul & mortem gignere dicitur: non quidem ex seipsa, sed propter naturae nostrae vitiositatem, quae ut Legi repugnat, ita ex semetipsa non aliud quam peccare potest, & peccando mortem toti homini accersere. Quapropter cum Christus Legem impleverit & simul ius eius abrogarit, ne posthac peccata nobis imputari queant, haec quoque simul sustulit atque expiavit. Quod si vero peccatum simul & Legem e medio sustulit, utique mortifero illo aculeo diabolum exarmavit, quo is contra nos non alio iure saeviebat, quam quod peccatores essemus, & propterea morte digni iudicaremur.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who shows more clearly, so that this consolation may be more certain and effective, what that sting of death is, and likewise what the victory over the underworld is, and by what means their power has been overthrown and the poison of death taken away and extinguished. "The sting of death," he says, "is sin; and the strength of sin is the Law. But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." He compares the devil, the common enemy of the human race, to a huge serpent or beast, which kills all men with the sting of death, that is, with its deadly venom. And he says that this sting is sin. For through sin death entered, and just as Satan, hidden in the serpent, killed our first parents when he persuaded them to transgress God's command, so he is the author of sinning for all their posterity, from which our destruction flows. But whence, you may ask, comes such great power in sin? Paul teaches this in one word, by naming the Law: not that the Law is by its own nature deadly or destructive, but because sin (as the Apostle John defines it) is a transgression of the Law, which deserves death. Indeed, if you consider the Law in itself, it is holy, just and good. But since where there is no law there is no transgression, and we do have the Law but cannot obey it or satisfy it, the Law is said to produce both sin and death: not from itself, but on account of the vitiated state of our nature, which, as it opposes the Law, so from itself can do nothing but sin, and by sinning bring death upon the whole man. Wherefore, since Christ has fulfilled the Law and at the same time abrogated its right, so that sins can no longer be imputed to us, he has also removed and expiated these things together. And if he has indeed taken away both sin and the Law from the midst, he has certainly disarmed the devil of that deadly sting, by which he raged against us with no other right than that we were sinners and therefore judged worthy of death.

units.la: Voluit autem Paulus hoc loco Legis quoque mentionem facere propter eos, qui huius studio addicti, se ei propriis viribus obedire, & proinde ex huius operibus iustitiam atque salutem consequi posse sibi persuadebant. Docet ergo ipsos adeo falli[?]pe sua, ut potius per Legem accusentur, peccati communicantur, & hoc ex Lege gravius atque letalius fiat. Quia enim ei nemo satisfacere potest, rata semper manebit, quoad nos & nostra opera, gravis illa & plus quam cruenta sententia: Maledictus, qui non fecerit omnia, quae scripta sunt in libro Legis huius. Quae causa est, quod Paulus hanc partem dulci & plena consolationis [?]διαλογία concludit, qua salutem nostram solius Dei gratiae acceptam fert per IESUM CHRISTUM. Itaque totum hunc locum argumento tali poteris completi: Quod omnes homines morti & poenis infernalibus obnoxii sunt, id omne ex peccato est: At Deus peccatum sustulit per Christum: Ergo in eodem mors quoque exarmata, & inferi prorsus expugnati sunt. Continetur his universa salutis doctrina, cuius partes singulas saepius inspexisse prodest.
units.tr: Paul wished in this place to mention the Law also, on account of those who, devoted to its study, persuaded themselves that they could obey it by their own powers, and so obtain righteousness and salvation from its works. He therefore teaches that they are so deceived in their own estimation that they are rather accused through the Law, made partakers of sin, and that this becomes more grievous and deadly through the Law. For since no one can satisfy it, that heavy and more than bloody sentence will always remain valid as far as we and our works are concerned: "Cursed is everyone who does not do all the things written in the book of this Law." This is why Paul concludes this part with a sweet and full consolation, by a kind of dialogue [διαλογία], in which he ascribes our salvation to the grace of God alone, received through Jesus Christ. Therefore you may summarise this whole passage in such an argument: All men are subject to death and to infernal punishments; all this comes from sin; but God has taken away sin through Christ; therefore death too is disarmed in the same, and the underworld has been utterly overcome. The whole doctrine of salvation is contained in these points, and it is useful to examine its individual parts often.

units.la: Prima est, qua nos mortis & damnationis reos esse, docemur. Causa in promptu est, quia omnes peccatores sumus. Testatur hoc omnis Scriptura, & si quis id negare audet, eum propria conscientia suo testimonio convincet. Quis enim non sentit cordis sui figmenta mala esse ab ineunte aetate? Aut quis negare poterit, pravas cogitationes sibi etiam invito obrepere? Imo quis tam perfricta frontis est, ut se illis non interdum indulgere, & ex iis quantulamcunque voluptatem capere inficiatur? Taceo nunc dicta improba, quae vel iratus, vel alio affectu abreptis, vel perigno rantiam temere nobis excidunt. Taceo item facta, quae contra Legis divinae praescriptum designamus. Verumtamen si ista omnia dissimulare lubeat, quid de infantibus praematura morte (ut vulgo aiunt) extinctis dicemus? Certe, nisi hos ex parentibus peccatores nasci fateamur, Deum iniustitiae insimulabimus, qui nihil huius meritis peccati poenam infligat. Debent ista saepe & diligenter considerari, & ab his Scripturae passim exordiuntur, quando de salutis nostrae causa disserunt, ut de nostris viribus atque meritis nos desperare cogant, quod salutis principium esse, alibi diximus.
units.tr: The first part is that by which we are taught that we are guilty of death and damnation. The cause is at hand, because we are all sinners. All Scripture bears witness to this, and if anyone dares to deny it, his own conscience will convict him by its testimony. For who does not feel that the imaginations of his heart are evil from his earliest youth? Or who can deny that wicked thoughts creep upon him even against his will? Indeed, who is so brazen-faced as not to admit that he sometimes indulges in them, and takes some pleasure from them? I say nothing now of the wicked words that escape us rashly, whether in anger, or carried away by some other passion, or through wantonness. I say nothing either of the deeds which we commit against the precept of the divine Law. Yet if we are willing to overlook all these things, what shall we say of infants snatched away by an untimely death (as people commonly say)? Certainly, unless we confess that they are born sinners from their parents, we shall accuse God of injustice, since he inflicts the punishment of sin on them though they have deserved nothing of it. These matters ought to be considered often and carefully, and Scripture everywhere begins from them when it discourses on the cause of our salvation, so that they may compel us to despair of our own powers and merits, which, as I have said elsewhere, is the beginning of salvation.

units.la: Ita enim hanc extra nos quaerere incipiemus, ubi nobis solius Dei gratia, vel potius misericordia gratuita occurret. Is enim occidit, ut vivificet. Idem peccatorum nostrorum molem atque atrocitatem arguit, ut gratiae suae & misericordiae divitias inexhaustas aliqua ex parte aestimare possimus. De eo nos Paulus per gratiarum actionem admonet, dicens: Sed Deo sit gratia, qui dedit nobis victoriam per Dominum nostrum IESUM CHRISTUM. Loquitur autem de uictoria, qua mors exarmata, & inferi expugnati sunt: Illam non nos obtinuisse, aut ex hoste re-tulisse, sed à Deo nobis datam esse ait, eoq; nomine gratias illi agens, hoc gratuitum misericordiæ diuinæ beneficium esse fatetur. Etenim si uictoriam contra hostes à Domino dari, gentes quoque olim agnouerunt, & ideo bellis exortis ad Deos suos votis & precibus solicitis conuersi sunt: ni-mirum impudens fuerit, qui peccatum, mortem, diabolum & inferos nostros uiribus uinci posse di-xerit. Quid enim hic faciant, qui ne ad cogitandum quidem sunt idonei?
units.tr: For thus we shall begin to seek this outside ourselves, where the grace of God alone, or rather his free mercy, will meet us. For he kills in order to make alive. The same God exposes the mass and atrocity of our sins, so that we may in some measure estimate the inexhaustible riches of his grace and mercy. Paul reminds us of this by giving thanks: "But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." He speaks of the victory by which death has been disarmed and the underworld overcome. He says that we did not obtain it or win it from the enemy, but that it was given to us by God; and in thanking him for this, he confesses that it is a free benefit of divine mercy. For the nations too of old recognised that victory over enemies is given by the Lord, and therefore, when wars broke out, they turned to their gods with vows and anxious prayers. Surely he would be shameless who said that sin, death, the devil and our underworld can be overcome by our own strength. For what could those do who are not even fit to think?

units.la: Quis verò ille est, per quem nobis uictoriam hanc salutiferam Deus dedit? Filius eius, Dominus noster JESVS CHRISTVS. Is enim nobis ab illo factus est sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio & redemptio. In eodem uictoria quoque plena nobis obtigit. Nam benedictum illud & à multis seculis optatum mulieris semen est, quod serpentis caput contriuit, & diaboli potentiam omnem euertit. Idem nobis quoque uires suggerit, quibus serpentem illum, quantumuis adhuc sibilare pergat, sub nostris quoque pedibus conculcat, ut Paulus alibi ait. Denique qui Christo per fidem uere sunt insiti in eodem possunt omnia. Unde Joannes dicebat: Omne quod natum est ex Deo, uincit mundum: & hæc est uictoria quæ uincit mundum, nempe fides nostra. Quis est qui uincit mundum, nisi qui credit quòd JESVS est Filius Dei? Quo loco sub mundi uocabulo huius etiam principem unà cum peccato & morte comprehendi, manifestius est, quàm ut demonstrari oporteat. Quis enim mundum ab eo deuictum dixerit, in quo mundi princeps per peccatum & mortem adhuc dominatur? Itaque uniuersa nostræ salutis gloria solius Dei gratuita misericordiæ debetur per CHRISTVM IESVM, qui hanc nobis meruit. Et quàmuis iam nunc nobis salus illa parta sit, plena tamen & omnibus numeris absoluta erit eius possessio, quando Christus aduentu suo glorioso Satanam æternis inferorum carceribus constringet, mortem abolebit, nosq; à mortuis excitatos aut subita mutatione incorruptibiles fastos[?] ad se recipiet. Interim quoad in hac carne uiuimus, perpetuò nobis luctandum erit, usque quò latus ille & felix triumphi universalis dies illucescet.
units.tr: Who, then, is he through whom God has given us this saving victory? His Son, our Lord JESUS CHRIST. For he has been made to us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. In him also we have obtained full victory. For that blessed seed of the woman, longed for through many ages, is the one who crushed the serpent's head and overthrew all the power of the devil. The same Christ also supplies us with strength by which we tread that serpent under our feet, however much it may still go on hissing, as Paul says elsewhere. Finally, those who have truly been grafted into Christ through faith can do all things in him. Hence John said: "Whatever is born of God overcomes the world; and this is the victory that overcomes the world, namely our faith. Who is it that overcomes the world, except he who believes that JESUS is the Son of God?" That under the name of the world the prince of this world is also included, together with sin and death, is more evident than it needs to be demonstrated. For who would say that the world has been overcome by him in whom the prince of the world still rules through sin and death? Therefore the whole glory of our salvation is owed to the free mercy of God alone, through CHRIST JESUS, who has merited it for us. And although that salvation has already been secured for us, our possession of it will be full and complete in every respect when Christ, by his glorious coming, will bind Satan in the eternal prisons of the underworld, abolish death, and receive us, raised from the dead or changed in an instant into incorruptible beings, to himself. Meanwhile, as long as we live in this flesh, we shall have to struggle continually, until that blessed and happy day of universal triumph dawns.

units.la: Ex his apparet totam humanæ salutis rationem eiusque principia conuelli atque euerti ab iis, qui resurrectionem ex mortuis & qui cum ea coniunctus est nouissimum Christi ad iudicium aduentum negant, aut scurrilibus dictis in dubium uocant. Nisi enim mortui resurgant & corpora nostra incorruptibilitate & immortalitate donentur, salua manebit & integra fem-[?]per morti sua potestas, quam per peccatum in nos obtinuit. Quòd si verò mortis potestas & imperium manserit, peccati quoque noxa maneat necesse est. Itaque & peccato & morti obnoxii adhuc erimus. Quid ergo de iustitia & uita dicemus, quam suæ mortis merito Christus nobis acquisiuit? Aut quid porrò ex illo sperare possumus? Vel qua de causa illum in mundum uenisse & hominem factum esse dicemus? Quid verò idem ille suâ morte & resurrectione meruit? Imò fatendum erit, aut fabulosa esse quæcunque de illo in Scripturis traduntur, aut quòd nulla sit prorsus mortis & resurrectionis ipsius utilitas. Quid verò magis impium excogitari, aut quod conuitium in Deum atrocius dici poterat? Diuinis & humanis legibus mortis supplicium iis decernitur, qui temerarium in Deum, in Filium eius JESVM CHRISTVM conuicitum dixerint, aut illius nomine ad impias execrationes fuerint abusi. At quanto grauior eorum culpa est, qui mortuorum resurrectionem scurriliter negant, & ita uno quasi ictu religionem Christianam prorsus euertunt? Sed quæ nostri seculi est calamitas, pauci istos qua decet seueritate coercent, multi etiam ex eorum dicteriis[?] uoluptatem uenantur. Sunt hi nouissimorum temporum mores, quos nosse quidem oportet, cùm de iis nos olim Spiritus Sanctus admonuerit: at iisdem pii nequaquam moueri debent, multò minus eorum exempla imitari, qui ita loquuntur & sentiunt. Oremus autem Deum Patrem, ut læta beatæ resurrectionis spe confirmati, per omnia salutis obstacula fide constanti eluctemur, ut ipsi quoque in magno illo die peccato, morte & inferis superiores facti cum JESV CHRISTO redemptore nostro triumphemus, uiuamus & regnemus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: From these things it is clear that the whole plan of human salvation, and its foundations, are overturned and destroyed by those who deny the resurrection of the dead and Christ's final coming to judgement, which is bound up with it, or who call it into doubt with scurrilous words. For unless the dead rise and our bodies are endowed with incorruptibility and immortality, the power of death, which it obtained over us through sin, will remain safe and entire for ever. But if the power and dominion of death remain, the harm of sin must also remain. So we shall still be subject both to sin and to death. What then shall we say of the righteousness and life which Christ won for us by the merit of his death? Or what more can we hope for from him? Or for what reason shall we say that he came into the world and was made man? What, moreover, did he merit by his death and resurrection? Indeed, we must confess either that everything that is handed down about him in the Scriptures is fabulous, or that his death and resurrection have no usefulness at all. What could be imagined more impious, or what reproach could be spoken against God more atrocious? By divine and human laws the penalty of death is decreed for those who have spoken rashly against God, against his Son JESUS CHRIST , or who have abused his name for impious curses. But how much graver is the guilt of those who scurrilously deny the resurrection of the dead, and so by a single blow utterly overthrow the Christian religion! Yet it is a calamity of our age that few restrain these men with the severity they deserve, while many even hunt out pleasure in their jests. These are the customs of the last times, which indeed we ought to know, since the Holy Spirit warned us of them long ago; but the godly ought in no way to be moved by them, much less to imitate the examples of those who speak and think in this way. Let us pray, however, to God the Father, that, strengthened by the joyful hope of the blessed resurrection, we may struggle through all the hindrances to salvation with a steadfast faith, so that we too, on that great day, made superior to sin, death and hell, may triumph, live and reign with JESUS CHRIST our Redeemer, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXXVIII.
units.tr: Homily 88.

units.la: Itaq; fratres mei dilecti, firmi estote, immoti, abundantes in opere Domini semper: cùm sciatis laborem vestrum non esse inanem in Domino.
units.tr: Therefore, my beloved brothers, be firm and immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, since you know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord. (1 Cor. 15:58)

units.la: Dei Filius, IESVS CHRISTVS Dominus noster, ideo in mundum venit & homo factus est, vt miseros mortales ex peccati noxa & diaboli tyrannide liberatos Patri consecraret, nosq; ei sisteret genus electum, regale sacerdotium, gentem sanctam, populum acquisitum & proprium, qui ipsius virtutes praedicet. Quare religio Christiana in duobus potissimum consistit. Primum est, vt Christum agnoscamus redemptorem vnicum, inq; eo solo omnem salutis spem collocemus, quando nec ipse gloriam suam dat alteri, neque aliud nomen sub coelo hominibus datum est, in quo nos seruari oporteat. Alterum, vt vitam viuamus vere Christianam, quae fidei nostrae professioni respondeat. Nec enim omnis (ait ille) qui mihi dixerit, Domine Domine, ingredietur in regnum meum: sed qui fecerit voluntatem Patris mei, qui in coelis est. Vrgent duo haec capita passim Apostoli, & ad ista Paulus doctrinam de mortuorum resurrectione hactenus prolixè expositam potissimum accommodat. In iis enim, quae proximè praecesserunt, futuri seculi conditionem ita descripsit, vt aperte omnis beatitatis nostrae authorem esse docuerit IESVM CHRISTVM. Nunc verò, quia Corinthij non solum in isto articulo vacillabant, sed vitam quoque viuebant Christiani nominis professione indignam, adeò vt periculum esset, ne impostorum fallacijs & illusorum dicacitate decepti à fide prorsus deficerent, tractationem hanc ita concludit, vt totam ipsis applicet, & ostendat, quis ipsis eius vsus esse debeat tam in religione quàm in vitae totius consuetudine & moribus. Partes loci huius duae sunt, de quibus ex ordine dicemus.
units.tr: The Son of God, Jesus Christ our Lord, came into the world and was made man so that he might free miserable mortals from the harm of sin and the tyranny of the devil, and present them consecrated to the Father: a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, who proclaim his virtues. Therefore the Christian religion rests chiefly on two things. The first is that we acknowledge Christ as the one Redeemer and place all our hope of salvation in him alone, since he does not give his glory to another, and there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). The second is that we live a life truly Christian, which corresponds to our profession of faith. For, as he says, not everyone who says to me, "Lord, Lord," will enter the kingdom of my Father, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven (Matt. 7:21). The apostles everywhere press these two heads, and to these Paul now applies the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead, which he has so far expounded at length. For in what immediately preceded, he described the condition of the age to come in such a way as to teach plainly that Jesus Christ is the author of all our blessedness. But now, since the Corinthians were not only wavering on this article, but also living a life unworthy of the name of Christian, so that there was danger that, deceived by the deceits of impostors and the mockery of scoffers, they would utterly fall away from the faith, he concludes this discussion so as to apply it wholly to them, and to show what use of it they ought to make, both in religion and in the whole course of their life and conduct. The parts of this passage are two, and we shall speak of them in order.

units.la: Prima hortatione graui constat, sed paucis verbis comprehensa: Itaque fratres mei dilecti, firmi estote, immoti, abundantes in opere Domini semper. Amicè & non sine pathetica amoris significatione eos compellat, fratres suos dilectos dicens, vt correptiones, quibus hucusq; acrioribus fuerat vsus, leniat, neue ipsum iniquius de ipsorum Ecclesia sentire putent. Ex iis autem, quae proximè scripserat, haec inferens, ita vult dicere: Cùm ergo constet, nos per Christum vere redemptos esse, qui victoriam nobis eiusmodi acquisiuit, vt neque mors neque inferi obstare possint, quo minus ad beatam immortalitatem resurgamus, etiam atque etiam nobis videndum erit, vt tantum Filij Dei beneficium qua decet diligentia & gratitudine expendatis, & tales sitis porrò, quos ipse in magno illo die possit pro suis agnoscere. Et ne quarant, quid facto opus sit, duo praescribit.
units.tr: The first part consists of a weighty exhortation, but it is compressed into few words: "Therefore, my beloved brothers, be firm and immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord." He addresses them kindly and with a touching expression of love, calling them his beloved brothers, so as to soften the rebukes with which he had hitherto dealt rather sharply, and so that they should not think he judged their Church too unfairly. He draws this conclusion from what he had just written, and his meaning is this: since it is established that we have been truly redeemed through Christ, who has won for us such a victory that neither death nor hell can prevent us from rising to blessed immortality, we must take care again and again that you weigh the benefit of the Son of God with the diligence and gratitude it deserves, and that you be such people as he may then be able to acknowledge as his own on that great day. And so that they should not ask what needs to be done, he prescribes two things.

units.la: Primum, firmi (inquit) estote, & immoti. Constantiam siue perseuerantiam in veritate agnita requirit, & ab ea orditur, partim quia multi erant, qui fidem eorum varijs tentationibus aut machinationibus labefactabant, & quia natura leues atque nouitatis amantes sumus: partim quia sine constantia nihil recte fit. Exempla sunt, quae de hoc nos admoneant. Qui in bonis aliquò vsque progressi studia sua non continuant, nunquam ad eruditionem solidam peruenient, & paulatim dediscunt quae prius non infeliciter didicerant. Opifices similiter, nisi in labore suscepto perseuerent, opus inceptum cum laude non perficiunt. In re autem militari absq; constantia adeò nihil proficitur, vt partam quoque victoriam saepe ex manibus suis turpiter amittant, qui remissius agere incipiunt, aut hostem clade aliqua consternatum non feruidè persequuntur, sed vires nouas eum colligere permittunt. Quod in Annibale olim Maharbal desiderabat, cùm post praelium Cannense Romam festinare nolenti diceret: Vincere scis Annibal, victoria vti nescis. Imprimis autem in religione & aeternae salutis negotio hoc requiritur. Ibi enim suam scholam nobis Deus aperit, in qua quod discamus nunquam deerit, quoad vita hac frui datur. Ibi opus illud pulcherrimum fidei homines inchoant, quod solum suos artifices Deo commendat, si illud ad suum finem deduxerint. Ibi turris illa & domus spiritualis extruitur, quam Deus ipse inhabitet, si nos in aedificando constanter pergere videat. Ibi bellum geritur Christi auspiciis, cui in baptismo nomen dedimus, in quo aut vincere oportet, aut aeternae salutis & patriae coelestis possessione cedere. Omnes ergo sibi applicent quod Dominus dixit: Qui vbi manum ara-tro admouit, respexerit a tergo, non est idoneus ad regnum Dei: Qui vero perseuerauerit in finem vsque, saluus erit. Item, In perseuerantia vestra possidebitis animas vestras. Docet praeterea idem ille, eorum qui ab agnita veritate deficiunt, fortem posteriorem longe deteriorem fore, quam prior fuerit. Huc enim pertinet, quod de septem pessimis daemonijs dicitur, qui hominem oscitantem & salutis suae securum inuadant. Petrus autem Apostolus de talibus inter alia scribit: Satius fuisset illis, non cognouisse viam iustitiae, quam illa cognita regredi a sancta doctrina ipsis tradita. Et quia defectione & leuitate ista nihil turpius aut foedius est, bestijs quoq; tur-pissimis illos confert, dicens: Accidit eis quod vero proverbio dici solet: Canis reuersus est ad suum ipsius vomitum: & Sus lota ad volutabrum caeni. Poterat hoc multis exemplis probari, sed veterum commemoratione non opus est, cùm huius generis multa fiant quotidie, quae hos possunt fidem facere. Etenim qui fidem in Christum abnegant, aut ab Euangelio IESV CHRISTI deficiunt, vt mundo magis propitio vtantur, ij & in superstitionum observatione aliis studiosiores, & in morum licentia deteriores fiunt, omnesq; modestiae metas transgrediuntur, ne ijs suspecti fiant, quibus placere cupiunt.
units.tr: First, he says, "be firm and immovable." He requires constancy, or perseverance, in the truth once known, and he begins with this, partly because there were many who undermined their faith by various temptations and schemes, and because we are by nature light and fond of novelty; and partly because nothing is done rightly without constancy. There are examples that warn us of this. Those who have advanced to some point in good studies but do not continue them will never attain to solid learning, and gradually unlearn what they had not unhappily learned before. Likewise craftsmen, unless they persevere in the work they have undertaken, do not finish the task begun with credit. In military affairs, too, nothing is achieved without constancy: those who begin to act more half-heartedly, or who do not vigorously pursue an enemy dismayed by some defeat but let him gather fresh strength, often shamefully lose from their hands even a victory already won. Maharbal once demanded this of Hannibal, when after the battle of Cannae he said to him, who was unwilling to hasten to Rome: "You know how to conquer, Hannibal; you do not know how to use victory." (Livy 22) Above all, this is required in religion and in the business of eternal salvation. For there God opens his school to us, in which there will never be lack of things to learn, as long as this life is given us to enjoy. There men begin that most beautiful work of faith, which alone commends its craftsmen to God, if they bring it to its end. There that spiritual tower and house is built, which God himself will inhabit, if he sees us going on steadily in the building. There a war is waged under the leadership of Christ, to whom we gave our name in baptism, in which we must either conquer or yield to the possession of eternal salvation and the heavenly homeland. Let all therefore apply to themselves what the Lord said: "He who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is not fit for the kingdom of God" (Luke 9:62); but "he who perseveres to the end will be saved" (Matt. 10:22; Luke 21:19). Likewise: "In your perseverance you will possess your souls" (Luke 21:19). That same Lord also teaches that those who fall away from the truth once known will have a later condition far worse than the first. To this pertains what is said of the seven worst demons, which attack a man who is careless and secure about his salvation (Matt. 12:45). The apostle Peter, moreover, writes of such people, among other things: "It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than, having known it, to turn back from the holy doctrine delivered to them." And because nothing is more shameful or foul than this fickleness and levity, he compares them even to the most filthy beasts, saying: "It has happened to them according to the true proverb: The dog has returned to his own vomit, and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire" (2 Pet. 2:21–22). This could be proved by many examples, but there is no need to recall the ancients, since many things of this kind happen every day which can bear witness to this. For those who deny the faith in Christ, or fall away from the gospel of Jesus Christ, so that they may enjoy the world's favour more, these become more zealous than others in observing superstitions, and worse in licentiousness of manners, and they overstep all the bounds of decency, lest they become suspect to those whom they wish to please.

units.la: Recte ergo & non sine gravibus causis Paulus Corinthios hortatur, vt firmi sint & immoti. Et consulto eiusmodi verbis vtitur, quae veram constantiae rationem nobis describunt. Primò ἀσάλευτους[?] esse iubet, quod non firmos modo, sed bene fundatos significat, metaphora a columnis petita, quae basibus firmis & solidis nituntur. Ita vero monet, vt non in inani & otiosa professione fidei acquiescamus, sed firmiter teneamus eius fundamentum: CHRISTVM IESVM videlicet, qui se petram illam inuictam esse testatur, super quam credentium Ecclesiam aedificari oporteat. Eundem Paulus alibi fundamentum Prophetarum & Apostolorum dicit, eò quod illum vnum omnes isti praedicarunt. Huic ergo nos constanter insistere conuenit, neque in vllo alio salutis fiduciam collocare: quia hoc relicto, aliud fundamentum poni non potest, sicuti supra cap.3. prolixè ostendimus. Deinde ἀμετακινήτους[?], id est, immotos siue immobiles aut stabiles vult esse aduersus omnes assultus, quibus fides nostra oppugnatur. Neminem ergo doctorum falsorum artes decipiant, neminem mundi huius exemplum moueat, nemo item tyrannorum minis aut persecutionum procellis terreatur, vt quam semel ex Dei verbo concepit sententiam mutet. Facit ad huius expositionem, quod Apostolus alibi monet, ne puerorum similes fluctuemus, & quouis vento doctrinae circumferamur. Quod autem de doctrina dicit, ad omnia alia extendi debet, quae nos vel ad defectionem, vel ad aliquam mutationem fidei & religionis solicitant. Quàm verò turpe est, hominem in eo leuem & inconstantem deprehendi, vbi constantissimum esse oportebat? Christus certe Ioannem commendaturus, hoc de illo imprimis praedicat, quod neque arun-dinis instar fuerit, quae à vento agitatur, neque mollicului aut leuis, quales in regum aulis habentur. Num ergo illi eos placere posse putabimus, qui in horas mutantur, & omni foro sese accommodant? Inter huius seculi filios praecipua quidem haec sapientia esse putatur, vt quis omnibus placere studeat, à nemine dissentiat, facilem deniq; sese praebeat ad omnia, quae maiori eorum, quibus cum versatur, parti placere viderit. At longè alia est Christianorum hominum sententia, quorum sapientia Christus est, à quo illi vel latum vnguem deflectere nefas esse sciunt, cùm solus verba vitae aeternae habeat. Et quis obsecro vel amicis hominibus, vel suo principi, vel alicui mortalium fidelem fore putauerit, si quid grauioris periculi incidat, cui lusus videtur fidem aeterno Dei filio datam fallere? Vidit hoc Constantius, Constantini Magni pater, qui (vt supra quoque diximus) exauthorandos esse censuit milites, qui leui comminatione territi superstitioso idolorum cultu sese contaminauerant. At hodie plerique Reges & principes populum suum se non aliter in officio continere posse putant, quàm si omnes Christum abnegare & in religionis causa perfidos fieri compellant.
units.tr: Rightly, then, and not without weighty reasons, Paul exhorts the Corinthians to be firm and immovable. And he deliberately uses words that describe for us the true measure of constancy. First he bids them be ἀσαλεύτους [asaleutous], which means not merely firm but well founded, a metaphor taken from columns, which rest on firm and solid bases. He warns them not to rest in an empty and idle profession of faith, but to hold firmly to its foundation, namely Christ Jesus, who testifies that he is that unconquered rock on which the Church of believers ought to be built. Paul elsewhere calls the same Christ the foundation of the prophets and apostles, because all of them preached him alone. We ought therefore to cling to him constantly, and place our trust for salvation in nothing else; for, this being set aside, no other foundation can be laid, as we have shown at length above in chapter 3. Then he wishes them to be ἀμετακινήτους [ametakinētous], that is, immovable, or stable, against all assaults by which our faith is attacked. Let therefore no false teachers' arts deceive anyone, let no example of this world move anyone, nor let anyone be terrified by the threats of tyrants or the storms of persecution, so that he changes the judgement he has once formed from God's word. To the explanation of this pertains what the apostle elsewhere warns, that we should not be like children tossed about, and carried around by every wind of doctrine (Eph. 4:14). What he says of doctrine ought to be extended to all other things that solicit us to defection, or to any change of faith and religion. How shameful it is, however, to find a man light and inconstant in that very matter where he ought to be most constant! Christ, certainly, when about to commend John, praises him chiefly in this, that he was not like a reed shaken by the wind, nor soft and effeminate, such as are found in royal courts (Matt. 11:7–8). Shall we then think that those can please God who change by the hour and accommodate themselves to every marketplace? Among the sons of this age, indeed, the chief wisdom is thought to be this: that one should strive to please everyone, dissent from no one, and in the end show himself pliable in all things that he sees pleasing to the greater part of those with whom he lives. But the opinion of Christians is quite different; their wisdom is Christ, from whom they know it is wrong to deviate even a hair's breadth, since he alone has the words of eternal life. And who, I ask, would think that a man would be faithful to his friends, his prince, or any mortal, if some graver danger befell him, when he seems to think it a joke to betray the faith given to the eternal Son of God? Constantius saw this, the father of Constantine the Great, who (as we also said above) judged that soldiers should be dismissed from service who, frightened by a slight threat, had defiled themselves with superstitious worship of idols. But today most kings and princes think that they cannot keep their people in obedience except by compelling them all to deny Christ and to become faithless in the cause of religion.

units.la: Sed ad alterum transfeamus, quod in praesenti Paulus Corinthijs praecipit: Nimirū vt abun-dantes sint semper in opere Domini. Opus Domini proprie dicitur Fides in IESVM CHRISTVM. Ita enim ipse interpretatur, quando Iudæis quærentibus, Quid faciemus vt operemur opera Dei? respondet: Hoc est opus Dei, vt credatis in eum quem ille misit. Est hoc opus omnium quæ à nobis fieri possunt, præstantissimum & saluberrimum: quia omnes homines vires & captum fides superat, & proinde non nisi Deo dante nobis obtingit, & quia ea sola Christum apprehendimus, in quo vno iustitia, vita & salus habetur. At fidei nomine audito, nemo inanem aut otiosam animi persuasionem animo concipiat, sed firmum certumq; animi assensum, quo Dei promissiones & secundum has exhibitum nobis IESVM CHRISTVM ita apprehendimus, vt nos totos illi mancipemus, & ab eo vno pendeamus. Nequit ergo fides absq; charitate consistere, qua & Deum supra omnia, & proximum vt nosipsos diligimus. Quis enim non diligat eum, cui vni fidit, & per quem solum se seruari posse intelligit? Quis vero non eos quoq; complectatur, quos huic charissimos esse, & ab eodem sibi quàm diligentissimè commendari audit? Hinc ergo obedientia vera manat, quæ hominem totum Dei seruitio vendicat, vt nihil illi antiquius sit, quàm ei obsequi, in quo spem salutis omnem habet collocatam. Ideo Paulus in CHRISTO IESV neq; Circumcisionem neq; præputium quicquâ valere dicebat, sed solam fidè, quæ per charitatem agit, quam alibi totius Legis impletionem siue consummationem esse scribit. Quod ergo in præsenti de opere Domini admonet, id per omnem vitam extenditur, quæ ita à nobis debet in-stitui[?], vt in omnibus actionibus nostris constet, nos Dei seruos esse, huius spiritu & verbo duci, neq; nostrum, sed eius negotium agere.
units.tr: But let us pass to the other point, which Paul in the present passage enjoins on the Corinthians: that they should always abound in the work of the Lord. The work of the Lord is properly called faith in Jesus Christ. He himself explains it so when the Jews asked, "What shall we do that we may work the works of God?" and he answered, "This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent." This is the most excellent and most healthful of all the works that can be done by us, because faith surpasses all human strength and understanding, and so it is granted to us only by God's gift, and because by faith alone we lay hold of Christ, in whom alone righteousness, life and salvation are found. But when the name of faith is heard, let no one conceive an empty or idle persuasion in the mind, but a firm and certain assent of the mind, by which we so lay hold of God's promises, and of Jesus Christ set before us according to them, that we give ourselves wholly to him and depend on him alone. Faith therefore cannot stand without love, by which we love God above all things and our neighbour as ourselves. For who would not love him in whom alone he trusts, and through whom alone he understands he can be saved? Who would not embrace also those whom he hears are most dear to Christ and are most diligently commended to him by Christ? From this true obedience flows, which claims the whole man for the service of God, so that nothing is more important to him than to obey him in whom he has placed all his hope of salvation. Therefore Paul said that in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails anything, but only faith which works through love, which he elsewhere writes is the fulfilment or completion of the whole Law. What he now admonishes about the work of the Lord therefore extends through the whole of life, which ought to be ordered by us in such a way that in all our actions it is evident that we are servants of God, led by his Spirit and Word, and do not do our own business but his.

units.la: Rursus autem obseruari debet Apostoli locutio, qui nos in opere Domini semper abundantes esse iubet. Ea enim admonet, ne inani fuco contenti simus, vt olim Pharisæi, & hodie hypocritæ omnes, qui religionem in externis ceremonijs & corporalibus exercitijs consistere arbitrantur, quæ idem ipse in priori ad Timothæum parum aut nihil prodesse ait, omnibus autem illis pietatem præfert, quæ promissiones præsentis & futuræ vitæ habeat. Itaque ad Christi verba alluditqui in Euangelio discipulis dicebat: Nisi abundauerit vestra iustitia plus quàm Scribarum & Pharisæorum, nequaquam ingrediemini in regnum cœlorum. Item: Estote perfecti, vt Pater vester, qui est in cœlis, perfectus est. Adhæc semper abundare iubet, vt intelligamus nos indies proficere debere, ne (quod malæ frugis seruì facere solent) nobisipsis ferias indicamus, priusquam vitæ huius pensum absoluerimus. Quia enim hæc tota Dei domum est, in quo viuimus & mouemur, totum quoq; eius tempus Dei seruitio destinari debet: quando nemo est, qui pro acceptis beneficijs dignam gratiam illi referre possit.
units.tr: Again, the Apostle's phrase should be noted, when he bids us always to abound in the work of the Lord. For it warns us not to be content with empty show, as the Pharisees of old and all hypocrites today are, who think religion consists in external ceremonies and bodily exercises. The same Apostle, in his first letter to Timothy, says these profit little or nothing, and he prefers to all of them that piety which holds promises for the present and the future life. Thus he alludes to the words of Christ, who said to his disciples in the Gospel: "Unless your righteousness abounds more than that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will by no means enter the kingdom of heaven." Likewise: "Be perfect, as your Father who is in heaven is perfect." Moreover, he bids us always to abound so that we understand we ought to make progress every day, lest (as worthless slaves are wont to do) we declare holidays for ourselves before we have finished the task of this life. For since this whole world is God's house, in which we live and move, all its time too ought to be devoted to the service of God, since there is no one who can make a worthy return of thanks for the benefits received.

units.la: Sunt autem aliæ etiam rationes minimè leues, quæ vt in Dei opere omni momento exercemur atq; abundemus exigunt. Inter has prima occurrit peccandi assiduitas, siue peccatorum nostrorum multitudo. Constat enim nos in peccato concipi & nasci, figmenta itèm cordis nostri à puericis prava esse, denique in multis (vt Apostolus scribit) labimur omnes, adeò vt delicta nostra ne ipsi quidem omnia possimus agnoscere. Æquum ergo est, vt è contra boni quoque operibus, ex vera fide manantibus, abundemus, ne in diaboli seruitio seruitiores esse deprehendamur, quàm in Dei obsequio, qui vt se ex toto corde, tota mente & omnibus viribus diligamus & colamus præcipit. Quam enim excusationem proferemus, si in congerendis huius seculi opibus indesessi, nullum laborem, nullas curas, nulla pericula subterfugiamus, nihil autem ferre veli-mus, vt æternis regni Dei thesauris potiamur? Aut num veniam aliquam sibijpsis possunt, qui libidinis igne accensi nihil non faciunt, vt illicitis amoribus potiri queant, in Dei autem dilectione adeò frigent, vt illius causa neminem offendere, & ne minimam quidem suorum bonorum iacturam facere velint? Deinde salus nostra hoc exigit, vt in opere Domini abundare studeamus. Vt enim artium omnium principia discentibus difficilia & molesta sunt, studio autem & consuetudine leuia atque iucunda fiunt: Ita verae fidei & pietatis exerci-tia initiò carni asperrima esse solent, & vix vnquam ea adduci posse videtur, vt omnibus, quæ in mundo eximia & iucunda habet, relictis, ab vno Deo pendeat, vnum diligat, & illi vnî-ueriat. At vbi his studere cœperimus, vt carnis quantùmuis reluctantis affectus subigere, & in hac pulcherrima palæstra nos indies exercere pergamus: mox nobis adlubescet, quod initio tam arduum videbatur, & quam inde sentiemus saluberrimorum fructuum dulcedo nos traket[?], vt & quotidie proficiamus in bono, & vita anteacta nos pudeat atque pigeat. Postremo ipsa fides nos ad istud obstringit. Ea enim Dei donum est, ut alibi demonstrauimus. At Domini mandatum est, ne eius dona humi defodiamus, aut otiosa corrumpi patiamur, sed ut illis faeneremur, & no-ta est illa Christi lex: Cui multum datum est, ab eo plura requirentur. Item: Omni habenti dabitur: ab eo autem qui non habet, etiam id quod habet auferetur. Frustra ergo fide gloriabuntur, qui non toti in eo fuerint, ut maiores in diem progressus faciant, & dona Spiritus sancti iugi pieta-tis exercitio auctiora reddant. Haec ut ab omnibus Christianis diligenter considerari debent, ita maxime ad eos publice pertinent, qui Ecclesiam & Reipub. ex Dei verbo bene constitutam habent, ne quae vel antecessorum studio parta, vel ab ipsis bene instituta sunt, sua ignauia collabi patiantur, aut ipsi etiam scelerate dissipent. Nam qui id fecerint, ij & suorum maiorum exemplo condemnabuntur, & apud posteritatem omnem infames fient, quae merito de ipsorum ignauia aut perfidia queretur.
units.tr: There are also other reasons, not at all slight, which require that we be exercised and abound in God's work at every moment. Among these the first to occur is the constancy of our sinning, or the multitude of our sins. For it is certain that we are conceived and born in sin, that the imaginings of our heart are evil from childhood, and that in many things (as the Apostle writes) we all stumble, so that we cannot even recognise all our offences. It is therefore fair that, conversely, we also abound in good works flowing from true faith, lest we be found more diligent servants of the devil than of God, who commands us to love and worship him with the whole heart, the whole mind and all our strength. For what excuse will we offer if, tireless in amassing the wealth of this age, we shun no toil, no cares, no dangers, yet are unwilling to bear anything so that we may obtain the eternal treasures of God's kingdom? Or can those have any excuse who, burning with the fire of lust, do everything to obtain illicit loves, yet are so cold in the love of God that they will not offend anyone for his sake, nor suffer even the smallest loss of their goods? Furthermore, our salvation demands that we strive to abound in the work of the Lord. For just as the first principles of all the arts are difficult and troublesome to learners, but become light and pleasant through study and practice, so the exercises of true faith and piety are usually most harsh to the flesh at first, and it seems scarcely possible to bring anyone to leave behind all the outstanding and pleasant things in the world, to depend on the one God, to love him alone and to devote himself wholly to him. But when we begin to labour at these things, to subdue the affections of the flesh however much they resist, and go on exercising ourselves daily in this most beautiful wrestling-ground, soon what seemed so arduous at the beginning will begin to please us, and the sweetness of the most wholesome fruits we then feel will draw us on, so that we both advance daily in good and are ashamed and grieved at our former life. Finally, faith itself binds us to this. For it is a gift of God, as we have shown elsewhere. But it is the Lord's command that we do not bury his gifts in the ground nor allow them to be spoiled through idleness, but that we make them yield interest; and that saying of Christ is well known: "To whom much has been given, of him more will be required." Likewise: "To everyone who has, more will be given; but from him who has not, even what he has will be taken away." Those, therefore, who have not wholly devoted themselves to this, that they may make ever greater progress and render the gifts of the Holy Spirit more abundant by constant exercise of piety, will boast in faith in vain. All Christians ought to consider these things carefully, but they especially pertain publicly to those who have the Church and the commonwealth well established according to the Word of God, lest they allow what was won by the zeal of their forefathers, or what they themselves have well instituted, to collapse through their own sloth, or even wickedly squander it themselves. For those who do so will be condemned by the example of their own ancestors, and will become infamous to all posterity, which will rightly complain of their sloth or treachery.

units.la: Caeterum quia natura ad bonum tardi sumus, altera huius conclusionis parte stimulum acrem & vehementem Paulus adhibet, dicens: Cum sciatis laborem vestrum non esse inanem in Domino. Opponit illud duabus remoris, quae carnem in tota hac causa imprimis absterrent, & quibus sibi ipsi patrocinari aut delitias facere solet, si quando suam ignauiam corripi sentiat. Aut enim impossibile putat eam, quam Deus exigit, obedientiam praestare, aut inutiliter praestari, eo quod Deus praemio nullo suos cultores remuneret, & vulgo constet, hominum in hoc seculo miserrimos esse eos, qui in Christo pie volunt viuere. Vtrisq; (inquam) hoc tam breui dicto Paulus remedium praesens & efficacissimum adhibet.
units.tr: Moreover, since we are slow by nature to what is good, Paul applies a sharp and vehement goad at the other part of this conclusion, saying: "Since you know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord." He sets this against two hindrances, which chiefly deter the flesh in this whole matter, and by which it is wont to excuse itself and indulge itself whenever it feels its sloth being rebuked. For it either thinks that the obedience God requires is impossible to render, or that it is rendered to no purpose, since God rewards his worshippers with no recompense, and it is commonly held that those who wish to live godly in Christ are the most wretched of men in this age. Against both of these, I say, Paul applies in this brief saying a present and most effective remedy.

units.la: Quoad primos enim, dum laborem nostrum non inanem esse ait in Domino, non obscure te-statur, nos nequaquam in vanum laboraturos sed plus quam putemus profecturos esse. Nam et-si obstet nobis naturae nostrae vitiositas, ut nihil boni ex nobis ipsis agere possimus, imo ne ad co-gitandum quidem idonei simus, Christi tamen spiritu confirmati in eodem possumus omnia, ut alibi Apostolus ait. Neque is solum nobis eam spem facit, sed ipsum Christum ad eadem nos excitare scimus, qui in ultima Caena discipulis inter alia dixit: Ego sum vitis illa vera, & Pater meus agricola est. Omnem palmitem in me non ferentem fructum tollit: & omnem qui fert fructum, purgat, ut fructum copiosiorem afferat. Iam vos puri estis propter sermonem, quem locutus sum vobis. Manete in me, & ego in vobis. Sicut palmes non potest ferre fructum a semetipso, nisi in vite manserit: ita neque vos, nisi in me manseritis. Ego sum vitis, vos palmites. Is qui manet in me, & in quo ego maneo, hic fert fructum multum. Et paulo post: Si manseritis in me, & verba mea in vobis manserint, quicquid volueritis, petite, & fiet vobis. In hoc glorificatus est Pater meus, ut fructum multum afferatis, & fietis mei discipuli. Quibus verbis fatetur quidem nos ex nobis ipsis fructum nullum ferre, imo dignos esse; qui aridorum palmitum instar refecti abijciamur: verumtamen non omnem spem negat, sed qua ratione ex steri-libus foecundi efficiamur, docet. Summa eius doctrinae est, ut verbum suum audiamus & ipsius simus discipuli. Qui id faciunt, ijs agnata carnis vitiositas nocere non potest. Vt enim palmes viti adhuc haerens aut insitus; ex ea succum & vigorem attrahit, ex quo fructus gignitur: ita in nos quoque per Christum Dei spiritus deriuatur, qui bonorum operum fructus in nobis procreat. Deus item bonus ille & industrius vinitor est, qui in horas nos putat & purgat, dum partim verbo & spiritu suo, partim castigationibus externis luxuriantes carnis affectus resecat, aut coercet, ne enasciturus fidei fructus praefocetur. Idem quia pater est indulgentissimus, imperfectionem & labes quae in bonis operibus concurrunt, nobis non imputat propter Christum, qui quae nobis desunt, abunde farcit. Accedit his precandi fiducia & libertas, quam nobis Christus fecit, ut preces nostrae irrita non sint. Cur enim Pater nos ea petentes negligat, quibus ipse glorificatur? Neminem ergo vel tanti negotij difficultas, vel propriae infirmitatis sensus absterreat, quo minus opus Domini forti & constanti animo aggrediatur: & mox sentiet, laborem suum non esse irritum in Domino.
units.tr: As to the first, then: when he says that our labour is not in vain in the Lord, he clearly testifies that we shall by no means labour in vain, but shall make more progress than we think. For although the corrupt nature we have stands in our way, so that we can do nothing good of ourselves, and are not even fit to think, yet strengthened by the Spirit of Christ we can do all things in him, as the Apostle says elsewhere. Nor does he give us this hope alone, but we know that Christ himself stirs us to the same, who at the last supper said to his disciples, among other things: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away; and every one that bears fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit. Now you are clean through the word which I have spoken to you. Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it abides in the vine, so neither can you unless you abide in me. I am the vine, you are the branches. He who abides in me, and in whom I abide, bears much fruit." And a little later: "If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you will, and it shall be done for you. In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and become my disciples." By these words he indeed confesses that we bear no fruit of ourselves, and that we deserve rather to be cut off like dried branches; yet he does not deny all hope, but teaches by what means the barren are made fruitful. The sum of this teaching is that we hear his word and are his disciples. For those who do this, the corruption of the flesh inherent in them cannot harm them. Just as a branch still clinging to the vine, or grafted into it, draws from it sap and vigour, from which fruit is produced, so the Spirit of God is also drawn down to us through Christ, who produces the fruits of good works in us. God too is that good and diligent vinedresser, who thinks to prune and cleanse us from time to time, while partly by his word and Spirit, partly by outward chastisements, he cuts away or restrains the rank affections of the flesh, lest the fruit of faith about to spring up be choked. Since he is also a most indulgent Father, he does not impute to us, for Christ's sake, the imperfection and blemishes that occur in our good works, since Christ abundantly supplies what is lacking in us. To these is added the confidence and freedom in prayer which Christ has given us, so that our prayers may not be in vain. For why would the Father neglect us when we ask for the things by which he himself is glorified? Let no one therefore be deterred either by the difficulty of so great a business or by a sense of his own weakness from undertaking the work of the Lord with a brave and steadfast spirit; and soon he will feel that his labour is not in vain in the Lord.

units.la: Eadem ratione dictum hoc Pauli alteri etiam remorae opponamus. Equidem si carnis sensum audias, nullū virtuti aut pietati praemium propositum, & hominum calumniatorissimi esse videntur, qui in opere Domini præ aliis laborant. Audiuntur ergo impiorum & illusorum voces, quarum Propheta quoque meminit: Frustra seruitur Deo: Quæ enim utilitas, quod custodiuimus eius custodiuimus, & quod humiliati coram Domino exercituum incedimus? Quin nunc beatos dicimus superbos: imò impietatem patrantes ædificantur, & qui Deum tentant, liberantur. Imò pios quoque interdum graviter tentari stimus[?], quando aut seipsos aut alios fidei verae cultores in exilium eiici, egere, de vita periclitari, omnibus inuisos & exosos esse, è contra autem impios Dei contemptores honoribus, diuitijs, clientelis superbire, & omni voluptatum genere diffluere vident. Nota sunt enim super hac re insignium Prophetarum, Asaphi, Ieremiæ, Habakuki & similium querelæ. At non propterea suo præmio caret pietas, neque inani labore fatigan-tur, qui Domino fidelem operam nauant. Nam ipsæ afflictiones amplissimi & multiplicis præmij instar sunt. His enim carnis inordinata desideria coercentur, ne illis circumuenti in scelera exi-tialia ruamus. His castigati ad mentem meliorem redimus, ne cum mundo contumaci & pe-nitere nescio condemnemur. Eadem patientiam in nobis pariunt, dum eius exercendæ materiam propinant, patientia vero diuinæ bonitatis experientiam sibi coniunctam habet, cuius dul-cissimo gustu fideles inter medias calamitatum undas recreantur: hæc spem gignit invictam, quæ nos pudefieri non sinit, quando charitas Dei in cordibus nostris diffusa nos salutis certos atque securos facit. Num ergo piorum labor inanis dici poterit, qui huius seculi afflictiones illis incundas & salutares facit, quæ impijs intolerabiles & exitiales sunt? Accedit his maius quid & præstantius, quod crucem & aduersa ferendo Filio Dei conformes efficimur, vt eiusdem olim cum eo gloriæ & felicitatis hæredes simus. Nam si cum eo moriamur, cum eo etiam viuemus: si cum eo toleremus, cum eodem regnabimus. Eius enim promissio est: Volo, vbi sum ego, ibi etiam sit minister meus. At quæ in hoc seculo agentibus gloria maior potest obtingere, quam si Christi socij & commilitones fiant? quæ item felicitas maior, quod præmium excellentius sperari potest, quam si cœlestium bonorum participes fiant, quæ (vt Propheta docet) omnem sensum & intellectum hominis excellunt? Quem ergo tanti præmij promissio non excitet? quem tantæ remunerationis spes non confirmet, vt ad omnia alacrem & intrepidum sese præbeat? Aut quis tam querulus aut insatiabilis fuerit, vt se frustra Domino seruire dicat, quando se eiusdem præmij cum æterno Dei Filio participem fore audit?
units.tr: By the same reasoning let us also set this saying of Paul against another obstacle. Indeed, if you listen to the sense of the flesh, no reward seems to be set before virtue and piety, and those who labour more than others in the work of the Lord seem the most foolish of men. So there are heard the voices of the impious and mocking, of which the Prophet also makes mention: "It is vain to serve God; what profit is it that we have kept his charge, and that we have walked humbly before the Lord of hosts? Indeed, now we call the proud blessed; yea, those who work wickedness are built up, and those who tempt God are delivered." Yes, and we sometimes see the pious too severely tried, when they see themselves or other true worshippers of the faith cast into exile, in want, in danger of their lives, hated and detested by all; while, on the other hand, they see the impious despisers of God grow proud with honours, riches and clients, and flow over with every kind of pleasure. For the complaints of the illustrious Prophets on this matter are well known: of Asaph, Jeremiah, Habakkuk and others like them. Yet piety is not for this reason deprived of its reward, nor do those who faithfully labour for the Lord toil in vain. For afflictions themselves are like a very great and manifold reward. By them the disordered desires of the flesh are restrained, lest, ensnared by them, we fall headlong into destructive crimes. Chastened by them, we return to a better mind, lest we be condemned together with the stubborn and unrepentant world. They also produce patience in us, while they offer us the matter for exercising it; and patience has joined to it the experience of divine goodness, by the sweetest taste of which the faithful are refreshed amid the waves of calamities. This produces an unconquered hope, which does not let us be put to shame, since the love of God poured into our hearts makes us certain and secure of salvation. Is, then, the labour of the godly to be called empty, when it makes the afflictions of this age pleasant and wholesome to them, which are intolerable and deadly to the impious? Added to these is something greater and more excellent: by bearing the cross and adversities we are made conformed to the Son of God, so that we may be heirs with him of the same glory and happiness. For if we die with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure with him, we shall also reign with him. For this is his promise: "I will that where I am, there my minister also may be." But what greater glory can fall to those who live in this age than to become companions and fellow soldiers of Christ? What greater happiness, what more excellent reward can be hoped for, than to become partakers of heavenly goods, which (as the Prophet teaches) surpass all the sense and understanding of man? Who then would not be stirred by the promise of so great a reward? Who would not be confirmed by the hope of such a recompense, so as to show himself eager and fearless for all things? Or who would be so querulous or insatiable as to say that he serves the Lord in vain, when he hears that he will share in the same reward with the eternal Son of God?

units.la: At hic non ofcitanter obseruari debet, Paulum nobis omnia ista, de quibus iam dictum est, in ipso Domino monstrare. Vt enim ex nobis ipsis ad nihil idonei sumus, ita si qua in re idonei efficimur, id omne ex Deo est, qui (vt ad Phil.dicit Apostolus) & velle & facere in nobis efficit pro gratuita sua in nos benevolentia. Idem remunerator quoq; fidelis est, & tantæ liberalitatis, vt quæ ipse in nobis egit nobis imputet, & pro iis præmia, quæ ipsi non meruimus, retribuat. Neminem igitur suarum virium aut proprij meriti fiducia inebriet.
