Nulla enim superbia Deo magis inuisa, nulla arrogantia exitialior est, quam si sibi ex operibus suis eam gloriam vendicent homines, quæ soli Deo debetur. Semper ergo cogitemus, nos in opere Domini versari, non modò quod quæ ille præcepit facimus, sed quod ipsius in nobis agentis sumus instrumenta: & laborem nostrum non inanem fore, non quia ipsi aliquid mereamur, sed quia merces nobis in Domino reposita est, qui nos seruorum, imò amicorum suorum loco habere dignatur. Quibus adde, quod supra cap.4. dixit Apostolus: Quid habes, quod non accepisti? Quòd si accepisti, quid gloriaris, quasi non acceperis?
units.tr: But here it must not be noticed carelessly that Paul shows us all those things of which we have spoken in the Lord himself. For just as we are of ourselves fit for nothing, so if we are made fit in any matter, all of that is from God, who (as the Apostle says to the Philippians) works in us both to will and to do, out of his free goodwill toward us. The same God is also a faithful rewarder, and of such great generosity that he reckons to us what he himself has done in us, and rewards with prizes those things which we did not deserve. Let no one, therefore, be intoxicated with confidence in his own strength or his own merit. For no pride is more hateful to God, and no arrogance more destructive, than when men claim for themselves from their own works that glory which is due to God alone. Let us therefore always consider that we are engaged in the work of the Lord, not only because we do what he has commanded, but because we are the instruments of him who works in us. And our labour will not be in vain, not because we deserve anything ourselves, but because the reward is laid up for us in the Lord, who deigns to hold us in the place not of servants only but even of his friends. To these add what the Apostle said above in chapter 4: "What have you that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you glory, as if you had not received it?"

units.la: Postremò hoc etiam obseruemus, vniuersum salutis negotium, cuius nobis author & vnicum fundamentum est IESVS CHRISTVS, eò tendere, vt toti Deo consecrati vitam viuamus Christiana professione dignam, vt ille olim nos pro suis discipulis & fratribus possit agnoscere. Vociferantur quidem aduersarij, nos bonorum operum inimicos esse, & per nos fieri, vt qui suapte natura ad malum proclives sunt, prorsus securi facti[?] indomita quiduis audendi licentia proteruiant. Id verò hanc vnam ob causam dicunt, quod salutis humanæ fontes in gra-tuita Dei misericordia monstramus, qui miseros nos & indignos priusquam mundus hic conde-retur, absque omni nostro merito elegit in Filio suo IESV CHRISTO, qui præsi-nito tempore homo factus ex Maria virgine, nos suæ mortis merito ex peccatorum noxa & eorundem pœna redemit. At si rem ipsam propius inspiciamus, doctrina hac adeo non tolluntur vitæ Christianæ & sanctæ officia, vt potius singulæ eius partes nos ad illa argumentis efficacissimis, ceu vinculis adamantinis, obstringunt. Quia enim nos in CHRISTO IESV Deus elegit, vt suus populus suumq; peculium simus, nostrum vtique fuerit, illi vni seruire & nos sanctos præbere, sicuti & ipse sanctus est. Si item nos ille ex gratia adoptauit & adoptionis spiritu dignatus est, nos illum vicissim vt patrem diligere, & eidem in omnibus obedire debemus. Ita quia per Christum à peccatis liberati & abluti sumus, nefas fuerit porrò vitam peccatis deditam viuere. Quòd si Christus ex mortuis resurrexit, conuenit, vt qui ab eo denominantur ex peccatis resurgant, neque locum dent ijs operibus, quibus mors æterna debetur. Similiter, si in Christo renati & noua creatura facti sumus, veterem Adamum exuere debemus, neque eius consilia posthac audire. Denique si spiritus sui virtute nos ille donauit, æquum fuerit, vt ea armati carnis desiderijs resistamus, & fructus feramus ex quibus spiritus efficacia possit agnosci. Quia autem hæc facere ex debito tenemur, non licebit in ijs aliquam meriti gloriam quærere, sed illud Christi agnoscere: Si feceritis omnia, quæ iniuncta sunt vobis, dicite: Serui inutiles sumus, quod debuimus facere, fecimus. Non ergo nobis cum quoquam de operibus bonis lis est, neque ea fieri debere negamus: sed eorum oppugnamus sententiam, qui quæ solius Christi merito debetur gloriam eis tribuunt, dum illis se iustificari & seruari contendunt. At quia de hac re sæpe dictum est, nunc dicendi finem facimus. Discant autem singuli diligenter meditari beatam illam spem vitæ cœlestis & æternæ, quam olim in resurrectione obtinebimus: & ea confirmati constanter tueantur fidem in IESVM CHRISTVM, in quo vno nobis salus reposita est, & qui suorum laborum inanes esse non sinet. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Finally, let us also observe this: the whole business of salvation, whose author and sole foundation is Jesus Christ, tends to this, that we who are wholly consecrated to God should live a life worthy of the Christian profession, so that he may one day acknowledge us as his disciples and brothers. Indeed our opponents cry out that we are enemies of good works, and that through us those who are by their own nature prone to evil become utterly secure and, with unrestrained licence for daring anything, run riot. They say this for the one reason that we point to the fountains of human salvation in the free mercy of God, who chose us, wretched and unworthy as we were, before the world was made, without any merit of our own, in his Son Jesus Christ, who, at the appointed time, made man from the Virgin Mary, redeemed us by the merit of his death from the harm of sins and the punishment of the same. But if we look more closely at the matter itself, the duties of Christian life and holiness are not at all removed by this doctrine; rather, each part of it binds us to them by the most effective arguments, like chains of adamant. For since God has chosen us in Christ Jesus, that we may be his people and his own possession, it is surely our part to serve him alone and to show ourselves holy, as he himself is holy. Likewise, since he has adopted us out of grace and has deigned to give us the spirit of adoption, we ought in turn to love him as Father and obey him in all things. Thus, since we have been freed and washed from sins through Christ, it would be wrong to live any longer a life given over to sins. And if Christ has risen from the dead, it is fitting that those who are named from him should rise from sins and give no place to those works for which eternal death is due. Similarly, if we have been born again in Christ and made a new creature, we ought to put off the old Adam and no longer listen to his counsels. Lastly, if he has given us gifts by the power of his Spirit, it will be fitting that, armed with it, we resist the desires of the flesh and bear fruits by which the efficacy of the Spirit may be recognised. But since we are bound to do these things as a debt, it is not permitted to seek any glory of merit in them, but rather to acknowledge that saying of Christ: "When you have done all the things that are enjoined on you, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done." Therefore we do not quarrel with anyone about good works, nor do we deny that they ought to be done; but we oppose the opinion of those who ascribe to them the glory which is due to the merit of Christ alone, while they contend that by them they are justified and saved. But since this matter has often been spoken of, we now make an end of speaking. Let each one diligently learn to meditate on that blessed hope of the heavenly and eternal life which we shall one day obtain in the resurrection; and being confirmed by it, let them steadfastly keep the faith in Jesus Christ, in whom alone salvation is laid up for us, and who will not allow our labours to be vain. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XVI. HOMILIA LXXXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER 16. HOMILY 89.

units.la: Porro de collecta in sanctos, quemadmodum constituit Eccle-siis Galatiæ, ita & vos facite. Primo quoque die hebdomadis vnusquisque vestrum apud se reponat, recondens quod pro Dei benignitate licuerit: ne cum venero, tunc collectæ fiant.
units.tr: Now concerning the collection for the saints: as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also are to do. On the first day of the week let each of you set something aside at home, storing up whatever he can by God's goodness, so that the collections need not be made when I come.

units.la: E ijs hucusque paulus disseruit, quæ ad generalem Ecclesiæ Corinthiacæ institutionem pertinebant, errores que & vitia, quæ in illam irrepserant, multa diligenter correxit. Sequitur postrema epistolæ pars peculiaria quædam continens, de quibus ad monendi erant pro temporum illorum ratione. Primum ex illis est Collecta siue publica pecuniarum contributio, quibus fratrum in Iudæa agentium egestatem subleuari oportebat. Quem locum vt rectius & maiori cum fructu intelligamus, ea repetere oportet, quæ Lucas in Actis Cap. 11. & 12. narrat. Statuerat Deus mundum ingratum & tam propriæ salutis quàm Filij sui dilecti, IESV CHRISTI, contemptorem fame punire, quam mox regnante Claudio Imperatore exortam fuisse historici produnt. Idem tamen pro suo more Ecclesiam suam per Agabum præmonuit, vt facilius Christiani homines, qui ethnicis & Iudæis permixti habitabat, sibi & suis prospicerent. Itaq; Antiocheni fideles primi de subsidio fratribus, qui in Iudæa erant, mittendo consilium cœperunt, quorum exemplum mox aliæ etiam ecclesiæ monentibus Apostolis secutæ sunt; & vt hoc facerent, causæ erant non leues. Nam grauior illos egestas premebat, cum inter hostes acerrimos Christiani nominis agerent, & iam ante direptionem suarum facultatum passi essent, sicuti in Epistola ad Hebraeos narratur. Deinde se illis hoc officium debere agnoscebant, ex quibus Euangelij praedicatio ad gentes per totum orbem terrarum erat propagata. At diutius durante rerum penuria, eo usque inualuit necessitas, ut Apostoli hanc rem prae aliis cordi haberent, adeo, ut cum Paulo Apostolatum ad gentes diuinitus commissum uiderent, de hoc uno tam ipse quam collega eius Barnabas admonendus uideretur, ut Iudaeos fratres commendarent Ecclesijs inter gentes dispersis. Ne ergo fidei suae deesset Paulus, ea in re diligentissimus fuit, et causam iam magno studio egit apud omnes, et imprimis quidem apud eos, qui et pace fruebantur, et opibus abundabant, quales tunc temporis erant Macedones, Achaii, et praeomnibus aliis Romani orbis terrarum domini. Et quia Achaiae totius emporium celeberrimum erat Corinthus, qui illic erant fideles quam maxime vrgendi esse visi sunt. Id ergo prima huius Capitis parte facit Apostolus, in genere admonens, quid ipsos facere deceat, eosdem vero in posteriori epistola pluribus et gravioribus rationibus hortatur, ne se in re omnium sanctissima ab aliis Ecclesijs patiantur superari.
units.tr: Up to this point Paul has discussed matters that pertained to the general arrangement of the Corinthian Church, and he has carefully corrected many errors and faults that had crept into it. Now follows the last part of the letter, containing certain particular matters on which he had to give advice according to the circumstances of those times. The first of these is the collection, or public contribution of money, by which the poverty of the brothers living in Judea was to be relieved. So that we may understand this passage more correctly and with greater profit, we must recall what Luke narrates in Acts chapters 11 and 12. God had decided to punish an ungrateful world, one that despised both its own salvation and his beloved Son Jesus Christ, with famine, which the historians report broke out soon after, in the reign of the Emperor Claudius. Yet God, in his usual way, forewarned his Church through Agabus, so that Christians, who lived mixed among pagans and Jews, might provide for themselves and their households. Therefore the faithful of Antioch were the first to begin sending aid to the brothers in Judea, and other churches soon followed their example at the urging of the Apostles. There were no slight reasons for doing this. The brothers were pressed by greater want, since they lived among the most bitter enemies of the Christian name, and they had already suffered the plundering of their goods, as is related in the Epistle to the Hebrews. Then the Gentile churches recognised that they owed this duty to those through whom the preaching of the gospel had spread across the whole world. But as the scarcity lasted longer, the need grew so pressing that the Apostles held this matter dearer than all others. So much was this so that Paul, to whom the apostleship to the Gentiles had been divinely committed, and his colleague Barnabas seemed bound to press this one point alone: that they commend the Jewish brothers to the churches scattered among the Gentiles. So, lest Paul be wanting in his duty to the faith, he was most diligent in this matter and pleaded the cause with great zeal before all, and especially before those who enjoyed peace and abounded in wealth, such as at that time the Macedonians, the Achaeans, and above all the lords of the Roman world. And since Corinth was the most famous trading centre of all Achaea, the faithful there seemed especially in need of pressing. So in the first part of this chapter the Apostle does this, advising in general what it befits them to do; and in the later letter he urges the same with more numerous and weightier arguments, not to let themselves be outdone by other churches in a matter most holy of all.

units.la: Admonemur nos Apostolorum exemplo, pauperum curam imprimis ad Ecclesiarum ministros pertinere. Sunt enim illi non minima Ecclesiae pars, quos ut nunquam defuturos esse Dominus in Veteri simul et Nouo Testamento praedixit: ita eosdem nobis ea conditione commendauit, ut in suas rationes se adscribere velle polliceatur quicquid in eos confertur. Quod Apo-stolos haud dubie olim monuit, ut sub nascentis Ecclesiae principia illorum curam vna cum pecuniarum ecclesiasticarum dispensatione ad se reciperent. Etsi vero crescente indies fidelium numero viderent, se tot negotijs simul non posse sufficere, diaconos quidem ex communi Ecclesiae sententia constituerunt, verum tamen curam hanc non omnem prorsus depositerunt, quo minus apud Ecclesias (ut modo dictum est) causam hanc magno studio agerent. Imitentur hoc illorum studium hodie etiam ministri Ecclesiarum, neque pudeat eos pauperum nomine mendicare, quando hoc ipsum olim Apostolos fecisse constat. At quid Apostolos dico, quando Christum hoc facere non puduit, qui olim quoque, quando toti mundo maiestatem suam manifestabit et totius mundi index erit, pauperum tamen personam induet, dicens: Ego esuriui, et non dedistis mihi cibum: ego sitiui, et non dedistis mihi potum, etc. Turpe quidem fuerit, si seipsos in pauperum locum substituant, qui Ecclesiarum ministri haberi volunt, et sibi petant dari (quod in papatu fratres mendicantes non minus impudenter quam impie faciunt sub voluntariae pauperta-tis praetextu) at pro egenis apud Ecclesiam intercedere, et opulentiores quosque monere, rogare, hortari et vrgere, ut liberaliter largiantur quod illis alendis sufficiat, id verae pietatis opus est. Id olim Apostoli fecerunt, et Paulus qui manibus propriis potius victum sibi parare et egere maluit, quam alicui molestus esse in debito sibi stipendio exigendo, pauperum tamen causam tanto studio suscepit, ut pro illis mendicare non erubescat.
units.tr: We are reminded by the example of the Apostles that the care of the poor belongs above all to the ministers of the churches. For they are no small part of the Church, and the Lord foretold in both the Old and the New Testament that they would never be lacking. He also commended them to us on this condition: that he promises to count as done to himself whatever is given to them. The Apostles without doubt were once taught this, so that in the early days of the infant Church they took the care of the poor upon themselves together with the distribution of the church's money. Yet, although as the number of the faithful grew daily they saw that they could not suffice for so many tasks at once, they did indeed appoint deacons by the common consent of the Church, but they did not wholly lay down this care, so that they continued to plead this cause with great zeal before the churches, as has just been said. Let the ministers of the churches today imitate this zeal of theirs, and let them not be ashamed to beg in the name of the poor, since it is established that the Apostles did this of old. But why do I speak of the Apostles, when Christ himself was not ashamed to do this? He who will one day reveal his majesty to the whole world and be the judge of all the world will nevertheless take on the person of the poor and say: "I was hungry, and you gave me no food; I was thirsty, and you gave me no drink," and so on. It would indeed be shameful if those ministers of the churches who wish to be held in honour were to put themselves in the place of the poor and ask for gifts for themselves, as the mendicant friars in Papistry do, no less shamelessly than impiously, under the pretext of voluntary poverty. But to intercede for the needy before the church, and to admonish, ask, exhort and urge the wealthier to give generously what suffices to feed them, that is a work of true piety. The Apostles did this of old, and Paul, who preferred to earn his own living by his own hands rather than be a burden to anyone by demanding the stipend owed to him, nevertheless took up the cause of the poor with such zeal that he did not blush to beg on their behalf.

units.la: Simul etiam primitiuae Ecclesiae exemplo eorum iniquitas arguitur, qui Ecclesiae opes adsque rapiunt, et omne in illas ius ita sibi vendicant, vt Verbi ministros prorsus excludant: imo indigne et inique eos facere arbitrantur, si de fideli et iusta illarum dispensatione et pauperum subuentione verba faciant. Regnat hoc vitium apud multos, qui Euangelij doctrinam atque fidem profitentur, quibus ad pietatem videtur sufficere, si monachos et sacrificulos ex bonorum Ecclesiasticorum possessione deiciant, vt vero eadem in suos vsus conuertantur, parum solliciti sunt. Hinc fit, ut maxima illorum pars male dissipetur, et ex ijsdem fere ditescant, qui religionem omnem oderunt, et Ecclesiae Christianae labes sunt. Sed non dormitat Dominus, qui aliquando Euangelij et nominis sui prophanationem dignis supplicijs vlcisceretur. Porro his praemissis ad Pauli verba accedamus, qui etsi hoc loco de extraordinarijs collectis agat, ita tamen de his loquitur, vt simul doctrinam generalem comprehendat de pauperum subuentione: quae cum nunquam debeat negligi, singulas partes ex ordine considerabimus.
units.tr: At the same time, by the example of the early Church, the wickedness of those is exposed who plunder the church's wealth and claim every right over it in such a way as to exclude the ministers of the Word altogether. Indeed they think it unworthy and unjust that these ministers should speak about the faithful and just distribution of those goods and the relief of the poor. This vice reigns among many who profess the doctrine and faith of the gospel, who think it enough for piety if they drive out monks and little priests from possession of the church's goods, but are little concerned that those goods should be turned to their proper uses. Hence it happens that the greatest part of them is squandered, and that those very men grow rich from them who hate all religion and are a disgrace to the Christian Church. But the Lord does not sleep; he will sometime avenge the profanation of his gospel and of his name with fitting punishments. Now, with these things premised, let us come to the words of Paul. Although in this place he treats of extraordinary collections, he speaks in such a way that he also takes in the general teaching about the relief of the poor, which must never be neglected. We shall therefore consider its parts in order.

units.la: Primo summam totius negotij proponit, quae est, vt quoad collectam pro subleuanda fan-ctorum, id est, fidelium Christi inopia idem faciant, quod in Galatarum Ecclesijs iampridem constituerit. Dicitur enim λογία Apostolo τὸ ἐκ τῶν ὑμῶν συνεισφερόμενον, id est, quod a multis in vnum conferatur, siue iam collatum est: quod alio nomine Symbolum vocant. Latini collectam dixerunt,quo vocabulo Ciceronem quoq; vsum fuisse scimus. Ecclesiastici scriptores illud ad sa-cras contributiones transtulerunt, quibus pecunia in pauperum Ecclesiae alimoniam colligitur: quas posteri in cantiunculas non minus superstitiosas quàm ineptas commutarunt, quae fortassis ita dici possunt, quia sub harum praetextu aucupium quaestuosissimum instituerunt, quo pecunia multa ex vulgo conflari potuit. Cùm verò simpliciter mandare posset Apostolus quid fieri debeat, exemplum Galatarum adducit, vt aduersariorum calumniis occurrat, qui ipsum hoc nomine vulgo suspectum facere conabantur, quòd Corinthios multis statutis grauaret, quae in aliis Ecclesiis non essent recepta: adhaec Galatarum potius quàm aliorum meminit, vt pudeat ipsos in charitatis officio ab illis superari, qui vulgo pro barbaris habebantur, eò quòd ex Gallia oriundi in ea Asiae parte consedissent. Id autem se constituisse dicit, quia boni doctoris est, non modò docere quid facto opus sit, verumetiam illud effectum dare, & ex Dei verbo ea instituere, quae ad pietatem & Ecclesiae aedificationem faciunt. Nec temere ab Apostolis hoc obseruatum fuit, vt vna eademq; esset apud omnes Ecclesias tam doctrinae quàm rituum aliarumq; constitutionum for-mula, ne dissimilitudo dissensionis suspicionem & simultates pareret:quod facilè fit,eò quòd vul-gus fere ab externis pendeat. Debebant huius meminisse hodie, qui nouitati student, & tunc demum sibi ipsis placent, si ab aliis omnibus dissentiant, aut saltem dissentire videantur.
units.tr: First he sets forth the sum of the whole business, which is that they should do concerning the collection for the relief of the saints, that is, of the poor faithful of Christ, the same thing he had long ago ordained for the churches of Galatia. For the Apostle calls it logia [λογία], that is, what is contributed by you [τὸ ἐκ τῶν ὑμῶν συνεισφερόμενον], that is, what is gathered together from many into one, or already gathered; others call it by another name, a "contribution." The Latins called it a collecta, a word which we know Cicero also used. Ecclesiastical writers transferred this term to the sacred contributions by which money is gathered for the support of the church's poor. Later generations changed these into little chants no less superstitious than foolish, which perhaps are so called because under the pretext of them they set up a most profitable fowling-trap, by which much money could be scraped together from the common people. But although the Apostle could have simply commanded what ought to be done, he brings forward the example of the Galatians, so as to meet the calumnies of his opponents, who tried to make him suspect to the people on this very account, because he burdened the Corinthians with many rules which were not received in other churches. Moreover, he mentions the Galatians rather than others, so that the Corinthians might be ashamed to be surpassed in the duty of charity by those who were commonly regarded as barbarians, because they were of Gallic origin and had settled in that part of Asia. He says that he has laid this down because it is the mark of a good teacher not only to teach what needs to be done, but also to see that it is carried out, and to establish by God's word those things which serve piety and the building up of the Church. Nor did the Apostles observe this rashly: that there should be one and the same form, both of doctrine and of rites and other arrangements, in all the churches, lest difference breed suspicion of dissension and enmity. This happens easily, because the common people for the most part depend on outward things. Those who pursue novelty should remember this today; they please themselves only when they differ from all others, or at least seem to differ.

units.la: Praecipuum autem huius loci caput est, quòd ex eo constat, Apostolorum temporibus collectas in Ecclesiis passim factas fuisse, ex quibus pauperes siue egeni publicè alerentur. De primitiua Ecclesia, quae statim post Ascensionem Domini & Spiritus sancti missionem coaluit, non opus est dicere, quando Lucas id in Actorum libro disertis verbis testatur. Et quia videmus in Ecclesiis extraordinarias collectas interdum institutas fuisse propter exteros, qui alieno subsidio opus habebant, quis dubitet singulas multo magis suis prospexisse, quos Paulus ad Galatas scribens domesticos fidei dicit? Durauit autem mos ille, quem Apostoli instituerunt apud posteros quoque, vt Tertullianus & Iustinus testantur, imò alij quoque ex orthodoxis scriptoribus, qui istos[?] vno & altero seculo secuti sunt.
units.tr: The chief point of this passage is that it shows that in the apostles' time collections were made in the churches everywhere, from which the poor, or the needy, were supported at public expense. There is no need to say anything about the primitive Church, which took shape immediately after the Lord's Ascension and the sending of the Holy Spirit, since Luke bears clear witness to this in the Book of Acts. And since we see that in the churches special collections were sometimes made for foreigners who needed outside help, who could doubt that each church provided even more for its own members, whom Paul, writing to the Galatians, calls the household of faith? That custom, which the apostles instituted, continued among their successors as well, as Tertullian and Justin testify, and indeed other orthodox writers too, who followed them in the next century or so.

units.la: Finis autem collectarum fuit, quem Lucas in Actis indicat, ne quis esset in Ecclesia egenus siue mendicus: qui videlicet oftiatim mendicando publicum esset & ignominiosum egestatis exemplum. Id verò cum veteri Lege conuenit, qua sancitur, ne fit mendicus in Israele: non quòd Deus egenos eijci velit, sed quòd eos ita prospicere debent qui eius populus censeri volunt, ne hinc inde vagari & victum quaerere cogantur. Et sunt Legis istius rationes multae & graues. Primò enim pugnat hoc cum sine beneficentiae, qui est, vt pauperes non spectaculum fiant, sed vt eis subue-niatur, quò suas res agere possint. Deinde est illud à charitatis ingenio alienissimum. Ea enim Dei exemplum imitatur, qui ab Apostolo ipsa charitas dicitur, & qui ne rogatus quidem benefacit, adeoq; dignos & indignos, bonos & malos benignissimè pascit & alit. Et Christus in Samaritani parabola, ita nos erga egenos affectos esse iubet, vt solo affectu alienae miseriae commoueamur, etiamsi miser ille neque nobis notus sit, neque opem à nobis flagitet. Praeterea qui suos mendicare sinunt, aut potius sua inhumanitate sive negligentia id facere cogunt, ij in leges sanctissimae illius communionis siue societatis peccant, quae credentibus omnibus in Christo intercedit, qui nos eiusdem Patris coelestis filios, & eiusdem corporis membra fecit. Cur ergo fratrem negligat? Aut quis membrum sui corporis quantumuis morbidum & exulceratum pertire sinit, si sit quo medeatur? Adde, quòd iniuria ista in ipsum Christum redundat, qui nos sui corporis, cuius ipse caput est, membra fecit. Itaque pauperem & egentem negligentes Christum negligimus, cuius ille membrum est. Et huc facit, quod Paulus in praesenti de collecta in sanctos loquitur, ita nimirum vocans eos pauperes, quos Christus per fidem sibi insitos Deo Patri consecrauit. Sufficit hoc vere Christiano aduersus iniqua & inhumana carnis iudicia, quae ma-lignius egentium vitia obseruat, vt aliquo praetextu charitatis officium illis negare possit. San-ctis, qui in terra sunt (inquit Dauid) toto animo delector. Quis ergo Dauidis spiritu eum regi dixerit, qui propter egestatem aut quodcunque aliud vitium eos negligit, qui Christi nomen profitentur, & quos ille in nouissimo die pro suis agnoscet? Accedit his, quod mendicandi licentia disciplinae Christianae quàm maximè officit. Quia enim mendicantibus pudor inutilis est, ferè illo abstersò quiduis sibi licere putant. Itaque qui mendicationi assueuerunt, ij reuera ἀτακτοι[?] illi siunt, quos ad Thessalonicen. scribens Paulus procul ab Ecclesia arcere iubet: qui videlicet otio inerti & ignauo dediti aliena modò curiose inspiciunt, inuident, cauillantur, nullis legibus continentur, quia egestas à politicis immunes facit, Ecclesiasticas verò ipsi negligunt, nisi quoad suo otio illas seruire sentiunt. Itaque neque coetibus sacris intersunt, ut suas preces cum aliorum precibus coniungant, neque Dei verbum audiunt, neque Sacramentis digne utuntur, ideoque labes sunt Ecclesiarum, & publica simul charitatis procul exulantis testimonia, ex quibus calumniandi occasionem arripiunt aduersarij, qui Veritatis doctrinam oderunt. Accedit malis istis, quòd ijdem liberos suos pessimè educant, & multos alios suo exemplo corrumpunt, ut ignauum hoc & iners vitae genus ipsi quoque sectari incipiant, & ita hominum eiusmodi numerus indies augetur. Vere ista dici res ipsa clamat hodie, & de iis vulgò omnes conqueruntur. Ista ergo Apostolos moverunt, ut veterem Dei legem de mendicis coercendis reductam voluerint, quae paulò ante Christi tempora Sacerdotum culpa interciderat, cùm illi sacrilega auaritia accensi ad se-ra-perent[?] ea, ex quibus pauperes ali debebant.
units.tr: The purpose of the collections, which Luke indicates in Acts, was that there should be no one in the Church who was needy or a beggar, that is, one who went from door to door begging and so became a public and shameful example of want. This agrees with the old Law, which orders that there be no beggar in Israel. This is not because God wishes the needy to be cast out, but because those who wish to be counted his people ought to provide for them, so that they are not forced to wander here and there seeking their living. There are many weighty reasons for this law. First, begging is contrary to beneficence, whose aim is that the poor should not become a spectacle, but that they should be helped so that they can manage their affairs. Second, such begging is most alien to the nature of charity. For charity imitates God, who is called charity itself by the Apostle, and who does good even without being asked, and in his kindness feeds and nourishes the worthy and unworthy, good and evil alike. And Christ, in the parable of the Samaritan, bids us to be so disposed towards the needy that we are moved by feeling alone at another's misery, even if that wretched man is not known to us and does not beg help from us. Moreover, those who allow their own people to beg, or rather, by their inhumanity or negligence force them to do so, sin against the laws of that most holy communion or fellowship which exists among all believers in Christ, who has made us sons of the same heavenly Father and members of the same body. Why then should anyone neglect his brother? Or who would allow a limb of his own body, however diseased and ulcerated, to perish, if there were a means of healing it? Add that this wrong reaches Christ himself, who has made us members of his body, of which he is the head. Therefore, in neglecting the poor and needy, we neglect Christ, whose member he is. Paul's words in the present passage about the collection for the saints bear on this, for he calls them poor, that is, those whom Christ, by faith, has grafted into himself and consecrated to God the Father. This is enough for a true Christian against the unjust and inhuman judgements of the flesh, which look more spitefully at the faults of the needy, so that under some pretext of charity they can refuse them this duty. "I take my whole delight in the saints that are on the earth," says David. Who then would say that he has the spirit of David if he neglects, on account of poverty or any other fault, those who profess the name of Christ, and whom Christ will acknowledge as his own on the last day? To these things is added that the licence to beg is most harmful to Christian discipline. For since shame is useless to beggars, they commonly think they may do anything once shame has been wiped away. Thus those who have grown accustomed to begging become truly disorderly [ἀτακτοι], those whom Paul, writing to the Thessalonians, bids to be kept far from the Church. They are given over to idle and lazy leisure, and they only pry curiously into others' affairs, envy them and carp at them; they are restrained by no laws, because poverty frees them from civil obligations, while they themselves neglect ecclesiastical ones, unless they feel that these serve their own idleness. Thus they neither attend the sacred assemblies, so as to join their prayers to those of others, nor hear the Word of God, nor partake of the sacraments worthily; and so they are a blot on the churches and a public proof that charity has fled far away. From these things adversaries, who hate the doctrine of truth, seize the chance to slander. Besides these evils, such people bring up their children very badly and corrupt many others by their example, so that they too begin to follow this idle and slothful way of life, and so the number of such people grows daily. The matter itself today clearly cries out that these things are true, and everyone commonly complains of them. These, then, are the things that moved the apostles to want the old law of God concerning the restraint of beggars restored, a law which had fallen into disuse shortly before Christ's time through the fault of the priests, who, inflamed by sacrilegious greed, seized for themselves what should have been used to support the poor.

units.la: Atqui debebant ista etiam hodie movere Christianos principes, ut de scandalo tam igno-miniso tamque noxio tollendo serio cogitarent. Sed obstat quod apud omnes hominum ordines regnat privati commodi studium: quod ut aliquo honestiori praetextu excusetur, plerique ut egentibus aliter prospiciatur, impossibile esse aiunt. At iidem primitivae Ecclesiae exemplo convincuntur, quando inter atrocia Imperatorum edicta, persecutionum grauissimarum tumultus, facultatum direptiones singuli non suos modo aluerunt, sed exteris & longo locorum interuallo abse dissitis vitae subsidia transmiserunt. Arguuntur item exemplo Judaeorum, qui cum hodie in omnes gentes dispersi, neq; rempub. neque templum & certas Ecclesias habeant, tamen ita suis prospiciunt, ne a nobis, quos illi odioso vocabulo Goijm vocant, vitae emendicare cogantur. Quid de Judais aut veteri Ecclesia dico, quando propriis exemplis nostri illi convincuntur? Nam si Papistica superstitionis sectatores inspiciamus, quam inanes sumptus faciunt horum Episcopi, Abbates, Cardinales, qui luxu & fastu cum regibus certant? Quam ingens pauperum numerus ex iis alipos-set, quae illi in canes, equos, accipitres, agasones, muliones, mimos, scurras, ludiones, scorta & voluptates inhonestas atque illicitas insumunt? Quàm multis item sufficerent fruges, quae ab inerti monachorum & sacrificulorum turba devorantur, de quibus verissimè illud Satyricum dixeris: Nos numerus sumus, & fruges consumere nati? Adde his, quae tam Papistae quàm evangelici inutiliter, imò turpiter & non sine scandalo dilapidant in luxuriosis comessationibus, alea, vestitu fastuoso, bellis non necessarijs, venatione, insanis aedificijs, & sexcentis aliis, quae cumme-morare longum foret. Quo igitur ore pauperum subventionem, ut impossibilem, neglígimus[?], quibus ad omne genus vitiorum abunde suppetit, quod carni & mundo lasciuienti impendatur? An ergo plura à nobis Christus in suis membris, quàm Satan in suis exigit? Fallimur, si hoc putamus. Ille enim necessarijs contentus est, hic autem nisi cum opibus te quoque totum ei mancipes, non potest quiescere. Desinant ergo inanes praetextus quaerere, qui tam manifestè indicijs se produnt, quod non facultate, sed voluntate in hac causa non minus necessaria quàm honesta destituantur.
units.tr: Yet these same things ought to move Christian princes today to think seriously about removing so shameful and so harmful a scandal. But what stands in the way is that among all orders of men the pursuit of private advantage reigns; and to excuse this under some more respectable pretext, many say that it is impossible to provide for the needy in any other way. But the example of the primitive Church refutes them, since, amid the savage edicts of emperors and the uproar of the most severe persecutions, and the plundering of property, individuals not only supported their own, but also sent means of life to foreigners living far away across long stretches of land. The example of the Jews also refutes them, for although today they are scattered among all nations and have neither a commonwealth, nor a temple, nor fixed congregations, still they provide so well for their own that they are not forced to beg a living from us, whom they call by the hateful name of gentiles, Goyim [גוים]. But why do I speak of Jews or the ancient Church, when our own people are refuted by their own examples? For if we look at the followers of Papist superstition, how vain are the expenses of their bishops, abbots and cardinals, who vie with kings in luxury and pride! How great a number of the poor could be fed from what they spend on dogs, horses, hawks, grooms, muleteers, mimes, buffoons, jesters, dancers, prostitutes and dishonourable and unlawful pleasures! How many, too, would be sufficed by the crops which are devoured by the idle crowd of monks and little priests, of whom one may most truly say what the satirist said: "We are a mere number, born to consume the crops." Add to these what both Papists and evangelicals squander uselessly, indeed shamefully, and not without scandal, on luxurious feasts, dice, showy clothing, unnecessary wars, hunting, mad buildings, and six hundred other things, which would take too long to recount. With what face, then, do we neglect the support of the poor, on the grounds that it is impossible, when there is more than enough money for every kind of vice, to be spent on the flesh and the wanton world? Or does Christ demand more from us in his members than Satan demands from his? We are mistaken if we think so. For the one is content with what is necessary, while the other, unless you give yourself up entirely to him along with your wealth, cannot rest. Let them stop, then, seeking empty pretexts, those who betray themselves so plainly by their evidence, that in this matter, which is no less necessary than honourable, they lack not means but will.

units.la: Sed pergamus in Pauli verbis, qui quid ex eius constitutione apud Galatas fiat, & quid Co-rinthij quoq; facere debeant, exponit: Primo quoq; die hebdomadis unusquisq; vestrum apud se reponat recondens quod pro Dei benignitate lucuerit[?]: ne cùm venero, tunc collecta fiant. Paucis verbis praecipua & summa totius negotij capita comprehendit. Primo, unusquisque vestrum, inquit. Nemo igitur excipitur, aut immunitate donatur, sive mas fuerit sive foemina, liber aut seruus, nobilis aut plebeius, doctus aut indoctus, imò sive dives aut pauper fuerit. Ut enim omnes eiusdem corporis membra sumus, ita eadem charitatis lege omnes sumus obstricti. Et quamuis plura ab iis merito exiguntur, qui facultatibus abundant, nullam tamen excusationem pauperes habent, qui quales quales sint, habent tamen hi quoque quod in commune conferant, sicuti exemplo viduae docemur, cuius obulos aut minuta Christus pluris fecit, quàm magnifica divitum donaria, quae ex magnis opum aceruis cum ambitiosa ostentatione conferebant. Et si tibi ne teruncius quidem neque panis frustulum sit quod egenti des, attamen corporis fortassis vires sunt, quibus laboranti opem feras, ægrotantem subleues, aut fatigatum recrees. Neque verba deesse possunt, quibus afflictum & mærentem consoleris. Quòd si ista quoque deficiant, saltem voluntas benigna sit, & cures ne Ecclesiæ præter causam oneri sis, neue quæ aliis multò te pauperioribus debentur, tu intercipias. Erat hoc diligentius cogitandum iis, qui se à lege charitatis exemptos putant, & quasi in mendicatione salus consistat, hinc inde discurrunt, & quibusuis[?] obuijs petendo molesti sunt, adeoque per ostia quoque omnia in quorumuis ædes irrumpunt, & in cubicula remotissima penetrant. At melius est dare, quàm accipere, ut alibi Apostolus monuit. Nec multò leuius scelus est ab aliis petere, quæ tu vel labore proprio vel parcius viuendo obtinere poteras, quàm inuitum per vim spoliare. Imò sacrilegium dici meretur, si qui seipsum alere potest alijs eleemosynam præripiat, ipse iners & otiosus. Quod non male à Turcarum sapientibus obseruatum est, qui ut eleemosynæ meritum supra omnia opera alia extollant: itaq; homini salutarius esse docent, ut proprias carnes arrodat atq; deuoret, quàm ut eleemosynam nulla necessitate coactus accipiat. Discant ergo singulí seipsos & fortunas suas diligentius excutere & examinare, ne vel in largiendo tenaciores sint, vel ad accipiendum impudentius ruant, & ita sacrilegi siant, dum inter pauperes Ecclesiæ censeri volunt.
units.tr: But let us go on with Paul's words, in which he sets out what is to be done about this under his arrangement among the Galatians, and what the Corinthians too ought to do: "On the first day of the week let each of you lay something aside at home, storing up what he has prospered by God's goodness, so that collections need not be made when I come." In a few words he sums up the principal points and the whole of the business. First, "each of you," he says. No one is therefore excepted or granted immunity, whether male or female, free or slave, noble or common, learned or unlearned, rich or poor. For just as we are all members of the same body, so we are all bound by the same law of charity. And although more is rightly required of those who abound in means, the poor have no excuse either, for whatever they are, they too have something to contribute to the common good, as we are taught by the example of the widow, whose two small coins Christ valued more highly than the magnificent gifts of the rich, which they gave with ostentatious display out of great heaps of wealth. And if you have not even a penny, nor a crumb of bread to give the needy, yet perhaps you have bodily strength by which you may help the labouring man, lift up the sick, or refresh the weary. Nor can words be lacking by which you may console the afflicted and the grieving. But if even these fail, let at least your willingness be kind, and take care that you are not a burden to the Church without cause, or that you do not intercept what is owed to others who are much poorer than you. This should have been considered more carefully by those who think themselves exempt from the law of charity, and who run hither and thither as if salvation lay in begging, and who are a nuisance to whomever they meet by asking, and so break into every house through all the doors and penetrate into the most remote bedrooms. "It is better to give than to receive," as the Apostle reminds us elsewhere. Nor is it much less wicked to ask others for what you could have obtained by your own labour or by living more sparingly, than to rob someone of his goods by force against his will. Indeed, it deserves to be called sacrilege if someone who is able to support himself, being idle and lazy, snatches alms from others. The Turks' wise men have observed this well, for they so extol the merit of almsgiving above all other works, yet teach that it is more wholesome for a man to gnaw and devour his own flesh than to accept alms when he is not compelled by any necessity. Let each person therefore learn to examine and scrutinise himself and his means more carefully, so that he is neither too stingy in giving, nor too shameless in rushing to receive, and so does not become a sacrilegious person while wishing to be counted among the poor of the Church.

units.la: Deinde modum quoque exponit, qui in collectis faciendis debeat obseruari. Primo quoq; die hebdomadis (inquit) vnusquisque vestrum apud se reponat, recondens, &c. Dicit autem ista de collecta illa extraordinaria, quæ (vt initio monuimus) in subuentionem fratrum in Iudæa egentium fieri debebat: & summa præcepti huius est, vt quisque singulis diebus Dominicis pro suarum facultatum ratione priuatim domi suæ aliquid seponat, quod postea cùm ipse venerit, in publicum aut commune conferat. Ita vero fieri iubet certas & graues ob causas. Primam ipse in præsenti adducit, ne tumultuariam collationem facere cogantur, si res ista in suum vsq; aduentum differatur. Quod vt multis incommodè accidere potuisset, ita moram quoque attulisset, quam abrumpere omnem oportebat. Voluit item hac moderatione tenuioribus consulere, qui multa simul conferre non possunt, pudet autem paucula dare. Ita enim horum quoque eleemosyna per aliquot menses absque aliquo grauamine collecta ad summam aliquam non omnino aspernandam ascendere potuit. Adijcit his causam tertiam ipse in posteriori epistola, ne qui de ipsorum liberalitate apud alias Ecclesias magnificè gloriatus fuerat, pudore suffundatur si cum aliquo comitatu aduéniens illos imparatos deprehendat.
units.tr: Next he also sets out the manner in which the collections are to be made. "On the first day of the week," he says, "let each one of you put something aside at home, storing it up," and so on. He is speaking of that special collection which, as we noted at the outset, was to be made for the relief of the poor brothers in Judaea. The substance of this command is that on each Lord's Day every person should privately set aside at home something in proportion to his means, to be brought into the common fund when he himself arrives. He orders this for certain serious reasons. The first he gives in the passage itself: that they should not be forced to make a hurried collection if the matter were postponed until his arrival. Such a delay would have been inconvenient for many and would also have caused a pause that had to be broken off. He also wished by this arrangement to consider the poorer folk, who cannot give a large sum all at once but are ashamed to give only a little. In this way the alms of these people too, gathered over several months without any burden, could amount to a sum not to be despised. He adds a third reason in his second letter: that those who had boasted grandly of their generosity to the other Churches should not be covered with shame if he arrived with a company and found them unprepared.

units.la: Quod autem de extraordinaria collecta dicitur, haud dubiè tunc temporis publicè in Ecclesijs fuit obseruatum: Vt videlicet primo die hebdomadis pecuniam in cœtibus colligerent, ex qua suos egenos alerent. Ita vero eum diem dixit Apostolus ex Iudæorum more (vt in resurrectionis Christi historia apud Marcum & Lucam est videre) quem postea Dominicum dixerunt Christiani, cum quod eo Dominus ex mortuis resurrexit, tum quod in Sabbati locum successit, vt eo cœtus sacri haberentur. Voluerunt autem tunc collectas illas fieri Apostoli, ne veterem Legem negligerent fideles, quæ mandat, ne vacui veniamus in conspectum Domini. Nam etsi sacrificia iampridem abrogata sint, quæ olim ex pecoribus & frugibus offerebantur, successerunt tamen his longè præstantiora, preces nimirum, laus & gratiarum actio, quodq; vnusquisque seipsum Deo viuentem hostiam sistit, quibus beneficentia quoque & eleemosyna adnumeratur, vt Paulus in epistola ad Hebræos annotauit. Et hæc quidem optimo iure sacrificium dicitur, quando constat, Christum sibi factum putare quicquid egenis in suo nomine conseritur. Multum præterea confert huic causæ temporis circumstantia, vnà cum iis, quæ diebus dominicis in cœtu sacro fieri consueuerunt. Tunc enim Verbum Dei auditur, quod passim nobis charitatis & beneficentiæ studium commendat. Tunc preces fiunt publicæ, quæ & ipsæ nos excitant, ne duriores simus erga nostræ opis indigos, quàm Deum erga nos esse velimus. Multùm quoque nos mouent aliorum exempla, vt liberalius conferamus, & vt pudeat nos solos inueniri asymbolos, qui nihil in pauperum vsum largiamur. Et quod de Corinthijs nuper diximus, hodie etiam locum habet, quòd absque magna molestia non contemnendam summam pecuniæ paulatim conferimus, quæ non sine incommodo & rei domesticæ iactura simul dari posset. Denique, quod Chrysostomus annotauit, quia hoc die Christus resurrexit,quæ salutis & omnium bonorum radix est, conuenit, vt ipsi quoque liberaliores simus in eos, qui à nostra ope toti pendent. Adde, quòd Cænæ mysticæ vsus nos hic imprimis officij admonet, quod[?] & mens à laboribus quiescens, & huius seculi curis libera, egentium facilius miseretur.
units.tr: As for what is said about the special collection, there is no doubt that at that time it was observed publicly in the Churches: namely, that on the first day of the week they gathered money in their assemblies from which to support their needy. The Apostle called that day the first day of the week in the Jewish manner (as can be seen in the accounts of Christ's resurrection in Mark and Luke). Later Christians called it the Lord's Day, both because the Lord rose from the dead on it and because it took the place of the Sabbath as the day for holy assemblies. The Apostles wished these collections to be made then so that the faithful would not neglect the old Law, which commands: "Let us not appear before the Lord empty." For although the sacrifices that were once offered from flocks and fruits have long since been abolished, they have been replaced by things far more excellent: prayers, praise and thanksgiving, and the fact that each person presents himself to God as a living sacrifice. To these, beneficence and almsgiving are also reckoned, as Paul noted in his letter to the Hebrews. And these are rightly called a sacrifice, since it is certain that Christ regards as done to himself whatever is contributed to the needy in his name. The circumstance of the time also contributes much to this purpose, together with what is customarily done in the holy assembly on the Lord's Days. For then the Word of God is heard, which everywhere commends to us zeal for love and beneficence. Then public prayers are made, which themselves stir us up, lest we be harder toward those who need our help than we would wish God to be toward us. The examples of others also move us greatly to give more generously, and it shames us to be found alone contributing nothing for the use of the poor. And what we said recently about the Corinthians also applies today: we gather, without great hardship, a sum of money not to be despised, little by little, which could not be given all at once without inconvenience and loss to our household. Finally, as Chrysostom noted, because Christ rose on this day, which is the root of salvation and of all good things, it is fitting that we ourselves be more generous toward those who depend wholly on our help. Add to this that the use of the mystical Supper reminds us especially of this duty, since a mind at rest from labours and free from the cares of this age more readily shows pity toward the needy.

units.la: Debet præterea hic obseruari recondendi verbum, quod de thesauris proprie dicitur, & ideo in Græco verbum ἀποθησαυρίζειν[?] ponit Apostolus, quod Latina inflexione thesaurizare diceremus. Eo enim vti voluit, vt doceat non amitti ea, quæ pauperibus dantur, sed potius ceu thesaurum recondi, quem olim non sine fœnore magno recipiamus. Quo sensu in priori quoque ad Timoth. diuites admonet, vt faciles sint ad impartiendum, & ita sibi ipsis recondant fundamentum bonum in posterum, & vitam æternam apprehendant. Id vero ex Christo didicerat Apostolus, qui in Euangelio monet, vt thesaurum nobis in cælo recondamus, vt denique ex huius seculi diuitiis, quas Mammona iniquitatis dicit, nobis amicos paremus, qui nos vbi defecerimus, in æterna tabernacula recipiant. Et huc imprimis promissiones illæ magnificæ faciunt, quibus Deus ipse quasi fideiussorem se sistit pro pauperibus. In Lege enim dicit: Si pauperi non maligne dederis, locupletabit & fortunabit te Dominus Deus tuus in omnibus operibus tuis, & in omnibus ad quæ admoueris manum tuam. Et per Isaiam ipse Deus ait: Frange esurienti panem tuum, affligetos vagos introduc domum, si videris nudum, vestito eum, & à carne tua ne te abscondas. Tunc erumpet velut aurora lux tua, & salus tua protenus germinabit, iustitia anteibit faciem tuam, & gloria Domini colliget te. Et paulò post: Si effuderis esurienti animam tuam, & animam afflictam saturaueris, tum orietur in tenebris lux tua, & erit caligo tua sicut meridies: Et deducet te Dominus semper, & saturam reddet in siccitatibus animam tuam, & ossa tua saginabit: & eris vt hortus irriguus, & sicut fons aquarum, cuius aquæ nunquam fallunt, &c. Recte ergo à Solomone dictum fuit: Domino fœnerat, qui[?] fquis benefacit pauperi: secundum beneficium eius rependetur ei. Et huius pater Dauid multa experientia edoctus dicebat: Iustus beneficus est quotidie, & mutuum dat, & posteri eius optime habent. Item: Spargit, ac dat pauperibus, iustitia eius æternum perstabit, & cornu eius exaltabitur cum gloria. Taceo nunc, quod Christus egenos sibi substituit, de quo sæpe iam diximus. Ista vero arguunt auarorum & tenacium hominum peruersam & stultissimam sorditiem: qui ne quidem in contractibus pecuniarum iacturam faciunt, homines fideiussores sibi dari volunt, & si hi ipsis diuites & opulenti sistantur, multa millia aureorum mutuò dant, neque eorum exemplis prorsus absterrentur, quibus tam debitores quàm sponsores fidem suam fefellerunt: Quod si vero in pauperes aliquid erogare oportet, ne Deum quidem pro his spondentem admittunt. Est hoc euidens argumentum, quo se à fide alienissimos esse producunt, quæ etiam causa est, quòd in charitate sint frigidiores.
units.tr: Here we should also observe the word "store up", which is properly used of treasures; and so the Apostle uses the Greek word for storing up treasure [ἀποθησαυρίζειν], which in Latin we would express by the verb thesaurizare. For he wished to use this word to teach that what is given to the poor is not lost, but is rather stored up like a treasure, which we shall one day receive back with great interest. In this same sense, in his first letter to Timothy, he admonishes the rich to be ready to share, and so to lay up for themselves a good foundation for the future and lay hold on eternal life. The Apostle had learned this from Christ, who in the Gospel bids us store up a treasure for ourselves in heaven, and to make for ourselves friends from the riches of this age, which he calls the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when we fail, they may receive us into everlasting dwellings. And especially to this purpose are those magnificent promises, by which God himself presents himself as a surety for the poor. For in the Law he says: "If you give to the poor not with a grudging heart, the Lord your God will enrich and prosper you in all your works and in all that you put your hand to." And through Isaiah God himself says: "Break your bread to the hungry, bring the homeless poor into your house; if you see the naked, clothe him, and do not hide yourself from your own flesh. Then your light shall break forth like the dawn, and your health shall spring up at once; righteousness shall go before your face, and the glory of the Lord shall gather you in." And a little later: "If you pour out your soul to the hungry, and satisfy the afflicted soul, then your light shall rise in darkness, and your gloom shall be like midday. And the Lord shall guide you always, and satisfy your soul in dry places, and fatten your bones; and you shall be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water whose waters never fail," and so on. Rightly, then, Solomon said: "He who is kind to the poor lends to the Lord; and what he gives will be repaid to him." And his father David, taught by much experience, said: "The righteous man is generous every day, and lends, and his children do very well." Again: "He scatters and gives to the poor; his righteousness endures for ever, and his horn shall be exalted with glory." I say nothing now of the fact that Christ has made the needy his own substitutes, as we have often said already. But these passages expose the perverse and most foolish stinginess of avaricious and tight-fisted men, who will not suffer any loss even in money-lending: they want men to stand surety for them, and if these are rich and well off, they lend many thousands of gold pieces; nor are they in the least deterred by the examples of those who have broken faith both as debtors and as sureties. But if they must give anything to the poor, they will not even admit God as a surety for them. This is clear evidence by which they show themselves most alien to faith, and this is also the reason why they are colder in love.

units.la: Postremò quia multi quærunt, quid & quantum dare debeant, & ea etiam ratione prætextu quærunt, quibus suam sorditiem sive tenacitatem excusent, quæstiones iflas omnes vno verbo Paulus abrumpit, singulos dare iubens quod pro Dei benignitate licuerit, id est, quantum ferunt facultates, quas ex Dei benedictione accepit. Quam partem Tobias filio suo prolixius exponens sic ait: Prout fueris ad copiam instructus, benignitatem exerceas: Si multum tibi fuerit, largè tribuas: quòd si parum fuerit tibi, ne verearis ex pauco præstare beneficentiam. Etenim non omnia possumus omnes: neque hoc exigit Deus, vt cum nostro luculento damno rei domesticæ iacturam alios ditemus. Et huc referri debet, quod in posteriori epistola dicetur: Non vt aliis relaxatio fit, vobis autem afflictio, &c. Hoc enim solum requirit Dominus, vt nostra abundantia tenuiorum & egentium inopiam subleuet. Rursus ergo omnis excusationis prætextus illis negatur, qui se nō habere queruntur, quod pauperibus magno subsidio esse queat, & ideo prorsus à benefaciendo abstinent. Atqui non petit Deus, vt quantum illis necesse est largiaris, sed quantum tuæ facultates, & rei domesticæ ratio ferre possunt. Et vt olim, quando ad tabernaculi fabricam dona sua Israelitæ conferebant, alij aurum, alij argentum, alij gemmas, alij purpuram, æs, sericum largiebantur, interim verò non minus grati aut accepti Deo erant, qui caprarum pilos atque pelles dabant: ita hic quoque non muneris pretium, sed dantis animus æstimatur, & Deus gratum sibi habebit quicquid pro tuarum facultatum ratione animo pio atque syncero largitus fueris. Facit prætereà locus iste ad confutandum eorum superstitionem, qui nisi omnibus abiectis facultatibus nudi & omniū inopes, paupertatem voluntariam profiteantur, se saluos fore negat. Sunt inter hos primi Monachi, qui interim sub istius professionis titulo multis fucum faciunt, cum omnibus abundent, quae vitae suauiter transigenda seruiunt: astutiores nimirum gentium philosophis, qui suis bonis in mare proiectis vitae genus vt stultissimum ita miserrimum sectati sunt. Sed omissis infelicibus illis, discamus, pauperum curam ad Ecclesias publice, & priuatim ad singulos Christianos pertinere. Illos ergo sibi commendatos habeant, quicunq; ex eorum numero censeri volunt, vt olim in magno illo die eos pro suis agnoscat aeternus Dei Filius, Dominus & redeptor noster IESVS CHRISTVS: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: Finally, since many ask what and how much they ought to give, and seek this pretext in order to excuse their meanness or stinginess, Paul cuts off all these questions with a single word, bidding each to give as much as God's goodness has allowed, that is, as much as their means, which they have received by God's blessing, can bear. Tobias, explaining this point more fully to his son, says: "According to your abundance, practise kindness. If you have much, give generously; but if you have little, do not be afraid to give a kindness from what is little. For we cannot all do everything, and God does not require that we enrich others with our own great loss to our household." And to this should be referred what will be said in the second letter: "Not that others may be eased and you burdened," and so on. For the Lord requires only this, that our abundance relieve the want of the poor and needy. Therefore, once again, every pretext of excuse is denied to those who complain that they have nothing that could be a great help to the poor, and so altogether refrain from doing good. Yet God does not ask that you give what they need, but what your means and your household's circumstances can bear. And just as once, when the Israelites brought their gifts for the building of the tabernacle, some gave gold, others silver, others gems, others purple, bronze, and silk, yet those who gave goats' hair and skins were no less pleasing and acceptable to God, so here too it is not the price of the gift but the mind of the giver that is weighed, and God will regard as pleasing whatever you give with a pious and sincere heart in proportion to your means. This passage also serves to refute the superstition of those who declare that unless they give up all their possessions and become naked and destitute of everything, professing voluntary poverty, they will not be saved. Among these were the first monks, who under the title of this profession often deceive many, although they abound in all the things that serve to live pleasantly: more cunning, no doubt, than the philosophers of the nations, who, having thrown their goods into the sea, pursued a way of life as foolish as it was wretched. But, leaving aside those unhappy men, let us learn that the care of the poor belongs to the Churches publicly and to each Christian privately. Let those who wish to be counted among their number therefore commend them to themselves, so that the eternal Son of God, our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, may acknowledge them as his own on that great day. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XC.
units.tr: HOMILY XC.

units.la: Postquam autem aduenero, quoscunque probaueritis, per epistolas hos mittam, vt perferant gratiam vestram in Hierusa-lem. Quòd si res digna fuerit, vt ipse proficiscar, mecum proficiscentur.
units.tr: "And when I have come, I will send whomever you approve with letters to carry your gift to Jerusalem. And if it seems fitting that I should go too, they will go with me."

units.la: QVoniam res hominum in hoc seculo ita comparatae sunt, vt nunquam desint pauperes & opis aliena indigi, Deus olim suo populo rationem commodissimam praescripsit, qua in illis alendis atque sustentandis vti debeant. Finis eius praecipuus est, ne mendici sint, qui hinc inde oberrando victum quaeritent. Hoc enim vt inhumanitatis argumentum est euidentissimum: ita disciplinae & morum honestati cumprimis officit, vt nuper demonstrauimus. Ideo Apostoli olim causam istam diligenter egerunt, neque illis satis fuit, si vnaquaeq; Ecclesia suos egenos siue pauperes aleret, & ἀτάκτως seu inordinatè viuentes arctiori disciplina coercerent: sed vt exterorum quoque curam haberent monuerunt. Itaq; cum illo tempore Christiani, qui per Syriam & Iudaeam dispersi erant, prae aliis rerum penuria ac fame premerentur, in gentium Ecclesiis passim collectas instituerunt extraordinarias, vt laborantibus subsidium mitteretur. De his in praesenti cum Corinthijs quoque Paulus agit, utpote hominibus opulentis & in pace securiori agentibus. Et quia res ista aliquibus ad rem nimium attentis difficilior videri poterat, id absque molestia fieri posse ostendit, si vnusquisq; singulis hebdomadibus pro suarum facultatum ratione aliquid seponat, quod postea cum aliorum eleemosynis collectum in Iudaeam mittatur.
units.tr: Since the affairs of men in this world are so arranged that there are always poor people who lack help from others, God long ago prescribed to his people the most suitable method by which they ought to support and sustain them. Its chief aim is that those who wander about from place to place seeking food should not become beggars. For this is the clearest evidence of inhumanity, and it is especially harmful to discipline and to the honourable conduct of life, as we showed recently. Therefore the Apostles long ago pleaded this cause with care. They did not think it enough for each congregation to feed its own needy or poor and to restrain by stricter discipline those who lived in a disorderly way [ἀτάκτως]. They also urged that the care of outsiders be taken up. Accordingly, when at that time the Christians who were scattered through Syria and Judaea were pressed by want and famine beyond the others, they arranged special collections in the churches of the Gentiles everywhere, so that help might be sent to those in distress. Paul now deals with this matter also with the Corinthians, since they were wealthy people living in greater security in peace. And because this business might seem more difficult to some who are too concerned with their own affairs, he shows that it can be done without trouble if each person sets aside something every week, according to his means, which afterwards, gathered together with the alms of others, may be sent to Judaea.

units.la: Porrò etsi institutum hoc omnes probent, & necessarium esse ducant, multos tamen absterret, aut saltem parciores reddit dispensatorum improbitas, & quòd metuunt, ne quae ipsi piè & liberali-ter conferunt, minus digne distribuatur. Ideo Paulus nunc ad ista quoq; huius tractationis partem accedit, docens quid ipse de collectis istis iam constituerit. Postquam (inquit) aduenero, quoscunq; probaueritis, per epistolas hos mittam, vt perferant gratiam vestram in Hierusalem, &c. Tria dicit. Primùm, ne ipsi temere mittant collectas pecunias Hierosolymam, sed illas apud se seruent in suum vsq; ad ipsos aduentum. Voluit enim videre quantum contulissent, vt ex eo posset iudicare de sui ministerij profectu. Multos etiam hoc excitare poterat, vt liberalius largirentur. Deinde ex ipsis & ipsorum consensu ordinandos tunc ait homines probatae fidei, qui hac ipsorum gratia ad Hierosolymitanos deferant. Gratiam vero dicit pecunias illas, partim quòd eas ex gratuita misericordia conferrent, & suum eo facto erga Iudaeorum Ecclesias fauorem testaretur: partim, quòd hoc omne gratiae Dei opus erat, qui hominum corda mouet, vt aliorum miserijs tangatur, & illis subuentum velint. Tertiò literas commendatitias pollicetur legatis eò profecturis, ne rerum ignari in homines male fidos incidant. Imò si (inquit) res digna fuerit, & id vel pecuniarum collectarum summa metiatur, aut necessitas ipsa postulet, ego ipse meam operam in illis deferendis vobis offero, & legatos vestros comitabor, vt & tutius & commodius illuc perueniant. Fuit ergo res ista Apostolo vehementer cordi: quia & mandato diuino vrgebatur, quod ab Apostolis acceperat, vt ad Galatas scribens testatur: & cum non fucato suae gentis amore arderet, graue ei fuit, tot credentium familias cũ tenellis liberis inter quotidiana, quae illis ab hostibus manifestis imminebat, pericula, insuper cũ fame cõflictari. Quidnis ergo facere & subire paratus erat, vt miseris & egentibus succurreretur,
units.tr: Yet although all approve this arrangement and consider it necessary, the wickedness of the stewards deters many, or at least makes them more sparing; they fear that what they give out of piety and generosity may be distributed less worthily. Therefore Paul now turns to this part of the subject as well, teaching what he himself has already decided about these collections. "When I have come," he says, "I will send whomever you approve with letters to carry your gift to Jerusalem," and so on. He says three things. First, that they should not rashly send the collected money to Jerusalem, but keep it with themselves until his arrival. For he wished to see how much they had contributed, so that from this he could judge the progress of his ministry. He could also thus stir many to give more generously. Second, he says that men of proven faith should then be appointed from among them, with their common consent, to carry this gift of theirs to the Jerusalemites. He calls the money a "gift" partly because they gave it from free mercy, and by doing so bore witness to their goodwill toward the churches of the Jews, and partly because this whole work was a work of God's grace, who moves men's hearts to be touched by the miseries of others and to wish to help them. Third, he promises letters of recommendation to the envoys who are going there, so that they do not fall among untrustworthy men through ignorance of affairs. Indeed, he says, if the matter is worthy, whether because of the size of the sum collected or because necessity itself demands it, then I myself offer my labour in carrying it to you, and I will accompany your envoys, so that they may reach that place more safely and conveniently. This matter was therefore very dear to the Apostle's heart. It was urged upon him by the divine command he had received from the Apostles, as he attests when writing to the Galatians. And since he burned with a genuine love for his own nation, it was grievous to him that so many families of believers, with their tender children, should also be struck by hunger, amid the daily dangers that hung over them from open enemies. Why, then, should he not be ready to do and to undergo whatever was needed to help the wretched and needy?

units.la: Ad hoc exemplum suos mores examinent Pontifices & Episcopi, qui cum Apostolici dici & haberi velint, adeò tamen non mouentur egentium & famæ pereuntium aspectu atq; clamoribus, vt ipsi plerunq; præcipui penuriæ & famis authores sint, dum vel suarum ditionum hominum immodicis & iniquis exactionibus expilat, vt fit quod ipsorum luxui plus quàm Sybaritico & fastui sufficiat: vel etiam bella inter reges serunt non necessaria, quæ totis gentibus exitia & horribilem regionum fertilissimarum vastitatem pariunt. Exempla hic commemorare non est opus, quando de illis omnes historiæ testantur, & nos quotidie illis consultoribus ea fieri cernimus, quæ boni omnes merito detestantur, & de quibus totus terrarum orbis queritur. Sed vt pergamus in præsentis argumenti tractatione, de bonorum Ecclesiæ & eleemosynarum dispensatoribus aliqua dicenda sunt, vt nimirum demonstremus primò iis omnino opus esse in Ecclesiis bene constitutis: deinde quales illi esse debeant: postremò qua authoritate eosdem muniri necesse sit.
units.tr: Let the Popes and bishops examine their own conduct by this example. Although they wish to be and to be called apostolic, they are so unmoved by the sight and cries of the needy who perish from hunger that they are often the chief authors of want and famine themselves. They plunder the people of their dominions with excessive and unjust exactions, so that there is enough for their luxury, more than Sybaritic, and their pride. Or they stir up unnecessary wars between kings, which bring ruin on whole nations and a dreadful devastation of the most fertile regions. There is no need to recall examples here, since all histories bear witness to them, and we see daily done, with these men as their advisers, the things that all good people rightly detest, and over which the whole world complains. But to continue with the treatment of the present subject, something must be said about the stewards of the Church's goods and alms, namely to show, first, that there is an absolute need for them in well-ordered churches; second, what sort of men they ought to be; and last, by what authority such men must be invested.

units.la: Quoad primum, longa demonstratione opus non est, quando communis sensus & experientia quotidiana docent, pecunias publicas absque dispensatoribus certis neque colligi, neq; in suos vsus commodè distribui posse. Nam nisi illi sint, iam aut nemo quicquam conferet, aut quod collatum est omnium libidini patebit, dum quisque pro suo arbitrio rapiet quod volet, vnde non tam Platonica omnium bonorum communio, quàm horribilis ac seditiosa rerum omnium confusio oriretur. Fuerunt itaque semper in Ecclesia dispensatores, & initiò quidem hoc munus penes Apostolos fuit, qui certa cum ratione illud administrarunt. De eo Lucas in Actis ita scribit: Quotquot possessores agrorum & ædium erant, iis venditis afferebant pretium eorum, & deponebant ad pedes Apostolorum: distribuebatur autem singulis prout cuique opus erat. At paulò postquam crescente cre-dentium numero Apostoli tot simul negotiis non sufficerent, & murmura atque querelæ indiet [?] audirentur eorum, qui se aut suos negligi dicebant, ex Apostolorum sententia & communibus Ecclesiæ totius suffragiis diaconi septem constituti sunt, qui pecunias publicas reciperent, & easdem digne distribuerent. Qua in re non dubito Apostolos in Christi exemplum respexisse, qui inter ipsos prius œconomiam constituerat, & loculos Judæ commiserat tanquam communi ipsorum omnium œconomo. Et hunc morem ab eo tempore in Ecclesiis omnibus passim receptum fuisse ex iis appareret, quæ in Paulinis epistolis de diaconis & eorum officio scribuntur, quos ab Episcopis & pastoribus aperte distinguit.
units.tr: As to the first point, no long demonstration is needed, since common sense and daily experience teach that public money cannot be collected, nor fairly distributed for its proper uses, without appointed stewards. For unless there are such men, either no one will contribute anything, or what has been contributed will lie open to the greed of all, since each will take whatever he wants according to his own judgement, whence would arise not so much Plato's communion of all goods as a dreadful and seditious confusion of everything. There have therefore always been stewards in the Church, and at first this office belonged to the Apostles, who administered it with a sound plan. Luke writes of this in Acts: "As many as were owners of lands or houses sold them and brought the price and laid it at the Apostles' feet; and distribution was made to each as he had need." But a little later, as the number of believers grew and the Apostles could not cope with so many affairs at once, and murmurs and complaints were heard daily from those who said that they or their people were being neglected, seven deacons were appointed, by the Apostles' decision and the common vote of the whole Church, to receive the public money and distribute it rightly. In this matter I do not doubt that the Apostles looked to the example of Christ, who had earlier appointed a steward among themselves and entrusted the purse to Judas as the common steward of them all. And that this custom had from that time been received everywhere in all the churches is clear from what Paul's epistles write about deacons and their office, whom he plainly distinguishes from the bishops and pastors.

units.la: Id vero diligentius admonemus propter eos, qui vt vetustatis ignari sunt, ita collectas in Ecclesia fieri indignè ferunt, & totum illud diaconorum siue dispensatorum institutum damnant. Vna illis omnibus ratio est, se eleemosynam suam dare velle quibus lubeat, neq; aliorum fidei commissuros ea, quæ ipsi pauperibus largiri statuerint. Belli certè homines, qui se plus Apostolis, plusquam Ecclesia primitiva sapere sibi persuaserunt. Quin ergo aperte Christum stultitiæ accusant, quem suas eleemosynas per Judam distribuisse ex vltimæ Cænæ historia apparet? Cum enim hunc di-xisset, Quod facis, fac citius: & nemo discumbentium id intellexisset, quidam hoc ei dictum fuisse putarunt, quia loculos gestabat, vt vel ea emeret quæ ad diem festum opus erant, vel vt pauperibus aliquid daret. At quam de postremo hoc cogitandi occasionem habere poterant Apostoli, si Dominus non ita facere consuevisset? Sunt ergo isti homines stultissimi, dum præ aliis sapere volunt. Poterant equidem idem Paulo respondere Corinthij, Galatæ, Macedones, Romani & alij, ad quos eadem scripsit: Nos ne quæ nostro labore & industria parta sunt, cuiusquam alterius fidei committamus, vt ipse ea pro suo arbitrio cui velit distribuat? Aut num tibi tuisque in longinquas oras deferenda dabimus, quæ egentibus constituimus largiri? At nihil horum dixerunt homines opulentissimi, sed quia quod Paulus monebat, cum exemplo & instituto Christi & cum more apud omnes Ecclesias recepto conuenire videbant, Dei ordinationi sese volentes subiece-runt. Et vt ita vbique locorum fiat, necessitas ipsa iubet. Nam principio si ubiam [?] alibi, hic imprimis delectu opus est, ne otiosi ventres & eleemosyna indigni eam dignioribus præripiant, sed potius (quod Paulus alibi monet) ad laborem relegentur, vt ipsi victum sibi parent. At vt priuatus aliquis omnes norit impossibile est, neque etiam eidem tutum fuerit aut commodum in omnium vitam atque mores inquirere. Et vt id quàm diligentissimè faciat, idem tamen præ-fractos & impudentes illos coërcere & ad laborandum cogere non poterit: quia homini priuato nunquam parebunt. Nisi ergo sint certi homines, qui publica totius Ecclesiae authoritate armati id faciant, plura semper intercipient improbi & temerarij nequam, quos ab Ecclesijs procul arcere iubet Apostolus, egentibus interim bonis & pijs, quos pudor & modestia impedit, quò minus in petendo tam audaces ac importuni sint. Deinde, nisi collectarum vsus retineatur, & diaconi constituantur, qui singulis, prout opus esse viderint, distribuant, obstari non poterit, quò minus mendicatio & mendicabula locum habeant, imò vt ea instituantur necesse est, & ad rem Christiano nomine indignissimā (vt antea demonstrauimus) etiam optimi redigentur, cùm nulla vitae sustentandae ratio appareat: & ita multis pudor paulatim perit, qui in officio facile contineri poterant, si ea ratione illis prospiceretur, quae Ecclesijs Apostoli ex Spiritus sancti suggestione praescripserunt. Praeterea non obstat ea ratio, quò minus priuatim quoq; omnibus benefacias, quos vel in vicinia tua inopia pati, aut morbis detineri, aut aliqua necessitate oppressos esse nouisti: vel qui aliunde aduenientes bonorum virorum testimonio commendati, vel etiam sine eo tibi digni videntur, quos aliquo subsidio iuues. Denique, quia Christo teste, pauperes nunquam deerunt, in singulas horas sese occasio bene de ali-quo merendi offert. Hoc solum in praesenti agitur, ne quis dum suo sensu abundare vult, ordinem Ecclesiae publicum turbet, disciplinam labefactet, & mendicationi fenestram aperiat contra Dei institutū, adhaec confusionem illam inuehat, qua proterui & validi mendici alijs se multò digniori bus alimenta praeripiant. Quae omnia quàm necessaria sint obseruatu, nemo pius & cordatus non vider: ideoque inexcusabilis est eorum pertinacia, qui ordinationi tam sanctae, tam vtili, tam necessariae sese opponunt.
units.tr: We stress this more carefully because of those who, being ignorant of antiquity, take it ill that collections are made in the Church, and condemn that whole institution of deacons or stewards. Their one reason is that they wish to give their alms to whomever they please, and will not entrust to others the distribution of what they have decided to give to the poor. Surely these are fine men, who persuade themselves that they are wiser than the Apostles and wiser than the primitive Church! Do they not then openly accuse Christ of folly, since the account of the last Supper shows that he distributed his alms through Judas? For when he had said to him, "What you do, do quickly," and none of those reclining understood it, some thought that it had been said to him because he carried the purse, that he should buy the things needed for the feast day, or give something to the poor. But how could the Apostles have had occasion to think of this last point, if the Lord had not been accustomed to act in this way? These men, then, are most foolish in wishing to be wiser than others.
