The Corinthians, Galatians, Macedonians, Romans and the others to whom he wrote the same thing could indeed have answered Paul: "Shall we entrust to anyone else what we have acquired by our own labour and industry, so that he may distribute it at his own discretion to whom he pleases? Or shall we give to you and yours, to be carried to distant shores, what we have set aside to give to the needy?" But the wealthiest men said none of these things. Seeing that what Paul urged agreed with the example and ordinance of Christ and with the custom received in all the churches, they willingly submitted themselves to God's appointment. And wherever else it may be, necessity itself requires it. For first, if anywhere else, here above all a selection is needed, lest idle bellies and those unworthy of alms snatch them from the more deserving, but rather (as Paul elsewhere warns) they be sent back to work, so that they may provide food for themselves. But no private individual can know everyone; nor would it be safe or convenient for him to inquire into the lives and morals of all. And however diligently he might do so, he would still be unable to restrain the headstrong and shameless and compel them to work, because they would never obey a private man. Unless there are certain men who do this, armed with the public authority of the whole Church, the wicked and reckless rascals, whom the Apostle bids be kept far from the churches, will always intercept more, while the good and pious, whom shame and modesty hinder from being so bold and importunate in asking, go without. Next, unless the use of the collections is maintained and deacons are appointed to distribute to each as they see fit, there will be no way to stop begging and begging-bags from taking hold. Indeed, if these things are not instituted, even good men will be reduced to that practice, which is most unworthy of the Christian name (as we showed before), since no means of sustaining life appears. And so shame gradually perishes in many who could easily have been kept in their duty, if provision had been made for them by the method that the Apostles prescribed to the churches under the prompting of the Holy Spirit. Moreover, this arrangement does not prevent you from also doing good privately to all whom you know to be suffering want in your neighbourhood, or held down by sickness, or oppressed by some necessity; or to those who arrive from elsewhere, commended by the testimony of good men, or even without it, whom you think worthy to be helped in some way. Finally, since, as Christ witnesses, the poor will never be lacking, the opportunity to do good to someone is offered at every hour. The only thing being dealt with here is that no one, while wanting to abound in his own opinion, should disturb the public order of the Church, weaken its discipline, and open a window to begging against God's institution; and further, that he should not introduce that confusion by which bold and strong beggars snatch food away from others who are far more deserving. No pious and sensible person fails to see how necessary all these things are to observe. Therefore the obstinacy of those who oppose so holy, so useful, so necessary an ordinance is inexcusable.

units.la: Transeamus ergo ad alterum caput institutae tractationis, Quales nimirum esse conueniat dispensatores siue œconomos Ecclesiae. Id in praesenti Paulus vno verbo expedit, dicens: Quoscunq; probaueritis. Qui vero probati, & idonei ad hoc munus censeri debeant, Apostoli diligentius in ea oratione docet, quam de Diaconis ordinandis ad Ecclesiam Hierosolymitanam habuerunt in hunc modum: Dispicite fratres, ex vobis viros septem, idoneo testimonio ornatos, plenos Spiritu sancto & sapientia, quos praeficiamus huic negotio. Iubet vt ex ipsis tales dispiciant atq; eligant. Debent enim ex ipsa Ecclesia deligi, nec admitti ad munus hoc homines ignoti aut peregrini, quorum fides merito suspecta aliquibus esse possit, aut qui odium & inuidiam facilius sibi conflent. Ideo Paulus nullum hic sibi ius sumit in Corinthiorum Ecclesiam, nec ipse aliquem ex ijs nominat, quos illic notos & amicos habebat, sed, Quos vos probaueritis (inquit) hos mittam. Fuit ergo in hoc etiam multum alienus à Pontificum moribus, qui in omnium nationum atq; gentium Ecclesias sibi ius vendicant, & in illis pro suo arbitrio omnia constituunt, imò suos mulliones, agasones, parasitos & quoscunque alios, plerunque illiteratos quoque & vitae illaudatae homines, illis obtrudunt, vt pastores siue parochos & mysteriorum Dei dispensatores agant. Conquesti sunt de hac tyrannide tam se-culis aliquot optimi quiq;, sed frustra verba fiunt illis, qui toti venter sunt, quem auribus & oculis destitui, olim Cato dicebat. Sed videamus singula, quae in dispensatoribus Ecclesiae Aposto-li requirunt.
units.tr: Let us now pass to the second head of this treatment: what kind of stewards or managers of the Church they ought to be. Paul settles this in the present passage with a single phrase, saying: "Whomever you shall approve." The Apostles teach more fully what kind of men ought to be counted approved and fit for this office in the speech they gave about ordaining deacons for the Church of Jerusalem, in these words: "Look out, brothers, from among you seven men of good report, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, whom we may appoint to this business." He bids the congregation look out for such men from among themselves and choose them. For they ought to be chosen from the Church itself, and men who are unknown or foreign should not be admitted to this office, since their faith may rightly be suspected by some, or they may more easily stir up hatred and envy against themselves. So Paul claims for himself no right over the Corinthian Church, and he does not name any of them himself, though he had known and befriended some of them there, but says, "Those whom you approve, I will send." In this he was far removed from the ways of the Papists, who claim rights over the churches of every nation and people and settle everything there at their own pleasure. They even foist on them their muleteers, grooms, parasites and whoever else, often illiterate men of disreputable life, to act as pastors or parish priests and dispensers of God's mysteries. Some of the best men have complained of this tyranny for several centuries, but their words are wasted on those who are all belly, and who, as Cato once said, are deprived of ears and eyes. But let us look at the individual qualities which the Apostles require in the stewards of the Church.

units.la: Primum est, vt idoneo siue bono & honesto testimonio ornati sint. Loquitur autem de publico simul totius Ecclesiae testimonio, deque priuatis, quae singuli de ipsis ferant. Est hoc ante omnia alia necessarium: quia nisi tales sint, multos suspicio sinistra absterrebit, vt in collectis Ecclesiae parcius conferant: facilius quoque murmura & querelae excitentur ab illis quibus nihil sufficit. Peccant ergo hic grauiter, qui hodie bonorum Ecclesiae administrationem ijs committunt, qui nullo bonorum virorum testimonio commendantur, & quos ne ipsi quidem ab honestate morum aut frugalitate laudare possunt, quosque nemo prudens suae domus dispensatores faceret: vt qui sua prius turpiter & inhonestè dilapidarunt ebrietate, alea, scortatione, aut saltem ignaua & inerti socordia. Volunt hi deinde ex alieno ditescere, & plerunque hominum auarissimi fiunt, quibus lu-cribonus est odor ex re qualibet. Cùm autem aliena pecunia contrectatio per se periculosa fit, & ea interdum boni quoque in nassam pertrahantur, quid de talibus speres, si eius functionis cura illis committeatur, vbi tot fallendi viae & rationes sunt, quas ne Argus quidem omnes observare possit? Certè quanto cum periculo id fiat, vnius Iudae exemplum abunde docet, cuius vestigijs vtinam hodie non multi insisterent.
units.tr: First, they should be adorned with a good and honest testimony. He speaks both of a public testimony from the whole Church and of the private testimonies that individuals give about them. This is necessary above all else, because unless such men are chosen, a bad suspicion will deter many from giving generously to the Church's collections, and murmurings and complaints will more easily be stirred up by those who are never satisfied. Those therefore sin gravely who today entrust the administration of the Church's goods to men who are commended by no testimony from good people, whom not even they themselves can praise for uprightness of life or frugality, and whom no prudent man would make stewards of his own household. Such men have first shamefully and dishonourably squandered their own goods in drunkenness, gambling, whoring, or at least in idle and sluggish laziness. They then want to grow rich at others' expense, and they very often become the greediest of men, for whom any source of gain smells sweet. But since handling other people's money is in itself dangerous, and good men too are sometimes dragged into its snares, what can you hope of such men if the care of that office is committed to them, where there are so many ways and methods of deceit that not even Argus could watch them all? Certainly, how great a danger this carries is amply taught by the example of Judas alone, whose footsteps, would that many did not follow today.

units.la: {Dispensatores quales esse debeant} (marginal note beside paragraph two, opening line: "Dispensatores quales esse de-ceant[?]")
units.tr: Which kind of stewards they ought to be.

units.la: Secundò, vt Spiritu sancto pleni sint, monent. Sumus enim natura nostri ipsorū[?] amantes, qui fere omnis mali fons atque fomes est. Opus igitur est nobis Spiritus sancti luce, qui charitatis & misericordiæ ignem in cordibus nostris accendat, & ex philautia enascentes cupiditates suo freno coerceat. Non debent ergo ordinari homines superbi, quos confidentia sua pauperum contemptores & osores reddit: non feroces & immites, qui in asperis & minacibus dictis, torvo oculorum intuitu, fastuoso incessu & ad terrorem incutiendum compositio totius corporis incessu, omnem fortitudinis laudem sibi tam esse arbitrantur: non item vino multo pleni, ebriosi & intemperantes. Quàm enim absurdum & indecorum fuerit, eum immitem & ferocem conspici, qui pauperum curam habere debet, quos egestas formidolosiores facit, & qui blando alloquio non minus quàm pecuniola aliqua recreantur? Quid verò turpius, quid inhonestius, quid sceleratius potest fingi, quàm multis cum inopia victus & dira fame conflictantibus, eos inebriari & luxu diffluere, qui illis consecratas opes dispensant? Quid item crudelius, quàm homines intemperantissimos insuper ditescere etiā ex sacrilegiis, dum pretiosa Christi membra fame pereunt? Sunt hæc non Christianis modo hominibus indigna, sed quouis supplicio & pœnis infernalibus dignissima sunt, quas procul dubio a talibus iudex ille iustissimus & acerrimus pauperum vindex exiget.
units.tr: Second, they advise that they be full of the Holy Spirit. For we are by nature lovers of ourselves, and this is almost the source and fuel of every evil. We therefore need the light of the Holy Spirit, who kindles in our hearts the fire of love and mercy, and restrains with its bridle the desires that spring from self-love. Proud men should not be ordained, for their self-confidence makes them despisers and haters of the poor. Nor should the fierce and harsh be chosen, who think it the height of courage to speak roughly and threateningly, with a grim look, a haughty stride, and a whole body posture designed to strike terror. Nor likewise those full of wine, drunkards and intemperate men. For how absurd and unseemly it would be to see a harsh and savage man, when he ought to care for the poor, whom want makes more fearful, and who are refreshed by a kind word no less than by a little money! What could be imagined more base, more dishonourable or more wicked than that, while many are struggling with lack of food and dire hunger, those who dispense the consecrated wealth should be drunk and wallow in luxury? What is also more cruel than that the most intemperate men should grow rich even by sacrilege, while the precious members of Christ perish of hunger? These things are not only unworthy of Christian men, but deserve any punishment and the torments of hell, which without doubt that most just and most stern judge, the avenger of the poor, will exact from such men.

units.la: Tertiò sapientia instructos esse volunt. Est autem sapientia (vt alias monuimus) rerum diuinarum & humanarum, causarumq;, quibus hæc res continentur, scientia siue cognitio. Et sanè absurdum foret hominibus a rerum diuinarum cognitione alienis aliquam ex ecclesiasticis functionibus committere, cùm hæ omnes præcipuè ad Deum spectent. At qui hominum necessitatibus prospicere debent, rerum quoq;, humanarum gnari atq; periti sint necesse est. Quid enim hic facient, qui œconomicam nesciunt, qui item quomodo rationes acceptorum & expensorum ineunde & subducendæ sint, ignorant? Accedat his prudentia, quæ circumspectos facit, vt quibus & quando largiri, quando item mitius, quando durius agere debeant, obseruent. Est horum omnium vsus perquàm necessarius: quia si ab Oeconomis siue dispensatoribus peccetur, id in totam Ecclesiam redundat, cuius nota vel inhumanitatis, vel leuitatis, vel etiam iniquitatis inuritur: abstterrentur præterea a beneficentia studio multi, quod pauperibus atque egenis imprimis officit: culpa autem omnium in iis hæret, qui tales constituerunt, aut deprehensa fraude & improbitate eorum, nihilominus tamen illis patrocinantur.
units.tr: Thirdly, they want them to be furnished with wisdom. Wisdom is (as we have said elsewhere) the knowledge or understanding of divine and human things and of the causes by which these things are held together. And indeed it would be absurd to entrust any ecclesiastical function to men who are strangers to the knowledge of divine things, since all of these look chiefly to God. But those who must provide for human needs must also be versed and experienced in human affairs. For what will those do here who do not know household management, and who do not know how accounts of receipts and expenses are to be drawn up and reckoned? Add to these prudence, which makes men circumspect, so that they observe to whom and when they ought to give, and when to act more gently or more harshly. The use of all these things is very necessary. If the stewards or managers do wrong, it reflects on the whole Church, and a mark either of inhumanity, levity or even injustice is branded upon it. Moreover, many are deterred from the zeal of beneficence, which above all harms the poor and needy. The blame for all this clings to those who appointed such men, or who still defend them when their fraud and wickedness has been detected.

units.la: Restat postrema huius tractationis pars, vt videamus, quomodo dispensatoribus authoritas conciliari debeat. Ad hanc pertinet, quod Paulus illis, qui publico Ecclesiæ consensu probati & delecti fuerint, literas ad Iudæos commendatitias pollicetur. Quod nemo eum arrogantius facere putauerit. Vt enim literis eiusmodi opus erat apud gentem peregrinam & homines ignotos: ita Paulus illas debuit dare, cùm maxima eius esset apud Ecclesias omnes authoritas. Interim admonemur, diaconos siue dispensatores publica authoritate creari simul & muniri debere. Est enim paupertate nihil inquietius & magis querulum, atq; rara admodū est τῆς αὐταρκείας virtus, quæ vnumquenq; suæ fortunæ contentum reddit. Experti sunt hoc non sine molestia & aliqua contumeliæ nota Apostoli, quando ipsis rem hanc administrantibus aliqui murmurasse dicuntur, quòd suas viduas negligi putarent. At quis alicuius doli siue fraudis suspectos habeat Apostolos? Et cur aliena surriperent, qui sua omnia propter Christum reliquerant? Non potuerunt tamen effugere, quò minus de illorum administratione querela spargerentur. Nunquam ergo satis tuti erunt dispensatores, nisi publica authoritate defendantur. Et debet exemplum illud omnes admonere, ne facile aures præbeant morosis & querulis, qui dispensatorum fidem suspectam facere conantur. Fiat potius diligens inquisitio, & si illis iniuria fiat, defendantur: Quòd si verò fraudem admiserunt, puniantur. Neq; hic indulgentius agant Christiani principes. Si enim peculatoribus & sacrilegis pœnas capitales constituunt leges Cæsareæ, quanto grauiores subire debent, qui ciuitatis & reipub. Christianæ thesauros surripiunt, nec ex templi solum ærario pecunias furantur, verum insuper authores sunt, vt qui vera & viua Christi templa sunt, egestate & fame pereant? Cessant quidem frequenter in illis puniendis principes, quia lupus lupinam non est: at non dormitat Dei iudicium, quo isti simul omnes damnantur. Et horrenda sunt, quæ in historijs proponuntur, exempla, quibus Deus impiorum sacrilegia & fraudes puniuit. Babylonijs vasorum templi direptio & eorundem prophanatio exitium attulit. Pompeius postquam temerario in templi adytum ingressu Dei sacrarium violà-uit, mox huic sibi aduersum sentire coepit, cuius fauore antea munitus res maximas terra marique gesserat. Secuta est enim consiliorum incertitudo, quae bellum ciuile excitarunt, & postea clades a-liquot ille infelix in Aegyptiaco littore, quasi in conspectu templi, proditorie & crudeliter occisus est. Manifestior fuit M. Crassi calamitas, qui cum etiam ipse in Sacrarium illud ingressus esset, & ex eo auri ingentem summam abstulisset, à Parthis una cum filio caesus est, qui occiso quoque insatiabilem auri sitim exprobrarunt. Quid de Iuda dicemus, qui cum à sacrilegio tepuisset, tan-dem Christi proditor quoque factus, & propriae conscientiae testimonio ad desperationem horribi-lem adductus, pecuniam sacrilegam ipse abiecit, seque ipsum suspendens animam simul cum cor-pore perdidit? Est etiam memorabilis Ananiae & Sapphirae interitus, qui cum in proprijs pecu-niis fraudem facere instituissent, & Ecclesiae, atque Spiritui sancto mentirentur, repentina morte conciderunt. Quid Iudaeorum sacerdotes post diuturna sacrilegia & pauperes inhumaniter abs-se neglectos cum tota sua gente, quae illorum improbitatem non coercuit, passi sint, longum esset commemorare.
units.tr: There remains the last part of this treatment, that we see how authority ought to be secured for the stewards. To this belongs what Paul promises to those who have been approved and chosen by the public consent of the Church: letters of commendation to the Jews. No one would think he did this too arrogantly. For just as such letters were needed among a foreign people and men unknown to them, so Paul ought to give them, since his authority among all the churches was very great. Meanwhile we are reminded that deacons or stewards ought to be appointed, and at the same time fortified, by public authority. For nothing is more restless and more querulous than poverty, and the virtue of self-sufficiency (τῆς αὐταρκείας), which makes each man content with his lot, is very rare. The Apostles experienced this not without trouble and some mark of insult, when some are said to have murmured against them while they administered this business, because they thought their widows were being neglected. But who would hold the Apostles suspect of any trickery or fraud? And why should those steal others' goods who had left everything of their own for Christ? Yet they could not escape complaints being spread about their administration. Therefore stewards will never be safe enough unless they are defended by public authority. That example ought to warn everyone not to lend ready ears to fretful and querulous people who try to make the stewards' good faith suspect. Rather let a diligent inquiry be made, and if they suffer wrong let them be defended; but if they have committed fraud, let them be punished. Nor should Christian princes act more leniently here. For if the Caesarean laws establish capital punishments for embezzlers and sacrilegious men, how much heavier should those suffer who steal the treasures of the Christian commonwealth, and who not only steal money from the temple's chest but also cause those who are the true and living temples of Christ to perish of want and hunger? Princes indeed often cease to punish them, because a wolf is no enemy to a wolf; but God's judgment does not sleep, and by it all of these are condemned together. The examples set out in histories of how God punished the sacrileges and frauds of the impious are dreadful. For the Babylonians the plundering of the temple's vessels and their profanation brought ruin. Pompey, after he rashly entered the inner sanctuary of the temple and violated God's holy place, soon began to feel opposition from that same quarter whose favour had previously protected him, and by which he had accomplished very great deeds on land and sea. For uncertainty of counsels followed, which stirred up civil war, and afterwards that unhappy man, after some defeats, was treacherously and cruelly killed on the Egyptian shore, almost in sight of the temple. The calamity of M. Crassus was more evident: when he too had entered that sanctuary and carried off from it a huge sum of gold, he was slain by the Parthians together with his son, and they, as he was killed, also taunted him with his insatiable thirst for gold. What shall we say of Judas, who, having cooled from sacrilege, at last became also the betrayer of Christ, and, driven to dreadful despair by the testimony of his own conscience, cast away the sacrilegious money himself, and hanging himself lost his soul together with his body? The death of Ananias and Sapphira is also memorable, who, when they had set about practising fraud with their own money and lied to the Church and to the Holy Spirit, fell dead suddenly. To recount at length what the priests of the Jews suffered, along with their whole nation which did not restrain their wickedness, after long-standing sacrileges and the inhuman neglect of the poor, would take too long.

units.la: Est horum consideratio hodie plus quam necessaria, quando crescente vbique gentium nume-ro pauperum, disciplina quoq; omnis Ecclesiarum corruit, & ex harum bonis fere opes sibi conge-runt & voluptuantur, qui non minima Christiani nominis labes sunt. Quibus malum medicinam inuenire multis impossibile videtur: sed nihil facilius esset, si Apostoli consilio parere & primitiuae Ecclesiae morem imitari liberet. Ita ergo ista consideremus, vt ea, in quibus hucusq; peccatum est emendentur, ne quando vindicem manum Deus magno nostro malo adhibeat. Pertinet cura ista ad principes imprimis, quia hic non tam Ecclesiae quam reipub. negotiu agitur. Interim singuli pri-uatim beneficentiae in egenos studeant, vt ita sibi ipsis tabernacula aeterna parent, & thesaurum in caelis incorruptibilem recondant, quo olim laeti & immortales fruantur cu IESV CHRISTO Domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: It is more than necessary today to consider these things, since the number of the poor is growing everywhere, and discipline in all the churches is also collapsing; and men who are no small stain on the Christian name grab wealth for themselves from the churches' goods and live in luxury on it. Many think a remedy for this evil is impossible to find, but nothing would be easier, if we were willing to obey the Apostles' counsel and imitate the custom of the primitive Church. Let us therefore consider these matters so that those things in which we have sinned up to now may be amended, lest God at some time lay his avenging hand upon us to our great harm. This care belongs above all to the princes, since here the business concerns the commonwealth rather than the Church. Meanwhile let individuals privately devote themselves to beneficence toward the needy, so that they may thus prepare for themselves everlasting tabernacles and lay up an incorruptible treasure in heaven, which they may one day enjoy with joy and immortality together with Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XCI.
units.tr: HOMILY XCI.

units.la: Veniam autem ad vos cum Macedoniam transiero (Macedo-niam enim pertransibo) apud vos autem fortasis permanebo, aut etiam hybernabo: Vt vos me prosequamini quocunque proficiscar. Nolo enim vos nunc in transcursu videre: sed spero aliquantum temporis mansurum me apud vos, si Dominus permiserit. Permanebo autem Ephesi vsque ad Pentecosten. Nam ostium mihi apertum est magnum & efficax, & aduersarij multi.
units.tr: But I will come to you when I have passed through Macedonia (for I am going through Macedonia). Perhaps I will stay with you, or even spend the winter, so that you may send me on my way, wherever I go. For I do not want to see you now in passing, but I hope to stay with you for some time, if the Lord permits. But I will remain at Ephesus until Pentecost. For a great and effective door has been opened to me, and there are many adversaries.

units.la: Postquam Paulus ex fidi pastoris officio diligenter de omnibus ijs disseruit, quae ad publicam totius Ecclesiae aedificationem & singulorum emendationem faciebant, postremo loco de Collecta pro fratribus in Iudaea fame atq; penuria laborantibus facienda admonuit. Quo exemplo admonemur, Christianos homines, ita de sua salute solicitos esse debere, vt ne alios in necessitate constitutos negligant. Caeterum absolutis his omnibus, nunc ad ea transit Apostolus, quae ad ipsius personam propius spectabant. Erat inter ea primum, quod se Corinthum venturum esse non semel promiserat, & eius praesentia opus fuisse apparet ex ijs, quae hucusq; audiuimus. Vt vero ipsum optimi quique magno cum desiderio expectabant, ita aemulus eius ac disciplinae oforibus [?] nihil molestius accidere poterat. Idem tamen, vt eius authoritati derogarent, moram ipsius odiose accusabant, & quasi nunquam aduenturum esse scirent, insolentius proteruiebant. Ideo nunc de eo diligentius agit occasione sumpta ex ijs, quae nuper de Collecta Hierosolymam deferenda dixerat, & moram hanc rationibus idoneis excusat.
units.tr: After Paul had carefully discussed, as a faithful pastor, all those matters that contributed to the public building up of the whole Church and to the correction of individuals, he finally urged the collection to be made for the brothers suffering famine and want in Judea. From this example we are reminded that Christians ought to be as concerned for their own salvation as they are not to neglect others who are in need. Now that these matters are settled, the Apostle turns to those things that concerned his own person more closely. First among these was that he had promised more than once that he would come to Corinth, and it is clear from what we have heard so far that his presence was needed. While the best people eagerly awaited him, nothing could be more troubling to his rival and to the enemies of discipline. Yet they kept criticizing his delay in order to undermine his authority, and, as if they knew he would never come, they grew more and more insolent. So now he deals with this more carefully, taking the occasion from what he had recently said about carrying the collection to Jerusalem, and he excuses this delay with suitable reasons.

units.la: Iusserat enim, vt in aduentum suum praeparârent pecunias illas, quae postea per delectos nun-tios Hierosolymam mitterentur, & se vna cum his eo profecturum promiserat, si ita opus esset. Poterat ergo aliquis maleuolus obijcere: Cur vero non aduenis [?] nunc, & nos in pecunijs hisce conficiendis adiuuas? cur promissis subinde [?] inanibus nos suspendis & laetas? Itaque per Praeoccupationem respondet: Veniam ad vos cum Macedoniam transfiero (Macedoniam enim pertransibo) apud vos autem fortasse permanebo, aut etiam hybernabo. Solebant enim Apostoli (ut Act.14. & aliis locis indicatur) abs se constitutas Ecclesias frequentius invisere: & ut idem hodie fiat a viris gravibus & singulari authoritate praeditis, valde necessarium est. Nam nihil in statu bono diu perseverat, & quemadmodum singulae mundi huius partes ad suam corruptionem finemque tendunt: ita homines natura ad malum propendent, & ideo in peius plerunque proficiunt. Nocet hic quoque plurimum innata nobis securitas, ex qua occasionem venatur Satan, ut incautos opprimat. Fit ergo in Ecclesiis idem quod in corporis valetudine. Ut enim illic morborum materia in nobis latet, & facile commouetur, si gula & palato intemperantius & incautius indulgeamus: ita mox optima Ecclesiae constitutio sive forma vitium contrahit, si qui securiori animo suis defixi derijs obsequuntur. Vehementer ergo errant, qui sufficere arbitrantur, si Veritatis doctrina semel bene tradita sit, & proinde non satis aequo animo ferunt, si qui ordinarij sunt Ecclesiarum pastores singula diligentius obseruent, & in mores hominum atque praesentem rerum statum inquirant. Quid enim hoc aliud est, quam nolle, ut pastor gregis sui curam habeat, aut speculatoris praecipere ne excubias agat, neue portis appropinquantes hostes obseruet, vel signo dato indicet? Atqui doctores populo pastores & speculatores a Deo datos esse, notius est quam ut demonstrari oporteat.
units.tr: For he had ordered that the money be prepared for his arrival, to be later sent to Jerusalem by chosen messengers, and he had promised to go there with them, if that should be necessary. Someone ill-disposed could therefore object: "Why are you not coming now, and helping us to gather this money? Why do you keep us in suspense and cheer us with empty promises?" So he answers in advance: "I will come to you when I have passed through Macedonia (for I am going through Macedonia). Perhaps I will stay with you, or even spend the winter." For the Apostles, as is shown in Acts 14 and elsewhere, were accustomed to visit the Churches they had founded fairly often, and it is very necessary that this be done today by serious men endowed with singular authority. For nothing in a good state lasts long, and just as each part of this world tends towards its own corruption and end, so men are naturally inclined to evil and for the most part go from bad to worse. Innate complacency also does great harm here, and from it Satan looks for an opportunity to overwhelm the unwary. So it happens in the Churches just as it does in bodily health. For just as the seeds of disease lie hidden in us and are easily stirred up if we indulge our gullet and palate too intemperately and carelessly, so the best constitution and form of a Church soon contracts faults if people, with a careless mind, follow their own pleasures. Therefore those greatly err who think it is enough if the doctrine of the truth has once been well taught, and who therefore bear it with poor grace when the ordinary pastors of the Churches observe each matter more carefully and inquire into the morals of people and the present state of affairs. For what else is this than not wanting a shepherd to care for his flock, or ordering a watchman not to keep guard, nor to watch for enemies approaching the gates, nor to give a signal? Yet it is better known than it needs to be shown that teachers are given by God as pastors and watchmen to the people.

units.la: Sed ut ad locum praesentem redeamus, se tunc demum Corinthum venire velle Paulus dicit, ubi Macedoniam invaserit. Nondum ergo Macedoniam ingressus erat, cum haec scriberet, sicuti ex posteriori Epistolae Cap. primo colligi potest. Nam expositis illic gravissimis periculis atque certaminibus, quae in Asia sustinuerat, pollicetur, se per Corinthum in Macedoniam transire, & inde ad ipsos redire constituisse, ut ab eis in Iudaeam deduceat. Quod obiter perstringimus, ne quis epistolae huius subscriptioni fidem habeat, quae eam Philippis missam fuisse testatur. Illam enim suppositiciam esse, praesentis loci argumentu & Paulinae historiae series satis evidenter ostendit. Quare verisimilior est eorum sententia, qui Chrysostomum secuti, epistolam hanc Ephesi scriptam esse dicunt. Enimuero Asiae fratrum postea meminit, quorum nomine Corinthios salutat. Sed quicquid illud fit, in praesenti hoc dicit, se nolle nunc ad ipsos venire, quia causis iustis & gravibus impediatur.
units.tr: But to return to the present passage: Paul says that he wishes to come to Corinth only when he has entered Macedonia. So he had not yet entered Macedonia when he wrote this, as can be gathered from the first chapter of the later Epistle. For there, after setting out the very grave dangers and struggles he had endured in Asia, he promises that he is passing through Corinth into Macedonia, and that he has decided to return from there to them, so that they might send him on to Judea. We touch on this in passing, so that no one will put faith in the subscription of this letter, which claims that it was sent to Philippi. For the present passage and the sequence of Paul's history show quite clearly that it is spurious. Hence the opinion of those who follow Chrysostom and say that this letter was written at Ephesus is more probable. Indeed, he later mentions the brothers of Asia, in whose name he greets the Corinthians. But whatever the case, in the present passage he says that he does not want to come to them now, because he is prevented by just and serious causes.

units.la: Primam his verbis exponit: Nolo vos nunc in transcursu videre, sed spero me aliquantum temporis mansurum apud vos, si Dominus permiserit. Ita vero suum erga illos studium declarat, qui nolit quasi aliud agens ex instituto itinere ad ipsos diuertere, & ita eis molestiam exhibere absque omni fructu: sed ita venire, ut aliquandiu apud ipsos haerere, & beneficium aliquod spirituale in eos conferre possit. Eo enim proposito Apostolos Ecclesias invisisse supra diximus, & in primo Cap. ad Roman. idem Paulus testatur. Expeto (inquit) videre vos, ut aliquod impertiar vobis donum spirituale ad vos stabiliendos. Et ut ita Corinthi fieret, omnino opus erat, cum multa illic essent [?], quae emendatione opus habebant, in Macedonia autem non item, cuius gentis Ecclesias in fide & aliis rebus optime constitutas fuisse, Pauli ad Philippenses & Thessalonicenses epistolae testantur. Simul autem docet in praesenti, quantum sibi ipsi de Corinthiorum erga se fide & studio polliceatur, quando ab ipsis deduci cupiat.
units.tr: He explains the first of these in these words: "I do not want to see you now in passing, but I hope to stay with you for some time, if the Lord permits." In this way he shows his affection towards them: he does not wish, as if doing something else, to turn aside from his planned journey to visit them, and so cause them trouble without any profit; rather he wants to come in such a way that he can remain with them for some time and bestow some spiritual benefit upon them. For we said above that the Apostles visited the Churches with this purpose, and Paul himself testifies to it in the first chapter of Romans: "I long to see you," he says, "that I may impart to you some spiritual gift, to establish you." For this to happen at Corinth it was altogether necessary, since many things there needed correction, whereas this was not the case in Macedonia, whose Churches were very well established in faith and other matters, as Paul's letters to the Philippians and Thessalonians bear witness. At the same time he indicates here how much he promises himself from the faith and eagerness of the Corinthians towards him, since he desires to be escorted on his journey by them.

units.la: Obseruabis autem piam Apostoli circumspectionem, qui cum certo constituerit Corinthum proficisci, dubitanter tamen de ea profectione loquitur, & euentum Deo permittit. Spero (inquit) me aliquantum temporis mansurum apud vos, si Dominus permiserit. Nam (ut alias monuimus) non semper certo sciuerit Apostoli, quid de ipsis statuisset Deus: sed frequenter nouis oblatis vocationibus & peculiari Spiritus sancti revelatione praeter suum institutum alio vocari fuerunt. Exemplum huius rei evidens Lucas proponit, de Paulo & comitibus eius sic scribens: Peragrata Phrygia & Galatica regione prohibiti sunt a Spiritu sancto loqui sermonem in Asia: Cumq; venissent in Mysiam, tentabant ire in Bithyniam: sed non permisit eis Spiritus. Et ibidem mox causam eius rei indicat, quod Paulu Deus Macedonibus destinauisset, ad quos per visionem extraordinariam vocatus est. Et Philippi ab angelo iussum fuisse legimus, ut ex Samaria in eu locu proficisceretur, ubi in eunuchu Aethiope incidit, qui per ipsum in fide Christiana instituì debebat. Sed & Petrũ visione peculiari[?] citauit Deus vt Cæsarea profectus Centurioni Cornelio Euangelium prædicaret. Debent exempla ista diligenter considerari, quia multum faciunt ad doctrinæ Apostolicæ commendationem & fidei Christianæ confirmationem: quando illam non temere in orbe terrarum prædicatam, neq; Apostolos erronum instar fuisse docent, qui pro sui animi libidine hinc inde discurrerint: sed qui Spiritu sancto duce nunc hic nunc illic prædicarint, quem Christus ipsis fidum aduocatum promiserat.
units.tr: You will notice the Apostle's godly caution: although he had firmly decided to set out for Corinth, he speaks hesitantly about that journey and leaves the outcome to God. "I hope," he says, "to stay with you for some time, if the Lord permits." For (as we have pointed out elsewhere) the Apostles did not always know for certain what God had decided about them, but often, when new calls presented themselves and by a special revelation of the Holy Spirit, they were called elsewhere, contrary to their own plan. Luke offers a clear example of this, writing thus about Paul and his companions: "When they had gone through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to preach the word in Asia. And when they had come to Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit did not allow them." And immediately afterwards he states the reason for this: God had destined Paul for the Macedonians, to whom he was called by an extraordinary vision. We also read that Philip was told by an angel to go from Samaria to the place where he met the Ethiopian eunuch, whom he was to instruct in the Christian faith. And God summoned Peter by a special vision to go to Caesarea and preach the gospel to the centurion Cornelius. These examples ought to be carefully considered, for they greatly help to commend the apostolic doctrine and to confirm the Christian faith. They teach that it was not preached rashly throughout the world, nor were the Apostles like vagabonds who ran hither and thither at the whim of their own minds; rather, with the Holy Spirit as their guide, they preached now here, now there, the Spirit whom Christ had promised them as a faithful advocate.

units.la: Admonet præterea Pauli exemplum, neminem de suis consiliis temere aut arroganter statuere debere, quasi illorum euentum in sua potestate habeat. Quis enim scit, quid ferus vesper vehat? Etsi inter os & offam (vt prouerbio dicitur) multa incidunt, quid de illis certò statui possit, ad quæ conficienda temporis aliqua mora opus est? In Domino viuimus, mouemur & sumus. Et si Paulus in re sanctissima, & quæ cum ipsius officio coniuncta erat, hac moderatione vsus est, nimium arrogantes sunt, qui in prophanis rebus, vel etiam in illicitis & quæ ab officio ipsorum alienissima sunt, pronuntiare audent quid facturi sint. Qui si meminissent, quàm incerta sit rerum humanarum conditio, & quàm fallaces sint spes, quibus sæpè deluduntur, qui omnia videntur posse, humilius multò de semetipsis sentirent atque loquerentur. Semper ergo Christianorum animus occurrat Iacobi Apostoli admonitio, quam non sine increpationis specie proponit, dicens: Age nunc qui dicitis: Hodie vel cras ibimus in illam vrbem, & transigemus ibi annum, & mercabimur & lucrabimur: qui ignoratis quid postero die futurum sit (quæ est enim vita vestra? Vapor equidem est, qui ad exiguum tempus apparet, & deinde euanescit) pro eo quòd dicere debebatis: Si Dominus voluerit, & si viuamus, faciemus hoc & illud: Nunc autem gloriamini de arrogantia vestra: omnis eiusmodi gloriatio mala est. Mala dicit gloriationem eiusmodi, quia ina nisi ipsius fiducia homines inflat, & non tam fortis suæ quàm prouidentiæ Dei omnia gubernantis immemores facit. Quòd si vero in hanc respicere & ab ea sola pendere discamus, mox procul arcebitur consiliorum temeritas, nec facile aliquid conabimur, quod à Dei voluntate dissentire sciemus. Ad preces quoque vehementer excitat ista consideratio, quando cogitamus sine Deo nihil feliciter inchoari, nedum absolui posse. Vide Psalmum CXXVII.
units.tr: Moreover, Paul's example reminds us that no one should decide rashly or arrogantly about his plans, as if he had their outcome in his power. For who knows what the wild evening will bring? Even though, as the proverb says, many things fall in between the cup and the lip, how can anything be decided with certainty when some delay is needed to bring it about? "In the Lord we live, move, and have our being." And if Paul, in a most holy matter that was bound up with his office, used this moderation, those are far too arrogant who dare to pronounce what they will do in worldly affairs, or even in unlawful matters and things utterly foreign to their office. If they remembered how uncertain the condition of human affairs is, and how deceptive the hopes are by which those are often deluded who seem able to do everything, they would think and speak of themselves far more humbly. Therefore let the mind of Christians always call to mind the admonition of the Apostle James, which he sets before us, not without a note of rebuke, saying: "Come now, you who say, 'Today or tomorrow we will go into such and such a city, and spend a year there, and trade and make a profit'; you who do not know what will happen tomorrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapor that appears for a little while and then vanishes. Instead you ought to say: 'If the Lord wills, and if we live, we will do this or that.' But now you boast in your arrogance; all such boasting is evil." He calls such boasting evil because it puffs men up with their own confidence, and makes them forget not so much their own strength as the providence of God, who governs all things. But if we learn to look to this and to depend on it alone, the rashness of our plans will soon be kept far away, and we will hardly undertake anything that we know is at odds with the will of God. This consideration also powerfully stirs us to prayer, when we reflect that nothing can be begun happily without God, much less brought to completion. See Psalm 127.

units.la: Porrò altera adhuc causam Paulus adduxit, quæ ipsum quò minùs nunc Corinthi veniat, re-moretur. Permanebo Ephesi (inquit) vsq; ad Pentecosten. Ne vero Ephesios Corinthijs anteponere putetur, huius etiam morae ratione reddit: Nam ostium mihi apertum est magnum et efficax, & aduersarij multi. Ostium dicit Metaphorice pro occasione prædicandi Euangelij. Magnum vero vocat ostium, quia multi parati erant ad recipiendu doctrinam de fide in Christum, adeo, (vt ipse Dominus loquitur) messis erat multa & copiosa. Efficax quoque erat ostium, quia occasiones eiusmodi sese offerebant, quibus non sine profectu & luculento fructu prædicabat, multis indies ad fidem Christi accedentibus. Addit tamen non deesse simul aduersarios multos, qui sese opponat & Euangelij prædicationem impedire conentur. Horum autem meminit, vt offendat, se magna necessitate cogi, vt illic adhuc subsistat, quia multum proficiat stationem illam tenendo, non posset autem absque periculo & detrimento Ecclesiarum illarum discedere: quando ita occasionem daret aduersarijs ea destruendi, quæ iam erant probè ædificata. Voluit autem ad Pentecosten vsque manere, quando cœtus fiebant frequentiores, & propter Iudæos ex variis gentibus Hierosolymam profiscentes maior sese offerebat pluribus prædicandi occasio. Facit autem ad loci huius expositionem pleniorem totū caput decimū nonū in Actorū libro. Eo enim describit Lucas, vt Paulus totū biennū Ephesi docuerit ex toto Asia Iudæis simul & Græcis ad ipsum confluentibus, vt Dei Verbum audirent: vtque doctrinam eius signis non vulgaribus confirmauerit, ita vt etiam super ægrotos deferrentur à corpore Pauli sudaria seu semicinctia, & morbi ab eis recederent, & spiritus mali exirent. Adiuuit quoque Veritatis causam non mediocriter tristis & infelix filiorum Sceuæ casus, qui cum à fide alieni nihilominus IESV CHRISTI nomine ad dæmones expellendos abuterentur, ab his pessimè multati sunt. Eo enim omnes perterriti sunt, & multi ad apertam suorum delictorum confessionem compulsi, adeò, vt qui artes magicas hucusque exercuerant, libros maximi pretij comportatos publicè exusserint. Iam ergo magnis incrementis illic surgebat regnum Dei, & non pauci Asiæ principum ad fidem conuersi & Paulo amici facti fuerunt. Non potuit ergo tam lætum veritatis propagandæ successum diutius ferre Satan, sed Demetrium quendam,qui ex delubrũ Dianæ Ephesiæ argenteis quæstum faciebat, excitauit, & per hunc ciuitatem totam tumultu seditioso commouit, qui tamen mox repressus est. Verè ergo Paulus scribit, ostium sibi magnum & efficax apertum esse, non autem deesse aduersarios, quorum improbitati ipsum adhuc detineat. Paulus vero hisce verbis multa comprehendit, quæ ad illustrandam doctrinam de Euangelij ministerio & ad ministrorum confirmationem faciunt.
units.tr: Paul adduced yet another reason which keeps him from coming to Corinth now. "I will remain at Ephesus," he says, "until Pentecost." Lest anyone think he is preferring the Ephesians to the Corinthians, he also gives the reason for this delay: "For a great and effective door has been opened to me, and there are many adversaries." He speaks of a door metaphorically, meaning the opportunity of preaching the gospel. He calls the door great because many were ready to receive the teaching about faith in Christ; the harvest, as the Lord himself puts it, was great and abundant. The door was also effective, because opportunities of this kind presented themselves, in which he preached not without progress and rich fruit, as many came to faith in Christ every day. Yet he adds that there were at the same time many adversaries who set themselves against him and tried to hinder the preaching of the gospel. He mentions them so as to make clear that he is under great necessity to stay there for the present: he advances much by holding that position, and he could not leave without danger and harm to those churches, since he would thereby give the adversaries an opening to destroy what was already well built. He wished to remain until Pentecost, when the assemblies became more crowded, and because of the Jews from various nations travelling to Jerusalem, a greater opportunity of preaching presented itself to many. The whole of the nineteenth chapter of the Acts of the Apostles contributes to a fuller explanation of this passage. There Luke describes how Paul taught at Ephesus for the whole of two years, with Jews and Greeks from all Asia flocking to him to hear the word of God; and how he confirmed his teaching with no ordinary signs, so that handkerchiefs and aprons were carried from Paul's body to the sick, and diseases departed from them and evil spirits went out. The sad and unhappy fate of the sons of Sceva also helped the cause of truth not a little: since they, being strangers to the faith, nevertheless abused the name of Jesus Christ to cast out demons, they were most severely punished by them. All were terrified by this, and many were compelled to make open confession of their sins, so much so that those who had practised magic arts up to then publicly burned books of the greatest value which they had gathered together. Now therefore the kingdom of God was rising there with great increase, and not a few of the princes of Asia were converted to the faith and became friends of Paul. Satan could not bear such a happy success for the spreading of the truth for long, so he stirred up a certain Demetrius, who made profit with silver from the shrine of Diana of Ephesus, and through him moved the whole city to seditious tumult, which was however soon suppressed. Paul therefore truly writes that a great and effective door had been opened to him, and that there were not lacking adversaries, by whose wickedness he was still being detained there. In these words Paul comprehends many things which serve to illustrate the doctrine of the ministry of the gospel and to strengthen ministers.

units.la: Inter ea primum occurrit, quòd ostium sibi apertum esse scribit. Nam si quæras, à quo illud fuerit apertum, non alius id fecisse dici poterit quàm Deus. Is enim solus est ex cuius æterno consilio salus nostra dependet, quæque[?] eius occasiones, quando vult, nobis offert, & sæpe Euangelii ex improuiso mittit nihil tale expectantibus, sicuti Macedonibus accidisse, paulò ante diximus. Et nunquam non verum erit illud Apostoli: Quomodo prædicabunt, nisi missi fuerint? Vt verò ille ministros & prædicatores Verbi sui mittit, ita idem ille tam in his quam in auditoribus agit, vt illi quidem apte & utiliter prædicent, hi verò aures & animos Verbo suo accommodent, & audito credant. Prodest ergo ipsa ista[?] sapius & diligentius consideravisse, vt vtrinque in Deum respiciant omnes, & hinc precibus assiduis solicitent, vt ministris quidem occasiones commodas offerat & linguas eorundem regat, auditorum verò corda illuminet atque trahat ad verum fidei obsequium. Et huc pertinet quod Paulus ad Colossen. scribit: Orate etiam pro nobis, vt Deus aperiat nobis ostium sermonis, vt loquamur mysterium Christi, propter quod & vinctus sum, vt (inquam) ita illud patefaciam, sicut oportet me loqui. Quibus consentiunt, quæ ad Ephesios sub finem epistolæ illius ab eodem Apostolo scribuntur.
units.tr: Among these, the first to occur is that he writes that the door was opened to him. For if you ask by whom it was opened, no one other than God can be said to have done it. He alone is the one on whose eternal counsel our salvation depends, and he offers us its opportunities when he wills, and often sends the gospel unexpectedly to those who expect nothing of the kind, as we said a little earlier happened to the Macedonians. And that saying of the Apostle will always be true: "How shall they preach unless they are sent?" Just as he sends the ministers and preachers of his Word, so too he works both in them and in the hearers, so that the former preach aptly and profitably, and the latter fit their ears and minds to his Word and believe what they hear. It is useful, therefore, to have considered this more often and more carefully, so that all may look to God on both sides, and from this may with constant prayers seek that he would offer suitable opportunities to the ministers and govern their tongues, and enlighten and draw the hearts of the hearers to true obedience of faith. To this belongs also what Paul writes to the Colossians: "Pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am also in bonds; that I may make it manifest, as I ought to speak." What is written to the Ephesians by the same Apostle near the end of that letter agrees with these words.

units.la: Deinde Euangelij fortem Paulus his verbis exprimit. Ostium mihi apertum est (inquit) magnum & efficax, & aduersarij multi. At quod illi apud Ephesios accidit, id ubique locorum & semper fieri solet: vt quo maiori cum professu Euangelium prædicatur, eò magis Satan aduersus illud tumultuetur. Docet hoc Christus in fortis armati parabola, quæ quiescere dicit domi suæ, quoad res eius salvæ sunt, & extra periculum constituta: at si fortior aliquis superveniens domum illius diripere conetur, mox certamen oritur, neque finis est tumultuandi, donec ille vinctus & vinculis alligatus victori loco cederit. Typus huius rei in Davidis regno præcessit. Cum enim hic à Saule obitu illud obtinuisset, mox gentes fremere, populi inania meditari, & reges tumultuare coeperunt, & bellis horrendis petitus est, qui à Saulina persecutione vix dum respiraverat. Non potuit enim regni eius reformationem & cultus divini instaurationem ferre Satan, qui sub Saule latenus regnaverat. Idem verò factum fuisse sub veri illius Davidis, IESV CHRISTI, adventum, historia testantur. Nam tunc quoque totum orbem terrarum mirifice & horribiliter diabolus turbavit, Romanis omnia longe lateque vastantibus. Et non multo ante Filij Dei incarnationem Aristobulo & Hircano ducibus Iudæi in partes distracti & bello civili inter se commissi sunt, quod toti genti servitutem & postremo excidium peperit. Adhæc Parthorum armis res Romanorum graviter afflictæ sunt, vt iam de civilibus bellis primum inter Iulium & Pompeium, postea inter Augustum & Antonium exortis nihil dicamus. Voluit enim ea ratione Satan omnem promissi Messiæ expectationem omnibus iis invisam & exosam facere, qui prius in illum totis animis intenti fuerant. Rursus cum postea Euangelium in toto orbe per Apostolos & horum successores prædicaretur, communis ille hostis humanæ salutis Romanos Imperatores in rebiem egit, qui ostium illud regni Dei minacibus edictis & armis crudelibus claudere, denique fidem Christianam funditus extirpare conati sunt. Exercuerunt per hos excitatæ persecutiones Ecclesiam veterem per annos paulò minus trecentos usque ad Constantini Magni tempora, quibus tantum sanguinis humani effusum est, quantum ab orbe condito nunquam orbis terrarum vidit. Debemus autem in veterum historiarum consideratione frequenter versari, ne offendamur, si quid huius etiam hodie nobis accidat, & publici tumultus ad Euangelicæ doctrinæ prædicationem subito excitentur. Nam quod pulchrè annotavit Chrysostomus, vt serpens calcatus sibilare & mordere incipit, scorpius item non nisi tactus aut irritatus ferit: ita Satan, qui dum nemine obstante securus regnat, quiescere videtur, mox dente & cauda furit, & undique arma sua exerit, quando per Euangelium Christus eum expossessione sua deturbare incipit. Itaque præparent sese ad certamina & pugnas, quicunque opus hoc aggredi volunt, neque eos periculi metus aliqui absterrat. Nam ut boni milites fere cruenti, sæpe autem & saucij ex pugna redeunt, victoriæ & triumphi gloria metum & dolorem omnem procul profligante: ita non semper absque sanguine sanctissimum illud certamen Euangelij contra mundum & principem eius decertatur, certa tamen triumphi cælestis spes nobis proposita est, quæ nos ad omnem periculi imminentis metum intrepidos facere debet. Qui enim remissius agunt, ut mundo probentur, & hostibus quoque placeant, ij Christi serui non sunt.
units.tr: Next, Paul expresses the fortune of the gospel in these words: "A door has been opened to me," he says, "great and effective, and there are many adversaries." But what happened there among the Ephesians happens everywhere and always: the more openly the gospel is preached, the more Satan rages against it. Christ teaches this in the parable of the strong armed man, who is said to rest in his house as long as his goods are safe and outside danger; but if someone stronger comes and tries to plunder his house, a struggle immediately arises, nor is there an end to the tumult until he is conquered, bound in chains, and gives way to the victor. A type of this matter went before in the kingdom of David. For when he had obtained it after the death of Saul, at once the nations raged, the peoples devised vain things, and kings began to rage, and he who had scarcely yet recovered from the persecution of Saul was assailed by dreadful wars. For Satan, who had reigned widely under Saul, could not bear the restoration of David's kingdom and the re-establishment of divine worship. Histories bear witness that the same thing happened at the coming of that true David, Jesus Christ. For then too the devil wonderfully and dreadfully disturbed the whole world, with the Romans laying waste everything far and wide. And not long before the incarnation of the Son of God, under the leaders Aristobulus and Hyrcanus, the Jews were divided into parties and plunged into civil war among themselves, which brought servitude and at last destruction upon the whole nation. Besides this, the affairs of the Romans were grievously shaken by the arms of the Parthians, not to mention the civil wars that arose first between Julius and Pompey, and afterwards between Augustus and Antony. For by this means Satan wished to make the whole expectation of the promised Messiah hateful and odious to all those who had previously been wholly intent upon him. Again, when afterwards the gospel was preached throughout the world by the Apostles and their successors, that common enemy of human salvation drove the Roman emperors into a frenzy, and they tried by threatening edicts and cruel arms to shut that door of the kingdom of God, and finally to root out the Christian faith utterly. The persecutions stirred up by these men harassed the ancient Church for almost three hundred years, down to the times of Constantine the Great, and so much human blood was shed in them that the world had never seen so much since the foundation of the world. We ought, moreover, to dwell frequently on the consideration of the histories of old, so that we are not offended if anything of this kind happens to us today too, and public tumults are suddenly stirred up against the preaching of the evangelical doctrine. For Chrysostom aptly observed that as a trodden serpent begins to hiss and bite, and likewise the scorpion strikes only when touched or provoked, so Satan, who seems to rest while he reigns unopposed, soon rages with tooth and tail and puts forth his weapons on every side, when Christ begins through the gospel to drive him out of his possession. Therefore let those who wish to undertake this work prepare themselves for battles and struggles, and let no fear of danger deter them. For as good soldiers often return from battle bloodied, and often wounded, the glory of victory and triumph putting to flight all fear and pain: so the most holy struggle of the gospel against the world and its prince is not always fought without blood; yet a sure hope of heavenly triumph is set before us, which ought to make us fearless against every threatening danger. For those who act more carelessly, so as to be approved by the world and to please its enemies as well, are not servants of Christ.

units.la: Ergo Pauli exemplum imitentur omnes, quibus Euangelij prouehendi munus commissum est. Is propter pericula & labores non sibi ex Asia discedendum, sed potius manendum esse putauit, quàmuis multa posset prætexere, & per honestas occasiones alio vocaretur. Magis enim eum mouit oblata magni & insperati profectus occasio, quam imminentium undique periculorum terror. Et ut ita faciamus, non obscure Christus monuit iam mortem adituru s, quando discipulis ad montem oliueti dicebat: Manete hic, vigilate & orate. Id enim ad omnes pertinet, qui illius serui esse volunt, ut scilicet stationem suam constanter tueantur, in eadem vigilent, & à Deo vires atque robur sibi dari postulent. Omnes ergo in periculis & laboribus sibi ipsis illud poeticum occinant: Tu ne cede malis, sed contra audentior ito. Peccant autem vehementer, qui pro sua commoditate sibi ipsis locum deligunt, vbi in otio & pace agant, relictis Ecclesijs, quibus suam operam nauare debebant. Fecerunt hoc olim Anachoretæ, qui persecutionum tempore in loca deserta secesserunt, pio quidem instituto, sed inconsiderato, & quod posteris exempli pessi-mi occasionem præbuit. Nam qui ex Monachis hodie optimi sunt, ij sub vita contemplatiuæ prætextu ita viuunt, ut neque sibi ipsis neque aliis vtiles sint. Sed & inter Euangelij professores inueniuntur, qui nulla aut perquam exigua suæ vocationis ratione habita, sibi ipsis ferias indicunt, & pericula atque labores imminentes cum ijs, quæ iam diu sustinuerint conferendo, se iam meruisse clamant, ut rudè donentur. Atqui ignauus nimium miles est, qui periculo viso de fuga citius quàm de illo fortiter propulsando aut vincendo cogitat. Stultus autem est, qui non videt, quòd quò magis pericula & labores amplificat, eò magis seipsum accusat, qui præter fidem datam ex acie discesserit, & ut mercenarius viso lupo oues turpiter atque proditorie reliquerit.
units.tr: Therefore let all those to whom the task of advancing the Gospel has been entrusted imitate Paul's example. Because of dangers and labours, he judged that he should not withdraw from Asia but rather remain there, although he could have put forward many pretexts and could have been called elsewhere on honourable grounds. For the opportunity of great and unhoped-for progress moved him more than the terror of dangers threatening on every side. And to put it in this way, Christ clearly warned that he was about to face death, when he said to the disciples at the Mount of Olives: "Stay here, watch and pray." For this applies to all who wish to be his servants: that they should constantly keep their post, stay watchful at it, and ask God to give them strength and vigour. Therefore, let all of us in dangers and labours sing to ourselves that line of the poet: "Do not yield to misfortunes, but advance all the more boldly against them." Those people sin gravely who, for their own convenience, choose for themselves a place where they may live in leisure and peace, abandoning the congregations to which they ought to devote their labour. The Anchorites did this long ago; they withdrew into desert places in times of persecution, from a pious but ill-considered purpose, and this gave later generations a most pernicious example. For those who are today the best of the monks live under the pretext of the contemplative life in such a way that they are useful neither to themselves nor to others. But among the professors of the Gospel too there are some who, with little or no regard for their calling, declare holidays for themselves, and, comparing the dangers and labours that threaten with those they have already endured for a long time, cry out that they have already earned their discharge, so that they may be given leave. Yet he is too cowardly a soldier who, on seeing danger, thinks of flight more quickly than of repelling or conquering it bravely. And he is foolish who does not see that the more he magnifies the dangers and labours, the more he condemns himself, since he has left the battle line in breach of the pledge he gave, and, like a hired hand who sees a wolf, has shamefully and treacherously abandoned the sheep.

units.la: Non tamen hæc ita dicimus, ut Tertulliani sententiam probemus, qui omnem fugam illicitam esse putauit. Nec enim illud Christi ignoramus: Si vos persecuti fuerint in vna ciuitate, fugite in aliam. Hoc solum dicimus, non deserendos esse eos locos, in quibus præsens necessitas nostram operam requirit, & eadem non omnino inutilis est. Alia eorum ratio est, qui vel ab hostibus apertis, vel ab illis ipsis eiiciuntur, qui cum Christum aliquandiu professi sint, porrò eius oues esse nolunt. Quid enim pastor faciat sine ouibus? Sunt etiam, quos ab Ecclesijs discedere vtile est: quando nimirum ipsos solos petit hostium rabies, & ipsis digressus sua tamen pax Ecclesijs integra manet, neque fidei libertas impeditur. Quod autem de Verbi mini-stris dicitur, id ad se illi quoque transferant, qui ad reipub. gubernacula sedent. Quid enim turpius dici potest, ex repub. honores & opes sperare, pro eadem vero periclitari nolle? Vti-nam vero hæc tam facile omnibus persuaderi possent, quàm confessa sunt omnibus. Oremus ergo Deum Patrem Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, vt vs[?] Ecclesiæ & Reipub. pastores excitet, qui in officio suo strenui & constantes ita se gerant, vt seipsos & suæ fidei creditos olim sistere possint intrepidos & integros in aduentu Filij sui, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Yet we do not say these things so as to endorse the opinion of Tertullian, who thought that every flight was unlawful. For we are not unaware of that saying of Christ: "If they persecute you in one city, flee into another." We say only this: that those places should not be deserted in which present necessity calls for our work, and where that work is not altogether useless. The case is different for those who are driven out either by open enemies or by those very people who, after professing Christ for some time, are unwilling to be his sheep any longer. For what does a shepherd do without sheep? There are also those for whom it is useful to withdraw from the congregations: namely, when the rage of enemies seeks only them, and by their departure the congregations remain whole in their peace, and the freedom of the faith is not hindered. What is said of the ministers of the Word, let those also apply to themselves who sit at the helm of the commonwealth. For what could be more shameful than to hope for honours and wealth from the commonwealth, yet be unwilling to face danger on its behalf? Would that these things could be persuaded to all as easily as they are admitted by all. Let us therefore pray to God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ that he may raise up pastors for the Church and the commonwealth who, vigorous and steadfast in their office, may so conduct themselves that they may one day be able to present themselves, fearless and blameless, to their own souls and to those entrusted to their faith, at the coming of his Son, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XCII.
units.tr: Homily XCII.

units.la: Quòd si venerit Timotheus, videte vt tuto sit apud vos: Opus enim Domini operatur, vt & ego. Ne quis igitur illum pro nihilo habeat, sed prosequimini eum cum pace, vt veniat ad me. Expecto enim eum cum fratribus. Por-rò quoad Apollo fratrem, multum precatus sum eum, vt i-ret ad vos cum fratribus: sed omnino non fuit ei voluntas nunc eundi, venturus est autem cum tempus opportunum habuerit.
units.tr: "If Timothy comes, see that he is safe among you, for he works the work of the Lord, as I also do. Let no one therefore despise him, but send him on his way in peace, that he may come to me; for I expect him with the brethren. As for Apollos our brother, I greatly urged him to go to you with the brethren, but it was by no means his will to go now; he will come when he has an opportune time."

units.la: Dominus & Seruator noster, IESVS CHRISTVS, iam mortem aditurus inter alia discipulis & Apostolis dixit: Ego elegi vos, et constitui vos, vt abeuntes fructum afferatis, & fructus vester maneat. Huius ergo dicti illi probè memores, non modò homines Dei & veritatis ignaros Christo adducere, & vbique gentium Ecclesias colligere studuerunt, sed toti simul in eo etiam fuerunt, vt eos seruarent, quos semel Christi cognitione ac vera fide imbutos esse videbant: ne qui vel periculorum metu succumberent, vel ab impostoribus seducerentur. Quae causa fuit, quòd Ecclesias frequenter inuiserunt, & si id illis per negotia non licuit, tunc per epistolas & nuntios fidos illas confirmarunt, & singulos fui[?] admonuerunt officij. Factum hoc etiam apud Corinthios. Qualis enim eius Ecclesia facies fuerit, iam saepe diximus. Non potuit autem Paulus ad eos accedere, cum à Deo subinde alio vocaretur, & noua quotidie impedimenta ipsi obijcerentur. Ergo epistolam hanc scripsit, qua diligenter omnia comprehendit, de quibus eos admoneri necesse erat: & eandem mittit per hominem fidissimum, Timotheum, cuius fides atque industria ei multis argumentis iampridem perspecta erat. Vt verò vt maiori cum fructu apud eos posset agere, hunc locum interserit, quo primum diligentissimè eum ipsis commendat, deinde cur hunc potius quàm Apollo aut quemuis alium miserit, docet.
units.tr: Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, about to face death, said among other things to his disciples and Apostles: "I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain." Mindful of this saying, the Apostles took great pains not only to bring to Christ men ignorant of God and the truth, and to gather churches throughout the nations, but also were wholly intent on preserving those whom they saw had once been imbued with the knowledge of Christ and true faith, lest any should either give way through fear of dangers or be seduced by impostors. This was the reason they often visited the churches, and if business did not allow this, they strengthened them through letters and trusted messengers, and admonished each one of his duty. This was also done among the Corinthians. For we have often said what kind of church it was. Paul could not go to them, since God kept calling him elsewhere and new obstacles were thrown in his way every day. So he wrote this letter, in which he carefully covered everything about which they needed to be admonished, and sent it by a most faithful man, Timothy, whose faith and diligence had long since been well proven to him by many tokens. But so that Timothy might act among them with greater profit, Paul inserts this passage, in which he first commends him most diligently to them, and then explains why he sent this man rather than Apollos or anyone else.

units.la: Quòd primum, sic ait: Quòd si venerit Timotheus, videte vt tuto sit apud vos: Opus enim Domini operatur, vt & ego: Ne quis ergo illum pro nihilo habeat: sed prosequimini eum cum pace, vt veniat ad me, &c. Est commendatio haec breuis quidem, sed grauis admodum, quia tria petit. Primum, Videte (inquit) vt tuto sit apud vos. Nam praeter apertos fidei hostes, erant etiam falsi fratres, de quibus non vno loco Paulus queritur, & homini peregrino difficile est pericula atque insidias omnes cauere. Vult ergo, vt ei diligenter prospiciant, ne quid mali accidat homini ingenuo & non vulgari Christi seruo. Alterum: Ne quis eum pro nihilo habeat. De eo admonere eos opus erat, quòd iuuenis esset Timotheus, & plerunque iuuentuti coniuncta sit leuitas, indicij inopia, ignorantia & quae alia sunt eius generis vitia. Monet ergo, vt non aetatem eius respiciant, sed dona potius, quibus illum Deus ornauerit. Sic ad ipsum Timotheum scribens, ait: Nemo tuam iuuentutem despiciat. Postremum, vt eum prosequantur & cum pace deducant, vt saluus atque incolumis ad ipsum posset redire, qui eum cum fratribus alijs simul expectet. Ista verò postulationibus vna ratio adijcitur, quae multarum instar esse potuit: Opus enim Domini operatur, vt & ego. Intelligit autem per opus Domini praedicationem Euangelij & regni Dei propagationem. Nam ipso Christo teste, opus Dei est proprie, vt credamus in eum, quem ille misit. Ergo opus Dei agunt, quicunque fidem in Christum docent, & in huius cognitionem eos adducunt, qui prius sub tenebrarum potestate per errores & vitia omnis generis volutabantur. Huc facit, quòd ministri siue praecones Euangelij in vinea Domini laborare dicuntur, & quòd supra Paulus scripsit: Dei sumus administri: Dei aruum, Dei aedificatio est. Fuit ergo haec magna & non vulgaris Timothei laus, quòd illum opus Domini agere dicit, & sibi quidem parem facit, quem vas siue organum Domini selectissimum fuisse scimus. Seruit huius loci illustrationi, quod in epistola ad Philippenses scribitur: Spero in Domino IESV, me Timotheum breui missurum vobis, vt & ego bono sim animo, vbi quis vester status sit cognouero. Neminem enim habeo pari animo praedictum, qui germanè res vestras curaturus sit. Nam omnes, quae sua sunt, quaerunt, non quae CHRISTI IESV. Porrò probationem eius nostris, quòd veluti cum patre filius, mecum seruierit in Euangelio. Fuit ergo hoc magni amoris argumentum, quòd eum ad Corinthios mitte-re voluit Paulus, cuius operae siue ministerio ipse non commodè carere poterat. Ita enim abunde testatus est, se maiorem Ecclesiae ipsorum, quàm suijpsius rationem habere.
units.tr: As to the first point, he says: "If Timothy comes, see that he is safe among you, for he works the work of the Lord, as I also do. Let no one therefore despise him, but send him on his way in peace, that he may come to me," and so on. This commendation is brief but very weighty, for it asks three things. First, "see," he says, "that he is safe among you." For besides the open enemies of the faith there were also false brethren, about whom Paul complains in more than one place, and it is hard for a stranger to guard against all dangers and snares. He therefore wants them to look after him carefully, so that no harm befalls a man of good character and no ordinary servant of Christ. Second, "let no one despise him." They needed to be warned about this, because Timothy was young, and youth is generally joined with levity, lack of judgement, ignorance and other faults of that kind. So he urges them not to look at his age but rather at the gifts with which God has endowed him. Writing to Timothy himself, he says: "Let no one despise your youth" (1 Tim. 4). Last, that they should send him on his way in peace, so that he might return safe and sound to the one who waits for him with the other brethren. To these requests is added one reason, which could count for many: "for he works the work of the Lord, as I also do." By "the work of the Lord" he means the preaching of the Gospel and the spreading of the kingdom of God. For, as Christ himself bears witness, the work of God is properly this: that we believe in him whom God has sent (John 6). Therefore those who teach faith in Christ, and lead to the knowledge of him those who before wallowed under the power of darkness in errors and vices of every kind, are doing the work of God. To this point also belongs the fact that the ministers, or heralds, of the Gospel are said to labour in the vineyard of the Lord, and what Paul wrote above: "We are God's servants; you are God's field, God's building" (1 Cor. 3). So this was a great and no ordinary praise of Timothy, that Paul says he does the work of the Lord, and by saying so makes him equal to himself, whom we know to have been the most chosen vessel or instrument of the Lord. The following passage in the epistle to the Philippians serves to illustrate this: "I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you shortly, so that I too may be of good cheer when I learn how you are doing. For I have no one of like mind who will genuinely care for your affairs. For all seek their own, not the things of Christ Jesus" (Phil. 2). Moreover, the proof of his worth to our people is that, like a son with a father, he has served with me in the Gospel. So it was a great proof of love that Paul wished to send Timothy to the Corinthians, although he himself could not conveniently do without Timothy's labour or ministry. For he thus openly testifies that he has greater regard for their church than for himself.

units.la: Apparet autem simul in eo admirabili & dignissima imitatu Pauli modestia, qui Timotheum, hominem iuuenem adhuc & suum discipulum sibi parem fiue aequalem facit. Sic alibi Sylvanum & Sosthenem, & hunc ipsum Timotheum in epistolarum inscriptionibus sibi coniungit. Quam procul ergo illum ab eorum fastu abfuisse putas, qui omnes alios Ecclesiarum ministros ex alto despiciunt, & tantumnon pedibus suis subiectos esse volunt: adhæc in ipsum Euangelium sibi ius quoddam vendicant, dum illud suum esse dicunt, & non pœnitendi Christi seruis hoc tam scripto quàm viua voce exprobrare audent, quod Euangelium fœtere fecerint, si quis aliquid quantumuis pium & necessarium ipsis non prius consultis, non tamen absque fructu tentauerit. Possem hic fa-fatuosi[?] cuiusdam Theologi factum recitare, qui præstantissimos Ecclesiarum superioris Germaniæ ministros cotumeliosissime habuit: sed præstat facinus insolentissimum silentio tegere. Meminerint tamen omnes, quibus datum est in Ecclesia Dei donis præclaris excellere, ad eius ædificationem nihil utilius esse modestia & humilitate, qua olim Apostoli floruerunt: neque vnquam illis excidat, quod Petrus ait: Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam.
units.tr: At the same time, in this passage there appears Paul's admirable modesty, most worthy of imitation, for he makes Timothy, still a young man and his own disciple, his equal. So elsewhere he joins Silvanus and Sosthenes, and this same Timothy, with himself in the greetings of his letters. How far, then, do you think Timothy was from the pride of those who look down from on high on all other ministers of the churches, and wish them to be almost at their feet. Moreover, they claim for themselves a certain right over the Gospel itself, calling it their own, and dare to reproach the servants of Christ, not to be repented of, both in writing and by word of mouth, for having made the Gospel stink, if anyone has attempted something, however pious and necessary, without first consulting them, though not without profit. I could here recount the deed of a certain foolish theologian, who treated the most distinguished ministers of the churches of Upper Germany with the greatest insolence; but it is better to pass over so outrageous a deed in silence. Yet let all those to whom it has been given to excel in the Church of God with notable gifts remember that nothing is more useful for its edification than the modesty and humility in which the Apostles once flourished; and let them never forget what Peter says: "God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble" (1 Pet. 5).

units.la: Docet prætereà hæc Timothei commendatio, quod sit præcipuum ministrorum Ecclesiæ officium: hoc nimirum, vt opus Domini agant. Ergo nihil ab eorum officio magis alienum est, quàm si suas res agant, & (quod ad Philippenses scribens in nonnullis Paulus reprehendit) quæ sua ipsorum sunt, quærant. Nemo, qui militat (ait Apostolus) implicatur vitæ negotijs, vt ei qui se in militiam delegit, placeat. Et supra de seipso loquens ministros athletis similes esse vult, qui vt coronam breui perituram accipiant, continentissimi sunt, & ab omnibus abstinent, quæ vires ipsorum eneruare aut attenuare poterant. Quantò magis ergo Christi ministros, qui in hoc felicissimo Ecclesiæ stadio contra diabolum & mundum certant, decet, vt omnibus aliis curis relictis, solius Dei negotium agant? Vehementer ergo peccant, qui relicta Euangelij prædicatione, circa frigidas & inutiles superstitiones occupantur, imagines ornant & vestiunt, lampades & cereos accendunt, organorum concentu aures demulcent, peregrinationibus vacant, vestitu portentoso religionem simulant, ieiunijs non necessarijs sese enecant, & sexcenta alia faciunt, quæ nusquam Dominus mandauit, & quæ Domini opus nullo modo dici merentur. Sunt hîs proximi, qui in inani cognitione acquiescunt, & nescio quam vitam contemplatiuam sectantur, quæ præter otiosas speculationes & ad inanem sanctitatis simulationem instituta orationes nihil continet. At non in sermone situm est Regnum Dei, sed in virtute Spiritus ea agentis, quæ ad opus Domini faciunt. Debent hîs conumerari, qui simul res alienas & Christi ministro indignas agunt, dum videlicet ludis & aleæ infami dediti tempus inutiliter consumunt, dum cum ebriosis & lurconibus comessantur, venationibus studeant & aucupijs, aut animi gratia hinc inde vagantes totis hebdomadibus à grege suæ fidei cômisso absunt, & tunc se officio suo probè defunctos esse putant, si diebus Dominicis concjones[?] habeant ad populum, & illis finitis ad sua illa studia non minus turpia quàm vana reuertantur. Sunt hi nequam illi serui, de quibus Matthæi 24. Cap. Christus loquitur, & quibus suam fortè cum hypocritis & proditoribus iampridem ille constituit. Quid verò de illis dicendum, qui cùm primi Ecclesiæ antistites & columnæ videri volunt, ac insuper Apostolicæ successionis titulo gloriantur, adeo tamen non agunt opus Domini, vt id etiam omni conatu impediant, simulq; obstent, ne qui sint, qui fida Euangelij prædicatione homines Christo adducant? Sunt hi Scribarum similes, qui clauem scientiæ è medio sustulerant, & nec ipsi in Regnum Dei ingrediebantur, neque alios ingredi sinebant.
