units.tr: Furthermore, this commendation of Timothy teaches that the chief duty of the ministers of the Church is this: that they do the work of the Lord. Therefore nothing is more foreign to their office than to attend to their own affairs and (as Paul rebukes some in writing to the Philippians) to seek their own things. "No one who serves as a soldier," says the Apostle, "is entangled in the affairs of this life, so that he may please the one who enlisted him" (2 Tim. 2). And speaking of himself above, he wants ministers to be like athletes, who, to win a crown that will soon perish, are most self-controlled and abstain from everything that could weaken or wear down their strength (1 Cor. 9). How much more, then, is it fitting for the ministers of Christ, who in this most happy arena of the Church contend against the devil and the world, to leave aside all other cares and attend only to the business of God? Those therefore sin grievously who, neglecting the preaching of the Gospel, busy themselves with cold and useless superstitions: they adorn and clothe images, light lamps and candles, soothe the ears with the harmony of instruments, devote themselves to pilgrimages, feign religion by strange clothing, wear themselves out with unnecessary fasts, and do six hundred other things which the Lord nowhere commanded and which in no way deserve to be called the work of the Lord. Close to these are those who rest in empty knowledge and pursue some kind of contemplative life, which, apart from idle speculations and prayers arranged for a vain show of holiness, contains nothing. But the kingdom of God does not consist in talk, but in the power of the Spirit who effects the things that belong to the work of the Lord (1 Cor. 4). Among these must be counted those who at the same time attend to other people's affairs and do things unworthy of a minister of Christ, namely, when given over to games and disreputable dice they waste their time uselessly, when they revel with drunkards and gluttons, when they devote themselves to hunting and fowling, or when, wandering here and there for the sake of amusement, they are absent for whole weeks from the flock committed to their faith, and then think they have discharged their office well if they hold sermons for the people on the Lord's Day and, when these are over, return to those pursuits no less shameful than they are vain. These are those wicked servants of whom Christ speaks in Matthew 24, and to whom he long ago assigned their place with hypocrites and traitors. But what should be said of those who, although they wish to be seen as the first leaders and pillars of the Church, and moreover boast of the title of Apostolic succession, nevertheless do not do the work of the Lord, but even by every effort hinder it, and at the same time obstruct others from being brought to Christ by the faithful preaching of the Gospel? These are like the Scribes, who had taken away the key of knowledge, and who neither entered into the kingdom of God themselves nor allowed others to enter (Luke 11).

units.la: Admonemur etiam hoc loco, quid ministris fidis debeant Ecclesiæ, & quotquot Christiani ut[?] ri haberi volunt. Primum est, vt eos tueantur, non prodant: adhæc vt ijsdem adsint auxilio, consilio, aut saltem studio atque fauore, si nihil præterea possint. Fecerunt hoc olim primitiuæ & Apostolicæ Ecclesiæ fideles. Cùm enim Apostoli in carcerem coniecti essent, & commune periculum immineret, non de illorum temeritate aut importunitate conquesti sunt, neque prædicandi libertatem certis legibus circumscribere multò minus illorum capitibus pacem redimere voluerunt, vt hodie aliqui faciendum esse censent: sed precibus illos iuuarunt, & hoc præcipuè à Deo petierunt, vt Spiritu suo eos armaret, vt intrepida & constanti fiducia Verbum Dei prædicare pergerent. Et cùm Herodes Iacobo prius occiso Petrum quoque in vincula coniectum perdere instituisset, Ecclesia cōuentus noctumos[?] habuit, & pro illius liberatione preces fudit ad Dominum. Etenim, si parentum salus filijs cordi esse debet, non possunt Christiani homines eos negligere, quorum ministerio ipsi in Dei filios regenerati sunt. Exigitur etiam, ne eosdem propter vilem speciem contemnant. Nam si hanc spectemus, semper erit, quod eos contemptibiles faciat, & ex quo calumniandi occasionem homines improbi arripiant. Exemplum eius rei memorabile in Judaorum gente proponitur, qui ut Joannem Baptistam calumniati sunt, & à dæmonio sustentari dixerunt, quòd vitam vineret au-steram, neque vitu & amictu usitato ac vulgari uteretur: ita JESUM CHRISTUM bel-luonem & bibonem esse clamarunt, quòd invitatus ad convivia accederet, seq; omnibus facilem atq; commodum præbereret. Et huius generis multa hodie fiunt, dum infelix mundus alios propter genus & opes exosos habet, alios superbè despicit, quòd obscuro loco nati, vitam in inopia & egestate transfigunt. Nihil ergo hic tutius fuerit, quàm in Dei institutum respicere, qui ut miseris mortalibus consuleret, qui divinæ maiestatis splendorem ferre non possunt, ex nostro genere ministros deligit, quos Spiritu suo illuminat & regit, ut Verbum suum nobis annuntient, et ad Regni sui hæreditatem nos adducant. Itaque simul doctrina inspiciatur, quæsi ex Dei ore, id est, ex scripturis sacris desumpta fuerit, audiri ac recipi meretur, neq; ei quicquam decedit propter vilem ac ignobilem prædicantis sive doctoris speciem. Ut enim gemma non mutatur, sive nudam, sive auro, sive cupro aut aliquo viliori metallo inclusam circumferas: ita nobilis illa Regni Dei margarita, Euangelium, natiuam suam vim retinet, quisquis tandem ille fit, qui eam nobis syncere ac fideliter proponit. Merentur ergo honorem debitum ministri, ut alibi Paulus admonet: & eum quidem bonorem, qui cum obedientia, quam Dei Verbo omnes debent, coniunctus fit. Quare impios & malafi-dei Christianos merito eos dicimus, qui illos scurriliter contemnunt: qui item dum res Christiana in tuto est, illorum amicitia & authoritate ad res suas agendas abutuntur, ut primum vero per-secutionum pericula imminent, rabie noua accensi, otium suum & mundi huius amicitiam capi-tibus illorum pactione non minus sacrilega quàm turpi & inhonesta redimunt.
units.tr: We are also reminded here what faithful ministers are owed by the churches, and by all who wish to be regarded as Christians. The first duty is to defend them and not betray them; next, to stand by them with help, counsel, or at least zeal and goodwill, if they can offer nothing more. The faithful of the early apostolic Church did this. When the apostles were thrown into prison and common danger threatened, the believers did not complain of their rashness or importunity, nor did they wish to hem in the freedom of preaching with fixed laws, much less to buy peace for the apostles' heads, as some think should be done today. Instead they helped them with prayers, and above all asked God to arm them with his Spirit, so that they would keep preaching the Word of God with fearless and steadfast confidence. And when Herod, having already killed James, decided to destroy Peter as well by putting him in chains, the church held nightly gatherings and poured out prayers to the Lord for his release. For if the safety of parents ought to be dear to children, Christians cannot neglect those through whose ministry they themselves have been born again as sons of God. It is also required that they not despise ministers for their lowly appearance. For if we look at that, there will always be something to make them contemptible, and wicked men will seize on it as an occasion for slander. A memorable example of this is set before us in the Jewish nation: they slandered John the Baptist, saying he was possessed by a demon, because he lived a harsh life and did not use ordinary and common food and clothing; and so they cried out that Jesus Christ was a glutton and a drunkard, because he accepted invitations to banquets and made himself agreeable and accessible to all. Many things of this kind happen today, while the unhappy world holds some in hatred on account of birth and wealth, and proudly despises others because they were born in obscure places and pass their lives in want and poverty. Nothing is safer here, then, than to look to God's own appointment. To care for wretched mortals who cannot bear the splendour of his divine majesty, he chooses ministers from our own kind, whom he enlightens and governs by his Spirit, so that they may announce his Word to us and lead us to the inheritance of his kingdom. Therefore, let the teaching be weighed: if it has been drawn from the mouth of God, that is, from the holy Scriptures, it deserves to be heard and received, and nothing is lost from it because of the lowly and humble appearance of the preacher or teacher. For a gem is not changed whether you carry it bare, or set in gold, or copper, or some cheaper metal; so that noble pearl of the kingdom of God, the Gospel, keeps its native power, whoever he may be who sets it before us sincerely and faithfully. Ministers therefore deserve the honour due to them, as Paul admonishes elsewhere, and that honour which is joined with the obedience that all owe to the Word of God. Hence we rightly call impious and faithless those Christians who scornfully despise them; likewise those who, while the Christian cause is safe, abuse the ministers' friendship and authority to advance their own affairs, but as soon as the perils of persecution loom, inflamed with fresh rage, they buy off their leisure and friendship with the world at the cost of those ministers' heads, by a bargain no less sacrilegious than shameful and dishonourable.

units.la: Sed ut ad præsentis loci tractationem redeamus, obiicere poterant aliqui ex Corinthiis: Cur vero mittis ad nos juvenem, nobis hucusque ignotum & rerum nostrarum imperitum? Cur non Apollo venit, qui ut ætate provectior est, ita aliquando apud nos egit & docuit? Fuit enim Apollo (ut Lucas in Actis scribit) vir eloquens, in Scripturis egregiè exercitatus, & disputator acutus atque vehemens, quem ex Ephesofo Corinthum profectum fuisse, & à Paulo illic plantatam Ecclesiam fiam rigavisse, supra ostendit. Tantæ etiam apud Corinthios existimationis fuit, ut quidam illum Paulo anteponerent, & ab illo potius quàm ab hoc denominari vellent. Ne igitur Paulus putaret illum consulto neglexisse, quòd vel eius gloriæ invideret, vel Corinthiorum desiderium frustrari cuperet, excusat sese, & id quidem tanta cum modestia, ut simul ipsum quoq; Apollo omni culpa liberet. Sic enim scribit: Porrò quoad Apollo fratre, multum precatus sum eum, ut iret ad vos cum fratribus: sed omnino non fuit ei voluntas nunc eundi: venturus est autem, cum tempus opportunum habuerit. Se illum rogavisse dicit, ut offendat, non per se flectisse, quò minus Apollo ad ipsos nunc veniat, sed hunc noluisse profectionem iam suscipere. Ne autem sic scribendo invidia conflet fratri bene de Ecclesia merito, quasi animum à Corinthiis alienavisset, ipsum quoque excusat & venturum pollicetur, quàm primùm occasio commodior sese offerat.
units.tr: But to return to the treatment of the present passage: some of the Corinthians might object, "Why do you send us a young man, hitherto unknown to us and inexperienced in our affairs? Why did Apollos not come, who, being older, has at other times worked and taught among us?" For Apollos was (as Luke writes in Acts) an eloquent man, well trained in the Scriptures, and a keen and vigorous disputer, who, as shown above, went from Ephesus to Corinth and watered the church that Paul had planted there. He was held in such high esteem among the Corinthians that some preferred him to Paul and wished to be named after him rather than after Paul. So lest Paul should think that Apollos had deliberately neglected them, either because he envied Paul's glory or wished to frustrate the Corinthians' longing, Paul excuses himself, and does so with such modesty that he at the same time clears Apollos of all blame. For he writes: "As for our brother Apollos, I strongly urged him to go to you with the brothers, but he was altogether unwilling to go now; he will come, however, when he has a suitable opportunity." He says that he asked Apollos to go, and that he did not himself dissuade him from coming to them now, but that Apollos was unwilling to undertake the journey at this time. And lest such writing should stir up envy against a brother who deserved well of the Church, as if he had alienated his mind from the Corinthians, Paul also excuses him and promises that he will come as soon as a more convenient occasion presents itself.

units.la: Quo loco rursus observari debet Apostolorum modestia, qui aliorum ministeriis, non pro im-perio abusi sunt, sed ergo quosvis præstiterunt, quod Petrus ab omnibus episcopis sive Ecclesiæ præfectis exigit: ut nimirum non dominium exerceant in Clerum, id est, in Ecclesiam, quæ Domini sors est atque hæreditas, sed potius exemplaria sint, quæ totus grex possit imitari. Paulus equidem Apollo rogat & precatur, munus verò hoc detrectantem non odiosè accusat apud Corinthios, sed potius suspicione omni ipsum liberare studet. Quod si Pontifices spectes, qui se eius successores esse gloriantur, longè alios eorum mores esse videbis. Nam in omnes omnium Ecclesiarum pastores sibi jus & imperium vindicant, eosdem in verba sua jurare cogunt, invitis & reluctantibus mandant quid velint fieri. Quid autem de his dicere attinet, quando ne Regibus quidem parcunt, qui pro ipsorum nutu fœdera inire, fidem datam violare, conjugia contrahere & rursus dissolvere, bella denique externa & civilia suscipere, & rursus quando ipsi volunt ab armis discedere coguntur? Exempla eius insolentiæ in historijs passim occurrunt, & nostris temporibus multa facta videmus, quæ ipsis possunt fidem facere.
units.tr: Here again we must note the modesty of the apostles, who did not abuse their authority over the ministries of others, but served them in every way, as Peter demands of all bishops or overseers of the Church: that they not lord it over the clergy, that is, over the Church, which is the Lord's lot and inheritance, but rather be examples that the whole flock may imitate. Paul indeed asks and entreats Apollos, and does not bitterly accuse him before the Corinthians when he declines this task, but rather takes pains to free him from all suspicion. But if you look at the Pontiffs, who boast that they are his successors, you will see that their manners are very different. For they claim for themselves right and rule over all the ministers of all the churches; they force them to swear to their words, and they command, against their will and in spite of their resistance, what they want done. But why speak of these things, when they do not even spare kings, whom they compel to make treaties at their nod, to break faith once given, to contract and again dissolve marriages, and finally to undertake foreign and civil wars, and again to lay down arms when they themselves wish? Examples of such insolence occur everywhere in histories, and in our own times we see many deeds that can bear witness to this.

units.la: Deinde admonemur huius loci exemplo, non semper eandem esse sanctorum hominum voluntatem in omnibus, quamvis quoad communem fidei causam & religionis Christianæ principiæ probè consentiant, & in ijs eodem spiritu regantur. Vult Paulus, vt Apollo Corinthum profectus afflictis illic Ecclesiae rebus opem ferat, & vt id faciat precibus quoque contendit. Sed eius voluntati reluctatur ille, & nullis precibus aut argumentis sese ab instituto dimoueri finit. Simile quid inter Paulum & Barnabam accidit, quando hic quidem Marcum profectionis ad Ecclesias institutae comitem assumere vult, ille vero indignum putat, eo quod prius ipsos temere reliquisset. Quae contentio eo vsque exarsit, vt abs se diuellerentur, qui prius amici coniunctissimi & innumerabilium laborum atque periculorum socij fuerant. Quibus adnumerari potest, quod Antiochiae Paulus Petrum publicè corripuit, quasi non recto pede incederet secundum Euangelij veritatem, quando propter Iudaeos eorum consuetudinem declinabat, qui ex gentibus ad Christum conuersi fuerant.
units.tr: Next, we are reminded by the example of this passage that the will of holy men is not always the same in all matters, even though they agree thoroughly on the common cause of the faith and the principles of the Christian religion, and are governed by the same Spirit in these things. Paul wishes that Apollos, having gone to Corinth, should bring help to the afflicted affairs of the church there, and he urges this with prayers too. But Apollos resists his wish, and lets himself be turned from his purpose by no prayers or arguments. Something similar happened between Paul and Barnabas, when the latter wished to take Mark as a companion on the journey to the churches that had been founded, while Paul thought him unworthy, because he had rashly left them earlier. This contention blazed up so far that those who had been very close friends and companions in countless labours and dangers were torn apart from each other. To these may be added the fact that at Antioch Paul publicly rebuked Peter, as if he were not walking straight according to the truth of the Gospel, because he was withdrawing, for fear of the Jews, from the custom of those who had been converted from the Gentiles to Christ.

units.la: Debent exempla ista obseruari, ne hodie doctorum celebrium dissensionibus offendamur, & propter eas de Euangelij veritate dubitemus. Accidit hoc multis hodie, quos infelix illa inter Lutherum & Zuinglium, fortissimos & immortali laude dignos fidei & religionis Christianae instauratores, exorta de Coena Domini controuersia vsque adeo offendit, vt se intra papisticas sordes mansuros dicant, donec litem illam diremptam & è medio sublatam viderint. Quid vero illi ipsi facturi fuerant, si in Apostolorum tempora incidissent, & in Ecclesijs factiosa audiuissent Paulinorum, Cephistarum & Apollonistarum nomina? si item hos quidem pro sola fide iustificante contra Legis iustitiam acerrimè pugnare, illos vero eandem non minus pertinaciter defendere, vtrinque autem Christianum nomen prætendi vidissent? Sunt hæc Ecclesiæ fata, vt dissensionum certaminibus exerceatur, quibus nemo ceu nouis & insolitis offendi debet. Habent enim ista quoque suum vsum, & quidem non pœnitendum. Nam ista occasione diligentius venitatur Veritas, & multa excutiuntur, in quibus boni quoque inconsulcius [?] aut superstitiosius hærent, nisi in controuersiam & disputationem traherentur. Quod olim factum fuisse constat, quando vtile fuit Legis vsum profundius scrutari, à cuius superstitiosa obseruatione pauci discessissent, nisi controuersiæ illæ ostendissent eam cum fide iustitia non posse consistere. Idem de Sacramentaria contentione dicere possumus, quæ ad detegendum & euertendum fictitij illius & noui Dei Mayzim cultum vehementer profuit, vt de aliis fructibus, qui inde enati sunt, nihil dicamus. Est præterea hic quoque certaminum istorum vsus, quod Euangelij præconis suspicionem liberant, ne quid ex composito & dolo malo agere videantur. Quis enim sui priuati commodi ergo eos inter se coniurauisse putet, quos in multis aliis dissentire, in solis autem ijs consentire videt, quæ ad Dei gloriam & Christi meritum illustrandum faciunt? Ita ergo nostris infirmitatibus atque vitijs bene vtitur Dominus, cuius sapientiam nos exosculari decet, non temere nos ipsos scandala obijcere.
units.tr: These examples should be observed, so that today we are not offended by the disagreements of famous teachers, nor doubt the truth of the Gospel because of them. This has happened to many today, whom that unhappy controversy over the Lord's Supper, which arose between Luther and Zwingli, most courageous men and restorers of the Christian faith and religion worthy of immortal praise, has so offended that they say they will remain within the Papist filth until they see that quarrel settled and removed from the midst. But what would those very men have done if they had lived in the times of the apostles, and had heard in the churches the names of Paulines, Cephasites and Apollonians, and had seen that some fought most fiercely for faith alone as justifying, against the righteousness of the Law, while others defended the same with no less stubbornness, and that on both sides the Christian name was claimed? Such is the fate of the Church, that it is exercised by the struggles of dissensions, and no one should be offended by these as if they were new and unusual. For these too have their use, and indeed one not to be regretted. For on such an occasion the truth is more diligently sifted, and many matters are examined, in which even good people cling too carelessly or superstitiously, unless they were drawn into controversy and disputation. This is known to have happened in the past, when it was useful to search more deeply into the use of the Law, from whose superstitious observance few would have withdrawn, unless those controversies had shown that it cannot agree with faith and justice. We may say the same of the sacramentarian contention, which greatly helped to expose and overthrow the worship of that fictitious and new god Mayzim, not to mention the other fruits that have sprung from it. Moreover, there is also this use of those contests: they free the herald of the Gospel from suspicion, that he might seem to act by prior arrangement and with evil guile. For who would think that they had conspired among themselves for their own private advantage, when he sees them disagree in many other matters, but agree only in those things that serve the glory of God and the illustration of Christ's merit? Thus the Lord makes good use of our weaknesses and faults, and it is fitting for us to embrace his wisdom, and not rashly to put stumbling blocks before ourselves.

units.la: Postremò, opportunitate oblata demum Apollo Corinthum venire voluit. Debent hu-ius etiam studiosi & diligentes obseruatores esse ministri: & de eo Christus admonet, quando dispensatorem constituit, qui non fidelis modo verumetiam prudens sit, & familiæ suæ dimensum suum depromat ἐν καιρῷ, id est, tempore opportuno, dum doctrinam pro temporis & loci ratione auditoribus accommodat. Erat hoc morosis illis & præcipitis ingenij rixatoribus obseruandum, qui tunc demum se zelo ardere & in Domini negotio feruere sibi persuadent, quando nulla vel locorum vel hominum ratione habita, omnia quam importunissimè faciunt. Sunt isti multos offendere & Euangelium illis exosum facere, qui si commodius tractarentur, lucrifieri, aut saltem contineri poterant, vt minus nocerent. Interim minimè eos probamus, qui cum ignaui & malæ frugis serui sint, prudentiæ titulum sibi vendicant, & opportunitatem nescio quam expectant, quam sibi ad Calendas Græcas dari vellent, ne quid fortiter & constanter agere cogerentur. Sunt hi cunctatores nocentissimi: quia dum prudentes & commodi videri volunt, pulcherrimas rei gerendæ occasiones præterlabi patiuntur. Singuli ergo opus Domini sedulò ac strenuè faciant, & in eo operas suas fideliter conferant, vt olim boni illi & fideles serui fuisse inueniantur, quos in gaudij sui societatem ingredi iubebit æternus Dei Filius, IESVS CHRISTVS: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Lastly, when the opportunity was at length offered, Apollos wished to come to Corinth. Ministers too ought to be eager and diligent observers of this same thing; and Christ admonishes about it when he appoints a steward who is not only faithful but also prudent, and who brings forth the portion for his household ἐν καιρῷ [en kairō], that is, in due time, while he adapts his teaching to the circumstances of time and place for his hearers. Those peevish and hot-headed brawlers ought to have observed this, who persuade themselves that they then burn with zeal and glow in the Lord's business, when, with no regard for places or people, they do everything as unseasonably as possible. Such men offend many and make the Gospel hateful to them, whereas, if they had been handled more suitably, they could have been won over, or at least restrained so that they did less harm. Meanwhile we by no means approve of those who, though they are lazy and worthless servants, claim for themselves the title of prudence and wait for some opportunity or other, which they would like to be given to them at the Greek Calends, so that they are never forced to act boldly and steadfastly. These laggards are most harmful, since, while they wish to seem prudent and considerate, they allow the finest occasions for doing their work to slip by. Let each one therefore carry out the work of the Lord diligently and vigorously, and devote his labours to it faithfully, so that he may be found to have been one of those good and faithful servants whom the eternal Son of God, JESUS CHRIST, will bid enter into the fellowship of his joy: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XCIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XCIII.

units.la: Vigilate, state in fide, viriliter agite, estote fortes. Omnia vestra cum charitate fiant.
units.tr: Watch, stand fast in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all your things be done in love.

units.la: Disseruit hucusque Paulus de omnibus iis, quae in Corinthiorum Ecclesia emendationem opus habebant, & postremo moram suam excusauit, qua suum ad ipsos aduentum hu-usque distulerat, commendauit autem quam diligentissime discipulum suum & collegam fidelissimum, Timotheum, quem ideo cum literis hisce misit, ut quaedam apud eos in memoriam restitueret. His in praesenti doctrinam generalem subijcit, quam antidoti instar vitiis illorum omnibus opponit, & quae paucis capitibus siue aphorismis omnia complectitur, quae hucusque prolixius dicta sunt. In eo autem fidei praeceptoris, vel potius pij parentis officio fungitur, dum memoriae eorum consulit, & ea tradit, quae ipsi sibi subinde occinant, ne de rebus obseruatu necessarijs cogitandi occasio unquam ipsis desit. Quia autem iisdem vitiis hodie etiam passim laboratur, eadem praecepta non minus ad nos pertinere putabimus, ut secundum ea vitam & mores instituamus.
units.tr: Up to this point Paul has discussed all those matters which needed correction in the congregation of the Corinthians. Finally he excused his delay in coming to them until now, and he commended most earnestly his disciple and faithful colleague Timothy, whom he sent with this letter so that he might bring certain things back to their memory. Here he adds a general teaching, which he sets against all their faults as an antidote, and which sums up in a few heads or maxims everything said at greater length so far. In doing this he acts as a teacher of the faith, or rather as a loving parent, when he takes care of their memory and hands on the things they should repeat to themselves from time to time, so that they never lack occasion to think about the matters that must be observed. Since these same faults are still widespread today, we shall judge that these same precepts apply no less to us, so that we may order our life and conduct according to them.

units.la: Principio vigilare iubet. Non loquitur autem de corporis vigilia aut Monachorum matutinis, quae cum nihil aliud quam corporalem exercitationem habeant, parum aut nihil prosunt in aeternae salutis negotio. Itaque ad animum hoc praeceptum transferri debet, & similitudine constat, quae ex re militari desumpta causa praesenti probe seruit. Est enim vita haec nostra instar militiae, & ut in bello propter hostium insidias & improuisas incursiones atque assultus excubijs perpetuis opus est: ita ut nos quoque semper vigilemus necesse est, quando nobis certamen est perpetuum cum Satana, qui nunquam quiescit, sed leonis rugientis instar semper obambulat, & quaerit quem deuoret. Opponitur ergo vigilia, quam Paulus nobis mandat, somno animi, qui non alius est, quam securitas, qua interni sensus & animi vires constringuntur, ut officio suo non possint defungi. Ut enim somnus corporis ex vaporibus in caput euectis nascitur, qui cerebri frigiditate repressi per corpus totum diffunduntur, & sensuum organa inuadunt atque ligant, ut ad tempus in officio cessent: ita in anima hominis simile quid fieri solet. Surgunt enim ex hereditaria natura nostra prauitate enati pessimarum cupiditatum atque noxiorum affectuum vapor[?]es: qui nisi mox vehementiori aliquo spiritu & mentis diuina motu excutiantur, ipsam rationem atque intellectum inuadunt & occupant, denique impediunt, ne per necessarias cogitationes discurrere, & ea meditari possit, sine quibus salus nostra non consistit. Et quemadmodum dormientibus animae vis imaginatiua siue phantastica omnis generis insomnia gignit, quae plerunque ridicula & ludicra sunt, aut inanibus terriculamentis nos exagitant (de naturalibus somnijs loquor, non de iis, quae Deus interdum immittit, ut de malis impendentibus aut aliis rebus cognitu necessarijs admoneat, qualia Pharaonis, Iacobi, Solomonis, Nabuchodonozoris, & multorum aliorum fuerunt) ita quorum animas sopor ille spiritualis siue securitas occupauit, ij nihil quidem eorum meditantur & agunt, quae hominem Christianum decent, circa ea autem occupantur, quae aut voluptati & libidini seruiunt, aut animos curis & terroribus vanis atque inutilibus fatigant. Fit ergo tunc quod in zizaniorum parabola Christus docet: ut nimirum hoc somno exitiali oppressis diabolus pessimarum cupiditatum suggestiones aspergat, dogmata falsa inuehat, superstitionibus fascinet, & infinita alia obijciat, quae saluti nostrae officiunt. Et hoc Corinthijs accidisse scimus, qui si probe vigilauissent, neque locum dedissent huic securitati, nunquam tot vitijs & erroribus Ecclesiam illorum aggrauauisset diabolus per suos satellites, pseudoapostolos nimirum, sectarios & mundo carnique addictos homines. Opponit ergo hunc aphorismum illorum socordiae Paulus, & ut in posterum vigilantiores sint admonet.
units.tr: First he bids them watch. He is not speaking of bodily watchfulness or of the monks' matins, which, since they have nothing but bodily exercise, do little or no good in the business of eternal salvation. This precept must therefore be transferred to the mind, and the comparison, taken from military affairs, serves the present purpose well. For this life of ours is like a campaign. As in war, because of the enemy's ambushes and unforeseen attacks and assaults, there is need of constant sentries, so we too must always keep watch, since we have a perpetual struggle with Satan, who never rests but, like a roaring lion, always prowls about seeking whom he may devour. Paul therefore sets the watchfulness he commands against the sleep of the mind, which is nothing other than carelessness, by which the inner senses and the powers of the soul are bound so that they cannot perform their duty. For just as bodily sleep arises from vapours carried up into the head, which, held back by the coolness of the brain, spread through the whole body and invade and bind the organs of the senses, so that for a time they cease from their work, so something similar usually happens in the soul of man. For from our hereditary corruption there arise vapours of the worst desires and harmful passions, which, unless they are soon shaken off by some more vehement breath and by a divine movement of the mind, invade and occupy reason and understanding itself, and finally prevent it from running through the necessary thoughts and meditating on those things without which our salvation does not stand. And just as in sleepers the imaginative or fantastic power of the soul produces dreams of every kind, which are mostly silly and playful, or else trouble us with empty terrors (I am speaking of natural dreams, not of those which God sometimes sends to warn of impending evils or other matters needful to know, such as those of Pharaoh, Jacob, Solomon, Nebuchadnezzar and many others), so those whose souls that spiritual drowsiness or carelessness has seized do not indeed think about or do those things which befit a Christian man, but busy themselves with things that serve either pleasure and lust, or wear down their minds with vain and useless cares and terrors. Then happens what Christ teaches in the parable of the tares: the devil, of course, sprinkles upon those oppressed by this deadly sleep the suggestions of the worst desires, introduces false doctrines, bewitches them with superstitions, and throws in countless other things that stand in the way of our salvation. We know that this happened among the Corinthians, who, if they had kept watch properly and not given room to this carelessness, the devil would never have burdened their Church with so many vices and errors through his henchmen, namely false apostles, sectaries and men given over to the world and the flesh. Paul therefore sets this maxim against their laziness and warns them to be more watchful in future.

units.la: At nos meminisse debemus, praeceptum hoc generale esse, & imprimis nostro saeculo conuenire. Huic enim Christus exitialem illam somnolentiam tribuit, quando nouissimorum temporum homines eorum similes fore dicit, qui olim ante diluuium & Lothi saeculo vixerunt. Et si mores spectes quibus hodie vivitur, non tam dormire, quam stupore plus quam belluino plerique superati & oppressi videri possunt. Grassatur enim passim impietas, & impune dicuntur & fiunt, quæ Dei gloriam imminuunt atque impediunt. Dogmata subinde noua inuchunt homines ambitiosi & superstitionibus editi. In mille locis monstratur Christus, & in mille sectas scissi sunt, qui omnes sub illo, seu vnico capite, consentire debebant. Ferent[?] passim bella cum externa tum ciuilia: nihil à proditionibus & insidijs tutum est. Fiunt prodigia omnis generis, & in cunctis mundi partibus signa ea apparent, de quibus nos Christus præmonuit, & quibus visis iussit capita attollere. Quotus vero quisque est, qui ista excitetur, vt de salute vel publica vel priuata seriò cogitet? Omnes fere ista negligunt, & vel fortuita esse arbitrantur, vel naturales rerum causas scrutantur, veras autem & in nostris moribus hærentes supina oscitantia[?] prætereunt. Fit ergo, vt quoad aliquas spes, vel potius inanis species quietis affulget, quæ nos à malis impendentibus nonnihil respirare finit, somno huic nos dedamus, & discipulos imitemur, qui ad montem Oliueti dormiebant interea, dum Christus cum horrendis mortis appropinquantis[?] terroribus luctabatur. Quid ergo miramur, si Iudas & pontificum cohortes nobis submittat Deus, qui nos armata manu excitent, & vel inuitos vigilare cogant? Nobis igitur Paulum loqui putemus, vt & Christum, qui idem monens discipulis dicebat: Quod vobis dico, omnibus dico: Vigilate. Est autem hæc vere salutaris atque necessaria vigilantia, vt procul reliquis mundi huius curis atque studijs, ea meditemur & quæramus quæ Dei sunt, & saluti æternæ næ seruiunt.
units.tr: But we ought to remember that this precept is general and especially suited to our own age. Christ attributes this deadly drowsiness to this age, when he says that the men of the last times will be like those who lived in the days before the flood and in the days of Lot. And if you look at the morals by which people live today, many can be seen to be overcome and oppressed not so much by sleep as by a stupor more than bestial. Impiety rages everywhere, and things that diminish and obstruct the glory of God are said and done with impunity. Ambitious men, puffed up with superstitions, bring in new doctrines from time to time. Christ is shown in a thousand places, and men are split into a thousand sects, though all of them ought to agree under that one Head. Wars, both foreign and civil, are waged everywhere; nothing is safe from betrayals and ambushes. Portents of every kind appear, and in all parts of the world those signs appear of which Christ forewarned us and at whose sight he bade us lift up our heads. But how few are roused by these things to think seriously about salvation, whether public or private? Almost everyone neglects them, and either judges them to be accidents or inquires into the natural causes of things, while they pass by the true signs that cling to our morals with idle yawning. So it happens that, as some hope, or rather an empty semblance of quiet, shines forth which allows us to breathe a little from the evils hanging over us, we give ourselves over to this sleep and imitate the disciples who slept on the Mount of Olives while Christ wrestled with the dreadful terrors of approaching death. Why then do we wonder if God should send us a Judas and the cohorts of the chief priests, who rouse us with armed hand and compel us to keep watch even against our will? Let us therefore take it that Paul is speaking to us, as Christ also did when, giving the same warning to his disciples, he said: What I say to you I say to all: Watch. This watchfulness is truly salutary and necessary, so that, far from the other cares and pursuits of this world, we may meditate on and seek those things which belong to God and serve eternal salvation.

units.la: Secundum huius loci præceptum est: State in fide. Perseuerantiam & constantiam requirit, & hanc opponit ipsorum leuitati, qua se tam cito passi erant adduci, vt reliqua simplici Veritatis doctrina incertis opinionibus fluctuarent. Etenim vt omnia alia nunc omittamus, leuitas magna & euidens fidei turpiter vacillantis argumentum fuit, quod ijs locum dabant, qui mortuorum resurrectionem in dubium vocare audebant, deque ea non absque scurrili dicacitate philosophabantur. Merito igitur constantiam in illis requirit, quæ vt in omnibus aliis institutis necessaria est; ita imprimis in fide & religione exigitur. Nam Christo teste, qui vbi manum aratro admoue-runt, à tergo respectant, non sunt idonei ad Regnum Dei, sed is demum saluus erit, qui in finem vsque perseuerauerit. Qui vero à Veritate agnita deficiunt, & fidem turpiter negant, eorum postrema primis deteriora fiunt. Solet enim fere leuitas illa abnegandi in peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum degenerare, nisi mox denuo collectis animi viribus ad mentem redeamus.
units.tr: The second precept of this passage is: Stand fast in the faith. It requires perseverance and constancy, and sets it against their fickleness, by which they had been so quickly led to let go of the simple teaching of the truth and to waver in uncertain opinions. For, to pass over all other things for now, that great and obvious fickleness was a sign of faith shamefully wavering, since they gave room to those who dared to call the resurrection of the dead into doubt and debated about it with no small amount of scurrilous wit. Rightly therefore he requires constancy from them, which is necessary in all other undertakings and is especially demanded in faith and religion. For Christ bears witness that those who put their hand to the plough and look back are not fit for the kingdom of God, but he alone will be saved who perseveres to the end. Those who fall away from the truth once known and shamefully deny the faith end up worse at the last than at the first. For that fickleness of denying usually degenerates into sin against the Holy Spirit, unless we quickly return to our senses by gathering the strength of our minds again.

units.la: Obseruabis autem, quòd nos non stare modo, sed in fide stare iubet. Atqui fidei fundamentum est Christus, extra quem aliud poni non potest, vt alibi prolixè satis demonstrauimus: Fidei autem regula Verbum Dei est, ex quo illa nascitur, secundùm illud Pauli: Fides ex auditu est, auditus autem ex Verbo Dei. Ergò in fide stant, qui Christo vni fidunt & adhærent, sicuti Dei Verbo edocentur, ideò vt ab huius præscripto se neque ad dextram neque ad sinistram abduci patiantur. Huc enim imprimis pertinet, quod Moses in Lege dicit: Ne deflectas à cunctis sermonibus, quos ego præcipio vobis hodie, neque ad dextram neque ad sinistram, vt eas post Deos alios, & eos colas. Dicuntur autem ad sinistra deflectere, qui aperta contumacia à Dei præceptis resiliunt, nè debitam illi obedientiam præstent. Ad dextram verò deflectunt, quotquot bona animi intentione nouos cultus sibi fingunt, vel etiam Christum longè alium fabricant, quàm in Euangelio ille describitur. Fecerunt hoc olim multi, & quàm difficile sit vtrumque diuerticulum cauere, exemplo nostri sæculi infinita docent. Nam etsi plerique intelligant; nulla venia dignos esse eos, qui Deum omnino negant & obsequium omne detrectant, ijdem tamen fere suis rationibus decipiuntur, & dum sibi licere putant, vt ex suo cerebro fidei articulos nouos constituant, nomen quidem Christi plenis buccis iactant, eiusdem verò merito seipsos spoliant, dum non illi vni fidunt, sedque illi vni debetur, gloriam, vel sibi ipsis & operum suorum meritis, vel creaturis tribuunt. Non temere ergo Deus tot Legis suæ monumenta in postibus, ianuis & vestibus extare voluit, quæ illam Israëlitis in mentem reuocarent. Et hodie magnus huius aphorismi vsus est, quando vndique omnis generis tentationes nobis obiiciuntur, quibus fides nostra oppugnatur. Debent autem in illis nos intrepidos facere promissiones, quibus nos Deus armauit. Apud Isaiam certè, cùm de lapide illo pretioso disseruisset, qui Zionis aut Ecclesiæ fundamentum esse debuit, addit tandem: Quisquis credit in eum, non pudefiet. Et Christus de seipso pronuntiat: Super hanc petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam, & portae inferorum non praevalebunt aduersus eam. Item: In mundo afflictionem habebitis, sed estote bono animo, ego vici mundum. Ecce ego vobiscum sum usque in consummationem saeculi. Ioan.16. Matth. 28.
units.tr: Notice, moreover, that he bids them not merely to stand, but to stand in the faith. Now the foundation of the faith is Christ, beside whom no other can be laid, as we have shown at length elsewhere. The rule of faith is the Word of God, from which faith is born, according to Paul's words: Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the Word of God. Therefore those stand in the faith who trust in and cling to Christ alone, as they are taught by the Word of God, so that they do not allow themselves to be drawn away from its prescription either to the right or to the left. To this belongs above all what Moses says in the Law: Do not turn aside from any of the words which I command you today, neither to the right nor to the left, that you go after other gods and serve them. Those are said to turn aside to the left who openly rebel with stubbornness against God's commands, so as not to render him the obedience they owe. Those turn aside to the right who, with a good intention of mind, invent new forms of worship for themselves, or even fashion a Christ quite different from the one described in the Gospel. Many have done this in former times, and the examples of our own age teach us countless things about how hard it is to guard against either byway. For although most men understand that those who utterly deny God and refuse all obedience deserve no pardon, yet nearly the same men are deceived by their own reasonings, and while they think it lawful to set up new articles of faith out of their own brains, they boast of the name of Christ with full cheeks, yet rightly strip themselves of him, since they do not trust in him alone, and they give to creatures or to themselves and the merits of their works the glory that is due to him alone. It was not without reason, then, that God wished so many monuments of his Law to stand on doorposts, gates and clothing, to call it back to the minds of the Israelites. And today this maxim is of great use, when temptations of every kind are thrown at us from all sides, by which our faith is assailed. In such cases we ought to be made fearless by the promises with which God has armed us. In Isaiah, certainly, after he had spoken of that precious stone which was to be the foundation of Zion or the Church, he finally adds: Whoever believes in him will not be put to shame. And Christ pronounces of himself: Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. Likewise: In the world you will have tribulation, but be of good cheer, I have overcome the world. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age. John 16. Matt. 28.

units.la: Pertinet huc etiam tertius aphorismus, quo nos viriliter agere & fortes esse iubet. Ἀνδρίζεσθε[?] Graecus significat ea facere, quae viros decent. At viri est, non pusillanimis, neq; molliculum aut formidolosum esse, sed res honestas & factu necessarias magno animo aggredi, neq; ullis periculis succumbere. Ideo expositionis loco subiicit, κραταιοῦσθε[?], id est, fortes estote, aut robusti. Id vero ad constantiam, de qua modo diximus, imprimis facit, sicuti ad Ephesios Cap.4. Paulus ipse docet, vt hunc ministerij Ecclesiastici finem omnibus nobis propositum esse vult, vt omnes euadamus in vi-rum perfectum, in mensuram staturae adulti Christi, & ne amplius simus pueri, qui fluctuemus & circumferamur quouis vento doctrinae, denique vt veritatem sectantes cum charitate, adolesca-mus in illum per omnia, qui est caput, nempe Christus.
units.tr: This also belongs here: the third maxim, by which he bids us to act manfully and be strong. The Greek word means to do the things that befit men [Ἀνδρίζεσθε]. But it is the mark of a man not to be faint-hearted or timid, but to undertake honourable and necessary things with a great spirit and not to give way to any dangers. So, by way of explanation, he adds, "be strong" or "be robust" [κραταιοῦσθε]. This especially serves the steadfastness of which we have just spoken, just as Paul himself teaches in Ephesians 4, where he sets this as the goal of the ecclesiastical ministry for all of us: that we all grow into a perfect man, into the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ; that we be no longer children, tossed about and carried along by every wind of doctrine; and finally, that pursuing the truth in love, we grow up in all things into him who is the head, namely Christ.

units.la: Peccant ergo in hoc Apostoli praeceptu: Primo, qui nihil certi habent in fide & religione, sed omnia in dubium vocant, & proinde in horas mutantur: quales hodie multos esse videre, qui tunc demum se prae aliis sapere putant, si quotidie novum aliquid in medium proferant, quo euangelicae doctrinae Veritas labefactatur. Et hi seipsos sponte impostoribus ludificandos praebent. Deinde peccant etiam, qui ad quamuis periculi qualiscunque mentionem trepidant, neque consolationes admittunt, quas Deus in Scripturis solidas & efficaces nobis offert. Cadit quidem in sanctissimos quoque Dei seruos interdum metus & trepidatio, sicuti in Mose, Iosua, Dauide, prophetis & Apostolis videmus: & Paulus supra se apud Corinthios cum timore & tremore multo versatum fuisse fatetur. In eo autem pij a prophanis differunt, quod hi omnes consolationem respuunt, & in periculis mox desperant, si nullum in humanis praesidium appareat: illi vero Deum consolatorem audiunt, & licet aliquando carnis infirmitate tententur, mox tamen spe nova concepta, eo firmius Deo adhaerent, quo minus spei in hominibus reliquum esse vident. Et hi reuera sese viros praebent, cum degeneres animos (vt Poeta verbis vtar) timor arguat. Nec minor eorum hic culpa est, qui animos effeminatos et pueriles producunt morum leuitate, vestitu molliori, incessu fracto, gestibus ad lasciuiam compositis, dictis item & factis petulantioribus. Erant omnia haec nimis vulgaria apud Corinthios, cum luxu & libidine diffluerent, & inter sacra habitu prophano ethnicos imitarentur, sicuti Cap. Vndecimo audiuimus. Quàm vero incerti rerum in religione fuerint, vnicus resurrectionis mortuorum articulus abunde ostendit, de quo illos dubitasse constat. Quis autem satis animosos & fortes in periculis eos fuisse crediderit, quibus praecipua adeoque vnica salutis spes dubia atque incerta fluctuabat? Recte ergo illis hoc antidotum Apostolus adhibet, vt animos viriles induant, & fortes sint in Domino. Et debent hodie etiam a Christianis principibus alienissima esse, quae modo in Corinthiorum moribus reprehendimus. Illorum enim est salem[?] illum Euangelicum spirare, & eo condire dicta factaq; sua omnia, vt in ipsis glorificetur Pater ille coelestis, qui illos totos sibi consecratos esse vult.
units.tr: Those who sin against this apostolic precept are, first, those who have nothing certain in faith and religion, but call everything into doubt, and so change with the hour. Many such people are to be seen today, who think themselves wiser than others only if they bring something new into the open every day, by which the truth of the evangelical doctrine is undermined. Such people willingly expose themselves to be deceived by impostors. Next, those also sin who tremble at the mere mention of any sort of danger and do not accept the consolations which God offers us in the Scriptures as solid and effective. Fear and trembling sometimes fall even upon the holiest servants of God, as we see in Moses, Joshua, David, the prophets and the apostles; and Paul confesses that he himself was among the Corinthians "in fear and much trembling." The difference between the godly and the profane, however, is this: the latter all reject consolation and at once despair in dangers if no human help appears; the former hear God as their comforter, and although they are sometimes assailed by the weakness of the flesh, yet, once a new hope has been conceived, they cling to God all the more firmly, the less hope they see remaining in men. These are truly showing themselves to be men, whereas fear betrays degenerate spirits (to use the poet's words). Nor is the fault of those less who produce effeminate and childish spirits by the frivolity of their manners: by softer clothing, broken gait, gestures composed for wantonness, and likewise by more wanton words and deeds. All these things were far too common among the Corinthians, who were steeped in luxury and lust and, among the sacred things, imitated the heathen in their profane conduct, as we heard in chapter eleven. How uncertain they were about the matters of religion, the single article of the resurrection of the dead clearly shows, for it is evident that they doubted it. Yet who would believe that they were sufficiently spirited and brave in dangers, when their one and only, and therefore chief, hope of salvation was wavering and uncertain? Rightly, then, the Apostle applies this antidote to them, that they may put on manly spirits and be strong in the Lord. And today, too, those things which we have just rebuked in the morals of the Corinthians ought to be utterly alien to Christian princes. For it is theirs to breathe that evangelical salt and to season all their words and deeds with it, so that the heavenly Father, who wishes them wholly consecrated to himself, may be glorified in them.

units.la: Vtinam vero huius praecepti apostolici perpetuo memores essent omnes ij, qui nomen Christia-num profitentur. Etenim si plerosque propius contemplemur, mox videbis, quàm procul ab illis animi illi viriles recesserint. Renascente primum Euangelij luce passim inueniebantur inter principes viros & vrbium magistratus, inter doctores item & plebeios homines, qui contemptis omnibus periculis nihil non audebant pro instauranda Veritatis doctrina: Condebantur ab illis ipsis hominibus leges contra luxum, intemperantiam, libidinem & alia vitia, quae cum Christiani nominis professione pugnant: nec minori zelo & feruore iidem leges abs se conditas defendebant. At quae nostri saeculi est infelicitas, hodie ad vnius Monachi vocem & Episcopi alicuius personati omnes terrentur, & ceruorum instar arrectis auribus & corde palpitante astant, quidq; faciant nesciunt. In vitijs vero & sceleribus plerique nimium audaces legum omnium laqueos, seu aranearum telas, perrumpunt. Incessus, colloquia, cantilenae animos libidini & voluptatibus deditos arguunt. Vestitus vero non mollitiem modo plus quàm muliebrem refert, sed portentosam proteruitatem spirat: quo fit, vt hodie Turcis aliisque nationibus exteris ludibrio sint Germani, qui olim a virilitate nomen accepisse nonnullis dicuntur, quod Germani, id est, toti viri sint, & nihil in semetipsis muliebre aut effœminatum habeant.
units.tr: Would that all who profess the Christian name were always mindful of this apostolic precept. For if we look more closely at most people, you will soon see how far those manly spirits have departed from them. When the light of the Gospel was first reborn, such men were found everywhere: among princely men and the magistrates of cities, among teachers likewise and among plebeian folk, who, despising all dangers, dared everything to restore the doctrine of the truth. Laws against luxury, intemperance, lust and other vices which conflict with the profession of the Christian name were enacted by these very men, and with no less zeal and fervour they defended the laws they had enacted. But such is the unhappiness of our age that today, at the voice of a single monk or some bishop in disguise, everyone is terrified and stands like stags, ears pricked and hearts pounding, not knowing what to do. Yet in vices and crimes many are far too bold, and they break through all the snares of the laws, or the spiderwebs. Their gait, conversations and songs betray minds given over to lust and pleasures. Their clothing not only displays a softness more than womanly, but breathes a monstrous shamelessness. As a result, today the Germans, who are said by some to have received their name from manliness, because "Germani" means "wholly men" and they have nothing womanly or effeminate in themselves, have become a laughingstock to the Turks and to other foreign nations.

units.la: Restat postremus aphorismus, quem sic enuntiat Paulus: Omnia vestra cum charitate fiant. Oportuit autem hunc prioribus adijci, quia in Corinthijs charitas imprimis desiderabatur, qui eam potissimum ob causam tam turpiter degenerauerant, quod à charitate iampridem alieni fuissent. Etenim si huic fluduissent[?], tum neque in sectas suam Ecclesiam distrahi passi fuissent, neque lites moviissent fratribus apud infidelium iudicum tribunalia, neque idolothytorum esu & sacrorum gentilium communione fratres infirmiores offendissent, neque in Cœna Domini mystica egenos neglexissent, multo minus autem donis spiritualibus abusi fuissent cum publico totius Ecclesiæ scandalo & fratrum suorum contemptu. Ideo graviter admodum de hac re præcipit. Omnia vestra, inquit: & ita omnes illorum actiones, studia, consilia, vitam denique universam uno verbo comprehendit.
units.tr: There remains the last maxim, which Paul states thus: "Let all your things be done in love." This had to be added to the earlier ones, because love was especially lacking among the Corinthians, who had degenerated so shamefully for this very reason: that they had long been strangers to love. For if love had flowed into them, they would neither have allowed their church to be torn into factions, nor stirred up lawsuits against their brothers before the tribunals of unbelieving judges, nor offended weaker brothers by eating idol-meats and taking part in pagan sacrifices, nor neglected the poor at the mystical Lord's Supper; much less would they have abused the spiritual gifts to the public scandal of the whole church and the contempt of their brothers. Therefore he instructs about this matter very earnestly. "All your things," he says; and so with one word he embraces all their actions, pursuits, counsels and, in short, their whole life.

units.la: Item, Fiant cum charitate. Non dicit: In omnibus charitatem simulate, aut huius officia inuicem verbis blandiusculis pollicemini: sed omnia fiant cum charitate, id est, ita fiant, ut charitatem factis et re ipsa testemini. Facit ad huius loci expositionem, quod dilectus ille discipulus, Ioannes, scribit: Filioli mei, ne diligamus verbo, neq; lingua, sed opere & veritate. Item: Si quis habuerit facultates mundi, & viderit fratrem suum egentem, & clauserit viscera sua coram eo, quomodo charitas Dei manet in eo? Quibus consentit quod Iacobus de charitate, vero fidei viuentis indicio sive argumento, dicit: Quod si frater aut soror nudi fuerint, & egentes quotidiano victu: dicat autem eis aliquis vestrum, Abite cum pace, calescite & saturemini: non autem dederitis eis quæ sunt apta corpori, quæ erit utilitas? Itaque ij demum omnia cum charitate faciunt, qui suarum actionum & consiliorum hunc sibi scopum proponunt, ut ijs prosint & subueniant, quos opus indigos esse vident. Et proprijssime hoc de charitate dicitur: quia quamuis ea in unimi affectione cosistat, tanta tamen eius vis est, ut totum hominem in eius, quem complectitur, obsequium rapiat, & ideo otiari non potest, sed semper cum ἔργῳ[?] coniuncta est, sicuti in parabola Samaritani docemur, qua Christus illius ingenium & effecta omnia depinxit.
units.tr: Likewise, "Let them be done in love." He does not say, "Pretend love in all things, or promise one another the duties of love with flattering words," but let all things be done in love, that is, let them be done in such a way that you bear witness to love by your deeds and in reality. The beloved disciple John writes something that bears on the exposition of this passage: "My little children, let us not love in word or in tongue, but in deed and in truth." Again: "If anyone has the goods of the world, and sees his brother in need, and shuts up his bowels against him, how does the love of God abide in him?" Such things agree with what James says about love, the true sign or proof of living faith: "If a brother or sister is naked and in lack of daily food, and one of you says to them, 'Go in peace, be warmed and filled,' but you do not give them the things that are needed for the body, what good is it?" Thus those alone do all things in love who set this aim before themselves in their actions and counsels: that they may benefit and help those whom they see to be in need. And this is said most properly of love, because although it consists in an affection of the mind, its power is so great that it draws the whole man into the service of the one it embraces; and so it cannot be idle, but is always joined with works [ἔργῳ], as we are taught in the parable of the Good Samaritan, in which Christ depicted its nature and all its deeds.

units.la: Obseruabis autem, hic quoque generalem doctrinam proponi, quæ ad omnis loci & ordinis homines pertinet. Est enim charitas propria & communis omnium Christianorum nota siue tessera, ex qua illi dignoscuntur. Hoc est præceptum meum (inquit Dominus) ut diligatis alij alios, prout dilexi vos. Item: Mandatum nouum do vobis, ut alij alios diligatis: sicut (inquā) dilexi vos, ut etiā diligatis alij alios. Ex hoc omnes cognoscent vos esse discipulos meos, si charitate habueritis alij in alios. Et in magno illo die, quo omnes ad Christi tribunal sistemur, ex charitatis operibus suos agnoscet ille, qui ipsum fide vera amplexi sunt atq; coluerunt. Quibus adde, quod ne præstantissimis quidem donis quicquam proficitur absq; charitate, qua de re supra Cap. decimo tertio abunde est dictum. Hæc enim (ut Chrysostomus scripsit) vinculum est perfectionis, radix item atque fons bonorum omnium. Hæc sola affectus prauos corrigit, æmulationem, inuidiam, odium, simultates, iram & huic coniunctam vindictæ cupiditatem reflinguit: hæc auaritiæ insatiabiles motus frænat, fraudes, impostoras, rapinas & quæ alia sunt huius generis prohibet: eadem superbiæ spiritus deprimit, & proximi contemptum procul arcet. Per illam denique Lex impletur, quæ tota (ut ipse Christus docuit) sub charitatis gemina, Dei nimirum & proximi, præcepto comprehenditur. Debet ergo hæc nobis esse totius vitæ atq; actionum nostrarum omnium regula atq; gubernatrix.
units.tr: You will observe, moreover, that here too a general doctrine is set forth, one that pertains to people of every place and rank. For love is the proper and common mark or token of all Christians, by which they are recognised. "This is my commandment," says the Lord, "that you love one another, as I have loved you." Again: "I give you a new commandment, that you love one another; as I have loved you, so also you should love one another. By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another." And on that great day, when we all are brought before the judgment-seat of Christ, he will recognise by the works of love those who embraced and worshipped him with true faith. To these add that not even the most excellent gifts profit anything without love, a matter which has been discussed at length above in chapter thirteen. For love (as Chrysostom wrote) is the bond of perfection, and likewise the root and fountain of all good things. It alone corrects depraved affections, restrains emulation, envy, hatred, quarrels and anger, and the desire for revenge joined with it; it bridles the insatiable movements of avarice and forbids frauds, deceits, robberies and other things of this kind; it likewise humbles the spirit of pride and keeps far away the contempt of one's neighbour. Finally, through love the Law is fulfilled, which as a whole (as Christ himself taught) is comprehended under the twofold command of love, namely of God and of neighbour. Therefore this should be for us the rule and guide of our whole life and of all our actions.

units.la: Cæterum elucet hoc loco humani ingenij vitiositas & peruersitas. Fatentur enim ipsud, quod modò diximus, omnes homines: sed quam pauci charitatis norma in studijs atque actionibus suis vrantur, res ipsa loquitur. Regnat vbique insaturata habendi cupido, quæ omnis generis vitia parit. Comitatur hanc luxus & intemperantia, cum impio pauperum contemptu coiuncta. Multis verò non satis est hos contempsisse, nisi insuper eosdem deprædentur, spolient, deglubant, ut luxui et fastui suo possint sufficere. Sequitur licentia morum & effrenis legum sanctissimarum coculcatio. Quid verò de vagis libidinibus dicam, in quibus nulla amicitiarum, hospitalis iuris, affinitatis, cognationis, & sæpe ne religionis quidem ratio habetur? Et cùm hæc communia vitia sint, quibus plerique laborant, alij tamen alijs inuident, quæ causa est odiorum, simultatum, calumniarum, dissidiorum, quæ plerunque ad Ecclesiam & Rempub. redundant, ut lites non necessariæ moveantur, & inter se hostiliter digladiantur, quorum vnanimi coofilio[?] atque consensu pax publica conservari debebat. Accedunt his mala ius venale, exactiones immodicae, bella non necessaria, in quibus quaestus honestissimus iam putatur homines innoxios ingulare, praedas agere, sacra et prophana diripere, viduas et orphanos affligere, caedibus deniq; incendijs et stupris omnia miscere. Et horum fere authores sunt potentissimi orbis Monarchae, quibus deinde ad tam nefaria flagitia operam suam locant homines venales, quibus illic ius esse videtur, vbi maxima merces. Quis ergo de nostri seculi Christianus dicere possit, eos (quod hic Apostolus monet) omnia cum charitate facere? Quis non potius ea tempora agnoscat, de quibus Christus pronuntiauit: Quia multiplicata erit iniqui-tas, refrigescet charitas multorum? Item: Cum venerit Filius hominis, num reperturus est fidem in terra? Queruntur de his omnes, sed qui de remedio cogitent serio, paucissimi sunt. Remedium vero vnicum et praesentissimum erit, Charitas, si huius ignem omnes animis suis conci-piant, et conceptu mutuis officijs fouere et conseruare pergant. Vbi multum proderit expendisse diligenter Dei bonitatem et quae nobis in Christo contulit beneficia. Horum consideratio nos illius amore accender, quem proximi dilectio mox sequetur. At illorum cognitio ex Dei Verbo hauritur. Huic ergo omnes studeant, et eidem preces coniungant ardentes, vt Deus suam charitatem per omnium corda diffundere dignetur, nobisque largiri, vt ipsius dictata atque iussa secu-ti olim a Filio suo dilecto, IESV CHRISTO, pro fratribus germanis et coheredibus agnoscamur, cumque eo in caelis viuamus, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria et potestas in aeter-num, Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, the wickedness and perversity of the human mind come to light here. All men admit what we have just said, but how few use the rule of charity in their pursuits and actions the facts themselves show. Everywhere an insatiable desire for possession reigns, and it gives birth to every kind of vice. Luxury and intemperance accompany it, joined with a cruel contempt for the poor. For many it is not enough to despise them, unless they also plunder them, strip them and flay them, so that they can satisfy their luxury and pride. Lawlessness of conduct follows, and the unbridled trampling of the most holy laws. And what shall I say of wandering lusts, in which no regard is had for friendship, the law of hospitality, kinship, blood relationship, and often not even for religion? Although these are common vices from which most people suffer, some envy others, and this is the cause of hatreds, quarrels, slanders and dissensions, which for the most part spill over into the Church and the commonwealth, so that unnecessary lawsuits are started and men fight one another like enemies, when public peace ought to have been preserved by their united counsel and agreement. To these are added the evils of venal justice, immoderate exactions, and unnecessary wars, in which it is now thought a most honourable gain to slaughter innocent men, carry off booty, plunder sacred and profane things alike, afflict widows and orphans, and finally mix everything up with murders, fires and rapes. The authors of these things are for the most part the most powerful monarchs of the world, and they then hire out their services for such nefarious crimes to men who sell themselves, for whom justice seems to lie wherever the greatest reward is. Which Christian of our age, then, could say that they do (as the Apostle here warns) all things in charity? Who does not rather recognise those times of which Christ pronounced: "Because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold"; and again: "When the Son of man comes, shall he find faith on the earth?" All complain of these things, but very few think seriously about a remedy. The only and most immediate remedy will be charity, if all kindle its fire in their minds, and once kindled, go on cherishing and preserving it by mutual services. Here it will be very helpful to weigh carefully the goodness of God and the benefits he has bestowed on us in Christ. The consideration of these things kindles us with love for him, and love of neighbour will soon follow. But the knowledge of these things is drawn from the Word of God. Let all therefore strive for this, and join to it fervent prayers, that God may deign to pour out his charity into the hearts of all, and grant us that, following his precepts and commands, we may be acknowledged by his beloved Son, JESUS CHRIST, as brothers and fellow heirs, and live with him in heaven, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XCIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XCIIII.

units.la: Precor autem vos fratres, nostis familiā Stephanae esse primi-tias Achaiae, et seipsos in ministerium sanctis ordinauisse: Vt et vos subijciamini talibus, et cuiuis operam suam conferenti et la-boranti. Gaudeo autem de aduentu Stephanae et Fortunati et Achaici: quoniam absentiam vestram hi suppleuerunt: Refece-runt enim spiritum meum et vestrum. Agnoscite itaque eos, qui sunt huiusmodi.
units.tr: I beg you, brothers, you know that the household of Stephanas is the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have devoted themselves to the ministry of the saints. Submit yourselves to such people, and to everyone who contributes effort and labours with them. I rejoice at the coming of Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus, because they have made up for your absence. For they have refreshed my spirit and yours. Acknowledge, therefore, those who are of this kind.

units.la: Paucis aphorismis nuper Paulus vniuersam doctrinam complexus est, quam tota hac episto-la prolixe ac diligenter tradidit: ijdem vero tam fidei quam vitae Christianae summam atq; regulam perfectissimam comprehendunt. Postremum in illis fuit commendatio diligens fraterna charitatis, quae nobis actionum omnium et totius vitae regula atque scopus esse debet. At non sa-tis est doctrinam fidei et salutis in genere proposuisse, nisi eadem locis et personis praesentibus accommodetur. Ideo quod de charitate dixit Paulus, nunc Corinthijs propius applicat, et com-mendationem subijcit fratrum quorundam, quorum haud vulgaria tam in ipsum quam totam Co-rinthiorum Ecclesiam beneficia extabant. Videbat enim non sine dolore aemulos suos remeo addu-xisse, vt minus diligerentur et in nullo pretio essent ij, qui de Ecclesia optime meriti erant, et quo-rum praecipua debebat esse authoritas. Quod ergo de charitate dixerat, nunc vt quoad istos impri-mis observent, admonet. Debet itaque ex hoc loco generalis doctrina peti, vt bonam gratiam refe-ramus benefactoribus. Vt enim gratitudinem natura ipsa commendat, quae huius legem brutis quo-que animalibus insevit, sicuti in iumentis, canibus, imo bestijs quoq; truculentioribus est videre:ita homine ingrato nihil sceleftius aut nocentius inveniri potest. Imprimis tamen videndum est, vt in honore et precio habeatur, quicunque publice de aliqua Ecclesia aut Repub. bene merentur. Nam praeter quam quod Lex naturae hoc iubet, idem salus publica requirit. Ita enim plures alij ad pul-cherrimorum exemplorum imitationem excitantur, et illi ipsi in suo studio magis feruent, si hoc agnosci et gratum esse videant. Quibus adde, quod ijdem prudentia instructi sunt, quam et diu-turnus rerum usus confirmauit, et proinde melius possunt in commune consulere. Sed praemissis his singulas huius loci partes ex ordine videamus. Prima Stephanam & familiam eius commendat. Dictum de his supra Capite primo, vbi eos ab ipso Paulo baptizatos fuisse audiuimus. Magno autem studio & singulari animi vehementia rem hanc agit, dicens: Precor autem vos, fratres, noftis familiam Stephanæ esse primitias Achaiæ, & seipsos in ministerium sanctis ordinauisse: Vt & vos subijciamini talibus, &c. Supra pliciter agit, & perinde ac si ipsius res ageretur, precibus id impetrare studet, quod iure & pro imperio mandare poterat: ita nimirum suo exemplo docens, quàm nobis curæ esse debeant ij, quorum præclara virtus in Ecclesia & Repub. cum publico aliquo emolumento elucet. Quid verò petit? Vt illis subijciantur. Et ne Stephanæ feruilius blandiri, aut primatum quendam ambitiosius instituere videatur, orationem non ad illum solum restringit, sed ad omnes etiam alios extendit, quorum idem sit de Ecclesia & publica salute meritum. Nam dicit: Vt & vos talibus subijciamini, & cuius operam sua conferenti & laborati. Ex quibus verbis apparet, illum non agere de subiectione seruili, qualem posteris temporibus Pontifices inuexerunt, qui ad pedum osculan-non modò vulgus Christianorum, verumetiam reges & Imperatores vocant, & eorundem col-la impuris pedibus calcare non verentur: omnibus denique pro sua libidine præscribunt & mandant: Sed de legitima obedientia agit, quæ cum reuerentia coniuncta sit, quæque omnibus debetur, qui Ecclesiæ fideliter seruiunt, & negotium Domini agunt, sicuti nuper de Timotheo dixerat. Itaque non aliud vult Apostolus, quàm vt eos, qui tales sunt, pro fidis Christi & Ecclesiæ eius ministris agnoscant, eosdem amentreuereantur, & eorum pijs monitis, vel potius Dei Verbo ab ipsis prædicato obtemperent. Meretur hoc donorum Dei excellentia, quæ suam existimationem siue honorem habere non possunt, si eos contemnamus, qui illis prædicti sunt. Et cum Christianorum hominum sit officium, vt vnusquisq; alium se præstantiorem esse existimet, aliq; alios honorepræueniant, quanto magis hoc erga eos obseruari debet, quos singularia Dei dona & propria merita commendant? Sed præstat rationes, quibus hic Paulus vtitur, diligentius excutere.
units.tr: Not long ago Paul summed up his whole teaching in a few aphorisms, which he set out at length and with care throughout this letter. These aphorisms contain the sum and the most perfect rule of both faith and the Christian life. The last of them was a diligent commendation of brotherly love, which ought to be the rule and aim of all our actions and of the whole of our life. But it is not enough to have set out the doctrine of faith and salvation in general terms, unless it is also fitted to the places and persons at hand. So what Paul said about love he now applies more closely to the Corinthians, and he adds a commendation of certain brothers, whose benefits to himself and to the whole Corinthian Church were not small. For he saw, not without grief, that his rivals had brought it about that these men, who had deserved very well of the Church, and whose authority ought to have been especially high, were less loved and held in no esteem. So he now admonishes them, above all, to observe in this matter what he had said about love. From this passage, then, a general doctrine should be drawn: that we ought to show a good return of gratitude to our benefactors. For nature itself commends gratitude, which has implanted this law even in brute animals, as can be seen in beasts of burden and dogs, and indeed even in the fiercer wild beasts. Thus nothing more wicked or harmful can be found than an ungrateful man. Yet first we must consider that those who have deserved well publicly of any Church or commonwealth should be held in honour and esteem. For, apart from the fact that the law of nature commands this, the public welfare also requires it. In this way many others are stirred up to imitate the finest examples, and those very people grow more eager in their zeal when they see that their work is recognised and welcomed. Add to this that such people are endowed with prudence, which long experience of affairs has confirmed, and therefore they are better able to counsel for the common good. But, these points being set down, let us look in order at the separate parts of this passage. First, he commends Stephanas and his household. We have spoken of these people above, in the first chapter, where we heard that Paul himself had baptised them. He treats this matter with great earnestness and singular warmth of spirit, saying: "I beg you, brothers, you know that the household of Stephanas is the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have devoted themselves to the ministry of the saints. Submit yourselves to such people," and so on. He speaks as a suppliant, and as if the matter concerned himself, he takes pains to obtain by entreaty what he could have commanded by right and authority. In this way he teaches, by his own example, how much care should be given to those whose outstanding virtue shines forth in the Church and commonwealth with some public benefit. But what does he ask? That they submit to them. And lest he seem to flatter Stephanas too servilely, or to set up some primacy in an ambitious way, he does not confine his request to him alone but extends it to all others whose service to the Church and public welfare is the same. For he says: "that you also submit to such people, and to everyone who contributes effort and labours." From these words it is clear that he is not speaking of a servile subjection, such as the Pontiffs in later times introduced, who not only call the common mass of Christians to kiss their feet, but even kings and emperors, and do not hesitate to tread their necks with unclean feet; and who, in short, prescribe and command everything at their own pleasure. He is speaking of a lawful obedience, joined with reverence, which is owed to all who faithfully serve the Church and carry on the work of the Lord, as he said recently of Timothy. Therefore the Apostle wants nothing else than that those who are such be acknowledged as faithful ministers of Christ and his Church, that they be held in reverence, and that their godly admonitions, or rather the Word of God preached by them, be obeyed. The excellence of God's gifts deserves this, for those gifts cannot keep their esteem or honour if we despise those who possess them. And since it is the duty of Christians that each one should consider the other more excellent, and that some should go before others in honour, how much more should this be observed towards those whom God's singular gifts and their own proper merits commend? But it is better to examine carefully the reasons which Paul uses here.

units.la: Prima est: Scitis eos esse primitias Achaiæ siue Græciæ; id est, primos esse, qui in Achaia ad fidem Christi concesserunt, relictis superstitionibus & illicitis Deorum cultibus. Et facit ad huius argumenti confirmationem, quòd ipsos testes sistit, ne quid ex gratia aut alio affectu fingere putetur. Consultò autem primitiarum vocabulo vtitur, vt partim ostendat, hoc ad Dei cultum & honorem pertinere (nam vt supra Cap.15. diximus, primitiæ Deo sacræ erant, & alibi gentes ad Christum adductæ oblatio siue victima dicuntur) partim illos suo exemplo alijs occasionem dedisse, qua etiam illi ad fidem conuersi & salutis participes facti sint. Vt enim primitias frugum mox messis tota sequitur: sic vbi vnus & alter in aliqua gente fidem Christi recipiunt, mox alij quoque sequuntur, & longe latèq; serpit semel admissa Euangelij prædicatio. Docet hoc Christus parabola fermenti, quod farinæ conspersa admixtum totam massam breui temporis spatio penetrat, & acore suo sapidiorem reddit. Fuit ergo hæc non vulgaris laus istius familiæ, quòd primi Christum recipiendo Dei gloriam in sua gente illustrarunt, cultum huius inuexerunt, & multis alijs salutis occasionem præbuerunt: & debent merito tales magni fieri ab omnibus. Si enim gentes in Deorum numerum eos referendos esse putarunt, qui alicuius rei vtilis & necessariæ inuentores erant, aut reipub. primi constituerant: quanto magis honor & reuerentia illis debetur, per quos non huius modo vitæ feliciter transfigendæ regulâ, verumetiâ salute æternam nobis Deus offert? Nemo tamen hoc ita dictum putet, quasi eorum superstitionem probemus, qui in Dei seruos eam gloriam transtulerunt, quæ solius Christi est, dum ex illis aduocatos siue mediatores fingunt, & salutis patronos, quibus preces & vota nuncupant. Est enim honor ille certis finibus circumscriptus, & in obedientia illa consistit, quæ Dei Verbo, cuius illi præcones siue administri sunt, debetur.
units.tr: The first is: "You know that they are the firstfruits of Achaia," that is, of Greece; in other words, they were the first in Achaia to come to the faith of Christ, having abandoned superstitions and the unlawful worship of the gods. And to confirm this argument he calls them as witnesses, so that no one may think he is inventing anything out of favour or some other feeling. He deliberately uses the word firstfruits, partly to show that this pertains to the worship and honour of God (for, as we said above in chapter 15, firstfruits were holy to God, and elsewhere the Gentiles brought to Christ are called an offering or sacrifice), and partly to show that by their example they gave others an occasion by which those also were converted to the faith and made partakers of salvation. For just as the whole harvest follows soon after the firstfruits of the crops, so when one or two in some nation receive the faith of Christ, others soon follow, and the preaching of the gospel, once admitted, spreads far and wide. Christ teaches this in the parable of the leaven, which, mixed into the flour, penetrates the whole mass in a short space of time and makes it more savoury with its tang. So this was no ordinary praise of that household, that by being the first to receive Christ they brought glory to God among their own people, introduced his worship there, and gave many others an occasion of salvation; and such people rightly ought to be held in high regard by all.
