For if the nations thought that those should be counted among the gods who were the inventors of some useful and necessary thing, or who first established a commonwealth, how much more honour and reverence are owed to those through whom God offers us not only a rule for living this life happily, but also eternal salvation? Yet no one should think this has been said as if we approved of the superstition of those who transfer to the servants of God that glory which belongs to Christ alone, when they make these people into advocates or mediators and patrons of salvation, and address prayers and vows to them. For that honour is confined within definite limits, and consists in that obedience which is owed to the Word of God, whose heralds and ministers they are.

units.la: Interim officij sui meminerint ij, quibus hoc à Deo datum est, vt primi in sua gente Veritatis cognitione illuminati Christo nomen dederint: Est illud, vt in fide semel concepta constanter perseuerent, & indies in melius proficientes dignos sua professione fructus ferant. Nam nisi id fiat, primi tandem fient nouissimi: quod Iudæis accidisse scimus, qui cum olim soli essent Dei pecu-lium & regnum illud sacerdotale, hodie ne vltimi quidem sunt, sed in Ecclesia locum omnino nullum habent: eò quòd leuitate, inconstantia, ingratitudine & contumacia dignitatem suam proflituerunt. Erat hoc nobis obseruandum & viri Germani, quos cum Antichristianæ tenebræ totum orbem longè lateque occupauissent, Deus primos Euangelicæ virtutis luce illustrare & in libertatem filiorum suorum transferre dignatus est. Fuit hæc præcipua nostræ gentis gloria, quam mox multa & præclara alia ornamenta subsecuta sunt. Adhæc multis aliis nationibus occasio data est, qua & ipsæ ad Christi cognitionem adductæ sunt: paucis tamen hoc datum, ut simili libertate & pace fruantur, & principes habeant veros atque fideles Ecclesiæ nutritios. At dum alij populi sub duro episcoporum imperio & regum Euangelio aduersantium tyrannide luctantur, plerique ex nostris securi stertunt, & laudis suæ maiorumque virtutis immemores in pejus quotidie proficiunt: quò fit, ut dormientes libertatem diuinitus nobis concessam improborum hominum artibus circumscribi & nobis eripi patiamur: ut de iis nunc nihil dicam, qui illam turpiter produnt, & ut tam viuunt Christiana professione indignam, adeò ut propter illos Euangelium male audiat apud eos, qui illud nondum intelligunt. Quid ergo nobis aliud pollicebimur, quàm fore, ut ipsi quoque tandem postremi simus, & à nobis Regnum Dei transferatur ad gentem, quæ Dei beneficium maiorus faciat?
units.tr: Meanwhile, those to whom this has been given by God, that as the first in their nation to be enlightened by the knowledge of the truth they have given their name to Christ, should remember their duty. It is this: that they persevere constantly in the faith once received, and, advancing daily towards better things, bear fruits worthy of their profession. For unless this is done, the first will in the end become the last. We know this happened to the Jews, who, though once alone were God's peculiar people and that priestly kingdom, today are not even the last, but have no place at all in the Church, because by levity, inconstancy, ingratitude and obstinacy they squandered their dignity. This ought to be observed by us, the German men, whom God deigned to make the first to be illuminated by the light of evangelical truth and transferred into the liberty of his sons, when the darkness of Antichrist had occupied the whole world far and wide. This was the outstanding glory of our nation, and many other splendid ornaments soon followed it. Moreover, an occasion was given to many other nations, by which they too were brought to the knowledge of Christ; yet it has been granted to only a few that they should enjoy a similar liberty and peace, and have princes who are true and faithful nurses of the Church. But while other peoples struggle under the harsh rule of bishops and the tyranny of kings who oppose the gospel, most of our people snore in security, forgetful of their own praise and of the virtue of their ancestors, and grow worse every day. As a result, while we sleep, we allow the liberty granted to us by God to be circumvented by the tricks of wicked men and snatched from us. I say nothing now of those who shamefully betray it, and who live so unworthily of the Christian profession that, because of them, the gospel is badly spoken of among those who do not yet understand it. What else, then, shall we promise ourselves, than that we too shall in the end become last, and that the kingdom of God will be transferred from us to a nation that will value God's benefit more?

units.la: Altera ratio, cur Stephanam & familiam eius obseruare debeant, hæc est, quòd seipsos in ministerium sanctis ordinauerint. Quo loco multi curiosè potius quàm necessario quærunt, annon peccarint ipsi seipsos ordinando, cùm nemo istum honorem (ut in epistola ad Hebræos scribitur) sibi ipsi vendicare debeat, et alibi damnetur, qui sponte currebant, non expectata Dei vocatione? Atqui nō loquitur hic Paulus absolutè aut expressè de solo Ecclesiæ ministerio, sicuti ex eo apparet, quòd de tota familia Stephanæ agit, in qua haud dubiè fœminæ etiâ & pueri vel minores natu fuerunt, quorum alios ætas, alios sexus à ministerio Ecclesiastico excludebat. Nam supra prohibet, ne mulieres in Ecclesia loquantur. Deinde non ait, quòd seipsos violenter intruserint, aut imperiosè sibi honorem istum vendicarint: sed ordinandi verbo vtitur, quod erroris aut disputationis causam præbuit, eò quòd posteriùs temporibus illud ad ordines suos Ecclesiasticos, quibus nihil minus ordinatum inueniri potest, transtulerint Pontifices: In præsenti tamen Apostolos non aliud vult dicere, quàm quòd sponte se addixerint Ecclesiæ ad quæuis officia præstanda, quæ ipsos decebant, & quibus obeundis sufficere poterant. Itaque sensus est: Stephanam & eius domesticos, postquam ad fidem Christianam peruenerunt, se totos Ecclesiæ consecrauisse, ut sanctis, id est, credentibus, qui per fidem in Christum sanctificati sunt, omni officiorum genere pro viribus inseruiant. Hoc sensu Caius Ecclesiæ totius hospes dicitur, eò quòd domus eius Christianis omnibus paterēt, qui vel incertis sedibus vagabantur, vel certas ob causas professionem aliquam instituebant. Et ex alijs locis constat, Apostolorum temporibus viduas quoque fuisse, quæ ministeria quædam publico Ecclesiæ nomine obibant, in ægrotis curandis, hospitibus excipiendis, alijsq; officijs, quæ per mulieres melius & commodius, quàm à viris præstari possunt. De his ergo omnibus in præsenti agitur. Quòd si præterea Stephanas, aut aliquis ex eius familia, ad docendi munus accessit, id procul dubio non absque legitima vocatione & manuum impositione factum est. Rursus autem est hoc præclarum pietatis non vulgaris argumentum, quòd isti Ecclesiam Christi tanti fecerunt, ut non modo fidem cum alijs profiteri voluerint, sed simul omnibus seruire, quos suo obsequio & opera opus habere videbant. Procul ergo abfuerunt ab eorum ingenio & moribus, qui non alio proposito ad Ecclesiam veniunt, quàm ut ex ea ditescant & publicis dignitatibus ornentur, cùm interim ignauos fucos agant, neque Deo neque hominibus vtiles.
units.tr: A second reason why they ought to honour Stephanas and his household is this: they have devoted themselves to the ministry of the saints. Here many ask, more out of curiosity than necessity, whether they sinned by ordaining themselves, since no one should claim that honour for himself (as is written in the epistle to the Hebrews), and elsewhere those are condemned who ran of their own accord without waiting for God's call. But Paul does not speak here absolutely or expressly of the ministry of the Church alone. This is clear from the fact that he is speaking of the whole household of Stephanas, which without doubt included women and children or younger people, whom age in some cases and sex in others excluded from the ecclesiastical ministry. For above he forbids women to speak in the Church. Next, he does not say that they forced their way in, or domineeringly claimed that honour for themselves. He uses the word "ordained", which has caused error and dispute, because later the Pontiffs transferred it to their own ecclesiastical orders, although nothing less ordained can be found in them. At present, however, the Apostle means nothing other than that they willingly gave themselves to the Church, to perform whatever duties befitted them and for which they were able. So the sense is this: Stephanas and his household, after they came to the Christian faith, consecrated themselves wholly to the Church, so that they might serve the saints, that is, believers who have been sanctified through faith in Christ, in every kind of office, as far as their strength allowed. In this sense Gaius is called host of the whole Church, because his house was open to all Christians who either wandered without a fixed abode or pursued some occupation for certain reasons. Other passages also make clear that in the times of the Apostles there were widows who performed certain ministries in the name of the public Church: caring for the sick, receiving guests, and other duties which women can perform better and more fittingly than men. It is all these things that are under discussion here. If, moreover, Stephanas or someone from his household took up the office of teaching, that was certainly not done without lawful calling and the laying on of hands. Again, this is a notable proof of no common piety: they valued the Church of Christ so highly that they wished not only to profess the faith with others, but at the same time to serve all those whom they saw had need of their obedience and labour. Far, then, were they from the disposition and manners of those who come to the Church with no other purpose than to grow rich from it and be adorned with public dignities, while meanwhile they play the idle drones, useful neither to God nor to men.

units.la: Admonentur hoc exemplo Christiani homines, quibus virtutibus laudem siue gloriam veram atque solidam mereri possint. Primò scilicet, si Deum vocantem facilè audiant, neque se aliorum exemplo detineri sinant, qui moras nes[?]tunt, dum præ alijs sapere volunt: quin potius altoi[?] in hoc stadio salutis præuenire studeant, ut Deo sint primitiæ optatæ & sanctæ. Deinde, si in eo quod bene cœperunt, constanter perseuerent, & indies in melius proficiant: ne ex eorum numero sint, qui vbi manum aratro admouerunt, à tergo respiciunt, quos Christus ad Regnum Dei idoneos esse negat. Postremò, si se totos sanctorum ministerio addicant & consecrent. Sanctorum nomine Christiani omnes censentur, siue iam pridem mortui, siue adhuc superstites sint: & idèo Ecclesia catholica in Symbolo communio Sanctorum dicitur, eò quòd ad eius societatem omnes pertineant, pertinēant, quos Christus sanctificauit. In praesenti tamen de solis viuentibus sermo est: quia qui iam è viuis excesserunt, vt suo seculo seruierunt & omnibus officijs suis defuncti sunt: ita nostris ministerijs nequaquam opus habent. Inter eos ergo qui viuunt quaeri debent quibus ministremus, quiq; nostra ope subleuentur. Facit huc quod Christus iam mortem aditurus officia ista corporalia, quae olim ipsi in terris agenti à pijs praestari potuerunt, abs se non in Diuos caelites, sed in pauperes & egenos transtulit. Qua in re efficacissimum stimulum nobis ipsis poterimus adhibere, si cogitemus illos Christo consecratos siue sanctos esse, & proinde male conferri non posse quae in illos conferuntur. Et hæc causa est, quod initio huius Cap. de subuentione pauperum Syriæ fratrum loquens Apostolus, illos sanctorum titulo commendat. At quae nostri seculi calamitas est, hodie homines superstitiosi multa in Diuos conferunt, qui in caelis vitam vere beatam agunt, neq; vllo officio nostro indigent, neglectis interim viuis Christi membris, quae fame & siti & frigore perire sinunt. Fit ergo, quod olim in Babylone factum fuisse Danielis historia testatur, vt impensae omnes, quas illi in Diuos sefacere putant, à crassis monachis & sacrificis intercipiantur, qui & ignaui ventres sunt, & plerunq; turpissima Bacchi atq; Veneris mancipia.
units.tr: Christians are admonished by this example as to the virtues by which they may earn true and solid praise or glory. First, if they readily hear God calling, and do not allow themselves to be held back by the example of others who spin out delays while wanting to be wiser than everyone else. Rather, they should strive to outstrip others in this race of salvation, so that they may be the desired and holy firstfruits to God. Next, if they persevere constantly in what they have begun well and make daily progress for the better, so that they are not among those who, having put their hand to the plough, look back, and whom Christ declares unfit for the kingdom of God. Last, if they devote and consecrate themselves wholly to the ministry of the saints. All Christians are counted under the name of saints, whether they have long since died or are still living; and therefore the catholic Church in the Creed is called the communion of saints, because all whom Christ has sanctified belong to its fellowship. In the present passage, however, the talk is only of the living, for those who have already departed this life, having served their age and discharged all their offices, have no need of our ministries at all. Among the living, therefore, we must look for those to whom we may minister, and who are relieved by our help. To this purpose belongs the fact that Christ, about to undergo death, transferred those bodily offices, which in former times had been performed for him by the godly while he was living on earth, from himself not to the heavenly saints but to the poor and needy. In this matter we can apply a most effective spur to ourselves, if we consider that those consecrated or holy in Christ are such that what is bestowed on them cannot be badly bestowed. This is also why the Apostle, at the beginning of this chapter, speaking of the relief of the brethren in Syria, commends them by the title of saints. But what a calamity of our age it is that today superstitious men bestow many things upon the saints, who in heaven lead a truly blessed life and need none of our services, while meanwhile the living members of Christ are neglected and allowed to perish with hunger, thirst and cold. So it happens that what the history of Daniel testifies was once done in Babylon takes place again: all the expenses which men think they make for the saints are intercepted by fat monks and priests, who are both idle bellies and, for the most part, the most shameful slaves of Bacchus and Venus.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui Stephanæ coniungit Fortunatum & Achaicum, quos similiter Corinthijs commendat. Venerant hi ad ipsum in Asiam Ephesum vsq;. Num vero ab Ecclesia missi fuerint, aut sponte sua & Pauli visendi desiderio profectionem illam suscepérint, à nonnullis dubitatur. At mihi minimè dubium est, quin eos Corinthij miserint, & vt ita sentiam, rationibus non levibus adducor. Prima est, quod ex Cap. 7. constat, publico totius Ecclesiæ nomine ad Paulum literas datas fuisse, quibus eius sententiam requirebant de coniugio & cælibatu, de diuortijs, de Virginitate & alijs causis ad coniugium pertinentibus. Quia autem per hos ipsos, qui hic nominantur, epistolam hanc ad Corinthios missam fuisse subscriptio testatur (quamuis ea quoad loci notationem mendosa sit, vt alibi extendimus) eosdem ego prius ab Ecclesia amandatos fuisse arbitror. Deinde pro delatoribus habiti fuissent, si sua sponte excurrissent ad Paulum, nec is prudenter per illos epistolam tam grauem & multa reprehensione plenam misisset. Sed & verba Pauli nostram sententiam confirmant, qui illis legationis fideliter peractæ testimonium reddit, sic dicens: Gaudeo autem de aduentu Stephanæ & Fortunati & Achaici: quoniam absentiam vestram hi suppleuerunt: Refecerunt enim spiritum meum & vestrum. Quid vero opus erat hæc toti Ecclesiæ commemorare, nisi ex huius voluntate & sententia ad ipsum venissent? Gratum vero & iucundum sibi fuisse ipsorum aduentum, duobus argumentis docet. Primum est: Quoniam absentiam vestram hi suppleuerunt: Vel vt Graeca sonant, Quod mihi deerat quoad vos, isti farciuerunt suis erga me officijs, adeo vt vos omnes in illis videre & completi mihi visus sim. Alterum: Refecerunt, siue recrearunt spiritum meum & vestrum, id est, meum spiritum, qui totus vester, & commodis vestris pro monendis addictus est. Potest etiam posterior particula de Corinthiorum spiritu exponi, quod horum quoq; votis fit satisfactum, quando legationem laboris & periculi plenam pro totius Ecclesiæ salute feliciter obierunt. Et huc probè facit reficiendi aut refocillandi verbum, quo illos omni suspicione liberat, ne Ecclesiam ab eis accusatam aut diffamatam esse putet. Ita enim neq; Pauli neq; Corinthiorum spiritum refecissent, sed potius vtrofq; perturbassent. Infert ergo commendationis huius statu[?]: Agnoscite itaq; eos, qui sunt huiusmodi, id est, obseruate & vt fidos Christi seruos complectiminí[?].
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who joins Fortunatus and Achaicus with Stephanas, whom he likewise commends to the Corinthians. These had come to him as far as Ephesus in Asia. Some doubt whether they were sent by the Church, or undertook that journey of their own accord out of desire to see Paul. To me it is by no means doubtful that the Corinthians sent them, and, to say what I think, I am led by no weak reasons. The first is that it is clear from chapter 7 that letters were sent to Paul in the public name of the whole Church, asking his opinion about marriage and celibacy, divorces, virginity and other matters pertaining to marriage. Now, that this epistle was sent to the Corinthians through the very men named here is attested by the subscription (although it is faulty as to the note of place, as I have elsewhere explained). So I think these men were first sent by the Church. Next, they would have been regarded as informers if they had run off to Paul of their own accord, and he would not have prudently sent through them so grave an epistle, full of much reproof. But Paul's own words also confirm our view, for he bears witness to their faithfully discharged mission, saying: "I rejoice at the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus, for these have supplied your absence; for they have refreshed my spirit and yours." But why would there have been any need to commemorate these things to the whole Church, unless they had come to him at its wish and by its decision? He shows in two ways that their coming was pleasing and welcome to him. The first is: "for these have supplied your absence", or, as the Greek sounds, "what was lacking to me on your part, these men made up with their services towards me, so that I seemed to see you all in them and to be made complete." The second is: "they have refreshed, or revived, my spirit and yours", that is, my spirit, which is wholly yours and devoted to your advantage in giving warning. The latter part can also be explained of the spirit of the Corinthians, in that their wishes too were satisfied when these men successfully performed a mission full of labour and danger for the salvation of the whole Church. The word "refreshed", or "revived", fits this well, for by it he frees them from all suspicion, lest anyone think that the Church had been accused or defamed by them. For in that case they would not have refreshed the spirit of Paul or of the Corinthians, but rather disturbed both. Therefore he adds a commendation of this kind: "Acknowledge therefore those who are such", that is, observe them, and embrace them as faithful servants of Christ.

units.la: Est autem multa laude dignissima hæc Pauli mansuetudo, qui Ecclesiæ tot modis distractæ & vitijs pluribus laborantis legatos tanti fecit, vt eos non amice modo & humaniter exceperit, verumetiam eosdem tanto studio vicissim Corinthijs commendet, & se per illos refocillatum esse publicè fateatur. At qui hodie Apostolorum successores aut Apostolici haberi volunt, tales nunquam admitterent, cùm ne regum quidem potentissimorum legatos in conspectum admittat, nisi prius cernui & canum instar adrepant, vt pedes eorum exosculentur. Nihil nunc de ea insolentia dicimus, quæ seculis aliquot totius orbis Christiani de ipsorum intolerabili tyrannide quiritantis vota per ludibrium frustrati sunt, adeò vt ex mille oneribus ne vnū quidem ab infelicis populi humeris remouerint. Et qui Euangelicæ doctrinæ instauratores se esse gloriantur, celebrium Ecclesiarum ministris apud se congregatis dicere ausi sunt: Vos foetere fecistis Euangelium nostrum. Nescio cuius spiritus istæ voces sint: apostolicum certè nihil spirant aut redolent.
units.tr: This gentleness of Paul is most worthy of praise: though the Church was torn apart in many ways and laboured under many faults, he held its envoys in such high regard that he not only received them in a friendly and humane manner, but also commended them in turn to the Corinthians with great earnestness, and publicly confessed that he had been refreshed by them. But today those who wish to be called the successors of the Apostles, or Apostolic men, would never admit such envoys; they do not even admit the envoys of the most powerful kings into their presence unless they first grovel face down and crawl like dogs to kiss their feet. I say nothing now of that arrogance which, for some centuries, has frustrated, in mockery, the prayers of the whole Christian world complaining of their intolerable tyranny, so that they have not removed even one of a thousand burdens from the shoulders of the wretched people. And those who boast that they are the restorers of evangelical teaching have dared to say to the ministers of famous Churches gathered before them: "You have made our Gospel stink." I do not know whose spirit these words come from; they certainly breathe and smell of nothing apostolic.

units.la: Singularem vero considerationem hoc loco meretur veterum Christianorum mos. Soliti fuerunt frequenter de rebus agendis Apostolos consulere, si quæ causa grauior incidisset. Exemplum eius rei memorabile extat Actorum 15.cap. vbi controuersiam de Lege ijs obtrudenda, qui ex gentilismo ad Christum conuersi erant, Ecclesiæ ad Apostolos retulerunt. Ita vero mos ille obtinuit, vt Corinthij, etsi multa apud eos præter decorum fierent, & Ecclesiæ eius facies esset depravatissima, illum tamen noluerint negligere, quo minus per longa & periculosa itinera legationem ad Paulum miserint. Debebat hoc ipsum hodie etiam observari in Ecclesijs. Nam etsi non amplius in terris hisce viuant Apostoli, neq; eos coram conuenire liceat, extant tamen eorum scripta, quibus nos de Dei voluntate certiores faciunt, & quibus totam Filij Dei doctrinam luculenter & perfectè amplectuntur. Accedunt his Mosis & Prophetarum libri, qui & ipsi dictante Spiritu Dei scripti sunt. Itaq; quoties libet, Concilium cogere licet, in quo de controuersijs articulis siue quæstionibus Deum ipsum per seruos suos loquentem audiamus, de quorum fide & authoritate nemo pius aut orthodoxus vnquam dubitauit. Quid autem fit? Priuatim homines superstitiosi ad loca fictis aut fucatis sanctorum reliquijs nobilitata concurrant, vbi vel offa mortua, vel laceras vestes, vel etiam arma nefariæ impietatis instrumenta, quibus illi occisi esse creduntur, deosculantur & colunt, eorundem vero libros & doctrinam, quam sanguinis sui testimonio obsignarunt, secure negligunt, vel etiam mendacij & hæresis accusant, dignosque iudicant, qui ex omnium manibus excussi exurantur: Publicè vero Concilia coguntur Pontificum, qui se Apostolicos esse dicut [?], cum nihil sit in eorum vel vita vel doctrina, quod spiritum apostolicum referat. Quid ergo mirum, si errores erroribus cumulentur, & in peius passim omnes proficiant? Remedium mali huius vnicum est, vt secundum æterni Patris præceptum, Filium eius IESVM CHRISTVM per suos Apostolos & Prophetas loquentem audiamus, quem ille nobis Regem & Sacerdotem dedit. Huic debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: The custom of the ancient Christians, however, deserves particular consideration here. They were accustomed often to consult the Apostles about matters to be done, if some more serious cause arose. A memorable example of this stands in Acts, chapter 15, where the Churches referred to the Apostles the controversy over imposing the Law on those who had been converted to Christ from the Gentiles. This custom so prevailed that the Corinthians, although many things among them were done contrary to propriety and the face of their Church was most corrupt, nevertheless were unwilling to neglect it, and so sent an embassy to Paul over long and dangerous journeys. This same practice ought to be observed in the Churches today. For although the Apostles no longer live on these lands, and it is not permitted to meet them face to face, their writings still exist, by which they make us more certain of God's will, and in which they set out the whole doctrine of the Son of God clearly and perfectly. To these are added the books of Moses and the Prophets, which were also written under the dictation of the Spirit of God. And so, whenever it pleases, a council may be convened in which we may hear God himself speaking through his servants on controverted articles or questions, whose faith and authority no pious or orthodox person has ever doubted. But what happens instead? Superstitious people privately flock to places made famous by fabricated or spurious relics of the saints, where they kiss and worship dead bones, torn garments, or even the weapons of wicked impiety by which those saints are believed to have been killed, while they carelessly neglect the books and teaching of those same men, which they sealed with the testimony of their blood, or even accuse them of falsehood and heresy, and judge worthy of being wrested from everyone's hands and burned. Publicly, meanwhile, councils are convened by the Pontiffs, who say that they are Apostolic, although there is nothing in their life or doctrine that reflects an apostolic spirit. What wonder, then, if errors are piled upon errors, and everyone makes progress everywhere for the worse? The only remedy for this evil is that, according to the command of the eternal Father, we hear his Son JESUS CHRIST speaking through his Apostles and Prophets, whom the Father has given us as King and Priest. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XCV.
units.tr: Homily 95.

units.la: Salutant vos Ecclesiæ Asiæ. Salutant vos in Domino multum Aquila & Priscilla, cum Ecclesia, quæ est domi ipsorum. Salutant vos fratres omnes. Salutate alij alios osculo sancto. Salutatio manu mea Pauli. Si quis non amat Dominum IESVM CHRI-STVM, sit anathema, maranatha. Gratia Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI sit vobiscum. Charitas vestra cum omnibus vobis in CHRISTO IESV. Amen.
units.tr: The churches of Asia salute you. Aquila and Priscilla salute you much in the Lord, together with the church that is in their house. All the brothers salute you. Greet one another with a holy kiss. The salutation of me, Paul, with my own hand. If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema, maranatha. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen.

units.la: Postrema epistolæ huius parte Paulus duo omnino agit. Primum eos commendat, qui pro aliis de Ecclesia bene meriti erant, vt nimirum honorem sibi debitum habeant, neq; audiantur homines maligni & ambitiosi, qui illos vulgò inuisos & suspectos facere studebant, vt ipsi facilius omnia pro suo arbitrio versarent. Et sane vix aliud in Ecclesia & Repub. tam est necessarium, quàm vt eorum authoritas defendatur, qui cum longo rerum vsu induxerunt coniunxerunt. Deinde in eo est Apostolus, vt amorem mutuum inter Corinthios accendat & foueat. Ad primum pertinet, quòd nuper Stephanam, Fortunatum & Achaicum commendauit. Ad alterum salutationes, quas modò recitauimus, vnà cum epistolæ totius conclusione. Solent enim Apostoli (vt Chrysostomus quoq; annotauit) Ecclesias & harum membra salutationibus mutuis colligere & conglutinare. Nam sunt hæc symbolum amoris, quia bene precando alijs animi nostri propensionem declaramus. Et debet exemplum apostolicum diligenter obseruari, ne in hoc officij genere nos eorum pudeat, qui nobis multò inferiores sunt. Nam vt quidam non inepte dixit, comis & blanda salutatio conciliat amicitiam, inimicitiam diluit, certè mutuam beneuolentiam auget aliquantùm. Ea denique occasione frequenter qui procul dissiti sunt, neq; se mutuò vnquam viderunt, ita coalescunt, vt in posterum separari nullo modo possint. Quod ideo admonemus, ne cui videamur operam luderem [?] in hisce salutationibus excutiendis.
units.tr: In the final part of this letter Paul does two things. First, he commends those who had deserved well of the Church on behalf of others, so that they may have the honour owed to them, and so that malicious and ambitious men are not listened to. These men were eager to make such people generally hated and suspect, so that they could more easily manage everything as they pleased. And indeed, there is hardly anything in the Church and the commonwealth so necessary as defending the authority of those who, by long experience in affairs, have established and united them. Second, the Apostle aims to kindle and foster mutual love among the Corinthians. To the first belongs his recent commendation of Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus. To the second belong the greetings we have just recited, together with the conclusion of the whole letter. For the Apostles (as Chrysostom also noted) were accustomed to bind together and cement the churches and their members by mutual greetings. For these are a sign of love, since by blessing others well we show the inclination of our hearts. And we ought to observe carefully the apostolic example, lest we be ashamed to perform this kind of duty even towards those who are far below us. For, as someone aptly said, a courteous and friendly greeting wins friendship, dissolves enmity, and at least increases mutual goodwill. Indeed, on such occasions, people who live far apart and have never seen one another often become so united that they can never afterwards be separated. We mention this so that no one may think I am wasting effort in examining these greetings.

units.la: Prima est: Salutant vos Ecclesiæ Asiæ. Atqui magnum fuit inter Corinthiorum urbem & Asiæ Ecclesias, quarum caput erat Ephesus, interuallum. Accedebat huic acerba veterum iniuriarum memoria ex bellis Persicis enata, quibus tota Græcia crudeliter afflicta fuerat: & victissim Græci postea Alexandro duce Asiam totam diripuerant atque vastarant. At postquam vtrinque Christo nomen dederunt, omnium iniuriarum oblivi, nunc se inuicem salutant & mutuo amore complectuntur: idque non publicè modò, verumetiam priuatim singuli, sicuti ex eo apparet, quòd Paulo post fratrum quoque, id est, singulorum credentium nomine illis salutem dicit. Vere ergo nunc in istum locum habuit, quod Christus de vno ovili & vno grege dicit, ad quem omnes credentes ex diuersis gentibus colligi oportet. Admonemur itaque hoc exemplo, quam parum adhuc in religione Christiana profecerint, qui iniuriarum acceptarum nimis bene memores odia fovent, & iampridem obducta vulnera refricant mutuis exprobrationibus. Est vitium hoc nimis vulga-re hodie, & vt olim apud Græcos odioso Barbarorum nomine (quod Persicorum bellorum tempore exortum fuisse alibi diximus) peregrini omnes notabantur: ita apud omnes fere nationes vocabula quædam in vsu sunt, quibus exteri in contemptum & odium adducuntur. Nec satis hoc est multis, si priuatis odijs indulgeant, sed insuper sibi licere arbitrantur, vt Ecclesias totas malitiosè insectentur, adeoque Veritatis doctrinam propter gentem, quæ ipsis inuisa est, temere damnent. At quia Ecclesiarum omnium vnum caput, vnus pastor, vnus Dominus est, IESVS CHRI-STVS, in quo non est Iudæus aut Græcus, Scytha aut barbarus, Germanus aut Italus, Gallus aut Hispanus, non poterit aliqua illarum contemni vel abijci, nisi in ipsum Christum iniuria illa redundet. Nimium autem stultè & inique de iniurijs, quæ maiores sui olim passi sint, homines conqueruntur, vt odia sua atque simultates excusent. Cùm enim recentes iniurias & quæ nobisipsis facta sunt condonare oporteat (siquidem Filij Dei & coheredes Christi censeri volumus) quantò magis eas toto animo expuere & æterna obliuione sepelire debemus, quas ipsi nunquam sensimus, & quæ Christi cognitionem longo multorum annorum spacio præcesserunt.
units.tr: The first is: "The churches of Asia salute you." Yet there was a great distance between the city of the Corinthians and the churches of Asia, whose head was Ephesus. To this was added the bitter memory of old injuries, born of the Persian wars, by which all of Greece had been cruelly afflicted; and afterwards the Greeks, under Alexander as leader, had plundered and laid waste the whole of Asia. But after both sides had given their name to Christ, they forgot all injuries and now greet one another and embrace in mutual love, and not only publicly but also privately, each person individually, as is clear from the fact that Paul afterwards greets them also in the name of the brothers, that is, of individual believers. Truly, then, what Christ says about one fold and one flock now has its place, since all believers from different nations ought to be gathered into it. We are therefore admonished by this example how little progress they have made in the Christian religion who, too mindful of injuries received, nourish hatreds and reopen wounds long since closed by mutual reproaches. This vice is too common today; and just as the Greeks once marked all foreigners with the hateful name of "barbarians" (which, as I have said elsewhere, arose at the time of the Persian wars), so among almost all nations certain words are in use by which outsiders are brought into contempt and hatred. Nor is it enough for many people to indulge private hatreds, but they further think it permissible to attack whole churches maliciously, and so rashly condemn the doctrine of truth on account of the nation that is hateful to them. But since the one head of all the churches, the one minister, the one Lord, is Jesus Christ, in whom there is neither Jew nor Greek, Scythian nor barbarian, German nor Italian, Frenchman nor Spaniard, none of them can be despised or cast aside without that injury redounding upon Christ himself. Yet people complain very foolishly and unjustly about the injuries their forefathers once suffered, in order to excuse their hatreds and quarrels. For since we ought to pardon recent injuries and those done to ourselves (since we wish to be counted sons of God and co-heirs with Christ), how much more ought we to cast out with our whole heart, and bury in eternal oblivion, those injuries which we ourselves never felt, and which came before the knowledge of Christ by a long span of many years.

units.la: Secundo loco Aquilam & Priscillam nominat, dicens: Salutant vos in Domino Aquila & Priscilla, cum Ecclesia, quæ est domi ipsorum. De his Lucas quædam annotauit Actio.18.cap. Fuit Aquila Ponticus genere, & Claudij Cæsaris edicto Roma pulsus, Corinthum concesserat, vbi Paulo illuc venienti hospitium præbuit. Inde Ephesum venit, sicuti ex hoc loco apparet. Estque hic quasi in transitu obseruandum, non nouum aut insolens esse hodie, si Christiani homines incertis sedibus vagentur, vt sicuti triumphos & magistratus suos numerant homines ambitiosi, qui sæculo huic per omnia addicti viuunt: ita illi exilia sua & fugas numerare possint. Ita enim suos exercet Deus, vt discant, se in terris peregrinos esse, patriam autem & ciuitatem permanentem habere in cælis, ad quam omni studio contendere debeant. Voluit autem Paulus Aquilam nominatim ponere, vtpote hominem Corinthijs probè notum, & vt hunc ipsorum adhuc memorem esse ostendat. Simul vero nouum gratitudinis exemplum hoc loco occurrit. Fuit enim Aquila tentoriorum textor, qui manuum labore victum sibi parabat. Non tamen eius pudet tantum Apostolum, imò dignum iudicat, cuius nomine salutem adscribat Corinthijs, qui in diuitijs & delitijs enutriti inter Græcos alijs multùm præstabant. Ita vero Deus remuneratur quæ suis feruis præstantur officia. Nec enim temere à Christo dictum est: Quisquis vni ex meis discipulis dederit poculum aquæ frigidæ, is non amittet mercedem suam. Cuius promissionis fides cum infinitis exemplis confirmata sit, vnum hoc multorum instar censeri potest. Quàm enim pulchrè fœneratum est Aquilæ beneficium hoc, quod in Paulum hospitem Corinthi contulit? Immortalem certè gloriam & æternam nominis sui memoriam eo sibi parauit, quam multi insanus [?] pyramidum ædificijs, cruentis & periculi plenis victorijs, & triumphis magnificentissimis nequicquam quæsiuerunt.
units.tr: In the second place he names Aquila and Priscilla, saying: "Aquila and Priscilla salute you much in the Lord, with the church that is in their house." Luke has noted some things about them in Acts 18. Aquila was a Pontian by birth, and having been expelled from Rome by the edict of the Emperor Claudius, he had come to Corinth, where he gave lodging to Paul when Paul came there. From there he came to Ephesus, as appears from this passage. And here, as it were in passing, it should be observed that it is not new or unusual today if Christians wander with uncertain dwelling places; so that just as ambitious men, who live wholly devoted to this age, count up their triumphs and their offices, so these might count up their exiles and flights. For God so trains his own that they learn that they are strangers on earth, and have an abiding fatherland and city in heaven, towards which they ought to strive with all zeal. Paul wished to name Aquila by name, as a man well known to the Corinthians, and to show that he is still remembered by them. At the same time, a new example of gratitude appears here. For Aquila was a weaver of tents, who earned his living by the labour of his hands. Yet the Apostle is not ashamed of him; rather he judges him worthy that greetings be sent to the Corinthians in his name, though the Corinthians, reared in riches and luxury, greatly surpassed others among the Greeks. Thus God rewards the services rendered to his servants. For it was not rashly said by Christ: "Whoever gives a cup of cold water to one of my disciples will not lose his reward." The faithfulness of this promise has been confirmed by infinite examples, and this one may be counted as equal to many. For how finely has this kindness been repaid, which Aquila showed to Paul, his host at Corinth? He certainly prepared for himself immortal glory and an eternal memory of his name, which many have sought in vain by the building of pyramids, by bloody and perilous victories, and by most magnificent triumphs.

units.la: At præ aliis, quæ hic dici poterant, obseruari debet, quod Ecclesiæ domesticæ meminit Paulus, quam Aquila & vxor eius Priscilla domi suæ habuerint. Exponunt hoc nonnulli de ijs, qui apud illum conuenire & cœtus sacros agere solebant. Sed cum Paulo ante omnium Ecclesiarum Asiæ nomine Corinthijs salutem dixerit, vix credibile est, quòd aliquam hic præ alijs nominare, adeoque alijs omnibus præferre voluerit. Scimus enim Apostolos passim humilitatis & modestiæ studium commendare, & imprimis cauere, ne quæ inter Christianos æmulatio ex ambitione exoriatur. Rectius ergo locus iste meo iudicio de familia Aquilæ exponitur, quam homo opulentus & artificium manuarium exercens procul dubio magnam & numerosam habuit. Estq; hæc laus minimè vulgaris, quòd domesticos suos ita instituit, vt Ecclesiam quasi priuatâ referrent, & à tato Apostolo ecclesia dici mererentur. Docet autem locus hic, quales esse debeant domus aut familiæ Christianorum hominum. Est enim Ecclesia proprie cætus fidelium, qui sub vno eodemque capite, IESV CHRI-STO, coalescit, cuius Verbo atq; Spiritu viuificatur atq; regitur. Quia autem piorum familiæ Ecclesia esse debent, prima vtique in illis debet fidei in Christum cura esse, vt in ea omnes confi-tiant. Deinde vt ex Dei Verbo renata eodem regantur atq; gubernentur necesse est: quia nisi id fiat, nemo illorum Christianus dici aut censeri merebitur. Quæ causa est, quòd Deus olim paren-tes aut patresfamilias inter domesticos suos frequenter de Verbo suo aut Lege, de iudiciorum suorum exemplis, deq; externorum sacrorum mysterijs differere voluit, vt iuniores ex priuata seu domestica institutione edocti ipsum timeant & colant. Itaq; is demum paterfamilias laudem merebitur, qui domi suæ episcopum siue parochum (vt sic loquar) priuatum egerit: sicuti D.quoq; Augustinus alicubi monet. Tales olim patriarcharum domus fuerunt, templa nimirum & schola religionis: quod de Abrahamo non obscurè Deus ipse testatur, quando excidium illud horribile, quod Sodo-mis & vicinis vrbibus imminebat, illi reuelaturus, inter alia dicit: Hoc scio, quod mandaturus sit filijs suis, & domui suæ post se, vt custodiant viam Domini, faciantq; iustitiam & iudicium, &c. Et in nouo Testamento domus eiusmodi fuisse scimus. Lazari Bethaniensis & sororum eius, Simeonis, & procul dubio Zachæi, Nicodemi, Iofephi Arimathaï & similium, qui ad Christum conuersi fuerunt: quibus merito hunc Aquilam nostrum cum sua Priscilla adnumerauerit. Debebant istorum exempla hodie imitari Christiani homines. Inter gentes certè hoc omnibus persuasum fuit, familias diuinitus conseruari, & ideo penates & Lares suos colebant. At inter eos, qui Christi nomen profitentur, Paucos inuenire licet, qui de hac re serio cogitent: & quàmuis culpam hanc plerique in semetipsis minimè agnoscant, imò pertinaciter negent, moribus tamen & studijs suis ita produntur & conuincuntur, vt nemo non videat, eos religionis cura nulla teneri. Si enim de Dei voluntate cogitarent, & domesticos suos Ecclesiæ Christi membra esse cuperent, nunquam suæ vel auaritiæ vel petulantiæ atq; libidini tantum indulgerent.
units.tr: But beyond the other things that could be said here, it must be noted that Paul mentions the household church which Aquila and his wife Priscilla had in their house. Some explain this of those who used to gather with them and hold sacred assemblies. But since Paul had greeted the Corinthians in the name of all the churches of Asia, it is scarcely credible that he wished to name one church above the others, and thus to prefer it to all the rest. For we know that the Apostles everywhere commend a concern for humility and modesty, and above all take care that no rivalry arise among Christians out of ambition. Therefore, in my judgment, this passage is more rightly explained of the household of Aquila, which, being a wealthy man who practised a manual craft, undoubtedly had a large and numerous household. And this is no ordinary praise, that he so trained his household members that they might act as a private church and deserve to be called a church by so great an Apostle. Moreover, this passage teaches what the houses or families of Christian people ought to be like. For a church is properly an assembly of the faithful, who are joined together under one and the same head, Jesus Christ, and are quickened and ruled by his Word and Spirit. And since the families of the godly ought to be churches, the first care in them must surely be faith in Christ, so that all may confess it. Next, since they have been born again by the Word of God, they must necessarily be guided and governed by the same; for unless this is done, none of them will deserve to be called or counted Christian. This is why God in former times wished parents or heads of households to speak frequently among their household about his Word or Law, about examples of his judgments, and about the mysteries of the outward sacred rites, so that the younger ones, taught by private or domestic instruction, might fear and worship him. Thus that head of a household will at last deserve praise who has made his own house a private bishop or parish minister (if I may so speak), as St Augustine also warns somewhere. Such were the households of the patriarchs of old, which were certainly temples and schools of religion. God himself bears clear witness to this about Abraham, when, about to reveal to him that horrible destruction which hung over Sodom and the neighbouring cities, he says among other things: "I know that he will command his sons and his household after him to keep the way of the Lord, and to do justice and judgment," etc. (Gen. 18). And we know that in the New Testament there were households of this kind: those of Lazarus of Bethany and his sisters, of Simon, and surely of Zacchaeus, Nicodemus, Joseph of Arimathea and others like them, who were converted to Christ; and rightly does Paul count our Aquila with his Priscilla among them. Christian people today ought to imitate their examples. Among the nations, indeed, this was held by all as a conviction, that families are preserved by divine providence, and therefore they worshipped their household gods and their Lares. But among those who profess the name of Christ, one may find few who think seriously about this matter; and although most do not recognise this fault in themselves, but even stubbornly deny it, yet by their manners and pursuits they so betray and convict themselves that everyone sees they are held by no concern for religion. For if they thought about God's will and desired that their households be members of the Church of Christ, they would never indulge so much in their avarice, their wantonness, or their lust.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui postquam Aquilæ & Priscillæ fratres omnes subiecit, ne quem præterisse aut contempsisse putetur, addit: Salutate alij alios osculo sancto. Quibus verbis monet, vt quam alij ipsis precentur salutem, ipsi sibi mutuò non inuideant, sed potius mutuo amore sese complectantur. Osculi autem meminit (vt etiam in priori ad Thessalonicenses) vel propter remptum eius seculi morem, qui tamen apud Hebræos magis in vsu fuit, quàm apud alias gentes: vel propter ritum, quo Christiani in Cœnæ mysticæ celebratione sese mutuò osculari solebant, cuius Iustinus Martyr libro secundo sui Apologetici meminit. Ac osculo animorum coniunctionem denotari alibi diximus. In præsenti sanctum osculum requirit, vt impura & lasciua excludat, imprimis autem dolum & hypocrisin fraudis atque proditionis plenam, qualia loabi olim & Iudæ proditoris oscula fuerunt. Vult ergo, vt quam externis signis profitentur animorum coniunctionem & consensionem sanctè colant atque tueantur. Interim minimè opus est, vt ex huius loci authoritate osculandi mos in Ecclesiam reducatur apud nos, qui illum semper ignoraumus. Conantur hoc Anabaptistæ, ineptum & importunum hominum genus: sed quàm ridiculè, imò quanto cum scandalo id faciant, non opus est dicere, cùm hoc abunde notum sit omnibus. Nec mutari debent temere gentium mores, si modesti sint, & nihil à pietate alienum habeant: vt nec peregrini inuehi debent, qui sua nouitate aliquem poterant offendere. Papistæ quidem osculum pacis ad osseas[?] & pilas tabellas transtulerunt, quæ in Missa circumferri solent. At nihil huius in Cœna sua Christus instituit, neque satis tutum est ab eius institutione discedere. Obseruetur potius mutuum charitatis studium, quod Christus discipulis suis commendatissimum esse voluit, & cuius vinculum externum nobis in Cœna adhibetur, à qua dolum omnem procul remouere debent, quotquot CHRI-STI IESV, qui ipsissima s Veritas, discipuli germani esse volunt. Restat postrema Epistolæ pars, quæ tribus membris constat.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who, after greeting all the brothers, Aquila and Priscilla included, so that no one would think he had passed anyone over or despised him, adds: "Greet one another with an holy kiss." By these words he urges that those whom others wish well should not begrudge them the same wish among themselves, but should rather embrace one another in mutual love. He mentions the kiss (as he also does in his first letter to the Thessalonians) either because it was the custom of that age, which was more common among the Hebrews than among other nations, or because of the rite by which Christians used to kiss one another at the celebration of the mystical Supper, a practice Justin Martyr mentions in the second book of his Apology. We have said elsewhere that a kiss signifies the joining of minds. Here he requires a holy kiss, so that it excludes whatever is impure and wanton, and above all deceit and hypocrisy full of treachery, such as the kisses of Joab of old and of Judas the traitor. His meaning, then, is that the union and agreement of minds, which they profess by outward signs, should be honestly kept and maintained. Yet there is no need to bring back into our Church the custom of kissing on the authority of this passage, since we have always been without it. The Anabaptists, an unseemly and troublesome breed of men, try to do this; but how ridiculous, indeed how scandalous, their doing so is, there is no need to say, since it is well known to everyone. Nor should the customs of nations be changed rashly if they are decent and contain nothing foreign to godliness, just as foreign customs should not be introduced, since by their novelty they could give offence. The Papists have indeed transferred the kiss of peace to little bone plates and tablets, which are customarily carried round in the Mass. But Christ instituted nothing of this kind in his Supper, and it is not safe to depart from his institution. Rather, let the mutual zeal for charity be observed, which Christ wished to be most strongly commended to his disciples, and whose outward bond is used for us in the Supper. All who wish to be true disciples of CHRIST JESUS, who is truth itself, must remove all deceit far from it. There remains the last part of the Epistle, which consists of three members.

units.la: Prima subscriptionem habet, propria Pauli manu factam. Nam Amanuensi vsum fuisse, ex vltimo ad Romanos apparet, vbi Tertius nominatur, qui epistolam illam scripserit. Sub finem autem ipse subscribere solebat, & quidem verbis semper iisdem, vt ad Colossenses ipse testatur, vbi ista leguntur: Salutatio, mea manu Pauli, quod est signum in omni epistola: ita scribo, &c. Vsus subscriptionum est, partim vt literis fides haberetur, quae dubia esse poterat, maxime, si aliena manu sint exaratae: partim vt caveantur falsarij: quod quàm vtile quamque necessarium sit, facile vident hodie, quibus cum hominibus huius seculi res est, quando mille artibus oculatissimi quique interdum falluntur. Et arguit Apostoli tanti diligentia eorum supinam oscitantiam, qui nihil pensi habent, & quiduis fieri patiuntur. Est autem boni viri officium cavere, ne quis sub nomine sui praetextu fallatur. Equidem non superuacaneam fuisse Apostolorum in hac re diligentiam, ex eo constat, quod illis adhuc viuentibus inuenti sunt, qui eorum nomine abusi dogmata falsa spargebant, & turbas dabant in Ecclesiis: posteris vero temporibus prodierunt homines non minus impij quàm audaces, qui Canones quosdam Apostolicos obtruserunt, quorum plerique tam absurdi & ridiculi, & ab apostolica gravitate adeo alieni sunt, vt mirum sit, aliquem repertum fuisse, qui illis fidem habuerit.
units.tr: The first is the subscription, written in Paul's own hand. For that he used a scribe is clear from the last chapter of Romans, where Tertius is named as the one who wrote that letter. At the end, however, he himself used to subscribe, and always in the same words, as he himself testifies to the Colossians, where these words are read: "The salutation by the hand of me, Paul, which is the sign in every epistle: so I write, etc." The use of subscriptions is partly so that a letter may be trusted, since its authenticity could be doubtful, especially if it was written by another hand; and partly so that forgers may be guarded against. How useful and how necessary this is, people see easily today, when they have to deal with men of this age, since the most watchful are sometimes deceived by a thousand tricks. The great care of the Apostle also reproaches the careless drowsiness of those who take no thought and allow anything to happen. It is the duty of a good man to take care that no one is deceived under his name or pretext. Indeed, that the Apostles' diligence in this matter was not superfluous is clear from the fact that, while they were still alive, there were people who abused their names, spread false doctrines and caused disturbances in the Churches. In later times there arose men no less impious than bold, who foisted upon the world certain Apostolic Canons, most of which are so absurd and ridiculous, and so foreign to Apostolic dignity, that it is a wonder anyone was found who gave them credit.

units.la: Secunda parte contra falsos fratres sententiam profert admodum grauem: Si quis non amat Dominum IESVM CHRISTVM, sit anathema, maranatha. Causa huius sententiae fuit, quod Corinthiorum Ecclesia eiusmodi hominibus abundabat, qui cùm fidem in Christum profitentur, omnia tamen dolo malo agebant, & animis à Christo erant alienissimis. Ex horum numero sectarij erant, qui si Christi fuissent amantes, Ecclesiam eius nunquam in partes lacerassent, quam ille vnâ esse voluit. Tales etiam erant improbi illi & muti canes, qui vagas libidines & incestus permittebant: quotquot item sacris alienis communicabant cum fratrum infirmiorum scandalo: omnes deniq; qui suam potius gloriam & commoda privata, quàm Ecclesiae aedificationem spectabant. Istis ergo omnibus in praesenti horribile Dei iudicium denuntiat.
units.tr: In the second part he pronounces a very grave sentence against false brothers: "If anyone does not love the Lord JESUS CHRIST, let him be anathema, maranatha." The cause of this sentence was that the Church of Corinth abounded in men of this kind, who, while professing faith in Christ, nevertheless acted in all things with evil deceit, and whose minds were most alien from Christ. Among their number were the sectarians, who, if they had loved Christ, would never have torn his Church into parties, though he wished it to be one. Such too were those shameless and dumb dogs who permitted wandering lusts and incest; likewise all who took part in strange rites to the scandal of weaker brothers; and finally all who looked to their own glory and private advantage rather than to the building up of the Church. For all these, then, he now declares the terrible judgment of God.

units.la: At nos hic ante omnia observare debemus, quod expressè solius dilectionis Christi meminit, & eos anathema pronuntiat, qui illa destituuntur, qualescunque illi sint, aut videri velint, quoad alia. Etenim dicere poterat: Si quis non credit in Christum, si quis ritus sacros non sancte seruauerit, anathema sit. Sed quia in externis hypocritae omnium sanctissimi & optimi videntur, adhaec fidei professio vt plurimum fallit, praesertim quando res secundae sunt, dilectionem potius quàm quiduis aliud requirit. Haec enim nunquam fallit, sed vt in secundis inuiolata manet, ita in aduersis & periculis potissimum sese prodit, vt quae tunc occasionem & materiam habeat sibi conuenientem. E contra proprius impietatis fons est, animum à Christo alienauisse, ita vt aliquid illo charius & praestatius habeamus. Nec temere propterea ille Regno Dei indignum pronuntiat eum, qui parentes, vxorem, liberos, fratres, vitam denique propriam magis quàm ipsum amauerit. Lucae 14.
units.tr: But here we must first of all observe that he expressly mentions the love of Christ alone, and pronounces anathema upon those who lack it, whatever they may be or wish to appear in other respects. For he could have said: "If anyone does not believe in Christ, if anyone has not kept the sacred rites faithfully, let him be anathema." But because hypocrites seem most holy and upright in outward things, and a profession of faith for the most part deceives, especially when things go well, he requires love rather than anything else. For this never deceives; as it remains unbroken in prosperity, so it shows itself most clearly in adversity and dangers, when it finds its fitting occasion and matter. On the contrary, the true source of impiety is to have estranged the mind from Christ, so that we hold something dearer and more valuable than him. Nor is it without reason that he declares unworthy of the kingdom of God the one who loves parents, wife, children, brothers, and finally his own life more than him (Luke 14).

units.la: Neque quis tamen hic seipsum inani perfuasione fallat, meminisse oportet dilectionis affectum non otiosum esse, neque illam vel in verbis vel inani contemplatione consistere, sed hominem totum Christo vendicare, vt huic obtemperet. Eius enim verba sunt: Si diligitis me, praecepta mea seruate. Item: Qui habet praecepta mea, & seruat ea, is est qui diligit me. Et rursus: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum seruabit. Qui non diligit me, sermones meos non seruat. Et alibi: Si praecepta mea seruaueritis, manebitis in dilectione mea. Vt enim ij filij demum patrem suum syncero amore complecti putantur, qui eius monitis obtemperant, & quibus nihil grauius accidere potest, quàm si illum offensum videant: ita Christi verè amantes sunt, qui huic obediunt & placere student, frustra autem fide & dilectione eius gloriantur, quibus lusus & iocus est praecepta eius transgredi, quiq; irae eius indicia atq; comminationes contemnunt. At praeceptorum Christi (vt alibi docuimus) haec summa est, vt in ipsum credamus, & exemplum, quo nobis praeiuit, sedulò imitemur. Isti ergo studere debent, quotquot illo propitio vti, & salutis illius merito partae participes fieri cupiunt.
units.tr: Yet let no one deceive himself here with empty persuasion. We must remember that the affection of love is not idle, nor does it consist in words or empty contemplation, but claims the whole man for Christ, so that he obeys him. For his words are: "If you love me, keep my commandments." Again: "He who has my commandments and keeps them, he is the one who loves me." And again: "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; he who does not love me does not keep my words." And elsewhere: "If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love." For just as those sons are thought truly to embrace their father with sincere love who obey his admonitions, and for whom nothing can be more grievous than to see him offended, so those are truly lovers of Christ who obey him and strive to please him. But those who boast in vain of his faith and love, and think it sport and a joke to transgress his commandments, and despise the signs of his anger and his threats, are not. Now the sum of Christ's commandments (as we have taught elsewhere) is that we believe in him and diligently imitate the example he has set before us. Therefore all who wish to enjoy his favour and to share in the salvation won by his merit ought to strive for this.

units.la: Excitet autem nos, quod in praesenti Paulus minatur, dicens: Si quis non amat Dominum IESVM CHRISTVM, sit anathema, maranatha. De anathemate diximus in epistola ad Romanos Cap. 9. Ita enim non ea modo dicuntur, quae Deo soli consecrata esse debent, verùmetiam ta,qua ille sic abominatur,vt ijs coli nolit,sed potius gratissimi cultus loco habeat,si prorsus excindantur & aboleantur. Quo sensu de Deorum sculptilibus & eorum auro atq; argento Moses loquens, voce Herem vtitur, quam Graeci per anathema reddiderunt. Sic enim scribit: Sculptilia Deorum igne exures: argentum & aurum, quod in illis est; ne concupiscas, vt tibi tollas, ne forte impingas in eo: quoniam abominatio est Domino Deo tuo. Ne ergo inferas abominationem in domum tuam, ne fias Herem fiue anathema, quemadmodum illud est: Omnino execreris illud, plane ab eo abhorreas: Herem enim est, id est, res eiusmodi, quae omnino aboleri debet, ne in rerum natura porro locum habeat. Itaq; Hiericho quoq; Herem fiue anathema dicitur, quòd Deus illam funditus excindi & exterminari vellet. Itaq; hoc loco Paulus ijs, qui Dominum IESVM non diligunt, horribile Dei iudicium denuntiat, quo ex Ecclesia excindi & aeterna salutis haereditate prorsus excludi eos velit.
units.tr: Now what Paul threatens here should stir us, when he says: "If anyone does not love the Lord JESUS CHRIST, let him be anathema, maranatha." We spoke of anathema in the epistle to the Romans, chapter 9. For things are called by this name not only those that ought to be consecrated to God alone, but also those that he so abhors that he will not be worshipped with them, but holds their complete extermination and abolition to be the most pleasing worship. In this sense Moses, speaking of the graven images of the gods and their gold and silver, uses the word Herem, which the Greeks rendered by anathema. For he writes: "You shall burn with fire the graven images of the gods; you shall not covet the silver and gold that is on them, to take it for yourself, lest you be ensnared by it, since it is an abomination to the LORD your God. Therefore do not bring an abomination into your house, lest you become Herem, or anathema, like it: you shall utterly detest it and utterly loathe it, for it is Herem," that is, a thing of such a kind that it must be utterly destroyed, so that it has no further place in the nature of things. So also Jericho is called Herem, or anathema, because God wished it to be utterly cut off and exterminated. Thus in this place Paul declares to those who do not love the Lord JESUS the terrible judgment of God, by which he wishes them to be cut off from the Church and utterly excluded from the inheritance of eternal salvation.

units.la: Adijcit Paulus anathematis denuntiationi, Maranatha. Quam vocem Syriacam & ex duobus compositam esse, D. Hieronymus ad Marcellam docet, & idem esse, quod, Dominus venit. At aliquibus ridiculum, aut saltem mirum videtur, voluisse Apostolum Graeco vocabulo & omnibus noto peregrinum atque ignotum subijcere. At nemo hoc insolens esse putet, quando constat in Euangelij libris voces aliquot Hebreas inueniri, quas primitiua Ecclesia (vt D. quoq; Augustinus testatur) non mutari, neque Graecas aut Latinas illarum loco supponi voluit, partim propter sanctiorem authoritatem, partim quod in sua lingua emphasim quandam habent, quae nulla alia tam commodè & proprie exprimi potest. Nec obscura aut ignota esse potuit tunc eiusmodi vocum significatio, cum ijs qui ex gentilismo conuersi erant, passim cohabitarent & eiusdem fidei socij essent Iudaei, apud quos illae erant vsitatissimae. Videntur autem non falli sua coniectura, qui Hebraos existimant voces istas Maran-atha solenni anathematismo subijcere solitos fuisse, vt ostenderent, hunc minime inanem aut irritum fore: eo quod Dominus Ecclesiae suae & eius ordinario ministerio coniunctus sit, imo venturus sit suo tempore iudex & vindex omnium, qui illud insolentius contemnunt. Et fauet huic sententiae, quod supra Capite quinto Paulus Spiritum suum, imo ipsius Christi potestatem, cum Corinthiorum spiritu coniungit, vbi de exclusione hominis incesti agitur. Vobis (inquit) & meo Spiritu in nomine Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI con-gregatis, cum potestate Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, tradatur ille Satanae, &c. In summa ergo hoc vult dicere Paulus, eos qui in Christiani nominis professione ludunt, & fucum faciunt Ecclesiae, Deo exosos esse, qui nunquam passurus sit, vt eis in Regno suo locus sit; & proinde indignos esse, quibus cum homines Christiani commercia habeant: nec inanem fore, quam contra tales Ecclesia pronuntiat sententiam: quia IESVS CHRISTVS certò venturus sit iudex, apud cuius tribunal omnes sisti oporteat, vt dignas suis scelleribus poenas exoluant. Conuenit cum his quod Ioannes Baptista dixit: Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam aeternam: Qui vero non credit (siue non paret) Filio, non videbit vitam: sed ira Dei manet super eum. Adde his ipsius Christi dictum: Qui crediderit, & baptizatus fuerit, saluus erit: Qui vero non crediderit, condemnabitur. Terreant nos ista, ne quid per hypocrisim fiat, neue ex eorum numero simus, quos Dominus per Prophetam hoc nomine reprehendit, quod ore quidem appropinquant, & labijs ipsum honorat, corde autem longius ab eo absint. Nihil enim simulatione turpius, nihil illa Deo magis exosum est, quando ne homines quidem probi & ingenui eam ferre possint.
units.tr: Paul adds to the proclamation of anathema the word Maranatha. Jerome, in his letter to Marcella, teaches that this Syriac word is composed of two words and means "the Lord comes." Some people find it ridiculous, or at least strange, that the Apostle should add a Greek word that is foreign and unfamiliar to everyone. But no one should think this unusual, since it is established that some Hebrew words occur in the books of the Gospels, which the early Church (as Augustine also testifies) did not wish to change or replace with Greek or Latin words, partly because of their more sacred authority, and partly because they have in their own language a certain emphasis that no other word can express so fittingly and precisely. Nor could the meaning of such words have been obscure or unknown then, when Jews, among whom these words were in most common use, lived everywhere among converts from paganism and were partners in the same faith. Those who think that the Hebrews were accustomed to attach these words, Maranatha, to a solemn anathema, to show that it would not be empty or void, seem not to be mistaken in their conjecture, because the Lord is joined to his Church and to its ordinary ministry, and indeed will come at his appointed time as judge and avenger of all who scorn it too insolently. This opinion is supported by the fact that above, in chapter five, Paul joins his Spirit, indeed the power of Christ himself, with the spirit of the Corinthians, where the exclusion of the incestuous man is discussed: "When you are gathered together, and my spirit, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, let such a one be handed over to Satan," and so on. In sum, then, Paul means this: those who play at the profession of the Christian name and deceive the Church are hateful to God, who will never allow them a place in his kingdom; therefore they are unworthy to have dealings with Christian men; and the sentence the Church pronounces against such people will not be empty, because Jesus Christ will certainly come as judge, before whose tribunal all must appear to pay penalties worthy of their crimes. This agrees with what John the Baptist said: "He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who does not believe (or obey) the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him." Add to these the saying of Christ himself: "He who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who does not believe will be condemned." Let these things terrify us, lest anything be done in hypocrisy, and lest we be among those whom the Lord rebukes through the prophet, because they draw near with their mouth and honour him with their lips, but their heart is far from him. For nothing is more shameful than pretence, and nothing is more hateful to God, since even honest and well-bred men cannot bear it.

units.la: Tertia & postrema parte fausta omnia Corinthijs precatur, & simul omnia sua officia illis defert, dicens: Gratia Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI sit vobiscum. Charitas mea cum omnibus vobis in CHRISTO IESV. Ista vero mitigat & emollit correptiones omnes, quibus tota haec epistola erga eos vsus fuit, suiq; animi benevolentiam testatur, ne de suo erga ipsos amore aut studio posthac dubitent: suo deniq; exemplo eos ad mutuam dilectionem excitat. Est autem obseruatu dignissimum Pauli exemplum, qui post tam acres tamq; iustas correptiones suum amorem & omnia Christiana amicitiae officia in commune omnibus tam liberaliter offert. Discamus ergo nos quoq; ita irasci hominum vitijs, vt interim dilectionis fraternae non obliuiscamur. Nam qui alios corripiunt, ij medicos agere debent. Hi dum amara pocula propinant, aut etiam vrunt atque secant, non tamen oderunt aegrotos, qui tam duris remedijs opus habent, sed potius salutis[?] eorum consulere student. Ita illos facere conuenit, & correptiones suas sic moderari, ut animum amicum & beneuolum non obscuris indicijs deprehendere liceat. E contra qui corripiuntur, hanc animorum medicinam esse cogitent non minus necessariam quam salutarem, & proinde patienter eam ferant, atque monitoribus fidis sese obsequentes & gratos praebeant. At quia de hac re alibi dictum est, nunc ista sufficiant, & quia hic Paulus epistolae suae finem fecit, nos quoque dicendi finem faciamus.
units.tr: In the third and final part, he wishes all good things to the Corinthians, and at the same time offers them all his services, saying: "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. My love be with you all in Christ Jesus." These words soften and mollify all the rebukes with which this whole letter has dealt with them, and bear witness to his goodwill, so that they may not henceforth doubt his love and zeal for them; and finally, by his own example, he stirs them to mutual love. Paul's example is most worthy of notice: after such sharp and just rebukes, he so generously offers his love and all Christian offices of friendship to all of them together. Let us therefore learn to be angry at men's vices in the same way, yet meanwhile not forget brotherly love. For those who rebuke others ought to act as physicians. While they offer bitter draughts, or even burn and cut, they do not hate the sick who need such harsh remedies, but rather strive to look after their health. It is fitting that they act so, and moderate their rebukes so that a friendly and kindly mind may be perceived through no obscure signs. On the other hand, those who are rebuked should think that this medicine for the soul is no less necessary than it is salutary, and so bear it patiently, showing themselves obedient and grateful to faithful admonishers. But since this matter has been dealt with elsewhere, let these things suffice; and since Paul has here made an end of his letter, let us too make an end of speaking.

units.la: Meminerint autem omnes, Apostolum hoc scripto errores & vitia Corinthiorum ad Verbi Dei regulam ita correxisse, ut simul generalem doctrinae Christianae & Apostolicae summam complexus sit: quae non minus nobis seruit, & plus quam necessaria est, quando eadem vitia hodie etiam ubique regnant. In sectas scissi sunt, qui fidem in Christum profitentur, & in omnium ore sunt factiosa Benedictinorum, Bernhardinorum, Iacobitarum, Franciscanorum, Dominicanorum & plurium aliorum nomina: quibus inter puriora doctrinae sectatores accedunt Lutherani, Zuingliani, Caluinistae, Synergistae & alij innumeri, in quos Ecclesia misere distrahitur. Morum di-sciplina prorsus extincta iacet, & qui fratres eundem tum ipsis Christum profitentes propter leui-culam aliquam dissensionem, & saepe propter dissensionis speciem, ferre nolunt, ijdem scortatores, adulteros, ebriosos, milites mercenarios, aleatores & grauissimis aliis sceleribus infames facile ferunt, & pro patronis habent. Litibus iniquis, & morosis potius quam necessarijs tribunalia o-mnia perstrepunt. Ambidextri in religione passim dominantur, & summa prudentia censetur fidem cum superstitionibus, & verum Dei cultum cum idololatria miscere. Libidine & luxu omnis ordinis & loci homines diffluunt. Inter Euangelicae doctrinae professores, papistici ritus in precan-do & aliis fidei exercitijs retinentur. Coena Domini mystica, alijs quaestus, alijs contentionum materia, alijs horribilis animorum atque conscientiarum carnificina facta est. Et cum nostrum seculum linguarum cognitione, eruditione, eloquentia, aliisq; donis praestantissimis Deus exorna-rit, illis plerique ambitiosa contendendi libidine ad suam ipsorum & aliorum pernitiem abutuntur. Quid de resurrectione ex mortuis & vita aeterna plerique sentiant, mores eorum corruptissimi & effrenis quiduis patrandi licentia testantur. Pauperes Christi ubiq; locorum neglecti oberrant, & illis fame contabescentibus, ex Ecclesiarum bonis belluantur, superbiunt & ditescunt, qui fere aterrimi sunt religionis hostes & scandalorum nocentissimorum authores. Et ista quidem in omnium conspectu sic fiunt, ut pudorem omnem abstulerit, qui ea negare audeat. Nemo igitur epistolam hanc nihil ad nos pertinere existimet. Eadem est seculis omnibus Dei voluntas, eadem semper Spiritus sancti sententia.
units.tr: Let all remember, however, that the Apostle in this writing corrected the errors and vices of the Corinthians by the rule of God's Word, and at the same time embraced the general sum of Christian and apostolic doctrine. This serves us no less, and more than is needed, since the same vices reign everywhere today. Those who profess faith in Christ are torn into sects, and on everyone's lips are the names of the factious Benedictines, Bernardines, Jacobites, Franciscans, Dominicans and many others; to these are added, among the followers of purer doctrine, Lutherans, Zwinglians, Calvinists, Synergists and countless others, by whom the Church is wretchedly torn apart. The discipline of morals lies utterly extinct. Those who profess the same Christ as ourselves, and who will not bear with one another over some trifling disagreement, and often over the mere appearance of disagreement, easily tolerate whoremongers, adulterers, drunkards, mercenary soldiers, gamblers and others infamous for the gravest crimes, and even treat them as patrons. All the law courts resound with unjust and vexatious lawsuits rather than necessary ones. Double-dealers hold sway everywhere in religion, and it is thought the height of prudence to mix faith with superstitions and the true worship of God with idolatry. Men of every rank and place are sunk in lust and luxury. Among the professors of the evangelical doctrine, papist rites are retained in prayer and in other exercises of faith. The mystical Lord's Supper has become for some a source of profit, for others a matter of quarrels, and for others a dreadful butchering of souls and consciences. Although God has adorned our age with knowledge of languages, learning, eloquence and other most outstanding gifts, many use these for their own and others' ruin, with an ambitious lust for contention. What most people think about the resurrection of the dead and eternal life, their most corrupt morals and unbridled licence for doing whatever they please bear witness. The poor of Christ wander neglected everywhere, and while they waste away with hunger, those who are almost the most bitter enemies of religion and the most harmful authors of scandals gorge themselves on the goods of the churches, grow proud and grow rich. And these things are done in the sight of all, in such a way that anyone who dares to deny them has lost all shame. Let no one therefore think that this letter does not concern us. The will of God is the same in all ages, and the mind of the Holy Spirit is always the same.

units.la: Simus ergo in illius meditatione assidui, & eius doctrinam nobis applicemus, ut & vitia nostra corrigamus, & totis cordibus innouati, dilectione non fucata complectamur Dominum nostrum IESVM CHRISTVM, dilectionem vero eius praeceptorum obseruatione diligenti testemur, ut & ille nos vicissim diligat, & una cum Patre & Spiritu suo manßionem apud nos faciat. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeter-num, Amen. [illegible, ~60 letters]
units.tr: Let us then be diligent in meditating upon it, and apply its teaching to ourselves, so that we may both correct our vices and, renewed in our whole hearts, embrace our Lord Jesus Christ with undisguised love, and bear witness to our love for his precepts by diligent observance, so that he in turn may love us, and together with the Father and his Spirit make his dwelling with us. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, Amen. [remainder illegible in the scan]
